topic: adolescent sleep timing and school start times
title: The Late Shift of Adolescence
subtitle: Should schools reorganise their timetables around the teenage body clock?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few complaints are as familiar to parents as the difficulty of getting a teenager out of bed. For generations this reluctance was treated as a failing of character, the product of late nights, poor discipline or simple idleness. Over the past three decades, however, a growing body of research has suggested that the problem lies less in adolescent attitudes than in adolescent biology. If that interpretation is correct, then the early start times adopted by many secondary schools are not merely inconvenient; they may be actively undermining the education they are designed to deliver. The argument has gained considerable momentum, and several regions have already moved their opening bells later. Yet the evidence is less uniform than campaigners sometimes imply, and the policy questions it raises are genuinely difficult.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The biological case rests on the timing of melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that night has arrived. Dr Aurelia Kowalczyk, a chronobiologist at the Baltic Institute of Sleep Medicine, has measured melatonin in saliva samples from more than two thousand young people. Her data indicate that, around puberty, the evening rise in the hormone shifts later by as much as two hours, and does not return to its childhood pattern until the early twenties. A fifteen-year-old who is sent to bed at nine o'clock, in other words, may lie awake for hours not out of defiance but because the internal signal for sleep has not yet arrived. Kowalczyk also notes that the pressure to sleep, which builds steadily during waking hours, accumulates more slowly in adolescents than in younger children, making it easier for them to stay alert late into the evening.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If teenagers cannot fall asleep early, an early school start inevitably cuts their sleep short. The economist Desmond Achterberg, of the Rhineland Centre for Education Policy, has studied districts that delayed their start times by between forty-five and seventy minutes. He found modest but consistent improvements in attendance and in test scores, particularly in lessons scheduled for the first period of the day. Achterberg goes further, calculating that the long-term gains in earnings associated with better qualifications would exceed the cost of rearranging bus timetables many times over. Such projections should be treated with caution, since they depend on assumptions about future labour markets that no one can verify. Nevertheless, the immediate improvements he documents are difficult to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that biology is the whole story. A research group at Hokkaido Metropolitan University, led by the psychologist Kenji Morimoto, followed a cohort of Japanese secondary pupils for six years and concluded that evening use of phones and tablets explained a substantial part of their delayed bedtimes. Light from screens, Morimoto argues, suppresses melatonin and so exaggerates a natural tendency that would otherwise be relatively mild. On this view, moving school start times later treats the symptom rather than the cause, and may even encourage teenagers to stay up later still. It is a provocative claim, but it sits uneasily with the observation that the adolescent delay in sleep timing has been recorded in societies with little access to electric lighting, let alone personal devices.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Practical objections carry more weight. Folasade Oyelaran, who studies family policy at the Lagos School of Public Affairs, has interviewed parents in districts that changed their timetables. Many welcomed the reform in principle but reported unexpected strains: younger siblings whose primary schools still opened early, part-time jobs that now clashed with the end of the school day, and sports fixtures that finished after dark in winter. Oyelaran does not oppose later starts, but she maintains that they succeed only when transport, childcare and extracurricular activities are reorganised at the same time. Reforms imposed on schools alone, she warns, tend to shift the burden onto households least able to absorb it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This concern has been sharpened by the sociologist Rafael Quintanilla, whose work at the University of Valparaíso examines how sleep varies with income. Quintanilla has found that teenagers from poorer households already sleep less than their wealthier peers, often because of crowded housing, noisy neighbourhoods or caring responsibilities. A later start time, he suggests, could therefore narrow educational gaps, since the pupils who gain the most extra sleep would be those who currently have the least. Interestingly, his figures also show that the benefits disappear if families respond by delaying bedtimes by the same amount, which happened in roughly a fifth of the households he surveyed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should schools do? The weight of evidence suggests that early starts impose a real cost on adolescents, and that this cost is rooted at least partly in physiology rather than habit. To dismiss the research because some teenagers misuse their phones would be to confuse an aggravating factor with an underlying cause. At the same time, a later bell is not a cure-all. The most successful reforms appear to be those introduced gradually, with the cooperation of transport authorities, employers and parents. The question is no longer whether adolescent sleep deserves attention, but whether communities are prepared to rearrange their routines to accommodate it.

topic: sleep and memory consolidation, including targeted memory reactivation
title: Rehearsing in the Dark
subtitle: How much does the sleeping brain really do for memory?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early twentieth century, psychologists noticed something curious: people who slept after learning a list of nonsense syllables remembered more of it than those who stayed awake for the same period. For decades the explanation seemed obvious. Sleep, it was assumed, simply protected new memories by shutting out the stream of fresh experiences that would otherwise interfere with them. Today that passive account has largely been abandoned. Most researchers now believe that the sleeping brain actively processes recent experience, selecting, strengthening and reorganising what was learned during the day. This is one of the most significant shifts in modern neuroscience, although, as this article will argue, the more ambitious claims made on its behalf deserve closer scrutiny.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the evidence comes from recordings of the hippocampus, a structure deep in the brain that is essential for forming memories of events. In rodents that have run through a maze, cells that fired in a particular sequence during the run fire again in the same order during subsequent deep sleep, though many times faster. The neuroscientist Margit Solheim, who leads a laboratory at the Trondheim Centre for Memory Research, describes this as 'replay' and believes it allows information to be transferred gradually from the hippocampus to the outer layers of the brain, where it can be stored for the long term. Disrupting replay with brief electrical pulses, her team has shown, impairs the animals' performance the next day. Solheim acknowledges that rodents navigating a maze are a long way from students revising history, but she argues that the basic machinery of memory has changed remarkably little in the course of mammalian evolution.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Human studies point in a similar direction. Brief bursts of electrical activity known as sleep spindles, which occur mainly in the lighter stages of non-dreaming sleep, increase in number after intensive learning, and people with more spindles tend to remember more. The psychologist Arjun Venkataraman of the Pune Institute of Cognitive Science has found that the relationship is strongest for factual material, such as vocabulary, and weakest for motor skills like typing. He suggests that different stages of sleep may specialise in different kinds of memory, a hypothesis that, while attractive, rests on a relatively small number of experiments.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most striking development has been the attempt to influence memory during sleep deliberately. In a technique called targeted memory reactivation, participants learn information while a particular sound or smell is present; the same cue is then presented quietly while they sleep. Lucía Barrientos and her colleagues at the Montevideo Sleep Laboratory report that items associated with replayed cues are remembered noticeably better than those that were not cued, apparently because the cue prompts the brain to rehearse that specific material. Barrientos is careful to stress that the effects are modest and that cues must be soft enough not to wake the sleeper, which in practice requires constant monitoring of brain activity. Her group has also found that cueing appears to work only during deep sleep; when the same sounds are played during lighter sleep or after the volunteers wake, any advantage vanishes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such findings have inevitably attracted commercial interest. Several companies now market headbands that claim to detect deep sleep and play sounds that enhance learning overnight. This is where enthusiasm begins to outrun evidence. Laboratory studies typically involve a few dozen volunteers, carefully selected and monitored throughout the night, learning simple material shortly before sleep. Whether the same effects can be achieved at home, over months, with the complex knowledge students actually need to acquire, is simply unknown. It would be premature to recommend such devices to anyone preparing for an examination.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some scientists doubt that the active account is complete. Nino Kapanadze, a cognitive scientist at the Caucasus University of Science, has re-examined dozens of published studies and argues that many reported benefits of sleep are smaller than they first appeared, partly because experiments with negative results are less likely to be published. She does not deny that sleep matters for memory, but she maintains that its effects are often exaggerated, and that much of what is attributed to active consolidation could still be explained by reduced interference. Her critique has been unwelcome in some quarters, yet it is a useful corrective to a field that has sometimes been too eager to announce breakthroughs.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What can be said with confidence? Sleep after learning is clearly beneficial, and losing sleep before a test is likely to do more harm than the extra hours of revision can repair. Beyond this, the picture is less certain. Researchers still disagree about which stages of sleep matter most, how long the benefits last and whether they differ between children, adults and the elderly. The idea that the brain sorts and files its experiences overnight is supported by an impressive range of evidence, but the hope of turning that process into a tool for effortless learning remains, for now, more a matter of speculation than of science.

topic: night shift work and internal circadian desynchrony
title: Working Against the Clock
subtitle: Night work keeps modern economies running, but at what cost to the people who do it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Roughly one in five employees in industrialised countries works outside conventional daytime hours, whether in hospitals, factories, transport networks or the call centres that serve customers in distant time zones. The round-the-clock economy depends on them, and for most of the twentieth century the main concern about their working patterns was fatigue: tired workers make mistakes, and mistakes in a chemical plant or an intensive care ward can be catastrophic. That concern remains valid. Over the past twenty years, however, attention has turned to a subtler and potentially more serious problem, namely the long-term consequences of forcing the body to operate at times when its internal systems are preparing for rest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Almost every cell in the human body contains a molecular clock, a set of genes whose activity rises and falls over a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours. These peripheral clocks are coordinated by a small region of the brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which is itself kept in time chiefly by light entering the eyes. Under normal conditions the system works in harmony: the liver prepares to process food during the day, body temperature falls at night, and hormones are released in a predictable sequence. Night work disrupts this coordination. The master clock responds to artificial light only slowly, while organs such as the liver and gut take their cues partly from mealtimes, so a worker who eats at three in the morning may end up with different parts of the body keeping different times. Physiologists call this condition internal desynchrony, and Dr Joaquim Esteves of the Porto Institute of Chronobiology compares it to an orchestra in which each section follows a different conductor.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What follows from such disorder is the subject of considerable dispute. Large studies of nurses and factory workers have linked long-term night work to higher rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The epidemiologist Eszter Balogh, who has analysed health records from more than ninety thousand Hungarian shift workers, believes the evidence now justifies treating prolonged night work as a recognised occupational hazard, comparable to exposure to noise or dust. Others are less certain. People who choose night work may differ from day workers in ways that affect their health, such as income, smoking habits or access to medical care, and no statistical technique can remove such differences entirely. Balogh's position is, in my view, broadly correct, but the size of the risks she reports may well be overstated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If disruption cannot be eliminated, can it be reduced? Esteves has experimented with carefully timed exposure to bright light during the early part of a night shift, combined with dark glasses on the journey home in the morning. In volunteers who followed this routine for a week, the master clock shifted by several hours, allowing them to sleep more soundly during the day. The difficulty, as he readily admits, is that most workers revert to a daytime schedule on their days off, undoing the adjustment almost immediately. A clock that is pushed back and forth every week may suffer more than one that is never moved at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This observation lies at the heart of a long-running argument about how shifts should be organised. Dr Tavita Faleolo, an occupational physician in Auckland, has advised several hospitals to replace rotating rosters with permanent night teams, on the grounds that people who work only at night have a better chance of adapting fully. Her critics point out that permanent night workers rarely adapt completely, because they still encounter daylight and wish to spend time with their families. Faleolo accepts this but argues that partial adaptation is preferable to the constant upheaval of rotation. Where rotation is unavoidable, she recommends that shifts move forward, from mornings to afternoons to nights, rather than backward, since the body finds it easier to delay its clock than to advance it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from Wanjiru Kamau, whose team at the Nairobi Centre for Industrial Health studies workers in manufacturing and logistics. Kamau argues that discussion of shift work has been dominated by research on nurses and other professionals, whose working conditions differ substantially from those of warehouse staff on short-term contracts. For these workers, she contends, the main problem is not the timing of shifts but their unpredictability: rosters are often published only days in advance, making it impossible to plan sleep, meals or childcare. Her surveys suggest that giving staff a fixed schedule two weeks ahead does more for their well-being than any adjustment to lighting.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these perspectives suggest that the health of night workers cannot be protected by biological solutions alone. Bright lights and carefully designed rosters have their place, but they are of limited use if employers treat working hours as something to be altered at short notice. Societies that rely on night work have an obligation to make it as tolerable as possible, and that obligation extends beyond the laboratory into the realm of employment law.

topic: the evolutionary origins and function of sleep across animal species
title: The Oldest Habit
subtitle: From jellyfish to dolphins, sleep appears to be almost universal. Biologists are still arguing about why.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: From an evolutionary perspective, sleep is a puzzle. An animal that is unconscious for hours each day cannot feed, cannot reproduce and cannot defend itself against predators. If sleep served no essential purpose, natural selection would surely have eliminated it long ago. Instead, it appears in virtually every animal that has been carefully studied, from fruit flies to elephants. This persistence strongly suggests that sleep provides some benefit which outweighs its considerable risks. Identifying that benefit, however, has proved remarkably difficult, and the search has produced a crowd of competing theories rather than a settled answer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The universality of sleep was underlined by a discovery that surprised even specialists. Dr Mirela Dragomir, a marine biologist at the Constanța Institute of Oceanography, spent two years observing a species of small jellyfish that rests on the sea floor and pulses rhythmically to move water over its body. At night the pulsing slowed considerably, and the animals took longer to respond to a sudden change in their surroundings, such as food being dropped near them. When Dragomir disturbed them repeatedly through the night, they were noticeably less active the following day, as though catching up on lost rest. These are the standard criteria by which scientists define sleep, and the jellyfish has no brain at all, only a loose network of nerve cells. If sleep exists in such a creature, then its origins must lie very far back in evolutionary history, and its purpose cannot be connected solely with the functioning of a complex brain.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the oldest explanations holds that sleep exists to save energy. Kaveh Rostami, a physiologist at the Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, points out that body temperature and metabolic rate fall during sleep, and that small mammals, which burn energy quickly, tend to sleep for longer than large ones. He argues that sleep is essentially a programmed period of reduced activity that keeps animals out of harm's way while conserving resources at times when foraging would be unproductive. The theory has the merit of simplicity. Its weakness is that the savings are modest: a sleeping human uses only around ten per cent less energy than one lying quietly awake, which seems a small reward for the vulnerability involved.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second family of theories focuses on maintenance. During waking hours, nerve cells accumulate chemical by-products and minor damage, and sleep may provide an opportunity to clear these away. Sigrún Einarsdóttir of the Reykjavík Neuroscience Unit has shown that in fruit flies deprived of sleep, a particular type of molecular damage builds up in nerve cells, and that flies genetically altered to repair this damage more efficiently need less sleep. In her view, the restoration of cells is the core function of sleep, and other benefits, such as improved memory, are secondary developments that appeared much later. This is an elegant proposal, though it remains to be seen whether findings in insects apply to mammals.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most compelling evidence that sleep is indispensable comes from animals whose way of life seems incompatible with it. Dolphins must surface regularly to breathe, and some seabirds remain airborne for weeks while crossing oceans. Ana Paula Tavares, a zoologist at the Federal University of Recife, has recorded brain activity in both groups and found that they sleep with one half of the brain at a time while the other half stays alert. Tavares notes that frigatebirds over the open ocean sleep for less than an hour a day, compared with twelve hours on land, but she does not believe this shows that sleep can be largely dispensed with. Rather, the extraordinary adaptation of sleeping one hemisphere at a time suggests that evolution found it easier to modify sleep than to abolish it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Lindiwe Mthembu, an ecologist at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, approaches the question from a different direction. She argues that it is a mistake to look for a single biological function, because the amount and timing of sleep vary enormously with an animal's ecology. Grazing animals exposed to predators on open plains sleep in short bursts, while predators such as lions may sleep for most of the day. Even within a single species, she has found, sleep shortens when food is scarce or when animals move into unfamiliar territory, and lengthens again once conditions become more secure. For Mthembu, sleep is best understood as a flexible strategy shaped by the dangers and opportunities of each environment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Mthembu's argument is persuasive as far as it goes, but it explains the pattern of sleep rather than its existence. The jellyfish evidence suggests that sleep arose to meet some basic cellular need, and that later functions were added to it as nervous systems grew more complex. The question 'what is sleep for?' may therefore have several correct answers, each belonging to a different stage of evolution. Searching for one universal purpose, as many researchers have done, is likely to prove fruitless.

topic: artificial light at night and its effects on human sleep and wildlife
title: The Vanishing Night
subtitle: Artificial light has transformed the hours of darkness. Scientists are only beginning to measure what has been lost.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1807, when gas lamps were first installed along a London street, crowds gathered to marvel at the spectacle. Within a century electric lighting had spread to cities across the world, and the night, which for most of human history had been a time of enforced rest, became an extension of the working and social day. Few innovations have been welcomed with such unqualified enthusiasm. Yet the brightening of the night sky has come at a cost that was not recognised until recently, and that is still frequently underestimated by the planners and engineers responsible for lighting our streets.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the change is now measurable. Bogdan Hryhorenko, an astronomer at the Lviv Observatory, has combined satellite images with thousands of ground-based readings to produce a map of artificial sky brightness. According to his estimates, more than eighty per cent of the world's population, and almost everyone living in Europe and North America, now lives under skies polluted by artificial light. One third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from home. Hryhorenko has also found that sky brightness has continued to increase by around two per cent a year, despite the replacement of older street lamps with supposedly more efficient designs. He attributes this partly to the fact that cheaper lighting encourages people to install more of it, so that gains in efficiency are absorbed by increases in use.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The switch to light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, has raised particular concerns. Early LED street lamps produced a cold, bluish light, and the light-sensitive cells in the human eye that signal to the body clock are most responsive to precisely these short wavelengths. Dr Seo-yeon Baek, a sleep physiologist at the Daegu Institute of Health Sciences, exposed volunteers to light of identical brightness but different colours in the two hours before bedtime. Blue-rich light suppressed melatonin, the hormone that promotes sleep, by roughly twice as much as warmer, amber light, and delayed the onset of sleep by around forty minutes. Baek cautions that indoor lighting and screens expose most people to far more light in the evening than street lamps do, and she considers outdoor lighting a relatively minor factor in human sleep. Her findings have nonetheless been cited in campaigns against bright street lighting.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For wildlife, the consequences may be more serious. Many animals rely on natural light cycles to time feeding, migration and reproduction, and artificial light can disrupt all three. Migrating birds, which navigate partly by the stars, are drawn towards illuminated buildings, where large numbers die in collisions. Newly hatched sea turtles, which instinctively head towards the brighter horizon over the sea, crawl inland towards roads instead. Joost van Wieringen, an ecologist at the University of Groningen, has spent a decade studying insects around street lamps. In experimental plots lit at night, he recorded a fall of almost half in the number of moth caterpillars compared with plots kept dark, and a corresponding decline in the plants that depend on moths for pollination.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Van Wieringen argues that light pollution should be ranked alongside pesticides and habitat loss as a cause of the widely reported collapse in insect numbers. This is probably going too far. His experiments were conducted in rural areas where the contrast between lit and unlit ground is sharpest, and the effect in already degraded urban environments may be considerably smaller. Nevertheless, the direction of his findings is consistent with a growing body of research, and the problem is one that, unlike many environmental threats, could be addressed quickly and cheaply. Once a lamp is switched off, its effect on the surrounding environment ends immediately, whereas chemical pollutants may persist in soil and water for decades.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical remedies are not difficult to identify. Lamps can be shielded so that light falls only where it is needed rather than spreading upwards and sideways; warmer colours can be chosen; and lights can be dimmed or switched off in the early hours when streets are empty. Ximena Aráoz, an urban planner in Córdoba, Argentina, has overseen a programme that reduced public lighting by forty per cent in several districts. Residents' initial fears about crime proved unfounded, she reports, and recorded offences did not rise. Aráoz is candid, however, that public acceptance depended on extensive consultation, and that a similar scheme imposed without discussion in a neighbouring town was abandoned within months.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Darkness, it seems, has become a resource that must be actively managed. Unlike clean air or clean water, it is rarely protected by law, and its loss attracts little public concern because it happened so gradually. A generation that has never seen a truly dark sky is unlikely to miss one, and campaigners for darker cities often find that their concerns are dismissed as aesthetic preferences rather than matters of health or ecology. Yet the evidence now suggests that the night is not simply empty time awaiting illumination, but an essential part of the environment for humans and other species alike.

topic: chronotypes, social jet lag and flexible working hours
title: Larks, Owls and the Tyranny of the Alarm Clock
subtitle: Are individual body clocks a matter of biology or habit, and should employers care?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Consider two colleagues in the same office. One wakes naturally before six, is at her most productive by mid-morning and is ready for bed soon after ten. The other struggles to function before eleven, reaches his peak in the late afternoon and does his best thinking close to midnight. Conventional wisdom tends to praise the first and criticise the second, associating early rising with virtue and late rising with indulgence. Research on what scientists call chronotype, an individual's natural preference for the timing of sleep and activity, suggests that this moral judgement is largely misplaced, and that a society organised around early starts may be unfairly penalising a sizeable minority of its members.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Chronotype is distributed across the population roughly in the shape of a bell curve: most people fall somewhere in the middle, with extreme 'larks' and 'owls' at either end. Annika Väisänen, a geneticist at the University of Turku, has analysed the DNA of nearly half a million volunteers and identified more than three hundred genetic variants associated with morning or evening preference. Many of these lie in or near genes known to regulate the body clock. Väisänen estimates that genes account for between a third and a half of the variation in chronotype, with the remainder explained by age, sex and environment. Chronotype also shifts over the course of a lifetime, becoming progressively later through adolescence, peaking at around twenty, and then gradually moving earlier again in middle and old age.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The consequences of a mismatch between biological and social time were first described systematically by Matteo Bellandi, a chronobiologist at the University of Bologna. Bellandi coined the term 'social jet lag' to describe the difference between the timing of a person's sleep on working days and on free days. A late chronotype who must rise at seven during the week but sleeps until ten at weekends effectively flies across three time zones every Friday and back again every Monday. In surveys of more than sixty thousand Europeans, Bellandi found that around two-thirds experienced at least one hour of social jet lag, and that each additional hour was associated with a higher likelihood of obesity, smoking and low mood.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These associations are striking, though they do not prove that social jet lag causes poor health. People who stay up late may also be more likely to smoke or drink for reasons unrelated to their body clocks. Bellandi accepts this limitation but points to laboratory studies in which volunteers forced to live out of step with their internal rhythms showed rapid changes in blood sugar and appetite hormones. Within a few days, some of these volunteers displayed patterns more typical of people at risk of diabetes, although the changes reversed once normal routines were restored. Taken together, the evidence makes a causal link plausible, even if its strength remains uncertain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the problem lies in the mismatch, one solution is to change working hours rather than people. Gulnara Abdrakhmanova, an organisational psychologist at the Almaty School of Management, persuaded a steel company to allow workers on its rotating shifts to choose schedules matching their chronotypes. Early types were excused from night shifts and late types from early mornings. Those in the middle of the range, who formed the majority, continued to rotate as before, which allowed the company to keep its factories running around the clock. Over the following year, the workers slept on average almost an hour longer on working days, and reported greater satisfaction with their jobs. Abdrakhmanova readily admits that the arrangement was easier to introduce in a large workforce, where there were enough people of each type to cover every shift, than it would be in a small business.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that chronotype should be treated as fixed. Emeka Nwachukwu, a sleep researcher at the University of Ibadan, took a group of self-described night owls on a week-long camping trip with no artificial light. By the end of the week, their sleep had moved almost two hours earlier and the differences between them and the morning types in the group had largely disappeared. Nwachukwu concludes that many late chronotypes are not born but made, by evening exposure to electric light and a lack of daylight during the day. His experiment is ingenious, but it was small and brief, and it is not clear that its results would survive a return to ordinary urban life.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Both perspectives contain some truth. Chronotype is partly inherited and partly shaped by circumstance, and the balance between the two will vary from person to person. What seems beyond dispute is that rigid schedules which ignore individual differences carry real costs. Allowing people a degree of choice over when they work is not an indulgence of the lazy; it is a sensible response to biological diversity, and one that may benefit employers as much as employees.

topic: segmented (first and second) sleep in pre-industrial history
title: The Lost Hour Between Two Sleeps
subtitle: Did our ancestors sleep in two shifts, and does it matter if we no longer do?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Scattered through letters, court records, medical handbooks and diaries from early modern Europe are references to something that sounds strange to modern ears: a 'first sleep' and a 'second sleep'. Writers mention waking in the middle of the night, sometimes for an hour or more, before settling down again until dawn. The interval was apparently put to many uses. People prayed, tended fires, checked on livestock, talked quietly with their partners or simply lay reflecting on their dreams. To those who recorded them, these waking hours seem to have been entirely unremarkable, which is perhaps the most intriguing thing about them. Nobody thought it necessary to explain the practice, any more than a modern diarist would explain the habit of eating lunch.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The historian Cormac Ó Faoláin, of the Galway Centre for Social History, spent more than a decade collecting such references and has found over two thousand of them in sources written in at least six languages. He argues that divided sleep was the normal pattern for most Europeans before the spread of artificial lighting, and that it disappeared during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as street lamps, gas and then electricity encouraged people to go to bed later. With less time available for sleep, Ó Faoláin suggests, the night was compressed into a single block, and the memory of the older pattern faded so completely that historians had overlooked hundreds of references in documents they had read many times.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Support for this idea seemed to come from an experiment conducted some years earlier by the psychiatrist Rune Haugaard at the Aarhus Sleep Clinic. Haugaard asked a group of healthy volunteers to spend several weeks in conditions where they were exposed to darkness for fourteen hours each night instead of the usual eight. After an initial period in which they slept for long stretches, apparently repaying accumulated sleep debt, most of the volunteers settled into a pattern of two sleeps separated by one to three hours of quiet wakefulness. Haugaard concluded that segmented sleep might be the natural human pattern, revealed only when the long nights of winter are not shortened by artificial light.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficulty with this conclusion emerged when anthropologists began to study communities living without electricity today. Amaru Quispe, an anthropologist at the National University of San Marcos in Lima, fitted motion sensors to members of three hunter-gatherer and farming communities in South America and Africa. Contrary to expectation, very few of them showed any regular pattern of two sleeps. They typically fell asleep some hours after sunset, slept in a single block and woke around dawn, waking briefly during the night but rarely for long. Quispe suggests that segmented sleep is not a universal biological pattern but a cultural practice, perhaps linked to the cold, long nights of northern latitudes and to the habit of retiring to bed very early to save fuel and candles.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Itzel Necoechea, a cultural historian at the Autonomous University of Puebla, takes this argument a step further. In her view, the European evidence shows how deeply sleep is shaped by social expectations, including religious ones: several Christian orders required members to rise in the middle of the night for prayer, and lay people may have imitated this practice. She warns against the temptation to treat any historical pattern as more 'natural' than our own, pointing out that this assumption has led some writers to romanticise the past and to blame modern life for problems that existed long before it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever its origins, the history of segmented sleep has found an unexpected application in medicine. Dr Yaël Benhamou, a specialist in insomnia at a clinic in Lyon, routinely tells patients who wake at three in the morning about the first and second sleep. Many of them, she reports, are less anxious once they learn that night waking was once considered normal, and anxiety about being awake is itself one of the main factors that prevent people from falling asleep again. Benhamou is careful not to claim that her patients' waking is natural, only that it need not be treated as a disaster. She encourages them to get up, read quietly in dim light and return to bed when they feel drowsy, rather than lying in the dark watching the clock and calculating how many hours remain before the alarm.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate illustrates the risk of drawing biological conclusions from historical evidence alone. Ó Faoláin's documentary research is impressive and has rightly changed how historians think about the night, but the leap from 'our ancestors often slept in two phases' to 'humans are designed to sleep in two phases' was always a large one, and Quispe's data suggest that it cannot be sustained. Still, Benhamou's work shows that history can have practical value even when it does not reveal some lost natural state. Knowing that the way we sleep is not the only way people have ever slept may be reassuring enough.

topic: theories of the function of dreaming and REM sleep
title: The Purpose of Dreams
subtitle: Do the stories we experience at night serve any function, or are they simply noise?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every night, most adults spend around two hours in rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, the stage most closely associated with vivid dreaming. During this time the brain is almost as active as when awake, the eyes dart beneath closed lids and the muscles of the body are temporarily paralysed, apparently to prevent sleepers from acting out their dreams. Such an elaborate arrangement seems unlikely to exist without a reason, and theories of what dreams are for have multiplied accordingly. Yet it is worth remembering that REM sleep and dreaming are not the same thing: dreams also occur in other stages of sleep, and an explanation of one is not automatically an explanation of the other.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, scientific opinion was dominated by the view that dreams have no function at all. According to this account, which Dr Kwabena Asante of the University of Ghana continues to defend in a modified form, dreams are a by-product of the brain's attempt to make sense of random signals generated during REM sleep. The brain, Asante argues, is a storytelling organ that cannot help imposing narrative on whatever activity it encounters. REM sleep itself may well be important, perhaps for maintaining neural connections, but the content of dreams is, in his phrase, 'the noise of the machine, not its output'. Asante points out that people who take certain antidepressants, which drastically reduce REM sleep, suffer no obvious harm even after years of treatment.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This minimalist position has been challenged from several directions. Professor Tariq Benali, a neuroscientist at the Rabat Institute of Brain Sciences, argues that REM sleep helps people cope with emotional experiences. During REM, levels of noradrenaline, a chemical linked to stress, fall almost to zero, while regions of the brain involved in emotion become highly active. Benali believes this combination allows painful memories to be reactivated in a safe neurochemical environment, so that their emotional intensity is gradually reduced while their content is retained. In one of his studies, volunteers who had a period of REM-rich sleep after viewing distressing images rated those images as less upsetting the next day than volunteers who had remained awake.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An alternative theory concentrates on the content of dreams rather than their chemistry. Dr Hana Dvořáková, a psychologist at Charles University in Prague, has analysed thousands of dream reports and found that threatening situations, such as being chased, falling or being attacked, appear far more often in dreams than in everyday waking life. She proposes that dreaming evolved as a kind of rehearsal, allowing our ancestors to practise responses to danger without real risk. Children who have experienced trauma, she notes, dream of threats more frequently than other children, which is consistent with a system that becomes more active when danger is perceived to be high. The theory has an obvious appeal, but critics observe that most dreams are mundane, and that rehearsing a response to a monster is of limited value in learning to escape a real predator.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Clinical work has added a practical dimension to these debates. Dr Aroha Ngata, a psychiatrist in Wellington who specialises in recurrent nightmares, teaches patients to rewrite the ending of a frightening dream while awake and to rehearse the new version repeatedly during the day. Patients do not need to recall the original dream in detail; a rough outline is usually sufficient, and the new ending need not be a happy one, only a different one. Many patients report that their nightmares become less frequent and less distressing within a few weeks. Ngata is cautious about what this shows, however. The success of the technique, she argues, demonstrates that dream content can be influenced, but not that dreams serve any particular purpose in the first place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Each of these theories captures something. Asante is right to insist that not every feature of a biological process must have a function, and that our instinct to find meaning in dreams may say more about us than about the brain. However, the evidence that REM sleep softens emotional memories is now considerable, and his dismissal of it is unconvincing. The observation about antidepressants is less decisive than it appears, since the patients concerned are, by definition, already being treated for emotional difficulties.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Dvořáková's rehearsal theory is the hardest to test, and for that reason the least satisfactory scientifically, however intuitive it may seem. The most probable conclusion is that REM sleep serves several functions, at least one of them emotional, while the stories we remember on waking are partly meaningful and partly accidental. That answer will satisfy neither those who see dreams as messages nor those who see them as meaningless, but it is the one that best fits the available evidence. It also points to where research should go next, particularly towards the dreams that occur outside REM sleep, which have so far received comparatively little attention.

topic: plant circadian clocks and their applications in agriculture
title: Gardens of Time
subtitle: Plants keep time with remarkable precision. Can farmers learn to work with their clocks?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the eighteenth century, a French astronomer placed a mimosa plant in a dark cupboard and observed that its leaves continued to open in the morning and fold at dusk, even though no light reached them. It was the first demonstration that living organisms possess an internal sense of time, independent of the environment. For two centuries the observation remained little more than a botanical curiosity. Today, however, plant clocks are the subject of intense scientific interest, and some researchers believe they could transform the way crops are bred, grown and stored. That optimism is, I think, broadly justified, although its more enthusiastic advocates sometimes underestimate the obstacles.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The plant clock is built from a network of genes that switch one another on and off in a cycle lasting approximately a day. Unlike animals, plants have no central controller equivalent to the brain; instead, each cell keeps its own time, and the clocks in different tissues can run at slightly different speeds. The clock allows a plant to anticipate dawn rather than merely react to it, so that the machinery of photosynthesis is ready the moment light arrives. It also governs the timing of flowering, since many species measure the length of the day in order to bloom in the right season. Dr Imogen Treharne of the Cambrian Institute of Plant Science has shown that plants whose internal cycle matches the length of the external day grow faster and survive longer than those whose clocks run too fast or too slow. In her experiments, mismatched plants fixed less carbon and produced fewer seeds, even when given ample water and nutrients.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The clock also appears to have played an important role in the history of agriculture. When crops such as rice, barley and tomatoes were carried away from the regions where they were first domesticated, they encountered different patterns of day length. Professor Ravindra Gunasekara, a geneticist at the University of Peradeniya, has traced how early farmers, without any knowledge of genetics, selected plants carrying mutations that slowed or weakened their clocks. These mutations allowed crops to flower at appropriate times far from the equator. In Gunasekara's view, adjustment of the clock was one of the decisive steps in domestication, as significant as the familiar changes in seed size and the loss of natural seed dispersal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If the clock has been altered unconsciously in the past, it might now be adjusted deliberately. Gunasekara argues that, as the climate warms and crops are grown in new latitudes, breeders will need to tune flowering time with far greater precision. Some go further. Dr Verónica Ibarguren, an agricultural scientist at the University of the Basque Country, has coined the term 'chronoculture' for the practice of timing farm operations to match the plant's internal rhythms. Plants' defences against insects, for example, peak at particular times of day, and Ibarguren has found that spraying pesticides when a crop's own defences are at their weakest allows farmers to use substantially smaller quantities. She believes similar gains could be made with the timing of irrigation and fertiliser application.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One of the more surprising discoveries is that the clock does not stop when a plant is harvested. A team at the Ghent Horticultural Research Station found that cabbages and lettuces kept in supermarket conditions continued to cycle for several days, provided they were exposed to alternating light and darkness. Vegetables kept in constant darkness or constant light lost their rhythm and, with it, some of their capacity to resist decay and to produce compounds that protect against disease. The researchers suggest that storing vegetables under a simulated day-night cycle could extend their shelf life and preserve their nutritional value.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not every expert is persuaded. Jarrah Whitlock, a horticultural engineer who advises vertical farming companies in Brisbane, points out that in fully enclosed, artificially lit facilities, growers can impose any light cycle they choose. In such systems, he maintains, the internal clock becomes far less important, because the plant never has to anticipate an unpredictable environment. Whitlock's experiments with lettuce grown under continuous light found that yields increased, at least for the first few weeks, although leaves eventually showed signs of damage. He concludes that the clock is a constraint to be managed, not a resource to be exploited.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whitlock's point has some force for the small proportion of food grown indoors, but it does not apply to the vast majority of crops, which will continue to be grown in open fields under the sun. Even his own results indicate that overriding the clock carries a cost over time. The more serious obstacle to chronoculture is practical: farmers already work long hours, and asking them to time every operation to the hour may be unrealistic without automated machinery. The science, in short, is ahead of the practice, which is not an argument against the science.

topic: consumer sleep-tracking devices: accuracy, anxiety and population research
title: Counting Sheep by Numbers
subtitle: Millions of people now measure their sleep every night. Is the data helping them rest, or keeping them awake?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A decade ago, information about the quality of a person's sleep could be obtained only in a laboratory, where volunteers spent the night wired to electrodes under the eye of a technician. Today, tens of millions of people wear rings, watches or wristbands that produce a detailed report each morning, complete with scores, graphs and estimates of time spent in each stage of sleep. The appeal is understandable. Sleep is one of the few areas of life that we cannot observe directly, and devices promise to make the invisible visible. Whether this promise is being fulfilled is another matter, and the answer depends very much on what is being measured, and by whom.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Most consumer devices do not measure sleep at all, at least not in the sense that a laboratory does. Laboratory recordings, known as polysomnography, track electrical activity in the brain, which is what defines the stages of sleep. Wrist-worn trackers, by contrast, infer sleep from movement and heart rate, using algorithms that the manufacturers rarely disclose. Professor Dimitrios Karalis, a biomedical engineer at the University of Patras, has compared several popular devices with simultaneous laboratory recordings. He found that they estimated total sleep time reasonably well in healthy young adults, usually within twenty minutes, but were far less accurate at distinguishing between light, deep and dreaming sleep. They also tended to mistake lying still while awake for sleep, a serious weakness for people with insomnia, who often spend long periods motionless in bed without sleeping.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For some users, the numbers themselves have become a source of distress. Dr Amaal Warsame, who runs a sleep clinic in Minneapolis, describes a growing number of patients who arrive with months of tracker data and a conviction that their sleep is seriously disordered, even when they feel well during the day. Some go to bed earlier, or stay in bed longer, in an attempt to improve their scores, behaviour that can actually worsen sleep by weakening the association between bed and sleep. Clinicians have begun to use the term 'orthosomnia' for this preoccupation with achieving perfect sleep data. Warsame stresses that such patients remain a minority of tracker users, but she argues that manufacturers have a responsibility to present their scores with more caution than they currently do.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others see considerable value in the devices, particularly when their data are combined across large populations. Dr Lê Thu Hà, an epidemiologist at the Hanoi School of Public Health, has worked with anonymised records from more than two hundred thousand tracker users in eleven countries. Her analysis has revealed patterns that would be almost impossible to detect in a laboratory, including the way sleep shortens during heatwaves and after the clocks change in spring. Such effects are small for any individual, often amounting to only a few minutes a night, but they become clearly visible when averaged across an entire country. Because errors in individual nights tend to cancel each other out across thousands of people, she argues, the data are far more reliable for studying populations than for judging the sleep of any one person.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further argument concerns behaviour. Kalani Akana, a behavioural scientist at the University of Hawaiʻi, ran a trial in which office workers were given trackers along with weekly feedback on their bedtimes. Over three months, the group went to bed on average twenty-five minutes earlier and reported feeling more alert than a control group without devices. Akana attributes the change not to the accuracy of the measurements but to the simple act of paying attention: once people could see how late they habitually went to bed, many chose to change. He concedes, however, that the improvement faded in the months after the feedback stopped, suggesting that the devices may need to be combined with longer-term support if the benefits are to last.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings are not as contradictory as they might first appear. The trackers appear to be most useful when their limitations are understood, either by researchers working with very large samples or by users who treat the data as a rough guide to habits rather than a precise verdict on their health. They are least useful, and occasionally harmful, when users place more trust in a sleep score than in their own sense of how rested they feel. In my view, the responsibility for this confusion lies largely with manufacturers, whose marketing frequently implies a level of precision that their products cannot deliver.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that people should abandon their devices. A tracker that encourages a regular bedtime is doing something worthwhile, regardless of whether its estimate of deep sleep is correct. Nor should the limitations of current devices be taken as permanent; sensors are improving rapidly, and independent testing of the kind Karalis carries out is becoming more common. But the best measure of a good night's sleep remains, as it always has been, how a person feels the next day.

topic: birth mode, early colonisation and the infant gut microbiome
title: First Colonists
subtitle: Does the way a baby enters the world shape the microbes it carries for life?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the womb was assumed to be sterile, and a newborn's encounter with bacteria was thought to begin at the moment of delivery. That assumption has been challenged in recent years by reports of microbial DNA in placental tissue, though most specialists now regard these traces as contamination introduced during sampling rather than evidence of genuine colonisation. What is not in dispute is that the first days of life represent an extraordinary period of microbial settlement. Within a week, the infant gut, previously almost empty, is home to billions of bacterial cells, and the species that arrive first may influence which others are able to follow. In my view, it is this question of order, rather than simple presence or absence, that deserves the most attention.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Babies born vaginally are exposed to their mother's vaginal and intestinal microbes during birth, whereas those delivered by caesarean section first encounter bacteria from skin and the hospital environment. A study coordinated by Dr Ingrid Solvang at the Bergen Institute of Child Health compared stool samples from nearly six hundred infants and found that caesarean-born babies had markedly lower levels of Bacteroides, a genus associated with the digestion of complex carbohydrates. Solvang's team also noted that the gap had largely closed by the age of nine months. She therefore cautions against describing the caesarean microbiome as 'damaged', arguing that the differences she observed were a matter of timing rather than permanent loss.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others interpret the same pattern less reassuringly. The epidemiologist Rafael Quintero-Baez of the Andean Centre for Population Health points to large registry studies linking caesarean delivery with modestly higher rates of asthma, obesity and coeliac disease in later childhood. If early colonisation trains the developing immune system, he reasons, then even a temporary delay could have lasting effects, much as a missed stage in language development may be difficult to make up later. Quintero-Baez acknowledges that these associations do not prove causation. Mothers who undergo caesarean sections differ in many ways from those who do not: they are more likely to receive antibiotics, to be older and to be overweight, and each of these factors might independently influence a child's health.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Such uncertainty has not prevented the emergence of a practice known as vaginal seeding, in which a gauze swab is placed in the mother's vagina before surgery and then wiped over the newborn's mouth, face and skin. Small trials have shown that seeded infants acquire a microbial profile somewhat closer to that of vaginally born babies. Yet the procedure is not without risk. The swab can transmit pathogens such as group B streptococcus or herpes simplex virus, which may cause serious infection in newborns. Several professional bodies have advised against seeding outside research settings, and this caution seems entirely sensible given how little is known about its long-term benefits.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from Dr Yuki Hanamura, a microbial ecologist at the Kansai University of Life Sciences, who argues that the focus on delivery mode is too narrow. In her longitudinal work, which tracked more than a thousand families, feeding method exerted a stronger and more persistent influence on gut composition than the route of birth. Breast milk contains complex sugars that human infants cannot digest themselves; their main function appears to be to nourish particular bifidobacteria, which in turn crowd out less desirable species. Hanamura therefore suggests that supporting breastfeeding may achieve more than any intervention in the delivery room. Her data are impressive, although they come largely from a single region, and it remains to be seen whether her conclusions hold in populations with different diets and medical practices.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most ambitious research programme is that of Professor Oluwaseun Adewale at the Lagos Centre for Microbial Medicine, who is investigating whether tiny quantities of maternal faecal material, carefully screened, could be given orally to caesarean-born infants. An early feasibility study involving seventeen babies reported no adverse effects and a rapid shift towards a typical vaginal-birth profile. Adewale himself describes the results as preliminary and has emphasised that any wider application would require rigorous screening of donors for viruses and drug-resistant bacteria. Even so, the idea has provoked considerable unease among parents and clinicians alike, some of whom feel that the enthusiasm surrounding the microbiome has begun to outpace the evidence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this debate is less a set of answers than a lesson in humility. The infant microbiome is shaped by delivery, feeding, antibiotics, older siblings and even household pets, and isolating the influence of any single factor has proved extraordinarily difficult. It would be a mistake, I believe, to make mothers who require caesarean sections feel that they have harmed their children. The more productive task is to identify which early exposures genuinely matter, and that will require studies that follow children not for months but for decades.

topic: faecal microbiota transplantation: evidence, mechanism and regulation
title: The Unlikeliest Medicine
subtitle: Faecal transplants work remarkably well against one stubborn infection. The question is what else they can, and should, be used for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few treatments in modern medicine provoke quite the same reaction as the faecal microbiota transplant, in which stool from a healthy donor is introduced into the intestine of a patient. The idea is far older than its current popularity suggests. Accounts from fourth-century China describe physicians administering preparations of faecal matter to patients with severe diarrhoea, and in the mid-twentieth century a small number of surgeons reported dramatic recoveries using faecal enemas. For decades, however, these reports were treated as curiosities. It was only when a particularly persistent intestinal infection began to resist conventional drugs that the procedure moved, somewhat reluctantly, from the margins of medicine towards its centre.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The infection in question is caused by Clostridioides difficile, a bacterium that tends to flourish when antibiotics have stripped away much of the gut's normal community. Further courses of antibiotics often clear the symptoms temporarily, only for the infection to return weeks later, sometimes repeatedly over a period of years. In a trial led by Dr Mateus Albuquerque at the Porto Institute of Digestive Medicine, patients with recurrent infection were assigned either to standard antibiotic treatment or to a faecal transplant. The trial was stopped early because the difference between the groups was so large that continuing to withhold the transplant was judged unethical: around nine in ten transplant recipients were cured, compared with roughly a third of those receiving antibiotics alone.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why the procedure works remains less clear than its success might imply. The prevailing explanation is that donor bacteria re-establish a diverse community that outcompetes the invader for nutrients and restores the conversion of certain bile acids into forms that inhibit its growth. However, Dr Signe Haraldsdottir, a microbiologist at the Reykjavik Centre for Molecular Medicine, reported that a small group of patients recovered after receiving donor material that had been filtered to remove living bacteria altogether. She suggests that viruses which infect bacteria, or chemical products left in the filtrate, may be doing much of the work. Her sample was tiny, and the finding awaits replication, but it raises an awkward possibility: that the word 'transplant' may describe the procedure less accurately than is generally supposed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These uncertainties feed directly into an unresolved regulatory question. In some countries, donor stool is classified as a medicinal product, subject to the same approval processes as a new drug; elsewhere it is treated more like donated blood or tissue. Professor Kwame Molander, a specialist in health law at the Accra School of Public Policy, argues that the drug model is poorly suited to a living, variable material that no manufacturer can patent, and that it has left patients in some regions unable to obtain an effective treatment. His critics counter that the risks are real: there have been reported cases of patients developing serious infections from drug-resistant organisms present in donor material that had not been adequately tested. On balance, the case for rigorous screening seems unanswerable, though it does not follow that the full apparatus of drug regulation is the only means of achieving it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Screening has made suitable donors surprisingly scarce. Stool banks routinely reject the great majority of volunteers, because of recent travel, medication use or the presence of potentially harmful microbes. Among those who are accepted, some appear to be more valuable than others. Dr Lucia Echeverria of the Montevideo Gut Research Group has observed that transplants from certain individuals succeed considerably more often than those from others, a pattern that has given rise to the notion of the 'super-donor'. Echeverria is careful to stress that the data come from small trials, in which a few unusually good results could arise by chance. The concept is intriguing, but it has spread through popular accounts of the microbiome rather faster than the evidence warrants.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most contentious issue concerns the use of faecal transplants beyond recurrent infection. Trials in ulcerative colitis have produced modestly encouraging results, while those in irritable bowel syndrome and obesity have been inconsistent, and claims regarding neurological and developmental conditions rest on very limited evidence. Nevertheless, online forums offer detailed instructions for home transplants, often using material from friends or relatives who have undergone no testing whatsoever. That patients with chronic and poorly understood conditions should be drawn to such methods is understandable; that they are doing so largely without medical supervision is a cause for genuine alarm.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Partly in response to these concerns, several companies are now developing standardised products containing defined mixtures of bacteria grown in the laboratory, which would eliminate the variability and infection risk of donor stool. Such products would undoubtedly be easier to regulate and to manufacture at scale, and they might also prove more acceptable to patients who find the original procedure distasteful. Yet if Haraldsdottir's findings are confirmed, a carefully selected set of bacterial strains may omit precisely those components on which the treatment's effectiveness depends. It would be ironic if, in making the procedure more acceptable, medicine were to strip away the very complexity that made it work.

topic: the gut-brain axis and psychobiotics
title: Thinking from the Gut
subtitle: Intestinal bacteria have been credited with influencing mood and behaviour. How strong is the evidence?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When mice are raised in sterile isolators, entirely free of microbes, they behave in curious ways. Compared with ordinary laboratory animals, these so-called germ-free mice explore open spaces more readily, yet they also show an exaggerated hormonal response when placed under stress. More striking still, when germ-free animals are colonised with gut bacteria taken from particularly timid mice, they tend to become timid themselves. Results of this kind have given rise to an entire field devoted to the idea that intestinal microbes influence the brain, and to a new category of supplements, sometimes called psychobiotics, marketed as aids to mood and mental clarity. The animal findings are genuinely remarkable. It should be remembered, however, that mice are not small humans, and behaviour in a laboratory cage is at best a crude proxy for human emotion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Several routes by which gut bacteria might communicate with the brain have been proposed. Microbes produce short-chain fatty acids and other compounds that enter the bloodstream; they influence the immune system, whose signalling molecules can affect neural tissue; and some manufacture the chemical building blocks of neurotransmitters. It is often pointed out that around ninety per cent of the body's serotonin is produced in the gut, a fact frequently cited, misleadingly, as evidence that intestinal bacteria govern mood: serotonin made in the intestine cannot pass the blood-brain barrier. A more direct pathway is the vagus nerve, which links the gut to the brainstem. Professor Henrik Aalto of the Turku Institute of Neurobiology found that a strain of Lactobacillus that reduced anxious behaviour in mice had no such effect once the vagus nerve had been surgically cut, and he regards this nerve as the principal channel of communication.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Establishing whether anything comparable happens in people is considerably harder. Dr Priyanka Raghunathan, who leads a population study at the Chennai Centre for Behavioural Medicine, analysed stool samples from more than a thousand volunteers and found that those reporting symptoms of depression carried lower levels of several bacteria that produce butyrate, a fatty acid with anti-inflammatory properties. Raghunathan is cautious about what this shows. Depression alters appetite, sleep and physical activity, and is often treated with drugs that themselves affect gut bacteria. It is therefore quite possible, she argues, that the illness shapes the microbiome rather than the other way round.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Intervention trials ought to resolve such questions, since they can test whether deliberately altering gut bacteria changes mental state. Dr Tariq Al-Mansouri of the Gulf University of Health Sciences pooled the results of over thirty trials in which volunteers took probiotic supplements. The overall effect on self-reported mood was small, and it was concentrated among participants who already had symptoms of anxiety or depression; healthy volunteers showed little benefit. Al-Mansouri also noted that a substantial proportion of the trials had been funded by supplement manufacturers. This is a pattern that, in my view, ought to temper any enthusiasm for the more positive results.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Popular accounts of this research frequently describe the gut as a 'second brain'. The phrase refers to the enteric nervous system, a genuine network of some five hundred million neurons lining the digestive tract, but as a description of the microbiome it does more to confuse than to inform, since it implies that bacteria possess something resembling intention. Dr Gabriela Szymanska, a psychiatrist at the Krakow Medical Academy, goes further, arguing that the field as a whole suffers from small samples and a tendency to publish only positive findings. She also points out that germ-free mice have severely underdeveloped immune systems, so that comparing them with normal animals is likely to magnify any apparent effect of bacteria. Her criticisms deserve to be taken seriously, but to conclude from them that the gut-brain connection is an illusion would be premature.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most promising applications may in fact lie not in capsules but in the kitchen. In one trial, adults with moderate depression who adopted a Mediterranean-style diet, rich in vegetables, legumes and whole grains, reported greater improvement over twelve weeks than a comparison group who received social support alone. The diet group also showed some reduction in anxiety, although the trial was too small to allow firm conclusions on this point. Whether the benefit arose through changes in gut bacteria is unknown. Yet this uncertainty matters less than it might appear, because such a diet is beneficial for the heart and metabolism regardless of its effect on the microbiome.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The study of the gut-brain axis thus occupies an awkward position. Its central idea is plausible and supported by a growing body of animal research, but the human evidence remains thin, and commercial interest has run well ahead of the science. The challenge for the coming decade is to conduct large, independently funded trials capable of distinguishing genuine effects from wishful thinking. Until such trials report, consumers would be well advised to treat the claims printed on supplement packaging with considerable scepticism, and to regard a varied, fibre-rich diet as the safer investment.

topic: antibiotics and the recovery of the gut microbiome
title: After the Storm
subtitle: Antibiotics save lives, but what happens to the gut's resident community once the course is finished?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a study that has become something of a reference point in the field, a group of healthy adult volunteers at the Tartu Clinical Microbiology Unit agreed to take a four-day course of three broad-spectrum antibiotics simultaneously, a regimen far more aggressive than anything a doctor would normally prescribe. The researchers, led by Dr Margit Kallas, sampled the volunteers' stool before treatment, daily during it, and at intervals for six months afterwards. By the end of the four days, the bacterial population had collapsed to a small fraction of its original size. Within six weeks, most of the major groups had returned. Yet even after six months, nine species that had been commonly present before treatment could no longer be detected in any of the participants.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: How should such results be interpreted? Kallas herself emphasises the resilience of the gut community: an ecosystem subjected to an almost unthinkable assault had, in large measure, rebuilt itself within weeks. Others focus on what failed to return. Professor Diego Valdivia, an ecologist at the University of Valparaiso, compares the gut to a forest recovering after a fire. A forest may regain its canopy within a few decades, he notes, while certain slow-growing or specialised species vanish permanently. In his view, total bacterial numbers, which most clinical studies measure, are a poor indicator of whether an ecosystem has genuinely recovered, since the disappearance of a few uncommon species with distinctive functions may matter more than the overall count.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Valdivia's analogy is illuminating, but it can be pushed too far. Unlike an isolated forest, the gut is continually exposed to new arrivals through food, water and contact with other people, and species lost during treatment may in time be reacquired from the environment. Whether this actually happens is a question that few studies have followed participants for long enough to answer. The limited long-term data that do exist, however, are not encouraging: they suggest that repeated courses of antibiotics are followed by progressively less complete recovery, with each course leaving the community somewhat less diverse than the one before.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This cumulative effect is of particular concern in early childhood, when antibiotics are prescribed more often than at almost any other stage of life. Dr Noor Hamidi of the Kuala Lumpur Paediatric Research Centre followed eight hundred children from birth and found that those who had received three or more courses before the age of two had markedly less diverse gut bacteria at the age of five. They were also somewhat more likely to be overweight, a finding that recalls the long-standing agricultural practice of adding low doses of antibiotics to animal feed to make livestock grow faster. Hamidi is careful not to claim that antibiotics cause childhood obesity, since children who are frequently ill may differ from their peers in many respects. She does, however, argue strongly for reducing prescriptions that serve no medical purpose, such as those given for viral infections, against which antibiotics are entirely ineffective.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A common response to concerns about antibiotic damage is to take probiotic supplements during or after treatment, in the expectation that they will speed recovery. A study by Dr Jae-won Ryu at the Seoul Institute for Microbial Health casts doubt on this practice. Volunteers who took a multi-strain probiotic after a course of antibiotics needed up to five months to regain their original microbial composition, whereas those who took nothing returned to their baseline within about three weeks. Ryu suggests that the probiotic strains occupied ecological niches that would otherwise have been reclaimed by the volunteers' own bacteria. In the same study, a third group received a transplant of their own stool, collected and frozen before treatment began, and recovered within days. The result is striking, but the procedure is expensive, and the need to store stool in advance of an illness that cannot be foreseen makes it impractical for most people.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For Dr Thandiwe Mokoena of the Cape Town Centre for Infection Control, attempts to repair the microbiome after the event address the problem from the wrong end. The more effective solution, she argues, is to avoid unnecessary damage in the first place by developing narrow-spectrum antibiotics that target specific pathogens, combined with rapid diagnostic tests that identify the cause of an infection within hours rather than days. Her argument is persuasive in principle. In practice, though, the commercial incentives run in the opposite direction: a drug that kills only one species of bacterium has a far smaller market than one that kills many, and few pharmaceutical companies have shown much appetite for developing such products.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this should be taken as an argument against antibiotics themselves, which remain among the most important tools in medicine and have prevented countless deaths from infections that were once routinely fatal. The lesson is rather that every course carries a cost that has, until recently, been largely invisible. Recognising that cost may encourage both doctors and patients to treat antibiotics as a precious resource, to be used decisively when needed and withheld when it is not.
