topic: the hygiene hypothesis and its 'old friends' revision
title: Too Clean for Our Own Good?
subtitle: The hygiene hypothesis has been revised so often that its original author might barely recognise it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1980s, Dr Sunniva Eide, an epidemiologist analysing a national birth cohort at the Trondheim Centre for Population Studies, noticed a curious pattern. Children who had several older brothers and sisters were noticeably less likely to develop hay fever and eczema than first-born or only children. Eide proposed that infections passed around within large families during the first years of life somehow protected younger siblings against allergic disease. The suggestion was quickly labelled the 'hygiene hypothesis', and it offered an appealingly simple explanation for one of the most puzzling trends in modern medicine: the steep rise in allergies and asthma across wealthy countries during the second half of the twentieth century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: As the evidence accumulated, however, the original version of the idea began to look increasingly fragile. Common childhood infections such as measles turned out to offer no protection against allergies, and in some studies appeared to increase the risk. Moreover, asthma has risen sharply in several rapidly growing cities where crowded living conditions mean that respiratory infections remain widespread. In my view, the name given to the hypothesis has also proved unfortunate. By implying that cleanliness itself is to blame, it has encouraged the mistaken belief that washing hands or cleaning the kitchen might harm children, a message that is not only unsupported but potentially dangerous.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more sophisticated reformulation was put forward by Professor Ruslan Abenov of the Almaty Institute of Immunology. According to his 'old friends' account, what matters is not exposure to infectious diseases, most of which became established in human populations only after the rise of cities, but contact with organisms that have accompanied our species throughout its evolution. These include the microbes of soil, water and animals, as well as certain parasitic worms. Abenov argues that such organisms stimulate the production of regulatory cells that teach the immune system to tolerate harmless substances like pollen and food proteins. Some of the strongest support for this view comes from studies of children raised on traditional dairy farms, who spend time in cowsheds from infancy and are roughly half as likely to develop asthma as children from the same rural areas who grow up away from livestock.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Further evidence has come from what might be called natural experiments. Dr Farida Colquhoun of the Tunis Institute of Public Health compared two neighbouring communities separated by a national border. The populations share a common ancestry and similar climate, yet one lives largely in modern apartment blocks while the other retains an older, more rural way of life. Allergy rates among children on the modern side of the border were around four times higher, and Colquhoun found that dust collected from their homes contained a much narrower range of microbes. The comparison is a valuable one, but it is not as clean as it first appears: the two communities also differ in diet, air pollution and access to health care, any of which might contribute to the gap.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If a lack of microbial diversity is partly responsible, it might be possible to restore some of what urban life has removed. Dr Isabela Furtado, an ecologist at the Sao Paulo Centre for Urban Health, tested this idea by replacing the gravel and artificial surfaces of several nursery playgrounds with turf, soil and patches of forest floor. Within a month, the children's skin carried a more diverse bacterial community, and blood tests showed changes in several markers associated with immune regulation. Furtado regards the trial as a proof of principle. It is certainly encouraging, but a shift in blood markers is not the same as a reduction in allergic disease, and only much longer studies will show whether the one leads to the other.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, then, should parents and public health authorities conclude? The most sensible response, it seems to me, is what some specialists call targeted hygiene. Hands should be washed before preparing food and after using the toilet, and surfaces cleaned where raw meat has been handled, because these are the moments when dangerous germs are most likely to spread. Beyond such situations, there is little reason to attempt to sterilise the home, and good reason to encourage children to play outdoors, to spend time with animals and to come into contact with the varied microbial world from which modern life has gradually separated them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The repeated revision of the hygiene hypothesis is sometimes cited as evidence that it was misguided from the outset. That conclusion seems to me mistaken. Eide's original observation was accurate; it was the explanation that required refinement, and the process by which that refinement occurred is precisely how science is meant to work. The difficulty lies elsewhere, in the gap between the careful language of researchers and the simplified slogans that reach the public. Researchers could help by abandoning the word 'hygiene' altogether in favour of a term that conveys what the evidence now suggests: that the immune system needs not dirt as such, but a rich diversity of the right kinds of microbial company.

topic: the skin microbiome and the cosmetics industry
title: Living on the Surface
subtitle: Cosmetics companies have discovered the skin microbiome. Scientists are less certain what has been found

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every square centimetre of human skin is home to as many as a million bacteria, together with fungi, viruses and microscopic mites. These communities are far from uniform. Oily regions such as the face and upper back are dominated by a small number of species able to feed on the fatty secretions of sebaceous glands; moist areas like the armpit favour different groups altogether; and the dry skin of the forearm, perhaps surprisingly, supports the most diverse populations of all. For much of the twentieth century, the organisms living on the skin were regarded chiefly as a source of infection, to be scrubbed away whenever possible. That view now seems badly mistaken. Some resident bacteria produce antimicrobial compounds that suppress dangerous competitors, and others appear to help regulate the immune responses of the skin itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The commercial world has been quick to respond. Shelves now carry cleansers, creams and sprays promoted as 'microbiome-friendly', and a growing number of products claim to contain live bacteria intended to colonise the skin. Some go further, promising to 'restore' a microbial balance that, according to the advertising, has been disrupted by pollution, stress or modern hygiene, although the nature of this ideal balance is rarely specified. The difficulty is that the phrase 'microbiome-friendly' has no agreed scientific definition. In the absence of any standard for testing such claims, it functions as little more than a marketing device, reassuring consumers without telling them anything they could verify.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Serious therapeutic interest centres on atopic dermatitis, or eczema, a condition in which flares are typically accompanied by a surge in Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium capable of damaging the skin barrier. Professor Lior Ben-Ami of the Haifa Institute of Dermatology took harmless strains of related bacteria from the unaffected skin of eczema patients, grew them in the laboratory and applied them as a lotion to the patients' inflamed areas. In a small trial, levels of S. aureus fell and symptoms eased within weeks. The trial involved only a few dozen patients, however, and the improvement was not seen in all of them. Ben-Ami regards the results as a model for what he calls bacteriotherapy, but insists that such treatments be prescribed and monitored by doctors, not sold over the counter like ordinary cosmetics.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more sobering perspective on everyday products comes from Dr Saoirse Breathnach of the Galway Centre for Skin Biology, who sampled the skin of volunteers at regular intervals over three years. She found that each person's microbial community was remarkably stable over time, despite daily washing, changes of season and the use of a wide variety of soaps and cosmetics. Most products altered the community for a few hours at most. Breathnach's conclusion seems to me sound, and it cuts both ways. If ordinary washing cannot destroy the skin's resident bacteria, as some campaigners against soap have alleged, then a cream is equally unlikely to 'rebalance' them in any lasting way.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even where products contain bacteria, the organisms may not survive. Dr Lan Phuong Trinh, a pharmacologist at the Hanoi University of Pharmacy, tested forty commercially available products labelled as containing live microbes and found that most held no viable organisms by the time they reached the consumer. Several contained heat-killed bacteria or the products of bacterial fermentation, sometimes marketed as 'postbiotics'. Trinh does not dismiss these products entirely; certain fermentation products, she notes, appear to improve the moisture content of the skin, an effect that would be independent of whether any living microbes were present. What she objects to is the gap between the claims made on the packaging and what the bottle actually contains.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: At the other end of the spectrum are individuals who have abandoned soap and shampoo altogether in the belief that their skin will reach a healthier natural balance. Professor Marisol Etxeberria, a dermatologist at the University of Bilbao, monitored a group of volunteers who stopped using such products for three months. Many reported that their skin felt less dry after an initial period of adjustment, but measured changes in their bacterial communities were modest, and Etxeberria warns that the practice could be risky for people whose skin barrier is already compromised. Such personal experiments are intriguing, but there is as yet no evidence that giving up soap brings any benefit to health.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In response to the proliferation of claims, the Dermal Ecology Consortium, an international network of academic laboratories, has proposed a set of standards specifying what a manufacturer would need to demonstrate before describing a product as supporting the skin microbiome. The consortium has no legal authority, though, and depends on manufacturers adopting its guidance voluntarily. The proposal is to be welcomed. However, cosmetics are regulated far less strictly than medicines in most countries, and experience suggests that regulators are likely to move slowly. Until they do, consumers would be wise to regard most microbiome claims as aspirations rather than established facts.

topic: industrial diets, migration and the loss of gut microbial diversity
title: The Vanishing Inner Ecosystem
subtitle: Are industrial diets driving gut microbes towards extinction, and should the survivors be preserved?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When researchers began comparing the gut bacteria of people in different parts of the world, one finding stood out above all others. Individuals living in rural, non-industrialised communities, whether foragers, herders or small-scale farmers, typically carry a far wider range of microbial species than city-dwellers in wealthy nations, in some studies by as much as forty per cent. Entire groups of bacteria that are common in the former are rare or absent in the latter. It is tempting to conclude that the non-industrial microbiome represents a natural human state from which industrialised populations have strayed. That temptation should be resisted. There is no single ancestral microbiome to return to, and the gut communities of foraging peoples differ widely from one another, reflecting differences in climate, diet and local environment.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Several features of modern life have been blamed for the loss of diversity, including antibiotics, caesarean births and sanitation, but diet has attracted the most attention. A typical industrial diet provides perhaps fifteen grams of dietary fibre a day, a small fraction of the quantities consumed by some foraging groups, and fibre is the main food source for many gut bacteria. Professor Mette Kjaergaard of the Aarhus Institute of Nutrition Science colonised laboratory mice with human gut bacteria and then fed them a low-fibre diet over four generations. With each generation, more species disappeared. When mice were returned to a high-fibre diet after a single generation, most of the missing species re-emerged; after four generations, however, restoring fibre was no longer enough, and the lost bacteria could be recovered only by deliberately reintroducing them. Kjaergaard concludes that losses can accumulate silently across generations until they become irreversible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Evidence that something similar happens in people comes from Dr Kaveh Fragoso of the Vancouver Centre for Migrant Health, who followed immigrants from Southeast Asia during their first years in North America. Within months of arrival, many of the participants' original bacterial strains had been displaced by strains typical of their new country, and genes associated with breaking down plant fibres became less common. The changes were greater still among children born after their parents had migrated. Rates of obesity among the immigrants rose steadily with the number of years spent in the new country. Fragoso, however, is careful not to overstate the connection: diet, physical activity and working patterns all changed after migration, and the microbiome may be only one of several routes through which these changes affected body weight.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies point to a possible public health concern, yet the step from 'less diverse' to 'less healthy' is not as straightforward as is often assumed. Within wealthy populations, a more diverse microbiome is associated with better health, but some highly diverse gut communities in other parts of the world also harbour parasites and disease-causing bacteria. Diversity, in other words, is not a virtue in itself; what matters is which organisms are present and what they do. A community rich in species but dominated by organisms that provoke inflammation may well be of less benefit to its host than a simpler one composed of well-adapted residents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For Dr Abebe Tadesse, a nutritionist at Addis Ababa University, the debate among scientists in wealthy countries risks overlooking where the most rapid change is taking place. In fast-growing cities across Africa and Asia, he points out, diets are shifting within a single generation from whole grains, legumes and fermented foods towards refined flour, sugar and processed products. Tadesse argues that protecting traditional food systems would achieve far more than any commercial supplement, since such diets nourish a broad community of microbes rather than the handful of strains that a capsule can contain.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious proposal comes from Dr Paulina Nadeau of the Lima Institute of Microbial Ecology, who has called for an international microbial vault, modelled on the seed banks that preserve the genetic diversity of crops. Samples from communities whose gut bacteria are still highly diverse would be frozen and stored, so that strains lost elsewhere could one day be studied or restored. The idea has drawn criticism on ethical grounds. Critics ask whether communities would genuinely understand what they were agreeing to, and whether they would share in any profits if their microbes were used to develop commercial products. Nadeau herself insists that contributing communities must retain control over how their samples are used. The concerns are legitimate, and the long history of researchers removing biological material from indigenous peoples without fair return gives communities every reason to be suspicious. They are not, however, a reason to abandon the idea, but rather to design it with unusual care.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For most people in industrialised countries, the practical implications are considerably less dramatic. Whatever the long-term prospects for microbial vaults or the restoration of lost species, there is already good evidence that eating more fibre, from a wide variety of plant foods, increases the range of bacteria in the gut within weeks. It is a modest recommendation, and an unglamorous one, but it is among the few in this field that rest on solid ground.

topic: gut bacteria and the metabolism of medicines
title: The Hidden Pharmacists
subtitle: The bacteria in our intestines may help to explain why the same medicine helps one patient and fails another

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Any doctor who has prescribed the same medicine to a hundred patients knows that it will not affect them all equally. Some will respond well, some hardly at all, and a few will suffer side effects severe enough to stop treatment. For decades, such differences have been attributed to age, body weight, kidney and liver function, and inherited variation in the enzymes that process drugs. These factors matter, but even when all of them are taken into account, a substantial share of the variation remains unexplained. A growing body of research suggests that part of the answer lies in the gut, where trillions of bacteria are capable of chemically transforming the medicines that pass through it. Of all the discoveries to emerge from microbiome research, this may well prove the most useful in practice, considerably more so than the much-publicised claims about bacteria and mood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest examples have been known for years without attracting much attention. Digoxin, a long-established heart medication, is converted into an inactive form in certain patients by a gut bacterium, with the result that they require higher doses to achieve the same effect. Intriguingly, what matters is not merely whether the species is present but which strain a patient carries, since only strains possessing a particular cluster of genes can carry out the conversion. A similar process affects levodopa, the main treatment for Parkinson's disease. Bacterial enzymes can break the drug down in the intestine before it reaches the brain, which may help to explain why some patients need ever larger doses as their treatment continues.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How widespread is this phenomenon? Dr Ondrej Hruby of the Brno Institute of Pharmacology exposed seventy-six common gut bacterial species to some two hundred and seventy drugs in the laboratory and found that around two-thirds of the drugs were chemically altered by at least one species. The figure is striking, but Hruby himself urges caution in interpreting it. Bacteria grown in isolation in a laboratory dish behave quite differently from those competing in the crowded and oxygen-poor environment of the intestine, and many of the reactions he observed may not occur in the body on a scale large enough to make any clinical difference.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In other cases, bacterial activity turns a medicine into a poison. The cancer drug irinotecan is inactivated in the liver, which attaches a sugar molecule to it so that it can be excreted via the gut. There, however, certain bacteria strip off the sugar to use as food, reactivating the drug inside the intestine and causing severe diarrhoea that can force doctors to reduce or abandon treatment. Professor Wanjiru Kamau of the Nairobi Cancer Research Institute has developed a compound that blocks the bacterial enzyme responsible without killing the bacteria themselves. In mice, it substantially reduced intestinal damage. Kamau argues that disabling specific bacterial enzymes is preferable to giving antibiotics, which harm the entire gut community. Her approach is an elegant one, since it treats the bacteria not as enemies to be eliminated but as a system to be adjusted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The relationship also runs in the opposite direction. Dr Yasmin Haddadin, a clinical pharmacologist at the Amman University Hospital, has shown that a surprising number of medicines not designed as antibiotics nevertheless inhibit the growth of gut bacteria, among them metformin, which is widely used for diabetes, and drugs that reduce stomach acid. Haddadin's work suggests that some of metformin's benefits for blood sugar may arise through changes it produces in the microbiome, and that certain side effects of other drugs may be explained in the same way. This finding has an uncomfortable implication for the field as a whole. Many studies that compare the gut bacteria of sick and healthy people fail to account for the medicines that the sick participants are taking, and some apparent links between bacteria and disease may in fact reflect the effects of treatment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Could doctors one day analyse a patient's gut bacteria before choosing a medicine or its dose? Dr Rohan Wickramasinghe of the Colombo Institute of Clinical Sciences believes that routine stool testing could become as standard as blood tests within a generation. Professor Teodor Iliescu, a pharmacologist at the University of Cluj, is unconvinced. The composition of the microbiome shifts with diet, illness and travel, he notes, so that a single sample may give a misleading impression, and few doctors are trained to interpret such results. Iliescu's reservations are well founded as far as most medicines are concerned. For drugs such as digoxin, however, where the margin between an effective and a dangerous dose is narrow, the case for testing seems considerably stronger.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is already clear is that the traditional picture of drug metabolism, in which the patient's own liver and kidneys do all the work, is incomplete. Medicines enter an ecosystem as well as a body. Recognising this will not transform prescribing overnight, but it may help to explain some of the puzzling failures of treatment that doctors have long been obliged simply to accept.

topic: ancient dental calculus and the history of the oral microbiome
title: Written in Plaque
subtitle: Hardened deposits on ancient teeth are giving scientists an unexpected window onto the microbial past

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Dental calculus, the hard yellowish deposit that forms when plaque mineralises on the surface of teeth, has never enjoyed much respect. Dentists remove it routinely, and for most of the twentieth century archaeologists did the same, scraping it from excavated skulls so that the teeth beneath could be measured and photographed. That practice, in retrospect, destroyed an irreplaceable resource. Calculus forms in layers throughout a person's life, and as it hardens it traps bacteria, fragments of food, pollen, particles of smoke and even proteins from the person's own body. Unlike bone, which absorbs chemicals from the surrounding soil after burial, calculus seals in material while its owner is still alive. It is arguably the richest single source of biological information in the entire archaeological record.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Among the first to exploit this potential systematically was Professor Zeynep Aksoy of the Ankara Institute of Archaeological Science, whose team extracted bacterial DNA from the calculus of more than three hundred skeletons spanning roughly seven thousand years at sites across the eastern Mediterranean. Her results suggest two major transitions. The first accompanied the adoption of farming, when diets rich in cereal carbohydrates encouraged bacteria associated with tooth decay. The second, and more dramatic, followed the spread of industrially refined sugar and flour in the nineteenth century, after which the diversity of oral bacteria fell sharply. People living today, Aksoy concludes, have less varied oral communities than any earlier population her team has examined.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts such conclusions without reservation. Dr Matteo Ferrandi, a molecular archaeologist at the University of Bologna, points out that ancient DNA is invariably fragmented and that calculus samples are easily contaminated, both by soil bacteria after burial and by modern DNA introduced during excavation and handling. He also notes that the skeletons that survive to be studied are rarely a representative sample of the populations from which they came, since burial customs often favoured the wealthy. Ferrandi accepts that the broad trends identified by Aksoy are probably real, but regards more specific claims, such as estimates of how common particular diseases were, as considerably less secure. His caution about the finer details is justified, although it would be wrong to let it obscure how much has already been learned.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Calculus has proved valuable for reasons that go well beyond bacteria. Starch grains preserved in the teeth of Neanderthals have shown that they ate cooked plant foods, contradicting the long-held image of them as almost exclusively meat-eaters. Milk proteins identified in calculus have revealed that dairying began earlier in some regions than archaeological evidence had previously indicated. Dr Hamish Rennie of the Edinburgh Centre for Bioarchaeology found particles of a red mineral pigment embedded in the calculus of several individuals buried at a medieval settlement, and has suggested that they worked with dyes, perhaps in the production of textiles, and repeatedly drew threads or brushes between their lips. In this way, calculus can record not only what people ate but how they spent their working lives.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers hope that this ancient evidence will also inform modern medicine. Bacteria from the mouth have been detected in the arterial plaques of people with heart disease, and gum disease has been statistically linked with diabetes and other chronic conditions. Dr Esperanza Villasenor of the Guadalajara Dental Research Institute argues that by comparing ancient and modern calculus, researchers can distinguish bacteria that have lived in human mouths for thousands of years from those that have become common only recently, and that the latter may be the most appropriate targets for treatment. The proposal is an ambitious one. However, whether oral bacteria actually cause heart disease, rather than simply being present where it occurs, remains a matter of genuine dispute, and building treatments on that assumption would be premature.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The study of calculus also raises ethical questions. Sampling is destructive: once a deposit has been removed and dissolved for analysis, it cannot be restored, and many skeletal collections are finite and irreplaceable. Some descendant communities have objected to the analysis of their ancestors' remains without consultation. Several museums holding large skeletal collections have begun to draw up guidelines on these matters, although practice still varies widely from one institution to another. It seems to me that sampling should be kept to the minimum needed to answer clearly defined questions, and that the views of descendant communities should be sought before, rather than after, the work is done.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For a material once scraped away and discarded, dental calculus has had a remarkable change of fortune. It now offers a record of diet, disease, work and microbial change spanning tens of thousands of years, and new techniques for extracting proteins and genetic material are extending its reach every year. The challenge for researchers is to use that record carefully, recognising both what it can reveal and the limits of what fragmentary evidence from the dead can tell us about the living.

topic: consumer microbiome testing and personalised nutrition
title: A Diet Written for One
subtitle: Companies now promise nutritional advice based on the bacteria in your gut. Can the science bear the weight of the claims?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Two people eat an identical slice of white bread. In one, blood sugar climbs steeply within half an hour; in the other, it barely changes. Observations of this kind lie at the heart of the movement known as personalised nutrition. In a study that did much to launch the field, Professor Benedikt Strobl of the Vienna Centre for Metabolic Research fitted nine hundred volunteers with continuous glucose monitors and recorded their responses to thousands of meals. Reactions to the same foods varied enormously from person to person. Strikingly, a computer model that took account of each volunteer's gut bacteria, alongside conventional information such as age and body weight, predicted their responses far more accurately than the standard approach of counting calories or carbohydrates. In a follow-up trial, volunteers who followed diets tailored by the model achieved better control of their blood sugar than those given conventional advice.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Within a few years, a commercial industry had grown up around such findings. Consumers can now order a kit, post a small stool sample to a laboratory and receive, for a fee, a report describing the bacteria in their gut together with dietary recommendations, often as part of a monthly subscription. Prices range from the cost of a restaurant meal to several hundred dollars for repeated testing, and some companies also sell supplements supposedly matched to the results. The marketing frequently invokes research like Strobl's. Yet the distance between a carefully controlled scientific study, with its glucose monitors, standardised meals and expert analysis, and a product delivered by post is far greater than the advertising implies.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One way to test the reliability of such products is simply to send them the same sample. Dr Mirela Kovac of the Zagreb Institute of Laboratory Medicine divided single stool samples into portions and posted them to five different companies. The reports she received diverged substantially. One company described a sample as having low diversity while another, analysing material from the same specimen, rated its diversity as excellent; a species flagged as a cause for concern by one laboratory was not detected at all by another. Kovac attributes these discrepancies not to dishonesty but to differences in laboratory methods, from the way DNA is extracted to the reference databases used to identify bacteria. Whatever their cause, the effect for the consumer is the same: the result depends to a worrying degree on which company is chosen.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even accurate results may be difficult to interpret. Dr Leyla Mammadova, a nutritional scientist at the Caspian Institute of Nutrition, objects to the practice, common in consumer reports, of classifying bacteria as 'good' or 'bad'. A given species, she points out, may be associated with health in one population and with disease in another, depending on diet and on which strains are involved; one widespread genus has been linked both with improved glucose control and with inflammation. Mammadova argues that reports should describe what a person's bacteria are capable of doing, such as fermenting fibre or producing particular compounds, rather than listing species as if they were heroes or villains. I find her argument entirely convincing; a list of names, however colourfully presented, tells the consumer very little.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further problem concerns the standards against which individuals are compared. Dr Pita Havili of the Auckland Pacific Health Unit found that participants of Pacific Island descent were frequently told that their gut bacteria were 'outside the normal range', even when they were in good health. The explanation was straightforward: the reference ranges used by the companies had been drawn almost entirely from volunteers of European and North American origin. Havili has since helped one company to develop ranges based on Pacific populations, but most providers have yet to follow its example. This is not a minor technical flaw. A test that labels healthy people as abnormal because of their ancestry or diet is not merely inaccurate but potentially harmful, encouraging unnecessary anxiety and inappropriate changes in diet.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the industry argue that even imperfect information has value, since customers who receive a report tend to eat more vegetables and fibre afterwards. The Consumer Genomics Review Panel, an independent advisory body, has taken a more cautious line, recommending that tests be clearly labelled as being for information only and that they refrain from offering anything resembling medical advice. The motivational effect is plausible, but it could almost certainly be achieved by far cheaper means, such as general dietary guidance, and it hardly justifies charging consumers for results that may not be reproducible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the idea of personalised nutrition is mistaken. The variation in individual responses to food is real, and research of the kind Strobl pioneered suggests that gut bacteria help to explain it. What is premature is the attempt to sell that insight to the public before the measurements are standardised, the reference ranges made representative and the advice shown to improve health. Until then, the most reliable dietary recommendations remain the familiar, unglamorous ones.

topic: corvid problem-solving and the stone-dropping (Aesop's fable) paradigm
title: Pebbles in the Pitcher
subtitle: Do crows that solve puzzles understand the physical world, or have they simply learned what works?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Aesop's fable of the thirsty crow dropping stones into a pitcher was long read as a moral tale about ingenuity rather than as a description of real behaviour. Over the past two decades, however, it has become the basis of one of the most widely used experimental paradigms in animal cognition. In the standard version, a bird is presented with a narrow transparent tube partly filled with water, on which floats a piece of food just out of reach of its beak. Stones are placed nearby. Rooks, New Caledonian crows and Eurasian jays have all learned to drop the stones into the tube, raising the water level until the reward can be seized. The results have been widely reported as evidence that corvids grasp the principle of displacement, but the interpretation of such experiments is considerably less settled than popular accounts suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The optimistic reading is championed by Professor Mateo Iriarte of the Institute for Comparative Behaviour in Bilbao. In a series of studies, his team offered crows a choice between tubes containing water and tubes containing sand, and between heavy stones and light objects that floated. Most birds came to prefer sinking objects and water-filled tubes, the combinations that actually brought food closer. Iriarte argues that these preferences reflect an understanding of cause and effect comparable to that of a child of five to seven years. He places particular weight on the speed with which some individuals selected the effective option, often within a handful of trials, which in his view is too rapid to be explained by gradual reinforcement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Saoirse Kavanagh, who studies learning in birds at the Western Isles Field Station, is unconvinced. She points out that in nearly every experiment the birds could see the food rising after each stone was dropped, so that each successful action was immediately rewarded by visible progress. Under such conditions, she contends, a bird with no concept of displacement at all could quickly learn to repeat whatever produced movement of the reward. Kavanagh's own studies included a version of the task in which the water level was hidden from view until the end of each trial. Performance in this condition fell to chance. For Kavanagh, this suggests that the crows were tracking feedback rather than reasoning about volume.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most revealing evidence may come from experiments designed to be counter-intuitive. In one apparatus, devised by Dr Hiroshi Takemura at the Kansai Centre for Animal Minds, a wide tube was connected out of sight to a narrow one by a hidden U-bend, so that stones dropped into the wide tube raised the water in the narrow tube, where the food was. No bird could have predicted this from the physical appearance of the apparatus. Several crows nonetheless learned to solve it, although more slowly than the standard task. Takemura interprets this as a sign that the birds were flexible learners, capable of adapting to arbitrary rules, rather than as proof either for or against causal understanding. His conclusion seems the most defensible of the three, since it accounts for both the speed of success in the standard task and the persistence of success in a task that no physical principle could have predicted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that the debate is often framed as a choice between two options: either the birds understand physics as humans do, or they are mechanically repeating rewarded actions. This framing is unhelpful. Human children themselves do not acquire an understanding of displacement in a single step; they combine trial and error with expectations built up through experience of objects. There is no reason to assume that a crow must be either a miniature physicist or a simple conditioning machine, and the more productive question is what kind of expectations it brings to a problem before it begins.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Methodological concerns also deserve more attention than they usually receive. Most studies test fewer than ten birds, and many of these have previously taken part in other experiments, so that it is difficult to separate innate ability from accumulated experience. Moreover, the birds that perform best are frequently highlighted while the others receive only a brief mention. Kavanagh has argued that results should be reported for every individual tested, and that pre-registration of hypotheses, now common in human psychology, should become standard in comparative cognition as well. Iriarte accepts the case for larger samples but warns that wild-caught corvids are difficult to keep, and that insisting on large numbers could make the research impossible in practice.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the achievements of the birds themselves. Whatever is going on in their heads, corvids solve problems that defeat many other species, and they do so with brains no bigger than a walnut. What the controversy does illustrate is how easily a compelling story can run ahead of the data. Aesop's crow was invented to make a point about human cleverness; the danger for researchers is that the real birds are recruited to make a similar point about themselves.

topic: the mirror mark test and the measurement of self-recognition in animals
title: Who Is in the Mirror?
subtitle: Half a century after it was devised, the best-known test of animal self-recognition is facing growing criticism

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than half a century, the standard method for asking whether an animal recognises itself has involved little more than a mirror and a spot of paint. In the classic version of the so-called mark test, an animal that has had time to become familiar with a mirror is marked, usually while asleep or distracted, on a part of the body it cannot see directly, such as the forehead. The dye used has no smell and cannot be felt. If the animal, on seeing its reflection, touches or investigates the mark on its own body rather than on the glass, it is said to have passed. Chimpanzees and orangutans typically do so; most monkeys, despite years of exposure to mirrors, never do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For decades the list of species that passed remained short and dominated by great apes, which helped to sustain the view that self-recognition was a rare capacity confined to animals with large brains and close evolutionary ties to humans. That picture has since become more complicated. Bottlenose dolphins, which have no hands, have been seen twisting their bodies in front of mirrors to inspect marks. One Asian elephant out of three tested passed in a widely discussed study, and magpies have scratched at coloured stickers placed beneath their beaks. Most controversially, a small tropical fish, the cleaner wrasse, has been reported to scrape its throat against the floor of its tank after seeing a mark there in a mirror.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ayşe Demirtaş, a comparative psychologist at the Anatolian Institute of Behavioural Science, remains a firm defender of the test. Its great strength, she argues, is that it relies on behaviour which independent observers can score, rather than on an experimenter's impression of what an animal is thinking. In her view, an animal that uses a reflection to locate a mark on its own body must at some level connect the image with itself, and no simpler explanation has yet been found. Demirtaş accepts that the test can produce false negatives, but she insists that a positive result is meaningful. It is easy to see why the test has endured: it is cheap, quick and requires no training of the animal. Simplicity, however, is not the same as validity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Tendai Mukwena of the Zambezi Centre for Animal Behaviour believes the mark test is biased in favour of animals that, like humans, depend heavily on vision. Dogs, he notes, almost universally fail it, yet they live in a world organised largely by smell. Mukwena's team developed what he calls a scent mirror: dogs were presented with samples of their own urine, some of which had been altered by the addition of another odour. The animals spent significantly longer investigating their own modified scent than unmodified samples, a response Mukwena interprets as a form of self-recognition. The design is ingenious, although it is less clear than he suggests that investigating a familiar but altered smell requires any concept of self.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Valentina Rocha, a marine biologist at the Atlantic Institute of Oceanography, has been closely involved in the debate over the cleaner wrasse. She does not question that the fish behaved as reported; her objection concerns what the result means. If a fish can pass, she argues, the test cannot be measuring the sophisticated self-awareness it has traditionally been taken to show. A more modest interpretation is that it detects the ability to use a reflection as a source of information about one's own body. Some primatologists have responded by suggesting that the fish findings must be the product of flawed procedures, but this reaction seems motivated more by a wish to protect the special status of apes than by any problem actually identified in the experiments.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication comes from research with humans. Children in Western countries generally pass the mark test between eighteen months and two years of age. Yet when Dr Piotr Zawadzki of the Vistula University child development unit tested toddlers in several rural communities, many children of the same age looked at the mark in the mirror and then did nothing. Zawadzki suspects that these children recognised themselves perfectly well but did not regard an unexpected mark as something that needed removing, perhaps because they had been taught not to interfere with their appearance in front of adults. If he is right, the test measures motivation as well as recognition.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these criticisms makes the mirror worthless. A positive result remains a striking piece of behaviour that demands explanation. What the evidence no longer supports is the assumption that failure indicates the absence of a sense of self, or that passing places an animal in an exclusive club. The mark test is best regarded as one instrument among several, and its results should be weighed alongside studies that take account of each species' senses and way of life.

topic: numerical cognition in bees and other insects
title: Counting Without a Cortex
subtitle: Experiments suggesting that insects can handle numbers are forcing a rethink of what small brains can do

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A honeybee's brain occupies about one cubic millimetre and contains fewer than a million neurons, against the roughly 86 billion of a human brain. For most of the twentieth century it was taken for granted that anything resembling numerical competence required a large brain, and probably a cerebral cortex as well. Insects, with their apparently rigid and instinct-driven behaviour, were considered the least likely candidates. That assumption first came under pressure from field experiments in which bees were trained to collect sugar from a feeder placed after the third of four identical tents along a route. When the tents were moved closer together, the bees landed earlier, as though they were counting landmarks rather than measuring distance flown.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: More ambitious claims have followed. At the Institute of Sensory Ecology in Mérida, Professor Rafael Nightingale-Obi and his colleagues trained bees to approach cards displaying different numbers of black shapes. Bees that chose the card with fewer shapes found a drop of sugar solution; those that chose the other card met a bitter solution of quinine. After about fifty training visits, most bees reliably selected the smaller quantity, even with displays they had never seen before. The most striking result came when a blank card was introduced. Offered a choice between a card with one shape and a card with none, the bees chose the empty card, treating nothing as less than one. Nightingale-Obi concluded that bees possess a rudimentary understanding of zero, an idea that took human civilisations thousands of years to formalise.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts such conclusions at face value. Dr Nomvula Dlamini, who studies insect vision at the Highveld Research Institute, has pointed out that number rarely varies on its own. A card with more shapes usually has a greater total area of black, a longer combined outline and a different density of elements, and any of these could guide a bee's choice. When Dlamini re-examined five published studies, she found that three had not controlled for the combined perimeter of the shapes. In her own experiments, in which perimeter was held constant, bees still chose correctly, but their accuracy fell from around 80 per cent to 63 per cent. Since chance performance would be 50 per cent, she concludes that bees probably combine a crude sense of number with other visual cues.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different challenge comes from computational modelling. Dr Jarkko Väisänen of the Boreal Institute for Neural Computation built a simulated circuit of just four neurons and found that it could solve the same less-than tasks given to real bees. The key, he argues, is that the model does not need to perceive all the items at once. Instead, it inspects them one at a time and accumulates a signal with each item encountered. Because such a circuit is so small, he adds, it would be inexpensive for evolution to build and could easily be embedded in the brain of almost any animal. Väisänen notes that high-speed video recordings show bees flying slowly along displays and appearing to examine individual shapes in turn, behaviour consistent with this sequential strategy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Väisänen's model is elegant, but it is sometimes presented as though it settled the matter, which it does not. Showing that a task can be solved by four neurons establishes that a simple mechanism is possible; it does not demonstrate that bees actually use it. Equally, the existence of a simple solution does not make the bees' behaviour any less impressive. Human counting can also be described as sequential accumulation, and no one regards it as trivial for that reason. As for Nightingale-Obi's claim about zero, there is a real distinction between treating an empty display as the lowest value on a scale and grasping zero as a number in its own right. His bees appear to have achieved the first; whether they have achieved the second remains unproven.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The ecological question is arguably more interesting than the philosophical one. A forager that can estimate how many flowers remain in a patch, or recognise a flower species by its number of petals, has a clear advantage. Spiders of several species appear to keep track of how many prey items are wrapped in their webs and search longer when more have been removed. Fish choosing between shoals of different sizes, and frogs responding to the number of notes in a rival's call, provide further examples from animals with similarly modest neural resources. Such abilities need not depend on anything like abstract arithmetic; they need only be good enough to improve decisions in the conditions an animal actually faces.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the insect research has done, above all, is undermine the idea that cognitive ability scales neatly with brain size. Large brains may permit greater memory capacity or more flexible combinations of skills, but specific competences, including some numerical ones, can apparently be achieved by remarkably small networks. This should make researchers cautious about ranking species on a single ladder of intelligence, with humans at the top and insects at the bottom.

topic: dogs' ability to follow human pointing gestures: domestication versus learning
title: Following the Finger
subtitle: Why can dogs understand a simple gesture that baffles our closest relatives?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a person points at one of two upturned cups, a pet dog will usually walk straight to the cup that has been indicated and find the treat hidden beneath it. Chimpanzees, despite their far closer kinship with humans and their impressive skill at solving mechanical puzzles, often perform no better than chance in the same test unless they have been trained extensively. This contrast, first documented around the end of the last century, launched a wave of research into canine social cognition and has turned the domestic dog into one of the most intensively studied animals in comparative psychology. The question at the heart of this work is deceptively simple: where does the dog's skill come from?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential answer is that it was shaped by domestication. Professor Emeka Nwachukwu of the Institute for Canine Science in Enugu argues that during the thousands of years in which dogs lived alongside people, selection favoured individuals that paid close attention to human signals, since these animals were more useful and more likely to be fed. He points out that puppies as young as eight weeks follow pointing gestures despite having had limited exposure to people, whereas wolf cubs reared by hand in human homes generally fail at the same age. Nwachukwu also draws on a long-running breeding programme in which foxes were selected solely for tameness. After many generations, these foxes began to follow human gestures as readily as dogs, even though this ability had never been a goal of the breeders. For Nwachukwu, this suggests that responsiveness to people may have arisen as an accidental consequence of selection for calm, friendly behaviour.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Oren Galili of the Carmel Centre for Animal Learning takes a very different view. In his opinion, the dog's ability is largely acquired during each animal's lifetime. Wolves that have been raised intensively by humans, he notes, can learn to follow points as adults, while dogs that have had little contact with people often perform poorly. In one of Galili's studies, only about a third of forty dogs living in an animal shelter followed a pointing gesture on their first day of testing. After three days in which each dog spent a short time interacting with a volunteer, however, most of them succeeded. Galili concludes that what dogs inherit is not a specialised understanding of human gestures but a general ability to learn from whatever happens around them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third position, associated with Dr Ilse Vandermeulen of the Flanders Institute of Ethology, shifts attention from understanding to temperament. Vandermeulen has found that dogs gaze at human faces for much longer than wolves do, and show far less fear of unfamiliar people. Wolves, by contrast, tend to look away from a person's face, so that they rarely notice where a hand is pointing. On her account, domestication reduced fear, and reduced fear made it possible for dogs to attend to people long enough to learn from them. This explanation strikes me as the most promising of the three, because it accepts a role for both evolutionary change and individual experience instead of forcing a choice between them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some of the evidence used in this debate is weaker than it first appears. The puppies cited by Nwachukwu are often described as inexperienced, yet most of them were born in human homes and had been handled by people from their first days of life. Limited exposure is, in other words, a relative term, and eight weeks of daily contact may be ample time to learn a great deal. A more general problem is that the pointing test captures only one narrow aspect of social behaviour. Dogs respond to gaze, tone of voice and body posture as well, and a species that failed the pointing test might still be highly sensitive to signals of other kinds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recent research has also asked whether some breeds are better at the task than others. A large online project, in which thousands of owners tested their own dogs at home and submitted the results, found that breeds developed for close cooperation with handlers, such as herding dogs, did not consistently outperform breeds kept mainly as companions. The project's organisers have estimated that genetic differences account for a modest share of the variation between individual dogs. Such large samples are valuable, but data collected by owners must be treated with caution, since few owners can avoid unintentionally guiding their pets with a glance or a movement of the head.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the findings suggest that the familiar contrast between nature and nurture is misleading in this case. What evolved in dogs may not have been an ability to read gestures as such, but a disposition that allows them to learn about humans unusually quickly and from unusually early in life. If that is correct, the success of the domestic dog lies less in any single inherited skill than in the combination of an inherited temperament with an environment that rewards paying attention to people.

topic: octopus intelligence, distributed nervous systems and the evolution of cephalopod minds
title: Minds in Eight Parts
subtitle: The octopus has become a test case for theories about how and why intelligence evolves

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: An octopus possesses around five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, but roughly two-thirds of them are located not in its head but in its arms. The animal's last common ancestor with humans, which lived some six hundred million years ago, is thought to have been a small worm-like creature with only a rudimentary nervous system. Whatever intelligence the octopus has must therefore have evolved quite separately from our own, which is precisely what makes it so valuable to scientists. Popular accounts of octopus behaviour are full of memorable stories: animals escaping from aquarium tanks at night, unscrewing the lids of jars, or squirting water at lights that annoyed them. Such anecdotes are entertaining, but they are a poor foundation for scientific claims, since they are rarely recorded systematically and the failures are seldom reported.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Controlled research has nevertheless confirmed that the octopus is a remarkable animal, and much of it has focused on the unusual relationship between the brain and the arms. Professor Dimitris Kostopoulos of the Hellenic Marine Station has shown that an arm separated from the body will still reach towards and grasp a piece of food, and that the suckers can detect chemicals in the water in a manner similar to taste. In his view, the central brain issues only broad instructions, such as an order to explore a crevice, while each arm works out for itself how to carry them out. Kostopoulos goes further, suggesting that the octopus may not experience the world as a single, unified self at all, but as something closer to a loose federation of partly independent agents.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Mariam Haddad of the Levantine Institute of Neuroscience accepts that the arms are capable of considerable independence, but she rejects the stronger version of this claim. In her experiments, octopuses had to guide a single arm through a transparent maze to reach food on the other side. They succeeded only when they could see the arm; when the maze was made opaque, the arm wandered aimlessly. Haddad concludes that the arms take care of routine movements, but that unfamiliar problems require coordination by the central brain using visual information. Her results are persuasive, though what they reveal is the limit of the arms' independence rather than its absence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A deeper puzzle concerns why the octopus became intelligent at all. Most species live for only one or two years, spend their lives largely alone and die soon after breeding, so that no parent ever teaches its offspring. This sits uncomfortably with the widely held view that complex minds evolve in long-lived animals that live in social groups. Dr Aroha Petrucci of the Southern Ocean Research Institute in Wellington proposes an ecological explanation instead. The ancestors of octopuses, she points out, had protective shells, which were lost over evolutionary time. A soft-bodied animal with no armour is exposed to a wide range of predators, and Petrucci argues that this vulnerability placed a premium on flexible foraging, camouflage and rapid decision-making.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Sun-hee Bae of the Korea Institute of Marine Behaviour questions whether octopuses are really as solitary as is usually assumed. At two sites off the coast of Australia, where unusually large numbers of octopuses live close together, her team recorded animals darkening their skin and raising their bodies as signals to rivals, and occasionally sharing dens. Some encounters ended in chases or grappling, while others appeared to be tolerated without any conflict. Bae believes that the social abilities of octopuses have been seriously underestimated because most observations have been made in places where they are scarce. These findings are intriguing, yet the sites she studied are exceptional, and it would be unwise to generalise from them to the species as a whole.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Laboratory research faces difficulties of its own. Almost all experimental work has been carried out on a handful of the roughly three hundred known species, most of all the common octopus, which is easy to obtain and to keep. Individual animals also vary considerably. Dr Lucas Ferreira, who has tested octopuses at a public aquarium in Brazil, reports that bold individuals approach new objects within seconds, while shy ones may hide for hours, so that the same test can produce very different results depending on which animals happen to be chosen. Ferreira argues that the temperament of each animal should be recorded before testing begins, a modest step that would make results from different laboratories far easier to compare.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These scientific debates have practical consequences. Growing recognition of octopus intelligence has led several countries to include them in animal welfare legislation, and proposals to farm octopuses commercially have met with strong opposition. Some argue that legal protection should await a clearer understanding of what octopuses actually experience. That position is mistaken. The evidence that octopuses learn, remember and respond flexibly to their surroundings is already strong, and when there is a serious possibility that an animal can suffer, the burden of proof should fall on those who wish to treat it as though it cannot.

topic: culture and social learning in whales and dolphins
title: Songs Across the Ocean
subtitle: Can the behaviour of whales and dolphins properly be described as culture?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, culture was regarded as an exclusively human possession. Anthropologists defined it in terms of language, symbols and shared systems of meaning, and few thought to look for it elsewhere. Biologists, however, have increasingly adopted a broader definition: culture consists of behaviour that is learned from others rather than inherited genetically, that is shared by members of a group, and that differs from one group to another. This definition has the great advantage of being testable, and it has opened up a productive field of research. Yet it also carries a risk, for in making culture easier to detect in animals, it may obscure precisely those features that make human culture so distinctive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most striking evidence comes from the oceans. Male humpback whales sing long, complex songs during the breeding season, and at any one time all the males in a population sing essentially the same song, which changes gradually over the months. Using a network of underwater microphones spread across the South Pacific, Professor Mahina Kealoha of the Pacific Cetacean Research Centre in Honolulu has tracked what happens when a new song appears. Over roughly two years, songs that originated off eastern Australia travelled eastwards from one population to the next, until they had completely replaced the songs previously sung thousands of kilometres away. Kealoha describes these episodes as cultural revolutions, since nothing in the whales' genes or surroundings could explain such rapid and wholesale change.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sperm whales offer a different kind of evidence. They communicate using codas, short patterns of clicks, and Dr Anders Fjeldstad of the Arctic Marine Institute in Tromsø has identified several vocal clans, each containing thousands of animals and each defined by a distinctive set of codas. Clans often share the same stretches of ocean, yet members of different clans rarely associate with one another. They also differ in their patterns of movement and in how successfully they find food in particular conditions. Fjeldstad argues that these clans are in some respects comparable to human ethnic groups, held together by shared traditions and marked out by recognisable ways of speaking.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Leticia Bustamante of the Valparaíso Institute of Marine Ecology urges caution. Most claims of whale culture, she notes, are reached by a process of elimination: researchers rule out genetic and environmental explanations for a difference between groups and conclude that what remains must be cultural. Bustamante argues that this method is unreliable, because subtle genetic or ecological differences may easily go undetected, and she maintains that only controlled experiments could settle the matter. The difficulty is that such experiments are impossible with animals that range across entire oceans. Her standard of proof is so demanding that the cultures of many human societies, studied by the same observational methods, could not meet it either.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The case of the sponging dolphins illustrates how hard it can be to separate these influences. In one large bay in Western Australia, a minority of bottlenose dolphins carry marine sponges on their beaks to protect them while searching for fish on the sea floor. The habit is passed down mainly from mothers to daughters, and genetic studies show that spongers tend to belong to the same maternal line, a finding sometimes cited as evidence that the behaviour is inherited. Dr Aminata Diallo, who has studied the population for more than a decade, has shown that spongers are concentrated in the deeper channels of the bay, where sponges are abundant. She argues that social and genetic inheritance are difficult to disentangle because both travel along family lines. Her point is important: that a behaviour follows family lines is not, in itself, evidence against a cultural explanation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The debate has practical implications. If whales and dolphins depend on knowledge acquired from others, then the loss of older individuals may remove information that cannot easily be replaced. Among killer whales, for instance, older females appear to lead their groups to feeding grounds during years when food is scarce, suggesting that they hold knowledge on which the survival of the group depends. Conservation plans should therefore consider culturally distinct groups, and not merely the total number of animals in a population. At the same time, there is a danger that the language of culture will be used chiefly as a means of attracting public sympathy and funding, and the concept will lose its value if it is applied too loosely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, the question is not simply whether whales have culture, but in which respects their social learning resembles our own and in which it does not. One crucial difference concerns accumulation. Human cultures build on previous achievements, so that tools and techniques become more effective over generations. There is little sign of this in cetaceans. Humpback songs change constantly, but there is no evidence that they become better or more sophisticated as they do so; they are replaced rather than improved.

topic: the scientific debate over pain and sentience in fish
title: Do Fish Feel Pain?
subtitle: A long-running scientific dispute has consequences for billions of animals every year

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Tens of billions of fish are farmed every year, and estimates of the number caught in the wild run into the hundreds of billions. Whether these animals are capable of feeling pain is therefore not an academic curiosity but one of the most consequential questions in animal welfare. For most of the twentieth century, the prevailing assumption was that fish respond to injury in a purely mechanical way, much as a hand withdraws from a hot surface before its owner has noticed anything. That assumption has been seriously challenged in recent decades. Because pain is a private experience, the question can never be settled with complete certainty in any animal other than ourselves. It does not follow, however, that science has nothing to say: evidence can be gathered and weighed, as it is in countless other areas where certainty is unavailable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first step was anatomical. Researchers examining rainbow trout found receptors in their faces that respond to heat, pressure and irritant chemicals, and which closely resemble the nociceptors that detect potentially damaging stimuli in mammals. This discovery was important, but it is frequently overstated. Nociception, the detection of harmful stimuli, is not the same as pain, which is a conscious experience of suffering. Humans under general anaesthesia still show nociceptive reflexes, even though they feel nothing. The presence of nociceptors in fish shows that they can detect injury; it does not show that injury hurts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This distinction lies at the heart of the argument put forward by Professor Wilhelmina Brandsma of the Northern Netherlands Institute for Neurobiology. In humans, she points out, the conscious experience of pain depends on activity in the neocortex, the folded outer layer of the brain. Patients with damage to certain cortical areas may react to injury without reporting any feeling of pain. Since fish have no neocortex at all, Brandsma concludes that whatever happens when they are injured cannot involve conscious suffering. Their responses, however complex they may appear, are in her view the product of unconscious processing in the brainstem and spinal cord.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Ananya Pruitt-Adebayo of the Coromandel Institute of Aquatic Biology believes that the behavioural evidence tells a different story. In her experiments, trout injected in the lips with a mild acid rocked from side to side and rubbed their lips against the gravel on the floor of the tank, and they delayed feeding for around three hours. When the fish were given morphine, these behaviours largely disappeared. Pruitt-Adebayo also found that injured trout became less wary of unfamiliar objects placed in their tanks, as though the injury was occupying their attention. Such prolonged and flexible responses, she argues, are difficult to reconcile with the idea of a simple reflex.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Brandsma's anatomical argument has been challenged directly by Dr Faisal Isaksson-Bree, a comparative neuroanatomist at the Gulf Centre for Brain Research. Birds, he observes, also lack a neocortex, yet they display sophisticated cognition, because other brain structures perform equivalent functions. Fish possess a region known as the pallium which, in his view, may play a similar role. To insist that pain requires a neocortex, Isaksson-Bree argues, is like insisting that flight requires feathers: it mistakes one way of achieving a function for the function itself. This argument is compelling as far as it goes, but it establishes only that fish could feel pain, not that they do.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most persuasive evidence comes from experiments that ask whether fish are willing to pay a cost to avoid an unpleasant state. Dr Mirela Popescu of the Transylvanian Institute of Animal Behaviour allowed zebrafish to choose between two tanks: one furnished with plants and gravel, which zebrafish normally prefer, and a barren tank in which a painkiller had been dissolved in the water. Uninjured fish chose the furnished tank. Fish that had been given a painful injection, however, swam into the barren tank. Studies of this kind come closer than any others to revealing what an animal feels, yet they have so far been carried out in only a few laboratories, often with small numbers of fish, and they need to be repeated far more widely before firm conclusions can be drawn.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the meantime, decisions about how fish are treated cannot wait for a consensus that may never arrive. Many fish are still killed by being left to suffocate in air or by being chilled on ice, methods that may take several minutes to cause death. Electrical and percussive stunning, which renders fish unconscious almost instantly, is already used on some farms, and the costs of adopting it more widely appear modest. Recreational angling raises more contentious questions, since it involves millions of people for whom fishing is a valued pastime. Wherever the line is eventually drawn, the uncertainty that surrounds fish pain should be treated as a reason for care rather than as an excuse for doing nothing.

topic: episodic-like memory and future planning in scrub jays and great apes
title: Thinking Ahead
subtitle: Can animals remember the past and plan for the future, or is mental time travel a uniquely human gift?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Human beings spend a great deal of time in places other than the present. We recall particular episodes from our past, complete with details of what happened, where and when, and we imagine situations that have not yet occurred in order to prepare for them. Psychologists refer to this pair of abilities as mental time travel. For much of the twentieth century it was widely held that animals possess nothing comparable: they might learn from experience, but they were thought to be stuck in the present, unable to recall specific events or to anticipate needs they did not currently feel. This view was influential, yet it was never well supported. It rested largely on the absence of evidence to the contrary, and that absence owed more to a lack of suitable experiments than to any demonstration that animals lacked the abilities in question.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious challenge came from studies of scrub jays, birds that hide food in thousands of separate locations and retrieve it later. Professor Ludmila Sokolova of the Siberian Institute of Comparative Zoology allowed jays to cache two kinds of food: wax-moth larvae, which they prefer but which decay within a few days, and peanuts, which last much longer. When the birds were allowed to search after a short interval, they went first to the larvae. When they had to wait five days, however, they ignored the larvae and searched for peanuts, apparently because they had learned that the larvae would by then be inedible. The jays, in other words, seemed to remember what they had hidden, where and how long ago. Sokolova is careful to describe this as episodic-like memory, since there is no way of knowing whether the birds consciously relive the experience of caching as a human would.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Remembering the past is one thing; planning for the future is another. In an experiment designed by Dr Kofi Agyeman of the Ashanti Institute of Behavioural Ecology, jays spent alternate nights in two different compartments. In one of them they were always given breakfast the next morning; in the other they were not. When the birds were later offered food in the evening and allowed to cache it, they stored significantly more in the compartment where breakfast had never been provided. Crucially, they were not hungry when they did so. Agyeman argues that the jays were preparing for a future state of hunger that they did not experience at the time, which is exactly what animals were once said to be incapable of.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Tariq Hussaini, a cognitive scientist at the Indus Centre for Mind and Behaviour, is unconvinced that these results reveal anything general. Caching, he points out, is a specialised behaviour that evolution has refined over millions of years, and a jay's skill in this narrow area may tell us little about its mental life as a whole. Genuine planning, in his view, should be flexible, applying across many different situations rather than being confined to a single activity. Hussaini is more impressed by experiments with great apes, in which orangutans and bonobos selected a suitable tool from several options and carried it with them so that they could use it to obtain food the following day, even though no reward was on offer at the moment of choice.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Mei-ling Kuo of the Formosa Institute of Psychology approaches the debate from the human side. Her studies suggest that people are often surprisingly poor at anticipating their own future needs: shoppers who are hungry buy far more food than they will eat, and those who are full buy too little. In Kuo's opinion, researchers routinely require animals to meet standards of foresight that many humans would fail. She has a point, but the comparison is not entirely fair. Humans can describe their memories and plans in words, which gives researchers a means of checking what is going on in their minds; with animals, behaviour is the only evidence available, and so stricter controls are inevitable.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Hussaini's objection also deserves closer scrutiny. It is true that caching is specialised, but human abilities are products of evolution too, and nobody concludes that human memory is not genuine memory simply because natural selection shaped it for particular purposes. The fact that an ability evolved to serve a specific function is no reason to deny that it involves real cognition. A more productive question is whether the mechanisms underlying the jay's behaviour resemble those that support planning in mammals, and that is a matter for investigation rather than definition.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of the researchers involved claims that a jay or an ape experiences the past and future in the rich, narrative way that humans do. What has changed is the burden of proof. The old assumption that animals live entirely in the present can no longer be defended, and the task now is to map the many forms that mental time travel may take, rather than to ask whether animals possess it at all.
