topic: metacognition and uncertainty monitoring in animals
title: Knowing What You Don't Know
subtitle: Experiments on uncertainty raise the question of whether any creature but ourselves can think about its own thinking

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of us know the sensation of being unsure: the hesitation before answering a difficult question, or the awareness that a name is on the tip of the tongue but cannot quite be retrieved. Psychologists call the ability to monitor one's own knowledge in this way metacognition, and in humans it is closely bound up with consciousness and self-reflection. For a long time it was assumed to be uniquely human. Over the past thirty years, however, researchers have devised ingenious tasks intended to detect it in animals. The attempt is worthwhile, but it faces a formidable obstacle. An animal cannot tell us what it is thinking, and so researchers must find some way of distinguishing behaviour that reflects the monitoring of an inner state from behaviour that is simply a response to features of the outside world.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic approach was first applied to a bottlenose dolphin. The animal was trained to press one paddle when it heard a high tone and another when it heard a low one. A third paddle allowed it to skip the trial altogether and move on to an easy one, earning a small but guaranteed reward. On trials where the two tones were almost impossible to tell apart, the dolphin increasingly chose the third paddle, and it swam towards the response paddles slowly and hesitantly, much as a doubtful human might. Professor Rémi Lacombe of the Institute of Animal Cognition in Lyon later extended this method to rhesus monkeys. His monkeys opted out of difficult perceptual trials in the same way, and in memory tests they chose to skip trials more often when they had apparently forgotten the item they had been shown. Lacombe argues that the monkeys were monitoring their own internal states of knowledge.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Nadia Beaudry, a computational psychologist at the Atlas Institute for Cognitive Science in Rabat, offers a more economical interpretation. In these tasks, she observes, the opt-out response is reliably rewarded whenever the stimulus is ambiguous. An animal could therefore learn a straightforward association, choosing the escape option whenever tones are close together, without any need to reflect on its own mind. Beaudry has built mathematical models based solely on such associations, and they reproduce the animals' choices with considerable accuracy. These models are elegant, but demonstrating that a simpler explanation is possible is not the same as demonstrating that it is correct.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lacombe has responded with experiments designed to rule out associative learning. In one version, monkeys had to decide whether to take a memory test before the test itself appeared on the screen. Since there was no stimulus for them to react to at the moment of decision, an association between stimulus and response could not guide the choice. The monkeys nonetheless declined the test more often after long delays, when their memory would have been weaker. In another series, monkeys trained to use the opt-out option on one task used it appropriately on entirely new tasks from the very first trial. These findings are much harder to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The picture became more complicated when Dr Ivo Marković of the Adriatic Centre for Behavioural Research reported that rats, too, show uncertainty responses. Given the option of declining difficult discrimination trials, his rats did so in patterns strikingly similar to those of the monkeys. For some researchers the result was an embarrassment, since rats are rarely credited with a capacity for reflection. Marković himself draws a cautious conclusion: either metacognition is far more widespread among mammals than was assumed, or the tests are not measuring what they were designed to measure. The rat findings are best read as a reminder that the tests may be detecting something more modest than the reflective awareness that humans experience.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Neuroscience offers a possible way forward. Dr Rohan Svensgaard of the Lanka Institute of Neural Science has recorded neurons in the monkey brain whose activity tracks how confident the animal is in a decision. He suggests that such a confidence signal could be computed automatically, without the animal being aware of it, and that metacognition is best understood as a continuum extending from unconscious estimates of reliability at one end to fully reflective awareness at the other. Not every species, however, seems to possess even the simpler forms. Dr Camila Arruda of the Paraná Institute of Ethology has found that pigeons repeatedly fail uncertainty tasks, which is notable because pigeons are excellent at the perceptual discriminations involved. Their failure, she argues, cannot therefore be attributed to poor perception, and suggests that differences between species are genuine.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has undoubtedly improved the design of experiments in comparative psychology. It has also exposed a problem of vocabulary. The word metacognition carries with it assumptions derived from human introspection, including the idea of a conscious self examining its own thoughts, and these assumptions may not apply to a monkey, let alone a rat. It would be more accurate to speak of uncertainty monitoring, a term that describes what the experiments actually measure without implying more than the evidence can support.

topic: the Clever Hans effect and unconscious cueing in animal cognition research
title: The Horse That Could Not Count
subtitle: More than a century after Clever Hans, unintended signals from researchers remain a hidden hazard in the study of animal minds

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early years of the twentieth century, crowds in Berlin gathered to watch a horse known as Clever Hans answer questions in arithmetic by tapping his hoof. His owner, a retired schoolteacher, was entirely sincere in his belief that he had taught the animal to calculate, and a commission of experts who examined Hans found no evidence of deliberate trickery. A later, more careful investigation revealed the truth. Hans was responding to tiny, involuntary movements made by his questioners, who relaxed their posture or raised their heads slightly when he reached the correct number of taps. When the questioner did not know the answer, Hans failed. The story is usually told as a warning about human gullibility. What this version tends to overlook is that the horse's ability to detect such faint signals was itself a remarkable achievement.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The episode gave its name to a phenomenon that every student of animal behaviour is now taught to guard against. The standard remedy is blinding: the person who presents a task to an animal and records its response should not know what the correct response is. In principle, this rule is universally accepted. In practice, it is followed far less consistently. Dr Signe Vestergaard of the Aarhus Institute of Behavioural Biology reviewed some six hundred studies of animal cognition published over a decade and found that fewer than a third reported any form of blinding. More worryingly, studies that did not use blinding reported, on average, considerably stronger effects than those that did.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Hamid Tillmann, who studies primate behaviour at the Zagros Field Research Station, acknowledges the problem but argues that blinding is not always practical. In field studies, a researcher may be the only person present, and with many animals a familiar handler is needed to keep them calm. In such situations, the person conducting a test will inevitably know what the animal is expected to do. Tillmann favours alternative safeguards, including automated equipment such as touchscreens that present tasks and deliver rewards without human involvement, and video recordings scored afterwards by observers who do not know the purpose of the study. Automation is certainly valuable, but it is not a complete solution. Machines produce sounds and vibrations of their own, and an attentive animal may learn to respond to these just as Hans responded to the people around him.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Bayarmaa Ganbold of the Steppe Institute of Animal Science believes the danger is greatest with domesticated species. Dogs and horses, she points out, have been bred for thousands of years to pay close attention to people, which makes them especially likely to pick up signals that their handlers are unaware of giving. In one of her studies, handlers of detection dogs were told, falsely, that a target scent had been hidden at locations marked with small red cards. In reality no scent was present anywhere. The dogs nevertheless indicated far more often at the marked locations than elsewhere, apparently responding to their handlers' expectations rather than to anything they could smell. Ganbold notes that the effect was strongest among the most experienced teams, whose dogs had spent years working closely alongside the same handler.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Findings of this kind ought to be taken more seriously than they often are. Among some researchers there is a tendency to treat unintended cueing as a historical curiosity, a problem identified and solved more than a century ago. This confidence is misplaced: as Vestergaard's review shows, the precautions that are supposed to prevent cueing are frequently not taken. At the same time, it would be wrong to discard every study that lacked blinding. Many such studies used other forms of control, and their conclusions have been confirmed by later work carried out under stricter conditions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Vestergaard has proposed that journals should require authors to state clearly whether blinding was used and, if not, why not. Her proposal is sensible and would cost very little. A further development is perhaps more surprising. Rather than treating sensitivity to human cues simply as a source of error, some researchers have begun to study it as a subject in its own right, asking how animals detect posture, gaze and tone of voice, and how this ability differs between species. This line of research is a welcome one, since the capacity that misled observers of Hans may reveal a great deal about how animals understand the people they live alongside.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson of Clever Hans, then, is not that animals are less intelligent than enthusiasts claim. It is that their intelligence may lie somewhere other than where we look for it. Hans could not do arithmetic, but he could read the bodies of strangers with a precision that few humans could match. Researchers who keep this in mind are less likely to be deceived, and more likely to recognise the abilities that animals genuinely possess.

topic: airborne volatile signals and eavesdropping between neighbouring plants
title: Whispers on the Wind
subtitle: Damaged plants release chemical warnings into the air, but scientists disagree about who the messages are really for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a caterpillar begins to chew a leaf, the plant does not suffer in silence. Within minutes, the damaged tissue releases a cocktail of volatile organic compounds, the small airborne molecules that give freshly cut grass its distinctive smell. For decades these emissions were regarded as little more than a by-product of injury. Since the early 1980s, however, a growing body of evidence has suggested that undamaged plants nearby can detect these chemicals and respond by strengthening their own defences before any insect arrives. The notion that plants might talk to one another was initially greeted with ridicule, and the first experiments were dismissed as poorly controlled. That reaction arguably revealed more about the assumptions of the time than about the quality of the data.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The chemistry is now reasonably well understood. Among the most studied compounds are green leaf volatiles, released within seconds of mechanical damage, and terpenes, which are produced more slowly and in blends that vary according to the species of attacker. Dr Aditi Raghavan of the Deccan Institute for Chemical Ecology has shown that maize seedlings exposed to the air surrounding caterpillar-damaged plants accumulate higher concentrations of defensive proteins in their leaves. Crucially, they do not activate these defences fully. Instead, they enter what Raghavan calls a primed state, in which the response is held in reserve and deployed far more rapidly if the plant is subsequently attacked. Priming, she argues, makes economic sense: defensive chemicals are expensive to manufacture, and a plant that produced them at full strength every time it detected a warning would waste resources on threats that never materialised.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that this amounts to communication. The plant physiologist Lars Tvedt, of the Nordfjord Botanical Institute, points out that a damaged plant gains nothing obvious by alerting its neighbours, which are frequently its competitors for light and water. In his account, the signal is not sent for the benefit of others at all; it is primarily a message from one part of a plant to another. Because the internal connections between distant branches transmit information slowly, airborne compounds may be the quickest way for a wounded leaf to warn the rest of the same individual. Neighbours, on this reading, are simply eavesdropping on a private conversation. Experiments on sagebrush appear to support this view: branches that were sealed inside plastic bags, so that air could not circulate around them, failed to respond when other branches on the same shrub were damaged.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The eavesdropping interpretation does not settle every question, however. Mariana Quiroga, who directs a field station in the Patagonian steppe run by the Austral Ecology Foundation, has found that plants respond more strongly to volatiles emitted by close relatives than to those from unrelated individuals of the same species. Over five growing seasons, shrubs exposed to cues from genetically similar neighbours suffered roughly a third less leaf damage than those exposed to cues from strangers. Quiroga interprets this as evidence that the blend of compounds carries information about identity, and that natural selection may have favoured signals which benefit kin. The finding is intriguing, but it should be treated with caution. Her sample was drawn from a single population, and the difference in damage, while statistically significant, varied considerably from one year to the next.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more practical limitation concerns distance. Volatile compounds disperse and break down quickly in the open air, particularly in warm, sunny conditions when ozone levels are high. Measurements by the atmospheric chemist Tunde Abiodun at the Gulf of Guinea Centre for Environmental Sciences suggest that in polluted air, some key signalling molecules travel less than a metre before being chemically altered beyond recognition. Abiodun warns that rising ozone concentrations near cities and major roads may be quietly disrupting a communication system on which plants have relied for millions of years. Whether this disruption has measurable consequences for crop yields or for wild plant populations has yet to be established, although he regards it as one of the most pressing questions for future research.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The prospect of harnessing these signals has naturally attracted agricultural interest. If crops could be primed artificially, by releasing synthetic volatiles across fields at the right moment, farmers might reduce their dependence on pesticides. Small trials with tomatoes and rice have produced encouraging results, but the approach faces real obstacles. Priming carries a cost of its own, and plants kept in a permanent state of alert tend to grow more slowly than those left undisturbed. Raghavan's laboratory has found that repeated exposure can reduce the grain harvest of maize by as much as eight per cent, which would cancel out much of the benefit. The timing of any treatment would therefore have to be extremely precise.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should this phenomenon be called? The word communication remains controversial, and Tvedt's objection that it implies intention is not without merit. Yet insisting on a narrow definition risks obscuring what is genuinely remarkable: plants detect and interpret chemical information from their surroundings and adjust their behaviour accordingly. Whether the sender intends to be heard matters less than the fact that the message is received. Future research would benefit less from debates over terminology than from careful field studies that measure how often, and over what distances, these signals actually operate under natural conditions.

topic: mycorrhizal networks and the contested idea of resource sharing between trees
title: The Network Beneath the Forest Floor
subtitle: Fungal threads connect the roots of neighbouring trees, but what flows through them is far less certain than popular accounts suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Beneath almost every forest lies a dense tangle of fungal threads. Known as hyphae, these filaments are often finer than a human hair, yet a single teaspoon of woodland soil may contain several kilometres of them. Many belong to mycorrhizal fungi, which form intimate partnerships with plant roots, and around ninety per cent of land plant species are thought to enter such associations. The arrangement is essentially a trade. The fungus, which cannot photosynthesise, receives sugars manufactured by the plant; in return it delivers water and mineral nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, gathered from a volume of soil far larger than the roots alone could explore. Because one fungus can colonise the roots of several plants at once, and one plant may host many fungi, neighbouring trees can become physically connected through what ecologists call a common mycorrhizal network.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It is what is said to travel through these networks that has captured the public imagination. In the late 1990s, a field experiment using carbon isotopes as tracers appeared to show that carbon moved from birch to fir seedlings, and that the transfer was greatest when the fir seedlings were shaded. From such findings grew a compelling narrative. Large, old trees, sometimes described as mother trees, were said to nourish their offspring through the network, to recognise their own kin and even to send warnings of insect attack to their neighbours. The story has been retold in best-selling books and television documentaries, and the phrase wood wide web has entered everyday speech. Yet in the view of a growing number of ecologists, public enthusiasm has run well ahead of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most systematic challenge has come from Ingrid Halvorsen, a forest ecologist at the Finnmark Boreal Research Station. Halvorsen and her colleagues re-examined twenty-six field studies that are frequently cited in support of resource sharing. They concluded that only a handful demonstrated transfer in quantities large enough to make a meaningful difference to a seedling's growth. More fundamentally, most experiments had not ruled out alternative explanations: carbon released by one root could, for instance, leak into the soil and be absorbed by another plant without ever passing through fungal tissue. Halvorsen also noted that in many forests seedlings growing close to large trees perform worse, not better, than those further away, which is difficult to reconcile with the image of generous parents. Her review does not deny that networks exist; it questions whether they do what has been claimed for them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the network hypothesis point to other kinds of evidence. Hiroshi Nakagawa, a plant pathologist at the Kanto Institute of Agricultural Science, has conducted a series of greenhouse experiments with tomato plants. Pairs of plants were separated by mesh barriers with holes wide enough to let fungal hyphae through but too small for roots to penetrate, and the containers were sealed so that no airborne chemicals could pass between them. When one plant was infected with a leaf blight, its connected neighbour activated defence genes within days, whereas plants without a fungal link showed no such response. The design is ingenious, and the results have been repeated in his laboratory several times. However, a few square centimetres of sterilised compost bear little resemblance to a forest floor, where hundreds of fungal species compete and the signal from any single plant would be diluted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different perspective emerges when the fungi themselves are placed at the centre of the story. Grace Ochieng, a microbiologist at the Rift Valley Centre for Soil Biology, argues that much of the popular account treats fungi as passive cables, conveying whatever plants choose to send. In reality, she points out, fungi are organisms with interests of their own. Her experiments suggest that they allocate phosphorus preferentially to the plants that supply them with the most sugar, behaving less like a postal service than like a trader seeking the best return. If carbon does move from one tree to another, it may be because the fungus has redistributed its own resources, not because the donor tree is behaving altruistically. This reframing is arguably the most valuable contribution to the debate in recent years, although Ochieng perhaps underestimates how difficult it will be to test in mature forests.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These disputes are not merely academic. Several forestry agencies have revised their guidelines in recent years, recommending that large old trees be retained during logging partly on the grounds that they support surrounding seedlings through fungal links. The policy analyst Zoltan Szabo, of the Danube Institute for Environmental Governance, contends that such guidelines are sensible but that they do not need the network hypothesis to justify them. Old trees, he observes, store large quantities of carbon, provide habitat for countless species and help to stabilise soils, all of which is firmly established. The point is well made, but it overlooks a risk. If policies are publicly defended with claims that later prove exaggerated, the credibility of the science, and of the policies themselves, may suffer when those claims are withdrawn.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the network beneath the forest floor is a myth. Fungal connections between trees are real, and they almost certainly influence how forests function. What remains uncertain is the scale and significance of whatever passes through them. Resolving that uncertainty will require long and expensive field studies capable of tracing materials through intact ecosystems, together with a willingness on all sides to accept results that may prove less dramatic than the story which made the subject famous.

topic: electrical signalling inside plants after wounding
title: Currents Without Nerves
subtitle: Plants send electrical signals between their leaves, but researchers are still arguing about what those signals mean

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Animals owe their speed of response to nerves, specialised cells that carry electrical impulses from one part of the body to another in a fraction of a second. Plants possess nothing of the kind, and for most of the history of botany it was assumed that they communicated internally only by means of slowly diffusing hormones. There were, admittedly, awkward exceptions. As early as the nineteenth century, physiologists recorded bursts of electrical activity in the leaves of the Venus flytrap and of the sensitive plant, whose leaflets fold when touched. But these were treated as curiosities, peculiar to a handful of unusual species with unusually rapid movements, and of little relevance to the plant kingdom as a whole. That judgement now looks distinctly premature.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The flytrap remains the most vivid illustration. Each lobe of its trap bears a few stiff trigger hairs, and when an insect brushes against one of them, an electrical impulse spreads across the leaf. A single touch, however, is not enough. The trap snaps shut only if a second hair is stimulated within roughly thirty seconds, which prevents it from wasting energy on raindrops or falling debris. Once closed, the plant begins producing digestive enzymes only after further stimulation, as the struggling prey triggers the hairs repeatedly. Researchers frequently describe this behaviour as counting, and the term is a convenient shorthand. It should not, however, be taken to imply any kind of awareness: the plant is responding to accumulating electrical charge, not keeping a tally.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The more significant discovery is that electrical signalling is not confined to such specialists. Dr Ewa Langhorne of the Vistula Institute of Plant Physiology has spent a decade studying thale cress, a small weed that has become a standard laboratory organism. When her team crushed a single leaf, they detected a change in electrical potential that travelled through the plant's veins to distant leaves within a few minutes. Those leaves, although they had not been touched, began manufacturing defence hormones that make their tissue less palatable to insects. The signal moves at around a millimetre per second, thousands of times more slowly than an impulse in a human nerve. Comparisons with the animal nervous system are therefore misleading; what plants possess is a distinct system that evolved to meet very different needs.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Exactly what generates the signal is disputed. The biophysicist Mateo Benítez, at the Andean Institute of Biophysics, argues that the electrical change is not a message in its own right. In his view, wounding releases tension in the water-conducting tissue, sending a pressure wave through the plant, and the electrical activity is simply a consequence of this hydraulic disturbance, much as the sound of an engine reflects, rather than drives, its motion. Langhorne rejects this interpretation. She points out that mutant plants lacking the genes for certain ion channels, the pores through which charged particles cross cell membranes, fail to pass the signal on, even though the pressure wave still occurs. The debate is far from settled, but her evidence is difficult to explain on Benítez's account.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Further complexity has emerged from studies of the chemistry at the site of injury. Damaged cells release glutamate, an amino acid that also acts as a messenger between nerve cells in the human brain, and this triggers a wave of calcium ions that moves alongside the electrical signal. Some commentators have seized upon the finding as proof that plants have a primitive nervous system. This conclusion does not follow. Molecules such as glutamate are extremely ancient and are found throughout living things; their presence in both plants and animals reflects a shared cellular inheritance, not a shared function. Insulin-like molecules, after all, occur in organisms that have no pancreas.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical applications are already being explored. Aino Aaltonen, an agricultural engineer at the Baltic Centre for Agri-Technology, has developed sensors that clip onto the stems of greenhouse tomatoes and record electrical activity continuously. Her trials suggest that changes in the signal can reveal water shortage or insect attack several hours before any symptoms become visible to growers. The main obstacle, she acknowledges, is interpretation. Electrical readings fluctuate with temperature, light and watering, and different stresses can produce similar patterns, making it hard to identify which problem a plant is actually facing. Some firms already market such devices as a means of letting crops tell farmers what they need, which overstates what the technology can currently achieve.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings demand a more generous view of what plants can do, without requiring anyone to imagine that they think. Plants integrate information from their surroundings and transmit it rapidly between their organs using mechanisms that are only beginning to be understood. Much remains to be learned about how a single leaf decides which signals to pass on, and how plants combine electrical, chemical and hydraulic messages into a coordinated response. That is remarkable enough without borrowing a vocabulary that was designed for animals.

topic: self and kin recognition by plant roots
title: Family Ties Underground
subtitle: Can a plant tell whether the roots beside it belong to a relative, a stranger or itself?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Competition among plants is usually imagined as a contest for light, fought out by stems and leaves racing upwards. Yet much of the struggle takes place out of sight. Roots compete fiercely for water and dissolved nutrients, and the outcome below ground can determine which plants survive above it. Some decades ago, agronomists working with beans noticed something puzzling: plants grown with a neighbour produced considerably more root mass than plants given exactly the same volume of soil on their own. Each plant, it seemed, was investing in roots not to gather more resources but to prevent its rival from obtaining them. For an individual, this may be a rational strategy. For the pair, it is wasteful, since energy spent on surplus roots is unavailable for seeds or fruit. The observation raised a question that has occupied plant ecologists ever since: can a plant tell who is growing next to it?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first part of the answer concerns the distinction between self and other. Yusuf Falconer-Odu, a plant ecologist at the Levant Institute for Plant Ecology, grew pea plants whose root systems had been divided between two pots. Roots belonging to the same individual tended to avoid one another, sparing the plant from competing with itself. Falconer-Odu then took cuttings to create genetically identical copies of a plant and grew them side by side. Despite sharing every gene, the copies treated one another as competitors once they had been physically disconnected for several weeks. Falconer-Odu concluded that self-recognition in roots relies not on genetic identity but on some internal physiological signal that can pass only between connected tissues, perhaps a rhythm of electrical or hormonal activity unique to each individual.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more provocative claim followed. Kirsten Sørensen, of the Jutland Coastal Ecology Centre, studied a small annual plant that grows along sandy shorelines and whose seeds tend to fall close to the parent, so that neighbours are often siblings. When she grew seedlings in pots shared either with siblings or with strangers from a different population, the plants grown among strangers produced markedly more roots. Sørensen interpreted this as restraint: plants appeared to limit competition with relatives, a behaviour that would make evolutionary sense if it improved the chances that shared genes were passed on. It is not difficult to see why the study attracted such attention. It seemed to show that plants, long regarded as passive, could behave in ways that resembled the co-operation familiar from animal societies.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The enthusiasm was not universal. Ryo Takeda, a statistician working in plant science at the Setouchi University of Agriculture, re-analysed several kin-recognition experiments and argued that their results could be produced by differences in size rather than relatedness. Siblings tend to germinate at similar times and grow at similar rates, whereas seedlings from different populations vary more; and pairs of unequal plants, he showed, allocate resources differently from evenly matched ones. A number of attempts to replicate the original findings also failed. Takeda's objections deserve to be taken seriously, and some early claims were undoubtedly overstated. Yet they do not dispose of the matter entirely, since later experiments that carefully matched plant size still detected kin effects in several species, though not in all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If plants do recognise relatives, how do they do it? Attention has focused on root exudates, the complex mixture of sugars, acids and other compounds that roots release into the soil. In laboratory trials, roots exposed to exudates collected from siblings responded much as they did to living siblings, while exudates from strangers provoked greater root growth. Recognition may not be confined to the soil, either. Some plants detect changes in the colour of light reflected from nearby leaves, and there is evidence that seedlings arrange their leaves to avoid casting shade on relatives while shading strangers more aggressively. Which signal matters most in natural conditions is not yet known.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings have prompted speculation about agriculture. Wanjiru Mwangi, a crop scientist at the Highlands Institute of Crop Science, points out that plant breeding has traditionally selected individuals that perform well, often by outcompeting their neighbours. A field of such plants, she argues, may squander resources in a constant underground contest. Mwangi has proposed that crops could instead be bred for reduced competitiveness towards related plants, and small trials with rice have produced modest increases in yield. The idea is appealing, but its potential may be limited. Most modern crop varieties are already close to genetically uniform, so that every plant in a field is, in effect, a close relative of its neighbours; if kin recognition were going to restrain competition, it would presumably be doing so already.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The study of kin recognition illustrates a recurring pattern in plant science: a striking result, a wave of excitement, a sceptical response and, gradually, a more nuanced picture. The current evidence suggests that some plants, in some circumstances, adjust their growth according to the identity of their neighbours. That is a more modest conclusion than early headlines implied, but it is still a significant one, and it is all the more convincing for having survived serious criticism.

topic: plant bioacoustics: sounds emitted by stressed plants and responses to sound
title: Do Plants Make a Sound?
subtitle: After decades of neglect, the study of plants and sound is returning to the laboratory

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the idea that plants might respond to sound belonged to the fringes of science. Popular books claimed that houseplants flourished when spoken to kindly or when exposed to classical music, and wilted when subjected to loud rock. The experiments behind such claims were rarely controlled with any care: plants given music were often also given more attention, more light or more water than those left in silence. When the claims collapsed, they took the reputation of the whole subject with them. For decades, few botanists who valued their careers would admit an interest in plant acoustics. This was unfortunate, because beneath the exaggeration lay genuine scientific questions that went unasked for a generation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Those questions are now being asked again, with considerably better instruments. Dmitri Volkonsky and his team at the Caspian Institute of Plant Biophysics placed tomato and tobacco plants inside soundproofed boxes fitted with sensitive microphones. Plants that had been deprived of water emitted between thirty and fifty brief ultrasonic clicks every hour, whereas well-watered plants produced fewer than one. Plants whose stems had been cut also clicked, though in a slightly different pattern. The sounds lie far above the range of human hearing but within that of many insects, bats and small mammals. Using computer analysis, the team found that recordings could be sorted reliably according to whether a plant was thirsty or injured. The most likely source of the clicks is cavitation: as water in the plant's vessels comes under increasing tension, tiny bubbles of air form and burst.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Volkonsky is careful not to describe the clicks as a form of communication. In his view they are a mechanical by-product of stress, no more intended than the creak of a drying timber beam. Nevertheless, he suggests that other organisms could exploit them. A moth searching for somewhere to lay its eggs might, for example, avoid plants that sound dehydrated, since they would offer poor food for its caterpillars. The suggestion is plausible, but it remains entirely untested; no one has yet shown that any animal pays attention to these sounds in the wild. Testing it would be far from simple, since it would require researchers to separate the effect of sound from the many visual and chemical cues that a stressed plant also gives off.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns how plants might respond to sound rather than produce it. Paola Ianni, of the Ligurian Centre for Pollination Ecology, exposed flowers of a coastal primrose to several recordings: silence, high-pitched tones, and the low hum of a flying bee. Within three minutes of hearing the bee, the flowers increased the sugar concentration of their nectar by around a fifth, but high-pitched tones had no such effect. Ianni found that the bowl-shaped petals vibrated mechanically at the frequencies of bee wingbeats, and she proposes that they act as a kind of ear, collecting vibrations and transmitting them to the rest of the flower. Sweeter nectar, produced only when a pollinator is nearby, would allow the plant to avoid wasting sugar.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced. Femi Oyelaran, a plant physiologist at the Niger Delta Institute of Plant Science, points out that many studies in the field rely on small numbers of plants, report modest effects and have seldom been repeated by independent laboratories. He also notes that no one has explained how a vibration could be converted into a chemical response inside a plant cell. Oyelaran is right that standards must rise, and the field would benefit from experiments whose methods are declared in advance. Yet to dismiss plant acoustics until every mechanism is understood would be to repeat the error of the past, when an entire area of inquiry was abandoned because of the excesses of a few.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most intriguing evidence comes from roots. Léa Castellane, of the Rhône Valley Agronomy Institute, grew pea seedlings in branching tubes in which one arm contained a recording of running water and the other was silent. When moisture was evenly distributed, the roots grew preferentially towards the sound; when a moisture source was present, they followed the moisture instead. The experiment was repeated with several hundred seedlings, and the pattern held throughout. Castellane concludes that sound may help roots locate water at a distance, before chemical cues become detectable. Roots that force their way into underground pipes are a familiar problem for engineers, and her findings offer one possible explanation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It may be too soon to speak of plants listening. But it is no longer reasonable to assume that they inhabit a silent world. Plants both emit and react to vibrations, and the challenge for the coming decade is to establish how much of this matters outside the laboratory, where wind, rain and the activity of countless animals create a far noisier environment than any soundproofed box.

topic: honesty and deception in floral signals to pollinators
title: Advertising in Bloom
subtitle: Flowers send signals to the animals that pollinate them, but not all of those signals can be trusted

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A flower is, among other things, an advertisement. Its colours, patterns and fragrances exist largely to attract animals that will carry pollen from one plant to another, and in most cases the animal is paid for its services with nectar or surplus pollen. The comparison with commercial advertising is a useful one, but it is imperfect: plants do not decide what to display, and their signals are the product of millions of years of selection rather than design. What the analogy does capture is a central question in pollination biology. Advertisements may be truthful or misleading, and producing them is expensive. How honest, then, are flowers with the animals that serve them?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: There is good evidence that many flowers are scrupulously honest. In a large number of species, individual flowers change colour after they have been pollinated, turning from yellow to red, for instance, or from white to purple, while remaining on the plant for several days. Bees quickly learn to ignore the altered flowers, which typically contain little or no nectar. The arrangement benefits both parties: the insect wastes less time on empty flowers, and the plant directs visitors towards blooms that still need pollen, while the old flowers continue to make the whole plant conspicuous from a distance. Pieter Tangerud, of the Wadden Institute for Pollination Biology, has catalogued such colour changes in species belonging to more than seventy plant families. In his view, honesty is the norm because pollinators are quick learners: a plant that repeatedly disappoints its visitors will soon be avoided.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet deception is far from rare. Roughly a third of all orchid species offer no reward whatsoever. Some resemble nectar-producing flowers growing nearby; others mimic the appearance and scent of female insects so convincingly that males attempt to mate with them, collecting pollen in the process. Chiamaka Nwosu, an evolutionary botanist at the Enugu Centre for Evolutionary Botany, has studied how such trickery persists. Her models and field data suggest that deceptive flowers succeed only while they are scarce relative to the honest species they imitate; if they become too common, pollinators learn to avoid the whole category. Nwosu has also found that deceptive orchids are often unusually variable in colour, which makes it harder for insects to recognise and avoid them. Deception, in other words, is not a curious exception to the rule of honesty but a sophisticated strategy in its own right.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some floral signals were unknown until recently. As bees fly, friction with the air gives them a positive charge, whereas flowers, connected to the ground through their stems, tend to carry a slight negative charge. When a bee lands, some of its charge is transferred, altering the flower's electric field for a minute or more. Ignacio Fonteyne, at the Atacama Institute of Sensory Ecology, has shown that bumblebees can detect these fields through fine hairs on their bodies, which bend in response, and can be trained to distinguish artificial flowers by electric pattern alone. Fonteyne describes the field as an especially honest signal, since a flower cannot fake the change caused by a recent visit. The finding is fascinating, but the language is questionable. A signal, strictly speaking, is a trait that has evolved because it influences the receiver; the electric field is better described as a cue, an unavoidable physical consequence that bees have learned to exploit.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more sceptical view of the honesty debate comes from Aya Hamada of the Seto Institute of Chemical Ecology. Hamada has measured scent emission in dozens of species and found that while many reduce their fragrance within hours of pollination, others carry on producing it at the same rate until the flower withers. She argues that this inconsistency reflects the costs and constraints of each plant's physiology rather than any strategy of truth-telling. More broadly, Hamada suggests that biologists have overstated the influence of pollinators, and that many floral traits are inherited from distant ancestors and persist simply because nothing has removed them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever the balance between honesty and deception, floral signalling now faces pressures that no plant has evolved to meet. Rising temperatures are shifting flowering times, sometimes out of step with the emergence of the insects that visit them. Less widely recognised is the effect of air pollution on scent. Laboratory studies indicate that ozone and the nitrogen oxides in diesel exhaust react with floral compounds, degrading the scent plumes that insects follow and reducing the distance over which a flower can be detected. This threat has received far less attention than it deserves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Flowers, then, do not speak with a single voice. Some are reliably truthful, some systematically deceptive, and many display traits that may owe more to history than to any message at all. Treating honesty as the only organising principle of floral signals would obscure this diversity, and the richness of the subject lies precisely in the variety of solutions that plants have found to the problem of attracting, and sometimes exploiting, the animals on which their reproduction depends.

topic: plants summoning parasitic wasps and the push-pull farming system
title: Calling in the Bodyguards
subtitle: How the chemical distress calls of plants are being put to work in the maize fields of eastern Africa

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Across much of eastern Africa, maize is both the main source of food and the main source of income for millions of small farmers. It is also the favourite food of the stem borer, a moth whose caterpillars tunnel into the stalks and can destroy a large part of a harvest. Chemical pesticides are effective but expensive, and for families farming a hectare or two they are frequently beyond reach. Over the past three decades, however, many of these farmers have adopted a system that relies not on chemicals bought from a shop but on chemicals produced by plants themselves. Known as push-pull, it has in many cases doubled maize yields, and it rests on one of the most remarkable discoveries in plant ecology: that plants under attack can summon the enemies of their enemies.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: When a caterpillar chews a leaf, compounds in its saliva trigger the plant to release a distinctive blend of volatile chemicals. These blends attract parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs inside the caterpillar; the wasp larvae then consume their host from within. Significantly, the response is not simply a reaction to injury. Leaves torn mechanically, without any insect involved, give off a different and much less attractive mixture, which suggests that plants can identify not only that they are being damaged but by what. Writers often describe the wasps as bodyguards hired by the plant. The image is vivid, though only partly accurate: the wasps are not paid to protect anything, and they would respond to the scent whether or not the plant benefited.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The push-pull system was refined over many years by a team led by Daniel Mutua at the Lake Basin Centre for Agroecology. Between the rows of maize, farmers plant a low-growing legume whose volatile emissions repel egg-laying moths and attract parasitic wasps: this is the push. Around the edge of the field they plant a fodder grass that moths find even more appealing than maize: this is the pull. Moths lay their eggs on the grass, but when the caterpillars hatch, most fail to survive, because the grass responds to their feeding by producing a sticky substance that traps them. The legume has a further benefit. Chemicals released from its roots suppress a parasitic weed that attacks cereal crops and that has long been one of the most serious problems facing farmers in the region. Mutua estimates that the technique has now been taken up by many thousands of smallholders.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the role of wasps in the system is less straightforward than early accounts implied. Chiara Esposito, of the Apennine Institute of Insect Behaviour, has spent years studying how parasitic wasps interpret plant odours. Her experiments show that the insects rely heavily on experience: wasps that have previously found a host near a particular scent are strongly drawn to it, whereas inexperienced individuals respond only weakly. In landscapes containing many plant species, moreover, the signal from an attacked plant may be masked by competing odours. Esposito concludes that relying on wasps alone would be risky, and that their contribution is most valuable as one element in a system that also deters pests in other ways.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Another line of research concerns the crop itself. Some traditional maize varieties, it has emerged, begin releasing wasp-attracting volatiles as soon as a moth lays its eggs on their leaves, before any caterpillar has hatched. Most modern commercial hybrids appear to have lost this ability, probably because breeders selecting for yield under pesticide protection had no reason to preserve it. Tobias Grünfeld, a plant breeder at the Upper Rhine Institute of Crop Genetics, has proposed crossing the trait back into high-yielding lines. The proposal is a sensible one, though it will take many years to deliver results, and there is no guarantee that the trait will function as well in a new genetic background.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most important debate, however, is economic rather than biological. Nadeesha Ranasinghe, an agricultural economist at the Kandy Institute of Rural Development, points out that push-pull demands more labour than conventional cultivation, requires farmers to give over part of their land to grass and legumes, and depends on knowledge that must be passed on through training. Its benefits, she argues, are greatest for households that keep cattle, since both companion plants make valuable animal feed; for farmers without livestock, the gains are considerably smaller. Ranasinghe warns against promoting the method as a universal solution. Her caution is justified, but it should not obscure the strength of the evidence: the system has delivered substantial benefits in a wide range of soils, climates and farming communities.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Push-pull demonstrates that the chemical conversations of plants are not merely a scientific curiosity. Understood well enough, they can be put to work. The broader lesson is perhaps that agricultural progress need not always mean replacing natural processes with manufactured inputs; sometimes it means learning to listen more carefully to what is already being said.

topic: root exudates and the recruitment of soil microbes by plants
title: Conversations in the Rhizosphere
subtitle: Plants pour a large share of their carbon into the soil around their roots, and the microbes there appear to be listening

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every root is surrounded by a thin sleeve of soil, rarely more than a few millimetres thick, that is unlike any other environment on earth. Known as the rhizosphere, it may contain billions of microorganisms in a single gram, many times the density found in the surrounding soil. The reason for this abundance is food. Plants release a substantial share of the carbon they capture through photosynthesis, by some estimates between a tenth and a fifth, into the soil through their roots, in the form of sugars, amino acids, organic acids and a bewildering variety of other compounds. For much of the twentieth century these root exudates were regarded as leakage, an unavoidable loss. That view is no longer tenable. A plant does not give away so much of its hard-won carbon by accident; the exudates are better understood as an investment, and increasingly as a language.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-known example has been studied for well over a century. Legumes such as peas, beans and clover form partnerships with rhizobia, soil bacteria that can convert nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. The partnership begins with an exchange of chemical messages. The root releases compounds called flavonoids; bacteria of the appropriate species detect them and reply with signalling molecules of their own; and the root then forms small swellings, or nodules, in which the bacteria are housed and supplied with sugar. The dialogue is so specific that a given legume will typically accept only particular strains. For decades it was treated as a special case, a curiosity confined to one plant family. It now seems more likely to be simply the best-documented instance of a far more general phenomenon.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Evidence for that broader view has come from research on how plants respond to disease. Hanne Bjørnstad, of the Fjellheim Institute of Soil Ecology, infected the leaves of thale cress with a fungal pathogen and then analysed what the roots released. Within days, the plants had increased their secretion of malic acid, a compound that attracts a particular group of soil bacteria. Once established on the roots, these bacteria triggered a state of heightened resistance throughout the plant, including in leaves far from the site of infection. Bjørnstad describes the process as a cry for help: a plant under attack above ground alters its chemistry below ground to recruit microbial allies.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kenta Ikeda, at the Hokuriku Centre for Plant-Microbe Research, has extended the idea in a surprising direction. Working in experimental field plots, his team grew wheat infected with a leaf disease, removed the plants, and then sowed a fresh crop in the same soil. The second generation suffered noticeably less disease than plants grown in soil that had never hosted an infection, and the protective effect persisted for three growing seasons. Ikeda argues that the infected plants had enriched the soil with beneficial microbes, leaving behind a kind of memory from which their successors profited. Farmers have long known of so-called suppressive soils, in which certain crop diseases mysteriously fail to take hold; Ikeda suspects that some of them may have arisen in precisely this way.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all specialists accept this interpretation. Rosa Mendoza-Ruiz, a microbiologist at the Pampas Institute for Soil Microbiology, observes that most experiments on microbial recruitment have been conducted in sterilised soil, to which researchers add only a handful of bacterial species. Real soil contains thousands of species competing for every available resource, and subtle changes in exudates might well be swamped. She also questions whether the changes are targeted at all; a stressed plant, she suggests, may simply leak different compounds, with any benefit arising by chance. Her objection to sterilised-soil experiments is well founded. It does not, however, account for Ikeda's results, which were obtained in ordinary field soil.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The commercial world has been quicker to embrace these ideas than the scientific one. A rapidly growing market now offers farmers microbial inoculants, preparations of supposedly beneficial bacteria and fungi to be applied to seeds or soil. Results in the field have been strikingly inconsistent. Oluwaseun Adebayo, of the Savanna Institute of Agricultural Microbiology, believes the reason is ecological: introduced microbes are generally outcompeted by the resident community within weeks. Rather than adding microbes, he argues, breeders should develop crops that are better at recruiting helpful organisms already present in the soil. Much of the marketing of inoculants promises considerably more than the evidence can support.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There are signs that such recruitment ability has been eroded. Ioana Borodina, of the Carpathian Institute for Crop Science, has compared the root microbiomes of modern wheat with those of its wild relatives and found that cultivated varieties host markedly less diverse communities. Generations of breeding under generous applications of fertiliser, she suggests, removed any advantage in maintaining costly microbial partnerships. If that is correct, then breeders can no longer afford to ignore what happens beneath the soil surface, and restoring the conversation between crops and soil may prove as important to future agriculture as any new chemical or machine.

topic: plant learning experiments and the debate over plant neurobiology terminology
title: Can a Plant Learn?
subtitle: Experiments suggesting that plants can learn and remember have provoked a fierce argument about evidence and about words

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Lucia Kovács, a plant physiologist at the Danube Bend Institute of Plant Behaviour, built a simple apparatus that lowered potted sensitive plants along a rail and then let them drop fifteen centimetres onto a padded surface. The sensitive plant folds its leaflets within seconds when disturbed, a defence thought to deter grazing animals. At first, every drop caused the plants to close. After a few dozen repetitions, however, they stopped responding and kept their leaves open. To rule out the possibility that the plants were simply exhausted, Kovács then shook them horizontally, a disturbance they had not encountered before; they folded immediately. When the plants were dropped again a month later, most still ignored the fall. The design was elegant, and the results were difficult to explain away.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In animals, this pattern, a declining response to a repeated stimulus that proves harmless, is known as habituation, and it is generally regarded as the simplest form of learning. Kovács concluded that her plants had learned that falling was not dangerous, and that they remembered the lesson for weeks. Not everyone accepts the vocabulary. Edwin Thorne, of the Severn Institute of Plant Physiology, argues that memory implies a dedicated structure in which information is stored and retrieved, and that plants possess nothing of the kind. He prefers to speak of a stress imprint, a lasting change in a plant's chemical state that alters how it responds to later events. Kovács replies that such objections define learning by the machinery rather than by the behaviour, and that the same reasoning would deny learning to single-celled organisms, which are known to habituate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious claim came from Samir Al-Masri at the Mashreq Centre for Plant Sciences. Al-Masri grew pea seedlings in Y-shaped tubes, with a small fan and a light placed together at the end of one arm. Seedlings naturally grow towards light, and in the first phase of the experiment they duly bent towards the illuminated arm. After several days of training, he removed the light and found that many seedlings now grew towards the arm containing the fan, as if they had come to associate moving air with the light that usually accompanied it. If confirmed, this would represent associative learning, a capacity once thought to require a nervous system, and the study was widely reported as evidence that plants can be trained much like animals.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Confirmation has proved elusive. A team led by Ibiere Sekibo at the Calabar Institute for Experimental Botany repeated the experiment with roughly five times as many seedlings and detected no association whatsoever. Al-Masri has responded that subtle differences in seed variety, lighting and temperature may explain the discrepancy, and this is possible: plants are notoriously sensitive to small variations in their growing conditions, and experiments in plant behaviour are harder to standardise than many in animal psychology. A failed replication does not by itself prove that the original result was mistaken. But the burden of proof rests with those making extraordinary claims, and until the effect can be reproduced reliably by independent groups, it should be regarded as unconfirmed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Behind these experimental disputes lies a quarrel about words. Over the past two decades, a group of researchers has promoted the field of plant neurobiology, arguing that plants process information in ways that parallel animal nervous systems. Its supporters contend that borrowing concepts from animal science can encourage researchers to ask questions that might otherwise never occur to them. Critics, including a number of senior botanists who signed an open letter on the subject, object that the term wrongly implies that plants possess nerve cells, or even awareness. A reasonable position lies between these extremes. Learning, if it is defined in terms of observable behaviour, is a perfectly acceptable term for what Kovács's plants did; neurobiology, by contrast, is inappropriate, because plants have no neurons.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The debate is not merely about labels; it has practical consequences. How a field describes itself affects which journals publish its work, which agencies fund it and how the public understands its findings. It has even begun to influence ethics, with some commentators asking whether, if plants can learn and remember, they might deserve some form of moral consideration. Such discussions are, at best, premature. The capacities demonstrated so far, however intriguing, offer no evidence that plants experience anything at all. To build ethical arguments on such foundations risks discrediting both the science and the ethics.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most useful outcome of the controversy has been to sharpen the questions. Rather than asking whether plants are intelligent, a question with no agreed answer, researchers are increasingly asking more precise ones: which stimuli plants can distinguish, how long changes in their behaviour last, and what physiological mechanisms sustain them. Those questions can be answered by experiment, and the answers are likely to prove more interesting than any label that might be attached to them.

topic: allelopathy and the novel weapons hypothesis of plant invasion
title: Poison in the Soil
subtitle: Do plants wage chemical warfare on their neighbours? After a century of argument, the answer is beginning to emerge

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Roman naturalists noted that little would grow beneath the canopy of a walnut tree, and farmers in many parts of the world have long held that certain plants sour the ground for others. In the early twentieth century, such observations acquired a name: allelopathy, the release by one plant of chemicals that inhibit the germination, growth or survival of another. The idea is intuitively appealing. Plants are prolific chemists, producing many thousands of compounds, and it would be surprising if none of them were used against competitors. Yet despite its long history, allelopathy remains one of the most contentious ideas in plant ecology, admired by some researchers as a key to understanding plant communities and dismissed by others as a theory that has never been properly demonstrated in the field.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in the evidence. A plant that suppresses its neighbours may do so simply by taking more than its share of water, light or nutrients, and separating chemical interference from ordinary competition is extraordinarily hard. For decades, the standard approach was to grind up leaves or roots, soak them in water and apply the resulting extract to seeds in a laboratory dish. Germination was frequently inhibited, and the results were taken as proof of allelopathy. Critics pointed out that such extracts typically contained compounds at concentrations far higher than any found in natural soil, where chemicals are broken down by microbes, bound to clay particles or washed away by rain. As one sceptic put it, these experiments showed only that almost anything is toxic at a sufficient dose. Much of this criticism was justified, and a large part of the early literature has deservedly been set aside.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More convincing methods have since been developed. Céline Lefebvre, of the Loire Institute of Plant Ecology, has made extensive use of activated charcoal, a material that readily absorbs organic compounds. If adding charcoal to the soil allows neighbouring plants to recover, the suppression was probably chemical rather than the result of competition for resources. In her experiments with spotted knapweed, a Eurasian plant that has invaded vast areas of North American grassland, native grasses grew substantially better in soil treated with charcoal. The method has its own complications, since charcoal can also change the availability of nutrients in the soil. Lefebvre acknowledges the problem and now includes additional controls in which nutrients are adjusted separately, an approach that has considerably strengthened her conclusions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Knapweed lies at the centre of an influential idea known as the novel weapons hypothesis. Vikram Anand, at the Western Ghats Institute of Ecology, argues that some invasive species are so successful because the chemicals they release are new to the communities they invade. In their native range, neighbouring plants have had thousands of years to evolve tolerance; in a new continent, they are defenceless. Anand points to experiments in which a compound produced by knapweed roots severely inhibited grasses from North America but had little effect on closely related grasses collected from the plant's home range in eastern Europe. If the hypothesis is correct, it would help to explain why some plants that are unremarkable at home become overwhelmingly dominant abroad.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis has attracted sharp criticism. Marta Wójcik, of the Masurian Centre for Invasion Biology, notes that when other laboratories measured the key knapweed compound in field soils, they generally found concentrations far lower than those originally reported, and in several cases could not detect it at all. She also argues that invasive success is more readily explained by escape from natural enemies: plants introduced to a new region frequently leave behind the insects and diseases that controlled them at home. Wójcik's objections are serious, but they are not fatal. Measuring short-lived compounds in soil is notoriously difficult, and results vary greatly with the timing and method of sampling. Moreover, escape from enemies and chemical interference are not mutually exclusive; an invader may well benefit from both.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Interest in allelopathy is not confined to ecologists. Sipho Tshabalala, an agronomist at the Highveld Institute of Agronomy, has investigated whether crops with allelopathic properties could reduce farmers' dependence on herbicides. Residues of rye left on the soil surface after harvest, for example, release compounds that suppress the germination of many small-seeded weeds, and sorghum roots exude a substance that inhibits a range of competing plants. Tshabalala cautions, however, that the same chemicals can damage the crop that follows, so that rotations must be planned with care. The approach is promising, but its benefits are likely to be modest; it may complement chemical weed control, but there is little prospect of it replacing herbicides altogether.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: After a century of debate, it seems reasonable to conclude that allelopathy is real but highly dependent on circumstances: on soil type, on microbial activity, on the species involved and on their evolutionary history. The question that now matters is not whether plants wage chemical warfare, but under what conditions their weapons are effective, and that question can only be answered in the field.

topic: prenatal famine exposure and lifelong health (famine birth cohorts)
title: Hunger's Long Shadow
subtitle: Can a famine experienced in the womb leave a mark that lasts a lifetime, or even longer?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the closing winter of a European war in the 1940s, a blockade cut food supplies to a densely populated coastal region for roughly seven months. Official rations, which had already been meagre, fell to fewer than seven hundred calories a day at their lowest point, and thousands of people died of starvation. Yet the episode had one feature that makes it unusually valuable to scientists: it began and ended abruptly, and the population affected was served by a well-organised health system that kept detailed birth records. Children who were in the womb during the famine can therefore be compared with siblings conceived before or after it, providing something close to a natural experiment on the effects of early nutrition.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first follow-up studies, conducted when these children reached the age of military service, found few differences between those who had been exposed and those who had not. It was only decades later, when the cohort entered middle age, that a pattern emerged. A team led by the epidemiologist Annelies Vroomans at the Institute for Perinatal Health reported that individuals exposed during the first three months of pregnancy had higher rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease and raised cholesterol than their unexposed siblings, whereas exposure late in pregnancy was associated mainly with lower birth weight and, later, with impaired glucose tolerance. The timing of the deprivation, in other words, appeared to matter at least as much as its severity.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such findings fit the broader hypothesis that the foetus 'reads' its environment and adjusts its development accordingly, preparing for a world of scarcity if nutrients are in short supply in the womb. When the world into which the child is born turns out to be one of abundance, the mismatch may cause disease. What remained unclear was the mechanism. A group led by the molecular biologist Tobias Heggland at the Bergen Centre for Developmental Biology examined DNA from blood samples taken from cohort members some sixty years after the famine. They found that a gene involved in growth carried fewer methyl groups, chemical tags that help to regulate gene activity, in those exposed around the time of conception. The difference was small, but it was striking that it had persisted for six decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Writers of popular science seized upon the result as evidence that famine had 'rewritten' the genome of a generation. This is an exaggeration. Methylation does not alter the underlying DNA sequence, and the changes identified affected only a modest proportion of the cells sampled. Moreover, blood is an imperfect proxy: the tissues most relevant to metabolic disease, such as the liver and pancreas, cannot easily be sampled from living volunteers, and patterns of methylation differ markedly from one tissue to another. Heggland himself has always described his findings as an association rather than proof that the methylation changes cause ill health.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: More controversial still is the claim that the effects extend to the next generation. Several analyses have reported that the children of women exposed in the womb were themselves more likely to be overweight, and some researchers have interpreted this as transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. The health economist Mireille Faucompré argues that such conclusions are premature. She points out that a woman who was herself exposed may experience complications during her own pregnancy, so that her child develops in a womb that is already compromised. In that case the 'inheritance' would be a direct physiological effect on a new foetus, not a mark transmitted through the egg. Families also share diets, habits and incomes, and these can pass on disadvantage just as effectively as any molecule.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Faucompré's objection is, in my view, a fair one, but it can be pushed too far. Studies in laboratory animals, where diet and environment can be controlled precisely, have shown that nutritional stress in one generation can alter metabolism in grandchildren that never encountered it, even when the offspring of the stressed animals are raised by unaffected foster mothers. Human evidence is unlikely ever to reach that standard of control, but it would be odd to dismiss the possibility merely because it is difficult to demonstrate. The developmental biologist Ngozi Adebanjo-Kerr has suggested that the most promising route is to combine historical cohorts with detailed records of family diet, so that social and biological explanations can at least be weighed against one another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the famine cohort undoubtedly shows is that the months before birth deserve far more attention from public health policy than they have traditionally received. Programmes aimed at improving adult health have largely concentrated on behaviour in later life: diet, exercise and smoking. If a substantial share of the risk is set before birth, then the nutrition of women who are, or may soon become, pregnant is not merely a matter of maternal welfare but an investment in the health of the population decades into the future. That conclusion does not depend on whether epigenetic marks are inherited; it would hold even if the effects ended with the generation that went hungry.
