topic: diet, DNA methylation and caste determination in honeybees
title: Born to Rule?
subtitle: How a special diet turns an ordinary bee larva into a queen, and why the explanation is less simple than it once seemed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a honeybee colony, the queen and her workers could hardly lead more different lives. The queen may survive for several years and, at the height of summer, lay as many as two thousand eggs a day. Her workers, by contrast, live for only a few weeks during the busy season and are, for practical purposes, sterile. Yet the two castes are not genetically distinct: any fertilised egg can become either. What decides the outcome is food. Larvae destined to become queens are fed generously on royal jelly, a secretion produced by glands in the heads of young workers, throughout their development. Larvae destined to become workers receive royal jelly for only about three days before being switched to a mixture of pollen and nectar.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, biologists assumed that royal jelly must contain a single 'queen substance' responsible for this transformation. Chemists separated it into its many components, among them sugars, fats, vitamins and an unusually rich assortment of proteins, and fed them to larvae one at a time, but none reliably produced queens on its own. Several candidates were announced with confidence, only to fail when other laboratories tried to repeat the results. The persistence of this search, which lasted for decades, is revealing. It reflects a habit of mind that is still common in biology and medicine: the expectation that a complex outcome must have a single, identifiable cause that can be isolated in a test tube.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A different approach emerged when attention shifted from the food itself to the way the larva's genes respond to it. A team led by the geneticist Rangi Tawhiri at the Southern Apiculture Institute used a laboratory technique to reduce the activity of an enzyme that attaches methyl groups to DNA. Methyl groups are small chemical tags that can influence whether a gene is switched on or off. When the enzyme was suppressed in newly hatched larvae, around seven in ten developed into queens with fully formed ovaries, even though they had been raised on the standard worker diet. Tawhiri concluded that methylation normally acts as a kind of brake on queen development, and that royal jelly may work, at least in part, by releasing it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The experiment was elegant, but it should not be read as the final word. Other laboratories attempting similar work have obtained less consistent results, and methylation in insects is far sparser than in mammals, which makes its role harder to interpret. The developmental biologist Lucía Barrientos argues that methylation is only one layer of a much larger regulatory system. Hormones that control growth and the signals by which cells sense the availability of nutrients are, in her view, at least as important. She compares the process to an orchestra, in which silencing one section changes the music without explaining how the whole piece was composed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more radical challenge comes from the entomologist Kwame Ofori-Atta, who suggests that biologists may have been asking the question the wrong way round. Instead of looking for something in royal jelly that creates queens, he has investigated what the worker diet contains that might prevent them. His group has identified compounds in pollen that appear to slow the development of the ovaries. On this view, queens represent the default path and workers are the result of a dietary restriction. The reframing is valuable precisely because it overturns an assumption that had gone largely unquestioned, although much of the supporting evidence comes from larvae reared in laboratories rather than in living hives.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Outside the laboratory, the story of the queen has proved commercially irresistible. Royal jelly is widely sold as a dietary supplement for people, often with suggestions that it can extend life or restore vitality, an idea plainly borrowed from the queen's remarkable lifespan. Ilse Vandermeulen, a consumer researcher at the Flemish Institute for Food Policy, examined the marketing of over a hundred such products and found that most referred, directly or indirectly, to bee research. Such claims have no sound basis. The bee's response depends on receiving the jelly during a narrow window early in development, and there is no evidence that adult humans, whose biology differs in countless ways, gain any comparable benefit.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the honeybee does demonstrate is that a single genome can support strikingly different bodies and behaviours, depending on the conditions encountered while an organism is developing. Rather than a fixed blueprint, the genome is better understood as a repertoire of possibilities from which the environment helps to select. The lesson most worth drawing from the hive, then, concerns not a miraculous food but the importance of timing: the same signal that transforms a larva in its first days would have no such effect a week later. Seen in this light, the honeybee offers developmental biology a model whose value extends well beyond the hive, since the same principle is now being explored in organisms ranging from ants to mammals.

topic: epigenetic clocks and the measurement of biological age
title: Reading the Body's Calendar
subtitle: Epigenetic clocks promise to reveal how fast we are really ageing, but what exactly are they counting?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask people how old they are and they will report the number of birthdays they have celebrated. Physicians have long known, however, that two sixty-year-olds can differ enormously in health and vigour, and the idea of a 'biological age', distinct from the chronological one, has a long history. Turning that idea into a measurement has proved surprisingly difficult. Earlier candidates, including the length of the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, grip strength and blood pressure, each turned out to be only loosely related to age when considered on their own, and none could be relied upon for an individual patient. Combining several such markers improved matters only slightly, and by the end of the twentieth century many researchers had concluded that ageing was simply too varied a process to be captured by any single number.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the early 2010s, the statistician Dagny Sørbø at the Arctic Institute for Computational Biology took a different route. Rather than starting from a theory of why organisms age, she supplied a computer algorithm with methylation measurements, readings of the chemical tags attached to DNA, from hundreds of thousands of sites across the genome, and asked it to find the combination that best predicted the age of the person who had provided the sample. The resulting 'clock' relied on fewer than four hundred sites, yet it could estimate the age of tissue from many different organs to within about four years on average. Sørbø was careful to describe her creation as a measuring instrument rather than an explanation. She admitted openly that she had no idea why these particular sites changed as the years passed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Attention soon turned to the cases in which the clock was wrong. When a person's predicted age exceeds his or her actual age, the difference is described as 'age acceleration', and a second generation of clocks was developed to capture it. Instead of being trained to predict the number of years a person has lived, these newer tools were trained on records of disease and death. A team led by the gerontologist Valentina Rusnak at the Adriatic Centre for Ageing Research reported that individuals whose clocks ran fast were considerably more likely to die over the following decade, even after smoking, body weight and income had been taken into account. For Rusnak, this demonstrates that the clocks are capturing the ageing process itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That conclusion goes further than the evidence allows. A measure that predicts death is not necessarily a measure of what causes it. Grey hair is a reasonably good indicator of advancing years, but no one imagines that dyeing it makes a person younger. The biochemist Tariq Bianconi argues that most of the sites used by epigenetic clocks are likely to be 'passengers' rather than 'drivers': changes that accompany ageing, such as the gradual drift in methylation that occurs whenever cells divide, rather than changes that bring it about. If he is right, an intervention that reversed these marks might be no more meaningful than a bottle of hair dye.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This distinction matters because epigenetic clocks have moved rapidly out of the laboratory. Several companies now sell tests directly to consumers, and a growing number of diets, supplements and drug trials claim to have turned back the clock by several years. The genomicist Obinna Eze and colleagues at the West African Genomics Network sent identical saliva samples to a number of these companies and received age estimates that differed by more than a decade. Even when the same company analysed the same sample twice, the results sometimes varied by several years. Until such inconsistencies are resolved, a reported reduction of two or three years in biological age tells us essentially nothing, since it lies within the range of ordinary measurement error.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the clocks should be dismissed. Their real value lies in research rather than in personal testing. Studies of ageing face an obvious practical obstacle: if the outcome of interest is death, investigators may have to wait decades for results. A clock, however imperfect, offers a cheap means of comparing large groups over a few years. Using this approach, researchers in the Montevideo Ageing Consortium found that adults who had experienced severe hardship in childhood tended to show accelerated clock ages decades later. If confirmed, that finding would provide a biological link between social circumstances and later health that has long been suspected but rarely measured.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the best analogy for an epigenetic clock is a thermometer. A high temperature reliably signals that something is wrong, but it does not reveal whether the cause is an infection, an injury or something else entirely, and lowering it does not necessarily cure the patient. The danger, then, lies less in the technology itself than in the language used to promote it. Advertising a clock reading as a person's 'true age' implies a precision and a depth of understanding that, at present, nobody possesses.

topic: genomic imprinting and the parental conflict theory
title: A Tug of War in the Genome
subtitle: Why do some genes behave differently depending on which parent they came from?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse; a hinny is the result of the reverse cross, a male horse and a female donkey. In principle the two animals carry the same mixture of genes, yet they are noticeably different. The hinny is usually smaller, with a thicker mane and shorter ears, and breeders have long regarded the two as distinct animals. This is more puzzling than it might appear. The laws of inheritance worked out in the nineteenth century, using careful crosses of garden peas, rest on the assumption that it makes no difference whether a particular version of a gene is inherited from the mother or from the father. For most genes that assumption holds. For a small but important group, it does not.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence came from experiments on mice in the 1980s. Researchers succeeded in creating embryos whose chromosomes came entirely from two mothers, and others whose chromosomes came entirely from two fathers. Neither kind survived. Embryos with only maternal chromosomes developed reasonably well at first but formed a poor placenta, while those with only paternal chromosomes produced a large, vigorous placenta surrounding very little embryo. The explanation is that certain genes are 'imprinted': they are marked, largely through the attachment of methyl groups, while still in the egg or the sperm, so that in the offspring only the copy from one parent is switched on. Around two hundred such genes have now been identified in mammals, and a striking number of them influence growth or the development of the placenta.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should such a system exist? The most influential answer, often called the conflict theory, has been developed in detail by the evolutionary biologist Ayodele Fashola of the Institute for Evolutionary Genetics. In species in which a female may have offspring by several different males over her lifetime, Fashola argues, the interests of the parents' genes diverge. A gene inherited from the father gains by drawing as many resources as possible from the mother for the current offspring, since the father may not be related to her future young. A gene inherited from the mother, by contrast, gains from a more even distribution of her resources among all her offspring. The theory therefore predicts that genes active only when inherited from the father will tend to promote growth, while those active only when inherited from the mother will tend to restrain it. A number of well-studied genes behave in exactly this way.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Much of the theory's appeal lies in its elegance, but its real strength is that it makes predictions which could, in principle, prove it wrong. If imprinting arises from a struggle over maternal resources after conception, it should be rare or absent in animals in which the mother provides all the nourishment for her young before the egg is fertilised. Birds are just such a case, and imprinting appears to be virtually absent in them. In my view, this is the most persuasive evidence for the theory yet produced.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The theory is not without critics, however. The molecular geneticist Pham Minh Chau points out that many imprinted genes have no obvious connection with growth; some are active mainly in the brain and appear to influence behaviour. The conflict theory can be stretched to cover such genes, she argues, but only through increasingly complicated arguments that become difficult to test. Gustavo Arriaga, a developmental physiologist, has proposed an alternative. Because a gene inherited from the mother is guaranteed to match one of the mother's own versions, he suggests, switching on only the maternal copy may help the foetus to coordinate its development with its mother's body. Arriaga's hypothesis has merit for certain genes active in the placenta, but it cannot explain why other genes are active only when they come from the father.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The subject is not merely of theoretical interest. When imprinting goes wrong, the consequences can be serious: two rare disorders arise from damage to the same region of one chromosome, yet they produce very different symptoms depending on whether the faulty copy came from the mother or from the father. Some studies have also reported a slightly higher rate of imprinting disorders among children conceived through assisted reproduction. The clinical geneticist Siobhán Ní Bhriain advises caution in interpreting these figures. The absolute risk remains very low, she notes, and the underlying fertility problems of the parents, rather than the laboratory procedures, may be responsible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Imprinting challenges the familiar image of the genome as a harmonious team of genes working towards a shared goal. It looks instead like a negotiated settlement between parties whose interests only partly overlap. For all its gaps, the conflict theory remains the most productive framework available, chiefly because it has generated predictions that researchers can check. It would be surprising, though, if a single idea accounted for every imprinted gene; a system that has evolved over many millions of years has probably been put to more than one use.

topic: paternal diet and inheritance through sperm-borne RNA
title: The Forgotten Parent
subtitle: Evidence is growing that a father's life before conception may shape the health of his children

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, a father's biological contribution to the next generation was thought to consist of half of his child's DNA and nothing more. The sperm cell, which sheds almost all of its cytoplasm as it matures, seemed physically incapable of carrying anything else. Mothers, by contrast, nourish the embryo for nine months, and it is hardly surprising that the study of influences before birth has concentrated almost entirely on them. Advice about diet, alcohol and smoking around the time of conception has been addressed overwhelmingly to women. This imbalance is understandable, but it has left a significant gap in our knowledge, and the gap is now beginning to close.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first indications came from laboratory animals. Male mice fed a diet high in fat for several weeks before mating fathered daughters whose bodies handled sugar poorly, even though the offspring never encountered their fathers and were raised by mothers eating a normal diet. The reproductive biologist Javad Karimzadeh, working at the Caspian Institute of Reproductive Science, obtained comparable results by feeding male mice a diet low in protein. In the livers of their offspring, he found altered activity in genes involved in the processing of cholesterol. Because the fathers had contributed nothing to their young except sperm, the information responsible must, it seemed, have travelled in the sperm itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question was how. Part of the answer appears to lie in small RNA molecules, short strands of genetic material that do not code for proteins but can regulate the activity of genes. Sperm turn out to acquire a cargo of these molecules as they pass through the epididymis, a long coiled tube in which they complete their maturation. The cell biologist Teodora Vasilescu and her colleagues extracted small RNAs from the sperm of males fed a high-fat diet and injected them into ordinary fertilised eggs. The resulting offspring developed metabolic problems similar to those seen in the young of the overfed fathers. Vasilescu regards this as the clearest demonstration so far that information acquired during a father's life can be passed on through sperm. The experiment is impressive, although it is worth remembering that the quantities of RNA injected may well have exceeded those that a single sperm would naturally deliver.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evidence from humans is considerably weaker. The historical demographer Henrike Oosterveld analysed two centuries of harvest records and church registers from an isolated northern parish, where good and bad years could be identified with some precision. She reported that men whose paternal grandfathers had enjoyed abundant harvests in the years shortly before puberty tended to die younger than other men. Oosterveld proposed that the period of slow growth preceding adolescence, when sperm-producing cells are first being established, is a particularly sensitive window. Her findings are tantalising, but they rest on a few hundred individuals and a long chain of assumptions about who ate what and when, and they have proved difficult to replicate elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Larger studies are now under way, designed specifically to avoid the weaknesses of historical records by gathering information before children are even born. The Hokkaido Paternal Health Cohort is following some ten thousand families, recording fathers' diets and body weight before conception and storing samples of their sperm. Early results suggest that obesity in men is associated with measurable differences in the small RNAs their sperm carry. What the project cannot yet say is whether these differences affect the children, who are still too young for their long-term health to be assessed. Until such data become available, claims about the scale of paternal effects in people remain largely speculative. Even then, separating biological transmission from the many habits that fathers share with their children will be far from straightforward.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The prospect of such findings has already prompted debate about how they should be communicated. The sociologist Akosua Darkwa notes that extending responsibility for children's health to fathers could, in principle, relieve some of the pressure that has fallen on mothers alone. In practice, she warns, it may simply add a new layer of blame, and the heaviest burden would fall on poorer families, who have the fewest opportunities to change what they eat. Her concern is legitimate, but it is not a reason to withhold information. Men have as much right as women to know how their health before conception might affect their children.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The field therefore needs to resist two opposite temptations. One is to dismiss paternal effects because the human evidence remains thin; the animal research is too consistent to be ignored. The other is to announce, on the strength of a handful of studies, that a father's every meal is written into his child's future. The most important consequence of this research may turn out to be conceptual rather than practical: it suggests that health before conception is a matter for both parents, and that the long-standing habit of addressing advice to women alone was never as well founded as it appeared.

topic: maternal care, stress responses and epigenetic marks in rats and humans
title: A Mother's Touch
subtitle: Experiments with rats suggest that early care can change how genes respond to stress, but how far can the findings be stretched?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who watches laboratory rats for long enough will notice that mothers differ. Some spend a great deal of time licking and grooming their newborn pups; others do so far less often. For many years these differences were regarded as little more than background noise, the kind of natural variation that experimenters try to average out. In the 1990s, however, the behavioural neuroscientist Benedikt Aschauer at the Alpine Institute for Behavioural Neuroscience observed that the offspring of the most attentive mothers grew into noticeably calmer adults. They were less easily startled, released smaller quantities of stress hormones when briefly restrained, and were more willing to explore unfamiliar surroundings.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The obvious objection was that calm mothers might simply pass on genes for calmness. To separate the effects of genes from those of care, Aschauer's team carried out cross-fostering experiments, moving pups shortly after birth from one mother to another. Pups born to mothers that rarely licked them, but raised by mothers that did so frequently, grew up calm; pups moved in the opposite direction grew up anxious. In each case, the adult behaviour followed the foster mother rather than the biological one. More remarkably, females raised by attentive mothers became attentive mothers themselves, so that a style of care was transmitted from one generation to the next without any genetic involvement at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The search for a mechanism led to the hippocampus, a region of the brain that helps to regulate the body's reaction to stress. A group led by the molecular neurobiologist Anjali Raghunathan found that in pups that had been licked frequently, a gene coding for a receptor that detects stress hormones carried fewer methyl groups, chemical tags that tend to silence genes. As a result, more of the receptor was produced. Raghunathan explains that a brain with more of these receptors detects stress hormones more readily and therefore switches off the stress response sooner, much as a sensitive thermostat turns off the heating before a room becomes too hot. The differences in methylation emerged during the first week of life and persisted into adulthood. Furthermore, when a drug that removes methyl groups was infused into the brains of adult rats raised by inattentive mothers, their stress responses came to resemble those of well-licked animals.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That final result is perhaps the most significant of all, because it suggests that marks laid down early in life are not necessarily permanent. It should not, however, be mistaken for a treatment. The effect was achieved by delivering chemicals directly into the brain, and drugs of this kind act on thousands of genes at once, with consequences that are impossible to predict. What the experiment demonstrates is a principle, not a practical remedy. Nonetheless, the principle matters. If a molecular mark can be removed in adulthood, then the window during which care shapes the brain may be less firmly closed than was once assumed, and gentler ways of influencing the same pathways may one day be found.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Inevitably, researchers asked whether something similar happens in people. The neuropathologist Nomvula Khumalo examined brain tissue donated after death and reported that individuals who had suffered severe abuse in childhood showed more methylation of the same receptor gene than those who had not. The study was widely reported as proof that childhood trauma leaves a 'scar' on the genome. The developmental psychologist Selin Karaca urges caution. The samples were small, she points out, and the people compared differed in many respects besides their early experiences, including their use of medication, their histories of drug and alcohol use and the circumstances of their deaths. She also doubts that the licking of rat pups is a meaningful model of human parenting, which involves language, play and relationships that extend over many years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Karaca's reservations are well founded, but they underestimate what the animal work has achieved. The rat studies do not show that human experience operates in the same way, and no serious researcher claims that they do. What they establish is that it is possible for social experience to produce lasting molecular changes in the brain. Before these experiments, many biologists would have regarded such a claim as implausible; afterwards, the question was no longer whether experience could leave a biological trace, but how often and under what conditions it does so.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is, finally, a risk that the research will be used to blame parents, and mothers in particular, for their children's difficulties. It is worth remembering a detail that is often omitted from popular accounts. In the original studies, the mothers that licked their pups least were frequently those that had been kept in stressful conditions, and when they were moved to calmer surroundings the quality of their care improved. If the rat studies carry any lesson for human societies, it is not that individual parents are at fault, but that parents who are themselves under pressure need support if they are to give their children the care they would wish to provide.

topic: temperature-dependent sex determination in sea turtles under climate warming
title: Hot Sands, Missing Males
subtitle: For many reptiles, the warmth of the nest decides whether an egg hatches as male or female. A warming world is putting that system to the test

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Shortly before dawn on a tropical beach, volunteers kneel beside a nest and count the hatchlings scrambling towards the sea. On some beaches, more than nine out of every ten of these young turtles are now female. In mammals and birds, the sex of an individual is fixed at fertilisation by the chromosomes it inherits. In many turtles, all crocodiles and alligators, and a number of lizards, however, there are no sex chromosomes at all. Instead, the temperature at which the egg is incubated during a critical period, roughly the middle third of development, determines whether it becomes male or female. In sea turtles, warm nests produce mostly females and cool nests mostly males; the 'pivotal temperature', at which equal numbers of each sex emerge, lies at around 29 degrees Celsius.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Exactly how a temperature is converted into a sex remained a mystery for decades. Recent work by the molecular biologist Bjarne Thorsrud at the Nordic Institute of Comparative Genomics has gone a long way towards solving it. Studying a freshwater turtle, his team found that warmth alters the activity of an enzyme that removes chemical marks from the proteins around which DNA is wound. In cool eggs, the enzyme is active at a key gene that triggers the development of testes, leaving the gene accessible and setting the embryo on the male path. Higher temperatures suppress production of the enzyme, the gene remains tightly packed away, and ovaries develop instead. Thorsrud describes the arrangement as 'a thermometer built into the packaging of the genome'. It is an elegant discovery, and a textbook illustration of how an environmental signal can be translated into a lasting developmental decision without any change to the genetic code.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What has made the discovery urgent rather than merely interesting is climate change. If average nest temperatures rise by one or two degrees, many populations may begin to produce almost no males. The Coral Coast Turtle Project, which has monitored one of the largest nesting populations in the Pacific for twenty years, found that among young turtles originating from the warmer northern beaches, around ninety-nine per cent were female. Members of the project warn that the population could appear healthy for many years, sustained by older males hatched in cooler times, and then decline abruptly once those males die.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The population ecologist Leilani Kahananui considers such warnings premature. Male sea turtles typically breed far more often than females: a male may mate with several females in a single season, whereas a female usually nests only once every two to four years. A population can therefore tolerate a strongly female-biased ratio among its hatchlings, and in the short term, she argues, such a population may even grow faster, since it is the number of females that limits the number of eggs. Kahananui's arithmetic is sound, but it assumes that males will continue to find females. As males become scarcer and more widely scattered across the ocean, that assumption may not hold. There is also a harder limit: above a certain temperature, embryos do not develop at all, so the danger lies not only in a shortage of males but in a shortage of hatchlings of either sex.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Can the turtles adjust? The marine biologist Mariana Cicognani has spent a decade investigating this question. Females return to nest on the beaches where they themselves hatched, but there is evidence that some populations have begun nesting earlier in the year, during cooler months, and individual females differ in how deeply they dig and whether they choose shaded spots. Cicognani believes that such behavioural flexibility offers more hope than any genetic change in the pivotal temperature itself, because turtles may take twenty-five years or more to reach breeding age, and evolution acting over so few generations would be far too slow.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the meantime, conservationists have begun to intervene: shading nests with cloth, sprinkling them with water, or moving eggs to hatcheries where temperatures can be controlled. The conservation biologist Farah Zabala warns that such measures could do harm if pursued without care. Hatchlings from artificially cooled nests may differ from naturally incubated ones in their size, strength and swimming ability, and nobody knows what the 'natural' sex ratio of a healthy population ought to be. Zabala favours a less direct approach: protecting beaches that are naturally cooler and preserving the vegetation behind beaches, which provides shade.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Zabala's caution is justified, yet waiting for perfect knowledge before acting would itself carry risks. The sensible course is to treat each intervention as an experiment, monitoring its results closely and abandoning it if the costs prove greater than the benefits. Temperature-dependent sex determination has served turtles for more than a hundred million years, through periods considerably warmer than today, so the animals are hardly defenceless. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that they will cope as easily with the present warming, which is proceeding far faster than any of the changes their ancestors survived.

topic: the reputation of Lamarck and the history of ideas about inheriting acquired traits
title: The Return of Lamarck?
subtitle: Epigenetics has revived an old and much-mocked idea about heredity, but historians of science doubt that the comparison is a fair one

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early nineteenth century, the French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed that living things change over time, and that characteristics acquired during an individual's lifetime can be passed on to its offspring. For much of the twentieth century, his name served as little more than shorthand for scientific error. Biology textbooks routinely set him alongside Charles Darwin as the man who had got evolution wrong, and illustrated the contrast with the image of a giraffe stretching its neck to reach higher leaves and passing on the slightly longer neck to its young. Students learned Lamarck's name chiefly so that they could learn why he was mistaken.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The historian Hana Kubota, of the Institute for the History of the Life Sciences, has spent much of her career arguing that this picture is a caricature. The inheritance of acquired characteristics, she points out, was not Lamarck's invention at all. It was taken for granted by almost every naturalist of his day, and Darwin himself later proposed a mechanism by which it might occur. What was genuinely original, and genuinely controversial, in Lamarck's work was his claim that species are not fixed but transform gradually over long periods. It is an irony of history, Kubota suggests, that he is remembered chiefly for the part of his thinking that he shared with everyone else.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The idea fell from favour towards the end of the nineteenth century. In a famous experiment, a German biologist cut off the tails of mice over several generations and found that their descendants were still born with tails of normal length. The experiment is often presented as a decisive refutation, but it proved less than is commonly claimed: the loss of a tail through injury is hardly the kind of response to an animal's needs that Lamarck had in mind. A more powerful objection was theoretical. Biologists came to believe that the cells which give rise to eggs and sperm are set aside early in development and sealed off from the rest of the body, so that nothing an organism experiences could reach them. This barrier was later reinforced by the principle, central to molecular biology, that information flows outwards from DNA but never back into it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, however, research in epigenetics has produced cases that seem to breach the barrier. In plants, worms and mice, states induced by the environment, such as tolerance of drought or altered metabolism after a change in diet, have been observed to persist in offspring that never experienced the original conditions. In one widely discussed study, the offspring of mice trained to fear a particular smell were themselves unusually sensitive to it, although they had never been exposed to the training. Several popular books have greeted these findings with the declaration that 'Lamarck was right'. The philosopher of biology Rodrigo Saavedra welcomes the comparison. In his view, it acts as a useful corrective to a rigidly gene-centred view of heredity and encourages scientists to take seriously possibilities that were dismissed for much of the last century.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The geneticist Kasimir Wójcik objects strongly. In mammals, he notes, the great majority of epigenetic marks are erased in each generation, during two waves of reprogramming that occur in the developing embryo. The few cases in which marks do survive usually fade within two or three generations. Moreover, the changes are rarely adaptive in Lamarck's sense: stress experienced by parents is at least as likely to produce harmful traits in offspring as useful ones. To describe such phenomena as Lamarckian, Wójcik argues, misleads the public into imagining that animals can pass on improvements they have worked to acquire.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Between these positions stands the historian Isabeau Lemaire. Labels borrowed from history, she argues, should be used to shed light on present debates rather than to settle old scores. Asking whether Lamarck was 'right' is, in her view, the wrong question, since his framework also included ideas, such as the continual spontaneous generation of simple life and an inner drive towards ever greater complexity, that no modern biologist accepts. What epigenetics revives is not Lamarck's theory but one strand of a much older and more widespread way of thinking about heredity. Recognising this, she suggests, would allow scientists to discuss the new findings on their own merits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Of the three views, Lemaire's seems closest to the truth, although Wójcik is too dismissive of the evidence from plants, in which certain epigenetic states have been documented across many generations. The episode carries a broader lesson. The barrier between reproductive cells and the rest of the body was a reasonable hypothesis, but it was treated as an established law long before the evidence justified such confidence, and observations that did not fit were too readily set aside. The story of Lamarck's reputation is less about the vindication of one individual than about the ease with which a scientific consensus can harden into dogma.

topic: epigenetic memory of winter and stress in plants and its use in crop breeding
title: Memories in the Seed
subtitle: Plants can 'remember' winters and droughts. Whether that memory can be handed down, and put to work by farmers, is fiercely disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A plant cannot run away from hardship, and so it has evolved elaborate ways of recording what it has experienced. The best understood of these is vernalisation. Many plants that germinate in autumn will not flower until they have been exposed to a prolonged spell of cold. During those weeks, a gene that holds back flowering is gradually silenced through chemical changes to the proteins around which the DNA is packaged, and it stays silent after warmer weather returns. The plant, in effect, remembers that winter has passed and flowers at the right moment in spring. Crucially, this memory is wiped clean in the seed, so that each new generation must experience winter for itself. The reset makes good sense: a seed cannot know what kind of winter it will face, and inheriting its parent's memory would risk flowering at the wrong time.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Vernalisation is uncontroversial. Far more disputed is the possibility that plants pass other kinds of experience to their offspring. It is well established that a plant exposed to mild drought or to a minor infection often responds more quickly when the stress recurs later in its life, a phenomenon known as priming. The question is whether this readiness can be inherited. The crop scientist Mahlet Tesfaye at the Highland Crop Research Centre grew a wild relative of millet under dry conditions and found that the seeds it produced germinated more successfully when water was scarce than seeds from well-watered parents. The advantage, however, was detectable in only one generation and disappeared in the next unless the drought was repeated.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The plant physiologist Harsha Wickramasinghe suspects that results of this kind often have a simpler explanation. A mother plant under stress, he notes, may provision its seeds differently, packing them with altered quantities of stored food or hormones. Any advantage enjoyed by the offspring might therefore reflect the contents of the seed rather than a mark inherited on the chromosomes. Distinguishing between these explanations requires experiments that control for the composition of the seed, and such controls are rarely carried out. This is an important objection, and a substantial proportion of the published studies claiming inherited stress memory fail to address it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are, nonetheless, cases of epigenetic inheritance in plants that are far more durable. Some heritable variants, known as epialleles, differ not in their DNA sequence but in the pattern of methylation attached to it, and a few have remained stable for centuries. One such variant, which alters the shape of a wild flower, was first described by botanists in the eighteenth century and can still be found growing today. The plant geneticist Yoon Seo-yeon and her colleagues surveyed several hundred wild populations of a small weed collected across a wide geographical range. They found that patterns of methylation corresponded to the climate in which each population grew, even after differences in DNA sequence had been taken into account. Yoon believes that epigenetic variation may provide plants with a rapid, supplementary source of adaptation, allowing populations to respond to change faster than mutation alone would permit.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Plant breeders have been slower to share this enthusiasm. Ana Luísa Correia, who has developed several commercial varieties of wheat, points out that a trait is useful to farmers only if it is reliable. Some epialleles revert to their original state in a few plants out of every hundred in each generation, and a farmer who buys seed expects the crop to behave in the same way every year. Correia's concern is understandable, but it is overstated. Conventional varieties are themselves far from uniform in their performance, which varies with soil and weather, and some epigenetic traits have proved to be as stable over many generations as ordinary genetic ones.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is one of language. Several companies now sell 'primed' seed which, they claim, has been prepared to withstand drought or disease. In most cases, the seeds have simply been soaked in water or treated with chemicals before sale, a technique that has been used for decades and that affects only the seed being treated. It has nothing to do with memory inherited from a parent plant. The use of the fashionable word 'epigenetic' in the marketing of such products confuses a quite separate issue and risks discrediting genuine research.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is a picture of plant memory that is real but, in most cases, short-lived. That brevity is probably an advantage rather than a flaw. Conditions in the wild fluctuate from one year to the next, and a memory that lasted too long would mislead offspring into preparing for hardships that never come. For agriculture, the most valuable contribution of the field may lie less in quick technological fixes than in a better understanding of how crops sense and respond to their surroundings, knowledge that could inform breeding programmes for decades to come.

topic: epigenetic divergence between identical twins with age
title: Same Genes, Different Lives
subtitle: Identical twins grow apart as they age, and not only in personality. What drives the divergence?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Identical twins develop from a single fertilised egg that splits in two, and they therefore share virtually the same DNA. Yet they are rarely as alike as their genes might suggest. If one twin develops schizophrenia, type 1 diabetes or multiple sclerosis, the other frequently does not. For many such conditions, the concordance between identical twins, meaning the proportion of pairs in which both are affected, is well below one hundred per cent and often less than half. For most of the twentieth century these differences were attributed to 'the environment', a label that, in truth, explained very little, since it covered everything from diet and infection to accidents of upbringing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the mid-2000s, the geneticist Aleksi Virtanen at the Finnish Centre for Population Genetics set out to look for differences at the molecular level. His team compared patterns of DNA methylation, the chemical tags that help to switch genes on and off, in identical twins of various ages. Pairs aged around three were almost indistinguishable. Pairs in their fifties, by contrast, showed differences several times greater, and the most divergent were those who had lived apart for the longest period and had adopted the most different ways of life. Virtanen concluded that the twins' experiences were, quite literally, being written onto their genomes as they aged.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The biostatistician Beatriz Lacerda soon challenged this interpretation. Every time a cell divides, she pointed out, its pattern of methylation must be copied, and the copying is imperfect. Small errors accumulate over a lifetime regardless of how a person lives, a process known as epigenetic drift. Using a mathematical model, Lacerda showed that chance alone could account for a large share of the differences Virtanen had observed. Her point is crucial. The fact that twins diverge with age does not, in itself, show that their environments are responsible, since any two people, identical or not, would be expected to drift apart over time simply as a result of random errors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Separating the influence of chance from that of experience required a different kind of study. Researchers working with the Baltic Twin Archive followed some two thousand pairs of twins for twenty years, taking blood samples at regular intervals and recording details of their health and habits. They found that both factors played a part. Smoking, for example, produced distinctive and consistent changes at particular sites in the genome, so that a smoker could be distinguished from a non-smoking twin with considerable accuracy. Most of the other differences, however, were scattered across the genome in no discernible pattern, just as random drift would predict. Because it tracked the same individuals over two decades rather than comparing different people at a single moment, this study offers the most reliable evidence available.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most pressing question is whether such differences help to explain why one twin falls ill while the other remains healthy. The immunologist Sione Fifita studied pairs of twins in which only one had developed an autoimmune disease, and found consistent differences in methylation in the immune cells of the affected twins. The difficulty lies in interpreting this result. The disease itself, and the drugs used to treat it, are known to alter methylation, so the differences might be a consequence of illness rather than its cause. Fifita openly describes the problem as one of 'chicken and egg'. Resolving it would require samples taken from twins before the onset of disease, which are scarce, although the large collections of stored blood now held by many health services may eventually make such studies possible.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The study of twins has long been used to argue that genes do not dictate destiny, and the epigenetic findings appear to strengthen that case. There is a danger, however, of replacing one form of determinism with another. If every methylation difference is assumed to carry meaning, the epigenome simply takes the place once occupied by the genes, as a hidden script that determines a person's fate. Much of the variation between twins may be nothing more than noise, the unavoidable randomness of biological processes. Lacerda argues that this randomness should not be dismissed as a nuisance, since it may itself contribute to the individuality that makes even identical twins recognisably different people.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Biology has traditionally framed questions about human differences as a contest between nature and nurture, with each new finding claimed as a victory for one side or the other. The twin studies suggest that chance deserves to be recognised as a third factor of equal standing. This is not an especially comfortable conclusion, because chance, unlike diet or smoking, cannot be modified by individuals or targeted by public health campaigns. It is, however, a more honest account of the evidence than one in which every difference must have an identifiable cause. Accepting the role of chance would also encourage researchers to report how much of the variation they study remains unexplained, rather than presenting every pattern as a discovery.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: smallpox variolation before Jennerian vaccination
title: Before the Cow
subtitle: Historians are reassessing the long tradition of smallpox inoculation that came before vaccination

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most textbook accounts of immunisation begin in rural England in 1796, when a country doctor scratched material from a cowpox blister into the arm of a young boy and later showed that the child could not be infected with smallpox. The episode is usually presented as the moment at which humanity first learned to protect itself against infectious disease. Yet this familiar story leaves out a practice that had been in use for centuries. Variolation, the deliberate introduction of matter from the sores of a smallpox patient into a healthy person, was known in China, India, the Ottoman Empire and many parts of Africa long before any European physician took an interest in it. In China, dried and powdered scabs were blown into the nostrils; elsewhere, the material was rubbed into small cuts in the skin. Any history of immunology that treats 1796 as its starting point is therefore not merely incomplete but misleading.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Where the practice first arose remains disputed. The traditional assumption has been that it spread outwards from a single point of origin, most often placed in China or India. Dr Farida Gulliksen, a historian at the Lagoon Institute for Medical History, rejects this view. Having gathered oral testimony from communities in West Africa and compared it with written descriptions from Asia and the Middle East, she argues that variolation was invented independently in several regions. The techniques, she points out, differed too greatly to have come from a common source: some groups used fresh fluid, others aged scabs, and the chosen site of the incision varied from the hand to the thigh. Her case is a strong one, and it corrects an unhelpful tendency to treat medical innovation as something that travels in only one direction. However, the evidence for the earliest dates she proposes remains thin, since oral traditions are notoriously difficult to place in time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What is not in doubt is that variolation worked, at least most of the time. Smallpox caught in the ordinary way killed between a fifth and a third of those infected, whereas only one or two in every hundred people who were deliberately inoculated died. The procedure produced a milder illness, perhaps because the virus entered through the skin rather than the lungs, and survivors were protected for life. But it carried a hidden cost. Professor Anders Halvorsen of the Nordic Institute for Epidemiological History has examined parish records from eighteenth-century Scandinavia and concludes that inoculated individuals were fully contagious while they were ill. In towns where the procedure became fashionable, he found, outbreaks sometimes began among people who had never chosen to be inoculated at all. For this reason, some authorities insisted that patients be confined in isolated houses until their sores had healed, and others banned the practice except during epidemics.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The arrival of variolation in western Europe in the 1720s is often told as a triumph of rational enquiry, but the reality was rather different. Reports of the technique had reached learned societies from Constantinople years earlier and had been largely ignored. What changed was not the quality of the evidence but the status of those who promoted it: once aristocratic and royal households had their children inoculated, the practice acquired a respectability that no scientific paper had been able to give it. Admittedly, physicians soon began compiling tables that compared death rates among the inoculated with those among people who caught the disease naturally. These tables were crude, but they represent one of the earliest attempts to settle a medical question by counting rather than by appeal to authority.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Shirin Tavakoli, who studies the history of public health at the Caspian University of Medical Sciences, believes that variolation did more than precede vaccination; it made vaccination possible. By the end of the eighteenth century, she argues, many communities were already familiar with the idea that a person might be made deliberately ill in order to be protected, and a network of practitioners skilled in making incisions and recording outcomes already existed. When cowpox inoculation appeared, it was absorbed into this existing system rather than having to create one from nothing. This argument is largely convincing, although it underestimates the resistance the newer method faced. Many people found the idea of introducing material from a diseased animal into a human body far more disturbing than the older practice, and cartoons of the period showed vaccinated patients sprouting horns.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why, then, has variolation been so thoroughly forgotten? Part of the answer lies in the interests of those who championed vaccination. Because cowpox did not make people contagious, its advocates had every reason to portray the older technique as dangerous and primitive, and their accounts became the basis of later histories. In 1840 Britain went further and made variolation illegal, and within a few generations it had been all but erased from popular memory. This erasure has a cost. It obscures the fact that communities with no knowledge of microbes or immune cells developed an effective, if risky, method of disease prevention through careful observation alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is to romanticise variolation, which killed many of those it was meant to protect and spread infection to many more. Nor does it diminish the importance of cowpox vaccination, which was safer by any measure. The point is rather that the history of immunisation is longer, and has many more centres, than the conventional narrative allows. Recognising this does not require us to rewrite the scientific achievements of the nineteenth century, only to acknowledge that they were built on foundations laid by people whose names have mostly not been recorded.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: the nineteenth-century cellular versus humoral immunity controversy
title: Cells Versus Serum
subtitle: A nineteenth-century quarrel about how the body defends itself still divides historians of science

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the final decades of the nineteenth century, a dispute broke out over a question that now seems almost too basic to ask: what, exactly, protects the body from infection? One camp held that the answer lay in cells. A zoologist working with transparent starfish larvae had observed mobile cells gathering around a thorn inserted into the animal and apparently consuming foreign material, and he proposed that similar 'eating cells' in the blood were the body's principal defence. The opposing camp, based largely in German laboratories, argued that immunity was a property of the fluid portion of the blood, the serum, which contained dissolved substances capable of neutralising bacteria and their poisons. For roughly two decades, each side produced experiments that seemed to confirm its own position and undermine the other's.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The conventional account holds that the humoral school, as the serum camp came to be known, won the argument decisively, and that cellular immunity was only rescued from obscurity in the second half of the twentieth century. Dr Ruslana Dovzhenko, a historian of science at the Dnipro Centre for Research Studies, regards this verdict as a product of politics as much as evidence. Following the Franco-Prussian War, she notes, scientific institutions in France and Germany saw themselves as national rivals, and the cellular theory, developed at a Paris institute, was received in Berlin with a hostility that went well beyond normal scientific scepticism. Dovzhenko's archival work is meticulous, and it is difficult to read her account without concluding that national pride coloured the judgements of leading figures. Yet she arguably goes too far in implying that the outcome would have been different in a more peaceful Europe. The humoral theory also had genuine practical successes, most notably the antitoxin treatments that saved thousands of children from diphtheria.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more positive interpretation is offered by Thiago Mattheus, who teaches the history of medicine at the Atlantic University of Recife. In his view, the rivalry was not an obstacle to progress but its engine. Each laboratory, determined to defeat the other, devised increasingly ingenious experiments, and techniques for culturing bacteria, measuring antibody levels and staining white blood cells were all refined in the heat of the controversy. It is a persuasive argument as far as it goes. Competition clearly did accelerate certain lines of work. But it also led to the neglect of observations that did not fit either camp's framework, and some promising findings lay unexamined for years because neither side had any interest in pursuing them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The sociologist Sigrun Haukeland has drawn attention to a different factor: the language in which the debate was conducted. Both sides, she observes, described immunity in military terms. Cells were 'defenders' and 'soldiers'; bacteria were 'invaders'; serum substances were 'magic bullets' fired at a precise target. Haukeland argues that these metaphors were not mere decoration but actively shaped what researchers looked for, encouraging them to think of immunity as a single decisive battle rather than a continuous process of regulation. There is considerable force in this claim, and the warlike vocabulary persists in immunology textbooks to this day. Whether it determined the course of the nineteenth-century dispute, however, is much harder to establish.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The philosopher Kenji Nakashima proposes a still more radical reading. The two schools, he contends, were not really disagreeing about the same thing. The cellular camp tended to study invertebrates and slow, chronic infections, while the humoral camp worked mostly with rabbits, guinea pigs and acute bacterial toxins. Under these conditions, it is hardly surprising that each found the mechanism it expected. Nakashima concludes that the controversy was less a contest between true and false theories than a misunderstanding produced by incompatible experimental systems.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Rafael Quintanar, an immunologist who has written widely on the history of his discipline, takes a more practical view. For Quintanar, the important point is that the eventual synthesis, which recognised that antibodies and cells work together, was delayed for decades. Antibodies, he notes, were later shown to coat bacteria in a way that makes them easier for cells to engulf, a finding that might have been made far earlier had the two schools collaborated. This seems to me the most valuable lesson of the episode. The quarrel was not wasted effort, but its cost is measured in the years during which an integrated understanding of immunity remained out of reach.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to treat the cells-versus-serum dispute as a cautionary tale about scientific vanity. That would be a mistake. Controversies of this kind are a normal feature of research, and they often sharpen thinking in ways that consensus does not. What the episode does show is that the resolution of a scientific debate depends not only on data but also on institutions, language and the choice of experimental organism. These are factors that rarely appear in the published record, and historians are only now beginning to examine them systematically.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: Victorian resistance to compulsory smallpox vaccination
title: The Reluctant Arm
subtitle: What the nineteenth-century campaigns against compulsory vaccination can, and cannot, teach us

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the spring of 1885, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of an English manufacturing town carrying banners, a child's coffin and an effigy of a doctor. They were protesting not against a war or a tax but against a medical procedure. For more than three decades, the law had required parents to have their infants vaccinated against smallpox, and those who refused faced fines and, if they could not pay, imprisonment. By the 1880s, thousands of prosecutions were being brought each year, and in some districts the courts struggled to cope. The protest was one of the largest of its kind, but it was far from unique: organised resistance to vaccination had appeared across Europe and North America almost as soon as the procedure became compulsory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, historians of medicine treated these movements as little more than an obstacle that science eventually overcame. Their members were portrayed as ignorant, superstitious or simply eccentric. This view has been decisively challenged. Dr Liesbeth Vestby of the Van Ruysdael Institute for Social History has analysed the membership lists of local anti-vaccination leagues and found that they were dominated not by the uneducated poor but by skilled workers, small shopkeepers and religious dissenters, groups with a long tradition of resisting interference by the state. For these people, she argues, the central issue was not whether vaccination worked but whether the government had the right to force it upon them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Wanjiru Fuentealba, a medical historian at the Rift Valley School of Public Health, emphasises a different, and more concrete, set of grievances. Until the 1890s, the standard method was arm-to-arm vaccination, in which fluid was taken from the blister of one recently vaccinated child and inserted into the arm of the next. Public vaccinators often worked quickly and with little supervision, and the technique could transmit other infections, including serious skin diseases and, on rare but well-publicised occasions, syphilis. Fuentealba points out that the parents who refused vaccination were frequently those who had already seen a child fall ill after the procedure. Their objections, in other words, were based on experience rather than fantasy. This is an important corrective, although it should not be pushed too far: some leaders of the movement also circulated claims that were demonstrably false, such as the assertion that vaccination caused the very disease it was designed to prevent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The town at the centre of the 1885 protest went on to develop an alternative approach. Instead of relying on universal vaccination, local health officials concentrated on rapid notification of cases, the isolation of patients in a fever hospital, and the quarantine and vaccination of their immediate contacts. For several decades, the town experienced remarkably few smallpox deaths, and its supporters held it up as proof that compulsion was unnecessary. The achievement was real, but it should be interpreted with caution. The town was surrounded by populations that were largely vaccinated, which limited the number of infections that could arrive from outside; whether the same method would have worked in isolation is far from certain. Interestingly, the strategy anticipated in some respects the targeted approach that was later used to eradicate smallpox worldwide.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Faced with mounting resistance, the government eventually gave ground. In 1898 a new law allowed parents to obtain exemption by declaring before magistrates that they conscientiously believed vaccination would harm their child, introducing the term 'conscientious objector' into the English language. Many magistrates, however, made the process deliberately humiliating, and the law had to be amended nine years later so that exemption became a simple matter of signing a declaration. Within a short time, the proportion of infants vaccinated had fallen considerably. Supporters of compulsion predicted disaster, but the expected epidemics did not materialise, partly because smallpox itself was by then becoming less common and a milder form of the disease was spreading.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to draw direct lessons from all this for the present day, and many commentators have done so. Professor Ignacio Castellanos, who studies the history of health policy at the University of the Southern Pacific, is wary of such comparisons. The Victorian movements, he notes, arose in a world where vaccination was crude, poorly regulated and sometimes genuinely dangerous, and where the state offered little in return for the obligations it imposed. Modern vaccines are subject to rigorous testing and monitoring, and their risks are far smaller. To equate the two situations, Castellanos argues, is to misunderstand both. His caution is well founded. Nevertheless, one lesson does seem to carry across the centuries: compulsion tends to harden opposition, and trust, once lost, is very difficult to restore.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most useful conclusion is a modest one. The opponents of compulsory vaccination were neither heroes nor fools. They were people responding, sometimes reasonably and sometimes not, to a policy that was imposed with little explanation and enforced with considerable harshness. Understanding why they acted as they did is not the same as agreeing with them, but it is a necessary first step for anyone who hopes to persuade rather than coerce.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: the 1954 polio vaccine field trial and the design of clinical trials
title: A Million Small Volunteers
subtitle: The great polio vaccine trial of 1954 is often hailed as a model of medical research, but the reality was messier

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the spring of 1954, more than a million American schoolchildren took part in what remains one of the largest medical experiments ever conducted. Over the following months, they received a series of injections intended to protect them against poliomyelitis, a viral disease that each summer left thousands of children paralysed and filled hospital wards with the iron lungs used to keep its victims breathing. The trial is usually remembered for its outcome: the announcement, a year later, that the vaccine was safe and effective. Historians of science, however, increasingly argue that its true importance lies in the way it was carried out. That claim deserves examination, because the trial's design was the product of compromise rather than principle, and its legacy is more ambiguous than celebratory accounts suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The trial was in fact two experiments running side by side. In some states, children were randomly assigned to receive either the vaccine or an identical-looking injection of salt water, and neither the children, their parents nor the doctors who examined them knew which they had been given. In other states, the vaccine was offered to all children in the second year of school, and the rates of polio among them were compared with those among unvaccinated children in the years above and below. Dr Aino Rautio, a statistician at the Lapland Centre for Biostatistics who has re-analysed the original records, argues that only the first design produced trustworthy results. In the second, the children whose parents agreed to vaccination tended to come from wealthier households, and polio, unusually for an infectious disease, caused paralysis more often among prosperous families, perhaps because children raised in cleaner conditions encountered the virus later in life. The comparison was therefore biased from the outset.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, was the weaker design used at all? Many state health officers refused to take part in an experiment that involved injecting children with a substance known to be useless. The bioethicist Sunil Bhattacharjee has argued that their objection, often dismissed as unscientific, was a serious moral position. In an epidemic year, a child given a placebo might be paralysed or die from a disease that the vaccine could have prevented. That concern deserves respect. Yet it is hard to avoid the conclusion that, had the entire trial relied on the observed-control method, its results would have been inconclusive, and the vaccine's approval might have been delayed by years, at a far greater cost in lives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The scale of the undertaking was extraordinary. The trial was funded not by government but by a charitable foundation that raised most of its money through small donations from the public, and it depended on the unpaid labour of tens of thousands of teachers, nurses and parents who recorded injections and tracked symptoms. Professor Mariana Ferreira-Lobo, a social historian at the Lisbon Institute of Contemporary Studies, describes it as a feat of public mobilisation as much as of science. Because ordinary families had paid for the research and helped to conduct it, she argues, they felt that the vaccine belonged to them, and this sense of ownership produced a level of public trust that later vaccination campaigns have rarely matched. The point is well made, though the same public enthusiasm also generated intense pressure for a rapid and positive verdict.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That pressure became apparent in April 1955. Within hours of the results being announced, the government licensed the vaccine, and manufacturers began distributing millions of doses. Weeks later, it emerged that batches produced by one company contained live, fully infectious virus. Children who received them developed polio, and some were left permanently paralysed. Dr Joseph Odhiambo, who studies the history of drug regulation at the Kisumu School of Law and Medicine, contends that it was this disaster, rather than the trial itself, that shaped modern vaccine policy, since it led directly to a far stricter system of government inspection of manufacturing. His argument is persuasive, and it suggests that the most lasting reforms in medicine are often driven by failure rather than success.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further corrective comes from Tomasz Tarrant, a historian of statistics at the Silesian Academy of Sciences. He points out that randomised controlled trials were not invented in 1954; a British study of an antibiotic for tuberculosis had used random allocation several years earlier. Among statisticians, Tarrant argues, the polio trial's mixed design was regarded not as a model but as a cautionary example of what happens when scientific requirements are diluted for political reasons. On the technical history he is largely right. What his account underplays is the trial's effect on public understanding. For millions of families, it was their first encounter with the idea that a treatment should be tested against a control before it is trusted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The 1954 trial, then, was neither the methodological triumph of popular memory nor a mere footnote. It showed what could be achieved when science and the public worked together, and also how fragile that partnership could be when expectations ran ahead of evidence.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: the global smallpox eradication campaign and surveillance-containment
title: The Ring Around the Virus
subtitle: Smallpox was eradicated not simply by vaccinating more people, but by changing how vaccination was used

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In May 1980, the World Health Assembly formally declared that smallpox had been eradicated. A disease that had killed an estimated three hundred million people in the twentieth century alone had been eliminated from nature, and it remains the only human disease to have suffered that fate. The achievement is often attributed simply to vaccination: an effective vaccine existed, and it was eventually delivered to enough people. This explanation is not wrong, but it is seriously incomplete. The vaccine had been available for more than a century and a half before eradication was achieved, and what finally made the difference was not a new technology but a new way of using an old one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: When the intensified eradication programme began in 1967, its strategy was mass vaccination. The aim was to immunise at least eighty per cent of the population in every affected country, on the assumption that this would be enough to stop transmission. In practice, the disease often continued to spread even where that target had been reached, particularly in densely populated regions where the unvaccinated minority still numbered millions. The alternative, which became known as surveillance and containment, emerged partly by chance. In eastern Nigeria, a shortage of vaccine forced field teams to concentrate their limited supplies on the villages where cases had been reported, vaccinating everyone around each patient to create a ring of immune people through which the virus could not pass. Outbreaks stopped, even though overall vaccination levels in the region remained low.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Mekdes Tesfaye, a historian at the Highland Institute of Public Health, argues that the success of this approach depended above all on local knowledge. Teams could only contain outbreaks they knew about, and in remote areas the most reliable source of information was not official reporting but villagers, market traders and schoolteachers. In several countries, cash rewards were offered to anyone who reported a new case, and the sums were steadily increased as the disease became rarer. Tesfaye contends that standard histories, written largely from the perspective of international agencies, have given too much credit to central planners and too little to the thousands of local workers who did the searching. Her argument is convincing, and it is reinforced by the programme's own internal reports, which repeatedly describe local recruits as indispensable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Lorenzo Marchetti, an epidemiologist at the Tyrrhenian School of Tropical Medicine, offers a more sobering perspective. Smallpox, he points out, possessed a rare combination of features that made it unusually vulnerable. It infected only humans, so there was no animal population in which it could survive unnoticed. Almost everyone who caught it developed a distinctive rash, making cases easy to identify, and people were not infectious before symptoms appeared. The vaccine, moreover, was cheap, gave long-lasting protection after a single dose, and could be freeze-dried so that it remained effective in tropical heat without refrigeration. Marchetti concludes that the smallpox campaign offers few lessons for other diseases, since almost none share these characteristics. On the biology, he is undoubtedly correct. But his conclusion is too pessimistic: the importance of rapid detection and targeted response is a principle that applies far beyond smallpox.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The campaign also took place in an unlikely political context. At the height of the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union, rivals in almost every other field, both supported the programme: one supplied much of the funding and expertise, the other donated hundreds of millions of doses of vaccine. Dr Selin Yilmazer, who studies the history of international health at the Bosphorus Centre for Global Affairs, regards this cooperation as a decisive factor, arguing that political commitment mattered as much as any technical innovation. There is some truth in this, although the relationship was less harmonious than her account implies. Each superpower was keen to claim credit, and rivalry as much as goodwill sustained their involvement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is a less comfortable side to the story. In the final stages of the campaign, when a single undetected case could undo years of work, pressure on field teams was intense, and in some places people were vaccinated against their will. There are accounts of houses being entered at night and of villagers being held down. Such episodes are sometimes justified by the scale of the prize. Yet they should not be quietly omitted from the record, not least because memories of coercion can undermine trust in health programmes for generations.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Four decades later, the campaign to eradicate polio has repeatedly come close to success without achieving it. The comparison is instructive. Polio lacks many of the features that made smallpox vulnerable, which supports Marchetti's caution. But where polio teams have relied on local knowledge and community trust, they have made the greatest progress, which suggests that the most important lessons of the smallpox campaign were never purely biological.
