area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: horse serum antitoxin therapy and biological standardisation
title: The Horses in the Laboratory
subtitle: Serum therapy saved thousands of lives before the age of antibiotics, and its influence is still felt today

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1890s, visitors to some of Europe's leading medical institutes were often surprised to find, behind the laboratories, rows of stables. The horses kept there were not used for transport. They were living factories for one of the first effective treatments for an infectious disease. Each animal was injected with gradually increasing doses of the toxin produced by diphtheria bacteria, which suffocated thousands of children every year. Over several months, the horse's blood came to contain large quantities of antitoxin, a substance that neutralised the poison. Blood was then drawn, the cells were removed, and the remaining serum was injected into sick children. Unlike vaccination, which trains the body to produce its own defences, this approach transferred ready-made protection from one organism to another. Its effect was immediate, but it faded within weeks, since the borrowed antitoxin was gradually cleared from the body.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Historians have traditionally told this story as one of laboratory genius, focusing on the scientists who first demonstrated the principle. Dr Callum Abernethy, a historian of veterinary science at the Grampian Institute of Animal History, argues that this neglects the animals on whom everything depended. Serum production, he shows, required large numbers of healthy horses, careful feeding and constant veterinary supervision, and a sick or poorly managed animal could yield weak or contaminated serum. Institutes competed to obtain suitable horses and employed specialist staff to care for them. This is a welcome corrective. Abernethy perhaps overstates the case, however, when he suggests that the horses deserve as much recognition as the researchers; animals were essential to the work, but they did not design it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the most serious difficulties facing early producers was that no two batches of serum were alike. The concentration of antitoxin varied enormously from horse to horse and even from one bleeding to the next, so that a dose which cured one child might be useless for another. The solution was to define a unit of antitoxin by comparison with a carefully preserved reference sample, against which every new batch could be tested. Dr Paloma Sutcliffe-Ade, who studies the history of pharmaceutical regulation at the Andean University of Health Sciences, argues that this system of biological standardisation was the most enduring legacy of serum therapy, since the same principle was later applied to vaccines, insulin and many other products whose strength cannot be measured by simple chemical analysis. Standardisation rarely features in popular histories of medicine, yet it is arguably one of the field's most important and least appreciated achievements.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Serum therapy also produced unexpected complications. Days after receiving an injection, some patients developed rashes, fever and painful joints, a condition that came to be called serum sickness. It was eventually understood as a reaction by the patient's own immune system to the foreign horse proteins in the serum. Dr Haruto Kuroda of the Kansai Institute for Immunological History contends that the study of serum sickness was crucial in establishing the idea that the body's defences could themselves cause disease, a concept that underlies modern understanding of allergy. Kuroda's account is illuminating, though it is worth remembering that most physicians at the time treated serum sickness as little more than an irritating side effect, and its theoretical significance was recognised by only a small number of researchers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How effective was the treatment? The question is more controversial than might be expected. Dr Elin Nyström, an epidemiologist at the Baltic Centre for Historical Demography, has re-examined national mortality records and notes that deaths from diphtheria had begun to fall in several countries before antitoxin was introduced, probably owing to improved living conditions. She concludes that the treatment's contribution has been exaggerated. Her analysis is careful, but her conclusion is difficult to accept. Hospital records from the period show that the proportion of diphtheria patients who died fell steeply, in some cases by more than half, within a year or two of the treatment becoming available, a change far too abrupt to be explained by gradual social improvement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: By the 1940s, serum therapy for diphtheria had largely been displaced by active immunisation with modified toxins and, later, by antibiotics. Yet Dr Folake Adeyemi, a pharmacologist at the Ogun Centre for Medicinal Research, insists that the approach never truly disappeared. Antivenoms for snakebite are still produced in horses by essentially the same method used in the 1890s, and the modern antibody treatments developed for cancer and viral infections rest on the same principle of supplying the body with protection it has not made itself. This continuity between nineteenth-century stables and twenty-first-century laboratories deserves far more attention than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Serum therapy occupies an awkward place in the history of medicine, overshadowed on one side by vaccination and on the other by antibiotics. But its story raises questions that remain relevant: how to guarantee the consistency of biological products, how to weigh benefits against side effects, and how to interpret historical statistics. It also reminds us that some of the most significant medical advances depended on partnerships, not always acknowledged, between humans and other animals.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: the history of vaccine preservation and the cold chain
title: Keeping It Cold
subtitle: The history of vaccines is usually told through their discovery, but getting them to patients intact has been just as difficult

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Histories of vaccination tend to be histories of discovery. They celebrate the moment when a protective substance was first identified and tested, and then move swiftly on to the next breakthrough. What they often leave out is the long and frustrating struggle to get vaccines from the places where they are made to the people who need them, without the vaccines losing their power along the way. A vaccine that spoils in transit protects no one. For this reason, the story of how vaccines have been preserved and transported deserves to be regarded as a central part of the history of immunisation, not as a technical footnote to it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The problem appeared almost as soon as vaccination itself. Material taken from cowpox blisters remained effective for only a few days, and early attempts to preserve it, by drying it on threads or sealing it between small plates of glass, were unreliable; much of what was sent over long distances arrived useless. The most famous solution was also the most disturbing. In 1803, an expedition sailed from Spain to carry vaccine to the Americas and Asia, and to keep it alive it took a group of orphaned boys who were vaccinated two at a time, each pair passing the infection to the next as the voyage continued. Dr Agnieszka Ostrowska, a historian at the Vistula Institute for the History of Science, describes the scheme as a remarkable piece of improvised engineering, a living chain that solved a problem no technology of the time could solve. She is right that it was ingenious, but ingenuity should not distract from the fact that the children themselves had no say in the matter.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Later in the nineteenth century, producers began growing vaccine on the skin of calves and mixing it with glycerine, which killed many contaminating bacteria and greatly extended the period over which the vaccine could be stored. State vaccine farms appeared in many countries, supplying clinics with standardised material. Even so, glycerinated vaccine deteriorated rapidly in warm conditions, and in tropical regions a large proportion of the doses that left the farms had lost their potency before they could be used.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A decisive advance came in the mid-twentieth century with freeze-drying, a process that removed water from the vaccine and turned it into a powder that could survive for long periods even in tropical heat. This technique was essential to the eventual eradication of smallpox. However, many of the new vaccines developed after the Second World War, against diseases such as measles and polio, were far more fragile, and could only be kept effective at low temperatures from the factory to the clinic. By the 1970s, health planners were speaking of a cold chain: a continuous sequence of refrigerators, insulated boxes and trained staff. Jean-Marc Baptiste, who studies the history of health logistics at the Antilles School of Public Policy, argues that in many low-income countries the cold chain built for childhood immunisation became the backbone of primary health care, providing clinics, transport and record-keeping systems that were later used for other purposes. His thesis is plausible, but the evidence for it remains patchy, drawn largely from a handful of well-documented countries.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Maintaining the cold chain proved far from straightforward. Early kerosene-powered refrigerators, used where there was no reliable electricity, frequently broke down, and spare parts were often unavailable for months. A less obvious problem was that some vaccines are damaged not only by heat but also by freezing. Dr Dilnoza Rahimova, an epidemiologist at the Samarkand Centre for Health Systems Research, has shown that training programmes stressed the dangers of warmth so strongly that many health workers packed vaccines directly against ice, believing that colder was always better. Surveys she conducted found that a substantial share of vaccines in some districts had been accidentally frozen. Her work makes an important point: in some cases, too much cold can do as much harm as too little.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most effective responses to these problems have been strikingly simple. In the 1990s, small heat-sensitive labels began to be printed on vaccine vials. The label changes colour gradually as the vial is exposed to heat, allowing a health worker to see at a glance whether the vaccine is still usable. Before their introduction, any vial suspected of having been warmed was supposed to be thrown away; afterwards, many doses that would once have been wasted could be used with confidence. Solar-powered refrigerators have similarly reduced dependence on fuel supplies. Such modest inventions rarely attract attention, yet they have arguably protected more children than some far more celebrated scientific discoveries.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson was learned again recently, when some newly developed vaccines required storage at temperatures far below those of an ordinary freezer, and many countries lacked the equipment to handle them. The science of making vaccines had moved forward faster than the means of delivering them. If the history of the cold chain teaches anything, it is that the two must advance together.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: vaccine adjuvants and the long gap between use and understanding
title: The Secret Ingredient
subtitle: For most of the twentieth century, vaccine makers relied on additives whose workings nobody could explain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people who have been vaccinated assume that the active ingredient in the injection is the part that resembles the disease: a weakened virus, a fragment of a bacterium or an inactivated toxin. Yet many vaccines contain something else as well. Adjuvants, from the Latin word meaning 'to help', are substances added to a vaccine to strengthen the body's response to it, and without them a number of widely used vaccines would barely work at all. What is remarkable about adjuvants is not that they exist but that, for roughly seventy years, they were used in hundreds of millions of doses without anyone being able to explain convincingly how they did their job.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The adjuvant effect was discovered, like many things in immunology, by accident. In the 1920s, a veterinarian responsible for producing diphtheria antitoxin in horses noticed that animals which developed abscesses, painful swellings at the site of injection, tended to yield considerably more antitoxin than those which did not. Rather than treating the abscesses as an unfortunate complication, he began to provoke them deliberately, mixing the toxin with irritating substances including tapioca and breadcrumbs. Around the same time, researchers working on modified toxins for human vaccines found that precipitating them with aluminium salts made them markedly more effective. Aluminium compounds had obvious practical advantages: they were cheap, easy to prepare and stable over long periods. Within a few years they had become a standard component of vaccines against diphtheria and tetanus, and they remain in use today.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To explain why aluminium worked, researchers proposed what became known as the depot theory. The salts, it was suggested, held the vaccine at the injection site and released it slowly, giving the immune system prolonged exposure. The idea was intuitive and widely taught. Dr Freja Sundqvist, an immunologist and historian at the Lake Vänern Institute for Biomedical History, points out that experiments as early as the 1950s had cast doubt on it: when the injection site was surgically removed a few hours after vaccination, the immune response was largely unaffected, which would not have been expected if a slow-release depot were essential. Sundqvist argues that the theory survived not because the evidence supported it but because aluminium worked, and nobody had a strong incentive to find out why. This is a fair criticism of a field that, in this instance at least, allowed a convenient explanation to go unchallenged for far too long.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The real explanation emerged only in the late 1980s and 1990s, with the discovery that cells of the innate immune system carry receptors which recognise molecular patterns typical of microbes and of damaged tissue. Adjuvants, it became clear, work largely by triggering these alarm signals, persuading the immune system that a genuine threat is present and that a strong response is required. Professor Kwabena Owusu of the Volta Institute of Immunology regards the adjuvant story as evidence that medicine can make real progress without complete understanding, and that practical success running ahead of theory is not in itself a weakness. There is something in this, but it ignores the cost of ignorance. Because no one knew how adjuvants worked, there was no rational basis for designing new ones, and for most of the twentieth century aluminium salts were the only adjuvants permitted in vaccines in several major markets.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ignorance also made it harder to address public concern. Over the past few decades, aluminium in vaccines has attracted periodic waves of anxiety, with campaigners linking it to a range of neurological conditions. Dr Itziar Iturbe, a toxicologist at the Basque Centre for Pharmaceutical Safety, has reviewed the research and concludes that these fears are not supported by evidence; the quantity of aluminium in a typical vaccine is small compared with what an infant absorbs from food over the same period. She also argues, however, that regulators responded poorly, dismissing concerns rather than explaining them. Her conclusion about safety is sound. It is worth adding that reassurance is difficult to give convincingly when scientists themselves have only recently been able to say what an ingredient actually does.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Today, a new generation of adjuvants is in use. They include oil-and-water emulsions, compounds extracted from the bark of a South American tree, and synthetic molecules designed to stimulate specific receptors. Their great practical advantage is that they allow a vaccine to contain a smaller amount of the active ingredient while still producing strong protection, so that limited supplies can be stretched to cover more people, a property that becomes critical during a pandemic. They can also improve responses in older people, whose immune systems often react weakly to conventional vaccines.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of adjuvants offers a lesson in humility. Vaccines have saved countless lives, but the confidence with which they are discussed can conceal how much remains uncertain. Even now, the mechanisms of some widely used adjuvants are only partly understood. Acknowledging this openly is not a sign of weakness in the science; it is the most effective way of maintaining public trust in it.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: the discovery of immunological tolerance and the idea of self and non-self
title: Learning What Belongs
subtitle: How scientists came to understand why the immune system usually leaves the body's own tissues alone

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Why does the immune system not destroy the body it is meant to protect? Its cells are capable of recognising and attacking an almost unlimited variety of foreign substances, yet in most people, most of the time, they ignore the tissues around them. For the first half of the twentieth century, this puzzle was largely set aside. A common assumption was that an organism was simply incapable of making an immune response against itself, as if some fundamental biological law forbade it. That assumption was eventually overturned by the recognition that a range of serious illnesses are caused precisely by the immune system turning on the body, but the question of how such attacks are normally prevented took decades to answer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: An important clue came from an unexpected direction. In the 1940s, a geneticist studying cattle breeding found that non-identical twin calves frequently carried mixtures of each other's red blood cells throughout their lives. The explanation was that the twins had shared a blood supply in the womb, so that cells from each had become established in the other before birth. Later work showed that such twins would also accept skin grafts from one another, something that unrelated cattle would never do. Dr Eleni Petrakis, a historian of biology at the Aegean Institute for the Life Sciences, argues that medical historians have consistently underestimated the contribution of agricultural research of this kind, which was driven by the practical needs of farmers rather than by any interest in human disease. Her point is well taken; the boundary between applied and fundamental science was far more porous than conventional histories suggest.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, wartime surgeons treating burn victims had observed that skin grafted from another person was always rejected, and that a second graft from the same donor was rejected more rapidly than the first, indicating that the immune system remembered its earlier encounter. Building on both lines of evidence, researchers in the early 1950s injected newborn mice with cells from a donor of a different strain. When these mice reached adulthood, they accepted skin from the same donor, while rejecting skin from any other. Dr Hamid Zuberi, who writes on the history of immunology at the Karachi Institute of Biomedical Sciences, regards this as the decisive turning point, because it demonstrated that tolerance is learned rather than inherited. That is undoubtedly its significance. It should be remembered, however, that the experiments were difficult to reproduce and worked only if the cells were introduced within a very narrow period around birth.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: From these findings emerged a powerful theory. During development, it proposed, the immune system learns to distinguish 'self' from 'non-self', eliminating or silencing those cells that react against the body's own molecules. The idea shaped immunology for half a century. Dr Mathilde Lemaire, a philosopher of biology at the Rhône Centre for the Study of Science, contends that it is nonetheless misleading. The body routinely tolerates things that are plainly foreign, including trillions of gut bacteria and, during pregnancy, a foetus that is genetically half different from the mother; and it sometimes attacks itself. Lemaire argues that the immune system responds to context and signs of damage rather than to a fixed boundary of identity. Her critique is valuable, but it does not follow that the older framework should be discarded. As an approximation, the distinction between self and non-self still explains a great deal, and it remains the starting point for most teaching in the field.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The practical consequences were felt most strongly in transplant surgery. The first successful kidney transplants, in the 1950s, were performed between identical twins, whose tissues the immune system could not tell apart. Transplants between unrelated people became possible only with drugs that suppressed the immune response. Dr Rawiri Gilchrist-Obi, a transplant surgeon at the Aotearoa School of Medicine who has written on the history of his specialty, argues that this progress owed far more to drugs discovered largely by trial and error than to tolerance theory. Gilchrist-Obi is substantially right. Yet theory has not been irrelevant: the long-term goal of transplant medicine remains the induction of genuine tolerance, which would free patients from a lifetime of medication, and that goal comes directly from the experiments of the 1950s.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also an uncomfortable ethical dimension to this history. Many early transplant operations were performed on patients who were already close to death and had little prospect of survival, and the majority died within weeks. Dr Einar Hallgrímsson, a medical ethicist at the Reykjavík Centre for Bioethics, believes that historians have been too forgiving of the surgeons involved, treating their failures as the inevitable price of progress. His argument raises important questions, but it is easy to condemn with hindsight. Any judgement of these early experiments must take into account the standards of consent and the alternatives that existed at the time.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The riddle of self has been partly solved. Scientists now understand many of the mechanisms by which harmful immune cells are removed or restrained. Yet the continuing rise in autoimmune conditions and allergies suggests that the body's capacity to judge what belongs to it is more fragile, and more dependent on environment, than the early theorists imagined.

area: the history of immunology and vaccines
topic: the BCG tuberculosis vaccine and its disputed effectiveness
title: A Century of Doubt
subtitle: The world's most widely given vaccine against tuberculosis has puzzled researchers for a hundred years

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The vaccine known as BCG was developed in France in the early twentieth century from a strain of tuberculosis bacteria that normally infects cattle. Over a period of thirteen years, researchers grew the bacteria again and again on a medium containing potato, glycerine and bile, transferring them to fresh cultures more than two hundred times until the strain had lost its ability to cause disease. The vaccine was first given to a newborn infant in 1921. A century later, it has been administered to several billion people and remains one of the most widely used vaccines in the world. It is all the more surprising, then, that scientists still cannot agree on how well it works.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: BCG's early history was overshadowed by catastrophe. In 1930, in the German port city of Lübeck, roughly 250 newborn infants were given an oral dose of the vaccine, and more than seventy of them died of tuberculosis within a year. An investigation established that BCG itself was not to blame: the vaccine had been contaminated with a virulent strain of tuberculosis in the local laboratory where it was prepared. Nevertheless, confidence in BCG collapsed in Germany and was shaken across Europe. Dr Konrad Brandauer, a historian at the Hanseatic Institute for the History of Medicine, argues that the disaster had one lasting positive consequence. The trial that followed, in which two doctors were convicted of negligence, established the principle that the procedures of laboratories producing biological medicines must be open to detailed external scrutiny, a principle that now underpins vaccine regulation everywhere.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A less dramatic but more persistent problem arose from the way the vaccine was distributed. In the decades after 1921, cultures of BCG were sent from Paris to laboratories around the world, and each laboratory maintained its own supply by continuing to grow the bacteria in successive cultures. Over many years, these separate lines accumulated genetic changes, so that by the middle of the century there were numerous distinct daughter strains, some of which differed noticeably from one another. The practice of preserving fixed batches by freeze-drying, introduced from the 1950s onwards, eventually halted this drift. Dr Njeri Kimathi, a microbiologist at the Great Rift Institute of Infectious Diseases, contends that differences between strains go a long way towards explaining why BCG has performed so inconsistently. Her argument is plausible, but it cannot be the whole story, since trials using the same strain in different places have also produced sharply contrasting results.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Those contrasting results are the heart of the BCG puzzle. A large trial conducted in Britain in the 1950s, involving schoolchildren aged fourteen and fifteen, found that the vaccine reduced the risk of tuberculosis by around eighty per cent. Yet a vast trial begun in southern India in the late 1960s found that it offered virtually no protection against the lung disease in adults. Other studies have produced figures scattered across almost the entire range between these extremes. The explanation favoured by Dr Duarte Lisboa, an epidemiologist at the Atlantic School of Tropical Health, is that people in tropical regions are constantly exposed to harmless relatives of the tuberculosis bacterium that live in soil and water. This exposure may give them some natural immunity, so that the vaccine adds little, or it may even block the vaccine's effect by causing the immune system to eliminate it before it can do its work. Of the explanations proposed, this is the most convincing, although it has not yet been conclusively demonstrated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Despite these uncertainties, a broad consensus has emerged on one point. BCG reliably protects young children against the most severe forms of tuberculosis, including tuberculous meningitis, an infection of the membranes surrounding the brain that is frequently fatal. Its protection against the common lung form of the disease in adults, which is responsible for most transmission, is far less dependable. As tuberculosis became rare in wealthy countries in the second half of the twentieth century, many of them ended routine vaccination of all children, reserving BCG for groups at higher risk. In countries where tuberculosis remains common, it is still given to infants shortly after birth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In recent years, BCG has attracted attention for an entirely different reason. Several studies in West Africa reported that vaccinated infants were less likely to die from infections unrelated to tuberculosis, and laboratory work suggested that the vaccine might train parts of the innate immune system to respond more vigorously to a range of threats. These findings are intriguing, and they have generated considerable excitement. A degree of caution is warranted, however. Later trials designed to test such effects have produced mixed results, and the history of BCG itself should serve as a warning against drawing firm conclusions from a small number of promising studies.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: BCG thus occupies a strange position in medicine: indispensable yet imperfect, familiar yet still not fully understood. The search for a more effective tuberculosis vaccine continues, but for the moment, the century-old vaccine remains the only one available.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: cheating, punishment and partner choice in cleaner fish mutualism
title: The Honest Cleaner
subtitle: Why do small reef fish that remove parasites from larger ones usually resist the temptation to cheat?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On coral reefs across the Indian and Pacific Oceans, a small striped fish known as the bluestreak cleaner wrasse operates what biologists often describe as a service station. Larger fish, from groupers to parrotfish, visit the wrasse's territory, adopt a characteristic motionless posture and allow it to pick parasites, dead skin and mucus from their bodies, and sometimes even from inside their mouths. A single cleaner may receive more than two thousand visits a day. At first sight the arrangement seems an uncomplicated example of mutual benefit: the client is relieved of parasites, and the cleaner obtains a meal. Yet closer observation has revealed that the relationship is far more fragile, and far more interesting, than this simple picture suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that cleaners do not actually prefer parasites. Laboratory experiments conducted by the marine biologist Ingrid Halvorsen at the Coastal Behaviour Institute offered wrasse a choice between plates of parasites and plates of client mucus, and the fish consistently chose the mucus, which is more nutritious. Since feeding on mucus requires biting the client, which responds with a visible jolt, every cleaning interaction contains a conflict of interest. Because these jolts are easy to see and count, the system has proved unusually convenient to study. The cleaner gains most by cheating, while the client gains only if the cleaner restrains itself. Halvorsen argues that cleaning should therefore be understood not as a harmonious partnership but as a negotiation in which each side constantly monitors the other.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How, then, do clients keep cleaners honest? Field studies have identified several mechanisms. Clients that are bitten may chase the cleaner aggressively, and after such punishment cleaners tend to behave more cooperatively for the rest of the encounter. Clients that can travel between reefs have another option: they simply swim away and visit a different cleaner next time. Observations suggest that cleaners treat these mobile clients with noticeably greater care than resident fish, which have access to only one station and must accept whatever service is on offer. In economic terms, the cleaners appear to respond to market conditions, behaving best towards customers who can take their business elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further mechanism depends on observers. Kwame Adeyemi, a behavioural ecologist at the University of the Gulf of Guinea, has shown that waiting clients watch the interactions between a cleaner and its current client, and that they are more likely to approach a cleaner they have seen behaving cooperatively. Cleaners, in turn, appear to adjust their behaviour when they are being watched, cheating less often in front of an audience. Adeyemi describes this as a form of reputation management, and he suggests that it may represent a simple precursor of the image-scoring processes once assumed to be unique to humans. This is an intriguing proposal, though it should be treated with some caution: a fish that cheats less when other fish are nearby need not have any representation of what those fish think of it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most surprising findings concern pairs of cleaners. Wrasse sometimes clean a client together, typically a male and a female, and in this situation a bite by either partner may cause the client to leave, depriving both of a meal. Studies have recorded that males respond to cheating by their female partners by chasing them, and that females subsequently cheat less. Elena Castellanos of the Mediterranean Institute of Ethology notes that the males, which are larger, are punishing behaviour that harms their own feeding prospects rather than the client's interests. In her view, this demonstrates that third-party punishment need not arise from any sense of fairness; it can be explained entirely by self-interest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Castellanos goes further, warning against the widespread habit of describing cleaner wrasse as possessing sophisticated social intelligence. She points out that the species has a very small brain and that many of its apparently strategic behaviours could result from relatively simple learned rules. Adeyemi disagrees, citing experiments in which wrasse outperformed chimpanzees on a task that required them to choose which of two food plates would disappear first. The comparison has been widely reported, but I suspect it reveals more about how the task was designed than about the relative intelligence of fish and apes, since the problem closely resembled the decisions wrasse make every day on the reef.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever the cognitive mechanisms involved, the cleaning system offers a valuable lesson for students of cooperation. It is sometimes assumed that cooperation requires either close kinship or advanced mental abilities. The cleaner wrasse possesses neither in any obvious sense, yet it sustains a relationship with hundreds of unrelated species. What makes this possible is not goodwill but structure: partner choice, punishment and observation together create conditions in which honesty usually pays. The same combination of incentives can be found in many human institutions, from village markets to online trading platforms, where buyers who can easily switch suppliers tend to receive the most attentive service. Rather than asking whether animals are capable of cooperation, researchers would do better to ask which features of their environment make cooperation worthwhile.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: food sharing in vampire bats: reciprocity, kinship and social bonds
title: Blood Debts
subtitle: Do vampire bats really repay favours, or has a famous example of animal reciprocity been misunderstood?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For several decades the common vampire bat has occupied a curious position in the study of cooperation. Textbooks frequently present it as the clearest example outside the human species of reciprocal altruism, the exchange of favours between unrelated individuals in which help given today is returned at some later date. The basis for this reputation is a single striking behaviour. Vampire bats feed exclusively on blood, and a bat that fails to find a meal on two or three consecutive nights is at serious risk of starvation. Roost-mates that have fed successfully, however, will often regurgitate part of their meal into the mouth of a hungry companion. Few behaviours seem so obviously generous, and it is easy to see why the species became a favourite illustration for theorists.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theoretical difficulty that reciprocity was meant to solve is well known. Natural selection should, in principle, eliminate any tendency to bear costs for the benefit of others, unless those others are relatives who share the helper's genes. An exchange of favours escapes this problem only if help is reliably returned and if individuals who accept help without giving any are excluded. Early field observations seemed to satisfy both conditions, but they were based on small numbers of animals, and the extent to which donations were directed towards kin was difficult to establish with the methods then available.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It was this uncertainty that prompted Dr Lajos Szabo of the Pannonian Centre for Behavioural Biology to argue, in an influential review, that the bat case had been overstated. Szabo pointed out that most donations in wild colonies occur between mothers and their offspring, and he maintained that kinship alone could account for the great majority of the sharing observed. In his view, the remaining cases between unrelated bats were too infrequent to demonstrate that reciprocity played any meaningful role. His critique was valuable in exposing how much had been assumed rather than measured, but I believe he was too quick to dismiss the minority of non-kin donations, since rare behaviours can nevertheless have significant evolutionary consequences.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More recent work has relied on captive colonies, which allow researchers to control feeding and record every interaction. In a series of fasting experiments, Grace Wanjiru and her colleagues at the Rift Valley Institute of Zoology withheld food from individual bats overnight and then observed who fed them on their return to the roost. Her team found that the amount of blood a bat had previously donated to a particular partner predicted the amount it later received from that partner more accurately than did genetic relatedness. Bats that had shared with many roost-mates were also fed by a wider range of individuals when they themselves were in need. Wanjiru interprets these results as evidence that bats form something comparable to long-term relationships, investing in a network of partners rather than keeping a precise record of debts.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This interpretation represents a significant departure from the original model of reciprocity, which imagined individuals carefully tallying favours given and received. Rodrigo Ahlberg, a theoretical biologist at the Atlantic Institute of Ecology, argues that such tallying would place heavy demands on memory and that a looser strategy, in which bats simply prefer partners with whom they have a history of mutual grooming and sharing, would be both easier to maintain and more robust to occasional mistakes. Ahlberg's models suggest that this relationship-based form of cooperation can remain stable even when individuals occasionally fail to reciprocate. His argument is persuasive, and it has the additional merit of making bat behaviour look less like an exotic exception and more like the social bonds documented in many primates.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that captivity reveals natural behaviour. Marta Goldaracena, who has studied wild colonies in Central America for many years, warns that captive bats live at unusually high densities, with no opportunity to leave the group, and that these conditions may encourage sharing between individuals who would rarely interact in the wild. She also notes that fasting experiments impose hunger artificially, whereas in nature the risk of a failed night depends on factors such as the availability of livestock and the weather. Goldaracena does not deny that unrelated bats share food, but she believes the frequency reported in captive studies is likely to be inflated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has implications beyond bats. If cooperation between non-relatives depends less on accurate bookkeeping than on durable social bonds, then researchers searching for reciprocity in other species may have been looking for the wrong thing. Instead of testing whether animals return favours promptly and precisely, they might ask whether individuals build up preferred partnerships over time. Such a shift would not settle every question raised by Szabo's critique, but it offers a more realistic picture of how cooperation might operate in animals whose cognitive resources are limited. It also suggests, perhaps uncomfortably, that the mental arithmetic once thought essential to reciprocity is not especially prominent in our own species either.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: cooperative breeding and helpers at the nest in birds
title: Staying Home to Help
subtitle: Why do some young birds put off breeding in order to raise chicks that are not their own?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In roughly nine per cent of the world's bird species, the task of raising chicks is not left to the parents alone. Young adults, often the offspring of previous seasons, remain on their natal territory and assist with feeding nestlings, defending the nest against predators and maintaining the territory's boundaries. To early naturalists, this behaviour was puzzling. A bird that postpones its own reproduction to rear the young of others appears to be sacrificing the very thing natural selection is supposed to favour. Explaining why such 'helpers at the nest' exist has occupied ornithologists for more than half a century, and the answer has turned out to be considerably more varied than first expected.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest and most influential explanation relies on kinship. Because helpers are usually raising their own younger brothers and sisters, with whom they share many genes, they can pass on copies of their genes indirectly even when they do not breed themselves. Professor Haruto Iwasaki of the Kansai Institute of Ornithology, who has studied bee-eaters for over two decades, has found that helpers in his population direct their efforts preferentially towards nests belonging to close relatives, and that they reduce their assistance sharply when relatedness is low. Bee-eaters are well suited to such work because they nest in dense colonies in riverbanks, allowing many families to be monitored at once. For Iwasaki, these patterns leave little doubt that kin selection is the principal force maintaining cooperative breeding.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kinship, however, cannot be the whole story. In a number of species, a substantial proportion of helpers are unrelated to the chicks they feed. Dr Fiona Bramwell, an evolutionary ecologist at the Western Isles Field Station, has argued that ecological constraints matter more than family ties. Where suitable breeding territories are scarce, she points out, a young bird that leaves home may be unable to find a place to breed at all, and its chances of survival outside a group are poor. Staying and helping, on this view, is a way of making the best of a bad situation: the helper gains safety, access to food and the possibility of inheriting the territory when the dominant breeder dies. Bramwell's 'waiting in the queue' hypothesis is supported by experiments in which vacant territories were made available and helpers rapidly left to occupy them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third group of researchers emphasises social benefits. Sipho Ndlovu, who works at the Highveld Centre for Animal Behaviour, has observed that in some groups helpers seem to work hardest when dominant birds are watching, and that lazy helpers are sometimes attacked or driven from the group. Ndlovu interprets this as a form of 'pay-to-stay', in which helping is the rent subordinates pay for permission to remain on the territory. His observations are suggestive, but the evidence for punishment of idle helpers remains patchy, and it has proved difficult to show that attacks are a response to laziness rather than to other kinds of conflict within the group.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These explanations are often presented as rivals, but in my view this framing is unhelpful. The three hypotheses address different questions: why helpers stay, why they help rather than simply remain idle, and whom they choose to assist. A helper may remain at home because territories are scarce, choose to feed its siblings because they are related, and work harder when watched because it risks expulsion if it does not. There is no logical reason why all three factors should not operate at once, and studies that set out to identify a single 'correct' explanation risk oversimplifying a complex phenomenon.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Comparative studies across many species have added a further dimension. Cooperative breeding is particularly common in environments where rainfall is unpredictable, such as the semi-arid regions of Australia and southern Africa. It has been proposed that in such habitats, the extra assistance provided by helpers acts as a kind of insurance, allowing groups to raise young successfully even in poor years when a pair alone would fail. In such places a pair breeding without help may lose its entire brood during a single dry spell, whereas a larger group can often continue to find enough insects to keep its chicks alive. This idea has attracted considerable support, although it is not yet clear whether harsh climates encourage cooperation or whether cooperative species are simply better able to colonise such environments in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, the study of helpers offers a useful corrective to the assumption that cooperation must be either selfless or selfish. Helpers frequently benefit themselves while also benefiting others, and the boundary between the two is often impossible to draw. This mixture of motives may well be the normal condition of social life rather than an exception to it, and researchers who insist on classifying every cooperative act as one or the other are likely to misunderstand what they observe. Seen in this light, helpers at the nest are less a paradox to be solved than a reminder that evolution rarely produces the neat categories that human observers prefer.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: costly punishment, fairness norms and the ultimatum game across cultures
title: The Price of Fairness
subtitle: Experiments in which strangers divide sums of money have transformed debates about human cooperation, but what do they really measure?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few laboratory procedures have been as influential in the social sciences as the ultimatum game. Its rules are simple. One participant, the proposer, is given a sum of money and must offer some portion of it to a second participant, the responder. If the responder accepts, the money is divided as proposed; if the offer is rejected, neither player receives anything. Standard economic theory predicts that proposers will offer the smallest possible amount and that responders will accept it, since even a tiny sum is better than nothing. In practice, offers below about a third of the total are frequently refused, and most proposers, apparently anticipating this, offer something close to half.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The willingness of responders to sacrifice money in order to punish an unfair offer has been interpreted as evidence of a distinctively human sense of fairness. Proponents of this view, among them the economist Astrid Lindahl of the Uppsala School of Behavioural Economics, argue that what they call 'costly punishment' is the key to large-scale cooperation. In groups where free riders, those who benefit from collective efforts without contributing, can be penalised by others, cooperation tends to remain high; where punishment is impossible, it typically collapses within a few rounds. Lindahl contends that a disposition to punish unfairness, even at personal cost, must have been favoured during human evolution precisely because it allowed groups of unrelated individuals to work together.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This argument depends heavily on the assumption that laboratory behaviour reflects a universal human trait. The early experiments, however, were almost all carried out with university students in wealthy industrialised countries. When the anthropologist Folake Larouche of the Lagos Institute for Comparative Social Research coordinated a project administering the same games in fifteen small-scale societies, including foragers, herders and subsistence farmers, the results varied enormously. In some communities, proposers routinely offered more than half; in others, offers were low and rarely rejected. Among one group of whale hunters, whose large catches can only be secured by crews of unrelated men, offers were among the most generous recorded anywhere. Larouche found that the strongest predictors of behaviour were the degree to which a society depended on market exchange and on cooperation with non-relatives in everyday economic life. Fairness norms, she concluded, are learned rather than innate.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Larouche's findings are among the most important in the field, yet it would be a mistake to treat them as a refutation of evolutionary accounts. A capacity to acquire and enforce local norms is itself something that might have evolved; what varies across cultures is the content of the norms, not the underlying ability to learn and uphold them. Seen this way, the cross-cultural data and Lindahl's theory are less incompatible than is often supposed. Both, after all, agree that humans are unusually sensitive to how resources are shared; they differ mainly over where the standards of fair division come from.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different challenge comes from those who question whether rejections in the ultimatum game represent punishment at all. Paolo Warrender, a psychologist at the Laboratory of Social Decision-Making in Bologna, has shown that many responders reject low offers even when the proposer will never learn of the rejection, a condition in which punishment cannot change anyone's future behaviour. Warrender suggests that rejections may express emotional reactions such as anger or a wish to avoid feeling humiliated, rather than a strategic attempt to enforce fairness. This is an important finding, but I am not persuaded that it undermines the punishment hypothesis as much as Warrender claims. Emotions such as anger may themselves be the mechanism through which evolution has produced a willingness to punish; the fact that a response is emotional does not mean it lacks a function.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Others have raised concerns about the experimental setting itself. Beatriz Duarte, an economist at the Lisbon Centre for Field Experiments, points out that participants in laboratory games interact anonymously and only once, conditions that rarely occur in real life. In her own field studies, conducted in fishing communities where people could observe one another's choices, punishment of free riders was far less common than in the laboratory, and disputes were more often settled through gossip, exclusion from future partnerships or negotiation. In one village, a fisherman who repeatedly kept more than his share of a communal catch was never confronted directly; instead, his neighbours quietly stopped inviting him to join their boats. Duarte argues that the laboratory may exaggerate the importance of direct punishment simply because it removes the alternatives people ordinarily use.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Duarte's point deserves wider attention than it has received. Much of the theoretical literature treats punishment as the primary mechanism sustaining human cooperation, yet direct punishment is risky: it can provoke retaliation and escalate conflict. Ethnographic accounts suggest that in many societies, reputation and the threat of being left out of future cooperation do most of the work. The ultimatum game remains a valuable tool, but its very simplicity, which made it so attractive to researchers, may also have encouraged them to see the whole of human cooperation through a single, rather narrow window.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: the evolution of eusociality in insects and the kin selection controversy
title: Sisters and the Superorganism
subtitle: A long-running and sometimes bitter dispute over how the societies of ants, bees and termites came into being

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the most remarkable achievements of evolution are the societies of ants, bees, wasps and termites. In a mature colony of leafcutter ants, millions of workers divide their labour among foraging, defence, waste disposal and the cultivation of underground fungus gardens, while a single queen produces almost all the offspring. The workers themselves rarely or never reproduce. Biologists refer to such societies as eusocial, and their existence posed what nineteenth-century naturalists recognised as a serious difficulty for the theory of natural selection. If evolution favours individuals that leave the most descendants, how could it produce creatures that leave none at all, and that do so in their millions?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely accepted answer for many decades came from the theory of kin selection. Its central insight is that a gene can spread not only by helping its bearer reproduce but also by helping relatives who carry copies of the same gene. In ants, bees and wasps, an unusual system of sex determination means that females develop from fertilised eggs and males from unfertilised ones. As a result, sisters who share the same father are more closely related to each other than they would be to their own daughters. For a time, this 'three-quarters relatedness' was thought to explain why sterile female workers devote their lives to raising sisters: in genetic terms, it seemed, they gained more by doing so than by breeding.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The elegance of this explanation helped make it a textbook standard, but it soon ran into difficulties. Termites, which are equally social, do not share the unusual genetic system. Many queens mate with several males, which reduces the relatedness between workers considerably. And numerous species with the same genetic system have never become social at all. Sawflies, for instance, possess exactly the same method of sex determination as honeybees, yet they live entirely solitary lives. By the 1990s most specialists had abandoned the three-quarters argument as a specific explanation, while retaining the broader framework of kin selection. In the words of Dr Tomáš Hrabal of the Moravian Institute of Entomology, 'the special arithmetic turned out to be a red herring, but the general principle that relatedness matters has survived every test'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A far more radical challenge appeared in the following decade. Professor Willemijn Riegler, a mathematical biologist at the Utrecht Centre for Evolutionary Theory, published a series of papers arguing that kin selection theory was not merely incomplete but unnecessary. Her models suggested that eusociality could be explained by ordinary natural selection acting on the colony, together with ecological conditions such as the need to defend a valuable nest. In her view, relatedness was a consequence of colony life rather than its cause. The papers provoked an extraordinary response: more than a hundred researchers signed a letter defending kin selection, and the dispute became unusually personal, spilling over from academic journals into conferences and the popular press.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Looking back, much of the heat in this controversy appears to have been generated by misunderstanding rather than by genuine disagreement. Riegler's models and kin selection models are, in many cases, mathematically equivalent ways of describing the same processes; they divide the costs and benefits of behaviour differently but yield the same predictions. Where they differ is largely in emphasis, and in the ease with which particular problems can be analysed. Kin selection draws attention to who is helped, whereas Riegler's approach highlights the ecological circumstances in which helping becomes advantageous. Both perspectives are useful, and it is regrettable that so much energy was spent defending territory rather than exploring how the two might complement each other.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Riegler's emphasis on ecology has nonetheless had a lasting effect. Field biologists such as Rosa Quispe of the Andean Institute of Natural History have documented that almost all eusocial species share one feature: a defensible nest containing food or other resources worth protecting. Quispe's studies of social wasps show that colonies frequently arise when a few females, often sisters, cooperate to guard a nest site that none could hold alone. She argues that this ecological requirement is necessary but not sufficient: a valuable nest makes cooperation worthwhile, but relatedness determines whether cooperators can resist the temptation to reproduce selfishly. Without close kinship, her observations suggest, such alliances tend to dissolve into conflict over who will lay the eggs.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Quispe's position strikes me as the most balanced currently available, although it leaves important questions open. It does not explain, for example, why the transition to full eusociality, with permanently sterile castes, has occurred only a handful of times in the history of life, despite the abundance of nesting animals. Nor does it settle how far insights from insect colonies can be applied to vertebrates such as naked mole-rats, whose social systems resemble those of termites in some respects but differ in others. The story of eusociality is, in short, a reminder that elegant theories may prove fragile, and that scientific disputes can obscure as much as they reveal.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: public goods, cheating and cooperation in bacteria and other microbes
title: Cheats in the Petri Dish
subtitle: Bacteria face the same dilemmas of cooperation as animals and people, and studying them may even help in the fight against infection

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It may seem strange to speak of cooperation among organisms that have no brains, no memory of past encounters and no capacity for intention. Yet over the past three decades, microbiologists have come to regard bacteria and yeasts as among the most valuable model systems for studying the evolution of cooperation. Many microbes survive by releasing substances into their surroundings that benefit not only the producer but every cell nearby. Bacteria secrete enzymes that break down food outside the cell, molecules that scavenge scarce iron, and slimy compounds that bind cells together into protective layers known as biofilms. Because these products are costly to make and are available to all, they are what economists call public goods, and they create exactly the same temptation that confronts any human community: the opportunity to benefit without contributing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Such opportunism is not merely theoretical. In laboratory populations of the bacterium Pseudomonas, mutants regularly arise that have lost the ability to produce iron-scavenging molecules but retain the ability to absorb them. These so-called cheats save the metabolic cost of production and, when they are rare, grow faster than the cooperators around them. Dr Aino Tabacchi, a microbial ecologist at the Helsinki Institute of Evolutionary Microbiology, has tracked such populations over hundreds of generations. Her experiments show that when cheats are introduced into well-mixed cultures, they spread rapidly, and in some cases the population as a whole declines because too few cells remain to supply the shared resource. Tabacchi describes this outcome as a microbial 'tragedy of the commons', and she argues that it demonstrates the fragility of cooperation in the absence of any mechanism to restrain exploitation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, does microbial cooperation persist in nature? The most important factor appears to be population structure. In a shaken flask, every cell has equal access to the public goods produced by every other cell. In soil, on leaves or in the tissues of a host, however, microbes typically grow in dense clusters descended from a single ancestor. Under these conditions, the benefits of cooperation fall mainly on the cooperator's relatives, which are themselves likely to be cooperators. Experiments in which cultures were grown on solid surfaces rather than in liquid have confirmed that cheats spread far more slowly when cells cannot move freely. Here, in other words, the same logic of kinship that has been invoked to explain helping in birds and social insects appears to apply to organisms that cannot recognise their relatives at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other mechanisms have also been proposed. Lorenzo Benedetti of the Turin Laboratory of Microbial Genetics has studied a system in which bacteria produce cooperative compounds only when their population reaches a certain density, a process known as quorum sensing. He argues that this regulation reduces the opportunities for exploitation, since public goods are made only when enough cells are present to benefit. Benedetti has also identified cases in which the genes for cooperation are physically linked to genes that confer a private advantage, so that a mutant which stops cooperating loses something it needs for itself. Such 'policing by linkage', in his view, may be as important as population structure, although direct evidence from natural environments remains limited.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers, however, warn against drawing too close an analogy between microbes and animals. Njeri Mwangi, an evolutionary biologist at the Nairobi Centre for Pathogen Research, points out that many apparently cooperative traits in bacteria may have evolved for reasons unrelated to cooperation. An enzyme released outside the cell, for instance, may simply leak from the producer rather than being 'shared' in any meaningful sense, and the fact that neighbours benefit may be incidental. Mwangi believes that the language of cheating and cooperation, borrowed from human social life, can lead researchers to see strategic interactions where there are only chemical ones. This caution is reasonable, but it can be taken too far. Whether or not the products were originally 'intended' for others, once they benefit neighbours, the evolutionary dynamics of cheating follow, and it is these dynamics that experiments measure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The study of microbial cheats has an unexpectedly practical dimension. Many disease-causing bacteria depend on public goods to establish infections, releasing toxins or iron-scavenging molecules that benefit the whole bacterial population within a patient. Several research groups have proposed deliberately introducing cheat strains into infections. Because cheats do not produce the harmful compounds, a population increasingly dominated by them should become less damaging to the host. Early experiments in insect larvae have produced encouraging results. It is too early to predict whether such approaches will reach clinical use, but the idea of turning bacterial social conflict against the bacteria themselves is a strikingly original one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Microbial research has thus reversed the usual direction of influence in the study of cooperation. Concepts first developed to explain the behaviour of animals and humans, such as kinship, free-riding and policing, have been tested more rigorously in microbes than in any other organism, because microbial populations can be manipulated and followed over thousands of generations in a matter of weeks. The results have generally confirmed the theory, which is a considerable achievement. Yet they also serve as a reminder that cooperation does not require any of the cognitive abilities that are often assumed to underpin it in humans.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: reputation, gossip and indirect reciprocity in human cooperation
title: Good Deeds and Good Names
subtitle: Why do people help strangers who will never be in a position to repay them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A traveller who leaves a generous tip in a roadside café she will never visit again presents a small puzzle for evolutionary theory. Direct reciprocity, the principle of 'you help me and I will help you', explains cooperation between people who meet repeatedly, but it cannot account for kindness towards strangers who will never return the favour. Over the past thirty years, a growing number of researchers have argued that the solution lies in reputation. According to the theory of indirect reciprocity, people help others not because they expect the recipient to repay them, but because they expect to be helped in turn by third parties who have observed, or heard about, their generosity. Helping, on this view, is an investment in one's good name.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theory received early support from computer simulations. Dr Ilinca Klaasen, a mathematician at the Bucharest Institute for Complex Systems, modelled populations in which each individual carried an 'image score' that rose whenever it helped and fell whenever it refused. When individuals chose to help only those with good scores, cooperation could become established even among strangers. Klaasen's later work, however, revealed a complication. If refusing to help a person with a bad reputation itself lowers one's own score, then justified refusals are punished as harshly as selfish ones, and the system becomes unstable. Stable cooperation, she concluded, requires that observers judge not only what a person did but also whom they did it to.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This finding has an important implication: indirect reciprocity places considerable demands on the information available to a community. People must know not only who helped whom, but also the reputations of those involved at the time. It is perhaps no coincidence, then, that humans are such enthusiastic gossips. The anthropologist Kalani Onyango, who has spent many years among pastoralist communities in East Africa, estimates that a substantial share of everyday conversation concerns the behaviour of absent third parties, and that much of it is evaluative, praising or condemning the generosity of others. Onyango argues that gossip is not a trivial pastime but a mechanism for distributing the information on which cooperation depends. I find his argument broadly convincing, although it would be a mistake to suppose that all gossip is accurate; reputations can be damaged as easily by rumour as by real misconduct.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Laboratory experiments have provided further support. In studies run by the psychologist Sigrún Eriksdóttir at the Reykjavík Centre for Social Psychology, participants who knew their decisions would be revealed to future partners donated considerably more to others than participants whose choices remained private. Eriksdóttir also found that people who had built a good reputation were more likely to receive donations from those who had never interacted with them before. In a follow-up study, participants were allowed to pass on written comments about one another, and cooperation remained high even when only a minority of interactions could be directly observed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some of the most widely publicised findings in this area have proved less robust. Early studies reported that merely displaying a picture of a pair of eyes, for example beside an honesty box for coffee payments, increased the amount people contributed, as if the image triggered an unconscious sense of being watched. These results attracted enormous media attention. Subsequent attempts to replicate them, including a large project coordinated by Farid Hakimi at the Casablanca Laboratory of Behavioural Science, found that the effect was either very small or absent altogether. Hakimi suggests that the original studies, which typically involved small samples, may have produced false positives. The episode is a useful warning that striking findings deserve particular scrutiny before they are accepted, especially when they appear to confirm an attractive theory.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Today, reputation systems operate on a scale that would have been unimaginable to our ancestors. Online marketplaces depend on ratings that allow buyers to trust sellers they will never meet, and ride-sharing services rely on drivers and passengers evaluating one another. These systems are, in effect, deliberate engineering applications of indirect reciprocity. Their success is often cited as confirmation of the theory, but they also reveal its weaknesses. Ratings tend to cluster at the top of the scale, making genuine differences difficult to detect, and they can be manipulated by fake reviews.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, however, to conclude that the human concern for reputation is purely calculating. Many people behave generously even when they are certain that nobody will ever know, and some forms of kindness appear to be motivated by sympathy rather than by any expectation of return. Reputation may explain why such dispositions were favoured during our evolutionary history, but it does not follow that every act of helping is a disguised attempt to improve one's standing. The distinction between the evolutionary origins of a behaviour and the motives of the individual performing it is easily overlooked, and it deserves to be kept firmly in view.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: cooperative hunting in chimpanzees, wolves and killer whales
title: Hunting Together
subtitle: When predators join forces, are they truly cooperating or simply chasing the same prey at the same time?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Images of lions encircling a herd of buffalo, or of wolves running down an elk in deep snow, have long encouraged the belief that group hunting is a sophisticated cooperative enterprise. Predators that hunt together, it is often assumed, must coordinate their movements, adopt distinct roles and share the rewards of success. In recent years, however, field researchers have begun to question how much of this picture survives close examination. The answer appears to differ markedly between species, and the debate has shed light on a broader question: what exactly should count as cooperation?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for genuine coordination is strongest among chimpanzees in the Taï Forest of West Africa. Over three decades of observation, researchers have recorded hunts of red colobus monkeys in which individual chimpanzees appear to take on specialised roles. Some act as 'drivers', pushing the monkeys in a particular direction through the canopy; others serve as 'blockers', climbing trees to cut off escape routes; and an 'ambusher' may wait ahead of the fleeing prey. Dr Valentina Arbeláez of the Bogotá Institute of Primate Studies, who has analysed hundreds of these hunts, reports that experienced males tend to occupy the same role repeatedly and that learning the ambusher role may take up to twenty years. She also notes that hunters who participated in a successful chase receive larger shares of meat than bystanders, which, she argues, discourages individuals from waiting on the ground for others to do the work.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Strikingly, chimpanzees elsewhere hunt differently. In East African populations, where the forest canopy is lower and more broken, hunts are typically less organised, with individuals pursuing prey independently and success depending largely on numbers. Arbeláez attributes this contrast to habitat: in the tall, continuous canopy of Taï, a single chimpanzee has almost no chance of catching an agile monkey, whereas in more open forest the prey can more easily be cornered. The difference is a valuable reminder that the degree of cooperation in a species is not fixed but may vary with ecological circumstances.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Wolves present a more contested case. Lars Sundqvist, a wildlife biologist at the Norrland Wildlife Research Station, has used GPS collars to track packs hunting moose and deer. His analysis suggests that much of the apparent coordination in wolf hunts can be reproduced by two simple rules: each wolf moves towards the prey until it reaches a safe distance, and then moves away from other wolves. Computer simulations based on these rules generate encircling patterns very similar to those observed in the wild. Sundqvist concludes that the impression of a planned strategy may be misleading, and that wolves may be cooperating only in the limited sense that each benefits from the presence of others. Moreover, his data show that the amount of food each wolf obtains actually declines in packs larger than four, which suggests that large packs exist for reasons other than hunting efficiency, such as defending territory and carcasses against rival packs.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sundqvist's analysis is elegant, but I would argue that it proves less than it might appear to. That a pattern can be generated by simple rules does not show that the animals involved are actually following those rules; it shows only that complex reasoning is not strictly required. Detailed observations of individual wolves adjusting their positions in response to the movements of particular pack members are difficult to reconcile with the simplest version of his model. Nor does the model explain why some packs consistently succeed against large prey that neighbouring packs rarely attempt to tackle.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most remarkable example of coordinated hunting comes from the ocean. Killer whales in Antarctic waters have been filmed creating waves to wash seals off floating ice. Several whales swim side by side towards the floe, then dive simultaneously beneath it, producing a wave that tips the seal into the water. Nomvula Tshabalala of the Cape Marine Mammal Institute, who has documented more than a hundred such attacks, observes that the technique appears to be confined to a small number of family groups and is apparently passed on from older to younger animals. She describes it as a cultural tradition rather than an instinct. Notably, the whales sometimes release seals unharmed after capturing them, a behaviour whose purpose remains unknown.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these cases suggest that the question 'do predators cooperate?' is too crude to be useful. Cooperation in hunting ranges from mere aggregation, in which animals happen to pursue the same prey, through simple rules of thumb, to the role specialisation and cultural transmission seen in chimpanzees and killer whales. Placing each species somewhere on this continuum, rather than forcing it into one category or another, seems to me the most productive way forward. Lions, whose hunts were mentioned at the outset, have yet to be studied with comparable precision, and they may well occupy several points along it, depending on the prey and the terrain. It also cautions against treating human cooperation as uniquely complex simply because we have studied it most closely.
