area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: inequity aversion in monkeys and dogs and the evolutionary roots of fairness
title: A Sense of Injustice?
subtitle: Animals that reject unequal rewards have been hailed as proof that fairness has deep evolutionary roots, but the interpretation remains disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a now celebrated series of experiments, pairs of capuchin monkeys were trained to hand a small stone to a researcher in exchange for a piece of food. As long as both monkeys received the same reward, a slice of celery, they continued the exchange contentedly. But when one monkey began receiving a fig, a far more desirable food, while its partner continued to receive celery, the disadvantaged monkey often refused to take part, sometimes throwing the celery back at the experimenter. The procedure was simple enough to be repeated in many laboratories, and footage of an indignant monkey hurling food at a scientist has since been viewed by millions of people. The findings, first reported by the primatologist Dr Márta Kovács of the Budapest Primate Research Unit, were widely interpreted as evidence that monkeys possess a sense of fairness, and they were quickly adopted as a cornerstone of arguments about the evolution of morality.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Kovács herself has argued that such reactions, which researchers call inequity aversion, are likely to evolve in species that cooperate with non-relatives. If an individual consistently accepts a worse deal than its partners, it will be exploited; a tendency to protest, or to withdraw from partnerships that are persistently unequal, protects cooperators from being taken advantage of. Consistent with this idea, she and her colleagues have found the strongest responses in species that frequently cooperate, such as capuchins and chimpanzees, and weaker or absent responses in more solitary species such as orangutans.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The interpretation was challenged almost immediately. Critics noted that the monkeys might simply have been frustrated at seeing a better food that they could not have, regardless of what their partner received. In one variant of the experiment, figs were placed visibly nearby but given to no one, and some monkeys still refused celery. Others pointed out that the animals occasionally rejected celery even in early trials, before any figs had appeared, suggesting that their motivation varied considerably from day to day. Arjun Ramaswamy, a comparative psychologist at the Institute of Animal Cognition in Pune, argues that this 'frustration effect' accounts for much of the original result. In his view, what looks like a response to unfairness may be a response to disappointed expectations: a monkey that has seen figs simply no longer finds celery acceptable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Subsequent studies have produced a mixed picture. Some replications have confirmed that the reaction is stronger when a partner actually receives the better reward than when the food is merely visible, which supports Kovács's interpretation. Others have failed to find any reaction at all. The differences may reflect variation in experimental details, such as how long the animals had been trained or whether they could see each other clearly. It seems to me that the contradictory results have been reported too selectively by both sides, each emphasising the studies that support its position while passing quickly over those that do not.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Interest in the question has extended beyond primates. Hélène Delacroix, an animal behaviour specialist at the Lyon Institute of Comparative Ethology, has tested domestic dogs in a similar procedure, asking them to give a paw in exchange for a reward. Dogs that received nothing while a neighbouring dog was rewarded eventually stopped cooperating, but they did not react when both dogs were rewarded with foods of different quality. Delacroix concludes that dogs are sensitive to the presence or absence of a reward but not to its quality, and she suggests that this simpler form of inequity aversion may have been shaped by thousands of years of living alongside humans. This is a plausible hypothesis, although it would be difficult to test without comparable data from wolves raised in similar conditions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A crucial difference between animal and human responses concerns the advantaged individual. People frequently feel uncomfortable when they receive more than others and sometimes act to correct the imbalance, a reaction known as advantageous inequity aversion. Among non-human animals, evidence for this is extremely scarce. Monkeys receiving figs very rarely share them with a partner who has been given celery. In human experiments, by contrast, a substantial minority of participants who are handed an unfairly large share choose to give some of it back. Kovács has reported a few such cases in chimpanzees, but even she admits that they are too infrequent to support firm conclusions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, can be concluded? It would be premature to claim that capuchins share a human sense of justice, and the term 'fairness' is perhaps best avoided when describing their behaviour. Nonetheless, the research has made an important contribution by showing that the building blocks of human moral reactions, such as sensitivity to how one's rewards compare with those of others, are not unique to our species. The greater challenge now is to understand how these simple reactions were transformed, over the course of human evolution, into concern for others who are treated unfairly, even when we ourselves have nothing to gain or lose.

area: the evolution of cooperation in animals and humans
topic: cultural group selection, religion and institutions in large-scale human cooperation
title: Cooperation on a Grand Scale
subtitle: How did humans come to cooperate with millions of strangers? A controversial theory points to competition between cultures

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: No other animal cooperates on the scale that humans do. Ant colonies may contain millions of individuals, but they are families; human societies routinely involve millions of people who are unrelated, who will never meet, and who nevertheless pay taxes, observe traffic laws and contribute to collective projects whose benefits they may never personally enjoy. Kinship and reciprocity, the mechanisms that explain most cooperation in other species, operate effectively only in small groups where individuals know one another. Explaining how cooperation was extended to entire nations is therefore one of the central puzzles of the human sciences.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One influential answer is the theory of cultural group selection, developed most fully by the anthropologist Professor Chidi Okwuosa of the Enugu Centre for Human Evolutionary Studies. Okwuosa argues that humans, unlike other animals, transmit large amounts of behaviour through social learning, and that this allows groups to develop distinctive norms and institutions. Groups whose norms promote internal cooperation, such as rules about sharing, punishing cheats or defending the community, tend to outcompete groups whose norms do not, whether by winning conflicts, growing faster or being imitated by their neighbours. Over thousands of years, according to Okwuosa, this process of competition between cultures has gradually favoured norms that support cooperation on ever larger scales.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The theory has an obvious appeal, and historical evidence offers some support. Dr Eleni Lazaridis, a historian at the Thessaloniki Institute for Comparative History, has compiled data on more than two hundred pre-modern societies and found that those exposed to frequent warfare with neighbouring groups were more likely to develop complex institutions, such as formal councils and systems of taxation. Lazaridis is careful to note, however, that correlation does not establish cause: complex societies might have been more warlike rather than warfare producing complexity. She also observes that conquest typically spread institutions by force rather than by the voluntary imitation that some versions of the theory emphasise.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A particularly contentious strand of the debate concerns religion. Some researchers have proposed that belief in powerful, moralising gods, deities who observe human behaviour and punish wrongdoing, helped societies to grow by encouraging cooperation among strangers who shared the same faith. Samuel Whitcombe, a cognitive scientist at the Bristol Laboratory for the Study of Religion, has challenged this view using a large database of historical societies. His analysis indicates that moralising gods generally appeared after societies had already become large and complex, not before. If so, such beliefs cannot have been the cause of social expansion, though they may have helped to stabilise societies that had already grown. Supporters of the original hypothesis have responded that the written records on which Whitcombe relies tend to appear late, so that earlier beliefs may simply have gone unrecorded.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Both sides make reasonable points, and in my view the question cannot be settled with the evidence currently available. What the dispute does show is how difficult it is to establish the order of events in societies that left few written traces. Archaeological finds such as temples and ritual objects can show that religion was present, but they rarely reveal whether the gods worshipped were believed to care about human morality. Claims about the role of religion in the growth of early civilisations should therefore be presented with more caution than has sometimes been the case.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: More fundamental objections have come from evolutionary biologists. Lucía Ibarra of the Madrid Centre for Evolutionary Biology contends that the term 'group selection' causes confusion, since it is easily mistaken for the discredited idea that animals act 'for the good of the species'. She argues that the processes Okwuosa describes could equally be described as individuals copying successful neighbours, without any need to treat groups as units of selection. Ibarra's criticism is partly a matter of terminology, but it is not trivial: unclear language has repeatedly hindered progress in the study of cooperation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A different alternative is offered by Dariush Mirzaei, an economist at the Tehran Institute of Political Economy, who places the emphasis on markets and states rather than on competition between cultures. In his view, large-scale cooperation is sustained primarily by institutions such as courts, contracts and police forces, which make cheating costly for individuals regardless of their cultural values. Mirzaei points out that the same people who cooperate readily in a country with effective courts may behave quite differently when such institutions break down. He cites cases from several regions in which the collapse of central government was followed within months by a sharp rise in theft and a decline in trade between communities.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: These perspectives need not be mutually exclusive. Institutions such as courts did not appear from nowhere; they had to be invented, maintained and accepted, and cultural evolution offers a plausible account of how that happened. Equally, the norms emphasised by Okwuosa would be fragile without the enforcement that formal institutions provide. The most persuasive account of human cooperation is likely to combine cultural transmission, competition and institutional enforcement, rather than relying on any one of them alone.

subtitle: Cold-water corals were discovered almost by accident; deciding how to protect them is proving far more deliberate work

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the notion that reef-building corals could flourish in near-freezing water hundreds of metres beneath the surface would have struck marine biologists as improbable. Corals were associated with warm, shallow, sunlit seas, where they rely on symbiotic algae for much of their energy. Fishermen working the continental margins of the North Atlantic had nonetheless been hauling up fragments of a brittle white coral for generations, and when remotely operated vehicles began surveying these slopes systematically, they revealed reef structures stretching for several kilometres. The species responsible contain no algae at all. They feed instead on zooplankton and on organic particles swept past them by currents, which allows them to grow in permanent darkness. That such extensive habitats escaped scientific notice for so long is a sobering reminder of how little of the ocean floor has actually been seen.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first question researchers asked was how old these reefs might be. Ingrid Solbakken, a marine geologist at the Institute for Continental Margin Studies, has used radiocarbon dating on cores drilled through reef mounds and concludes that the living coral extends its branches by only a few millimetres a year. Some of the mounds she has sampled began forming shortly after the last ice age, roughly ten thousand years ago. On this evidence, Solbakken describes the reefs as effectively non-renewable: a structure flattened today would not regain its present form for many human lifetimes. Her phrasing has been criticised as alarmist, but it seems to me an accurate summary of what the dating shows, and policymakers would do well to take it literally.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The reefs are also strikingly rich in life. Surveys have recorded well over a thousand animal species living among the coral branches, from sponges and brittle stars to commercially valuable fish such as redfish. Kwabena Belinskaya, a benthic ecologist, urges caution in interpreting such figures. Most of the species found on reefs, he points out, also occur on the surrounding seabed, so the reefs may concentrate biodiversity rather than generate it. The distinction is a genuine one, yet I think it is easily overstated. Even if few species are confined to reefs, a habitat that gathers so many organisms into a small area provides shelter, feeding grounds and nursery sites that the open sediment around it cannot.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most immediate threat comes from bottom trawling. Heavy nets dragged across the seabed can reduce a reef to rubble in a single pass, and surveys off Norway and Ireland have documented broad scars where coral once stood. Representatives of the Coastal Fisheries Federation argue that recent closures of fishing grounds are excessive, since experienced skippers deliberately avoid reefs that would tear their gear. This argument has some force for large, well-mapped reefs, but it collapses for the many smaller patches that appear on no chart. A skipper cannot steer around a structure that nobody knows is there, and the scars recorded by underwater cameras suggest that avoidance has been far from universal.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Deciding which areas to protect depends partly on how reefs are connected to one another. Mariana Esquivel, a larval biologist, has reared coral larvae in the laboratory and found that they can swim upwards and survive for up to two months before settling. Combining these observations with models of ocean currents, she estimates that larvae released on one reef may colonise sites several hundred kilometres away. In her view, isolated protected areas are therefore of limited value; what is needed is a network of sites spaced closely enough for larvae to travel between them. The argument is persuasive, although it rests on laboratory behaviour that has yet to be confirmed in the open sea.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A slower but potentially more serious threat is ocean acidification. As seawater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes less saturated with aragonite, the mineral from which coral skeletons are built. Below a certain depth, known as the saturation horizon, water is corrosive to aragonite, and this horizon is gradually rising towards the surface. Projections by Haruto Nishimoto, an ocean modeller, indicate that a majority of known cold-water reefs could lie in corrosive water by the end of this century. Laboratory experiments suggest that living polyps can sometimes continue to build skeleton under such conditions. The weakness lies in the dead framework beneath them, which has no living tissue to protect it and may dissolve until the reef collapses under its own weight.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to conclude that, with acidification beyond the reach of local action, efforts to restrict fishing are futile. That conclusion is mistaken. Reefs that are already fragmented by trawling will be less able to withstand chemical stress, and the larval networks Esquivel describes cannot function if their stepping stones have been destroyed. Protecting reefs from physical damage will not make them immune to changing ocean chemistry, but it is the one measure that can be taken immediately, and it may determine which reefs survive long enough to benefit from any future reduction in emissions.

topic: whale falls and the communities they support
title: A Feast on the Abyssal Plain
subtitle: When a whale dies and sinks, it creates an oasis that may last for decades, and raises questions about how deep-sea life spreads

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some decades ago, the pilots of a research submersible exploring a basin off the Pacific coast of North America came across something they had not been sent to find: the skeleton of a large whale, lying on the sediment more than a kilometre down and coated in a whitish film of bacteria. Clams and snails clustered around the bones, and tiny worms grew from their surfaces. At the time, the deep seabed was generally pictured as a food-poor desert, sustained only by a thin drizzle of organic particles sinking from above. The skeleton suggested something different. A single carcass, it seemed, could deliver to one small patch of seabed the equivalent of thousands of years of ordinary food supply in a single event.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Biologists have since learned to recognise a broad sequence in the life of such a 'whale fall'. Leilani Kahananui, who has studied carcasses sunk deliberately at known depths, has used time-lapse cameras to document the first stage, in which mobile scavengers such as hagfish and sleeper sharks strip away the soft tissue. Depending on the size of the animal, this can take anything from a few months to two years. A second stage follows in which dense populations of worms and crustaceans exploit the organic matter that has enriched the surrounding sediment. Finally, bacteria begin to break down the oils stored inside the bones, releasing sulphide that supports communities of a kind otherwise associated with hydrothermal vents. This last stage may continue for fifty years or more.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most remarkable inhabitants of whale falls are bone-eating worms. They possess neither a mouth nor a gut; instead, they send root-like tissues into the skeleton and rely on bacteria living within those tissues to digest the fats and proteins locked inside. Kahananui was surprised to find these worms colonising her experimental carcasses within weeks of their arrival on the seabed. Since the nearest natural whale fall might lie many kilometres away, she infers that their larvae must be drifting through the deep water in enormous numbers, waiting for a chance encounter. That inference seems reasonable, although nobody has yet sampled the water column with sufficient intensity to confirm it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whale falls have also been proposed as a solution to a long-standing puzzle. Hydrothermal vents are separated by hundreds of kilometres, yet many vent animals appear on newly formed vents surprisingly quickly. If whale carcasses provide temporary islands of sulphide-rich habitat, they might act as stepping stones, allowing vent species to spread across otherwise inhospitable distances. Chidinma Eze, a deep-sea ecologist at the Lagos Institute of Ocean Sciences, considers the idea attractive but poorly supported. Of the hundreds of species recorded on whale falls, she notes, only a handful also live at vents. I share her doubts about the more ambitious versions of the hypothesis, but even a small number of shared species would be significant if those species were otherwise unable to disperse.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The history of whaling adds a sobering dimension. During the twentieth century, industrial fleets killed nearly three million large whales, reducing some populations by more than ninety per cent. Fewer whales inevitably means fewer carcasses reaching the seabed, and the distance between successive whale falls must have grown considerably. Bogdan Vasilescu, a palaeontologist, has argued that some species which depended on whale falls may therefore have disappeared before scientists ever had the opportunity to describe them. The suggestion is plausible, but it is, by its nature, almost impossible to test, and it should be treated as a warning rather than an established fact.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Vasilescu's own research suggests that whale-fall communities are far older than whaling, or indeed than whales themselves. He has described fossilised whale skeletons, some more than thirty million years old, surrounded by the shells of molluscs similar to those found on modern carcasses. More surprisingly, comparable assemblages have been identified on the bones of large marine reptiles that lived in the age of the dinosaurs. The fossil evidence is fragmentary, and critics point out that molluscs of this kind also gather around natural seeps, so their presence near a skeleton does not prove that they were feeding on it. If he is correct, the specialists of today descend from animals that exploited sunken carcasses long before the first whale entered the sea, switching from one kind of carcass to another as the ocean's large animals changed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: As some whale populations recover, the number of carcasses reaching the deep seabed should increase once more. In the meantime, a few coastal authorities have begun towing whales that strand on beaches out to sea and sinking them, partly to avoid the cost of disposal on land. This practice deserves wider adoption: it returns nutrients to the ecosystem in which the animal lived and provides scientists with valuable natural experiments. It is, however, no substitute for allowing whale populations to rebuild, since a handful of sunken carcasses near the coast cannot replicate the scattered supply that once covered entire ocean basins.

topic: explanations for deep-sea gigantism
title: Why Grow Large in the Dark?
subtitle: More than a century after giant deep-sea animals were first described, scientists still disagree about what makes them so big

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the creatures hauled up by the great oceanographic expeditions of the nineteenth century were some that seemed to belong to another world: isopods, relatives of the woodlouse, as long as a man's forearm; sea spiders whose legs spanned the width of a dinner plate; amphipods many times the size of their shoreline cousins. Since then, the list has grown to include squid with eyes the size of footballs and single-celled organisms several centimetres across. The tendency of some deep-sea animals to reach enormous proportions, known as deep-sea gigantism, has attracted explanations almost as varied as the animals themselves. What is striking is how little agreement has emerged after more than a century of speculation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest explanation links size to temperature. Tavita Sunderland, a comparative physiologist at the Southern Pacific Marine Laboratory, points out that in cold water, cells tend to grow larger and development proceeds more slowly, so that animals mature later and continue growing for longer. The same pattern is seen in polar seas, where many invertebrates are larger than their tropical relatives, and Sunderland regards deep-sea and polar gigantism as two expressions of a single physiological rule. The argument is elegant, but it struggles to explain why only certain groups grow large in the deep while countless others, living in exactly the same frigid water, do not.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A related hypothesis emphasises oxygen. Cold water dissolves more oxygen than warm water, and larger animals, which have relatively less body surface through which to absorb oxygen, may only be viable where supplies are plentiful. Experiments on shallow-water crustaceans reared at different oxygen levels have shown that the largest individuals are the first to suffer when supplies fall. Ignacio Barrientos, who compiled body-size measurements for nearly two thousand species of amphipod, found that maximum size rose with the oxygen content of the water in which each species lived. His data are impressive, yet they leave a puzzle: some of the largest deep-sea crustaceans have been collected from regions where oxygen is far from abundant, a fact that suggests oxygen sets an upper limit on size rather than driving animals towards it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third school of thought looks to food. The deep seabed receives only a fraction of the organic material produced at the surface, and much of it arrives unpredictably, in the form of dead fish or whales. Oksana Hrytsenko, a behavioural ecologist, argues that a large body is an advantage under such conditions: it allows an animal to travel long distances between scattered meals, to store substantial energy reserves and to survive extended periods without feeding. Giant isopods kept in aquariums have reportedly gone several years without eating. Of the explanations considered here, this seems to me the most persuasive for scavengers, though it says little about filter-feeders or predators.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Any account of gigantism must also confront an awkward fact. In many groups, including snails and bivalve molluscs, deep-sea species are on average smaller than their shallow-water relatives. Mehmet Karaduman, who has studied these molluscs for two decades, describes this as abyssal dwarfism and contends that it is at least as widespread as gigantism. He argues that scarce food favours small bodies in sedentary animals that feed on sediment, since they cannot move to find more, while favouring large bodies in mobile animals that can. This proposal has the considerable merit of explaining both trends with a single principle, and in my view it represents the most promising direction for future research.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some scientists question whether the phenomenon is as widespread as its reputation suggests. Researchers belonging to the Pacific Benthic Census Consortium point out that the trawls and nets used by early expeditions had wide meshes that retained large animals while allowing small ones to escape. Spectacular specimens were also more likely to be described, displayed and reported in the press. The consortium suggests that much of what passes for gigantism is an artefact of how the deep sea has been sampled. This is a valuable corrective, but it should not be pushed too far. Baited traps and cameras, which do not discriminate by size in the same way, have confirmed that certain scavenging amphipods genuinely are far larger than their shallow relatives.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate is not merely academic. If temperature and oxygen shape body size, then the warming of deep water and the expansion of zones with little oxygen, both of which are now being documented, might gradually favour smaller species and alter food webs in ways that are hard to foresee. Smaller animals generally have higher metabolic rates and shorter lives, so such a shift could change the speed at which energy and nutrients pass through deep-sea ecosystems. Some commentators have already predicted the decline of the deep sea's giants. Such forecasts are premature. Until researchers understand why gigantism appears in some groups and not others, predictions about how deep-sea body sizes will respond to a changing ocean amount to little more than guesswork.

topic: the functions of bioluminescence in the twilight zone
title: Signals in the Twilight
subtitle: Most animals of the open ocean's middle depths can make their own light. Working out why has proved surprisingly difficult

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has watched the wake of a ship at night will have seen the sea glow as plankton disturbed by the hull emit tiny flashes of light. That display, striking as it is, gives only a faint impression of what happens further down. In the open ocean between about two hundred metres and a kilometre below the surface, where sunlight fades to a dim blue twilight and then disappears altogether, the great majority of fish, squid, shrimp and jellyfish are able to produce light of their own. Measured by the number of species and individuals involved, bioluminescence may well be the most widespread form of communication on the planet. It is also, remarkably, one of the least understood, and the reasons for that ignorance are largely practical.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Studying behaviour in the dark presents an obvious paradox: to watch an animal, an observer needs light, and light changes what the animal does. The powerful white floodlights fitted to early submersibles caused many animals to flee or freeze, while specimens brought to the surface in nets usually arrived damaged or dead, their light organs exhausted. A breakthrough came when the engineer Ayelet Ben-Haim designed a camera system that used faint red illumination. Because most deep-sea animals are sensitive only to blue light, they appear to be unaware of red, and Ben-Haim's recordings captured displays that no human had previously witnessed. Her work demonstrated, perhaps more clearly than any theoretical argument could, how much earlier observations had been distorted by the act of observing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The function about which there is least dispute is camouflage. Seen from below, an animal swimming in the twilight zone forms a dark silhouette against the faint light filtering down from the surface, making it an easy target for predators with upward-looking eyes. Many species have rows of light organs along their undersides that emit a glow matching the light above, effectively erasing their outline. Ilse Brandsma, working with hatchetfish kept in darkened tanks, showed that the fish adjust the brightness of their glow within seconds when the intensity of overhead light is altered. Few findings in the field are as firmly established, and it is reasonable to treat this form of camouflage, known as counter-illumination, as the benchmark against which other proposed functions should be judged.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more surprising idea is that light can be a call for help. When attacked, some jellyfish produce spinning, pinwheel-like displays of blue light. According to Anjali Raghunathan, a sensory ecologist, the purpose is not to frighten the attacker but to attract a larger predator that may eat it, in the same way that a burglar alarm summons the police. To test this, her team deployed a ring of blue lights programmed to imitate a distressed jellyfish, and within hours a large squid approached the device. The result is intriguing, but a single encounter cannot carry the weight that has sometimes been placed on it, and the claim that such displays regularly save the animals that produce them has yet to be demonstrated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Light also appears to play a role in finding a mate. Tomasz Wierzbicki, who has catalogued the arrangement of light organs in more than two hundred species of lanternfish, found that each species possesses a distinctive pattern, and that in many species males and females differ. He argues that these patterns allow individuals to recognise suitable partners in darkness, much as birds use plumage. The argument is plausible, yet I am not entirely convinced by it. Differences between species could equally arise because each has adapted its camouflage to slightly different depths and light conditions, and a pattern that differs between the sexes is not proof that it is being used as a signal.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Predators, too, exploit light. Several species of deep-sea anglerfish dangle glowing lures in front of their jaws, drawing curious prey within reach. More ingenious still are certain dragonfish, which possess light organs below their eyes that emit red light. Since their prey cannot perceive red, the dragonfish can illuminate potential victims without being detected, rather as a hunter might use a telescopic sight. Ben-Haim's camera, in other words, was not entirely original: evolution had arrived at the same solution millions of years earlier. That predators and prey have both shaped their use of light around the limitations of each other's vision is, to my mind, the most compelling illustration of how central light has become to life in the deep.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These discoveries have acquired new practical significance. Proposals to mine minerals from the deep seabed would generate clouds of sediment that could drift for many kilometres through midwater, and artificial lighting from mining equipment may add further disruption. If bioluminescence is essential to camouflage, defence and reproduction, such disturbances could affect animals far beyond the immediate mining area. Environmental assessments rarely consider this possibility. They ought to, and the gaps in our understanding of what light actually does for deep-sea animals should be treated as a reason for caution rather than as permission to proceed.

topic: proposals to harvest mesopelagic (twilight zone) fish
title: The Last Untapped Fishery?
subtitle: The ocean's twilight zone may hold more fish than the rest of the sea combined. Whether they should be caught is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each evening, as the light fades, vast numbers of small fish, shrimp and squid rise from depths of several hundred metres to feed in the productive surface waters, returning to the darkness before dawn. This daily migration, repeated throughout the world's oceans, is thought to be the largest regular movement of animals on the planet. Most of the travellers belong to the mesopelagic, or twilight, zone, and the most abundant among them are lanternfish, few of which grow longer than a finger. Until recently they attracted little interest outside academic circles. That has changed, because a growing body of evidence suggests that the twilight zone may contain more fish than the rest of the ocean put together, and some in the fishing industry have begun to see it as one of the last great untapped resources.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Estimates of how many fish live there have varied dramatically. Early figures, based on the catches of research nets towed through the twilight zone, put the total at around one billion tonnes. In the past two decades, however, acoustic surveys, which measure the echoes returned from sound pulses sent down from ships, have produced far larger numbers. Nkosana Dlamini, a fisheries acoustician at the Benguela Ocean Institute, has argued that the true biomass may be ten times higher than the net-based estimate. Lanternfish, he notes, have sensitive eyes and good hearing, and appear to detect and avoid approaching nets, so that net samples capture only a small proportion of the fish actually present.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts these higher figures. Lucía Etxeberria, a marine biologist, points out that acoustic methods depend on assumptions about how strongly each type of animal reflects sound. Many lanternfish possess gas-filled swim bladders that produce particularly strong echoes, and some jellyfish-like organisms with small gas floats do the same, so an echo cannot always be attributed with confidence to a fish of known size. In her view, the acoustic estimates may substantially overstate the quantity of fish. What is striking about this exchange is that both sides accept that the uncertainty spans roughly a factor of ten. A resource whose size cannot be estimated more precisely than that is hardly one on which to build an industry.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Advocates of harvesting nonetheless argue that the numbers are on their side. A report by Meridian Marine Resources, a fisheries consultancy, contends that even if only a small fraction of the twilight zone's fish were caught each year, the catch could supply a large share of the fishmeal and fish oil used to feed farmed salmon and shrimp. This, the report suggests, would ease pressure on overexploited coastal species such as anchovies, which are currently ground up for feed in enormous quantities. The proposal is presented as an environmental benefit as much as a commercial one, but its central claim, that harvesting would be sustainable, depends entirely on the larger of the disputed biomass figures being correct.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also practical obstacles. Kiri Te Awa, a resource economist, observes that lanternfish are small, oily and spoil rapidly once caught, and that their bodies contain waxy compounds that make them unsuitable for direct human consumption. Several national fleets experimented with twilight-zone fishing in the late twentieth century and abandoned the effort, largely because processing the catch cost more than it earned. Te Awa doubts that this situation will change soon. I am less confident than she is. Demand for aquaculture feed is rising steeply, and technologies for processing small fish at sea have improved considerably, so the economics that defeated earlier attempts may not hold for long.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even if harvesting became profitable, it would carry a cost that does not appear in any balance sheet. Farhad Rezaei, a biogeochemist, has studied how migrating animals transport carbon. Fish that feed near the surface at night digest their food and release carbon-rich waste and carbon dioxide at depth during the day, effectively moving carbon out of contact with the atmosphere. Rezaei estimates that this process may account for between a tenth and a quarter of the carbon carried into the deep ocean by biological activity. Removing large numbers of migrating fish would weaken this transport, and the consequences for the climate would be borne by everyone, not merely by those who profit from the catch.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The twilight zone also supports much of the ocean's larger wildlife. Tuna, swordfish, seabirds, dolphins and several species of whale feed heavily on lanternfish, and a decline in their prey could affect populations far beyond the zone itself. Most twilight-zone waters lie on the high seas, beyond national jurisdiction, where fisheries regulation has historically been weak. For once, however, regulators have an opportunity rarely granted to them: the chance to set rules for a fishery before it exists rather than after it has collapsed. That opportunity should not be wasted, and until the size and ecological role of twilight-zone fish are far better understood, large-scale harvesting ought not to be permitted.

topic: recolonisation of hydrothermal vents after volcanic eruptions
title: Life After Lava
subtitle: When an undersea eruption wiped out a field of hydrothermal vents, scientists were given a rare chance to watch life return

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the spring of an otherwise unremarkable year, instruments on a section of the East Pacific Rise recorded a swarm of small earthquakes. When a research vessel arrived several weeks later, its cameras revealed that a volcanic eruption had buried an entire field of hydrothermal vents beneath fresh black lava. The tubeworms, mussels and crabs that had crowded around the hot, mineral-rich springs only months before had vanished. For the biologists involved, the loss was also an opportunity. Cameras and sensors installed by the Ridge Observatory Network, a consortium of research institutions, had documented the community in detail before the eruption, so that researchers could now observe how life returns to a site where it has been completely eliminated. Such natural experiments are rare, and the results have challenged several long-held assumptions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first return visit, about a year after the eruption, found that new vents had already opened in the lava and that their surfaces were coated with thick mats of bacteria. Émilie Garnier, who led the survey, was more surprised by what came next. Among the earliest animals to arrive was a small snail that had not been recorded at the site before the eruption; its nearest known population lived more than three hundred kilometres away. Within three years, giant tubeworms had formed dense thickets, growing at rates that make them among the fastest-growing invertebrates known. Garnier concluded that the pioneers of a new vent are not necessarily the species that lived there previously, but whichever larvae happen to arrive first.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How larvae travel such distances remains contentious. Valentina Rossetti, a physical oceanographer, has combined current measurements with computer models to track particles released from vents. Her simulations suggest that larvae rising a few hundred metres above the ridge can be captured by large swirling eddies, which carry them along the ridge for months before releasing them. Some vent larvae feed on plankton as they drift and could survive long enough to complete such journeys. Others carry a supply of yolk that allows them to go without feeding for weeks, and slow their metabolism in the cold water to make that supply last. If Rossetti is right, the water above the ridge functions less as a barrier than as a highway, and the isolation of individual vent fields has been considerably exaggerated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Abebe Farrugia, a benthic ecologist, takes a more cautious view. In his own surveys, most new arrivals at disturbed vents belonged to species found at small vents that had survived the eruption only a few kilometres away, and he maintains that the majority of larvae settle close to the place where they were produced. Long-distance colonists, he argues, are the spectacular exceptions rather than the rule. Both positions may be correct for different species, since larvae vary greatly in how long they can survive in the water. Nonetheless, Farrugia's conclusion rests on surveys confined to a relatively small area, and an approach that does not look far is unlikely to detect arrivals from far away.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Genetic evidence offers an independent test. Seo-yeon Perrault, a population geneticist, compared the DNA of mussels and tubeworms collected from dozens of vent fields. Along continuous stretches of ridge, populations of the same species were almost genetically identical, which implies that individuals move between them frequently. Where the ridge is broken by major fracture zones, however, populations on either side were clearly distinct, suggesting that such features obstruct the movement of larvae. Perrault's results therefore support neither extreme. They indicate that vent animals are well connected over large distances, but only along particular routes, and that the geography of the seafloor shapes those routes in ways that are still poorly mapped.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These questions have acquired commercial importance. Vent fields deposit mineral-rich crusts containing copper, zinc and gold, and several companies have expressed interest in mining them. Proponents argue that mining should concentrate on inactive vents, where the springs have ceased to flow, and that vent communities in any case recover quickly from eruptions. The Ridge Observatory Network rejects both claims. Inactive vents, its members point out, support their own distinctive animals, and recovery after an eruption depends on the survival of nearby populations to supply larvae. Mining, unlike an eruption, removes the seafloor structure itself. I find the network's argument convincing: comparing a natural disturbance to which vent life has adapted with an industrial one to which it has not is misleading.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The return of life to buried vents is a striking demonstration of resilience, but it is resilience of a conditional kind. It depends on a network of populations, linked by currents along particular pathways, remaining intact enough to provide colonists. Remove too many links in that network and the recovery observed on the East Pacific Rise might not be repeated elsewhere. Moreover, the rapid recovery documented so far concerns a handful of conspicuous species; for most of the smaller animals living at vents, scientists simply do not know how quickly, or whether, they return.

topic: marine snow and the biological carbon pump
title: The Slow Snowfall
subtitle: A constant drift of particles carries carbon from the ocean surface to the deep. Measuring it, let alone improving it, is proving far from simple

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Below the sunlit surface layer of the ocean, a continuous shower of pale particles drifts slowly downwards. Oceanographers call it marine snow. Each flake is an aggregate of dead and dying plankton, the faecal pellets of small animals, grains of mineral and the sticky mucus that binds them together, and most are no more than a few millimetres across. A particle may take several weeks to reach the seabed four kilometres below. Marine snow is the principal source of food for much of the deep-sea community, but it matters well beyond the deep. By carrying carbon fixed by plankton away from the surface, it forms the core of what is known as the biological carbon pump, which is estimated to export between five and twelve billion tonnes of carbon from surface waters every year. Only around one per cent of that carbon, however, is eventually buried in seabed sediments.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Measuring this flux has proved surprisingly difficult. Since the 1970s, the standard tool has been the sediment trap, a funnel-shaped container moored at a fixed depth that collects whatever falls into it. Traps have yielded most of what is known about the pump, but they suffer from well-documented biases. Small swimming animals enter them and are counted as sinking material, while currents flowing across the opening can carry particles past the funnel before they settle. Matías Quiroga, an oceanographer at the Humboldt Institute of Marine Science, developed traps that float freely at a set depth and drift with the surrounding water, reducing the effect of currents. In side-by-side deployments, his drifting traps recorded fluxes that differed from those of moored traps by as much as fifty per cent.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cameras offer a complementary approach. Aigerim Seitkali, a marine optics specialist, has lowered camera systems through the water column to photograph particles where they are, without disturbing them. Analysing several million images, her team found that large aggregates, more than half a millimetre across, were far more common in deep water than trap studies had implied. They also found that sinking speeds varied enormously, from a few metres to several hundred metres per day. Size alone proved a poor guide: many of the largest aggregates were loose and porous, and sank more slowly than compact faecal pellets a fraction of their size.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever the method, measurements agree that most marine snow never reaches the deep seabed. The greater part of the organic matter leaving the surface is consumed or broken down within the upper five hundred metres. Bacteria colonise falling particles and digest them, and zooplankton graze on them. Scientists working with the Southern Ocean Flux Programme have argued that zooplankton play a further, less obvious role: by feeding on large aggregates, they break them into smaller fragments that sink more slowly and are therefore more likely to be consumed before reaching depth. According to the programme's estimates, fragmentation of this kind may account for as much as half of the loss of sinking material in some regions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why some particles survive the journey while others do not is a matter of lively dispute. Renata Vasconcelos, a biogeochemist, has drawn attention to a close relationship, observed in deep traps around the world, between the quantity of organic carbon arriving and the quantity of minerals such as chalk, silica and wind-blown dust. She argues that these minerals act as ballast, making particles denser so that they sink faster and spend less time exposed to consumers. Critics respond that the relationship could equally run in the opposite direction, with sticky organic matter gathering up mineral grains as it falls. The data are consistent with both interpretations, and the question of which is cause and which effect remains, in my view, genuinely open.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The pump has attracted interest from those who hope to enhance it deliberately. In many parts of the ocean, the growth of plankton is limited by a shortage of iron, and over a dozen experiments have added dissolved iron to patches of sea to stimulate blooms. Blooms duly appeared, but in most cases little additional carbon could be detected sinking to depth. Eero Kivimäki, an advocate of the technique, attributes this to the small scale and brief duration of the trials and calls for larger experiments. I am not persuaded. The weak link in the pump appears to lie not in the production of organic matter at the surface but in its rapid consumption on the way down, and adding iron does nothing to address that.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the pump is likely to change without deliberate intervention. As the surface ocean warms, it becomes more strongly layered, which reduces the supply of nutrients from deeper water and tends to favour smaller species of plankton. Smaller cells produce smaller, slower-sinking particles, so a warmer ocean may export less carbon to depth, at precisely the moment when that service is most needed. Predictions of this kind remain uncertain, but they are a powerful argument for improving measurement of the pump before attempting to manipulate it.

topic: mining polymetallic nodules on the abyssal plain
title: Metals from the Abyss
subtitle: The seabed holds vast reserves of metals needed for clean energy. The question is what would be lost in collecting them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Scattered across the abyssal plains of the central Pacific, four or five kilometres below the surface, lie trillions of dark, potato-sized lumps known as polymetallic nodules. Each began as a small object on the seabed, perhaps a fragment of shell or a shark's tooth, around which metals dissolved in seawater gradually precipitated in concentric layers. The process is extraordinarily slow: a nodule grows by only a few millimetres every million years. The result, however, is a deposit of remarkable richness, containing manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper, metals needed in large quantities for the batteries of electric vehicles and the storage of renewable energy. For a growing number of companies, the nodules represent the most important untapped source of these metals on the planet.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The commercial case is put most forcefully by Pelagos Metals, one of several firms seeking permission to begin collection. Its executives point out that mining nickel and cobalt on land frequently involves clearing tropical forest, displacing communities and producing large volumes of toxic waste. Nodules, by contrast, lie loose on the surface of the seabed and can be gathered by robotic collectors without drilling or blasting, in a region where no people live. Opponents of deep-sea mining have sometimes dismissed this argument as mere public relations. That is a mistake: the harms of mining on land are real and well documented, and any honest assessment of seabed mining must weigh them against its alternatives.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that the nodules are not simply lying on the seabed; they are part of it. Nguyen Thi Lan, a deep-sea biologist at the Institute of Pacific Benthic Ecology, notes that the abyssal plain is largely covered by soft mud, so that hard surfaces are scarce. The nodules provide almost the only places where sponges, soft corals, anemones and other animals can attach themselves. In her surveys, more than half of the larger animal species recorded depended on nodules in this way. Because nodules take millions of years to form, their removal amounts to the elimination of that habitat on any timescale relevant to human beings. Nguyen also points out that roughly nine out of ten specimens collected in a recent survey belonged to species new to science.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evidence on how the seabed recovers comes largely from small experiments. In the late 1980s, researchers ploughed a section of seabed off the coast of South America to simulate the effects of mining. Anneliese Vogt, a marine ecologist, led a return expedition to the site more than a quarter of a century later. The plough tracks, she reported, looked almost as fresh as on the day they were made. Many groups of animals, particularly those that filter food from the water, had not returned, and microbial activity in the disturbed sediment remained well below that of undisturbed areas nearby. If this is the pace of recovery from a disturbance far smaller than commercial mining would cause, the damage should be regarded as permanent for all practical purposes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The effects would not be confined to the mined area itself. Collectors moving across the seabed stir up clouds of fine sediment, which may drift for considerable distances before settling and smothering animals that feed by filtering water. Further plumes would be created when ships at the surface discharge the water and fine particles separated from the nodules. Mining companies tend to describe the footprint of their operations in terms of the area directly collected. This is misleading, since the area affected by settling sediment could prove several times larger, and its boundaries are almost impossible to predict in advance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nor is the argument that seabed metals are indispensable as straightforward as it appears. Imran Qureshi, a materials economist, observes that battery manufacturers are already shifting towards designs that use little or no cobalt or nickel, partly because of the high cost and ethical concerns associated with those metals. Recycling of batteries, he adds, is expanding rapidly. In his view, forecasts of demand on which the case for seabed mining rests are likely to prove exaggerated. I would add a qualification: recycling cannot meet demand while the total quantity of metal in use is still growing, so some new supply will be needed for decades. But the claim that the energy transition depends on the seabed is considerably overstated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Responsibility for regulating mining in international waters rests with a single intergovernmental authority, which has been charged both with enabling the exploitation of seabed minerals and with protecting the marine environment from harm. These two duties sit uneasily together, and the authority has come under pressure to finalise rules that would allow commercial collection to begin. Given how little is known about the species of the abyssal plain, and how slowly the seabed recovers, it would be wiser to delay mining until scientists can say with some confidence what would be lost.

topic: the backlog of undescribed deep-sea species and new identification methods
title: Nameless in the Deep
subtitle: Most of the animals living on the deep seabed have never been formally described. Can technology close the gap before it is too late?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the basement of a natural history museum on the Mediterranean coast, rows of glass jars line metal shelves from floor to ceiling. Each contains animals collected from the deep sea: worms, crustaceans, sea cucumbers and fish, preserved in alcohol and labelled with little more than the name of the ship, the date and the depth at which they were caught. Some were gathered over half a century ago. Eleni Papadakis, the museum's curator of marine invertebrates, estimates that the collection contains several thousand species that have never been formally described, and that at the rate her small team can work, describing them all would take several hundred years. Her museum is not unusual. Similar backlogs exist in collections around the world.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the problem is difficult to exaggerate. Some biologists have suggested that more than ninety per cent of the species living on the deep seabed remain unnamed. Describing a new species is laborious: a specialist must examine specimens in detail, compare them with every closely related species already known, prepare illustrations and publish a formal account, a process that can take months for a single animal. Meanwhile, the number of people trained to do this work is falling. Retiring taxonomists are frequently not replaced, and young scientists are drawn towards fields that attract more funding and more prestigious publications. It is tempting to blame the shortage on money alone, but the deeper problem is that the classification of organisms has come to be regarded as old-fashioned, a service activity rather than a science in its own right.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One proposed solution is to let genes do much of the work. Juan Pablo Ocampo, a molecular ecologist, uses a technique known as DNA barcoding, in which a short, standard section of an organism's genetic code is sequenced and compared with those of other specimens. Specimens whose sequences differ by less than a set threshold are grouped together as probable members of the same species. Ocampo's laboratory can process thousands of specimens a year in this way, and he argues that the genetic groups can be used immediately for ecological studies, with formal names attached later, as and when specialists are available to provide them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Zsófia Kertész, a taxonomist with forty years' experience of deep-sea crustaceans, regards this approach with considerable suspicion. A genetic cluster, she argues, tells us nothing about what an animal looks like, how it lives or what it eats. Moreover, the thresholds used to separate clusters are partly arbitrary: set them slightly differently and one species becomes two, or two become one. She warns of a future in which lists of genetic codes stand in for knowledge of real organisms. These concerns are legitimate, but I think Kertész underestimates how much barcoding can contribute. A provisional genetic grouping is far more useful than a jar of unsorted animals, and it can guide specialists towards the specimens most in need of their attention.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second technological shortcut relies on images rather than genes. Remotely operated vehicles now return millions of photographs and hours of video from the deep seabed, far more than any human could examine. A single dive can generate tens of thousands of images, most of which are never looked at by a specialist. Researchers in the Abyssal Imaging Collaborative have trained computer programs to recognise animals in these images, and the best programs can identify common species with an accuracy rivalling that of experts. Their performance declines sharply, however, for animals that appear only rarely, since there are too few examples from which the programs can learn. This creates an awkward paradox, because it is precisely the rare and unfamiliar animals that are of greatest interest to science and conservation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The backlog has acquired particular urgency because of proposals to mine the deep seabed. Before mining can begin, contractors are expected to survey the animals living in the areas concerned, so that the effects of disturbance can later be measured. Tendai Moyo, an adviser on environmental regulation, points out that these surveys cannot wait for formal names. At present, however, each contractor tends to label unnamed animals in its own way, so that a sea cucumber known as 'species 12' in one survey may be 'morphotype C' in another, and results cannot be compared. Moyo proposes a shared catalogue of provisional names and reference images. This is an eminently sensible suggestion, and it is remarkable that nothing of the kind is yet in place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these approaches will eliminate the need for trained specialists. Barcodes must eventually be linked to physical specimens, image-recognition programs must be trained on images that experts have identified, and provisional catalogues require someone to decide what counts as a distinct form. Technology can make taxonomists far more productive, but it cannot replace them. Unless more are trained, many deep-sea species will disappear, whether through mining, warming or other pressures, before anyone has recorded that they existed.

topic: underwater noise and deep-diving beaked whales
title: A Noisy Silence
subtitle: Sound travels far in the sea, and human activity is filling it with noise. For the ocean's deepest-diving mammals, the consequences can be fatal

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over two days in the spring of an otherwise ordinary year, more than a dozen beaked whales stranded on beaches along a chain of islands in the Atlantic. Several were dead when they were found; others died despite attempts to return them to the water. Strandings of whales are not in themselves unusual, but beaked whales are among the least frequently encountered large animals on Earth. They are the most extreme divers of all mammals, regularly descending more than a kilometre to hunt squid and remaining submerged for over an hour, occasionally for more than two. They spend so little time at the surface that some species are known only from a handful of dead specimens. That so many should come ashore together demanded an explanation, and investigators soon learned that naval vessels had been using powerful sonar nearby during an exercise.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first clues came from the bodies themselves. Catalina Ferreyra, a veterinary pathologist, conducted detailed examinations of several of the stranded animals and found bleeding around the ears and brain, together with gas bubbles in the liver and other organs. These injuries closely resembled those of human divers suffering from decompression sickness, a condition caused when gas dissolved in the blood forms bubbles as a diver rises too quickly. The finding was unexpected. Deep-diving mammals had long been assumed to be immune to the condition, since they possess physiological adaptations, including the ability to collapse their lungs at depth, that limit the amount of gas absorbed by their tissues.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How could sound cause such injuries? Putu Wirawan, a behavioural ecologist, has attached suction-cup tags to beaked whales that record their movements and the sounds around them. In controlled experiments, whales exposed to sonar signals at volumes far below those previously considered harmful stopped making the clicks they use to locate prey, swam silently away from the source and, in some cases, rose towards the surface far faster than normal. Wirawan suggests that the whales perceive sonar much as they would the calls of killer whales, their principal predator, and that their flight disrupts the carefully controlled dive patterns that ordinarily protect them. This account has the great merit of linking behaviour to the injuries Ferreyra observed, and if it is correct, the noise levels currently regarded as safe are set far too high.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Navies, which regard sonar as essential for detecting submarines, have adopted a range of precautions. According to the Naval Acoustics Advisory Panel, ships now post lookouts during exercises and reduce or suspend transmissions when marine mammals are seen nearby, and they increase the power of sonar gradually so that animals have time to move away. The panel concludes that, with these measures in place, the risk to whales is low. The difficulty is obvious. A safeguard that depends on observers sighting whales is poorly suited to animals that surface briefly, are inconspicuous when they do, and spend most of their lives far below. I find the panel's confidence difficult to share.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sonar is dramatic, but it is intermittent and confined to particular areas. The noise of commercial shipping, by contrast, is constant and almost everywhere. Ruairí Ó Briain, an acoustic oceanographer, points out that the low-frequency sound generated by large ships travels across entire ocean basins and overlaps with the frequencies used by many whales to communicate. When shipping traffic in one busy bay was halted for several days, he and his colleagues found that levels of stress hormones in the resident whales fell noticeably. Because shipping noise affects so many species so continuously, it may well prove a greater threat overall than the occasional sonar exercise, even though it rarely leaves dead whales on beaches.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The engineer Mariam Haddad has investigated how such noise might be reduced. Most underwater noise from ships, she has found, is produced by cavitation, the formation and collapse of tiny bubbles around a rotating propeller. Cavitation increases sharply with speed, so that a modest reduction in speed can produce a disproportionate fall in noise while also lowering fuel consumption. Improved propeller designs can achieve further reductions. This is a rare instance in which environmental and commercial interests point in the same direction. Even so, it would be naive to expect the industry to act on its own: voluntary slowdown schemes have so far attracted only limited participation, and some form of regulation will almost certainly be required.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Noise has one great advantage over most other forms of pollution. Unlike chemical contaminants, which may persist in the environment for decades, sound disappears the moment its source is switched off. The ocean could, in principle, become quieter almost overnight. Restricting sonar exercises in the habitats where beaked whales are known to live, and requiring ships to slow down in important feeding and breeding areas, would not solve every problem, but they are measures whose benefits would be felt immediately.

topic: measuring insect decline: monitoring data, baselines and their limits
title: Counting the Vanishing
subtitle: How scientists are trying to establish whether, and how fast, the world's insects are disappearing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone old enough to have driven long distances in the 1970s or 1980s is likely to remember stopping to scrub the remains of insects from the car windscreen. Today, many drivers report that their windscreens stay almost clean even after a summer journey through the countryside. This so-called windscreen phenomenon has been repeated so often in newspapers and online that it has acquired the status of common knowledge. As evidence, of course, it is almost worthless: cars have become more aerodynamic, roads have changed, and memory is notoriously selective. Yet it would be a mistake to dismiss the anecdote entirely, because the systematic data that have emerged over the past decade suggest that the drivers were noticing something real.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study that transformed the debate came not from a university but from a society of amateur naturalists. For almost three decades, its members had set tent-like Malaise traps in nature reserves, collecting every flying insect that blundered into them and weighing the catch. When the records were finally analysed, they revealed a fall in the total biomass of flying insects of more than 75 per cent. Liesbeth Kraaijeveld, a statistician at the Lowlands Institute for Ecology who led the reanalysis, tested whether changes in weather, vegetation or land use at the trapping sites could account for the decline. None of them could. What made the result so alarming was its setting: these were protected areas, where insects might have been expected to fare comparatively well.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepted the wider conclusions drawn from such findings. Rafael Quintanilla, an ecologist at the Iberian Biodiversity Observatory, pointed out that the trapping sites had not been selected at random; many had been chosen precisely because they were rich in insects at the start, so some decline was statistically likely. He also noted that almost all long-term insect records come from western Europe and North America, while the tropics, which hold the majority of insect species, have barely been surveyed. On this basis, Quintanilla argued, headlines warning of a global 'insect apocalypse' went far beyond the evidence. His criticism of the headlines is fair, but his argument contains a weakness of its own. The absence of data from much of the world is not evidence that insects there are thriving; it is simply an absence of data.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more nuanced picture emerged when a team under Sunniva Haugland at the Bergen Centre for Ecological Synthesis combined more than 160 separate monitoring studies. Their analysis suggested that land-dwelling insects had declined by roughly nine per cent per decade on average, a rate lower than the most dramatic estimates but still substantial when compounded over a century. Surprisingly, insects that spend part of their lives in fresh water showed the opposite trend, increasing in many regions. Haugland attributes this partly to legislation that has improved water quality in rivers and lakes since the 1970s. The variation between habitats and regions is more instructive than any single global figure, because it hints at which pressures matter and which interventions work.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even the longest records, however, may understate what has been lost. Systematic monitoring generally began after the great intensification of agriculture in the mid-twentieth century, when hedgerows were removed, wetlands drained and synthetic pesticides introduced on a vast scale. Researchers therefore risk treating an already impoverished state as the natural baseline. To look further back, Kofi Adjei-Boateng of the Accra School of Natural History has turned to museum collections, comparing the abundance of species in drawers of specimens gathered over 150 years. The approach is ingenious, but it has obvious limitations, since collectors tended to pursue rare or beautiful specimens and largely ignored the common species that make up most insect biomass.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That distinction between rarity and abundance lies at the heart of a further disagreement. Conservation has traditionally focused on species threatened with extinction, and the number of species recorded at a site can remain stable even while the total number of individuals collapses. For ecosystem functions such as pollination, pest control and the feeding of birds, however, it is the sheer quantity of insects that counts, and a handful of common species often perform most of the work. Protecting rare insects remains worthwhile, but policies that measure success solely by preventing extinctions will miss the more widespread loss of ordinary insects on which farming and wildlife depend.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The obvious response to these uncertainties is better monitoring, and here volunteers are once again proving indispensable. Schemes in which members of the public count insects on standard routes or photograph visitors to flowers are now generating data across large areas at minimal cost, although their value depends on consistent methods being followed year after year. What should not happen is that the gaps in knowledge become an excuse for inaction. The causes most often blamed for insect decline, namely habitat loss, pesticides, light pollution and climate change, are already known to harm insects individually, and measures to address them are justified regardless of the precise rate at which populations are falling.
