topic: neonicotinoid insecticides and sublethal harm to bees
title: Doses and Doubts
subtitle: The long argument over whether a widely used class of insecticides is harming the bees on which farmers depend

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When regulators restricted the outdoor use of three neonicotinoid insecticides, environmental campaigners hailed the decision as a victory for science over commercial interest. Manufacturers, by contrast, complained that it rested on laboratory experiments bearing little relation to conditions in real fields. Both camps overstated their position. The evidence was neither as conclusive as campaigners claimed nor as flimsy as the industry suggested, and the episode arguably reveals more about the difficulty of detecting subtle forms of harm than about the chemicals themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Neonicotinoids are systemic: rather than remaining on the surface of a plant, they are absorbed into its tissues and carried to every part, including the pollen and nectar. Introduced in the 1990s, they were typically applied as a coating on seeds, so that the growing crop was protected from within. This was regarded at the time as a considerable advance, since it appeared to remove the need to spray insecticide indiscriminately across whole fields. The concentrations that reach nectar are tiny, measured in parts per billion, and they rarely kill bees outright. For this reason, early safety assessments, which focused on how much of a substance is needed to kill an insect, concluded that the risk was low.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That conclusion began to unravel when researchers turned their attention to effects short of death. Ewa Szczepańska, of the Carpathian Apiculture Institute, fitted bumblebees with miniature radio tags and released them near colonies that had been given nectar containing field-level doses. Exposed foragers took longer to return from each trip, a larger proportion never returned at all, and the colonies went on to rear markedly fewer new queens, the individuals on which the next generation depends. In Szczepańska's interpretation, the chemicals do not poison colonies so much as erode them, through the accumulated effect of small impairments to the navigation and learning of individual bees.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tadashi Morikawa, an entomologist at the Kansai Agricultural Research Station, has been among the most prominent sceptics. He points out that many laboratory studies used doses higher than bees would normally encounter, and that captive insects were given no alternative food. In a real landscape, he argues, foragers visit a variety of flowers, most of them untreated, so that their intake of the chemical is diluted. Large field trials conducted in several countries produced results that Morikawa describes as inconsistent: harm was detected in some locations and not in others. He therefore concludes that the evidence is too contradictory to justify a blanket prohibition. Yet inconsistency is not the same as the absence of an effect. Differing outcomes are exactly what one would expect if the impact of a pesticide depends on local conditions such as weather, disease and the availability of other forage.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection to the original assessments concerns the choice of test species. Chidinma Kolstad, who coordinates the West African Pollinator Network, notes that safety testing has relied overwhelmingly on the honeybee, a species whose colonies may contain tens of thousands of workers and can absorb the loss of many foragers without collapsing. Most of the world's twenty thousand bee species, however, are solitary: each female builds and provisions her own nest, and if she is impaired, her offspring suffer directly. Kolstad argues that the honeybee is therefore a poor stand-in for wild bees. Her argument is difficult to dispute, and it applies well beyond this particular class of chemicals. The same reasoning could equally be directed at fungicides, herbicides and any other substance whose risks have been judged mainly through experiments on a single, unusually resilient insect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The case against neonicotinoids was strengthened further by the work of the Agrochemical Assessment Panel, an independent body advising the regulator. Its investigators found that only a small fraction of the insecticide applied to a seed is actually taken up by the crop. The remainder enters the soil, where it may persist for several years and dissolve into water that is absorbed by wildflowers growing along field margins. Bees foraging on these flowers, which had never been treated, were thus exposed even when they avoided the crop altogether, a finding that undermined the assumption that exposure could be controlled simply by timing applications carefully.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Restrictions, however, have had consequences of their own. Joaquín Altamirano, an economist at the Andean Institute of Agricultural Economics, has studied farms in the years following the ban. He found that many growers of oilseed rape, deprived of seed treatments, returned to spraying older pyrethroid insecticides, which kill a broader range of insects on contact. In some regions, damage by flea beetles also reduced yields sharply, and a number of farmers abandoned the crop. Altamirano's findings show that a ban introduced without support for alternative methods of pest control can produce perverse results. They do not, however, amount to an argument for lifting the restrictions; rather, they suggest that prohibition should be the beginning of a policy rather than the whole of it, accompanied by investment in crop rotation, natural predators and the monitoring of pest numbers.

topic: managed honeybees versus wild bees: competition and disease spillover
title: Too Many Hives?
subtitle: Why the boom in beekeeping may be doing little for the bees that most need help

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past fifteen years, beehives have appeared on the roofs of offices, hotels, schools and even museums in cities across the world. Companies advertise them in their annual reports as evidence of a commitment to biodiversity, and urban beekeeping courses are frequently booked months in advance. The motivation is undoubtedly genuine, prompted by widely reported losses of honeybee colonies. Nevertheless, the enthusiasm is largely misdirected. The western honeybee is not an endangered species but a managed animal, kept for its honey and its pollination services much as cattle are kept for milk, and the number of managed colonies worldwide has actually grown over the past half century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The bees that are in trouble are mostly wild ones. There are around twenty thousand known bee species, and the honeybee is only one of them. The rest include bumblebees, mining bees, mason bees and many others, a considerable proportion of which are declining in range or abundance. Because they attract little commercial interest, however, their fortunes are far less closely monitored than those of honeybees, whose losses are counted every winter by beekeepers' associations. These insects are not merely of interest to naturalists. Wild bees contribute substantially to the pollination of crops, and for certain crops they are more efficient than honeybees: a single mason bee, for example, may pollinate as many apple blossoms as dozens of honeybee workers, because of the way it carries pollen loosely on its body.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The concern is that honeybees, introduced in large numbers, may deprive wild bees of food. Margarida Fonseca, an ecologist at the Lisbon Institute of Urban Ecology, surveyed flowers in several European cities over six years. Where the density of hives increased, she found that the number of wild bee species visiting flowers fell. A single strong honeybee colony, she calculates, may gather in one season as much pollen as would be needed to rear many thousands of solitary bees. Fonseca argues that some cities have exceeded the number of hives their green spaces can support, and she has called for hives to be registered so that their density can be monitored and, if necessary, limited.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Competition for food is not the only risk. Thandiwe Mokoena, who heads the Cape Pollinator Health Unit, has detected viruses long associated with honeybees, including one that causes deformed wings, in bumblebees foraging near apiaries. Flowers, she suggests, act as meeting points where pathogens pass from one species to another when bees visit the same blooms. Mokoena is careful, however, not to cast honeybees solely as the source of infection. Some of her samples indicate that viruses also travel from wild bees to managed colonies, and she admits that the direction in which most transmission occurs has yet to be established.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers accept that urban beekeeping poses a serious threat. Ivo Petrović, a beekeeper and researcher at the Dalmatian Beekeeping College, points out that much of the evidence of competition comes from studies of large commercial apiaries placed in natural habitats, where hundreds of hives may be gathered in one spot. A few hives on a city rooftop, he maintains, are a different matter. He also notes that hobby beekeepers are often among the most active campaigners for planting wildflowers, and he warns that treating them as enemies of conservation is likely to backfire. On this last point he is right: hostility towards beekeepers achieves little. But the uncertainty he highlights cuts both ways, and the onus should be on those who wish to place hives where wild bees are already scarce to show that no harm will result.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question is most pressing in protected areas. In some nature reserves, migratory beekeepers set out hundreds of hives each summer to take advantage of flowering heathland or wild herbs. Fonseca and others have recommended exclusion zones around populations of threatened wild bees. Enforcing such zones, though, is far from straightforward, since honeybee workers routinely fly several kilometres from the hive in search of nectar and pollen, and a zone small enough to be practical may offer little real protection. Some reserve managers have responded by negotiating voluntary agreements with beekeepers, who are offered alternative sites in return for keeping their hives away from the most sensitive areas. Such arrangements depend heavily on goodwill, and their success has so far been uneven.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If adding hives is not the answer, what is? The needs of wild bees are well understood. They require a continuous supply of flowers from early spring to late autumn, and, just as importantly, places to nest: patches of bare ground for mining bees, dead wood and hollow plant stems for others. Simply mowing parks and verges less frequently can make a measurable difference. A rooftop planted with native wildflowers would almost certainly do more for pollinators than one crowded with hives. The public's affection for bees is a valuable resource, and the task now is to channel it towards measures that actually help the species in decline.

topic: artificial light at night and nocturnal moth pollination
title: The Lost Night Shift
subtitle: Artificial lighting is quietly disrupting the insects that pollinate flowers after dark

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The sight of moths circling a lamp on a summer evening is so familiar that it has rarely been regarded as a matter of scientific concern. Yet moths outnumber butterflies by roughly ten species to one, and many of them visit flowers, carrying pollen from plant to plant while most of the world sleeps. Some plants, such as certain campions and honeysuckles, release their scent mainly after dusk, a sign of how long they have depended on these nocturnal visitors. Until recently, the study of pollination concentrated almost exclusively on bees, butterflies and other insects active in daylight. This imbalance arguably reflected the working hours of researchers rather than the relative importance of the insects themselves, and it has left a large gap in our understanding of how plants reproduce.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the first attempts to measure what artificial light does to nocturnal pollination was carried out by Ayşe Korkmaz of the Anatolian Institute of Ecology. Her team installed portable streetlamps in mountain meadows that had previously been entirely dark, and compared them with unlit plots nearby. Under the lamps, visits by insects to flowers during the night fell by more than sixty per cent. More strikingly, a common meadow plant produced around thirteen per cent fewer seeds in the lit plots, even though bees and hoverflies continued to visit it during the day. The implication was that daytime pollinators could not simply take over the work that night-flying insects had stopped doing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several mechanisms appear to be involved. Many moths that encounter a bright light fly around it repeatedly until they are exhausted or are picked off by bats and birds that have learnt to hunt beneath lamps. Those that escape this fate may still be affected: illumination suppresses feeding, and in some species it reduces the production of pheromones, the chemical signals by which females attract mates. The development of caterpillars, which in many species is timed according to day length, can also be thrown into confusion. Lorcan Ó Dálaigh, an entomologist at Western Seaboard University, found that hedgerows beneath modern LED streetlights supported roughly half as many caterpillars as comparable hedgerows left in darkness, a difference large enough to affect the birds that feed their young on them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The timing of this research is significant, because towns and cities around the world are currently replacing their old orange sodium lamps with white LEDs, which use far less electricity. White LEDs, however, emit much more blue light, to which most insects are especially sensitive. Ananya Raghunathan of the Deccan Centre for Sensory Ecology warns that municipalities may be intensifying the problem without realising it, and she recommends amber or filtered LEDs that remove the shorter wavelengths. The energy savings offered by LEDs are too large to be sacrificed, and no serious case can be made for returning to older technology. What matters is not the switch to LEDs itself but the colour, brightness and direction of the light they produce, all of which can be adjusted at modest cost.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A broader approach is promoted by the Lumen Ecology Consortium, an alliance of researchers and local authorities. It argues that much outdoor lighting is simply unnecessary, and that streetlamps could be dimmed or switched off in the early hours of the morning, or fitted with sensors that activate them only when someone approaches. Trials in a number of towns found no increase in road accidents or crime after such measures were introduced. Objections on grounds of safety are frequently raised but seldom backed by evidence. Even so, it would be unwise to dismiss them entirely: the trials so far have been small, and if residents feel unsafe walking in darker streets, that perception has real consequences for how they live, whatever the statistics show.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not every scientist believes that light deserves so much attention. Pablo Echeverría, a conservation biologist at the Southern Cone Biodiversity Trust, argues that the loss of habitat and the intensification of agriculture are far more important causes of insect decline, and that limited funds would be better spent on those problems. He is correct that light is rarely the principal driver of losses. However, his argument overlooks one crucial difference. Restoring a drained wetland or a cleared meadow may take decades, whereas a lamp can be dimmed or redirected overnight. Few environmental pressures are so easily reversible, and that alone makes lighting an unusually cost-effective target for action.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Much remains unknown, including how light interacts with other stresses such as pesticides and rising temperatures, and how quickly moth populations recover once darkness returns. Reliable long-term counts of moths are also lacking for most tropical countries, precisely where artificial lighting is spreading fastest and insect diversity is greatest. What is clear is that the night itself has become a threatened habitat. Across large parts of Europe, North America and Asia, truly dark skies have all but disappeared, and with them the conditions in which a vast and largely unseen community of insects evolved.

topic: cities, gardens and brownfield land as refuges for pollinators
title: Bees in the Concrete Jungle
subtitle: Towns and cities may be better places for pollinators than anyone expected, but how much better is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, ecologists regarded cities as little more than biological deserts, places where nature survived only in a few neglected corners. That view has been seriously challenged by a series of surveys comparing the insects of urban areas with those of the surrounding countryside. In several countries, researchers have found that cities support a greater variety of bee species than nearby farmland, and in some cases almost as many as protected nature reserves. The finding has been greeted with understandable enthusiasm by gardeners and urban planners alike. It is a genuinely encouraging result, but it needs to be interpreted with considerable care, since the number of species recorded tells only part of the story.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The reasons why cities can be so attractive to bees are not hard to find. Private gardens, parks and allotments together contain an enormous range of flowering plants, many of them imported from other continents, and their flowering periods overlap to provide food from early spring until late autumn. Modern farmland, by contrast, is often dominated by a few crops that flower briefly and simultaneously, producing a short glut of food followed by what beekeepers call the hunger gap, a period in which almost nothing is in bloom. Cities are also warmer than the surrounding land because buildings and roads absorb and release heat, which allows bees to remain active for longer each year. The picture is not uniformly positive, however: some gardeners apply pesticides more heavily per square metre than any farmer would.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not every garden plant is equally useful. Halima Ouédraogo, a botanist at the Institute of Tropical Urban Studies, has examined hundreds of popular ornamental varieties and found that many offer pollinators almost nothing. Plants bred to produce showy double flowers, in which the parts that would normally make pollen have been converted into extra petals, often provide little or no food, and their complex shape can prevent insects from reaching what nectar there is. Ouédraogo therefore advises gardeners to choose single-flowered varieties wherever possible. Interestingly, her research does not support the common belief that only native plants are worth growing; many introduced species proved valuable, particularly those that flower late in the season when native plants have finished.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some of the richest urban habitats are not gardens at all. Stellan Vikander of the Northern Polytechnic has spent a decade surveying brownfield sites, the abandoned railway yards, demolished factories and disused quarries that most cities contain. These sites typically have ground that is bare and nutrient-poor, conditions that suit the many bee species which dig their nests in the soil, and they are colonised by a succession of wild plants. Vikander found that a single derelict site could hold more bee species than several hectares of well-kept parkland. Yet such places are routinely described as wasteland and are among the first to be selected for new housing or landscaped into neat lawns. Vikander is right to argue that this represents a failure of perception: tidiness is too often mistaken for ecological value.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more sceptical view is offered by Mei-Ling Tsao of the Pacific Rim Ecology Laboratory. She points out that the bees which flourish in cities are mostly generalists, species that can feed on a wide range of flowers and tolerate heat and disturbance. Specialists, which depend on a single family of plants or require particular nesting conditions, are largely absent. Moreover, Tsao's comparison of insect records from cities on three continents suggests that urban bee communities are becoming increasingly similar to one another, dominated by the same adaptable species wherever they are found. This is an important corrective. High species counts in cities may conceal a loss of the distinctive local communities that make the countryside irreplaceable, and urban areas can never be a substitute for it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The way in which urban green spaces are arranged also matters. Volunteers taking part in the Urban Pollinator Census, a long-running citizen science project, have recorded bees in thousands of locations over many years. Their data suggest that isolated gardens, however well planted, support fewer species than those connected to a wider network of green land. Strips of vegetation alongside railways and rivers appear to act as corridors along which bees can move between larger patches of habitat, allowing populations to recover after a poor year. The Census organisers now urge city authorities to plan green spaces as linked systems rather than as separate ornaments.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that cities can solve the problem of pollinator decline on their own. Urban land covers only a small fraction of most countries, and the fate of most bee species will be decided in the countryside. Nevertheless, municipal authorities have more influence than they often realise. Mowing roadside verges less often, leaving some dead wood in parks and restricting the cosmetic use of pesticides on public land are inexpensive measures. The last of these, in particular, is a straightforward step that many cities have postponed for far too long.

topic: the economic valuation of pollination services
title: Pricing the Pollinators
subtitle: Economists have tried to put a figure on the work insects do for agriculture. The numbers are striking, but what do they really mean?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few environmental statistics are quoted as often as the claim that pollinating animals contribute hundreds of billions of dollars to global food production every year. Figures of this kind have proved remarkably effective in attracting the attention of finance ministries and agricultural agencies, which tend to respond more readily to sums of money than to appeals on behalf of insects. Their very persuasiveness, however, is a reason to examine them closely. A headline number can create an impression of precision that the underlying calculations do not justify, and it may conceal more than it reveals about where the real costs of pollinator decline would fall.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Most global estimates rely on what is known as the dependence ratio method. For each crop, researchers estimate the proportion of its yield that would be lost without animal pollinators: close to all of it for almonds or melons, a modest share for oilseed rape, and none at all for wheat, rice and maize, which are pollinated by the wind. This proportion is then multiplied by the market value of the crop. Calculations of this sort show that around three quarters of the leading types of food crop benefit to some extent from animal pollination, yet these crops account for only about a third of global food production by volume, because the staple cereals need no insects at all. Kaveh Rostami, an economist at the Caspian School of Economics, argues that the method is fundamentally flawed. It assumes, he points out, that pollinators disappear overnight and that nothing else changes, whereas in reality farmers would switch to other crops and prices would adjust.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To capture these responses, Rostami and his colleagues have built models of entire agricultural markets in which a fall in pollination raises the price of affected foods and prompts producers to change what they grow. Their results suggest that the losses suffered by farmers are considerably smaller than the dependence ratio method implies, but that consumers bear a heavy burden through higher prices, particularly for fruit, vegetables and nuts. This approach is undoubtedly more realistic. It nonetheless shares a weakness with the method it seeks to replace, in that it typically models the complete loss of pollinators rather than the gradual and uneven decline that is actually taking place.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more direct approach has been pioneered by Kadri Tammsaar of the Baltic Agricultural University. Instead of imagining the total disappearance of pollinators, her team compares flowers that are left to natural pollination with flowers on the same plants that are pollinated by hand, ensuring that every flower receives ample pollen. Any difference in the resulting yield reveals a pollination deficit, the harvest that is being lost because insects are too few. Across several hundred fruit and seed farms, Tammsaar found such deficits on roughly one farm in three. The significance of this work is that it shifts attention from a hypothetical catastrophe to losses that farmers are already incurring, and that might be reduced by measures as simple as planting flowering margins.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For Wanjiru Muthoni-Gathii of the East African Smallholder Research Institute, even these refinements miss the most important point. Valuations based on world market prices, she observes, are dominated by high-value export crops grown in wealthy countries. In much of the tropics, however, pollinator-dependent crops such as beans, pumpkins and mangoes are grown on small plots and eaten by the households that produce them, so that they scarcely appear in market statistics. Since fruits, vegetables and nuts supply a large share of essential vitamins and minerals, a decline in pollination could damage nutrition long before it registered as an economic loss. Of all the arguments for protecting pollinators, this is perhaps the most compelling.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some scholars question whether nature should be priced at all. Felipe Arancibia, a philosopher at the Institute for Environmental Ethics in Valparaíso, warns that once the contribution of wild insects is expressed in monetary terms, it becomes natural to ask whether a cheaper substitute could be found. In certain fruit-growing districts, orchards are already pollinated by teams of workers using brushes, and engineers are developing robotic alternatives. If such methods ever cost less than conserving habitat, Arancibia argues, the economic case for wild pollinators would collapse. The danger he identifies is real. Yet refusing to value pollination would leave it invisible in decisions where everything else, from fertiliser to labour, carries a price, and that would hardly serve the insects better.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In one respect, markets are already putting a price on pollination. Almond growers in some regions rely on more than a million honeybee colonies, transported by lorry each spring, and the fees charged for renting hives have risen several-fold over two decades as demand has outstripped supply. Such prices offer a clearer signal of scarcity than any global estimate. The most valuable use of economic analysis may therefore lie not in producing ever larger headline figures but in informing specific local choices: which hedgerow to plant, which field margin to leave uncultivated, and which crops a region can realistically expect to grow.

topic: robotic and artificial pollination as a substitute for insects
title: Mechanical Bees
subtitle: Engineers are building machines to pollinate crops. Should we welcome them, or worry about what they represent?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a spring morning in a pear orchard, a small drone hovers a metre above the blossom, releasing a fine mist of pollen suspended in liquid. Within minutes it has moved on to the next row, guided by cameras and software that identify open flowers. Demonstrations like this one are frequently reported under headlines announcing that robot bees will soon rescue agriculture from the decline of insects. Such headlines misunderstand both the technology and the problem it is supposed to solve. Machines may well have a role in pollination, but it is a far narrower one than enthusiasts suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Artificial pollination is not in itself a new idea. Date palms have been pollinated by hand for thousands of years, with growers climbing the trees to dust female flowers with pollen gathered from male ones. Vanilla, when grown outside its native region, depends entirely on human labour, because the insect that pollinates it in the wild is absent; each flower opens for only a single day and must be pollinated individually with a slender stick. In some regions, kiwifruit growers routinely supplement the work of bees by blowing pollen over their vines. What these examples have in common is that hand pollination has remained confined to crops valuable enough to justify the labour it demands.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Hyun-woo Baek, who leads a robotics group at the Hanbit Institute of Agricultural Engineering, believes that automation could change this calculation. His team's drones are designed to provide a form of insurance in seasons when insects are scarce, and to work in greenhouses, where commercial bumblebee colonies are currently bought in to pollinate tomatoes and peppers. Commercial bumblebees are not without problems of their own: colonies are shipped across borders in large numbers, and workers that escape may spread diseases to wild populations. Baek claims that a small fleet of drones could cover a hectare of greenhouse crops more quickly than the colonies now used. It is in such enclosed environments, where conditions are controlled and the plants are arranged in regular rows, that the case for machines is at its most convincing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Outdoors, however, the challenge is of an entirely different order. Zsófia Kertész, an ecologist at the Pannonian University of Ecology, has estimated that wild insects and honeybees together make billions of flower visits every day during the flowering season in a single agricultural region. To replace them with machines would require fleets of a size that is difficult to imagine, each unit consuming energy and requiring maintenance. Even the most sophisticated drones currently fly for less than half an hour before their batteries must be replaced, and strong winds can ground them entirely. Bees, by contrast, reproduce themselves without any cost to the farmer. They also perform their task with a sensitivity that no current robot can match, responding to the scent, temperature and nectar of each bloom and thereby detecting whether it is receptive to pollen at that moment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers are troubled less by the practical limitations of the technology than by the message it sends. Itzel Huerta-Cano, of the Mesoamerican Centre for Agroecology, argues that the promotion of mechanical substitutes risks weakening the political will to protect insects, by implying that their loss can be compensated for with investment. She also observes that funding tends to flow towards solutions that can be patented and sold, rather than towards habitat conservation, from which no single company profits. Most importantly, the great majority of wild flowering plants depend on animals for pollination, and no machine will ever move through a meadow pollinating wildflowers. Pollination is not merely a service to agriculture but a process that sustains entire ecosystems, and any discussion that loses sight of this is fundamentally misguided.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Those developing the technology do not always make the extravagant claims attributed to them. The Orchard Robotics Initiative, a partnership between growers and engineers, explicitly describes its aim as supplementing insect pollination rather than replacing it. In a cold or wet spring, bees may barely leave their hives during the brief period when fruit trees are in flower, and a well-timed application of pollen can rescue a harvest. In the Initiative's trials, supplementary spraying increased the proportion of cherry blossoms that developed into fruit by around a fifth in years of poor weather, but made no measurable difference when conditions were favourable. This modest account of what the machines can achieve is considerably more credible than the claims found in newspaper headlines.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Viewed in this light, pollinating machines are a tool like any other, useful in particular circumstances and irrelevant in many others. The genuine risk lies not in the technology itself but in the way it is presented. The question that matters is not whether machines can pollinate flowers, which in limited settings they plainly can, but whether societies will treat their existence as a reason to stop caring about the insects that have done the job, without charge, for millions of years.

topic: climate change, phenological mismatch and range shifts in pollinators
title: Out of Step
subtitle: As springs grow warmer, are flowers and their pollinators drifting apart?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Across much of the temperate world, spring now arrives measurably earlier than it did a century ago, and many plants flower several days sooner with each passing decade. This raises an obvious question: are the insects that pollinate them keeping pace? If a plant comes into flower before its pollinators have emerged, it may set little seed; if bees emerge before there is anything to feed on, they may starve. The notion of such a mismatch has an intuitive appeal and has featured prominently in warnings about climate change. The evidence for it, however, turns out to be considerably more ambiguous than the warnings imply.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most comprehensive data come from Aino Kettunen of the Lapland Institute of Arctic Biology, who compared the dates recorded on pressed plant specimens and pinned bees in museum collections spanning more than 120 years. On average, she found, flowers and bees had both shifted their timing forward, and at broadly similar rates. Had the analysis stopped there, it might have seemed that fears of mismatch were exaggerated. Yet the averages concealed considerable variation. For roughly a quarter of the plant and bee pairs that Kettunen examined, the interval between flowering and the emergence of the insect had widened by more than a week, enough in some cases to leave a plant with few visitors at the height of its bloom.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should partners that have evolved together drift apart? Part of the answer lies in the signals each relies upon. Most plants time their flowering according to accumulated warmth, but insects use a variety of cues. Some respond to air temperature, others to day length, and others to the melting of snow. Many solitary bees spend the winter as adults sealed inside underground nest cells, so the moment at which they emerge depends on the temperature of the soil rather than of the air above it, and the two do not necessarily change at the same rate. When plants and insects respond to different cues, a warming climate is likely to pull them in different directions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Farid Benmoussa, an ecologist at the Atlas Mountains Research Station, believes that the consequences of such shifts are often overstated. Most plants, he points out, are visited by several pollinator species, and most bees feed on a range of plants, so the loss of any single partner is rarely catastrophic. His computer simulations of pollination networks suggest that they can tolerate the loss of many connections before their overall function declines. This is reassuring as far as it goes. But redundancy of this kind can be eroded without anyone noticing, since each lost connection reduces the capacity of the network to absorb the next disturbance, and a system that appears stable may be approaching a point at which it suddenly fails.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Climate change affects not only when pollinators are active but also where they can live. Valentina Rocchetti of the Apennine Ecology Institute has mapped the distribution of bumblebees, which are adapted to cool conditions, across two continents over several decades. Her data show that the southern limits of many species have moved northwards by as much as three hundred kilometres, while their northern limits have barely shifted. The result is a steady contraction of the area they occupy. For species that were already confined to small areas, such as isolated uplands or particular islands, the losses may prove irreversible. Why these species have failed to spread into newly suitable territory remains unclear; a lack of appropriate habitat and the limited distances that queens disperse have both been suggested. Rocchetti has proposed that colonies might be deliberately moved to cooler regions, an idea that has provoked considerable debate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In mountainous areas, species can respond to warming by moving uphill, but only until they reach the summit. Plants near the peaks have nowhere further to go, and neither do the insects that feed on them. Researchers in the Alpine Phenology Network, which maintains monitoring plots across several mountain ranges, have recorded a further change. Because the snow now melts earlier, flowering in high meadows begins sooner, yet it ends at much the same time, so that the season available to pollinators has become compressed. The Network has also found that during heatwaves many alpine flowers secrete markedly less nectar, an effect that has received far less attention than shifts in timing but may matter just as much to the insects that depend on it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done? Climate change rarely acts alone; its effects are compounded by the loss of habitat and the use of pesticides. Landscapes that offer a variety of local conditions, such as north-facing slopes, shaded valleys and damp hollows, allow species to find cooler refuges without travelling far, and protecting such variety is among the most effective responses available. Moving colonies to new regions may eventually prove necessary for some species, but it carries risks of spreading disease and disrupting existing communities, and it should be regarded as a last resort rather than a first response.

topic: wildflower strips and agri-environment payments for pollinators on farmland
title: Margins of Hope
subtitle: Farmers are paid to grow flowers for insects at the edges of their fields. Is the money well spent?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than thirty years, governments in Europe and elsewhere have paid farmers to sow strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields. The sums involved are considerable, running to hundreds of millions in some countries each year, and the results are undeniably attractive: bands of poppies, cornflowers and clover now brighten landscapes that were once uniformly green. Yet a basic question has received surprisingly little attention, given the amount of public money at stake. Do these strips actually increase the number of pollinating insects, or do they merely gather together insects that would have been living in the area anyway?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Ecologists refer to this as the distinction between attraction and production. Bogdan Lupescu, of the Danube Institute of Agroecology, was among the first to test it directly. Counting bees on farms with and without flower strips, he found that the strips themselves were crowded with insects, but that the total number of bees across the wider landscape had not risen during the first two years of the scheme. In his interpretation, the strips were acting as magnets, concentrating existing populations rather than enlarging them. Such counts are laborious, requiring observers to walk fixed routes repeatedly throughout the season, which may explain why so few studies of this kind had previously been attempted. Lupescu also raised a more troubling possibility: if strips are in full bloom at the same moment as a crop, they might draw pollinators away from the very fields that need them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A longer study by Nadia Haddad, of the Levant University of Agriculture, produced a more encouraging picture. Over six years, she tracked bumblebee colonies on farms with established strips and found that colonies near the flowers produced more new queens, and that the density of nests rose in subsequent seasons. Production, in other words, does occur, but it takes several years to become apparent. Haddad also found that location mattered: strips without suitable nesting sites nearby, such as hedge banks or rough grassland, provided food but produced no lasting rise in bee numbers. Her findings suggest that schemes assessed after only a year or two may be judged far more harshly than they deserve.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even where strips can work in principle, many fail in practice. Kristjan Ólafsson, of the Nordic Agricultural College, surveyed several hundred strips established under government schemes and found that only about a third remained in good condition after five years. Many had been sown with cheap seed mixtures containing just a few species that flower briefly in early summer, offering far less than more diverse mixtures. Others had been invaded by vigorous grasses that gradually crowded out the flowers. Ólafsson attributes much of this decline to the way in which schemes are designed. Because farmers are paid for sowing seed rather than for what grows, there is little incentive to manage strips carefully once they have been established.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One proposed remedy is to pay farmers according to results. Under such arrangements, an inspector counts the number of indicator flower species present, and payment rises with the richness of the strip. The inspections add to administrative costs, but they reward farmers for what they achieve. In a trial organised by the Lowland Farmers' Conservation Forum, participants reported that the approach transformed their attitude: many began experimenting with different management techniques and learning to identify plants they had previously ignored. Results-based payment is a promising idea, but it is not suitable everywhere. Farmers working on poor or waterlogged soils may struggle to produce rich strips however hard they try, and a system that rewards outcomes could penalise them for conditions beyond their control.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Amani Lukumay, of the Kilimanjaro Centre for Smallholder Agriculture, questions whether the model should be exported at all. Wildflower strips, she argues, were designed for the vast, uniform fields of industrial agriculture in Europe and North America, where little natural vegetation remains. On the small farms of East Africa and much of Asia, by contrast, fields are often already interspersed with hedges, fallow plots and patches of native scrub. She points to farms where old hedgerows were cleared in order to qualify for modern subsidies, removing the very habitats on which local bees depended. In such landscapes, Lukumay contends, the priority should be to protect existing diversity, which is far cheaper than attempting to recreate it once it has been lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that wildflower strips are a waste of money. Where they are well sited, well managed and given time to work, they clearly benefit pollinators, and they bring the additional advantages of supporting insects that prey on crop pests and of reconnecting farmers with the wildlife on their land. They remain worthwhile, but they cannot by themselves compensate for intensive management of the remaining ninety-five per cent of a farm. A narrow band of flowers alongside a field that is heavily sprayed and ploughed is at best a partial remedy, and policies that treat it as a complete one will continue to disappoint.

topic: interacting stressors in bee decline: parasites, pesticide mixtures and nutrition
title: No Single Culprit
subtitle: Bees rarely face one threat at a time, and scientists are only beginning to understand what happens when pressures combine

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Whenever reports of collapsing bee colonies reach the news, the search for a culprit begins. At various times, pesticides, parasitic mites, mobile phone signals and climate change have each been presented as the principal cause. The appetite for a single explanation is understandable, since a single cause suggests a single remedy. It has nevertheless done considerable harm to the science. By encouraging researchers to study one factor at a time and to defend it against rival explanations, the hunt for a villain has obscured the most important feature of the problem: in the real world, bees are almost always exposed to several pressures at once, and these pressures interact.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The clearest illustration is provided by the varroa mite. Originally a parasite of the Asian honeybee, it transferred to the western honeybee during the twentieth century and has since spread to almost every continent. The mite attaches itself to developing bees and feeds on their fat body tissue, an organ that plays a central role in immunity and the storage of nutrients. More damaging still, it acts as a carrier of viruses. Deformed wing virus had long been present in honeybee colonies, usually at low levels and with mild effects. Once varroa became established, however, the virus was injected directly into the bloodstream of the bees, and it was transformed into one of the leading causes of colony death. Neither the mite nor the virus alone would have produced such devastation; it was their combination that proved lethal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Similar interactions occur between chemicals. Radomir Hájek, a toxicologist at the Bohemian Institute of Apidology, has shown that certain fungicides, which are applied to crops to control fungal disease and are almost harmless to bees on their own, can make some insecticides many times more toxic. The fungicides appear to inhibit the enzymes that bees use to break down toxins, so that an otherwise tolerable dose of insecticide accumulates in the body. Since farmers commonly spray several products together, such mixtures are a routine feature of agricultural landscapes. Yet regulatory systems almost everywhere evaluate each substance separately, and the combinations that bees actually encounter are seldom examined. Hájek argues that the most frequently used mixtures should be tested as a matter of course, a proposal that seems difficult to oppose on scientific grounds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Leilani Anscombe, who directs the Pacific Islands Pollinator Laboratory, approaches the question from a different angle. In her experiments, bees fed on pollen from a single crop mounted weaker immune responses than those given pollen from a variety of plants, and they were less able to survive exposure to both parasites and pesticides. Anscombe regards nutrition as the foundation on which all other aspects of bee health rest, and she argues that improving the quality and diversity of forage would raise the resilience of colonies to every other threat. Her emphasis is valuable, not least because the planting of flowers is something that farmers, councils and gardeners can undertake immediately.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are convinced that interactions are as dramatic as some studies suggest. Junaid Qureshi, a statistician at the Indus Institute of Quantitative Ecology, reviewed more than a hundred experiments that claimed to have detected harmful combinations. In most of them, he found, the effects were simply additive: the combined harm was roughly equal to the sum of the individual harms, rather than greater. Genuine synergy, in which the whole exceeds the sum of its parts, appeared in only a minority of cases. Qureshi also suggests that studies reporting striking interactions are more likely to be published than those finding none. His caution is warranted. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that additive effects are of little consequence. A colony facing three or four moderate stresses at once may be pushed beyond the point of recovery, even if no single stress, and no pair of them, would have been fatal.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious attempt to capture this complexity in the field has been made by the Integrated Bee Health Consortium, which has monitored several hundred apiaries over a decade. For each colony, its researchers recorded the number of mites, the pesticide residues in stored pollen, the quality of the surrounding forage and the local weather. When they analysed the data, no individual factor reliably predicted which colonies would die over the winter. A combination of heavy mite infestation and poor forage, by contrast, proved a strong predictor of loss. The Consortium now encourages beekeepers and farmers in each district to share information, so that problems can be identified before they combine.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Recognising that bee decline has many interacting causes has clear implications for policy. Regulatory frameworks designed around individual substances will need to be revised, and research funding will need to support long-term studies that track several factors at once. There is, however, a danger in all this. Complexity can easily become an excuse, and the claim that the problem is too complicated to address has sometimes been used to deflect criticism of particular products. That several factors are involved is no reason to delay action on those already known to cause harm; if anything, it strengthens the case for reducing each of them wherever possible.

topic: the search for the magnetic sensor in migratory birds
title: The Missing Compass
subtitle: Birds clearly sense the earth's magnetic field, but scientists still disagree about how they do it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every autumn, songbirds weighing less than twenty grams leave the forests of northern Europe and fly several thousand kilometres to wintering grounds in Africa, and many return the following spring to within a few metres of the place where they hatched. To achieve this they draw on an array of cues: the position of the sun, the rotation of the night sky, familiar landmarks and possibly even smells. Of all these sources of information, the earth's magnetic field is the most puzzling. Birds plainly use it, yet the organ that detects it has never been identified with certainty. It is a remarkable fact that, more than half a century after magnetic orientation was first demonstrated in the laboratory, the question of where the sensor lies remains unresolved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The early experiments were simple in design. Migratory robins were placed in circular cages during the season when they would normally be travelling, and the direction in which they hopped was recorded. When coils around the cage altered the magnetic field, the birds altered their preferred heading accordingly. Further trials produced an unexpected result: the birds were indifferent to the polarity of the field and responded instead to the angle at which its lines meet the earth's surface. In other words, a bird can distinguish 'towards the pole' from 'towards the equator', but not north from south in the sense that a hand-held compass would. The sense also proved to operate only within a narrow range of field strengths, although birds kept for several days in an unfamiliar field gradually adjusted to it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first serious candidate for a receptor was magnetite, an iron oxide that aligns itself with magnetic fields. Rasmus Thorbecke of the Lindholm Institute for Sensory Ecology reported clusters of iron-rich cells in the upper beak of pigeons, apparently linked to a nerve that carries signals to the brain. Such a structure, he proposed, would register variations in field intensity and so give birds a kind of map rather than a compass. The idea suffered a severe setback when a team under Amaia Zubizarreta examined the same tissue in far greater detail and concluded that most of the iron-rich cells were immune cells of a type found throughout the body, with no connection to the nervous system. Thorbecke has accepted this finding, but he maintains that some form of magnetic map must exist, since birds transported hundreds of kilometres eastwards correct their course in a way that cannot be explained by a compass alone. The episode is a cautionary tale. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that the magnetite hypothesis has been disproved; it has merely lost its most visible evidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Attention has since shifted to the eye. According to the so-called radical pair hypothesis, light striking proteins called cryptochromes in the retina generates pairs of molecules, each carrying an unpaired electron, whose subsequent chemical behaviour depends on their alignment with the magnetic field. If this is correct, the compass should work only in light and should be vulnerable to weak radio-frequency noise. The second prediction received dramatic support from Mireille Fontanaud and her colleagues, who found that robins housed in wooden huts on a city campus could not orient themselves at all. When the huts were lined with earthed aluminium sheets, which block electromagnetic interference, the birds recovered their sense of direction at once. The noise responsible was far weaker than the levels permitted by safety regulations for humans.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Fontanaud's result is striking, but it should be treated with some caution. Other laboratories have struggled to reproduce it, and wild migrants crossing large cities do not appear to lose their way in large numbers. There are theoretical objections, too. The physicist Yusuf Karaoğlan points out that the earth's field is extraordinarily weak, and that for it to influence the reaction at all, the electrons would have to remain in a delicate quantum state for far longer than such states usually survive in warm, wet living tissue. Karaoğlan does not dismiss the hypothesis, but he argues that it demands a degree of molecular protection that has never been observed in any biological system.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty concerns method rather than mechanism. Tuva Hjelmeland, a behavioural ecologist, argues that the hopping of a caged bird is a poor guide to what happens during a real journey, since the restlessness birds display in captivity is only a rough substitute for genuine navigation. She favours fitting wild birds with miniature tracking devices after experimental treatment and following them along their actual routes. Her case is a strong one, yet cage experiments should not be abandoned. They remain the only means by which the magnetic environment can be controlled precisely enough to test a specific hypothesis.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What seems increasingly likely is that birds possess more than one magnetic sense, with a light-dependent compass in the eye and a map sense located elsewhere. Resolving the matter will require physicists, neurobiologists and field ecologists to work far more closely than they have done in the past. The question also has a practical dimension. If electromagnetic noise from human activity really can disable an animal's compass, then its effects on wildlife deserve considerably more attention than they have so far received.

topic: natal homing and geomagnetic imprinting in sea turtles
title: The Long Way Home
subtitle: How do sea turtles find the beach where they hatched after decades at sea?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For a loggerhead turtle, life begins with a frantic scramble. Within minutes of emerging from the sand, hatchlings no larger than a matchbox cross the beach, plunge into the surf and swim continuously for a day or more until they reach the open ocean. Many will spend the next decade or longer drifting and feeding in the vast circular currents of the North Atlantic, travelling thousands of kilometres from land. Yet when the females reach maturity, a large proportion return to nest on the same stretch of coast where they themselves hatched, sometimes within a few kilometres of the exact spot. How an animal that left as a hatchling can find its way back decades later, across an ocean with no visible landmarks, is one of the most intriguing problems in animal navigation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation is known as geomagnetic imprinting. Every point on the earth's surface has a distinctive combination of magnetic field intensity and inclination, the angle at which field lines meet the ground. The hypothesis holds that hatchlings record the magnetic signature of their natal beach and later search for it as adults. Support came from an unusual source. Lucía Olabarrieta and her colleagues at the Institute of Marine Behaviour in Antofagasta analysed nearly twenty years of nesting records along a long, straight coastline. Because the earth's field drifts slowly, the magnetic signatures of particular beaches shifted over the study period. Where the lines marking equal field values moved closer together, nests became more densely packed; where they spread apart, nests thinned out, exactly as the hypothesis would predict.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Laboratory work points in the same direction. Nomvula Ntshangase, working with young turtles in large circular tanks, reproduced the magnetic fields found at various points along the route that loggerheads follow around the Atlantic. Hatchlings that had never been to sea responded to each field by swimming in the direction that, in the real ocean, would keep them within the warm current and away from cold waters where they would perish. This suggests that turtles inherit a crude magnetic map at birth, and that imprinting on the home beach adds a specific destination to this inborn framework. Ntshangase compares the arrangement to a traveller who is born with a rough outline of a continent and later writes a single address on it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Persuasive as this research is, it should not be mistaken for proof. The evidence concerning adult turtles is largely correlational, for the obvious reason that no one can capture a hatchling, alter the field it experiences and then wait twenty-five years to see where it nests. Some indirect support comes from genetic studies, which show that turtles nesting on beaches with similar magnetic signatures tend to be more closely related than those on beaches with different ones, even when the beaches are far apart. This pattern fits the imprinting hypothesis well, but it could equally arise if the populations simply share common ancestors.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other researchers emphasise the final stage of the journey. Keoni Kalanikau, a sensory biologist, argues that magnetic cues may bring a turtle to the right region of coast, but that the field changes too little over short distances to identify an individual beach. In his view, chemical cues carried in coastal water, perhaps from particular sediments or vegetation, guide females during the last few kilometres. This two-stage model seems to me the most plausible account currently available, since it is common for migratory animals to switch from one sense to another as they approach their goal.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The imprinting hypothesis has implications for conservation. Where beaches are threatened by predators, poaching or erosion, eggs are frequently moved to protected hatcheries, some of which are surrounded by metal fencing or built close to buildings containing steel and electrical cables. Piet Oosterhuis, a conservation scientist, warns that such structures could distort the local field, causing hatchlings to imprint on a false signature and making it harder for them to return as adults. He has called for magnetic surveys of hatchery sites to become routine. His concern is legitimate, and the surveys he proposes would be cheap. However, there is as yet no direct evidence that hatchery turtles fail to come home, and it would be a serious mistake to suspend hatchery programmes, which save very large numbers of eggs, until such evidence exists.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A broader question is how turtles will cope with a changing world. Rising sea levels are expected to drown many existing nesting beaches, and warmer sand produces a higher proportion of female hatchlings, so populations may need to move in any case. Meanwhile, the earth's magnetic field will continue to drift, and over decades a population that faithfully follows a magnetic signature will gradually shift its nesting grounds along the coast. Far from being a weakness, this flexibility may prove valuable, allowing turtles to track suitable habitat rather than returning stubbornly to beaches that have become unusable. Understanding how turtles find their way home is therefore no longer merely an academic curiosity; it may determine how successfully these ancient animals can be protected.

topic: sun-compass orientation and the multi-generational migration of monarch butterflies
title: Inheritance on the Wing
subtitle: No monarch butterfly that reaches the Mexican mountains has ever been there before. How it finds its way remains one of the great puzzles of animal navigation

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave breeding grounds across eastern North America and fly as far as 4,000 kilometres to a handful of fir-covered mountain slopes in central Mexico, where they cluster on trees in such densities that branches can bend under their weight. What makes this journey remarkable is not merely its length but its peculiar pattern of inheritance. The butterflies that arrive in Mexico are the great-grandchildren of those which left the previous spring, and none has made the trip before. Whatever guides them cannot have been learned from experience or from older companions; it must, in some sense, be carried in the insect's own body. For that reason, the monarch has become something of a test case for anyone who wishes to understand how navigational ability can be encoded without instruction.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first component of the system to be identified was a sun compass. In flight simulators, in which tethered butterflies are suspended inside drums so that their preferred heading can be recorded, autumn migrants consistently orient towards the south-west on sunny days. The difficulty with the sun as a reference, of course, is that it moves across the sky. A butterfly that simply kept the sun at a fixed angle would trace a long curve rather than a straight line. The insect must therefore compensate for the time of day, and experiments in which captured monarchs were kept under artificially shifted light cycles confirmed this: butterflies whose internal clocks had been advanced by six hours altered their headings by a predictable amount, flying towards the south-east instead. Dr Gudrun Skjoldager of the Lakeshore Institute of Insect Physiology describes this as one of the clearest demonstrations of time-compensated orientation in any invertebrate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Where the clock resides proved more surprising. It had long been assumed that timekeeping was confined to the brain, but work by Skjoldager's group indicated that the antennae contain their own circadian clocks, and that butterflies whose antennae were painted black, so that the clocks there could not be reset by light, lost their ability to correct for the sun's movement. The finding was striking enough to be widely reported, and it has since been replicated in several laboratories. Yet it is worth being cautious about the conclusion sometimes drawn from it, namely that the antenna is the seat of navigation. The more modest inference, that the antennal clock supplies information which is integrated elsewhere in the nervous system, fits the evidence equally well and requires fewer assumptions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cloudy days posed a further problem. Monarchs continue to migrate under overcast skies, which implies the existence of a back-up mechanism. Researchers led by the biologist Teodoro Garmendia at the Central Plateau Ecological Station reported that monarchs held in simulators with the sun obscured could orient using the inclination of the earth's magnetic field, provided they had previously been exposed to ultraviolet light. The claim has proved contentious. A subsequent study by an independent team failed to reproduce the magnetic response, and Garmendia has suggested that the difference lies in subtle variations in the experimental lighting. The disagreement has not been resolved, and while it is possible that both results are correct under different conditions, the episode illustrates how fragile behavioural evidence for magnetic sensing can be.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns what happens once the butterflies leave the simulator. The field biologist Chidimma Anyaegbunam argues that laboratory studies, however elegant, describe a system that may not explain the routes actually taken in the wild. Tracking individual monarchs with radio tags weighing well under a tenth of a gram has shown that butterflies frequently drift with the wind, pause for days at a time, and make substantial detours around mountain ranges and large bodies of water. In Anyaegbunam's view, the compass sets a general heading, but the landscape, and particularly the funnelling effect of coastlines and valleys, does much of the work of delivering the insects to their destination. This is a reasonable corrective, but it should not be overstated: a butterfly with no compass at all would be scattered by the wind rather than funnelled anywhere.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How the insects locate a destination only a few hundred square kilometres in size remains the least understood part of the puzzle. A compass, after all, provides direction but not position. Some researchers propose that the butterflies simply fly south-west until they encounter the mountains, at which point local cues, such as the cool, humid air of the fir forests, take over. Others suspect a more sophisticated map sense. Neither hypothesis has yet been subjected to a decisive test, partly because the experiments required, such as displacing butterflies hundreds of kilometres and observing whether they correct their course, are logistically formidable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These questions have recently acquired an unwelcome urgency. Overwintering numbers have declined steeply since the 1990s, a fall commonly attributed to the loss of milkweed, the only plant on which monarch caterpillars feed, as well as to the degradation of the Mexican forests. Some conservation groups have responded by rearing monarchs in captivity and releasing them in large numbers. Recent research suggests, however, that captive-reared butterflies often fail to orient correctly in simulators, perhaps because they develop without the natural light and temperature cues that trigger migratory behaviour. If so, well-meaning efforts may be adding insects to the population that are unable to complete the very journey they are meant to sustain. Understanding the navigation system, in other words, is not an academic luxury but a precondition for effective conservation.

topic: the oceanic spawning migration of the European eel
title: The Eel's Last Journey
subtitle: For more than two thousand years, the breeding grounds of the European eel have resisted discovery

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few animals have kept their secrets as stubbornly as the European eel. Ancient naturalists, unable to find eggs or young in any river, concluded that eels arose spontaneously from mud, and the belief persisted in various forms for centuries. It was not until the early twentieth century that a Danish expedition, by collecting ever-smaller larvae across the Atlantic, traced the tiniest specimens to the Sargasso Sea, a vast region of warm water east of the Bahamas. That conclusion is still widely accepted. Remarkably, however, no one has ever observed a European eel spawning in the wild, nor collected a single egg there. The textbook account of the eel's life cycle rests, to a greater degree than is usually admitted, on inference.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The outline of that account is as follows. Larvae, transparent and shaped like willow leaves, drift with the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current towards Europe, a journey that may take anything from several months to three years. On reaching the continental shelf they transform into 'glass eels', enter estuaries, and gradually darken into the yellow eels that inhabit rivers, lakes and coastal lagoons, sometimes for decades. Finally, they undergo a second metamorphosis into 'silver eels': their eyes enlarge, their digestive tract shrinks, and they stop feeding altogether. They then leave fresh water and set out on a return journey of 5,000 to 7,000 kilometres, powered entirely by stored fat.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How they find their way across an ocean that they have previously crossed only as passive larvae is the central question. Research by Dr Saskia Oudendijk and her colleagues at the North Sea Fisheries Laboratory suggests that eels possess a magnetic map. In tank experiments, glass eels exposed to magnetic fields resembling those at different points along their larval route oriented in directions that would carry them into the Gulf Stream. Oudendijk interprets this as evidence that eels imprint on the magnetic signature of their oceanic birthplace, which adult silver eels later use to steer home. The experiments are ingenious, but they involved young eels rather than adults on the return journey, and it should not simply be assumed that a sense present in a juvenile operates in the same way decades later.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Satellite tags have provided the first direct evidence about the adult migration. A team under the marine ecologist Rodrigo Albarracín fitted pop-up tags, which detach after a set period and transmit stored data, to several hundred silver eels released off the coasts of France and Ireland. The results were unexpected. The eels did not head directly south-west but followed a variety of routes, many travelling south towards the Azores first. Most strikingly, they performed daily vertical migrations, spending daylight hours at depths of up to 1,000 metres and rising to around 200 metres at night. Albarracín believes this behaviour serves two purposes: the cold of the deep water slows sexual maturation until the eels are near their destination, while darkness at depth protects them from predators. His team's tracks also suggested that, at the speeds recorded, most eels would not reach the Sargasso Sea in time for the spring spawning season that had been assumed, and he has proposed that spawning may in fact take place a year later than once thought.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This interpretation has been challenged by the oceanographer Selamawit Gebreyesus. She argues that the tags themselves impose drag on the eel, which slows the animals and makes such estimates unreliable. Moreover, many tags detached prematurely, frequently because the eels had been eaten by sharks or toothed whales, whose stomach temperature was registered by the tag. In her view the data are better read as evidence of how hazardous the migration is than as a guide to its timing. Of her two objections, the point about drag seems the stronger, since it applies to every tagged eel, whereas predation removes only a proportion of them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The uncertainty matters because the European eel is now critically endangered. The number of glass eels reaching European rivers has fallen by more than ninety per cent since the 1980s. Proposed causes include overfishing of glass eels, many of which are exported illegally to be raised on Asian farms; dams and turbines that block or kill migrating silver eels; a parasitic worm introduced from Asia which damages the swim bladder; and changes in ocean currents that may carry larvae off course. The fisheries economist Tiberiu Dragomirescu argues that, because the oceanic phase lies beyond any national jurisdiction, management should concentrate on what can be controlled in rivers: removing obstacles and limiting catches. This is sensible as far as it goes, but it would be a mistake to treat the ocean as irrelevant; if shifting currents are part of the problem, river measures alone may never be enough.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most telling indication of how much remains unknown is that, despite decades of attempts, no one has yet succeeded in breeding European eels commercially in captivity. Every farmed eel began life as a wild glass eel. Until the conditions under which eels spawn are understood, the species will remain dependent on a journey that it alone knows how to make, and that science has, so far, only partly reconstructed.
