topic: olfactory navigation in ocean-going seabirds
title: Following the Scent of the Sea
subtitle: The idea that birds find their way by smell was once dismissed as eccentric. Experiments on ocean-going seabirds have forced a rethink

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, ornithologists regarded birds as creatures of sight and sound, equipped with a sense of smell so feeble as to be virtually irrelevant. The assumption owed something to anatomy, since the olfactory bulbs of songbirds are small relative to the rest of the brain, and something to the sheer difficulty of designing experiments to test it. Tube-nosed seabirds, the group that includes albatrosses, petrels and shearwaters, were always an awkward exception. Their nostrils are housed in prominent tubes along the top of the bill, and their olfactory bulbs are among the largest, proportionally, of any bird. Even so, the suggestion that such species might use odours not merely to locate food but to navigate across thousands of kilometres of featureless ocean was, until fairly recently, treated with polite disbelief.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first breakthrough concerned foraging. Dr Begoña Irigoyen of the Southern Ocean Research Unit drew attention to dimethyl sulphide, or DMS, a compound released into the air when microscopic animals graze on phytoplankton. Because grazing is most intense where nutrients are abundant, concentrations of DMS are elevated over continental shelves, seamounts and other productive areas. The ocean, which appears uniform to a human observer, may therefore present a seabird with an odour landscape of considerable complexity. To test this, Irigoyen's team released DMS from floating platforms and recorded which birds approached. Several petrel species arrived in large numbers, while others ignored the scent entirely; the strongest responses came from species that nest in burrows and return to their colonies under cover of darkness.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Finding food, however, is not the same as finding home. The most influential navigation experiments were carried out by a team under the behavioural biologist Ettore Pacchierotti, working with shearwaters breeding on a Mediterranean island. Adult birds were captured at the colony and divided into three groups. One group was made temporarily unable to smell by means of a nasal wash; a second had small magnets attached to the head, intended to disrupt any magnetic sense; and a third was left untreated. All were released several hundred kilometres away at sea and followed with miniature GPS loggers. The birds carrying magnets returned as quickly and directly as the untreated controls. The birds deprived of smell, by contrast, wandered over the open sea in no consistent direction and reached the colony only after they had encountered a stretch of coastline they apparently recognised, often days later. Pacchierotti concluded that smell is essential for navigating over the open ocean and that magnetic information plays no part.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The work did not go unchallenged. The sensory ecologist Feodora Lisitsyna argued that the original nasal treatment might have had side effects, leaving the birds unwell or simply less motivated to fly home. A sick bird, she pointed out, might fail to home even if its navigation system were entirely intact. Pacchierotti's group responded with a second series of experiments using a short-acting local anaesthetic, which blocks smell for only a few hours. The results were similar, and the anosmic birds were observed diving and feeding at sea in the normal way, which suggests that they were not generally impaired. This does not settle the matter entirely, but it does make the illness explanation considerably harder to sustain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How odours could supply a map remains an open question. One proposal, originally developed for homing pigeons, holds that birds at their home site learn to associate particular smells with the direction of the wind that carries them. When displaced, a bird that detects a familiar odour can infer which way home lies. For this to work at sea, the odour landscape would need to be reasonably predictable. Modelling by the atmospheric chemist Kalolaine Hufanga indicates that it may be: because DMS hotspots are tied to fixed features of the seabed, the broad pattern remains fairly stable over periods of several weeks. Hufanga cautions, though, that strong winds can smear scent plumes across hundreds of kilometres, so a bird's picture of the landscape must be relatively coarse.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the evidence that smell is necessary for ocean navigation in these birds now appears strong. Whether it is sufficient is another matter, and it seems likely that seabirds combine odour with other cues, such as the position of the sun and the sight of land, much as human sailors once combined several imperfect instruments. Pacchierotti's dismissal of magnetic information, moreover, goes further than his data allow. Magnets attached to the head may disrupt one kind of magnetic sense while leaving another unaffected, so the failure of the treatment to alter behaviour shows only that one possible mechanism was not needed in that particular experiment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The research has acquired practical significance. Investigators at the Coastal Debris Observatory have shown that floating plastic, once colonised by algae, gives off DMS, which may explain why tube-nosed seabirds swallow so much of it: to a bird that hunts by smell, plastic can quite literally smell like food. Warming seas, too, are altering the distribution of phytoplankton, and with it the odour landscape on which these species appear to rely. If the map is changing, birds that depend on it could find navigation increasingly unreliable. That possibility deserves far more attention than it currently receives.

topic: miniature tracking devices and their limitations in the study of songbird migration
title: Small Devices, Long Journeys
subtitle: Miniature tracking tags have revealed migrations that no one suspected, but the technology brings blind spots of its own

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until a few decades ago, almost everything known about the routes of small migratory birds came from ringing: fitting a numbered metal band to a bird's leg and hoping that someone, somewhere, would find it again. Recovery rates for songbirds were typically well below one per cent, and the few records that came back revealed where a bird had been at two points in its life, but nothing about the journey in between. Migration was thus mapped largely through inference, with arrows drawn between breeding and wintering areas whose connections were assumed rather than demonstrated. The arrival of miniature tracking devices has changed this picture more profoundly than any development since ringing itself began.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first of these devices to be widely used on small birds was the light-level geolocator. It contains no transmitter; instead, it records the intensity of daylight at regular intervals. Because the timing of sunrise and sunset varies with location, day length indicates latitude and the time of solar noon indicates longitude, so a bird's approximate position can be reconstructed once the device is retrieved. Geolocators weighing under a gram allowed researchers, for the first time, to follow birds as small as warblers across continents. Their limitations are considerable, however. Positions are accurate only to within roughly 150 to 200 kilometres, latitude cannot be estimated at all around the equinoxes, when day length is much the same everywhere, and the bird must be recaptured, usually a year later, before any data can be obtained.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even so, the results have overturned several long-standing assumptions. A programme coordinated by the ornithologist Dr Aurelio Santangelo, which fitted geolocators to more than a dozen species of European songbird, found that many birds believed to fly more or less directly to Africa in fact paused for weeks at a time in regions that had never been regarded as important. Some populations even divided the winter between two widely separated areas, moving between them in midwinter. Santangelo argues that conservation planning, which has traditionally concentrated on breeding and wintering grounds, has overlooked stopover sites where birds may spend as much as a third of their migratory period, and where the loss of a single wetland could affect an entire population.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Geolocators are now being supplemented, and in some cases replaced, by GPS tags and satellite transmitters, which offer far greater precision and send their data remotely, so that the bird need never be caught again. Until recently such devices were too heavy for anything smaller than a large gull, but receiving systems in orbit are now being designed to collect signals from tags weighing only a few grams. The electronics engineer Wouter Haesaerts, who works on these systems, predicts that within ten years it will be routine to follow individual insects across continents. His enthusiasm is understandable, but it underestimates the stubborn physics involved: a transmitter needs power, power requires a battery or a solar panel, and both add weight that the smallest animals simply cannot carry.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Weight is also at the centre of an ethical debate. Field researchers have long worked to a convention that a device should weigh no more than three per cent of an animal's body mass. The behavioural ecologist Golnaz Daneshvar reviewed several hundred tracking studies and found that tagged birds had, on average, slightly lower survival and breeding success than untagged ones. More strikingly, she found that the three per cent figure had never been tested experimentally, and that the method of attachment, whether by harness, glue or leg loop, often mattered more than the device's weight. She proposes that the single rule be replaced by assessments tailored to each species. Her argument is persuasive, although a simple threshold does have the merit of being easy to enforce, and the more flexible alternative would demand expertise that ethics committees do not always possess.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A subtler problem lies in what tracking data leave out. Geolocators reveal the journeys only of birds that survive to be recaptured; the devices carried by birds that die along the way are almost never recovered. Studies based on them therefore describe successful migrations, and may underestimate how dangerous particular routes are. This survivorship bias is arguably the most serious weakness of such research, and it is one that published studies too rarely acknowledge. Satellite tags reduce the problem, since they continue to transmit until the battery fails, but they are still largely restricted to larger species, so that the smallest migrants remain the least understood.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes what the new technology has achieved. Yet it would be a mistake to imagine that tags can replace traditional fieldwork. A geolocator can show that a warbler spent three weeks in a particular valley; it cannot explain what the bird was eating there, whether the habitat was adequate, or why that site, rather than another, was chosen. Answering such questions still requires people on the ground with binoculars and notebooks, and the most revealing studies of recent years have been those that combined both approaches.

topic: radar studies of high-altitude insect migration
title: Rivers in the Sky
subtitle: Trillions of insects migrate high above our heads every year. Radar has only recently begun to reveal the scale of the movement, and its consequences

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a warm night in late summer, the air a few hundred metres above the farmland of southern England may contain more travellers than any motorway. Moths, beetles, lacewings and aphids drift, flap and glide past in their millions, almost all of them invisible from the ground. For a long time, insect migration was regarded as a curiosity confined to a handful of conspicuous species, of which the monarch butterfly was the standard example. That view has now been comprehensively overturned. It appears that insect migration is, by sheer weight of numbers and of biomass, the most important annual animal movement on land, dwarfing the far better-known seasonal journeys of songbirds.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the evidence comes from specialised radars that point straight upwards and record the insects passing through their beams. Over a decade of continuous monitoring, a team led by the entomologist Dr Crispin Haverstock at the Rothmere Agricultural Research Station estimated that some three and a half trillion insects, with a combined mass of more than three thousand tonnes, cross the skies of southern Britain each year. The radars can detect and characterise individual insects heavier than about ten milligrams, recording their size, speed and heading. The far more numerous smaller species, which are invisible to the radar, are sampled instead with nets suspended from tethered balloons, and their numbers are then extrapolated.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most surprising finding concerns the larger moths. Far from being blown about at random, they appear to select the altitudes at which winds are fastest and are blowing in the seasonally appropriate direction, northwards in spring and southwards in autumn. Moreover, their headings are often offset from the wind direction in a way that partly corrects for drift. Haverstock's group concludes that the moths possess some form of compass and can, remarkably, sense the direction of the wind even at night and hundreds of metres above the ground, perhaps by detecting the subtle patterns of turbulence within the air. Individual radar tracks, they report, show moths adjusting their headings within minutes of a change in wind direction.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this interpretation. The theoretical ecologist Ondřej Kratochvíl argues that much of the apparent selectivity could arise without any sophisticated sensing at all. Insects that happen to take off on nights when the winds are favourable will travel further and spend longer aloft than those that do not, and so will be over-represented in radar samples. The pattern, in other words, may say more about which insects the radar happens to record than about the decisions the insects make. Kratochvíl's warning is a valuable methodological caution, and it should make researchers wary of reading purpose into aggregate data. It does not, however, easily account for the individual tracks, in which the same moth can be seen changing course as the wind shifts.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Daytime migrants have attracted rather less attention, which is unfortunate, since some of them perform services of considerable value. The ecologist Zanele Sithebe has studied hoverflies, which travel south across Europe each autumn in their billions. As adults they pollinate a wide range of crops and wild flowers along their route; as larvae, many species feed voraciously on aphids, among the most damaging of agricultural pests. Sithebe estimates that the larvae produced by these migrants consume several trillion aphids annually in Britain alone. She argues that the economic contribution of such insects is greatly underestimated, and that agricultural policy ought to take them into account, for example by protecting the flowering field margins on which the adults feed during their journey.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Migration is not, of course, always beneficial to farmers. Several serious crop pests are long-distance migrants, arriving suddenly and in vast numbers from hundreds of kilometres away. The agricultural forecaster Henrique Coelho points out that the national weather radar networks operated in many countries already detect such insect swarms, but that the signals are routinely filtered out as clutter by software designed to measure rainfall. Coelho believes that this information could form the basis of an early warning system, giving farmers several days to prepare for an invasion. It is remarkable that data of such obvious potential value are discarded as a matter of routine.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The radar studies have also been drawn into the wider debate about insect decline. Reports from ground-level surveys in several countries have suggested alarming reductions in insect abundance over recent decades. Haverstock's data, by contrast, show no clear downward trend in the numbers of high-flying migrants over the monitoring period. This finding has occasionally been cited as reassuring, but it should not be read in that way. Ten years is a short period in which to detect a trend in populations that fluctuate enormously from one year to the next, and the migrants that dominate the radar record tend to be adaptable species that thrive in intensively farmed landscapes. Their persistence tells us little about the fate of more specialised insects.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is a picture of an entire layer of the ecosystem that has, until recently, gone almost entirely unnoticed. As the climate warms and wind patterns shift, the timing and direction of these aerial movements are likely to change, with consequences for pollination, pest control and crop damage that no one is yet in a position to predict.

topic: learned migration and cultural transmission in hoofed mammals
title: Knowing the Way
subtitle: Some large mammals are not born knowing where to migrate. They have to learn, and what is learned can be lost

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the seasonal movements of hoofed mammals such as deer, wild sheep, elk and antelope were assumed to be largely instinctive. Every spring, herds in mountainous regions climb from sheltered winter ranges in the valleys to summer pastures high above, and every autumn they return, often along the same paths their ancestors followed. The regularity of the pattern seemed to speak of a fixed inheritance, comparable perhaps to the inborn programmes that guide young songbirds on their first journey south. Over the past two decades, however, evidence has accumulated that for many of these animals migration is not so much inherited as learned, and that the knowledge on which it depends is passed from one generation to the next.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A useful starting point is the question of why such animals migrate at all. In spring, new plant growth begins in the lowlands and gradually advances uphill as the snow retreats. Young shoots are far richer in protein and easier to digest than mature vegetation, and an animal that moves upward in step with this advancing wave of growth can feed on high-quality forage for weeks longer than one that stays in a single place. Ecologists describe this behaviour as surfing the green wave, and the benefits it brings can be measured directly. The ecologist Tadhg Ó Murchú, who has tracked several thousand animals with GPS collars, has shown that individuals that surf the wave most closely gain more weight over the summer and are more likely to raise offspring successfully.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The decisive evidence for learning came from an unplanned experiment. Throughout the last century, wildlife agencies reintroduced wild sheep and moose into regions from which they had been eliminated by hunting, releasing animals into landscapes that were entirely unfamiliar to them. Ó Murchú's team compared the movements of herds that had been released at different times, from a few years to more than a century earlier. Recently translocated animals rarely migrated, and those that did tracked the green wave poorly. Herds that had occupied their new range for many decades, by contrast, migrated almost as precisely as native populations. The implication is that migration routes are built up gradually, as each generation explores and refines what the previous one discovered. These findings have significant implications for wildlife management, yet they have received far less attention outside specialist circles than they deserve.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The behavioural ecologist Boglárka Vámosi has examined how such knowledge spreads. Her observations suggest that calves and lambs learn routes principally by accompanying their mothers during their first year, and that adults occasionally adopt new routes after travelling with other members of the herd. She describes the accumulated knowledge of a herd as a form of animal culture. The term remains contested, with some researchers arguing that it should be reserved for behaviour that is more complex or more clearly variable between groups. Yet the dispute over vocabulary should not distract from the central point, which is that an essential survival skill can exist only so long as it is transmitted socially.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every researcher accepts that learning tells the whole story. The population geneticist Daniyar Zhaksybekov notes that many reintroduced herds were drawn from source populations that did not themselves migrate, and suggests that an inherited predisposition to stay put may have slowed the development of migration in their descendants. This is a reasonable hypothesis, and it is probable that genes contribute something to the tendency to explore. It cannot, though, explain why herds taken from strongly migratory populations also failed to migrate when first released, and on balance the case for learning as the dominant factor remains considerably stronger.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practical consequences are considerable. In many regions migration routes are being cut by fences, highways and energy developments. The wildlife manager Rosalía Pomareda warns that once a migration has been abandoned, removing the barrier that caused its loss will not necessarily restore it, because the animals that knew the route may no longer be alive to lead others along it. She argues that the most effective strategy is to identify and protect existing corridors before they are severed. Her point exposes a weakness in conventional planning, which tends to treat areas of habitat as interchangeable, so that land lost in one place can be compensated for by land protected elsewhere. That assumption is mistaken where migration is concerned: a herd cannot simply transfer its knowledge to an unfamiliar landscape.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Similar findings have emerged from other groups of animals. Captive-reared cranes released without older companions, for example, have been reported to wander aimlessly rather than follow traditional flyways, and conservationists have resorted to guiding young birds south behind light aircraft in an attempt to teach them a route. Some whale populations, too, appear to inherit their feeding grounds from their mothers rather than through their genes. The assumption that migration is simply instinctive made it easy to overlook how fragile such behaviour can be. If an inherited programme can survive a temporary collapse in numbers, a learned tradition may not, and some of the migrations that have disappeared in recent decades may already be beyond recovery.

topic: climate change and timing mismatch in long-distance migratory birds
title: Arriving Too Late
subtitle: As European springs arrive earlier, many migratory birds are struggling to keep pace. But the idea of 'mismatch' may be less straightforward than it sounds

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A small songbird spending the winter in West Africa has no way of knowing what the weather is like in the European woodland where it will breed. It cannot feel the warmth of an early spring five thousand kilometres away, nor see the oak leaves opening. Instead, the timing of its departure is governed by an internal annual clock, which is calibrated by changes in day length on its wintering grounds. For thousands of years this arrangement served long-distance migrants well, because spring in Europe arrived at roughly the same time each year. As the climate warms, however, that reliability has broken down. Spring now comes earlier in much of the continent, and birds that keep to their traditional schedule risk arriving after the moment of greatest food abundance has passed. Ecologists call this phenomenon phenological mismatch.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-documented case comes from Kessenholt, a mixed woodland in which pied flycatchers have been monitored for more than three decades by a team under Dr Hedda Valkonen. Over that period, the annual peak in the abundance of caterpillars, the food on which the birds feed their nestlings, has advanced by around two weeks. The flycatchers' arrival date, by contrast, has moved forward by only a few days. The birds have partly compensated by starting to lay eggs sooner after their arrival, compressing the interval between the end of migration and the beginning of breeding. Even so, in the parts of the woodland where the caterpillar peak is earliest, Valkonen's team recorded population declines of up to ninety per cent, while in areas with a later peak numbers remained comparatively stable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why do the birds not simply leave Africa earlier? The physiologist Tafadzwa Mukarumbwa argues that they are constrained by the very mechanism that once made them so punctual. Because the departure signal is day length, and day length is unaffected by global warming, a bird's internal clock offers no information about conditions at its destination. Only an evolutionary change in the clock itself, or in its sensitivity to day length, would allow migrants to set off sooner. Mukarumbwa points out, however, that some species have managed to advance their arrival without leaving earlier, by travelling faster and spending less time at stopover sites along the way, which suggests that the constraint is not absolute.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are convinced that mismatch deserves the prominence it has acquired. The population ecologist Léonie Cassagnou argues that the concept rests on an oversimplified picture in which each species depends on a single, sharply defined food peak. In reality, she observes, many migrants feed their young on a wide variety of prey, and the decline of several species has coincided with drought in their African wintering grounds and the loss of wetlands on their migration routes. A review of more than sixty species that she conducted concluded that mismatch could explain population trends in only a minority of them. Cassagnou is right to resist explanations that blame a single cause for complex declines. Her review, however, grouped together species with very different diets, an approach that may well have diluted the effect of mismatch in those species that genuinely depend on a brief food peak.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also some cause for cautious optimism. If individuals that arrive early raise more young, natural selection should favour earlier arrival, and the trait appears to be at least partly heritable. The evolutionary biologist Rhoswen Penhallow has analysed arrival records from a northern population of flycatchers and found that the average date has advanced over twenty years at a rate consistent with genetic change, rather than with individual birds merely adjusting their behaviour. This is an encouraging result, but it would be unwise to treat it as a solution. Evolution of this kind takes place over many generations, and there is little reason to expect it to keep pace with a climate that is changing as quickly as the present one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Long-distance migrants also face a problem that has attracted less attention than it deserves. Species that winter within Europe, such as many tits, can respond directly to local temperatures and have advanced their breeding far more than their long-distance competitors. Where both compete for the same nest holes, earlier-breeding residents may occupy the best sites before the migrants arrive, and there are records of flycatchers being killed by tits in disputes over nest boxes. The consequences of such shifts in competitive balance remain poorly understood, and it is not yet clear whether they will prove more or less damaging than mismatch itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, can be done? Some conservationists propose improving the condition of stopover sites, so that birds can refuel more quickly and complete their journeys sooner. Others suggest that woodland managers could influence the timing of the caterpillar peak by altering the mix of tree species, since caterpillars emerge at different times on different trees, thereby extending the period during which food is plentiful. Such measures are worth pursuing, and they may buy valuable time. None of them, though, can substitute for reducing the warming that created the problem in the first place.

topic: competing explanations for the long-distance migrations of baleen whales
title: The Long Swim to Warm Water
subtitle: Every year, great whales abandon rich polar feeding grounds for warm but food-poor tropical seas. Why they do so is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Humpback and grey whales undertake some of the longest migrations of any mammal, travelling up to 8,000 kilometres each way between feeding grounds near the poles and breeding areas in the tropics. At first sight the behaviour makes little sense. The cold waters of high latitudes are rich in krill and small fish, while tropical seas offer almost nothing a large whale can eat. For several months of every year, therefore, the animals fast, living on reserves of blubber and losing as much as a third of their body mass. Moreover, some polar regions remain productive well into the winter. An animal that simply stayed where the food was would, one might suppose, be better off. The fact that so many whales do not has given rise to a long-running debate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The traditional explanation concerns the young. Newborn calves have relatively thin layers of blubber, and it has long been argued that they would lose heat dangerously quickly in polar seas. The marine mammal physiologist Dr Kaito Hirasawa has refined this argument, suggesting that the problem is not survival as such but efficiency: a calf born in warm, calm water can devote energy to growth that would otherwise be spent on keeping warm. This version of the hypothesis is more sophisticated than the original, but the argument as a whole is less persuasive than it first appears. Whale calves are large at birth, and because large bodies lose heat slowly relative to their volume, models suggest that even newborns could tolerate cold water for extended periods.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second explanation emphasises danger rather than temperature. Killer whales, which prey on the calves of larger species, are considerably more abundant at high latitudes, and the biologist Yesenia Cutipa argues that giving birth in the tropics substantially reduces the risk of attack. In support, she points to the parallel tooth marks found on the tails of many adult humpbacks, most of which appear to have been acquired when the animals were very young. The hypothesis is plausible, but it is extremely difficult to test, since researchers can hardly compare the survival of calves born in different waters under controlled conditions. It should also be noted that killer whales are by no means absent from tropical seas.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most recent proposal is also the most unexpected. A group led by Tormod Lysgaard at the Southern Cetacean Institute has suggested that whales migrate in order to maintain their skin. In cold water, a whale restricts circulation to its skin to conserve body heat, and Lysgaard argues that this slows the regeneration of skin cells. Travelling to warmer water, he suggests, allows circulation to resume, so that old skin can be shed together with the films of algae that accumulate on it. Tracking data show that not only pregnant females but also juveniles and adults with no breeding role make the journey, and some whales visit tropical waters only briefly before heading back towards the poles. Whales photographed in warm water, Lysgaard's group reports, also tend to have noticeably cleaner skin than those in polar regions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The strength of this hypothesis is that it explains something the calving explanation cannot: why animals that will not give birth undertake such costly journeys. Its weakness is that the central mechanism has not yet been demonstrated. No one has measured the rate at which whale skin regenerates at different temperatures, and the evidence for the theory remains largely circumstantial. Critics also point out that seals, which face similar problems, solve them by leaving the water to moult on land or ice, rather than by travelling vast distances. These objections are reasonable, but they do not show that the theory is wrong, only that it is incomplete.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Indeed, it is increasingly doubtful whether any single explanation will suffice. Underwater microphones moored in polar waters have recorded humpback song throughout the winter months, indicating that a proportion of the population does not migrate at all. Those that stay appear to be mainly juveniles and females that are not pregnant. This pattern suggests that migration is not a fixed rule but a strategy whose costs and benefits differ between individuals, and it seems likely that warmth, safety and skin maintenance all contribute in varying degrees. To treat the competing hypotheses as rivals, of which only one can be correct, is probably a mistake.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question is not merely academic. As sea ice retreats and prey species shift their ranges in response to warming oceans, the balance of costs and benefits that shapes whale migration is changing. Coastal communities in the tropics that depend on the seasonal arrival of whales for tourism have an obvious interest in whether those visits will continue. Only by understanding why whales migrate in the first place will scientists be able to anticipate how their behaviour may alter, and the answer is likely to involve several factors rather than one.

topic: the diet-heart hypothesis and the reassessment of saturated fat
title: The Long Shadow of the Fat Hypothesis
subtitle: Decades after saturated fat was cast as the chief villain of heart disease, scientists still argue about how the original case was built

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the second half of the twentieth century, few nutritional ideas enjoyed greater authority than the claim that saturated fat, found abundantly in butter, cheese and fatty meat, raised blood cholesterol and thereby caused heart disease. The proposition, usually called the diet-heart hypothesis, shaped official guidelines, led to the reformulation of thousands of supermarket products and altered the eating habits of entire nations. In recent years, however, it has become fashionable to describe the hypothesis as a scientific blunder, the product of flawed studies and forceful personalities. That revisionist account contains some truth, but it is at least as oversimplified as the orthodoxy it seeks to replace.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The original case rested on three kinds of evidence. Laboratory feeding experiments showed that replacing saturated fat with vegetable oils lowered cholesterol in the blood within a matter of weeks. Comparisons between countries revealed that populations eating the most animal fat tended to suffer the highest rates of coronary disease. And long-term studies of individuals linked high cholesterol to later heart attacks. Each strand, taken alone, was open to objection; the persuasiveness of the hypothesis came from the way the strands appeared to converge. According to the historian of medicine Ilse Kasprzyk of the Institute for Health Policy History, it was this convergence, rather than any single decisive experiment, that convinced the committees drafting dietary advice in the 1970s.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics have directed most of their fire at the international comparisons. The epidemiologist Tobias Halvorsrud of the Centre for Evidence Review argues that the countries chosen for the most influential of these studies were not a random sample, and that including others would have weakened the apparent relationship considerably. He also notes that nations with rich diets differed from poorer ones in smoking rates, physical activity and sugar consumption, any of which might explain their higher mortality. Halvorsrud's point about confounding is well taken. Yet his further suggestion that the selection of countries was deliberately manipulated is not supported by the archival record, which shows the researchers working with whatever reliable statistics happened to be available at the time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of criticism concerns the randomised trials of the 1960s and 1970s, in which patients in hospitals and care homes were assigned either a normal diet or one in which saturated fat had been replaced by vegetable oils. Several of these trials were never fully published, and when the raw data from one large study were recovered and reanalysed decades later, the group eating vegetable oils showed lower cholesterol but no reduction in deaths; if anything, the oldest participants fared slightly worse. Some commentators have treated this finding as fatal to the hypothesis. That conclusion seems premature. The trials were short, many participants left before completing them, and the margarines of the era contained trans fats, now known to be harmful in their own right.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of mainstream advice, among them the cardiologist Amara Okereke of the Lagos Cardiovascular Research Unit, emphasise a different body of evidence. Modern genetic studies, she points out, have found that people who inherit variants causing lifelong low cholesterol have markedly fewer heart attacks, while drugs that lower cholesterol reduce cardiac events roughly in proportion to the reduction achieved. For Okereke, these findings settle the question of whether cholesterol in the blood causes heart disease. What they do not settle, she concedes, is how much any particular dietary change will alter cholesterol in a free-living population, where people who give up one food tend to compensate by eating more of another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This question of substitution may be the most important lesson of the whole controversy. When manufacturers removed fat from biscuits, yoghurts and ready meals, they frequently added refined starch and sugar to preserve flavour and texture. A diet that is low in saturated fat but rich in white bread and sweetened drinks is unlikely to protect the heart, and studies that compare saturated fat with all other sources of calories combined therefore tend to find little effect. The nutritionist Paulo Ferreirinha of the Coimbra School of Public Health has shown that the apparent benefit depends heavily on the replacement: substituting unsaturated oils, nuts or whole grains is associated with lower risk, whereas substituting refined carbohydrate is not.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the general public? The temptation, encouraged by a number of popular books, is to conclude that the experts got everything wrong and that butter has become a health food. Such a conclusion misreads the evidence just as badly as the original simplifications did. What the controversy really exposes is the difficulty of turning findings about single nutrients into advice about whole diets. Guidelines that speak of foods and eating patterns, rather than isolated components, are harder to summarise in a slogan, but they are considerably less likely to be overturned by the next generation of research.

topic: the reliability of self-reported diet and food frequency questionnaires in nutritional epidemiology
title: Remembering What We Ate
subtitle: Much of what we are told about diet and health depends on people describing their own meals. How far can such reports be trusted?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every newspaper story claiming that coffee protects the liver or that eggs harm the heart can be traced back to a simple research tool: the food frequency questionnaire. Participants are given a list of perhaps 120 foods and asked how often, over the previous year, they consumed each one. Because the questionnaire is cheap and can be completed at home, it can be distributed to hundreds of thousands of people and repeated over decades, which is why it dominates large studies of diet and disease. It is also widely mocked. My own view is that the method deserves neither the blind trust of those who publish such headlines nor the contempt it increasingly attracts from its critics.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulties are easy to list. People forget what they ate, struggle to estimate portion sizes and, consciously or not, report the diet they think they ought to have rather than the one they actually have. Teodora Valkanova of the Plovdiv Institute of Nutrition has measured the scale of the problem by comparing the energy intake people report with their energy expenditure, which can be measured accurately using a harmless form of labelled water. Her studies reveal that energy intake is typically under-reported by between a fifth and a third, and that the gap is widest among participants with higher body weight. Because the errors are not random, she argues, they can create or conceal associations between foods and disease.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cormac Feeheny, a statistician at the Galway Centre for Population Health, draws a more radical conclusion. Reviewing a national survey, he found that a large proportion of the reported intakes were physiologically implausible, being too low to keep a living adult alive. Data of this quality, in his opinion, should no longer be used to guide public policy at all. Feeheny has done valuable work in exposing the extent of misreporting, but his conclusion goes too far. Food frequency questionnaires were never designed to measure exactly how much a person eats. Their purpose is to rank people relative to one another, distinguishing those who eat a great deal of a food from those who eat little, and for that task they can perform reasonably well.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This is the position taken by Haruki Tamashiro, an epidemiologist at the Ryukyu Cohort Study. Validation studies, he notes, compare questionnaire answers with detailed weighed food records kept over several days and with biomarkers, objective measurements such as the nitrogen excreted in urine, which reflects protein intake. The correlations are usually moderate rather than strong, but they are high enough to separate the highest consumers from the lowest. Tamashiro also advocates calibration, in which a subgroup of participants provides biomarker data that are then used to correct the errors of the whole sample. He concedes, however, that the technique can only be applied to the handful of nutrients for which reliable biomarkers exist.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different weakness lies not in the questionnaire but in what researchers do with it. When hundreds of foods are tested against dozens of diseases, some striking associations will appear by chance alone. Wanjiru Oduya of the Nairobi School of Public Health argues that the real problem is a publication culture that rewards surprising findings, and she has called for researchers to register their planned analyses before examining the data. Oduya has also pointed out that questionnaires developed in Europe and North America often omit staple foods eaten elsewhere, so that the diets of whole populations are poorly captured. Of the reforms currently proposed, I believe her call for pre-registration is the most urgent, since better measurement achieves little if results are selectively reported.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Technology is frequently presented as the answer. Lucia Garavito, who designs dietary tracking software, predicts that smartphone photographs and small wearable cameras will soon make questionnaires obsolete, because they record meals as they are eaten instead of relying on memory. Some systems already use image recognition to estimate portion sizes automatically, although their accuracy with mixed dishes such as stews, soups and curries remains disappointing. These tools undoubtedly reduce the burden on recall. Yet they introduce a problem of their own, known as reactivity: people who know that their meals are being recorded tend to simplify their diets or eat less, so the act of measurement alters the very behaviour being measured. It is therefore unlikely that any device will remove inaccuracy entirely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that self-reported data are worthless. The obvious alternative, randomised trials in which people are assigned different diets and followed for decades until they develop disease, would be impractical and, in many cases, unethical. Nutritional science therefore has to combine imperfect sources: questionnaires, biomarkers, shorter feeding trials and studies of genetic variation. The sensible response is to treat any single questionnaire-based study as a starting point for further investigation rather than a conclusion, and to grow suspicious when a headline announces that one food has suddenly become dangerous or miraculous.

topic: salt reduction policy and the disputed J-shaped curve of sodium intake
title: A Pinch of Controversy
subtitle: Health authorities urge almost everyone to eat less salt, but a determined minority of researchers questions whether the advice should apply to all

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few pieces of dietary advice have been repeated as consistently as the instruction to eat less salt. International health bodies recommend that adults consume no more than five grams a day, roughly a level teaspoon, yet in many countries average intake is close to double that figure. Contrary to popular belief, the salt cellar is a minor culprit: around three-quarters of the salt in a typical Western diet is already present in bread, processed meat, sauces and ready meals by the time they are bought. The scientific dispute over salt is narrower than its tone would suggest. Few nutritional debates, in fact, have generated so much heat in proportion to the actual size of the disagreement.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for reduction begins with blood pressure. Sodium, the component of salt that matters physiologically, causes the body to retain water and raises the pressure in the arteries, and high blood pressure is a leading cause of stroke and heart disease. In carefully controlled feeding trials, in which participants ate prepared meals for a month at a time, lowering salt reliably reduced blood pressure, with the largest falls among older people and those already diagnosed with hypertension. Eleni Mavropoulou of the Hellenic Institute for Cardiovascular Prevention also points to a national programme launched in a northern European country in the 1970s, during which salt intake fell by about a third over three decades while deaths from stroke declined dramatically. She considers it the strongest real-world evidence available. It is persuasive, but smoking rates and cholesterol levels also fell during the same period, so the share of the improvement attributable to salt is impossible to determine precisely.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The challenge to the consensus comes from a series of large observational studies that estimated the sodium intake of tens of thousands of people in many countries and then tracked their health. Several reported a J-shaped curve: cardiovascular events were least common at moderate intakes and rose not only at high intakes but also at low ones. Nalin Abeywardena of the Kandy Centre for Population Studies, who led one such study, suggests that very low sodium intake may activate hormonal systems that constrict blood vessels and strain the heart. In his view, advice to cut salt should be targeted only at populations whose consumption is high, rather than applied to everybody.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics have identified two weaknesses in these studies. First, most estimated sodium intake from a single sample of urine collected in the morning, yet the amount of sodium a person excretes varies greatly from day to day, so a single measurement is a poor guide to habitual diet. Second, people who are already ill often eat less, or have been advised by their doctors to reduce their salt, which could make low intake appear dangerous when it is in fact a consequence of poor health. Gunnar Arnasson of the Reykjavik Institute of Epidemiology re-examined data from a trial in which participants had provided several complete twenty-four-hour urine collections. When intake was measured in this way, risk rose steadily with sodium, and the upturn at low intakes disappeared. Arnasson's analysis is the more convincing of the two, although its participants were mostly middle-aged Europeans, which limits how far its conclusions can be applied elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective shifts attention away from sodium alone. Kalala Mbuyamba of the Kinshasa School of Public Health argues that the ratio between sodium and potassium predicts cardiovascular risk more accurately than sodium by itself. Potassium, abundant in fruit, vegetables and pulses, helps the kidneys to excrete sodium and appears to counteract some of its effects on blood pressure. In a trial conducted across hundreds of rural villages, households that replaced ordinary salt with a substitute in which part of the sodium chloride was swapped for potassium chloride experienced significantly fewer strokes. This result, which costs very little to put into practice, ranks among the most important in nutrition research for decades. Substitutes of this kind are not suitable for everyone, however, since people with kidney disease may be unable to excrete excess potassium safely.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In practice, most governments have relied on persuading manufacturers to reformulate their products. Because taste preferences adapt within a few weeks, the salt content of bread can be lowered in small annual steps without customers noticing, and several countries have achieved substantial reductions in this way. Voluntary targets, though, tend to be met by some companies and ignored by others, which has led some public health researchers to call for legally binding limits. Whatever the eventual resolution of the J-curve dispute, its practical relevance to policy is slight: very few populations anywhere consume salt at the low levels where the alleged danger is supposed to begin.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The salt controversy illustrates a recurring pattern in nutrition science, in which observational studies with imperfect measurements are set against trials that are too short to record deaths. Neither kind of evidence is decisive alone. Until a trial large and long enough to settle the question is funded, the balance of evidence still favours moderate reduction for most people, combined with a greater emphasis on the fruit and vegetables that supply potassium.

topic: non-nutritive sweeteners and their disputed effects on weight and metabolism
title: Sweetness Without Sugar
subtitle: Once hailed as a solution to obesity, low-calorie sweeteners now attract suspicion. What does the evidence really show?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ingredients have travelled as strange a path through public opinion as non-nutritive sweeteners. Compounds such as aspartame, sucralose and purified extracts of the stevia leaf are hundreds of times sweeter than table sugar, so a minute quantity can sweeten a drink while contributing virtually no energy. When they first appeared in mass-market products, they were welcomed as an elegant technical answer to rising rates of obesity: the pleasure of sweetness could, it seemed, be separated from its metabolic cost. Today the same substances are routinely described as hidden threats to health. In my view, both the original enthusiasm and the current alarm have run well ahead of what the evidence can support, and the debate has suffered from a tendency to treat a family of chemically unrelated compounds as if they were a single substance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case in favour rests largely on simple arithmetic. A can of sugar-sweetened soft drink contains roughly 140 kilocalories; its artificially sweetened equivalent contains almost none. If people make the substitution and do not compensate by eating more elsewhere, they should gradually lose weight. Professor Ingrid Brekkhus of the Bergen Institute of Nutrition has pooled the results of randomised controlled trials in which participants were assigned either to sweetened or to sugary beverages, and reports small but consistent reductions in body weight over periods of up to eighteen months. Brekkhus concedes that the effect is modest, amounting to little more than a kilogram on average, but she insists that, applied across an entire population, a shift of this size would be far from trivial.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Large observational studies tell a different story. When researchers follow tens of thousands of adults for a decade or more, those who drink artificially sweetened beverages most often turn out to be more likely to gain weight and to develop type 2 diabetes than those who rarely consume them. The most widely accepted explanation is reverse causation: people who are already overweight, or who have been warned that their blood sugar is rising, are precisely the ones most likely to switch to diet products. Statistical adjustment can reduce this bias but never eliminate it entirely. I find this explanation largely convincing, yet it would be a mistake to treat it as a reason to ignore the observational data altogether, since the association has appeared too consistently, across too many populations, to be dismissed out of hand.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Several biological mechanisms have been proposed to account for a genuinely harmful effect. Dr Mateus Vilaverde, a physiologist at the Paraná Centre for Metabolic Research, has argued that tasting sweetness without receiving the expected calories may weaken the body's learned association between sweet flavours and energy, so that appetite is regulated less accurately and more food is eaten later. In laboratory experiments, rats given saccharin-sweetened yoghurt gained more weight than rats given yoghurt sweetened with glucose. These results are intriguing, but the doses involved were often far higher, relative to body weight, than any human would plausibly consume, and people, unlike laboratory animals, encounter sweetness in a bewildering variety of foods and contexts. Whether such a finely tuned learning process survives the complexity of a normal human diet remains entirely open.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more recent line of inquiry concerns the trillions of bacteria that inhabit the human gut. A team led by Dr Folasade Adeyinka-Bello at the Ibadan Centre for Gut Health gave volunteers daily doses of one of four sweeteners, within officially permitted limits, for a fortnight. Two of the compounds altered the composition of participants' gut bacteria, and in a subset of individuals this change was accompanied by a measurable decline in glucose tolerance. Strikingly, the response varied enormously from person to person: some volunteers showed pronounced changes, while others showed none at all. Adeyinka-Bello herself warns against reading too much into the findings, noting that the trial involved only around 120 people and lasted barely two weeks, but she believes they help to explain why population averages may conceal effects confined to particular groups.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Public understanding has not been helped by the way official assessments are communicated. When an international agency recently placed one widely used sweetener in a category described as 'possibly carcinogenic', the announcement generated alarming headlines around the world. Few reports noted that a separate expert committee, reviewing the same evidence, left the acceptable daily intake unchanged, or that the category in question also contains certain pickled vegetables. Dr Selim Karamanlı, who studies risk communication at the Ankara Institute of Public Policy, argues that classifications describing whether something could cause harm under any circumstances, its hazard, are routinely misread as statements about how likely it is to cause harm at normal levels of exposure. He contends that agencies should abandon such categories in public announcements altogether, a proposal that seems to me too drastic, since the remedy for poor explanation is surely better explanation rather than less information.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should consumers conclude? The most useful question is probably not whether sweeteners are good or bad in themselves, but what they are replacing. For a habitual drinker of sugary beverages, switching to a sweetened alternative is very likely to be an improvement, even if water would be better still. For someone who would otherwise drink water, there is little reason to begin consuming them. Above all, research should stop treating sweeteners as interchangeable. Sucralose, stevia extracts and aspartame differ in chemical structure, in how they are absorbed and in how they interact with gut bacteria, and it would be surprising if they all had identical effects on health.

topic: whether breakfast really is the most important meal of the day
title: The Most Important Meal?
subtitle: A century-old slogan about breakfast is finally being tested, and the results are more complicated than the cereal packet suggests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: 'Breakfast is the most important meal of the day' must be one of the most frequently repeated pieces of nutritional advice in the world. Parents recite it to reluctant children, and it appears on cereal packets, in school leaflets and in the guidance of numerous health authorities. Its history, however, is less distinguished than its ubiquity might suggest. The phrase was popularised in the early twentieth century by manufacturers of ready-to-eat cereals, who had an obvious interest in persuading households that the morning meal was indispensable. A commercial origin does not, of course, make a claim false. It should, however, make us cautious about accepting it simply because it is familiar, and over the past two decades researchers have begun to subject the slogan to the scrutiny it was long spared.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest support has come from observational research. Dr Bérénice Fauconnet, an epidemiologist at the Lyon Institute of Population Nutrition, has examined data from cohorts in eleven countries and finds that adults who regularly skip breakfast are, on average, heavier and more likely to develop heart disease than those who eat it. Breakfast skippers also tend to smoke more, drink more alcohol and sleep less, and sceptics have argued that these habits, rather than the missed meal, account for their poorer health. Fauconnet accepts that such factors explain part of the difference, but she reports that a significant association remains even after they have been statistically controlled for, and she interprets this as evidence that going without food in the morning disrupts the body's regulation of appetite and blood sugar.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Randomised trials have produced a rather different picture. Dr Kofi Abrokwah of the Kumasi Centre for Clinical Nutrition has combined the results of studies in which adults were instructed either to eat breakfast or to skip it for several weeks. Those assigned to breakfast consumed on average around 260 more kilocalories a day and did not compensate by eating less at lunch; if anything, they ended the trials slightly heavier. Abrokwah concludes that recommending breakfast as an aid to weight control has no basis in experimental evidence, and on that narrow point he is surely right. The trials were brief, however, and largely confined to healthy volunteers, so they reveal little about long-term cardiovascular risk. To read them as proof that breakfast confers no health benefits of any kind would be to ask more of them than they can deliver.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third perspective shifts attention from whether people eat in the morning to when they eat more generally. Dr Akane Mizushima, who studies biological rhythms at the Hokkaido Institute of Chronobiology, has shown that the body's sensitivity to insulin is typically higher early in the day. In her experiments, volunteers given an identical meal at eight in the morning and at eight in the evening showed markedly higher blood sugar after the evening meal. Mizushima argues that what matters is the distribution of energy across the day: consuming the bulk of one's calories late in the evening appears to be more harmful than skipping a morning meal, provided the largest meal is still eaten relatively early.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For children, the evidence carries a different emphasis. Dr Rodrigo Escalada, an education researcher at the Montevideo School of Social Policy, has evaluated free breakfast schemes in low-income districts of several South American cities. Attendance rose and performance in arithmetic tests improved, but the gains were concentrated almost entirely among pupils who arrived at school hungry; for children who had already eaten at home, an additional meal made no measurable difference. This suggests that school breakfast programmes are best understood as a means of tackling hunger rather than as proof of a universal rule about the morning meal.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Others question whether 'breakfast' is a meaningful category at all. Dr Laleh Farahmandi, a dietitian at the Shiraz Nutrition Research Unit, points out that the term covers everything from a bowl of sugary cereal or a pastry to eggs with wholegrain bread, and argues that the composition of a meal is far more important than the hour at which it is eaten. In her view, studies that simply compare eaters with skippers lump together such dissimilar diets that their results are almost impossible to interpret. This is a valuable corrective, but it goes too far to dismiss timing altogether, given the consistency of the findings on how the body responds to food at different points in the day.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Individual variation further complicates matters. People differ in their natural daily rhythms: so-called morning types wake early and feel hungry soon after rising, while evening types often have little appetite until mid-morning. Requiring the latter to eat at dawn may simply add an unwanted meal to their day, which is precisely the outcome the trials recorded. A single piece of advice applied to everyone is therefore hard to justify.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Why, then, has the slogan proved so durable? Part of the answer is that it is simple, memorable and appears harmless. Yet simplicity has a cost when it misleads. A more defensible message would be less quotable: for most adults, eating breakfast is a matter of preference rather than necessity; the quality of food matters more than the clock; and very late, heavy meals deserve more concern than an empty morning. For hungry children, by contrast, a reliable breakfast remains one of the most effective interventions available.

topic: the rise and reassessment of vitamin D supplementation
title: The Sunshine Vitamin on Trial
subtitle: Vitamin D was once expected to prevent everything from cancer to depression. Large trials have told a more sobering story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the space of little more than a decade, vitamin D went from being a minor topic in bone medicine to one of the best-selling supplements in the world. Newspaper articles described it as a near-miraculous protector against cancer, heart disease, infection and low mood, and in some countries sales increased more than tenfold. The story of how this happened, and of what large clinical trials subsequently revealed, is worth telling in detail. It is, I would argue, one of the clearest modern examples of commercial enthusiasm racing ahead of the evidence, and of the hazards of moving too quickly from an observed association to a recommendation for millions of people.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Unlike most vitamins, vitamin D is obtained mainly not from food but from sunlight: the skin manufactures it when exposed to ultraviolet B radiation. At high latitudes, the winter sun is too weak for this process to occur at all for several months of the year, which is why blood levels in northern populations commonly fall between November and March. The vitamin's role in absorbing calcium has been understood since the early twentieth century, when it was found to prevent rickets, a disease that deforms children's bones. Interest broadened dramatically after Professor Anneliese Vortkamp, of the Bremen Institute for Preventive Medicine, compiled observational studies showing that people with low blood levels of the vitamin were more likely to develop a strikingly wide range of conditions, including several cancers, cardiovascular disease and multiple sclerosis. Vortkamp suggested that raising levels across the population might prevent a substantial share of these illnesses.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such a sweeping claim demanded testing, and in time large randomised trials were organised. The most ambitious, led by Dr Mirela Dumitrascu at the Cluj Centre for Clinical Trials, followed more than 25,000 middle-aged and older adults for five years, half of whom received a daily vitamin D supplement and half a placebo. At the end of the study, there was no reduction in the incidence of cancer, heart attacks or strokes among those taking the vitamin. A small decrease in cancer deaths was observed, but it was not statistically robust and might easily have arisen by chance. Dumitrascu concluded that routine supplementation of healthy adults could not be justified on the basis of her results.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How could the observational evidence have been so misleading? Dr Tariq Bensouda, an epidemiologist at the Rabat School of Public Health, argues that low vitamin D is frequently a consequence of poor health rather than a cause of it. People who are ill, overweight or physically inactive tend to spend less time outdoors, and fat tissue absorbs the vitamin, reducing the amount circulating in the blood. Inflammation, too, appears to lower measured levels. In Bensouda's memorable phrase, vitamin D behaves 'more like a thermometer than a thermostat': it records the state of the body without controlling it. The analogy is apt as far as it goes, but it cannot account for everything, since the vitamin's effect on bone is beyond dispute and plainly causal.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of vitamin D have raised a different objection. Dr Ximena Caporaletti, a nutritionist at the Rosario Institute of Food Science, points out that most participants in the large trials already had adequate blood levels when the studies began. A nutrient, she argues, is not like a drug: giving more of it to people who already have enough should not be expected to do anything, and any benefit is likely to be confined to those who are genuinely deficient. This is a fair criticism of the way the trials were designed. Even so, the argument carries a danger of its own. If every disappointing result can be explained away by pointing to the wrong participants, the original hypothesis becomes impossible to refute, and smaller trials restricted to deficient people have so far produced mixed results.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more practical view comes from Dr Obinna Ezeakor of the Enugu Centre for Community Health, who believes that the debate over universal supplementation has distracted attention from the people who need help most. People with darker skin living at high latitudes, elderly people who rarely go outside, and breastfed infants are all at considerably higher risk of deficiency. Ezeakor argues that resources would be better spent on identifying and supplying these groups than on general advice aimed at everyone. Nor are very high doses harmless: excessive intake can raise calcium in the blood to dangerous levels, and some products on sale contain many times the recommended daily amount.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that vitamin D is useless. It remains essential for healthy bones, and correcting real deficiency is clearly worthwhile. The lesson is rather about the standard of proof required before a message is directed at whole populations. The early observational findings were genuine and deserved attention; what they did not deserve was to be treated as settled before anyone had tested them. If nutrition science is to retain public trust, it must become far more willing to say, at an early stage, that a promising association is just that, and no more.

topic: the classification of ultra-processed foods and the dispute over what makes them harmful
title: Beyond the Nutrition Label
subtitle: The idea that the degree of processing, not just the nutrients, determines a food's effect on health has transformed nutrition research. Can it bear the weight now placed on it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, the phrase 'ultra-processed food' was virtually unknown outside a small circle of specialists. Today it appears in government reports, newspaper headlines and the marketing of products that boast of containing nothing artificial. In several wealthy countries, such foods are estimated to supply more than half of the energy that people consume. The concept has undoubtedly done valuable work, forcing researchers to look beyond the nutrient panel on the back of the packet and to ask how the way food is made might influence the way it is eaten. Yet its rapid rise has obscured a definitional problem that its advocates, in my view, consistently underestimate, and which becomes more pressing the closer the idea comes to being written into law.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The concept was formalised by a team under Professor Renata Taborda at the Recife Centre for Food Systems, who proposed a four-tier classification based not on the nutrients a food contains but on the extent and purpose of the industrial processing it has undergone. At one end lie unprocessed or minimally processed foods such as fresh vegetables, milk and eggs; at the other are ultra-processed products, defined as formulations made largely from substances extracted or refined from foods, typically combined with additives such as emulsifiers, colourings and flavour enhancers that are rarely found in domestic kitchens. Taborda's group argued that decades of nutrient-focused advice had failed, pointing to the low-fat products of the 1990s, many of which compensated for the missing fat with large quantities of sugar. It is a criticism that, in my view, is fully justified: by concentrating on single nutrients, earlier advice allowed products of dubious value to be marketed as healthy choices.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Since then, a large body of observational research has linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods with obesity, type 2 diabetes, depression and earlier death. Taborda points to what epidemiologists call a dose-response relationship: in study after study, the risk of these outcomes rises progressively as the proportion of ultra-processed food in the diet increases. Such gradients are often regarded as one of the stronger signs that an association may reflect a genuine causal effect, although they cannot by themselves rule out the possibility that people who eat these foods differ in other important ways from those who avoid them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most influential attempt to test causation directly was conducted by Dr Wirat Somboonsuk at the Chiang Mai Clinical Nutrition Unit. Twenty adults lived in a metabolic ward for four weeks, spending two weeks on an ultra-processed diet and two on a minimally processed one. The meals offered were matched for calories, sugar, fat, fibre and salt, and participants could eat as much or as little as they wished. On the ultra-processed diet they consumed around 500 more kilocalories a day and gained weight; on the other, they lost it. The experiment is elegant, but its scale and duration are modest, and while it demonstrates that something about ultra-processed meals encourages overeating, it does not reveal what that something is.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Ilona Szendrői, a sensory scientist at the Debrecen Institute of Food Physics, believes the answer lies in texture. Many ultra-processed products are soft and require little chewing, so they can be eaten very quickly. In her laboratory, volunteers ate energy-dense, soft meals markedly faster than firmer meals of equal nutritional content, and consumed more before reporting that they felt full. Szendrői argues that rapid eating allows large amounts of energy to be absorbed before satiety signals have time to take effect. If she is right, it is the physical properties of these foods, rather than the fact of their industrial manufacture, that matter most.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental challenge comes from Dr Joona Kivistö, a food technologist at the Tampere Centre for Food Innovation. He notes that the ultra-processed category places mass-produced wholemeal bread, flavoured yoghurt and infant formula alongside sugary soft drinks and processed meats, products with very different nutritional profiles. Moreover, when he asked trained nutritionists to classify a list of common supermarket items, they frequently disagreed about which tier particular foods belonged to. This is a serious objection. A category that experts themselves cannot apply consistently is a weak foundation for regulation, whatever its usefulness as a research tool.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Representatives of food manufacturers have unsurprisingly rejected the notion that processing is inherently harmful. Dr Matías Lezcano, a nutrition scientist who advises an industry association, contends that the problems identified in the research can be addressed by reformulation: reducing salt and sugar, adding fibre and adjusting recipes to slow the pace of eating. Working with manufacturers, he maintains, will achieve more than warning labels that merely alarm consumers. The record of voluntary reformulation does not inspire much confidence, as most past programmes have achieved only modest reductions in salt and sugar. Nevertheless, to dismiss reformulation altogether would be unwise, given how much of the food supply is now industrially produced.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the concept? It seems to me that ultra-processing is best treated as a valuable signal, one that has pointed researchers towards questions they had previously ignored, rather than as a ready-made basis for dietary rules. The likeliest outcome of the current research is that a handful of specific properties, such as texture, energy density and the combinations of fat, sugar and salt that make foods hard to stop eating, will turn out to explain most of the effect. Identifying them would allow advice to target the genuinely harmful products without condemning a loaf of bread for the crime of having been baked in a factory.
