topic: red and processed meat, cancer risk and the dispute over how to grade nutritional evidence
title: Weighing the Meat Evidence
subtitle: When experts reach opposite conclusions from the same studies, the problem may lie less in the data than in how certainty is judged

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When an international health agency announced that processed meat was 'carcinogenic to humans', placing bacon and sausages in the same category as tobacco smoke, the reaction was immediate. Headlines suggested that a ham sandwich was as dangerous as a cigarette, and butchers in several countries reported falling sales. The classification, however, described only how confident the agency was that processed meat could cause cancer, not how much cancer it caused. In my view, the episode revealed a deep and persistent confusion, shared by journalists and the public alike, between the strength of the evidence for a risk and the size of the risk itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: On the question of size, the figures are less dramatic than the headlines implied. Professor Thandiwe Mthembu-Sithole, an epidemiologist at the Durban Institute of Cancer Epidemiology, has pooled data from cohorts on four continents. She estimates that every 50 grams of processed meat eaten daily, roughly two rashers of bacon, is associated with an increase of about 18 per cent in the relative risk of bowel cancer. Because the disease is fairly uncommon, this translates into a rise in lifetime risk from around five per cent to around six. Mthembu-Sithole stresses, however, that when such products are eaten by hundreds of millions of people, even a small individual effect amounts to thousands of additional cases a year, a burden she describes as considerable. Plausible mechanisms exist: compounds formed from nitrites added as preservatives can damage the lining of the gut, as can the haem iron that gives red meat its colour.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A very different conclusion was reached by an international panel led by Dr Radim Šebesta of the Brno Evidence Review Group. Applying a formal system for grading the quality of evidence, the panel judged nearly all the studies on meat and health to be of 'low' or 'very low' certainty, and advised that most adults could continue eating meat at their current levels. The recommendation provoked fierce criticism. Opponents argued that the grading system had been designed for evaluating drug trials, and that it automatically downgrades evidence from observational studies, however large and consistent, simply because participants were not randomly assigned to their diets. Some also questioned whether the panel had given sufficient weight to laboratory findings on how cancer develops, which are largely consistent with the epidemiological picture. Šebesta replied that his group had simply applied, transparently and without favour, the same standards used in every other field of medicine.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Both sides, I believe, are partly right. The grading system reflects genuine weaknesses: people who eat a lot of processed meat also tend to smoke more, exercise less and eat fewer vegetables, and no statistical adjustment can fully separate these influences. But the alternative that the system implicitly favours is unrealistic. Cancer develops over decades, and no one could persuade thousands of people to follow an assigned diet faithfully for thirty years. To demand trial-quality evidence for long-term dietary effects is, in practice, to demand the impossible. At the same time, Šebesta's panel was right to emphasise that the benefit to any one person of cutting down on meat is small, a point that public health messages have often obscured.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe the health argument is a distraction. Dr Ana Lucía Zubiaurre, who studies food systems at the Bilbao Centre for Environmental Nutrition, contends that the strongest reasons for eating less meat concern greenhouse gas emissions, water use and the conversion of forests to pasture, and that nutritionists should say so plainly. Her environmental case is well founded, but combining it with health claims is a risky strategy. If people suspect that uncertain health findings are being emphasised to serve an environmental agenda, they may come to distrust both. Each argument should stand or fall on its own evidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that most of the research comes from wealthy countries where meat consumption is high. Dr Weiyuan Qiao, a nutritionist at the Kunming Institute of Public Nutrition, points out that in populations where diets are largely plant-based and iron deficiency is common, a modest increase in meat consumption can improve the health of young children, pregnant women and the elderly. Advice suited to a high-consumption country may therefore be actively harmful when applied elsewhere, and Qiao argues that dietary guidelines should be developed locally rather than borrowed wholesale. Her own surveys suggest that national advice copied from abroad is often ignored precisely because it bears little relation to local eating habits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What would better communication look like? First, it should distinguish clearly between processed meat, for which the evidence of harm is reasonably consistent, and unprocessed red meat, for which it is considerably weaker. Second, it should express risks in absolute terms. Telling people that bacon raises their cancer risk by 18 per cent is technically accurate but misleading; telling them that it raises a lifetime risk of five in a hundred to six in a hundred allows them to make an informed choice. Such messages may make for less striking headlines, but that is a price well worth paying.

topic: personalised nutrition based on individual glucose responses and genetic testing
title: A Diet of One
subtitle: Personalised nutrition promises advice tailored to each individual's biology. The science behind it is real, but so are its limits

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of its history, dietary advice has been addressed to an imaginary average person. Guidelines specify how much fibre, salt or saturated fat 'adults' should consume, as though a sixty-kilogram office worker and a hundred-kilogram labourer were metabolically interchangeable. It is hardly surprising, then, that the promise of personalised nutrition, advice based on an individual's own genes, gut bacteria or blood chemistry, has attracted enormous interest from scientists, investors and the public. The appeal is understandable, and the underlying insight, that people genuinely differ in how they respond to food, is correct. What remains far less clear is whether those differences can yet be measured reliably enough to justify the confident claims now being made.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the excitement can be traced to a study directed by Dr Yael Hirschfeld at the Haifa Institute of Metabolic Science. Around 800 volunteers wore continuous glucose monitors, small sensors attached to the arm, for a week while recording everything they ate. The results were striking: the same standardised meal produced a sharp rise in blood sugar in some participants and barely any change in others. Some people responded more strongly to bread than to ice cream; for others the reverse was true. Factors that dietitians had long assumed to be decisive, such as the amount of carbohydrate in a meal, explained only part of this variation. Hirschfeld's team then developed a computer algorithm which, using information about each volunteer's gut bacteria, lifestyle and blood tests, predicted individual responses considerably more accurately than conventional methods based on counting carbohydrates. It was a genuine and important discovery, and it challenged the assumption that a given food has a fixed effect on everyone.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Subsequent work has complicated the picture. Dr Bjarke Sønderskov, a physiologist at the Aarhus Centre for Nutrition Research, asked volunteers to eat identical breakfasts on several different mornings under carefully controlled conditions. He found that a single person's glucose response to the same meal could vary almost as much from one day to the next as it varied between different people, depending on factors such as sleep, stress and the previous evening's meal. Sønderskov does not dispute that individual differences exist, but he argues that a single week of monitoring cannot distinguish a person's stable characteristics from day-to-day fluctuation. Reliable personal profiles, he concludes, would require repeated testing over much longer periods than most commercial services provide.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Genetic testing, offered by numerous companies directly to consumers, rests on even weaker foundations. Dr Nurul Aisyah Kamaruddin of the Penang Institute of Nutrigenomics led a trial in which overweight adults were randomly assigned either to a diet matched to their genetic profile or to standard healthy-eating advice. After a year, the two groups had lost almost exactly the same amount of weight. Nor did the genetically matched group report finding their diet any easier to follow, which might have been expected if the advice suited their bodies better. Although particular genes influence how people metabolise caffeine, lactose or certain fats, the evidence that genotype-based advice improves overall health is, at present, close to non-existent, and the confident language used in the marketing of such tests is difficult to defend.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet the story does not end with biology. Dr Inês Valadares, a behavioural scientist at the Coimbra Laboratory for Health Psychology, has studied why people abandon diets. In one experiment, she gave participants either a plan genuinely tailored to their glucose responses or a generic plan that they were told had been personalised. Both groups followed their plans for longer than a control group who knew they were receiving standard advice, and the difference between the two 'personalised' groups was negligible. Valadares concludes that much of the benefit of personalised nutrition may come from the sense of ownership and commitment it creates, rather than from the biological precision of the recommendations themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such findings raise awkward questions for a fast-growing industry. Dr Ruslan Tokhtarbekov, who studies health regulation at the Almaty School of Public Policy, has reviewed the websites of more than sixty companies selling personalised diet plans and found that most made claims about weight loss or disease prevention that went well beyond any published evidence. Because these services are generally classified as lifestyle products rather than medical tests, they face little scrutiny. Several of the companies he examined charged annual subscriptions costing more than a typical family's monthly food budget. It seems to me that companies offering such advice should be obliged to demonstrate, through properly conducted trials, that it produces better outcomes than the free guidance already available, a modest requirement that few of them could currently meet.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that personalised nutrition is a dead end. For people with diabetes, who must manage their blood sugar carefully every day, continuous monitoring has already proved its worth, and finer insight into which foods affect them most could be genuinely valuable. For the general population, however, the gap between the simple advice everyone already receives and the way most people actually eat is far larger than any gain likely to come from individual tailoring. Until that gap narrows, the most effective 'personalised' advice for most people may well be the familiar recommendation to eat more vegetables and fewer heavily processed foods.

topic: intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating as a weight-loss method
title: The Science of Not Eating
subtitle: Restricting meals to a narrow daily window has become a global trend. Does the evidence justify the enthusiasm?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Fasting is among the oldest of human practices. It features in many of the world's religious traditions, from the month-long daytime fast of Ramadan to the abstinence of Lent and the regular fast days observed in Hinduism and Judaism. In the past decade, however, it has acquired a new identity as a scientific weight-loss technique. Under labels such as 'intermittent fasting' and 'time-restricted eating', millions of people now confine their meals to a window of eight hours or fewer, or eat very little on two days a week. The practice spread largely through books, podcasts and the endorsements of celebrities, well before rigorous trials in humans had been completed. Its long pedigree is often cited in its favour, but the fact that people have fasted for centuries for spiritual reasons tells us nothing about its effects on metabolism.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scientific case originated in animal research. In an experiment that attracted wide attention, Dr Seo-yeon Hwangbo of the Daejeon Institute of Metabolic Biology fed two groups of mice an identical high-fat diet, containing the same number of calories, but allowed one group to eat at any time and restricted the other to an eight-hour window. The unrestricted mice became obese and developed signs of diabetes; those on the restricted schedule remained relatively lean and healthy. Hwangbo proposed that giving the body a long daily break from digestion allows it to switch to burning stored fat and to carry out cellular repair. The results are striking, but mice are not small humans. They are active at night, their metabolism runs many times faster than ours, and a sixteen-hour fast for a mouse is physiologically far more demanding than for a person.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Human trials have proved much less dramatic. Dr Augustin Mbarga of the Yaoundé Centre for Clinical Nutrition randomly assigned 140 adults with obesity either to time-restricted eating or to conventional calorie restriction, carefully ensuring that both groups consumed the same total amount of energy. After a year, the two groups had lost similar amounts of weight, and there were no meaningful differences in blood pressure, cholesterol or blood sugar. Mbarga concludes that fasting regimes work chiefly because they lead people to eat less, not because of any special effect of timing. I find his trial persuasive. Yet this does not make fasting worthless: a method that helps people reduce their intake is useful whatever the mechanism.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are also potential drawbacks. Dr Elżbieta Wróblewska-Kurek, who studies muscle physiology at the Poznań Institute of Sports Medicine, has analysed body composition in fasting trials and found that, in some, a considerable proportion of the weight lost came from muscle rather than fat. She suspects that when protein is eaten in only one or two large meals, the body is less able to use it to maintain muscle tissue. This concern is particularly relevant to older people, for whom loss of muscle increases the risk of falls and frailty, and it suggests that fasting is not a regime to be adopted lightly by everyone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, do so many people report success? Dr Anjali Thekkedath, a health psychologist at the Kochi Centre for Behavioural Research, interviewed several hundred people who had followed fasting regimes for at least six months. Most said that what they valued was not a particular biological effect but simplicity: instead of counting calories or weighing portions, they had only to remember a single rule about when to stop eating. For people who find conventional dieting exhausting, this clarity may be decisive. Thekkedath notes, however, that a sizeable minority found the rule socially isolating, since it prevented them from joining family meals or eating out with friends.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more intriguing line of research concerns timing relative to the body's internal clock. Dr Kristjan Põder of the Tartu Centre for Chronobiology argues that eating late in the evening, when the body is preparing for sleep, may disrupt the daily rhythms that govern hormone release and glucose metabolism. In his studies, shift workers who ate mainly at night showed poorer blood sugar control than day workers eating the same food. If he is correct, the question is less how long people go without food than when they choose to eat, an issue that, in my view, deserves far more attention than it has so far received.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should we conclude? On present evidence, fasting appears to be one reasonable way of reducing calorie intake rather than a metabolic shortcut. Its effects in humans are modest, its benefits beyond weight loss are unproven, and for some groups it carries real risks. What is now needed are longer studies, involving a broader range of participants, including older adults and people from different cultures, that compare fasting directly with other approaches. Until such studies are available, those who find that a fixed eating window helps them eat less have no reason to stop, but nor should anyone be persuaded that the clock holds the secret to good health.

topic: calorie restriction and lifespan extension
title: The Lean Hypothesis
subtitle: Can eating less really slow the clock of ageing? Decades of experiments have produced a less tidy answer than enthusiasts suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1930s, nutritionists working with laboratory rats noticed something unexpected: animals given roughly a third less food than they would normally eat lived considerably longer than their well-fed companions. In the decades since, the effect has been reproduced in yeast, nematode worms, fruit flies and mice, making calorie restriction one of the most frequently confirmed findings in the biology of ageing. It is hardly surprising, then, that the idea has escaped the laboratory. Diet books, fasting apps and wellness clinics now promise that eating less will add years to a human life. Yet the leap from a caged rodent to a free-living person is far longer than such promises imply, and it deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty lies in explaining why restriction works at all. Dr Ottilie Brannvik, a molecular biologist at the Baltic Institute of Gerontology, has spent much of her career on the cellular pathways that respond to nutrient scarcity. In her view, a shortage of food acts as a signal that switches cells from growth to maintenance: damaged proteins are recycled more efficiently, and resources are diverted towards repair rather than reproduction. Brannvik argues that this response evolved because it allowed animals to survive famines and breed once conditions improved. The theory is elegant, but it carries an awkward implication. If the benefit is essentially a strategy for waiting out hard times, there is no particular reason to expect a long-lived species such as our own, which already invests heavily in maintenance, to gain as much from it as a mouse.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most eagerly awaited evidence came from primates. Two long-term studies of rhesus monkeys, begun in the late 1980s, were expected to settle the question. Instead, they appeared to contradict each other. One reported that restricted monkeys lived longer and developed fewer age-related diseases; the other found improvements in health but no gain in lifespan. Professor Kwabena Asante-Mensah of the Coastal Primate Research Station, who has re-examined both datasets, believes the discrepancy is largely explained by diet. The control animals in the first study were allowed to eat as much as they wanted of food rich in sugar, so the restricted group was being compared with monkeys that were, in effect, overweight. In the second, even the controls were fed a healthier and carefully measured diet. Asante-Mensah's conclusion is that restriction protects mainly against the harm caused by overeating, rather than slowing ageing itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This interpretation is, to my mind, the most persuasive yet offered, and it has uncomfortable consequences for laboratory research generally. Most experimental mice are housed with unlimited access to food and little opportunity for exercise. If such animals are already unhealthy, then many apparent 'anti-ageing' effects observed in them may simply be the correction of a condition that scientists themselves created. Some gerontologists have begun to call for standard laboratory diets to be redesigned, although there is little agreement yet on what a 'normal' diet for a mouse should look like.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Human evidence is necessarily indirect, since no trial can follow volunteers for an entire lifetime. Dr Marisol Arrizabalaga, an endocrinologist who coordinated a two-year trial at the Iberian Centre for Metabolic Health, measured markers that are thought to track the pace of ageing, such as blood pressure, inflammation and insulin sensitivity. Participants who reduced their intake by around twelve per cent showed improvements on most of these measures. Arrizabalaga is careful not to overstate the results: the markers, she notes, predict disease reasonably well in populations but have never been shown to predict how long a particular individual will live. She also reports that a significant minority of volunteers abandoned the regime within months, citing constant hunger, irritability and a loss of interest in social occasions centred on food.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That last observation points to a problem which the enthusiasm for restriction tends to ignore. A treatment that few people can sustain is of limited value, however impressive its effects in principle. For this reason, attention has shifted towards alternatives that might deliver some of the benefits without the hardship. Intermittent fasting, in which people eat normally on most days but sharply reduce their intake on others, is one such option. Another is the search for drugs that mimic the cellular effects of scarcity. The pharmacologist Lucjan Wierzbowski of the Southern Ageing Consortium is among those testing compounds of this kind in older dogs, a species that shares human environments and many human diseases. Wierzbowski admits, however, that a drug which tricks the body into believing it is starving might also blunt its ability to fight infection or heal wounds.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the original finding was mistaken. In simple organisms, at least, restriction genuinely extends life, and the pathways it acts upon are real and worth studying. What the research does not support is the confident claim that ordinary people can expect to live dramatically longer by skipping meals. The more modest lesson, that avoiding chronic overeating protects health, is less marketable, but it is the one the evidence actually supports.

topic: age verification and the reliability of longevity hotspot claims
title: Counting the Centenarians
subtitle: Regions famed for extraordinary longevity have inspired a global industry. Some demographers now ask whether the birthdays were real

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in popular health writing have proved as attractive as the notion of the longevity hotspot: a remote island or mountain valley where an unusual proportion of inhabitants reach their hundredth birthday. Such places are typically credited with a combination of plant-based diets, daily physical labour, strong family ties and a sense of purpose that persists into old age. Over the past two decades, the concept has generated best-selling books, television series and even town-planning schemes designed to recreate the conditions supposedly found there. Yet beneath the appealing narrative lies a basic statistical question that has received surprisingly little public attention: are the people in these regions really as old as they claim to be?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Verifying extreme age is far harder than it sounds. In countries where civil registration was introduced late, or where records were lost in wars and fires, a person's stated birth date may rest on nothing more than family memory. Teodora Brancoveanu, a demographer at the Danube Institute for Population Studies, has examined thousands of claims of exceptional longevity over the past twenty years. Her research indicates that the proportion of supposed centenarians tends to be highest precisely in regions where documentation is weakest, a pattern she regards as a warning sign rather than a coincidence. In her experience, when birth certificates, baptismal entries and military service records are cross-checked, a substantial share of claims collapse. Errors arise in many ways: a child might be given the name of an older sibling who died in infancy, for example, and later inherit that sibling's birth date.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Financial incentives can compound the problem. Brancoveanu points to cases in which pensions continued to be collected long after the recipient's death, and others in which individuals deliberately added years to their age to qualify for benefits earlier. In one region she studied, the number of registered centenarians fell by more than half after authorities began requiring documentary proof of age. She does not claim that every longevity hotspot is fictitious, but she argues that the burden of proof should lie with those making extraordinary claims. This seems to me an entirely reasonable standard. In any other field of science, a finding that disappeared when its underlying measurements were checked would be regarded as discredited, and it is difficult to see why longevity research should be treated differently.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the hotspot concept respond that the best-known regions have, in fact, been subjected to rigorous validation. Aksel Fjelstad, an anthropologist at the Northern Institute for Ageing and Society, spent several years in a mountain community where he and his colleagues traced every claimed centenarian through parish registers going back to the eighteenth century. According to Fjelstad, the ages there were confirmed in almost all cases, and the community's longevity is genuine. He accepts that some celebrated hotspots may not survive close examination, but insists that discarding the whole concept on that basis would be a serious mistake. Fjelstad's evidence is impressive, but it is worth noting that a single verified community cannot vouch for the others, and several of the regions most often cited in popular books have never undergone comparable checks.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even where ages are accurate, the explanation for long life remains contested. The lifestyle factors listed in popular accounts are rarely measured directly; more often they are inferred from interviews conducted with the survivors themselves, who are, by definition, an unrepresentative group. Professor Yusuf Karaosmanoglu, a gerontologist at the Anatolian Centre for Longevity Research, points out that the elderly residents of such regions grew up in conditions very different from those of their grandchildren, and that the diets now promoted in their name often bear little resemblance to what they actually ate in youth. He also notes that emigration may play a role: if younger, healthier people leave a region in search of work, while frailer ones remain, the age structure of the population can be distorted in ways that have nothing to do with diet or social life.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Karaosmanoglu's alternative explanation centres on early-life conditions. He has compared birth cohorts in several Mediterranean villages and found that those who reached extreme old age were disproportionately likely to have been born in years when local harvests were good and infectious disease was relatively rare. In his view, the foundation of exceptional longevity may be laid in childhood rather than in old age, which would make it far harder to reproduce through adult lifestyle changes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these findings implies that diet, exercise and social connection are unimportant; a large body of evidence links each to better health in later life. What the debate does show is how easily a compelling story can run ahead of the data supporting it. If the longevity hotspot is to remain a useful idea, it will need to be rebuilt on verified records and careful comparison, rather than on the anecdotes that first made it famous. Policymakers, too, should be wary of building programmes around lessons drawn from places whose very statistics remain in doubt.

topic: cellular senescence and senolytic drugs
title: Clearing Out the Zombies
subtitle: Drugs that destroy ageing cells have raised hopes of treating many diseases at once, but the early results call for patience

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 1960s, a young biologist culturing human cells noticed that they did not divide indefinitely, as was then widely believed. After about fifty divisions, the cells stopped multiplying, yet they did not die. They remained metabolically active, enlarged and flattened, persisting in the culture dish for months. For decades this state, which came to be called cellular senescence, was regarded as a laboratory curiosity, or at most as a defence against cancer: a cell that can no longer divide cannot form a tumour. Only relatively recently has it been recognised that senescent cells accumulate in the body with age and may contribute to many of the disorders associated with growing old.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The key insight was that senescent cells are not merely idle. They release a cocktail of inflammatory molecules, enzymes and growth factors, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Professor Emeka Obiorah of the West African Institute of Cell Biology has compared the effect to a single rotten apple spoiling a barrel: a small number of senescent cells, he argues, can disrupt the function of the healthy tissue around them and even push neighbouring cells into senescence themselves. On this view, the damage done by senescent cells is out of all proportion to their numbers, which rarely exceed a few per cent of the cells in any tissue.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If this is correct, removing such cells ought to be beneficial, and experiments in mice have been striking. When researchers engineered animals in which senescent cells could be selectively destroyed, the mice remained active for longer, their kidneys and hearts functioned better in old age, and their median lifespan increased. These results prompted a search for drugs, termed senolytics, that could achieve the same effect without genetic modification. Several candidates have since been identified, including a combination of a cancer drug and a plant pigment found in apples and onions. Because senescent cells take weeks to reaccumulate, such drugs might be given intermittently, perhaps once every few months, which would limit side effects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The excitement surrounding senolytics has been considerable, and some of it is justified. Unlike treatments that target one disease at a time, these drugs promise to act on a process that underlies many conditions at once, from osteoarthritis to lung fibrosis. Nevertheless, enthusiasm has outpaced evidence. Dr Signe Vuorikari, a clinical pharmacologist at the Nordic Unit for Ageing Medicine, notes that the first human trials have been small, short and designed mainly to establish safety. One trial in patients with knee osteoarthritis found no improvement in pain or joint function compared with a placebo, a result that she believes should temper expectations rather than end the field.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also reasons to doubt that senescent cells are simply harmful. Dr Paloma Fedorchuk, an immunologist at the Andean Centre for Regenerative Research, points out that senescence plays a vital role in wound healing: cells at the edge of an injury temporarily enter the senescent state and release signals that recruit repair processes. Senescent cells are also involved in the development of the embryo and in limiting scar formation in the liver. Fedorchuk therefore warns that indiscriminately eliminating them could slow recovery from injury, particularly in older people, whose healing is already impaired. In her opinion, the goal should be to modify the harmful secretions of senescent cells rather than to kill the cells outright.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Fedorchuk's position is a valuable corrective, although I suspect she underestimates the problem of persistence. Senescent cells that contribute to healing are normally cleared by the immune system within days or weeks; it is the cells that linger, because the ageing immune system fails to remove them, that seem to cause harm. If senolytics were given only periodically, healthy temporary senescence might be largely spared. Whether this is true in practice is an empirical question that only careful trials can answer.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty concerns measurement. There is no single marker that identifies a senescent cell with certainty; researchers rely on combinations of features, each of which is also found in some non-senescent cells. This makes it hard to confirm that a drug has actually cleared its target in human patients, rather than merely producing a measurable change in the blood. Obiorah's group is developing imaging techniques to address the problem, but he concedes that reliable tools may be years away.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Senolytics, then, represent a genuinely new approach to the diseases of ageing, and it would be a mistake to dismiss them because the first trials have disappointed. It would be an equal mistake to treat them as the long-sought remedy for old age. The history of medicine contains many treatments that worked wonderfully in mice and modestly or not at all in humans, and the burden now lies with the field to show that this one is different. What the coming decade requires, in short, is patience rather than either hype or premature dismissal.

topic: the free radical (oxidative damage) theory of ageing, the failure of antioxidant supplements and the hormesis alternative
title: An Oxidised Idea
subtitle: For half a century, ageing was blamed on chemical damage caused by oxygen. The decline of that theory says much about how science treats an attractive idea

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1956 a chemist studying the effects of radiation proposed an idea that would shape research on ageing for the next fifty years. Cells, he suggested, generate energy by burning oxygen, and in doing so they release free radicals: unstable molecules carrying an unpaired electron, which react with almost anything they encounter. Over a lifetime, the damage these molecules inflict on proteins, fats and DNA gradually accumulates, and ageing is simply its visible result. The theory had obvious appeal. It seemed to explain why small animals with rapid metabolisms tend to die young while larger, slower-living species survive for decades, and it pointed directly to a remedy: if oxidation caused ageing, then antioxidants, substances that neutralise free radicals, ought to slow it down. By the 1990s, antioxidant supplements had become a multi-billion-dollar industry. Few theories in biology, I would suggest, have travelled so far beyond the laboratory on so little direct evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For a time, the evidence did appear to accumulate in its favour. Professor Fiammetta Scardigli of the Apennine Centre for Biogerontology was among those who documented it. Her group, and others, reported that strains of fruit flies engineered to produce additional quantities of antioxidant enzymes sometimes lived noticeably longer than ordinary flies, and that long-lived species generally show lower levels of oxidative damage in their tissues than short-lived ones. Scardigli has remained a defender of the theory, if a more cautious one than in her early career. The relationship between oxidative damage and lifespan across the animal kingdom, she maintains, is far too consistent to be dismissed as a coincidence, whatever individual experiments may show.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most serious challenge came from genetic studies in mammals. A team at the Masovian Institute of Experimental Gerontology, led by Dr Witold Ostrzeszewicz, bred mice that lacked one copy of the gene for a key antioxidant enzyme. As predicted, these animals carried substantially more oxidative damage in their cells than normal mice. Yet they lived just as long. Mice engineered to produce extra antioxidant enzymes, meanwhile, showed no gain in lifespan at all. Similar results have since been obtained in worms, in one case with a strain whose lifespan actually increased when it was exposed to a chemical that raised free radical production. Ostrzeszewicz concludes that oxidative damage is a by-product of ageing rather than one of its causes. This strikes me as going somewhat further than the evidence permits. To show that extra damage is not enough to shorten life is not the same as showing that damage plays no part in ageing whatsoever.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In humans, the decisive evidence came from clinical trials. During the 1990s and 2000s, large randomised studies tested whether vitamin E, vitamin C, beta-carotene and similar compounds could prevent heart disease, cancer or early death. Dr Minae Hitotsuyanagi, an epidemiologist at the Shinshu School of Public Health, has pooled the results of dozens of such trials, involving well over two hundred thousand participants. She found no reduction in mortality among those taking supplements and, for some compounds taken in high doses, a slight increase. In one trial, beta-carotene raised the incidence of lung cancer among smokers. Hitotsuyanagi points out that the original enthusiasm rested largely on observational studies, which found that people with diets rich in fruit and vegetables lived longer. Such people, however, also tend to smoke less, exercise more and earn higher incomes, any of which could account for their better health.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If antioxidants do not help, why not? An intriguing answer has been proposed by Dr Kwadwo Amankrah-Boateng of the Kumasi Institute of Cell Biology. In small quantities, he argues, free radicals are not merely harmful waste but signals, warning the cell of stress and prompting it to strengthen its own defences and repair systems. This principle, known as hormesis, would explain why physical exercise, which temporarily increases free radical production, is nonetheless one of the most reliable ways of improving health in later life. Amankrah-Boateng cites a study in which volunteers who took high doses of vitamins C and E during a training programme gained fewer metabolic benefits from their exercise than volunteers who took no supplements. On this view, antioxidant pills may suppress the very signals that make the body more resilient. I find this the most persuasive of the current accounts, though it is still far from established.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Scardigli does not accept that the original theory has been refuted. Laboratory mice, she observes, live in warm, sheltered cages, free from infection and predators and supplied with as much food as they want. Under such conditions, she suggests, the costs of extra oxidative damage may simply never become apparent, whereas in the wild they could be considerable. The argument deserves to be taken seriously, but it is difficult to test, and it is hard to see how it could explain the disappointing results of human trials, whose participants were not living in cages.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong to treat the history of the free radical theory as a story of scientific folly. The theory made clear predictions, researchers tested them, and when the predictions failed, most of the field revised its views. That is how science is meant to work. What is more troubling is how little of this revision has reached the public. Antioxidants are still widely marketed with the promise of slowing ageing, and the gap between what specialists now believe and what is sold in pharmacies seems unlikely to close soon.

topic: the grandmother hypothesis and the evolution of post-reproductive lifespan
title: Life After Fertility
subtitle: Why do women live for decades beyond menopause? Evolutionary biologists are still divided

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the many peculiarities of the human life course, few have puzzled evolutionary biologists as much as menopause. In most mammals, females remain capable of reproducing until shortly before they die; a chimpanzee in the wild, for instance, rarely outlives her fertility by more than a few years. Women, by contrast, typically lose the ability to bear children around the age of fifty, yet may live for three or four decades afterwards. Humans are not entirely alone in this respect: killer whales and short-finned pilot whales also have a prolonged post-reproductive phase. But the trait is extremely rare, and its existence seems to defy a basic principle of evolution. Natural selection favours characteristics that help organisms to pass on their genes, so it is not obvious why it should maintain a body that has stopped reproducing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential answer is known as the grandmother hypothesis. Its origins lie in fieldwork carried out by the anthropologist Kristen Aasvangen among a community of hunter-gatherers in the savanna of East Africa. Aasvangen noticed that the hardest-working foragers were often women past childbearing age, who spent long hours digging up starchy tubers buried deep in rocky soil. Much of this food went to their grandchildren, particularly when the children's mothers were occupied with newborn babies. Supported in this way, younger women could wean their infants earlier and give birth again sooner than would otherwise have been possible. A grandmother who remained vigorous into her sixties, in other words, could increase the number of descendants who carried her genes. Computer simulations later suggested that even a modest amount of such help, accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years, would be enough to stretch an ape-like lifespan into a human one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Historical records offer a further test. Dr Tendai Chikowore, a demographer at the Southern Africa Population Institute, has analysed parish registers of births, marriages and deaths kept by churches in several farming communities during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Her results show that children whose maternal grandmother was alive and living in the same village were significantly more likely to survive to adulthood. Intriguingly, the advantage disappeared once the grandmother passed the age of about seventy-five, perhaps because she then required care herself rather than providing it. The presence of a paternal grandmother had a weaker effect, and in some communities none at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that menopause needs an adaptive explanation. Dr Ramón Iturbide of the Iberian Centre for Evolutionary Studies argues that long post-reproductive lives are largely a product of modern nutrition and medicine. In his view, our ancestors seldom lived beyond fifty, so there was never strong selection on what happened after that age. Menopause, he suggests, is simply the consequence of women being born with a fixed supply of eggs that was sufficient for the short lives of the past. The difficulty with this argument is that it rests on a misreading of ancient life expectancy. Average lifespans in pre-industrial populations were low mainly because so many children died; studies of contemporary foragers show that individuals who survive childhood frequently live into their sixties and seventies. A lengthy life beyond fertility, then, is not a recent invention, and Iturbide's position is hard to sustain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more serious challenge comes from Dr Anwen Prydderch, a behavioural ecologist at the Cambrian Marine Research Unit, who has spent two decades observing killer whales. Prydderch found that when a mother and her adult daughter produced calves at the same time, the older female's calves were far less likely to survive. Stopping reproduction, she argues, allows older females to avoid competing with the next generation for limited resources. She believes a similar logic applies to humans, because in many traditional societies young women moved into their husband's family, where they would compete with their mother-in-law rather than with their own mothers. Prydderch presents her reproductive conflict hypothesis as an alternative to grandmothering, but I am not persuaded that the two are rivals. Conflict may explain why reproduction comes to an end, while the benefits of grandmothering explain why the body continues to function afterwards.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What does this debate reveal about ageing more generally? Perhaps most importantly, it suggests that the pace at which a species ages is not fixed but can be shaped by social relationships. If grandmothers made a difference to the survival of their descendants, there was a selective reward for bodies that stayed robust for longer, and some researchers believe this may help to explain why humans age more slowly than other primates in many respects.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A note of caution is nevertheless necessary. Evolutionary explanations describe the pressures that shaped our ancestors; they do not prescribe how anyone ought to live now. It would be a mistake to conclude from the grandmother hypothesis that the proper role of older women is to look after grandchildren, just as it would be absurd to argue that women without grandchildren have somehow failed to fulfil their biological purpose. The value of a long life after fertility lies in what individuals choose to make of it.

topic: compression versus expansion of morbidity in longer-lived populations
title: Longer Lives, Healthier Lives?
subtitle: As life expectancy rises, researchers disagree about whether the extra years are being spent in good health or in sickness

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the course of the twentieth century, life expectancy in wealthy countries rose by roughly three months every year, and in most places the increase has continued, if somewhat more slowly, into the present century. This achievement is usually reported as an unambiguous triumph. Yet a longer life is not necessarily a better one, and the question of whether the extra years are spent in good health or in sickness is, I would argue, the single most important issue facing those who plan health and social care. The answer determines how many hospital beds, carers and pension payments a society will need, and it shapes the experience of growing old for hundreds of millions of people.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most optimistic answer was proposed more than four decades ago by Professor Ilse Vandekerckhove of the Leuven Institute of Public Health. She argued that the human lifespan has a natural ceiling of around eighty-five years, beyond which few people can expect to survive whatever medical care they receive. If that ceiling is fixed, and if healthier diets, less smoking and more exercise could delay the onset of chronic illness, then the period of sickness at the end of life would be squeezed into an ever shorter span. Vandekerckhove called this the compression of morbidity, morbidity being the technical term for ill health. In its ideal form, people would remain vigorous until shortly before death and then decline rapidly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others have drawn a much gloomier picture. Dr Mikko Haapalainen, a health economist at the Tampere Centre for Health Economics, contends that modern medicine has been most successful not in preventing chronic disease but in preventing people from dying of it. A heart attack that would once have been fatal is now frequently survived; diabetes, once a rapid killer, can be managed for decades. Haapalainen describes these outcomes as hollow victories, because each life saved is often a life lived with a long-term condition. On his account, rising life expectancy brings an expansion rather than a compression of morbidity, and societies should prepare for a growing number of years spent in poor health.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third position attempts to reconcile these views. Dr Thandiwe Nxumalo of the Cape Institute of Gerontology points out that both earlier theories treat disease as a single category, whereas a diagnosis and a disability are very different things. A woman whose high blood pressure is detected at fifty and controlled with daily tablets technically lives with a chronic condition for the rest of her life, yet she may experience no limitation whatsoever. Nxumalo suggests that people are indeed spending more years with diagnosed illnesses, partly because screening detects them earlier, but that those illnesses are becoming less disabling. She calls this a dynamic equilibrium.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Long-term studies have begun to test these competing predictions. A team led by Dr Dae-hyun Kwak at the Seoul Healthy Ageing Panel followed more than twenty thousand adults aged sixty and over for fifteen years, recording both their medical diagnoses and their ability to carry out daily activities such as dressing, bathing and shopping without help. The number of years lived free of disability rose broadly in step with life expectancy. The number of years lived with at least one diagnosed chronic condition, however, grew considerably faster. These findings fit Nxumalo's account better than either of the older theories. There was one notable exception: for dementia, years of severe impairment appeared to be lengthening, a trend that no amount of earlier diagnosis can explain away.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Much of the disagreement, it seems to me, arises from definitions. Whether morbidity is expanding or contracting depends heavily on whether it is measured by counting diagnoses, by asking people to rate their own health, or by assessing what they are able to do. Of these, counts of diagnoses are arguably the least meaningful, since they rise automatically whenever screening improves; how people judge their own health is a far better guide to the quality of their lives. I am also sceptical of the fixed ceiling on which Vandekerckhove's theory depends. The age reached by the oldest people in many countries has continued to climb, which suggests that the limit, if there is one, is not where she placed it. Her central insight, that postponing illness is at least as valuable as treating it, nonetheless remains sound.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most troubling finding of recent research concerns who benefits. In several countries, gains in disability-free life have been concentrated among people with university degrees and professional occupations, while among manual workers they have barely changed. National averages, which combine these groups, can therefore suggest a general improvement that many people have not experienced.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: So are longer lives healthier lives? The honest answer is that it depends on which people, which conditions and which measures are being considered. This may seem an unsatisfying conclusion after four decades of debate, but it is more useful than a confident generalisation in either direction.

topic: comparative biology of exceptionally long-lived animals such as naked mole-rats and bats
title: Lessons from the Long-Lived
subtitle: A handful of animals break the usual rules of ageing. What can they tell us about our own?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among mammals, one of the most dependable rules in biology is that bigger animals live longer. A house mouse is old at two or three years; a horse may reach thirty, and an elephant seventy. The pattern holds across hundreds of species and has a plausible explanation: large animals generally have slower metabolisms and are less vulnerable to predators. Yet the rule has striking exceptions. Some bats weighing less than ten grams have survived in the wild for over forty years, and a small burrowing rodent from East Africa can live ten times longer than its size would predict. In my view, it is these anomalies, rather than the rule itself, that have the most to teach us about why bodies age and whether that process can be slowed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The rodent in question is the naked mole-rat, a hairless, nearly blind creature roughly the size of a mouse that lives in large underground colonies, each with a single breeding queen, rather like those of bees or ants. Mole-rats in captivity have survived beyond thirty years, but their longevity is not the most remarkable thing about them. Dr Isidora Vranjes of the Adriatic Institute of Comparative Physiology has analysed records from thousands of animals kept in laboratory colonies over three decades. In almost every other species studied, including our own, the risk of dying roughly doubles at regular intervals once adulthood is reached. Vranjes found that in naked mole-rats it does not: a twenty-five-year-old animal is about as likely to die in a given year as a two-year-old. They are also exceptionally resistant to cancer, which is otherwise common in ageing rodents.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What accounts for this? Dr Nnamdi Ezeagwu, a cell biologist at the Niger Delta Research University, has drawn attention to an unusually large form of a sugar molecule found in the spaces between mole-rat cells. In laboratory dishes, this substance causes cells to stop dividing as soon as they become crowded, a property that would make tumours difficult to form. When Ezeagwu's team engineered mice to produce the molecule, the animals developed fewer tumours and lived somewhat longer. This is an elegant result, but the gain in lifespan was modest, around ten per cent, which falls far short of what the mole-rat achieves. It seems more likely that the molecule is one contributor among many, alongside other features such as unusually stable proteins and an ability to survive long periods with very little oxygen. Ezeagwu himself acknowledges this, describing the molecule as 'a piece of the puzzle, not the picture on the box'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Bats present a different puzzle. Flight is extremely demanding, and the high metabolic rate it requires produces chemical by-products that damage DNA and proteins. By the logic that once linked fast metabolism with short life, bats ought to age rapidly. Researchers from the Tasman Comparative Biology Group, who have spent fifteen years capturing and releasing wild bats, argue that the opposite has happened precisely because of these demands. To cope with the stress of flight, bats evolved highly efficient systems for repairing damaged molecules and controlling inflammation, and long life, the group suggests, is essentially a by-product of these adaptations. Not everyone is convinced. Vranjes points out that many bats spend months of each year hibernating, during which their metabolism slows almost to a standstill, and she suspects that these long periods of inactivity contribute at least as much to their longevity as any repair system. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, and the truth may well involve both.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Evolutionary theory offers a broader account of why such exceptions exist. If most members of a species are killed by predators, disease or accident while still young, there is little advantage in investing in a body that could last for decades, because few individuals would live long enough to benefit. Where external dangers are low, by contrast, natural selection can favour slower ageing. Mole-rats are protected by their tunnels, bats by their ability to fly and tortoises by their shells, and all three age unusually slowly. Many seabirds, which nest on remote cliffs and islands beyond the reach of most predators, fit the same pattern. This explanation is persuasive as far as it goes, but it says why slow ageing evolved, not how it is achieved in the body, which is the question that matters most to medicine.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That question has inspired hopes that drugs could reproduce the tricks of long-lived animals in people. Such hopes should be treated with caution. The mechanisms that protect the mole-rat or the bat evolved together, over millions of years, within a particular body and way of life, and it would be surprising if a single feature could be lifted out and transplanted into human beings with similar effect. Even so, the comparative approach has already made one invaluable contribution. By showing that evolution has slowed ageing many times, in many different ways, it has demonstrated that ageing is not a fixed and inevitable process but one that can, in principle, be changed. That conclusion alone justifies the effort of studying creatures that might otherwise seem little more than biological curiosities, and it offers some grounds for hope that human ageing, too, may prove more flexible than was once assumed.

topic: cognitive reserve and resilience to brain ageing
title: The Resilient Brain
subtitle: Why do some people whose brains show extensive damage never develop the symptoms of dementia?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late twentieth century, researchers examining the donated brains of elderly people noticed something puzzling. A substantial minority of those who had shown no sign of memory loss or confusion during their lives turned out, at post-mortem, to have brains riddled with the protein deposits known as plaques and tangles, the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease. In some cases the damage was as extensive as in patients who had died with severe dementia. To explain how a brain could carry so much pathology without obvious symptoms, scientists proposed the idea of cognitive reserve: a capacity, built up over a lifetime, that allows some people to keep functioning despite damage that would disable others. The concept has since become one of the most influential in the study of brain ageing. It is, I would suggest, also one of the most useful and one of the most slippery.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the early evidence came from the work of Professor Leopold Ostendorp at the Rhine Institute for Clinical Neurology. Following several thousand older adults over two decades, his team found that those with more years of education, more mentally demanding occupations and, in some analyses, fluency in more than one language were diagnosed with dementia later than their peers. Ostendorp's most striking finding, however, concerned what happened after diagnosis. Highly educated patients, once diagnosed, declined considerably faster than those with less schooling. Far from undermining his theory, he argues, this is exactly what reserve would predict: if a well-protected brain can conceal damage for longer, then by the time symptoms finally emerge the underlying disease will be more advanced, and the decline that follows will be steeper.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Researchers have since drawn a distinction between two forms of protection. Brain reserve refers to physical characteristics, such as a larger brain or a greater number of neurons and connections, which provide a kind of buffer: more can be lost before a critical threshold is reached. Cognitive reserve, by contrast, concerns how flexibly and efficiently the brain uses the resources it has. Dr Hiwot Gebremariam of the Horn of Africa Neuroscience Centre has used brain imaging to study people performing memory tasks. Those with high reserve, she reports, tend to draw on alternative networks of brain regions when the usual ones are damaged, rather like a driver who knows several routes around a blocked road. For Gebremariam, reserve is therefore better understood as something a person does than as something a person has.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are comfortable with the concept. Dr Valentina Urquiaga, an epidemiologist at the Basque Centre for Cognitive Epidemiology, raises two objections. The first is that reserve has often been inferred after the event: whenever someone shows fewer symptoms than their brain damage would predict, they are said to have high reserve, which makes the idea impossible to disprove. The second is that education is closely bound up with other advantages, including higher income, better diet and readier access to medical care, any of which might protect the brain independently. Her second objection deserves serious attention. The first, though fair as a description of early studies, is now overstated. Many researchers today measure reserve in advance, using independent indicators such as vocabulary and occupational history, and then test whether those measures predict how people cope with later damage. Defined in this way, the idea can certainly be tested, and it could in principle be shown to be wrong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more practical question is whether reserve can still be built in later life. Dr Suresh Kottarathil and colleagues in the Malabar Ageing Brain Study followed some three thousand adults over the age of sixty for twelve years. Participants who took up new and demanding activities, such as learning a musical instrument or a language, showed slower cognitive decline than those who did not. Kottarathil is careful to acknowledge a complication. The earliest, still undetected stages of dementia may themselves cause people to withdraw from challenging pursuits, so that inactivity could be an effect of decline rather than its cause. When his team used statistical methods to allow for this possibility, the apparent benefit of new activities became smaller, but it did not disappear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such findings have been eagerly seized upon by the makers of brain-training games, which promise to sharpen memory and attention in a few minutes a day. The evidence here is disappointing. Players reliably improve at the games themselves, but there is little sign that these gains carry over to the mental demands of everyday life, such as remembering appointments or managing finances. It is worth distinguishing such narrow exercises from the rich, sustained and socially engaging activities examined in studies like Kottarathil's, which may well be a different matter.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Cognitive reserve, then, is best seen not as a shield against disease but as a means of postponing its consequences. Reserve does not prevent plaques and tangles from forming; at most, it allows people to live well with them for longer. That distinction matters for a further reason. There is a risk that the concept will be used to imply that those who develop dementia simply failed to keep their minds active enough. Given how strongly reserve appears to depend on early education, which few people choose for themselves, such an implication would be both unfair and mistaken.

topic: telomeres, telomerase and the rise and fall of a single-cause theory of ageing
title: The Ends of the Matter
subtitle: Telomeres were once hailed as the key to ageing. The truth has turned out to be considerably more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the tip of every human chromosome sits a stretch of repetitive DNA known as a telomere. Telomeres are often compared to the plastic caps on the ends of shoelaces: they carry no genetic instructions of their own, but they prevent the chromosome from fraying or becoming fused to its neighbours. Their significance for ageing stems from a quirk of cell division. The molecular machinery that copies DNA cannot reproduce the very end of a chromosome, so each time a cell divides its telomeres become slightly shorter. After fifty or so divisions they reach a critical length, and the cell stops dividing altogether. An enzyme called telomerase can rebuild telomeres, but in most adult tissues it is barely active. It is switched on mainly in reproductive cells, in some stem cells and, significantly, in the great majority of cancers, where it allows cells to keep multiplying indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the late 1990s this picture seemed to offer a simple explanation of ageing. A team led by Professor Mirela Iordachescu at the Carpathian Institute of Cell Biology inserted the gene for telomerase into ordinary human skin cells growing in the laboratory. Whereas untreated cells stopped dividing after the usual number of generations, the treated cells continued to divide well beyond that point and showed no sign of becoming cancerous. Newspapers greeted the results as the discovery of a biological fountain of youth. The excitement was understandable, but it was misplaced. Iordachescu herself was careful to point out that her cells had been grown in a dish, and a dish is not a body. Most of the cells in an adult human, including those of the heart and brain, rarely divide at all, so it was never likely that the shortening of telomeres could account for every aspect of growing old.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Attention then turned to large population studies. Dr Yerlan Tleuberdiyev of the Central Asian Institute of Human Genetics measured telomere length in the white blood cells of more than forty thousand adults and followed their health for ten years. People in the shortest fifth of the distribution were significantly more likely to develop heart disease and to die during the study period than those in the longest fifth. Telomere length was also associated with a range of social and behavioural factors: it tended to be shorter in smokers, in people living in poverty and in those reporting long periods of psychological stress. Tleuberdiyev has suggested that telomere length might therefore serve as a kind of biological record of the hardships a person has experienced, summarising in a single number the wear and tear of a lifetime.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others are much less confident. Dr Kawika Nakoa, a geneticist at the Pacific Institute for Genome Biology, notes that laboratory mice have telomeres many times longer than ours yet rarely live beyond three years, which suggests that length on its own cannot be what sets the limits of a lifespan. More importantly, he argues, telomere length varies enormously between individuals from birth, and most of that variation is inherited. A single measurement taken in middle age, on this view, says more about a person's parents than about how they have lived. I find Nakoa's argument decisive as far as individuals are concerned: one reading of an inherited trait cannot reveal much about one person's experience. It does not follow, however, that average differences between large groups, such as smokers and non-smokers, are meaningless, since inherited variation tends to cancel out when thousands of people are compared.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An even more unexpected complication emerged from genetic research. People who inherit variants that give them unusually long telomeres turn out to have a higher risk of several cancers, including melanoma and certain brain tumours. Dr Elina Ruusuvuori of the Nordic Cancer Genetics Unit argues that this makes sense once telomere shortening is seen not as a defect but as a defence. Every division carries a small risk of introducing a harmful mutation, and limiting the number of divisions a cell can undergo reduces the chance that a damaged cell will multiply into a tumour. The price of this protection, she suggests, is the gradual loss of tissue renewal in old age. This idea of a trade-off between cancer and degeneration seems to me the most illuminating insight the field has produced, because it explains why evolution has not simply given us longer telomeres.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this has deterred the sellers of supplements claiming to activate telomerase and thereby slow ageing. There is no reliable evidence that these products lengthen telomeres in people, and if they did work as advertised, the link between telomerase and cancer would give users good reason for concern. Supporters sometimes cite experiments in which gene therapy delivering telomerase extended the lifespan of mice. Those results are genuinely interesting, but the animals involved had been genetically engineered to be unusually resistant to cancer, so they tell us little about what the same treatment would do in an ordinary animal, let alone in a human being.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Telomeres, then, are neither the villain nor the saviour they were once portrayed to be. Their gradual erosion is a real feature of ageing and almost certainly contributes to some age-related diseases, particularly those of the blood and immune system, but it is one process among many, interacting with others in ways that are still poorly understood. Perhaps the most lasting lesson of the telomere story is a cautionary one: a single, elegant mechanism can attract far more hope than the evidence warrants, and the complexity of ageing tends to reassert itself sooner or later.

topic: parabiosis and the search for rejuvenating factors in young blood
title: Borrowed Time
subtitle: Experiments that join old and young animals have revived an old question: is there something in young blood that can turn back the clock?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the nineteenth century, a French physiologist devised an unusual surgical procedure. By stitching together the skin of two living animals along their flanks, he found that their blood vessels would eventually grow into one another, so that the pair shared a single circulation. The technique, known as parabiosis, was used for decades to study how substances travel through the body. In the 1950s, researchers in North America applied it to the question of ageing by joining old rats to young ones, and reported that the older animals in these pairs lived longer than old rats that had not been connected. The findings attracted little attention at the time, and for nearly half a century parabiosis was largely forgotten, regarded by many as a crude and ethically uncomfortable relic of an earlier era of physiology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its revival began in the early 2000s, when Professor Shirin Dastmalchi of the Elburz Institute for Regenerative Medicine joined pairs of old and young mice and examined their tissues in detail. In the older partners, injured muscles healed more effectively than expected, liver cells divided more readily, and new neurons appeared in regions of the brain associated with memory. The effect also worked in reverse: young mice that shared blood with old partners repaired damaged tissue less efficiently than normal. Dastmalchi concluded that the blood of young animals must contain factors capable of restoring youthful function to ageing organs, and that identifying these factors could lead to entirely new treatments for the diseases of old age.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The search that followed produced some dramatic claims. One laboratory announced that a single protein, abundant in young blood and scarce in old, could reverse the thickening of heart muscle in elderly mice and restore strength to their skeletal muscles. Within a few years, however, other groups reported that they could not reproduce the results. It emerged that the test used to measure the protein had also detected a different molecule, and that levels of the protein might not decline with age at all. There is no suggestion that anyone acted dishonestly; the error appears to have been purely technical. Nevertheless, the episode is a reminder that a single striking result in this field should be treated as a hypothesis rather than a discovery.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental challenge to Dastmalchi's interpretation came from Dr Corentin Abgrall at the Armorican Centre for Ageing Biology. Abgrall noticed that in parabiosis the old animal not only receives young blood but also has its own blood diluted. To separate the two effects, his team removed half of the blood plasma from old mice and replaced it with a simple saline solution containing albumin, a common protein that carries no known rejuvenating properties. The treated mice showed improvements in muscle repair, liver function and memory comparable to those seen in parabiosis. Abgrall argues that old blood contains substances that actively suppress repair, and that the benefit comes from reducing them rather than from adding anything youthful. I believe this reframing is the most important advance the field has made, because it moves attention away from young donors and towards the possibility of cleaning old blood, a procedure that hospitals already perform routinely for certain immune disorders.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such subtleties have not prevented the commercial exploitation of young blood. Several private clinics have offered infusions of plasma taken from donors aged between sixteen and twenty-five, charging thousands of dollars per treatment, until regulators warned that there was no proof of benefit. The only controlled trial so far, involving eighteen patients with mild Alzheimer's disease, found that the infusions were safe but had little measurable effect on memory or thinking. Charging vulnerable people large sums for a treatment with no demonstrated benefit is, in my view, indefensible, however sincere the providers may be.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Akosua Owusu-Bempah of the Volta Institute of Transfusion Medicine raises a different concern. Supplies of donated plasma are already stretched, she points out, and are needed for patients with burns, bleeding disorders and immune deficiencies. If plasma from young donors were ever shown to slow ageing, the demand from wealthy older people could be enormous, creating a market that would draw on the young and the poor while diverting supplies from those in urgent need. She therefore argues that research should concentrate on identifying the active molecules so that they can be manufactured synthetically. Her worry is entirely legitimate, though if Abgrall is right, it may never arise: a treatment based on diluting or filtering a patient's own blood would require no donors at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever the eventual outcome, the revival of parabiosis has changed how researchers think about ageing. It has shown that the condition of old tissues depends in part on the environment in which they are bathed, and that at least some of the decline associated with age may be reversible. Whether that insight can be turned into safe and effective treatments for people remains, for now, an open question.
