area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the genetic origins of maize from teosinte
title: A Grass Transformed
subtitle: How an unpromising wild grass became the world's most productive cereal, and why the genetic story may be less simple than it first appeared

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Teosinte, a wild grass of the Balsas River valley in south-western Mexico, looks very little like maize. It branches profusely, produces dozens of small ears, and each ear holds only five to twelve kernels sealed inside hard, stony cases. For much of the twentieth century, some botanists refused to accept that such a plant could be the ancestor of maize at all, proposing instead an extinct wild maize that had left no trace in the landscape. Genetic evidence has since settled the question decisively: maize was domesticated from teosinte roughly nine thousand years ago, apparently in a single region. What remains contested is how the transformation occurred, and in particular whether it was driven by a few genes of large effect or by thousands of small changes accumulating gradually over time.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for a few major genes rests largely on the work of a team at the Highland Institute of Plant Genetics led by Itzel Coaquira. By crossing maize with teosinte and tracking which chromosomal regions accompanied particular traits in the offspring, her group found that a small number of regions accounted for a surprisingly large share of the differences between the two plants. One gene, which controls branching, appears to explain much of why maize grows a single stalk topped by a tassel rather than a bushy cluster of stems. Another determines whether kernels are enclosed in a hard casing or exposed on the surface of the cob. Coaquira argues that early farmers, by selecting a few conspicuous variants, could have produced a recognisably maize-like plant within a few centuries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Notably, the branching gene variant favoured in maize did not arise during domestication. Coaquira's group detected the same variant in wild teosinte populations, where it occurs at low frequency. Its effect in maize stems not from a change to the protein the gene produces but from a stretch of DNA, located a considerable distance away, that increases the gene's activity. The finding illustrates a principle that has since been confirmed in many crops: domestication frequently worked by altering when and how strongly existing genes are switched on, rather than by creating new genes. In this sense, early cultivators were not inventing novelties but amplifying variation that wild populations already contained.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that this picture is complete. Dávid Szabolcsi, a population geneticist at the Danube Centre for Evolutionary Studies, has compared whole genomes from modern maize varieties with those of teosinte and identified hundreds of regions that bear the signature of selection. Most, he contends, have individually tiny effects on yield, kernel size or flowering time, and their combined contribution may rival that of the celebrated major genes. Szabolcsi's view is that the focus on a few large-effect genes is partly an artefact of the experimental methods used: crossing studies are good at detecting genes with big effects and poor at detecting the many with small ones. There is some force in this argument, although it does not overturn the earlier findings so much as place them in a broader context.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Archaeological material has added a further complication. Cobs recovered from dry caves in the Mexican highlands, some of them more than five thousand years old, have yielded ancient DNA. Analyses by Kanokwan Ruangsri and colleagues at the Pacific Archaeogenomics Laboratory show that some of these early cobs already carried the maize form of the branching gene, but retained the teosinte form of genes affecting kernel quality and starch content. Domestication, in other words, was not a single event completed in a few centuries but a process that continued for thousands of years, with different traits fixed at different times and in different places. Ruangsri has also found evidence that maize repeatedly exchanged genes with a highland teosinte after it spread from the lowlands, acquiring variants that may have helped it tolerate cold.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings matter for more than historical reasons. Plant breeders today face the challenge of adapting crops to hotter, drier and less predictable climates, and wild relatives are an obvious source of useful genetic variation. If domestication depended mainly on a handful of switches, it might be relatively straightforward to transfer resilience traits from teosinte into modern maize. If, as Szabolcsi suggests, crop performance depends on thousands of interacting variants, any such transfer will be far more laborious. The truth probably lies between these positions, but breeders would be unwise to assume that the simple version of the story will serve them well.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is also worth reflecting on what the maize story reveals about the people who began it. The first cultivators had no knowledge of genetics, yet over many generations they consistently favoured plants whose kernels were easier to harvest and process. Whether they did so deliberately, or whether such plants simply prospered in tended fields, is impossible to establish. What seems clear is that the remarkable productivity of modern maize is the cumulative achievement of countless anonymous farmers rather than the result of any single decisive step.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the origins of the domestic dog as revealed by ancient genomes
title: Tracing the First Dogs
subtitle: Ancient genomes have answered some long-standing questions about the origins of the dog and raised several new ones

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few questions in the study of domestication have generated as much disagreement as the origin of the dog. It is generally agreed that dogs descend from wolves, and that they were the first animals to be domesticated, well before the arrival of farming. Beyond that, almost everything has been disputed: when domestication happened, where it happened, how many times, and whether humans or wolves took the initiative. For several decades, researchers tried to answer these questions by examining the DNA of living dogs. That approach, it is now clear, was always going to struggle, because thousands of years of movement and interbreeding have blurred the genetic traces of the earliest events.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The arrival of ancient DNA has changed the field considerably. Bones and teeth from archaeological sites can now yield entire genomes, allowing researchers to observe dog populations as they existed thousands of years ago rather than inferring them from their modern descendants. One unexpected result is that none of the wolf populations alive today appears to be the direct ancestor of dogs. Instead, dogs seem to have descended from a population of wolves that has since vanished, leaving only its domesticated offshoot behind. This explains why earlier efforts to identify a single region of origin by comparing dogs with modern wolves produced such contradictory answers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question of whether dogs were domesticated once or more than once remains open. Ingrid Halvorsrud, of the Northern Institute for Ancient Genomics, has argued that the deep genetic division between dogs of eastern Asia and those of western Eurasia reflects two independent domestications, one at each end of the continent. In her account, the western population was later largely replaced by dogs arriving from the east, which would explain why early European dogs look genetically distinct from modern European breeds. Other researchers find this explanation unnecessarily complicated. Chukwuemeka Ezeanyika, at the Lagos Centre for Evolutionary Biology, maintains that a single origin followed by a split into eastern and western lineages accounts for the same evidence more economically. On present data, Ezeanyika's simpler model seems the more defensible, though a single well-preserved genome from the right site and period could easily reverse that judgement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dating the process is equally difficult. Genetic estimates have placed the separation of dogs from wolves anywhere between fifteen thousand and more than thirty thousand years ago. Part of the problem is that the rate at which mutations accumulate, on which such estimates depend, is itself uncertain. Another difficulty is that separation from wolves is not the same thing as domestication; a population might have begun to diverge genetically long before it lived closely with people. Archaeologists, meanwhile, debate whether some very early canid skulls belong to dogs or to unusual wolves, and since skull shape changes gradually, there may be no clear line to draw. Some specialists have suggested that the earliest relationship may have been a loose partnership in which wolves scavenged around human camps for generations before any deliberate control was exercised over their breeding.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What happened after domestication is in some ways better understood. Hiroshi Kawabuchi and his colleagues at the Kansai Molecular Zoology Unit have studied a gene involved in digesting starch. Wolves usually carry two copies of it, whereas many dogs carry far more, which appears to help them digest the starchy food scraps left by farming communities. Kawabuchi found, however, that the number of copies varies widely: dogs traditionally associated with hunting peoples or with herders in cold regions often have few, while dogs from long-established farming regions have many. This suggests that the change occurred after agriculture spread, and well after domestication itself, a reminder that dogs continued to adapt to human ways of life for thousands of years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Interbreeding complicates the picture further. Dogs and wolves can produce fertile offspring, and genomes show that genes have flowed in both directions throughout their shared history. Some researchers regard this as noise that obscures the true story. It seems more accurate to treat it as part of the story: the dog was never a sealed lineage separated once and for all from its wild ancestor, but a population that remained in contact with wolves over a very long period. Similar patterns have since been reported in pigs, goats and cattle, which suggests that the dog is typical rather than exceptional in this respect. Domestic populations in general appear to have been far less isolated from their wild relatives than early models assumed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate over dog origins is sometimes presented as a contest between rival teams, each defending its preferred location. This framing is unhelpful. The evidence increasingly points to a long, messy process involving several populations of both wolves and people, and it is unlikely that any single site will ever be identified as the place where the dog began. Accepting that uncertainty is not a failure of science but a more honest reflection of how domestication actually occurs. Nor does it make the subject any less interesting; if anything, it brings the history of the dog closer to the complicated history of the people who lived alongside it.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the nineteenth century, naturalists noticed something curious about domestic mammals. Animals as different as pigs, rabbits, dogs and cattle tend to share a cluster of traits rarely seen in their wild ancestors: drooping ears, patches of white fur, shorter faces, smaller teeth, reduced brain size and a tendency to retain youthful behaviour into adulthood. This pattern later became known as the domestication syndrome. Its existence posed an awkward question. It is easy to understand why early herders might have preferred calm animals, but much harder to see why they would have deliberately chosen spotted coats or smaller brains in so many species at once.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One answer, which has attracted considerable interest over the past decade, concerns a group of embryonic cells known as the neural crest. Early in development, these cells migrate through the body and give rise to a remarkable variety of tissues, including pigment cells, parts of the skull and jaw, the teeth and the adrenal glands that govern the response to fear. Elena Amundarain, a developmental biologist at the Basque Institute of Comparative Anatomy, argues that selecting animals for tameness would have favoured individuals with slightly fewer or less mobile neural crest cells, and therefore a muted fear response. Because the same cells shape the face, the ears and the coat, the other features of the syndrome would have followed as unintended side effects. The idea has an undeniable elegance: one developmental mechanism appears to account for a whole bundle of apparently unconnected traits.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporting evidence has come from comparisons of genomes. Obinna Nwokedi, at the West African Centre for Evolutionary Genetics, has examined published scans for signs of selection in more than a dozen domestic species and found that genes involved in neural crest development appear repeatedly among the regions that changed. Yet Nwokedi is careful not to overstate the case. Several hundred genes participate in neural crest development, he points out, so a degree of overlap would be expected purely by chance, and the analyses carried out so far have not always controlled adequately for this.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental challenge comes from Karen Lindebjerg, a zoologist at the Øresund Institute of Animal Science, who questions whether the syndrome exists in any meaningful sense. Having reviewed descriptions of domestic animals across many centuries, she concludes that few of the supposed traits occur consistently across species, and that several, such as the extreme short faces of some dog and pig breeds, appeared only with the specialised breeding of the past two hundred years. Lindebjerg is right that the syndrome is a looser collection of tendencies than textbooks imply. To abandon the concept entirely, however, would be to discard a genuine pattern simply because it is imperfect.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much of the enthusiasm for the neural crest hypothesis stems from a long-running Siberian experiment in which foxes were bred over many generations solely for their friendliness towards people. Within a few decades, the tamest lines had begun to show floppy ears, curly tails and patches of white fur. Lindebjerg, however, notes that the founding animals were obtained from commercial fur farms, where they had already experienced some selection for tolerance of captivity, and where coat variation was not unknown. The experiment, she argues, may therefore reveal less about the very beginnings of domestication than is often claimed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different line of evidence comes from animals that have never been deliberately bred at all. Rodolfo Quispealaya, of the Andean Institute of Urban Ecology, has compared museum skulls of wild foxes and other carnivores collected over the past century with those of animals now living in cities. He reports that urban populations show slightly shorter snouts and smaller braincases, which he interprets as the early stages of a self-domestication driven by the advantage of being less fearful near people. The observation is intriguing, but caution is required: a change of diet towards softer, human-derived food could alter skull shape just as readily as any change in temperament.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Anahit Sarkisyan, a theoretical biologist at the Caucasus Centre for Evolutionary Studies, offers yet another interpretation. In her view, many features of the syndrome reflect not selection but its absence. Once animals lived under human protection, the natural pressures that had maintained camouflage colouring, keen senses and large brains were relaxed, allowing mutations affecting these traits to accumulate without penalty. This explanation and the neural crest hypothesis are often presented as rivals, but there is no reason why both processes could not have operated together, perhaps to different degrees in different species.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Where, then, does the debate stand? It would be premature to declare the neural crest hypothesis either confirmed or refuted. Its chief merit lies in the fact that it makes specific predictions that can be tested: for instance, that tamer animals should show measurable differences in the number or movement of neural crest cells during development. Experiments of this kind are now under way. Until their results are known, the term domestication syndrome is perhaps best used with some caution, as a convenient label rather than as proof of a single underlying cause.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: single versus multiple origins of Asian rice (indica and japonica)
title: One Grain, Many Histories
subtitle: Geneticists and archaeologists still disagree about how many times Asian rice was domesticated, and about what the answer means for the crop's future

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Rice provides a greater share of the calories consumed by humanity than any other single crop, yet the story of how it came to be cultivated remains surprisingly contested. Asian rice is divided into two main groups, indica and japonica, which differ in grain shape, in the stickiness of the cooked grain and in the climates to which they are suited. Indica tends to produce long, separate grains and thrives in the humid lowlands of South and Southeast Asia, whereas japonica, with its shorter and more glutinous grains, extends into cooler temperate zones. For much of the twentieth century, botanists took it for granted that plants so distinct must have been tamed separately, from different wild ancestors in different places. The question is not merely one of historical curiosity. Where and how a crop originated determines where plant breeders search for useful genetic variation, and for a grain on which billions of people depend, that is a matter of real practical consequence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea of two separate origins seemed, at first, to be confirmed by the arrival of large-scale genetic sequencing. When researchers compared the complete genomes of hundreds of rice varieties, indica and japonica turned out to differ at an enormous number of positions, and each resembled particular wild populations more closely than it resembled the other. Lucien Fabregat, a plant geneticist at the Mediterranean Centre for Crop Evolution, has been the most forceful defender of this interpretation. In his view, the degree of divergence between the two groups is simply too great to have accumulated in the few thousand years since farming began. They must, he argues, have been separated long before people started to cultivate them, which implies that each was domesticated independently from its own wild stock.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This conclusion was soon complicated by research into the small number of genes responsible for the traits that distinguish a crop from its wild relative. Wild rice scatters its seeds as soon as they ripen, a useful strategy for a wild plant but a disaster for a farmer trying to harvest a field. Domesticated rice holds on to its grain, and the change is controlled largely by a single gene. A team led by Sachiko Otomura at the Institute of Paddy Genomics found that indica and japonica carry exactly the same mutated version of this gene, and the same proved true of a second gene that makes the plant grow upright rather than sprawling along the ground. Otomura points out that the chance of an identical mutation arising twice, in two separate populations, is extremely small. The more economical explanation, she contends, is that these genes arose once, in japonica, and were later passed on to indica.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The two findings appear contradictory, but a model proposed by the population geneticist Thandeka Mobeng offers a way of reconciling them. Mobeng suggests that japonica was domesticated first, probably in southern China, and was carried by farmers westwards and southwards into South Asia. There, it was repeatedly crossed with local wild or semi-cultivated rice. Over many generations, most of the genome of the resulting plants came from the local populations, which accounts for the large differences Fabregat identified. The handful of genes that made the plants easy to harvest, however, came from japonica, because farmers consistently favoured plants that kept their grain. This account explains both sets of evidence more convincingly than either rival theory, although it should be acknowledged that the dates it proposes for these crossings rest on very limited archaeological data.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Archaeologists, for their part, have raised a more fundamental objection. When the spikelet bases left behind after threshing are examined under a microscope, it is possible to tell whether the grain fell naturally or was torn from the plant. Marisol Echeverlarra, an archaeobotanist who has analysed thousands of such remains from sites in the lower Yangtze valley, has found that the proportion of non-shattering forms rose only gradually, over a period of perhaps two or three thousand years. For Echeverlarra, talk of an 'origin' encourages people to imagine a single moment of invention, when the reality was a slow drift in which wild and cultivated plants grew side by side. Her point is well taken, but it does not follow that the genetic question is meaningless. A process can be gradual and still have begun in one region rather than several.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A useful comparison is provided by African rice, an entirely separate species domesticated in the inland delta of the Niger River roughly three thousand years ago. West African farmers selected for the same characteristics as their Asian counterparts, including grain that stays on the plant, yet the genetic changes responsible are different. When people in different places domesticated rice independently, in other words, they did so through different mutations. This lends weight to Otomura's reasoning: had indica and japonica been domesticated quite separately, they too would be expected to carry different versions of the key genes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate matters because domestication narrows genetic diversity. Each time farmers selected a few desirable plants, much of the variation present in the wild population was left behind, and some of it may hold the key to resisting new diseases or coping with a changing climate. Some researchers have argued that if japonica originated in southern China, wild populations there deserve priority in conservation programmes. That reasoning is understandable, but it is mistaken. Wild rice is disappearing across its entire range as wetlands are drained and converted to housing and industry, and whatever the true history of the crop turns out to be, the genetic resources of every remaining population will be needed.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the origins of the domestic horse: Botai, Przewalski's horse and the steppe lineage
title: Riding into History
subtitle: Ancient genomes have overturned several confident accounts of where and when the horse was first domesticated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few animals have altered the course of human history as profoundly as the horse. Before it was domesticated, nothing on land could carry a person faster than his or her own legs; afterwards, messages, armies, goods and ideas could cross a continent in a matter of weeks. It is no exaggeration to say that the ridden horse did more to shrink the ancient world than any innovation before it. Yet the question of where and when horses were first tamed has proved remarkably difficult to answer. People hunted wild horses for tens of thousands of years before they began to keep them, and the bones of a hunted animal look much like those of a herded one. For most of the twentieth century, archaeologists could do little more than argue over ambiguous scraps of evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: By the 1990s, one site had come to dominate the discussion. At settlements of the Botai culture in the grasslands of northern Kazakhstan, dating from around 5,500 years ago, excavators recovered hundreds of thousands of horse bones, far more than those of any other animal. Bolat Ermekbayuly, an archaeologist at the Steppe Archaeology Institute, assembled what remains the most detailed argument that the Botai were herders rather than hunters. Fragments of pottery from the sites, he showed, carried fat residues whose chemical signature matched that of mare's milk. Rings of post holes near the dwellings suggested corrals, and a number of horse teeth displayed a pattern of wear that he attributed to the use of a bit. Taken together, these strands of evidence made an impressive case, and for two decades Botai was widely cited as the birthplace of the domestic horse.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That consensus was overturned when the palaeogeneticist Ingrid Haavardsholm and her colleagues sequenced the genomes of horses from Botai sites. The animals proved to be only distantly related to the domestic horses of today. Instead, they were the direct ancestors of Przewalski's horse, the stocky animal of the Mongolian steppe long celebrated as the last truly wild horse on earth. If the Botai horses were indeed herded, then Przewalski's horses are not wild at all but the feral descendants of domesticated stock, a finding with uncomfortable implications for the conservation programmes built around them. Haavardsholm herself interprets the results as evidence of an early domestication that led nowhere: the Botai, she suggests, kept horses for meat and milk, but their lineage was eventually abandoned and its animals reverted to life on the open steppe.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the Botai kept horses at all. The zooarchaeologist Valeria Montescudo has examined teeth from Ice Age horses that lived thousands of years before any human could have handled them, and found that some display damage almost identical to the supposed bit wear at Botai. Such marks, she argues, can arise from natural abnormalities in the way the teeth meet. She also notes that fat residues degrade over time and are difficult to attribute confidently to a single source. In her reading, the Botai were specialised hunters who drove wild herds into enclosures for slaughter. This scepticism is a useful corrective to an account that was accepted too readily. Yet it is difficult to dismiss every strand of the original evidence, and the most plausible conclusion is perhaps that the Botai practised a loose form of management somewhere between hunting and herding.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If modern horses did not descend from Botai, where did they come from? The answer emerged from an ambitious study coordinated by the statistical geneticist Siosaia Taufahema, which compared the genomes of more than two hundred ancient horses from sites across Eurasia. The lineage that gave rise to virtually all living domestic horses appears in the archaeological record around 4,200 years ago, in the steppe close to the lower reaches of the Volga and Don rivers. What followed was astonishingly rapid. Within a few centuries this lineage had spread from the Atlantic coast to Mongolia, almost entirely replacing the varied local populations that had existed before. Its expansion coincides with the appearance of spoked wheels and light chariots, which would have given communities possessing the new horses a considerable advantage.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taufahema's team also identified regions of the genome that had changed sharply under selection. One is associated with reduced anxiety and greater tolerance of handling; another with the strength and structure of the back. Taufahema takes this as evidence that the decisive step in domestication was not the supply of meat but the creation of an animal that could be controlled and ridden. The interpretation is plausible, but it should be held with some caution, since the functions of these genes have largely been inferred from studies of mice and humans rather than of horses themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The new findings have also disturbed a theory about the history of language. It has long been proposed that herders known as the Yamnaya, who expanded westwards from the steppe some 5,000 years ago, carried early Indo-European languages into Europe, and their success was often attributed to their mastery of the horse. The genetic evidence suggests, however, that Yamnaya horses did not belong to the lineage that later conquered Eurasia, which emerged several centuries after their expansion. The Yamnaya may instead have relied on heavy wagons pulled by oxen. This does not refute the linguistic theory itself, which rests on other evidence, but it removes one of its most romantic elements. In the space of a decade, ancient DNA has dismantled three confident stories about the horse, and that record ought to make researchers wary of embracing a new one too quickly.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the domestication of the chicken from junglefowl and its link to cereal farming
title: The Accidental Bird
subtitle: New genetic and archaeological evidence suggests that the chicken was domesticated later, and less deliberately, than once believed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: There are more chickens on earth than any other bird; at any given moment, more than twenty billion of them are alive, most of them in vast commercial sheds. Yet for an animal so familiar, the chicken has a surprisingly obscure past. Its very ordinariness has worked against it: archaeologists have tended to pass over small bird bones in favour of the remains of cattle, sheep and pigs, and geneticists turned their attention to its history only relatively recently. This neglect is regrettable, because the story of the chicken reveals a good deal about how domestication can happen almost by accident, without any intention on the part of the people involved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That the chicken descends mainly from the red junglefowl, a shy forest bird of South and Southeast Asia, has long been suspected, and genome sequencing has now confirmed it. More precisely, the closest match is a subspecies found today in southwestern China, northern Thailand and Myanmar. The picture is not entirely simple, however. The chicken genome also contains contributions from other species of junglefowl, and the gene responsible for the yellow skin of many breeds appears to have come from the grey junglefowl of the Indian subcontinent. Torvald Ekhagen, an avian geneticist at the Uppland Centre for Bird Genomics, regards this genetic mosaic as a sign that chickens were domesticated in several regions independently. Most of his colleagues favour a different explanation: a single domestication, followed by repeated interbreeding with wild birds as chickens were carried into new territories.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question of when this happened has proved even more contentious. For several decades, textbooks reported that chickens were being kept in northern China as much as ten thousand years ago, on the basis of bird bones recovered from early farming villages. When these bones were re-examined with modern techniques, many turned out to belong to pheasants and other wild birds, and it was pointed out that the region would in any case have been too cold and dry for junglefowl to thrive. Such errors were understandable, since the bones of small game birds are notoriously difficult to tell apart, but it is unfortunate that they were repeated without question for so long.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more persuasive account has been put forward by the zooarchaeologist Kanokwan Siriphatthana. In her surveys of sites in central Thailand, the earliest reliable chicken bones date to around 3,500 years ago, and they appear only at settlements where dry rice and millet cultivation had recently arrived. Siriphatthana argues that wild junglefowl were drawn to the grain growing in fields and stored in villages, and that over many generations the boldest birds came to live alongside people, becoming steadily tamer. On this view, the chicken was a by-product of cereal farming rather than a deliberate undertaking, and it spread across Asia and beyond in the company of the crops that had first attracted it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Equally revealing is what happened once chickens reached the far west of Eurasia. Ottilie Brannagh, a historian of early European farming, has studied chicken remains from Iron Age sites and found that, for several centuries after their arrival, the birds were rarely eaten. Skeletons are frequently found complete, sometimes buried alongside human beings, and very few bear the marks of butchery. A number of the birds evidently lived to an advanced age, and several cockerels show healed injuries to the legs of a kind associated with fighting. Brannagh concludes that chickens were initially prized for cockfighting, for their striking appearance or for religious reasons, and that they became an everyday food only much later, under Roman rule. The lesson is an important one: the purpose for which an animal is first kept may bear little relation to the uses it eventually serves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Siriphatthana's model is elegant, but it is not beyond question. Its central argument rests on the absence of earlier chicken remains, and absence is a fragile foundation in tropical Southeast Asia, where acidic soils and high humidity destroy bone far more quickly than in temperate regions. Older chickens may well have existed and simply failed to survive in the archaeological record. Ekhagen has made a similar point, adding that if domestication occurred in several places, the Thai sites need not be the earliest. The cereal hypothesis therefore deserves to be treated as the best current explanation rather than a settled conclusion.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These debates have practical consequences. Modern commercial chickens descend from a remarkably narrow genetic base, which leaves them vulnerable to diseases such as avian influenza. A single pathogen able to exploit a weakness shared by most commercial flocks could spread with alarming speed, and breeders searching for genetic resistance have few places to look. Wild junglefowl represent a reservoir of the diversity that domestic flocks have lost, yet in much of their range they are interbreeding with village chickens and gradually losing their distinct genetic identity. The protection of genuinely wild junglefowl populations is therefore an urgent task, and it is one that has so far attracted remarkably little attention from conservation bodies.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the self-domestication of the cat and the spread of its lineages
title: The Cat That Walked In
subtitle: Is the domestic cat a domesticated animal at all? Genetics and archaeology suggest that the answer depends on what we mean by the word

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Cats share homes with several hundred million people, yet a surprising number of biologists hesitate to describe them as fully domesticated. Unlike dogs, cats perform no task on command; for most of their history they have chosen their own mates, and millions of feral cats survive perfectly well without any human assistance. This hesitation, however, says more about our definitions than about cats. The standard idea of domestication was developed with livestock in mind, and it assumes an animal whose breeding, movement and food are controlled by people. Judged by that measure, the cat will always appear to be an anomaly, and the measure is arguably too narrow to capture the different routes by which animals have come to live with humans.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Genetic studies have at least settled the question of ancestry. All domestic cats descend from the African wildcat, a small tabby-coloured predator whose range extends across North Africa and the Near East. What is striking is how little the two have diverged. Comparisons of their genomes reveal only a modest number of regions that appear to have been shaped by selection, several of them linked to memory, fear and the seeking of rewards. To the behavioural ecologist Paulette Ravoahangy, this is precisely what one would expect of an animal that has never been fully brought under human control. She describes cats as semi-domesticated, living in an arrangement with humans that either party can walk away from at any time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How the arrangement began is usually explained by what is known as the commensal pathway. The grain stores of the first farming villages in the Near East attracted mice and rats, and the rodents in turn attracted wildcats, the boldest of which grew accustomed to human company. People had no reason to drive away an animal that protected their harvest, and so a relationship developed in which neither side needed to plan anything. Yet one discovery complicates this picture. On the island of Cyprus, archaeologists found a human grave around 9,500 years old in which a cat had been buried close to the body. Since wildcats are not native to Cyprus, they must have been brought there by boat. For the archaeologist Yusuf Karadağlı, this shows that people were actively involved with cats from the very beginning, and that the idea of cats domesticating themselves has been overstated. The objection is an important one, but carrying an animal across the sea is not the same as controlling its breeding, and the Cyprus burial does not demonstrate the latter.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ancient DNA has added a further dimension to the story. A team led by the palaeogeneticist Henrike Oosterbaan analysed genetic material from more than two hundred cat remains spanning some nine thousand years. Their results point to two distinct waves of expansion. The first carried cats out of the Near East with early farmers, into Anatolia and south-eastern Europe. The second, thousands of years later, began in Egypt and moved rapidly around the Mediterranean along maritime trade routes, perhaps because cats were kept on board ships to keep down rodents. It was this Egyptian lineage, Oosterbaan found, that contributed disproportionately to the ancestry of cats around the world today.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The same study shed light on one of the few visible differences between domestic cats and their wild ancestors. The blotched tabby pattern, with its swirling bands of dark fur, is now extremely common, yet the mutation responsible was rare until the medieval period and became widespread only in the last few centuries. This suggests that deliberate breeding for appearance is a very recent phenomenon in the history of the cat. For most of the nine thousand years that cats have lived among people, it seems, humans exercised little control over which cats reproduced, a finding that lends considerable support to the view that cats largely domesticated themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most intriguing evidence comes from northern China. Linghu Zhuoran, an archaeozoologist, examined cat bones from a farming village occupied around 5,300 years ago. Chemical analysis indicated that the animals had eaten rodents which had themselves fed on the millet grown by the villagers, exactly the kind of relationship the commensal model describes. Yet the bones belonged not to the African wildcat but to the leopard cat, an entirely different species. Leopard cats never became domestic animals, and they were eventually replaced by descendants of the African wildcat arriving from the west. Linghu interprets the episode as an independent attempt at domestication that was abandoned, and argues that it shows that living close to farmers is not, by itself, sufficient to turn a wild animal into a domestic one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, this evidence suggests that domestication is better understood as a continuum than as a simple division between wild and tame, with the cat occupying an intermediate position along it. Ravoahangy's term is useful in this respect, though the prefix 'semi' implies something unfinished, when the cat's status may in fact be a stable arrangement that has suited both parties for millennia. That arrangement is now changing, as breeders develop pedigree varieties with increasingly exaggerated features. Whether this represents progress is far from clear: several of the most fashionable breeds suffer from serious inherited disorders affecting their breathing, joints and hearts.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the hybrid origin of bread wheat and the revival of synthetic wheat
title: A Weed in the Loaf
subtitle: Bread wheat was born from an unplanned cross between a crop and a wild grass, and plant breeders are now trying to repeat the accident

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Bread wheat supplies roughly a fifth of the calories eaten by the world's population, yet in genetic terms it is one of the strangest plants in cultivation. Its genome is about five times the size of the human genome, and each of its cells contains not two sets of chromosomes, as in most plants and animals, but six. These six sets come from three different ancestral species, which merged in two separate events thousands of years apart. The emergence of such a plant was not the result of any plan, and it surely ranks among the most remarkable accidents in the history of agriculture.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The story begins in the Fertile Crescent, where wild emmer wheat grew on the hillsides of what are now Turkey, Syria and Iraq. Emmer was itself a hybrid, formed naturally long before the advent of farming when two wild grasses crossed and their chromosome sets combined. Farmers began cultivating it around 10,500 years ago, gradually favouring plants whose ears did not shatter when ripe. As emmer cultivation spread eastwards into the region south of the Caspian Sea, the crop encountered a weedy wild grass known as goat grass, which flourished at the margins of fields. At some point between eight and nine thousand years ago, pollen from one plant reached the other, and the offspring, carrying the chromosomes of both, became the ancestor of bread wheat. Unlike emmer, therefore, bread wheat has never existed as a wild plant: it was born in a farmer's field.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Which goat grass plants were involved has become the subject of lively disagreement. By comparing the portion of the wheat genome inherited from goat grass with samples of the wild grass collected across Central Asia, the geneticist Mehrnoush Daryabari has traced the donor lineage to populations that still grow near the south-western shore of the Caspian. She also found that this portion of the wheat genome is remarkably uniform, suggesting that only a handful of goat grass plants ever contributed to it. Tobiah Ellenbogen, a plant evolutionary biologist, accepts the Caspian origin but maintains that the hybridisation must have happened more than once, since certain traditional wheat varieties carry rare variants that are absent from the main lineage. Daryabari counters that these variants could have entered the crop later, through occasional crossing with wild goat grass growing nearby. At present the dispute cannot be resolved, because wild goat grass has been sampled only patchily across its enormous range.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever the details, the contribution of goat grass was decisive. Its chromosomes gave the new crop tolerance of cold winters and salty soils, allowing wheat to spread far beyond the Fertile Crescent into continental Europe and the steppes of Central Asia. Just as importantly, goat grass supplied proteins that make dough elastic, enabling it to trap the gas produced by yeast and rise into a light loaf. Emmer and other earlier wheats could be made into flatbreads and porridge, but not into bread as most people now understand it. It is no exaggeration, then, to say that the modern loaf owes its existence to a weed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The manner of bread wheat's birth has also left it with a weakness. Because so few goat grass plants were involved, the part of the genome they provided is the least varied of the three, and this genetic narrowness leaves the crop exposed to new strains of disease and to rising temperatures. For several decades, breeders have tried to address the problem by producing what is known as synthetic wheat. They cross durum wheat, a modern descendant of emmer, with wild goat grass under laboratory conditions, recreating the original hybridisation with fresh partners. The programme run by the plant breeder Wairimu Gathecha in East Africa has used such synthetic lines to introduce resistance to stem rust, a devastating fungal disease, together with greater tolerance of drought, into varieties grown by local farmers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not every specialist is convinced that this is the best route. Rémi Castagnède, who has worked on wheat improvement for many years, points out that synthetic lines tend to bring unwanted characteristics along with useful ones: tall, weak stalks, grain that is difficult to thresh and flour of poor baking quality. Removing these traits requires years of repeated crossing with established varieties. Castagnède argues that gene editing, which can alter a single targeted gene directly, offers a far quicker alternative. His point about speed is fair, but it overlooks a basic limitation. Editing works only when breeders know which gene to change, and for complex traits such as drought tolerance, which depend on many genes acting together, that knowledge is often lacking. In such cases, the untapped variation of a wild relative cannot easily be replaced.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This makes the fate of wild goat grass a matter of real concern. Many of its populations around the Caspian are under pressure from overgrazing by sheep and goats and from the expansion of towns and roads, and the world's seed banks hold only a fraction of the diversity that survives in the wild. Conservation efforts tend to favour species that capture the public imagination, and an unremarkable grass growing at the edge of a field is unlikely ever to do so. Yet the plant that made bread possible deserves at least as much protection as many more charismatic wild species.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: the cost of domestication: the accumulation of harmful mutations in crops and domestic animals
title: The Hidden Price of Taming
subtitle: Domesticated plants and animals may carry a genetic burden that their wild relatives have largely avoided

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Domestication is usually described as a story of improvement. Wild grasses with tiny seeds became cereals with heavy, nutritious grains; nervous, unpredictable animals became docile companions and dependable sources of meat and milk. Over the past two decades, however, genetic research has revealed a less flattering side to this transformation. Many domesticated species appear to carry substantially more harmful mutations than their wild relatives, a phenomenon that geneticists have come to call the cost of domestication. The idea is still debated, but it offers a valuable correction to a narrative that has too often treated domestication as an unbroken march of progress.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two processes are thought to be responsible. The first is the population bottleneck. Domestication generally began with a small number of founding individuals, and in small populations the influence of chance outweighs that of natural selection, so that mildly damaging mutations can drift to high frequencies instead of being weeded out. The second is the selective sweep. When breeders strongly favour a valuable gene, the stretch of chromosome surrounding it tends to be inherited along with it, and any harmful variants lying nearby are carried along as unwelcome passengers. Plants that are propagated from cuttings rather than seed face an additional handicap. Because they rarely reproduce sexually, they miss out on recombination, the reshuffling of chromosomes that normally allows harmful mutations to be separated from beneficial ones and gradually removed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cassava, a starchy root crop that feeds hundreds of millions of people in Africa, Asia and South America, has been grown from stem cuttings for thousands of years, and it has become an important test case. A team led by the population geneticist Akosua Frimpomaa compared the genomes of cultivated cassava with those of its wild ancestor and found that the crop carries a markedly greater number of mutations predicted to impair the function of genes. Many of these are concealed, because each plant usually possesses one working copy of the gene alongside the faulty one. Frimpomaa argues that this explains a long-standing puzzle: when cassava plants are inbred, the faulty copies are frequently paired together and the offspring are weak and unproductive. Her view is that crops propagated in this way, among them potatoes, bananas and grapes, are likely to bear the heaviest burden of all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Animals tell a broadly similar story. Sunniva Kjeldaas, a geneticist who studies canine evolution, compared the genomes of domestic dogs with those of grey wolves and found that dogs carry a higher proportion of potentially damaging variants in the genes that code for proteins. Strikingly, the proportion is highest in modern pedigree breeds, most of which were created through intense selection from small numbers of animals during the last two centuries. Kjeldaas links this pattern to the high rates of inherited disease recorded in many breeds. Her results suggest that the second, recent bottleneck imposed by formal breeding has done more genetic harm than the original domestication of the dog thousands of years earlier.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are persuaded that the cost is as large as these studies imply. Dragoș Albulescu, a quantitative geneticist, points out that mutations are usually classified as harmful by computer programs, which predict their effects from how strongly the relevant section of a gene has been conserved during evolution. Very few of these predictions have been tested experimentally. Moreover, a variant that would be damaging in the wild may be harmless, or even useful, in a field where plants are fertilised, irrigated and protected from competitors. Albulescu's caution is justified as far as it goes. Yet the weakness of inbred cassava and the disease burden of pedigree dogs are not computer predictions; they are observable facts, and they are difficult to explain without some genuine accumulation of harmful mutations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If the cost is real, it may also be reversible. The plant breeder Ignacio Barrenechea has proposed using genomic data to identify the individuals carrying the fewest harmful variants and to favour them as parents, a strategy he calls genomic purging. In preliminary trials with maize, lines selected in this way produced higher yields than lines chosen by conventional means. The approach is promising, but it relies on precisely the predictions whose accuracy Albulescu questions, and if applied carelessly it could narrow the genetic base of crops still further by concentrating breeding on a small number of favoured lines.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that domestication should be regarded as a failure. The crops and animals that humans have shaped over ten thousand years remain extraordinarily productive, and the cost identified by geneticists is a matter of degree rather than a fatal flaw. What the research does underline is the value of wild relatives, which in many cases retain healthier genomes than their domesticated descendants and could help breeders to repair some of the damage. Protecting those wild populations is perhaps the most practical response to a problem that domestication itself created.

area: the genetics of domestication (plants and animals)
topic: de novo domestication of wild plants using gene editing
title: Domestication on Fast-Forward
subtitle: Gene editing may allow scientists to turn wild plants into crops in a few years rather than a few thousand, but the obstacles are not only technical

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The domestication of the world's major crops took thousands of years, and it came at a price. As early farmers selected plants with larger seeds or fruits, they left behind much of the genetic diversity of the wild populations, including traits that helped plants to withstand drought, salt and disease. For over a century, breeders have tried to recover some of that diversity by crossing crops with their wild relatives, a slow process that often introduces undesirable characteristics along with useful ones. A group of plant scientists now proposes reversing the procedure: instead of adding wild traits to crops, they would add domestication traits to wild plants. This approach, known as de novo domestication, has been made feasible by gene-editing tools that can alter specific genes with great precision. It is one of the most intriguing ideas in contemporary plant science, although the claim that it will rapidly transform world agriculture is, at the very least, premature.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most celebrated demonstration so far was carried out by a team led by Tamar Gvaramia. Her group began with the wild ancestor of the tomato, a straggling plant from the coastal valleys of Peru and Ecuador that produces fruits no bigger than a currant. Drawing on decades of research into the genes that changed during the original domestication of the tomato, the team edited six of them, controlling fruit size, the number of fruits, the compactness of the plant and its sensitivity to day length. Within a single generation, the edited plants bore fruits three times larger and ten times more numerous than their wild parents. Crucially, they retained the wild plant's tolerance of salty soil and contained a higher concentration of lycopene, a pigment valued for its antioxidant properties, than most cultivated tomatoes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Haruto Kisaragi has applied similar methods to a different kind of plant. His interest lies in what are sometimes called orphan crops: species that are gathered or grown locally, often in large quantities, but that were never fully domesticated and have attracted little attention from commercial breeders. One example is the groundcherry, a relative of the tomato whose sweet fruits are popular in parts of the Americas but which sprawls untidily and drops its fruit to the ground before it can be harvested. By editing the genes responsible for these traits, Kisaragi's group produced plants that were more compact and bore larger fruits. He argues that de novo domestication will prove most valuable not as a means of replacing established crops but as a way of improving species like these, for which no other breeding effort is likely to be made.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kisaragi's emphasis seems sensible. The major crops benefit from centuries of accumulated improvement in a wide range of characteristics, including flavour, storage life and uniformity, many of which are controlled by hundreds of genes whose identity is still unknown. Editing a handful of well-understood genes produces what is, at best, a partially domesticated plant. Gvaramia's tomatoes, impressive as they are, still yield considerably less per hectare than commercial varieties, and closing that gap would require knowledge that does not yet exist. To suggest that a few precise edits can replicate what farmers and breeders achieved over thousands of years is to underestimate the complexity of the task.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other concerns are regulatory and ecological. Lorenza Bassignani, a specialist in the governance of biotechnology, notes that edited wild species occupy an awkward legal position. They are neither conventional crops nor genetically modified organisms in the traditional sense, since no foreign DNA has been inserted, and in many countries it is unclear which rules apply to them. She also warns that a newly domesticated plant growing near its wild relatives could cross with them, with consequences that are difficult to predict. Bassignani therefore recommends field trials lasting several seasons before any edited wild plant is released for general cultivation. This caution is reasonable, but the risk of edited genes escaping from small, closely monitored trials appears modest, and prolonged legal uncertainty is likely to deter publicly funded researchers, who lack the resources to navigate it, far more than large companies.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further question concerns who will benefit. Inti Quillahuaman, an anthropologist who works with farming communities in the Andes, points out that many wild relatives and orphan crops come from regions whose indigenous inhabitants have cultivated, gathered and studied them for generations. It was often their knowledge that first identified which plants were worth eating or growing. If edited varieties are patented by universities or companies elsewhere, Quillahuaman argues, the communities that made them known may receive nothing in return. He calls for agreements that guarantee such communities a share of any benefits and a voice in deciding which traits are developed. This is surely right: a scientific achievement that ignores the people whose knowledge made it possible can hardly be regarded as a complete success.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: De novo domestication, then, is unlikely to replace conventional breeding, but it may offer a valuable complement to it. Its most realistic successes are likely to come from orphan crops and from hardy wild species that could be grown on marginal land, where existing crops struggle and where a changing climate is making conditions harsher still. Whether that promise is fulfilled will depend as much on decisions about regulation and ownership as on progress in the laboratory.

topic: bacteria-based self-healing concrete
title: The Concrete That Mends Itself
subtitle: Concrete laced with bacteria promises cracks that seal themselves, but its supporters and sceptics disagree about what it can realistically achieve

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Concrete is the most widely used manufactured material on the planet, and after water it may be the most heavily consumed substance of any kind. Its weakness is not a lack of strength but a vulnerability to cracking. As concrete dries, bears loads and expands and contracts with the seasons, fine fissures inevitably appear. On their own these are rarely dangerous, but they provide a pathway for water and dissolved salts to reach the steel bars that reinforce most modern structures. Once the steel begins to corrode, it swells, splitting the surrounding concrete and accelerating the damage. Governments spend vast sums each year inspecting and patching bridges, car parks and tunnels, and it is arguably the hidden cost of maintenance, rather than the price of construction, that should dominate discussion of how we build.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One response to this problem has been to give concrete the ability to repair itself. The best-known approach, developed over the past two decades, mixes dormant bacterial spores into the concrete along with a food source, usually calcium lactate, sealed inside tiny clay capsules. The spores belong to species that tolerate the extremely alkaline conditions inside concrete and can remain inactive for many years. When a crack forms and water seeps in, the capsules break open, the bacteria revive and, as they consume the nutrient, they produce calcium carbonate, essentially limestone, which gradually fills the gap. Ottilie Thorvaldsrud, a microbiologist at the Hallgrim Institute of Building Materials, reports that in her laboratory trials cracks up to 0.8 millimetres wide were completely sealed within three weeks, a result she describes as 'well beyond what conventional sealants achieve without human intervention'.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that such results will transfer to real structures. Kwabena Oduro-Mensah, a structural engineer at the Coastal Infrastructure Laboratory, points out that laboratory specimens are kept at stable temperatures and are regularly wetted, whereas bridges and walls experience freezing winters, scorching summers and long dry spells. Because the bacteria need a steady supply of moisture over a period of weeks, he suspects that in arid regions many cracks would simply never heal. He also notes that the capsules occupy space that would otherwise be filled by aggregate, and early versions reduced compressive strength by as much as a quarter. His caution about climate is well founded. On strength, however, his objection now looks dated: newer capsule designs, which are smaller and bond more effectively with the surrounding cement, have cut the loss to a few per cent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The more stubborn obstacle may be economic rather than technical. Self-healing concrete currently costs considerably more than the conventional material, with estimates ranging from thirty to fifty per cent extra, and that premium is paid at the moment of construction. Mariela Achával, an economist at the Institute for Construction Economics, argues that the true comparison should be made over a structure's entire life, since the savings appear only decades later, when repairs that would otherwise have been needed are avoided. The difficulty, she says, is that the firm which builds a structure is rarely the organisation responsible for maintaining it, and tendering processes typically reward whoever offers the lowest initial price. On this point Achával is surely right: until the way contracts are awarded changes, even a flawless product will struggle to find buyers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Bacteria are not the only route to self-repair. Some research groups embed networks of thin tubes filled with liquid polymer, which flows into cracks and hardens when the tubes are ruptured; others add crystalline chemicals that react with water to form insoluble deposits. Advocates of these methods argue that they are simpler to manufacture and less sensitive to environmental conditions. Yet they have a significant limitation. A ruptured polymer tube cannot be refilled, so each section can heal only once, whereas a bacterial system may respond to repeated cracking for as long as viable spores remain in the vicinity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Given the cost, few engineers expect self-healing concrete to replace ordinary concrete across the board. Its most persuasive applications lie in places where inspection and repair are difficult, dangerous or extremely expensive: tunnel linings, underground water tanks, the foundations of tall buildings and offshore structures exposed constantly to seawater. In such locations a modest reduction in maintenance can justify a substantial increase in the initial outlay. Targeting the technology at these settings, rather than promoting it as a universal improvement, seems the most sensible way to build confidence among clients who are, by nature, conservative.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Supporters also present self-healing concrete as an environmental technology. Cement manufacture is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and structures that last longer should, in principle, reduce the need for new construction. This argument deserves to be treated with some care. Extending the life of a bridge does nothing to lower the emissions produced when its cement was made, and there is a danger that the promise of durable concrete could distract attention from the harder task of decarbonising cement production itself. Self-healing materials are a valuable contribution to the problem of ageing infrastructure; they are not, on their own, a solution to the climate impact of building.

topic: bioplastics and the meaning of 'biodegradable'
title: The Trouble with 'Biodegradable'
subtitle: Plastics made from plants were supposed to solve the waste crisis. The reality is considerably more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the first plastic bags labelled 'biodegradable' appeared in supermarkets, they seemed to offer an easy escape from a growing environmental embarrassment. Three decades later, the market for so-called bioplastics is expanding rapidly, yet confusion about what the term actually means has, if anything, deepened. Part of the difficulty is that it covers two quite separate properties. A plastic is 'bio-based' if it is made from plant material rather than oil; it is 'biodegradable' if microorganisms can break it down into water, carbon dioxide and biomass. The two need not coincide. Polyethylene manufactured from sugarcane is chemically identical to the fossil-fuel version and persists just as long, while certain oil-derived polymers are readily consumed by microbes. Much public misunderstanding stems from treating these categories as if they were interchangeable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely used bioplastic, polylactic acid (PLA), illustrates the problem. Made from fermented corn starch or sugarcane, it is both bio-based and, under the right circumstances, compostable. Halina Kaczanowska, a polymer chemist at the Baltic Institute of Macromolecular Research, emphasises how narrow those circumstances are. PLA breaks down within about twelve weeks in industrial composting plants, where the material is held at around 58°C in moist conditions; in a garden compost heap, which rarely becomes so hot, or in cold seawater, it may survive largely intact for years. The label 'compostable' is therefore accurate in a technical sense but potentially misleading, all the more so because industrial facilities willing to accept such packaging remain scarce in most countries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Labels matter because they shape behaviour. In a series of experiments, the behavioural scientist Tamsin Harcourt of the Westmoor Centre for Consumer Studies gave volunteers drinks in cups marked either 'biodegradable' or with no environmental claim, then observed what happened to the cups at an outdoor event. Those holding the labelled cups were noticeably more likely to leave them on the ground, apparently assuming that the material would simply disappear. If this finding holds, it is troubling: a label designed to reduce harm could end up increasing litter. Harcourt's studies were, however, conducted with a few hundred participants in a single city, and it would be premature to build policy on them before they have been repeated elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different problem arises once bioplastics enter the waste system. Emeka Okonjo-Adeyemi, who studies municipal recycling at the Gulf of Guinea Waste Research Institute, points out that PLA bottles look almost exactly like those made from PET, the plastic most commonly recycled. When they are mixed together, even small quantities of PLA can weaken the recycled PET, lowering its value. Sorting machines equipped with near-infrared sensors can tell the materials apart, but many local authorities cannot afford them. Okonjo-Adeyemi proposes that compostable packaging be given a distinctive colour so that it can be separated by eye. The idea is sensible, though it depends on the willingness of manufacturers, who have so far shown little enthusiasm for any requirement that limits their freedom of design.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Questions also surround the origins of bioplastics. Inés Valdivieso, who carries out life-cycle assessments at the Andean Centre for Industrial Ecology, has found that while plant-based plastics usually generate fewer greenhouse gases than their fossil equivalents, the crops from which they are made require land, water and fertiliser. In several of the products she examined, fertiliser washing from fields into rivers meant that the bio-based option performed worse on measures of water pollution. It would be wrong to conclude from this that bio-based plastics should be abandoned. What her work does show is that the choice of raw material deserves far closer scrutiny, and that feedstocks such as crop residues and food-processing waste, which require no additional farmland, are likely to be preferable.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe the solution lies in entirely different polymers. Riku Vuorinen, a microbiologist at the Lakeland Bioprocess Laboratory, works on polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), materials that certain bacteria produce naturally as energy stores. Unlike PLA, PHAs decompose in soil and even in seawater, typically within a few months. Their drawback is price: they currently cost three to five times as much as conventional plastics. Vuorinen is confident that costs will fall as production expands, much as the price of solar panels did. The comparison is less convincing than it appears. Solar panels became cheaper largely through improvements in manufacturing, whereas most of the cost of PHA lies in the sugars and oils on which the bacteria are fed, and these are unlikely to become dramatically cheaper.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that bioplastics have no future, but it does suggest that their role should be more modest than their early champions imagined. Replacing one single-use material with another leaves the underlying culture of disposability untouched, and reduction and reuse will always deliver larger benefits. Compostable plastics make most sense where an item will inevitably end up mixed with food: tea bags, coffee pods and the liners of food-waste bins, for example, which can be composted together with their contents. In these cases biodegradability is not a marketing claim but a genuine practical advantage.

topic: nickel-titanium shape-memory alloys in medical devices
title: Metal with a Memory
subtitle: How a temperamental alloy of nickel and titanium found its place inside the human body

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few materials have had a stranger career than the alloy of nickel and titanium known as nitinol. In the early 1960s, metallurgists at a naval research laboratory noticed that a strip of the metal, bent out of shape at room temperature, would snap back to its original form when gently heated. The discovery was greeted as a curiosity, and for almost two decades it remained one: the alloy was difficult to melt, harder still to machine, and so sensitive to its exact composition that two batches made to the same recipe could behave quite differently. This long neglect contradicts the popular assumption that superior materials find their own markets. The history of nitinol suggests that performance on its own guarantees nothing; what matters is whether engineers can find a setting in which a material's peculiarities become virtues.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation for this behaviour lies in the alloy's crystal structure. At lower temperatures, nitinol adopts a form known as martensite, in which the atoms are arranged in layers that can slide past one another with little resistance, allowing the metal to be bent or twisted with ease. When it is heated above a certain point, it shifts into a more rigid arrangement called austenite and, in doing so, recovers the shape it was given during manufacture. Crucially, the temperature at which this change occurs can be adjusted. Altering the proportion of nickel by a fraction of one per cent can move it by tens of degrees, so that wire can be made to transform at body temperature. A related property, known as superelasticity, allows the austenite form to be stretched by up to eight per cent and still return to its original dimensions, whereas ordinary stainless steel is permanently deformed by a strain of less than one per cent.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It was in medicine that nitinol finally found its niche. Self-expanding stents, the tiny mesh tubes used to hold open narrowed blood vessels, can be compressed into a thin catheter, guided through an artery and then released, at which point the warmth of the body causes them to spring open. In orthodontics, nitinol archwires have largely replaced steel ones. Dr Ottavia Brancaleoni, a biomaterials engineer at the Adriatic Institute of Biomaterials, argues that shape memory itself is a less important reason for this success than is commonly supposed. What dentists value, she contends, is that a superelastic wire exerts an almost constant, gentle force as the teeth move, whereas a steel wire pushes hard at first and then quickly slackens, requiring frequent adjustment. Her point is well made, although it perhaps underplays the convenience of a wire that can be fitted cold and allowed to tighten itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone has welcomed the alloy into the body. Roughly half of nitinol by weight is nickel, one of the most common causes of skin allergy, and there has long been concern that nickel ions might leach from implants into surrounding tissue. Professor Sigrún Hallvarðsdóttir, who studies corrosion at the Reykjavík Centre for Surface Science, has found that the thin layer of titanium oxide which forms naturally on the metal is generally an effective barrier. Her experiments suggest, however, that the quality of this layer depends heavily on how the device is finished: poorly polished surfaces, or those scratched during insertion, release far more nickel than smooth ones. She believes the industry has focused too much on composition and too little on surface treatment. The fears expressed in some popular accounts appear exaggerated where the majority of patients are concerned, yet for devices intended to remain in the body for decades, closer scrutiny is surely justified.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more pressing difficulty is fatigue. A stent placed in an artery of the leg may be bent, twisted and compressed more than a million times a year. Data gathered by the Antofagasta Vascular Implant Registry, under the direction of Dr Ximena Quilodrán, indicate that stents in the leg fracture considerably more often than those in the coronary arteries of the heart. Quilodrán attributes this not to defects in the metal but to the nature of the loads involved: laboratory tests have traditionally subjected devices to simple, repeated bending, whereas a leg artery imposes a combination of twisting, stretching and crushing that such tests do not reproduce. It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that regulatory testing has lagged behind clinical experience.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe the answer lies in new alloys altogether. Dr Haruki Momoyama, a computational materials scientist at the Miyagi Advanced Alloys Laboratory, uses computer simulations to screen thousands of possible compositions, adding small quantities of elements such as copper and hafnium to the basic nickel-titanium mixture. Several of the alloys his group has produced have survived more than ten million loading cycles without failure. Such results are encouraging, but they should be treated with caution. Endurance in a testing machine is not the same as durability in a human limb, as Quilodrán's findings make clear, and elements such as hafnium are expensive and scarce.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Beyond medicine, nitinol has found a scattering of other uses, from actuators that adjust the shape of aircraft engine inlets to spectacle frames that recover after being sat on. Enthusiasts have occasionally proposed it as the basis for heat engines that would turn waste warmth into motion, but these schemes have foundered on a basic limitation: such devices convert only a few per cent of the heat they absorb into mechanical work. Nitinol did not succeed because it was extraordinary, but because, after a long search, engineers found tasks for which its odd combination of properties was exactly what was required.
