topic: metamaterials beyond the invisibility cloak
title: Beyond the Cloak
subtitle: Engineered materials that bend waves in unnatural ways have been judged by the wrong standard

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of history, the properties of a material were dictated by its chemistry: copper conducts because of the way its electrons behave, and glass bends light because of how its atoms are bound together. Metamaterials break this rule. They are artificial structures built from repeating elements, each smaller than the wavelength of the waves they are designed to manipulate, and their behaviour derives from the arrangement of those elements rather than from what they are made of. Correctly designed, they can steer light or sound in directions that no natural substance permits. Yet public discussion of the field has been dominated by a single idea, the invisibility cloak, and this fixation has arguably done metamaterials research more harm than good, encouraging expectations that no laboratory could hope to meet.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The cloak's reputation rests on demonstrations from the mid-2000s, in which a ring of carefully patterned copper elements guided microwaves around a small cylinder so that it barely disturbed them. The achievement was genuine, but it worked at a single frequency and in only two dimensions. Approached from another angle, or illuminated at a different frequency, the cylinder was as conspicuous as ever. Professor Dagny Rustad, a theoretical physicist at the Lofoten Institute for Wave Physics, argues that these limitations are not teething troubles but consequences of fundamental physics. To hide an object, a cloak must send light around it along a longer path while making it emerge as if it had travelled straight through, which is possible only over a narrow band of wavelengths. Concealing a large object across the full visible spectrum, she concludes, is ruled out in principle. Her reasoning is sound, and it deserves wider circulation than it has so far received.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even modest optical metamaterials are difficult to make. To manipulate visible light, the individual elements must be only tens of nanometres across, and the standard method of fabricating them, electron-beam lithography, writes each feature one at a time; patterning a single square centimetre can take several days. Dr Wiesław Grzyb and his colleagues at the Wrocław Nanophotonics Centre have pursued an alternative in which nanoparticles are coaxed into assembling themselves into ordered arrays. The method is far cheaper, but the resulting structures are never perfect. Grzyb has turned this apparent weakness into an argument: a controlled degree of disorder, his group reports, can actually broaden the range of wavelengths over which a device functions, at the cost of some loss of precision.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, metamaterials have been quietly succeeding elsewhere. Compact antennas in mobile phones and satellites are one example; so-called metalenses, flat surfaces studded with nanoscale pillars that can focus light in place of a stack of curved glass elements, are another, and both are already reaching the market. Dr Lorcan Ó Fearghail, an engineer at the Limerick Centre for Applied Electromagnetics, observes that the most commercially important applications are precisely those that consumers never notice. He goes further, suggesting that the word 'metamaterial' should be abandoned, since many of these devices amount to clever engineering of periodic structures that predates the term. This seems a step too far. Whatever its origins, the label has brought together physicists, chemists and engineers who previously worked in isolation, and that shared identity has value in its own right.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Similar ideas have been extended from light to sound and even to the ground beneath our feet. In one widely reported field trial, engineers drilled a grid of boreholes into soil and found that vibrations passing through it were substantially reduced, prompting speculation that cities might one day be shielded from earthquakes. Dr Tupac Huamaní, a geophysicist at the Cusco Seismic Observatory, is unconvinced. The trial, he points out, used artificially generated vibrations at relatively high frequencies, whereas the most destructive earthquake waves are slow, low-frequency undulations. Deflecting these would require structures tens of metres deep, spread over areas comparable to entire districts. He does not dismiss the idea entirely, conceding that smaller arrays might protect sensitive installations, such as precision laboratories, from the vibrations of nearby traffic or machinery.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mechanical metamaterials, by contrast, are delivering tangible results. By arranging tiny struts in particular geometries, designers have produced materials that grow fatter rather than thinner when pulled, a property that makes them useful in protective padding and in medical implants that must expand evenly inside the body. Other lattices have been tuned to absorb the energy of an impact and then recover their shape, something that conventional foams cannot do more than once.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is as dramatic as a vanishing cloak, and that is precisely the point. Funding agencies tend to reward proposals that promise spectacular outcomes, and researchers have learned to frame their work accordingly, often describing incremental progress as a step towards invisibility. Flat camera lenses, quieter machinery and lighter protective equipment may lack the glamour of science fiction, but they are what the discipline is actually producing. A field ought to be judged not by its most theatrical ambitions but by the accumulation of modest, reliable advances, and by that measure metamaterials are thriving.

topic: cross-laminated timber in tall buildings
title: Building Upwards in Wood
subtitle: Engineered timber is reshaping city skylines, but its environmental credentials deserve a closer look

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, the tall building has been a creature of steel and concrete. Wood, it was assumed, belonged to houses and barns: too weak, too flammable and too prone to rot for anything more ambitious. That assumption is now being overturned. Using a product known as cross-laminated timber, or CLT, architects have erected residential and office towers of eighteen storeys or more, and designs for considerably taller structures are under discussion. Advocates present these buildings as a powerful weapon against climate change. Their enthusiasm is understandable and, to a degree, justified, but the environmental case for building in wood is considerably more complicated than its supporters usually acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: CLT is made by gluing together layers of kiln-dried boards, each layer laid at right angles to the one below, and pressing them into large, solid panels. Because wood swells and shrinks far more across the grain than along it, alternating the direction of the boards greatly reduces the tendency of the panel to change size as humidity rises and falls. Panels are manufactured in factories, where computer-controlled machines cut openings for windows, doors and service pipes with millimetre accuracy, and they arrive on site ready to be lifted into place. As a result, a timber frame can be assembled far more quickly than a concrete one, with fewer lorry deliveries and markedly less noise and dust for those living nearby.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The central environmental argument concerns carbon. As a tree grows, it absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and locks the carbon into its wood, where it remains for as long as that wood survives. Professor Solveig Ånestad of the Hedmark Institute of Building Ecology points out that a timber building therefore functions as a kind of carbon store, while at the same time displacing materials whose production is notoriously polluting: the manufacture of cement and steel together accounts for a substantial share of global industrial emissions. Her life-cycle analyses of completed projects suggest that the emissions embodied in the structure of a timber building may be roughly half those of an equivalent concrete design.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts such figures. Dr Mateus Cordovil, who studies forest policy at the Minho Forest Policy Unit, argues that the carbon stored in a building has merely been moved from one place to another, and that whether this represents a genuine gain depends on what happens in the forest. If trees are felled faster than they regrow, or if long-established natural woodland is cleared and replaced with plantations, the atmosphere may be no better off. Much also depends on the fate of the timber once the building is demolished: if it is burned or left to decay, the stored carbon returns to the air. Cordovil is right that forests must be included in any honest calculation. It does not follow, however, that timber buildings offer no climate benefit at all, as he concludes, for there are many well-managed forests in which harvesting is carefully balanced against growth.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For the public, the most immediate concern is fire. Here the evidence is more reassuring than intuition might suggest. Dr Kwame Nyantakyi, who leads fire testing at the Tamale Fire Engineering Laboratory, has shown that when a thick CLT panel is exposed to flames, its outer few centimetres are converted into charcoal. This blackened layer shields the wood beneath from heat, so that the panel retains its structural strength for a predictable period, a behaviour that engineers can design around. Nyantakyi has, however, identified one serious weakness. Under intense heat, the adhesive that bonds the layers can soften, causing charred layers to fall away and exposing fresh wood, which can then cause a dying fire to flare up again. Newer, heat-resistant adhesives appear to reduce this risk, although they are more expensive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A less publicised but perhaps more significant obstacle is financial. Dr Emiko Tsurumaki, who analyses construction risk at the Sapporo Centre for Construction Risk, notes that insurers frequently charge higher premiums for timber buildings, or decline to cover them altogether. In her view, this reluctance stems less from fear of fire than from the absence of long-term data: few tall timber buildings are more than a decade old, and insurers cannot yet judge how they will perform over fifty or a hundred years. Water is a particular worry, since panels left exposed to rain during construction may develop mould or decay that remains hidden for years. Tsurumaki believes that this uncertainty, rather than any technical shortcoming, is the main factor holding the industry back.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that timber construction should be abandoned. It does suggest, though, that wood is best regarded as one sensible option among several, rather than as a solution in itself. The material appears to be at its most effective in buildings of moderate height, perhaps six to twelve storeys, where its lightness reduces the need for heavy foundations and where fire and insurance requirements are least demanding. The image of wooden skyscrapers rescuing the climate is an appealing one, but the real contribution of timber is likely to be quieter and more modest.

topic: graphene and the gap between laboratory promise and commercial reality
title: The Wonder Material That Wasn't (Yet)
subtitle: Two decades after its isolation, graphene's slow progress tells us as much about our expectations as about carbon

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When graphene was first isolated in 2004, peeled from a lump of graphite with ordinary adhesive tape, it seemed to possess every virtue a material could have. A sheet of carbon only one atom thick, it was stronger than steel by weight, conducted electricity and heat better than copper, and was almost perfectly transparent. Predictions followed swiftly: graphene would replace silicon in computer chips, transform batteries, purify seawater and make flexible, unbreakable screens commonplace. Two decades later, the products that actually contain it are rather less dramatic: tennis rackets, bicycle frames, conductive inks and a handful of specialist sensors. It is tempting to conclude that graphene has failed. The more accurate judgement is that the disappointment reveals more about the expectations placed upon it than about any deficiency in the material itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first obstacle has been manufacture. The adhesive-tape method yields flakes of exceptional quality but microscopic size, useful for experiments and useless for industry. Growing graphene on copper foil from carbon-containing gases produces sheets many centimetres across, but these must then be transferred to another surface, a delicate process that tends to leave them wrinkled, torn and contaminated. Cheaper techniques that shear graphite apart in liquids generate large quantities of powder, though what they produce is often a mixture of fragments several layers thick. Dr Ksenia Voronikhina of the Novosibirsk Centre for Carbon Materials analysed samples from dozens of commercial suppliers and found that a large proportion of what was being sold as graphene consisted mainly of ordinary graphite, with very few genuine single layers. She has campaigned for internationally agreed definitions, and she is surely right to do so: without them, buyers have had no means of knowing what they were paying for, and confidence in the entire market has suffered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Electronics presented a different difficulty. A transistor, the basic switch of a computer chip, must be able to stop the flow of current as well as allow it, and silicon can do this because of a property known as a band gap. Graphene has no band gap, and although researchers have devised ways of creating one, each method sacrifices much of the conductivity that made the material attractive in the first place. Professor Aurelio Scarpellini of the Padua Institute of Solid-State Physics maintains that this rules graphene out of digital logic permanently. He argues that its future in electronics lies instead in high-frequency communication devices and in sensors, where its sensitivity to anything touching its surface is an advantage rather than a nuisance. On the evidence available, this assessment seems difficult to dispute.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some observers regard the whole story as entirely normal. Dr Olumide Fasawe, a historian of technology at the Abeokuta Centre for Innovation Studies, notes that aluminium and carbon fibre each took twenty to thirty years to progress from laboratory curiosity to mass-market product. By that standard, he suggests, graphene is not late at all. The comparison is partly reassuring, but it should not be pressed too far. Aluminium was obviously useful from the outset; the barrier was cost, and once cheap production methods appeared, demand was assured. In many of graphene's proposed applications, by contrast, its advantages over existing materials are often marginal, and saying that it is merely following a familiar schedule assumes the very success that remains in doubt.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more pragmatic view comes from economists. A group led by Dr Ha-eun Gwak at the Daejeon Materials Economics Group has examined where graphene is actually generating revenue, and finds that the most promising market is not pristine sheets but bulk additives. Mixing a fraction of one per cent of graphene powder into plastics, coatings or even concrete can noticeably improve strength, durability or resistance to corrosion. Such uses demand neither perfect crystals nor single layers, and so sidestep the manufacturing problems described above. Gwak's group concludes that graphene's commercial destiny is likely to be as an ingredient, sold in large volumes at modest prices, rather than as the foundation of revolutionary devices.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Wider use raises questions of safety. Dr Ilinca Moraru, a toxicologist at the Timișoara Institute of Nanotoxicology, has drawn attention to laboratory studies in which the sharp edges of graphene flakes appeared to pierce cell membranes. Little is known about what happens when such particles are inhaled or released into rivers, and she argues that their incorporation into everyday consumer goods should proceed cautiously until more is understood. Her concern is reasonable, but the findings so far come largely from isolated cells exposed to high doses, and it would be a mistake to allow preliminary evidence of this kind to bring development to a halt.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most damaging consequence of the early excitement was financial. Governments launched large research programmes in the expectation of rapid industrial returns, and a number of start-up companies raised substantial sums on the strength of promises they could not keep. When those returns failed to appear, graphene acquired a reputation for over-promising that it has struggled to shake off. Yet the material's most lasting contribution may lie elsewhere. Its isolation demonstrated that crystals only one atom thick could exist and be studied, opening an entire family of two-dimensional materials with properties of their own. Judged by that legacy, graphene has been anything but a failure.

topic: the quest to manufacture artificial spider silk
title: Spinning a Better Thread
subtitle: Why the effort to copy spider silk has taken far longer than anyone expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some years ago, a museum put on display a shimmering golden textile woven entirely from the silk of wild spiders. Producing it had required the work of dozens of people over several years and the silk of more than a million spiders, each collected, gently 'milked' and then released. The textile was beautiful, but its real message was one of impossibility. Spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms: they are solitary, fiercely territorial and inclined to devour their neighbours. If the remarkable properties of spider silk are ever to be exploited on an industrial scale, the material will have to be made without spiders. For more than thirty years, scientists and investors have been confidently announcing that this goal lies just five years away, a forecast that has so far proved consistently wrong.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The source of the excitement is dragline silk, the thread from which a spider hangs and which forms the frame of its web. Weight for weight, it rivals high-grade steel in strength, and it can absorb more energy before breaking than the synthetic fibres used in body armour. The silk is made of proteins known as spidroins, long chains built largely from short, repeating sequences. Some of these sequences fold into tightly packed crystalline regions that give the thread its strength; others form looser, disordered regions that allow it to stretch. Equally important is the way the thread is produced. The spider stores the protein as a concentrated liquid and draws it through a narrowing duct, where changes in acidity and in the concentration of dissolved salts, combined with the pulling force, cause the molecules to line up and solidify into a fibre.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Since spiders themselves are unsuitable, researchers have inserted spider genes into a variety of other organisms, including bacteria, yeast and silkworms, in the hope that these would produce the protein instead. Dr Nilufar Rashidova of the Tashkent Institute of Molecular Biotechnology argues that the chief difficulty has never been persuading these organisms to make spider protein, but persuading them to make enough of it in its full length. Natural spidroins are enormous, and the highly repetitive genes that encode them are unstable in bacteria, which tend to produce shortened versions. Fibres spun from these truncated proteins have generally been far weaker than the real thing. Rashidova's laboratory has developed a technique in which bacteria manufacture shorter segments that are then stitched together into proteins of natural length, and fibres made in this way have matched natural silk in some mechanical tests.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Eliseo Barragán-Tuz of the Yucatán Centre for Biomimetic Engineering takes a different view. In his opinion, obtaining the right protein is only half the battle, and the less important half. Most artificial spinning methods dissolve the protein in harsh chemical solvents and force it through a nozzle, producing fibres that lack the intricate internal organisation of natural silk. His team has instead built microscopic channels that imitate the gradually narrowing duct of the spider, reproducing its chemical gradients as closely as possible. Each researcher has identified a genuine problem, but the debate between them is somewhat artificial. The properties of silk emerge from the interaction of protein and process, and to treat either as the sole obstacle is to misunderstand how the material works.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the commercial record has been sobering. Several companies have announced consumer products containing recombinant silk, among them a running shoe, a knitted hat and a luxury jacket. Most were either quietly withdrawn or sold only in tiny numbers, and in several cases the silk made up a small fraction of a blend dominated by conventional fibres. Professor Anselm Kreuzberger of the Kassel Textile Research Institute believes that the industry has been chasing the wrong market. Silk proteins, he points out, are tolerated well by the human body and break down slowly and harmlessly, which makes them attractive for surgical stitches, scaffolds that guide the regrowth of damaged nerves, and coatings for implants. Such applications require only small quantities of material and can justify high prices, whereas the clothing market demands enormous volumes at low cost.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recombinant silk has also been marketed as an environmentally friendly alternative to nylon and polyester, which are derived from oil. The claim is appealing but, at present, difficult to substantiate. The microorganisms that produce silk protein must be fed on sugar, which has to be grown, and the fermentation and purification processes consume considerable amounts of energy and water. Independent life-cycle assessments are scarce, and those that exist depend heavily on assumptions about the scale of future production. Until fuller evidence is available, claims that artificial silk is greener than synthetic fibres should be regarded as premature.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to read this history as a catalogue of failure. That would be unfair. In trying to copy the spider, researchers have learned a great deal about how proteins assemble themselves into ordered structures, knowledge that is already informing work on other biological materials. Even if artificial silk never appears in a bulletproof vest, the effort to make it will have been well spent.

topic: high-entropy alloys and the exploration of compositional space
title: Metals in Equal Measure
subtitle: A radical recipe for alloys has overturned an ancient habit of metallurgy, but turning it into useful products is proving harder

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly five thousand years, the recipe for an alloy has followed the same basic pattern. A metallurgist begins with one principal metal and adds modest quantities of one or two others: a little tin to copper produces bronze, a pinch of carbon turns iron into steel. In the early years of this century, a handful of researchers asked what would happen if this habit were abandoned altogether, and five or more elements were combined in roughly equal proportions. Conventional theory predicted a brittle jumble of compounds. Instead, some of these mixtures formed surprisingly simple crystal structures with unexpected properties. The resulting materials, known as high-entropy alloys, represent one of the most important conceptual departures in metallurgy for a century, even if their practical impact has, so far, been rather limited.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The name refers to a thermodynamic explanation. When many different atoms are distributed randomly across the sites of a crystal, the number of possible arrangements is enormous, and this disorder, or entropy, was thought to stabilise a single uniform structure, particularly at high temperatures. Professor Kaveh Tabrizchi of the Isfahan Institute of Metallurgy argues that the role of entropy has been considerably exaggerated. His experiments show that many supposedly uniform alloys gradually separate into several distinct phases when held for long periods at moderate temperatures, precisely the conditions many engineering components experience. He prefers the term 'complex concentrated alloys', which makes no claim about mechanism. Tabrizchi's criticism goes further than a dispute over terminology. By encouraging researchers to search almost exclusively for single-phase materials, the original label arguably steered the field away from multi-phase alloys that may ultimately prove more useful.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whatever the explanation, some of the properties discovered have been striking. One alloy containing equal parts of cobalt, chromium, iron, manganese and nickel becomes both stronger and tougher as it is cooled towards the temperature of liquid nitrogen, whereas most metals grow brittle in the cold. Such behaviour suggests possible uses in tanks for storing liquefied gases or in equipment designed for space. At the other extreme, alloys built from metals with very high melting points, such as tungsten, molybdenum and niobium, retain much of their strength above 1,000 degrees Celsius, which has made them candidates for the hottest parts of gas turbines.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in finding the best combinations. With around fifty elements that might reasonably be used, the number of possible five-element mixtures in equal proportions runs into the millions, and once unequal proportions are admitted the possibilities become effectively limitless. Dr Odalys Fuenmayor of the Maracaibo Centre for Combinatorial Materials believes that traditional trial and error is hopeless in the face of such numbers. Her group deposits thin films in which the composition varies gradually across a single wafer, so that thousands of slightly different alloys can be tested at once, and feeds the results into machine-learning programs that predict which compositions deserve closer study. Fuenmayor expects this approach to identify alloys that outperform today's best turbine materials within a decade. Her optimism is not easily shared. A film a few millionths of a metre thick does not necessarily behave like a cast component weighing several kilograms, and models trained on relatively small datasets cannot yet be relied upon to make accurate predictions far beyond the examples they have seen.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also questions of supply. Dr Aleksi Rautiainen, who leads the Lappeenranta Circular Materials Laboratory, observes that many of the best-known high-entropy alloys depend on cobalt, most of which is mined in a handful of countries, sometimes under conditions that raise serious ethical concerns. The high-temperature varieties frequently require scarce elements such as hafnium and tantalum. Rautiainen is equally concerned about what happens at the end of a component's life. Scrap from conventional steel can be melted down and reused with relative ease, but an alloy containing five or more elements in similar proportions is extremely difficult to separate back into its constituents. He argues that future research should concentrate on alloys made from metals that are abundant and inexpensive, such as aluminium, iron, manganese and titanium.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Industrial adoption faces its own obstacles. In aerospace, a new alloy typically undergoes ten to fifteen years of testing before it is approved for use in an engine, and the nickel-based superalloys it would replace have been refined continuously for more than half a century. A newcomer must therefore be substantially better than the incumbent, not merely comparable, to justify the cost and risk of switching. A few high-entropy materials have nevertheless found niche roles, notably as hard, wear-resistant coatings on cutting tools. Coatings of this kind may well be the most realistic route to wider use in the near term, since a thin surface layer requires only a small quantity of expensive material and avoids many of the problems of producing large, flawless castings.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The greatest contribution of high-entropy alloys may ultimately be intellectual rather than commercial. For millennia, metallurgists explored only the corners of what might be called compositional space, the regions dominated by a single element. The new approach has opened up its vast and largely unexplored centre. That achievement deserves to be celebrated, but the field would do well to learn from other materials that were once hailed as revolutionary, and to resist the temptation to promise more than it can deliver.

topic: aerogels as insulation and the economics of a lightweight solid
title: Frozen Smoke Comes Down to Earth
subtitle: The world's lightest solids have spent decades in laboratories and spacecraft. Can they become an everyday building material?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Hold a piece of aerogel up to the light and it seems scarcely to be there at all. Pale blue and translucent, it has been nicknamed 'frozen smoke', and with good reason: some varieties consist of more than 99 per cent air, making them among the lightest solids ever produced. They are also extraordinary insulators, able to protect a flower from the flame of a blowtorch held beneath them. Space agencies have used aerogel to insulate equipment on planetary rovers and to trap dust from a passing comet without destroying the fragile grains. Yet although the material was first made in the 1930s, it remains largely confined to specialist applications. The usual explanation is that aerogel is simply too delicate for ordinary use. In fact, the principal obstacle has always been cost rather than any technical limitation, and that obstacle is now slowly being eroded.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Most aerogels begin as a wet gel, in which a sponge-like network of silica is filled with liquid. The challenge is to remove the liquid without destroying the network. If the gel is simply left to dry, the retreating liquid exerts capillary forces that crush the tiny pores, and the result is a dense, cracked lump. The traditional solution is supercritical drying. The gel is placed in a sealed vessel and heated under intense pressure until the liquid passes into a state in which it is neither liquid nor gas, and can be released without collapsing the structure. The process works, but it requires costly equipment that must withstand dangerously high pressures, and it can only be carried out in batches. Even when successful, it yields a brittle material that crumbles easily and sheds a fine dust.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much effort has therefore gone into avoiding supercritical drying altogether. Dr Bénédicte Kerhervé of the Rennes Institute of Porous Materials has refined a method known as ambient-pressure drying, in which the inner surfaces of the gel are chemically treated so that they repel water. The network still shrinks as the liquid evaporates, but instead of collapsing permanently, it springs back once drying is complete. Kerhervé estimates that the technique could reduce production costs by as much as 80 per cent. This is a promising development, but it comes at a price: aerogels made in this way tend to be slightly denser than conventional ones and, as a consequence, insulate somewhat less effectively.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The problem of fragility has largely been solved by combining aerogel with other materials. In commercial blankets, aerogel particles are embedded in flexible fibre mats that can be cut, rolled and wrapped around awkward shapes. Such blankets have become common in the oil and gas industry, where they insulate pipelines and processing equipment, and they are increasingly used to renovate older buildings, where a thin layer can achieve the same effect as a much thicker conventional board. This is particularly valuable in historic properties, where bulky insulation would conceal mouldings or reduce the size of already small rooms. Professor Rahim Sarwari of the Dundee Institute of Occupational Health warns, however, that cutting and fitting the blankets releases clouds of fine silica dust, and that the risks to installers have been given far less attention than they deserve. His concern is legitimate, although the form of silica in aerogel appears to be considerably less hazardous than the crystalline form associated with serious lung disease.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all aerogels are made from silica. Researchers have produced versions from polymers, from carbon and, increasingly, from cellulose, the main structural component of plants. Dr Marta Iriondo of the Gipuzkoa Biomaterials Centre makes cellulose aerogels from agricultural waste such as straw and the pulp left over from fruit processing. Her materials are flexible rather than brittle, and they decompose naturally at the end of their lives. Iriondo believes they could eventually replace expanded polystyrene, the white foam widely used to protect goods during shipping. The environmental advantages of turning farm residues into insulation are plausible enough, but cellulose readily absorbs moisture, and in humid conditions these aerogels can lose much of their insulating ability.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental question concerns how much difference aerogel insulation actually makes. Dr Takumi Ōsawa of the Asahikawa Building Physics Laboratory has modelled the performance of renovated homes and concludes that the energy savings claimed for aerogel retrofits are frequently overstated. Once the walls of a house are well insulated, he argues, most of the remaining heat escapes through thermal bridges: the junctions around window frames, floor joists and balconies, where heat finds a path around the insulation. Adding a more effective material to the walls therefore produces diminishing returns. Ōsawa's analysis is a useful corrective to some of the more extravagant marketing claims, although it applies chiefly to buildings that are already reasonably well insulated, rather than to the many older properties that are not.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The future of aerogel, then, depends less on scientific breakthroughs than on the patient work of reducing costs and adapting the material to particular settings. If the price continues to fall, it is likely to spread gradually from pipelines and specialist renovations into mainstream construction and packaging. Should that happen, a material once reserved for spacecraft may come to seem as unremarkable as the foam it is beginning to replace.

topic: perovskite solar cells and the problem of durability
title: Brilliant but Fragile
subtitle: Perovskite solar cells have broken efficiency records at astonishing speed. Whether they can survive on a rooftop is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Silicon has dominated solar power for half a century. A typical commercial panel today converts around 22 per cent of the sunlight falling on it into electricity, and the theoretical ceiling for a single layer of silicon lies at roughly 29 per cent. Into this mature market has burst a family of materials known as perovskites. The name refers to a particular crystal structure, first identified in a mineral discovered in the Ural Mountains in the nineteenth century; the versions used in solar cells are synthetic compounds that typically combine lead, a halogen such as iodine and a small organic molecule. When perovskites were first tested in a solar cell in 2009, they converted just 3.8 per cent of light into electricity. Within little more than a decade, laboratory cells had passed 25 per cent, a rate of improvement unmatched by any earlier photovoltaic technology. The achievement is genuinely remarkable, yet efficiency records alone reveal very little about whether a technology can succeed commercially.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The appeal of perovskites goes beyond efficiency. Silicon must be purified and crystallised at temperatures above 1,400 degrees Celsius, an energy-intensive process requiring vast factories. Perovskites, by contrast, can be dissolved in solvents and coated or even printed onto a surface at temperatures not much higher than those of a domestic oven. The resulting layers are hundreds of times thinner than a silicon wafer, light enough to be deposited on flexible plastic sheets. Perhaps most significantly, a perovskite layer can be placed on top of a conventional silicon cell to create a so-called tandem, in which each material absorbs a different portion of the solar spectrum. Laboratory tandems have exceeded 33 per cent efficiency, comfortably beyond the limit of silicon alone.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is durability. Perovskite crystals are vulnerable to moisture, oxygen and heat, and, rather awkwardly for a solar material, to light itself. Dr Yerlan Tokhtarbay, who directs an outdoor testing station on the Karaganda steppe, reports that the best cells now retain about 90 per cent of their initial output after a year of exposure. That represents enormous progress, but it should be set against the standard for silicon panels, which manufacturers routinely guarantee for 25 years with losses of less than half a per cent annually. Tokhtarbay is also critical of the accelerated ageing tests used by the industry, in which panels are held at 85 degrees Celsius and 85 per cent humidity for a thousand hours. These procedures, he argues, were devised for silicon and fail to detect some of the ways in which perovskites deteriorate. Under illumination, for instance, charged atoms drift through the crystal, reducing its output during the day, only for much of the loss to reverse at night, a pattern that short laboratory tests can easily miss.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Rayén Nahuelpán, a packaging engineer at the Pichilemu Solar Materials Centre, takes a more optimistic view. In her opinion, the stability problem is essentially one of encapsulation: if perovskite cells are sealed between sheets of glass with sufficiently robust edge seals, moisture and oxygen are excluded and lifetimes increase dramatically. Her own sealed cells have survived conditions that destroyed unprotected samples within hours. Encapsulation is undoubtedly part of the answer, but Nahuelpán's position seems too sanguine. A seal can keep out water and air, but it cannot shield the crystal from the heat and light that a solar panel must, by definition, endure, and the drifting of charged atoms that Tokhtarbay describes is a property of the material itself rather than of its surroundings.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further concern is lead. The amount in a perovskite panel is small, less than a gram per square metre, but the lead compounds involved dissolve readily in water. Dr Henrik Østergaard, an environmental chemist at the Odense Institute for Environmental Chemistry, points out that a panel cracked by hail and then exposed to rain could release lead into the soil beneath it. He does not regard this as a reason to abandon the technology, noting that conventional silicon panels also contain lead in their solder, but he recommends that perovskite modules incorporate layers designed to capture lead if the panel is damaged. Attempts to replace lead with tin have so far produced cells that are both less efficient and markedly less stable than their lead-based counterparts.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of scale. Most record-breaking cells are tiny, frequently smaller than a single square centimetre, because depositing a film of even thickness over a large area is far more difficult than over a small one. As cells are enlarged into full-size modules, minor defects multiply and efficiency falls appreciably. A small number of manufacturers have nonetheless established pilot production lines, most of them producing tandem modules rather than panels made of perovskite alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This choice is telling, and probably wise. The most likely route to commercial success is not for perovskites to displace silicon but to enhance it, allowing manufacturers to build on an existing industry, its supply chains and its customers' trust. Stand-alone perovskite cells may find their place in less demanding settings, such as indoor sensors powered by artificial light, where temperatures are mild and exposure to the elements is minimal.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Above all, the field would benefit from a change of priorities. For more than a decade, academic prestige has attached to efficiency records, which make headlines and are easily compared. Durability, by contrast, is slow and unglamorous to demonstrate. Unless funding bodies and journals begin to reward evidence of longevity as highly as gains in efficiency, perovskites risk remaining what they have been for much of their short history: brilliant in the laboratory and fragile everywhere else.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: hot Jupiters and theories of planetary migration
title: The Planets That Should Not Exist
subtitle: Giant worlds orbiting closer to their stars than Mercury does to the Sun forced astronomers to rethink how planetary systems are built

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the first planet around a Sun-like star was confirmed in the mid-1990s, it was not the discovery anyone had predicted. The object was roughly half the mass of Jupiter, yet it completed an orbit in just over four days, circling so close to its star that its upper atmosphere must have been heated to well over a thousand degrees. Textbook theory, built almost entirely on the example of our own solar system, held that giant planets could only form far from their stars, beyond the so-called snow line, where temperatures are low enough for water to freeze into solid grains. Close in, there simply should not have been enough solid material to assemble a planetary core large enough to capture a massive envelope of gas. The new world, and the many similar 'hot Jupiters' found soon afterwards, were in this sense impossible objects.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation that quickly became orthodox was migration. According to this view, hot Jupiters were born in the cold outer regions just as theory required, but subsequently travelled inwards. Professor Annelise Skaugvoll of the Tromsø Institute for Planetary Dynamics was among the first to model the process in detail. Her simulations showed that a young planet embedded in the disc of gas and dust surrounding a newborn star exchanges momentum with that disc, gradually losing energy and spiralling towards the centre. Skaugvoll argues that this 'disc migration' is gentle and orderly, and that it should leave planets on nearly circular orbits aligned with the rotation of their star. For roughly a decade, observations seemed to bear her out.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The picture became more complicated once astronomers learned to measure the angle between a planet's orbit and its star's spin. By tracking subtle distortions in the starlight as a planet crosses the stellar disc, a team led by Dr Ramiro Quisbert at the Altiplano Observatory found that a substantial fraction of hot Jupiters travel on tilted orbits, some of them even circling backwards relative to the star's rotation. Such misalignments are difficult to reconcile with a smooth journey through a flat disc. Quisbert contends that many hot Jupiters must instead have arrived by a more violent route: gravitational encounters with other planets flung them onto highly elongated orbits, after which tidal forces from the star gradually circularised and shrank those orbits. In his view, the disc model describes the exception rather than the rule.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It would be tempting to treat this as a simple contest between two mechanisms, but the evidence does not divide so neatly. Dr Sipho Mbatha, an observational astronomer at the Karoo Centre for Stellar Studies, has pointed out that misaligned orbits appear predominantly around hotter stars, whereas cooler stars tend to host aligned hot Jupiters. Mbatha interprets this pattern not as proof of two separate migration routes but as a consequence of stellar structure: cooler stars have thicker outer layers that may, over time, drag a planet's orbit back into alignment. If he is right, the present-day orientation of an orbit tells us less about a planet's history than was once assumed. This seems to me a genuinely important caution, because it suggests that one of the field's favourite diagnostic tools may have been overinterpreted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third possibility, once regarded as heretical, is that some hot Jupiters never migrated at all. Dr Liisa Talvitie of the Oulu Planetary Formation Group has argued that, under certain conditions, enough solid material could drift inwards through the disc to build a giant core close to the star. Her calculations indicate that 'in situ' formation is feasible if the inner disc is unusually massive. Critics respond that such discs would be rare, and that the theory struggles to explain why hot Jupiters so often lack close planetary neighbours. Talvitie accepts that her mechanism cannot account for every case, but she maintains that dismissing it outright reflects the field's habit of assuming that the solar system is typical.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That habit deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. Hot Jupiters are, in fact, relatively uncommon: surveys suggest that only around one Sun-like star in a hundred hosts one. They dominated early discoveries because the techniques then available were biased towards large planets on short orbits, which produce the strongest and most frequent signals. A statistical survey conducted by Dr Mirela Soeharto at the Bandung Astrophysical Archive estimated that, once such biases are corrected for, compact systems of several small planets are far more common than hot Jupiters. Soeharto concludes that theorists devoted a disproportionate effort to explaining a minority phenomenon, while the more typical architecture of planetary systems received comparatively little attention.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Her point is fair, although I would not go as far as to call the attention lavished on hot Jupiters misplaced. Extreme cases often illuminate general processes, and the effort to explain these planets has forced theorists to accept that planetary systems are dynamic rather than fixed, that planets can move great distances after they form, and that our own solar system may have been shaped by such movements too. The deeper lesson is one of humility. A theory derived from a single example, however carefully constructed, can describe only what that example happens to show; it took a planet that 'should not exist' to reveal how narrow the original model had been.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: direct imaging of exoplanets: coronagraphs versus starshades
title: Blotting Out the Stars
subtitle: Photographing a planet beside its star is like spotting a firefly next to a lighthouse, and engineers disagree about the best way to do it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost all of the several thousand exoplanets catalogued so far have never actually been seen. Their existence has been inferred indirectly, from the slight dimming of a star as a planet passes in front of it or from the tiny wobble a planet's gravity induces in its host. Direct imaging, which captures the light of the planet itself, has produced only a few dozen detections, nearly all of them young, hot giants orbiting far from their stars. The difficulty is one of contrast. In visible light, a planet like the Earth is roughly ten billion times fainter than the Sun, and from a distance of many light years the two would appear separated by a tiny fraction of a degree. Yet direct imaging remains, in my view, the method that matters most for the future of the field, since it is the only one that could allow astronomers to study the atmospheres of rocky planets in the zones where liquid water might exist.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The established approach is the coronagraph, an instrument placed inside a telescope that blocks the light of the central star before it reaches the detector. Early coronagraphs, developed to study the Sun's outer atmosphere, used a simple opaque disc. Modern versions employ carefully shaped masks and deformable mirrors that adjust their surfaces thousands of times per second to cancel out residual starlight. Dr Ines Quinlan-Moss, an optical engineer at the Basque Institute for Astronomical Instrumentation, has spent much of her career refining such systems. She argues that coronagraphs have a decisive practical advantage: because they travel with the telescope, they can be pointed at a new target in minutes. Quinlan-Moss believes that steady improvements in mirror control will eventually bring Earth-like planets within reach, though she concedes that the required stability, with mirror surfaces held steady to within a fraction of the width of an atom, has never been demonstrated in space.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An alternative is to block the starlight before it enters the telescope at all. A starshade is a separate spacecraft, shaped like a giant flower with petals tens of metres across, that would fly in formation with a telescope tens of thousands of kilometres away, casting a precisely positioned shadow. Professor Tendai Nyirenda of the Zambezi Space Systems Laboratory, a leading advocate of the concept, points out that a starshade places far less demanding requirements on the telescope itself, which need not be built with exotic optical precision. The petals' shape is designed so that light bending around the edges cancels out rather than spilling into the shadow. Nyirenda's group has tested scaled-down models in desert conditions at night and reports contrast levels close to those needed to detect an Earth twin.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The drawbacks of starshades are, however, considerable. Moving the shade from one target to another means relocating a large spacecraft across thousands of kilometres, a manoeuvre that could take days or weeks and consumes fuel that cannot be replenished. A mission might therefore observe only a few dozen stars over its lifetime. Nyirenda acknowledges this limitation but contends that a carefully chosen target list matters more than sheer numbers. I find this argument only partly convincing. When so little is known in advance about which nearby stars host rocky planets, the ability to survey widely and revisit promising targets seems more valuable than he allows.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third voice in the debate belongs to Dr Pavel Hakobyan, a mission analyst at the Yerevan Centre for Space Policy, whose interest lies less in the optics than in the economics. Hakobyan notes that budget overruns on large space telescopes have repeatedly delayed or cancelled other projects, and he warns that a flagship mission carrying either technology could absorb resources for two decades. His preferred strategy is incremental: smaller missions that test key components, followed by a larger observatory only once the technology has matured. Critics reply that incremental programmes are themselves vulnerable to cancellation because each stage must be justified separately.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, ground-based observatories are pursuing their own route. The next generation of extremely large telescopes, with mirrors more than thirty metres across, will gather enough light to image some planets around nearby small, cool stars, where the contrast problem is less severe. The atmosphere blurs starlight, but adaptive optics systems that correct this distortion in real time have improved dramatically. Some astronomers suggest that the ground could deliver the first images of temperate rocky worlds before any space mission does.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, though, to frame the coronagraph and the starshade as rivals in which only one can win. The two technologies are suited to different tasks, and a telescope designed to work with both would combine the flexibility of one with the deep contrast of the other. What is truly at stake is not which instrument prevails but whether funding agencies are prepared to sustain a programme over the decades such a goal requires. The engineering challenges are formidable, but history suggests that long-term political commitment, rather than technical ingenuity, is the scarcer resource.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: transit surveys, false positives and the statistical validation of planets
title: Shadows Across the Star
subtitle: The transit method has produced thousands of planets, but deciding which dips in starlight are real is a matter of statistics as much as observation

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a planet passes in front of its host star, as seen from Earth, it blocks a minute fraction of the star's light. For a planet the size of Jupiter crossing a star like the Sun, the dimming amounts to about one per cent; for an Earth-sized world, it is closer to one hundredth of that. Detecting such transits requires photometers of extraordinary stability, and it was only when space telescopes began staring continuously at the same patch of sky for years on end that the technique came into its own. The result has been a flood of candidates numbering in the thousands. Yet the sheer abundance of these signals has created a problem that is less widely appreciated than the discoveries themselves: a dip in brightness is not, in itself, a planet.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many astrophysical phenomena can mimic a transit. The most notorious is the eclipsing binary, a pair of stars orbiting one another so that each periodically hides part of the other. If such a pair lies behind or very close to a brighter foreground star, its eclipses are diluted, and the resulting shallow dip may look exactly like the shadow of a small planet. Starspots rotating into view, instrumental glitches and even cosmic rays striking the detector add further confusion. Traditionally, the remedy was confirmation by a second, independent method, most often the measurement of the slight wobble induced in the star by an orbiting body's gravitational pull. Such follow-up, however, demands time on large ground-based telescopes, and for faint stars or small planets the wobble may be too slight to measure at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Faced with a backlog that conventional confirmation could never clear, a group at the Aurelian Institute for Astrophysics led by Dr Cosmin Vartolomei developed what has come to be called statistical validation. Rather than proving that a signal is a planet, the approach estimates the probability of every alternative explanation, using models of how common eclipsing binaries and background stars are in that region of sky, and declares a candidate 'validated' when the planetary interpretation is overwhelmingly more likely than all the others combined. Vartolomei's team has argued that a threshold of 99 per cent is sufficient, and hundreds of planets in the published catalogues owe their status to this reasoning alone. The method was a pragmatic innovation, and without it our census of small planets would be far poorer. But it should be recognised for what it is: an inference about likelihoods, not an observation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most forceful critique has come from Professor Halldóra Eysteinsdóttir, who contends that validation is only as sound as the population models on which it depends. If the frequency of faint background binaries has been underestimated in a particular field, she argues, then every probability derived from that assumption will be inflated, and the errors will not be random but systematic, affecting many candidates at once. Her group re-examined a sample of validated planets using higher-resolution imaging and found previously unseen companion stars near a notable proportion of them. In most cases the planetary interpretation survived, but the estimated sizes of the planets had to be revised upwards, since some of the light previously attributed to the host star belonged to its neighbour. To my mind, this is a more troubling finding than the occasional outright impostor: a planet may be real and yet be described wrongly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Machine learning has added a further layer. Dr Obinna Ezeugwu, at the Coastal Observatory Consortium, trained neural networks on thousands of signals previously classified by human experts, and the resulting software can now sort new candidates in seconds. Ezeugwu insists that such tools are best used for triage, ranking signals so that scarce telescope time can be directed towards the most promising. Some enthusiasts have gone further, proposing that algorithms should be allowed to validate planets without human review. I find this proposal premature. A network trained on past classifications inherits whatever biases those classifications contained, and it is poorly equipped to recognise a genuinely novel phenomenon, which it will tend to force into a familiar category.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The stakes are not merely a matter of bookkeeping. Dr Teodora Ruskova, who models planetary populations at the Danubian Space Research Centre, points out that estimates of how common Earth-sized planets are in the temperate zones of Sun-like stars rest heavily on the statistical properties of transit catalogues. If even a few per cent of small validated planets are in fact impostors, or are systematically larger than reported, she calculates, then the frequency of rocky, temperate worlds may be noticeably overstated. Since future missions are being designed, and their budgets justified, partly on the basis of such figures, errors in the catalogues could shape decisions about which instruments are built for decades to come.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the transit catalogues are untrustworthy. The great majority of confirmed and validated planets are almost certainly genuine, and independent checks have repeatedly upheld them. What the debate does show is that the boundary between 'candidate' and 'planet' is a matter of convention rather than of nature, and that the convention deserves to be stated more plainly. A catalogue that recorded, alongside each planet, the method by which it was accepted and the probability attached to it would allow researchers to choose for themselves how much uncertainty they were willing to tolerate. That modest change would cost little and would do more for the credibility of the field than any single new discovery.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: the radial velocity method and the problem of stellar jitter
title: The Trouble with Wobbles
subtitle: Measuring the tiny back-and-forth motion of stars revealed the first planets around Sun-like stars; now the stars themselves are getting in the way

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before anyone could photograph a planet beyond the solar system, astronomers realised that they might detect one indirectly. A star and its planet both orbit their common centre of mass, so as the planet circles, the star traces a small loop of its own. Seen from Earth, this motion alternately carries the star slightly towards us and slightly away, compressing and stretching its light by minute amounts. By splitting starlight into thousands of narrow colour bands with an instrument called a spectrograph, and tracking the shift of dark absorption lines, astronomers can infer the star's velocity along the line of sight. This is the radial velocity method. The first planet found in this way around an ordinary Sun-like star, a giant world completing an orbit every four days, astonished astronomers who had expected nothing of the kind, and for more than a decade the technique remained the principal means of finding exoplanets.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The precision required is remarkable. Jupiter pulls the Sun around at roughly twelve metres per second, about the pace of a sprinter; the Earth's effect is a mere nine centimetres per second, scarcely faster than a tortoise. Over the past three decades, spectrographs have improved from a precision of several metres per second to well below one, thanks to vacuum-sealed, temperature-controlled designs and calibration using laser frequency combs. Engineers at the Vestmark Observatory, under Dr Rasmus Kjeldgaard, claim that their latest instrument is stable to within ten centimetres per second over a single night. On paper, then, the detection of a true Earth analogue around a nearby Sun-like star is within reach.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In practice, a different obstacle has emerged, and it lies not in the instruments but in the stars. The surface of a star is not a smooth, still sphere. Hot gas rises in vast convection cells and sinks back at their edges, producing a granulated pattern that shifts every few minutes. Dark spots and bright magnetic regions rotate across the visible disc over days and weeks, while the star's overall level of magnetic activity waxes and wanes over cycles lasting years. Each of these processes distorts the shapes of absorption lines and imitates a velocity change. Astronomers refer to the combined effect as stellar 'jitter', and for a quiet Sun-like star it typically amounts to between one and several metres per second, swamping the signal of an Earth-like planet many times over.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Researchers disagree about how to deal with this. One school, associated with Professor Wairimu Gachanja at the Karoo Plateau Centre for Stellar Physics, argues that jitter can be modelled and subtracted. Because spots and magnetic regions alter line shapes in characteristic ways, and because they also leave traces in other indicators such as the brightness of particular calcium lines, it should be possible, she maintains, to build a detailed model of each star's activity and remove its contribution. Her group has had some success: in tests using simulated planets injected into real data, they recovered signals of around forty centimetres per second. Supporters point out that comparable strategies have transformed other branches of astronomy, where sources of noise once thought intractable are now corrected as a matter of routine.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Others are more pessimistic. Dr Itzel Xicoténcatl, an astrophysicist who has spent years observing the Sun as if it were a distant star, notes that even for our own star, the one we can study in unparalleled detail, the relationship between activity indicators and apparent velocity is far from straightforward. Some magnetic features produce large velocity shifts with little change in brightness, and vice versa. If the behaviour of the Sun cannot be fully predicted from its own indicators, she reasons, there is little hope of doing so for stars observed only as points of light. Xicoténcatl advocates instead an observing strategy of very frequent measurements over many years, so that jitter averages out statistically rather than being modelled away.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Both positions contain an element of truth, but I believe the second underestimates the cost involved. Averaging requires enormous quantities of telescope time, and a programme devoted to a single star for a decade means fewer stars surveyed overall. The modelling approach, despite its difficulties, at least offers a route to studying many systems. That said, Gachanja's claim of forty-centimetre sensitivity should be treated with caution until it has been reproduced with real rather than simulated planets, since artificial signals are, by construction, perfectly regular in a way that nature rarely is.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A third possibility is to sidestep the problem by choosing different targets. Small, cool red dwarf stars are more numerous than Sun-like ones, and a planet orbiting one of them produces a larger wobble because the star is less massive. Kjeldgaard's team has argued that the near-term future of radial velocity work lies with such stars. The attraction is obvious, but the conclusion is, in my view, too hasty: many red dwarfs are, if anything, more magnetically active than the Sun, and the goal of finding a genuine twin of the Earth around a twin of the Sun cannot simply be abandoned because it is difficult. The wobble method, which once opened the field, may yet determine whether its most ambitious question can be answered at all.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: atmospheric biosignatures, false positives and chemical disequilibrium
title: Reading the Air of Other Worlds
subtitle: Astronomers hope to detect life on distant planets from the gases in their atmospheres, but no single molecule may be enough

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine an astronomer on a planet orbiting a distant star, examining the Earth through a powerful telescope. She could not see forests or cities, but by analysing the starlight that filtered through our atmosphere, or the sunlight reflected from it, she might detect the chemical fingerprints of the gases it contains. Among them she would find abundant oxygen, a highly reactive gas that would vanish within a few million years if it were not continually replenished by photosynthesis. Oxygen has therefore long been regarded as the most promising 'biosignature': an atmospheric feature that betrays the presence of life. Now that a new generation of telescopes is beginning to probe the atmospheres of small, rocky exoplanets, the question of what such a signature would actually prove has moved from philosophy to practical planning.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that oxygen can accumulate without any biology at all. Dr Nuno Albergaria, a planetary chemist at the Lusitanian Institute of Space Sciences, has modelled several such 'false positive' scenarios. On a planet that has lost most of its water, for instance, ultraviolet radiation from the star can split water vapour high in the atmosphere; the light hydrogen escapes to space while the heavier oxygen remains behind. Over hundreds of millions of years, this process could in principle build up an atmosphere as rich in oxygen as our own. Albergaria's simulations suggest that planets orbiting small red dwarf stars, which emit intense ultraviolet light during their youth, are particularly vulnerable to such non-biological build-up. Since these are precisely the planets that current telescopes are best placed to study, his warning is especially pertinent.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Ewa Grzelczak of the Vistula Centre for Astrobiology argues that the solution is to look not for a single gas but for combinations. Oxygen accompanied by methane, she points out, is far harder to explain without life, because the two react with one another and should not coexist in large quantities unless both are being supplied continuously. This concept of chemical disequilibrium, an atmosphere held far from the state it would settle into if left alone, has become the dominant framework in the field. Grzelczak's group has calculated how much of each gas would be needed for the combination to be considered convincing, and she maintains that, given favourable conditions, the pairing could be detected within the next two decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet disequilibrium has its critics too. Dr Laleh Mirhosseini, who studies the early Earth at the Kavir Geoscience Laboratory, observes that for most of our planet's history its atmosphere would have failed the test. For roughly two billion years after life emerged, oxygen was present only in trace amounts, and an alien observer would have seen a world dominated by nitrogen, carbon dioxide and perhaps methane, gases that volcanoes and other geological processes can also produce. In Mirhosseini's view, a strict focus on oxygen and methane risks overlooking inhabited planets that resemble the young Earth far more than the present one. She argues that the search should be broadened to include gases released by microbial life under oxygen-poor conditions, even if such signals are inherently more ambiguous.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is a certain irony here. The more inclusive the list of possible biosignatures becomes, the harder it is to treat any one of them as decisive; the more exclusive it becomes, the more likely we are to miss life that does not resemble our own. My own view is that this tension cannot be resolved by choosing a better molecule. What matters is the context in which a gas is detected: the type of star, the planet's size and temperature, the presence or absence of oceans, and the geological activity that might be expected. A gas that would be an ambiguous signal on one world might be compelling on another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This contextual approach has been formalised by Dr Tupac Huaraca and colleagues at the Andean Observatory for Planetary Systems, who propose a probabilistic framework. Rather than declaring a planet inhabited or uninhabited, astronomers would assign a likelihood to each possibility, revising it as new observations accumulate. Huaraca likens the process to a medical diagnosis, in which no single symptom is conclusive but a pattern of findings gradually narrows the possibilities. The framework has been widely praised, though it is worth noting that its outputs depend heavily on how probable life is assumed to be in the first place, a figure about which we know almost nothing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever approach prevails, the first claims of a biosignature are certain to be contested. Detection itself will be at the edge of what instruments can achieve, with signals barely distinguishable from noise. Some commentators have suggested that astronomers should agree in advance on a scale of confidence, so that tentative results are not reported to the public as discoveries of alien life. Such a scale would be valuable, but it should not become a reason for silence. Science advances through the open discussion of uncertain results, and an announcement framed honestly as provisional does less damage to public trust than the impression that information is being withheld.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: the habitable zone concept and its limitations
title: Beyond the Goldilocks Line
subtitle: The habitable zone has guided the search for life-bearing planets for decades. Is it still the right map?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in astronomy have captured the public imagination as thoroughly as the habitable zone. The concept is simple: around every star there is a band of orbits within which a planet would receive just enough warmth for liquid water to persist on its surface, not so close that oceans boil away and not so far that they freeze solid. Popularly nicknamed the 'Goldilocks zone', after the fairy-tale character who preferred porridge neither too hot nor too cold, it offers a neat way of sorting the thousands of known exoplanets into those worth a closer look and those that are not. News reports of a newly discovered planet almost invariably mention whether it lies inside this band, as though that settled the question of whether life might exist there.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea has a longer history than is often realised. Early versions in the mid-twentieth century were crude, defining the zone simply by the temperature a bare, airless rock would reach at a given distance. Later work incorporated the effects of atmospheres, in particular the warming produced by carbon dioxide and water vapour, and the cooling produced by clouds that reflect sunlight back into space. The most widely cited modern estimates for our solar system place the inner edge just inside the Earth's orbit and the outer edge somewhere beyond Mars. Each refinement, however, has also exposed how much the boundaries depend on assumptions about the planet itself rather than about its star.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This dependence lies at the heart of a critique advanced by Professor Radka Hlaváčková of the Svratka Institute for Planetary Climate. She argues that the habitable zone, as usually drawn, is really a description of where an Earth-like planet with an Earth-like atmosphere could keep surface water. Change the atmosphere and the zone moves. A planet with a thick hydrogen envelope, for instance, could retain enough heat to keep water liquid far beyond the conventional outer edge, while a world with very little carbon dioxide might freeze even in the middle of the zone. In Hlaváčková's view, the familiar band on diagrams conveys a false precision: it looks like a property of the star, when in fact it is a property of an imagined planet.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others push the critique further. Dr Baltasar Echazarreta, a planetary scientist at the Magellanic Centre for Ice and Ocean Worlds, points out that some of the most promising places for life in our own solar system lie well outside the habitable zone. Several moons of Jupiter and Saturn are thought to harbour oceans of liquid water beneath thick shells of ice, kept warm not by sunlight but by the flexing caused by the gravity of their giant hosts. If such subsurface oceans are common elsewhere, Echazarreta argues, then a search restricted to the habitable zone is looking in only a small fraction of the places where life might arise. The difficulty, of course, is that an ocean hidden under kilometres of ice would be almost impossible to detect from light-years away. Even within our own solar system, establishing that such oceans exist has required spacecraft to fly close by and measure subtle variations in gravity and magnetic fields.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the concept accept many of these points but argue that they miss its purpose. Dr Sione Lolohea, who helps to plan target lists for space telescopes at the Pacific Exoplanet Survey, emphasises that the habitable zone was never intended as a boundary marking where life can exist. It is, he says, a practical filter, and one whose boundaries are routinely revised as climate models improve. Telescope time is scarce, and astronomers need a defensible way of deciding which planets to observe first. A planet with surface water would interact with its atmosphere in ways that could, in principle, be detected; a buried ocean would not. Choosing planets in the habitable zone is therefore a bet on detectability as much as on habitability.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Lolohea's argument is persuasive as far as it goes, and I think the critics sometimes underestimate the practical constraints he describes. Yet the distinction he draws between a working tool and a scientific claim is rarely respected outside specialist circles. When a planet is announced as lying 'in the habitable zone', many readers understandably conclude that it is likely to be habitable, and some press releases do little to correct the impression. The concept is not at fault for this misunderstanding, but scientists who use it carry some responsibility for how it is communicated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A more nuanced approach is beginning to emerge. Instead of a single band with sharp edges, some researchers now present the habitable zone as a range of probabilities, shaded according to the variety of atmospheres that a planet might plausibly have. Others have proposed separate zones for different kinds of planet, such as rocky worlds, ocean worlds and worlds with dense hydrogen atmospheres, each with its own boundaries. These refinements make the diagrams less tidy, and they will undoubtedly be harder to explain in a headline. But a map that admits its uncertainties is, in the end, more useful than one that hides them, particularly when the territory it describes is as unexplored as this.
