area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: the habitability of planets orbiting red dwarf stars
title: Living with a Restless Star
subtitle: Red dwarf stars host most of the galaxy's rocky planets. Whether any of those planets can support life is one of astronomy's most contested questions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: If one were to choose a star at random from the Milky Way, the odds are roughly three in four that it would be a red dwarf: a small, cool, dim star with between a tenth and a half of the Sun's mass. Such stars are too faint to be seen with the naked eye, even the nearest of them, yet surveys suggest that rocky planets are common around them, and that many orbit at distances where they receive about as much energy as the Earth does from the Sun. Because red dwarfs also burn their fuel extremely slowly, they will continue to shine for trillions of years, long after stars like the Sun have died. On numbers alone, then, if life exists elsewhere in the galaxy, it might be expected to be found most often on worlds such as these.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Numbers, however, are not everything. A red dwarf's habitable zone lies very close to the star, typically at a fraction of the distance between Mercury and the Sun. At such proximity, the star's gravity is likely to slow the planet's rotation until one hemisphere permanently faces the star and the other is plunged into perpetual night, much as the Moon always presents the same face to the Earth. Early calculations suggested that on such a 'tidally locked' world, the atmosphere would freeze out on the dark side, leaving the day side as an airless, scorched desert. For decades this conclusion led many astronomers to dismiss red dwarf planets as candidates for life.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That pessimism has since been largely reversed, thanks in part to climate models developed by Professor Bayarmaa Tsend-Ayush at the Orkhon Institute for Atmospheric Physics. Her simulations show that even a moderately thick atmosphere would carry enough heat from the day side to the night side, via powerful winds, to prevent it from freezing. In some models, an ocean on the day side would generate a thick layer of cloud directly beneath the star, reflecting much of its light and keeping temperatures moderate. Tsend-Ayush concludes that tidal locking, far from ruling out habitability, might in certain circumstances help to stabilise a planet's climate. Her work has been influential, and rightly so, though it rests on the assumption that the planet retains its atmosphere in the first place, an assumption that is by no means secure.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the most serious threat comes not from the star's gravity but from its temperament. Red dwarfs are magnetically turbulent, especially when young, and they unleash frequent flares that can briefly increase their brightness many times over, accompanied by bursts of charged particles. Dr Cathal Ó Duibhginn, who leads a monitoring programme at the Connacht Observatory, has recorded flares on some nearby red dwarfs occurring several times a day. Over hundreds of millions of years, he argues, this onslaught could strip away the atmosphere of a close-in planet altogether, and with it any surface water. His group's observations of one nearby system, in which a rocky planet appears to lack any substantial atmosphere, are often cited in support of this view.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone draws the same conclusion from such evidence. Dr Leilani Keawekane, a planetary geologist at the Mauna Research Centre, points out that the Earth's own atmosphere is not a fixed inheritance but has been continually replenished by gases released from volcanoes. A planet with vigorous geological activity, she suggests, might rebuild an atmosphere once the turbulent youth of its star had passed. She also notes that a single airless planet tells us little about the population as a whole: it may simply be smaller, or closer to its star, than others in the same zone. In my view Keawekane is right to resist generalising from one case, but her alternative depends on geological processes that cannot at present be observed on any exoplanet, and it is therefore, for now, equally speculative.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also intriguing suggestions that flares need not be wholly harmful. Ultraviolet radiation, in moderate doses, may drive chemical reactions thought to be important in the origin of life, such as the formation of the building blocks of genetic molecules. Some researchers have even proposed that organisms living beneath a protective layer of water or rock could harness the occasional bursts of light. These ideas are imaginative, but they remain hypotheses without experimental support, and it would be unwise to let them colour our expectations.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Fortunately, the question is one that observations may soon begin to settle. The latest space telescopes are able, for the first time, to detect whether some of the rocky planets orbiting nearby red dwarfs have atmospheres at all, by measuring how heat is distributed between their day and night sides. A planet whose night side is almost as warm as its day side must have air to carry the heat around; one with a stark contrast is likely to be bare. The first results have been mixed, which is itself instructive: it suggests that red dwarf planets are not a single class with a single fate. That, more than any model, should temper both the enthusiasm and the gloom that this subject has tended to provoke.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: citizen science and volunteer contributions to exoplanet discovery
title: Many Eyes on Distant Suns
subtitle: Volunteers with no formal training have helped to discover planets around other stars. What does their contribution tell us about how science is done?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early years of the large transit surveys, a retired schoolteacher spending her evenings at a home computer noticed something odd in a stream of data from a space telescope. Among thousands of graphs showing the brightness of stars over time, one displayed a series of irregular dips that no automated program had flagged. Her observation, posted to an online discussion forum, eventually led to the identification of a planet orbiting a pair of stars. Episodes of this kind have become surprisingly common. Online projects now invite members of the public to inspect light curves, the records of how a star's brightness changes, and to mark any features that might indicate a passing planet. Tens of thousands of people have taken part, and dozens of planets have been credited, at least in part, to their efforts.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The rationale for involving volunteers is partly a matter of scale. Modern telescopes produce far more data than professional astronomers could ever examine by hand. Yet the more interesting argument concerns the kind of attention people bring. Dr Fenella Ashcombe, who coordinates a volunteer platform at the Wessex Centre for Public Astronomy, points out that computer algorithms are designed to find what they have been told to look for: regular, evenly spaced dips of a particular shape. Human observers, by contrast, are good at noticing patterns that do not fit expectations, such as the irregular, the lopsided and the unexpected. In her experience, the most significant volunteer discoveries have been precisely those that automated searches were never designed to detect. She cites planets whose transits vary in depth or timing because of the gravitational tug of unseen neighbours, signals that a search tuned for perfect regularity would simply discard as noise.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all astronomers share this enthusiasm. Professor Oumar Sangaré of the Sahel Institute for Data Astronomy argues that the advantage of human pattern recognition is shrinking rapidly. Modern machine-learning systems, he notes, can now be trained to detect anomalies rather than specific patterns, flagging anything that departs from the ordinary behaviour of a star. He accepts that volunteers have made genuine contributions in the past, but believes their role in discovery will soon be largely symbolic, valuable chiefly as a means of engaging the public rather than as a source of new findings. Sangaré's argument deserves to be taken seriously; however, I suspect it underrates how difficult it is to train a machine to recognise the significance of an anomaly, as opposed to its mere existence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different concern relates to reliability. Volunteers vary greatly in skill and attentiveness, and an individual's classifications may be inconsistent. Most platforms address this by showing each light curve to many people and combining their judgements, often giving greater weight to participants whose previous classifications agreed with expert assessments. Dr Yuliya Prokopchuk, a statistician at the Poltava Observatory who has studied such systems, found that the combined verdict of around fifteen volunteers was, on average, as accurate as that of a single trained astronomer. Interestingly, she also found that accuracy did not continue to rise as more volunteers were added beyond that number, suggesting that some errors are shared rather than random. Prokopchuk attributes this to features of the data that mislead almost everyone in the same way, such as the brief dimming caused by a spacecraft adjusting its orientation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Beyond discovery itself, many advocates stress the educational and social value of such projects. Dr Ximena Urquidi, who has surveyed thousands of participants for the Cordillera Science Engagement Network, reports that most join out of curiosity rather than any expectation of finding a planet, and that many go on to read more widely about astronomy and to encourage friends and relatives to take part. A smaller number become deeply involved, developing expertise that rivals that of professionals in narrow areas, such as the recognition of particular kinds of instrumental fault. Urquidi argues that such projects should be judged on these broader outcomes rather than on the number of planets found.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This is, in my view, a sensible position, but it risks a certain complacency. If the scientific contribution of volunteers becomes negligible, then presenting their work as discovery would be misleading, and participants who realised as much might reasonably feel that their goodwill had been exploited. Projects therefore have an obligation to be honest about what volunteers are actually achieving. It is also worth noting that questions of credit have not always been handled well: in some early cases, volunteers who identified candidates were thanked in acknowledgements but not listed as authors of the resulting papers, a practice that has since become less common.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever the future balance between human and machine, volunteer astronomy has already altered the relationship between professional science and the public. Above all, it has shown that meaningful contributions to research are not confined to those with formal qualifications, and it has created a large community of people with a personal stake in the search for other worlds. That community may prove valuable in ways that are hard to measure, not least in sustaining public support for the expensive missions on which the field depends.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: retracted claims and the first confirmed exoplanets around a pulsar: historians' interpretations
title: False Dawns and Unlikely Worlds
subtitle: The history of exoplanet discovery is littered with withdrawn claims. Historians disagree about what those failures reveal

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Today the existence of planets beyond the solar system is so well established that it is easy to forget how recently it was in doubt. For most of the twentieth century, claims to have detected such planets appeared every decade or so, and almost all were eventually withdrawn. In several mid-century cases, astronomers reported that nearby stars appeared to wobble across the sky in a manner suggesting unseen companions, basing their conclusions on decades of photographic plates. Later analysis traced the apparent wobbles to changes in the telescopes themselves: a lens remounted here, a new type of photographic emulsion there. Some of these announcements came from respected observers at established institutions and were reported with considerable fanfare. By the 1980s, many astronomers had come to regard announcements of exoplanets with weary suspicion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first discovery that withstood scrutiny came from a quarter almost no one expected. In the early 1990s, radio astronomers timing the pulses of a pulsar, the rapidly spinning remnant of an exploded star, noticed tiny, regular variations in the arrival times of its signals. Because pulsars emit beams of radio waves with a regularity rivalling that of the best atomic clocks, even minute delays can be measured with confidence. The variations were best explained by a small family of planets, each of only a few Earth masses, orbiting the dead star. The finding was greeted with caution, partly because only shortly before, a similar pulsar claim had been publicly retracted after its authors discovered that they had failed to correct properly for the Earth's own motion around the Sun. This time, however, independent observations confirmed the result, and the planets' gravitational interactions with one another were later detected, exactly as predicted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Historians have offered contrasting interpretations of this sequence. Professor Henrike Abendroth, a historian of science at Halden College, argues that the earlier retractions were not failures of method but evidence of science working correctly. Claims were made, tested and discarded, and the community's scepticism ensured that the eventual genuine discovery was accepted only after rigorous checks. In her account, the long string of false alarms was simply the price of an open system in which tentative results could be published and challenged, and she warns against judging the astronomers involved by the standards of instruments that did not yet exist.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Kasimir Ostrowicz takes a less comfortable view. He points out that some of the mid-century claims persisted for decades, during which they were cited in textbooks and used as evidence that planetary systems were common, despite warnings from a minority of observers that the data were unreliable. In his reading, the episode illustrates how a result that confirms widely shared expectations can escape the scrutiny that a surprising result would receive. The pulsar planets, he notes, were treated far more harshly precisely because nobody had expected planets to survive around such objects. Ostrowicz has also examined correspondence from the period and found that doubts about the earlier claims were often expressed privately but seldom in print.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective, from the sociologist Dr Sunniva Tveitnes, emphasises the role of instruments and institutions. Planet-hunting in the mid-century, she observes, was a marginal activity, pursued by a handful of individuals at small observatories without the resources to check their own equipment thoroughly. The pulsar discovery, by contrast, arose from a well-funded radio programme with no particular stake in finding planets. Tveitnes argues that the reliability of a field depends less on the virtues of individual scientists than on whether it has the money and the independent groups needed to replicate results. She adds that purpose-built instruments transformed the field less by making astronomers more careful than by making their errors easier to catch.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Each of these accounts captures something real, and they are not mutually exclusive. Yet I think Abendroth's is too generous. It is true that the false claims were eventually corrected, but 'eventually' conceals a great deal: decades in which flawed results shaped expectations and, arguably, influenced how later evidence was received. A system that corrects itself only slowly is not obviously working well, and the cost of that delay falls on everyone who builds on the mistaken work in the meantime. Ostrowicz's emphasis on the asymmetry between expected and unexpected findings seems to me the most instructive lesson, not least because the same asymmetry may affect today's search for Earth-like planets, where the desire to find a second Earth is intense.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a final irony. The pulsar planets, which so few had anticipated, remain among the strangest worlds known: bathed in radiation, orbiting a star that no longer shines in any ordinary sense. They told astronomers little about the prevalence of planets like our own, and for several years after their discovery they were regarded as curiosities; even now, few popular histories of the subject give them more than a passing mention. It was only with the detection of a giant planet around an ordinary Sun-like star a few years later that the modern era of exoplanet research is usually said to have begun. That conventional dating is itself revealing: the first planets to be confirmed were, in a sense, written out of the story because they did not fit the narrative that everyone wanted.

area: astronomy and the search for exoplanets
topic: gravitational microlensing and the census of free-floating planets
title: Planets Without Suns
subtitle: A technique based on the bending of light has revealed worlds drifting alone through the galaxy, and raised the question of how many there might be

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of exoplanet research, a planet has been defined in part by its relationship to a star. The techniques that found the first thousands of exoplanets all depend on that relationship: a planet is detected because it makes its star wobble, because it dims its star's light, or because it can be photographed in the star's glare. Yet theorists have long suspected that the galaxy contains another population altogether, made up of planets that have no star at all and drift through interstellar space in perpetual darkness. Such objects emit almost no light of their own, and until recently there seemed no realistic way of finding them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The solution came from an idea that predates the discovery of exoplanets by decades. According to the theory of general relativity, mass bends the path of light. When a massive object passes almost exactly between an observer and a more distant star, it acts as a lens, focusing the background star's light and causing it to brighten temporarily. This phenomenon, known as gravitational microlensing, does not depend on the lensing object emitting any light; it reveals mass, not brightness. A star acting as a lens produces a brightening that may last for weeks. A lone planet, being far less massive, produces an event lasting only a day or two, or in the case of an Earth-mass object, a matter of hours.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The technique has unusual strengths and weaknesses. Because microlensing events require an extremely precise alignment, they are rare and unpredictable, and each one happens only once; there is no possibility of repeating the observation. Surveys therefore monitor hundreds of millions of stars towards the crowded centre of the galaxy, night after night, waiting for brightenings, and networks of smaller telescopes spread across several continents stand ready to follow any event around the clock as soon as it begins. Yet microlensing is uniquely sensitive to planets far from their stars or with no star at all, objects that every other method misses. It is, in effect, the only census tool capable of counting the galaxy's dark population.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The first surveys produced a startling result. A collaboration led by Professor Ilona Szabadkai at the Tisza Astronomical Institute reported a large number of short events which, if interpreted as lone Jupiter-mass planets, implied that such objects might outnumber stars in the galaxy by nearly two to one. The claim attracted considerable attention, not least because it suggested that planet formation is a far more wasteful process than had been assumed, with systems routinely ejecting giant planets into space. Szabadkai has defended the result as a natural consequence of the violent gravitational interactions that, according to many models, take place in young planetary systems.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Subsequent surveys have not been kind to this figure. A team under Dr Kaveh Ardalani at the Caspian Sky Survey, using a larger sample and improved methods for distinguishing genuine short events from noise, found far fewer free-floating giants, perhaps one for every four or five stars. Ardalani suggests that some of the earlier events may have been caused by planets that do orbit stars, but at such great distances that the host star's own lensing effect went unnoticed. The difference is not trivial: a planet in a wide orbit and a planet with no star at all imply quite different histories.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: At the same time, the newer surveys have found evidence of a population of much smaller rogue planets, perhaps comparable in mass to the Earth or Mars, that may be more numerous still. Dr Nomvula Mthimkhulu, a theorist at the Drakensberg Centre for Theoretical Astrophysics, argues that this is exactly what models of planet formation predict: small bodies are ejected more easily than large ones, because they are more readily flung away during close encounters with their neighbours. If she is right, the galaxy may contain billions of Earth-sized worlds wandering in darkness, some of which may retain thick atmospheres or ice-covered oceans warmed by internal heat.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to treat each new survey as having overturned the last, but I think that would be a mistake. The disagreement between Szabadkai and Ardalani is, at bottom, a disagreement about how to interpret a small number of very brief and unrepeatable events, and both teams have been admirably open about the uncertainties involved. What has changed is not the underlying reality but the quality of the data. Nor should Mthimkhulu's speculations about potentially habitable rogue planets be dismissed out of hand, although they currently rest on theoretical possibility rather than on any direct evidence.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The next decade should bring greater clarity. A new generation of space telescopes, observing from above the blurring effect of the Earth's atmosphere and monitoring the galactic centre continuously, is expected to detect hundreds of free-floating planets, including many of Earth mass, and to measure their masses far more precisely than ground-based surveys can. For the first time, astronomers may be able to say with confidence how common such objects are. Whatever the answer, it seems likely that the familiar picture of a planet as something that belongs to a star will need to be revised. A significant share of the galaxy's planets, perhaps even the majority, may have no sun at all.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the caloric theory of heat and its reputation
title: The Fluid That Never Was
subtitle: Why the caloric theory of heat deserves more respect than it usually receives

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the closing decades of the eighteenth century, most natural philosophers who thought seriously about heat agreed on what it was. Heat, they held, was a subtle fluid called caloric: weightless, invisible, and composed of particles that repelled one another while being attracted to ordinary matter. When a hot object warmed a cold one, caloric was simply flowing from where it was abundant to where it was scarce. So respectable was the idea that Antoine Lavoisier included caloric in the table of elements published in his chemistry textbook of 1789. Modern textbooks, when they mention the theory at all, tend to present it as a cautionary tale: an imaginary substance that held back progress until experiment exposed it. This portrayal is both unfair and historically misleading.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The caloric theory was not a vague speculation but a working tool. It explained why bodies expand when heated, since the self-repelling particles of caloric pushed the particles of matter apart. It accounted for the so-called latent heat absorbed when ice melts, which was interpreted as caloric becoming chemically bound to water. Duarte Valcárcel, a historian at the Mediterranean Institute for the History of Science, has catalogued dozens of quantitative predictions made within the caloric framework, many of which were confirmed. His most striking example is Sadi Carnot's analysis of steam engines, published in 1824, which treated the work done by an engine as analogous to water falling over a mill wheel, with caloric descending from a hot body to a cold one. Valcárcel concludes that for roughly half a century caloric was not merely tolerated but was the most successful account of heat available.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, is it remembered as a blunder? Much of the answer lies in a famous episode. In 1798 Benjamin Thompson, better known as Count Rumford, observed that the boring of cannon barrels at a Munich arsenal produced heat in apparently unlimited quantities, as long as the drilling continued. If heat were a material substance, he reasoned, it should eventually be exhausted. Popular histories treat this as the moment caloric was refuted. Ingrid Solheimsen of the Nordic Centre for Science Studies disputes this reading. Contemporaries, she points out, did not regard Rumford's observations as decisive, and defenders of caloric proposed several ways of accommodating them, for instance by suggesting that the metal drew caloric from its surroundings. Solheimsen argues that every successful theory lives alongside unexplained anomalies, and that scientists who set aside a puzzling result are not necessarily being dogmatic. Her point is well taken, although it should not be pushed too far: some defenders of caloric clearly did resist the evidence longer than was reasonable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The theory's eventual decline was gradual rather than sudden. During the 1840s, James Joule's careful experiments showed that a fixed amount of mechanical work always produced the same quantity of heat, and the principle of the conservation of energy began to take shape. Even so, caloric lingered in textbooks for another generation. Kwabena Boaduo, who studies the history of thermodynamics, argues that no single experiment overturned the older view. What mattered instead was the emergence of a rival framework, in which heat was understood as the motion of particles, that could explain everything caloric explained while also accounting for the conversion of work into heat. On this account, scientists abandoned caloric not because it was disproved but because something better had become available.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes this more generous assessment. The philosopher Renske Duivesteijn has warned that historians who stress the achievements of discarded theories risk implying that scientific truth is merely a matter of fashion. Caloric, she insists, was simply wrong: there is no such fluid, and no amount of contextual sympathy changes that fact. Her concern is understandable, but it rests on a confusion. To recognise that a theory was productive and rationally held is not to claim that it was true. Indeed, the history of caloric is a powerful illustration of how science corrects itself, precisely because its replacement had to match and then exceed a genuinely impressive rival.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a more subtle reason to take caloric seriously: parts of it survived. We still speak of heat flowing from one body to another and of the heat capacity of a substance, phrases that make most sense if heat is a kind of stuff. More significantly, Carnot's conclusions about the efficiency of engines did not have to be thrown away. Around 1850, Rudolf Clausius showed that they could be preserved, with modifications, within the new theory of energy. The structure of an argument, it seems, can outlive the picture of nature that first inspired it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This has consequences for the way physics is taught. Research by a group of science educators at the Coastal Institute of Education suggests that many secondary-school pupils spontaneously think of heat as a substance that moves between objects, much as eighteenth-century scientists did. The group recommends using the history of caloric to help pupils examine their own intuitions. The idea is attractive, although the evidence so far comes from a small number of classrooms and should be treated with caution. What seems clear is that presenting caloric as a simple mistake teaches students the wrong lesson about science: that good scientists are those who happen to be right, rather than those who reason carefully from the evidence available to them.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the luminiferous aether and the historiography of its abandonment
title: Weighing the Invisible Medium
subtitle: The aether vanished from physics around 1905, but historians still argue about what removed it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a lecture delivered in 1900, Lord Kelvin spoke of two clouds that obscured the otherwise clear sky of physics. The first concerned a puzzle about the luminiferous aether, the invisible medium through which light waves were thought to travel: how could the earth move through it without leaving any detectable trace? Within a few years the medium itself had disappeared from mainstream physics. The usual explanation is brief and dramatic. A single experiment found no evidence of the aether, and a young Albert Einstein drew the obvious conclusion. Like many stories that are retold in textbooks, this one is far too tidy, and it obscures a more interesting process by which an idea that had seemed indispensable became, quite quietly, unnecessary.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for the aether rested on a powerful analogy. By the 1820s the wave theory of light had largely displaced the older view that light consisted of particles, and waves, as everyone knew, required something to wave in: sound travels through air, ripples through water. Yet the properties demanded of this medium grew steadily stranger. Because light was shown to be a transverse wave, vibrating at right angles to its direction of travel, the aether had to possess the rigidity of a solid, while the planets somehow passed through it without the slightest resistance. Hartwig Lomnitz, a historian of nineteenth-century physics, insists that the scientists concerned were not naive. They recognised these oddities perfectly well, he argues, and their insistence on a physical medium reflected a commitment to explaining phenomena mechanically rather than an uncritical attachment to tradition. On this point Lomnitz is surely right: to demand a mechanism for the transmission of light was a mark of rigour, not credulity.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell showed that light could be understood as an electromagnetic wave, and the aether was reinterpreted as the seat of electric and magnetic fields. Yaretzi Amezcua, who works on the history of field theory, sees this triumph as double-edged. In the short term, she argues, it made the aether more secure than ever, since it now underpinned the most impressive physical theory of the age. Over the following decades, however, physicists increasingly worked directly with Maxwell's equations and paid less and less attention to the mechanical structure that was supposed to lie beneath them. Amezcua describes the result as a slow evaporation: the aether remained in the vocabulary of physics long after it had ceased to do any real explanatory work.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It was against this background that Albert Michelson and Edward Morley carried out their celebrated experiment of 1887. If the earth was moving through a stationary aether, they reasoned, it should experience an aether wind, and light travelling with and against this wind should take measurably different times to cover the same distance. They detected no such difference. The result was not, at first, interpreted as a refutation. George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz independently proposed that bodies moving through the aether contract slightly in the direction of motion, by exactly the amount needed to cancel the expected effect. This proposal has often been ridiculed as a convenient patch. Teodor Zaharescu disagrees, pointing out that Lorentz connected the contraction to his theory that the forces holding matter together were themselves electromagnetic. Zaharescu's defence has merit. Yet it remains true that the hypothesis was constructed so that no experiment of Michelson's kind could ever reveal it, which is hardly a comfortable position for a physical theory.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In 1905 Einstein proposed that the speed of light is the same for all observers moving uniformly relative to one another, and declared that the introduction of a luminiferous aether would prove superfluous. Historians have argued for decades about how far the Michelson-Morley result shaped his thinking. Losaline Teixeira-Bom regards this debate as misconceived. The opening of Einstein's paper, she notes, is concerned with a theoretical asymmetry in the way electrodynamics treated moving magnets and conductors, not with any particular measurement. In her view the experiment's central place in the story was largely created afterwards by textbook writers who wanted a decisive turning point. Teixeira-Bom's reading is plausible as far as it goes, but she goes too far if she implies that experiment was irrelevant. The repeated failure of many attempts to detect the earth's motion through the aether formed part of the background that made a radical solution thinkable.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nor did the aether vanish overnight. Many senior physicists continued to use the concept for years after 1905, and Lorentz himself never entirely gave it up, preferring to interpret the new equations within a framework that retained a privileged state of rest. More recently, some commentators have suggested that the aether has returned in disguise, since modern physics attributes measurable properties to apparently empty space. The comparison is superficial. The old aether was a material substance with a definite state of motion; the vacuum of contemporary physics has no such state and singles out no observer as being truly at rest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, killed the aether? The best answer may be that nothing did. It was not so much refuted as made idle: once a new framework could account for every relevant observation without it, the concept simply had nothing left to do. This pattern is arguably more common in the history of science than the dramatic overthrow celebrated in popular accounts. Ideas tend to fade when they stop being useful, and the experiments later remembered as decisive are often those that came to symbolise a change that was already under way for other reasons.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the late acceptance of the reality of atoms around 1900
title: Counting the Uncountable
subtitle: Why did it take until the twentieth century for physicists to agree that atoms are real?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the close of the nineteenth century, a student of chemistry could hardly avoid atoms. Formulae such as H2O presupposed them, and the periodic table arranged the elements according to their atomic weights. Yet a surprising number of eminent physicists and chemists declined to accept that atoms actually existed. For the Austrian physicist Ernst Mach, the atom was at best a convenient fiction, a bookkeeping device that should not be confused with a description of nature. Wilhelm Ostwald, a founder of physical chemistry, went further, proposing that energy rather than matter was the fundamental reality. Within little more than a decade, however, both the scepticism and most of its advocates had fallen silent. How this shift occurred has become one of the most closely examined episodes in the history of science, and the answers offered say as much about the historians as about the atom.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The textbook account is straightforward. In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that the erratic jiggling of tiny particles suspended in a liquid, known as Brownian motion, could be explained by the impacts of invisible molecules, and he predicted how far such particles should wander in a given time. Three years later the French physicist Jean Perrin confirmed these predictions with painstaking measurements under the microscope, and the doubters conceded defeat. Ostwald himself announced in 1909 that the existence of atoms had been established. On this view, a single decisive experiment resolved a long-running dispute, exactly as an idealised picture of science would lead us to expect.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This account is not false, but it is far too tidy. Dr Ottilie Braekhus, a historian of physics at the Arctic Institute for the History of Science, has examined the correspondence of more than thirty physicists active between 1890 and 1914. She found that many of those who accepted atoms after 1908 cited not Perrin's work on Brownian motion alone but the agreement between it and a dozen other, quite unrelated, methods of estimating the number of molecules in a given quantity of substance. Perrin himself emphasised this point: calculations based on the colour of the sky, the radiation emitted by hot bodies, radioactive decay and the viscosity of gases all yielded roughly the same value. According to Braekhus, it was this convergence, rather than any individual result, that persuaded the hesitant. I find her argument convincing. A single experiment can always be explained away as the product of some unsuspected error; it is far harder to dismiss thirteen independent routes arriving at the same destination.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second strand of recent scholarship concerns the sceptics themselves. It was once customary to portray Mach and Ostwald as stubborn conservatives standing in the way of progress. Professor Santiago Irarrázabal of the Andean Centre for Philosophy of Science rejects this caricature. He argues that their reluctance rested on a coherent principle: that science should admit only entities which could, at least in principle, be observed or measured. Before 1900, he points out, atomic theories had generated a bewildering variety of models, many of which contradicted one another, and none had predicted a quantity that could be checked independently. To withhold belief under those circumstances was not obstinacy but caution. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that the sceptics were simply right for their time. Mach's insistence on observability, applied consistently, would have ruled out much of the physics that later proved most fruitful, and some of his followers clung to it long after the evidence had changed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more provocative interpretation comes from Dr Haruka Tsunemori, a sociologist of science at the Pacific Institute for Science Studies. Tsunemori notes that the most committed anti-atomists were, by 1908, mostly in their sixties, while the physicists who embraced atoms most enthusiastically were considerably younger and had built their careers on research into radioactivity and electrons. In her view, the dispute was resolved less by evidence than by the passage of a generation, as younger scientists who had always worked with atoms took control of journals, professorships and textbooks. There is something to this, since few scientific arguments are entirely insulated from questions of career and influence. Yet the generational explanation struggles with Ostwald's conversion: here was an elderly and celebrated opponent who changed his mind publicly, explicitly citing the experimental results.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Part of what made the new evidence so powerful was its directness. Earlier arguments for atoms had been largely inferential: chemists noted that elements combined in fixed proportions and reasoned that discrete particles offered the simplest explanation. Perrin's work, by contrast, allowed observers to watch, through a microscope, the effects of molecular collisions on particles large enough to be seen. Within a few years, the cloud chamber made the paths of individual charged particles visible as trails of droplets, and counting devices registered the arrival of single alpha particles as distinct clicks or flashes. Atoms had not been seen, strictly speaking, but their individual actions had been, and that distinction mattered a great deal to scientists trained to distrust what could not be counted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, does the case teach? The most important lesson, in my view, is that scientific consensus is rarely the product of one crucial experiment, however much popular accounts favour such dramatic moments. The acceptance of atoms depended on independent lines of evidence reinforcing one another, on new instruments, and, to some degree, on generational change. It is worth adding that the sceptics left a valuable legacy. Their demand that theoretical entities justify themselves through measurable predictions pushed atomists to sharpen their claims, and it is arguably because of this pressure that the eventual case for atoms was so robust.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: Maxwell's demon and the debate over the physical cost of information
title: The Demon That Would Not Die
subtitle: For more than a century, an imaginary creature has forced physicists to ask what knowledge has to do with heat

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1867 the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell described, in a private letter, a being so small that it could follow individual molecules. Stationed beside a tiny door in a wall dividing two chambers of gas, it would allow fast-moving molecules to pass in one direction and slow ones in the other. Over time one chamber would grow hot and the other cold, apparently without any work being done, in flagrant defiance of the second law of thermodynamics, which holds that heat does not flow unaided from cold to hot. Maxwell's purpose, most scholars agree, was not to overturn the law but to demonstrate that it was statistical in character: true with overwhelming probability rather than with absolute certainty. Yet the creature, soon christened a 'demon' by William Thomson, quickly escaped its author's intentions and acquired a career of its own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why has the demon proved so durable? Dr Ilse Kvarnström, a historian at the Baltic Institute for the History of Physics, contends that its longevity owes less to the difficulty of the puzzle than to its adaptability. Each generation, she argues, has 'exorcised' the demon using whatever concepts happened to be fashionable. In 1929 Leo Szilard proposed that the act of measuring a molecule's speed must itself generate entropy; in the 1950s Léon Brillouin argued that the demon would need light to see the molecules, and that producing this light would cost more than the demon could gain. For Kvarnström, the history of the demon is less a sequence of refutations than a mirror reflecting physicists' changing preoccupations. Her reading is illuminating, but it understates the extent to which genuine understanding accumulated along the way, since later accounts did not merely replace earlier ones but exposed specific flaws in them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most influential of these accounts emerged from research into computing. In 1961 Rolf Landauer suggested that processing information carries an unavoidable thermodynamic price only when information is destroyed, and two decades later Charles Bennett showed that measurement, contrary to Szilard and Brillouin, could in principle be carried out at no cost at all. The catch lies elsewhere. A demon that records the speed of every molecule must store those records somewhere, and since no memory is infinite, it must eventually wipe its records clean. That erasure, according to what became known as Landauer's principle, releases at least a minimum quantity of heat, enough to cancel whatever the demon has gained. By the 1990s this analysis had become orthodoxy, and many textbooks still present it as the definitive solution.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is satisfied. Professor Desmond Vlietstra, a philosopher of physics at the Lowlands Centre for Foundational Studies, maintains that the standard exorcism is circular. Proofs of Landauer's principle, he observes, typically assume the second law in order to derive the cost of erasure, which is then invoked to rescue the second law from the demon. An argument of this kind, Vlietstra insists, cannot be a solution; at best it shows that the law and the principle are consistent with each other. The charge has real force. It is weakened, though not removed, by a series of laboratory experiments conducted since 2012, in which the heat released by erasing a single bit of memory was measured and found to approach the predicted minimum. Such results do not settle the logical question Vlietstra raises, but they make it considerably harder to treat the principle as a mere assumption.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Nnamdi Ezeoguine, a physicist at the Gulf of Guinea Institute of Technology, takes a more pragmatic line. The demon matters today, he argues, chiefly because engineers can now build it. Microscopic 'information engines' have been constructed in which a feedback system observes a particle and adjusts a barrier according to its position, extracting small amounts of useful work from random motion, and biologists suspect that certain molecular machines inside cells operate on related principles. For Ezeoguine, the philosophical dispute over whether the demon has truly been exorcised is a distraction from such engineering questions. I cannot agree. How efficiently these devices can operate depends precisely on which account of the cost of information is correct, so the conceptual and the practical are far more tightly bound together than he allows.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different concern is raised by Dr Svetla Boyanova, who studies science education at the Thracian University of Applied Sciences. Having surveyed the treatment of the demon in some sixty undergraduate textbooks, she found that almost all describe it as a solved problem, usually in a single paragraph that cites Landauer and Bennett. Students, she concludes, come away believing that a question which specialists continue to debate was closed decades ago. Boyanova's point is well taken, although it should be said that introductory courses cannot present every unresolved controversy, and some simplification is the price of teaching anything at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, finally, has the demon achieved? Its most significant contribution, in my judgement, has been to establish that information is not an abstraction floating free of the material world but something that must be stored in physical systems and is therefore subject to physical laws. That insight now underpins research in fields as varied as computing and molecular biology. Some enthusiasts have gone much further, claiming that the universe is, at bottom, made of information. Such claims may one day be vindicated, but they go well beyond anything the demon itself demonstrates, and they deserve to be treated with corresponding caution.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: Galileo's falling-bodies thought experiment and the epistemology of thought experiments
title: Experiments Without Apparatus
subtitle: How can reasoning alone tell us anything about the physical world? A famous argument of Galileo's still divides philosophers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In his final book, published in 1638, Galileo Galilei set out one of the most celebrated arguments in the history of physics. Aristotle had taught that heavy objects fall faster than light ones. Suppose, said Galileo, that a heavy stone and a light stone are tied together and dropped. If Aristotle were correct, the light stone, falling more slowly, ought to hold back the heavy one, so that the pair would descend more slowly than the heavy stone alone. Yet the combined object is heavier than either stone, so by the same reasoning it should fall faster. Since the pair cannot fall both faster and slower, Aristotle's theory must be wrong, and objects of different weights must fall at the same rate. What makes the argument remarkable is that it appears to establish a fact about nature without anyone touching a stone, and philosophers have puzzled ever since over how such a feat is possible.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Popular histories tend to add a more theatrical episode: Galileo dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa before an astonished crowd of professors. Most historians doubt that this happened. The story first appears in a biography written by Galileo's young assistant Vincenzo Viviani many years after the supposed event, and Galileo's own writings never mention it. What Galileo certainly did do was roll balls down gently sloping wooden channels, timing their descent again and again in order to work out how speed increases during a fall. The persistence of the tower legend, despite its doubtful origins, seems to me revealing: we prefer our scientific heroes to triumph through spectacular demonstrations rather than through patient measurement or careful argument.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The philosophical debate concerns what thought experiments actually achieve. Dr Anneke Grobbelaar, a philosopher at the Cape Institute for Logic and Science, holds a deflationary view. Every thought experiment, she argues, is simply an argument in disguise. Its conclusion can always be reconstructed as following from a set of premises, and those premises are ultimately drawn from ordinary experience. On her account there is nothing mysterious about Galileo's reasoning; the vivid imagery of tied stones merely dresses up a piece of logic. This is an elegant position, but it does little to explain why thought experiments are so much more persuasive than the bare arguments to which they supposedly reduce. Few readers would be gripped by Galileo's case if it were presented as a list of numbered premises.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: At the opposite extreme stands Professor Bogumił Starzak of the Vistula Academy of Philosophy, who maintains that the best thought experiments offer a kind of intellectual perception. In Galileo's case, he claims, we do not merely deduce that all bodies fall alike; we grasp the law of nature directly, much as we might see a mathematical truth. Starzak's view has the merit of taking seriously the sense of sudden insight that a good thought experiment produces. It nevertheless asks too much of the imagination. History records many thought experiments that seemed equally compelling and turned out to be mistaken; for centuries, for instance, ingenious arguments convinced scholars that a vacuum could not exist. A faculty that can mislead so thoroughly hardly deserves the name of perception.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach comes from cognitive science. Dr Marisol Huarachi, who directs a reasoning laboratory at the Altiplano Centre for Cognitive Research, suggests that thought experiments work by running simulations on mental models built up from everyday physical experience. In a series of studies, she asked participants to predict the outcomes of imagined physical scenarios. Their predictions were generally accurate for situations involving objects of familiar size moving at familiar speeds, but became unreliable for scenarios involving very small particles or speeds approaching that of light. Huarachi concludes that our intuitive physics is tuned to the scale of ordinary life, which would explain why thought experiments have served physicists well in some domains and poorly in others.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Huarachi's account also sheds light on a weakness in Galileo's argument. The reasoning works only if the speed of a falling body depends on its weight alone. If speed depended on some other property, such as the material an object is made of or its shape, the contradiction would disappear, and indeed a feather and a stone dropped through air do not land together. Galileo was aware of air resistance and dealt with it carefully elsewhere, but the tied-stones argument itself silently assumes that it can be ignored. The episode suggests that thought experiments are only as reliable as the hidden assumptions on which they rest, and that Galileo's real achievement lay in combining imaginative reasoning with systematic experiment rather than in either one alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the thought experiment? Physicists continue to rely on it, and some of the most important theories of the twentieth century began as imagined scenarios. The most defensible view, I would suggest, is that thought experiments are best understood as tools for exposing contradictions within our existing beliefs rather than as independent sources of new facts about the world. That may sound like a modest role, but it is not: revealing that a widely accepted theory is inconsistent has often been the first and most difficult step towards replacing it.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the shift from action at a distance to the concept of the physical field
title: Filling the Empty Spaces
subtitle: The field is now among the most basic ideas in physics. For much of its history, it was regarded as little more than a picture

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Modern physicists speak of electromagnetic and gravitational fields as if they were as tangible as furniture. A field, in the contemporary sense, is something that exists at every point in a region of space, carrying energy and transmitting influences from one object to another. Yet the concept had a remarkably difficult birth. For most of the eighteenth century, the dominant model of physical explanation was action at a distance, inherited from Isaac Newton's theory of gravitation, according to which the sun simply pulls on the earth across the intervening void. Newton himself was uneasy about this. In a letter of 1693 he described the notion that one body could act upon another at a distance, through a vacuum and without anything to convey the action, as so great an absurdity that no competent thinker could accept it. His successors, however, proved far less troubled than he was.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Rasmus Thorbjørnsen, a historian at the Skagerrak Institute for the History of Science, argues that the eighteenth-century embrace of action at a distance should not be dismissed as intellectual laziness. It was, he contends, a deliberate and pragmatic choice. Newton's inverse-square law predicted the motions of planets and comets with unprecedented precision, and questions about the mechanism behind the attraction could be set aside as speculative without any loss of predictive power. When Charles-Augustin de Coulomb formulated the law of electrical attraction in the 1780s, he followed exactly the same pattern. Thorbjørnsen's defence is persuasive as far as it goes. Nevertheless, the pragmatic attitude carried a hidden cost, because by declaring questions about the intervening medium unanswerable, it discouraged precisely the kind of inquiry that would eventually transform physics.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That inquiry came from an unexpected quarter. Michael Faraday, the son of a blacksmith, had received little formal education and almost no training in mathematics. Studying electricity and magnetism in the 1830s and 1840s, he came to picture the space around magnets and electric currents as filled with curving 'lines of force', patterns that could be made visible by scattering iron filings on a sheet of paper. Most of his mathematically trained contemporaries regarded these lines as, at best, a convenient illustration. Dr Amaru Tupayachi, of the Andean School of Science Studies, has argued that Faraday's lack of mathematics was in fact an advantage, since it freed him from the formal habits of thought that made action at a distance seem natural. The suggestion is attractive but somewhat romantic. Many people of the period lacked mathematical training without producing anything comparable; what distinguished Faraday was an experimental ingenuity of an almost unparalleled kind.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell translated Faraday's lines of force into a set of equations. Among their consequences was the prediction that disturbances in the electromagnetic field should travel through space as waves, moving at the speed of light, and two decades later Heinrich Hertz generated and detected such waves in his laboratory. The significance of this was profound. If an electromagnetic influence takes a finite time to pass from one object to another, then during that interval its energy must be located somewhere other than in either object. The field, in other words, could no longer be regarded as a mere bookkeeping device; it had to be a carrier of energy in its own right.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Or so it seems in retrospect. Professor Ebru Sarıgöl, a philosopher of science at the Bosphorus Centre for Theoretical Studies, contends that the reality of the field remained unsettled for decades after Maxwell. Most nineteenth-century physicists, Maxwell among them, understood fields not as independent entities but as states of strain or motion in a mechanical aether that was assumed to fill all space. Only when the aether was abandoned in the early twentieth century, Sarıgöl argues, did the field come to be regarded as a fundamental constituent of the world. On her account, the victory of the field belongs to the twentieth century rather than the nineteenth. I find her analysis largely convincing, though the precise date assigned to such a gradual shift is surely a matter of emphasis rather than fact.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, moreover, to conclude that the field simply defeated action at a distance once and for all. In the twentieth century several physicists attempted to reformulate electromagnetism without fields, describing interactions directly between particles separated in space and time, and certain correlations predicted by quantum theory have revived serious debate about whether physical influences must always pass continuously through space. None of this undermines the extraordinary success of field theories, which remain the foundation of modern physics. But it does suggest that the history of physics is not a straightforward march from inferior concepts to superior ones; abandoned ideas have a habit of returning in altered form.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable lesson of this history concerns intellectual humility. The field, now treated as one of the most basic ingredients of physical reality, was for decades regarded by leading scientists as a helpful picture with no claim to truth. Recognising this ought to make us more cautious about the confidence with which we now dismiss certain ideas as mere metaphors or calculating devices. Some of them may, in time, prove to be considerably more than that.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the eighteenth-century particle theory of light and the reception of the wave theory
title: In the Shadow of Newton
subtitle: Did reverence for a great name really delay the wave theory of light by a hundred years?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A familiar story is told about the history of optics. In the late seventeenth century, Isaac Newton argued that light consists of tiny particles, or corpuscles, while his Dutch contemporary Christiaan Huygens proposed that it is a wave spreading through a subtle medium. Because of Newton's immense prestige, the story goes, the particle theory dominated the eighteenth century, and the wave theory was neglected until Thomas Young and Augustin Fresnel revived it in the early nineteenth. The moral usually drawn is that scientific authority can obstruct progress. There is some truth in this account, but it is misleading in important respects, and recent historical work has made it considerably more complicated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Sigrun Fjellanger, a historian of optics at the Fjord Institute for Science History, argues that eighteenth-century physicists preferred the particle theory for sound scientific reasons rather than out of deference. The particle view gave a satisfying explanation of why light travels in straight lines and of how it is reflected and refracted. Huygens' wave theory, by contrast, could not easily explain why light casts sharp shadows. Sound waves, after all, bend around corners, so that a person can be heard but not seen through a doorway; if light were a wave, it seemed, it should behave in the same way. Given the evidence available, Fjellanger concludes, choosing the particle theory was entirely rational, and the scientists who did so should not be portrayed as slaves to a famous name.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Between 1801 and 1803, Thomas Young presented experiments showing that light passing through two narrow openings produces a pattern of bright and dark bands, which he explained as the result of waves reinforcing and cancelling one another. His work was poorly received in Britain, and he was subjected to a series of anonymous reviews ridiculing his ideas. The traditional explanation is that Young was challenging Newton and paid the price. Professor Ikechukwu Anyaoha of the Niger Delta Centre for the History of Ideas offers a different view. Young, he points out, presented his findings largely in qualitative terms, without the mathematical detail that would have allowed others to test them, and his prose was notoriously difficult to follow. In Anyaoha's view, Young's ideas suffered at least as much from the manner in which they were communicated as from any loyalty to Newton. This seems to me a fair correction, although it would be naive to suppose that Newton's reputation played no part at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The decisive developments occurred in France. In 1818 Fresnel submitted a mathematically rigorous wave theory to a competition organised by the French Academy of Sciences. One of the judges, Siméon Denis Poisson, a supporter of the particle theory, worked through Fresnel's equations and derived what he took to be an absurd consequence: if the theory were correct, a bright spot should appear at the very centre of the shadow cast by a small circular disc. When another judge, François Arago, performed the experiment, the spot was there. The episode is often told as the moment the wave theory triumphed. Dr Mateus Brum, of the Atlantic Institute for Philosophy of Science, considers this a considerable exaggeration. Many supporters of the particle theory, he notes, remained unconvinced for years afterwards. What finally won them over, he argues, was Fresnel's explanation of polarisation, which required him to propose that light consists of transverse waves, vibrating at right angles to the direction of travel.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A fourth perspective concerns institutions rather than individuals. Dr Yuki Shiraume, a sociologist of science at the Kansai Institute for Science and Society, observes that the wave theory gained acceptance in France well before it did in Britain. She attributes this to the education of French scientists, many of whom had been trained as engineers at the École Polytechnique in precisely the kind of advanced mathematical analysis that Fresnel employed. British natural philosophers, educated in a different tradition, were less equipped to evaluate his work. Shiraume's account is illuminating, but institutional factors can explain only so much. They tell us why a theory found a receptive audience in one country, not why particular individuals, often after long resistance, eventually changed their minds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The story does not end with the victory of the wave theory. In 1905 Albert Einstein proposed that light is absorbed and emitted in discrete packets of energy, later called photons, and quantum physics went on to attribute both wave-like and particle-like properties to light. It is sometimes said that Newton was therefore right after all. This is an anachronism. Photons share almost nothing with the corpuscles Newton imagined beyond the fact that they come in separate units, and to describe twentieth-century physics as a vindication of his theory is to misunderstand both.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the history of optics really shows, I believe, is that the authority of great names rarely explains, on its own, why a theory is accepted or rejected. Each of the rival theories possessed genuine strengths and weaknesses, and the balance between them shifted as new experiments, new mathematical techniques and new institutions emerged. To blame eighteenth-century physicists for failing to see what became obvious only after Fresnel is to judge them by standards they could not possibly have met.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the steady-state versus Big Bang cosmology debate, 1948-1965
title: A Universe Without a Beginning
subtitle: For nearly two decades, a theory of an eternal cosmos competed on equal terms with the Big Bang. Its defeat is more instructive than its critics allow

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1948 three scientists working in Cambridge, Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle, put forward a bold alternative to the idea that the universe had a beginning. They accepted that the universe is expanding, as observations of distant galaxies had shown since the 1920s, but proposed that new matter is continuously created in the gaps between galaxies, so that the overall density of the cosmos never changes. On this steady-state view, the universe has no birth and no end. The rival hypothesis, developed from the work of Georges Lemaître and George Gamow, held that everything had emerged from an extremely hot, dense state at some finite time in the past. It was Hoyle himself who gave that rival its enduring name: in a radio broadcast in 1949 he referred to it as the 'Big Bang'. The phrase is often said to have been intended as mockery, though Hoyle later insisted that he had merely been searching for a vivid image.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The steady-state theory had considerable attractions. Its authors grounded it in what they called the perfect cosmological principle: the assumption that the universe presents the same overall appearance not only from every location but at every moment in time. It also offered a way out of an embarrassing difficulty. In the late 1940s, the measured rate of cosmic expansion implied that the universe was only about two billion years old, younger than the earth itself according to geological evidence. Dr Oksana Zavgorodnia, a historian of astronomy at the Dnieper Institute for the History of Science, argues that the theory should be remembered as thoroughly respectable. Because it insisted that the universe never changes, she points out, it made unusually firm predictions, and any evidence that the distant, and therefore ancient, universe differed from the nearby one would count decisively against it. I would go further: its very vulnerability to observation was a scientific virtue, and in this respect it compared favourably with its rival in those early years.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first blow fell indirectly. In 1952 the astronomer Walter Baade revised the scale used to measure distances to other galaxies, roughly doubling the estimated age of the universe and removing much of the embarrassment over its age. More direct evidence came from the new science of radio astronomy. A group at Cambridge led by Martin Ryle counted radio sources at different distances and reported that faint, and presumably distant, sources were more numerous than a steady-state universe would allow, implying that the cosmos had changed over time. Early counts contained significant errors, and Hoyle and his allies contested them vigorously. Professor Yohannes Gebremeskel, of the Horn of Africa Centre for Science Studies, has argued that the dispute was shaped as much by personal rivalry between neighbouring Cambridge groups as by the data. There is evidence of genuine animosity, but personal factors seem to me to have intensified the dispute rather than determined its outcome; by the early 1960s, improved counts pointed clearly in one direction.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The decisive evidence, in the eyes of most cosmologists, arrived in 1965, when Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, two radio engineers at Bell Laboratories in the United States, detected a faint microwave signal coming uniformly from every direction in the sky. Physicists quickly interpreted it as the cooled afterglow of the hot early universe that the Big Bang theory required. Defenders of the steady state proposed alternative explanations, suggesting for example that the radiation might be starlight scattered by dust, but these proposals struck most observers as contrived, invented solely to rescue a failing theory.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet was the steady-state theory actually refuted? Dr Lucía Echenique, a philosopher of science at the Río de la Plata Institute for Advanced Study, contends that it was not, at least in any strict logical sense. A theory's supporters, she notes, can almost always modify it to accommodate awkward evidence, and Hoyle and his collaborators were still developing a revised 'quasi-steady-state' model in the 1990s. What actually happened, in Echenique's analysis, was that the scientific community gradually ceased to regard such modifications as worth pursuing. The distinction between refutation and abandonment is a valuable one, and it captures something that tidy textbook accounts of crucial experiments tend to obscure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The defeated theory also left a remarkable legacy. Because it denied that the universe had ever passed through a hot, dense phase, the steady-state model needed some other way to account for the origin of chemical elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. This requirement helped to motivate Hoyle's most enduring contribution to science: the explanation, set out in a celebrated 1957 paper written with three colleagues, of how such elements are forged by nuclear reactions inside stars. That account remains a cornerstone of modern astrophysics. It is a considerable irony that a theory now remembered chiefly as a mistake should have prompted one of the most durable achievements of twentieth-century science.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Histories written by the victors tend to treat losing theories as detours. The steady-state episode suggests a different judgement. A rival that makes sharp predictions forces its competitors to sharpen their own, and even in defeat it may generate ideas that outlive it. Defeated theories, in short, deserve a more generous place in the history of science than they are usually given.

area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: why the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics became orthodoxy and hidden-variable theories were neglected
title: The Questions Nobody Asked
subtitle: For decades, most physicists treated the meaning of quantum theory as settled. Historians are now asking why

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between 1925 and 1927, a small group of physicists created quantum mechanics, a theory whose predictions about atoms and light have since been confirmed to an extraordinary degree of precision. What the theory says about reality, however, was disputed from the start. The view associated with Niels Bohr and his circle in Copenhagen held that particles do not possess definite properties, such as a precise position, until they are measured, and that it is meaningless to ask what happens between measurements. By the 1930s this outlook had become orthodoxy. Alternatives were quietly dropped. When the American physicist David Bohm showed in 1952 that a theory in which particles always have definite positions could reproduce every prediction of quantum mechanics, the great majority of his colleagues simply ignored him. The reasons for this collective indifference have become a lively topic of historical research.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the explanation lies in a mathematical proof. In 1932 the mathematician John von Neumann published what was widely taken to be a demonstration that no theory with 'hidden variables', that is, additional properties underlying the quantum description, could ever reproduce the theory's predictions. In 1935 the German philosopher Grete Hermann identified a flaw in the argument, but her objection went almost unnoticed until John Bell independently made the same point in 1966. Dr Henrike Osterwalder, a historian at the Alpine Institute for the History of Science, has traced citations of the proof and concludes that its authority rested largely on von Neumann's formidable reputation, since very few physicists seem to have worked through it themselves. That a proof could be invoked so often and examined so rarely is, to my mind, one of the most striking features of the whole affair.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious explanation has been advanced by Professor Kodzo Agbenyega of the Volta Centre for Science and Culture. He argues that the intellectual climate of Germany in the 1920s, marked by widespread hostility towards mechanistic thinking and the idea of strict causality, predisposed physicists to welcome a theory in which chance appeared to be fundamental. According to Agbenyega, the Copenhagen interpretation succeeded partly because it suited the cultural mood of its time. The suggestion is intriguing, but it remains speculative. Cultural influences of this kind are notoriously hard to demonstrate, and the Copenhagen view won adherents just as readily in countries whose intellectual climates were very different.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Rania Shuqair, a historian of physics at the Levant Institute for Advanced Study, emphasises a later and more practical factor. After the Second World War, physics in the United States grew at an unprecedented pace, fuelled by government funding for nuclear research and the development of new technologies. Students were trained in large classes, and the emphasis fell overwhelmingly on calculation: on solving problems in nuclear and solid-state physics rather than on reflecting about what the equations meant. Textbooks dropped the philosophical discussions that earlier generations had considered essential, and interpretive questions came to be regarded as a waste of valuable time. I find this the most persuasive of the available explanations, because it accounts not only for why the Copenhagen view was accepted but also for why its rivals were never seriously examined at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Bohm's own case illustrates how several factors could combine. In the early 1950s he was investigated during the anti-communist campaigns of the period and lost his position at Princeton, eventually moving to Brazil, which left him isolated from the centres of American physics. His theory also had features that many found unappealing, notably the implication that a measurement in one place could instantaneously influence events far away. It is tempting to attribute the neglect of his work entirely to politics, but this would be a mistake: physicists in Europe, who were unaffected by American political pressures, showed hardly more interest than their American counterparts.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Since the 1970s, the situation has changed considerably. Bell's work showed that questions about hidden variables could be translated into predictions testable in the laboratory, and a series of increasingly refined experiments followed. The foundations of quantum mechanics, once a subject that could damage a young physicist's career, have become respectable again, and research into quantum computing and secure communication has made them commercially relevant as well. It seems significant that this revival coincided with the emergence of practical applications. It suggests, perhaps, that physicists are most willing to take conceptual questions seriously when those questions promise to lead somewhere tangible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What should we conclude from this history? The dominance of the Copenhagen interpretation, it now appears, reflected not only the evidence available but also judgements about which questions were worth asking, judgements shaped by reputations, institutions and the demands of a rapidly expanding profession. This does not mean that the Copenhagen view was mistaken, and historians who imply otherwise overstep the limits of their discipline. The question of what quantum mechanics tells us about reality remains open; what the history shows is that, for several decades, physicists largely chose not to pursue it.
