area: the history of ideas in physics
topic: the N-ray affair, pathological science and the myth of automatic self-correction
title: Rays That Were Never There
subtitle: A century-old episode in French physics raises awkward questions about how science corrects its mistakes

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1903 René Blondlot, a distinguished physicist at the University of Nancy, announced the discovery of a new form of radiation, which he named N-rays in honour of his city. The rays, he reported, were emitted by many sources, including flames, heated metals and even the human body, and they could be detected by the slight increase in brightness they produced in a small electric spark or a faintly glowing screen. Coming only eight years after the discovery of X-rays, the claim seemed entirely plausible, and within little more than a year well over a hundred papers on the new rays had appeared, the great majority by French scientists. Yet researchers in Britain, Germany and the United States repeatedly failed to observe the effect. In 1904 the American physicist Robert Wood visited Blondlot's laboratory and, while measurements were being taken in the darkened room, quietly removed an aluminium prism on which the apparatus supposedly depended. Blondlot went on reporting the same readings. Wood's account of the visit, published shortly afterwards, effectively ended interest in N-rays outside France.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The episode is usually retold as a parable of fraud exposed by sceptical ingenuity. Dr Margit Szentiványi, a historian of physics at the Danube Institute for Science Studies, considers this framing seriously misleading. Having examined Blondlot's notebooks and correspondence, she finds no trace of deliberate deception. The effects he sought lay at the very threshold of human perception, and judging by eye whether a faint spark had brightened by a few per cent was precisely the kind of task in which expectation shapes what is seen. In Szentiványi's view, Blondlot was the victim of self-deception rather than its perpetrator. Her reading is, I think, the right one. Nothing in the record suggests that Blondlot was anything other than sincere, and the more unsettling conclusion is that a careful and honest scientist could be misled so completely.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why did the rays survive so much longer in France than elsewhere? Professor Chidiebere Nwaogwugwu, of the Enugu Centre for the Sociology of Knowledge, points to national rivalry. X-rays had been discovered in Germany, and French physicists, he argues, were eager for a comparable triumph of their own; this eagerness made them reluctant to abandon N-rays even after Wood's report. There is surely something in this, but the argument is overstated. Several prominent French physicists expressed doubts from the outset, and interest declined rapidly within France as well once careful repetitions failed, which suggests that the evidence ultimately carried more weight than patriotism.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For Dr Ignacio Valderrama-Pino, a philosopher at the Pacific Coast Institute for Advanced Study, the affair is a reassuring demonstration that science corrects itself. A false claim, endorsed by a respected scientist and repeated in dozens of publications, was discarded within a few years. This conclusion deserves to be qualified. The correction depended heavily on a single sceptic's decision to travel to Nancy and on a simple trick that happened to be available to him; had Wood stayed at home, the rays might have lingered considerably longer. Moreover, the correction was far from costless, since many researchers devoted months of work to a phenomenon that did not exist.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more recent case invites comparison. In 1989 two electrochemists announced that they had achieved nuclear fusion at room temperature in a simple tabletop apparatus. Laboratories around the world attempted to repeat the experiment within weeks, and within months the consensus was that the claim could not be sustained. Dr Thongchai Sirisombat, who studies research communication at the Chao Phraya Institute of Technology, argues that faster communication explains the difference in speed between the two episodes: where news of N-rays travelled by post and printed journals, reports of failed repetitions in 1989 circulated almost instantly by fax and electronic mail. Yet Sirisombat also notes that a small community of researchers continued to pursue the phenomenon for decades, which suggests that correction is rarely complete. It is worth adding that rapid communication is a double-edged instrument: the same networks that spread refutations also spread the original excitement, along with numerous premature confirmations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Episodes of this kind share certain features. The claimed effects are typically close to the limits of detection; their advocates often report surprisingly high precision; and failures to reproduce the results are explained away by special circumstances, as when Blondlot's supporters suggested that only observers with especially sensitive eyes could see the rays. Such patterns provide useful warning signs. They cannot, however, be applied mechanically, because genuine discoveries frequently display some of the same characteristics in their early stages, before techniques have been refined.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most lasting legacy of such affairs may be methodological. Procedures in which the person taking a measurement does not know which condition is being tested, now routine in many sciences, were developed partly in response to episodes in which expectation had distorted observation. This points to what I take to be the real lesson of the N-ray affair. Science does not correct itself automatically, as if by some internal mechanism; it corrects itself when its practitioners deliberately construct procedures that guard against their own hopes and expectations.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the self-healing chemistry of Roman marine concrete and its relevance to low-carbon cement
title: The Stone That Mends Itself
subtitle: Roman concrete has outlasted the empire that built it. Can its chemistry help an industry with an enormous carbon problem?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few human-made objects have survived two thousand years of weather as well as the harbour walls and domes of ancient Rome. The Pantheon's unreinforced concrete dome, completed in the second century AD, remains the largest of its kind in the world, while piers built along the Mediterranean coast have endured centuries of pounding by seawater that would reduce many modern structures to rubble within decades. For a long time, this durability was treated as a historical curiosity, attributed vaguely to superior craftsmanship or to the selection of particularly good stone. Over the past two decades, however, chemists have begun to treat Roman concrete as a laboratory problem, and what they have found challenges some basic assumptions about how a building material ought to behave.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Modern concrete is a mixture of aggregate, such as sand and gravel, bound together by Portland cement, which is made by heating limestone and clay to around 1,450°C. When water is added, the cement forms crystalline compounds that harden into a rigid mass. Since its development in the nineteenth century, this material has dominated construction because it sets quickly and predictably. Roman builders worked differently. They combined lime with volcanic ash, much of it gathered from the region around the Bay of Naples, and in marine structures they packed the mixture into wooden frames submerged in the sea. The ash reacted with lime and water to produce a binder that was, by modern standards, relatively weak when new. Its strength lay elsewhere: in its capacity to keep changing chemically long after it had set.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Oksana Hrabovska, a mineralogist at the Adriatic Institute of Materials, has examined cores drilled from ancient piers using high-resolution X-ray techniques. She reports that seawater percolating through the concrete dissolved components of the volcanic ash, and that new minerals, including a rare platy crystal called aluminous tobermorite, grew in the pores and cracks. In effect, the sea that destroys modern harbours was reinforcing the Roman ones. Similar crystals have been synthesised in laboratories, but only at high temperatures that would make industrial manufacture prohibitively expensive. Hrabovska is careful to stress that the process unfolded over centuries, and she warns against the assumption that it could be reproduced in a structure expected to carry loads within months of construction.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns the small white lumps of lime that are scattered through many samples of Roman concrete. These were long dismissed as evidence of careless mixing. A team led by Professor Losaline Vaipulu at the Southern Pacific School of Engineering has proposed a different explanation. In their view, Roman builders mixed quicklime directly with ash and water, a process known as hot mixing, and the heat released left behind brittle lime clasts. When a crack later forms and water seeps in, the clasts dissolve and recrystallise as calcium carbonate, sealing the fracture. Vaipulu's group has produced modern samples containing such clasts and reports that cracks in them closed within two weeks, while cracks in control samples did not close at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These findings have generated considerable enthusiasm, some of it, in my view, premature. The cement industry is responsible for around eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, partly because of the energy required to fire kilns and partly because heating limestone itself releases carbon dioxide. It is tempting to conclude that a return to Roman methods offers a ready solution. Yet lime production also involves heating limestone, albeit at lower temperatures, and suitable volcanic ash is found only in particular regions. Transporting it across continents would cancel out much of the environmental advantage. Several start-up companies are already marketing 'Roman-inspired' cements, and their promotional claims tend to run well ahead of the published evidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The structural engineer Ignacio Arrieta-Zubiri, who advises several European standards bodies, puts the objection more bluntly. Roman concrete, he argues, survived largely because it was never asked to do what modern concrete does. Roman structures were massive and worked in compression; they contained no steel reinforcement, which in modern concrete corrodes when water penetrates and causes the surrounding material to crack from within. Arrieta-Zubiri contends that what matters for modern engineering is not ancient concrete itself but the self-healing principle it illustrates, which might be applied to reinforced structures using entirely different chemistry. This seems to me the most realistic position in the debate, although it risks understating how much ancient builders actually knew.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That last point deserves emphasis. The Romans left few technical manuals, and the most detailed surviving treatise on architecture from the period is ambiguous about mixing methods. But the consistency of the evidence across sites from Spain to the Levant suggests a body of practical knowledge passed on through workshops rather than written down. Researchers at the Kestrel Building Research Group have argued that modern laboratories should treat ancient recipes as hypotheses to be tested rather than as relics. Whether or not Roman techniques return to building sites, the willingness to learn from a material once regarded as primitive is itself an advance.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the rise of synthetic coal-tar dyes and their social and environmental consequences
title: The Colour of Coal
subtitle: Synthetic dyes transformed what people wore within a single generation. Historians disagree about whether the change deserves celebration

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before the middle of the nineteenth century, every coloured fabric in the world owed its hue to a plant, an insect or a mollusc. Madder roots yielded reds, the indigo plant supplied blues, and a deep purple could be extracted from Mediterranean sea snails, though so many thousands were needed for a single garment that the colour remained a symbol of rank for centuries. Natural dyes were often unpredictable: the shade obtained from a harvest depended on soil, rainfall and the skill of the dyer, and many faded rapidly in sunlight or washing. Dyeing was also a skilled and often secretive trade, with recipes handed down within families and guilds and jealously guarded from competitors. Colour, in other words, was expensive, variable and, for most people, scarce.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That situation changed with remarkable speed after 1856, when a young chemistry student in London, attempting to synthesise the anti-malarial drug quinine from compounds found in coal tar, instead obtained a vivid purple substance that would dye silk. Coal tar was a waste product of the gas works that lit Victorian cities, and chemists soon realised that it contained a wealth of molecules which could be transformed into colours. Within two decades, laboratories had produced synthetic reds, greens and yellows, and by the end of the century a commercially viable synthetic indigo had reached the market. Colours that had once required months of cultivation and processing could now be manufactured in a factory in a matter of days. Germany, with its well-funded university laboratories and close ties between academic chemists and manufacturers, soon came to dominate production, and its firms eventually supplied most of the synthetic colours sold around the world.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The economic consequences were dramatic. Dr Anaïs Rochebrune, a textile historian at the Rhône Institute for Industrial Heritage, has traced the collapse of natural dye cultivation, from the madder fields of southern France to the indigo plantations of South Asia. She argues that the change is too often described simply as technological progress, when it also destroyed the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of farmers who had no part in the decision. I find this point well made, though it should be remembered that indigo cultivation under colonial rule was itself notorious for coercive working conditions, so the old order hardly represented a golden age.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other historians emphasise the gains. Dr Sunniva Jaroslawski, an economic historian based in Reykjavik, points to price records showing that brightly coloured cloth, once a luxury, became affordable to working households within a generation. Labourers and factory hands who had previously dressed almost entirely in undyed fabric or dull browns and greys could, for the first time, buy garments in vivid shades. In her account, synthetic dyes were among the first products of the chemical industry to alter the daily experience of ordinary people, and she suggests that they did more to shape modern consumer culture than many inventions that receive far greater attention. Her claim is difficult to test, but the evidence of mail-order catalogues and surviving garments lends it considerable weight.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective concerns the environmental legacy. Professor Kofi Ampofo-Darko, an environmental chemist at the West African Water Institute, notes that the dye works of the late nineteenth century discharged effluent directly into rivers, and that some early synthetic colours were based on arsenic compounds or generated toxic by-products. Today the textile industry is estimated to be among the largest industrial polluters of fresh water, with untreated effluent from factories in some regions turning rivers red, blue or black according to the season's fashions. Ampofo-Darko argues that the problem lies less in the molecules themselves than in weak regulation: modern treatment methods can remove most dyes from waste water, but they add costs which manufacturers in highly competitive markets are reluctant to bear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is sometimes suggested that the answer is a return to natural dyes. This view, in my opinion, misunderstands the scale involved. Supplying the world's textile industry with plant-based colours would require vast areas of farmland, much of it diverted from food crops, and natural dyeing typically depends on mordants, the metal salts that fix colour to the fibre, some of which are themselves harmful. Plant-based colours also vary from one batch to the next, which makes it extremely difficult to match shades across the vast numbers of identical garments that modern retailers demand. Natural dyes have a valuable place in craft production, but they cannot replace synthetic ones without creating serious problems of their own.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The more promising route lies in chemistry itself. Researchers are developing dyes that bind more completely to fibres, so that less is lost in rinsing, as well as dyeing processes that use pressurised carbon dioxide in place of water. Some groups are engineering microorganisms to produce pigments by fermentation. None of these methods is yet cheap enough to transform the industry, and it would be naïve to expect market forces alone to bring them into widespread use. The history of synthetic dyes shows that chemical innovation can spread astonishingly fast once it becomes profitable; the task now is to ensure that cleaner innovation becomes profitable too.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the chemical weathering of glass, from medieval windows and museum vessels to vitrified nuclear waste
title: The Patience of Glass
subtitle: Glass looks permanent, but conservators and nuclear engineers alike are learning how slowly, and how surely, water wears it away

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visitors to medieval churches are often told that the old window panes are thicker at the bottom because glass is really a very slow liquid that has sagged over the centuries. The story is attractive, but it does not survive scrutiny. Calculations based on the viscosity of glass at room temperature indicate that any measurable flow would take far longer than the age of the universe, and the uneven panes are better explained by the way they were made: sheets blown by hand were rarely uniform, and glaziers often set the heavier edge at the bottom. The real enemy of old glass is not gravity but chemistry. Glass appears inert, which is why laboratories store aggressive reagents in it, yet over long enough periods even this familiar material is attacked by the water around it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Most everyday glass consists of a disordered network of silicon and oxygen atoms, into which other elements are introduced to lower the melting temperature. Sodium, potassium and calcium, the so-called network modifiers, sit loosely within this framework. When water touches the surface, hydrogen ions gradually change places with these modifier ions, which are drawn out of the glass, leaving a thin leached layer that is chemically different from the material beneath. How quickly this happens depends heavily on composition. Roman craftsmen used a mineral soda that produced a relatively stable glass, whereas many medieval workshops north of the Alps relied on the ash of burnt beech and bracken, which is rich in potassium. This so-called forest glass was cheap to produce, but it is markedly more vulnerable to attack, and some of the most celebrated windows of northern Europe are made of it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Itzel Bocanegra, a conservation scientist at the Cantabrian Heritage Laboratory, has spent much of her career examining the brown crusts and pitted surfaces that disfigure such windows. Her measurements have led her to a conclusion that surprised many restorers: the most serious damage is caused not by rain on the exterior but by condensation forming on the inside of the glass, where moisture lingers for hours on cold mornings. Bocanegra also links the acceleration of decay during the twentieth century to sulphur dioxide from coal burning, which reacts with the leached ions to form crusts of gypsum and other salts. The remedy she favours is protective glazing, in which a modern pane is fitted outside the historic window, leaving a ventilated gap so that the old glass stays at the temperature of the interior. This approach has slowed deterioration at many sites, although it inevitably alters how the windows look from the street, a cost that is seldom acknowledged.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Glass in museum collections faces a related problem. Some vessels made in the late seventeenth century, when glassmakers experimented with recipes containing too much alkali and too little lime, suffer from what curators call crizzling: a network of fine cracks that slowly renders the glass cloudy and eventually causes fragments to flake away. Professor Halvard Eikrem, a museum chemist in Trondheim, argues that the key variable is relative humidity. If the air is too damp, leaching speeds up; if it is too dry, the hydrated surface layer shrinks and fractures. He recommends a narrow band of around forty to forty-five per cent. In principle this is straightforward, but glass is often displayed alongside metals, which corrode in moist air, and wood, which cracks in dry conditions, so a single case may contain objects with incompatible requirements.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The durability of glass has acquired a quite different urgency in the nuclear industry. Several countries immobilise their most radioactive waste by melting it into borosilicate glass, which is sealed in steel canisters and destined for burial deep underground. Engineers must show that the glass will retain its contents for tens of thousands of years, a period far beyond the reach of any laboratory experiment. The Vitreous Futures Consortium, a network of geochemists and engineers from six countries, has responded by studying natural and archaeological analogues: volcanic glasses that have lain in the ground for millions of years, and Roman glass recovered from shipwrecks. Their findings suggest that alteration is fastest at first and then declines steeply, because the leached layer reorganises into a dense gel that shields the glass underneath.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is reassured. Dr Laleh Farzanegan, a geochemist who has worked on waste repositories for two decades, points out that no analogue matches the composition of waste glass exactly, and that conditions on the seabed differ greatly from those in a sealed repository. More troubling, in her view, is evidence from long-running experiments that the protective gel can fail abruptly when certain minerals begin to crystallise within it, causing corrosion to resume at close to its original rate. These objections are serious, and the consortium has perhaps been too quick to treat its analogues as proof. Yet it would be a mistake to discard them. Imperfect as they are, ancient glasses are the only direct record we possess of how such materials behave over very long periods, and the sensible course is to use them alongside, rather than instead of, laboratory studies and computer models.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these very different fields is a single lesson: the durability of glass is not a fixed property of the material but the outcome of a relationship between a particular composition and a particular environment. A forest-glass window might survive for centuries in a dry, unpolluted building yet decay within decades in a damp, smoky one. It is striking, then, that conservators and nuclear engineers, who confront essentially the same chemistry, so rarely read one another's research. Each community has accumulated knowledge that the other could use, and closer exchange between them is overdue.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the chemistry of soap and synthetic detergents, phosphate pollution and low-temperature washing
title: Coming Clean
subtitle: The story of how we wash our clothes is also a story of unintended consequences

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of history, getting things clean meant soap, and soap meant boiling animal fat or vegetable oil with an alkali, traditionally obtained by soaking wood ashes in water. The reaction, known as saponification, produces molecules with a curious double nature. One end of each molecule is attracted to water, while the other, a long chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms, avoids water and dissolves readily in oil. When soap is added to dirty fabric, the oil-loving tails bury themselves in greasy deposits, and the molecules arrange themselves into tiny spheres, called micelles, with the grease trapped inside and the water-loving heads facing outwards. These spheres can then be rinsed away, carrying the dirt with them. The principle has hardly changed in four thousand years, and modern chemistry has largely refined rather than replaced it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Soap has one serious weakness. In areas where the water supply is rich in dissolved calcium and magnesium, the heads of soap molecules bind to these minerals and form an insoluble grey scum. Much of the soap is wasted, and the residue clings to clothes and basins. For centuries this was simply tolerated, but in the first half of the twentieth century two pressures combined to change matters. Washing machines were becoming common, and during two world wars, fats were needed for food and munitions and could not be spared for cleaning. Chemists responded by developing synthetic detergents from petroleum, whose molecules work in much the same way as soap but are far less inclined to react with the minerals in hard water.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To improve performance further, manufacturers added so-called builders, of which the most effective were phosphates. These compounds lock up calcium and magnesium so that the detergent itself can concentrate on the dirt, and by the 1960s they made up as much as half the weight of some washing powders. The consequences for rivers and lakes soon became apparent. Phosphorus is a nutrient, and when it reaches still water it fuels explosive growth of algae, which then die and decompose, using up the oxygen that fish require. Dr Wanjiru Gathoni, a limnologist at the Lake Basin Water Institute, has reconstructed this history from layers of sediment and concludes that detergents were a major contributor to the crisis, although never the only one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Many countries eventually restricted or banned phosphates in household detergents, but the measures remain contested. Professor Joost Terpstra, an industrial chemist who spent many years in the detergent industry, regards the bans as largely symbolic. The substitutes, he argues, were less efficient at softening water, so consumers compensated by using more powder, and in any case the fertiliser running off farmland delivers far greater quantities of phosphorus. Terpstra is right about farms, which today account for most of the phosphorus entering lakes in many regions. But his wider claim does not hold up: several lakes recovered measurably within a decade of the bans, which would hardly have happened if the restrictions had been a mere gesture.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more recent development is the addition of enzymes, proteins that speed up particular chemical reactions. Proteases break down stains such as blood and egg, lipases attack fats, and amylases dissolve starch. Dr Yerlan Zhaksylykov, a biochemist at the Steppe Institute of Applied Enzymology, argues that enzymes are the most significant advance in washing since the synthetic detergent itself, because they work efficiently in cool water. Since heating the water accounts for the greater part of the energy used in a typical wash, a shift from forty degrees to twenty could reduce household energy consumption considerably. The obstacle, he admits, is psychological: many people remain convinced that clothes washed in cold water cannot really be clean. His figures may be somewhat optimistic, since older machines and heavily soiled work clothes still require warmer cycles, but the broad argument seems to me difficult to dispute. Persuading the public is another matter, and advertising that has spent decades associating steaming water with hygiene has not made the task any easier.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The history of detergents offers at least one example of a problem solved cleanly. The first synthetic detergents were made from molecules with branched carbon chains, which bacteria in sewage works could not easily digest. In the 1950s, rivers downstream of large towns were sometimes covered in banks of foam several metres high. Manufacturers switched to straight-chain molecules, which microorganisms break down readily, and within a few years the foam had largely disappeared. This episode deserves to be better known, as it shows that an environmental problem caused by chemistry can sometimes be reversed by chemistry alone, without any change in public behaviour.

paragraphs.label: G

If that is so, the most effective step towards a cleaner wash may lie not in new chemistry but in persuading people to use less of the products they already have.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: fluoropolymer non-stick coatings and the regulation of persistent PFAS chemicals
title: The Price of Slipperiness
subtitle: The chemistry that keeps eggs from sticking to the pan has left a legacy that may outlast us all

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1930s, a young chemist working on new refrigerant gases opened the valve of a storage cylinder and found that nothing came out. The cylinder had not leaked; when it was cut open, the gas inside was found to have transformed itself into a white, waxy solid. The material, later known as polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE, turned out to be one of the most unreactive substances ever made. It withstood boiling acids, did not melt at the temperatures of a domestic oven and was so slippery that almost nothing would adhere to it. These properties derive from the bond between carbon and fluorine atoms, the strongest in organic chemistry. Within a few decades PTFE and its chemical relatives were coating frying pans, insulating aircraft cables and making outdoor clothing repel rain.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The same bond, however, lies at the heart of a growing environmental concern. PTFE belongs to a family of several thousand synthetic compounds, collectively known as PFAS, which share chains of carbon atoms surrounded by fluorine. Because few natural processes are capable of breaking these chains, the compounds do not break down in the environment, earning them the popular label of 'forever chemicals'. For decades, the manufacture of fluoropolymers relied on smaller fluorinated acids as processing aids, and these escaped from factories into rivers and groundwater. Being small and soluble, they travelled far. Today PFAS can be detected in rainwater on every continent, in the livers of Arctic seals and in the blood of almost every person who has been tested for them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Teodora Vasilache, a toxicologist at the Siret Valley Institute of Public Health, has reviewed hundreds of studies of exposed populations. She regards the evidence linking certain PFAS to raised cholesterol, weakened responses to vaccines and some cancers as sufficiently strong to justify urgent action. More controversially, she argues that regulators should restrict the entire class of compounds instead of assessing them one at a time. Her reasoning is historical: when the best-known fluorinated acids were phased out, manufacturers replaced them with molecules of slightly shorter length, which were initially presumed safe but have since been found in drinking water and linked to similar effects. Assessing thousands of substances individually, she contends, would simply allow this cycle of substitution to repeat itself indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Rafael Montiel-Ochoa, a polymer chemist, considers this approach scientifically crude. A finished PTFE coating, he points out, consists of enormous molecules, far too large to pass through cell membranes, and is about as biologically active as a piece of glass. Grouping such materials with small, mobile acids would, in his view, threaten applications for which no substitute exists, including medical implants and equipment used to make semiconductors. The distinction he draws is real, but it considers the polymer only while it is in use. Its production has historically depended on the very acids that cause most concern, and when coated products are burned at the end of their lives in incinerators that do not reach sufficiently high temperatures, they can release smaller fluorinated compounds. A pan may be harmless on the stove and still contribute to the problem before and after its working life.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Removing PFAS once they are in the environment is extraordinarily expensive. Water companies can capture them using filters of activated carbon or high-pressure membranes, but these methods only concentrate the chemicals; the spent filters must then be destroyed, which requires temperatures well above a thousand degrees. The Nordwater Utilities Partnership, an association of public water suppliers, has estimated that treating contaminated supplies across its member regions will cost billions over the coming decades, and it insists that the manufacturers responsible should pay. The principle is fair, but applying it is far from simple. Much of the contamination dates back half a century, and many of the companies concerned have since merged, been sold or ceased to exist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One proposal that has gained support among regulators is to distinguish between essential and non-essential uses. Fluorinated compounds might remain permitted in surgical equipment or fire-fighting foams used at chemical plants, where alternatives are inadequate, while being banned from stain-resistant carpets, food wrappers and the waxes applied to skis. This seems to me the most workable compromise available. It accepts Montiel-Ochoa's point that some applications are genuinely irreplaceable, while recognising that a large share of PFAS use serves convenience rather than necessity, and that these uses should be the first to go.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The wider lesson concerns the way new materials are judged. PTFE was celebrated for precisely the qualities that now cause anxiety: its resistance to heat, chemicals and time. It has been suggested that chemists should in future design substances to break down as rapidly as possible once released. That would be going too far. Nobody wants a heart valve or a waterproof roof membrane that disintegrates within months. What is needed instead is for the fate of a material after its useful life to be considered as seriously as its performance during it, before it is manufactured on a vast scale rather than afterwards.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the chemistry of rust and the methods used to protect steel structures from corrosion
title: The Quiet Return of Iron
subtitle: Corrosion rarely makes headlines, yet it consumes a remarkable share of the wealth invested in our buildings, bridges and ships

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Rust is so familiar that it is easy to forget how much it costs. Studies in several industrialised countries have put the annual expense of corrosion, including repairs, replacements and protective measures, at around three per cent of national output, and since these estimates leave out indirect losses such as traffic diverted around closed bridges, the true figure is, if anything, higher. The process itself is best seen as a kind of homecoming. Iron is almost never found in its metallic form in nature; it occurs in ores as oxides, and a great deal of energy must be spent in a blast furnace to separate the metal from the oxygen. Corrosion is simply that energy being released as the iron recombines with oxygen and returns to the state from which it was taken.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Rusting requires both water and oxygen, and it is electrochemical in nature. On a wet steel surface, one area acts as an anode, where iron atoms give up electrons and dissolve, while another acts as a cathode, where those electrons combine with oxygen and water. Salt accelerates the process dramatically because dissolved salt allows the water to conduct electricity more easily, which explains why cars in snowy regions, where roads are salted, and structures beside the sea suffer so badly. What makes rust particularly destructive is its bulk. Iron oxide occupies more volume than the metal it replaces, so it cracks and flakes away, constantly exposing fresh metal to attack. Aluminium, by contrast, forms an extremely thin, tightly bonded oxide film that seals the surface and prevents further reaction.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The traditional defence is to separate steel from its environment with paint. A more sophisticated method is galvanising, in which steel is dipped into molten zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so where the coating is scratched it corrodes in preference to the steel, sacrificing itself to protect the metal beneath. Dr Ifeoluwa Olatunbosun, a corrosion engineer who has inspected hundreds of failed structures, believes that the industry's attention is often misdirected. In her experience, the most expensive failures are seldom caused by inferior coatings. They are caused by details of design, such as ledges, crevices and poorly drained joints, where water collects and remains for long periods. A structure shaped to shed water quickly, she argues, will outlast a badly designed one, however well the latter is painted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An ingenious alternative is weathering steel, which contains small quantities of copper, chromium and nickel. Instead of flaking, its rust forms a dense, stable layer that dramatically slows further corrosion, so the steel can be left unpainted. Professor Ragnhild Ostvedt, an architectural historian, admires the material not only for its practicality but for its appearance: the deep orange-brown surface, which changes with the seasons, has become a favourite of sculptors and architects, and she sees in it a rare honesty about the passage of time. Dr Paulo Cavaco-Sequeira, a bridge engineer, is more cautious. Where steel is exposed to salt spray or remains damp for long periods, he points out, the protective layer never stabilises, and the metal corrodes much like ordinary steel. Several coastal bridges built of weathering steel have had to be painted at considerable expense. His warning is justified, but these cases reflect poor choices of location rather than a flaw in the material, which performs well in the conditions for which it was intended.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Corrosion also threatens structures in which the steel cannot be seen at all. Reinforcing bars inside concrete are normally protected by the alkalinity of their surroundings, which keeps a passive film on the steel's surface. That protection can be lost, either as carbon dioxide from the air gradually neutralises the concrete or as chloride from sea water and de-icing salts penetrates it. The steel then rusts, and because rust expands, it splits the concrete apart from within. The Harbourline Infrastructure Survey, a long-term study of ports and sea walls, found that chlorides were responsible for the large majority of serious deterioration in the structures it examined, and recommended that sensors be embedded in new concrete to detect the danger before cracks appear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ships, pipelines and offshore platforms are often protected by a technique known as cathodic protection. Blocks of a more reactive metal, usually zinc or magnesium, are attached to the structure, or a small electric current is applied, so that the steel is forced to act as a cathode and does not dissolve. It is one of the cleverest applications of electrochemistry in everyday engineering. It is not, however, a solution that can be installed and forgotten: the blocks are gradually consumed and must be replaced, and systems that rely on electric current need regular checking.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, corrosion is less a problem of materials than of maintenance. The chemistry has been understood for more than a century, and effective protective methods exist for almost every situation. What is frequently missing is the will to pay for inspection and repair. Governments find it easier to win support for a new bridge than for the unglamorous repainting of an old one, and maintenance budgets are among the first to be cut when money is short. This is not to say that every ageing structure should be preserved, since some are cheaper to replace than to repair. But in general, a small sum spent regularly on upkeep prevents a much larger bill later.

topic: acid paper, the brittle books crisis and the chemistry of library preservation
title: Books That Eat Themselves
subtitle: Why a library's nineteenth-century volumes may crumble long before its medieval manuscripts

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Any librarian who has handled both will confirm a curious paradox. A book printed in Venice in the 1490s can usually be opened and read without risk; its pages are supple and often barely discoloured. A novel printed in 1900, by contrast, may be so brittle that a corner snaps off when a page is turned. Surveys carried out in large research libraries during the second half of the twentieth century suggested that a substantial proportion of their holdings from the period between about 1850 and 1950 were becoming too fragile to use, and the phenomenon came to be known simply as the brittle books problem. That newer documents should be in worse condition than older ones seems to defy common sense, but the explanation lies in a change in the chemistry of paper itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, European paper was made from linen and cotton rags, which were beaten into a pulp of long, strong cellulose fibres. As literacy spread and newspapers multiplied, rags could no longer meet demand, and manufacturers turned to wood pulp, whose fibres are much shorter and which brings with it other substances, notably lignin, that discolour over time. The most damaging change, however, was in the sizing, the treatment that prevents ink from spreading. Papermakers adopted a mixture of rosin and alum, and in the presence of moisture, alum generates sulphuric acid. The acid attacks the long chain-like molecules of cellulose, cutting them into shorter and shorter pieces, so that the paper steadily loses its ability to bend without breaking. Worse still, the reaction produces further acidic compounds, so that decay speeds up rather than slowing as the paper ages.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first large-scale response was microfilming. During the 1980s, libraries photographed millions of deteriorating volumes, and in many cases the originals were discarded once a film copy existed. Dr Ewa Szczygielska, a book conservator who has written extensively on this period, regards it as one of the great self-inflicted losses in the history of libraries. Many of the books thrown away, she argues, could have been stabilised, and the films that replaced them were not always durable: some made on acetate film have since begun to shrink and give off a smell of vinegar as they break down. It is difficult to disagree with her. Decisions taken in the belief that the originals were doomed now look hasty, and a film image cannot record the paper, binding and handwritten notes that give a particular copy much of its historical interest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious approach, developed from the 1970s onwards, is mass deacidification. Instead of being treated one at a time by hand, hundreds of books are placed in large chambers and soaked in a liquid that carries fine particles of an alkaline compound, typically magnesium oxide, deep into the paper. The particles neutralise the acid already present and leave behind an alkaline reserve that will counteract acid formed in future. Dr Gyöngyi Halmosi, head of research at the Balaton Paper Conservation Centre, has subjected treated and untreated samples to artificial ageing in heated chambers. Her results indicate that treatment can extend the useful life of paper by a factor of three to five. But it cannot restore strength that has already been lost, and Halmosi therefore insists that books must be treated while they can still be handled safely, not once they have become brittle.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Since no library can afford to treat everything, the question of selection is unavoidable. Professor Kojo Amponsah-Wiredu, an information scientist, argues that digitisation has changed the calculation. Once a text is available online, he points out, the physical book will rarely be consulted, so resources should be concentrated on volumes that have value as objects, such as those with rare bindings or annotations by their owners, while ordinary printed books, of which many copies supposedly survive elsewhere, can be left to take their chances. The logic is appealing, yet it rests on an assumption that is often false. When libraries have compared their holdings, they have repeatedly found that titles each institution believed to be safely kept elsewhere in fact survive in only one or two copies, or in none at all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For large collections, the most cost-effective measure may also be the least dramatic: controlling the environment. Like most chemical reactions, the breakdown of cellulose slows as temperature falls, and a widely used rule of thumb holds that reducing storage temperature by five degrees roughly doubles the expected life of paper. Keeping humidity low also helps, because water takes part in the reaction, although air that is too dry can cause paper and parchment to shrink and distort. Some libraries now keep their most vulnerable material in cold stores. The drawback is access: a book removed from cold storage must be allowed to acclimatise for many hours before it is opened, or moisture will condense on its pages, and readers must therefore order material well in advance.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Since the 1980s, much of the world's printing and writing paper has been produced under alkaline conditions, with calcium carbonate added as a filler, and such paper is expected to last for centuries. Conservationists campaigned hard for this change, but it was hastened above all by economics: calcium carbonate is cheaper than wood pulp, so substituting it for part of the fibre lowered manufacturers' costs. There is some irony in the fact that a problem created by the pursuit of cheap paper should have been largely resolved by the same pursuit. Yet the books printed during the century of acid paper remain on library shelves, and the chemistry at work inside them has not stopped.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: plant-based and biodegradable plastics such as PLA, and the gap between their promise and their behaviour after disposal
title: Green in Name Only?
subtitle: Plastics made from plants are often presented as the answer to plastic pollution, but their chemistry tells a more complicated story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Supermarket shelves increasingly carry cups, cutlery and packaging described as bioplastic, a word that suggests a material which comes from nature and will return to it harmlessly. The term, however, covers two quite different ideas. A plastic may be bio-based, meaning that it is made from plants rather than petroleum, or it may be biodegradable, meaning that microorganisms can break it down. The two properties do not necessarily go together. A version of the plastic used for drinks bottles can be manufactured from sugar cane, yet it is chemically identical to the fossil-fuel product and lasts just as long, while certain plastics derived from oil are readily digested by bacteria. Much of the confusion surrounding these materials begins with this single, overloaded word.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-known material that is both plant-based and biodegradable is polylactic acid, or PLA. It is made from the starch in maize or the sugar in sugar cane, which microbes ferment into lactic acid, the same substance that accumulates in tired muscles. The lactic acid molecules are then linked together into long chains to form a clear, rigid plastic. In principle, water can break these chains apart again, but in practice the reaction proceeds at a useful speed only when the material is held at temperatures above about fifty-five degrees and high humidity for several weeks. Such conditions exist in industrial composting plants. In a garden compost heap, in soil or in the sea, PLA may persist for years.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Kiyoshi Furuhata, a marine chemist, placed samples of PLA and conventional plastics in tanks of circulating seawater and found that, after twelve months, the PLA had lost almost none of its mass. He is particularly concerned about labelling. Consumers who read the word biodegradable, he argues, may conclude that an item can be thrown away anywhere without consequences, and so labels intended to reassure may actually encourage littering. Furuhata is surely right that the word is widely misunderstood. Whether the misunderstanding actually leads people to drop more rubbish is a separate question, and on that point the evidence so far is thin.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Nomvula Vilakazi, who advises municipal authorities on waste management, has encountered a more immediate difficulty. To the eye, a PLA cup is almost indistinguishable from one made of the conventional plastic used in drinks bottles, and when the two are mixed in recycling streams, even small amounts of PLA weaken the recycled material. At the same time, many composting plants refuse to accept PLA at all, because their processing cycles have been shortened to a few weeks to handle large volumes of food and garden waste, and the plastic does not break down quickly enough. The result, she says, is that a large share of PLA ends up being burned or buried, the very fate it was designed to avoid.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics have also raised the question of land. If plastics are to be made from crops, will they compete with food? Professor Rocio Lizarraga, an agricultural economist, considers the concern overstated, noting that all the bioplastics currently produced require only a tiny fraction of the world's farmland. This is accurate as far as it goes, but it describes the present rather than the future. Bioplastics make up only around one per cent of plastic production today; if they were to replace a significant share of conventional plastics, as their supporters hope, the area of land required would rise considerably, and the comparison with food would become far more pressing. Supporters respond that future plastics could be made from agricultural waste such as straw rather than from food crops, an approach that is promising but still far from commercial scale.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Life-cycle assessments, which attempt to account for all the environmental effects of a product from raw material to disposal, offer a mixed picture. The Circular Packaging Observatory, an independent research network, has compared dozens of such studies and concludes that the main advantage of PLA lies in its manufacture: because the plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, producing PLA generally releases less greenhouse gas than producing fossil-based plastics. After use, however, the benefits largely disappear unless the material reaches an industrial composter, and in landfill it behaves much like any other plastic. The Observatory also cautions that results vary widely depending on assumptions about fertiliser use and the energy consumed in farming, so single headline figures should be treated with care.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that bioplastics are worthless. They seem to me genuinely valuable in particular situations, above all where packaging is likely to be contaminated with food, such as tea bags, coffee capsules or the liners used in food-waste bins, since these items can go to a composting plant together with their contents instead of polluting recycling streams. As a general substitute for conventional plastic, however, they promise more than they can deliver, and they risk distracting attention from the less fashionable but more effective strategies of using less packaging and reusing what we already have.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the light-induced darkening and fading of artists' pigments and the dilemma of museum lighting
title: The Colours We Never See
subtitle: Many celebrated paintings no longer look as their creators intended, and the light that lets us admire them is partly to blame

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: We tend to assume that a painting in a gallery shows us what the artist saw on the day it was finished. Often it does not. A number of pigments widely used in past centuries are chemically unstable, and over decades they have shifted in ways that can alter the balance of an entire composition. Brilliant red lakes, made from insects or plant roots, have faded to pale pink or vanished altogether, leaving skies and draperies oddly lifeless. Smalt, a blue made from powdered cobalt glass, has turned a dull grey in many seventeenth-century canvases. Perhaps the most closely studied case is chrome yellow, a lead-based pigment adopted enthusiastically by painters in the nineteenth century for its intensity, which in some works has darkened to an unattractive olive brown.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The chemistry of this darkening is now reasonably well understood. Light, and particularly its shorter wavelengths at the blue and ultraviolet end of the spectrum, triggers a reaction in which chromium atoms at the surface of the paint lose part of their bond with oxygen and are converted into a different, brownish compound. Not all chrome yellows are equally vulnerable. The pale, lemon-coloured varieties, which manufacturers produced more cheaply by incorporating sulphur-containing compounds, deteriorate far more readily than the deep orange-yellow forms. Importantly, the change affects only a very thin outer layer; beneath it, the paint frequently retains much of its original brilliance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ilona Vaskelyte, a heritage scientist who uses powerful X-ray beams to map the chemistry of paint layers, has found that the altered zone is often only a few thousandths of a millimetre deep. She regards this as a reason for optimism. By analysing the unaltered paint underneath and measuring the extent of the surface change, she argues, it is possible to calculate the colours a painting originally displayed and to recreate them digitally, allowing viewers to compare the work as it is with the work as it was. Such reconstructions are valuable tools for scholars. They become more problematic when presented to the public as the true appearance of a painting, since each one depends on assumptions about the original paint that cannot be fully verified, and a confident image on a screen can conceal a great deal of uncertainty.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Prevention, of course, is preferable to reconstruction. Professor Amaru Condori, who has advised several national museums on conservation policy, points out that although curators cannot change the paint on a canvas, they can decide how much light falls on it, and this is the factor most directly within their control. He recommends low lighting levels for sensitive works and the removal of ultraviolet radiation by filters. Condori has also raised questions about the light-emitting diodes that have replaced older lamps in most galleries. Many common types produce a pronounced peak of blue light, precisely the region of the spectrum most damaging to chrome yellow, and he has called for these lamps to be assessed more rigorously before being installed beside vulnerable paintings.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The Lumen Display Working Group, an association of lighting designers and curators, accepts the chemistry but disputes some of the conclusions. Galleries that are kept very dim, its members argue, are uncomfortable to visit, make fine detail difficult to see and may discourage the public from coming at all. Modern adjustable lamps, they maintain, allow the most harmful wavelengths to be removed while the overall level of illumination stays the same, so that a general reduction in brightness is unnecessary. The technology they describe is real and welcome. Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to conclude that any form of lighting is entirely safe. Damage of this kind is cumulative, and even carefully filtered light contributes to it over the decades a painting spends on display.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A quite different objection comes from Dr Fenna Brouwershaven, an art historian who studies painters' working methods. Some artists, she notes, were warned that certain pigments were unstable and chose to use them regardless, so the changes we now observe are part of the history of the object rather than an error to be corrected. Efforts to recover a supposed original state, whether physically or on screen, risk erasing that history. Her point deserves respect, yet it can be pushed too far. That a painter accepted a risk does not mean the result would have pleased them, and the letters of several nineteenth-century artists suggest they would have been dismayed to see their colours turn brown.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Behind these disagreements lies an unavoidable tension between preservation and access. Every hour a painting spends under gallery lights consumes a small part of its future, yet a painting locked permanently in darkness serves no one. Rather than pretending that this dilemma can be resolved by better technology alone, museums ought to state openly how much change they are prepared to accept in a given work over a given period, and to plan their displays accordingly. Some institutions have begun to do so. It is an uncomfortable exercise, but it is more honest than the comforting fiction that the colours on the wall will last for ever.

area: the chemistry of everyday materials (glass, concrete, dyes, etc.)
topic: the chemistry of adhesives, from animal glue and epoxy to debond-on-demand and mussel-inspired wet glues
title: Holding Things Together
subtitle: Glue is among the oldest of human technologies, and the question of how to make it let go is now as pressing as how to make it stick

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Adhesives are older than our own species. Archaeologists have found stone tools attached to wooden handles with tar extracted from birch bark by Neanderthals more than 150,000 years ago, a process that required careful control of heat. For most of recorded history, however, the glue of choice was made from animals. Hides, bones and hooves were boiled for hours until the protein collagen they contain broke down into a sticky gelatine, which was applied warm and set firm as it cooled. Such glues held together centuries of furniture and musical instruments. Crucially, they could also be undone: warmth and moisture soften them again, which is why a skilled restorer can take apart an antique chair, replace a broken leg and reassemble it without damaging the original wood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Every adhesive must perform two tasks in sequence. First, while still liquid, it must spread across a surface and flow into the microscopic hills and valleys that exist even on materials that feel perfectly smooth, a property chemists call wetting. Then it must harden, whether by cooling, by the evaporation of a solvent or by a chemical reaction. A successful joint depends both on adhesion, the attraction between the glue and the surfaces it joins, and on cohesion, the internal strength of the hardened glue itself. Modern epoxy resins excel at both. They are supplied as two separate components which, when mixed, react to form a dense network in which every molecule is chemically linked to its neighbours. The result is so strong that epoxies now bond the wings of aircraft and the enormous blades of wind turbines.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That strength comes at a price, because a joint designed never to fail is also a joint that can never be opened. Many smartphones have batteries glued into their cases, making replacement difficult and recycling laborious, and most wind turbine blades that reach the end of their working lives are cut up and buried in landfill, since the materials bonded within them cannot easily be separated. The Disassembly Design Network, a group of engineers and product designers, argues that the solution lies in adhesives that hold firmly in normal use but release on command. Prototypes already exist that lose their grip when heated to a specific temperature or when a small electric current is passed through them, allowing components to be separated cleanly at a recycling plant.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Liesbeth Grevink, a materials scientist who tests structural joints, is unconvinced. An adhesive designed to let go, she warns, may do so at the wrong moment, for example when a device is left on the dashboard of a car on a hot day. In aircraft, vehicles or buildings, where a failed joint could cost lives, that risk is unacceptable. For consumer goods, she argues, the better answer is to return to mechanical fasteners such as screws and clips, which can be undone repeatedly without any special equipment. Grevink is clearly right about applications where safety is at stake. But it does not follow that screws are the answer everywhere. They add weight, require thicker casings and increase assembly costs, and in thin, lightweight products they are often simply impractical.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different frontier concerns glues that work in water. Most adhesives fail when wet because a thin film of water coats the surface and prevents the glue from making direct contact with it. Mussels, however, anchor themselves to wave-battered rocks using threads tipped with proteins rich in an unusual amino acid whose chemical structure allows it to displace water and bind tightly to wet minerals. Dr Seo-yeon Maeng, a bioengineer, has developed synthetic adhesives that mimic this chemistry for use inside the body. She hopes that they will one day replace stitches in delicate operations, such as sealing blood vessels or repairing internal organs, where needles can cause further damage. Several of her formulations are now in clinical trials.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Maeng's work illustrates a broader point about learning from nature. Early attempts to exploit mussel glue involved harvesting the proteins directly, but a single gram required the processing of thousands of animals, and the approach was quickly abandoned. Progress came only when researchers identified the specific chemical feature responsible for the glue's performance and reproduced it in molecules that could be manufactured in quantity. In my view this is typical: imitating the principle behind a natural material is generally far more fruitful than trying to reproduce the material itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a certain irony in the direction adhesive research is now taking. For a century, chemists strove to create glues that were ever stronger and more permanent, and they succeeded spectacularly. Now some of the most inventive work aims to recover a property that the humble animal glues of the past possessed all along: the ability to be undone. Those old glues were weaker, less resistant to damp and unpleasant to prepare, and nobody would wish to build an aircraft with them. But their reversibility was a genuine virtue, and modern adhesives, for all their advantages, have lost something that we are only now learning to value.

topic: earthquake early warning systems
title: Racing the Waves
subtitle: Earthquake early warning systems promise precious seconds of notice, but what those seconds are worth remains disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: No one can yet predict when an earthquake will strike, but once a rupture has begun it is possible to warn people before the most violent shaking reaches them. The opportunity arises from a quirk of physics. An earthquake releases several kinds of seismic wave, and the first to arrive, known as primary or P waves, travel considerably faster than the secondary and surface waves that cause most of the damage. An early warning system places sensors close to active faults; when they detect P waves, computers calculate the location and size of the event and broadcast an alert to areas further away. The warning rarely exceeds a minute and is often just a few seconds. Supporters describe these systems as the most important advance in seismic safety for a generation, and on the whole that description is deserved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central technical difficulty lies in judging the size of an earthquake from its opening moments. Dr Oriana Castellví, a seismologist at the Institute for Pacific Geophysics, points out that a large rupture may continue to spread along a fault for a minute or more, whereas an alert must be issued within the first few seconds. Algorithms that rely on conventional seismometers therefore tend to underestimate the very largest events, a problem known as magnitude saturation. Castellví's team has instead experimented with satellite positioning stations, which record how far the ground has actually moved rather than how rapidly it is vibrating, and which therefore do not saturate in the same way. The drawback is cost: such stations are expensive to install, and their measurements are too imprecise to be useful for small and moderate earthquakes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second limitation is less often acknowledged. Because the alert must be computed and transmitted, places very close to the epicentre receive it too late or not at all. This so-called blind zone is precisely where the shaking is strongest, and it is an uncomfortable fact that advocates of early warning have sometimes played down. Denser networks of sensors can narrow the zone, since the nearest instrument will be closer to any given rupture, and faster processing helps further. Yet no amount of investment can remove it entirely, because the information can never outrun the waves themselves by more than the difference in their speeds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For Ruslan Temirkhanov, a railway engineer who has designed automatic braking systems, the greatest value of early warning lies not in alerting people but in alerting machines. A computer controlling a high-speed train can begin to brake within a fraction of a second of receiving a signal, and ten seconds of deceleration can remove a substantial proportion of the train's speed before the shaking arrives. Lifts can be halted at the nearest floor, valves on gas pipelines closed and delicate manufacturing processes paused. Human beings, by contrast, need time to understand a message and decide what to do. Temirkhanov's emphasis on automation is persuasive, but it would be a mistake to conclude from it that warnings to the public are worthless.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The evidence on public response is nonetheless sobering. Lior Hadassi, a social psychologist who has interviewed recipients of alerts in several countries, found that many people spent their few seconds of notice looking at their phones, telephoning relatives or simply asking those around them what was happening. In one survey conducted after a moderate earthquake, fewer than a third of respondents reported having taken any protective action. Hadassi concludes that the recommended response of dropping to the ground, taking cover and holding on must be rehearsed until it becomes automatic. He has also challenged the widespread assumption that false alarms destroy public confidence: in his data, people were far more forgiving of an unnecessary alert than officials feared, provided that an explanation followed promptly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Every system must also settle on a threshold, the level of expected shaking at which an alert is sent. Set it too low and people receive frequent warnings for tremors they barely feel, which may teach them to ignore future alerts; set it too high and a damaging earthquake may go unannounced. Some agencies have resolved the dilemma by sending alerts at a lower threshold to industrial users than to the general public. A group at the Centre for Risk Communication led by Matías Echeverrigaray goes further, arguing that thresholds involve judgements about acceptable risk and should therefore be decided with local communities rather than by seismologists alone. This is a sensible principle, although consultation inevitably slows the introduction of systems that could save lives in the meantime.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be made of early warning overall? It is best understood as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, buildings that can withstand strong shaking. Ten seconds of notice offers little protection to someone inside a structure that is destined to collapse. The risk is that a visible, high-technology system attracts funds and political attention more readily than the unglamorous work of reinforcing schools and apartment blocks, even where the latter would prevent far more deaths. Early warning deserves support, but not at the expense of the slower task of making cities safe to begin with.

topic: slow slip events at subduction zones and their link to large earthquakes
title: The Quiet Faults
subtitle: Some faults move without shaking the ground at all, and seismologists disagree about whether this silent movement is a warning or a reprieve

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, seismologists assumed that a fault could do one of two things. It could remain locked, accumulating strain until it ruptured in an earthquake, or it could creep steadily, releasing strain so gradually that no earthquake ever occurred. The arrival of dense networks of satellite positioning stations around the turn of the millennium complicated this tidy picture. Instruments began to record episodes in which sections of a fault slipped over days or weeks, sometimes moving several centimetres and releasing as much energy as a moderately large earthquake, yet producing no shaking that anyone could feel. The discovery of these slow slip events ranks among the most consequential in modern seismology, not least because it dismantled an assumption that had shaped the discipline for generations.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the earliest and most persuasive evidence came from Takeshi Odagiri at the Southern Margin Geodetic Observatory. Analysing a decade of positioning data from stations above a subduction zone, where one tectonic plate descends beneath another, Odagiri noticed that the stations periodically reversed their usual direction of travel for a few weeks before resuming their normal motion. More remarkably, the reversals recurred at intervals of roughly fourteen months and coincided with bursts of faint, low-frequency seismic signals now called tremor. Odagiri recalls that his first presentations were met with suspicion: several colleagues assumed that the reversals reflected a malfunction in the receivers, and it took corroborating data from a separate network to convince them otherwise.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should a fault slip slowly rather than suddenly? Paulina Szczepankowska, who directs a rock mechanics laboratory at the Baltic Institute of Earth Physics, has sought an answer by shearing samples of fault rock under carefully controlled temperatures and pressures. Her experiments suggest that slow slip arises in a transitional band at depth, between the shallow locked portion of a fault and the deeper region where rock flows freely. There, water released from minerals in the descending plate raises the pressure of fluids within the rock, weakening the fault enough for it to move but not enough for a rupture to accelerate. Notably, she could reproduce slow slip only within a narrow window of conditions; outside it, her samples either stuck firmly or failed violently. The work is elegant, but a degree of caution is in order. Her samples measure a few centimetres across, whereas the fault zones they are meant to represent extend for tens of kilometres, and there is no guarantee that behaviour observed at one scale holds at the other.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question that matters most to the public is whether slow slip has anything to do with destructive earthquakes. Each slow event transfers stress to the neighbouring locked section of the fault, and it is natural to wonder whether this might occasionally push that section past breaking point. Obiora Ekwueme, a geophysicist at the Gulf of Guinea Seismological Centre, has compiled cases in which large subduction earthquakes were preceded by weeks or months of slow slip near their point of origin. In his view, continuous monitoring of such activity could eventually allow authorities to issue short-term forecasts, raising the alert level when slow slip appeared close to a locked segment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Henrike Vassbotn, a statistician who specialises in earthquake probabilities, is unconvinced. For every large earthquake preceded by slow slip, she notes, there are dozens of slow slip episodes after which nothing of consequence happened. Moreover, several of the precursory episodes cited by Ekwueme were identified only by re-examining data once the earthquake had already occurred, a procedure that makes patterns easy to find. On her calculations, observing slow slip raises the probability of a large earthquake in the following weeks only slightly. Vassbotn's caution is well founded, yet her conclusion that monitoring therefore has little practical value does not follow. Even a small rise in probability may justify inexpensive precautions, such as checking emergency supplies or postponing hazardous maintenance work, provided the public understands that a forecast is not a prediction.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication comes from Ignacio Raffo-Lagos and his modelling group at the Andean Centre for Geodynamics. Their simulations suggest that slow slip may, in some circumstances, act as a safety valve, relieving stress that would otherwise accumulate until it was released in a single large rupture. If they are correct, frequent slow slip might indicate a fault that is less, not more, dangerous. It is tempting to treat this view and Ekwueme's as rival hypotheses, only one of which can survive. A more plausible reading is that both effects occur, with the outcome depending on where along the fault the slow slip takes place and how close the adjacent locked section already is to failure.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Resolving the issue will require better observations, and here geography poses a serious obstacle. The slow slip of greatest concern frequently occurs beneath the sea floor, far beyond the reach of land-based positioning stations. Instruments placed on the ocean floor can measure movement directly, but they are costly to build, difficult to maintain and must transmit their data through kilometres of water. At present only a small number are in operation worldwide. Until such networks are expanded considerably, the debate is likely to remain unsettled.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Slow slip has not brought earthquake prediction any closer in the sense that the public might hope. What it has done is reveal that faults behave along a continuum, from silent creep to catastrophic rupture, with a range of intermediate behaviours in between. That insight alone justifies the effort devoted to studying it.
