topic: paleoseismology: reconstructing prehistoric earthquakes from fault trenches and lake sediments
title: Reading the Scars in the Ground
subtitle: Paleoseismologists dig across faults to recover earthquake histories that no instrument was ever present to record

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Seismometers capable of recording distant earthquakes have existed for little more than a century. For the purposes of understanding a single fault, that is a remarkably short window. Large earthquakes on many faults recur only every few hundred or even few thousand years, so the instrumental era may capture no more than a fragment of a fault's behaviour, and often nothing at all. Written records extend the picture in a handful of regions with long literary traditions, but for much of the world they are fragmentary or entirely absent. It is this gap that paleoseismology, the study of earthquakes that occurred before the age of instruments, sets out to fill. Its importance is frequently underestimated: it is no exaggeration to say that modern hazard maps rest as heavily on the spade as on the seismometer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic technique is disarmingly simple. Researchers excavate a trench, typically several metres deep, across the line of a fault, scrape its walls clean and record every layer of sediment exposed. When an earthquake rupture reaches the surface, it breaks and displaces the layers that existed at the time. Sediments deposited afterwards are laid down across the break, undisturbed. By identifying the youngest layer that has been cut and the oldest layer that has not, investigators can bracket the date of the event between the two. Fragments of charcoal or plant material within those layers are then dated using radiocarbon methods. A single well-chosen trench may reveal evidence of four to eight separate ruptures, extending the history of a fault back over several millennia.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Results of this kind have encouraged some researchers to make bold claims about the predictability of faults. Oriane Kesselbrink, of the Institute for Continental Deformation, compiled data from twenty trenches along a major strike-slip fault running through a mountain range. She found that, over the past three thousand years, the fault had ruptured on average every 330 years, and that individual intervals departed surprisingly little from that figure. In her view, such regularity justifies what are known as time-dependent forecasts, in which the probability of a future earthquake is assumed to grow steadily as the time since the last one lengthens. A fault that has been quiet for longer than its typical interval, she argues, should be treated as overdue.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the ground can be read with such precision. Bakhyt Zhumagaliyev, a geochronologist at the Steppe Geological Survey, points out that each dated event typically carries an uncertainty of fifty to a hundred years. When analysts plot the midpoint of each range, he suggests, a sequence that was in reality quite erratic can be made to look orderly. He raises a second difficulty as well: a trench samples only one point on what may be a fault hundreds of kilometres long. If a rupture died out before reaching the trench site, it leaves no trace there, and the earthquake simply vanishes from the record. His objection is a serious one, but it cuts both ways. If events have been missed, the true interval between earthquakes must be shorter than the trenches indicate, and the danger correspondingly greater than reported.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Partly in response to such concerns, paleoseismologists have looked beyond faults themselves. Coastal marshes that drop suddenly during an earthquake preserve buried soils and sheets of sand washed in by tsunamis. Lakes offer another archive. Leocadia Ferraz-Ugalde, who studies lake cores in the high Andes, explains that strong shaking causes sediment on the steep underwater slopes of a lake to collapse, producing distinctive layers in which coarse grains settle first and fine ones last. Because lake floors accumulate sediment without interruption, their cores provide a continuous record in a way that a trench rarely can. The difficulty is that floods and storms can produce deposits that look much the same. Ferraz-Ugalde therefore attributes a layer to an earthquake only when deposits of the same age appear in at least three separate lakes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most unsettling idea to emerge from the field concerns the way earthquakes are distributed over time. A team led by Ingvild Torrestad at the Polar Margin Research Unit has argued that some faults do not behave regularly at all, but alternate between active phases, when several large earthquakes strike within a few decades, and dormant phases lasting thousands of years. If this is correct, an average recurrence interval may be misleading: a fault in a dormant phase could be judged more hazardous than it really is, while one entering an active phase could be badly underestimated. The model deserves to be taken seriously, yet the evidence for it is still thin, resting on a small number of faults that happen to have unusually long records.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever the outcome of these debates, the practical value of the discipline is not in doubt. Paleoseismic evidence has influenced decisions about where to build dams, power stations and hospitals, and in several countries faults once regarded as inactive have been reclassified after trenches revealed ruptures within the past few thousand years. Arguably, however, the greatest contribution of paleoseismology is a kind of humility: it reminds engineers and planners that a fault which has been silent throughout living memory is not necessarily a safe one. It is all the more regrettable, then, that trenching projects attract only a small fraction of the funding devoted to instrument networks, an imbalance that ought to be corrected.

topic: induced seismicity from wastewater injection and geothermal projects
title: Earthquakes of Our Own Making
subtitle: As fluid injection triggers tremors in regions once thought stable, scientists disagree about how far the risk can be controlled

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, certain continental interiors were regarded as among the most seismically tranquil places on earth. Within a few years in the early twenty-first century, some of them were recording hundreds. The cause, investigators eventually concluded, lay not in the slow movement of tectonic plates but in the disposal of vast quantities of salty wastewater produced by oil and gas extraction, which was being pumped into porous rock deep underground. That human activity can trigger earthquakes had been known for decades, from reservoirs, mining and geothermal schemes. What changed was the scale. Induced seismicity can no longer be treated as a geological curiosity; it is a hazard in its own right, and it demands to be managed as one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physics behind the phenomenon is now reasonably well understood. Many faults in the earth's crust are already loaded almost to breaking point by tectonic stresses accumulated over thousands of years, and they remain locked only because friction between the two sides prevents them from slipping. When fluid is forced into the surrounding rock, it raises the pressure in the tiny pores and fractures that the rock contains. This rising pressure partly counteracts the force clamping the fault together, and if it climbs high enough the fault gives way. The crucial point is that the injected fluid does not supply the energy of the resulting earthquake. That energy was stored in the crust long before any well was drilled; the fluid merely acts as a trigger. It is for this reason that a modest industrial operation can, in principle, unleash an earthquake out of all proportion to its own size.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Public anxiety has tended to focus on hydraulic fracturing, the technique in which fluid is injected at high pressure to crack open rock and release gas. Fracturing does occasionally cause felt tremors, but the great majority of significant induced earthquakes have been linked instead to wastewater disposal. The difference lies in duration and volume: fracturing typically involves injection for a matter of hours or days, whereas disposal wells may operate continuously for years, steadily pressurising an ever larger volume of rock. The tendency to treat the two activities as interchangeable has, in my view, distorted the debate, directing attention towards the more visible technology rather than the more consequential one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How large an induced earthquake can be is a question of more than academic interest, since the answer determines what regulators can realistically demand. Dr Mirela Caragiale of the Institute of Applied Geomechanics has argued that the maximum magnitude at a site is governed chiefly by the total volume of fluid injected there. Her model implies that capping volumes would effectively cap the size of any resulting earthquake, and its simplicity has made it attractive to regulatory agencies, which can monitor injection volumes far more easily than they can measure conditions deep underground.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Efua Nsiah-Brempong, a seismologist at the Geophysical Hazards Laboratory, considers this reassurance misplaced. Once a rupture begins, she contends, it need not remain within the zone that has been pressurised by injection; it can run on along a fault that was already close to failure, in which case the eventual magnitude is limited only by the dimensions of the fault itself. She points to a number of induced earthquakes that were considerably larger than volume-based calculations would permit. On the largest events, the evidence appears to favour Nsiah-Brempong. It would nonetheless be a mistake to discard the volume model entirely, since it continues to describe the behaviour of the many small tremors that make up the bulk of induced seismicity reasonably well.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In practice, many jurisdictions now rely on so-called traffic-light systems. Operators monitor seismic activity around their wells: at the green level injection continues normally, an amber level requires the rate to be reduced, and a red level obliges the operator to stop. These schemes are sensible, but they rest on the assumption that halting injection halts the danger. Research by Sayuri Kazamatsuri and colleagues at the Coastal Crust Observatory casts doubt on this. Examining dozens of injection projects, they found that roughly a third of the largest earthquakes occurred after pumping had ceased, because pressure continued to spread outwards through the rock for months. A red light, in other words, may arrive too late to prevent the very event it is designed to avoid.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The social dimension of the problem has received less scientific attention. Several geothermal projects intended to supply heat or electricity to cities have been abandoned after triggering tremors that cracked walls and alarmed residents, leaving their developers facing costly compensation claims. Tobiah Rautenstrauch, a sociologist who has interviewed communities near such projects, maintains that public tolerance depends less on the size of the tremors than on whether residents feel that they were consulted beforehand and stand to gain something in return. This matters well beyond the energy industry, because deep geothermal heat is one of the few low-carbon sources capable of providing continuous power, and a collapse in public trust could set its development back by a generation.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done? The most defensible approach would be to require operators to map the faults near a proposed site, and to estimate how close they are to failure, before any injection is permitted, rather than relying on monitoring after the fact. Such surveys are expensive, but the cost is small compared with that of a damaging earthquake or an abandoned project. Induced seismicity also offers grounds for cautious optimism. Unlike natural earthquakes, which no human decision can prevent, the earthquakes we cause can at least partly be avoided by choosing where, and how, we inject.

topic: the search for reliable earthquake precursors (animal behaviour, radon, foreshocks, satellite signals)
title: The Elusive Warning Sign
subtitle: Can anything reliably announce an earthquake before it strikes? The search for precursors has a long and chequered history

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Stories of strange events preceding earthquakes are almost as old as written history. Animals are said to have fled their stables, wells to have risen or fallen without explanation, and unusual lights to have flickered in the sky. Such accounts have encouraged a persistent hope that earthquakes might one day be predicted, in the strict sense of specifying in advance the time, place and magnitude of a coming event. This is quite different from forecasting, which merely estimates the probability of an earthquake over a period of years or decades. It must be admitted that the scientific record of prediction is, for the most part, a record of failure. Yet to abandon the search altogether would be premature.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Animal behaviour is the most popular candidate, and also the most problematic. Anecdotes are plentiful, but nearly all of them are collected after an earthquake has occurred, and they are distorted by a form of memory bias: an owner whose dog barked all night will recall it vividly if the ground shook the next morning, and forget it entirely if nothing happened. To avoid this trap, Dr Rosalind Sjoerdsma of the Behavioural Ecology Unit fitted motion sensors to cattle, sheep and goats on a farm close to an active fault and recorded their movements continuously for several years. The animals did become noticeably more active in the hours before a number of moderate earthquakes. However, similar bursts of activity occurred on many occasions when no earthquake followed. Sjoerdsma concludes that the animals may well sense something, but that their behaviour is far too inconsistent to serve as a warning. Her careful work shows that this field, so often treated as a joke, deserves to be taken more seriously than it has been.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns radon, a radioactive gas that escapes from rock when it is stressed and cracked. Sudden increases in the radon content of groundwater have been reported before several destructive earthquakes. Tavita Leaupepe, a hydrogeologist at the Pacific Groundwater Institute, monitored a network of wells for a decade. He found that radon peaks preceded only a small proportion of the earthquakes in his region, and that many peaks had nothing to do with seismic activity at all, being caused instead by heavy rain or changes in air pressure. In his view, radon readings on their own are as likely to mislead as to inform, and they become useful only when interpreted alongside other kinds of measurement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Foreshocks, the smaller tremors that sometimes come before a large earthquake, might seem the most obvious warning of all. Around half of all major earthquakes are preceded by them. The difficulty is that a foreshock can be recognised only in hindsight; at the moment it occurs, it looks exactly like any other small earthquake, and the vast majority of small earthquakes are not followed by anything larger. Ximena Uriarte-Bolaños of the Seismic Statistics Group nevertheless argues that foreshocks have value. The chance that a given small earthquake will turn out to be a foreshock is only a few per cent, she acknowledges, but that is many times higher than the normal background probability, and even a modest temporary increase in risk can justify practical steps such as checking emergency equipment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious attempt to catch precursors in the act ended in disappointment. A segment of fault that had produced moderate earthquakes at fairly regular intervals was selected for intensive study, on the assumption that the next event was due within a few years. Researchers from the Consortium for Fault Observation surrounded it with instruments to detect any change in ground movement, water levels or electrical properties. The earthquake eventually arrived more than a decade later than expected, and the instruments detected no clear sign that it was coming. The consortium concluded that precursors, if they exist, may not appear in any consistent form. The experiment is sometimes described as a costly mistake, but this judgement is unfair; it was a hard lesson, and a necessary one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: More recently, attention has turned to signals detected from space. Professor Bogomil Stoyanchev claims that satellite measurements reveal disturbances in the upper atmosphere several days before large earthquakes. His critics respond that the atmosphere is disturbed constantly, and that by selecting the anomalies that happen to precede earthquakes while ignoring the rest, almost any data set can be made to look predictive. Claims of this kind should not be accepted simply because they have not been disproved. They must be subjected to blind testing, in which predictions are formally registered before the events they describe. So far, no proposed method has passed such a test.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Despite this record, public demand for prediction remains strong, and self-declared predictors regularly attract media attention with confident warnings that are rarely fulfilled. Scientists have a responsibility to explain clearly why probabilities, rather than precise dates, are the best they can honestly offer. The future of earthquake safety almost certainly lies in long-term forecasting, building standards and early warning systems. Basic research into precursors, however, still deserves modest support, for the history of science suggests that questions once dismissed as hopeless are occasionally answered after all.

topic: when plate tectonics began on the early Earth
title: When the Plates Began to Move
subtitle: Geologists agree that plate tectonics shapes the modern planet, but not on how long it has been doing so

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The outer shell of the earth is broken into about a dozen major plates, which drift across the planet's surface at a few centimetres a year, colliding, separating and sliding past one another. Where one plate descends beneath another, at a subduction zone, old crust is dragged down into the mantle and recycled. As far as can be determined, this arrangement is unique among the rocky planets of the solar system: neither Venus nor Mars shows evidence of plate tectonics operating today. Yet when the process began on earth remains a matter of fierce dispute. Published estimates range from more than four billion years ago to less than one billion, a span that covers most of the planet's history. Few questions in the earth sciences are at once so fundamental and so poorly constrained.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies partly in the nature of the evidence. Ocean floor, which would provide the most direct record of plate movement, is itself consumed at subduction zones, and none of it survives for long in geological terms; the oldest oceanic crust still in place is only around 180 million years old. Geologists must therefore rely on the continents, whose oldest rocks are scarce, scattered and heavily altered by later heating and deformation. Some of the most important clues come from zircons, tiny crystals so resistant to weathering and chemical change that individual grains have survived for as long as 4.4 billion years, long after the rocks in which they originally formed have disappeared.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Saskia Ondrejkova of the Institute of Early Earth Studies belongs to what might be called the early-start camp. Her analyses of the oxygen and trace elements within ancient zircons indicate that they crystallised from magma containing material that had once been at the surface and had interacted with liquid water. Today, the main way in which such material is carried down to depths where it can melt is subduction. Ondrejkova therefore argues that processes resembling modern plate tectonics were already operating by about 4.2 billion years ago, remarkably soon after the planet formed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Halldor Sigvaldason, a geodynamicist, is unconvinced. The same chemical signature, he points out, could have been produced in other ways: by dense lower parts of a thick crust peeling away and sinking into the mantle, or by large meteorite impacts that melted wet surface rock. More fundamentally, he notes that the early mantle was considerably hotter than it is now, perhaps by two or three hundred degrees. Plates sitting on such a mantle would have been weaker and more buoyant, and might have broken apart rather than sinking as coherent slabs. Sigvaldason favours a 'stagnant lid' model, in which the young earth was encased in a single rigid shell pierced by volcanoes, and he places the onset of true plate tectonics at around three billion years ago, once the interior had cooled sufficiently.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Evidence for a change at about that time is considerable, including a shift in the chemical composition of continental crust and the first appearance of paired belts of rock that seem to record subduction. Dr Nkiruka Obiaga-Faure, however, argues for a much later start. She focuses on blueschists, rocks that form when crust is carried rapidly to great depths while remaining relatively cool, as occurs in modern subduction zones. Such rocks are almost entirely absent from the record before about 800 million years ago, and she concludes that subduction of the modern, cold type began only then. This argument is weaker than it first appears, since it rests on the absence of evidence. Blueschists are easily altered when they are reheated or brought back to the surface, and older examples may simply have been destroyed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the question itself is badly framed. The search for a single starting date assumes that plate tectonics switched on once, globally and permanently. It may instead have begun in particular regions, stopped and restarted several times, and become a worldwide system only gradually. Computer simulations by the Geodynamics Modelling Collective lend some support to this picture, showing an early earth that alternates between stagnant-lid conditions and brief episodes of subduction. The transitional view is attractive, not least because it reconciles much of the conflicting evidence. Its weakness is that a model flexible enough to accommodate almost any observation is correspondingly difficult to test.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The issue matters far beyond geology. Plate tectonics helps to regulate the earth's climate over long periods through the carbon cycle: carbon dioxide released by volcanoes is gradually drawn out of the atmosphere by the weathering of rock, and the carbon is eventually buried and carried into the mantle at subduction zones. Plate movement also builds continents and replenishes the supply of nutrients to the oceans, and some researchers link its onset to the rise of atmospheric oxygen and the emergence of complex life. Astronomers searching for habitable planets around other stars also have a stake in the debate, since whether earth-sized planets are likely to develop plate tectonics affects estimates of their habitability. It is quite possible that the decisive evidence will come not from ancient rocks at all, but from comparisons with other worlds.

topic: seismic building codes, enforcement and retrofitting of vulnerable buildings
title: It Is Buildings That Kill
subtitle: The death toll of an earthquake depends less on its size than on the structures in which people happen to be standing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Engineers who study earthquakes are fond of a blunt saying: earthquakes do not kill people; buildings do. The evidence for it is stark. Two earthquakes of almost identical magnitude can strike within a few years of each other, one in a wealthy region where it causes a few dozen deaths, and the other in a poorer one where the toll runs into tens of thousands. Differences in geology and population density account for some of the gap, but by far the greater part is explained by how buildings were designed and constructed, and by whether the rules governing their construction were actually followed. This is surely the most important lesson that the study of earthquakes has to offer, because it means that the great majority of earthquake deaths are, in principle, preventable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Building codes set out how structures should be designed to withstand shaking. They specify the amount and placement of steel reinforcement, the strength of the connections between beams and columns, and the ability of a frame to bend without snapping, a property engineers call ductility. What many people do not realise is that most modern codes do not aim to keep buildings undamaged. Their central purpose is to prevent collapse, so that occupants have time to escape. A building that fully complies with the code may therefore be left so badly cracked after a strong earthquake that it must be demolished. This is a reasonable objective, given the enormous cost of making buildings truly earthquake-proof, but it is one that the public deserves to have explained to them more honestly than it usually is.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Codes, moreover, apply mainly to new construction, whereas most of the buildings in older cities were erected before modern standards existed. Two types are particularly dangerous: masonry buildings constructed without any reinforcement, and concrete-framed blocks whose ground floors are left open for shops or car parks, creating a weak lower storey that can collapse while the floors above remain intact. Strengthening such buildings, a process known as retrofitting, is costly, and no city can afford to retrofit everything at once. Dr Kaveh Dastgheib-Nouri of the Urban Structural Safety Centre has estimated that strengthening the most vulnerable tenth of the buildings in a typical city would prevent the majority of deaths, and he argues that schools and hospitals should be dealt with first.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In many fast-growing cities, the problem is not the absence of codes but the failure to apply them. Much new housing is built informally by owners and local builders without the involvement of qualified engineers, and inspections, where they happen at all, can be undermined by bribery. Professor Amara Kollie-Venn, an economist who studies urban housing, argues that simply tightening enforcement can backfire. When official approval becomes slow and expensive, she observes, construction shifts further into the informal sector, beyond the reach of regulators altogether. She advocates instead training the masons and small contractors who actually make decisions on building sites, and several programmes of this kind have produced measurable improvements in the quality of everyday construction.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every solution requires advanced engineering. Confined masonry, in which brick walls are tied together by slender bands of reinforced concrete, adds relatively little to construction costs and has performed well in a number of earthquakes. Dr Elif Tozkoparan, an architectural historian, goes further, arguing that many traditional techniques, such as walls laced with horizontal timber beams, were developed precisely because communities had learned from repeated earthquakes, and were abandoned only because concrete came to be seen as a symbol of modernity. Her research is valuable, but there is a danger of romanticising the past. The traditional buildings that stand today are, by definition, those that survived; countless others did not. Nor can such methods be adapted to the tall apartment blocks in which a growing proportion of city dwellers now live.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even where the technical solution is clear, someone must pay for it. Owners seldom retrofit voluntarily, since the costs are immediate while the benefits are uncertain and may never materialise during their ownership; tenants, meanwhile, bear much of the risk without any say in the decision. Some cities have responded by making the strengthening of the most hazardous buildings compulsory, with fixed deadlines, while offering tax relief and low-interest loans. A review by the Metropolitan Resilience Office of one such city found that its mandatory programme had achieved over ninety per cent compliance within seven years, whereas an earlier voluntary scheme had persuaded fewer than one owner in twenty to act.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The knowledge needed to make cities far safer already exists; the obstacles are largely political and economic. Destructive earthquakes in any particular place are rare, while political terms of office are short, so retrofitting offers leaders little visible reward. Money spent on strengthening a school produces no ribbon-cutting ceremony, and its success can only be measured by a disaster that does not happen. Governments that postpone such programmes are, in effect, gambling with their citizens' lives. Seismic safety may be the clearest example of an investment whose value lies in the fact that, if it works, nobody will ever notice it.

topic: aftershock forecasting and the public communication of earthquake probabilities
title: After the Mainshock
subtitle: Forecasting aftershocks is one of seismology's genuine successes; explaining those forecasts to a frightened public is a different matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a large earthquake strikes, it is never the end of the story. In the hours, weeks and months that follow, the surrounding crust adjusts to the sudden shift, producing a succession of smaller earthquakes known as aftershocks. Their number can run into the thousands, but it declines in a remarkably consistent way, roughly in inverse proportion to the time elapsed since the main event, a pattern first described more than a century ago. The largest aftershock is typically about one unit of magnitude smaller than the mainshock, although individual sequences vary considerably around that figure. Because these regularities hold across so many earthquakes, aftershock forecasting has become one of the very few areas in which seismology can make genuinely dependable statements about the future, a point that is too rarely acknowledged when the discipline is criticised for its failure to predict earthquakes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Statistical models can now generate forecasts within hours of a large earthquake, expressing, for example, the probability of an aftershock above a given magnitude during the following week. Such forecasts have obvious practical uses. Rescue teams must decide how much risk to accept when entering collapsed structures; engineers must judge when damaged buildings can safely be reoccupied; and families must decide whether to return home or remain in temporary shelter. There is also a small but real possibility, usually put at around five per cent, that what has been called a mainshock will be followed by an even larger earthquake, in which case the first event is reclassified, after the fact, as a foreshock.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Researchers differ over how such forecasts are best produced. Dr Folasade Ogunwusi of the Centre for Crustal Mechanics favours physics-based models, which calculate how the mainshock has altered the stresses on surrounding faults. Areas where stress has increased, she argues, are where aftershocks will concentrate, and such models can therefore say something about location that purely statistical approaches cannot. Professor Radim Holoubek takes the opposite view. In blind tests, he notes, statistical models have often outperformed physics-based ones, largely because stress calculations depend on the precise geometry of faults deep underground, which is rarely known with any confidence. In forecasting, he maintains, simplicity is a virtue. This rivalry has been healthy rather than damaging: hybrid models combining the two approaches now appear to perform better than either does alone.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Producing an accurate forecast, however, is only half the task. Probabilities are notoriously difficult for non-specialists to interpret. A ten per cent chance of a damaging aftershock may be heard as a reassurance by one listener and as a warning of imminent disaster by another. Dr Ottilie Skarsgjerd, a psychologist who studies risk perception, has found that people grasp forecasts more readily when they are expressed as frequencies, for instance by saying that in a hundred situations like this one, a damaging aftershock would be expected in about ten. Her interviews with residents of earthquake-affected towns also revealed that numbers alone were seldom what people wanted. Above all, they wanted to know what they should actually do.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Communication has been further complicated by the question of blame. In one widely reported case, scientists who had made reassuring public statements shortly before a deadly earthquake were put on trial, and although their convictions were later overturned, the episode left a lasting mark. Some researchers became reluctant to speak to journalists at all, and certain agencies began to release forecasts only in written form, after approval by a committee. Such caution is understandable, but it is mistaken. When experts fall silent after a disaster, the gap is quickly filled by rumour and by self-appointed prophets, whose claims are far more likely to cause harm than any carefully worded probability.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some institutions have taken the opposite approach. The Regional Seismic Advisory Panel ran a trial in which aftershock forecasts were published automatically on a public website within minutes of any significant earthquake, and updated as the sequence developed. An evaluation of the trial found that public trust in the panel rose, and that newspaper and television reports of aftershock risk became noticeably more accurate. A minority of users, however, said they found the constantly changing figures confusing. Automatic publication is, on balance, the right course, but it cannot be a substitute for explanation; numbers released without context risk being misunderstood as easily as numbers withheld.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It must also be remembered that a forecast is a statement of probability, not a promise. A one per cent chance is not a zero per cent chance, and on rare occasions the unlikely outcome will occur. Judging forecasters by whether they happened to anticipate a particular damaging aftershock is therefore misguided. The proper test is whether their forecasts helped emergency managers, engineers and ordinary people make better decisions than they would otherwise have made. By that standard, a forecast that is technically flawless but widely misunderstood has failed just as surely as one that is simply wrong.

topic: fibre-optic cables, smartphones and low-cost sensors as new seismic monitoring networks
title: Listening Through Glass
subtitle: Telecommunications cables and everyday devices are being turned into seismic instruments, but more data does not automatically mean better data

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A modern broadband seismometer is a marvel of precision, able to register ground movements far smaller than the width of an atom. It is also expensive to buy, install and maintain, and for that reason such instruments are usually spaced tens of kilometres apart, even in well-funded networks. Elsewhere the gaps are far larger. The oceans, which cover around seventy per cent of the planet, are almost entirely unmonitored, and many earthquake-prone countries can afford only a handful of stations. The uneven global distribution of seismic instruments is one of the least discussed inequalities in science, yet it determines which earthquakes are studied in detail, which faults are mapped, and which populations receive timely warnings.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most promising attempts to close these gaps relies on infrastructure that already exists. In a technique known as distributed acoustic sensing, pulses of laser light are sent along an optical fibre. Microscopic imperfections in the glass scatter a tiny fraction of the light back towards the source, and when passing seismic waves stretch or compress the fibre, the pattern of this returning light changes. By analysing it, researchers can turn a single cable into thousands of virtual sensors, spaced every few metres along a length of fifty kilometres or more. Crucially, the method can make use of so-called dark fibre: spare strands within the cables laid by telecommunications companies, including those running across the sea floor.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Early results have been striking. Dr Anahí Mamani-Ruelas of the Andean Seismic Imaging Laboratory connected equipment to a forty-kilometre stretch of seafloor cable and, within months, had detected hundreds of small offshore earthquakes that no land-based station had recorded. The density of measurements also allowed her team to map the structure of an offshore fault in far finer detail than had previously been possible. Because the fibre was already in place, the only significant costs were the laser unit at the shore station and the time needed to process the data. Mamani-Ruelas is openly enthusiastic, arguing that the thousands of kilometres of cable already crossing the world's oceans could provide seismic coverage of the sea floor at a fraction of the cost of conventional instruments.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others urge caution. An optical fibre responds only to stretching along its own length, so it is largely blind to ground motion at right angles to the cable. Its sensitivity also depends on how firmly it is attached to the ground: a cable lying loosely in a plastic pipe may rattle and produce misleading signals. Professor Severin Achleitner, a geophysicist, points out that because these factors vary from one section of cable to the next, the instruments are difficult to calibrate, and estimates of earthquake magnitude derived from them can be seriously wrong. He regards the technique as a valuable complement to conventional seismometers rather than a replacement for them, and on the present evidence that assessment seems correct.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second strand of innovation turns ordinary consumer devices into instruments. Almost every smartphone contains an accelerometer sensitive enough to detect strong shaking, and several systems now gather readings from millions of phones to identify earthquakes and issue alerts. Low-cost sensors, costing a few hundred dollars rather than tens of thousands, have also been installed in homes and schools. Dr Nomvula Zikhali, who coordinates a school seismometer programme, acknowledges that the quality of the data is modest. She argues, however, that the programme's real value lies elsewhere: it brings students into contact with genuine scientific work and builds public awareness of earthquake risk. In regions without any professional network, she adds, imperfect measurements are far better than none.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Phones, of course, were not designed for seismology. A phone carried in a pocket or placed on a vibrating table generates constant background noise, and a phone that is dropped can produce a signal resembling a nearby earthquake. To avoid false alarms, the computer scientist Ravshan Tursunkulov has developed algorithms that declare an earthquake only when a large number of phones in the same area register shaking at almost the same moment. Such systems also raise questions of privacy, since they depend on knowing where each phone is located. These concerns are genuine, but they are manageable: location data can be made anonymous and stored only briefly, and the systems already in operation have shown that this is achievable in practice.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these developments are producing seismic data in quantities that would have been unimaginable a generation ago. A single fibre-optic installation can generate several terabytes in a day, far more than any team of analysts could examine, and storing it all, let alone sharing it with other research groups, presents formidable practical problems of its own. Machine-learning tools are therefore indispensable, although there is a risk that researchers will come to rely on algorithms whose workings they do not fully understand. The greatest benefit of these new methods will probably be felt not in wealthy countries that already possess dense networks, but in those regions where monitoring is currently sparse. There is, however, a danger that must be guarded against: cheap networks should never become an excuse for governments to avoid investing in the professional monitoring that remains essential.

topic: intraplate earthquakes in stable continental interiors
title: Trouble in the Middle of the Plate
subtitle: Earthquakes far from plate boundaries are rare, but they defy the models that explain most of the world's seismic activity

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Plate tectonics provides an elegant explanation for why most earthquakes occur where they do. The great majority are concentrated along the boundaries between plates, where vast slabs of rock grind past, collide with or pull away from one another. A small proportion, however, strike in the interiors of plates, hundreds or even thousands of kilometres from the nearest boundary. Such events are infrequent, but they can be powerful, and their effects are often felt over remarkable distances. The crust beneath continental interiors is typically old and cold, and seismic waves pass through it with little loss of energy, so an intraplate earthquake may shake an area many times larger than a boundary earthquake of the same magnitude. Because buildings in these regions are seldom designed with earthquakes in mind, intraplate events pose a danger out of all proportion to their frequency.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In broad outline, the cause is reasonably well established. Forces generated at plate boundaries are transmitted through the rigid interior of a plate, and where the crust contains ancient zones of weakness, this stress can be released. Typical examples include failed rifts, where a continent once began to split apart but never completed the process, and the sutures where separate landmasses were welded together hundreds of millions of years ago. The difficulty is that continental interiors are criss-crossed by countless such structures, most of which show no sign of activity. Explaining why intraplate earthquakes happen in general is one thing; determining which of these innumerable ancient faults will rupture next is quite another, and at present it cannot be done.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Part of the problem is time. Measurements from satellite positioning systems indicate that most continental interiors are deforming at less than one millimetre per year, far more slowly than plate boundaries. Dr Mehrnoush Kiani-Asl, a seismologist at the Institute for Lithospheric Studies, argues that this has profound consequences. Where strain builds up so slowly, she contends, the interval between large earthquakes on any one fault may amount to tens of thousands of years. Moreover, aftershock sequences, which near plate boundaries die away within a few years or decades, may continue for centuries in slowly deforming crust. Much of the minor seismic activity recorded in some interior regions today, in her view, may therefore consist of the aftershocks of large earthquakes that took place long ago.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If Kiani-Asl is right, hazard maps based on recent seismicity may be pointing in the wrong direction, highlighting the places where large earthquakes have already happened rather than those where the next will strike. Professor Tiberiu Oancea goes a step further. He argues that intraplate seismicity tends to migrate: once one fault has released its accumulated strain, stress is transferred to neighbouring faults, so that activity shifts from one structure to another over thousands of years. On this view, the next major intraplate earthquake in a region is more likely to occur on a fault with little recorded history than on one that has ruptured recently. The idea is an unsettling one, because it implies that areas currently regarded as safe may be nothing of the kind.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some support for these interpretations comes from the Continental Interior Geodesy Network, a consortium that has installed high-precision positioning stations across one continental interior. Its measurements have revealed almost no detectable deformation in the area of a famous sequence of large earthquakes that occurred some two centuries ago, a finding consistent with the view that the region is not currently storing strain for a comparable event. Other researchers caution that the instruments may simply not be precise enough to detect strain accumulating at very low rates. This is a fair point. The failure to measure deformation does not prove that none is occurring, and the network's results, while suggestive, cannot settle the question.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An additional influence may come from changes at the surface. During the last ice age, thick ice sheets pressed down on large parts of the northern continents. When the ice melted, the crust began to rebound, altering the stresses on faults beneath. Dr Yolanda Ruiterbos, a geologist who has studied fault scarps in formerly glaciated regions, has found that many of them formed within a few thousand years of the ice retreating, which she interprets as evidence of a burst of earthquakes triggered by the removal of this enormous load. She suggests that the process may still be affecting some faults today, and that erosion and large changes in groundwater levels could have similar, if smaller, effects elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What should be done in the face of so much uncertainty? Because the historical record in most continental interiors is far too short to reveal the true pattern of activity, critical facilities such as dams and power stations have often been sited on the basis of a few centuries of observation. The prudent course, in my view, would be to assume that a damaging earthquake could occur almost anywhere within a stable continental interior, and to design the most important structures accordingly, even at considerable cost. It would be a mistake, however, to spread resources for earthquake protection evenly between such regions and the areas near plate boundaries, where large earthquakes are far more frequent and the need for investment remains far more pressing.

topic: the 1815 Tambora eruption and how far the hardships of 1816 can be blamed on it
title: The Summer That Never Came
subtitle: Two centuries on, scholars still disagree about how much of the misery of 1816 can be laid at the door of a single volcano

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted with a violence unmatched anywhere on earth in recorded history. The explosion, heard more than two thousand kilometres away, hurled an estimated 150 cubic kilometres of rock and ash into the air and killed tens of thousands of people on Sumbawa and neighbouring islands. Its more distant consequences arrived a year later. In 1816, snow fell in New England in June, frosts damaged crops in every month of the summer, and harvests failed across much of western Europe, where the price of grain roughly doubled. The connection with an eruption on the far side of the world was not proposed until more than a century later. Today the 'year without a summer' is a standard illustration of how volcanoes can alter climate. Yet the very neatness of that story deserves more suspicion than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physical mechanism is well understood. A powerful eruption injects sulphur dioxide high into the stratosphere, where it combines with water vapour to form a haze of tiny sulphate droplets. Because there is no rain at that altitude to wash them out, the droplets can linger for one or two years, reflecting a portion of incoming sunlight back into space. By measuring the sulphate that settled on the polar ice sheets, Henrike Vasstrand, a palaeoclimatologist at the Tromsø Polar Archive, has shown that Tambora's deposit is among the largest of the last two thousand years in both Greenland and Antarctic cores. Her models suggest that average global temperatures fell by between 0.4 and 0.7 degrees Celsius. This modest-sounding figure helps to explain why the eruption's role went unnoticed for so long, but it is also misleading. An average of this kind conceals striking regional extremes: in parts of central Europe, summer temperatures in 1816 were several degrees below normal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that Tambora did not act alone. Ice cores record another large eruption around 1809, whose source has never been identified, and the decade that followed was already one of the coldest in several centuries. The sun, too, was unusually quiet during these years, a period of reduced activity known as the Dalton Minimum. Ruben Aldecoa-Urrutia, a solar physicist at the Valparaíso Institute of Astronomy, argues that this weak sun had already pushed temperatures downwards before 1815, so that Tambora struck a climate that was primed for cold. Vasstrand counters that changes in solar output at the time were too small to explain more than a fraction of the cooling. On balance, the evidence favours Vasstrand, but Aldecoa-Urrutia is surely correct that the eruption cannot sensibly be studied in isolation from the conditions that preceded it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The human toll is more complicated still. Chidinma Onwuachi, an economic historian at the Accra Centre for Historical Demography, points out that 1816 came only a year after the end of the Napoleonic Wars. Europe was crowded with demobilised soldiers, public finances were exhausted, and several states responded to poor harvests by banning grain exports, which drove prices even higher across their borders. Comparing regional records, Onwuachi found that areas served by well-functioning grain markets endured steep prices but relatively few deaths, whereas parts of Switzerland and southern Germany, cut off from imports, saw mortality rise sharply. In her phrase, the weather pulled the trigger, but poverty and politics had loaded the gun. This distinction between a natural shock and the vulnerability of the society it strikes is perhaps the most valuable insight to have emerged from recent scholarship.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Most accounts of 1816 remain stubbornly European, a bias that Tatsuo Kirihara, a historical geographer at Kyushu Coastal University, has set out to correct. Drawing on provincial chronicles, he has documented three consecutive years of failed rice harvests and famine in Yunnan, in south-western China, and has linked a disrupted monsoon in Bengal to the emergence of a virulent strain of cholera that later spread across Asia and beyond. Kirihara contends that the worst suffering caused by the eruption probably occurred in Asia rather than Europe. His argument is plausible, but it is extremely difficult to test, since population records for these regions in this period are fragmentary. The connection with cholera, in particular, remains speculative: outbreaks of the disease had occurred in Bengal long before 1815.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The eruption has also been credited with reshaping the map of North America. Lucja Wierzbowska, a historian of migration at the Baltic Institute of Social History, has traced a surge in departures from Vermont and Maine to the Ohio valley in 1817, which she attributes largely to the crop failures of the previous year. The timing is certainly suggestive. However, the westward movement of New England farmers had begun decades earlier, driven by exhausted soils and cheap land on the frontier, so the cold summer seems more likely to have hastened an existing trend than to have started a new one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be concluded from the events of 1816? Eruptions on Tambora's scale are thought to occur only once or twice in a thousand years, and it is tempting to assume that a modern, globally connected food system would absorb such a shock with ease. That assumption may be complacent. Today, a large proportion of the world's grain is produced in a handful of regions, and simultaneous failures there could strain international markets severely. The deeper lesson of the year without a summer is less about volcanoes than about the societies they affect: nature supplies the shock, but it is human arrangements that determine how much it costs.

topic: dating and attributing past eruptions from sulphate and tephra in polar ice cores
title: Reading the Ice
subtitle: Layers of ancient snow have become the leading archive of past eruptions, but the archive is harder to read than it looks

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each year, the snow that falls on the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica traps a little of the atmosphere in which it formed. Buried and compressed by later snowfall, these layers turn to ice, building up an archive that in places stretches back hundreds of thousands of years. Among the most valuable things this archive preserves is a record of volcanic eruptions. When a large eruption sends sulphur gas into the stratosphere, the resulting sulphate gradually settles out over the polar regions, leaving a distinct spike of acidity in that year's snow. For historians of climate, these spikes have become indispensable. Yet the apparent precision of the ice-core record can be deceptive, and the methods used to interpret it deserve closer scrutiny than they generally receive outside the specialist literature.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first task is dating. Because summer and winter snow differ in their chemistry and dust content, the layers can, in principle, be counted like the rings of a tree. Near the surface this works well. Deeper down, however, the weight of overlying ice squeezes the layers until they become extremely thin, and two years may merge into what looks like one. Small errors of this kind accumulate, so that a chronology which is accurate to within a year for recent centuries may have drifted by a decade or more two thousand years back. For a long time, researchers tried to limit this drift by anchoring their counts to eruptions known from written history, the most famous being the destruction of Pompeii by Vesuvius in AD 79.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The weakness of that approach was exposed by an unexpected source of evidence. Some time around AD 774, an intense burst of radiation from space struck the earth, leaving a sudden rise in radioactive carbon in tree rings and a corresponding peak of beryllium in polar ice. Since the same event is recorded in both archives, and tree rings can be dated to the exact year, it provides a fixed point against which ice chronologies can be checked. A team led by Ingrid Eikesdal at the Kvaløya Ice Laboratory used this marker to recalibrate the Greenland record and found that it had drifted by about seven years. One consequence was that the sulphate peak long attributed to Vesuvius turned out to belong to a different, unidentified eruption. The recalibration settled several long-running disputes about the timing of cold episodes, and it represents one of the genuine advances of the field in recent decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dating an eruption is not the same as identifying the volcano responsible. Sulphate is chemically identical whatever its source, so a spike in the ice reveals that an eruption occurred, but not where. The most reliable way of linking the two is through tephra: microscopic shards of volcanic glass whose chemical composition acts as a fingerprint for a particular volcano. Mateus Carvalhal, a geochemist at the Azores Volcanological Observatory, has spent much of his career matching such shards to their sources. He notes, however, that tephra particles are often scarce or absent in cores drilled far from the eruption, and he argues that without them any attribution of an ice-core signal to a named volcano amounts to little more than educated guesswork.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Where tephra is lacking, researchers often rely on a different clue. Aerosols from tropical eruptions tend to be carried by stratospheric winds towards both poles, whereas those from eruptions at high latitudes generally remain in their own hemisphere. A sulphate spike that appears simultaneously in Greenland and Antarctica is therefore usually taken to indicate a tropical source. Noor Faizabadi, an atmospheric modeller at the Lahore Institute for Climate Studies, warns that coincidence can mislead: two unrelated eruptions, one in each hemisphere and within a year of each other, would leave a pattern indistinguishable from that of a single tropical event. The danger she describes is real, but it is probably small, and for the very largest spikes the method remains robust.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The final step, estimating how much an eruption cooled the climate, introduces further uncertainty. The size of a sulphate spike is used to calculate the total quantity of sulphur released, which in turn feeds models of temperature change. But deposition on the ice is patchy: variations in wind and snowfall mean that one core may receive several times as much sulphate as another drilled only a few kilometres away. Eikesdal's group therefore recommends combining results from as many cores as possible. The advice is sound, though for many periods only a handful of cores exist, and drilling new ones is costly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these difficulties diminishes what ice cores have achieved. They have shown, for instance, that clusters of eruptions coincided with some of the most severe cold periods of the last two millennia, offering an explanation for episodes that once seemed mysterious. What does need to change is the way such findings are communicated. Popular accounts frequently present ice-core dates as if they were exact, omitting the margins of error that specialists take for granted. Making those uncertainties visible would not undermine confidence in the science; on the contrary, it would strengthen it.

topic: the mismatch between tree-ring records and climate models over volcanic cooling
title: Written in Wood
subtitle: Tree rings and computer models tell different stories about how much great eruptions cooled the planet. Which should we believe?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1257, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Lombok produced one of the largest eruptions of the past several thousand years, leaving a deposit of sulphate in polar ice greater than that of Tambora in 1815. When climate models are supplied with this sulphate record, they predict that summers across the northern hemisphere should have cooled by between one and two degrees Celsius in the years that followed. Temperature reconstructions based on tree rings, however, show a cooling of perhaps half that amount. The same discrepancy appears, to a greater or lesser degree, after almost every major eruption of the last millennium, and it has become known as the problem of the 'missing cooling'. It might be dismissed as a technical quarrel between specialists, but resolving it matters a great deal, because the models whose performance is in question are the same ones used to project the climate of the coming century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Trees growing near the northern limit of forests, or high on mountainsides, are useful thermometers because their growth is restricted mainly by summer warmth. In a warm summer they lay down a wide ring of dense wood; in a cold one the ring is narrow and light. Eszter Barsodi, who directs the Pannonian Tree-Ring Laboratory, argues that ring width is a flawed measure of sudden cold because of what she calls biological memory. A tree that has enjoyed a favourable year stores sugars in its roots and needles and draws on them the following spring, so that the effect of a single cold summer is spread over several years and its peak is flattened. Measurements of wood density, which reflect conditions in the late summer of one year only, are much less affected, and the cooling they record lies closer to the models. On this point the evidence is now strong: density is plainly the more trustworthy guide to short-lived temperature shocks.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more provocative explanation comes from Joaquim Brandão-Seixas, a dendroclimatologist at the Atlantic Forest Institute. He suggests that in exceptionally cold summers, trees at the treeline may produce almost no growth at all, leaving a ring so thin that it cannot be seen. If such missing rings go undetected, the dates assigned to later rings in that tree are shifted by a year, and when many trees are averaged together the sharp cold signal is blurred. Barsodi objects that the routine cross-checking of patterns among thousands of samples would expose any missing rings. Brandão-Seixas replies that his simulations show that misdating in only a small percentage of trees is enough to weaken the signal noticeably. The dispute remains unresolved, yet even if the hypothesis proves wrong, it has already served a purpose by prompting laboratories to re-examine collections that had not been scrutinised for decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An alternative possibility is that the fault lies not with the trees but with the models. Arvid Knutsby, an aerosol physicist at the Nordic Centre for Earth System Modelling, points out that most simulations assume that cooling increases in proportion to the amount of sulphur released. In very large eruptions, he argues, this assumption breaks down. When the stratosphere is crowded with sulphate, the tiny droplets collide and merge, forming larger particles. These fall out of the atmosphere more quickly and reflect less sunlight for their mass, so that doubling the sulphur produces considerably less than double the cooling. When his particle-growth scheme is included in a model, the predicted cooling after 1257 falls by roughly a third. The argument is persuasive because it rests on well-established physics, but it has a clear limitation: it cannot account for the mismatch after moderate eruptions, where particle growth should be insignificant.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the quality of the light reaching the trees. Selin Arıkan, a plant physiologist at the Anatolian Centre for Ecosystem Research, notes that volcanic haze scatters sunlight, increasing the proportion of diffuse light, which penetrates forest canopies more effectively than direct sunshine. Leaves that would normally sit in shade therefore photosynthesise more, partly offsetting the effect of lower temperatures on growth. If she is right, tree rings would systematically understate post-eruption cooling. The idea is intriguing, but the supporting measurements come largely from dense temperate forests studied after the eruption of Pinatubo in 1991, and it is far from clear that they apply to the scattered conifers at the treeline on which most temperature reconstructions depend.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In recent years the gap has narrowed. Reconstructions that rely on density rather than width, that have been checked for missing rings and that are compared with models incorporating particle growth now agree for most eruptions within their stated margins of error. It would nevertheless be premature to declare the problem solved. For the very largest events, including that of 1257, a significant difference remains. More troubling is the manner in which agreement has been reached: tree-ring specialists and modellers have each revised their methods partly in light of the other's results, and convergence achieved in this way carries an obvious risk of circular reasoning.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The stakes extend beyond the medieval past. Large eruptions are among the few natural experiments available for testing how quickly the climate responds to a sudden change in incoming sunlight. They are also directly relevant to proposals for deliberately injecting sulphate into the stratosphere to counter global warming: if Knutsby's physics is correct, such schemes would become less efficient the more sulphur was used. What the missing cooling debate teaches above all is humility about the confidence with which any single source of evidence, whether living or digital, can be read.

topic: the 1991 Pinatubo eruption as a natural analogue for stratospheric solar geoengineering
title: A Volcano as a Laboratory
subtitle: What can a single eruption in 1991 reveal about the risks of deliberately dimming the sun?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In June 1991, after five centuries of near silence, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted with a force unmatched anywhere on earth for decades. The explosion lifted around fifteen million tonnes of sulphur dioxide more than twenty kilometres into the stratosphere, where the gas was gradually converted into a fine haze of sulphate droplets. Carried by high-altitude winds, the haze encircled the globe within weeks and reflected a small but measurable fraction of incoming sunlight back into space. Over the following year, average surface temperatures fell by roughly half a degree Celsius. For advocates of solar geoengineering, the proposal to offset global warming by releasing reflective particles into the upper atmosphere on purpose, the eruption has since become a kind of founding text: evidence, supplied by nature itself, that the idea could work. The appeal of this argument is easy to understand, but the analogy is considerably weaker than its constant repetition suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest case for taking the comparison seriously has been made by Renske Hoogeveen, an atmospheric physicist at the Rhine Delta Institute for Climate Research. She stresses that, shortly after the eruption, a team of modellers published a forecast of the cooling it would cause, and that the temperatures later observed fell within a tenth of a degree of their prediction. In Hoogeveen's view, this demonstrates that the basic physics of stratospheric aerosols is understood well enough to support serious planning. The forecast was indeed a remarkable achievement, and it deserves more credit than sceptics usually give it. Yet predicting a global average is a very different matter from predicting what will happen in any particular region, and it is regional changes, not global ones, that determine whether harvests succeed or fail.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Here the evidence is far less comforting. Kwabena Asiedu-Frimpong, a hydrologist at the Volta Basin Water Observatory, has examined river records from the year after the eruption and found that the total volume of fresh water flowing from the continents into the oceans dropped sharply, with some of the largest declines in tropical basins. Since cooling the surface reduces evaporation from the sea, and therefore the moisture available to fall as rain, he argues that a sustained geoengineering programme could weaken the monsoons on which billions of people depend. His reasoning is plausible, though it is not the only possible explanation: an El Niño event was also under way during the period, and El Niño is known to disrupt rainfall across much of the tropics. Separating the two influences has so far proved impossible.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns time. A volcanic eruption is a pulse: most of its aerosols drift down out of the stratosphere within about two years, and the climate quickly returns to its former state. Solar geoengineering, by contrast, would require particles to be replenished continuously for decades, perhaps for more than a century. Ilkka Vuorenmaa, a climate modeller at the Boreal Centre for Earth System Science, points out that a brief disturbance cools only the upper layer of the ocean, whereas a permanent reduction in sunlight would eventually alter the deep circulation, with consequences no eruption could reveal. To my mind this argument is decisive. Pinatubo can tell us a good deal about how the climate responds quickly, and almost nothing about how it responds slowly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Chemistry adds further uncertainty. In the two years after the eruption, the ozone layer over the middle latitudes thinned noticeably, because the sulphate droplets provided surfaces on which chlorine compounds, then abundant in the atmosphere from industrial refrigerants, could destroy ozone. Amaru Ccahuana, an atmospheric chemist at the Cusco Laboratory for Atmospheric Chemistry, notes that chlorine concentrations have been falling since those refrigerants were banned, so the damage caused by deliberate injection today might be smaller. He also warns, however, that continuous release would cause droplets to merge into larger ones that reflect sunlight less efficiently and settle more rapidly. Each additional tonne of sulphur would then achieve less cooling than the one before.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some critics object less to the science than to the way the eruption is invoked. Members of the Climate Ethics Forum, a group of philosophers and social scientists based in Nairobi, argue that repeatedly describing geoengineering as an imitation of a natural event lends it an undeserved air of safety, as though anything a volcano can do must be harmless. There is something to this concern, but it is overstated. The researchers who cite Pinatubo most often are, in my experience, also the most careful to list its limitations, and it is hard to see how public debate would be improved by ignoring the only large-scale test available.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should the eruption be taken to show? It confirms that a veil of particles in the stratosphere can cool the planet, and that the size of the global effect can be predicted with some confidence. It does not show that such a veil could be maintained safely for generations, nor that its benefits and harms would be fairly shared between regions. Pinatubo is best treated not as a rehearsal for geoengineering but as a single, imperfect experiment, valuable precisely because it reminds us how much remains to be learned.

topic: the 1257 Samalas eruption and the debate over volcanic triggers of the Little Ice Age
title: The Mountain That Started an Ice Age?
subtitle: A forgotten thirteenth-century eruption has reshaped the argument over what cooled the medieval world

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For several decades, glaciologists drilling into the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica kept encountering the same puzzle. In layers dating from around 1258, both hemispheres recorded a spike in sulphate so large that it ranks among the greatest of the past two thousand years. Sulphate of this kind is the signature of a major volcanic eruption, and its presence at both poles pointed to a tropical source, since only eruptions near the equator distribute their gases efficiently into both hemispheres. Yet no historical document described such an event, and candidates proposed in Mexico, Ecuador and New Zealand were each ruled out when their deposits proved to be of the wrong age or chemistry. The 'mystery eruption' became a fixture of textbooks, an effect in search of a cause.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The cause was eventually traced to Samalas, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Lombok whose summit is now occupied by a crater lake several kilometres across. Thick layers of pumice on the island's flanks matched the chemical fingerprint of the glass shards in the polar ice, and radiocarbon dates from trees buried by the eruption placed it in the mid-thirteenth century. Ketut Wirasana, a geographer at the Rinjani Geohazard Centre, has drawn attention to a further line of evidence: chronicles written on palm leaves in the Old Javanese language, which describe the burial of a royal settlement beneath falling ash and fire. Wirasana argues that scholars of the eruption have concentrated almost entirely on its global climatic effects while neglecting the society that was obliterated by it, a criticism that seems entirely fair.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The identification of Samalas has, however, revived a much larger question: whether volcanoes were responsible for the Little Ice Age, the period of cooler conditions that affected much of the Northern Hemisphere between roughly 1300 and 1850. During these centuries Alpine glaciers advanced over farmland, the Thames in London froze over on numerous occasions, and growing seasons in Scandinavia shortened. Average temperatures across the hemisphere seem to have fallen by no more than half a degree, but in a pre-industrial economy even modest cooling could mean repeated harvest failures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficulty for any volcanic explanation is one of timing. The aerosols produced by an eruption remain in the stratosphere for only two or three years, whereas the Little Ice Age lasted for centuries. Ásdís Hrafnkelsdóttir, who leads the North Atlantic Climate Dynamics Group, believes she has resolved this paradox. Samalas, she points out, was not an isolated event but the first of four large eruptions within roughly thirty years. In her simulations, the repeated cooling allowed Arctic sea ice to spread further each winter, and because ice reflects more sunlight than open water, the extra ice preserved the cold that had created it. Some of the ice drifted south into the North Atlantic and melted, leaving a layer of fresher, lighter water at the surface that weakened the ocean currents carrying heat northwards. Once established, she argues, this arrangement could persist for centuries without further volcanic assistance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Her case draws support from an unusual source. On Baffin Island in the Canadian Arctic, small ice caps that are now retreating have exposed mosses that were killed when the ice first advanced over them. Radiocarbon dating shows that a large proportion of these plants died within a few decades of 1275, suggesting an abrupt onset of cold rather than a gradual decline. Hrafnkelsdóttir's model is elegant, and the Baffin evidence is striking, but it should be remembered that the feedback she describes has been reproduced convincingly only in simulations; whether the real ocean behaved in the same way remains extremely difficult to test.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all specialists accept that volcanoes deserve the leading role. Tiberiu Lupsoreanu, a solar physicist at the Bucegi Solar Observatory, points to a sequence of prolonged lows in sunspot activity that coincided with the coldest phases of the period, the best known of which lasted from about 1645 to 1715. The reduction in solar output during these lows was tiny, perhaps a tenth of one per cent, but Lupsoreanu maintains that its effect was magnified through changes in stratospheric ozone that altered wind patterns over Europe. Most modelling studies nonetheless find the solar contribution to be smaller than the volcanic one, and on present evidence Lupsoreanu's position looks difficult to sustain as anything more than a secondary influence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A different challenge comes from historians. Dorottya Bárándy, who studies medieval European weather records at the Szeged Centre for Historical Climatology, notes that documentary sources from 1258 and 1259 describe poor weather and famine in some regions but entirely ordinary conditions in others. She warns that once a dramatic cause has been identified, there is a temptation to attribute every misfortune of the following years to it. Her caution extends to the term 'Little Ice Age' itself, which she regards as misleading because the coldest decades arrived at different times in different places.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: On this last point, Bárándy is surely right. The evidence now points to a period of unstable climate in which volcanic eruptions, a weaker sun and the internal rhythms of the ocean all played a part, their relative importance varying from region to region. Samalas may well have set the process in motion. But to call it the cause of the Little Ice Age would be to replace one oversimplification with another.
