topic: the volcanic climate shock of 536 CE and how far it explains sixth-century social crises
title: The Darkened Sun of 536
subtitle: Historians and scientists disagree over how much a sixth-century climate shock changed the course of history

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the year 536, writers on opposite sides of the known world recorded something strange. A Byzantine official in Constantinople complained that the sun gave out its light without brightness, like the moon, for more than a year. Irish monastic annals noted a failure of bread, and chronicles in China described snow falling in late summer. For a long time, historians treated such reports with suspicion, assuming that chroniclers had exaggerated a few bad seasons or borrowed apocalyptic language from religious texts. That suspicion now looks misplaced. Over the past three decades, natural archives have confirmed that the mid-sixth century witnessed one of the most abrupt climatic downturns of the last two millennia.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first clue came from tree rings. Oaks and pines from Ireland to Siberia laid down exceptionally thin growth rings in 536, and again in the early 540s, indicating short and cold growing seasons. Ice cores later revealed why: layers of volcanic sulphate showed that a large eruption, probably in the Northern Hemisphere, occurred in 536, and that a second, even larger one, probably in the tropics, followed around 540. Eilidh MacQuarrie, who directs the Hebridean Dendrochronology Laboratory, argues that this sequence is the key to the episode. A single eruption, she points out, cools the climate for only a few years; the damage in this case came from the second blow arriving before the first had faded. Summer temperatures in Europe in the following decade may have been two degrees lower than normal, and some researchers now speak of a 'Late Antique Little Ice Age' lasting until about 660.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to link this cooling to the other great catastrophe of the age. In 541 bubonic plague reached the Mediterranean, and over the following years it killed a large proportion of the population of the Eastern Roman Empire. Some scholars have suggested that hunger weakened people's resistance or that cooler, wetter conditions altered the behaviour of the rodents carrying the disease. These ideas are not unreasonable, but they have not been demonstrated, and it should be said plainly that the coincidence of two disasters in the same decade is not in itself evidence that one caused the other.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In some regions, by contrast, the evidence of a climate-driven crisis is hard to dismiss. Folasade Akinwumiju, an archaeologist at the Ogbomoso Centre for Comparative Archaeology, has studied pollen preserved in Swedish lake sediments. Around the middle of the sixth century, pollen from cereals and grazing plants declines sharply while that of birch and other trees returns, suggesting that farmland was left to revert to forest. Settlement surveys in the same districts indicate that as many as half of the farms may have been deserted. Akinwumiju also notes that unusually large numbers of gold objects were buried in this period, which she interprets as offerings intended to persuade the gods to restore the sun. Taken together, her findings make a persuasive case that parts of Scandinavia suffered a genuine demographic disaster.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other claims are more speculative. Yerlan Tolegenuly, a historian at the Steppe Research Centre in Almaty, argues that colder and drier conditions on the Central Asian grasslands reduced pasture for herds and pushed nomadic groups westwards, setting off movements of peoples that reached the borders of Europe within a generation. He points to archaeological signs that a number of steppe cemeteries fell out of use in the mid-sixth century, and to the sudden appearance of new groups on the frontiers of the Eastern Roman Empire during the 550s. The idea is ambitious, but it rests on a chain of inferences, from climate to grass, from grass to herds and from herds to migration, each of which is uncertain, and written sources from the steppe for this period are almost non-existent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable contribution to the debate has come from the Late Antiquity Resilience Project, a group of historians and economists who emphasise how many societies came through the crisis intact. The Eastern Roman Empire, they observe, continued to collect taxes, pay its armies and complete ambitious buildings throughout the cold decade. Even in the worst years, they add, shipments of Egyptian grain continued to reach Constantinople, cushioning the capital against failures elsewhere. In their view, what determined the impact of the downturn was not the severity of the cold itself but the capacity of institutions to respond, through grain reserves, trade networks and the ability to move food from regions that had harvested well to those that had not.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This seems to me the right lesson to draw. The events of 536 show that a volcanic shock can be devastating, but they do not show that climate alone decides the fate of societies. Where food could be stored and moved, the cold was endured; where it could not, communities were abandoned. The sixth century offers a sobering reminder that the distribution of vulnerability matters as much as the scale of the hazard. None of this diminishes the scale of what happened. It simply suggests that historians should ask not only how cold it became, but also who was in a position to absorb the loss.

topic: the Deccan Traps eruptions versus the asteroid impact as causes of the end-Cretaceous extinction
title: Fire from Below, Fire from Above
subtitle: Decades after the asteroid hypothesis won the argument, the volcanic explanation for the end of the dinosaurs refuses to go away

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the disappearance of the dinosaurs some 66 million years ago was attributed to slow changes in climate and sea level. That consensus was overturned in 1980, when a thin clay layer marking the end of the Cretaceous period was found to be enriched in iridium, an element rare in the earth's crust but common in meteorites. The subsequent discovery of a buried crater nearly two hundred kilometres wide beneath the coast of Mexico seemed to settle the matter: an asteroid had struck, and life on earth had paid the price. Yet throughout these decades a minority of geologists continued to point to another candidate, the Deccan Traps of western India, where eruptions produced lava flows that are today more than two kilometres thick in places and once covered perhaps half a million square kilometres.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Eruptions of this kind, known as large igneous provinces, are unlike anything witnessed in human history. Rather than explosive blasts from a single mountain, they consist of fissures that pour out lava for centuries at a time, repeated over hundreds of thousands of years. Their significance lies less in the lava than in the gases: carbon dioxide, which warms the climate over the long term, and sulphur dioxide, which cools it abruptly. Several of the other great extinctions in the geological record, including the largest of all at the end of the Permian period, coincide closely with eruptions of this type. That pattern, in my view, is the strongest argument for taking the Deccan seriously; it would be a remarkable coincidence if the one mass extinction that happened to coincide with an impact were the only one in which volcanoes played no part.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The debate has therefore turned on timing. Anouk Verbrugghe, a geochronologist at the Kortrijk Laboratory for Isotope Geology, has dated crystals of zircon trapped in ash beds between successive lava flows. Her results suggest that the Deccan eruptions came in four main pulses and that the largest began some tens of thousands of years before the extinction. A rival laboratory using a different dating method has concluded that most of the lava erupted after the impact. The disagreement is not trivial, but it should not be exaggerated either: both techniques now carry uncertainties of a few tens of thousands of years, which is extraordinarily precise by geological standards yet still too coarse to determine whether the volcanoes struck the first blow or the last.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ocean sediments offer another perspective. Members of the Marine Proxy Working Group, which analyses the chemistry of microscopic shells from deep-sea cores, have identified a warming of around three degrees that began roughly 150,000 years before the boundary and which they attribute to volcanic carbon dioxide. Strikingly, however, this warming was accompanied by only modest losses among marine organisms. The group concludes that the Deccan eruptions placed ecosystems under stress but did not, on their own, cause a collapse.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This conclusion is welcomed by Rafael Cuartas-Mosquera, a palaeontologist at the Magdalena Museum of Natural History, who has spent two decades collecting fossils from rock sequences in the Americas. In his sections, he says, ammonites, plankton and many other groups persist in abundance right up to the iridium layer and then vanish within it. For Cuartas-Mosquera, an extinction so sudden can only have had a sudden cause. The objection carries weight, but it addresses only the final act. A sudden death does not rule out the possibility that ecosystems had already been weakened, in the way that a storm brings down more easily a forest already thinned by drought.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Others have proposed that the two explanations are linked. Hamid Rezvanpour, a geophysicist at the Yazd Institute of Earth Dynamics, has calculated that seismic waves from the impact would have shaken the entire planet with great intensity, possibly enough to destabilise magma chambers beneath India and accelerate the eruptions already under way. The idea has obvious appeal, since it allows both camps to claim a share of the truth. That appeal, however, is precisely why it should be treated with care: a hypothesis that satisfies everyone is not thereby more likely to be correct, and the mechanism by which distant shaking could release such vast volumes of magma remains largely theoretical.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the gases themselves. Thandiwe Dlamuka, a volcanic geochemist at the Mpumalanga Centre for Volcanic Geochemistry, argues that the volume of lava is a poor guide to environmental damage, because much of the sulphur and carbon may have escaped from magma before it reached the surface, in quiet releases that left no lava flows to date. If she is right, the climatic effects of the Deccan could have been concentrated in periods that the lava record barely registers.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What emerges is less a contest between two theories than a question about how they combined. The long-running quarrel over whether an asteroid or volcanoes killed the dinosaurs has been fuelled as much by professional rivalry as by evidence, and it has arguably delayed the more interesting enquiry: how a world already stressed by volcanic warming responded to a sudden catastrophe from space. Answering that will demand dating methods even more precise than those now available, and a willingness on both sides to abandon the language of victory.

topic: measuring volcanic carbon dioxide emissions and the silicate weathering thermostat
title: The Planet's Slow Breath
subtitle: Measuring how much carbon volcanoes release has proved surprisingly hard, and the answer matters for more than one reason

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few claims about climate are repeated as confidently, or as wrongly, as the assertion that a single volcanic eruption releases more carbon dioxide than all human activity. The reality is the reverse. The best current estimates put the world's total volcanic output of carbon dioxide at somewhere between 0.3 and 0.4 billion tonnes a year, while the burning of fossil fuels and the manufacture of cement release roughly a hundred times as much. Even the largest eruption of recent decades emitted, over its entire course, less carbon dioxide than human activity produces in a few hours. That such a misconception persists says something about how vividly people perceive eruptions compared with the invisible emissions of everyday life, but it is not the most interesting aspect of the subject. The more searching question is why scientists themselves have found it so difficult to agree on how much carbon volcanoes release.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty begins with the gas itself. Carbon dioxide is already abundant in the atmosphere, so a volcanic plume adds only a small amount to an enormous background, and measuring that increment is rather like trying to pick out a single extra voice in a stadium crowd. For many years, global estimates were extrapolated from a handful of easily accessible volcanoes, most of them in wealthy countries. Itziar Larrañaga, a volcanologist at the Donostia Laboratory for Volcanic Gas Studies, has led a campaign to change this by flying small drones carrying gas sensors directly through plumes at remote volcanoes in Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and the Andes. Her measurements show that a small number of persistently active volcanoes, rather than occasional large eruptions, account for most of the carbon released from volcanic vents. She argues that targeting these few emitters would improve global estimates more than any other single step, and her results so far bear that out.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all volcanic carbon emerges from craters. Oğuzhan Tekeli, a geochemist at the Anatolian Rift Observatory, has spent a decade measuring gas seeping quietly from soils, springs and fractures along continental rifts, where the earth's crust is being pulled apart. In parts of the East African Rift, he has found that carbon escaping through the ground over thousands of square kilometres rivals the output of active volcanoes. Tekeli maintains that because such diffuse emissions have been almost entirely ignored, the global volcanic total may have been underestimated by as much as half. This is an important finding for geologists, but it does nothing to rescue the popular claim with which this article began: even doubling the volcanic figure would leave it a tiny fraction of human emissions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The greatest uncertainty lies beneath the sea. Most of the earth's volcanic activity takes place along the mid-ocean ridges, where new crust is formed, and on thousands of submarine volcanoes that have never been visited. Siosaia Fonua, a marine geologist at the Pacific Seafloor Institute in Nuku'alofa, notes that carbon released at the ridges dissolves into seawater rather than entering the air, and so cannot be measured with instruments designed for plumes. Estimates instead rely on analysing the gas content of glass formed when lava is quenched by cold water, a method that she regards as useful but prone to large errors. The problem is compounded by variety: some ridges spread slowly and erupt only rarely, while others are almost continuously active, so sampling a few sites reveals little about the rest. Her view is that the submarine contribution will be known only to within a factor of two or three for the foreseeable future, an assessment that seems, if anything, a little optimistic.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why should any of this matter, if volcanoes are so minor a source compared with human activity? The answer lies in geological time. Over millions of years, the carbon released by volcanoes is removed from the atmosphere mainly by the chemical weathering of rocks, as rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide breaks down silicate minerals and carries the products to the sea, where they are eventually locked into limestone. Because weathering speeds up in a warmer, wetter climate and slows in a cooler one, the process acts as a natural thermostat. Researchers in the Deep Carbon Accounting Initiative argue that this balance explains why the earth has remained habitable for billions of years, and that the rate of volcanic outgassing is therefore one of the key settings of the planet's long-term climate. Some commentators have taken comfort from the existence of this thermostat, suggesting that the earth will correct human disturbance unaided.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That comfort is misplaced. The weathering thermostat works, but it works on a timescale of hundreds of thousands of years; it will eventually absorb the carbon released in the industrial era, but not before many thousands of generations have lived with the consequences. If the study of volcanic carbon teaches anything, it is that the planet's natural cycles are both remarkably stable and remarkably slow. Human emissions have overwhelmed the slow breath of the earth not because they are unprecedented in kind, but because they are unprecedented in speed. Volcanoes, in other words, are not the villains of the climate story, but they are among its most revealing witnesses.

topic: volcanic eruptions, failed Nile floods and social unrest in Ptolemaic Egypt
title: When the River Failed
subtitle: Can distant volcanic eruptions help to explain hunger and rebellion in ancient Egypt?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the autumn of 44 BCE, the Nile failed to rise. Each summer, monsoon rains falling on the Ethiopian Highlands swelled the river, which spilled across the floodplain of Egypt and left behind the moisture and silt on which the country's harvests depended. When the flood was poor, fields went unwatered and granaries emptied. Contemporary accounts describe famine and disease in the years that followed, during the reign of the last Ptolemaic ruler, Cleopatra VII. For centuries such crises were explained by local factors: unusual weather, misgovernment or simple misfortune. Over the past decade, however, a different explanation has been proposed, one that traces the failure of the flood to volcanic eruptions on the other side of the world.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The argument rests on a chain of physical reasoning. Large eruptions in the Northern Hemisphere inject sulphur into the stratosphere, cooling the land more than the ocean and weakening the temperature contrast that drives the African monsoon. Less rain in the highlands means a lower flood downstream. Jonas Ellingsgaard, a palaeoclimatologist at the Limfjord Institute for Polar Research, has compared the dates of volcanic sulphate layers in Greenland ice with the Egyptian historical record. Such a comparison has only recently become possible, because volcanic signals in the ice can now be dated to within a year or two. He reports that in the years following major eruptions, documents mentioning poor floods, tax relief and unrest become markedly more frequent. A large eruption in Alaska in 43 BCE, he argues, helps to explain why the crisis of Cleopatra's reign was so prolonged. The statistical association he describes is impressive, and it would be perverse to dismiss it as chance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporting evidence comes from a later and better-documented period. From the seventh century CE onwards, officials in Cairo recorded the height of the Nile each year on a Nilometer, a graduated column set in a stone basin. Mwajuma Kombo, a hydrologist at the Zanzibar Centre for River Studies, has analysed more than a thousand years of these readings and found that flood levels fell, on average, in the years immediately after large tropical and northern eruptions. For Kombo, the medieval record confirms that the volcanic mechanism is a persistent feature of the region's climate rather than an artefact of ancient sources. Her analysis is the more persuasive for being based on direct measurement rather than inference from texts.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that the link to unrest is so straightforward. Hoda Abdelrazek, a papyrologist at the Alexandria Centre for Papyrus Studies, points out that the surviving documents from Ptolemaic Egypt are scattered and uneven: some decades are illuminated by thousands of texts, others by a handful. A rise in references to hardship after an eruption might therefore reflect the chance survival of papyri as much as any real change in conditions. She does not reject the volcanic hypothesis, but she insists that it be tested against the gaps in the record as well as the entries in it. This is a reasonable demand, though it should not be allowed to become an argument for doing nothing; every historical source is incomplete, and the question is whether the patterns are stronger than the gaps can account for.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second objection concerns the step from hunger to revolt. Benedek Fazakas, an economic historian at the Eger Institute for Ancient Economies, notes that Egypt had experienced poor floods throughout its history, and that earlier rulers had long maintained granaries to tide the population over lean years. Under the Ptolemies, he argues, the burden of taxation on farmers was unusually heavy, and grain was shipped abroad to finance wars and the royal court. He also points out that in years when the authorities remitted taxes after a poor flood, reports of disorder seem to have subsided. A low flood became dangerous, in his view, only because the state had reduced the margin that allowed ordinary people to absorb it. If Fazakas is right, the eruptions acted not as causes of unrest but as triggers that exposed a weakness created by policy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Field archaeology adds a third perspective. Members of the Theban Survey Team, who have mapped settlements along the edge of the floodplain in southern Egypt, have found that several villages at the margin of cultivation were abandoned during the late third century BCE, when a serious revolt broke out in the region. The team is cautious about attributing this to climate, since the villages could equally have been deserted because of fighting. Pottery collected at the abandoned sites shows no signs of burning, but the team regards this as weak evidence either way. Yet they note that settlements on the highest ground, which a weak flood would be the first to miss, were the earliest to be left.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The volcanic hypothesis, then, is best understood not as a rival to political explanations but as a complement to them. It seems clear that eruptions far from Egypt could reduce the flood, and that a reduced flood placed pressure on society. Whether that pressure led to famine or rebellion, however, depended on decisions made in Alexandria. The value of the new research lies precisely in showing how a natural shock and a political system interacted, and it would be a mistake for either historians or climate scientists to claim the story as wholly their own. Such collaboration will not always be comfortable, since the two disciplines work with very different kinds of evidence and different standards of proof.

topic: the Toba supereruption and the hypothesis of a human population bottleneck
title: After the Ash
subtitle: Did a colossal eruption 74,000 years ago bring early humans close to extinction?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: About 74,000 years ago, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumatra produced the largest eruption of the past two million years. The collapse of Toba left a crater lake some 100 kilometres long, and ash from the eruption has been found as far away as India, where in places it lies several metres deep. Fine ash also settled across the floor of the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, forming a layer that geologists use as a convenient time marker. Estimates of the volume of material ejected run to around 2,800 cubic kilometres, thousands of times more than the eruption of Mount St Helens in 1980. It is hardly surprising that so vast an event should have been linked to one of the great questions of human prehistory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the late 1990s it was proposed that Toba had triggered a 'volcanic winter' lasting several years, followed by a millennium of colder conditions, and that this had reduced the human population to a few thousand breeding adults. The idea offered an elegant explanation for a puzzle in human genetics: compared with chimpanzees, people living today are remarkably similar to one another, as if descended from a small group in the not-so-distant past. For a time the hypothesis was widely repeated in textbooks and documentaries. It is an attractive story, but the evidence gathered over the past twenty years has not been kind to it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first challenge came from climate science. Sunniva Skjeldrum, a climate modeller at the Sognefjord Centre for Earth Simulation, has run simulations of the eruption using a range of assumptions about the quantity of sulphur released. Her results suggest a global cooling of several degrees in the first year or two, but a rapid recovery thereafter, with no sign of the prolonged cold the original hypothesis required. Skjeldrum also notes that the cooling would have been most severe at high latitudes, far from the tropical regions where most humans then lived. Models are only as reliable as their inputs, and the sulphur yield of Toba remains uncertain; even so, it is difficult to construct a plausible scenario in which a single eruption cools the planet for a thousand years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Archaeology has added further doubts. Revathi Anbalagan, an archaeologist at the Kaveri Institute of Prehistory, has excavated sites in southern India where stone tools lie both beneath and above the Toba ash. The tools on either side of the layer are made in the same way and from the same kinds of stone, which she interprets as evidence that the same population remained in the area after the eruption. Critics have asked whether the tools might have been made by a different species of human, since no bones have been recovered from the sites, and Anbalagan accepts that this remains an open question. On the southern coast of Africa, meanwhile, members of the Agulhas Coast Excavation Group have identified microscopic shards of volcanic glass from Toba in cave sediments, a technique that allows the eruption's arrival to be pinned to a precise layer. They found that human activity at the site not only continued after the ash fell but actually increased, perhaps because a drier climate concentrated people and animals near the coast.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings make a global catastrophe unlikely. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that the eruption had no effect on people at all. The South African and Indian sites are both thousands of kilometres from Sumatra, and evidence that communities survived there tells us little about what happened closer to the volcano, where ash falls would have been heaviest and where very little excavation has been carried out. Regional devastation remains entirely possible, and the absence of evidence from South-East Asia should be read as a gap in knowledge rather than as reassurance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, then, of the genetic puzzle? Mateus Rocha-Bentes, a population geneticist at the Braga Centre for Human Genomics, argues that the low diversity of living humans is real but has been misinterpreted. In his view, it does not reflect a single sudden collapse but a series of smaller reductions as groups left Africa and settled new continents, each founding population carrying only part of the genetic variety of the group it came from. Supporting this, he observes that genetic diversity among living populations declines steadily with their distance from Africa, just as such a sequence of departures would predict. Methods that estimate past population sizes from genomes, he notes, show no sharp drop at the time of the eruption. This explanation fits the evidence better than the original hypothesis, although such methods are poor at detecting very short-lived declines, and a crash lasting only a few generations might escape them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever its eventual fate, the debate over Toba has been productive. It has spurred the development of techniques for finding ash layers invisible to the naked eye, which can now be used to link archaeological sites across continents with a precision that radiocarbon dating cannot achieve for this period. And it offers a useful lesson about how scientific stories gain currency: the hypothesis spread so widely not because the evidence was strong but because the narrative was so compelling.

topic: the debate over whether the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) is weakening or heading for collapse
title: The Faltering Engine?
subtitle: Scientists agree that the great overturning circulation of the Atlantic matters; they disagree sharply about what it is doing now

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every second, the Atlantic Ocean moves an immense volume of warm, salty water northward from the tropics. As it travels towards Greenland and Norway, this water gives up its heat to the atmosphere, becomes colder and denser, and eventually sinks to the depths, from where it creeps slowly back towards the south. Oceanographers call the whole system the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, usually shortened to AMOC, while popular accounts tend to describe it as a great conveyor belt. The image is memorable, but it is also misleading. The real circulation is not a single tidy loop but a shifting patchwork of wind-driven currents, swirling eddies and deep flows that split and recombine, and treating it as one machine with one switch encourages the belief that it can simply be turned off.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That belief is at the heart of current anxieties. As the climate warms, the Greenland ice sheet is shedding increasing quantities of meltwater, and rainfall over the North Atlantic is also rising. Fresh water is less dense than salt water, so its arrival at the surface makes it harder for northern waters to sink, potentially weakening the engine that drives the overturning. Almost all climate models project some decline in the AMOC over the present century. What remains fiercely disputed is whether that decline has already begun, how far it might go, and whether it could ever pass a threshold beyond which the circulation would collapse into a much weaker state.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Answering the first question ought to be straightforward, since the circulation has been measured directly for two decades. Since 2004, a line of moored instruments stretched across the subtropical Atlantic has recorded the temperature, salinity and velocity of the water from the surface to the sea floor. The record has been revealing, though not in the way many expected. Rather than a smooth trend, it shows that the strength of the flow can change dramatically from one year to the next; in one winter it fell by around a third before largely recovering, a dip that was later linked to unusual winds. For the physical oceanographer Mireille Dauphas of the Institut Littoral de Brest, this variability is precisely the problem. Twenty years of data, she argues, are simply too few to distinguish a genuine long-term decline from the natural oscillations that the ocean is known to undergo over periods of several decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others have looked further back, using indirect evidence. Rafael Ochandiano, a climate scientist at the Valdivia Centre for Ocean Studies, points to a persistent patch of the North Atlantic, south of Greenland, that has cooled over the past century while almost every other part of the world's oceans has warmed. He interprets this 'cold blob' as a fingerprint of reduced northward heat transport, and combines it with sediment cores from the sea floor, in which the size of the silt grains reflects the speed of the deep currents that deposited them, since faster flows are able to carry coarser particles. On this evidence he concludes that the circulation is weaker now than at any point in the past thousand years. His critics accept the data but question the interpretation: the cooling south of Greenland, they note, might equally be explained by changes in cloud cover or atmospheric pollution rather than by anything happening in the ocean below.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most dramatic claims, however, have come from statisticians. Tadashi Imagawa of the Hokuriku Institute for Complex Systems has applied techniques developed to study abrupt transitions in ecosystems and financial markets. Systems that are approaching a tipping point, he explains, often show characteristic warning signs: their fluctuations grow larger and they take longer to recover from disturbances. Detecting these signals in reconstructed temperature records, Imagawa has suggested that a collapse could occur as early as the middle of this century. The reasoning is ingenious, yet the confidence placed in such dates is hard to justify. The method assumes that the ocean behaves like a simple system with a single tipping point, and the temperature series on which it depends are themselves indirect estimates. That a precise year has dominated newspaper headlines says more about the appetite of the media than about the strength of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Paradoxically, one of the strongest arguments for taking collapse seriously comes from those who distrust the models most. Ilse Brønnum-Kjær, a modeller at the Faroe Bank Oceanographic Laboratory, has compared the salt transport simulated by leading climate models with observations, and found that many models move salt in a way that artificially stabilises the circulation. If she is right, the models that reassure us that collapse is unlikely this century may be underestimating how easily the AMOC could weaken. Her findings do not prove that a collapse is imminent, but they do suggest that the comforting projections should not be accepted at face value.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Faced with such conflicting evidence, it is tempting to conclude that nothing can be said until the science is settled. That would be a mistake. The consequences of a collapse would be severe: harsher winters in north-western Europe, a southward shift in the tropical rain belts on which hundreds of millions of farmers depend, and an additional rise in sea level along the north-east coast of North America. A risk of this magnitude deserves attention even if its probability is low. Yet the most valuable response is not another headline-grabbing forecast. It is the patient, unglamorous work of keeping instruments in the water for decades to come, so that future scientists have the long record that the present debate so conspicuously lacks.

topic: autonomous profiling floats and the strengths, blind spots and fragile funding of global ocean observation
title: Robots Adrift
subtitle: A fleet of drifting instruments has transformed our picture of the ocean interior, but its achievements conceal both scientific gaps and political fragility

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the closing years of the twentieth century, almost everything known about conditions beneath the surface of the open ocean came from instruments lowered over the side of research ships. Such voyages were slow and expensive, and their routes were dictated by convenience: measurements clustered along busy shipping lanes and in the calmer months of the northern summer, while the stormy Southern Ocean in winter went almost entirely unobserved. Textbook maps of temperature and salinity in the deep sea looked authoritative, but they were in truth elaborate interpolations stretched across vast empty spaces. It is no exaggeration to say that much of what oceanographers believed about the interior of the sea before 2000 rested on a remarkably thin foundation of evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That situation changed with the arrival of the autonomous profiling float. Roughly two metres long and weighing about as much as a large suitcase, a float spends most of its life drifting at a depth of around one kilometre. Every ten days it pumps oil into an external bladder to alter its buoyancy, sinks to two kilometres, and then rises slowly to the surface, recording temperature and salinity as it ascends. Once at the surface it relays its readings by satellite and descends again. Some four thousand floats are now operating at any one time, spread across the world's oceans at intervals of a few hundred kilometres, and each profile costs a small fraction of the equivalent ship-based measurement. Ships have not become redundant, however; they remain indispensable both for deploying floats and for the precise reference measurements against which float sensors are checked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The scientific dividends have been considerable. Henrike Albersmeyer, a physical oceanographer at the Kattegat Marine Institute, argues that floats have settled what was once a contentious question: where the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases actually goes. Float records show that the great majority of it has been absorbed by the ocean rather than the atmosphere, and Albersmeyer contends that the record is now long enough to reveal a warming trend in the upper two kilometres beyond reasonable doubt. Her assessment that this is the programme's single greatest achievement is difficult to dispute. Even so, it is worth remembering that the early years of the record had to be corrected after a batch of floats was found to carry faulty pressure sensors, an episode which demonstrates that a large and well-run observing system is not thereby immune from error.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other shortcomings are built into the design. Because floats cannot be steered, their positions depend entirely on the currents that carry them. They are swept rapidly out of fast-moving regions and tend to accumulate in places where surface waters converge, so that sampling is densest exactly where the ocean is least dynamic. Floats also avoid shallow continental shelves, where they risk running aground, and in polar seas they cannot reach the surface while it is covered by ice, though newer models can store their data until open water returns. Joaquín Larrañeta of the Cantabrian Oceanographic Centre regards the first of these weaknesses as the most serious. The narrow boundary currents along the western edges of ocean basins carry a disproportionate share of the heat moved by the sea, he points out, yet floats pass through them so quickly that they are scarcely measured. He advocates supplementing the array with gliders, which can be piloted remotely to hold a position.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second gap lies in the depths. Standard floats descend no further than two kilometres, leaving roughly half the volume of the ocean unmonitored. Thandeka Ntshingila, who leads a deep-ocean research group at the Agulhas Institute of Marine Science, has assembled evidence that the abyssal waters around Antarctica are warming measurably, and that this warming expands the water enough to make a meaningful contribution to sea-level rise. In her view, extending the array to the sea floor, using floats rated to six kilometres, should be the programme's highest priority. The difficulty is cost: a deep float is several times more expensive than a standard one, and its pressure housing must withstand forces that would crush conventional designs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Pyotr Volnyansky, a chemical oceanographer at the Barents Sea Research Station, makes a competing case. He argues that the most urgent questions now concern the chemistry and biology of the ocean rather than its temperature, and that adding sensors for oxygen, nitrate, acidity and chlorophyll to existing floats is the cheapest way to track the loss of oxygen and the gradual acidification of seawater. He acknowledges that such sensors drift over time and need careful correction. Presented as a straight contest between depth and chemistry, the argument is in one sense artificial, since both kinds of measurement are plainly valuable and neither replaces the other. In practice, though, the choice is real enough, because the budgets that sustain the array have barely grown in a decade.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Indeed, the greatest threat to the system may be financial rather than technical. The array is maintained by voluntary contributions from around thirty countries, with no binding international agreement to guarantee its future, and a decision by a single major contributor to cut its funding could open large holes in coverage within a few years, as floats reach the end of their working lives and are not replaced. Weather stations and meteorological satellites are generally treated as essential public infrastructure, funded year after year without serious debate. Observations of the ocean deserve the same status, not least because the forecasts and climate projections on which governments depend increasingly rely on them.

topic: lost cargo, drift bottles and beachcombing as accidental evidence for mapping surface ocean currents
title: Messages from the Tide Line
subtitle: What can objects lost at sea tell scientists about the movement of the ocean's surface?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, storms knock hundreds of shipping containers off the decks of cargo vessels. Most sink, but some burst open and release their contents into the sea: plastic toys, trainers, ice-hockey gloves and countless other floating goods. Months or years later, these objects begin to appear on beaches, sometimes thousands of kilometres from the place where they were lost. For oceanographers, such accidents amount to unplanned experiments in the movement of the sea surface, and a few of them have become famous. They are genuinely useful, but the enthusiasm of popular accounts, which sometimes suggest that a container of bath toys rewrote our understanding of the Pacific, goes well beyond what the evidence supports.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scientific appeal of a drifting object is easy to explain. An instrument fixed to the sea floor records the water flowing past a single point, whereas an object carried by the sea reveals the route that a parcel of water actually follows, summed over weeks or months. Long before the age of container shipping, scientists exploited this principle deliberately. During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, hundreds of thousands of sealed bottles were thrown overboard, each holding a printed card that asked the finder to record where and when it had been found and to return it. Recovery rates were low: typically fewer than one bottle in ten was ever reported, and many of those had spent unknown periods lying on a beach before discovery.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kazimierz Wierzbołowicz, a modeller at the Baltic Institute of Ocean Physics, has made the most systematic use of accidental spills. He ran a computer simulation of surface currents in the North Pacific and compared its predictions with the dates and places at which spilled consumer goods came ashore. The model reproduced many arrival times to within a few months. Wierzbołowicz argues that the real worth of such spills lies in their duration. Instruments built for the purpose, he notes, seldom survive more than a year or two at sea, whereas a durable plastic object may circulate for over a decade, allowing a model to be tested across an entire ocean basin.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is, however, a serious complication. An object that floats high in the water catches the wind as well as the current, a property known as windage. A hollow toy bobbing on the surface will be driven by the breeze far more than a waterlogged shoe that floats almost submerged. Lieselotte Vanbrabant of the Scheldt Coastal Research Unit maintains that, because the proportion of wind and current in any object's track is unknown, spilled goods can tell us very little about currents as such. Only purpose-built drifters fitted with drogues, submerged fabric sails that anchor them to the moving water, provide reliable data, she argues. Her caution is reasonable but overstated. When a single spill releases several kinds of object with different shapes, their contrasting paths can be compared, and the effect of the wind can then be estimated rather than merely guessed at.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty concerns the people who find the objects. Amaru Quispecahua coordinates a network of volunteer beachcombers along the Pacific coast of South America who log and photograph everything they find. He freely admits that their records are uneven. Finds are concentrated on beaches near towns and roads, and they cluster after winter storms, when more debris is thrown ashore and more people go looking for it. A remote stretch of coastline with no reports may simply be a coastline that nobody visits. Nevertheless, Quispecahua contends that volunteers patrol thousands of kilometres of shore that no funded research programme could ever hope to survey, and that patchy coverage is far better than none.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recently, interest in drifting objects has shifted from physics to biology. The Kermadec Drift Collective, a group of marine ecologists working across several Pacific island nations, has used drift records to show that floating plastic serves as a raft for barnacles, crabs, molluscs and other organisms, carrying them to coasts they could never otherwise reach. Because plastic lasts far longer than the driftwood and seaweed on which such creatures once travelled, it may be greatly increasing the number of species that cross oceans. This change of emphasis is, to my mind, the most significant development in the field, since it turns a curiosity of oceanography into a question with real consequences for coastal ecosystems.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Today, satellites measure the height of the sea surface precisely enough to calculate currents across the whole globe, and purpose-built drifters report their positions every hour. It might seem, therefore, that accidental drifters have had their day. Yet they continue to offer something that the newer methods do not: long journeys recorded at almost no cost. They should be treated as a supplement to proper instruments rather than as a substitute for them. Perhaps their most lasting contribution, though, is a simple one. By turning up on distant shores, they remind us that the world's coastlines are connected by the sea far more quickly and closely than intuition suggests.

topic: mesoscale ocean eddies: their discovery, their physical and biological roles, and the problem of representing them in climate models
title: The Ocean's Weather
subtitle: Swirling eddies were once dismissed as noise in oceanographic records; they now appear to shape the behaviour of entire ocean basins

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the circulation of the ocean was pictured as a set of broad, sluggish gyres: vast rotating systems that turned slowly and steadily across entire basins. Measurements that did not fit this picture were usually attributed to faulty instruments or local disturbances. That view began to unravel in the early 1970s, when a large multinational survey moored dozens of current meters in the western North Atlantic for several months. The instruments revealed an ocean filled with swirling vortices, typically between fifty and two hundred kilometres across, drifting and spinning for weeks or months at a time. More startling still, the kinetic energy contained in these eddies was found to exceed that of the mean currents many times over. The ocean, it turned out, has weather of its own, and the tidy gyres of the textbooks were merely its long-term average.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Satellites later confirmed how widespread eddies are. Because the water in a rotating eddy piles up or sags slightly, an eddy shows up as a bump or a hollow of a few tens of centimetres in the height of the sea surface, which radar altimeters orbiting the earth can measure with remarkable precision. Since the 1990s, tens of thousands of eddies have been identified and tracked in this way. Many travel westward at a few kilometres per day, and the most persistent survive for more than two years. Some of the best known are the rings that break away from the current flowing south along the coast of Africa, near its southern tip. Each ring encloses a lens of warm, salty water from the Indian Ocean and carries it into the South Atlantic, a leakage that may influence the overturning circulation of the Atlantic as a whole.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The physical importance of eddies goes beyond such transfers. Sigrún Þorgrímsdóttir of the Reykjanes Institute for Ocean Dynamics has studied the Southern Ocean, where the westerly winds encircling Antarctica have strengthened over recent decades. Most climate models of an earlier generation predicted that stronger winds would intensify the overturning circulation there. Observations suggested that it had changed far less than expected, and Þorgrímsdóttir attributes the discrepancy to eddies: as the winds strengthened, the eddy field became more energetic, and the eddies transported water in a direction that largely cancelled the extra wind-driven flow. If she is correct, a process absent from many models acts as a powerful brake on one of the ocean's responses to climate change.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Eddies matter for living things too. Obiora Nwankpa-Eze, a biological oceanographer at the Niger Delta Marine Laboratory, has shown that eddies rotating in one direction draw cold water rich in nutrients upward towards the sunlit surface layer, where it can fuel dense blooms of phytoplankton in otherwise barren waters. Eddies rotating in the opposite direction tend to push surface water downward, starving the surface of nutrients. Eddies can also trap fish larvae and other drifting organisms and carry them hundreds of kilometres from where they were spawned. Predators have learned to exploit these structures: satellite-tagged tuna and seabirds concentrate their feeding along the edges of eddies, where prey is gathered by converging water, rather than in their centres.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These discoveries pose an awkward problem for climate modelling. Most models used for long-term projections divide the ocean into grid cells roughly one hundred kilometres wide, too coarse to represent eddies directly. Instead, their combined effect is approximated by simplified formulas, a technique known as parameterisation. Valentina Kostadinova, a modeller at the Black Sea Centre for Climate Simulation, argues that this compromise is no longer acceptable. When she reran simulations with cells a tenth of the size, fine enough to resolve eddies, features such as the point at which the Gulf Stream leaves the American coast shifted substantially, and with them the projected pattern of warming. Coarse models, she concludes, may be adequate for global averages but cannot be trusted for the regional projections that governments increasingly want. The obstacle is cost: halving the size of the grid cells multiplies the computing time required by roughly ten.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mateus Bettencourt-Sarmento of the Azores Laboratory of Earth System Science accepts Kostadinova's results but draws a different conclusion. He argues that parameterisations can be greatly improved by training them, using machine-learning techniques, on the output of short high-resolution simulations, so that a coarse model learns to behave much like a fine one at a fraction of the computational price. Moreover, he contends, running many coarse simulations with slightly different starting conditions reveals the range of possible futures far better than a single expensive high-resolution run, which may give a misleading impression of precision. Several modelling centres are now experimenting with this approach, although none has yet used it for official projections.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Both positions have merit, and the choice between them is partly a matter of what questions models are expected to answer. What neither side can escape, however, is the scarcity of observations below the surface. Satellites see only the surface signature of an eddy; its vertical structure, which determines how much heat and how many nutrients it carries, is known from a relatively small number of ship surveys and floats that happened to pass through. Until eddies are measured as thoroughly at depth as they are at the surface, any model, whether coarse or fine, will rest on assumptions that cannot be fully tested, and the debate between the two camps is unlikely to be resolved.

topic: coastal upwelling systems, their fisheries and the dispute over how climate change will alter them
title: Where the Deep Rises
subtitle: A handful of narrow coastal strips feed a large part of the world. Will a warming climate strengthen them or undermine them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Along the western coasts of the Americas and Africa lie four narrow bands of ocean that punch far above their weight. Off California, Peru and Chile, north-west Africa and south-west Africa, steady winds blow along the shore towards the equator. Combined with the effect of the earth's rotation, these winds push the surface water offshore, and it is replaced by cold water welling up from below, laden with nutrients that have accumulated in the dark depths. The result is an explosion of plankton, and of the fish that feed on it. Together these upwelling systems occupy less than two per cent of the ocean's surface, yet they yield roughly a fifth of the world's wild-caught fish. They are arguably the most productive marine ecosystems on the planet, and how they respond to a changing climate is one of the weightiest questions in oceanography.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Their productivity has always been precarious. Off Peru, where a small fish called the anchoveta once supported the largest single-species fishery in the world, the periodic warming known as El Niño weakens the winds and spreads a layer of warm, nutrient-poor water across the coast. In the early 1970s, a strong El Niño coincided with record catches, and the fishery collapsed spectacularly, taking decades to return to anything like its former size. This episode is still widely described as a natural disaster, but that account lets the fishing industry off far too lightly. The fish population had already been depleted by years of intensive fishing; the warming merely delivered the final blow to a stock that had lost its capacity to recover.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Over the longer term, a more intriguing possibility has been raised. In the 1990s, it was proposed that global warming might actually intensify upwelling. Because land heats up faster than the sea, the argument runs, the difference in air pressure between continent and ocean will grow, driving stronger winds along the coast and therefore lifting more deep water to the surface. Paloma Etcheverry-Rojas, a physical oceanographer at the Instituto del Mar de Paracas, believes the evidence is now accumulating in favour of this idea. Wind records from coastal stations and ships, she reports, show that alongshore winds off Peru have strengthened over the past half-century, and sea-surface temperatures near the shore have cooled slightly even as the open ocean has warmed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards this as good news. Tendai Musarurwa, who studies the system off south-west Africa at the Walvis Bay Marine Research Centre, points out that upwelling can be too vigorous. When winds are very strong, plankton may be swept offshore before fish larvae can feed on them. More worryingly, the deep water brought to the surface is naturally low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide. Off Namibia, episodes in which oxygen almost disappears from the bottom water have become more frequent, occasionally releasing toxic gas and killing large numbers of fish and lobsters. More intense upwelling, in Musarurwa's view, could expand these lifeless zones and expose shellfish to increasingly acidic water.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Khalid Benjelloun-Tazi of the Atlantic Institute of Fisheries Science in Agadir urges caution of a different kind. In the system off north-west Africa that he studies, the evidence is mixed: winds have intensified in some areas but weakened in others. He also notes a countervailing process. As the surface ocean warms, it becomes more strongly layered, with a warm, light upper layer sitting on top of colder, denser water, and this makes it harder for winds to bring deep water upward, even if they blow harder. For Benjelloun-Tazi, each upwelling system has its own geography and its own balance of forces, and any global generalisation about their future is premature.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third possibility comes from computer simulations. Annika Vesterlund-Holm, a climate modeller at the Gothenburg Centre for Marine Futures, finds that in most models the zones of strongest upwelling migrate towards the poles, intensifying at their high-latitude ends and weakening nearer the equator. Fish populations would follow, crossing the maritime boundaries between countries. Fleets that have depended on a stock for generations could find it moving into a neighbour's waters, a recipe for conflict. This, rather than the remaining scientific uncertainty, strikes me as the most pressing aspect of the problem. Scientists may disagree about the details, but the institutions needed to share migrating stocks fairly scarcely exist.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Given how much remains unknown, the sensible response is to manage these fisheries in a way that can adjust quickly to changing conditions. Peru offers an instructive example. Its authorities now survey the anchoveta stock regularly and close the fishery at short notice when the proportion of young fish in catches rises, protecting the next generation from being caught before it can breed. Such responsive management is demanding and sometimes unpopular with fishing communities, but it deserves to be adopted far more widely. Whatever the future holds for the winds, the lesson of the 1970s is that the greatest danger lies in fishing a stock as though conditions will never change.

topic: internal waves, deep-ocean mixing and the 'missing mixing' problem in the return of deep water to the surface
title: Waves Beneath the Surface
subtitle: Invisible to sailors, the ocean's internal waves may hold the key to how its deepest waters find their way back to the light

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Beneath the calm surface of the open ocean, waves far larger than any storm breaker rise and fall unseen. These internal waves travel along the boundaries between layers of water of different density, and because the density contrast between such layers is tiny compared with that between water and air, they can reach heights of two hundred metres while producing barely a ripple above. They are now understood to lie at the heart of one of the great unresolved puzzles of physical oceanography. Cold, dense water sinks near the poles and spreads slowly through the abyss; for the circulation to continue, that water must eventually be made lighter and returned to the surface. Without some process to achieve this, the deep basins would gradually fill with frigid water, and the overturning circulation that redistributes heat around the planet would grind to a halt. Explaining where and how the return journey happens is arguably among the most consequential questions that climate science has yet to answer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The process responsible is thought to be mixing, in which turbulence blends dense deep water with the lighter water above it. The energy for this turbulence comes largely from two sources: the tides, which drag water back and forth across ridges and seamounts and in doing so generate internal tides, and the wind, which sets the upper ocean oscillating. Internal waves can carry this energy for thousands of kilometres before they steepen and break. Yet when researchers first lowered free-falling microstructure profilers, instruments sensitive enough to detect centimetre-scale fluctuations in temperature and velocity, into the open ocean, they found mixing roughly ten times weaker than the circulation seemed to require. Because the profilers must be deployed from research vessels, each survey covers only a narrow strip of ocean, and some argued that the missing turbulence was simply occurring elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That suspicion was strengthened by the work of Ilse Vranckaert and her colleagues at the Flanders Institute for Marine Physics. Surveying an abyssal basin in the South Atlantic, they found that mixing over the rough flanks of a mid-ocean ridge was up to a hundred times more intense than over the smooth plains nearby. Vranckaert concluded that turbulence in the deep ocean is concentrated in hotspots above uneven terrain, which explained why earlier surveys, conducted largely over flat seafloor, had recorded so little. But the discovery created a fresh difficulty. If mixing is strongest near the seabed and weakens with height, theory implies that water in the interior above the hotspots should become denser and sink, rather than lighter and rise.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tavita Seumanutafa, a physical oceanographer at the Pacific Centre for Ocean Dynamics, has proposed an ingenious resolution. In her account, the bulk of the deep ocean does indeed sink slowly, while the upwelling the circulation requires takes place within thin boundary layers, perhaps only tens of metres deep, that hug the sloping sides of ridges and continents. Net upward flow, on this view, is the small difference between widespread descent and intense ascent at the margins. The theory is elegant, and it has the considerable merit of reconciling the hotspot observations with the need for deep water to return to the surface. It would be premature, however, to treat it as established. The direct evidence so far consists of a handful of experiments in which dye was released near the seabed and tracked for several months, and the number of sites examined is too small to support conclusions about the ocean as a whole.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different challenge comes from Rafael Uribarren of the Andean Institute of Oceanography, who argues that mixing has been asked to do more than its share. Around Antarctica, he points out, strong westerly winds drive surface water northwards, and deep water rises along steeply tilted density surfaces to replace it, with comparatively little mixing involved. On his estimate, this wind-driven route returns the greater part of the deep water formed in the North Atlantic. Supporters of the mixing and wind-driven explanations have tended to present them as rival theories, but the opposition is largely artificial. Both mechanisms almost certainly operate, and the more useful question is how their relative contributions vary between ocean basins.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These debates are not merely academic. Global climate models cannot resolve internal waves directly, so most represent mixing with a single fixed coefficient applied across vast regions. Marit Skjeldrup, a modeller at the Nordic Climate Modelling Consortium, has shown that when this constant is replaced with a pattern that varies according to the roughness of the seafloor, simulations produce noticeably different rates of ocean heat uptake and a different strength of overturning. She is now combining satellite measurements of tidal energy loss with data from autonomous floats in an attempt to build a global map of mixing. Given what is now known, the continued reliance on a uniform value is difficult to defend, whatever its convenience.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have gone further, suggesting that during the ice ages, when sea levels were more than a hundred metres lower, tidal energy that is now dissipated in shallow coastal seas would have been diverted into the deep ocean, intensifying mixing there. The idea is intriguing, but it rests on reconstructions of ancient tides that carry very large uncertainties. What the internal-wave story demonstrates more clearly is how processes occurring at the scale of centimetres can govern circulation at the scale of ocean basins. Progress will depend less on ever more sophisticated models than on the patient, expensive business of measuring the deep ocean directly, an activity that rarely attracts the funding it deserves.

topic: the history of tide prediction, from local rules of thumb to harmonic analysis and tide-predicting machines, and the problem of changing tides
title: Tides of Reckoning
subtitle: How sailors, mathematicians and machines learned to forecast the rise and fall of the sea, and why the task is not yet finished

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the motions of the sea, the tides are the most regular, and for that reason they were among the first natural phenomena that people attempted to forecast. A ship entering a shallow estuary needed to know not merely that the water would rise, but by how much and at what hour, since an error of half a metre could mean grounding on a sandbank. Yet regularity is not the same as simplicity. The tide at any given harbour is shaped by the shifting positions of the moon and sun, by the outline of the coast and by the depth of the surrounding sea, so that two ports only a few dozen kilometres apart may experience strikingly different patterns. The history of tide prediction is therefore the story of how a phenomenon that anyone could observe proved remarkably difficult to calculate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Until the nineteenth century, most tide tables were produced by local experts using rules of thumb. A harbour master might note that high water arrived a fixed interval after the moon crossed the meridian, and adjust that interval through the month according to long experience. Some of these methods were surprisingly accurate, and the families who devised them often guarded them closely, selling printed tables for profit while revealing nothing of how the figures were obtained. The drawback was that each method applied only to the port for which it had been developed; it could not be transferred elsewhere, and when the experienced practitioner died, the knowledge frequently died too.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The breakthrough came with harmonic analysis, a technique that treats the tide as the sum of many simple, regular oscillations, each linked to a particular astronomical cycle. Once a year or more of observations had been collected at a port, mathematicians could work out the size and timing of each component and then add them together to forecast the tide indefinitely into the future. The arithmetic, however, was formidable. To ease the burden, engineers in the 1870s built tide-predicting machines: cabinets of gears and pulleys in which each wheel represented one component, while a wire running over the pulleys traced the combined curve onto a roll of paper. A machine of this kind could produce a whole year of predictions for a port in a few hours.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These devices have long been celebrated as triumphs of Victorian ingenuity, but the historian Ottilie Klaverstijn of the Leiden Centre for the History of Navigation believes their importance has been exaggerated. In her view, the accuracy of the predictions depended overwhelmingly on the quality and length of the observations fed into them; the machines merely speeded up a calculation that skilled clerks could already perform. There is some truth in this, though it underestimates the effect of speed itself. Before the machines existed, few authorities could afford to compute tables for more than a handful of major ports, whereas afterwards predictions for hundreds of harbours became routine.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Kwame Ofosuhene, of the Gold Coast Institute of Maritime History, draws attention to a different neglected group: the human computers, many of them young women, who analysed tidal records by hand before the machines could be set. He also notes that the expansion of tide prediction followed the routes of empire, with tables for colonial ports compiled chiefly to serve naval and commercial shipping rather than local fishing communities. This is a valuable corrective to accounts that focus solely on the inventors, although it would be a mistake to conclude that the science was nothing more than a tool of imperial power, since the same methods were soon adopted by newly independent nations to chart their own coasts.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mechanical predictors remained in service in some countries until the 1960s, when electronic computers finally replaced them, and modern tide tables are still based on the harmonic method. That method rests on an assumption, however: that the components measured at a port remain constant over time. Lucía Goikoetxea, an oceanographer at the Cantabrian Coastal Observatory, has compared century-long records from several estuaries and found that the tidal range at some of them has increased by as much as a fifth, largely because channels were deepened to admit larger ships. Takeshi Inukai, a harbour engineer, regards such changes as manageable, arguing that tables can simply be recalculated every few years and that the errors involved are small beside the surges produced by storms. For navigation, he is probably right. For coastal flood defence, where a few centimetres can determine whether a barrier is overtopped, the argument is far less convincing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Tide prediction is often presented as one of the earliest successes of mathematical forecasting, and with justification: few other natural events can be anticipated years ahead with such precision. Yet its history also offers a warning. The method worked so well for so long that its central assumption came to be taken for granted, and only now, as harbours are reshaped and sea levels rise, is it becoming clear how much the tides themselves can change. The lesson extends beyond oceanography. Any forecast built on the patterns of the past is only as reliable as the stability of the system it describes, and that stability is precisely what human activity has begun to undermine.

topic: marine heatwaves: how to define them, their atmospheric and subsurface causes, lasting ecological damage and the limits of forecasting
title: The Ocean's Hottest Days
subtitle: Marine heatwaves have become one of the most closely watched phenomena in oceanography, but scientists still disagree about what exactly they are measuring

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the last decade, a vast expanse of unusually warm water spread across the north-east Pacific and lingered there for the better part of two years. Its effects rippled through the food web: seabirds starved in their hundreds of thousands, toxic algae forced the closure of shellfish harvests, and forests of kelp that had sheltered fish for generations thinned and disappeared. Events of this kind, now known as marine heatwaves, have moved in little more than a decade from the margins of oceanography to its centre. The usual definition is a period of at least five days during which the water is warmer than ninety per cent of previous observations for that place and time of year. It is a deliberately relative yardstick, and that choice has proved more contentious than its authors could have anticipated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that the oceans are warming steadily. Mireia Casademunt, a climatologist at the Balearic Institute of Ocean Science, points out that if the threshold is fixed to temperatures recorded in, say, the 1980s, then within a few decades many regions will be in a near-permanent state of heatwave, a result she considers meaningless. She therefore advocates removing the long-term warming trend before identifying events, so that the term continues to describe short-lived extremes. Babajide Olumuyiwa, a marine ecologist at the Gulf of Guinea Research Station, takes the opposite view. Organisms, he argues, respond to the temperature of the water around them, not to its deviation from a moving average, and a definition that adjusts to warming risks concealing exactly the harm it ought to reveal. Both arguments have force, and the dispute is less about which definition is correct than about which question is being asked: a physicist studying the causes of extremes needs one measure, an ecologist assessing damage the other.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Those causes are themselves more varied than early studies assumed. Many surface heatwaves begin when a persistent area of high atmospheric pressure calms the winds, reducing the mixing that would normally bring cooler water up from below while allowing the sun to heat a thin surface layer. Others are driven by the ocean rather than the atmosphere. Pyeon Hyun-woo and colleagues at the Tongyeong Institute of Marine Dynamics used temperature profiles from autonomous floats to show that some of the most persistent events occur well below the surface, at depths of one to two hundred metres, where warm water is carried in by shifting currents. Because satellites measure only the skin of the ocean, such subsurface heatwaves can pass entirely unnoticed, and Pyeon estimates that existing catalogues may omit a substantial proportion of them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The ecological consequences depend heavily on whether a species can move. Fish and other mobile animals often shift towards the poles or into deeper water, sometimes appearing hundreds of kilometres beyond their usual range, and may return once conditions ease. Organisms fixed to the seabed have no such option. Signe Kallaste of the Baltic Centre for Ecosystem Research has documented cases in which a single severe event killed kelp so extensively that grazing sea urchins occupied the bare rock and prevented the kelp from returning even after temperatures fell. These so-called urchin barrens have persisted at some sites for more than a decade. Kallaste concludes that the damage done by a heatwave cannot be judged by its duration, since a brief event may push an ecosystem into an alternative state from which recovery is extremely slow.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such findings have encouraged efforts to forecast heatwaves before they arrive. Seasonal prediction systems, which combine ocean observations with computer models, can now anticipate some events several months in advance, particularly where they are linked to large-scale climate patterns. In principle, this would allow fish farmers to harvest stock early or move cages to cooler water, and fishery managers to adjust catch limits before a population collapses. The progress is real, but its value should not be overstated. A forecast is useful only if those who receive it have both the authority and the means to act, and many fisheries operate under quotas that are set annually and cannot be revised at short notice.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a risk that the vivid imagery of heatwaves distracts attention from the slower, less dramatic warming on which they are superimposed. A collapse of kelp forests makes headlines; the gradual retreat of a fish stock towards the poles over thirty years rarely does. Yet the two are closely connected, since each degree of background warming makes the extremes both more frequent and more intense. Treating heatwaves as isolated disasters, to be managed through emergency responses, is therefore a mistake. They are better understood as the sharpest expression of a long-term trend, and the most effective response to them remains the reduction of the emissions that drive that trend. Better definitions, deeper observations and earlier warnings are all worth pursuing, but none of them, on its own, will make the ocean's hottest days any less frequent.
