topic: forecasting El Niño: the ocean-atmosphere mechanism, the spring predictability barrier, machine-learning forecasts and communicating uncertainty
title: Reading the Pacific's Moods
subtitle: Forty years of attempts to predict El Niño reveal both the power and the limits of climate forecasting

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years, the surface of the eastern tropical Pacific warms by several degrees, and the consequences are felt far beyond the ocean itself. This phenomenon, known as El Niño, shifts the paths of rainfall across half the globe: it tends to bring drought to Indonesia and eastern Australia, heavy rains to the coastal deserts of Peru and Ecuador, and milder winters to parts of North America. Because farmers, water authorities and insurers all stand to gain from advance warning, El Niño has become the most intensively studied mode of natural climate variability, and the attempt to forecast it is one of the oldest and most instructive projects in climate science. Its record of success and failure says a good deal about what prediction of the climate system can and cannot achieve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Under normal conditions, the trade winds blow steadily from east to west along the equator, piling warm surface water up in the western Pacific, where the sea surface stands around half a metre higher than off South America. In the east, meanwhile, cold water rises from below. An El Niño begins when the trade winds slacken. Warm water drifts back towards the east, reducing the temperature difference across the ocean that drives the winds in the first place, so the winds slacken further and yet more warm water spreads across the basin. The process, in other words, feeds on itself. Crucially, it seems to require a precondition: in the months before most events, a large store of warm water builds up beneath the surface of the western Pacific, ready to be released.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This understanding gave forecasters grounds for confidence. In the mid-1980s, a comparatively simple computer model successfully predicted an event more than a year in advance, and it was widely assumed that reliable long-range forecasts would soon be routine. In retrospect, that optimism was premature. A powerful event earlier in the decade had developed almost entirely unobserved, catching scientists by surprise, and its lesson was that no model could succeed without continuous measurements from the ocean itself. Over the following years, a network of around seventy moored buoys was installed across the equatorial Pacific, transmitting temperature and wind data by satellite every day. Yet even with this array in place, forecasts continued to fail at critical moments.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Much of the difficulty lies in what has become known as the spring predictability barrier. Forecasts issued before the northern hemisphere spring are markedly less reliable than those issued after it, regardless of the model used. Luseane Kupu, of the South Pacific Climate Centre, attributes this to the state of the ocean at that time of year, when the temperature contrast across the Pacific is at its weakest and the coupling between ocean and atmosphere is therefore loose. In these conditions, she argues, short bursts of westerly wind, essentially unpredictable weather events lasting a week or two, can tip the system towards or away from El Niño. If she is right, the barrier is a property of the climate itself, and no improvement in models will remove it entirely.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Gunnhild Rasten, a modeller at the Arctic Institute for Climate Prediction, is less pessimistic. She points out that the barrier has narrowed noticeably in models that assimilate more detailed observations of the subsurface ocean, which suggests that at least part of it reflects the limitations of the forecasting systems rather than of nature. More striking still are recent forecasts produced by machine-learning methods, which have been trained on thousands of years of simulated climate and claim useful skill up to eighteen months ahead. These results are impressive, but they deserve caution. A method trained on simulations may inherit the biases of the models that produced them, and the instrumental record contains only around two dozen El Niño events, too few to verify any claim of long-range skill with confidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even a perfect forecast of whether an event will occur would leave an important question unanswered. Ignacio Barbagelata of the Humboldt Current Research Station has drawn attention to the diversity of El Niño. In some events the strongest warming occurs near the South American coast; in others it is concentrated in the central Pacific, and the effects on rainfall can differ sharply, so that a region expecting drought may instead receive normal rains. Barbagelata suspects that global warming may be altering the balance between the two types, though he acknowledges that the observational record is too short to be sure. Predicting which kind of event will develop, not merely whether one will, is arguably the next real frontier for forecasters.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, there is the problem of communication. Forecasts are issued as probabilities, but they are frequently reported as certainties. When a widely anticipated event failed to materialise a few years ago, the resulting headlines damaged public trust in a way that the forecasters' cautious wording did nothing to prevent. Further gains in skill will undoubtedly come, but they will matter less than a clearer explanation of what a seventy per cent chance actually means. A forecast that is understood is worth more than a slightly better one that is not.

topic: ocean acoustics: the deep sound channel, acoustic thermometry, the marine-mammal controversy and earthquake-based ocean temperature measurement
title: A Thermometer Made of Sound
subtitle: Sound can cross whole ocean basins, and with it the means of measuring how fast the deep sea is warming. Why has the idea struggled to win acceptance?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Light fades within a few hundred metres of the ocean surface, and radio waves penetrate scarcely at all. Sound, by contrast, travels through seawater with remarkable ease, and under the right conditions it can cross entire ocean basins. The reason lies in the way its speed varies with depth. Near the surface, where the water is warm, sound moves relatively fast; at great depths, the immense pressure has the same effect. Between the two, typically at around a thousand metres, lies a layer where sound travels most slowly. Waves that stray upwards or downwards from this layer are bent back towards it, so that low-frequency sound becomes trapped in a natural channel and loses very little energy as it spreads. The deep sound channel was identified in the middle of the twentieth century, and for decades its principal uses were military: navies exploited it to track submarines and to locate aircraft that had come down at sea.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It was only later that oceanographers recognised its scientific potential. Because the speed of sound in seawater increases with temperature, the time a pulse takes to travel between a source and a distant receiver depends on how warm the water along its path is. Measure the travel time precisely enough, and the average temperature across thousands of kilometres can be calculated. Delphine Cazaubon, an acoustician at the Biscay Ocean Acoustics Laboratory, has long argued that this property makes acoustic thermometry uniquely valuable for monitoring climate change. A thermometer placed at a single point, she notes, is at the mercy of passing eddies and seasonal fluctuations, whereas a sound pulse automatically averages out such local disturbances, leaving the slow, basin-wide warming trend that matters most.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The method's early history was nonetheless troubled. When large-scale experiments were proposed in the 1990s, involving loud transmissions repeated over several years, they provoked fierce opposition from those who feared the sound would disturb whales, many of which communicate at similar frequencies. Aigerim Tlegenova, a marine biologist at the Caspian Institute of Marine Mammal Studies, remains firmly opposed to such transmissions. In her view, the low-frequency noise produced by commercial shipping has already risen so sharply in recent decades that any deliberate addition is indefensible. The concern for marine mammals was legitimate and deserved a hearing, but the monitoring programmes that followed found little evidence that the transmissions altered animals' behaviour in any lasting way. Tlegenova's argument also has an awkward implication. If shipping is the dominant source of underwater noise, it is shipping, rather than a handful of scientific instruments, that ought to be the focus of regulation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Acoustic thermometry suffered a further setback with the arrival of autonomous profiling floats, several thousand of which now drift through the world's oceans, rising and sinking to record temperature over the upper two kilometres. Nkiruka Obiozor, of the West African Centre for Ocean Observation, contends that these floats have made acoustic methods redundant, providing far more detailed information at a fraction of the cost. It is easy to see why this view has gained ground, but it overlooks important gaps. Floats measure individual points, which must be combined statistically to estimate averages; they cannot operate beneath sea ice, where they are unable to surface to transmit their data; and most never descend below two thousand metres, leaving more than half of the ocean's volume unsampled.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One recent development may give acoustics a new lease of life, while sidestepping the controversy over artificial sources altogether. Teodor Prisăcaru, a seismologist at the Danube Geophysical Institute, has shown that undersea earthquakes can serve as natural transmitters. Where earthquakes recur at almost exactly the same location, the sound waves they generate travel along the same path each time, and differences in arrival time at distant listening stations reveal how the intervening water has warmed. Because suitable recordings exist from stations established decades ago to detect nuclear tests, the technique can reconstruct past changes without any new equipment. It is an ingenious and inexpensive approach. Its limitation is equally plain: measurements can be made only where the earth happens to provide earthquakes, so the coverage it offers is dictated by geology rather than by scientific need.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The Arctic illustrates where acoustics may prove most useful. With sea ice preventing floats from surfacing and satellites unable to see beneath it, the region remains among the most poorly observed parts of the ocean, at precisely the moment when it is changing fastest. Cazaubon and her colleagues have deployed moored sources and receivers in the deep strait between Greenland and Svalbard, through which most of the Arctic's exchange of water with the Atlantic takes place, and argue that sound is the only practical way to monitor such ice-covered regions continuously.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of ocean acoustics is in some ways a cautionary tale about the fashions of science. A method was championed, then largely abandoned, partly for good reasons and partly because a newer technology seemed to make it obsolete. Yet no single instrument can observe an ocean that is vast, deep and in places permanently frozen over. The most reliable picture of how the oceans are warming is likely to come from combining floats, satellites and sound, each compensating for the blind spots of the others.

topic: ensemble forecasting and the communication of forecast probabilities
title: The Arithmetic of Uncertainty
subtitle: Ensemble forecasting has changed what meteorologists know about the limits of prediction, but not yet how the public hears about them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, a weather forecast was a single statement about the future: tomorrow will be wet, the temperature will reach eighteen degrees, the wind will veer westerly by evening. Behind this confident tone lay an assumption that the atmosphere, given enough data and sufficiently powerful computers, would eventually yield to precise calculation. That assumption has not survived. Since the 1960s it has been understood that the atmosphere is a chaotic system, in which tiny differences in starting conditions grow until they overwhelm any forecast. A gust unrecorded over the Atlantic today may, within a week, separate a calm afternoon from a gale. The practical consequence is that there is a horizon beyond which detailed prediction becomes impossible, and no improvement in instruments will push it back indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The response of forecasting centres has been the ensemble. Rather than running a computer model once, they run it perhaps fifty times, each time nudging the initial conditions slightly to reflect the inevitable gaps and errors in the observations. If the fifty runs agree closely, forecasters can be confident; if they diverge, the spread itself is information, signalling that the atmosphere is in a sensitive state. Dr Folasade Arowolo, who leads the predictability group at the Meridian Institute for Atmospheric Science, describes the ensemble as a way of forecasting the forecast. Her group's analysis of a decade of European winter storms found that ensemble spread predicted forecast error well in the first five days, but that the relationship weakened noticeably thereafter, so that by day ten a narrow spread was no guarantee of accuracy.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This finding matters because the ensemble is often presented as the solution to chaos rather than a way of living with it. Ensembles do not abolish the forecast horizon; they map it. Indeed, there is a persistent risk that the members of an ensemble share the same systematic flaws, since they are all produced by the same model. Where a model consistently underestimates, say, the strength of sea breezes, fifty runs of it will underestimate them fifty times, and the apparent agreement will be misleading. Some centres have tried to address this by combining ensembles from different models, a so-called multi-model approach, which tends to produce better-calibrated probabilities, though at considerable computational expense.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The more contentious question is what to do with the probabilities once they exist. Torvald Ekhaugen, a social scientist who studies risk communication at the University of Bergsfjord, argues that the public is far more capable of handling probabilities than forecasters assume. In surveys conducted with his colleagues, most respondents correctly interpreted a seventy per cent chance of rain as meaning that rain was more likely than not, and a clear majority said they preferred forecasts that admitted uncertainty to those that did not. Ekhaugen contends that withholding probabilistic information is not merely paternalistic but counterproductive, because a single deterministic forecast that turns out wrong damages trust more than an honest probability that does.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Marisol Quiñones-Abad, a former emergency planner who now advises a national weather service, points out that what people say in surveys and what they do in emergencies are rather different things. In her experience, officials responsible for closing schools, cancelling events or evacuating coastal towns want a clear recommendation, not a percentage, and a forecast that reads 'forty per cent chance of severe flooding' can leave them paralysed, uncertain whether that figure is alarmingly high or reassuringly low. She has proposed that probabilities be translated into tiered action levels, each linked to specific steps that authorities have agreed in advance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Both positions contain an important truth, but Quiñones-Abad's proposal seems the more workable of the two. Ekhaugen's surveys measure comprehension in calm conditions, when nothing is at stake; it is quite another matter to weigh a probability at three in the morning with a river rising. At the same time, tiered warnings carry a danger of their own. If the thresholds are set cautiously, warnings will be issued for events that never materialise, and repeated false alarms are known to erode the willingness of communities to respond. The design of such systems is therefore as much a question of politics and local experience as of meteorology.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is that the very meaning of a probability forecast is often unclear even to those who issue it. A thirty per cent chance of rain might refer to the likelihood that rain falls somewhere in a region, or at a particular point, or that it falls for a certain proportion of the day. A survey of national forecasting practice by a team at the Coastal Forecasting Laboratory, led by Dr Yusuke Hanamoto, found that weather services in different countries used at least four distinct definitions, frequently without stating which one applied. Until such basic matters are settled, debates about whether the public can understand probabilities are somewhat premature: it is hard to understand a figure whose meaning has never been defined.

topic: the scientific testing of traditional weather lore
title: Wisdom in the Wind
subtitle: Can centuries-old weather sayings survive the scrutiny of modern meteorology?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before satellites and supercomputers, farmers, sailors and shepherds relied on a body of weather lore handed down from one generation to the next. Red skies, low-flying swallows, cattle lying down in the fields and the sharp smell of approaching rain were all read as signs of what the coming hours or days would bring. For much of the twentieth century, professional meteorologists tended to dismiss this inheritance as little more than superstition, a relic of an age before instruments. That dismissal was always too hasty. Some traditional sayings encode genuine and careful observation, even if many others do not, and the interesting question is not whether weather lore is true or false as a whole, but which parts of it work, and why.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Short-range sayings tend to fare best. The familiar claim that a red sky in the evening promises fine weather has a plausible physical basis: in the middle latitudes, weather systems generally travel from west to east, and a red sunset indicates clear air to the west, the direction from which tomorrow's conditions are likely to arrive. Dr Rūta Kalinauskas, a climatologist at the Baltic Institute of Applied Meteorology, tested twenty traditional short-term sayings from her region against forty years of station records. Roughly a third of them performed noticeably better than chance, and the most successful concerned cloud types and shifts in the wind. A halo around the moon, produced by ice crystals in high, thin cloud, was followed by rain within twenty-four hours in around sixty per cent of cases. That such sayings should work is hardly surprising, since they describe the same features that forecasters themselves examine.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sayings based on animal behaviour performed less well. In Kalinauskas's study, almost none of them did better than guesswork. Professor Somchai Thammavongsa, a biologist at the Mekong Valley Research Station who studies insect behaviour, considers this verdict unfair. Many animals, he points out, respond to falling air pressure or rising humidity, both of which commonly precede storms. Swallows fly lower before rain, for example, because the insects they feed on are carried downwards in damp, heavy air. In his view, the fault lies not with the animals but with the sayings, many of which were recorded carelessly by collectors who stripped them of the local circumstances in which they had once been useful. It is a reasonable objection, and one that should make researchers cautious about drawing sweeping conclusions from a single regional survey.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Long-range lore is a different matter. Sayings that claim to predict an entire season from the weather on a single day, such as the belief that rain on a particular feast day will be followed by weeks of wet weather, show no measurable skill at all. Their credibility is further undermined by history: the calendar reform of the eighteenth century shifted many dates by about eleven days, so a number of these sayings now refer to days quite different from those their originators had in mind. Yet it is a mistake to subject such proverbs to statistical tests as though they were scientific hypotheses. They are better understood as cultural artefacts, expressing the anxieties of communities whose survival depended on the harvest, than as forecasts in any modern sense.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious defence of traditional knowledge comes from Dr Thandeka Mukwevho, an anthropologist who has spent many years documenting weather knowledge among farming communities in southern Africa. She argues that treating folk forecasting as a list of proverbs to be checked one by one fundamentally misunderstands it. In the villages she has studied, prediction relies on many signs at once, including the flowering of certain trees, the direction of seasonal winds, the appearance of particular birds and the behaviour of termites, all interpreted together by experienced individuals. No single sign is decisive. Her work has encouraged several national weather services to hold regular meetings with local forecasters in order to produce joint seasonal outlooks for rural districts.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These co-production schemes have their critics. Armen Tavitian, a statistician responsible for evaluating forecast skill at a national meteorological agency, accepts that traditional knowledge has cultural value, but warns that without systematic verification there is no way of knowing whether joint outlooks are any better than scientific ones alone. He notes that human memory is a poor judge of accuracy: people readily recall the occasions when a sign proved correct and quietly forget the many times it failed. Tavitian therefore insists that both kinds of forecast be written down in advance and scored against what actually happens, using the same methods that are applied to computer models.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Tavitian's demand for evidence is entirely reasonable, but it ought to apply in both directions. Scientific seasonal forecasts for many tropical regions have only modest skill themselves, and they are rarely held up to the same scrutiny in public debate. Moreover, the value of joint outlooks may lie less in accuracy than in trust: farmers appear more willing to act on advice that comes partly from people they know and respect. Perhaps the real lesson of weather lore is not that our ancestors were either right or wrong, but that close attention to local conditions remains valuable, something that an era of global models and automated forecasts is in danger of overlooking.

topic: the telegraph and the origins of national storm warning services
title: Signals Along the Wire
subtitle: How the telegraph turned weather from a local experience into a national forecast, and why the first warnings caused such controversy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, news of the weather could travel no faster than the weather itself. A storm crossing a country might advance at forty or fifty kilometres an hour, comfortably outpacing any rider or mail coach that set out to warn the towns in its path. Observers could record what had already happened, and some kept meticulous diaries of pressure and rainfall, but they could do almost nothing to anticipate what was coming. The electric telegraph changed this almost overnight. For the first time, reports from widely separated places could be gathered in a single office within hours. It is arguable that this, rather than any refinement of the barometer or thermometer, was the most important single development in the history of forecasting.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: During the 1850s and 1860s, governments in several countries established networks of observing stations that sent their readings by telegraph each morning to a central office. There, clerks plotted pressure, wind direction and temperature onto outline maps. These charts, which showed conditions across a broad area at a single moment, revealed that storms were vast rotating systems that moved in broadly predictable directions. Dr Ingrid Gjermundsen, a historian at the University of Tromsvik, stresses that such maps were as much a product of bureaucracy as of science. Instruments had to be standardised, reporting times fixed and codes agreed, and this required years of negotiation between national telegraph authorities. In her account, the first international agreements on when observations should be taken were driven partly by the timetabling requirements of railway companies, which had their own reasons for wanting clocks across a country to agree.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most visible result of the new networks was the storm warning. Coastal signal stations began hoisting large cones or drums on tall masts to alert vessels when a gale was expected, the orientation of a cone indicating the likely direction of the wind. The reaction of fishing communities was mixed. Dr Ákos Szarvas, who has examined harbour records from a dozen ports, finds that in the decades after warnings were introduced, fewer small vessels were wrecked. He is careful, however, to add that this period coincided with the spread of steam-powered boats, which were far less vulnerable to sudden changes in the wind, so that the precise contribution of the warnings is difficult to isolate. Shipowners, meanwhile, complained that cautious signals kept their vessels in harbour on days when they could safely have sailed, at considerable cost.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More damaging was the hostility of the scientific establishment. Several prominent learned societies argued that weather prediction lacked any theoretical foundation and amounted to little more than guesswork presented as science. In one country, warnings were suspended for several years after an official committee concluded that the predictions were insufficiently reliable to justify public funds; they were restored only after sustained protests from coastal communities. The critics were not entirely wrong. Early forecasters relied on rules of thumb derived from the sequence of pressure changes, not on any understanding of atmospheric physics. What the critics failed to appreciate was that a warning does not need a complete theory behind it to be useful; it needs only to be right more often than it is wrong, and to be acted upon.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Chukwuemeka Ifeanyichukwu, a historian of science, interprets the dispute as a contest over who had the authority to speak about the future. The first forecasters were frequently naval officers or civil servants rather than university scientists, and their public, daily predictions exposed them to ridicule whenever they failed. Newspapers took evident pleasure in printing each mistake. Ifeanyichukwu suggests that the reluctance of academic science to engage with forecasting delayed the emergence of a theoretical meteorology by several decades. This claim is harder to sustain. The mathematical tools required for physically based forecasting did not exist until well into the twentieth century, and the computing power needed to apply them arrived later still; it is difficult to see how greater academic enthusiasm could have overcome such obstacles.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Montserrat Ruscalleda has drawn attention to a dimension that national histories often neglect. Telegraph networks were extended into colonial territories in South Asia, the Caribbean and elsewhere, largely to protect shipping and trade. Cyclone warnings issued from ports around the Bay of Bengal were among the earliest of their kind outside Europe. Ruscalleda notes that observations supplied by local clerks and observers were essential to these systems but were rarely acknowledged in official reports. She also argues that the warnings were organised around harbours and commercial routes, while the inland and low-lying villages, where flooding caused the greatest loss of life, received little or no notice of approaching storms.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The principle established in this period, that observations must be collected rapidly and exchanged across borders, still underpins every forecast issued today. The free international exchange of weather data, maintained even between countries that are otherwise hostile to one another, is one of the more remarkable examples of sustained global cooperation. Such cooperation should not, however, be taken for granted. Growing pressure to treat observations as commercial products, to be sold rather than shared, threatens an arrangement that has served the world well for more than a century and a half.

topic: machine-learning weather models and their relationship to physics-based forecasting
title: Learning the Sky
subtitle: Machine-learning models now rival traditional forecasting systems. Does that mean the physics no longer matters?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than half a century, weather forecasting has rested on a single method, known as numerical weather prediction. The atmosphere is divided into millions of grid boxes, and the equations that govern the motion of air, the transfer of heat and the behaviour of water vapour are solved for each box, step by step, into the future. The approach demands enormous computing resources: a ten-day global forecast can occupy one of the world's largest supercomputers for around an hour. In the past few years, however, a different kind of system has appeared. Models trained on decades of historical weather records can now produce global forecasts of comparable accuracy in less than a minute on a single processor. This is probably the most significant shift in the field since computers were first applied to the weather, although not entirely for the reasons usually given.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: These new models do not solve any equations. Instead, they learn statistical relationships between the state of the atmosphere at one moment and its state six hours later, and then apply what they have learned repeatedly to build a forecast extending days ahead. Dr Emir Duraković, who led the development of one such system at the Adriatic Centre for Computational Meteorology, reports that his model outperformed the leading physics-based system on roughly four-fifths of the standard verification measures for forecasts of up to ten days. Just as importantly, its speed makes it possible to produce ensembles of thousands of forecasts rather than the fifty or so that current supercomputers can manage, giving a far more detailed picture of the range of possible outcomes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Leena Kivirauma, an atmospheric dynamicist, argues that such headline scores conceal important weaknesses. Machine-learning forecasts, she observes, tend to become smoother and less detailed as they extend further into the future. The reason is that a model trained to minimise its average error learns, when it is uncertain, to predict something close to the average of all the possibilities, which is the safest choice statistically but a poor representation of reality. As a result, the intensity of extreme events, precisely those that matter most to the public, tends to be underestimated; in her tests, the peak winds of the most severe storms were systematically too weak. She raises a second concern as well: a model trained on the climate of the past may not cope with a warming world in which conditions arise that never appeared in its training data.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Of these two objections, the second is by far the more serious. The tendency to blur is essentially a technical problem, and newer designs already address it by training models to reproduce realistic variability rather than simply to minimise average error. The difficulty of extrapolation, by contrast, is a fundamental limitation of any system that learns from examples: a model cannot learn what it has never seen. Even so, the problem should not be exaggerated. Record-breaking weather rarely involves entirely novel processes; it usually consists of familiar ingredients combined in unusual strength, and a well-trained model may handle such combinations better than its critics expect.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also an irony in the claim that machine learning might make physics redundant. Dr Farida Sunderji, a data scientist at a national weather service, points out that the historical records on which the new models are trained are not raw observations at all. They are reanalyses, reconstructions of past weather produced by physics-based models that combine scattered measurements into a complete and consistent picture. Furthermore, every machine-learning forecast must begin from a description of the current atmosphere, and that starting point is prepared using the same traditional methods. Without the physical models, Sunderji argues, there would be nothing for the new systems to learn from and nothing for them to start from. The real question, in her view, is not one of replacement but of how the work should be divided.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The economic consequences may prove as important as the scientific ones. Dr Rafael Bechara, an economist who studies the forecasting industry, suggests that cheaper forecasts could allow countries with modest meteorological budgets to run high-quality models of their own, reducing their reliance on a handful of wealthy centres. He also warns, however, that many of the most capable systems have been developed by large technology companies rather than public agencies, and that the terms on which they are made available could change at any time. Bechara's optimism about poorer nations seems premature. Running a trained model is cheap, but training one in the first place still requires vast quantities of computation and data, resources that remain concentrated in a few places.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most likely outcome, for the foreseeable future, is a hybrid arrangement in which physical models supply the starting conditions and the training data, machine-learning systems produce rapid forecasts and large ensembles, and human forecasters interpret the results and communicate them to the public. What has changed is less the practice of forecasting than its philosophy. The boundary between understanding the atmosphere and predicting it has become harder to draw. Some meteorologists regret this, but forecasting has always been a pragmatic discipline, judged by whether its predictions prove useful rather than by the elegance of the methods that produce them.

topic: the skill and usefulness of seasonal climate forecasts
title: Beyond the Fortnight
subtitle: Seasonal forecasts claim to tell us whether next summer will be dry or next winter severe. How far should we believe them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Because the atmosphere is chaotic, detailed day-to-day forecasting runs into a wall at around two weeks. Beyond that point, nobody can say whether it will rain in a given town on a given afternoon. Yet every month the major forecasting centres issue predictions for the coming three months, stating whether a season is likely to be warmer, colder, wetter or drier than usual. This looks like a paradox, but it is not. Seasonal forecasts make no attempt to predict the weather on particular days. What they predict is a shift in the odds, driven by components of the climate system that change far more slowly than the atmosphere itself: the temperature of the oceans, the moisture stored in soils, and the extent of snow cover and sea ice.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oceans are by far the most important of these influences. Periodic warming and cooling of the tropical Pacific alters rainfall patterns across much of the tropics, and when such an episode is strongly developed, forecasts for parts of eastern Africa, South-East Asia and South America can be genuinely useful. Dr Wanjiru Mwangangi, a climate scientist at the East African Climate Applications Centre, has evaluated two decades of seasonal rainfall forecasts for her region. She found that predictions for the short rains, which fall between October and December, showed considerable skill, whereas those for the long rains of March to May were scarcely better than simply assuming an average season. She attributes the difference to the stronger influence of ocean temperatures on the later of the two seasons.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the middle latitudes, including most of Europe, the picture is much less encouraging, because the atmosphere there is dominated by its own internal fluctuations and the ocean signal is comparatively weak. Nevertheless, Dr Henrik Lindroos of the Nordic Centre for Climate Dynamics has reported a curious result. Winter forecasts of the large-scale pressure pattern over the North Atlantic turned out to be more skilful than expected, yet the predictable signal within the models was oddly faint, so that the forecasts matched the real world better than they matched their own individual ensemble members. Lindroos concludes that the models must be missing some physical process. This is perhaps the most intriguing puzzle in contemporary climate science, and it is less comforting than it first appears: if models are better than they themselves indicate, the probabilities they issue cannot be taken at face value.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The value of any forecast, of course, depends on how it is used. Dr Ximena Carvajal-Teng, an agricultural economist, has studied how farmers in the Andes respond to seasonal outlooks. Such outlooks are commonly expressed as three probabilities, for instance a forty-five per cent chance of above-normal rainfall, thirty-five per cent for normal and twenty per cent for below normal. Carvajal-Teng found that these figures were widely misunderstood: many farmers took a forty-five per cent chance of a wet season to mean that a wet season was assured. However, farmers who had received forecasts together with training in how to interpret them made planting decisions that raised their average yields modestly. She argues that seasonal forecasts justify their cost only when they are accompanied by sustained engagement with the people who use them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Professor Babatunde Oyelowo, a statistician, points to a deeper difficulty. A forecast of modest skill, applied to a single decision, will frequently be wrong. A farmer who reduces planting because drought has been predicted, only for good rains to arrive, may lose a substantial part of the year's income. Over many years the gains may outweigh such losses on average, but a poor household may not survive the bad years in order to enjoy the average. Oyelowo therefore suggests that seasonal forecasts are best suited to organisations such as governments, aid agencies, insurers and hydropower operators, which make many decisions and can absorb occasional failures.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Oyelowo's argument is compelling, but it should not be taken to mean that smallholders are better left out altogether. One promising approach, often described as forecast-based financing, allows the risk to be shared. Several humanitarian organisations now commit funds in advance to be released to vulnerable communities as soon as a forecast crosses an agreed threshold, so that households can buy food, move livestock or protect stored grain before a drought or flood arrives, rather than waiting for aid after the damage has been done.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Climate change adds a further complication. Seasonal forecasts are judged against a definition of normal based on thirty-year averages. In a warming climate, a forecast of above-normal temperatures will turn out to be correct in most years, regardless of whether the forecasting system has any real insight into the season ahead, and this inevitably flatters the scores by which forecasts are assessed. Forecasting centres ought to state openly how much of their apparent success arises simply from the long-term warming trend, rather than allowing it to be counted as evidence of skill.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Seasonal forecasting, then, is neither the triumph that its promoters sometimes proclaim nor the illusion that its sceptics suggest. In some regions and seasons it offers real, if limited, guidance; in others it adds little to what an average year would suggest. Its future credibility depends on whether those who produce it are willing to be as clear about its limitations as they are about its successes.

topic: citizen weather observations from home stations and smartphones
title: A Million Thermometers
subtitle: Readings from garden weather stations and mobile phones are reshaping how the atmosphere is observed, but their value remains disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, measuring the weather was a task for professionals. National meteorological services operated networks of stations built to exacting standards: thermometers housed in ventilated white screens, mounted at a fixed height above short grass and well away from buildings. Such stations are expensive to install and maintain, and even in wealthy countries they are often spaced tens of kilometres apart. Over the past fifteen years, however, a parallel network has emerged almost by accident. Hundreds of thousands of inexpensive weather stations now sit in gardens and on rooftops, uploading readings to the internet every few minutes, while billions of smartphones contain sensitive pressure sensors originally intended to help with navigation inside tall buildings. In terms of sheer quantity, this flood of information is arguably the most important change in how the atmosphere is observed since the launch of the first weather satellites. Quantity, though, is not the same as usefulness, and the question of what such data are actually worth has divided the meteorological community.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulties are easy to list. Consumer stations are rarely calibrated, and their owners place them wherever is convenient: against sunny walls, on balconies or beside air-conditioning units. When Ilona Szentmiklósi, a data scientist at the Carpathian Institute of Atmospheric Physics, compared readings from some 30,000 private stations in a single capital city with values from nearby official instruments, she found that more than a fifth reported afternoon temperatures at least two degrees too high. Yet Szentmiklósi draws an optimistic conclusion from this result. The errors, she points out, are largely systematic rather than random: a station fixed to a south-facing wall overheats in a predictable way, day after day. Errors that behave consistently can be recognised by comparing each station with its neighbours and with computer model output. Her quality-control procedure discards stations whose readings repeatedly disagree with the surrounding pattern, typically retaining around sixty per cent of the network.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kwame Adjei-Brobbey, who leads a research group at the Gulf of Guinea Atmospheric Centre, is more interested in pressure than temperature. Pressure has one great advantage: unlike temperature, it is scarcely affected by where an instrument is located, so a phone lying on a desk indoors records much the same value as one held outside. The main obstacle is altitude. Because pressure falls with height, a phone's reading can only be interpreted if its elevation is known, and the satellite positioning systems in phones are notoriously imprecise in the vertical dimension; an error of ten metres in height produces an error of roughly one hectopascal, a large discrepancy in meteorological terms. Adjei-Brobbey's solution is to concentrate not on absolute values but on how quickly pressure changes, averaged across many devices in the same area. Sudden jumps in pressure often accompany developing thunderstorms, and in trials his team found that feeding such data into short-range models produced modest but measurable improvements in forecasts of severe storms.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares this enthusiasm. Paulina Ostaszewska, a former director of observations at a national weather service, warns that the attraction of free data may tempt governments to cut spending on professional stations. Official networks, she observes, do more than support daily forecasts: they provide long, consistent records stretching back more than a century, which are essential for detecting climate change. A garden station may be moved, replaced or abandoned at its owner's whim, and much citizen data passes through commercial platforms whose terms of use could change at any time. Her concern about funding is entirely justified, and it deserves more attention than it has received. However, Ostaszewska also argues that amateur readings should be kept out of operational forecasting until their reliability is proven beyond doubt, and here she goes too far. Forecasters routinely work with imperfect data, from satellite estimates to ship reports, and the relevant question is whether a new source adds information, not whether it is flawless.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The case for citizen data is strongest in cities. Official stations tend to be located at airports or in parks on the urban fringe, so they say little about conditions in the dense neighbourhoods where most people actually live. Private stations, for all their faults, are concentrated precisely in those areas, and they have revealed differences of several degrees between streets only a few hundred metres apart. Such detail matters to public health authorities, since the risks of extreme heat fall unevenly on different districts.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different philosophy is promoted by the Haverleigh Weather Circle, a volunteer association of several hundred amateur observers. Its members regard statistical correction as a poor substitute for good practice, and they ask participants to follow simplified siting rules, use shaded radiation shields and submit photographs of their installations. Because quality is built in from the start, the Circle claims, far fewer readings need to be rejected later. The two approaches are complementary rather than competing, but the Circle's emphasis on volunteers highlights something that purely statistical methods overlook: contributors who see their observations being used remain engaged, whereas those whose readings vanish silently may simply lose interest. Weather services that rely on such data should therefore explain to contributors when, and why, their measurements have been excluded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a certain irony in all this. In the nineteenth century, many national weather records depended on unpaid volunteers, among them clergymen, schoolteachers and farmers, who read their instruments each morning and posted the results to a central office. Professionalisation later pushed such amateurs to the margins of the science. Their return, in digital form, is unlikely to be reversed, and the important question is therefore not whether citizen observations will be used, but on what terms.

topic: impact-based forecasting and severe weather warnings
title: Forecasting Consequences
subtitle: Weather services are learning to predict what the weather will do, not merely what it will be, and discovering that the change raises awkward questions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the evening before a severe storm struck a medium-sized river town some years ago, the national weather service issued a forecast that, by any technical standard, was excellent. It predicted between 100 and 130 millimetres of rain within twelve hours, and the total eventually recorded was 118. Yet the following morning several drivers were trapped in a flooded underpass and dozens of homes were inundated, largely because residents had not grasped what such a figure would mean for their streets. Episodes of this kind have persuaded many meteorological agencies to change the way they communicate. Instead of warning that a certain quantity of rain will fall, they increasingly state that roads are likely to become impassable or that low-lying properties may flood. This move from forecasting weather to forecasting its consequences is, in my view, long overdue, and for the most part it is to be welcomed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The behavioural case for the change has been made most forcefully by Fenella Oudshoorn, a social scientist at the Leeuwarden Centre for Risk Communication. Oudshoorn argues that people respond to consequences rather than to quantities, and her surveys suggest that recipients of impact-based warnings were nearly twice as likely to report taking protective action as those who were given rainfall totals alone. Her findings are persuasive, but they should be treated with some caution. Surveys record what people say they did or intend to do, and there is a well-documented gap between stated intentions and actual behaviour, particularly when acting involves inconvenience or expense.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Predicting impacts also demands knowledge that meteorologists have rarely possessed. Whether heavy rain causes harm depends not only on the weather but on exposure and vulnerability: which roads lie in hollows, which drains are blocked, which neighbourhoods house large numbers of elderly residents. Such information is held, if at all, by local councils, emergency services and utility companies. Rohan Jayawickrema, a hydrometeorologist at the Southern Monsoon Hazards Office, has spent several years building what his team calls impact tables, colour-coded grids that combine the likelihood of an event with the severity of its expected effects. He contends that the grid forces forecasters to be more honest about uncertainty, since an event that is unlikely but potentially catastrophic can justify a higher warning level than a probable but minor one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that weather services should take on this role. Ainura Sydykova, a legal scholar at the Tien Shan Institute of Public Law, points out that forecasting impacts blurs the boundaries of responsibility. A prediction of rainfall concerns a natural phenomenon, but a prediction that a bridge will close depends on human decisions about maintenance, traffic management and emergency response. If an impact forecast proves wrong, Sydykova asks, who is accountable: the forecaster, the engineer or the council? Her concern is legitimate, and agencies would be unwise to dismiss it. However, the appropriate response is to clarify the legal frameworks within which warnings are issued, not to retreat into forecasts that are technically accurate but practically ignored.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A related worry is the so-called cry-wolf effect, the fear that a public exposed to repeated false alarms will eventually disregard warnings altogether. Esperanza Villacorta-Ruiz, an emergency planner who has analysed a decade of warnings and public responses across three countries, argues that the evidence for this effect is considerably weaker than is commonly assumed. In her data, people generally forgave warnings that did not materialise, provided they understood why the warning had been issued in the first place. This is reassuring, although her sample covers regions where serious false alarms were relatively infrequent, and it would be rash to assume that public patience is unlimited.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most serious weakness of impact forecasting, however, lies in verification. A conventional forecast can be checked against measured rainfall from a network of gauges, so that its accuracy can be tracked from year to year. An impact forecast, by contrast, can only be verified if there is a reliable record of what actually happened on the ground, and records of flooded roads, damaged buildings and closed schools are patchy and inconsistent. Some services have begun to collect photographs and reports posted on social media, but these come disproportionately from cities and from younger, wealthier residents. Without systematic verification, impact forecasting risks becoming an exercise that cannot be held to account, which would undermine the very trust it is meant to build.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is clear is that the change alters the nature of the forecaster's job. A meteorologist who once described the state of the atmosphere is increasingly expected to act as a kind of risk adviser, weighing probabilities against consequences and negotiating with partners who have different priorities. This calls for skills in communication and judgement that traditional training in physics and mathematics does not provide. A few services have started placing meteorologists within local emergency planning teams for months at a time, an arrangement that appears to build mutual understanding, although it is still too early to say whether it improves outcomes for the public. The transition will be uncomfortable, but the alternative, a series of accurate forecasts that nobody acts upon, is considerably worse.

topic: weather balloons, aircraft reports and the upper-air observing network
title: The Balloons That Still Matter
subtitle: In an age of satellites, weather balloons and passenger aircraft remain surprisingly important sources of information about the upper atmosphere

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twice a day, at the same moment all over the world, staff at several hundred observing stations release balloons filled with hydrogen or helium. Each carries a radiosonde, a small package of instruments that measures temperature, humidity and pressure as it rises, while its changing position reveals the speed and direction of the wind. Over roughly two hours the balloon climbs to around thirty kilometres, expanding as the air thins until it finally bursts, and the instrument parachutes back to earth, where it is seldom recovered. The basic procedure has changed little since the 1930s, and beside the satellites that now circle the planet it can look like a relic of an earlier era. That impression, however, is mistaken: the weather balloon remains one of the most valuable observing tools that forecasters possess.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The reason lies in the difference between looking down and passing through. Satellites infer temperature and moisture from radiation emitted by thick layers of the atmosphere, so the vertical profiles they produce are inevitably somewhat blurred. A radiosonde, by contrast, samples the air directly as it ascends, capturing sharp changes over a few tens of metres, including the shallow layers of warm air above cooler air that can suppress or trigger thunderstorms. Oyuunchimeg Batsaikhan, a physicist at the Steppe Atmospheric Observatory, emphasises a second, less obvious role. Satellite instruments drift and degrade, she notes, and their readings must constantly be checked against something more trustworthy. Radiosondes act as anchors for the whole system: without them, gradual biases in satellite data could accumulate unnoticed and quietly contaminate forecasts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Balloons are not the only source of direct measurements aloft. Many commercial airliners automatically report temperature and wind during their flights, and because reports are especially frequent as aircraft climb away from and descend towards airports, they supply thousands of vertical profiles every day, far more than the balloon network. Their coverage, though, is very uneven: reports are concentrated along busy routes over North America, Europe and East Asia and are sparse over Africa and the oceans. When air traffic collapsed in the spring of 2020, the number of aircraft reports fell by around three-quarters, and forecasting centres detected a small but measurable loss of accuracy, most clearly in predictions of winds at high altitudes. For Graciela Etchebarne of the Rioplatense Centre for Numerical Prediction, the episode amounted to an accidental experiment, revealing how heavily modern forecasting relies on a source of data that nobody pays for and nobody controls.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The balloon network, meanwhile, faces financial pressure. Each launch requires an instrument that will almost certainly be lost, a supply of gas and trained staff, and for many lower-income countries these costs are a heavy burden. Across parts of Africa, stations launch irregularly or have closed altogether. Jean-Pierre Kanyinda, who coordinates observing programmes for a regional meteorological association, argues that wealthy countries should help to fund these stations, because weather systems cross borders and forecasts in Europe or Asia depend partly on observations taken thousands of kilometres upstream. Studies of forecast sensitivity suggest that a single observation from a data-sparse region can have a far greater influence than one from an area that is already well observed. Kanyinda's argument is sound, and it should be stressed that such funding would be a matter of self-interest rather than charity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more sceptical voice belongs to Matthias Trübenbach, who assesses observing systems for a consortium of European weather services. In so-called denial experiments, in which particular observations are deliberately withheld from a forecasting model, he has found that removing a substantial share of radiosonde stations produces only a slight decline in average forecast quality, provided the remaining stations are carefully chosen. He therefore suggests that resources might be better devoted to new satellite instruments. His results are carefully obtained, but they rest on averages, and averages conceal precisely the cases that matter most. A single sounding taken upstream of a rapidly developing storm can transform a forecast, yet such occasions are too rare to register in figures calculated over many months.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practice is not without environmental costs. Hundreds of thousands of burst balloons, together with instruments containing batteries and circuit boards, fall into forests, farmland and seas each year. Some services have switched to biodegradable materials or offer small rewards for returned instruments, and automated launchers, which can fill and release a balloon without a technician present, have reduced staffing costs at remote stations. Drones capable of flying vertical profiles and returning to base are also being tested, although they cannot yet reach the altitudes that balloons attain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The upper-air observing system of the future will almost certainly be a mixture of satellites, aircraft, balloons and newer platforms. The danger is that the cheapest and most traditional components are taken for granted precisely because they have always been there. The present arrangement was not designed as a whole; it accumulated piece by piece, shaped by history and commercial convenience. Perhaps the clearest lesson of 2020 is that a network on which so much depends ought to be planned deliberately rather than inherited by accident.

topic: cloud seeding and the difficulty of proving that weather modification works
title: The Rainmakers' Dilemma
subtitle: Eighty years after scientists first coaxed snow from a cloud, nobody can say with confidence how much extra water cloud seeding produces

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1940s, laboratory researchers made a discovery that seemed to place the weather within human control. Clouds frequently contain droplets of water that remain liquid at temperatures well below freezing, and the experimenters found that introducing tiny particles of dry ice or silver iodide into such supercooled clouds caused ice crystals to form almost instantly. Since ice crystals grow at the expense of the surrounding droplets and may become heavy enough to fall, the implication was obvious: seed the right clouds and more rain or snow would reach the ground. Within a decade, commercial operators were selling seeding services to farmers, power companies and ski resorts across several continents. Yet few technologies have promised so much and demonstrated so little. Today seeding programmes operate in dozens of countries, but the central question of how much additional precipitation they generate remains stubbornly unresolved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is fundamentally statistical. Precipitation varies enormously from one storm to the next, and even from one valley to its neighbour, whereas the increases claimed for seeding are typically modest, often in the region of ten to fifteen per cent. Detecting so small a signal against such a noisy background is extraordinarily demanding. Hamdiya Al-Ruwaili, a statistician at the Arabian Gulf Institute for Water Studies, insists that only randomised experiments can separate a genuine effect from chance. In such trials, each suitable cloud or storm is either seeded or left alone according to a random decision, so that any systematic difference in the resulting precipitation can be attributed to the treatment. Her calculations suggest that reliably detecting a ten per cent increase would require several hundred cases gathered over at least five winters, a scale that very few projects have attempted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Teófilo Banchero, an engineer who has directed operational seeding programmes in the Andes for over twenty years, regards this standard as unrealistic. The water authorities and farmers who pay for seeding, he points out, expect every promising storm to be treated, and they are unlikely to accept that half of them should be deliberately ignored for the sake of an experiment. Banchero relies instead on comparisons between target areas, where seeding takes place, and nearby control areas, where it does not, using decades of historical records to estimate what precipitation would have been without intervention. His frustration is understandable, but such comparisons cannot settle the matter. Changes in land use, in the placement of rain gauges or in regional climate can all alter the relationship between target and control areas, producing apparent effects that have nothing to do with seeding.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different kind of evidence has emerged from the work of Mihaela Gherghiceanu, a cloud physicist who combines radar with instrumented research aircraft. Rather than counting rainfall totals, her team tracks the physical chain of events that seeding is supposed to set in motion. In several winter clouds over mountainous terrain, radar revealed narrow zigzag bands of snow whose shape precisely matched the flight paths of the seeding aircraft, a fingerprint that natural processes could hardly have produced. This is, to my mind, the most persuasive evidence yet that seeding can affect clouds. Gherghiceanu herself is careful to note its limits, however. Her observations show what happened in a handful of particular clouds; they reveal little about how much extra snow seeding might add over a whole season, which is the figure that matters to anyone deciding whether to pay for it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Seeding also raises questions of fairness that are independent of its effectiveness. Ochieng Wafula, who studies the governance of shared water resources, has documented disputes in which communities accused upwind neighbours of stealing their rain. The physical basis for such accusations is weak. Clouds convert only a small fraction of the moisture passing through them into precipitation, so there is little reason to think that seeding in one place substantially reduces rainfall further downwind, and I find this evidence convincing. Wafula's point, though, is that perception matters as much as physics. Suspicion flourishes where operations are secret, and he argues that every programme should publish the times, locations and quantities of each seeding operation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Concerns about the environment have proved easier to address. The quantities of silver iodide released are tiny, and studies of soils and streams in long-running project areas have generally found concentrations well below levels considered harmful. The economic case is more complicated. If seeding does increase precipitation by ten per cent, the cost of each additional cubic metre of water would compare favourably with the cost of building new reservoirs or transferring water between river basins. If the true effect is close to zero, the money is simply wasted. Some farmers' associations have meanwhile called for seeding to be extended to summer thunderstorms, which pose quite different physical challenges.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: After eight decades, then, the case for cloud seeding remains unproven rather than disproven, and that distinction matters. As droughts become more frequent in many regions, governments will be tempted to fund seeding because it offers the appearance of action at relatively little cost. The sensible course is neither to abandon it nor to expand it uncritically, but to require that operational programmes include a randomised component, so that the clouds left untreated can finally show what the treated ones have achieved.

topic: forecasting the rapid intensification of tropical cyclones
title: When Storms Accelerate
subtitle: Forecasters can now predict where a tropical cyclone will go with impressive accuracy; predicting how strong it will become is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, forecasts of the paths taken by tropical cyclones have improved remarkably. The typical error in a storm's predicted position three days ahead has fallen by more than half, allowing coastal authorities to target evacuations far more precisely than before. Forecasts of intensity, however, have improved much more slowly, and their weakest point is a phenomenon known as rapid intensification, in which a storm's maximum sustained winds increase by at least 55 kilometres per hour within a single day. When this happens shortly before a storm reaches land, the consequences can be severe: residents who have prepared for a modest storm may find themselves facing a far more destructive one, with little time left to leave. Rapid intensification is arguably the most important unsolved problem in tropical forecasting, and understanding why it has resisted solution reveals much about the limits of prediction.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that intensification depends on processes operating at very different scales. Certain large-scale conditions are known to favour it: unusually warm sea water, light winds in the upper atmosphere and moist air surrounding the storm. Yet these conditions are frequently present without rapid strengthening taking place. What seems to decide the outcome are events within the storm's inner core, such as bursts of towering cloud near the eye, many of which are smaller than the grid boxes used by most forecasting models. Yusuf Kaplanoğlu, a modeller at the Anatolian Centre for Atmospheric Modelling, argues that resolution is therefore the key. Experimental models with a grid spacing of one kilometre or less, he reports, reproduce episodes of rapid intensification far more faithfully than coarser ones, although running them over large areas demands computing power that few centres can yet afford.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Soraya Benhaddou, an oceanographer at the Maghreb Institute of Marine Science, believes that too much attention has been paid to the atmosphere and too little to the sea beneath it. Sea surface temperature, she argues, can be misleading. A strong storm stirs the upper ocean, drawing cooler water up from below, and if the warm layer is thin the storm effectively cuts off its own supply of energy. The crucial quantity is not how warm the surface is but how far the warmth extends downwards. Benhaddou has shown that several notorious cases of rapid intensification occurred when storms passed over deep pools of warm water that satellite images of the surface alone had failed to identify. She is right that the ocean has been neglected, and the floats and gliders that measure it deserve more investment. It does not follow, however, that better knowledge of the ocean would by itself solve the problem, since the inner-core processes described above would remain just as difficult to capture.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third approach avoids simulating the physics directly. Trương Quang Vinh, who leads the South China Sea Storm Research Unit, has developed statistical tools that estimate the probability of rapid intensification from a set of environmental indicators, including ocean heat, wind shear and humidity. In several recent seasons this guidance has identified upcoming episodes more reliably than the physics-based models. Trương argues that a probability is a more honest product than a single predicted wind speed, because it conveys the genuine uncertainty involved. Such guidance is undoubtedly valuable to forecasters, who can weigh it against other evidence; conveying it to the public is a harder task, since many people find a forty per cent chance of sudden strengthening difficult to translate into a decision.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That problem of communication is the focus of Inmaculada Ferrándiz, a sociologist who studies evacuation behaviour. Her interviews suggest that people tend to fix on the category of storm announced when they first hear a warning and are slow to revise their plans afterwards. She therefore proposes that authorities should advise residents to prepare for a storm one category stronger than the official forecast. The idea has obvious drawbacks: evacuations are expensive and disruptive, and repeatedly preparing for storms that fail to materialise could erode public trust. Nevertheless, in low-lying coastal regions where moving large populations takes several days, her proposal seems a sensible precaution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Direct observations of the inner core would help all of these approaches, but they are scarce. Specially equipped aircraft can fly through a storm and release instruments that measure conditions as they fall towards the sea, yet such flights are carried out routinely in only a few ocean basins. The majority of the world's tropical cyclones, including many that strike densely populated coasts in Asia, are never sampled in this way. This inequality is rarely discussed, but it is surely one reason why forecast quality varies so widely between regions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There are, nonetheless, grounds for cautious optimism. Average errors in intensity forecasts have begun to fall over the past decade, helped by higher-resolution models and better use of ocean data. The improvement is real, but it is uneven, and the most extreme episodes, in which a storm strengthens by several categories overnight, remain the hardest to anticipate. Since such episodes are precisely the ones that cause the greatest loss of life, the task is far from complete.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: base-rate neglect and the interpretation of medical screening results
title: The Arithmetic of Alarm
subtitle: Why a positive screening result so often means less than patients, and even doctors, assume

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine a screening test for a disease that affects one person in a hundred. The test correctly identifies ninety per cent of those who have the condition, and wrongly flags nine per cent of those who do not. A patient receives a positive result. What is the chance that she is actually ill? When this question is put to medical students, the most common answer lies somewhere around ninety per cent. The correct figure is roughly nine per cent. Out of every thousand people screened, about nine of the ten who are ill will test positive, but so will around eighty-nine of the 990 who are healthy, so fewer than one in ten positive results reflects genuine disease. The error has a name, base-rate neglect, and in my view it is one of the most consequential misunderstandings in modern medicine, precisely because it is made not only by patients but by the professionals advising them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The phenomenon was first documented in laboratory settings, where volunteers asked to estimate probabilities routinely ignored information about how common an event was in favour of vivid, case-specific details. Ottilie Ravnsborg, a cognitive psychologist at the Nordland Institute for Decision Research, argues that the mistake is not a sign of carelessness but a predictable feature of human reasoning: people treat the accuracy of a test as if it were the answer to the question they are really asking. "A test that is right ninety per cent of the time sounds as though it gives you a ninety per cent answer," she explains. "The prevalence of the disease seems like background noise, when in fact it is half of the calculation." Her experiments indicate that greater intelligence or mathematical training offers surprisingly little protection against the error.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Daniel Kiplagat, a medical educator at the Rift Valley College of Health Sciences, has pursued a more optimistic line of enquiry. He has found that when the same problem is presented as counts rather than percentages (of 1,000 people, ten have the disease; nine of these test positive; eighty-nine of the remaining 990 also test positive), the proportion of doctors who reach the correct answer rises from under a fifth to well over half. Kiplagat contends that the difficulty lies less in people's minds than in the format in which statistical information is conventionally delivered, and he has campaigned for leaflets and consent forms to be rewritten accordingly. This is, I believe, the single most practical finding in the field, and it is remarkable how slowly it has been adopted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that reformatting is enough. Marisol Benavidez, who studies health communication at the Andean School of Public Health, points out that natural frequencies work well on paper but are harder to convey in a hurried consultation, where the patient is anxious and the doctor has perhaps ten minutes. In her surveys of general practitioners, many admitted that they had never been taught to interpret screening statistics at all, and some regarded such calculations as the business of laboratory specialists rather than clinicians. She argues that the deeper problem is institutional: medical curricula devote years to anatomy and pharmacology but only a handful of hours to probability. Her diagnosis is persuasive, although I suspect she underestimates how much could be achieved by better materials alone, even without reform of medical training.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences of misunderstanding extend beyond individual anxiety. A false positive typically triggers further investigation, such as a biopsy, a scan or sometimes surgery, each of which carries its own risks and costs. Tadeusz Szczepanik, a health economist at the Baltic Centre for Health Policy, has estimated that in some national mammography programmes the follow-up procedures generated by false alarms consume a larger share of the budget than the initial screening itself. He is careful not to argue that screening should be abandoned; rather, he maintains that the decision to screen a population should take account of these downstream costs, which are frequently left out of official evaluations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a subtler issue, concerning what counts as a genuine positive. Some screening programmes detect abnormalities that meet the technical definition of disease but would never have caused symptoms during the patient's lifetime. This overdiagnosis is invisible in individual cases: a woman whose small tumour was removed cannot know whether it would have harmed her, and she is likely to credit screening with saving her life. Ravnsborg notes that such stories, sincerely told, create powerful public support for programmes whose overall benefit may be modest. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that the public are simply being misled. The benefits of early detection for certain cancers are real, and the task is to weigh them honestly rather than to replace enthusiasm with cynicism.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done? The minimum requirement is that anyone invited for screening should receive the relevant figures in a form they can grasp: not a list of percentages, but a clear statement of how many people out of a given number will be helped, harmed or worried unnecessarily. Kiplagat's research suggests this is achievable at little cost. Whether patients will then make different choices is another matter; early evidence suggests that most still opt to be screened. But the purpose of informed consent was never to reduce uptake. It is to ensure that a decision about one's own body rests on an accurate picture of what the test can and cannot reveal.
