area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: mortality tables and the historical development of life insurance
title: Pricing the Unknowable Hour
subtitle: How records of death turned life insurance from a wager into a science, and what that transformation concealed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of its early history, insuring a life was barely distinguishable from gambling. In the coffee houses of eighteenth-century European ports, merchants could take out policies on the lives of strangers, including politicians and celebrities whose illnesses were reported in the newspapers, and premiums rose and fell with the latest rumours. Contracts were typically short, often covering a single year or a single voyage, and the price was set by negotiation rather than calculation. Governments, meanwhile, raised money by selling annuities, regular payments for the rest of the buyer's life, at prices that frequently took no account of the buyer's age, so that a purchaser of twenty paid the same as one of sixty. It was, in hindsight, an arrangement that rewarded anyone shrewd enough to nominate a healthy child as the life on which the payments depended.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The change came from an unlikely source: the lists of burials and baptisms kept by parish clerks. From the mid-seventeenth century, a handful of enthusiasts began compiling these records into tables showing how many people, out of a given number born, survived to each age. The historian Hester Aldwinckle, of the Thameside Institute for the History of Calculation, argues that the significance of these early life tables lay less in their accuracy, which was poor, than in the idea they embodied: that while no one could predict when a particular individual would die, the deaths of a large population followed patterns regular enough to be relied upon. "The individual remained a mystery," she writes, "but the crowd became legible."

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Turning that insight into a business took nearly a century. The first societies to price policies according to age, founded in the second half of the eighteenth century, charged level premiums: the same annual sum throughout the policy, set high enough in the early years to build a reserve against the greater likelihood of death later on. This required not only a mortality table but also assumptions about the interest the reserve would earn, and the early actuaries were notoriously cautious on both counts. Ingeborg Solheimsdal, an economic historian at the Skagerrak School of Economics, has examined the ledgers of several such societies and found that their tables substantially overstated death rates among their own members, who were mostly prosperous townspeople. The result was large surpluses, which were eventually returned to policyholders as bonuses. Solheimsdal regards this caution as the foundation of the industry's reputation for reliability; competitors who priced more aggressively, she notes, were far more likely to collapse.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the very success of mortality tables raised a question that has never been fully settled: whose deaths should a table describe? A population-wide table averaged together rich and poor, healthy and sick, and so was too pessimistic for some applicants and too optimistic for others. Insurers soon learned to refine their tables, first by sex and occupation, later by medical examination, and to refuse or surcharge those who seemed likely to die early. Rafael Teixidor, a sociologist at the Mediterranean Institute for Social Research, describes this as a gradual shift from pooling risk to sorting it. In his account, the early mutual societies saw themselves as communities in which the fortunate subsidised the unfortunate, whereas the modern insurer aims to charge each customer a price matching his or her own expected cost.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Teixidor's critique is pointed. Every refinement in classification, he argues, makes insurance cheaper for those who need it least and dearer, or simply unobtainable, for those who need it most. The historical record lends some support to this view: in several countries during the early twentieth century, insurers charged higher premiums to entire ethnic groups on the basis of aggregate mortality figures that largely reflected poverty and poor housing rather than anything inherent in the people concerned. It does not follow, however, that classification is inherently unjust. If an insurer ignores information that its competitors use, it will attract a disproportionate number of high-risk customers, and its prices will rise for everyone. Some sorting is therefore unavoidable; the real question is which characteristics a society is prepared to allow insurers to consider.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That question has become sharper with the arrival of genetic testing. An applicant who knows from a test that she carries a gene associated with early heart disease has information her insurer lacks, and may buy more cover as a result. Insurers fear this asymmetry; patient groups fear the opposite, namely that test results will be used to exclude people. Several governments have responded with temporary agreements under which insurers undertake not to ask for genetic results below a certain level of cover. Aldwinckle sees in this a curious return to the eighteenth century, when ignorance about individuals was a practical limitation; today, she observes, it is becoming a deliberate policy choice.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of life insurance is often told as a story of progress from superstition to science, and in one sense it is. But the statistical methods that made the industry stable also changed what insurance was for. A table can tell an insurer, with remarkable precision, how many of a thousand forty-year-olds will die within a decade. It cannot tell anyone whether those who die ought to have been charged more, and that remains a moral question rather than a mathematical one.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: statistical significance thresholds, p-values and the replication crisis
title: The Tyranny of Nought Point Nought Five
subtitle: A single number has come to decide which scientific findings reach print. Should it be abolished, tightened or simply ignored?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many branches of science, a result is considered worth reporting only if it passes a test of 'statistical significance', conventionally defined as a p-value below 0.05. Roughly speaking, the p-value measures how surprising the observed data would be if there were in fact no real effect; a value of 0.05 means that results at least as extreme would turn up about one time in twenty by chance alone. The threshold was originally proposed as a rough guide for deciding whether an experiment merited further investigation. Over the course of the twentieth century, however, it hardened into something closer to a rule of admission: journals favoured significant findings, researchers learned that their careers depended on producing them, and a number intended as a prompt for judgement became a substitute for it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The consequences became difficult to ignore in the early 2010s, when large collaborative projects attempted to repeat well-known experiments in psychology and other fields. In many cases the original effects either disappeared or proved far smaller than first reported. Ludmila Karpenko, a methodologist at the Volga Centre for Research Integrity, argues that the significance threshold was a central cause. Because a result just below 0.05 is publishable and one just above it is not, researchers face a constant temptation to make small analytical choices, such as excluding an awkward participant, trying an alternative measure or stopping data collection once the desired result appears, that nudge borderline findings across the line. None of these decisions need be dishonest in isolation, Karpenko stresses; it is their cumulative effect that fills journals with false positives. She has also shown, using published datasets, that reported p-values cluster suspiciously just below 0.05 in several disciplines, a pattern that is hard to explain unless results are being steered towards the line.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Karpenko's proposed remedy is radical: she would abandon the threshold altogether and require researchers to report exact p-values alongside estimates of how large an effect is and how uncertain that estimate remains. Readers, rather than an arbitrary cut-off, would then decide how much weight a finding deserves. The proposal has attracted wide support among statisticians, and I find its logic compelling. A difference between p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 is, in evidential terms, trivial, and it is absurd that it should determine whether years of work see the light of day.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Sefa Yildirimkaya, who edits a leading journal of experimental economics at the Bosphorus Institute of Social Science, takes a more conservative view. Thresholds, he argues, exist because editors and reviewers must make yes-or-no decisions about what to publish, and because many readers lack the training to interpret a raw p-value sensibly. Remove the line, and the space it occupied will be filled not by careful judgement but by rhetoric, with authors describing ever weaker evidence in confident language. His alternative is to keep a threshold but make it stricter, moving from 0.05 to 0.005 for claims of new discoveries. Simulations conducted by his group suggest that this would cut the rate of false positives substantially, though at the cost of requiring much larger samples.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yildirimkaya's concern about rhetoric deserves to be taken seriously; experience suggests that, given room for interpretation, authors seldom underestimate their own findings. Yet a stricter threshold seems to me to treat the symptom rather than the disease. The fundamental problem is not that the line is in the wrong place but that so much depends on which side of it a result falls. Moving the line to 0.005 would simply relocate the incentive to cross it, and researchers working with rare populations or expensive equipment, who cannot easily enlarge their samples, would be disadvantaged.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third approach shifts attention away from the statistics and towards the process by which research is conducted. Noor Habibullah, a psychologist at the Indus Valley University of Sciences, has championed 'registered reports', a publishing format in which journals agree to publish a study on the basis of its question and methods before any data are collected. Because acceptance no longer depends on the result, there is no reason to massage the analysis. Critics have objected that the format suits laboratory experiments better than exploratory or observational work, where the most interesting questions often emerge from the data themselves. Early evaluations by Habibullah's team found that registered reports produced positive results in under half of cases, compared with over ninety per cent in conventionally published papers in the same fields, a contrast that says a great deal about how the usual literature has been filtered.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these reforms is a complete answer, and they are not mutually exclusive. A journal could, for instance, adopt registered reports for confirmatory studies while asking all authors to report effect sizes and uncertainty in full; such combinations are already being tried in a few fields. But the debate has already achieved something valuable: it has reminded scientists that statistics is a tool for reasoning under uncertainty, not a machine for producing certainty. A field that treats a single number as a verdict will eventually be embarrassed by its own record, as several have already discovered. The more encouraging lesson is that the recent crisis was detected by scientists themselves, using the very statistical tools whose misuse had caused it.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: the psychology of risk perception: dread, familiarity and public priorities
title: Fear by Numbers
subtitle: The risks that frighten us most are rarely the ones most likely to harm us. But is that really irrational?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the year following a serious rail accident, one European country recorded a marked fall in train travel and a corresponding rise in journeys by car. Because driving is, mile for mile, many times more dangerous than rail travel, analysts later estimated that the switch had caused more road deaths than the original crash. Episodes of this kind are frequently cited as proof that public attitudes to risk are hopelessly at odds with the evidence. People fear flying more than driving, nuclear power more than coal, and rare diseases more than common ones, even though the statistics point in the opposite direction in every case. The temptation for experts is to conclude that the public simply cannot count. That conclusion, I shall argue, is both too hasty and too convenient.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The systematic study of risk perception began in the 1970s, when psychologists asked members of the public to rate dozens of hazards, from bicycles to pesticides, on a range of characteristics. Matthias Oberholzer, of the Alpine Institute for Behavioural Science, has spent much of his career refining this approach. His work suggests that people's judgements are organised around two main dimensions. The first he calls 'dread': whether a hazard is perceived as uncontrollable, catastrophic and likely to kill many people at once. The second concerns familiarity: whether the risk is well understood, observable and long established. Hazards that score high on dread and low on familiarity, such as nuclear accidents or novel viruses, provoke demands for strict regulation regardless of how many deaths they actually cause. These ratings have proved remarkably stable across countries, although later surveys found that groups with less social and economic power tend to rate most hazards as more serious, a finding that hints at the role of vulnerability in shaping fear.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Oberholzer is careful to present these patterns as descriptions rather than errors. Others have been less restrained. Ilse Dahlqvist, a decision scientist at the Oresund School of Economics, argues that dread and unfamiliarity are classic sources of bias that distort public spending. She points to estimates that, in several wealthy countries, the cost of preventing one statistical death varies by a factor of a thousand or more between different government programmes, with the most expensive measures concentrated on dreaded risks such as radiation, while cheap and effective interventions, such as improving dangerous road junctions, remain underfunded. If resources were allocated purely by lives saved per unit of money, she calculates, many thousands more people could be kept alive each year at no additional cost.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dahlqvist's arithmetic is difficult to dispute, and the inconsistencies she documents are real. However, her argument rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that the only thing that matters about a risk is the expected number of deaths it causes. Amara Tamboura, an anthropologist at the Sahel Centre for Social Research, rejects this premise. In her fieldwork among communities living near industrial sites, she found that residents were less concerned with the probability of harm than with who had imposed it, whether they had been consulted, and whether anyone would be held accountable if things went wrong. A risk accepted voluntarily, such as skiing, is morally different, she argues, from one imposed by a distant company, even if the numbers are identical.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This seems to me an important corrective. It is not irrational to care about fairness, consent and trust, and a society that weighed every hazard solely by its death toll would be making a value judgement of its own, merely one that happens to suit those who produce the statistics. Catastrophic risks raise a further point. A single event killing a thousand people may disrupt a community far more profoundly than a thousand separate deaths spread over a decade, and the public instinct to treat it as worse may reflect this rather than a failure of arithmetic.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that public perceptions should simply be accepted as they are. Joost Haverkamp, a communication researcher at the Lowlands Institute for Media Studies, has shown that perceptions of risk are strongly shaped by media attention, which in turn is driven by novelty and drama rather than by frequency. In one analysis, he found that a rare hazard received several hundred times more news coverage per death than a common one such as heart disease. Coverage also tends to fade quickly once a hazard ceases to be new, even if it continues to claim lives at the same rate. Haverkamp argues that this does not reflect irrational audiences so much as an information environment that systematically distorts what they see, and that the remedy lies with journalists and editors rather than with campaigns to 'correct' the public.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The rail example with which this article began illustrates both sides of the problem. The travellers who abandoned trains were, in a narrow sense, mistaken: they exchanged a small risk for a larger one. But their reaction was shaped by vivid coverage, by a sense that the railway had failed them, and by the comforting illusion of control that comes from holding a steering wheel. Any serious attempt to improve decisions about risk must engage with these factors rather than dismissing them. Experts who wish to be heard would do better to ask why people fear what they fear than to repeat, ever more loudly, that they are wrong.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: the hot hand in sport, the gambler's fallacy and the statistical bias in streak analysis
title: Hot Hands and Cold Logic
subtitle: How a celebrated example of human irrationality was overturned by a flaw hidden in its own arithmetic

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has watched a basketball game will be familiar with the idea that a player can become 'hot'. After three or four successful shots in a row, team-mates look for that player and the crowd expects the next attempt to succeed as well. The mirror image of this belief is found in casinos, where a gambler who has seen a long run of red may conclude that black is now 'due'. For several decades both convictions were treated by psychologists as classic errors in reasoning about chance. The story of how one of them came to be rehabilitated is, in my view, among the most instructive episodes in modern behavioural science, not least because the mistake that was eventually uncovered lay with the experts rather than with the public.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against the hot hand was first set out by a team led by the cognitive psychologist Corentin Lavasseur at the Ardennes Institute for Cognitive Science. Lavasseur's group examined the shooting records of professional players across an entire season and compared two figures: the proportion of shots scored immediately after a run of three hits, and the proportion scored after a run of three misses. The first figure was not higher; if anything, it was slightly lower. The team concluded that the hot hand was an illusion, generated by a mistaken intuition about what randomness looks like. They cited experiments in which volunteers asked to write down an imaginary sequence of coin tosses switch between heads and tails far too often, producing fewer long runs than a genuinely random process would. Faced with real sequences, which inevitably contain such runs, people see patterns where none exist. The argument was elegant and economical, and it is easy to understand why it was quickly absorbed into textbooks as a model demonstration of human bias.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Doubts emerged first from those who knew the sport well. A match, they pointed out, is hardly a controlled experiment. A player who believes himself to be on a streak may attempt more ambitious shots from greater distances, while opponents who notice his success are likely to defend him more closely. Either change would lower his chances on each attempt, so a flat success rate could conceal a genuine improvement in skill. To remove these complications, the sports scientist Thandeka Mabuyakhulu studied free throws and organised shooting contests in which the position and difficulty of every attempt were fixed in advance. She found a modest tendency for success to follow success. Her samples, however, were small, and supporters of the original finding dismissed the effect as statistical noise.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yevgenia Strelbitska, a statistician at the Podillia School of Mathematics, noticed that the method used by Lavasseur's team contained a subtle bias. When one looks at a finite sequence and selects only the attempts that immediately follow a run of successes, the expected proportion of successes among them is lower than the true underlying rate, even if each attempt is entirely independent of the others. Strelbitska illustrated the point with a simple case: if a fair coin is tossed four times, and one records, for each sequence, the proportion of heads among tosses that come straight after a head, the average of those proportions is roughly forty per cent rather than fifty. So finding no difference between the two figures was not evidence against streaks at all; it was what one would expect if a real positive effect were being masked by the bias. It would be wrong to regard this as a careless oversight. The error escaped the attention of highly competent researchers and reviewers for almost thirty years, which is a humbling reminder of how counter-intuitive probability can be even for specialists.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Once the bias was corrected, the original records showed a hit rate after a streak several percentage points higher than after a run of misses. Hamid Shahbazfar, who directs the Elburz Sports Analytics Laboratory, accepts that the effect is real but warns against overstating it. Surveys of supporters and coaches, he notes, suggest that they believe a hot player's chances improve by something like fifteen or twenty points, several times more than the data support. Some commentators have declared that the original researchers were simply wrong about human cognition. I find this conclusion too hasty. The public's intuition was correct in direction but greatly inflated in size, and an exaggerated belief remains a bias even when it contains a grain of truth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The gambler's fallacy has fared differently. A roulette wheel has no memory. Yet casino records show that, after a long run of one colour, bettors increasingly place their chips on the other. Mabuyakhulu has proposed that the two beliefs are linked by a single principle: people expect momentum from sources they regard as animate, such as athletes, and self-correction from those they regard as mechanical, such as wheels and dice. The idea is attractive, since it would explain why the same person can hold both views simultaneously, but it has so far been tested only with laboratory tasks rather than with real wagers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The broader lesson concerns how claims of irrationality are evaluated. Researchers who identify a flaw in ordinary thinking rely on statistical tools, and those tools can themselves contain hidden flaws. The hot hand was rescued only because the original shot-by-shot records had been preserved for others to examine. This argues strongly for the routine publication of data and analysis methods alongside findings. More generally, it suggests that confident verdicts about public error deserve the same scrutiny that researchers apply to the beliefs they criticise.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: Simpson's paradox: aggregation reversals, confounding and the causal interpretation of combined data
title: When the Whole Contradicts Its Parts
subtitle: Combining figures from different groups can reverse what each group shows, and deciding which picture to trust is not a purely statistical question

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a hypothetical but entirely realistic comparison, two hospitals each treat a thousand patients for the same condition. At Northgate, 90 per cent survive; at Riverside, only 84 per cent do. Few people would hesitate to choose Northgate. Yet when the patients are divided into mild and severe cases, Riverside turns out to achieve the better survival rate in both groups. The explanation is that Riverside, as a regional referral centre, receives a far larger share of severe cases, which drag down its overall figure. This reversal, in which a trend present in every subgroup disappears or is inverted when the groups are combined, is known as Simpson's paradox. It is often presented in textbooks as a curiosity, a puzzle to entertain students. That presentation is, I believe, seriously misleading, because reversals of this kind turn up regularly in the data on which public decisions are based.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanism is straightforward once it has been identified. Severity of illness affects both the choice of hospital and the chance of survival, and because it is unevenly distributed between the two hospitals, it distorts the overall comparison. Statisticians call such a factor a confounding variable. How often it produces outright reversals is harder to establish, but a review of published hospital performance data by the health-services researcher Iolo Gwalchmai, of the Usk Institute for Health Evaluation, suggested that roughly one comparison in eight might change direction if patient mix were properly taken into account. Gwalchmai himself regards this estimate as provisional, since it depends on which patient characteristics are recorded in the first place; differences between patients that never appear in the records cannot be adjusted for.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The obvious lesson might seem to be that data should always be broken down as finely as possible. The statistician Aurelio Fontecilla, of the Andes Centre for Statistical Science, argues that this advice is not merely incomplete but sometimes dangerous. Whether disaggregation clarifies or distorts, he points out, depends entirely on the causal relationships among the variables. Suppose a new drug works by lowering blood pressure. If patients are grouped according to their blood pressure after treatment, the comparison within each group removes the very pathway through which the drug acts, and the drug may appear useless or even harmful. In such a case it is the combined figure that tells the truth. Fontecilla's point seems to me the single most important insight in this whole area, and it is striking how rarely introductory statistics courses address the question of when, rather than how, data ought to be divided.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences extend well beyond medicine. Ragnhild Svartdal, an education researcher at the Telemark School of Social Inquiry, examined the published results of a secondary school whose overall examination performance had risen steadily for five years. When she separated pupils by their level of attainment on entry, she found that results had fallen within every band. The apparent improvement was due entirely to a change in the school's intake, which had come to include a higher proportion of pupils who were already high achievers. Svartdal has argued that performance tables should routinely report results by entry band so that families can see whether a school is adding value or merely recruiting well.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Economic statistics are equally vulnerable. Edem Dzokoto, a labour economist, has documented periods in which the median wage across a whole economy fell even though wages rose for workers at every level of education. The overall decline reflected the arrival of a large number of younger and less qualified workers, not a deterioration in anyone's pay. Dzokoto's concern is less with the arithmetic than with its use: governments, he observes, tend to cite the subgroup figures when these flatter them and the aggregate when it does, and opposition parties do the reverse. I would go further. The principal danger posed by aggregation paradoxes is not that people fail to understand them, but that those who do understand them can choose the level of analysis that suits their argument.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Can ordinary readers be equipped to resist such manipulation? Nadezhda Kolomiytseva, a cognitive psychologist, gave participants tables of the hospital kind and asked them which option they would choose. Even participants with statistical training generally favoured the option with the better aggregate figures, regardless of what the subgroups showed. When the same information was accompanied by a simple diagram indicating which factors influenced which, however, the proportion of sound decisions roughly doubled. These results are encouraging, but they should not be overstated. A diagram helps only if its arrows are drawn correctly, and in many real disputes it is precisely the causal structure that is contested.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the paradox ultimately reveals is that data do not speak for themselves. Deciding which comparison is meaningful requires assumptions about cause and effect that cannot be read from the numbers alone. Advanced statistical techniques can refine an analysis, but they cannot supply those assumptions. For that reason, the most valuable habit any analyst can cultivate is not technical sophistication but candour: stating plainly what has been assumed about how the world works, so that others can judge whether the conclusions follow.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: opinion polling: falling response rates, weighting and the accuracy of election polls
title: The Missing Respondents
subtitle: Opinion polls are more accurate than their critics allow, but the problems they face are changing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years, after an election result defies the final opinion polls, a familiar chorus declares that polling is broken. Newspapers that commissioned the surveys publish columns denouncing them, and politicians who trailed in the polls but won insist they never believed the numbers. These obituaries are, in my view, premature. A comparison of several thousand pre-election polls across more than thirty countries, carried out by the political scientist Rodrigo Albornoz and colleagues at the Cuyo Institute of Electoral Studies, found that the average error in polls conducted in the final week of a campaign has remained roughly constant for half a century. Polling has not become worse; what has changed is how much attention its failures receive, and the methods required to keep it accurate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theory behind the opinion poll is simple. If every member of a population has an equal chance of being selected, and every person selected agrees to take part, a sample of around a thousand people will estimate the share of the vote for a party to within about three percentage points on nineteen occasions out of twenty. This figure, the familiar 'margin of error', is printed beneath almost every published poll. The second condition is the one that has broken down. In the era of landline telephones, pollsters could expect a reply from more than a third of the households they called. Today, with unknown numbers screened by caller identification and many people simply unwilling to talk to strangers, response rates for telephone surveys frequently fall below one in twenty.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A low response rate is not in itself fatal, however. Sunniva Kjaervik, a survey methodologist at the Hardanger Centre for Survey Research, has shown that what matters is not how many people decline, but whether those who decline differ from those who take part in ways that are related to how they vote. To deal with such differences, pollsters use weighting: if young men are under-represented in the sample, the answers of the young men who did respond are counted more heavily. Weighting by age, sex and region has long been standard. The difficulty, Kjaervik notes, is that it works only if the pollster has chosen the right characteristics. Several notable misses in recent years were later traced to the failure to weight by educational qualifications, at a time when graduates were both more willing to answer surveys and more likely to support particular parties.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Albornoz believes that a more intractable problem lies behind these episodes. People who distrust journalists, politicians and official bodies, he argues, are also less willing to give their time to a polling company, and in several countries the same group has been disproportionately attracted to parties that campaign against the political establishment. He supports this with evidence from post-election studies in which voters were contacted repeatedly: those reached only after many attempts were markedly more likely to have backed anti-establishment candidates. Because no census records a person's level of trust, this bias cannot be corrected by weighting to known population totals. I find his argument both persuasive and troubling, precisely because the standard remedies of the profession cannot reach it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One response has been to abandon random selection altogether. Many polls are now conducted through online panels whose members have volunteered to complete surveys in return for small payments. Such panels are cheap and can supply samples of tens of thousands, and a team led by Ilan Gefen at the Carmel School of Data Science has argued that, combined with sophisticated statistical modelling, they can match or even outperform traditional methods. Their record in several recent elections is genuinely impressive. Yet the models depend on assumptions about how volunteers relate to the wider population that are difficult to test until after the votes have been counted, and no quantity of data can by itself remove a bias in the way respondents were recruited. A larger self-selected sample is simply a more precise estimate of the wrong quantity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The way polls are reported adds a further layer of confusion. A shift of two points between surveys is routinely presented as news, though it lies well within the stated margin of error. Readers, understandably, assume that the printed margin covers every possible source of error. In fact it accounts only for the chance variation that comes from sampling, not for non-response, flawed weighting or late changes of mind. Kjaervik estimates that, once these sources are included, the realistic uncertainty in a single poll is roughly double the published figure. Pollsters would serve the public better by publishing these wider ranges, even if the resulting headlines are less dramatic.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that polls should be abandoned. The alternatives proposed by their critics, from betting markets to counts of supportive messages on social media, have generally performed worse when tested against actual results. It would also help if commentators remembered that a poll describes opinion at the moment it was taken and is not a forecast of a vote that may be weeks away. The task is rather to treat a poll as what it is: a carefully constructed estimate, whose precision depends on assumptions that deserve to be stated as openly as the numbers themselves.

title: The Price of a Life Not Yet Lost
subtitle: Governments routinely attach a monetary value to statistical lives. The figure is indispensable, but what it measures is widely misunderstood

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a transport ministry decides whether to install crash barriers on a stretch of rural road, or an environmental agency considers tightening limits on an industrial pollutant, someone must eventually compare the cost of the measure with the deaths it is expected to prevent. To make that comparison, governments in many countries use a figure known as the value of a statistical life, which in wealthy economies typically lies somewhere between three and ten million dollars. Whenever the practice comes to public attention, it provokes indignation: officials, it is said, are putting a price on human life. The indignation is understandable but, I would argue, misplaced. Every decision about safety spending implies some valuation, since no society can spend without limit on preventing death. Refusing to state the figure does not avoid placing a value on life; it merely conceals the value that has been placed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the confusion arises from the word 'life'. The figure does not represent what any identifiable person is worth, and no one proposes that a government should refuse to rescue a trapped miner because the operation costs more than the official number. It describes instead how much people are willing to pay for very small reductions in risk. Suppose that each of a hundred thousand people would pay fifty dollars a year for a measure that lowers their annual chance of dying by one in a hundred thousand. Between them they would pay five million dollars, and on average one death would be prevented. The value of a statistical life in this case is therefore five million dollars. In practice, economists estimate such figures in two ways: by observing the choices people actually make, or by asking them what they would choose.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first approach is associated above all with the labour economist Soo-ah Yeom, whose studies compare the wages of workers in occupations with different fatality rates. Other things being equal, she finds, people in more dangerous jobs are paid a premium, and the size of that premium reveals how they trade money against risk. Critics object that workers frequently have little idea of the actual hazards they face, and that in many labour markets they lack the bargaining power to demand proper compensation; both factors would tend to make the resulting estimates too low. Yeom accepts these limitations, but maintains that figures drawn from real decisions, made with real money at stake, are inherently more trustworthy than answers to hypothetical questions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Those hypothetical questions are the province of the second approach, in which large samples of the public are asked directly how much they would pay for a given reduction in risk. The economist Benedetta Ghisolfi has spent much of her career designing such surveys, and her own findings have exposed their central weakness. Respondents typically offer almost the same sum for a reduction of one in a hundred thousand as for a reduction three times as large, which implies valuations differing by a factor of three for the same life. Ghisolfi concludes that most people cannot meaningfully distinguish between tiny probabilities, and she has shown that presenting risks as grids of coloured dots makes answers more consistent. The improvement is real but partial. In my view, her results are a reason to interpret survey estimates with caution, not to discard them, since the alternative sources of evidence are flawed in other ways.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Further difficulties emerge when the logic of willingness to pay is followed to its conclusion. Because richer people can afford to pay more for safety, a strictly consistent approach would assign higher values to lives in wealthy regions than in poor ones. Most governments sidestep this by applying a single national figure to everyone, a choice that is ethically defensible even if it sits awkwardly with the theory. Dragos Patrascanu, a health economist, has pressed a different refinement: since preventing the death of a child secures many more years of life than preventing that of a very old person, he argues that policies should be assessed in terms of life-years saved. When one ministry adopted a version of this approach, protests from pensioners' organisations forced its withdrawal within months. Patrascanu's reasoning is internally coherent, yet I do not believe it should prevail. A method of valuing lives that large sections of the public regard as unjust cannot provide a durable basis for policy, however rigorous its arithmetic.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The philosopher Sieni Fa'asavalu raises a different objection. A single figure, she points out, treats all deaths as interchangeable, whereas people care a great deal about how they might die. Surveys consistently show that deaths from cancer, or from deliberate attacks, are dreaded far more than deaths in road accidents. Fa'asavalu contends that these preferences are legitimate and that regulators should be willing to spend more to prevent deaths that people particularly fear. Others reply that this would allow public anxiety, however poorly founded, to distort the allocation of limited resources.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the strongest argument for the value of a statistical life, however, concerns consistency rather than any particular number. At present, different agencies within the same government often use very different figures, or none at all. The result is that some regulations costing many millions per death averted go ahead while cheaper measures that would save more lives elsewhere are never adopted. The greatest failure of current practice lies not in the existence of a price for risk, but in the inconsistency with which it is applied.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: the economics and psychology of state lotteries: expected value, regressivity and earmarked revenue
title: A Tax on Hope?
subtitle: State lotteries raise vast sums for public causes, but who pays for them, and why do people keep playing?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In almost every country that operates a national lottery, players as a group receive back in prizes only around half of what they spend. The rest goes to the state, to designated causes and to the operator. By the standards of conventional economics, then, a lottery ticket is a poor purchase: its expected value is well below its price, and anyone who buys tickets regularly can be almost certain to lose money over time. For decades economists have treated the persistence of lottery playing as a puzzle, and many have been content to label players irrational. That label, I believe, is applied too quickly. It overlooks what people may actually be buying, and it diverts attention from the more troubling question of who pays for lotteries and who benefits from them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economist Rosalía Quispecahuana, of the Altiplano Institute for Economic Research, argues that a ticket buys more than a chance of a prize. In interviews with regular players, she found that many valued the days between purchase and draw, during which they planned how they would spend their winnings. On this view, the ticket is partly a licence to daydream, and the pleasure of anticipation is a genuine benefit that conventional calculations ignore. Quispecahuana adds a second point. For a household on a low income, no realistic programme of saving can produce a life-changing sum, so a lottery may be the only route, however improbable, to a dramatic change in circumstances. These arguments make lottery playing intelligible. They do not, in my view, make it a wise use of scarce money, particularly for those who can least afford the losses.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Psychologists offer explanations of a different kind. Teodor Parvulescu, a cognitive psychologist, has shown that people consistently overweight very small probabilities, treating a one-in-ten-million chance as though it were far larger. Lottery design, he argues, exploits this tendency. In one of his experiments, participants who had chosen their own numbers demanded a significantly higher price to sell their ticket than those whose numbers had been assigned at random, even though the chance of winning was identical. The freedom to pick numbers, Parvulescu concludes, creates an illusion of control that makes the game feel more like a test of skill than a pure gamble. Near misses, such as matching five of six numbers, appear to have a similar effect, encouraging players to buy again rather than to conclude that the odds are hopeless.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever the motives of individual players, the aggregate pattern is clear. Studies in several countries have found that households with the lowest incomes spend a considerably larger share of their income on lottery tickets than wealthier ones. Part of the explanation lies in geography: Nkandu Chilufya, a specialist in public finance, has mapped ticket outlets and found them heavily concentrated in poorer districts, where they are more accessible than banks. Chilufya describes the lottery as an implicit tax, and one more regressive than almost any other in the public finances. Defenders reply that, unlike a tax, buying a ticket is voluntary. The distinction is real, but I think it carries less weight than they suppose when lotteries are promoted through extensive advertising campaigns funded by the state itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Governments often justify lotteries by pointing to the good causes they support, such as schools, sport and cultural heritage. Yet research on earmarked revenues suggests that lottery money frequently replaces funding that would otherwise have come from general taxation, so that total spending on the favoured causes rises far less than the publicity implies. There is also the question of who uses what is funded. Opera houses, museums and heritage sites, which receive substantial lottery support, are visited disproportionately by people with higher incomes and education. The combination of revenue drawn largely from poorer households and spending that favours the better-off amounts to a transfer from poorer citizens to richer ones, and this, to my mind, is the most serious charge against lotteries as currently run.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Several alternatives have been proposed. Quispecahuana is an enthusiastic advocate of prize-linked savings accounts, in which the interest that would normally be paid to depositors is pooled and distributed as prizes in regular draws, while every saver retains the original deposit. Trials in a number of countries have found that such accounts attract households that previously saved little or nothing. Parvulescu is more cautious, warning that the appeal of a new product may fade once the novelty wears off. His caution is reasonable, but the evidence so far seems to me strong enough to justify offering these accounts far more widely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Abolishing lotteries outright would almost certainly be counterproductive, since the demand they satisfy would simply move to unregulated and often illegal forms of gambling. Nor is there any need to treat players with condescension: people are entitled to spend money on hope, just as they spend it on other kinds of entertainment. The more productive approach is to recognise lotteries for what they are: instruments for raising public revenue. Judged in that way, they should be held to the same standards of fairness and transparency that we expect of any tax.

area: statistics, probability and risk in society
topic: regression to the mean and the misattribution of improvement to interventions
title: The Pull of the Average
subtitle: Why extreme results tend to be followed by ordinary ones, and how this simple fact has misled coaches, doctors and policy-makers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At a football academy in a mid-sized European city, coaches kept careful notes on how young players responded to feedback. Those who received warm praise after an outstanding match, the notes showed, usually played less well the following week, while those who were sharply criticised after a poor performance tended to improve. The coaches drew the natural conclusion: praise made players complacent, and criticism sharpened them. The conclusion was almost certainly wrong. The pattern in their notes would have appeared even if the coaches had said nothing at all, because it reflects a statistical phenomenon known as regression to the mean. In my judgement, this is one of the most widespread and least recognised sources of error in the evaluation of almost anything, from medical treatments to government policy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle is simple to state. Any measured performance can be thought of as the sum of two parts: a relatively stable component reflecting underlying ability or conditions, and a fluctuating element of chance. A result that is exceptionally good or bad is likely to have been produced by an unusually large contribution from chance, in one direction or the other. Since that contribution is not repeated on the next occasion, the following result will typically lie closer to the average. The more strongly a measurement depends on luck, the more pronounced the effect becomes. It is often said that extreme results are 'pulled' back towards the mean, but the metaphor is unhelpful. Nothing is pulling. The apparent movement arises solely because the extreme case was selected for attention at the very moment when chance happened to favour, or disfavour, it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The consequences for public policy can be substantial. Road authorities commonly install speed cameras at locations that have recently experienced a cluster of serious accidents. In the following years, accident numbers at those sites almost invariably fall, and the cameras receive the credit. Eirik Skjelbred, a transport statistician at the Vestland Institute of Road Safety, pointed out that sites chosen because of an unusually bad period would be expected to record fewer accidents afterwards whether or not anything was done. By comparing camera sites with similar locations that had suffered comparable spikes but received no cameras, he estimated that between a third and a half of the reduction previously attributed to cameras was due to regression alone. Skjelbred is careful to stress that the remaining effect is genuine and that cameras save lives. The real cost of the overestimate, however, is that it distorts comparisons between safety measures, favouring those that happen to be introduced in response to bad years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Medicine provides perhaps the most consequential examples. People tend to seek treatment when their symptoms are at their worst, whether the problem is back pain, headaches or high blood pressure, and many such conditions fluctuate naturally. Improvement after a visit to the doctor is therefore likely regardless of what the doctor does. The clinical epidemiologist Chiamaka Obidike argues that this explains why numerous ineffective remedies retain loyal followings, and why only trials that compare treated patients with an untreated control group can separate genuine effects from natural recovery. She goes further, suggesting that a considerable part of what is routinely described as the placebo effect is in fact regression to the mean, since patients enrolled in trials are typically selected because their readings are unusually high. This claim is plausible, but it remains disputed by many researchers who study placebos and who point to measurable physiological responses to inactive treatments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Education offers a further illustration. Maialen Gorostiaga, an educational researcher, has examined programmes that direct additional support to the lowest-performing schools in a given year. Many of these schools leave the lowest category the following year, and their improvement is frequently cited as evidence that the support worked. Gorostiaga shows that a large share of this improvement would have occurred anyway. She is equally concerned about the opposite case: schools that achieve outstanding results one year often decline the next, and their head teachers may be criticised or even dismissed for what is largely a statistical inevitability. Her recommendation is that schools be judged on averages taken over several years rather than on single annual results.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Averaging certainly reduces the influence of chance, but it carries a cost that Gorostiaga's proposal tends to understate. A school whose results are genuinely deteriorating, perhaps because of the departure of experienced staff, may go unnoticed for two or three years while a multi-year average slowly catches up with reality. I would therefore not dismiss a single bad year as mere noise. The sensible response is to treat it as a signal worth investigating, while declining to draw firm conclusions until further evidence is available.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What unites these cases is a single structural feature: something is selected for attention because of an extreme value, and its subsequent change is then interpreted as the effect of whatever was done in the meantime. Wherever this sequence occurs, regression should be suspected, and the remedy is almost always the same: compare the selected cases with similar ones that received no intervention. Basic instruction in this principle ought to be part of the training of every manager, doctor and policy-maker. It would cost very little, especially when set against the resources currently wasted on interventions that receive credit for improvements they did not cause.

topic: satellite-based quantum key distribution and its practical limits
title: Secrets from Orbit
subtitle: Sending quantum keys by satellite promises communication that cannot be cracked, but the engineering and the economics remain hotly contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of the encryption that protects online banking, medical records and diplomatic messages depends on mathematical problems that conventional computers find extremely hard to solve. Quantum key distribution, usually shortened to QKD, takes a fundamentally different approach: its security rests on physics rather than on mathematics. Two parties exchange individual particles of light whose polarisation encodes the digits of a secret key, and because measuring a quantum state inevitably disturbs it, any eavesdropper introduces errors that the legitimate users can detect. The principle was demonstrated in laboratories in the 1980s, and commercial systems running over optical fibre have been available for nearly two decades. Their weakness is distance. Photons are absorbed and scattered by glass, and since quantum states cannot be copied, the signal cannot simply be amplified as in ordinary telecommunications. Beyond roughly a hundred kilometres, the rate at which key material can be generated falls to impractically low levels.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Satellites appear to offer an escape. Most of the path between orbit and the ground passes through near-vacuum, and only the final ten kilometres or so cross dense atmosphere. Over the past decade, a series of experiments has used spacecraft in low orbit to share keys between ground stations more than a thousand kilometres apart. Dr Wanjiku Kipchumba, who leads the optical ground station programme at the Highland Institute of Photonics, describes these results as proof that 'the distance problem has been solved in principle'. Yet the phrase 'in principle' carries considerable weight. A satellite in low orbit passes over any given station for only a few minutes at a time, the links function only at night and under cloudless skies, and the volume of key exchanged during a single pass is measured in kilobits rather than gigabits.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such limitations have led some engineers to question the whole enterprise. Ferenc Szabadi, a network architect at the Danubian Telecommunications Laboratory, argues that weather alone makes satellite QKD unsuitable for anything resembling a dependable service. His group modelled a network of ground stations in central Europe and found that, even with stations spread across several countries, there would be prolonged spells in winter when no link could be established anywhere. Szabadi's figures are sobering, but they rest on an assumption that may not hold: that keys must be generated at the moment they are needed. In practice, key material can be stockpiled during clear nights and consumed gradually, much as a reservoir stores rainfall for the dry months.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A deeper objection concerns trust. Many current satellite schemes use the spacecraft as a so-called trusted node: it generates one key with a ground station, another with a second station, and then combines them so that the two stations end up sharing a secret. The arrangement is safe only if the satellite itself is secure, which means that users must place their confidence in whoever builds and operates it. Cristina Ulloa, a cryptographer at the Pacific Coast Institute for Information Security, points out that this reintroduces precisely the kind of dependence that QKD was supposed to eliminate. Her preferred alternative is entanglement-based distribution, in which the satellite sends pairs of linked photons to the two stations and never learns the key at all. Entanglement-based links have been demonstrated, but their key rates are lower still, by a factor of several hundred in the trials Ulloa cites.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Then there is the matter of cost. A single quantum satellite, including its launch, has been estimated to cost between fifty and one hundred and fifty million dollars, and a constellation large enough to offer continuous coverage would require dozens. Gunnar Bjarnason, an economist who advises a northern European space agency, believes such sums are justifiable only for a narrow range of clients, namely governments, central banks and perhaps the operators of critical infrastructure, whose secrets must remain confidential for decades. For ordinary commercial traffic, he argues, the newly standardised 'post-quantum' algorithms, which run on existing hardware and are designed to resist attack by future quantum computers, will be sufficient and vastly cheaper.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to treat the two technologies as rivals. Post-quantum algorithms rest on mathematical problems that are believed, not proven, to be hard; an unexpected advance in mathematics could undermine them, just as it might undermine the schemes they are replacing. QKD, by contrast, offers security that does not depend on assumptions about an attacker's computing power. The sensible course for organisations with long-lived secrets is to layer the two, so that an adversary would have to defeat both. Kipchumba's team has already tested such a hybrid link, combining a satellite-delivered key with a post-quantum exchange, and reported no measurable loss in performance.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is less often acknowledged is that the security proofs for QKD apply to idealised equipment. Real detectors and lasers have imperfections, and over the years researchers have exploited several of them in laboratory attacks, for instance by blinding detectors with bright light so that they register only what the attacker chooses. Manufacturers have patched each vulnerability as it emerged, but this history should temper claims that the technology is 'unhackable'. Satellite QKD is a remarkable scientific achievement and a valuable addition to the security toolkit; it is not, and probably never will be, a universal replacement for the cryptography on which the internet already relies.

topic: optical atomic clocks and the proposed redefinition of the second
title: Beyond Caesium
subtitle: A new generation of optical clocks could force a change in the definition of the second, but scientists disagree about when, and why, it should happen

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since 1967 the second has been defined by the behaviour of caesium atoms: it is the duration of a fixed number of oscillations of the radiation absorbed when those atoms switch between two energy states. The best caesium clocks would neither gain nor lose a second in roughly a hundred million years. For most purposes, from satellite navigation to financial trading and the synchronisation of power grids, that is more than adequate. Over the past two decades, however, a rival has emerged. Optical clocks, which exploit transitions in atoms such as strontium or ytterbium, oscillate at frequencies around a hundred thousand times higher, dividing time into far finer slices. The most accurate of them would drift by less than a second over a period longer than the present age of the universe.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Such precision has made the caesium definition look increasingly dated, and the international body responsible for measurement standards has drawn up a plan for replacing it. Yet the transition is less straightforward than the raw performance figures suggest. Professor Annelie Esterhuizen of the Southern Metrology Institute notes that a definition must be not only accurate but reproducible in many countries. At present only a handful of laboratories operate optical clocks of the highest quality, and their results must be compared with one another before any of them can serve as a reference. Comparing clocks on different continents is itself a formidable task, because the satellite links used to connect them introduce uncertainties larger than those of the clocks themselves. Links through optical fibre perform far better, but they cannot yet cross oceans.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is also the awkward question of which atom to choose. Strontium, ytterbium, aluminium ions and several other candidates each have champions, and each has particular strengths. Dr Takeshi Hoshino, who directs a frequency standards group at the Kanto Institute of Physical Measurement, has proposed sidestepping the dispute by defining the second through a weighted average of several transitions. His scheme would avoid tying the unit to a single element whose limitations might become apparent only later. Critics reply that an average is harder to explain and to realise in practice. Hoshino's idea is more elegant than it first appears, but it seems likely to remain a fallback rather than the first choice.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One of the most intriguing consequences of optical clocks has little to do with timekeeping. According to general relativity, clocks run more slowly in stronger gravitational fields, so a clock raised by a single centimetre ticks very slightly faster. Optical clocks are now sensitive enough to detect this difference. Beatriz Quaresma, a geophysicist at the Atlantic Geodesy Centre, sees in this a new tool for mapping the Earth's gravitational field, with possible applications in monitoring volcanoes, tracking underground water and determining height above sea level more precisely than conventional surveys allow. Her team has used a transportable clock to compare heights between mountain and lowland sites hundreds of kilometres apart. Such measurements could be particularly valuable in remote regions, where traditional levelling surveys are slow and expensive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This sensitivity, however, cuts both ways. If a clock's rate depends on its height, then a definition of the second must specify the gravitational conditions under which it is realised, and those conditions must be known to an accuracy matching that of the clock itself. In effect, metrologists will need to know the Earth's gravitational field better than geodesists currently do, which means that the two disciplines are becoming dependent on each other in ways that neither anticipated. Quaresma herself regards this as an opportunity rather than an obstacle: a worldwide network of optical clocks, she suggests, could serve at once as a timekeeping standard and as a continuously updated map of gravity. Whether national laboratories, which are funded to keep time rather than to survey the planet, would accept such a dual role is another matter.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some observers question whether a redefinition is needed at all. Lars Nordgren, an engineer who advises a European telecommunications regulator, argues that no industrial application currently demands more precision than caesium provides, and that the cost of upgrading national timing infrastructure would be borne by taxpayers for the benefit of a small scientific community. His concern about cost is reasonable, but the argument from present needs is weak. When caesium itself was adopted, few could have predicted that satellite navigation would one day depend on it. Standards are, in a sense, infrastructure for applications that do not yet exist.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most persuasive case for change may in fact be a modest one. A definition based on an optical transition would not immediately alter the clocks in homes or phones; it would simply ensure that the official unit reflects the best measurement humanity is capable of making. Allowing the definition to lag far behind laboratory capability creates the odd situation in which the most accurate clocks on Earth must be calibrated against less accurate ones. That anomaly, rather than any immediate practical gain, is reason enough to proceed, though carefully, and only once comparisons between laboratories are secure.

topic: migrating to post-quantum cryptography before quantum computers can break current encryption
title: The Long Migration
subtitle: Replacing the cryptography that underpins digital life before quantum computers can break it may prove the largest software upgrade ever attempted

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1990s, organisations around the world spent vast sums checking computer systems for the so-called millennium bug, a programming shortcut that threatened to make software misread the year 2000. The effort was widely mocked afterwards when little went wrong, although many engineers insist that little went wrong precisely because of the effort. A comparable undertaking now looms, and in some respects it is far more demanding. Much of the public-key cryptography that secures web browsing, software updates and electronic payments relies on the difficulty of factoring very large numbers or of solving related mathematical problems. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer, running an algorithm devised in the 1990s, could solve these problems quickly. No such machine yet exists, but the prospect has prompted standards agencies to publish replacement algorithms, known collectively as post-quantum cryptography, and to urge that the transition begin at once.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why the urgency, if the threat remains hypothetical? The answer most often given is the risk of 'harvest now, decrypt later'. An adversary who records encrypted traffic today can store it until a capable quantum computer becomes available, and then read it at leisure. For information that must stay confidential for many years, such as medical histories, intelligence sources or long-term commercial plans, the danger is therefore already present. Dr Itziar Arismendi, who studies information security policy at the Cantabrian School of Governance, has formalised this into a simple rule: if the time needed to migrate a system, added to the period for which its data must remain secret, exceeds the time until quantum computers arrive, the organisation is already too late. The rule is useful as a prompt to action, but it lends the problem a misleading air of precision, since none of its three quantities can be estimated with any confidence.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Forecasts of when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer might be built certainly vary wildly. Professor Marek Kowalewski, a physicist at the Vistula Institute of Technology, points out that today's largest machines contain at most a few thousand physical qubits, each prone to errors, whereas breaking a standard key is thought to require several million. He considers it unlikely that such a machine will exist within twenty years, and warns that exaggerated timelines may encourage hasty and poorly tested deployments. Others are less sanguine. A survey of specialists conducted by the Lakeshore Quantum Forum found that roughly a third believed there was at least an even chance of a code-breaking machine within fifteen years. Surveys of this kind measure opinion rather than evidence, but the spread of answers is itself a reason not to wait.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The practical obstacles to migration have little to do with physics. Cryptography is embedded in hardware and software in ways that are often undocumented. Achieng Okeyo, who runs a security consultancy in Nairobi, reports that when her firm audits large organisations, it routinely discovers encryption in places nobody remembered: in payment terminals, in industrial controllers installed decades ago, in code libraries buried within other libraries. Her firm's first task is therefore an inventory, and she estimates that for a large bank this stage alone may take two years. Devices with long service lives pose a particular difficulty, since a sensor or satellite built today may still be operating in the 2050s, yet may have no means of receiving a software update.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The new algorithms bring complications of their own. Many produce keys and digital signatures considerably larger than those they replace, which can slow connections and overwhelm devices with limited memory. More worrying is that they are young. Ruedi Leutwyler, a mathematician at the Alpine Cryptography Centre, notes that one of the candidates evaluated during the standardisation process was broken in a single weekend by researchers using an ordinary laptop, after years of scrutiny had found no flaw. In Leutwyler's view, the episode demonstrates that the process works, because flawed designs are being caught before they are deployed. That is a fair point, though it hardly inspires confidence in the survivors. For this reason, many agencies recommend 'hybrid' schemes that pair a new algorithm with an established one, so that security fails only if both are broken.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical position is taken by Yelena Varaksin, a software engineer at the Baltic Open Systems Foundation. She argues that the real lesson of the post-quantum transition is that cryptographic choices should never again be hard-wired into systems. Instead, software should be designed with what she calls 'crypto-agility', so that one algorithm can be replaced by another with minimal disruption. Varaksin regards the coming upgrade less as a one-off emergency than as an opportunity to repair a structural weakness that would eventually have caused trouble anyway, quantum computers or not.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Her argument is surely correct in principle, although agility has costs of its own: systems that can switch algorithms easily may also be tricked into switching to weaker ones, a vulnerability that attackers have exploited in the past. Still, the broader point stands. The quantum threat may materialise in ten years, in thirty or not at all, but the work required to prepare for it, namely knowing where cryptography is used and being able to change it, is valuable regardless. Unlike the millennium bug, this problem comes with no fixed deadline, which makes it all too easy to postpone.

topic: claims of quantum advantage and the classical-simulation counterattack
title: The Moving Finish Line
subtitle: Each time a quantum computer is said to have beaten a conventional one, classical programmers fight back. What does the contest really show?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the race to build useful quantum computers, few milestones have attracted as much attention as 'quantum advantage': the point at which a quantum device completes a task that no conventional computer could finish in any reasonable time. Announcements of such advantage have appeared several times over the past decade, usually accompanied by striking comparisons. A calculation that took a quantum processor a few minutes, one press release might claim, would occupy the world's fastest supercomputer for thousands of years. Such figures make arresting headlines. They also tend to have a short shelf life. Behind the publicity, however, lies a serious scientific question: whether any physical device can genuinely outperform the best possible classical computation, a question that has proved surprisingly difficult to settle.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The pattern has become familiar. Within months of an announcement, teams of classical programmers publish improved algorithms that perform the same task on ordinary hardware far faster than predicted, sometimes in days rather than millennia. Dr Milena Zarkovic, a computer scientist at the Adriatic Centre for Computation, has catalogued a dozen such episodes. In her analysis, the original estimates were rarely wrong in a technical sense; rather, they assumed that the classical simulation would be carried out using the best method known at the time. Classical computing, she points out, is not a fixed target but an active research field, and setting it a public challenge is perhaps the surest way to stimulate improvements. Zarkovic does not regard this as an embarrassment for the quantum teams; in her view, it is simply how competitive science ought to operate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The tasks chosen for these demonstrations have also drawn criticism. Most involve sampling from the output of a randomly configured quantum circuit, an exercise selected precisely because it is easy for a quantum device and believed to be hard for a classical one, but which has no known practical use. Professor Ilkka Saarinen of the Boreal University of Technology compares such experiments to a sprinter racing a car over a course full of obstacles that only a human can step over. The victory may be genuine, he argues, but it reveals little about which is the better means of transport. Saarinen's analogy is entertaining, but it understates what the experiments achieve. Demonstrating that a machine built from fragile quantum components can be controlled precisely enough to perform any computation at this scale is a substantial engineering accomplishment, whatever the usefulness of the computation itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more technical objection concerns noise. Present-day quantum processors are imperfect: their qubits lose their quantum properties within fractions of a second, and errors accumulate as calculations proceed. Dr Hye-jin Rhee, a theoretical physicist at the Han River Institute for Advanced Study, has shown that, beyond a certain level of noise, the output of a random circuit can be approximated by relatively simple classical methods. Paradoxically, then, building larger noisy machines may not strengthen claims of advantage, because the additional errors make their output easier to imitate. Rhee's results do not rule out advantage altogether, but they imply that convincing demonstrations will require much lower error rates than current devices achieve. Reaching such rates is expected to depend on error correction, in which many physical qubits are combined to represent a single, more reliable one, a technique that remains extremely costly in hardware.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some observers regard the entire contest as a distraction. Gaëtan Brisebois, who manages a technology investment fund in Montreal, argues that the competition between quantum and classical teams has encouraged companies to put publicity ahead of substance. Investors, he says, should ignore claims of advantage and ask instead whether a machine can solve a problem that someone would pay to have solved. His impatience is understandable, yet the demand for immediate commercial relevance may be premature. The first transistors were laboratory curiosities too, and early judgments of their value proved spectacularly wrong. Nobody examining those early devices could have foreseen the industries that would eventually grow up around them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, then, has the contest achieved? Arguably its greatest product has been an improvement in classical algorithms, several of which have found applications well beyond the problems they were designed for. Methods developed to simulate quantum circuits, for example, are now used in chemistry and in the analysis of complex networks. It is an irony worth savouring that the attempt to show classical computers to be obsolete has made them noticeably more capable. The episodes also illustrate a broader truth about scientific claims: a result is only as strong as the effort others have made to overturn it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The likeliest outcome is not a single decisive moment but a gradual shift. As techniques for correcting errors improve, quantum machines will begin to tackle problems of genuine scientific interest, such as simulating molecules for drug design, where classical methods face difficulties that are fundamental rather than merely technical. Even there, the boundary will be contested, and it would be wise to treat any announcement of victory as an opening statement rather than a final verdict. The finish line, it turns out, moves whenever someone approaches it.
