topic: wearable brain scanners based on optically pumped quantum magnetometers
title: Listening to the Brain's Magnetic Whisper
subtitle: Quantum sensors small enough to wear could change how brain activity is recorded, but the obstacles are not where many expected them to be

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The electrical currents carried by nerve cells generate magnetic fields that are around a billion times weaker than the magnetic field of the earth, and for half a century the only instruments capable of detecting them have been superconducting quantum interference devices, known as SQUIDs. The technique built on them, magnetoencephalography or MEG, has always come with awkward conditions attached. SQUIDs work only when cooled to about minus 269 degrees Celsius, so they must be bathed in liquid helium inside a bulky insulated vessel. The patient has to lie or sit perfectly still with their head inside this fixed helmet, which is built in a single adult size. Despite these drawbacks, conventional MEG has earned a secure place in hospitals, notably for pinpointing the area of the brain from which epileptic seizures arise before surgery.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The device that may change this situation is the optically pumped magnetometer, or OPM. At its heart is a small glass cell containing a vapour of alkali atoms such as rubidium. A laser beam passing through the cell aligns the spins of the atoms. When an external magnetic field is present, it disturbs this alignment and alters the amount of light that passes through the cell, so that measuring the transmitted light reveals the strength of the field. A complete sensor is now little larger than a sugar cube and requires no cryogenic cooling. Crucially, it can be placed directly against the scalp. Because magnetic signals weaken rapidly with distance, sensors that sit a few millimetres from the head rather than a few centimetres can record noticeably stronger signals than their superconducting predecessors.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ragnhild Østvik, whose group at the Trøndelag Institute of Neurophysics was among the first to mount OPMs in a lightweight helmet, believes that sensitivity is not the most important gain. Her team has recorded brain activity from volunteers who were nodding, drinking tea and even bouncing a ball, activities that would ruin a conventional recording. In Østvik's view, the technology's real promise lies in allowing researchers to study the brain during natural behaviour, and in opening MEG to people who cannot keep still for long periods, such as infants, young children and patients with movement disorders. Of all the arguments advanced for the new sensors, this is the most compelling, since it addresses a limitation that no refinement of the old technology could ever have removed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the sensors have a demanding requirement of their own. They function properly only in an almost perfectly zero magnetic field, which means that the earth's field, along with disturbances from traffic and machinery, must be almost entirely cancelled. This is achieved partly by recording inside a room lined with layers of a special nickel-iron alloy and partly by surrounding the subject with electrical coils that counteract whatever field remains. Professor Tadeusz Wroblicki, an engineer at the Silesian Technical University, points out that if a subject moves through even a weak residual field, the sensors register the motion as a large signal that can swamp the brain's activity. His team has designed coil systems that reduce the residual field to a tiny fraction of its original strength. Wroblicki now argues that the shielded room, rather than the sensor, has become the chief barrier to wider adoption, since a room typically costs more than the sensors it contains. For the present that judgement is probably accurate, although it may underestimate how quickly lighter and cheaper shielding designs are emerging.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whether the new systems are ready for routine clinical use is another matter. The neurologist Dr Amaru Ttito compared OPM and SQUID recordings in a group of patients with epilepsy and found that the wearable system detected abnormal discharges in nearly every case where the conventional one did. In several children, it identified discharges that the conventional system had missed altogether, presumably because the sensors sat closer to the brain. Ttito nonetheless stresses that his study involved only thirty patients and that hospitals should not abandon proven equipment on the strength of such limited evidence. Current wearable systems also carry fewer sensors than a SQUID helmet, limiting coverage of the head. His caution is well judged: a technology that performs impressively in the hands of its developers must still prove itself in ordinary clinics.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental reservation is expressed by Dr Siosaia Taumoepeau, a physicist who has worked with both types of sensor. He notes that OPMs respond relatively slowly and are therefore less able than SQUIDs to capture rapid, high-frequency brain activity; they also lose accuracy in stronger fields. On this basis he predicts that the wearable sensors will complement superconducting systems rather than replace them. Taumoepeau may well be right in the short term, but his argument assumes that the performance of OPMs will remain roughly where it is today, and the recent history of the field gives little reason to accept that assumption. Commercial sensors have become markedly quieter and smaller within a decade.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The economic case may ultimately prove decisive. Liquid helium has become steadily more expensive and less reliably supplied, forcing some hospitals to suspend MEG services. A consortium of clinical centres coordinated by Dr Noor Al-Habsi has estimated that a wearable system installed in a compact shielded room could be operated at well under half the annual cost of a conventional one, bringing MEG within reach of many more hospitals. Such projections are encouraging, but they should not be confused with the confident forecasts, heard occasionally at industry conferences, that MEG will soon be as commonplace as the electrical recordings taken from scalp electrodes. That day, if it comes, is still some way off.

topic: quantum gravimeters based on atom interferometry for underground surveying and navigation
title: Weighing the Ground Beneath Us
subtitle: Instruments that use falling atoms to measure gravity are leaving the laboratory, but what they can reveal is often overstated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The pull of gravity is not quite the same everywhere. Above a body of dense rock it is fractionally stronger; above a cave, a buried pipe or a pocket of loose soil it is fractionally weaker. The differences are minute, often less than one part in a hundred million, but measuring them, a practice known as gravimetry, has long helped geologists to search for oil and mineral deposits. The instruments traditionally used for the purpose rely on a tiny mass suspended from a spring. They are remarkably sensitive, yet they share an inconvenient flaw: over hours and days the spring slowly changes its properties, so the readings wander and must be corrected by returning repeatedly to a reference point whose gravity is already known. Surveys carried out in this way are slow, painstaking and expensive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Quantum gravimeters take an entirely different approach. Inside a vacuum chamber, a cloud of atoms is chilled with lasers to a few millionths of a degree above absolute zero and then released, so that it drops freely for a fraction of a second. During the fall, carefully timed pulses of laser light split the quantum wave associated with each atom so that it travels along two separate routes, before recombining it. The way the two halves interfere with each other depends on how much the atoms have been sped up by gravity during their descent. Because every atom of a given element is identical, and because the measurement is referenced to the wavelength of laser light, the instrument does not drift in the way that a spring does. In effect, it calibrates itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first commercial applications are appearing in civil engineering. Dr Ludmila Strnadová, a geophysicist at a Prague-based engineering consultancy, recently used a quantum gravimeter to survey the route of a planned railway line and discovered a disused mine shaft that appeared on no historical map. In her view, the instruments' greatest value lies not in finding such dramatic hazards but in reducing the number of exploratory boreholes that engineers must drill. Each borehole is costly, and because it samples only a single point, a hazard lying a few metres away can be missed entirely. A gravity survey, by contrast, examines the whole area between boreholes. Of all the uses proposed for quantum gravimetry, this is the one most likely to generate income in the near term, because the cost of an unexpected void beneath a construction site is so obvious to those who pay for it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Field conditions, however, are rarely kind to delicate instruments. A single measurement may require the device to remain perfectly still for several minutes, and vibration from passing traffic or machinery can spoil the result. Professor Kwabena Twumasi, a physicist at the Gold Coast Institute of Technology, has addressed this problem by building a gradiometer, which drops two atom clouds simultaneously, one above the other. Since ground vibration shakes both clouds in exactly the same way, subtracting one measurement from the other removes the disturbance while preserving the tiny difference in gravity between the two heights. Twumasi expects gradiometers, rather than single gravimeters, to become the standard tool for surveying. That expectation seems reasonable, although current prototypes are still large enough to require a van for transport, which limits where they can be used.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second set of applications concerns navigation. Satellite positioning signals are weak and easily jammed, and they do not penetrate water, so submarines and many ships rely on inertial systems that calculate position from measurements of acceleration. Unfortunately, small errors in these measurements accumulate, and after several days a vessel's estimated position may be kilometres from the truth. Quantum accelerometers, based on the same principle as gravimeters, drift far less. A further idea is to compare gravity readings taken on board with an existing map of the gravity field, in much the same way that a walker matches visible landmarks to a chart. Dr Itzel Tlapanco, a navigation specialist, doubts that this second technique will succeed at sea, because the gravity maps available for most of the world's oceans are too coarse to allow a precise position to be fixed. Her objection is well founded: no matter how good the instrument, the result can be no better than the map against which it is compared.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Popular accounts of the technology frequently claim that it allows users to 'see' underground as if with an X-ray. Such descriptions are misleading. A gravimeter measures differences in mass, and many different arrangements of material below the surface can produce exactly the same reading: a small, shallow cavity and a larger, deeper one may look identical. For this reason, a review published by the Andean-Pacific Geophysics Network concluded that quantum gravimeters should always be combined with other methods, such as ground-penetrating radar or borehole sampling, before conclusions are drawn. The instruments, in other words, are powerful at indicating where something unusual lies, but much weaker at revealing what it is.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the scale of the achievement. Only twenty years ago, atom interferometers occupied entire laboratory rooms and were tended by teams of doctoral students. The fact that they can now be operated beside a railway embankment by an engineer with a few days' training represents a remarkable feat of miniaturisation and robustness. Whether quantum gravimetry becomes a routine part of surveying will depend less on further gains in sensitivity than on whether the instruments become cheaper, lighter and easier to interpret.

topic: the overhead of quantum error correction and competing strategies for reducing it
title: The Price of Reliability
subtitle: Before quantum computers can do anything useful, they must learn to correct their own mistakes, and the cost of doing so is staggering

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The basic components of a quantum computer, its qubits, are astonishingly delicate. Stray heat or slight imperfections in their control pulses can corrupt the information they hold, and even the best devices built so far make roughly one mistake in every thousand operations. That might sound respectable, but the algorithms that would make quantum computers genuinely valuable require billions of operations to run without error. The proposed solution is quantum error correction, in which the information belonging to a single 'logical' qubit is spread across many physical ones. Errors cannot be found simply by inspecting the qubits, because measuring a quantum state directly destroys the information it contains. Instead, auxiliary qubits are used to check, again and again, whether neighbouring qubits still agree with one another, revealing that an error has occurred without revealing the data itself. A key theoretical result, known as the threshold theorem, states that if the physical error rate can be pushed below a certain critical level, then enlarging the code will cause the error rate of the logical qubit to fall dramatically.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in the arithmetic. Under the most widely studied scheme, the surface code, achieving the reliability needed for useful algorithms may require around a thousand physical qubits for every logical one. A machine capable of breaking widely used encryption has been estimated to need several million physical qubits, while the largest processors in existence today contain little more than a thousand. This ratio is arguably the single most important number in quantum computing, yet it seldom appears in the announcements with which companies publicise their latest processors, which tend to emphasise the total number of qubits as though every one of them were available for computation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There has nonetheless been real progress. A team led by Professor Ximena Escalona at the Pacific Institute for Quantum Engineering recently showed that, as the size of a surface code was increased, the error rate of the logical qubit decreased, which is the behaviour the threshold theorem predicts. Escalona regards the result as a turning point: in her view, the fundamental science has now been settled, and what remains is a matter of engineering. That claim is correct in a narrow sense, but it makes the remaining task sound more routine than it is. Every physical qubit in a superconducting machine needs its own control wiring, and each wire carries heat into a refrigerator that must be held close to absolute zero. Scaling from a thousand qubits to a million is therefore not simply a matter of repetition; the practical obstacles involved may prove every bit as formidable as the scientific ones that preceded them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Several groups are trying to reduce the overhead itself. Dr Jun-seo Jegal, a theorist at the Hangang Centre for Quantum Information, has studied a family of codes known as low-density parity-check codes, which in principle protect the same amount of information with perhaps a tenth of the physical qubits that the surface code requires. The catch is that these codes demand connections between qubits that may be far apart, whereas superconducting chips are laid out as flat grids in which each qubit interacts only with its immediate neighbours. Jegal therefore believes that platforms in which qubits can be physically moved, such as individual atoms held and shuttled by laser beams, may ultimately prove better suited to large-scale error correction than the superconducting machines that currently dominate the field.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different strategy is to build qubits that are less prone to error from the start. Dr Mirela Dobrescu and her colleagues store information not in a single circuit but in particular states of microwave light trapped inside a tiny cavity, so-called cat qubits. Such states are naturally resistant to one of the two main kinds of quantum error, the so-called bit flip, so that only the other kind needs to be actively corrected. Dobrescu calculates that this could cut the number of physical components required several times over. The idea is elegant and the early results are encouraging, but they have so far been obtained with individual qubits, and it remains to be seen whether the protection survives when many cat qubits are made to interact.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious approach of all is being pursued by the research division of Halcyon Systems, which hopes to create topological qubits whose information would be protected by the physical structure of the material itself. If successful, such qubits would make much of the elaborate machinery of error correction unnecessary. Yet this is also the approach with the least convincing experimental record: several earlier claims to have observed the necessary physical effects have been withdrawn or disputed, and even sympathetic observers concede that a working topological qubit has yet to be demonstrated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the meantime, some researchers favour a more modest technique called error mitigation. Rather than correcting errors as they occur, it runs a calculation many times under deliberately varied levels of noise and uses statistical methods to estimate the answer a perfect machine would have produced. Dr Safiya Mbarek, who has developed several such methods, readily admits their limitation: the number of repetitions required grows exponentially as calculations become longer, so mitigation is practical only for relatively short computations. She describes it as a bridge to fault-tolerant machines rather than an alternative to them. Although it will never replace error correction, mitigation has already allowed noisy processors to produce results of scientific interest. What should matter to anyone judging progress in the coming decade, however, is not how many qubits a machine contains but how few physical qubits it needs for each reliable logical one.

topic: training a workforce for the quantum technology industry
title: Who Will Build the Machines?
subtitle: Governments are pouring money into quantum technology, but finding the people to develop it may prove harder than funding the research

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past decade, more than thirty countries have launched national programmes to develop quantum technologies, together committing tens of billions of dollars to research centres, start-up companies and university laboratories. Alongside the announcements, one complaint has been heard with growing frequency: there are not enough skilled people to do the work. Industry surveys regularly report that vacancies in quantum companies outnumber suitably qualified graduates by as much as three to one. These figures deserve to be treated with some caution, since they are typically compiled by industry associations whose members stand to benefit from public spending on training. Nevertheless, few people working in the field doubt that recruitment has become a serious constraint. Start-up companies in particular report losing months of progress while positions remain unfilled, and larger firms complain that salaries have risen so quickly that smaller competitors can no longer match them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What kind of people are actually needed? Popular accounts tend to picture the industry as a gathering of theoretical physicists working out equations on blackboards. Dr Folasade Ekpenyong, an analyst at the Lagos Centre for Technology Policy, set out to test this picture by examining several thousand job advertisements published by quantum companies over three years. She found that fewer than one in five positions required a doctorate in quantum physics. Far more common were requests for expertise in microwave engineering, cryogenics, control electronics and software development. Her study suggests that the familiar image of the industry is largely mistaken: building a quantum computer, it turns out, is chiefly a task for engineers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Universities have responded by creating specialised master's degrees in quantum engineering, and Professor Aurelio Castellanza of the Ligurian Polytechnic is among their most energetic advocates. Traditional physics degrees, he argues, give students a thorough grounding in theory but very little experience of the laboratory techniques that companies rely on, such as assembling vacuum systems or programming the electronics that control qubits. His own programme includes a six-month placement in industry, and he reports that almost all of its graduates have found relevant employment within half a year of completing the course. Castellanza also maintains that such programmes help to retain talented students who might otherwise leave science altogether after an undergraduate degree, because they offer a visible route into well-paid work rather than an uncertain academic career.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that narrow degrees of this kind are wise. Dr Parisa Gholamzadeh, who studies the economics of higher education, points out that emerging technologies often pass through cycles of enthusiasm and disappointment, and that the quantum industry may well contract if commercial applications arrive later than investors hope. In that event, she warns, graduates whose training is tied to a single sector may struggle to find employment. She would prefer students to take broad degrees in electrical engineering or computer science, with optional modules on quantum devices. Her caution is sensible, but the danger she describes is smaller than it first appears. Many of the skills that quantum companies value, cryogenics and microwave engineering in particular, are equally sought after in medical imaging, telecommunications and the space industry, so a quantum engineer would rarely be left without options.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much of the debate concerns graduates, yet the most acute shortage may lie elsewhere. Quantum laboratories depend on technicians who assemble and maintain refrigeration systems, wire control lines and repair delicate optical equipment, and the vocational colleges that train technicians for other industries seldom offer anything comparable. A group of firms and colleges known as the Northern Lakes Quantum Skills Partnership has begun to address this gap with apprenticeships that allow trainees to work on real machines while studying part-time. Initiatives of this kind deserve far more attention than they receive; a shortage of technicians has been the most neglected aspect of the entire discussion.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The competition for talent is also international. Several governments have introduced fast-track visas intended to attract foreign specialists, while at the same time imposing export controls that restrict the sharing of certain quantum technologies on grounds of national security. Dr Henrik Aasland, a physicist who has worked in four countries, argues that these two policies pull in opposite directions. Progress in the field, he observes, has historically depended on researchers moving freely between laboratories and carrying their expertise with them, and controls that discourage such movement could slow innovation in exactly the countries that impose them. Aasland accepts that some technologies may need protection, but he insists that the boundaries should be drawn narrowly and reviewed regularly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these perspectives suggest that the workforce problem will not be solved by any one type of qualification. Specialised degrees, broad engineering courses, apprenticeships and sensible immigration rules all have a part to play. There is also a less obvious remedy. Students deciding whether to enter the field need honest information about how long useful quantum machines are likely to take to arrive; exaggerated promises may attract them in the short term but leave them disillusioned later. Clearer communication about realistic timescales would probably do as much for the industry's future workforce as any new degree programme. Universities, companies and governments have each tended to address the issue in isolation, and better coordination between them is overdue.

topic: quantum computing for chemistry, with the nitrogenase enzyme as a flagship problem
title: The Fertiliser Promise
subtitle: Quantum computers are often said to be on the verge of transforming chemistry, but the most famous example of their potential tells a more complicated story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Roughly half of the world's population is fed by crops grown with synthetic fertiliser, and almost all of that fertiliser depends on a single industrial reaction. The Haber-Bosch process combines nitrogen from the air with hydrogen to make ammonia, but it does so only at temperatures of around 450 degrees Celsius and at pressures some two hundred times that of the atmosphere. As a result it consumes a significant fraction of the world's energy supply. Certain soil bacteria, by contrast, accomplish the same chemical feat at ordinary temperatures and pressures, using an enzyme called nitrogenase. At the heart of this enzyme lies a small cluster of iron, molybdenum and sulphur atoms, and chemists have long hoped that understanding exactly how it works might suggest ways of making ammonia far more efficiently.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That hope has been frustrated by the limits of conventional computing. In the metal cluster, the behaviour of each electron depends intimately on the behaviour of all the others; in the language of chemistry, the electrons are strongly correlated. Describing such a system exactly requires computing resources that increase exponentially with the number of electrons involved, so classical computers must fall back on approximations, and different approximate methods have yielded contradictory accounts of the cluster's chemistry. A quantum computer, which is itself governed by the same quantum rules, could in principle represent these states directly. Some years ago, a group led by Professor Rasmus Toftegaard at the Jutland Institute for Theoretical Chemistry estimated that a fault-tolerant quantum computer with a few million physical qubits could complete the decisive calculation in a matter of days. Nitrogenase quickly became the flagship example of what quantum computing might achieve.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: As a choice of illustration, it was shrewd. The problem combines genuine scientific difficulty with obvious humanitarian significance, and it is easily explained to politicians and the public. Its very success, however, has encouraged a misleading impression: that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer would, on its own, cut the energy cost of feeding the world. Even a perfect description of the electrons in nitrogenase would not tell engineers how to construct an industrial catalyst that is cheap, durable and capable of operating at the scale of a fertiliser plant. Those are problems of materials science and chemical engineering, and they would remain after the quantum calculation had been completed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, classical methods have not stood still. Dr Bao Ngoc Truong, a computational chemist at the Mekong Institute of Molecular Science, has shown that newer classical techniques, which compress the description of a quantum system by discarding the least important connections between its parts, now produce increasingly consistent accounts of the nitrogenase cluster. In Truong's view, such progress has seriously weakened the claim that chemistry will be the first field transformed by quantum computers. She adds that most molecules of industrial interest are not strongly correlated at all and are already handled well by existing software. Her argument is an important corrective, but it does not settle the question. There remain systems, including some catalysts and magnetic materials, whose complexity appears to place them beyond the reach of any foreseeable classical method.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Estimates of what a quantum computer would need have also changed. Successive improvements to quantum algorithms have reduced the predicted cost of the nitrogenase calculation by a factor of several hundred since the original estimate was published. Toftegaard interprets this as evidence that the field is maturing, as researchers learn to exploit the structure of chemical problems more cleverly. That interpretation is reasonable as far as it goes, yet the falling estimates cut both ways. If the figures can shrink so dramatically in a few years, they were clearly far less certain than they appeared at the time, and the same may be true of the figures now being quoted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Outside the field of fertiliser production, claims about drug discovery deserve similar scrutiny. Dr Anahí Colque, who leads a computational group at a pharmaceutical company, points out that the great majority of candidate medicines fail in clinical trials, usually because they prove toxic or ineffective in human patients rather than because their chemistry was miscalculated. No calculation of a single molecule's electronic structure, however exact, can predict how a drug will behave in the immensely complicated environment of the human body. Colque does see a role for quantum computers, but a modest one: producing highly accurate reference results against which faster classical methods, including machine-learning models, can be checked and trained.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This more modest vision is probably the most realistic. If quantum computers contribute to chemistry within the next two decades, they are likely to do so indirectly, by improving the tools that chemists already use rather than by delivering discoveries of their own. Such a contribution would attract fewer headlines than a revolution in fertiliser manufacture, but it could prove valuable nonetheless, and it has the considerable advantage of being achievable. The danger is that, by promising too much, advocates of the technology will make its genuine achievements look like failures.

topic: quantum repeaters and quantum memories for a ground-based quantum internet
title: Holding Light Still
subtitle: A quantum internet would need devices that can store fragile quantum states, and building them is proving to be one of the hardest problems in physics

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The phrase 'quantum internet' is often taken to mean nothing more than a highly secure way of sending encrypted messages. Its ambitions are in fact much broader. The aim is to share entanglement, the peculiar quantum connection in which two particles behave as a single system however far apart they are, between machines in different cities or even on different continents. A network of this kind could link several modest quantum processors so that they work together as one larger machine, synchronise atomic clocks with unprecedented precision, or combine light collected by widely separated telescopes to produce far sharper images of distant stars. None of these applications is yet close to reality, and all of them depend on solving the same fundamental problem.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That problem is loss. Quantum information is usually carried by single particles of light, or photons, and even the best optical fibre absorbs or scatters them steadily: over a hundred kilometres, roughly ninety-nine out of every hundred photons disappear. Ordinary telecommunications networks overcome similar losses by placing amplifiers at intervals along the cable to boost the signal. Quantum networks cannot do this, because a basic law of quantum physics forbids the copying of an unknown quantum state, and amplification is a form of copying. This prohibition, more than any other single fact, explains why constructing a quantum internet is so much more difficult than constructing the classical one. The proposed solution is the quantum repeater, a chain of stations that first create entanglement across short sections of fibre and then join these sections together through a process known as entanglement swapping, until the two ends of the chain are entangled with each other.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Repeaters, however, need somewhere to keep quantum states while they wait. Because each short link succeeds only occasionally, a station must hold its share of an entangled pair until the neighbouring link has also succeeded, and that requires a quantum memory. Several materials are being explored for the purpose, including clouds of cold atoms and crystals doped with rare-earth ions. Dr Saule Zhakupova and her team at the Steppe Institute of Photonics recently stored a quantum state in such a crystal for more than an hour, a record that attracted considerable attention. Zhakupova argues that storage time is the essential benchmark by which memories should be judged, since a network spanning a continent will require states to survive for long periods. That emphasis is understandable but too narrow. A memory that holds a state for an hour yet returns it successfully only once in every ten attempts would be of limited use; efficiency, and the speed at which a memory can be loaded and read, matter just as much.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have concentrated on building small working networks. Professor Olumide Fagbemi, whose group at the Niger Delta Quantum Laboratory connected three nodes across a city using tiny defects in diamond as memories, has found that the hardest difficulty lies somewhere unexpected. The light emitted by many memory materials has a wavelength that optical fibre absorbs strongly, so it must be converted to a different wavelength before it can travel any distance. In Fagbemi's experience, it is this conversion step, which adds both loss and unwanted noise, that currently limits performance most severely.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone believes that repeaters are urgently needed. Dr Kaimana Pahukoa, a network engineer who has advised several telecommunications companies, points out that so-called trusted nodes are already in use. These are secure stations at which an encryption key is decoded and then re-encrypted before being passed on. Pahukoa argues that such stations are sufficient for the great majority of security applications and that the effort devoted to repeaters is premature. As far as secure communication is concerned, his point has some force. Yet it overlooks the wider purposes described above: linking quantum processors or telescopes requires genuine entanglement between the end points, which a trusted node, by decoding the information along the way, is unable to provide.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further group is concerned less with hardware than with organisation. The Quantum Network Protocols Forum, an alliance of universities and companies, has argued that common standards for how quantum networks exchange information should be agreed now, before rival systems become established and turn out to be unable to communicate with one another. Its members point to the early history of computer networking, when several incompatible systems competed for years before a shared set of rules emerged. Planning ahead in this way seems prudent, provided that the standards remain flexible enough to accommodate technologies that have not yet been invented.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is the realistic outlook? The likeliest first step is a patchwork of small networks within individual cities, connected to one another, if at all, by trusted nodes or satellite links. A quantum internet spanning continents, by contrast, depends on memories and repeaters far better than any yet demonstrated, and claims that it will be running within a few years should be treated with scepticism. It would be a mistake, though, to conclude that the effort is misguided. The scientific foundations are sound, and the history of the classical internet suggests that useful applications tend to emerge once a network exists, often in forms that its builders never anticipated.

topic: beaver reintroduction and its effects on river flow, water quality and landowners
title: Engineers of the Floodplain
subtitle: The return of the beaver to European rivers is reshaping not only waterways but also the way scientists think about managing water

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By the end of the nineteenth century, the Eurasian beaver had been all but eliminated from western Europe. Prized for its dense fur, its meat and a scented secretion once used in medicine and perfume, the animal survived only in a handful of scattered refuges, perhaps numbering no more than a thousand individuals in total. Its recovery since then has been remarkable. Following legal protection and a series of deliberate releases beginning in the 1920s, beavers now occupy rivers in more than two dozen European countries, and their population is estimated to exceed one million. This is rightly regarded as one of the outstanding achievements of modern conservation. Yet the real significance of the beaver's return lies less in the survival of the species itself than in the changes it brings about in the landscapes it recolonises.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Those changes stem from a single behaviour. Beavers fell trees and use branches, mud and stones to build dams across streams, creating ponds deep enough to keep the underwater entrances to their lodges submerged throughout the year. A single family may construct a whole sequence of dams along a few hundred metres of watercourse. The consequences for the movement of water are considerable. Dr Ilona Szabados, a hydrologist at the Carpathian Freshwater Institute, compared measurements taken on a number of small streams before and after beavers settled there. She found that the highest flows recorded after heavy rainfall fell by as much as a third downstream of the dams, because water was held back and spread out across the floodplain rather than rushing straight down the channel. Equally important, in her view, was what happened in dry weather: the ponds released their stored water gradually, so that streams which had previously dried up in late summer continued to flow.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Findings of this kind have encouraged some campaigners to present the beaver as a cost-free substitute for engineered flood defences. Such claims go too far. The effects Szabados recorded were strongest on small streams in the upper parts of catchments; on large rivers, and during the most extreme storms, beaver dams are typically overtopped or swept away altogether. Professor Rune Torsvik, an engineer at the Western Fjords University, has gone further, warning that a chain of dams may fail one after another in a severe flood, releasing a large volume of stored water in a single surge. Torsvik concedes that documented cases of such collapses causing serious damage remain rare, and his warning is perhaps best understood as an argument for careful observation rather than for opposition to beavers as such.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further claimed benefit concerns water quality. Because the current slows as it enters a beaver pond, fine particles of soil settle on the bottom, along with some of the nutrients washed off neighbouring farmland. A team led by Dr Yaw Ofosu-Brandt at the Lowland Rivers Observatory reported that water leaving beaver wetlands carried markedly less suspended sediment than water entering them, and lower concentrations of phosphorus, a nutrient that in excess causes algae to multiply in lakes downstream. The picture is not entirely positive. Stagnant ponds can emit methane, and Ofosu-Brandt himself acknowledges that the nutrients locked away in pond sediments may be released again when a dam is eventually abandoned and breaks down. These reservations do not cancel out the gains, but they do suggest that monitoring needs to continue for decades rather than for the few years that most research grants allow.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For the people who own land along recolonised rivers, the beaver's talents can be decidedly unwelcome. Flooded pasture, blocked drainage pipes and felled fruit trees are common complaints. A range of management techniques has been developed in response, the most widely used being the flow device, a pipe inserted through a dam that allows water to pass while keeping the pond at an agreed height. Where such measures fail, dams may be removed, and in some countries the authorities issue licences for animals to be killed. Interestingly, research by Dr Siobhán Carrabine, a rural sociologist, suggests that hostility towards beavers is not necessarily strongest where the damage is greatest. Instead, it was most intense among landowners who felt that the original releases had been carried out without their knowledge. If her findings are confirmed elsewhere, they imply that early consultation may matter as much as financial compensation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Beyond these practical questions lies a more fundamental one. Historical and geological evidence indicates that, before widespread drainage, many lowland valleys contained not a single neat channel but a shifting network of pools, side channels and marshes, much of it created and maintained by beavers. What most people today picture as a natural river, confined between firm banks, is in fact the product of centuries of human engineering. Ecologists have long described the beaver as an ecosystem engineer, noting the frogs, dragonflies, bats and wading birds that flourish in its wetlands. Arguably, though, its most profound effect may be on human perception, forcing us to reconsider what a healthy river should actually look like.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the beaver should be treated as a solution to every problem facing rivers. It is a valuable ally in managing water, but not a replacement for planning, investment or the regulation of pollution at its source. Whether its return is ultimately judged a success will depend less on the animals themselves than on whether landowners and governments are prepared to allow water, and the creatures that shape it, a little more room.

topic: wolf reintroduction and the contested evidence for trophic cascades
title: The Wolf and the Willow
subtitle: A celebrated account of predators restoring a landscape has become one of ecology's most hotly disputed stories

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few stories in ecology have travelled as far as the tale of the wolves that changed a landscape. In the version retold in documentaries and on social media, the return of wolves to a national park in the northern Rocky Mountains in the mid-1990s set off a chain of consequences: elk, no longer free to graze at leisure, abandoned the valley floors; willows and aspens grew back along the streams; songbirds and beavers returned; even the course of the rivers shifted as vegetation stabilised their banks. Ecologists call such a sequence, in which effects pass down the food chain from predators to plants, a trophic cascade. The story is compelling, and it has been invoked in support of reintroducing large carnivores everywhere from the Scottish Highlands to the Iberian plateau. Its appeal, however, owes at least as much to its shape as a narrative, with a single hero restoring order, as to the strength of the evidence behind it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most influential explanations for the recovery of streamside trees comes from Dr Teodora Vlašić, a field ecologist who spent eight seasons tracking elk fitted with satellite collars. Her data suggest that the elk did not simply decline in number; they changed their behaviour. Animals spent less time in narrow gullies and on riverbanks bordered by fallen timber, places from which a fleeing animal could not easily escape a pursuing pack, and it was precisely in such locations that young trees grew most vigorously. Vlašić describes this as a 'landscape of fear', in which the mere risk of predation reshapes where herbivores feed. The idea is elegant because it implies that a relatively small number of predators can exert an influence out of all proportion to the number of animals they actually kill.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Professor Kenji Hayakawa, a quantitative ecologist, has re-examined several of the datasets on which the cascade story rests and identified what he regards as a serious methodological flaw. Many surveys, he notes, measured the tallest stems in each stand of willow or aspen, on the reasonable assumption that these best reflected the absence of browsing. But because the tallest stems are, almost by definition, the ones that have escaped grazing, the approach tends to overstate how widely trees have recovered. When Hayakawa's group sampled stems at random, the recovery appeared patchy and considerably more modest. He also points out that elk numbers were falling during the same period for reasons unrelated to wolves, including hunting by people outside the park boundary and the growing populations of bears and cougars.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Hayakawa's critique is a valuable corrective, and advocates of reintroduction would do well to take it seriously. It does not, however, demonstrate that wolves were irrelevant. Even his own random samples show more young trees in areas where wolves are most active than in areas they rarely visit, and few ecologists now doubt that predators played some part in the change. The more defensible conclusion is that the wolves were one cause among several, and that the original account compressed a slow, uneven and multi-causal process into a tidy fable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different complication is raised by Dr Lerato Hlongwane, who studies river systems. In her view, the decades without wolves did not merely allow elk to multiply; they transformed the streams themselves. Without trees to supply them with timber, beavers disappeared from many valleys, their dams collapsed and the water table dropped, leaving channels deeply cut into dry soil where willows struggle to take root. Such an ecosystem, Hlongwane argues, may have settled into what ecologists call an alternative stable state. Returning the predator removes one pressure, but it cannot by itself reverse the physical changes that followed its loss, and in some places active intervention, such as the construction of artificial dams, may be needed before trees can recover.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whether any of this applies to Europe is still more uncertain. Dr Gustavo Pinheiro, who has studied wolves recolonising farmland in the Iberian Peninsula, notes that European landscapes are crowded with roads, villages, fences and hunters. In his study areas, red deer and roe deer adjusted their movements far more in response to human activity than to the presence of wolves, which themselves avoided people and kept largely to the night. Where humans are the dominant source of danger, Pinheiro suggests, the subtle redistribution of grazing pressure seen in the American case is unlikely to be repeated. This does not make reintroduction pointless, but it does mean that the ecological benefits promised by campaigners may prove far smaller than expected.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For this reason, the Highland Carnivore Group, an alliance of conservation organisations, has proposed that the case for returning large predators should no longer rest on predicted cascades at all. Instead, its members argue, carnivores should be restored simply because they belong in their native ecosystems and because societies have an obligation to repair the losses they caused. There is something to be said for this candour, since promises of dramatic ecological change that fail to materialise may undermine public trust. Yet to abandon ecological arguments altogether would be a mistake. Predators do influence the animals they hunt, even if the outcome varies from place to place, and the task for researchers is to establish under what conditions those effects are strong, rather than either to celebrate or to dismiss them.

topic: assisted colonisation: moving species beyond their historical range in response to climate change
title: A New Home for an Old Species
subtitle: As the climate shifts, some conservationists are proposing to move threatened species to places they have never lived

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a cool upland valley several hundred kilometres south of its natural range, a team of biologists recently released forty young tortoises belonging to a species whose lowland wetland home is steadily drying out as rainfall declines. Releases of captive animals are nothing new in conservation, but this one was different in an important respect. Conventional reintroduction returns a species to a place where it once lived and from which it was lost. The tortoises, by contrast, were taken to a location where, as far as anyone knows, the species has never existed. The practice, known as assisted colonisation, is still rare, but it marks a profound shift in conservation thinking: from protecting nature where it is to deciding where it ought to be.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for intervention rests on speed. Climatic conditions are shifting across the globe faster than many organisms can follow, and the routes by which they might once have moved are increasingly blocked by roads, cities and intensively farmed land. Dr Aroha Rangihuna, a conservation biologist who works on threatened reptiles and freshwater invertebrates, argues that for species which disperse poorly and occupy small ranges, a decision to wait is itself a decision with consequences. By the time a decline becomes undeniable, she points out, too few individuals may remain to found a healthy population elsewhere. She therefore advocates the early establishment of so-called insurance populations, created while the source population is still large enough to spare animals. This argument seems to me difficult to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The objections, however, are serious. The history of species introduced beyond their native ranges, whether deliberately or by accident, contains many expensive disasters. Professor Agnieszka Wróblewska-Hart, who studies biological invasions, warns that a species which is harmless at home may behave very differently once freed from the competitors, predators and diseases that normally keep its numbers in check. Translocated animals may also carry parasites to which local wildlife has no resistance. She has proposed strict criteria: movements should be confined to the same continent, should cover the shortest distance possible, and should involve only species with little capacity for rapid spread. Her caution is justified, yet the parallel with invasive species is imperfect. Most of the worst invaders were carried across oceans to entirely unfamiliar ecosystems, whereas assisted colonisation typically involves modest distances into habitats adjoining a species' present range.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Choosing a destination raises problems of its own. Dr Ikenna Udeagbala builds what are known as climate envelope models, which identify the temperature and rainfall conditions a species currently experiences and then predict where similar conditions will be found in fifty or a hundred years. Such models are indispensable, but they rest on a questionable assumption: that the range a species occupies today reflects the full set of conditions it can tolerate. Many species are in fact confined by competitors, by the loss of habitat or by centuries of human persecution, and could thrive in places a model would reject. Udeagbala himself insists that his maps should be treated as a means of identifying candidates for small experimental releases, which can then be monitored, rather than as a guide to final destinations.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Beneath these technical disputes lies a philosophical one. Critics worry that moving species around undermines the very idea of a native ecological community, and some fear that conservation could slide into a kind of planetary gardening, with scientists arranging wildlife according to their own preferences. The environmental philosopher Sindre Fjellstad responds that the notion of a fixed, authentic community was always something of a fiction. Species ranges have expanded and contracted repeatedly with past climatic changes; after the last ice age, for instance, entire forests advanced northwards over several thousand years. This is a fair point, but it is not decisive. What distinguishes the present situation is both the pace of change and the fact that humans are its cause, and the real question is therefore not whether to intervene but how far intervention should go.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In practice, few projects have yet been attempted. In many countries the law forbids the release of animals outside their recorded native range, and obtaining permission can take years. Landowners in the receiving area may object, and the costs of breeding, transport and long-term monitoring are considerable. Most trials so far have involved plants and insects, which are cheaper to move and less likely to provoke public controversy. The tortoise project remains one of the few involving a vertebrate, and its early results are encouraging but incomplete: most of the released animals survived their first three winters, although breeding in the wild has yet to be confirmed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Assisted colonisation should, in my view, be reserved for species that have no realistic alternative, and every proposal should be judged on its own evidence. To rule it out altogether, though, would be to accept the loss of species that could have been saved. It demands a degree of humility that conservation has not always shown, but the alternative may be to watch, carefully and scientifically, as species disappear.

topic: passive rewilding of abandoned farmland in European uplands: fire, open-habitat species and rural communities
title: When the Farmers Leave
subtitle: Millions of hectares of European farmland are reverting to the wild without any plan. Is this an opportunity or a loss?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Across large parts of Europe, farming is quietly retreating from the land. In the mountain valleys of the Iberian interior, the Balkans and the Carpathians, younger generations have moved to the cities over the past seventy years, and the terraces, hay meadows and upland pastures their families once worked are being left to themselves. Estimates vary widely, but some projections suggest that an area larger than Portugal could fall out of agricultural use by the middle of this century. Many conservationists have welcomed this trend under the label of 'passive rewilding': the idea that nature, if simply left alone, will restore itself. The phrase is appealing, but it is also misleading. To call the process passive implies that nothing is being decided, when in fact the choice not to manage land is a decision like any other, and one with consequences that fall unevenly on different species and different people.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for optimism rests largely on the work of Professor Mirela Zavoianu of the Institute for Landscape Dynamics, who has spent two decades comparing historical aerial photographs with recent satellite images. Her results show that fields left untended are typically colonised by scrub within a decade and by young woodland within thirty to forty years. Over the same period, red deer, wild boar and, in some regions, wolves have returned to areas from which they had been absent for generations. Zavoianu argues that abandonment has done more to expand Europe's forest cover than any deliberate planting programme, and that it has done so at almost no expense to the public. Her data are difficult to dispute, but the claim that the process is free deserves scrutiny. The costs have not disappeared; they have simply been postponed and transferred to others, notably to rural fire services and to the residents who remain.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Fire is the most immediate of those costs. For centuries, grazing animals and the cutting of hay and firewood kept the quantity of flammable vegetation in check. Once these activities stop, continuous stretches of shrubs accumulate across hillsides, and fires that would once have burned out in a patchwork of fields can now spread for many kilometres. Anselm Grevholt, a fire ecologist at the Mediterranean Wildfire Research Unit, has shown that blazes in abandoned landscapes tend to be both larger and more intense than those in actively farmed areas. His proposed remedy is to release semi-wild herds of horses and hardy cattle, which he describes as 'living firebreaks' capable of thinning the undergrowth without human labour. The idea is attractive, and it fits neatly with the broader rewilding agenda. However, most of the supporting evidence comes from small, fenced trial plots, and it remains unclear whether free-ranging animals would choose to graze in the places where fuel is most dangerous.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second concern is that the benefits of abandonment are distributed very unequally among wildlife. Dr Ludmila Vrbenská, who studies butterflies at the Centre for Grassland Ecology, points out that a large proportion of Europe's threatened species depend not on wilderness but on open habitats maintained by centuries of low-intensity farming. Flower-rich meadows, grazed heaths and the larks and orchids associated with them decline rapidly as scrub closes in. In Vrbenská's view, unmanaged reversion risks exchanging species that are rare for species that are already common, such as those typical of young woodland. Rewilding advocates sometimes respond that such meadows are artificial, the product of human activity rather than nature. This seems to me a weak argument. A hay meadow that has been cut every summer for a thousand years is part of the ecological history of a region, and there is no good reason to regard the woodland that replaces it as inherently more natural.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The human dimension is easily overlooked. The rural sociologist Ruy Esteireiro has interviewed residents of more than sixty mountain villages, many of whom are elderly and live in settlements that have lost most of their population. Few of them describe the advancing vegetation as the return of nature. Instead, they tend to see it as a visible sign of their community's decline and of the erasure of work done by earlier generations. Ecotourism is frequently promoted as a source of new income, but Esteireiro found that in most villages it had so far created only a handful of jobs, the majority of them seasonal. Conservationists, for their part, have too often described these regions as empty, a habit of language that renders invisible the people who still live there.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that abandoned land should be returned to farming, which in most cases would be neither economically realistic nor desirable. A more promising approach is to plan for a mosaic: allowing some areas to revert to woodland while keeping others open through subsidised grazing, and deliberately maintaining breaks in vegetation where fire risk is greatest. Such an arrangement could accommodate both the species of the forest and those of the meadow. Its main weakness is practical rather than ecological. A mosaic only works if it is designed across whole regions, since decisions taken farm by farm cannot produce a coherent pattern, and coordination on that scale remains rare.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Abandonment will continue whatever conservationists think of it, because the forces driving it, from falling farm incomes to the attraction of urban employment, lie largely outside their control. The real question, therefore, is not whether these landscapes will become wilder but what kind of wildness will emerge, and who will bear its costs. Treating abandonment as a conservation strategy in its own right would be a mistake. It is better understood as an opportunity which, without careful planning, could just as easily become a loss.

topic: lynx reintroduction and the social roots of opposition among farmers and rural communities
title: The Cat Nobody Sees
subtitle: Plans to return the lynx to the forests of western Europe reveal that the hardest part of reintroduction may have little to do with ecology

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the animals proposed for return to the forests of north-western Europe, the Eurasian lynx is perhaps the most paradoxical. A medium-sized cat weighing around twenty kilograms, it hunts mainly at dusk and dawn, ambushing roe deer in dense woodland, and it is so secretive that people living within its range may go a lifetime without seeing one. Lynx disappeared from much of western Europe centuries ago, largely as a result of hunting and the clearance of forests, but since the 1970s they have been returned to several mountain regions of the continent, and proposals to release them in further areas are now debated with surprising intensity. The creature at the centre of these arguments poses no recorded threat to human safety. That it nonetheless provokes such strong feeling suggests that the debate is not really about the animal at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The ecological case has been made most forcefully by Dr Tove Ekerholm of the Nordic Institute for Forest Ecology. Her field studies, which tracked radio-collared lynx over several winters, indicate that a single adult kills roughly one roe deer a week. At the scale of a whole landscape, she concedes, this has only a modest effect on deer numbers, which in many regions have grown so large that browsing prevents young trees from becoming established. For Ekerholm, however, controlling deer was never the main point. What matters, she argues, is the restoration of a natural process, predation by a large carnivore, that has been missing from these forests for hundreds of years.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sheep farmers have been the most vocal opponents of reintroduction, and their concern is easy to understand. Yet Ekerholm's analysis of data from continental Europe suggests that lynx rarely take livestock. Most attacks occur where flocks graze unattended close to forest edges, and losses tend to be concentrated on a small number of farms rather than spread across a region. She is confident that once farmers are shown these figures, much of their opposition will fade. This optimism seems to me misplaced. Statistics rarely change minds when a dispute is really about something other than the facts being counted, and there is good reason to think that the lynx debate is a dispute of exactly this kind.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That reason comes from the work of Professor Eilidh MacCrimmon, a social scientist who has spent several years interviewing farmers, gamekeepers and village residents in areas where releases have been proposed. Many of those she spoke to were less worried about the animals than about who was making decisions. Reintroduction, in their eyes, was a project designed by urban conservation charities and distant officials, and the lynx had become a symbol of outsiders' control over the countryside. MacCrimmon also examined compensation schemes, which typically pay farmers for livestock proven to have been killed by a predator. Proof is often hard to obtain, since carcasses may be scavenged or never found. More strikingly, several farmers described compensation as an admission that their livelihoods were negotiable. Payments of this kind are clearly necessary, but they are by no means sufficient.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences of this alienation can be severe. In several reintroduced populations, illegal killing has been the largest single cause of death among adult lynx, and MacCrimmon interprets this not simply as criminal behaviour but as an expression of the same resentment. She points to one Alpine valley where farmers were invited to run the network of camera traps used to monitor the cats, and where reports of poaching subsequently fell. The lesson appears clear: no reintroduction, however sound its ecological basis, can be imposed successfully on a population that is determined to resist it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different kind of caution comes from the conservation geneticist Dr Andrius Žemaitaitis. Several of Europe's reintroduced lynx populations, he notes, are descended from a handful of founders, in some cases fewer than ten animals, and they now show worryingly low genetic diversity. Inbreeding can reduce fertility and leave a population vulnerable to disease. Žemaitaitis therefore recommends releasing larger numbers of animals drawn from several different source populations, and linking isolated groups through wildlife corridors. He goes further, arguing that no new release should take place until a corridor plan has been agreed. His concerns are well founded, but this final condition is too strict. Waiting for ideal conditions risks postponing reintroduction indefinitely, and genetic diversity can be improved later by releasing additional animals into an established population.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the end, the success of any lynx reintroduction will be measured less by the number of cats in the forest than by whether the people who live alongside them come to accept their presence. The animal's elusiveness cuts both ways: it means that conflict with humans is rare, but it also means that the lynx exists for most people as an idea rather than as an animal, and ideas are easily made into symbols. If ecologists want the lynx to be welcomed, the most useful thing they can do may be to spend less time presenting evidence and more time listening.

topic: eradicating introduced rats and cats from islands to restore seabird colonies
title: Clearing the Islands
subtitle: Removing introduced predators from islands has transformed seabird conservation, but the easy victories may now be over

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Islands occupy a small fraction of the earth's land area, yet they have witnessed a disproportionate share of recorded extinctions. Much of the blame lies with animals that arrived alongside people: rats that came ashore from ships, cats brought to control them, and goats and pigs released as a source of food for passing sailors. Seabirds have suffered especially badly. Many species nest in burrows or on open ground and evolved in the absence of mammalian predators, so they have few defences against a rat that eats eggs and chicks. Since the 1980s, introduced mammals have been removed from several hundred islands around the world, and the results have been remarkable. It is arguably the most effective conservation tool developed in the past half-century, and certainly one of the few whose successes can be measured with confidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Professor Hallvard Strømsnes, a seabird ecologist, has monitored breeding colonies on a group of North Atlantic islands for more than two decades, both before and after rats were removed. Within fifteen years, he reports, the number of burrow-nesting petrels had increased several times over, and species that had abandoned the islands altogether had begun to return. Strømsnes is particularly interested in what happens beyond the shoreline. Seabirds feed at sea but deposit their droppings on land, and the nutrients washed from these deposits fertilise the surrounding waters. Around islands where colonies have recovered, he argues, algae grow more vigorously and reef fish grow faster. This is a compelling idea, but it should be treated with some caution: such effects on marine life have so far been documented at only a handful of sites.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The techniques of eradication have improved considerably. On most islands, poison bait is scattered from helicopters guided by satellite navigation, so that every square metre of ground receives a dose. Dr Ignacio Etxaniz, who has planned operations on islands in three oceans, stresses that the aim is not to reduce numbers but to remove every last animal. A rat population can recover from a few survivors within a couple of years, so a partial success is, in practical terms, a failure. Nevertheless, the proportion of operations that achieve complete removal has risen steadily, and islands of tens of thousands of hectares are now being attempted. In Etxaniz's view, the size of island that can be cleared is no longer limited by technique; it is limited by the money available to pay for helicopters, bait and years of follow-up monitoring.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The poisons themselves are a source of concern. Most baits contain anticoagulants, which can also kill birds of prey, ground-feeding songbirds and land crabs that eat the pellets or the poisoned rodents. Dr Njeri Gathogo, an ecotoxicologist, has documented deaths among several native species following large-scale bait drops, and on some islands rare birds have had to be captured and kept in temporary captivity until the poison has degraded. Gathogo favours greater use of bait stations, which release poison only to animals that enter them, even though this approach is slower and requires teams on the ground. Her findings deserve attention. Even so, the losses she describes are generally temporary, whereas the damage done by an established predator continues for as long as it remains on the island.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental change is that the remaining candidates for eradication are increasingly inhabited. Most of the small, uninhabited islands where operations are straightforward have already been cleared. On islands with resident communities, cats are household pets, pigs may carry cultural significance, and spreading poison near homes and water supplies requires consent that cannot simply be assumed. The anthropologist Dr Kalolaine Mailau has studied eradication proposals on several Pacific islands and concludes that projects succeed where islanders themselves define what restoration is supposed to achieve. In her experience, a programme presented as a gift from outside experts is likely to be quietly undermined. For the next generation of projects, then, understanding communities will be at least as important as the logistics of bait and helicopters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Eradication can also produce unexpected results. On one sub-Antarctic island, the removal of cats allowed rabbits, which the cats had previously kept in check, to multiply rapidly, and the rabbits then stripped large areas of vegetation on which nesting birds depended. Cases like this have persuaded the Southern Islands Restoration Trust, a consortium of conservation agencies, to argue that all the introduced mammals on an island should be removed in a single coordinated operation, rather than one at a time. The Trust also emphasises biosecurity, since a cleared island can be reinvaded by a single pregnant rat that escapes from a visiting boat. The point is well made: the investment in an eradication is wasted if the arrival of new predators is not prevented.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Looking further ahead, some researchers, Etxaniz among them, have expressed enthusiasm for genetic techniques that could spread infertility through a rodent population without the use of poison. Such methods might one day make it possible to clear islands that are currently too large or too densely populated for conventional operations. Yet the enthusiasm seems premature. A modified organism, once released, cannot be recalled, and rodents have a long history of travelling on ships to places where nobody intended them to go. Until it can be shown that such changes would remain confined to their target island, the poison and the helicopter are likely to remain the main instruments of island restoration.

topic: preparing captive-bred animals for release: behavioural deficits, adaptation to captivity and soft release
title: Learning to Be Wild
subtitle: Breeding endangered animals in captivity is one thing; teaching them to survive outside it is quite another

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past fifty years, captive breeding has rescued a number of birds and mammals that at one point survived only in zoos and specialist breeding centres. Such programmes attract public support because their achievements are easy to count: so many chicks hatched, so many cubs raised. Yet producing animals in captivity is considerably easier than returning them successfully to the wild, and for many species the second task has proved far harder than anticipated. A programme that breeds thousands of animals which then die within weeks of release has achieved very little. The proper measure of success, in other words, is not how many animals leave the breeding centre, but how many survive, and eventually reproduce, outside it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the difficulty became clear when the Translocation Outcomes Consortium, an international network of conservation biologists, reviewed the records of more than three hundred releases. Animals bred in captivity were, on average, markedly less likely to survive their first year than wild animals that had simply been caught in one place and moved to another. The main causes of death were predation, starvation and failure to find adequate shelter, and in a minority of programmes fewer than one released animal in ten was still alive after twelve months. These figures need to be interpreted with care, however. Captive-bred animals are often used precisely because no wild source population remains, and they are frequently released into degraded habitats where any animal, whatever its origin, would struggle to survive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even so, there is clear evidence that captivity changes behaviour. Dr Pernille Hvidbjerg, a behavioural ecologist, has observed captive-raised animals of several species and finds that many show little or no reaction when a predator approaches, and some actively approach people. Their foraging skills are also limited, since they are used to finding food in the same place each day. Hvidbjerg has experimented with predator-aversion training, in which a model fox or hawk is presented together with recorded alarm calls. Trained animals respond more strongly to danger than untrained ones, but the effect fades within a few weeks unless it is regularly reinforced. Such training is clearly worth doing, but it cannot replace the experience that wild-born animals acquire over a lifetime.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more troubling possibility has been raised by Professor Chidera Achugbu, a geneticist who studies zoo populations. In captivity, she points out, the individuals that breed most successfully are often those that are calm, tolerant of crowding and unafraid of keepers, traits that are of little value in the wild. Over a few generations, natural selection in reverse may therefore produce populations that are genetically suited to captivity. Achugbu has found measurable changes after as few as three or four generations. She recommends keeping the captive phase as short as possible and regularly bringing wild-born individuals into breeding programmes where they are available. Of all the problems discussed here, this seems the most serious, because no amount of training can undo a change that is written into an animal's genes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have concentrated on the moment of release itself. Dr Rocío Tintaya has studied the reintroduction of a ground-nesting parrot in the foothills of the Andes. Some birds were released immediately on arrival, a method known as hard release; others were kept for several weeks in pens at the release site, where the supply of food was gradually reduced. The birds given this soft release survived their first year at roughly twice the rate of those set free immediately, and they tended to remain closer to the release area. Tintaya acknowledges that soft release is expensive, and that prolonged contact with keepers can make animals too comfortable around people. Nonetheless, her results have attracted considerable interest, not least because the pens themselves cost little compared with the years of breeding that precede any release.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most promising approach involves using animals to teach other animals. In some programmes, captive-bred individuals are released alongside older animals, or into areas where a wild population of the same species still exists, so that they can learn where to find food and how to recognise danger by watching their companions. Animals that learn in this way appear to acquire skills more quickly and to retain them for longer than those trained by humans. The obvious limitation is that the approach depends on wild animals being available to act as teachers, and for the most endangered species they may no longer exist.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that captive breeding should be abandoned. For some species it remains the only option, and without it several would already have vanished entirely. However, it should be treated as a last resort rather than a substitute for protecting habitats, and where it is used, preparation for release ought to be built into a programme from the very beginning, not added at the end. An animal that has spent its whole life being fed and protected is, in a real sense, a different animal from its wild ancestors, and returning it to the wild requires far more than opening the door of a cage.
