topic: Pleistocene rewilding: using living species as ecological proxies for extinct megafauna
title: Ghosts of the Ice Age
subtitle: Should living animals be recruited to perform the work of giants that disappeared thousands of years ago?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until relatively recently in geological terms, every continent apart from Antarctica supported a remarkable variety of very large animals. Mammoths and mastodons roamed the northern grasslands, giant ground sloths browsed the forests of the Americas, and wild horses and camels grazed plains where none are found today. Between roughly fifty thousand and ten thousand years ago, most of these creatures vanished. Whether the principal cause was a changing climate, hunting by expanding human populations or some combination of the two is still argued over, and the evidence differs from one continent to another. What is less often appreciated is that the loss involved more than a list of species. When the giants disappeared, the work they had performed in their ecosystems disappeared with them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The palaeoecologist Professor Magnus Torfason has devoted much of his career to reconstructing that work. Large herbivores, he argues, kept vegetation open by trampling and browsing, carried nutrients from fertile valleys to poorer uplands in their dung, and dispersed the seeds of plants too large for any smaller animal to swallow. He draws particular attention to several trees in Central and South America whose heavy fruits fall to the ground and rot, apparently waiting for animals that will never return. Torfason calls them 'anachronisms', survivors of a partnership whose other half has gone. The evidence for this specific claim is largely circumstantial, since no one can observe an extinct sloth eating fruit. The wider picture he paints, however, of landscapes still shaped by the absence of animals that once lived there, is persuasive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: From this insight emerged one of the boldest proposals in modern conservation. Under the banner of 'Pleistocene rewilding', a group of ecologists suggested that elephants, camels, cheetahs and lions might be introduced to large, fenced reserves in the grasslands of North America, where they would stand in for their extinct relatives. Such animals, it was claimed, would restore missing ecological processes and at the same time provide secure populations of species threatened in their native ranges. The idea was imaginative, but in its full form it was never realistic. The costs, the risks to people and livestock and the likely reaction of rural communities made it a gift to critics, and the ridicule it attracted diverted attention from more modest versions of the same idea that deserved far more serious consideration.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One such version uses animals that are already present. In the deserts of the south-western United States, feral donkeys descended from animals abandoned by miners are routinely culled as nuisances. Yet a team led by Dr Ilka Raudsepp found that during dry periods these donkeys dig wells up to two metres deep in dry stream beds in order to reach groundwater. The wells were subsequently visited by dozens of other kinds of birds, mammals and insects, and once abandoned they became sites where tree seedlings took root. Wild equids that once lived in the region probably behaved in the same way. Raudsepp concludes that animals currently managed as unwanted intruders may in fact be performing functions that were lost with the extinct megafauna.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced. Dr Shirin Golpayegani, who studies biological invasions, argues that a proxy is simply an introduced species described in more flattering terms. The history of deliberate introductions, she notes, is full of animals that behaved quite differently in their new homes from what their sponsors had predicted. In her view, the 'functional equivalence' of a living species and an extinct one is usually assumed rather than demonstrated; donkeys, for instance, also trample stream banks and may compete with native bighorn sheep for scarce water. Her caution is valuable, but her argument proves too much. It is not reasonable to treat every non-native animal alike, regardless of whether its ecological role was filled by a close relative for millions of years until very recently. On one point, though, she is surely right: the burden of proof should rest with those who want to introduce a proxy, not with those who doubt it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is raised by Dr Kwabena Sarpong-Kumi, who has spent fifteen years studying elephants in the savannas of West and southern Africa. Their effects, he has found, depend heavily on local conditions. In one reserve, a given density of elephants converted dense woodland into open grassland within two decades; in another, with different rainfall and fire patterns, a similar density made little visible difference. If the impact of elephants cannot be reliably predicted on the continent where they evolved, Sarpong-Kumi asks, how could anyone forecast their behaviour on a different one? He does not reject proxies outright, but favours small, closely monitored trials that can be reversed if necessary, with criteria for removing the animals agreed before any are released.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It seems unlikely that lions will ever hunt camels on the prairies of North America, and probably that is just as well. Yet the debate has been valuable for reasons that have little to do with any particular release. It has shown that the ecosystems conservationists work to protect, and often describe as natural, may themselves be impoverished remnants of something far richer. Once that is recognised, the question of what restoration should aim for becomes considerably more complicated, and considerably more interesting.

topic: back-breeding cattle to resemble the extinct aurochs for use as large grazers in rewilding
title: Breeding Back the Aurochs
subtitle: Europe's great wild ox died out four centuries ago. Can selective breeding bring back something like it, and does it matter if the result is not quite the real thing?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For thousands of years, the aurochs was the largest land animal in much of Europe. A wild ox standing up to one metre eighty at the shoulder, with long forward-curving horns, it appears in cave paintings and was the ancestor of almost all modern cattle. As forests were cleared and hunting increased, its range contracted steadily, and the last known aurochs died in a royal hunting reserve in Poland early in the seventeenth century. Today, several breeding projects across Europe are attempting to produce animals that resemble it, with the intention of releasing them into rewilding areas. Whatever their scientific merits, these projects have achieved something unusual: the idea of bringing back a lost giant has captured public imagination in a way that the protection of soil or wetland rarely does, and conservation as a whole has benefited from the attention.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method is known as back-breeding. Because the genes of the aurochs did not vanish entirely but survive, scattered and diluted, in its domestic descendants, it should in principle be possible to reassemble at least some of them. Dr Gerrit Oosterwolde, who leads one of the largest programmes, crosses primitive breeds from southern and eastern Europe that retain features of their wild ancestor, and then selects offspring for characteristics such as horn shape, body size and coat colour. His team now also compares the DNA of candidate animals with genetic material extracted from aurochs bones found in archaeological sites, using the results to decide which animals should be bred together. Progress is inevitably slow, since a cow produces only one calf a year and each generation takes several years to reach breeding age. After six generations, he reports, some bulls are already strikingly similar in appearance to the animals depicted in prehistoric art.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Halina Chmielarczyk, a palaeogeneticist, is unimpressed by such comparisons. Resemblance, she argues, is a poor guide to ancestry: two animals can look alike while differing in thousands of genes that affect behaviour, digestion and resistance to disease, none of which is visible in a photograph. In her view, back-breeding produces a new breed of cattle that happens to look like an extinct one, and the projects should say so plainly. On this point she is right. To describe these animals as aurochs, or even as recreated aurochs, is to promise something that selective breeding cannot deliver, and such claims are likely to damage the credibility of rewilding when the public eventually learns the truth.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the grazing ecologist Dr Teodoro Valdeolmillos, however, the argument about authenticity misses the point. What rewilding areas need, he says, is not a historical replica but an animal that does the job the aurochs once did: grazing and trampling vegetation in an uneven pattern that maintains a mixture of woodland, scrub and open grassland. The most important criterion is therefore hardiness, above all the ability to survive winter without supplementary feeding, and several existing breeds already meet it. There is much to be said for this practical view. Even so, it underestimates the importance of appearance. Rewilding depends on public support, and an animal that looks wild and impressive is far more likely to win that support than an ordinary-looking cow, however well it grazes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most difficult questions are legal rather than biological. Dr Aino Peltokangas, who specialises in animal welfare law, points out that in many countries livestock owners are obliged to give their animals winter fodder and veterinary care. Free-roaming cattle in a rewilding area occupy an uncertain position between wild and domestic, and managers are often unsure which set of rules applies. The consequences became painfully clear in a large reserve in the Low Countries, where a series of hard winters led to the deaths of hundreds of grazing animals from starvation. Images of the dying animals provoked a public outcry, and the reserve's managers were forced to begin feeding and culling. Peltokangas argues that the status of such animals must be clearly defined in law before further releases take place, a view that seems difficult to dispute.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters of back-breeding point to economic as well as ecological benefits. Herds of large, wild-looking cattle attract visitors, and in several remote regions they have become the focus of small tourism businesses offering guided walks and photography. One upland estate in northern Spain reports that income from visitors now covers roughly a third of the annual cost of keeping its herd. Grazing by these animals may also reduce the cost of managing vegetation that would otherwise have to be cut by machine. Nevertheless, the economic case remains largely untested, and most projects still depend heavily on grants from charities and public bodies.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to dismiss back-breeding as a romantic indulgence, and some of the claims made for it deserve that criticism. Yet the underlying aim, to return a large grazing animal to European landscapes that have lacked one for centuries, is a sound one. If the programmes are honest about what they are producing, and if the legal status of the animals is settled, the cattle that emerge from them may prove genuinely useful, even if no one ever mistakes them for the real thing.

topic: sea otter recovery on the North Pacific coast: kelp forests, shellfish fisheries and historical baselines
title: The Otter and the Urchin
subtitle: The return of the sea otter to the North Pacific is often told as a simple success story. The reality involves difficult trade-offs

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the fur of the sea otter, the densest of any mammal, made it one of the most valuable commodities in the North Pacific. Ships from several nations pursued the animals along the coasts of Asia and North America, and a population that may once have numbered in the hundreds of thousands was reduced to perhaps two thousand individuals, surviving in a few isolated colonies. An international treaty signed in 1911 brought commercial hunting to an end. From the late 1960s onwards, several hundred otters were captured and moved by boat and aircraft to stretches of coast from which they had disappeared, and in a number of these places their descendants now form substantial populations.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The ecological consequences have been studied in detail by the marine ecologist Dr Marisol Echepare. Unlike whales and seals, sea otters have no layer of blubber and depend for warmth on their fur and a very high metabolic rate, which obliges them to consume roughly a quarter of their body weight every day. Sea urchins form an important part of their diet. Where otters are absent, urchin numbers grow rapidly and the urchins graze kelp down to bare rock, creating what divers call urchin barrens. Where otters return, Echepare has found, kelp generally recovers within a few years. Kelp forests shelter young fish, dampen the energy of incoming swells and absorb large quantities of carbon, and Echepare has attempted to calculate the value of this carbon in monetary terms. Her account of the otter as a guardian of the kelp is one of the clearest examples of a predator restoring an entire habitat. The carbon figures, however, should be treated with caution, since they depend on how much kelp is eventually buried in deep sediments rather than decomposing, and this remains poorly understood.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone has welcomed the otters back. Besides urchins, they eat crabs, clams and abalone, all of which support valuable fisheries, and in several recolonised areas shellfish harvests have fallen sharply. Professor Isak Haugseth, a fisheries economist, argues that the costs of otter recovery fall heavily on a small number of fishing families, while the benefits, including more abundant finfish, tourism and carbon storage, are spread thinly across society as a whole. He proposes that those who benefit should fund compensation for those who lose. This is a fair argument, although calculating appropriate compensation would be far from simple. It also overlooks an important point. The abundance of shellfish that these fisheries relied upon was itself largely a consequence of the otters' absence, and fisheries built on that abundance were, in a sense, living on borrowed time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That point is complicated, however, by the work of Dr Seo-yun Hyeon, an anthropologist who has examined archaeological shell deposits left by coastal communities over several thousand years. The deposits, she argues, show that people living along these coasts hunted otters regularly, keeping their numbers near villages low enough to protect the shellfish beds on which those communities depended. If she is right, the situation that conservationists now seek to restore, with abundant otters and scarce shellfish, may itself have been unusual for much of human history. Hyeon proposes that coastal communities should share in the management of otter populations, including, in some places, a limited harvest. Her proposal is controversial, since sea otters remain legally protected across most of their range, but it raises an uncomfortable question about which past a restoration project should be trying to recreate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other evidence suggests that otters cannot always restore kelp on their own. Researchers in the Pacific Kelp Monitoring Network have recorded sites where urchin barrens have persisted despite the presence of otters. In recent years, prolonged periods of unusually warm water have weakened kelp along parts of the coast, while a mass die-off of predatory sea stars has removed another important check on urchin numbers. In such conditions, the Network concludes, otters alone are insufficient, and recovery may also require divers to remove urchins by hand and, in some cases, the replanting of kelp.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The otters' own expansion has also been slower than many expected. Female sea otters tend to remain close to the area where they were born, and established populations typically extend their range by only a few kilometres each year. As a result, large gaps remain along the coast, and some biologists have proposed further translocations to speed up recolonisation. Such proposals have met strong resistance from fishing organisations, which fear a repetition of the losses experienced elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The return of the sea otter is frequently cited as a triumph of species reintroduction, and in many respects it deserves that reputation. Yet it is better understood as a lesson in trade-offs than as a simple success. Restoring a predator restores its effects, both welcome and unwelcome, and the decision about which of those effects matter most is ultimately not a scientific one. It is a decision about whose coast is being restored, and for whom.

topic: rapid evolution of plants and animals in cities
title: Evolution in the Concrete Jungle
subtitle: Cities were once thought to be evolutionary dead ends; a growing body of research suggests they may be among the fastest-changing environments on the planet

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, biologists treated cities as places where nature was diminished rather than transformed. Urban areas appeared as blank spaces on distribution maps, and the species that persisted in them were regarded as tolerant generalists simply making the best of poor conditions. Evolution, it was assumed, operated on timescales of thousands or millions of years, far too slowly to register in settlements that had existed for only a few centuries. That assumption has now collapsed. Over the past two decades, studies on several continents have documented heritable changes in urban populations of plants, insects, birds and mammals, some of which appear to have arisen within a few dozen generations. Cities, it turns out, are not merely places where wildlife survives; they are places where it is being reshaped.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most compelling evidence comes from white clover, a small plant found in lawns and verges throughout the temperate world. Many clover plants produce hydrogen cyanide when their leaves are damaged, a chemical defence against grazing animals. The trait carries a cost in places with severe frosts, however, because freezing ruptures the plant's cells and releases the toxin into its own tissues. A research consortium coordinated by the plant geneticist Wanjiru Ndiritu at the Highland Institute of Ecology sampled clover along gradients running from city centres to the surrounding countryside in more than a hundred cities. In a majority of them, cyanide-producing plants became steadily rarer towards the urban core. Ndiritu's explanation is counterintuitive: because cities often have less insulating snow cover, ground-level temperatures in winter can actually fall lower than in rural fields, favouring plants that do not produce the toxin. The pattern was not universal, she acknowledges, but its repetition across so many independent locations makes chance an unlikely explanation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Animals offer equally striking examples. The ornithologist Bence Szekeres of the Danube Field Station has spent twelve years comparing blackbirds in central parks with those in nearby forests. City birds, he reports, begin singing earlier in the morning, breed several weeks sooner and are noticeably less fearful of approaching humans. Similar contrasts have been found in lizards, whose limbs and toe pads have altered in ways that seem to improve their grip on smooth walls and painted surfaces. In Szekeres's view, however, such findings demand caution. Many differences between urban and rural animals, he argues, may reflect flexible responses to the environment rather than genetic change. A blackbird hatched in a forest might, if moved to a city as a chick, behave exactly like its urban neighbours.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This distinction lies at the heart of the field's methodological debate. Demonstrating genuine evolution requires showing that a trait is inherited, not merely displayed, and that usually means rearing animals or plants from both environments under identical conditions. Such common garden experiments are slow and expensive, especially for long-lived species, and so they remain comparatively rare. Eleni Arvanitaki, an evolutionary biologist at the Aegean University of Life Sciences, has reviewed nearly two hundred published claims of urban adaptation and concludes that fewer than a third provide convincing evidence of a genetic basis. She does not dispute that urban evolution occurs; her concern is that the excitement surrounding the subject has encouraged researchers to announce adaptation where only difference has been shown. This is a fair criticism, and one the discipline has been slow to confront.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all urban evolution, moreover, is adaptive. Roads, buildings and railways divide populations into small, isolated fragments, and in small populations genes can be lost or become fixed purely by chance, a process known as genetic drift. Studies of white-footed mice in a large North American city, conducted by a team under Hiroshi Takamura, found that populations living in separate parks, sometimes only a few kilometres apart, had become genetically distinct from one another. Takamura stresses that much of this divergence carries no apparent benefit to the animals; it is simply the signature of isolation. Indeed, he warns that the loss of genetic variety may leave such populations less able to respond to future challenges, such as new diseases or a warming climate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why should any of this matter beyond academic biology? One answer is that cities offer something close to a natural experiment repeated hundreds of times. Because urban environments share many features, including heat, artificial light, pollution and hard surfaces, researchers can ask whether different cities push species in the same direction, a question that bears directly on how predictable evolution is. A second answer is practical. If pest species such as rats, pigeons or mosquitoes are evolving resistance to control measures in cities, as some evidence suggests, then urban managers can no longer treat these populations as fixed targets. The research group led by Armen Petrossian has argued that conservation planning should incorporate evolutionary thinking, for example by designing green corridors that allow isolated populations to exchange genes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that urban evolution offers grounds for complacency about the loss of wild habitat. The species that adapt successfully to cities are a small and unrepresentative minority; for every clover or blackbird that thrives, many more organisms simply disappear when land is built upon. What the research does demonstrate is that cities are ecosystems in their own right, with their own evolutionary dynamics, and that the decisions made by planners and architects are, whether they intend it or not, acting as agents of natural selection. Recognising this does not make cities any less damaging to biodiversity, but it does make them far more interesting to study.

topic: green roofs: stormwater, cooling and biodiversity claims
title: Gardens in the Sky
subtitle: Green roofs are spreading rapidly across the world's cities, but the benefits claimed for them are not always the ones they deliver

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Look down on the centre of almost any large European or East Asian city today and you would notice a quiet transformation. Flat roofs that were once covered in bitumen and gravel are increasingly planted with grasses, sedums and wildflowers. Some cities now require green roofs on new commercial buildings above a certain size, and many offer subsidies for converting older ones. Supporters credit them with an impressive list of benefits: cooler buildings, cleaner air, reduced flooding, habitat for wildlife and even improved wellbeing for office workers who can see them from their desks. Such enthusiasm is understandable, but it has sometimes run ahead of the evidence, and a clearer picture of what green roofs actually achieve is only now emerging.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest case concerns rainwater. In a city, most rain falls on impermeable surfaces and rushes straight into drains, which can overflow during heavy storms and discharge untreated sewage into rivers. A green roof acts like a sponge. Its growing medium and plants hold water and release it slowly, partly through evaporation. Measurements by the hydrologist Neema Mwakasege at the Coastal Cities Laboratory indicate that a typical extensive roof, with a substrate only eight to ten centimetres deep, retains around half of the annual rainfall that lands on it. Mwakasege is careful to add a qualification, however. During the most intense storms, which are precisely the events that overwhelm drainage systems, the substrate quickly becomes saturated, and the roof's capacity to hold back water falls sharply. Green roofs, in her words, are "excellent at managing ordinary rain and modest at managing extraordinary rain".

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Claims about temperature are similarly mixed. A planted roof certainly insulates the building beneath it, and on a summer afternoon the surface of a green roof can be dozens of degrees cooler than a dark conventional one. Yet the effect on energy use depends heavily on the building. Lars Eskildsen, an engineer who has monitored offices across Scandinavia, found that savings in modern, well-insulated buildings were negligible, because the roof added little to insulation that was already effective. Older buildings with poor insulation, by contrast, showed substantial reductions in cooling costs. The effect on the city as a whole, rather than on individual buildings, is harder still to establish. Because roofs sit high above the street, a green roof may do little to cool the pavements where pedestrians actually feel the heat.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The biodiversity argument has proved the most contentious of all. Many early green roofs were planted almost entirely with sedum, a hardy succulent that needs little water or care and tolerates the thin soils and fierce exposure of rooftops. The ecologist Valentina Aldana argues that such monocultures offer wildlife little more than a bare roof would. Her surveys of rooftops in three Latin American cities found that roofs with deeper and more varied substrates, planted with native wildflowers and incorporating logs, stones and patches of bare sand, supported several times as many species of insects and spiders. Aldana believes that building regulations should specify the ecological quality of green roofs, not merely their area. It is hard to disagree, although such roofs are heavier and more costly, and some buildings simply cannot bear the additional weight.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty concerns what happens after installation. Green roofs are often presented as low-maintenance, and the impression lingers that once planted they will look after themselves. In reality, roofs that are never weeded, watered during droughts or checked for blocked drains can deteriorate within a few years. Henrik Bergqvist, who advises municipal governments on urban greening, has inspected hundreds of subsidised roofs and estimates that roughly a quarter are in poor condition. He attributes this not to the technology but to funding structures, which typically pay for installation but make no provision for upkeep. A roof that has reverted to bare substrate delivers none of the benefits that justified the subsidy in the first place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The claim that green roofs clean the air deserves particular scrutiny. Plants do capture fine particles on their leaves and absorb small quantities of gases such as nitrogen dioxide, and laboratory studies have confirmed both processes. The difficulty is one of scale. Most air pollution in cities is generated at street level by traffic, and it is breathed at street level by people; a few hundred square metres of sedum on top of a ten-storey building is poorly placed to intercept it. Calculations for entire districts suggest that even widespread installation would reduce pollutant concentrations by a fraction of one per cent. Cleaner air is a welcome side effect, in other words, rather than a sound reason for building a green roof.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that green roofs are a fashionable mistake. On balance, they deliver genuine improvements, particularly for stormwater, and they put to use surfaces that would otherwise be entirely wasted. But they are not a universal remedy, and policy should reflect what they do well rather than everything they might conceivably do. A city seeking to reduce street-level heat would probably achieve more by planting trees; a city worried about extreme floods will still need larger engineering solutions such as storage tanks and wider channels. The most useful contribution of the research so far may be to replace an all-purpose enthusiasm with a more modest and better-targeted one.

topic: unequal street tree canopy and urban heat
title: The Shade Divide
subtitle: Why the distribution of urban trees has become a question of fairness as well as ecology

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the hottest afternoons of a recent summer, researchers carrying handheld sensors walked two routes through the same city, a few kilometres apart. One passed along avenues lined with mature plane trees in an affluent district; the other crossed a neighbourhood of low-rise apartment blocks where trees were scarce and car parks plentiful. The difference in air temperature between the routes was more than six degrees Celsius, and the difference in the surface temperature of pavements was greater still. Findings of this kind, now replicated in dozens of cities, have turned the humble street tree into an object of intense political debate. Shade, it seems, is not distributed equally, and the inequality follows familiar lines of income and, in many places, ethnicity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Trees cool cities in two distinct ways. Most obviously, their canopies intercept sunlight before it reaches the ground, keeping pavements, walls and people in shadow. Less visibly, they draw water from the soil and release it through their leaves, a process called transpiration that consumes heat in the same way that evaporating sweat cools the skin. According to the urban climatologist Thandiwe Mahlangu, it is the second mechanism that explains why a park of mature trees can lower temperatures in the surrounding streets, not merely beneath its own branches. Mahlangu's measurements suggest, however, that this effect depends on a canopy cover of roughly forty per cent across a neighbourhood; below that threshold, scattered trees cool little more than the spot where they stand.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why are some districts so much leafier than others? The obvious explanation is that wealthier residents can afford to plant and maintain trees on private land, and that their neighbourhoods tend to have larger gardens. But historical research points to deeper causes. Studies led by the urban historian Kerem Ozturan have traced present-day canopy cover back to planning decisions made in the early twentieth century, when municipal investment in parks and boulevards was concentrated in districts judged desirable by lenders and officials. Areas classified as high-risk, often those housing migrants and minorities, received little. A century later, Ozturan argues, the map of urban shade still largely mirrors those discriminatory classifications. His work is persuasive, though it should be remembered that later decisions, such as road-widening schemes that removed mature trees, have also shaped the pattern.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Many city governments have responded with ambitious planting programmes, promising to add hundreds of thousands of trees, often with priority given to the most deprived areas. The intention is admirable, but the results have been uneven. Rosalind Fitzwalter, an arborist who has audited planting schemes in several English-speaking countries, found that in some programmes more than a third of young trees died within five years. Saplings planted along busy roads face compacted soil, salt spray, vandalism and damage from vehicles, and without regular watering during their first summers many simply do not survive. Fitzwalter maintains that cities would achieve more by planting fewer trees and caring for them properly than by chasing headline numbers. Counting trees planted, she notes, is easy; counting trees that grow up is not.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is a further complication. In some neighbourhoods, residents have opposed new trees, an attitude that planners have sometimes dismissed as ignorance. Research by the sociologist Mirela Gvozdenović suggests a more complicated picture. In interviews with residents of low-income districts, she found that objections were rarely to trees as such. Instead, people worried about falling branches, leaves blocking drains, roots lifting pavements and, above all, the possibility that greening would make the area attractive to wealthier newcomers and push up rents. Gvozdenović argues that tree programmes imposed without consultation are likely to fail, whereas those designed with residents, including decisions about species and locations, tend to enjoy greater support and survive longer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The concern about rising rents deserves to be taken seriously. Several studies have linked major greening projects with increases in property values, and in cities with weak tenant protections such increases can displace the very households the projects were intended to help. Yet it would be wrong to conclude that deprived areas should therefore be left unshaded. The health costs of heat are real and fall most heavily on the elderly, on outdoor workers and on people without air conditioning. A more defensible approach is to combine planting with measures that protect existing residents, such as rent stabilisation or community ownership of land.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Trees alone will not make cities bearable in a warming climate. Reflective roofing, better building design and changes to working hours during heatwaves all have a role. But trees offer something that engineered solutions rarely do: they improve with age, provide habitat for birds and insects, and make streets more pleasant to walk along. The real challenge, then, is not simply to plant more trees but to plant them where they are most needed, in ways that local people support, and with a commitment to looking after them for decades rather than a single growing season. Measured against that standard, few cities have yet succeeded.

topic: urban beekeeping and competition with wild pollinators
title: Hives on High
subtitle: The fashion for keeping honeybees on city rooftops may be doing less for pollinators than its supporters believe

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past fifteen years, honeybee hives have appeared on the roofs of hotels, banks, museums and corporate headquarters in cities across Europe and North America. In some districts of large capitals, the number of registered colonies has multiplied several times over. The motivation is generally benign. Hives are relatively inexpensive to install, beekeeping courses are oversubscribed in many cities, and specialist firms now offer to manage colonies on behalf of clients who never handle a frame themselves. Alarmed by reports of declining insect populations, businesses and individuals have taken up beekeeping as a visible contribution to environmental protection, and companies frequently advertise their rooftop hives in annual sustainability reports. Yet a growing number of ecologists argue that this boom rests on a misunderstanding, and that in some places it may even be harming the creatures it is intended to help.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The misunderstanding concerns which bees are actually in trouble. The western honeybee is a domesticated animal, managed by humans for honey production and crop pollination, and its global numbers have in fact risen over recent decades, even though individual beekeepers suffer serious colony losses from parasites and disease. The species facing real decline are wild pollinators: the hundreds of species of solitary bees and bumblebees, along with hoverflies, moths and beetles, that receive no human care. "Keeping honeybees to save bees," says the entomologist Leilani Tuiasosopo, "is rather like keeping chickens to save wild birds." Her comparison is deliberately provocative, but it captures an important point that public campaigns have often obscured.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The concern is not simply that urban beekeeping fails to help wild species but that it may actively compete with them. A strong honeybee colony can contain fifty thousand workers in summer, and these foragers collect vast quantities of nectar and pollen from flowers within several kilometres of the hive. Where hives are dense and flowers limited, wild bees may find little left. A study by Agnieszka Sokolowska and colleagues, carried out in parks across a central European capital, found that the number of wild bee species recorded at flower patches fell as the density of nearby hives rose. Sokolowska is careful not to overstate the result: her data show an association, not proof of cause, and other features of densely populated districts might also have played a part. Nevertheless, the pattern matches findings from experiments in rural areas, where introducing hives has reduced the foraging success of bumblebees.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Disease presents a second risk. Honeybees carry a range of viruses, some of which have been detected in bumblebees feeding on the same flowers, apparently picked up from contaminated pollen or nectar. Bumblebee colonies are far smaller and shorter-lived than those of honeybees, and a single infected queen in spring can mean the loss of an entire nest, so even modest rates of infection could matter more than raw numbers suggest. How much harm this transmission causes to wild populations remains uncertain, but the possibility has led some researchers to recommend minimum distances between apiaries and important habitats for rare species. In cities, where hives are often placed close to the few remaining patches of wildflower meadow, such guidance is rarely followed, partly because few municipal authorities monitor where hives are kept at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this critical view. Daniel Ostrander, who chairs an association of urban beekeepers, points out that cities offer a remarkable diversity of flowering plants in gardens, parks and street plantings, often flowering over a longer season than intensively farmed countryside. In his opinion, competition is likely only where hives are packed unusually closely together. He also argues that beekeeping has educational value, introducing city dwellers to the lives of insects and encouraging them to plant flowers. These points have some merit; the problem is that the educational benefits are rarely accompanied by any clear message about the needs of wild species, so that the public comes away believing that installing hives is the best thing they can do.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, then, would genuinely help urban pollinators? The answer is less glamorous than a rooftop hive. Wild bees need a continuous supply of flowers from early spring to late autumn, and many species need bare soil, dead wood or hollow stems in which to nest. Mowing roadside verges less frequently, allowing lawns to flower, planting native shrubs and leaving untidy corners in parks would all do more, at lower cost, than adding colonies of a domesticated species. Some cities have begun to act accordingly: a few have introduced registration schemes that limit the number of hives in particular districts, while redirecting funds towards habitat improvement.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that people should stop keeping bees. Honeybees are fascinating animals, and well-managed hives in areas with plentiful forage are unlikely to cause harm. Several wildlife charities have reached a similar conclusion in their own advice, urging supporters to think first about flowers and nesting places and only afterwards about whether a hive suits their circumstances at all. But the rooftop hive should be recognised for what it is: a hobby or a source of honey, not a conservation measure. For organisations keen to demonstrate their environmental credentials, planting a meadow is less photogenic than unveiling a hive, but it is far more likely to make a difference.

topic: sponge cities: nature-based urban drainage and flood management
title: Cities That Drink the Rain
subtitle: Can planting, soaking and storing water replace the pipes on which cities have relied for two centuries?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the past two hundred years, urban drainage has been built on a single principle: remove rainwater from streets and roofs as quickly as possible. Gutters, sewers and concrete-lined channels carry it away to the nearest river or sea, and for a long time the approach worked well enough. As cities have expanded and paved over the fields and marshes that once soaked up rainfall, however, the volume of water rushing into these systems has grown, and flash flooding has become a familiar hazard in places that rarely experienced it. The response that has attracted most attention in the past decade is the so-called sponge city, in which the urban landscape itself is redesigned to absorb, store and slowly release rain. Permeable paving, planted roadside channels, rain gardens and constructed wetlands are intended to hold water where it falls rather than sending it elsewhere. The concept marks a genuine change of direction in urban engineering. The difficulty is that its slogans have advanced considerably faster than the evidence behind them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most careful measurements have been made by Ayodele Fagbenro, a civil engineer at the Gulf of Guinea Institute for Water Engineering. Over six years, her team instrumented permeable car parks and rain gardens in three coastal cities and recorded how much runoff they prevented. For the ordinary showers that make up the great majority of rainy days, the results were impressive: the features captured almost all of the water that would otherwise have entered the drains. During the most intense downpours, by contrast, the soils became saturated within an hour, after which the surfaces behaved little differently from conventional asphalt. Fagbenro concludes that such measures should be treated as a complement to pipes and storage tanks, not as a substitute for them. In her view, presenting them as a complete solution risks leaving cities exposed to precisely the events that cause the greatest damage.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The urban planner Zhuang Mingyuan approaches the subject from a different angle. He contends that judging rain gardens or pavements one at a time, as engineers tend to do, misses the real promise of the idea, which lies in reorganising whole districts around the movement of water. His proposals include reopening streams that were buried in culverts a century ago and designing parks to flood deliberately: playing fields and lawns that serve as recreational space in dry weather can be lowered slightly so that they become temporary reservoirs during a storm. One such park, completed in a southern river city, is designed to fill several times a year and to drain within two days. Zhuang's vision is undoubtedly attractive, but it depends on something that many cities lack, namely open land. Space is scarcest in the dense older neighbourhoods that tend to flood most often, and it is there that his approach would be hardest to put into practice.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A less publicised concern relates to what happens to water once it soaks into the ground. Runoff from streets is far from clean; it carries oil, tyre particles, heavy metals and, in colder climates, large quantities of salt from winter road treatment. Signe Hovdenak, a hydrologist at the Fjordland Groundwater Centre, sampled soils beneath rain gardens in a northern European city and found that salt had accumulated in them and was migrating into shallow groundwater, which in some areas supplies wells. Hovdenak does not oppose infiltration, but she argues that features built on contaminated sites or above vulnerable aquifers need filtering layers and regular monitoring. It is a point that enthusiasts for green infrastructure have, on the whole, been slow to acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of upkeep. Permeable paving gradually clogs as fine sediment fills the gaps between its blocks, and unless it is cleaned with specialised vacuum equipment its capacity to absorb water may fall by more than half within ten years. Rain gardens need weeding, replanting and the removal of litter. Bakhyt Kadyrbekov, an economist who has examined municipal budgets in several countries, notes that construction is commonly paid for by national grants, while maintenance is left to local authorities that have no additional income to cover it. The likely outcome, he warns, is a generation of green infrastructure that functions only on paper. His forecast is probably too gloomy, since a number of cities have introduced charges on property owners in proportion to the paved area they drain, and these fees provide a steady source of revenue. Nevertheless, the underlying mismatch he identifies is real.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where sponge features have a clear advantage is in their adaptability. Conventional drains are sized according to historical rainfall records, and as storms become more intense, a pipe that was adequate when it was laid may be overwhelmed. Replacing buried pipes is costly and disruptive, whereas planted channels, permeable surfaces and storage areas can be added street by street as conditions change. This flexibility is arguably the most compelling argument in their favour, and it has received less emphasis than the more photogenic benefits of greenery.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the sponge metaphor itself deserves reconsideration. A sponge, after all, absorbs water only until it is full; beyond that point, any further water simply runs off. Cities will continue to need large-scale storage and conveyance for extreme events, combined with the green measures that deal so effectively with everyday rain. The more useful question is not what proportion of rainfall a city manages to retain, a figure many programmes publish as their headline target, but how far the combination of approaches reduces harm to people, homes and livelihoods.

topic: urban carnivores such as foxes and coyotes, human-wildlife conflict and coexistence
title: Neighbours with Teeth
subtitle: Foxes, coyotes and other carnivores have moved into the city. How should their human neighbours respond?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Within living memory, a fox seen in a city garden would have been a talking point for weeks. Today, in many European capitals, foxes trot along pavements in the early evening and raise their cubs beneath garden sheds, while coyotes have established themselves in almost every large city in North America, and raccoons, badgers and even jackals have followed similar paths elsewhere. These animals are no longer occasional visitors wandering in from the surrounding countryside; they are resident, breeding populations, and in some suburbs they live at higher densities than in any rural habitat. The colonisation of cities by medium-sized carnivores is one of the most remarkable ecological shifts of recent decades, yet it has received far less scientific attention than it deserves, perhaps because researchers have traditionally preferred to study predators in wilder places.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The attractions of the city are not difficult to identify. Food is plentiful, whether in the form of household rubbish, pet food left outdoors or scraps offered deliberately by sympathetic residents. Hunting is prohibited, and there is ample shelter beneath buildings and along railway embankments. Dorottya Halmagyi, a behavioural ecologist who has fitted satellite collars to more than two hundred foxes, has shown that urban animals occupy much smaller home ranges than their rural relatives, become almost entirely nocturnal and tend to cross major roads in the quietest hours before dawn. In her view, these differences reflect behavioural flexibility rather than any inherited change. Individual foxes, she argues, learn the rhythms of the city in the same way that a commuter learns a train timetable, and young animals acquire much of this knowledge by following their mothers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Living at close quarters inevitably produces friction. Coyotes occasionally kill cats and small dogs, foxes tear open rubbish bags and dig up lawns, and on rare occasions a person is bitten. Such incidents attract intense media coverage, which can create the impression of a growing menace. Mateus Sobreira, a social scientist who has surveyed residents in two coastal cities, found that people's attitudes to coyotes depended far less on their own encounters than on what they had read or watched. Remarkably, residents who had actually seen a coyote near their homes were, on average, more tolerant of the animals than those whose knowledge came entirely from news reports. If this finding holds more widely, it suggests that well-designed information campaigns may do more to reduce hostility than any programme of removal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Disease is a more serious concern. Urban foxes are frequently afflicted by mange, a painful skin condition caused by mites, and in some regions carnivores carry parasites and viruses that can be passed to pets or, more rarely, to people. Sunil Deshmane, a wildlife veterinarian, argues that deliberate feeding is the main factor increasing this risk, because it draws animals together at the same spots and encourages contact between individuals that would otherwise keep apart. He has called for feeding to be prohibited by law. The logic is sound, but such bans are notoriously difficult to enforce, not least because a great deal of feeding is unintentional: an unsecured compost heap or a bowl of cat food left on a doorstep is as attractive to a hungry fox as a plate of scraps set out on purpose.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the standard response to troublesome carnivores was to trap and kill them. The evidence against this approach is now substantial. Removing the residents of a territory simply creates a vacancy, which is usually filled by young animals from neighbouring areas within a matter of weeks. Among coyotes, there is some evidence that heavy culling causes the survivors to produce larger litters, so that populations recover quickly. As a long-term strategy, then, culling is largely futile, although it may still be justified in the case of a particular individual that has lost its fear of people and become aggressive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An alternative is being tested by the Northshore Coexistence Project, a partnership between a city council and a local university. Its staff train residents in a technique known as hazing: when a coyote approaches, people are encouraged to shout, wave their arms and make loud noises, so that the animal learns to associate humans with discomfort and to keep its distance. The project also distributes animal-proof bin lids and runs an online system through which sightings and incidents can be reported. Over three years, complaints to the council fell by about a third. The result is encouraging, but because there was no comparable city without the programme, it is impossible to be certain that the project itself was responsible for the decline.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever policies are adopted, carnivores are now a permanent feature of urban life. Their presence brings some benefits, including the control of rats and rabbits, and for many city dwellers a fox glimpsed under a streetlight offers a rare and welcome encounter with wild nature. The real question is therefore not whether people and predators will share the city, but on what terms that sharing will take place, and whether those terms can be set by evidence rather than by headlines.

topic: green gentrification: new urban parks, rising property values and displacement
title: When Parks Push People Out
subtitle: New green spaces are meant to benefit everyone, but in some neighbourhoods they may hasten the departure of the very residents they were built for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few urban investments seem as uncontroversial as a new park. Green space is associated with lower rates of heart disease and depression, it cools surrounding streets during heatwaves, and it gives children somewhere to play. In recent years, cities have converted disused railway lines into elevated walkways, uncovered rivers that had been hidden in concrete channels and turned derelict industrial land into meadows. Yet in a number of these places a troubling pattern has emerged. As the neighbourhood becomes more attractive, rents and house prices climb, and the low-income households who lived there before the improvements find that they can no longer afford to stay. The phenomenon has come to be known as green gentrification. The irony it describes is real, but the term is now invoked so readily that it is sometimes applied to cases where the evidence for displacement is thin.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for concern rests largely on studies of property markets. Ximena Ugarteburu, an urban geographer, compared neighbourhoods within walking distance of eighteen newly created parks across several cities with similar neighbourhoods located further away. Over the following decade, house prices close to the parks rose between fifteen and twenty per cent faster, and the proportion of low-income residents fell noticeably. Ugarteburu describes parks as amenities whose value is absorbed into the price of nearby land. On this view, the principal beneficiaries of public spending on green space are not the people who use the parks but those who own property around them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The economist Joonas Hirvisalo regards such conclusions as premature. Cities, he points out, rarely choose the sites for new parks at random; they frequently invest in districts where young professionals are already arriving and prices are already rising. To separate cause from coincidence, Hirvisalo examined a group of parks whose construction had been postponed for several years because of budget shortfalls. He found that a substantial share of the increase in nearby prices had occurred before the parks opened, and in some cases before construction had even begun. His methodological point is important and too often overlooked. It does not, however, dispose of the problem altogether. Even if a park merely accelerates a change that was already under way, the speed of that change matters a great deal to a family that must find a new home within a single year rather than over a decade.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Housing statistics capture only one dimension of the issue. Prakriti Bhattarai, a sociologist who has spent three years interviewing long-standing residents of neighbourhoods near new parks, describes what she calls cultural displacement. Even people who manage to keep their homes may come to feel that the park is not intended for them. New cafes charge prices they cannot afford, events are advertised in ways that reach newcomers, and activities that were once common, such as informal food stalls or large family barbecues, are discouraged or forbidden. Several of her interviewees said that they avoided a park they had campaigned for. This form of exclusion leaves no trace in census figures, which is precisely why policymakers so seldom take it into account.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One response, advocated by a number of planners, is a strategy sometimes summarised as 'just green enough'. Rather than building a single spectacular park that attracts visitors and investors from across the city, authorities would scatter modest improvements, such as small pocket parks, tree planting and community gardens, through a neighbourhood, delivering health benefits without triggering a surge in property values. The approach has some merit, particularly in districts where pressure on housing is intense. But it also contains an uncomfortable implication: that poorer neighbourhoods should accept green spaces of lower quality than wealthier ones in order to avoid becoming more desirable. That is a troubling bargain to ask anyone to make.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more promising route is to combine greening with measures that protect housing. In one mid-sized city, a community land trust, a non-profit body that owns land on behalf of local residents, acquired several dozen houses along the route of a planned riverside trail before construction began, and has since let them at rents tied to local incomes. Early surveys suggest that most of the households living there when the project started have been able to stay. Other cities have introduced rent stabilisation or required developers to include affordable homes in schemes near new parks. The lesson of these experiments, however, is that timing is everything: protective measures must be in place before plans are announced, because speculation in property tends to begin the moment a new park is made public, long before the first tree is planted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this debate is that green space is not, in itself, the source of the problem. Parks become engines of displacement only where housing markets are left largely unregulated, so that any improvement to a neighbourhood is quickly converted into higher rents. To treat greening as the culprit is to blame the wrong thing, and it risks persuading cities to withhold from deprived districts the very amenities they most need. The task is to plan parks and housing together, so that the benefits of a greener city are shared by those who have waited longest for them.

topic: urban green space and mental health: evidence behind 'green prescriptions'
title: The Prescription Outdoors
subtitle: Doctors are increasingly advising patients to spend time in parks. How strong is the evidence that city greenery protects the mind?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a growing number of countries, family doctors can now issue what are informally called green prescriptions. Instead of, or alongside, medication, a patient with mild anxiety or low mood may be advised to walk in a local park several times a week, join a conservation volunteering group or take part in community gardening. Health services have welcomed the idea because it is cheap, has few side effects and seems intuitively right: most people report feeling calmer among trees than among traffic. The policy rests on a large body of research linking urban greenery to psychological wellbeing. The enthusiasm is understandable, but the science is considerably less settled than the speed of its adoption would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two theories have dominated the field. The first, attention restoration theory, proposes that modern urban life constantly draws on our capacity for directed attention, which is depleted by tasks such as monitoring traffic or working at a screen, and that natural scenes allow directed attention to recover because they hold our interest effortlessly. The second, stress reduction theory, holds that green environments trigger an immediate physiological calming, reflected in slower heart rates and lower levels of stress hormones. Laboratory and field experiments offer some support for both. The experimental psychologist Tadeusz Wrzosek has repeatedly found that volunteers who walk for fifty minutes through a park perform better on memory tasks and report less anxiety than those who walk along a busy street. Wrzosek is candid about the limits of these results, however: the improvements are modest and typically fade within a few hours.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Larger claims depend on population studies. Siriporn Kaewkanya, an epidemiologist, linked the health records of some nine hundred thousand urban residents to measures of vegetation around their homes derived from satellite images. Those living in the greenest surroundings were around twelve per cent less likely to be prescribed antidepressants than those in the least green. Findings of this kind are striking, but they are vulnerable to an obvious objection. Wealthier households tend to live in leafier districts, and wealth itself protects mental health. Kaewkanya adjusted her analysis for income and education, yet it is far harder to account for self-selection: people who already enjoy good mental health, or who like to exercise outdoors, may deliberately choose to live near parks.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most persuasive evidence so far comes from a different kind of study. Researchers known as the Greenmind Cohort team took advantage of a programme in one post-industrial city to clean up abandoned plots of land. Working with the city authorities, they randomly assigned a number of vacant lots to be cleared of rubbish, planted with grass and a few trees and given a low fence, while comparable lots were left untouched. Residents living near the greened plots subsequently reported feeling depressed substantially less often than those near the neglected ones, with the largest improvements in the poorest streets. Because the allocation was random, self-selection cannot explain the result. Randomised designs of this kind represent a major advance, but they remain rare, and a single city cannot settle the matter.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that not all green space is equal. Lucía Echeverry, a landscape architect who has surveyed visitors to more than sixty parks, argues that researchers have focused too heavily on how much greenery a neighbourhood contains and too little on what it is like. A poorly lit, littered park in which people do not feel safe may increase rather than reduce anxiety. In her surveys, how tranquil visitors judged a park to be predicted their wellbeing far better than the park's size, and parks with a greater variety of plants and birdsong were rated most restorative. If she is right, simply counting trees or hectares may tell planners very little.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a question of fairness. The people most likely to benefit from contact with nature, including those on low incomes and those with existing mental illness, often have the least access to good green space and the least free time in which to use it. Critics have warned that green prescriptions place the burden of recovery on individual patients, who are told to walk more, while leaving untouched the structural causes of poor mental health, such as insecure housing, debt and unemployment. This criticism deserves to be taken seriously. A walk in the park, however pleasant, cannot compensate for overcrowded accommodation or the strain of not knowing whether the rent can be paid.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this suggests that city greenery is unimportant. Taken together, the evidence indicates that well-designed, well-maintained green space produces real, if modest, psychological benefits, and that these may be greatest for the most disadvantaged. But it should not be treated as a substitute for clinical care. Green space is better understood as part of a city's public health infrastructure, in the same category as clean water or safe streets, which should be provided for everyone as a matter of course rather than dispensed to individuals as a form of medicine.

topic: tiny urban forests created by dense native planting (the Miyawaki method) and the evidence for their claimed benefits
title: Forests the Size of a Tennis Court
subtitle: Densely planted miniature woodlands are springing up in schoolyards and on roadsides. Do they live up to the claims made for them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past decade, small patches of dense woodland have appeared on school grounds, beside motorways and in the corners of city parks across Europe and Asia. Most are no larger than a tennis court, and many are planted in a single day by volunteers. They are based on a technique devised by a Japanese botanist in the 1970s, originally to re-establish native vegetation around factories and temples. The ground is first dug deeply and enriched with compost, and saplings of thirty or more native species are then planted close together, typically three to every square metre. For the first three years the plots are weeded and watered; after that, they are left to fend for themselves. Promotional materials commonly state that such forests grow ten times faster, are thirty times denser and support a hundred times more biodiversity than conventional plantations. These figures are repeated widely, yet it is remarkably difficult to establish where they originally came from or what they were compared with.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Independent measurements have begun to fill the gap. Anjali Hazarika, a forest ecologist, has monitored forty tiny forests in five European cities for five years. Her results confirm that the plots establish themselves quickly: in most, the leaves of neighbouring saplings had met overhead to form a closed canopy within three years, and the number of insect species recorded was considerably higher than on the mown lawns beside them. When Hazarika compared the tiny forests with conventionally planted woodland of the same age, however, the difference in growth was far smaller than advertised. Trees in the dense plots were on average around half as tall again as their conventional counterparts, a respectable advantage, but nothing like a tenfold one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The forester Ignasi Puigdollers is more sceptical still. Dense planting, he observes, inevitably produces fierce competition for light, and many saplings are soon overshadowed and die, a process foresters call self-thinning. In some of the plots he examined, more than half of the original trees had died within eight years. Conventional forestry, by contrast, plants far fewer trees per hectare and expects relatively modest losses. Puigdollers argues that whatever rapid growth the tiny forests achieve is mostly the result of the deep soil preparation and the careful watering of the early years, rather than of the crowding itself. His explanation is plausible, but it has not yet been tested in a controlled experiment that separates the effects of soil, water and density.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The economics are also open to question. Because of the soil improvements, the large number of saplings and the intensive maintenance required at first, a tiny forest typically costs many times more per square metre than ordinary tree planting. Advocates sometimes present the plots as a contribution to tackling climate change, but here the case is weakest. Even if each tree grows quickly, the area involved is so small that the carbon absorbed by all the tiny forests in a city amounts to a negligible fraction of its emissions. As a climate measure, the approach is unpersuasive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ewa Zawadzka, a social scientist who studies community environmental projects, believes critics are judging tiny forests by the wrong standard. Their real value, she argues, lies less in carbon or timber than in what they do for the people who plant them. Schoolchildren learn to identify dozens of tree species, neighbours who have never spoken work together, and the sense of ownership that results appears to protect the plots: in her surveys, forests planted by local volunteers suffered noticeably less vandalism than those planted by contractors. Participants were also more likely to join other environmental initiatives in the following years. This is a fair point, and it explains much of the method's appeal, although it does not justify the ecological claims that are still routinely made on its behalf.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some ecologists raise a more fundamental objection. The method aims to recreate what its originator called the potential natural vegetation of a site, meaning the plant community that would develop if human influence ceased. That concept is a theoretical construct rather than an observed state, and critics argue that it is often estimated crudely from regional maps. Where the original landscape was grassland, heath or wetland, planting a dense woodland may replace one valuable habitat with another that never existed there. In drier climates, moreover, the young trees can require so much irrigation during their first summers that the scheme makes heavy demands on scarce local water supplies.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these criticisms means that tiny forests should be abandoned. They bring shade, birdsong and a little wildness into places that badly lack them, and they give city dwellers a practical way to take part in environmental work. But the movement would be better served by citing measured results than by repeating striking figures whose basis no one can identify. Exaggerated promises are easy to make in the early years of any popular idea; they become a liability once the evidence arrives and fails to match them.

topic: urban agriculture and community food growing: self-sufficiency claims, food miles and land security
title: Can Cities Feed Themselves?
subtitle: Rooftop farms and community plots are flourishing, but the case for growing food in cities may rest on the wrong arguments

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Growing food in cities is not a new idea. During both world wars, governments in Europe and North America urged citizens to turn lawns, parks and railway embankments into vegetable plots, and by some estimates these wartime gardens supplied a substantial share of the fresh produce eaten in several countries. When peace returned, most of the plots were grassed over again, and for half a century urban food growing was largely confined to allotment holders and enthusiasts. Today it is enjoying a revival on a far larger scale. Rooftop farms supply restaurants, community gardens occupy vacant lots, and city governments publish strategies promising to strengthen local food security. The wartime example shows that cities can produce a meaningful quantity of food, but it is worth remembering the circumstances: imports were disrupted, labour was mobilised by national campaigns, and people accepted a monotonous diet that few would tolerate now.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: How much could a modern city actually grow? Folasade Akinwunmi, an urban geographer, set out to answer this question by mapping every piece of land in one large city that might plausibly be cultivated, including vacant plots, flat roofs, private gardens and the grass around apartment blocks. Her calculations indicate that, if all of this space were farmed intensively, the city could in principle supply most of the vegetables its residents eat. Vegetables, however, provide only a small fraction of the calories in a typical diet, and the staple crops that supply the rest, such as wheat, rice and maize, require far more land than any city possesses. Akinwunmi also found that small, carefully tended urban plots often produce more per square metre than commercial farms, chiefly because they receive so much more manual labour per square metre. That labour is usually unpaid, which is one reason why the figures cannot simply be scaled up.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A common argument for local food is that it reduces 'food miles', the distance produce travels from field to plate, and therefore cuts carbon emissions. The economist Ondrej Pospichal believes this argument has been badly overstated. For most foods, he points out, transport accounts for only a small proportion of total emissions; the way the food is grown matters much more. A tomato raised in a heated city greenhouse in winter may be responsible for far more emissions than one grown outdoors in a sunny region and shipped across a continent. Pospichal's analysis is convincing as far as high-technology operations are concerned, particularly indoor farms that rely on artificial lighting. It is less relevant to the majority of community gardens, which use unheated beds, compost made on site and rainwater, and whose environmental footprint is correspondingly modest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: City soils pose a problem of their own. Decades of leaded petrol and lead-based paint have left many urban sites contaminated, and Akinwunmi's tests found lead concentrations above recommended limits in several of the plots she sampled. The risk, however, is often misunderstood. Plants absorb relatively little lead into their edible parts; most exposure comes from contaminated soil dust clinging to leaves and roots. Washing produce thoroughly removes much of the danger, and growing in raised beds filled with clean soil removes most of the remainder.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If cities cannot feed themselves, what is urban agriculture for? Refilwe Tshabangu, a public health researcher, has followed participants in community gardens in three low-income neighbourhoods for four years. She reports that gardeners eat noticeably more fresh vegetables than their neighbours, that children involved in growing are more willing to try unfamiliar foods, and that the gardens function as meeting places in districts with few other shared spaces. Tshabangu is careful to note that people who choose to garden may already be more health-conscious than those who do not, so the differences cannot all be attributed to gardening. That caveat is important, and some published claims about the health benefits of community gardens have ignored it entirely.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the greatest threat to urban agriculture is not contamination or low yields but insecurity of tenure. Many community gardens occupy land that is empty only because no one has yet found a more profitable use for it, and they operate under leases that can be ended at short notice. When a neighbourhood becomes more desirable, often partly because of the gardens themselves, the land is sold for development and the plots are bulldozed. Temporary leases may suit landowners, but they leave gardeners unable to invest in soil, buildings or long-term planting. Cities that claim to value food growing should demonstrate it by giving established gardens permanent protection in their planning rules.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate over urban agriculture has too often been framed as a contest over tonnes: supporters exaggerate how much food cities can produce, and critics respond by pointing out how little they do. Both sides miss what matters. Measured by output alone, urban farming will always disappoint. Its real contribution lies in diet, education and the strengthening of community ties, and it should be judged and funded accordingly. Advocates would strengthen their case by abandoning the promise of self-sufficiency and arguing instead for what their gardens demonstrably achieve.
