paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the shallow waters off many tropical coasts, divers can be seen tending structures that resemble washing lines, hung not with clothes but with small fragments of living coral. The technique, known as coral gardening, borrows its logic from horticulture: pieces broken from healthy colonies are raised in underwater nurseries until they are large enough to be transplanted onto damaged reefs. Over the past two decades it has spread from a handful of experimental sites to hundreds of projects in more than fifty countries. Its appeal is easy to understand. Unlike many conservation measures, which ask people to refrain from fishing, building or polluting, gardening offers volunteers, tourists and governments something tangible to do, and its results can be photographed within months. Popularity, however, is not the same thing as effectiveness, and the question of what coral gardening really accomplishes deserves closer scrutiny than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method rests on a natural process. Many reef-building corals, particularly branching species such as staghorn and elkhorn, reproduce asexually through fragmentation: when storms snap off their branches, the broken pieces can reattach to the reef and grow into new colonies. Ileana Varvaressos, who directs the Caribbean Reef Nursery Network, explains that fragments suspended in mid-water nurseries are shielded from the sediment, predators and diseases that kill so many young corals on the sea floor, and may grow several times faster than colonies in the wild. In her network's nurseries, a fragment no longer than a finger can become a colony the size of a football within eighteen months. For species whose wild populations have fallen by more than ninety per cent, she argues, these nurseries function as living gene banks, holding genetic material that might otherwise vanish altogether.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulties begin once the corals leave the nursery. The survival of transplanted colonies varies enormously from one project to the next. A review by the Coastal Futures Institute of more than two hundred projects found that on average around sixty per cent of outplanted corals were still alive after two years, but that individual results ranged from almost total success to near-complete loss. More revealing was the discovery that most projects had monitored their sites for less than eighteen months, often because funding came to an end once the planting was complete. The institute's authors concluded that published figures probably exaggerate long-term success, since the greatest threats to transplanted corals, marine heatwaves and outbreaks of disease, may strike only once every few years. This is a reasonable inference, but it should not be mistaken for proof that gardening fails; what it demonstrates is that, for the moment, nobody really knows.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns scale. Signe Tveiteraas, a reef ecologist at the Nordhavn Marine Laboratory, has calculated that even the most ambitious gardening programmes restore only a few hectares of reef each year, whereas reefs worldwide are losing thousands of hectares annually to bleaching alone. In her view, the money spent on nurseries would achieve more if it were used to reduce local pressures such as sewage discharge and overfishing, which determine whether any coral, planted or wild, can survive at a site. Her arithmetic is difficult to dispute, but the conclusion she draws from it does not necessarily follow. Coral gardening was never intended to rebuild entire reef systems. Its more thoughtful defenders present it as a way of sustaining populations of key species at carefully chosen locations, from which natural recovery might eventually spread.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further concern is genetic. Early projects frequently took fragments from a small number of donor colonies, chosen simply because they grew well in nurseries, with the result that some restored reefs were populated largely by clones. A genetically uniform population is unusually fragile: a disease or heatwave to which one colony is susceptible is likely to affect them all. Many nurseries now deliberately maintain dozens of distinct genotypes, and some test their corals for heat tolerance before transplanting them. Varvaressos regards this shift as the most important development in the field over the past decade. She is right to do so, although there is an irony here, since choosing only the most heat-tolerant corals could itself narrow the genetic variety that restoration is meant to protect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some practitioners believe that the ecological debate misses the point. Siaosi Leiataua, who has worked with fishing villages in Samoa for many years, argues that the real value of gardening lies less in the corals than in the people who look after them. In the communities where he has worked, fishers who helped to maintain nurseries later supported the creation of protected zones that they had previously resisted. He warns against judging projects purely by the number of corals that survive, because such counts ignore shifts in attitude that may matter more in the long run. Tveiteraas responds that similar engagement could be achieved through cheaper activities that do not consume scarce conservation funds. Both may have a point, but it is worth noting that the social returns of coral gardening are at least as poorly documented as its ecological ones.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What does seem clear is that coral gardening cannot substitute for tackling the underlying causes of reef decline, above all the warming of the oceans. Corals raised in nurseries die in a heatwave just as surely as wild ones. Used as one tool among many, at well-chosen sites and accompanied by long-term monitoring, it may buy time for a number of vulnerable species. Presented as a solution in its own right, it risks becoming exactly what its critics fear: a reassuring image that distracts attention from the far harder decisions about emissions on which the future of reefs ultimately depends.

topic: assisted evolution: breeding heat-tolerant corals and hardened symbiotic algae
title: Breeding for a Hotter Sea
subtitle: Should scientists deliberately speed up the evolution of corals to help them survive warming oceans?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Natural selection has always been the means by which species adjust to changing environments, but it operates over generations, and for many corals a generation may last a decade or more. The oceans, by contrast, are warming within a single coral lifetime. Since the 1980s, mass bleaching events, in which heat-stressed corals expel the symbiotic algae that supply most of their energy, have shifted from rare catastrophes to near-annual occurrences on some reefs. It is against this background that a once marginal idea has drifted towards the mainstream: that humans should deliberately accelerate the evolution of corals, using a set of techniques known collectively as assisted evolution. The proposal is unsettling, and it ought to be. Yet the alternative, waiting for natural adaptation to catch up with a climate that is changing at unprecedented speed, is arguably no less of a gamble.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most straightforward method is selective breeding. Liesl Dornbusch, a coral geneticist at the Southern Reef Genomics Centre, collects spawn from colonies that came through recent heatwaves with little or no bleaching and crosses them, sometimes with partners from warmer reefs hundreds of kilometres away. In her trials, the offspring of such crosses have tolerated temperatures roughly one degree higher than the offspring of ordinary parents before bleaching. One degree may sound trivial, but Dornbusch points out that it corresponds to several decades of projected warming under moderate emissions scenarios. She is careful to stress that breeding is not meant to make reefs immune to heat, only to give them enough time for reductions in emissions to take effect.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second approach targets the algae rather than the coral. A coral's tolerance of heat depends partly on which strains of algae it hosts, and some strains cope with high temperatures far better than others. Hamid Zarrinkalam, a microbiologist at the Institute for Marine Symbiosis, has spent ten years culturing algae in progressively warmer water, so that over hundreds of algal generations, each lasting only a few weeks, they become more resistant to heat. When these strains were introduced into juvenile corals, the corals bleached less severely in laboratory heat trials. Zarrinkalam argues that because algae reproduce so rapidly, they offer by far the quickest route to adaptation. The results are striking, though they have so far been obtained almost entirely in aquaria; whether the hardened algae would persist inside corals on an open reef, where they must compete with native strains, remains uncertain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yolanda Ixcoy, an ecologist who has studied the reefs of Central America for two decades, warns that heat tolerance rarely comes free. In several species, colonies that resist bleaching grow more slowly or produce fewer eggs, presumably because energy devoted to coping with stress is unavailable for other purposes. If restoration programmes were to plant large numbers of such corals, she suggests, the outcome could be reefs that survive heatwaves but build their skeletons too slowly to keep pace with rising sea levels or erosion. Ixcoy does not oppose assisted evolution outright; rather, she argues that candidates should be assessed on growth and reproduction as well as on heat tolerance. This seems an entirely reasonable demand, and one that the field has been slow to meet, largely because trials measuring growth take years rather than weeks.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other objections are ethical as much as scientific. The Reef Ethics Forum, a coalition of marine scientists and conservation lawyers, has questioned whether people should be altering wild populations at all. Its members point out that corals bred from distant parents may carry traits poorly suited to local conditions other than temperature, such as light levels or prevailing diseases, and that once organisms have been released, they cannot be recalled. The Forum has called for international rules on the movement of coral larvae between countries, comparable to those governing genetically modified crops. Such concerns deserve serious attention, but the comparison with genetically modified crops is misleading. Selective breeding and algal culturing do not insert foreign genes; they merely concentrate variation that already exists in nature, much as farmers have done with livestock for thousands of years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even enthusiasts acknowledge that the practical obstacles are formidable. The Great Barrier Reef alone comprises around three thousand individual reefs, and producing enough hardened corals to influence even a small proportion of them would require hatchery capacity many times greater than anything that currently exists. Dornbusch's answer is not to replant entire reefs but to seed heat-tolerant corals at a limited number of well-connected sites, whose larvae would then carry the beneficial traits to neighbouring reefs through natural spawning. Computer models suggest that this strategy could succeed within a few decades, provided that the planted corals survive long enough to reproduce, a condition that is far from guaranteed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this alters the central fact that assisted evolution treats symptoms rather than causes. If warming continues unchecked, temperatures will eventually exceed what even the hardiest bred corals can withstand. The genuine case for these techniques is therefore a modest one: they may preserve enough genetic and ecological diversity to allow reefs to recover once temperatures stabilise. Judged by that standard, the research deserves support. Judged as a way of postponing difficult choices about emissions, it would be a dangerous illusion.

topic: larval reseeding: capturing mass coral spawn to restore reefs
title: Catching the Coral Snowstorm
subtitle: Mass spawning offers reef restorers billions of potential new corals every year, if only more of them can be kept alive

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Once a year on many reefs, usually a few nights after a full moon in late spring, corals release their eggs and sperm at almost the same moment, in an event that divers compare to an upside-down snowstorm. The tiny bundles float to the surface, where fertilisation takes place, and gather into pinkish slicks that can stretch for kilometres. Within days the fertilised eggs develop into larvae, which drift with the currents until they find a surface on which to settle. The quantities involved are staggering: a single large colony may release hundreds of thousands of eggs in one night. Yet only a minute fraction of them ever grow into adult corals. Most are eaten, carried out into open water or settle in places where they cannot survive. It is this enormous wastage that has inspired a newer approach to restoration, known as larval reseeding, which aims to capture a small share of each year's spawn and improve its chances.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The appeal of reseeding becomes clearer when it is compared with coral gardening, the method that currently dominates restoration. Gardening has two well-known limitations. Every fragment that is transplanted is a genetic copy of the colony it was cut from, and each one must be fixed to the reef by hand, which in practice confines most projects to a few hundred square metres. Reseeding, by contrast, produces genetically diverse offspring, since each larva is the product of sexual reproduction, and it can in principle be carried out over much larger areas. Thandiwe Mkhabela, a larval ecologist at the Mozambique Channel Reef Station, has described reseeding as restoration at last matching the size of the problem, observing that a single night's collection can yield millions of larvae.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of the necessary equipment was developed by Raffaele Scognamiglio, a marine engineer at the Adriatic Institute of Ocean Technology. His floating pools, large mesh-lined enclosures moored above the reef, allow collected spawn to be reared in calm, clean water until the larvae are ready to settle. At that point there are two options. The larvae can be released beneath mesh tents pegged over damaged patches of reef, which hold them in place for several days, or they can be allowed to settle on small ceramic tiles inside the pools, which are later wedged into crevices in the reef. Scognamiglio's team reports that settlement under the tents can be up to a hundred times higher than on comparable untreated reef.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Malin Ekdahl, a coral demographer at Kattegat University, cautions that settlement is merely the first hurdle. During their first year, newly settled corals, barely a millimetre across, are extraordinarily vulnerable: they are scraped away by grazing fish and sea urchins, overgrown by algae or buried under sediment. In her surveys, fewer than one settled larva in a thousand was still alive a year later, even on reseeded plots. High settlement rates, she concludes, reveal very little about how many adult colonies will eventually result. Her point is important, and some advocates of reseeding have indeed been guilty of reporting settlement figures as if they were measures of success. It is not, however, an argument against the method itself. Even at one in a thousand, a million larvae would produce a thousand colonies, at a far lower cost per colony than gardening can achieve.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Researchers are now looking for ways to improve the odds during that perilous first year. Some raise settled corals on tiles in protected nurseries for several months before placing them on the reef; others introduce herbivorous snails to keep algae under control. The Indo-Pacific Spawning Consortium, a network of twelve projects, found that tiles moulded with microscopic ridges, which give young corals shelter from grazing fish, tripled survival compared with flat surfaces. These results are encouraging, although every additional stage of handling erodes some of the cost advantage that made reseeding attractive in the first place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more stubborn problem is timing. Spawning occurs within narrow windows, often on a single night, and the date varies between species and between locations; a team that misses it must wait another year. Mkhabela notes that many reefs have never been studied closely enough for anyone to predict when their corals will spawn. Several groups are therefore experimenting with inducing spawning in aquaria by carefully controlling light and water temperature, so that larvae could be produced whenever they are needed. If these experiments succeed, they could prove the most significant advance of all, freeing restoration from the constraints of the natural calendar.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that reseeding can protect reefs from the effects of warming any more than other techniques can. Larvae settled on a reef that bleaches the following summer will die alongside everything else. But in offering both genetic diversity and the prospect of working at a meaningful scale, the method addresses the two most obvious weaknesses of gardening. It therefore deserves a considerably larger share of restoration funding than it currently attracts, provided that projects report survival over years rather than settlement over days.

topic: crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks: causes and culling
title: The Starfish Problem
subtitle: Periodic plagues of a coral-eating predator have prompted decades of culling, yet scientists still disagree about what sets them off

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few animals inspire such ambivalence among reef scientists as the crown-of-thorns starfish. It feeds by spreading its stomach over living coral and digesting the soft tissue. At ordinary densities of a few individuals per hectare, the starfish is an unremarkable member of the reef community, and it may even play a useful role: because it prefers the fast-growing branching corals that would otherwise overshadow their slower neighbours, its feeding helps to keep a variety of species in place. Every so often, however, its numbers explode, reaching hundreds or even thousands per hectare, and a reef that took decades to grow can be stripped of most of its living coral within a single season. On some reef systems, outbreaks now rival marine heatwaves as a cause of coral loss, yet they receive only a fraction of the attention that bleaching attracts, an imbalance that is difficult to justify.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why outbreaks begin remains a matter of dispute. The most widely cited explanation is associated with Dr Ingrid Valstadbakken of the Coral Sea Research Institute, who studies the starfish's larval stage. A female may release tens of millions of eggs, but in the clear, nutrient-poor water typical of tropical reefs, the larvae find very little of the microscopic algae on which they feed, and almost all of them starve. Valstadbakken's laboratory experiments indicate that when algal concentrations double, the proportion of larvae surviving to settle on the reef rises many times over. She links this to rivers carrying fertiliser from coastal farmland: after heavy rain, plumes of nutrient-rich water trigger algal blooms, and with them, she argues, the conditions for an outbreak.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second school of thought shifts the focus from the beginning of the starfish's life to a later stage. Professor Tupou Kaufana, a fisheries biologist at the Pacific Marine Science Consortium, notes that young starfish are eaten by a range of predators, including emperor fish, triggerfish and the giant triton, a large sea snail prized by shell collectors. Many of these predators have been heavily exploited. In Kaufana's surveys, outbreaks occurred considerably less often on reefs within no-take zones, where fishing is prohibited, than on comparable reefs open to fishing. The two hypotheses are frequently presented as rivals. This seems to me a false choice. It is entirely plausible that nutrients increase the number of larvae while overfishing removes the predators that would otherwise thin out the young starfish, the two effects together producing outbreaks that neither would cause alone.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical position is taken by Dr Marisol Llanque, a palaeoecologist who has drilled cores from the sediments that accumulate behind reefs. These cores contain tiny skeletal fragments of starfish, and Llanque interprets layers rich in such fragments as evidence of outbreaks that took place thousands of years before the arrival of industrial agriculture. In her view, outbreaks are a long-established natural phenomenon to which reefs have always eventually adjusted. Her critics point out that burrowing worms and crustaceans constantly churn the sediment, so that fragments may be displaced from the layers in which they were originally deposited, making their dates unreliable. But even if her dating is accepted, the conclusion does not follow. To show that outbreaks happened in the past is not to show that they happened as often as they do now, and reefs that once had decades to recover between outbreaks may now be granted only a few years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For half a century the main response to outbreaks has been culling. Early efforts were laborious: divers removed starfish by hand or injected each animal many times with poison, so that a team might deal with only a few hundred in a day. The discovery that a single injection of bile salts, or later of ordinary household vinegar, is enough to kill a starfish transformed the economics of control. The Reef Response Collective, an alliance of tour operators and conservation groups, now runs teams of divers who concentrate on sites of particular ecological or commercial value. The Collective reports that coral cover at its regularly treated sites has held steady while that of untreated reefs nearby has collapsed. Such results are encouraging, but they should be kept in proportion. Divers can treat only a small fraction of a large reef system, and culling is better understood as a way of defending selected sites than as a means of ending an outbreak.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: New technology may extend that reach. Prototype underwater robots have been trained to recognise starfish from camera images and to deliver a lethal injection without human help, although their cost has so far confined them to trials. The molecular ecologist Dr Anselm Okoroafor takes a different approach. His team filters seawater for traces of starfish genetic material shed into the environment, which can reveal a rising population long before adults become visible to divers. Okoroafor argues that this matters because culling is far more effective in the first stages of an outbreak, when the animals are still few enough to be removed, than once they have multiplied across a reef.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Yet none of these tools addresses the conditions that allow outbreaks to occur. If Valstadbakken and Kaufana are even partly correct, the most effective long-term measures are improved water quality and the restoration of predator populations. These are considerably harder to achieve than culling, because they require farmers far inland to change how they use fertiliser and fishing communities to accept restrictions on their catch. Culling, by contrast, is visible, immediate and politically uncontroversial. There is nothing wrong with defending the most valuable reefs in this way, but it would be a mistake to confuse the treatment of a symptom with a cure.

topic: herbivorous reef fish, seaweed overgrowth and the management of grazing
title: Grazers on the Reef
subtitle: Could protecting plant-eating fish help coral reefs resist being smothered by seaweed?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On any tropical reef, corals and seaweeds are engaged in a slow contest for space. On a healthy reef, the contest is kept in check by herbivorous fish such as parrotfish, surgeonfish and rabbitfish, which crop algae almost continuously, keeping it short and leaving bare surfaces on which the larvae of corals can settle. When grazing declines, seaweed can spread rapidly, shading and scraping neighbouring corals and releasing chemicals that harm them. Once established, a carpet of seaweed may persist for decades, a condition scientists describe as a 'phase shift'. The recognition that a reef's fate depends partly on its grazers is, in my view, one of the more hopeful insights of modern reef science, because unlike ocean temperature, fishing is something that coastal communities can directly control.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the evidence for this idea comes from long-term monitoring. Dr Béatrice Kasongo of the Indian Ocean Reef Observatory has surveyed thirty reefs at regular intervals for more than fifteen years. After a severe cyclone flattened large areas of coral across her study region, she found that reefs with a high weight of herbivorous fish had regained much of their coral cover within a decade, whereas heavily fished reefs nearby were taken over by seaweed and showed little sign of recovery. Kasongo is careful to stress that her results show a strong association rather than proof of cause, but similar patterns have since been reported from several other oceans. One reason the pattern is so consistent, she suggests, is that seaweed, once it gains a foothold, makes the reef less attractive to the very fish that might remove it, so that grazing early in recovery is worth far more than intervention later.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such findings have encouraged some governments to ban the capture of parrotfish altogether. Professor Ryota Nakamatsu, a fisheries economist, regards this as a well-meant mistake. In many island communities, herbivores make up a large share of the catch and provide much of the protein that families eat. Unlike many reef species, they can be caught close to shore with simple traps and spears, which makes them especially important to households without boats. Bans that ignore this, he argues, cause real hardship and are widely ignored as a result. Nakamatsu favours restrictions on fishing gear, such as minimum mesh sizes for traps, which allow the largest grazers to escape while fishers continue to land smaller fish and so keep their income. His argument deserves more attention than it has received, since rules that people refuse to obey protect nothing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all herbivores do the same job, however. Dr Ignacio Riquelme, a marine ecologist, divides them into functional groups. Scrapers remove fine algal turf from the reef surface; excavators, mainly large parrotfish, bite off chunks of dead coral, creating fresh surfaces and producing sand in the process; browsers, such as certain rabbitfish and unicornfish, feed on large, fleshy seaweed. Riquelme's experiments show that once seaweed has grown tall, most parrotfish avoid it, and only the browsers, a small number of species, will eat it. A target based on the total weight of herbivores could therefore be met while the very species capable of reversing a phase shift continued to decline. This complicates the simple targets favoured by some managers, but it does not weaken the case for managing herbivores; if anything, it strengthens the case for doing so with care.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more sceptical voice comes from the Leeward Fisheries Council, an organisation representing small-scale fishers. The Council argues that protecting herbivores distracts from the real threat, rising sea temperatures, and points to fully protected reserves whose corals bleached just as severely as those on fished reefs. Its members also complain that restrictions are usually imposed by distant officials who have never fished for a living, and that the costs fall on the poorest households while the benefits are enjoyed largely by tourists and dive operators. It is true that grazing fish cannot prevent bleaching. But the question that matters is not whether a reef is damaged by heat, but what happens afterwards. Herbivores cannot save a reef from a heatwave; they may, however, decide whether it recovers from one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also concerns that protection may sometimes do harm. Large parrotfish occasionally bite living coral as well as dead surfaces, and some researchers have warned that increasing their numbers on reefs where little coral remains could expose the few surviving colonies to damaging bites. Kasongo considers this risk minor compared with the benefits of grazing, but the evidence on either side is still thin, and it would be premature to dismiss the concern. Equally uncertain is the role of sand production: the material excavated by parrotfish helps to build beaches and low-lying islands, yet few studies have measured how much of this supply is lost when the fish are overexploited.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this makes herbivore management a substitute for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, which remain the only lasting solution to coral bleaching. What it offers is something rarer: a measure that can be taken locally, at modest cost, and whose results can be observed within years rather than generations. Whether it succeeds, though, will depend less on the quality of the science than on the cooperation of fishers, and the most promising programmes are those in which fishing communities help to design the rules they are asked to follow.

topic: artificial reef structures: sunken objects, engineered modules and electrified frames
title: Reefs by Design
subtitle: Artificial structures are being lowered onto the seabed in growing numbers, but whether they create new marine life or merely relocate it is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: People have been placing objects in the sea to attract fish for centuries. Fishing communities in several parts of Asia sank bundles of brushwood weighted with stones, returning weeks later to harvest the fish that had gathered around them. In the twentieth century the practice expanded dramatically and became far less discriminating: old cars, railway carriages, decommissioned ships and, notoriously, millions of discarded tyres were dumped offshore in the name of habitat creation. Many of the tyre reefs proved disastrous. Bound together with straps that soon corroded, the tyres broke loose, rolled across the seabed in storms and battered the natural corals they had been intended to supplement, and some are now being recovered at a cost far exceeding that of their original placement. The episode is instructive. Good intentions, it turns out, are no substitute for engineering, and an object that happens to be lying on the seabed is not thereby a reef.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Modern artificial reefs are designed with considerably more care. Concrete modules perforated with holes, ceramic tiles and structures produced by large-scale 3D printing are all now in use, many of them shaped to imitate the irregular forms of natural reefs. What these designs have in common is an emphasis on structural complexity: the crevices, overhangs and tunnels that shelter juvenile fish and invertebrates from predators. Dr Folasade Akinwande, a coastal engineer at the Gulf of Guinea Marine Laboratory, argues that complexity matters far more than the choice of material. In her trials, modules pierced with holes of many different sizes hosted roughly twice as many fish species as smoother modules of the same volume, regardless of whether they were made of concrete or clay.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most persistent controversy, however, concerns not how artificial reefs are built but what they actually achieve. Professor Eirik Sørhaug, a fisheries scientist, contends that most structures simply concentrate fish drawn from the surrounding area. Because the fish are gathered in one known location, they become easier to catch, and an artificial reef that is open to fishing may therefore accelerate the decline of the very populations it was meant to support. Others respond that for species whose numbers are limited by a shortage of shelter, additional habitat genuinely allows more fish to survive. In all probability the answer differs from species to species. Yet Sørhaug's central warning holds whichever view proves correct: a structure that gathers fish together without any restriction on fishing is at least as likely to harm stocks as to help them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious approach involves electrified structures. In a technique known as mineral accretion, a weak electric current is passed through a steel frame on the seabed, causing minerals dissolved in seawater to be deposited on the metal as a layer of limestone. Corals attached to the frame are said by the technique's supporters to grow faster and to survive heat stress better than corals elsewhere. Dr Paloma Yrigoyen, a marine chemist, is unconvinced. The trials reporting such benefits, she observes, were mostly small, short and carried out by the developers of the method themselves, while independent studies have found only modest improvements or none at all. She also points out that the structures stop working the moment their supply of electricity is interrupted, a serious obstacle at remote sites. Her scepticism is justified, but it would be a mistake to abandon the technique before it has been properly tested in large, independent trials.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever the structure, the arrival of corals cannot be taken for granted. A new surface is usually colonised first by algae, sponges and other fast-growing organisms, and corals appear only if their larvae can reach it. Akinwande stresses that the location of a structure is therefore as important as its design. A module placed on open sand far from any healthy reef may remain largely free of coral for years, however intricate its shape, whereas one placed within reach of a thriving reef will normally receive a steady supply of coral larvae.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also an ecological cost that is rarely counted. Researchers in the Benthic Ecology Group at Lagos Coastal University point out that the seabed on which artificial reefs are placed is not empty. Sand and mud support worms, burrowing shrimps, flatfish and, in shallow water, seagrass, all of which are displaced or buried. Environmental assessments, the group argues, routinely treat these habitats as worthless simply because they are less visually appealing than a reef. The criticism seems to me well founded. Replacing one habitat with another is not the same as creating habitat from nothing, and the gains should be weighed against what is lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that artificial reefs are without value. Submerged structures can protect coastlines by breaking the force of waves, they can draw recreational divers away from fragile natural reefs, and they offer researchers a controlled setting in which to study how reef communities assemble. What they cannot do is replace the natural reefs now being lost. Those reefs were built over thousands of years, and the area that could realistically be covered by artificial structures is tiny compared with the area of coral that is disappearing each decade.

topic: economic valuation of coral reefs and reef insurance schemes
title: Pricing the Reef
subtitle: Putting a monetary value on coral has opened new ways of paying for its protection, and new reasons for unease

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Coral reefs perform a remarkable range of services for the people who live beside them. A healthy reef crest absorbs the great majority of the energy of incoming waves, shielding beaches, towns and roads from storms. Reefs also sustain fisheries that feed millions of people and attract tourists whose spending supports whole regional economies. For several decades economists have attempted to express these services in monetary terms, and the resulting estimates vary enormously, from a few thousand to several hundred thousand dollars per hectare per year. Such variation is sometimes held up as proof that the whole exercise is meaningless. In my view, it is less a sign of incompetence than a reflection of how genuinely difficult the task is: a reef beside a crowded resort coast and a remote reef visited only by local fishers simply do not perform the same services.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the more influential approaches has been developed by Dr Oyuunaa Batbayar, an environmental economist at the Institute for Coastal Economics. Her method, known as avoided damages, estimates what storms would cost a stretch of coastline if its reef were absent, by combining models of wave behaviour with data on the value of buildings and infrastructure near the shore. In one study of a densely developed coast, she calculated that the reef reduced annual flood losses by a sum many times greater than the cost of maintaining it. Batbayar argues that figures of this kind are the most effective means of persuading finance ministries to treat reefs as infrastructure, comparable to sea walls, rather than as scenery to be admired.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If a reef protects valuable property, it follows that those who insure that property have an interest in keeping the reef intact. This logic has inspired a new kind of policy known as parametric insurance. Unlike conventional insurance, which pays out only after losses have been assessed, a parametric policy pays automatically once a measurable event, such as wind speed exceeding an agreed threshold within a defined area, has occurred. The money is used to dispatch repair teams who clear debris and reattach broken coral fragments in the weeks after a hurricane. Dr Leila Bakhtiyari, a risk analyst who has helped to design several such schemes, says that speed is their decisive advantage: fragments left lying on the seabed are soon buried or swept away, and most die if they are not secured within a few weeks.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The ingenuity of these arrangements is undeniable. Their limitations, however, deserve more attention than they usually receive. The policies cover storm damage, but the gravest long-term threat to most reefs is not wind but water temperature. Marine heatwaves now occur so frequently that, as Bakhtiyari herself acknowledges, no insurer could cover them at a premium that any government would be willing to pay. The result is that reef insurance offers protection against the hazard least likely to determine whether reefs survive the present century, while leaving the most serious hazard entirely uninsured.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection is raised by Professor Nimal Abeysekera, an anthropologist who has worked for many years with fishing communities in South Asia. Assigning a price to a reef, he argues, invites the conclusion that a reef worth less than a proposed harbour or hotel may reasonably be sacrificed. Moreover, much of what reefs mean to coastal communities, including their place in customary law, religious practice and local identity, cannot be translated into money at all. He also notes an uncomfortable consequence of the avoided damages method: because it measures the value of property protected, a reef sheltering a poor fishing village will always appear to be worth less than one sheltering luxury resorts. For Abeysekera, these problems are serious enough that valuation should be abandoned as a basis for policy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Between these positions stands the Coastal Commons Alliance, a network of community organisations that has campaigned on reef finance. The Alliance does not object to valuation as such, but to the question of who benefits from it. At present, insurance payouts and conservation funds are usually channelled through national agencies, while the fishing communities who accept restrictions on their catch receive little. The Alliance argues that a share of any money raised in the name of reefs should be paid directly to the communities that manage them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Abeysekera's criticisms are telling, but his conclusion does not follow from them. Declining to attach any number to a reef does not protect it from being traded away; in practice it means that, when a harbour or a hotel is being planned, the reef is quietly given a value of zero. The more sensible course is to treat economic estimates as a lower limit, a statement of the minimum that a reef is worth, rather than as a complete account of its value. Used in that spirit, valuation allows reefs to be discussed in the language that finance ministries understand without pretending that this language captures everything that matters.

topic: a fast-spreading coral tissue-loss disease: causes, transmission and treatment
title: An Epidemic Under Water
subtitle: A disease that strips corals of their living tissue has spread across a whole region, and the search for its cause and cure has divided scientists

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The first reports came from recreational divers, who noticed bright white bands spreading across large brain corals near a busy commercial port. Within months, similar patches had been found dozens of kilometres along the coast, and within a few years the disease had reached reefs throughout the region. Earlier coral diseases had typically attacked one or two species and progressed slowly. This one has been recorded in more than twenty species, and it can kill a colony that is several centuries old within a matter of weeks. In hindsight, the early response was too slow. The first sightings were widely assumed to be ordinary bleaching, which also turns coral white, and by the time the distinctive pattern of tissue loss had been recognised and a monitoring programme funded, the disease had spread far beyond any area that could have been contained.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What causes the disease remains uncertain. Dr Agnieszka Kowalczuk, a microbiologist at the Caribbean Reef Health Laboratory, showed in aquarium experiments that placing fragments of diseased coral next to healthy colonies transmitted the infection, and that treating the water with antibiotics halted its progress. Her results strongly suggest that bacteria are involved, although no single species has yet been identified as responsible. Professor Hendrik Rautenbach, a virologist, offers a different interpretation. Using an electron microscope, his team found virus-like particles inside the symbiotic algae of diseased corals, particles that were rare in healthy colonies. Rautenbach believes the virus is the primary cause and that bacteria merely invade tissue already weakened, which would explain why antibiotics slow the disease without preventing new infections.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whatever the agent, the question of how it travels has proved easier to answer. Dr Sefo Tauvaga, an oceanographer, mapped the dates and locations of new outbreaks and found that many appeared first near ports and along shipping routes, sometimes hundreds of kilometres from the nearest known infection. Ships take on seawater as ballast to keep them stable and discharge it at their destination; water taken on near an infected reef may therefore carry the disease to a distant one. In laboratory trials, Tauvaga's group showed that ballast water containing material from diseased corals could infect healthy fragments, though treatment with chlorine prevented this. Several port authorities now require ships to disinfect ballast water before releasing it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: On the reef itself, the main weapon is an antibiotic. Divers apply a paste containing amoxicillin along the advancing edge of each lesion, the narrow band where living tissue meets bare skeleton. In field trials, more than 80 per cent of treated lesions stopped advancing. The treatment does not, however, protect the rest of the colony: new lesions frequently appear elsewhere on treated corals, so that colonies must be revisited every few weeks or months. An earlier technique, in which divers chiselled a trench around each lesion and filled it with a chlorinated compound, proved considerably less effective.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The use of antibiotics in the open sea has caused unease. Dr Yerlan Aldabergenov, a microbial ecologist, warns that releasing these drugs into the marine environment could encourage the growth of resistant bacteria, both among the microbes that normally live on corals and in the surrounding water. In sediment close to frequently treated colonies, his team has detected genes associated with resistance, although he stresses that these findings are preliminary. Supporters of treatment reply that the quantities involved are tiny and confined to a few square centimetres of coral. Both sides have a point. The risk is real, but so is the prospect of losing entire species from the region, and it seems to me that treatment is justified for the rarest and most vulnerable corals while being difficult to defend as a routine measure across whole reefs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Aldabergenov's own group is pursuing an alternative. They have cultured bacteria from colonies that remained healthy while their neighbours died and applied these beneficial microbes to susceptible corals in aquaria, where infection rates fell by roughly half. Translating this result to the reef is proving difficult, since bacteria released into open water are quickly carried away by currents. The team now encloses individual colonies in weighted plastic bags for several hours so that the microbes have time to become established.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For some species, these efforts may come too late. Pillar coral, which forms tall columns and was always uncommon, has disappeared from much of the region. The Windward Reef Disease Network, a partnership of aquariums, universities and government agencies, has therefore removed hundreds of colonies of the most susceptible species from the reef and placed them in land-based tanks, a living gene bank from which reefs might one day be restocked. Several of these captive colonies have now spawned, the first time this has been achieved for some of the species. The epidemic carries a broader lesson. Reefs face threats other than rising temperatures, and preventing the spread of disease, as the ballast-water rules attempt to do, is likely to be far cheaper than attempting to cure it once it has arrived.

topic: acoustic enrichment: playing healthy-reef sounds to attract young fish to degraded reefs
title: The Sound of Recovery
subtitle: Recordings of healthy reefs are being broadcast underwater in an attempt to lure young fish back to damaged ones

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: To a diver, a coral reef may seem a place of silence, but to a hydrophone it is anything but quiet. On a healthy reef, the clicking of countless snapping shrimps, small crustaceans that stun their prey with a jet of water, merges into a constant crackle, over which fish add a repertoire of grunts, pops and whoops that rises to a peak at dawn and dusk. This chorus can be detected several kilometres away. Reefs that have been degraded by bleaching or storms are markedly quieter, since many of the animals responsible for the noise have died or moved away. The difference matters because many reef fish begin life as larvae drifting in the open ocean for several weeks before they must find a reef on which to settle, and a growing body of evidence suggests that they rely heavily on sound for navigation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: If young fish follow the sound of a healthy reef, it ought to be possible to attract them to a damaged one by playing them that sound. This was the reasoning behind an experiment led by Professor Sigrun Fagerheim of the Northern Institute of Marine Acoustics. Her team built small patches of dead coral rubble on open sand and placed underwater loudspeakers on some of them, broadcasting recordings made on thriving reefs nearby. Over forty days, the patches with loudspeakers attracted roughly twice as many young fish as silent patches, and the number of species present was around fifty per cent higher. The new arrivals included species from every major feeding group, from plankton-eaters to predators. The result is striking, and it is, as far as I am aware, the first convincing demonstration that sound could be used as a practical tool in reef management rather than simply as a subject of study.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is enthusiastic. Dr Mere Pohatu, a behavioural ecologist, warns that acoustic enrichment risks creating what ecologists call an ecological trap: a place that appears attractive to an animal but in which its chances of survival are poor. A degraded reef may offer less shelter and less food than a healthy one, so fish drawn to it by an artificial signal could be worse off than if they had settled elsewhere. The warning is a sensible one, but it has not so far been borne out. In subsequent trials, young fish on enriched patches survived at rates similar to those on unenriched patches, although these trials lasted only a few months and longer studies are clearly needed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are also practical obstacles. Loudspeakers require a power supply, and batteries must be replaced every few weeks, which makes large-scale use expensive in remote locations. Dr Esteban Apaza, an acoustic engineer, has developed cheaper, solar-powered units, but he believes the content of the broadcast matters as much as the hardware. A single recording played continuously, he argues, may gradually lose its effect, because a natural reef never sounds the same from one hour to the next. Apaza is therefore building playback systems that vary through the day, reproducing the louder choruses of dawn and dusk and the quieter periods in between.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers think the effort is directed at the wrong end of the problem. The Marine Noise Working Group, a coalition of acousticians and conservation bodies, points out that the sounds of many reefs are increasingly drowned out by boat engines, coastal construction and seismic surveys. Rather than adding recorded sound to quiet reefs, the group argues, managers should reduce the human noise that prevents young fish from hearing the real thing, for example by imposing speed limits on boats near reefs. The two approaches are not really in competition, and both have a place. Of the two, however, noise reduction is arguably the more valuable, because its benefits extend to every animal that relies on hearing, from shrimps to whales.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is important to be clear about what acoustic enrichment can and cannot achieve. Sound attracts fish; it does not rebuild coral. A larger fish community can help a reef to recover, particularly by grazing the seaweed that would otherwise smother young corals, but if the surrounding water remains too warm, no recording will bring the reef back. Several teams are now testing whether broadcasting sound alongside the transplanting of coral fragments produces better results than either approach alone. Acoustic enrichment is best seen as a means of accelerating recovery where conditions already permit it, not as a remedy in itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, some critics have expressed unease at the idea of manipulating the behaviour of wild animals with artificial signals. The objection deserves a hearing, but in this case it seems misplaced. The fish on degraded reefs are already being manipulated, by the silence that bleaching leaves behind and by the noise of human activity. Playing them the sound of a living reef restores a signal that people helped to remove; it does not introduce a false one.

topic: coral cryopreservation and biobanking of reef genetic material
title: A Frozen Insurance Policy
subtitle: Scientists are storing coral reproductive cells at extremely low temperatures, but a gene bank raises as many questions as it answers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For decades, botanists have guarded against the loss of crop varieties by storing their seeds in cold vaults, from which lost strains can be regrown. Corals produce no seeds, and a living colony cannot simply be placed in a freezer. Their reproductive cells, however, can be preserved. Since the early years of this century, researchers have stored the sperm of dozens of coral species in liquid nitrogen at minus 196 degrees Celsius, and sperm thawed after more than a decade has successfully fertilised fresh eggs. Biobanking has attracted only a fraction of the publicity given to coral gardening or the breeding of heat-tolerant strains, yet it is, I believe, among the most valuable investments that can currently be made in the future of reefs. Every severe bleaching event removes genetic variation that cannot be recovered, and a frozen collection is the only means yet devised of keeping that variation in existence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Sperm, though, has obvious limitations. It carries the genetic material of only one parent, and it cannot by itself regenerate a colony; fresh eggs must be available whenever the sperm is used. Freezing eggs or larvae would be far more useful, but coral eggs are large and rich in fat, and when they are frozen conventionally, ice crystals form inside them and tear them apart. Dr Darlene Tsosie, a cryobiologist at the Pacific Biorepository, has spent ten years on this problem. Her team cools larvae so rapidly that the water inside them solidifies into a glass-like state without forming crystals. Rewarming proved the greater challenge, since crystals can form as easily during thawing as during freezing. The solution was to mix the larvae with microscopic gold particles that absorb a pulse of laser light, heating each larva in a fraction of a second. A proportion of larvae treated in this way have survived, settled and grown into young polyps, and Tsosie expects that whole fragments of coral could be stored within the next decade.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Frozen material also opens up possibilities that go beyond storage. Professor Ioane Sapolu, a reef geneticist, has proposed using banked sperm to transfer heat tolerance between populations. Corals on reefs that already experience high temperatures may carry genetic variants that would help populations living in cooler waters to survive future warming. Moving live colonies between distant reefs risks spreading disease, but frozen sperm can be shipped in sealed flasks and used to fertilise the eggs of local corals. In trials, crosses between populations several hundred kilometres apart produced healthy offspring. The proposal is an attractive one, but it is not without risk. Local populations are adapted not only to temperature but to many other conditions, from water chemistry to the timing of spawning, and repeated crossing could dilute these adaptations. Sapolu accepts this possibility but considers it small compared with the threat posed by rising temperatures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some observers are uneasy about the whole enterprise. Dr Kristin Søreide, an environmental ethicist, argues that frozen collections may create a form of moral hazard: if governments come to believe that reefs can always be restored from the freezer, they may feel less pressure to cut the emissions that are destroying them. A gene bank, she warns, could become an excuse rather than a safeguard. The concern is understandable, but the argument proves less than it appears to. Closing the collections would not make governments act any faster on emissions; it would merely ensure that, if they fail to act, the genetic material is lost as well. What Søreide's argument does show is that scientists should be careful about how they describe biobanks in public.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also questions about who controls the collections. Most coral material is currently stored in a handful of institutions in wealthy countries, while the reefs from which it comes lie overwhelmingly in tropical nations with far fewer resources. The Global Coral Seed Vault Consortium, a network of laboratories and reef agencies, argues that freezing facilities should be built in the countries that possess the reefs, with local scientists trained to run them, and that those countries should retain legal ownership of any genetic material collected. The practical difficulties are considerable, since a steady supply of liquid nitrogen can be hard to secure on remote islands, but the principle seems difficult to dispute.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even the most complete collection has limits. A frozen sample is of no value unless there is somewhere suitable to return it to; if ocean conditions remain hostile, thawed corals will simply die again. Moreover, a coral does not live alone. Dr Wanjiru Kamau-Ochieng, a microbial ecologist, points out that corals depend on the symbiotic algae in their tissues and on communities of bacteria, and that colonies raised without their usual partners often grow poorly. Her laboratory is therefore building a parallel collection of frozen algal and bacterial cultures, on the grounds that a coral banked without its partners is only part of the organism that needs to be saved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the case for biobanking; it simply clarifies what the banks are for. They cannot save reefs, but they can buy time, preserving options that would otherwise disappear while the world decides whether to reduce emissions quickly enough for those options to be used. The cost of maintaining the collections is trivial compared with the value of what they hold, and they should be expanded without delay.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: mangrove blue carbon credits and the voluntary carbon market
title: Selling the Tide Forest
subtitle: Carbon markets promise to pay for mangrove protection, but the arrangement raises awkward questions about measurement and ownership

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Mangroves occupy a narrow band of tropical and subtropical coastline, where salt-tolerant trees grow in the zone between low and high tide. For centuries coastal communities have relied on them for timber, firewood, fish and crabs, and for protection against storm surges. Their more recent celebrity, however, stems from something less visible. Because the waterlogged sediments beneath mangrove stands contain little oxygen, fallen leaves and roots decay extremely slowly, and carbon builds up in the mud to depths of several metres. Per hectare, a mature mangrove forest may hold several times as much carbon as an inland tropical forest, most of it below ground. This so-called 'blue carbon' has made mangroves an attractive prospect for the voluntary carbon market, in which companies purchase credits to offset their own emissions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The logic is straightforward. A project developer, often working with a non-governmental organisation, agrees with local communities to protect or replant an area of mangrove. The carbon that would otherwise have been lost through clearing, or that new trees are expected to absorb, is calculated and sold as credits, and part of the revenue is returned to the community. Supporters argue that this finally attaches a price to services that mangroves have always provided free of charge. Since the 1980s, by most estimates, a significant proportion of the world's mangroves have been cleared, chiefly for shrimp ponds, rice fields and coastal development, and conventional conservation funding has done little to slow the loss. If carbon finance can reverse that trend, it deserves a serious trial.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Measurement is the first difficulty. Dr Ilse Hjelmstad, a coastal geochemist at the Institute for Tropical Shorelines, has spent a decade coring mangrove sediments in South-East Asia and East Africa. Her work shows that carbon stocks vary enormously, not only between regions but between neighbouring stands only a few hundred metres apart, depending on tidal range, sediment supply and the age of the forest. Many projects, she notes, rely on default values drawn from published averages rather than local sampling, because coring is slow and expensive. In Hjelmstad's view, this practice could lead to credits that overstate the carbon actually protected by a factor of two or more in some sites. She does not oppose blue carbon markets, but she insists that no credit should be issued until the soil beneath it has been measured directly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second problem concerns what economists call additionality: the requirement that a project protects carbon that would otherwise have been lost. Professor Kwame Asamoah-Dery, who studies environmental markets at the Coastal Economics Unit in Accra, points out that some projects have been established in areas where clearing was never likely, because the land was too remote or too strictly protected by law to be converted. Credits from such sites, he argues, reward developers for nothing more than drawing a boundary on a map. The difficulty is that additionality depends on predicting a future that never happens, and different assumptions about it can produce wildly different results. Asamoah-Dery's criticism is well founded, yet it applies to almost all forest carbon schemes, and it would be unfair to single out mangroves as uniquely vulnerable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Replanting raises different issues. Planting seedlings is visibly productive and easy to report, which may explain why many projects favour it over the less photogenic work of protecting existing forest. Teodora Valcescu, an ecologist with the Delta Restoration Network, has surveyed planting schemes across several countries and found that survival rates are frequently poor. Seedlings are often placed on mudflats that are too low in the tidal frame, where they are submerged for too long each day, or a single fast-growing species is planted where several once grew together. Valcescu advocates instead restoring the hydrology of abandoned shrimp ponds, after which mangroves frequently recolonise naturally from nearby seed sources. Her approach is cheaper and generally more successful, although it yields fewer of the images that donors and buyers like to see.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most contentious question is who owns the carbon. In many countries, the intertidal zone is legally state property, even where families have harvested crabs and wood there for generations. Ravindu Sooriyabandara, a legal anthropologist who has worked with fishing villages in Sri Lanka and Mozambique, describes cases in which communities signed agreements without understanding that they were surrendering rights to future carbon revenue, or in which access to traditional harvesting grounds was restricted in the name of carbon protection. He maintains that unless benefit-sharing arrangements are written into law, blue carbon risks repeating the pattern of earlier resource booms in which outside investors captured most of the value.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these objections is fatal. Taken together, though, they suggest that the enthusiasm surrounding blue carbon has run well ahead of the evidence. The most credible projects so far are small, carefully measured and designed with the full participation of local people, and they have tended to emphasise fisheries and coastal protection rather than carbon alone. That may be the most useful lesson. Mangroves are worth protecting for many reasons, and a financing model that values them solely as stores of carbon is likely to misunderstand both the forests and the people who depend on them.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: managed realignment of sea walls to recreate salt marsh
title: Giving Ground
subtitle: Deliberately breaching sea walls to recreate salt marsh is now an accepted tool of coastal management, but its outcomes are more ambiguous than its advocates admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a grey morning in late autumn, a mechanical excavator cuts a gap twenty metres wide through an earth embankment that has kept the sea off a stretch of farmland for over two hundred years. Within hours, the incoming tide spreads across fields that once grew wheat, and the land begins its slow return to salt marsh. Scenes like this, once unthinkable to engineers whose professional purpose was to hold the line against the sea, have become a familiar part of coastal policy in north-west Europe and, increasingly, elsewhere. The practice, known as managed realignment, rests on a simple observation: salt marsh in front of a sea wall absorbs wave energy, so a wall fronted by a wide marsh needs to be far less massive than one exposed directly to the waves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The rationale has gained force as sea levels rise. Many embankments were constructed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries to reclaim marsh for agriculture, and in the process the marshes that once buffered the coast were lost. Squeezed between rising water and fixed defences, the remaining fringes of marsh are gradually drowning, a process described as 'coastal squeeze'. Realignment offers a way out by allowing marsh to re-establish landward. Dr Edem Ahiakpor, a coastal engineer at the Shoreline Adaptation Institute, has compared the long-term costs of maintaining existing walls with those of building smaller defences further inland. Over a fifty-year period, his figures suggest, realignment is cheaper at most of the sites he examined, chiefly because repairing ageing walls exposed to stronger storms becomes progressively more expensive. Ahiakpor is careful to add that these savings assume the new marsh develops as expected, an assumption that is not always borne out.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Physically, the early signs are often encouraging. Hanne Torvund, a sedimentologist who has monitored more than a dozen realigned sites over fifteen years, reports that mud accumulates rapidly once the tide is admitted, sometimes by several centimetres a year, as sediment-laden water slows and drops its load. Yet she has also found that the former farmland behaves differently from natural marsh. Decades of ploughing and drainage have compacted the soil and destroyed the network of fine creeks that carries water in and out of a natural marsh. Without these channels, water can stagnate on the surface, and plant colonisation is patchy. Torvund now recommends that engineers excavate artificial creek systems before breaching, a step that adds cost but seems to accelerate recovery considerably.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ecologically, the picture is more complicated still. Marisol Saldivar, who studies marsh biodiversity at the Iberian Coastal Ecology Group, has compared plant and invertebrate communities on realigned land with those on neighbouring natural marshes. Even after twenty years, she finds, the restored sites contain fewer species of plants typical of the upper marsh and a noticeably different mix of burrowing invertebrates. In her judgement, the restored marshes should be regarded as a new kind of habitat rather than a replica of what was lost. This is not necessarily a failure: the realigned sites are heavily used by feeding waterbirds, which is often what conservation agencies wanted. But it does undermine one of the claims frequently made for realignment, namely that it compensates in full for natural marsh destroyed elsewhere, for instance by port expansion.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That claim matters because, under some regulatory systems, developers who damage protected intertidal habitat are required to create an equivalent area somewhere else. Realignment has become a convenient means of doing so. If Saldivar is right, the habitat created is not equivalent, and the accounting that permits the original damage rests on a false premise. It would be going too far to suggest that compensation schemes are therefore worthless; a new marsh, even an imperfect one, is plainly preferable to none at all. What seems unjustifiable is treating hectares created and hectares destroyed as interchangeable, when two decades of evidence show they are not.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of public consent. Realignment usually means surrendering farmland, footpaths and, occasionally, houses to the sea, and it has met fierce local opposition. Policymakers have generally assumed that such opposition is about money, and have responded with compensation payments. Nikos Kapoulas, a rural sociologist, conducted interviews in coastal villages affected by realignment and reached a different conclusion. Residents, he found, frequently described the embankments as part of their inheritance, built and maintained by their ancestors, and regarded breaching them as an admission of defeat. Financial offers, in his view, may even deepen resentment by appearing to put a price on something residents regard as beyond price.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Kapoulas's findings help to explain why some schemes that looked sound on paper have stalled, and they deserve wider attention among engineers, who still tend to see consultation as a matter of explaining decisions already made. A more productive approach, adopted in a handful of recent projects, involves residents in deciding where new defences should go and how the restored land will be accessed. Such processes are slow, and they do not always produce agreement. But a strategy that depends on communities accepting the loss of land their families have defended for generations cannot succeed if it treats their attachment as an obstacle rather than a legitimate concern.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Managed realignment, then, is neither the panacea its champions sometimes present nor the capitulation its opponents fear. It is a sensible response to a coastline that cannot be held everywhere indefinitely, but its benefits depend heavily on site preparation, honest accounting and the patience to let natural processes work over decades rather than years.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: constructed treatment wetlands for cleaning wastewater
title: The Living Filter
subtitle: Artificial marshes are cleaning sewage in thousands of communities, but their champions may be promising more than they can deliver

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the treatment of sewage was regarded as an engineering problem to be solved with concrete tanks, pumps and chemical dosing. The idea that a shallow bed of gravel planted with reeds might do the same job was treated, at best, as a curiosity. Yet constructed wetlands, artificial basins designed to reproduce the purifying processes of natural marshes, now serve thousands of villages, farms and small industrial sites across several continents. Their appeal is easy to understand: they use little or no electricity, require few specialist staff and can be built largely from local materials. What remains disputed is how far their reach should extend, and whether the enthusiasm they currently enjoy rests on evidence or on a rather romantic view of nature.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanisms involved are more varied than the popular image of plants 'drinking' pollution suggests. As wastewater moves slowly through the system, suspended particles settle out, while bacteria attached to gravel and root surfaces break down organic matter. Reeds contribute less by absorbing contaminants themselves than by pumping small amounts of oxygen down through their hollow stems into the root zone, creating pockets where oxygen-dependent microbes can thrive alongside those that do without it. Dr Aurelio Benvenga, a microbial ecologist at the Subalpine Institute of Water Studies, argues that the plants are best understood as 'scaffolding for bacteria'. In his trials, beds planted with reeds removed roughly a third more nitrogen than identical unplanted beds, but he attributes almost all of the difference to the microbial communities that the roots supported rather than to uptake by the plants.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Performance, however, varies widely with design. Surface-flow wetlands, in which water moves across open ponds much like a natural marsh, are cheap to build and attractive to wildlife, but they need large areas of land. Subsurface systems, in which effluent passes through gravel beneath the surface, occupy perhaps a fifth of the space and avoid problems with odour and insects, though their pores gradually clog with solids and bacterial film. The hydrologist Mirela Dragomanu, who has surveyed more than two hundred systems in south-eastern Europe, found that clogging, rather than any failure of the biology, was the main reason subsurface beds stopped working. Many had been built with gravel that was too fine, or had received effluent that had not been adequately screened. Her conclusion is that the technology is far more forgiving of neglect than conventional plants, but far less forgiving of poor initial design.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cold climates have provided a further test. Since microbial activity slows sharply at low temperatures, sceptics long assumed that wetlands would be of little use where winters are severe. Monitoring in northern Scandinavia and Canada has partly overturned this assumption: insulated beds, covered with a layer of mulch or snow, continue to remove organic matter through the winter, although nitrogen removal falls considerably. The lesson, it seems to me, is not that climate is irrelevant but that designers must decide in advance which pollutants matter most at a given site and size the system accordingly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Advocates frequently go further, presenting constructed wetlands as a replacement for conventional treatment in towns and even cities. Here the case becomes much weaker. Joost Zwijsen, an engineer with the Lowlands Sanitation Consortium, calculates that a wetland serving a town of 50,000 people would need an area in the order of 200 hectares, land which near a growing urban area is rarely available and never cheap. Zwijsen does not dismiss wetlands altogether; he proposes instead that they be used as a final 'polishing' stage after mechanical treatment, removing residual nutrients before the water is released into rivers. This hybrid role is, in my view, where the technology's greatest future lies, at least in densely populated regions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A separate concern is that wetlands may simply move pollution rather than eliminate it. Phosphorus, for example, is not broken down but bound to gravel and sediment, and once these materials are saturated, removal declines abruptly. Heavy metals and some pharmaceutical compounds also accumulate in sediments, raising the question of what should eventually be done with them. Wanjiru Kibicho, who studies treatment systems on flower farms in East Africa, has shown that replacing the saturated gravel every ten to fifteen years restores phosphorus removal, but adds a cost that early budgets rarely included. It would be wrong to treat this as a fatal objection; it is, rather, a reminder that no treatment system is maintenance-free, however natural it may appear.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most intriguing claims concern benefits that have nothing to do with water quality. Surface-flow wetlands attract birds, amphibians and insects, and some have become valued local amenities with footpaths and observation hides. Yet these benefits come with tensions. Wildlife drawn to a treatment pond is exposed to whatever contaminants it contains, and few studies have followed the health of such animals over time. Until that evidence exists, describing these systems as nature reserves seems premature. Constructed wetlands deserve their growing reputation, but they will be served best by advocates who are candid about what they cannot do.
