area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: dredging estuaries for shipping: tidal amplification, turbidity and saltwater intrusion
title: Dredged to the Limit
subtitle: Deepening estuaries for ever-larger ships may be changing the way these waterways behave

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Estuaries have always attracted ports. Sheltered from the open sea yet connected to it, they offered early traders safe anchorage and access by river to inland markets. But the ships that call at them today bear little resemblance to those for which most harbours were built. The largest container vessels now draw more than sixteen metres of water, and every increase in their size has been followed by demands that the channels leading to inland ports be deepened yet again. Over the past century, the navigation channels of many of the world's busiest estuaries have been dredged to two or three times their natural depth. Only recently has it become clear that such interventions do not merely make room for ships; they can change the fundamental behaviour of the estuary itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most striking consequence is a change in the tide. In a shallow, natural estuary, friction against the bed and banks drains energy from the incoming tide, so that its range diminishes as it travels upstream. Deepening reduces this friction, and in some cases the tidal range far inland has grown by a metre or more within a few decades. Ottavia Rambaldi, a geomorphologist at the Ligurian Coastal Dynamics Laboratory, has reconstructed tidal records stretching back to the nineteenth century for six European and Asian estuaries. In each case, she argues, the timing of the increase corresponds more closely to successive dredging campaigns than to the gradual rise in sea level, which has been far too small to explain it. Her findings matter because a larger tidal range raises high-water levels upstream, increasing the risk of flooding in cities whose defences were designed for a different estuary.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Deepening can also set off a chain of effects that is harder to reverse. With stronger flood tides, more fine sediment is carried landward than is flushed out by the ebb, and it accumulates in the upper estuary. The water becomes so laden with suspended mud that in extreme cases it forms a dense, fluid layer near the bed. Light no longer penetrates, algae cannot grow, and bacteria consuming organic matter in the mud strip the water of oxygen, sometimes over stretches of many kilometres. Rambaldi describes this as a 'tipping point': beyond a certain depth, the estuary shifts into a turbid state from which it may not return even if dredging stops, because the accumulated mud itself further reduces friction. Not all of her colleagues accept that the shift is irreversible, but the evidence that it can happen with surprising speed seems to me hard to dispute.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Salt is a further concern. A deeper channel allows denser seawater to creep further upriver along the bed, and freshwater intakes once comfortably beyond the reach of the sea have begun to draw brackish water during dry summers. Farmers who irrigate from tidal rivers have reported damage to crops, and in at least one delta, municipal water supplies have had to be moved several kilometres upstream at considerable expense. Chiamaka Eze-Uzor, an estuarine ecologist, points out that the changing salinity also redistributes wildlife: species adapted to fresh water retreat while marine organisms advance, and the brackish zone on which many fish depend for spawning is compressed into a narrower band.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Port authorities, unsurprisingly, see matters differently. Torbjørn Haugaland, an economist who has advised several harbour boards, argues that ports which fail to accommodate the largest ships will lose traffic to competitors, with severe consequences for employment and regional economies. In his view, the environmental costs, while real, are routinely exaggerated by opponents who ignore the fact that most estuaries have been heavily modified for centuries. There is some force in this point: for many estuaries there is no pristine baseline to which they could return. Yet it hardly follows that further modification is harmless. If anything, an estuary already under stress may be closer to the thresholds that Rambaldi describes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some engineers believe the conflict can be resolved through design. A group at the Hanseatic Institute for Hydraulic Engineering has proposed measures intended to restore friction without reducing navigable depth: underwater sills that slow the tide, the reconnection of side channels and former floodplains that absorb tidal energy, and the creation of tidal storage areas into which water spills at high tide. Early results from pilot schemes are encouraging, although the areas involved remain modest compared with the scale of the problem. The approach also requires land, and in estuaries lined with industry and housing, land is the scarcest resource of all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Underlying the debate is a question of who bears the costs. The benefits of deeper channels accrue largely to shipping companies and port operators, whereas the costs, in the form of higher flood risk, saltier water and degraded fisheries, fall on communities scattered along the estuary, many of which were never consulted. Eze-Uzor has argued that any future deepening should be conditional on a long-term commitment by ports to fund monitoring and restoration. That seems a modest and reasonable demand. The deeper difficulty is that the effects of dredging may emerge only decades after the decisions that caused them, long after those responsible have moved on, and no system of accountability yet devised has proved capable of bridging so wide a gap in time.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: the mangrove nursery hypothesis: do mangroves really supply young fish to coastal fisheries?
title: A Cradle Among the Roots?
subtitle: The belief that mangrove forests feed the world's coastal fisheries is widely held, but surprisingly hard to prove

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask a fisher in a village on the edge of a mangrove forest why the trees matter, and the answer is likely to be the same almost anywhere in the tropics: without the forest, there would be no fish. The belief that mangroves act as nurseries for young fish and shrimp, sheltering them during their most vulnerable stage before they move offshore to join commercial stocks, has become one of the central arguments for conserving them. It appears in government policy documents, conservation campaigns and economic valuations that attribute a sizeable share of coastal fisheries' income to the forests. Yet when researchers have tried to demonstrate the connection directly, it has proved surprisingly elusive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case rests on observations that are not in doubt. Juveniles of many species are far more abundant among mangrove roots than on nearby open mudflats or sandy shores. The tangle of prop roots offers protection from larger predators, which find it hard to manoeuvre in the shallow, cluttered water, and the murky conditions make small fish harder to see. Decaying leaves fuel a food web rich in small invertebrates. Bunyamin Saragih, a fisheries biologist who has sampled mangrove creeks in eastern Indonesia for nearly twenty years, has recorded juveniles of more than ninety species, several of which are later caught by trawlers far out at sea. To him, the pattern is unmistakable: remove the forest and the supply of young fish to offshore stocks will dwindle.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty, as Rosalind Tavake-Pahulu of the Pacific Reef and Lagoon Institute has pointed out, is that abundance is not the same as contribution. A habitat may contain large numbers of juveniles and yet supply few of the adults that eventually reach the fishery, perhaps because survival there is poor or because growth is slow. A true nursery, in her definition, is one that contributes more adults per unit area than other habitats in which the same juveniles occur. By this stricter test, she argues, the evidence for most species remains incomplete, since few studies have tracked young fish from the mangroves to the populations that are actually harvested. In some regions, seagrass beds appear to perform the nursery role at least as effectively, and in others young fish spend only a brief and possibly non-essential period among the roots.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tracing fish from one habitat to another was until recently almost impossible, because tags small enough for juveniles were unavailable. Chemical methods have begun to change this. The chemist Esteban Iturralde has analysed the ear stones, or otoliths, of adult snapper caught on offshore reefs. These tiny structures grow in daily layers and incorporate traces of elements and isotopes from the surrounding water, so that the core of an adult's otolith preserves a chemical record of where it lived as a juvenile. Iturralde's results show that, on the reefs he studied, a majority of adult snapper had spent their early lives in mangrove-fringed waters. In my view, this is the strongest evidence yet produced for the nursery hypothesis, but it applies to a handful of species and locations, and it would be rash to generalise from it to the many fish that have not been examined.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Large-scale comparisons offer another line of evidence. Studies across several countries have found that fisheries catches tend to be higher along coastlines with more extensive mangroves. Such correlations are suggestive but difficult to interpret. Coasts with large mangrove forests also tend to have large river systems delivering nutrients, broad shallow shelves and particular tidal regimes, any of which might independently support productive fisheries. Separating the influence of the trees themselves from these other factors has proved extremely difficult, and some apparent relationships weaken considerably once they are taken into account.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that mangroves are unimportant for fish, and it would be a serious misreading of the debate to suggest so. The question is rather one of precision. Lalaine Dimaculangan, who studies small-scale fisheries in the Philippines, warns that overstated claims can backfire. When governments are promised that restoring a stretch of mangrove will revive collapsing fish stocks, and the catch fails to recover within a few years, support for conservation may evaporate. She also notes that many coastal households depend less on offshore stocks than on species caught within the forests themselves, such as mud crabs and shellfish, whose reliance on mangroves is not in dispute.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The nursery debate illustrates a broader tension in environmental science. Simple, memorable arguments are powerful tools for persuading policymakers, but they can harden into assumptions that are rarely tested. Mangrove forests have many other values, from protecting shorelines against erosion to storing carbon, and the case for them does not depend on the nursery function alone. A more honest account would acknowledge where the evidence is strong, where it is merely plausible, and where it is still missing; that, rather than any single persuasive slogan, is the firmer foundation for protecting them.

topic: reclamation of Yellow Sea tidal flats and the decline of migratory shorebirds
title: The Vanishing Stepping Stones
subtitle: Tidal flats thousands of kilometres from where they are counted may hold the key to the fate of migratory shorebirds

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every spring, millions of shorebirds leave their non-breeding grounds in Australia and New Zealand and fly north to breed on the Arctic tundra of Siberia and Alaska. Few can complete a journey of more than 10,000 kilometres without stopping. Instead, they break it at a small number of staging sites, where they spend several weeks feeding intensively on worms, clams and crustaceans buried in intertidal mud, in some cases almost doubling their body weight before departing on the next leg. For many species, the most important of these sites lie along the shores of the Yellow Sea, between China and the Korean peninsula, where vast tidal flats are exposed twice a day by a tidal range that in places exceeds eight metres.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Those same flats have for decades been regarded as land waiting to be claimed. Building sea walls across the intertidal zone and filling the enclosed area creates level coastal ground suitable for ports, industrial zones, aquaculture ponds and farmland. Analysis of satellite imagery suggests that, between the 1950s and the early 2010s, well over half of the tidal flats along parts of the Yellow Sea coast were lost in this way, much of it with the active encouragement of governments that regarded the flats as unproductive and the new ground as essential to economic growth. Over the same period, counts on Australian beaches recorded steep declines in several migratory species, in some cases of more than three-quarters within three decades.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Linking the two trends is less straightforward than it might seem. Shorebirds face threats throughout their range: disturbance on beaches, hunting in some regions, and changing conditions on the breeding grounds, where warming may be altering the timing of the insect emergence on which chicks depend. Alinta Coolbardie, who has coordinated volunteer counts on the north-west coast of Australia for twenty-five years, notes that the declines have been steepest in species that rely most heavily on the Yellow Sea, while species that stage elsewhere have fared comparatively well. In her view, this pattern points clearly to the loss of staging habitat as the principal cause. The inference is a reasonable one, although a pattern of this kind cannot on its own establish cause and effect.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lieke Vossenberg, an ecologist who studies energy budgets in migratory birds, has approached the problem from the birds' perspective. Using small radio tags, her group found that individuals arriving at reclaimed sections of coast did not simply move to neighbouring flats, as had been widely assumed; many lingered on remaining fragments where feeding was already intense and food had become scarce. These birds put on weight more slowly and departed later, or lighter, than those staging on intact flats, and their survival over the following year was markedly lower. The implication, Vossenberg argues, is that the remaining flats were unable to absorb displaced birds: the loss of one site could not be compensated for by crowding into another. To my mind, this is the most compelling piece of the puzzle, because it connects the disappearance of mud to the fate of individual birds.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the case is closed. Seo-yeon Bahk, an ornithologist at the West Coast Wetland Observatory, has cautioned that the counts on which the declines are based were made by different observers using varied methods, and that some apparent losses might reflect birds shifting to sites that are not surveyed. She also points out that some reclaimed areas, such as salt pans and certain aquaculture ponds, are used by shorebirds as roosts at high tide, so that the effects of reclamation are not uniformly negative. Bahk does not dispute that habitat loss has caused harm; her concern is that overstating the certainty of the evidence leaves conservationists exposed when individual figures are challenged. Her caution is worth heeding, though it is difficult to see how a shift to unsurveyed sites could explain declines of this size across so many species.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Policy has shifted noticeably. In the late 2010s, authorities in the region announced restrictions on new commercial reclamation, and several sections of the coast were nominated for international protection. Yet halting reclamation does not by itself secure the flats that remain. Many are being colonised by an invasive cordgrass, a salt-marsh plant deliberately introduced decades ago to stabilise coastlines, which converts open mud into dense vegetation where shorebirds cannot feed. Reduced sediment supply from dammed rivers may also mean that some flats will slowly erode. Protection, in other words, may need to be supplemented by active management.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The story of the Yellow Sea shows how the conservation of migratory species depends on places far from where the animals are most visible. Australians who watch shorebirds on their beaches had little reason to think about the coast of another continent, and the agencies responsible for one end of a flyway rarely have influence over the other. International agreements exist, but their effectiveness will depend on whether governments are willing to give mudflats the protection they now routinely extend to forests and reefs. That would require a change in perception as much as in law, since a muddy shore, unlike a rainforest, is rarely seen by the public as something worth saving.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: wetlands, mosquitoes and disease: the history of draining marshes against malaria and fears about restored wetlands
title: Marsh Fever
subtitle: Wetlands were once drained in the name of public health. Does restoring them bring the old dangers back?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of European history, marshes were associated not with wildlife but with sickness. The very word 'malaria' derives from the Italian for 'bad air', reflecting the long-held belief that fevers rose from the foul-smelling vapours of stagnant water. Communities living beside fens and coastal lagoons suffered recurrent outbreaks, and life expectancy in some low-lying districts was markedly lower than in neighbouring uplands. Drainage was therefore presented not only as a means of creating farmland but as a public health measure, and the engineers who reclaimed marshes were celebrated as benefactors of the poor. Some of the most ambitious drainage schemes of the early twentieth century were justified almost entirely on these grounds.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The discovery at the end of the nineteenth century that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes rather than by air seemed at first to confirm the wisdom of drainage: remove the standing water, and the insects would have nowhere to breed. Graciela Ferrandiz, a historian at the Iberian Centre for the History of Medicine, has examined parish and hospital records from three European regions and argues that the story is more complicated. In several places, she finds, malaria had begun to retreat before large-scale drainage was completed. Better housing that kept mosquitoes out of sleeping quarters, the movement of cattle into stables close to homes, which diverted the insects towards animals, and wider access to quinine all played a part. Drainage, in her account, was one contributor among several, and in some places a minor one. Some historians have questioned her conclusions, pointing out that records from the period are patchy, but the pattern she describes recurs in all three regions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This historical revision matters today because wetlands are now being restored on a large scale, and the old fears have not entirely vanished. Residents near restoration schemes frequently raise concerns about mosquitoes, and planning objections citing nuisance and disease are common. Anahit Harutyunyan, a medical entomologist, has spent a decade sampling mosquitoes in restored and degraded wetlands. Her surveys show that the species which breed in large numbers in healthy marshes are often not those capable of transmitting human diseases. Many of the most troublesome species prefer small, temporary pools, such as blocked gutters, discarded tyres and puddles in disturbed ground, to the permanent, well-vegetated water of a functioning wetland. In her samples from restored sites, the proportion of disease-carrying species was, if anything, lower than in the ditches of surrounding farmland.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The ecological explanation lies largely in predation. Permanent wetlands support fish, dragonfly larvae, water beetles and other animals that feed on mosquito larvae, and their complex vegetation provides habitat for these predators. Water movement also matters: where water flows gently through reedbeds, larvae are more easily dislodged and exposed to predators than in stagnant hollows. A poorly managed or partially drained marsh, by contrast, may consist of shallow, fluctuating pools that dry out too often for predators to persist, but not quite often enough to prevent mosquitoes from completing their brief development. Harutyunyan's conclusion, which seems to me well supported, is that a degraded wetland can produce more biting insects than either a fully drained or a fully restored one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This does not mean that restoration carries no risk. Kalombo Ilunga, a public health specialist who has advised on wetland projects in Central Africa and southern Europe, warns that conditions vary greatly between regions. Where efficient carriers of disease are present and the human population lacks access to treatment, even modest increases in mosquito numbers may have serious consequences. He points out, too, that the critical period in a restoration project is often the first few years, when water levels are still being adjusted and predator populations have not yet become established. Ilunga advocates mosquito monitoring as a standard part of restoration planning, together with the design of channels and shorelines that prevent water from stagnating in shallow margins.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some restoration managers resist such recommendations, arguing that they add cost and delay to projects already struggling for funding, and that fears about mosquitoes are exaggerated by people who oppose restoration for other reasons. There is something to this: complaints about insects can be a convenient way of objecting to schemes that residents dislike for quite different reasons, such as the loss of farmland or changes to a familiar landscape. Yet dismissing public concern is unwise. A single outbreak attributed, rightly or wrongly, to a restored marsh could set back support for wetland conservation across an entire region, and the cost of that would far exceed the modest expense of monitoring.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of malaria and marshes offers a cautionary lesson. A simple explanation, that wetlands cause disease, gave rise to policies that destroyed vast areas of valuable habitat, while the actual reasons for the decline of the disease were more varied. Today there is a risk of the opposite simplification: the belief that healthy wetlands pose no threat at all. The evidence suggests that the truth depends on the type of wetland, the species of mosquito and the circumstances of the people living nearby, and policy is likely to work best when it takes all three into account rather than relying on slogans from either side of the debate.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: putting a monetary value on the services provided by wetlands
title: What Is a Marsh Worth?
subtitle: Economists have tried to show that wetlands earn their keep. The results have been revealing, but not always in the way they intended

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a city council weighs a proposal to drain a marsh for a housing estate, the arithmetic usually seems one-sided. The houses have a market value that can be calculated to the nearest unit of currency; the marsh, which produces nothing that is bought or sold, appears on the balance sheet as zero. Over the past three decades, a growing community of environmental economists has set out to correct this imbalance by estimating the monetary value of the services that wetlands provide: absorbing floodwater, filtering pollutants, supporting fisheries, sheltering wildlife and offering places for recreation. Their figures, which in some cases run to tens of thousands of dollars per hectare per year, have been cited in planning disputes, government reports and international negotiations. Whether they have actually saved many wetlands is a different matter.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The methods involved are diverse. Some services can be valued by reference to what it would cost to replace them: if a marsh removes nitrogen that would otherwise have to be removed by a treatment plant, the cost of the plant provides a rough measure of the marsh's worth. Flood protection can be estimated from the damage avoided in storms. Other benefits are harder to capture. The pleasure people take in birdwatching, or their satisfaction in knowing that a rare frog survives, has no market price, and economists have to rely on surveys asking people how much they would pay to preserve them. Yevgenia Pashkevich, who has conducted such surveys around lakes and floodplains in eastern Europe, acknowledges that the answers can be sensitive to how questions are phrased, but maintains that a carefully designed survey produces figures that are consistent and repeatable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics have focused on a practice known as benefit transfer. Original valuation studies are costly and slow, so analysts frequently take figures from a study of one wetland and apply them to another, sometimes in a different country and decades later. Fumiko Takaoka, an economist at the Pacific Rim Institute of Resource Economics, has compared transferred values with those obtained from new studies of the same sites and found discrepancies that in some cases exceeded a factor of ten. A marsh beside a large city, she points out, provides far more flood protection and recreation than an identical marsh in an empty landscape, simply because there are more people and more property to benefit. To my mind, her work does not invalidate benefit transfer, but it should make anyone wary of global totals assembled largely from borrowed figures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection is philosophical. Babacar Gueye, who has worked with fishing and herding communities in the inland deltas of West Africa, argues that converting a wetland into a sum of money misrepresents the relationship that many people have with it. For these communities, he contends, a floodplain is a source of livelihood, identity and spiritual meaning, and its loss cannot be compensated for by a payment of any size. He has documented cases in which communities were offered cash for the loss of seasonal grazing and fishing grounds, only to find that the money could not buy access to comparable land anywhere nearby. Valuation, in his view, implies that a wetland may legitimately be destroyed whenever a more profitable use can be found, which is precisely the outcome it was meant to prevent.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of valuation reply that decisions about land are made in monetary terms whether economists take part or not, and that assigning no value at all to a wetland is itself a valuation: an implicit judgement that it is worthless. Rainer Kesselring, who advises regional planning authorities in central Europe, argues that the real purpose of valuation is not to set a price at which a marsh may be sold, but to make visible costs that would otherwise be ignored. He cites cases in which the estimated cost of replacing a floodplain's water storage with engineered defences persuaded authorities to abandon plans to build on it. This seems to me the most persuasive defence of the approach, although it depends on valuation being used to inform decisions rather than to settle them mechanically.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The evidence on whether valuation changes outcomes is surprisingly thin. Studies of planning decisions suggest that monetary estimates are frequently commissioned but rarely decisive; they tend to be cited when they support a decision already favoured on other grounds and quietly set aside when they do not. Valuation studies are also concentrated in wealthy countries, where funds for research are available, while the most rapid wetland losses are occurring elsewhere. In some of those countries, the agencies responsible for wetlands lack the legal authority to block development, so that even a compelling estimate has nowhere to go. There is a risk, therefore, that the effort devoted to refining estimates has outstripped the attention paid to the institutions that would need to act on them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the enterprise should be abandoned. Economic valuation has helped to shift public discussion, so that wetlands are now widely described as infrastructure rather than wasteland, and that change in language is not trivial. But the numbers should be treated as arguments rather than facts, and presented alongside the ecological and cultural reasons for protection rather than in place of them. A wetland that is saved only because its price is high enough remains vulnerable to the next calculation.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: restoring lost oyster reefs in estuaries: baselines, water filtration and living shorelines
title: Reefs of Shell
subtitle: Oyster reefs once dominated many estuaries. Bringing them back is proving both more valuable and more difficult than expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Early European accounts of estuaries on both sides of the Atlantic describe oyster reefs so extensive that they posed hazards to navigation. Ships ran aground on them, and in some bays they were mapped alongside sandbanks as features to be avoided. Heaps of discarded shell on the shores of some estuaries, accumulated over thousands of years, show how long people had harvested them without exhausting the supply. Little of this remains. Centuries of dredging for oysters, which were once among the cheapest foods in many coastal cities, followed by pollution, sedimentation and disease, have reduced the world's oyster reefs to a small fraction of their former extent, and many bays now retain effectively none. Because the decline happened gradually and long ago, few people living near these estuaries today are aware that anything has been lost.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That historical blindness is the focus of Tadeusz Wroblewski, an ecologist who reconstructs past ecosystems from harbour surveys, fishing logs and archaeological shell mounds. He argues that each generation of scientists has tended to treat the estuary it first encountered as the natural baseline, so that the standard of what counts as healthy has slipped steadily downward. Restoration targets, in his view, are consequently far too modest: a project that re-establishes a few hectares of reef may be celebrated as a success even though the original reefs covered thousands. I find his argument broadly convincing, though there is a practical difficulty he tends to understate. Estuaries have changed in so many other respects since the reefs were lost that the historical state may no longer be achievable, even in principle.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Interest in restoring oysters has nonetheless surged, driven by the many functions a healthy reef performs. Oysters are filter feeders: a single adult can process dozens of litres of water a day, removing algae and suspended particles and so improving the clarity of the water. Healthy reefs may also remove some nitrogen permanently, either by locking it into shell and tissue or by encouraging bacteria in reef sediments to convert it into harmless gas. Reefs provide complex three-dimensional habitat for crabs, small fish and the young of commercially important species. And, perhaps most attractively for coastal authorities, reefs built close to the shore can break the force of waves and reduce erosion, an approach often described as a 'living shoreline'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It is this last function that has attracted the attention of engineers. Thabiso Mokgethi, a coastal engineer who has designed reef breakwaters in southern Africa and the Gulf of Mexico, points out that, unlike a concrete sea wall, a living reef grows upward as new oysters settle on older shells, and so may keep pace with gradual rises in sea level. In his trials, reef structures reduced the wave energy reaching the shore by up to half in moderate conditions. Because the reefs are porous, they also allow water and animals to move freely between the open estuary and the marshes behind them, something a solid wall prevents. He is careful, however, to distinguish moderate conditions from severe storms, during which waves pass over low reefs with little reduction, and he regards reefs as a complement to conventional defences rather than a substitute for them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The claims about water quality have proved more contentious. Early advocates suggested that restoring oysters could reverse the excessive growth of algae in polluted estuaries, a condition fed by nutrient run-off from farms and cities. Delphine Arsenault-Roy, a marine ecologist at the Atlantic Estuarine Research Station, has calculated that, in most large estuaries, the oyster populations that could realistically be restored would filter only a modest proportion of the total volume of water. Oysters can make a noticeable difference in small, enclosed creeks, she concludes, but they cannot take the place of reducing the nutrients that enter the estuary in the first place. This seems to me an important corrective. Promising that oysters will clean up a bay risks giving polluters an excuse to postpone more expensive measures.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Restoration itself is far from straightforward. Oyster larvae need hard surfaces on which to settle, and in many estuaries the shell that once provided these has been removed or buried under sediment. Projects therefore lay down 'cultch', a base of recycled shell, limestone or broken concrete, to give larvae a foothold. Disease presents a further obstacle. Sigrun Ellefsen, who studies shellfish pathogens, notes that two parasites have devastated oyster populations in several regions, and that restored reefs can become reservoirs of infection if they are stocked with susceptible animals. She advocates the use of oysters bred for resistance, although this raises concerns about reducing the genetic diversity of wild populations.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most underrated obstacle is social. In some estuaries, restored reefs sit uncomfortably beside commercial harvesting, and fishers may regard sanctuaries closed to harvest as the loss of traditional grounds. Elsewhere, residents worry that reefs will obstruct boating or produce unpleasant smells at low tide. Disputes over who owns the seabed, and who is liable if a reef damages a vessel, have stalled some projects for years. Projects that involve local people from the outset, for instance by recruiting restaurants to return used shells or schoolchildren to monitor growth, appear to fare considerably better. Oysters, in other words, can help to rebuild an estuary, but only if the communities around it want the job done.

area: wetlands, estuaries and mangroves (not peatland carbon)
topic: intermittently closed coastal lagoons and the artificial opening of their sand barriers
title: The Closing Mouth
subtitle: Many coastal lagoons are naturally sealed off from the sea for long periods. Should we keep digging them open?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Along many of the world's wave-dominated coastlines, small rivers do not flow freely into the sea. Instead, they end in shallow coastal lakes and lagoons whose entrances are periodically sealed by sand pushed ashore by waves. For months or even years, such a lagoon may be cut off from the ocean, its water level slowly rising as rivers and rainfall fill it. Eventually, after heavy rain, the water spills over the sand barrier, scours a channel and drains rapidly to the sea, after which the tides flow in and out until waves close the entrance once again. These intermittently open systems are common in south-eastern Australia, southern Africa, parts of India and the Mediterranean, yet they have received far less scientific attention than permanently open estuaries, and they are, I would argue, among the most misunderstood of all coastal environments.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The misunderstanding stems partly from the fact that their natural behaviour conflicts with the expectations of the people who live beside them. When a lagoon is closed and its level rises, low-lying gardens, roads and septic systems may be flooded, sometimes long before any natural breakout occurs. The response in many places has been artificial opening: mechanical excavators dig a channel through the sand barrier whenever the water reaches a set height. In some lagoons this is now done several times a year, so that the system spends far more of its time open, and at lower water levels, than it would naturally.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kirra Maddigan, a coastal geomorphologist who has studied more than seventy such lagoons in south-eastern Australia, argues that frequent artificial opening has subtle but cumulative effects. Because channels are dug when water levels are relatively low, the outflow is weaker than in a natural breakout, and it fails to scour sediment from the lagoon's entrance. Sand therefore accumulates in the entrance area, the barrier rebuilds more quickly, and closures become more frequent, which in turn prompts more openings. Maddigan describes this as a self-reinforcing cycle, in which the management intervention gradually creates the very conditions that make it seem necessary.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The ecological consequences are debated. Corrado Albanesi, who studies Mediterranean lagoons, has found that the fringing wetlands of salt marsh and reed which surround many closed lagoons depend on periods of high water to flood them; when lagoons are opened early and often, these wetlands are inundated less frequently and begin to be colonised by dry-land plants. Opening also exposes the lagoon bed, and when organic-rich sediments that have been underwater are suddenly drained, they can release acids and deplete the water of oxygen, occasionally causing large fish kills. Albanesi concludes that the burden of proof should lie with those who wish to open a lagoon, not with those who wish to leave it alone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Others take a more cautious line. Priyamvada Kulasekaran, a fisheries scientist working on lagoons along India's east coast, points out that many fish and prawns spend part of their life cycle at sea and depend on open entrances to move between the lagoon and the ocean. For communities who fish these lagoons for a living, a prolonged closure can mean the failure of the catch for an entire season, and fishers have long dug channels themselves for this reason. In her view, artificial opening is not inherently damaging; what matters is its timing relative to the migrations of key species. This is a valuable reminder that opening is not solely a modern engineering response, though it does not, it seems to me, weaken Maddigan's case against the frequent, level-triggered openings now common in suburban settings.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Climate change is likely to make the dilemma sharper. Rising seas will raise the height of beaches and sand barriers, so that closed lagoons will fill to higher levels before breaking out, flooding more property. At the same time, changes in rainfall may lengthen the periods during which lagoons stay closed. Isabeau Montferrand, a planner who advises coastal municipalities in south-western France, argues that the long-term answer cannot be ever more frequent excavation. She advocates moving the most vulnerable infrastructure away from lagoon shores and prohibiting new building below a level that allows for natural fluctuations in water level. Such policies are, unsurprisingly, unpopular with property owners, and few authorities have so far adopted them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to present the issue as a straightforward contest between nature and development, but that would oversimplify it. Some artificial opening is likely to remain necessary where homes were built long before the dynamics of these lagoons were understood. The more serious failing has been the absence of clear rules: in many places, decisions about when to open have been made case by case, often under pressure from residents, without reference to the condition of the lagoon or the life cycles of its inhabitants. What these systems need is not a ban on intervention but a recognition that they are meant to close, and that a lagoon which spends long periods cut off from the sea is not malfunctioning.

topic: corporate zero-deforestation commitments in commodity supply chains (soy, cattle, cocoa)
title: Promises in the Supply Chain
subtitle: Corporate pledges to remove deforestation from commodity production have multiplied, but their effect on the world's forests remains fiercely disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past fifteen years, hundreds of the world's largest food and consumer-goods companies have announced that the palm oil, soy, beef and cocoa they buy will no longer be linked to the clearing of tropical forests. These so-called zero-deforestation commitments were greeted, when they first appeared, as evidence that market pressure might achieve what decades of government regulation had not. Because a handful of trading firms handle the bulk of the global trade in each commodity, campaigners reasoned that persuading those firms to change their purchasing rules would ripple outwards to millions of producers. The logic was attractive, and it is not without foundation. Yet the record so far suggests that the pledges have been far less transformative than either their authors or their early admirers hoped.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited success is the Amazon Soy Moratorium, an agreement under which major traders undertook not to purchase soy grown on land cleared after a fixed date. Research by Dr Lucía Sarmiento at the Institute for Tropical Land Studies found that, in the decade after the moratorium began, the proportion of new soy fields planted on recently cleared forest in the Brazilian Amazon fell from roughly a third to around one per cent. Sarmiento attributes this largely to the fact that the agreement was simple to monitor: soy fields are large and easily identified from satellite images, and the cut-off date left little room for argument. She is careful, however, to warn against assuming that the same model can be transplanted to other commodities, since few combine such visibility with such a concentrated buyer base.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics point to a less comfortable effect known as leakage. The economist Piotr Kaczmarczyk of the Centre for Commodity Economics argues that when one region or product is subjected to strict rules, the demand for land does not disappear but relocates. His analysis of farm-level data indicates that as soy expansion slowed in the Amazon, clearing intensified in the neighbouring Cerrado savanna, which was not covered by the agreement, and that cattle ranchers displaced by soy farmers moved deeper into forested areas. Kaczmarczyk does not dispute that the moratorium reduced clearing for soy itself; his claim is that the net benefit for native vegetation as a whole was much smaller than headline figures implied. This seems to me a fair challenge, although the size of the displacement remains difficult to measure with any precision.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second problem concerns traceability. For a company to guarantee that its products are free of deforestation, it must know where its raw materials originate, and in many supply chains this information simply does not exist. Cattle offer the clearest illustration. An animal may pass through several ranches during its life, and while slaughterhouses can often verify the final farm that sold it, the earlier 'indirect' suppliers, where much of the clearing actually happens, typically remain invisible. Amara Gyamfi, who studies cocoa supply chains at the West African Forest Policy Unit, reports a comparable difficulty: cocoa is grown by hundreds of thousands of smallholders and traded through intermediaries who rarely keep records of individual farms. In her view, traceability is not merely a technical gap but a political one, because the intermediaries who hold the information often have little incentive to share it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers question whether the pledges were ever intended to be met. A survey led by Henrik Strandberg of the Nordic Business and Environment Group examined more than two hundred corporate commitments and found that fewer than a quarter included measurable targets, independent verification or penalties for non-compliance. Many simply expressed an aspiration to reach zero deforestation 'by 2020', a deadline that passed with little comment from the companies concerned. Strandberg interprets this as evidence that a large share of commitments functioned primarily as reputational insurance. That conclusion is probably too sweeping. Vague wording can reflect genuine uncertainty about what is achievable rather than cynicism, and several firms that missed their targets have since invested heavily in monitoring systems.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important objection is that private commitments cannot reach the producers who matter most. Tendai Mutasa, an agricultural geographer at the Southern Land Use Observatory, has shown that a substantial share of commodities grown on recently cleared land is sold in domestic markets or to buyers in countries where consumers exert little pressure on corporations. A pledge by a European chocolate manufacturer, she observes, has no bearing on a farmer who sells to a local mill supplying a national market. On this reading, supply-chain commitments may simply divide producers into a 'clean' segment serving demanding buyers and an unregulated segment serving everyone else.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means the commitments have been worthless. They have generated monitoring tools, satellite alert systems and public datasets that governments and journalists now use routinely, and they have shifted expectations about what responsible business looks like. But it is increasingly clear that voluntary pledges work best alongside, rather than instead of, public regulation. New laws requiring importers to demonstrate that goods were not produced on recently cleared land represent a recognition of this. Whether such laws avoid the weaknesses of the voluntary approach will depend on how seriously they address leakage and the needs of smallholders, who risk being excluded from lucrative markets simply because they cannot afford the paperwork.

topic: natural regeneration of secondary forests versus tree-planting campaigns
title: Letting the Forest Return
subtitle: Tree-planting campaigns attract headlines and funding, but a growing body of research suggests that forests often recover best when left largely to themselves

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In recent years, planting trees has become one of the most popular responses to the climate crisis. Governments announce targets measured in billions of seedlings, corporations sponsor planting days for their employees, and smartphone applications allow users to fund a sapling with a single tap. The appeal is easy to understand: a tree is a tangible symbol of renewal, and the act of planting one offers a sense of direct, personal contribution that few other environmental actions can match. Yet a growing number of ecologists warn that this enthusiasm, however well intentioned, is frequently misdirected. In many landscapes, they argue, the most effective way to bring back a forest is not to plant one at all, but to step aside and allow it to return by itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The evidence for this view comes largely from the study of secondary forests, which grow back on land that has been cleared and later abandoned. Across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, millions of hectares of former pasture and cropland have been left to regenerate as rural populations have moved to cities. A comparison led by Wanjiru Obuya of the East African Restoration Research Centre examined more than sixty such sites alongside tree plantations of similar age. Her team found that naturally regenerating forests stored, on average, comparable or greater quantities of carbon above ground, and supported several times as many species of birds and plants. Crucially, they did so at a fraction of the cost, since no nurseries, seedlings or labour for planting were required.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Natural regeneration depends on mechanisms that are easy to overlook. Seeds may lie dormant in the soil for years, the stumps and roots of felled trees can send up new shoots, and birds and bats carry seeds from nearby woodland as they feed. The forest ecologist Mateus Oyarzun, who has mapped regrowth across southern Chile, emphasises that this last process is highly sensitive to distance. Where abandoned land lies within a few hundred metres of an intact forest, he reports, a closed canopy can form within two decades; beyond that distance, the arrival of seeds declines steeply and recovery may stall for a generation or more. Oyarzun's work suggests that the location of restoration efforts matters at least as much as the method chosen.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tree-planting schemes, by contrast, have a mixed record. An audit of planting projects carried out by Ingrid Holmgren at the Scandinavian Forest Monitoring Programme found that in roughly half of the cases she examined, the majority of seedlings had died within five years, typically because they were planted in the wrong season, left unprotected from grazing animals, or simply never tended after the initial ceremony. Many surviving projects consisted of a single fast-growing species, often eucalyptus or pine, chosen for timber value rather than ecological suitability. Even more troubling, some campaigns have planted trees on natural grasslands and savannas, ecosystems that were never forested and whose rich biodiversity is destroyed by afforestation. To describe such projects as restoration is, in my view, a misuse of the word.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, however, to conclude that letting nature take its course is always the better option. Dragan Vukovic, a soil scientist who has worked on degraded mining land in the Balkans, points out that natural regeneration assumes conditions that many sites no longer possess. Where topsoil has been eroded, where aggressive grasses have taken hold, or where repeated fires sweep across the landscape, seedlings may fail to establish for decades. On some Pacific islands, the problem is different again: the conservation biologist Kalani Kamaka notes that many of the birds which once dispersed the seeds of native trees have become extinct, so that forests cannot spread without human assistance. In such places, active planting of native species is not an indulgence but a necessity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further weakness of secondary forests is their impermanence. Because they often grow on private farmland and lack the legal status of 'primary' forest, they are frequently cleared again as soon as agricultural prices rise. Studies in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest have found that a significant proportion of regrowth is cut down before it reaches twenty years of age, long before it has recovered much of its carbon or biodiversity. This is a failure of policy rather than of ecology, yet it seriously undermines the case for relying on regeneration alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most persuasive position, then, is that the choice between planting and natural regrowth has been presented as a stark alternative when it should not be. Practitioners increasingly favour what is known as assisted natural regeneration: fencing out livestock, clearing competing grasses, creating firebreaks and planting a small number of trees only where seed sources are lacking. Such an approach takes advantage of whatever capacity for recovery a site retains while intervening where that capacity has been lost. Adopting it widely, though, would require funders to abandon their attachment to the number of trees planted as a measure of success, and to accept that some of the most valuable restoration work involves no planting at all.

topic: forest fragmentation and edge effects in tropical forests
title: The Trouble with Edges
subtitle: Why the shape of a forest may matter almost as much as its size

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When governments and campaign groups report on the state of the world's forests, the figure that dominates is almost always area: so many million hectares cleared in a given year, so many remaining. Such statistics are indispensable, but they conceal as much as they reveal. A forest that has been cut into a hundred scattered pieces may cover the same total area as one that remains a single block, yet ecologically the two are hardly comparable. Fragmentation, rather than outright clearance, may now be the defining condition of tropical forests, and it is a condition that headline numbers are poorly equipped to capture.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The reason lies at the boundary between forest and cleared land. Along a newly created edge, sunlight penetrates beneath the canopy, temperatures rise, humidity falls and wind gusts reach trees that grew up sheltered from them. The consequences were first documented systematically by a long-term experiment begun in the 1980s, in which ranchers clearing land in the central Amazon agreed to leave isolated reserves of one, ten and a hundred hectares. Dr Lucia Marquezini, who has directed the project for the past two decades, reports that tree mortality in the outer hundred metres of these reserves has remained persistently higher than in continuous forest. The losses fall disproportionately on the largest canopy trees, which are snapped by wind or die of drought stress, and these are precisely the trees that hold the most carbon. Their place is taken by fast-growing pioneer species with light, short-lived wood.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How much this matters globally depends on how much forest lies close to an edge, and recent mapping suggests the answer is a great deal. A team led by the remote-sensing specialist Ingrid Haldorsen at the Bergen Institute for Landscape Analysis combined high-resolution imagery with Marquezini's mortality figures and concluded that roughly a fifth of the world's remaining tropical forest lies within a hundred metres of a boundary. On their calculations, the carbon released from degrading edges could add between a quarter and a third to the emissions conventionally attributed to deforestation. These estimates rest on the assumption that edges everywhere behave like those in the central Amazon, which is far from certain. Even so, the broad conclusion is difficult to dismiss: emissions accounts that look only at cleared land are almost certainly too low.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that edges are as damaging as this research implies. Kwabena Amankwah, a forest ecologist at the Volta Forest Research Station, points out that the studies most often cited come from a single type of forest, one in which species evolved beneath an unbroken canopy. In West Africa, by contrast, forests have long existed as mosaics interspersed with savanna, and many of their plants and animals appear well adapted to abrupt boundaries. Amankwah has also observed that, after a decade or so, dense secondary growth along an edge can form a kind of living wall that shields the interior from wind and drying. His argument is a valuable corrective to the assumption that findings from one region apply to all, but it should not be stretched too far. A naturally patchy landscape is not the same as one carved up by roads and pasture within a single generation, and the protective wall he describes is easily breached when the surrounding land is burned for grazing.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If fragments are inevitable, can they at least be reconnected? Corridors of forest linking isolated patches have become a favourite tool of conservation planners, and work by Siriporn Ruttanapong and colleagues in southern Thailand has shown that some mammals, including several species of primate, do travel along them. Yet Ruttanapong is cautious about their value. A corridor fifty metres wide, she notes, consists almost entirely of edge, and the species most in need of connection, those dependent on deep, humid interior conditions, are the very ones least likely to use it. Corridors also have a political appeal that has little to do with their ecological performance: they allow a development to proceed while appearing to mitigate its effects. The danger is that they come to be treated as a substitute for keeping large blocks intact rather than as a supplement to it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Land-use law can make matters worse. In several tropical countries, landowners are required to keep a fixed proportion of each property under forest. The intention is admirable, but because the rule is applied farm by farm, the outcome is frequently a scatter of small woodlots, each surrounded by pasture and each consisting largely of edge. A more effective arrangement would allow landowners to pool their obligations, so that the same total area is conserved as a few large blocks rather than hundreds of fragments. Proposals along these lines have been resisted, partly because they require cooperation between neighbours and partly because they leave some farms with no forest at all, which is politically awkward even if ecologically sensible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the area of forest is unimportant; clearing remains the single greatest threat. But measuring forests only by their extent is rather like assessing a person's health solely by their weight. Satellite programmes now make it technically straightforward to report the length of forest edge and the proportion of core habitat lying far from any boundary, and there is little excuse for continuing to leave such measures out of national statistics. Until shape is counted alongside size, much of the damage that fragmentation causes will remain invisible to the people charged with preventing it.

topic: indigenous and community land rights as a tool for slowing deforestation
title: Who Guards the Forest?
subtitle: The evidence that secure land rights slow deforestation is strong, but the reasons behind it are less straightforward

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, protecting a tropical forest meant drawing a boundary around it and declaring it a national park. People who had lived in and from the forest for generations were frequently moved out or forbidden to hunt, farm and gather within it. Over the past two decades, however, a growing body of research has suggested that forests formally owned and managed by indigenous and local communities are cleared more slowly than comparable land, sometimes even more slowly than strictly protected reserves. This is among the more encouraging findings in modern conservation. It has also, unfortunately, been turned too readily into a slogan, as if handing over a title deed were enough in itself to save a forest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most persuasive evidence comes from the geographer Rosa Huerta-Valle, of the Andean Institute of Territorial Studies, who compared satellite records for titled indigenous territories in the Peruvian Amazon with untitled land nearby. Over a fifteen-year period, she found, the rate of deforestation within titled territories was about two-thirds lower. What distinguishes her study is its design. Remote land tends to be cleared less whoever owns it, simply because it is expensive to reach, so Huerta-Valle paired each territory with untitled areas at a similar distance from roads and navigable rivers. Earlier comparisons that ignored accessibility may well have exaggerated the benefits of title, and it is this careful matching that makes her results considerably more convincing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The economist Ilze Kalnberza, who has examined land records from the lowlands of Bolivia, accepts the overall pattern but questions what lies behind it. In her view, a legal document makes little difference unless a community is able to enforce it, by patrolling its boundaries, expelling intruders and pursuing cases in court. Where such capacity was lacking, she found, titled and untitled land were cleared at almost identical rates. More surprisingly, a handful of communities actually increased their clearing after receiving title, apparently because the security it offered encouraged them to invest in cattle. These cases are important reminders that ownership changes incentives in more than one direction. They do not, however, overturn the broader picture, since they represent a small minority of the territories studied.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different perspective is offered by the anthropologist Mariama Ndiaye, whose fieldwork has taken her to forest communities in both West Africa and South America. Ndiaye argues that the decisive factor is not title but the strength of a community's own rules. In her experience, forests are best protected where communities possess functioning customary institutions, such as councils that allocate land and settle disputes over who may cut which trees. She is also critical of the tendency among outsiders to portray forest peoples as natural conservationists. Communities, she insists, respond to economic pressures like anyone else, and where young people see no prospect of earning a living from standing forest, the temptation to sell timber or rent land to ranchers can become very strong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Policy specialists have tended to focus on cost. According to Duarte Vitorino, a legal analyst who advises several regional governments, the expense of surveying and registering community land works out at a small fraction of the annual cost per hectare of staffing and equipping a national park. The economic case is hard to argue with. Yet Vitorino is equally clear about the obstacles. Applications for title can remain unprocessed for decades, during which time settlers and companies may move onto the land. In addition, some governments grant ownership of the surface while retaining the rights to underground minerals and timber, leaving communities unable to refuse a mining concession on what is nominally their own property.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: International interest in the issue has grown rapidly since forest carbon became a tradeable commodity. Several funds now channel money towards titling programmes on the grounds that they are a cheap source of avoided emissions, and climate negotiators increasingly cite community territories as evidence that forest protection can be compatible with development. This attention is welcome, but it brings risks of its own. When payments are tied to measured reductions in deforestation, communities whose forests were never under much threat may be rewarded generously, while those on the frontier of agricultural expansion, where the pressures are greatest and success is hardest to achieve, may find themselves judged as failures. A system designed to reward results can, in this way, end up penalising precisely the communities doing the most difficult work.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that secure tenure is best understood as a necessary condition for community protection of forests rather than a sufficient one. Donors who wish to support it should therefore fund the less glamorous work that follows the paperwork: training in boundary monitoring, legal aid and help in developing forest-based livelihoods. It would also be a mistake to evaluate land rights purely in terms of the hectares of forest they preserve. The recognition of a people's claim to the land they have occupied for centuries is first and foremost a question of justice, and it would remain so even if its environmental benefits proved smaller than current research suggests.

topic: near-real-time satellite deforestation alerts and whether they reduce forest loss
title: Alarms in the Canopy
subtitle: Satellites can now report the felling of a forest within days, but knowing is not the same as acting

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the early years of this century, most tropical countries measured deforestation once a year at best. Analysts compared satellite images taken twelve months apart, mapped the areas that had changed, and published national totals that were often more than a year out of date by the time they appeared. By then the cleared land had usually been burned, fenced and planted with pasture or crops, and there was little that any authority could do except record the loss. Today, freely available imagery and automated software produce alerts within days of the first trees falling, and these are distributed to governments, companies and campaign groups across the tropics. This is arguably the most significant change in forest governance in a generation. It would be naive, however, to imagine that information alone can stop a chainsaw.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Most alert systems rely on optical satellites, which record sunlight reflected from the earth's surface. When a patch of canopy is removed, its reflectance changes, and software that compares each new image with the statistical history of the same location can flag an abrupt departure from the norm. The weakness of this approach is cloud. Over parts of the Congo Basin and Borneo, cloud cover can hide the ground for most of the wet season, leaving optical systems effectively blind for months at a time. Radar satellites, which send out microwave pulses that pass through cloud, offer a solution, and Dr Aino Toivonen of the Nordic Earth Observation Laboratory has developed an alert system based on them. In the cloudiest regions she has studied, it has reduced the average delay before a clearing is detected from several months to less than two weeks. Radar is not without problems of its own: its signal is sensitive to soil moisture and heavy rain, and Toivonen's team estimates that roughly one in ten of the alerts it issues during the wet season turns out to be false.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Improvements in resolution have also changed what can be seen. The first generation of alert systems generally missed clearings smaller than about a hectare, which happens to be the typical size of a plot opened by a smallholder farmer. Newer sensors can detect gaps of a tenth of that area. Even so, one important form of degradation remains largely invisible. In selective logging, only the most valuable trees are removed, and the gaps they leave in the canopy are usually closed by surrounding vegetation within a year, so that the damage below, from roads, skid trails and crushed saplings, is hidden from above.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whether alerts actually reduce deforestation is a separate question, and the evidence is more mixed than their advocates sometimes admit. The environmental economist Hery Rasolofo examined twenty-two countries on three continents in which government agencies had begun to receive alerts. Averaged across his sample, forest loss fell modestly in the two years after subscription, but in a majority of the countries he could detect no measurable effect at all. The reductions were concentrated in places where alerts were passed directly to enforcement units that had vehicles, trained staff and the legal power to halt clearing and impose fines. Where alerts simply arrived in the inbox of an under-resourced ministry, they changed very little.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The political scientist Kenji Ishikawa has raised a more troubling possibility: that people who clear forest learn to evade the systems designed to catch them. He cites cases in which clearing has been timed to coincide with the cloudy season, or carried out in small increments, each just below the size that would trigger an alert. Monitoring, in his account, becomes an arms race in which every improvement provokes a new form of evasion. Ishikawa's concern deserves to be taken seriously, but it is hardly an argument for abandoning alerts. If anything, it is a case for continual investment in the technology, since clearing that is forced into smaller and slower increments is already clearing that has been reduced.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most promising results have come from combining satellites with people on the ground. Researchers led by Lucía Ballester worked with indigenous communities in the western Amazon, supplying patrols with smartphones that received alerts for their territory, along with small payments for verifying each alert on foot. In the first year, participating communities lost roughly half as much forest as similar communities without the scheme. In the second year, after the payments ended, the difference faded. Ballester nevertheless regards local verification as indispensable, because a satellite can show that trees have disappeared but cannot reveal whether their removal was authorised.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That final point is easily overlooked. An alert identifies change; it says nothing about legality. In many countries, clearing is permitted on part of every property, and the records showing who holds a licence to clear where are incomplete, scattered across agencies or treated as confidential. Without them, even a perfectly accurate alert cannot distinguish a farmer acting within the law from a land-grabber acting outside it. The next major gains in forest protection are therefore likely to come not from better satellites but from making permit information public, a reform that requires no new technology at all, only political will.

topic: the Amazon dieback hypothesis: deforestation, drought and fire pushing rainforest towards a degraded state
title: A Forest on the Brink?
subtitle: Scientists disagree about whether the Amazon could suddenly collapse, but perhaps that is not the most important question

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 2000s, a handful of computer simulations produced a startling result: by the end of the century, large parts of the Amazon rainforest might give way to open, savanna-like vegetation. The reasoning behind this prediction rests on a feature that sets the Amazon apart from most other forests. A substantial share of the rain that falls on the basin has already passed through trees, drawn up from the soil by their roots and released through their leaves before condensing again into cloud. The forest, in other words, helps to make its own weather. If enough of it is cleared, rainfall declines, the dry season lengthens, fires spread more easily, and the remaining forest may eventually be unable to sustain itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The obvious question is how much clearing would be enough. Professor Elena Soberanis, a climate modeller at the Institute for Tropical Climate Dynamics, has spent a decade trying to answer it. Her simulations suggest that, when the effects of global warming are combined with those of deforestation, the southern and eastern parts of the basin could cross a critical threshold once around a fifth to a quarter of the original forest has been lost. Roughly seventeen per cent has already disappeared. Soberanis also points to observations showing that the dry season in the southern Amazon is now several weeks longer than it was in the 1980s, a change she interprets as an early warning that the system is losing stability.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are persuaded that the forest is so fragile. The plant physiologist Dimitris Hatzidakis argues that the models underestimate the capacity of trees to withstand drought. Many Amazonian species have roots reaching many metres underground, allowing them to draw on deep reserves of water, and higher concentrations of carbon dioxide may allow leaves to lose less water for each unit of growth. In a long-running experiment, Hatzidakis and his colleagues installed plastic panels beneath the canopy of a forest plot to divert roughly half of the rainfall away from the soil. For several years the trees coped remarkably well. Only after about seven years did large trees begin to die in significant numbers. Hatzidakis interprets this as evidence of slow decline rather than sudden collapse. The distinction is a real one, but it is arguably of more interest to modellers than to the forest itself: whether the loss takes a decade or half a century, the trees are lost all the same.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Fire is the element that links drought to lasting damage. Unlike the trees of fire-prone savannas, most rainforest species have thin bark and have never needed to survive regular burning, so even a slow-moving fire at ground level can kill a large proportion of them. Worse, a forest that has burned once is more likely to burn again, because dead wood and fallen leaves accumulate on the ground and the opened canopy allows the understorey to dry out. After three or four fires, what was once tall forest may be reduced to a tangle of grasses, vines and scattered surviving trees. The fire ecologist Joseph Kiprotich objects to describing such places as savanna at all. Genuine savannas, he notes, are rich in plant and animal species that have evolved alongside fire over millions of years; burned Amazonian forest has neither that diversity nor those adaptations. To call it savanna, in his view, gives a misleadingly reassuring impression of what is being created.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The risk is not distributed evenly. The western Amazon, close to the Andes, receives heavy rainfall throughout much of the year and appears considerably less vulnerable than the south-east, where the dry season is already long and the agricultural frontier is advancing fastest. Yet the hydrologist Amélie Laurentin warns against treating these regions as independent. Moisture blown in from the Atlantic, she explains, is recycled repeatedly as it moves westward, falling as rain and evaporating again from the forest several times over. Rainfall in the west therefore depends partly on the survival of forest in the east, and losses at one end of the basin could be felt at the other. Her work makes a strong case for managing the basin as a single system rather than as a collection of national territories.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How the tipping-point idea should be used in public debate is itself contested. Some campaigners welcome it because it conveys urgency in a way that gradual decline does not. Others fear it may encourage fatalism if people come to believe the threshold has already been passed. A further danger is less often discussed. Talk of a single critical point implies that deforestation below that level is harmless, and this is simply not the case. Every hectare cleared reduces rainfall recycling, increases the area exposed to fire and weakens the forest's capacity to recover from drought.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is, moreover, some room for optimism. Because the forest's resilience depends partly on human choices, it can be strengthened as well as weakened. Allowing degraded land to regrow, preventing the use of fire to clear pasture and protecting the remaining large blocks of forest would all push any threshold further away. The precise location of that threshold may never be known with confidence, and it does not need to be. The case for halting deforestation in the Amazon is overwhelming whether the forest is approaching a cliff edge or merely a long and damaging slope.
