topic: forests as sources of rainfall for distant regions: moisture recycling, the contested biotic pump theory and its governance implications
title: Rain Made Elsewhere
subtitle: Forests may supply the rainfall of places far beyond their borders, a possibility that raises awkward scientific and political questions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A grain farmer on the plains of a continental interior is unlikely to spend much time thinking about forests a thousand kilometres away. Yet a considerable part of the rain that waters such farms may have begun its journey as moisture released by trees far upwind. Atmospheric scientists now speak of a region's 'precipitationshed', the area of land and sea from which its rainfall is ultimately drawn, by analogy with the watershed that feeds a river. The idea has a significance that extends well beyond meteorology. If the rain falling in one place depends on forest standing in another, then clearing that forest ceases to be a purely local matter and becomes a concern for every community downwind, including those on the other side of a national border.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the evidence comes from moisture-tracking models, which follow parcels of water vapour backwards in time from the place where they eventually fall as rain. Using this technique, Dr Itziar Aranguren of the Iberian Atmospheric Research Centre has estimated that in several major farming regions of South America and Africa, more than a third of the rain that falls during the growing season evaporated from forest upwind. Her models also suggest that, over large forested areas, the same moisture may fall and evaporate again as many as five times as it travels across a continent. Such figures should be treated with caution. The models must estimate how much water forests release under different conditions, and when Aranguren compared her results with those of other groups, she found that estimates for the same region sometimes differed by a factor of two.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A far more radical claim has been advanced by a small group of physicists led by Pieter Duvenhage. According to their 'biotic pump' theory, forests do not merely recycle moisture but actively draw it inland. When water vapour released by trees condenses into cloud, the volume of gas in the air falls, lowering the atmospheric pressure above the forest and sucking in moist air from the ocean. Duvenhage points out that over unforested land, rainfall typically declines steadily with distance from the coast, whereas over large continuous forests it can remain high thousands of kilometres inland. If the theory is correct, the clearing of coastal forest could cut off the supply of rain to entire continental interiors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Most meteorologists remain sceptical. Hiroshi Takeuchi, who studies atmospheric circulation, accepts that condensation lowers air pressure but argues that the effect is small compared with the pressure differences produced by uneven heating of land and sea, which conventional models already represent well. Climate simulations that include the proposed mechanism, he notes, do not reproduce observed winds any more accurately than those that leave it out. The debate has not always been conducted calmly, and some of the hostility towards the theory appears to reflect the fact that its authors are outsiders to the discipline rather than any careful assessment of their arguments. That said, a proposal that would overturn a central assumption of atmospheric science requires correspondingly strong evidence, and so far that evidence has not been produced. The theory has not been disproved, but nor has it earned the confidence that some environmental campaigners already place in it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even without the biotic pump, conventional moisture recycling has substantial economic implications. The environmental economist Selin Yerlikaya has attempted to put a value on the rainfall that forests supply to downwind agriculture and to hydroelectric dams, whose output depends on the volume of water reaching their reservoirs. Her calculations suggest that, in some regions, a hectare of forest is worth more for the rain it helps to generate elsewhere than it would be as cleared farmland. The difficulty is that this value is invisible to the person who owns the forest. The farmers and power companies who benefit are often hundreds of kilometres away, and sometimes in another country, while the landowner who refrains from clearing receives nothing for the service.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Thandiwe Mbekwa, a specialist in international environmental law, has examined whether existing agreements could address this imbalance and concluded that they cannot. Treaties on shared water resources deal with rivers, lakes and aquifers; none covers water while it is still in the air. Mbekwa therefore proposes agreements between the countries that share a precipitationshed, modelled on the arrangements that already govern international river basins. In the present political climate, the prospect of governments accepting obligations to protect forests for the sake of their neighbours' rainfall seems remote. Her proposal is nonetheless worth developing, if only because many precipitationsheds lie largely within a single country, where national policy could act on the same principle without any treaty at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a certain irony in all of this. In several countries, agricultural organisations have been among the most powerful advocates of opening forest land to cultivation. If the research on moisture recycling is even approximately correct, the expansion they promote may be reducing the rainfall on which their own members depend. Forests, it seems, are not simply consumers of land that could otherwise be farmed; they may be part of the infrastructure that makes farming possible in the first place.

topic: timber forensics (wood anatomy, isotope and DNA tracing) in enforcing laws against illegal logging
title: Reading the Grain
subtitle: Scientists can increasingly tell where a plank of timber was grown, but whether the law can make use of that knowledge is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Estimates of the proportion of the world's timber trade that is harvested illegally vary widely, from around one tenth to well over a third, and the uncertainty itself reveals the nature of the problem. Once a tree has been felled, sawn and shipped, its origin becomes almost impossible to establish from paperwork alone. Permits can be forged, logs from protected reserves can be mixed with legally cut wood at a sawmill, and a single false declaration at a border may launder an entire consignment. Over the past two decades, several importing regions have passed laws requiring companies to show that their timber was harvested legally. Such legislation, however, is only as strong as the means of checking compliance, and for many years those means consisted largely of inspecting documents that were themselves the weakest link in the chain.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest forensic technique is also the simplest. Wood anatomists examine a cross-section of timber under magnification and identify it from the arrangement of its vessels, fibres and rays. Gulnara Ospanova, who trains customs officers at the Central Asian Institute of Wood Science, argues that this approach remains underrated. A skilled examiner with a hand lens, she points out, can often identify a sample at the port within minutes, at almost no cost. Its limitation is that anatomy usually reveals the genus rather than the species, and it says nothing at all about where a tree grew. Since many timber laws protect particular species only in particular countries, knowing that a plank is mahogany of some kind may not be enough to bring a prosecution.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To answer the question of origin, researchers have turned to chemistry and genetics. As a tree grows, it absorbs water and nutrients whose isotopic composition reflects local rainfall, geology and climate, and these signatures are locked into the wood. By comparing a sample with reference material collected from known locations, laboratories can estimate where it was harvested, sometimes to within a few hundred kilometres. DNA analysis offers a complementary approach: populations of the same species in different regions carry distinctive genetic markers, and in favourable cases a log can be matched not merely to a region but to an individual stump left in a forest. Mateo Cienfuegos, a geneticist at the Andean Timber Tracing Laboratory, describes the latter achievement as transformative, because it allows investigators to link timber seized in a foreign port directly to the scene of a crime.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These methods share a crucial dependence, however. A chemical or genetic signature means nothing unless it can be compared with reliable samples of known origin, and building such reference collections is slow, expensive and unglamorous work. Aru Tamaruk, who coordinates a sampling network across South-East Asia, estimates that adequate coverage for even the twenty most traded tropical species would require hundreds of thousands of verified samples, many from remote areas where collection is dangerous. At present, she notes, the databases are patchy: dense for a handful of commercially prominent species and almost empty for the rest. This, in my view, is the most serious obstacle facing timber forensics, and it is one that receives far less funding than the development of new laboratory techniques, which attract more attention from both journals and donors.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty arises in the courtroom. Scientific evidence of origin is probabilistic: an isotope test may indicate that a sample is far more likely to have come from one region than another, but it rarely excludes all alternatives. Defence lawyers have been quick to exploit this. Renata Paixão, a legal scholar who has studied timber prosecutions in several jurisdictions, found that judges unfamiliar with statistical reasoning often treated any residual uncertainty as reasonable doubt. Paixão nonetheless rejects the view that forensic science has failed the law. In her analysis, the principal value of these techniques lies less in securing convictions than in deterring fraud, since companies that know their declarations can be tested are less inclined to falsify them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Paixão's argument is attractive, and there is some evidence to support it: following the introduction of routine random testing at certain European ports, the proportion of consignments with false declarations of species appears to have fallen. Yet deterrence depends on the credibility of the threat, and that credibility is easily undermined if testing remains rare. If only a tiny fraction of shipments is ever examined, a rational trader may calculate that the risk is worth taking. It seems to me that the case for deterrence has been somewhat overstated by those who wish to justify modest testing budgets; a deterrent that is seldom applied is not much of a deterrent.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that forensic tools are unimportant. On the contrary, they have shifted the balance of power, however slightly, away from those who rely on paperwork that nobody can check. But technology alone cannot compensate for weak governance in producer countries, where the same officials who issue permits may profit from illegal harvests. The most promising future probably lies in combining laboratory methods with satellite monitoring of logging roads and with stronger legal protections for the forest communities who are often the first to witness illegal felling. Science can tell us where a piece of wood came from; whether anyone acts on that knowledge remains a political choice.

topic: the forest transition theory: why some countries regain forest cover as they develop, and the displacement critique
title: After the Clearing
subtitle: Many nations have watched their forests shrink and then return. Is this a pattern the rest of the world can count on?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early nineteenth century, barely a seventh of France was covered by woodland. Today the figure is close to a third, and similar recoveries have been documented in Switzerland, Denmark, parts of the north-eastern United States and, more recently, in several countries in East Asia. Geographers refer to this sequence of decline followed by recovery as the forest transition, and the idea has become one of the most influential in the study of land use. It is easy to see why: it offers an optimistic narrative in which deforestation is a temporary stage rather than a permanent loss. Yet a description of what happened in some places is not a law of what must happen everywhere, and treating it as one carries real dangers.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-known explanation for the transition emphasises economic change. Valtteri Koskimies, an environmental historian at the Northern Institute for Landscape Studies, argues that industrialisation drew rural labour into the cities, leaving remote and unprofitable farms without the workers needed to maintain them. At the same time, improvements in agriculture meant that fertile valleys could produce far more food than before, so the steep and stony hillsides that had been cultivated out of necessity were no longer required. On abandoned land, trees returned of their own accord. In Koskimies's account, the recovery of Europe's forests was largely an unplanned by-product of prosperity.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Danica Brezovar, who studies forest policy at the Adriatic Centre for Environmental Governance, offers a rather different story. In her view, recovery frequently began not when societies became rich but when the consequences of losing their forests became intolerable. Shortages of timber and firewood drove up prices, while bare slopes suffered erosion and downstream towns were repeatedly inundated. In several alpine regions, she notes, strict controls on grazing and large planting programmes were introduced only after catastrophic floods had destroyed bridges and villages. Brezovar sees the same logic in the vigorous reforestation campaigns undertaken by some Asian governments in the second half of the twentieth century. Both pathways, it seems to me, have genuinely operated, and the evidence does not allow one to be dismissed in favour of the other. The distinction nevertheless matters, because the first implies that forests will look after themselves once growth arrives, whereas the second implies that recovery requires deliberate intervention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more troubling challenge has come from Marco Ferraiuolo, a land-use scientist who has traced the flows of timber and agricultural products between countries. His central claim is that many nations which have regained forest have done so partly by importing from elsewhere the wood, food and animal feed that their own land once supplied. When the clearance associated with those imports is taken into account, Ferraiuolo calculates, a substantial share of the apparent gain disappears; in one case he examined, it exceeded half. This is, to my mind, the most uncomfortable finding in the entire debate, since it suggests that a transition celebrated at the national level may conceal continued, or even accelerated, loss at the global one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The ecologist Aminata Bassolé raises a further objection, concerning what is actually being counted. Official statistics generally record any land with a certain density of tree cover as forest, regardless of its character. As a result, a rich, mixed woodland and a plantation of a single fast-growing species may appear identical in national inventories. Bassolé argues that much of the recent increase in forest area reported by several countries consists of precisely such plantations, which support only a fraction of the wildlife found in natural forest, and she calls for the two to be subject to separate reporting. Her criticism is well founded, although it can be pushed too far. Plantations, managed responsibly, can supply timber that would otherwise be extracted from natural forests, and in that sense they may protect the very ecosystems with which they are unfavourably compared.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practical stakes become clear when the theory is applied to the tropics. Some development economists have implied that countries now clearing their rainforests will eventually follow the European path, so that deforestation can be regarded as a regrettable but passing phase. This conclusion seems to me deeply mistaken. Tropical forests contain a large proportion of the world's terrestrial species, many of which have extremely restricted ranges, and a species lost during a period of clearance does not return when the trees do. Moreover, the mechanism Koskimies describes depended on demand for food being met by more productive land within the same country. In a globalised market, farmland abandoned in one region can simply be replaced by new clearance in another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Nor is it clear when recovery should be expected. A review of historical land-use records compiled by the Land Change Observatory found that the lowest level of forest cover reached before recovery began varied enormously between countries, from under a tenth of their territory to more than half. No single threshold, in other words, marks the point at which decline gives way to regrowth. The authors concluded that the transition is better used to interpret the past than to forecast the future.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the forest transition is a myth. The recoveries in Europe and elsewhere are real, and they demonstrate that the loss of forest is not inevitably permanent. But the conditions that produced them were specific, and some of them cannot be repeated in a world where trade links distant landscapes. If tropical countries are to experience a transition, it is likely to be one that is deliberately brought about, and brought about far sooner, than those of the past.

topic: shifting cultivation (swidden farming): whether rotational slash-and-burn agriculture is a cause of deforestation or a sustainable land use
title: Fire and Fallow
subtitle: Shifting cultivation has long been blamed for the destruction of tropical forests. A closer look suggests the charge is too simple

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, few farming practices had a worse reputation than shifting cultivation. In its classic form, a household cuts down the vegetation on a small patch of forest, burns it, grows crops for two or three years and then moves on, leaving the plot to regrow before returning to it a decade or more later. Colonial foresters regarded the system as wasteful and primitive, and the governments that succeeded them frequently shared that view. Officials also complained that smoke from burning fields damaged valuable timber and endangered nearby settlements. Across South-East Asia, Africa and Latin America, programmes were launched to persuade or compel shifting cultivators to adopt permanent farms in fixed locations. Looking back, it is hard to avoid the conclusion that these judgements rested less on careful observation than on a prejudice against people who lived on the margins of the state and whose way of life was difficult to tax or administer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Research over the past few decades has painted a more nuanced picture. The burning of cleared vegetation releases a pulse of nutrients, as the ash enriches otherwise poor tropical soils, and during the long fallow that follows, regrowing trees draw minerals up from deeper layers and rebuild the organic matter in the topsoil. Souksavanh Keomany, an agronomist at the Mekong Upland Research Station, has spent years measuring carbon and biodiversity in highland villages where fallows of twelve to fifteen years are still common. Her surveys show that older fallows support a surprising variety of birds, insects and useful plants, and that, averaged over the full cycle, a landscape farmed in this way holds considerably more carbon than one converted to permanent fields or plantations. Keomany is careful, however, to stress that these benefits depend entirely on the length of the fallow. Where the land is cultivated again after only three or four years, the forest has no time to recover, and the system begins to unravel.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That is precisely what has happened in many regions. As populations have grown and large areas have been allocated to commercial plantations, mining concessions and protected reserves, shifting cultivators have been squeezed into smaller and smaller territories. With less land available, they have had little choice but to return to each plot sooner, and the shortened fallows have led to declining yields, invasive grasses and eroded slopes. Ingeborg Rønnestad, a geographer at the Nordic Centre for Development Geography, argues that much of the degradation attributed to shifting cultivation is therefore a product of the very restrictions placed upon it. Her argument is, in my view, largely correct, and it exposes an uncomfortable irony: policies intended to protect forests from farmers have often created the conditions that make farming destructive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that shifting cultivation has been unfairly maligned. A remote-sensing team led by Ilmari Vuorela has used decades of satellite imagery to identify the causes of forest disturbance across the tropics, and its findings indicate that small-scale clearance for cropping accounts for a large share of disturbance in parts of central Africa. Vuorela insists, however, that the figures must be interpreted carefully. Rotational systems, in which farmers return to the same plots, are quite different from pioneer clearance, in which migrants push into old-growth forest that has never been farmed. In most statistics the two are lumped together. A family returning to a plot it last cleared fifteen years ago and a newcomer felling ancient trees for the first time are thus recorded in exactly the same way. This distinction is, I believe, the key to the whole controversy, since the first can be broadly sustainable while the second results in a net loss of primary forest.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What happens when shifting cultivation is abandoned also deserves attention. In several countries, bans on burning have pushed farmers towards permanent cash crops such as maize, cassava or rubber, grown year after year on the same land with chemical fertilisers. Studies suggest that this transition has frequently resulted in more lasting forest loss, not less. The anthropologist Wilka Condorcanqui, who has worked with communities in the western Amazon, points to another cost: the erosion of detailed knowledge about forest plants, soils and the signs that tell a farmer when a fallow is ready to be cleared again. It would nonetheless be a mistake to romanticise the practice. Swidden farming involves heavy physical labour and uncertain harvests, and many young people in upland villages would rather earn a cash income than continue it. Not every community, in short, wishes to preserve the system its grandparents used.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The lesson for policy is not that shifting cultivation should be promoted everywhere, but that it should be judged by its outcomes rather than its appearance. A plot that is cleared, burned and abandoned to regrow may look alarming from the air, yet it can be far less harmful than a neat plantation that never returns to forest. Where fallows remain long, the practice may be among the less damaging ways of producing food in tropical forests. The most effective support governments could offer is probably secure rights to land, since farmers who are confident that their fallows will not be taken from them have every reason to let those fallows grow old.

topic: no-till farming: erosion control, yield penalties and disputed soil carbon gains
title: Leaving the Plough in the Shed
subtitle: No-till farming promises healthier soils, but its record on harvests and carbon is more contested than its advocates admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly ten thousand years, turning the soil has been almost synonymous with farming. The plough buries weeds, mixes crop residues and manure into the ground, and leaves a loose seedbed into which seeds can easily be sown. Yet over the past half-century a growing number of farmers have abandoned it. In no-till systems, the stubble of the previous crop is left on the surface and seed is placed directly into undisturbed ground by specialised drills that cut a narrow slot. The practice now covers well over a hundred million hectares worldwide, concentrated in the Americas and Australia. To its supporters it amounts to nothing less than a revolution; to its critics it is a useful technique that has been oversold. Both camps, arguably, have treated a question that depends heavily on local conditions as though it had a single answer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The original case for abandoning the plough was erosion. Bare, freshly tilled fields are exposed to wind and rain, and the dust storms that devastated parts of North America in the 1930s left a lasting impression on agricultural scientists. A surface mulch of residues shields the soil from the impact of raindrops, slows run-off and allows water to soak in rather than carry topsoil away. On this point, the evidence is about as strong as agronomy ever produces. Facundo Poblete, who has studied farms in the Argentine pampas for over two decades, reports that soil losses on long-term no-till fields there are frequently less than a tenth of those on comparable ploughed land. Poblete also emphasises a benefit that farmers themselves tend to mention first: fewer passes with heavy machinery mean substantial savings in fuel and labour.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty arises with yields. A large synthesis of field trials compiled by Wanjiru Kamotho and colleagues at the Equatorial Agronomy Institute found that, averaged across all sites, no-till produced slightly lower harvests than conventional cultivation, with the penalty most pronounced in the first few years after conversion. Crucially, however, the average concealed great variation. In dry climates, where the mulch conserves scarce moisture, no-till frequently matched or exceeded ploughed yields, whereas in cool, wet regions it often fell well short, partly because residue-covered soils warm slowly in spring and seeds germinate late. Kamotho concludes that the technique should be targeted at the environments where it performs best rather than promoted universally. This is the most sensible reading of the data, although it sits uncomfortably with campaigns that present no-till as a solution for every farm.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Weeds pose a further challenge. Without the plough to bury them, farmers have relied heavily on herbicides, and the spread of herbicide-resistant weeds in several no-till regions has forced some to return to occasional cultivation. Advocates respond that this is a problem of poor management rather than of the system itself, and that cover crops and diverse rotations can suppress weeds without chemicals. That may be true in principle, but it is hardly a minor qualification: a system that functions well only when accompanied by a sophisticated set of additional practices is considerably more demanding than its simple name implies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most heated dispute, however, concerns carbon. For years no-till was promoted as a means of drawing carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and storing it in the soil, and some carbon-offset schemes still reward farmers for adopting it. Sigrun Hallvardsdottir, a soil chemist at the Northern Institute for Land Research, has challenged this claim. Most early studies, she points out, sampled only the top twenty or thirty centimetres of soil. When her team sampled to a depth of one metre, they found that no-till had largely redistributed carbon rather than increased it: more was concentrated near the surface, but less was found lower down, where ploughing would previously have buried residues. Her findings do not show that no-till has no climate benefit, but they do suggest that the figures used by offset markets may be considerably inflated.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this interpretation. A group of researchers at the Prairie Soil Consortium argues that deep sampling introduces errors of its own, since carbon concentrations at depth are low and highly variable, making small differences difficult to detect. They maintain that the surface gains are real and that soil structure improves in ways that carbon measurements alone fail to capture, notably through larger populations of earthworms and more stable aggregates of soil particles. Both arguments have merit, but the burden of proof should rest with those selling carbon credits, not with those questioning them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be concluded? No-till is neither the miracle its champions describe nor the failure some critics suggest. Its benefits for erosion control and farm costs are well established; its effects on yields depend on climate; and its contribution to climate mitigation remains uncertain. Rather than asking whether no-till is good or bad, researchers and policymakers would do better to ask where, and in combination with which other practices, it makes sense. That is a less inspiring message than the one that has often accompanied the technique, but it is a more honest one.

topic: biochar as a soil amendment and a method of carbon removal
title: Charcoal in the Furrow
subtitle: Biochar has been hailed as a way to enrich soils and lock away carbon for centuries; the evidence points to a more modest role

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When organic material such as wood chips, crop husks or manure is heated in the near absence of oxygen, it does not burn away but is converted into a porous, carbon-rich solid. Spread on fields, this substance, known as biochar, has attracted extraordinary claims over the past two decades. It has been described as a substitute for fertiliser, a remedy for degraded land and, most ambitiously, a means of removing carbon from the atmosphere on a scale large enough to matter for the climate. Few agricultural products have been asked to do so much. That alone ought to make observers cautious, for materials promoted as solutions to several unrelated problems at once rarely live up to all of them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The appeal rests on chemistry. Because the carbon in biochar is arranged in stable, ring-like structures, soil microbes find it difficult to break down. Whereas a crop residue ploughed into the ground may return most of its carbon to the air within a few years, a large fraction of the carbon in biochar can persist for centuries. Its vast internal surface area, meanwhile, can hold water and nutrients and provide shelter for microorganisms. In principle, therefore, a single application could improve the soil while also storing carbon that plants originally drew from the air.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Field results, however, have been strikingly uneven. Tomas Ossandon, an agronomist at the Andean Institute of Soil Studies, has compiled data from several hundred trials. He finds that the most dramatic yield increases occur on acidic, nutrient-poor tropical soils, where the alkaline nature of biochar counteracts acidity much as agricultural lime does. On the fertile, near-neutral soils of temperate farmland, by contrast, effects on yields are typically small and occasionally negative. Ossandon concludes that biochar is best understood not as a universal soil improver but as a specialised treatment for particular problems. It is a reasonable conclusion, though one that greatly narrows the market that early enthusiasts imagined.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The climate case faces difficulties of its own. Mwila Bwalya, who studies carbon accounting at the Southern African Climate Policy Unit, argues that the benefits of biochar depend almost entirely on what would otherwise have happened to the raw material. If crop wastes that would have been burnt in open fields are converted instead, the gain is substantial. If, on the other hand, forests are cut to supply feedstock, or the residues would have been returned to the soil anyway, the net effect may be negligible or even harmful. Bwalya also notes that the heating process itself consumes energy unless the gases it releases are captured and used, as they are in well-designed modern kilns but rarely in traditional pits. These caveats are often absent from promotional literature, which tends to report the carbon content of the char as though all of it represented a pure gain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of permanence. Laboratory incubations, which typically last a few years at most, are used to predict how long biochar carbon will persist over centuries. Aino Vaisanen, a soil physicist at the Boreal Centre for Environmental Science, regards this as a considerable leap. Her experiments suggest that the stability of biochar varies widely with the temperature at which it is produced: material made at high temperatures is far more resistant to decay than that made at lower temperatures, which may lose a significant share of its carbon within decades. Since buyers of carbon credits are paying for storage that lasts, she argues, credits should be linked to production conditions rather than awarded at a flat rate per tonne. This proposal is both sensible and overdue.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters of biochar respond that such objections apply to almost every method of carbon removal, and that biochar at least has the advantage of producing something useful. A consortium of producers known as the Lowland Carbon Initiative claims that improved water retention alone justifies its use in drought-prone areas, and points to farms where irrigation needs have fallen after application. The evidence for this is suggestive rather than conclusive, since few of the farms in question have been compared with untreated controls. Yet it would be a mistake to dismiss the claim entirely: if the agricultural value of biochar can be confirmed even in limited settings, the economics of producing it would look considerably more attractive.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Scale presents the final obstacle. Estimates of the potential of biochar to remove carbon dioxide frequently assume that vast quantities of residues could be collected, transported and processed. In practice, residues are scattered, bulky and often already used for animal bedding, fuel or soil cover. Collection costs rise steeply with distance from a kiln, and small farmers in particular may lack the capital to take part. None of this means that biochar has no future. It means that its future is likely to be local and specialised: a useful tool on acidic soils, a sensible use for wastes that would otherwise be burnt, and a modest contribution to carbon removal rather than a cornerstone of it.

topic: soil salinisation caused by irrigation in dry regions and competing remedies
title: The Salt Beneath the Harvest
subtitle: Irrigation turned deserts into farmland; now the salt it brings is quietly taking that land back

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some of the earliest written records of farming come from southern Mesopotamia, and among the most intriguing features of these documents is a gradual change in the crops they describe. Over several centuries, wheat appears less and less often, while barley, which tolerates salty soil far better, becomes dominant. Many historians have interpreted this as evidence that irrigation slowly poisoned the land on which the first cities depended. The story is often told as a warning about civilisations that destroy their own foundations, but such tidy morality tales deserve some suspicion. The shift in crops could equally reflect changes in taste, trade or taxation, and the documentary evidence is too fragmentary to settle the matter. What is not in doubt is that the underlying process is real, and that it is happening today on a far larger scale.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanism is straightforward. All irrigation water contains dissolved salts, even when it tastes fresh. When water is applied to fields in hot, dry climates, much of it evaporates or is taken up by plants and released through their leaves, leaving the salts behind. Over the years, these accumulate in the root zone. A second route is less obvious. Where irrigation raises the water table, groundwater that is often naturally salty can rise to within a metre or two of the surface; capillary action then draws it upward, and as it evaporates it deposits a white crust on the ground. Estimates vary, but a substantial share of the world's irrigated land is thought to be affected to some degree, with yields reduced long before the salt becomes visible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Hemant Ranjitkar, a soil scientist who has worked on irrigation schemes across South Asia, believes that the scale of the problem has been consistently underestimated because most monitoring relies on visible symptoms. By the time a crust appears, he argues, yields may already have fallen by a third. Ranjitkar has championed the use of electromagnetic sensors that can map salinity across entire fields in a single day, and he maintains that such mapping should be a routine part of managing any large irrigation scheme. His case is convincing, although sensors alone do nothing to remove the salt; they simply reveal the extent of a problem that still requires a remedy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The conventional remedy is leaching: applying more water than crops need, so that the excess flushes salts below the root zone. Leaching works, but only if the water can drain away. Where drainage is poor, extra water merely raises the water table further and makes matters worse. Engineers have therefore installed networks of buried pipes and open ditches to carry salty water off the land. Askar Zhunusov, a hydrologist at the Steppe Water Institute, points out that this simply moves the problem elsewhere. Drainage water must go somewhere, and in many basins it ends up in rivers or lakes, raising their salinity for users downstream. In his view, no drainage project should be approved without a clear plan for where its salt will finally end up.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different school of thought, represented by the plant geneticist Ottavia Morandi, holds that agriculture must learn to live with some salt rather than fight it everywhere. Morandi's group has screened thousands of varieties of wheat, barley and rice for their ability to grow in saline conditions, and has identified genes that allow some plants to exclude salt from their leaves. She also points to halophytes, plants that naturally thrive in salty environments, some of which produce edible seeds or useful fodder. Critics object that salt-tolerant crops treat the symptoms rather than the cause and may encourage farmers to keep irrigating unsustainably. That objection has some force, but it overlooks the fact that much salinised land cannot realistically be reclaimed at any acceptable cost.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most instructive experience comes from basins where authorities have tried to coordinate action across many farms. In one large river basin, a regional body, the Lower Plains Water Commission, introduced a system in which every new irrigation development had to be offset by measures that reduced the salt entering the river elsewhere, such as pumping saline groundwater into evaporation basins. Salinity in the river fell measurably over the following two decades. Yet the scheme depended on strong institutions, reliable data and the willingness of farmers to accept restrictions, conditions that are absent in many of the regions where salinisation is advancing fastest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson, then, is less about technology than about time. Salinisation is slow, and its costs fall largely on future farmers, while the benefits of irrigation are immediate. Every remedy, whether drainage, leaching, breeding or regulation, demands investment today to prevent losses that may not become apparent for decades. Societies have rarely been good at making such trade-offs. Still, it would be wrong to conclude that the outcome is inevitable: the experience of well-managed basins shows that the advance of salt can be slowed, provided that the problem is recognised before the crust appears.

topic: invasive earthworms in previously glaciated northern forests of North America
title: The Unwelcome Gardeners
subtitle: Earthworms are celebrated as friends of the farmer, but in the forests of northern North America they are reshaping ecosystems that evolved without them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few animals enjoy a reputation as benign as that of the earthworm. Gardeners welcome them, farmers regard a spadeful of soil teeming with worms as a sign of good health, and nineteenth-century naturalists praised their role in burying stones and turning over the land. By pulling dead leaves into their burrows and passing soil through their guts, earthworms mix organic matter into the ground, create channels through which water and air can move, and release nutrients in forms that plants can use. On farmland, these services are real and valuable. It is precisely because the reputation is so well deserved in fields and gardens, however, that the behaviour of worms in other settings has been so slow to attract concern.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: During the last ice age, glaciers covered much of what is now Canada and the northern United States, and scientists generally believe that any native earthworms in these areas were wiped out. When the ice retreated around twelve thousand years ago, forests re-established themselves without them, and worms from unglaciated areas further south spread back only very slowly, perhaps a few metres per year. For millennia, the forest floor in these regions was covered by a thick, spongy layer of decomposing leaves, known as the duff, which fungi and insects broke down gradually. Then, from the seventeenth century onwards, European settlers arrived, bringing soil, potted plants and livestock that carried European earthworm species with them. In the twentieth century, anglers discarding unused bait at the edges of lakes added a further route of introduction.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The consequences were first documented systematically by Freya Lindblom, a forest ecologist then working with a long-term research programme in the Great Lakes region. Lindblom compared plots where worms had arrived with neighbouring plots they had not yet reached. In invaded areas, the duff layer, sometimes ten centimetres deep, had disappeared within a few years, leaving bare mineral soil. Several species of wildflower and many tree seedlings, which depend on the duff for germination and moisture, had declined sharply, and the ground-nesting birds and salamanders that sheltered in the leaf litter were also less abundant. Lindblom describes the arrival of the worms as a slow-motion invasion whose effects are easy to miss, because the animals responsible spend almost their entire lives out of sight.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe the story is more complicated. Oleksandr Kovalchuk, a soil biologist at the Institute of Temperate Ecology, points out that the effects vary greatly with the species involved. Some European worms live mainly in the leaf litter, others burrow deeply, and a third group feeds within the mineral soil; only certain combinations produce the dramatic loss of the duff layer. Kovalchuk also notes that some plants appear to benefit from the changes, particularly grasses and sedges. In his opinion, describing invaded forests simply as damaged ignores the fact that they are becoming different ecosystems rather than impoverished ones. This argument has some merit, but it should not be allowed to obscure the losses: a forest in which native wildflowers are replaced by a few hardy grasses is different in a way that most ecologists would regard as worse.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more recent development has added urgency to the debate. Since the early 2000s, several Asian species, often called jumping worms because of their violent thrashing when handled, have spread rapidly through parts of the United States. They reproduce without mating, mature within a single season and turn the topsoil into a loose, granular material resembling coffee grounds, which washes away easily in heavy rain. Tavita Fonoti, who leads a monitoring network of volunteers, reports that the species are now found in many states, transported largely in mulch, compost and nursery plants. Unlike the European species, which spread at a few metres a year on their own, jumping worms can travel hundreds of kilometres in a single delivery of garden products.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of carbon. Because northern forest soils store large quantities of carbon, some scientists feared that worms would release much of it into the atmosphere by speeding up decomposition. Field studies have produced mixed results. Worms certainly accelerate the breakdown of the duff, but they also mix carbon into the mineral soil, where some of it becomes bound to clay particles and is protected from further decay. Whether invaded forests store more or less carbon overall appears to depend on soil type, and no consensus has yet emerged.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Eradicating earthworms from a forest is effectively impossible, so management focuses on slowing their spread. Measures include advising anglers to dispose of bait in rubbish bins rather than on the ground, encouraging heat treatment of compost and mulch before sale, and washing soil from vehicles, tyres and boots. These steps are modest, and it is tempting to regard them as futile given how widespread the worms already are. That conclusion would be premature. Large areas of northern forest remain uninvaded, and because natural spread is so slow, preventing a single introduction may protect a site for centuries. Prevention, in this case, is not merely better than cure; it is the only option available.

topic: cover crops and the reasons for their slow adoption by farmers
title: Fields That Never Lie Bare
subtitle: Cover crops are among the most widely recommended conservation practices, yet most farmers still do not plant them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In much of the world's grain belt, fields lie bare for months between one harvest and the next sowing. During that time, rain and wind strip away topsoil, and nitrogen left over from fertiliser washes out into streams and groundwater. The solution most frequently recommended by agronomists is disarmingly simple: plant something else in the gap. Cover crops, such as rye, clover, vetch or radish, are not grown to be sold but to protect and enrich the soil until the main crop returns. Government agencies promote them, environmental groups praise them and research papers on their benefits number in the thousands. Yet in some of the most intensively farmed regions, they are grown on less than a tenth of cropland. This gap between recommendation and practice is the real puzzle, and it deserves more attention than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The benefits themselves are not seriously disputed. A living cover holds soil in place, and its roots create channels that improve the infiltration of water. Legumes such as clover and vetch host bacteria in their roots that capture nitrogen from the air, reducing the need for synthetic fertiliser in the following season. Grasses such as rye are particularly effective at absorbing nitrogen that would otherwise be lost; in some catchments, widespread planting has measurably reduced nitrate concentrations in drinking water supplies. Over time, the extra roots and residues add organic matter to the soil, although this process is slow and may take a decade or more to become detectable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, are farmers reluctant? Marguerite Thibodeaux, an agricultural economist at the Midcontinent Farm Policy Centre, argues that the answer is largely financial. Seed and planting cost money now, while the benefits accrue gradually and often to people other than the farmer, such as residents downstream whose water is cleaner. In her surveys, many farmers who had tried cover crops abandoned them after two or three years, when yields of the main crop had not visibly improved. Thibodeaux contends that subsidies for the first several years are essential to carry farmers through this period. Her analysis is persuasive as far as it goes, but it treats farmers as purely financial decision-makers, which they are not.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Pernilla Holmqvist, a rural sociologist, has explored this other dimension. Through interviews with farming families, she found that attitudes towards cover crops were shaped as much by identity and reputation as by profit. A clean, bare field after harvest has long been regarded as a sign of a diligent farmer, and some respondents admitted feeling uncomfortable with fields that neighbours might consider untidy. Holmqvist also found that farmers were far more likely to adopt the practice if someone they knew personally had done so successfully. Information from government leaflets, by comparison, had little influence. Her findings suggest that peer networks may achieve more than further payments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Practical difficulties also matter, and these are sometimes underestimated by those who promote the practice from a distance. In regions with short growing seasons, there may simply be too little time after harvest for a cover crop to establish itself before winter. In dry areas, cover crops can use water that the following cash crop needs, and in some trials yields of the main crop fell as a result. Rutendo Mapondera, who has studied smallholder farms in southern Africa, points out that livestock owners may graze cover crops, removing much of the benefit, and that seed for suitable species is often unavailable locally. In her view, recommendations developed on large, mechanised farms in temperate regions cannot simply be transferred to other settings.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not every obstacle is insurmountable, however. A farmer-led network known as the Groundcover Alliance has developed techniques for sowing cover crops into standing cash crops before harvest, extending the time available for establishment. Members also share equipment and buy seed collectively, reducing costs. The Alliance claims that its members achieve higher profits than neighbouring farms within five years. Such claims should be treated with care, since farmers who join a network of enthusiasts are likely to differ from those who do not; they may already be more skilled or better resourced. The real question, then, is not whether such groups help at all, but how much of their apparent success would survive a carefully controlled comparison.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is that the slow uptake of cover crops is not primarily a failure of knowledge. Farmers generally know what cover crops do; what they lack is a combination of financial support during the early years, practical methods suited to local conditions and a social environment in which the practice is regarded as normal. Policies that address only one of these are unlikely to succeed. Arguably, the most effective programmes will be those that pay farmers to experiment while also creating opportunities for them to learn from one another, so that the first successful adopters in a district can persuade the rest more effectively than any official ever could.

topic: phosphorus scarcity, phosphorus waste and nutrient recovery from wastewater
title: The Finite Nutrient
subtitle: Phosphorus has no substitute in farming. The real question may be not whether the world is running short, but why so much of it is wasted

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every living cell depends on phosphorus. It forms part of the backbone of DNA, and plants deprived of it grow stunted and yield poorly. Unlike nitrogen, which fertiliser factories can draw from the air, phosphorus cannot be manufactured; it must be dug from the ground, almost all of it from deposits of phosphate rock laid down on ancient sea floors. Yet for a substance of such importance, phosphorus has received remarkably little public attention, and when it has attracted notice, the discussion has tended to centre on whether the world is running out. That emphasis, it will be argued here, has distracted attention from a more immediate difficulty: not how much phosphorus remains, but how carelessly it is used.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea of 'peak phosphorus' gained prominence in the late 2000s, when the price of phosphate rock rose several-fold in little more than a year. Dr Henrike Daalgaard, a resource analyst at the Institute for Material Flows, was among those who drew a parallel with oil. Applying the same kind of model that had been used to forecast the peak of petroleum output, she projected that phosphate production would reach a maximum within a few decades and then decline, leaving farmers to compete for a dwindling resource. Her analysis was widely cited, and it lent the neglected subject of soil nutrients an unaccustomed urgency.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The forecast was soon challenged. Olumide Akinsete, an economic geologist at the Lagos School of Earth Resources, pointed out that estimates of global reserves had been revised sharply upwards after one of the largest producing countries reassessed its deposits, and that reserves are in any case a moving target, expanding whenever prices rise or extraction techniques improve. On his reckoning, the rock still in the ground could sustain current rates of use for several centuries. Akinsete is almost certainly correct about the geology, but his reassurance overlooks two important matters. First, the bulk of the remaining reserves lies within a small number of countries, which leaves importing nations exposed to export restrictions and political upheaval far more than to physical exhaustion. Second, the richest and cleanest ores have largely been worked, and much of what remains contains cadmium and other contaminants that must be removed at considerable expense if they are not to accumulate in farmland.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If supply is less precarious than once feared, waste is more serious than is generally acknowledged. Only a minority of the phosphorus extracted each year ends up in the food that people actually eat. Large quantities are washed from fields into rivers and lakes, where they feed the algal blooms that starve water of oxygen; more is lost in livestock manure, which tends to pile up in regions of intensive animal farming far from the arable land that could use it. Paradoxically, decades of generous application have left the soils of many wealthy farming regions with substantial reserves of their own. Yuval Shalgi, a soil chemist at the Negev Centre for Dryland Agriculture, has run field trials in which crops grown on such land without any added phosphorus produced undiminished yields for up to eight years. Shalgi is careful, however, to stress that his results cannot be extended to the heavily weathered soils of much of the tropics, which bind phosphorus so tightly that plants struggle to obtain it, and where farmers typically apply far too little rather than too much.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Attention has also turned to wastewater. In a growing number of treatment plants, phosphorus is recovered in the form of struvite, a crystalline mineral that can be sold as a slow-release fertiliser. Plant operators have their own reasons to welcome the technology, since struvite otherwise forms hard deposits that block pipes and pumps. Phosphorus can also be extracted from the ash left behind when sewage sludge is burned. The Baltic Nutrient Forum, an alliance of water utilities and municipal authorities, has campaigned for recovery to be made compulsory at all large treatment works, arguing that voluntary schemes will never attract the investment required. The Global Phosphate Producers' Association has questioned whether recovered products can match the consistency of conventional fertiliser, and surveys suggest that some farmers remain uneasy about spreading material derived from sewage on their fields.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Wastewater recovery is a worthwhile innovation, but its importance is frequently exaggerated. Human excreta accounts for only a modest share of the phosphorus moving through the food system, and even complete recovery from every treatment plant would leave the larger losses, from eroding fields and surplus manure, largely untouched. Greater gains are likely to come from less glamorous measures, such as matching fertiliser to the needs of each field and moving manure to arable regions. Daalgaard herself has since moderated her original position. She now concedes that the timing of her forecast was wrong, but maintains that the language of 'peak phosphorus' served a purpose by alerting policymakers to a neglected issue. That defence is not without merit, although alarming predictions that fail to come true can easily leave the public more sceptical of the next warning, however well founded it may be.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is that the phosphorus problem is essentially one of management rather than of geology. The fundamental weakness of the present system is that the element travels in a single direction, from mine to field to sea, with little of it ever returning to the land. A sustainable approach would treat phosphorus as something to be circulated rather than consumed, and it would also have to confront a striking inequality: while some soils are saturated with phosphorus accumulated over generations, others, often those farmed by the world's poorest households, are starved of it.

topic: soil compaction by heavy farm machinery and controlled traffic farming
title: The Weight of the Harvest
subtitle: As farm machines have grown heavier, the damage they cause beneath the surface has become harder to ignore

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the twentieth century, a typical tractor on a European or North American farm weighed around three tonnes. Today a fully loaded combine harvester can exceed thirty, and the grain trailers that accompany it at harvest are scarcely lighter. The reasons for this growth are not hard to find. Larger machines allow a single operator to cover far more ground in a day, which matters both because skilled farm labour has become scarce and expensive and because the periods when fields are dry enough to sow or harvest are often short. Yet the weight that makes these machines so productive is transmitted directly into the ground beneath them. Soil compaction, the squeezing together of soil particles under pressure, is arguably among the most underrated threats to agricultural land, and it is underrated largely because it happens out of sight.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Healthy soil is roughly half empty space: a network of pores through which water drains, air circulates and roots extend. Compaction collapses this network. Near the surface, the damage is partly reversible, since cultivation, the burrowing of earthworms and the expansion of freezing water all help to reopen the soil. Deeper down, recovery is far slower. Ingeborg Torvanger, a soil physicist at Halsvik Agricultural University, has found dense layers more than forty centimetres below the surface persisting for decades after heavy machines were driven across wet fields. Her measurements also indicate that the depth to which compaction penetrates is governed chiefly by the total load carried on each axle, whereas tyre pressure mainly affects the upper layers. The consequences of deep compaction include poor drainage, increased surface run-off and, under waterlogged conditions, higher emissions of nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Machinery manufacturers have responded with a range of technical fixes. Wider tyres inflated to lower pressures, and rubber tracks in place of wheels, spread a vehicle's weight over a larger area and undoubtedly reduce damage close to the surface. They are often marketed, however, as if they solved the problem altogether, and in the light of Torvanger's findings such claims seem overstated: a heavy machine on soft tyres still delivers its full load into the subsoil. Another option, deep ripping, uses steel tines dragged through the ground to shatter compacted layers. Farmers frequently report improved crop growth afterwards, but the loosened soil is structurally weak, and unless traffic is changed it tends to be re-compacted within a season or two, sometimes to a greater density than before.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical approach is to accept that compaction will occur, but to decide where. In controlled traffic farming, every machine on a farm is driven along the same permanent lanes year after year, leaving the land between them untouched by wheels. Aurelio Quintrileo, an agricultural engineer at the Litoral Institute of Farm Mechanisation, has followed several dozen farms through the transition. He reports that typically around four-fifths of each field ceases to be driven on, and that yields on the untrafficked strips tend to rise as the soil structure recovers. Fuel use also falls, since tractors travelling on firm, compacted lanes waste less energy than those sinking into loose ground. The system relies on satellite guidance precise to within a few centimetres, so that wheels follow exactly the same tracks on every pass.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the benefits are so evident, why has adoption remained modest? Thandiwe Mavundla, a farm economist at the Drakensvale Centre for Agricultural Policy, argues that the principal obstacle is not cost as such but incompatibility. Tractors, sprayers and harvesters made by different manufacturers come in different widths, and a functioning system requires all of them to share the same wheel spacing. Converting may therefore mean modifying or replacing much of a farm's fleet, and contractors who harvest for dozens of farms have little incentive to adapt their machines to the needs of one client. Where farmers have acted together, the picture changes. The Western Grains Cooperative persuaded its members to agree on a common set of machine widths, and it reports that the proportion of member farms using permanent lanes has risen steeply since the agreement was made.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Enthusiasts sometimes present controlled traffic as a solution for virtually every farm, and here a note of caution is needed. On small or irregularly shaped fields, permanent lanes are difficult to lay out efficiently, and crops such as potatoes and sugar beet are lifted by machines whose dimensions rarely match those used for cereals. Moreover, much of the evidence for yield gains comes from dry regions, where improved infiltration of scarce rainfall makes a large difference. In wetter climates the advantages appear to be smaller and less consistent, and they deserve more careful study before confident promises are made to farmers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, the problem of compaction is bound up with the economic forces that have made machines larger in the first place, and those forces show no sign of weakening. It is curious that public roads have long been protected by legal limits on axle loads, while the soil on which food production depends enjoys no comparable protection. Introducing such limits would be contentious and difficult to enforce, but the anomaly is at least worth debating, because damage done to the subsoil today may still be reducing harvests a generation from now.

topic: microplastics in agricultural soils from mulch film, sewage sludge and coated fertilisers
title: Hidden in the Furrows
subtitle: Plastic pollution is usually pictured at sea, but farmland may be quietly accumulating far more of it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When people picture plastic pollution, they tend to imagine beaches strewn with bottles or seabirds entangled in fishing line. Far less attention has been paid to farmland, yet a number of researchers now suspect that agricultural soils receive a larger quantity of microplastics each year than the world's oceans. The sources are varied. In much of East Asia and the Mediterranean, crops are grown beneath thin sheets of polyethylene known as mulch film, which retain moisture, suppress weeds and warm the soil in spring; after harvest, torn fragments are often left behind and ploughed in. Sewage sludge, spread on fields as a fertiliser in many countries, carries fibres shed when synthetic clothing is washed. Even some fertiliser granules are coated in polymers designed to release nutrients slowly. The comparison with the oceans is now widely repeated, but it rests on estimates so rough that it should be treated as a hypothesis rather than an established fact, although its general direction is probably correct.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence of accumulation comes from Haruki Nakabayashi, an environmental chemist at the Tottori Institute for Agro-Environmental Studies. Sampling fields in which mulch film had been used for periods ranging from five to thirty years, his team found that the concentration of plastic fragments rose steadily with the number of seasons the film had been laid. Nakabayashi attributes much of the problem to the thinness of the film itself. Sheets thinner than a hundredth of a millimetre are cheap, but they tear into small pieces that are almost impossible to gather. If manufacturers were required to produce thicker film, he argues, farmers could lift it intact at the end of each season and send it for recycling, as already happens in a few regions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What the plastic does once it is in the soil is far less clear. Leocadia Furtuna, a soil ecologist at the Bihor Institute of Soil Ecology, has carried out laboratory experiments suggesting that synthetic fibres loosen the clumps of particles that give soil its structure, increase the rate at which water evaporates, and affect the organisms that live there; in one study, earthworms kept in contaminated soil showed reduced growth over several weeks. Critics have pointed out, however, that experiments of this kind often use concentrations many times higher than those recorded in the field, and that they typically employ spherical beads of a single size rather than the ragged fragments and fibres found on real farms. Such objections are largely justified, and many of the more alarming headlines on the subject can be traced to studies with exactly these limitations. Furtuna accepts the point but replies that in the most heavily mulched fields, concentrations are already approaching the levels used in her experiments.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Underlying these disagreements is a more basic problem: there is still no agreed method for extracting and counting plastic particles in soil. Unlike seawater, soil is full of organic matter that resembles plastic under the microscope and interferes with chemical identification, and laboratories using different procedures can produce results that differ by orders of magnitude. The smallest particles, known as nanoplastics, are scarcely detectable at all, which is unfortunate, since these are the ones small enough to be taken up by plant roots. Until measurement is standardised, it will be impossible to say with confidence how much plastic farmland contains or whether it is increasing, and this, more than any shortage of experiments on worms, is the principal obstacle to progress.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Disagreement extends to remedies. Some environmental groups have called for a ban on spreading sewage sludge, but Ximena Chuquimia, an agronomist at the Altiplano University of Agricultural Sciences, considers this a mistake. Sludge returns organic matter and nutrients to the land that would otherwise have to be replaced by manufactured fertiliser, with its own environmental costs. Chuquimia proposes instead that fibres be stopped at their source, by requiring new washing machines to be fitted with filters. The proposal is sensible, but its effects would be gradual rather than immediate: the machines already in homes may remain in use for a decade or more, and the existing stock of synthetic garments will continue shedding fibres for years after any new rule takes effect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mulch film presents a different choice. Biodegradable films, made from polymers that microorganisms can break down, are increasingly promoted as a solution, but they cost between two and three times as much as conventional polyethylene. The Agricultural Plastics Recovery Network, which represents film suppliers and farmers' organisations, favours collecting and recycling conventional film instead, pointing to trials in which supposedly biodegradable products degraded fully only under warm, moist conditions and persisted for years in cool northern soils. The Network is hardly a disinterested party, but its point about cold soils is supported by independent research. The sensible conclusion is that neither approach will suffice on its own.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important difference between plastic in the sea and plastic in the soil is that the latter cannot be cleaned up. There is no practical way to sieve fragments from millions of hectares of farmland. That is why uncertainty about the scale of the harm should not be an excuse for delay. When a pollutant accumulates in a way that is effectively irreversible, the sensible response is to limit what goes into the soil now, rather than to wait for proof of damage that, once established, can no longer be undone.

topic: soil sealing: the loss of fertile farmland to urban expansion and planning responses
title: Concrete Over Clay
subtitle: Every year, cities spread across some of the world's most fertile soil. Can the loss be halted without halting growth?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Soil is formed with extraordinary slowness. Depending on climate and parent rock, a single centimetre of fertile topsoil can take several centuries to develop, as minerals weather and organic matter accumulates. It can be lost in an afternoon. When a field is covered by houses, roads or car parks, the soil beneath is sealed: rain can no longer soak into it, the organisms that inhabit it die, and it ceases to produce anything at all. Of all the forms of degradation that soil suffers, from erosion to salinisation, sealing is arguably the most permanent, since land that has been built on is very rarely returned to cultivation. It is therefore surprising how seldom the subject features in discussions of food security, which tend to concentrate on crop yields, water supplies and the effects of climate change.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The damage is compounded by geography. Towns and cities were overwhelmingly founded in fertile valleys, river plains and coastal lowlands, precisely because the surrounding soil could feed their inhabitants. As they expand outwards, they inevitably consume the very land that made their growth possible. Farida Baimukhanova, a soil scientist at the Irtysh Institute of Soil Science, has mapped the spread of more than twenty cities over half a century and found that in the great majority of cases new development took place on soils of above-average quality. As a result, she argues, figures that record only the area of land lost understate the decline in productive capacity. It is sometimes claimed that such losses are offset by bringing new land into cultivation elsewhere, but the replacement land is generally less fertile, and preparing it may require clearing forest or building costly irrigation schemes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Bérénice Courtemanche, a land-use geographer at the University of the Middle Loire, believes that the root of the problem lies in how planning systems view the ground. In most countries, proposals for new development are assessed for their impact on landscape, wildlife and traffic, but the quality of the soil to be built upon is rarely considered; land is treated as a surface rather than as a living resource. Courtemanche proposes that planners be obliged to consult detailed soil maps and to direct development towards poorer land wherever possible. The idea is a sensible one, but it is not without cost. The best soils frequently lie close to existing cities, where the demand for housing is greatest, so pushing construction elsewhere could lengthen journeys to work and spread settlements more thinly across the countryside.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Several European governments have adopted a more ambitious goal of 'no net land take', under which any newly sealed land must be balanced by restoring an equivalent area elsewhere. Imre Bakonyi, an urban economist at the Pannonian School of Economics, is sceptical of firm limits of this kind. Restricting the supply of building land, he argues, inevitably raises its price, and the burden falls most heavily on young and low-income households trying to find somewhere to live. He favours instead a charge on sealing, so that developers would pay for the soil they destroy and would have an incentive to build more compactly. The Federation of Housebuilders, for its part, rejects any additional restriction, insisting that land is in plentiful supply. That claim misses the point: what matters is not the quantity of land but the quality of soil, and the most fertile soil is anything but plentiful.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much of the pressure on farmland could be relieved by building upwards rather than outwards and by reusing brownfield sites, land previously occupied by factories, railway yards and other industrial activity. Such sites should be the first choice for new housing, but it would be naive to treat them as a cost-free alternative. Many are contaminated with heavy metals or chemical residues that are expensive to remove, and a number of abandoned sites have developed into valuable habitats for insects and birds, which conservationists understandably wish to protect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A newer idea is desealing, the removal of asphalt and concrete so that the ground beneath can function as soil once again. Several cities have replaced car parks and disused roads with gardens and planted areas, and the benefits are real: unsealed ground absorbs heavy rainfall, reducing the risk of flooding, while vegetation helps to lower summer temperatures in crowded districts. Baimukhanova warns, however, that desealed land seldom recovers its original fertility. The topsoil was usually stripped away during construction, and the layers beneath were compacted by heavy machinery, so what remains is better suited to recreation and drainage than to growing food. This has implications for policy. If restored urban land is counted as equivalent to the farmland lost to new building, targets such as 'no net land take' risk concealing a continuing decline in the land's capacity to feed people.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that cities should stop growing; populations rise and people need homes. The real question is where and how densely that growth takes place. Water, forests and minerals are all recognised in planning law as resources to be managed for future generations. Soil, which underpins most of the food that humanity consumes, deserves to be treated with the same seriousness, and its quality should be weighed explicitly whenever a decision is made to build.
