topic: breeding perennial grain crops and their potential to protect soil
title: Roots That Stay
subtitle: Grain crops that live for years rather than months could transform farming's relationship with the soil, provided they can be made productive enough

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every grain that feeds humanity comes from an annual plant. Wheat, rice, maize and barley complete their life cycle in a single season, so that each year the land must be prepared, sown and harvested afresh, and for weeks or months between crops it often lies bare, exposed to wind and rain. Natural grasslands work very differently. They are dominated by perennial species whose roots persist from one year to the next, binding the soil, drawing water from deep underground and capturing nutrients that would otherwise drain away. The notion of a grain crop that behaves like a prairie grass, regrowing after each harvest without being replanted, is frequently presented as a modern invention. In fact it is considerably older: plant breeders in several countries attempted to cross wheat with its perennial wild relatives in the middle of the twentieth century, before abandoning the effort as impractical.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why did the first farmers domesticate annuals in the first place? One explanation is that annual plants, which must reproduce within a single season, devote a large share of their energy to seed, the part that humans eat, whereas perennials divert much of theirs into roots and other structures that allow them to survive the winter. Anneliese Kropfitsch, an agronomist at the Styrian Agricultural Research Station, regards this as an unavoidable trade-off. In her view, a plant that invests heavily below ground can never match the grain output of one that does not, and perennial grains will therefore always yield less than their annual counterparts. Teodoro Villasanta, a plant breeder at the Cordillera Institute of Plant Breeding, rejects this conclusion. He points out that perennials begin growing earlier in spring and continue later into autumn, intercepting more sunlight over the course of a year, and argues that this longer growing period could in principle offset the resources they allocate to their roots.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Practical results so far lie somewhere between these positions. Intermediate wheatgrass, a wild relative of wheat, has been the subject of intensive breeding for some two decades. Its grain yield has increased several-fold over that period, yet it still produces only around a quarter as much as annual wheat grown in comparable conditions, and its small seeds are difficult to separate from their husks. Perennial rice has fared better: in trials in parts of East Asia it is reported to have yielded about as much as annual varieties for several consecutive harvests, although output declined after the fourth year and the fields then had to be replanted. These achievements demonstrate that progress is possible, but for wheatgrass, at least, the gap in yield remains far too wide for the great majority of farmers to contemplate switching.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The case for perennials rests largely on what happens beneath the surface. Kalinda Burrangong, a soil ecologist at the Riverina Centre for Soil Ecology, has traced wheatgrass roots to depths of more than three metres, compared with roughly one metre for annual wheat. In her field trials, losses of nitrate to groundwater were dramatically lower under the perennial crop, and soil organic carbon rose steadily. Burrangong is careful to add, however, that most of the additional carbon accumulated in the uppermost layers of soil, and that if a field is ploughed to re-establish the crop once yields fall, a large part of it could be released again within a short time. This qualification is seldom mentioned by enthusiasts for perennial grains, who tend to describe carbon storage as though it were permanent.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For farmers, perennials offer obvious savings: no seed to buy each year, and far less fuel and labour spent on cultivation. The difficulty lies further along the supply chain. The Prairie Seed Growers' Cooperative, whose members have planted wheatgrass on an experimental basis, reports that finding buyers has been a persistent struggle. Millers and bakers depend on large and consistent supplies of grain with predictable properties, and wheatgrass flour, which is low in gluten, behaves quite differently from wheat flour in the oven. A handful of food companies have launched products that advertise the crop's environmental credentials and sell them at a premium. Such ventures provide valuable publicity, but a high-priced specialist market cannot by itself support cultivation on the scale that would make a meaningful difference to the soil.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more promising route may be to use perennials for more than one purpose. Because the plants remain green after the grain harvest, they can be grazed by livestock in autumn and early spring and then left to produce grain the following summer. Villasanta argues that this combination could make perennial grains financially viable even if their yields remain well below those of annual crops. The argument is persuasive for mixed farms that keep both animals and crops. Many of the world's major grain-producing regions, however, have become highly specialised over the past century, and farmers there have neither the livestock nor the fencing and water supplies needed to take advantage of grazing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perennial grains, then, are unlikely to displace annual crops in the foreseeable future, and it does the cause no favours when advocates suggest otherwise. Their real value probably lies in a more targeted role: on steep slopes, easily eroded soils and land bordering rivers and streams, where annual cultivation causes the greatest harm, even a lower-yielding perennial may be the better choice. Realising that potential will require breeding programmes lasting decades. Private seed companies have little incentive to fund them, since farmers who grow perennials need not purchase new seed every year, and it is difficult to see how the work will continue without sustained public investment.

topic: offshore wind farms and their coexistence with commercial fishing
title: Sharing the Sea
subtitle: As offshore wind farms multiply, fishing communities and energy developers are being forced to negotiate over the same stretch of water

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, offshore wind was a marginal technology, confined to a handful of shallow sites close to the coasts of Denmark and the Netherlands. Today turbines taller than most cathedrals stand in clusters across the North Sea, and governments from East Asia to the eastern seaboard of North America have announced targets that would multiply installed capacity several times over within two decades. The appeal is easy to understand: winds at sea are stronger and steadier than on land, and large arrays can be built far from the homes of people likely to object to them. Yet the sea is not empty. Much of the water now being leased to developers has been fished for centuries, and the question of how the two industries can share it has become one of the more contentious aspects of the energy transition.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The concerns of fishing communities are partly practical. Once a wind farm is built, the cables that link turbines to one another and to the shore must be protected, and in many jurisdictions trawling within the site is either prohibited or effectively discouraged by insurers. Vessels that once worked these grounds must travel further, burning more fuel and spending longer away from port. Dr Rehana Moosajee, a fisheries economist at the Institute for Maritime Livelihoods, has calculated that for small inshore boats the additional costs can absorb a substantial share of annual profits. She stresses, however, that the losses are unevenly distributed. Large, mobile vessels can usually relocate to other grounds, while smaller operators, who lack the range to do so, may be squeezed out of the industry altogether.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all the evidence points towards conflict. The foundations of turbines, along with the rock placed around them to prevent erosion, form hard surfaces in areas where the seabed is otherwise sandy, and these are rapidly colonised by mussels, anemones and other organisms. Professor Anders Kvalheim, a marine ecologist who has surveyed wind farms off the Norwegian and Scottish coasts for over a decade, reports that fish such as cod and pouting congregate around the structures in numbers far greater than on nearby open ground. Because fishing is restricted inside the arrays, he argues, the sites may function as unofficial marine reserves, allowing stocks to recover and eventually spill over into surrounding waters where they can be caught.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This 'reef effect' has been enthusiastically adopted by developers, and it is not hard to see why: it allows an industrial installation to be presented as a gift to marine life. The evidence, though, is less conclusive than the publicity suggests. Kvalheim's own data show that fish are attracted to the turbines, but attraction is not the same as production. A structure may simply draw fish from elsewhere without increasing their total number, in which case concentrating them in one place could even make them easier to overexploit once restrictions are lifted. Spillover, moreover, has been convincingly demonstrated for only a few protected areas, most of them in warm, shallow seas quite unlike the turbid waters of the North Sea. It would therefore be premature to count the reef effect as a reliable benefit.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The social dimension of the dispute has received less attention. Dr Anouk Dekkerhuis, an anthropologist who has spent three years with fishing families on the Dutch and Belgian coasts, argues that the conflict is not primarily about money. Fishing grounds, she observes, carry knowledge passed down through generations: skippers know where particular species gather at particular times of year, and the loss of a ground represents the loss of that inherited expertise. Compensation payments, which treat the problem as purely financial, therefore tend to leave fishers feeling that their concerns have been misunderstood. In Dekkerhuis's view, what communities want most is a meaningful say in where turbines are placed, ideally before sites are put out to tender rather than after the decisions have effectively been made.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some attempts at coexistence are already under way. In parts of the German Bight, developers have experimented with permitting static gear, such as pots for crabs and lobsters, between turbines, since these pose little risk to buried cables. Elsewhere, wind farms have been paired with seaweed or shellfish cultivation, using the turbine foundations as anchoring points. The Baltic Fleet Liaison Group, an association representing fishing cooperatives in several countries, has welcomed such trials but warns that they benefit only a narrow segment of the industry. A trawler crew, it points out, cannot simply convert to pot fishing; the vessels, licences and skills involved are entirely different.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is that offshore wind and fishing are neither natural enemies nor natural partners. The outcome depends heavily on decisions about where arrays are sited, which activities are permitted inside them, and who is consulted when such choices are made. Marine spatial planning, in which governments map the competing uses of an area of sea before allocating it, offers a framework for these decisions, but in practice it has often been conducted at a speed dictated by energy targets. That urgency is understandable, given the scale of the climate challenge. Even so, the transition will be both fairer and, in the long run, more politically durable if those whose livelihoods depend on the sea are treated as participants rather than obstacles.

topic: loss of grid inertia as wind and solar replace conventional power stations
title: The Weight of Spinning Metal
subtitle: Why the disappearance of heavy rotating generators poses a subtle challenge to electricity grids, and how engineers propose to meet it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, electricity grids have relied on a property that few of their users have ever heard of. In conventional power stations, whether fired by coal, gas or nuclear fuel, electricity is produced by enormous turbines and generators spinning in step with the frequency of the grid: fifty or sixty cycles per second, depending on the country. These machines, some weighing hundreds of tonnes, store a considerable amount of kinetic energy. When a large power station suddenly fails, or demand jumps unexpectedly, that stored energy is automatically released as the machines slow fractionally, cushioning the grid against an abrupt fall in frequency. Engineers call this property inertia, and for most of the history of electrification it came free, as an incidental by-product of the way power was generated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Wind turbines and solar panels do not supply inertia in the same way. Solar panels have no moving parts at all, and although wind turbines rotate, they are connected to the grid through power electronics known as inverters, which decouple the speed of the blades from the frequency of the network. As the share of electricity from these sources rises, the total inertia of a grid falls, and frequency can change more rapidly after a disturbance. Dr Joaquín Altuna, a power systems engineer at the Basque Institute for Grid Studies, compares the situation to driving a lighter car: the vehicle responds faster to every push, but it is also more easily knocked off course. In a low-inertia system, he notes, protective equipment has less time to act before frequency falls to a level at which customers must be automatically disconnected to prevent a wider collapse.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The risk is not hypothetical. Several large blackouts in recent years have been attributed, at least in part, to frequency falling faster than control systems could respond, and grid operators in places with high shares of renewable generation, such as islands with weak connections to their neighbours, have occasionally been forced to keep fossil-fuelled plants running solely to provide stability. This practice, sometimes described as 'must-run' generation, is expensive and undermines the purpose of building renewable capacity in the first place. In one island grid studied by Altuna's team, as much as a fifth of the wind energy available on windy nights was wasted because conventional plants could not be switched off.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Two broad responses have emerged. The first is to preserve physical inertia by other means. Synchronous condensers, essentially large generators that spin without producing power, can be installed from new or created by converting retired power stations, providing inertia without burning fuel. Professor Yewande Akinsanmi, who advises a national grid operator, favours this approach because it relies on well-understood technology whose behaviour under stress has been observed for decades. 'Operators are rightly conservative,' she argues. 'When the cost of failure is a regional blackout, proven hardware is worth paying for.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The second response is more radical. Inverters, after all, are controlled by software, and in principle they can be programmed to mimic the behaviour of a spinning machine, injecting power within milliseconds when frequency starts to fall. Batteries connected through such 'grid-forming' inverters can, according to their advocates, respond faster and more precisely than any conventional generator. Dr Priyamvada Kotturi, whose group at a technical university has tested grid-forming systems on a microgrid serving several thousand homes, goes further, arguing that the very concept of inertia is a relic of an older technology. What a grid needs, she contends, is not spinning mass as such but a rapid and reliable response to disturbances, and electronics can provide this more cheaply than steel.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Kotturi's argument is persuasive in principle, yet it underestimates the difficulty of the transition. Grid-forming inverters have performed impressively in small systems and in trials, but there is limited experience of operating them in very large networks, where thousands of devices from different manufacturers must interact without destabilising one another. Problems of this kind tend to reveal themselves only at scale, and often at the worst possible moment. Akinsanmi's caution therefore appears better founded than her critics allow, even if it is unlikely to remain the right answer indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further complication is commercial rather than technical. Because inertia was historically provided at no charge, most electricity markets have no mechanism for paying for it. The Eastern Interconnection Operators' Forum, which brings together several regional grid companies, has proposed creating separate markets for 'stability services', in which any technology, spinning or electronic, could compete to supply rapid frequency response. Such markets would at least ensure that the service is valued explicitly, rather than being assumed to exist. Whether they will reward the cheapest solution or merely the most familiar will depend on how carefully the rules are written.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake to treat the inertia problem as an argument against renewable energy. It is, rather, a reminder that an electricity system is more than a collection of generators, and that properties once taken for granted must now be deliberately engineered. The challenge is real but manageable, provided that it is recognised early, before the last conventional plants close and the cushion they quietly provided disappears with them.

topic: mining the critical minerals needed for batteries and renewable technologies
title: The Metal Beneath the Transition
subtitle: Clean energy requires vast quantities of lithium, copper and nickel. Can they be supplied without repeating the mistakes of the fossil-fuel era?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is often said that renewable energy frees societies from dependence on resources dug out of the ground. Sunlight and wind, unlike coal and oil, cannot be exhausted or monopolised. The claim contains an important truth, but it is also misleading. The machines that capture and store renewable energy are themselves made of materials that must be mined, and in quantities far greater than those required by the systems they replace. An electric car contains roughly six times the mineral content of a conventional one, much of it in its battery, while an onshore wind farm requires several times as much mineral resource per unit of capacity as a gas-fired power station. The transition, in other words, swaps a dependence on fuels for a dependence on metals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the expected increase is striking. Professor Halima Mwakikagile, a resource geologist at the East African Institute of Earth Sciences, estimates that demand for lithium could grow more than tenfold over the next two decades, with copper, nickel, cobalt and graphite following similar, if less dramatic, trajectories. The difficulty, she argues, is not primarily that the earth lacks these elements; known deposits of most of them would be sufficient for decades. The bottleneck lies in the time it takes to bring new mines into production, which, from initial discovery to first output, typically exceeds fifteen years. Exploration, permitting, financing and construction all take time, and none can be greatly accelerated without cutting corners. Mining companies, moreover, are often reluctant to commit billions to projects whose returns depend on metal prices that have proved notoriously volatile.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cutting corners, however, is precisely what critics fear. Many of the richest deposits lie in regions where environmental regulation is weak, and the history of extraction offers little reason for optimism. Dr Tomasz Szczepaniak, who studies mining governance at a European policy institute, points to the high-altitude salt flats of South America, where lithium is extracted by pumping brine into vast evaporation ponds. Local farming and herding communities, he notes, have long complained that the process draws down scarce groundwater, although the companies involved dispute the extent of the effect. In Szczepaniak's view, the absence of reliable independent monitoring makes it almost impossible to settle such disputes, and this uncertainty itself erodes public trust.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some observers argue that the solution lies in shorter supply chains. Several governments in Europe and North America have announced plans to open or reopen domestic mines, partly to reduce reliance on imports and partly in the belief that stricter local rules will produce cleaner extraction. Yet this strategy has encountered an awkward obstacle: local opposition. Proposed mines in Scandinavia and the Iberian Peninsula have met fierce resistance from residents who support renewable energy in principle but object to its material consequences arriving on their doorstep. It is difficult not to see an element of hypocrisy here, since consumers in wealthy countries have long been content for the damage associated with their purchases to occur out of sight.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different strategy is to reduce the need for new extraction altogether. Recycling is the most obvious route, and batteries in particular contain metals valuable enough to justify recovery. Dr Renata Inzunza, a materials engineer, has shown that modern hydrometallurgical processes can recover more than ninety per cent of the lithium, cobalt and nickel in a spent battery. Recycling, however, cannot meet growing demand on its own, for the simple reason that the metals now needed are locked inside products that will remain in use for many years. Until the volume of retired batteries catches up with the volume being manufactured, which Inzunza expects to take at least two decades, mining will remain indispensable. Recycling plants, moreover, need a steady flow of material to operate profitably, and that flow does not yet exist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Engineers are also attempting to design around scarce materials. Battery chemistries based on iron and phosphate, which avoid cobalt and nickel entirely, have rapidly increased their share of the market, and sodium-ion batteries, which use one of the most abundant elements on earth, are now in commercial production. Erik Bergkvist, an industry analyst, regards such substitution as the most underrated tool available. Over the history of mining, he observes, predicted shortages have repeatedly failed to materialise because high prices stimulated both new supply and alternative technologies. This argument has some force, but it should not be pushed too far. Substitution reduces pressure on particular minerals, but it does not eliminate the need to mine; it simply moves the burden elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be concluded? Not that the energy transition is unsustainable, as some of its opponents claim. The total quantities of material extracted for clean energy remain small compared with the billions of tonnes of coal and oil burned each year, which, unlike metals, cannot be recovered once used. But the transition will be judged not only by the emissions it avoids but also by the conditions under which its materials are produced. Ensuring that those conditions are acceptable will require international standards, transparent monitoring and a willingness among wealthier nations to bear part of the cost. None of this will happen automatically, and it would be naive to assume that market forces alone will deliver it.

topic: community-owned renewable energy cooperatives and local acceptance
title: Owning the Wind
subtitle: Community energy projects promise a fairer and more popular transition, but can they survive in a market built for large investors?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1990s, residents of a farming district in northern Germany formed a cooperative, pooled their savings and bought a single wind turbine. Two decades later, the cooperative owns eleven turbines and a solar park, pays dividends to several hundred members and funds a local bus service from its profits. Stories of this kind are frequently told by advocates of community energy, the model in which renewable installations are owned, wholly or in part, by the people who live near them. In Denmark and Germany, such projects once accounted for a substantial share of new renewable capacity, and their supporters claim that they offer not only cleaner power but a more democratic energy system, one in which the benefits of the transition are shared by those who live alongside its infrastructure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central argument concerns acceptance. Wind farms in particular often provoke local hostility, and projects owned by distant corporations are frequently opposed on the grounds that the community bears the visual and environmental costs while the profits flow elsewhere. Dr Aino Kilpeläinen, a sociologist at a Nordic university, has surveyed residents living near more than sixty wind installations. She found that those near community-owned turbines were markedly more likely to describe them positively, even when the turbines were similar in size and number to commercially owned ones. Interestingly, the effect was not confined to people who had invested: non-members living in the same villages also expressed greater approval, which Kilpeläinen attributes to a perception that the planning process had been fair.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Declan Halloran, an energy economist, accepts these findings but questions how much they matter. Community projects, he points out, are typically small, and the transition requires investment on a scale that only large utilities and institutional investors can supply. A cooperative that takes ten years to raise funds for a handful of turbines is admirable, in his view, but it cannot be the main vehicle for building the hundreds of gigawatts of capacity needed. Moreover, small projects often pay more for equipment, finance and grid connections than large developers do, so that the electricity they produce tends to be more expensive. Halloran also notes that professional developers can spread the risk of failure across dozens of projects, a luxury unavailable to a village cooperative with a single site.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is something to Halloran's objection, but it rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: namely, that cost per unit of electricity is the only relevant measure. If local opposition delays or blocks large commercial projects, and in several European countries a significant proportion of proposed onshore wind farms have been abandoned for this reason, then a model that wins consent may deliver more capacity in practice, even if each project is individually more expensive. The cheapest turbine, after all, is of little value if it is never built.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The decline of community energy in some countries is nonetheless real. In Germany, where citizens once owned close to half of all installed renewable capacity, the share of new capacity owned by citizens fell sharply after the government replaced fixed payments for renewable electricity with competitive auctions. Dr Folasade Daramola, a political scientist who studies energy policy, argues that this outcome was predictable. Auctions favour bidders who can absorb the costs of preparing complex applications and the risk of losing, and small cooperatives, which may stake their entire capital on a single project, are poorly placed to do either. In Daramola's view, policymakers designed the auctions with efficiency in mind and gave little thought to who would be excluded by them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all the difficulties are external. The Rural Power Collective, a network of cooperatives in Britain and Ireland, has acknowledged that many community projects depend on a small number of committed volunteers, often retired professionals, whose departure can leave an organisation without the expertise it needs. Membership, moreover, tends to be drawn disproportionately from wealthier and older residents, since buying shares requires savings that many households lack. A model promoted as democratic may therefore reproduce existing inequalities, a point that its advocates have been slow to acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Several responses to these problems are being tried, with varying degrees of success. Some countries now reserve a portion of auction capacity for community bidders or offer them grants to cover early-stage costs such as wind measurements and environmental surveys. Others require commercial developers to offer local residents the option of buying a share in new projects. Such hybrid arrangements are sometimes dismissed as a diluted form of community ownership, but this criticism seems misplaced: a minority stake that gives residents a real voice and a real return may achieve much of what full ownership would, while drawing on the capital of large investors.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Community energy will probably never supply most of the electricity in any large economy, and its advocates do their cause no favours by suggesting otherwise. Its significance lies elsewhere: in demonstrating that the energy transition can be something that communities participate in, rather than something that simply happens to them. In an era when the costs of decarbonisation are increasingly contested, that may prove to be worth more than any number of cheaply built turbines.

topic: agrivoltaics: combining solar panels and crop farming on the same land
title: Harvesting Sunlight Twice
subtitle: Can a single field produce both food and electricity, or is the promise of agrivoltaics too good to be true?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As solar power has become the cheapest source of new electricity in much of the world, a less obvious problem has come into view: land. A large solar farm requires roughly two hectares for every megawatt of capacity, and the flat, sunny, accessible sites that developers prefer are frequently the same sites that farmers prize. In parts of Europe and North America, proposals to cover arable fields with panels have prompted protests about the loss of productive farmland, and some governments have begun to restrict ground-mounted solar on high-quality soils. Against this background, a once obscure idea has attracted considerable attention. Agrivoltaics, the practice of combining solar panels and agriculture on the same land, promises to resolve the conflict by allowing a single field to yield both crops and electricity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The concept is older than its current popularity suggests. It was first proposed in the early 1980s by two German physicists, who calculated that panels raised several metres above the ground and spaced widely apart would leave enough light for crops beneath. For decades the idea remained largely theoretical, since solar panels were too expensive to justify the additional cost of elevated structures. Only with the dramatic fall in panel prices over the past fifteen years have commercial agrivoltaic installations become viable, and there are now several thousand around the world, from vineyards in southern France to rice paddies in Japan. Early installations were mostly small research plots, however, and many of the practical questions that matter to farmers, such as how tractors and harvesters would manoeuvre between the supporting posts, were left unanswered until larger commercial projects obliged engineers to confront them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of the enthusiasm rests on a counter-intuitive finding: for some crops, partial shade is beneficial. Dr Lucia Ambrosetti, an agronomist who has run field trials in central Italy for eight years, has found that lettuce, spinach and several soft fruits grown beneath panels produced yields comparable to, and in hot, dry summers higher than, those grown in full sun. The panels, she explains, reduce heat stress on the plants and slow the evaporation of water from the soil, so that irrigation needs fall by as much as a fifth. Ambrosetti believes that as summers in southern Europe grow hotter, shading will turn from a compromise into a positive advantage for many growers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Kenji Matsuura, a plant physiologist, cautions against generalising from such results. Most staple crops, he points out, including wheat, maize and soya, are adapted to full sunlight, and their yields typically fall when light is reduced. In his trials, maize grown beneath panels yielded up to a third less than in neighbouring open plots. Matsuura does not dispute Ambrosetti's findings for leafy vegetables, but he notes that such crops occupy only a small fraction of farmland. If agrivoltaics is to make a meaningful contribution to both food and energy supply, he argues, it must work for the crops that dominate agriculture, and for these the evidence is far less encouraging.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The economic picture is also complicated. Dr Hélène Thibodeau, a land-use economist, has compared the income of farms with and without agrivoltaic installations. Her research suggests that for many farmers the electricity is far more valuable than the crop: a hectare of panels can earn several times what the same land would yield from cereals. This creates an obvious temptation. Thibodeau has documented installations in which the agricultural activity appears to be largely symbolic, maintained only to satisfy planning rules, while the real business of the site is the generation of power. In her view, regulations that define agrivoltaics loosely risk turning the term into a label that allows solar developers to build on farmland under a more acceptable name.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This concern is well founded, and it suggests that the credibility of the whole field depends on clear standards. Some jurisdictions now require that crop yields beneath panels remain above a fixed proportion, often two-thirds, of the yields expected on comparable open land, and that this be independently verified at regular intervals. Such rules are a sensible start, although they may need to vary between crops and regions if they are not to exclude combinations that are genuinely productive. A threshold suitable for lettuce in a Mediterranean climate, for instance, may be quite unrealistic for grain grown under the cloudier skies of northern Europe.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, however, to conclude that agrivoltaics is merely a marketing device. Even sceptics such as Matsuura accept that the combination can work well for grazing, particularly for sheep, which are small enough to move freely beneath panels and benefit from shade on hot days. And in arid regions where water, rather than land, is the main constraint on farming, the reduced evaporation beneath panels may prove more significant than any loss of light. The approach is unlikely to be the solution to the competition between food and energy, but it can be one of several, provided it is judged by what it produces in the field rather than by what it is called.

topic: green hydrogen and the decarbonisation of steelmaking
title: Iron Without Coal
subtitle: Hydrogen promises to clean up one of the world's dirtiest industries, but the hardest obstacles may lie outside the furnace

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few materials are as fundamental to modern life as steel, and few are as difficult to produce cleanly. The industry is responsible for somewhere between seven and nine per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Much of this is not, as is often assumed, a matter of burning fuel for heat. In a conventional blast furnace, iron ore is mixed with coke, a form of purified coal, and the carbon it contains pulls oxygen away from the iron, leaving metal behind and releasing carbon dioxide as an unavoidable by-product of the chemistry itself. Supplying the furnace with renewable electricity would therefore leave the bulk of its emissions untouched. It is for this reason that steel is arguably the most demanding test of whether heavy industry can be decarbonised at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely discussed alternative replaces carbon with hydrogen. In a process known as direct reduction, hydrogen gas is passed over heated pellets of ore; it combines with the oxygen to form water vapour, and the solid product, called sponge iron because of its porous texture, is then melted in an electric arc furnace. The principle is hardly novel. Direct reduction plants running on natural gas have operated in the Middle East and Latin America since the 1970s. What is new is the ambition to use hydrogen made by splitting water with renewable electricity, a route that could cut emissions from ironmaking by more than ninety per cent. Several northern European pilot plants have produced small quantities of steel this way, and engineers at the Kemijoki Pilot Works have reported that the iron behaves somewhat differently in the arc furnace, requiring changes to the mineral additives used to remove impurities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For Sigrun Stavnheim, a process engineer at the Nordkapp Institute of Metallurgy, such changes are routine. In her assessment, the furnace technology is essentially ready, and the real constraint lies elsewhere: in the sheer quantity of electricity required. Producing hydrogen by electrolysis is energy-intensive, and she calculates that converting a single large steelworks to the new process would demand as much power as a medium-sized city. Multiplied across a national industry, the requirement could amount to a substantial fraction of a country's present electricity consumption, all of it from new wind and solar capacity and grid connections that do not yet exist. This point has been strangely neglected in public debate, which tends to dwell on the novelty of the furnaces rather than on the infrastructure that must feed them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of cost. Kwabena Bediako, an industrial economist at the Takoradi Centre for Industrial Economics, estimates that steel made with green hydrogen currently costs between twenty and thirty per cent more per tonne than conventional steel. Yet he argues that this premium looks less alarming from the end of the supply chain. The steel in a typical family car accounts for only a small part of its retail price, so even a substantial increase in the cost of the metal would add little more than one per cent to the price of the vehicle. Bediako therefore proposes long-term purchasing agreements in which carmakers and other manufacturers commit in advance to buying low-emission steel. The argument is sound as far as it goes, but it applies mainly to high-value products. Much of the world's steel ends up as reinforcing bars and structural beams, which are traded as commodities on thin margins, and in these markets a price difference of a quarter cannot be quietly absorbed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more radical proposal concerns where steel should be made. Mariam Tolegenova, an economic geographer at the Pavlodar Institute of Regional Studies, observes that hydrogen is expensive and awkward to store or transport, whereas iron is not. It would be more rational, she suggests, to reduce ore in places where both ore and cheap renewable energy are plentiful, such as parts of Australia, Brazil and North Africa, and then ship the iron in compressed briquettes to established steelmaking countries for final processing. Her economic reasoning is difficult to fault, but it implies that regions which have built their identity around ironworks for two centuries would surrender the most valuable stage of production, and it is far from clear that their governments, or their workers, would accept such a loss.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different objection is raised by Tomás Urrestarazu of the Basque Foundry Research Council, who regards the enthusiasm for hydrogen as premature. Melting scrap steel in electric arc furnaces, he points out, already avoids most of the emissions of the blast furnace route and requires no new chemistry; investment, in his view, should go first to expanding recycling. There is merit in this, but it cannot be the whole answer. The available scrap is limited by how much steel was made decades ago, and it falls well short of demand in developing economies that are still building their roads, railways and cities. Recycled steel also tends to be contaminated with copper from wiring and motors, which weakens it and makes it unsuitable for the most demanding applications. Newly made iron will be needed for the foreseeable future.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this makes hydrogen steel a fantasy, but it does suggest that its arrival will depend far more on policy than on metallurgy. Without mechanisms that make carbon-intensive imports more expensive, early producers of green steel will be undercut by cheaper conventional metal, and the plants now being planned may never move beyond the demonstration stage. The decisive question for the coming decades is not whether clean steel can be made, but who will be willing to pay for it while it remains more expensive.

topic: long-duration energy storage: pumped hydro and its newer rivals for covering week-long renewable shortfalls
title: Water Uphill
subtitle: Batteries can carry solar power into the evening, but keeping the lights on through a windless winter week is a far harder problem

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When politicians speak of the transition to renewable energy, they usually mean generation: the rapid spread of wind turbines and solar panels that now supply a growing share of electricity in many countries. Far less is said about what happens when the wind drops and the sky darkens at the same time. Lithium-ion batteries, whose cost has fallen dramatically, are well suited to shifting solar power from the afternoon into the evening, but they typically discharge within four hours. Northern Europe, by contrast, regularly experiences winter spells of a week or more in which cold, still, overcast weather sharply reduces renewable output just as demand peaks. Covering such periods requires storage on an altogether different scale, and it is, arguably, the least resolved technical and economic problem of the entire transition.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest answer is also, by a wide margin, the largest. Pumped hydroelectric storage relies on two reservoirs at different heights. When electricity is plentiful and cheap, it is used to pump water from the lower reservoir to the upper one; when power is scarce, the water is released downhill through turbines that generate electricity once more. Roughly three-quarters of the energy used for pumping is recovered, a respectable figure for any storage method. The first schemes were built in the Alps in the 1890s, and today pumped hydro accounts for more than ninety per cent of the energy storage capacity installed worldwide, a dominance that is rarely acknowledged in discussions that treat storage as synonymous with batteries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, has pumped hydro not been built more widely? The usual objection is that it needs dramatic topography and large dams, and that new schemes would flood valleys and disrupt rivers that are already under pressure. Dr Milica Draganić, a hydrologist at the Sava Institute of Water Engineering, believes this image is outdated. Her group used satellite elevation data to search for so-called closed-loop sites, in which both reservoirs lie away from existing rivers, often in disused quarries or on pairs of neighbouring hilltops, and water simply circulates between them. The survey identified hundreds of thousands of technically feasible locations around the world, far more than any plausible demand for storage would require. If her figures are even roughly correct, the challenge is not a shortage of suitable land but the choice of which few sites to develop.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Shoichi Takeshima, who models electricity markets at the Sendai Energy Systems Laboratory, is concerned less with geography than with money. A large pumped hydro plant can take a decade to plan and build and may cost several billion dollars, and its income depends on the difference between the low price at which it buys power and the high price at which it sells. As batteries spread, Takeshima argues, they will flatten precisely the daily price swings on which pumped hydro has relied, and private investors will be unwilling to commit capital over such long periods without guaranteed returns. His analysis exposes a deeper flaw. Electricity markets reward flexibility over hours, but they place almost no value on resilience against a rare, week-long shortfall, which resembles an insurance policy more than a trading opportunity. Unless governments decide to pay for that insurance directly, it will probably not be provided.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, a range of newer technologies is competing for the same role. Compressed air can be pumped into underground salt caverns and released through turbines when needed; heat can be stored in large insulated tanks of sand or crushed rock; and so-called iron-air batteries store energy by repeatedly rusting and un-rusting iron pellets, using some of the cheapest materials on earth. A team led by Andris Kalnins at the Baltic Energy Storage Centre in Riga argues that the low efficiency of several of these methods, which may return less than half of the energy put into them, matters far less than is usually supposed. For a reserve that might be called upon only a few times a year, Kalnins contends, what counts is the cost of each unit of storage capacity, not the proportion of energy lost along the way.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This is correct in principle, but it carries a hidden cost. Every unit of energy wasted in storage must be generated in the first place, which means building additional wind and solar farms, with all the land and grid connections they require. A different school of thought, represented by the Nordic Grid Reliability Forum, maintains that much of the need for storage could be avoided by linking national grids across a continent, on the grounds that the weather is rarely calm and overcast everywhere at once. Stronger interconnections would certainly help, yet they cannot eliminate the problem: large weather systems sometimes cover much of a continent, and international transmission lines have proved notoriously slow to approve and build.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No single technology seems likely to win. A sensible system will probably combine batteries for daily cycles, pumped hydro where geography allows, and one or more cheaper but less efficient options for the rare extended crisis. What is clear is that the decisions cannot wait. Given lead times of a decade or more, the storage that grids will need in the 2040s has to be planned now, while the shortfalls it is meant to cover still seem remote.

topic: replacing gas boilers with heat pumps in homes: performance, retrofitting, running costs and grid impacts
title: The Quiet Machine in the Garden
subtitle: Heat pumps could remove the carbon from home heating, yet their progress depends on much more than engineering

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Heating buildings accounts for a remarkably large share of the energy used in cold and temperate countries, and in much of northern Europe that heat still comes overwhelmingly from gas boilers. The leading low-carbon replacement is the heat pump, a device that uses electricity not to generate heat directly but to move it from the outside air or ground into a building, by compressing and expanding a refrigerant fluid. Because it relocates heat rather than creating it, a well-installed unit typically delivers around three units of warmth for every unit of electricity it consumes. None of this is new. The principle was described by physicists in the mid-nineteenth century, and every domestic refrigerator works in the same way, merely in reverse. The obstacles to heat pumps, in other words, are no longer chiefly technical; they are economic, institutional and, to a surprising degree, psychological.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One persistent belief is that heat pumps struggle in genuinely cold weather. The experience of Scandinavia, where they now heat a majority of detached houses in some countries, suggests otherwise. Dr Lærke Grønbech, a building physicist at the Jutland Building Research Institute, has analysed monitoring data from some 1,200 homes over five winters. During severe cold spells, she found, efficiency did fall, but it rarely dropped below two units of heat per unit of electricity, which is still twice as good as a conventional electric heater. Far more important than the weather, in her analysis, was the quality of installation. Units that had been wrongly sized, radiators that were too small for the rooms they served, and controls set to deliver water at unnecessarily high temperatures together explained most of the poorly performing systems. Grønbech concludes that training installers properly would achieve more than any improvement to the machines themselves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Her findings bear directly on the question of older housing. Heat pumps work most efficiently when they circulate water at moderate temperatures, which in a draughty building may require larger radiators or underfloor heating. Matteo Pellegrinetti, an energy economist at the Po Valley Institute for Housing Studies, therefore advocates what is known as a 'fabric first' approach: walls, roofs and windows should be thoroughly insulated before a heat pump is fitted, or households will face high running costs and disappointing comfort. The logic is attractive, but applied rigidly it becomes self-defeating. Deep insulation of an old house can cost several times as much as the heat pump itself, and making it a precondition would postpone the replacement of boilers in millions of homes for decades. Grønbech's data, moreover, include many modestly insulated houses that perform perfectly adequately after nothing more than a few radiators have been upgraded. Insulation is valuable in its own right; it should not be treated as an entry ticket.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more stubborn difficulty is the price of energy itself. In several European countries, a unit of electricity costs three or four times as much as a unit of gas, partly because the levies that fund renewable energy and social programmes have been placed largely on electricity bills. Where that ratio is high, a heat pump's efficiency advantage is largely cancelled out. Selma Hadžić, an energy policy analyst at the Sarajevo Centre for Regulatory Studies, argues that moving these levies from electricity to gas would be the most effective single measure available to governments, more powerful than the installation grants on which most have relied. The point is well made. A grant reduces the cost of buying a heat pump, but no household will willingly switch if the machine then costs more to run than the boiler it replaced.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also the matter of the grid. Heating demand peaks on cold winter mornings, and Rokas Vaitkus, a power systems engineer at the Kaunas Network Planning Unit, has modelled what would happen if most homes in a district switched to heat pumps simultaneously. In some areas, he finds, the local winter peak could roughly double, overloading cables and neighbourhood transformers designed for a much lighter load. Vaitkus proposes that homes be warmed in advance during quieter hours, using hot-water tanks and smart controls, so that demand is spread more evenly. His warning deserves attention, but it should not become an argument for delay. Network reinforcement is a familiar engineering task that can be carried out street by street as uptake grows, and nobody suggests waiting for the cables before people buy electric cars.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some voices in the gas industry promote a different route altogether: boilers that burn hydrogen, delivered through the existing network of pipes. The appeal of avoiding disruption is obvious, but the physics is unforgiving. Producing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it for warmth requires roughly five to six times as much electricity as supplying the same heat with a heat pump. Proposed trials in which whole villages were to be converted to hydrogen have been abandoned after local opposition, and few independent analysts now regard it as more than a marginal option for homes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is that the heat pump's future will be decided less by engineers than by householders. People replace a boiler perhaps two or three times in their lives, usually in a hurry when the old one fails, and they tend to choose whatever is familiar and quick to install. Persuading them to do otherwise requires trustworthy installers, predictable running costs and an honest account of the upheaval involved. The transition in heating, it seems, will be won or lost in kitchens and living rooms rather than in laboratories.

topic: end-of-life waste from wind turbine blades and solar panels: recycling, reuse and design for disassembly
title: When the Turbines Come Down
subtitle: The first generation of wind and solar equipment is reaching retirement, raising awkward questions about what happens to it next

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few images have been used more effectively by critics of renewable energy than photographs of enormous wind turbine blades stacked in landfill sites, awaiting burial. The pictures suggest an industry that preaches sustainability while quietly generating mountains of unrecyclable waste. They are, however, misleading about scale. Projections indicate that by the middle of the century the world may need to dispose of tens of millions of tonnes of blades and solar panels, a large figure in isolation but a small one beside the ash produced each year by coal-fired power stations or the debris of the construction industry. That said, the problem is real, it will grow rapidly as early installations retire, and an industry whose appeal rests on environmental credentials cannot afford to ignore it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Blades are difficult to deal with precisely because they are so well made. Most consist of glass or carbon fibres embedded in a thermoset resin, a material that hardens permanently when it cures and cannot afterwards be melted and reshaped as many plastics can. This is what allows a blade to flex through storms for twenty-five years without failing, but it also means that the composite cannot simply be separated into its ingredients. At present, the most widely used alternative to landfill is to shred blades and feed them into cement kilns, where the resin serves as fuel and the glass replaces some of the sand and clay used as raw material. Dr Corina Tanasescu, a materials chemist at the Iasi Polytechnic Institute, regards this as the most practical option currently available, and notes that it slightly reduces the emissions of cement production. She is candid, however, that it is a form of downcycling: the fibres, the most valuable component, are destroyed rather than recovered for further use.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More ambitious approaches aim to retrieve the fibres intact. A group led by Ignasi Llorente at the Valencia Composites Laboratory has developed solvents that dissolve the resin, leaving fibres that can be woven into new products. The method works well at laboratory scale, but it demands large quantities of energy and the recovered fibres tend to be shorter and weaker than new ones. Llorente himself believes the lasting solution lies further upstream, in blades designed from the outset to be taken apart, for instance by using resins that can be softened by heat and recovered at the end of a blade's life. Prototype blades of this kind have already been installed on several turbines. The argument is persuasive, yet it offers little comfort in the near term, since a whole generation of conventional blades is due to be decommissioned over the next fifteen years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In the meantime, some designers have found imaginative uses for old blades as they are. The architect Torstein Sørhus has incorporated blade sections into pedestrian bridges, bicycle shelters and playground equipment, arguing that their strength and curved forms make them ideal structural elements. Such projects are admirable and attract considerable publicity. But it would be naive to see them as a general answer: even if every town in Europe built a blade bridge, the projects would absorb only a fraction of the blades coming out of service, and there is a danger that a handful of eye-catching structures will create the impression that the problem has been solved.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Solar panels present a different challenge. By weight, they are composed mostly of glass and aluminium, materials that conventional recycling plants already handle with ease. The difficulty is that the most valuable substances in a panel, notably silver and high-purity silicon, make up only a tiny fraction of its mass and are bonded tightly within its layers, so extracting them is complicated and costly. As a result, in many countries it currently costs more to recycle a panel than to send it to landfill. Njambi Gathuru, an environmental economist at the Nyeri Institute for Resource Policy, argues that the only reliable way to close this gap is to make manufacturers responsible for disposal and to collect the necessary fees at the moment a panel is sold, rather than when it is discarded decades later, by which time the original producer may no longer exist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A complicating factor is that many panels are removed long before they stop working. Because newer models are considerably more efficient, owners of large solar farms often replace functioning equipment in order to generate more power from the same land. Gathuru points out that a growing number of these used panels are sold abroad, frequently to buyers in lower-income countries, where they can supply electricity for many more years. This trade has obvious benefits, but unless the receiving countries have the facilities to deal with the panels when they finally fail, it risks merely relocating the waste problem to places less equipped to manage it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these difficulties undermines the case for renewable energy, whose environmental benefits far outweigh the burden of its waste. They do, however, reveal a habit that the industry would do well to abandon: treating the end of a product's life as somebody else's concern. The lesson of the first generation of turbines and panels is that the question of disposal has to be addressed when equipment is designed, not when it is dismantled.

topic: the 'just transition' for coal-mining regions: job losses, replacement industries and the fate of mining towns
title: After the Last Shift
subtitle: Closing coal mines is essential to the energy transition, but history suggests that the communities around them pay a heavy price

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every energy transition creates winners and losers, and the losers are rarely spread evenly across a country. They are concentrated in particular places: the valleys and plains where coal has been mined and burned for generations, and where the pits and power stations provided not only well-paid work but a shared identity. The last great wave of closures, in the industrial regions of western Europe during the 1980s and 1990s, offers a sobering precedent. Many former mining districts still record higher unemployment, poorer health and lower life expectancy than their national averages more than thirty years after the final shifts ended. Whether today's transition retains public support may depend, to a considerable degree, on whether that experience is repeated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The phrase most often used to express this concern is 'just transition', a term that originated in the labour movement several decades ago and now appears in international climate agreements and in the plans of many governments. Its spread is welcome, but its very popularity carries a risk. A phrase that can be endorsed by trade unions, energy companies and finance ministries alike is in danger of meaning very little, and there is a temptation for governments to announce a just transition fund, attach a modest sum to it and consider the matter settled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What, then, actually harms a mining community when the mine closes? Dr Bożena Wojtaszek, a labour economist at the Katowice Institute of Regional Economics, has followed former miners and their families in a dozen towns over two decades. The direct loss of mining jobs, she found, was only the beginning. Each closure removed demand from local suppliers, hauliers and shops, so that the eventual fall in employment was often twice as large as the number of miners laid off. Equally damaging was the quality of the work that replaced it. Former miners who found new jobs typically earned far less, frequently in insecure warehouse or call-centre positions that carried none of the status of their previous occupation. Retraining schemes, in Wojtaszek's view, too often prepared people for vacancies that existed elsewhere in the country rather than in the towns where they lived.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A popular response is to steer the new energy industries towards the old coal regions, for example by offering subsidies to manufacturers of batteries, wind turbines or solar components that agree to build factories there. Dr Youssef Marzouki, an economic geographer at the Sfax Centre for Territorial Studies, is doubtful. Modern factories of this kind are highly automated and employ far fewer people than mines once did, and companies choose locations according to transport links, the availability of skilled labour and access to markets rather than the wishes of politicians. Plants attracted mainly by subsidies, he warns, have a habit of closing once the payments stop. Marzouki's scepticism is healthy, but it should not be pushed too far. Some former industrial areas have succeeded precisely because their workforce already possessed relevant skills; shipyards that once built vessels have been converted to fabricate the foundations of offshore wind turbines, employing welders and engineers whose expertise transferred almost directly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The European experience, moreover, is not the whole story. Harpreet Tiwana, a policy analyst at the Ranchi Institute for Development Research, points out that in several large coal-producing countries in Asia and Africa, the industry supports not only formally employed miners but an enormous informal workforce of transport workers, traders and people who collect coal by hand. Many regional governments, she adds, depend on coal royalties for a substantial share of their revenue, which funds schools and hospitals. Transition funding that compensates individual workers but ignores the collapse of public budgets will, in her judgement, fail. This is a dimension that European discussions, focused on miners' pensions and retraining, have largely overlooked.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where the transition is managed at all, it usually involves a fixed date for the final closure of mines and power stations, announced years in advance. The Council of Mining Municipalities, which represents local authorities in several coal-producing countries, argues that the most effective use of transition funds is generous early retirement for older workers, since retraining people in their late fifties for entirely new careers seldom succeeds. Such packages undoubtedly protect individuals, but they do little to protect places. A town whose older residents are comfortably pensioned off while its young people move away in search of work is not being transformed; it is being slowly emptied. Ironically, the falling cost of renewable electricity may now undermine even the planned approach, as coal plants become unprofitable and close well ahead of the dates negotiated with unions and municipalities.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important lesson is that success cannot be measured simply by counting jobs replaced. A former mining town that gains a new factory but loses its younger generation has not been rescued. What matters is whether such places can offer their residents a credible future and a sense of purpose that does not depend on looking backwards. Money is necessary for that, but it is the easier part of the problem; the harder part is giving communities a genuine say in deciding what that future should be.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: ship-breaking: dismantling end-of-life ocean vessels on tidal beaches
title: The Last Voyage
subtitle: Most of the world's retired ships end their lives on a handful of tidal beaches. Must they?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, several hundred large ocean-going vessels reach the end of their working lives. A container ship or oil tanker is, among other things, an enormous store of steel: a single large vessel may contain tens of thousands of tonnes of high-grade metal, much of which can be rolled into reinforcing bars for the construction industry. In principle, then, the dismantling of ships ought to be a model of the circular economy, returning materials to productive use rather than leaving them to rust. In practice, the industry has become a byword for danger and pollution. The great majority of retired tonnage is cut up not in dry docks or purpose-built yards but on open tidal beaches in South Asia, where vessels are driven ashore at high tide and then taken apart, piece by piece, largely by hand.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The beaching method owes its dominance to economics rather than engineering. Intermediaries known as cash buyers purchase ships from their owners and resell them to whichever yard offers the highest price per tonne of steel, and beach yards, with low labour costs, minimal infrastructure and a large domestic market for re-rolled steel, can consistently outbid their competitors. Rasmus Overgaard, a shipping economist at the Baltic Institute of Maritime Trade, has calculated that an owner selling to a beach yard may receive several million dollars more for a large tanker than one selling to a facility in Europe or East Asia. Shipowners, he notes, are rarely penalised for this choice. Vessels are frequently re-flagged shortly before their final voyage to registries in states with little interest in enforcing environmental rules, which places them outside the reach of the stricter regulations that would otherwise apply.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The human cost of this arrangement is considerable. Workers, many of them seasonal migrants from poorer inland districts, slice through hulls with gas torches, often without adequate protective equipment, and accidents involving falling steel plates, fires and explosions in residual fuel tanks are frequent. Older vessels also contain asbestos insulation, paints laced with heavy metals and oily sludges, and on a tidal beach there is no barrier to prevent these substances from being carried out to sea. Professor Anwar Talukdar, an environmental engineer who has sampled sediments along one of the largest breaking coasts, has found concentrations of some metals many times higher near the yards than at comparable sites further along the shore. He stresses, however, that the data remain patchy, as access to the yards for independent researchers is tightly controlled.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: International regulation has struggled to keep pace. A convention specifically addressing ship recycling was adopted in 2009 but took more than fifteen years to gather enough ratifications to come into force, and campaigners have criticised it for accepting beaching in principle, demanding only that individual yards meet certain standards. The Lisbon-based Maritime Responsibility Forum, a coalition of environmental and labour organisations, argues that no beach can ever be made safe, because heavy sections cannot be lifted by cranes on soft sand and spills cannot be contained in intertidal mud. For the Forum, the only acceptable solution is to require all dismantling to take place on impermeable floors fitted with drainage systems, whether in dry docks or on specially built slipways.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this verdict. Dr Saoirse Kilbride, who studies maritime law at a university in western Ireland, contends that a blanket prohibition would be both unenforceable and counterproductive. If beach yards were simply excluded from the market, she argues, owners would find ways to send vessels there regardless, and the yards that had invested in improvements would lose any incentive to continue. Kilbride points to several yards in western India that have laid concrete platforms behind the tideline, brought in mobile cranes and begun training workers in the handling of hazardous materials; these, in her view, demonstrate that conditions can be transformed without moving the industry elsewhere. Her argument is partly convincing. The improvements she describes are real, but they have so far been adopted by a minority of yards, and they leave the cutting of the hull's lowest sections on the beach itself, where the problem of containment has not been solved.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What is often overlooked in this debate is the role of the steel itself. Countries with large breaking industries depend on recovered plate for a significant proportion of their construction steel, and the re-rolling mills that process it employ far more people than the yards do. Any reform that raised the cost of dismantling in these countries would therefore have consequences well beyond the beaches. This is not an argument for leaving things as they are. It is, rather, a reason to ensure that the expense of safer methods is borne by those who profit most from the current arrangement, namely the shipowners who sell their vessels at inflated prices and walk away from the consequences.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One promising proposal would do precisely that. Under a ship recycling fund, owners would pay a small levy each time their vessels called at ports in participating countries, and the money would be refunded only when the ship was dismantled at an approved facility. Overgaard estimates that a levy of this kind would close most of the price gap that currently favours the beach. The scheme has yet to be tried, and its success would depend on the cooperation of the major port states. Nonetheless, it has the considerable merit of tackling the economic incentive at its source rather than relying on the goodwill of individual owners, and it is difficult to see how the problem will ever be solved by any approach that does not.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: deposit-return schemes for drinks containers
title: Paying for the Return Journey
subtitle: Deposit schemes for drinks containers are spreading rapidly. Do they deserve their reputation?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few environmental policies enjoy such broad support as the deposit-return scheme. The principle is simple: when a consumer buys a drink in a bottle or can, a small sum is added to the price, and this is refunded when the empty container is brought back to a shop or collection machine. Schemes of this kind have operated in parts of northern Europe and North America for decades, and in recent years they have been adopted or announced by a growing number of countries. Their appeal lies partly in their visible results. Where deposits are charged, return rates for containers commonly exceed ninety per cent, compared with figures closer to half in places that rely on household recycling bins. Yet popularity is not the same as effectiveness, and it is worth asking what exactly these schemes achieve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious benefit is the quality of the material collected. Containers placed in household bins are mixed with paper, food scraps and other packaging, and much of what reaches sorting plants is contaminated. Bottles returned through a deposit system, by contrast, arrive separately and relatively clean, which means they can be turned into new bottles rather than downgraded into lower-value products such as fibres for carpets. Dr Ilse Brakenhoff, a materials engineer at a recycling research centre in the Netherlands, argues that this is the schemes' true value. In her view, the headline return rates matter less than the fact that the plastic can be recycled repeatedly in a closed loop, reducing the need for newly manufactured polymer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters also point to a reduction in litter. Studies in several regions have recorded sharp falls in the number of drinks containers found on beaches and roadsides after deposits were introduced, and the effect is easy to understand: a discarded bottle now has a cash value, and it is frequently collected by someone other than the original purchaser. Professor Tadeusz Kobierski, a behavioural economist, regards this as a striking illustration of how small financial incentives can alter behaviour, but he warns against overstating it. Drinks containers, he points out, make up only a fraction of litter by volume, and cigarette ends, food wrappers and takeaway packaging are untouched by any deposit.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The costs of running such a scheme are less often discussed. Retailers must accept returned containers, store them and, in many cases, install reverse vending machines that read barcodes and crush the items. Small shops have complained that these obligations fall disproportionately on them, since they have little space for storage and handle relatively low volumes. A spokesperson for the Federation of Independent Grocers has described the requirement as an unfunded burden. Most schemes do pay retailers a handling fee for each container, but the Federation contends that the fee rarely covers the true expense. This complaint deserves to be taken seriously. A scheme which depends on convenient return points cannot succeed if the shops that provide them withdraw.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also an awkward question about unredeemed deposits. Not every container is returned, and the deposits that are never claimed usually remain with the organisation that operates the scheme, where they help to fund its operations. Dr Neo Kgositsile, who studies waste policy in Cape Town, notes that this creates a curious tension: the scheme's finances are healthiest when its environmental performance is weakest. She does not suggest that operators deliberately discourage returns, but she believes that unclaimed money should be directed to independent environmental programmes, so that the operator gains nothing when consumers fail to bring their containers back.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A broader criticism concerns what deposit schemes leave unchanged. By making recycling easier and more rewarding, they may reinforce the assumption that single-use packaging is acceptable as long as it is collected afterwards. Some campaigners would prefer schemes built around refillable bottles, which are washed and reused many times, as was once common for milk and beer. Refillable systems, however, require standardised containers and a network of washing facilities, and reviving them would be a far more demanding task than collecting containers for recycling. The two approaches need not be in competition: a well-designed deposit system could provide the logistical foundation on which a refill system is later built.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Deposit-return schemes are therefore neither the cure-all that their advocates sometimes imply nor the distraction that their critics fear. Much of the disagreement surrounding them arises because supporters and opponents are, in effect, asking different questions. Supporters ask whether more containers are being recovered, and the answer is plainly yes; opponents ask whether the schemes alter the culture of disposability that produces so much waste in the first place, and here the evidence is far less encouraging. Both questions are legitimate, but only the first is one that a deposit was ever designed to answer. The schemes solve a specific problem, the low quality and low quantity of recycled drinks packaging, remarkably well, and governments that introduce them should be candid about this limited purpose rather than presenting them as a comprehensive response to the packaging crisis. They should be judged on that basis, and not on whether they can cure every ill associated with packaging waste.
