area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: chemical recycling of plastics: depolymerisation, pyrolysis and mass-balance accounting
title: Breaking the Chain
subtitle: Chemical recycling promises to turn almost any plastic back into raw material. The reality is considerably more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The recycling of plastic has traditionally been a mechanical affair. Bottles, trays and films are sorted, shredded, washed and melted, and the resulting pellets are moulded into new products. The method works tolerably well for clean streams of a single polymer, but each cycle shortens the long molecular chains that give plastic its strength, so that the material is gradually degraded until it can no longer be used. Coloured, layered and food-soiled items are frequently rejected altogether. Mechanical recycling, whatever its merits, cannot on its own deal with the bulk of the plastic that societies throw away, and this is the gap that chemical recycling claims to fill. The term covers a family of processes that break polymers down into smaller molecules, which can then, in theory, be reassembled into plastic of a quality indistinguishable from the original.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two broad approaches dominate. Depolymerisation uses heat, solvents or enzymes to split certain polymers, notably the polyester used in drinks bottles and clothing, back into their constituent building blocks, which are purified and repolymerised. Pyrolysis, by contrast, heats mixed plastics in the absence of oxygen until they decompose into an oily liquid that can be fed into the steam crackers of petrochemical plants. Dr Yevgenia Starodub, a chemical engineer who has worked on both technologies, regards depolymerisation as by far the more promising, because it can recover material of virgin quality from items, such as dyed fabrics or opaque bottles, that mechanical recyclers turn away. She readily concedes, however, that it is suited only to a narrow range of polymers and that most packaging plastics cannot be treated in this way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It is pyrolysis, nonetheless, that has attracted most investment, largely because it promises to accept the mixed and dirty waste that no other process wants. Here the criticism has been fiercest. The Plastics Transparency Network, an alliance of environmental researchers, examined the published output of several commercial facilities and concluded that a large proportion of what they produced was burned as fuel rather than turned into new plastic. Even when pyrolysis oil does reach a cracker, only part of it emerges as the small molecules from which plastics are made; the remainder becomes fuel gases and other by-products. The Network maintains that describing such a process as recycling is fundamentally misleading.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication lies in the accounting. Because pyrolysis oil is blended with fossil feedstock inside a cracker, it is physically impossible to trace which molecules end up in which product. Companies therefore use a system known as mass balance, under which a quantity of recycled input can be allocated, on paper, to particular products. Dr Itzel Sarabia, a life-cycle analyst in Monterrey, defends this system, comparing it to the purchase of renewable electricity from a shared grid. Mass balance is legitimate, she argues, provided that the rules prevent the same tonne of recycled input from being counted more than once. The analogy is a fair one as far as it goes. Yet a shopper who picks up a bottle advertised as containing thirty per cent recycled plastic may be holding one that contains none at all, and few labels make this clear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The environmental case is also contested. Pyrolysis requires sustained high temperatures, and life-cycle studies of its emissions have reached strikingly different conclusions, partly because they make different assumptions about what would otherwise have happened to the waste: landfill, incineration or export. Professor Teodor Haraszti, a process engineer, argues that it is unfair to judge the technology by its present performance, since existing plants are small and inefficient, and larger installations would be expected to improve markedly, as many industrial processes have done before. This is possible. But an argument based on future gains is difficult to test, and it has a convenient tendency to postpone scrutiny indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most telling evidence concerns the waste that pyrolysis plants actually accept. Mixed plastic often contains PVC, whose chlorine corrodes equipment and can form harmful compounds during heating, as well as food residues and paper that lower the quality of the oil. A team led by Dr Achieng Nyamweya at a polymer research laboratory in Nairobi compared the feedstock specifications published by commercial operators and found that many of them closely resembled those of conventional mechanical recyclers. If that is so, the two industries may end up competing for the same relatively clean waste, rather than chemical recycling taking on the difficult material that mechanical methods cannot handle.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that chemical recycling has no future. For specific, well-defined streams, depolymerisation in particular may recover material that would otherwise be lost, and it deserves continued research. The danger lies elsewhere. A technology that is said to be capable of processing any plastic can easily become an argument for producing more of it, and for postponing the harder work of reducing demand and designing packaging that can be reused. Chemical recycling should be treated as a complement to those measures, not as a substitute for them. Its supporters would strengthen their own case if they published clearer figures on how much of what they collect becomes new plastic.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: the right-to-repair movement and product repairability
title: Built to Be Mended?
subtitle: The campaign for a right to repair has moved from hobbyists' workshops into parliaments. What will it actually change?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the twentieth century, a new radio or washing machine was often sold with a folded circuit diagram tucked inside the casing. Products were expected to break down from time to time, and when they did, they were taken to a local repair shop or opened up at the kitchen table. The contrast with today is striking. Many smartphones and laptops are now glued rather than screwed together, fastened with screws that require specialist tools, or controlled by software that refuses to recognise a replacement part unless it has been authorised by the manufacturer. Electronic waste has become one of the fastest-growing categories of household rubbish, and a considerable share of what is thrown away could, in principle, have been mended.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The right-to-repair movement grew out of frustration with this state of affairs. Its early members were an unlikely coalition: electronics hobbyists, independent repair businesses and farmers whose tractors could no longer be fixed without a visit from an authorised dealer. Over the past decade, legislators in several jurisdictions have responded by requiring manufacturers of certain goods to make spare parts and repair manuals available for a fixed number of years after a model is withdrawn from sale. Given the determined opposition of some of the world's largest companies, the movement's success in reaching the statute book is remarkable. Yet the laws themselves are narrower than the enthusiastic headlines suggest, covering only particular categories of appliance and often allowing manufacturers to restrict certain parts to professional repairers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Manufacturers have resisted on three main grounds: safety, security and the protection of intellectual property. Dr Halvard Rønningen, a product-safety engineer, accepts that some of these concerns are real. A badly fitted lithium battery can overheat and catch fire, and a carelessly replaced fingerprint sensor might compromise a device's security. He points out, however, that comparable risks are routinely managed in other sectors; motor vehicles, for instance, are serviced every day by independent garages working to recognised standards. Some of the industry's concerns are legitimate, then, but the safety argument has been stretched well beyond what the evidence supports, and it has been invoked against the repair of products that contain no hazardous components whatsoever.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Access to parts is, in any case, only half the battle. Professor Lucía Ugarteche, an economist who studies household consumption, argues that repair will remain unattractive unless it is affordable. A legal obligation to supply spare parts, she notes, can be quietly undermined if those parts are priced so high that buying a new product is the more sensible choice. Her survey of repair quotes for common household appliances found that, for cheaper items such as kettles, toasters and vacuum cleaners, the cost of a professional repair frequently exceeded half the price of a replacement, at which point most consumers chose to replace. In her view, a meaningful right to repair must therefore be accompanied by products designed from the outset to be taken apart cheaply.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One attempt to encourage such design is the repairability index, a score displayed at the point of sale that rates how easily a product can be dismantled and how readily its parts can be obtained. Dr Faisal Al-Rawahi, a design researcher, has investigated whether these scores influence what people buy. His findings suggest only a modest effect, as most shoppers continue to give priority to price, brand and features. The more significant response, he found, came from manufacturers, several of whom redesigned products specifically to improve their scores. This is perhaps the most important lesson of the index: it works less by changing the decisions of individual consumers than by exposing companies to public comparison.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Alongside legislation, a grassroots movement of community repair cafés has spread across many countries. Volunteers with practical skills help visitors to fix broken lamps, toasters, bicycles and clothing, usually free of charge. Records kept by one such network, the Mend It Collective, indicate that roughly six in ten items brought in leave in working order. The organisers argue that the cafés do more than divert objects from landfill; they change how participants think about their belongings, encouraging them to see a broken item as a problem to be solved rather than a reason to shop. Such initiatives are valuable, but they cannot substitute for a professional repair trade, and the number of trained technicians in many countries has been falling for decades as repair work has become less profitable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, the debate has so far concentrated on hardware, while an equally serious threat to product lifespans has received less attention. A smartphone in perfect physical condition becomes effectively useless once its manufacturer stops providing security updates, since continuing to use it exposes the owner to fraud and data theft. Physical repairability alone, in other words, cannot guarantee that a device will remain in use. If the right to repair is to fulfil its promise, the next generation of legislation will need to require minimum periods of software support as well as the availability of screws, screens and batteries.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: landfill mining: excavating old waste sites to recover materials and reclaim land
title: Digging Up the Dump
subtitle: Old landfill sites are being reimagined as stores of valuable material, but whether excavating them makes sense remains fiercely contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the landfill was regarded as the end of the line. Household and industrial refuse was tipped into excavated pits or former quarries, compacted by heavy machinery and covered with soil, after which the site was expected to be forgotten. Europe alone is estimated to contain somewhere between 150,000 and 500,000 such sites, the majority of which predate modern rules on lining and the collection of contaminated liquid. In recent years, however, a small but vocal group of engineers and economists has begun to argue that these buried heaps should be seen not as liabilities to be contained but as deposits to be worked. The practice they propose, known as landfill mining, involves excavating old waste, sorting it and recovering whatever can be sold, burned for energy or reused. It is an appealing idea, and one that deserves more serious attention than it has so far received; yet the enthusiasm surrounding it has at times outpaced the evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The concept is not new. Small excavations were carried out as early as the 1950s, usually to free up space at a site that was nearly full or to remove waste that threatened a local water supply. What has changed is the justification. Dr Renske Hooijberg, a resource geologist at the Institute for Secondary Materials in Utrecht, points out that some older landfills contain concentrations of copper and aluminium comparable to those of low-grade natural ores. In her view, the rising cost of virgin metals and growing anxiety about the security of supply mean that the economic calculation is gradually shifting. She does not claim that every site is worth opening, but she argues that national surveys should at least identify the small number that are.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics respond that the composition of buried waste is far less promising than such comparisons imply. Professor Ion Vranceanu, an environmental engineer at the Carpathian Polytechnic, has analysed material excavated from eleven sites and found that the largest fraction by weight, often more than half, consists of a fine, soil-like residue that has little value of any kind. Plastics recovered from landfills, meanwhile, are typically so contaminated with dirt and moisture that recycling them is impractical; at best they can be burned as fuel. Vranceanu concludes that, except in unusual cases, landfill mining will remain a costly form of waste management rather than a profitable source of raw materials. His figures are hard to dispute, but his conclusion rests on an assumption that the only benefits worth counting are those that appear on a balance sheet.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That assumption is precisely what a team at the Baltic Resource Recovery Consortium has challenged. Rather than asking whether recovered materials can pay for an excavation, the consortium's researchers have tried to place a value on everything else a project achieves. Old, unlined sites frequently leak polluted water into the ground and emit methane as organic matter decays; excavating them removes these hazards permanently instead of requiring decades of monitoring. Land that was previously unusable can be returned to housing, industry or parkland, which in crowded regions may be worth more than any metal retrieved from it. When these gains were included, the consortium found, roughly a third of the projects it modelled moved from loss to profit. This seems to me the more honest way of framing the question, although such estimates depend heavily on the value assigned to land, which varies enormously from one place to another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The technology itself has advanced considerably. Early projects relied on simple rotating drum screens that separated material by size, leaving most of the sorting to manual labour. Current pilot plants combine screens with magnets, eddy-current separators that repel non-ferrous metals, and optical sensors capable of distinguishing between types of plastic. Dr Satoshi Tsukamura, who directs a pilot programme in northern Japan, argues that the decisive factor is no longer separation but excavation: digging into a mass of compacted waste is slow, releases odours and gases, and can destabilise the remaining slopes. He estimates that excavation and handling account for well over half the cost of a typical project, and he believes that research funding is currently directed at the wrong stage of the process.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Health and safety concerns add a further complication. Older landfills may contain asbestos, clinical waste or industrial chemicals that were never recorded, and workers can be exposed to dust and to gases released when the waste is disturbed. Dr Chidinma Anyaoku, an occupational health specialist, has documented cases in which excavation crews were not informed about the likely contents of a site because no reliable records existed. She argues that a detailed historical investigation, combining archive research with test drilling, should be compulsory before any large-scale excavation begins. It is difficult to see how anyone could object to such a requirement, yet it would add considerably to the cost and duration of projects whose financial margins are already narrow.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done with the hundreds of thousands of forgotten heaps beneath European soil? The answer is unlikely to be either wholesale excavation or continued neglect. A more defensible strategy would be to treat landfill mining as one tool among several, used where a site poses an environmental threat or occupies valuable land, and where the recovery of materials helps to offset costs that would have to be met in any case. Framed in this way, the practice looks less like a gold rush and more like a long-delayed clean-up. That may be a less exciting prospect than the one its promoters sometimes describe, but it is considerably more likely to be realised.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: food date labels ('use by' and 'best before') and household food waste
title: Reading the Small Print
subtitle: The dates stamped on food packaging are often blamed for household waste, but the evidence suggests a more complicated story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In most wealthy countries, a remarkable proportion of the food that households buy is never eaten. Some estimates put the figure at around one fifth of all purchases, and in many national surveys private kitchens, rather than farms, factories or supermarkets, emerge as the largest single source of food waste. Among the culprits most frequently named is the small date printed on almost every package. Campaigners argue that confusing labels persuade people to discard perfectly edible food, and several governments have responded with public information campaigns and new guidance for manufacturers. Labels certainly deserve scrutiny. Yet to treat them as the principal cause of household waste, as some commentators do, is to misunderstand both how the labels came about and how people actually behave in their kitchens.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Date marking was not originally intended for consumers at all. When it spread through grocery retailing in the middle of the twentieth century, its purpose was to help shop staff ensure that older items were sold before newer deliveries. The codes were deliberately concealed, often as strings of numbers that only employees could interpret. It was consumer campaigns in the 1970s that demanded so-called open dating, arguing that shoppers had a right to judge freshness for themselves. What had begun as a tool of stock control thus came to be read, in the public mind, as a signal of safety. Two quite different marks are now in common use. A 'use by' date applies to highly perishable products such as fresh meat and fish, and food should not be eaten after it. A 'best before' date, by contrast, is concerned only with how food looks, tastes and feels; after it has passed, a product may be less crisp or flavourful, but it is generally safe.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: According to Dr Liesl Pfannhauser, a food scientist at the Alpine Institute of Nutrition, the trouble is that many shoppers do not grasp this distinction. Her surveys suggest that a large proportion of consumers treat the two marks as interchangeable, routinely throwing away yoghurt, eggs and bread on the day the 'best before' date is reached. Pfannhauser proposes that such dates be abolished altogether for goods that deteriorate extremely slowly, such as dry pasta, rice and tinned vegetables, where the printed date conveys almost no useful information. Some retailers have already gone further, removing 'best before' dates from fresh fruit and vegetables and inviting customers to rely on their own judgement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Tomasz Golebiowski, a behavioural economist, accepts that confusion exists but doubts that it matters as much as surveys imply. In a study he led, several hundred households weighed and recorded everything they discarded over four weeks, noting the reason each time. The dominant explanations were buying more than was needed, failing to plan meals and cooking larger portions than were eaten; date labels were cited for less than a fifth of the food thrown away. Golebiowski's method is, I think, more trustworthy than a questionnaire, since people asked about their habits tend to give answers that make them sound responsible. Even so, keeping a detailed diary is likely to change behaviour, and participants who know they are being observed probably waste less than they normally would. His figures may therefore understate the problem as a whole, though not necessarily the share attributable to labels.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Technology offers another possible solution. Researchers at the Consumer Food Behaviour Unit have tested labels containing indicators that change colour according to the temperature a product has experienced since packing. Unlike a printed date, which assumes that food has been stored correctly, such indicators reflect what has actually happened to it. In trials, shoppers found them easy to understand and said they trusted them more than conventional dates. The difficulty is cost: each indicator is several times more expensive than a printed date, and manufacturers of everyday goods with slim profit margins have shown little interest. The idea is a promising one, but it seems unlikely to reach the cheaper end of the market for many years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from the anthropologist Dr Amaru Huamantica, who has studied food habits in Andean villages and in several northern European cities. He observes that older people in both settings tend to assess food by smell, appearance and taste, whereas younger people increasingly hand that decision to the label. In his view, the date has become a substitute for practical knowledge that was once passed down within families, and he argues that schools should teach children how to judge whether food is still good to eat. There is much to be said for this, but it should not be taken too far: some dangerous bacteria produce no change in smell or appearance, which is precisely why 'use by' dates must remain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Date labels, then, are a modest lever rather than a master switch. Simplifying them is cheap, and removing meaningless dates from long-lasting products is plainly worth doing. But expecting better labelling to transform household behaviour is unrealistic. The larger gains are more likely to come from changes to the way food is sold, from pack sizes suited to small households to the multi-buy promotions that encourage shoppers to take home more than they can possibly use.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: the afterlife of donated clothing: sorting, the second-hand export trade and fibre-to-fibre textile recycling
title: Loose Threads
subtitle: Dropping unwanted clothes into a collection bin feels like recycling, but the journey that follows rarely ends in a new garment

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By some estimates, the number of garments manufactured worldwide doubled in the first fifteen years of this century, while the average number of times each item was worn fell sharply. Faced with overflowing wardrobes, many consumers in wealthy countries take comfort in the collection bins that stand in car parks and outside supermarkets. Depositing a bag of old shirts there feels like a responsible act, and the bins themselves often carry slogans about recycling. The reality is rather different. Only a modest fraction of donated clothing is resold in the country where it was given; most is baled and shipped abroad, and it is commonly estimated that less than one per cent of the material collected is ever turned back into fibre for new clothes. The comforting picture of a closed loop, in other words, is largely an illusion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first stop for most donations is a sorting plant, where workers grade each item by hand, often in a matter of seconds, into well over a hundred categories according to type, fabric, condition and the market for which it is suited. The best pieces, sometimes called the 'cream', are sold in charity shops and vintage outlets at home; middle grades are pressed into bales for export; and the lowest are cut into industrial rags, shredded for insulation or sent to landfill. Dr Sunniva Aaberge, an economic geographer who has spent several years inside such plants, describes sorting as the hidden engine of the entire system. In her analysis, the profits of sorting firms depend overwhelmingly on the small share of high-value cream. As the quality of new clothing declines, she warns, that share is shrinking, and the economics of the whole operation are becoming precarious.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Exported bales travel principally to East and West Africa, Eastern Europe and parts of Asia, where they are bought by importers who are usually unable to inspect the contents before paying. Dr Nomvula Gqola, who has studied one of the largest second-hand markets on the West African coast, emphasises that the trade supports a vast informal economy of traders, tailors, repairers and washers. Yet she has also recorded a steady rise in the proportion of each bale that cannot be sold at all, which traders now estimate at a third or more. These unwanted items end up on open dumps, in drainage channels or on beaches. Gqola argues that exporting countries should accept responsibility for this outcome by funding waste management in the places where their discarded clothing finally comes to rest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A longer-running controversy concerns the effect of the trade on local manufacturing. Critics have long maintained that cheap imported clothing destroyed textile industries in several African countries during the 1980s and 1990s. Professor Arkady Prokhorenko, a development economist, disputes this. He contends that the decline of local mills owed more to currency crises, the removal of trade protections and competition from new Asian factories, and that banning second-hand imports, as some governments have proposed, would not revive domestic production but would simply raise prices for the poorest consumers. The evidence seems to me to favour Prokhorenko over his opponents. But the argument is increasingly beside the point if what is being shipped is no longer clothing that people want to buy, but waste.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Turning old clothes into new ones is, in principle, the obvious answer. Mechanical recycling, which shreds fabric back into fibre, shortens the fibres in the process, so recycled cotton generally has to be blended with new material to produce yarn of acceptable strength. Chemical methods can separate cotton from polyester, but blended fabrics, stretch fibres, dyes and finishes all complicate the chemistry. Dr Bilal Ghaznavi, a materials engineer, believes that these technical barriers are steadily being overcome in the laboratory. The real bottleneck, he argues, lies earlier: recyclers need to know exactly what a garment is made of, yet sorting by fibre content is still done largely by eye, and the labels sewn into clothes are frequently inaccurate. Ghaznavi expects scanners that identify fibre composition automatically to be in widespread use within a decade.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the industry's own designers are attempting to address the problem at source. The Northern Garment Collective, an association of independent clothing makers, encourages its members to produce garments from a single material wherever possible and to attach zips, buttons and labels in ways that allow them to be removed easily before recycling. Several large retailers, meanwhile, have introduced take-back schemes that accept worn clothing in their stores. These initiatives are welcome, but the take-back schemes in particular deserve some suspicion. Many reward customers with discount vouchers redeemable against new purchases, which risks encouraging precisely the kind of consumption that created the problem in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, the difficulty is one of volume. No sorting system, export market or recycling technology can keep pace with production that continues to grow at its present rate. A number of governments are now introducing schemes under which producers pay a fee for every garment they place on the market, with the proceeds used to fund collection and recycling. This is a sensible step, but the fees ought to vary according to how long a garment is designed to last, so that durable clothing becomes cheaper to produce than disposable fashion. Without such incentives, the collection bin will remain what it largely is today: a way of moving a problem out of sight rather than solving it.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: informal waste pickers and their place in municipal recycling systems
title: The Invisible Recyclers
subtitle: Millions of informal workers recover the materials that cities throw away. Policymakers are only beginning to decide what to do about them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a great many cities across Africa, Asia and Latin America, recycling is carried out not by municipal authorities but by informal waste pickers, who collect, sort and sell the materials that others discard. Estimates of their number vary widely, but figures of fifteen to twenty million people worldwide are frequently cited. In some cities they are thought to recover a larger proportion of recyclable material than the costly, highly mechanised systems of many European countries. Yet for most of their history they have been ignored or treated as a nuisance, moved on by police and excluded from official plans. The value of their work has long been underestimated, and that is at last beginning to change, though not always in ways that serve the pickers themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economics of picking are straightforward but unforgiving. Pickers gather paper, plastic, glass and metal from streets, bins and dumps, and sell it to small neighbourhood dealers, who accumulate larger quantities before passing them on to wholesale traders and eventually to manufacturers. Prices are set at the top of this chain, and the pickers at the bottom receive only a small fraction of the final value. Dr Lucía Bermeo, a sociologist who has worked for many years with pickers' organisations in Andean cities, argues that the problem is not a lack of skill, since pickers are often remarkably expert at identifying grades of material. It is a lack of bargaining power: individuals selling a few kilograms at a time cannot negotiate. In the cooperatives she has studied, members pool what they collect, store it until prices improve and sell directly to industry, and their incomes have risen by as much as half as a result.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some municipalities have gone further and formally contracted cooperatives to provide door-to-door collection of recyclables, paying them a fee for each tonne recovered. Professor Folasade Olatubosun, an urban planner, has evaluated several such arrangements. She concludes that integration is considerably cheaper than introducing fleets of collection vehicles, and that it preserves employment for people with few alternatives. In one city she examined, the payments to cooperatives amounted to less than half of what private contractors had quoted for the same service. Critics point out, however, that such contracts tend to reach only the minority of pickers who already belong to organised groups, leaving the majority as marginalised as before.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Paradoxically, the greatest threat to many pickers comes from efforts to modernise waste management. The closure of open dumps, the construction of engineered landfills and incinerators, and the privatisation of collection can all cut pickers off from the materials on which they depend. Dr Senthil Ilangovan, an environmental economist, studied the closure of a vast dump on the edge of a South Asian city and found that several thousand people lost their livelihoods almost overnight; the limited compensation that was offered went only to those who appeared on an official register, which most did not. Ilangovan insists that no dump should be shut without a transition plan for those who work there. This seems entirely reasonable. Open dumps catch fire, poison groundwater and endanger the people who live around them, and closing them is often unavoidable; what deserves criticism is the manner in which closures are carried out, not the fact that they happen.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A newer challenge arises from so-called extended producer responsibility laws, which require manufacturers to pay for the collection and recycling of the packaging they put on the market. In principle, such laws could channel substantial funds towards the people who already do this work. In practice, companies may find it simpler to contract a handful of large, formal waste firms. Researchers at the Urban Livelihoods Observatory have warned that producer responsibility could end up excluding pickers from the very sector they built, and they recommend that legislation explicitly require the participation of pickers' organisations. How these laws are drafted is, in my view, the most important question now facing informal recyclers anywhere.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this should obscure the harshness of the work. Pickers face cuts, burns and respiratory illness, and they often endure considerable social stigma; in some places, children work alongside their parents. For these reasons, some campaigners argue that the aim of policy should be to bring waste picking to an end, on the grounds that no one ought to have to do it. The sentiment is understandable, but the conclusion is mistaken. Abolishing picking without providing alternative sources of income would leave many families poorer than before. A better course is to improve conditions through protective equipment, covered sorting centres, identity cards that confer legal recognition, and access to healthcare.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Seen in this light, waste pickers are not a problem to be solved but part of the solution to the growing quantity of rubbish that cities produce. Treating them as service providers who deserve payment and protection, rather than as an embarrassing reminder of poverty, would benefit both the workers and the municipalities that rely on them, often without acknowledging it. Wealthy countries, whose own recycling rates depend on expensive collection systems, might even find something to learn.

area: waste, plastics and the circular economy
topic: waste-to-energy incineration: climate impact, contractual lock-in and air quality
title: Burning Questions
subtitle: Plants that turn rubbish into electricity and heat are hailed by some as a clean solution and condemned by others as an obstacle to recycling

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The modern waste-to-energy plant bears little resemblance to the smoking municipal incinerator of the past. Many are designed by celebrated architects; one in northern Europe even has an artificial ski slope on its roof. Their promoters present them as a clean and efficient alternative to landfill, turning rubbish that would otherwise rot in the ground into electricity and heat. Their opponents regard them as monuments to waste, swallowing materials that ought to be recycled and locking cities into dependence on a steady diet of refuse. Having followed this argument for some years, I have come to believe that both camps overstate their case, and that the more useful question is not whether incineration is good or bad but under what conditions it makes sense.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The arguments in favour are substantial. Landfilled organic waste generates methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, for decades after it is buried, and even well-managed sites capture only part of it. Burning shrinks the bulk of rubbish by around nine-tenths, although its weight is reduced by considerably less, and the energy released can be put to use. Dr Hanne Thorsager, an energy engineer who has advised several Scandinavian municipalities, points out that the efficiency of a plant depends overwhelmingly on what is done with its heat. A facility that generates electricity alone may convert little more than a quarter of the energy in its fuel into something useful; one that also supplies hot water to a district heating network can exceed eighty per cent. Thorsager argues that, in cold climates with such networks, burning the residual waste that cannot be recycled is the least damaging option available.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics focus on carbon. When plastics are burned, the carbon they contain, which originated in oil or gas, is released as carbon dioxide just as surely as if the fossil fuel had been burned directly. Professor Kenji Ishikure, an atmospheric scientist, has calculated that some plants already emit more carbon dioxide for each unit of electricity than a modern gas-fired power station. Worse, he argues, the situation will deteriorate over time. As recycling and composting remove more paper and food from the waste stream, what remains is increasingly dominated by plastic, so each tonne burned releases more fossil carbon, even as national grids shift towards wind and solar power. Ishikure's analysis is persuasive, but it applies with greatest force to plants that produce electricity only; facilities that displace fossil-fuelled heating perform considerably better.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A subtler problem is financial. Incinerators are extremely expensive to build and are typically financed over twenty-five or thirty years, often under contracts that guarantee the operator a minimum annual quantity of waste. If a municipality delivers less than the agreed tonnage, it must pay a penalty. Dr Lorenza Scalabrini, a policy analyst who has examined such contracts, argues that they create a powerful incentive to keep waste volumes high, undermining efforts to reduce and recycle. In one region she studied, the construction of several plants left so much spare capacity that operators began importing rubbish from neighbouring countries to keep their furnaces running. Of all the objections to incineration, this seems to me the most compelling reason for caution before any new plant is commissioned.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Public anxiety, by contrast, tends to centre on air pollution. Older incinerators were notorious sources of dioxins and heavy metals, but modern filtration systems have reduced regulated emissions to a small fraction of earlier levels. Dr Babajide Ogunsanya, a public health researcher, nonetheless questions whether official figures tell the whole story. Dioxins at many plants are sampled only a few times a year, he notes, and the highest emissions tend to occur during start-up and shutdown, when furnace temperatures are unstable and measurements are least likely to be taken. He advocates continuous sampling at every plant. This is a sensible precaution, although it should be stressed that Ogunsanya's work identifies a gap in monitoring rather than evidence of actual harm.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Incineration also leaves a residue. Bottom ash, which accounts for roughly a fifth to a quarter of the original weight of waste, can be processed once iron and aluminium have been extracted, and is then commonly used as an aggregate beneath highways. Fly ash, the fine material captured by the filters, is another matter: it contains concentrated toxic compounds and must be stabilised and sent to specially engineered disposal sites.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, the technology does not travel well. Waste in many lower-income cities is wet and rich in food scraps, which gives it a low energy content; some incinerators built in such places have struggled to burn it without supplementary fuel, and several have been abandoned within a few years of opening. Composting and anaerobic digestion, which thrive on precisely this kind of material, are usually better suited. Incineration, then, has a legitimate role as a means of treating genuinely residual waste, especially where its heat can be used. But new capacity should be sized for the smaller quantity of residual waste that a serious recycling policy would leave, not for the quantity cities produce today.

topic: industrial symbiosis: exchanging by-products between neighbouring firms and the limits of planned eco-industrial parks
title: One Firm's Waste
subtitle: Turning the by-products of one factory into the raw materials of another sounds simple. Decades of experience suggest otherwise

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in environmental policy have proved as attractive as industrial symbiosis, the notion that the waste of one enterprise can become the raw material of another. Its best-known illustration is a small port town in Denmark, where, over several decades, a power station, an oil refinery, a pharmaceutical manufacturer and a plasterboard factory came to share steam, cooling water and by-products such as gypsum. The arrangement now features in countless textbooks as a model of the circular economy. It is genuinely impressive. Yet it has frequently been misread. The network did not arise from a master plan; it grew piece by piece out of separate commercial agreements between pairs of firms, each of which made financial sense on its own terms long before anyone thought to describe the whole as a system.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That distinction matters, because since the 1990s governments in many countries have tried to reproduce the Danish success by building planned eco-industrial parks, selecting tenants whose material flows complement each other. The results have been largely disappointing. Dr Mathilde Ravenel, an industrial ecologist, surveyed dozens of such parks in Europe and Asia and found that most had established no more than one or two exchanges, while several had failed to attract suitable tenants at all. In her view, symbiosis cannot be designed from above, because the processes, ownership and markets of individual firms change far faster than planners anticipate. When a key partner relocates or closes, the companies that relied on its by-products may suddenly find themselves without an essential input.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Jaroslaw Kedzierski, an economist, accepts that top-down planning has a poor record, but insists that the alternative is not simply to leave matters to chance. He points to a national programme in which publicly funded advisers organised workshops at which managers from local firms described the materials they used and discarded, and then searched together for possible matches. Over a decade, the programme reportedly arranged thousands of exchanges and diverted millions of tonnes of material from landfill, at a modest cost to the public purse. These figures are striking, but they should be treated with some caution. Many of the exchanges were small or occurred only once, and it is difficult to know how many would have taken place without any official involvement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Legal obstacles are a recurring complaint. In many jurisdictions, any material classed as waste is subject to permits, record-keeping and restrictions on transport, even when it is harmless and useful. Dr Wanjiru Wambugu, an environmental lawyer, observes that legal definitions of waste were written primarily to prevent illegal dumping, and that they now obstruct the very reuse that policymakers claim to support; a company wishing to use a neighbour's by-product may first have to obtain a licence to handle waste. She proposes clear end-of-waste criteria under which materials that meet agreed quality standards would be reclassified as products. The proposal is sensible, but it needs careful drafting. Loosening the definition of waste could all too easily create a loophole through which unscrupulous operators disguise dumping as trade.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Equally important, though less often discussed, is the question of trust. Firms are frequently reluctant to reveal the composition of their waste streams, fearing that competitors could learn something about their processes. The Westfjord Industrial Exchange, a cooperative of manufacturers in western Norway, has tried to overcome this by maintaining a database in which members list surplus materials anonymously; a coordinator then contacts potential partners and introduces them only when both sides agree. Members report that the coordinator's personal knowledge of local businesses has been far more valuable than the software itself, which suggests that a trusted intermediary matters more than sophisticated technology.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Geography imposes further limits. Dr Emre Sarigul, an economic geographer, emphasises that the materials most often exchanged, such as sand, ash, waste heat and steam, are bulky and of low value, so that moving them is economic only over short distances; steam, in particular, cannot be piped economically beyond a few kilometres. Symbiosis therefore favours dense clusters of heavy industry and may have little to offer regions whose economies are dispersed or dominated by services. Sarigul also notes an awkward irony: many celebrated networks are anchored by coal- or gas-fired power stations, whose steam and flue-gas gypsum feed the other partners. As these plants close in the name of climate policy, the networks lose their foundations. The irony is real, but it is hardly an argument for keeping fossil-fuelled plants open longer than necessary.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that industrial symbiosis should be abandoned. Exchanges that make commercial sense deserve encouragement, and the environmental gains, though rarely as large as advocates suggest, are real. But the lesson of the past three decades is that governments achieve more by removing barriers than by drawing up blueprints. Clarifying the law on by-products and funding the unglamorous work of local intermediaries are likely to yield greater returns than another landscaped park waiting in vain for tenants whose waste happens to match.

topic: individual transferable fishing quotas: ending the race to fish and the consolidation of ownership
title: Owning the Catch
subtitle: Tradeable fishing quotas have ended the race to fish in many places, but critics ask who has paid the price

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the standard way to prevent overfishing was to set a total allowable catch for a fishery and then close it once that limit had been reached. The flaw in this arrangement soon became obvious. Because every vessel competed for a share of a single common limit, each skipper had a powerful incentive to land as much as possible before the others did. Owners invested in larger engines and bigger nets, seasons that had once lasted months shrank to a few frantic days, and crews went to sea in weather they would otherwise have avoided. Economists came to call this pattern 'the race to fish', and it was widely regarded as wasteful, dangerous and, in the long run, self-defeating.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The solution proposed by a number of resource economists in the 1970s and 1980s was to divide the total catch into individual portions, each assigned to a particular fisher or company. If these portions could also be bought and sold, the argument ran, the industry would reorganise itself efficiently: the least productive operators would sell their shares and leave, while those who remained would no longer need to rush. Gustavo Arrieche-Montalvo, an economist at the Southern Institute for Marine Resource Economics, has been among the most consistent advocates of the system. In his view, transferable quotas give fishers a stake in the future health of the stock, because the market value of a quota rises when the fish population recovers. A fisher who holds a permanent share, he argues, behaves less like a hunter and more like a farmer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is considerable evidence that the system works, at least by some measures. Studies of fisheries that adopted transferable quotas have generally found that the race to fish disappears, that seasons lengthen and that accidents at sea decline. Because fishers can choose when to land their catch, they can also time their deliveries to meet demand for fresh rather than frozen fish, which typically fetches a higher price. A comparative review led by Ingrid Valtonen-Aasheim at the Baltic Fisheries Policy Centre found that the proportion of stocks fished beyond safe limits was lower in quota-managed fisheries than in comparable fisheries managed by other means. Valtonen-Aasheim is careful to point out, however, that the countries which introduced quotas tended to have stronger scientific monitoring in the first place, so the quotas themselves may not deserve all the credit.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most persistent criticism concerns what happens to the ownership of quota over time. Since shares can be traded, they tend to accumulate in the hands of those with the greatest access to capital. Within two decades of quotas being introduced in several fisheries, the number of quota holders had fallen by half or more, and in some places a handful of companies controlled most of the catch. The anthropologist Miriama Lealaiauloto of the Pacific Coastal Livelihoods Project has documented the effects on small harbour communities, where young people who might once have bought a boat and entered the fishery now face quota prices far beyond their means. Many end up leasing quota from owners who never go to sea, sometimes paying more than half the value of their catch for the privilege. Fishing, Lealaiauloto observes, has turned into a kind of tenant farming on water.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong to dismiss these concerns as merely sentimental. A fishing community is not simply a collection of businesses; it supports processing plants, boatyards and schools, and when quota is sold to companies based elsewhere, the income it generates leaves with it. Yet it would be equally mistaken to conclude that the quota system itself is to blame. The problem lies less in the principle of tradeable rights than in the way those rights were first allocated. In most cases, quota was handed out free of charge to existing boat owners on the basis of their recent catches, which turned a public resource into a private asset almost overnight. Those fortunate enough to be fishing at the time received a windfall; everyone who came after had to pay them for access.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Several reforms have been proposed to address this. Some governments now cap the share of the total catch that any single owner may hold, while others require that quota be owned only by active fishers rather than by investors. A more radical idea, promoted by the fisheries lawyer Teodora Kalinowska, is to issue quota for a fixed period, perhaps fifteen years, after which it returns to the state and is reallocated, possibly by auction. Kalinowska argues that this would allow the public to share in the value of the resource and would give newcomers a realistic route into the industry. Opponents counter that fishers who own quota only temporarily would lose precisely the long-term stake that made the system attractive in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This objection deserves to be taken seriously, but it is probably overstated. Fifteen years is longer than the term of most commercial loans, and a fisher with a reasonable expectation of renewal is unlikely to plunder a stock on which his or her livelihood depends. What the history of transferable quotas suggests, above all, is that the design of a property right matters as much as its existence. Markets in fishing rights can end the race to fish; they cannot, on their own, decide who ought to benefit from the sea.

topic: satellite tracking of fishing vessels, 'dark' fleets and at-sea transshipment: what remote monitoring can and cannot achieve
title: Watching the Fleet from Orbit
subtitle: Satellites have made the high seas more visible than ever before, but visibility is not the same thing as control

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some four hundred nautical miles from the nearest coast, two ships lie alongside one another in the dark. One is a fishing vessel that has been at sea for many months; the other is a refrigerated cargo carrier, or reefer, which takes on the fishing boat's catch and supplies it with fuel and food in return. Such meetings, known as transshipments, are not in themselves illegal, and they allow fishing fleets to remain on distant grounds without the expense of returning to port. But they also make it extremely difficult to know where a catch was taken, by whom and under what conditions. Fish caught without a licence can be mixed with legal catch in the reefer's hold, and crews who never come ashore are beyond the reach of labour inspectors.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of fishing, what happened on the high seas was effectively invisible to anyone not present. That has begun to change, largely because of a technology that was never intended for the purpose. The Automatic Identification System, or AIS, was introduced so that large ships could broadcast their position, speed and identity to one another and thus avoid collisions. There is a certain irony in the fact that a safety device has become the principal means of monitoring fishing worldwide. Satellites now collect billions of these messages each year, and the data scientist Kaito Morimatsu, of the Institute for Maritime Analytics, has trained algorithms to recognise fishing from the shape of a vessel's track alone: trawlers move back and forth at low, steady speeds, whereas longliners set their gear in long straight lines and then drift. Morimatsu's group claims that its models can distinguish fishing from mere transit in the great majority of cases.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The resulting maps, which show fishing effort across the world's oceans almost in real time, are undeniably impressive. Yet they should not be mistaken for a complete picture. AIS is required only on larger vessels, it can be switched off, and its signals can be falsified to suggest that a ship is somewhere it is not. The remote-sensing specialist Inés Quiñonero-Lasarte has sought to find these 'dark' vessels by combining several other sources: radar satellites, which detect metal hulls through cloud and at night, and optical sensors that pick up the powerful lamps some fleets use to attract squid. Her surveys suggest that a substantial minority of industrial fishing vessels in some regions do not broadcast at all. Radar, however, has a basic limitation: it reveals that a ship is present, but not which ship it is.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Transshipment can be detected in a similar way. When two vessels travel side by side at very low speed for several hours, the most likely explanation is that cargo is being transferred. A non-profit organisation, the Open Waters Transparency Collective, publishes such encounters online, naming the vessels involved. Its members argue that disclosure is itself a form of enforcement: supermarkets, seafood importers and insurers are sensitive to their reputations, and few wish to be linked publicly with a ship suspected of illegal activity. This is a plausible argument, and there are anecdotal cases of companies cutting ties with particular suppliers after a report. Whether publicity has reduced illegal transshipment overall, though, has not yet been convincingly shown.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Lawyers are more cautious still. Benedikte Hjortsvang, a specialist in the law of the sea, points out that outside national waters a fishing vessel is normally subject only to the jurisdiction of the country whose flag it flies. A number of states offer their flags cheaply and show little interest in what the vessels registered with them actually do. Moreover, she notes, satellite evidence is rarely sufficient to secure a conviction on its own: courts generally expect proof gathered by boarding the vessel, inspecting its hold and examining its logbooks. A track that looks suspicious from orbit, in her words, is grounds for investigation, not proof of an offence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For coastal states with limited resources, the value of the new data depends on what they can do with it. Nomvula Mabhena, who has advised several West African fisheries agencies, observes that a country with two patrol boats and an exclusive economic zone the size of a European nation cannot inspect more than a fraction of the vessels it sees on a screen. Even so, she argues, satellite data allows those few boats to be sent where they are most needed rather than on routine patrols. Mabhena also raises a less obvious concern: if the most advanced monitoring is provided by foreign organisations, it may be they, rather than the coastal states themselves, who decide which problems receive attention.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these perspectives suggest that the transparency revolution at sea, though real, has been somewhat oversold. Seeing a crime is not the same as stopping it. In my view, the most promising application of satellite data lies not on the open ocean but in port. Every catch must eventually be landed somewhere, and a port that refuses entry to vessels with unexplained gaps in their tracking history, or with records of suspicious encounters, can achieve far more than a patrol ship searching thousands of square kilometres of water. The technology has made the ocean more visible; whether it becomes better governed will depend on ordinary, unglamorous inspections on the quayside.

topic: harmful fisheries subsidies: fuel support, overcapacity, measurement problems and trade negotiations
title: Paying for Empty Nets
subtitle: Governments spend billions supporting their fishing fleets. Economists disagree over how much of that money is doing harm

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each year, governments around the world transfer an estimated thirty-five billion dollars to their fishing industries. The sum is large, but what is more remarkable is how rarely it has been examined. Agricultural support has been debated in public for half a century, and payments to fossil-fuel producers now attract regular criticism, yet fisheries subsidies have, until recently, received attention mainly from a small circle of specialists. This neglect matters because, unlike most forms of public spending, money given to fishing fleets acts directly on a shared natural resource that is already under severe strain: by most assessments, more than a third of the world's commercially exploited fish stocks are now harvested beyond biologically sustainable levels.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Not all of this money is the same, and much of the debate turns on how it should be classified. Economists commonly distinguish between support that increases a fleet's ability to catch fish, such as grants for building new vessels or exemptions from fuel tax, and spending that serves broader public purposes, such as scientific surveys, the policing of fishing grounds or the management of marine reserves. Halvard Strømnes, of the North Atlantic Resource Economics Group, has argued that fuel subsidies are the most damaging category of all. Fuel is typically the largest single cost for vessels that travel far from port, and by reducing it, governments make voyages profitable that would otherwise never leave the harbour. In his analysis, a considerable share of fishing on the high seas would cease to pay for itself if fuel were sold at its full price.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The underlying logic is straightforward. In an unsubsidised fishery, falling catches eventually make fishing unprofitable, and some boats withdraw, giving stocks a chance to recover. Subsidies interrupt this feedback. By keeping costs artificially low, they allow fleets to continue operating long after declining returns should have forced a reduction in effort, so that too many vessels end up chasing too few fish. Economists describe the result as overcapacity, and its consequences extend beyond the fish themselves: the potential wealth of the resource is gradually consumed by the expense of maintaining fleets far larger than the stocks can support. It is difficult to quarrel with this reasoning in principle, and the historical record of collapsed fisheries offers ample illustration of it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Where the consensus begins to fracture is over who would bear the cost of reform. Amaru Condoruna, a development economist at the Andean Centre for Coastal Livelihoods, warns that blanket condemnations of subsidies overlook millions of small-scale fishers in poorer countries, for whom subsidised fuel can make the difference between a viable living and destitution. Removing such support, he contends, would fall hardest on precisely those communities least able to adapt, while industrial operators would simply pass on higher costs or relocate. His concern for vulnerable fishers deserves to be taken seriously. Nevertheless, the argument sits uneasily with the evidence on how fuel support is actually distributed. Because most schemes are tied to the volume of fuel consumed, the largest vessels, which burn the most, collect by far the greatest share of the benefit, and small boats receive comparatively little.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that nobody is entirely sure how large the problem is. Liesl Brandtner, who leads a data project at the Vienna Centre for Trade Statistics, has spent several years trying to reconcile the figures that governments report. She has found that countries define subsidies inconsistently, that some payments are omitted altogether, and that certain arrangements are almost impossible to classify. A prominent example is the access agreement, under which a wealthy nation pays a coastal state for permission for its fleet to fish in that state's waters. Whether such payments amount to a subsidy for the distant fleet is fiercely disputed. Brandtner believes that, taken together, these gaps mean published totals understate the true level of support. Yet uncertainty about the exact figure should not be mistaken for a reason to delay action, since no plausible correction would make the sums involved insignificant.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: International efforts to curb harmful subsidies have moved slowly. After roughly two decades of negotiation, members of the World Trade Organization agreed to prohibit support for illegal fishing and for fishing on stocks already recognised as overfished. Teodora Brankovan, a specialist in trade law, describes the agreement as a foundation on which stronger rules can now be built, noting that it was the first trade deal to be framed around environmental sustainability. That assessment seems somewhat generous. The deal postponed the most consequential question, namely how to restrict subsidies that expand fishing capacity in general, and its effectiveness depends heavily on governments reporting their own spending honestly, which, as Brandtner's work suggests, they have rarely done.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this implies that governments should stop spending money on fisheries altogether. A growing number of economists propose that existing budgets be redirected rather than abolished: towards monitoring and enforcement, towards research, or towards schemes that pay fishers to retire their vessels. Such buy-back programmes, however, illustrate how easily good intentions can go wrong. In several cases, fishers who sold their boats used the proceeds to buy newer and more efficient ones, leaving the fleet's overall capacity unchanged or even greater. Redirection will therefore work only if it is accompanied by firm limits on how much fishing is permitted. The real question, in other words, is not whether public money should flow to the sea, but what it is being asked to achieve once it arrives.

topic: regional fisheries management organisations and shared tuna stocks: consensus voting, allocation and pre-agreed harvest rules
title: Fish Without Passports
subtitle: Tuna cross dozens of maritime borders in their lifetimes. The bodies that manage them are only as strong as their most reluctant member

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A single yellowfin tuna may begin its life in the warm waters of one country's exclusive economic zone, feed for several years in the open ocean, and end up on the deck of a vessel registered on the other side of the world. Fish of this kind pay no attention to political boundaries, and no individual government can conserve them alone. The solution adopted over the second half of the twentieth century was the regional fisheries management organisation, a body through which all the states that fish a particular stock agree on catch limits, gear restrictions and closed seasons. The principle is unquestionably sound. The results, however, have been uneven, and for several of the world's most valuable tuna populations they have been frankly disappointing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty most often blamed is the way such bodies make decisions. Most operate by consensus, which means that a proposal is adopted only if no member formally objects. Sigrún Eyvindardóttir, a political scientist who has studied the minutes of more than two hundred annual meetings, argues that this rule systematically weakens conservation. Because any single delegation can block an agreement, the measures eventually adopted tend to reflect the preferences of the member most reluctant to cut its catch. In her sample, recommendations from scientific committees to reduce catches were followed in full in fewer than one case in five; far more commonly, a proposed reduction was diluted during negotiation until it no longer threatened anyone's fleet.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Folau Fakatulolo, who advised island governments in the Pacific for many years, offers a less damning interpretation. Consensus, he argues, is the price that must be paid for keeping all fishing nations inside the system. If decisions were taken by majority vote, states that were outvoted could simply invoke the so-called objection procedure, a provision found in most founding agreements that exempts a member from any measure it has formally rejected. A dissatisfied state might even withdraw altogether, leaving its vessels free to fish without any restriction. There is force in this argument, but it is weaker than it first appears. The objection procedure already exists under consensus rules and has been used repeatedly, so consensus does not, in practice, guarantee the universal participation that Fakatulolo values.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Beneath the procedural arguments lies a more fundamental quarrel over who is entitled to the fish. Allocation has traditionally been based on historical catch: nations receive a share in proportion to what their fleets have taken in the past. Critics point out that this arrangement rewards precisely those countries which fished most heavily, often before the stock was regulated at all, while penalising coastal developing states whose own fleets are only now being built. Shirin Golestaneh, an expert in the law of the sea, has proposed that shares should instead reflect zonal attachment, meaning the proportion of its life cycle that a stock spends within each country's waters. The principle is fairer, yet it rests on tagging and survey data that remain patchy for many species, and every party will naturally favour the estimate that enlarges its own share.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Optimists frequently cite the recovery of a heavily depleted bluefin tuna stock as proof that the system can work. After years in which catches far exceeded scientific advice, the responsible organisation introduced strict quotas, a minimum landing size and a scheme requiring every fish to be documented from capture to sale. Within little more than a decade, estimates of the spawning population had risen considerably. Researchers at the Pacific Commons Policy Unit, however, argue that the credit belongs elsewhere. In their view, a sustained campaign by environmental organisations, together with the threat of a ban on international trade in the species, created pressure that the management body could not resist. Both explanations probably contain some truth: outside pressure supplied the motive for reform, but without an institution capable of setting and monitoring quotas, that motive would have had nowhere to go.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more recent innovation attempts to take the annual bargaining out of the process altogether. Under what are known as management procedures, members agree in advance on a formula that converts indicators of a stock's condition into a catch limit, so that when the indicators fall, quotas are cut automatically. Rémi Quellenec, a fisheries modeller, has run simulations suggesting that stocks governed in this way fluctuate far less than those managed through yearly negotiation, and that the fishing industry benefits from the greater predictability. The approach is undoubtedly promising. Even so, agreeing on the formula is itself a negotiation, and a procedure designed to avoid painful cuts will produce no better outcomes than the bargaining it replaces.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is that the weaknesses of regional management are rarely scientific. Stock assessments for the major tuna species are among the most sophisticated in fisheries science, and the advice they generate is usually clear. The obstacle lies in persuading sovereign states to accept short-term losses for the sake of long-term gains that will be shared with their competitors. No redesign of voting rules or allocation formulas can remove that tension entirely; at best, it can make the cost of ignoring the evidence more visible.

topic: shifting baselines in fisheries: using archives, photographs, menus and fishers' memories to reconstruct past fish abundance
title: Remembering a Fuller Sea
subtitle: Historians and ecologists are searching old ledgers, photographs and memories for evidence of what the oceans once held

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the mid-1990s, a fisheries biologist coined a phrase that has since travelled far beyond his discipline. Each generation of researchers, he observed, tends to accept as normal the state of a fish stock at the beginning of its career, and to measure later declines against that reference point. As stocks diminish, the reference point itself slips downward, so that a sea emptied over centuries can appear, to those studying it, to be only slightly depleted. The notion of the 'shifting baseline' is now so familiar that it is cited in debates about everything from birdsong to urban air quality. Familiarity, however, has arguably blunted its force: the idea is widely acknowledged, but its practical consequences for how fisheries are managed have barely been absorbed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One response has been to look for evidence of what the oceans contained before scientific monitoring began. Ottilie Gravenhorst, a marine historian at the Hanseatic Archive Project, has spent two decades extracting figures from customs registers, market ledgers and the account books of religious houses that once bought fish in bulk. Her colleagues have turned to less conventional sources. One team compared photographs of prize fish displayed by sport anglers at a single harbour between the 1950s and the 2000s and found that the average length of the largest specimens had fallen by more than half, while the anglers in the later pictures appeared every bit as proud as their predecessors. Restaurant menus have been used in a similar way: when a species disappears from the menu, or reappears at a much higher price, it may signal growing scarcity.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Living memory offers a further window. The anthropologist Mireille Abadjian interviewed fishers from three generations in a group of coastal villages and asked each of them to name the largest catch they could remember and the species that had once been common. The oldest respondents listed many species that the youngest had never seen, and some of the younger fishers expressed disbelief at the sizes their grandparents described. For Abadjian, these interviews show the shifting baseline operating within individual families. Such testimony must be treated with care, since memories of exceptional days tend to be exaggerated with time. Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to dismiss it, for it frequently records changes that no official dataset ever captured.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that historical reconstruction can bear the weight placed upon it. Bohdan Lysenchuk, a stock assessment scientist, points out that early records were compiled for purposes quite unrelated to ecology. A sudden fall in recorded landings, for example, may reflect a change in how a port was taxed rather than any change in the fish population, and improvements in fishing gear mean that a given catch in 1900 represents a very different level of abundance from the same catch in 1980. Lysenchuk also warns that if recovery targets are set according to inflated historical estimates, they may prove impossible to meet, and the resulting failures could undermine public confidence in management. His caution about the quality of the evidence is justified. Yet to reject old data entirely is not a neutral choice: it means accepting, by default, the most degraded baseline of all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In practice, the most convincing historical studies rely not on any single source but on the agreement between several independent ones. If tax records, photographs and the recollections of elderly fishers all point towards the same decline, the likelihood that each is distorted in exactly the same way is small. Researchers have also begun to use statistical techniques that assign explicit levels of uncertainty to each type of evidence, so that a figure derived from a medieval ledger is given less weight than one from a modern survey, but is not discarded.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The policy implications are considerable. In many jurisdictions, legal targets for rebuilding fish stocks are calculated from data covering only the past few decades, a period during which most commercially important populations were already heavily exploited. Historical studies suggest that some of these targets correspond to a small fraction of former abundance. This does not mean that managers should attempt to restore the seas of the Middle Ages, an ambition that would be both unrealistic and, given the demands of modern populations, arguably undesirable. It does mean that they should be aware of how far present conditions lie from earlier ones, and be honest with the public about the gap.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the deepest lesson of this research is that ecological loss can be invisible to the very people best placed to notice it. The scientists, fishers and officials who deal with the sea every day are, precisely because of their experience, at risk of mistaking a diminished ocean for a natural one. Recovering the past is therefore not a matter of nostalgia but a necessary correction to the limits of human perception, and a reminder that what looks normal to us may be nothing of the kind.
