topic: community-based management of small-scale fisheries: territorial use rights, co-management committees and their unequal effects
title: Rights to the Rocks
subtitle: Giving fishing communities control over their own coasts has produced striking successes. It has also raised awkward questions about who is left out

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of the roughly sixty million people who earn some part of their living from catching fish, the great majority work not on industrial trawlers but in small boats, on foot along the shore, or with nets set from beaches and riverbanks. Yet for most of the twentieth century, fisheries science and policy were built around the industrial fleet. Catch limits were calculated in distant capitals, licences were issued by central ministries, and enforcement depended on inspectors who were rarely seen on remote coasts with hundreds of landing sites. It is hardly surprising that such a model failed small-scale fisheries; it was designed for a different world. Since the 1990s, an alternative has gained ground: handing a share of responsibility, and of rights, to fishing communities themselves. The shift was driven partly by principle and partly by necessity, since many governments simply lacked the resources to manage their coasts in any other way.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely studied version of this idea is the territorial use right, under which a fishing association receives exclusive access to a defined stretch of seabed and, with it, the duty to manage the resources found there. One South American country pioneered the approach on a national scale for a prized sea snail that had been fished almost to commercial extinction. Ximena Larraguibel, a marine ecologist at the Pacific Littoral Institute, has surveyed more than fifty of these managed areas for nearly twenty years. She reports that densities of the snail inside them are typically several times higher than in neighbouring open-access waters, and that associations voluntarily spend considerable sums on patrol boats and guards. In her interpretation, secure rights give fishers a reason to protect stocks that open access never could: what one leaves in the water today will still be there tomorrow.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Haruto Iwashimizu, a resource economist, accepts these findings but questions what they reveal. The success of the managed areas, he argues, has been partly purchased at the expense of the coast around them. Fishers excluded from the territories, or members seeking extra income, concentrate their effort on the remaining open-access grounds, which in several regions have become noticeably more depleted than before the reform. Membership of the associations, moreover, is often closed, so that young people and newcomers cannot easily join, and shoreline gatherers, many of them women, have lost access to areas they once used freely. These are serious objections, and they suggest that comparisons between inside and outside the territories may overstate the overall benefit.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A related concern has emerged from studies of co-management elsewhere. Anneke Swartbooi, who has spent a decade observing the committees through which fishing communities around several large African lakes share authority with government agencies, found that the committees were frequently dominated by boat owners and local notables. Hired crew, who make up the bulk of the workforce, were seldom represented, and the women who buy, process and trade most of the catch had almost no voice in decisions about it. Swartbooi concludes that co-management, far from empowering communities, can harden the inequalities that already exist within them. Her evidence is difficult to dispute. It does not follow, however, that a return to central control would be preferable, since the ministries that once ran these fisheries consulted crew members and traders even less.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why do some community arrangements flourish while others falter? Researchers at the Shoreline Tenure Observatory have compiled a database of more than one hundred and thirty cases from five continents in an attempt to answer this question. Their analysis suggests that the precise legal form of the rights matters less than two other factors: the degree of trust and cooperation that existed in a community before the reform, and the match between the size of the managed area and the movements of the species being fished. Territories work best for creatures that stay put, such as shellfish and seaweed, and far less well for fish that roam across many kilometres and therefore cannot be protected by any single association. This finding deserves more attention than it has received, because it implies that territorial rights are a tool for particular circumstances rather than a universal remedy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of these models allows the state to step aside. Communities can patrol their own grounds against members who break the rules, but they are seldom able to resist outsiders with larger boats and political connections. In one widely reported case, a fishing village that had managed its reef carefully for over a decade watched helplessly as industrial trawlers entered the area, while the authorities that had formally recognised the village's rights declined to intervene. Rights that cannot be defended are of little value, and the willingness of governments to back communities against powerful intruders is arguably the single most important condition for success.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The experience of the past three decades therefore offers a lesson in humility rather than a blueprint. Handing authority to fishers has produced some of the clearest conservation successes in small-scale fisheries, but also exclusion, displaced pressure and the entrenchment of local elites. The task now is less to promote any particular model than to understand, case by case, who gains and who loses when the sea is divided up, and to design arrangements flexible enough to be corrected when the answer proves uncomfortable.

topic: reducing bycatch of seabirds, turtles and other non-target animals: gear fixes, hard caps, electronic monitoring and discard bans
title: The Unwanted Catch
subtitle: Every year, fishing kills vast numbers of animals that nobody intended to catch. Can better gear and smarter rules change that?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every fishing method catches more than it is meant to. Longlines set for tuna hook albatrosses diving for bait; trawls dragged for shrimp scoop up sea turtles and young fish; gillnets entangle porpoises and seals. This unintended harvest, known as bycatch, is among the most serious pressures that fishing places on marine wildlife, yet estimates of its scale vary enormously, from under a tenth of the global catch to well over a third. Much of the variation stems from definition. Some researchers count only animals that are thrown back dead; others include unwanted fish that are landed and sold for low prices; still others exclude any species that is legally permitted. The dispute may sound pedantic, but it is not: the choice of definition largely determines whether bycatch appears to be a contained technical problem or a vast and systemic one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For some species, technical solutions have proved remarkably effective. Seabirds are typically caught when they seize baited hooks in the seconds before a longline sinks out of reach. Mateus Tavira, a seabird ecologist, tested three simple measures on commercial vessels: streamer lines that flutter above the baited hooks and scare birds away, small weights that make the line sink faster, and setting the lines at night, when most seabirds are not feeding. Used individually, each measure reduced bird deaths substantially; used together, they cut them by more than ninety per cent, with no measurable loss of the target fish. Because every hook taken by a bird is a hook that cannot catch a tuna, the measures also save fishers money. Bycatch reduction rarely offers such a neat alignment of conservation and commercial interest, which is precisely why this case is so often quoted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The history of the turtle excluder device is less straightforward. The device, a metal grid fitted inside a shrimp trawl, allows shrimp to pass through to the back of the net while deflecting larger animals out through an escape hatch. Trials showed that it released the great majority of turtles at the cost of only a small fraction of the shrimp catch. Yet fishers resisted it for years, convinced that it would empty their nets, and in some fleets the hatches were routinely sewn shut. Kalinda Burrage, a gear technologist who has worked with trawler crews for two decades, argues that the resistance had less to do with the actual losses than with the way the device was introduced: it was designed by outsiders and imposed by regulation. Her conclusion is that new equipment should be developed alongside the fishers who will use it, since a device that crews distrust will eventually be disabled.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Technology alone cannot solve problems that arise from incentives. The economist Grzegorz Sobczynski has championed a different instrument: a hard cap on the quantity of a protected species that a fleet may catch in a season, with the entire fishery closing once the cap is reached. Because a single careless vessel can end the season for everyone, fishers acquire a powerful collective interest in avoiding bycatch. In fleets where such caps operate, Sobczynski notes, skippers have begun sharing the locations of bycatch hotspots in real time, an innovation that no regulator required. The approach is impressive, but it depends entirely on knowing how much bycatch is actually being taken, and that is where most fisheries fall short.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In the majority of the world's fleets, fewer than five per cent of trips carry an independent observer, and some carry none at all. Electronic monitoring, in which cameras record activity on deck and the footage is reviewed later, promises far broader coverage at lower cost. Teuila Aumaivao, a policy analyst who works with Pacific island fleets, cautions that the technology raises genuine questions of privacy for crews who live on board for weeks, and that the cost of installation could be prohibitive for small operators. If requirements designed for wealthy fleets were applied universally, she warns, less prosperous fishers might be forced out of the industry. These concerns are legitimate, although the price of the equipment has fallen steeply in recent years and is likely to continue doing so.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The consequences of rules without monitoring are well illustrated by attempts to ban discarding. Several jurisdictions now require fishers to land everything they catch, rather than throwing unwanted fish back, in the hope that the cost of bringing worthless fish ashore will push crews to fish more selectively. In practice, compliance has been poor and difficult to verify, and the rules have accumulated so many exemptions that their effect is uncertain. The principle behind them is sound; without the means to check what happens at sea, however, it has remained largely symbolic.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the deepest difficulty is that bycatch occurs out of sight. Consumers see the fish on their plates, not the birds, turtles and juveniles that died alongside it. Labelling schemes that report the bycatch associated with particular products remain rare, yet making these hidden costs visible to those who buy seafood may ultimately do more to change fishing practices than any single regulation.

topic: the maximum sustainable yield concept in fisheries management and its scientific, ecological, economic and climate-related critics
title: The Elusive Surplus
subtitle: For seventy years, fisheries have been managed according to a single elegant number. Is it time to let it go?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in environmental science have shaped policy as profoundly as maximum sustainable yield. Its logic is elegant. A fish population that is far below its natural maximum grows quickly, because individuals have abundant food and space; a population close to that maximum grows slowly, because it is limited by competition. Somewhere between these extremes, typically at around half the population's unfished size, the annual increase is greatest, and this surplus can in principle be harvested indefinitely without depleting the stock. By the 1950s the concept had become the guiding principle of fisheries management, and it was later written into international agreements on the law of the sea. Its enduring appeal lies in its simplicity: a single number that tells managers how much may be taken. That same simplicity, however, is the source of its most serious weaknesses.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic model rests on assumptions that rarely hold in the real ocean. It supposes that the environment remains unchanging from year to year, that the population is close to a stable equilibrium, and that each species can be treated as if it existed alone. Linnea Bjurström, a stock assessment specialist at the Baltic Institute of Fisheries Science, has drawn attention to a more practical difficulty. Calculating the yield requires estimates of how fast a population grows and how large it would be if left unfished, and both quantities are notoriously hard to measure. Her simulations show that modest errors in these estimates can lead managers to overstate the sustainable catch considerably. Because the penalty for overestimation, a collapsing stock, is so much greater than the penalty for underestimation, a slightly smaller catch, she argues that fishing at the calculated maximum is, in practice, a recipe for gradual overfishing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the concept accept many of these criticisms but contend that they apply to an outdated version of it. Anouk Wijnbergen, a population modeller, points out that since the early 2000s many authorities have treated maximum sustainable yield not as a target to be reached but as a ceiling that must not be exceeded, with actual catches set some distance below it to allow for uncertainty. Several stocks managed in this way, she notes, have recovered substantially. The point is fair, and the recoveries are real. Yet the reinterpretation concedes much of what the critics originally argued: if the calculated yield must routinely be discounted because it cannot be trusted, its claim to identify the best possible catch has largely been abandoned.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection comes from ecologists who study whole food webs. Ebo Quansah-Turkson, a marine ecologist, notes that managers typically calculate a separate maximum yield for each commercially important species, as though the cod did not eat the herring and the herring did not eat the plankton on which young cod depend. Adding these figures together, he argues, produces a total catch that the ecosystem could never actually deliver, since reducing a prey species to half its natural size inevitably reduces the food available to its predators. The problem is especially acute for small, abundant forage fish such as sardines and anchovies, which sustain seabirds, marine mammals and larger fish. The case for harvesting these species well below their single-species maximum seems compelling, even if precisely how far below remains a matter of debate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Economists have raised a different challenge. Mariela Bidegaray, who studies the economics of natural resources, observes that the catch which maximises profit is generally reached at a lower level of fishing effort than the catch which maximises tonnage. Beyond a certain point, each additional boat adds more to costs than it adds to revenue. Managing for maximum economic yield therefore implies fewer vessels, larger fish stocks and higher returns, a combination that would seem to satisfy conservationists and industry alike. The principal objection is that fewer vessels mean fewer jobs, a serious matter in communities with few other sources of employment. That concern is not without substance, but it is worth noting that many of those jobs are currently sustained by public subsidies rather than by the fish themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Climate change adds a further layer of difficulty. As waters warm, the productivity of many stocks is shifting, rising in some places and falling in others, and some species are moving towards the poles altogether. Reference points calculated from decades of past data may therefore describe a stock that no longer exists in the same form. Some researchers now propose dynamic reference points, recalculated regularly as conditions change. Whatever their merits, the very need for them makes the notion of a single, permanent sustainable yield increasingly untenable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Why, then, does the concept persist? Part of the answer is institutional: it is embedded in legislation and treaties that are difficult to amend. Part is practical: managers need a figure, and alternatives such as ecosystem models are complex and themselves uncertain. Abandoning maximum sustainable yield entirely would be unwise, since it remains a useful benchmark against which to judge whether a stock is being fished too hard. What should be abandoned is the belief that it can, on its own, tell us how much of the sea's productivity humanity is entitled to take.

topic: ghost gear: lost and abandoned fishing nets, retrieval, gear marking, no-fault reporting, producer responsibility and biodegradable nets
title: Nets That Never Stop Fishing
subtitle: Lost and abandoned fishing gear goes on killing for years. Preventing it is proving harder than cleaning it up

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a fishing net is lost at sea, it does not stop working. Drifting with the currents or snagged on a reef, it continues to entangle fish, turtles, seals and seabirds, whose struggling bodies in turn attract scavengers that become trapped themselves. This process, known as ghost fishing, can persist for years, and in cold, deep water where nets degrade slowly, possibly for decades. Abandoned, lost and discarded gear is thought to make up a significant proportion of the large plastic debris floating in the oceans, and studies suggest that several per cent of all nets in use are lost each year. What sets ghost gear apart from most other marine litter is that it was designed specifically to capture animals, and it goes on doing exactly what it was made to do long after anyone has any use for the catch.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Understanding why gear is lost is essential to preventing it. Nets and pots may be torn away by storms, become caught on rocks or wrecks, or be destroyed when trawlers towing nets along the seabed drag through static gear set by other fishers. Some gear is also dumped deliberately, particularly where ports charge high disposal fees or lack facilities for receiving old nets. Ignatius Mchomvu, who has surveyed more than two thousand fishers across four oceans, insists that accidental loss accounts for the overwhelming majority of cases, and that policies which portray fishers as careless polluters are therefore misdirected. His evidence is persuasive, and the stereotype of the irresponsible fisher deserves to be retired. Nonetheless, in certain regions where disposal is costly and inspection rare, deliberate dumping is far from negligible, and any honest account of the problem must acknowledge it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most visible response has been retrieval. Volunteer divers, community groups and specialist organisations now recover many tonnes of gear every year, using sonar to locate nets on the seabed and lifting equipment to haul them to the surface. The Tidewrack Recovery Network, one of the largest such organisations, argues that its work does more than remove hazards: by recording where gear is found and what type it is, the network has built up a map of accumulation zones that can guide future prevention efforts. Critics note that retrieval is expensive, sometimes costing thousands of dollars per tonne, and that it addresses the consequences of loss rather than its causes. Both points are valid, but they do not make retrieval pointless. For the vast quantity of gear already lying on the seabed, recovery is the only remedy available, even if it can never keep pace with the rate at which new gear is lost.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Prevention begins with knowing whose gear is whose. Many authorities now require nets, buoys and pots to carry marks identifying their owner, so that lost items can be traced. Delwyn Prothero, a former fisheries inspector who now researches compliance, argues that marking on its own achieves little. In his experience, fishers who lose gear rarely report it, because they fear being fined or blamed for the damage it causes; marking simply makes them more anxious about being identified. Prothero proposes instead a system of no-fault reporting, in which fishers who promptly declare a loss face no penalty and may even receive help with recovery. Such an approach runs against the instinct of regulators to punish, but it reflects the reality that information is more valuable than fines when the aim is to find and remove lost gear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Economic instruments offer another route. Under deposit schemes, fishers pay a small charge when buying new gear and recover it when they return old gear to port. A more ambitious idea, extended producer responsibility, makes manufacturers financially responsible for their products at the end of their working lives. Ottavia Ravasenga, a specialist in environmental law, argues that this would give producers a strong reason to design nets that are easier to collect and recycle, for example by using a single type of plastic rather than mixtures that cannot be separated. Opponents point out that manufacturers will simply add the cost to the price of gear, so that fishers end up paying after all. Some passing on of costs is inevitable. Even so, the incentive to redesign products would remain, and that is the part of the scheme that matters most.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Technological optimists place their hopes in biodegradable gear, made from materials that break down after a period in the water so that lost nets eventually stop fishing. Trials have produced mixed results. Some experimental nets have shown lower catch efficiency than conventional ones, which makes fishers reluctant to adopt them, and the rate at which they degrade appears to vary greatly with water temperature, so that a net designed to disintegrate in two years in warm seas may last far longer in polar waters. The idea is attractive, but it is not yet ready to be required by regulation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No single measure will end ghost fishing, and the most effective strategies combine retrieval, marking, reporting and economic incentives. If one step deserves priority, however, it is probably the least glamorous: making it free and easy for fishers to dispose of old gear in port. Where that has been done, deliberate dumping has largely ceased, at a cost far below that of hauling nets from the seabed.

topic: seafood fraud and mislabelling: DNA barcoding surveys, traceability ledgers and the limits of ecolabels
title: What's Really on the Plate?
subtitle: Genetic testing has revealed that a surprising amount of seafood is not what its label claims. Stopping the substitution is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Seafood is the most heavily traded food commodity in the world. A fish caught off West Africa may be landed in Spain, filleted in China, frozen, breaded and sold in a supermarket in Canada, passing through the hands of a dozen companies on the way. At each stage the product loses some of the features that might reveal what it is: the head and skin are removed, the flesh is coated or cooked, and the original label is replaced. Long and opaque supply chains of this kind create countless opportunities to substitute one species for another, and when a cheap fish can be sold as an expensive one with little chance of detection, it would be surprising if nobody did so.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years, suspicions of seafood fraud were difficult to prove. That changed with the arrival of DNA barcoding, a technique that identifies a species by reading a short, standardised stretch of its genetic code and comparing it with a reference library. Dozens of surveys have since been carried out, reporting mislabelling rates ranging from a few per cent to more than a third of samples. One of the largest, led by the geneticist Ondine Kervella, analysed some twelve hundred samples bought from restaurants, fishmongers and supermarkets in nine cities. Just over a fifth were not the species stated on the label or menu. Mislabelling was most common in restaurants, particularly those serving raw fish, and in the great majority of cases the substitute was a cheaper species, frequently a farmed fish sold in place of a wild one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such figures make striking headlines, but not everyone accepts them at face value. Arvid Leinonen, an economist who studies the international seafood trade, argues that many surveys are designed in ways that inflate the apparent problem. Researchers naturally concentrate on species already known to be vulnerable to substitution, such as red snapper or tuna, rather than sampling the market at random. Moreover, a single species may be sold under different common names in different countries, and a label that is legally correct in one jurisdiction may be recorded as fraudulent in another. Leinonen's methodological objections are reasonable, and survey results should not be read as estimates for the seafood market as a whole. Yet even studies that sample randomly and apply local naming rules have found rates of substitution well above what could be explained by honest error.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences extend beyond consumers paying too much for an inferior product. Some substitutes carry health risks: escolar, an oily fish occasionally sold as white tuna, can cause unpleasant digestive problems, and species from regions where certain natural toxins are common may be passed off as safer alternatives. The conservation implications are arguably more serious still. When the identity of fish can be falsified at the point of sale, so can its origin, and fish caught illegally, or taken from overexploited stocks, can be laundered into legitimate markets under false names. Fraud at the fish counter is thus closely linked to the problem of illegal fishing far out at sea.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most widely promoted solution is traceability: a continuous record that follows each batch of fish from the vessel that caught it to the shop that sells it. Several governments now require catch documentation for imported fish, and some companies have experimented with digital ledgers that cannot be altered once an entry has been made. The Harbourside Seafood Integrity Consortium, an alliance of processors and retailers, ran a two-year pilot in which every box of fish carried a code linked to such a ledger, allowing buyers to view its entire history. The consortium reports that the system was popular with retailers and reduced paperwork. However, a record that cannot be altered is not the same as a record that is accurate. If the species or catch location is entered incorrectly at the first step, whether by mistake or by design, the system will faithfully preserve the error all the way to the consumer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ecolabels, which certify that seafood comes from a fishery assessed as sustainable, have also been presented as a defence against fraud. The consumer researcher Thandeka Mvelase found, however, that fewer than one shopper in five could correctly explain what the most common label meant, and that most did not look for it when buying fish. In her view, ecolabels function chiefly as a tool for large retailers, who use certification to meet procurement commitments, rather than as a guide for individual consumers. The premium that certified products command at the till is typically small. One encouraging finding is that certified products appear to be mislabelled far less often than others: DNA tests of several hundred certified items found substitution in fewer than one per cent of cases, presumably because certification requires chain-of-custody checks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No system based purely on paperwork, whether printed or digital, can by itself guarantee that the fish matches its label. What makes fraud unattractive is the realistic prospect of being caught. Regular, unannounced DNA testing at every stage of the supply chain, combined with penalties large enough to outweigh the profits of substitution, would do more to protect consumers and fish stocks than any number of labels.

topic: the Great Green Wall: tree planting versus farmer-managed natural regeneration in the Sahel
title: A Wall That Is Not a Wall
subtitle: Africa's most ambitious response to desertification has quietly abandoned its founding idea, and may be better for it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When African heads of state endorsed the Great Green Wall in 2007, the image at its centre was strikingly simple: a belt of trees some fifteen kilometres wide, stretching almost eight thousand kilometres from Senegal in the west to Djibouti in the east, holding back the advance of the Sahara. The image was persuasive precisely because it was visual. A wall suggests a front line, an enemy and a defensive structure that can be built, measured and photographed. Yet the premise on which it rested, that the desert is a single body moving steadily southwards, had already been questioned by dryland scientists for two decades, and the history of the project since then is largely the story of that premise being dismantled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most direct evidence came from the ground. Adjovi Kpodar, a forester at the Sahelian Institute for Woody Resources, spent six years revisiting plantations established during the project's first phase. Of the seedlings she was able to trace, she estimates that fewer than one in five was alive after three dry seasons. Kpodar does not attribute these losses mainly to drought. Instead she points to the way planting was organised: seedlings were raised in distant nurseries, delivered at whatever time suited the transport schedule rather than the rains, and left without anyone responsible for watering them or protecting them from livestock. In her view, the failures were administrative rather than ecological, which is in one sense encouraging, since administration is easier to change than climate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of evidence came from above. Lars Strandskogen, who leads a remote-sensing group at the Bergen Centre for Earth Observation, has compared satellite imagery of the Sahel over four decades and found that many districts are considerably greener now than in the drought years of the 1980s. Crucially, however, the densest new tree cover does not coincide with official plantations. It appears instead on ordinary farmland, where cultivators have allowed stumps and roots left in the soil to resprout, selecting and pruning the strongest shoots. This practice, usually called farmer-managed natural regeneration, costs almost nothing, uses species already adapted to local conditions, and produces trees that belong to the people who tend them. Strandskogen goes so far as to argue that the bulk of the Sahel's recent regreening has taken place despite large planting schemes rather than because of them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That claim deserves some caution. Satellite sensors detect vegetation, not its cause, and a wetter run of years since the 1990s has undoubtedly contributed to the greening that Strandskogen describes. To credit farmers with the whole of it is to replace one simple story with another. Nevertheless, the broad point stands: where trees have actually returned, they have generally been grown by local people on their own land, not imposed upon it from outside.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, did natural regeneration take so long to spread? Ricardo Terrazas-Bello, a legal scholar at the Iberian Institute of Agrarian Law who specialises in land tenure, locates the answer in colonial forestry codes, several of which survived independence almost unchanged. Under these laws, trees on farmland were the property of the state, and a farmer who cut a branch without a permit could be fined. The rational response was to remove young trees before they became valuable enough to attract official attention. Terrazas-Bello notes that the districts where regeneration expanded most rapidly were those in which the law was reformed, or at least ceased to be enforced, during the 1980s and 1990s. Ownership, he concludes, did more to restore the land than any seed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Partly in response to such findings, the Great Green Wall was formally redefined in the 2010s. It is now described not as a line of trees but as a mosaic of land-use interventions, including water harvesting, grazing management, regenerated farmland and village woodlots, spread across a broad zone. Most specialists welcomed the change. Zarina Ismatova, a political economist at the Steppe Institute for Development Policy, is less convinced that it amounts to more than a change of vocabulary. She observes that the image of the wall remains central to the project's fundraising, because donors find a continental belt of trees easier to support than thousands of small, unglamorous local schemes. In her assessment, the project is now caught between what works on the ground and what attracts money abroad.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ismatova's analysis is perceptive, although it underplays the value of a powerful symbol. Without the drama of a wall, it is doubtful that dryland restoration would have secured anything like the attention it now receives at international summits. The more serious difficulty lies elsewhere. Progress reports continue to measure success in hectares 'treated' and seedlings planted, figures that say nothing about whether the trees survive or whether the households living among them are any better off. Until the indicators change, the incentives that produced the empty plantations Kpodar documented will remain firmly in place.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of this means the original vision was worthless. It drew attention to a region that had long been neglected, and it brought eleven governments into a common framework for the first time. But the experience offers a broader lesson about environmental policy. The most effective interventions are often those that remove obstacles to what people already know how to do, and these are, almost by definition, the hardest to display on a map.

topic: biological soil crusts in drylands: their functions, fragility and restoration
title: The Crust Beneath Our Feet
subtitle: A barely visible layer of microbes, lichens and mosses may matter more to the health of deserts than the plants that grow above it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most visitors to a desert walk across a dark, slightly crunchy surface without giving it a second thought. What they are treading on is a biological soil crust: a community of cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses and fungi that lives in the top few millimetres of the ground. Such crusts are thought to cover around a tenth of the earth's land surface, and in some arid regions they occupy most of the open ground between shrubs. For much of the twentieth century they were dismissed by range managers as dirt, or at best as a curiosity for specialists. That neglect is difficult to justify, because the crust performs functions on which almost everything else in a dryland depends.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The microbiologist Yusra Al-Hadrami, of the Gulf Institute of Arid Microbiology, has spent much of her career documenting those functions. Cyanobacteria, she explains, produce long filaments coated in sticky sugars, which wind between sand grains and bind them into a coherent mat that resists being lifted by the wind. Many crust organisms also take nitrogen from the air and convert it into a form plants can use; in some deserts, this is the principal source of nitrogen available to vegetation. Al-Hadrami goes further, arguing that because crusts respond to disturbance faster than shrubs or grasses do, a decline in crust cover may reveal that land is degrading years before any change in the plants becomes apparent.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The crust's great weakness is its fragility. Its organisms are active only when moist, and in many deserts they may remain dry and dormant for months at a time. In that state they are brittle, and a single footstep or tyre track can shatter structures that took decades to form. Cyanobacteria may recolonise a damaged patch within a few years, but lichens and mosses can take far longer, sometimes centuries in the driest regions. Livestock are a particular concern. Brecht Vossaert, a grazing ecologist with the Flemish Rangeland Research Group, recorded steep declines in crust cover as herd densities rose. Significantly, though, the damage depended on timing: animals grazing during the wet season, when crusts were damp and pliable, did far less harm than the same animals in the dry months. Vossaert therefore recommends restricting grazing to the wetter part of the year rather than removing livestock altogether. His proposal is sensible, but on communally owned land, where no single authority decides when herds move, it would be very hard to put into practice.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Climate change presents a less obvious threat. A team led by Aisha Nankoma at the Kalahari Field Station has spent nine years manipulating experimental plots, warming some and altering the pattern of rainfall on others. The most striking result concerned mosses. When rain arrived as frequent light showers rather than occasional heavy downpours, mosses died in large numbers, even where the total amount of water was unchanged. Each brief wetting appears to wake the plants, which then use up stored carbon in resuming activity but dry out again before they can photosynthesise enough to replace it. As the mosses disappear, they are replaced by paler cyanobacterial crusts, so the ground reflects more sunlight than before. Some commentators have suggested that this might slightly offset local warming. It would be a mistake to treat this as good news, since the change also reduces the crust's capacity to capture nitrogen and hold soil in place.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Can lost crust be put back? Earlier attempts, which simply scattered crushed crust collected from intact sites, merely moved the damage from one place to another.Tomasz Przybylek, who directs a restoration programme at the Silesian Centre for Dryland Ecology, has developed methods for growing crust organisms in greenhouse nurseries and spreading them over degraded ground. In cooler, moister drylands the results have been encouraging, with treated plots developing a stable crust within two or three years. In the hottest deserts, however, much of the material has been scorched before it could establish. Przybylek acknowledges that the technique is currently expensive but is confident that costs will fall sharply once production is scaled up. Even if he is right, restoration will remain slow and uncertain, and the more effective use of limited funds is surely to protect the crusts that still exist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the broadest lesson of crust research is how much of a dryland's functioning is concentrated in a layer thinner than a coin. Land managers routinely count shrubs, measure grass cover and estimate the number of animals the land can support, yet crusts rarely appear in their surveys at all. Part of the reason is practical: crust cover is hard to estimate from a moving vehicle, and distinguishing a healthy lichen crust from a disturbed one requires training that few field staff receive. Another part is cultural, since a landscape is still judged largely by what grows tall enough to be seen from a distance. Neither obstacle is insurmountable. Simple photographic methods, developed in several national parks, allow untrained volunteers to record crust condition in a matter of minutes. Monitoring that ignores them is, in a real sense, measuring the wrong thing.

topic: overgrazing, herd mobility and the equilibrium versus non-equilibrium debate in dryland rangelands
title: Grazing on Shifting Ground
subtitle: Are pastoral herders the cause of dryland degradation, or its most experienced managers?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the explanation for degraded rangelands seemed self-evident: there were simply too many animals. Colonial administrators, and later the development agencies that succeeded them, observed bare ground around villages, counted the livestock nearby and concluded that herders kept more animals than the land could feed. An influential theoretical argument lent weight to this conclusion. Because grazing land was held in common, it ran, each herder gained the full benefit of an extra animal, while the costs of overgrazing were shared by all; the rational individual would therefore keep adding stock until the pasture collapsed. Policies followed naturally from the diagnosis, in the form of destocking campaigns, fencing schemes and programmes to settle mobile families in permanent villages. The logic was admirably neat. Its record in practice, however, is far less impressive, and over the past four decades the assumptions behind it have been steadily eroded.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The original view still has able defenders. Dirk Ellerbroek, a modeller at the Low Countries Institute for Rangeland Science, treats each pasture as having a carrying capacity: the number of animals it can support indefinitely without deteriorating. Sustained grazing above that level, he argues, removes perennial grasses, whose deep roots hold the soil, and allows them to be replaced by unpalatable shrubs or by bare ground. Ellerbroek accepts that capacity rises and falls from one year to the next, but insists that a long-term average remains a valuable guide when governments come to set stocking limits. He is right that heavy grazing can degrade land, and few ecologists would seriously dispute it. The question is how often, and where, the conditions his models assume actually hold.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Oyunchimeg Enkhjargal, who has worked for twenty years at the Gobi Steppe Research Station, believes those conditions are rarer than is generally supposed. In the regions she studies, annual rainfall can easily double or halve from one year to the next, and the amount of grass available tracks the rain far more closely than it tracks the number of animals. Severe droughts and harsh winters periodically kill a large proportion of the livestock, so herds seldom stay at high densities long enough to inflict lasting harm. In such systems, which ecologists call non-equilibrium, Enkhjargal argues that a fixed carrying capacity is close to meaningless: an average figure describes a year that never actually occurs. After good rains, she has found, even heavily grazed pasture recovers within a single season.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, though, to conclude that grazing pressure is irrelevant in variable environments. Enkhjargal herself notes that during the dry season animals crowd around permanent water sources such as wells and boreholes, and that the degradation in these places is both severe and persistent. Such key resource areas help to reconcile the two positions. The steppe as a whole may behave as a non-equilibrium system, but the patches on which herds depend in the leanest months behave much more like the pastures in Ellerbroek's models.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If concentration is the problem, mobility may be the solution, and this is the argument advanced by Nadia Bouhafsi, an anthropologist at the Maghreb Centre for Pastoral Studies. Herders, she points out, have traditionally moved between seasonal pastures, following the rain and avoiding prolonged pressure on any single area. In her fieldwork, the most badly damaged land coincided not with unusually large herds but with the loss of movement, as families settled near schools, clinics and new boreholes funded by development programmes. The irony, in Bouhafsi's account, is that settlement and fencing, introduced to protect pasture, generated exactly the concentrated grazing they had been intended to prevent. Her evidence is persuasive, yet she perhaps romanticises mobile life. Many families settle for entirely sensible reasons, such as education and health care, and no policy is likely to reverse that choice.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication comes from markets. Amaru Ebersole, an economist at the Altiplano Institute of Applied Economics, has examined the rapid growth in herd sizes that followed the privatisation of state livestock in parts of Central Asia during the 1990s. He links much of this growth to international demand for cashmere, which has encouraged herders to keep ever larger numbers of goats. Goats are especially damaging to fragile pasture, because their sharp hooves break up the surface and because they tend to pull plants up by the roots rather than cropping them. In this case, Ebersole argues, herd growth reflects a response to global prices rather than a failure to manage shared land. His work makes it clear that the degradation question cannot be settled by ecology alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has therefore shifted from apportioning blame towards a more varied picture, in which the same herd may be harmless on one pasture and destructive on another. The practical implication is that policies ought to be judged primarily by whether they preserve the ability of herders to move, rather than by counts of animals alone. That is not to say that numbers never matter; where goat herds have multiplied in response to distant markets, some reduction may well be unavoidable. But the old reflex of blaming the herder has done considerable damage of its own, and it deserves to be retired.

topic: satellite monitoring of dryland degradation: vegetation indices, Sahel greening and the limits of remote sensing
title: Reading the Land from Orbit
subtitle: Satellites have transformed the measurement of dryland degradation, but what they reveal depends on how their data are interpreted

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, estimates of how much of the world's dryland was turning into desert varied so widely that they were almost meaningless. Some assessments suggested that as much as seventy per cent of agricultural drylands had been degraded; others put the figure at less than a fifth. Most relied on the judgement of regional experts, who were asked to classify the land they knew on a simple scale from 'light' to 'extreme' degradation, and their answers inevitably reflected local preoccupations as much as measurable change. When satellite records of vegetation became available in the early 1980s, many scientists hoped that the question would at last be settled by observation rather than opinion. Four decades later, that hope has been only partly fulfilled. Satellites have certainly replaced guesswork with data, but the data have turned out to be far less self-explanatory than their early advocates assumed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely used measure is a vegetation index derived from the way leaves interact with sunlight. Healthy green plants absorb most of the red light that falls on them, using it for photosynthesis, while strongly reflecting light in the near-infrared part of the spectrum. By comparing the two, a sensor orbiting hundreds of kilometres above the ground can estimate how much living vegetation each patch of land supports. When researchers assembled these images into a continuous record, the result was a surprise. Across large parts of the Sahel, the belt of semi-arid land south of the Sahara, the land had become noticeably greener since the catastrophic droughts of the early 1980s. Dr Saule Tursynbekova of the Steppe Observation Institute regards this as decisive evidence that the popular image of an advancing desert was exaggerated from the start. In her view, the region's vegetation has demonstrated a resilience that earlier, more pessimistic accounts failed to anticipate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the greening represents genuine recovery. Rainfall in the Sahel also increased over the same period, and since plant growth in drylands is closely tied to precipitation, a greener landscape may simply be a wetter one. To separate the two influences, Dr Mateus Quintela and colleagues at the Lusophone Centre for Arid Studies developed what has become known as the residual method. They first calculate how green a given area ought to be, given the rain it received, and then compare this prediction with what the satellite actually recorded. Land that consistently produces less vegetation than its rainfall would predict is flagged as degraded, even if it appears to be greening in absolute terms. Applying this technique, Quintela's team identified scattered pockets of decline concealed within the broader trend of improvement, particularly around market towns and along major roads.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns what the index actually measures. Greenness is not the same as ecological health, still less as usefulness to the people who depend on the land. In parts of southern Africa, the rangeland ecologist Dr Adaeze Ezenwa has documented the spread of thorny shrubs into former grassland, a process that makes the land greener from above while sharply reducing the grazing available to cattle. Invasive grasses can produce a similar illusion. Ezenwa insists that satellite trends must be checked against measurements taken on foot, and her own transects revealed several sites that the imagery had classed as improving but that local herders regarded as ruined. Of all the limitations of remote sensing, this seems to me the most serious, because it cannot be solved by better sensors or cleverer statistics: it arises from the gap between what a machine can detect and what a landscape is worth.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also the awkward matter of where any trend begins. The satellite record starts at almost exactly the moment when the Sahel was at its driest in living memory, so nearly any subsequent change was bound to look like an improvement. Had continuous observation begun in the wetter 1950s, the same landscape might appear to have declined. This does not invalidate the greening findings, but it does mean that the choice of baseline can quietly determine the conclusion, and researchers ought to state explicitly which years they have used and why.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Spatial resolution poses a further difficulty. The sensors that provide the longest records divide the earth into cells several kilometres across, and within each cell the readings are averaged. Severe but localised damage, such as the bare ground that often forms around a borehole where herds gather to drink, may be invisible at this scale, diluted by healthier land nearby. Newer instruments can distinguish features only ten or twenty metres wide, yet their records extend back little more than a decade, which is too short to separate lasting change from the ordinary fluctuations of a variable climate. Researchers are therefore forced to choose between long but coarse records and detailed but brief ones, and neither option is entirely satisfactory.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that satellites have failed. They have exposed the weakness of the older expert assessments and have made it impossible to claim, without evidence, that deserts are spreading relentlessly. Tursynbekova has called for international agencies to agree on a single global estimate of degraded land derived from satellite data, arguing that policymakers need one authoritative number. The appeal of such a figure is obvious, but I believe it would be a mistake. A single number would conceal precisely the disagreements over method, baseline and meaning that the past four decades have brought to light. Maps that show where estimates are confident and where they remain doubtful would be less convenient, but considerably more honest.

topic: desert dust storms: long-range transport, ecological fertilisation, human contribution and health effects
title: The Wandering Soil
subtitle: Dust lifted from the world's drylands crosses oceans and continents, and scientists disagree about how much of it is our own doing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, winds lift somewhere between one and three billion tonnes of mineral dust from the world's drylands and carry it into the atmosphere. Satellite images regularly show tawny plumes streaming westward from the Sahara across the Atlantic, or eastward from the deserts of central Asia over the Pacific. For most of the twentieth century, such events were treated as little more than a local nuisance, a matter of grit in machinery and reduced visibility at airports. Today dust is recognised as an active component of the earth system, affecting climate, ocean chemistry and human health. This change of perspective is welcome and overdue. Yet it has also encouraged some rather simplistic stories, in which dust is cast either as a hidden benefactor of distant ecosystems or as an unambiguous symptom of human mismanagement of the land.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dust emission begins when the wind blowing across a dry surface exceeds a critical speed, at which point loose particles start to bounce along the ground and dislodge finer material. Vegetation, stones and the living crusts formed by microorganisms all raise this threshold, which is why undisturbed land releases relatively little dust even in strong winds. Once airborne, coarse grains fall back within a few kilometres, but the finest particles, smaller than a hundredth of a millimetre, can remain aloft for a week or more and travel several thousand kilometres. A disproportionate share of the global total comes from a handful of hotspots, most famously the Bodélé Depression in Chad, a dried lake bed whose powdery sediments are scoured by funnelled winds for much of the year.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The atmospheric chemist Dr Sawsan Elbadawi, of the Nile Basin Atmospheric Laboratory, has spent much of her career tracing what happens when this material comes down. Desert dust is rich in phosphorus and iron, nutrients that are scarce in many ecosystems. Elbadawi's measurements suggest that dust deposition supplies a significant fraction of the phosphorus used by parts of the Amazon rainforest, whose ancient, heavily leached soils retain little of their own, while iron falling on remote oceans can stimulate the growth of plankton. She warns that efforts to suppress dust could therefore have unforeseen consequences for ecosystems on the other side of the world. The caution is reasonable as far as it goes, but it should not be stretched into an argument against soil conservation. Much of the dust that matters most for distant forests comes from natural hotspots that no conservation programme is likely to touch.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of how much dust humans are responsible for is more contentious. Professor Tomasz Brzezinski, a palaeoclimatologist at the Baltic Institute of Earth History, has analysed layered sediments from West African lakes and coastal seabeds, which preserve a year-by-year archive of the dust that settled on them. His records show deposition rising sharply from the mid-nineteenth century onwards, a period that coincides with the expansion of commercial agriculture across the Sahel and North Africa. On this basis, he estimates that land use may now account for between a quarter and a half of the region's dust output, and he regards the ploughing of marginal land as the principal driver.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Kamran Durrani, who models dust emissions at the Institute for Desert Meteorology, finds these figures implausible. In his simulations, the great natural hotspots dominate so heavily that changes in farming could only ever make a modest contribution to the total. He also points out that the nineteenth-century increase in Brzezinski's sediments overlaps with a series of severe droughts, and that drier conditions alone would be expected to raise dust levels whether or not the land was being farmed. Durrani is especially critical of policies that single out smallholder farmers as the culprits, arguing that they are being blamed for a phenomenon that is largely beyond their control.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third perspective shifts attention from quantities to consequences. Dr Ines Larrain, an environmental epidemiologist, studies the effects of dust on the people who breathe it. Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs, and in several West African cities hospital admissions for respiratory illness climb steeply during the dusty months. Outbreaks of meningitis also tend to occur in the dry, dusty season, although whether dust plays a direct role remains uncertain. Larrain's key observation is that the origin of dust matters as much as its volume: particles blown from farmland on the edges of towns are released close to where people live, whereas dust from remote hotspots is often diluted by the time it reaches populated areas.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It seems to me that Larrain's point largely dissolves the dispute between Brzezinski and Durrani. Even if Durrani is right that human activity contributes only a small share of the global total, that share is generated precisely where it does most harm to human health. The case for reducing dust from cultivated land does not depend on resolving how large that share is. Nor should the debate over global budgets distract from simpler measures, such as forecasting systems that warn residents and hospitals of approaching storms, which several countries have begun to introduce.

topic: fog harvesting in coastal deserts: collector design, site selection and community maintenance
title: Drinking from the Clouds
subtitle: Nets that capture fog can supply water in places where it almost never rains, but their promise has often been overstated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Along a few stretches of coastline, the driest places on earth sit beside the ocean. In the Atacama of northern Chile, the Namib of south-western Africa and the Atlantic fringe of southern Morocco, rain may not fall for years, yet banks of fog roll inland from the cold sea on most mornings. Some desert organisms depend on it entirely. A species of beetle in the Namib, for example, stands on dune crests with its back tilted into the wind, allowing droplets to gather on its shell and trickle towards its mouth. Engineers have long hoped to imitate such creatures on a human scale, and since the 1980s hundreds of fog-collecting nets have been erected in coastal drylands. Fog harvesting has, I think, been oversold as an answer to the world's water problems. Yet in the right places, and under the right conditions, it can make a real difference to people's lives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle is simple. A fog collector is essentially a vertical sheet of fine mesh stretched between two posts and positioned at right angles to the prevailing wind. Fog droplets, each a small fraction of a millimetre across, are carried through the mesh, and some collide with its fibres. There they merge with other droplets until they become heavy enough to run down into a gutter and from there into a storage tank. The difficulty is that the standard polyethylene mesh captures only a modest proportion of the water passing through it. Making the mesh denser might seem an obvious remedy, but a tighter weave acts more like a wall: the wind, and the fog it carries, is deflected around the edges instead of passing through. A mesh that is too open, by contrast, lets most droplets slip between its fibres untouched.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For Dr Valentina Huanca, a hydrologist who has measured fog in the Atacama for more than two decades, the design of the net matters far less than where it is placed. Her records show that yields can differ tenfold between sites only a few hundred metres apart, depending on altitude, the angle of the slope and exposure to the sea breeze. The most productive locations tend to be ridges that face the ocean at the height where the fog bank typically meets the land. Huanca recommends that no full-scale installation be built until small standard collectors have been operated on the site for at least a full year, since fog varies markedly from season to season and a few weeks of promising readings can be badly misleading.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others have concentrated on improving the collectors themselves. At the Nordic Laboratory for Surface Engineering, the materials scientist Dr Pernille Arvidsson has developed meshes coated to imitate the Namib beetle's shell, which combines water-attracting bumps with water-repelling channels that speed drainage. Her team has also tested designs made of parallel vertical wires, rather like the strings of a harp, which are less prone to clogging. Under controlled conditions in a wind tunnel, some of these designs captured roughly three times as much water as conventional netting. These are impressive results, but they should be treated with caution. Laboratory winds are steady and the air is clean, whereas in the field collectors face dust, intense ultraviolet light and occasional storms, all of which can degrade delicate coatings. Until the new materials have survived several years outdoors, claims that they will transform fog harvesting are premature.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A quite different perspective comes from Professor Lahcen Zerrouki, a social scientist at the Institute of Saharan Studies, who has followed a fog-harvesting project in the mountains of south-western Morocco for over a decade. He attributes its success above all to the involvement of local women, who had traditionally walked for hours each day to fetch water and therefore had the strongest interest in keeping the nets in good repair. Zerrouki contrasts this with earlier schemes in other countries, many of which collapsed once the external funding ran out, leaving torn nets and rusting posts behind. In his view, the technology is the easy part; the harder task is ensuring that someone feels responsible for it after the engineers and donors have left.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even well-run projects produce limited quantities. A typical large collector yields a few hundred litres on a good day, and much less during the clear months when fog is scarce. This is enough to supply drinking water to a small village, to support a school, or to keep tree seedlings alive while their roots become established. It is nowhere near enough for the irrigation of commercial crops, which demand vastly greater volumes. Some enthusiasts have suggested that arrays of fog nets could one day supply entire coastal cities. Such proposals, in my view, ignore the arithmetic: the quantities involved are simply too small, and the land suitable for collectors too scarce, for fog ever to rival conventional sources of supply.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A final uncertainty is climate change. Coastal fog depends on a delicate balance between cold ocean water and warmer air above, and there are indications that fog has become less frequent along some coastlines over recent decades, although the records are patchy. If fog patterns shift, sites selected on the basis of past measurements may become far less productive. This seems to me a strong argument for favouring small, inexpensive installations that can be moved or abandoned without great loss, rather than large fixed systems whose costs can only be recovered over many years.

topic: the history of the 'advancing desert' idea: colonial origins of the desertification narrative and its later critics
title: The Desert That Never Marched
subtitle: How a vivid image of creeping sand came to shape a century of policy, and why rejecting it carries its own risks

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few environmental images have proved as durable as that of the desert on the march. Politicians, journalists and textbook writers have described sand dunes advancing across farmland at a steady rate of several kilometres a year, swallowing villages as they go. The picture is dramatic, easy to grasp and apparently self-evident. It is also, for the most part, wrong. What is remarkable is not that the image arose, since drylands can indeed deteriorate badly, but that it has survived for so long when the evidence supporting it has always been so thin. Understanding why requires a look at where the idea came from and whose purposes it served.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The notion of an encroaching desert took shape in the 1920s and 1930s among colonial foresters and administrators in West and North Africa. Many of them were convinced that the Sahara was expanding southwards and that the cause lay in indigenous land use: the burning of grassland, the clearing of woodland for shifting cultivation and, above all, the grazing of livestock by nomadic herders. Professor Nino Tsereteli, a historian of science at the Caucasus Institute for Environmental History, has examined the reports these officials produced. She argues that their conclusions owed less to measurement than to conviction, and that the narrative was convenient for colonial governments, since it justified the creation of forest reserves, restrictions on the movement of herds and greater administrative control over land that had previously been managed by local communities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Doubts surfaced early. A survey expedition sent to the southern edge of the Sahara in the late 1930s found little evidence that sand was moving into cultivated areas, and reported that the vegetation fluctuated with rainfall rather than retreating steadily. Its findings, however, made little impression on official thinking. The narrative returned with full force during the catastrophic Sahel droughts of the late 1960s and 1970s, when images of dying cattle and abandoned villages reached a global audience. Widely quoted estimates suggested that the desert edge was moving south by several kilometres a year. Many of these figures, it later emerged, rested on comparisons between surveys carried out in unusually wet years and observations made at the height of the drought, so that a temporary contraction of vegetation was mistaken for a permanent advance.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most direct challenge came once long satellite records became available. Dr Ebere Amadi, a geographer at the West African Centre for Land Observation, used these records to reconstruct the position of the boundary between desert and semi-desert over several decades. Her reconstruction shows no steady southward front. Instead, the boundary swings back and forth by tens or even hundreds of kilometres in step with rainfall, expanding in dry years and retreating in wet ones. Where lasting damage does occur, Amadi found, it appears as scattered patches around wells, towns and heavily used tracks, rather than as a line moving across the map. Amadi does not deny that the droughts caused immense suffering, but she argues that describing them as the leading edge of an expanding desert confused a temporary climatic shock with a lasting transformation of the landscape.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These findings have prompted a reassessment of the policies that the narrative inspired. Professor Oskar Kvasnicka, a development economist, has traced their effects across several countries: belts of trees planted along the supposed desert margin, programmes to persuade nomadic herders to settle in permanent villages, and bans on the use of fire. He concludes that such measures frequently undermined the livelihoods of the very people they were meant to protect, since mobility and controlled burning were often sensible responses to an unpredictable climate. Yet Kvasnicka also acknowledges that the alarm brought international investment into regions that had previously received almost none. He is right to make this concession, because a purely negative account of the period would be as one-sided as the narrative it criticises.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Indeed, the revisionist case carries a risk of its own. Having discovered that the desert is not marching, some commentators have slipped into implying that dryland degradation is largely imaginary. Dr Ayşe Karaoglu, a soil scientist at the Anatolian Research Station for Arid Lands, warns against this conclusion. Her long-term field plots record substantial losses of topsoil and organic matter on overcultivated land in several regions, even where satellites show little change in overall greenness. On this point, Karaoglu seems to me entirely correct: the fact that degradation does not take the form of an advancing front does not mean it is not happening.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The international definition of desertification has since been revised. It now refers broadly to land degradation in drylands resulting from various factors, including climatic variations and human activities, and makes no mention of moving sand. Some researchers now avoid the word altogether, preferring more neutral phrases, although these have attracted even less public interest. This is undoubtedly more accurate than the old image. It is also so broad that it can be stretched to cover almost any unwelcome change in a dry landscape, and it lacks the power to capture public imagination. Accuracy has been gained, but at the cost of the attention that a vivid image once commanded.

topic: controlling mobile sand dunes: straw checkerboards, chemical stabilisers, planting and living with moving sand
title: Taming the Dunes
subtitle: Engineers and ecologists have devised many ways of stopping sand from burying roads and fields, but none of them works for long on its own

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In parts of northern China, the Arabian Peninsula and the Sahel, roads, railways and irrigation canals are periodically buried by sand. A single crescent-shaped dune can move tens of metres in a year, and a field of such dunes can engulf an oasis within a generation. Here, at least, the familiar image of encroaching desert has a basis in fact: whatever the doubts about the wider idea of a desert spreading along a front, individual dunes undeniably travel. The response has typically been to fight them with engineering, and a remarkable range of techniques has been developed. Yet most of these methods deal with the symptom rather than the cause, since they do little about the loss of vegetation that set the sand moving in the first place. The most lasting results, I would argue, come from combining physical barriers with living plants.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To understand why dunes move, it helps to follow a single grain. When the wind is strong enough, grains are lifted briefly into the air and land a short distance downwind, knocking other grains loose in turn. On a dune, this process carries sand up the gentle windward slope to the crest, where it accumulates until it becomes unstable and avalanches down the steep slip face on the other side. Repeated millions of times, this transfer of sand from one side of the dune to the other causes the whole structure to advance. Small dunes contain less sand and therefore travel faster than large ones, and because the quantity of sand moved rises steeply with wind speed, a few stormy days can account for most of a year's movement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the most widely used defences is strikingly simple. Workers press bundles of straw vertically into the sand to form a grid of squares, each about a metre across, with stalks protruding some fifteen centimetres above the surface. These checkerboards add surface roughness, slowing the wind close to the ground so that it can no longer lift grains. Dr Batzorig Dorjsuren of the Gobi Institute of Applied Ecology has monitored checkerboards beside desert railways for many years. He has found that the sheltered sand inside each square soon develops a thin biological crust, and that wind-blown seeds lodge there and germinate, gradually binding the surface. The weakness, he notes, is that straw decays within five to ten years, so the grids must be replaced repeatedly unless plants have taken hold in the meantime, and in remote areas obtaining enough straw can itself be expensive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A quicker alternative is to spray the surface with a chemical binder. Oil-based mulches were once common, but their environmental effects have made them unpopular, and attention has shifted to biodegradable polymers that glue grains together into a thin, porous layer. Dr Hamid Esfahani, a soil engineer at the Plateau Centre for Arid Engineering, has tested several such products. He does not claim that they can halt dunes indefinitely; rather, he sees them as a way of holding the surface still for a season or two, long enough for seedlings to become established. That seems to me the right way to regard them. As a temporary aid to planting they have obvious value, but as a permanent solution they are at best a costly stop-gap, since the layer breaks down and must be renewed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Planting, then, is central to almost every long-term strategy, but what is planted matters greatly. The ecologist Dr Giulia Ricciardelli has studied shelterbelts in several dryland regions and is critical of schemes that rely on fast-growing trees with high water requirements. In some districts, she reports, such plantations have lowered the water table to the point where both the trees and nearby crops began to die. She recommends native shrubs and drought-tolerant grasses instead, which are less conspicuous but far more likely to survive without irrigation. Her concern is well founded, for survival rates among planted trees in dry regions are often disappointingly low.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical position is taken by Dr Moses Kipruto, a geomorphologist who questions whether dunes should always be stopped at all. Mobile sand, he points out, is a natural feature of many deserts and provides habitat for specialised insects, reptiles and plants that cannot survive on stabilised ground. Kipruto argues that new infrastructure should be designed to coexist with moving sand: routing roads around the most active dune fields, building elevated roads that allow sand to blow underneath without accumulating, and placing fences upwind to trap sand before it arrives, accepting that such fences must be raised as they fill.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Kipruto's approach is attractive, and for new projects it deserves serious consideration. For towns and farms that already exist in the path of moving dunes, however, it offers little; nobody can reroute an oasis. In such places, the combination of checkerboards and carefully chosen vegetation remains the most reliable defence available. What all these methods share is a need for long-term maintenance, and it is here, rather than in the techniques themselves, that most sand control projects fail. Grids are installed with great publicity, funding ends, and within a decade the straw has rotted and the sand is moving once more.
