topic: ancient runoff farming in the Negev highlands: dating the terraces, the purpose of stone mounds and the causes of abandonment
title: Harvesting the Desert Rain
subtitle: The ruins of ancient farms in one of the driest corners of the Middle East raise questions about who built them, how they worked and why they failed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Negev highlands receive, on average, around a hundred millimetres of rain a year, less than a quarter of what conventional rain-fed cereal farming normally requires. Yet the valleys of this stony plateau are crossed by thousands of low stone walls, and the slopes above them are scored with channels and scattered with heaps of rubble. These are the remains of an agricultural system that once supported towns, monasteries and vineyards in a landscape that today supports little more than seasonal grazing. They are, by any measure, one of the most impressive achievements of dryland farming anywhere in the world. What they reveal about the relationship between people and arid environments, however, remains a matter of lively dispute.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle behind the system, known as runoff farming, is now well understood. The hillsides of the region are covered with a fine, wind-deposited soil called loess, which forms a thin, almost impermeable crust when it is wetted by the first drops of rain. As a result, even light showers do not soak into the slopes but flow across them. Ancient farmers built channels to gather this water from large areas of hillside and lead it down to small fields on the valley floors. Because the catchment was often twenty or more times larger than the field it fed, a plot in a year of average rainfall might receive the equivalent of three or four hundred millimetres. Walls built across the valleys slowed the resulting floods, so that the water had time to sink in, and the silt it carried settled behind them, gradually building up a deep, fertile soil.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the terraces were attributed to the Nabataeans, the Arab traders who controlled the incense routes across the region around two thousand years ago. Recent dating work has complicated this picture considerably. Dr Leora Avital of the Institute for Desert Archaeology has applied a technique called optically stimulated luminescence to the sediments trapped behind the terrace walls. The method measures the time that has elapsed since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight, and therefore indicates when a layer of soil was buried. Avital's results show that a few terraces are considerably older than the Nabataean period and some were built in the early Islamic centuries, but that the great majority were constructed between the fourth and seventh centuries AD, when the region formed part of the Byzantine Empire. She concludes that runoff farming reached its peak not under the Nabataeans but several centuries later.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The heaps of stones on the hillsides have proved even harder to explain. Arranged in long rows, they number in the hundreds of thousands. An early hypothesis held that grapevines were grown on the mounds, which supposedly gathered dew during cool nights. Dr Omar Rawashdeh, a hydrologist at the Levantine Water Research Unit, set out to test this idea. Over several seasons he found that the mounds collected negligible quantities of dew, far too little to sustain a vine. He then compared experimental plots from which surface stones had been removed with plots left untouched, and found that the cleared slopes produced substantially more runoff, apparently because the exposed loess formed its crust more readily. Rawashdeh therefore argues that the stones were piled up simply to clear the surface and increase the flow of water to the fields below. His case is persuasive, though it does not exclude the possibility that the heaps served more than one purpose.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why the farms were abandoned is the most contested question of all. Professor Sigrun Lindblad, a palaeoclimatologist, has analysed stalagmites from caves in the region, whose chemical layers record changes in rainfall over many centuries. Her data suggest that the climate became noticeably drier during the sixth and seventh centuries, and she believes this was enough to tip a finely balanced system into decline. The economic historian Dr Darius Tavakkoli offers a different explanation. He points out that the Negev farms specialised in producing wine for export to markets around the Mediterranean, and that this trade collapsed after a devastating epidemic in the mid-sixth century and the political upheavals that followed. Excavated rubbish dumps at one of the region's towns, he notes, stopped growing around the time of the epidemic, well before any drying trend would have been severe. In his view the farms failed not because the rain stopped but because their customers disappeared.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the mid-twentieth century, researchers reconstructed several ancient farms using the original channels and walls, partly to understand how they worked and partly to see whether runoff farming could be revived. The experimental farms successfully grew almonds, olives, grapes and cereals with no water other than runoff, even in dry years. Yet the technique has been adopted on only a small scale. The walls and channels require constant repair after every flood, which demands a large and reliable labour force, and the yields, while respectable for a desert, are modest compared with those of modern irrigated agriculture.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings suggest that the ancient system cannot be understood purely as a feat of engineering. It flourished when there were markets for its produce, institutions such as monasteries able to organise labour, and enough people to maintain thousands of walls. The romantic notion that ancient techniques can simply be transplanted into the present to solve modern food shortages is therefore misleading. Runoff farming may still have a role, particularly for tree crops and small-scale restoration of degraded valleys, but its history is a reminder that the success of any dryland technology depends as much on the society that operates it as on the cleverness of its design.

topic: utility-scale solar farms in deserts: ecological disturbance, microclimate, panel-cleaning water and siting
title: Sun on the Sand
subtitle: Deserts look like the perfect place for vast solar power stations, but they are not the empty spaces they are often imagined to be

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: To the planners of large solar power stations, deserts appear to offer everything: intense sunshine on almost every day of the year, cheap land and very few residents to object. Over the past two decades, installations covering several thousand hectares each have appeared in the drylands of North America, the Middle East, North Africa and western China. Promotional material often describes such places as wasteland or empty space, as if nothing of value were being displaced. That description is plainly inaccurate. Deserts support distinctive plants and animals, many found nowhere else, and their soils hold structures that have taken centuries to form. Yet it does not follow that solar power should be kept out of drylands altogether. The real question is not whether to build there but how.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the damage, according to the restoration ecologist Dr Benedetta Ferrante, occurs before a single panel is installed. On many projects the entire site is scraped bare and levelled by heavy machinery, a practice that destroys perennial shrubs, some of them centuries old, along with the fragile biological crusts that hold desert soils in place. Burrowing animals are evicted or relocated, and the bare ground becomes a source of dust for years afterwards. Ferrante has run trials on sites where vegetation was cut down to a low height rather than removed, leaving roots and crusts intact, and panels were mounted on posts driven into undisturbed ground. On these plots, most shrubs resprouted within two growing seasons and dust emissions were a fraction of those from cleared sites. The extra cost, she argues, is small relative to the total value of a project.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Once built, a solar park alters its own climate. By day the panels shade the ground beneath them, keeping the soil several degrees cooler than the surrounding desert. At night the pattern reverses: the panels and their supporting structures release the heat they have absorbed, and measurements at some sites have found air temperatures over the installation several degrees warmer than over nearby undeveloped land. The ecological consequences are mixed. Certain plants and small animals appear to benefit from the shade and from the moisture that collects where rain drips off the panels, while others that depend on cool desert nights may be disadvantaged. In my view, it is simply too early to say whether the overall effect is harmful or beneficial; most sites have been monitored for only a few years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dust poses a practical problem for operators as well as an ecological one. A film of dust on a panel can cut its output considerably within a few weeks, and the traditional remedy is to wash the panels with water, a scarce commodity in any desert. Dr Kavitha Ramaswami, an engineer at the Institute for Solar Durability, has evaluated alternatives including robotic brushes that sweep panels dry each night and coatings that make it harder for dust to stick. The robots greatly reduce water use, she reports, but over years of operation their bristles can leave fine scratches on the glass that permanently lower its efficiency. Ramaswami calculates that even conventional washing uses far less water per unit of electricity than coal or gas power stations, which require large volumes for cooling. That comparison is valid, but it should not be taken to mean that cleaning water is of no consequence: where a solar park draws on the same small aquifer as local farms and settlements, even modest withdrawals can matter.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: At the largest scale, some researchers have asked whether solar power could affect the climate of an entire region. The climate modeller Dr Rebwar Barzani has simulated what might happen if a substantial fraction of the Sahara were covered with panels. Because the panels are darker than sand, they would absorb more sunlight and warm the surface, and in his models this warming draws in moist air, increasing rainfall and vegetation across the region. The same simulations, however, suggest that rainfall could decline in other parts of the world as atmospheric circulation adjusts. Barzani concludes that installations on such a scale could not be treated as a purely local matter. These scenarios involve areas many hundreds of times larger than anything currently planned, and they are better regarded as a thought experiment than as grounds for hesitating over present projects.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where, then, should desert solar parks be built? The strongest candidates are land that has already been disturbed: abandoned farmland, former mining sites and ground alongside existing roads and power lines, where connection costs are lower and little intact habitat remains to be lost. Several governments have begun to map zones where development is encouraged and others where it is discouraged, an approach that deserves to be far more widely adopted than it currently is. Developers often prefer untouched sites because they are larger and simpler to acquire, but such convenience is a poor reason to sacrifice irreplaceable habitat.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these concerns amounts to an argument against solar energy, which remains one of the most important tools for reducing carbon emissions. They are, rather, an argument against treating deserts as blank spaces on a map. Built with care, on the right land and with the least possible disturbance, a solar park can be a reasonably good neighbour to the ecosystem around it.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: glacier surges: competing thermal and hydrological explanations for sudden glacier advances
title: Glaciers That Gallop
subtitle: Why a small minority of the world's glaciers periodically race forward, and what their behaviour might reveal about ice in a warming climate

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most glaciers move at a pace imperceptible to the human eye, creeping downhill by a few tens of metres a year. A small minority, however, behave very differently. For decades, sometimes for a century, a surge-type glacier appears to be stagnant or even shrinking; then, over a period of months or a few years, it accelerates to speeds ten or a hundred times its normal rate, its surface shattering into a maze of crevasses as the front advances by several kilometres. Only around one per cent of the world's glaciers are known to surge, and they are concentrated in a handful of regions, notably Svalbard, Alaska, the Yukon and the Karakoram mountains of Central Asia. Why these particular glaciers should behave so erratically, while their neighbours do not, remains one of the more stubborn puzzles in glaciology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first accounts of surges came not from scientists but from the communities whose lives were disrupted by them. In the Karakoram, herders long told of glaciers that 'walked' across valleys, and in the nineteenth century advancing ice repeatedly blocked rivers, creating lakes that later drained in catastrophic floods. Such reports were often dismissed by European travellers as exaggeration or folklore. It is now clear that they were accurate, and the episode is a reminder that local knowledge, however unsystematic it may appear, has frequently anticipated scientific findings by generations.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Scientific explanations have traditionally fallen into two camps. The first emphasises heat. Ingrid Hallvardsen, of the Arctic Cryosphere Institute, argues that in Svalbard surges are governed by the temperature at the glacier bed. During the long quiet phase, ice builds up in the upper reaches of the glacier, and this thickening layer acts rather like a blanket, preventing heat that rises from the earth from escaping. The base gradually warms until it reaches melting point. Once a film of meltwater appears beneath the ice, friction is reduced and the glacier begins to slide. In her view, this explains why Svalbard surges tend to begin slowly and may continue for as long as a decade, since the warm zone at the bed spreads only gradually.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The second camp emphasises drainage. Rustam Tokhtarov, a hydrologist at the Pamir Mountain Research Station, has studied surges in the Karakoram, where events often start and finish abruptly, sometimes within a single season. He maintains that the critical factor is not the quantity of meltwater but the way in which it escapes. In winter, he suggests, the tunnels beneath the ice close up under the weight of the glacier, so that water is trapped at high pressure and effectively lifts the ice from its bed. A surge ends, by this account, when an efficient network of channels reopens and the water drains away, often in a sudden flood from the snout.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For many years these explanations were treated as rivals, and the debate between their supporters became somewhat entrenched. More recently, Joseph Ochuodho, a modeller at the Centre for Earth System Dynamics in Nairobi, has proposed that both can be understood within a single framework based on the balance of energy at the glacier bed. Heat and water, he points out, are not independent of one another: melting produces water, and moving water both carries and generates heat through friction. A surge, on this account, occurs whenever a glacier cannot dispose of energy as fast as it accumulates it, whether by conduction or by drainage. Ochuodho's model has been widely praised for its elegance, and I believe it represents a genuine advance. It should be said, however, that a model which can account for every surge may simply be too flexible to be tested, and its supporters have yet to show that it can predict which glaciers will surge next.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question has acquired new urgency because of climate change. A team led by Laila Grinvalds at the Baltic Remote Sensing Laboratory has used satellite records spanning four decades to catalogue surges worldwide. Their data suggest that in some regions surges have become less frequent as glaciers thin, because thinner ice may never accumulate enough mass to trigger the cycle. In the Karakoram, by contrast, surges appear to have become more common, a pattern that Grinvalds tentatively links to increasing snowfall at high altitude. It would be a mistake, though, to treat surges as a symptom of global warming, as some media reports have done. Surges are an internal property of certain glaciers, and they were occurring long before human influence on the climate became significant.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even so, surges matter in practical terms. A surging glacier may advance across a road, a pipeline or a river, and lakes dammed by the ice can burst without warning. In the Karakoram, such floods have destroyed bridges and farmland many kilometres downstream. Better monitoring is therefore essential, and here satellite imagery has transformed what is possible, allowing changes in surface speed to be detected months before a surge reaches its peak. In my view, however, the most valuable lesson of surge research is a broader one. If glaciers that look almost identical can respond to the same climate in entirely different ways, then forecasts of ice loss based on the average behaviour of glaciers should be treated with considerable caution.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: the marine ice cliff instability hypothesis and the debate over rapid Antarctic ice loss
title: The Cliff Edge
subtitle: Could the Antarctic ice sheet collapse through a mechanism that has never been directly observed? Glaciologists remain divided

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Projections of sea-level rise have long contained an uncomfortable asymmetry. Scientists can say with some confidence how much the oceans will expand as they warm and how much water mountain glaciers will contribute, but the behaviour of the great ice sheets, and of West Antarctica in particular, remains the largest source of uncertainty. Much of that uncertainty now centres on a single hypothesised process, known as marine ice cliff instability, whose importance has divided the glaciological community for more than a decade.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea rests on a simple physical limit. Where an ice sheet terminates in the ocean, it usually does so through a floating ice shelf, which acts as a buttress, restraining the flow of ice from the interior. If the shelf disintegrates, the grounded ice behind it is left exposed as a vertical cliff. Ice, however, has finite strength, and calculations suggest that a cliff standing more than about ninety metres above the waterline cannot support its own weight; it will fracture and topple into the sea, exposing a taller cliff behind it, which in turn collapses. Because the bedrock beneath much of West Antarctica deepens inland, the cliffs would grow ever higher as the ice retreats, potentially producing a retreat that feeds on itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most prominent advocate of the mechanism's significance is Kenji Kuroiwa, of the Southern Ocean Modelling Group. When his team incorporated cliff failure into a model of the Antarctic ice sheet, the projected contribution to sea level by 2100 under high emissions roughly doubled compared with earlier estimates, a result that attracted enormous public attention. Kuroiwa argues that the model was also better able to reproduce sea levels during past warm periods, notably the Pliocene, some three million years ago, when the oceans stood well above their present height. In his view, a model that cannot explain the past has little claim to describe the future.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics have questioned almost every link in this chain. Astrid Brannstedt, a glaciologist at the Nordic Institute for Polar Studies, points out that when ice cliffs collapse, the debris does not simply disappear. In fjords such as those in Greenland, fallen ice combines with sea ice to form a dense mixture known as mélange, which can press against the cliff and slow further collapse. Brannstedt's group has also shown that cliff failure is less abrupt in models that allow ice to deform slowly before it fractures. Re-running Kuroiwa's simulations with these modifications, they found that the additional sea-level rise was considerably smaller. Moreover, Brannstedt contends that the Pliocene evidence is weaker than it appears, because estimates of sea level at that time vary by tens of metres depending on how far the land is assumed to have risen or sunk since.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is that the process has never been observed in its fully developed form. The tallest ice cliffs now in existence, at Greenland's largest outlet glaciers, rise only around a hundred metres, close to the theoretical limit. Chidi Iwunze, who leads a field programme at the Centre for Cryospheric Observation, has spent several seasons filming calving at such sites with time-lapse cameras. Her recordings show that very tall faces do collapse in large slabs, but also that the rate of collapse is strongly influenced by the temperature of the water at their base. Iwunze is careful not to take sides; she argues that the debate has been conducted too much through models and too little through measurement, and that a few well-instrumented sites would do more to settle it than any number of new simulations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It may be tempting to conclude that, because the mechanism is unproven, it can safely be set aside. That would, I think, be a serious error. The absence of observations reflects the fact that the conditions in which it might operate, namely very thick ice suddenly losing its shelf, do not currently exist, not that the process is impossible. At the same time, the dramatic figures from the earliest studies should not be repeated uncritically, as they still sometimes are in public discussion. The honest position is that the probability of rapid collapse this century is low but not negligible, and that its consequences, were it to occur, would be severe.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: How should such uncertainty be handled by those who must plan for the future? Natalia Kazantseva, a risk analyst who advises coastal authorities, argues that the question is less scientific than ethical. Engineers designing a sea wall expected to last a century, she observes, routinely account for floods with a one-in-a-thousand chance of occurring in any given year; there is no obvious reason why ice-sheet collapse should be treated differently simply because it is harder to model. She therefore recommends that long-lived infrastructure be built to accommodate a high-end scenario, or at least designed so that it can be adapted later. Some scientists fear that this risks spreading alarm on the basis of a contested idea. Yet her proposal seems to me entirely reasonable: the planners she advises are not being asked to believe the worst, only to avoid being unprepared for it.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: glacial lake outburst floods: triggers, trends and the competing ways of protecting mountain valleys
title: When the Ice Lets Go
subtitle: Glacial lakes are multiplying in the world's high mountains, and so is the argument over how to protect the valleys below them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the high valleys of the Himalaya, the Andes and the Alps, the retreat of glaciers is leaving behind something more immediately dangerous than bare rock. As the ice withdraws, meltwater collects in the hollows it has carved, forming lakes that are often held in place by nothing more substantial than moraine, the heaps of loose boulders, gravel and sand that a glacier pushes ahead of it or drops along its margins. Such barriers were never formed to hold water, and they can fail abruptly, releasing millions of cubic metres in a matter of hours. The resulting torrents, known as glacial lake outburst floods, can sweep away bridges, farmland and entire villages. In my view, the hazard has grown considerably faster than our ability to understand it, and certainly faster than the institutions responsible for managing it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What actually causes a dam to give way is less straightforward than it might appear. The most common trigger is a mass of ice or rock breaking away from the slopes above and plunging into the lake, generating a wave that surges over the crest of the moraine and begins to erode it. In other cases the dam is weakened from within, as blocks of ice concealed inside the moraine slowly melt and leave cavities behind. Earthquakes, too, can shake an unstable barrier apart. Dr Tashi Norgyal of the Himalayan Glacial Hazards Unit argues that these triggers deserve far more attention than they currently receive. Hazard assessments, he notes, have traditionally ranked lakes by their volume, on the assumption that the largest bodies of water pose the gravest danger. Norgyal contends that size alone is a misleading guide: a modest lake beneath a steep, crumbling ice cliff may be far more likely to burst than a much larger one surrounded by stable slopes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is little doubt that the number of glacial lakes is rising. Satellite inventories suggest that their combined area in the world's major mountain ranges has expanded by roughly half since 1990. It does not automatically follow, however, that floods are becoming more frequent, and Professor Elvira Mamanchura, a geographer at the Andean Institute of Mountain Studies, has been prominent among those urging caution. Historical records of outburst floods, she points out, are patchy at best; many events in remote valleys were simply never documented, and the apparent rise in reported floods may partly reflect the fact that far more people are now watching. Her caution is reasonable, but it should not be mistaken for reassurance. Even if floods occur no more often than they did a century ago, the number of people and the value of infrastructure in their path have multiplied, as hydropower plants, roads and tourist lodges have spread into valleys that were once sparsely inhabited.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most direct way of reducing the danger is to lower the level of the lake itself. Engineers have done this by cutting outlet channels through moraines or installing siphons. In parts of the Andes, programmes of this kind began in the mid-twentieth century after a series of deadly floods, and they are widely credited with having prevented further disasters. Marten Oosterhuizen, a hydraulic engineer who has advised on projects in several countries, accepts that such works can be highly effective. His concern is that they are frequently treated as a single, finished intervention. Because many lakes continue to grow as the glaciers feeding them retreat, a channel that was adequate when it was dug may be insufficient twenty years later, and Oosterhuizen argues that budgets rarely allow for the repeated deepening and repair that this demands.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Where lowering a lake is impractical, authorities have increasingly turned to early warning systems, in which sensors detect a sudden rise in water level or a surge of debris and set off sirens in the villages downstream. These systems are often presented as an inexpensive technological solution, but their record has been decidedly mixed. Equipment at high altitude is exposed to extreme cold and avalanches; some stations have failed for lack of power, while others have been dismantled by residents who were never told what they were for. More fundamentally, a warning may provide only minutes of notice, and whether those minutes save lives depends entirely on whether people know where to go and are prepared to act at once.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This is the central argument of the Mountain Risk Collective, a network of researchers and community organisations based in Kathmandu. The Collective maintains that the most durable protection comes not from equipment but from local preparation: mapping likely flood paths with residents, rehearsing evacuations, and discouraging new construction on the lowest ground near rivers. It also stresses that herders and farmers often notice changes in lakes and glaciers long before they appear in official data. I find much of this persuasive, but the emphasis on restricting building strikes me as somewhat optimistic. In narrow mountain valleys, flat land beside the river is frequently the only land suitable for homes, schools and fields, and asking families to abandon it is a great deal easier on paper than in practice.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, outburst floods do not respect national borders. A lake that forms in one country may drain into the river systems of another, and effective warning requires that data be shared quickly across frontiers that are sometimes politically sensitive. Agreements of this kind remain rare. The science of glacial hazards has advanced impressively, and tools for monitoring lakes from space are now widely available. What is lacking, I would argue, is less a matter of technology than of trust, and of the institutional arrangements that allow neighbouring governments to act together on a shared threat.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: the darkening of the Greenland ice sheet: glacier algae, ancient dust and soot as competing causes of reduced reflectivity
title: A Shadow on the Ice
subtitle: Why parts of Greenland's ice sheet are turning grey, and why scientists cannot agree on who or what is to blame

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Fresh snow is among the most reflective natural surfaces on earth, returning as much as ninety per cent of incoming sunlight to the sky. Bare glacier ice reflects considerably less, and ice that has been discoloured may reflect barely a third. This property, known as albedo, matters enormously for the Greenland ice sheet, because every fraction of sunlight that is absorbed rather than reflected becomes energy available for melting. Each summer, as the winter snow retreats, a broad band along the western margin of the ice sheet turns a dull grey, and satellite images show this so-called dark zone expanding in warm years. Discussions of ice loss tend to be framed almost entirely in terms of rising air temperatures, and in my judgement this emphasis has caused the question of surface brightness to be seriously neglected.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years the discolouration was attributed largely to inorganic particles: wind-blown mineral dust from exposed land, together with soot carried from distant fires and industrial chimneys. Such material was assumed to settle on the ice passively, darkening it in much the same way that grime darkens a city pavement. Over the past decade, however, this picture has become considerably more complicated, as researchers have recognised that the surface of the ice sheet is not a sterile slab but a habitat, and that its inhabitants may be doing much of the darkening themselves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The microbiologist Ayumi Tsurugaoka, of the Polar Microbial Ecology Laboratory, has led the case for living organisms. Her teams have counted cells in thousands of surface samples and found that microscopic algae, growing in the thin film of meltwater on bare ice, can reach densities of tens of thousands of cells per millilitre. These algae produce a purple-brown pigment that protects them from intense ultraviolet light, and it is precisely this protective pigment that causes the ice to absorb more heat. Tsurugaoka describes a self-reinforcing cycle: melting supplies the liquid water the algae require, the algae darken the ice, and the darker ice melts faster still. On her estimates, algae account for the greater part of the darkening observed in the dark zone during a typical summer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that biology is the principal driver. The glaciologist Bjarke Solvhoj argues that the position of the dark zone is fixed less by algae than by geology. As ice flows slowly from the interior towards the coast, layers of dust deposited during the last glacial period, when the climate was drier and windier, are carried along within it and eventually emerge at the surface. In Solvhoj's view, this ancient dust supplies the phosphorus and other nutrients on which algae depend, so that blooms flourish where the dust outcrops and are scarce elsewhere. The algae, he concludes, are better understood as a symptom of the dust than as an independent cause. The disagreement is often presented as a contest between two rival explanations, but this seems to me to be misleading: if Solvhoj is right about nutrients, then dust and algae are partners in a single process, and the real question is how much each contributes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Answering that question matters because of the models used to forecast sea-level rise. Most ice sheet models assign bare ice a single, fixed albedo, ignoring the way it varies from place to place and from one summer to the next. The Ice Surface Energy Consortium, a group of modellers from several countries, has experimented with adding biological darkening to these simulations, and reports that doing so raises projected surface melt from the western margin by between ten and thirteen per cent. The Consortium itself stresses that this range rests on assumptions about how readily algae will colonise newly exposed ice further inland, about which very little is yet known. Even so, it is hard to avoid the conclusion that models which leave biology out altogether are more likely to be understating future melt than overstating it, although the precise figures should be treated with considerable caution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from the atmospheric chemist Folasade Akintoye, who has traced soot on the ice to its sources using chemical fingerprints. She finds that soot arrives in pulses, with exceptional deposits following summers of large forest fires in Canada and Siberia, and she argues that it deserves particular attention because, unlike dust or algae, it can be reduced by human action through cleaner combustion and better fire management. The point about policy is a fair one, yet I am not convinced that what can most easily be controlled should determine where research effort is directed. By Akintoye's own measurements soot accounts for a modest share of the darkening in most years, and an agenda shaped mainly by what is politically actionable risks leaving the larger processes poorly understood.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It has occasionally been suggested that the darkening could be countered directly, by scattering reflective particles across the dark zone or by treating the surface to suppress algal growth. Such schemes strike me as fanciful. The dark zone covers tens of thousands of square kilometres, it shifts from year to year, and any material spread on it would be buried, washed away or carried into the ocean within a single season. The more realistic contribution of this research is to sharpen our forecasts, and to remind us that an ice sheet is not merely a block of frozen water responding to the thermometer, but a complex surface on which physics, geology and biology are tightly intertwined.

subtitle: In the cold deserts of the high Himalaya, villagers are freezing water in winter to save it for spring. How much can such schemes really achieve?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the high valleys on the northern side of the Himalaya, rain is almost unknown and farming depends on meltwater from glaciers and snowfields. For centuries this arrangement worked well enough, but it has always contained an awkward mismatch. Barley and wheat must be sown in April and May, when the nights are still cold and the streams carry only a trickle, whereas the main flow of glacial meltwater does not arrive until the heat of June and July. As the glaciers that feed these valleys shrink and retreat higher up the mountainsides, the spring shortage has become more severe, and in some villages fields that were cultivated for generations now lie abandoned.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One response has been to manufacture ice. The older technique, practised in the region for several decades, involves diverting a stream in late autumn onto a shaded, north-facing slope, where low stone walls slow the water and allow it to freeze in successive thin sheets. By spring, a long ribbon of ice has accumulated close to the village, and its gradual melting supplies water just when sowing begins. A more recent variant takes a different form. Water is piped from a point far upstream and, driven only by gravity, is sprayed upwards into the freezing night air through a vertical pipe. As it falls, it freezes into a tall cone. The shape is the key to the design: a cone exposes a relatively small surface to the sun for the volume of ice it contains, and so it melts more slowly than a flat sheet.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Kunzang Yangdol, a hydrologist at the Trans-Himalayan Field Station, has spent five winters measuring the output of these ice towers. Her results show that a single large cone can hold several million litres of water and continue releasing it well into May. They also show how unpredictable the towers are. In winters with frequent warm spells or strong winds, some cones grew to barely a fifth of their intended size, and one collapsed before spring. Yangdol therefore insists that ice towers should be regarded as a supplement to existing water sources rather than as a substitute for them, and she warns against plans that assume a reliable volume of stored water every year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A sharper criticism comes from the glaciologist Ilse Verhoolen, who objects to the very name 'artificial glacier'. A true glacier, she points out, is a body of ice that persists over many years and flows under its own weight; the structures being built in the Himalaya disappear every summer and are more accurately described as seasonal ice reservoirs. Verhoolen also worries that striking images of villagers building ice towers may give the public the impression that the retreat of real glaciers can be offset by local ingenuity, and so weaken the pressure to cut emissions. On the first point she is surely correct: the terminology has run well ahead of what the structures actually do. Her second concern, however, seems to me overstated. There is no evidence that communities who build ice towers, or the audiences who admire them, become any less aware of the causes of glacial retreat.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A less obvious difficulty concerns who owns the water. Mateo Carrasquedo, an economist who studies irrigation institutions in mountain regions, notes that winter water was traditionally regarded as having little value, because it could not be used. Ice towers change that calculation. Water that once flowed downstream through the winter, recharging springs and wetlands used by other villages, is now captured upstream by whoever has the equipment to freeze it. Long-established rotation systems, which divide spring water among households and villages according to carefully negotiated rules, make no provision for this new resource, and Carrasquedo has documented several disputes in which downstream communities accused upstream builders of taking water that was rightfully theirs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Advocates of the technique, notably the Himalayan Water Commons Group, emphasise its social benefits. Building a tower requires dozens of people to lay pipes and keep them clear through the coldest nights, and the Group argues that this shared effort strengthens communities that have been weakened by migration to the cities. Ice towers have also become a modest attraction for visitors, and their construction costs are a small fraction of those of a concrete reservoir. Even the Group acknowledges, however, that volunteer enthusiasm tends to fade after the first two or three winters, once the novelty has worn off, and that several towers have been abandoned for lack of willing labour.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that ice towers are a mistake. In valleys where a few extra weeks of spring water can decide whether a field is sown or left fallow, they offer a cheap and ingenious form of storage. The greatest threat to the technique may in fact come from its admirers, since claims that it can save the glaciers or solve the water problems of the mountains invite disappointment and, eventually, disillusion. What the schemes need is patient, independent measurement over many winters. Photographs of gleaming cones against a blue sky have done much to publicise the idea, but they reveal nothing about how much water was delivered, when, or to whom.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: the search for million-year-old Antarctic ice and what it might reveal about the Mid-Pleistocene Transition
title: The Deepest Archive
subtitle: Scientists are drilling ever further into Antarctica in search of ice old enough to solve one of the great puzzles of the planet's climate history

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ice cores are among the most valuable archives in the earth sciences. As snow accumulates on an ice sheet and is compressed into ice, it seals tiny bubbles of air, and these bubbles preserve samples of the ancient atmosphere that can be analysed for carbon dioxide and other gases. The longest continuous record recovered so far extends back roughly 800,000 years. That span is impressive, but it stops short of a period that has long perplexed climate scientists. Until about a million years ago, the great ice ages came and went roughly every 41,000 years; afterwards, the cycle lengthened to around 100,000 years, and the cold phases became considerably more severe. Nothing in the pattern of the earth's orbit, which paces these cycles, changed at that time, and the cause of this shift, known as the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, remains disputed. Recovering air from before and during the transition is, in my view, one of the most worthwhile undertakings in contemporary climate research.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Finding such air is far from simple. The oldest ice lies at the very bottom of an ice sheet, where the weight above has squeezed annual layers until a single metre may represent tens of thousands of years. Heat escaping from the earth's interior can warm the base sufficiently to melt it, destroying the oldest record altogether, while the slow flow of the ice can fold and shear the lower layers. The ideal site is therefore a paradox: the ice must be thick enough to have accumulated a long record, yet not so thick that it insulates the bed and allows it to thaw, and it must lie on a gentle dome where horizontal movement is minimal. Professor Giedre Vaitkute, who has led radar surveys across the East Antarctic plateau, argues that a combination of airborne radar and computer modelling has now pinpointed several locations meeting these conditions, and she is confident that at least one holds an unbroken sequence stretching back 1.5 million years.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Drilling at such sites takes several summer seasons, each a few weeks long, and the boreholes reach depths approaching three kilometres. Dr Ebo Kwarteng-Addo, a specialist in ice deformation, has urged caution about what the bottom of these cores will show. Near the bed, he notes, layers can be stretched, overturned or even repeated, so that a section which appears to be continuous may in fact contain gaps or segments in the wrong order, and independent methods of dating ice of this age are imprecise. His warning deserves to be taken seriously. Whatever is extracted from the lowest few metres should be published with its uncertainties stated explicitly, rather than presented as a clean continuation of the existing record.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have pursued a quite different route. In parts of Antarctica known as blue ice areas, persistent winds strip away the surface snow and the flow of ice brings ancient layers up to the surface, where fragments more than two million years old have been sampled with relatively shallow drilling. Professor Teodor Wierzchowski is the leading advocate of this approach, pointing out that it is far cheaper than deep drilling and allows researchers to return repeatedly to collect fresh samples. The value of such material is undeniable, but its limitations should not be understated. Blue ice yields isolated snapshots of the ancient atmosphere, not a sequence, and snapshots alone cannot show how the rhythm of the ice ages changed from one form to another. The two approaches are best regarded as complementary.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What might the deep cores reveal? One leading hypothesis holds that a gradual decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide pushed the climate system past a threshold, allowing ice sheets to survive the warm phases of the shorter orbital cycles and grow into the larger, longer-lasting ice sheets of the later period. A rival explanation focuses on the ground beneath the northern ice sheets. Over millions of years, it is argued, earlier glaciations scraped away the layer of soft, weathered sediment that had covered much of North America; once the ice rested directly on hard bedrock, it could no longer slide so easily and was able to build up to far greater thicknesses. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, but a well-dated record of carbon dioxide across the transition would show whether a fall in the gas coincided with the change in rhythm.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even if the ice is intact, analysing it will stretch existing techniques to their limits. The Basal Ice Working Group, an international team of laboratory scientists, has pointed out that at the depths in question a sample the length of a finger may span several thousand years, so that conventional methods, which melt or crush comparatively large pieces of ice to release their air, would blur together periods that need to be distinguished. The Group has therefore been developing laser-based systems that extract gas from tiny portions of a core, though these remain experimental and have not yet been tested on ice of comparable age.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be unwise to expect the new cores to settle the argument over the transition decisively; the record may prove ambiguous, and both camps are likely to find something to support their position. That does not diminish the significance of the work. The deep past offers a natural experiment in how the climate responds to changing levels of carbon dioxide, a question of more than academic interest to a world in which the gas is now rising faster than at any time recorded in the ice. The oldest air on earth may, in the end, have a good deal to say about the air of the coming century.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: Antarctic subglacial lakes: their connections, microbial life and the ethics of drilling into them
title: Sealed Worlds?
subtitle: Hundreds of lakes lie hidden beneath the Antarctic ice. Should we be in a hurry to reach them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When pilots and scientists first flew radar equipment over the Antarctic ice sheet in the 1960s and 1970s, they noticed something unexpected: in places, the signal bouncing off the bottom of the ice returned as a flat, unusually bright reflection, the signature of liquid water. More than four hundred such subglacial lakes have since been identified, ranging from shallow ponds to one body of water comparable in area to some of the largest lakes on the surface of the planet. They remain liquid, despite temperatures above them far below freezing, because the immense weight of the overlying ice lowers the melting point of water and because geothermal heat rising from the rock beneath keeps the base of the ice warm. It is no exaggeration to count their discovery among the most remarkable achievements of polar science in the twentieth century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years the lakes were imagined as sealed time capsules, cut off from the rest of the world for perhaps millions of years. That picture has been revised. Dr Iñaki Gorostidi, a geophysicist who uses satellites to measure tiny changes in the height of the ice, found that the surface above certain lakes rose and fell by several metres over periods of months. The only plausible explanation was that water was moving between lakes, draining from one and filling another through channels beneath the ice. Gorostidi has also shown that when such water reaches the edge of a glacier it can act as a lubricant, temporarily increasing the speed at which the ice slides towards the sea. Some of these drainage events, he estimates, released volumes of water comparable to a large river in flood, though because they occur several kilometres beneath the ice, they leave almost no trace at the surface apart from the subtle changes in height that his instruments record.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question that has attracted most public interest is whether anything lives in these dark, cold waters. In the past decade, hot-water drills have penetrated the ice above two shallow lakes, and samples analysed by the microbiologist Oksana Zhovtobriukh contained thousands of microbial cells in every millilitre. With no light to support photosynthesis, these organisms appear to obtain their energy from chemical reactions involving minerals in the rocks over which the water flows. Zhovtobriukh suggests that such communities offer a model for the kind of life that might exist in the oceans thought to lie beneath the ice-covered moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The comparison is intriguing, but some of the headlines it has inspired go far beyond what the evidence can support: finding microbes beneath Antarctica tells us that life can survive in such places on earth, not that it exists anywhere else.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Reaching the lakes poses a serious technical and environmental challenge. Older boreholes drilled into the ice for climate research were kept open with fluids based on kerosene, which would pollute any lake they reached. Hot-water drilling avoids such chemicals, but the water and equipment can still carry surface microbes into an environment that has never encountered them. The engineer Wanjiru Mbogori has designed a system that passes the drilling water through fine filters and exposes it to ultraviolet light before it enters the borehole. Her tests indicate that the number of cells introduced in this way can be reduced to well below the number naturally present in the lake water itself, so that any contamination would be too small to distort the results.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is reassured. The Antarctic Environmental Ethics Panel, an advisory body of scientists and philosophers, argues that the largest and deepest lakes, which are likely to have been isolated for longest, should not be entered until clean drilling methods have been proven repeatedly on smaller, shallower lakes. Contamination, the Panel points out, cannot be reversed: once foreign organisms have been introduced, the scientific value of a pristine environment is lost permanently. I agree with the principle, although Gorostidi's findings complicate it. If many lakes are connected and exchange water, they are less pristine than was once assumed, and the notion of a perfectly untouched environment may apply only to a minority of the very largest lakes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also practical considerations. The most isolated lakes lie beneath three or four kilometres of ice, in the coldest and most remote parts of the continent, where even a short season of fieldwork demands elaborate preparation. Each drilling campaign requires tonnes of fuel and equipment to be hauled across hundreds of kilometres of ice, and a single season can consume a large share of a national polar programme's budget. Given the irreversible nature of contamination and the fact that the lakes have waited for millions of years, a delay of a decade or two while methods improve seems a modest price to pay. Exploration of the smaller, connected lakes can continue in the meantime, and will in any case supply the experience on which any later attempt must depend. The lakes are not going anywhere.

area: glaciers, ice sheets and polar regions
topic: glacial isostatic adjustment: the slow rebound of land after the ice ages and its consequences for sea level and ice-loss estimates
title: Rising Ground
subtitle: Ten thousand years after the great ice sheets melted, the land beneath them is still moving, with consequences that reach from Baltic harbours to the Antarctic coast

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Along the shores of the Gulf of Bothnia, between Sweden and Finland, medieval harbours now stand some distance from the water, and mooring rings once used by fishing boats can be found on rocks in the middle of fields. In the eighteenth century, naturalists carved marks on coastal rocks to record the level of the sea and returned decades later to find the water well below them. Most concluded that the sea itself was gradually draining away. The true explanation is the opposite: it is the land that is rising, in places by almost a centimetre a year. During the last ice age, Scandinavia lay beneath an ice sheet some three kilometres thick, and since the ice disappeared roughly ten thousand years ago, the ground has been slowly recovering from its weight.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The process, known to geophysicists as glacial isostatic adjustment, depends on the behaviour of the mantle, the layer of hot rock beneath the earth's crust. Over short periods the mantle behaves as a solid, transmitting earthquake waves, but over thousands of years it flows like an extremely thick liquid. The weight of an ice sheet pressed the crust down into it, displacing mantle rock sideways and raising a broad bulge of land around the margins of the ice. Now that the load has gone, the centre is rebounding while the surrounding bulge is sinking back. Large parts of the Netherlands, southern England and the east coast of North America lie on such former bulges, and their subsidence adds to the rise in sea level caused by warming oceans and melting ice. It is a contribution that, in my experience, local planners too often leave out of their calculations.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Measuring the movement precisely has become possible only recently. Tide gauges, some operating for more than two centuries, record changes in sea level relative to the land, and ancient beaches stranded high above the present shore can be dated to reconstruct the longer history. Satellite positioning now allows the vertical motion of the ground to be tracked directly. Professor Liisa Haapakoski, who coordinates the Fennoscandian Uplift Network of several hundred permanent receivers, reports that uplift rates near the former centre of the ice sheet closely match those predicted by standard models, but that at the margins the measured motion departs from predictions by a substantial margin. She argues that the mantle's resistance to flow must vary from region to region far more than the models assume, which treat it as broadly uniform at any given depth.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These details matter well beyond Scandinavia. Since the early 2000s, satellites have measured changes in the earth's gravity field to estimate how much ice the polar ice sheets are losing. Rebounding land, however, also changes the gravity field: as mantle rock flows back beneath a region, the mass there increases, which can partially mask a loss of ice or even mimic a gain. The satellite data must therefore be corrected using a model of isostatic adjustment, and in Antarctica, where the history of the ice is poorly known, this correction is both large and uncertain. Dr Mekdes Woldegiorgis has argued that differences between correction models may explain a considerable part of the disagreement among published estimates of Antarctic ice loss.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Antarctica may also hold a surprise of a more hopeful kind. Seismic surveys indicate that beneath parts of West Antarctica the mantle is unusually hot and therefore far less resistant to flow than beneath Scandinavia, which means the ground there could respond to ice loss within decades rather than over thousands of years. Professor Hamish Tolquhoun has used computer models to explore the consequences. As glaciers thin, he suggests, the bedrock beneath them would rise, raising the floor at the grounding line, the point at which the ice leaves the bed and begins to float, and this could slow the retreat of the ice. Other researchers accept the mechanism but contend that the uplift would be too gradual to make much difference to sea-level rise during the present century, and that it would at best delay rather than prevent the loss of ice. On present evidence the sceptics seem to me to have the stronger case, although the possibility surely deserves closer study than it has so far received.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: On the Bothnian coast, meanwhile, rebound has practical and even legal consequences. Each generation, new strips of land emerge from the sea, and under long-established rules in parts of the region the emerging land is allotted to the owners of the adjoining shore. Harbours must be dredged or relocated, and some coastal towns have moved their quays several times since the Middle Ages. Shallow bays are gradually turning into lakes, then into wetlands, and eventually into dry ground, creating a landscape that is visibly younger than the rocks beneath it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The broader lesson is that the ground beneath our feet is not the fixed reference point that most discussions of sea level assume. A global average figure for sea-level rise conceals enormous local variation: a coastal city on a sinking former bulge may face several times the average increase, while a town on rebounding land may see the sea retreat. Projections intended to guide coastal defence ought to be made locally, and should incorporate the slow movement of the land as routinely as they do the expansion of warming water.

topic: glacial geoengineering: proposals for seabed barriers and curtains to shield polar outlet glaciers from warm ocean water
title: Curtains for the Ice?
subtitle: Some engineers believe that giant underwater barriers could slow the collapse of polar glaciers. Others regard the idea as a dangerous distraction

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The glaciers that drain the polar ice sheets into the sea are not, for the most part, being melted by warm air. Their main enemy lies beneath the surface. In parts of Antarctica and Greenland, a layer of relatively warm, salty water flows along deep troughs in the seabed and reaches the underside of floating ice tongues and ice shelves, melting them from below. As these floating sections thin, they hold back less of the ice behind them, and the glaciers accelerate. If the warm water could be kept away, the argument goes, the glaciers might be stabilised. A decade ago, the idea of intervening physically in this process was confined to the margins of glaciology. It is now discussed at major scientific conferences, and in my view it is right that it should be examined seriously, if only so that its weaknesses can be properly understood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two broad designs have been proposed. The first, put forward by the engineer Sigrun Aaltvedt, would involve piling up ridges of gravel on the seabed in front of a glacier, raising the sea floor enough to block the deepest and warmest water. Aaltvedt herself has since shifted her preference to a second design: a flexible, buoyant curtain, anchored to the seabed and rising several hundred metres towards the surface, which would deflect warm water while allowing colder surface water to pass over it. Her reasons are partly practical, since a curtain would require far less material than a gravel ridge, and partly ethical. Unlike a ridge, a curtain could in principle be taken away again if it caused unforeseen harm, a feature she regards as essential for any intervention in so poorly understood an environment.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The scale of what is proposed is daunting. A curtain protecting one of the largest Antarctic glaciers might need to stretch for eighty kilometres across water more than six hundred metres deep, in a sea crowded with icebergs and covered for much of the year by sea ice. Aaltvedt's preliminary estimates put the cost in the tens of billions of dollars, a sum she compares favourably with the expense of raising sea defences along the world's coastlines. The oceanographer Tariq Bahlawan is unconvinced on more fundamental grounds. The computer models used to predict how warm water would respond to a barrier, he argues, are still crude, and there is a real possibility that water blocked in one trough would simply find its way to a neighbouring glacier, transferring the problem rather than solving it. He also points out that the troughs support rich communities of marine life whose response to altered currents is entirely unknown.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the idea accept that much remains uncertain, and they propose to proceed in stages. Laboratory experiments in large water tanks have already tested scaled-down curtains, and a field trial in a sheltered fjord, with a curtain a few hundred metres long, has been planned. Such modest steps seem to me entirely reasonable. A trial in a fjord poses negligible risk, and it is difficult to see how the questions Bahlawan raises could ever be answered without some experiment of this kind.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For the Southern Ocean Stewardship Alliance, a coalition of environmental organisations, the danger lies elsewhere. The Alliance argues that the mere prospect of an engineering fix for melting ice weakens the political will to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, offering governments and industries a convenient reason to delay. This concern is a legitimate one, and it has been raised about every form of climate engineering. It does not, however, strike me as a sufficient reason to block research. A substantial amount of further sea-level rise is already unavoidable, whatever happens to emissions, and refusing even to investigate options for limiting it would be a curious form of caution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of who would decide. Most of the glaciers concerned lie in Antarctica, which is governed under a treaty that prohibits many kinds of activity and gives decisive influence to a relatively small group of nations. Dr Mirela Vlasceanu, a specialist in international environmental law, observes that the consequences of any intervention, whether successful or harmful, would be felt by low-lying coastal states across the globe, many of which have no voice in Antarctic governance. She argues that a decision of this magnitude would require a far more inclusive process than any that currently exists. In Greenland, the situation is different again, since several of the fjords under consideration are used by local communities for fishing and hunting.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even on the most optimistic assumptions, underwater barriers would not reverse the loss of polar ice; at best, they would slow it, buying time for societies to adapt and for emissions to fall. They would also have to be inspected, repaired and eventually replaced for as long as the ocean remained warm, which might mean several centuries. No engineering project in history has been maintained over such a period, and that commitment, rather than the technical challenge of building the structures, may be the most sobering aspect of the whole proposal.

subtitle: Is the shrinking of Arctic sea ice responsible for harsher winters and longer heatwaves further south? Two decades of research have produced more argument than agreement

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Arctic is warming roughly three to four times faster than the planet as a whole, and the extent of summer sea ice has fallen by around forty per cent since satellite records began in the late 1970s. That the region is changing dramatically is beyond dispute. What remains fiercely contested is whether these changes are reaching out to affect the weather of Europe, North America and Asia. According to one influential hypothesis, the rapid warming of the Arctic reduces the temperature difference between the pole and the middle latitudes, which is what drives the jet stream, the band of strong winds that steers weather systems around the hemisphere. A weaker jet stream, the argument runs, meanders in larger loops and moves more slowly, so that spells of cold, heat or rain remain over the same region for longer. The hypothesis is elegant and easily communicated, and it has, I would suggest, attracted a degree of media attention out of all proportion to the strength of the evidence behind it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its most prominent advocate is the climatologist Rosalind Trevarthen, whose analyses of weather observations indicate that the jet stream has tended to be wavier in years when Arctic ice was unusually scarce. Trevarthen has paid particular attention to the Barents and Kara Seas, north of Scandinavia and Russia, where autumns with little ice have frequently been followed by severe winters in Siberia and eastern Asia. She proposes that the connection operates partly through the stratosphere, the layer of the atmosphere above the one in which weather occurs: heat escaping from open water disturbs the ring of cold winds that circles the pole high above the surface, and when that ring weakens, frigid air can spill southwards weeks later.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The atmospheric dynamicist Dariusz Grzybowicz is not persuaded. The reliable observational record, he points out, covers barely four decades, while the jet stream varies enormously from one year to the next for reasons that have nothing to do with sea ice. In so short and noisy a record, he argues, patterns that look meaningful can arise purely by chance. Grzybowicz also draws attention to a competing influence. At high altitudes, the tropics are warming faster than the poles, which tends to increase rather than reduce the temperature contrast that powers the jet. The jet stream is thus caught in a kind of tug of war between surface warming in the Arctic and upper-level warming over the tropics, and it is far from obvious which will prevail.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Computer models ought, in principle, to settle the matter, since they allow researchers to change one factor while holding everything else constant. The Polar Linkages Modelling Group, a collaboration of climate modelling centres, has run hundreds of simulations in which nothing but the amount of Arctic sea ice was altered. The results show an effect in the expected direction, with cold Eurasian winters becoming slightly more likely when ice is reduced, but the effect is many times smaller than the observational studies imply. Either the models are failing to capture some important process, or the apparent link in the observations owes more to coincidence than to cause. Both possibilities remain open. Some commentators have treated this persistent disagreement as an embarrassment for climate science; I would argue the reverse, since it reflects the genuine difficulty of detecting a modest signal amid the natural turbulence of the atmosphere.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection has been raised by the statistician Thandeka Sibisi, who questions the direction of cause and effect. Certain large-scale atmospheric patterns, she notes, carry warm, moist air into the Arctic, where it melts sea ice, while simultaneously drawing cold air out of the Arctic over the continents. If such patterns are responsible for both the low ice and the cold winters, then the two will appear together in the records without the first having caused the second. Of all the contributions to the debate, Sibisi's seems to me the most important, not because it disproves the hypothesis, which it does not, but because it shows that the observational correlation on which so much has been built is open to more than one interpretation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question is not purely academic. Energy companies, farmers and insurers would all benefit if the state of Arctic ice in autumn could improve forecasts of the following winter. There is a communication problem too. Each exceptionally cold winter now prompts headlines blaming the melting Arctic, and when the next winter turns out mild, those who doubt that the climate is changing at all are quick to point out the apparent contradiction. Scientists would be better served by stating plainly how uncertain the link remains than by allowing every cold spell to be presented as further proof.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Time may resolve what argument so far has not. If the connection is real, it should become more apparent as the ice continues to retreat and the observational record lengthens, and within two or three decades the signal ought either to have emerged clearly from the noise or to have faded into insignificance. Until then, the most honest answer to the question of whether a cold winter in Beijing or Chicago can be traced to the open waters north of Russia is that, at present, no one knows.

topic: biodiversity offsetting, the mitigation hierarchy and the accounting behind 'no net loss'
title: Losing Ground Without Losing Count?
subtitle: Biodiversity offsets promise that development can go ahead with no net loss of nature. The arithmetic is less straightforward than it appears

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The idea is appealingly simple. When a road, mine or housing estate destroys a patch of habitat, the developer pays for an equivalent area of habitat to be created, restored or protected elsewhere, so that the overall stock of biodiversity remains unchanged. Known as biodiversity offsetting, the practice has spread from a handful of wetland programmes in the 1970s to policies in more than a hundred countries, and it is now written into the lending conditions of several major development banks. Its supporters present it as a pragmatic compromise between economic growth and conservation. Its critics see it as a licence to destroy. Both camps, I would argue, have tended to argue about the principle while paying too little attention to the accounting on which the whole enterprise depends.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Offsetting was never meant to stand alone. In its original formulation it sits at the bottom of what is called the mitigation hierarchy: developers are expected first to avoid damage altogether, then to minimise whatever damage cannot be avoided, then to restore affected land on site, and only as a last resort to compensate for residual losses elsewhere. Dr Mirela Stoicovici, an ecological economist at the Danube Institute for Environmental Accounting, has examined planning files from over three hundred projects that relied on offsets. In her sample, fewer than one in five contained any documented consideration of whether the damage could have been avoided by redesigning or relocating the project. Offsetting, she concludes, has quietly migrated from the end of the sequence to the beginning, because it is the step that allows a scheme to proceed unchanged.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Equivalence is the second problem. To claim no net loss, one must show that what is gained matches what is lost, and that requires a common currency. Most schemes use a metric that multiplies the area of a habitat by a score for its condition, producing units that can be added and subtracted. The approach has the virtue of being transparent, but Professor Tancredi Bellomo, who studies grassland ecology at the University of Trento, argues that such metrics reward what is easy to count. A meadow that has existed for centuries, with fungal communities and soil invertebrates that no surveyor records, may score exactly the same as a recently sown field of similar extent and floristic quality. 'Every metric is a decision about what to ignore,' he writes, 'and the things these metrics ignore are disproportionately the things that take longest to replace.'

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Time is indeed the third difficulty, and perhaps the least appreciated. Habitat destroyed by a bulldozer disappears in a day; habitat created to replace it may need decades to reach comparable condition, and some types, such as ancient woodland, cannot realistically be recreated on any timescale relevant to policy. Many schemes attempt to address this with multipliers, requiring developers to provide more units than they remove in order to cover the delay and the risk that restoration fails. The Oranmore Biodiversity Audit Group, an independent team which revisited 112 offset sites a decade after their approval, found that only 34 had reached the condition promised in their management plans, while 19 could not be located with any confidence at all. In fairness, a few sites had exceeded expectations, but the overall pattern suggests that the multipliers commonly applied, which rarely exceed two, are too low to cover the risk of failure.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A subtler problem concerns the baseline against which gains are measured. Many offsets do not create new habitat at all; instead, they protect existing habitat that is said to be under threat, and the gain claimed is the loss that would otherwise have occurred. Yet this counterfactual is inherently uncertain, and there is an obvious incentive to exaggerate it. If the protected forest would not in fact have been cleared, the offset delivers nothing, and the development it permitted represents a straightforward net loss. Hamid Farahzadi, a planning lawyer who has represented community groups in offset disputes, points out that the party estimating the threat is frequently the same consultancy that has been paid by the developer. He does not allege dishonesty, he says, merely that such an arrangement would never be tolerated in financial auditing.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that offsets should be abandoned. Before they existed, most of the habitat lost to development was simply lost, with no compensation of any kind, and it would be naive to imagine that a ban on offsetting would restore a world in which damaging projects were routinely refused. Stoicovici herself is no abolitionist; she favours stricter enforcement of the avoidance step, with planning authorities required to publish the alternatives they considered before any offset is accepted. Bellomo goes further, proposing that certain categories of habitat be declared irreplaceable and therefore ineligible for offsetting altogether. That seems to me a sensible proposal, although the list of such habitats would need to be drawn up by ecologists in advance rather than negotiated case by case.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the evidence suggests is that offsetting is better understood as a promise than as a transaction. A developer who buys units has not acquired biodiversity; it has acquired a commitment, often lasting thirty years or more, that someone will manage a piece of land in a particular way. Whether that promise is kept depends on monitoring, funding and legal enforcement that extend long after the original project has been completed and its builders have moved on. Policies that treat the purchase of credits as the end of the matter are, in this sense, not offsets at all, but merely an expensive form of hope.
