topic: debt-for-nature swaps: converting sovereign debt into conservation funding
title: Trading Debt for Forests
subtitle: Swapping a country's foreign debt for conservation commitments has become fashionable again. Does it help either the debtor or the environment?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1984 a biologist writing in a conservation journal made a suggestion that seemed, at the time, almost whimsical. Many tropical countries, he noted, were heavily indebted to foreign banks and governments, and the same countries contained much of the world's remaining biodiversity. Why not allow them to pay off part of what they owed by protecting their forests instead? Within a few years the first so-called debt-for-nature swaps had been agreed, and in the decades since, dozens of transactions have converted billions of dollars of debt into funding for parks, marine reserves and conservation trusts. After a quiet period in the 2000s, the idea has returned with remarkable force, and some of the largest swaps ever arranged have been signed in the last five years.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic mechanism varies little from deal to deal. A conservation organisation, a development bank or a creditor government buys a portion of a country's debt, usually at a discount, because loans to struggling economies trade below their face value. The debt is then cancelled or restructured, and in exchange the debtor government commits to spending an agreed sum, in local currency, on conservation over a fixed period. Often this money is placed in an independent trust fund governed by a board on which government, scientists and civil society are all represented. The debtor pays less than it owed; the environment, in principle, receives funding that would not otherwise exist. Negotiating such an arrangement can take several years, and the legal and advisory fees involved are rarely trivial, which is one reason why smaller deals have often struggled to justify their costs.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters emphasise this rare combination of benefits. Professor Ingrid Scandurra, who advised on several early swaps and now teaches environmental finance at the Bergen School of Economics, argues that the trust funds created by these deals have been their most valuable legacy. Unlike government budgets, which can be cut overnight, a well-endowed trust can pay park rangers' salaries for decades. She points to protected areas that have survived political upheaval largely because their running costs were met from a fund that ministers could not easily raid. In her view the actual amount of debt relief is secondary; what matters is the creation of predictable, long-term finance.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Economists who study sovereign debt are less enthusiastic. Dr Esteban Aramburu of the Corviglia Sovereign Debt Observatory has calculated that even the largest swaps have reduced the total debt of the countries involved by only a few per cent. A country that remains heavily indebted, he argues, may still be forced to cut public spending in ways that harm the environment more than the swap helps it, for instance by shrinking the budget of the environment ministry or encouraging the expansion of export crops into forested land. Aramburu also notes that the discount at which debt is bought partly reflects a market expectation that it would never be fully repaid. Cancelling debt that would not have been paid anyway, he suggests, is less generous than the headline figures imply.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also questions of sovereignty. Because the conservation commitments are written into international agreements, they can bind future governments for twenty years or more. Dr Nomvula Sedgwick, a political scientist who has interviewed officials in several debtor countries, found that many felt the conservation priorities had been set largely by foreign organisations, with local communities consulted late or not at all. In some cases, fishing grounds were closed under marine protection commitments without any agreement on compensation for the families who depended on them. Sedgwick does not oppose swaps, but she insists that their legitimacy depends on who decides how the money is spent. Without that clarity, she warns, even well-funded programmes may provoke resentment among the very people whose cooperation conservation ultimately requires.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The truth, it seems to me, lies between these positions. It would be unrealistic to expect swaps to solve the debt crises of poor countries; they were never designed to do so, and judging them by that standard is unfair. Equally, however, they should not be marketed as a remedy for biodiversity loss on a global scale. The total sums involved, though large in headline terms, are modest compared with the estimated annual funding gap for conservation. Their genuine strength is narrower: they can provide stable funding for specific places over long periods, which is exactly what conservation projects most often lack.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If swaps are to fulfil that promise, several conditions seem necessary. The trust funds they create must be governed transparently, with independent audits published regularly. Local communities, especially those whose livelihoods are affected, should be involved before the terms are fixed rather than after. And the most recent generation of deals, which increasingly include targets for climate as well as biodiversity, need to be monitored with care, since it is far from clear that a single transaction can be held accountable for so many goals at once. A tool that was once almost an afterthought now carries considerable expectations; whether it can bear their weight remains to be seen.

topic: trophy hunting as a source of conservation finance: revenue distribution, quotas and import bans
title: The Price of a Trophy
subtitle: Can selling the right to shoot a few animals pay to protect a great many more?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few conservation issues provoke such strong feeling as trophy hunting. When photographs of a hunter posing beside a dead lion circulate online, public reaction is swift and almost uniformly hostile, and airlines, retailers and legislators have all responded with prohibitions of one kind or another. Among conservation economists, however, the question is far less settled. Their concern is not whether killing animals for sport is appealing, since few of them think it is, but whether the money it generates protects habitat that would otherwise disappear. Framed in this way, the issue becomes one of incentives rather than ethics, and the evidence turns out to be considerably more ambiguous than either side is usually willing to admit.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economic case rests on a simple observation. Across large parts of eastern and southern Africa, wildlife shares land with people who bear the costs of living alongside it: elephants trample crops, lions kill cattle, and land set aside for animals cannot be ploughed. Unless wildlife produces some income for these communities, the argument runs, they have every reason to convert the land to agriculture. Hunting, it is claimed, can earn revenue from areas that are too remote, too dry or too lacking in scenery to attract photographic tourists. Dr Thandeka Mbuyazi, an economist at the Limpopo Institute for Rural Development, estimates that in some countries hunting concessions cover an area several times larger than the national parks. If those concessions ceased to pay, she argues, much of that land would be fenced for livestock within a decade.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics question both the size of the revenue and where it ends up. Professor Rasmus Edelgaard of the Øresund Centre for Development Studies spent three years analysing the financial records of hunting operators and government agencies in four countries. He found that only a small fraction of hunting fees reached the villages in or near the concessions; most was absorbed by operators, ministries and intermediaries in the capital. Communities that receive almost nothing, he observes, can hardly be expected to tolerate predators for the sake of an industry that enriches others. Edelgaard does not deny that hunting earns money, but he regards the claim that it funds conservation on a large scale as resting more on assertion than on audited data.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ecologists have raised a different objection. Dr Nino Vashakidze, who has studied lion populations for more than two decades, found that where quotas were set too high, or where hunters targeted males in their prime, the social structure of prides was disrupted. Incoming males killed the cubs of their predecessors, and populations fell far faster than the number of animals shot would suggest. In her view the fault lies not with hunting as such but with quotas fixed by officials eager to maximise licence income rather than by scientists. Where she has seen age-based rules enforced, permitting only males older than six years to be taken, lion numbers have remained stable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A rather different perspective comes from the Northern Rangelands Councils Network, an association of village councils that manage wildlife on communal land. Its members argue that the decision whether to permit hunting should rest with the communities that live with the animals, not with distant governments or overseas campaigners. Where councils control both the quota and the revenue, the network reports, poaching has declined, because residents themselves have a stake in the animals' survival. Its leaders are openly scornful of import bans introduced by wealthy countries, which they describe as decisions about African land taken without African voices.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: My own view is that the debate has been distorted by an assumption shared by both camps: that the choice is between hunting and photographic tourism. In reality, many concessions hold no attraction for tourists, and the realistic alternative to hunting there is not a safari lodge but a cattle ranch. Opponents of hunting who ignore this are, in effect, gambling that land will stay wild without any income to sustain it. That said, supporters of hunting cannot claim that the industry is well run merely because it could, in principle, be beneficial. Edelgaard's findings on the distribution of revenue are damning, and they have not been convincingly rebutted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Nor is it obvious that bans achieve what their advocates intend. When one country suspended hunting nationwide several years ago, operators abandoned a number of concessions, and later surveys recorded a rise in poaching in those areas, apparently because the anti-poaching patrols that operators had paid for were withdrawn. It would be unwise to draw sweeping conclusions from a single case; other factors, including a severe drought, may have played a part. But the episode illustrates how removing one source of funding without replacing it can leave wildlife more exposed rather than less.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What seems clear is that trophy hunting is neither the conservation lifeline its defenders claim nor the unmitigated evil its critics describe. Its value depends almost entirely on governance: on who sets quotas, who receives the money, and whether either is independently monitored. A blanket judgement, for or against, is less useful than the slow and unglamorous work of discovering where hunting has worked, where it has failed, and why.

topic: conservation auctions: reverse tenders for landholder stewardship contracts
title: Bidding to Protect
subtitle: Borrowed from the world of government procurement, the conservation auction promised to stretch scarce budgets further. Has it delivered?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, governments that wanted farmers to manage land for wildlife relied on a simple instrument: a fixed payment per hectare, offered to anyone willing to sign up. The approach was easy to administer and politically uncontroversial, but economists had long suspected that it wasted money. A farmer whose land happened to contain a rare orchid meadow received exactly the same rate as one whose fields contributed little to biodiversity, and landholders who would have looked after their land in any case were paid as generously as those who needed persuading. From the 1990s onwards, a number of agencies began experimenting with an alternative adapted from the way governments buy roads and office supplies: the conservation auction.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanism is known as a reverse auction, because the agency is buying rather than selling. It announces a budget and a set of environmental goals, and landholders then submit sealed bids describing the actions they would undertake, such as fencing a creek or withdrawing sheep from a patch of woodland, together with the payment they would require. Each bid is scored using an index that combines the expected ecological benefit with the price, and the agency funds the bids offering the best value until its money runs out. Because nobody knows in advance where the cut-off will fall, each bidder has an incentive to ask for something close to his or her real costs; asking for too much risks rejection altogether.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Early results were striking. Dr Haruto Hattamura, an agricultural economist at the Murray Basin Policy Unit, compared a pilot auction in a temperate grassland region with what a conventional fixed-rate scheme would have achieved on the same budget. By his calculations, the auction secured between two and three times the ecological gains. The savings arose because many landholders bid well below the standard rate, either because their costs were genuinely low or because they valued conservation for its own sake and were content simply to have their expenses covered. Hattamura has described the auction as the most significant advance in agri-environmental policy in a generation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others are more guarded. Dr Corazon Ancheta, a behavioural economist, has run repeated auctions both in the laboratory and with real farmers, and has found that bidders learn. In a first round, bids broadly track costs. In later rounds, however, participants who have worked out the approximate cut-off raise their bids towards it, and after three or four rounds much of the initial cost advantage has disappeared. Ancheta does not conclude that auctions are futile. Instead, she argues that agencies should keep varying the rules, altering the budget, the scoring formula or the timing, so that bidders cannot easily infer where the threshold lies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third concern relates to who takes part. Professor Eeva Ruokolainen studied participation in forest conservation tenders in northern Europe and found that owners of small properties, and older owners in particular, were far less likely to submit bids than large commercial estates. Preparing a competitive bid, she discovered, demanded time, technical knowledge and confidence in dealing with officials. Since small holdings sometimes contain the most valuable habitat, including fragments of old-growth forest, this imbalance meant that the auctions tended to select the most capable bidders rather than the most important land. In trials where an adviser visited small owners before a tender opened, participation among them roughly doubled.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It seems to me that both the enthusiasm and the scepticism have been overstated. The laboratory evidence of learning is persuasive, but real auctions are held infrequently, often years apart, and landholders rarely have the detailed feedback available to an experimental participant. I suspect, therefore, that the erosion of savings in the field is slower than Ancheta's experiments imply. On the other hand, Hattamura's comparison flatters the auction, because it ignores the considerable expense of designing scoring systems, assessing sites and processing hundreds of individual bids. Fixed-rate schemes are cheap to run precisely because they are crude, and any fair comparison must account for that.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A deeper difficulty concerns what happens once contracts end. Most auction contracts run for between five and ten years, and there is remarkably little evidence about whether landholders maintain the changes after the payments stop. If fences are taken down and grazing resumes, the gains bought so efficiently may prove to be temporary. Some agencies are now experimenting with permanent covenants attached to the title of the land, which bind future owners as well as current ones, although landholders understandably demand much higher sums before agreeing to such terms.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Auctions, then, are not the magic formula their early champions suggested. Yet they do achieve something that is easily overlooked: they reveal information. A fixed payment tells an agency nothing about what conservation actually costs on different farms, whereas an auction, even an imperfect one, shows who can deliver environmental benefits cheaply and where. That knowledge, which can guide future spending of every kind, is arguably worth as much as the savings themselves.

topic: voluntary biodiversity credit markets: contribution claims, measurement metrics and the problem of demand
title: A Market for Nature Itself?
subtitle: Biodiversity credits promise to do for wildlife what carbon credits claimed to do for the climate. The comparison may be more revealing than their promoters intend

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the past few years, a new commodity has begun to appear in the brochures of financial consultancies and on the agendas of international summits: the biodiversity credit. The idea is to do for living species what carbon markets claimed to do for the atmosphere, turning an environmental improvement into a unit that can be measured, certified and sold. A landowner who restores a wetland or protects a stretch of forest would receive credits representing the gain in biodiversity, and companies, governments or private individuals could then buy them. Advocates speak of mobilising hundreds of billions of dollars a year. Sceptics see only the latest instalment in a long series of attempts to put a price on nature, few of which have lived up to the expectations that surrounded their launch.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Proponents are careful to distinguish credits from offsets. An offset is purchased to compensate for specific damage elsewhere, such as a new road that destroys a meadow, and is intended to cancel that damage out. A biodiversity credit, by contrast, is generally presented as a 'contribution': the buyer pays for conservation without claiming that its own impacts have thereby been neutralised. Dr Ilze Ozolina, who helped to draft one of the early voluntary standards at the Baltic Centre for Nature Finance, regards this distinction as essential. Offsetting, she notes, has always been dogged by the suspicion that it licenses destruction; contribution credits escape that trap because nobody can use them to justify harm.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: I find this distinction less reassuring than its authors intend. Whatever the formal wording, companies that buy credits will naturally wish to publicise the fact, and consumers are unlikely to grasp the subtle difference between contributing to nature and compensating for its loss. Experience from carbon markets suggests that the language of contribution slides easily into claims of neutrality once marketing departments become involved. Unless the rules governing public claims are strictly enforced, the line Ozolina draws may turn out to exist mainly on paper.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The deeper challenge is measurement. Carbon has one great advantage as a commodity: a tonne of carbon dioxide has the same effect on the climate wherever it is emitted or removed. Biodiversity has no such common currency. A hectare of restored bog in Scotland and a hectare of protected cloud forest in Ecuador differ in their species, their ecological functions and their rarity. Dr Kwabena Gyamerah, an ecologist at the Volta Basin Ecological Survey, has tested several of the metrics proposed by credit developers and found that they could rank the same set of sites in almost opposite order, depending on whether they emphasised the sheer number of species, the presence of threatened ones, or the intactness of the habitat. In his view, any single metric conceals choices that are fundamentally about values, and those choices are seldom acknowledged.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Gyamerah does not conclude that measurement is impossible, only that it must be local. He proposes that credits be tied to particular ecosystems and assessed against baselines established through independent field surveys, with satellite imagery used to supplement observation on the ground rather than to replace it. Such surveys are expensive, however, and here the economics become awkward. Professor Meenal Sabharwal, who studies environmental markets at the Deccan School of Public Policy, estimates that in the pilot projects she reviewed, monitoring and verification consumed between a third and a half of the revenue from credit sales. When so much is spent proving that a benefit exists, she observes, relatively little is left for the work that creates it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Sabharwal's broader concern relates to demand. Carbon markets grew largely because regulation in some regions obliged firms to buy credits, or because firms had made public commitments to reach 'net zero'. No comparable obligation exists for biodiversity, and voluntary purchases so far have been tiny in comparison with the sums predicted. She doubts that a market resting purely on corporate goodwill can ever reach the scale its promoters describe, and suggests that public funding, though less fashionable, would be a more dependable source of finance for conservation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That judgement seems to me too pessimistic. Purely voluntary markets are certainly fragile, but they can serve as testing grounds in which methods of measurement and verification are refined before governments decide whether to make them mandatory. The early carbon markets, after all, were also small, chaotic and widely derided. Moreover, credits may channel money to places that public budgets rarely reach, such as land held by indigenous communities, provided that those communities, rather than intermediaries, receive the bulk of the payments.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Whether biodiversity credits become a significant force for conservation or merely a footnote in its history will depend less on the ingenuity of their design than on the integrity of those who use them. A market in nature can function only if buyers are prevented from overstating what they have bought, and if the people who actually manage the land are rewarded fairly for doing so. Neither condition can be taken for granted, and both will require a degree of oversight that the enthusiasm of the market's promoters has so far tended to obscure.

topic: paying for human-wildlife conflict: compensation, conditional payments, performance payments and wildlife damage insurance
title: The Cost of a Wild Neighbour
subtitle: Paying farmers for the damage done by protected animals seems only fair. Making it work is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When an elephant walks through a field of maize at night, a family may lose a season's food in a few hours. Across Africa and Asia, conflict between people and wildlife ranks among the most serious threats to large mammals, not because farmers are by nature hostile to animals, but because the costs of living alongside them are distributed so unevenly. A tourist who photographs an elephant in a national park enjoys the benefit; the farmer on the park boundary absorbs the loss. One response has been to compensate people for damage caused by protected species. The principle seems just, and many governments have adopted it. Yet decades of experience suggest that compensation is far harder to do well than it first appears.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious difficulty is verification. Before paying a claim, an agency must confirm that the damage was caused by a protected species and not, for instance, by stray cattle or disease, and it must then estimate the value of what was lost. In remote areas this may require an official to travel for days. Dr Pieter Bezuidenhoudt, who evaluated compensation programmes in four countries for the Kavango Conservation Economics Group, found that the average delay between a claim and its payment exceeded fourteen months in two of them, and that many farmers had simply stopped reporting their losses. A payment that arrives more than a year late, he argues, does little to change how a farmer feels about the animal responsible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second problem is what economists call moral hazard. If losses are fully reimbursed, farmers may have less reason to guard their crops, build sturdy enclosures for livestock or avoid planting next to the forest edge. Dr Agnieszka Kuczera, who studied wolf predation in central Europe, found that herders receiving generous compensation were less likely to use guard dogs or night-time enclosures than those in regions where payments were modest. She is careful, however, not to blame the herders themselves. In her view the fault lay with schemes that paid out whether or not any precautions had been taken; where payment was made conditional on basic protective measures, losses fell by almost half.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some specialists would abandon compensation altogether in favour of approaches that reward the presence of wildlife rather than the damage it causes. In parts of Scandinavia, reindeer-herding communities have been paid according to the number of carnivore offspring confirmed on their grazing lands, regardless of how many reindeer are actually killed. Professor Sipho Ndlovana of the Highveld Centre for Environmental Policy, who has called for this model to be adapted for southern Africa, maintains that it aligns incentives: the community gains when predators thrive, yet it still has every reason to keep its own losses low through careful herding. Critics respond that such payments can feel like being asked to sell one's tolerance, and that they offer nothing to an individual family whose herd suffers a particularly severe attack.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further alternative is insurance. In several pilot projects in South Asia, farmers pay a small premium, often subsidised by conservation organisations, in return for cover against wildlife damage. The Terai Smallholders' Alliance, a federation of farming cooperatives that has run such a scheme for more than a decade, reports that paying premiums gives members a sense of ownership that state compensation never achieved. Because the cooperative's own assessors know both the land and the farmers, claims are settled within weeks rather than months. The alliance insists that local control, rather than the size of payments, is the real reason for its success.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In my view, the debate has too often been framed as a contest between rival mechanisms, when the more important question is one of trust. Compensation, insurance and performance payments can each work, but only if farmers believe that their claims will be handled fairly and promptly. Where they have that confidence, even modest sums can substantially reduce retaliatory killing of animals; where they lack it, generous budgets achieve remarkably little. It is no coincidence that the most successful schemes involve local institutions in assessing damage.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is also worth remembering that money is not the only cost that farmers bear. Families who guard their fields through the night lose sleep, children may miss school to help them, and the fear of meeting an elephant on a path at dusk is not something a cheque can easily offset. Researchers have only recently begun to measure these hidden costs, and they are very probably larger than the financial losses that schemes are designed to cover. Any honest assessment of coexistence with wildlife must take them into account.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of this means that compensation should be abandoned. For many rural communities it remains the only tangible acknowledgement that their losses matter to anyone outside the village. But it should be regarded as one tool among several, designed with care, monitored honestly, and linked wherever possible to the measures that prevent damage from occurring in the first place.

topic: wildlife-friendly certification of crops such as shade-grown coffee: price premiums, consumer behaviour and additionality
title: Does the Label Pay?
subtitle: Wildlife-friendly certification promised to fund conservation through the supermarket checkout. The results have been mixed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk down the coffee aisle of a large supermarket and you will find packets decorated with birds, frogs and rainforest canopies, each carrying a logo that promises the beans were grown in ways that protect wildlife. Certification schemes of this kind emerged in the 1990s from a simple proposition: if consumers would pay a little more for products grown without destroying habitat, farmers would have a financial reason to conserve it. Rather than relying on governments to regulate land use, or on donors to purchase land for reserves, conservation would be funded at the checkout. Three decades later, wildlife-friendly labels appear on a significant share of the coffee, cocoa, tea and bananas traded internationally. Whether they have achieved what their founders hoped is a different and more difficult question.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The ecological rationale is strongest in the case of coffee. Traditionally, coffee bushes were grown beneath a canopy of taller trees, which provided shade and, incidentally, habitat for birds, insects and the orchids and bromeliads that grow on branches. From the 1970s onwards, however, many farmers in Latin America cut down their shade trees and switched to sun-tolerant varieties. These yield more beans in the short term, but they demand larger quantities of fertiliser and support far fewer species. Field surveys in the region have recorded up to twice as many bird species on shaded farms as on sun plantations. The most demanding certification standard therefore requires farms to maintain a canopy containing at least ten species of tree, reaching a minimum height of twelve metres.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For farmers, the decisive issue is the price premium. Dr Mateo Sancho-Villalobos, an agronomist at the Cordillera Agrarian Research Station, tracked the accounts of more than three hundred smallholdings over eight years. He found that certified farmers did receive higher prices, typically between five and ten per cent above the conventional rate, but that the premium often failed to cover the additional costs of certification. These include annual inspection fees, the time spent keeping detailed records, and the beans forgone by retaining shade trees. For the smallest farms, the net financial effect was frequently negative. Many stayed in the scheme nonetheless, because certification gave them access to buyers who offered more stable, long-term contracts, a benefit that had little to do with conservation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consumer side of the equation is no more straightforward. Dr Eleni Mavridou, a consumer economist who has conducted purchasing experiments in Europe and North America, found that shoppers questioned in surveys claim to be willing to pay substantially more for wildlife-friendly products, yet in trials conducted in real shops only a minority actually did so. The proliferation of labels has added to the confusion: in one of her surveys, fewer than one in five respondents could correctly explain what any of the logos guaranteed. Mavridou concludes that much of the premium is captured not by farmers but by retailers and roasters, who use the labels principally to distinguish their brands from those of competitors.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most uncomfortable findings concern ecological outcomes. Professor Aino Rautavaara, an ecologist, compared certified and uncertified farms in three countries. On average, certified farms had more tree cover and more bird species, as the schemes' promoters would hope. On closer inspection, however, most of these farms had been shaded long before they joined. The schemes had largely recruited farms that already met their standards rather than persuading owners of sun plantations to replant, so that, in the terminology economists use, their additionality was low. There was one notable exception. In a region where a cooperative had supplied seedlings and technical advice, a number of sun farms converted back to shade within six years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Rautavaara's result is often cited as proof that certification has failed, but I would argue that it is less damning than it first appears. Rewarding farmers who have kept their shade trees despite every temptation to clear them is not worthless; without the premium, some of them might well have followed their neighbours into sun cultivation, and preventing a loss is as valuable as reversing one. Nonetheless, it is difficult to see how labels could ever become the main pillar of conservation finance. The volumes of certified produce actually sold at a premium are too small, and the premium itself too unreliable, to sustain that role.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Recent proposals attempt to address some of these weaknesses. One is landscape certification, in which whole districts rather than individual farms are assessed. The Highland Growers' Federation, which represents several thousand smallholders, argues that farm-by-farm inspection is both expensive and ecologically naive, since birds and pollinators move freely across property boundaries. A district certified as a unit, it maintains, could share the costs of monitoring and plan corridors of forest between farms. Critics reply that landscape schemes dilute accountability, because a single careless landowner can undermine the efforts of many without bearing any individual penalty.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Wildlife-friendly labels, then, have proved to be a modest instrument rather than a transformative one. Their greatest achievement may lie less in the money they have raised than in the awareness they have created: millions of consumers now know that the way a crop is grown matters to the animals that live among it. Turning that awareness into reliable funding on the scale conservation requires, however, remains a problem that no logo has yet solved.

topic: visitor entry fees as a source of funding for protected areas: willingness to pay, two-tier pricing, revenue retention and dependence on tourism
title: The Price of Admission
subtitle: Could the people who visit national parks pay to keep them protected, and should they?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of the world's protected areas are chronically short of money. Surveys of park managers repeatedly report too few rangers, crumbling roads and visitor centres, and budgets that cover only a fraction of what effective management would require. Conservationists even have a name for the result: 'paper parks', areas that are protected in law but scarcely at all in practice. One obvious source of additional income stands at the gate. Yet in many countries entry to national parks is free or nearly so, and proposals to raise charges tend to provoke heated argument, because they expose deep disagreements about whom parks are for and who should pay for them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economic case for higher fees is straightforward. Dr Aigerim Nurmagambetova, an environmental economist at the Steppe Institute for Resource Economics, has measured what visitors are prepared to pay at a dozen parks in Central Asia and East Africa, and has found that charges are typically set far below that level. For international tourists, who may have spent thousands on flights and accommodation, the entry fee represents a negligible share of the cost of the trip, so raising it considerably would barely affect the number who come. By her calculations, fees at several of the parks she studied could be tripled without any measurable fall in foreign arrivals, and the extra revenue would be enough to pay for the entire ranger service. Domestic visitors, she acknowledges, are far more sensitive to price, which is why her proposals apply chiefly to foreigners.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Many parks already charge foreign visitors more than their own citizens, sometimes ten times as much. The usual justification is that residents contribute to parks through taxation, generally have lower incomes than international tourists, and have a stronger claim to what is, after all, their national heritage. Critics occasionally describe such pricing as discriminatory, but the case for it seems to me broadly sound. There is, however, a complication that its defenders rarely acknowledge. If prices for residents are kept extremely low, the main beneficiaries may turn out to be affluent city-dwellers with cars and leisure time, while the rural families who live beside a park, and who bear most of the costs of its existence, gain almost nothing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns what dependence on fees does to the way parks are managed. Dr Tomasz Wojtasik, a geographer who studies tourism in the mountain parks of central Europe, describes what he calls a 'revenue trap'. Where a park relies heavily on ticket sales, its managers come under pressure to attract ever more visitors, by widening roads, enlarging car parks and permitting new hotels, and this development can degrade the very ecosystems the park was established to protect. In two parks he examined, the share of the budget derived from tickets rose from under a fifth to more than three-fifths within a decade, and spending shifted steadily away from habitat management towards visitor facilities. In his view, fees should supplement public funding, never replace it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even where fees are collected, they do not always reach the park. In many countries all entry charges are paid into the central treasury and redistributed, if at all, through the general budget. Dr Lerato Moipolai, who has advised protected-area agencies across southern Africa, found that where parks were allowed to retain at least half of their fee income, managers had a strong incentive to improve both visitor services and the enforcement of anti-poaching laws. Where every cent went to the treasury, by contrast, there was little reason to collect fees efficiently, and informal payments to gate staff were widespread. Moipolai also argues that a fixed proportion of fee income should be passed directly to neighbouring communities, a measure that would go some way towards addressing the imbalance described earlier.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is that tourism revenue is highly concentrated. A handful of famous parks, with spectacular scenery or easily seen large animals, earn the great majority of fee income, while most protected areas, remote and lacking charismatic wildlife, receive very few visitors at all. However efficiently fees are set and collected, they will never fund such places. Some countries therefore pool entry charges across their whole park system, so that the most popular sites subsidise the least visited. This arrangement strikes me as entirely sensible, but it is also politically fragile, since managers of the successful parks understandably resent surrendering money their own efforts have earned. Without such pooling, however, the parks that most need money, often those protecting little-known but ecologically irreplaceable habitats, would be left almost entirely dependent on whatever their governments chose to allocate.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Visitor fees, then, are part of the answer to the funding crisis in protected areas, but they cannot be the whole of it. Perhaps the greatest danger is that finance ministries, observing a rise in fee revenue, will cut their own allocations by a corresponding amount, leaving parks no better off than before and considerably more exposed to the fortunes of the tourist industry. As sudden collapses in international travel have repeatedly demonstrated, that is among the least predictable sources of income a park could have. Fees work best when they add to a stable foundation of public money rather than substituting for it.

topic: conservation triage: prioritising threatened species by cost-effectiveness, evolutionary distinctiveness and cultural value
title: Choosing Which to Save
subtitle: With money for conservation far short of what is needed, some scientists argue that species must be ranked. Others find the very idea intolerable

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, conservation agencies around the world spend a sum that is generally estimated to be a small fraction of what would be needed to halt the decline of threatened species. The consequence is uncomfortable but unavoidable: every decision to fund the recovery of one species is, implicitly, a decision not to fund another. Some researchers have begun to describe this situation using a term borrowed from battlefield medicine, where doctors faced with more casualties than they can treat must decide whom to help first. 'Conservation triage', as it has become known, proposes that these choices be made openly and systematically rather than left to chance, habit or public sentiment. Few ideas in the discipline have provoked such fierce resistance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Among the most prominent advocates of explicit prioritisation is Dr Marjatta Isokangas, a decision scientist at the Kvarken Centre for Decision Analysis. Her framework ranks recovery projects according to three quantities: the expected benefit to a species, the probability that the project will succeed, and its cost. When she applied the method to the threatened plants of a northern archipelago, she found that following the ranking would have secured almost twice as many species against extinction as the existing pattern of spending, which tended to concentrate resources on the very rarest and most precarious. Isokangas is unapologetic about the implications. Declining to set priorities openly, she argues, does not avoid triage; it merely ensures that triage is carried out arbitrarily, by default, and without anyone taking responsibility for it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The core logic of this argument is difficult to dispute. If resources are fixed, a method that saves more species with the same money would seem self-evidently preferable to one that saves fewer. My reservation concerns the numbers on which such rankings depend. For well-studied mammals and birds, the costs and likely success of a recovery programme can be estimated with some confidence. For an obscure moss or freshwater snail, however, these figures are frequently little more than informed guesses, and a neatly ordered list can lend them a precision they do not possess. A ranking is only as trustworthy as its least reliable input, and that input is often very unreliable indeed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different objection holds that species should not be treated as interchangeable units at all. Dr Rustam Farahbod, an evolutionary biologist, maintains that some species embody far more unique evolutionary history than others. A beetle with hundreds of close relatives is, in his view, not equivalent to a reptile that is the sole surviving member of a lineage stretching back a hundred million years. When the former disappears, much of its genetic heritage survives in its relatives; when the latter is lost, an entire branch of the tree of life is cut away. Farahbod has therefore championed priority lists that weight each species by its evolutionary distinctiveness as well as by the degree of threat it faces, an approach that has already influenced the allocation of funds by several international bodies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Professor Sione Leavasa, an anthropologist who has worked for many years with island communities in the Pacific, regards both approaches as excessively technocratic. Many species, he points out, carry cultural meanings that no formula captures: particular birds whose feathers are used in ceremonies, or trees that feature in genealogies and oral histories. When priorities are set by experts in distant institutions, the species that matter most to the people who live alongside them may be the very ones quietly abandoned. Leavasa does not reject ranking as such, but he insists that communities must take part in deciding the criteria, rather than merely being informed of the results.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A fourth position challenges the premise that any species need be written off. The Vanishing Lineages Consortium, an alliance of zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks, argues that triage is premature because off-site conservation can preserve species until conditions in the wild improve. Storing the seeds of a plant species, it notes, can cost less per year than a single field survey, and captive breeding has already rescued several animals that had disappeared entirely from their natural habitats. On this view, the choice is not between saving a species and losing it, but between protecting it in the wild now and safeguarding it in storage for the future.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The consortium's position is appealing, but I believe it overstates what off-site conservation can achieve. Captive populations of animals are expensive to maintain, tend to lose genetic diversity over successive generations, and in many cases can never be returned to the wild because the threats that drove them out persist. Seed banking works admirably for most plants, yet a significant minority produce seeds that die when dried or frozen. It is also sometimes claimed that publishing lists of species judged not worth saving would deter donors. That may be so, but it is an argument for careful communication, not for pretending that choices are not being made.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The real question, then, is not whether conservation should prioritise, since it already does, but how it should do so and who should decide. A defensible approach would combine estimates of cost-effectiveness with measures of evolutionary distinctiveness and cultural value, state its assumptions openly, and revise its rankings as better information becomes available. Such a system would not make the choices any less painful. It would, however, make them visible, and visibility is the precondition for holding anyone to account for them.

topic: natural capital accounting: recording ecosystems in national statistics, physical versus monetary accounts
title: Counting the Uncounted
subtitle: Governments measure their economies in meticulous detail but have rarely kept track of the forests, wetlands and soils on which those economies depend. A new kind of accounting aims to change that

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Economists have long pointed out a peculiar blind spot in the way nations measure their prosperity. A country that cuts down its forests and sells the timber records an increase in gross domestic product, while the disappearance of the forest itself appears nowhere in the national statistics. The same is true of a fishery harvested beyond its capacity to recover, or of farmland whose topsoil is steadily washed into rivers. Natural capital accounting is an attempt to correct this omission. Alongside the conventional accounts of production and income, it records the stocks of natural assets a country possesses, such as forests, wetlands, groundwater and soils, together with the flows of services they provide, from the filtering of drinking water to the protection of coasts against storms. An internationally agreed statistical standard for such accounts was adopted only recently, and dozens of countries are now experimenting with it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The accounts come in two broad forms. Physical accounts record the extent and condition of ecosystems: how many hectares of wetland remain, for example, and how healthy they are. Monetary accounts go further, attaching a financial value to these assets and services. Dr Ama Baptiste-Ondo, who led a pilot programme at the Gulf of Guinea Statistical Office, believes the physical form is by far the more important. Her team's accounts revealed that the country's mangrove forests had shrunk by a quarter in fifteen years, a loss that had not been captured by any previous official statistic. Ministers took notice, she recalls, largely because the figure appeared in the same publication as the growth figures they routinely consulted. In her view, attaching prices to such findings is unnecessary and risks provoking arguments that distract from the evidence of decline.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Florencia Etchegaray, an environmental economist, takes the opposite view. Real decisions about land use, she argues, are made in finance ministries, and finance ministries think in money. Only when nature appears in the same units as roads, factories and tax revenue will it be weighed against them on equal terms. In one study she estimated the value of the water purification provided by a forested catchment and found that it exceeded the annual revenue of the hydroelectric dam downstream, which depended on that clean water to function. Etchegaray readily concedes that such estimates are uncertain. Nevertheless, she maintains that a rough figure is preferable to the value nature is implicitly assigned at present, which is zero.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Bayarmaa Tserendorj, an ecological economist, is among the most forceful critics of monetary accounts. To remain consistent with conventional national accounts, she explains, the methods used value ecosystems at the prices that would apply if their services were bought and sold, which deliberately excludes much of the benefit people actually derive from nature, including the satisfaction of knowing that a species or landscape continues to exist. The resulting figures therefore systematically understate nature's worth. More troubling still, in her view, is that once a forest has a price, it becomes easier to argue that a more profitable use of the same land justifies its destruction. Some processes, such as the slow formation of soil over centuries, have no meaningful market equivalent at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It seems to me that the debate between physical and monetary accounting has become needlessly polarised. Physical accounts are indispensable in any case; without reliable data on the extent and condition of ecosystems, any monetary value is built on sand. Tserendorj's fear that prices encourage substitution is understandable, but it attributes too much power to the accounts themselves. Forests were cleared on a vast scale long before anyone attempted to price them, and the absence of a price did nothing to protect them. A monetary figure, used carefully and accompanied by physical data, can at least ensure that a loss is acknowledged rather than ignored.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical obstacles are considerable. Accounts are only useful if they are updated regularly and consistently, yet many countries lack the resources for sustained ecological monitoring. Satellite imagery has made it far easier to measure the extent of forests and wetlands, but it is much less informative about their condition: a forest may look intact from space while having lost most of its large animals to hunting. There is also a tendency for accounts to be compiled once, as donor-funded pilots, and then quietly abandoned. Of the dozen or so pilot accounts produced in one region over the past decade, only a handful have been updated since their initial funding came to an end.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even well-maintained accounts matter only if somebody uses them. A treasury that publishes natural capital accounts but continues to appraise new projects without reference to them has gained little beyond a statistical curiosity. The real test, therefore, is whether the accounts influence budgets and planning decisions, and here the evidence remains thin. A few countries now require proposals for major infrastructure, such as dams and highways, to state their likely effects on natural capital, but it is too early to know whether this has altered which projects are approved.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Natural capital accounting will not, by itself, halt the degradation of ecosystems; it is a measuring instrument, not a policy. Yet measurement has a power of its own. Losses that are recorded year after year in official publications are harder to dismiss than those that remain invisible, and a government that knows the condition of its natural assets can no longer plead ignorance when they decline. In that sense, accurate accounts are a necessary, if far from sufficient, condition for managing nature as seriously as nations already manage their money.

topic: cool roofs and reflective pavements for reducing urban heat
title: The Case for Paler Cities
subtitle: Painting roofs and roads in light colours is one of the cheapest ways to cool an overheating city, but its benefits are less straightforward than they first appear

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has walked barefoot across a dark car park on a summer afternoon understands the basic problem. Asphalt, tar and dark roofing materials absorb most of the sunlight that strikes them, store it during the day and release it slowly through the night, so that dense urban districts can remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside long after sunset. The proposed remedy is disarmingly simple: make these surfaces paler, so that more sunlight is reflected back towards the sky before it can be converted into heat. The idea is hardly new, since the whitewashed villages of the Mediterranean and the pale mud walls of desert towns embody the same principle. What is new is the ambition to apply it to entire cities. Its simplicity is precisely what makes the approach so appealing to municipal authorities, but it is also, I would argue, what has allowed some of its drawbacks to escape proper scrutiny.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physics, at least, is uncontroversial. The proportion of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects is known as its albedo, and it ranges from about five per cent for fresh asphalt to more than eighty per cent for a newly applied white coating. Dr Marisol Ugartemendia, who studies building physics at a research institute in Valencia, has recorded the temperatures of more than two hundred roofs over five summers. On a clear afternoon, she found, a conventional dark roof may exceed seventy degrees Celsius, while a white roof beside it remains only a few degrees above the temperature of the air. For the occupants of the building, the difference is considerable. Ugartemendia's data suggest that the demand for air conditioning in top-floor flats falls by between ten and twenty per cent once a reflective coating is applied, although she is careful to point out that the effect diminishes sharply on lower floors, which are shielded from the roof by the storeys above them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whether brighter roofs can cool a whole city, rather than individual buildings, is a harder question, because it cannot be answered by direct measurement; no city has yet transformed enough of its surfaces to provide a convincing test. Researchers have therefore turned to computer simulations. A group led by the climate modeller Hamid Zarrinkoob has estimated that if most of the roofs in a large, densely built city were made reflective, average afternoon air temperatures during heatwaves could fall by between one and two degrees. That may sound modest, yet Zarrinkoob notes that mortality during extreme heat rises steeply with each additional degree, so that even small reductions could prevent a significant number of deaths among elderly residents.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Roads and pavements are a different matter. Because they make up a large share of the urban surface, several cities have experimented with grey or white coatings on streets, and early reports of lower surface temperatures were greeted with enthusiasm. The work of Tuulikki Rahkonen, an environmental physiologist, has complicated this picture. Rather than measuring the temperature of the ground or the air, Rahkonen measured the total heat load experienced by a person walking along a street, which includes sunlight reflected upwards from below. On coated streets at midday, she found, this load was frequently higher than on untreated ones, because the light that the pavement no longer absorbed was being redirected onto the bodies of pedestrians. In other words, a street can become cooler by conventional measures and at the same time more uncomfortable for those who use it. This finding deserves more attention than it has received, since it is people, not thermometers, who suffer during a heatwave.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is that bright surfaces rarely stay bright. Dust, soot and the growth of algae gradually darken reflective coatings, and in polluted cities they may lose a third of their reflectivity within three years unless they are regularly cleaned or recoated. Cost estimates for cool-roof programmes frequently overlook this maintenance burden, and they are more optimistic as a result. Some scientists have raised more speculative concerns. Simulations produced by the Andean Urban Climate Consortium suggest that brightening on a very large scale could weaken the sea breezes that carry moisture inland, reducing rainfall in surrounding regions. These results are worth noting, but they assume a degree of adoption far beyond anything currently planned, and they are not, in my view, a reason to delay modest programmes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The social dimension of cool surfaces is in some respects their strongest argument. Poorly insulated top-floor flats, often rented by low-income households who cannot afford air conditioning, are among the most dangerous places to be during a heatwave, and a reflective coating is one of the cheapest interventions available to protect their occupants. Yet those who would benefit are rarely those who decide. Landlords bear the cost of recoating a roof while tenants enjoy the lower temperatures, and voluntary subsidy schemes have consequently attracted few applicants in the poorer districts where they are most needed. Incorporating reflectivity standards into building regulations, so that every replacement roof must meet them, would seem a more reliable route than continuing to offer grants that so few landlords take up.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that paler cities are a mistake. Reflective roofs, in particular, offer a rare combination of low cost, rapid installation and measurable benefit. But they are best understood as one element of a broader strategy that also includes street trees, shaded walkways and better-insulated housing, and reflective streets should be introduced only where few people walk, such as car parks and service roads. The most valuable contribution of the debate so far may simply be the reminder that cooling a city is not the same as cooling the people who live in it.

topic: heat-health action plans: heatwave alerts, cooling centres and reaching vulnerable residents
title: Warnings in the Heat
subtitle: Cities have learned to sound the alarm when temperatures soar, but whether the alarm reaches those most at risk is another question

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the hazards associated with weather, heat is perhaps the most deceptive. Floods and storms leave visible destruction in their wake, but the victims of a heatwave usually die quietly, often alone in overheated flats, and their deaths are frequently recorded as heart attacks or respiratory failure rather than as consequences of the temperature. Following a series of devastating summers, hundreds of cities have now adopted what are known as heat-health action plans. When forecasts indicate that temperatures will pass a predetermined threshold, an alert is issued, public messages are broadcast, air-conditioned buildings are opened as cooling centres and social services are instructed to contact vulnerable residents. The spread of these schemes is undoubtedly welcome. Yet the confidence with which they are promoted rests, I believe, on rather thinner evidence than their advocates usually acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty lies in deciding when an alert should be triggered. Dr Lalaina Ravelomanana, an epidemiologist at the Indian Ocean Institute for Urban Health, examined daily mortality records from thirty cities and found that the temperature at which deaths begin to climb differs enormously from place to place. In cities with cool climates, mortality may start to rise at temperatures that residents of hotter regions would consider pleasant. Ravelomanana concludes that thresholds should be calibrated for each city individually, and she adds that they ought to include minimum night-time temperatures, since it is the absence of relief during the hours of darkness that exhausts the body's capacity to cope. Her case seems to me unanswerable. A single national threshold, which several governments still use, is bound to issue warnings too late in some places and too often in others, and frequent false alarms teach the public to disregard them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whether the alerts actually save lives is a more contentious matter. A number of studies have reported that heat-related mortality fell after cities introduced action plans. Mikko Hiltunen, a statistician who specialises in the evaluation of public health programmes, regards such comparisons as deeply unreliable. Over the same period, he observes, air conditioning became far more common, the general health of older people improved, and populations may have grown physiologically accustomed to hotter summers. Once these factors are taken into account, Hiltunen estimates that the plans themselves explain only a modest share of the decline. His scepticism is a useful corrective, but it would be a mistake to infer from it that the plans achieve little. The more accurate conclusion is that most of them were never designed in a way that would allow their effects to be measured, which is a failing of evaluation rather than evidence of futility.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cooling centres illustrate the gap between intention and outcome particularly clearly. A team led by the geographer Shirin Esfandiari surveyed visitors to such centres in four cities and found that attendance was generally low and that those who did come were, for the most part, younger and in reasonably good health. The people at greatest risk, such as the very old, the housebound and those living with chronic illness, were rarely present. Esfandiari identifies several reasons. Travelling across a city in extreme heat is itself hazardous for a frail person; many centres refuse entry to pets, which some elderly residents will not leave behind; and opening hours commonly end in the early evening, just as poorly ventilated flats reach their highest temperatures. Her recommendation is that authorities should shift resources from bringing people to the cool towards bringing coolness, or at least contact, to people in their homes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A subtler obstacle is the way in which people perceive their own vulnerability. Surveys repeatedly show that many people in their seventies and eighties do not think of themselves as elderly, and so pay little attention to advice addressed to 'older people'. Kawika Kekumu, who researches risk communication, compared the responses of several thousand participants to different versions of a heat warning. Messages that urged recipients to check on a neighbour or relative prompted considerably more intended action than those that emphasised the danger to the recipient personally. The finding is intriguing, and it may point towards more effective campaigns. It should be noted, however, that Kekumu recorded what participants said they would do, not what they subsequently did, and the gap between the two is notoriously wide.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some cities have tried to reach vulnerable residents directly by maintaining registers of people who wish to receive a telephone call whenever an alert is issued. Anna Strzelecki, who studies social policy, points out a fundamental weakness in this approach: enrolment is voluntary, and the socially isolated people who face the highest risk are precisely those least likely to put their names forward. Health services often hold the information that would identify such individuals, but data protection rules generally prevent it from being passed to the local authorities who run the registers. Strzelecki suggests that consent to be contacted during heatwaves could be requested routinely when patients register with a doctor, a modest administrative change that might greatly extend the reach of these schemes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these measures addresses the underlying cause of most heat deaths, which is that many people live in buildings that become dangerously hot. Action plans treat a heatwave as an emergency to be managed for a few days, and in that role they are valuable. The danger is that they come to be seen as a sufficient response in themselves, allowing governments to postpone the far more expensive task of insulating, shading and ventilating the housing in which vulnerable people spend their summers. Warnings can tell people that their homes are unsafe; they cannot make those homes any cooler.

topic: managed retreat: government buyouts and relocation of flood-prone urban neighbourhoods
title: Stepping Back from the Water
subtitle: Paying people to leave flood-prone neighbourhoods was once politically unthinkable. Is it now becoming unavoidable?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a number of riverside towns, there are streets where the houses have vanished. The pavements and lamp posts remain, but the plots between them have been grassed over and are mown each summer by the local council. These empty lots are the legacy of buyout programmes, in which public authorities purchase homes that have flooded repeatedly, demolish them and return the land to open space that can be inundated without harming anyone. The practice is generally known as managed retreat, and until recently it was rarely mentioned by politicians, who feared being seen to abandon their own voters. It now features in almost every serious discussion of how cities should adapt to rising flood risk. In my view, retreat deserves the attention it is finally receiving, but its progress has been slowed by the very phrase used to describe it, which suggests defeat rather than foresight.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economic argument is the easiest to make. In most flood insurance systems, a small minority of properties is responsible for a disproportionate share of claims, because the same houses are damaged and rebuilt again and again. Dr Neema Mbwambo, an economist at the Coastal Economics Unit in Dar es Salaam, analysed two decades of claims data and concluded that for the most frequently flooded properties, a single purchase by the state would have cost considerably less than the repairs that were actually funded over the period. Her calculations are convincing as far as they go. However, they concern the worst cases, and it would be unwise to assume that the same logic can be extended to whole districts, where land values are higher, flooding is less frequent and the costs of relocation rise sharply.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A less obvious difficulty arises from the voluntary nature of most programmes. Because each household decides independently whether to accept an offer, buyouts tend to produce what planners call a chequerboard pattern, with occupied homes scattered among vacant plots. The urban planner Julien Pelletreau has documented the consequences in several such neighbourhoods. Roads, drains and street lighting must still be maintained for the households that remain, but the local tax base has shrunk, and those who stay find themselves increasingly isolated as shops and neighbours disappear. Pelletreau argues that programmes should offer additional incentives when all the households on a street agree to leave together, so that entire blocks can be cleared and the land restored as a coherent floodplain rather than a patchwork.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Questions of fairness are harder still. The sociologist Oyunchimeg Bayarsaikhan, who has interviewed more than three hundred households offered buyouts, found that those most willing to accept were typically owners with savings or relatives elsewhere, people for whom moving was a manageable disruption. Tenants, by contrast, often received nothing, since payments were made to the owners of the property rather than to its occupants. Bayarsaikhan also draws attention to the way offers are calculated. Most programmes pay the market value of a home before the flood, but in poorer neighbourhoods that value may be too low to buy anything comparable in a safer location. Some families therefore end up moving to cheaper areas that are themselves at risk, which merely relocates the problem.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Beyond money lies the question of what is lost when a community disperses. The anthropologist Eleni Anagnostou has compared cases in which residents moved individually with cases in which whole communities relocated together to a new site. Where residents were involved in choosing and designing the destination, she found, social networks largely survived, and satisfaction several years later was markedly higher. Collective relocations of this kind are slow, sometimes taking a decade from first proposal to completion, and critics argue that people living in danger cannot wait that long. The objection has some force, but I would maintain that the delay is a price worth paying when the alternative is the slow disintegration of a community.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The vocabulary of retreat has itself become a subject of debate. Some agencies now prefer terms such as strategic relocation or managed realignment, hoping to avoid the military associations of the older phrase. A change of name alone, however, is unlikely to persuade anyone to leave a family home. What appears to matter more is whether relocation is presented as a move towards something, such as better housing, secure tenure or a stronger local economy, rather than simply as an escape from danger. Several successful programmes have combined buyouts with investment in the receiving neighbourhood, so that those who leave and those who welcome them can both see a benefit.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this suggests that retreat will become the principal way in which cities respond to flooding. Most urban land is far too valuable, and most residents far too attached to it, for anything other than defence to be considered in the majority of cases. But to rule retreat out entirely is to commit public budgets to ever-rising costs in the places where defence makes least sense. The most important lesson from existing programmes concerns timing. Decisions taken in the weeks after a disaster, when emotions run high and the desire to rebuild is strongest, tend to favour reconstruction on the same site. Retreat works best when it is planned calmly, years before the next flood arrives.

topic: urban ventilation corridors: planning cities to channel cool night air and wind
title: Letting the City Breathe
subtitle: Planners in many hot cities now try to steer cool air through the streets, but the science of urban airflow is less settled than the maps suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a still summer night, the air in a city that lies in a valley can become oppressively stagnant. The surrounding hills may be several degrees cooler, and in principle that cooler air ought to drift downhill into the streets below. In practice, it frequently fails to arrive, because rows of tall buildings, raised motorways and dense industrial estates stand across its path and cause it to pool on the outskirts. For several decades, a handful of European municipalities have responded by protecting so-called ventilation corridors: strips of parkland, railway land, river banks and broad avenues aligned with the direction in which air naturally flows, kept free of large buildings so that cool air can penetrate the urban core. The concept has recently been written into the planning guidance of many fast-growing cities in Asia and the Middle East. It is an elegant idea, and the maps that accompany it are persuasive. However, the enthusiasm with which it has been adopted has, I suspect, run some way ahead of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The underlying physics is well understood. After sunset, grass and woodland on the slopes around a city lose heat rapidly, and the air in contact with them becomes cooler and therefore denser than the air above the built-up area. This heavier air slides downhill at roughly walking pace, and where it is able to enter the city it can lower night-time temperatures in nearby streets by several degrees. Dr Aino Pohjanpalo, a climatologist who has spent a decade tracking such flows with sensors mounted on bicycles, confirms that the effect is real but finds that it is strikingly local. Close to the edge of a corridor the cooling is pronounced; a few hundred metres away, among closely packed buildings, it is barely detectable. In her view, corridors mainly cool their immediate surroundings and should not be marketed as a means of cooling an entire city.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters of corridors point out that cold-air flows are strongest on calm, cloudless nights, which are precisely the conditions that accompany the most dangerous heatwaves. This is a genuine strength: a measure that works best when it is most needed is rarer than one might expect. The wind engineer Farid Ishaqzai, however, believes that attention to a few large corridors distracts from the influence of ordinary buildings. Using scale models in a wind tunnel, he has shown that a district of uniformly tall blocks behaves almost like a solid wall, deflecting air over the top, whereas a district in which buildings vary in height generates turbulence that draws cooler air down to street level. The size of the gaps between buildings and their orientation to the wind, he argues, matter at least as much as any corridor. His experiments are illuminating, but a wind tunnel contains neither traffic nor the heat given off by air-conditioning units, and its results should be treated as indicative rather than conclusive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Corridors are also frequently promoted as a way of flushing polluted air out of cities. The environmental health researcher Chiamaka Nzeribe is cautious about this claim. Many corridors, she observes, follow railway lines or major roads, simply because these are the long, open spaces that a city already possesses. Air moving along them may collect exhaust fumes and carry them into residential districts rather than removing them. Where the incoming air has first passed over a port or an industrial zone, improved ventilation may actually import pollution. Nzeribe does not oppose corridors, but she insists that air quality must be modelled alongside temperature before any route is designated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The sharpest controversy concerns land. Most cities are simultaneously trying to become more compact, building on vacant sites to reduce car use and protect the countryside, and those vacant sites are often exactly the ones a ventilation corridor requires. The urban economist Rodrigo Jaramillo has calculated that strict corridor protections in one metropolitan region removed from development enough land for tens of thousands of homes, contributing to a rise in housing costs. On this basis, he concludes that the cooling benefits do not justify the economic price. His figures are carefully assembled, yet the comparison is misleading, because the same land also serves as public parkland, flood storage and habitat for wildlife. To value a corridor solely for the degrees of cooling it provides is to understate what is lost when it is built over.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even where the case for a corridor is accepted, protecting it is difficult. Cool air is generated largely on hillsides and farmland beyond the city boundary, in areas governed by separate authorities with their own development plans, and regional cooperation of the necessary kind is rare. A single warehouse or housing estate built across the mouth of a valley can block a flow on which an entire district depends. Many cities now produce detailed climate maps showing where cool air originates and how it moves, but these are usually advisory rather than binding, and they carry little weight when a profitable development is proposed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It seems to me that ventilation planning is most valuable not as a grand gesture involving a few spectacular corridors, but as a set of modest principles applied to everyday decisions: varying building heights, leaving gaps between blocks and avoiding construction across the routes by which air descends from the hills. These principles cost almost nothing when they are applied before a district is built, and they are almost impossible to introduce afterwards.
