topic: amphibious and floating architecture as a response to urban flooding
title: Houses That Rise with the Flood
subtitle: Architects are designing homes that float when the water comes. Are they a practical answer to urban flooding or an elegant distraction?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a quiet suburb on the edge of a river delta, a row of ordinary-looking houses hides an unusual feature. When the river overflows, the houses lift gently off the ground, rising as much as two metres with the water, and when the flood recedes they settle back exactly where they stood. These are amphibious houses, and alongside their cousins, the permanently floating homes moored in former docks and canals, they have moved in the space of two decades from architectural curiosity to serious proposal. Their appeal is easy to understand. Instead of attempting to keep water out with ever-higher walls, they accept that some land will flood and adapt the building to that fact. I believe that such designs have a genuine role to play in urban adaptation, but a considerably narrower one than their most enthusiastic promoters suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The engineering is less exotic than it appears. An amphibious house rests on a buoyant base, usually a hollow concrete shell or a frame filled with dense foam, which sits in a shallow pit when the ground is dry. As water enters the pit, the base begins to float, and the house is kept in place by vertical steel guideposts that allow it to move up and down but not sideways. Water, electricity and sewage lines are connected through flexible pipes that can stretch as the building rises. Dr Ingrid Bjornstad, an architect who has designed several prototypes, argues that one of the technology's main advantages is that it can be fitted to existing homes. According to her estimates, converting a typical detached house costs roughly a third as much as raising it permanently on stilts or a concrete plinth, and the house retains its original appearance at street level.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Permanently floating buildings raise different questions. Several port cities have built small floating neighbourhoods in disused harbours, where residents reach their homes along jetties and the water level changes only with the tide. Stavros Sakellariou, a marine engineer, considers these schemes technically sound but warns against assuming that they can be replicated elsewhere. In sheltered docks, he points out, the water is calm. On open coasts or wide estuaries, floating platforms would be exposed to waves and storm surges that could snap their moorings or make them uninhabitable, and the cost of protecting them with breakwaters would largely cancel out their advantages.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For many architects, the most frustrating obstacles are not physical but administrative. Building codes generally assume that a house is fixed to its foundations, and insurers are often uncertain whether a floating home should be treated as a building or as a vessel. Banks, in turn, are frequently reluctant to offer mortgages on a property that is not permanently attached to land. Losa Tauiliili, a legal scholar who specialises in planning law, argues that these regulatory gaps rather than any engineering limitation are what currently prevent amphibious housing from spreading, and she has proposed that governments create a distinct legal category for buildings designed to move with water. I am inclined to agree with her: the technical problems have largely been solved, while the legal ones have barely been addressed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more pointed criticism comes from the urban geographer Ruslan Mukhametov. In his view, floating architecture has become a form of adaptation as spectacle: striking waterfront developments, often marketed to affluent buyers, that generate international publicity but do nothing for the millions of poorer residents who live in flood-prone informal settlements. There is some truth in this complaint, since many of the best-known projects are indeed expensive. Yet it overlooks a quieter tradition of low-cost floating structures. In several river deltas, communities have built schools and health clinics that float on recycled oil drums lashed beneath bamboo platforms, allowing children to continue their education through the flood season.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important limitation concerns everything outside the front door. A house that floats safely is of limited use if the surrounding roads are impassable, the electricity substation is under water and the sewers have overflowed. The hydrologist Nadia Fakhoury has studied neighbourhoods in which amphibious homes were built individually, without changes to the surrounding infrastructure, and found that during prolonged floods many residents had to be evacuated regardless, because they could neither reach shops nor receive medical care. This seems to me the crucial point. Amphibious homes keep possessions dry, but unless they form part of a district-wide plan, they may offer residents little more than a comfortable place in which to be stranded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the evidence suggests that amphibious design suits places where floods are short and relatively shallow, lasting days rather than weeks, and where the wider urban systems can be made to cope. It is no substitute for drainage, for flood defences where they make sense, or for relocation where the water is likely to become permanent. Its greatest contribution may ultimately be cultural rather than technical, in encouraging cities to regard water as something to live with rather than an enemy to be held back at any cost.

topic: land subsidence in coastal cities caused by groundwater pumping
title: The Slow Descent
subtitle: Rising seas dominate discussion of coastal cities, yet in many of them the more urgent problem is that the ground itself is sinking

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the future of coastal cities is discussed, attention almost always turns to the oceans. Global sea level is currently rising by a little under four millimetres a year, and projections for the end of the century are alarming. Yet in a number of large delta cities, the land is falling far faster than the water is rising, in some districts by several centimetres annually, or roughly ten times the rate of sea-level rise. For the residents of these neighbourhoods, what matters is not the absolute height of the sea but its height relative to the ground on which they live, and by that measure subsidence is often the dominant factor. It is, in my view, the neglected half of the problem, and adaptation plans that address only the oceans are likely to underestimate the danger considerably.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Although land can subside for several reasons, including the natural settling of young delta sediments and the weight of new buildings, the principal cause in most rapidly sinking cities is the pumping of groundwater. The sediments beneath a typical delta consist of layers of sand and gravel, which hold water readily, separated by layers of clay. When wells draw water from the sandy aquifers, the pressure within them falls, and water is slowly squeezed out of the adjacent clay, which compacts as it drains. Crucially, this process is largely irreversible: sand may recover some of its volume if water levels rise again, but clay that has been compressed does not rebound. Dr Päivi Laukkanen, a hydrogeologist who models aquifer systems, has shown that because clay releases its water so slowly, a city would continue to sink for years and possibly decades even if all pumping ceased tomorrow.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, subsidence could be measured only by repeated surveys of fixed markers, a laborious process that left large areas unmonitored. Satellite radar has transformed the picture. By comparing images taken weeks or months apart, the technique can detect vertical movements of a few millimetres across an entire metropolitan area. A research group led by Arundhati Goswami, a specialist in remote sensing, has used it to map a dozen coastal cities in Asia and Africa. Their maps reveal that subsidence is strikingly uneven. Some of the fastest sinking is found around industrial zones, which extract large volumes of water, but much of it occurs in densely populated low-income districts that lack a municipal water supply, where households and small businesses depend on private wells, most of which are unregistered.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is encouraging evidence that the problem can be halted. During the decades of rapid industrial growth that followed the Second World War, parts of one large East Asian city sank by several metres, leaving some districts below the level of high tide. The authorities responded by imposing strict limits on groundwater extraction while simultaneously building a network of pipelines to deliver river water to factories and homes. Within roughly a decade, the sinking had almost stopped. The lesson usually drawn from this case is that regulation works. I would put it differently: regulation worked because an alternative source of water was provided at the same time, and a ban on pumping without such a source would have been both unenforceable and unjust.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That point is central to current debates about policy. The economist Chukwuemeka Ugwuanyi observes that in many sinking cities groundwater is pumped at little or no cost to the user, and that the absence of any register of wells makes regulation almost impossible. He has proposed a system of charges that would vary according to the zone in which a well is located, with the highest rates applied in areas where subsidence is most severe. In principle the idea is sound, since it would encourage large users to reduce their extraction. However, critics point out that the heaviest burden would fall on poor households who have no other way of obtaining water, and I share their concern: charges of this kind would be unfair unless an alternative source of water were made available first.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Engineering responses have so far concentrated on the coast itself. Several cities are planning, or have begun building, enormous sea walls to protect their low-lying districts. The civil engineer Kristaps Dravnieks argues that such walls are futile so long as the ground continues to subside, because the wall sinks along with the land it stands on and must be raised repeatedly at growing expense. In his view, every coastal defence project in a sinking city should be made conditional on measures to reduce pumping. Some authorities are also experimenting with artificial recharge, in which treated water is injected back into aquifers to restore their pressure. This can slow further compaction, but because compressed clay does not rebound, it cannot recover the height that has already been lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is, finally, a reason for cautious optimism. The rate at which the oceans rise depends on global emissions of greenhouse gases and therefore lies largely beyond the control of any single city. Subsidence, by contrast, is overwhelmingly a local problem with local causes, and a city that secures an alternative water supply and controls its wells can bring it to a halt within its own boundaries. Of all the threats facing low-lying coastal cities, it may be the one they are best placed to defeat.

topic: protecting outdoor workers from extreme heat in cities: working hours, platform work and cooling technology
title: Labour Under a Hotter Sun
subtitle: As cities warm, those who build, clean and deliver in them face the greatest risks. How should their working lives change?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every city depends on people who work outdoors: the labourers on its building sites, the crews who collect its rubbish and repair its roads, the vendors who sell food on its pavements and, increasingly, the riders who deliver meals and parcels to its doorsteps. As urban summers grow hotter, these workers are exposed to heat more directly and for longer than almost anyone else. Yet public debate about urban heat has concentrated overwhelmingly on the dangers faced by elderly people in overheated homes. Those dangers are real, but the relative neglect of the outdoor workforce is, in my view, a serious oversight, and one that adaptation policies have only recently begun to correct.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physiological problem is straightforward. Hard physical work generates a great deal of internal heat, which the body sheds mainly through the evaporation of sweat. In hot, humid conditions, sweat evaporates poorly, core temperature climbs and the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke rises steeply. Repeated exposure over many summers has also been linked to lasting damage to the kidneys. Dr Oksana Kovalenko, an occupational physiologist, fitted construction workers with sensors over three summers and found that their output began to decline well before any of them reported feeling unwell. The workers, she concluded, were instinctively slowing down and taking short, unofficial pauses to keep their body temperature under control. Kovalenko regards this self-pacing as a vital form of protection, and she criticises payment systems based on the quantity of work completed, which effectively penalise workers for listening to their own bodies.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most widely adopted response has been to change the hours of work. In several hot countries, outdoor work is prohibited by law during the middle of the day for part of the summer, and many employers in other places now begin shifts at dawn. The labour economist Sione Moengangongo, who has examined compliance with midday bans in four countries, found that they were frequently ignored wherever inspections were infrequent and penalties small. He also noted that most bans apply between fixed calendar dates, so that an exceptionally hot week in late spring may go unregulated while a cool spell in midsummer brings needless disruption. It seems to me that restrictions of this kind would command more respect if they were triggered by measured conditions, such as a combination of temperature and humidity, rather than by the date.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second approach requires employers to provide shade, drinking water and regular rest. Such rules are now common, but Rania Khoury, a former labour inspector who now researches occupational health, points out that they protect only those who are legally classed as employees. Street vendors are usually self-employed, and many delivery riders are treated as independent contractors by the digital platforms that allocate their work. For riders, the difficulty is compounded by the way in which these platforms reward speed: those who stop to rest may lose bonuses or receive fewer orders. Khoury argues that platforms should be legally obliged to suspend delivery-time targets whenever an official heat alert is in force, a proposal that would cost little and could protect a very large number of workers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Technology offers a third option. Engineers have developed vests containing cooling packs or circulating water, as well as wearable sensors that monitor heart rate and estimate core temperature, alerting a worker or supervisor when danger approaches. Tomas Hrdlicka, a mechanical engineer, has designed a vest that costs a fraction of earlier models and has been tested on road crews, where it reduced measured heat strain by a modest but consistent margin. Such devices undoubtedly have value. However, I am uneasy about the tendency to treat them as the answer, because they risk transferring responsibility for safety from the employer, who controls the pace and timing of work, to the individual who wears the equipment. Sensors that record a worker's physical condition might also be used to monitor productivity, and no vest can replace the need to stop and rest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Moving work into the night might appear to be an obvious solution, and some cities already schedule road repairs and refuse collection after dark during heatwaves. But night work brings costs of its own. It disrupts sleep, which is itself associated with poorer health; it increases the risk of accidents, since fatigue and poor visibility make heavy machinery more dangerous; and it generates noise that disturbs nearby residents. Moreover, because buildings and pavements release stored heat after sunset, city nights are becoming warmer, and the relief that darkness once offered is steadily diminishing in the densest districts.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Advocates of better protection frequently emphasise the economic costs of heat, pointing to estimates of the billions of working hours that may be lost as temperatures rise. The argument is understandably attractive to finance ministries. Nevertheless, I believe it is a double-edged one. If the case for protecting workers rests chiefly on productivity, it implies that protection is worthwhile only when it pays, and it may be abandoned whenever the figures appear to point the other way. The stronger foundation is a simpler one: that nobody should have to risk their health in order to earn a living.

topic: flood insurance pricing, subsidies and property markets as signals for urban climate adaptation
title: What the Premium Knows
subtitle: Rising insurance costs in flood-prone districts are often treated as a problem to be solved. They may also be one of the clearest warnings a city receives

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before most homeowners notice any change in the weather, insurers have begun to adjust their prices. Their business depends on estimating the likelihood of damage, and in many riverside and coastal districts the numbers have moved decisively in one direction. Premiums have climbed steeply, some companies have stopped offering cover altogether, and householders who once took insurance for granted now struggle to obtain it. Two broad views of this development compete. One holds that rising prices are a valuable signal, steering people and investment away from places that are becoming dangerous. The other treats affordable insurance as a social necessity that governments must protect. My own position is that insurance pricing could be among the most powerful instruments of urban adaptation, but only if it is permitted to tell the truth about risk, and at present it seldom is.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for prices that reflect risk has been made most forcefully by Dr Timur Bekmuratov, an economist who studies housing markets. When a household pays the true expected cost of flooding, he argues, it has every reason to install flood barriers, raise electrical sockets or choose a home on higher ground, and developers have a corresponding reason to avoid building on floodplains. Bekmuratov examined a region in which controls on premiums were removed and found that, within five years, the number of new homes approved in high-risk zones had fallen by about a third. The finding is striking, although it should be noted that the same period saw a tightening of planning rules, which may account for part of the change.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The objection to this approach is a matter of fairness. Many governments operate schemes that cap premiums for existing homes, and Halla Thorsteinsdottir, who researches social policy, regards them as indispensable. Large numbers of low-income owners, she points out, bought their homes long before the scale of the danger was understood, and her modelling suggests that under fully risk-based pricing the annual premium for some of them would exceed their annual income. Critics reply that such subsidies encourage people to remain and rebuild in places they ought to leave. In my view both sides are right, and the conflict can be eased by attaching assistance to the household rather than to the building: current owners would remain protected, but the subsidy would end when the property was sold, so that each new buyer faced the real price of the risk.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whether house prices themselves reflect flood risk is a contested question. Kekoa Lopaka, a real-estate economist, tracked sales in several flood-prone neighbourhoods over two decades. He found that prices fell sharply after a major flood but typically recovered within three or four years, even though the underlying risk had not diminished and in some cases had grown. Buyers, it appears, respond to vivid recent experience rather than to long-term probabilities, and memories of a disaster fade quickly once the damage has been repaired. If Lopaka's results are representative, the property market cannot be relied upon to register flood risk unaided, and buyers need better information than they currently receive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One obvious remedy is to require sellers to disclose a property's exposure to flooding, something many jurisdictions still do not demand. The data scientist Yuki Kanazawa, however, warns that the official maps on which such disclosure would depend are often unreliable. Many were drawn using rainfall records from previous decades rather than projections of future climate, and they are frequently produced at a scale too coarse to distinguish between neighbouring streets, let alone individual houses. A home might therefore be labelled safe when it is not, or stigmatised when its risk is low. Kanazawa's criticisms are well founded, yet they argue for improving the maps rather than for withholding them. An imperfect warning is still more useful to a buyer than none at all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most troubling scenario arises when insurers withdraw from an area entirely. Because mortgage lenders generally insist that a property be insured, homes that cannot be insured become difficult to sell, and their value can collapse within a few years. Falling property values reduce the local taxes on which many cities depend, which in turn limits their ability to pay for drainage and flood defences, making the area still riskier and still less attractive to insurers. Such a cycle, once established, is extremely difficult to reverse, and it is far better prevented through early public investment than repaired after the fact.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Insurance, then, can reveal risk, but it cannot by itself reduce it. Premiums tell a city where its defences, its planning rules and its housing are failing to keep pace with a changing climate; they do not build embankments or move homes. Governments that respond to rising premiums simply by capping them indefinitely resemble a recipient of bad news who blames the person who delivered it. The message is unwelcome, but suppressing it merely postpones the moment at which it must be acted upon, and the cost of acting rises with every year of delay.

topic: urban drought and 'Day Zero' water crises: restrictions, desalination, water recycling and leakage
title: The Day the Taps Nearly Ran Dry
subtitle: Prolonged droughts have brought several large cities close to cutting off their water supply. What have they learned?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A few years ago, after three successive winters of unusually low rainfall, the authorities of a large southern-hemisphere city announced that within months the municipal supply might have to be switched off. On that date, which the press quickly christened Day Zero, residents would have been required to collect a daily ration of water from public distribution points. Queues formed at natural springs, bottled water disappeared from the shops, and households were urged to restrict themselves to a few dozen litres a day. Remarkably, the city's consumption fell by almost half within a year, and when the rains finally returned, the shutdown was averted. The episode is usually recounted as a triumph of civic cooperation, and in part it was. But that account is incomplete, and the omissions matter for the many other cities now facing similar prospects.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Aline Ndikumana, a water economist who studied the crisis in detail, believes that the most effective single measure was the countdown itself. A regularly updated estimate of the number of days remaining before the taps ran dry turned an abstract hydrological risk into something immediate and personal, and consumption fell most sharply in the weeks after each revision of the date. Ndikumana also warns, however, that such campaigns produce fatigue, and that once a crisis has passed, household use tends to creep back towards its former level. Moreover, the burden of saving water was far from evenly distributed. Steeply rising tariffs weighed most heavily on poorer households, while many wealthy residents simply drilled private boreholes in their gardens and carried on much as before. The story of a city pulling together, in other words, conceals a great deal of inequality.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Faced with such scares, many cities turn to desalination, which converts seawater into drinking water and is therefore independent of rainfall. The engineer Paolo Ferraresi regards it as a valuable safeguard but not as a solution in itself. Desalination consumes large amounts of energy, and the concentrated brine it discharges can harm marine life near the outflow. Ferraresi proposes that plants should function as a reserve, kept running at reduced output during wet years and expanded only during droughts. The difficulty is that a plant operating at low capacity costs almost as much to maintain as one working at full capacity, and this makes it an easy target for budget cuts. Several plants built in the aftermath of earlier droughts have stood idle for years and some have been mothballed entirely.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An alternative is to treat wastewater to a standard at which it can be drunk. The technology has been proven for decades, and the water it produces often exceeds the quality of conventional supplies. The principal obstacle is psychological: many people find the idea of drinking recycled sewage repellent, however thoroughly it has been purified. The psychologist Ragnheidur Ingolfsson has found that acceptance rises considerably when treated water is first released into a lake or underground aquifer and only later withdrawn for drinking, even though this step adds nothing to its safety. This reaction is not strictly rational, but I would argue that policymakers should accommodate it rather than dismiss it with ridicule, since a supply that the public refuses to drink provides no security at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers favour a more decentralised approach. Kyriaki Gerasimou, a hydrologist, argues that cities become more resilient when they draw on many small sources, including rainwater tanks attached to houses, systems that reuse water from baths and washing machines for flushing toilets, and schemes that channel stormwater into underground storage. A city with diverse sources, she contends, is less vulnerable to the failure of any one of them. Critics respond that household tanks are of little help during a drought lasting several years, since they empty within weeks once the rain stops. This objection is fair as far as it goes, but it misses the point: the chief value of such systems lies in reducing demand on the central supply in ordinary years, so that reservoirs enter a drought fuller than they otherwise would.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The least glamorous source of additional water is also, in many places, the cheapest. In numerous cities, a quarter or more of the treated water that enters the distribution network is lost through leaking pipes before it reaches a single tap. Finding and repairing these leaks typically yields new supply at a fraction of the cost of building a desalination plant or a recycling facility. Yet leak reduction rarely attracts political enthusiasm, perhaps because a repaired pipe buried beneath a road offers none of the opportunities for public ceremony that a gleaming new treatment works provides.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If the near-miss of Day Zero teaches anything, it is that no single measure can protect a city against prolonged drought. The most secure cities will combine reduced leakage, efficient use, recycled water and some drought-independent supply, and they will distribute the costs of restriction fairly. Above all, they will plan for droughts more severe than any in the historical record, since a changing climate has made the past an increasingly unreliable guide to the future.

topic: the air-conditioning dilemma: mechanical cooling as life-saving adaptation or urban maladaptation
title: The Cooling Paradox
subtitle: Air conditioning saves lives in hot cities, yet it may also be making those cities hotter. Is it an adaptation or a trap?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Within living memory, air conditioning was a luxury confined to cinemas, department stores and the homes of the wealthy. Today it is spreading through the cities of the tropics and subtropics at extraordinary speed, as rising incomes coincide with ever more frequent heatwaves, and one widely quoted projection suggests that the number of units in use worldwide could triple by the middle of the century. Among climate specialists, this trend is often described as a textbook case of maladaptation: a response that protects individuals in the short term while aggravating the very problem it is meant to address. The label contains an important truth. Nevertheless, I believe it is too crude to guide policy, because it obscures both the benefits of mechanical cooling and the specific ways in which its harms might be reduced.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The benefits are not in serious doubt. Dr Mbuyi Tshiamala, an epidemiologist, has examined more than a century of mortality records from several countries and found that the relationship between hot days and deaths weakened dramatically over the second half of the twentieth century. After allowing for improvements in medical care and other factors, he attributes the greater part of this decline to the spread of air conditioning in homes. His conclusion is difficult to dispute, and it has an uncomfortable implication for those who would discourage mechanical cooling on environmental grounds. To deny poorer households in hot countries a technology that wealthier nations adopted long ago, and in the name of a climate crisis they did little to create, would be indefensible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The harms, however, are equally real. An air conditioner does not destroy heat; it moves it from inside a building to the outside, adding the heat generated by its own motor in the process. Inés Paniagua, who builds computer models of urban climate, has simulated densely built districts in which most households use air conditioning and found that the waste heat expelled by the units can raise night-time street temperatures by as much as two degrees. The result is a feedback loop in which those who cool their homes make the city hotter for everyone else, including those who cannot afford cooling, and thereby increase demand for still more units. Electricity demand also peaks during heatwaves, placing grids under severe strain at exactly the moment when a power failure would be most dangerous.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That danger is magnified by the way in which modern buildings are designed. The architect Henrik Lindemark points out that glass-clad offices and lightweight apartment blocks are constructed on the assumption that mechanical cooling will always be available, whereas traditional buildings in hot regions relied on thick walls, shaded courtyards and cross-ventilation to remain tolerable without any power at all. In a prolonged blackout, he warns, a modern flat can become lethally hot within hours. Lindemark therefore argues that building regulations should require new homes to remain safe for several days without electricity. His argument is persuasive as far as ordinary heatwaves are concerned. It should be acknowledged, though, that in the most humid tropical cities, where temperatures are expected to approach the limits of human tolerance, no amount of passive design will be sufficient on its own.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further set of problems arises from the machines themselves. Many of the units sold in rapidly growing markets are inefficient, and the refrigerants that circulate inside them are often potent greenhouse gases that escape through leaks and careless disposal. Siriporn Kaewkla, an energy policy analyst, has studied the introduction of minimum efficiency standards in several Asian countries and found that within a decade they had roughly halved the electricity consumed by new units while adding only slightly to their purchase price. She regards such standards as the single most effective policy available. I agree that they are essential, but their impact is blunted by the flourishing trade in second-hand units, many of them imported from countries that have already banned their sale, which continue to operate for years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Access to cooling is also profoundly unequal. The sociologist Adebayo Olawuyi has found that in the cities he studies, ownership of air conditioners closely tracks household income, and that even ownership does not guarantee protection. Many low-income families who possess a unit cannot afford to run it for long, a condition Olawuyi describes as energy poverty, and he has documented households switching their machines off during the hottest periods in order to save money. He proposes that electricity be supplied at reduced rates to vulnerable households whenever an official heat alert is in force.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Air conditioning, then, is neither a villain to be resisted nor a solution to be embraced without reservation. The sensible goal is to reduce how much cities need it, through shading, trees, better building design and efficient machines, while ensuring that everyone can use it when it is genuinely required. For moderate heat, electric fans, which use a fraction of the power, are often adequate, and they deserve more attention than they receive. What cities must avoid is a future in which their residents can survive the summer only so long as the electricity keeps flowing.

topic: the recognition heuristic and the 'less-is-more' effect in judgement
title: The Uses of Ignorance
subtitle: Can simply recognising a name be a better guide to the world than knowing a great deal about it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Which of two cities has the larger population: a provincial capital the reader has heard of, or one whose name means nothing to them? Most people, asked such questions, simply pick the city they recognise, and a surprising body of research suggests that they are often right to do so. The strategy, which psychologists call the recognition heuristic, rests on a simple observation: in many environments, the things we have encountered are not a random sample of the world. Large cities appear more frequently in news reports, successful companies are discussed more often than failing ones, and famous athletes are famous partly because they win. Recognition, in other words, may carry information that a more deliberate analysis would struggle to extract.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea was given its most provocative form by the cognitive scientist Lucía Barandiarán and her colleagues at the Institute for Adaptive Cognition in Bilbao. In a series of experiments, they asked participants to compare the sizes of cities in their own country and in a foreign one. Counter-intuitively, people who knew only about half of the foreign cities sometimes outperformed those who knew almost all of them, a result Barandiarán labelled the 'less-is-more effect'. Her explanation was that partial ignorance allows recognition to do its work: when someone has heard of every city, recognition can no longer discriminate between them, and they must fall back on patchy factual knowledge that is often less reliable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For Barandiarán, the finding was more than a curiosity. It challenged an assumption, widespread in economics and in much of psychology, that good decisions require gathering as much information as possible and weighing it carefully. On her account, the mind possesses an 'adaptive toolbox' of simple rules, each suited to particular environments, and the rationality of a rule cannot be judged in isolation from the setting in which it is used. This is an attractive position, and I believe it is broadly correct, though its advocates have sometimes been too quick to treat a laboratory demonstration as evidence of how people actually reason in daily life.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most sustained criticism has come from Haruto Isozaki, a decision researcher at the Kansai Behavioural Sciences Centre, who argues that people rarely rely on recognition alone. In his studies, participants who recognised a city but also knew something unflattering about it, such as the fact that it had no major airport, frequently abandoned the recognised option. Isozaki concludes that recognition is better understood as one cue among many, integrated with other knowledge, rather than as a stand-alone rule that stops the search for information. Barandiarán's supporters respond that the heuristic was never meant to describe every decision, only those in which recognition is a strong indicator and other information is scarce.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of inquiry concerns how well the heuristic travels beyond city sizes. Ekow Mensa-Bonsu, an economist at the University of Cape Coast, examined whether amateur investors who selected shares solely on the basis of company names they knew could match the returns of professional fund managers. Over a two-year period, portfolios built in this way performed respectably, outperforming roughly half of the managed funds he examined. Mensa-Bonsu is careful, however, to stress that the period studied was one of rising markets, and that recognition is likely to favour large, established firms whose shares tend to do well only in particular conditions. Similar studies of sports forecasting, in which ordinary fans predicted the winners of tennis matches, have produced comparable results, although the effect appears weakest among the lower-ranked players whom few people have heard of.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important question is when recognition misleads. The heuristic works only when what people recognise is correlated with the quantity they are trying to judge, and that correlation can be broken or even deliberately manipulated. Mirela Stanciulescu, who studies consumer behaviour in Cluj, has shown that advertising can make unfamiliar brands feel familiar after only a few exposures, and that shoppers then attribute qualities to them which they have done nothing to earn. In such cases, the very environment on which the heuristic depends has been engineered by those who stand to gain from it. It seems to me that this vulnerability is underestimated by the heuristic's champions, who tend to describe environments as if they were natural rather than shaped by commercial interests.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the recognition heuristic should be dismissed. What the debate has made clear is that the value of a simple rule lies not in the rule itself but in its fit with the structure of the world. A strategy that serves a traveller well when guessing which of two unfamiliar towns is larger may serve a consumer badly in a supermarket designed to exploit exactly the same tendency. The real achievement of Barandiarán's work, in my view, is not the discovery that ignorance can be useful, a claim that has proved fragile in several replications, but the demonstration that rationality must be assessed relative to environments rather than in the abstract. That insight is likely to outlast any particular experimental result, and it deserves a wider audience among economists and policymakers than it has so far received.

topic: anchoring effects in numerical judgement, sentencing and negotiation
title: The Weight of the First Number
subtitle: Arbitrary figures shape judgements from courtrooms to car showrooms, but how, and how much, is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Any experienced car buyer knows that the first price mentioned in a negotiation matters, even when everyone involved understands that it is only an opening move. Psychologists call the phenomenon anchoring: the tendency of an initial number, even one known to be irrelevant, to pull subsequent estimates towards it. Decades of research have documented the effect in settings as different as property valuation, salary negotiations and wine auctions, and it is now one of the most frequently cited findings in behavioural science. Yet familiarity has bred a certain complacency. Anchoring is often described as if it were a single, well-understood mechanism, when in fact researchers still disagree about why it happens and how large it is outside the laboratory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The standard laboratory procedure is simple. Participants are first asked whether some quantity, such as the height of a mountain or the age at which a historical figure died, is higher or lower than a given number, and are then asked for their own estimate. In a widely replicated version devised by Ottilie Krogsgaard at the Aarhus Centre for Judgement Research, the comparison number was generated in front of participants by rolling dice, so that they could have no reason to think it informative. Even so, those who saw a high number gave estimates that were, on average, around a third larger than those who saw a low one. Krogsgaard interprets this as evidence of 'insufficient adjustment': people start from the anchor and move away from it, but stop too soon, once they reach a value that seems plausible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this account. Rafael Quintanilha, a psychologist at the University of Coimbra, argues that adjustment cannot explain why anchors influence people even when they are told to ignore them, or when the anchor is wildly implausible. In his view, the comparison question prompts people to search their memories selectively for information consistent with the anchor. Asked whether a river is longer than 5,000 kilometres, they call to mind facts suggesting that it is very long, and this biased sample of knowledge then shapes their final answer. Quintanilha's 'selective accessibility' model predicts that anchors should be strongest when people know a little about a topic, enough to retrieve supporting facts but not enough to be confident, and his experiments broadly bear this out.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The two explanations are not necessarily rivals. It seems likely that adjustment dominates when people generate their own starting points, while selective recall matters more when the anchor is supplied by someone else. What is harder to resolve is the question of expertise. One might expect professionals to be largely immune, yet studies of experienced estate agents found them just as susceptible as students when valuing houses, although the agents insisted that the listing price had played no part in their judgement. This combination of influence and denial is perhaps the most troubling aspect of the research, because a bias that people cannot detect in themselves is one they are unlikely to correct.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nowhere is this more consequential than in the courts. Ingrid Haavikko, a legal scholar at the University of Turku, reviewed sentencing decisions in which prosecutors' demands varied for broadly similar offences. She found that higher demands were associated with longer sentences, even after accounting for the severity of the crime and the defendant's record. Haavikko is cautious about concluding that judges are simply anchored, since prosecutors may ask for more in cases that are more serious in ways her data cannot capture. Nevertheless, she argues that sentencing guidelines, which provide a recommended range before any party speaks, could act as a counter-anchor. I find this proposal sensible, though it carries a risk: a guideline is itself a number, and it may simply replace one anchor with another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The commercial world has drawn its own conclusions. Negotiation trainers routinely advise clients to make the first offer, and to make it ambitious. A team at the Lagos Business Institute led by Chinonso Ebubedike tested this advice in simulated salary negotiations involving several hundred business students and managers. First offers did predict final agreements, but only up to a point. Extreme opening demands frequently caused the other side to walk away altogether, or to respond with an equally extreme counter-offer that left both parties further apart than before. Ebubedike's team concludes that an anchor works best when it is ambitious but defensible, a finding that complicates the simple advice to aim as high as possible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: More recently, the size of the anchoring effect itself has come under scrutiny. Large-scale replication projects have confirmed that the basic effect is real, but have found it considerably smaller in some versions than the original studies reported, particularly those relying on incidental anchors, such as random numbers that are never explicitly compared with the target. This should not be surprising, since early studies in any field tend to overestimate effects. But it suggests that popular accounts, which present anchoring as an almost irresistible force, have overstated the case. A more accurate picture is of a genuine but variable bias, strongest when people are uncertain and the anchor is plausible, and weaker when they have firm knowledge of their own.

topic: choice overload: the jam-tasting study, failed replications and the conditions under which too many options discourage choosing
title: Too Many Jams?
subtitle: The idea that abundant choice paralyses consumers became a cultural commonplace. The evidence turned out to be more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few findings in behavioural science have escaped the laboratory as successfully as the claim that more choice can be bad for us. It has been invoked to justify slimmer restaurant menus, smaller product ranges in supermarkets and simplified pension schemes, and it fits comfortably with a widespread sense that modern life offers more options than anyone can reasonably evaluate. The notion has an appealing paradox at its heart: freedom of choice, which economists have long treated as an unambiguous good, appears to become a burden once it exceeds a certain point. Yet the story of how this idea rose to prominence, and of what happened when researchers tried to reproduce it, is a useful lesson in how scientific claims travel and how they are transformed along the way.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The founding study was conducted by the consumer psychologist Amadou Kouyaté in a large food hall in Dakar. On alternate days, a tasting stall offered shoppers either six or twenty-four varieties of fruit preserve. The larger display attracted more visitors, but far fewer of them went on to buy anything: around three per cent of those who stopped at the extensive display made a purchase, compared with nearly thirty per cent of those who saw the limited one. Kouyaté proposed that a large set of alternatives makes the act of choosing more effortful and raises the prospect of regret, since the more options one rejects, the more likely it seems that one of them would have been better. Faced with that prospect, many people prefer not to choose at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The result was striking, and it spread rapidly through business books and popular lectures, often stripped of its qualifications. In retelling, a single study of fruit preserves became a general law about human nature. It was not until a decade later that a systematic attempt was made to test how robust the effect really was. A team led by Gulnara Yusupova at the Kazan Federal Research Institute gathered every study they could find, published or not, that had compared decisions made from small and large assortments. Combining the results of more than fifty experiments, they found that the average effect of assortment size on satisfaction and willingness to choose was close to zero. Some studies showed strong overload; others showed the opposite, with larger assortments making people happier and more likely to buy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to conclude from this that choice overload was simply an illusion, but that interpretation seems to me mistaken. An average of zero can conceal large effects in opposite directions, and the real question is what distinguishes situations where abundance discourages choice from those where it encourages it. Lorenzo Ferrandini, a decision scientist at the University of Bologna, has spent several years trying to answer exactly this question. His analysis identifies four conditions under which overload becomes likely: when the options are difficult to compare because they differ on many attributes at once; when people have no clear prior preference; when they are under time pressure; and when they expect to have to justify their choice to others. When none of these conditions holds, more options tend to be welcomed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ferrandini's framework has the merit of explaining both the original finding and the failures to replicate it. Shoppers tasting preserves on a busy afternoon, with no strong attachment to any flavour, were in precisely the circumstances his model predicts. Someone choosing a book in a well-organised shop, with a firm sense of what they enjoy, is not. The framework is less successful, however, at predicting how large any effect will be, and critics have pointed out that its four conditions are general enough to accommodate almost any result after the fact. A theory that can explain every outcome, in this view, risks explaining none.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question matters most where the stakes are high. Mere Paewai, an economist at Victoria University of Wellington, examined enrolment in workplace pension schemes and found that, for every ten additional investment funds an employer offered, the proportion of employees who joined fell by a small but consistent amount. Paewai is reluctant to attribute this entirely to overload, noting that companies offering many funds also tended to provide less guidance to their staff. Even so, her work suggests that, in complex financial decisions, reducing the number of options or providing a sensible default may help people who would otherwise put off the decision indefinitely, sometimes at considerable cost to their future income.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be made of the jam study? It was neither wrong nor representative. It captured a genuine phenomenon under particular conditions, and its greatest weakness lay not in the experiment itself but in the eagerness with which others generalised from it. The broader lesson concerns the way behavioural findings enter public life. Ideas that are simple, counter-intuitive and commercially useful travel fastest, and they tend to lose their caveats as they go. Researchers cannot entirely prevent this, but they can do more to report the boundaries of their results as prominently as the results themselves.

topic: the sunk cost effect in humans, animals and organisations, and whether persisting with past investments is always irrational
title: The Pull of What Is Already Spent
subtitle: Letting past investment guide future choices is a textbook error. But is it always one?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every large organisation seems to have its own version of the story: a building, a software system or a weapons programme that should have been abandoned years earlier but was kept alive because so much had already been invested in it. Economists regard such behaviour as an elementary error. Money, time and effort that have already been spent cannot be recovered whatever one decides, so they should have no bearing on what happens next; only future costs and benefits ought to count. The tendency to let past investment shape present choices is known as the sunk cost effect, and textbooks usually present it as one of the clearest examples of human irrationality. Yet the closer researchers have looked, the less clear-cut that verdict has become.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The effect is easy to demonstrate. In a typical study, participants are told that they have paid a large sum for one weekend trip and a smaller sum for a different trip they would enjoy more, only to discover that the two trips fall on the same dates. A majority choose the more expensive trip, even though the money is gone in either case. Similar patterns appear in everyday life: people who have paid full price for a season ticket attend more games than those who received the same ticket at a discount, at least in the first months after purchase. The effect seems to fade over time, as though the pain of the original payment gradually wears off.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Biologists have long been interested in whether animals show the same tendency, which some of them call the Concorde fallacy, after the famously unprofitable supersonic airliner. Early field studies appeared to suggest that they did: parent birds whose nests were threatened were observed defending older clutches more vigorously than newer ones. Signe Lehtisalo, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Oulu, argues that these observations were misinterpreted. An older clutch, she points out, is not merely one in which more has been invested; it is also closer to hatching and therefore more valuable in terms of future reproductive success. When her team controlled for this by experimentally swapping eggs between nests, the parents' defensive effort tracked the age of the eggs, not the length of time the parents had spent incubating them. Animals, in her view, are better economists than humans.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other evidence complicates this neat conclusion. Oleksandr Prokopovych, a neuroscientist at the Kyiv Institute of Physiology, has trained rats to forage in an arena where food is delivered after a delay at each of several stations. A rat can abandon a wait at any moment and move on to the next. Prokopovych found that the longer an animal had already waited, the more likely it was to continue waiting, even when the remaining delay was identical, and the same pattern appears when humans perform an equivalent task for short video rewards. Because the behaviour is found in species separated by tens of millions of years of evolution, he suggests that it may reflect a deep feature of how brains value effort, rather than a cultural habit or a misunderstanding of accounting principles.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In organisations, the stakes are greater and the motives more tangled. Élodie Corriveau, who studies management decisions in Montreal, distinguishes the sunk cost effect proper from what she calls escalation of commitment, in which managers continue to back failing projects partly to protect their own reputations. In her experiments, executives who had personally initiated a project were far more willing to approve further funding than colleagues who had inherited it, even when both groups were given identical information about its prospects. Corriveau therefore recommends that the decision to continue a large project should be taken by someone other than the person who began it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers agree that persistence is a mistake. Thandiwe Khumbuza, a developmental psychologist in Johannesburg, notes that young children appear largely immune to sunk costs, and that the sensitivity becomes strong only in adolescence, at around the age when concerns about consistency and reputation intensify. She interprets this as evidence that honouring past commitments is a learned social strategy: people who abandon projects at the first sign of difficulty may be regarded as unreliable partners. On this view, what looks like an error in an isolated laboratory task may be a sensible rule in a world where others are watching and remembering.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: I find this argument persuasive up to a point. There are certainly situations in which persisting with a costly course of action conveys useful information to others, or in which abandoning it would carry hidden costs that a simple calculation ignores. To label every such decision a fallacy is to mistake a narrow model of rationality for the whole of good judgement. But the social explanation cannot be stretched to cover the most expensive cases. When public infrastructure projects run years late and billions over budget, it is rarely because continuing serves any genuine signalling purpose; more often it is because no one wishes to be the official who wrote off the investment. Here Corriveau's advice seems to me not merely sensible but urgent.

topic: default effects and opt-out organ donation systems: registration, actual transplants, ethics and mandated choice
title: Consent by Default
subtitle: Switching organ donation to an opt-out system looks like an effortless way to save lives. The reality is more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In two neighbouring European countries with similar cultures, languages and health systems, the proportion of citizens registered as potential organ donors once differed dramatically. In one, fewer than one person in eight had signed up; in the other, almost everyone was counted as a donor. The explanation lay not in public attitudes, which surveys showed to be broadly alike, but in the design of a form. In the first country, people became donors only if they actively chose to register, an arrangement known as opt-in. In the second, everyone was presumed to consent unless they took steps to withdraw. Comparisons of this kind, repeated across many countries, made organ donation the most famous illustration of what behavioural scientists call the default effect: the tendency of people to stay with whatever option has been pre-selected for them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Three explanations for the power of defaults are generally offered. The first is effort: changing a default requires time and attention, however minimal, and people tend to postpone tasks that bring no immediate reward. The second is that a default can be read as an implicit recommendation, a signal of what policymakers consider normal or desirable. Iñaki Igartua, a psychologist at the University of the Basque Country, found that when participants were told a default had been chosen at random, its influence fell by around half, suggesting that much of its power comes from this perceived endorsement. The third explanation draws on the observation that people evaluate options relative to a reference point, so that departing from the default feels like giving something up.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: On the strength of such findings, a number of governments have switched from opt-in to opt-out systems over the past two decades. The results have been less dramatic than the early comparisons implied. Henrike Ostendarp, a health economist at the University of Münster, compared deceased-donation rates in countries before and after such a switch with those in similar countries that did not change their law. In most cases, she found, registration rose sharply but the number of organs actually transplanted increased only modestly, and in a few countries not at all. One reason is that registration is not the same as donation. In practice, doctors in nearly every country consult the family of a potential donor, and relatives may refuse even where the deceased never opted out.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ostendarp also notes that the countries with the highest donation rates, including some with opt-out laws, tend to share other features: a dense network of trained transplant coordinators in hospitals, sufficient intensive-care capacity, and well-established procedures for identifying potential donors. One country frequently cited as a success story for opt-out legislation had in fact introduced its law some ten years before donation rates began to climb; the increase coincided instead with a national reorganisation of its transplant services. It is therefore difficult to know how much credit the legal default deserves.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics also raise ethical objections. Rosalind Mavhunga, a bioethicist based in Harare, argues that consent inferred from silence is not consent in any meaningful sense, particularly for groups who may be less aware of the law, such as recent migrants, people with limited literacy, or those who rarely engage with official documents. Mavhunga does not oppose organ donation; rather, she maintains that a system relying on inertia treats the bodies of the least informed citizens as available unless they object. She favours what is known as mandated choice, in which everyone is required to record a decision, for example when applying for a driving licence or renewing an identity card.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters of opt-out systems reply that mandated choice has its own problems. Kristjan Põldma, who advises a Baltic health ministry, points out that when people are forced to decide quickly at an administrative counter, a significant minority select 'no' simply to end the conversation, and such refusals may be harder to reverse than the mere absence of a registration. In a trial he oversaw, a prompted-choice system, in which the question is always asked but answering is optional, produced higher registration than either compulsory choice or the previous opt-in arrangement, though still lower than opt-out.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These debates are sometimes presented as if the future of transplantation depended on the wording of a single form. It does not. The evidence suggests that defaults have a real but limited influence on donation, and that their effect is easily swamped by the quality of hospital systems and by the willingness of families to agree at the bedside. That is not an argument against reform. A law that signals that donation is the normal, expected choice may, over time, shift the conversations families have, and it is in those conversations, rather than in registers, that most decisions are actually made. But governments that change the law and expect organs to follow, without investing in the people and procedures that turn consent into transplants, are likely to be disappointed. The default effect is a genuine and useful discovery; it is simply not a substitute for the slower, costlier work of building a transplant system that functions well.

topic: decision fatigue: the parole-board study, the ego depletion theory and their re-examination
title: Justice Before Lunch
subtitle: Does the quality of our decisions really decline as the day wears on?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine two prisoners who appear before the same parole board on the same day, with similar records and similar prospects of rehabilitation. One is heard at half past nine in the morning, the other shortly before lunch. According to one of the most widely discussed studies in recent social science, the first has a far better chance of being released. The study, and the theory used to explain it, gave rise to the notion of 'decision fatigue': the idea that the quality of our choices deteriorates as we make more of them, because each decision draws on a limited mental resource that must be periodically replenished.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study in question was conducted by Paweł Dziedzic, an economist at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, who analysed more than a thousand rulings made by experienced judges sitting on parole panels. At the start of each session, roughly two-thirds of applications were granted. As the session wore on, the proportion fell steadily, reaching almost zero just before the judges took a scheduled food break. After the break, the rate of favourable rulings jumped back to its original level, only to decline again. Dziedzic argued that as judges grew mentally tired, they increasingly took the easier option, which in parole hearings is to maintain the status quo and refuse release.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This interpretation drew heavily on a theory known as ego depletion, which holds that self-control and effortful thinking consume a common pool of mental energy. In early laboratory experiments, participants who had been asked to resist temptation, for instance by refusing freshly baked biscuits, gave up sooner on a subsequent puzzle than those who had not. Some researchers went further, proposing that the resource in question was literally blood glucose, and that a sugary drink could restore flagging willpower. The parole findings seemed to offer dramatic real-world confirmation of an elegant laboratory theory.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The foundations of that theory have since been shaken. A consortium of more than twenty laboratories coordinated by Margarida Lobato, a psychologist at the University of Lisbon, conducted a pre-registered replication of a standard ego depletion procedure, with every laboratory following an identical protocol agreed before any data were collected. The combined effect was very small and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Lobato is careful not to claim that mental fatigue does not exist; people plainly feel tired after demanding work. Her conclusion is rather that the specific laboratory paradigm on which the resource model was built does not reliably produce the effect it was said to demonstrate, and that the glucose hypothesis in particular has little support.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The parole data have faced a separate challenge. Nasrin Farahani-Doust, a legal statistician at Leiden University, examined how the panels in question organised their days and found that the order of cases was not random. Prisoners without legal representation, whose applications were far less likely to succeed, tended to be heard at the end of each session, because their hearings were shorter and could be fitted in before the break. Farahani-Doust also points out that the size of the reported decline is implausibly large: if fatigue really reduced the chances of release from two-thirds to almost nothing within a couple of hours, its effects would be obvious in virtually every area of professional life.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That last argument strikes me as particularly telling. Effects of such magnitude rarely go unnoticed by the people who experience them, and judges are not generally known for believing that their verdicts depend on how recently they have eaten. Yet it would be wrong to dismiss the broader pattern entirely. Pualani Kauwila, who studies workplace behaviour at the University of Hawaii, analysed the decisions of loan officers at a large bank and found a modest but consistent tendency to approve fewer applications as the working day progressed, even after allowing for the type and quality of the applications received. The effect was a fraction of the size reported in the parole study, but it was there.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What might explain such smaller effects, if not a depleted store of energy? Kauwila suggests that motivation, rather than capacity, is the key variable. As the day goes on, people become less willing to invest effort in any one decision, not because they are unable to, but because the perceived value of doing so declines relative to other demands, such as finishing work on time. On this account, fatigue is less like an emptying fuel tank and more like a shifting set of priorities, which might be altered by changing incentives or simply by reminding people of what is at stake.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The story of decision fatigue is a cautionary one, but its lesson is not that the original researchers were careless. Their findings were striking, plausible and consistent with a respected theory, and they were embraced for exactly those reasons. The difficulty is that self-help advice built on these studies, such as scheduling important choices for the morning, keeping a snack handy before meetings or reducing the number of trivial decisions one makes, has spread far faster than the evidence warrants. Some of that advice may be harmless, even sensible. But institutions that decide people's liberty or livelihoods would do better to examine how cases are scheduled and allocated than to place their faith in biscuits.

topic: the wisdom of crowds: independence, social influence, select crowds and prediction markets in aggregating judgements
title: Many Minds, One Number
subtitle: When does pooling the guesses of ordinary people produce better answers than asking an expert?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visitors to a science museum in Gothenburg are invited each summer to guess how many marbles fill a large glass cylinder in the entrance hall. Individual guesses are often wildly wrong, some by a factor of ten. Yet when the museum's staff calculate the median of several thousand entries at the end of the season, the figure has, in most years, come within five per cent of the true number, closer than all but a handful of individual guesses. The phenomenon, usually called the wisdom of crowds, has been reproduced with estimates of distances, dates, prices and weights, and it has inspired forecasting tournaments, prediction markets and online platforms that pool the judgements of thousands of contributors.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The statistical logic is straightforward. Every individual estimate contains some truth and some error. If the errors are random and unrelated to one another, those that overshoot and those that undershoot tend to cancel out when the estimates are combined, leaving an average closer to the truth than most of its components. This logic, however, depends on a crucial condition: the errors must genuinely be independent. When people share the same misconceptions, consult the same sources or influence one another, their errors point in the same direction, and averaging no longer eliminates them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The fragility of this condition was demonstrated vividly by Torunn Ravndal, a social psychologist at the University of Bergen. Participants in her experiments answered factual questions in several rounds; in some groups, they were shown the average of the others' previous answers before each new round. Exposure to this information made the group's estimates converge, and the range of answers narrowed dramatically, but it did not make them more accurate. In many cases the collective estimate drifted further from the truth, while participants reported growing confidence in it. Ravndal concluded that social influence undermines crowd wisdom twice over: it reduces the diversity of opinions on which aggregation depends, and it creates an illusion of consensus that discourages further thought.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every researcher accepts that independence must be preserved at all costs. Sakshi Prajapati, a cognitive scientist at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru, has found that allowing people to discuss a question in small groups of four or five before submitting estimates can improve the accuracy of the final average. Discussion, she argues, lets people share relevant facts and correct obvious mistakes, as long as each group reaches its own conclusion without contact with the others. Her results suggest that what damages crowds is not interaction as such but the unstructured, large-scale influence that occurs when everyone watches the same signal, such as a running average or a widely shared post.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: I find Prajapati's distinction persuasive, and it exposes how loosely the independence condition has often been stated. Ordinary life is full of interaction, and a theory that required people to form judgements in complete isolation would apply to almost nothing outside the laboratory. What matters is the structure of influence: small, diverse, separate conversations may enrich a crowd, whereas a single shared reference point is likely to impoverish it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A second debate concerns who should be included. Ottavia Castelvetri, a decision scientist at the University of Padua, analysed several years of results from an international forecasting competition and found that the average of the best-performing ten per cent of forecasters consistently beat the average of all participants. She argues that a 'select crowd', chosen on the basis of past accuracy, combines the error-cancelling benefits of aggregation with the advantages of expertise. Critics respond that past accuracy is a noisy guide to future performance, especially when the questions being asked change, and that small crowds lose much of the diversity that makes large ones robust. Castelvetri accepts the point in part, recommending that select crowds be refreshed regularly with new members.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Prediction markets, in which participants buy and sell contracts whose value depends on future events, are often promoted as the most refined form of crowd wisdom. Folake Egbetokun, an economist at the University of Ibadan, compared the forecasts of such markets for elections and commodity prices with simple averages of surveyed opinion and found the markets only marginally more accurate, despite their being far more costly to run and vulnerable to manipulation by wealthy traders. In my view, the enthusiasm for markets has run well ahead of the evidence; their main advantage may simply be that they attract participants who already follow the subject closely.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Finally, it is worth remembering what the wisdom of crowds cannot do. It works for questions that have a correct answer, at least in principle, such as the number of marbles in a jar or the result of an election. It offers no guidance on questions of value, such as whether a policy is just or a work of art is beautiful, where there is no truth for errors to cancel around. Popular discussions sometimes blur this distinction, treating majority opinion as if it carried the same statistical authority as a well-constructed average. It does not, and confusing the two risks lending the language of science to what are, in the end, matters of judgement and debate.
