topic: framing effects in medical and public health decisions: survival versus mortality wording, information leakage, numeracy and gain/loss messages
title: The Same Facts, Told Differently
subtitle: Why does describing an outcome in terms of gains or losses change what people choose, and should it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A patient facing surgery asks her doctor about the risks. One doctor replies that ninety per cent of patients are alive five years after the operation; another, describing exactly the same data, says that ten per cent have died within five years. Logically, the two statements are identical. Psychologically, they are not. A large body of research shows that people are considerably more willing to accept a treatment described in terms of survival than one described in terms of mortality, a phenomenon known as the framing effect. Since its first demonstrations, it has been cited as evidence that human preferences are unstable, shaped less by the facts themselves than by the words in which those facts happen to be wrapped.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most influential studies of medical framing was carried out by Matteo Trevisan and his colleagues at the University of Turin. They presented several hundred participants, among them practising physicians, with a choice between surgery and radiation therapy for a serious illness, and varied only the way in which the short-term outcomes of surgery were described. When these were expressed as the proportion of patients who survived the immediate post-operative period, around three-quarters of participants chose surgery; when the identical figures were expressed as the proportion who died, fewer than half did. Strikingly, the physicians were no less affected than anyone else. Trevisan concluded that framing reflects a deep asymmetry in how people respond to outcomes: losses loom larger than equivalent gains, and words that draw attention to death make any risk feel more threatening.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This interpretation, which treats framing as a departure from rational choice, has dominated the field for decades, but it has been challenged in an interesting way. Chiamaka Anozie, a cognitive scientist at the University of Nigeria, argues that the frames speakers choose are rarely arbitrary. In one series of experiments, she asked participants to describe a glass that had been half filled from empty, or half emptied from full; the former was far more often described as 'half full'. Listeners, it turns out, are sensitive to this pattern. When a doctor speaks of survival rather than death, she may be implicitly signalling that the treatment has improved, or that she personally regards it favourably. On Anozie's account, responding to the frame is not an error but a reasonable inference about information the speaker has not stated explicitly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: I think Anozie's argument deserves more attention than it has received, because it shifts the question from whether people are irrational to what frames actually communicate. Yet it does not dissolve the problem entirely. Even when participants are told explicitly that a description was chosen at random, framing effects tend to shrink but do not disappear. Something beyond inference about the speaker's intentions seems to be at work, and the asymmetry Trevisan identified remains a plausible candidate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Individual differences complicate the picture further. Sunniva Brekkeflat, a psychologist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, has found that people with high numeracy, meaning the ability to understand and work with numbers, are markedly less susceptible to framing than those who struggle with numerical information. In her studies, numerate participants appeared to translate a statement such as 'ten per cent die' into its complement without conscious effort, so that both descriptions came to mean the same thing. Brekkeflat suggests that improving numeracy, rather than banning particular forms of words, might be the most effective protection against manipulation, although she concedes that such skills take years to develop and that many adults never fully acquire them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Outside the clinic, framing has been enthusiastically adopted by those who design public health campaigns. A popular rule of thumb, derived from early research, holds that messages emphasising losses, such as warnings that skipping a screening appointment may mean missing a tumour, work best for behaviours that detect illness, whereas messages emphasising gains, such as reminders that exercise helps people live longer, work best for behaviours that prevent it. Laleh Moshiri, an epidemiologist at the University of Tehran, conducted a review of more than ninety trials testing this rule and found the differences between gain and loss messages to be small and inconsistent, often vanishing altogether in larger studies. In her judgement, the choice of frame matters far less than whether a message is clear, credible and repeated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Her conclusion seems to me well supported, and it should temper the confidence with which campaign designers invoke framing research. A finding that is robust in a controlled experiment involving a single hypothetical decision need not translate into measurable changes in behaviour when people encounter many competing messages over months or years. This is a familiar pattern in behavioural science, and framing is no exception.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Where, then, does this leave the doctor? The most defensible practice, many medical ethicists now argue, is to present both frames: to say that ninety per cent of patients survive and that ten per cent do not. Some worry that this will simply confuse patients, but the available evidence suggests that presenting both versions reduces the effect of either one without noticeably reducing understanding. Framing cannot be avoided altogether, since every description emphasises something at the expense of something else. What can be avoided is the pretence that one particular choice of words is neutral, and that the person who chose it bears no responsibility for its consequences.

topic: the planning fallacy, strategic underestimation and reference class forecasting in projects
title: The Optimism of Plans
subtitle: Why projects so often overrun, and whether studying other people's failures is the cure

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost anyone who has renovated a kitchen, written a thesis or managed a construction project knows the experience: the work takes longer and costs more than expected, and the same thing happens on the next project despite the lesson of the last. Psychologists call this the planning fallacy, the tendency to underestimate the time, cost and risk of future actions while overestimating their benefits. What makes it puzzling is not that predictions are sometimes wrong, since the future is uncertain, but that the errors run overwhelmingly in one direction. If forecasters were merely imprecise, overruns and underruns would roughly cancel out across many projects. They do not.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic demonstrations involve students. In studies conducted by Marisol Urkiaga at the University of the Basque Country, final-year undergraduates were asked to estimate when they would submit their dissertations, both under realistic conditions and on the assumption that everything went as badly as it possibly could. Fewer than a third finished by their realistic estimate, and a substantial minority missed even the pessimistic one. Strikingly, when the same students were asked to predict how long a classmate would take, their estimates were noticeably more accurate. Urkiaga concludes that the bias arises from the way people think about their own plans: they construct a step-by-step scenario of how the task will unfold, and in doing so they concentrate on the specific case in front of them while neglecting their own past record of delays.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This explanation implies a remedy. If the problem is excessive attention to the particular case, which has been called the inside view, forecasters should adopt an outside view, setting the details aside and asking how similar projects have actually turned out. The technique built on this idea, known as reference class forecasting, requires planners to identify a group of comparable past projects, establish the distribution of their outcomes, and then position the new project within that distribution. Tomasz Grabczewski, who has studied transport infrastructure in more than twenty countries, has been its most energetic advocate. His database of rail and road schemes shows average cost overruns of around 45 per cent for rail, and he argues that public bodies which apply an uplift derived from such data produce budgets far closer to final costs than those relying on engineers' detailed estimates.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Grabczewski goes further than many psychologists in one respect. He contends that optimism is only part of the story; in large public projects, underestimates are frequently strategic. Promoters competing for limited funds have every incentive to present low costs and high benefits, knowing that once construction has begun a project is seldom cancelled, however far its budget has drifted. On this account, the planning fallacy in the public sector is less a cognitive illusion than a predictable response to approval systems that reward appearing cheap. I think this is broadly right, and it explains why repeated appeals to planners to be more realistic have achieved so little: telling people to correct a bias is pointless when the bias is, in effect, being paid for.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the outside view is a reliable cure. Haruki Nishizono, an operations researcher in Osaka, points out that the method depends entirely on choosing the right reference class, and that this choice is itself open to manipulation and disagreement. Is a new metro line in a dense historic city comparable to all metro lines, to all urban rail projects, or only to those built under similar geological conditions? Each answer yields a different forecast. In a series of exercises in which experienced planners were given the same project description, Nishizono found that their chosen reference classes differed so widely that the resulting forecasts varied by a factor of two. The outside view, he concludes, replaces one kind of judgement with another rather than removing judgement altogether.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third line of research asks whether the bias is always harmful. Ingrid Hjartardóttir, a social psychologist in Reykjavik, has followed several hundred small business founders over a period of years. Her data suggest that optimistic timelines encourage people to begin ventures they would otherwise never attempt, and that those who set ambitious deadlines often complete tasks sooner in absolute terms than those who set cautious ones, even though they miss their own targets more frequently. In her view, a forecast serves two purposes, predicting and motivating, and the two may pull in opposite directions. A perfectly calibrated estimate, she suggests, might be a perfectly discouraging one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This is an important observation, but it should not be overstated. A private individual who misjudges how long it will take to paint a fence bears the cost alone, and if optimism gets the fence painted, so much the better. The calculation changes when a forecast is used to allocate public money or to commit others to a timetable; there, the motivational benefits accrue to the planner while the costs fall on taxpayers or passengers. Nor does Nishizono's objection, valid as it is, undermine the case for the outside view. A disputed reference class still anchors debate in evidence about real outcomes, which is more than can be said for a detailed plan that has never been tested against anything. The sensible conclusion, in my view, is that the two perspectives should be combined: the inside view to understand what makes a project distinctive, and the outside view to limit how far that distinctiveness is allowed to shift the estimate.

topic: satisficing versus maximising: decision styles, well-being, search costs and stopping rules
title: The Case for Stopping Early
subtitle: Is it wiser to hunt for the best option or to settle for the first one that is good enough?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When economists first described human beings as rational agents, they imagined a decision-maker who surveyed every available option, calculated the value of each and selected the one that came out on top. It was an elegant picture, but critics soon pointed out that no real person could meet its demands. Information is costly, time is limited and the mind can hold only a handful of possibilities at once. In the 1950s a different word entered the vocabulary of the behavioural sciences: satisficing, a blend of 'satisfy' and 'suffice'. A satisficer, in this sense, does not seek the best option; instead, they set a threshold of acceptability and take the first option that clears it. What began as a description of how organisations cope with complexity has since become a lens through which psychologists examine individual personality.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That shift owes much to the work of Rosalind Kerkhoven, a psychologist at the University of Groningen, who developed a questionnaire distinguishing maximisers, people who habitually try to find the best possible option, from satisficers. Respondents were asked how far they agreed with statements such as 'When I watch television, I flick through the channels even while I am watching something' or 'I often find it hard to choose a gift for a friend'. In surveys of several thousand adults, those scoring high on maximising reported lower life satisfaction, more frequent regret and more depressive symptoms than those who scored low. Kerkhoven's interpretation was that the habit of comparing every choice against an imagined ideal makes contentment difficult to achieve: whatever is chosen, the maximiser remains conscious that something better might have been found.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A later study by a team at Seoul National University, led by Ji-hoon Sohn, added a twist. Following graduates as they entered the job market, Sohn's group found that maximisers secured starting salaries roughly 20 per cent higher than satisficers, apparently because they applied for more positions and negotiated harder. Yet the same maximisers reported feeling less satisfied with the jobs they took, more anxious during the search and more inclined to wonder afterwards whether they had made the right decision. The result was widely summarised as showing that maximisers 'do better but feel worse', a phrase that quickly captured the public imagination and has been repeated in countless magazine articles and self-help books.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The phrase is memorable, but I suspect it has been accepted too readily. A subsequent analysis of Kerkhoven's questionnaire by Teodora Bărbulescu, a psychometrician in Cluj, showed that it measures at least two distinct things. Some items capture high standards, the wish to obtain a genuinely good outcome, while others capture difficulty in deciding and a tendency to keep searching even after a choice has been made. When Bărbulescu separated these components, high standards on their own were unrelated to unhappiness and were even modestly associated with greater well-being; it was the indecisive, restless searching that predicted regret and low mood. If she is right, the problem is not wanting the best but being unable to stop looking for it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Context matters too. Lungile Gumede, a behavioural economist in Durban, argues that whether maximising pays depends on what is riding on a decision and on the cost of searching. When choosing a house or a medical treatment, a thorough search may be well worth the effort; when choosing a breakfast cereal, it almost certainly is not. In laboratory tasks in which participants could pay a small fee to inspect additional options, Gumede found that people on average adjusted their effort sensibly to the stakes, but that self-described maximisers continued to search when the expected benefit of further inspection had fallen below its cost. In his view, the error lies not in a fixed personality type but in a failure to recognise when enough is enough.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The growth of online shopping has given these questions new urgency. A shopper once limited to the stock of a few local stores can now compare thousands of products, read hundreds of reviews and return unwanted items with little effort. Some commentators have argued that this abundance turns everyone into a maximiser, with predictable costs to well-being. There is something to this argument, but the evidence is thinner than the claim suggests. Most studies of online shopping measure how long people spend searching, not whether they end up less content with what they eventually buy.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should an individual take from this research? It would be a mistake to conclude that satisficing is always the wiser strategy. A threshold that is set too low leads to choices that are genuinely poor, and some decisions deserve far more care than others. The more useful lesson, I would argue, concerns stopping rules. Deciding in advance how much time a choice deserves, and what would count as good enough, allows a person to keep high standards while avoiding the endless comparison that seems to do the damage. Satisficing, understood in this way, is not a lowering of ambition but a means of protecting it from the costs of perpetual doubt.

topic: eyewitness identification and the design of police line-up procedures
title: Pointing the Finger
subtitle: Psychologists disagree about how police line-ups should be run, but they agree that a witness's memory must be handled with care

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the courtroom, few forms of evidence carry as much persuasive weight as a witness who points to the defendant and declares, with evident conviction, that this is the person they saw. Jurors find such testimony compelling, and for much of the twentieth century the legal system shared their faith. Yet reviews of convictions later overturned on the basis of DNA evidence have repeatedly found that mistaken identification played a part in a majority of cases. The lesson is not that witnesses lie; the overwhelming majority are honest people doing their best. It is rather that human memory was never designed to function as a recording device, and procedures that treat it as one are bound to fail.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Memory for a face is formed under conditions that are often far from ideal. Crimes tend to be brief, frightening and unexpected, and the presence of a weapon draws attention away from the perpetrator's features, a phenomenon psychologists call 'weapon focus'. Identification across ethnic lines is also notably less accurate than identification within them. But the original encoding is only the first stage. Between the event and the moment a witness views a line-up, weeks or even months may pass, during which the memory can be altered by conversations, media reports and, crucially, by the identification procedure itself. It is this final stage, the one under the direct control of the police, that has attracted most attention from reformers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Orsolya Szentkirályi of the Pannonian Institute of Cognitive Science has spent over a decade comparing the two main formats. In a simultaneous line-up, the witness sees all the members together, usually six, and picks one. In a sequential line-up, members are presented one at a time, and the witness must reach a decision about each before seeing the next. Szentkirályi's early experiments indicated that the sequential method substantially reduced the number of innocent people chosen, because witnesses could no longer simply select whoever looked most like their memory of the culprit, a strategy she terms 'relative judgement'. On the strength of such findings, a number of police forces adopted sequential procedures during the 1990s and 2000s.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That consensus has since come under challenge. Professor Dumisani Lekgetho, a statistician at the Highveld Centre for Legal Psychology, argues that the apparent superiority of sequential line-ups was partly an artefact of the way results were analysed. Sequential procedures, he points out, make witnesses more cautious overall: they pick fewer innocent suspects, but they also fail to pick more guilty ones. When Lekgetho re-examined the data using methods borrowed from medical diagnostics, which weigh both kinds of error together, the simultaneous format performed as well as, or better than, its rival. Szentkirályi accepts that caution accounts for some of the difference but maintains that sequential presentation still discourages guesswork. In my view, both researchers are right about something important: the choice of format matters less than the conditions under which either is carried out.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Chief among those conditions is the behaviour of the officer running the procedure. Studies by the Kesteven Working Group, a collaboration of police trainers and academic psychologists, found that administrators who knew which line-up member was the suspect often communicated this unintentionally, through a pause, a change in tone or a remark such as 'take your time with number three'. Witnesses were rarely aware of having received such cues. The group's recommendation, that line-ups should be conducted by someone who does not know the suspect's identity, is simple and inexpensive, and it is difficult to understand why it has not been universally adopted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A second condition concerns confidence. It has long been held that a witness's certainty is a poor guide to accuracy, and courts have been warned accordingly. Dr Rafael Zubiría of the Andean School of Forensic Studies has complicated this picture. His analysis suggests that confidence recorded immediately at the first identification is in fact a reasonably good predictor of accuracy: witnesses who hesitate are much more likely to be wrong than those who respond quickly and firmly. The problem, Zubiría argues, is that confidence is not stable. A witness who is told 'good, you identified our suspect' typically becomes more certain over time, so that by the trial a tentative choice has hardened into unwavering conviction. Zubiría's findings are sometimes presented as a rehabilitation of the eyewitness, but this goes too far; they rehabilitate only the initial statement, and only when it has been properly recorded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is less a single reform than a philosophy: memory should be treated like physical trace evidence, which can be contaminated and must therefore be collected carefully, documented at once and tested only once. Repeated identification attempts, for instance, are especially harmful, because a face seen in an earlier line-up becomes familiar and may be chosen again for that reason alone. Some legal scholars worry that such reforms will make prosecution harder. That may be true in a narrow sense, but a justice system that convicts fewer innocent people is surely not weakened by the change.

topic: memory reconsolidation and its proposed use in treating traumatic and fearful memories
title: Rewriting on Recall
subtitle: The discovery that memories become unstable each time they are retrieved has raised therapeutic hopes and awkward questions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists described memory formation in terms that would have been familiar to any printer. A new experience was thought to leave a fragile trace which, over a period of hours, was gradually stabilised through the synthesis of proteins in the brain, a process known as consolidation. Once this had happened, the memory was considered fixed, much as ink becomes permanent once it has dried. It might later fade or become hard to retrieve, but its content was not expected to change. The appeal of this model is easy to understand, since it matches our subjective sense that remembering is a matter of looking something up. It is, however, increasingly difficult to defend.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The challenge came from a series of animal studies around the turn of the millennium. Rats were trained to associate a tone with a mild electric shock, and they duly froze whenever the tone sounded. Days later, long after consolidation should have been complete, the researchers played the tone again and immediately injected a drug that blocks protein synthesis. When tested subsequently, the animals showed little fear. The implication was startling: the act of recalling a memory appeared to return it to an unstable state, from which it had to be stored all over again. Professor Henrike Asmussen of the Odense Institute of Neurobiology, who has studied this 'reconsolidation' for two decades, argues that it is not a flaw but a feature. Memories, she contends, are reopened on retrieval so that they can be revised in the light of new information, keeping our knowledge of the world current. If she is right, and I believe she largely is, then the distortions to which human memory is prone are not a separate defect but the price paid for its adaptability.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It did not take long for clinicians to see the therapeutic possibilities. If a memory becomes malleable each time it is recalled, it might be possible to weaken the emotional force of a traumatic recollection by intervening during that window. Dr Yerlan Kopbosynov of the Steppe Centre for Clinical Psychology has conducted several trials in which patients with long-standing anxiety disorders were asked to describe a distressing memory after taking propranolol, a drug commonly prescribed for high blood pressure that dampens the body's response to stress hormones. In follow-up sessions, many showed markedly reduced heart rate and sweating when the memory was revisited. Significantly, they could still recount what had happened in detail; what had diminished was the visceral sense of dread that accompanied it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Enthusiasm, however, has been tempered by inconsistent results. A number of laboratories have failed to reproduce the effect, and it has become clear that reconsolidation is subject to strict boundary conditions. Dr Mateus Arrudão of the Porto Alegre School of Neuroscience has shown that memories which are very old or were formed under intense stress tend to resist destabilisation altogether. More importantly, Arrudão argues that simple recall is not sufficient: the memory is reopened only when the reminder contains an element of surprise, some mismatch between what the person expects and what actually occurs. A reminder that is too short may fail to trigger the process, while one that is too prolonged appears to produce something quite different, namely extinction, in which a new, competing memory is laid down alongside the original rather than replacing it. Since the original memory survives extinction intact, symptoms often return. This narrow window explains much of the inconsistency in the literature, and it makes the clinical application of reconsolidation far more delicate than early reports implied.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Alongside these practical difficulties, bioethicists have raised a different kind of objection. Some fear that techniques for editing memory could be used to blunt a perpetrator's guilt, or to soften the recollections of soldiers in ways that make further violence easier. Others warn that our memories, including painful ones, are integral to personal identity. These concerns deserve a hearing, but talk of 'memory erasure' badly misrepresents what the treatments actually do. Kopbosynov's patients did not forget their experiences; they remembered them with less anguish. A more serious worry, in my view, concerns the courtroom, where a witness whose memory has been treated in this way might give testimony that has been altered in ways no one can detect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A research group at the Malabar Institute of Behavioural Science, led by Dr Ananya Thottathil, has explored whether the same window can be exploited without drugs. In their procedure, participants are briefly reminded of a feared object, and then, after a pause of about ten minutes, they undergo standard exposure therapy. The idea is that the new, safe information is incorporated into the reopened memory rather than stored separately. Early results with spider phobia were encouraging, though subsequent trials have produced a more mixed picture, and Thottathil herself cautions that the timing must be calibrated to each individual.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever its clinical future, reconsolidation research has implications that reach well beyond the clinic. If every act of recall is also an act of rewriting, then a memory that has been recounted many times is less a record of the original event than a record of its most recent retelling. This does not mean that memory is worthless as evidence, but it does suggest that the confidence we place in vivid, frequently rehearsed recollections is often misplaced.

topic: flashbulb memories of shocking public events and their accuracy over time
title: The Flash That Fades
subtitle: Vivid recollections of where we were when momentous news broke are less dependable than they feel

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask people where they were when they first heard about a major public catastrophe, and many will answer without hesitation, supplying a wealth of detail: the room they were standing in, the person who broke the news, even what they happened to be eating. Such recollections were labelled 'flashbulb memories' in the 1970s, a term intended to capture both their brilliance and the apparent instantaneousness of their formation, as though the shock of the news had triggered a mental camera. The label has proved remarkably durable, appearing in textbooks and popular writing alike. Yet the metaphor at its heart has, in my opinion, done more to mislead than to illuminate, because it implies a permanence that the evidence simply does not support.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most telling evidence comes from studies that capture memories soon after an event and then revisit them. On the morning after a widely televised industrial disaster, Professor Teodora Vlaicu of the Carpathian University of Cluj asked over a hundred students to write down how they had learned of it. When she contacted the same students three years later, fewer than one in ten produced an account that closely matched the original, and roughly a quarter gave versions that differed in every significant respect. Remarkably, the students' confidence in their later accounts was high, and several who were shown their original handwritten statements insisted that it was the earlier version, not their current memory, that must be mistaken. Vlaicu has since repeated the exercise after two further public tragedies, with broadly similar results, which suggests that the original finding was not a quirk of one unusual event or of one unusually forgetful group of students.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such findings raise the question of whether flashbulb memories are really special at all. Dr Hrafnhildur Ketilsdóttir of the Reykjavík Centre for Cognitive Research addressed this directly by asking participants, on the day after a shocking news event, to record both how they had heard the news and an ordinary event from the preceding days, such as a meal with friends. Over the following year, the two kinds of memory declined in accuracy at almost exactly the same rate. What differed was how they felt: the flashbulb memories were rated as more vivid and were held with far greater conviction. Ketilsdóttir concludes that the distinctive feature of these memories is the belief that surrounds them rather than any unusual accuracy, a conclusion that seems to me essentially correct.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts so deflationary a view. Dr Benedetta Zanforlin, a neuropsychologist at the Padua Laboratory of Emotion and Memory, points out that studies of this kind tend to lump together two quite different types of information. The central facts of the event itself, what happened and roughly when, are retained remarkably well, she argues, and emotional arousal genuinely strengthens memory for them. It is the peripheral details of personal circumstance, such as who delivered the news or what one was wearing, that drift over time. Zanforlin's distinction is valuable, but it does less to rescue flashbulb memory than she suggests, since it is precisely these personal details that people feel most certain about.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Part of the explanation for this drift lies in what happens after the event. A five-country study by the Tasman Memory Consortium examined recollections of a single international crisis and found that the people who discussed it most often, and watched the most news coverage, showed the greatest changes in their accounts over time. Each retelling, the researchers suggest, tends to smooth the story into a more coherent narrative, and details absorbed from later broadcasts are gradually incorporated as though they had been personally experienced. A number of participants, for example, remembered watching live footage of events that had not in fact been broadcast until the following day. Interestingly, participants from the country most directly affected by the crisis gave the most consistent accounts.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why, then, should such unreliable memories be held with such confidence? One plausible answer is that their function is social rather than archival. Shared memories of a dramatic event allow individuals to locate themselves within a collective history, and the act of telling one's own story of that day strengthens a sense of belonging to a community. Families and nations rehearse such stories at anniversaries, and the memories become part of a shared inheritance that is passed on even to those too young to have experienced the event themselves. Seen in this light, confidence is not a malfunction; a story that is told hesitantly does little to bind people together. The difficulty arises when these narratives are treated as documentary evidence, whether by historians compiling oral testimonies or by courts.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that people who recall where they were on a momentous day are deceiving themselves entirely. Their memories usually preserve the outline of events, and sometimes a good deal more. But the vividness of a recollection is not a guarantee of its truth, and the sense of certainty that accompanies it may be the least trustworthy element of all. Perhaps the most useful lesson of flashbulb research is that even our most treasured memories deserve to be held with a little humility.

topic: the reliability of oral traditions as long-term collective memory and historical evidence
title: Spoken Across the Centuries
subtitle: Can stories passed by word of mouth preserve accurate information for a thousand years or more?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the modern era, professional historians regarded oral tradition with suspicion. Written documents could be dated, compared and archived; stories passed from mouth to mouth, by contrast, seemed hopelessly vulnerable to embellishment and decay. Experimental psychology appeared to confirm this prejudice. If individuals misremember events from a few weeks earlier, it seemed absurd to suppose that a community could preserve an accurate account across dozens of generations. Over the past three decades, however, a body of evidence has accumulated which suggests that, under certain conditions, oral traditions can carry information across spans of time that would once have been thought impossible.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most striking cases come from the Pacific. Professor Losaline Vainikolo, a geographer at the Pacific Institute of Coastal Studies, spent several years recording narratives on a group of small islands, one of which tells of a mountain that 'split open and threw down burning stones' on a neighbouring island, driving its inhabitants into the sea. The neighbouring island has been uninhabited for as long as anyone can remember, and the story was long regarded as myth. When volcanologists later examined the island, they found ash deposits that radiocarbon dating placed at roughly thirteen hundred years old, together with buried house foundations. Equally significant, the narrative described the eruption as beginning on the island's southern flank, which is exactly where the geological evidence indicates the main vent was located.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How could such detail survive? Laboratory studies of 'serial reproduction', in which a story is passed along a chain of participants, typically show it becoming shorter, simpler and more conventional within a handful of retellings. Dr Ingeborg Fjæreide, a cognitive anthropologist at the Nordic Institute of Cognitive Anthropology, argues that these experiments misrepresent how traditional knowledge was actually transmitted. Participants in a laboratory hear a prose passage once and pass it on to a stranger. Traditional narratives, by contrast, were frequently cast in verse, set to music or tied to particular landscapes, and each of these features acts as a constraint that limits the range of possible errors: a substituted word that breaks the metre or the rhyme is quickly noticed. In her own experiments, verses that combined rhyme, rhythm and vivid imagery were reproduced with almost no loss across ten links of a chain, whereas prose versions of the same content had lost most of their detail by the fourth.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Social institutions provided further safeguards. In many societies, the recitation of important narratives was entrusted to trained specialists, performances took place in public before audiences familiar with the material, and mistakes were openly corrected. Knowledge was sometimes deliberately divided among different families, so that no single version could be altered without the others noticing. Yet not all researchers share this optimism. Dr Kwabena Kyerematen, a historian at the Kumasi Centre for Oral Archives, has spent much of his career comparing royal genealogies with independent sources such as trade records kept by foreign merchants. He finds that genealogies are routinely revised to legitimise those currently in power: inconvenient ancestors disappear, and the middle generations of a lineage are often compressed, a process sometimes called 'telescoping', so that the founding of a dynasty appears more recent than it was.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These positions are less incompatible than they first appear. What Vainikolo and Kyerematen document are different kinds of information. Knowledge about the physical environment, such as the location of fresh water, the behaviour of the sea or the danger posed by a volcano, has practical value for everyone and little political significance, so there is every incentive to preserve it accurately. Genealogies, on the other hand, are claims to authority, and their content is under constant pressure from those whose interests they serve. It would therefore be a mistake to judge oral tradition as a whole to be either reliable or unreliable; the more useful question is what a particular story was for.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The arrival of writing complicated matters further. When missionaries and colonial administrators began to transcribe oral traditions in the nineteenth century, they often recorded a single version from a single informant, sometimes chosen because he was willing to cooperate rather than because he was regarded locally as an authority. Once printed, that version acquired a fixity it had never possessed, and rival accounts were dismissed as corruptions. In some cases, the very act of preservation removed the social mechanisms that had kept a tradition accurate, since performance and public correction were no longer thought necessary.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The value of oral tradition is not merely historical. When a tsunami struck parts of the region early in the present century, several long-established coastal communities whose stories warned of the sea retreating before a great wave moved to higher ground in time, while many recent settlers, who did not share those stories, were caught unprepared. Such episodes suggest that scientists concerned with natural hazards would do well to treat traditional narratives not as folklore to be catalogued, but as data to be tested.

topic: cognitive offloading: how search engines, saved files and cameras affect what we remember
title: Memory in the Machine
subtitle: Are digital devices weakening our memories, or simply changing what we choose to remember?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Human beings have always stored memories outside their own heads. Notches cut into bone, knotted cords, written ledgers and pocket diaries all served to relieve the mind of information it could not, or did not wish to, retain. What distinguishes the present moment is the scale and ease of the arrangement. A smartphone holds a person's appointments, contacts, photographs and directions, and a search engine answers almost any factual question in seconds. Not surprisingly, commentators have begun to warn of 'digital amnesia', a generation that remembers nothing because it never needs to. The alarm is understandable, but in my view it is largely misplaced, although, as I shall argue, not entirely so.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The modern research began with a deceptively simple experiment. Dr Hye-jin Byun of the Hanbit Institute of Cognitive Science asked participants to type a series of unusual facts into a computer. Half were told that their entries would be saved; the other half were told they would be deleted. When later asked to recall the facts, those who believed the information had been saved remembered considerably fewer of them. Yet when Byun asked the same participants which folder each fact had been saved in, they performed remarkably well. In other words, when people expect information to remain available, memory appears to shift its effort from the content itself to the means of finding it again. Byun is careful to stress that this is a reallocation of effort rather than a loss of capacity.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Iñaki Aizpurua, a social psychologist at the Basque Centre for Behavioural Research, interprets such findings through the concept of 'transactive memory'. Long-standing couples, families and work teams, he notes, routinely divide the task of remembering: one partner keeps track of birthdays, another of finances, and each knows who knows what. A device, on this view, is simply another member of the team, and a highly dependable one. Aizpurua's own work suggests that offloading can bring a positive benefit. Participants who saved one list of words on a computer before studying a second list remembered the second list significantly better than those who had to keep the first list in mind, presumably because their mental resources were no longer occupied. This seems to me a persuasive account of why offloading is often sensible, though it assumes that the device will always be available when needed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Photography offers a particularly vivid illustration of the trade-offs involved. In a study conducted in a large art museum, Dr Liisa Kärkkäinen of the Tampere Laboratory of Applied Cognition directed visitors to view some objects and to photograph others. The next day, visitors recalled fewer of the photographed objects, and remembered fewer details about them, than of the objects they had simply observed. Kärkkäinen attributes this to a kind of mental handover: once the camera has recorded an object, the viewer stops processing it. Intriguingly, however, the effect disappeared when visitors were told to zoom in on one particular feature of an object before taking the picture. In that case, their memory for the whole object, including parts that did not appear in the photograph, was as good as that of people who had not used a camera. What matters, it seems, is not the device but whether it replaces attention or directs it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is so relaxed. Dr Obiageli Ezeokoli, who studies learning at the Lagos Institute of Educational Psychology, argues that the analogy with a human team breaks down at a crucial point. Expertise, she contends, depends on a rich store of knowledge held in long-term memory, because new ideas arise from connections between things one already knows. A fact that sits on a server cannot be combined with another fact in the mind of someone who has never learned it. Ezeokoli's studies of university students found that those who routinely looked up information while writing essays produced work that was accurate but noticeably less original than that of students who had studied the material in advance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ezeokoli has also identified a more subtle danger. In one experiment, participants who had used a search engine to answer a set of questions subsequently rated their own knowledge more highly, even on topics they had not searched for, than participants who had answered the same questions from a printed encyclopaedia. Access to the internet, it appears, can blur the boundary between what we know and what we merely know how to find. I find this the most troubling finding in the field. The risk of the digital age is not so much that we will forget facts as that we will lose the ability to judge accurately what we actually remember, and an inflated sense of one's own knowledge is a poor basis for decisions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this suggests that people should abandon their devices or return to memorising telephone numbers. Offloading routine information is, for the most part, an efficient use of limited mental resources. What it does suggest is that remembering has become a matter of choice rather than necessity, and that the choice deserves more thought than it usually receives. Schools that teach students to search efficiently might do well to teach them, too, which knowledge is worth carrying in their own heads.

topic: cryptomnesia: unintentional plagiarism and the failure to remember where ideas came from
title: The Unwitting Borrower
subtitle: Why do honest people sometimes present other people's ideas as their own, and what does this reveal about memory?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years a songwriter, novelist or academic is accused of plagiarism and responds with an unusual defence: they did not knowingly copy anything. The melody or the phrase, they insist, simply came to them. Such claims are easily dismissed as convenient excuses, and some of them doubtless are. Yet psychologists have long recognised a genuine phenomenon, known as cryptomnesia, in which a memory returns without the sense of familiarity that normally accompanies it, so that a person experiences a recollection as a fresh idea. The question that now divides researchers is not whether cryptomnesia occurs, but how often it occurs, under what conditions, and how far it should excuse those who are guilty of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The phenomenon was first studied systematically through a simple group game. Participants took turns generating examples from a category, such as types of musical instrument, and were later asked either to recall the items they themselves had produced or to come up with entirely new ones. Dr Mele Fakatava of the Tongan Institute for Memory Studies has refined this procedure over two decades. In her experiments, between three and nine per cent of the items people claim as their own were in fact produced by someone else, and the proportion of supposedly new ideas that turn out to be repetitions is higher still. Notably, participants were most likely to appropriate the contributions of the person who had spoken immediately before them. Fakatava concludes that the error arises when attention is divided between listening to others and preparing one's own response, so that the source of what is heard is never properly encoded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Bohuslav Zatloukal of the Olomouc Centre for Cognitive Research argues that cryptomnesia is not a distinct quirk but an instance of a much more general weakness: memory stores content well but records its origin poorly. On his account, the brain does not attach a permanent label to each memory stating where it came from. Instead, people infer the origin of a thought at the moment of retrieval, from clues such as its vividness and the effort that went into it. An idea that one has heard, considered and elaborated upon may therefore come to feel as though it had been generated internally. Zatloukal's studies show that participants who were asked to improve on other people's suggestions were later far more likely to claim the improved ideas, and crucially the originals as well, as their own. I find this account convincing as far as it goes, because it explains why the most engaged listeners, rather than the most careless, are often the ones who borrow.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Parvaneh Ghaffarzadeh, who studies creativity at the Isfahan School of Applied Psychology, has argued that laboratory games understate the problem. In everyday life, she points out, the interval between encountering an idea and reproducing it may be months or years, and the original context, whether a conversation at a conference or an article read late at night, is quickly lost. In a survey of more than four hundred professional composers, nearly a third reported having discovered, usually through a colleague, that a melody they had believed original closely resembled an existing work. Ghaffarzadeh accepts that self-reports of this kind cannot be verified, but she argues that their sheer frequency suggests unintentional borrowing is a normal by-product of creative work rather than a rare lapse.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are persuaded. Dr Henrike Osterkamp of the Kiel Laboratory of Experimental Psychology has noted that in most experiments the rate of cryptomnesia falls sharply when participants are offered a small reward for accuracy, or are simply warned that their answers will be checked against those of others. In her view, this shows that much apparent cryptomnesia reflects a lack of effort rather than an inability to remember: people who are motivated to monitor their sources generally can. Her findings are important, but I think she draws the wrong conclusion from them. That an error can be reduced by effort does not mean it was deliberate when the effort was absent. People also make fewer spelling mistakes when they are paid to be careful, yet no one regards ordinary misspellings as intentional.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The distinction matters because cryptomnesia increasingly arises in courtrooms and disciplinary hearings. Courts in several countries have held that copying may infringe copyright even when it is subconscious, on the reasoning that the original creator suffers the same loss either way. Universities, by contrast, tend to treat intention as central to whether misconduct has occurred, although they rarely have reliable means of establishing it. Zatloukal himself has warned that expert testimony about cryptomnesia may be used too freely as a defence, and he recommends that it be admitted only when there is evidence that the accused had genuinely encountered the original long before, and in a setting unlikely to be remembered.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should writers, composers and scholars do? The research offers no means of eliminating cryptomnesia, but it does suggest ways of reducing it. Keeping records of where ideas were first encountered, allowing time to pass between gathering material and producing work, and asking others to check drafts for unconscious echoes are all simple precautions. More fundamentally, the phenomenon should temper the moral outrage that tends to greet accusations of plagiarism. Originality, it seems, is in part an illusion created by a memory that is far better at preserving what we have learned than at reminding us where we learned it.

topic: déjà vu and what the false feeling of familiarity reveals about how memory monitors itself
title: The Strange Familiarity of the New
subtitle: Scientists are finally taking déjà vu seriously, but they do not agree on what it is

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people know the sensation. Walking into a café for the first time, or hearing a remark in a conversation, they are suddenly gripped by the conviction that they have lived through this exact moment before, while knowing perfectly well that they cannot have done. Surveys suggest that around two-thirds of adults experience déjà vu at some point in their lives, usually for no more than a few seconds. The experience is reported across cultures and age groups, although the French term for it has become the standard name in most languages. For much of the twentieth century the phenomenon was left to mystics, who saw it as evidence of past lives, and to psychiatrists, who suspected it of signalling mental disturbance. Neither interpretation has survived scrutiny. My own view is that déjà vu is best understood not as a malfunction at all, but as a rare glimpse of the system by which memory continually checks its own output.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential modern account treats déjà vu as familiarity without recollection. Dr Amaru Ccori of the Andean Institute of Cognitive Science in Cusco notes that recognising something involves two separate processes: a quick sense that a thing is familiar, and a slower retrieval of the specific occasion on which it was met. Déjà vu, he proposes, occurs when the first process fires without the second. To test the idea, Ccori had volunteers explore a series of rooms in virtual reality. Later, they toured new rooms that contained entirely different furniture and objects but whose spatial arrangement copied that of an earlier room. Volunteers reported déjà vu far more often in these rooms, particularly when they failed to recall the earlier room they resembled. The study is elegant, and it plainly captures something real, but I doubt that it explains more than a portion of cases; many people describe déjà vu in settings that resemble nothing they have ever seen.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A quite different explanation comes from neurology. Professor Zbigniew Sobiepan of the Lublin Medical Academy has spent many years working with patients whose epileptic seizures originate in the temporal lobes, the region of the brain most closely involved in memory. Many of these patients report intense déjà vu immediately before a seizure, and the sensation can sometimes be produced by mild electrical stimulation of the same region during surgery. From this, Sobiepan concludes that all déjà vu, including that of healthy people, is a brief misfiring of neurons and has nothing to do with any earlier experience. This, in my opinion, takes a sound observation too far. Patients often say that their seizure-related déjà vu is longer, stronger and more frightening than the ordinary kind, which suggests that the two may differ in nature and not only in degree.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most surprising work has come from Dr Folasade Adegbenro at the Ibadan Centre for Brain and Behaviour. Using brain imaging, she induced déjà vu in the laboratory by means of word lists designed to create a false sense of familiarity. When participants reported déjà vu, the most active areas were not those that store memories but frontal regions associated with decision-making and error detection. Adegbenro interprets déjà vu as the moment at which the brain's checking system notices that a feeling of familiarity is mistaken. Her survey data fit this picture: déjà vu is most common between the ages of fifteen and twenty-five, declines steadily thereafter, and is reported more often by people who travel frequently and by those with better memories, not worse ones. Adegbenro is careful to add, however, that a sensation produced with word lists in a laboratory may be only a pale imitation of the spontaneous experience.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One puzzling feature of déjà vu is the feeling that often accompanies it, that one knows what is about to happen next. Dr Ingeborg Lysaker of the Bergen Laboratory for Memory Research set out to test whether this feeling has any substance. Participants followed a route through a virtual town and, at each junction, were asked whether they could predict the next turn. When they were experiencing déjà vu, they felt strongly that they could, but their predictions were correct no more often than chance would allow. Lysaker concludes that the sense of foreknowledge is itself part of the illusion. Her findings, it seems to me, go a long way towards explaining why so many people have regarded déjà vu as supernatural: an experience that feels like a glimpse of the future is difficult to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If Adegbenro is right, the fact that déjà vu becomes rarer with age has an interesting implication. It may be that the brain's checking system becomes less vigilant over time, so that false feelings of familiarity are accepted rather than noticed. Elderly people who no longer experience déjà vu need not be worried by its absence, since there is no evidence that it predicts memory problems. Still, the research as a whole points to a striking conclusion. Memory is not a passive store from which recollections are simply withdrawn; it is constantly assessing whether the impressions it produces can be trusted, and déjà vu is one of the few occasions on which we catch it doing so.

topic: internalised false confessions: how police interrogation can lead innocent suspects to distrust and rewrite their own memories
title: Believing the Unbelievable
subtitle: Why do some innocent suspects come to remember crimes they never committed?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few kinds of evidence carry as much weight in a courtroom as a confession. It seems self-evident that no one would admit to a serious crime they had not committed, and juries, judges and the public tend to treat a confession as the end of the matter. Yet the steady stream of convictions overturned in recent decades, many of them on the basis of later DNA analysis, has shown that a surprising proportion of wrongly convicted defendants had confessed. Most such confessions are what psychologists call compliant: the suspect knows they are innocent but admits guilt simply to bring an exhausting interrogation to an end. Only a minority are internalised, meaning that the suspect comes genuinely to believe in their own guilt. It is this second group that seems to me the most unsettling demonstration we have of how fragile human memory can be.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Professor Ruairí Ó Muirgheasa of the Sligo Institute of Forensic Psychology has described the process through which such beliefs arise as 'memory distrust'. A person, he argues, does not abandon confidence in their memory all at once. Rather, it is eroded by a combination of circumstances: isolation from friends and family, lack of sleep, repeated insistence by interrogators that the evidence against them is overwhelming, and, crucially, the suggestion that they may have committed the crime without being aware of it, perhaps because they suffered a blackout or were affected by alcohol. Once a suspect accepts that their own recollection cannot be relied upon, Ó Muirgheasa contends, they begin to depend on external sources of information, and the most readily available source is the interrogator.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Studying this process directly is impossible, since no ethics committee would permit researchers to accuse volunteers of genuine crimes. Instead, investigators have relied on milder analogues. In one well-known design, Dr Thandeka Sibiya of the Pietermaritzburg School of Psychology asked participants to type letters read aloud to them, warning them not to press a particular key because it would cause the computer to crash. The computer was in fact programmed to crash regardless, and participants were accused of pressing the forbidden key. When a confederate claimed to have witnessed the error, a majority signed a written confession, and some went on to describe precisely how they had made the mistake, supplying details that could not have been true. The effect was strongest when letters were read at a fast pace, which made participants less certain of what they had actually done. Critics point out that the stakes in such experiments are trivial compared with those of a criminal investigation. This is true, but it does not render the studies worthless; if anything, one would expect real interrogations, with their far greater pressures, to produce stronger effects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More recent work has attempted to go further. Dr Corina Dobrogeanu of the Iași Institute of Legal Psychology reported that, over the course of three interviews in which researchers combined accurate details from participants' adolescence with a fabricated account of a minor crime, around seventy per cent of participants came to describe committing the offence. The result attracted considerable attention, but it has also been challenged. Dr Keoni Puahala, a methodologist at the Honolulu Centre for Behavioural Science, argues that the criteria used to classify responses were too generous, counting as a false memory any account in which a participant merely accepted the suggestion. When he recoded the transcripts using stricter criteria, which required vivid and detailed recollection, the figure fell to roughly thirty per cent. Puahala's correction is a valuable one, but even his lower figure ought to alarm anyone who places faith in confessions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Who is most at risk? Research consistently identifies juveniles, people with intellectual disabilities and those who score highly on measures of suggestibility as especially vulnerable. Ó Muirgheasa, however, insists that the problem cannot be confined to such groups, and that ordinary adults of normal intelligence can be led to doubt their memories if they are subjected to sufficient pressure. I am inclined to accept this in principle, but it should be acknowledged that the claim rests largely on laboratory studies; the real cases in which internalised confessions have been documented involve, disproportionately, suspects from the vulnerable groups.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Several reforms have been proposed. The most widely adopted is the electronic recording of entire interrogations, which allows courts to see how a confession was obtained. Some jurisdictions have also banned the practice of falsely telling suspects that incriminating evidence, such as fingerprints, has been found, while others still permit it. A number of police services have moved towards a model of investigative interviewing whose purpose is to gather accurate information rather than to secure an admission of guilt. Puahala doubts, however, that recording is enough on its own. His studies of mock jurors show that people who watch a recorded interrogation continue to give heavy weight to the resulting confession, even when the questioning they have observed was plainly coercive.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No single measure will remove the danger, because its roots lie not in police misconduct alone but in the nature of memory itself. What the research does suggest is that confessions should lose their special status. Rather than being treated as decisive, a confession ought to be regarded as one piece of evidence among others, and courts should be reluctant to convict on its basis unless there is independent corroboration. That would not prevent every wrongful conviction, but it would at least acknowledge what psychologists have shown: a person's account of their own past can be reshaped by others more easily than most of us would like to believe.

topic: childhood amnesia: why adults cannot recall their earliest years
title: The Vanishing Years
subtitle: Almost nobody remembers the first years of life. Explaining why has become one of the more revealing puzzles in memory research

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask a room of adults to describe their earliest memory and a curious pattern emerges. Very few can recall anything that happened before the age of three, and the handful of fragments that survive from the following year or two tend to be isolated, wordless snapshots: the colour of a bedroom wall, a moment of fear at the edge of the sea. Psychologists call this blank stretch at the start of life childhood amnesia, and it was noted as early as the late nineteenth century. Long treated as a mere curiosity, it deserves far more attention, because the gap sits precisely in the years when the brain is learning faster than it ever will again.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One early assumption was that babies simply cannot form lasting memories. That idea has not survived experimental scrutiny. A group led by Liesbeth Vroonhoven at the Zeeland Infant Cognition Laboratory taught infants to move a brightly coloured mobile by kicking a leg attached to it with a soft ribbon. Six-month-olds retained the trick for up to two weeks, and when a brief reminder was given, with the mobile simply jiggled in front of them, infants who appeared to have forgotten it entirely began kicking again. Such results reframe the question. The difficulty is evidently not that early experiences fail to register, but that they somehow become inaccessible as the child grows up.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Of the competing explanations, the most intuitive concerns language. Sefa Adjeman, a developmental psychologist at Akosombo Lakeside University, argues that an experience encoded before a child possesses the words to describe it is stored in a format that the verbal adult mind can no longer use. In one of her studies, toddlers played with an unusual machine that turned coloured balls into a stream of bubbles. When they were interviewed six and twelve months later, many could still operate the device, yet in describing the episode they used only words that had been in their vocabulary at the time of the original game; terms learned afterwards almost never appeared. Adjeman concludes that memories seem to be 'frozen' in the language available when they were formed. The finding is elegant, but it cannot be the whole story.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The chief difficulty is that childhood amnesia is not confined to our own species. Young rats and mice also forget early learning far more rapidly than adults do, and they have no language to lose. Mirela Constandache and her colleagues at the Danube Centre for Neural Plasticity have proposed that the explanation lies in the hippocampus, a structure central to memory for events. In infancy, new neurons are produced there at an extraordinary rate, and Constandache suggests that as these cells are wired into existing circuits, they overwrite the connections in which earlier memories were held. In support, her team found that when the production of new neurons was slowed in infant mice, the animals retained what they had learned for considerably longer, whereas stimulating neuron growth in adult mice made them more forgetful. Caution is needed, of course, in transferring conclusions from rodents to children, whose brains mature over a far longer period. Nevertheless, the account has the considerable merit of explaining why the forgetting appears across species.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third group of researchers places the emphasis not on brain cells but on the developing sense of self. Tomasz Wierzbinski of the Masurian Centre for Memory Studies maintains that an autobiographical memory requires an 'I' around which events can be organised, and that this only begins to emerge at around eighteen months to two years, when children first recognise their own reflection. The way adults talk to children also appears to matter. Wierzbinski's longitudinal research found that youngsters whose parents discussed shared experiences in rich detail later reported first memories that dated from earlier in life than those of children whose parents spoke about the past only briefly. Comparisons across societies point in the same direction: in cultures that encourage individuals to tell stories about themselves, the average earliest memory dates from several months earlier than in cultures that stress the group over the individual. The implication is that the boundary of childhood amnesia is not set by biology alone.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This raises an uncomfortable question about surviving memories. Many of the episodes people confidently describe as their earliest may in fact be reconstructions, assembled from photographs, home videos and stories repeated at family gatherings. In a large survey conducted by Constandache's institute, almost two in five respondents claimed to remember events from before the age of two, and a significant number dated memories to their first year. Given everything known about early forgetting, the researchers regard most of these as fictional, however vivid they feel. It would be wise, therefore, for all of us to treat our earliest recollections with a degree of humility: their sincerity is no guarantee of their accuracy.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to see the three explanations as rivals, but the evidence suggests that each describes part of a single process. Neural turnover, the absence of language and an unformed self all belong to the same developmental period, and they probably combine to make early episodes unrecoverable. What should be firmly rejected is the popular conclusion that, because the first years are forgotten, they matter little. The loss of specific episodes is not the loss of everything learned. Early experience shapes language, emotional responses and expectations about other people, and these persist long after the events that formed them have disappeared from conscious memory. Childhood amnesia, in this sense, is less a failure of memory than evidence of how much memory does without our knowing.

topic: collaborative remembering and the social contagion of memory in groups, couples and co-witnesses
title: Minds in Company
subtitle: Most remembering happens in conversation with other people, and research is revealing how much those conversations reshape what we recall

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, the experimental study of memory has largely been the study of solitary individuals. A volunteer sits alone in a quiet room, learns a list of words or a set of pictures, and is later tested on how much he or she can reproduce. The method has yielded a great deal, but it bears little resemblance to the way memory operates in daily life. Families reminisce over dinner, colleagues reconstruct what was agreed at a meeting, and witnesses to an accident compare notes while waiting for the police. In each case, what is eventually remembered is the product of a conversation rather than of one mind working in isolation. The laboratory's preference for the lone rememberer has, in my view, left researchers with a lopsided picture of what memory is for.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: When psychologists did begin to study remembering in groups, the first results were counterintuitive. Ingrid Skaugrud and her team at Fjordheim University compared groups of three people recalling material together with 'nominal groups': the same number of people working separately, whose answers were later pooled with duplicates removed. Real groups consistently produced more than any single member could manage, but noticeably less than the nominal groups. Skaugrud attributes this shortfall, known as collaborative inhibition, to a clash of retrieval strategies. Each person has an idiosyncratic route through what they have learned, and listening to others recite items in a different sequence disrupts that route. Her most telling evidence is that the deficit largely disappeared when members were asked to take turns recalling whole categories in their own preferred order rather than contributing items at random. This does not mean that group remembering is futile; it means that its benefits depend heavily on how the conversation is organised.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Conversation does not only suppress memories; it can also implant them. Chinyere Mbanefo-Ude, of the Ikenga Institute of Behavioural Science, has studied what she calls the social contagion of memory. Participants viewed photographs of household scenes alongside a partner who, unknown to them, was a member of the research team. During a joint recall session, the partner casually mentioned objects that had not appeared in the photographs, such as a toaster in a kitchen or a lamp in a study. In a later individual test, participants frequently reported these items as part of what they had seen, often with considerable confidence. The effect was markedly stronger when the partner had been introduced as an interior designer, suggesting that people are especially willing to absorb the errors of someone they believe to be knowledgeable. The relevance to legal settings, where witnesses routinely discuss what they observed, is obvious.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the picture is not uniformly bleak. Paulo Arrabal-Quintas, at the Tagus Centre for Ageing Research, has examined couples who have been married for several decades. Asked to recall shared holidays or the plots of films they had watched together, many such pairs remembered considerably more jointly than the two partners did on their own, reversing the usual pattern of collaborative inhibition. The successful couples cued each other, picked up on half-finished sentences and knew which of them was likely to hold which kind of detail. Crucially, however, the advantage was confined to couples who communicated smoothly; those who repeatedly contradicted each other over minor details actually recalled less together than apart. One sobering implication, which I find hard to dismiss, is that the death of a long-term partner may deprive the survivor not only of companionship but of part of his or her own past, since some memories were only ever retrievable in the other person's company.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Groups do more than share memories; over time, they come to forget the same things. Ji-ho Seomun of the Hanbyeol Institute of Social Cognition has shown that when one person selectively recounts parts of a shared experience, listeners later find the unmentioned but related details harder to retrieve, just as the speaker does. A conversation, in other words, both rehearses some memories and quietly weakens others in every participant. Seomun argues that this mechanism helps to explain how communities converge on a common version of the past. The idea is intriguing, but the leap from laboratory word lists to the collective memory of entire nations is considerable, and the experiments so far say little about how such effects accumulate across years of public debate, commemoration and education.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practical question is what to do with these findings, particularly in the justice system. Courts have traditionally regarded any discussion between witnesses as contamination, and police are often advised to keep witnesses apart. As a counsel of perfection, this is sensible; as a practical policy, it is largely unworkable. Witnesses to a crime are frequently friends or relatives who travel home together, and many will have talked about the event long before an officer arrives. A more realistic safeguard would be to obtain a brief written or recorded account from each witness as early as possible, before extensive discussion, so that later statements can be compared with what each person reported independently.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the research suggests that it is misleading to ask whether social remembering improves or corrupts memory, as though the answer were the same in every case. Remembering with others can fill gaps, correct errors and preserve experiences that no individual could retain alone; it can equally spread falsehoods and erase inconvenient details. Which outcome prevails depends on who we remember with, how much we trust them and how the exchange is structured. Memory, it seems, is less a private archive than a shared and continually negotiated resource.
