topic: the crowding-out (overjustification) effect: whether external rewards undermine intrinsic motivation
title: When Payment Spoils the Game
subtitle: Do rewards weaken the enthusiasm they are meant to encourage? Half a century of research has produced a less tidy answer than its popularisers suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Common sense holds that if you want people to do more of something, you should reward them for doing it. Since the early 1970s, however, a substantial body of psychological research has challenged this assumption, at least for activities that people already find enjoyable. Offering a reward for such an activity, the argument runs, can diminish the pleasure people take in it, so that once the reward is withdrawn they engage in it less than they did before. The phenomenon, usually described as 'crowding out', has since travelled far beyond the laboratory. It features prominently in management handbooks, parenting columns and debates about school policy, where it is frequently stated with a confidence that the underlying evidence does not justify.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic experiments followed a simple design. Volunteers were given an absorbing task, such as a set of spatial puzzles, and some of them were paid for each puzzle they solved. The researcher then left the room on a pretext, and observers behind a screen recorded whether participants carried on with the puzzles or turned to magazines left on a nearby table. Those who had been paid typically spent less of this unsupervised interval on the task. The standard interpretation is that people infer their own motives partly from their circumstances: once payment is involved, an activity that had seemed worth doing for its own sake comes to be seen as a job. Ilse Haugmoen of the Nordfjord Institute of Psychology has refined this account. In her view, what matters is not the reward itself but the message it sends. A reward experienced as an attempt to control behaviour tends to weaken interest, whereas one that conveys recognition of competence may actually strengthen it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Subsequent work has confirmed that rewards are far from equivalent. Meta-analyses, which pool the results of dozens of experiments, indicate that the strongest negative effects arise from rewards that are tangible, announced in advance, and contingent merely on taking part in the task rather than on performing it well. Verbal praise, by contrast, tends to raise intrinsic motivation, while rewards that arrive as a surprise appear to have almost no effect either way, presumably because they cannot have shaped a person's reasons for starting. Such distinctions matter, because the rewards most commonly used in schools and workplaces, from stickers to attendance bonuses, frequently belong to the most damaging category.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evidence from outside the laboratory is scarcer but suggestive. Dumisani Khoza, an economist at the Cape Centre for Applied Economics, studied a coastal town in which volunteers had cleared litter from the beaches every weekend for more than a decade. When the municipality began paying a small fee for each bag collected, participation by long-standing volunteers fell by almost a third, while the number of newcomers attracted by the payment was negligible. Interviews revealed that many veterans felt their efforts had been reclassified as poorly paid labour. Khoza is careful to note that a single case cannot establish a general rule, but he argues that it illustrates how a payment can alter the meaning of an activity for those already committed to it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the effect deserves the attention it receives. Renata Szaboova, a behavioural psychologist, contends that crowding out is modest in size, short-lived and largely confined to tasks that are interesting to begin with. For the dull and repetitive tasks that make up much of working life, she points out, rewards reliably increase effort, and there is little intrinsic motivation to undermine. She also regards the free-choice measure as artificial, since a few minutes alone with some puzzles reveals little about how people behave over months or years. Her point about uninteresting work is well made. To treat the entire phenomenon as a laboratory curiosity, though, is to go too far, given that field studies such as Khoza's point in the same direction.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the size of the reward. A team led by Matteo Castelvecchi found that, in a series of experiments involving charitable fundraising and simple data-entry work, small payments produced worse results than no payment at all, whereas large payments increased performance. His explanation is that a trivial sum signals that the task has little value, without being generous enough to compensate for the loss of satisfaction. If this non-linear pattern is genuine, it goes a long way towards explaining why so many studies of rewards appear to contradict one another: researchers using different amounts of money may simply have been observing different points on the same curve.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings have obvious relevance for schools, many of which reward pupils with points or tokens for the number of books they read. The results of such schemes have been mixed. In some cases pupils read more during the scheme, but there are also reports of children choosing shorter and easier books in order to accumulate rewards more quickly. This suggests that the chief danger of such schemes is not that rewards destroy enjoyment but that they redirect effort towards whatever happens to be counted, which is rarely the thing teachers actually care about.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The practical lesson, then, is not that rewards should be abandoned, but that they should be designed with attention to how they will be interpreted. A bonus that recipients regard as an acknowledgement of good work is likely to have very different consequences from an identical sum that feels like a bribe. What remains uncertain is how durable any of these effects are, since the great majority of studies have followed participants for weeks rather than years, and it is precisely the long-term consequences that matter most to teachers, managers and parents.

topic: performance-related pay for schoolteachers: test-based bonuses, gaming, value-added measures and recruitment effects
title: Bonuses in the Staffroom
subtitle: Linking teachers' pay to their pupils' results sounds like common sense. The evidence tells a more complicated story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, governments in many countries have experimented with linking teachers' pay to the test results of their pupils. The appeal of the idea is easy to understand. In most professions, rewarding good performance is taken for granted, whereas teachers' salaries have traditionally risen according to years of service and formal qualifications. Supporters of reform argue that such a system rewards time-serving rather than talent, and that it gives the most effective teachers little reason to stay in the classroom. Yet the record of performance-related pay in schools is considerably more uneven than its advocates tend to admit, and the reasons for this tell us a good deal about the limits of financial incentives in complex jobs.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the earliest evidence came from a programme analysed by Hiroshi Oshiro, an economist at the Kansai Institute for Education Policy. Schools in one region received bonuses if their average mathematics scores rose. Over the first two years scores did improve, but by a modest amount, and almost all of the gains were concentrated among pupils who had previously been just below the pass mark. Teachers, it appeared, had focused their attention on these borderline pupils, whose progress would make the greatest difference to the school's figures. Oshiro does not regard this as dishonest; in his view it was a rational response to the incentive on offer. This seems a fair judgement, but it means that the improvement partly reflected a redistribution of attention rather than better teaching overall.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A less flattering picture emerges from the work of Aigerim Kerimova, a sociologist who interviewed more than two hundred teachers working under bonus schemes. Many reported that the time devoted to test preparation had increased sharply, while subjects that were not tested, such as music, art and history, had been squeezed out of the timetable. Some described this as a betrayal of their professional values, and several said that their enthusiasm for the job had declined. Kerimova also argues that performance pay damages cooperation within schools, because colleagues who once shared lesson plans become competitors for a limited pool of money. Her evidence on this point is persuasive, but it relates almost entirely to schemes that reward individual teachers. Bonuses paid to an entire school appear to avoid much of the problem.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Designers of later schemes have tried to learn from these difficulties. One important change has been the use of 'value added' measures, which assess pupils' progress from their starting point rather than the raw scores they achieve. Since raw scores largely reflect pupils' family backgrounds, value-added measures are widely regarded as fairer to teachers in disadvantaged areas. The statistician Selam Dagnachew, however, warns that such estimates are unreliable when applied to individual teachers. Because a single class contains relatively few pupils, the same teacher may be ranked near the top one year and near the bottom the next, for reasons that have nothing to do with the quality of their teaching. Dagnachew recommends averaging results over at least three years. This is sensible, but it delays any reward for so long that much of its motivational effect may be lost.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some economists believe that the most important effect of performance pay lies not in changing the effort of existing teachers but in altering who chooses to enter the profession in the first place. Jean-Paul Tuyishime, a labour economist, surveyed several thousand university students about their career plans and found that high-achieving graduates were noticeably more likely to express interest in teaching when salaries were described as linked to performance. Whether these students would actually have become teachers, and remained in the job, is unknown. The possibility is an intriguing one, but it is far too early to build national policy around it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The underlying difficulty is that teaching involves a wide range of goals, only a few of which can be captured by tests. Teachers are expected to develop pupils' curiosity, social skills and character as well as their knowledge, and when only some of these outcomes are rewarded, effort naturally drifts towards them. This does not mean that incentives can never work. In areas where tests measure the relevant skills reasonably well, such as early reading, the results of bonus schemes have been rather more encouraging. Even there, however, much depends on how the tests are constructed. A reading assessment that rewards the rapid decoding of unfamiliar words, for instance, may encourage drills of exactly that skill at the expense of the wider reading for pleasure that most specialists regard as the foundation of later success. The lesson is not that measurement should be abandoned, but that whatever is measured will tend to become the curriculum.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate is often presented as a choice between rewarding results and trusting professionals to do their best. This is a false choice. The most promising schemes appear to be those that combine modest bonuses awarded at school level with peer observation and professional development, so that money supports improvement rather than substituting for it. Pay alone is unlikely to transform the quality of teaching, but it would be equally mistaken to conclude that it is irrelevant.

topic: contrafreeloading: why animals choose to work for food when identical food is freely available, and its use in animal welfare
title: Working for Lunch
subtitle: Why do so many animals labour for food that they could have for nothing?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: According to a long tradition in the study of behaviour, animals should behave like careful accountants, obtaining the food they need for the least possible expenditure of energy. An experiment conducted in the early 1960s appeared to contradict this principle. Rats that had been trained to press a lever for pellets continued to press it even when a dish of identical pellets was placed freely available beside them. Researchers coined the rather awkward term 'contrafreeloading' to describe this preference for earned over free food, and in the decades since, it has been documented in pigeons, chickens, gerbils, fish, several species of primate, parrots and even giraffes in zoos. The sheer variety of species involved is striking, and it means that the phenomenon can no longer be dismissed as an oddity of laboratory rodents.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation treats contrafreeloading as a form of information gathering. Elena Ortolani, a behavioural ecologist at the Adriatic Institute of Behavioural Ecology, points out that in the wild, food sources rarely remain reliable for long. An animal that occasionally samples alternatives to its usual supply learns where else food may be found, knowledge that becomes invaluable when the familiar source is exhausted. Several observations fit this account. Animals contrafreeload more in environments that change unpredictably, and considerably less when they are very hungry, presumably because the immediate need for calories then outweighs the longer-term value of information. Severely food-deprived animals, in fact, generally take the free food.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second explanation holds that the work itself is rewarding. Aleksi Kallio, an animal welfare scientist, argues that many species have a strong drive to perform the behaviours through which they would naturally obtain food, such as scratching, rooting or probing, and that captivity frequently denies them the opportunity to do so. Food that must be extracted or searched for satisfies this need in a way that food in a bowl does not. He notes that chickens will scratch through litter for scattered grain even when the same grain is available in a feeder, and that pacing and other repetitive behaviours in captive animals tend to decline when foraging opportunities are introduced. The two explanations are often presented as rivals, but there is no reason why both should not be true at once: a drive to forage could itself have evolved because foraging yields information.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every species conforms to the pattern. In one study of domestic cats, almost all of the animals ignored a puzzle feeder and ate from a freely available tray. Grace Ruhumuliza, a veterinary behaviourist, offers two possible explanations. The feeders used may simply have been poorly suited to cats, having been adapted from devices designed for dogs. Alternatively, the result may reflect the fact that cats are ambush hunters, which obtain food in short bursts of activity rather than through prolonged searching. Whichever explanation proves correct, the cat study is a useful reminder of how risky it is to generalise from one species to another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The strength of contrafreeloading also depends on circumstances. It declines as the amount of work required increases, and animals that have received extensive training on a task tend to show it more strongly than those with little training. This last observation has prompted criticism. Nikos Mavrogordato, a comparative psychologist, argues that many laboratory findings are artefacts of training history: animals that have repeatedly been rewarded for pressing a lever may simply continue doing so out of habit, rather than because they prefer to work. When he tested animals that had not been trained beforehand, the effect was weaker, although it did not disappear. His critique has usefully forced researchers to design more careful experiments, but it falls well short of explaining the phenomenon away.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever its causes, contrafreeloading has had practical consequences. Many zoos and some farms now practise 'feeding enrichment', scattering food, hiding it, or presenting it in devices that must be manipulated before the food can be reached. Several studies report a reduction in repetitive behaviours following such changes, and keepers frequently describe animals as more active and alert. Yet enrichment is not automatically beneficial. Devices that are too demanding can produce frustration rather than engagement, and where animals are housed in groups, dominant individuals may monopolise the feeders while subordinate ones go without. Enrichment, in other words, needs to be adapted to the species and to the individuals concerned rather than applied as a standard package.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to draw lessons from all this about human motivation. People, too, often appear to value rewards they have earned more highly than those handed to them, and some commentators have presented contrafreeloading as evidence that the desire for meaningful work is deeply rooted in biology. Such parallels should be treated with caution. The animal evidence concerns foraging specifically, a behaviour shaped by millions of years of selection in particular environments, and the leap from a rat pressing a lever to an employee seeking a fulfilling career is a long one. What the research does demonstrate convincingly is that, for a great many animals, simply being fed is not the same as being satisfied.

topic: gamification of apps: streaks, badges and leaderboards in language-learning, fitness and workplace software
title: Keeping the Flame Alive
subtitle: Points, badges and daily streaks have spread from video games into almost every kind of app. Do they build lasting motivation, or merely a habit of checking?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Open almost any language-learning programme, fitness tracker or even banking application today and you are likely to encounter devices borrowed from video games: points for completing tasks, badges for reaching milestones, leaderboards ranking users against one another, and counters recording how many consecutive days a person has used the service. The companies that build these features report dramatic rises in what they call engagement, and 'gamification' has become a standard element of software design. Whether such techniques foster genuine, lasting motivation or simply encourage compulsive checking is far less clear, and it is a question that has received much less scrutiny than its commercial importance would warrant.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Of all these devices, the streak counter appears to be the most powerful. Its effect seems to depend on what psychologists call loss aversion: people are typically more troubled by losing something they already possess than they are pleased by gaining something of equal value, and a streak of a hundred days quickly comes to feel like a possession. Carla Santesso, a consumer psychologist at the Ligurian Business School, analysed the usage records of some two million learners on a popular language application. Those with streaks longer than thirty days were far more likely than others to open the app every day. Much of this activity, however, was minimal: a large proportion of long-streak users completed only the shortest lesson available, apparently for no other reason than to keep their record intact. Santesso describes this as 'maintenance behaviour'. Her findings suggest that daily-use statistics, which companies routinely cite as evidence of success, give an inflated impression of how much learning is actually taking place.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Santesso's data also revealed what happens when a long streak comes to an end. A substantial minority of users whose streaks were broken after several months stopped using the application altogether within a fortnight, as though, with the record gone, there was no longer any point in continuing. Some companies have responded by selling 'streak freezes', which allow users to miss a day without losing their count. Others send increasingly insistent reminders as midnight approaches, warning users that their progress is about to be lost. Such messages are undoubtedly effective in the narrow sense that they bring people back to the app, but interviews with users suggest that many experience them less as encouragement than as a nagging obligation. One participant compared her streak to a pet that had to be fed every evening, regardless of whether she had any desire to study. From a commercial perspective the logic is impeccable, but there is something troubling about a business model that profits directly from the anxiety its own design has created.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Points and badges raise different issues. Kenji Matsukawa, a former games designer who now researches digital motivation, argues that points are effective when they give people informative feedback about their progress towards a goal they genuinely hold, and ineffective when they seem arbitrary. Leaderboards, in his view, are a particularly blunt instrument: they tend to energise those near the top while discouraging those near the bottom, who may conclude that they have no realistic chance of improving their position. He cites a pilot scheme at a customer-service call centre, where a leaderboard displaying each employee's daily output raised average productivity during its first month. Within six months, however, productivity had fallen back to the level recorded before the scheme began, and staff turnover among the lowest-ranked employees had risen noticeably.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of gamification point to more encouraging results. Wanjiru Nyambura, a public health researcher, conducted a twelve-week trial of a step-counting application among office workers who had previously taken little exercise. Participants who used a version that organised them into teams competing in weekly challenges walked, on average, around 1,500 more steps a day than a control group using a basic version without game features. More strikingly, about half of this difference persisted three months after the trial ended and the game features were switched off. Nyambura attributes the effect less to the points themselves than to the social commitments the teams created: participants reported not wanting to let their teammates down. Her results are genuinely encouraging and point to the social dimension as the crucial ingredient. It should be borne in mind, though, that participants volunteered for the trial, and people willing to sign up for an exercise study may well be more motivated than the population at large.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Gamification, then, is neither the transformative tool its promoters describe nor the cynical manipulation its critics allege. Its value depends on whether the game elements serve the user's own goals or merely the company's preferred measures of success. A language application that keeps people opening it every day without improving their fluency has succeeded only on its own terms. If designers were judged by the outcomes users actually care about, such as the ability to hold a conversation or a measurable improvement in fitness, rather than by the number of daily visits, the features that survived would probably look rather different from those that dominate today.

topic: paying schoolchildren for achievement: cash incentive experiments for test scores, reading and attendance
title: Cash for Grades
subtitle: Should pupils be paid to learn? The experiments that tried it produced results neither side of the argument expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past two decades, education authorities in a number of cities have tried something that many teachers regard as unthinkable: paying pupils for their achievements. Depending on the scheme, money has been offered for higher test scores, better report cards, regular attendance or the number of books read. The reaction has been predictably polarised. Opponents warn that such payments turn learning into a transaction and teach children to expect a fee for every effort. Supporters reply that the rewards of education, such as higher lifetime earnings, are so distant that they mean little to a fourteen-year-old, particularly one from a poor household, and that a more immediate incentive simply corrects this imbalance. What is striking is how often both camps have argued from principle while paying little attention to what the experiments actually found, which turns out to be more interesting than either side predicted.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious research programme was analysed by Ahmet Bakirci, an education economist at the Anatolian Centre for Policy Research. Across several cities, pupils were offered payment either for outputs, such as their scores in standardised tests, or for inputs, such as reading books, attending classes or completing homework. The output-based schemes produced almost no measurable improvement. The input-based schemes, by contrast, led to modest but genuine gains in achievement. Bakirci's explanation is that most pupils offered money for test scores were keen to earn it but had no clear idea how to raise their scores; a pupil can be told to read a book, but cannot easily be told how to become better at mathematics. This is arguably the most important finding in the entire field, because it moves the debate away from whether pupils are motivated and towards whether they know what to do with their motivation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The fear that payments destroy a love of learning has been examined by Chidinma Uchendu, a developmental psychologist. She followed pupils for two years after the end of one reading incentive programme and compared their attitudes with those of a control group. Pupils who had been paid reported no less enjoyment of reading than those who had not, although they reported no more either. Uchendu herself urges caution in interpreting this result. Questionnaires about enjoyment are an imperfect guide to how people really feel, she notes, and the pupils in her study were older teenagers, whose attitudes towards reading may already have been relatively settled.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How rewards are delivered seems to matter as much as whether they are offered at all. Lev Vashchenko, a behavioural economist, found that payments made at the end of a school year had very little effect, whereas those made immediately after a test produced noticeably better results. In one of his experiments, pupils who were handed money before a test and told that they would have to return it if their score did not improve outperformed pupils who were promised the same sum afterwards. He also found that, among younger children, inexpensive trophies were just as effective as cash. The finding about returning money is certainly striking, but it is difficult to see how a policy of taking money back from children could be justified, however effective it might be.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Another important question is which pupils benefit. The sociologist Hemi Tamatea has shown that incentive schemes help mainly those pupils who are already close to the required standard. Those who are furthest behind gain little, presumably because the target seems unattainable, and in some households the money is absorbed into the family budget, which weakens the connection between effort and reward. Tamatea argues that incentives should be combined with tutoring, so that pupils receive both a reason to work harder and the means of doing so. This is entirely consistent with Bakirci's findings, and it is hard to disagree with.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even successful schemes must be judged against the alternatives. Ingrid Ahlgren, a specialist in public finance, has compared the cost of raising achievement by a given amount through different policies. Input-based incentives, she found, compare reasonably well with reductions in class size, which are notoriously expensive. They are, however, far less cost-effective than intensive small-group tutoring. In other words, the real choice facing education authorities is not between paying pupils and doing nothing, but between paying pupils and spending the same money in other ways. Ahlgren adds that her calculations probably flatter incentive schemes, since they exclude the considerable administrative effort of verifying attendance, checking that books have really been read and distributing payments to thousands of pupils. Several programmes, she points out, were quietly abandoned not because they failed to work but because the schools running them found the paperwork unmanageable. Political considerations play a part as well: a scheme that visibly hands cash to teenagers attracts hostile newspaper coverage in a way that an equally expensive tutoring programme rarely does.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Payment for learning, then, is neither the moral catastrophe that its critics feared nor the inexpensive solution that its advocates hoped for. Its lasting contribution may lie elsewhere. By isolating motivation from other factors, the experiments have demonstrated something that teachers have long suspected but could rarely prove: that a desire to succeed, without the knowledge of how to succeed, achieves very little.

topic: curiosity as an intrinsic reward: paying for useless information, the information-gap theory, curiosity and memory, and its exploitation
title: The Itch to Know
subtitle: Why do people pay, wait and even suffer for information that is of no use to them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Traditional economic theory treats information as a tool. Knowledge is worth acquiring, the reasoning goes, only to the extent that it helps a person make a better decision, so that the value of learning the weather forecast depends entirely on whether one is planning to go outdoors. Everyday experience suggests otherwise. People stay up late to finish a detective novel, search their phones to settle a trivial argument, follow gossip about strangers and check the results of matches on which nothing depends. None of this information changes what they will do next. It is more illuminating, I would suggest, to regard curiosity not as a means to some further end but as a reward in its own right, sought for much the same reasons as food or warmth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Laboratory studies have tested this idea by offering people information that is, by design, of no practical use. In a typical experiment, participants take part in a lottery whose outcome is already fixed, and are offered the chance to pay a small sum to learn the result immediately rather than at the end of the session. Since nothing they can do will alter the outcome, a strictly rational participant should refuse. Many, however, pay. Marta Ibarrola, a cognitive scientist at the Basque Institute for Cognitive Science, found that participants were willing to pay most when uncertainty was greatest, as with an even chance of winning or losing, and least when the outcome was nearly certain. Brain imaging has added a further dimension: the anticipation of such information activates some of the same regions as the anticipation of food or money. This overlap has been widely reported as proof that curiosity is a form of hunger, but the fact that the same areas are active in two situations does not mean that the two are experienced in the same way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What triggers curiosity in the first place? The most influential answer is the so-called information-gap theory, according to which curiosity arises when people become aware of a gap between what they know and what they would like to know. People who know almost nothing about a subject are rarely curious about it, because they cannot perceive any gap at all, while those who already know nearly everything have little left to discover. Curiosity should therefore peak somewhere in between. Nadia Sokolnikova, an education researcher, tested this prediction by asking volunteers to rate their confidence in answering trivia questions, and found that curiosity was greatest at intermediate levels of confidence. She concludes that teachers should open lessons with questions that pupils can partly but not fully answer, rather than with material that is either entirely familiar or entirely new.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Curiosity also appears to affect memory. In a series of experiments, volunteers were shown trivia questions, rated how curious they were about each, and then waited several seconds before seeing the answer. A day later, they recalled the answers to high-curiosity questions considerably better than the others. More surprisingly, they also remembered better the photographs of unfamiliar faces that had been shown to them during the waiting period, even though these were entirely unrelated to the questions. Desmond Fenwright, a neuroscientist, interprets this as evidence that curiosity places the brain in a general state of readiness to learn, which benefits whatever happens to be encountered at the time. The finding about faces is the most intriguing in this area of research, but attempts to repeat it have produced only partial success, and it would be premature to build educational practice on it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Curiosity has a less attractive side. People frequently choose to look at disturbing images or to read detailed accounts of crimes, and in one study a number of participants accepted mild electric shocks in exchange for learning the answers to questions that had been left unresolved. The commercial world has not been slow to exploit this appetite. So-called 'clickbait' headlines deliberately withhold a key fact in order to persuade readers to visit a page filled with advertising. Such techniques are more corrosive than they might appear: if curiosity is repeatedly aroused only to be disappointed, there is a real danger that people will learn to suppress it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is often said that curiosity declines with age. Ibarrola disputes this, arguing that what changes is not the amount of curiosity but its direction. Older adults in her surveys expressed less interest than younger ones in novel trivia, but more interest in subjects related to their existing knowledge and concerns. Her reframing is plausible, yet it rests on comparisons between different people of different ages rather than on studies that follow the same individuals over time, and such data cannot separate the effects of ageing from differences between generations.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If curiosity is genuinely rewarding, schools and workplaces may be able to harness it rather than relying so heavily on grades, bonuses and other external incentives. It would be a mistake, however, to assume that curiosity can simply be switched on. Confronting people with a gap that is too large tends to produce anxiety rather than interest, and an environment in which questions are discouraged will soon extinguish the impulse altogether. Curiosity, in short, is a powerful motive, but also a fragile one.

topic: commitment contracts: self-imposed financial and social penalties for failing personal goals (saving, smoking, exercise) and who benefits from them
title: Tied to the Mast
subtitle: Contracts that punish people for breaking promises to themselves are becoming big business. Whether they help is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the classical story, a sailor who wished to hear the song of the sirens without steering his ship onto the rocks had himself bound to the mast and ordered his crew to ignore every plea he made. Behavioural economists have adopted this image to describe what they call commitment devices: arrangements that people enter into voluntarily in order to restrict their own future choices. The logic rests on a well-documented tendency known as present bias. Asked today whether they would prefer to exercise or to relax next Thursday, most people choose exercise; asked on Thursday itself, a good many choose the sofa. A person who recognises this pattern may reasonably decide to remove the tempting option before the moment of choice arrives. What is new is that such devices have recently been turned into a commercial product.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Several online services now allow users to set a goal, such as losing weight or finishing a thesis chapter, and to stake a sum of money on achieving it. If they fail, the money is forfeited, sometimes to a charity and sometimes to an 'anti-charity', an organisation whose aims the user finds objectionable. Many services also invite users to nominate a referee who confirms whether the goal has been met. Their founders report impressive rates of success. Such figures should be treated with caution. People who sign up are, almost by definition, unusually determined, and the companies' statistics rarely separate the effect of the contract from the resolve that led people to choose one in the first place.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More rigorous evidence comes from field experiments. Ottilie Grimelund, a behavioural economist at the Sognevik Centre for Household Finance, worked with a cooperative bank to offer a randomly selected group of customers a savings account from which no withdrawals could be made until a date or a balance of the customer's own choosing had been reached. Roughly a quarter of those offered the account opened one, and a year later the average savings of the group that had received the offer were noticeably higher than those of a comparison group that had not. Grimelund interprets this as evidence that many people are aware of their own weaknesses and are willing to sacrifice flexibility to guard against them. This is a reasonable reading, although it is worth noting that most customers declined the account, so the effect averaged across everyone who was offered it was far smaller than the gains made by those who accepted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A similar pattern appears in research on smoking. Kwabena Asante-Darko, a public health researcher, invited smokers to deposit their own money in an account over six months; the full amount, plus a small bonus, would be returned only if urine tests confirmed that they had stopped. Those who took part quit at more than twice the rate of smokers offered conventional support. Yet only around one smoker in nine accepted the invitation. Asante-Darko concludes that the main obstacle facing commitment contracts is not that they fail but that so few people want them, and he has proposed that smokers should be enrolled automatically, with the right to withdraw. Here, I think, he goes too far. A contract that a person has not chosen is no longer a commitment device in any meaningful sense; it becomes a penalty imposed by someone else, and there is little reason to expect it to draw on the same psychological resources.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more troubling objection has been raised by Marisol Zubeldia-Ruiz, who studies consumer finance. Economic theory distinguishes 'sophisticated' individuals, who correctly anticipate their own lapses, from 'naive' ones, who overestimate their future self-control. Commitment devices, she argues, are useful to the first group but potentially harmful to the second, who may set ambitious targets, fail to meet them and lose their stakes. Her analysis of anonymised records from one commitment website found that a substantial minority of users forfeited money repeatedly, and that these losses were concentrated among people on lower incomes. For such users, she suggests, the device works less as a mast than as a tax on optimism. Her concern deserves to be taken seriously by anyone who promotes these products, even if it does not apply to the majority of their customers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all commitments need involve money. Teodora Vulpescu, a social psychologist, compared exercise programmes in which participants either staked cash or simply agreed that a named friend would be told each week whether they had kept to their plan. Over the first two months the reputational stake proved about as effective as the financial one, and nobody lost any money. Vulpescu notes, however, that the effect weakened markedly once the friend began to lose interest and stopped responding to the weekly reports. Social pressure, in other words, depends on an audience that is itself motivated to keep watching.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should we conclude? Commitment devices are neither a cure for weakness of will nor a mere gimmick. They seem to work best when the goal can be verified without ambiguity: a cigarette is either smoked or not, a balance either reached or not. For vaguer aims, such as becoming a more patient parent, there is nothing a referee can check, and the contract adds anxiety without adding clarity. I would also argue that the services should encourage modest stakes rather than large ones, since the users most attracted to dramatic penalties may be precisely those least able to bear them. Above all, the value of these devices should be judged not by the success of the determined few who sign up, but by what they achieve for the population as a whole.

topic: the goal-gradient effect: accelerating effort near a goal, loyalty cards, progress indicators, the small-area hypothesis and post-reward slowdowns
title: The Final Stretch
subtitle: Effort tends to quicken as a goal comes into view. Businesses have learned to exploit this, but the effect is less generous than it looks

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1930s an animal psychologist named Lucjan Sobieraj noticed something curious about the rats in his laboratory. Animals running along a straight alley towards a food box did not move at a steady pace: they ran faster the closer they came to the reward. Sobieraj called this pattern the goal gradient and suggested that the pull of a reward grows stronger as it draws near. For several decades the observation remained a minor footnote in the study of animal learning, cited in textbooks but rarely tested in human beings. It is only in recent years that researchers interested in human motivation, and the businesses that fund some of them, have rediscovered it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-known modern demonstration comes from Nayeli Atzimba, a consumer psychologist who worked with a chain of cafés. Customers were given one of two loyalty cards. The first had ten empty spaces, one to be stamped with each coffee bought, after which a free drink was given. The second had twelve spaces, but two had already been stamped on the day it was issued. In both cases, then, ten purchases were needed. Yet customers with the second card completed it noticeably sooner, and in both groups the intervals between visits grew shorter as the card filled up. What mattered, it seems, was not the amount of progress actually made but the impression of having made a start. The finding suggests that people respond to how far they feel they have come, which is not always the same thing as how far they have travelled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Similar patterns have since been observed online. Users of a music website who earned a reward for rating a fixed number of songs rated them more quickly as they approached the target, and people completing questionnaires often speed up when a progress bar shows that they are nearly finished. The effect even appears in competitive sport, where distance runners commonly record their fastest kilometre at the end of a race despite mounting fatigue. Progress indicators are not, however, always helpful. When the early questions in a survey are long and the bar moves only slowly, respondents are more likely to give up altogether. A progress indicator, in short, is only as motivating as the news it delivers, and designers who add one to every task may be doing more harm than good.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should effort increase near the end? One influential answer is the 'small-area hypothesis' proposed by Daewon Seok, a decision researcher. Seok argues that people are most motivated when their attention is directed to whichever quantity is smaller: the work already done or the work still to do. At the beginning of a task, emphasising what has been achieved ('you have finished two of ten stages') makes progress seem substantial; towards the end, emphasising what remains ('only two stages to go') has the same effect. Charities have used the idea when reporting the progress of fundraising campaigns. The hypothesis is an elegant one, but most of the supporting evidence comes from short laboratory tasks, and in everyday life people may pay far less attention to such framing than experiments assume.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more sceptical note is sounded by Obiageli Anyaduba, an economist who examined several years of purchase records from a supermarket loyalty scheme. She confirms that shoppers buy more frequently as they approach a reward. But she also documents what she calls a 'post-reward reset': once the reward has been claimed, customers wait considerably longer than usual before their next purchase, and a minority never return to the scheme at all. Over a full year, she argues, the burst of buying before each reward and the lull after it largely cancel each other out. This is an important corrective, though it does not show that such schemes are worthless; a business may value the timing of purchases, for example during a quiet season, as much as their total number.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Outside commerce, the goal gradient has influenced the design of education and health programmes. Long courses are increasingly divided into short units, each with its own certificate, so that learners always have a nearby target to aim at. Physiotherapists sometimes structure exercise programmes in the same way, setting weekly milestones rather than a single distant target of full recovery. There is a risk here, too. When a goal is broken into too many small pieces, people may begin to treat each piece as an end in itself and lose sight of the larger purpose, finishing units without acquiring the skill they were meant to build. The art lies in placing goals close enough to pull people forward but not so close that reaching them becomes the whole point.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Nearly a century after Sobieraj watched his rats, the goal gradient has proved to be one of the more robust findings in the psychology of motivation. Its limits, however, deserve as much attention as its strength. The effect describes the shape of effort over time rather than its quantity: it tells us when people try hardest, not whether they try harder overall. Those who use it to boost sales or completion rates should remember that a sprint at the finish is often paid for by a slower walk afterwards.

topic: innovation inducement prizes: paying for solutions rather than funding research, who wins, wasted effort, entrants' motives and milestone prizes
title: The Price of a Breakthrough
subtitle: Offering a reward for solving a problem, rather than paying someone to work on it, is an old idea enjoying a revival. Its record is more mixed than its champions admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: There are, broadly speaking, two ways of persuading people to tackle a difficult technical problem. The first, and today by far the more common, is to pay them in advance: a government or foundation awards a grant to a researcher whose proposal looks promising and hopes that something useful results. The second is to announce a reward that will be paid only to whoever actually solves the problem. Economists call these 'push' and 'pull' incentives. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, pull incentives were widespread, with states and learned societies offering prizes for everything from a reliable way of preserving food for armies to a dye that would not fade in sunlight. During the twentieth century such prizes fell out of favour as research became institutionalised, but over the past three decades foundations, companies and government agencies have rediscovered them with considerable enthusiasm.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Enthusiasts often point to the history of prizes as proof of their power. The historian Ingrid Wahlgrenn, who has examined the archives of several prize-giving bodies, urges caution. Many historical prizes, she found, were never awarded at all, and those that were often became the subject of bitter disputes between judges and claimants. More strikingly, the winners were usually individuals who had been working on the problem long before the prize was announced, which suggests that the reward did more to publicise existing efforts than to call new ones into being. This is a valuable reminder that the popular image of the unknown outsider who claims a fortune owes more to legend than to the archives. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that the money made no difference: a reward that publicises a problem may still attract resources and attention that it would otherwise have lacked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Modern evidence paints a somewhat different picture. Piotr Kaluzny, a management scholar, analysed several hundred problems posted by companies on an online platform where anyone could submit a solution in return for a cash award. Contrary to what might be expected, successful solvers were disproportionately drawn from fields far removed from the one in which the problem arose: a chemical puzzle might be solved by a physicist, a biological one by an engineer. Kaluzny argues that such people succeed because they bring techniques that are routine in their own discipline but unfamiliar to the specialists who were stuck. If he is right, the chief advantage of an open prize is not that it increases effort but that it widens the range of minds applied to a question.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Economists have been less enthusiastic. Bat-Erdene Tsogtbaatar points out that a prize can induce competitors to spend, in total, far more than the reward itself, since many teams invest heavily and only one is paid. From the point of view of society, he argues, much of this effort is duplicated and therefore wasted. He has also shown that adding more entrants to a contest tends to reduce the effort each one makes, because the chance of winning falls; the exception is a problem whose solution is highly uncertain, where a larger field raises the likelihood that someone will find an unusual answer. Tsogtbaatar's notion of waste is, I believe, too narrow. Losing entrants frequently acquire skills, contacts and partial results that they go on to use elsewhere, and none of this appears in a calculation that counts only the winning entry.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why do people enter such contests at all, given that most will receive nothing? The psychologist Hana Ondruskova surveyed entrants to a range of open competitions and found that relatively few named the money as their main motive. More often they mentioned the intellectual challenge, the chance of recognition from peers or the opportunity to demonstrate their abilities to potential employers. In her view, the size of a prize matters chiefly as a signal of how important the sponsor considers the problem to be. This account is plausible for software competitions, whose entrants typically hold salaried jobs and compete in their spare time. It is much less convincing for small firms, which must justify every investment to owners or lenders and cannot afford to treat a contest as a hobby.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That point is central to the concerns of Lindiwe Mbatha-Rowe, a development economist who has studied prizes intended to encourage new technologies for poorer countries, such as cheap diagnostic tests and drought-tolerant seed varieties. Because a prize pays only at the end, she notes, it favours organisations that can finance years of work from their own resources, which in practice means large companies and wealthy universities. Teams from the very regions the prizes are meant to benefit are rarely able to compete. Mbatha-Rowe recommends 'milestone' prizes, in which smaller sums are paid for intermediate achievements. The proposal is sensible, but it carries a cost. The more often a sponsor pays for progress rather than results, the more a prize comes to resemble a grant, and the more it loses the distinctive feature that made it attractive in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that prizes are a fashion that will soon pass. They appear to work best when the goal can be specified precisely in advance but the route to it is unknown, so that the sponsor knows exactly what it wants without knowing who is best placed to provide it. They are poorly suited to basic research, where the most valuable outcome may be a question no one had thought to ask. Prizes, in other words, should be seen as a complement to grants rather than a replacement for them, and a sponsor that treats them as a cheap way of buying innovation is likely to be disappointed.

topic: piece-rate pay: paying workers per unit of output, sorting versus effort effects, quality and inspection costs, restriction of output and rate cuts, safety risks, and algorithmic platform rates
title: Paid by the Piece
subtitle: Piece rates promise to reward effort directly, but their long history suggests that the relationship is rarely so simple

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Paying people according to how much they produce, rather than how long they work, is one of the oldest ways of linking effort to reward. In the eighteenth century, hand-loom weavers were paid by the length of cloth they delivered; in the nineteenth, women sewing shirts at home were paid by the dozen; and today, couriers working through smartphone applications are paid per parcel. A worker who produces more earns more, so the incentive to work hard is built into the wage itself, and an employer who pays only for results has less need to watch over the workforce. Yet the simplicity of the system is deceptive, and the history of piecework is, to a remarkable degree, a history of consequences that nobody intended.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely cited evidence in its favour concerns raw output. Teodora Cotoveanu, a labour economist at the Danube School of Economics, examined the records of a forestry contractor that replaced daily wages with a payment for every sapling planted. Within a season, output per worker rose by almost forty per cent. Cotoveanu, however, also tried to explain where this increase came from. Only about half of it, she calculated, reflected existing employees working harder. The remainder arose because the slowest planters gradually left for jobs elsewhere, while the new pay system attracted applicants who knew themselves to be fast. In Cotoveanu's view, a firm that introduces piece rates is not merely motivating its staff differently; it is in effect choosing a different staff. This distinction is more important than it might appear. A gain that depends on attracting the quickest workers can benefit one company, but it cannot be repeated across an entire economy, since the fast planters recruited by one contractor have been lost by another.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second difficulty concerns quality. When earnings depend on quantity alone, workers have every reason to cut corners, and the forestry contractor soon found many saplings planted too shallowly to survive. Ekow Darkwa-Ofori, of the Accra Institute of Organisational Studies, observed the same pattern in garment workshops, where the switch to piece rates was followed by a rise in faulty seams. The workshops responded by employing inspectors, and Darkwa-Ofori found that the cost of inspection frequently consumed the greater part of what had been saved by reducing supervision. He concludes that piece rates make sense only for tasks whose quality can be verified cheaply and quickly. The argument is sound as far as it goes, but it is perhaps too sweeping. Digital tracking, barcode scanning and automated testing have made the checking of output far less expensive in many industries than it was a generation ago, and the range of tasks for which piece rates are workable has widened accordingly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Particularly instructive is the practice that sociologists called 'restriction of output'. Observers in machine shops in the middle of the twentieth century repeatedly found that workers produced well below what they were capable of, and that the group enforced an unofficial ceiling on each person's daily output. Anyone who exceeded it might be mocked or ignored. Managers tended to interpret such behaviour as idleness. Lorenzo Quaglierini, a historian at the Emilian Institute of Social History, offers a different reading. Employers of the period, he notes, routinely cut the rate paid per item whenever workers began to earn what was considered too much, so that extra effort was rewarded with a lower price for every subsequent piece. Seen in this light, the informal ceiling was not laziness but a reasonable defence against the conduct of management. Quaglierini is surely right, and the lesson extends well beyond the machine shop: an incentive is only as strong as the promise that stands behind it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Piece rates also raise questions of health and safety. Fruit pickers paid by the crate are known to skip rest breaks in hot weather. Ingrid Aaslestad, an occupational health researcher at the Bergen Centre for Work and Health, compared two groups of urban couriers and found that those paid for each delivery were injured at work considerably more often than those paid an hourly wage. Such findings have led some campaigners to call for piece rates to be banned outright in hazardous occupations. That response, in my view, is a blunt instrument. A guaranteed hourly minimum combined with a modest payment per unit would remove the pressure to work at a dangerous pace while preserving much of the incentive that makes piece rates attractive in the first place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The arrival of digital platforms has given these old debates a new form. On many applications the rate per task is set by an algorithm and may change weekly without explanation. Quaglierini argues that this has revived precisely the suspicion that once prevailed on the factory floor: workers who cannot see how their pay is calculated tend to assume that any rise in their earnings will soon be taken away. Unlike machine-shop workers, however, platform workers rarely meet one another, which makes it almost impossible for them to agree on a shared limit to output or to resist cuts collectively.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that piece rates are either the ideal incentive that some economists have imagined or the instrument of exploitation that their fiercest critics describe. Their effects depend heavily on what exactly is being measured, on who sets the rate and how openly, and on whether workers believe that the rate will be honoured. Where those conditions are met, paying by the piece can reward effort fairly; where they are not, it tends to produce exactly the behaviour it was designed to prevent.

topic: statistical learning and how infants segment words from continuous speech
title: Finding the Gaps in Speech
subtitle: How do infants work out where one word ends and the next begins, when spoken language offers almost no pauses?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has listened to a conversation in an unfamiliar language will recognise the sensation: speech seems to arrive as an unbroken torrent, with no obvious indication of where one word stops and another starts. Acoustic analyses of natural speech show that silences are as likely to occur inside words, as between them. Yet by their first birthday most infants recognise dozens of words, and they must somehow have extracted those words from the continuous stream. For much of the twentieth century it was assumed that parents solved the problem for them by presenting new words in isolation. Recordings of family life have undermined that assumption: words spoken on their own make up only around one utterance in ten of the speech addressed to infants. The segmentation problem, as it is known, is arguably one of the most underappreciated achievements of infancy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential answer to emerge in recent decades is that infants are sensitive to statistics. In a now classic type of experiment, eight-month-olds listen for just two minutes to an artificial language consisting of four three-syllable nonsense words, strung together by a speech synthesiser without pauses or variations in stress. Within each word, one syllable always predicts the next; across the boundaries between words, the next syllable could be any of several. Afterwards the infants are played either the words themselves or 'part-words', sequences that straddle a boundary, and they listen reliably longer to the part-words, a novelty preference which indicates that they have distinguished the two. Professor Liis Tamsalu of the Baltic Institute of Cognitive Development, who has replicated the finding in three languages, argues that babies are tracking the likelihood that one sound will follow another, and that this computation is powerful enough to account for much of early segmentation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics have been quick to point out how far the laboratory languages are from the real thing. Every word is the same length, and each is repeated dozens of times in a flat, mechanical voice. Dr Chidi Ikeogu, a computational linguist at the Lagos Centre for Speech Sciences, tested the idea by running a statistical segmentation algorithm over transcripts of speech recorded in ordinary homes. The program correctly located the boundaries of fewer than half the words; it frequently broke longer words into fragments and fused common pairs such as 'do you' or 'look at' into a single unit. Ikeogu concludes that statistics alone would leave infants with a mental lexicon cluttered with errors. This is a valuable corrective, but it does not follow that statistical learning is unimportant. What his results show is that it cannot be the whole story.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second source of information is the rhythm of speech. In English, the great majority of content words carry stress on their first syllable, as in 'table' or 'baby'. Haruka Kurokawa, a developmental psychologist at Sendai University of Education, has shown that nine-month-olds learning English treat a stressed syllable as the beginning of a word. They at first mis-segment words with stress on their second syllable, so that the 'tar' of 'guitar' is attached to whatever follows it. Infants learning Japanese, a language without strong stress, appear instead to rely on patterns of pitch, which suggests that the rhythmic cues infants exploit are tuned to their native language. Most intriguingly, when stress and statistics were set in conflict, seven-month-olds sided with statistics, while nine-month-olds favoured stress. Her interpretation is that infants first use statistics to discover which stress pattern their language prefers and then adopt that pattern as a shortcut. It is an elegant account that turns two rival explanations into partners.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third cue lies in words the child already knows. Morten Brodsgaard, who directs the infant laboratory at the Nordic Centre for Child Studies, has found that babies as young as six months use highly familiar words, such as their own name or the word for their mother, to locate the boundary of the word that follows. A novel word heard immediately after an infant's name is later recognised more readily than the same word heard after an unfamiliar name. Brodsgaard argues that segmentation therefore snowballs: every word that is reliably identified becomes an anchor that makes the next word easier to isolate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A broader controversy concerns whether the capacity Tamsalu describes is specific to language at all. Similar learning has been demonstrated with sequences of musical tones and visual shapes, and even in tamarins and rats. Tamsalu regards this as a strength of her account, since it means that language can draw on a mechanism already shared with other forms of perception. Others take the opposite view, arguing that if a rat can perform the computation, it cannot explain what is distinctive about human language. That objection, in my view, misreads the claim. Nobody supposes that tracking syllable sequences explains grammar or meaning; the claim is merely that it helps solve one early problem, and the generality of the mechanism is a reason to take it seriously rather than to dismiss it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some researchers report that children later diagnosed with developmental language disorder perform less well on statistical learning tasks, and commercial programmes promising to sharpen these abilities have begun to appear. Here caution is essential. The findings are inconsistent, and it remains unclear whether weak statistical learning is a cause of language difficulties or a consequence of them. Until these questions are resolved, it would be premature to build interventions on the idea. What can be said with some confidence is that no single cue solves the segmentation problem; infants appear to assemble a solution from several imperfect strategies, each compensating for the weaknesses of the others.

topic: infant-directed speech ('parentese'): infant preferences, vowel hyperarticulation, attention and cultural variation
title: The Sing-Song Register
subtitle: Adults everywhere seem to change their voices when they talk to babies, but what this special way of speaking actually achieves is far from settled

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In almost every society that has been studied, adults speak to babies in a manner quite unlike the way they speak to one another. Their pitch rises, its contours swoop and dip, the tempo slows, vowels are drawn out and utterances are short and frequently repeated. For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries this 'baby talk' was regarded with suspicion: child-rearing manuals warned that it would retard a child's progress and advised parents to address infants as they would an adult. Today the pendulum has swung the other way, and infant-directed speech, as researchers now call it, is widely promoted as a powerful aid to language learning. The reversal is instructive, but there is a risk that the new enthusiasm will prove as overstated as the old disapproval.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That infants like being spoken to in this way is not in doubt. In preference experiments, babies only a few weeks old will turn their heads or suck harder on a dummy to hear infant-directed speech rather than ordinary adult conversation, and they do so even when the language is foreign to them. The most convincing demonstration came from a collaboration coordinated by Dr Sigrun Kristiansdottir of the Reykjavik Institute for Developmental Science, in which sixty-seven laboratories in seventeen countries tested more than two thousand infants using a common procedure. The preference proved robust, and it was somewhat stronger in older infants than in younger ones. In a discipline where many celebrated findings have failed to survive repetition, a result confirmed on this scale is unusually secure.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Liking, however, is not the same as learning. Kristiansdottir has argued that infant-directed speech functions as a kind of built-in tutorial, pointing to the fact that caregivers stretch their vowels apart, so that sounds such as 'ee', 'ah' and 'oo' become acoustically more distinct. Dr Amani Mwangaza, a phonetician at the East African Institute of Phonetics, is unconvinced. Her measurements show that while the average vowels in infant-directed speech are indeed further apart, individual examples are also far more variable, with the result that the categories overlap almost as much as they do in adult speech. Mwangaza further suggests that much of the apparent exaggeration is a side effect of smiling and of raised pitch, both of which alter the shape of the vocal tract. In her words, the exaggeration may be 'emotional rather than instructional'. This does not show that infant-directed speech has no linguistic value, but it does seriously weaken the idea of a deliberate lesson hidden in the vowels.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An alternative account places attention and emotion at the centre. Professor Declan Delahunty of the Munster Centre for Child Development contends that the primary function of the register is to capture and regulate an infant's attention. He notes that particular melodies carry consistent messages: a rising-falling contour signals approval, while short, sharp bursts signal prohibition, and infants respond appropriately to these patterns even in languages they have never heard. On this view, any benefit to learning is indirect, because a baby who is attending closely is better placed to absorb whatever is said. Delahunty's own word-learning studies are consistent with this. Toddlers aged around twenty-one months learned new words presented in infant-directed speech but not those presented in an adult style, whereas children six months older learned equally well from both. Delahunty concludes that the register matters most when a child's capacity to process speech is still limited.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the strongest challenge comes from anthropology. Dr Eleni Arvanitis of the University of Thessaloniki has spent a decade documenting communities in which caregivers rarely address pre-verbal infants directly. Babies there are carried throughout the day amid busy conversation among siblings, neighbours and relatives, yet they appear to become competent speakers at broadly the usual age. Arvanitis argues that the belief that infant-directed speech is essential reflects the narrow range of families, mostly Western and middle-class, on which the research has been based. Her point is well taken, although it should be said that the evidence about the timing of development in these communities rests on relatively informal observation, which makes subtle delays difficult to rule out.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even within a single household the register is not uniform. Fathers tend to raise their pitch less than mothers but use a greater proportion of words that a young child is unlikely to know, which some researchers believe may stretch children's vocabularies. Older siblings, meanwhile, simplify their speech in ways that only partly resemble the adult version, shortening sentences but rarely altering their pitch.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that parents should abandon the sing-song voice that most adopt instinctively. Campaigns encouraging them to use it are harmless and probably beneficial. But the more consistent finding across studies is that what predicts later language is responsive interaction, in which an adult notices what has caught a child's interest and talks about it, waiting for and building on the child's replies. A melodious stream of speech delivered at a baby who is looking elsewhere is unlikely to accomplish much, however high its pitch.

topic: the 'word gap': quantity of language input, family income and children's vocabulary
title: Counting Words
subtitle: A famous estimate of how much language children hear at home has shaped public policy for decades. Does it deserve its reputation?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In waiting rooms and on buses in many cities, parents are greeted by posters urging them to talk, read and sing to their babies. Some families are offered small recording devices that clip onto a child's clothing and report, at the end of each day, how many words the child has heard. Behind these campaigns lies the idea of a 'word gap': the claim that children from poorer homes hear millions fewer words before they start school than children from wealthier ones, and that this shortfall explains much of the later difference in their educational achievement. Rarely can a single number have exerted so much influence on the way governments think about early childhood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The figure can be traced to the work of the psychologist Raimo Lehtovaara, who in the 1980s visited thirty-eight families once a month for two and a half years, recording an hour of everyday life on each occasion. Extrapolating from these samples, he calculated that by the age of four, children in the most advantaged professional households had heard around thirty million more words than those in families living on state benefits. Their vocabularies at age three, he found, were closely related to their performance at school several years later. Lehtovaara concluded that the sheer quantity of talk a child receives is the decisive factor in language development. It was a striking result, but it rested on a remarkably slender base. Thirty-eight families is a small sample by any standard, and projecting four years of experience from a single hour a month requires the assumption that the observed hour was typical, something that cannot easily be checked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Recent technology has made it possible to test the claim on a far larger scale. Wearable recorders now capture everything a child hears over an entire day, and software can estimate the number of adult words automatically. When Dr Ngozi Iwuchukwu and her colleagues at the Centre for Early Childhood Research in Abuja analysed recordings from almost two thousand children in several countries, they found that differences between income groups did exist, but were a fraction of the size Lehtovaara had reported. More striking still, the variation within each group was far larger than the variation between them: some low-income households were among the most talkative in the sample, and some affluent ones among the quietest. Iwuchukwu argues that a family's income is therefore a poor guide to what an individual child actually experiences.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second complication is that not all words are equal. Professor Tomislav Vrabec of the Adriatic Institute of Developmental Studies has shown that, in the homes he studied, only speech addressed directly to a child predicted the size of its vocabulary; talk between adults, or from a television in the background, contributed almost nothing. His distinction is a useful one, and it has encouraged researchers to separate types of input rather than lumping them together. Yet it would be unwise to treat his conclusion as universal. In societies where infants spend their days amid lively conversation among many relatives, children seem to learn a good deal from what they overhear, and Vrabec's findings may say more about the quiet, small households in which he worked than about children in general.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have shifted attention from words to exchanges. Dr Sushila Pradhanang of the Himalayan Centre for Cognitive Science has found that the number of conversational turns — moments when an adult speaks and the child responds, or vice versa — predicts later vocabulary better than the total number of words a child hears. In her view, what matters is not how much language flows past a child but how often the child is drawn into it. The argument is persuasive, though it carries a difficulty of its own. Children who are naturally more vocal will tend to provoke more replies from adults, so a high number of turns may partly reflect the child's own temperament rather than anything the parents are doing.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The sharpest criticism of the word gap, however, is not methodological but cultural. Critics point out that the standard vocabulary tests used in such research favour the kind of words valued in classrooms, and overlook the storytelling, verbal games and inventive teasing that flourish in many working-class communities. To describe such children as linguistically deprived, they argue, is to mistake difference for deficiency. There is real force in this objection, and the tests are certainly not neutral measures of linguistic ability. It does not follow, however, that the gap is imaginary. Because the tests reflect what schools reward, a shortfall in school-style vocabulary has genuine consequences for the children concerned, whatever its cause.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should policy make of all this? Trials of programmes that give parents word counts and coaching have generally produced modest gains, and these tend to fade within a year or two. The underlying message of the research — that frequent, responsive conversation helps children's language to grow — is sound. But reducing that message to a daily total risks placing the burden entirely on parents, many of whom have little control over the long working hours, insecure housing and financial stress that eat into the time and energy available for talk. A policy that addressed those pressures might do more for children's vocabularies than any number of posters.
