topic: overregularisation errors ('goed', 'mouses') and the rules-versus-associations debate in grammar learning
title: The Instructive Mistake
subtitle: When a toddler announces that she 'goed' to the park, she is revealing something about how grammar is learned — though researchers still disagree about exactly what

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere between the ages of two and four, many English-speaking children begin to say things they have almost certainly never heard. They report that they 'goed' outside, that the dog 'eated' its dinner, or that there are 'mouses' in the garden. What makes these errors especially intriguing is that the same children have often used the correct forms, 'went' and 'ate', for months beforehand. Performance thus follows a U-shaped curve: accurate, then error-prone, then accurate again. Because adults do not say 'goed', such forms cannot be the product of imitation, and they have therefore become a crucial piece of evidence in a long-running dispute about how the mind represents grammar. Few phenomena in developmental psychology have been asked to carry quite so much theoretical weight.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation is the so-called words-and-rules theory, championed by Professor Owen Hartigan of the Galway Institute of Linguistics. On this account, regular past tenses are generated by a mental rule — add '-ed' — while irregular forms such as 'went' are stored individually in memory, like ordinary vocabulary. The two systems compete, and the rule applies whenever retrieval of the stored form fails. Hartigan explains the U-shaped curve as follows: a very young child memorises 'went' as an unanalysed whole; once the child has extracted the regular rule, it occasionally overrides irregular forms that are not yet firmly stored. He emphasises that such errors are less common than parents imagine, accounting for only about four per cent of irregular verbs in the speech samples he has analysed, which in his view shows that memory usually wins the contest.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the late twentieth century this account was challenged by researchers working with artificial neural networks. Dr Keiko Matsuzawa of the Kansai Institute for Computational Cognition trained networks to map the sounds of present-tense verbs onto their past-tense forms, without building in any rule at all. Her networks not only reproduced the U-shaped curve but also produced errors such as 'brang', formed by analogy with 'sing' and 'sang', which real children also make and which a simple '-ed' rule cannot explain. Matsuzawa concluded that a single system of associations between sounds could account for both regular and irregular verbs. Critics replied that the curve in some early networks appeared only because the experimenters had suddenly enlarged the vocabulary on which they were trained, an artefact with no obvious parallel in childhood. Matsuzawa maintains that her later models, which received a gradually expanding vocabulary, show the same pattern.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evidence from children's surroundings has added a further dimension. Dr Irina Dubrovskaya of the Siberian Centre for Child Language examined thousands of hours of recorded family conversation and found that verbs which parents frequently use in the past tense are overregularised far less than verbs heard only occasionally. Children rarely say 'goed' for long, but may persist with 'stinged' for years. The finding is robust, yet it does less to resolve the debate than is sometimes claimed. Both camps predict a frequency effect: for Hartigan, frequent forms are stored more securely; for Matsuzawa, frequent forms create stronger associations.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the rule-based view have looked beyond English for decisive cases. In German, the plural ending '-s' is used with only a small minority of nouns, yet children readily apply it to unfamiliar words, names and borrowed terms, much as English-speaking children apply '-ed'. Since a pattern this rare should, on an associative account, exert little pull, the behaviour has been presented as evidence that children can treat a form as a default regardless of how often they hear it. Dr Paulo Zeferino of the Lusophone Centre for Language Research, who has studied German-speaking children extensively, urges caution here. He reports that the children he recorded actually overgeneralised the far more common '-n' ending more often than '-s', a pattern that fits rather awkwardly with the claim that '-s' functions as the true default.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Neurological studies have also been recruited. Dr Ragnheidur Gunnlaugsson of the Reykjavik Neurolinguistics Unit has documented patients with damage to different brain regions, some of whom struggle mainly with regular forms and others mainly with irregular ones. At first sight this supports the existence of two separate systems. Gunnlaugsson herself, however, points out that regular past forms in English tend to end in more complex clusters of consonants, as in 'walked' or 'jumped', and that when patients are tested on words matched for difficulty of pronunciation, much of the apparent separation disappears.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: After several decades, the dispute has become noticeably less polarised. Many associative models now produce behaviour that looks rule-like, and many supporters of rules accept that stored forms and frequency play a large part. Neither side can claim outright victory, but the contest has been remarkably productive, generating experimental methods and data that would not otherwise exist. I would go further and suggest that the original question — rules or associations? — may have been poorly posed, since the distinction becomes blurred once either system is described in sufficient detail. For parents, at least, the practical lesson is clear: there is no need to correct these errors, which fade of their own accord, and which are better understood as a sign of progress than of confusion.

topic: perceptual narrowing: infants' declining ability to distinguish non-native speech sounds in the first year
title: Tuning In, Tuning Out
subtitle: Babies begin life able to hear distinctions between the sounds of any language. Within a year, much of that ability has faded. Should we regret it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Young infants have sometimes been described as 'citizens of the world'. At six months, a baby growing up in an English-speaking home can typically hear the difference between two 't' sounds that are distinct in Hindi but treated as the same by English speakers, and a Japanese baby can distinguish the English 'r' and 'l', a contrast that many Japanese adults find extremely difficult. By the end of the first year, however, this broad sensitivity has largely gone. Infants become steadily better at telling apart the sounds of the language around them and markedly worse at distinguishing those of other languages. The phenomenon, known as perceptual narrowing, is often presented as a loss. That framing seems to me misleading: it is more accurately understood as a form of specialisation, in which the infant gives up a capacity it does not need in exchange for greater efficiency with the language it will actually use.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the early evidence came from experiments in which infants are trained to turn their heads when a repeated sound changes, and rewarded with a moving toy when they do so correctly. Using this method, Dr Nadeesha Fonseka of the Colombo Institute of Infant Perception found that most English-learning babies of six to eight months detected a change between the two Hindi sounds, whereas only a small minority of ten- to twelve-month-olds did. Yet Fonseka also discovered an important exception. Click sounds from certain southern African languages remained easy to distinguish, even for adults who had never heard them. Her explanation is that clicks resemble nothing in the English sound system and are therefore not absorbed into an existing category. Narrowing, she argues, is not a general deterioration of hearing but a process in which unfamiliar sounds are drawn into familiar categories.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Can the process be delayed? In a widely cited experiment, Dr Andreas Kiriakou of the Hellenic Centre for Child Development arranged for nine-month-old English-learning infants to spend twelve short play sessions with a Mandarin speaker. Afterwards, these infants could distinguish a Mandarin contrast as well as babies raised in Taiwan. A second group received exactly the same Mandarin input from video recordings, and a third from audio recordings alone; neither showed any benefit at all. Kiriakou concludes that social interaction acts as a 'gate' for early language learning. The result is striking, but it has arguably carried more weight than a single, fairly small study should bear, and later attempts to repeat it have produced mixed results.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Narrowing is not confined to speech. Six-month-olds can tell individual monkey faces apart almost as easily as human ones, but by nine months most have lost this ability — unless they have been shown picture books of monkeys at regular intervals in the meantime. Similarly, infants raised with Western music notice disruptions to the irregular rhythms of Balkan folk music at six months but not at twelve. Dr Litia Siwatibau of the Pacific Centre for Developmental Science argues on this basis that narrowing is a general property of how perception develops rather than a mechanism peculiar to language. Her proposal has considerably broadened the field, encouraging researchers to see language as one instance of a wider pattern of learning from experience.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nor does narrowing appear to be entirely permanent. Japanese adults who receive intensive training on English 'r' and 'l' do improve, though few ever reach the accuracy of native speakers. More intriguing is research by Dr Karim Abdelrahim of the Nile Institute of Cognitive Science on adults who were adopted in infancy from one country to another and who no longer have any conscious knowledge of their birth language. When taught the sounds of that language, they learned them faster than comparison groups with no early exposure. Abdelrahim suggests that traces of early experience survive long after the language itself has been forgotten. This is an encouraging finding, although the advantage he measured was modest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe that the timing of narrowing matters for later development. Fonseka has followed infants into their second year and found that those whose perception of native sounds sharpened early tended to have larger vocabularies at the age of two. She interprets this as evidence that an early commitment to the native language speeds up word learning. The correlation is real, but the interpretation is not the only one available: babies who mature more quickly in general might be expected to show both earlier narrowing and faster vocabulary growth, without one causing the other.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings are sometimes used to promote foreign-language classes for babies, on the grounds that the window for learning closes within the first year. That conclusion goes well beyond the evidence. Narrowing chiefly affects the perception of individual sounds, and therefore pronunciation; it says little about the ability to acquire vocabulary or grammar, at which older learners often excel. Exposure in infancy may well confer some advantage, but it is clearly not a requirement for later success.

topic: language mixing (code-mixing) in bilingual toddlers: confusion, differentiation and the unitary-system hypothesis
title: Two Languages, One Mind?
subtitle: When a bilingual toddler blends two languages in a single sentence, is the child confused, or demonstrating an unexpected kind of skill?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Parents who raise a child with two languages frequently become anxious when, at around the age of two, the child begins to produce sentences such as 'I want more leche', combining English with Spanish. For much of the twentieth century, this kind of blending was interpreted as a symptom of confusion. Paediatricians, speech therapists and teachers routinely advised families to abandon one of the languages, usually the one spoken by the minority community, so that the child could build a single secure foundation. In my view, that advice rested on a misreading of the evidence, and it caused genuine harm: countless children grew up unable to speak with their grandparents, having lost a language that, as we now know, they were perfectly capable of acquiring alongside the other.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The intellectual basis for the old advice was the so-called unitary-system hypothesis. Its most prominent advocate was Professor Ansgar Bergaust of the Trondheim Institute of Developmental Linguistics, who kept detailed diaries of his own two children as they grew up speaking Norwegian and German. Bergaust observed that in their second year the children combined words from both languages freely and, more strikingly, seemed to lack translation equivalents: a child who knew the German word for 'milk' would not use the Norwegian one, and vice versa. He concluded that young bilinguals begin with one merged store of words and only later, perhaps around the age of three, separate it into two distinct languages.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This conclusion was challenged when researchers began recording children with each parent separately rather than relying on observations made at home by a single adult. Dr Marit Zwanepoel of the Leiden Centre for Bilingual Development found that children as young as twenty months used noticeably more of their mother's language when speaking with their mother and more of their father's language with their father, and that they even adjusted their choice when introduced to unfamiliar adults. On the question of translation equivalents, Zwanepoel argues that the missing words reflect the different settings in which each language is used: a word learned at bath time with one parent may simply never have been heard from the other. In her account, children mix most often when they lack a word in the language of the moment, a strategy she terms 'gap-filling'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of research has examined the speech children hear. Dr Kacper Woloszyn of the Poznan Child Language Laboratory compared bilingual families in three countries and reported that the rate at which children mix closely mirrors the rate at which their parents do. In households where adults switch between languages constantly, children do the same; in households that follow a strict policy of one parent, one language, children mix far less. Woloszyn interprets mixing as a learned social practice rather than a sign of confusion. His argument is attractive, but I am not convinced that his data settle the matter. The relationship could run in the opposite direction, with parents beginning to mix more because their child prefers one language, and a correlation of this kind cannot by itself tell us which comes first.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most persuasive evidence of all comes from the structure of mixed sentences themselves. Dr Rosario Huanacuni of the Andean Linguistics Laboratory in Cusco analysed the speech of children growing up with Quechua and Spanish, two languages whose grammars differ considerably. She found that the children's switches were far from random. They rarely occurred at points where the two grammars conflict, for example between a verb and its suffix, but clustered at boundaries where both languages allow a change, much as adult bilinguals' switches do. That three-year-olds respect constraints of this subtlety suggests that, far from lacking two systems, they are already managing the relationship between them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more practical concern has centred on vocabulary. When bilingual children are tested in only one of their languages, they often know fewer words than monolingual children of the same age, a finding that once fuelled fears of delay. Dr Nirmala Abeywardane of the Colombo Institute of Child Studies has argued that such tests are misleading, because they ignore the words a child knows only in the other language. When she combines both languages into a measure of conceptual vocabulary, the number of distinct ideas a child can name, bilingual children match or exceed their monolingual peers. I accept her point about measurement, but it would be wrong to dismiss the concern entirely. A child who enters a school taught in one language may still find that the smaller vocabulary in that language matters, at least during the first years of formal education.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Today, few specialists defend the unitary-system hypothesis, and the consensus is that bilingual children distinguish their languages from a very early stage. Families can therefore be reassured that mixing is not a cause for alarm, and that there is no reason to give up a language for the sake of the other. Yet differentiation should not be confused with balance. Most bilingual children have a dominant language, usually the one used at school and among friends, and unless the minority language receives deliberate support at home, many grow up as passive bilinguals, able to understand their parents' language but reluctant or unable to speak it themselves.

topic: infant pointing and gesture as precursors of first words and two-word speech
title: Before the First Word
subtitle: Long before they can speak, infants point at the world around them. Some researchers believe these gestures are where language truly begins

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At some point between nine and twelve months of age, most infants extend an arm and an index finger towards something that has caught their interest: a dog in the street, an aeroplane overhead, a biscuit on a high shelf. For many years developmental psychologists regarded this behaviour as charming but peripheral, a minor milestone on the way to the real business of speech. Over the past two decades, however, a number of researchers have proposed a far more ambitious view, arguing that gesture is the scaffold on which spoken language is built. The claim deserves to be taken seriously, in my opinion, although some of its more enthusiastic versions go considerably further than the evidence allows.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the impetus for this view comes from long-term studies of individual children. Dr Xochitl Tlatelpa of the Puebla Institute of Developmental Science followed more than two hundred infants from their first birthday until the age of three and a half. Children who pointed at a wider range of objects at fourteen months went on to have larger spoken vocabularies, even when their parents' education and the amount of speech they heard were taken into account. More remarkable was a pattern at the level of individual items. The particular objects a child pointed at tended to enter that child's spoken vocabulary around three months later, as though the gesture were a rehearsal for the word. Tlatelpa describes pointing as the gateway through which most early words pass.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should a gesture help a child learn a word? Professor Yaw Agyekum of the Kumasi Centre for Cognitive Development believes the answer lies not inside the child's head but in conversation. When an infant points, adults almost irresistibly respond by naming the object: 'Yes, that's a dog!' In Agyekum's recordings of family life, parents supplied a label within two seconds of a point in the great majority of cases. In effect, the child selects the topic of the lesson, and the adult delivers the relevant word at exactly the moment the child's attention is fixed on its referent. Of the explanations on offer, I find this conversational account the most convincing, because it explains not merely why frequent pointers learn more words in general but why they learn the specific words for the things they point at.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Gesture also appears to anticipate grammar. Before children can produce two-word sentences, many combine a single word with a gesture, and these combinations come in two kinds. Some simply reinforce each other, as when a child points at a cup and says 'cup'. Others add information, as when the child points at the cup and says 'mine', expressing an idea that neither element conveys alone. Dr Dinara Kerimbayeva of the Almaty Institute of Child Language found that the age at which a child first produced the second, information-adding kind of combination predicted the age at which the same child began to put two words together. Combinations of the reinforcing kind had no such predictive value.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These findings have attracted the interest of clinicians. A marked lack of pointing at twelve months is one of several early signs that specialists consider when assessing a child's risk of later language difficulties, and it also features in screening for autism. Dr Sanna Paavola of the Oulu Centre for Paediatric Communication, who has studied such screening extensively, nevertheless warns against treating low pointing as a diagnosis in itself. Many infants who point rarely go on to become entirely ordinary talkers, and a single observation of a shy or tired baby can be highly misleading. I share her caution, and would add that parents gain nothing by anxiously counting their infant's gestures; the behaviour is informative across large groups of children far more than it is for any individual.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Cultural comparisons add a further complication. Pointing has been observed in every society in which it has been studied, but its form varies: in some communities people point with their lips or chin, in others with the whole hand, and the frequency of pointing differs widely. Agyekum himself has noted that in communities where adults seldom name objects for infants, preferring to involve children in shared activity, children nonetheless acquire language at a normal pace. Labelling in response to a point, then, is clearly one route into vocabulary rather than the only one. Since the great majority of the research described above was carried out with urban families in Europe and North America, its conclusions cannot simply be assumed to hold everywhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The practical question is whether encouraging gesture can accelerate language. In one trial, Tlatelpa's team coached parents to respond promptly and consistently whenever their infants pointed. Their children showed modest vocabulary gains at the age of two, but by the age of four the difference between them and a comparison group had disappeared. This does not make the programme worthless, but it does suggest that gesture is better understood as a window than as a lever. Watching what an infant points at tells us a great deal about what that child is ready to learn; it does not follow that multiplying the gestures will multiply the words.

topic: fast mapping and the mutual exclusivity bias: how toddlers work out what new words refer to
title: One Word, One Glance
subtitle: Young children seem able to learn a new word after hearing it just once. A closer look suggests the truth is slower, stranger and more social

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine a toddler who hears an adult say 'rabbit' while a rabbit hops across the lawn. To us the meaning is obvious, but logically the word could refer to the whole animal, its ears, its brown colour, the act of hopping, or even 'rabbit-on-grass'. This is the problem of reference, and it is far more formidable than most adults, who solved it long ago, ever notice. Yet between the ages of two and six, children add new words to their vocabulary at an astonishing rate, by some estimates around ten a day. Explaining how they narrow down the possible meanings so efficiently has become one of the central puzzles of developmental psychology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: An influential answer emerged from experiments of deceptively simple design. Dr Lajos Szentgyorgyi of the Debrecen Centre for Cognitive Science placed two objects in front of two-year-olds, one familiar, such as a cup, and one they had never seen, such as an oddly shaped kitchen gadget. When asked to 'give me the dax', a made-up word, the great majority handed over the unfamiliar object. Remarkably, when tested a week later, many could still pick out the 'dax' from a new set of objects. Szentgyorgyi concluded that children can form a connection between a word and its meaning on the basis of a single encounter, a capacity that came to be known as fast mapping, and he argued that this ability largely explains the explosive growth of vocabulary in the preschool years.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why do children choose the unfamiliar object? Professor Hanta Rakotobe of the Antananarivo Institute of Developmental Psychology proposed that they operate with a built-in assumption that each object has only one name. If the cup is already called 'cup', the new word must belong to something else. This mutual exclusivity bias, Rakotobe argued, drastically reduces the number of hypotheses a child must consider. He also pointed to its costs: a child who already calls the family pet a 'dog' may at first resist the suggestion that it is also a 'poodle', or insist that a 'flower' cannot be a 'daisy'. Such resistance, he maintained, is exactly what an inborn constraint of this kind would predict.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The claim that the bias is inborn was soon tested by researchers working with children who hear more than one language. Dr Agnieszka Trzaskowska of the Lublin Institute of Child Language found that bilingual toddlers showed a markedly weaker preference for the unfamiliar object, and trilingual toddlers a weaker one still. Since such children routinely hear two or three names for the same thing, she concluded that the assumption of one name per object is shaped by linguistic experience rather than fixed from birth. Rakotobe responded that the bias is merely a default setting, which experience can adjust. This reply is logically coherent, but it carries a cost of its own: if any result, whether a strong bias or a weak one, can be accommodated, it is difficult to see what evidence could ever count against the theory.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Doubts have also been raised about how much is actually learned in these experiments. Dr Meenakshi Duraisamy of the Madurai Child Cognition Laboratory repeated the classic procedure but added a test only five minutes later, in which the new object appeared among other unfamiliar items rather than beside a familiar one. Many children who had chosen correctly at first now performed no better than chance. Duraisamy draws a distinction between referent selection, working out in the moment which object a speaker means, and genuine word learning, which requires that the link be stored and retrieved later. The first, she argues, is fast; the second is not. Retention improved substantially when children met the same word on several occasions over a number of days, particularly when they had slept between sessions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other researchers suggest that children rely less on assumptions about words than on their understanding of people. Dr Armen Gevorgyan of the Yerevan Laboratory for Social Cognition arranged for an experimenter to say a new word while looking steadily at the familiar object rather than the novel one. In this situation, most two-year-olds attached the word to whatever the speaker was looking at, even when it already had a name. The children, in other words, abandoned mutual exclusivity as soon as social cues pointed elsewhere. For Gevorgyan, the toddler's main resource is an awareness that speakers use words to refer to the things they are attending to.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings suggest to me that the rapid expansion of children's vocabularies does not depend on one-shot learning at all. It is more plausibly the product of gradual accumulation, as children meet each word in many situations and slowly refine their sense of what it does and does not mean. Fast mapping is real, but it is a first step rather than the whole journey, and the label has arguably done some damage by encouraging the belief, common among teachers, that a single clear presentation of a new word is normally sufficient. This is not to say that biases such as mutual exclusivity play no role; they plausibly help children make a reasonable first guess. But the guess must then be tested and revised, a process that takes time and, above all, repetition.

topic: the 'video deficit': whether toddlers can learn words from screens, video chat and touchscreen apps
title: The Screen and the Speaker
subtitle: Toddlers today spend hours in front of screens. Can they learn language from them, and if so, under what conditions?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Around the turn of the century, a wave of videos and, later, apps appeared that promised to accelerate the language development of babies and toddlers. Their packaging showed smiling infants and their advertising spoke of vocabulary gains and 'brain-building'. Parents bought them in large numbers, and in many households screens are now a routine part of a two-year-old's day. Yet the marketing ran far ahead of the evidence. When researchers began to test whether children under three could actually learn words from a screen, the results were considerably less encouraging than the boxes suggested, and the reasons for this have turned out to reveal a great deal about how language is learned in the first place.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The foundational studies were carried out by Dr Solveig Kvistad of the Tromso Centre for Early Learning. She taught children aged between fifteen and twenty-four months a set of new words, either through a person sitting with them in the room or through a recording of the same person saying exactly the same things on a television screen. Children in the live condition learned roughly twice as many words as those who watched the recording. The gap was not permanent: it narrowed steadily with age and had almost disappeared by about the age of three. Kvistad named the phenomenon the 'video deficit', a term that has since been applied to the learning of actions and problem-solving as well as words.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should a screen be so much less effective than a person? Dr Kofi Amegashie of the Accra Institute for Child Development has argued that the crucial missing ingredient is responsiveness. A real conversational partner reacts to what the child does, pausing when the child looks away, following the child's gaze and answering the child's sounds. A recording cannot. To test this idea, Amegashie compared video chat, in which an adult on screen responded to the child in real time, with prerecorded footage of the same adult delivering identical content. Toddlers learned nearly as well through video chat as they did face to face, but learned little from the recording. Because the two screen conditions differed only in whether the adult could respond, the study offers strong support for his explanation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second explanation focuses not on the screen's partner but on the child's understanding of images. Dr Lucia Ochoa-Pinzon of the Bogota Laboratory of Cognitive Development points out that very young children struggle with the idea that a picture can simultaneously be an object in its own right and a representation of something else. Eighteen-month-olds will sometimes try to pick up a pictured cup or scratch at a photograph of a flower. If a child does not fully grasp that the person on the screen stands for a real person, the argument runs, the words that person speaks may not be connected to objects in the child's world. Consistent with this, Ochoa-Pinzon found that toddlers who had been read picture books more often showed a smaller video deficit. It is worth stressing that her account and Amegashie's need not be rivals; both factors could well operate at once.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The spread of touchscreen devices has raised the possibility that interactivity might overcome the deficit. Dr Shirin Yazdanpanah of the Tehran Centre for Media and Development compared three ways of presenting the same story with new words. In one version children simply watched. In another, the story advanced only when the child touched the specific object being named. In a third, any touch anywhere on the screen moved the story on. The version requiring children to touch the named object produced clearly better word learning than passive watching. The version in which any touch would do, however, produced no benefit at all, and children using it often tapped repeatedly and at random. Interactivity, Yazdanpanah concludes, helps only when the action the child performs is relevant to the word being learned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most practically useful findings concern the role of other people in the room. Dr Ilze Liepina of the Riga Institute of Family Studies has shown that when a parent watches alongside a toddler and talks about what is happening on screen, naming characters, asking questions and linking the programme to the child's own experience, the video deficit largely disappears. In effect, the parent converts the screen into the subject of a shared conversation. Liepina's household surveys contain a less welcome message, though. Families report watching television together quite often, but shared use of phones and tablets is much rarer, because the small screen tends to be handed to a child to use alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should parents be told? Complete avoidance of screens before the age of three is sometimes recommended, but in my view such a ban is neither realistic for most families nor necessary. The research does not show that screens are inherently harmful to language; it shows that they are a poor substitute for the responsive conversation through which young children learn. The sensible advice is therefore to make screen time social where possible, by watching together and talking about what is seen. Video chat with distant relatives appears to be a reasonable exception to the general rule, given Amegashie's results, though I would add that his samples were small and that the conversations in his laboratory were rather more attentive than many family calls.

topic: late talkers: whether toddlers slow to start speaking catch up, predicting persistent difficulty, and wait-and-see versus early intervention
title: Waiting for Words
subtitle: Most toddlers who are slow to start talking eventually catch up, but deciding which ones will not has proved far harder than expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every parent of a two-year-old is aware of the milestones. By the second birthday, a typical child is expected to produce at least fifty words and to have begun combining them into short phrases. Yet roughly one child in seven falls noticeably short of this benchmark while otherwise developing normally: such children hear well, understand much of what is said to them and show no sign of broader cognitive difficulty. Clinicians call them 'late talkers', and for decades they have posed a deceptively simple question. Is a slow start to speech a harmless variation in timing, or an early warning of a lasting language disorder? The answer matters, because it determines whether families are reassured and sent home or referred for therapy at a time when, many believe, the brain is at its most adaptable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for patience rests largely on longitudinal studies. A group at the Tromsø Centre for Child Development led by Professor Ilse Brakvatne followed more than six hundred late talkers from the age of two until they started school. By five, around three-quarters had vocabulary and grammar scores within the normal range, and many were indistinguishable from children who had begun speaking early. Brakvatne concludes that most late talkers are simply at the tail end of a wide but healthy distribution, and that routinely referring them for treatment would overwhelm already stretched speech therapy services. Her data are impressive, and the reassurance they offer is, for most families, entirely justified. But a figure of three-quarters also implies that one late talker in four does not catch up, and an approach that works well on average can still fail a substantial minority of individual children.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Moreover, 'catching up' may be a less complete recovery than the term suggests. Rustam Tazhibayev, a psycholinguist at the Almaty Institute of Developmental Science, has re-examined several cohorts in which former late talkers appeared to have reached normal levels by school age. Using more demanding measures, such as the ability to repeat complex sentences, to tell a coherent story or to understand passive constructions like 'the dog was chased by the cat', he found that as a group they continued to score slightly below their peers into adolescence, even though most remained within what is conventionally regarded as the average band. Tazhibayev describes this as 'illusory recovery'. Critics respond that the differences are small and of uncertain practical significance, and that standard tests are designed precisely to detect difficulties that affect everyday life. Both positions have some merit, though it seems to me that a persistent disadvantage, however modest, ought not to be dismissed simply because it falls below a clinical threshold.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If not every late talker should be treated, the obvious alternative is to identify those most at risk. Here the research has been more productive than is sometimes acknowledged. The strongest single predictor appears to be comprehension: toddlers who understand few words, as opposed to merely saying few, are far less likely to catch up unaided. Other warning signs include limited use of gesture, a family history of language or reading difficulties, and a small repertoire of consonant sounds in babbling. Lucía Ospital, a screening specialist in Valencia, argues that combining such indicators allows clinicians to sort late talkers into groups with very different prospects. Yet even her most refined checklists misclassify a considerable number of children, labelling some as at risk who later develop normally and missing others who go on to struggle.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that the most useful information can only be gathered over time. Ospital has therefore championed what she calls 'active monitoring': rather than deciding at a single appointment, clinicians see a child at intervals of three or four months and refer for therapy only if progress stalls. Early evaluations suggest that parents find it less distressing than either immediate referral or blanket reassurance. Its weakness is cost. Repeated assessments demand clinicians' time, and in health systems where waiting lists already stretch beyond a year, the theoretical benefits of monitoring may never reach the families who need them most.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A rather different perspective comes from the speech therapist Aiyana Thornquist, who questions the framing of the entire debate. In her view, the choice between waiting and treating is a false one, because the most effective early support is not therapy delivered by a professional but coaching for parents. In programmes she has helped design, parents learn to follow their child's focus of attention, to pause long enough for the child to respond and to expand short utterances into slightly longer ones. Thornquist's trials report gains in children's expressive vocabulary within six months, and the method is cheap enough to be offered to every late talker regardless of predicted outcome. Sceptics note that the families who volunteer for such trials tend to be highly motivated, which may inflate the results; how well the method works among parents who are exhausted, overworked or doubtful about its value remains largely untested.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these competing accounts is less a verdict than a shift in emphasis. The question is no longer simply whether late talking is benign, since for most children it plainly is, but how resources can be allocated so that the minority who will struggle are not lost among the majority who will not. Approaches that are inexpensive and carry little risk of harm, such as parent coaching, seem to me the most defensible starting point, with specialist therapy reserved for children whose difficulties persist. A child who is slow to speak presents genuine uncertainty, and both confident reassurance and immediate intervention offer the comfort of decisive action in a situation that, in truth, calls for watchful patience.

topic: the incubation effect: why setting a problem aside can lead to creative solutions
title: Stepping Back to Leap Forward
subtitle: Psychologists have spent decades trying to explain why solutions so often arrive after we stop looking for them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost everyone has had the experience of struggling with a problem for hours, abandoning it in frustration, and then finding the answer arriving unbidden while doing something else entirely: walking, showering or drifting towards sleep. Accounts of this kind fill the memoirs of mathematicians and composers, and they inspired one of the earliest theories of creative thought, which divided problem-solving into four stages: preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. Of these, incubation, the period during which a problem is set aside, has proved both the most intriguing and the most elusive. Anecdotes, however vivid, cannot establish that the break itself achieved anything. The solver may simply remember the occasions on which time away was followed by a breakthrough and forget the far more numerous occasions on which it produced nothing at all. For that reason, the phenomenon has had to be brought into the laboratory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Participants work on a problem, such as finding a single word that links three apparently unrelated words, or listing as many unusual uses as possible for a brick. One group works continuously; another is interrupted for a fixed interval and then returns to the task. A review of more than a hundred such studies by Agnes Kertvari at the Institute for Cognitive Research in Szeged concluded that interrupted groups do perform better on average, though the advantage is modest. More revealing, in Kertvari's view, was the variation between studies. The benefit was largest for open-ended tasks with many possible answers and considerably weaker for problems with a single correct solution. It was also greater when participants had already worked on the problem for some time before the break, a finding which suggests that incubation cannot substitute for initial effort but can only build upon it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Explaining why a pause helps has proved harder than demonstrating that it does. One long-standing account holds that a break simply allows people to forget. When we attack a problem, we frequently become fixated on an inappropriate approach, returning to the same unproductive idea again and again. Hiroshi Saegusa, a psychologist at Kansai University of Behavioural Sciences, has shown that when participants are deliberately misled at the start of a task, for instance by being offered unhelpful hints, those who take a break recover from the misdirection far more successfully than those who persist. On this view, nothing constructive happens during incubation at all. The mind merely sheds its mistakes, so that the problem can be seen afresh when the solver returns to it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A rival explanation is altogether more ambitious. It proposes that the mind continues to work on the problem outside conscious awareness, exploring remote associations that deliberate thought would reject as irrelevant. Supporters point to experiments in which the activity performed during the break turns out to matter a great deal. Ngozika Mbanefo and her colleagues at the Niger Delta Institute of Psychology found that participants who spent the interval on an undemanding task, such as sorting cards by colour, later produced more original ideas than those who either rested quietly or tackled a mentally taxing puzzle. If incubation were merely a matter of forgetting, Mbanefo argues, quiet rest should have been at least as effective as light activity. That it was not implies that some form of unconscious processing is taking place, and that it thrives when the conscious mind is occupied but not overloaded.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This conclusion has been challenged, most forcefully by Peter Rydberg of the Uppsala Centre for Experimental Psychology. Rydberg contends that 'unconscious work' is a label rather than an explanation, since it specifies no mechanism and is therefore almost impossible to disprove. His own attempts to repeat the light-task experiments produced inconsistent results: the advantage appeared in some samples but vanished in others. He also notes that, when questioned afterwards, many participants admit to having thought about the problem during the supposed break, so that what looks like unconscious progress may in fact be brief, half-noticed conscious reconsideration. Rydberg's scepticism is a valuable corrective to some of the more extravagant claims made on behalf of the unconscious mind. Nevertheless, it goes too far to dismiss unconscious processing altogether. The evidence that the type of break matters has emerged in too many laboratories to be explained away by occasional failures to replicate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Particular interest has centred on whether sleep is an especially effective form of incubation. In several studies, participants who slept between two attempts at a numerical task were more likely to discover a hidden rule that made the task far easier than those who remained awake for the same period. Such results are frequently cited as proof that sleep generates creative insight, but they have arguably been over-interpreted in popular accounts. Closer inspection shows that the advantage appeared chiefly among participants who had already partly grasped the structure of the task before sleeping; sleep, it seems, refines insights that are already forming rather than creating them from nothing. The benefits of sleep are also hard to separate from the effects of fatigue on the group kept awake.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The research offers a more qualified message than the self-help literature tends to suggest. Breaks do not replace hard work; they are most effective after a period of sustained effort, and on problems that admit many possible solutions rather than one. The choice of activity during the interval also seems to matter, even if the reasons remain disputed. Perhaps the most useful lesson is that persistence and withdrawal are not opposites but partners. Knowing when to stop working on a problem may be as much a creative skill as knowing how to begin.

topic: whether constraints and limitations stimulate or stifle creativity
title: The Freedom of Limits
subtitle: Do rules and restrictions make people more inventive? Psychologists are discovering that the answer depends on the kind of limit involved

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Poets have long worked within strict forms, such as the fourteen lines of the sonnet or the seventeen syllables of the haiku, and many insist that such rules liberate rather than confine them. The idea that limitations spur invention has become a commonplace of management literature too, where 'constraint-driven innovation' is promoted as a cure for complacent teams. Until recently, however, the claim rested largely on anecdote: memorable stories of engineers improvising with scraps or film-makers turning a tiny budget into an asset. Psychologists are now testing it systematically, and the picture that is emerging is considerably more complicated than the slogans suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why might a restriction help? One influential explanation is known as the 'path of least resistance'. When people generate ideas freely, they tend to retrieve the most accessible and typical examples first, and then stop. Laure Duquesnoy, a cognitive psychologist at the Lyon Institute of Cognitive Science, illustrated this by asking volunteers to invent creatures that might live on another planet. Left to their own devices, most produced animals with two eyes, four limbs and a symmetrical body, closely modelled on species found on Earth. When instructed that their creature must lack a feature common to Earth animals, such as eyes, the designs became markedly more original, according to independent judges. In Duquesnoy's view, a constraint works by blocking the obvious route, so that the mind is forced to search less familiar territory.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kenji Takeshita, who studies innovation at the Osaka Graduate School of Management, has taken the question out of the laboratory and into the workplace. Following product development teams over several years, he found that teams given smaller budgets and fewer materials tended to produce more novel product ideas, but only up to a point. Moderate scarcity was stimulating; severe scarcity was stifling, because teams spent their energy simply getting by rather than exploring new possibilities. Takeshita also discovered that the type of constraint mattered. Restrictions on materials were frequently productive, whereas tight deadlines generally reduced creativity, since pressure of time narrowed attention to the most familiar solutions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This distinction between kinds of constraint is crucial, and it is too often ignored in advice offered to businesses. Telling a team that it must work with less is not the same as telling it that it must finish sooner. The first may provoke fresh thinking; the second is more likely to produce hurried repetition of what has worked before. Managers who conflate the two may conclude, wrongly, that constraint as such is unhelpful, when it was only one particular form of it that failed. Organisations that cut budgets and shorten deadlines simultaneously in the name of innovation are therefore likely to achieve the opposite of what they intend.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further question concerns who sets the limit. Adaeze Ogunleye of the West African Centre for Design Research has interviewed architects, weavers and furniture makers about the rules they work under. She found that self-imposed restrictions, such as a decision to use only local timber or a palette of three colours, were associated both with high job satisfaction and with work that peers rated as original. Constraints imposed by clients or managers were a different matter. These raised originality only when the person concerned perceived them as a challenge to be met; when they were experienced as a threat or an insult to professional judgement, the effect was reversed. Ogunleye concludes that the psychological meaning attached to a constraint matters as much as its content.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced by the research. Rumyana Velikova, a social psychologist at the Balkan Institute for Social Psychology, argues that many laboratory studies measure originality in a very narrow way. An idea is usually scored as original simply because few other participants produced it, regardless of whether it would actually work. When Velikova asked judges to rate usefulness as well as novelty, the ideas generated under constraint were sometimes less practical than those produced freely. She also suspects that striking positive results are more likely to be published than disappointing ones. Her point about usefulness is well taken. Yet she goes too far in implying that the benefits of constraint are merely an artefact of measurement, since the central finding, that blocking typical features leads to less predictable ideas, has been repeated across a wide range of tasks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson, then, is that constraints are tools rather than magic formulas. What matters is matching the type and degree of restriction to the task and to the people doing it. A blank page is not always the freedom it appears to be, but neither is every limit a gift. A restriction that blocks an obvious solution can open up new ground; one that exhausts people or questions their competence is likely to close it down. Designers of workplaces and classrooms would do well to ask not whether to impose limits, but which limits, how many, and who should choose them. The sonnet works for poets not because it is restrictive, but because it is restrictive in a way they have chosen and can master.

topic: group brainstorming versus individual idea generation
title: Many Heads, Fewer Ideas?
subtitle: Group brainstorming remains a fixture of working life, despite decades of evidence that it rarely delivers what it promises

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the twentieth century, an advertising executive popularised a technique he called brainstorming. Its rules were simple: participants were to withhold criticism, welcome unusual suggestions, aim for quantity rather than quality and build freely on one another's contributions. Groups that followed these principles, he claimed, would produce roughly twice as many ideas as the same people working alone. The technique spread rapidly through corporations, schools and government departments, and the brainstorming session, with its flip charts and coloured sticky notes, remains a familiar feature of office life. Yet almost from the beginning, laboratory research told a very different story. The inferiority of group brainstorming is one of the most robust findings in social psychology, and it is also one of the most widely ignored.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The standard experiment compares two arrangements. In one, a group of, say, four people brainstorms together. In the other, four individuals work separately, and their ideas are afterwards pooled, with duplicates removed; researchers call this a 'nominal group'. Nominal groups consistently generate more ideas than interactive ones, and frequently more good ideas as well. Matvei Zelenko of the Kharkiv Institute of Social Cognition regards a phenomenon known as production blocking as the principal culprit. Only one person can speak at a time, and while waiting for their turn, group members forget ideas or decide that they are no longer relevant to the direction the discussion has taken. In one of Zelenko's experiments, participants working alone were required to wait for a signal before voicing each idea, as if they were in a group. Their output fell almost to the level of interactive groups, suggesting that the need to take turns accounts for much of the shortfall.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Other researchers stress social rather than mechanical causes. Lucía Ibarguen, an organisational psychologist at the Pacific Institute of Organisational Psychology in Valparaíso, points to what she terms evaluation apprehension. Despite the official ban on criticism, people remain anxious about how their suggestions will be judged, particularly when someone more senior is present. In her studies, junior employees who brainstormed in front of a manager offered fewer ideas, and those they did offer were noticeably more conventional. Ibarguen also identifies a tendency for effort to decline when individual contributions cannot be identified, a pattern sometimes described as social loafing. Both effects, she found, were most pronounced among staff who had recently joined an organisation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Given such evidence, the survival of group brainstorming is at first sight puzzling. Part of the explanation, however, is that people in groups feel more productive than they are. Sigrún Gísladóttir of the Reykjavík Centre for Behavioural Research has documented what she calls the illusion of group productivity. Members of brainstorming groups consistently overestimate their own contribution, rate their sessions as more enjoyable than solitary work, and later recall some of their colleagues' ideas as their own. The enjoyment is not trivial; a pleasant shared experience may strengthen relationships within a team. But it should not be confused with creative output, and too many organisations appear to make exactly that mistake.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of brainstorming argue that the laboratory evidence is beside the point. Kwame Oppong of the Accra School of Management Studies observes that most experiments involve strangers spending fifteen or twenty minutes on trivial problems, such as suggesting improvements to a doorknob. Real teams, by contrast, share expertise and a history of working together, and they tackle complex problems over weeks or months. His field studies of design consultancies found that brainstorming sessions served purposes beyond the generation of ideas: they spread technical knowledge across the firm, impressed clients and fostered a culture of experimentation. Oppong is right that the laboratory is an artificial setting. His argument, however, quietly changes the terms of the debate. If brainstorming is valuable mainly for reasons other than producing ideas, then it ought to be promoted honestly on those grounds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, researchers have developed alternatives designed to keep the benefits of collaboration while avoiding its costs. In electronic brainstorming, members type ideas simultaneously into a shared system, which removes production blocking at a stroke; with large groups, this method can outperform even nominal groups. Giulia Anselmi of the Bologna Laboratory for Applied Cognition has examined how individual and group work can best be combined. The most effective sequence in her studies began with individuals generating ideas alone, followed by a meeting to combine and evaluate them, and finally a further period of solitary work. Exposure to other people's ideas can indeed be stimulating, Anselmi argues, but only when people then have time to think without being interrupted. In her view, the problem lies not with groups as such but with the way they are usually run.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of brainstorming is, in one sense, a cautionary tale about how intuitive appeal can outlast evidence. It would be wrong, though, to conclude that collaboration should be abandoned. What the research points to is not solitude in place of teamwork, but a more careful structuring of the two. The best ideas probably come neither from the lonely genius nor from the noisy meeting room, but from people who move deliberately between working alone and working together.

topic: the 'mad genius' hypothesis: the relationship between creativity and mental illness
title: The Tormented Genius Reconsidered
subtitle: Is there a genuine link between creative brilliance and mental illness, or is it a romantic story we like to tell?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The image of the tormented artist is among the most enduring in Western culture. Ancient philosophers suggested that no great mind had ever existed without a touch of madness, and the Romantic poets turned suffering into something close to a qualification for genius. Today the idea survives in films and biographies that dwell on the despair of painters and the breakdowns of composers. But is there any real connection between creativity and mental illness? The question is not merely academic. If such a link exists, it may have implications for how creative people are supported and treated. If it does not, the myth may be doing harm, by romanticising suffering and discouraging people from seeking the help they need.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest evidence came from biographical studies of eminent figures. Researchers combed through the lives of celebrated poets, novelists and painters for signs of mood disorders, and reported strikingly high rates. Ilona Varkonyi, a historian of psychology at the Budapest Centre for Historical Psychology, has argued that these studies suffer from serious weaknesses. The diagnoses were made long after the subjects' deaths, on the basis of letters, diaries and anecdotes that are often incomplete. Biographers, moreover, are naturally drawn to dramatic lives, and samples restricted to the famous cannot tell us whether equally creative but less troubled people were simply overlooked. Varkonyi's objections are decisive against the biographical method. They do not, however, show that the link is false; they show only that this kind of evidence is incapable of establishing it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more rigorous approach became possible when several Nordic countries began to link national health registers with records of occupation. Eero Ruokonen of the Turku Institute of Population Psychiatry analysed the records of more than a million people. Because the registers include everyone, whether celebrated or obscure, this method avoids the bias towards fame that undermined the biographical studies, and diagnoses are recorded by clinicians at the time rather than inferred centuries later. Contrary to popular belief, those working in creative professions, a category that included writers, visual artists, musicians and scientists, were not, taken as a whole, more likely to have received a psychiatric diagnosis than the rest of the population. There were, however, two notable exceptions. Writers showed elevated rates of depression and bipolar disorder, and close relatives of people with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia were over-represented in creative occupations, even though they themselves had no diagnosis.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The finding about relatives has prompted what is sometimes called the shared vulnerability model. Marie-Claire Tchamba, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Central African Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience, proposes that certain mental traits may be beneficial in mild forms and harmful in severe ones. One example is a reduced tendency to filter out information that seems irrelevant. In moderation, Tchamba suggests, this may widen the range of ideas and associations available to a person; in an extreme form, and combined with other risk factors, it may contribute to illness. Whether the outcome is creativity or disorder may depend on protective qualities such as high intelligence and a strong working memory, which may allow people to make use of an unusual openness to ideas without being overwhelmed by it. On this view, creativity and mental illness are not cause and effect, but share some of their roots.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The model is attractive, and it fits the data on relatives well, but it should be treated with caution. The statistical associations on which it rests are small. The great majority of people with mental illness are not unusually creative, and most creative people are not mentally ill. It is also clear that severe episodes of illness generally make creative work harder rather than easier. Writers who experience depression, for instance, typically report that they produce very little during their worst periods, and much of their best work is done when they are well.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For Daniel Galeano of the Montevideo Institute for Arts and Health, the most pressing issue is not whether the link exists but what the belief in it does to people. In surveys of art and music students, he found that a considerable minority believed that psychiatric treatment would dull their creativity, and some admitted to having postponed seeking help for that reason. Yet when Galeano interviewed professional musicians who had received treatment, most reported that the quality of their work had either improved or remained unchanged. This is the strongest reason of all to challenge the romantic myth. Whatever its literary charm, a belief that encourages people to avoid effective treatment can cause real harm.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from a century of research is not the simple story of madness breeding genius, but a modest and complicated relationship that applies to some groups and not to others. Popular culture, which prefers the dramatic exception to the unremarkable rule, has been slow to absorb this more nuanced picture. It may be time to change the question. Rather than asking whether suffering is the price of creativity, researchers and the public alike might more usefully ask how creative people who are struggling can best be helped to go on working, and to live well.

topic: the measurement of creativity with divergent thinking tests and its limitations
title: The Trouble with Tallying Ideas
subtitle: For seventy years psychologists have tried to measure creativity with pencil-and-paper tests. How much do the scores really tell us?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the decades after the Second World War, a number of psychologists grew frustrated with intelligence tests. Such tests, they complained, rewarded convergent thinking, the capacity to home in on the single correct answer to a well-defined problem, while ignoring the ability to generate new possibilities. Their solution was to measure divergent thinking instead. In the best-known example, the Alternative Uses Task, people are asked to list as many uses as they can for an everyday object such as a paperclip or a tin can. Responses are scored for fluency, the total number of ideas; flexibility, the number of different categories into which they fall; originality, usually defined as statistical rarity; and elaboration, the amount of detail provided. The task soon became the most widely used measure of creativity in research, and was adopted by many schools to help select pupils for programmes for the gifted. Its popularity, however, has always owed more to its convenience than to any firm evidence that it captures what we ordinarily mean by creativity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One difficulty became apparent early on. Rosa Pellegrini, a psychometrician at the Turin Institute for Psychometrics, has shown that originality scores are closely tied to fluency. Someone who lists forty uses is bound to include more unusual ones than someone who lists ten, simply by the law of averages, so that the originality score largely duplicates the fluency score. Pellegrini's remedy is to ask participants to nominate their two best ideas and to score only those. This not only removes much of the statistical overlap, she argues, but also tests a neglected part of creativity: the ability to recognise which of one's own ideas are worth pursuing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental weakness lies in the definition of originality itself. Because an idea is scored as original when few others in the sample produce it, the same answer may count as highly original among teenagers and entirely ordinary among engineers. Originality, in other words, is not a fixed property of a response; it depends on who else happened to be tested. One alternative is to rely on human judgement. Sigríður Thorsdóttir of the North Atlantic Centre for Assessment Research has championed a method known as consensual assessment, in which experts independently rate the creativity of products such as poems or drawings. Judges agree with one another to a surprising degree, she reports, but the method is slow and costly, and experts drawn from different fields frequently disagree about what deserves to be called creative.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recent technology offers a way around the expense. Navid Ebrahimi of the Caspian Institute of Computational Psychology has developed software that calculates the semantic distance between the object named in the task and each response, drawing on statistical models of how words are used in vast collections of text. A response that is rarely mentioned in the same context as 'paperclip' scores as distant. Ebrahimi's distance scores correlate well with human ratings of originality, and thousands of responses can be scored in seconds. This is a genuine advance in efficiency. Yet distance is not the same as creativity: a word chosen at random would be extremely distant from 'paperclip' without being in the least inventive. Ebrahimi accepts the point and has added a filter for appropriateness, though how well such a filter performs remains to be established.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even a perfectly scored test would be of limited value if it did not predict creative behaviour outside the laboratory. Tomasz Kaczmarek of the Kraków Centre for Developmental Research has followed a group of children who were tested at the age of ten for more than thirty years. Their divergent thinking scores did predict later creative accomplishments, such as published writing, patents and exhibited artwork, and did so somewhat better than IQ in certain domains. But the relationship was modest, accounting for only a small proportion of the differences between individuals. The strongest predictor of adult achievement, Kaczmarek found, was not any test score but whether a child had shown a sustained passion for one particular activity. Such a result should not be dismissed, but it falls well short of what has sometimes been claimed for these tests.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical critique comes from Anahit Mirzoyan of the Armenian Institute of Applied Psychology. She argues that divergent thinking tests assume the existence of a general creative ability, when creativity is in fact largely specific to particular domains: an inventive physicist need not be an inventive cook. Mirzoyan advocates assessment through real tasks within a domain, such as writing a short story, composing a collage or designing a simple device. Her emphasis on domain-specific skill is a useful corrective, but her position is too extreme. Studies that compare performance across many domains do find a general component, even if it is smaller than the designers of the original tests assumed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that divergent thinking tests should be discarded. In research, where they are used to compare groups or to study the mental processes involved in generating ideas, they remain valuable tools. The danger arises when a single score is used to make decisions about individuals. Selecting children for special programmes on the basis of how many uses they can find for a paperclip places far more weight on these tests than the evidence can bear. Creativity is better judged through several measures, gathered over time and in the activities that people actually care about.

topic: creativity across the lifespan: the age at which creative achievement peaks
title: The Myth of the Young Genius
subtitle: Is creative achievement really the preserve of youth, or have we misread the careers of the great innovators?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask most people when creative genius flourishes and they will point to youth. The image of the precocious poet who burns brightly and dies young, or the mathematician who does his finest work before thirty, has become so familiar that it is rarely questioned. Yet the belief owes far more to the romantic imagination of the nineteenth century than to any systematic body of evidence. Over the past few decades, psychologists, economists and historians have begun to examine the careers of creators in a more methodical way, and what they have found is considerably more complicated, and in some respects more encouraging, than the popular myth suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most extensive of these investigations has been carried out by Dr Ilse Ostrowiecka of the Northern Institute for Historical Psychology, whose team compiled the publication and exhibition records of more than four thousand composers, painters, writers and scientists who worked between 1500 and 1950. Across the whole sample, creative output tended to climb steeply during the twenties, reach its highest point at around the age of forty, and then fall away gradually rather than abruptly. However, Ostrowiecka stresses that this average conceals striking differences between disciplines. Lyric poets and pure mathematicians typically produced their most celebrated work in their late twenties or early thirties, while historians, philosophers and novelists frequently did so in their fifties or even later. In fields where success depends on accumulating a large body of knowledge, she concludes, the creative peak arrives late.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should some creators flourish early and others late? One influential answer comes from the economist Rafael Brannigar, who originally developed his theory by studying the prices paid at auction for paintings produced at different stages of artists' lives. Brannigar distinguishes between two types of innovator. 'Conceptual' innovators set out with a clear idea that they wish to express and tend to make dramatic breakthroughs when young, before habits of thought have set in. 'Experimental' innovators, by contrast, proceed by trial and error, refining their methods slowly over many years, and their greatest achievements therefore come late. Brannigar has since applied the same distinction to scientists. The scheme is elegant, but it is surely too tidy: a great many artists, on close inspection, alternate between the two approaches over the course of a single career, and some seem to belong to neither.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different line of research questions whether the timing of great work needs any special explanation at all. Analysing the citation records of several thousand scientists, the sociologist Mireille Sauvageot found that the proportion of a researcher's papers that went on to become highly influential remained remarkably constant from the beginning of a career to its end. Her 'equal-odds' principle implies that creators produce their best work at the point when they produce the most work: masterpieces cluster in mid-career simply because output does. An older scientist who continues to publish at the same rate as a young colleague has, on this account, just as good a chance of producing a landmark study with each attempt. To my mind, this is the most important finding in the field, because it moves attention away from age itself and towards the conditions that allow people to remain productive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What, then, causes output to fall? Hiroto Kanemura and his colleagues at the Osaka Centre for Lifespan Studies argue that the main culprits are circumstantial rather than biological. In mid-life, they note, creators typically take on administrative obligations, teaching loads and family responsibilities that leave little time for original work. In one study, senior researchers who were relieved of committee duties for two years increased their output substantially, despite receiving no additional funding. This is not to deny that the mind changes with age. Fluid intelligence, the capacity to reason about unfamiliar problems, begins to weaken from early adulthood, whereas crystallised intelligence, the store of accumulated knowledge and expertise, continues to grow until at least the sixties. The evidence that working conditions matter more than cognitive decline is, in my judgement, stronger than the case for a purely biological explanation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that the age of peak achievement is not fixed but shifts over time. Researchers at the Lisbon Institute for Science Policy have shown that the average age at which Nobel-winning discoveries were made rose by roughly six years during the twentieth century. Their explanation is what they call the 'burden of knowledge': as each field accumulates more information, newcomers must spend longer mastering it before they can contribute anything original. The argument is plausible, but it is unlikely to be the whole story. The same period saw doctoral programmes lengthen and permanent posts become harder to obtain, so that many young scientists were simply denied the independence needed to pursue their own ideas until later in life.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that age is irrelevant to creativity, but it does suggest that the popular myth may be actively harmful. If funding bodies assume that the best work is done by the young, they may withdraw support from older applicants; and if creators themselves believe that their best years are behind them, they may stop attempting ambitious projects, thereby making the prediction come true. The lesson of the research is not that every career will end in a late flowering, but that the decline so often attributed to ageing is, to a considerable degree, something that societies and institutions create.
