topic: expertise and creative fixation: whether deep knowledge helps or hinders original thinking
title: The Expert's Blind Spot
subtitle: Knowledge is the raw material of creative work, yet it can also stop us seeing what is in front of us

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is almost an article of faith in education that creativity depends on knowledge. Nobody, the argument runs, can compose a symphony without understanding harmony, or design a bridge without a grasp of mechanics. Yet there is an equally persistent folklore that celebrates the outsider: the amateur who solves a problem that has defeated the professionals precisely because he or she has never been taught how it ought to be approached. Each of these accounts contains an element of truth, and the research of the last two decades has done much to show when each applies. Neither picture, however, is adequate on its own, and the more interesting question is not whether expertise helps or hinders creative thought, but how it can do both at once.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The hindering effect has a name: the Einstellung effect, from the German for 'attitude' or 'set'. When a familiar method comes to mind, it tends to block the search for better ones. Ksenia Lavrentyeva, a cognitive scientist at the Volga Institute of Psychology, demonstrated this with experienced chess players. Presented with a position that could be won by a well-known five-move sequence, most failed to notice a quicker three-move solution, though they found it easily when the familiar option was removed from the board. More revealingly, eye-tracking equipment showed that the players' gaze kept returning to the squares associated with the familiar plan, even while they insisted they were looking for alternatives. Only grandmasters of the very highest rank escaped the trap, and even they took noticeably longer than when no familiar solution was available.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If knowledge can blind, perhaps there is an optimum amount of it. This is the view of the economist Ugo Pascarella, who analysed several hundred thousand patents and found that the most original inventions, judged by how often later patents cited them, came from inventors with an intermediate depth of experience in the relevant field. Newcomers lacked the tools to contribute, while veterans tended to refine existing designs rather than replacing them. Pascarella's data are impressive, but his conclusion may be less secure than it appears. Citation counts reward inventions that open up crowded fields, and long-serving inventors are more often found in mature areas where fewer new patents are filed; the downturn at the top of his curve may therefore owe something to how originality was measured rather than to the inventors themselves.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The case of the successful outsider has been examined most closely by Folasade Ilesanmi of the Port Harcourt Business School, who studied thousands of entries to online contests in which companies post unsolved technical problems and offer prizes for solutions. Strikingly, the further a solver's own discipline lay from the domain of the problem, the more likely that solver was to win. A chemist might crack a problem in biology, or a physicist one in materials engineering. Ilesanmi is careful to point out, however, that the winners were rarely novices; most possessed deep specialist training, simply in a different field. This qualification tends to vanish from popular retellings, which prefer the story of the gifted amateur, and the loss is not trivial: it turns a finding about the transfer of expertise into a misleading argument against expertise itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of knowledge have their own evidence. Henrik Strandquist, a psychologist at the Trøndelag Centre for Creative Studies, points to what is often called the ten-year rule: in a survey of celebrated composers, painters and scientists, almost none produced a major work without roughly a decade of intensive preparation. Fixation, in Strandquist's view, is a genuine cost, but it is a modest price for the competence that makes any significant contribution possible. The argument has force, but the evidence on which it rests is narrower than it looks. Surveys of famous creators include only those who succeeded; those who trained for ten years and produced nothing of note, and those who made an impact after a much shorter apprenticeship but were later forgotten, are invisible in such samples.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most practical contribution comes from Yuriko Tachibana and her colleagues at the Sendai Design Laboratory, who have asked whether the rigidity of experts can be loosened deliberately. In one series of experiments, professional engineers were asked to redesign everyday objects. Those instructed first to describe each component in terms of its function, as 'something that joins two surfaces' rather than 'a screw', generated nearly twice as many novel designs as those given no such instruction. Working in teams that combined different specialisms produced a similar, though smaller, benefit. These results are encouraging, but some caution is needed: none of the techniques has yet been tested on projects lasting longer than an afternoon, and it is not obvious that a trick which works in a short laboratory session would survive months of real design work.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is that the important variable is less the quantity of knowledge a person possesses than the way in which it is held. Expertise that is organised around rigid procedures tends to produce the fixation Lavrentyeva observed; expertise that is organised around underlying principles can be carried into unfamiliar domains, as Ilesanmi's prize-winners carried theirs. If this is right, then education and professional training should aim not merely at accumulating knowledge but at teaching people to see it from more than one angle. That is a harder goal to assess, but it is the one most likely to produce genuinely creative work.

topic: cultural differences in how creativity is understood: novelty versus the reworking of tradition
title: Whose Idea of Originality?
subtitle: Research across cultures is challenging the assumption that creativity means breaking with the past

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most psychology textbooks define creativity in two parts: a creative product must be both novel and appropriate, original and in some way useful. The definition appears neutral, almost technical, and it underpins decades of research. Yet in practice the second criterion has received far less attention than the first, and novelty has come to be understood chiefly as a break with what came before. This emphasis is presented as though it were a universal truth about the human mind. In reality, it reflects a particular intellectual history, and a growing body of cross-cultural research suggests that other societies have weighed the two criteria rather differently. Because most of the foundational studies were carried out on university students in a handful of wealthy nations, this narrow emphasis was rarely noticed, let alone questioned.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited evidence comes from a survey conducted by Bolat Temirkhanuly of the Shymkent Institute of Social Research, who asked over six thousand adults in eight countries to rate a series of paintings, inventions and pieces of music. Respondents in East Asian countries tended to give their highest marks to work that reinterpreted inherited forms, while those in North America and Western Europe preferred work that departed radically from convention. These results are often quoted as proof of a sharp divide between cultures. Less often mentioned is Temirkhanuly's further observation that the variation within each country was almost as great as the variation between them, a finding that deserves far more attention than it has received.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Part of the apparent contrast may be historical rather than geographical. The cultural historian Marguerite Desrosiers has argued that the European cult of originality is surprisingly young. Medieval craftsmen were admired for faithfully reproducing approved designs, and Renaissance painters spent years copying the canvases of the masters who trained them, both as an apprenticeship and as a form of homage. Only in the eighteenth century, as copyright laws were introduced and the figure of the solitary genius took hold in literature, did originality become the chief measure of artistic worth. Seen in this light, a comparison between modern Western and traditional Eastern attitudes is, to a considerable degree, a comparison between two different centuries.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have questioned whether creativity should be located in individuals at all. Mele Akoteu, an anthropologist who has worked for many years in Pacific Island communities, describes societies in which songs are composed collectively and are credited to ancestors rather than to the people who actually composed them. In such settings, she argues, an instrument that scores individuals for the originality of their ideas is simply measuring the wrong thing. Her point is important, but it carries a risk of romanticising the communities concerned. Akoteu's own field notes record that particularly gifted composers were widely known and informally honoured, which suggests that individual contribution is recognised even where it is not formally claimed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The question is not merely academic, because assessment tools travel. Standard divergent thinking tests, which ask people to produce as many unusual uses as possible for an everyday object, were developed in the United States and are now used in schools and companies around the world. When Do-yeon Gweon and her colleagues at the Busan Centre for Educational Measurement gave such tests to students in South Korea and Canada, the Korean students scored lower on originality. However, when the scoring was revised to give credit for elaboration and for the appropriateness of ideas, the difference between the two groups disappeared entirely. The implication, I believe, is that such tests measure not creativity as such but the degree to which a person's thinking matches one cultural ideal.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that cultural differences run so deep. The psychologist Rodrigo Condarco, whose team has studied judgements of creativity in fourteen societies, points out that people in every culture he examined drew a line between work that was creative and work that was merely competent, and that they largely agreed about which examples fell on each side of it. In his view, what varies is emphasis rather than substance. He adds that the qualities people mentioned when explaining their judgements, such as surprise, technical command and emotional power, were remarkably similar from one society to the next. This seems to me broadly correct: cultures appear to differ less in what they understand creativity to be than in how much weight they place on its separate features.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If so, the practical lesson is one of balance. Education systems in many countries have recently adopted programmes that encourage children to challenge convention and to think 'outside the box', often borrowing teaching materials designed elsewhere. There is nothing wrong with that ambition, and it would be a mistake to abandon it. The aim should rather be to widen the definition so that it also recognises the quieter forms of invention that many traditions have long prized. But a conception of creativity that values only rupture risks overlooking the patient reworking of tradition through which much of the world's art, craft and science has in fact advanced.

topic: mood and creativity: whether positive or negative emotions foster creative thinking
title: Feeling Inventive
subtitle: Does a good mood make us more creative, or is the link between emotion and originality more complicated than it first appeared?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask people to picture a creative person at work, and two quite different images tend to emerge. One is the tormented artist, whose best work is wrung from despair; the other is the buoyant inventor, sketching ideas on a whiteboard in a burst of enthusiasm. Psychology has, for most of its history, sided firmly with the second image. A series of laboratory studies beginning in the 1980s found that participants who had been put in a good mood were noticeably more likely to solve puzzles that require a sudden insight. These findings were taken up with remarkable speed by management consultants and the authors of self-help books, who presented them as proof that happy employees are inventive employees. In my view, that enthusiasm ran well ahead of the evidence, and the story that has emerged since is considerably more interesting.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation of the early results was developed by Ksenia Ruskule of the Daugavpils Institute of Cognitive Science. Ruskule proposes that pleasant feelings widen the scope of attention, so that ideas only loosely connected to the task at hand are more likely to come to mind. In one of her best-known experiments, participants who had just recalled a happy memory produced far more unusual responses on a word-association task than those who had recalled a neutral one. Yet Ruskule herself has always been careful about the limits of this effect. Her data show that a cheerful mood helps most when a problem demands switching between different perspectives, and that it offers little advantage, and sometimes even a slight disadvantage, when success depends on sticking doggedly to a single line of attack.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That qualification is the starting point for a rival account put forward by Tadeusz Pstrokoński at the Wielkopolska University of Social Sciences. Pstrokoński argues that negative moods act as a signal that something in the environment is amiss, and that they consequently push people towards careful, systematic thought. In his studies, participants made mildly sad by a melancholy film generated fewer ideas than their cheerful counterparts in the first few minutes. When they were allowed to keep working for half an hour, however, the ideas they eventually produced were judged by independent raters to be of higher quality. It is tempting to treat Ruskule and Pstrokoński as opponents. But their findings are less contradictory than they seem: one describes a route to creativity through breadth, the other a route through persistence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third group has argued that both camps have been asking the wrong question. Lerato Ntsoane and her colleagues at the KwaZulu Centre for Behavioural Research point out that moods differ not only in how pleasant they feel but also in how strongly they energise the body and mind. Happiness and anger are both high-energy states, while contentment and sadness are low-energy ones. When the team pooled the results of more than a hundred published experiments, they found that the pleasant-unpleasant distinction made only a modest difference to creative performance, whereas the energising quality of a mood made a considerable one. Anger proved especially revealing: angry participants produced a rush of ideas, though not particularly original ones, and this advantage evaporated within minutes. This reframing is, I think, the most useful contribution the field has made in a generation. It does, however, rest almost entirely on laboratory work, and that is a significant limitation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The problem is that the moods induced in experiments are, by necessity, mild and fleeting. Film clips and remembered birthdays tilt feelings for a few minutes, but such manipulations are far weaker and shorter-lived than the emotions people actually bring to their working lives. To address this gap, Ingrid Bjørnevik of the Stavanger Institute of Organisational Psychology asked 220 employees in seven companies to complete a brief diary every evening for four months. Positive mood on a given day reliably predicted creative thinking not only on that day but also on the next, as if good feelings set in motion a process that continued overnight. Days of frustration were occasionally followed by a breakthrough, but this pattern was rare, and Bjørnevik regards it as too infrequent to support any general conclusion.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Diary studies also leave open the question of which way causation runs. Mateo Choquehuanca, a psychologist who studies amateur musicians and painters in Bolivia, argues that in everyday life creative activity is at least as likely to improve mood as the reverse. Becoming absorbed in a demanding piece of work, he notes, tends to leave people feeling more cheerful afterwards, much as a session of physical exercise does. If he is right, some of the association recorded by Bjørnevik may reflect creative days producing good moods rather than good moods producing creative days. Choquehuanca's argument does not overturn the laboratory evidence, where mood is deliberately manipulated before any task begins, but it ought to make anyone interpreting workplace data considerably more cautious.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Many organisations have responded to the popular message by installing games rooms, organising team outings and otherwise attempting to keep their staff in a permanent state of good cheer. Such efforts are harmless enough, but they are founded on a misunderstanding. If different moods favour different kinds of thinking, then a team that is always buoyant may be well equipped to generate possibilities and poorly equipped to scrutinise them. A more realistic aim would be to recognise that the ebb and flow of emotion across a project has its uses, and that the unsettled feeling which accompanies a stubborn problem is not always something to be eliminated. Emotions, in short, are better regarded as instruments of creative work than as obstacles to it.

topic: boredom as a possible spur to creativity: daydreaming, replication doubts, types of boredom and smartphones
title: The Uses of Tedium
subtitle: Psychologists disagree over whether boredom is a hidden creative resource or simply an unpleasant waste of time

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a study that has since been cited thousands of times, volunteers at the Opole Institute of Applied Psychology spent fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory before being asked to think of as many uses as they could for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with a group who had moved directly to the cup task, the copiers came up with significantly more ideas, and more unusual ones. The study's author, Agnieszka Sobolewska, was cautious about what it showed, but the popular press was not: headlines declared that boredom was the secret of creative genius. Such claims were exaggerated, yet they did have the merit of challenging a long-standing prejudice. For centuries, boredom has been treated by moralists as a sign of idleness or weak character, and that reputation is, in my view, only partly deserved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Psychologists today tend to regard boredom not as a failing but as a signal. According to this functional account, the unpleasant feeling of being bored arises when an activity seems to lack meaning or challenge, and it motivates us to look for something better to do. I find this view persuasive: boredom appears to work much as pain or hunger do, as an uncomfortable state whose purpose is to make us change what we are doing. Sobolewska has suggested one route by which this search might lead to creative thinking. When the outside world fails to hold our interest, attention drifts inwards, and the resulting daydreams allow distant ideas to meet. Consistent with this, her later experiments found the effect to be strongest when the dull task was passive, such as reading a list, rather than one requiring active effort, such as writing it out.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all attempts to repeat these findings have been successful. Kayode Ajibewa of the Osun Centre for Experimental Psychology coordinated a replication involving more than six hundred participants in five laboratories, using identical instructions and an analysis plan registered in advance. He did find that bored participants scored higher on the creative task, but the advantage was only about a third the size of the one originally reported. Ajibewa also offers a less flattering explanation for it. Anyone who has just endured a tedious exercise, he argues, is likely to welcome almost any other activity, and may therefore throw themselves into it with greater energy; the higher scores, on this reading, reflect relief rather than inspiration. This is a serious objection, and it should temper the more extravagant claims. It does not, however, dispose of the effect altogether, since a smaller but genuine benefit remains in his own data.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that boredom comes in more than one form. The Chilean psychologist Marisol Undurraga distinguishes between what she calls restless boredom, an agitated state in which people actively search for stimulation, and apathetic boredom, in which they become listless and withdrawn. In her studies, only the restless kind was associated with creative output. The apathetic kind was linked instead with low mood and, when it persisted for months, with symptoms of depression. Undurraga suspects that which form a person experiences depends partly on whether they believe they could escape the dull situation if they wished. This distinction matters a great deal, because it shows how risky it is to present boredom as an unqualified good. For people trapped in monotonous jobs or in long periods of unemployment, boredom is rarely a spur to invention; it is more often a source of real distress.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe that modern technology is changing the role boredom plays in our lives. The sociologist Dávid Szendrei points out that the smartphone has made it possible to banish idle moments almost entirely, whether in a queue, on a train or in a waiting room. In a survey of 2,400 adults, he found that those who habitually reached for their phones whenever they had nothing to do reported having fewer original ideas in daily life. Szendrei concludes that constant distraction is depriving people of the mental wandering that boredom once encouraged. The argument is plausible, but I am not convinced that his evidence supports it. A survey of this kind cannot establish which way the influence runs, and many people use their phones precisely to find material that sparks new ideas.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What practical lessons follow? Some educators have proposed that children should occasionally be left with nothing to do, in the hope that they will learn to entertain themselves imaginatively. There may be something in this, but it would be a mistake to conclude that dullness should be engineered for its own sake. The value of boredom, if it has any, lies not in the feeling itself but in what it prompts people to do. A bored child who is free to wander, invent a game or take something apart may indeed discover something new; one confined to a desk with no alternatives will simply be miserable. The crucial ingredient, in other words, is not boredom but the freedom to respond to it.

topic: the universality of facial expressions of emotion across cultures
title: Reading the Face
subtitle: Is a scowl understood as anger everywhere in the world? A long-standing assumption about emotion is under renewed scrutiny

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in psychology have seemed as secure as the claim that a smile means the same thing everywhere. According to the view that dominated the field for much of the late twentieth century, a small set of emotions, usually listed as happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, are biologically hard-wired, and each is accompanied by a distinctive facial configuration that people in every culture produce and recognise without instruction. The theory had an elegant simplicity, and it shaped not only academic research but also airport security training, lie-detection courses and, more recently, commercial software. Yet over the past two decades its foundations have been questioned so persistently that it can no longer be treated as settled fact.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The original evidence came largely from recognition studies. Participants were shown photographs of actors posing exaggerated expressions and asked to choose a matching emotion word from a short list. In early studies conducted in Europe, North America and Japan, agreement rates were impressively high, often exceeding eighty per cent. Researchers then took the photographs to remote communities with little exposure to Western media and reported similar, if somewhat lower, levels of agreement. To supporters such as Professor Ilse Skjervheim of the Bergen Institute for Behavioural Science, these results remain compelling. When people who have never seen a film or a magazine interpret a scowl as anger, she argues, the most economical explanation is that the link between the two is part of our shared biology rather than something acquired from the surrounding culture.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics, however, have focused on the method rather than the results. The anthropologist Dr Kofi Adomah-Kwarteng points out that offering participants a short list of words effectively hands them the answer: with only six options, a person can reach the expected choice by elimination, even if the face itself conveys very little. When his team repeated the procedure in two villages in northern Ghana but asked participants to describe each face in their own words, agreement collapsed. A face posed as fearful was frequently described as showing surprise, threat or even readiness to attack, and many participants described what the person was doing rather than what they were feeling. In Adomah-Kwarteng's view, the high agreement scores of earlier studies were produced less by the faces than by the format of the questions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of criticism concerns the faces themselves. Posed expressions are caricatures, deliberately exaggerated to be unmistakable, and they may bear little resemblance to the movements people actually make when they experience an emotion. A large analysis led by Dr Mariela Zaldua at the Bilbao Centre for Affective Studies examined thousands of video recordings of people in real situations, from sporting victories to bereavements. Her group found that people scowled when angry only around a third of the time, and that they scowled frequently when they were not angry at all, while concentrating hard, for example, or squinting in bright sunlight. The relationship between an inner state and an outward expression, she concludes, is real but far looser and more dependent on context than the classic theory allows.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, though, to conclude that facial expressions are entirely arbitrary. Some findings have proved remarkably durable. Smiles are associated with positive situations in virtually every society that has been studied, and infants born blind produce smiles and frowns despite never having seen them. What seems to be emerging is not a straightforward victory for either side but a more nuanced picture, in which certain broad dimensions of feeling, such as whether an experience is pleasant or unpleasant, calm or agitated, are signalled fairly reliably, while the finer distinctions between specific emotions depend heavily on learning and circumstance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Skjervheim accepts some of this. She concedes that posed photographs exaggerate the consistency of real expressions, but maintains that the critics have overcorrected, treating the noisiness of everyday behaviour as proof that no universal signals exist. Her position deserves more sympathy than it sometimes receives: variation in how often a signal is used does not by itself show that the signal has no biological basis, any more than the existence of different accents proves that humans lack an inborn capacity for speech. Nevertheless, the burden of proof has shifted. The confident claim that six emotions can be read from six faces now looks much harder to defend than it did a generation ago.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate matters well beyond the laboratory. Several technology companies sell systems that claim to detect emotions from images of faces, and these have been marketed for uses ranging from job interviews to classroom monitoring. Such products typically rest on the assumption that a particular arrangement of facial muscles corresponds to a particular feeling, which is precisely the assumption that recent research has weakened. Until the science is far more certain than it is today, the use of these tools to make decisions about people's lives should be regarded with considerable suspicion. The study of the face, it turns out, has as much to teach us about the limits of scientific confidence as about emotion itself.

topic: emotional granularity: describing feelings precisely and its links to coping and wellbeing
title: The Words for What We Feel
subtitle: Does a precise emotional vocabulary help people cope with adversity, or has a promising idea run ahead of its evidence?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask a group of people how they are feeling and many will offer a single, broad word: good, bad, stressed, fine. Others reach for something more exact, describing themselves as irritated rather than angry, wistful rather than sad, apprehensive rather than anxious. Psychologists have a name for this difference. 'Emotional granularity' refers to the precision with which a person distinguishes between their own feelings, and over the past fifteen years it has moved from a curiosity of personality research to a subject of intense interest in clinical psychology. The reason is a series of findings suggesting that people who describe their feelings in fine detail cope better with adversity. If those findings hold, granularity may be one of the more teachable components of emotional health. Whether the case has yet been made, however, is far less certain than its enthusiasts suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Granularity is usually measured through a technique known as experience sampling. Participants carry a phone that prompts them several times a day, over a period of weeks, to rate how strongly they are feeling each of a list of emotions. Statisticians then examine how closely the ratings move together. A person whose scores for anger, sadness and fear rise and fall in unison is assumed to be experiencing a general sense of feeling bad; one whose scores diverge is assumed to be drawing finer distinctions. The method has the advantage of capturing emotion as it happens, rather than relying on memory, but it measures granularity only indirectly, through patterns in numbers rather than through anything a participant actually says about their experience.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Using this approach, Dr Nadia Velkarova and her colleagues at the Sofia Laboratory for Emotion Research followed more than four hundred adults through a difficult period in their lives, such as a divorce, a redundancy or the illness of a parent. Those with high granularity scores were noticeably less likely to respond to their distress by drinking heavily or behaving aggressively towards others. Velkarova's explanation is that a precise label works rather like a diagnosis. Knowing that one is disappointed rather than merely upset points towards particular remedies, whereas an undifferentiated sense of distress offers no guidance about what to do next.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Hemi Amadou-Bey of the Wellington School of Psychology goes further, arguing that granularity does not merely describe emotions but helps to create them. On this 'constructionist' account, the brain continually predicts what bodily sensations mean, drawing on concepts acquired through language and culture; a person with a richer stock of emotion concepts can therefore construct a wider range of experiences. Amadou-Bey points to languages that contain emotion words with no exact English equivalent, and suggests that learning such words may allow speakers to feel things they could not previously identify. It is an intriguing hypothesis, but the evidence for it remains thin: showing that people can learn a new word for a feeling is not the same as showing that the word has changed the feeling itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics have raised more basic concerns. Dr Sunil Amarasekera, a statistician at the Colombo Institute of Health Sciences, notes that the standard measure of granularity is sensitive to how participants use rating scales. Some people simply avoid extreme numbers, or give every item a similar rating when they are tired or bored; such habits can make a person appear to have low granularity even if their emotional life is highly differentiated. Amarasekera has also found that granularity scores correlate with verbal intelligence and years of education, raising the possibility that some of its apparent benefits reflect these broader advantages rather than emotional precision as such. His work does not demonstrate that granularity is meaningless, but it does suggest that some of the more striking findings should be treated as provisional.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication is cultural. A team led by Oksana Kovalchyk at the Kyiv Centre for Cross-Cultural Psychology compared participants in several countries and found that the benefits associated with granularity were weaker in societies where emotions are typically understood in terms of relationships rather than as private inner states. Where the question 'how do you feel?' is seldom asked, Kovalchyk suggests, the ability to answer it precisely may matter less. This finding is a useful corrective to the tendency to treat a Western model of emotional self-awareness as a universal ideal.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this has prevented the concept from being taken up enthusiastically by therapists, schools and the wellbeing industry. Mobile applications now offer 'emotion wheels' with dozens of labels, and some school programmes encourage children to expand their emotional vocabulary from an early age. Whether these interventions actually increase granularity, as distinct from increasing the number of words children can list, has rarely been tested. Velkarova's own small trial found that a six-week training course raised scores on her measure, but the improvement had largely disappeared three months later.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It would nonetheless be unfortunate if justified scepticism led to the idea being abandoned altogether. The core intuition, that understanding what one feels is a step towards managing it, is plausible and is supported by more than one line of evidence. What is needed now is not more enthusiasm but better measurement, longer follow-up studies and greater attention to cultural difference. Until then, a richer emotional vocabulary is best regarded as a promising tool rather than a proven cure.

topic: interoception: perceiving the body's internal signals and its role in emotional experience
title: Listening to the Heart
subtitle: An old idea about the bodily roots of emotion has returned, but measuring what people sense inside themselves is proving harder than expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: More than a century ago, one influential school of thought proposed a counter-intuitive sequence of events: we do not tremble because we are afraid; we are afraid because we tremble. On this view, emotions are perceptions of changes in the body, such as a racing heart or a tightening stomach, rather than the cause of those changes. For much of the twentieth century the idea was regarded as little more than a historical curiosity, undermined by experiments showing that quite different emotions could be accompanied by very similar physiological changes. In recent years, however, it has returned in a modified form, under the banner of a field known as interoception: the study of how the brain senses the internal state of the body.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Interoception covers signals from the heart, lungs, gut and bladder, as well as sensations such as temperature and itch. The brain receives a constant stream of such information, most of which never reaches conscious awareness. Researchers have become particularly interested in individual differences in how accurately people perceive these signals, which they most often assess with heartbeat tasks. In the commonest version, participants are asked to count their heartbeats silently over several short intervals, without touching their wrist or chest, and their counts are compared with a recording of their actual heart rate. Some people turn out to be remarkably accurate; others miss more than half of their beats.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Liisa Laaksovirta of the Tampere Centre for Psychophysiology has spent a decade exploring what these differences mean. In a series of studies, she found that people who counted their heartbeats accurately rated emotional photographs as more intense than poor counters did, and showed larger changes in skin conductance while viewing them. She argues that interoceptive accuracy acts rather like the volume control on a radio: the more clearly a person perceives their body, the more vividly they experience emotion. Her group has also linked poor accuracy to alexithymia, a trait characterised by difficulty in identifying and describing one's own feelings.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The heartbeat counting task, however, has come under sustained attack. Professor Ikenna Mbadiwe, a physiologist at the University of Port Harcourt, notes that many participants do not actually perceive their heartbeats at all but estimate them from what they know about typical heart rates. Someone who believes the heart beats around seventy times a minute can produce a fairly accurate count simply by guessing, and when Mbadiwe's team supplied participants with false information about average heart rates, their counts shifted in the direction of the misleading figure. In his view, a large part of the literature on interoceptive accuracy measures knowledge and beliefs about the body rather than perception of it. The criticism is a serious one, and it has not yet been fully answered.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Alternative measures do exist. In heartbeat discrimination tasks, participants hear a series of tones and judge whether they are in time with their pulse or slightly delayed. Such tasks are much harder to solve by guessing, but they are also so difficult that many participants perform no better than chance, which makes differences between individuals hard to detect. Dr Ayaka Nakashiba of the Osaka Institute of Cognitive Science suggests that the field has placed too much weight on the heart, largely because it is the organ whose activity is easiest to record. Signals from the stomach and lungs may be just as important for emotion, she argues, and breathing is unusual in being under both automatic and voluntary control, which makes it a promising route for research and perhaps for therapy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Clinical researchers have taken a keen interest in these debates. People with panic disorder, for instance, appear to be unusually watchful of sensations from the heart, and may interpret a harmless skipped beat as the onset of a heart attack, setting off a spiral of fear. A team led by Emre Kerimoğlu at the Ankara Clinical Psychology Unit has trialled a form of training in which anxious patients practise detecting their heartbeat while receiving feedback on their accuracy. Early results suggested a reduction in symptoms. Kerimoğlu himself stresses that his trials were small and lacked a convincing comparison group, an admirable caution, given that patients who receive any kind of attention from a therapist often report feeling better.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where, then, does the field stand? It would be premature to claim that interoception explains emotion. The relationship between body and feeling plainly runs in both directions: emotions alter heart rate and breathing, and those changes in turn feed back into experience. What the revival has achieved is to restore the body to a central place in the study of emotion, after decades in which emotions were treated mainly as thoughts or judgements. That shift is welcome, whatever becomes of the specific claims currently attached to it. Yet the field's progress will depend less on bold theory than on the unglamorous work of developing measures that genuinely capture what they claim to capture.

topic: emotion regulation strategies: cognitive reappraisal versus expressive suppression and the case for flexibility
title: The Art of Feeling Differently
subtitle: Psychologists once ranked the ways people manage their emotions from best to worst. The evidence now suggests that the question was badly posed.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Everyone attempts, at least occasionally, to change what they feel. A student calms herself before an examination by telling herself that the result will not decide her future; a manager listens to an infuriating complaint with a fixed, neutral smile. Psychologists group such efforts under the heading of emotion regulation, and for roughly three decades a single comparison has dominated the field. On one side stands cognitive reappraisal, which involves reinterpreting a situation so that its emotional meaning changes. On the other stands expressive suppression, the attempt to conceal an emotion that has already arisen. The prevailing verdict has been unambiguous: reappraisal is healthy, suppression is costly. That verdict contains a good deal of truth, but it has hardened into a slogan, and slogans are poor guides to the messy business of everyday feeling.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against suppression rests on a substantial body of laboratory work. In a typical experiment, volunteers watch a distressing film while some of them are instructed to keep their faces perfectly still. Dr Lieve Vranckx, whose group at the Scheldt Institute for Affective Science has run dozens of such studies, reports that suppressors feel just as bad as those who watch freely, yet show greater activation of the sympathetic nervous system, as measured by blood pressure and skin conductance. They also remember less of what they saw, presumably because monitoring one's own face consumes attention that would otherwise be devoted to the film. Reappraisers, by contrast, report reduced distress with no comparable physiological penalty. Vranckx concludes that suppression treats the symptom while leaving the underlying emotion intact, and so imposes a double burden on the person who relies on it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Large-scale surveys appeared to confirm the laboratory picture. People who say they habitually hide their feelings tend to report lower life satisfaction, fewer close relationships and more symptoms of depression than those who habitually reinterpret events. Yet correlations of this sort are notoriously difficult to interpret. It may be that suppression erodes wellbeing; it may equally be that people who are already unhappy or socially isolated simply have more feelings they wish to hide. In my view, the field moved too quickly from experiments lasting a few minutes to confident claims about lifelong habits, and the second inference was never as secure as the first.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more serious challenge has come from cultural psychology. Professor Kwabena Akuffo-Twene of the Accra Centre for Behavioural Research compared students from societies that prize emotional restraint with students from societies that encourage open expression. Among the latter, habitual suppression was associated with poorer mood, exactly as earlier research had predicted. Among the former, the association largely disappeared. Akuffo-Twene argues that where restraint is a widely shared value, concealing anger or disappointment is experienced not as a lonely act of self-denial but as an ordinary courtesy that others recognise and return. On this account, the costs of suppression documented in the laboratory partly reflect the cultural assumptions of the participants who happened to be tested, most of whom were undergraduates at a small number of Western universities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Reappraisal, meanwhile, has proved less uniformly beneficial than its reputation suggests. Dr Mirela Stănculescu, a clinical psychologist at the Transylvanian Clinic for Mood Disorders, followed adults who were coping with different kinds of stress. When the stressor was something they could not alter, such as a relative's terminal illness, those who reappraised more often fared better. When the stressor lay within their power to change, for example an exploitative employer, frequent reappraisal predicted worse outcomes, since persuading oneself that a bad situation is acceptable may remove the motivation to improve it. Stănculescu's findings have not yet been widely replicated, but they expose an awkward assumption in much of the earlier work: that feeling better is always the goal. Sometimes an unpleasant emotion is precisely the signal that action is required.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Results of this kind have encouraged a shift from asking which strategy is best to asking how flexibly people choose among strategies. A team at the Nordic Centre for Emotion Studies led by Ingrid Haugseter proposes that regulatory flexibility has three components: sensitivity to the demands of the context, a broad repertoire of strategies, and the capacity to notice when a chosen strategy is failing and to switch to another. In the team's longitudinal studies, it was this flexibility, rather than a preference for any single technique, that best predicted resilience after bereavement or the loss of a job. The idea is attractive, and it accords with ordinary experience, since few people would wish to reinterpret a fire alarm as a pleasant surprise. Its weakness is that flexibility is far harder to measure than a questionnaire item asking how often someone hides their feelings, and the early tasks designed to capture it rely heavily on artificial choices made in the laboratory.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the original findings were wrong. Suppression maintained over long periods probably does carry costs for many people, and reappraisal remains one of the most useful techniques that therapists teach. What has changed is the recognition that a strategy cannot be evaluated in isolation from the person using it, the situation in which it is used and the culture that gives it meaning. That is a less tidy conclusion than the one psychology offered a generation ago, but it is a considerably more honest one, and it may ultimately prove more helpful to anyone who is trying to manage a difficult feeling.

topic: nostalgia: from a diagnosed illness to a studied emotion with psychological functions and possible costs
title: A Longing for Yesterday
subtitle: Once classified as a disease, nostalgia is now studied as a psychological resource, though perhaps not an unlimited one

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late seventeenth century, a Swiss medical student coined the word 'nostalgia', joining the Greek terms for homecoming and pain, to describe an illness he had observed among soldiers serving far from their native valleys. The symptoms he recorded included fever, loss of appetite and persistent weeping, and for the next two hundred years physicians treated the condition as a genuine and potentially fatal disorder. Some army doctors even banned the singing of certain folk songs that were believed to trigger it. By the twentieth century the medical label had faded, but nostalgia retained a faintly disreputable air, regarded by psychologists as a form of depression and by social critics as a sentimental refusal to face the present.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That reputation has been substantially revised over the past two decades. Dr Despina Pelekanos, a social psychologist at the Cycladic Institute of Human Development, was among the first to collect large numbers of written accounts in which people described nostalgic episodes. Analysing several thousand of these narratives, her team found that they followed a characteristic pattern. They often began with a disappointment or a loss but tended to end on a note of warmth, typically featuring the writer surrounded by family or friends at a significant occasion such as a wedding or a holiday. Pelekanos describes nostalgia as a 'redemptive' emotion: bittersweet, certainly, but with the sweetness usually outweighing the bitterness. Her team also noted that nostalgic narratives were considerably more likely than ordinary autobiographical stories to mention other people by name.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experimental studies have since suggested that nostalgia performs identifiable psychological functions. When participants in laboratory studies are induced to feel lonely, for instance by being told that their personality profile predicts a solitary future, they spontaneously report more nostalgic thoughts, and those who are then prompted to recall a cherished memory subsequently describe themselves as more socially supported. Professor Ruwan Gunawardana of the Kandy Institute of Psychological Science has extended this work to physical sensations. In one study, volunteers who sat in a cool room reported more nostalgia than those in a warm one, and nostalgic recollection appeared to make them feel slightly warmer. Gunawardana interprets nostalgia as a kind of regulatory mechanism, summoned automatically whenever people feel cold, isolated or uncertain about the meaning of their lives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These findings are intriguing, and the consistency with which they have been reported across different countries is impressive. Yet the methods deserve some scrutiny. Many of the experiments rely on participants rating their own feelings minutes after a brief manipulation, and the effects, though statistically reliable, are often modest in size. Few studies have followed participants beyond a single session, and fewer still have examined whether repeated nostalgic reflection produces any lasting change. It would be a mistake, in my opinion, to conclude from such evidence that nostalgia is a dependable remedy for loneliness, still less that it could replace the human contact it seems to stand in for. The laboratory shows that a pleasant memory can lift the mood of someone who has briefly been made to feel alone; it says rather less about the person who has been isolated for years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Indeed, there are reasons to think that nostalgia has a darker side. Dr Bożena Kaczmarska, who studies emotion and ageing at the Mazovian Centre for Social Research, distinguishes between personal nostalgia, which concerns one's own past, and what she calls 'historical nostalgia', a longing for an era that the individual may never have experienced. She has found that people who frequently idealise a collective past tend to view the present more negatively and are more likely to express distrust of outsiders. Kaczmarska is careful to point out that her data are correlational and cannot show which comes first. Nonetheless, the political uses of a romanticised history are hardly a new phenomenon, and it seems reasonable to worry that the comfort of a remembered past can be turned against the actual present.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have also questioned whether personal nostalgia is beneficial for everyone. Among people who score highly on measures of anxiety, recalling happier times can apparently prompt painful comparisons, leaving them feeling worse rather than better. Pelekanos acknowledges this pattern but argues that it affects only a minority and that, for most people, the emotion's net effect is positive. This seems to me a fair summary of the present evidence, provided that it is not taken as a licence to recommend nostalgia indiscriminately.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the commercial world has drawn its own conclusions. Advertisers routinely deploy the music, typefaces and colours of earlier decades, and the revival of vinyl records, instant cameras and reissued video games suggests that the past is an exceptionally marketable commodity. Film studios remake the children's programmes of their audiences' youth, and entire radio stations broadcast nothing but the songs of a single decade. Whether this represents a healthy use of a valuable emotion or a cynical exploitation of it is a question that psychology alone cannot answer. What the research does make clear is that nostalgia is neither the illness it was once thought to be nor the simple tonic it is sometimes now presented as, but something more interesting than either: an emotion that draws on the past in order to manage the present.

topic: measuring emotional states in non-human animals: judgement bias tests, positive welfare and the problem of animal feelings
title: The Optimistic Rat
subtitle: Scientists have devised ingenious ways of asking animals how they feel. Interpreting the answers is another matter.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Nineteenth-century naturalists wrote freely of dogs that were jealous, parrots that sulked and elephants that grieved. For much of the twentieth century, however, such language was banished from serious biology. Under the influence of behaviourism, scientists were trained to describe only what an animal did, not what it might feel, and to attribute emotions to other species was dismissed as sentimental anthropomorphism. The caution was understandable, given how easily observers project their own moods onto creatures they are fond of. But the pendulum swung too far. By refusing even to ask whether animals have emotional lives, researchers left a question of obvious moral importance to be settled by intuition and advertising rather than evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central difficulty is that animals cannot describe their experiences. Dr Aarne Hautala of the Boreal Institute of Animal Welfare proposes a pragmatic solution. Emotions, he argues, have components that can be measured objectively: changes in heart rate and stress hormones, characteristic postures and vocalisations, and shifts in attention and decision-making. Science should concentrate on these 'affective states' and leave aside, at least for now, the philosophical question of whether any conscious feeling accompanies them. The proposal has made the field respectable, and much useful work has followed from it. Yet it quietly sidesteps the very issue that concerns most people who care about animal welfare, since an animal's suffering matters morally only if there is something it is like, for that animal, to suffer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the most influential techniques to emerge from this approach is the judgement bias test. In a typical version, rats are trained that one tone signals the delivery of food while another signals a mildly unpleasant burst of noise, and they learn to respond differently to each. They are then played a tone pitched halfway between the two. Rats housed in large, stimulating enclosures tend to treat the ambiguous tone as a promise of food, while those kept in small, barren cages are more likely to treat it as a warning. The pattern mirrors a well-established finding in humans, among whom anxious or depressed individuals interpret ambiguous situations more negatively. Versions of the test have since been applied to sheep, dogs, chickens and even honeybees: bees that had been vigorously shaken, in a manner intended to simulate an attack by a predator, became less inclined to approach an odour that lay between one associated with sugar and one associated with a bitter taste.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It was the bee experiments that prompted Dr Camila Gjesdal, a comparative psychologist at the Patagonian Centre for Animal Cognition, to question what the test really measures. A change in the threshold at which an organism decides to approach or avoid, she points out, could be produced by a very simple mechanism, one that might equally be built into a robot. Such a shift in response bias does not in itself demonstrate that any emotion is present, let alone that it is felt. Her argument is logically sound, but it arguably proves too much. Applied consistently, it would also oblige us to doubt the emotions of other human beings, whose inner lives we likewise infer from behaviour rather than observe directly. What Gjesdal's critique really shows is that no single test can carry the whole weight of the argument.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of research has focused on pleasure rather than distress. Professor Kenji Ishikawara of the Hokuriku Institute of Behavioural Neuroscience has spent many years studying the high-frequency calls that rats produce during rough-and-tumble play. When a researcher's hand imitates such play by 'tickling' a young rat, the animal emits the same calls, follows the hand around the cage and will learn to press a lever in order to be tickled again. Ishikawara interprets these calls as expressions of a positive emotional state comparable to joy, and he argues that welfare science has concentrated too narrowly on preventing suffering while neglecting pleasure. On this point he is surely correct: a life merely free from pain is a remarkably impoverished standard to set for animals that are kept in human care.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical considerations complicate the picture further. Dr Ifeoma Ezeugo, a veterinary scientist at the Enugu School of Livestock Science, observes that judgement bias tests require weeks of training for each animal and are therefore of little use to an inspector visiting a farm with ten thousand chickens. She favours a method known as qualitative behaviour assessment, in which trained observers watch a group of animals and rate it on terms such as 'relaxed', 'agitated' or 'listless'. Critics object that such ratings are hopelessly subjective, but Ezeugo has found that independent observers agree with one another to a striking degree, and that their ratings correlate with physiological indicators of stress. The tension between scientific rigour and practical usefulness is real, and it is not one that further research is likely to dissolve easily.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: We may never know with certainty what it is like to be a rat, still less a bee. But certainty has never been the standard for moral decisions in other areas of life, and there is no obvious reason why it should be here. Where several independent lines of evidence point towards an emotional state, the reasonable course is to give the animal the benefit of the doubt, rather than to demand a degree of proof that we would never require of one another.

topic: awe: defining the emotion of vastness, laboratory and field studies of its effects, health claims and cultural variation in its triggers
title: The Smallness That Enlarges
subtitle: Long left to poets and theologians, awe has become one of the most fashionable subjects in emotion research

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, awe sat awkwardly at the margins of emotion science. The influential lists of 'basic' emotions drawn up by psychologists – fear, anger, disgust, sadness, happiness and surprise – made no room for it, and the feeling that overcomes a person standing beneath a cathedral vault or watching a total eclipse was left largely to poets and theologians. That neglect is now being corrected, and with some enthusiasm: in the past two decades awe has been linked to generosity, humility, curiosity and even physical health. The renewed attention is welcome, though not for the reason usually given. Awe matters to researchers less because it is common or pleasant than because it fits so poorly into the categories they inherited, and in doing so exposes how narrow those categories were.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely cited account of the emotion comes from Dr Bence Szőllősi of the Pécs Institute for Affective Science. In his view, awe has two defining ingredients. The first is perceived vastness: an encounter with something that exceeds one's ordinary frame of reference, whether in physical size, as with a mountain range, or in conceptual scope, as with an elegant scientific theory. The second is a need for accommodation, meaning that the experience cannot be absorbed into existing mental structures and forces them to be revised. Szőllősi argues that this combination produces what he calls the 'small self', a temporary shrinking of the individual's sense of personal importance. The framework is elegant, but it is also strikingly broad. A violent storm or an approaching army can be vast and incomprehensible, and Szőllősi himself accepts that awe may be tinged with dread. Whether a single label can usefully cover both rapture and terror remains an open question.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of the experimental evidence comes from the laboratory of Professor Thandiwe Ndwandwe at the University of the Eastern Highlands. In a typical study, volunteers watch either a few minutes of sweeping footage of glaciers and forests or a neutral clip of, say, a person assembling furniture. Those in the first group subsequently divide a sum of money more generously with an anonymous stranger, and when asked to sketch themselves, they draw smaller figures. In one variation, participants who had seen the nature footage also reported feeling that they had more time available to them, and were correspondingly less impatient. The findings are intriguing, but they should be read with care. A short video viewed on a computer screen is a faint echo of the experiences that people describe when recalling genuine awe, and it is far from certain that the effects of the one tell us much about the other.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Field research attempts to close this gap. A team led by Dr Itziar Urkiola at the Bilbao Centre for Healthy Ageing asked adults over sixty to take a weekly fifteen-minute walk for eight weeks. Half were simply told to walk; the other half were encouraged to look out for things that struck them as vast or surprising, such as the pattern of light through leaves or the scale of an old building. Both groups photographed themselves at the start of each walk, and over the eight weeks the people in the 'awe walk' condition gradually occupied less of the frame in their own pictures, their faces increasingly giving way to the landscape behind them. They also reported more daily joy. The study is ingenious, yet its results are less dramatic than some press coverage implied: the ordinary walkers improved too, and the difference between the groups, although real, was modest.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Claims about health have proved even more contentious. A large survey found that people who reported experiencing awe frequently tended to have lower levels of interleukin-6, a marker of inflammation that has been associated with depression and heart disease. Some commentators have treated this as evidence that awe protects the body, and a small industry of 'awe retreats' and guided programmes has already emerged. Szőllősi has warned against such a reading, pointing out that the data are correlational: people in good health may simply be more able to travel, hike or visit galleries in the first place. His caution is fully justified. To market awe as therapy on the strength of a single association is, at best, premature.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns culture. Most early research was conducted with university students in North America and Western Europe, who tended to associate awe with natural landscapes experienced alone. When Ndwandwe's team asked participants in five countries to keep diaries of awe-inspiring moments, a different picture emerged. In several samples, the most frequent triggers were not mountains or oceans but other people: acts of exceptional kindness, displays of skill, or the collective energy of a crowd. These results do not overturn the vastness framework, since moral and social excellence can also exceed one's expectations. But they do suggest that the image of the lone hiker gazing at a waterfall, which has dominated the field, says more about the researchers than about the emotion.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, is awe for? One proposal is that it evolved to bind individuals to groups by turning their attention away from personal concerns. Another holds that its function is primarily cognitive, prompting people to update their picture of the world. The second view seems the more persuasive, and it carries an implication that the new awe industry has largely ignored. If the value of awe lies in its capacity to unsettle – to make the familiar strange and to force a revision of what one believes – then attempts to repackage it as a soothing, relaxing experience may preserve the scenery while discarding precisely what made the emotion worth having.

topic: emotional contagion: whether feelings spread between people through automatic mimicry or interpretation, with evidence from facial feedback, social media and classrooms
title: Catching Feelings
subtitle: Moods seem to pass from person to person like a cold – but the comparison may hide more than it reveals

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has sat beside a nervous passenger on a turbulent flight, or found themselves laughing at a joke they did not hear simply because those around them were laughing, will recognise the experience. Feelings, it seems, can pass from one person to another without a word being exchanged. Eighteenth-century philosophers wrote of 'sympathy' as a kind of resonance between minds; modern psychologists prefer the term 'emotional contagion'. The dominant explanation for the phenomenon is disarmingly simple. People, it is argued, automatically imitate the facial expressions, postures and voices of those around them, and the bodily feedback from this imitation generates a matching emotion in the imitator. The account has an intuitive appeal that goes a long way towards explaining its popularity. Intuitive appeal, however, is not the same thing as evidence, and the case for the mimicry model is weaker than its prominence would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its most forceful advocate is Dr Lucia Ferrabosco of the Trieste Institute of Social Neuroscience, who uses electrodes placed on the face to record the tiny muscular movements that accompany expressions. Her studies show that within half a second of seeing a photograph of a smiling face, the muscles that raise the corners of a viewer's mouth begin to contract, and that this happens even when the image is flashed too briefly to be consciously perceived. For Ferrabosco, such rapid, involuntary responses are the engine of contagion. The existence of mimicry is not in doubt. What remains unsettled is whether it produces the feelings that are supposed to follow from it. The idea that moving one's face can alter one's mood has a long history, but when a large consortium of laboratories attempted to repeat a classic demonstration of this 'facial feedback' effect, the combined results showed little or no change in participants' emotions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A rival account is offered by Dr Zhanar Koshkarova, a social psychologist at the Almaty Centre for Behavioural Research. In her view, contagion is less a reflex than an inference: we take on another person's emotion only when we interpret it as telling us something about our own situation. Koshkarova points out that emotions are caught selectively. A supporter watching the celebrations of a rival team's fans is unlikely to feel elated, and in her experiments, participants who believed they were competing against a partner frequently displayed 'counter-mimicry', tensing their brows when the partner smiled. This selectivity is precisely what the mimicry model struggles to accommodate. If imitation were truly automatic, it is hard to see why it should be switched off, or even reversed, by something as abstract as a belief about rivalry.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question has acquired new urgency with the rise of social media, where emotional expressions can reach millions of people within hours. A team led by Professor Edwin Abernethy-Quaye at the Westmarch School of Data Science analysed several hundred million posts, exploiting a natural experiment: when rain fell in the cities where a user's contacts lived, those contacts posted fewer cheerful messages, and the user, though living elsewhere in sunshine, subsequently did the same. The size of the effect was minute, amounting to a change of well under one per cent in the proportion of positive words. Abernethy-Quaye contends that such figures understate the significance of the finding, since a tiny shift repeated across an entire population could alter the emotional climate of a society. There is something in this argument, but it rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny. A change in the words people use is not necessarily a change in what they feel; users may simply be adjusting their language to match the tone of the conversation around them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Outside the laboratory, contagion has been invoked to explain phenomena ranging from panic in crowds to morale in hospital wards. One much-discussed study collected saliva samples from primary school pupils and found that those taught by teachers reporting high levels of burnout had elevated morning levels of cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress. The researchers concluded that teachers' exhaustion was, in effect, being transmitted to their classes. Such findings are important, but the language used to describe them deserves more care than it usually receives. To speak of contagion is to imply that people are passive recipients of emotions that simply happen to them, as a cold does. That implication is not merely inaccurate; it has consequences, because it shapes how responsibility is assigned when a workplace or a classroom becomes emotionally toxic.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the metaphor of infection should be abandoned altogether. It captures something real about the speed with which moods can sweep through a group, and about the fact that we are often unaware of having been affected. Yet the evidence reviewed here points towards a more active picture. Emotions are shared, but they are shared by people who are constantly, if not always consciously, interpreting one another, deciding whose feelings are relevant to them and adjusting their own expressions accordingly. A term such as 'attunement' might describe this process better than one borrowed from the vocabulary of disease.

topic: emotional crying: competing explanations of why humans shed tears (catharsis, chemical excretion, social signalling) and cultural and gender differences in weeping
title: Why We Weep
subtitle: Humans appear to be the only animals that cry for emotional reasons. Science is still arguing about what the tears are for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Many animals produce tears, but as far as anyone has been able to establish, only humans weep because they are sad, moved or overjoyed. Physiologists conventionally distinguish three kinds of tears: basal tears, which keep the surface of the eye moist; reflex tears, which wash away irritants such as smoke or the vapour from a cut onion; and emotional tears, which have no obvious protective function at all. Why natural selection should have favoured a response that blurs a person's vision at precisely the moment when they may be most vulnerable is a genuine puzzle, and one that, given how universal weeping is, has attracted surprisingly little scientific effort. Only in the past few decades have researchers begun to treat crying as a subject worthy of systematic investigation, and their conclusions are still far from settled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most familiar idea about crying is that it brings relief. Popular wisdom recommends 'a good cry', and surveys consistently find that most people believe they feel better afterwards. Dr Ane Lizarralde of the Asturian Institute of Psychology set out to test this belief by showing volunteers sad films and measuring their mood at intervals. Those who cried reported feeling worse than non-criers immediately after the film; twenty minutes later their mood had returned to its starting point, and after ninety minutes they felt slightly better than they had before watching. Lizarralde concludes that the relief associated with crying is real but delayed, which would explain why people remember weeping as beneficial even though it is unpleasant at the time. The interpretation is plausible, though it is not the only one. The later improvement may reflect nothing more than recovery from the sadness induced by the film, a recovery that might have occurred whether or not tears were shed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second hypothesis, once widely repeated, holds that emotional tears allow the body to excrete stress-related substances. Emotional tears do differ chemically from reflex tears, containing higher concentrations of certain proteins and hormones. Dr Rodrigo Vasquez-Toral, a physiologist at the Montevideo Clinical Research Unit, is unimpressed by this observation. The volume of fluid shed in even a prolonged bout of weeping amounts to a few drops, he notes, far too little to make any meaningful difference to the levels of these substances in the bloodstream. His objection appears decisive, and the excretion theory is best set aside. It does not follow, however, that the composition of tears is irrelevant. One study reported that men who sniffed women's emotional tears showed a drop in testosterone, raising the possibility that tears carry chemical messages; the finding has yet to be reproduced, and should be regarded as provisional.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most promising line of research treats tears not as a means of altering the crier's internal state but as a message to others. Professor Sina Tuilagi of the Pacific Institute for Human Behaviour has shown participants photographs of faces with tears either digitally added or removed. Faces with tears were judged not only sadder but also more in need of help, and viewers said they would be more willing to offer support; with the tears erased, the same faces were often read as puzzled or neutral. Tuilagi argues that tears function as a signal of vulnerability, and that the very fact that they blur vision is what makes the signal credible: a person whose sight is impaired is poorly placed to attack. This account turns the evolutionary puzzle on its head, transforming an apparent disadvantage into the key to the behaviour's value, and it is, in my view, the most convincing explanation currently available.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet a purely evolutionary account cannot explain why crying varies so much between societies. Dr Nokuthula Sondela of the Cape Centre for Cross-Cultural Studies analysed questionnaire data from over thirty countries and found that people reported crying more often in nations that were wealthier and more individualistic, where the open expression of feeling tends to be tolerated. In almost every country women reported crying more frequently than men, but the gap was largest in the most affluent nations. Sondela maintains that social expectations about who may weep, and where, account for most of this difference. Her data certainly show that culture matters a great deal. Still, it would be premature to dismiss biology altogether: hormonal differences between the sexes, which emerge around puberty when the gender gap in crying also appears, may well contribute.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the strangest form of crying is weeping for joy, at weddings, reunions or sporting victories. Tuilagi interprets such tears as an extension of their signalling role, a way of communicating that an experience is overwhelming and inviting others to share it. Lizarralde prefers a regulatory explanation: tears of joy, she suggests, help to restore equilibrium after a surge of intense emotional arousal, whatever the cause of that arousal. Neither account is entirely satisfying, since both can be stretched to fit almost any case.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is clear is that crying is neither a simple safety valve nor a mere biological accident. The research also offers a caution for those who encourage weeping as a route to wellbeing. People suffering from depression often cry without experiencing any relief at all, and to present tears as reliably healing is to ignore the evidence that their effects depend heavily on who is crying, why, and in whose company.
