topic: affective forecasting: why people overestimate how strongly and how long future events will affect their feelings (impact bias, focalism, immune neglect) and the practical consequences
title: Forecasting Our Future Feelings
subtitle: We are surprisingly poor judges of how much the events in our lives will affect us – and that matters more than it might seem

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every significant decision a person makes rests on a prediction about feelings. We choose a career, a partner or a house partly because we expect it to make us happy, and we avoid risks because we anticipate the misery that failure would bring. Psychologists call these predictions 'affective forecasts', and over the past three decades a substantial body of research has examined how accurate they are. The broad conclusion is that people are reasonably good at predicting whether an event will feel pleasant or unpleasant, but consistently poor at judging how intensely they will feel it and for how long. This tendency to overestimate the emotional impact of future events, known as the impact bias, might seem a curiosity of laboratory psychology. It is in fact a matter of considerable practical importance, with implications for fields as diverse as medicine, economics and public policy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence comes from a study conducted by Professor Anouk Delacroix-Ibe at Lake Annecy University, where first-year students are assigned to halls of residence by lottery, a system that creates a natural experiment. Before the lottery, 212 students were asked to predict how happy they would be in each of the university's twelve halls; most expected to be substantially happier in the handful of desirable buildings near the centre of campus than in the remainder. When they were surveyed again a year after moving in, however, those in the popular halls were no happier than those in the unpopular ones. Delacroix-Ibe traced the error to what the students had attended to when forecasting. They had concentrated on visible physical features such as location and architecture, which varied greatly between halls, while overlooking social factors such as friendships with neighbours, which varied little and turned out to matter far more.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Sevan Mardirossian of the Yerevan Institute of Decision Science offers a more general account of such mistakes, which he terms focalism. When people imagine a future event, he argues, they picture it in isolation, forgetting that it will be embedded in a life full of other activities and concerns that will compete for their attention. In one study, he asked supporters of two rival football clubs to predict how they would feel in the days after a decisive match. Those who had first been asked to write a detailed account of a typical day, listing their work, meals and conversations, made far more moderate predictions than those who had not. The remedy is elegant in its simplicity. Whether people would ever apply it spontaneously, outside an experiment, is another matter; focalism is powerful precisely because those in its grip are unaware of it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A complementary explanation comes from Dr Bounmy Kittikhoun of the Mekong Centre for Behavioural Research, who argues that people underestimate their own capacity to recover from setbacks. Humans, she contends, possess a kind of psychological immune system, a set of largely unconscious processes, such as rationalisation and reinterpretation, that soften the blow of misfortune. In one experiment, volunteers were told they had been rejected for a desirable task either by a single assessor or by a panel. Those rejected by an individual recovered their mood more quickly, apparently because they could dismiss the decision as one person's prejudice. Yet when asked in advance, participants predicted that both forms of rejection would hurt equally. We fail, Kittikhoun suggests, to foresee the very defences that will protect us.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These findings take on a sharper edge in medicine. When healthy people are asked to imagine living with a serious chronic condition, they typically predict a dramatic and lasting fall in their quality of life. Yet patients who actually have such conditions often report levels of everyday wellbeing that are not far below those of the general population; in one frequently cited survey, people undergoing regular kidney dialysis rated their mood as roughly equal to that of healthy volunteers. Since the methods used to allocate health resources frequently rely on the judgements of the healthy public, this gap is potentially troubling. Nevertheless, patients' reports cannot simply be taken at face value. People who adapt to illness may revise the standard against which they judge their lives, so that a rating of 'fairly happy' means something different after diagnosis from what it meant before.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards forecasting errors as defects. Dr Sigrid Ystgaard of the Tromsø Laboratory for Motivation Research argues that they may serve a useful function. If people accurately anticipated how quickly the pleasure of a promotion would fade, she observes, they might be less inclined to work hard for it; and an exaggerated dread of failure helps them steer clear of genuinely dangerous situations. On this view, correcting the impact bias could sap motivation. There is some force to this argument, but it underestimates the costs. Forecasting errors also lead people into bad choices with lasting consequences, as when families buy a larger house far from their workplaces, expecting the extra space to compensate for a long daily commute, only to find that it does not.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most practical finding in the field concerns a remedy that people seem determined to ignore. In a study of 'surrogation', participants predicted how much they would enjoy an experience more accurately when they read a short report from a stranger who had just been through it than when they read a detailed description of the experience itself. Yet when offered the choice, a large majority preferred the description. The research on affective forecasting is usually presented as revealing errors about the future. Its deepest lesson may instead concern the present: our curious reluctance to believe that other people's feelings can tell us anything about our own.

topic: re-examining the classic line-judgement conformity experiments: decline over time, cultural differences and compliance versus private belief
title: The Weight of the Majority
subtitle: Seventy years after a famous series of experiments on group pressure, researchers still disagree about what the results actually show

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 1950s, a series of laboratory studies conducted in the United States produced one of the most frequently cited findings in social psychology. Volunteers were seated among a group of strangers and asked to state aloud which of three lines matched a reference line in length. The task was so easy that, when tested alone, almost nobody made a mistake. Unknown to the volunteer, however, the other members of the group were actors who had been instructed to give the same wrong answer on certain trials. Faced with a unanimous majority, roughly a third of responses went along with the obvious error, and around three-quarters of participants conformed at least once. The experiments are usually presented in textbooks as a demonstration of how readily people abandon the evidence of their own eyes. That interpretation, I would argue, has always been more dramatic than the data warrant.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first reason for caution is that most responses were not conforming at all. Even under the strongest pressure, two-thirds of answers were correct, and a substantial minority of participants never yielded once. Ilse Ellingboe, a social psychologist at the Nordkapp Institute of Behavioural Science, has re-examined the original reports and points out that the researchers themselves were more impressed by independence than by submission. "The story that reached the public," she says, "was almost the reverse of the one the experimenters thought they had told." It is a fair point, although it should not be pushed too far: a situation in which one person in three denies something plainly visible is still remarkable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second question concerns whether the effect has changed over time. During the 1970s and 1980s, dozens of replications were carried out in Europe and North America, and some reported far lower rates of conformity than the original work. A meta-analysis led by Haruki Takahara at the Kansai Centre for Social Research combined results from more than a hundred such studies and found a gradual decline in conformity across the decades. Takahara attributes this to broad cultural change, in particular the growing value placed on individual self-expression in post-war societies. The pattern is real, but the explanation is harder to confirm than it appears. Later studies often used university students tested by researchers of the same age, whereas the earliest volunteers faced a formal, authority-laden laboratory setting; changes in procedure, rather than in national character, may account for part of the decline.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The same meta-analysis revealed striking differences between countries. Studies conducted in societies usually described as collectivist, where obligations to family and community are emphasised, tended to produce higher conformity than those in more individualist nations. Dewi Ramdhani, a cultural psychologist at the Java Institute of Behavioural Studies, cautions against reading these figures as evidence that some populations are simply more submissive. In her view, agreeing with a group in public may be understood in many cultures as a form of tact, a way of preserving harmony with people one will meet again, rather than a failure of judgement. Going along with others, she suggests, can be a socially intelligent decision.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This raises a deeper problem about what the original experiments measured. Psychologists distinguish between compliance, in which people outwardly agree while privately retaining their own view, and internalisation, in which their actual perception or belief changes. Petteri Kivisto, of the Baltic Laboratory for Cognitive Science, has argued that line-judgement studies capture almost nothing but compliance. When participants are allowed to write their answers privately rather than announce them, conformity drops sharply, which suggests that most of those who agreed with the actors never believed them. Kivisto concludes that the experiments reveal a reluctance to cause embarrassment, not a vulnerability of perception. Yet this reassuring reading overlooks evidence from brain-imaging work in which exposure to a mistaken majority appeared to alter activity in regions associated with visual processing, hinting that, for some people at least, the group may genuinely change what they see.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, researchers have begun to ask whether the classic findings hold outside the laboratory. A team directed by Grace Sakwa at the East African Institute for Social Inquiry staged everyday versions of the task in markets and bus stations in Nairobi, asking passers-by to judge quantities or distances after hearing several confederates give a wrong estimate. Conformity appeared, but it was weaker than in laboratory studies, and it almost disappeared when a single bystander disagreed with the majority. Sakwa believes this last finding is the most practically important result in the whole field: the presence of one ally, even one who gives a different wrong answer, appears to release people from pressure to agree.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should we conclude? It would be a mistake to treat the line experiments as proof that human beings are fundamentally sheep, but it would be equally misleading to dismiss them as artefacts of an unusual era. People clearly weigh the views of others when forming their own, and in an uncertain world that is often a sensible strategy, since a crowd frequently knows more than any one individual. The real lesson may be that independence is fragile but easily supported. Institutions that want honest judgement from their members, such as juries, committees and scientific panels, would do well to ensure that disagreement is voiced early, because a lone dissenting voice appears to be far more powerful than anyone in the original experiments suspected.

topic: groupthink in committees and organisations: critiques of the original theory, leadership, assigned versus genuine dissent and hierarchy
title: The Comfort of Consensus
subtitle: The idea that close-knit groups make reckless decisions has become management folklore. Does the evidence support it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a committee of intelligent, experienced people approves a plan that later proves disastrous, observers often reach for a single word: groupthink. The term, coined by a political scientist in the early 1970s, describes a mode of thinking in which the desire for unanimity overrides a realistic appraisal of alternatives. Members of a tightly knit group, the theory holds, come to believe in their own invulnerability, dismiss warnings, put pressure on doubters and censor their own misgivings, until the group arrives at a decision that none of them, considered individually, might have endorsed. The concept has proved enormously popular. It appears in business school curricula, official inquiries and newspaper editorials, and it has the appeal of an explanation that seems to fit almost every fiasco. That very versatility, however, ought to make us suspicious.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The original theory was built on a handful of historical case studies, mostly foreign-policy decisions that had gone badly wrong. Adaeze Umeadi, a historian of institutions at the Lagos School of Governance, argues that this method was flawed from the start. Because the cases were chosen precisely because they ended in failure, she says, the symptoms of groupthink were identified with the benefit of hindsight. Cohesion, confidence and the rejection of dissenting advice can be found in many successful decisions too; we simply do not label them as defects when things turn out well. Umeadi's critique is, I think, largely correct, although it does not follow that the phenomenon is imaginary, only that the case-study method cannot demonstrate it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experimental studies have produced a more complicated picture. The theory places group cohesiveness at the heart of the problem: the more members like one another, the greater their reluctance to disagree. Yet laboratory groups made up of friends do not consistently make worse decisions than groups of strangers, and some studies find the reverse, since people who trust one another may feel freer to argue. Marta Zaborowska, an organisational psychologist at the Vistula Institute of Management, has reviewed several decades of this research and concludes that cohesion matters far less than leadership style. In her analysis, the most reliable predictor of a poor decision is a leader who announces a preferred option at the outset, which signals to everyone else which conclusion is welcome.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If Zaborowska is right, the remedy lies less in the composition of groups than in their procedures. One widely recommended technique is to appoint a "devil's advocate", a member whose task is to argue against the emerging consensus. Experiments by Jonas Nordqvist at the Malaren Centre for Decision Research suggest that this practice is less effective than it appears. When participants know that the critic has been assigned the role, they discount the objections as theatre; the group may even become more confident in its original choice, having apparently survived a challenge. Genuine dissent, by contrast, from a member who actually holds a contrary view, prompted groups to search more widely for information and to consider more options, even when the dissenter turned out to be wrong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Research outside the laboratory points in a similar direction. A group led by Einar Hallgrimsson at the North Atlantic Institute of Human Factors analysed transcripts from flight simulators and from hospital surgical teams and found that junior members frequently noticed errors but phrased their concerns so indirectly that they were easily ignored. A co-pilot might ask whether the captain was "comfortable" with the fuel level instead of stating plainly that it was too low. The researchers argue that the obstacle was not a shared illusion of invulnerability but a steep hierarchy, in which challenging a superior felt riskier than staying silent. Training programmes that teach junior staff a standard formula for raising concerns have, according to their data, reduced the number of errors that go unchallenged.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Anjali Mukherji, who studies corporate boards at the Deccan Institute of Business Research, takes a different view of what goes wrong. In her interviews with directors, few reported feeling pressured to agree; rather, many admitted that they had simply not prepared adequately and deferred to colleagues who seemed better informed. What looks like conformity, she contends, is often rational ignorance: individuals reasonably rely on others' judgement because examining every proposal in depth would be impossible. This argument deserves more attention than it has received, although it describes a problem of workload that is quite distinct from the social pressures the original theory emphasised.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the concept? It would be wrong to discard it entirely. The pressures it describes are real, and anyone who has sat through a meeting in which an objection died unspoken will recognise them. But as a scientific theory groupthink has fared poorly: its components do not reliably appear together, and its central causal claim about cohesion has not been confirmed. Its lasting value may be as a warning label rather than an explanation, reminding organisations that agreement is not evidence of correctness, and that the absence of dissent in a meeting should prompt questions, not reassurance.

topic: the bystander effect: laboratory intercom studies versus CCTV evidence of intervention in real public conflicts
title: Safety in Numbers?
subtitle: The belief that crowds of onlookers discourage anyone from helping is being challenged by evidence gathered on real streets

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few findings in social psychology have travelled as far beyond the laboratory as the so-called bystander effect: the proposition that a person in distress is less likely to receive help when many people are present than when there is only a single witness. It appears in countless textbooks as a settled fact about human nature. In its popular form, however, the finding has acquired a meaning that its original authors never intended. What began as a careful observation about how the presence of others shapes individual decisions has been retold as a story of moral decline, in which city dwellers are portrayed as too selfish or too indifferent to come to one another's aid. That version is not merely exaggerated; it is close to the opposite of what the best current evidence shows.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the classic experiments, participants who believed they were taking part in a discussion over an intercom suddenly heard another speaker apparently suffering a seizure. Those who thought they were the only listener almost always left their booth to seek help, and did so quickly; those who believed that four others could also hear were slower and less likely to respond at all. Researchers proposed three mechanisms to account for the pattern. The first, diffusion of responsibility, holds that the obligation to act is felt to be shared out among everyone present, so that each individual carries only a fraction of it. The second, audience inhibition, reflects a fear of looking foolish by overreacting in front of others. The third, often termed pluralistic ignorance, arises when uncertain witnesses glance at one another for clues, observe apparent calm, and conclude that nothing serious is happening, when in fact everyone else is equally uncertain and is simply concealing it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Later laboratory work has refined rather than overturned these results. A review of more than a hundred studies by Teodora Carstoiu of the Institute for Behavioural Inquiry found that the inhibiting effect of other people was real but varied considerably with circumstances. It was strongest when an emergency was ambiguous and the cost of intervening was low, and it shrank markedly when the danger was obvious and severe, apparently because a clear threat removes the uncertainty on which pluralistic ignorance depends.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most serious challenge to the popular story, however, comes from outside the laboratory altogether. A team led by Kwabena Asumadu-Sarpong at the Urban Conflict Observatory examined closed-circuit television footage of more than two hundred public disputes and assaults recorded in three countries with very different levels of crime. In roughly nine incidents out of ten, at least one bystander stepped in, whether by placing themselves between the parties, calming an aggressor or comforting a victim. Moreover, the chance that someone would intervene rose, rather than fell, as the number of onlookers increased. Asumadu-Sarpong concluded that people in public spaces are remarkably willing to help, and that the image of the passive crowd owes more to a handful of widely publicised cases than to systematic observation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: At first sight, these results seem to contradict the laboratory tradition, but the conflict is more apparent than real. The original experiments measured the likelihood that any particular individual would help; the street studies measured the likelihood that a victim would receive help from someone. Even if each witness becomes a little less inclined to act as a crowd grows, a larger crowd contains more potential helpers, and the probability that at least one of them will act can still increase. Much of the confusion surrounding the bystander effect stems from a failure to distinguish between these two questions. The laboratory studies, then, should not be dismissed; they correctly identify pressures that operate on individuals, even if they say little about the overall fate of victims.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further strand of research asks who the bystanders are. Signe Strandskov, a sociologist at the Nordic Centre for Public Life, has argued that onlookers who know one another, or who share a sense of belonging to the same group, intervene far more readily than strangers, because helping becomes something the group does together rather than a solitary risk. The argument is plausible, but caution is needed: much of the evidence comes from nightlife districts, where witnesses are disproportionately young and often out with friends, and it is not yet clear that the pattern holds in workplaces, on public transport or in quiet residential streets.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question has acquired new urgency online, where harassment may be witnessed by thousands of people at once. Hamid Rezvanifar of the Centre for Networked Society reports that only a small proportion of users who see abusive messages respond to them in any way. Yet such figures are difficult to interpret, since it is far from settled what should count as intervention in a digital setting: reporting a post, sending a private message of support and publicly challenging an abuser involve very different levels of effort and risk. Until researchers agree on definitions, comparisons between online and offline behaviour are likely to mislead.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the bystander effect is a myth, but it does suggest that the moral lesson usually drawn from it is mistaken. Many programmes that train people to intervene open by warning participants that people tend to stand by and do nothing. Such warnings may be counterproductive, since telling people that inaction is normal risks making it appear acceptable. A more promising approach would be to emphasise how often ordinary people do help, and to concentrate on the practical skills, such as how to interrupt a confrontation safely, that turn willingness into effective action.

topic: social-norm messaging in public policy: descriptive versus injunctive norms, the boomerang effect in energy reports, persistence and ethics
title: What Everybody Else Is Doing
subtitle: Governments increasingly try to change behaviour by telling people about their neighbours, but the technique is less straightforward than it appears

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the water authority of a large coastal city launched a campaign during a prolonged drought, its posters carried a stark message: tens of thousands of households, they announced, were still watering their gardens in defiance of restrictions. The intention was to shame offenders into compliance. Instead, according to an internal evaluation, consumption in the following weeks rose slightly in the districts where the posters were most densely displayed. The episode illustrates a recurring trap in public communication. Officials who wish to provoke concern naturally emphasise how widespread a problem has become, and this instinct is understandable, since a problem that seems rare hardly seems worth addressing. Yet the same message carries a second, unintended meaning: that the undesirable behaviour is what most people do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Social psychologists distinguish between two kinds of norm. Descriptive norms concern what people actually do; injunctive norms concern what people think ought to be done. Lucía Olabarria, of the Institute for Applied Social Research, has spent a decade documenting what happens when the two pull in opposite directions. In one of her field trials, conducted across a network of public libraries, reminder notices that lamented how many borrowers kept books past the due date were followed by more late returns than notices carrying no social information at all, while notices stating that the great majority of borrowers returned items on time produced a clear improvement. Her conclusion is that a message which condemns a behaviour while simultaneously advertising its popularity will tend to be heard as permission rather than as a warning.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most extensively studied application of these ideas involves household energy. Utility companies in several countries now send customers periodic reports comparing their consumption with that of similar homes nearby. Such reports reliably reduce use among households that consume more than their neighbours, but early trials uncovered an awkward side effect: households already using less than the average tended to drift upwards, as though the comparison had informed them that they had room to spare. Torvald Rimstad, an economist at the Institute for Public Economics, found that this so-called boomerang effect largely disappeared when frugal households also received a simple symbol of approval, such as a smiling face, beside their figures. The finding is elegant, but its practical significance should not be overstated: the average reduction produced by comparative reports is in the region of two per cent, which is worthwhile across millions of homes but scarcely transformative.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more pressing question is whether such effects endure. Researchers at the Baltic Policy Laboratory, who followed tens of thousands of households for several years, found that the response to each individual report faded within days, yet repeated reports produced savings that accumulated over time and persisted for a period even after the letters stopped. They attributed this persistence to changes in physical capital, such as the replacement of inefficient appliances or the installation of insulation, rather than to lasting shifts in attitude. Whatever the mechanism, durability ought to be the central test of any intervention of this kind, since a small saving that lasts for years is worth considerably more than a dramatic one that vanishes in a week.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The choice of comparison group also matters. Ebube Nwachinemere, a sociologist at the Centre for Community Studies, argues that norms exert the greatest pull when the people being described are perceived as similar to the recipient, so that a comparison with residents of the same street is more persuasive than one with a national average. Nwachinemere has also noted, however, that comparisons can become too local. In a survey of people receiving street-level reports, a substantial minority said they felt watched, and some suspected that their neighbours could see their figures. Precision, in other words, can provoke resentment, and a message that is resented is unlikely to be heeded.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some critics object to norm-based messaging on principle. Saskia Verhaegen, a philosopher who works on the ethics of public policy, contends that such messages influence behaviour by exploiting the desire to fit in rather than by offering reasons, and that they are therefore a form of manipulation. She points in particular to the practice of selecting whichever reference group happens to yield the most flattering statistic. On the second point she is surely right: a comparison chosen solely because it produces a favourable impression is misleading, however accurate the underlying figures. Her broader objection is less convincing. Telling people truthfully what others do gives them information they are free to weigh, and it is not obvious why a wish to behave like one's peers should be considered a less legitimate motive than any other.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Two limitations remain. The first is that descriptive norms are of little use when the desired behaviour is genuinely uncommon: announcing that only a small fraction of commuters cycle to work is unlikely to recruit many more. Olabarria has suggested that in such cases messages should describe a trend rather than a state, emphasising that growing numbers of people are changing their habits, although the evidence for this approach is still thin. The second limitation is political. Because letters and posters are cheap, they can tempt governments to favour them over costlier measures such as pricing, regulation or investment in infrastructure. Social norm messages can usefully complement such measures, but they cannot replace them.

topic: the myth of mass panic: how crowds actually behave in emergencies, shared identity, evacuation delay and crowd modelling
title: Keeping Calm in the Crush
subtitle: The image of the stampeding, panic-stricken crowd is deeply rooted, but research on real emergencies tells a very different story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a fire breaks out in a crowded building or a crush develops at a stadium, news reports reach almost automatically for the language of panic. Crowds are said to have stampeded, people to have trampled one another in a blind rush for the exits. The image has a long history. Writers on crowd psychology in the late nineteenth century argued that individuals who join a mass lose their capacity for reason and become prone to primitive, contagious emotion. Their ideas were rarely tested against systematic evidence, yet they passed into common sense, and they have shaped the design of buildings and the conduct of emergency services to a degree that the evidence does not justify.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, researchers who have actually spoken to survivors have found remarkably little of the behaviour the traditional picture predicts. Efua Tamakloe, of the Centre for Disaster Research, has interviewed more than four hundred people who escaped from fires, transport accidents and collapsing structures. Uncontrolled, selfish flight, she reports, was rare. Far more often, people helped strangers who had fallen, held doors open, guided others through smoke and even waited their turn at narrow exits. Tamakloe has also re-examined official accounts of crowd disasters and concludes that most deaths at such events are caused not by people trampling one another but by compression: when the density of a crowd passes a critical level, the pressure of bodies alone can make breathing impossible, regardless of how anyone behaves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should cooperation be so common among people who have never met? Kristin Sigurdardottir, a social psychologist at the Reykjavik Institute of Behavioural Science, argues that shared danger transforms a collection of individuals into a psychological group. Faced with a common threat, strangers begin to see themselves as members of a single 'we', and norms of mutual help that normally apply only among friends and family are extended to the crowd as a whole. In a series of experiments using virtual evacuations, Sigurdardottir found that participants who reported a strong sense of identity with the people around them were more likely to stop and assist others, and less likely to push, than those who did not.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If panic is the wrong diagnosis, what is the real problem? Increasingly, specialists point to delay. In many emergencies people do too little, too late: they finish a telephone call, collect their belongings or look for more information before moving. A study led by Haruki Inoue at the Institute of Fire Safety Engineering, which analysed video recordings of unannounced evacuation drills in office buildings, found that occupants typically waited several minutes after an alarm sounded before heading for the stairs, and that one of the strongest predictors of when an individual set off was whether colleagues nearby had already done so. In this situation, the tendency to look to others before acting works directly against survival.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These findings have uncomfortable implications for those in charge. Officials have often been reluctant to give crowds full information about a danger, for fear of provoking the very panic the research suggests is uncommon. Tamakloe argues that this caution is misplaced, and that clear, specific instructions about what is happening and where to go shorten the time people take to leave. She is right, and the point can be taken further: by withholding information, authorities may generate exactly the uncertainty and disorder that they hope to prevent, since people who do not know what is happening will spend precious time trying to find out.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The research has also begun to influence the engineers who model crowd movement. Many computer simulations used in the design of stations and stadiums treat pedestrians as independent particles, each seeking the shortest route to an exit. Neema Mwakalinga, whose group at the Coastal Institute of Technology develops such models, argues that they must take account of the fact that people tend to move in clusters, as families or friends who refuse to be separated, a pattern that can slow the overall flow considerably. This is a welcome step towards realism, although it comes at a price: each additional layer of social behaviour makes the models harder to check, and reliable data from real emergencies against which they could be tested are scarce.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this should lead us to romanticise crowds. Cooperation is not guaranteed, and competitive behaviour does sometimes appear, particularly when people come to believe that an exit is about to be blocked and that escape will soon be impossible. But such breakdowns are the exception, and they usually follow from conditions that could have been foreseen. For that reason, the word 'panic' ought to disappear from official reports into crowd disasters. It places the blame on the victims, and in doing so it draws attention away from the overcrowding, poor design and inadequate management that, far more often, turn an emergency into a tragedy.

topic: group polarisation: from the risky shift to persuasive-argument, social-comparison and identity explanations, and the echo-chamber debate
title: Talking Ourselves to the Edge
subtitle: Discussion was long expected to make groups more moderate. Why does it so often do the opposite?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, it was taken almost for granted that groups make more moderate decisions than individuals. Committees, juries and boards were valued precisely because the eccentricities of any one member would, it was assumed, be smoothed away by discussion, leaving a sensible middle course. The first serious challenge to this assumption came from an unexpected direction. In the early 1960s, a series of studies asked participants to advise fictional characters facing risky choices, such as whether to leave a secure job for an uncertain venture. When people who had answered privately were brought together to agree on a joint recommendation, their advice was consistently bolder than the average of their private answers. The so-called 'risky shift' was greeted with some astonishment, and rightly so, for it suggested that the reassuring logic behind collective decision-making was, at best, incomplete.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Later work showed that the original label was misleading. When the dilemmas were altered so that most participants initially favoured caution, discussion made groups more cautious still. What groups did, it emerged, was not to seek risk as such but to move further in whichever direction their members already leaned. The phenomenon was renamed group polarisation, and it has since been documented in a remarkable range of settings. Mock juries inclined to award modest damages tend, after deliberation, to award larger sums, and people with slight prejudices can leave a discussion with stronger ones. In each case, the group does not split the difference between its members but amplifies their shared tendency.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Two explanations have dominated the debate. The first, associated most closely with Ilse Kortevaara of the Lakeland Institute of Social Cognition, focuses on the information exchanged during discussion. If most members of a group lean one way, Kortevaara argues, then most of the arguments voiced will support that position, and each member is likely to hear reasons which had not previously occurred to them. Since the pool of arguments is lopsided from the outset, the net effect of discussion is to persuade people further in the direction they were already heading. In her experiments, the extent of the shift could be predicted with some accuracy simply by counting the number of novel arguments on each side that participants encountered.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The second explanation, championed by Teodoro Arrizabalo at the University of Valdemora, emphasises social comparison rather than reasoning. People, he suggests, like to see themselves as holding the socially admired position somewhat more firmly than the average person. When discussion reveals that others are just as cautious, or as daring, the members shift further to restore their sense of being slightly ahead of the crowd. In support, Arrizabalo has shown that merely informing participants of other members' views, without any arguments being exchanged, is enough to produce a measurable shift. Supporters of the two camps have often written as though only one account could be correct. That seems to me a false choice: the evidence suggests that both mechanisms operate, and that their relative importance depends on whether the issue is primarily one of fact or one of values.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from Sipho Mabuzane and colleagues at the Karoo Centre for Group Processes, who argue that members do not move towards an extreme as such but towards what they perceive as the typical position of their own group. Because that typical position is defined partly by contrast with outsiders, it tends to be exaggerated whenever a rival group is in view. This account has the considerable merit of explaining why polarisation intensifies when people are reminded of an opposing camp. It is less convincing, however, as an explanation of the shifts observed among groups of strangers with no shared identity to speak of, who were, after all, the participants in many of the original studies.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Interest in polarisation has grown enormously with the spread of social media, which is widely blamed for sorting people into 'echo chambers' where they hear only views that confirm their own. The laboratory findings make this fear intuitively plausible, but field evidence paints a more complicated picture. Mirela Draganescu, a computational sociologist at the Iron Gate Centre for Network Research, analysed the browsing histories of several thousand volunteers and found that most were exposed to a broader range of political content online than they encountered offline. Sharp increases in partisanship, her data suggest, are concentrated among a small minority of very active users, who seek out like-minded communities rather than being trapped in them by recommendation algorithms. The more alarming claims about social media dividing entire societies therefore appear to outrun the evidence. Yet it would be premature to dismiss the concern altogether, since a small and highly vocal minority can exert an influence on public debate out of all proportion to its size.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, can be done to keep deliberation productive? The most reliable safeguard is diversity of initial opinion, since polarisation depends on a shared leaning in the first place. Where this cannot be arranged, procedural measures can help. Asking members to record their views privately before any discussion begins is among the most effective, because it prevents early speakers from defining what the group appears to believe. None of this means that discussion is harmful; it means only that it has no inherent tendency to moderate. Whether talking leads a group towards wisdom or towards excess depends less on the act of talking itself than on who is in the room.

topic: minority influence: how consistent dissenters change private opinion, behavioural style, indirect effects and the value of dissent for group thinking
title: The Power of the Persistent Few
subtitle: Research on conformity has mostly asked how majorities sway individuals. A smaller tradition asks how minorities change majorities

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of the famous experiments on conformity share a single underlying question: how far will an individual bend in order to agree with a group? The answer, repeated in countless textbooks, is that people bend a surprising amount. Yet the history of ideas tells a rather different story. The view that the earth moves around the sun, the abolition of slavery and the right of women to vote all began as the convictions of small and often ridiculed minorities. If social influence flowed only from the many to the few, such changes would be very hard to explain. For several decades, conformity research largely ignored this problem, and in my view that neglect was a serious blind spot rather than a mere difference of emphasis.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the studies that first drew attention to minority influence used a deceptively simple task. Groups of six were shown a series of slides, all of them clearly blue, and asked to name the colour aloud. Two members of each group were secretly working for the researchers and consistently described every slide as green. Only a small fraction of the genuine participants ever repeated this judgement in public. When they were later tested alone, however, on a task in which colours gradually shaded from blue into green, many of them showed that their private colour boundary had moved: they now labelled as green shades they would previously have called blue. For Ludovica Sannazzaro, a social psychologist at the Po Valley Institute of Social Psychology, findings like this reveal a fundamental asymmetry. Majorities, she argues, typically produce public compliance without private change, whereas minorities tend to produce the reverse, a slow and often unacknowledged conversion of what people actually believe.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not every minority succeeds, of course. Kwabena Adjepong of the Accra Institute for Social Research has spent many years studying what he calls the behavioural style of dissenters. Consistency, he has found, is essential: a minority that wavers is simply dismissed. But consistency can be overdone. Minorities that refuse to make any concession at all are perceived as dogmatic, and their arguments are then explained away as a product of stubbornness rather than conviction. The most persuasive dissenters, according to Adjepong, are those who hold firmly to their central position while appearing reasonable and willing to negotiate on matters of detail.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How large are these effects? Haruto Kanemaru, who has combined the results of nearly a hundred experiments, concludes that minorities seldom change people's opinions on the specific issue being debated, at least not immediately. Their impact is more likely to appear on related questions, or on measures taken days or weeks later, a pattern he describes as indirect influence. Sceptics point out that the effects in question are modest, and they are right to do so. It does not follow, though, that such effects are trivial. A small shift in private opinion, repeated across many people and many conversations, may accumulate into precisely the kind of gradual change that the historical record shows.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of research has asked not whether minorities win converts but what dissent does to the quality of group thinking. In a series of problem-solving studies, a team at the Laugarvatn Decision Laboratory found that groups exposed to a persistent dissenting voice considered more alternatives and generated a wider range of solutions than groups in which everyone agreed. Strikingly, this benefit appeared even when the dissenter was wrong. Exposure to disagreement, it seems, prompts people to think more broadly instead of settling on the first acceptable answer. Of all the findings in this field, this is the one with the greatest practical significance, since it suggests that dissent can be valuable whether or not it is correct.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The neat contrast between majority and minority influence has not gone unchallenged. Folake Olumodeji, who studies persuasion at Ogun Valley University, argues that the distinction has been drawn too sharply. Majorities, she notes, can also prompt careful scrutiny of arguments, particularly when their position is unexpected, and minorities sometimes win simple public agreement. In her view, a single account of persuasion, in which the amount of thought people give to a message depends on circumstances, explains the evidence better than two separate processes. Olumodeji is probably right that the dichotomy is overdrawn. Even so, as a rough guide to the typical effects of being outnumbered and of being challenged, the distinction remains a useful one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings matter well beyond the laboratory. Organisations frequently treat disagreement as a problem to be managed, and those who persist in raising objections may find their careers suffering as a result. The research suggests that this is short-sighted. Yet it also contains a warning for dissenters themselves. A minority rarely wins the argument on the day it is made; its influence works quietly and over time, often without those who have been persuaded recognising where their new opinions came from. That is exactly why it is so easy to underestimate.

topic: informational cascades and herding: copying earlier choices in laboratory guessing tasks, online music downloads and comment ratings
title: Following the Queue
subtitle: When people copy the choices of those who went before them, popularity can become self-fulfilling

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine arriving in an unfamiliar town and having to choose between two restaurants on the same street. One is almost empty; the other is crowded. Most people choose the crowded one, and it is tempting to dismiss this as mindless imitation. But the decision can be perfectly reasonable. The diners already seated may know something that the newcomer does not, perhaps from a recommendation or a previous visit, and their presence is a form of evidence. Economists who formalised this intuition in the early 1990s gave it the name 'informational cascade', and their central insight deserves more recognition than it usually receives: copying others is not necessarily a sign of weak character or poor judgement, and in many circumstances it is the rational thing to do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in what happens next. Each person in a sequence, the theory supposes, has some private information of uncertain quality, as well as the public record of earlier choices. Once a few people have chosen the same option, a newcomer may sensibly conclude that the weight of public evidence outweighs his or her own hunch and follow the crowd regardless. At that point the cascade has begun, and something curious occurs: because later individuals no longer act on their private information, their choices reveal nothing new, and the crowd stops learning. A long queue may therefore rest on the judgements of only the first two or three people in it. For the same reason, cascades are fragile. Since they are built on so little information, a small amount of new public evidence, such as a single critical review, can bring them to an abrupt end.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Laboratory studies have confirmed that such sequences arise readily. In a series of experiments at the Mazovia School of Economics, Dariusz Wolanczyk asked participants to guess, one after another, which of two urns a set of coloured balls had been drawn from. Each saw a single private draw and heard the guesses of everyone before them. In roughly seven out of ten sequences in which the mathematics made a cascade possible, one duly formed, with participants overriding the evidence of their own draw. About a quarter of these cascades settled on the wrong urn, a striking proportion given that the information held by the group as a whole was usually sufficient to identify the correct one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whether such effects matter outside the laboratory was tested on a far larger scale by Tomás Echevarne of the Meseta Institute of Technology. He recruited around twelve thousand people to an online site where they could listen to and download songs by unknown bands. Participants were randomly assigned to one of eight independent 'worlds', each a self-contained market in which they could see how many times each song had been downloaded by others, while a control group saw no such figures. The best songs, as judged by the control group, rarely did badly and the worst rarely did well, but for the great majority in between, success varied enormously from one world to another. A song that topped the chart in one world might languish near the bottom in the next. iisible download counts also made the most popular songs far more dominant, increasing the gap between hits and failures.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nkiruka Anyanwu, a consumer researcher at the Lagos Centre for Digital Behaviour, extended this work to online ratings. Working with a news website, her team randomly gave some newly posted comments a single artificial positive vote, others a single negative vote, and left a third set untouched. Comments that received an early positive vote were substantially more likely to end up with a high overall score, an effect that persisted for months. Artificial negative votes, by contrast, tended to be cancelled out, as other readers stepped in to correct what appeared to be unfair treatment. Herding, in other words, seems to operate more powerfully in the direction of approval than of disapproval.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that these findings reveal widespread irrationality. Henrik Saltvedt, an economist who has written extensively on consumer markets, argues that much apparent herding is simply people tracking quality. In real markets, he points out, consumers usually have far more independent information than laboratory participants, from detailed written reviews to the advice of friends, and cascades are correspondingly easier to break. Saltvedt is right that laboratory designs, which deliberately starve participants of information, may exaggerate how easily cascades take hold. However, his argument underestimates how much digital platforms have changed matters. By displaying sales figures, star ratings and download counts at the very moment of choice, they make earlier decisions more visible than at any time in history, and thereby create precisely the conditions in which cascades flourish.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some platforms have begun to respond. A number now hide popularity figures until an item has accumulated a minimum number of ratings, and others ask users to submit their own rating before revealing those of other people. Such measures will not eliminate herding, nor should they try to, since following others is often sensible. The real problem is not that people copy, but that copying discards information that would otherwise have been shared. Popularity is, at best, weak evidence of quality, and the more a system encourages people to set aside their own judgement, the weaker that evidence becomes.

topic: behavioural mimicry and rapport: unconscious copying of gestures, its effects on liking, tipping and helping, cultural limits and replication doubts
title: The Unwitting Mirror
subtitle: We copy one another's gestures without noticing. Does this hidden form of conformity really bring people closer?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Watch two friends talking in a café for a few minutes and a curious pattern often emerges. When one leans forward, the other soon does the same; when one folds her arms or touches her hair, her companion follows a moment later. Neither is aware of what is happening. Research on conformity has traditionally concentrated on opinions and judgements, on whether people will publicly agree with a group they suspect is mistaken. Yet a great deal of social alignment takes place below the level of conscious thought, in posture, gesture and tone of voice, and it seems to me that this bodily form of conformity deserves a far more central place in the field than it has generally been given.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most widely cited evidence comes from the laboratory of Margit Csepregi at the Tisza Institute of Behavioural Science. In her first study, participants took turns describing photographs with a partner who, unknown to them, was employed by the researchers. Throughout the conversation, the partner either rubbed her face or repeatedly shook her foot. Video recordings showed that participants performed whichever action their partner displayed noticeably more often, yet when questioned afterwards, almost none had any awareness of having copied it. In a second study, the roles were reversed: the partner discreetly imitated the participant's own posture and movements. Compared with those who had not been imitated, these participants judged that the conversation had flowed more smoothly and rated their partner as more likeable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Field studies soon appeared to confirm that the effect extended beyond the laboratory. Diego Condori-Yupanqui, who teaches at a hospitality college in Cusco, persuaded restaurant staff to alternate between two ways of taking orders: either repeating the customer's words exactly, or responding with a polite paraphrase. Customers whose orders had been echoed word for word left tips that were, on average, around a fifth larger. Other experiments suggested that people who have been imitated become more generous in general. In one, participants who had been mimicked were more likely to help pick up a handful of pens that someone dropped, even when that person was not the one who had imitated them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should copying have such effects? One explanation is evolutionary: mimicry is described as a kind of 'social glue' that helped our ancestors maintain cooperative relationships in small groups. Another emphasises the close link between perception and action in the brain, since watching someone perform a movement partly activates the same processes involved in performing it oneself. These accounts are not incompatible, and both may be correct. What is often overlooked, however, is that the direction of cause and effect is far from settled. People who already like each other mimic one another more, so mimicry may be as much a consequence of rapport as a cause of it, and in everyday life the two probably reinforce each other in a continuous loop.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Kaori Inamura of the Sendai Institute for Cultural Psychology has shown that the effects of mimicry also depend heavily on context. In her cross-cultural comparisons, the link between being imitated and liking was strongest among participants from societies that place a high value on group harmony, and considerably weaker elsewhere. More strikingly, imitation that was noticed tended to backfire. When participants realised that a partner was copying them, they rated that partner as less trustworthy and the interaction as less comfortable than if there had been no imitation at all. Mimicry by a member of a group the participant regarded as different from their own was particularly likely to be resented.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: More recently, the field has faced the same doubts about reliability that have affected much of social psychology. A large replication project coordinated by Anneliese Vrolijk brought together eleven laboratories and some thirteen hundred participants. The participants did imitate their partners, confirming that unconscious copying is a robust phenomenon. However, the effect of being imitated on liking was far smaller than in the original studies, and in several laboratories it was close to zero. Some commentators have taken this to mean that the social benefits of mimicry were an illusion. That conclusion seems premature. A brief encounter with a stranger in a laboratory is arguably a poor test of a process that normally unfolds over long relationships. Nevertheless, the more confident claims made in the past clearly need to be scaled back.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this has prevented mimicry from being marketed as a technique. Sales trainers and self-help authors advise readers to mirror the posture and phrases of clients in order to win their trust. Such advice misunderstands the phenomenon. Mimicry appears to work, when it works at all, precisely because neither party intends it or notices it; deliberate imitation is likely to be clumsy, and, as Inamura's findings indicate, imitation that is detected can do more harm than good. A salesperson who copies every gesture of a customer is, in effect, conducting a version of the noticed imitation that participants in the laboratory found so off-putting. The lesson of this research is not that we should manipulate others by imitating them, but that the ordinary, unplanned coordination of bodies is one of the quieter ways in which people signal that they belong together. The unwitting mirror, in short, cannot easily be turned into a tool.

topic: ostracism and social exclusion as a driver of conformity: brief laboratory exclusion, the social pain hypothesis, strategic re-inclusion and chronic shunning
title: The Sting of Exclusion
subtitle: Being ignored or left out appears to hurt in ways that shape how readily people fall into line

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every human society has found ways of punishing its members by withdrawing their company. Ancient Athens voted to send prominent citizens into exile, religious communities have shunned those who break their rules, and schoolchildren have always understood the force of refusing to speak to a classmate. The universality of such practices points to something fundamental: people depend so heavily on acceptance by others that the mere threat of losing it can regulate their behaviour. Studies of conformity have generally treated the wish to be liked as a background assumption rather than a subject of investigation. In my view this has been a mistake, since the fear of exclusion is arguably the engine that drives much of the conformity those studies describe.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Systematic research on exclusion became possible with the development of a remarkably simple procedure. In the version used by Fiachra Mac Suibhne at Shannonside College, participants play an online game in which three players toss a virtual ball to one another. After a few throws, the other two players, who are in fact controlled by a computer program, stop passing the ball to the participant altogether. The whole episode lasts barely three minutes. Yet participants who are left out report lower mood, a weaker sense of belonging and reduced self-esteem compared with those who are included. Mac Suibhne found that these effects persisted when participants were told beforehand that the other players were not human, and even when the excluders were said to belong to a political group the participants despised. That such brief and trivial rejection should matter at all is striking; that it should matter regardless of who is doing the rejecting is more striking still.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should exclusion hurt so much? Researchers involved in the Jostedal Social Pain Project have proposed that the pain is more than metaphorical. Using brain imaging, they have reported that being left out activates regions also associated with the distress component of physical pain. In a widely publicised follow-up, volunteers who took a common over-the-counter painkiller every day for three weeks reported fewer hurt feelings in their daily lives than those given a placebo. The findings are intriguing, but they have been interpreted more boldly than they deserve. The regions in question respond to many kinds of unexpected or significant event, not only painful ones, and the fact that two experiences produce overlapping patterns of brain activity does not show that they feel alike to the person undergoing them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The link between exclusion and conformity was examined directly by Malgorzata Brzezicka of the Wroclaw Institute of Psychology. Participants first played the ball-tossing game and were then asked to make simple perceptual judgements alongside a group whose members unanimously gave the same incorrect answers. Those who had just been excluded went along with the erroneous majority considerably more often than those who had been included. Crucially, however, this difference appeared only when participants announced their answers aloud. When they recorded their judgements privately, the excluded and included participants performed almost identically. Brzezicka concludes that conformity after exclusion is less a change of belief than a bid to win back acceptance, and the evidence strongly suggests that she is right: the behaviour is calculated, not a mindless reflex.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nyasha Mushonga, who studies social behaviour at the Harare Institute of Social Behaviour, has refined this picture further. In her experiments, excluded participants were noticeably warmer and more cooperative towards new partners whom they expected to meet again. When there was no realistic prospect of being accepted, however, the same participants frequently became hostile, for example allocating unpleasant tasks to strangers who had played no part in the original rejection. Mushonga argues that people respond to exclusion by trying to restore whatever they feel they have lost most acutely. Where belonging seems attainable, they seek it through compliance; where it does not, they reassert control in other ways.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: All of this research, however, concerns exclusion lasting a matter of minutes. Bakhtiyor Turdaliev, a sociologist who has interviewed people shunned by their families or communities for many years, argues that long-term ostracism follows a quite different course. After the initial pain and a period of attempting to regain acceptance, those who remain excluded tend to enter a stage of resignation marked by alienation, depression and a pervasive sense of helplessness. Laboratory studies, by their nature, can capture only the first of these stages, and they almost certainly underestimate the damage that prolonged exclusion inflicts.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings have obvious relevance to schools and workplaces, where the 'silent treatment' is often dismissed as a lesser form of mistreatment than open aggression, and to online communities, where users can be ignored or blocked with a single click. They also invite a reconsideration of how conformity is judged. People who go along with a group are frequently portrayed as weak or lacking in principle. If conformity is often the price people pay to avoid the sting of exclusion, then we should perhaps be slower to condemn individuals who conform, and more attentive to the social arrangements that make dissent so costly.

topic: personality change across adulthood and the maturity principle
title: The Settling Self
subtitle: Adult personality turns out to be far less fixed than psychologists once believed, but explaining why it changes has proved contentious

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, psychologists broadly accepted that adult personality was essentially fixed. A person might acquire new skills, change careers or move across the world, but the underlying dispositions – how sociable, anxious, orderly or curious they were – were assumed to have hardened by the age of thirty, much as plaster sets once it has been poured. This assumption was convenient: it allowed researchers to treat personality as a stable backdrop against which more interesting changes took place. It was also, as the evidence accumulated over the past three decades now makes clear, largely mistaken. The question today is not whether adults change, but how much, in what direction, and why.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential answer has come from longitudinal studies that track the same individuals for decades. Marit Rønneberg and her colleagues at the Bergen Lifespan Panel have followed more than eleven thousand Norwegians since 1987, assessing them every five years on the five broad traits most psychologists now recognise. Their data reveal a consistent pattern: between early adulthood and late middle age, people on average become more conscientious, more agreeable and less prone to anxiety and moodiness. Rønneberg calls this the 'maturity principle', arguing that personality shifts towards the traits that societies tend to value in responsible adults. Importantly, the largest changes occur not in adolescence, as was once supposed, but between the ages of twenty and forty.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should this happen? Rønneberg favours what is sometimes called social investment theory: as people commit themselves to adult roles – a stable job, a long-term partner, parenthood – the expectations attached to those roles gradually reshape their behaviour, and eventually their dispositions. Someone who must arrive at work on time every morning for years, the argument runs, does not merely behave more conscientiously; they become more conscientious. In support of this, her team found that young adults who entered paid employment early showed correspondingly early rises in conscientiousness compared with peers who remained in full-time education.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Sorin Teodorescu, a behavioural geneticist at the Cluj Institute for Developmental Science, points out that twin studies show much of the change in adult personality is itself partly heritable. If identical twins raised apart mature at similar rates, he argues, then maturation may reflect an intrinsic biological programme rather than a response to social roles. On this view, people do not become conscientious because they take on jobs and families; rather, the same underlying process that makes them more conscientious also makes them more inclined to accept such commitments. Teodorescu accepts that the correlation between role entry and personality change is real, but he insists that its direction has never been convincingly established.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from cross-cultural research. Itziar Whitlam, working with collaborators at the Altiplano Institute of Social Research, compared personality trajectories in sixty-two countries. She found the maturity pattern almost everywhere, but noted that its timing varied: in countries where people typically marry and begin working at younger ages, the rise in conscientiousness also began earlier. To Whitlam, this is strong evidence for the social investment account, since a purely biological clock should tick at roughly the same rate everywhere. Teodorescu's response is that nutrition and health, which also vary considerably from one country to another, could influence the pace of biological maturation, so the cultural data do not settle the matter.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In my view, the two positions are less opposed than their advocates suggest. Genes and roles are unlikely to operate independently: a person's inherited temperament influences which roles they seek, and the roles in turn amplify or dampen that temperament. What the debate has sometimes obscured is the sheer size of individual differences. The averages hide enormous variation; a substantial minority of adults become less conscientious or more anxious over time, often following divorce, unemployment or serious illness. Dov Sharabi, a clinical psychologist who studies such cases, warns that the cheerful message of the maturity principle can lead people to assume that personal growth is automatic. It is not, and treating it as such risks overlooking those whose trajectories move in the opposite direction.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Later life brings further complications. Data from people over seventy, though still relatively scarce, suggest that some of the gains of middle age may partially reverse: agreeableness tends to remain stable, but conscientiousness and openness to new experience often decline, a pattern Rønneberg attributes to retirement and the loss of structured roles. Whether this decline is inevitable is unclear. It seems at least plausible that older adults who remain engaged in demanding activities preserve their conscientiousness for longer, although this has yet to be tested rigorously.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What, then, should we conclude? The image of personality as plaster is clearly wrong, but it would be equally mistaken to replace it with an image of endless plasticity. Personality is better described as moderately stable: rank orders between individuals remain fairly consistent, so that the most anxious twenty-year-olds are usually still among the more anxious sixty-year-olds, even as the whole group becomes calmer. Change is real, but it is slow, cumulative and, for the most part, unnoticed by the people undergoing it.

topic: animal personality: consistent individual differences in boldness and their evolution
title: The Bold and the Cautious
subtitle: Behavioural ecologists once dismissed individual differences in animal behaviour as noise. Now they are trying to explain them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Place a novel object – a brightly coloured plastic block, say – into a tank of sticklebacks, and the fish will not respond as one. Some approach within seconds and nudge it; others retreat to the vegetation and stay there for the rest of the afternoon. Repeat the test a week later and, remarkably often, the same individuals behave in the same way. Similar consistency has since been documented in creatures as different as octopuses, jumping spiders, red squirrels and songbirds, which suggests that it is not a quirk of one group of animals but a widespread feature of animal life. For behavioural ecologists, observations of this kind have become the foundation of a field that would have seemed faintly absurd fifty years ago: the study of animal personality.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Earlier generations of researchers were not unaware of such differences, but they tended to treat them as noise. Natural selection, it was assumed, should push each population towards a single optimal behaviour, and individual departures from that optimum were regarded as measurement error or as the product of temporary circumstances such as hunger. Researchers therefore averaged across individuals and reported the mean, a practice that conveniently made the variation disappear from the published record. Journal editors, for their part, showed little appetite for studies that seemed merely to catalogue the quirks of particular animals. Only in the 1990s did a handful of ecologists begin to argue that consistent individual differences were themselves a phenomenon requiring explanation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Among the most prominent of these is Liene Strautmane of the Riga Centre for Behavioural Ecology, whose long-term work on great tits has become a reference point for the field. Strautmane measured how quickly wild-caught birds explored an unfamiliar room and found that the trait was not only repeatable but also partly inherited: fast explorers tended to produce fast-exploring offspring. More strikingly, neither type was consistently more successful. In years when beech trees produced abundant seed, bold birds fared better, perhaps because they competed more aggressively for territories; in poor years, cautious birds survived at higher rates. Strautmane argues that this fluctuating selection explains why both personalities persist: because conditions vary from year to year, no single strategy wins out permanently.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Paavo Ruusunen, an evolutionary theorist at the Oulu Institute of Ecology, offers a complementary explanation that focuses on trade-offs within an individual's life. In his model, animals that have accumulated valuable assets – a good territory, for example, or substantial body reserves – have more to lose and should therefore behave cautiously, whereas those with little to lose can afford to take risks. Because early differences in assets tend to persist, behavioural differences become self-reinforcing over time. Ruusunen's model has the attraction of explaining why boldness and aggression so often go together, a correlation that is hard to account for if each trait evolved separately. It is an elegant theory, though the empirical support for it remains patchy, and in several studies the predicted link between assets and caution has simply failed to appear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are comfortable with the vocabulary being used. Grace Ombati, who studies reef fish at the Mombasa Marine Behaviour Station, accepts that consistent individual differences exist but objects to calling them 'personality'. The term, she argues, imports assumptions from human psychology – about inner mental states, for instance – that cannot be tested in a fish. She prefers the more neutral phrase 'behavioural syndromes'. This is more than a quibble over words: Ombati worries that the attractive language has helped the field win media attention and funding while encouraging overconfident claims. Her concern is understandable, but I think it is overstated. Researchers who use the word 'personality' are, almost without exception, careful to define it operationally, in terms of measurable behaviour, and the label has the advantage of signalling continuity with a large body of human research.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever it is called, the phenomenon has practical consequences. Conservation programmes that breed endangered animals in captivity have discovered that captive conditions can unintentionally favour certain personalities. Bold individuals often thrive in enclosures, where food is plentiful and predators are absent, but when released into the wild they may approach predators too readily. Some reintroduction projects now test animals' responses before release and aim to send out a mix of temperaments. In fisheries, too, there is evidence that passive fishing gear such as traps preferentially captures bolder fish, so that heavily exploited populations may gradually become shyer – a change that could, in turn, make them harder to catch and to monitor.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The study of animal personality also raises questions about how we interpret experiments generally. If individuals respond in consistently different ways, then a laboratory study that happens to draw on a sample of unusually bold animals may produce results that do not generalise. There is a growing suspicion that some failures to replicate findings in animal behaviour stem from exactly this problem. Some laboratories have responded by screening animals for boldness before assigning them to experimental groups, a modest precaution that costs little and may prevent a good deal of confusion. It would be an exaggeration to say that personality research has overturned behavioural ecology, but it has certainly forced the discipline to take seriously something it once preferred to ignore: that in animals, as in people, the individual matters.
