topic: the lexical hypothesis and whether the five-factor model of personality is universal across languages and cultures
title: Written in the Dictionary
subtitle: Can the structure of human personality be read from the words people use to describe one another?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every language contains hundreds, sometimes thousands, of words for describing what other people are like. English speakers can call someone punctual, boastful, timid, warm-hearted or quarrelsome, and they expect to be understood. In the early twentieth century, a small number of psychologists proposed that this vocabulary was not merely a convenience but a scientific resource. Their reasoning, which became known as the lexical hypothesis, was that any difference between people important enough to matter in daily life would sooner or later acquire a name. The dictionary, on this view, is a kind of archive in which generations of ordinary speakers have recorded the dimensions of personality that they found worth noticing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Putting this idea into practice was laborious. Researchers combed dictionaries for descriptive adjectives, discarded those referring to temporary moods or physical appearance, and then asked large samples of people to rate themselves or acquaintances on the remaining terms. Statistical techniques were used to discover which words tended to be applied to the same people. If those described as 'talkative' were also usually described as 'outgoing' and 'energetic', the words could be grouped together as indicators of a single underlying dimension. After decades of such work, conducted mainly with English-speaking university students, five broad clusters emerged repeatedly, and these eventually became the basis of the model that now dominates personality psychology.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The success of the five-factor model rests partly on the claim that it is universal. Fabrizio Galeotti, a psychometrician at the Turin Centre for Personality Assessment, has spent much of his career translating standard questionnaires and administering them in more than forty countries. In the great majority, he reports, the familiar five dimensions reappear with remarkable fidelity. Galeotti regards this as evidence that the five factors reflect something deep about human nature, perhaps even a biological inheritance shared by the whole species.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics point out, however, that translating an existing questionnaire is not the same as testing the lexical hypothesis afresh. If researchers begin with English categories and simply render them into other languages, they may find those categories because they have built them into the instrument. Pornthip Thanarat, a linguist at the Chao Phraya Institute of Social Sciences, has therefore advocated what she calls 'indigenous lexical studies': starting from scratch with the descriptive vocabulary of each language, without reference to English. When this approach has been followed, the results are less tidy. Studies of several European and Asian languages have produced a sixth factor, broadly concerned with honesty and humility, which the English-based model distributes awkwardly across other dimensions. In some languages, moreover, only two or three broad factors can be recovered reliably.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Thanarat's position is more radical than it might first appear. She argues that the very notion of a trait – a stable inner disposition that travels with a person from one situation to another – may be more central to some cultures than to others. In communities where behaviour is described chiefly in terms of social roles and relationships, people may simply have fewer words for context-free characteristics, so the lexical method will reveal less structure. If she is right, the dictionary is not a neutral archive at all but a reflection of what a particular culture considers worth describing.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third line of criticism concerns who is studied. Kofi Abubakari, an anthropologist at the Tamale Centre for Comparative Psychology, notes that the populations in which the five factors replicate best tend to be literate, urban and accustomed to completing questionnaires. In a study of rural farming communities, his team found that the five-factor structure fitted poorly, with items intended to measure different traits correlating with each other in unexpected ways. Abubakari cautions against reading this as evidence that personality is organised differently in such communities. The problem, he suspects, may lie partly in the method: unfamiliar response formats and abstract questions may produce data too noisy to reveal any structure.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What should we make of these disputes? It seems to me that Galeotti's cross-national data, impressive as they are, cannot by themselves establish universality, precisely because the instruments were designed in one language and imported into others. At the same time, Thanarat's critique risks proving too much. The fact that some languages emphasise different features does not mean there is no common structure beneath them; the repeated appearance of something like sociability and conscientiousness in otherwise very different vocabularies is hard to dismiss as coincidence. The most defensible position is that a few broad dimensions are probably universal, while the finer details of personality structure are shaped by language and culture.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: There is a practical dimension to this debate. Personality questionnaires are increasingly used around the world in recruitment, education and clinical practice, often in translation and with little local validation. If the five-factor model fits some populations poorly, decisions based on it may be unfair to those who are least well described by it. The lexical hypothesis began as an elegant intuition about words; a century later, it has become a test of whether psychology can describe humanity as a whole rather than the small portion of it that has been most convenient to study.

topic: the person-situation debate: cross-situational consistency of behaviour, aggregation and if-then signatures
title: Character or Circumstance?
subtitle: Half a century after psychologists questioned whether stable traits exist at all, the argument about consistency has been reshaped rather than resolved

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, psychologists took it for granted that people possess stable traits, such as honesty, sociability and conscientiousness, which reliably shape what they do. In the late 1960s that assumption came under sustained attack. Reviewing dozens of studies, critics observed that a person's behaviour in one setting predicted their behaviour in another only weakly; the typical correlation hovered around 0.3, meaning that knowing how someone acted at a party said very little about how they would act in a seminar. Children who were scrupulously honest in one test cheated readily in another. If traits were real, the critics asked, why were they so poor at forecasting conduct? The question provoked a dispute that occupied the discipline for two decades, and its echoes can still be heard today.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The situationist position, as it came to be known, held that behaviour is governed principally by the immediate features of a setting: who is present, what is at stake, what norms apply. On this view, the impression that others have fixed characters is largely an illusion created by the observer. Agnieszka Zawilska, a social psychologist at the Kraków Institute of Behavioural Studies, has argued that the illusion is sustained because we usually encounter acquaintances in a narrow range of circumstances. The colleague is seen only at work, the neighbour only on the street, so that consistency of setting is mistaken for consistency of person. It is an elegant argument, and there is undoubtedly something in it. But it proves less than its advocates suppose, because it cannot explain why people who are observed across many different settings are still judged with notable agreement by independent raters.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most influential reply came from researchers who questioned the statistics rather than the theory. Rómulo Huamanchumo, at the Andean Centre for Personality Research in Lima, pointed out that a single act is an extremely unreliable measure of anything. One afternoon's helpfulness may reflect a headache, a deadline or a chance remark; a trait, by contrast, is a tendency that shows itself only over many occasions. When his team aggregated behaviour across two weeks of daily diary reports, the correlations between traits and conduct rose dramatically, in some cases above 0.6. Huamanchumo likens the situation to forecasting the weather: no one can say whether a particular July day in a temperate city will be warm, but anyone can say that July will be warmer than January. This, in my view, was the decisive move of the whole debate, since it showed that weak prediction of single acts was entirely compatible with strong traits.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Aggregation did not settle everything, however. Ingvild Sæterdal, of the Bergen Laboratory for Social Cognition, has drawn attention to a pattern that neither camp anticipated. When she tracked participants across a variety of situations, she found that individuals differed not only in their average level of a trait but in the shape of their responses. One person might be talkative with strangers yet withdrawn among friends; another might show precisely the reverse. These 'if-then' signatures, Sæterdal argues, are themselves remarkably stable over time, and they represent the true core of personality. Her proposal is attractive because it accommodates both variability and stability within a single framework. Yet it carries a practical cost: signatures can be identified only by observing someone across many situations, which makes them far harder to measure than conventional trait scores.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective focuses on how people choose situations rather than simply responding to them. Noor Hamdani, a psychologist at the Gulf Institute for Human Development, emphasises that adults are seldom passive recipients of circumstances. The sociable person accepts invitations; the anxious person avoids crowded rooms; the curious person seeks out unfamiliar places. Over the years, these choices build environments that reinforce the dispositions which produced them in the first place. Hamdani's longitudinal data from more than three thousand adults suggest that such selection may account for much of the apparent stability of personality in later life. If she is right, the opposition between persons and situations that dominated earlier debate was always somewhat artificial, since situations are partly the creations of the persons who occupy them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, though, to conclude that the situationists lost the argument entirely. Their critique forced personality researchers to abandon careless habits, such as inferring a broad trait from a single questionnaire item or a single laboratory task. It also served as a reminder that powerful situations, such as an emergency, a strict institution or a crowd in panic, can override individual differences almost completely. Few researchers now dispute that strong situations reduce the variation between people, while weak or ambiguous situations allow it to emerge. The real question is not whether persons or situations matter, but how much each matters in a given context.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What remains unresolved is how this hard-won consensus should be applied outside the laboratory. Employers, courts and schools routinely make judgements about individuals on the basis of a brief encounter: an interview, a single incident, an hour of observation. The research of the past fifty years suggests that such judgements are bound to be fragile, not because character is a myth, but because so little behaviour has been sampled. A modest proposal follows. Wherever decisions about people carry serious consequences, they should rest on observations gathered across time and settings. That this principle is so rarely followed is perhaps the clearest sign that the lessons of the debate have yet to travel beyond academic journals.

topic: twin studies, the heritability of personality and the puzzle of the non-shared environment
title: The Siblings Who Grow Apart
subtitle: Twin studies show that personality is substantially heritable, but the more puzzling finding concerns what families fail to share

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few findings in psychology are as robust, or as quietly unsettling, as those produced by twin studies of personality. The method is simple in principle. Identical twins share all of their genes, whereas fraternal twins share on average about half; if identical pairs resemble each other more closely on a trait than fraternal pairs do, the difference can be attributed to genetic influence. Applied to the broad dimensions of personality, such as extraversion, anxiety and conscientiousness, this logic consistently yields heritability estimates of between 40 and 50 per cent. That genes matter is hardly surprising. What is surprising is the fate of the remainder. Almost none of the environmental influence on personality appears to come from what siblings have in common: the same parents, the same house, the same neighbourhood and income. Adopted children raised in the same family turn out, as adults, to be scarcely more alike in personality than people chosen at random.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Eszter Kovácsházy, who directs the Danube Twin Registry in Budapest, has analysed data from more than nine thousand twin pairs in six countries and finds the pattern remarkably consistent across them. In her view, the near absence of shared environmental effects is no statistical artefact but one of the most secure results in the behavioural sciences. It is worth being precise about what this does and does not mean. It does not mean that parents have no influence on their children. It means, rather, that whatever influence they exert does not make their children resemble one another. A parent's warmth or strictness may shape each child, but apparently in different directions, so that the effect disappears when siblings are compared.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Attention has therefore turned to what geneticists call the non-shared environment: the experiences that differ between children growing up in the same household. Plausible candidates are not hard to list. Parents may treat one child more indulgently than another; siblings make different friends, have different teachers and suffer different illnesses. Ioana Brâncoveanu, a developmental psychologist at the Cluj Institute for Family Studies, spent a decade trying to measure such factors directly. The results were sobering. Differences in parental treatment explained only a modest fraction of the personality differences between siblings, typically less than five per cent, and longitudinal data suggested that much of this differential treatment was itself a reaction to traits the children already displayed. A more irritable child, in other words, tends to receive harsher discipline, rather than becoming irritable because of it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Faced with such meagre returns, some researchers have embraced what has been called the 'gloomy prospect'. Chiamaka Ijeomah, of the West African Centre for Behavioural Genetics in Ibadan, argues that the non-shared environment consists largely of idiosyncratic events: a chance encounter, an accident, a particular book read at a particular age. She goes further, suggesting that random variation in the way the brain develops before birth may contribute too, which would explain why even identical twins raised together differ noticeably in temperament. If she is correct, much of what makes individuals distinctive is intrinsically unpredictable. The argument deserves serious consideration, but it carries a danger: once unexplained variance is labelled as chance, the incentive to look for its causes weakens. It should also be remembered that the non-shared estimate is calculated as a residual, the variance left over once genes and shared environment are accounted for, and so it inevitably absorbs measurement error as well.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics of the twin method raise a different set of objections. Dokgo Min-seo, a statistician at the Seoul Centre for Population Health, points out that the method assumes identical and fraternal twins experience equally similar environments. If identical twins are dressed alike, mistaken for each other and treated as a unit, some of their extra similarity may be environmental rather than genetic, and heritability will be overstated. Dokgo also stresses that heritability describes a particular population at a particular time, not a fixed property of a trait. On this last point the critics are entirely right; a highly heritable trait is not thereby immune to change, as the dramatic rise in average height over the past century demonstrates. Their first objection is weaker than it appears, however. Studies of twins whose zygosity was misjudged by their parents suggest that being treated alike adds little to their resemblance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The arrival of molecular genetics was expected to resolve these disputes. Instead, it has opened a new one. Genome-wide studies have found that personality is influenced by thousands of genetic variants, each with a minuscule effect, and scores combining all of them currently explain only a small fraction of the variation that twin studies attribute to genes. Kovácsházy is confident that this 'missing heritability' will shrink as samples grow larger; Dokgo regards it as evidence that twin estimates were inflated from the start. At present, the data do not allow either position to be dismissed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be concluded about the family? The claim, popular in some accounts, that upbringing is irrelevant goes considerably further than the evidence permits. Shared environment does have measurable effects on some adult outcomes, notably religious affiliation and political attitudes, even if it leaves personality largely untouched. Moreover, twin and adoption samples rarely include families at the extremes of neglect or poverty, so their conclusions apply to the ordinary range of homes rather than to all possible ones. The more defensible lesson is a humbler one: within that ordinary range, parents influence their children profoundly, but they cannot determine which kind of people those children will become.

topic: birth order and personality: niche theory, within-family designs and the age confound in parents' ratings
title: First, Middle, Last
subtitle: The belief that our position among our siblings shapes who we become has proved far more durable than the evidence for it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas about personality are as widely held as the belief that birth order shapes character. Firstborns, it is said, are responsible, ambitious and conscientious, the natural leaders who identify with their parents' authority. Youngest children are charming, carefree and inclined to rebel, while middle children, overlooked by everyone, become diplomats and peacemakers. Such claims fill parenting magazines and popular psychology books, and many people find them confirmed in their own families. The notion that a child's position in the family leaves a lasting mark on personality goes back at least to the early twentieth century. What is remarkable is not that the idea is popular, but how little its popularity has been dented by a century of research that has largely failed to support it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious modern version of the theory was put forward by Thorvald Eikeland of the Nidaros Centre for Family Research. Drawing on evolutionary thinking, Eikeland argued that siblings compete for a limited supply of parental attention and resources. Rather than competing head-on, he suggested, each child carves out a distinct niche within the family. The firstborn, being larger and more capable, aligns with the parents and adopts conventional values; later children, unable to win on those terms, cultivate openness and a willingness to challenge authority. In support, Eikeland assembled biographical data on thousands of historical figures and reported that laterborns were far more likely than firstborns to champion radical ideas in science. The theory is undeniably ingenious. However, the historical data were collected and coded by a single team, and they have never been independently re-examined, which makes the striking results difficult to evaluate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of the earlier research suffered from a more basic flaw. Most studies compared firstborns from some families with laterborns from others, a design that confuses the effects of birth order with those of family size. Large families contain, by definition, more laterborns, and in many countries they have also tended to be poorer and less educated, so differences attributed to birth order may in fact reflect background. Shirin Ghorbani of the Zayandeh Institute of Social Statistics addressed this problem by analysing three national panel studies involving more than twenty thousand participants, comparing siblings within the same family. She found no meaningful effects of birth order on extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness or conscientiousness. The one consistent difference was small: firstborns had slightly higher intelligence scores, by around one and a half points on average.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why, then, does the belief persist? Yuki Tsubouchi of the Kobe Laboratory of Child Development has proposed an answer that is as simple as it is persuasive. When parents describe their children, they inevitably compare them with one another at the same moment, and at that moment the eldest is also the oldest. An eight-year-old is more responsible than a five-year-old, not because of birth order but because of three extra years of development. In Tsubouchi's studies, parents consistently mistook age differences for personality differences, rating the elder child as more conscientious even when independent measures taken at matched ages showed no gap. Families, in other words, do observe real differences, but they are snapshots of development rather than permanent features of character.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone has abandoned the field. Inés Altuzarra of the Bilbao Centre for Lifespan Studies defends a narrower claim. Birth order, she argues, does shape behaviour, but chiefly within the family itself: elder siblings tend to dominate, instruct and protect younger ones, and these roles can persist into adulthood whenever the siblings are together. Outside the family, however, the effects fade. This is a plausible position and one that fits much everyday experience. Yet it should be recognised that it is a much more modest claim than the popular one, which holds that birth order moulds personality in every sphere of life.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is also possible that the absence of effects is partly a product of where the research has been done. Ghorbani herself notes that almost all large-scale studies come from wealthy Western societies in which children are, at least formally, treated as equals. In cultures where land and property pass to the eldest son, birth order directly determines inheritance and occupational choices, and it would be surprising if this had no consequences for how individuals see themselves. The question deserves proper investigation; the fact that no effects have been found in one kind of society does not show that they are absent everywhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Does any of this matter? Arguably it does, because beliefs about birth order are not merely harmless entertainment. A parent who expects the youngest child to be irresponsible may give that child fewer opportunities to prove otherwise, and a teacher who assumes the eldest is a natural leader may overlook quieter talents in a younger sibling. The damage is probably modest, but it is real. The evidence suggests that a child's place in the family tells us very little about who that child will become, and the folklore deserves to be treated with considerably more scepticism than it usually receives.

topic: computational personality assessment: inferring traits from digital footprints, smartphone sensing and personality-targeted advertising
title: Personality by Proxy
subtitle: Algorithms can now estimate our character from the traces we leave online. What they actually reveal is a more modest, and more awkward, question

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the measurement of personality meant asking people about themselves. Respondents rated how well a series of statements described them, and their answers were summed into scores on broad traits. Over the past fifteen years, however, another source of information has emerged. Every endorsement of a web page, every online purchase, every message typed into a phone leaves a trace, and a growing field known as computational personality assessment sets out to infer character from these traces without asking a single question. The approach has been greeted with a mixture of excitement and alarm. My own view is that both reactions have run ahead of the evidence: the techniques are less powerful than their admirers suggest, and the most serious problems they raise have little to do with their power.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study that brought the field to public attention was conducted by a team at the Halden Institute for Social Computing under the direction of Ottilie Fjærestad. Some 58,000 volunteers completed a hundred-item personality questionnaire and also gave the researchers access to the list of pages they had publicly endorsed on a social networking site. A model trained on these endorsements then predicted each person's questionnaire scores. With around seventy endorsements to work from, the model's predictions agreed with the volunteers' self-ratings more closely than did ratings supplied by a friend; with three hundred, it matched the judgements of a spouse. Newspapers announced that computers now knew us better than our partners did. That conclusion, though understandable, misread what had been measured. The model and the spouse were both judged by how well they reproduced the volunteer's own answers, and self-reports are themselves an imperfect guide to how a person actually behaves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In fact, the accuracy figures are respectable rather than remarkable. In Fjærestad's data, openness to experience was the trait predicted most successfully and agreeableness the least. Iñaki Larrazabal, of the Cantabrian Institute of Behavioural Data, later pooled the results of twenty-six studies and found an average correlation of about 0.34 between predicted and self-reported scores, a level he compares to that of a single, reasonably well-chosen questionnaire item. More troubling, in Larrazabal's view, is that such models age badly. Platforms change their design, fashions shift, and the meaning of a particular endorsement drifts; in one analysis, a model built on 2012 data was markedly less accurate on comparable data from four years later. This decay has received far less attention than it deserves, since any commercial system would have to be retrained continually to remain useful.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second strand of research looks not at what people endorse but at what they write and do. Analyses of millions of social media posts have found that extraverts use more words associated with social occasions, while people scoring high on neuroticism refer to themselves more often and use more words expressing anxiety or sadness. Smartphones offer still richer material. At the Baltic Centre for Mobile Sensing, Taavi Kõrvits and his colleagues collected sensor data from the phones of 600 university students over four weeks. The number of calls a student made, together with the number of conversations detected by the phone's microphone, predicted sociability; conscientiousness was linked to the regularity of daily routines, such as how consistently the phone was first unlocked at the same hour each morning. Kõrvits argues that sensing records what people actually do rather than how they wish to present themselves, and that for some purposes it may therefore be superior to the questionnaire.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This argument deserves a hearing, but it rests on an easily overlooked assumption. Behaviour is not the same thing as personality. A student who rarely leaves home may be introverted, but she may equally be unwell, short of money or caring for a relative. Across hundreds of people, such circumstances can be expected to cancel out, revealing the link between behaviour and trait. For any single individual, there is no such guarantee. The distinction between validity at the level of a group and accuracy at the level of a person is, I would argue, the most important point that public discussion of these methods has missed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It matters most when inferences are put to practical use. In one set of field experiments, advertisements for a cosmetics brand were written in an extravert and an introvert version and shown to users whose personality had been estimated from their online activity. Matched advertisements attracted up to 40 per cent more clicks and 50 per cent more purchases than mismatched ones. Kgomotso Sibanyoni-Ruele, of the Centre for Digital Rights in Johannesburg, contends that the real danger lies not in how accurate such inferences are but in the fact that nobody consented to them, and that even a wrong estimate can cause harm if it is used to screen applicants for loans or jobs. On the question of manipulation, the experimental results are less alarming than the percentages imply: click rates rose from a tiny fraction of one per cent to a slightly larger tiny fraction. Fears of mass manipulation are therefore overstated. Her argument about consent, however, does not depend on effect sizes at all, and it seems to me unanswerable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Regulation aimed at particular techniques is likely to be overtaken quickly, given how rapidly models decay; rules governing the purposes for which personality may be inferred, and requiring that people be told when it is, would prove more durable. There is also an irony worth noting. A field that set out to bypass the questionnaire may end up improving it, by forcing psychologists to confront how much of what they call personality has always been measured through people's descriptions of themselves.

topic: faking and impression management on personality questionnaires used in job selection
title: Putting On a Good Face
subtitle: Job applicants routinely present a polished version of themselves on personality questionnaires. The real question is whether that matters

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine applying for a sales position and meeting the statement 'I sometimes put off tasks I find dull.' For most people the honest response is yes, but few applicants need to be told which answer the employer would prefer. Personality questionnaires are now a routine part of recruitment in many large organisations, and for as long as they have been used, critics have argued that this transparency makes them worthless: if candidates can simply give the answers they think are wanted, the scores reveal nothing. In my view this objection is partly right, but it is largely aimed at the wrong target.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That applicants do adjust their answers is no longer in serious doubt. The clearest evidence comes from studies in which the same people complete a questionnaire in two different settings. Signe Ulvestad, an occupational psychologist at the Vestland School of Work Psychology, tested some 1,200 people first when they applied for jobs at a logistics company and again, a year later, as anonymous participants in a research project. Their conscientiousness scores were on average about half a standard deviation higher when a job was at stake, and emotional stability rose by a similar amount. Openness to experience, by contrast, barely changed. Ulvestad concludes that applicants do not inflate their scores indiscriminately; they raise the traits they believe the position demands and leave the others alone.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the questionnaires accept these findings but deny that they are damaging. Lorenzo Vacchelli, of the Turin Institute for Personnel Selection, points out that the correlation between questionnaire scores and supervisors' later ratings of job performance is almost as strong among real applicants as in low-stakes research samples. If faking destroyed the usefulness of the scores, he argues, this would not be the case. His explanation is that working out what an employer is looking for is itself a valuable skill, and one that tends to serve people well once they are in the job. The argument is plausible, and it probably explains part of the pattern, but it does not tell the whole story.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The problem is that a correlation summarises an entire group of applicants, while hiring decisions concern only those at the top. Even if faking leaves the overall relationship between scores and performance largely intact, it can reshuffle the order of candidates in the highest-scoring band, where the people who exaggerated most will be overrepresented. Kenji Morooka, at the Osaka Institute for Assessment Research, modelled this effect using realistic levels of faking. He found that when an employer hired only one applicant in ten, as many as a third of those appointed would not have been chosen had everyone answered honestly. For organisations that recruit a few people from a large pool, therefore, reassurance based on overall validity figures is misleading, and this, rather than whether the questionnaires work at all, is the issue that deserves attention.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Various remedies have been tried. Warning applicants that their answers will be checked for dishonesty reduces score inflation, but only modestly, and there is some evidence that it makes honest candidates more anxious. Another approach is the 'lie scale', a set of statements such as 'I have never resented anyone' that hardly anyone could truthfully endorse. The difficulty is that some people who agree with them are not lying at all; they are simply unusually scrupulous, and penalising them would be unjust. More promising is the forced-choice format, in which applicants see pairs of statements matched for how desirable they appear and must indicate which describes them better. A team led by Marijke Wijdeveld at the Northern Netherlands Assessment Centre found that this format cut score inflation by roughly two-thirds. Its drawback is technical: the scoring of such responses requires sophisticated statistical models, and older versions produced results that allowed traits to be compared within one person but not between different applicants.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Forced-choice designs seem to me the most encouraging development in the field, but no change of format removes the need to ask what a questionnaire is for. Used as one source of information alongside interviews, references and samples of actual work, it can add genuine value. Used as a single gate through which every candidate must pass, it is poorly suited to the task, precisely because of the effects Morooka describes. None of this supports the conclusion some critics draw, that personality testing should be abandoned altogether. The interview, which those critics rarely question, is at least as open to self-presentation as any questionnaire, and arguably more so, since a confident and likeable manner can easily be mistaken for competence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Every stage of recruitment, from the covering letter to the final conversation, invites candidates to show themselves in the best possible light, and it would be strange if they did not. Singling out the questionnaire for this reason makes little sense. What matters is not whether applicants present a favourable picture of themselves, since almost all of them will, but whether a selection procedure has been designed with that tendency in mind.

topic: the dark triad of Machiavellianism, narcissism and psychopathy: one core or three traits, short-scale measurement and evolutionary explanations
title: Shades of Darkness
subtitle: Psychologists have spent two decades studying the unpleasant side of ordinary personality. They still disagree about what exactly they have been measuring

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Early this century, personality researchers began to treat three socially undesirable traits as a family. Machiavellianism, a cynical readiness to manipulate others for personal gain; narcissism, an inflated sense of one's own importance and a hunger for admiration; and psychopathy, a combination of callousness and impulsive thrill-seeking, became known collectively as the 'dark triad'. The label proved enormously successful. Thousands of studies have since appeared, and the phrase has migrated into management handbooks and self-help guides on spotting manipulative colleagues. Yet the speed of this success has, I suspect, concealed how loosely the concept was defined at the outset.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The three traits came from strikingly different intellectual traditions. Machiavellianism was derived from political philosophy by way of questionnaires about cynical attitudes; narcissism originated in clinical psychiatry; and psychopathy was a concept of criminology, developed to describe offenders. Only later were they reimagined as continuous dimensions on which everyone, not merely patients or prisoners, could be placed. Paloma Ezcurdia of the Madrid Centre for Personality Science argues that, whatever their origins, the three overlap so heavily that they should be understood as variations on a single theme. In her data, measures of Machiavellianism and psychopathy frequently correlate at 0.5 or above, and all three share a central element of callousness and willingness to exploit. Ezcurdia proposes that this shared 'dark core' also underlies other aversive tendencies, including spitefulness and sadism, which she believes belong in the same family.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dariusz Krzemień, of the Silesian Institute of Social Psychology, accepts that the traits share a callous centre but insists that their differences are just as important. People high in narcissism are typically sociable and crave attention, and they react with unusual sensitivity to criticism. Psychopathy is marked by impulsiveness, Machiavellianism by patience and careful planning. To merge them, Krzemień argues, would be to throw away information that matters: in his workplace studies, Machiavellianism predicted elaborate long-term deception, whereas psychopathy predicted reckless short-term risk-taking. In my view the two positions are less opposed than they appear. Whether one sees one core or three distinct traits depends largely on the level of detail a particular question requires, and much of the dispute dissolves once that is acknowledged.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A less tractable problem concerns measurement. A large share of dark triad research relies on very brief questionnaires, the shortest containing only twelve statements, four for each trait. Such instruments are attractive because they can be added to almost any online survey at little cost. Ifeoma Onyejekwe, at the West African Centre for Psychometrics, examined one widely used short scale and found that its Machiavellianism items correlated more strongly with established measures of psychopathy than with longer, well-validated measures of Machiavellianism itself. The implication is uncomfortable. A substantial body of published findings about Machiavellianism may, in effect, be findings about psychopathy, and convenience appears to have been allowed to take priority over validity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of why such traits persist at all. Kaveh Esfandiarpour, an evolutionary psychologist at the Caspian Institute for Behavioural Ecology, proposes that the dark triad represents a 'fast' life strategy: a tendency to exploit immediate opportunities, including short-term relationships, that would have paid off in unpredictable environments where the future could not be relied upon. He cites evidence that people with higher dark triad scores report a stronger preference for brief relationships and a greater willingness to take risks. The account is ingenious, but its evidential base is thin. Almost all of it comes from self-report surveys of university students, and Esfandiarpour himself concedes that his data cannot distinguish a genuine adaptation from a by-product of other traits. As it is currently framed, it is difficult to see what result could ever count against the theory.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Popular interest has focused above all on the workplace. Here the most robust finding concerns narcissism, which is consistently associated with being chosen as a leader in groups of strangers, but not with leading effectively. Hanne Vähämäki and her colleagues followed student project teams over a twelve-week term: members high in narcissism were rated as the most leader-like after the first meeting, but by the end of the term their ratings had fallen below the group average, as teammates came to know them better. The confidence and charm that make a stranger seem a natural leader, it appears, are far less impressive once colleagues have watched the same person respond to setbacks and criticism. Such findings are more modest than the claims of best-selling books warning of psychopaths in the boardroom, which typically rest on a handful of small and unrepresentative samples of executives.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the dark triad should be discarded. It has served a real purpose in drawing attention to traits that, in milder forms, are present throughout the ordinary population, rather than confined to clinics and courtrooms. It has also encouraged contact between fields that once had little to say to one another, so that clinical, criminological and social psychologists now read each other's work. But it is better treated as a provisional sketch than as a finished map, one that researchers should feel free to redraw as better measures become available. The most useful next steps would be unglamorous ones: longer, carefully validated questionnaires, tested on samples drawn from well beyond the university campus, and studies that follow people over many years rather than surveying them once.

topic: conscientiousness as a predictor of health and longevity: health behaviours, life paths, common causes and cultural context
title: The Dutiful Survive
subtitle: People who are organised and self-disciplined tend to live longer. Explaining why has proved harder than establishing that they do

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the broad dimensions of personality, conscientiousness sounds the least dramatic. It describes how organised, dependable and self-disciplined a person is, and it rarely features in conversation the way that extraversion or anxiety do. Yet over the past three decades it has emerged as one of the more reliable psychological predictors of how long people live. The basic finding has now been replicated so often that it can be regarded as secure. What remains far less settled, and what is too often glossed over in popular accounts, is why the connection exists.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most striking evidence comes from the Kestrel Bay cohort, a group of around 1,500 schoolchildren whose personalities were rated by their parents and teachers in the late 1930s and whose lives were later traced through official records. Because the ratings were made decades before any of the children fell ill, they cannot have been coloured by knowledge of who would later become unwell. Children judged most conscientious had roughly a 30 per cent lower risk of dying at any given age during adulthood than their least conscientious classmates. Mireille Assoumou, of the Lyon Institute of Health Psychology, has since combined data from twenty cohorts in eleven countries, covering more than 80,000 people. In her analysis the association survived statistical adjustment for education and family income, and its size was broadly comparable with that of socio-economic status itself, a factor normally regarded as one of the most powerful influences on health.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The obvious explanation is behaviour. Conscientious people smoke less, drink more moderately, drive more carefully and are more likely to take medication as prescribed. Tomasz Rybczak, at the Poznań Centre for Behavioural Medicine, estimates, however, that such habits account for only about a third of the link. The rest, he argues, comes from the long-term shape of people's lives. Conscientious individuals are more likely to stay in education, to hold steady jobs and to form stable partnerships, and these circumstances in turn provide income, social support and lower stress. Each of these advantages, modest on its own, accumulates over decades. On this view, personality influences health less through daily choices than through the environments people gradually build for themselves. The idea is persuasive, but it is difficult to test, because the routes it describes are so closely intertwined that separating their contributions is almost impossible.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Farid Qassemlou, of the Doha Institute for Lifespan Studies, offers a different interpretation. He suggests that some early biological disadvantage, such as low birth weight or serious illness in infancy, might impair both the development of self-control and long-term physical health. If so, conscientiousness would be less a cause of longevity than a marker of an underlying condition. Qassemlou points to studies in which children born prematurely scored somewhat lower on measures of self-regulation in adolescence and also showed higher rates of chronic illness in middle age. The hypothesis deserves investigation, but at present the evidence for it is indirect. It also struggles to explain why, in the Kestrel Bay data, childhood ratings of conscientiousness continued to predict mortality even after researchers had taken account of the children's health at the time they were assessed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The relationship is not uniform. It has sometimes been claimed that extreme conscientiousness, shading into perfectionism, carries its own health risks, but the evidence for harm at the upper end of the scale is weak. More convincing is research on cultural context. Aiko Takamine, at the Kyushu Institute of Gerontology, found that conscientiousness predicted survival much less strongly among older adults in Japan than in comparable European samples. Her explanation is that where social norms already require regular meals, punctual appointments and close attention to health, individual differences in self-discipline have less room to make a difference. This is an important reminder that the consequences of a trait depend on the setting in which it is expressed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If conscientiousness is good for health, can it be increased? Several short programmes that teach planning skills, such as forming specific intentions about when and where to exercise, have produced modest gains in self-reported conscientiousness over a few months. Whether such changes last, or whether they translate into longer lives, is not yet known. Self-reports are also an uncertain guide here, since participants who have just completed a course on planning may simply have learned to describe themselves in more organised terms. In my judgement, public health policy would achieve more by altering environments so that conscientious behaviour becomes easier for everyone: automatic enrolment in screening programmes, reminders for medication and well-designed default options demand very little self-discipline from the individual.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The longevity findings are a useful corrective to the assumption that health is determined purely by medical care and material resources. They should not, however, become a basis for moral judgement. To attribute a person's poor health to a lack of discipline is to ignore how much of that discipline, and of the stable life it supports, depends on circumstances that were never under the individual's control. Recognising that conscientiousness matters for health is one thing; using it to apportion blame is quite another.

topic: deliberate practice versus innate talent: the ten-thousand-hour claim, meta-analytic evidence and multifactorial models of expertise
title: Counting the Hours
subtitle: Is expert performance simply the product of enough of the right kind of practice?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas from psychology have travelled as far, or been simplified as thoroughly, as the claim that ten thousand hours of practice will turn anyone into an expert. The figure originated in a study of violin students at a European music academy, which found that those judged by their teachers to be the most accomplished had, by the age of twenty, accumulated considerably more hours of solitary practice than their less distinguished peers. In popular books and motivational talks, this observation has been transformed into something close to a law of nature: a fixed quantity of effort that guarantees mastery in any field. The original researchers never made such a claim, and the number itself was an average rather than a threshold. Yet the appeal of the idea is easy to understand, since it promises that excellence is available to anyone prepared to work for it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most forceful modern defender of the practice account is Anneliese Kvalsund, a cognitive psychologist at the Bergen Institute for Performance Studies. Kvalsund insists that the crucial variable is not the total time spent on an activity but the amount of what she calls deliberate practice. In her definition, this is not mere repetition of things a learner can already do. It consists of tasks that lie just beyond the performer's current ability, that target particular weaknesses, and that are accompanied by feedback which arrives immediately, usually from a teacher or coach who designs the exercises. Such practice is rarely enjoyable, she notes, which is why so few people sustain it for years. As for innate talent, Kvalsund regards it largely as a label attached after the fact: we observe that someone performs brilliantly and then infer a gift that explains nothing the history of their training does not already explain.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This position has been tested most directly by a group led by Teodor Vaszary at the Pannonian University of Applied Psychology, which pooled the results of eighty-eight studies covering games, music, sport, education and professional work. Their analysis concluded that differences in accumulated practice accounted for roughly a quarter of the variation in performance in games such as chess, about a fifth in music, and considerably less in sport. In professional domains the figure was close to one per cent. Vaszary interpreted these results as evidence that practice, while important, leaves most of the differences between individuals unexplained. In my view, the findings neither vindicate nor demolish either side of the debate as decisively as commentators have suggested. Most of the studies relied on adults recalling how many hours they had practised years or even decades earlier, and such estimates are notoriously unreliable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have looked for the factors that practice leaves out. Mirela Albescu, a behavioural geneticist at the Carpathian Institute of Behavioural Genetics, analysed data from more than ten thousand pairs of twins and found that musical aptitude was moderately heritable. More surprisingly, the tendency to practise was itself partly heritable: identical twins resembled one another in the number of hours they chose to devote to an instrument more closely than non-identical twins did. If this is correct, the clean separation between nature and effort on which the popular debate depends begins to dissolve, since the willingness to work hard may be part of what is inherited. It is worth stressing, however, that a heritable trait is not an unchangeable one. Height is highly heritable, yet average heights have risen substantially over the past century as nutrition has improved.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Kvalsund has responded vigorously to these challenges. The pooled analysis, she argues, grouped together many activities that do not meet her strict definition, such as playing music for pleasure or competing in tournaments, and so it inevitably underestimated the contribution of genuine deliberate practice. There is some force in this objection, since lumping all forms of activity together does blur an important distinction. But it carries a danger of its own. If every case in which practice fails to predict performance can be dismissed on the grounds that it was the wrong sort of practice, the theory becomes impossible to refute, and a theory that cannot be shown to be wrong is of limited scientific value.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more promising direction, in my opinion, is offered by researchers who reject the choice between talent and practice altogether. Joaquín Ledesma, who directs the Andean Centre for Learning Research, has proposed what he terms a multifactorial model, in which practice interacts with starting age, personality, working memory capacity and access to good instruction. His team's study of competitive chess players found that those who began playing before the age of twelve reached higher ratings than late starters, even when the total number of hours they had practised was the same. Working memory capacity also predicted performance, although its influence was strongest among novices and diminished as players became more experienced. Such findings suggest that the question is not whether talent or practice matters more, but how the two combine at different stages of development.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The practical stakes of this debate are considerable. The belief that talent is fixed can discourage learners who conclude, after early difficulty, that they simply lack the necessary gift. But the opposite belief has costs as well: if practice alone determines success, those who fail to reach the top may be blamed for insufficient effort when other factors were at work. The most defensible message for teachers and parents is that practice is necessary but not sufficient. Rather than counting hours, schools and coaches would do better to attend to the quality of practice, and to accept that two learners who work equally hard may still end up in very different places.

topic: chunking, template theory and perceptual pattern recognition in chess expertise
title: What the Master Sees
subtitle: Decades of research on chess players have reshaped scientific ideas about the nature of expert memory

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a series of experiments first carried out in the mid-twentieth century and repeated many times since, chess players of varying strength were shown a position from a real game for about five seconds and then asked to reconstruct it on an empty board. Masters typically replaced almost every piece correctly; club players managed perhaps half; beginners could recall only four or five. On its own, this might suggest that strong players simply have superior memories. The decisive twist came when the pieces were arranged at random. Faced with positions that could never arise in an actual game, masters performed scarcely better than novices. Whatever the experts possessed, it was evidently not a general capacity to remember, but something tied closely to the structure of the game itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation that came to dominate the field is known as chunking. According to this view, years of play allow experts to build up a vast store of familiar patterns, such as a chain of pawns or a castled king with its protective pieces, each of which can be recognised and remembered as a single unit. Ilona Ferenczi of the Budapest Institute for Cognitive Science has estimated, on the basis of computer simulations of learning, that a master holds somewhere between fifty thousand and one hundred thousand such chunks in long-term memory. The estimate is often quoted, and it captures something important about the scale of expert knowledge. Nonetheless, it should be treated with caution, since the figure depends on assumptions built into the simulations about how chunks are formed, and those assumptions are extremely hard to check against real players.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Chunking also faced a more concrete difficulty. If experts encode a position as a handful of chunks held briefly in short-term memory, then their recall ought to be limited by the small capacity of that system, which is usually put at no more than a few items. Yet masters can be shown several boards in quick succession and still recall most of them, and their memory for a position survives even when they are distracted by an unrelated task before being tested. Kenji Takamori, a cognitive scientist at the Kansai Institute of Technology, proposed a solution in what he called template theory. Chunks that are encountered very frequently, he argued, develop into larger structures with a fixed core and a number of open slots, into which the positions of particular pieces can be inserted. Because templates already reside in long-term memory, filling their slots allows a new position to be stored there within seconds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even the famous finding about random positions has been refined. When Wanjiku Mwenesi and her colleagues at the Nairobi Centre for Cognitive Studies combined the results of dozens of experiments, they found that experts did retain a small but consistent advantage for random boards. Their explanation was that even a random arrangement will, purely by chance, contain the occasional configuration that resembles something from real play, and experts are able to exploit these fragments. Some commentators presented this as a blow to chunking theory, but that interpretation seems to me mistaken. A modest advantage which is proportional to the number of accidental familiar patterns is exactly what the theory would predict, and the result therefore strengthens it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Memory experiments, however, tell us only indirectly how experts choose their moves. Research using eye-tracking equipment has attempted to close this gap. Studies conducted by Margaux Lachance at the Laurentian Laboratory of Perception found that strong players directed their first glances at the pieces most relevant to the position far more often than weaker players did, and frequently fixed their gaze on empty squares between pieces, apparently taking in the relations among several of them in one look. On the basis of such evidence, Lachance has argued that chess skill is at root perceptual: the master, in her phrase, sees the right move before calculating it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts so strong a conclusion. Harriet Vellacott, who studies decision-making at the Thamesmead School of Psychology, points out that grandmasters still spend long periods analysing variations during serious games. In her experiments, when players were forced to move under severe time limits, the quality of their decisions fell only slightly in simple positions but declined sharply in complicated ones. If recognition were sufficient, she argues, a lack of time to think should hardly matter. Both positions contain a good deal of truth. A more plausible account is that recognition supplies a small number of promising candidate moves, which calculation then tests, and that the balance between the two shifts according to how complex the position is.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Similar patterns of expertise have since been found well beyond the chessboard, among radiologists scanning images, musicians reading unfamiliar scores and programmers inspecting code. What these studies share is the conclusion that expert knowledge is highly specific to its domain. This has an implication that enthusiasts are often reluctant to accept. Chess is frequently promoted in schools on the grounds that it sharpens general reasoning and improves mathematical ability, but the evidence for such transfer is weak, and the better-controlled studies have generally found little or no benefit. Learning chess makes people better at chess; it is far from clear that it does much more.

topic: tacit knowledge in traditional crafts and whether apprenticeship can be replaced by explicit instruction or digital archives
title: Knowledge in the Hands
subtitle: Can the skills of a master craftsperson ever be written down, and does it matter if they cannot?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In workshops where violins are made, stone is carved or bread is shaped by hand, there is a familiar saying that a craft cannot be learned from books. Master craftspeople often struggle to explain what they do; asked how they know that a joint is tight enough or that a dough has been worked for long enough, they will say only that it feels right. Philosophers have long described this as tacit knowledge: understanding that a person possesses and uses with confidence but cannot fully put into words. For much of the twentieth century the idea was treated as little more than a curiosity. It has now become central to a lively argument about how skills are passed on, and about whether the traditional apprenticeship, with its years of watching and imitating, still has a place in an age of manuals, videos and formal qualifications.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for the apprenticeship model has been made most forcefully by the anthropologist Kwabena Kyeremateng, who spent four years working alongside weavers and blacksmiths in West Africa. He reports that novices there were rarely given instructions at all. Instead, they were assigned simple, peripheral tasks, such as sweeping, fetching charcoal or preparing thread, while the master worked nearby, and only gradually moved towards the central activities of the trade. In Kyeremateng's account, this apparently idle period was in fact a crucial stage of learning: by being constantly present, apprentices absorbed the rhythms, sounds and postures of skilled work long before they were allowed to attempt it. He concludes that the knowledge in question is not hidden inside the master's head but distributed across the whole setting of the workshop.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that such knowledge lies beyond description. Dr Orsolya Ferencvári, a cognitive scientist at the Institute for Applied Expertise in Budapest, argues that much of what is called tacit is merely knowledge that nobody has yet tried hard enough to articulate. Her team used a technique known as cued recall, in which craftspeople watch video recordings of their own work and are asked to comment on each decision as it occurs. Working with a group of stonemasons, the researchers extracted more than two hundred distinct rules of thumb, many of which the masons themselves had never consciously formulated. When these rules were taught to beginners, the beginners made noticeably fewer errors in their first months than a comparison group who learned by observation alone.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ferencvári's findings are impressive, but they do not settle the matter as neatly as she suggests. A follow-up study two years later found that the advantage enjoyed by the rule-trained beginners had largely disappeared, and that the most accomplished masons in both groups were those who had spent the longest hours at the stone. It seems, then, that explicit rules may help novices avoid costly early errors without substantially changing where they end up. This is not a trivial benefit, since in trades that work with expensive materials a reduction in early mistakes can save a great deal of money. It is, however, a far narrower claim than the assertion that tacit knowledge can be fully translated into words.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third position is taken by Professor Ilse Brandsæter, a sociologist at Sognefjell University College who studies traditional boat-builders. She argues that the real threat to craft knowledge is economic rather than educational. Apprenticeships are expensive: a master who spends hours supervising a novice produces less, and in many countries the small workshops that once trained the next generation have closed. According to Brandsæter, the question of whether tacit knowledge can be written down matters less than whether anyone will still be practising a trade in twenty years' time to pass it on. Her interviews with Norwegian boat-builders revealed that most were over sixty, and that few had trained a successor.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Enthusiasts for digital tools believe that technology can fill this gap. Rodrigo Valdepeñas, who directs a craft-documentation project in Spain, has filmed master potters and guitar makers using multiple cameras and motion sensors, building an archive which he hopes will allow future learners to study techniques after the masters have retired. The ambition is admirable, and such archives are undoubtedly valuable as historical records. I doubt, however, that they can serve as a substitute for a living teacher. A recording can show what a master's hands do, but it cannot respond when a learner makes an error, nor can it adjust the next task to the learner's progress, and it is precisely this responsiveness that the best apprenticeships provide.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is not a choice between words and practice but a recognition that each does different work. Explicit instruction is efficient in the early stages, when beginners need to avoid basic mistakes; prolonged practice under supervision remains essential for the subtler judgements that distinguish an expert. The more pressing danger, in my view, is the one Brandsæter identifies. Debates about the nature of tacit knowledge will remain largely academic if the workshops in which it lives continue to disappear.

topic: when expert intuition can be trusted: recognition-based decisions, statistical prediction and the role of environmental regularity and feedback
title: The Limits of the Expert's Hunch
subtitle: Some professionals can trust their gut feelings; others merely believe they can. What makes the difference?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The story is often retold. A senior fire officer leads his crew into a burning house, directs water at what appears to be a kitchen fire, and then, for no reason he can articulate, orders everyone outside. Seconds later the floor on which they had been standing collapses into a blazing basement. Asked afterwards what had alerted him, he could say only that something felt wrong: the room was too hot for so small a fire, and too quiet. Anecdotes of this kind have done much to popularise the idea that experienced professionals possess a kind of sixth sense. They are vivid and memorable, but they are a poor guide to the question that actually matters, which is not whether intuition can ever be accurate but under what conditions it deserves to be believed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One influential answer comes from the field known as naturalistic decision-making. Matías Ondarroa and his colleagues at the Centre for Field Cognition interviewed more than sixty fire commanders, intensive-care nurses and military officers about the most difficult incidents of their careers. To their surprise, the researchers found that these professionals almost never weighed alternative courses of action against each other. Instead, they recognised the situation as an instance of a familiar type, adopted the first plausible response that occurred to them, and rehearsed it mentally to check for problems, turning to another option only if the first seemed likely to fail. Ondarroa argues that the formal comparison of options, as taught on management courses, is not merely slower under time pressure but frequently produces worse decisions than the expert's rapid recognition.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A very different picture emerges from research in the tradition that studies errors in human judgement. Yetunde Olabisi-Crane, a psychologist at the Halberd Institute for Decision Research, has reviewed several hundred studies in which the forecasts of professionals were compared with those of simple statistical formulas. The tasks ranged from predicting which offenders would commit further crimes to judging which applicants would succeed at university and estimating the future price of newly produced wines. In the great majority of cases, the formula equalled or outperformed the experts, who were, moreover, consistently more confident than their records justified. Olabisi-Crane's conclusion is blunt: in many professions, what feels like expert insight is largely an illusion created by fluency and experience.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: At first sight these two bodies of work seem irreconcilable, but the conflict is more apparent than real, because the two groups of researchers have largely been studying different kinds of work. A fire commander operates in an environment that, for all its danger, follows physical laws, and the consequences of a decision become clear within minutes. A university admissions officer, by contrast, may wait years to learn how a student performs and will never discover how a rejected applicant might have fared. The organisational psychologist Halvard Sandvold has proposed that intuition can be trusted only when two conditions are met: the environment must be regular enough to be predictable, and the practitioner must have had prolonged opportunity to learn its regularities through timely feedback. This seems to me the most useful framework yet offered, chiefly because it shifts attention from the individual expert to the setting in which expertise was acquired.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sandvold's own experimental work lends the framework considerable support. He trained volunteers on two computer-based tasks over several weeks. In one, outcomes followed a stable pattern and participants were told immediately whether each judgement had been correct; in the other, feedback was delayed and often misleading. Participants' confidence rose at the same rate in both conditions, yet their accuracy improved only in the first. The implication is uncomfortable. Experience, it seems, will make almost anyone feel more expert, regardless of whether it has made them any better. If there is one practical lesson to be drawn from the entire debate, it is this: a professional's certainty, however sincerely felt, tells us very little about whether he or she is right.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some commentators have drawn a more radical conclusion. The economist Declan Hollingrake contends that, wherever a reliable formula exists, professional discretion should be removed altogether, since human judgement can only add noise. This, I believe, goes too far. Statistical rules perform well on the cases they were designed for, but they cannot recognise the exceptional case that falls outside them, such as the patient whose symptoms are typical but whose circumstances are not. Formulas also depend on experts to decide which factors are worth measuring in the first place. It must be conceded, however, that in fields where feedback is scarce and outcomes are unpredictable, the formula ought to be the default, and the burden of proof should lie with anyone who wishes to override it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The more constructive response is to change the environments in which professionals learn. Weather forecasters, who discover every day whether their predictions were correct, are among the best-calibrated experts ever studied, and there is no obvious reason why other occupations could not borrow from their example. Some hospitals now routinely inform radiologists of the results of later tests on patients whose scans they have read, giving them the kind of feedback that their work does not naturally supply. Rather than asking whether experts in general can be trusted, then, we should ask a narrower question about each of them: did the conditions under which they gained their experience allow them to become genuinely skilled?
