topic: the expert blind spot: why highly skilled people struggle to teach novices, and remedies such as cognitive task analysis and near-peer tutoring
title: Forgetting the View from the Bottom
subtitle: Why the people who know a subject best are not always the people best placed to teach it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It seems reasonable to assume that the person who knows most about a subject will be the best person to teach it. Universities appoint distinguished researchers to lecture first-year students; hospitals ask their most skilful surgeons to train junior doctors; companies promote their top performers to supervise newcomers. Yet a growing body of research suggests that deep expertise can make teaching harder rather than easier. Psychologists call this the expert blind spot: the tendency of highly skilled people to lose sight of what it is like not to know. In my view, the phenomenon is still poorly understood by the very institutions that are most affected by it, and many of them continue to treat skill and the ability to pass it on as though they were the same thing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence comes from the cognitive psychologist Sunniva Ekeland. She asked three groups, university mathematicians, experienced secondary-school teachers and trainee teachers, to rank a set of algebra problems according to how difficult fourteen-year-old students would find them. The students then attempted the same problems. The mathematicians proved the least accurate of the three groups. Most of them assumed that problems expressed purely in symbols would be easier for students than the same problems presented as short stories, but the students actually performed better on the word problems, which allowed them to reason informally. Ekeland's explanation is that, for an expert, the intermediate steps in solving a problem have become so automatic that they are no longer noticed, and what cannot be noticed cannot easily be taught.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Joseph Ssempala, a specialist in medical education, has documented the same pattern in surgery. When he asked experienced surgeons to describe how they perform common operations, he found that their accounts left out as many as seven in ten of the decisions they actually made during the procedure. To recover the missing knowledge, Ssempala uses a method known as cognitive task analysis, in which trained analysts conduct lengthy interviews with several experts and combine their accounts into a single, detailed guide. Junior doctors taught from such guides made significantly fewer errors than those taught in the conventional way. Ssempala would like the method used throughout medical training. It is, however, expensive and slow, demanding many hours from scarce specialists; it is clearly justified for high-risk procedures, but it is hard to see how it could be applied to the routine teaching that fills most of a trainee's day.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every researcher accepts that the blind spot is an inevitable consequence of expertise. Pita Mahuika, an education researcher, compared experts who rarely met beginners with experts whose work brought them into daily contact with them, such as ski instructors and music teachers. The second group predicted learners' difficulties almost as well as the learners themselves. Mahuika concludes that the problem lies not in knowing a great deal but in having drifted away from people who know very little. I find this a hopeful conclusion, because it implies that the blind spot is not a fixed cost of mastery but something that regular exposure to novices can reduce.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A related approach has been tested in engineering faculties by Itziar Zabaleta, who trains students in their second or third year to act as tutors to first-year classes. Because these near-peer tutors encountered the same obstacles only recently, they are often better than professors at recognising where a newcomer has become stuck. In Zabaleta's studies, first-year pass rates rose noticeably in courses that adopted the scheme. She is frank about its weaknesses, however: tutors who are only slightly ahead of their students may pass on their own misconceptions, and they rarely have the depth of knowledge needed to answer difficult questions. It seems likely, therefore, that the most effective arrangement is one in which near-peers and experts work alongside each other rather than one replacing the other.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The blind spot is not confined to the classroom or the operating theatre. It shapes textbooks that skip the step a reader most needs, assembly instructions that assume familiarity with the tools, and software manuals written by the engineers who built the program. In each case the author is too close to the material to see where a newcomer will stumble. The remedy, I would argue, is not to make experts any less expert, which would be absurd, but to give them both the motivation and the means to recover a beginner's perspective, whether by testing their explanations on real learners or by working with colleagues who still remember being confused.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the ability to perform a skill and the ability to explain it are distinct, and that the second does not develop automatically from the first. This is not an argument against expert teachers; a novice taught only by other novices would soon reach the limits of what they could offer. It is, rather, an argument for treating explanation as a skill in its own right, one that must be practised, observed and given feedback in the same way as any other. Institutions that recognise this will continue to value their experts, but they will stop assuming that expertise alone qualifies someone to teach.

topic: surgical learning curves and whether simulation training can move skill acquisition out of the operating theatre
title: Practice Without Patients
subtitle: Simulators promise to move the surgeon's learning curve out of the operating theatre. How far can they deliver?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, surgeons were trained according to a principle summed up in the phrase "see one, do one, teach one". A trainee watched an experienced surgeon perform an operation, then carried out the same procedure under supervision, and before long was expected to instruct those who came after. The system produced many fine surgeons, but it rested on an awkward fact: the earliest operations of every career were performed on real patients. That the outcomes of these first cases tend to be worse is well documented. When keyhole removal of the gallbladder was introduced in the late 1980s, for example, injuries to the bile duct, a rare but serious complication, occurred several times more often in the technique's early years than they did once surgeons had gained experience with it. There is something ethically uncomfortable about a system in which patients, rather than the profession, bear the cost of learning, and it is to the credit of surgical educators that they have stopped regarding this as inevitable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Practical pressures have reinforced the ethical ones. Limits on working hours, introduced in many countries over the past three decades, have sharply reduced the time trainees spend in the operating theatre; in some European systems a trainee now accumulates roughly half the operating experience that a predecessor would have gained a generation ago. At the same time, hospitals face growing public scrutiny of their results, and surgeons' individual outcomes are increasingly published. Together these developments have created strong demand for ways of acquiring skill that do not depend on the patient.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Simulation is the most prominent answer. At its simplest, it involves a box trainer, a closed container in which trainees practise manipulating instruments on rubber or synthetic tissue while watching a screen. More sophisticated virtual-reality simulators reproduce entire procedures and record measures such as the time taken, the number of errors and the total distance travelled by the tips of the instruments. In a widely cited trial, the surgical educator Anouk Verbeelen divided thirty-two junior trainees into two groups, one of which trained on a virtual-reality simulator before all of them performed a real gallbladder operation. Assessors who did not know which group each trainee belonged to found that the simulator-trained group worked twenty-nine per cent faster and made fewer errors. Verbeelen attributes much of this success to a single design choice: trainees were required to keep practising until they reached a fixed performance benchmark, rather than for a set number of hours.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The surgeon and researcher Kaveh Arjomand has questioned how much such results really show. He points out that the measured benefits of simulation are concentrated in basic hand movements and in a trainee's first few operations, and that no simulator can yet reproduce the sudden bleeding, unusual anatomy or tense communication within a team that make real surgery demanding. In his review of the literature, Arjomand found that few studies had followed trainees beyond their first ten operations, and none had demonstrated a reduction in patient deaths. This is a fair challenge, although the second point is less damaging than it first appears. Deaths during routine procedures are, fortunately, so uncommon that a trial large enough to detect a difference would require many thousands of patients, and the lack of such evidence partly reflects that difficulty rather than any proven failure of simulation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection concerns cost. A commercial virtual-reality simulator can cost as much as a mid-range car, placing it beyond the reach of many hospitals. Achieng Ndege, who trains surgeons in East Africa, has responded by building box trainers from plastic storage containers, desk lamps and inexpensive webcams connected to a laptop. In her study, trainees who practised on these devices improved their scores on standard skills tests by a margin similar to that reported for commercial machines. Her results suggest that the sophistication of the equipment matters far less than whether it is used in a structured and systematic way, a conclusion with obvious implications for health systems with limited budgets.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Simulation addresses the beginning of a career, but the work of Hamish Corrieston suggests that the learning curve does not end with qualification. Corrieston asked experienced surgeons to watch recordings of colleagues performing the same weight-loss operation and to rate their technical skill. When these ratings were compared with the patients' subsequent outcomes, surgeons placed in the lowest quarter turned out to have almost three times as many complications as those in the highest. The study is striking for two reasons: it shows that technical ability varies widely even among fully qualified specialists, and it implies that peer assessment could become a powerful tool for continuing improvement.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that simulation can replace experience in the operating theatre. The most realistic hopes for it are more modest: that it can ensure trainees arrive at their first real operation having already mastered the basic movements, so that supervisors can concentrate on judgement rather than technique. The learning curve, in other words, can be shortened and partly shifted away from patients, but it cannot be abolished. That is still a considerable achievement, and arguably the most significant change in surgical education since the apprenticeship model was first established.

topic: the contextual interference effect: blocked versus random practice schedules in motor skill learning, the challenge point principle and learners' misjudgement of their own progress
title: Mixing It Up
subtitle: Why the training schedule that feels most productive may be the one that teaches least

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk into almost any training session, whether on a tennis court, in a music studio or on a factory floor, and you are likely to see the same method at work. A learner repeats a single movement many times, refining it until it runs smoothly, and only then moves on to the next. Psychologists call this blocked practice, and its appeal is easy to understand: improvement within a session is rapid and plainly visible, which reassures learner and instructor alike. Yet over the past half-century, research on motor learning has produced a finding that sits uneasily with this tradition. When several skills are practised in a mixed or random order, performance during training tends to be worse, but what is retained days or weeks later is frequently better. This phenomenon, known as the contextual interference effect, is surely among the most counterintuitive results in the study of skill, and its implications have still not been fully absorbed by those who design training.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the original series of experiments, conducted by the movement scientist Ragnhild Hovland at the Trondheim Institute of Human Performance, volunteers learned three different arm movements, each requiring them to knock down a set of small wooden barriers in a prescribed sequence as quickly as possible. One group practised each pattern in a separate block; another encountered the three patterns in an unpredictable order. During the training phase the blocked group was consistently faster. When both groups returned ten days later, however, the position was reversed: the random group not only performed the original patterns more quickly but also coped better with a fourth pattern they had never attempted before. Hovland's conclusion, that the conditions which flatter performance in practice may be precisely those which undermine durable learning, has since been replicated in dozens of laboratory studies.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should mixing tasks help? Two accounts have dominated the debate. The first, the elaboration hypothesis, holds that when different skills are practised side by side, learners naturally compare them, noting what is distinctive about each, and so build richer and more clearly separated memory representations. The second, championed by the cognitive scientist Haruki Ishibashi of the Hokuriku Institute of Technology, proposes a quite different mechanism. On his reconstruction account, switching to a new task causes the plan for the previous one to be partly forgotten, so that each time it reappears the learner must assemble it again from scratch. It is this repeated effort of rebuilding, Ishibashi argues, rather than any act of comparison, that strengthens memory. The two camps have spent decades designing experiments to separate their predictions, with inconclusive results. It seems likely that both processes contribute, and for practical purposes the distinction may matter rather less than its proponents assume: either way, the learner benefits from being made to work harder.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Outside the laboratory, the picture becomes less tidy. Aurelio Castellvi, a sports scientist at the Mediterranean Institute of Sport Sciences, recently reviewed more than sixty studies carried out in applied settings, from volleyball serves to welding. He found that the advantage of random practice, while real, was considerably smaller than laboratory work had suggested, and in several studies involving complete beginners it disappeared altogether or was even reversed. Castellvi interprets this through what he calls the 'challenge point' principle. Every learner, he suggests, has an optimal level of challenge, and this depends on both the learner's existing experience and the complexity of the task. A novice attempting a difficult skill is already stretched to capacity; adding the burden of constant switching may simply overwhelm them. For such learners, a period of repetitive practice may be needed before variation becomes useful.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This is an important correction, and it exposes a weakness in the way the research has often been communicated. Coaching manuals and popular books have tended to present random practice as a universal improvement, implying that any instructor still using blocked drills is behind the times. That conclusion goes well beyond the evidence. Contextual interference appears to be a powerful tool for learners who have already grasped the basic form of a movement, but it is no substitute for judgement about when a learner is ready for it. The most sensible schedule is probably one that begins with repetition and introduces variety progressively as competence grows.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further obstacle is psychological. Because blocked practice produces smooth, rapid gains, learners tend to believe it is working better. A survey led by Nomvula Mukanya at the Centre for Coaching Research in Durban asked several hundred amateur athletes to rate different training schedules after using them. The majority judged blocked practice the more effective, even when their own retention tests showed the opposite. Mukanya warns that this preference cannot simply be disregarded, since athletes who find training frustrating may train less often or give up entirely. That is a fair point, but it should not lead coaches to let learners' impressions dictate how practice is arranged. A better response is to explain openly why practice that feels harder is likely to pay off later.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable legacy of this research lies not in any particular schedule but in the distinction it draws between performance and learning. What a learner can do at the end of a session is an unreliable guide to what he or she will be able to do next month. This has uncomfortable consequences for anyone who judges instructors by the visible progress made within lessons, a habit that, if the evidence is taken seriously, may reward exactly the wrong kind of teaching.

topic: perceptual anticipation in elite sport: occlusion studies, the 'quiet eye', laboratory versus on-field testing, perceptual training and deception
title: The Split-Second Forecast
subtitle: Elite athletes seem to react impossibly fast. In truth, they are not reacting at all

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A professional tennis player returning a serve struck at over 200 kilometres per hour has roughly half a second before the ball arrives. Since it takes most of that time simply to detect the ball's direction and initiate a movement, a player who waited for the ball to leave the racket before responding would rarely make contact at all. The popular explanation is that elite performers are blessed with exceptional reflexes or unusually sharp eyesight. That explanation is almost certainly wrong. When experts and novices are given standard laboratory tests of simple reaction time or visual acuity, the differences between them are trivial, and sometimes favour the novices. What distinguishes the expert is not the speed of the nervous system but the ability to anticipate: to extract, from the opponent's body before the ball is even struck, information about what is about to happen.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of what is known about this ability comes from a deceptively simple technique. In temporal occlusion studies, pioneered by the sports psychologist Siobhan Fitzallan at the Western Isles Centre for Performance Science, players watch filmed sequences of an opponent serving or striking, but the screen goes blank at a chosen moment, after which they must predict where the ball will go. Experts predict with accuracy well above chance from clips cut off before racket and ball even meet; novices perform no better than guessing until they have seen part of the ball's flight. In a later variant, Fitzallan masked particular regions of the opponent's body. Hiding the racket and arm made surprisingly little difference to experts, whereas concealing the rotation of the hips and trunk sharply reduced their accuracy. Her interpretation is that the expert's advantage lies less in seeing more than in knowing which sources of information are worth attending to.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Eye-tracking research has added a further dimension. Skilled performers generally make fewer fixations, each of longer duration, than less skilled ones, as if they have learned to settle quickly on the most informative locations. The kinesiologist Aino Tervonen has drawn particular attention to what she terms the 'quiet eye', the final steady fixation made just before a critical action such as a golf putt or a basketball free throw. In expert performers this fixation begins earlier and lasts longer, and Tervonen maintains that it is a cause of superior performance rather than a mere symptom of it, pointing to studies in which training athletes to prolong their final fixation improved their accuracy. The evidence is suggestive, but it falls short of settling the question: it remains entirely possible that a longer quiet eye is a by-product of the calm and control that skill brings, and that training it works partly by encouraging athletes to slow down in general.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that laboratory studies capture the phenomenon they claim to measure. Kwabena Adjei-Mensah, who studies movement at the Accra Institute of Applied Kinesiology, argues that asking a seated participant to watch a screen and press a button severs the natural link between perceiving and acting. When players are filmed actually moving to intercept a ball, he reports, the gap between expert and novice is considerably wider than in screen-based tests, suggesting that much expert knowledge is embedded in movement itself and simply cannot be expressed through a keyboard. This critique deserves to be taken seriously, but it does not render the laboratory obsolete. The very artificiality that Adjei-Mensah objects to is what allows researchers to isolate individual cues, and no field study could have revealed the importance of hip rotation with comparable precision.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If anticipation is learned, can it be taught more efficiently than through years of play? Mariko Kanemoto and her colleagues at the Kansai Sports Research Centre trained junior football goalkeepers using occluded clips of penalty kicks. The goalkeepers improved markedly on the laboratory task, and their saves on the pitch increased modestly, though the gain largely faded within two months unless the training was repeated. More revealing was a comparison between two forms of instruction. Goalkeepers who were given explicit rules, such as watching the angle of the kicker's standing foot, improved fastest but tended to perform poorly when placed under pressure, while those guided to discover the relevant cues for themselves improved more slowly but proved far more robust. Approaches of this second kind seem to me the more promising direction for coaches.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Anticipation, however, has a vulnerability that opponents are quick to exploit. Because experts commit to an action on the basis of early cues, those cues can be faked. Johan Strandqvist, who analyses deception in rugby, has shown that experienced defenders are much better than inexperienced ones at distinguishing genuine changes of direction from feints, yet even they can be fooled by exaggerated movements of the head and shoulders, which attackers learn to produce precisely because defenders have learned to read them. The result is a continual contest in which each side adapts to the other, and it implies that anticipation should be understood not as a fixed possession but as a skill perpetually renegotiated against particular opponents.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to extend these findings to radiologists, drivers or police officers, all of whom must predict events from partial information. Some caution is required. Perhaps the most robust result in the entire field is that perceptual expertise is narrowly tied to its domain: an elite tennis player shows no special ability to anticipate badminton shots, let alone traffic. For that reason, commercial programmes promising to improve anticipation in general, through abstract visual exercises unrelated to any particular activity, are unlikely to deliver what they advertise.

topic: choking under pressure in skilled performers: distraction versus explicit-monitoring theories, analogy learning, pressure acclimatisation and reappraisal of arousal
title: When Skill Deserts the Skilled
subtitle: Psychologists are divided over why experts sometimes fall apart at the very moment that matters most

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every sport has its legends of collapse: the golfer who squanders a commanding lead on the final holes, the footballer who sends a decisive penalty high over the bar. Psychologists use the term 'choking' for such episodes, but they define it more narrowly than everyday speech does. Choking is not simply performing badly; it is performing below one's own established level precisely because the stakes are high. The distinction matters, since commentators are inclined to describe almost any defeat in a big match as a choke, when the more mundane explanation is often that the opponent was better. The phenomenon is genuine, but it is rarer than its popularity as a label would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One influential account treats choking as a problem of distraction. Revati Tamboli, a cognitive psychologist at the Institute for Learning Sciences in Pune, argues that pressure fills the mind with worries about failure and its consequences, and that these worries occupy working memory, the limited mental workspace in which information is held and manipulated. With less capacity left over for the task itself, performance suffers. Her most striking finding concerns who is most affected. In experiments involving difficult arithmetic, participants with the largest working memory capacity performed best under relaxed conditions but showed the steepest decline under pressure, apparently because their usual strategies depend most heavily on the very resource that anxiety consumes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A rival account, developed by the sport scientist Etienne Sauvageau at the Quebec Centre for Human Movement, proposes almost the opposite mechanism. Rather than attending too little to the task, Sauvageau suggests, the pressured performer attends to it too much. Highly practised skills run largely automatically, without step-by-step conscious control; under pressure, experts try to make sure nothing goes wrong by monitoring each component of the movement, and in doing so they break apart an action that functions best as a single unit. In one of his studies, experienced golfers instructed to concentrate on the movement of their club during a putt became less accurate, whereas novices given the same instruction improved. It would be a mistake, however, to treat the two theories as mutually exclusive. The more plausible view is that distraction chiefly damages tasks that demand reasoning, while excessive monitoring chiefly damages well-learned physical skills.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If conscious knowledge of technique is what pressure exploits, one remedy might be to learn skills with as little of it as possible. Oleksandr Kovalyshyn, a motor learning specialist at the Lviv Academy of Physical Culture, has tested what he calls analogy learning, in which a single image replaces a list of technical instructions. Table tennis beginners, for example, were told to strike the ball as though tracing the side of a triangle rather than being given detailed guidance on the angle of the bat. Compared with conventionally instructed learners, they could report far fewer explicit rules afterwards and their performance held up considerably better when pressure was introduced. The results are encouraging, but the studies are small and have largely involved novices in laboratory settings; whether the approach would protect professionals who have already accumulated years of explicit instruction remains an open question.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have concentrated on preparing performers for pressure rather than changing how they learn. Mette Lindholt, who works with Danish national squads, has studied acclimatisation training, in which athletes regularly practise under mildly stressful conditions such as being filmed, judged or rewarded. Her athletes showed less deterioration in competition than controls, but she emphasises one condition: the pressure in training must feel real, and artificial stakes rapidly lose their effect once athletes realise nothing depends on them. In the academic sphere, Tamboli's group has reported that students who spend ten minutes writing about their anxieties immediately before an examination score higher than those who do not, presumably because putting worries on paper releases some of the capacity they would otherwise occupy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most underrated insight in this field is that pressure itself is not the enemy. Racing heartbeat, quickened breathing and heightened alertness are the same bodily responses whether a performer experiences them as dread or as excitement. Studies in which participants were encouraged to interpret these signals as signs that their body was preparing to perform, rather than as warnings of disaster, have reported improvements in both sporting and academic tasks. This helps to explain why some performers seem to thrive in decisive moments: it is the meaning they attach to arousal, not its intensity, that appears to determine whether it helps or hinders.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What choking ultimately reveals is that expertise is not a fixed store of ability that can simply be drawn upon at will. It depends on a delicate balance between conscious attention and automatic control, and that balance can be upset in seconds. This also means that the many popular books promising to make anyone immune to choking claim far more than the evidence allows. The research offers useful tools, but no technique yet devised removes the risk entirely.

topic: skill decay after periods of non-use: which skills fade fastest, overlearning and refresher training, automation and pilots' cognitive skills, overconfidence and relearning
title: The Fading Edge
subtitle: Hard-won skills begin to erode the moment we stop using them, and the professions that can least afford this are often the most exposed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A paramedic certified in advanced resuscitation, an airline pilot trained to handle an engine failure on take-off and a reservist instructed in field medicine share an uncomfortable predicament. Each has acquired, at considerable expense, a skill that may be needed only once in several years, and each is likely to have lost a substantial portion of it by the time that moment arrives. Psychologists call this process skill decay: the gradual loss of trained capabilities during periods when they are not exercised. Although it has been documented for over a century, it remains strikingly neglected in the design of professional training, which still tends to treat certification as the end of learning rather than the beginning of a long struggle against forgetting. In occupations where the most critical skills are also the most rarely used, that neglect is difficult to justify.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most comprehensive synthesis of the evidence comes from Ingvild Haakonsen, a training researcher at the Nordic Institute for Workplace Learning, who pooled the results of more than a hundred retention studies. After a year without practice, she found, average performance had fallen by roughly a third, but the rate of loss varied enormously with the type of skill. Tasks involving continuous control, such as cycling, swimming or steering a vehicle, proved remarkably durable, and could often be performed almost as well after years of inactivity as on the day they were learned. Procedural tasks made up of discrete steps, such as an emergency checklist or the assembly of a piece of equipment, decayed far more quickly. Haakonsen attributes the difference to the demands such tasks place on memory: a continuous skill is a single flowing pattern, whereas a procedure is only as reliable as the weakest link in a chain of steps that must each be recalled in the correct order.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Haakonsen also identified the factor that best predicted how well a skill would survive. It was not the ability of the learner or the length of the original course, but the amount of practice that continued after the learner had first reached the required standard, a phenomenon known as overlearning. The implications for training are less straightforward than they might appear, however. Thandiwe Dlamini-Shezi, who directs simulation training at the Durban School of Emergency Medicine, found that resuscitation teams given extensive extra practice at certification did lose their skills more slowly, but lost them nonetheless, and that the benefits of each additional hour diminished rapidly. Her alternative is what she calls low-dose, high-frequency training: sessions of six or seven minutes on a manikin, repeated monthly. In her trials, staff who followed this regime outperformed those who attended a traditional full-day course once a year, despite spending considerably less time in training overall.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Automation adds a further complication. As aircraft, ships and power plants have become increasingly self-regulating, operators have fewer opportunities to practise the very skills they would need if the automated systems failed. It is widely assumed that the principal casualty is manual dexterity, the physical handling of controls. Yet research by Tomasz Zielonka, a human factors specialist at the Baltic Aviation Safety Institute, suggests otherwise. When he tested airline pilots in a simulator with the autopilot disconnected, their hand-flying was generally adequate. What had deteriorated, particularly among pilots who rarely flew manually, were cognitive skills: the ability to maintain a mental picture of the aircraft's position and to recognise quickly that a situation was becoming abnormal. If his findings are confirmed, much of the current debate about automation has been directed at the wrong target.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Compounding the problem is the fact that people are poor judges of their own retention. Dlamini-Shezi asked nurses to rate their resuscitation skills before testing them, and found that confidence remained high long after competence had declined; those who had lost most skill were frequently the most assured. Confidence, in other words, decays more slowly than ability, and the widening gap between the two is precisely what makes skill decay dangerous. It follows that organisations which rely on employees to report when they need retraining are building their safety arrangements on an unreliable foundation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards the picture as so bleak. Rafael Ochoa-Brandt, an economist who advises defence ministries on training budgets, points out that skills which have faded are typically regained much faster than they were originally learned, since some underlying structure persists even when performance has collapsed. On this basis he argues that continuous refresher programmes are often wasteful, and that brief, intensive retraining immediately before a skill is needed offers far better value. For tasks that can be scheduled in advance, such as a planned deployment or a seasonal operation, this argument is persuasive. But the skills that matter most in emergency professions are, by definition, needed without warning, and a refresher course cannot be arranged in the seconds between an engine failing and the aircraft leaving the runway.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that skill decay should be seen as a flaw in human memory. A memory that preserved every skill indefinitely, regardless of use, would be cluttered and inefficient; forgetting what is not used is, in most circumstances, a sensible economy. The difficulty arises only when the environment changes faster than the brain's assumptions, so that skills which are rarely exercised nonetheless remain vital. The solution is to engineer the opportunities for practice that ordinary work no longer provides. Requiring that automated systems be periodically switched off, so that operators can rehearse the tasks they would otherwise never perform, would be a modest price for a substantial gain in safety, and regulators should be prepared to insist on it.

topic: hedonic adaptation and the set-point theory of happiness: twin studies, long-term panel data and uneven recovery from life events
title: Back to Baseline?
subtitle: The belief that people always return to a fixed level of happiness after good or bad fortune is coming under growing pressure

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in the psychology of wellbeing have proved as durable as the 'hedonic treadmill'. According to this view, people react strongly to good and bad events - a promotion, a new car, a divorce, a serious injury - but within a surprisingly short time they drift back to a personal baseline, rather as a walker on a treadmill stays in the same place however fast the belt turns. That baseline, or 'set point', is held to be largely fixed by temperament, so that the pursuit of happiness through changing one's circumstances is ultimately futile. The theory has an obvious consoling symmetry: if good fortune fades, so too does misfortune. Yet the appeal of an idea is no guarantee of its truth, and over the past two decades the evidence on which the set point rests has begun to look considerably less secure than its admirers assume.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest support has come from behavioural genetics. Ingrid Leuenberger, of the Bergen Institute for Social Research, has compared the wellbeing scores of thousands of identical and non-identical twins and concludes that roughly half of the variation in happiness between individuals reflects genetic differences. In her view, attempts to raise one's happiness permanently are rather like trying to make oneself taller. The comparison is memorable, but it rests on a common misunderstanding. A heritability estimate describes how much of the variation within a particular population is associated with genes; it says nothing about how fixed any one person's level is, nor about how far that level could be shifted by a change of environment. Short-sightedness is also strongly heritable, and spectacles correct it perfectly well.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more direct test is to follow the same people over many years. Tadeo Villasante and colleagues at the Valencia Centre for Wellbeing Studies drew on a national survey in which more than twenty thousand households answered questions about their lives annually for two decades. Their analysis suggests that some events leave a lasting mark. Satisfaction fell sharply among those who lost their jobs and, strikingly, remained lower even after most of them had found new work, as though the experience had permanently altered how secure they felt. After the death of a spouse, satisfaction recovered on average over about seven years, but Villasante stresses that this average conceals two very different groups: most widows and widowers returned close to their earlier level, whereas around a quarter never did.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should adaptation be complete in some cases and partial in others? Nkechi Onwuzurike, a psychologist at the West African Centre for Behavioural Research, argues that the answer lies in attention. Gains in income or possessions quickly become part of the background of daily life and cease to be noticed. By contrast, conditions that are unpredictable or intermittent - traffic noise, a long and unreliable commute, chronic pain that comes and goes - keep forcing themselves back into awareness, and so resist adaptation. Onwuzurike illustrates the point with housing: a family that moves to a larger home soon stops registering the extra rooms, whereas one that moves to a quieter street may continue to benefit for years, because each night of undisturbed sleep is experienced afresh.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers accept that the survey evidence can settle the question. Rustam Tursunbekov, an economist at the Institute for Applied Social Measurement in Almaty, points out that people answer life satisfaction questions on numerical scales - typically from zero to ten - and that the meaning of those numbers may itself change. Someone who becomes disabled might, after a period of time, judge their life by different standards, so that a score of seven means something different from what it meant before. If so, an apparent recovery might reflect a shift in the yardstick rather than in the person's actual experience. This is a serious objection, and it deserves more attention than it usually receives. Taken to its logical conclusion, however, it would imply that self-reported wellbeing is meaningless, and that seems an overreaction: people's ratings of their own happiness correspond reasonably well with the judgements of friends and family and with observable behaviour such as smiling or social engagement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practical implications are considerable. If people recover only partially from certain adversities, then preventing those adversities should be a priority for governments - a strong argument, for instance, for policies that reduce long-term unemployment rather than merely compensating those affected. The findings also suggest ways in which individuals might slow their adaptation to positive changes. In one study at the Ostrava Wellbeing Laboratory, participants who were encouraged to vary how and when they used a recent purchase remained more satisfied with it than those given no such advice. The result is intriguing, but the study followed participants for only six weeks, which is far too short to say whether the effect persists.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is not a refutation of adaptation but a more nuanced picture of it. Human beings clearly do adjust, often remarkably well, to both good and bad fortune; this capacity is real and, in the face of tragedy, frequently admirable. But the adjustment is uneven, depending on the kind of change involved and on the individual concerned. Paradoxically, this conclusion is more hopeful than the original theory. If circumstances were irrelevant to lasting happiness, there would be little point in trying to improve them; the evidence that they do matter means that both personal choices and public policy can make a lasting difference.

topic: the income paradox: rising national income, flat average happiness, relative income, aspirations and the business-cycle critique
title: Richer, But No Happier?
subtitle: Half a century after it was first noticed, the puzzle of rising incomes and stagnant happiness continues to divide economists

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, economists assumed that the connection between money and wellbeing required little investigation: higher incomes allowed people to buy more of what they wanted, and so, it was presumed, made them better off. The first large surveys asking people directly how happy they were seemed to confirm this. Within any given country, wealthier individuals reported greater satisfaction with their lives than poorer ones, and citizens of rich nations tended to be happier than those of poor nations. But when researchers began to track average happiness within a single country over several decades, a puzzle emerged. Incomes adjusted for inflation had in some cases doubled, yet the proportion of people describing themselves as 'very happy' had scarcely moved. This apparent contradiction, often called the income paradox, deserves more attention than it receives outside academic circles, because it calls into question whether economic growth ought to be the central objective of government policy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation focuses on comparison. Margit Szendrey, of the Central European Institute for Economic Studies in Budapest, argues that people judge their income less by what it can buy than by how it ranks against the incomes of those around them. If everyone becomes richer at the same rate, nobody's relative position improves, and so average happiness stays the same. Szendrey cites a survey in which participants were asked to choose between two imaginary worlds: in the first they would earn twice as much as everyone else, while in the second they would have a larger income in absolute terms but only half that of other people. A clear majority chose the first world, giving up wealth for rank. Her analysis of neighbourhood data points the same way: holding their own income constant, people whose neighbours earn more report lower satisfaction.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second account emphasises aspirations rather than rivals. Kwame Anokye, an economist at the Accra School of Development Economics, has examined surveys asking respondents how much money a household like theirs would need simply to get by. He found that this figure climbs almost in step with what households actually earn, so that the gap between what people have and what they think they need hardly narrows as they grow richer. Material gains, on this view, are absorbed into a rising standard of what counts as normal. Anokye presents his explanation as an alternative to Szendrey's, but the distinction may be less sharp than he suggests. Our expectations are shaped largely by what we observe others possessing, and it is quite possible that rising aspirations and social comparison are simply two descriptions of the same underlying process.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that there is a paradox to explain. Liesbeth Doornbos and her colleagues at the Rhine Institute for Wellbeing Economics contend that the original finding was an artefact of limited data. Using surveys from more than a hundred countries, they report that happiness generally does rise as nations grow richer, although the effect is modest. The key, they argue, is that wellbeing responds to the proportional rather than the absolute change in income: a rise of one thousand dollars transforms the life of a poor family but makes little impression on a wealthy one. In already prosperous countries, then, even substantial growth produces only small gains, which are easily missed. As for the flat trend in the large, wealthy country that originally gave rise to the debate, Doornbos attributes it not to the limits of income but to a sharp increase in inequality and a decline in trust between citizens over the same period.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the paradox have responded vigorously. Eero Pihlaja, a statistician at the Tampere Centre for Social Statistics, observes that happiness is highly sensitive to the business cycle: it falls sharply during recessions, when jobs are lost and insecurity spreads, and recovers as the economy improves. Studies covering only a decade or two, he suggests, mistake these temporary fluctuations for a lasting relationship. When the analysis is restricted to trends of at least ten years, the connection between growth and happiness largely disappears. Pihlaja's distinction is an important one, and any serious study must now take it into account. Nevertheless, it does not settle the matter. Many of the countries in which long-term growth does seem to have raised happiness were emerging from widespread poverty, and it seems likely that the paradox holds for rich societies but not for poor ones, where additional income still meets urgent needs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the measuring instrument itself. Happiness is usually recorded on a scale from zero to ten, and some critics have suggested that average scores cannot keep rising, because a population whose members already rate their lives at seven or eight has little room left on the scale. This is a reasonable concern in principle, but it is unlikely to explain the paradox, since average scores in a number of countries have risen by a full point or more in recent decades, showing that the upper end of the scale is not a fixed barrier.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should policymakers conclude? It would be a mistake to treat the income paradox as proof that growth is worthless; the tax revenue it generates pays for health care, education and social protection, all of which matter a great deal to how people feel about their lives. But growth is clearly not sufficient in itself. Unemployment, poor health and loneliness are consistently associated with large and persistent falls in life satisfaction, far larger than those accompanying modest changes in income. A government genuinely concerned with the wellbeing of its citizens would therefore give these matters at least as much weight as the rate at which national output expands.

topic: measuring national wellbeing beyond GDP: single composite index versus indicator dashboard versus life satisfaction, and targets in wellbeing budgeting
title: Budgeting for Contentment
subtitle: Governments are experimenting with new ways of measuring national progress, but agreeing on what to count is proving harder than rejecting the old yardstick

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a finance minister rises to present a national budget, the figure most likely to dominate the following day's headlines is the forecast rate of economic growth. In recent years, however, a small number of governments have begun to present their spending plans differently, justifying each major decision by reference to its expected effect on citizens' health, social connections, security and satisfaction with life. Supporters describe this as the most significant change in public accounting since national income statistics were first compiled in the middle of the last century. Whether it represents a genuine shift in priorities, or merely a new vocabulary for old decisions, is a question that researchers are only beginning to answer. Early results suggest that the answer may depend less on the choice of indicators than on what governments are prepared to do with them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against relying on gross domestic product is by now familiar, but it bears repeating. GDP records the market value of goods and services produced; it was designed to help governments manage production in wartime and recession, not to measure how well people live. It counts the cleaning up of an oil spill as a contribution to output, ignores unpaid care within families entirely, and says nothing about how income is distributed. None of this would matter if GDP were treated as one specialised statistic among many. The difficulty is that, over several decades, it has acquired the status of a general verdict on national success, a role for which it was never intended and is poorly suited.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is far less agreement about what should replace it. Ana Tuimavave of the Oceania Policy Institute argues that any alternative must take the form of a single headline index, combining measures of health, education, environment and income into one number. Her reasoning is strategic rather than technical. GDP owes much of its power to its simplicity: a single figure, rising or falling, can be reported in a sentence. Rates of inflation and unemployment enjoy the same advantage, which is partly why they too are reported so prominently. An alternative presented as a long list of statistics, Tuimavave contends, will never compete with it for the attention of journalists and voters.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Zofia Brzozowska, who directs the Krakow Centre for Social Indicators, regards this approach as fundamentally misguided. To merge dozens of measures into one figure, she points out, statisticians must decide how much each component counts: whether, say, a year of additional life expectancy is worth more or less than a ten per cent fall in crime. Such weights are inevitably arbitrary, and in her view they involve value judgements of a political kind that should not be concealed within a formula. She favours instead a dashboard of separate indicators, each reported in its own right. The objection to composite indices is a serious one, but the alternative carries its own risk. Several governments that have published dashboards of forty or fifty measures have found that ministers and journalists simply ignore most of them, and a display that shows everything can end up highlighting nothing.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third position avoids the weighting problem by a different route. Mikko Ollikainen, an economist at the Helsinki Unit for Wellbeing Economics, proposes that the headline measure should be people's own evaluations of their lives, gathered through large annual surveys. When a person rates their satisfaction on a scale of zero to ten, Ollikainen argues, they are already weighing health, income, relationships and work according to their own priorities, so no expert needs to impose a formula. Critics reply that people in persistent hardship often lower their expectations and may therefore report reasonable contentment with circumstances that are plainly unacceptable. This is a genuine difficulty, and it means that self-reported satisfaction cannot be the only guide to policy. It is not, however, a reason to abandon such measures altogether, since the same surveys reveal large and consistent differences that correspond closely to objective conditions such as unemployment and ill health.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever is measured, there remains the question of what happens once the measure becomes a target. Rania Fakhouri, of the Levant School of Public Administration, studied twelve municipal authorities that had adopted formal wellbeing objectives. In most of them, she found, departments shifted resources towards indicators that could be improved within a single electoral term, such as attendance at public events or the number of residents using parks, while longer-term goals, including mental health services for adolescents, received less attention than before. Fakhouri does not conclude that wellbeing targets are harmful, but she insists that the measures chosen must reward slow, durable improvements as well as quick ones. One of the authorities she studied did exactly this, pairing each short-term indicator with a longer-term counterpart, and it was the only one in which longer-term goals did not lose ground.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The evidence so far suggests that changing the measure of progress does not, by itself, transform how governments spend money; in the countries that pioneered wellbeing budgets, the share of spending allocated to each ministry has altered only slightly. Yet it would be wrong to dismiss the experiment on these grounds. A budget framed around wellbeing obliges ministers to explain how a proposal will improve people's lives, not merely how much it will add to output, and over time such questions may change what is regarded as a respectable argument in public debate.

topic: gratitude diaries and positive psychology interventions: control groups, replication, frequency of practice, cultural fit and person-activity fit
title: Counting Blessings
subtitle: The gratitude diary has become one of the most popular tools of the wellbeing industry, but the research behind it tells a more modest story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few psychological techniques have travelled as far or as fast as the gratitude diary. The idea is disarmingly simple: once a week, or sometimes every evening, a person writes down a handful of things for which they feel thankful. In the space of two decades the exercise has moved from the psychology laboratory into self-help books, corporate wellness schemes, school curricula and dozens of smartphone apps that send nightly reminders. Its appeal is easy to understand, since it costs nothing, takes a few minutes and carries no obvious risk. Yet the enthusiasm with which it has been adopted has run considerably ahead of the evidence, and the research of the past decade suggests a more modest, and more interesting, story than the one usually told.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The early findings were striking. In a study that is still widely cited, Claire Vinet and her colleagues at the Rhone Institute of Psychology asked participants to spend ten weeks keeping one of several kinds of weekly record. Those who listed things they were grateful for reported greater satisfaction with life, more optimism about the coming week and even fewer physical complaints than those who recorded daily hassles. The difficulty lies in that comparison. Writing about irritations may well make people feel worse, so a gap between the two groups could reflect a decline among the complainers rather than any genuine improvement among the grateful. A study designed in this way cannot reveal which of the two has occurred.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To address such problems, fourteen laboratories formed the Multi-Site Replication Network and ran a common protocol with more than three thousand participants. Crucially, the control group did not dwell on annoyances but instead described neutral events from the previous week, such as journeys or meals. The Network also registered its analyses in advance, stating exactly which outcomes it would examine, so that favourable results could not be selectively reported. The gratitude exercise still produced a measurable improvement in wellbeing, which suggests that the effect is real. However, it was only about a third of the size reported in the original studies, and when participants were contacted a month after they had stopped writing, the difference between the groups had largely vanished.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should such a simple activity work at all, and why so weakly? Reto Gwerder, a psychologist at the Zurich Centre for Applied Emotion Research, believes that part of the answer lies in how often people practise it. In his experiment, students who listed their blessings once a week showed larger gains than those who did so three times a week. Gwerder argues that frequent repetition causes the exercise to degenerate into a chore, completed mechanically and without the emotional engagement that makes it effective. The idea is plausible and has obvious implications for the design of apps that prompt users every night. Nevertheless, it rests so far on a single study of university students, and it would be premature to assume that the same pattern holds for other groups.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dinara Nazarbekova, of the Eurasian Institute of Social Psychology in Astana, has drawn attention to a different limitation. Most research on gratitude has been carried out in North America and Western Europe, where thanking others is generally experienced as purely pleasant. In many other societies, however, receiving help creates an obligation to repay it, so that dwelling on what others have done for us may provoke a sense of debt as well as warmth. In Nazarbekova's studies, participants who wrote letters of thanks to people who had helped them showed smaller gains in wellbeing than comparable North American samples, and a notable minority reported embarrassment rather than pleasure. This does not imply that gratitude is less valued in such societies; rather, it suggests that an exercise developed in one cultural setting cannot simply be exported to another without adaptation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A related line of research concerns the match between person and activity. Tunde Olowokere and his team at the Ibadan Centre for Behavioural Health found that participants who were allowed to choose a gratitude exercise from a menu of options benefited more than those who were simply assigned one. They also found that those who began the study with low wellbeing gained the most, while people who were already highly content improved very little, presumably because they had less room for improvement. The second finding is persuasive. The first is harder to interpret, since people who opt for an exercise may simply be more motivated to persist with it, and motivation rather than choice may explain their greater progress.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that gratitude exercises are worthless. An intervention that is free, safe and capable of reaching millions of people can do considerable good even if its effect on any one individual is small. What the evidence does not support is the claim, made by some commercial providers, that keeping a gratitude diary can take the place of professional treatment for depression or anxiety. The techniques of positive psychology are best regarded as modest aids to wellbeing, and the field will serve the public better by saying so plainly.

topic: the U-shaped curve of life satisfaction across the lifespan: the midlife dip, statistical controls, cohort effects, ape studies and unmet expectations
title: The Midlife Dip
subtitle: Is there really a low point in the middle of life, and if so, what causes it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The notion of the midlife crisis entered popular culture long before anyone had attempted to measure it. The image of the restless forty-five-year-old who abandons a steady career or buys an unsuitable sports car became a staple of novels and films in the second half of the twentieth century, despite the fact that early psychological studies found little sign of a sudden emotional upheaval at any particular age. It was therefore something of a surprise when, around the turn of the millennium, economists analysing large surveys reported a pattern that seemed to vindicate the popular idea, albeit in a gentler form. Life satisfaction, they found, tends to decline gradually from early adulthood, reach a low point in middle age and then rise again into the sixties and seventies, tracing a shape like a shallow letter U.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most comprehensive analysis to date was carried out by Kofi Amankwaah at the Kumasi Institute of Applied Economics, who pooled responses from about one and a half million people in seventy countries. To isolate the effect of age itself, Amankwaah compared people who were alike in income, education, marital status and number of children. On this basis, satisfaction reached its lowest point at an average age of forty-seven, although the trough occurred as early as forty in some countries and as late as fifty-five in others. The size of the decline was modest, about a third of the drop typically associated with becoming unemployed, but its appearance in such different societies suggested to Amankwaah that it reflected something fundamental about the human life course.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone was persuaded. Paulina Kasprzycka, a demographer at the Gdansk Institute for Population Research, objected that removing the influence of income, health and family circumstances was the wrong procedure. These, she argued, are precisely the means by which age shapes people's lives; holding them constant is like asking how tall children would be if they did not grow. When she repeated the analysis without such adjustments, the U became much flatter, and in several countries satisfaction simply declined with age after about sixty. The objection is a fair one, but it does not prove that Amankwaah was wrong. The two methods address different questions - one about the effect of ageing in itself, the other about how people of different ages actually fare - and both are legitimate, provided that it is clear which question is being asked.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental problem is that most of the evidence comes from surveys that interview different people at a single point in time. A comparison between today's forty-year-olds and today's seventy-year-olds may reveal less about ageing than about generations that grew up in very different economic and social conditions. The only way to disentangle the two is to follow the same individuals over many years. Yelena Tarkhanova of the Siberian Centre for Population Studies did exactly this, tracking nine thousand adults for twenty-five years. She did find a dip in middle age, but it was roughly half the size suggested by single-time surveys, and among two of the five generations she studied it could not be detected at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some of the most intriguing support for a biological explanation has come from an unexpected source. A team led by Martin Iribarne at the River Plate Primate Research Station asked keepers at zoos on three continents to rate the wellbeing of more than five hundred chimpanzees and orangutans. When the scores were plotted against the animals' ages, a similar U-shape emerged, with the lowest point at an age equivalent to middle age in humans. Since apes have neither mortgages nor careers, Iribarne concludes, the pattern cannot be explained entirely by the pressures of modern life. The study is ingenious, but its conclusions should be treated with caution: keepers' impressions of an animal's mood are a long way from a human's considered evaluation of his or her life as a whole.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Among psychological accounts, the most promising centres on expectations. Surveys asking people to predict how satisfied they will be in five years' time show that young adults consistently forecast a better future than they actually experience. As the years pass, the shortfall between hope and reality accumulates, and in middle age it produces a pervasive sense of regret. Older respondents, by contrast, make forecasts that are, if anything, too pessimistic; having scaled back their ambitions, they find their lives turning out rather better than anticipated. This account sits comfortably alongside laboratory evidence that older adults attend more to pleasant than to unpleasant information, recalling cheerful images more readily and dwelling less on setbacks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What follows from all this? Above all, it would be a mistake to exaggerate the midlife dip. It is an average tendency of moderate size, it appears to be smaller when the same people are followed over time, and many individuals never experience it. Yet there may be some value in knowing that it exists. People who find themselves unaccountably dissatisfied in their late forties may take comfort from the evidence that such feelings are common and, for most, temporary.

topic: experienced versus remembered happiness: experience sampling, memory bias in evaluating episodes, which measure should guide policy, and the day reconstruction method
title: Moments and Memories
subtitle: New methods of tracking feelings throughout the day have revealed a gap between how people live and how they remember living

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask people how happy they are and you may receive two quite different kinds of answer. One is a considered judgement: a person steps back, surveys their circumstances, and rates their life as a whole, perhaps as a seven out of ten. The other is a report of feeling: how cheerful, anxious, bored or irritated they are at this precise moment. For many years, wellbeing research relied almost entirely on the first kind of answer, largely because it is cheap to collect through conventional surveys. The arrival of mobile technology changed this, allowing researchers to ask people about their feelings at random moments as they go about their lives. The resulting distinction between how people evaluate their lives and how they actually experience them is arguably the most important conceptual advance in the field during the past thirty years.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technique, known as experience sampling, typically involves a smartphone that sounds an alert several times a day, prompting the user to record what they are doing, who they are with and how they feel. Emilie Bellefleur and her colleagues at the Montreal Laboratory for Everyday Experience used this method with some two and a half thousand adults, each of whom was contacted six times a day for a fortnight. The least pleasant moments of the day were reported during commuting, housework and time spent with a manager; the most pleasant during socialising, eating with friends and exercise. Perhaps the most striking finding concerned money. Household income was a strong predictor of how satisfied people said they were with their lives, yet it had almost no bearing on how they felt at any given moment.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The gap between the two kinds of measure is partly explained by the workings of memory. Oleh Lukashuk, a cognitive psychologist at the Lviv Centre for Cognitive Studies, asked travellers to rate their mood every evening throughout a holiday and then, a month after returning, to give an overall assessment of the trip. The later assessments bore little relation to the average of the evening ratings. Instead, they were predicted mainly by the single best day and by the last day of the holiday; how long the travellers had been away made almost no difference. Memory, in other words, does not store a faithful record of experience but a highly selective summary, and that summary can misrepresent the experience in systematic ways.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Which of the two, then, should count as a person's 'real' happiness? Lukashuk argues that the remembered evaluation deserves priority, because it is memory rather than momentary experience that guides our decisions: people choose their next holiday on the basis of how they remember the last one. Thandiwe Mokgadi, of the Pretoria Institute for Wellbeing Research, takes the opposite view. Life, she points out, is lived moment by moment, and a society that cares about the welfare of its citizens should aim to reduce the share of their waking hours spent in unpleasant states such as pain, anxiety or boredom. Mokgadi's position has considerable force, but it goes too far when it treats people's reflective evaluations as nothing more than distortions. A sense that one's life has purpose, for example, may emerge only when a person reflects on it as a whole, and is no less real for being invisible from moment to moment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Experience sampling also has practical limitations. Being interrupted several times a day is tiresome, and many participants drop out before the end of a study; those who remain may differ from those who leave, perhaps by being more conscientious or simply less busy. More subtly, the act of reporting a feeling can alter it; people who are repeatedly asked whether they are anxious may become more aware of, or even more prone to, anxiety. A further problem has been identified by Armen Sahakyan, a survey methodologist at the Caucasus Institute of Social Measurement. By comparing the timing of missed alerts with information from participants' calendars, he found that people were considerably less likely to respond during arguments, emergencies or periods of intense work. Since difficult moments are underrepresented, studies may present a calmer picture of daily life than is really the case.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One response has been the day reconstruction method, in which participants divide the previous day into episodes, such as breakfast, a journey or a meeting, and describe how they felt during each in turn. It is less intrusive and far cheaper than experience sampling, and its results are broadly similar, although it inevitably relies on memory, the very faculty whose distortions motivated moment-by-moment measurement in the first place. Researchers who have compared the two methods directly suggest that each has its place, with sampling better suited to small, intensive studies and reconstruction to large national surveys.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, the choice between these measures is not merely technical. A government that judged its success solely by life evaluations might concentrate on raising incomes and status, while one guided by momentary experience might give priority to shortening commutes, reducing noise and creating opportunities for people to spend time together. Both sets of goals are worth pursuing, and the most sensible course is for public bodies to monitor both kinds of measure rather than to choose between them.
