topic: loneliness as a public health issue: isolation versus loneliness in mortality evidence, reverse causation, the 'epidemic' claim, social threat vigilance and interventions
title: A Crowded Solitude
subtitle: Loneliness is now treated as a threat to public health, but the evidence behind the most popular claims deserves closer scrutiny

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Not long ago, loneliness was regarded as a private misfortune, a matter for poets and advice columnists rather than for health ministries. That has changed remarkably quickly. Several governments have appointed officials with responsibility for social connection, public health campaigns urge people to check on isolated neighbours, and medical journals regularly describe loneliness as a risk factor comparable to obesity or physical inactivity. The most widely repeated claim of all is that being lonely is as damaging to health as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. The comparison is memorable, and it has undoubtedly helped to attract attention and funding to a neglected problem. It is also, on closer examination, seriously misleading.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The claim derives from an analysis by Giulia Pellizzari and colleagues at the Emilia Institute of Epidemiology, who combined the results of some 140 studies involving more than three hundred thousand people. Those with weak social relationships were, on average, about a quarter more likely to have died by the end of the follow-up period than those with strong ones. However, the studies in question measured quite different things. Some recorded objective circumstances, such as living alone or seeing friends rarely; others asked people whether they felt lonely, a subjective state that can occur even among those surrounded by others. When Pellizzari separated the two, it was objective isolation, rather than the feeling of loneliness, that showed the stronger link with early death. A slogan about loneliness, in other words, rests largely on evidence about something else.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of which way the causal arrow points. Wanjiru Wanjau, of the Nairobi Centre for Social Epidemiology, notes that serious illness often leads people to withdraw from social life: someone with heart disease or chronic pain may stop attending clubs or visiting friends simply because doing so has become difficult. If so, part of the apparent effect of isolation on health may in fact be an effect of health on isolation. When Wanjau reanalysed several large studies after excluding participants who were already ill when they were first surveyed, the association between weak social ties and mortality fell by about a third. Her caution is justified, but the finding cuts both ways: the association that survives such adjustment is still large enough to be of real public health concern.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Equally questionable is the frequent assertion that modern societies are in the grip of a loneliness epidemic. Bat-Erdene Gombosuren, a sociologist at the Ulaanbaatar Centre for Comparative Sociology, compared surveys conducted over four decades in twelve countries and found no consistent increase in loneliness across the population as a whole. In several countries it had risen among young adults while falling among the elderly, so that the overall level remained roughly stable. The rise among the young deserves attention, but the language of epidemics is unhelpful. Presenting loneliness as a contagious disease risks making those who experience it feel abnormal or ashamed, and shame is precisely the emotion most likely to discourage them from seeking company.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Research on the psychology of loneliness helps to explain why it can be so persistent. Sione Taukei, a neuroscientist at the Pacific Centre for Behavioural Research, argues that loneliness evolved as a signal, rather like hunger or thirst, whose function was to prompt our ancestors to repair damaged relationships, since survival outside the group was precarious. In the short term, the signal is useful. When it persists, however, it appears to produce a state of heightened vigilance for social threat. In Taukei's experiments, chronically lonely participants judged neutral faces to be less friendly than other participants did and remembered critical remarks more readily than kind ones. Such a bias leads people to expect rejection and to withdraw, which in turn deepens their isolation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This insight has implications for how loneliness should be tackled. Many schemes simply increase opportunities for contact, through lunch clubs, befriending services or referrals from doctors to community groups. Yet reviews of such programmes suggest that their effects on loneliness are generally modest. Ardita Sulejmani, a clinical psychologist at the Prishtina Centre for Applied Psychology, compared a group activity programme with a course designed to help participants recognise and challenge negative assumptions about other people. Six months later, loneliness had fallen considerably more among those who took the course. Such results are encouraging, but they should not be used to dismiss practical forms of support. Psychological courses reach relatively few people, and for someone who is housebound, a weekly visitor may be the only regular human contact available.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the research makes clear above all is that isolation and loneliness are different problems that require different responses. Some people live alone and see others rarely yet feel perfectly content; others feel desperately lonely in the middle of a busy family or workplace. Policies that treat these groups as one, or that measure success simply by counting social contacts, are unlikely to help either of them much. Nor is there any reason to expect a single solution. The evidence reviewed here points instead towards a range of approaches: practical help for those who are genuinely cut off from others, psychological support for those whose loneliness has become self-perpetuating, and greater care over the claims made about both, so that public concern is directed to where it can do the most good.

topic: commuting and wellbeing: the commuting paradox, travel mode and unpredictability, the commute as a transition, unequal commuting burdens and remote work
title: The Price of the Journey
subtitle: Why do so many people accept long journeys to work that appear to make them less happy?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every working day, hundreds of millions of people spend an hour or more travelling between home and work. To an economist, this is not in itself a puzzle. People choose where to live and work, and if they accept a long journey, it is presumably because they are compensated in some other way: by a higher salary, a larger house, a garden, or a neighbourhood with better schools. In a well-functioning market, the argument runs, these gains should exactly offset the time and inconvenience of travel, so that people with long commutes ought, on average, to be neither more nor less satisfied with their lives than those who live next door to their workplace. Any lasting difference in wellbeing would imply that people were systematically making choices that left them worse off, a possibility that standard economic models are reluctant to accept.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The evidence does not bear this out. Hendrik Bezuidenhout, of the Stellenbosch Unit for Labour Economics, analysed fifteen years of data on some thirty thousand workers and found that each additional twenty minutes of travel in each direction was associated with a fall in life satisfaction comparable to that produced by a substantial cut in pay. Crucially, he could find no evidence that long-distance commuters were rewarded with incomes or homes sufficient to make up the difference. Bezuidenhout attributes this 'commuting paradox' to a systematic error in decision-making. When choosing a home, people are drawn to tangible advantages such as an extra bedroom, which they can see and imagine enjoying, while they underestimate the cumulative cost of hours spent in traffic, which is harder to picture in advance. This seems the most plausible explanation, not least because similar errors have been documented in many other kinds of decision.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all commutes are equally harmful, however. Selin Yildirimer, who leads the Izmir Centre for Mobility Research, surveyed commuters in eight cities about how they travelled and how they felt on arrival. Those who walked or cycled were the most contented group, even when their journeys took longer than average, while passengers on crowded buses reported the lowest levels of satisfaction. Among drivers, Yildirimer found, the length of the journey mattered less than its unpredictability: a forty-minute drive that always took forty minutes was tolerated far better than one that might take twenty minutes or an hour depending on the traffic. Rail commuters, whose services were generally punctual in the cities studied, fell somewhere between these extremes.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some researchers go further and argue that commuting has hidden benefits. Ingvild Nordhagen, an occupational psychologist at the Hordaland Institute for Work Psychology, suggests that the journey provides a transition between the roles of employee and parent or partner, allowing people to leave the concerns of the office behind before they arrive home. She points out that during the pandemic, when millions of people suddenly began working from home, a number of them devised artificial 'commutes', walking around the block before and after work in order to recreate the boundary they had lost. Nordhagen's argument is plausible, but its implications are limited. A transition of this kind can be accomplished in ten or fifteen minutes, and it can scarcely be used to justify journeys of an hour or more.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A dimension of the issue that has been largely overlooked is its unequal distribution. Kaarel Lepp, of the Tartu Centre for Urban Research, has shown that rising housing costs in city centres push lower-paid workers towards the outskirts, so that those least able to afford a car often face the longest and least reliable journeys. Lepp has also found that women with caring responsibilities are more likely than men to turn down job offers that involve a long commute, because they need to remain close to schools or elderly relatives. Since better-paid jobs are often concentrated in particular districts, this reluctance may contribute to differences in pay between men and women. These findings deserve far more attention from policymakers than they have so far received.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The spread of remote working might seem to offer a simple solution. Yet the evidence here is mixed. Employees who work entirely from home avoid the journey altogether, but surveys suggest that they report greater loneliness than those who travel to a workplace, and some miss the informal conversations that office life provides. Arrangements in which people work from home on some days and in the office on others appear to combine many of the advantages of both, although most studies of such hybrid patterns have so far covered only a few years.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For individuals, the lesson of this research is that the time cost of a journey deserves more weight than it usually receives when deciding where to live. For planners, it is that reliability matters at least as much as speed. Transport investment is too often judged by the minutes it will save on an average journey, when reducing uncertainty may do more for the wellbeing of those who travel. A railway line that runs on time, or a bus lane that keeps services moving through congested streets, may thus be worth more to commuters than a costly scheme that shortens the typical trip by a few minutes but leaves them as unsure as ever about when they will arrive.

topic: prosocial spending and happiness: whether spending on others makes people happier, cross-cultural evidence, replication, conditions for benefit, self-image and workplace giving schemes
title: The Rewards of Giving
subtitle: Experiments suggest that spending money on others makes people happier than spending it on themselves, but the effect is more fragile, and more revealing, than it first appears

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: 'It is better to give than to receive' is a sentiment found, in one form or another, in almost every moral tradition. Over the past two decades it has also become the subject of a substantial body of experimental research. In the best-known design, participants are approached in the street or on a university campus and handed an envelope containing a modest sum of money. Half are instructed to spend it on themselves by the end of the day, the other half to spend it on someone else, whether by buying a gift or giving to charity. When they are contacted that evening, those who spent the money on others typically report being happier than those who treated themselves. Findings of this kind have been widely reported, and in contrast to a number of celebrated results in social psychology that have failed to survive closer scrutiny, they have proved remarkably durable. What they mean, however, is less clear than is often supposed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most striking features of the effect is its breadth. Hanta Rasoanaivo, of the Indian Ocean Institute for Behavioural Science, coordinated studies in nine countries, ranging from wealthy industrial economies to societies where many households struggle to meet basic needs. Participants were asked to recall an occasion on which they had spent money either on themselves or on another person, and then to rate their current mood. In every country, those who recalled spending on others reported feeling happier, even in places where such spending represented a genuine sacrifice. Rasoanaivo concludes that the emotional reward of generosity may be a universal feature of human psychology, perhaps one that evolved because cooperation was essential to survival in small groups.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Universality, however, says nothing about size. Radu Dumitrache, of the Transylvanian Laboratory for Social Psychology, organised a large replication involving some eighteen hundred participants and an analysis plan registered before any data were collected. The effect was present, but it was roughly half as large as in the original studies, and it was noticeably weaker when participants actually spent money than when they performed recall tasks of the kind used by Rasoanaivo. Such shrinkage is common when early findings are tested more rigorously, and it does not mean that the original researchers were mistaken; it means rather that the benefits of generosity are real but modest, and should not be oversold.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all giving appears to be equally rewarding. Eleni Kanellopoulou, a psychologist at the Thessaloniki Centre for Decision Research, has identified three conditions under which the effect is strongest. Givers benefit most when they can see the difference their gift has made, when the gift strengthens a relationship with another person, and when the decision to give is made freely. In her studies, donations to large charitable organisations that provided no feedback produced little improvement in mood, while contributions that people felt pressured to make, such as collections organised by an employer, produced none at all. Spending money on a friend over a shared meal, by contrast, delivered among the largest gains she recorded.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why should giving make people feel good? Aigerim Mukhametova, an economist at the Volga Centre for Experimental Economics, argues that much of the benefit lies in the giver's self-image: in acting generously, people confirm to themselves that they are good and caring individuals. To test this, she designed an experiment in which a computer, rather than the participants themselves, sometimes decided whether money would be passed to another person. When participants could not regard the gift as their own choice, the improvement in mood disappeared, even though the recipient benefited just as much. Some commentators have taken this as evidence that generosity is fundamentally selfish. That conclusion does not follow. A motive that is partly self-regarding does not make an act less valuable to the person who receives it, and a disposition that rewards people for helping others is surely preferable to one that does not.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The research has not escaped the attention of business. Several companies have introduced so-called prosocial bonuses, in which employees receive money that they must spend on colleagues or donate to charity. Sigrid Bjelland, of the Bergen School of Organisational Studies, studied sales teams in which members were given small sums to spend on one another, and found that they went on to achieve higher sales than teams whose members had spent the same amount on themselves. When the scheme was repeated over several months, however, the advantage gradually faded. There is a further danger here. Generosity encouraged in order to raise productivity risks becoming merely another management technique, and employees who sense that their kindness is being harnessed for profit may well lose the very satisfaction that made it effective.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The evidence, then, supports a modest version of the traditional maxim. Spending on others does tend to make people somewhat happier, particularly when the gift is freely chosen and its effects are visible. Yet there is an irony at the heart of these findings. If the pleasure of giving depends on the act being genuinely generous, then those who give chiefly in order to improve their own mood may find that the reward eludes them.

topic: cultural differences in the meaning and measurement of happiness: word origins, ideal emotions, reluctance to report happiness, anchoring vignettes and international rankings
title: Lost in Translation?
subtitle: International happiness rankings assume that people everywhere mean the same thing by a good life. Cross-cultural research suggests otherwise

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each year, the publication of international happiness rankings attracts a flurry of headlines. The countries at the top are congratulated on their contentment, those near the bottom are pitied for their gloom, and commentators speculate about what the leaders might teach the rest of the world. These league tables are based on surveys that ask people in more than a hundred countries to rate their lives on the same numerical scale, usually from zero to ten. The results are then arranged in order, from the most contented nation to the least. The method rests on an assumption that is rarely stated: that people everywhere understand the question in the same way and use the scale in a similar manner. A growing body of cross-cultural research suggests that this assumption deserves far more scrutiny than it has received.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty begins with language. Farai Chikwanha, of the Zambezi Institute of Cross-Cultural Psychology, examined historical dictionaries in thirty languages to trace the origins of the words now used to translate 'happiness'. In about two-thirds of them, the earliest recorded meaning was connected with luck or good fortune, implying that happiness was something that befell a person rather than something they could achieve. In others, the word was associated with inner balance or harmony with one's community. Chikwanha argues that these origins continue to colour how people respond when asked how happy they are. The research is fascinating, but the conclusion drawn from it is open to question, since the meaning of a word centuries ago is an uncertain guide to how it is understood by the people who use it today.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more direct approach is to ask people not only how they feel but how they would like to feel. Melanie Tchoukoua, a psychologist at the Yaounde Centre for Psychological Research, has found striking differences in what she terms 'ideal emotions'. Participants in North America consistently said they wished to feel excited, enthusiastic and energetic, whereas many participants in East Asia and Central Africa valued calm, peacefulness and contentment above excitement. These preferences shaped everyday choices: asked to choose between holidays, those who valued calm favoured quiet retreats, while those who prized excitement selected adventurous trips. Perhaps most significantly, Tchoukoua found that the gap between how people actually felt and how they wished to feel predicted symptoms of depression more accurately than how positive their feelings were in absolute terms.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cultural differences may also affect how willing people are to report happiness at all. Ignacio Elizalde, of the Andean Institute for Social Psychology, points out that in a number of societies intense happiness is regarded with suspicion, as something that may invite misfortune or provoke the envy of neighbours. People who hold such beliefs may be hesitant to describe themselves as extremely happy even when they are content, and in Elizalde's surveys they were noticeably less likely to choose the highest points on the rating scale. If he is right, the scores recorded in these countries may understate how happy their citizens really are, and some of the apparent gaps between nations may be a matter of modesty rather than misery.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Survey researchers have not ignored these problems. One proposed solution is the use of 'anchoring vignettes'. Zoltan Gyurcsik, of the Pannonian Centre for Survey Research, has led studies in which respondents first rate the lives of several imaginary people, described in short paragraphs, before rating their own. Because everyone rates the same imaginary lives, differences in their ratings reveal how each group uses the scale, and these differences can then be used to adjust the scores people give themselves. When Gyurcsik applied this correction to data from twenty countries, several moved five or more places in the rankings, although Gyurcsik himself acknowledges that the adjusted figures should be regarded as estimates rather than definitive scores. The technique is ingenious, but it is not a complete solution. It assumes that people in different cultures interpret the descriptions of the imaginary lives in the same way, which is precisely the kind of assumption that the method was designed to avoid.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that international comparisons are worthless. It is a notable fact that, across very different societies, people's ratings of their lives are related to much the same circumstances: income, health, having someone to rely on in times of trouble, and the freedom to make important choices. This consistency strongly suggests that the surveys are capturing something that people everywhere share. Even so, the rankings deserve to be read with care. A difference of a few hundredths of a point between countries that are adjacent in the table is far too small to bear the weight of interpretation that is often placed on it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The practical implications extend beyond league tables. A wellbeing policy designed around the ideal of an energetic, excited citizen may be poorly suited to a society in which calm is more highly prized, and programmes exported from one country to another may need substantial adaptation. Perhaps the most valuable contribution of cross-cultural research, then, is not a better ranking but a degree of humility among those who study, and seek to promote, human happiness. Nor should the findings be taken as a reason to abandon measurement altogether: without surveys of this kind, the very differences described here would never have come to light.

topic: the contested 'bilingual advantage' in executive control: replication failures, publication bias and measurement problems
title: Two Tongues, One Controller?
subtitle: For two decades the idea that speaking two languages sharpens the mind enjoyed wide acceptance. It now faces a crisis of evidence

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, bilingualism was regarded with suspicion by educators and psychologists alike. Early intelligence testing, often conducted on immigrant children in a language they barely knew, appeared to show that those raised with two languages lagged behind their monolingual peers, and parents were sometimes advised to abandon the home language altogether. The reversal of this view, when it came, was dramatic. By the early 2000s a series of laboratory studies had suggested not merely that bilingualism did no harm but that it conferred a hidden benefit: an enhanced capacity for what psychologists call executive control, the set of mental processes that allow us to focus attention, ignore distraction and switch flexibly between tasks. The so-called bilingual advantage quickly escaped the laboratory and became a staple of parenting magazines and language-school advertising.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theoretical case for the advantage is elegant. Research on word recognition has shown that a bilingual's two languages are never completely switched off; even when a Spanish-English speaker is conversing purely in English, Spanish words are activated in the background. To avoid producing the wrong word, the speaker must continually suppress the language not in use. Dr Ingrid Haraldsrud, whose group at the Institute for Cognitive Development in Trondheim produced several of the early findings, argued that this constant juggling amounts to a lifelong training regime for the brain's control system. In her studies, bilingual children responded more quickly than monolinguals on tasks such as the Simon task, in which participants must press a button on the side indicated by an arrow's direction while ignoring the side of the screen on which the arrow appears.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that the effect has proved stubbornly hard to reproduce. When the cognitive psychologist Chidi Ozoemena and his colleagues attempted to replicate the classic findings with samples several times larger than the originals, they found no reliable difference between bilinguals and monolinguals on any of the standard measures. Ozoemena went further, pointing to evidence of publication bias: conference abstracts reporting a bilingual advantage were, according to his analysis, considerably more likely to be published in full than those reporting null or negative results. If positive findings are systematically favoured, the published literature will overstate an effect that may in reality be tiny or non-existent. His conclusion, that the advantage is at best confined to specific and poorly understood circumstances, has been widely cited, though not universally accepted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Haraldsrud's defenders respond that the failures to replicate tell us less than they appear to. One problem is that 'bilingual' is not a single category. A person who acquired two languages from birth and uses both daily differs profoundly from someone who studied a second language at school and rarely speaks it, yet many large studies have lumped such people together. Another is that the advantage may be most visible in groups whose control systems are still developing or already declining, namely young children and older adults, rather than in the university students who make up the bulk of participants in experimental psychology. These objections carry real weight. Nevertheless, there is a danger that they render the hypothesis unfalsifiable: if every negative result can be explained away by pointing to the wrong sample, it is unclear what evidence would ever count against it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the tasks themselves. Lucía Achucarro, a psychometrician at the Southern Institute of Psychometrics, has shown that measures such as the Simon task and the flanker task correlate surprisingly weakly with one another, even within the same individual tested on the same day. If two tests supposedly tapping the same underlying ability barely agree, she argues, it is doubtful whether either is measuring a stable trait at all. On this view, the debate has been conducted with instruments too blunt to settle it, and the contradictory findings reflect noise in the measurement rather than genuine differences between people. Her critique is perhaps the most damaging of all, because it applies equally to studies on both sides.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also the matter of confounding variables. Bilinguals and monolinguals frequently differ in socioeconomic status, immigration history and cultural background, any of which might influence performance on cognitive tests. Studies conducted in Canada, where bilinguals often come from relatively advantaged families, have tended to report benefits; studies in some other settings, where bilingualism is associated with economic hardship, have not. Researchers attempt to control for these differences statistically, but such adjustments are only as good as the measures of background on which they rely, and these are often crude.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the field? Maarten Dijkgraaf, who has reviewed more than a hundred studies, proposes abandoning the question of whether bilinguals are 'better' in favour of asking how specific patterns of language use shape specific cognitive processes. Someone who switches between languages many times within a single conversation, he suggests, may develop quite different skills from someone who keeps the two strictly apart. This reframing seems to me the most promising way forward, not least because it treats bilingual experience as varied rather than uniform. It does, however, carry an awkward implication for the public: the simple message that learning a language will make children cleverer is not one that the evidence currently supports. That should not matter as much as it might. The case for bilingualism has never really depended on reaction times; it rests on the access to people, cultures and opportunities that a second language provides.

topic: first-language attrition in adult emigrants: word retrieval, grammatical interference, age at emigration and emotional factors
title: The Language Left Behind
subtitle: Can people really forget the language they grew up speaking? Research on emigrants suggests the answer is more complicated than either yes or no

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people assume that a language learned in childhood is permanent, a possession that, once acquired, can never be taken away. Emigrants who have spent decades abroad often discover otherwise. They hesitate over everyday words, find themselves borrowing expressions from their new language, and are told by relatives on visits home that they now speak with a faint foreign accent. Linguists call this process first-language attrition. Although it has been studied far less than second-language learning, it raises fundamental questions about how languages are stored in the mind and whether, once learned, they can ever truly be lost.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest systematic research focused on vocabulary. Farida Kassymova, working with Kazakh and Russian speakers who had settled in Germany, found that the most obvious symptom of attrition is difficulty in retrieving words, particularly less frequent ones, under time pressure. Crucially, however, her participants could usually recognise the words they had failed to produce, and they performed almost as well as speakers who had never left home when they were given time to think. Kassymova concluded that what declines is not knowledge itself but access to it: the words remain stored but become harder to reach, much as a seldom-used path through a forest gradually becomes overgrown.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Grammar appears to be more resistant. Studies of long-term emigrants have found that the core grammatical system of the first language usually remains intact, even after forty or fifty years abroad. Where changes do occur, they tend to affect areas in which the two languages overlap or conflict, such as the use of pronouns or the order of words in subordinate clauses. Lorcan Ditchfield, who has recorded the speech of Dutch-born emigrants in Canada over three decades, argues that these changes are better described as the influence of the second language than as loss: speakers are not forgetting their grammar so much as allowing the patterns of another language to seep into it. This distinction is more than a matter of terminology. If attrition is largely a matter of interference, it should be at least partly reversible, and there is some evidence that emigrants who return home regain their former fluency within a year or two.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Age at emigration turns out to be one of the strongest predictors of what happens. Sione Lemalu compared adults who had left their country of birth at different stages of life and found a sharp contrast. Those who had emigrated after puberty generally retained their first language well, whatever their circumstances, whereas some who had left before the age of about ten appeared to have lost it almost completely, being unable as adults to understand even simple sentences. Yet Lemalu also discovered that such people, when they later tried to relearn the language, distinguished its sounds more accurately than learners who had never been exposed to it. In his view, early experience leaves a lasting imprint even when conscious knowledge has vanished. Whether such an imprint deserves to be called knowledge of a language is, however, open to debate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: More surprising is the finding that the sheer amount of first-language use may matter less than common sense would predict. In a study of Lithuanian emigrants in Norway, Vytautas Navickas found that how often participants spoke their first language was only a weak predictor of how well they had preserved it. A stronger predictor was their attitude towards the country they had left. Those who had departed under painful circumstances, such as political persecution, showed markedly greater attrition, which Navickas interprets as a form of emotional distancing from a past they preferred not to revisit. The explanation is plausible, but it is difficult to disentangle from other factors: people who flee their homeland often have fewer opportunities to stay in touch with it, so their weaker first language may reflect isolation rather than any psychological rejection.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mihaela Vrabie has raised a more basic objection to the way attrition is usually measured. Emigrants are generally compared with speakers who stayed at home, but the language at home does not stand still. Over several decades it acquires new vocabulary, new idioms and new patterns of pronunciation, so that an emigrant who left in the 1980s may sound old-fashioned rather than deficient. Vrabie suggests that a considerable part of what is labelled attrition is in fact the result of this mismatch. She is surely right that the benchmark matters, although it would be going too far to conclude that attrition is simply an illusion, since the difficulties emigrants report with retrieving words cannot be explained in this way.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Research on attrition has practical as well as theoretical significance. Elderly emigrants who develop dementia sometimes revert to their first language, which can leave care staff unable to communicate with them, and an understanding of how first languages are stored may help in designing better support. More generally, the evidence suggests that, for those who emigrate as adults, the first language is far more durable than they tend to fear. What looks like loss is more often a reorganisation, in which one language yields some ground to another without disappearing. The worry, common among emigrants, that their mother tongue is slipping irretrievably away is for most of them unfounded.

topic: whether lifelong bilingualism delays the onset of dementia: clinic-based versus community-based evidence
title: A Second Language Against Forgetting?
subtitle: Claims that bilingualism postpones dementia have attracted enormous interest. The evidence behind them is more fragile than the headlines suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the neurologist Henrik Ottesen and his colleagues examined the records of around six hundred patients diagnosed with dementia at a single memory clinic in Copenhagen, they noticed something unexpected. Patients who had spoken two or more languages throughout their adult lives had first shown symptoms, on average, more than four years later than those who had spoken only one. The two groups had received similar amounts of education, and the difference persisted when occupation was taken into account. A delay of that size would exceed anything achieved by the drugs then available, and the finding was reported around the world as evidence that a second language could protect the ageing brain.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation offered draws on the concept of cognitive reserve. It has long been known that the amount of physical damage in a brain does not correspond neatly to the severity of a person's symptoms; some individuals whose brains show extensive disease at post-mortem examination had functioned normally until death. Reserve is the name given to whatever allows such people to compensate. Ottesen proposed that the continual effort of managing two languages builds up this capacity. Brain scans carried out by his group seemed to support the idea: bilingual patients with the same level of symptoms as monolingual patients showed more advanced shrinkage of brain tissue, implying that they were coping with greater damage. This point is frequently misunderstood. If the theory is correct, bilingualism does not prevent the disease; it postpones its visible effects, and there is some evidence that, once diagnosed, bilingual patients decline more rapidly than others.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sceptics have focused on how the original studies were conducted. Parisa Sadeghipour, an epidemiologist, notes that the age at which symptoms began was usually reconstructed from the recollections of family members, which are notoriously imprecise. Moreover, people who reach a specialist clinic are not a random sample of those with dementia, and in a city with a large immigrant population, bilingual patients may differ from monolingual ones in many ways, including their health before migration. Sadeghipour therefore led a study that recruited more than three thousand healthy adults over the age of sixty-five and followed them for a decade. By the end of that period, the proportion who had developed dementia was almost identical among bilinguals and monolinguals.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the hypothesis argue that such large studies often define bilingualism too loosely. Claudine Mukamana, working in a region where many people speak three or more languages, classified participants not by how many languages they knew but by how often they used them. Those who used at least two languages every day developed symptoms around two years later than monolinguals, whereas those who used a second language only occasionally showed no benefit at all. A dose-response pattern of this kind, in which greater exposure brings a larger effect, is precisely the sort of evidence that strengthens the case for a causal link. Her study, however, involved fewer than three hundred people, and its results await confirmation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different challenge comes from the psychologist Gábor Szentesi, who points out that the direction of cause and effect is far from certain. Children of higher ability may be more likely to learn additional languages successfully and to keep using them, so that bilingualism could be a marker of a well-functioning brain rather than its cause. To test this, Szentesi traced a group of adults whose intelligence had been assessed at school at the age of eleven. Once these childhood scores were taken into account, the association between bilingualism and cognitive performance in old age shrank by roughly half, but it did not disappear. It is a finding that both camps have claimed as support, which perhaps says more about the debate than about the data.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most comprehensive picture so far comes from a review that combined the results of twenty-five studies. It found that the apparent protective effect depended heavily on the type of research. Clinic-based studies, which look back through the histories of people already diagnosed, generally reported a substantial delay in symptoms. Community-based studies, which follow healthy people forward in time, generally did not. To my mind, this contrast is the most telling clue that the effect may be at least partly an artefact of method, although it falls short of proof, since the two kinds of study also tend to define bilingualism differently.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What should older adults conclude? Some trials have offered language classes to people in their sixties and seventies, and these have produced modest short-term improvements in attention, but no trial has yet run long enough to show any effect on dementia. Learning a language later in life is plainly worth doing for the pleasure and social contact it brings; it would be irresponsible, however, to promote it as a means of avoiding dementia on the basis of the current evidence. At the same time, the research should not be abandoned. Even a modest delay in the onset of symptoms, spread across a whole population, would spare millions of people years of illness.

topic: the foreign-language effect: how using a second language changes moral judgements and susceptibility to decision biases
title: Thinking at a Distance
subtitle: People appear to make different choices when they reason in a language that is not their own. Psychologists disagree about why

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Would you make the same decision in a language you learned at school as in the language you grew up speaking? Most people would answer yes without hesitation, yet a substantial body of experimental work now suggests otherwise. Over the past fifteen years, researchers have reported that people who consider a problem in a foreign language are less prone to certain well-known biases in judgement and more willing to accept harmful actions that produce a greater overall good. The phenomenon has become known as the foreign-language effect, and it raises uncomfortable questions for a world in which millions of people routinely make important decisions in a second language, from business negotiators and diplomats to doctors and their patients.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the earliest demonstrations used a classic framing problem. Participants are told that a disease threatens six hundred people and are asked to choose between a programme that will certainly save two hundred and a gamble that might save everyone or no one. When the options are described in terms of lives saved, most people prefer the certain option; when exactly the same options are described in terms of lives lost, most prefer the gamble. A team led by Pieter Oosthuizen at the Centre for Decision Science in Stellenbosch found that this inconsistency was greatly reduced when participants read the problem in a foreign language. Oosthuizen argued that because a foreign language is processed more slowly and with greater effort, it pushes people away from rapid intuition and towards careful analysis.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That explanation has been challenged by the psychologist Dewi Tjandra, who contends that the effect arises not from extra deliberation but from reduced emotion. She points out that participants working in a foreign language perform no better on standard reasoning puzzles designed to catch out hasty thinkers, which is hard to reconcile with the idea that they are thinking more carefully. On the other hand, physiological measures show that emotionally charged words, from terms of endearment to insults, provoke weaker bodily reactions when encountered in a second language. On Tjandra's account, when people are asked whether they would push one person off a bridge to save five others, more of them agree in a foreign language simply because the idea feels less repugnant. Her interpretation fits the available evidence considerably better than its rival.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Work by Irina Bryzgalova has refined this picture further. Using a statistical technique that separates the different considerations underlying moral choices, she showed that a foreign language weakens people's attachment to rules against causing harm without increasing their concern for the consequences of their actions. This finding matters because the effect is often described as making people more 'utilitarian', a term which implies a rational weighing of costs and benefits. The label is misleading. People in Bryzgalova's experiments were not calculating more; they were simply less restrained by moral norms, which is hardly a reassuring conclusion.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The size of the effect also depends on the speaker's history with the language. It is most pronounced among people who acquired the language in formal settings such as school classrooms and who rarely use it outside them. It becomes weaker as fluency increases and may disappear entirely in those who have spent many years abroad. The most plausible explanation is that a language gradually builds up emotional associations through lived experience: arguments, jokes, friendships and romance conducted in that language give its words the same power to move people as those of the mother tongue.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: As with many striking findings in psychology, the question of whether the effect is genuine has been put to a demanding test. Jon Arbeloa coordinated a project in which eighteen laboratories in different countries ran identical versions of the key experiments. The reduction in the framing effect was replicated, but it was considerably smaller than the original reports had suggested. The shift in responses to moral dilemmas proved more robust, though it too was modest. The effect is therefore real but less dramatic than early enthusiasm implied, and some of the more sweeping claims made in popular accounts can now be set aside. Arbeloa himself has cautioned that even this verdict applies mainly to university students in wealthy countries, who made up most of the participants, and that very little is known about how the effect operates among older adults or among people who use several languages every day.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some commentators have gone so far as to suggest that people should deliberately reason in a foreign language in order to make better decisions. This advice seems to me mistaken. If the effect works by dampening emotion rather than by sharpening reasoning, there is no guarantee that the resulting decisions will be wiser, since emotions often carry valuable information about what matters to us. The more pressing implications concern those who have no choice in the matter: patients giving consent to medical treatment in a second language, migrants negotiating contracts, and witnesses giving evidence through a language in which they are not at ease. For them, the foreign-language effect is not a curiosity of the laboratory but a factor that may quietly shape the course of their lives.

topic: whether bilinguals change personality when they switch languages: self-reports, translated questionnaires, therapy and age of acquisition
title: One Speaker, Several Selves?
subtitle: Many bilinguals say they become someone else when they change language. Researchers are divided over what, if anything, is really changing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask a group of bilinguals whether they feel like the same person in each of their languages and a surprising number will say no. One describes herself as blunt and decisive in German but gentle and hesitant in Portuguese; another claims to be funnier in English than in his native Tagalog. Such accounts are so common in the memoirs of writers who have changed languages that they have become almost a literary convention. When Ottilie Wrenshall surveyed more than a thousand bilingual adults, nearly two-thirds reported that they felt different when using their second language, and many said that friends had remarked on the change. The question that has divided researchers is not whether these reports are sincere, for there is no reason to doubt that they are, but what exactly they reveal.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Wrenshall herself is cautious about taking them at face value. A person's sense of self, she argues, is built up from the settings in which they habitually find themselves, and for most bilinguals each language is tied to a particular set of settings: one may be the language of childhood, family meals and religious festivals, the other the language of university, office meetings and official forms. When people feel more formal or more confident in one language, they may be responding to the situations with which that language is associated rather than to anything in the language itself. On this view, it is the context, not the grammar or vocabulary, that makes someone feel like a different person.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others believe that language plays a more active role. Nadim Abboud asked bilinguals to complete standard personality questionnaires twice, once in each of their languages, several weeks apart. Their scores shifted in consistent ways: Arabic-French bilinguals, for example, rated themselves as more sociable in one version and more reserved in the other, and the direction of the shift tended to match the way each culture is popularly imagined. Abboud interprets this as evidence of what he calls cultural switching. Because a language is learned together with the values and expectations of the people who speak it, using that language brings those expectations to mind, and people adjust their self-descriptions accordingly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Eszter Hegyesi, a specialist in psychological measurement, is unconvinced. She points out that personality questionnaires can never be translated perfectly: a word such as 'outgoing' may carry approving overtones in one language and faintly critical ones in another, so that a respondent who is in fact entirely consistent will appear to give different answers. When Hegyesi replaced questionnaires with direct observation, coding the behaviour of bilinguals in video-recorded conversations conducted in each language, the differences were far smaller than self-reports had suggested. Her point about translation is an important one, and it casts doubt on much of the questionnaire research. Her alternative, however, is not free of problems either. A conversation with a stranger in a laboratory, with a camera running, is a highly artificial situation, and it may not capture the way people behave at a family gathering or in a heated argument.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some of the most intriguing evidence comes from outside the laboratory. Hery Andrianasolo, a psychotherapist who works with refugees, has analysed recordings of therapy sessions conducted with clients who speak several languages. He found that clients frequently moved into their second language when describing traumatic events, apparently because the words felt less raw, and moved back into their first language when expressing affection for family members. Rather than treating this as an obstacle, Andrianasolo encourages therapists to make deliberate use of it, allowing clients to approach painful memories first in a language that offers some protection. This seems to me one of the most valuable practical applications of the whole field, and it has received far less attention than it deserves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The age at which a language is learned also appears to matter. Aino Paikkala compared people who had grown up with two languages from infancy with people who had learned their second language during adolescence or adulthood. Those in the first group reported markedly fewer differences between their 'selves' in each language. Paikkala's explanation is that a language learned later in life becomes attached to the identity a person was developing at that time, for instance a young migrant's struggle to fit into a new country. The sense of being another person in another language may thus be, in part, a record of an individual's history.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the question of whether language changes personality is badly posed. Personality is not a fixed essence that a language could either preserve or distort; everyone behaves differently with grandparents than with colleagues, and nobody regards this as a mystery. Bilinguals simply possess an additional and highly audible marker of such shifts, which makes them easier to notice. This does not make the phenomenon less interesting, but it should discourage some of the more romantic interpretations it has inspired. In particular, it would be a mistake to conclude that certain languages are inherently more emotional, more logical or more polite than others; the differences bilinguals feel belong to their experiences of a language, not to the language itself.

topic: mother-tongue-based multilingual education: early versus late transition, implementation problems and parental attitudes
title: Learning in the Language of Home
subtitle: Should children start school in the language they speak with their families? The evidence is encouraging, but turning it into policy has proved difficult

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On their first day at school, millions of children around the world are greeted by a teacher speaking a language they barely understand. In many countries, particularly those that were once colonies, the language of instruction is a national or international language that most pupils never hear at home. International estimates suggest that a large proportion of the world's children are taught in a language other than the one they speak best, and the consequences are visible in classrooms where pupils copy sentences from the board without grasping their meaning. Over the past three decades, an alternative known as mother-tongue-based multilingual education has gained ground. Under this approach, children learn to read and write first in their home language, while other languages are introduced gradually, initially as subjects and only later as a means of teaching other subjects.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the strongest evidence in its favour comes from a large pilot programme evaluated by the education researcher Ifeoma Uzodinma. In rural districts where a dozen local languages were spoken, pupils who were taught to read in their home language were twice as likely as those in comparison schools to read with understanding by the end of their second year. More strikingly, by their fifth year they had also overtaken the comparison group in the official language, despite having spent less classroom time on it. Uzodinma attributes this to the transfer of skills between languages: a child who has learned to decode written words and extract meaning from them in a familiar language does not need to learn these skills again. As she puts it, one only learns to read once.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all such programmes have produced results of this kind, and Hamid Rostampour believes he knows why. Many schemes move children into the official language after just two or three years, an arrangement known as early exit. In Rostampour's view, this is too soon. By that point children may have learned to read, but they have not yet learned to use reading as a tool for acquiring new knowledge, and their command of the second language is not yet sufficient to take over that role. Comparing programmes in several countries, he found that those which continued teaching in the home language for around six years produced the best outcomes, whereas early-exit programmes were often followed by a marked dip in achievement at the point of transition. The case for later transition is persuasive, but it is also politically awkward, since it requires governments to sustain teaching in local languages well into the upper years of primary school.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Practical obstacles are considerable. Ingeborg Vestli, who has studied the implementation of these programmes in a number of countries, notes that many local languages have no agreed spelling system and few printed materials, and that teachers are often posted to regions where they do not speak the local language at all. In rapidly growing cities, a single classroom may contain children from five or six language backgrounds, making instruction in one local language difficult to organise. According to Vestli, when programmes have disappointed, the cause has usually been poor execution rather than a flaw in the principle: textbooks arriving months late, teachers receiving a few days of training, and inspectors who continue to test pupils only in the official language. This is a crucial distinction. A badly run programme tells us about the quality of its management, not about the merits of the approach.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most powerful source of resistance is parents themselves. In his research in eastern Indonesia, Bambang Sulistyo found that many parents opposed teaching in local languages, fearing that it would hold their children back in a labour market where the national language, and increasingly English, opened doors to better-paid work. Yet Sulistyo also found that opposition fell sharply when parents were shown results from nearby schools in which children taught first in their home language went on to perform better in the national language. Parents' worries should not be dismissed as ignorance. Given the realities of the job market, they are entirely rational, and programmes that fail to address them are unlikely to survive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Cost is a further concern. Producing textbooks, readers and teacher guides in many languages requires substantial investment, and governments with limited budgets understandably hesitate. Advocates respond that these costs are offset by savings elsewhere: when children understand their lessons, fewer of them repeat school years or leave school early, and each repeated year represents an additional expense for the education system. Some economic analyses suggest that the savings exceed the initial costs within a decade. Such claims are plausible, but they rest heavily on modelling assumptions about future enrolment and repetition rates, and should be treated with appropriate caution.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The strongest argument for home-language education is not economic at all. It is simply that children cannot learn what they cannot understand. That said, mother-tongue-based education is not a universal remedy. In linguistically mixed urban schools, approaches sometimes described as translanguaging, in which teachers permit and encourage pupils to draw on every language they know, may prove more workable than choosing a single local language. What the research suggests above all is that language policy in education needs to be flexible, responsive to local circumstances, and judged by whether children are actually learning.

topic: simultaneous interpreting as extreme bilingual control: brain changes in trainees, specialised versus general skills, selection effects and anticipation strategies
title: Speaking While Listening
subtitle: Simultaneous interpreters perform one of the most demanding feats of language processing known. What it does to their minds is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Simultaneous interpreting is a surprisingly recent profession. Before the middle of the twentieth century, international meetings relied on consecutive interpreting, in which a speaker would pause every few minutes so that an interpreter could render what had been said. The arrival of headphones and microphone systems made it possible for interpreters to work while the speaker continued, sitting in soundproof booths and speaking into a microphone as they listened. The interval between hearing a phrase and producing its equivalent, known as the ear-voice span, is typically only two to three seconds. Because the task is so exhausting, interpreters at international organisations usually work in pairs, handing over to a colleague roughly every thirty minutes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Interpreting is often described as the most demanding linguistic task that human beings undertake, and that reputation is deserved. The interpreter must comprehend one language, hold its meaning in memory, reformulate it in another language and monitor their own output, all at the same moment and without the opportunity to go back. It is therefore natural that researchers interested in how bilinguals control their languages have turned to interpreters as an extreme case. Anouk Verstraelen and her colleagues scanned the brains of students at the beginning and end of a two-year master's course in conference interpreting, and compared them with students of written translation who had followed a course of similar length. The interpreting students showed changes in brain regions associated with auditory processing and with selecting between competing responses, changes that were absent in the translation group. Verstraelen concludes that intensive interpreting practice physically reshapes the networks that manage language.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sergei Lozhkin accepts that interpreting training alters the brain but warns against assuming that it produces general mental superiority. When he tested professional interpreters on non-verbal tasks, he found that they outperformed comparable bilinguals on tasks requiring them to hold information in mind and constantly update it. On tasks requiring them to suppress irrelevant information, however, they showed no advantage at all, and on some measures they performed slightly worse. Lozhkin explains this by pointing out that interpreters, unlike ordinary bilinguals, cannot afford to switch off either language, since they need both to be active at once. In his words, interpreters are specialists, not all-round champions of mental control.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lozhkin's findings deserve wider attention than they have received, because they complicate the debate over whether bilingualism improves general cognitive abilities. If even the most intensively trained bilinguals show benefits only on tasks that closely resemble what they practise, the case for broad advantages among ordinary bilinguals becomes harder to sustain. Brain changes, in other words, do not by themselves justify conclusions about general abilities; they show only that the brain has adapted to a particular set of demands.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is raised by Paora Hetaraka, who has studied admissions to interpreting schools. Entry to the most prestigious courses is fiercely competitive, and aptitude tests typically eliminate the large majority of applicants. Those who are admitted, Hetaraka argues, already possess exceptional abilities, so differences between professional interpreters and other people may reflect who is selected rather than what training does. Longitudinal studies such as Verstraelen's, which follow the same individuals over time, are the obvious answer to this objection, and her design is the best currently available. Even so, it cannot entirely dispose of the problem, since people who choose to train as interpreters may differ from translation students in motivation or temperament in ways that influence how their brains respond to training.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have been less concerned with what interpreting does to the brain than with how interpreters manage the task at all. Thandeka Khanyile analysed recordings of expert and novice interpreters working between German and English. Because German frequently places the main verb at the end of a sentence, interpreters into English face the problem of beginning a sentence before they know what action it describes. Experts, Khanyile found, rely heavily on anticipation, predicting the likely verb from context, or else split long sentences into shorter units that can be rendered safely. Novices, by contrast, tend to try to keep pace with the speaker word by word and quickly become overloaded. Khanyile concludes that training should concentrate on teaching such strategies rather than on attempting to expand students' raw mental capacity.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The working conditions of interpreters are also changing. Malin Lindhagen, who has measured interpreters' physiological stress during assignments, reports heart rates comparable to those recorded in other high-pressure occupations. Since many meetings moved online, a growing share of interpreting is done remotely, and Lindhagen argues that poor sound quality and the absence of visual cues from speakers have made the work considerably more tiring; she has called for shorter shifts for remote interpreters. At the same time, automatic speech translation systems are improving rapidly, and some commentators predict that human interpreters will soon be obsolete. Such predictions seem premature. Interpreting involves far more than converting words: it requires an understanding of tone, context and what a speaker means but does not say, and in diplomacy or courtrooms errors of that kind can carry serious consequences.

topic: linguistic relativity in bilinguals: whether bilinguals' perception of motion, colour and time shifts with the language they are using
title: Between Two Worldviews?
subtitle: If the language we speak shapes the way we think, what happens in the minds of people who speak two?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The idea that language shapes thought has had a turbulent history. In the middle of the twentieth century it was widely popularised, often in extravagant forms which suggested that speakers of different languages inhabited entirely different mental worlds. By the 1970s it had fallen out of favour, as research on colour naming appeared to show that human perception rests on universal foundations regardless of vocabulary. Since the 1990s, however, the idea has been revived in a more modest guise: few researchers now claim that language determines what we are able to think, but many believe it can influence what we notice, remember and attend to. Bilinguals offer an unusually revealing test of this claim. If language really does shape thought, does a bilingual person's thinking shift with the language in use, settle somewhere between the two, or remain unaffected?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most studied areas concerns the description of movement. English typically packs the manner of movement into the verb itself, as in 'stroll', 'dash' or 'crawl', and adds the direction with a separate word such as 'into' or 'across'. Spanish more often uses the verb to express the path, as in verbs meaning 'enter' or 'cross', and mentions the manner only when it is important. Osvaldo Peñaranda showed short video clips to speakers of both languages and asked them which clips seemed most alike. Monolingual speakers of each language tended to focus on the feature that their language placed in the verb. Spanish-English bilinguals, however, behaved differently depending on which language the instructions were given in, and bilinguals who were equally proficient in both languages produced judgements that fell midway between the two monolingual groups. Peñaranda concludes that the language a person is currently using guides their attention in real time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Colour has provided some of the most striking evidence. Greek, unlike English, has two basic words for blue, one for lighter and one for darker shades. Riikka Halttunen recorded the brain responses of Greek speakers living in Britain while they looked at different shades. Those who had lived in the country only briefly showed a sharp distinction between light and dark blue, but the distinction became progressively weaker the longer participants had lived there, as if their perception were gradually adjusting to the English pattern. Halttunen interprets this as evidence that prolonged immersion in a second language can recalibrate perceptual categories. The finding is impressive, but it should not be overstated. The differences were measured in milliseconds of neural activity, and nothing in the study suggests that Greek speakers actually see the colours of the world differently as they go about their daily lives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more sceptical voice is that of Avital Benyamini, who has investigated when such effects appear and when they do not. In her experiments, participants performed colour and motion tasks while simultaneously repeating a string of numbers aloud, a procedure that prevents people from silently naming what they see. Under these conditions, the differences between language groups largely disappeared. Benyamini concludes that language does not permanently restructure perception; rather, people draw on words as an aid when a task allows them to do so. In my view, this is the most important finding the field has produced, because it changes the question being asked. Language appears to function less as a lens through which everything is seen than as a tool that is picked up when it is useful.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Research on time points in a similar direction. Languages differ in the spatial metaphors they use for time: English speakers usually talk of the future as lying ahead and the past behind, while Mandarin also uses vertical terms, describing earlier events as 'up' and later ones as 'down'. Yelena Duvanova found that Mandarin-English bilinguals were more inclined than English monolinguals to arrange pictures of events in vertical sequences. Yet she also showed that English speakers who were given a brief training session in using vertical expressions began to display a similar tendency. Duvanova argues that such effects reflect habits of thought rather than deep and fixed differences, and that habits of this kind can be acquired in a short time.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the bilingual mind is neither locked into a single worldview nor wholly switching between two. Its patterns of attention are blended, flexible and sensitive to context. This picture sits uneasily with two popular positions. It does not support the familiar claim, beloved of language-learning advertisements, that acquiring a new language gives a person a completely new way of seeing the world; that is an exaggeration. But neither does it support those who dismiss any influence of language on thought as a myth, since the effects, though small and conditional, have been replicated many times.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some educators have begun to ask whether language teaching should explicitly train learners in the habits of attention associated with a new language, for instance by encouraging learners of Spanish to notice the paths of moving objects. The idea is intriguing but premature. A more pressing limitation is that the great majority of studies have examined a small number of European and East Asian languages. Until the research encompasses a far wider range of the world's languages, conclusions about how language and thought interact in bilingual minds should be held with some humility.

topic: age of acquisition and ultimate attainment in a second language: the critical period debate, exceptional late learners and the native-speaker benchmark
title: The Late Learner's Ceiling
subtitle: Is there an age after which a new language can never be fully mastered? The answer depends partly on what counts as mastery

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few beliefs about language are as widely held as the conviction that children absorb new languages effortlessly while adults are condemned to struggle. The scientific version of this belief, usually called the critical period hypothesis, holds that the capacity to acquire a language to native level is governed by a biological window which closes at around puberty. Yet the everyday evidence is more complicated than the slogan suggests. In classrooms, teenagers and adults frequently make faster progress in the early stages than young children, who take longer to master grammar and vocabulary. Researchers have therefore learned to distinguish between the rate of learning, at which older learners often excel, and ultimate attainment, the level a learner finally reaches after many years. It is in the second of these that the advantage of an early start is thought to lie.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: If a biological window really closes at puberty, one would expect a sharp drop in ultimate attainment among those who began learning after that point. Marek Zaleski tested this prediction using grammar test scores from more than thirty thousand immigrants, all of whom had lived in their new country for at least ten years. Attainment did decline with age of arrival, but the decline was steady and continued well into adulthood, with no abrupt break at adolescence or at any other age. In Zaleski's view, this pattern is difficult to reconcile with a discrete window and is better explained by gradual changes in learners' circumstances and in general cognitive abilities across the lifespan.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ama Boatemaa is not persuaded that a gradual decline rules out biological constraints. Many maturational processes, she notes, unfold gradually rather than switching off at a fixed moment; the ability to hear high-pitched sounds, for example, diminishes steadily over decades. She also points out that different components of language behave differently. Pronunciation appears to be the most sensitive to age, and those who arrive in a new country after early childhood almost always retain some detectable accent, whereas vocabulary can continue to grow throughout life. Boatemaa therefore proposes that there is not one critical period but several, each closing at a different age for different aspects of language.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Particularly revealing are studies of so-called exceptional learners: people who began learning a language as adults yet are taken for native speakers by those who meet them. Jean-Pierre Mpoyi recruited a group of such individuals who had been judged native by listeners in brief recordings. When he subjected them to more demanding tests, including judgements of subtle grammatical distinctions and the comprehension of speech against background noise, almost none performed entirely within the range of native speakers. Mpoyi concludes that complete native-likeness after childhood is extremely rare, if it exists at all. He is careful to add, however, that in ordinary conversation his participants were indistinguishable from native speakers. That qualification matters more than is often recognised. Differences that can be detected only with specialised laboratory tests may say something about the architecture of the mind, but they are of little consequence for how a person lives, works or is understood.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Leila Sabzevari has questioned the benchmark against which late learners are judged. Research in this area almost always compares learners with monolingual native speakers, yet even people who have grown up with two languages from birth do not perform exactly like monolinguals in either language, because each language subtly influences the other. Some of the gap between late learners and natives may therefore reflect the fact of being bilingual rather than the age at which learning began. When Sabzevari compared late learners with early bilinguals instead of monolinguals, the difference between the groups was considerably smaller. Her argument is a persuasive one. The monolingual speaker is a curious yardstick for measuring minds that, by definition, contain more than one language.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of experience. Children who arrive in a new country are typically placed in local schools, where they spend most of the day surrounded by the new language and make friends who speak it. Adults, by contrast, often work alongside speakers of their first language and use it at home. Sanna Pitkänen followed immigrant families for six years, recording how much each family member heard and used the new language. When the quantity of input was taken into account, the effect of age on most measures shrank considerably, although it remained substantial for pronunciation. Age, it seems, does matter, but much of what has been attributed to it may in fact reflect the very different lives that young and older newcomers lead.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings have implications beyond the laboratory. Many education systems have introduced foreign languages in the early years of primary school, often citing the critical period as justification. But a few hours of classroom teaching each week bears little resemblance to the immersion experienced by young immigrants, and studies comparing pupils who began a foreign language at eight with those who began at eleven have found that the later starters generally catch up within a few years. There may be good reasons to teach languages to young children, but the critical period is not one of them. Equally, adults should not be discouraged from learning a language by the belief that it is too late: for almost every practical purpose, it is not.
