topic: word retrieval in the bilingual mental lexicon: co-activation of both languages, slower naming, tip-of-the-tongue states and the measurement of bilingual children's vocabulary
title: The Crowded Mental Dictionary
subtitle: Bilinguals carry two vocabularies in one head. The small costs this brings reveal a great deal about how words are stored and found

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a typical experiment, Dutch-English bilinguals sit in front of a screen and decide, as quickly as possible, whether each string of letters that appears is a real English word. The task is conducted entirely in English, and participants are not told that their Dutch is of any relevance. Yet their responses betray it. Words such as 'room', which also exists in Dutch with a quite different meaning (cream), are recognised more slowly than comparable English words, while words that look alike and share a meaning in both languages, such as 'hotel', are recognised more quickly. The conclusion drawn from many studies of this kind is that a bilingual's languages are not stored in separate compartments that can be switched on and off. Both are active whenever words are being processed, even when only one language is relevant to the task.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: This constant co-activation appears to carry certain costs. Compared with monolinguals, bilinguals tend to be slightly slower at naming pictures, report more frequent experiences of having a word on the tip of the tongue without being able to produce it, and score lower on vocabulary tests in each of their languages taken separately. Weronika Krzemińska attributes these effects mainly to frequency of use. Because bilinguals divide their speaking time between two languages, they use each individual word less often than a monolingual does, and the mental connections that link a word's meaning to its sound are correspondingly weaker. In support of this view, she observes that the retrieval disadvantage is greatest for words that are seldom used and that it shrinks as bilinguals' exposure to a language increases.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Eero Ollikainen favours a different explanation, based on competition. When a bilingual attempts to name an object, he argues, the word for it in the other language is activated as well and must be suppressed before the intended word can be produced, rather as two people trying to pass through a doorway at the same time slow each other down. His evidence comes from experiments showing that naming becomes slower still when participants have just been using their other language, which should increase the strength of the competitor. The two accounts are usually presented as rivals, but this seems to me a false choice. The evidence for each is substantial, and it is entirely possible that weaker connections and competition both contribute to the delays that bilinguals experience.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of vocabulary size has practical consequences, particularly for children. Hallgerd Gudmundsen, who studies early language development in immigrant communities, points out that bilingual children's knowledge of words is often distributed across their languages according to where they encounter them. A child may know the words for kitchen utensils and family celebrations only in the home language, and the words for classroom activities and school subjects only in the language of school. Tested in either language alone, such a child appears to have a small vocabulary. When Gudmundsen counted the concepts that children could name in at least one language, however, bilingual children matched and sometimes exceeded their monolingual peers. This finding deserves to be widely known. Judging a bilingual child to be delayed in language on the basis of a test in only one language is a serious error, and it has led some children to be referred for therapy they did not need.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Further evidence on the source of retrieval difficulties has come from research on older adults, whose tip-of-the-tongue experiences become more frequent with age. Rupert Ainsworth compared older bilinguals and monolinguals and found that, although the bilinguals experienced more retrieval failures overall, they did not differ from monolinguals in their difficulty recalling people's names. Since proper names are usually identical in both languages, a bilingual uses them as often as a monolingual does, and Ainsworth presents the result as strong confirmation of Krzemińska's frequency account. The argument is an elegant one, but it is less conclusive than he suggests. Proper names also lack translation equivalents, so they face no competition from the other language, and the result is therefore just as consistent with Ollikainen's position.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is important to keep these costs in perspective. The delays observed in naming experiments amount to a few tens of milliseconds, far too little to be noticed in most conversations. Bilinguals also possess strategies that monolinguals lack. When speaking with other bilinguals, they frequently switch between languages within a single conversation, drawing on whichever word comes to mind first. Such switching has often been regarded by teachers and parents as evidence that a speaker has not properly mastered either language. That view is mistaken. Research on bilingual communities has shown that switching follows systematic rules and is used most skilfully by the most proficient speakers; it is better understood as an efficient use of the full resources available than as a symptom of deficiency.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is a picture of a single, integrated mental dictionary in which the words of two languages are interconnected and constantly interact. The occasional hesitation, the momentary failure to find a word, are not signs that something has gone wrong; they are the natural consequence of a store that is larger and more densely connected than a monolingual's. Seen in this light, the small costs of bilingual word retrieval are a modest price for the considerable advantages of commanding two languages, and one that most bilinguals would gladly continue to pay.

topic: language nests: immersion preschools staffed by elderly speakers as a tool of language revival
title: Raised in the Nest
subtitle: Immersion preschools have become a favourite tool of language revival, but their long-term effects are more contested than their supporters admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By the time a language has only elderly fluent speakers left, the chain of transmission from parent to child has usually been broken for decades. The language nest, a model first developed in the Pacific in the early 1980s, attempts to repair that chain at its weakest link. Very young children are placed in day-care settings where only the endangered language is spoken, typically by grandparents and other older members of the community. The idea spread quickly, and versions of it now operate on several continents. Its appeal is easy to understand: small children absorb languages with little visible effort, and a preschool requires neither a formal curriculum nor teachers trained to secondary level. Yet the very simplicity that makes the model so attractive has, in my view, encouraged unrealistic hopes about what it can accomplish by itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most detailed evidence comes from Dr Hemi Kawiti of the Southern Institute for Language Renewal, who followed some three hundred children through and beyond their years in immersion preschools. Those who had attended for at least two years understood the language well, and many could hold simple conversations with elders. Once they entered mainstream primary schools, however, the majority stopped using it within eighteen months, a pattern Kawiti describes as the 'cliff edge'. He is careful to insist that this does not mean the nests themselves have failed. The difficulty, he argues, lies in what follows them, and he has called for public funding to be extended so that children can continue their education in the language throughout primary school.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ilona Ferenczy, a developmental psychologist at Carpathian University, reads the evidence differently. In her own study, the decisive factor was not the kind of school a child later attended but whether the child's parents were themselves learning the language. Children whose mothers or fathers took evening classes alongside them retained the language far better than those whose parents did not, whatever school they went on to. Ferenczy therefore describes the nest as 'a family intervention disguised as a childcare service'. Her emphasis on parents is a welcome correction to the assumption that children can carry a language forward unaided. It should be noted, though, that her participants came from communities in which many adults already had some knowledge of the language, and her conclusions may not transfer to places where no parent speaks it at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Nests also depend on a resource that is shrinking every year: the elderly speakers who staff them. The anthropologist Obiageli Amaechina spent two years interviewing older carers in several programmes. Many told her that the work had given them a renewed sense of purpose, sometimes after years in which their language had been treated as a source of shame; almost all, however, also spoke of physical exhaustion. Amaechina found a further, less obvious obstacle. The traditional ways in which elders taught children, through storytelling, songs and frequent, direct correction, regularly collided with the licensing requirements imposed on childcare centres, which demanded formal qualifications that few elders possessed. Of all the problems nests face, this is the least discussed and probably the easiest to remedy, since it calls for nothing more than a change in administrative rules.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The cost of the model has attracted sharper criticism. A typical nest serves between ten and twenty children and needs several adult speakers to run it, which makes the expense per child considerable. The economist Farid Hakimzada has argued that the same money would produce more speakers if it were spent on intensive courses for adults, who could then use the language with their own children. His figures are carefully assembled, but the comparison he draws is, I believe, misleading. Adults who learn a language rarely attain the ease and accuracy of those who acquire it in early childhood, and the two approaches are not really alternatives at all; Ferenczy's research suggests that they work best when combined.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more unexpected debate concerns the kind of language the children end up speaking. The sociolinguist Ragnhild Sølvberg has recorded children who have passed through nests and found that their speech is noticeably simpler than that of their teachers, with grammar and sound patterns influenced by the dominant national language. Some elders find this variety, sometimes called a 'nest dialect', strange or even painful to hear. Sølvberg insists, however, that such features are ordinary signs of language change, the same processes that shape every living language, rather than evidence of corruption. On this point she is surely right. Revival movements that have demanded a pure, unchanging form of the language have tended to discourage the very learners on whom their survival depends.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this suggests that language nests should be abandoned. They remain one of the few methods that produce young speakers at all, and they give elderly speakers a valued role in their communities. But they are best seen as a necessary first step rather than a complete solution. The proper measure of their success is not how many children enrol, the figure most often cited by governments, but how many of those children go on to raise their own families in the language, and that is a question that only another generation can answer.

topic: reclaiming 'sleeping' languages from archival notebooks and wax-cylinder recordings
title: Waking the Sleepers
subtitle: Languages with no living speakers are being brought back from old notebooks and fragile recordings, raising difficult questions about evidence and ownership

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, a language whose last native speaker had died was described without hesitation as extinct. Increasingly, however, the communities whose ancestors spoke such languages reject that label, preferring to call them 'sleeping' or 'dormant'. The choice of word is not merely sentimental. It reflects a growing number of projects in which people with no living teacher have learned to speak, and in a few cases to raise children in, a language known to them only through documents and recordings. The materials in question were mostly assembled between the mid-nineteenth and mid-twentieth centuries by missionaries, colonial officials and early anthropologists, few of whom imagined that their notebooks would one day serve as textbooks.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The quality of these sources varies enormously. Written records were often made by people with no training in phonetics, who spelt unfamiliar sounds according to the conventions of their own languages, so that a single word may appear in a dozen different forms across several manuscripts. Sound recordings, which might be expected to settle such questions, present difficulties of their own. Many of the earliest were made on wax cylinders, each holding only two or three minutes of audio and prone to cracking, mould and wear each time they were played. When Dr Aoife Merrigan of the Western Seaboard Sound Archive began a project to digitise some 1,400 cylinders, she discovered that roughly a third could no longer be played on any mechanical equipment. Using an optical technique that reconstructs the groove from high-resolution images instead of tracing it with a stylus, her team recovered usable sound from about half of these damaged items.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even the best-preserved material leaves gaps. No archive records every word a language contains, and grammatical patterns are often only partially documented. To fill these gaps, the linguist Rimas Pakalnis has adapted the comparative method of historical linguistics, inferring missing forms from closely related languages that are still spoken, or that were better recorded. Pakalnis is unusually frank about the limits of the approach. A reconstructed word, he argues, is a hypothesis, and teaching materials should mark it as such so that learners know which forms are attested and which are inferred. Some community educators have objected that such labelling makes learners hesitant to use the language at all. Their concern is understandable, but I find Pakalnis's position the more defensible: a revival built on concealed guesses is vulnerable to precisely the charge of inauthenticity that its opponents are keen to make.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Who should control the archives is a still more sensitive matter. Many collections are held by universities and museums far from the communities concerned, and descendants have in the past had to pay copying fees or travel long distances simply to hear their great-grandparents' voices. The legal scholar Nimali Abeyratne has documented cases in which institutions restricted community access to recordings while making them freely available to visiting academics. Some collections also contain ceremonial songs that were never intended to be heard by outsiders, and which were recorded under conditions that would not now be regarded as genuine consent. Abeyratne argues that descendant communities should have the final say over access, including the right to withdraw material from public view. I share her view, though it is worth acknowledging the cost: a recording closed to the public is also closed to neighbouring communities whose own reclamation efforts might depend on it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What, then, do reclamation projects actually achieve? The numbers involved are modest. The sociologist Marisol Tolentino surveyed participants in twelve programmes across three continents and found that fewer than one in ten described themselves as able to hold an extended conversation in the language. Yet when asked what they valued about their involvement, most placed fluency well below other benefits, such as a stronger sense of identity and the ability to understand place names and family histories. Tolentino concludes that judging such projects by the number of fluent speakers they produce misunderstands their purpose.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more hostile line of criticism holds that what is produced is not the original language at all but a new creation, shaped by the dominant language that every learner already speaks. Such critics point out that pronunciation reconstructed from imperfect spellings is unlikely to match that of the last native speakers. This is probably true, but it proves less than they suppose. Every language revived after a break in transmission has changed in the process, and many languages that were never interrupted have changed just as much over a comparable period. Whether a reclaimed language is 'authentic' is, in the end, a question for the people who speak it rather than for outside observers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a certain irony in all this. Much of the material on which reclamation now depends was collected in the belief that the peoples concerned were destined to disappear, and that the purpose of recording their languages was to preserve a memory of them for science. The notebooks and cylinders that were meant to serve as a memorial have instead become, in the hands of those peoples' descendants, the raw material of a living future.

topic: measuring language endangerment: speaker counts, transmission scales, risk models and the politics of labels
title: Measuring Silence
subtitle: How do linguists decide which languages are in danger, and how far should their figures be trusted?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few statistics about language have travelled as widely as the claim that half of the world's seven thousand or so languages will cease to be spoken by the end of this century. It appears in newspaper articles, museum displays and funding applications, and it has probably done more than any other single figure to persuade the public that linguistic diversity is under threat. Yet the foundations of the prediction are considerably weaker than its popularity would suggest. To understand why, it is necessary to look at the surprisingly difficult business of deciding what a language is, how many people speak it, and what it means for one to be endangered.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first problem is one of definition. Linguists have long recognised that there is no purely linguistic way of separating a language from a dialect; the distinction is often settled by history, politics or national pride. Dr Zsófia Szakolczai, a dialectologist who has spent much of her career in mountainous border regions, has shown how much depends on the criterion chosen. In one valley system she studied, the number of distinct languages could be put at anywhere between four and eleven, depending on whether researchers relied on tests of mutual understanding or on the names that speakers themselves used for the way they talked. Since global totals are simply the sum of thousands of such local decisions, the denominator in the 'half of all languages' calculation is itself uncertain.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Counting speakers is scarcely easier. Most national figures come from censuses, which typically ask respondents whether they speak a particular language and accept whatever answer is given. Some people claim a heritage language out of pride although they know only a few phrases; others, particularly where a language has been stigmatised, deny speaking one they use every day. More importantly, a raw total says little about a language's prospects. A language with fifty thousand speakers, none of them younger than forty, is in far greater danger than one with five hundred speakers who are all still bringing up their children in it. Numbers, in other words, tell us how large a language community is, not whether it is renewing itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For this reason, most assessments now rely on graded scales that classify languages from 'safe' to 'extinct' according mainly to whether children are still acquiring them at home. Dr Chileshe Mwanakatwe, who helped to design one widely used regional scale, maintains that intergenerational transmission is the single most reliable indicator of a language's future, outweighing official status, the existence of written materials or even the size of the community. The logic is hard to dispute. The practical difficulty is that applying such a scale requires detailed fieldwork, and for a great many languages that work has never been done. Assessments in global databases are frequently based on reports that are decades old, so a language recorded as healthy in the 1970s may still be listed as such long after its children have stopped speaking it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different approach has been taken by the statistician Eero Kalliokoski, who has built models that estimate a language's risk from information available for almost every country: population, geography, the length of compulsory schooling, and the density of roads. One of his more striking findings was that the spread of roads and the number of years children are required to spend in school predicted language loss more accurately than the number of speakers did, presumably because both bring small communities into regular contact with a dominant language. The work is ingenious, but its limitations should be acknowledged. A model built on the losses of the past cannot easily anticipate the effects of revival movements, or of digital media that allow scattered speakers to stay in touch, and both of these may make future patterns quite different from earlier ones.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most fundamental objection comes from the anthropologist Lucia Corradetti, who questions the value of the whole exercise. Describing a language as 'moribund', she argues, can become a self-fulfilling prophecy: funding bodies may conclude that support would be wasted, while speakers, told by experts that their language is dying, lose the morale needed to keep using it. Several communities have formally objected to the categories assigned to their languages in international lists. Corradetti is right that such labels have consequences, and they should certainly not be applied casually. But I cannot accept that the answer is to stop measuring altogether, since that would leave governments and funders with no basis for deciding where limited resources should go. The better course is to make communities partners in the assessment of their own languages, so that the categories reflect local knowledge rather than outdated reports.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these difficulties means that the loss of languages is imaginary. Whatever the precise figures, there is no doubt that many communities around the world are ceasing to pass their languages on to their children, and that the pace of this change has increased over the past century. The famous prediction is best read as a warning about direction rather than as a forecast of a precise number. Treated as the latter, it invites the kind of scepticism that can be used to justify doing nothing; treated as the former, it remains an entirely reasonable call to act.

topic: digital technology and endangered languages: keyboards, social media, speech technology, data ownership and learning apps
title: Typing to Survive
subtitle: Can keyboards, apps and speech software keep small languages alive, or do they merely give an appearance of health?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a small island in the western Pacific, a fifteen-year-old girl sends her cousin a text message in the language of their grandparents. Until recently this would have been almost impossible: the phones sold locally offered no way of typing several of the language's characters, and young people simply wrote to one another in the national language instead. A keyboard application built by volunteers has changed that. Scenes like this are frequently held up as evidence that technology, so often blamed for the spread of a few global languages, might also be the means of rescuing small ones. The optimism is understandable, and there are genuine successes to report. It nonetheless deserves closer examination than it usually receives, because the relationship between digital tools and the survival of a language is far less direct than enthusiasts tend to assume.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for investment rests partly on the idea of 'digital language death'. The computational linguist Pieter Ottervanger has estimated that fewer than one in twenty of the world's languages has any meaningful presence online, in the sense of being usable for searching, messaging or reading the news. A language that cannot be used on the devices through which young people now conduct most of their social lives, he argues, will come to seem to them a relic, suitable for ceremonies and conversations with grandparents but irrelevant to the rest of their existence. Ottervanger therefore proposes that every language with a written form should be equipped with at least a basic set of tools, beginning with keyboards and spelling checkers, which are cheap to produce compared with the cost of other forms of language support.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Presence online, however, is not the same as use. The sociolinguist Sanduni Bulathsinhala analysed several thousand social media posts written by members of three minority-language communities and found that the heritage language appeared mainly in greetings, jokes, blessings and expressions of emotion, while anything requiring sustained argument or information was written in the dominant language. She describes this pattern as 'decorative use' and warns that counting the number of posts containing a language can give a seriously inflated impression of its vitality. Her analysis is a valuable corrective to the more breathless claims made for social media. Even so, I would hesitate to dismiss symbolic use entirely. Adult learners almost always begin with greetings and set phrases, and for a young person who has never spoken the language at home, a joke shared online may be the first step towards something more substantial.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More ambitious technologies, such as machine translation and speech recognition, have traditionally required vast quantities of text and recorded speech, which endangered languages by definition lack. The engineer Timur Imanaliev, who leads a project developing speech recognition for languages with only a few thousand speakers, believes this obstacle is disappearing. New techniques allow systems trained on major languages to transfer much of what they have learned, so that, in his account, a working recogniser can now be built from as little as a few hours of transcribed recordings. This has prompted concern about who controls the resulting data. Losana Manuatu, who researches data governance in Indigenous communities, has documented a case in which recordings donated by elders to a revival project were later incorporated, without the community's knowledge, into a commercial product. She insists that communities should retain legal ownership of any dataset built from their speech and should set the terms on which it may be used.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most popular technology of all is the language-learning app. The education researcher Bence Kerekes compared adults who studied an endangered language using an app alone with those who combined the same app with regular face-to-face practice. After a year, both groups had learned a similar number of words, but the app-only learners rarely attempted to speak, and most described themselves as unable to follow a conversation. Kerekes concludes that such tools function well as a supplement to human contact but poorly as a substitute for it. This seems to me entirely persuasive, yet it points to an awkward paradox. Apps are promoted most enthusiastically for precisely those languages whose speakers are fewest and most scattered, which is to say in the situations where face-to-face practice is hardest to arrange.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is that technology tends to amplify whatever social conditions already exist. Where families and communities are determined to use a language, digital tools can make that use easier and extend it into new areas of life. Where that determination is absent, no keyboard or app is likely to create it. There is also a less obvious danger. Because software is cheap compared with salaries, governments under financial pressure may be tempted to fund an app and declare the problem addressed, while the more expensive work of training teachers and supporting immersion schools goes unfunded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is an argument against building digital tools. They are relatively inexpensive, they signal that a language belongs in the modern world, and in some places they have made a real difference. But it is worth returning to the girl on the island. What makes her message significant is not, in the end, the keyboard that allowed her to type it. It is the fact that she has a cousin who can read it and reply, and that the two of them, for the moment at least, still choose to use their grandparents' language with each other.

topic: master-apprentice programmes: one-to-one immersion pairing elderly speakers with adult learners
title: One Teacher, One Learner
subtitle: Where only a handful of elderly speakers remain, revival may depend on pairing each of them with a single dedicated student

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a language is spoken fluently by only a dozen people, all of them over seventy, the ordinary tools of language teaching are of little use. There are too few speakers to staff classrooms, often no textbooks, and no time to train a new generation of teachers before the last native speakers are gone. The master-apprentice model was devised for exactly this situation. An elderly speaker and a younger adult learner agree to spend between ten and twenty hours a week together, for as long as three years, during which they use only the endangered language. They do not sit at desks. Instead, they cook, garden, repair fences, visit relatives and go shopping, so that the learner acquires the language of daily life in the settings where it is naturally used.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most thorough evaluation of the approach was carried out by Dr Itziar Oyarzabal, who followed forty pairs through their full three years. Most apprentices reached the point where they could sustain a conversation on familiar topics, an impressive result given that many began with no knowledge at all. More surprising was her finding about what distinguished the most successful pairs. It was not, as might be expected, the total number of hours they spent together. Rather, it was the range of their shared activities: pairs who regularly left the house and encountered new situations made far greater progress than those who spent the same time talking at a kitchen table. Oyarzabal attributes this to the way new contexts force speakers to reach for vocabulary they would otherwise never use, from the names of tools and plants to the expressions reserved for particular kinds of social occasion. A kitchen, however lively the conversation, offers only a limited stock of topics.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The demands on the elders, however, are considerable. Dr Chidi Ihejirika interviewed more than sixty of them and found that many initially struggled to remain in the language for long periods, having spent most of their adult lives switching automatically into the dominant language whenever a younger person was present. Some described feeling like performers rather than teachers. For others the difficulty was emotional: a number had been punished at school as children for speaking their language, and returning to it daily brought back painful memories. Ihejirika argues that programmes should offer elders more than gratitude, recommending both regular payments and access to counselling where it is needed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of payment divides communities. Some members feel that a heritage language should not be bought and sold, and that paying elders to speak it turns something sacred into a commodity. I understand this objection, but I do not find it convincing. The elders are giving up a large part of their week, often at some physical cost, and they possess knowledge that no one else can supply. Payment is a recognition of that expertise, not a sign of disrespect, and to expect people to provide hundreds of hours of skilled work for nothing is hardly a mark of reverence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Anahit Vardanyan has examined what happens after the three years are over. In her view, a programme should be judged not by the fluency of its apprentices but by whether they go on to pass the language to others, as teachers, as parents or as mentors to new apprentices. Measured in this way, the results are more modest. Only a minority of the graduates she traced were teaching the language five years later, and most of those who had stopped gave the same explanation: there were few paid positions available, and they needed to earn a living. Vardanyan's point is an important one, because it suggests that the bottleneck in many revival efforts lies not in producing speakers but in creating the conditions under which those speakers can afford to use what they have learned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more technical concern has been raised by the linguist Giorgio Pellicciari. Because each apprentice learns from a single person, he points out, they inevitably acquire that person's individual way of speaking, including words, expressions and habits of pronunciation that may be unusual even within the community. He has therefore proposed that apprentices should rotate between several elders. The suggestion has some merit where enough speakers are available, but the concern behind it seems to me overstated. In a language with only a handful of speakers, any variety that is passed on is valuable, and children who learn a language from their parents also absorb individual habits without any harm to the language as a whole.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Judged by cost per learner, the master-apprentice model is expensive, and it produces speakers slowly, one at a time. For many communities, however, there is simply no alternative. Where the remaining speakers are few and elderly, a method that is slow but effective is preferable to faster methods that cannot be put into practice at all. Its greatest value may in fact lie in something that evaluations rarely measure: the relationship that develops between two people of different generations, which often outlasts the programme itself and gives both a reason to keep the language in use.

topic: orthography and standardisation disputes in language revival: alphabets, dialect standards and literacy
title: Whose Spelling?
subtitle: Decisions about how to write an endangered language can unite a revival movement or split it apart

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has attended the early meetings of a language revival committee will know that few subjects generate as much heat as the question of how the language should be written. To an outsider, choosing between two ways of spelling a vowel may seem a minor technical matter. To those involved, it can feel like a decision about who owns the language and whose version of it will survive. My own view is that orthography debates usually absorb far more energy than they deserve, at the expense of the more pressing task of getting people to speak. Yet they cannot simply be avoided, because textbooks, signs and dictionaries all require some decision to be made, and a decision once printed is very difficult to reverse.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Broadly speaking, revivalists face a choice between two strategies. They can adopt the spelling conventions of the dominant national language, which has the advantage that almost every learner can already read them, or they can devise conventions of their own. The first option is practical but carries an unmistakable message of dependence, as if the smaller language were merely a regional variant of the larger one. The second asserts independence but asks learners to master an unfamiliar system. The historian of writing Tomasz Siemiradzki examined some thirty orthographic reforms in minority languages over the past century and found a striking pattern. The systems that departed most sharply from the dominant language's conventions were the ones most enthusiastically taken up by activists, yet they were also the ones least likely to be used by ordinary speakers in everyday writing. Siemiradzki calls this the 'distinctiveness trap'.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second set of disputes concerns dialects. Many endangered languages survive in scattered settlements, each with its own pronunciation and vocabulary, and a single written standard requires choosing between them. The benefits of standardisation are real: a common form makes it possible to produce one set of teaching materials, one dictionary and one broadcasting service. The costs, however, can be severe. The sociolinguist Lindiwe Ngcobozi has documented a case in which the speech of one village was selected as the basis of a standard, with the result that two neighbouring communities, offended at seeing their own speech treated as incorrect, withdrew from the revival programme entirely. Ngcobozi advocates instead what she calls a polycentric standard, in which several regional spellings and words are accepted as equally correct.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In principle this is an attractive solution, and it avoids the kind of rupture Ngcobozi describes. In practice, its costs are easy to underestimate. Teachers and publishers frequently report that materials offering several alternative forms confuse rather than reassure, and adult learners who have no home dialect of their own are left uncertain which forms to adopt. A more workable compromise, I would suggest, is a single shared written form combined with an explicit acceptance that people will pronounce it according to their own local traditions. Many large languages already operate in exactly this way without anyone regarding it as a problem.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe the debate should be settled by evidence about learning. The educational psychologist Hery Andriamanana has conducted a series of experiments with children learning to read endangered languages, comparing writing systems that differ in how consistently letters correspond to sounds. Children taught with a 'shallow' orthography, in which each sound is represented by one letter and each letter by one sound, learned to read noticeably faster than those taught with systems that preserved historical spellings. Andriamanana argues that ease of learning should take priority over every other consideration, including tradition and symbolism, because a writing system that children find difficult will simply not be used.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical position is taken by the anthropologist Sigrún Gudmundsen, who questions the assumption that revival requires standard literacy at all. Standardised spelling, she points out, emerged alongside the printing press and the modern nation-state, and many endangered languages belonged to cultures in which knowledge was transmitted through speech, song and performance. Insisting on written standards, in her view, imposes on these communities a model of what a 'proper' language looks like that is foreign to their own traditions. She proposes that revival should concentrate on audio and video materials rather than printed texts. Her historical argument is well founded, but I am not persuaded by her conclusion. Young people today expect any serious language to be readable and writable, and written forms confer a prestige that matters in a world dominated by print and screens. To confine a language to speech is to risk confining it to the past.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most humbling evidence comes from the sociolinguist Mateo Xiberras, who studied how young people actually write endangered languages in text messages and on social media. He found that most paid little attention to official spellings, devising their own conventions that were shaped largely by the layout of phone keyboards and by habits carried over from the dominant language. Rather than treating this as an error to be corrected, Xiberras suggests that committees should observe such usage closely and codify the forms that prove popular. Whether or not one accepts that proposal, his findings carry a clear lesson. An orthography is a tool, and like any tool it can be adjusted as the needs of its users change. Treating it as a monument to be defended is the surest way to ensure that it is admired by committees and ignored by everyone else.

topic: 'new speakers' versus traditional native speakers: authenticity, legitimacy and tension in revived languages
title: Native and New
subtitle: As revival movements produce more learners, relations between those who inherited a language and those who acquired it have become strained

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For decades, the central problem facing most minority languages was a shortage of speakers. In a number of places that problem is now, at least partly, being solved. Schools, evening classes and immersion courses have produced thousands of people who learned their language as teenagers or adults, and in some cases these so-called 'new speakers' already outnumber those who grew up speaking it at home. Yet success has brought difficulties of its own. The two groups often live in different places, belong to different social classes and speak noticeably different varieties of the language, and the relationship between them has become one of the most delicate issues in language revival. It is also one that official programmes, focused on enrolment figures and examination results, have been slow to acknowledge. The questions it raises are uncomfortable ones: who has the authority to decide what counts as 'good' usage, and whether a language learned in a classroom can ever carry the same weight as one absorbed in childhood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The sociolinguist Ane Beldarrain spent three years interviewing older native speakers in rural districts. Many told her that the speech of new speakers sounded artificial, describing it as 'bookish' and full of newly coined technical words that no one in their village would ever use. Some admitted that when addressed by a learner, they would switch to the national language almost without thinking, partly out of politeness and partly because the conversation simply felt easier that way. Beldarrain notes that new speakers frequently interpreted this habit as a rejection, even when it was not intended as one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The view from the other side has been explored by Darina Zelenkova, who surveyed more than eight hundred new speakers. A clear majority said they were reluctant to use the language with native speakers, chiefly because they feared that their speech would be criticised or corrected. Zelenkova calls this 'legitimacy anxiety': the sense that, however fluent one becomes, one has no real right to the language. Her data also contain a more encouraging finding. Those respondents who had persisted in speaking with native speakers reported that their confidence grew steadily, and several said that the older speakers had been far more welcoming than they had anticipated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These tensions should not surprise anyone. Many native speakers grew up in an era when their language was treated as a mark of poverty or backwardness, and some were punished for using it at school. They now watch as people from the cities are praised and even employed for learning what they themselves were once taught to be ashamed of. Some resentment is entirely understandable in the circumstances. Nevertheless, it would be a serious mistake to regard new speakers as a threat to the language. In many regions the native-speaking population is elderly and declining, and a language that depends on that population alone has, quite simply, no future.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Economic factors sharpen the divide. The economist Bolormaa Erdenebat has studied employment in sectors where knowledge of a minority language is required or rewarded, such as education, broadcasting and public administration. She found that such jobs were concentrated overwhelmingly in cities, far from the rural areas where most native speakers live, and that they were mostly filled by new speakers with university degrees. In the eyes of many traditional speakers, Erdenebat suggests, this has created the impression that the revival chiefly benefits an educated urban class rather than the communities in which the language survived. That impression is not entirely accurate, since many urban posts exist only because of campaigns that rural speakers themselves supported, but perceptions of fairness can matter as much as the facts in determining whether people continue to support a revival.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some scholars argue that the distinction itself is unhelpful. Paolo Quaglietti, a linguistic anthropologist, points out that many people classed as native speakers in fact have limited command of their language, while many new speakers go on to raise children who become native speakers in the fullest sense. He proposes that researchers abandon the two categories and think instead of a continuum of experience and ability. This is a useful corrective to rigid labelling, but it may underestimate how much the categories matter to the people concerned. For a native speaker who was punished at school, the difference between inheriting a language and choosing it is not an academic abstraction.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The future of many revived languages will depend less on government policy than on whether these two groups can find ways of meeting on equal terms. Some promising initiatives already exist, among them schemes in which older native speakers act as mentors to new speakers, helping them to acquire the idioms and rhythms of everyday speech. Such schemes work best, it seems, when the mentors are paid for their time, since this treats their knowledge as the valuable expertise it undoubtedly is. They also allow influence to flow in both directions: new speakers gain fluency and acceptance, while native speakers see their own way of speaking recognised as a model rather than dismissed as old-fashioned.

topic: official status and language legislation: whether legal recognition, signage, job requirements and translation duties help endangered languages
title: Written into Law
subtitle: Campaigners for minority languages have long fought for official recognition, but the evidence on what such recognition achieves is surprisingly mixed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past half-century, governments in many parts of the world have granted some form of legal recognition to minority languages. The measures vary widely: a clause in a national constitution, bilingual road signs, the right to use the language in court, quotas for broadcasting, or a requirement that public servants in certain regions be able to speak it. For the activists who campaign for them, often over several decades, such measures represent hard-won victories, and their passage is frequently celebrated as a turning point. Yet legal status is too often treated as the destination of a revival, when it is at best a means of reaching it and, in some circumstances, a distraction from the slower and less glamorous work of persuading families to speak the language at home.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most systematic attempt to measure the effects of recognition has been made by the political scientist Chinedu Okparaeke, who assembled data on some 120 minority languages over fifty years and compared trends in their transmission to children before and after they received official status. The results were sobering. Recognition had no consistent effect: for some languages the decline slowed or even reversed, while for others it continued at much the same rate as before. When Okparaeke looked more closely at the cases of improvement, he found that recognition had made a difference mainly where it was accompanied by sustained public funding for education through the medium of the language. Law, he concludes, is 'a permission, not an engine': it removes obstacles, but it does not in itself generate the energy that a revival requires.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The social psychologist Kseniya Kozhemyakin believes this conclusion undervalues the symbolic power of recognition. In her surveys, speakers living in regions with bilingual signs and official documents reported greater pride in their language and a greater willingness to use it in shops, offices and other public places than speakers in comparable regions without such measures. Visible recognition, she argues, alters the perceived status of a language, and perceived status strongly influences the decisions parents make about which language to pass on. The argument is plausible, and it may well be correct. It should be said, however, that her surveys measure attitudes and stated intentions rather than behaviour, and there is abundant evidence from other fields that pride in a language does not automatically translate into speaking it at the kitchen table.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recognition can also produce effects that its supporters did not intend. The legal scholar Kristoffer Annerstedt has studied regions where knowledge of a minority language became a condition of employment in the public sector. In several cases, the requirement provoked resentment among residents who spoke only the majority language, and in one region it fuelled a political campaign to repeal the law altogether. Annerstedt also found that the requirement had created a group of officials who had studied the language intensively to pass the necessary examination and then scarcely used it again. He argues that governments would achieve more by offering incentives, such as salary supplements for staff who use the language, than by imposing obligations.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Annerstedt's evidence is valuable, and the backlash he describes is a genuine risk. His preferred solution, however, rests on an optimistic assumption: that governments will fund incentive schemes generously and maintain that funding over many years. The history of minority-language policy gives little reason for such confidence, since programmes that depend on annual budgets are usually the first to be cut when public finances come under pressure. Requirements, whatever their drawbacks, have the considerable advantage of remaining in force without fresh expenditure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different kind of objection has been raised by the anthropologist Eleni Dimitrakos, who has worked with communities that greeted official recognition with suspicion rather than celebration. In several of these cases, the state now offering recognition was the same state that had once banned the language from schools, and older speakers were reluctant to trust its intentions. Their caution was not always misplaced. Recognition sometimes arrived together with a standardised form of the language devised by government agencies, so that decisions about grammar, spelling and vocabulary passed from the community to officials in the capital. Dimitrakos therefore argues for legal frameworks that transfer authority over a language to the communities that speak it, rather than to state institutions acting on their behalf.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, there is the question of cost. The economist Ádám Hollósi examined the obligation, common in language laws, to translate official documents into the minority language. In one country he studied, more than nine-tenths of the translated documents published online were never downloaded in their minority-language version, and Hollósi proposes that the money would be better spent on schools. Translations that nobody reads are certainly hard to defend, and some reallocation seems sensible. Yet counting downloads misses part of the point. A language that appears alongside the national language on every official form is being told, in effect, that it belongs in public life, and that message has a value which download figures cannot capture. Law, in the end, can open doors. Whether anyone walks through them depends on decisions made in millions of homes, which no legislature can dictate.

topic: ancestral language revival and community health: wellbeing, youth suicide and health programmes
title: The Healing Tongue
subtitle: A growing body of research links knowledge of an ancestral language with better health, but what that link means is far from settled

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Arguments for reviving endangered languages have traditionally been cultural ones. A language, it is said, carries a unique body of knowledge, a way of seeing the world and a connection to ancestors, and its loss diminishes both its speakers and humanity as a whole. In recent years a different kind of argument has gained ground. A series of studies in Indigenous communities on several continents has reported that where more people know their ancestral language, rates of youth suicide, depression and certain chronic illnesses tend to be lower. Such findings now appear regularly in applications for funding, and some health agencies have begun to support language programmes for the first time. The health argument is undeniably powerful, and it has opened doors that cultural arguments alone could not. It also carries risks that its advocates have been slow to recognise.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited evidence comes from the epidemiologist Marija Jovanoski, who analysed health records from around 150 small communities in a northern region. In communities where more than half of the members could hold a conversation in their ancestral language, the rate of suicide among young people was a small fraction of that in communities where fewer people had such knowledge. Crucially, the difference remained after Jovanoski had taken account of household income, remoteness and access to health services, factors that might otherwise have explained it. Jovanoski herself is careful to stress the limits of her work. Her data, she points out, show an association between language and health; they do not establish that one causes the other.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Two broad explanations have been offered for the association. The psychologist Aigerim Sadykova argues that language knowledge contributes to what she calls cultural continuity, a sense that one's own life is connected to the lives of past and future generations. Young people who possess this sense, she suggests, are better protected against the despair that can follow personal setbacks, because they can see themselves as part of a story larger than their present circumstances. In interviews with teenagers enrolled in language classes, Sadykova found that many described the classes as the first place in which they had felt they truly belonged. The sociologist Tomas Laurinavičius offers a different account. Communities that have kept their languages, he observes, tend also to be those that have won control over their own schools, land and health services. On this view, knowledge of the language may be less a cause of good health than a marker of a community's broader capacity to govern its own affairs.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Laurinavičius's point deserves to be taken seriously, because it has direct practical consequences. If language is merely an indicator of self-determination, then funding language classes alone, while leaving other conditions unchanged, is unlikely to produce any improvement in health. It does not follow, however, that the two explanations are rivals. A community that sets out to revive its language is, in that very act, exercising control over its own future, and it seems entirely possible that language revival both reflects and strengthens the wider sense of agency that Laurinavičius identifies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have sidestepped the question of cause altogether by asking whether language can make existing health programmes work better. The public health researcher Hanna Nussbaumer evaluated a diabetes prevention scheme in which sessions on diet and exercise were conducted in the ancestral language and built around the preparation of traditional foods. Compared with participants in a standard programme run in the national language, those in the language-based scheme attended sessions far more regularly and were much more likely to complete the full course. Nussbaumer argues that, whatever the deeper relationship between language and health, delivering services in a community's own language can make them more acceptable and therefore more effective. Several participants told her that, for the first time, the sessions had felt like something designed for them rather than imposed on them, and a number brought along relatives who had never previously attended any health programme.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For all its promise, the health argument has dangers. If language programmes come to be funded primarily as health interventions, they will be judged by health outcomes, and these may take a generation to appear. A government that expects falling suicide rates within a few years may conclude, when they fail to materialise, that the programme has failed, and withdraw its support. There is also a more fundamental objection. To present a language as a kind of medicine is to treat it as valuable only for what it does, rather than for what it is. The case for revival should not stand or fall on health statistics, however encouraging those statistics may currently be.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is to dismiss the research. The evidence that language matters to wellbeing is suggestive and has grown steadily stronger, and it would be foolish to ignore it. Health agencies that support language programmes are making a reasonable bet, and the partnerships they form with communities may prove valuable in their own right. But the most durable argument for revival remains the simplest: that communities have a right to the languages of their ancestors, whatever the measurable benefits of exercising it.

topic: restoring Indigenous place names on maps and signs as a strategy of language revival
title: Restoring the Map
subtitle: Returning original names to rivers, mountains and towns has become a favoured tool of language revival, but what it does for the languages themselves is disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, a quiet revision of the world's maps has been taking place. Mountains, rivers, bays and towns that for a century or more carried names imposed by colonial surveyors have, in growing numbers, had their earlier names officially restored. The surveyors rarely set out to erase anything; they recorded what they heard, often through interpreters, and the results were frequently garbled, shortened or attached to the wrong feature altogether. Today, renaming is widely promoted as a tool of language revival, and its advocates speak of 'returning the language to the land'. It would be a mistake to dismiss such projects as mere symbolism, yet the claims made for them as instruments of revival are considerably larger than the evidence currently supports.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most compelling case for restoration rests on what names contain. Marjatta Kivilahti, who leads a toponymy project at the Institute for Northern Place Studies, describes traditional names as 'compressed knowledge'. In a survey of some 1,200 names along a northern coastline, she found that more than sixty per cent referred to physical features or to resources: a stretch of shore where seals hauled out, a channel where the ice formed late. Only a small minority commemorated people or events. On this view, a restored name is not a decoration but a store of ecological and practical information, accumulated over generations and easily lost when the name disappears. The argument is persuasive as far as it goes. Its weakness is that such knowledge is available only to those who can analyse the grammar and vocabulary of the name; to the great majority of people who read it on a road sign, it remains an opaque label, no more informative than the colonial name it replaced.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kwesi Nkansah-Darteh, a geographer at the Centre for Landscape and Society, has approached the question from a different angle, asking not what names mean but whether people use them. He followed the official renaming of a river and fourteen villages in a coastal district over a ten-year period. By the end of the decade, a clear majority of local residents were using the restored names in everyday speech, including many who had no knowledge whatsoever of the language from which they came. Nkansah-Darteh regards this as evidence that names can act as an 'entry point': once a name is familiar, people become curious about what it means. In his follow-up interviews, roughly a quarter of residents reported having tried to find out the meaning of at least one name. Yet the trail grew faint after that. Fewer than three per cent had gone on to enrol in a language class of any kind.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the linguist Ileana Strâmbeanu, figures like these confirm her suspicion that renaming can become a substitute for substance. Changing signs, she points out, is cheap and highly visible, whereas training teachers and producing learning materials is expensive and slow, and governments eager to demonstrate goodwill may prefer the former. The result, she says, is 'a language of the landscape that nobody speaks'. She also objects that restored names are often chosen by committees which settle on a single standard form, flattening the variation that existed between communities; in one case she documents, three neighbouring groups had distinct names for the same lake, and only one was adopted. Her warning about substitution deserves to be taken seriously. However, the evidence that renaming actually diverts money away from teaching is thin: in the cases she cites, spending on language education had already begun to fall several years before any signs were changed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Practical difficulties also arise once a name moves from a community into an official register. Many endangered languages contain sounds with no equivalent in the dominant language, and their spelling may require letters or accents that older mapping software cannot display. A regional emergency dispatch service reported that, after one renaming programme, callers sometimes gave the restored name and sometimes the old one, causing delays in locating incidents. The usual compromise is dual naming, in which both names appear together, typically with the restored name placed first. The Coastal Names Working Group recommends dual naming as a transitional stage after which the colonial name would eventually be dropped. Dual naming is a sensible arrangement, although the question of which name comes first, which has provoked surprisingly bitter disputes, is far less important than whether people learn to pronounce the restored name correctly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is, finally, the question of who decides which names are restored, and whether some should be restored at all. Kivilahti notes that several communities she has worked with have deliberately kept the names of burial grounds and ceremonial sites out of official records, fearing that publication would attract unwanted visitors or expose sacred knowledge to outsiders. Officials sometimes interpret this reluctance as a lack of interest in the project. It is better understood as a reminder that restoration need not mean publication, and that the communities whose languages are involved are entitled to keep some names to themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that renaming is an empty gesture. A name that reappears on a map signals that a language was there first, and that recognition can matter a great deal. But a name alone teaches very little. Where restoration has been accompanied by explanatory panels, school lessons and recordings that allow listeners to hear a name spoken by those who know it, it appears to have stimulated genuine interest. Where it has not, the restored names risk becoming like labels in a museum whose doors remain closed: accurate, perhaps, but read by almost nobody able to understand them.

topic: the screen inferiority effect: whether reading comprehension is poorer on digital devices than on paper, and why
title: The Page and the Pixel
subtitle: Readers seem to understand less when they read from a screen, but researchers disagree sharply about why

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Within a single generation, the screen has displaced the printed page as the place where most adults in wealthy countries do most of their reading. Schools have followed, replacing textbooks with tablets in the belief that digital material is cheaper, lighter and easier to update. Yet a body of experimental work suggests that something may be lost in the transfer. When the results of fifty-four comparison studies were pooled in a recent analysis, readers who studied a text on paper answered comprehension questions slightly but consistently better than those who read the same text on a screen. The size of this so-called screen inferiority effect is modest, and nobody seriously proposes that digital reading is ruinous. What makes the finding worth taking seriously is not its magnitude but the competing explanations that have grown up around it, because each implies a quite different response.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely cited account comes from Liv Haugsrud, an educational psychologist at the Western Norway Institute of Education. Haugsrud argues that the difference lies less in the device than in the habits people bring to it. Because screens are used overwhelmingly for brief messages, news headlines and social media, readers have learned to approach them in a hurried, scanning mode, and they carry this mode over to demanding texts without noticing. Her laboratory has produced some telling evidence. When participants were allowed as much time as they wished, those reading on screens finished sooner and scored lower, yet they predicted that they had done better than the paper readers. In Haugsrud's view, the problem is therefore one of misjudged effort: screen readers stop working at a text before they have understood it, because they believe they already have.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A different explanation emphasises the physical object rather than the reader's state of mind. Teodoro Abellanosa, a cognitive scientist at the Visayas Centre for Learning Research, points out that a printed book offers a constant stream of spatial and tactile cues. A reader can feel how many pages remain, recall that a particular event occurred near the bottom of a left-hand page, and flick back to check. In one of his experiments, participants read a short detective story either as a paperback or on an e-reader. The two groups performed equally well on questions about the characters and on how absorbed they had felt, but the e-reader group was markedly worse at putting the main events of the plot into the correct order. The study is ingenious, though it involved only fifty volunteers and has yet to be repeated elsewhere, so its conclusions should be treated as provisional.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third camp regards the whole effect as a temporary phenomenon. Ruairí Ó Floinn, who studies media use at the Galway Institute of Technology, maintains that older participants simply have more experience of print, and that the gap will close as people who grew up with touchscreens come to dominate experimental samples. It is an attractive argument, but the evidence points the other way. The pooled analysis found that the advantage of paper was, if anything, larger in studies published in the last decade than in earlier ones, and it was present among university students who reported doing most of their reading on phones. Familiarity with a device, it seems, does not automatically translate into skill at reading from it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The effect is also far from uniform. For narrative fiction the difference between media is negligible, whereas for informational texts, such as scientific explanations or historical accounts, it appears reliably. Length matters as well: with passages of fewer than about five hundred words, the two groups generally perform alike. The way the text is presented on screen makes a further difference. Readers who must scroll continuously through a document tend to do worse than those who move through it in discrete pages, perhaps because scrolling deprives them of the fixed visual landmarks that Abellanosa considers so important. Time pressure, too, widens the gap, which is unfortunate given that many assessments are now delivered digitally and against the clock.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most hopeful line of research concerns simple interventions. A team led by Chidinma Uzowulu at the Lagos Centre for Literacy Studies asked students, before reading on a screen, to write down in one sentence what they hoped to learn from the text, and afterwards to produce a short summary. With these two steps in place, the disadvantage of the screen group disappeared entirely. Uzowulu interprets this as strong support for Haugsrud's position, since a change in the reader's approach removed the effect while the device stayed the same. The result is encouraging, but it should not be overstated. The exercises lengthen every reading session, students may abandon them once nobody is checking, and they say nothing about the difficulties with sequence and location that Abellanosa has identified.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should schools and universities conclude? The rush to replace printed textbooks entirely with tablets now looks premature, particularly for the kind of extended, information-dense reading on which academic success depends. Equally, there is little justification for treating screens as inherently harmful, since for short texts and stories they appear to do no damage at all. The sensible course is to match the medium to the purpose and to teach students explicitly how to slow down when a digital text demands it. Above all, the debate is a reminder that reading is not a single skill. Focusing narrowly on which surface the words appear on risks obscuring the more important question of what readers are trying to achieve when they read.

topic: the history of silent reading: word separation, ancient reading aloud as social custom, and inner speech
title: Reading Without a Voice
subtitle: When did people stop reading aloud, and did it matter? Historians are less certain than they once were

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most people today, reading is a silent and solitary activity, so much so that someone who moves their lips while reading a newspaper may be thought slightly odd. For a long time, however, historians assumed that the opposite was true of the ancient world, where reading was believed to be almost always performed aloud. A frequently repeated anecdote describes a visitor in the late fourth century who was astonished to find a bishop reading with his eyes alone, his voice and tongue at rest. The story has often been treated as proof that silent reading was then a rare curiosity. In my view it has been made to carry far more weight than a single observation can bear: the visitor may have been surprised less by the silence itself than by the bishop's refusal to share the text with the people waiting to speak to him.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic account of how silent reading became normal was developed most fully by Margarethe Oosterbroek of the Low Countries Institute for Book History. Her argument rests on the physical appearance of the written page. Greek and Latin texts were usually written without spaces between words, a style known as continuous script, and Oosterbroek contends that a reader faced with an unbroken line of letters needed to sound the words out in order to discover where one ended and the next began. From around the seventh century, scribes in Ireland and Britain, for whom Latin was a foreign language, began to separate words with spaces. The practice gradually spread to the continent, and by the thirteenth century, according to Oosterbroek, silent reading had become routine in monasteries and the new universities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This neat sequence has been challenged by Dimitra Kalogeropoulou, a classicist at the Aegean University. She has collected dozens of passages from ancient literature in which characters read letters, inscriptions or official documents without making a sound, and in which the silence is mentioned without any hint of surprise. For Kalogeropoulou, the ancient preference for reading aloud was a matter of social custom rather than mental limitation. Books were often performed for groups of listeners, and wealthy households kept trained readers whose task was to read to their owners. Her work persuasively separates two questions that had long been confused: whether ancient people were able to read silently, and whether they usually chose to. It does not, however, entirely dispose of Oosterbroek's case, since word spacing may still have made silent reading easier and therefore more common.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from Bahram Tavakkolian, a historian of manuscripts at the Institute of West Asian Studies, who argues that the debate has been too narrowly European. In many scholarly traditions of the Islamic world, he notes, the spoken transmission of a text was valued as a guarantee of its accuracy. Students learned important works by hearing them recited by a teacher, who had in turn heard them from his own teacher, and written copies were checked against this living chain of voices. Silent reading was certainly practised, but it existed alongside recitation rather than replacing it. Tavakkolian warns that presenting the shift from voiced to silent reading as a story of progress implies that cultures which continued to value recitation were somehow backward, an assumption he regards as both inaccurate and unhelpful.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever its timing, the spread of silent reading has been credited with remarkable consequences. Some scholars have claimed that it allowed readers to encounter dangerous ideas in private, encouraged personal interpretation of religious texts and made possible a new kind of inner life. Church authorities, it is sometimes said, became anxious about what people might be reading without supervision. These suggestions are plausible, and some contemporary complaints about private reading do survive. Yet it is extremely difficult to demonstrate that silent reading caused such changes rather than simply accompanying them, and the more ambitious claims about transformed inner lives seem to me to go well beyond what the evidence can show.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Modern psychology adds a further complication. Even fluent adults who read in apparent silence often experience an inner voice, and sensitive instruments can detect small movements in the muscles of the throat and tongue while people read to themselves. This phenomenon, known as subvocalisation, is frequently targeted by courses that promise to double or triple reading speed by teaching students to suppress it. Experiments suggest that such training can indeed increase speed, but usually at the cost of understanding, particularly when the text is difficult. If even silent readers are, in a sense, speaking under their breath, then the boundary between reading aloud and reading silently is far less sharp than the traditional history implies.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to see the current popularity of audiobooks and podcasts as a break with centuries of silent reading. The history outlined here suggests a different interpretation. The voiced and the silent modes have always coexisted, with the balance between them shifting according to technology, social habit and the purpose of reading. Parents still read aloud to young children, poetry is still written to be heard, and lawyers still read contracts slowly under their breath. Rather than a decline, the return of listening may be better understood as one more swing of a very old pendulum.
