topic: competing explanations of dyslexia: phonological, visual and multiple-deficit accounts, cross-linguistic differences and the value of diagnosis
title: One Label, Many Causes?
subtitle: After a century of research, scientists still disagree about what dyslexia is — and whether the answer should change how struggling readers are helped

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere between five and ten per cent of children find learning to read unexpectedly hard. They may be articulate, curious and capable in mathematics, and they may have received the same teaching as classmates who read fluently, yet print remains stubbornly resistant to them. For more than a century this puzzle has been known as dyslexia, but the consensus implied by a single name is largely illusory. Researchers continue to disagree about what lies behind the difficulty, and the disagreement is far from academic. Each theory points towards a different kind of help, and children, parents and schools are left to navigate between them, often with little guidance about which claims are backed by evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential account holds that the core problem lies not in vision but in the processing of speech sounds. Annelie Wubbolts, a developmental psychologist at the Northern Netherlands Reading Institute, has spent two decades documenting how children with dyslexia struggle with tasks such as deciding whether two words rhyme, or saying what remains of a word when one sound is removed. Because alphabetic writing maps letters onto these sounds, a child who cannot perceive them clearly will find the code almost impossible to crack. Critics once objected that weak sound awareness might be a result of poor reading rather than its cause, since learning to read is known to sharpen awareness of speech sounds. Wubbolts's most important contribution has been to answer this objection: her group tested children at the age of four, before any formal instruction, and found that difficulties with rhyme and sound segmentation predicted which of them would later struggle.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that sound processing tells the whole story. Tomasz Pawlikowski, a vision scientist at the Silesian Institute of Neuroscience, argues that many children with dyslexia suffer from visual crowding, a tendency for letters that are close together to interfere with one another. In his studies, simply increasing the space between letters allowed dyslexic children to read noticeably faster without any loss of accuracy. The finding is genuine and has been reproduced, but its significance is easily overstated. Extra spacing also helps typically developing readers who are slow, which suggests that it eases a general bottleneck rather than correcting a problem specific to dyslexia, and the gains, while measurable, are modest beside those produced by systematic teaching of letter–sound correspondences.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further challenge comes from comparisons across languages. Ananya Ghoshal, who leads a cross-linguistic project at the Bengal Centre for Cognitive Science, observes that most theories of dyslexia were built on studies of English, a language whose spelling is notoriously irregular. In languages such as Finnish or Italian, where each letter reliably represents one sound, dyslexic children eventually read accurately but remain painfully slow. Among readers of Chinese, whose characters represent meaningful units rather than individual sounds, difficulties with visual form and with the structure of words appear to matter at least as much as sound awareness. Ghoshal concludes that a theory derived from a single, unusual writing system cannot simply be assumed to apply to all others.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most significant shift in recent thinking has been away from the search for a single cause altogether. Rafael Tumiri, a geneticist at the Andean Institute of Developmental Research, is among the leading proponents of what is known as the multiple-deficit model. In this view, dyslexia results from an accumulation of small risks — many genes of minor effect, weaknesses in sound processing, attention or memory, and environmental factors such as the number of books in the home — none of which is sufficient on its own. Tumiri stresses that reading ability is distributed continuously across the population, so that any line separating dyslexic from merely weak readers is drawn by convention rather than by nature. The model fits the evidence better than any of its predecessors. It also, however, raises an uncomfortable question: if dyslexia is the lower end of a continuum, what exactly does a diagnosis identify?

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Uncertainty about causes has left room for remedies with little scientific support. Coloured overlays and tinted spectacles, for example, are widely sold to families on the basis that they reduce visual stress. Sigrún Kolbeinsdóttir, a clinical researcher at the Reykjavik Child Health Centre, conducted a series of carefully controlled trials in which neither the children nor the researchers knew which tint was supposedly beneficial. She found no improvement beyond what could be attributed to expectation. It is difficult to justify the continued marketing of such products to anxious parents, whose money and hope might be better invested in approaches that have been shown to work.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Given all this, some educators argue that the term dyslexia should be abandoned in favour of the more neutral phrase reading difficulty. I do not share that view. For many families, a diagnosis brings relief, removes the suspicion that a child is lazy or unintelligent, and in some education systems unlocks extra support and examination arrangements. The real problem is not the label but the way it is often used as a gate. Where help is reserved for children who have obtained a formal assessment, those whose parents cannot afford one, or who fall just above an arbitrary threshold, are left to fall further behind. Every child who struggles with reading deserves early, well-founded intervention, whatever name is eventually given to the difficulty.

topic: audiobooks and whether listening counts as reading: comprehension, mind-wandering, narration and support for struggling readers
title: Is Listening Reading?
subtitle: The rapid growth of audiobooks has revived an old question about what it really means to read a book

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Sales of audiobooks have risen steeply over the past decade, while those of printed books have remained broadly flat. Millions of people now get through novels, biographies and popular science on the train, at the gym or while cooking dinner. This shift has prompted a question that is asked with surprising frequency, and often with surprising heat: does listening to a book count as reading it? Some people clearly feel that those who listen are taking a shortcut, rather like watching the film instead of reading the novel. The question, however, is less straightforward than either side tends to assume, and the most useful answers come not from arguments about prestige but from research into what the mind actually does in each case.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Henrike Lüdemann, a cognitive psychologist at the Hanseatic University of Applied Sciences, points out that reading involves two broad components. The first is decoding, the process of turning marks on a page into words. The second is comprehension, which involves understanding sentences, linking ideas and building a mental picture of what is described. For skilled adult readers, decoding is so rapid and automatic that it places almost no demand on the mind, and what remains is essentially the same language system that is used for understanding speech. In Lüdemann's experiments, adults who listened to a story and adults who read it answered comprehension questions with almost identical accuracy. In her view, for a fluent reader the difference between the two experiences is far smaller than many people suppose.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ilaria Bressanin, who studies attention at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences in Padua, is more cautious. Reading, she observes, allows the reader to control the pace: one can slow down at a difficult sentence, pause to think or look back at an earlier paragraph. Listeners, by contrast, are carried along at the speed of the narrator. In Bressanin's studies, participants who listened to a complex scientific article reported that their minds had wandered more often than those who read it, and they later remembered less of the argument. With simple narratives, the gap largely vanished. Bressanin also notes that people rarely listen to audiobooks while doing nothing else. Her findings are convincing, but they seem to me to say more about divided attention than about listening as such: a reader who glanced at a page while preparing dinner would probably fare no better.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For children who are still learning to read, the picture is different again. Joost Haverkort, an educational researcher at the Twente Centre for Literacy, has studied the use of audiobooks with pupils who find decoding difficult. Such children, he argues, are often confined to simple books well below their intellectual level, which can leave them bored and starved of new vocabulary. Audiobooks give them access to the stories their classmates are enjoying. Haverkort insists, however, that listening must supplement rather than replace practice in decoding. His most promising results came from pupils who followed the printed text with their eyes while hearing it read aloud: over a school year, their reading fluency improved considerably more than that of pupils who simply listened.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difference concerns the voice of the narrator. A skilled performer conveys irony, emotion and emphasis through tone and timing, and this can make a demanding text easier to follow. Listeners new to Shakespeare, for instance, often find a good recording more accessible than the printed play. Yet the narrator's choices are also an interpretation, and the listener has no option but to accept it. A reader decides how a character sounds, where the stress falls in a line of dialogue and whether a remark is sincere or sarcastic. Something is lost when these decisions are made by someone else, although it is worth remembering that for most of history stories were experienced through the voice of a teller.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The suspicion that listening is somehow inferior has a familiar ring. In the eighteenth century, novels themselves were condemned as frivolous entertainment likely to corrupt young readers, and in the twentieth century paperbacks were dismissed as cheap and disposable. In each case, a new and more accessible form was judged less serious than the established one. Much of the current disdain for audiobooks is, I suspect, of the same kind, and it says more about social status than about the quality of the experience. That said, it would be equally mistaken to claim that the two forms are interchangeable for every purpose.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most sensible conclusion is that the question of whether listening is reading is the wrong one to ask. What matters is the purpose. For a gripping novel enjoyed on a long drive, an audiobook offers nearly everything a printed copy does. For a dense text that must be studied, analysed and remembered, the ability to pause, reread and annotate gives print a clear advantage. And for a child struggling with decoding, the two are best used together. Asking which format suits which task is likely to prove far more productive than ranking them.

topic: orthographic depth: why irregular English spelling slows children's early reading compared with transparent writing systems, and the case for and against spelling reform
title: The Price of Irregular Spelling
subtitle: Children learning to read English face a harder task than most of their European peers. Should the spelling system be blamed — or changed?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few writing systems attract as much affectionate exasperation as that of English. The same sequence of letters can be pronounced in strikingly different ways, as in 'though', 'through', 'cough' and 'bough', while a single sound may be spelled in half a dozen forms. Native speakers tend to regard these quirks as harmless curiosities, the price of a language with a rich and varied history. Over the past few decades, however, comparative research has made it increasingly clear that the inconsistency of English spelling imposes a measurable burden on those learning to read it. The burden is real, and it falls hardest on the youngest and most vulnerable learners. Whether anything can or should be done about it is a far more difficult question.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited evidence comes from a large comparative study coordinated by Kaarina Rintamäki at the Central Finland Institute for Educational Research. Her team assessed children in thirteen European countries towards the end of their first year of formal reading instruction, asking them to read aloud lists of simple, familiar words. In languages with highly regular spelling, such as Finnish, Greek, Italian and Spanish, most children read more than ninety per cent of the words correctly. Children learning English, by contrast, managed only around a third. Rintamäki estimated that English-speaking children required two and a half years or more to reach the level of basic decoding that their peers in regularly spelled languages attained within a single year.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These figures have not gone unchallenged. Ottavio Sanseverino, a developmental psychologist at the University of Northern Lombardy, points out that English-speaking children typically begin formal reading lessons at four or five, whereas Finnish children often start at seven, and that younger children may simply be less ready to learn. When Sanseverino compared groups matched for age rather than for years of schooling, the difference between English and more regular languages narrowed considerably. Crucially, though, it did not disappear. His work suggests that early starting age exaggerates the disadvantage of English spelling but cannot fully explain it away, a conclusion that is, in my view, the most balanced reading of the evidence currently available.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental defence of English spelling is offered by the linguist Declan Fennelly of the Munster Institute of Language Studies. Fennelly argues that critics misunderstand what the system is designed to do. English spelling, he contends, frequently preserves the visual identity of related words even when their pronunciation differs: 'sign' keeps its silent 'g' because of 'signature', and 'health' retains the 'ea' of 'heal'. The system therefore represents meaning as well as sound, and for the experienced reader this provides valuable clues to how words are connected. The argument is elegant and largely correct as far as skilled adults are concerned. It is, however, of little comfort to a six-year-old who has not yet encountered the word 'signature' and simply wants to know how to read 'sign'.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How English spelling came to be so irregular is the subject of work by Morwenna Treloar, a historian of language at the Cornwall Centre for Textual History. Treloar shows that the spelling of many words was fixed by early printers, some of them trained abroad, at a time when pronunciation was changing rapidly; the spoken language moved on while the written forms stayed put. Later scholars made matters worse by inserting letters to reflect the Latin origins of words, which is why 'debt' and 'doubt' contain a 'b' that has never been pronounced in English. Treloar also explains why repeated campaigns for spelling reform have failed. The most serious obstacle, in her account, is the absence of a single standard pronunciation: a spelling that is perfectly phonetic for a speaker in one region would be misleading for a speaker in another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If reform is impractical, attention turns to teaching. Lukáš Moravec, an education economist at the Brno Institute for Social Research, has attempted to estimate the cost of English spelling in terms of extra teaching time and remedial support, and concludes that it is substantial. He is nonetheless sceptical of shortcuts. In the 1960s, some schools experimented with simplified, regularised alphabets designed to be used for the first years of schooling before children switched to conventional spelling. Moravec's reanalysis of those programmes found that pupils initially learned to read more quickly, but that many struggled with the transition, and that by the age of eight their advantage had largely vanished. He argues instead for teaching letter–sound patterns systematically from the start and for introducing the meaning-based patterns that Fennelly describes explicitly, rather than leaving children to discover them by chance.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Wholesale reform of English spelling is, realistically, not going to happen. The language is spoken in too many varieties across too many countries, and centuries of printed material would instantly become old-fashioned. Nor is it obvious that reform would be desirable, since the meaning-based features of the system genuinely help mature readers. What can be changed is the way children are introduced to it. Schools in English-speaking countries should acknowledge that their pupils face a harder task than children elsewhere, allow them more time without labelling them as failures, and teach the hidden logic of the spelling system rather than presenting it as a list of exceptions to be memorised. A difficult system that is well taught may turn out to be considerably less daunting than its reputation suggests.

topic: whether reading fiction improves empathy and the understanding of other minds: short-term experiments, replication failures and lifetime reading
title: Does Fiction Make Us Kinder?
subtitle: The idea that novels improve our understanding of other people is an appealing one. The evidence is more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Defenders of literature have long claimed that reading novels makes people better at understanding one another. By entering the minds of characters very different from ourselves, the argument goes, we learn to imagine the feelings and motives of real people. In recent years this old idea has acquired a scientific gloss, as a series of psychological experiments appeared to show that fiction could sharpen what researchers call social cognition, the capacity to infer what others are thinking and feeling. The findings were widely reported and quickly cited by teachers, librarians and arts organisations seeking to justify their work. The claim is an attractive one, and it may even be true, but the evidence for it is considerably weaker than the headlines suggested.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study that attracted most attention was carried out by Nasrin Kashanifard and colleagues at the Institute for Social Psychology in Toronto. Participants were asked to read one of three kinds of short text: an extract from an acclaimed literary novel, an extract from a popular thriller or romance, or a passage of non-fiction. Immediately afterwards, they were shown photographs of people's eyes and asked to identify the emotion each person was experiencing. Those who had read literary fiction performed better than the other two groups. Kashanifard's explanation was that literary writing deliberately leaves gaps, describing characters indirectly and leaving much unsaid, so that readers are forced to work out for themselves what is going on in a character's mind. Popular fiction, by contrast, tends to state characters' feelings explicitly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that the effect has proved hard to reproduce. A consortium of laboratories in several countries repeated the experiment with several thousand participants, using the same materials and procedures, and found no reliable difference between the groups. It is hardly surprising that reading a few pages of a story should fail to alter a skill developed over a lifetime, and in retrospect the original claim looks implausibly strong. Yet the failure of the short-term effect does not settle the larger question. A single dose of medicine may do nothing, while a long course of treatment works; similarly, one story may change little, while years of reading might change a great deal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This longer-term possibility has been explored by Owain Gwilym of the Centre for Reading Research in Aberystwyth. Because asking people how much they read tends to produce inflated answers, Gwilym measures lifetime reading indirectly: participants are given a list of names and asked to tick those they recognise as real novelists, with invented names included to catch guessing. People who recognise more authors consistently score higher on tests of social understanding, and this relationship holds even after personality traits such as curiosity and openness to new experiences are taken into account. Gwilym is careful to acknowledge, however, that his data cannot show which comes first. It may be that reading fiction develops social understanding, but it is equally possible that people who are already interested in others are drawn to fiction.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach comes from neuroscience. Jelena Vuković, who directs a brain-imaging laboratory at the Belgrade Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience, has found that the regions active when people follow a narrative overlap substantially with those involved in thinking about the beliefs and intentions of real individuals. She proposes that fiction acts as a kind of simulator, allowing readers to rehearse social situations safely in the way that pilots practise in a flight simulator. The image is vivid, but the evidence is less decisive than it appears. That two activities use the same brain regions shows that they draw on similar processes; it does not show that practising one improves the other.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even if fiction does improve social understanding, it would be a mistake to assume that this makes readers kinder. Understanding what another person feels is not the same as caring about it, and a skilled manipulator may be very good at the former. Moreover, the effects of reading may depend heavily on how it is done. Several studies indicate that readers who become deeply absorbed in a story are more affected by it than those who read in a detached way, which may help to explain why the same novel can move one reader profoundly and leave another unchanged.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that reading fiction is socially worthless, and it seems reasonable to suppose that a lifetime of reading contributes in some modest way to our understanding of others. But defenders of literature would be unwise to rest their case on such claims. If the value of novels depends on their measurable effect on empathy, then any study that fails to find such an effect becomes a threat to literature itself. It is better to recognise that people read fiction for pleasure, for beauty and for the experience of another way of seeing the world, and that these are sufficient reasons in their own right.

topic: how learning to read reorganises the brain: neuronal recycling, adults who become literate late, mirror invariance and competition with face processing
title: Rewiring for the Written Word
subtitle: Reading is too recent an invention for evolution to have prepared us for it. So how does the brain make room for it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Writing was invented a little over five thousand years ago, and for most of the time since then only a tiny minority of people could read. This is far too short a period for natural selection to have equipped the human brain with a dedicated reading organ. Yet brain scans of literate people, whatever language they read, reveal a small region on the underside of the left hemisphere that responds strongly and selectively to written words. The most widely accepted explanation is known as the recycling hypothesis: reading, on this view, takes over circuits that evolved for other purposes, chiefly the recognition of objects, and retrains them for a new cultural task. It is one of the most elegant ideas in modern cognitive neuroscience. What it implies for teaching, and for those who learn to read late in life, is considerably more contested.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most revealing evidence has come from adults who never had the opportunity to attend school as children. Mariana Cotrim, a neuroscientist at the Lisbon Institute of Cognitive Neuroimaging, has studied three groups from rural communities: adults who had never learned to read, adults who had learned only in later life through evening classes, and adults who had learned as children. The word-responsive region was present in both literate groups, demonstrating that the adult brain retains enough flexibility to develop it. In those who had learned late, however, the response was weaker and their reading remained noticeably slower. This is genuinely encouraging news for adult literacy programmes, which have sometimes been regarded as a poor investment compared with schooling for the young.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ishwari Karandikar, of the Deccan Centre for Brain Research, went a step further by following a group of adults through a literacy course rather than comparing different people at a single point in time. Scanning her participants before the course and again after six months, she found changes not only in the outer layers of the brain but also in deeper structures that relay visual information, along with measurable improvements in visual attention. Karandikar concludes that literacy reshapes the entire route by which visual information travels through the brain. The study is impressive in its design, but it involved only around thirty learners, and changes in brain activity do not by themselves tell us how well those learners can actually read.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recycling also has costs, or at least side effects. Hélène Bouchardeau, a developmental psychologist at the University of Upper Normandy, points out that primate vision naturally treats an object and its mirror image as the same thing, a useful trait for an animal that needs to recognise a predator whether it approaches from the left or the right. Reading in the Latin alphabet requires this tendency to be suppressed, since 'b' and 'd', or 'p' and 'q', differ only in orientation. Bouchardeau has shown that adults who cannot read readily judge mirror-image shapes to be identical, whereas literate adults find it difficult to ignore orientation even when the shapes have nothing to do with letters. Her work also suggests that the letter reversals common among young children are a natural stage in development rather than a warning sign, a point that ought to reassure many anxious parents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A related concern involves faces. In people who cannot read, the region that later responds to words is partly devoted to recognising faces. As reading develops, Erling Ellingsen of the Bergen Laboratory for Visual Cognition has found, responses to faces in the left hemisphere decline and become more concentrated in the right. Some commentators have described this as literacy crowding out face recognition. Ellingsen, however, has found no evidence that literate people are any worse at recognising faces; the brain appears simply to redistribute the work. Talk of a cost seems to me misleading, since a change in where a task is performed is not the same as a loss of ability.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers are convinced that these differences are caused by reading itself. Wanjiru Gichohi, an anthropologist at the Rift Valley Institute of Social Research, argues that comparisons between literate and non-literate adults are inevitably confounded. People who never learned to read typically also received less schooling of any kind, often grew up with poorer nutrition and had less exposure to printed pictures, maps and screens. Some of the differences attributed to literacy may therefore reflect education or living conditions more broadly. This is an important objection. Studies that follow the same individuals over time, such as Karandikar's, partly answer it, but only partly, because literacy courses also involve regular attendance, social contact and other forms of mental effort.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Despite such uncertainties, the research carries at least two clear lessons. The first is that it is never too late to learn to read: the adult brain can and does reorganise itself when given the chance. Literacy programmes for adults should therefore be funded with confidence, but they should also allow learners far more time than is usually provided, since late readers may remain slow for years. The second lesson is one of caution. The phrase 'brain-based' is increasingly used to market reading programmes to schools, but nothing in the neuroscience of reading yet tells teachers which method to use in the classroom, and claims to the contrary should be treated with suspicion.

topic: readability formulas and the measurement of text difficulty: surface features, coherence, background knowledge and levelled reading in schools
title: Counting Syllables
subtitle: For a century, educators have tried to put a number on how hard a text is to read. The results have been useful, influential and frequently misused

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the early twentieth century, teachers, publishers and governments have searched for a reliable way of measuring how difficult a piece of writing is. The most enduring answer has been the readability formula, a calculation that combines the average length of sentences with the average length of words, usually measured in syllables, to produce a single score or an equivalent school grade. Such formulas are now built into word-processing software, used to select texts for school examinations and, in some jurisdictions, written into regulations that require documents such as insurance policies to fall below a certain level of difficulty. Their remarkable persistence shows how badly a simple measure of difficulty is wanted. It does not show that the measure is a good one, and on closer inspection the formulas capture only the surface of what makes reading hard.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The logic behind the formulas is not unreasonable. Long sentences often contain complex grammatical structures, and long words are frequently rare or technical ones, so both tend to be associated with difficulty. According to Corinna Wachtendorf, a historian of education at the University of Kassel, the early developers of these measures intended them only as rough guides to help librarians and teachers choose suitable books from existing collections. The trouble began, she argues, when the formulas were turned around and used as instructions for writing. Authors and editors, asked to produce material at a given level, began shortening sentences and replacing long words mechanically in order to reach the required score, without asking whether the text had actually become easier to understand.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experimental work suggests that it often had not. Augustin Ravelonjato, a psycholinguist at the Antananarivo Institute of Language Sciences, took a set of school texts and produced simplified versions with lower readability scores, chiefly by breaking long sentences into shorter ones. In the process, many of the small linking words that signal relationships between ideas, such as 'because', 'although' and 'therefore', disappeared. Young readers understood the simplified versions less well than the originals, since they now had to infer for themselves how one statement related to the next. Ravelonjato's research also highlights the importance of what readers already know. In one study, children with a strong interest in football understood a demanding article about the sport better than more able readers who knew little about it, even though the article's formula score predicted that it would be too hard for them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In response to such criticisms, researchers have developed far more sophisticated tools. Priyamvada Sethuraman, a computational linguist at the Institute of Language Technology in Chennai, has helped to build systems that analyse dozens of features of a text, including how frequently its words occur in everyday language, how clearly its sentences are connected and how deeply its grammatical structures are embedded. Trained on the results of thousands of comprehension tests, these systems predict how well readers will understand a passage considerably more accurately than the traditional formulas. Sethuraman is nonetheless frank about their limits. No measure based on the text alone, she points out, can take account of a reader's purpose or motivation, and a reader who badly wants to understand something will often persist with material that any formula would judge far too difficult.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Measurement of difficulty has had a particularly strong influence on the teaching of reading in primary schools. In many classrooms, children are assessed and then given books that match their measured level, the aim being to provide texts that are challenging but not discouraging. Chukwudi Ogbonnaya, an education researcher at the Enugu Centre for Literacy Studies, believes this practice may hold back the very children it is meant to protect. Pupils who are kept on texts at their current level, he argues, rarely meet the vocabulary and ideas they need in order to progress. In a year-long classroom study, he found that pupils who read texts intended for their age group, with substantial help from the teacher, made greater gains than similar pupils restricted to books at their measured level. The findings are persuasive, but the crucial phrase is 'with substantial help'. Simply handing struggling readers harder books and leaving them to cope is likely to do more harm than good.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Outside the classroom, readability formulas have played a valuable role in the movement for plain language in official documents. A formula can quickly reveal that a tax guidance leaflet consists of sentences sixty words long, and this alone can prompt a useful revision. Yet a low score is no guarantee that a document can be understood. The only dependable way to find out whether people can follow a set of instructions is to ask some of the people who must use them to try, and organisations that rely on formulas instead of testing with real readers are, in effect, measuring the wrong thing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of readability formulas illustrates a familiar problem with measurement. A number that is useful as an indicator can become harmful once it is treated as a target, because people learn to improve the number rather than the thing it was meant to reflect. Formulas, old and new, can usefully alert writers and teachers to possible difficulties. They should inform judgement, not replace it.

topic: historical literacy and economic growth: measuring past literacy from signatures, church-led reading campaigns, practical commercial schooling and the direction of causation
title: Did Reading Make Nations Rich?
subtitle: Development experts often assume that mass literacy leads to prosperity. The historical record tells a more tangled story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few propositions in development policy command such universal assent as the idea that literacy fuels economic growth. International agencies routinely justify spending on adult education and primary schooling by pointing to the higher incomes of literate populations, and history is frequently called upon as a witness: the nations that industrialised first, it is said, were those whose people had first learned to read. The connection is intuitively appealing, since a worker who can read instructions, keep accounts and follow written contracts would seem to be more productive than one who cannot. Yet when economic historians look closely at the past, the relationship between reading and wealth turns out to be far less direct than this account implies, and in some cases it appears to run in the opposite direction.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty is knowing how many people could read at all. For periods before national censuses asked about literacy, historians have relied heavily on marriage registers, counting the proportion of brides and grooms who signed their names rather than making a mark. Pieter Veldkamp, a demographic historian at the Groningen Institute for Historical Research, warns that this measure is ambiguous. In much of early modern Europe, reading and writing were taught as separate skills, with reading taught first and writing, which required paper, ink and a teacher's time, taught later or not at all. Many people who could read fluently may therefore never have learned to sign, while others could write their names and little else. Signature counts are a crude instrument, but because the same crude instrument was applied consistently over long periods, they remain valuable for tracing trends, if not for establishing exact levels.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Nowhere is the gap between reading and writing clearer than in Sweden. Ebba Tornérhjelm, of the Uppsala Centre for Nordic Social History, has examined the registers kept by Lutheran parish clergy, who visited every household once a year to test its members on their knowledge of religious texts and to record how well each person could read. Because the church made reading ability a condition of taking communion and of marrying, the pressure to learn was intense. By the middle of the eighteenth century, Tornérhjelm finds, the great majority of Swedish adults could read printed religious works, an achievement accomplished largely without schools, through instruction given at home, very often by mothers. The ability to write, however, remained rare until the following century. And despite this precocious mass literacy, Sweden remained among the poorer countries of Europe for roughly another hundred years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For Adaeze Nnabuife, an economist at the Lagos School of Development Studies, the Swedish case is a decisive refutation of the idea that literacy is sufficient to generate prosperity. Growth, she argues, also requires secure property rights, functioning markets, access to capital and transport networks, and none of these was in place in eighteenth-century rural Sweden. Nnabuife does not conclude, however, that the country's literacy was economically irrelevant. When those other conditions finally appeared in the late nineteenth century, she suggests, a population already accustomed to reading was able to adapt to industrial work with exceptional speed, so that literacy acted as a stored-up asset waiting to be used. It is an attractive interpretation, but one that is very hard to test, and it carries the risk of explaining whatever happens after the fact.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Haruto Ikegami, a historian at the Kansai Institute of Comparative History, believes that the nature of literacy matters as much as its extent. In Japan during the Edo period, a large proportion of children from ordinary families attended small private schools, many of them attached to temples, where the curriculum was overwhelmingly practical: pupils learned to write business letters, keep accounts and calculate with the abacus. Ikegami contrasts this commercial literacy with the devotional reading cultivated in Sweden, and argues that it was far better suited to supporting trade and manufacturing. The comparison is illuminating, but it may underestimate devotional reading. The discipline of regular study, and the habit of treating printed texts as a source of authority, may have had economic value even when the texts themselves were religious.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most uncomfortable evidence for the conventional view comes from England, the first nation to industrialise. In several of the textile towns at the heart of the early industrial revolution, signature rates stagnated or even fell during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, as factories drew children into employment at ages when they might otherwise have been at school. Early mechanised industry, in other words, does not seem to have required a highly literate workforce, and in some places it actively undermined literacy. Only later, as rising incomes allowed families to keep their children in school and governments introduced compulsory education, did literacy rise rapidly. On this evidence, wealth may have done at least as much to spread reading as reading did to create wealth.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this implies that literacy is economically unimportant in the modern world, where almost every form of skilled work depends on written information. What the history does suggest is that literacy works in combination with other conditions rather than as a lever that can be pulled on its own. Programmes that teach people to read without addressing the absence of jobs, credit or markets should not be expected to transform economies by themselves. There is also a deeper danger in defending literacy chiefly as an instrument of growth. The ability to read has value for the individual, in access to knowledge, to law and to the imaginative world of literature, that does not depend on whether it raises national income, and it should be defended on those grounds as well.

topic: book-gifting programmes and books in the home: correlation with later literacy, randomised gifting trials, shared-reading guidance and children's choice of books
title: A Library on Every Shelf?
subtitle: Giving free books to young children is a popular way of promoting literacy. But do the books themselves make the difference?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In dozens of countries, newborn babies now go home from hospital with a parcel of picture books, and charities post a new book every month to millions of young children. The reasoning behind these schemes seems unanswerable. Children who grow up surrounded by books tend to read earlier, do better at school and earn more as adults, so putting books into homes that lack them ought to narrow the gap between rich and poor. The generosity of such programmes is admirable, and many families clearly value them. Whether the books themselves cause the improvements attributed to them, however, is a question to which the research gives a far less confident answer than the promotional material for these schemes might suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence for the importance of books in the home comes from large international surveys. Margit Puusepp, a sociologist at the Tartu Institute of Social Studies, has analysed data from more than thirty countries in which adults were asked, among other things, roughly how many books there had been in their home when they were sixteen. The answers are strongly associated with adult literacy and numeracy, and the association remains even after parents' education and occupation are taken into account. Interestingly, the benefit rises steeply up to around eighty books and then levels off, so that a home with several hundred books confers little additional advantage. Puusepp interprets the number of books not as a cause in itself but as a sign of what she calls a scholarly culture: a family way of life in which reading, discussion and curiosity are taken for granted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This interpretation exposes the central weakness of the case for book gifting. If a shelf of books is a sign of a particular family culture, then supplying the books will not necessarily supply the culture. Nuno Carvalhais, an economist at the Porto School of Public Policy, tested this directly in a randomised trial involving some two thousand families with low incomes. Half received a free book every month from birth until the age of three, while the other half did not. When the children started school, those in the book group had only slightly larger vocabularies than the others. Parents in the book group did report reading aloud more often during the first year of the scheme, but by the third year this difference had largely disappeared. Carvalhais concludes that gifting alone produces small and short-lived effects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Inés Arocena, a developmental psychologist at the Montevideo Centre for Early Childhood, believes the crucial ingredient is not the book but the conversation around it. In what is known as dialogic reading, the adult asks open questions about the pictures, builds on the child's answers and gradually hands over the role of storyteller to the child. Arocena's own trial compared families who simply received books with families who also attended a few short sessions on this style of reading. The vocabulary gains in the second group were roughly three times as large. Books delivered without guidance, she argues, are often read in a hurried and passive way, or are not opened at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different emphasis comes from Thi Lan Phung, a researcher at the Hanoi Institute of Educational Sciences, who has studied children of primary-school age. Phung notes that many children read less during the long summer holiday and return to school with weaker skills than they had at the start. In her experiment, pupils from low-income areas were invited to choose a dozen books to keep before the summer break began. Compared with classmates who received no books, they read more over the holiday and lost noticeably less of their reading ability. Phung stresses that choice was essential: children were far more likely to read books they had picked themselves, and they frequently reread their favourites, something they rarely did with library loans that had to be returned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that books are necessary but not sufficient. A child cannot read without access to books, and in many households that access is genuinely lacking, but the books do most good when they are matched to the child's interests and accompanied by adults who know how to share them. Programmes that combine book gifting with brief guidance for parents are therefore likely to be considerably more effective than those that simply deliver parcels, and the additional cost of such guidance is small. I would add one caveat. Measured effects on vocabulary or test scores are not the only reason to give books. The pleasure a child takes in owning a book is worth something in itself, even if it never appears in a statistical table.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is harder to defend is the tendency of some organisations to promise that a box of books will transform a child's future. Such claims may help to raise funds, but they set expectations that the evidence cannot meet, and when the promised transformation fails to appear, public support for worthwhile programmes may be put at risk. A more modest message, that books help most when they are chosen with care and shared with enthusiasm, has the advantage of being true.

topic: the token theory of the origin of Mesopotamian cuneiform and its rivals
title: From Counters to Signs
subtitle: Did the world's oldest writing grow out of small clay objects used for bookkeeping?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some time around 3300 BCE, in the southern Mesopotamian city of Uruk, scribes began pressing marks into damp clay in a way that historians now recognise as the earliest form of cuneiform. The vast majority of the five thousand or so tablets recovered from this period have nothing to do with poetry, law or religion. They record rations of barley, the numbers of sheep in temple flocks and the labour owed by workers. This mundane character disappoints many museum visitors, who expect the first writing to preserve myths or the deeds of kings. Such expectations rest on a misunderstanding: writing in Mesopotamia was not invented to express ideas but to keep track of goods, and several centuries passed before anyone thought to use it for anything else.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation of how this accounting tool came into being is known as the token theory. Across the Near East, archaeologists have unearthed thousands of small clay objects, including cones, spheres, discs and cylinders, some dating back as far as 8000 BCE. For decades these were catalogued as toys, gaming pieces or amulets. Dr Lerato Mokgatle, an archaeologist at the Institute for Ancient Economies in Johannesburg, has spent much of her career arguing that they were in fact counters, each shape standing for a fixed quantity of a particular commodity: a cone for a small measure of grain, perhaps, or a cylinder for an animal. According to Mokgatle, the decisive development came in the fourth millennium BCE, when tokens began to be sealed inside hollow clay balls, known as envelopes, to guarantee the terms of a transaction. Because the contents could not be checked without breaking the ball, officials pressed the tokens into its surface before enclosing them. Eventually, she argues, it became clear that the markings alone were sufficient, the tokens themselves were abandoned, and the envelope was flattened into a tablet.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The appeal of this account lies in the visual correspondences on which it rests. The sign for a sheep on the earliest tablets, for example, is a circle containing a cross, and a disc-shaped token incised with exactly the same pattern is common at many sites. Mokgatle has documented dozens of similar pairings, and she points out that envelopes bearing impressions of the tokens they contain have been found at Susa, in present-day Iran, as well as in Mesopotamia itself. For her, the sequence from loose counters to impressed envelopes to flat tablets amounts to a gradual evolution in which no single individual can be credited with the invention of writing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all specialists are persuaded. Andreas Kallergis, an Assyriologist at the University of Thessaloniki, accepts that a handful of signs resemble particular tokens but argues that most of the roughly nine hundred signs in the proto-cuneiform repertoire have no plausible ancestor among them. He also notes that many tokens have been recovered from graves and domestic rubbish rather than from storerooms or administrative buildings, which in his view undermines the claim that they served a single accounting purpose. His most frequently cited objection, though, concerns chronology: if tokens were used in much the same form for some five thousand years, why should they have given rise to writing so abruptly? This argument is less damaging than it first appears. Long-established techniques often change rapidly once social circumstances shift, and the late fourth millennium saw Uruk grow into a city of perhaps forty thousand people, with temple institutions managing labour and produce on an unprecedented scale.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third position has been developed by Hiroko Yamauchi of the Kyoto Centre for Near Eastern Studies, who regards the search for a single precursor as mistaken. In her account, writing was assembled from several existing practices: the images carved on cylinder seals, the pictorial conventions of pottery decoration, and a class of so-called numerical tablets, which carry impressed numbers but no indication of what is being counted. Yamauchi draws particular attention to a later stage in which these numerical tablets acquired a second sign identifying the commodity. At that point, the number five no longer had to be represented by five separate marks for jars of oil; it could be written once and attached to any object. This separation of quantity from the thing being counted is arguably the true intellectual breakthrough, and it is one that the token theory, focused as it is on the shapes of individual signs, tends to overlook.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further puzzle is how a system for recording goods acquired the ability to represent spoken language. The key mechanism was the rebus principle, in which a sign is used for its sound rather than its meaning, much as a picture of an eye might stand for the English pronoun 'I'. Erik Sahlberg, a linguist at Uppsala, maintains that the pressure to adopt this device came from personal names. Administrators needed to record who had delivered or received goods, and names, particularly those of foreigners, could not easily be conveyed with pictures. Sahlberg's hypothesis is attractive, yet the evidence for it remains thin, since the readings of most names on the earliest tablets are still disputed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whichever account is preferred, the history of cuneiform offers a useful corrective to the image of writing as the creation of a lone genius. The token theory may not explain every sign, but it has permanently shifted attention towards the routine bookkeeping from which writing emerged. Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that writing had not one origin but several, and that asking which object was its true ancestor is rather like asking which tributary is the real source of a river.

topic: the debate over whether the Indus valley signs constitute a writing system
title: Signs Without Sounds?
subtitle: A century after their discovery, scholars still disagree about whether the Indus inscriptions are writing at all

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the ruins of the great Bronze Age cities of the Indus valley, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro among them, excavators have recovered more than four thousand small objects bearing rows of enigmatic signs. Most are square stamp seals carved from soft stone, typically showing an animal, often a one-horned bull, beneath a line of symbols. The inscriptions are strikingly brief: the average contains about five signs, and the longest known runs to barely two dozen. Since the 1920s, scores of scholars have announced decipherments, linking the signs to early forms of Dravidian, Sanskrit or languages long extinct, yet none has won general acceptance. This record of failure is hardly surprising. The most famous decipherments in history relied either on texts carrying the same message in a known language or on a large body of material written in a language whose descendants are still spoken. For the Indus signs, neither exists.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, a more radical possibility was put forward by Pierre Vaillancourt, a historian of early states based in Lyon. Perhaps, he suggested, the signs had never been decipherable because they did not record language at all. In his view they formed a system of emblems, comparable to heraldic badges or the symbols on modern road signs, which could convey information about clans, offices or deities without corresponding to particular words. Vaillancourt pointed to the brevity of the inscriptions and to the fact that a large proportion of the roughly four hundred known signs occur only once in the entire corpus, a pattern he considered inconsistent with any working script. He also dismissed the common argument that longer Indus texts once existed on palm leaves, cloth or wood and have simply rotted away. Such reasoning, he argued, makes the theory impossible to test, since any missing evidence can always be blamed on perishable materials.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The reaction was swift, and much of it was hostile. Nalini Abeysekara, a computational linguist at the University of Peradeniya, led a team that analysed the order in which signs appear. They found that certain signs cluster consistently at the beginning of inscriptions and others at the end, and that the sequences are neither rigidly fixed, as in a repeated pattern, nor random, but fall within the range of variability measured for known languages. Abeysekara also challenged the significance of brevity. Fully literate societies, she observed, produce enormous numbers of very short texts, from coins and stamps to labels on jars, and nobody concludes from these that their makers could not write.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the statistical case has its own weaknesses. Rustam Dzhumabayev, a computer scientist in Almaty, demonstrated that several systems known not to encode speech, including medieval coats of arms and certain kinds of ritual notation, produce figures within the same range. A measure of this kind, he concluded, may be consistent with language but cannot on its own prove that language is present. His critique is well founded, but it is often misread. Showing that a test is inconclusive does not, as some of Vaillancourt's supporters have claimed, make his alternative any more likely; it merely returns the debate to where it began.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The archaeologist Ingrid Kristoffersen has tried to move the discussion away from the inscriptions themselves and towards the places where they were used. Clay sealings, the lumps of clay that were impressed with seals and attached to bundles of goods, have been excavated in storerooms within the Indus cities and at trading sites as far away as the Persian Gulf. Some inscriptions also appear on pottery and on small copper tablets, which repeat the same short texts many times. To Kristoffersen, this distribution points to an administrative role linked to the movement of commodities, much like the role writing played in early Mesopotamia. If the seals carried the names or titles of officials, she argues, then at least part of the system must have represented spoken words, and the real question becomes not whether the signs were writing but to what degree.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This reframing seems to me the most productive way forward. The insistence on a simple choice between writing and non-writing owes more to modern assumptions than to the evidence, since the earliest Mesopotamian tablets themselves recorded only a narrow range of information and could not have been used to set down a story. Vaillancourt's assumption that a literate civilisation must leave lengthy texts is therefore difficult to sustain. It would also help if more effort were devoted to the inscriptions on pottery, copper and bone, which have received far less attention than the seals. As for the long-hoped-for discovery of a bilingual inscription, perhaps in a Mesopotamian trading post, the chances are slim, but they are not negligible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What makes the debate so heated is the assumption that literacy is a measure of civilisation. Some commentators fear that if the Indus signs are not writing, the Indus cities will be judged less advanced than their contemporaries in Egypt and Mesopotamia. That fear is misplaced. A society that built planned cities with covered drains, standardised weights and long-distance trade networks over several centuries hardly needs a script to demonstrate its sophistication.

topic: the invention of the first alphabet in Sinai and Egypt and the question of who created it
title: Letters from the Mines
subtitle: Who invented the alphabet, and why did it take so long to catch on?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every alphabet in use today, from the Latin letters of this page to Arabic, Hebrew and the scripts of South and Southeast Asia, descends from a single system devised in the second millennium BCE by speakers of a Semitic language living in contact with Egypt. It is difficult to think of an invention with more far-reaching consequences, and yet remarkably little is known about how it came about. The earliest substantial evidence consists of some forty short inscriptions scratched on rocks and statues at Serabit el-Khadim, a turquoise-mining site in the Sinai peninsula, together with two inscriptions found at Wadi el-Hol, on a desert route west of the Nile. Their dates are disputed, with estimates ranging across several centuries.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle behind the new script is now well understood. Its creators borrowed pictures from Egyptian hieroglyphs but ignored their Egyptian meanings and sounds. Instead, each picture was named with a word in the inventors' own language, and the sign was then used for the first consonant of that word. A drawing of an ox head, 'alp, represented a glottal stop; a simple house plan, bayt, stood for b. The method, known as acrophony, meant that around two dozen signs were enough to write any word, compared with the many hundreds required by the Egyptian system. Vowels were not marked at all, a gap that would not be filled until the Greeks adapted the script more than a thousand years later.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The identity of the inventors is far more contentious. Samira Tlili, an epigrapher at the University of Tunis, argues that they were not scribes but labourers, soldiers and caravan workers employed on Egyptian mining expeditions. Such people would have seen hieroglyphs carved on temple walls and monuments all around them without being able to read them. Tlili points out that the Sinai signs are irregular and clumsily formed, that their shapes vary considerably from one inscription to another, and that their inventors borrowed only the outlines of Egyptian signs, never their established sound values. Most of the inscriptions are brief dedications to a goddess, scratched in the mines themselves. Her conclusion is deliberately provocative: the alphabet, she maintains, was the creation of people who could not write.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Owen Fairweather, an Egyptologist at the University of Bristol, finds this implausible. Egyptian writing, he notes, already included a set of signs that each represented a single consonant, although scribes used them alongside hundreds of other signs rather than on their own. In Fairweather's view, the leap to a purely consonantal system is far more likely to have been made by someone who knew of this feature, perhaps a bilingual interpreter or a junior official attached to an expedition. He also stresses the setting of the Wadi el-Hol inscriptions, which lie on a road used by foreign troops serving the Egyptian state, where scribes would certainly have been present to record supplies and orders.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Both positions, it seems to me, depend on drawing too sharp a line between the literate and the illiterate. Literacy in the ancient world was rarely an all-or-nothing matter. A foreman who had learned to recognise a few dozen hieroglyphs in order to check deliveries would not count as a scribe, but nor would he be wholly ignorant of writing. Such partially literate individuals are exactly the kind of people one might expect to improvise a simpler system. Nor is the clumsiness of the Sinai signs as revealing as Tlili suggests. The local sandstone is hard and uneven, the inscriptions were often made in poorly lit mine shafts, and the tools available were probably no more than stones or metal points; an experienced scribe working under such conditions might well have produced something equally crude.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For Eleni Zografou, a historian at the University of Crete, the question of who invented the alphabet is less interesting than the question of why so little happened afterwards. On this point the evidence is clear: for perhaps five hundred years the new script left only a scattering of short inscriptions, while cuneiform and hieroglyphs remained the instruments of government, diplomacy and religion throughout the region. Zografou argues that the alphabet flourished only after the collapse of the Bronze Age palace economies around 1200 BCE, which had employed and trained the specialist scribes who maintained the older systems. In the smaller trading cities of Phoenicia that emerged afterwards, a cheap and easily learned script suddenly had no powerful rival.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to conclude from this history that the alphabet was an inherently democratic technology, which placed writing in the hands of ordinary people. That conclusion goes too far. Even in Phoenicia and in the kingdoms of the southern Levant, the ability to read and write appears to have remained confined to a minority for centuries. A script that can be learned in weeks rather than years removes one barrier to literacy, but schools, materials and, above all, a reason to write are needed as well. The alphabet's simplicity made a wider spread of literacy possible; it did not make it inevitable.

topic: why the decipherment of Maya hieroglyphic writing was delayed and who it has benefited
title: The Long Silence of the Glyphs
subtitle: Maya writing can now largely be read. Why did it take so long, and who has gained from the achievement?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For well over a thousand years before the Spanish conquest, Maya scribes recorded their world in an intricate script carved on stone monuments, painted on pottery and written in folding books of bark paper, only four of which survive. Today specialists can read the great majority of known inscriptions, yet most of that progress was made in a remarkably short period, roughly between the late 1950s and the 1980s. For much of the twentieth century, the prevailing view was that the glyphs recorded little beyond calendars, astronomy and religious ritual, and that they could not be read as language at all. The usual telling of the story celebrates a handful of brilliant individuals who overturned this view. Such accounts are not false, but they obscure more instructive lessons about how scholarly fields succeed and fail.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The irony is that a key to the script had existed since the sixteenth century. A Spanish bishop in Yucatán asked a Maya informant to write the letters of the Spanish alphabet in Maya signs, and dutifully recorded the result. What the informant actually produced were signs for syllables corresponding to the names of the Spanish letters, so that the letter 'b', pronounced 'be', was written with a sign for that syllable. Because the list did not behave like an alphabet, generations of scholars dismissed it as a misunderstanding. Meanwhile, the Maya calendar had been worked out in impressive detail by about 1900, and this very success did more harm than good: it encouraged the belief that the inscriptions were the work of priests absorbed in the passage of time rather than records of human affairs.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Iker Arbeloa, a historian of science at the University of the Basque Country, regards the subsequent delay as largely a social phenomenon. In the middle decades of the century, he argues, the field was dominated by one immensely respected authority who held that the glyphs were essentially symbols for ideas and who responded to phonetic proposals with open scorn. Younger scholars, dependent on that authority for positions and publication, hesitated to break ranks. When a convincing phonetic approach did emerge, it came from a linguist working far from the main centres of research, whose papers were initially ignored or ridiculed. Arbeloa describes the period as 'an extended case of a discipline deferring to a single voice'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Haruki Okuyama, an epigrapher at Sophia University, believes that this emphasis on personalities is overdone. Before the 1960s, he points out, relatively few inscriptions had been published in accurate drawings or photographs; many monuments lay deep in the rainforest and had been seen by only a handful of outsiders. Without a large body of reliable texts, proposed readings could not be tested by checking whether a sign behaved consistently across many contexts. Once systematic recording programmes made thousands of inscriptions available, progress accelerated sharply. A pivotal moment came when patterns of dates on the monuments at one site were shown to mark events in the lives of individual rulers, among them births, accessions and deaths. Okuyama's argument is persuasive as far as it goes, but it cannot explain why phonetic readings were resisted even after the evidence for them had begun to accumulate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third factor has received less attention than it deserves. The linguist Linnea Bergstrand of Lund University notes that around six million people speak Mayan languages today, yet most early epigraphers made little attempt to learn any of them. The grammar of the script, she argues, only began to yield once scholars with training in Mayan linguistics joined the effort, because a knowledge of the structure of modern Mayan languages proved essential to identifying verbs, pronouns and the endings that mark tense. On this point Bergstrand is surely right: the single most valuable resource for reading the inscriptions was being spoken in the villages around the ruins throughout the decades in which experts declared the script unreadable.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The anthropologist Leilani Kahale raises a different question: who has benefited from the decipherment? Since the 1980s, workshops have taught the glyphs to thousands of Maya speakers, and some communities now use the script on public signs and in school materials. Kahale welcomes these developments but warns that the overwhelming majority of research is still published in English and Spanish, and that academic careers and museum exhibitions built on Maya texts have rewarded outsiders far more than the descendants of the people who wrote them. Her concerns are legitimate, although the situation is arguably more encouraging than she allows, since a growing number of Maya scholars now hold university posts and lead their own research projects.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The decipherment remains incomplete; a minority of signs still resist interpretation. What the history so far suggests is that an ancient script is not unlocked by data alone, nor by insight alone, but by a field willing to test its assumptions, to listen to unfashionable voices and to treat the descendants of the original writers as partners rather than as sources of information.

topic: twentieth-century Chinese script reform: character simplification, Pinyin and why an alphabet never replaced characters
title: The Script That Refused to Die
subtitle: A century ago, many reformers expected Chinese characters to give way to an alphabet. Why did that never happen?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early decades of the twentieth century, a remarkable number of Chinese intellectuals came to regard their own writing system as an obstacle to national survival. Literacy rates were low, and reformers argued that a script requiring years of memorisation condemned most of the population to ignorance. Some went further, calling for characters to be abolished altogether and replaced with an alphabet, as had happened with Turkish and Vietnamese. One prominent writer of the period declared that if the characters did not perish, China itself would. A century later, Chinese characters are used daily by well over a billion people, and the predictions of their demise look not merely mistaken but curiously revealing of the anxieties of their age.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against characters was not without substance. Reading a newspaper requires familiarity with around three thousand of them, and the mechanical technologies of the time, from the telegraph to the typewriter, were designed for alphabets of a few dozen letters. When reform finally came in the 1950s, however, it took a more moderate form than the radicals had hoped. Thousands of characters were simplified by reducing the number of strokes needed to write them, and in 1958 a system of romanisation known as Pinyin was officially adopted. Pinyin was presented not as a replacement for characters but as a tool for teaching pronunciation and for promoting a standard national language. In the decades that followed, literacy on the mainland rose dramatically, and simplification was widely credited with the achievement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That credit is disputed. Ji-ho Seong, a historian of education at Pusan National University, argues that the gains owed far more to the expansion of compulsory schooling and to adult literacy campaigns than to any change in the script itself. His most telling evidence comes from Taiwan and Hong Kong, where the traditional, unsimplified characters remained in use and where literacy reached comparably high levels over the same period. If simplification had been decisive, Seong reasons, those societies should have lagged well behind.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Margaux Lafleur, a cognitive psychologist at the Université de Montréal, has approached the question from the perspective of the reader. Her experiments suggest that, for practised readers, the number of strokes in a character has little effect on how quickly it is recognised; what matters is familiarity with the recurring components from which characters are built. Simplification may, however, help beginners who are learning to write by hand, since fewer strokes mean less to memorise and reproduce. Lafleur also notes a cost that reformers underestimated: in several cases, two characters with quite different meanings were merged into a single simplified form, so that the new script introduced ambiguities which the old one had avoided. Her distinction between the demands of reading and those of writing seems to me essential, and much of the older debate went round in circles because it ignored it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, was the alphabet never adopted? The standard answer points to the structure of the language. Mandarin has only around four hundred distinct syllables, or roughly thirteen hundred if tones are counted, so large numbers of words sound identical; characters allow such words to be told apart on the page. Characters can also be read by speakers of varieties such as Cantonese and Hokkien, which are mutually unintelligible in speech. The linguist Chukwuemeka Nzeogwu, who compares writing systems at the University of Lagos, believes the first of these arguments is overstated. Spoken Chinese, he observes, functions perfectly well without characters, because listeners rely on context to resolve ambiguity, and readers of an alphabetic script would do the same. In his view, the decisive reasons were political and cultural: an attachment to an unbroken literary heritage stretching back more than two thousand years. Nzeogwu is right about everyday language, but his argument is less convincing for classical texts and personal names, where context offers far less help.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ironically, the technology that once seemed fatal to characters has turned out to be one of their strongest allies. Computers and mobile phones allow users to type a word in Pinyin and then select the intended character from a list, making the writing of Chinese as fast as that of English. Yet this convenience has its own consequences. Surveys conducted by Lafleur's team found that many adults who read fluently increasingly struggle to write familiar characters from memory, a phenomenon popularly called 'character amnesia'. In a sense, the alphabet has gained by stealth the everyday role it was denied by law. Even so, it would be premature to predict the end of handwriting, which remains central to schooling and to the cultural prestige of calligraphy.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of Chinese script reform suggests a broader lesson. Writing systems are rarely chosen, kept or abandoned on grounds of efficiency alone. They carry identity, memory and authority, and the arguments made about them, as the reformers of a century ago demonstrated, often say as much about the hopes and fears of those making them as about the scripts themselves.
