topic: the rongorongo tablets of Rapa Nui (Easter Island): independent invention, stimulus diffusion or memory aid
title: The Tablets of Rapa Nui
subtitle: Did the inhabitants of one of the world's most remote islands invent writing for themselves?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Rapa Nui, better known to outsiders as Easter Island, lies more than two thousand kilometres from the nearest inhabited land. Its famous stone statues have attracted most of the attention, but the island has also produced one of the most perplexing puzzles in the history of writing. Around two dozen wooden objects survive, now scattered among museums from Santiago to St Petersburg, bearing rows of small, carefully incised signs known as rongorongo. The lines run in alternate directions, and the reader must turn the tablet upside down at the end of each line to continue. When a missionary first reported the tablets to the outside world in 1864, the island's population had just been devastated by slave raids and by epidemics of disease, and nobody could be found who was able to read them. The stakes of the puzzle are high. If rongorongo was genuine writing created without any outside influence, it would join the very small group of scripts, among them those of Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, that were invented from scratch.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Karim Tarabay, a historian of Pacific contact at the American University of Beirut, doubts that it was. He draws attention to a Spanish expedition of 1770, during which island chiefs were invited to mark a document formally annexing their territory to the Spanish crown. None of the European visitors who arrived before or shortly after that date, Tarabay notes, made any mention of tablets or carved signs, even though several wrote detailed descriptions of island life. His proposal is that the islanders encountered the idea of writing at that ceremony and then devised a system of their own, a process sometimes called stimulus diffusion. The signs, on this view, are entirely original, but the concept behind them was borrowed. Tarabay compares the case with the nineteenth-century Cherokee syllabary, created by a man who could not read English but who had observed the power of written messages among European settlers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Aino Rimpiläinen, an archaeologist at the University of Turku, argues that the silence of the early visitors proves very little. Most of them stayed on the island for only a few days, communicated with its inhabitants through gestures, and were unlikely to have been shown objects that, according to later accounts, were regarded as sacred and kept in the houses of specialists. She also points to material evidence. Although several tablets are carved on driftwood or on European oars, suggesting late manufacture, the wood of at least one has been dated to a period well before the first European ships arrived. This is suggestive, but it falls short of proof: the age of a piece of wood is not the age of the signs carved on it, and timber on an almost treeless island may have been stored and reused over several generations.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different line of enquiry examines the internal structure of the inscriptions. Daisuke Matsuda, a computational epigrapher at Kyushu University, has catalogued long sequences of signs that recur, with small variations, on several different tablets, much as passages from a shared text might appear in several manuscripts. On one tablet he has identified a section in which signs resembling crescents appear at intervals that seem to correspond to the phases of the moon, and he believes this part at least served as a calendar. Matsuda is careful not to overstate his conclusions. The recurring sequences show that the signs carried structured information, he argues, but they do not reveal whether individual signs represented sounds, words or broader ideas.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The ethnologist Mirela Kovačić of the University of Zagreb has taken yet another approach, re-examining the accounts collected from islanders in the late nineteenth century. When elderly informants were asked to 'read' tablets, she observes, they frequently recited chants that bore little relation to one another, and on separate occasions the same person might offer quite different recitations for the same object. Kovačić concludes that the signs were prompts for memorised chants rather than a full record of them, comparable to the notched sticks and knotted cords used elsewhere in Polynesia to recall genealogies. Her reading of the sources is careful and important, yet the inconsistency she describes might equally reflect the partial knowledge of informants who had grown up after the island's trained experts had died.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Once again, the debate tends to be framed as a stark choice between true writing and mere memory aid, as though there were no intermediate possibilities. Many early scripts recorded only part of what a speaker would say and relied on the reader's knowledge to supply the rest. Whatever its nature, rongorongo poses a severe practical problem: the entire surviving corpus amounts to perhaps fifteen thousand signs, far less than was available for any successfully deciphered script. Most specialists believe that a full decipherment will remain impossible unless new material is found. Their pessimism is probably justified, but it need not mean the end of research. The most realistic goal is not to read the tablets aloud but to understand how the system was organised and what kinds of knowledge it was used to preserve.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For the people of Rapa Nui today, rongorongo is more than an academic puzzle. Local artists have revived the signs in carving and tattooing, and community organisations have asked museums abroad to return the tablets, or at least to share their images and research freely with the island. Questions about where the tablets belong, and who should have the final say over how they are studied and displayed, are not ones that scholars alone are entitled to settle.

topic: how and why the Greeks added vowel letters when adapting the Phoenician script
title: The Invention of the Vowel
subtitle: When the Greeks borrowed the Phoenician script, they changed it in one crucial respect. Was it a stroke of genius or a happy accident?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some time in the eighth century BCE, Greek speakers adopted the script used by Phoenician merchants and transformed it into the ancestor of the alphabets now used across Europe. Their most celebrated change was to give vowels letters of their own, placing them on an equal footing with consonants. This innovation is regularly described as the birth of the 'first true alphabet', and some twentieth-century theorists went further, crediting it with nothing less than the rise of democracy, philosophy and rational enquiry in the Greek world. The celebratory story is appealing, but almost every element of it deserves closer scrutiny than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanics of the change are not in dispute. The Phoenician script consisted of twenty-two letters, all representing consonants, and several of them stood for sounds that did not exist in Greek, including a glottal stop and a guttural sound produced deep in the throat. Rather than discarding these letters, the Greeks reassigned them. The letter called 'alep, for example, became alpha and was used for the vowel a, while others gave rise to epsilon, iota and omicron. The Greeks also attached a few entirely new letters to the end of the sequence, such as phi, chi and psi, for sounds or combinations of sounds that Phoenician did not need, although these additions have attracted far less attention than the vowels. What remains contested is how this happened, and in particular whether the result was the product of a deliberate plan.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sofia Antonakopoulou, a historical linguist at the University of Athens, believes that no plan was needed. Phoenician letters were taught by their names, and each name began with the sound the letter represented. A Greek learner hearing the name 'alep, she argues, would simply not have perceived the initial glottal stop, which had no equivalent in his own language, and would have heard the name as beginning with a vowel. Applying the same principle by which the Phoenicians themselves linked names and sounds, he would naturally have treated the letter as standing for a. On this account, the Greek vowels arose from a predictable mishearing. Antonakopoulou points out that the letters that became vowels are precisely those whose Phoenician sounds were absent from Greek, which is exactly what her hypothesis would predict.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tomasz Jaroszewicz of the Jagiellonian University in Kraków finds this explanation too passive. He argues that the vowel letters were the work of a single adapter who set out to solve a specific problem: recording poetry. Greek epic verse was built on patterns of long and short syllables, and a script that omitted vowels could not capture its rhythm. Jaroszewicz notes that several of the earliest surviving Greek inscriptions contain lines of verse, among them a drinking cup from a Greek settlement in southern Italy that bears three lines, two of them in the metre of epic poetry. He also emphasises that, although the local Greek alphabets of the period differ in many details, they assign the same letters to the same vowels, a uniformity that in his view points to a single act of invention.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The uniformity is indeed striking, and it does suggest that the vowels were established once rather than reinvented in different places. But a single origin does not require a deliberate design: one adapter mishearing the Phoenician names, exactly as Antonakopoulou describes, would produce the same consistent result. In this respect the two hypotheses are less incompatible than their supporters tend to assume. The poetic evidence is also weaker than it appears. Early Greek inscriptions include owners' names, dedications to gods and practice alphabets as well as verse, and the handful of verse examples is too small, and too likely to have survived by chance, to reveal what the first adapter had in mind.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental challenge comes from Rania Maalouf, a specialist in Semitic inscriptions at the Lebanese University in Beirut. She objects to the very assumption that the Phoenician script lacked something. In Semitic languages, she explains, words are built from roots of usually three consonants, with vowels varying according to grammatical function, so that a skilled reader can supply the vowels from context with little difficulty. Moreover, Phoenician and especially Aramaic scribes had already begun to use certain consonant letters to indicate long vowels in some positions. The Greek development, in Maalouf's view, was a systematic extension of an existing practice rather than a sudden conceptual leap. Her argument deserves wider acceptance than it has received, for describing consonantal scripts as defective reflects the assumptions of speakers of European languages rather than any genuine shortcoming in the scripts themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, of the larger claims made for the Greek alphabet? The notion that writing vowels transformed the Greek mind is very hard to sustain. Literacy in classical Athens appears to have been limited to a minority, and the Semitic consonantal scripts supported rich traditions of law, poetry and religious writing, as their continued use for Hebrew and Arabic demonstrates. Nor did the Etruscans, Romans and other peoples who later borrowed Greek letters undergo any sudden intellectual awakening as a result. The Greek innovation was clever, and its consequences for the later history of European writing were immense. It was not, however, a revolution in human thought.

topic: whether the knotted-cord khipus of the Inca Andes should be regarded as a form of writing
title: Knots That Speak?
subtitle: The Andean khipu has been called an accounting device, a memory aid and a lost form of writing. The evidence for each view is surprisingly hard to weigh

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When Spanish soldiers reached the Andes in the 1530s, they encountered a state that governed millions of people across some 4,000 kilometres of mountainous terrain without, apparently, any form of writing. What the Inca possessed instead were khipus: bundles of knotted cords, usually of cotton or the spun hair of llamas and alpacas, hanging from a thicker primary cord. Specialist record-keepers used them to track tribute, census figures and the contents of state storehouses, and several early colonial chroniclers reported that the same specialists could 'read' from them histories, genealogies and even songs. Around a thousand khipus survive today, most of them in museum collections far from the Andes, and almost all were dug up without any record of where or alongside what they were found. Whether these objects constitute writing remains a stubborn question, and the answer depends at least as much on how writing is defined as on the cords themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The numerical side of the puzzle was solved early in the twentieth century, when it was shown that many khipus record quantities in a decimal system. Knots placed furthest from the primary cord represent units, with tens, hundreds and thousands positioned progressively closer to it. Three kinds of knot are used: single knots for most values, 'long' knots with several turns in the units position, and a distinctive figure-of-eight knot for the number one. The absence of any knot in a given position signifies zero, a concept the Inca therefore handled in practice. On the strength of this discovery, it has been estimated that perhaps two-thirds of surviving khipus are essentially numerical. The remaining third, sometimes labelled 'anomalous' because their knots do not fit the decimal pattern, has become the focus of the debate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For Rafael Ccorimanya, an archaeologist at the Andean Institute of Cultural Studies, the case for a narrative function rests on more than the testimony of the chroniclers. Khipus, he points out, vary in many dimensions besides their knots: the colour of each cord, the type of fibre, the direction in which it was spun, and the way it is attached to the primary cord. Combining these variables, Ccorimanya calculates that a khipu-maker had well over a thousand distinct cord types available, a repertoire comparable in size to the sign inventories of some logographic scripts. To him, the conclusion is unavoidable: the Inca wrote in thread. This is an attractive argument, but a large stock of possible signs is not in itself proof that the signs recorded language; systems of heraldry and textile ornament can be equally rich without encoding a single word.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ottilie Taubmann, a historian at the Hanseatic Archive Institute, approaches the question through colonial documents. In the decades after the conquest, Spanish officials not only tolerated khipus but relied on them, and courts accepted their testimony in disputes over tribute and labour. In several cases Taubmann has found the same transaction recorded twice, once on a khipu read aloud by its keeper and once in a Spanish notary's transcription. Such pairs are, in principle, the Andean equivalent of a bilingual inscription. Her difficulty is that none of the cords mentioned in these documents has been securely identified among surviving collections. In 1583 a church council in Lima ordered that khipus be burned as instruments of idolatry, and although the order was unevenly enforced, it ensured that the cords most closely tied to Spanish records were also the most likely to be destroyed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach treats khipus as data. A team led by Dariusz Wolanin at the Kraków Laboratory for Computational Archaeology has built a database recording every measurable feature of more than 600 specimens and searched it for recurring sequences. The team has identified groups of khipus that appear to be copies or summaries of one another, with totals on one specimen matching the sums of values on others, which suggests a hierarchy of accounts passing upwards from local to regional administrators. Wolanin is cautious about the anomalous khipus, arguing that statistical regularities can reveal structure but cannot by themselves reveal meaning. Patterns that look like grammar, he warns, may equally be the product of bookkeeping conventions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most intriguing evidence comes not from museums but from living communities. In a few highland villages, khipus were kept as communal heirlooms into the twentieth century, and elders could partly explain how they had been used. The anthropologist Noor Elkadiri, working in one such village, recorded a tradition that certain cords stood for the names of family lineages, distinguished by colour and by the animal whose fibre had been used. If correct, this would mean that some khipus encoded the sounds of particular words, and not merely quantities or categories, which is precisely the threshold that most definitions of writing require. Elkadiri herself stresses that the cords concerned date from the colonial period or later and may reflect the influence of Spanish literacy.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The insistence that only systems which record spoken language count as true writing has been useful in separating scripts from pictures, but it sits awkwardly with the khipu, which may have done much of the administrative work that writing did elsewhere without necessarily representing speech. The more productive question is not whether khipus pass a test devised for Mesopotamian clay tablets, but how a large state managed to store and transmit information in a medium that was three-dimensional, tactile and coded by colour. Answering it will require the cords to be studied alongside the archives and the memories of the communities that preserved them; none of these sources, on its own, is likely to be sufficient.

topic: the creation of the Korean Hangul alphabet, the debate over its origins and its slow acceptance by Korea's elite
title: Letters by Royal Design
subtitle: Korea's alphabet is often hailed as the most rational script ever devised. Its history is more complicated than the praise suggests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few writing systems attract as much admiration as Hangul, the alphabet used today by around 80 million speakers of Korean. Linguists from many countries have described it as the most scientific script in the world, and its creation is commemorated each year with a national holiday in South Korea. Unlike most scripts, which evolved gradually over centuries and whose inventors are unknown, Hangul was devised deliberately, at a known date, under the direction of a single monarch. Much of the praise is deserved. Yet the celebratory story tends to pass quickly over two awkward facts: that the script may have borrowed more from its neighbours than is usually admitted, and that for several centuries after its invention the people who held power in Korea largely refused to use it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Before the fifteenth century, Koreans wrote in Classical Chinese, a language very different in grammar and sound from their own. Various methods had been developed for adapting Chinese characters to Korean, using some for their meaning and others for their pronunciation, but these remained cumbersome and required years of study. Literacy was therefore confined largely to a small aristocratic class. In 1443 King Sejong completed a new set of 28 letters, and three years later published them in a document whose title may be translated as 'The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People'. Its preface explains that ordinary people who wished to express themselves in writing were frequently unable to do so, and that the new letters were intended to be learned easily and used every day.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The design of the letters is remarkable. The basic consonant shapes are thought to represent the organs of speech as each sound is produced: the letter for 'k', for example, depicts the back of the tongue raised to block the throat, while the letter for 'm' outlines the closed mouth. Related sounds are then formed by adding strokes, so that a stronger or aspirated consonant visibly derives from a weaker one. Vowels are built from three elements, a dot, a horizontal line and a vertical line, said to represent heaven, earth and humanity. Letters are not written in a simple line but grouped into square blocks, each corresponding to a syllable. Aurelio Iturrioz, a phonetician at the Basque Centre for Language Sciences, argues that this 'featural' principle, in which the shape of a letter encodes how its sound is made, has no real parallel among scripts in widespread use. On this point he is surely correct, although it is worth remembering that the principle is not applied with complete consistency across the original inventory.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More controversial is the question of where the shapes came from. The historian Namgung Seo-yun of Hanbit University draws attention to a passage in a court record stating that the letters imitated 'ancient seal characters', a phrase usually taken as a vague reference to Chinese calligraphy. Namgung proposes instead that it may refer to the Phags-pa script, an alphabet devised in the thirteenth century for the Mongol rulers of China and known to Korean scholars of the period. Several basic consonants, she notes, resemble Phags-pa letters closely in outline. The argument is plausible, but it hardly diminishes the achievement. Borrowing a handful of outlines is a very different matter from borrowing a system, and nothing in Phags-pa resembles the derivation of related sounds by added strokes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What followed the invention was less triumphant. In 1444 a group of senior scholar-officials submitted a formal protest, warning that abandoning Chinese characters would cut Korea off from civilisation. For the next four centuries, official documents, examinations and serious scholarship continued in Classical Chinese, and the new letters were often dismissed as a 'vernacular script' fit only for women and the uneducated. In 1504 a king even banned their use after anonymous posters written in them criticised his rule. Hafsa Siddiqa, a sociolinguist at the Lahore Institute of Language and Society, argues that this low status should not be mistaken for failure. Excluded from public life, the alphabet flourished in private domains: in letters between family members, in Buddhist texts, in popular novels and in the diaries of aristocratic women, creating a large community of readers who had never been taught Chinese.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Hangul became the official script of government only in 1894, and for much of the twentieth century it was written alongside Chinese characters. North Korea abandoned characters entirely in 1949, while South Korea reduced their use more gradually. Today Korea's literacy rate is among the highest in the world, a fact often attributed directly to the simplicity of its alphabet. Mateus Baltazar, an economic historian at the Lisbon School of Social Sciences, disputes this explanation, pointing out that mass literacy arrived only with compulsory schooling in the second half of the twentieth century, five hundred years after the script was devised. His objection is fair, but it can be pushed too far. A script that can be learned in days does not create readers by itself; it does, however, make the task of a national school system considerably easier.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of Hangul, then, is not simply the story of a brilliant invention. It is also a reminder that the success of a writing system depends less on the elegance of its design than on who is permitted, or encouraged, to use it.

topic: the origins of the Germanic runic alphabet and the Viking-Age reduction of the futhark from 24 to 16 letters
title: Carved Against the Grain
subtitle: Where did the runic alphabet come from, and why did Scandinavians later choose to make it smaller?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a thousand years, the peoples of northern Europe wrote in runes, an alphabet of angular letters carved into wood, bone, metal and stone. The earliest securely dated inscriptions, from the second half of the second century AD, appear on portable objects such as combs, spearheads and brooches, many of them recovered from bogs in southern Scandinavia where captured weapons were deposited as offerings after battles. Most consist of a single word, often a personal name. The alphabet is known as the futhark, after the sounds of its first six letters, and in its oldest form it contained 24 characters arranged in a sequence quite unlike that of any Mediterranean script. Almost everything else about it, including where it came from, is disputed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That the runes were modelled on a Mediterranean alphabet is not in serious doubt: several letters closely resemble Latin or Greek counterparts in both form and sound value. The question is which one. Ildikó Szántó, a philologist at the Pannonian Institute of Early Literacy, favours the alphabets of the Alpine region, used by peoples in what are now northern Italy and southern Switzerland until around the first century BC. These scripts, she points out, share with runes certain letter shapes that are absent from Latin, and inscriptions in them sometimes run from right to left or alternate direction from line to line, as early runic texts also do. Their weakness as a source is chronological: the Alpine scripts had largely fallen out of use some two hundred years before the first runic inscriptions appear.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Gaspard Ollivier of the Rouen Centre for Medieval Studies argues that the Latin alphabet is the more likely model. Germanic warriors served in large numbers in the Roman army, and Roman coins, inscribed objects and trade goods circulated far beyond the imperial frontier. In Ollivier's view, the runes were created by someone familiar with Latin writing who adapted it deliberately rather than copying it, giving the letters new names and a new order so that the script would be recognisably Germanic. This account fits the dates better than Szántó's, but it leaves unexplained the letters with no Latin equivalent. Moreover, the chronological objection to the Alpine theory may be less damaging than it seems. If the earliest runes were cut mainly into wood, which rarely survives in the ground, the alphabet could be considerably older than its oldest surviving examples.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Wood may also explain the appearance of the letters. Runes consist almost entirely of vertical and diagonal strokes, and they lack the horizontal lines and curves found in Mediterranean scripts. A horizontal cut made along the grain of a wooden stick tends to split the surface or disappear into the natural lines of the wood, whereas a cut across the grain remains clear. The explanation is a sensible one, and it is consistent with the large numbers of inscribed sticks recovered from later medieval towns, though it cannot be tested directly for the earliest period, from which so little wood remains.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most puzzling episode in runic history came in the eighth century, when the alphabet used in Scandinavia was reduced from 24 letters to 16, producing what is now called the Younger Futhark. The change took place within a few generations at most, and it happened at a time when the spoken language was acquiring more distinct sounds, not fewer. As a result, a single rune frequently had to stand for several sounds: one letter served for both 'k' and 'g', another for 'u', 'o' and 'w'. Eeva Saarnio, a linguist at the Helsinki Institute of Nordic Philology, interprets the reform as a consequence of changes in pronunciation that had altered the names of several runes. Because each rune represented the first sound of its name, a rune whose name now began differently no longer indicated its original value and could be dropped. Oluwaseun Adekanbi, an archaeologist at the Centre for Comparative Archaeology in Ibadan, sees practical motives instead: a smaller set of simpler signs was quicker to carve and easier for traders and craftsmen to learn.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Neither account is wholly convincing. Saarnio's explains why particular letters disappeared but not why the reform was so drastic, while Adekanbi's assumes that writers were willing to accept considerable ambiguity in exchange for speed. What is clear is that the reduced alphabet did not hinder runic writing. The Viking Age and the centuries that followed produced several thousand rune stones, most of them in Sweden, commemorating the dead and recording journeys, inheritances and the building of bridges. Excavations at a medieval harbour in western Norway have uncovered more than six hundred inscribed sticks, among them owners' labels for goods, business messages and private notes. Runes continued in use alongside the Latin alphabet for several centuries after Christianity reached Scandinavia.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In popular culture, runes are usually presented as a mystical script, the preserve of magicians and fortune-tellers. Some inscriptions do contain formulas whose purpose seems to have been protective, and it would be wrong to dismiss this aspect altogether. Yet the humble sticks of the medieval towns point to a more ordinary picture, in which runes were above all a practical tool for everyday communication. It is a less romantic conclusion than the popular image, but it is far better supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, the proportion of students leaving university with the highest classes of degree has risen steadily in many countries. In some national systems the share of top grades has more than doubled within a single generation. The phenomenon has come to be known as grade inflation, a term borrowed from economics, where it describes money losing its purchasing power as prices rise. The metaphor is apt in one respect: when top grades become plentiful, each one buys less, in the sense that it tells an observer less about the person who holds it. In another respect, however, it is misleading, because it implies that there was once a stable standard against which today's grades can be measured, and that assumption is far harder to defend than is usually acknowledged.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely cited case against rising grades concerns information. Ilse Lacroix-Bah, an economist at the Northern Institute for Higher Education Studies, argues that a grade is essentially a signal, a compact message that allows employers and admissions panels to distinguish one applicant from another. If most graduates cluster in the top band, the signal is compressed against a ceiling and loses its power to discriminate. Employers do not simply give up, Lacroix-Bah notes; they turn to other indicators, such as the reputation of the university attended, unpaid internships and extracurricular achievements. These alternatives tend to favour students from wealthier families, who are more likely to have attended prestigious institutions and to be able to afford unpaid work. This consequence, it seems to me, is the most serious of all, yet it is rarely mentioned in public debate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that grades have become less meaningful. Rafael Paiwonsky, who researches learning and assessment at Halden Coast University, contends that rising marks may reflect genuine improvement. Teaching has become more professional, he points out, assessment criteria are now published in advance, and students have become far more strategic in directing their effort towards what is rewarded. To speak of inflation, in his view, is to assume without evidence that performance has stood still. This argument deserves a fair hearing, but the data offer it only limited support. When analysts compare cohorts with similar qualifications on entry, a substantial part of the increase remains unaccounted for. One study by Mark Tamarkin's group at the Centre for Assessment Research estimated that at least half of the rise in top grades over a fifteen-year period could not be explained by any measurable change in the students being admitted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tamarkin himself has been more interested in why marks rise than in whether they should. He identifies a set of institutional pressures that push in the same direction. National rankings frequently include the proportion of good degrees awarded as a measure of quality, so a university that marks strictly is penalised in the tables. Students who pay substantial fees increasingly regard themselves as customers and may challenge marks they consider unfair. Perhaps most subtly, lecturers are often evaluated partly through student satisfaction surveys, and there is evidence that those who mark generously receive more favourable ratings. None of these pressures, Tamarkin concedes, can be shown to have caused grade inflation on its own, but together they create an environment in which leniency carries few costs and strictness carries many.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A rather different perspective comes from the sociologist Halina Zdunek, who argues that grades have never been anchored to a fixed standard. Until the late twentieth century, many systems used what is known as norm referencing, in which only a fixed proportion of candidates could receive each grade, regardless of how well the group performed overall. The widespread shift towards criterion referencing, under which any student who meets a published description of achievement receives the corresponding grade, made an increase in top marks almost inevitable. On this account, much of what is called inflation is the predictable result of a deliberate change in policy. Zdunek's historical point is well made, but it does not settle the matter. Even under criterion referencing, the way markers interpret phrases such as 'excellent analysis' can drift gradually over time, and most systems have no mechanism for detecting such drift.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Proposed remedies are as varied as the diagnoses. Lacroix-Bah favours a partial return to quotas, limiting the share of students in any course who can receive the highest grade. Critics respond that this would set students against one another and discourage the collaboration that good learning often requires. A less drastic option is to report each grade alongside information about how it compares, for instance by showing the average mark awarded in that course. Yet transparency can have unintended effects. At one university that began publishing course averages online, enrolment shifted noticeably towards courses with a reputation for generous marking, which, if anything, intensified the pressure on strict markers to relent. Information on its own, it appears, is no cure.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, is the real problem? In my view, it is not that grades are high but that the same grade means different things in different places. A top grade from one department may represent a level of achievement that another would reward only modestly. The solution must therefore involve shared calibration: markers from different institutions regularly comparing samples of student work and agreeing what each grade represents. Such schemes are expensive and slow, and some versions of them have already fallen into neglect. But unless the meaning of a grade can be stabilised across institutions, debates about whether there are too many top grades will continue to miss the point.

topic: class size reduction: randomised experiments, problems of scaling up, teacher quality and changes in classroom practice
title: The Arithmetic of the Classroom
subtitle: Smaller classes are popular with parents and teachers alike, but the evidence for them is more complicated than their supporters admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few education policies enjoy such broad support as reducing the number of pupils in each class. Parents assume that their children will receive more individual attention, teachers report lower levels of stress, and politicians find the policy easy to explain and popular to announce. Yet it is also one of the most expensive interventions available to governments. Cutting the average class from thirty pupils to twenty does not require a modest adjustment; it requires half as many teachers again, together with the classrooms in which they will teach. A policy with such a price deserves closer scrutiny than it usually receives, and when that scrutiny is applied, the picture that emerges is considerably more complicated than either its champions or its critics tend to suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the optimism rests on a single large experiment conducted in the 1980s. A regional education authority randomly assigned several thousand children, at the start of their schooling, either to small classes of around fifteen pupils or to regular classes of around twenty-four, and kept them in those classes for four years. Teachers, too, were allocated to classes at random, so that differences in outcomes could not easily be blamed on the more skilful teachers choosing smaller groups. Researchers led by Beatriz Mascarenhas at the Institute for Educational Evaluation found that pupils in the small classes outperformed their peers by a margin equivalent to several months of learning, and that the gains were largest among children from low-income families. When the same pupils were traced into adolescence, those who had been in small classes were more likely to complete secondary school. Mascarenhas concluded that reducing class sizes in the earliest years is one of the very few interventions whose benefits endure long after it has ended.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The economist Juhani Koskinen does not dispute these findings, but he doubts that they can be reproduced across an entire school system. He points to the case of one large state which, shortly afterwards, reduced class sizes in all of its primary schools within the space of two years. To do so it had to recruit tens of thousands of new teachers, many of them inexperienced and some without full qualifications. Wealthier districts, able to offer better conditions, attracted the strongest candidates, while schools in poorer areas were left with whoever remained. Libraries and art rooms were converted into classrooms. The gains in achievement turned out to be far smaller than the experiment had predicted, and in the most disadvantaged schools they were barely detectable. For Koskinen, the lesson is that the quality of the teacher matters far more than the number of pupils in front of them, and that the money spent on smaller classes would achieve more if it were invested in developing the teachers already employed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Koskinen's warning is an important one, but his conclusion goes further than the evidence allows. What the state programme demonstrates is that a hurried reform, introduced without the teachers or buildings to support it, is likely to disappoint; it does not show that smaller classes are ineffective in themselves. A gradual introduction, matched to the supply of qualified staff, might well have avoided the problems he describes. Nor are class size and teacher quality straightforward alternatives. Smaller classes make teaching a more manageable job, and there are indications that they may persuade some teachers to remain in the profession who would otherwise leave.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why smaller classes help, when they do, is a question that Anahit Petrosyan, who studies classroom interaction, has tried to answer through direct observation. Her team spent hundreds of hours in classrooms of different sizes and found, somewhat unexpectedly, that many teachers given smaller classes continued to teach in much the same way as before, addressing the whole group from the front of the room. In such cases the benefits were slight. Where clear gains appeared, teachers had altered their practice: they gave more frequent individual feedback, noticed misunderstandings earlier and spent less time dealing with disruptive behaviour. Petrosyan therefore describes a reduction in class size not as a treatment in its own right but as an opportunity, one that produces little unless teachers are trained to make use of it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The debate is often framed as a simple choice between supporting and opposing smaller classes, but the more useful question is for whom, and at what stage of education, they make a difference. The evidence is strongest for the youngest children and for those from disadvantaged backgrounds; there is little to suggest that trimming a secondary school class from twenty-eight to twenty-five achieves very much. A targeted programme, concentrated in the early years in poorer areas and accompanied by training for the teachers involved, is therefore well justified. Blanket reductions across every year group, by contrast, are hard to defend on the basis of the research. A policy that helps everyone a little is easier to announce than one that helps some a great deal, but it is the latter that the evidence supports.

topic: grade retention (making pupils repeat a school year): flawed early studies, cut-off score comparisons, emotional costs and intensive support as an alternative
title: A Second Year in the Same Seat
subtitle: Making struggling pupils repeat a year is routine in some countries and almost unknown in others. What does the evidence say?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In some education systems, a fifth or more of pupils repeat at least one school year before the age of fifteen, and in certain regions the proportion is higher still. In others, promotion with one's age group is automatic, and repetition is reserved for exceptional circumstances such as a prolonged illness. Supporters of the practice, usually known as grade retention, argue that it gives a struggling child the time needed to master the foundations on which later learning depends. Opponents reply that it stigmatises children and wastes public money, since every repeated year costs the state the price of an additional year of schooling. What is striking is that such divergent practices persist among countries with broadly similar levels of wealth and similar school systems. This suggests that national tradition, rather than any careful weighing of evidence, is what largely determines whether children are held back.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For several decades, the research seemed to favour the opponents. Study after study compared pupils who had been retained with classmates who had been promoted, and found that the retained group fared worse in later years: their test scores were lower and they were more likely to leave school without qualifications. Dorota Lisowska, a statistician at the Centre for Evidence in Schooling, has argued that such comparisons are fundamentally misleading. Pupils are held back precisely because they are already struggling, so it is hardly surprising that they continue to do less well than their average peers. Comparing the two groups, she points out, confuses the effect of retention with the reasons it was imposed in the first place. Her criticism is, to my mind, decisive, and it means that much of the older literature can tell us very little.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Lisowska's own studies take advantage of systems in which the decision to retain is made according to a fixed cut-off score on an end-of-year test. Pupils who fall just below the line and those who scrape just above it are, for practical purposes, almost identical in ability, so any later difference between them can reasonably be attributed to retention itself. The results are more nuanced than either side of the debate would like. In the year after repeating, retained pupils showed clear gains, often outperforming those who had narrowly passed. Within three to four years, however, this advantage had faded, and by the end of compulsory education there was no measurable difference between the two groups.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Test scores, of course, are not the only consideration. The developmental psychologist Tafadzwa Tumbare has interviewed several hundred children who were held back, and her findings challenge a common assumption. The damage to a child's sense of self, she reports, arises less from the decision itself than from what follows it: separation from friends and placement among younger classmates, where the retained child may feel conspicuous. Adolescents were considerably more distressed than younger children, partly because friendships matter more to them and partly because the difference in age is more visible. Tumbare concludes that, if retention is used at all, it should be confined to the first years of school.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These emotional costs are real, but it would be a mistake to assume that the alternative is painless. A child who is promoted without having mastered basic reading or arithmetic may face a different kind of humiliation: years of sitting through lessons that he or she cannot follow, falling further behind with each term. The relevant comparison, in other words, is not between retention and some ideal outcome, but between retention and what actually happens to struggling pupils who move up with their class. Too often, critics of retention have compared it with an alternative that does not exist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That alternative can, however, be created. The policy analyst Henrik Nyquist has examined a system that abolished retention and redirected the money saved into intensive support, consisting of summer schools and small-group tutoring during the school year. Over the following decade, the achievement of the lowest-performing pupils improved more than it had under retention, and at a lower cost per pupil. Nyquist is careful to add that the benefits depended heavily on tutoring being provided by trained staff; where schools relied on volunteers, little was gained. Meanwhile, a team led by Samira Bokhari at a teacher-training college has investigated why retention remains popular with teachers despite such findings. Teachers, the team found, see the improvement of retained pupils at first hand, while the fade-out that follows occurs after those pupils have moved on to other classrooms.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the evidence suggests that retention is neither the disaster its critics describe nor the remedy its supporters hope for. It is, for the most part, a costly way of purchasing a temporary improvement. The money would generally be better spent on early, targeted support for children who are falling behind. Governments that wish to reduce their retention rates should therefore begin by building the kind of support that makes repetition unnecessary, and only then remove the option of holding pupils back. Abolishing retention without putting such support in place would simply leave the weakest pupils to drift through school, and that would be no improvement at all.

topic: international comparative assessments of fifteen-year-olds: league tables, policy borrowing, student effort on low-stakes tests and the value of within-country trends
title: Ranking the World's Classrooms
subtitle: International surveys of student achievement have become powerful instruments of education policy. Are they being asked to carry more weight than they can bear?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years, the results of large international surveys that test fifteen-year-olds in reading, mathematics and science are published, and education ministers around the world brace themselves. Countries that rise in the rankings celebrate; those that fall face newspaper headlines about national decline, and a drop of only a few places has been enough to trigger sweeping reforms. In little more than two decades, these surveys have become some of the most influential documents in education policy. Their influence, I would argue, now exceeds what the underlying data can reasonably support, and the reasons are worth examining.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The surveys are technically sophisticated. In each participating country, a sample of several thousand students is selected, and each student answers only a portion of a large pool of questions. Statistical models are then used to estimate how the whole population would have performed, and the results are reported on a common scale. The designers are careful to point out that countries lying close together on that scale often cannot be distinguished with any confidence; a country in twelfth place may not genuinely differ from one in twentieth. When the results are presented as a league table, however, this uncertainty disappears from view. The designers deserve credit for the rigour of their methods, but they could do considerably more to discourage the misleading uses to which their figures are routinely put.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Lucia Morandini, a researcher at the Institute of Comparative Pedagogy, has studied what happens after the results appear. Countries that perform poorly frequently send delegations to the top performers and return with ideas to copy: a particular style of textbook, a structure for training teachers, a longer or shorter school day. Morandini's research suggests that the features copied are often not the ones responsible for success. High-performing systems, she argues, rest heavily on cultural foundations, such as the value families place on education and, in some cases, extensive private tutoring outside school hours, none of which can be transplanted by a ministry. She cites the case of one country that adopted the mathematics textbooks of a leading performer almost wholesale; a decade later, its scores had scarcely moved.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different set of doubts concerns the tests themselves. Gábor Takacsy, a specialist in educational measurement, notes that the surveys are low-stakes for the students who sit them: their results have no bearing on their own grades or prospects. The effort that students invest may therefore vary considerably between countries, depending on attitudes to authority and to testing in general. In a series of experiments, Takacsy's team offered students small financial incentives for each correct answer. Scores rose noticeably in some countries but hardly at all in others, which suggests that the rankings partly reflect willingness to try hard on a test that does not matter personally. He has also found that certain questions appear to become harder when translated into particular languages, although the size of this effect remains disputed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The surveys nonetheless have able defenders. Inés Arvelo, an economist at a development research institute, argues that, whatever their flaws, they provide the only comparable evidence of what students in different countries can actually do. Before they existed, governments judged their school systems by their own national examinations, and these, as Arvelo rightly observes, have a tendency to show improvement year after year, partly because teachers become familiar with the style of the questions. The international surveys revealed uncomfortable truths, such as the discovery that in some countries with near-universal school enrolment, large numbers of students could not read a simple text. For Arvelo, the real value lies not in the rankings at all but in the detailed data on how a country's results change over time and on how performance relates to students' family backgrounds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Arvelo's case is persuasive, and abandoning the surveys would be a genuine loss. The difficulty is that it is the rankings, not the detailed data, that capture the attention of politicians and the press. One modest reform would be to publish results in broad bands rather than precise positions, and to give greater prominence to changes within each country than to comparisons between them. Much of this information already exists in the technical reports that accompany each round of results, but those documents run to hundreds of pages and are read by only a small circle of specialists. Giving the same information prominence in the published summaries would cost almost nothing. Critics object that this would make the results less newsworthy. That, surely, is precisely the point.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most useful way to think about the surveys is as a thermometer rather than a medicine. They can tell a country that something is wrong, and sometimes roughly where, but they cannot tell it what to do about the problem. Several of the countries whose results improved most markedly did so through reforms developed at home and sustained over many years, rather than through measures imported in haste. Such reform requires a far more patient understanding of a nation's own schools, teachers and communities than any international table can offer, and it is in the pursuit of such understanding, rather than in the search for a higher position, that the surveys can make their most valuable contribution.

topic: comparative judgement as an alternative to rubric-based marking of essays: reliability, feedback, bias and institutional obstacles
title: Better Judged Than Measured?
subtitle: A method that asks examiners to compare pieces of work rather than score them is challenging long-held assumptions about marking

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has marked a pile of essays knows how uncertain the process can be. Examiners are typically given a mark scheme, or rubric, listing the qualities they should look for and the number of marks each is worth. Yet when the same essay is given to several trained examiners, they frequently award it different marks, and the same examiner may award it different marks on different days. In subjects such as literature and history, disagreements of a full grade are far from rare. Rubrics were introduced precisely to reduce this kind of subjectivity, but in my view they have often succeeded only in creating an illusion of precision, dressing up uncertain human judgements in the language of measurement.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: An alternative known as comparative judgement abandons scores altogether. Judges are shown two pieces of work side by side and asked a single question: which is better? Each piece is compared many times with different partners by different judges, and a statistical model converts the thousands of resulting decisions into a scale on which every piece has a position. The principle behind the method is well established. People are poor at making absolute judgements but remarkably good at relative ones; it is far easier to say which of two parcels is heavier than to estimate the weight of either in grams.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Siobhan Prendiville, who leads assessment research at the Dunmore Institute, has run large trials of the method with samples of writing by primary-school pupils. The teachers who acted as judges agreed with one another considerably more closely than teachers using a conventional rubric, and each decision took them well under a minute. Prendiville argues that the method succeeds because it allows judges to respond to the overall quality of a piece rather than breaking it into fragments. Rubrics, she contends, reward the presence of particular features, such as a variety of linking words or a certain number of descriptive phrases, and pupils soon learn to insert these mechanically, whether or not they serve any purpose in the writing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The philosopher of education Karim Elbadri has raised a series of objections. The first concerns transparency. A rubric, whatever its faults, allows a student to see why a particular mark was awarded and what might be done to improve it; comparative judgement produces only a position on a scale, with no explanation attached. Elbadri also worries that judges making rapid decisions may be swayed by superficial characteristics, such as neat handwriting or sheer length. Most fundamentally, he insists that agreement among judges should not be mistaken for accuracy. A group of judges who share the same assumptions can agree perfectly and still be wrong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Elbadri's concern about feedback is a serious one, but it rests on an optimistic view of what rubrics provide. A comment such as 'shows some evidence of analysis' tells a student remarkably little about how to write a better essay. Comparative judgement, moreover, produces something rubrics do not: a ranked collection of real work. Pupils who can examine pieces from different points on the scale, and see concretely what distinguishes a strong argument from a weak one, may learn more than they would from any list of criteria.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question of superficial bias has been investigated by the statistician Lena Ramsauer. In a series of experiments, she presented judges with identical essays, some written in neat handwriting and others in untidy script. Neatly written essays did receive a small advantage, but Ramsauer found an effect of almost exactly the same size when the essays were marked with a conventional rubric. The bias, in other words, belongs to human readers, not to the method. Ramsauer is less enthusiastic on another point: because comparative judgement depends on a large number of comparisons, it offers little benefit to a teacher assessing a single class of twenty-five pupils, for whom the effort involved may outweigh the gain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If the method is as promising as its supporters claim, why has it not been adopted for national examinations? Kenji Yanagawa, who studies assessment policy, argues that the obstacles are institutional rather than technical. Examination boards are often legally required to justify every mark in the event of an appeal, which is far easier when a rubric can be pointed to. In addition, the professional identity of many experienced examiners has been built around their mastery of mark schemes, and a method that makes such expertise less central is unlikely to be welcomed. Yanagawa expects comparative judgement to spread first in classroom assessment, where the consequences of any single result are modest, before it is trusted with high-stakes decisions.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Comparative judgement does not remove human judgement from assessment; rather, it makes the role of that judgement more honest. A sensible approach may well combine the two methods, using comparison to establish the order of a set of scripts and written comments to explain it. Some caution is nevertheless required. Most of the impressive figures for reliability come from studies conducted by researchers closely associated with the method, and they need to be confirmed by independent investigators before examination systems are rebuilt around them.

topic: homework policy: weak links with achievement, task design and retrieval practice, home inequality, homework clubs and pupil wellbeing
title: The Work That Follows Pupils Home
subtitle: Arguments about homework flare up every few years. The research suggests that both its defenders and its opponents are asking the wrong question

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years, a campaign to abolish homework gathers pace. Some primary schools announce that they will no longer set it at all; parents write to newspapers either applauding the decision or warning that standards will collapse; and politicians are asked whether they are for homework or against it. Much of this debate, it seems to me, generates more heat than light, because the word 'homework' covers activities that have very little in common. Ten minutes of reading aloud to a parent, a page of arithmetic exercises, a month-long research project and an evening of revision for an examination are all homework, yet there is no reason to expect them to have the same effects, and lumping them together makes any general verdict almost meaningless.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The research, viewed broadly, offers only modest support to either side. Large reviews combining the results of many studies have found a positive but fairly weak association between homework and achievement among secondary-school students, and an association close to zero among younger children. Ramón Talavera, an educational psychologist at the Southern Institute of Learning Research, warns that even the positive finding must be interpreted with care. The studies are largely correlational, and it may simply be that able and motivated students choose to do more homework, rather than that homework makes them more able. Moreover, the benefits appear to level off beyond about an hour and a half a day for older students and may even decline. In Talavera's view, the length of time a student spends is far less important than the kind of thinking a task demands: homework that requires students to recall and apply what they have learned is valuable, while homework that merely keeps them busy is not.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Talavera's conclusion is a welcome one, but it is sometimes misused. Several schools have cited research on the weak link between time and achievement as grounds for abandoning homework entirely, which does not follow at all. A substantial body of laboratory and classroom research shows that brief, frequent self-testing, in which students try to recall information rather than simply reread it, is one of the most effective study techniques known. Such practice is ideally suited to being done at home in short sessions. The real problem, then, is not homework itself but homework that is poorly designed, and the remedy is better tasks rather than none.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different set of concerns relates to fairness. Friederike Kirschbaum, a sociologist who studies families and schooling, points out that homework is the one part of education that takes place entirely outside the school's control. Children in comfortable households typically have a quiet room, a reliable internet connection and parents who can help; children in poorer households may share a bedroom with siblings, look after younger brothers and sisters, or have no computer at all. Homework set without regard to these circumstances, Kirschbaum argues, tends to widen the gaps that schools are supposed to narrow. Her research also complicates the assumption that parental involvement is always beneficial. When parents helped directly with the content of assignments, results were sometimes worse, partly because parents used methods that differed from those taught in class and partly because some simply completed the work themselves. Parental interest and encouragement, by contrast, were consistently associated with better outcomes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One popular response has been the homework club, in which pupils can complete their assignments at school, under supervision, after lessons end. The education economist Chidi Nwachuku evaluated a programme of such clubs across a large urban district and found the results disappointing. The pupils who most needed a quiet place to work were often the least likely to attend, because of transport difficulties or responsibilities at home, and the measurable benefits were concentrated among pupils who were already motivated. Nwachuku concludes that homework should be redesigned so that success does not depend on resources at home, with tasks that need neither an internet connection nor an adult's assistance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is much sense in this proposal, but taken to its logical conclusion it risks narrowing what all pupils are asked to do. If every task must be completable by a child with no books, no computer and no help, then extended projects and independent research, which many pupils find among the most rewarding parts of their schooling, would largely disappear. A better approach would be to supply what is missing, by lending devices, keeping libraries open in the evening and providing printed materials, rather than to limit every child's homework to what the least advantaged can manage.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, there is the question of wellbeing. Surveys of older teenagers in several countries have found that heavy homework loads are associated with stress, headaches and lost sleep, particularly among students at highly selective schools. These findings are correlational too, but they are consistent enough to take seriously, and setting sensible upper limits on homework for this age group would be entirely reasonable. Abolition, however, would be the wrong lesson to draw. Homework that is brief, purposeful and designed so that completing it does not depend on a child's circumstances at home remains one of the more valuable tools that schools possess.

topic: test-optional university admissions: equity claims, institutional incentives, predictive validity of entrance tests and contextual interpretation of scores
title: Admission Without the Test
subtitle: Universities that abandoned standardised entrance tests promised a fairer system. The evidence on whether they delivered it is surprisingly mixed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, universities in a number of countries required applicants to submit scores from a standardised admissions test, a single examination taken by candidates from every kind of school. Over the past two decades, a growing number of institutions have made such tests optional: applicants may submit a score if they wish, but are not obliged to. The movement accelerated sharply when test centres were forced to close during a public health emergency, and for a time it seemed that the tests might disappear from admissions altogether. More recently, however, several prominent universities have reinstated their requirements. This swing back and forth, I would suggest, reveals less about the tests themselves than about the uncertainty of universities over what their admissions processes are actually meant to achieve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against compulsory testing was built largely on fairness. Critics pointed out that scores are closely correlated with family income, and that wealthier families can pay for private coaching that raises their children's results. Tests, on this view, do not so much measure ability as reproduce existing privilege. Removing the requirement, it was argued, would encourage talented applicants from poorer backgrounds who might otherwise be deterred, either by the cost of the examination or by the fear that a modest score would rule them out. Early reports appeared to support this optimism, with many institutions announcing record numbers of applications, including from groups that had traditionally been under-represented.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A closer look has tempered that enthusiasm. Astrid Lundmark, a sociologist at the Institute for Higher Education Access, followed a group of colleges for several years after they went test-optional. Applications from low-income students did rise, but the proportion of such students who actually enrolled changed very little. Part of the explanation, Lundmark suggests, is that applications rose among every group, so that the colleges simply became more selective. She also noticed a less obvious effect. Because applicants with low scores tended not to submit them, the average scores that colleges published rose, improving their position in national rankings. This finding should make us cautious about the more generous accounts of the movement: it seems unlikely that every institution adopting the policy was motivated purely by a concern for equity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the economist Oleksandr Ivanchuk has examined whether the tests predict anything useful. Using records from several universities, he found that test scores predicted students' first-year grades and their likelihood of graduating, even after their school grades had been taken into account, and that they did so about as well for disadvantaged students as for others. School grades, Ivanchuk points out, have become steadily more generous and vary greatly in meaning from one school to another, so that an excellent report from one school may represent a quite different standard from an excellent report from another. A common test provides a yardstick that school grades cannot. Without it, he argues, admissions officers lose one of the few ways of spotting a gifted student at a weak school, whose high score stands out against the record of classmates.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ivanchuk's argument is a strong one, but it does not establish that tests should be compulsory, only that the information they provide is valuable. The deeper difficulty with optional policies lies in who decides whether a score is submitted. Applicants with modest scores tend to withhold them, even when those scores are, in fact, impressive given the schools they attended. There are reports of advisers in poorer schools encouraging students to withhold scores that would have strengthened their applications. The result is that information is lost precisely where it might have helped the most.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A possible way forward is proposed by Eleni Matsoukas, who studies admissions practice. She argues that scores should be read in context, by comparing each applicant's result with the typical result at his or her school. A score in the middle range, achieved at a school where most students score poorly, may signal more ability than a higher score achieved at a well-resourced school with extensive coaching. When two universities trialled this approach, they admitted noticeably more students from disadvantaged backgrounds, without any reduction in graduation rates. For Matsoukas, the problem has never been the tests themselves, but the way in which their results are interpreted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Contextual reading does not answer every objection. Coaching still advantages those who can afford it, even if its effects are smaller than is often claimed, and some capable students perform poorly under examination conditions for reasons that have nothing to do with their ability. Assessing every applicant in context also requires detailed information about thousands of schools and considerable time from trained staff, resources that are unevenly distributed among universities.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The question that universities should be asking, then, is not whether to require a test but how to use every piece of available information as fairly as possible. Of the approaches currently on offer, reading scores in context appears to be the most promising, combining the predictive value that Ivanchuk identifies with the concern for disadvantaged applicants that motivated the test-optional movement in the first place. It would be naive, however, to expect it to spread quickly. It demands a degree of transparency about how decisions are made that many admissions offices have traditionally avoided, and smaller institutions may simply lack the staff and data needed to carry it out properly.

topic: school inspection regimes: single-word graded verdicts, effects of failing grades, bias linked to intake, inspector reliability and separating accountability from support
title: A Verdict in One Word
subtitle: School inspection is meant both to reassure the public and to help schools improve. Can it really do both?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most countries with publicly funded schools send someone to look at them. In some systems, inspectors arrive with only a day's notice, spend two days observing lessons, examining pupils' work and interviewing staff, and then publish a report that summarises the school in a single grade, ranging from 'outstanding' to 'inadequate'. In others, inspection is a gentler affair, closer to a conversation between professionals, and the findings are never reduced to a label. The contrast reflects two quite different views of what inspection is for: to hold schools to account on behalf of parents and taxpayers, or to help them improve. My own view is that a system attempting to do both at once, as most now do, will tend to do neither particularly well.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for graded verdicts rests largely on their effect on parents. A single word is easy to understand, and families who would never read a forty-page report will certainly notice when a local school is declared failing. Lucía Cardozo, an economist at the Institute for Public Service Research, has studied what happens to schools that receive the lowest grade. In the two years after such a verdict, she found, pupils' examination results rose measurably, and the improvement was concentrated among the weakest pupils. Cardozo attributes this to the shock of public failure, which forces governors and head teachers to act on problems they had previously tolerated. Her findings are robust, and they ought to give pause to those who claim that inspection achieves nothing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet it does not follow that the grade itself is accurate. Tomasz Przybylak, a statistician who has compared inspection outcomes with the characteristics of the schools concerned, points out that schools serving disadvantaged neighbourhoods are considerably more likely to receive poor grades, even after their pupils' prior attainment is taken into account. One interpretation is that such schools really are less well run, since able teachers and leaders tend to avoid them. Another is that inspectors, who rely heavily on test data when deciding which grade to award, are partly measuring the intake rather than the quality of teaching. Przybylak suspects that the second explanation accounts for much of the pattern, though he concedes that his data cannot settle the matter. He has proposed that inspectors be shown results adjusted for pupils' backgrounds before they visit, although inspectorates have so far been reluctant to adopt the suggestion.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further problem concerns consistency. In a study that has been widely discussed among inspectors themselves, a team led by Kenji Yamashiro sent pairs of inspectors to the same schools on the same days, with each inspector instructed to reach a grade independently. The pairs agreed in roughly three cases out of four. That may sound respectable, but it means that in a quarter of cases a school's public reputation depended on which inspector happened to arrive. Agreement was highest at the extremes and lowest for schools in the middle of the range, precisely where the difference between two adjacent grades can determine whether a head teacher keeps his or her job.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such consequences shape behaviour long before any inspector walks through the door. Aisling Brennock, an education researcher who spent a year observing staff in schools preparing for inspection, describes how much effort went into producing evidence for visitors rather than into teaching itself: lesson plans rewritten in an approved format, exercise books marked to a uniform standard, classroom displays refreshed overnight. Teachers she interviewed spoke of anxiety that persisted for months. Brennock does not argue that inspection should be abolished, but she believes that the threat of a damaging grade encourages schools to perform for the inspector instead of improving in ways that would become visible only over several years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Critics of graded inspection often point to systems in which judgements are given in narrative form only, as if this resolved the difficulty. I am not convinced that it does. Where there is no single grade, parents and journalists tend to construct their own, picking out the most critical sentence in a report and quoting it as though it were a verdict. Some systems that abolished grades have also found it harder to identify schools in genuine difficulty quickly, since a carefully worded report can soften a problem that a blunt grade would expose. Removing the label, in short, does not remove the appetite for one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A more promising approach would separate the two functions of inspection. Routine monitoring, based largely on published data and short visits, could identify the small number of schools where something is seriously wrong, and these would be subject to full inspection with clear consequences. The great majority of schools would instead receive developmental visits from experienced practitioners, whose reports would not be published in graded form and whose purpose would be to help staff reflect on their practice. This would not remove every weakness of the current arrangements; inspectors would still disagree, and data would still reflect intake as well as quality. But it would ensure that the anxiety generated by high-stakes judgement is reserved for the cases where it is actually justified.
