title: Sorting the Class
subtitle: Placing pupils in groups according to their attainment is one of the most common practices in schooling. Does it help those it is meant to help?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few decisions in schooling are made as routinely, or with as little public debate, as the decision to group pupils by attainment. In much of the English-speaking world, children are placed in 'sets' for mathematics by the age of eleven, and in many secondary schools the practice extends to most academic subjects. Elsewhere, notably in several Nordic countries, pupils are kept in mixed classes until the end of lower secondary school, at around sixteen. A third model, often called streaming or tracking, allocates pupils to entirely separate schools or programmes, sometimes as early as the age of ten. The justification offered for grouping is intuitive: a teacher facing a narrower range of attainment can pitch lessons more precisely, stretching the able without leaving the struggling behind. Intuitive arguments, however, have a poor record in education, and this one deserves far more scrutiny than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential evidence comes from comparisons across systems. Ingrid Ahlstrand, an economist at a Scandinavian research institute, examined what happened to pupils' attainment between primary and secondary school in countries that select early and in those that do not. In early-selecting countries, the gap between high and low attainers widened markedly over those years, while average attainment was no higher. Her conclusion is that early separation increases inequality without raising standards overall. The method is ingenious, since it compares each country with itself at two points in time, but it cannot exclude the possibility that early-selecting countries differ in other ways that also widen gaps, such as the way their schools are funded. Ahlstrand acknowledges this, but points out that the pattern holds across countries with very different spending levels, which makes funding an unlikely explanation on its own.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Studies conducted within schools tell a more complicated story. Dimitar Dobrev, working with records from more than two hundred secondary schools, found that pupils placed in top sets made modestly faster progress than comparable pupils in mixed classes, whereas pupils in bottom sets made slower progress. The net effect across all pupils was close to zero; grouping, in effect, redistributed attainment from the bottom to the top. Dobrev was also struck by how imprecise allocation tended to be. Roughly a third of pupils, he estimated, were placed in a set that did not match their prior test scores, and misallocated pupils from poorer families were far more likely to have been placed too low than too high.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should bottom sets fare so badly? Rosalind Seebohm, who has spent several hundred hours observing lessons, argues that the explanation lies less in the grouping itself than in what accompanies it. Lower sets, she reports, were more often taught by inexperienced or non-specialist teachers, were given less demanding work and experienced more frequent disruption. Teachers' expectations, moreover, appeared to adjust to the label: pupils in a set described as 'low ability' were assumed to be incapable of tasks that, in mixed classes, children of similar attainment completed without difficulty. To my mind, this is the most important finding in the field, because it implies that the harm done by grouping is not inevitable but a consequence of choices that schools could make differently.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That possibility has since been tested. A team led by Mariela Vasquez-Leal worked with schools that retained sets but agreed to follow three principles: allocation based on up-to-date assessment rather than a single test, regular review so that pupils could move between sets, and the assignment of the most experienced teachers to the lowest groups. After two years, the gap in progress between top and bottom sets had narrowed, though it had not disappeared. Surprisingly, the hardest principle to sustain was movement between groups; teachers worried that moving pupils would disrupt the sequence of the curriculum, and in practice few pupils changed set more than once.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Advocates of mixed-attainment teaching sometimes present these findings as an argument for abolishing sets altogether. That conclusion strikes me as premature. Mixed classes place heavy demands on teachers, who must provide work at several levels at once, and where teachers lack the training or time to do this, the result can be lessons aimed at the middle that suit almost nobody. There is also some evidence that the most able pupils lose a little ground in mixed classes, and although the loss is small it is not imaginary. The choice, in other words, is not between a harmful practice and a beneficial one, but between two arrangements, each of which can be done well or badly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the research does justify is scepticism about early and rigid separation. The case against placing ten-year-olds on separate educational paths is now strong, and the case for flexible grouping within a school, with genuine opportunities to move upwards, is considerably stronger than the case for permanent sets. Policymakers who wish to reform grouping would therefore do better to regulate how pupils are allocated and reviewed than to prohibit grouping by decree, a measure that tends merely to drive the practice underground. Above all, schools that group pupils need to be honest about who is teaching the lowest groups and what is expected of them, for that, rather than the label on the classroom door, seems to determine whether grouping helps or harms.

topic: the relative-age effect in schooling: birth date and attainment, over-diagnosis of attention disorders in the youngest pupils, selection in youth sport, delayed school entry and age-adjusted assessment
title: Youngest in the Class
subtitle: A child's month of birth can shape how he or she is judged at school. How much does it matter, and what can be done about it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In almost every school system, children start school in the same year if their birthdays fall within the same twelve-month period. A child born on the first day after the cut-off date will therefore be almost a full year older than a classmate born on the last day before it. At the age of five, a year represents a fifth of a child's life, and the difference shows: the oldest children in a class are, on average, taller, more articulate and better able to sit still than the youngest. That younger pupils perform less well in their first tests is neither surprising nor, in itself, a cause for concern. What has troubled researchers is the suggestion that the disadvantage does not simply fade as children grow up.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Pieter Groenewald, an economist who has analysed national test records spanning twelve years of schooling, found that the attainment gap between the oldest and youngest pupils in a year group was largest at the age of seven and narrowed steadily thereafter. By the end of compulsory education it was small, though still measurable, and the youngest pupils remained somewhat less likely to enter university. Groenewald stresses that the narrowing gap is good news: whatever the early disadvantage does, it does not set a permanent ceiling on achievement. Nevertheless, a small difference in average attainment can conceal larger effects at key decision points, such as the allocation of pupils to sets or selective programmes, where being placed a little too low can have lasting consequences.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns diagnosis. Signe Rasmusdottir, a paediatric epidemiologist, examined records from a national health database and found that children born just before the cut-off date were considerably more likely than those born just after it to have been diagnosed with attention disorders and prescribed medication. Since there is no reason to believe that birth month itself causes such disorders, she argues, the most plausible explanation is that teachers and doctors are comparing the youngest children with older classmates and mistaking ordinary immaturity for a medical condition. I find this argument persuasive, and it seems to me the most troubling finding in the whole literature, since a misdiagnosis can follow a child for years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Sport offers a striking parallel, and one in which the stakes are easier to see, because selection is explicit and records of birth dates are routinely kept. Arjun Anand-Ghosh, who studies talent development, has shown that in youth football academies the great majority of players are born in the first few months after the selection cut-off. Coaches choosing the best players at the age of nine or ten are, in effect, largely selecting the most physically mature, and these children then receive better coaching, which widens the gap further. Interestingly, Anand-Ghosh found that among the small number of relatively young players who are selected, a disproportionate share go on to professional careers, perhaps because they have had to develop superior technique in order to compete with bigger opponents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done? One popular response is to allow parents to delay their child's entry to school by a year. Margaux Leclercq, a sociologist, has studied the families who choose this option and found that they are disproportionately well-off and well-educated, partly because delaying entry usually means paying for an additional year of childcare. The policy may therefore benefit the children of privileged families while leaving disadvantaged younger children exactly where they were. Worse, since the delayed children become the oldest in their new class, it may even push the remaining younger pupils further down the ranking by age. Where the practice has become widespread, the cut-off date has, in effect, shifted for one section of society but not for another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An alternative is to change how children are assessed rather than when they start. Several researchers have proposed that test scores be adjusted for age within the year group, so that a child's results are compared with those of children of the same age rather than with the class as a whole. This is technically straightforward and would remove some of the bias in decisions about selection and special educational needs. It would not, however, change what happens in the classroom, where a five-year-old is still expected to keep up with classmates who are nearly a year older. Some countries have experimented with more flexible arrangements in the first years of school, allowing children to move through the early curriculum at different speeds, but such schemes are demanding to organise and their long-term effects have yet to be properly evaluated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: My own conclusion is that the relative-age effect deserves more attention than it currently receives, but that the remedies need to be modest and targeted. Since every system needs some cut-off date, there will always be a youngest child in every class; no rearrangement of the calendar can change that. What schools and doctors can do is to remember this fact whenever they make judgements with lasting consequences, such as when they label a child as slow, as disruptive or as lacking in talent. In the early years in particular, teachers might reasonably be told the age of each pupil in months, a small piece of information that could prevent a great many unfair conclusions.

topic: risky play: playground safety standards, children's self-regulation of risk and adult fear of blame
title: The Value of a Scraped Knee
subtitle: Decades of making playgrounds safer may have taken away something children need, but the case for risk is more complicated than its champions admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who compares a playground built in the 1970s with one built in the last twenty years will notice how much has changed. Tall metal slides and climbing frames set above concrete have given way to low platforms, rounded edges and thick rubber matting. In many parks the tallest structure a child can climb is barely higher than an adult's shoulder. These changes were introduced for understandable reasons, chiefly a wish to prevent the serious head and limb injuries that falls from height can cause. Yet a growing body of researchers now argues that the pursuit of safety has been carried too far, and that in removing almost every element of danger from children's play, adults may have removed something children genuinely need. On balance, I believe they are right, although the case is not quite as straightforward as some of its advocates suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential figure in this movement is Dr Ragnhild Grøttum of the Tromsø College of Early Childhood Education, who has observed children at play in kindergartens across northern Norway for almost two decades. Grøttum defines risky play as thrilling activity in which there is a real possibility of physical injury: climbing to heights, moving at speed, using tools such as knives or saws, or playing near water and fire. What struck her most, she says, was how carefully children manage such risks when left to themselves. A four-year-old climbing a tree typically ascends a little, pauses, looks down and decides whether to continue, gradually extending the limits of what she can do. Grøttum describes this as a process of self-regulation, in which the child repeatedly balances fear against exhilaration. In her view, children who are denied such experiences do not become safer; they simply never learn to judge what their bodies are capable of.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporting evidence has come from an unexpected direction. Dr Mateus Sobreiro, an epidemiologist at the Lisbon Institute of Child Health, examined hospital records before and after the renovation of more than two hundred playgrounds in which tall equipment had been replaced with lower structures. Contrary to expectation, the rate of injuries requiring treatment fell only slightly, and the rate of broken arms did not fall at all. Sobreiro suggests that children, finding the new equipment unchallenging, began to use it in unintended ways, jumping from the tops of slides. The finding is intriguing, but it should be treated with some caution. Hospital records reveal nothing about how children actually behaved, and Sobreiro's explanation, while plausible, remains an inference rather than an observation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A broader and more contentious claim concerns mental health. The developmental psychologist Professor Haruto Kuwabata of the Osaka Centre for Childhood Studies has argued that the steady decline in unsupervised outdoor play since the 1960s has contributed to the rise in childhood anxiety reported in many wealthy countries. Children who never face manageable fears, he contends, are poorly equipped to cope with larger ones later in life. Kuwabata's argument has been widely repeated in the press, but the evidence for it is largely correlational. Rates of anxiety have risen during a period in which a great many other things have changed, from the structure of family life to the spread of digital technology, and it is difficult to isolate the contribution of any single factor. The hypothesis deserves careful testing; it does not yet deserve the status of established fact.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded by the case for risk. Dr Clodagh Mulcahy, a consultant in paediatric emergency medicine in Cork, points out that researchers who praise the benefits of risky play rarely spend their working days treating fractured skulls. She does not, however, argue for a return to the most cautious designs. Instead she draws a distinction between risks, which a child can see and choose whether to take, and hazards, which are hidden and which the child cannot reasonably be expected to anticipate. Mulcahy believes that playground standards should eliminate hazards ruthlessly while tolerating risks. This seems to me the most useful contribution to the whole debate, since it shifts the question from how much danger is acceptable to what kind.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some local authorities and schools have begun to act on such ideas. In one trial organised by Dr Lucía Zalakain and colleagues at the Basque Institute for Educational Research, eighteen primary schools introduced so-called loose parts into their playgrounds at break time: old tyres, planks, crates and ropes that children could move and combine as they wished. After a year, teachers in these schools reported that pupils were more physically active and that fewer of them complained of having nothing to do. Recorded injuries did not increase. However, nearly half the teachers said that they had felt uneasy during the first months, chiefly because they feared being blamed by parents if a child was hurt.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That unease points to what is, in my view, the real obstacle to change. The design of playgrounds can be altered within a single summer, but the attitudes of the adults who supervise them are far harder to shift. As long as every injury is treated as evidence that someone has failed, adults will continue to favour caution, whatever the research suggests. None of this means that safety standards should be abandoned, and the most enthusiastic campaigners occasionally write as if a broken wrist were a valuable educational experience in itself. What is needed instead is a more honest public conversation about the trade-offs involved, one which accepts that a childhood without any risk at all carries dangers of its own.

topic: pretend play and whether it causes cognitive development: correlational evidence, play-training studies and cross-cultural comparison
title: Make-Believe on Trial
subtitle: Pretend play is widely credited with driving children's intellectual growth, but the evidence for that belief has come under unusually close scrutiny

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At some point around eighteen months of age, most children begin to pretend. A banana is held to the ear as though it were a telephone; an empty cup is tipped to a doll's lips. By the age of four, these isolated gestures have often grown into elaborate dramas involving several children, assigned roles and long-running plots. Few aspects of early childhood have been so warmly regarded by educators. Entire preschool curricula are built on the assumption that make-believe is not merely enjoyable but essential, a kind of engine that powers the growth of language, creativity, social understanding and self-control. It is an attractive idea, and it may well contain a good deal of truth. But it is held, in my view, with a confidence that the research has never quite earned.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic argument rests on what pretence demands of the mind. Dr Mirela Vukašinović, a cognitive psychologist at the Adriatic Institute for Developmental Science, points out that a child who treats a banana as a telephone must keep two representations in mind simultaneously: the object as it really is, and the object as it is being imagined. Vukašinović contends that this capacity to separate reality from supposition is the very same one that later allows children to grasp that another person may hold a belief which is false. In support, she cites a substantial body of studies showing that children who engage in more frequent pretend play tend to pass tests of false-belief understanding at a younger age than their peers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such correlations, however, cannot by themselves show which way the influence runs, or whether some third factor, such as language ability or a talkative home, lies behind both. This was the central point of a lengthy review by Professor Desmond Kloppenburg of the Utrecht School of Child Studies, who examined around one hundred and fifty published studies. The few experiments that had attempted to increase children's pretend play and then measure the consequences were, he found, beset by problems: samples were small, the researchers who assessed the children often knew which group they belonged to, and children in the play groups frequently received far more adult attention than those in comparison groups. Where studies avoided these flaws, the apparent benefits tended to shrink or vanish. Kloppenburg concluded that pretend play is probably one of several routes to the same developmental destinations, rather than an indispensable cause.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The review was a valuable corrective, and the profession needed it. Yet some commentators have drawn from it a conclusion it does not support, namely that make-believe has been shown to be developmentally irrelevant. A shortage of rigorous evidence for an effect is not the same as rigorous evidence that the effect is absent. It should also be acknowledged that the ideal experiment is almost impossible to carry out. Researchers cannot ethically or practically prevent a group of children from pretending for several years, and brief interventions lasting a few weeks are unlikely to reveal the influence of an activity that children pursue spontaneously, in countless small episodes, throughout their early lives.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Anthropology offers a different kind of test. Dr Yaretzi Tecuapetla, who has spent several years living in farming villages in southern Mexico, reports that adults there seldom encourage or join in their children's pretend play, regarding it as a pleasant but unremarkable way for the young to pass time. Children in these communities pretend less often than those in middle-class European or North American families, and much of what they do pretend imitates the daily work of adults: grinding maize, herding animals, selling goods at market. Nevertheless, Tecuapetla has found that they come to understand other people's thoughts and intentions on much the same timetable as children elsewhere. If make-believe were truly indispensable, she argues, this is not what we would expect to see.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One strand of research has produced more encouraging results. Dr Henrike Brasseur of the Liège Centre for Early Learning has investigated the claim that playing a role helps children govern their own behaviour. In her studies, four- and five-year-olds asked simply to stand still managed to do so for a short time, but when the same children were asked to stand guard at a pretend castle, they remained motionless for considerably longer. Brasseur believes that the rules implicit in a role give children a structure for restraining their impulses. The finding is striking, though it has not been reproduced consistently: some laboratories have confirmed it, while others have found no difference between the two conditions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave educators? The most sensible position, I would suggest, is that pretend play does not need to be justified as an instrument of intellectual progress at all. Children seek it out, take intense pleasure in it and organise much of their social lives around it; that alone gives it a claim on their time. Indeed, the eagerness to prove that play produces measurable gains carries a danger of its own, since it encourages adults to take over children's games and to see them harnessed to meet learning targets set by adults. None of this, however, is an argument for removing play from preschools in favour of formal lessons. The evidence that early academic instruction brings lasting benefits is, if anything, weaker still.

topic: forest kindergartens: outdoor nature preschools, motor development, school readiness and access
title: Lessons Under the Canopy
subtitle: Kindergartens without walls have spread far beyond their northern European origins. What do children actually gain from them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a typical forest kindergarten, there is no classroom. Children aged between three and six spend almost the entire day outdoors, whatever the weather, with only a simple shelter or heated cabin for the coldest hours. They build dens from fallen branches, follow animal tracks, cook over open fires and invent games with whatever the woodland provides. The model took shape in Scandinavia and Germany in the second half of the twentieth century and has since been adopted, in one form or another, from Scotland to South Korea. Its supporters make bold claims about physical health, concentration, independence and wellbeing. Their enthusiasm has, I think, run somewhat ahead of the evidence, but the evidence is nonetheless considerably more persuasive than the support offered for many of the educational fashions that come and go.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most consistent findings concern the body. Dr Sigrun Weitbrecht of the Black Forest Institute for Early Education followed some two hundred children for a full year, half of them in forest settings and half in conventional kindergartens nearby. At the start of the year, the two groups performed similarly on tests of balance, agility and hand–eye coordination. By the end, the forest children had improved markedly more, a difference Weitbrecht attributes to the constant demands of uneven ground, slopes and obstacles that no indoor play area can reproduce. Several smaller studies point in the same direction, and of all the benefits attributed to outdoor kindergartens, this one seems to me the most securely established. Claims that forest children also take fewer days off sick are more contested, partly because illness is recorded in very different ways from one institution to another.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Attention is another matter. Dr Akosua Nyamekye, a psychologist at the Accra Centre for Child Development who now works mainly in Denmark, tested children's ability to concentrate on puzzles and listening tasks after periods spent in woodland and after periods spent indoors. Performance was noticeably better after time among the trees. Nyamekye is careful, however, to acknowledge a difficulty that runs through the whole field: parents who choose a forest kindergarten are not a random sample of the population. They tend to be better educated, more interested in the outdoors and more involved in their children's lives, and any of these characteristics might influence how children perform. She attempted to reduce the problem by comparing families with similar backgrounds, but admits that no such matching can be complete.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most frequently voiced objection comes from primary school teachers, some of whom worry that children arriving from forest settings are less prepared for formal learning. They may know a great deal about beetles, the argument goes, but less about letters, and may struggle to sit still at a desk. Dr Pavel Hruška of the Brno Pedagogical Institute set out to test this concern by tracking forest and conventional kindergarten children through their first three years of school. In the first year, the forest group did indeed lag slightly behind in early reading. By the third year, however, the gap had closed entirely, and teachers rated the forest children more highly for their ability to work cooperatively with classmates. The results are reassuring, although Hruška's sample of eighty children is too small for them to be regarded as conclusive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different criticism concerns who benefits. The sociologist Dr Rafael Arrocha argues that, outside a few countries with generous public funding, forest kindergartens have become a largely middle-class phenomenon. Fees can be high, specialised waterproof clothing is expensive, and the sites are often reachable only by car. In Arrocha's view, the movement is in danger of turning a childhood in nature, once taken for granted by most families, into a privilege enjoyed by the few. This warning deserves to be taken seriously, but I am not convinced that such exclusivity is inevitable. Municipal programmes in parts of Denmark have shown that outdoor kindergartens can be run at lower cost than conventional ones, precisely because they do not require large buildings to be constructed, heated and maintained.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, many ordinary kindergartens have adopted a compromise, taking their children to a nearby wood or park for one day each week. Such schemes are popular with parents and staff, and they are certainly better than nothing. Whether they deliver the benefits reported for full-time forest kindergartens is, however, an open question. If the gains in coordination and concentration arise from long and continuous immersion in a natural environment, a weekly excursion may achieve rather little; if they depend mainly on a change of scene, it may achieve a great deal. At present, no study has compared the two arrangements directly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, then, to frame the debate as a choice between forest kindergartens and conventional ones, as though every child ought to spend the early years in the woods. The more productive question is what ordinary settings can learn from the forest model. The answer, on present evidence, seems to be that children benefit from far more time outdoors than most of them now receive, that rain and cold are far less harmful than adults tend to assume, and that an environment which is unpredictable and physically demanding may teach lessons that no carefully designed indoor space can offer.

topic: rough-and-tumble play in young children: distinguishing play fighting from aggression, preschool bans and the role of fathers
title: Fighting for Fun
subtitle: Many nurseries forbid children to wrestle and chase one another. Researchers who have watched such play closely are less sure that it should be stopped

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Watch any group of young children left to their own devices and, sooner or later, some of them will begin to wrestle, chase, pounce and tumble over one another. Rough-and-tumble play, as researchers call it, is common between the ages of three and eight, and although it is more frequent among boys, girls take part in it too. It is also widespread among other mammals, from rats to chimpanzees, which suggests that it has deep evolutionary roots. Yet in many nurseries and primary schools it is actively discouraged, and some operate what amounts to a complete ban, on the grounds that play fighting leads to injuries and, before long, to real fights. Such policies are well meant. They rest, however, on a misunderstanding of what rough play is and of what happens when children engage in it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty is simply telling play from aggression. Professor Olumide Fasoranti of the Lagos Centre for Child Observation spent several years filming children in playgrounds and coding their behaviour second by second. Playful fighting, he found, is marked by a characteristic set of signals: relaxed open-mouthed expressions, laughter, exaggerated movements and frequent changes of role, so that the chaser becomes the chased. Stronger children routinely hold back, allowing weaker partners to pin them down. Most tellingly, when an episode ends, the participants usually stay together and move on to another game, whereas genuine fights end with the children separating. When Fasoranti showed his recordings to children and to adults, the children identified play and real fighting with considerable accuracy; adults, particularly those with little experience of such play, were far more likely to mistake one for the other.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What of the fear that play turns into violence? Dr Ilse Vanderplaetse, a developmental psychologist at the Flemish Institute for Child Development, examined more than three thousand episodes of rough-and-tumble play and found that only around one in a hundred ended in genuine aggression. Among one group of children, however, the figure was many times higher: those already rejected by their classmates. Such children, Vanderplaetse suggests, may misread the signals of play, interpreting a playful shove as an attack, or may deliberately use the cover of a game to hurt others. This finding is important, and it exposes the weakness of blanket rules. A policy that treats all children in the same way ignores the fact that the risk is concentrated in a small minority.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others have focused on what children may gain. Dr Kamran Sohrabi of the Tehran Institute of Developmental Studies argues that rough play is an apprenticeship in emotional control. To keep a game going, a child must become excited without losing self-control, judge how hard to push and recognise from a partner's face when to stop. Sohrabi frequently cites laboratory studies in which young rats deprived of play-fighting grew into adults that responded inappropriately to other rats, either freezing or attacking. The parallel is suggestive, but it should not be pressed too far: the social lives of rats and of human children differ in so many respects that findings from one cannot simply be transferred to the other.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Rough play also takes place at home, often between children and their fathers. Dr Bronwyn Tillotson of the Western Australian Family Research Centre recorded fathers playing physically with their four-year-olds and then followed the children for two years. It was not the amount of rough play that mattered, she found, but its character. Where fathers played vigorously but also set clear limits, stopping the game when it became too wild and resuming once the child had calmed down, children later showed fewer behavioural problems. Where fathers allowed the child to dominate completely, never asserting themselves, children were later more aggressive with their peers. Tillotson's study is intriguing, although it says little about mothers, many of whom also engage in physical play with their children, or about families in cultures where such play takes different forms.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Could nurseries put such findings to use? A team at the Montreal Early Years Observatory persuaded twelve nurseries to replace outright bans with a set of simple rules: rough play was permitted on a designated mat, any child could end a game by saying a particular word, and staff were trained to recognise the signals Fasoranti had described. Over a school year, incidents of genuine aggression did not increase, and staff reported feeling more confident in deciding when to intervene. The trial was small and lacked a proper comparison group, but its results are difficult to reconcile with the assumption that permitting play fighting inevitably leads to harm.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that every nursery should welcome wrestling at all times, or that adults should never intervene. Reasonable rules, and staff who understand what they are watching, are essential. But a general prohibition has an unfortunate consequence that is seldom noticed. The children most likely to turn play into real aggression are precisely those who most need to learn how to read the intentions of others and to restrain their own strength. Excluding them from rough play removes the risk for a while, but it also removes the opportunity to learn. They would be better served by supervised practice than by a rule that keeps them away from such play altogether.

topic: block and construction play, spatial skills and later mathematics achievement
title: Building Blocks
subtitle: Wooden bricks have been a fixture of the nursery for two centuries. Are they also a foundation for mathematical thinking?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Wooden blocks were among the very first materials designed specifically for early education. The German educator Friedrich Froebel, who founded the first kindergarten in the 1830s, gave children sets of simple geometric shapes, believing that handling them would reveal the order underlying the natural world. For much of the twentieth century, blocks remained a standard feature of nursery classrooms, if a rather unglamorous one. In recent years, however, they have attracted fresh attention, largely because of growing evidence that spatial ability is closely connected with success in mathematics and science. This revival of interest is welcome. Less welcome is the flood of expensive construction kits now marketed to parents with the promise that they will turn toddlers into future engineers, claims that go far beyond anything the research can support.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Spatial ability refers to a cluster of skills, including the capacity to picture objects in the mind, to imagine how they would look if turned around, and to understand how parts fit together into a whole. Professor Ayane Uebayashi of the Kansai Institute for Learning Sciences followed more than four hundred children from the age of four until the end of primary school. At the start of the study, researchers rated the complexity of each child's block constructions, noting whether they built simple towers or elaborate structures with arches, enclosures and symmetrical wings. Those whose constructions were most complex at four went on to obtain higher mathematics scores at eleven, and the relationship held even when differences in family income and general intelligence had been taken into account.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Uebayashi's results are impressive, but they cannot by themselves establish that block play makes children better at mathematics. An equally plausible explanation is that children who are already strong at spatial reasoning find building more rewarding, spend more time doing it and produce more ambitious structures as a result. On this view, complex constructions would be a sign of spatial talent rather than its source. Uebayashi herself acknowledges this possibility, although she notes that the children who built most often were not always those who built most skilfully, which suggests that practice and talent can be at least partly separated. The question, however, can only be settled by studies in which researchers deliberately change the way children play and then observe the consequences.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Experiments offer a way round this problem. Dr Leandro Fattorini of the Bologna Centre for Early Childhood assigned five-year-olds to one of three groups for six weeks. The first group used blocks to copy models shown in photographs, which required them to translate a flat image into a three-dimensional structure. The second played freely with the same blocks, and the third did puzzles unrelated to construction. Only the first group showed a clear improvement on tests in which children had to work out how shapes would appear once rotated, even though the free-play group had spent at least as much time handling the blocks. Fattorini concludes that what matters is not contact with blocks as such, but the kind of challenge that building presents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Spatial skills are of particular interest because of a persistent gap between the sexes: on average, boys outperform girls on certain spatial tasks from middle childhood onwards. Dr Joanna Przybylska of the Kraków Institute of Developmental Psychology points out that boys also spend far more time with construction toys, partly because these are the toys they are given. In one study in twenty preschools, she ensured that girls had equal access to blocks and that staff actively invited them to build. After a term, the difference in spatial performance between boys and girls had narrowed considerably. The finding is promising, though it remains to be seen whether such gains persist once children leave the preschool environment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further line of research shifts attention from the blocks to the conversation around them. Dr Tendai Mupfumira of the Harare Centre for Family Studies recorded parents building alongside their children and counted the words they used to describe position, shape and direction, such as above, between, corner and curved. Children whose parents used such words more often scored higher on spatial tasks a year later. Mupfumira argues that spatial language gives children tools for noticing and remembering relationships they might otherwise overlook. If she is right, and I suspect she is, then the talk that accompanies building may matter at least as much as the building itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What follows for parents and teachers? Not, certainly, that they need to buy elaborate kits; ordinary wooden blocks seem to serve perfectly well. The research points instead to two inexpensive ingredients: an occasional challenge, such as copying a design or building something that will stand up to a particular test, and adults who talk about what is being made. There is, however, a danger in pushing this too far. Children build because they enjoy it, and if every session with the blocks is turned into a lesson, adults may destroy the very pleasure that makes children want to build in the first place.

topic: imaginary companions in early childhood: from clinical suspicion to normal development, theory of mind, unruly companions and the fantasy-reality question
title: Friends Nobody Else Can See
subtitle: Invisible companions were once treated as a warning sign. Researchers now disagree about what, if anything, they reveal about a child's mind

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere between the ages of three and seven, a remarkable number of children acquire a friend whom no one else can see. Some of these companions are wholly invisible: a girl who must have a place set for her at dinner, a dragon who sleeps under the stairs. Others are personified objects, such as a stuffed rabbit credited with opinions, a temper and a detailed family history. For much of the twentieth century, clinicians regarded such creations with suspicion. An invisible friend was taken to be a symptom of loneliness at best and, at worst, an early sign of a disordered grip on reality, and parents were sometimes advised to discourage the habit firmly. The source of this reputation is not hard to find. The children described in the early literature were almost all patients, referred to clinics because someone was already worried about them, and a sample assembled in that way was always likely to find trouble wherever it looked.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The picture began to change when researchers turned to ordinary families. The most ambitious of these surveys was conducted by Liisa Rantasalo and her colleagues at the Northern Institute of Developmental Science, who interviewed more than 1,200 children aged between three and nine, together with their parents. By the age of seven, they reported, roughly two children in every three had had an imaginary companion of one kind or another. Firstborn and only children were somewhat more likely to invent one, but the difference was modest, and companions were common in large, busy households too. Perhaps the most revealing result concerned the parents. In nearly a third of cases where a child described a companion in detail, the parents had no idea that it existed. Since most earlier estimates had depended entirely on what mothers and fathers reported, it seems likely that the phenomenon was for decades seriously underestimated.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If imaginary companions are normal, might they even be beneficial? Chidi Ezeonwuka, a developmental psychologist at the Coastal University of Education, believes they are. In a series of studies he found that children with companions performed better than their peers on tasks requiring them to work out what another person knows or believes, and that the stories they told were longer and more varied in perspective. Ezeonwuka argues that the companion serves as a kind of rehearsal space: in speaking for an invisible friend, the child practises imagining a point of view other than his or her own. The argument is attractive, but the data cannot carry the weight placed on them. It is equally plausible that children who are already unusually alert to other minds are more inclined to invent companions in the first place. Settling the question experimentally would be extremely difficult, since no ethics committee could assign a child an invisible friend.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more surprising line of work concerns how the companions behave. Ximena Arguedas of the Institute for Early Childhood Research in Valparaiso asked children not simply whether they had a companion but what it was like to spend time with. Around a third of the companions, it emerged, were far from compliant. They refused to come when called, interrupted conversations, spoke too loudly in the library or wandered off at inconvenient moments. Arguedas contends that this unruliness is precisely the point: in giving the companion desires that conflict with their own, children are constructing a mind which is independent of theirs. To my mind, this is the most illuminating finding in the field, not least because it undermines the long-standing assumption that companions are merely a form of wish fulfilment, an ideal friend who always does as it is told.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What, then, of the fear that children cannot tell their inventions from reality? Kenji Shirakawa, who has interviewed several hundred children in Osaka and Sapporo, finds little to support it. When asked directly, the great majority readily acknowledge that the companion is pretend, and many show visible irritation when an adult appears to take it too literally. Shirakawa concludes that adult anxiety on this score is misplaced, and on the evidence he is right. Yet it would be a mistake to infer that, because children know the companion is invented, it means little to them. Children can grieve when a companion moves away, and they can be genuinely hurt when a sibling mocks it. Knowing that something is imaginary and caring about it are not, after all, incompatible: adults weep at novels without ever believing in their characters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Most companions eventually depart without ceremony, often around the time a child starts school, and many adults have no memory of them at all. Some researchers have nonetheless looked for lasting effects. Novelists, for instance, report having had childhood companions at unusually high rates, and some describe their fictional characters as speaking with similarly independent voices. The comparison is intriguing, but the writers concerned volunteered for the studies, and those with a vivid story to tell about their childhood were presumably the most eager to take part. Rantasalo's team has also documented a smaller group of adolescents who create companions, often during periods of stress. She regards these as a coping strategy rather than a symptom, a judgement that deserves to be taken seriously by clinicians who still treat older children's companions as a cause for alarm.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What should parents do? On present evidence, neither deliberate encouragement nor suppression seems warranted; a polite, unforced interest is probably the wisest response. The larger lesson of this research, however, concerns science rather than parenting. The reputation of the imaginary companion did not change because children changed. It changed because researchers changed whom they asked, and how carefully they listened to the answers.

topic: loose parts play: open-ended movable materials versus fixed playground equipment and realistic toys, supervision, safety and cost
title: The Power of Junk
subtitle: Tyres, crates and cardboard boxes are finding their way into school playgrounds. How much do they really change the way children play?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visit a well-equipped modern playground and you will find slides, climbing frames and swings bolted firmly to the ground. Visit a school that has adopted what is known as 'loose parts' play and you may find something that looks, at first sight, like a scrapyard: stacks of old tyres, lengths of drainpipe, wooden crates, rope, fabric and cardboard boxes. The idea behind such collections is simple. Materials that can be carried, combined and rearranged, it is argued, invite children to invent their own games, whereas fixed equipment largely dictates how it will be used. A slide, after all, is for sliding. A crate can be a boat, a shop counter, a stage or a step. In my view, the movement deserves more serious attention than it usually receives from education authorities, which tend to dismiss it as a passing fashion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the strongest evidence comes from playground interventions. A team led by Sipho Mkhwanazi at the Highveld Centre for Childhood Studies introduced loose materials into the break-time areas of twelve primary schools, while a further twelve schools carried on as before. Over two years, children in the intervention schools spent markedly more of their break time in active movement, and teachers reported fewer disputes. Mkhwanazi attributes the fall in conflict partly to the fact that there was simply more to do: with fixed equipment, children often queue for a single popular item, and arguments about whose turn it is are frequent. Interestingly, the effects were strongest not in the youngest pupils but in those aged eight and nine, an age at which, he notes, interest in conventional playground equipment usually begins to fade.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Advocates also claim that open-ended materials foster creativity, and here the evidence is more mixed. Agnieszka Zablocka, a psychologist at the Baltic Institute of Education, observed pairs of four-year-olds playing either with realistic toys, such as a toy kitchen, dolls and a plastic tool set, or with unstructured objects such as boxes, cloth and wooden offcuts. With the unstructured materials, children engaged in more symbolic substitution, using one object to stand for another, and invented more varied storylines. Yet Zablocka also found that the youngest children she observed, those under three, often played less with unstructured materials, seemingly unsure what to do with them. Her conclusion is that realistic props provide a kind of scaffold that very young children need before they can make use of abstraction. This seems to me a sensible caution against treating any single type of material as universally superior.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that the materials themselves are what matter. Rohan Kirtikar of the Western Institute of Play Research points out that schools adopting loose parts play typically also change how adults supervise break time, with staff trained to step back rather than direct. In his view, it may be this shift in adult behaviour, and not the tyres and crates, that produces most of the reported benefits. It is a fair point, and one that intervention studies have rarely been designed to test. Still, the two changes are hard to separate in practice, since it is difficult to imagine adults standing back while children play on equipment that requires strict turn-taking and constant monitoring.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most common objection, at least among parents and school managers, concerns safety. Heavy tyres can trap fingers, and children stacking crates will sometimes fall. Mette Lindegaard, who advises local authorities in Denmark on play provision, argues that such fears are generally exaggerated. Injury records from schools she has worked with show no increase in serious accidents after loose materials were introduced, although minor scrapes and bruises became somewhat more frequent. Lindegaard maintains that these small injuries are part of how children learn to judge risk. That may well be true, but it does not follow that every school should accept them without question: a setting with very few supervising staff faces different constraints from one that is generously staffed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also the matter of cost, which, perhaps unexpectedly, favours loose parts. Much of the material can be obtained free from local businesses, and a box of donated offcuts costs a fraction of a single item of fixed equipment. Some schools have gone further, inviting families to contribute household objects, which has the added benefit of involving parents in what happens at break time. Paulo Mattos, an economist who has studied playground budgets in Brazil, notes that the main expense is not the materials but storage: without a dry shed, cardboard disintegrates and fabric becomes mouldy within weeks. Schools that underestimate this, he warns, often abandon the approach within a year.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that slides and climbing frames should be torn down. Fixed equipment offers forms of physical challenge, such as height, speed and swinging, that a pile of crates cannot easily replicate. The real lesson is that play spaces work best when they offer variety, including materials whose purpose has not been decided in advance by an adult designer. Children, given the chance, are remarkably good at deciding for themselves.

topic: guided play versus free play and direct instruction in early years education: shape-learning experiments, meta-analysis, definitional problems and teacher training
title: Between Freedom and Instruction
subtitle: Guided play promises to combine the best of child-led and teacher-led learning. Its critics are not yet convinced

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Debates about how young children should learn have long been framed as a contest between two camps. On one side stand the defenders of free play, who argue that children learn best when left to pursue their own interests, with adults keeping a respectful distance. On the other are the advocates of direct instruction, for whom the efficient transmission of knowledge requires a teacher to explain, demonstrate and correct. In recent years, however, a third position has gained ground. Known as guided play, it proposes that adults should arrange an environment with a particular learning goal in mind, but then allow children to take the lead in the activity that unfolds within it. Its supporters present it as the best of both worlds; its critics suspect that it is neither one thing nor the other.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited evidence for guided play comes from studies of how children learn about shapes. In one experiment at the Lakeshore Child Learning Laboratory, a team under Grace Kariuki taught four- and five-year-olds the defining features of triangles, rectangles and pentagons. One group received a lecture-style lesson using picture cards; a second was left to play freely with the same cards; a third was invited by an adult to act as 'shape detectives' and discover the 'secret' of what made a shape a real triangle. A week later, the children in the detective condition were substantially better at identifying unusual examples, such as long, thin triangles or triangles standing on one point. The children who had played freely learned little, while the instructed group performed well on typical shapes but were often misled by atypical ones.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kariuki interprets these results as evidence that guided play combines two ingredients that matter for learning: the active engagement that free play provides, and the focus on a specific goal that instruction supplies. A meta-analysis published in 2019 by researchers at Rhine Valley University, led by Tobias Kessling, appeared to support this view. Pooling data from 39 studies involving roughly 3,800 children, the team concluded that guided play produced larger gains than direct instruction in early mathematics and in shape knowledge, though not in literacy, where the two approaches performed similarly. Kessling himself acknowledges, however, that most of the studies in his analysis measured learning only days or weeks after the intervention had ended.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone has been convinced. Dilnoza Abubakirova, an educational psychologist at the Institute for Pedagogical Studies in Samarkand, has argued that the label 'guided play' covers activities so varied that it means almost nothing. In some studies, she points out, guidance involves an adult simply asking an occasional open question; in others, the adult controls nearly every step, and the child's freedom amounts to choosing which coloured card to pick up first. Grouping such activities together, Abubakirova argues, makes the impressive average effects reported in meta-analyses very difficult to interpret. This criticism seems to me largely justified. Until researchers agree on a definition, claims about the superiority of guided play will remain claims about an approach whose boundaries no one can draw.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection comes from the defenders of free play. Farida Dastoor, who has spent two decades observing children in nursery settings in Mumbai and Leeds, worries that the enthusiasm for guided play reflects an adult preoccupation with measurable outcomes. Free play, she argues, develops capacities such as negotiation, persistence and self-direction that are rarely captured by tests of shape recognition. When adults, however gently, steer play towards a curriculum goal, they risk teaching children that play is valuable only when it serves someone else's purpose. Her argument is difficult to test, precisely because the outcomes she values are hard to measure, but that is not a reason to dismiss it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a practical problem. Guided play makes heavy demands on adults. A teacher must design an environment rich enough to sustain children's interest, recognise the moments when a well-timed question might extend a child's thinking, and refrain from intervening when it would not. In Kariuki's laboratory studies, the guiding adults were trained researchers working with one or two children at a time. In a typical classroom of twenty-five, with a single teacher and perhaps one assistant, such sensitivity is far harder to achieve. A survey of 600 early years teachers conducted by Kessling's group found that while more than 80 per cent supported the idea of guided play, fewer than a third felt they had received adequate training to deliver it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that guided play should be abandoned. The laboratory evidence is consistent, and the underlying logic is persuasive: children learn more when they are actively engaged and when that engagement is directed towards something worth learning. But the approach is likely to be only as good as the adults implementing it, and policy makers who adopt it as a slogan, without investing in the training it requires, may find that they have achieved neither genuine play nor effective instruction.

topic: sex differences in young children's toy preferences: animal and hormonal evidence, parental and commercial socialisation, and children's self-socialisation through gender labels
title: Trucks, Dolls and the Question of Origins
subtitle: Why do so many young boys and girls choose different toys? Three explanations compete, and the answer may require all of them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By the age of three, a large proportion of children already show clear preferences in the toys they choose. On average, boys spend more time with vehicles, construction sets and toy weapons, while girls spend more time with dolls, tea sets and dressing-up clothes. These differences are among the largest psychological differences between the sexes found in early childhood, although the overlap is considerable and many children do not fit the pattern at all. For decades the toy aisles of shops were divided by colour, until campaigns by parents persuaded several large retailers to remove signs labelling products as being 'for boys' or 'for girls'. Behind such campaigns lies an old question: do toys simply reflect preferences that children already have, or do they help to create them? It is usually asked as though only one answer could be correct, and that, I believe, is where the debate has gone wrong.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for a biological contribution rests partly on studies of other species. Oskari Pirttijarvi, a primatologist at the Northern Primate Research Station, offered young monkeys a selection of plush animals and wheeled toys. Males spent noticeably more time with the wheeled toys, whereas females divided their attention fairly evenly between the two kinds. Since monkeys are exposed neither to advertising nor to parental expectations, Pirttijarvi argues, some predisposition must predate culture. Supporting evidence comes from girls exposed before birth to unusually high levels of male hormones because of a rare medical condition, who tend to show greater interest in vehicles than other girls. The animal findings are intriguing, but the samples involved are small, and it is far from clear what the monkeys were responding to. What is inherited may be nothing more specific than an attraction to objects that move, a preference that human cultures only later label as masculine.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others place the emphasis firmly on the social environment. The sociologist Nomvula Ntuli of the Cape Institute for Social Research filmed eighty families at play and found that parents, and fathers in particular, were far more likely to discourage a son from playing with a doll than a daughter from playing with a truck. Ntuli has also analysed toy catalogues across five decades and reports that the division of toys by gender was considerably sharper in the 2010s than in the 1970s, a change she attributes to manufacturers discovering that separate ranges for boys and girls allowed families to be sold the same product twice. The historical finding is striking, since a purely biological account would struggle to explain why the division should have grown so markedly in a few decades. Yet the evidence that marketing altered the toys children actually chose, rather than merely the colour of the packaging, remains thin.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third account gives children themselves the leading role. According to Armen Bagdasarian, a developmental psychologist at the Ararat Institute of Child Studies, children behave like 'gender detectives'. Once they are able to label themselves as a boy or a girl, usually at around two and a half, they begin actively searching for information about what people like them do, and their preferences become markedly stronger as a result. In one of his experiments, children were shown unfamiliar toys that had been described as intended either for boys or for girls. They played longer with the toys said to be for their own sex, and later remembered more about them, even though they had never encountered any of the toys before. Bagdasarian finds that this rigidity usually peaks at around five or six and relaxes by the age of seven or eight. Of the three explanations, his seems to me the most convincing, because it accounts for something the others cannot: the way preferences often intensify even in families that deliberately avoid stereotypes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Does any of this matter? Different toys plausibly encourage different skills. Construction toys exercise spatial reasoning, while dolls and pretend kitchens invite conversation and the rehearsal of caring roles. If children confine themselves to one category, they may miss opportunities that the other provides. Ntuli advocates gender-neutral marketing on these grounds. Pirttijarvi regards such efforts as harmless but doubts that they will change much, given the predispositions he has identified. He may be right about the size of the effect, but removing a label from a shelf costs very little, and a modest benefit obtained cheaply is still worth having.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most useful way to see the three accounts is not as rivals but as layers. A small initial difference in what attracts boys and girls may be amplified by children's own search for an identity and then reinforced by families and by the market. On this view, the more productive question is not where preferences come from but how flexible they remain. Here, one of Bagdasarian's observations is suggestive. Children left alone in a playroom were considerably more willing to play with toys associated with the other sex than when a classmate of the same age was present. Preferences that weaken so readily once no one is watching are surely less fixed than they first appear.

topic: the evolutionary function of play in young animals (practice, training for the unexpected, surplus energy, brain development) and what it implies for children's play time
title: Why the Young Play
subtitle: Almost all young mammals play, often at considerable cost. Biologists' attempts to explain why have implications for the way we treat children's play

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A young goat leaps into the air, twists and lands facing the opposite direction for no apparent reason. Two otter cubs take turns sliding down a muddy bank. A juvenile raven repeatedly drops a twig from a height and swoops to catch it before it reaches the ground. Play of this kind is found in nearly all mammals and in a number of birds, and it presents biologists with a genuine puzzle. Natural selection is generally thought to eliminate behaviour that consumes energy without bringing some benefit, yet play is expensive. It burns calories that a growing animal can ill afford, it distracts the player from approaching predators, and it frequently results in injury. Behaviour that persists despite such costs, it is reasonable to suppose, must be doing something useful. The difficulty lies in establishing what.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest and most intuitive answer is that play is practice. On this view, defended most vigorously in recent years by Irina Drozdova of the Volga Institute of Ethology, the kitten pouncing on a ball of wool is rehearsing the movements it will later need to catch mice, and the young deer racing in circles is preparing to escape wolves. The practice theory has the virtue of simplicity, but it fits the evidence less well than its popularity might suggest. Cats raised without any opportunity for object play, for instance, turn out to be perfectly competent hunters as adults. Moreover, much animal play bears little resemblance to any adult activity: there is no obvious adult skill for which a young goat's mid-air twist could be preparing it. A theory that explains only the play that happens to resemble adult behaviour is, in my view, too narrow to be the whole story.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious proposal comes from Lars Brannstrom, a behavioural ecologist at Baltic Coast University. Brannstrom argues that the function of play is to prepare young animals not for specific tasks but for the unexpected. He draws attention to the curious fact that playing animals often put themselves at a deliberate disadvantage. A stronger young wolf will roll onto its back and allow a weaker partner to pin it down; a young monkey will leap from an unsteady branch it could easily have avoided. Such self-handicapping, Brannstrom suggests, creates brief episodes of lost control, and so trains both the body and the emotions to recover quickly from surprise. Of all the explanations on offer, this one strikes me as the most promising, precisely because it accounts for the apparently pointless quality of so much play.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that play needs a dedicated function at all. Awa Seck, who has spent more than a decade observing wild meerkats in the Kalahari, points out that play is the first activity to disappear when conditions become hard. In years of severe drought, she found, juvenile play almost ceased, while foraging and watching for predators continued as usual. Seck interprets this as evidence that play is a by-product of surplus energy, something young animals do when their basic needs are met, rather than an adaptation in its own right. Her data are impressive, but the conclusion does not follow from them. That play is abandoned first under pressure shows only that it is less urgent than finding food; it does not show that it is useless. A family facing hardship may cancel music lessons before it stops buying bread, without anyone concluding that music lessons have no value.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further line of evidence comes from neuroscience. Eero Tauriainen, of the Nordic Centre for Brain Development, has compared the age at which play peaks in several species with the timing of brain growth. In mice, rats and cats, he reports, play is most frequent during a short window when connections in the cerebellum, a region involved in coordinating movement, are forming most rapidly. He also notes that in species with long childhoods, such as primates, the period of intense play is correspondingly extended. Tauriainen suggests that play helps to shape this wiring. The match in timing is suggestive, but a coincidence of timing is not proof of cause, and it remains possible that brain development and play are simply both products of the same stage of growth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What does any of this mean for human children? It is tempting to read the animal evidence as a straightforward endorsement of children's play, but Hery Rabearivelo, a developmental psychologist at the Indian Ocean Institute of Child Studies, urges caution. Human play includes forms such as pretending and the invention of games with agreed rules, which have no clear equivalent in other species, and theories built on goats and meerkats may tell us little about them. A game of shops or schools, for example, draws on social knowledge that no meerkat possesses. This is a fair warning, and it would be unwise to transfer conclusions from animal studies to classrooms without further evidence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even so, one lesson seems to survive the transfer. If play is costly yet has been preserved across so many species, the likelihood that it serves no purpose at all is small. Education systems that shorten break times or replace early play with formal lessons in pursuit of academic gains are therefore taking a considerable gamble, and on present evidence it is one they would be wise to avoid.

topic: the emergence of a new sign language among deaf schoolchildren in Nicaragua and competing explanations of how its grammar developed
title: A Language Born in the Playground
subtitle: The rapid appearance of a new sign language gave linguists a rare chance to watch grammar take shape, but what exactly they were watching is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Linguists rarely witness the birth of a language. The origins of even the youngest are usually hidden by a lack of written records. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, however, something unusual happened in Nicaragua. When the government expanded its special education programme, hundreds of deaf children who had previously lived in relative isolation, communicating with hearing relatives through a handful of improvised gestures, were brought together in schools in the capital. The official teaching focused on lip-reading and spoken Spanish, and by most accounts it achieved very little. Yet in the playgrounds and on the school buses, the children began to sign to one another, and within little more than a decade a fully fledged language had appeared. It is no exaggeration to say that this episode has become one of the most closely studied events in modern linguistics.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What made the case so valuable was that the language could be observed changing from one cohort of pupils to the next. Ilse Sotiriou, a linguist at the Institute for Comparative Grammar in Uppsala, has compared the signing of those who entered the schools in the first years with that of children who arrived later. In her analysis, the earliest signers produced long, rather loosely organised sequences, often acting out an event as a whole, whereas younger signers broke the same events into discrete units, using one sign for the manner of a movement and another for its direction, and combined these units according to consistent rules. Sotiriou concludes that the crucial grammatical innovations were introduced not by adults or teachers but by young children, who imposed structure on the less systematic input they received from older pupils.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This interpretation has proved influential because it appears to support the idea that children possess a special capacity for language which declines with age. If young learners can transform a rough communication system into a grammar within a few years, the argument runs, then something in the developing brain must be predisposed to seek out regularity. Sotiriou herself is careful not to claim that her findings prove the existence of an innate grammar, but others have been less cautious, and the case is frequently cited in textbooks as straightforward evidence for such a view. That reading strikes me as premature. The data are compatible with an inborn tendency towards structure, but they do not rule out other explanations, and several of these deserve more attention than they have so far received.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One such alternative is offered by Narine Arakelyan and her colleagues at the Centre for Language and Interaction in Yerevan, who argue that the role of the social network has been underestimated. In their account, what mattered was not so much the age of the learners as the density and frequency of their interactions. As the school population grew, each signer encountered a greater number of partners, and forms that were ambiguous or hard to perceive were gradually abandoned in favour of those that almost everyone could understand. Arakelyan points out that computer simulations of communicating agents, which possess no innate grammar whatsoever, display similar increases in regularity over successive generations. Structure, on this view, emerges from communication itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection comes from Juma Mwangoka, an anthropologist at the Kilimani Institute for Linguistic Anthropology, who questions the assumption that the children started from nothing. Many of them, he notes, had already developed private gesture systems with their families, some of considerable complexity, and a number of these families were in contact with one another before the schools opened. Moreover, documentation of the early years is sparse. Much of what is known about the first cohort comes from recordings made when those signers were already adults, a decade or more after they had first met. Mwangoka argues that it is therefore difficult to know what the original signing looked like, and that the apparent crudeness of the older generation's language may have been exaggerated by comparing adults who learned it late with children who acquired it from birth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These criticisms do not undermine the significance of the case, but they do complicate the neat story of children inventing grammar from scratch. I find Mwangoka's point about the evidence especially telling: confident claims about what happened in a playground forty years ago rest on a surprisingly slender foundation. At the same time, the alternatives are not necessarily incompatible with Sotiriou's position. Researchers at the Signed Languages Laboratory in Montreal, led by Hélène Dussault, have tried to separate the competing factors by comparing signers who entered the schools at the same age but at different points in the community's history. Those who joined later, when the community was larger, signed more systematically even when age of entry was held constant. Yet among pupils who arrived at the same moment, those under the age of ten mastered the newer grammatical devices far more fully than those who came later in childhood. Both age and community size, it seems, played a part.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is, finally, a question that the scientific debate has tended to overlook. Nicaraguan Sign Language is not a laboratory specimen; it is the everyday language of a community with its own associations and artists. Some Deaf Nicaraguans have objected to being described as the subjects of a natural experiment, as though their language existed chiefly to settle arguments among foreign academics. Their complaint deserves to be taken seriously. Research that treats signers merely as sources of data is likely to be ethically questionable, and it may also be scientifically poorer, since those who use a language every day are often best placed to notice its subtleties.
