topic: village sign languages and shared signing communities with high rates of hereditary deafness
title: When a Whole Village Signs
subtitle: Communities in which deaf and hearing people share a sign language challenge familiar ideas about disability, but they may be more fragile than they appear

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In most parts of the world, deaf people form a small minority who use a sign language largely among themselves, while the hearing majority knows little or nothing of it. There are, however, a number of communities where the situation is very different. In certain villages, a hereditary form of deafness has been passed down through generations of intermarrying families, so that deaf residents make up a much higher proportion of the population than usual, sometimes one person in fifty compared with roughly one in a thousand elsewhere. In such places a local sign language tends to develop, and, crucially, it is used not only by deaf people but by many of their hearing neighbours as well. Linguists refer to these as 'shared signing communities', and over the past few decades examples have been documented in Asia, Africa, the Americas and the Middle East.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first thing visitors tend to notice is how unremarkable deafness seems. Freya Ingvarsdóttir, an anthropologist at the Reykjavik Centre for Cultural Studies, spent two years in one such village and reports that deaf residents farmed, traded, married and held positions of local responsibility much as their hearing relatives did. Hearing children picked up the sign language in the same way as they learned the spoken one, through daily exposure rather than formal instruction, and adults switched between the two without apparent effort. When Ingvarsdóttir asked villagers how many deaf people lived there, several struggled to answer; they had simply never thought to count. For Ingvarsdóttir, this demonstrates that much of the disadvantage associated with deafness elsewhere is produced by social arrangements rather than by the condition itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This conclusion has been warmly welcomed by disability scholars, and it is persuasive as far as it goes. Yet it would be a mistake to romanticise these communities. Rohan Kapoorwala, a linguist at the Institute of Language Documentation in Pune, has found that while deaf villagers participate fully in everyday life, they are often excluded from areas that depend on literacy or on contact with the outside world, such as dealing with government officials or continuing their education beyond the village school. Moreover, hearing signers vary greatly in fluency. Many can manage a conversation about familiar matters but struggle to follow a complex story or argument, which means that deaf people may still find themselves on the margins of important discussions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The languages themselves raise intriguing questions. Because they arise in small, close-knit groups where everyone shares a great deal of background knowledge, they appear to rely heavily on context. Ana Mendibil and her team at the Andean Linguistics Laboratory compared three village sign languages with national sign languages used in large deaf communities, and found that the village languages made far less use of the space in front of the signer to keep track of who was doing what to whom, a device that is almost universal in urban sign languages. Mendibil suggests that this reflects the circumstances in which the languages are used: when signers know each other and their topics of conversation intimately, there is less need for grammatical machinery to make reference explicit. This, I believe, is an important insight, since it implies that some features previously regarded as universal to sign languages are in fact products of particular social environments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most pressing concern today, however, is survival. Many shared signing communities are under pressure from changes that would have seemed unconnected to language a generation ago. Improved roads and migration have reduced intermarriage within villages, and the incidence of hereditary deafness is falling as a result. At the same time, deaf children are increasingly sent to residential schools in cities, where they learn the national sign language and often bring it back home with them. Eleni Laskaridou, who studies language endangerment at the Aegean Institute for Minority Languages, has documented one village where the local sign language was used by most residents in the 1990s but is now known fluently only by a handful of older people.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Opinion on what should be done is divided. Laskaridou argues that recording the remaining fluent signers is an urgent task, and that village schools should teach the local language alongside the national one. Others, including some deaf villagers themselves, regard the national language as a passport to employment, higher education and a wider deaf community, and see little reason to preserve a local variety. Their view is difficult to dismiss. Nevertheless, the choice need not be absolute. Bilingualism is the norm in many parts of the world, and there is no obvious reason why deaf children should not acquire both a national sign language and the local one, provided that the latter retains a genuine role in village life.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever their future, shared signing communities have already taught researchers a valuable lesson. They show that the position of deaf people in society is not fixed by biology but depends on choices that hearing people make, often without realising that they are making them. That lesson has implications far beyond the villages themselves.

topic: homesign: gesture systems invented by deaf children of hearing parents and what they reveal about the child's contribution to language
title: Signs Without a Teacher
subtitle: Deaf children who receive no sign language input often invent gesture systems of their own; what these systems reveal about the human capacity for language is still contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most children, learning a language means absorbing the one spoken or signed around them. Some deaf children, however, grow up in hearing families who do not know a sign language and who, for one reason or another, do not expose them to one. Unable to hear the speech around them, and without access to a conventional signed language, many such children nonetheless develop a system of gestures with which to communicate with their families. These systems, known as homesign, have attracted intense interest because they seem to offer a glimpse of what a child brings to the task of communication when the usual linguistic input is missing. If certain properties of language appear in homesign, the reasoning goes, they cannot have been learned from a model and must originate in the child.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest systematic studies emphasised how much structure homesigners produce. Valentina Feodorova of the Institute of Developmental Linguistics in Kazan filmed ten deaf children in their homes over periods of up to four years. She found that the children combined gestures into strings with a consistent order, for example placing the gesture for the object acted upon before the gesture for the action, and that they used pointing to refer to people and things in much the way that pronouns are used in spoken languages. Some of the older children even used gestures to talk about events in the past or the future, rather than simply about the here and now. Feodorova argues that these features represent 'resilient' properties of language, which will emerge in a child's communication under even the most unfavourable conditions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An obvious objection is that the children might have copied their hearing parents, who gesture as they speak. Feodorova anticipated this and analysed the parents' gestures as well. Strikingly, the mothers' gestures were far less systematic than those of their children: they rarely combined more than one gesture at a time, and they showed no consistent ordering. The children, she concluded, were not simply reproducing a model but going well beyond it. This finding is genuinely remarkable, and it has survived repeated attempts at replication in different cultures. It is, in my view, the strongest part of the case.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers, however, have questioned how much should be read into it. Nimal Ranawaka, a psychologist at the Colombo Centre for Child Communication, points out that the parents' gestures were typically analysed on their own, stripped of the speech they accompanied. When a mother says 'Put the cup on the table' while pointing at the cup, the gesture may look fragmentary, yet the meaning she conveys to the child, who can see her face, her actions and the objects around them, is far richer than the gesture alone suggests. Ranawaka argues that homesigners are embedded in dense, routine interactions with caregivers, and that the contribution of this shared activity has been neglected. He does not deny that the children contribute something of their own, but he believes the contrast between impoverished input and rich output has been overstated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective concentrates on what homesign lacks. Giulia Lunardelli, who studies sign language acquisition at the Ligurian Institute for Cognitive Science, has compared homesign with established sign languages and with the signing of deaf children exposed to such languages from birth. She notes that homesign systems, although structured, remain limited in important respects: their vocabularies are small and partly idiosyncratic, and they show little of the complex grammatical marking found in mature sign languages. Moreover, because a homesigner's relatives usually understand the gestures but rarely produce them in return, the system is used productively by only one person. For Lunardelli, homesign demonstrates both the power and the limits of the individual child: some foundations of language can be laid alone, but a complete language requires a community of users.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practical stakes of this debate are considerable. Children who homesign into adolescence without learning a full language are at risk of lasting difficulties, and there is good evidence that late exposure to any language, signed or spoken, affects eventual fluency. Marcus Sorhaindo, an educational researcher at the Caribbean Institute for Deaf Education, has studied adults who learned a sign language only in their teens after years of homesigning. He reports that, while they communicate effectively, many continue to make grammatical errors that native signers do not, and that traces of their homesign habits persist in their signing decades later. Sorhaindo stresses that homesign should therefore be seen not as an adequate substitute for a language but as evidence of what children will attempt in its absence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to treat these positions as rivals, but they are better understood as answers to different questions. Feodorova asks what a child can create, Ranawaka asks how much help the child receives, and Lunardelli asks what remains beyond the child's reach. The answers are complementary rather than contradictory. What is far less defensible is the occasional suggestion, found in some popular accounts, that homesign shows that children need no linguistic environment at all. Nothing in the research supports such a claim, and the experience of Sorhaindo's participants points in exactly the opposite direction.

topic: co-speech gesture and thinking: whether gestures serve the listener or help the speaker think and learn
title: Thinking with the Hands
subtitle: Why do people gesture when they speak, even on the telephone? The answer may say as much about thought as about communication

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: People gesture when they talk. They do so in every culture that has been studied, they do so when speaking on the telephone to someone who cannot see them, and people who have been blind from birth gesture even when talking to other blind people. These observations pose a puzzle. If gestures exist to help listeners understand, why are they produced when nobody can see them? Over the past thirty years, a growing number of researchers have concluded that gestures serve the speaker as well as the listener, and that the hands may play a part in the process of thinking itself. This is a bolder claim than it might first appear, since it implies that some thoughts are partly formed in movement rather than being fully worked out in the mind and only then translated into words.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The listener-centred view nevertheless remains important. Aino Tuominen, a psycholinguist at the Turku Centre for Communication Research, has shown in a series of experiments that listeners extract information from gestures that is absent from speech. When a speaker describes a spiral staircase while tracing its shape in the air, listeners later recall details of the shape that the words alone never conveyed. Tuominen also found that speakers gesture more, and more elaborately, when they know their listener can see them, which suggests that gesture is at least partly designed for an audience. In her view, gestures made on the telephone are simply habits carried over from face-to-face conversation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others regard this explanation as incomplete. Kenji Takemori of the Kansai Institute of Cognitive Science investigated what happens when speakers are prevented from gesturing. In his studies, participants were asked to describe complex routes or the workings of machines while either moving freely or keeping their hands still. Those who could not gesture spoke more slowly, paused more often and produced more filler words such as 'um', particularly when describing spatial information. Takemori argues that gesture helps speakers retrieve words and organise spatial ideas into the linear form that speech requires. Restricting gesture, on this account, is rather like asking someone to do mental arithmetic without being allowed to write anything down.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most striking evidence for a cognitive role comes from studies of learning. Abena Agyeiwaa, an educational psychologist at the Accra Institute for Learning Sciences, has studied children solving mathematical equivalence problems such as 4 + 3 + 5 = 4 + _. She observed that some children who gave wrong answers nonetheless produced gestures reflecting a correct strategy, for instance pointing to the two sides of the equation as if grouping them, a phenomenon she calls a 'mismatch'. These children were significantly more likely than others to benefit from subsequent instruction. Agyeiwaa concludes that gesture can reveal knowledge that a learner cannot yet express in words, and that teachers who attend to their pupils' hands may be able to identify those who are ready to learn.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Agyeiwaa has gone further, arguing that asking children to gesture can actually help them learn. In one study, pupils who were instructed to copy a teacher's grouping gesture while solving problems retained what they had learned for several weeks longer than those who simply repeated the teacher's words. This is a remarkable result, though I would be cautious about generalising from it. The pupils were all of a similar age and drawn from a small number of schools, and the tasks involved were narrow and highly spatial, and it is not obvious that the same benefits would appear when learning history or a foreign language. Nonetheless, the finding challenges the common assumption that gestures merely decorate thoughts that have already been formed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this interpretation. Pavel Zeleny, a philosopher of cognitive science at the Brno Institute for Mind and Language, argues that much of the research confuses correlation with causation. Children who produce mismatches may simply be those whose understanding is already in transition, he suggests, with gesture acting as a symptom of this rather than a cause. Similarly, the speakers in Takemori's experiments may have hesitated because keeping their hands still demanded effort and attention, which would explain their difficulties without implying that gesture itself aids thinking. Zeleny's caution is healthy, but I think he underestimates the weight of the experimental evidence: studies in which gesture is deliberately induced, as in Agyeiwaa's work, are precisely the kind needed to establish causation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has practical implications. If gesturing aids thinking, classrooms that require pupils to sit still with folded hands may be working against learning, and online teaching in which only a teacher's face is visible may lose more than is commonly recognised. Conversely, if gesture serves chiefly to inform listeners, teachers might benefit from training in how to use their own hands more deliberately when explaining difficult ideas. The truth probably lies between the extreme positions: gestures serve listeners and speakers alike, and the balance between these functions varies with the task. What is clear is that the movements of the hands, long dismissed as a mere accompaniment to speech, deserve a central place in the study of language and mind.

topic: iconicity versus arbitrariness in sign languages: its extent, its role in learning signs and its erosion and renewal over time
title: The Shape of Meaning
subtitle: Sign languages are full of signs that resemble what they mean; for decades linguists played this down, but some now argue that it belongs at the centre of the study of language

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the early twentieth century, one of the founding principles of linguistics has been that the relationship between a word and its meaning is arbitrary. There is nothing about the sound of 'tree' that resembles a tree, and other languages use entirely different sounds for the same concept. Sign languages appeared to pose a problem for this principle. In many of them, the sign for 'drink' imitates raising a cup to the lips, and the sign for 'house' traces the outline of a roof. This resemblance between form and meaning, known as iconicity, was once taken by sceptics as proof that sign languages were merely elaborate pantomime rather than languages in the full sense.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The pioneering sign linguists of the 1960s and 1970s responded by emphasising arbitrariness. They pointed out that iconic signs vary from one sign language to another, with the sign for 'tree' in one language picking out the trunk and in another the branches, and that people who do not know a sign language usually cannot guess the meanings of signs, even highly iconic ones. They also showed that, over time, signs tend to become less iconic as they are streamlined for speed and ease of production. These arguments were strategically important: by demonstrating that sign languages shared the core properties of spoken ones, they helped to secure recognition for sign languages in education and law. But, as is now increasingly acknowledged, they also led researchers to neglect a pervasive feature of signed communication.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Leading the reassessment is Tamar Kutateladze, a linguist at the Tbilisi Centre for Visual Language, who argues that iconicity is not a peripheral curiosity but a fundamental resource. In her survey of four unrelated sign languages, she estimated that between a third and a half of all signs have some iconic motivation. More importantly, she argues, iconicity is not confined to individual signs but runs through the grammar: verbs of motion, for instance, can be modified to show the speed, path and manner of a movement simply by altering how the hands move. Kutateladze also notes that spoken languages are more iconic than traditionally assumed, citing the sound-symbolic words found in Japanese and in many African languages. The difference between spoken and signed languages, in her view, is one of degree rather than kind.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A natural question is whether iconicity makes signs easier to learn. Here the evidence is surprisingly mixed. Dilani Amarasuriya, a developmental psychologist at the Kandy Institute for Child Language, examined the first signs produced by deaf children acquiring a national sign language from their deaf parents. She found that iconic signs were indeed learned somewhat earlier than non-iconic ones, but that the effect was modest compared with other factors, above all how often parents used a particular sign. Moreover, very young children do not seem to notice iconicity at all: a toddler learning the sign for 'milk', which resembles squeezing an udder, has no idea of its origin. Amarasuriya suggests that iconicity may help older children and adults more than infants, since appreciating a resemblance requires knowledge of the world that infants lack.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For adult learners, the picture appears clearer. Studies of hearing adults taking sign language classes consistently show that iconic signs are remembered more easily. Yet Arturs Rozentals, who teaches and researches at the Riga Academy of Sign Language Interpreting, warns that this advantage has a cost. Learners who rely on iconicity, he observes, often assume that they can interpret unfamiliar signs from their appearance alone, and they make errors as a result, since the conventional form of a sign frequently differs from the gesture a newcomer would consider most natural. Rozentals argues that teachers should present iconicity as an aid to memory, not as a dependable guide to meaning.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, historical research has complicated the familiar story of declining iconicity. Zofia Walewska of the Kraków Institute of Historical Linguistics has compared films and drawings of signs spanning more than a century. She confirms that many signs have lost their once-obvious link with their meaning, but she also finds the reverse process: signs whose origins had become opaque were sometimes reanalysed by signers in the light of contemporary objects, acquiring a new visual motivation. The sign for 'telephone', for example, has changed shape in several languages to reflect the shift from handsets with separate earpieces to mobile phones. Walewska concludes that iconicity is continually eroded and renewed rather than steadily lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, this research suggests that the original emphasis on arbitrariness was understandable but overstated. I do not believe that recognising iconicity weakens the status of sign languages; on the contrary, it shows that they exploit the possibilities of the visual medium in ways that spoken languages cannot. What remains unclear is how much iconicity matters for the mind. Kutateladze's further claim that iconicity shapes the way signers think about space is intriguing, but it has yet to be tested rigorously, and it would be premature to accept it. What is certain is that a theory of language built only on spoken languages will be incomplete, and that sign languages, far from being an awkward exception, may turn out to be among the most revealing cases of all.

topic: cochlear implants and whether implanted deaf children should also be exposed to sign language (language deprivation and bimodal bilingualism)
title: Two Routes to Language
subtitle: Should deaf children who receive cochlear implants also be taught to sign? A long-running dispute is being reshaped by new evidence

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Around nine in ten deaf children are born to hearing parents, most of whom have never met a deaf person before their child's diagnosis. Within weeks or months, these families face a decision with lifelong consequences. Cochlear implants, electronic devices that stimulate the auditory nerve directly, can give many profoundly deaf children access to spoken language, especially if they are fitted early in life. Families are often told that they must also decide how their child will communicate: through speech alone, or through a sign language as well. For decades, this choice has been at the centre of one of the most bitter disputes in deaf education.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for concentrating exclusively on speech was made most forcefully by clinicians who argued that time spent signing is time taken away from listening. Mikko Lehtokari, an audiologist at the Helsinki Institute for Hearing Science, has long maintained that the brain's auditory pathways develop most rapidly in the first years of life, and that children who rely on visual communication during this period may make less effective use of their implants. In a study of 150 implanted children, he found that those whose families used only spoken language had, on average, better speech perception scores at the age of six than those whose families signed. Lehtokari concludes that parents should be encouraged to prioritise listening during this critical early period.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics have identified a serious flaw in such comparisons. Families do not choose sign language at random; they are more likely to turn to it when their child is struggling with the implant. As Nomvula Ntshona, an epidemiologist at the Durban Centre for Deaf Health, points out, it is therefore unsurprising that signing children perform worse on average: signing may be a response to poor outcomes rather than their cause. When Ntshona re-analysed comparable data, taking into account how well children had been progressing before their families began to sign, the apparent disadvantage largely disappeared. Her conclusion is not that signing improves speech, but that the evidence against it is much weaker than is often claimed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental concern drives the opposing camp. Implants work well for many children, but not for all, and outcomes are notoriously difficult to predict. Some children, despite early implantation and intensive therapy, acquire spoken language slowly and incompletely. Laia Pellicer, a psycholinguist at the Barcelona Institute for Language Development, has studied what she calls 'language deprivation', the lasting cognitive and social consequences of failing to acquire any language fully in early childhood. She argues that a child who has access to a sign language from the beginning is protected against this outcome, because whatever happens with the implant, the child will possess one complete language on which to build. For Pellicer, withholding sign language is a gamble with stakes that are simply too high.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Recent research on bilingual children offers some support for this position. Studies of hearing children who grow up with both a spoken and a signed language, typically the children of deaf parents, show no disadvantage in their spoken language development, and some evidence of benefits in tasks requiring attention control. Oleksandr Vereshchak, a cognitive scientist at the Kharkiv Centre for Bilingualism Research, found that implanted deaf children whose families signed fluently performed as well on spoken vocabulary tests as children exposed to speech alone. Crucially, however, he found this only when the parents' signing was fluent; children whose parents signed hesitantly, having learned only a limited number of signs, showed no advantage over either group and in some cases did worse.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This last finding deserves far more attention than it has received, because it exposes a practical difficulty that the debate frequently ignores. It is one thing to say that children should be exposed to a sign language; it is quite another to make that possible. Learning a sign language to a high level takes years, and most hearing parents begin from nothing while also managing hospital appointments, therapy and the ordinary demands of a young family. Classes are often expensive or unavailable outside cities. If the benefit of signing depends on fluency, then recommending sign language without providing serious support for families risks creating the worst of both worlds.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In my view, the evidence now favours offering both routes rather than forcing a choice. The fear that signing harms spoken language has not been substantiated, while the risks of language deprivation are well documented. But a recommendation is only as good as the resources behind it. Programmes that pair families with deaf adults, who can model sign language and offer reassurance, appear particularly promising, although their long-term effects have not yet been properly evaluated. What families need above all is not ideology from either side but honest information about what is known, what remains uncertain, and what help is actually available to them.

topic: sign language and the brain: left-hemisphere specialisation in deaf signers, evidence from stroke patients and neuroimaging, and the effect of late language exposure
title: Language in the Hands, Language in the Brain
subtitle: Studies of deaf signers have overturned long-held assumptions about why one side of the brain dominates language

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century after physicians first linked damage to the left side of the brain with the loss of speech, it was widely assumed that the left hemisphere specialised for language because of its role in hearing and controlling the vocal tract. Speech is a rapid sequence of sounds, and the left hemisphere was thought to excel at processing fast-changing auditory signals. Sign languages offered a natural test of this idea. They are perceived through the eyes rather than the ears, they are produced by the hands, arms and face, and they make heavy use of space, a domain traditionally associated with the right hemisphere. If the lateralisation of language were simply a by-product of hearing and vocal control, signers ought to rely on the right side of the brain far more than speakers do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first clear evidence came from deaf signers who had suffered strokes. Dr Sunniva Skjeldal, a neurologist at the Bergen Institute for Clinical Neuroscience, examined thirty-four such patients over a period of eleven years. Those with damage to the left hemisphere frequently produced signs with the wrong handshape or location, much as hearing patients with aphasia substitute incorrect sounds within words, and several could no longer follow signed sentences of moderate complexity. Patients with right-hemisphere damage, by contrast, often had difficulty copying drawings or finding their way around a hospital ward, yet their signing remained grammatically intact. To Skjeldal, the conclusion is unambiguous: the left hemisphere is specialised for language as such, whatever channel the language happens to travel through.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Particularly revealing were cases in which different abilities came apart within the same individual. One patient described by Skjeldal could no longer arrange objects on a table to match a simple diagram, but continued to use signing space accurately to keep track of who had done what to whom in a story. Another could imitate meaningless hand movements perfectly while being unable to produce the signs for common household objects. Such dissociations matter because they rule out the obvious objection that signing is merely a complex motor skill. If an impairment of sign language simply reflected clumsiness of the hands, the ability to copy arbitrary movements should have been lost as well.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Neuroimaging has added detail, and some complications, to this picture. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, Dr Mirela Cozmescu of the Danube Centre for Cognitive Imaging found that the classic language regions of the left hemisphere are activated when fluent signers watch signed sentences, in much the same way as when hearing people listen to speech. However, her scans also showed more right-hemisphere activity in signers than in speakers, particularly when sentences used space to describe the layout of a room or the movement of objects within it. Cozmescu does not believe this undermines the general finding. In her interpretation, the right hemisphere is recruited for the specific task of mapping signing space onto real space, a function with no close equivalent in spoken language, while the core grammatical work remains on the left.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the case is closed. Professor Kwabena Dokyi, a linguist at the Volta Institute of Linguistics, argues that imaging studies have relied on a narrow range of sentence types, chosen largely because they resemble the structures of English. Sign languages, he points out, contain a great deal that has no spoken counterpart: facial expressions that mark questions and conditions, the simultaneous use of both hands to represent two objects, and constructions that depict events rather than describe them. If researchers examined these features more often, Dokyi suspects, the right hemisphere would turn out to play a considerably larger part. This is a fair criticism of the experimental record, but it is not obviously a challenge to the main conclusion. The stroke studies observed patients signing naturally rather than responding to selected sentences, and they still found that grammar survived damage to the right hemisphere.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further question concerns the role of age. A team led by Hiroaki Tsutsumida at the Sendai Institute of Developmental Neuroscience compared deaf adults who had learned to sign in infancy with others who first encountered sign language in adolescence, having had little access to any language before then. The late learners showed weaker and more scattered activation in left-hemisphere language areas, and their comprehension of complex sentences was poorer even after decades of daily signing. Tsutsumida's group concluded that the specialisation of the left hemisphere is not fixed at birth but depends on exposure to a language during early childhood. The modality of that language, the evidence suggests, matters far less than its timing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings are of more than theoretical interest. In several countries, deaf children are still discouraged from signing on the assumption that it will interfere with the development of speech. The neurological evidence offers no support for that assumption; if anything, it suggests that withholding an accessible language in the early years carries real and possibly permanent costs. It would be a mistake, though, to imagine that brain scans can settle questions of educational policy on their own. Families make choices for many reasons, and research is most useful when it informs those choices rather than dictating them. What the study of signers has achieved, beyond doubt, is a change in how scientists think about language itself: not as a property of the ear and the mouth, but as a capacity of the brain that will use whatever channels it is given.

topic: automated sign language translation: sensor gloves, camera-based recognition, data shortages, signing avatars and deaf community objections
title: Can a Machine Learn to Sign?
subtitle: Engineers have spent decades trying to automate sign language translation, but deaf communities are asking whom the technology is really for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years a new invention is announced that promises to break down the barrier between deaf and hearing people. Often it is a glove fitted with sensors that converts finger movements into spoken words; more recently it has been software that reads signing through a phone camera and displays a written translation. Such announcements are reliably greeted with enthusiasm in the press and, almost as reliably, with weariness among deaf people themselves. Understanding why the two reactions differ so sharply says a good deal about what sign languages are, and about the limits of treating human communication as an engineering problem.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The sensor glove illustrates the difficulty well. Yeo Dong-geun, an engineer who built one of the more sophisticated prototypes at the Gyeonggi Institute of Applied Robotics, acknowledges that his device recognised around two hundred isolated signs with high accuracy in laboratory conditions. Yet a glove records only what the fingers do. In most sign languages, a large part of the grammar is carried elsewhere: in the direction and speed of movement, in the position of the hands relative to the body, and above all on the face, where raised or lowered eyebrows can turn a statement into a question. A device that ignores these signals is, at best, recognising vocabulary rather than language. Yeo himself now describes the glove as a useful lesson in what not to do, and his team has abandoned it in favour of camera-based methods.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Camera systems trained on large collections of video have certainly advanced. Dr Teodora Kubelíková, whose group at the Brno Centre for Machine Perception develops recognition software, reports that the best current systems can translate short, carefully signed sentences on restricted topics, such as weather forecasts, with reasonable accuracy. Her main obstacle, she says, is not the algorithms but the data. Spoken-language translation systems are trained on billions of words of text; most sign languages, however, have no written form, and the total amount of annotated video available for any one of them may amount to only a few hundred hours. Moreover, much of that video comes from interpreters and television presenters, whose signing is slower and more formal than everyday conversation between deaf people.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: To Kubelíková, the solution is to expand data collection, ideally by recording deaf signers in natural settings. This sounds straightforward, but it raises awkward questions. Recording conversations requires consent, and deaf communities are small enough that individuals may be identifiable from their signing style alone. Annotation, too, is skilled work: it must be done by fluent signers, of whom there are relatively few, and it is frequently paid poorly or not at all. It seems reasonable to ask who will benefit from the products built on this labour, and whether the communities supplying it will have any say in how it is used.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That question is pressed most forcefully by Dr Oyelade Fasanmi, a deaf sociolinguist at the Lagos Centre for Deaf Studies. Fasanmi observes that almost every translation device he has examined was designed to turn signing into speech or text for hearing users, rather than the reverse. The burden of making communication work, he argues, is thereby placed once again on deaf people, who are expected to sign clearly to a machine for the convenience of others. He is also concerned that institutions such as hospitals and courts might come to regard automated tools as a cheap substitute for human interpreters, with serious consequences when translations go wrong. These worries deserve to be taken seriously, though they should not be read as a case against the technology as such. Several projects led by deaf researchers have shown that the same tools can be designed for purposes the community itself values, such as searchable dictionaries or teaching materials for hearing parents.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some applications are less controversial. Signing avatars, animated figures generated by computer, are increasingly used to present fixed announcements on railway platforms and airport screens. Because the content is predictable, it can be checked in advance by deaf signers. Yet even here, deaf viewers frequently complain that avatars look stiff and lack the facial expression that conveys meaning, so that a message about a cancelled train may appear oddly cheerful. Avatars are, in this sense, a reminder that the challenge lies not only in recognising signs but also in producing them convincingly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the dream of a universal translator? It would be wrong to dismiss the research, which has already improved scientific understanding of how sign languages are structured. But the history of these projects suggests that technical success in the laboratory has repeatedly been mistaken for a solution to a social problem. The most valuable advances are likely to come not from devices that make deaf people's languages legible to hearing users, but from collaborations in which deaf signers decide what is worth building. For the foreseeable future, a well-trained human interpreter remains far more capable than any machine.

topic: the gesture-first hypothesis of language evolution: ape gesture, tool-making and the brain, the shift to speech and the multimodal alternative
title: Did Language Begin with the Hands?
subtitle: The idea that our ancestors gestured before they spoke has found new support, but its critics remain unconvinced

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Because spoken words leave no fossils, the origins of language have long been a field in which speculation outruns evidence. In 1866 the Linguistic Society of Paris went so far as to ban discussion of the subject at its meetings, and for much of the following century serious scholars kept their distance. Among the theories that have resurfaced in recent decades, one of the most persistent holds that the first human language was not spoken but gestured, and that speech took over only later. The appeal of this gesture-first hypothesis is easy to understand. Our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos, cannot be taught to speak, yet they learn to use manual signs with surprising facility; and the existence of fully developed sign languages demonstrates that the hands are entirely capable of carrying grammar.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence in its favour comes from the study of ape communication in the wild. Dr Anneliese Vorbrüggen, a primatologist at the Rhine Primate Research Station, spent twelve years observing wild chimpanzees and catalogued more than seventy distinct gestures, from an outstretched arm requesting food to a raised hand inviting play. What impresses her is not the size of this repertoire but the way it is used. Chimpanzees direct gestures at particular individuals, check whether they have been noticed, and repeat or modify a gesture when the first attempt fails. Their vocal calls, by contrast, appear largely fixed: a chimpanzee that finds food or sees a predator produces the relevant call almost automatically, whether or not anyone is listening. For Vorbrüggen, it is this flexible, intentional quality of gesture, rather than any resemblance in form, that makes it the more plausible ancestor of language.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of argument concerns the brain. Dr Nkemdirim Ugwuoke, who studies the neuroscience of tool use at the Enugu Institute of Human Evolution, has found that the regions of the left hemisphere involved in planning sequences of hand actions overlap substantially with those that support grammar in modern humans. In imaging experiments, skilled knappers recreating ancient stone-tool techniques showed activity in areas close to those used in processing complex sentences. Ugwuoke proposes that the control of precise, ordered hand movements, refined over hundreds of thousands of years of tool-making, may have provided the neural scaffolding on which language was later built. The suggestion is an intriguing one, though overlap in brain activity is notoriously difficult to interpret: two tasks may engage the same region for quite different reasons.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis faces an obvious problem, which its critics have been quick to point out. If language began in the hands, why did virtually every human community abandon it for speech? Professor Matías Uriarte-Goñi of the Bilbao Centre for Linguistic Research argues that no satisfactory answer has been given. The usual explanations, that speech frees the hands for work, can be used in darkness and does not require the listener to be watching, are plausible enough, but Uriarte-Goñi notes that they would seem to favour speech from the very beginning, which makes it puzzling that gesture should have come first at all. He also points out that the vocal control of apes, although limited, is greater than was once believed: recent recordings show that some orangutans can learn new sounds and vary their calls deliberately.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Uriarte-Goñi's objection is a serious one, but it is perhaps less decisive than he believes. Evolution does not work towards the best possible solution; it works with whatever is already available. If our ancestors' control of the voice was poor while their control of the hands was already highly developed, gesture would have been the readier channel, whatever the eventual advantages of speech. The switch could then have occurred gradually, as anatomical changes such as the lowering of the larynx and finer control of breathing made speech increasingly practical.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A growing number of researchers now reject the choice between gesture and speech altogether. A team led by Saule Baimukhamedova at the Almaty Centre for Comparative Cognition has filmed thousands of bonobo interactions and found that gestures and vocalisations are frequently combined, with the meaning of a call sometimes depending on the gesture that accompanies it. Human communication, Baimukhamedova notes, remains thoroughly multimodal: speakers gesture constantly, and the timing of gesture and speech is so tightly coordinated that the two appear to be planned together. On this view, language did not migrate from one channel to another; it emerged from the outset as a combination of both, and the question of which came first is simply badly posed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The multimodal view has much to recommend it, not least because it fits the behaviour of living humans. Yet it should not be mistaken for a solution. Saying that language began in both channels at once leaves open the question of why speech eventually became dominant almost everywhere, while gesture was relegated to a supporting role. Nor does it explain why sign languages arise so readily whenever deaf people are brought together, a fact which suggests that the capacity for manual language lies remarkably close to the surface. It may be that the origins of language will never be known with certainty. But the debate has at least moved beyond pure speculation, and the comparative study of gesture has made a lasting contribution, regardless of which theory eventually prevails.

topic: cultural variation in gesture: emblems, lip-pointing and the division of reference, gestures for time, and gesture habits of bilinguals and migrants
title: An Accent of the Hands
subtitle: Cultures differ not only in which gestures they use, but in what they use gesture for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Travellers are often warned that a gesture which is harmless at home may cause offence abroad. The thumbs-up, the circle formed by thumb and forefinger and the beckoning finger have all acquired a reputation as hazards for the unwary tourist. Such warnings concern what researchers call emblems: gestures with a fixed, conventional meaning that can be understood without any accompanying speech, much like words. Emblems vary from place to place in roughly the way vocabulary does, and they are learned in much the same way. Yet they make up only a small part of how people use their hands when they talk, and an exclusive focus on them has, arguably, given a misleading impression of what cultural variation in gesture really involves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Wanjiru Kiriinya, an anthropologist at the Nairobi Institute for Communication Studies, has spent much of her career compiling inventories of emblems in East African communities. She has recorded more than two hundred in a single town, a number comparable to those reported for southern Italy, which has often been described as the most gesture-rich region in the world. Kiriinya argues that the Italian reputation reflects not an unusually large repertoire but the attention of earlier, largely European observers, who documented gestures in societies familiar to them and neglected those elsewhere. Her point is well made: the apparent distribution of gestural richness may say more about where scholars have looked than about where gestures are genuinely most abundant.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More revealing, in many respects, are the gestures that accompany speech without having fixed meanings. Consider pointing. In many parts of the world, people point not with the index finger but with the lips, the chin or a movement of the head, and these forms are not simply substitutes for one another. Dr Thibault Essomba of the Douala Centre for Language and Interaction analysed hundreds of hours of recorded conversation in several communities and found that lip-pointing was used mainly for objects or places that were already being discussed, while finger-pointing was reserved for introducing something new or for emphasis. In other words, different forms of pointing divide up the work of reference in ways that may be invisible to an outsider, who notices only that people seem reluctant to use their fingers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Gesture can also reveal how a culture thinks about abstract ideas. Speakers of English and many other European languages tend to gesture forwards when talking about the future and over the shoulder when talking about the past, and to place earlier events to the left and later ones to the right, the direction in which they read. Dr Mereani Tuisawau, a cognitive scientist at the Suva Institute of Pacific Studies, has documented communities in which these patterns are reversed or altogether different. In some, the past is placed in front, since it is known and can therefore be 'seen', while the unknown future lies behind. In one community she studied, time was gestured along the course of a nearby river, so that later events were indicated downstream regardless of the direction in which the speaker happened to be facing.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Tuisawau draws a bold conclusion from such findings: that gesture provides a more reliable window on how people think about time than their language does, since spoken metaphors may be fossilised expressions whose original meaning speakers no longer notice, while spontaneous gestures are produced without reflection. This claim is attractive but, in my view, somewhat overstated. Gestures are themselves shaped by convention and by imitation of others; a child who grows up watching adults point downstream for 'later' may be copying a habit rather than expressing a private mental image. Gesture is certainly a valuable source of evidence about thought, but it is one source among several rather than a privileged one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different question is addressed by Professor Ilkka Peltomaa of the Turku Laboratory for Multimodal Research, who studies how gesture changes when people move between cultures. Peltomaa found that bilingual speakers often adjust the size and frequency of their gestures depending on which language they are using, gesturing expansively in one and sparingly in the other. Long-term migrants, however, tend to retain the gestural habits of their first culture for decades, even after their speech in the new language has become fluent and almost free of any foreign accent. Gesture, Peltomaa suggests, may be one of the last features of communication to adapt: a kind of accent of the hands that persists long after the spoken accent has faded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings have practical as well as theoretical implications. Teachers of foreign languages rarely say anything about gesture, and learners are left to discover the conventions for themselves, sometimes at the cost of embarrassing misunderstandings. Including gesture in language teaching would be a sensible step, although it is far from clear how much of it can be learned through instruction rather than immersion. What is clear is that the tourist's list of forbidden gestures captures only the surface of a much deeper variation. Cultures differ not only in which gestures they use, but in the jobs they ask their hands to do, and appreciating those differences requires attention to the ordinary, unremarkable movements that accompany everyday talk.

topic: dialect levelling in planned new towns: how children of migrants form a new local variety
title: Speaking Like Nowhere in Particular
subtitle: How the children of planned towns forge new ways of talking, and what that reveals about dialect change

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When governments in the mid-twentieth century built new towns to relieve overcrowded cities, planners thought carefully about roads, housing and schools. Few gave any thought to how the inhabitants would speak. Yet these settlements turned out to be natural laboratories for linguists. Families arrived from dozens of regions, each bringing its own vowels, vocabulary and grammatical habits, and within a generation something unexpected happened: the children of these migrants began to sound remarkably alike, and remarkably unlike their parents. The process, known as dialect levelling, offers one of the clearest views available of how a new variety of a language is born.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The pioneering work in this area was carried out by Ingrid Haraldstad, a sociolinguist at the Northern Coastal University. Recording children aged four, eight and twelve in a Scandinavian new town founded in the 1960s, she found that the youngest children still spoke much like their parents, but that by the age of eight the influence of the peer group had become dominant. Features that were strongly associated with a single region, such as a distinctive vowel or an unusual word for a common object, were the first to disappear. What survived tended to be forms that were shared by several of the incoming dialects, or that were simpler, in the sense of being more regular or easier to learn. Haraldstad concluded that the new dialect was essentially a compromise, a kind of lowest common denominator negotiated in the playground.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This picture has proved influential, but it has not gone unchallenged. Babatunde Olusesi, who has compared new settlements on three continents, argues that the compromise model makes the outcome sound far more predictable than it is. In his data, the proportions of migrants from different regions were a poor guide to which features would survive. Instead, he points to the importance of a small number of socially prominent families, whose children set the tone in schools and youth clubs. On this account, levelling is less a matter of arithmetic than of prestige: children adopt the speech of those they admire. Olusesi's argument is a useful corrective, although it is worth noting that the two explanations need not be mutually exclusive. A form may survive both because many people use it and because the 'right' people do.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns timing. According to the model developed by Haraldstad and later refined by others, the formation of a new dialect typically takes three generations. The first generation of adult migrants retain their original accents almost entirely, since the capacity to acquire a new accent declines sharply after adolescence. Their children produce a highly variable mixture, with individuals differing widely even within the same classroom. Only the grandchildren, it is claimed, inherit a stable and uniform variety. Marta Drozdowska of the Institute for Language and Society has questioned this timetable. Analysing recordings from a mining settlement established in the early twentieth century, she found that a recognisably distinct local accent had emerged within roughly twenty-five years, far quicker than the three-generation model predicts. She attributes the speed to the settlement's isolation: with few outside visitors and little travel, the children had no competing model to follow.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Drozdowska's findings carry an implication that is easy to overlook. If isolation accelerates the formation of a new dialect, then the opposite should also hold: a settlement closely connected to a large city should produce a dialect that drifts towards the city's speech rather than developing a character of its own. This appears to be precisely what has happened in several satellite towns built within commuting distance of capitals. Their young residents do not speak a distinctive local variety; they speak a version of the metropolitan accent, sometimes indistinguishable from that heard in the capital's outer suburbs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why should any of this matter beyond academic linguistics? One reason is that levelling is no longer confined to new towns. Increased mobility, the decline of lifelong employment in a single place and the expansion of higher education mean that many established communities now experience a similar mixing of dialects. In much of Europe, traditional rural dialects are retreating, and in their place regional varieties are forming that cover far larger areas. Some commentators describe this as the homogenisation of speech, and lament the loss of local distinctiveness. That reaction is understandable but, in my view, somewhat misplaced. What is emerging is not uniformity but a new layer of regional difference, coarser than the old village dialects, certainly, yet still clearly identifiable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is, finally, a methodological lesson. Most studies of language change must reconstruct the past from scattered written records, or infer change by comparing speakers of different ages at a single point in time. New towns allow researchers to watch the process unfold almost from its starting point, with a known date of foundation and known origins of the population. It would be a mistake, though, to treat them as perfect experiments. Migrants are rarely a random sample of their home regions, and the records of who settled where are often incomplete. The evidence from new towns is invaluable, but it should complement, rather than replace, the slower work of tracing change in older communities.

topic: the gender pattern in sound change: why women often lead new pronunciations, and competing explanations (status, childcare, social networks, interview artefacts)
title: Who Leads the Change?
subtitle: Women are frequently found to be ahead when pronunciation shifts, but the reasons remain fiercely contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since sociolinguists first began systematically recording urban speech in the 1960s, one finding has recurred with a regularity unusual in the social sciences. When a new pronunciation is spreading through a community, women typically adopt it earlier, and use it more often, than men of the same age and social background. At the same time, women in many of the same surveys were found to use fewer of the forms that their communities regarded as careless or uneducated, such as dropped consonants or non-standard verb endings. Women, in other words, appeared to be simultaneously more conservative and more innovative than men. This apparent contradiction, which has come to be known as the gender paradox, has generated a remarkable variety of explanations, none of which has yet commanded general assent.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest account focused on status. Agnieszka Kaczmarzyk of the Baltic Institute for Social Linguistics argued that women, historically excluded from many of the occupations through which men displayed their standing, relied more heavily on symbolic resources, including speech, to signal respectability. This explained their avoidance of stigmatised forms, but not their enthusiasm for new ones. Kaczmarzyk later extended her argument by observing that innovations in their early stages are seldom stigmatised; more often they carry connotations of youth, urban sophistication and mobility, and women adopt them as markers of a modern identity. The extension is ingenious, but it risks circularity: almost any form that women are found to favour can be relabelled, after the event, as carrying some kind of prestige.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A quite different approach shifts the question from who invents new forms to whose forms survive. Luca Bergamaschi, a historical linguist, points out that in nearly every society for which records exist, mothers have performed the greater part of early childcare. Children therefore acquire much of their speech from women. A change led by women will be passed directly to both daughters and sons, while a change led by men will reach the next generation less efficiently. On this view, women need not be more innovative at all; their innovations are simply more likely to be transmitted, and so more likely to appear in the historical record. The argument is elegant, and it carries a testable prediction, which Bergamaschi openly accepts: as fathers take on a larger share of childcare, the female lead should gradually narrow. The evidence gathered so far, however, is inconclusive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Teodora Zhelyazkova, whose fieldwork centres on south-eastern Europe, regards gender as little more than a stand-in for something else. In a study of a port city, she found that the speakers who led changes were those with loose, wide-ranging social networks, people who encountered many acquaintances but belonged to no tightly bound group. In that city, women were more likely to work in shops and offices, where they met strangers daily, whereas men were concentrated in dockside crews whose members spent their working and leisure hours together. In a farming village a short distance inland, the roles were reversed: men travelled to regional markets while women rarely left the village, and there it was men who led. Of all the accounts on offer, this is the most persuasive, since it identifies a mechanism rather than a correlation. Yet it struggles to explain why the female lead should appear in so many societies whose divisions of labour differ considerably.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers suspect that part of the pattern is manufactured by the methods used to detect it. A group led by Harlan Kittredge at the Pacific Coast Speech Laboratory noted that the fieldworkers who conducted the classic surveys were overwhelmingly men, and that interviews were typically formal encounters in which speakers might be expected to monitor their language. If women adjusted their speech more than men in the presence of a male stranger, the surveys would have exaggerated the difference between the sexes. When the group reanalysed archived recordings, comparing interviews in which speaker and fieldworker were of the same sex, the gap shrank by roughly a third. It did not, however, disappear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Elin Thorbjarnardottir has drawn attention to the cases that do not fit. Her survey of island and coastal communities in the North Atlantic identified a number of well-documented changes in which young men, not women, were in the lead. Strikingly, these tended to involve the revival or exaggeration of traditional local pronunciations, often among men who had chosen to remain in fishing or farming rather than move away. Thorbjarnardottir concludes that the direction of the gender difference depends on what a particular form signifies locally. Forms associated with outward mobility are taken up first by those with the strongest ties beyond the community; forms that signal loyalty to place are championed by those whose lives are most bound to it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these accounts suggest that the search for a single cause has probably been misguided. The female lead looks less like a fixed property of half of humanity than an outcome produced, in different places, by different combinations of status, childcare, working life and local meaning. If the debate has achieved anything lasting, it is to have moved attention away from individual speakers and their supposed tendencies towards the social structures in which speech is learned and used. That shift has made language change appear considerably less mysterious than it once did.

topic: the apparent-time method in studying language change, age grading, and panel studies showing that adults' speech continues to change
title: Hearing the Past in the Present
subtitle: Linguists often detect language change by comparing old and young speakers, but the assumption behind this shortcut is under growing strain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Language change is usually too slow to observe directly. A shift in the pronunciation of a vowel may take half a century to work its way through a community, far longer than most research careers or funding cycles. Linguists have therefore relied on an ingenious shortcut known as the apparent-time method. Instead of waiting decades, researchers record speakers of different ages at a single moment. If grandparents consistently use one form, their children use a mixture, and teenagers use a new form almost exclusively, it is inferred that the community is moving from the old form to the new. The method rests on a crucial assumption: that an individual's way of speaking becomes more or less fixed by the end of adolescence, so that older people preserve the speech of their youth in much the way that the rings of a tree preserve the conditions of past seasons.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For several decades the assumption was rarely questioned, partly because the method seemed to work. Renata Kalnina, who leads a dialect research group at the Daugava Linguistics Centre, has systematically compared the predictions of apparent-time studies with recordings and written descriptions made in the same communities many years earlier. In the great majority of cases, the direction of change suggested by the age differences matched what the older evidence showed. Kalnina describes the method as remarkably robust when it comes to identifying which way a language is moving, while conceding that it is a far less dependable guide to how fast that movement is taking place.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One long-recognised difficulty is what linguists call age grading. Some features of speech are associated not with a particular generation but with a particular stage of life. Faisal Noorani, a sociolinguist who has worked extensively with adolescents, points out that teenagers in many communities use more non-standard pronunciations than their parents, yet tend to abandon them in their twenties, when they enter the labour market and face pressures such as job interviews and dealings with clients. A researcher who recorded such a community only once would see the young using a form that the old avoid, and might wrongly conclude that a change was in progress. The only reliable way to tell the two situations apart, Noorani argues, is to return to the same community later.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Returning is exactly what real-time studies do, and they come in two forms. Trend studies revisit a community after an interval and record a fresh sample of speakers chosen by the same criteria as before. Panel studies, which are much rarer, track down and re-interview the very same individuals. The practical obstacles are formidable: participants die, move away or simply decline to take part again. Henrik Rosenqvist managed to locate only forty of the one hundred and twenty speakers originally recorded in a Baltic port twenty-eight years earlier. What he found in their recordings, however, was striking. A substantial number of these adults had altered their pronunciation over the intervening years, and they had done so in the same direction as the community as a whole, adopting the innovations of younger speakers, though never to the same extent.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The implication is uncomfortable for the apparent-time method. If older adults have themselves moved towards newer forms, their speech no longer faithfully records that of their youth, and the gap between generations will appear smaller than the change that has actually occurred. In other words, apparent-time comparisons may systematically understate the pace of change. Rosenqvist has described the stable adult as a 'useful fiction'. His challenge is a welcome one, but the scale of adult change should not be overstated. In his data the shifts were modest, and they varied considerably from one person to the next; some individuals had barely changed at all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why some adults change and others do not is the question addressed by Sofia Lazaridou. Comparing panel data from two cities, she found that the adults who altered their speech most were those whose social circumstances had changed: people who had moved up the occupational ladder, switched careers, or spent much of their working day with younger people, as teachers and youth workers do. Those whose lives had remained stable changed least. Lazaridou concludes that linguistic flexibility in adulthood depends less on age than on social experience. The argument is plausible, but her sample was small and entirely urban, and extending her conclusions to rural communities, where social networks tend to be denser and more stable, would be premature.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the apparent-time method should be discarded. It remains the only practical means of studying change in the many communities for which no earlier recordings exist, and Kalnina's comparisons show that it usually points in the right direction. What the real-time evidence demands is a degree of modesty: apparent-time results are best treated as approximate indications of where a language is heading, to be checked against real-time data wherever such data can be obtained. That, in turn, requires a willingness to invest in research whose rewards may not appear for decades. It is regrettable that funding bodies, which typically expect results within three or four years, have so rarely shown such patience.

topic: the myth that isolated communities preserve archaic speech: relic features, innovation in small populations, contact and heritage narratives
title: The Myth of the Frozen Tongue
subtitle: Remote communities are often said to speak as their ancestors did centuries ago. The reality is considerably more interesting

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visitors to certain remote valleys and islands are frequently told that the local people still speak the language of their seventeenth-century ancestors, or even of Shakespeare. The notion that isolation preserves speech, as a sealed tomb preserves its contents, has an obvious appeal. It promises a direct line to the past, and it gives small communities a distinctive and marketable heritage. Linguists, however, have long been sceptical, and with good reason: such claims almost invariably collapse under close examination. Yet dismissing them is not enough. It is worth asking why the idea has proved so durable, and whether it contains any kernel of truth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The kernel is real but small. Isolated communities do sometimes retain individual features that have disappeared elsewhere: an old word for a farm implement, an archaic past-tense form, a pronunciation once common across a whole region. Matteo Sabatino, who spent a decade documenting a dialect spoken in a cluster of high mountain villages, identified roughly a dozen such relics. Alongside them, however, he found a striking number of innovations entirely unknown in the region from which the villagers' ancestors had come, including a thoroughly reorganised system of verb endings. Preservation and innovation, Sabatino concluded, are not alternatives but companions. Isolation removes the levelling pressure that contact with outsiders exerts, and in doing so it allows old forms to linger and new, idiosyncratic ones to flourish.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should small, secluded communities innovate at all? One answer draws an analogy with population genetics. In a large, well-connected population, random variations tend to cancel each other out; in a small one, an innovation introduced by a single prominent household can sweep through the whole community within a generation. Hirut Tsegaye, a computational linguist, has modelled this process by simulating thousands of virtual communities of different sizes and degrees of contact. In her models, small and isolated populations changed faster, not more slowly, than large ones, and they did so in directions that were impossible to predict, whereas large, connected populations changed gradually and tended to converge. Simulations are, of course, only as sound as the assumptions built into them. Even so, Tsegaye's results match the evidence from fieldwork closely enough to be deeply uncomfortable for the preservation story.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further weakness of that story is that isolation is seldom as complete as it appears. Many communities now regarded as remote were once linked to the outside world by seasonal labour, trade or the sea. Jonas Baranauskas examined parish registers, shipping records and early dialect surveys relating to an island long celebrated for its archaic speech. He found that a considerable proportion of its supposedly ancient features had in fact arrived during the nineteenth century, carried by fishermen who settled there from a distant port. These features seemed archaic only because they were absent from the standard language of the nearby mainland. The episode illustrates how readily claims of antiquity arise when a dialect is measured against the wrong point of reference.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, does the myth persist? The anthropologist Ragnheidur Gudmundsdottir has studied how communities themselves deploy it. Beyond its value for tourism, the claim of antiquity can transform a stigmatised way of speaking, long ridiculed by outsiders as incorrect or uneducated, into a treasured inheritance. Gudmundsdottir argues that linguists should be cautious about debunking such narratives, because they perform real social functions and may encourage people to keep speaking a dialect that would otherwise be abandoned. Her account of the motives involved is illuminating, but her conclusion is harder to accept. Scholars cannot lend their authority to claims they know to be false, and the myth carries a hidden cost of its own. If a dialect is valued only as a relic, then every change it undergoes is liable to be condemned as corruption, and the young people who are actually keeping it alive may be told that they speak it badly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a basic problem of method. To show that a dialect has preserved the speech of its founders, one must know what that speech was like at the time of settlement, and this is frequently unknown. In practice, many claims of preservation rest on comparing a modern rural dialect with the modern urban standard. Since the standard has itself changed considerably over the same period, the differences between the two may reflect developments in the standard at least as much as any conservatism in the dialect. A rural form that strikes a city dweller as old-fashioned may simply be one that the city abandoned.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Every living dialect is a blend of the inherited and the newly invented, and isolated dialects are no exception. They are better understood not as museums, in which the past is displayed behind glass, but as laboratories in which language is free to develop on its own terms, unconstrained by the norms of a wider society. Their real value lies not in what they have kept but in what they reveal about the range of directions that a language can take when left to itself.
