topic: whether television and other media change people's accents: passive viewing, engaged viewers, vocabulary versus pronunciation, and interactive online gaming
title: Can the Screen Change the Way We Speak?
subtitle: Linguists have long insisted that broadcasting has little effect on accents. That certainty is beginning to look less secure

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few beliefs about language are as widespread as the idea that television is flattening regional accents. Every generation, it seems, fears that its grandchildren will end up sounding like newsreaders. Linguists have traditionally dismissed this fear. Accents, they point out, are acquired through interaction with real people, not through passive listening; a child may hear thousands of hours of broadcast speech, but nobody can hold a conversation with a television set. In broad outline, this orthodoxy is sound. Over time, however, it has hardened into something closer to dogma, and the confidence with which it was asserted has, for several decades, discouraged anyone from testing it properly.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The evidence for the orthodox position is nonetheless substantial. Ilaria Pellegatti followed several hundred children from early childhood into adolescence, recording both their speech and their viewing habits. Children who watched large amounts of programming presented in the national standard showed no greater tendency to adopt standard pronunciation than those who watched little; their accents tracked those of their friends and classmates almost exactly. Pellegatti also drew attention to a telling detail. The pronunciations spreading most rapidly among young people in her study were rarely those heard on national broadcasts at all. On the contrary, they were non-standard features that appeared to be moving from one city to another through personal contact, carried by students, workers and families on the move.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first serious challenge to this picture came from Daniyar Kozhakhmetov, who studied the audience of a long-running and very popular drama series set in a large city. Rather than simply counting hours of viewing, he measured how emotionally involved viewers were with the programme: whether they discussed its characters, identified with them, or followed the actors' lives off screen. After allowing for the amount of contact each person had with residents of the city, he found that strongly engaged viewers used certain pronunciations associated with that city more often than other viewers did. Among casual viewers there was no detectable effect. Kozhakhmetov does not claim that television introduces new features. He describes it instead as an accelerator: by presenting forms that people have already encountered in conversation in an attractive and familiar light, it may speed up their adoption.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kozhakhmetov's study is carefully designed, but its findings are correlational, and an alternative explanation cannot be ruled out. People who are already drawn to a fashionable urban identity might be more likely both to become devoted to a city-based drama and to adopt the city's speech, without the one causing the other. A longitudinal design, in which the same viewers were recorded both before and after they became attached to a series, would go some way towards settling the matter, although such studies are expensive and slow to yield results. Even so, the accelerator model seems far more plausible than either of the extreme positions, the popular belief that television transforms accents and the academic insistence that it has no effect whatsoever.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much depends, too, on which aspect of language is in question. Layla Aldabbagh has assembled extensive evidence that words and catchphrases spread readily through films and broadcasting, sometimes within weeks of a programme being aired. Vocabulary, she argues, is easy to borrow because speakers can adopt a word deliberately, often as a playful quotation. Pronunciation and grammar are different. They are acquired largely unconsciously in childhood and are deeply ingrained, so that even speakers who want to change them find it difficult. Aldabbagh proposes a hierarchy of susceptibility to media influence, with individual words at the top, set phrases next, pronunciation further down and grammatical structure at the bottom.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recent technological change complicates matters further. Much of the media that young people now consume is not broadcast at all, and some of it is interactive. Karim Nasrallah studied teenagers who spent several hours a week playing online games while talking to other players through voice chat, often with people from regions or countries they had never visited. He found clear evidence that the players adjusted their pronunciation towards that of their regular teammates during play, and that some of these adjustments appeared in their speech away from the game as well. This research blurs the very distinction between media and interaction on which the orthodox view was built; in such settings, one can talk back. Whether the effects Nasrallah observed will last into adulthood, however, it is still far too early to say.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is that the question 'Does television change accents?' was always rather too crude. The line between media and conversation is not a sharp boundary but a matter of degree, and what seems to matter most is not exposure as such but engagement and social meaning: whether listeners care about the speakers they hear and wish, in some sense, to be like them. Future research would do better to measure viewers' engagement than to keep counting the hours they spend in front of a screen. It would also be wise to abandon the assumption that a single answer will hold for every community, since the prestige attached to broadcast speech varies considerably from one society to another.

topic: grammaticalisation: how ordinary words become grammatical markers, frequency and phonetic reduction, the unidirectionality hypothesis and its counter-examples
title: From Words to Grammar
subtitle: How ordinary vocabulary slowly hardens into the machinery of a language, and whether the process ever runs backwards

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every language possesses a stock of grammatical words and endings, such as prepositions, auxiliary verbs and markers of tense and case, that carry little meaning of their own but hold sentences together. For a long time, the origins of this machinery were considered beyond recovery. Over the past half-century, however, historical linguists have shown that a great many grammatical items began life as ordinary nouns and verbs. The English auxiliary 'will' once meant 'want'; the phrase 'going to', which originally described physical movement, now signals the future and in casual speech has contracted to 'gonna'. The process by which content words harden into grammar is known as grammaticalisation. It is, I would argue, among the most valuable insights the discipline has produced, although, as will become clear, it has sometimes been asked to explain more than it can.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Three changes typically accompany the process. The word's original meaning fades, a development known as semantic bleaching; its range of use widens; and its pronunciation is reduced. Teodoro Abrantes, of the Lusitanian Institute of Language History, set out to establish the order in which these changes occur. Working with a corpus of private letters and court records spanning six centuries, rather than printed books, he traced dozens of constructions from their first appearance to their full grammatical use. In almost every case, a sharp rise in frequency came first, and phonetic shortening followed, typically within about a hundred and fifty years. Abrantes concludes that repetition is the engine of the whole process. Just as a pianist who practises a passage eventually plays it without conscious attention, speakers who produce the same sequence of words thousands of times begin to treat it as a single unit, compressing it in the process.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second, more controversial claim concerns direction. According to the unidirectionality hypothesis, items move from lexical to grammatical, and from less grammatical to more grammatical, but almost never in reverse. Sunniva Kvalsvik, at the Nordic Centre for Language Typology, has compiled a database of documented changes drawn from over four hundred languages and reports that reversals account for less than one per cent of them. For Kvalsvik, this asymmetry is close enough to a law to be used as a tool. When two related languages express the same idea, one with an independent verb and the other with a suffix, she argues, a reconstruction should assume that the verb represents the older stage, because the opposite development would be almost unprecedented.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Mirela Sarbulescu has spent much of her career challenging this reasoning. She has gathered a collection of apparent counter-examples, several of them from English: the suffix '-ism' has become a free-standing noun, as in talk of competing 'isms'; the preposition 'up' can now serve as a verb, as when a company decides to 'up' its prices; and the possessive ending has loosened its attachment to individual nouns, so that it can close an entire phrase. If such reversals are possible at all, Sarbulescu contends, unidirectionality is a tendency rather than a law, and using it to reconstruct the past risks circularity, since the hypothesis is then confirmed by the very histories it was used to create. Her logical point is well taken. Yet most of her examples are marginal, often playful coinages, and the overwhelming imbalance in the data still demands an explanation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most persuasive explanation so far has come from Kobina Essandoh, who locates the cause in the behaviour of speakers rather than in the structure of language. People, he observes, are constantly searching for vivid and forceful ways of expressing themselves. Emphatic expressions lose their impact through overuse and must be replaced, and the replacements are recruited from ordinary vocabulary. French negation illustrates the pattern. The word 'pas', originally meaning 'step', was first added to verbs of motion for emphasis before becoming a compulsory part of every negative sentence; in informal speech the older negative particle 'ne' is now frequently omitted altogether. Essandoh describes the result as a cycle of renewal. Crucially, worn-out grammatical forms hold little attraction for speakers in search of expressiveness, which is why material flows steadily into grammar but rarely back out.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Valuable as these accounts are, the field has a habit of treating grammaticalisation itself as an explanation. Strictly speaking, it is not one. The term describes an outcome, a recurring pathway from word to grammar; the causes lie elsewhere, in frequency, in the inferences listeners draw, and in the social spread of new forms. There is also a problem of evidence that deserves more attention than it receives. Written records are dominated by formal registers, and innovations typically circulate in speech for generations before writers consider them respectable enough to commit to paper. Abrantes's letters are less formal than most historical sources, but even they were written by people who had been taught to write carefully. His figure of a century and a half may therefore underestimate how long the process takes, since the real starting point probably lies earlier than the first written attestation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the central lesson, which has a direct bearing on present-day attitudes. Commentators who deplore forms such as 'gonna', or the use of 'like' to introduce reported speech, often present them as evidence that the language is decaying. In fact, they are products of exactly the processes that created the grammar such critics wish to defend. To complain about them is rather like a medieval scribe lamenting the arrival of a future tense that later generations would regard as perfectly correct. Language change is not a falling away from some earlier perfection; it is how grammar comes into being.

topic: accent prejudice in hiring: matched-guise evaluations, employer callbacks, listener perception, accent-reduction courses, training recruitment panels and legal protection
title: The Price of a Vowel
subtitle: Listeners judge speakers by their accents within moments. Researchers disagree about what, if anything, can be done about it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine two recordings of the same job applicant answering the same interview question. The words are identical, the hesitations fall in the same places, and the voice belongs to a single person; the only difference is that in one recording the speaker uses the accent of a prosperous capital city, and in the other the accent of an industrial region in decline. Listeners asked to rate the recordings consistently judge the first version more intelligent and more competent, and the second friendlier and more trustworthy. This technique, known as the matched-guise test, was devised in the mid-twentieth century and has since been repeated in dozens of countries. Its results are remarkably stable, and they reveal something uncomfortable: accent remains one of the few grounds of social judgement that many people still regard as acceptable to express openly.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Laboratory ratings, of course, are not decisions. Rafael Achurra, of the Institute for Applied Sociolinguistics, therefore moved the question into the workplace. He sent recorded voicemail messages from fictional applicants, identical except for accent, to some six hundred employers advertising vacancies. Applicants with the prestige accent received around thirty per cent more return calls for posts involving contact with customers, but for positions based in back offices the difference disappeared. Achurra interprets this as evidence that employers are often anticipating the prejudices of their clients rather than acting on their own. The distinction is analytically useful, but it offers little comfort to the applicant who is turned away, and it can hardly be treated as a defence: a prejudice that is merely passed along on someone else's behalf still does its damage.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Eun-ji Seonwoo has examined how quickly such judgements are made, and on what basis. In her experiments, listeners formed stable impressions of a speaker's social background within half a second, long before they could have processed the content of what was being said. More strikingly, when the same recording was paired with photographs of different faces, listeners reported hearing a noticeably stronger accent if the face appeared to belong to a member of an ethnic minority. Seonwoo concludes that what people call an accent is partly constructed by the listener. This finding deserves far wider attention than it has received, because it implies that teaching speakers to modify the way they talk will not, on its own, remove the discrimination they face.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That has not prevented the growth of a substantial industry offering accent reduction, with courses that promise clients a neutral or professional voice. Supporters of such courses argue that they are simply pragmatic: whatever the injustice, individuals must make their way in the labour market as it actually exists. Oluwaseun Adegbite followed adults through several of these programmes. Acoustic analysis showed measurable changes in a handful of vowels, yet when independent listeners rated recordings made before and after the course, their judgements of the speakers barely shifted. Many participants also reported a sense of having given up part of who they were. Adegbite stops short of condemning the courses, noting that some clients said they felt more confident afterwards. Even so, the industry as a whole places the burden of change on the wrong party.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An alternative is to work on the listeners. Thandiwe Mdletshe designed a programme for recruitment panels in which members listened regularly, over several weeks, to competent professionals speaking with a wide range of accents. By the end, the gap between panels' ratings of standard and regional speakers had narrowed by roughly half. When Mdletshe returned six months later, however, the effect had partly worn off. Her recommendation is therefore to combine exposure with structured interviews, in which every candidate answers the same questions and is scored against fixed criteria before the panel begins any discussion. Changing attitudes is slow and uncertain work; altering the procedures through which decisions are made appears to be a considerably more reliable route.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The law has been slow to engage with any of this. In most jurisdictions accent is not in itself a protected characteristic, although it frequently overlaps with nationality or ethnic background, which are. Some campaigners argue for explicit protection. Their opponents point out that certain roles legitimately require a speaker to be readily understood, air traffic control being the example most often cited. The objection rests on a confusion, however. Being easily understood and having a particular accent are not the same thing: a speaker with a strong regional accent may be entirely clear, while one with a prestigious accent may mumble. Any legislation worth having would need to protect accent while still allowing employers to test how well a candidate can be understood.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most troubling finding of all is that the prejudice is not confined to outsiders. In region after region, listeners rate speakers with their own local accent as less competent than those who use the prestige variety, a pattern that sociolinguists term linguistic insecurity. There are some grounds for cautious optimism. Broadcasters now feature a far wider range of regional voices than they once did, and younger listeners in several studies show smaller gaps in their ratings than their parents. But attitudes that have been absorbed over generations are unlikely to disappear of their own accord, and complacency would be a mistake.

topic: multiethnolects: new youth varieties in multilingual city neighbourhoods, learner-origin versus identity-style accounts, persistence into adulthood, stigma in schools and cross-city similarities
title: The Sound of the Mixed City
subtitle: In the most multilingual neighbourhoods of large cities, teenagers have created new ways of speaking. Are these dialects, slang or something else entirely?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the 1980s, linguists in a number of European cities have reported a distinctive way of speaking among adolescents in neighbourhoods where dozens of languages are in daily use. Its features vary from place to place, but certain traits recur: words borrowed from the languages of immigrant families, a simplified system of grammatical gender, unusual word order and a clipped, evenly stressed rhythm. What makes the phenomenon remarkable is that it is not restricted to the children of migrants. Teenagers whose parents grew up speaking only the national language use it too, provided that they have grown up in the same streets and attended the same schools. Researchers have coined the term 'multiethnolect' to describe such varieties. The label is a useful one, but, as I will suggest, it obscures almost as much as it reveals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Early accounts placed the origins of these varieties in second-language learning. Zeynep Ozdamarlar, whose recordings from the late 1980s are among the earliest systematic descriptions, argued that many of the distinctive features began as the approximations of adults acquiring the national language as newcomers. In her view, these forms were then passed on, not principally by parents, whose contact with their children's peer groups was limited, but by older brothers and sisters, who acted as linguistic models for younger children and their friends. Once established among one group of siblings, a feature could spread rapidly through an entire school.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dagny Kvernmo regards this explanation as incomplete at best. She points out that several of the most characteristic features, including the distinctive rhythm, are not found in the speech of adult learners at all and do not correspond to any of the heritage languages spoken in the neighbourhoods concerned. For Kvernmo, the variety is better understood as a style, assembled by young people to signal toughness, solidarity and attachment to a particular place. Her strongest evidence comes from recordings of the same teenagers in different settings: they used the features heavily when talking among themselves, but very sparingly in conversation with teachers, and hardly at all when taking part in mock job interviews.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If Kvernmo is right, one would expect the variety to fade as its speakers grow up, much as teenage slang usually does. Marcel Okpalaeke set out to test this by recording a group of speakers at intervals from the age of fifteen into their early thirties. Many features did decline as the speakers entered work and family life, which lends some support to the view that the variety is a youthful style. However, a number of features, notably the simplified gender system and certain vowel qualities, persisted, and Okpalaeke found them again in the speech of his participants' young children. He concludes that what began as an adolescent way of talking is hardening into a stable community dialect. Of all the work in this field, his is the most significant, since it suggests that linguists may be observing the birth of new urban dialects in real time.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Public discussion has generally been less curious. Newspapers describe the varieties as broken or impoverished language, comedians parody them, and politicians have occasionally blamed them for poor school results. Ines Sotomarino examined how teachers perceive pupils who use these forms. Shown samples of speech together with pieces of written work, teachers rated multiethnolect speakers lower in academic potential even when their written work had been judged equal to that of other pupils. Sotomarino argues that it is the stigma, rather than the variety itself, that damages pupils' prospects. She is surely right, although it would be naive to dismiss anxieties about the standard language altogether: examinations and most employers still demand it. The sensible goal is for pupils to add the standard to their repertoire, not to abandon the way they speak with their friends.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A team at the Centre for Urban Speech led by Lukas Vondracek has compared descriptions from five cities in different countries. Despite the very different national languages and heritage languages involved, the team found striking similarities: reduced gender marking, a preference for fixed word order and the frequent use of a small number of discourse particles. Vondracek interprets these parallels as universal consequences of intense linguistic contact among young people. The interpretation is attractive, but it should be treated with some caution. Researchers in each city have been guided by the earliest published descriptions, and it is quite possible that they have been searching for the same features, while traits which did not fit the established template have gone unreported.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question of whether these varieties are dialects or styles may ultimately be a false choice. Every dialect presumably began as some group's way of marking who they were, and the speech of many great cities was itself formed when migrants from numerous regions were thrown together. What multiethnolects offer is an unusual opportunity to watch that process as it happens, and they deserve the same careful description that linguists have long devoted to the speech of remote rural villages.

topic: mapping dialects: traditional dialect atlases and their informants, gradual boundaries versus isoglosses, smartphone crowdsourced surveys and the reliability of self-reported usage
title: Drawing Lines Through Speech
subtitle: For more than a century, dialectologists have tried to map how language varies across a territory. New technology is changing both the maps and the questions they raise

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The great dialect atlases of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were heroic undertakings. Fieldworkers travelled from village to village, often on foot or by bicycle, carrying questionnaires that ran to several hundred items. In each locality they would ask a carefully chosen informant what he called a particular farm implement, how he pronounced a given word, or which form of a verb he would use in a set phrase, and the answers were transcribed and later plotted as symbols on a map. The informants were not chosen at random. Fieldworkers sought out elderly men who had spent their whole lives in one place and had travelled little, on the assumption that such people preserved the most authentic local speech. Given the aims of the projects, this approach was understandable. Its result, however, was a portrait of a vanishing countryside, not a record of how the majority of the population actually spoke.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Gwilym Prys-Ellis, who has written extensively on the history of the discipline, believes that the atlases have been judged too harshly. Their compilers, he argues, were racing against time to document rural speech that would otherwise have disappeared without trace, and to criticise them for not studying cities is to fault them for failing to do something they never set out to do. Today, Prys-Ellis adds, the old maps are an irreplaceable baseline against which later change can be measured. On this last point he is clearly correct. It does not follow, though, that the atlases are beyond criticism, because their selective sampling is routinely forgotten when their maps are reproduced in textbooks and popular books, where they are presented simply as pictures of a nation's dialects.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second difficulty concerns the lines themselves. Where the answers given in one group of villages differed from those in a neighbouring group, mapmakers drew a boundary, known as an isogloss, between them. Bundles of such lines were taken to mark the borders of dialect areas. Mathilde Kerhervé decided to examine one such border in detail, interviewing several hundred residents of every age along a stretch of countryside that the atlases had divided neatly in two. She found no single dividing line. Instead, there was a belt some thirty kilometres wide in which both competing forms were in use, sometimes by the same speaker on different occasions. Kerhervé concludes that the sharp boundaries on dialect maps are largely a product of how the information was displayed: a symbol on a map can record only one answer per village, and so variation within communities simply disappears from view.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recent technology has transformed the scale of the enterprise. Jana Ostrovidova and her colleagues developed a smartphone application that asks users to choose between alternative words and pronunciations and to state their age and the place where they grew up. Within a few months the application had gathered more than seven hundred thousand responses, more than all the traditional surveys of the country combined. Because each answer is tagged with the user's age, the team can produce separate maps for different generations. Comparing them, Ostrovidova has shown that many regional forms that remain common among older users are retreating among younger ones, who increasingly favour variants associated with a handful of large cities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such data have obvious weaknesses. Users of the application are self-selected and tend to be younger, better educated and more urban than the population as a whole. More fundamentally, the application records what people say they say, which is not necessarily what they actually say. Tomasz Wielgosz investigated this by asking a sample of users to complete the survey and then recording them in conversation. For vocabulary, their answers agreed with their recorded speech in about eighty-five per cent of cases, but for pronunciation the figure fell to little more than half. People, it seems, are poor judges of the sounds they themselves produce. Maps of pronunciation derived from such applications should accordingly be read with considerable caution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The two researchers disagree about how serious this is. Ostrovidova maintains that errors of self-report are largely random and that, with hundreds of thousands of responses, they will tend to cancel each other out. Wielgosz replies that the errors are systematic rather than random: speakers consistently report the form they consider correct or typical of their region, and gathering more answers will not correct a distortion that runs in the same direction every time. Wielgosz has the stronger argument. A larger sample drawn from a biased population merely produces a more precise version of the wrong answer. None of this makes the applications worthless; for vocabulary, in particular, they appear to be a quick and reasonably reliable tool.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the history of dialect mapping teaches, above all, is that maps of speech are not mirrors but arguments. Every one reflects decisions about whom to ask, what to ask and how to display the answers, and those decisions shape the picture as much as the speech itself does. The most promising projects now combine methods, using large online surveys to identify patterns and targeted recordings to check them, and weighting results to compensate for who has and has not taken part. That is less dramatic than a coloured map of a nation's dialects, but it is a great deal more honest.

topic: whether languages change at a steady rate: lexical dating of language splits, word frequency and replacement rates, bursts of change at separation, contact-driven borrowing and computational dating methods
title: The Unreliable Clock
subtitle: Can the rate at which words are replaced tell us when two languages went their separate ways?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: All living languages change, but does change proceed at a uniform pace? In the middle of the twentieth century, a method known as lexical dating proposed that it did, at least for one part of the vocabulary. The idea was that a core list of basic meanings, such as parts of the body, low numbers, family relationships and features of the natural world, is resistant to fashion and borrowing, and that its words are therefore replaced at a roughly constant rate. If that rate were known, the proportion of shared core words in two related languages could be used to calculate how long ago they had separated, in much the same way that radioactive decay is used to date ancient objects. The method was adopted enthusiastically, but when it was applied to languages whose history is well documented it frequently produced dates that were badly wrong, and by the 1970s most specialists had abandoned it. That rejection was, in my view, too hasty. The method's central intuition, that some words are far more durable than others, was entirely sound; what failed was the assumption that durability could be converted into a single, fixed rate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Ragnhild Esmark has done more than anyone to explain why durability varies. Working with large comparative databases covering several language families, she measured how often each core meaning is expressed in everyday conversation and compared this with how frequently the corresponding word had been replaced. The relationship proved remarkably strong. The most commonly used words, among them low numbers and pronouns, may survive for ten thousand years or more, whereas less frequently used items on the same list are often replaced within a few centuries. Esmark argues that frequency of use accounts for most of the difference in replacement rates between meanings, because words that are constantly repeated are reinforced in the memory of every speaker and are correspondingly hard to dislodge.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kazuhiro Yamabuki has drawn attention to a different kind of irregularity, one that concerns time rather than meaning. Comparing pairs of closely related languages, he found that the divergence between them was not spread evenly across their histories. Instead, a substantial share of their differences, in some cases around a third, appeared to have arisen in a short burst at about the time the communities separated. Yamabuki attributes these bursts to the desire of a newly independent group to distinguish itself from its former neighbours, a process in which linguistic differences become markers of identity and are deliberately adopted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For Lucia Barrachina, irregularity goes deeper still. Her research focuses on periods of intense contact, such as conquest, large-scale migration and long-distance trade, during which a language may replace a significant part of even its basic vocabulary with borrowings in the space of a couple of centuries. Because such episodes depend on the accidents of political and economic history, she argues, no reliable clock of language change can ever be constructed. Language, in her memorable phrase, is not a clock but a weather system.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Obinna Chukwuneta takes a more optimistic view. He has applied computational methods originally developed in evolutionary biology, which do not assume a single rate but allow rates to vary from one word to another and from one branch of a language family to another. Rather than giving a precise date for the separation of two languages, these methods produce date ranges with an estimate of their probability. Chukwuneta reports that the ranges obtained for several language families are consistent with independent archaeological evidence about the movements of the populations concerned. This is a genuine advance on the original method. Yet the ranges are often wide, sometimes spanning several thousand years, and the calibration of the models relies partly on archaeological assumptions which are themselves disputed. There is a danger that linguists and archaeologists end up confirming each other's conjectures.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the variation in rates of change is patterned rather than chaotic. Frequency of use appears to provide a fairly steady background rate for each meaning, onto which are superimposed bursts of change at moments of separation and surges of borrowing during periods of contact. Barrachina's comparison with the weather is therefore apt in one respect but misleading in another. Weather is indeed irregular, yet meteorologists still produce useful forecasts expressed as probabilities, which is very much what the newer dating methods attempt to do.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It should be stressed that almost all of this work concerns vocabulary. Changes in sound systems and grammar are considerably harder to quantify, and attempts to date language splits on the basis of grammatical features have so far produced results that are far less consistent. The dream of a universal clock of language change has not been realised, and it probably never will be. What has replaced it, a set of probabilistic tools whose assumptions are stated openly, is less ambitious but far more defensible.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: the longitude problem at sea: marine chronometers versus the lunar-distance method, and why the two coexisted
title: Two Ways to Find a Ship
subtitle: The familiar story of how sailors learned their longitude leaves out much of what actually happened at sea

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of ocean navigation, a ship's latitude, its position north or south of the equator, could be found with reasonable confidence by measuring the height of the sun at noon or of the pole star at night. Longitude was another matter. Because the earth turns through fifteen degrees every hour, determining how far east or west a vessel had travelled amounted to knowing the time at two places at once: the local time on board, which could be read from the sun, and the time at some reference point such as a home port. The difference between the two gave the longitude. The difficulty lay entirely in the second figure. Without a reliable way of carrying the home time across thousands of kilometres of rolling sea, navigators relied on dead reckoning, estimating position from speed, heading and elapsed time, a method whose errors accumulated with each day of a voyage.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The popular account of how this problem was solved is a story of individual triumph. In the eighteenth century, so the story goes, a self-taught clockmaker built a series of timekeepers robust enough to keep accurate time despite the motion of a ship and the changing temperatures and humidity of a long voyage, and in doing so defeated the astronomers who favoured a rival celestial method. The account is not false, but it is badly incomplete, and its persistence says more about the appeal of the lone inventor than about the historical record.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The rival method was that of lunar distances. The moon moves against the background of fixed stars by roughly its own diameter every hour, so its position functions as a clock visible from anywhere on earth. By measuring the angle between the moon and a selected star with a sextant, and comparing the result with tables predicting that angle for the reference meridian, a navigator could deduce the home time. Dr Ana Mendonça, a maritime historian at the Lisbon Institute for Naval Studies, has examined more than three hundred logbooks from British, Portuguese and Dutch vessels and found that lunar observations remained the routine means of fixing longitude on most ocean-going ships until well into the 1830s. In her view, the method's reputation as a cumbersome failure is a retrospective invention, created once the chronometer had become cheap enough to make it unnecessary.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The reason it took so long, according to the economic historian Karel Morandi-Hale of the University of Zagreb, was price rather than performance. Early marine chronometers were handmade instruments that could cost as much as a third of the value of the vessel carrying them, and even the navy issued them only to a minority of its ships for several decades. Lunar distances, by contrast, required only a sextant, which a competent officer already owned, and a published almanac costing a few shillings. Morandi-Hale argues that it was the mechanisation of chronometer manufacture, not any single design breakthrough, that finally decided the matter. This interpretation is persuasive as far as it goes, but it underplays a genuine weakness of the lunar method: the calculations involved could take an experienced navigator up to four hours, and a single arithmetical slip could place a ship many kilometres from its true position.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Liesel Bergfeld, who studies the history of scientific instruments at the Hamburg Maritime Museum, emphasises a different point. The two methods, she contends, were never true competitors at sea, whatever rivalry existed between their advocates on land. Logbooks show that captains fortunate enough to possess a chronometer routinely used lunar observations to check it, since even the finest timekeeper might drift or stop altogether, and there was no other means of detecting the fault in mid-ocean. Bergfeld's evidence on this point is convincing, and it suggests that the question of which method won is, in a sense, the wrong one to ask.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other scholars have widened the focus still further. Chinedu Obiakor, a historian of science at the University of Ibadan, has drawn attention to the extent to which both methods depended on infrastructure on land. Almanac tables had to be computed by teams of human calculators, often working from home for modest fees, and chronometers had to be rated, that is, have their daily rate of gain or loss measured, at observatories before each voyage. Ports therefore began to display time signals, such as a ball dropped from a mast at a fixed hour, so that ships at anchor could set their instruments. For Obiakor, the solution to the longitude problem was less a matter of invention than of administration, and it is difficult to disagree with him.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the ingenuity of the early chronometer makers, whose instruments were extraordinary achievements of precision engineering. What the more recent scholarship does show is that historical change in technology is rarely a matter of one device simply replacing another. Old and new methods frequently coexist for generations, each compensating for the other's weaknesses, and the moment at which an innovation appears is often far less significant than the slower process by which it becomes affordable, reliable and supported by the institutions around it.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: railway time, the telegraph and the adoption of standard time zones in the nineteenth century
title: Whose Noon Is It?
subtitle: Standard time is often credited to the railways, but the full story involves telegraph wires, town councils and stubborn local pride

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, almost every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over that particular place, and since the sun appears to cross the sky from east to west, a town lying some distance to the west of its neighbour would reach noon a few minutes later. Within a small community this mattered little: church bells and public clocks were set to local solar time, and nobody needed greater consistency. A traveller moving at the pace of a horse could hardly notice that the clocks of successive towns disagreed by a minute or two.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The railway altered that situation dramatically. A train could cross a hundred and fifty kilometres in a few hours, and companies that published timetables had to choose which of the dozens of local times along the route to follow. Many simply adopted the time of their headquarters city, with the result that a single station might display several clocks, each belonging to a different company. Accidents caused by confusion over timing were reported, and passengers complained of missed connections. By the 1880s, standardised zones of time, each an hour apart, had been introduced across much of the industrial world, and the conventional explanation is that the railways forced this change upon reluctant societies.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Priya Varadarajan, a historian of technology at the Centre for Transport History in Leeds, accepts that the railways created the demand for uniform time but insists they could not have satisfied it alone. What made standard time workable, she argues, was the electric telegraph, which allowed a time signal generated at a central observatory to be transmitted instantly to distant stations. Without that technology, standard time would have remained an abstraction, since there would have been no practical way to ensure that clocks hundreds of kilometres apart actually agreed. This seems to me a necessary correction to the usual story; the railways supplied the motive, but the telegraph supplied the means.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more provocative argument comes from Tomasz Gorski, a social historian at the University of Kraków. Gorski points out that railway companies frequently ran on standard time for years while the towns they served continued to observe local time, so that a station clock and the clock on the town hall opposite might differ by a quarter of an hour. In his reading, the railways did not so much impose a new time on society as create a parallel time that coexisted with the old. Public adoption, he maintains, came much later and was driven by legislation, often after protracted debate in which opponents denounced standard time as an attack on local identity. Gorski's research is valuable, but he arguably overstates the separation between the two systems: once people grew used to catching trains, many began to set their own watches by the station clock long before any law required it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The resistance Gorski describes was nonetheless real. Dr Elodie Corbeil, who has studied municipal records in France and Switzerland, found that several towns maintained two sets of hands on their public clocks, one showing local and the other national time, for more than a decade. Some citizens regarded the national time as an imposition from the capital, a symbol of the centralising state; others objected on practical grounds, since farmers and labourers organised their day by daylight rather than by the clock. Corbeil interprets these disputes as evidence that time had become a political question rather than merely a technical one, and this interpretation is difficult to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The international dimension added further complexity. In 1884, delegates from more than twenty countries met to agree on a single prime meridian from which longitude, and therefore time zones, would be calculated. The decision to choose a meridian passing through an observatory near London was not unanimous; one major delegation abstained and continued to use its own meridian for almost three decades. Hiroshi Tanabe, a researcher at the Institute of Global History in Osaka, notes that adoption elsewhere was uneven and frequently driven by commercial or colonial interests rather than scientific logic. Some nations chose zones offset by half an hour, or even by odd numbers of minutes, a legacy that persists in a few places today. In Tanabe's view, the map of modern time zones is therefore better read as a record of past political and economic relationships than as the outcome of a rational plan.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What lessons can be drawn from this history? The most obvious is that technological standards rarely spread simply because they are efficient. Standard time was plainly more convenient for trade and transport, yet its adoption depended on a combination of infrastructure, law and public acceptance, and in many places it took half a century to complete. Much the same pattern can be seen in later disputes over units of measurement and electrical fittings, where obvious practical advantages did not prevent decades of disagreement. It is tempting to regard the result as inevitable, but that judgement is made with hindsight. Had the telegraph been slower to spread, or had local loyalties proved stronger, the patchwork of local times might have lasted considerably longer than it did.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: the 1582 Gregorian calendar reform and its slow, contested adoption across Europe and beyond
title: Days That Never Were
subtitle: The calendar reform of 1582 was an astronomical success, but persuading the world to accept it took more than three centuries

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The calendar inherited by medieval Europe rested on a small but consequential error. It assumed that the solar year, the interval between one spring equinox and the next, lasted exactly 365 and a quarter days, and it accommodated the extra quarter by adding a leap day every fourth year. In reality the year is roughly eleven minutes shorter. Eleven minutes is trivial over a lifetime, but it accumulates to a full day approximately every 128 years, and by the sixteenth century the calendar date of the equinox had drifted about ten days away from the astronomical event. For most people this was of no practical consequence. For the Church, however, it was a serious matter, because the date of Easter was calculated from the spring equinox, and a calendar that misplaced the equinox risked celebrating the most important festival of the year on the wrong day.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The remedy, introduced by papal decree in 1582, had two parts. First, ten days were simply removed: in the territories that adopted the reform immediately, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October. Second, the rule for leap years was modified so that the error would not recur. Century years would no longer be leap years unless they were divisible by 400, so that 1600 remained a leap year but 1700, 1800 and 1900 did not. The new rule leaves an error of only about one day in more than three thousand years, an accuracy that remains remarkable even by modern standards.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Technically, then, the reform was a triumph. Politically it was something else entirely. Catholic kingdoms such as Spain, Portugal and the Italian states adopted it within weeks or months, but Protestant territories regarded a calendar issued by the papacy with deep suspicion. Dr Marta Brzezinska, a historian of early modern Europe at the University of Wrocław, has documented the confusion that resulted in regions where Catholic and Protestant communities lived side by side. In some towns, she found, neighbours celebrated Christmas ten days apart, and merchants trading across confessional borders routinely recorded transactions with two dates. Brzezinska argues that the calendar became a badge of religious identity, and that its astronomical merits were largely irrelevant to the decision whether to accept it. That conclusion is broadly convincing, although it may underestimate the number of Protestant scholars who privately acknowledged that the reform was correct.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The Protestant German states eventually accepted a modified version of the reform in 1700, and Britain and its colonies followed in 1752, by which time the discrepancy had grown to eleven days. British history textbooks long reported that the change provoked riots, with crowds demanding the return of their 'eleven days'. Dr Joost Vermaak of the University of Stellenbosch has examined newspapers, court records and private diaries from the period and found almost no contemporary evidence of such disturbances. The story, he suggests, seems to derive largely from a satirical painting of an election campaign, in which a placard protesting about the lost days appears, and was later repeated by historians who took the image literally. Vermaak's work is a salutary reminder of how easily a vivid anecdote can harden into accepted fact.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Further east, the reform took far longer still. The Orthodox churches had never recognised papal authority, and the Russian Empire retained the older calendar until 1918, when the new revolutionary government adopted the reformed calendar as part of a broader programme of modernisation. Greece made the change in 1923. Even then, the Orthodox churches largely continued to calculate Easter by the older reckoning, a practice that persists today and means that Eastern and Western Easter frequently fall on different Sundays. Professor Eleni Dimitriadou, a historian of religion at the University of Thessaloniki, argues that this persistence should not be dismissed as mere conservatism. For many Orthodox communities, she maintains, the older calendar expresses continuity with an unbroken tradition of worship, and to abandon it would be to concede a theological point, not merely an astronomical one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Outside Europe, adoption was often bound up with commerce and diplomacy. Dr Selin Sevim, who studies the late Ottoman state, notes that the empire used several calendars simultaneously for different purposes, including a lunar calendar for religious observance and a solar calendar for financial administration, and that the reformed European calendar was introduced for civil use only in 1926. In Sevim's view, the decisive pressure came not from scientific argument but from the practical demands of international trade, banking and treaty-making, in which a shared calendar had become an unspoken requirement. Similar considerations, she suggests, shaped the timing of reform in several other states that had previously kept calendars of their own.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of the reform therefore offers a cautionary lesson to anyone who assumes that a technically superior solution will be adopted simply because it is superior. The reformed calendar was demonstrably more accurate than its predecessor, yet it took well over three centuries to become the global civil standard, and it has still not been universally accepted for religious purposes. Calendars, it turns out, are never merely instruments for measuring time. They encode authority, belief and community, and changing them requires persuading people to give up something that many regard as their own.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: the origins of the medieval mechanical clock: monastic, commercial and astronomical explanations
title: The Bell Before the Dial
subtitle: Did the rhythm of monastic prayer give birth to the mechanical clock, or is that story too neat?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The earliest mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the final decades of the thirteenth century, although nobody knows precisely where or by whom they were first built. Unlike the sundials and water clocks that preceded them, these machines were driven by a falling weight whose descent was regulated by a device known as an escapement, which repeatedly checked and released a toothed wheel. The result was a mechanism that advanced in small, regular steps, and the familiar tick of the clock is the sound of that interruption. Early examples were large iron frames installed in towers; most had no dial and no hands, but instead struck a bell at intervals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That last detail has encouraged one of the most enduring explanations of the clock's origins. Monastic communities followed a strict daily schedule of prayer, known as the canonical hours, which included services in the middle of the night. Someone had to wake the community at the right moment, and the task, traditionally entrusted to a monk who watched the stars or tended a water clock, was notoriously prone to error. On this account, the mechanical clock emerged as an alarm for monks: a device to ring a bell reliably, regardless of cloud or frost. Dr Siobhan Dunleavy, a medieval historian at University College Cork, has assembled an impressive body of evidence in support of this view, including monastic rule books that impose penalties on sacristans who rang the night office too late.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dunleavy goes further, suggesting that the discipline of the monastery shaped European attitudes to time more broadly. Monasteries, she argues, were the first institutions to divide the day into regular, collectively observed units and to treat punctuality as a moral virtue, and those habits gradually spread into secular life. The argument is elegant, and there is undoubtedly some truth in it. Yet it rests on a somewhat idealised picture of monastic life. Many monastic hours were not of fixed length at all: they were 'unequal hours', which divided the time between sunrise and sunset into twelve parts, so that an hour in midsummer was considerably longer than one in midwinter. A device that ticked in equal steps was, in that respect, poorly suited to monastic needs.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This mismatch is central to the case made by Professor Kenji Matsuoka of Kyoto University, who has compared the earliest surviving references to mechanical clocks across Europe. Matsuoka finds that the majority were commissioned not by monasteries but by town councils and cathedral chapters in prosperous commercial cities, where merchants needed a shared, public signal to regulate markets, working hours and the opening and closing of city gates. The equal hour, he points out, suited the rhythm of commerce far better than the rhythm of prayer. Matsuoka also observes that several of these cities had previously paid watchmen to sound the hours by hand from a tower, an expense that councils were understandably eager to reduce. In his view, the monastic thesis confuses the earlier history of timekeeping in general with the specific circumstances in which the mechanical clock flourished.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from Dr Ilse Westerlund, a historian of astronomy at Uppsala University, who argues that the escapement was a by-product of efforts to build mechanical models of the heavens. Several thirteenth-century scholars described ambitions to construct a wheel that would turn once a day in step with the stars, and Westerlund believes the earliest clocks were, in effect, simplified versions of such astronomical instruments. Some of the most elaborate early clocks did indeed display the positions of the sun, moon and planets, which lends her argument a certain plausibility. However, the instruments she cites are known mainly from written descriptions, and it is not clear that any of them actually worked. A design that existed only on parchment can hardly be considered the ancestor of a machine that was built and used, and Westerlund has yet to show that the craftsmen who made the first tower clocks had any contact with the scholars concerned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Radu Lazarescu of the University of Cluj takes a more sceptical position on the whole debate. The surviving evidence, he notes, is so fragmentary that the Latin word for clock, horologium, was applied without distinction to sundials, water clocks and mechanical devices alike, making it extremely difficult to know which kind of instrument a given document describes. In Lazarescu's view, attempts to identify a single origin are misguided; the mechanical clock is better understood as the product of several overlapping communities, monastic, civic and scholarly, whose needs happened to converge. This seems to me the most defensible conclusion, even if it is a less satisfying one than a story with a single hero or a single motive.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is clear is that, once established, the public clock transformed urban life. Within a century of the earliest examples, a striking clock had become a matter of civic pride, and towns competed to install ever more elaborate ones, complete with moving figures and astronomical displays. The accuracy of these early machines was poor by later standards, since they might gain or lose a quarter of an hour in a day, and they had to be corrected regularly against a sundial. Nevertheless, by making time audible across an entire city, they established the principle that time was something to be shared, regulated and, increasingly, sold.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: ancient Egyptian decan star clocks, diagonal star tables and the origin of the twenty-four-hour day
title: Counting the Night
subtitle: Why is the day divided into twenty-four hours? Part of the answer may lie in star tables painted inside ancient Egyptian coffins

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few conventions seem as natural, or are as arbitrary, as the division of the day into twenty-four hours. Nothing in astronomy requires it: the rotation of the earth could just as easily be split into ten, twenty or a hundred parts, and in the late eighteenth century revolutionary France briefly attempted exactly that with a decimal clock of ten hours. The number twenty-four has a long history, however, and most historians of astronomy trace it to ancient Egypt, where, more than four thousand years ago, priests developed a method of telling the time at night by observing the rising of particular stars.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method relied on groups of stars that later Greek writers called decans. The Egyptians selected thirty-six such stars or star groups, spaced around a band of sky roughly parallel to the path of the sun. Each decan rose on the eastern horizon shortly before dawn for about ten days, before being replaced in that position by the next, so that the full cycle of thirty-six covered the 360 days of the Egyptian civil year, to which five additional festival days were added. During any given night, a series of decans rose one after another, and their successive appearances could be used to mark divisions of the darkness. Because of the way the stars were spaced, twelve such divisions were typically observed between dusk and dawn.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The clearest evidence for this system comes from an unexpected source: the inside lids of wooden coffins dating from around 2100 BCE. These lids carry grids, now known as diagonal star tables, in which each column represents a ten-day period and each row an hour of the night, with the names of the relevant decans entered in the cells. Because the star for a given hour shifts by one row every ten days, the same names run diagonally across the grid, which gives the tables their modern name. Around two dozen examples survive, almost all from a relatively short period, after which the fashion for decorating coffins in this way seems to have faded. Dr Nadia Elmadani, an Egyptologist at Cairo University, argues that the tables were primarily religious rather than practical, intended to help the deceased navigate the night sky in the afterlife. She points out that copying errors in many tables would have made them useless for actual timekeeping, which suggests that the painters did not expect anyone to consult them for that purpose.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Fredrik Nordahl of the University of Oslo accepts that the coffin tables had a funerary function but maintains that they were copied from working documents used by temple astronomers. In his view, the errors are precisely what one would expect when a technical chart is reproduced by craftsmen who do not understand it, and they say nothing about the accuracy of the originals. This is a reasonable inference, though it remains an inference: no working table of the kind Nordahl describes has ever been found, and the case for its existence rests largely on the internal logic of the coffin versions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If twelve night hours came from the stars, where did the twelve hours of daylight come from? Here the evidence is thinner. Dr Teodora Jovanovska, who studies ancient scientific instruments at the University of Skopje, has examined surviving Egyptian shadow clocks, L-shaped devices on which the shadow of a raised bar fell across a marked scale. Several of these divide the day into ten parts, with an additional period of twilight at each end, giving twelve in total. Jovanovska suggests that the daytime count was adjusted to match the night-time count, producing a symmetrical day of twenty-four parts. On this view, the preference for twelve owed more to a desire for balance between light and darkness than to any property of the sun's movement. Her reconstruction is ingenious, although the small number of surviving instruments means that it should be treated with some caution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Crucially, these Egyptian hours were not equal. Twelve divisions of a summer night were much shorter than twelve divisions of a winter night, and the length of each hour varied throughout the year. Fixed hours of equal length emerged much later, and according to Dr Rafael Sandoval-Prieto of the University of Seville, they were the product of a cultural meeting rather than a single invention. Astronomers in the Hellenistic world, he argues, combined the Egyptian division of the day into twenty-four parts with the Babylonian practice of counting in sixties, and it was this combination, used initially for astronomical calculation rather than daily life, that gave rise to hours of sixty minutes. Ordinary people continued to use unequal, seasonal hours for well over a thousand years afterwards.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The story of the twenty-four-hour day illustrates how scientific conventions accumulate layers of history. A practice rooted in religious observation of the night sky was reshaped by Greek mathematics, preserved in medieval astronomy and finally fixed by the mechanical clock. It would be a mistake, though, to imagine that the Egyptians set out to create a universal standard. They were solving a local problem, and the persistence of their solution owes as much to historical accident as to any intrinsic merit. Had the scholars of Alexandria inherited a night divided into eight or sixteen parts instead, it seems likely that our clocks would look rather different today.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: the history of daylight saving time and the current debate over energy savings, health and abolishing clock changes
title: Borrowing an Hour
subtitle: Moving the clocks each spring and autumn began as a wartime economy. A century later, its justification is increasingly hard to find

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twice a year, in much of Europe and North America, clocks are moved forward or back by an hour, and hundreds of millions of people adjust their routines accordingly. The practice is so familiar that it is easy to forget how recent and how contested it is. The idea of making better use of summer daylight was floated, half in jest, by an American diplomat living in Paris in the 1780s, who calculated the number of candles that Parisians might save by rising earlier. A serious campaign began only in the early twentieth century, when a London builder, irritated that so many people slept through bright summer mornings, published a pamphlet proposing that clocks be advanced in stages during April and set back in September. Parliament debated the proposal repeatedly but declined to act.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It was war that turned the idea into law. In 1916, Germany and its allies advanced their clocks in order to reduce the consumption of coal for lighting, and Britain followed within weeks. Many countries abandoned the measure after the war, reintroduced it during the Second World War, and revived it again during the oil crises of the 1970s. According to the historian Luca Ottaviani of the University of Bologna, this pattern is revealing. Daylight saving, he argues, has always been justified as an emergency measure, adopted in moments of national crisis when governments sought visible ways to demonstrate thrift, and then retained largely through inertia once the crisis had passed. Ottaviani's account explains the timing of adoption well, although it pays rather less attention to the lobbying of retailers and sports organisations, who discovered that long summer evenings were good for business and campaigned vigorously to keep them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The central economic claim, that shifting the clock saves energy, has proved surprisingly hard to confirm. Dr Oskar Fagerlund, an energy economist at the Stockholm School of Economics, has reviewed more than forty studies conducted over half a century and concludes that any savings are small, typically well under one per cent of electricity use, and in some cases negative. The reason is that lighting now accounts for a much smaller proportion of household energy demand than it did in 1916, while the extra hour of evening daylight in hot regions can increase the use of air conditioning. In one region he examined, the introduction of daylight saving was followed by a modest rise in electricity consumption. Fagerlund's analysis is careful, and it seems fair to conclude that the energy argument, whatever its historical merits, no longer provides much justification for the practice.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If the economic case is weak, the health case against changing the clocks has grown stronger. Dr Wanjiru Chepkoech, a sleep researcher at the University of Nairobi, points to evidence that the spring transition, when an hour of sleep is lost, is followed by a short-term increase in heart attacks, workplace injuries and road accidents. Chepkoech stresses that the problem is not simply the lost hour but the misalignment between the body's internal clock, which is set largely by morning light, and the social clock that governs work and school. In her view, permanent daylight saving time, which would leave mornings dark for much of the winter, would perpetuate this misalignment throughout the year, and the healthier option would be to keep standard time permanently.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This last point is where the debate becomes genuinely difficult. Polls in several countries suggest that, if forced to choose, the public would prefer to keep the long summer evenings all year round rather than return permanently to standard time. Politicians have tended to follow this preference. Yet experience suggests it may be unwise. When one country adopted permanent summer time in the 1970s, the measure was so unpopular during the dark winter mornings that it was reversed within a year. Dr Gwen Cuthbertson, a political scientist at the University of Edinburgh, argues that such episodes show how poorly people predict their own reactions to changes in daily routine. Her argument is persuasive, though it would be wrong to dismiss public preference entirely; it simply needs to be informed by evidence about what dark mornings actually feel like.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Complicating matters further is the need for coordination between neighbouring states. When regions that share borders or trade closely adopt different rules, the result can be considerable confusion for transport, broadcasting and business, as anyone who has missed a connection at a border station can testify. In 2019 the European Parliament voted to end seasonal clock changes, but the proposal stalled because member states could not agree on which time each should keep, and many feared that a patchwork of time zones across the continent would disrupt the single market.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of daylight saving suggests that it has survived less because of any demonstrated benefit than because changing it requires agreement among many parties. That is not in itself a reason to keep it. The weight of current evidence, it seems to me, favours abolishing the twice-yearly change, and probably favours permanent standard time over permanent summer time. Whether governments will act on that evidence, given the enduring popularity of light summer evenings and the political risks of being blamed for darker mornings, is another matter altogether.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: the Maya calendar: the Long Count, the correlation problem with the European calendar and the calendar's political and social meaning
title: Anchoring the Long Count
subtitle: Reading Maya dates proved easier than placing them in history. The century-long effort to do so reveals much about how knowledge is established

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When European scholars began to study the carved monuments of the ancient Maya in the nineteenth century, they found inscriptions dense with numbers. Gradually it became clear that many of these numbers were dates, recorded in a calendrical system of remarkable sophistication. The Maya, it emerged, maintained several interlocking cycles at once. A ritual count of 260 days combined thirteen numbers with twenty named days, while a separate year of 365 days consisted of eighteen periods of twenty days followed by five days regarded as unlucky. Because the two cycles were of different lengths, any particular combination of positions recurred only once every fifty-two years, a period now known as the Calendar Round.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For recording events over longer spans, the Maya used what scholars call the Long Count, a tally of days elapsed since a fixed starting point. Its units were built largely on multiples of twenty: twenty days formed one unit, eighteen of these made a period of 360 days, twenty such periods made a unit of roughly twenty years, and twenty of those formed a cycle of about 394 years. A Long Count date was therefore a precise statement of how many days had passed since the beginning of the current era. The arithmetic was not difficult to reconstruct. The real problem, which occupied researchers for most of the twentieth century, was where that starting point lay in the European calendar.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This is known as the correlation problem, and its importance is hard to exaggerate. Without a reliable correlation, a Maya date can be placed precisely relative to other Maya dates but not anchored in absolute time, which makes it impossible to compare Maya history with events elsewhere. Several competing correlations were proposed, differing from one another by as much as two and a half centuries. Choosing between them was no mere technicality: a shift of that size would move the decline of the great lowland cities from one climatic episode to another, and so alter the explanations that historians could plausibly offer for it. The one eventually accepted by most specialists places the beginning of the current Long Count era in August 3114 BCE. Its original support came from documents written in the colonial period, when Spanish chroniclers recorded a handful of dates in both calendars.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Henrik Ekström of Lund University has long argued that these colonial documents are a weaker foundation than is generally acknowledged. The chroniclers, he points out, were writing several centuries after the Long Count had fallen out of use, and the correspondences they recorded relied on the shorter cycles, which repeat every fifty-two years and therefore cannot by themselves fix an absolute date. Ekström does not reject the standard correlation outright, but he insists that its acceptance owed as much to scholarly consensus as to evidence. That criticism had considerable force when he first made it, and it is to his credit that he pressed it at a time when questioning the consensus was unfashionable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most decisive test has come from radiocarbon dating. Dr Itzel Vasquez-Toro, an archaeologist based in Mexico City, led a project that dated wooden beams from temple doorways carved with Long Count dates. By measuring the growth rings preserved in the wood and the radiocarbon content of individual rings, her team was able to estimate when the trees had been felled with an uncertainty of only a few years. The results matched the standard correlation closely and ruled out most of its rivals. Vasquez-Toro regards the question as effectively settled, and it is hard to see how a reasonable sceptic could now disagree, although Ekström himself has suggested that a small adjustment of a day or two may still be needed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have turned their attention from the mechanics of the calendar to its social meaning. Dr Aiko Eguchi of Kyoto University argues that the Long Count was primarily a political instrument. Rulers, she notes, frequently timed their accessions and monuments to coincide with the completion of major calendrical periods and linked their own reigns to dates in the remote mythical past, presenting themselves as part of a cosmic order. Dr Paul Quenneville of Laval University accepts this interpretation for the monumental inscriptions but warns against extending it too far. The calendar, he observes, also governed agricultural and ceremonial life for ordinary people, most of whom never saw a carved monument, and the 260-day count in particular survived among some communities in the highlands of Guatemala long after the Long Count had been forgotten.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The modern fascination with the Maya calendar has not always been well informed. The completion of a major cycle in December 2012 was widely, and quite wrongly, presented as a Maya prediction of the end of the world, although no ancient inscription makes such a claim; on the contrary, several refer to dates far in the future. If anything, the episode demonstrated how readily a sophisticated system of thought can be reduced to a sensational story. Specialists who attempted to correct the misunderstanding at the time found that their explanations attracted a fraction of the attention given to the predictions they were trying to dispel. The real achievement of the Maya calendar lies in its precision and its intellectual ambition, and in the long scholarly effort needed to understand it.
