area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: water clocks from ancient Egypt to the medieval Islamic world: design, social uses and the limits of accuracy
title: Measured in Water
subtitle: For three thousand years, dripping water told people the time. Its history challenges the idea that timekeeping was always a quest for accuracy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before the first mechanical clock struck the hours in a European tower, people in many parts of the world measured time with water. The principle was simple: water flows out of, or into, a vessel at a reasonably steady rate, so the level inside can serve as a measure of elapsed time. The oldest surviving example, a stone bowl from an Egyptian temple dating from around 1400 BCE, has a small hole near its base and a series of marks on its inner surface. Its sides slope outwards towards the top, a feature that historians have long interpreted as a deliberate attempt to deal with the instrument's main weakness: as the water level falls, the pressure driving it through the hole decreases, and the flow slows down.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Professor Sunil Anandakumar, a historian of technology at the University of Madras, argues that this sloping design reveals a sophisticated grasp of the problem, achieved by trial and error rather than by theory. Others are less impressed. Dr Agnieszka Zielinska of the University of Gdańsk has calculated that the slope of the Egyptian vessel compensates only partially for the change in pressure, so that it would have run noticeably fast or slow at different stages of emptying. In her view, the device was intended more as a temple object, perhaps used to time rituals performed during the night, than as a precise instrument, and its accuracy was simply not a priority. Both interpretations are plausible, but Zielinska's has the merit of not assuming that ancient makers shared modern preoccupations with precision.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In classical Athens, the water clock served a very different purpose. Law courts used a simple vessel to limit the length of speeches made by prosecutors and defendants, and a court official would block the outlet whenever proceedings were interrupted, for example while documents were being read aloud. An expression used to describe a speaker wasting the court's time referred literally to the water running out. Important cases were allotted more water than minor ones, so the size of the vessel itself signalled the seriousness of the matter being judged. This was timekeeping not as a measure of the hour but as the allocation of a fair share, and it is a useful reminder that clocks have always served social as well as scientific ends.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most significant technical advance was the shift from outflow to inflow clocks. Rather than measuring the falling level of a draining vessel, engineers in Hellenistic Alexandria devised clocks in which water dripped into a receiving tank from a reservoir kept at a constant level by an overflow. Because the pressure at the outlet remained steady, so did the rate of flow, and a float rising in the receiving tank could drive a pointer or even simple moving figures. Similar designs appeared independently in China, where engineers developed systems of several stacked tanks, each feeding the one below, to smooth out variations still further. By the eleventh century, Chinese water-driven machinery was turning armillary spheres and celestial globes inside towers several storeys high, regulated by a mechanism that released a large wheel one bucket at a time. Some historians have described this device as an ancestor of the mechanical escapement, although there is no evidence that knowledge of it ever reached Europe.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Leyla Basaran, who studies the history of engineering at a university in Istanbul, argues that the water clocks built in the Middle East during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries reached a level of mechanical complexity that was not matched in Europe for another two hundred years. Some incorporated gears, valves and automata that struck cymbals or dropped metal balls into bowls to mark the passing hours. Basaran believes that these machines were as much displays of royal prestige as timekeepers, and she cautions against judging them solely by their accuracy. This seems right. To describe them simply as early clocks is to miss much of their purpose.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even the best water clocks, however, faced limits that no amount of ingenuity could fully overcome. Water flows more slowly when cold, because it becomes more viscous, and in northern winters it could freeze altogether. Dirt and mineral deposits gradually narrowed outlet holes, changing the rate of flow, and evaporation in hot climates reduced the volume of water. Dr Mikko Ikonen of the University of Helsinki argues that these difficulties explain why the mechanical clock, despite being less accurate than the best water clocks when it first appeared, spread so rapidly in northern Europe: it did not freeze. Ikonen's explanation is attractive in its simplicity, but it probably understates the role of cost and of the civic prestige that came with a large public clock.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the history of the water clock demonstrates most clearly is that the pursuit of accuracy has not been the sole, or even the main, force driving the development of timekeeping. Water clocks were used to regulate religious rituals, to allocate speaking time in court and to display the wealth and learning of rulers. Precision mattered in some of these contexts and scarcely at all in others. To read the history of timekeeping as a steady march towards ever more accurate instruments is to impose the values of the present on the past, and to overlook the many other purposes that these remarkable devices once served.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: industrial time discipline: factory clocks and fines, pre-industrial clock awareness, colonial labour and workers' use of the hour
title: Before the Factory Bell
subtitle: Did industrialisation teach working people to live by the clock, or had they already learned to do so?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It has become something of a commonplace among historians that industrialisation changed not only how people worked but how they experienced time. In pre-industrial societies, according to this view, work was organised around tasks rather than hours: a farmer milked the cows when they needed milking, a fisherman went out when the tide allowed, and a weaver working at home might labour intensely for several days and then rest. The factory replaced this rhythm with one dictated by the clock. Machinery was expensive and had to be kept running, so employers insisted that workers arrive at a fixed hour and remain until a fixed hour, and they enforced this discipline with bells, locked gates and fines for lateness.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: This account, often called the 'time-discipline' thesis, has been enormously influential, and it contains much that is true. Factory regulations from the early nineteenth century survive in large numbers, and many impose penalties that seem extraordinary today: a worker arriving five minutes late might lose a quarter of a day's wages, and in some mills the gates were locked promptly at the starting hour. Workers who complained that the factory clock had been deliberately set fast were rarely believed, and in several towns the mill clock became a focus of bitter resentment. Dr Harriet Fenwick of the University of Manchester, who has catalogued more than six hundred such rulebooks, argues that their very severity shows how alien clock time was to the workforce; rules are written, she points out, against behaviour that is common, not behaviour that is rare.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That inference is reasonable, but it is not the only one possible. Severe rules may also reflect employers' anxieties, or a desire to impress investors, rather than the actual behaviour of workers. More importantly, a growing body of research suggests that awareness of clock time was widespread well before the factory. Dr Ines Kristiansen of the University of Bergen has studied the statements of witnesses in English criminal trials between 1700 and 1800, which often required people to say when events had occurred. She found that ordinary labourers, servants and farmworkers routinely referred to clock hours, and sometimes to quarters of an hour, decades before the spread of factories. Kristiansen also points to inventories of personal property showing that ownership of watches among working people was far higher in the eighteenth century than historians had assumed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kristiansen's findings are striking, but they do not entirely overturn the older thesis. Knowing the time is not the same as having one's working day governed by it, and the testimony she cites shows familiarity with the clock rather than subordination to it. What the evidence does suggest is that the transition was gradual rather than abrupt, and that the factory intensified a process already under way rather than starting it. The distinction matters, because a change that unfolds over several generations is experienced quite differently from one imposed within a single working life.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The question takes on a different character outside Europe. Dr Chukwuma Okeke of the University of Lagos has examined how clock time was introduced in colonial mines and plantations in West Africa during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In these settings, he argues, punctuality was presented by employers and administrators as a sign of civilisation, and the alleged inability of local workers to keep time was used to justify low wages and harsh supervision. Okeke found that workers frequently adopted clock time very quickly when it served their own interests, for example in organising trade or religious meetings, while resisting it in the workplace. The supposed cultural barrier, he concludes, was largely a convenient myth. Okeke's work is a valuable reminder that claims about how other peoples experience time have often carried a political charge, and that historians who repeat such claims uncritically risk reproducing the prejudices of the sources on which they rely.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Professor Arturo Pacheco of the National University of La Plata takes the argument in another direction. He suggests that time discipline was never a one-way imposition, because workers learned to use the employer's clock against the employer. Once wages were calculated by the hour, he notes, organised labour campaigned for a shorter working day and for overtime pay, demands that only made sense in a world measured in hours. The campaigns for a ten-hour and later an eight-hour day, in Pacheco's view, show workers fighting not against clock time but over its distribution. This is an important corrective, although Pacheco perhaps underestimates how unequal the contest was in its early decades, when strikes were frequently illegal and dismissal could mean destitution.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Debates about time discipline have acquired new relevance in an age of digital monitoring, in which software can record the keystrokes of office workers and the movements of warehouse staff minute by minute. Some commentators argue that this represents a return to the most rigid forms of factory discipline. Others see something genuinely new, since the measurement now extends to individual tasks and gestures rather than simply to hours of attendance. Whatever the answer, the history of the factory clock suggests that such systems will be contested, adapted and reinterpreted by those subject to them, rather than simply accepted.

area: the history of timekeeping and calendars
topic: failed calendar reforms: the French Republican calendar, the International Fixed Calendar, the World Calendar and the Soviet continuous week
title: Tidying the Year
subtitle: For over two centuries reformers have tried to replace our irregular calendar with something more logical. Why have they almost always failed?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The calendar used across most of the world today is, by almost any rational standard, an untidy instrument. Its months vary in length from twenty-eight to thirty-one days for reasons that owe more to ancient Roman politics than to astronomy. A given date falls on a different day of the week each year, so that timetables, school terms and financial quarters have to be recalculated annually. The four quarters of the year are of unequal length, which complicates comparisons of business performance from one quarter to the next. For more than two centuries, reformers have proposed alternatives that would remove these irregularities, and for more than two centuries, almost all of those proposals have failed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most radical attempt was made in revolutionary France. In 1793, the new republic introduced a calendar of twelve months, each of exactly thirty days, with five or six additional days at the end of the year devoted to national festivals. Each month was divided into three periods of ten days, replacing the seven-day week, and the months were renamed after the weather and agricultural activities of the seasons. Dr Camille Delacourt, a historian at the University of Lyon, argues that the calendar's purpose was as much ideological as practical: by abolishing Sunday and the saints' days that structured the traditional year, the revolutionaries hoped to weaken the influence of the Church. In this, she suggests, the calendar was a failure. Many people continued to observe Sunday as a day of rest, and the ten-day cycle, which gave workers one rest day in ten instead of one in seven, was deeply unpopular. The calendar was abolished at the start of 1806.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more commercial vision inspired the International Fixed Calendar, which attracted considerable support in the 1920s. Its design was simple: thirteen months of exactly twenty-eight days, each beginning on a Sunday and ending on a Saturday, with one extra day at the end of the year belonging to no week and no month. Every month would be identical, and any given date would always fall on the same day of the week. A number of large businesses adopted the scheme for internal accounting, and one American photographic company continued to use it until the late 1980s. The advantages for bookkeeping were real, but the drawbacks were obvious to many: thirteen cannot be divided into halves or quarters, so the familiar divisions of the business year would have disappeared.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The World Calendar, promoted from the 1930s onwards, attempted to overcome this difficulty by dividing the year into four identical quarters of ninety-one days, each consisting of one month of thirty-one days followed by two of thirty. Like the Fixed Calendar, it required an extra day outside the weekly cycle at the end of each year, and a second such day in leap years. The proposal was taken seriously by international bodies and came close to formal consideration at the United Nations in the mid-1950s. According to Dr Jonas Birkeland, a historian of international organisations at the University of Trondheim, it was halted largely by religious objections. For Jewish, Christian and Muslim communities that observe a weekly day of worship, the insertion of days belonging to no week would mean that the sabbath drifted through the days of the reformed calendar. Several governments, including that of one major power, made clear that they would not accept such a change.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Birkeland regards these objections as decisive, and it is difficult to dispute that they were. Yet religious opposition alone may not explain why calendar reform has made so little progress since. Dr Rekha Dhillon, an economist at a university in New Delhi, argues that the deeper obstacle is coordination. The benefits of a reformed calendar would arrive only if almost every country adopted it simultaneously, whereas the costs of change, such as rewriting software, contracts and legal deadlines, would fall immediately on whoever moved first. No single government has an incentive to lead, and there is no international body with the authority to compel collective action. In Dhillon's view, this is a classic example of a system locked in by its own success: the existing calendar is not optimal, but it is universal, and universality is itself enormously valuable.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This argument seems to me broadly right, although it should not be taken to mean that calendars never change. The Soviet Union abolished the seven-day week in 1929, replacing it with a continuous working week in which rest days were staggered so that factories need never close. The experiment disrupted family and social life, since husbands, wives and children frequently had different days off, and it was abandoned in 1940. The lesson is not that reform is impossible, but that a calendar is woven into social life far more tightly than its critics often recognise.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Proposals for reform continue to appear. Some recent schemes preserve the seven-day week by adding an occasional extra week rather than days outside the week, thereby avoiding the religious difficulty. Whether any of them will ever be adopted is doubtful. For all its irregularities, the existing calendar does what most people require of it, and the history of reform suggests that efficiency alone has never been a sufficient reason for people to change the way they count their days.

topic: Neolithic obsidian exchange: chemical sourcing, the down-the-line model, direct seafaring voyages and obsidian as a social token
title: Black Glass, Long Distances
subtitle: Volcanic glass has given archaeologists their clearest view of prehistoric exchange, but what that view shows is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before metals were worked, one of the most sought-after materials in the ancient world was a volcanic glass. Obsidian forms when silica-rich lava cools so quickly that crystals have no time to grow, and when it is struck skilfully it breaks into blades with edges sharper than those of a modern scalpel. Its value to early farming communities is easy to understand. What makes it so valuable to archaeologists, however, is something its users could not have known: every volcanic source produces glass with its own chemical signature. Since the sources in south-west Asia and the Mediterranean are few in number and widely scattered, a blade found hundreds of kilometres from the nearest volcano is, in effect, a message about movement. No other prehistoric commodity offers so clear a record of how goods travelled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The techniques for reading that message have changed dramatically. Early analyses required a sample to be ground into powder, which meant that only a handful of artefacts from any site could be tested. Today, portable instruments can assign a piece to a particular lava flow within minutes, without damaging it. Dr Orsolya Kertvelyi, a geochemist at the Danube Institute of Archaeometry, estimates that more obsidian has been sourced in the past fifteen years than in the previous half-century. Yet she is notably cautious about this abundance. Many of the newly analysed pieces, she points out, come from old museum collections whose excavation records are incomplete, so that analysts know precisely where an object originated but have little idea where, or in what layer, it was found. In her view the field risks producing ever more precise answers to questions it has not properly asked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first great interpretive framework was built on far smaller data sets. In the 1960s and 1970s, researchers noticed that within roughly 300 kilometres of a source, obsidian made up most of the chipped stone at excavated villages, but that beyond this zone its share fell away steadily with distance. The pattern was explained by a 'down-the-line' model: each village obtained obsidian from its neighbour nearer the source, kept a proportion for its own use and passed the remainder on. Professor Davit Kipiani of the Caucasus Prehistory Unit has become the most outspoken critic of this reasoning. A smooth fall-off curve, he argues, could be produced by several quite different arrangements, including occasional long journeys by specialists, so the curve alone cannot reveal which mechanism was at work. The objection is sound as far as it goes, but Kipiani's conclusion that such curves are therefore worthless is surely too severe. Whatever produced them, they still establish the scale of the movement involved.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evidence from the Aegean suggests that at least some obsidian moved in a far more purposeful way. Glass from the island of Melos appears at sites on the Greek mainland in very early deposits, which implies that people were crossing open water to reach it before farming arrived. Researchers on the Aegean Exchange Project, directed by Marisol Ballivian-Pohl, argue that this reflects direct voyages by small groups of experienced seafarers rather than a chain of intermediaries. They point to two kinds of evidence: the presence of unworked cores, not merely finished blades, at sites far from Melos, and a few coastal settlements holding far more obsidian than their distance from the source would predict. Their case for the Aegean is convincing. It is much less clear that the same explanation can be extended to inland regions, where no sea separated communities and the opportunities for gradual, neighbour-to-neighbour transfer were correspondingly greater.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach questions whether obsidian should be treated as a practical commodity at all. Dr Yusuf Ozkardesler, who studies early villages in central Anatolia, notes that some communities imported it even though perfectly serviceable flint was available close at hand. Particular colours, such as a translucent green variety, seem to have been deliberately selected, and polished obsidian was occasionally made into mirrors. For Ozkardesler, the glass circulated chiefly as a sign of relationships between families and villages, its movement tracing marriages and alliances rather than demand for cutting tools. This is a welcome corrective to accounts that reduce prehistoric people to calculating consumers of raw materials. Its weakness is that it is difficult to test: almost any distribution of finds can be described as the outcome of social ties.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Experimental work has added a further complication. Modern stoneworkers have shown that a single good core can yield well over a hundred usable blades, which means that a modest quantity of raw glass, carried by one traveller, could supply a village for a long time. If so, the volumes of obsidian found at most sites do not demand any regular traffic at all, and long gaps between deliveries would have left little trace.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these debates suggest that the very image of an obsidian 'route', with its implication of a fixed path regularly travelled, may be misleading. What emerges instead is a shifting web of contacts in which seafaring specialists, neighbouring villages and the obligations of kinship all played a part, their relative importance varying from one region and period to another. More chemical analysis alone will not resolve the question of which mattered most. That will require sourcing laboratories and excavators to work together far more closely than they have done, so that every analysed fragment can be tied to the place where it was finally discarded.

topic: the Old Assyrian caravan trade recorded in the merchant archives of Kanesh and the debate over whether it was a market economy
title: Letters from a Merchant Quarter
subtitle: Clay tablets from central Anatolia record a trading system four thousand years old, and have revived an old argument about how ancient economies worked

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of what is known about early trade has been pieced together from objects: a bead found far from its source, a pot of foreign clay, a hoard of metal. The traders themselves are almost always silent. At Kanesh, a mound in central Anatolia, they are anything but. In the lower town beneath the ancient citadel, excavators have recovered more than twenty thousand clay tablets left behind by merchants from the city of Assur during the nineteenth and early eighteenth centuries BCE. The tablets include letters, contracts, debt notes and court records. Taken together they constitute what is arguably the most detailed record of private commerce to survive from any society before classical Greece, and they allow historians to follow individual traders, and sometimes their wives and children, across several generations.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic pattern of the trade is not in doubt. In Assur, merchants purchased tin, which had itself been brought from regions still further east, together with woollen textiles, some woven in the households of the merchants' own families. The goods were packed onto black donkeys, and caravans made a journey of roughly a thousand kilometres, lasting around six weeks, to Kanesh and other Anatolian towns. There the cargo was sold for silver and, less often, gold, which travelled back to Assur to finance the next shipment. Even the donkeys were usually sold on arrival rather than making the return trip. The margins could be considerable: tin might fetch nearly twice what had been paid for it in Assur, and the finest textiles more still, although tolls, guards and travel costs consumed much of the difference.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What has made Kanesh controversial is what this trade implies about ancient economies in general. For much of the twentieth century, an influential school of thought maintained that exchange in early societies was embedded in kinship, religion and the authority of palaces and temples, and that markets in the modern sense, where prices are set by supply and demand, scarcely existed. Professor Leocadia Kwiatosz of the Institute for Ancient Economies regards the tablets as a decisive refutation of that position. She draws attention to letters in which merchants urge relatives to sell quickly because a large caravan is expected, or to hold back textiles until a shortage drives prices up. Such behaviour, she argues, presupposes prices that moved in response to supply. It is difficult to see how this evidence can be explained away, and the older view, at least in its strongest form, can no longer be sustained.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Henrik Aalvik, an Assyriologist at the University of Bergsund, accepts that prices fluctuated but insists that the trade cannot be understood as a free market. The merchants, he points out, operated within a dense framework of institutions. The city assembly of Assur laid down rules for the trade and settled disputes; treaties with Anatolian rulers fixed the taxes that caravans paid and guaranteed their safety on the roads; and the business itself was organised through family firms, typically with a senior figure in Assur and sons or brothers stationed in Anatolia. Trust, in Aalvik's view, rested on kinship and civic law rather than on the impersonal dealings of strangers. His account is a valuable correction, but the opposition he draws is overstated. Every market that has ever functioned has depended on institutions of some kind, and the existence of rules and family loyalties at Kanesh does not make its prices any less real.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Particular interest has focused on a form of long-term partnership that the merchants called a 'bag'. A group of investors would entrust a quantity of gold to a single trader, who used it as working capital for a period that might last ten years or more, and at the end of which the investors received a portion of the profits rather than a fixed fee. Kwiatosz sees in this arrangement a striking anticipation of the commercial partnerships of medieval Italy. Researchers in the Kanesh Archive Group, led by Dr Sevgül Demirkapı, urge more caution. They observe that the tablets were not written to inform posterity: merchants put things in writing chiefly when a debt was disputed, a relative had died or a shipment had gone astray. Routine transactions, conducted face to face, may have left no trace at all, so that the archive inevitably gives exaggerated prominence to the moments when business went wrong.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One such source of trouble was smuggling. Several letters refer to an unofficial route through the hills that allowed caravans to avoid the tolls collected by local rulers, and others warn that goods discovered on it would be confiscated and their owners punished. These texts are revealing in two directions at once. They show merchants weighing the cost of a tax against the risk of being caught, which is precisely the kind of calculation that Kwiatosz emphasises. Yet they also demonstrate that the treaties Aalvik describes were enforced seriously enough to make evasion dangerous; regulations that nobody respected would hardly have been worth the trouble of avoiding.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The trade did not last. Political upheavals in both Assur and Anatolia during the eighteenth century BCE disrupted the routes, and the merchant quarter at Kanesh was eventually abandoned, its archives sealed beneath the debris of later occupation. Perhaps its most important legacy is a warning against asking whether ancient economies were 'market' or 'non-market' economies, as though these were the only possibilities. The merchants of Assur responded keenly to prices, and they relied just as heavily on family, city and treaty. The challenge is to explain how these elements fitted together, not to decide which of them was the real one.

topic: the Baltic amber routes to the Bronze Age Mediterranean: spectroscopic sourcing, the Adriatic corridor, spacer plates and how distance created value
title: The Resin Road
subtitle: How fossilised tree resin from the shores of the Baltic reached the graves and palaces of the Mediterranean

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Amber is the fossilised resin of ancient trees, and along the south-eastern coast of the Baltic Sea it is found in unusual abundance. Lumps of it are thrown up on the beaches by winter storms, and larger quantities lie in shallow deposits just inland. Light, warm to the touch and easily carved, it glows when held to the light and produces a fragrant smoke when burned. By the second millennium BCE it was reaching the eastern Mediterranean, where hundreds of amber beads were buried with members of the early Mycenaean elite in Greece. Rarely has so light a material carried so much weight in arguments about how distant societies were connected, and those arguments remain far from settled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty is knowing where a given piece came from. Amber-like resins occur in many regions, including Sicily, and a bead found in Greece cannot be assumed to be northern simply because it is amber. In the 1960s, chemists discovered that Baltic amber produces a characteristic pattern when examined by infrared spectroscopy, a feature linked to its relatively high content of succinic acid. Dr Clementine Ashdown-Farrah, who has spent two decades applying the technique to museum collections, concludes that the great majority of Bronze Age amber in Greece is of Baltic origin. She is careful to add, however, that amber which has been buried in damp or acidic soil gradually loses its signature, so that badly weathered pieces cannot be assigned to any source. Since the most fragile finds are also the least likely to have been tested, this caveat deserves far more attention than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If most of the amber was Baltic, how did it travel more than two thousand kilometres to the south? Professor Radomir Vuksanovic of the Adriatic Institute of Prehistory argues that the principal route ran down the river systems of central Europe to the head of the Adriatic, and then by sea along the coast to western Greece. He points to the concentration of amber finds along this corridor and to evidence of amber working at settlements in northern Italy. The case is a plausible one, yet distribution maps of this kind need to be read with care. They record where archaeologists have excavated as much as where amber was carried, and regions that have attracted little fieldwork will inevitably appear empty.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different line of evidence comes from a small group of unusual ornaments. Amber spacer plates, flat pieces pierced by several holes so that they could hold apart the strands of a necklace, have been found in southern Britain, southern Germany and Greece, and some of them share strikingly similar arrangements of drilled holes. For Dr Teodor Fjeldvik, a specialist in Bronze Age ornament at the University of Lindhavn, the resemblance is too close to be coincidental. He proposes that finished jewellery, rather than raw amber, was passed between ruling families as gifts, binding distant leaders together in a network of obligation. His critics reply that a limited number of practical ways exist to drill a flat plate, and that similar patterns could have been reached independently.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Surprisingly little attention has been paid until recently to the people who actually gathered the amber. Researchers working with the Vistula Delta Survey, led by Dr Jurgita Baltrusaitiene, have examined burials along the Baltic coast from the centuries when amber was most prized in Greece. They found that it appears only rarely among grave goods, far less often than bronze objects imported from the south. Their interpretation is that the local population regarded amber as something to be exchanged rather than kept. The finding supports a broader point: the worth of amber was not a property of the material itself but was created, to a great extent, by the distance it had travelled.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Much more is known about the trade in later centuries. Under the Roman Empire, an overland 'amber road' linked the Baltic coast with the Danube frontier and the city of Aquileia, whose workshops carved amber into small figures, flasks and charms for wealthy customers. A Roman writer of the first century CE described an expedition sent north specifically to obtain it. According to Dr Wendeline Opsahl, who studies the Roman frontier economy, this trade was run largely by private dealers, with the state providing roads and security. It is tempting to project this well-organised Roman system back into the Bronze Age, but the temptation should be resisted. Nothing in the earlier evidence suggests a regular, organised flow; the pattern is better explained by intermittent contacts that rose and fell with the fortunes of the elites who desired the material.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The study of amber thus illustrates a wider problem in the history of ancient exchange. Chemistry can tell us, with increasing confidence, where an object began its journey and where it ended, but it is silent about the route and the people in between. Those gaps are filled with models, and every model carries assumptions about trade that may owe more to later periods than to the societies being studied.

topic: the Bronze Age 'tin problem': locating the distant sources of tin used in Near Eastern and Mediterranean bronze
title: The Missing Metal
subtitle: Bronze transformed the ancient world, yet one of its two ingredients came from places archaeologists are still trying to find

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Bronze is an alloy of copper with roughly a tenth part of tin, and the addition makes an extraordinary difference. The resulting metal is considerably harder than copper alone, it melts at a lower temperature and it flows more readily into moulds. By the late third millennium BCE, tin-bronze had become the standard material for weapons, tools and vessels across Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Aegean. The difficulty is that copper ores are found in many places, whereas workable deposits of tin are rare, and none of these regions possessed any of their own. Archaeologists have called this the 'tin problem', but the label understates its significance. At its heart is the question of how some of the earliest urban societies came to depend for an essential material on suppliers they may never have seen.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Written sources offer only partial help. Cuneiform documents from Mesopotamia and Syria record tin arriving from the east, sometimes in large consignments, and describe it being sold on to buyers further west. Merchants based in the city of Assur purchased it in quantity before carrying it into Anatolia. Yet these texts reveal where traders acquired the metal, not where it was originally dug from the ground, and the place names they use for the lands beyond the eastern mountains have proved impossible to locate with confidence.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For several decades, attention has focused on Central Asia, where Bronze Age tin workings have been identified in the mountain valleys of present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. A team led by Professor Bakhtiyor Rahimjonov has excavated mining shafts, crushing stones and the camps of the workers, and argues that these sources supplied much of the tin used in the Near East. The difficulty is chronological: radiocarbon dates from the workings so far fall mostly in the second millennium BCE, several centuries after tin-bronze became common in Mesopotamia. This gap does not rule out the theory, since earlier workings may simply not yet have been found. It does mean, however, that the case for Central Asia remains circumstantial.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Chemistry has recently opened a new line of enquiry. Tin, like lead, occurs in several isotopic forms, and the proportions vary slightly between ore deposits. Dr Anahid Ter-Grigoryan, a geochemist at the Yerevan Centre for Archaeometallurgy, has analysed tin ingots recovered from Late Bronze Age shipwrecks off the coast of the eastern Mediterranean. Her results suggest that some of the ingots match ores from western Europe, including south-west Britain, while others are more consistent with sources in Central Asia. Ter-Grigoryan herself emphasises the limitations of the method. The isotopic ranges of different ore fields overlap, and once metal from several sources had been melted down together, its signature becomes a blend that points to none of them. Of these difficulties, the recycling of old bronze is surely the most underestimated, for in a world where metal was scarce, almost nothing was thrown away.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The western evidence has encouraged a reassessment of the Atlantic coast. Dr Lucas Ferreira-Moutinho of the Lusitanian Archaeology Institute argues that tin from the Iberian peninsula and the British Isles was reaching the Mediterranean considerably earlier than the shipwrecks themselves would indicate. He points to bronzes with unusually high tin content in Iberian settlements and to coastal sites where tin appears to have been processed, and suggests that the metal was passed along the Atlantic seaboard by a series of local intermediaries before entering Mediterranean exchange. His argument is attractive but rests heavily on the assumption that tin-rich bronzes must reflect easy access to the raw metal, an inference that is plausible rather than proven.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third candidate lies closer to the centres of demand. In the 1980s, a mine in the Taurus Mountains of southern Anatolia was proposed as a third-millennium tin source, and researchers associated with the Anatolian Mining Survey, led by Dr Selin Karaburun, continue to defend that identification. Critics have pointed out that the ore at the site contains very little tin, and that no tin-bronze workshops of matching date have been identified nearby. The dispute illustrates a broader obstacle. Most ancient tin was probably collected not from underground mines but from river gravels, in which heavy grains of tin ore accumulate after being washed out of the rock. Such workings leave few lasting traces, and the most important sources of the Bronze Age may therefore have vanished from the landscape altogether.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever its sources, the tin trade exposes a vulnerability in Bronze Age civilisation. The palaces and cities of the eastern Mediterranean relied on a material that had to be brought over immense distances through the hands of many intermediaries. When this world disintegrated around 1200 BCE, some historians have suggested that a shortage of tin, caused by disruption to the long supply chains, contributed to the collapse. That claim goes further than the evidence allows, since the shortage itself is hard to demonstrate. Nevertheless, the dependence that made such a shortage possible is undeniable, and it should give pause to anyone who regards the long-distance supply of critical materials as a modern phenomenon.

topic: the frankincense and myrrh caravan trade of southern Arabia: camels, the basis of south Arabian wealth, Nabataean middlemen and the causes of decline
title: Fragrance and the Desert
subtitle: The trade in frankincense is said to have made southern Arabia rich, but why it did so, and why it faded, is less certain than once believed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Frankincense and myrrh are aromatic resins obtained by cutting the bark of small, hardy trees that grow in a narrow belt of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa. Burned in temples, used in medicines and perfumes, and consumed in large quantities at funerals, they were in steady demand across the ancient Mediterranean and Mesopotamia. Greek and Roman writers spoke of 'Fortunate Arabia', a land so wealthy that its people supposedly built with gold and burned cinnamon for fuel. Such descriptions have shaped popular images of the trade for centuries. They ought to be treated with considerable suspicion, however, since they were written by outsiders who had almost certainly never travelled there, and who had every reason to embellish the mystery of a product whose origins were deliberately obscured by those who sold it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: From the producing regions, caravans carried the resins northwards along the western side of the Arabian peninsula, a journey of more than two thousand kilometres that ended at ports such as Gaza on the Mediterranean coast. The route linked a chain of oases and walled towns, and it depended on the domesticated dromedary, which can travel for days without water. When camels first came into general use as pack animals is disputed. Dr Nadira Bakhashwain, an archaeologist at the Red Sea Heritage Institute, has examined animal bones from dozens of sites and concludes that, although camels were known earlier, they were used widely for transport only from the end of the second millennium BCE. The camel was undoubtedly a precondition for the overland trade, but it can hardly have been its cause. Without organised demand, secure stopping places and agreements between the communities along the way, the animal alone would have created nothing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The kingdoms of southern Arabia, of which Saba was the most famous, have long been seen as the chief beneficiaries. Their impressive cities and monumental temples have often been explained as the product of incense revenues. Professor Ottavio Ruggerone, a historian of the ancient economy, regards this explanation as a distortion created by excessive reliance on classical authors. He emphasises instead the great irrigation systems of the region, which captured seasonal floods to water extensive fields, and argues that the kingdoms' prosperity rested primarily on agriculture. Ruggerone is surely right that the classical sources have coloured modern thinking, although his own conclusion may swing too far in the other direction; farming and trade were not alternatives, and the surplus from irrigated land is likely to have supported the very caravans that carried the resins north.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: New scientific techniques have added a further complication. Dr Signe Tvedegaard, who analyses chemical residues in ancient vessels, has examined small stone incense burners from sites in the southern Levant and Mesopotamia. A surprising number contained traces not of frankincense but of resins from trees that grew locally, such as wild pistachio. Her interpretation is that genuine Arabian frankincense was used mainly on special occasions or by the wealthy, while cheaper local substitutes served for everyday purposes. If this pattern proves typical, the volume of the overland trade may have been considerably smaller than is often assumed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever its scale, the trade enriched those who controlled its northern stretches. The Nabataeans, originally nomadic herders, came to dominate the desert routes east of the Jordan valley. Their particular advantage lay in their knowledge of water: they dug underground cisterns, sealed them and concealed their entrances, so that they could cross country that would defeat an enemy. From their rock-cut capital at Petra they supplied caravans with guides, water and protection, and charged substantial tolls for doing so. Their fortune was therefore made not by producing anything themselves but by managing the passage of goods that belonged to others.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The traditional account of the trade's decline is straightforward. Once sailors from the Roman Mediterranean learned to use the monsoon winds, cargoes could be shipped through the Red Sea, bypassing the caravan routes altogether. Recent fieldwork tells a more complicated story. Researchers with the Dhofar Landscape Project, directed by Dr Eithne O Ciarmhaic, have found that settlements in one of the main frankincense-producing areas continued to grow for several centuries after the sea route opened. The change of route, they argue, damaged the middlemen of the north far more than it damaged the producers of the south. Demand itself was later undermined by religious change, as incense lost its central place in temple ritual across much of the Mediterranean world.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The incense trade is often presented as a simple story of a precious commodity, a beast of burden and a route that rose and fell. The evidence now suggests something more interesting: a trade whose volume, beneficiaries and eventual decline all depended on factors that the classical writers did not see or chose not to describe. The role usually given to the sea route in that decline has been considerably overstated, and the producers of the south appear to have been more resilient than their customers ever imagined.

topic: the origins and organisation of the trans-Saharan gold trade: pre-Islamic contacts, coin evidence, desert processing towns and West African control of gold supply
title: Across the Sea of Sand
subtitle: Gold from West Africa crossed the Sahara for centuries, but when that traffic began, and who controlled it, remain contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Medieval geographers writing in Arabic described a land beyond the great desert where gold was so plentiful that it was exchanged, weight for weight, for salt. Several of them repeated a curious story about how the exchange was conducted. Merchants from the north, it was said, would lay out their goods on a riverbank and withdraw; the unseen inhabitants would then place a quantity of gold beside each pile and retire in turn, and the process continued until both sides were satisfied, without a word ever being spoken. This 'silent trade' has often been quoted as if it were a description of real practice. It almost certainly is not. Very similar stories were told by ancient writers about entirely different peoples on the edges of their known world, and the tale is best understood as a familiar literary device for conveying remoteness and strangeness rather than as a report of how business was done.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Until recently, most historians accepted that regular trade across the Sahara began only after the Arab conquest of North Africa in the seventh and eighth centuries CE, when Muslim merchants, mounted on camels, opened routes to the gold-producing lands of the south. That view has been challenged by the Fezzan Oasis Project, an international team directed by Dr Elettra Mazzoleni. Working in south-western Libya, the team has documented the oasis kingdom of the Garamantes, whose people farmed the desert using underground channels to bring water from distant aquifers. Their settlements have yielded Mediterranean pottery and glassware, but also beads and plant remains that Mazzoleni attributes to regions south of the desert, dating from several centuries before the rise of Islam. In her view, a network of trans-Saharan contacts was already in place long before the Arab merchants arrived.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ffion Pengelly, a numismatist at the Institute of Mediterranean Coinage, approaches the question from the other end of the route. She has analysed the gold content and trace elements of North African coins and finds that their volume rose sharply from the eighth and ninth centuries, while their chemical composition increasingly resembles gold from West African sources. For Pengelly, this marks the true beginning of the trans-Saharan gold trade. The two positions are less opposed than they first appear. The Fezzan evidence demonstrates that the desert was crossed in earlier centuries, but it says little about the quantities involved; the coins indicate when gold began to flow in large amounts. It is entirely possible that long-established, small-scale contacts were transformed into a major commercial artery only in the Islamic period.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What happened to the gold on its way north is the subject of work by Dr Mustapha Ouzzani, who has excavated a market town on the southern edge of the desert that flourished around a thousand years ago. Among the finds were clay moulds used to cast small gold blanks of standard weight, together with crucibles containing tiny droplets of gold. Ouzzani argues that such towns were not mere staging posts where caravans rested and changed animals, but centres where raw gold was refined, weighed and prepared for the mints of North Africa. Value, on this account, was added in the desert itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Professor Seydou Bakayoko of the Centre for Sahelian History has argued that much of the literature still views the trade from the north, as if the peoples of West Africa were simply waiting to supply whatever their visitors desired. He draws attention to evidence that the rulers of the early Sahelian states kept the location of the goldfields a closely guarded secret, and that, according to one medieval account, a king claimed every nugget found in his territory, allowing only gold dust to be traded. Bakayoko interprets this as a deliberate policy of restricting supply in order to keep prices high. He is right to insist on this point, and the image of passive African suppliers deserves to be abandoned entirely. The goldfields were not discovered by outsiders; access to them was negotiated with powerful states that understood the value of what they controlled.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different emphasis comes from the environmental historian Dr Kwabena Owusu-Ampem, who has reconstructed past rainfall from lake sediments and ancient dune systems. He finds that the Sahara passed through wetter and drier phases during the period in question, and that particular routes became usable or impassable as wells and pastures appeared or failed. His reconstruction is a valuable reminder that the desert was not a fixed barrier. However, environmental change can open or close possibilities without explaining why people chose to take them up, and it would be a mistake to treat climate as the principal driver of the trade's growth.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, this research replaces a simple narrative of northern merchants discovering southern gold with a more complex picture. The trade grew out of older connections, depended on processing centres in the desert and was shaped at least as much by decisions taken in the south as by demand in the north. The Sahara, in short, was less a barrier that outsiders managed to cross than a shared space, used and contested by many different peoples over many centuries.

topic: Bronze Age trade between the Indus civilisation (Meluhha) and Mesopotamia: carnelian beads, resident merchants, Gulf intermediaries and the missing return goods
title: The Ships of Meluhha
subtitle: Mesopotamian texts speak of a distant land called Meluhha; archaeologists are still debating how its goods reached the cities of Sumer

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Towards the end of the third millennium BCE, a Mesopotamian king boasted that ships from three foreign lands, Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha, were moored at the quay of his capital. Other cuneiform texts of the period list the goods associated with these places: copper from Magan, dates and pearls from Dilmun, and from Meluhha carnelian, ivory, hardwoods, gold and even exotic birds. Dilmun is now generally located on the island of Bahrain and Magan on the coast of Oman. Meluhha, the most distant of the three, is widely identified with the cities of the Indus valley, in what is now Pakistan and north-western India. That identification is almost certainly correct, but it is worth remembering that it rests on circumstantial evidence; no text from the Indus itself can confirm it, because the Indus script has never been deciphered.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The circumstantial evidence is, nevertheless, considerable. Square stamp seals in the Indus style, cubical stone weights made to the Indus standard and long, polished beads of red carnelian have all been found in Mesopotamian cities and at sites around the Gulf. Some of the most striking are etched carnelian beads, whose white decoration was created by painting an alkaline paste onto the stone and heating it, so that the surface was permanently bleached. Dr Mio Tanigawa, who studies ancient bead technology, has examined the drill holes of beads from royal graves in southern Mesopotamia using silicone moulds and electron microscopy. Many show the distinctive traces left by a type of hard stone drill known only from Indus workshops. Either the beads were made in the Indus valley, Tanigawa concludes, or they were made in Mesopotamia by craftsmen trained there.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The second possibility points to the presence of Indus people far from home. Dr Ishita Banerjee-Kolte, an archaeologist at the Institute of South Asian Antiquity, notes that one Mesopotamian text refers to a 'village of Meluhha' near the city of Lagash, and that a person described as an interpreter for the Meluhhan language appears on a cylinder seal. She also observes that some Indus-style seals found in Mesopotamia depart from Indus conventions, using unfamiliar motifs or arranging script signs in unusual sequences. In her view these were made by merchant families who had settled in Mesopotamia and gradually adapted to local practices while preserving elements of their own identity. This is a persuasive reading of fragmentary evidence, and it gives a human face to what is too often described simply as the movement of goods.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that Indus ships regularly sailed all the way to Mesopotamia. Professor Hamad Al-Mannai of the Gulf Maritime Archaeology Unit argues that most of the trade passed through intermediaries at Dilmun and Magan, whose merchants bought goods from one direction and sold them in the other. He points out that Dilmun adopted the Indus system of weights, which suggests close and regular dealings with the east, and that its own distinctive round seals are found across the region. Al-Mannai's emphasis on the Gulf is a valuable corrective, but it need not exclude direct voyages. Trading systems of this kind commonly combined long-distance specialists with local middlemen, and the balance between them is likely to have shifted over the centuries.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A puzzling feature of the evidence is its lack of symmetry. Indus objects are found in Mesopotamia, yet hardly any Mesopotamian objects have been recovered from Indus cities. Dr Corentin Kerbrat, an economic historian, offers an explanation: Mesopotamia paid for its imports chiefly with textiles, oils, grain and other perishable goods, which have long since decayed. Mesopotamian texts certainly record large-scale production of woollen cloth for export, so the suggestion is plausible. It is also, however, conveniently impossible to disprove. An argument that explains the absence of evidence by the perishability of what is missing should be handled with care, however reasonable it may seem.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever its organisation, the trade did not last indefinitely. After about 1900 BCE, references to Meluhha become increasingly rare in Mesopotamian sources, and its name eventually survives only as a poetic term for a remote and exotic land. This decline coincides broadly with the transformation of the Indus cities, many of which were reduced in size or abandoned as the population moved to smaller settlements further east. Dilmun, meanwhile, became the principal point of contact for Mesopotamian merchants, and the goods of the far east reached them only indirectly, if at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The study of Meluhha shows both how much and how little can be learned about ancient trade from material remains. The beads, seals and weights prove that contact took place, and careful technical analysis can even reveal where objects were made and by whom. But because one partner left texts that can be read and the other did not, our understanding of the relationship is unavoidably one-sided. We know what Mesopotamian kings and merchants thought of Meluhha; what the people of the Indus thought of Mesopotamia, we cannot yet say.

topic: Viking-age hoards of Islamic silver dirhams around the Baltic: the Volga route, a weight-based bullion economy, why hoards were buried, the slave trade and the end of the silver flow
title: Silver from the East
subtitle: Hundreds of hoards of Islamic coins buried around the Baltic reveal a remarkable long-distance exchange, and raise uncomfortable questions about what was traded for them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the Baltic island of Gotland, farmers ploughing their fields have for centuries turned up buried silver. More than seven hundred hoards from the Viking Age are now known from the island alone, and together they contain tens of thousands of coins struck not in Scandinavia but in the Islamic world: in Baghdad, in Samarkand and in other cities of Central Asia, several thousand kilometres to the south-east. Similar finds, though in smaller numbers, have been made across Sweden, the eastern Baltic and Russia. Most of the coins are dirhams, the silver currency of the caliphate, and the majority were minted in the ninth and tenth centuries. No other body of evidence shows so vividly how closely the far north of Europe was bound to the economies of the Islamic world during this period.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The silver travelled along the river systems of what is now Russia. Traders from Scandinavia, known in eastern sources as the Rus, carried their goods by boat and portage to the middle Volga, where a market town called Bulghar served as a meeting point with Muslim merchants arriving from the south. A tenth-century envoy from Baghdad who visited the region left a description of the Rus, noting their weapons, their ornaments and the care with which they conducted their business. From the Volga, the coins passed north and west in stages, and many had probably changed hands several times before they reached the Baltic.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Once there, the coins were not treated as coins at all, at least not in the sense familiar to their makers. Their Arabic inscriptions meant nothing to most of those who handled them; what mattered was their weight and purity. Payments were made by weighing silver on folding scales, many examples of which have been found in graves and settlements, and coins were frequently cut into pieces, known to archaeologists as hack-silver, so that exact amounts could be made up. Many dirhams also bear small nicks known as test marks, made with a knife to confirm that the coin was solid silver rather than a plated copy. The economy of the Viking north, in other words, was one of bullion measured by weight, and it would be misleading to describe the dirhams as money in the modern sense.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why so much of this silver was buried and never recovered is a long-running question. Professor Arvid Kallmyr of the Baltic Institute of Numismatics argues that hoards were essentially savings. Most of the Gotland hoards, he notes, were concealed beneath the floors or beside the walls of farmhouses, which suggests that their owners intended to retrieve them; those that remained in the ground were presumably left by people who died or were driven away before they could do so. Dr Sigrun Hjaltadottir, a historian of religion, takes a different view. She points to later Norse literature in which wealth buried during a person's lifetime could be used in the afterlife, and to hoards placed in bogs and at the boundaries of territories, where retrieval seems never to have been intended. On Gotland, at least, the location of the hoards weighs heavily in Kallmyr's favour. Elsewhere, however, a ritual purpose cannot be dismissed, and it is quite possible that both motives operated side by side.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What did the Scandinavians give in exchange? Furs, wax, honey and swords certainly travelled south. Dr Oksana Prytulenko, who has studied Arabic and Byzantine descriptions of the northern trade, argues that the most important commodity was people. Captives seized in raids on eastern Europe were sold at the Volga markets, and in her view the rise and fall of the silver flow closely follows the rhythm of this traffic. Iron shackles found at several trading sites lend her argument weight. This is an uncomfortable conclusion, and popular accounts of Viking enterprise have often preferred to pass over it. It must nevertheless be faced squarely, even though the surviving evidence does not allow the proportion of the silver paid for captives to be calculated.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: From around the 960s, the flow of dirhams into the Baltic dwindled and then almost ceased. Dr Yerlan Abdikarimov, a numismatist at the Institute of Central Asian Studies, links this to the silver mines of Central Asia, which he believes were approaching exhaustion. Coins struck in the late tenth century, he observes, contain noticeably less silver than earlier issues, as if the mints were struggling to obtain metal. Other scholars attribute the decline to political turmoil along the Volga, which disrupted the markets on which the trade depended. Abdikarimov's explanation accounts well for the declining quality of the coins, but by itself it struggles to explain why the supply to the north stopped so abruptly. Within a few decades, Scandinavian hoards were dominated instead by silver pennies from the German lands and England.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The dirham hoards are thus far more than collections of old coins. They record a network that linked the farms of Gotland to the caliphal capital, a way of handling money quite unlike our own and, less comfortably, a trade in human beings. Their testimony is all the more valuable because so little else from the period was written down by the people of the north themselves.

topic: rethinking the 'Silk Road': local exchange in oasis documents, Sogdian merchant networks, state-funded silk payments to frontier garrisons and the spread of ideas
title: A Road That Never Was?
subtitle: The image of camel caravans carrying silk from China to Rome is a powerful one; historians increasingly doubt that it describes anything real

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few phrases in the history of trade are as evocative as 'the Silk Road'. It conjures up a single highway across the heart of Asia, travelled by long caravans of camels laden with silk on their way from China to the markets of Rome. Yet the expression is surprisingly recent. It was coined by a German geographer in 1877 and became popular only in the twentieth century, when it was adopted by travel writers, museums and, eventually, governments. Its appeal is easy to understand. But as a description of how goods actually moved across Eurasia in the first millennium CE, the term has arguably done more to obscure the past than to illuminate it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the strongest evidence comes from the oasis towns that lay along the supposed road. In the dry climate of the Turfan basin in north-western China, thousands of documents on paper have survived, many of them recycled by later generations to make shoes and burial garments for the dead. Professor Anselm Heuvelink, who has spent much of his career studying these texts, finds that the great majority record local transactions: the sale of a camel or a slave between neighbours, a loan of grain, a dispute over a field. Caravans, where they appear at all, are small, often consisting of a handful of merchants with a few dozen animals. Rather than a single road, Heuvelink describes a mesh of shorter routes along which goods passed in stages from one trader to the next. It is now clear that few, if any, merchants made the whole journey from China to the Mediterranean.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Long-distance commerce was not absent, however, and its most famous practitioners were the Sogdians, a people whose homeland lay around Samarkand in present-day Uzbekistan. A bundle of letters written by Sogdian merchants in the early fourth century and lost in a watchtower west of Dunhuang reveals family firms with agents stationed in cities hundreds of kilometres apart. Dr Bolormaa Tsedendamba, a specialist in the Sogdian language, argues that these communities formed a commercial network that spanned much of Asia, held together by kinship, shared religion and regular correspondence. One letter, written by a woman left behind in Dunhuang by her husband, complains bitterly that she has no money and that nobody will help her; others discuss consignments of musk, pepper and silver. The letters certainly demonstrate an organised network, but they reveal little about the volume of goods it carried, and some describe trade on a strikingly modest scale.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If private trade was smaller than legend suggests, what accounts for the undoubted prosperity of the oasis towns in some periods? Dr Parisa Mahjoubian, a historian of the Tang dynasty, points to the state. In the seventh and eighth centuries, the Chinese government maintained large garrisons in the western regions and paid its soldiers partly in bolts of silk, which functioned there as a form of currency. Hundreds of thousands of bolts were sent west each year, and the soldiers spent them in local markets, stimulating trade of every kind. When a major rebellion in the mid-eighth century forced the withdrawal of the garrisons, the documents show local commerce shrinking rapidly. Mahjoubian's case is a compelling one. It implies that much of the traffic on the so-called Silk Road was driven not by the demand of distant consumers but by government spending.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Silk, in any case, was only one of the things that moved. Horses, paper, glass, spices and medicines travelled in various directions, and so did musicians, missionaries and diseases. Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China along these routes, carried by monks who often journeyed alongside merchants, and techniques such as papermaking passed westwards over several centuries. Measured by their long-term consequences, the exchanges of beliefs, skills and knowledge may well have been more significant than any trade in luxury textiles. Even the history of silk itself illustrates the point. By the sixth century, silkworms had been carried westwards in secret and silk was being woven in the eastern Mediterranean, so that by the time of the Tang garrisons the commodity which supposedly defined the route was no longer a Chinese monopoly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why, then, does the image of the Silk Road persist? Part of the answer lies in its usefulness. It provides an attractive brand for tourism and exhibitions, and in recent decades several governments have borrowed the name for modern infrastructure projects, presenting them as the revival of an ancient tradition of friendship between nations. The image also flatters a modern wish to see global connection as a natural and ancient condition rather than a recent and fragile achievement. As a convenient shorthand for the connections between East and West, the term is perhaps harmless. As history, it misleads, encouraging the belief that a single route existed and that a single commodity defined it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the peoples of Eurasia lived in isolation. The documents, letters and coins show a world in which goods, people and ideas did travel enormous distances, but they did so slowly, in short steps, and through the hands of many intermediaries, most of whom never saw either end of the journey. Historians who abandon the romantic image lose a good story; they gain a far more accurate and, in its own way, more interesting one.

topic: royal gift exchange versus private commerce in the Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean: diplomatic letters, a cargo shipwreck, standardised copper ingots and port-city merchants
title: Gifts Between Kings
subtitle: Was trade in the Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean an affair of palaces, or were merchants already doing business on their own account?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the fourteenth century BCE, the rulers of the great powers of the Near East wrote to one another on clay tablets in a shared diplomatic language. Several hundred of these letters, found at an Egyptian royal city on the Nile, record the correspondence between the pharaoh and the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, the Hittites and the island of Cyprus. The kings address each other as 'brother' and send one another gold, horses, chariots, fine textiles, copper and precious oils. They also complain, sometimes at length, when a gift falls short of expectations: one Babylonian king protests that the gold he received turned out, when melted down, to be mostly base metal. Such complaints make plain that every present created an obligation to respond with something of comparable value. These letters are among the most vivid documents to survive from the ancient world, and they have shaped the way historians imagine the commerce of the period, perhaps more than they deserve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Read at face value, the letters suggest that long-distance exchange was conducted by and for monarchs. Dr Theodora Stamatelou, a historian of the Aegean palaces, takes this view further. In her account, the language of gifts and brotherhood was a polite disguise for what was in effect trade, but trade that was planned, financed and controlled by palaces. Merchants existed, she accepts, but they acted as royal agents, travelling under the protection of their masters and carrying goods that belonged to the crown. Independent commerce, if it occurred at all, was marginal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Idris Mansaray of the Centre for Ancient Mediterranean Economies regards this picture as an artefact of the sources. Royal letters, he points out, were written by kings and their scribes, and naturally present the world from a royal perspective; a merchant's private dealings would hardly feature in a pharaoh's correspondence. He draws attention to other documents, including legal records from coastal cities, in which merchants lend money, form partnerships and pursue debts on their own behalf. Mansaray's point about the bias of the evidence is well made, and it cannot simply be set aside. Whether the private activity he identifies was substantial, however, is a separate question that the texts alone cannot answer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Archaeology has offered a different kind of evidence. A merchant ship that sank off the southern coast of Anatolia towards the end of the fourteenth century BCE was found to be carrying some ten tonnes of copper and about one tonne of tin, together with ingots of coloured glass, logs of ebony, ivory, amber beads and jars of resin. Dr Beatriz Lazcano-Witt, who has studied the wreck's contents, observes that the ratio of copper to tin almost exactly matches the proportions used to make bronze, and that the quantity would have been sufficient to equip a substantial army with weapons. She believes the main cargo was a royal consignment. Yet she also notes that the personal possessions recovered from the wreck, including seals, weights and cooking pots, come from several different cultures, indicating that the people on board were of more than one origin and that some of them may have been trading in smaller goods for themselves.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much of the copper on such ships took the form of so-called oxhide ingots: flat slabs with projecting corners, each weighing roughly thirty kilograms. Chemical analysis indicates that most of them were made from Cypriot ore. Dr Henrike Dalsgaard, a specialist in ancient metallurgy, has measured hundreds of these ingots and confirms that they are remarkably uniform. This uniformity has often been taken as a sign of production controlled by a central authority. Dalsgaard herself is more cautious. The distinctive shape, she suggests, may simply reflect the practical needs of carrying heavy slabs on the shoulder or lashing them in the hold of a ship, and standardisation of this sort could develop among independent producers without any official direction.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most illuminating evidence comes from the great port cities of the Levantine coast. Researchers working with the Coastal Levant Texts Project, led by Dr Nadim Zeidan, have examined archives from one such city and found merchants who served the king as agents in one transaction and traded for their own profit in the next. Some held the title of royal merchant while running family businesses that extended to Cyprus and Egypt. These findings suggest that the sharp distinction modern historians draw between public and private commerce may not have been one that people at the time would have recognised. A merchant could be the king's servant and an independent trader at the same moment, without any sense of contradiction.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Around 1200 BCE, this interconnected world collapsed. Palaces were destroyed or abandoned across Greece, Anatolia and the Levant, and the great diplomatic correspondence ceased. In the centuries that followed, the merchant cities of the Phoenician coast flourished, and some scholars treat their success as proof that private enterprise had been the real engine of trade all along. That conclusion does not follow. The Phoenicians may equally have developed new forms of commerce in response to the disappearance of the palaces. What the debate reveals most clearly, perhaps, is the difficulty of applying modern categories such as 'state' and 'market' to societies that organised exchange on quite different principles.
