area: the history of printing and books
topic: the persistence of woodblock printing in East Asia after the invention of movable type
title: Carved Once, Printed for Centuries
subtitle: Why East Asian printers kept faith with the woodblock long after movable type was available

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, Western histories of printing told a simple story. Movable type, perfected in Europe in the fifteenth century, was the decisive breakthrough, and any society that did not adopt it had somehow fallen behind. Printers in China were experimenting with ceramic type in the eleventh century, and metal type was in use in Korea by the fourteenth, well before it appeared in Europe. Yet woodblock printing, in which each page is carved in relief on a single board, remained the dominant method across the region until the nineteenth century. The explanation usually offered is that a script containing thousands of characters made movable type impractical: a printer needed tens of thousands of individual pieces, and locating the right one could take longer than carving a page from scratch. This account is not mistaken, but it is incomplete, and it rests on an assumption that deserves to be challenged: that woodblock printing was a primitive stage which East Asian printers simply failed to leave behind.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Sunjae Eogeum, a book historian at the Daejeon Institute of Material Texts, argues that the two methods rested on entirely different economic logics. With movable type, a printer had to decide in advance how many copies to produce, because once the pieces were returned to their cases the page ceased to exist; a second edition meant setting the whole text again. A carved block, by contrast, preserved the page indefinitely. Blocks could be stored for decades and brought out whenever orders arrived, so that a publisher might print twenty copies one season and fifty the next without spending anything further on preparation. In a market where demand for most titles was modest and difficult to predict, Eogeum contends, the ability to avoid unsold stock was worth far more than the speed with which a fresh page could be composed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question of labour points in the same direction. Carving was skilled work, but it was not scarce: apprentices could be trained in a matter of months, and they did not need to be fully literate, since they worked from a calligrapher's handwritten sheet that had been pasted face down onto the board and simply cut away the wood around the inked strokes. A compositor working with movable type, on the other hand, had to recognise and retrieve every character correctly. Liesel Ormerod-Taft, an economic historian, has examined surviving account books from several commercial publishers in the lower Yangzi region and found that carving a block typically accounted for a surprisingly small proportion of a book's total cost. By far the largest expense, in her figures, was paper. Her finding is striking, and it helps to explain why publishers saw little reason to change their methods. Nevertheless, the account books in question come from only a handful of firms, and it would be unwise to treat them as representative of the trade as a whole.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Aesthetic considerations also mattered. Because a woodblock reproduced the hand of a calligrapher, a printed page could retain the elegance that educated readers prized, and pictures could be carved on the same board as the text, allowing illustration and words to share a page with ease. Early movable type, by contrast, often produced uneven lines and characters that looked mechanical. Kofi Adzraku, who studies printing comparatively across Asia, believes that where movable type did flourish, it was for reasons that confirm rather than undermine this argument. In Korea, he points out, the principal customer for printed books was the royal court, which required a great many different titles but only small numbers of each for distribution among officials. Under those conditions, a set of reusable type was ideal, whereas carving thousands of blocks for works that would be printed only once would have been wasteful.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this is to suggest that woodblocks were free of drawbacks. The blocks for a single large work could fill an entire storeroom, and collections were vulnerable to warping, to insects and, above all, to fire, which could destroy in an afternoon what had taken carvers years to produce. Errors were also awkward to fix, although printers developed an ingenious remedy: the faulty character was chiselled out and a small plug of fresh wood, carved with the correct form, was glued into the gap.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more serious objection is raised by Pavol Hrubeš, a historian of the press, who argues that the long dominance of the woodblock slowed the emergence of periodicals in the region. Newspapers depend on speed: an issue must be composed, printed and distributed within hours. When periodicals did appear in East Asia in the nineteenth century, Hrubeš notes, they relied almost entirely on imported movable type and lithography. This is a fair point, but it does not show what it is sometimes taken to show. It demonstrates that the two technologies suited different purposes, not that one of them was superior in every respect.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should replace the old story of failure? The most useful lesson is that technologies ought to be judged against the needs of the people who used them, rather than against a single path of development drawn from European experience. Some scholars estimate that, before 1500, more printed pages were produced in China than in the rest of the world combined, a figure that is difficult to verify but one that sits uneasily with any claim of backwardness. The persistence of the woodblock tells us less about the limitations of East Asian printers than about the assumptions of the historians who described them.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: textual variation in early printed books: stop-press corrections, errata, piracy and the supposed fixity of print
title: No Two Alike
subtitle: Did the printing press really fix texts in place, or have historians overstated its power to standardise?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the claims most often made for the printing press, few have proved as durable as the idea that it fixed texts in place. Before print, so the argument runs, every manuscript was copied by hand, and each scribe introduced fresh slips, omissions and improvements of his own, so that a work drifted further from its original with every generation. The press, by contrast, is said to have produced hundreds of identical copies at a stroke, allowing readers across a continent to work from precisely the same words. There is genuine substance in this view, and it would be foolish to dismiss it. Yet the closer bibliographers look at the books themselves, the less identical those copies turn out to be.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The reason lies partly in the workings of the hand press. Sheets were printed one at a time, and errors were frequently noticed only after the run had begun. When that happened, the press would be stopped and the type corrected, but the sheets already printed were not thrown away: paper was far too expensive to waste. Corrected and uncorrected sheets were then stacked together and later folded and bound in no particular order, so that each finished copy contained its own unpredictable mixture of early and late states. Matthias Quellhorst, a bibliographer who has spent a decade collating copies of a seventeenth-century herbal, reports that among the sixty copies he examined, no two were textually identical in every respect.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Printers did have another remedy. Many books ended with a list of errata, inviting readers to correct their copies by hand. Ilvana Dervišević, who studies the traces left by early readers, has searched surviving copies for evidence that these instructions were followed. Her method involves comparing each printed list against the corresponding pages and noting any corrections made in ink in the margins or above the line. In her sample, fewer than one copy in five shows any correction corresponding to the printed list. Dervišević interprets this as a sign that readers were relatively tolerant of error. That conclusion may be right, but it goes further than the evidence allows: a reader who noted a correction mentally, or who simply never reached the faulty passage, would leave no mark at all on the page.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Variation also multiplied once a text left its first printer. Successful books were quickly reprinted, often without permission, and pirated editions routinely altered spelling, abbreviated difficult passages or added material of doubtful origin. In one notorious case, an unauthorised reprint of a popular travel narrative appeared with an entire chapter that its supposed author had never written. Tavita Fa'alogo, a historian of the book trade, argues that what later generations came to regard as textual stability was not a natural consequence of the press at all. In her account, it was produced over several centuries by other forces: copyright legislation, the commercial value of a publisher's reputation for accuracy, and the rise of scholarly editing, which treated the establishment of a correct text as a discipline in its own right.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this revision. Ruairí Mac Giollarnáth, a specialist in early scientific publishing, contends that critics of the traditional view have confused the existence of variation with its significance. The differences between copies of a printed edition, he insists, are usually trivial when set beside the wholesale divergence found among manuscripts of the same work. More importantly, print allowed a reader in one city and a reader in another to cite the same page numbers when they disagreed, and this simple possibility made indexes, footnotes and sustained scholarly debate far easier to manage. On this point he is surely correct. The weakness of his position is that it treats fixity as all or nothing, when it is better understood as a matter of degree.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: New technology is helping to measure that degree more precisely. Collation was once a painstaking business, carried out by laying two copies side by side and comparing them line by line, or with optical devices that superimposed one page upon another. A team at the Harbourne Collation Project now uses high-resolution imaging software to compare dozens of copies in the time it once took to examine two. Their early results suggest an intriguing pattern: variation is considerably more frequent in cheap, popular books such as almanacs and ballads than in expensive editions intended for wealthy buyers, presumably because printers took greater care where their reputation was at stake.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings matter beyond the history of printing. Major libraries are digitising their collections at remarkable speed, and in most cases a single copy of an edition is scanned and then presented online as if it stood for every other. The assumption that one copy can represent the whole edition is precisely the assumption that bibliographers have spent decades dismantling. At the very least, digital records should state which physical copy was photographed, so that readers know they are looking at one witness among many rather than at the book itself. Without such information, a scholar who notices a discrepancy between two digital versions may have no means of telling whether it reflects separate editions or merely different states within one.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: widows and other women running printing houses in early modern Europe despite guild restrictions
title: The Widow's Imprint
subtitle: Women ran printing houses across early modern Europe, yet for centuries their work went almost unrecorded

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the sixteenth, seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the guilds that regulated printing in European cities were, in principle, closed to women. A woman could not normally be admitted as a master printer in her own right, nor could she take on apprentices under her own name. Yet the title pages of the period tell a rather different story. Again and again, books appear with imprints announcing that they were printed by the widow of a named printer, and one survey of a single German city found that at any given moment roughly one printing house in ten was headed by a widow. This exception has often been treated as a legal curiosity. It is arguably considerably more than that: it offers one of the clearest windows we have onto the gap between what the rules of the trade said and how the trade actually worked.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Guild authorities tolerated widows for practical reasons. A printing house represented a substantial investment: presses, cases of type, stocks of paper and unsold books might together be worth more than the family home. Allowing a business to collapse on the death of its master would have harmed not only the family but also apprentices whose training was incomplete and creditors who were owed money. Moreover, the widow was rarely a newcomer to the work. Henrike Vosmaer, who has reconstructed the households of printers from inventories, marriage contracts and court records, argues that many wives were effectively co-managers of the business for years before they were widowed. They kept the accounts, dealt with paper merchants, supervised sales from the shop front and, in some cases, read proofs. Widowhood, in Vosmaer's phrase, did not create a female printer so much as reveal one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The position of a widow was nevertheless precarious. In many cities, the right to run the business passed to her new husband if she remarried, and the most likely candidate was a journeyman from the same workshop, for whom marrying the master's widow was the quickest route to a press of his own. Mercedes Etxegoien, studying printers in northern Spain, found that widows who did not remarry ran their businesses for an average of eleven years, and that several expanded them considerably. It is tempting to read such cases as deliberate choices of independence over marriage. That interpretation may sometimes be correct, but it should be treated with caution, since the decision not to remarry was also shaped by age, the number of children and the simple availability of suitable partners.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is that the records themselves conceal much of women's work. Imprints changed when a widow remarried or handed the business to a son, and the labour of wives and daughters who folded sheets, stitched pamphlets or helped in the shop was almost never recorded at all. Ásdís Snæbjarnardóttir has argued that even the work of widows is systematically undercounted, because library catalogues are generally organised under the name of a male printer. A book issued by a widow is frequently filed under her late husband's name, and imprints that refer only to the heirs of a printer give no indication of who was actually in charge. Such conventions were not intended to mislead, but their cumulative effect has been to make a substantial body of work disappear from view.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all historians share the enthusiasm that has accompanied this research. Kwabena Offei-Ansah cautions that the field risks building a heroic narrative on a handful of exceptional figures. Most widow-run presses, he points out, were small establishments that produced ballads, public notices, almanacs and printed forms rather than scholarly folios, and a good many widows sold the business within a year or two. His warning against romanticising the evidence is well founded. Less convincing is his implication that such modest output is of minor importance. Jobbing work of this kind was the economic backbone of most printing houses, and to treat it as marginal is to adopt the bias of collectors, who preserved handsome books and discarded everything else.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some widows achieved positions of real standing. A number held appointments as official printers to city councils, universities or bishops, and in several documented cases these contracts were renewed in the widow's own name rather than transferred to a male relative. Others moved into bookselling, a branch of the trade in which guild restrictions were often less strict and in which commercial skills could be put to good use without the need to manage a workforce of journeymen. Paradoxically, the decline of guild power in the late eighteenth century did not open the trade further to women. As mechanised presses spread in the following century, the capital required to establish a printing business rose sharply, and the trade unions that represented compositors frequently excluded women from their ranks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of the printing widow therefore cautions against reading the formal rules of any trade as a description of its practice. The regulations said that women could not be printers; the books say that many were. Recovering that history means reading the surviving records against the grain, paying attention to what they omit as much as to what they state, and resisting the temptation to replace one simplified story with another.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: chapbooks and cheap print: who read them, who wrote them and how they circulated in the eighteenth century
title: Reading for a Penny
subtitle: The cheap booklets sold by travelling pedlars were once dismissed as rubbish and later hailed as the voice of the people. Neither view quite fits

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For the price of a penny or less, a buyer in eighteenth-century Britain could acquire a small booklet of eight, sixteen or twenty-four pages, printed on a single folded sheet of coarse paper and often decorated with a crude woodcut. These chapbooks, named after the chapmen, or travelling pedlars, who sold them, contained an extraordinary miscellany: abridged romances, ballads, jokes, prophecies, accounts of notorious crimes and simplified versions of religious works. Comparable cheap literature circulated in France, the German lands and Scandinavia. For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, scholars ignored such material as worthless. Then, from the 1970s, the pendulum swung, and chapbooks were celebrated as the authentic voice of ordinary people. Both attitudes, it is now clear, misrepresent what these booklets were.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first question is who actually read them. Probate inventories, the lists of possessions drawn up after a death, are a standard source for book ownership, but they are of little help here, because objects as cheap as chapbooks were rarely thought worth recording. Gwenllian Prys-Ashdown has therefore turned to a different kind of evidence: names, dates and comments written into surviving copies, together with references in diaries and letters. Her findings complicate the familiar picture. Apprentices, domestic servants and farm labourers certainly appear among the owners, but so do clergymen, shopkeepers and the children of landed families, some of whom recalled chapbooks fondly in later life as their first encounter with reading for pleasure. Prys-Ashdown concludes that the chapbook was less the literature of a particular class than the literature of a particular price.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Equally contested is the question of who wrote them. Most chapbook texts were produced not by the rural communities in which they circulated but by poorly paid writers working in London and a handful of other cities, who frequently cut down older romances to fit the limits of a single sheet. A small number of printing centres turned them out in enormous quantities, and the same text might be reused, with only minor alterations, for half a century. Idriss Lahlouhi contends that this makes nonsense of the claim that chapbooks express popular culture. In his view, they reveal only what urban printers believed rural buyers would want: a culture made for the people rather than by them. There is much truth in this, yet it overlooks a crucial mechanism. Printers worked on narrow margins and had every reason to abandon titles that failed to sell, so that over time the repertoire was shaped, indirectly but powerfully, by the preferences of buyers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The routes by which chapbooks travelled have also attracted attention. Chapmen walked regular circuits through market towns and villages, and an inventory of one pack, preserved because its owner died on the road, lists several hundred booklets packed alongside ribbons, pins, needles and spectacles. Ondine Marchetaux, who has reconstructed the distribution networks of printers in eastern France, argues that cheap print reached rural areas far more effectively than historians once assumed. Using printers' account books and records of licences issued to pedlars, she has shown that new titles could reach remote mountain villages within a few weeks of leaving the press.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomed this traffic. Clergy and reformers repeatedly complained that chapbooks spread superstition and immorality, and from the 1790s religious societies began producing their own cheap tracts, deliberately imitating the format, woodcuts and even the titles of popular chapbooks in order to displace them. Millions of these tracts were distributed, many of them free of charge. Whether they succeeded in changing reading habits is doubtful: contemporary reports suggest that pedlars sometimes found tracts hard to sell, and that buyers who wanted adventure and humour were not easily persuaded to accept moral instruction instead.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Counting copies, however, tells us only part of the story. Chapbooks were commonly read aloud, by a literate member of a household to the rest of the family in the evening, or by one worker to others during repetitive tasks, so that a single booklet might reach a dozen listeners, some of whom could not read at all. Reading aloud also shaped the texts themselves, which often favour short sentences, repetition and dialogue, features that suit a listening audience. This has an important consequence. Historians who measure literacy chiefly by the ability to sign one's name in a marriage register are likely to underestimate, perhaps considerably, the number of people who regularly encountered printed stories.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the nineteenth century, the chapbook gradually lost its place. Cheap magazines, serialised fiction and the expansion of railway bookstalls offered new forms of inexpensive reading, and the surviving chapbooks were increasingly marketed to children or bought by antiquarian collectors. Those collectors, it should be remembered, kept what they found charming or curious and discarded much else, so the booklets that fill library shelves today are not a neutral sample of what was once sold. Perhaps the most accurate way to understand the chapbook, then, is neither as rubbish nor as the unmediated voice of the people, but as a meeting point where the commercial calculations of printers and the tastes of an enormous readership continually adjusted to one another.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: eighteenth-century book censorship and the clandestine trade in forbidden books
title: Married Sheets and Silent Censors
subtitle: Forbidden books circulated freely in eighteenth-century Europe. Does that mean censorship failed?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the eighteenth century, almost every European state maintained some apparatus for controlling the printed word. Manuscripts had to be submitted to official censors before publication; printers required licences or privileges to operate; and lists of prohibited titles were drawn up, revised and circulated to booksellers and customs officers. Yet the period is also notorious for the ease with which forbidden books circulated. Works condemned by the authorities were read in drawing rooms and coffee houses, discussed in correspondence and, on occasion, found on the shelves of the very officials charged with suppressing them. It is therefore tempting to conclude that censorship simply failed. Whether that conclusion is justified, however, depends on what one supposes censorship was meant to achieve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most visible obstacle to effective control was geography. Europe was a patchwork of jurisdictions, and a book banned in one capital could be printed legally, or at least safely, a few days' journey away, in a small principality, a free city or a republic whose authorities had little interest in policing their neighbours' morals. Printers in these places produced editions aimed specifically at markets where the books were forbidden. The sheets were then smuggled across borders, often concealed among the sheets of perfectly legal works, a technique the trade called 'marrying'. Customs officers were few, poorly paid and frequently open to bribery, and the sheer volume of legitimate goods crossing frontiers made thorough inspection impossible. Leocadia Brzostowska, who has studied the records of customs posts along several frontiers, estimates that perhaps one illicit consignment in twenty was ever seized.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some historians go further and argue that censorship actively promoted the books it targeted. Anselm Ruppertshofen points to booksellers' catalogues that advertised titles as having been condemned, and to evidence that prices rose sharply once a ban was announced. A prohibition, in his view, functioned as free publicity. This 'forbidden fruit' argument is plausible for the most notorious titles, whose condemnation became news in itself. But the great majority of banned books were obscure works that no ban could make famous, and for these the main consequences of prohibition were higher costs, greater risks and smaller sales. To generalise from the celebrated cases is to mistake the exception for the rule.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A rather different picture of the censors themselves has emerged from the work of Nkiruka Onwuasoanya, who has read thousands of their surviving reports. Far from being narrow-minded functionaries, many censors were writers, scholars and lawyers who corresponded with authors, proposed alterations that would make a manuscript acceptable and, in some instances, defended works against more hostile colleagues. In one case she describes, a censor spent several months exchanging letters with an author, suggesting how a controversial chapter might be reworded so that its argument survived while its tone was softened. Some states also developed a system of tacit permissions, under which a book could be sold without formal approval on the understanding that its printer would not be prosecuted. Onwuasoanya concludes that censorship is better understood as a process of negotiation than as a wall.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Thibault Esquerré approaches the question as an economic historian. In his view, the most damaging effect of strict censorship was not on readers but on domestic printers. Because demand for forbidden books was met by foreign presses, capital, skilled workers and profits flowed abroad, and in at least one large kingdom, he argues, native printers lost most of the market for new works of philosophy and politics to competitors across the border. He notes, for example, that several established printing families relocated their businesses to neighbouring territories during the middle decades of the century, taking their equipment and journeymen with them. His argument is compelling, but it depends heavily on fragmentary commercial records, and the proportion of the trade that was lost cannot be calculated with any confidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, exactly, were readers buying? A team at the Ledbury Centre for Book History has examined lists of seized books alongside the order books of booksellers who dealt in illegal titles. Their findings are sobering for anyone who imagines a public hungry for philosophy. Serious works of political theory and religious criticism were certainly present, but they were outnumbered by scandalous accounts of the private lives of courtiers, satirical libels and erotic fiction. This complicates the familiar claim that the clandestine trade carried new ideas directly to a receptive public. It does not, however, make that trade politically harmless. Stories that portrayed the powerful as corrupt and ridiculous may have done more to erode respect for authority than any treatise.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question of whether censorship worked has usually been answered by counting the books that slipped past it. That approach captures only part of the picture. Censorship shaped where books were printed, what they cost and who could afford them, and it surely influenced, in ways that are almost impossible to measure, what authors chose to leave unwritten. Authors who expected their work to be refused may simply never have written it. The most important effects of a censorship system may well be the ones that leave no trace in the archives.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: blackletter versus roman type and the long-running debate over the legibility of typefaces
title: The Shape of Letters
subtitle: For five centuries, printers and reformers have argued over which typefaces are easiest to read. The answer may lie less in the letters than in the reader

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the decades after printing spread across Europe, printers faced a choice of letterforms. On one side stood the gothic or blackletter types, dense and angular, modelled on the formal handwriting of medieval scribes. On the other stood roman types, rounder and more open, derived from the scripts favoured by Italian humanists. Over the following two centuries most of Europe settled on roman, but in the German-speaking lands and parts of Scandinavia and the Baltic, blackletter remained the everyday type for books and newspapers well into the twentieth century. Throughout this long coexistence, one argument recurred with remarkable persistence: that one style was simply easier to read than the other. That argument has never been settled, and the reason, it can be argued, is that it rests on a mistaken premise, namely that legibility is a fixed property of the letters themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against blackletter was made most often by its opponents in the nineteenth century, and it has an obvious appeal. In many blackletter faces, letters are built largely from short vertical strokes, so that combinations such as 'm', 'n', 'u' and 'i' can merge into a picket fence of near-identical marks. Roman letters, with their varied curves and wider spacing, seem to offer the eye more distinctive shapes. Some reformers went further, claiming that the strain of deciphering blackletter damaged children's eyesight, an assertion for which they offered little evidence. Elspeth Kinnaird-Rowe tested the basic intuition with modern adult readers, asking them to read comparable passages set in each style. Her participants read blackletter roughly a third more slowly and made more errors when asked to recall details.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These results are frequently cited, but they demonstrate less than is often claimed. Kinnaird-Rowe's readers had been educated entirely in roman type and had rarely, if ever, encountered blackletter; what the experiment measured, therefore, was largely the effect of unfamiliarity. More revealing are the records uncovered by Joaquim Quaresma-Lobo, who found reading tests administered to schoolchildren in the early twentieth century in regions where both styles were taught. Children who had learned blackletter first read it as quickly as roman type, and differences between the groups largely disappeared after a few months of practice in the second style.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If legibility alone cannot explain the persistence of blackletter, culture may. During the nineteenth century, the choice of type became entangled with questions of national identity. Blackletter was presented by its defenders as an expression of native tradition, while roman was associated with cosmopolitan scholarship and with neighbouring nations. In the early twentieth century, governments in several countries issued decrees on the matter, sometimes favouring one style and then, a few years later, abruptly reversing their position. Yaw Ankomah-Dwamena argues that typefaces have always functioned primarily as signals: a printer who chose one style over another was announcing an allegiance to tradition or to modernity, and readers registered that message before they had read a single word. On this view, the long debate about legibility was often a debate about identity conducted in technical language.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A milder version of the same controversy continues today in the argument over serifs, the small strokes that finish the ends of letters in many roman typefaces. It has often been claimed that serifs guide the eye along the line and therefore make long texts easier to read, while sans serif letters are said to be clearer at small sizes. Ingeborg Ystebø, who reviewed several decades of experimental studies, found no consistent advantage for either style. Where differences appeared, they were small compared with the effects of letter size, the spacing between letters and lines, and the length of each line. Her conclusion seems sound, and designers anxious about legibility would do better to attend to spacing than to argue about serifs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Technology has added a further twist. Early computer screens displayed text with a coarse grid of pixels, on which the fine details of serifs were rendered crudely, and sans serif faces became the practical choice for on-screen reading. Typefaces designed specifically for screens in that period, with generous spacing and simplified forms, were widely adopted and quickly became familiar to millions of readers, which may itself help to explain why many people now report finding them comfortable. Modern high-resolution displays have largely removed the original constraint, yet the association between screens and sans serif letters persists. Here, as in the earlier debates, claims about what is easy to read often appear to rationalise preferences that are really aesthetic or ideological.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that letterforms are irrelevant. A badly designed alphabet, with cramped spacing or ambiguous shapes, may defeat any reader, however experienced. But within the range of competent designs, legibility appears to be less a property of letters than a relationship between letters and the readers who have learned them. Recognising this does not make questions of design trivial; it simply places them in their proper context. What we find easy to read, in the end, is largely what we have read most often.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: marginalia and readers' annotations in early printed books as evidence for the history of reading
title: Pen in Hand
subtitle: The notes that readers scribbled in their books were once scrubbed away as damage. Historians now treat them as precious, but also slippery, evidence

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the history of the book was largely a history of production. Scholars reconstructed the workshops of printers, counted editions and traced the movement of books through the trade. Readers, by comparison, were elusive: we know what was printed and sold, but far less about what people did with the books once they owned them. One of the most promising sources for answering that question lies in the books themselves, in the underlinings, crosses, brief comments and small pointing hands, known as manicules, that readers added to their pages. Such marks were long regarded as defacement. Nineteenth-century collectors and librarians sometimes had annotated pages washed or their margins trimmed in order to restore a clean appearance, and a great deal of irreplaceable evidence was destroyed in the process. It is hard to regard this as anything other than a serious loss.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What the surviving notes reveal, above all, is that reading in the early modern period was frequently purposeful. Cosimo Pellizzaro has studied a set of histories annotated over many years by a scholar employed in the households of noblemen. The margins are crowded with cross-references to other authors, summaries of arguments and short notes drawing lessons from ancient events for contemporary politics. In one volume, a single page about a disputed royal succession carries more than forty separate notes, several of which compare the ancient case with events that had taken place only a few years earlier. Pellizzaro argues that this scholar read not for private enjoyment but in order to prepare advice for his employers, extracting from each text whatever might be useful in their affairs. Reading, in this account, was an activity aimed at action.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in knowing how far such cases can be generalised. Annelise Brøndum-Kjær points out that the great majority of readers left no marks in their books at all, and that those who did were drawn disproportionately from particular groups: scholars, students, lawyers and clergy, many of whom had been taught at school to read with pen in hand and to compile commonplace books of useful extracts. A handful of prolific annotators, whose copies have attracted intense study, may therefore have shaped our picture of reading far more than their numbers justify. This warning deserves to be taken seriously; a history of reading built on exceptional readers risks becoming a history of exceptions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second objection concerns the nature of the notes themselves. Temitope Adewusi-Clarke has shown that many annotations, far from recording a reader's spontaneous response, were copied from teachers' lectures, from printed commentaries or from the notes of earlier owners. Students in particular often transcribed the same remarks into their texts as their classmates, and copies of a single textbook now held in different libraries sometimes carry almost identical notes. In her view, marginalia tell us more about educational routines than about individual minds. This is a valuable corrective, but it goes too far. Even when the wording of a note was borrowed, the decision to mark one passage rather than another was the reader's own, and patterns of selection can reveal priorities that no single comment would disclose.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Recent work has attempted to place the study of marginalia on a more systematic footing. Rather than seeking out famous annotated copies, the Calderwood Marginalia Survey examined a random sample of several thousand books printed before 1700 and now held in libraries of different types and sizes. Roughly one copy in five contained some form of annotation, but most of these marks were simple underlinings, brackets or symbols rather than written comments. Rates of annotation also varied sharply by subject, being far higher in law and medicine than the average across the sample. The survey also found that annotations were concentrated in the opening chapters of many books, suggesting that numerous readers either lost interest or stopped marking their copies well before reaching the end.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Interpreting even these modest marks is not straightforward. Most notes are unsigned and undated, and a single copy may carry layers of annotation added by successive owners over two or three centuries. Historians have traditionally relied on the style of handwriting and the colour of ink to separate these layers, methods that depend heavily on individual judgement. Hyacinth Morganstern has proposed a statistical technique that compares the shapes of individual letters across many notes, allowing hands to be grouped and, where signed examples survive, identified. Her method is promising, though it works best where notes are long enough to supply a reasonable number of letters for comparison.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a final irony. Electronic reading devices now record, on an enormous scale, which passages readers highlight, and some services publish lists of the most frequently marked sentences in popular books. Future historians may therefore possess far more data about reading than their predecessors ever did. Yet these records strip each mark of its context, saying nothing about who made it, or why, and they are held by private companies rather than libraries. Historians of the future may know a great deal more about what was highlighted while understanding considerably less about how people actually read.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: Victorian circulating libraries and the three-volume novel: pricing, literary form, moral gatekeeping and collapse
title: Three Volumes and a Subscription
subtitle: How the commercial lending libraries of Victorian Britain shaped the price, length and content of the novel

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the Victorian period, a new novel in Britain was not something an ordinary reader expected to buy. Fiction was normally published first in three separate volumes at a combined price of thirty-one shillings and sixpence, a sum equivalent to a week's wages for many skilled workers. Very few private individuals paid it. Instead, readers borrowed new fiction from commercial circulating libraries, paying an annual subscription that entitled them to exchange volumes as often as they wished. The largest of these firms bought new novels by the hundred, and sometimes by the thousand, and their orders could determine whether a book succeeded or failed. The arrangement is usually remembered as a kind of cartel that kept books expensive and restricted what novelists could write. That account contains some truth, but it simplifies a system that was more complicated, and in some respects more productive, than its critics allowed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Philippa Strathdee, an economic historian of publishing, argues that the high price was not an accident but the keystone of the whole arrangement. By making private purchase almost unthinkable, it ensured that readers who wanted new fiction had little choice but to subscribe. Publishers, in turn, could rely on the libraries to take a substantial part of each edition, which made the cost of producing a novel far more predictable than it would otherwise have been. Cheaper single-volume reprints usually followed a year or so later, once library demand had been exhausted. Strathdee compares the system to the staggered release of films, which appear first in cinemas and only later in cheaper formats, and the comparison is illuminating.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The format also left its mark on the novels themselves. Authors frequently complained that they were obliged to stretch their material to fill three volumes, and many works of the period contain subplots that seem to exist mainly to occupy space. Chidozie Ezeigwe has analysed the final chapters of each volume in several hundred novels and found that they contain a disproportionate number of dramatic revelations, unexpected arrivals and unresolved crises, apparently designed to send the reader back to the library for the next instalment. The pattern is striking. It would be a mistake, however, to attribute it to the three-volume format alone, since many of the same novels first appeared in monthly parts in magazines, a form of publication that rewarded suspense in exactly the same way.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Most controversial was the libraries' role as moral guardians. The leading firms presented themselves as suppliers of reading suitable for the whole family, and they occasionally refused to stock novels they considered improper, a decision that could be ruinous for an author. Marit Holtegaard has argued that this influence has been greatly exaggerated: her search of trade records and correspondence uncovered only a few dozen outright refusals over half a century. Her figures appear accurate, but they count only open confrontations. Publishers who knew a library's preferences could advise authors to soften a scene before a manuscript ever reached the printer, and such quiet adjustments would leave little or nothing in the records she examined.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is, however, another side to the ledger. Because the libraries bought in bulk and needed a constant supply of new titles to satisfy their subscribers, publishers could afford to take chances on unknown writers whose first novels might never have found buyers on the open market. Dov Shapirovsky contends that the system consequently supported a greater variety of new fiction than a free market in cheap books would have done, and he points to the large number of first novels published during its peak decades. The argument is plausible, but the number of debut novels may also reflect broader changes, not least rising literacy and the growth of a middle-class reading public.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The system collapsed with remarkable speed. By the early 1890s the libraries were burdened with vast stocks of second-hand volumes that could no longer be sold on, while publishers were experimenting with new novels issued directly in a single volume at a much lower price. In 1894 the two largest libraries announced that they would pay less for three-volume novels and would delay buying them. Within a few years the format had all but disappeared, and the single-volume novel priced at six shillings became the norm. Many authors welcomed the change, which freed them from the obligation to pad their work, although some publishers feared that lower prices would reduce their profits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The episode offers a lesson that extends well beyond the Victorian period. We tend to think of the form of a book as something chosen by its author, but the three-volume novel shows how powerfully the institutions that distribute books can shape their length, their structure and even their content. Seen in this light, the history of the circulating library is not merely a chapter in the story of publishing but an early example of a pattern that recurs whenever a few large buyers dominate a market. Readers today who notice that television series have grown longer or shorter to suit the requirements of subscription services are observing the same process at work.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: the rag shortage in European papermaking and the slow search for alternative fibres before wood pulp
title: The Rag Famine
subtitle: For four centuries, printed books depended on a steady supply of old clothes. When that supply ran short, the search for something else proved surprisingly slow

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly four hundred years after printing reached Europe, almost every sheet of paper on which a book was printed began life as a piece of clothing. Paper was made from linen and, later, cotton rags, which were sorted, cut, left to ferment and then beaten into a pulp of fibres. As literacy grew and the output of the presses expanded, so did the appetite for rags, and by the eighteenth century much of Europe faced a chronic shortage. Governments banned the export of rags, licensed collectors and, in some cases, encouraged citizens to save worn-out linen rather than burn it. Histories of printing have traditionally been written around presses, typefaces and the people who operated them. Yet the supply of rags, it might be argued, imposed limits on the spread of print that were every bit as decisive, and it has received far less attention than it deserves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The rag trade was an industry in its own right. Rag-pickers gathered discarded cloth from households and streets; merchants bought it in bulk, graded it and sold it on to mills, with fine white linen reserved for writing paper and coarser, coloured material used for wrapping and cheap printing. Esperanza Villacañas, who has worked through the ledgers of rag merchants in several Mediterranean ports, found that the price of good-quality rags in the region she studied roughly tripled over the course of the eighteenth century, far outpacing the general rise in prices. Rag merchants who could secure reliable supplies became wealthy, and disputes over collecting rights were sometimes settled in the courts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Gottfried Ahlbeck goes further, maintaining that the scarcity of rags did more than any other factor to hold back the growth of cheap print. Since paper often accounted for half or more of the cost of producing a book or newspaper, rising rag prices fed directly into the price paid by readers. Printers responded by setting text in smaller type, reducing the width of margins and using thinner sheets, all ways of extracting more words from each page. Ahlbeck's argument is persuasive in outline. It is difficult, however, to separate the influence of rag prices from that of the heavy taxes many governments levied on paper and newspapers in the same period, and both probably contributed to keeping print expensive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The obvious solution was to find something other than rags. Throughout the eighteenth century, experimenters attempted to make paper from straw, nettles, thistles, cabbage stalks, bark and moss, inspired in part by the observation that wasps construct their nests from a kind of paper made of chewed wood. Some of these enthusiasts printed small books on their experimental sheets as proof of what could be done. Almost none of the materials succeeded commercially. The resulting paper was often weak, brittle or discoloured, and the processing required to break down tough plant fibres made it more expensive than the rag paper it was meant to replace.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nyokabi Gitonga has drawn attention to a puzzle in this story. The idea that wood might be used to make paper was in circulation by the late eighteenth century, yet wood pulp did not become commercially important until well into the nineteenth. The delay, she argues, reflected not a shortage of imagination but the absence of suitable technology: wood had to be ground mechanically or dissolved chemically before its fibres could be used, and neither process was practical on a large scale until the necessary machinery and chemistry had been developed. Ironically, another invention made the shortage worse in the meantime. The papermaking machine, which produced a continuous roll of paper rather than individual sheets, vastly increased the capacity of mills and therefore their demand for rags.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The transition to new fibres may have been less abrupt than it appears. A team working on the Tolland Watermark Survey has analysed the fibre content of several thousand dated sheets held in archives across northern Europe. Their results suggest that mills were adding cheaper materials, including straw and recycled waste paper, to their pulp decades before such practices were openly acknowledged. By the 1820s, according to the team, adulterated paper had become commonplace, even in sheets sold as pure rag. The finding matters because it implies that printers and readers were gradually becoming accustomed to inferior paper long before the arrival of wood pulp made the change official.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Once wood pulp became established, the cost of paper fell dramatically, helping to make possible the mass-circulation newspapers and inexpensive books of the later nineteenth century. There was a price to pay. Much of the wood-pulp paper of that era was chemically acidic and has since become yellow and brittle, so that libraries now face the expensive task of preserving millions of crumbling volumes. Leopold Szczepankiewicz contends that the bargain was nevertheless a good one: wider access to print for the many, he argues, was worth more than permanence for the few. That judgement is broadly persuasive, although it should be acknowledged that the cost of the bargain has fallen on later generations of librarians and readers rather than on those who made it.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The history of paper suggests that the story of printing cannot be told through technology and ideas alone. Presses and typefaces determined how books were made; the supply of raw material determined how many could be made at all. What could be printed, and for whom, depended to a remarkable degree on the humble business of collecting, sorting and pulping old cloth.

area: the history of printing and books
topic: the commercial failures of the first printers: overproduction, credit, survival strategies and distribution in the fifteenth-century book trade
title: Boom and Bust in the First Age of Print
subtitle: The printing press spread across Europe with astonishing speed, but many of the people who backed it were ruined

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to imagine that the printing press was an immediate and unqualified success. The speed with which it spread certainly seems to support that view: within about fifty years of the first printed books appearing in the German city of Mainz, presses had been established in more than two hundred and fifty towns across Europe. Yet behind these impressive figures lies a much less triumphant story. A large proportion of the early presses closed within a few years of opening, many printers fell into debt, and bankruptcies were common. Historians have long been aware of these failures, but they have tended to treat them as unfortunate footnotes to a larger narrative of success. Rather than a smooth march of progress, the first decades of printing are better understood as a speculative boom, followed, as such booms usually are, by a painful shake-out.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central difficulty was that early printers misjudged their market. Many assumed that the main demand would be for the texts that had dominated the manuscript trade: Latin classics, works of theology and law, and the large reference books used in universities. These were expensive to produce, and printers in the same city frequently issued competing editions of the same works within a few years of one another. In one Italian city during the early 1470s, several firms printed the same classical authors almost simultaneously, and prices fell so far that some editions could not be sold at a profit at all. Ottavia Bonvecchiato, who has examined inventories drawn up when printing businesses were wound up, estimates that the unsold stock held by a struggling firm could amount to several years of its output.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Overproduction was compounded by the economics of the trade. Paper, the largest single cost, had to be bought before printing began, and an edition of several hundred copies might take months to print and years to sell. Printers therefore depended on outside investors, usually merchants, lawyers or wealthy clerics, who expected to be repaid long before most of the books had found buyers. Erkki Ylitervo argues that early printing businesses failed not primarily because nobody wanted their books but because they ran out of cash before the books could be sold. This is a valuable insight, but it is hard to treat cash flow and overproduction as separate explanations. A printer whose books sold quickly would have had little difficulty repaying his investors; it was precisely the glut of competing editions that slowed sales to a crawl.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The printers who survived did so by adapting. Many shifted towards smaller and cheaper formats, towards texts in the local language rather than Latin, and towards devotional works, schoolbooks and calendars that could be sold to a wider public. Some also found a profitable sideline in printing indulgences, documents sold by the church that were issued in enormous numbers and required only a single sheet. Sefa Ahiable has drawn attention to another, less glamorous source of survival. Churches and governments required large quantities of printed forms, proclamations and certificates, and contracts for such work provided a steady income that was paid promptly. In Ahiable's view, it was this routine official printing that kept many workshops solvent, effectively subsidising the riskier business of publishing books.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Equally important were improvements in distribution. Early printers often had to sell their books largely in their own town, but by the end of the fifteenth century a network of booksellers, agents and great trade fairs allowed stock to be exchanged and sent across long distances. Rosalind Featherstonhaugh argues that the emergence of these wholesale networks did more to stabilise the trade than any refinement of the press itself, since a book that could not sell in one city might find buyers in another. This is a persuasive point, and it is consistent with the fact that the most successful printers of the next generation were frequently also major booksellers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Our picture of this period is shaped, however, by the books that happen to have survived. Large, expensive volumes were bound, stored in libraries and carefully preserved; cheap pamphlets, forms, calendars and schoolbooks were used until they fell apart and were then thrown away. Many such items are known only from a single copy or from a fragment recovered from the binding of another book, and many more have presumably vanished without trace. Even the survival of large books is uneven, since collections were broken up, burned or dispersed during later wars and religious conflicts. Estimates of the total number of editions printed before 1500 must therefore be treated as approximate, and the impression that early printing was dominated by scholarly works is almost certainly exaggerated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The early history of print has an obvious resonance today. New technologies tend to attract waves of investment based on optimistic assumptions about demand, and the pioneers are not always the ones who profit. The lesson is not that enthusiasm is misplaced, but that a technology's eventual importance offers little protection against the commercial misjudgements of its early years. The printing press transformed European culture over the long term, but in the short term it ruined a good many of the people who believed in it most enthusiastically.

topic: world map projections: Mercator, the equal-area campaign, compromise projections and web maps
title: The World Made Flat
subtitle: No map of the whole earth can be accurate, so the real question is which distortions we are willing to live with

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every flat map of the world is, in a strict sense, wrong. A sphere cannot be unrolled onto a plane without tearing or stretching, a fact proved mathematically in the early nineteenth century, and cartographers must therefore decide which of the globe's properties to sacrifice. A projection may preserve the true areas of landmasses, or their local shapes, or distances from a single point, but never all of these at once. Because the decision is usually made out of sight, by publishers and software designers rather than by map readers, it is tempting to regard it as a purely technical matter. That view is mistaken. The choice of projection is never neutral: it determines which regions look large and central and which appear marginal, and those impressions can outlast any amount of later correction.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most famous example is the projection devised by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. His aim was practical. On his map, a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line, so a navigator could lay a ruler between two ports, read off the angle and hold that course. For this purpose the design was brilliant. The price, however, was a dramatic inflation of area towards the poles. Greenland appears roughly as large as Africa, although Africa is some fourteen times bigger, and northern Europe seems to dwarf regions near the equator. Despite this, the projection became the standard wall map in many classrooms, and more recently it was adopted by web mapping services, partly because it can be cut neatly into square tiles and keeps the shapes of streets and buildings undistorted at every level of zoom.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s a vigorous public campaign set out to dethrone Mercator. Its supporters promoted an equal-area projection, arguing that the familiar map exaggerated the importance of high-latitude, largely wealthy nations at the expense of the tropics. The historian Mireille Daucourt, of the Institut d'Histoire Cartographique in Lyon, has argued that the campaign succeeded more as a political gesture than as a contribution to cartography. The map it championed, she points out, stretched Africa and South America vertically, distorting their shapes almost as severely as Mercator had distorted their size. More pointedly, Daucourt observes that professional cartographers had long since abandoned Mercator for world maps, so that the campaign was attacking a position few experts still defended. This is fair as far as it goes, but it underestimates how far classroom practice lagged behind professional opinion. Experts may have moved on decades earlier; the maps on school walls, and therefore the mental images of millions of pupils, had not.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whether those mental images matter is an empirical question, and it has been addressed by the cognitive psychologist Kaito Fujinami at the Hokuriku Institute of Spatial Cognition. Fujinami asked university students from several countries to estimate the relative areas of pairs of countries. Those who had grown up with Mercator wall maps overestimated the size of northern countries by around a third. Yet students educated with equal-area maps also made substantial errors, often enlarging their own nation and its neighbours. Fujinami concludes that a sense of geographical scale is assembled from many sources, including globes, news coverage and national pride, and that no single map can correct it. This conclusion seems sound, although it should not become a reason for indifference about which maps children are shown; one influence among several is still an influence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third position rejects the idea that any single property deserves priority. Sunniva Kvamsdal, a cartographer at the Bergen School of Geomatics, favours so-called compromise projections, which preserve neither area nor shape exactly but keep every kind of distortion moderate. In her view, the long quarrel over Mercator encouraged the public to believe that a 'correct' world map exists and is merely being withheld. Kvamsdal argues instead that the choice of projection should follow from what a map is for. Charts intended for navigation should preserve angles, as Mercator's did. Thematic maps, on the other hand, which shade regions according to population density, forest cover or rainfall, should always be equal-area, since readers instinctively judge the significance of a coloured region by how much of the page it occupies.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some commentators believe that digital technology has made the debate obsolete. Ottavio Rinaldesi, a software engineer who writes on the design of online maps, contends that most users now view maps at the scale of a city or a street, where the distortions of Mercator are negligible, and that when they zoom out, many applications now display the earth as a rotating globe. His argument has some force, but it is too optimistic. A great deal of global data, from climate-risk dashboards to maps of internet access, is still presented on flat Mercator backgrounds, and on these the high latitudes continue to appear far more extensive than they are. The problem has not disappeared; it has simply become less visible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done? Searching for the perfect projection is futile, since it does not exist. The more valuable goal is map literacy: teaching people, from an early age, to ask of any map what it has been designed to show and what it has been obliged to distort. Even the globe, the only representation of the earth that is free of distortion, cannot display the whole surface at once. Every way of picturing the world conceals something, and the most useful skill a map reader can acquire is the habit of wondering what that is.

topic: the purpose of medieval world maps (mappae mundi): devotional, encyclopedic and practical interpretations
title: Worlds on Calfskin
subtitle: Medieval world maps were long dismissed as failed geography. Historians now ask what they were really for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the great world maps of the European Middle Ages were treated as an embarrassment. Historians of cartography, writing in an age of triangulation and precise surveys, saw in them little more than evidence of ignorance: distorted continents, imaginary peoples and a geography apparently subordinated to religious doctrine. The usual story ran from the accurate maps of the ancient Greeks, through a long medieval eclipse, to a triumphant recovery in the Renaissance. Such a judgement, however, reveals more about the expectations of those historians than about the maps themselves. To ask whether a mappa mundi is accurate is rather like asking whether a stained-glass window is a reliable diagram of the weather.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic design of these maps is simple. Many follow what is known as the T-O scheme: the inhabited world is drawn as a circle, with east at the top, and the circle is divided by bodies of water that form the shape of a T. Asia fills the upper half, while Europe and Africa share the two lower quarters. Jerusalem frequently sits at or near the centre, and the earthly Paradise is placed at the far eastern edge, at the very top of the map. The largest surviving example, made around 1300, was drawn on a single calfskin more than one and a half metres tall and carries over a thousand inscriptions describing cities, rivers, animals and the strange peoples believed to live at the edges of the world.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What were such objects for? One influential answer has been offered by Halina Zawierucha, an art historian at the Kraków Institute of Medieval Visual Culture. She argues that mappae mundi were primarily devotional images, intended to be contemplated rather than consulted. On her reading, the map unfolds the story of salvation across space: creation begins in the east, at Paradise, and history moves westward towards the present, while the whole world is framed by images of judgement at its upper edge. Zawierucha stresses that several of the largest maps hung in churches, some of them close to altars, where their audience would have been worshippers rather than travellers. A map in such a setting, she suggests, was closer to an altarpiece than to an atlas.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Benedek Szalontai, a historian of science at the Esztergom Centre for Manuscript Studies, finds this account too narrow. He points out that the great majority of inscriptions on the maps are not prayers or scriptural verses but extracts from classical and early medieval writers on geography and natural history. In his view, the maps functioned as encyclopedias in visual form, gathering into one image everything a learned person was expected to know about the world, its peoples and its past. Szalontai's argument is persuasive as far as the content of the maps is concerned. Yet the opposition he draws between religious and scholarly purposes is one that their makers would probably not have recognised. For a medieval cleric, to understand the created world was itself an act of devotion, and the two readings are better seen as complementary than as rivals.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third line of research has asked whether the maps had any practical function at all. Leocadia Arizmendi, who has compared the place names on several maps with surviving lists of stages along pilgrimage roads, found that the sequence of towns along certain routes through France and Italy is largely correct, even though the distances between them bear little relation to reality. Arizmendi concludes that some compilers drew directly on travellers' itineraries. She is careful, however, not to overstate the point: nobody, she insists, could have used a mappa mundi to find the way from one town to the next, and the itinerary material seems to have been included as knowledge worth preserving rather than as guidance for journeys.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence that accuracy was simply not the aim comes from a different kind of map. In the late thirteenth century, at about the same time as the largest world maps were being made, sailors and chart-makers in the Mediterranean were producing portolan charts: sea charts whose outlines of coasts and harbours are remarkably close to those of modern maps. Medieval Europeans, in other words, were entirely capable of accurate cartography when accuracy was what they needed. That the two traditions existed side by side suggests that the makers of mappae mundi were answering a different question altogether.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: By the fifteenth century, world maps increasingly borrowed coastlines from the sea charts and incorporated the coordinates of Ptolemy's newly translated Geography, and the older form gradually faded away. It is natural to describe this as progress, and in many respects it was. But it should not be seen as a simple story of improvement, because something was also lost. The mappae mundi placed their viewers in time as well as in space, showing not only where things were but where they stood in a larger history. Modern maps answer the question 'where?' with extraordinary precision; they rarely attempt to tell us what a place means.

topic: counter-mapping: indigenous and community-made maps used to claim land rights, and their unintended effects
title: Maps from Below
subtitle: Communities that were once left off official maps are now drawing their own, with consequences that are not always predictable

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of their history, maps have been instruments of those in power. Colonial administrations surveyed land in order to tax it, grant it to settlers or open it to mining, and the territories of forest dwellers, herders and shifting cultivators were frequently drawn as blank spaces or labelled 'unoccupied'. A people whose hunting grounds and burial sites did not appear on any official sheet had, in the eyes of the law, no claim to them. It is no exaggeration to say that cartography was one of the quieter tools of dispossession: it did not seize land by force, but it made the seizure appear orderly and legitimate. Lines drawn by surveyors who might never have met the inhabitants became, in time, the boundaries of concessions, reserves and private estates.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Since the 1990s, however, the same tool has increasingly been turned in the opposite direction. In what has come to be called counter-mapping, communities, often working with sympathetic researchers or advocacy groups, produce maps of their own territories. These range from sketches drawn on the ground with sticks and stones to detailed surveys made with satellite positioning receivers. They record what official maps leave out: fishing spots, sacred groves, fields left fallow for years at a time, and the routes along which herds are driven between seasonal pastures. Such maps have been presented in land negotiations and, in a number of countries, accepted by courts as evidence that a territory was in continuous use.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How much difference do they make? Yaretzi Arrevillaga, a geographer at the Instituto de Geografía Social in Oaxaca, followed forty indigenous communities in Central America over twelve years. Those that had produced their own maps were roughly three times as likely as the others to have obtained formal title to their land by the end of the period. Arrevillaga is nonetheless reluctant to credit the maps alone. Communities that undertook mapping, she notes, usually did so with the support of lawyers and non-governmental organisations, and these partners may have been the decisive factor. Her caution is well placed; a map is rarely the only thing that changes when outsiders arrive to help draw it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental critique comes from Sinethemba Mthiyane, a legal anthropologist who has studied land claims in southern Africa. Customary arrangements for using land, she observes, are often flexible: several groups may share grazing at different times of year, rights may depend on kinship rather than location, and the edges of a territory may be deliberately left vague. A map, by contrast, demands boundaries. Once a line has been drawn, it invites the question of who is on which side of it, and Mthiyane has documented cases in which mapping projects provoked conflict between neighbouring villages that had previously coexisted without difficulty. In her view, counter-mapping translates local relationships into the language of state property, even when it is used to resist the state.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This danger is real, but Mthiyane goes too far when she implies that communities would be better off not mapping at all. The choice is rarely between a map and no map. Governments, mining companies and conservation agencies will survey a territory in any case, and a community that declines to produce its own version simply leaves the field to others. The more useful question is how mapping can be carried out so that it records shared and seasonal uses rather than erasing them, for instance by showing overlapping zones instead of single lines. Several projects have experimented with exactly this, marking areas of shared use in a separate colour and attaching written agreements that explain how access changes through the year. Such maps are messier to look at, but they are considerably more honest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: New technology has added a further complication. Joonas Ylitörmänen, a specialist in geographic information systems, points out that low-cost drones, smartphones and free mapping software have made it far easier for communities to survey their own land. Yet digital maps can be copied and circulated in ways that hand-drawn ones cannot. Once the location of a sacred site or a valuable stand of timber has been stored on a server, it may become available to looters or logging firms. Some communities have responded by keeping certain layers of their maps confidential, revealing them only when a court requires it. Ylitörmänen argues that such data should be held on servers that the communities themselves control, rather than by the universities or charities that helped to collect it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of who, within a community, holds the pen. Researchers at the Mekong Land Tenure Observatory reviewed more than two hundred community maps and found that the places used mainly by women, such as water points, gathering areas and medicinal plant sites, were missing from most of them unless separate mapping sessions had been arranged for women. The most authoritative-looking map may therefore reflect the knowledge of a few senior men. If counter-mapping is to be judged fairly, its success should not be measured only by the number of land titles it secures. Its greatest value may lie in the discussions it forces communities to have about what their land is, who uses it and what they want it to become.
