topic: phantom islands: why non-existent islands appeared on charts and why they persisted for centuries
title: Islands That Never Were
subtitle: For centuries, charts of the oceans included land that did not exist. Explaining why tells us a good deal about how maps are made

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 2012 a research vessel crossing the Coral Sea arrived at the position of an island that appeared both on nautical charts and on a widely used digital map of the world. Instead of land, the scientists on board found open water more than a kilometre deep. The episode attracted brief international attention, but it was far from unique. For five centuries, charts of the world's oceans were dotted with so-called phantom islands, some of which were reported only once and others of which were copied faithfully for hundreds of years. It is tempting to treat their long survival as evidence of carelessness among chartmakers. That interpretation is unfair. The persistence of phantom islands reflects not negligence but the peculiar logic of how charts were compiled, checked and trusted.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Their origins are varied. Sailors frequently mistook fog banks, icebergs, floating masses of volcanic pumice or low clouds on the horizon for land, and at a time when nobody could measure longitude reliably, a genuine island sighted by two different ships might be recorded in two different places and so appear twice. Copyists introduced further errors, misreading coordinates or transferring an island from one chart to another without its accompanying note of doubt. A minority of phantoms were deliberate inventions, devised by captains who wished to impress sponsors or to claim the honour of a discovery. Which of these causes was the most common is impossible to establish, since most phantoms were reported without any description of how they were seen.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, once suspected, were such islands not simply removed? The maritime historian Clemente Aguirrebeña has argued that the answer lies in an asymmetry of risk. If a hydrographic office deleted an island that turned out to be real, a ship might run aground on it at night and lives would be lost. If, on the other hand, it retained an island that did not exist, the only cost was that cautious navigators would steer around an empty patch of sea. Faced with this choice, chartmakers rationally preferred to leave doubtful islands in place, often marked 'existence doubtful', until a thorough search had been made. Aguirrebeña's reasoning is sound, but it explains only part of the story, since many phantoms survived long after searches had failed to find them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the rest, the geographer Halvard Nesheim looks to the economics of chart production. Until the late nineteenth century, he points out, most commercial charts were compiled in workshops from earlier charts rather than from fresh surveys, because sending ships to check every reported island was prohibitively expensive. Errors were thus inherited in much the same way as features are passed between generations of a family. In one study, Nesheim traced a single non-existent island through more than forty charts produced by different publishers over a century and a half, all of them ultimately derived from one sighting by a whaling captain. To his mind, a chart was less a record of observations than a record of earlier charts.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from Makerita Fonohema, who studies the encounter between Pacific Islander and European navigators. She has shown that a number of islands later dismissed as phantoms first entered European charts through conversations with island navigators, whose knowledge of distant islands was extensive but was expressed in terms of sailing directions, star paths and days of travel rather than coordinates. When this knowledge was converted into European positions, islands were frequently misplaced, and a later failure to find them at the recorded location led to their being declared imaginary. In Fonohema's view, the label 'phantom' has sometimes concealed real geographical knowledge that was simply mistranslated. This is an important corrective, although it would be unwise to extend it to every phantom in the Pacific, many of which clearly originated in European misperceptions alone.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Physical explanations have also been proposed. Oceanographers working with the Tasman Seafloor Survey have compared the reported positions of several dozen phantom islands with modern measurements of the ocean floor. In a number of cases, they found shallow banks or seamounts close to the reported position, where waves breaking over a reef might easily have been taken for a shoreline. They have also suggested that a few phantoms may have been genuine volcanic islands that were later eroded by the sea or collapsed below the surface. The idea is plausible, but in most cases it can be neither confirmed nor ruled out, because the original reports are too vague to be tested against the geological record.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It might be assumed that satellite imagery and digital mapping have finally consigned such errors to history. The case with which this article began suggests otherwise. Digital maps are not drawn from nothing; they are assembled from older datasets, which in turn draw on charts whose sources may be centuries old, and an error can travel quietly from parchment to server. If anything, a mistake on a screen is more dangerous than one on paper, because the crisp, seamless appearance of a digital map encourages a degree of trust that its sources do not always deserve. The lesson of the phantom islands is that every map is a compilation with a history, and that knowing that history is part of knowing how far to rely on it.

topic: remote volunteer mapping for disaster response: speed, data quality, local participation and maintenance
title: Mapping from a Distance
subtitle: Volunteers around the world now trace maps of disaster zones within hours. How much do these maps really help?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a powerful earthquake struck a densely populated Caribbean city in 2010, relief agencies arrived to find that much of it had never been properly mapped. Within days, several hundred volunteers scattered across the globe, most of whom had never visited the country, began tracing roads, buildings and open spaces from newly released satellite images onto a freely editable online map. Rescue teams soon downloaded the results onto their handheld devices. The episode has since become a founding story for what is now called remote humanitarian mapping, and the model it established has been formalised into a permanent network, with training courses, coordinating organisations and regular 'mapathons' held in universities and offices. Within a decade, volunteers had traced tens of millions of buildings in regions affected by floods, cyclones and epidemics, and the approach is now routinely activated within hours of a major emergency.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method is straightforward. Volunteers working at home trace the outlines of features visible from above; more experienced validators then check their work for obvious mistakes; and, where possible, people on the ground add the information that cannot be seen from space, such as street names, the purpose of a building or whether a road is passable in the rainy season. The great advantage is speed. A city of a million people can be outlined in a matter of days, a task that might take a national mapping agency many months. In the first hours after a disaster, that difference can determine whether relief convoys are sent along roads that still exist.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Speed, however, is not the same as usefulness. Folasade Oyerinde, a geographer at the West African Institute for Spatial Data, compared volunteer maps of three cities with detailed surveys carried out on foot. The outlines of buildings were impressively complete, with roughly nine in ten structures captured. Yet the attributes that responders most need, such as whether a building was a school, a clinic or a home, or how many storeys it had, were missing in the great majority of cases. A map that shows ten thousand anonymous rectangles, Oyerinde observes, tells a relief worker where people might be, but not where they are likely to gather or where the injured might be taken. Her findings expose a genuine weakness of mapping from a distance: what can be seen from orbit is rarely what matters most on the ground.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Edvin Sveinbjörnsson, who studies digital participation at the Reykjavik Centre for Information Ethics, raises a different objection. Remote mapping, he argues, concentrates the power to describe a place in the hands of people who live far from it. Categories chosen by distant volunteers, for instance the decision to label an entire district an informal settlement, can shape how aid is distributed and how residents are later treated by authorities. Sveinbjörnsson contends that the inhabitants of vulnerable areas should be trained and paid to map their own neighbourhoods, rather than serving merely as occasional sources of local detail for others.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third difficulty concerns what happens after the emergency has passed. Priscila Lustosa, a sociologist who has surveyed several thousand volunteers, found that participation rises steeply in the days following a well-publicised disaster and then collapses almost as quickly. Few volunteers return to update the maps they helped to create, and as cities grow and change, the data steadily become out of date. Lustosa proposes a shift towards preparedness mapping, in which vulnerable regions are mapped thoroughly and kept current before any disaster occurs, so that responders are not forced to rely on hurried work. Her proposal is a sensible one, even if it lacks the emotional appeal that draws volunteers to a crisis unfolding on the news.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Relief agencies themselves have been more ambivalent than the enthusiastic accounts of the 2010 response suggest. A survey of field staff conducted by the Geneva Humanitarian Data Forum found that many of them either did not know that volunteer maps of their area existed or did not trust them, preferring to wait for data produced by their own organisations. Some respondents argued that rapid information of uncertain quality could be worse than none, since it might send teams in the wrong direction. This position is understandable, but it underestimates the value of imperfect information in the early stages of a response. A road map with occasional errors remains far more useful than a blank screen when lorries are waiting to leave.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that remote mapping should be abandoned. It has repeatedly provided a basic picture of places that official cartography had neglected, and it has introduced many thousands of people to the practice of mapping. In several countries, the open data produced in emergencies have later been adopted by local governments for planning water supplies, vaccination campaigns and school building programmes. But the popular image of distant volunteers rescuing a stricken city from their laptops is appealing and misleading in equal measure. Satellite tracing can supply the skeleton of a map; only people who know a place can supply its substance. The most promising projects are those that treat remote volunteers as a support for local mappers rather than a substitute for them.

topic: mapping the global ocean floor: sonar versus satellite methods, the goal of complete coverage, priorities and the risks of detailed seabed data
title: The Unseen Seventy Per Cent
subtitle: An international effort aims to map the entire ocean floor within a few years. Whether it should, and how, is less straightforward than it sounds

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is often said that we possess better maps of the surface of Mars than of the floor of our own oceans. The statement is true in a narrow sense, but it gives a misleading impression of negligence. Mars has no ocean to hide its surface, and orbiting spacecraft can photograph or scan it directly. Seawater, by contrast, absorbs light and radar within a short distance, so the seabed cannot be seen from above at all. Every detailed measurement of its shape must be made from the water itself, usually by a vessel moving slowly across the surface, and that difference, rather than any lack of curiosity, explains why so much of the ocean floor remains poorly known.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two very different methods are used. The first relies on satellites, which measure the height of the sea surface with remarkable precision. Because a large seamount exerts a slightly stronger gravitational pull than the surrounding seabed, water piles up above it, producing a bulge of a metre or two on the sea surface; deep trenches produce corresponding dips. From these irregularities, scientists can infer the broad shape of the ocean floor across the entire globe. The resolution, however, is coarse: features smaller than several kilometres across are effectively invisible, and a seamount the size of a small mountain range may be missed entirely. Fine detail requires the second method, in which ships fitted with multibeam sonar send fans of sound pulses to the seabed and time their echoes. Only around a quarter of the ocean floor has so far been mapped in this way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In 2017, an international initiative set itself the goal of mapping the entire ocean floor at high resolution by 2030. The ambition has energised governments, research institutes and private companies, and the proportion of the seabed mapped in detail has risen considerably since its launch. It is nevertheless unlikely that the target will be met; by most estimates, completing the task with conventional survey ships would require several hundred years of vessel time. Yet it would be wrong to dismiss the goal as worthless on these grounds. Deadlines of this kind serve less as predictions than as rallying points, and without one the work would almost certainly proceed far more slowly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Given that resources are limited, where should surveying begin? Henrike Haverkorn, a hydrographer with long experience of national charting programmes, argues that the effort should be concentrated where detailed knowledge is most immediately useful: busy shipping lanes, coastal waters vulnerable to storm surges, and the routes of planned undersea cables. A uniform push to cover remote abyssal plains, she contends, spends scarce ship time on areas that few people will ever need to know in detail. Her approach has an obvious practical appeal, but it rests on the assumption that we already know which parts of the seabed matter. The marine geologist Chidera Obiechina-Faure challenges precisely this assumption. Accurate maps of the deep seabed, she points out, are essential for modelling how tsunamis travel, how heat and nutrients circulate in the deep ocean and where unusual ecosystems are likely to be found. Priorities chosen according to present needs, in her view, risk leaving future scientific questions without the data needed to answer them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards a complete map as an unqualified good. Valtteri Kuusikallio, who researches ocean governance, observes that detailed bathymetry is of great value to companies hoping to mine metal-rich nodules and crusts from the deep seabed, and to navies whose submarines depend on knowing the terrain below them. Partly for these reasons, some coastal states refuse to release survey data collected within their territorial waters. Kuusikallio's concern about mining is justified: a precise map can make an environmentally damaging industry considerably cheaper to establish. But secrecy is a poor remedy. Mining companies are well able to commission their own surveys, and the main effect of withholding data is to deprive scientists and smaller nations of information that wealthy interests can obtain anyway.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Technology may ease some of these tensions by lowering costs. Engineers at the Kerguelen Autonomous Systems Laboratory have been testing uncrewed surface vessels that can survey continuously for weeks, guided remotely from shore, at a fraction of the cost of a research ship with a full crew. Another approach gathers depth readings from the echo sounders already carried by fishing boats, cargo ships and private yachts, which, once corrected and combined, can fill gaps in the coastal record. The quality of such contributions varies widely, and they are concentrated along coasts and busy routes. Data from private vessels will therefore remain a supplement rather than a replacement for dedicated surveys of the open ocean, where few ordinary ships ever travel.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is easy to forget how recently the deep ocean floor was regarded as a featureless plain. Each improvement in mapping has overturned that assumption, revealing ridges, canyons and many thousands of seamounts that no one suspected. The value of a complete map, therefore, lies not only in the questions it can answer now but in the questions it will make it possible to ask. That is the strongest argument for persisting with the goal of full coverage, even if the deadline slips and the methods change.

topic: smartphone navigation apps and their effect on spatial learning and the mental maps people form of places
title: Following the Blue Dot
subtitle: Navigation apps have made getting lost almost impossible. Are they also making it harder to know where we are?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Within little more than a decade, the smartphone map has become the default way in which millions of people find their way around. A pulsing dot marks the user's position, a coloured line shows the route, and a calm voice announces each turn in advance. The convenience is undeniable, and so, according to a steady stream of newspaper articles, is the cost: we are told that satellite navigation is 'shrinking our brains' and producing a generation unable to read a map. Such headlines considerably exaggerate what the research has shown. Nevertheless, the underlying question of whether handing navigation over to a device changes how we learn about places is a legitimate one, and it deserves a more careful answer than either alarm or dismissal.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Psychologists distinguish between two broad ways of knowing an environment. Route knowledge consists of a sequence of actions linked to particular points, such as turning left at the bakery and continuing to the bridge. Survey knowledge, by contrast, resembles a map held in the mind: it represents the relative positions of places, so that a person can work out a shortcut or point towards a destination that is out of sight. Survey knowledge is slower to acquire and appears to depend heavily on the hippocampus, a brain structure also involved in forming memories of events. Studies of professional drivers who must memorise the layout of an entire city have found that this region can change in response to intensive navigational practice.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Margarethe Lindebrekke, a cognitive psychologist at the Bergen Laboratory for Spatial Behaviour, asked volunteers to walk through an unfamiliar district, some guided by a turn-by-turn app and others by a printed map. The app users reached their destinations more quickly and made fewer wrong turns. Afterwards, however, they drew far less accurate sketch maps of the area and, when asked to return to the starting point without help, took considerably longer than those who had used paper. Lindebrekke attributes the difference largely to attention. Eye-tracking recordings showed that app users spent much of the walk looking at their screens, glancing at their surroundings only when prompted to turn, and therefore noticed fewer of the landmarks from which a mental map is built.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A short experiment cannot show whether such effects accumulate over time. To investigate this, Ravindra Kulasekera of the Colombo Institute of Cognitive Ageing followed more than nine hundred adults for three years, recording how often they used navigation apps and testing their spatial memory annually. Heavier users showed a steeper decline in their scores. Critics objected that people with a poor sense of direction might simply rely more on apps, so that weak navigation skills cause app use rather than the reverse. Kulasekera, however, measured each participant's ability at the outset, and the association remained after this was taken into account. The study is carefully designed, but the effect it reports is small, amounting to a few percentage points over three years, and it hardly justifies the alarm with which it was greeted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers question whether any of this matters. Soledad Iparraguirre, a philosopher of technology, argues that delegating navigation to a device is no different in principle from relying on a calculator for arithmetic or on writing instead of memorising long texts. Skills that are no longer needed, she suggests, can fade without real loss, and the only practical risk arises when the battery runs out. This argument is persuasive for many tasks, but navigation is not quite like arithmetic. Knowing how places fit together underlies our ability to explore, to feel at home in a neighbourhood and, perhaps, to remember where events in our lives took place. If the brain systems that support navigation also support memory more generally, then their neglect might carry costs that extend well beyond the occasional wrong turn, although this possibility remains largely untested.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Encouragingly, the problem may lie less in navigation technology itself than in the way it has been designed. Interaction designers at the Aalborg Urban Cognition Studio have built experimental apps that deliberately keep the user engaged with the surroundings. Instructions refer to prominent landmarks rather than distances, an overview of the whole area is displayed with north always at the top, and every so often users are asked to predict the next turn before it is revealed. In trials, people using these versions formed noticeably better mental maps of a district, while their journeys took only slightly longer than with a conventional app.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The sensible conclusion, then, is neither to abandon navigation apps nor to accept them uncritically. The losses identified so far are real but modest, and they are not an unavoidable consequence of the technology; they follow from design choices that favour speed and ease over understanding. Users can help themselves by occasionally navigating without assistance, particularly in places they visit often. Developers, for their part, could offer modes that teach as well as guide. A device that tells us where to turn need not prevent us from knowing where we are.

topic: the local guides, porters, interpreters and surveyors behind nineteenth-century exploration, and the problem of recovering their contribution from the archives
title: The Hidden Hands of Exploration
subtitle: Nineteenth-century expeditions are remembered through the names of a few leaders. Historians are now asking who else was there, and what they contributed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The popular image of nineteenth-century exploration is of a solitary figure, usually European, pushing into unknown territory with little more than courage and a compass. Statues, biographies and the medals of geographical societies have all reinforced this picture. Yet almost no major expedition of the period was carried out by a handful of travellers. Most depended on dozens, sometimes hundreds, of local people: guides who knew the paths and water sources, porters who carried supplies, interpreters who negotiated passage through territories governed by others, and informants whose descriptions of lands further on were often the only basis for the maps that were later published. The lone-hero narrative is not merely incomplete. It misrepresents the way in which geographical knowledge was actually produced, presenting as individual discovery what was in reality a collective, and frequently unequal, enterprise.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of these contributors were highly skilled specialists in their own right. In the Himalaya, colonial survey departments recruited men from border communities and trained them to measure distances and directions while travelling in disguise through regions closed to Europeans. They counted their steps on prayer beads modified to have exactly one hundred beads instead of the usual number, and concealed their notes inside prayer wheels. The routes they recorded filled large blank areas on the official maps of the day, yet for decades their identities were concealed behind code names, partly for their own protection and partly because their achievements sat uncomfortably with assumptions about who was capable of scientific work.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How did so many contributors vanish from the record? The historian Adaobi Nwokoye-Rossi has compared the published narratives of more than thirty expeditions with the unpublished material that survives from them, including field diaries, letters and, most revealingly, the account books in which payments were recorded. The ledgers name hundreds of people who are absent from the printed books, and the diaries frequently acknowledge the advice of guides in terms that the published versions omit or attribute to the leader himself. Nwokoye-Rossi concludes that the disappearance occurred mainly at the stage of publication, as editors and publishers shaped raw material into the heroic narratives that the reading public expected and paid for.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tobias Wennerholm, a historical geographer, goes further. Local guides, he argues, were not simply helpers who executed a leader's plans; they actively shaped what expeditions saw. Guides chose routes that passed through villages with which they had trading or family ties, avoided the territories of rival groups and, on occasion, deliberately exaggerated the dangers of a particular direction to prevent outsiders reaching valuable resources. The resulting maps, in Wennerholm's view, recorded local political geography as much as physical terrain. This is a persuasive argument, and it restores a genuine agency to people previously treated as anonymous labour. It does, however, risk the opposite error of portraying every guide as an all-knowing insider. Many guides were themselves strangers to the regions through which they led expeditions, hired at the coast and relying, like their employers, on information gathered along the way.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more cautious note is struck by Nyarai Chigumba, who works on the archives of exploration in southern and eastern Africa. Almost all the surviving sources, she points out, were written by Europeans, so that the voices of guides and porters reach us only after being filtered through the perceptions, prejudices and linguistic limitations of their employers. Names were often misspelt or replaced by nicknames, making it difficult to trace individuals from one document to another. In Chigumba's assessment, careful archival work can establish that local people were present and what they did, but only rarely what they themselves thought of the enterprise. She has therefore begun recording oral histories in communities descended from expedition members. Such accounts are valuable, though they should be treated with caution, since memories transmitted across five or six generations inevitably change in the retelling.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Despite these obstacles, the scale of the hidden workforce is gradually becoming visible. The Coimbra Expedition Records Project has spent a decade indexing the names of non-European expedition members found in archives across three continents, and its database now contains more than four thousand individuals. One of its more surprising findings is that a substantial minority appear in the records of several expeditions, sometimes spanning twenty or thirty years. These were, in effect, professional travellers, whose accumulated experience of routes, languages and diplomacy made them sought after by successive expedition leaders, and who may, in some cases, have known more about the interior than any European of their time.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What follows from this research? It would be a mistake simply to replace one set of heroes with another, carving new names onto old monuments while leaving the underlying story unchanged. The more important lesson is that exploration was a cooperative undertaking, carried out by people with very different motives, rewards and degrees of freedom. Here honesty is essential. Not every participant was a willing one: some porters were forced into service, and others worked under conditions that would now be regarded as coercive. Any account of exploration that celebrates collaboration without acknowledging this would be as misleading, in its own way, as the lone-hero legend it seeks to replace.

topic: trap streets and paper towns: deliberate errors inserted into maps to detect copying, their legal value, ethics and decline in the digital age
title: Deliberate Mistakes
subtitle: For decades, mapmakers hid invented streets and towns in their work to catch copiers. Was the practice ever justified?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1930s, two employees of a small road-map company in the north-eastern United States invented a hamlet. They gave it a name formed from their own initials, placed it at a remote crossroads, and waited. Some years later the name turned up on a map published by a much larger rival, and the company prepared to accuse its competitor of copying. The rival, however, had a surprising defence: a general store had since been built at the crossroads and had adopted the name it found on the map, so that the imaginary hamlet had, in a modest way, become real. The story is often told as a curiosity, but it captures something important about maps. Because people trust them, what appears on a map has a way of shaping what exists on the ground.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The hamlet was an example of what cartographers call a paper town; its urban equivalent, a short invented street or cul-de-sac, is known as a trap street. Both were devices for detecting plagiarism, and the reason they were needed is straightforward. Producing an accurate map from fresh surveys is slow and expensive, whereas copying one that already exists is quick and cheap. Proving that copying has occurred, however, is surprisingly difficult, because two accurate maps of the same town will inevitably look very similar. A deliberate error solves this problem. If a feature that exists nowhere except on your own map appears on someone else's, the most plausible explanation is that they have copied it. Similar tactics have been used by the compilers of dictionaries, which have occasionally included invented words, and of telephone and trade directories, which have included fictitious entries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whether such traps actually win cases is another matter. Ottilie Barkworth, who teaches intellectual property law, notes that courts in several countries have held that facts cannot be owned: a publisher may protect the way a map is designed and presented, but not the location of a road. An invented street creates an awkward puzzle, since it is presented to readers as a fact, and some judges have concluded that copying it is evidence of copying in general but does not in itself infringe anything that the law protects. Barkworth points out, however, that this weakness matters less than it might appear, because most disputes over copied maps are settled through negotiation without a court ruling, and in negotiation the discovery of a trap street is a powerful bargaining tool.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Teodora Pârvulescu, a philosopher who writes on the ethics of information, objects to the practice on different grounds. A map, she argues, carries an implicit promise that what it shows is, to the best of the publisher's knowledge, true. A deliberate error breaks that promise, and it does so in a way that may have consequences for users: a delivery driver may waste time searching for a street that does not exist, or an ambulance may be directed to a non-existent address. Pârvulescu stops short of calling for a legal ban, but urges publishers to abandon the practice voluntarily. The practical harm, it should be said, has generally been slight, because traps were usually placed in obscure locations where few people would have reason to look. The more serious issue is one of principle: a publisher that knowingly includes falsehoods has weakened its claim to be trusted on everything else.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In the digital era, the trap street appears to be in decline. Bashir Qaderi, a data engineer who has worked for several commercial mapping firms, explains that companies now protect their datasets in subtler ways, for example by introducing tiny, systematic shifts in the coordinates of many features, invisible to users but statistically detectable if the data are copied wholesale. At the same time, the growth of openly licensed maps, which anyone may copy legally provided the source is acknowledged, has reduced the incentive to steal. Qaderi regards the trap street as effectively obsolete. This is broadly right, although it overlooks the fact that copying can still be exposed without any deliberate traps at all. Every map contains honest mistakes, and when an unusual error appears in two supposedly independent maps, it betrays copying just as clearly as an invented street.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How widespread was the practice? Researchers at the Ghent Centre for Information Law surveyed sixty map publishers in Europe and North America. Around a third acknowledged that they had used deliberate errors at some point in their history, although the great majority of these said that they no longer did so. Several respondents described the technique as a relic of a period when maps were expensive physical products sold in competitive markets. Others admitted that they had never once used a trap to take legal action, and suspected that the main effect had been to deter potential copiers who believed such traps might exist.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The trap street, then, belongs largely to a particular moment in the history of cartography, when maps were scarce, proprietary and costly to produce. Its legitimacy was always questionable, and its legal value turned out to be more limited than its inventors hoped. Yet the debate it provoked raises a question that remains relevant. People consult maps in the assumption that they are honest, and that assumption is the most valuable thing a mapmaker possesses. Protecting a map from copiers is a reasonable commercial aim, but it is not worth pursuing at the expense of the trust on which every map ultimately depends.

topic: persuasive cartography: how colour, classification and design choices in maps shape readers' conclusions, from wartime propaganda to election and data maps
title: Maps That Argue
subtitle: A map looks like a neutral picture of the world, but every map makes a case. The question is whether its readers can tell

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the night of a national election, television channels and news websites display a familiar image: a map of the country, each district coloured according to the party that won it. In many countries the result is striking, because sparsely populated rural districts cover most of the territory and therefore dominate the picture, while densely populated cities appear as small specks. A party that has won a clear majority of votes can look as though it has been overwhelmingly rejected. Nobody involved need have intended to mislead; the map simply shows land, and land does not vote. The example illustrates a point that is easy to forget. Maps do not merely display information. Through the choices built into them, they also suggest how that information should be understood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In some periods, this persuasive power has been exploited quite openly. During the first half of the twentieth century, governments and political movements produced maps designed to alarm or inspire: a nation shown in pale, vulnerable colours, encircled by dark and menacing neighbours; thick arrows sweeping across borders to suggest an imminent invasion; territories claimed by one state shaded as though they already belonged to it. Such maps were crude, but they made little pretence of objectivity. Their viewers could at least recognise them as propaganda, in the same way that they recognised a political poster or a slogan for what it was.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For a number of scholars, however, the distinction between propaganda maps and ordinary ones is less clear than it seems. Leandro Bramão, a geographer associated with the school known as critical cartography, argues that every map is persuasive. Each one, he points out, results from a series of decisions about what to include, what to leave out, how to group the data and which symbols and colours to use, and each decision reflects the purposes and assumptions of whoever made it. A neutral map, in his view, is a contradiction in terms. This is true in a limited sense, but taken to its conclusion it obscures a distinction that matters a great deal in practice: the difference between maps that are open about the choices they make and maps that conceal those choices in order to deceive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recent experimental work suggests that even well-intentioned maps can steer readers far more than either their makers or their readers realise. The cognitive scientist Ingvild Sæbø presented several hundred participants with maps showing the rate of a disease across the regions of an imaginary country. All the maps were based on exactly the same figures; the only difference was where the boundaries between colour categories had been set. When the cut-off points were placed one way, most participants concluded that the disease was concentrated in the north; when they were placed another way, most concluded that it was evenly spread. Sæbø also found that regions shaded red were judged to be in greater danger than regions with identical figures shaded in other colours, and that fewer than one participant in five consulted the legend before drawing a conclusion. These results are troubling, because the choices involved are of a kind that mapmakers make routinely and seldom explain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Can better designs correct such distortions? Rashida Elmahdi, who studies data visualisation at the Institute for Visual Statistics in Rabat, has tested alternatives to conventional election and population maps. Among the most promising are cartograms, in which each region is resized in proportion to its population, so that a crowded city expands while an empty desert shrinks. Cartograms present the distribution of people far more fairly than ordinary maps. Elmahdi's tests show, however, that readers find them disorienting: the familiar outlines of countries are distorted beyond recognition, and many participants struggled to locate even their own region. The difficulty is not a reason to abandon cartograms, but it does confirm that each solution introduces new costs, and that no design can remove the need for judgement on the part of its readers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical guidance has followed. A committee of the Nordic Data Journalism Network has drawn up standards for maps published in the news media, recommending that every map include a clear legend, that the method used to divide data into categories be stated, and that the underlying figures be made available to readers who wish to check them. Such guidelines are welcome and overdue. Yet it would be naive to suppose that rules alone could prevent misleading maps. The range of possible design choices is so large that no set of standards can anticipate them all, and the most effective safeguard remains a reading public that knows what questions to ask.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What makes maps unusually persuasive is the authority they appear to possess. A chart of figures invites scrutiny; a map, with its coordinates and careful shading, looks like a direct picture of reality and so tends to be accepted without question. The danger lies not in persuasion as such, which is an inevitable and often legitimate part of communication, but in persuasion presented as neutral description. Readers would do well to approach a map as they would approach any other argument, asking who made it, for what purpose, and what it might have been designed to leave out.

topic: the uneven adoption of surgical anaesthesia after 1846: selective use, fear of sudden death, the myth of religious opposition and its effect on surgical mortality
title: The Slow Conquest of Pain
subtitle: The arrival of surgical anaesthesia is usually told as a story of instant triumph, but historians now describe a hesitant and uneven acceptance

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of its history, surgery was an art of speed. Without any reliable means of dulling sensation, patients faced the knife fully conscious, held down by assistants, and the most admired operators were those who could complete an amputation in less than a minute. Unsurprisingly, many people who needed an operation refused it, preferring to live with a tumour or a crushed limb rather than endure the alternative. The situation appeared to change almost overnight in October 1846, when a dentist in Boston demonstrated publicly that a patient who had inhaled ether vapour could undergo surgery without apparent distress. Within months, ether was in use in London, Paris and Edinburgh. Later that year chloroform was introduced as an alternative; it acted more quickly and was easier to carry, but it was also considerably more likely to stop the heart.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The conventional account presents what followed as a straightforward victory: a grateful profession seized upon the discovery, and the age of agony came to an end. Faustyna Grzelczyk, a historian at the Centre for Medical Humanities in Kraków, regards this narrative as seriously incomplete. Having examined the operating registers of eleven European and American hospitals, she found that anaesthesia was used in fewer than half of major operations at most of them for at least a decade after 1846. Its use, moreover, was strikingly selective. Surgeons frequently withheld it from patients whom they believed to be less sensitive to pain, a category that, according to the assumptions of the period, included manual labourers, the elderly and members of certain ethnic groups. This is perhaps the most uncomfortable finding of recent scholarship, because it shows that relief from suffering was distributed according to prejudice rather than need.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some resistance had more respectable origins. A number of surgeons held that pain served a physiological purpose, stimulating the body and helping the patient to survive the shock of the operation; to remove it, they argued, was to remove a natural defence. The most powerful objection, however, was the risk of sudden death. In 1848 a fifteen-year-old girl in the north of England died within minutes of inhaling chloroform before a minor operation on her toe, and similar cases followed. Such deaths were rare in relation to the number of anaesthetics given, but each was reported in detail in the medical press, and their unpredictability made them far more alarming than the familiar dangers of surgery itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Popular histories often add a further obstacle: the claim that churchmen condemned the relief of pain in childbirth as a defiance of scripture. Kwabena Akrofi of the Institute for the History of Science in Accra has searched sermons, pamphlets and religious periodicals from the period and found remarkably little evidence of such opposition. In his view, the religious controversy was largely invented, or at least greatly exaggerated, by advocates of anaesthesia, who found it convenient to portray their opponents as superstitious. Akrofi also questions the significance usually given to the use of chloroform by Queen Victoria during the birth of her eighth child in 1853. While it undoubtedly made the practice fashionable among wealthy families who paid for private care, he finds no sign that it altered routine practice in the hospitals where the poor were treated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more provocative argument concerns the effect of anaesthesia on survival. The surgeon and historian Ansel Quarrington contends that, in its first two decades, anaesthesia did nothing to lower surgical mortality and may even have raised it. Freed from the need for haste, surgeons began to operate more slowly and to attempt longer and more ambitious procedures, including operations inside the abdomen that had previously been unthinkable. Wounds therefore remained open for longer, and in an era before the causes of infection were understood, the consequences were frequently fatal. Hospital figures from the 1850s and early 1860s, Quarrington notes, show death rates after amputation that were unchanged or higher than before. Only after antiseptic methods spread from the late 1860s did the potential of anaesthesia begin to be realised. His statistics are difficult to dispute, but his conclusion that anaesthesia represented a step backwards is harder to accept. Survival was never the only measure of its value: the removal of terror allowed patients to seek treatment earlier, when their conditions were more curable, and spared countless people an experience that many had considered worse than death.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What is beyond question is that the skill involved in giving anaesthesia was long underestimated. In the early years it was commonly administered by whoever happened to be available, often a junior student or even a hospital porter, using a handkerchief or sponge soaked in the liquid and with the dose judged largely by guesswork. Purpose-built inhalers that regulated the concentration of vapour were designed within a few years, yet they were slow to replace the handkerchief, and doctors who specialised in anaesthesia enjoyed little professional standing. In Britain, a society devoted to the subject was not founded until 1893, almost half a century after the Boston demonstration. It seems likely that this neglect cost many lives which careful administration might have saved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of anaesthesia is therefore less a tale of instant conquest than one of hesitant, uneven and sometimes unjust adoption. It demonstrates that even an innovation whose benefits seem self-evident is not accepted on the strength of evidence alone; its reception is filtered through beliefs about pain, assumptions about social class and the professional interests of those who control it. That lesson deserves a place in the training of doctors today, who are no less likely than their predecessors to assume that a good idea will simply speak for itself.

topic: the invention of the stethoscope and how listening to the body changed diagnosis, doctor-patient relations and medical authority
title: Listening Through a Tube
subtitle: Two centuries after its invention, the stethoscope still raises questions about what doctors should trust: the patient's words or the patient's body

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1816 a young physician in Paris was called to examine a woman thought to be suffering from heart disease. The accepted method of the time was to press an ear directly against the patient's chest, but he was reluctant to do so, partly out of modesty and partly because her build made the sounds hard to hear. Instead, he rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, placed one end on her chest and the other at his ear, and was surprised to find that the heartbeat came through more clearly than ever before. Within three years he had replaced the paper with a wooden cylinder and published a long treatise describing the sounds made by the heart and the lungs in health and disease. Early instruments were designed for a single ear; versions with flexible rubber tubing, allowing the doctor to listen with both ears, did not become common until the 1850s.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Before the stethoscope, diagnosis rested heavily on conversation. A physician would question the patient at length about symptoms, habits and history, and supplement the answers with a limited range of observations: the pulse, the appearance of the tongue, the colour of the urine. According to Marc Bellefontaine, a historian at the Montreal Institute for the History of Medicine, the new instrument began a fundamental change in this relationship. For the first time, a doctor could detect disease that the patient could neither feel nor describe, and the body itself, rather than the patient's story, became the principal source of medical truth. In Bellefontaine's account, the patient's own words were steadily pushed into a secondary position, and were increasingly treated with suspicion.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This is an important insight, but it is sometimes stretched into the claim that the stethoscope dehumanised medicine, and that claim seems overstated. Physicians had been sceptical of what their patients told them long before 1816; the stethoscope merely gave them an alternative. Moreover, many patients appear to have welcomed a doctor who could identify a condition that they themselves were unable to put into words. Even the distance created by the tube, so often interpreted as a symbol of detachment, originated in a wish to spare the patient embarrassment. Nor is there much evidence that skilled users of the instrument stopped asking questions; the most celebrated listeners of the period were frequently also the most patient interviewers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why the instrument succeeded where and when it did is a separate question. Leila Sadeqi, a historian of science at the Rhineland Institute for Clinical History, argues that the stethoscope could only have been developed in the great Paris hospitals of the early nineteenth century. These institutions held hundreds of patients, and post-mortem examinations were carried out routinely, so that a doctor could compare the sounds he had heard in a living chest with the damage he later found in the dead body. Without this constant matching of sound to lesion, Sadeqi points out, the noises transmitted by the tube would have meant very little. Her argument helps to explain why the device was adopted more slowly in Britain, where hospital autopsies were less common, and why some British physicians dismissed it as a passing French fashion.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The stethoscope also acquired meanings that had little to do with diagnosis. Neema Mwakyusa of the East African Centre for the History of Health has studied medical practice in East Africa in the early twentieth century and found that the instrument was often carried by doctors working in small clinics that had neither the drugs nor the equipment to treat what it revealed. In such settings, she argues, its main function was to display the authority of the person wearing it. It is tempting to regard this as a distortion of the instrument's real purpose, but the symbolic role should not be dismissed as trivial. A patient who feels that he or she has been properly examined is more likely to trust the doctor and to follow the advice given, and the stethoscope, hung around the neck, remains the most recognisable sign that such an examination has taken place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Today the instrument faces a challenge from technology. Ultrasound scanners small enough to fit in a pocket can now produce images of the beating heart at the bedside, and several studies have shown that trainee doctors are poor at identifying heart murmurs by ear. Some medical educators have therefore proposed that teaching stethoscope skills should be abandoned altogether. This proposal appears premature. Handheld scanners remain far more expensive than a stethoscope, require more training to interpret, and depend on batteries and software updates, all of which limit their usefulness in the clinics of low-income countries, where most of the world's patients are seen. A more sensible response to poor listening skills would surely be better teaching rather than no teaching at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the stethoscope will last for ever, and it may eventually become a largely ceremonial object. Its history, however, offers a lesson that extends beyond medicine. An instrument does not create knowledge by itself; it depends on institutions that give its signals meaning, and on the trust of those who are examined with it. Any technology intended to replace the stethoscope will need to earn both.

topic: medieval hospitals: religious houses or places of healing? Layout, eastern medical hospitals, skeletal evidence, spending priorities and selective admission
title: Beds Before the Altar
subtitle: Were medieval hospitals places of healing, of prayer, or of something else entirely?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the twelfth and the fifteenth centuries, several thousand hospitals were founded across Europe. Most were small, housing perhaps a dozen inmates, and almost all were established by religious orders, bishops or wealthy individuals seeking to secure the welfare of their souls. Two images of these institutions dominate popular understanding. In one, they are grim refuges where the destitute went to die, untouched by anything resembling medicine; in the other, they are the direct ancestors of the modern hospital, early experiments in organised clinical care. Neither picture survives close examination, and the more interesting question is why historians have found it so difficult to agree on what these places were actually for.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For Edith Marchbanks of the Northumbria Centre for Medieval Studies, the answer is clear: the medieval hospital was first and foremost a religious house. She draws attention to the architecture of surviving buildings, in which the beds were typically arranged along an open hall that led directly to a chapel, so that every inmate could see the altar and hear the daily services. Inmates were expected to attend prayers if they were able, and many foundation charters required them to pray for the souls of the founder and his family. In Marchbanks's view, applying the modern word 'hospital' to these institutions at all invites misunderstanding, since their central concern was the salvation of the soul rather than the cure of the body.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That interpretation, however, rests almost entirely on evidence from western Europe. Nino Dzhaparidze, a historian at the Caucasus Institute for Byzantine Studies, has shown that in the Byzantine Empire and the Islamic world the situation was quite different. A twelfth-century hospital in Constantinople, for instance, had separate wards for different kinds of illness, salaried physicians who worked in rotation, and a set of written rules specifying the duties of each member of staff. Large hospitals in Cairo and Damascus were similarly organised and also served as places where medicine was taught. Dzhaparidze argues that historians have taken conclusions drawn from English and French examples and treated them as if they described medieval hospitals in general. Her work is a valuable corrective, and it suggests that the religious character of western hospitals reflected local circumstances rather than any inevitable feature of the age.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even in the west, the absence of physicians does not mean the absence of care. The archaeologist Inés Valdecasas has analysed skeletons from cemeteries attached to hospitals in Spain and England. A high proportion show signs of long-term conditions such as tuberculosis of the bone, and many display fractures that had healed well, which would have required the injured person to be fed and sheltered for weeks while the bones mended. Valdecasas concludes that many inmates lived in hospitals for months or even years, and that the nursing they received, although basic, was sustained and effective in keeping them alive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The economic historian Ryo Nakagawara has approached the question through hospital accounts. These show that spending on bread, meat, ale, fuel and clean linen far exceeded anything spent on physicians or medicines. It would be easy to read this as evidence of medical neglect, but Nakagawara argues the opposite: given the limited effectiveness of medieval drugs, warmth, rest and a reliable diet were probably the most beneficial treatments available, and hospital administrators allocated their money accordingly. This is a persuasive argument, although it should not be taken to imply that every inmate was well fed. Accounts record what was purchased, not who consumed it, and there is evidence that some masters diverted funds for their own use. By the later Middle Ages, moreover, many hospitals had begun selling places to comfortable older people, known as corrodians, who paid a lump sum in return for board and lodging for life, so that a charitable institution gradually came to resemble a kind of retirement home.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone in need was welcome. Sigrun Inderhaug of the Western Fjords Centre for Social History has examined the admission rules recorded in foundation documents and found that a large number explicitly excluded pregnant women, the insane and people suffering from infectious diseases, while lepers were usually sent to separate institutions altogether. Fear of contagion played some part, she accepts, but the main reason was that such people threatened the orderly, prayerful routine on which a hospital's reputation with its benefactors depended. In Inderhaug's interpretation, hospitals helped to define who counted as the deserving poor, and were therefore instruments of social order as much as of charity.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is an institution that was neither a waiting room for death nor an early version of the modern hospital. It is a mistake to judge it by the standards of an era in which cure is expected; medieval hospitals were designed to provide shelter, food, comfort and spiritual reassurance, and by those measures many of them appear to have succeeded. There may even be something to learn from them. In an age in which a growing proportion of hospital patients are elderly people with conditions that cannot be cured, the medieval emphasis on comfort and companionship looks less like a failure of ambition than a recognition of what care can realistically achieve.

topic: maritime quarantine and lazarettos against plague in the Mediterranean, 1377-1750: origins of the forty-day rule, effectiveness, commercial politics and institutional legacy
title: Forty Days on the Island
subtitle: Quarantine was invented to keep plague out of Mediterranean ports. Whether it actually did so is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the Black Death swept across Europe in the late 1340s, it killed perhaps a third of the continent's population, and for the following three and a half centuries plague returned in recurring waves. Medical theory offered little help. Most physicians attributed the disease to corrupted air, and the remedies they recommended, from burning fragrant woods to fleeing the city, did little to halt its spread. In 1377 the Adriatic port of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, issued a decree that is often described as the first quarantine regulation: travellers arriving from places where plague was present had to spend thirty days on a nearby island before they were allowed into the city. Isolating the sick was nothing new; lepers had been kept apart for centuries. What was novel was the isolation of people who showed no symptoms at all, simply because of where they had come from. Within a few decades the period had been extended to forty days, quaranta giorni in Italian, which gave the practice its name.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why forty? It has occasionally been suggested that the figure reflected careful observation of how long the disease took to appear in a person who had been exposed. This seems improbable. The incubation period of plague is in fact a matter of days, not weeks, and no one in the fourteenth century was in a position to measure it. Forty was, however, a number heavy with meaning: it recalled the forty days of Lent, the forty days Christ spent in the wilderness, and an ancient medical doctrine holding that acute illnesses reached their crisis within forty days. The figure was almost certainly chosen for its symbolic and traditional authority, which may also explain why people were prepared to accept such a long confinement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Over the following century the system became more elaborate. In 1423 Venice opened a permanent isolation hospital, or lazaretto, on an island in its lagoon, and similar establishments soon appeared in Genoa, Marseille and Malta. Crews and passengers of suspect ships were held there for the required period, while their cargo was unpacked and exposed to the air, sometimes for weeks, in the belief that infection could cling to cloth and other materials. Letters were dipped in vinegar or passed through smoke before delivery. Ports also began to issue bills of health, documents certifying whether a ship had departed from a place free of disease, and permanent health boards were created with the power to close harbours, burn goods and confine suspects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whether any of this worked is a question that has divided historians. Eleni Stavridou of the Aegean Institute for Maritime History has assembled records of plague outbreaks in thirty-seven Mediterranean ports between 1500 and 1750, comparing those that enforced strict maritime quarantine with those that applied it loosely or not at all. Ports in the first group, she found, experienced outbreaks roughly half as often as those in the second. Stavridou acknowledges that the records are incomplete, but she argues that the pattern is too consistent across too many places to be dismissed as coincidence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Tomas Zubrickas, a historian of epidemics at the Baltic Centre for the Study of Disease, is more sceptical. Quarantine regulations, he points out, were concerned almost exclusively with people and goods arriving by sea, yet plague is primarily a disease of rodents, carried by their fleas, and it could travel overland in grain carts, baggage trains and the supplies of marching armies. Early rules made no provision whatever for rats. Zubrickas suggests that the eventual retreat of plague from western Europe in the eighteenth century may owe more to changes in rat populations, in building materials, or even in the bacterium itself than to any human policy. He is surely right that quarantine cannot by itself account for the disappearance of the disease. Yet to conclude that it achieved nothing goes too far. Stavridou's figures point to a genuine effect, and the great outbreak at Marseille in 1720, one of the last in western Europe, began when a ship's cargo was released early under pressure from merchants, which is hardly evidence that the rules were pointless.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Kenji Hoshizaki, an economic historian at the Kansai Institute of Trade History, draws attention to the costs of the system and to the uses to which it was put. Forty days of idleness was an expensive delay for any merchant, and records of bribery, forged bills of health and secret landings at night show that evasion was common. Governments, meanwhile, discovered that health regulations could serve commercial ends: a state could impose long quarantines on vessels from a rival port while waving through ships belonging to its allies, all in the name of public safety. In Hoshizaki's view, bills of health became instruments of diplomacy as much as of medicine.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most enduring legacy of quarantine, however, may lie less in the control of plague than in the institutions it created. The health boards of Renaissance Italy, with their inspectors, registers, licences and powers of enforcement, were the first permanent public health authorities in Europe, and their methods of collecting information about disease were inherited by the states that followed them. The arguments they provoked are equally familiar. Disputes over how to balance the protection of the public against the demands of trade and the liberty of individuals, and suspicion that health measures serve political purposes, would not have surprised a Venetian merchant waiting out his forty days.

topic: scurvy and the citrus cure that was found, lost and found again: the 1747 shipboard trial, naval adoption, the switch to limes, polar expeditions and the discovery of vitamin C
title: A Cure Found and Forgotten
subtitle: The history of scurvy shows that medical knowledge does not simply accumulate; it can also be lost

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For sailors in the age of long ocean voyages, few prospects were more dreaded than scurvy. After several weeks without fresh food, the first signs appeared: exhaustion, aching limbs and swollen, bleeding gums. Teeth loosened, old wounds that had healed years before opened again, and without treatment the victim eventually died. It is frequently claimed that scurvy killed more sailors than all the naval battles of the eighteenth century combined. Estimates of this kind vary enormously, and some of the most widely quoted figures rest on little more than guesswork, but there is no doubt that the disease could devastate a ship's company and that navies regarded it as one of their gravest problems.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 1747 a Scottish naval surgeon carried out an experiment on board a warship that is now often celebrated as the first controlled clinical trial. He took twelve sailors suffering from scurvy, divided them into six pairs and gave each pair a different remedy: cider, a dilute acid, vinegar, seawater, a paste of spices, or two oranges and a lemon each day. The pair receiving citrus fruit recovered so quickly that one of them was fit for duty within a week. Aino Pakarinen, a historian of science at the Nordic Institute for Maritime Medicine, regards the modern celebration of this trial as largely anachronistic. The surgeon himself, she points out, did not conclude that citrus fruit was a specific cure. In the long treatise he published several years later, he continued to attribute scurvy to damp air and blocked perspiration, and recommended a concentrate prepared by boiling the juice, a process now known to destroy much of its value. Pakarinen is right that the trial has been turned into a legend, but it would be unfair to blame its author for failing to see what no theory of his time could have explained.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The British navy did not make lemon juice a routine issue until 1795, almost half a century later. This delay is often presented as a scandal, a case of officials ignoring plain evidence. Chidi Cervantes-Mora of the Lagoon Centre for Naval History offers a more sympathetic reading. Lemons had to be imported from southern Europe at considerable expense, and the naval board responsible for sailors' health was receiving recommendations for numerous other remedies, among them fermented cabbage and an infusion of malted barley, each supported by its own reports of success. On the evidence available at the time, Cervantes-Mora argues, citrus fruit did not stand out as clearly superior. His account is convincing, and it suggests that the problem was not ignorance but the difficulty of distinguishing a genuine remedy from a crowd of plausible ones.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Once adopted, lemon juice was remarkably effective, and scurvy largely disappeared from the navy for several decades. Then, in the 1860s, the supply was switched from Mediterranean lemons to limes grown in Britain's own Caribbean colonies, which were cheaper and politically more convenient. Limes contain considerably less of the protective substance than lemons, and the juice was often stored in ways that degraded it further. For a time nobody noticed, largely because steamships had shortened most voyages to the point at which scurvy rarely had time to develop.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences became apparent on the polar expeditions of the late nineteenth century, when crews provisioned with lime juice spent many months away from fresh supplies and fell ill in large numbers. According to Maite Baraibar of the Biscay Institute for Polar Studies, these failures led many experts to lose confidence in citrus altogether. In its place they adopted a new explanation: that scurvy was a form of poisoning caused by tainted tinned meat. Ironically, the observation that some explorers avoided the disease by eating fresh seal meat was taken as support for this theory, rather than as a clue to the real cause. In Baraibar's words, the knowledge of the previous century was not merely neglected; it was actively unlearned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The way out of this confusion came from an unexpected direction. In 1907 two Norwegian researchers studying a different nutritional disease found that guinea pigs fed on a restricted diet of grain developed symptoms resembling scurvy. Lukas Feldbauer, a biochemist turned historian at the Styrian Institute for Nutritional Science, argues that this was the true turning point. Most laboratory animals, including the rats then widely used in nutrition research, produce the protective substance in their own bodies and therefore never develop scurvy, which is why earlier experiments had produced such confusing results. The guinea pig, by contrast, gave researchers a reliable means of testing which foods prevented the disease, and within twenty-five years vitamin C had been identified and isolated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The story of scurvy is sometimes told as a simple progression from ignorance to understanding, but it is better seen as a warning. A remedy that works for reasons nobody understands is fragile: it can be weakened by an administrative decision, abandoned in favour of a fashionable theory, or forgotten when circumstances change. Modern medicine still relies on a number of treatments whose mechanisms remain unclear, and the history of scurvy suggests that such knowledge deserves to be guarded with particular care.

topic: the clinical thermometer and the fever chart: how measuring body temperature created the idea of a 'normal' temperature and changed nursing and diagnosis
title: The Tyranny of Thirty-Seven
subtitle: How a glass tube and a column of mercury taught doctors to think about the body in numbers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of medical history, fever was not regarded as a symptom of disease but as a disease in its own right, and physicians judged it in the only way available to them: by laying a hand on the patient's forehead or chest. In the early seventeenth century an Italian physician adapted a recently invented device for indicating changes in heat and used it to examine his patients, but the instrument was large, slow to respond and had no agreed scale, so readings taken by one doctor could not be compared with those taken by another. For the next two hundred years, thermometers remained objects of scientific curiosity rather than everyday clinical tools, and the experienced hand remained the principal means of detecting a fever.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The decisive change came in 1868, when a German physician published the results of a vast programme of measurement involving around 25,000 patients and, by his own account, more than a million individual readings. From these he concluded that the healthy human body maintained a temperature of about 37 degrees Celsius, and that anything above 38 degrees indicated fever. Just as important was his demonstration that fevers were not uniform: each disease tended to follow its own characteristic course, with temperatures rising, falling or fluctuating in a recognisable sequence over days or weeks. To capture these sequences he promoted the fever chart, a graph kept at the bedside on which readings were plotted several times a day, so that the progress of an illness could be seen at a glance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Practical obstacles remained. The instruments of the period were about thirty centimetres long and had to be held in the armpit for up to twenty minutes, which made routine use cumbersome. In 1867 an English physician designed a version roughly half that length which gave a reading in about five minutes, and within a few decades compact thermometers were standard equipment in hospitals and in the bags of family doctors. Increasingly, though, it was nurses rather than doctors who took the measurements. Harleen Dosanjh, a historian of nursing at the Midlands Institute for Nursing History, argues that this transformed nursing itself. By recording temperatures as numbers on a chart, nurses acquired a defined and respected clinical task. At the same time, Dosanjh observes, their own observations of a patient's colour, breathing or mood came to count for less than a figure on a graph.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some historians see in the fever chart nothing less than a revolution in the concept of illness. Pascal Laviolette of the Alpine Centre for Medical Humanities contends that, before thermometry, disease was understood as a disturbance of the whole person, shaped by temperament, diet and circumstance; afterwards, it increasingly came to mean a measurable departure from a numerical norm. The idea of 'normal' itself, he suggests, entered medicine largely through the thermometer. There is much truth in this, but Laviolette tends to present as sudden a shift that in reality took generations. Medical textbooks went on discussing temperament and constitution well into the twentieth century, and many physicians combined the new numbers with the old ways of thinking without any apparent sense of contradiction.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The famous figure of 37 degrees has itself come under scrutiny. The German physician measured temperatures in the armpit, a site that typically gives lower readings than the mouth, and it has been suggested that his instruments were not perfectly calibrated. More intriguingly, a team led by Sunniva Kirkegaard at the Nordic Centre for Population Health Records has examined temperature records spanning more than a century and a half and concluded that the average body temperature in some populations has gradually fallen, to something nearer 36.6 degrees. Kirkegaard attributes the decline to reduced levels of chronic infection and inflammation, together with more comfortable living conditions. The finding is fascinating, but it should be treated with caution, because methods of measurement have changed so much over the period that some of the apparent decline may simply reflect better instruments.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more practical objection comes from the physician and historian Kaarel Tamkivi of the Baltic Institute of Clinical History. A single threshold for fever, he argues, can be seriously misleading. Body temperature varies with the time of day, with age and from one individual to another, and elderly people in particular often fail to develop a high temperature even when they have a dangerous infection. Relying on a fixed figure may therefore cause the most vulnerable patients to be overlooked. Tamkivi proposes that each person's usual temperature should be recorded when they are well, so that departures from it can be recognised. His concern is justified, yet fixed thresholds should not be abandoned altogether: in a crowded emergency department, a simple and universal rule allows staff to identify quickly those who need attention, and that value is not easily replaced.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most lasting effect of the clinical thermometer was perhaps not any particular discovery but a change in habit. It placed a number at the centre of the relationship between carer and patient, and accustomed generations of doctors and nurses to look first at a chart rather than at a face. Numbers have proved immensely useful in medicine, but the history of the thermometer is a reminder that they are tools for understanding patients, not substitutes for it.
