topic: interchangeable parts and the 'American system of manufactures': armoury subsidies, machinists, commercial relevance and why Britain differed
title: Parts That Fit
subtitle: The quest for interchangeable components is often told as a story of American ingenuity, but money, the state and measurement may matter more

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the Great Exhibition opened in London in 1851, the American section initially attracted more mockery than admiration. Within weeks, however, opinion had shifted. American reaping machines outperformed their rivals in field trials, an American locksmith picked supposedly unpickable British locks, and rifles whose parts could be exchanged between one weapon and another drew the attention of military observers. So impressed was the British government that in 1854 it dispatched a commission to examine American armouries. According to its report, workmen at one armoury took apart ten muskets made in different years, mixed the components together and reassembled the weapons, which then functioned perfectly. The commissioners coined a phrase for what they had seen: the 'American system of manufactures'.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The ideal behind the demonstration was simple to state. If every component were made so accurately that it would fit any example of the finished product, assembly would no longer require the skilled fitter who filed each part until it matched its neighbours, and a broken mechanism could be repaired with a spare rather than returned to a workshop. The idea was not American in origin. French military engineers had pursued interchangeable musket locks in the 1780s, but the project was abandoned, largely because the parts cost far more than conventionally made ones. The history of interchangeable parts is therefore less a tale of inspired invention than one of persistence: an old idea that waited decades for someone prepared to pay for it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That someone, according to Michiko Kurihashi of the Tohoku Centre for the History of Technology, was the United States government. Kurihashi has reconstructed the accounts of the federal armouries and shows that interchangeability was achieved only through decades of investment in specialised machine tools, together with elaborate systems of gauges against which every part was checked. Muskets produced in this way were considerably more expensive than hand-fitted weapons, a premium no private customer would have accepted. Only an institution indifferent to short-term cost, and concerned above all with repairing weapons in the field, could have sustained the effort. In Kurihashi's view, the American system was in its origins a creation of the state rather than of the market.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Gustavo Raposo, of the Porto Institute of Economic History, accepts this account but locates the armouries' significance elsewhere. What mattered commercially, he argues, was not interchangeability as such but the machine tools and the machinists that the armouries produced. Men trained in armoury workshops carried their skills into private industry, and the same basic operations of cutting, drilling and grinding metal proved applicable to sewing machines, bicycles and typewriters in turn. The armouries, on this reading, functioned as unintended training schools for an entire generation of mechanical engineers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Femi Adegoroye, a business historian, goes further, questioning whether interchangeability was necessary for commercial success at all. He points to the leading sewing-machine manufacturer of the 1860s and 1870s, which continued to employ skilled fitters to file its parts into shape long after some rivals had adopted armoury methods, yet came to dominate the market. Its success, Adegoroye argues, owed far more to aggressive advertising and to allowing customers to pay in instalments than to production technique. The label 'American system', he concludes, implies a uniformity of method that never existed. This criticism of the label is justified, but it would be wrong to infer that interchangeability was commercially unimportant. The moving assembly lines of the early twentieth century depended on it absolutely, since a line cannot keep moving if a worker must stop to file each component until it fits.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why did these methods take root in the United States rather than in Britain, then the world's leading industrial nation? Researchers at the Leipzig Manufacturing History Project, who compared the records of British and American firms making similar goods, emphasise differences in circumstances rather than in ingenuity. In America, skilled craftsmen were in short supply and commanded high wages, timber was plentiful, and a large rural market was content with plain, similar products. British manufacturers, by contrast, could hire skilled workers relatively cheaply and served customers who expected goods tailored to their individual requirements. Their reluctance to adopt machine methods was, the project concludes, a sensible response to British conditions rather than a symptom of conservatism.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where conditions were different, Britain adopted American methods readily enough. Following the commission's visit, the government armoury at Enfield purchased a complete set of American machinery, and within a few years it was producing rifles with interchangeable parts. The transfer was not entirely smooth: American mechanics had to be engaged to install the equipment and instruct British operatives, and early output fell short of expectations. Yet as at the American armouries, the state was the customer, and the state was willing to pay.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important lesson of the episode concerns measurement. No two manufactured parts are ever truly identical; they are interchangeable only within a tolerance, a permitted margin of error that must be defined, measured and enforced. The real achievement of the armouries was not identical parts but a culture in which every component was checked against a standard. Gauges, inspectors and written specifications allowed a part machined in one building to fit a product assembled in another. That culture, more than any individual machine, is the inheritance of modern manufacturing.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: Pacific island wayfinding: the drift theory, star compass, swells and seabirds, experimental canoe voyages and the long pause in eastward settlement
title: Reading the Ocean
subtitle: How did the first settlers of the remote Pacific find islands that no one had seen before?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When European ships first entered the central Pacific in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, their crews found that almost every habitable island, however remote, was already occupied. The people they met had reached these specks of land in double-hulled canoes, without compasses, charts or any written record of the routes, and the visitors struggled to account for the achievement. The explanation that gained most favour for the next three centuries was that the islands had been settled by accident, as fishing parties were swept out to sea and washed up on unknown shores. That view, it seems to me, reveals rather more about the observers than about the islanders. Sailors who relied on instruments found it hard to imagine that anyone could cross such distances without them, and so they concluded that nobody had.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The drift theory has not survived close examination. In one frequently cited study, Henrik Aasvold, a geographer at the Bergen Institute of Ocean History, used historical records of winds and currents to model several thousand imaginary voyages by canoes left entirely to the mercy of the weather. Hardly any of these simulated vessels reached the outer corners of the region, and none arrived at the most isolated archipelagos from the likely points of departure. Aasvold also pointed out that settlement broadly proceeded from west to east, against the prevailing trade winds, which is precisely the opposite of what passive drift would produce. His conclusion, now widely shared, is that the remote islands were found by people who were looking for them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How they looked is a question answered largely through the testimony of navigators in parts of Micronesia and Polynesia where traditional voyaging survived into the twentieth century. Central to their method is the so-called star compass. This was not an object but a mental model: the horizon was divided into a number of points, each named after a star that rises or sets there, and a canoe held its heading by steering towards a sequence of such stars. Yet Losana Lavemai, an anthropologist who has recorded the accounts of more than twenty elderly navigators, insists that the stars were only part of the picture. Ocean swells, generated by distant weather systems, travel in consistent directions for days, and an experienced navigator could detect their pattern through the motion of the hull. Several of her informants described lying down in the canoe at night to feel the swells more clearly. For Lavemai, the navigator's body rather than his eyes was the principal instrument.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further element concerns the target itself. A low island may be visible from a canoe only within fifteen kilometres or so, and a navigator aiming for it directly would need remarkable accuracy. Kofi Nketsiah, a marine ecologist who studies tropical seabirds, argues that this way of framing the problem is misleading. Certain species fly out to feed each morning and return to land at dusk, and a navigator who observed them could detect an island from perhaps fifty kilometres away. Stationary clouds above high islands, and the greenish tint that shallow lagoons reflect onto the underside of clouds, offered further clues. In Nketsiah's view, voyagers aimed not at individual islands but at entire chains, which presented a target hundreds of kilometres wide.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Since the 1970s these claims have been tested in practice. Reconstructed voyaging canoes, crewed by people trained in traditional methods, have completed long passages between island groups without instruments, and their success has done much to restore confidence in the old techniques. Some historians object that the modern crews knew exactly where their destination lay, whereas the first explorers did not, so the experiments prove less than their supporters suggest. This criticism is reasonable up to a point, but it is often pushed too far. The voyages were never intended to recreate the experience of discovery; what they establish is that deliberate navigation over such distances was possible. Whether it actually happened in a particular case is a separate question, and one that only archaeology can settle.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That evidence has itself shifted. Improved radiocarbon dating has led Daria Belokurova, an archaeologist at the Tallinn Centre for Maritime Studies, to argue that the eastern Pacific was settled much later and much faster than was once believed. After people had established themselves in the western islands, there appears to have been a pause of well over a thousand years, followed by a burst of expansion in which the remaining archipelagos were colonised within two or three centuries. Belokurova considers this long interruption a greater mystery than the voyages that ended it. One possibility she has explored is that a period of altered climate brought more frequent westerly winds, allowing canoes to sail eastwards with less effort. It is an intriguing proposal, but the records of past climate for the region are still too patchy to support it with any confidence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is not in doubt is that the knowledge involved was precise, cumulative and carefully transmitted. Because it was passed on orally, through long apprenticeships, it was also fragile; in many island groups it vanished within a few generations of European contact, and its partial revival owes much to a handful of navigators who agreed to share what they knew. To describe such expertise as instinct, as some early commentators did, is to misunderstand it entirely. It was a science of the ocean, built on observation and tested on every voyage, and it deserves to be studied as seriously as the instruments that replaced it.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: compass deviation in nineteenth-century iron ships: correcting magnets versus tabulation, wreck inquiries and the routines that solved the problem
title: The Wandering Needle
subtitle: When ships began to be built of iron, the most trusted instrument on board started to tell lies

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For several centuries the magnetic compass was the one instrument that a seaman could rely on absolutely. Its needle might be affected by the gradual variation of the earth's magnetic field from place to place, but that variation was charted and could be allowed for. In the first half of the nineteenth century, however, shipbuilders began to replace timber with iron, and the compass started to behave in alarming ways. An iron hull is itself a large magnet, and a needle placed within it responds partly to the ship rather than to the earth. There is a certain irony in this: the material that made vessels stronger, larger and cheaper to build was the same material that made it harder to know where they were heading.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The error introduced by the hull, known as deviation, proved peculiarly difficult to manage because it was not constant. It altered with the direction in which the ship was steering, so that a compass might be accurate on a northerly course and several degrees wrong on an easterly one. It changed again when the vessel heeled over under sail. Most puzzling of all, a new ship carried a magnetic imprint of its construction: the repeated hammering of iron plates in the shipyard left the hull magnetised according to the direction it had faced on the slipway, and this magnetism faded unpredictably during the first months at sea. Wooden ships had suffered small deviations from iron guns and fittings, but nothing on this scale.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A scientific answer arrived surprisingly early. In the late 1830s an astronomer conducted a series of experiments aboard an iron vessel moored in a river and proposed that the ship's influence could be cancelled by placing permanent magnets and pieces of soft iron close to the compass. When the correctors were properly arranged, the needle pointed true on every heading. Many naval officers were unconvinced. They argued that since the hull's magnetism shifted over time, fixed correctors that were accurate on the day of fitting might later add errors of their own, and a navigator who trusted them would have no idea that anything was wrong. In my view both camps were partly right, and the long argument between them was less a matter of ignorance than of genuine uncertainty.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The navy's preferred alternative was not to correct the error but to measure it. A ship would be 'swung' around all points of the compass in calm water, with its readings compared against distant landmarks, and the deviation on each heading recorded in a table that the navigator consulted throughout the voyage. Nadia Ferhati, a historian of science at the Lyon Maritime Archive, argues that the dispute between correction and tabulation was never purely technical. On one side stood men of science, confident that physical theory could eliminate the problem; on the other stood seamen, who believed that a known error was safer than a hidden one. In Ferhati's account, the debate became a contest over who possessed authority at sea.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, iron ships were being lost. Edmund Hollinrake, a former merchant officer who now researches maritime history, has examined the records of more than two hundred inquiries into wrecks between 1850 and 1880. He found that a large majority of the iron vessels involved had been fitted with correctors, but that very few had been swung again after their first voyage, even when they had been laid up for months or had loaded heavy iron cargo. The difficulty, Hollinrake concludes, was not a shortage of knowledge but the absence of any rule obliging owners to have compasses checked at regular intervals. Equipment that was installed once and then forgotten offered little real protection.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more provocative reading comes from Mirela Seferović of the Institute for Nautical Studies in Split, who suggests that the inquiries themselves deserve suspicion. Compass error, she points out, was a convenient verdict: it placed responsibility on an invisible physical force rather than on a master who had kept a poor lookout or an owner who had sent an overloaded ship to sea. Her analysis of the reports shows that deviation was frequently cited as a cause even when no compass had been examined after the loss. Seferović's argument is a useful corrective, but it would be wrong to conclude that the compass served merely as a scapegoat. Deviation was a real and serious hazard, and the instruments recovered from some wrecks were shown to be many degrees in error.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: By the end of the century the problem had largely been brought under control, though not by any single breakthrough. Compass needles became shorter and lighter, which made them easier to correct; housings were redesigned so that correctors could be adjusted at sea; and regulations began to require that compasses be inspected by qualified adjusters. Officers' examinations, too, came to include questions on deviation. What finally made iron ships safe to navigate, then, was the combination of a sound theory with dull but dependable routine. It is a lesson that the history of navigation teaches repeatedly: each new technology tends to create hazards of its own, and these are rarely overcome by better instruments alone.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: Norse navigation in the North Atlantic and the debate over the sunstone (Iceland spar) hypothesis
title: Light Through Stone
subtitle: Did Norse seafarers find their way across the North Atlantic with the help of a crystal?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the ninth and eleventh centuries, Norse seafarers crossed the North Atlantic from Scandinavia to the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland and, briefly, the coast of North America. They did so without the magnetic compass, which did not reach northern Europe until later, and in latitudes where the summer sky offers little help: for weeks around midsummer the stars are invisible in the long twilight, and cloud and fog are common. How these voyages were navigated has long intrigued historians, and one answer has proved especially attractive. A handful of medieval Icelandic texts mention a sólarsteinn, or 'sunstone', and some scholars have proposed that this was a crystal used to locate the sun when it was hidden. It is worth stressing at the outset that a remarkably large structure of argument has been built on a very small textual foundation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most likely candidate for such a stone is Iceland spar, a transparent form of calcite that splits light into two beams. Because daylight scattered by the atmosphere is polarised in a pattern centred on the sun, an observer rotating the crystal against the sky could, in principle, work out where the sun lay even behind cloud. Bodil Kjelstrup, a physicist at the Aarhus Centre for Optical History, tested this by asking volunteers to locate the hidden sun with calcite under overcast skies. Most were able to do so to within a few degrees. Her results are impressive, and they settle the question of whether the method could have worked. They do not, however, show that anyone in the Viking Age actually used it, and the two questions are too often run together.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kristín Eydal, a specialist in Old Norse literature at the University of Akureyri, is sceptical of the whole idea. She notes that the texts in which the sunstone appears were written down two or three centuries after the great voyages, and that none of them is set at sea. In the best-known passage, a king holds a stone up to a cloudy sky to confirm a claim made by one of his followers about the sun's position. For Eydal, the sunstone in these stories is a marvel attached to royal authority, comparable to other wondrous objects in the same literature, rather than a practical piece of equipment used by ordinary sailors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others have attempted to estimate how much difference the device could have made. Adebayo Akintunde, who builds computer models of historical voyages, simulated thousands of crossings from western Norway to southern Greenland under realistic weather conditions. Ships that used a sunstone to correct their heading reached their destination in a high proportion of cases, but only when readings were taken at least every few hours; with less frequent checks, the advantage almost disappeared. The work is ingenious, yet its conclusions depend entirely on an assumption about how often navigators consulted the stone, and on that point there is no evidence whatsoever.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever the truth about the sunstone, it was certainly not the only resource available. In clear weather a navigator could judge latitude from the length of the sun's shadow at midday, keeping to a chosen line of latitude by checking that the shadow remained constant. Seabirds, whales and the colour of the water indicated the approach to land. A fragment of a wooden disc marked with lines, found at a Greenland farm site, has been interpreted as a kind of sun compass. Matteo Scagliola, an archaeologist at the Venice Institute of Maritime Archaeology, warns against reading too much into it: the object is incomplete, and similar markings appear on items with no known navigational use. In his view, most Norse navigation rested on accumulated experience, preserved in the sailing directions recorded in later texts, which describe routes in terms of coastal landmarks and the number of days' sailing between them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: To my mind, the debate has become unnecessarily polarised. One side treats the sunstone as the key that unlocks Norse navigation; the other dismisses it as a literary invention. A more plausible position lies between them. Calcite was available in Iceland, the optical effect is real, and it would be surprising if experienced seafarers had never noticed it. Yet there is no reason to think the stone was indispensable. It was more probably a specialist tool, brought out on overcast days when other methods failed. Nor should the absence of sunstones from excavated Norse sites be taken as decisive, since calcite is a soft mineral that would rarely survive many centuries in damp, acidic soils.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important lesson concerns the questions historians choose to ask. Because modern navigation depends on instruments, researchers have tended to look for an instrument behind every historical achievement at sea. The Norse case suggests that this habit can distort our understanding. Norse voyagers succeeded above all because they combined many kinds of observation, of sun, sea, sky and wildlife, into a body of knowledge passed from one generation of sailors to the next. A single crystal, however intriguing, was at most one small part of that knowledge.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: who paid for lighthouses: light dues, private patents, state provision and the lighthouse as an economic example
title: Who Paid for the Light?
subtitle: The history of lighthouse finance is more complicated, and more interesting, than economics textbooks suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For generations of economics students, the lighthouse has served as the standard illustration of a good that markets cannot supply. The reasoning appears straightforward. A light shining over a dangerous coast helps every passing ship, and its keeper has no way of switching it off for vessels whose owners refuse to pay. Since nobody can be excluded from the benefit, the argument goes, nobody will volunteer to contribute, and a private lighthouse could never cover its costs. Only government, funded by compulsory taxation, can therefore be expected to build and maintain such structures. The example is elegant and easy to remember, and it has been repeated in introductory courses with remarkably little alteration for more than a century. Its chief weakness is that it was constructed with very little reference to how lighthouses were actually paid for.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In Britain, the earliest coastal lights were often maintained by religious houses or by local guilds of seamen, but from the seventeenth century onwards a large number were built by private individuals. An entrepreneur would petition the Crown for a patent granting the right to erect a light at a particular spot and to charge passing ships for its use. These charges, known as light dues, were not collected at sea, which would indeed have been impossible, but in port. Agents stationed at harbours calculated the sum owed according to each vessel's tonnage and the lights it had passed on its voyage, and a ship could not complete its business until the dues had been settled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Fintan Mulcreevy, an economic historian at the Galway School of Commerce, regards this system as decisive evidence against the textbook view. By linking payment to the use of ports, he argues, lighthouse owners neatly solved the problem of ships that would otherwise have enjoyed the light without contributing to it. Mulcreevy points out that by the early nineteenth century a substantial share of the lights around the British coast were in private hands, and that several of them returned handsome profits to their owners. For him, the episode demonstrates that private enterprise is capable of supplying goods that economists have too readily assigned to the state.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Rania Shirazian, who studies the history of regulation at the Institute for Public Economics in Leiden, accepts the facts but rejects the conclusion. The private lights, she observes, could not have existed without the state at every stage. It was the Crown that granted each owner an exclusive right to a stretch of coast, and it was the law that compelled shipmasters to pay at the harbour. What emerged, in Shirazian's view, was not a free market but a franchise, in which private capital operated under public protection. She adds that the profits were not universally admired: shipowners complained for decades that the dues were excessive, and eventually Parliament purchased the remaining private lights and placed them under a single public authority.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Shirazian's point seems to me largely correct, and it rather weakens the use that Mulcreevy makes of the British case. Yet it does not rescue the textbook argument either, which claimed that private financing was impossible rather than merely dependent on law. A different question concerns the quality of the service. Hugh Arbuthnott, a former engineer who has written widely on lighthouse construction, notes that many private lights in the eighteenth century were simple coal fires, dim and frequently obscured by smoke. However, he also finds that some private owners were among the first to adopt oil lamps with polished reflectors, while public bodies were at times slow to replace outdated equipment. In Arbuthnott's judgement, ownership by itself tells us little about how well a light was kept.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other countries chose different paths. In France, the state established a national lighthouse service in the early nineteenth century, financed from general taxation and planned as a single system covering the entire coastline. Ships paid nothing directly for the lights they passed. Engineers employed by the service drew up a classification of lights by range and importance, so that a navigator approaching the coast from any direction would encounter a predictable sequence of beams. The French arrangement produced a well-organised network that was much admired abroad, yet it depended on a strong central administration that few nations at the time possessed. Comparisons of this kind suggest that there is no universally superior model of lighthouse provision; what worked in one country reflected the particular institutions, legal traditions and public finances available there.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most valuable lesson of the lighthouse debate may therefore be a general one. Economists have often treated public and private provision as clearly separate alternatives, but the history of coastal lights shows how frequently they were intertwined. Private owners relied on state privileges; public authorities borrowed techniques and personnel from private ones; and in several countries light dues are still collected today to fund services that are publicly managed. Today, with satellite navigation available on almost every vessel and most lighthouses fully automated, the question of who should pay for the light has lost much of its practical urgency. Its value as a reminder of how institutions actually develop has not.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: radio navigation at sea: direction-finding beacons, hyperbolic positioning networks, their closure after satellites, and the debate over backup systems and seamanship skills
title: Signals in the Fog
subtitle: Radio transformed the way ships found their position, and its quiet disappearance has left questions that are still unresolved

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of maritime history, a navigator out of sight of land depended on the sky. The sun and stars could reveal a ship's position, but only when they were visible, and a week of overcast weather could leave even a skilled officer uncertain of his whereabouts by many kilometres. The arrival of radio in the early twentieth century changed this in a fundamental way. Within a few decades, shore stations were transmitting time signals and weather reports, and coastal beacons allowed a ship equipped with a rotating aerial to take a bearing on a known transmitter. Radio was, in effect, the first technology since the magnetic compass to give the navigator information that did not depend on what could be seen overhead.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Direction-finding was useful but imprecise, and the decisive advance came with what are known as hyperbolic systems, developed in the 1940s and widely adopted after the war. These relied on pairs of land stations broadcasting precisely synchronised signals. A receiver on board measured the tiny difference in the time at which the two signals arrived, and since every point with the same time difference lies on a particular curve, a hyperbola, the ship could be placed somewhere along that line. A second pair of stations provided a second curve, and the intersection gave a position. Near the coast, fixes could be accurate to within a few hundred metres. At night, however, accuracy deteriorated, because signals reflected from the upper atmosphere arrived alongside those travelling directly over the surface and confused the receiver.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Histories of these systems usually emphasise safety, but Annelie Bockhorst, a historian of technology at the Kiel Institute for Maritime History, argues that their most far-reaching effects were economic. Fishing skippers quickly realised that a receiver allowed them to return again and again to the exact spot where a good catch had been taken, and to record productive grounds with a precision their predecessors could only have dreamed of. In several fisheries, Bockhorst suggests, the result was a marked intensification of fishing effort on particular banks, with consequences for stocks that were not understood at the time. Navigation technology, in her phrase, quietly became fishing technology.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kenji Ishikane, who studies the history of telecommunications at the Kobe University of Maritime Science, draws attention to another neglected aspect: the systems' military origins. Several networks were planned by defence ministries, and the location of their transmitters reflected strategic priorities rather than the requirements of commercial shipping. Ishikane shows that some of the busiest merchant routes received poor coverage for years, while remote waters of naval interest were served well. In some regions, moreover, the precise specifications of the signals were for a time treated as confidential, which delayed the production of affordable receivers for civilian vessels. It is a useful reminder that infrastructure which appears neutral was often shaped by interests that had little to do with the people who eventually came to rely on it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: From the 1990s onwards, satellite positioning made the land-based networks look obsolete. Satellite receivers were cheaper, worked everywhere and were accurate to within metres, and one government after another switched off its transmitters. The decision seemed uncontroversial at the time, since maintaining ageing stations was costly and the number of ships still using them was falling year by year. Tunde Adeyanju, a navigation engineer at the Lagos Centre for Ocean Technology, believes this was a serious error. Satellite signals reach the earth extremely weak, he explains, and can easily be drowned out by a transmitter on the ground, or imitated so that a receiver displays a false position. Adeyanju has catalogued numerous incidents in which ships' instruments showed vessels to be sitting at inland airports or moving in impossible patterns. He argues for a modernised terrestrial network, operating on entirely different principles, as a backup.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Moira Callender, a former ship's master who now trains deck officers, shares Adeyanju's concern but locates the weakness elsewhere. In her view, the greater danger lies not in the absence of a second system but in the erosion of the skills needed to recognise when any system is wrong. Officers trained in recent years seldom practise taking positions from the sun or from coastal bearings, and a crew that trusts the screen implicitly may not notice that the position displayed has drifted. A backup network, she warns, will offer little protection if no one on the bridge can tell when it, too, is failing. Both arguments have force, but Callender's has received far less attention than it deserves, and it would also be considerably cheaper to act upon.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That said, the costs of a terrestrial backup are not as daunting as its opponents sometimes claim; several countries have reopened stations at modest expense. The deeper lesson of the radio era is that each improvement in accuracy has tended to encourage greater dependence on a single source of information. Navigators who once cross-checked the stars against their compass and log came to trust the hyperbolic receiver, and their successors now trust the satellite. Whether governments will choose to fund alternatives remains uncertain. What history makes clear is that safety at sea has rarely been secured by one perfect method, and far more often by several imperfect ones used together.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: dead reckoning in the age of sail: the chip log and traverse board, how accurate logbook estimates were, and navigators' judgement
title: Reckoning Without Stars
subtitle: The humble art of estimating a ship's position from speed, course and time deserves more respect than it usually receives

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Histories of navigation tend to celebrate instruments: the astrolabe, the sextant, the marine chronometer. Far less attention is paid to the method that, for most of the age of sail, determined where a ship was believed to be for most of the time. Dead reckoning is simple in principle. If a navigator knows the point from which the ship set out, the direction in which it has been steered, its speed and the time that has elapsed, he can calculate its present position. The method is often described as crude, and its results could certainly be wrong. Yet it would be a mistake to treat it as a primitive stage that later techniques left behind. Even after observations of the sun and stars became routine, dead reckoning carried the ship between those observations, and on cloudy days it was all the navigator had.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The equipment involved was modest. Speed was measured with the chip log, a weighted wooden board attached to a line on which knots were tied at regular intervals. The board was thrown over the stern and the line allowed to run out freely while a small sandglass emptied; the number of knots that passed through a sailor's hands gave the speed, which is why speed at sea is still expressed in knots. Courses steered were recorded every half hour by placing pegs in a traverse board, and the totals were later worked into the logbook. Each step introduced error. Glasses ran fast or slow, knots were spaced inaccurately, and the ship did not travel exactly where its bow was pointing: wind pushed it sideways, an effect known as leeway, while ocean currents carried it along without anyone on board feeling a thing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How large were the resulting errors? Rosalind Fairbrother, a historian at the Plymouth Institute of Maritime Records, has compared the positions recorded in several hundred eighteenth-century logbooks with the places where the same ships actually reached land. On short coastal passages, she finds, dead reckoning was often impressively accurate. Over long ocean crossings, however, small daily errors accumulated, and by the end of a voyage of several weeks a ship might be a hundred kilometres or more from where its navigator believed it to be. The errors were not evenly distributed: they were consistently larger in waters crossed by strong currents that had not yet been charted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Giulia Ferraguti, of the University of Genoa, cautions against reading the logbook figures as raw measurements. An experienced navigator, she argues, did not simply multiply speed by time. He adjusted his estimate for the leeway he judged the ship to be making, for the currents he expected in a given region, and for the known peculiarities of his own vessel. The positions entered in the logbook were therefore already the product of interpretation. For Ferraguti, this judgement, acquired over years at sea and rarely written down, was the true core of the navigator's craft, and its importance has been obscured by the attention historians lavish on instruments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Tomasz Cieślak, a historian of science in Gdańsk, is far less impressed. In his view, much of what passes for seamanly judgement was guesswork, and the apparent accuracy of some logbooks is an illusion. He has identified numerous cases in which entries were evidently revised after landfall, so that the reckoning appeared to have brought the ship precisely to its destination. Cieślak is surely right that logbooks were not neutral records and must be read with care. But he goes too far in implying that the navigator's skill was largely a myth. If adjustments had been mere guesses, they would have made estimates worse as often as better, and Fairbrother's data suggest that this was not the case.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the clearest evidence of skill lies in how navigators used their estimates. Aware that their reckoning could be wrong, many deliberately steered to one side of their destination, a practice known as aiming off. A ship approaching a coast in this way knew that, on sighting land, it should turn in one particular direction to find its harbour, whereas a ship that aimed directly at the harbour and missed it would not know which way to turn. Navigators also kept generous margins around known hazards, and slowed down at night when they believed land to be near. Such practices show that dead reckoning was less about achieving precision than about managing uncertainty intelligently.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The method has never entirely disappeared. Officers are still taught to keep a reckoning as a check on electronic positions, and modern inertial navigation systems, which calculate position from measurements of acceleration and rotation, are in essence an electronic version of the same idea. The persistence of dead reckoning is no accident. Any system that relies on external signals can be interrupted, and a method that requires nothing more than a known starting point, a compass, a clock and a measure of speed retains a value that no satellite can entirely replace.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: the origin of medieval portolan charts: compiled from sailors' compass bearings or derived from lost surveys
title: Lines Across the Middle Sea
subtitle: The earliest sea charts of the Mediterranean were astonishingly accurate, and nobody is quite sure how they were made

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late thirteenth century, a new kind of map began to circulate among the ports of the Mediterranean. Drawn in ink on a single sheet of vellum, the portolan chart showed the coasts of the inland sea with a precision that no earlier map had approached. Its surface was criss-crossed by a web of straight lines radiating from a ring of compass roses, and harbour names were written at right angles to the shore. The oldest surviving example, the so-called Carta Pisana, is usually dated to around 1275, and it is already fully formed. There is no earlier, cruder version from which it seems to have evolved, and this abrupt arrival is, in my view, one of the most stubborn puzzles in the history of cartography.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The puzzle has sharpened since historians began measuring the charts rather than merely admiring them. A team led by Ottavia Brusasco at the Institute of Mediterranean Cartography in Genoa scanned more than thirty medieval charts and digitally overlaid them on modern maps. The outline of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, they found, was frequently accurate to within a few per cent over distances of several thousand kilometres. Two systematic distortions stood out, however. First, the entire image is rotated roughly nine degrees anticlockwise, an error that closely matches the magnetic variation believed to have prevailed in the region at the time. Second, the scale of the western basin does not quite agree with that of the eastern, as though the chart had been assembled from separate parts that were never perfectly reconciled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The standard explanation has long been that the charts grew out of working sailors' experience, and Halvard Myrseth, a historian of navigation at Vestland Maritime University, remains its most energetic defender. According to this account, pilots noted the compass bearing and estimated distance between pairs of ports over generations of voyages, and chartmakers gradually stitched these observations into a single picture. The timing fits: the magnetic compass is known to have reached the Mediterranean by the late twelfth century, leaving roughly a hundred years for such information to accumulate. For Myrseth, the rotation measured by Brusasco is the decisive clue, since a chart compiled from compass bearings would inherit exactly that error, whereas one based on astronomical observation would not.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone finds this persuasive. Yusra Qalbani, a geodesist turned historian at the Amman Centre for the History of Science, points out that medieval pilots could judge distance only by estimating the speed of the ship, and such estimates could easily be wrong by a fifth or more. Errors of this size, she argues, would compound as observations were chained together across the sea, so that a chart built in this way ought to become steadily more distorted towards its edges. Since the portolan charts do not, Qalbani suggests that their makers drew on some earlier body of survey work, possibly Byzantine or Islamic, which has since been lost. Her objection deserves to be taken seriously. Less deserving of attention are the popular writers who have pushed the same reasoning much further, attributing the charts to a forgotten ancient civilisation with advanced surveying techniques. No document, instrument or archaeological find supports such claims, and it is surely for those who propose a lost source to demonstrate that it existed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Mathematics may offer a way out. Ricardo Valadim and colleagues at the Porto Institute of Applied Geography built a computer simulation in which hundreds of imprecise bearings and distances, each carrying random errors of the kind Qalbani describes, were combined by a simple process of averaging. Because the errors pointed in different directions, they largely cancelled one another out, and the resulting outline approached the accuracy of the real charts. The simulation shows that sailors' observations could in principle have produced such maps; it does not show how medieval chartmakers actually combined them, and no working drafts or tables of bearings have survived. Critics treat this silence as damning. I do not, because working papers of every kind seldom outlived their usefulness, and vellum was valuable enough to be scraped clean and reused.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How the charts were used is itself debated. In principle the procedure was simple: the navigator laid a ruler between the port of departure and the destination, found the line on the chart running most nearly parallel to it, and traced that line back to its compass rose to read off the bearing to steer. The method demanded no mathematical training whatever, which may explain why the charts spread so rapidly among Mediterranean pilots. Yet fewer than two hundred charts survive from before 1500, and many are lavishly illuminated with flags, cities and kings, decoration that seems out of place on a document exposed to salt spray. Myrseth argues that the charts actually used at sea were worn out and discarded, so that the survivors are mostly presentation copies commissioned by wealthy patrons. This neatly accounts for the pattern of survival, but it has the awkward property of being impossible to test, since a chart that has perished can never be produced as evidence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The origin of the charts may never be settled. What seems to me beyond dispute, however, is the kind of knowledge they represent. The learned world maps of the same period, produced in monasteries and universities, arranged the earth around Jerusalem and filled their margins with marvels. The portolan charts, by contrast, were the work of craftsmen serving a commercial clientele, and they were judged by a single test: whether a ship that followed them arrived where it intended. In that sense they are an early and striking case of practical knowledge outstripping the scholarship of its age.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: monsoon sailing in the pre-modern Indian Ocean: sailing calendars, the kamal, Arabic pilot manuals and the role of local pilots after European arrival
title: Riding the Seasonal Winds
subtitle: How the sailors of the Indian Ocean turned a predictable wind system into a navigational science

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twice a year, the winds over the northern Indian Ocean change direction. Between roughly November and March they blow steadily from the north-east, carrying dry air from the Asian landmass towards Africa; from about June to September they reverse, sweeping moist air from the south-west back towards India. For the sailors who traded between East Africa, Arabia, India and beyond, this regular alternation was the foundation of everything. A ship could ride one monsoon outwards and the next one home, completing a round trip within a year with little need to sail against the wind. It is for this reason that the Indian Ocean was arguably the most forgiving of the great oceans for navigators before the age of steam, and why long-distance seafaring developed there so early.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Exploiting the monsoon, however, demanded precise timing. Leave port too early and a vessel might meet the tail of the previous season's winds; leave too late and it risked the violent storms that accompany the height of the south-west monsoon, when many harbours on the western coast of India were effectively closed. Over centuries, sailors developed calendars that fixed the best days of departure for each route, counting from the start of the solar year. Faridah Lukmanji, a historian at the Coastal Archives Institute in Mombasa, has compared calendars preserved in several languages and found that the recommended dates for some routes shifted by only a few days over more than three hundred years. In her view, this stability reflects a body of shared knowledge refined by countless crews rather than the rules of any single authority.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Timing alone did not bring a ship to its destination. Navigators also needed to know how far north or south they were, and for this they relied on an instrument of striking simplicity, the kamal. It consisted of a small wooden board attached to a knotted cord, the end of which the navigator held in his teeth. By holding the board at the distance marked by a particular knot and aligning its lower edge with the horizon and its upper edge with the Pole Star, he could judge whether the star stood at the height expected for a given port. Anselm Kroonenberg of the Leiden School of Maritime Studies has shown that this was all that was required for the method known as latitude sailing, in which a ship first reached the latitude of its destination and then simply ran east or west along it. Some historians have treated the kamal as a crude forerunner of European instruments, but this misses the point: its very simplicity made it cheap, robust and easy to use on a rolling deck.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What we know of this navigational culture comes largely from pilot manuals written in Arabic from the fifteenth century onwards. These texts combine lists of stars and their rising points with descriptions of coastlines, depths and the signs that a ship was nearing land: changes in the colour of the water, particular species of seabird and, most reliably, the appearance of sea snakes. Many sections are composed in verse. Ravindu Hettiaratchi, who has edited several of these manuals at the Kandy Centre for Ocean History, believes the verse form reveals their purpose. Rhyme and metre, he argues, made long lists of bearings and landmarks easier to memorise, and the manuals were therefore primarily teaching texts studied ashore by apprentice pilots rather than reference works consulted at sea.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Mariam Al-Shidhani, a palaeographer at the Sohar Manuscript Library, disputes this. Several surviving copies, she notes, contain marginal notes in different hands correcting the depths of particular channels or adding warnings about newly formed sandbanks, which are exactly the kind of revisions a working pilot would make after a voyage. To my mind, the two positions are less opposed than they appear. A text learned by heart as an apprentice could easily become a pilot's companion in later life, and there is no reason to suppose that the manuals served only one function.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The arrival of Portuguese fleets at the end of the fifteenth century is often told as a story of European navigational mastery. Yet the Portuguese routinely hired local pilots once they had entered the Indian Ocean, and researchers at the Gulf Seafaring Archive have argued that the astrolabes and charts they brought offered little advantage in waters that regional navigators already knew intimately. I share this view. The decisive European contribution in the region was military and commercial, in the form of armed ships and fortified trading posts, rather than any superiority in the art of finding the way.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The monsoon system shaped Indian Ocean trade for well over a thousand years, and its grip was loosened only when steamships, indifferent to the direction of the wind, began to dominate the main routes in the late nineteenth century. Wooden sailing vessels continued to trade along the coasts well into the twentieth century, and a handful of elderly men who learned to navigate aboard them are still alive. Recording what they remember has become a matter of real urgency, and not merely for the sake of nostalgia. Their knowledge represents a sophisticated, tested way of understanding the sea, and it deserves to be studied on its own terms rather than as a quaint prelude to modern navigation.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: nineteenth-century coastal hydrographic surveying with lead lines and triangulation, its motives, its debt to local informants, and the old soundings still on modern charts
title: Sounding the Shallows
subtitle: The survey ships that charted the world's coasts in the nineteenth century left a legacy that is still printed on charts today

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the nineteenth century, most of the charts carried by merchant ships were compilations of hearsay. Publishers copied coastlines from one another, added soundings reported by passing captains, and rarely tested any of it. The consequences were measured in wrecks. Over the following decades, several maritime nations created official hydrographic offices and dispatched small, slow survey vessels to chart coasts systematically, a task that occupied some ships for twenty years or more. Taken together, this effort ranks among the largest scientific undertakings of the century, and it is curious how faintly it registers in popular histories of science, which tend to favour the voyages that discovered new species over those that measured the depth of a harbour entrance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The methods were laborious. Surveyors began ashore, measuring a baseline with chains and then extending a network of triangles along the coast with a theodolite, so that headlands and hilltops could be fixed with considerable accuracy. Offshore work was done from open boats. A crew member would cast the lead line, a heavy weight on a rope marked at intervals in fathoms, and call out the depth when it touched bottom. A hollow in the base of the weight was packed with tallow, to which particles of sand, shell or mud adhered, and the nature of the seabed was entered on the chart alongside the depth, because it told a captain whether an anchor was likely to hold. The position of every sounding was fixed by measuring angles with a sextant to marks on the shore. A single chart of a moderately complex stretch of coast might demand tens of thousands of soundings and several seasons of work.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why did governments pay for all this? Teodora Hristozova, a historian of science at the Varna Institute for Maritime Studies, argues that the answer lies in commerce and strategy rather than curiosity. Her analysis of survey records shows that the order in which coasts were charted closely followed the growth of trade routes and the location of naval bases, and that the naturalists who sometimes sailed with survey ships were tolerated as passengers rather than treated as part of the mission. Hristozova's case is largely convincing, yet it risks underestimating the scientific culture that grew up within the survey service itself. Many officers took pride in standards of precision that went well beyond anything their commercial masters required, and some devoted years to observations of tides and magnetism that had no immediate practical use.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kwabena Oteng-Boakye, of the Accra Institute of Atlantic Studies, has drawn attention to a less celebrated aspect of the work. Officers' journals, he shows, are full of references to local pilots and fishermen who pointed out hidden reefs, explained the behaviour of currents and supplied the names of headlands and creeks. Almost none of these informants are credited on the printed charts, and many of the names they provided were discarded in favour of names commemorating naval officers, ships or aristocratic patrons. The criticism is fair, although it should not be overstated: on a number of coastlines, from West Africa to the Pacific, surveyors did record indigenous names, sometimes carefully transcribed, and many of them survive on charts today.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How good were the results? Lisette Ruysdonck, a marine geophysicist at the Delft Centre for Seabed Mapping, has compared nineteenth-century charts with modern surveys made using multibeam sonar, which measures a continuous swathe of the seabed rather than a series of points. Across most of the areas she examined, the old depths proved remarkably reliable, typically agreeing with modern values to within a metre. The weakness lay between the lines of soundings. A lead line samples only the spot where it lands, and a narrow pinnacle of rock rising between two lines could pass entirely unnoticed. Ruysdonck found a number of such features, some shallow enough to endanger a modern vessel, that appear on no chart made before the age of sonar.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This matters because the Victorian surveys have never been entirely replaced. Resurveying is expensive, and hydrographic offices have concentrated their resources on busy shipping lanes and ports. According to the Coastal Charting Review, a monitoring group based in Wellington, in some remote regions more than half of the depths shown on current charts derive from measurements made before 1900. The danger, in my view, lies less in the age of the data than in the confidence with which it is now used. A navigator whose satellite receiver gives a position to within a few metres may assume that the chart beneath that position is equally precise, when its soundings may have been taken by a rowing boat a century and a half ago, and several recent groundings of cruise ships in poorly surveyed waters illustrate the consequences.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The surveyors themselves would hardly be surprised. Their charts often carried notes warning that a region had been only partially examined, an honesty that modern electronic displays, with their seamless coastlines, tend to conceal. As shipping moves into less familiar waters, the case for restoring that candour, and for funding the resurveys that would make it unnecessary, has rarely been stronger.

area: the history of navigation at sea
topic: training and licensing of navigators: early modern pilot examinations, pilots versus cosmographers, printed manuals and whether formal training made ships safer
title: Navigators by Examination
subtitle: When states began to license the people who steered their ships, an old craft collided with the new learning

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of history, the art of navigation was learned the way carpentry or weaving was learned: by watching, imitating and gradually taking on responsibility under the eye of an experienced practitioner. A boy went to sea, and if he survived and showed aptitude he might, after many years, be trusted to guide a vessel himself. In the sixteenth century, as Iberian fleets began to cross the Atlantic regularly, this informal system came under strain. The royal trading houses that controlled the transatlantic trade began to require that anyone wishing to serve as a pilot on the routes to the Americas attend a course of instruction and pass a formal examination. This is often described as the birth of navigation as a licensed profession. It was certainly a significant development, but its novelty can be exaggerated: guilds of coastal pilots in several European ports had long examined their own members on local waters, even if they asked nothing about the stars.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The new requirements were demanding on paper. A candidate had first to demonstrate that he had spent at least six years at sea, a condition intended to ensure that theory would be built on a foundation of practical experience. He then attended lectures given by a royal cosmographer, in which he learned to use the astrolabe and the quadrant and to calculate his latitude by measuring the height of the sun at midday and correcting it with printed tables. Finally, he faced an oral examination before a panel of senior pilots, who questioned him about routes, landmarks and the handling of instruments. Once licensed, a pilot was obliged on returning from each voyage to report any new coastlines, shoals or islands he had encountered, so that an official master chart could be kept up to date and copied for future fleets.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How well this system worked in practice is another matter. Ximena Urkizaga, a historian at the Bilbao Institute of Atlantic History, has examined the surviving examination registers and found that almost every candidate passed, often after only a few weeks of lectures. Letters from senior pilots complain repeatedly of licences granted to men who could barely read a chart, and there are hints that some candidates simply paid for their certificates. Urkizaga concludes that the main function of the system was not to raise standards but to give the Crown control over navigational information, by gathering reports from returning pilots and restricting access to the master chart. Her evidence is compelling, but I think her conclusion goes too far. Even lenient examinations obliged candidates to master a common set of techniques, and the very existence of a written standard gave senior pilots grounds on which to complain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The examinations also brought together two groups who did not always respect each other. Gunnhild Rasmo, of the Tromsø Centre for Early Modern Science, has studied the long-running quarrels between the university-educated cosmographers who taught the courses and the pilots who were expected to apply their lessons. Pilots ridiculed cosmographers who had never been to sea and whose charts placed islands where no sailor had found them; cosmographers, in turn, protested that pilots misused instruments they did not understand. Rasmo argues that this friction was ultimately productive, because complaints from the sea forced repeated corrections to tables and charts, and instruments were redesigned in response to practical criticism. On this point she is surely right.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Knowledge of the new methods soon spread beyond the Iberian Peninsula through printed manuals, written not in Latin but in everyday languages and quickly translated into English, French and Dutch. Researchers in the Antwerp Early Print Group have traced dozens of editions published within a century, and they argue that these books made navigational science available to anyone who could read, allowing ambitious sailors to teach themselves without attending any official course. This is an attractive idea, but it sits awkwardly with what we know about their readers. The manuals were costly, many ordinary seamen could not read at all, and surviving copies tend to bear the names of gentlemen, officials and merchants rather than working mariners.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Did formal training actually make ships safer? Chidubem Ifeagwu, an economic historian at the Lagos School of Maritime Economics, has tried to answer this question for a later period by analysing insurance records from the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Comparing voyages commanded by officers who had studied at navigation schools with those commanded by men trained entirely at sea, he found no significant difference in the rate of losses until the middle of the nineteenth century. Only after examinations became compulsory and their content was revised to include newer methods did trained officers begin to outperform the rest. Ifeagwu suggests that the value of instruction depended less on the fact of schooling than on whether what was taught matched the problems navigators actually faced.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The questions raised in the sixteenth century have never really gone away. Modern maritime academies debate how much time cadets should spend in simulators rather than at sea, and whether reliance on electronic positioning is eroding the ability to navigate when systems fail. These arguments are, in essence, a continuation of the old dispute between book learning and experience, and the early experiments in licensing pilots, with all their flaws, still have something to teach those who design training today.

area: the history of scientific societies and institutions
topic: collective witnessing of experiments in seventeenth-century scientific societies: gentlemanly testimony, critical meetings, written reports and invisible technicians
title: Seen and Signed
subtitle: How the first scientific societies turned private experiments into publicly accepted facts

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the second half of the seventeenth century, small groups of physicians, clergymen, merchants and landowners in several European cities began to meet regularly in order to perform experiments and discuss their results. The best known of these gatherings received a royal charter in London in 1662, but comparable circles existed in Florence, Paris and elsewhere. Their members confronted a difficulty that modern readers can easily overlook. A claim about nature produced by one individual, working privately with apparatus that few others possessed, had no obvious claim on anyone else's belief. Ancient authority was being abandoned as a guide, and nothing had yet replaced it. The solution that emerged, which historians now call collective witnessing, deserves more credit than it usually receives, for it established the principle that a finding must be capable of public demonstration before it can count as knowledge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The procedure was simple in outline. An experiment would be performed at a meeting in front of the assembled members, who would then record that they had seen it and, in some cases, sign a statement to that effect. According to the historian Eleni Valsamaki of the Institute for the History of Learned Bodies, the signatures mattered more than the apparatus. Valsamaki argues that what made a report credible was not the precision of the instruments but the standing of those who vouched for it: a gentleman's word was assumed to be disinterested, because his income did not depend on the outcome. On this reading, the early societies borrowed the conventions of honour that governed polite society and applied them, almost unchanged, to the study of nature.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this emphasis on social rank. Pavel Druzhinin, who has catalogued the minutes of more than two thousand meetings held before 1720, points out that many demonstrations failed, and that members frequently recorded their disagreements. In his view, the meetings resembled a workshop more than a ceremony: experiments were repeated, varied and sometimes abandoned, and the witnesses were active critics rather than passive guarantors. Druzhinin's archival work is impressive, and it corrects any impression that the fellows simply applauded whatever they were shown. Yet the two accounts are less opposed than their authors suggest. A gathering could be sharply critical in its internal discussion and still rely on the reputation of its members when it came to communicating results to the outside world.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That outside world was reached chiefly through print. Since only a few dozen people could fit around a table, the societies depended on detailed written reports that allowed distant readers to imagine they had been present. These accounts described the equipment, the sequence of operations and even the failures, often at a length that seems tedious today. Astrid Hvidberg, a specialist in the history of scientific publishing, describes this style as 'virtual witnessing', and she suggests that its purpose was to multiply the audience indefinitely. Engravings of instruments played a similar role. A reader in a provincial town who had never seen an air pump could, in principle, follow every step of a trial and judge for himself whether the conclusion was justified.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is, however, a group whose contribution this story tends to leave out. The experiments demonstrated at meetings were rarely prepared by the fellows themselves. Paid assistants built and repaired the apparatus, ran trial versions in advance and, quite often, worked out why an experiment had failed. Kwabena Amanquah, whose research focuses on these technicians, has found that their names almost never appear in the published accounts, even when surviving letters show that they proposed significant modifications to the procedures. Amanquah contends that the authority of the gentleman witness was possible only because this skilled labour remained invisible. I find his argument largely convincing, although it may overstate how deliberate the concealment was; omitting assistants was simply standard practice in many trades at the time.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Collective witnessing also had practical limits. Some phenomena could not be produced on demand in a meeting room: observations of comets, reports of unusual births or accounts of distant earthquakes arrived as letters from correspondents whom nobody in the society had ever met. For these, the members fell back on judging the reliability of the informant, frequently by asking whether other trusted individuals could vouch for him. In such cases the ideal of seeing for oneself gave way to a chain of personal recommendation, and errors could travel a long way before anyone noticed them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, then, to treat early witnessing as a simple triumph of observation over authority. In many respects it replaced one kind of trust with another. Still, its enduring legacy is real. The modern expectation that methods be described in enough detail for others to repeat them descends directly from those lengthy seventeenth-century reports, and the current concern about studies that cannot be reproduced is, in a sense, a return to the founders' original question. What has changed is the scale: no room, however large, could now hold everyone whose confidence a new finding needs to win.

area: the history of scientific societies and institutions
topic: the history of peer review in the journals of learned societies: editorial control, early referee reports and post-war adoption
title: A Younger Safeguard Than We Think
subtitle: Peer review is often described as science's oldest quality check, but its history is shorter and stranger than that

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few institutions in modern science are invoked as often as peer review. When a new finding is reported in the press, the phrase 'published in a peer-reviewed journal' is offered as a kind of guarantee, and the practice is frequently described as having accompanied science since the first journals appeared in the 1660s. This picture is misleading. Although scholars have always commented on one another's work, the routine use of outside experts to decide what a journal should print is, for most fields, a development of the twentieth century. Recognising how recent it is does not diminish its value, but it should make us more cautious about the claims made on its behalf.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest scientific periodicals were essentially the projects of individuals. The journal launched in London in 1665, for example, was for many years the private enterprise of the Royal Society's secretary, who selected its contents himself and kept any profits. Only in 1752 did the Society assume formal responsibility, setting up a committee of fellows to decide which papers should be printed. According to Mariam Tarkanian, a historian of learned institutions, this committee is often misread as an early form of peer review. In her analysis, its concern was the dignity of the Society rather than the accuracy of what it published, and she notes that each volume carried a statement disclaiming responsibility for the truth of the authors' claims.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more recognisable system emerged in the 1830s, when several London societies began asking individual fellows to write reports on submitted papers. Some of these early reports were even printed, so that members could read the referee's opinion alongside the paper itself. Johannes Ollendorp argues that this tells us something about the original purpose of refereeing: rather than serving as a confidential filter, it was intended to stimulate debate and make the society's proceedings livelier, and therefore more widely read. Only later, he believes, did the reports become private judgements on whether a paper deserved to appear. Ollendorp's account is plausible, but it rests on a fairly small number of surviving documents, and it may be that practices varied too much between societies for any single purpose to be identified.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What is striking is how slowly the practice spread. Throughout the nineteenth century and well into the twentieth, many respected journals were run by a single editor, or a small editorial group, who made decisions without consulting anyone outside. This was not necessarily negligence. Submissions were relatively few, the community of specialists in a given subject was small, and an experienced editor could reasonably claim to know the field as well as any referee. Indeed, some editors regarded outside review as an unnecessary delay, and a few prominent periodicals were still accepting papers on the editor's judgement alone in the 1960s. Authors, for their part, rarely complained; a quick decision from a trusted editor was often preferred to the uncertainty of waiting for the verdict of an anonymous stranger.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The decisive change came after the Second World War. Public spending on research expanded enormously, the number of scientists multiplied, and disciplines fragmented into specialisms that no editor could hope to master. Kalliope Sevastou, who studies the politics of research funding, argues that these practical pressures explain only part of the story. In her view, external review was adopted so widely because it offered a visible sign of accountability at a time when governments were asking what they were receiving in return for their money. It is revealing, she points out, that the expression 'peer review' itself only came into common use during the 1970s, initially in debates about how grant applications should be assessed rather than in discussions of journals.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This history matters for current arguments. Peer review is now criticised for failing to detect fabricated data, for slowing publication and for favouring established researchers. Some of these criticisms are fair, but the first rests on a misunderstanding. Referees have almost never had access to raw data or laboratory notebooks, and the system was never designed to catch deliberate fraud; expecting it to do so asks more than any reviewer could deliver. Other critics go further and propose that journals abandon review before publication altogether, relying instead on open commentary once a paper has appeared. Sevastou warns that such a move could undermine public confidence, since the label has become, for many non-specialists, the only available measure of reliability.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Both sides in this debate tend to appeal to tradition, whether to defend peer review as a time-honoured safeguard or to dismiss it as an outdated ritual. The historical record supports neither position. Peer review is too young to be regarded as an inheritance from the founders of modern science, yet it has proved too useful, across too many disciplines, to be discarded as a mere formality. What it reveals instead is an arrangement that has changed repeatedly in response to the size, funding and expectations of the scientific community. There is no reason to suppose that its present form is final, and proposed reforms ought to be judged on the evidence of what they achieve, not on whether they seem to honour or betray the past.
