area: the history of measurement and standards
topic: the standardisation of musical pitch: local organ pitches, nineteenth-century pitch inflation, the 1859 French standard and the 440-hertz agreement
title: Tuning the World
subtitle: The search for a single musical pitch reveals what makes artistic standards different from scientific ones

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before any orchestral concert begins, the principal oboist sounds a single note, the A above middle C, and the other players adjust their instruments to match it. Today that note is generally expected to vibrate 440 times per second, and the ritual appears so natural that few listeners give it a moment's thought. Yet the notion that music has one correct pitch is a surprisingly recent invention. For most of the history of Western music, the frequency of a given note was a local matter, and what counted as an A in one city might have been heard as something closer to a B flat or a G sharp in the next. The story of how a single number came to be accepted is, in many ways, a story about the limits of standardisation itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Until the nineteenth century, the pitch of a town's music was usually set by its church organ. Because organs were expensive to build and almost impossible to retune substantially, they fixed the pitch for generations, and neighbouring towns could differ by a semitone or more. Dr Henrike Vosskuhl, an organologist at the Hanseatic Institute for Musical Instruments, has measured hundreds of surviving organ pipes and early tuning forks to reconstruct these local pitches. She argues that the variation was far less troublesome than modern musicians imagine. Travelling performers carried instruments with interchangeable sections, and singers and players routinely transposed their music into a different key when they arrived somewhere new. Her reconstruction is meticulous, although it rests heavily on organs, and it is not obvious that the pitch of a cathedral instrument tells us much about the pitch used by a travelling theatre company or a household ensemble.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: During the nineteenth century, pitch began to climb. Orchestras in Vienna, Paris and London gradually tuned higher, apparently in search of a more brilliant sound, and by mid-century the A in some theatres had risen well above 450 vibrations per second. Professor Matteo Scarabelli, a music historian at the Conservatory of Brescia, attributes this rise above all to competition among manufacturers of wind instruments, who discovered that a slightly sharper instrument sounded more impressive when compared side by side with a rival's. This is a plausible account, but it overstates the case: audiences, too, rewarded brilliance, and conductors were quick to exploit their enthusiasm. Singers were the chief victims. Dr Joost Oudemans, a voice physiologist who has studied singers' letters from the period, believes that the strain of performing at ever higher pitches shortened a number of careers, though he admits that the evidence is anecdotal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The first serious attempt to halt the rise came from France. In 1859 a government commission, including composers and physicists, fixed the A at 435 vibrations per second and embodied the decision in an official tuning fork, which was kept as a legal reference in much the same way as the standard metre. Several other countries gradually adopted the French figure, but Britain resisted for decades, many of its orchestras continuing to play at a considerably higher pitch. The French standard was therefore less a universal settlement than one regional preference among several, albeit an influential one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The modern figure of 440 was agreed at an international conference in 1939. One motive was the spread of radio: broadcasters transmitting music across borders needed a common reference tone that listeners and performers everywhere could rely on. Dr Rosalind Fitzalan, an acoustician at the Northern College of Sound Engineering, argues that the decisive factor was technological. Tuning forks shift slightly with temperature and wear, so no physical object could guarantee a perfectly stable frequency; only electronic oscillators, which became widespread in the 1930s, allowed a pitch to be generated identically in any studio. Fitzalan is surely right that this technology was necessary, but it was not sufficient. An electronic signal could reproduce any frequency equally well, and it took negotiation, not engineering, to decide which one should be reproduced.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even now, the standard is far from universally observed. Many leading orchestras tune a little higher, at 442 or even 445, while ensembles specialising in Baroque music commonly tune to about 415, a semitone below the modern standard, in an attempt to recreate the sound of the period. Fitzalan regards this drift as evidence that the 1939 agreement has partly failed. Vosskuhl, by contrast, welcomes it as a return to the healthy diversity of earlier centuries. Neither interpretation seems entirely satisfactory. The value of 440 lies not in compelling every performer to adopt it but in providing a fixed point from which deliberate departures can be measured and described.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This points to a fundamental difference between scientific and artistic standards. A metre or a kilogram must mean exactly the same thing in every laboratory, because any discrepancy undermines the comparison of results. A musical pitch, however, only needs to be shared by the people who are playing together at a particular moment. Seen in this light, the variations that persist today are not errors awaiting correction but choices, and critics who treat every departure from 440 as a lapse in discipline have perhaps misunderstood what a musical standard is for.

area: the history of measurement and standards
topic: the ancient Egyptian royal cubit: surviving cubit rods, the question of a master standard, ceremonial stone rods and the fiscal role of measurement
title: Measured by the Forearm
subtitle: What surviving cubit rods reveal about how ancient Egypt kept its units of length in order

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The earliest units of length were taken from the human body. Fingers, palms, feet and forearms were always available and required no special equipment, but they suffered from an obvious defect: no two bodies are quite the same. The royal cubit of ancient Egypt is the oldest well-documented attempt to overcome this problem by tying a unit derived from the body, in this case the length of the forearm from elbow to fingertip, to a physical object that could be copied and checked. It is often celebrated as an early triumph of mathematics, but it deserves to be remembered chiefly as a feat of administration, since its real achievement was to persuade officials and workers across a long and narrow kingdom to measure in the same way.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The royal cubit measured roughly 52.4 centimetres. It was divided into seven palms, each of which was subdivided into four digits, and it was distinct from a shorter common cubit of six palms, which measured about 45 centimetres. Several dozen cubit rods have survived, the great majority recovered from tombs rather than from quarries or construction sites. Some are plain wooden rules, worn from handling; others are carved from stone and inscribed with lists of deities, divisions of the digit into fractions and dedications to the rulers of the day. These stone examples are often heavy and highly decorated, characteristics that hardly suggest daily use on a building site.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ilinca Draganova, a metrologist at the Institute for Ancient Technology in Sofia, has measured more than thirty surviving rods with modern instruments. She reports that many of them agree with one another to within one or two millimetres, even when they were found at sites hundreds of kilometres apart and made centuries apart. In her view, such consistency could only have been achieved if working rods were regularly copied from, and checked against, a master standard held by a central authority. Her results are striking, but they may be less representative than they appear. Rods placed in the tombs of officials were presumably of the finest workmanship available, whereas the everyday rods of builders, which would have rotted, broken or been reused as firewood, may well have varied considerably more.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different interpretation is offered by Dr Fabrizia Ravasio of the University of Pavia, who argues that the stone rods were never intended as measuring tools at all. Their inscriptions, she suggests, served a religious function, linking the act of measurement to the cosmic order that the king was obliged to maintain. On this view, the precision of Egyptian building was achieved by other means: knotted cords stretched between pegs, standard procedures handed down within workshops, and the repeated checking of new work against existing structures. The results were certainly remarkable; the four sides of the base of the Great Pyramid, each around 230 metres long, differ in length by only a few centimetres. Ravasio's reading of the stone rods is convincing, yet it is difficult to believe that cords, which stretch when wet and sag over long distances, could by themselves have delivered accuracy of this order.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach emphasises the economic purpose of measurement. Professor Hendrik Haarbosch of the Leiden Centre for Near Eastern Studies points out that the prosperity of Egypt depended on the annual flood of the Nile, and that the height of the river was recorded on graduated structures known as Nilometers, which were marked in cubits. Because a high flood promised a generous harvest, these readings were used to set the level of taxation for the coming year. The flood also washed away field boundaries, so surveyors had to measure the land again after the waters receded. For Haarbosch, the cubit was above all a fiscal instrument, and its standardisation was driven by the state's need to assess land and produce fairly and predictably.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Haarbosch's emphasis is a useful corrective to accounts that dwell only on monumental architecture. However, it would be a mistake to set economic motives against religious ones, as though the Egyptians themselves drew such a distinction. Temples owned vast estates, stored grain and employed scribes and surveyors; they were, in effect, economic institutions as much as places of worship. A rod inscribed with the names of gods may have carried authority precisely because the sacred and the administrative were inseparable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whether the Egyptian cubit influenced the units of later civilisations remains uncertain. Related cubits were used elsewhere in the ancient Near East, but their lengths differ, and attempts to trace a direct line from Egyptian rods to medieval or modern units are largely speculative. What the rods do demonstrate is that a measurement standard has never depended on a physical object alone. Its authority came from a combination of a reference artefact, institutions willing to enforce it and a shared belief that it ought to be respected, a combination that, as the long reverence for the international prototype of the kilogram suggests, has proved remarkably durable.

area: the history of measurement and standards
topic: the regulation of weights and measures in medieval markets: royal decrees, town standards, the bread assize and local variation in measures
title: A Fair Bushel
subtitle: Medieval markets are often imagined as places of confusion and fraud, but their system of measures had a logic of its own

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a medieval market town, almost every transaction involved an act of measurement. Grain was sold by the bushel, cloth by the ell, ale by the gallon and wool by the stone, and none of these units had a single fixed value. A bushel in one town might hold noticeably more than a bushel twenty miles away, and even within a single market, oats and wheat could be sold by containers of different sizes. To modern eyes, accustomed to the uniformity of the metric system, this looks like chaos, and it has frequently been described as such. Yet that judgement, in my view, misunderstands what medieval measures were meant to achieve. Their purpose was not to make every unit identical across a kingdom, but to ensure that buyers and sellers in a particular place could trust one another.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: This is not to say that rulers were indifferent to uniformity. In England, a famous charter of 1215 declared that there should be one measure of wine, ale and corn throughout the realm, and similar declarations were repeated by monarch after monarch over the following centuries. Dr Wiktor Kasprzycki, an economic historian at the University of Kraków, interprets this endless repetition as clear proof of failure. Local lords, he argues, had every reason to resist, since they often collected rents and dues in kind using their own measures, which tended to be generously large. The incentive to keep them was simply too strong for distant royal officials to overcome. Kasprzycki is right about the lords' motives, but repetition need not mean that the decrees achieved nothing; laws against theft are also reissued constantly, and no one concludes from this that they are ignored.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: At the level of the town, the system was considerably more effective. Most boroughs kept master weights and measures, usually cast in bronze or brass, in the guildhall or the parish church, and officials known as searchers were appointed to inspect the scales and containers used by traders. Merchants found using false weights could be fined, and repeat offenders might have their equipment publicly destroyed. Bakers were watched with particular care, because bread was the staple food of the poor. A baker who sold underweight loaves could be paraded through the streets or placed in the pillory, where neighbours could jeer at him. Under the regulation known as the assize of bread, the price of a standard loaf remained fixed, while its weight was adjusted up or down according to the current price of grain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: To modern readers, varying the weight rather than the price seems an odd choice. Professor Chidinma Nwaokolo of the Lagos School of Economic History argues that it was in fact an ingenious solution to a practical problem. Medieval economies suffered from a chronic shortage of small coins; the smallest silver penny was worth a considerable sum to a labourer, and there was often no convenient way to charge a fraction of it. By holding the price constant and allowing the loaf to grow or shrink, the assize functioned as an early form of price indexing that protected consumers without requiring coins that did not exist. Nwaokolo's case is persuasive, and it is a useful reminder that apparently strange institutions often make sense once the constraints of their time are understood.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A less flattering picture emerges from the work of Dr Ingrid Sunnanå, a social historian at the University of Bergen, who has examined thousands of entries in the records of local courts. She finds that prosecutions for false measures were extremely common, but that the fines imposed were generally small and that the same traders appeared year after year. In her view, the penalties operated less as a deterrent than as a kind of licence fee: traders paid them as a routine cost of doing business, and town authorities welcomed them as a dependable source of income. Her figures are difficult to dispute, but her conclusion is too cynical. The public shaming of dishonest bakers, which brought no revenue at all, suggests that communities regarded short measure as a genuine moral offence and not merely as an opportunity for profit.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Much of what looks like confusion also had a rational basis. Some goods were sold by heaped measure, with the grain piled above the rim, others by struck measure, levelled off with a straight stick, and custom determined which method applied to which commodity. Local measures often reflected local conditions, such as the typical density of a region's grain or the width of cloth produced on its looms. Experienced merchants carried the necessary conversions in their heads, and a trader moving between markets was no more confused by different bushels than a modern traveller is by different currencies.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Pressure for genuine national uniformity grew only gradually, as long-distance trade expanded and centralised states sought to tax production on a consistent basis. When the metric system was finally introduced in France at the end of the eighteenth century, its champions presented it as the replacement of medieval disorder with rational order. That story has shaped our view of the medieval market ever since. It would be better to recognise that earlier measures answered a different question. They did not ask whether a bushel was the same everywhere, but whether the bushel in front of the buyer was honest, and by that standard they were often remarkably successful.

area: the history of measurement and standards
topic: the failure to standardise clothing sizes: early anthropometric surveys, brand-specific sizing, vanity sizing and body scanning
title: One Size Fits None
subtitle: Why the numbers on clothing labels have resisted every attempt to turn them into a genuine standard

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has carried three garments marked with the same size into a fitting room, only to find that one is too tight, one too loose and one roughly acceptable, has encountered one of the strangest anomalies in modern measurement. In an age when the length of a second is defined by the vibrations of atoms, the numbers printed on clothing labels remain stubbornly unreliable. It is tempting to blame the complexity of the human body, and that complexity is real. Nevertheless, the persistent confusion of clothing sizes is, I believe, less a failure of measurement than a failure of incentives: the technical means of creating a workable standard have existed for decades, but those in a position to adopt one have rarely had a reason to do so.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, most clothing was made to measure, either at home or by a tailor, and the question of standard sizes scarcely arose. Ready-made garments spread first in menswear, helped by the experience of supplying uniforms to large armies, and men's clothing came to be labelled by direct body measurements such as chest and waist in inches, a practice that largely survives. Women's clothing followed a different path. Its size numbers were originally linked, loosely, to the age of the wearer, and they soon became abstract codes with no obvious relationship to any part of the body. This difference has had lasting consequences, since a label that states a measurement can be checked by the buyer, whereas an arbitrary number cannot.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious attempt to impose order came at the end of the 1930s, when a government survey in the United States measured nearly fifteen thousand women in an effort to give manufacturers and mail-order companies a reliable basis for their patterns. The project was undermined from the outset by its sample. Volunteers were paid a small fee, which attracted disproportionate numbers of poorer women, and the selection of participants excluded many groups altogether. The resulting commercial standard, published two decades later, was quietly withdrawn in the 1980s. Professor Miroslava Tsvetanova, an anthropometrist at the Balkan Institute of Human Measurement, argues that the deeper problem was conceptual. Any scheme that assigns a single number to a garment, she contends, must assume that bodies of a given size share the same proportions, an assumption that her own measurements repeatedly contradict. Her analysis explains convincingly why the standard fitted so few women, but it does not explain why the industry abandoned it rather than attempting to improve it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That question is better answered by Dr Iker Zubillaga, a business historian at the Basque School of Commerce. Zubillaga shows that, as the clothing market fragmented in the decades after the Second World War, manufacturers increasingly saw sizing not as a technical convention but as a commercial tool. A company aiming at younger customers might cut its garments slimmer; another, targeting older shoppers, might cut them more generously. Once customers learned that a particular label fitted them, they were likely to return to it. In Zubillaga's account, a distinctive sizing system became part of a brand's identity, and a shared standard would have destroyed that advantage.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Incentives also help to explain the phenomenon known as vanity sizing, the gradual reduction over several decades in the numbers attached to garments of the same physical dimensions. Dr Annelise Brakstad, a consumer psychologist at the Trondheim Business Institute, has conducted experiments in which participants tried on identical garments carrying different labels. Those told they were wearing a smaller size rated the clothes more highly and expressed greater willingness to buy them, although the effect was modest and faded when participants were reminded of the arbitrary nature of labels. Her experiments were carefully designed, but they took place in a laboratory, and it is far from clear that the same effect operates in a crowded shop. Even so, the sheer persistence of the practice suggests that retailers, at least, are convinced it boosts sales.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some observers believe that technology will soon make the whole debate irrelevant. Dr Haruto Kinugasa, who develops measurement software at the Osaka Centre for Digital Fit, argues that three-dimensional body scanners and smartphone measurement applications will allow every shopper to be matched to individual garments, rendering fixed size categories obsolete. The technology is undoubtedly impressive. However, the body data it gathers is typically held by individual retailers and software companies, each with its own methods and its own commercial interest in keeping customers loyal. Rather than producing a common standard, such systems seem more likely to replace one form of fragmentation with another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If there is a reason for cautious optimism, it lies in the economics of online shopping. A substantial proportion of clothes bought on the internet are returned, and poor fit is the most frequently cited reason. Returns are expensive to process, and the cost falls on the retailers themselves. For the first time, the industry may face a financial penalty for incompatibility large enough to outweigh the advantages of distinctive sizing. Whether this will be sufficient to produce a genuine standard remains uncertain; the history of clothing sizes suggests that the industry has a remarkable capacity to tolerate inconvenience, provided that someone else bears most of its cost.

area: the history of measurement and standards
topic: international paper sizes: the square-root-of-two ratio behind the A series, its institutional spread, and the survival of North American letter size
title: The Shape of a Page
subtitle: The ordinary sheet of office paper conceals one of the most elegant standards ever devised, and one of the most stubborn exceptions to it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people handle sheets of A4 paper every day without giving their dimensions a second thought. Yet those dimensions are the product of a remarkably clever idea. The ratio between the long side and the short side of every sheet in the A series is the square root of two, approximately 1.414. This particular proportion has a unique property: when a sheet is folded or cut in half across its longer side, the two halves have exactly the same shape as the original. The largest sheet, A0, has an area of one square metre, and each smaller size is half of the one before, so that an A4 sheet is one sixteenth of a square metre. It could be argued that the most successful standards of measurement are those that no one notices, and by that test the A series is among the best ever designed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The underlying idea is older than the standard itself. An eighteenth-century German scientist described the advantages of the square-root-of-two ratio in a letter, and in 1798 the French revolutionary government included formats based on the same principle in a law governing the taxation of paper. Neither proposal, however, came into general use. The system as it is known today was published by the German national standards body in 1922, spread to a number of European countries between the two world wars, and was adopted by many more after 1945. In 1975 it became an international standard, and it is now used officially in almost every country in the world.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why did a scheme that had languished for more than a century suddenly succeed? Dr Rafael Montesdeoca, a historian of printing at the University of Seville, insists that its mathematical elegance had little to do with it. The decisive factor, in his view, was institutional. Government departments consumed enormous quantities of printed forms, and once a national bureaucracy adopted the new formats, it required its suppliers to do the same, creating a market that private printers could not afford to ignore. This account is largely persuasive, but it underestimates the appeal of the design itself. The standards committees that recommended the system were composed largely of engineers, and it is hard to imagine that a proposal of such logical simplicity did not help to win their support.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Once adopted, the system brought practical benefits that went well beyond tidiness. Because all A-series sheets share the same proportions, a document can be enlarged or reduced from one size to another on a copier without leaving awkward margins or cutting off text. Envelopes in the related C series are designed to hold A-series sheets, either flat or folded, and filing cabinets, binders and printers can all be built to a predictable set of dimensions. Professor Pavel Hromádka, an economist at the Prague Institute of Applied Economics, has attempted to estimate the savings in paper and labour that resulted. His figures are impressive, but they should be treated with caution, since no one can know with any confidence how much would have been wasted had the standard never been introduced.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The great exception is North America, where the dominant office format is letter size, a sheet measuring eight and a half by eleven inches. Its origins are obscure: it has been suggested that the dimensions derive from the size of the moulds used to make paper by hand, but no conclusive evidence has been found. Canada experimented with metric paper formats during its conversion to metric units, before largely returning to the traditional size. Dr Lotte Brennecke, a historian of graphic design at the Hamburg Academy of Visual Communication, defends the American format, arguing that its wider proportions are better suited to certain page layouts, such as documents set in two columns, and that the elegance of the square-root ratio means nothing to the person actually reading a page. Brennecke is right that readers do not care about ratios, but she gives too little weight to the costs of incompatibility. Documents sent between continents are routinely printed with text cut off at the bottom or with large blank areas, and organisations working internationally must stock two kinds of paper and adjust their equipment accordingly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why, then, has the United States not switched? Hromádka offers a straightforward explanation. The costs of conversion, from replacing printing equipment and filing systems to redesigning forms, would have to be paid immediately and by identifiable organisations, whereas the benefits would arrive gradually and be spread thinly across the whole economy. In such circumstances, he argues, a superior standard can fail to displace an established one indefinitely, regardless of its merits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One might expect the rise of digital documents to make the whole question irrelevant. Much of what was once printed is now read on screens, and electronic files can in principle be displayed at any size. Yet paper formats have proved surprisingly persistent even in the digital world. Word-processing software opens with a default page size, electronic documents are formatted for printing whether or not they are ever printed, and the dimensions of a sheet of paper continue to shape the layout of countless screens. In this sense, a standard that began as a matter of physical convenience has become embedded in the infrastructure of digital technology, and it is likely to outlast much of the paper it was designed to describe.

area: the history of measurement and standards
topic: the nineteenth-century standardisation of electrical resistance: telegraph cable testing, rival wire and mercury units, the absolute ohm and international congresses
title: A Matter of Resistance
subtitle: How the telegraph industry and the physics laboratory together produced the ohm

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1860s, the crew of a cable ship searching for a fault in a submarine telegraph line faced a peculiar difficulty. The standard technique for locating a break was to measure the electrical resistance of the cable from the shore and, knowing the resistance of each mile of conductor, to calculate how far along the line the damage lay. The method was sound in principle, but it depended on figures supplied by different manufacturers, each of whom expressed resistance in a unit of its own devising. A number that meant one thing in a London workshop meant something else in Berlin. It is often said that the ohm was a gift of pure science to industry. The history of the unit suggests, on the contrary, that it was industry's urgent demands that first set scientists to work.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Before any common unit existed, many firms defined resistance as that of a specified length of copper wire of a particular thickness. The difficulty was that the resistance of copper varies considerably with its purity and temperature, so two coils made to the same specification could give noticeably different readings. A German manufacturer proposed an alternative: the resistance of a column of mercury one metre long and one square millimetre in cross-section, measured at the temperature of melting ice. Mercury could be purified relatively easily, and as a liquid it took the exact shape of its container. Dr Wendela Kooistra, a historian of physics at the University of Groningen, argues that this made the mercury unit far easier to reproduce reliably in any laboratory, and that British reluctance to adopt it owed much to national pride. That pride undoubtedly played a part, but it was not the whole story.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In 1861 a committee of British scientists was appointed to establish a standard of resistance. Its members wanted something more ambitious than a convenient reference object: an absolute unit, derived from the fundamental units of length, mass and time, so that electrical quantities could be related directly to mechanical work and heat. Determining such a unit required an elaborate experiment in which a coil was spun in the earth's magnetic field. Having carried it out, the committee distributed sets of wire coils whose resistance matched the value obtained. Professor Saeed Al-Mukhaini, of the Gulf Institute for the History of Science, maintains that the committee's motives were essentially theoretical, and that the needs of the telegraph companies were at most a secondary consideration. Al-Mukhaini is right that the theoretical ambition was genuine; nonetheless, several leading members of the committee had close financial links with cable companies, and it is implausible that commercial concerns carried as little weight as he suggests.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: By the late 1870s, however, more careful measurements indicated that the British coils differed from their intended absolute value by roughly one per cent, an error that was far from trivial for the engineers who depended on them. Dr Paulo Rebouças, a metrologist at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, regards this episode as a vindication of the mercury unit. In his view, the error demonstrated the danger of tying a unit to an experiment so demanding that few laboratories could repeat it, whereas a mercury column could be checked almost anywhere. The lesson is less clear-cut than he implies. What followed was not the defeat of the absolute principle but a compromise between the two approaches.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That compromise was worked out at a series of international meetings. A congress held in Paris in 1881 endorsed the absolute definition of the unit, but recognised that it could not be realised conveniently in everyday practice. A provisional standard agreed in 1884 therefore specified a mercury column 106 centimetres long, chosen to match the absolute ohm as closely as measurements then allowed. In 1893, a further congress in Chicago refined the figure to 106.3 centimetres and specified the mass of the mercury column as well as its length, removing the need to measure its cross-section directly. Dr Inés Coloma, a sociologist of science at the University of Zaragoza, stresses that these outcomes were shaped by diplomacy as much as by data. Delegates bargained over wording, and national committees were reluctant to accept definitions that appeared to favour a rival's instruments.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The history of the ohm is frequently presented as a contest between two philosophies of measurement, one practical and one theoretical, in which one side eventually triumphed. That framing seems to me mistaken. The eventual settlement retained a theoretical definition while relying on a practical object to embody it, and each approach compensated for the weakness of the other. The same pattern has recurred since. For much of the twentieth century, the international unit was maintained by carefully preserved resistors, and in 1990 a conventional value based on a quantum effect was adopted for practical use, even though it was not formally part of the international system of units until that system was revised in 2019.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the achievement of the nineteenth-century physicists, but it does call into question the tidy story in which science supplies standards and industry merely receives them. The ohm was produced by the interaction of commercial need, theoretical ambition and international negotiation, and an account that leaves out any one of these is likely to misrepresent how measurement standards are actually made. If anything, it is the cable engineer on the deck of a ship, rather than the scientist in the laboratory, who deserves to be remembered as the unit's first and most demanding customer.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: why people did not smile in nineteenth-century photographic portraits: exposure times, painting conventions, permanence and the rise of the snapshot smile
title: Faces Without Smiles
subtitle: The stern expressions of early portrait photography are usually blamed on slow cameras, but the full explanation is more interesting

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who leafs through an album of nineteenth-century portraits will be struck by the same thing: almost nobody is smiling. Men stare at the lens with set jaws, women hold their lips in a tight line, and even small children appear to have been instructed in solemnity. The explanation offered in most popular accounts is technical. Early cameras, it is said, required sitters to remain motionless for so long that a smile could not be sustained, and so people simply relaxed their faces into neutrality. This account has the appeal of simplicity, and it is not entirely wrong. But it is too tidy to bear the weight usually placed upon it, and the historians who have examined the question most closely disagree sharply about what else was involved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: There is no doubt that the first photographic processes were extraordinarily slow. A daguerreotype made in the early 1840s could demand an exposure of several minutes in strong daylight, and studios fitted iron stands behind their chairs to brace the sitter's neck and waist. Takeshi Iwabuchi, a historian of photographic technology at the Osaka Institute of Visual Media, argues that this physical ordeal remains the decisive factor. Even after the wet collodion process reduced exposures to a handful of seconds in the 1850s, he notes, a smile held for that long tends to collapse into something closer to a grimace, and any movement of the mouth registers as a smudge. Photographers, Iwabuchi contends, learned to discourage expressions that would spoil the plate, and their advice hardened into a habit that outlived its original cause.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ilona Querol, an art historian based at the Budapest Academy of Visual Culture, finds this argument incomplete. She points out that by the 1880s dry gelatine plates allowed exposures of a fraction of a second, yet broad smiles remained rare in studio portraits for at least another three decades. To explain this persistence, Querol looks to painting. For centuries, she argues, an open-mouthed smile in a portrait had signalled drunkenness, foolishness or low social standing; it belonged to tavern scenes and comic peasants, not to people of property. Early photographers, many of whom had trained as miniature painters, carried these conventions into the new medium, and their customers expected a likeness that conveyed composure and respectability rather than fleeting good humour.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third interpretation emphasises the meaning of the photograph itself. For Adebayo Sowunmi, a social historian at the Lagos Centre for Comparative History, the crucial point is that a studio portrait was, for most families, an expensive and infrequent purchase. It might be the only image by which a person would be remembered by grandchildren who never met them, and this sense of permanence encouraged sitters to present what they regarded as their true and lasting character. Sowunmi draws attention to the popularity of memorial portraits of the recently deceased, arguing that the boundary between commemorating the living and the dead was less distinct than modern viewers assume. His reading is persuasive, but it is also difficult to test, since sitters rarely recorded what they were thinking as they faced the camera.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One explanation that circulates widely can probably be set aside. It is often claimed that poor dental health made people reluctant to show their teeth. Gareth Tamblyn, who has studied dentistry in Victorian Britain, set out to find support for this idea and was surprised by how little he discovered. Etiquette manuals and private letters of the period, he reports, almost never mention teeth in connection with portraits, and in any case a closed-mouth smile would have concealed them perfectly well. Tamblyn concludes that the dental theory owes more to modern assumptions about the past than to any historical record, and on this point his scepticism seems entirely justified.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, then, brought the smile into photographs? The change gathered pace in the early twentieth century, when cheap roll-film cameras placed photography in the hands of ordinary people, who used it to record holidays, picnics and family gatherings rather than formal occasions. Lucia Mendizabal, a media historian at the Bilbao School of Communication, has examined the trade catalogues and order books of commercial studios from this period. She found that after about 1910 many studios began to advertise their ability to capture a 'natural and pleasant expression', and she argues that it was this marketing, together with the advertising of camera manufacturers, that taught the public to associate photographs with happiness. Her evidence is valuable, yet it seems unlikely that advertisers could have created such a shift on their own; more probably they amplified a relaxation of manners that was already under way.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If no single factor accounts for the unsmiling faces of the nineteenth century, the debate nonetheless carries a broader lesson. Photographs are frequently treated as transparent windows onto the past, but a portrait records a negotiation between sitter, photographer and convention as much as it records a face. To conclude from these sombre images that the Victorians were a joyless people would be a serious misreading. Their expressions tell us a good deal about what they believed a portrait was for, and very little about how they actually felt.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: colour in silent cinema: stencil colouring, tinting and toning, the loss of colour through black-and-white archive copying, and debates over colour restoration
title: The Forgotten Colours of the Silent Screen
subtitle: Early cinema is remembered in shades of grey, but audiences of the time saw something quite different

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask most people to picture a film from the 1910s and they will imagine a flickering image in shades of grey. The assumption is understandable but largely mistaken. A substantial proportion of the films shown in cinemas before the arrival of sound were coloured in some way, and in certain years and countries coloured prints were the norm rather than the exception. That this fact has been so thoroughly forgotten says less about early cinema than about the way its history has been preserved, and correcting the impression is arguably one of the more important tasks facing film archives today.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Three principal techniques were used. The most laborious was stencil colouring, in which workers, very often young women employed in specialist workshops, cut separate stencils for each colour and applied dyes to individual frames with fine brushes or velvet pads. Far more widespread were tinting and toning. Tinting involved immersing a length of developed film in dye, so that the lighter areas of the image took on a uniform hue, while toning replaced the silver of the image with a coloured compound, leaving the highlights clear. The two could be combined, giving, for instance, a sunset scene with orange skies and deep purple shadows. By the early 1920s, film manufacturers were selling pre-tinted stock in a range of named shades, which suggests how routine the practice had become.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, did colour vanish from collective memory? Part of the answer lies in the economics of preservation. When archives began copying deteriorating nitrate prints in the middle of the twentieth century, duplicating onto colour stock was expensive and, in the view of many curators, unnecessary. Countless tinted originals were therefore reproduced on black-and-white film and the originals discarded. Some coloured prints survived only because private collectors held on to them, often unaware that public archives had chosen to keep monochrome duplicates instead.Galina Kolomiets, a conservator at the Riga Moving Image Archive, estimates that in some national collections more than half of the surviving silent features exist today only in monochrome copies of what were once coloured prints. Television broadcasts and later home-video releases, which drew on these copies, completed the process of making grey seem authentic.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kolomiets argues that archives have a duty to restore the colours wherever documentary evidence allows. Many prints carried instructions scratched or written on their leaders, the blank strips at the start of each reel, and some distributors' catalogues specify which tint was to be used for each scene. Using such sources, her team has reconstructed the colour schemes of several dozen films, and audiences who see the results often report that the films seem less remote and more emotionally direct. For Kolomiets, presenting these works in black and white is a distortion comparable to exhibiting a painted medieval statue that has been stripped to bare stone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares her enthusiasm. Marc Duvernoy, a film historian at the Lyon Institute for Cinema Studies, maintains that tinting was largely a matter of routine convention rather than artistic choice. Blue indicated night, amber suggested lamplight, red signalled fire or danger, and these codes were applied by laboratory staff with little reference to directors. In his view, restorers who treat every tint as a deliberate aesthetic decision risk attributing to film-makers an intention they did not have. He concedes that a handful of directors supervised the tinting of their own films closely, but he regards them as exceptions. Duvernoy's point about the conventional nature of tinting is well taken, but it does not follow that the colours were unimportant. Conventions shape how audiences experience a film, and a night scene printed in grey loses information that viewers of the period would have taken for granted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more technical objection comes from Samir Elkholy, a chemist who studies the degradation of photographic dyes at the Alexandria Centre for Materials Conservation. The aniline dyes used for tinting, he explains, were notoriously unstable, and exposure to light and heat during repeated projection altered them in unpredictable ways. A surviving print that now looks pale pink may originally have been a strong red; one that appears brown may have been closer to green. Elkholy does not oppose restoration, but he warns that digitally recreated colours are, at best, informed estimates, and that archives should say so clearly rather than presenting them as recovered originals. He also notes that the same tint could look quite different depending on the lamp in the projector and the colour of the screen, so that even a perfectly preserved print would not guarantee an identical experience.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Elkholy's caution and Kolomiets's ambition are less opposed than they first appear. A restoration that is honest about its uncertainties is still a better guide to how early audiences saw these films than a monochrome copy that conceals the very existence of colour. What matters is that viewers understand what they are watching, and accompanying notes or introductions can make the basis of each reconstruction clear without spoiling the experience. The silent screen was never simply black and white, and the sooner that misconception is abandoned, the more clearly the achievements of early cinema will be seen.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: the decay of nitrate and acetate film and the debate between physical storage and digitisation in film preservation
title: Saving the Reels
subtitle: Most of the films made in cinema's first decades have disappeared, and archivists still disagree about how best to protect what remains

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is commonly estimated that the majority of feature films produced before 1930 no longer exist in any form. The usual villain in this story is cellulose nitrate, the highly flammable material on which films were printed until the early 1950s, and it is true that vault fires destroyed entire collections in a matter of minutes. Yet to blame the chemistry alone is to misunderstand what happened. Far more films were lost through indifference than through combustion. Studios regarded their productions as commercial goods with a short life in cinemas, and once a film had finished its run, the prints were frequently melted down to recover the silver they contained or simply thrown away to save the cost of storage.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Nitrate does, however, decay, and it does so in a recognisable series of stages. The image first begins to fade while the base takes on an amber tint; the film then becomes sticky and gives off a pungent odour; bubbles appear on its surface; and eventually the reel is reduced to a brown powder. Crucially, the gases released as the material breaks down speed up the decay of any other reels kept close by, so that a single neglected can may endanger an entire shelf. How quickly a reel passes through these stages depends heavily on where and how it has been kept.For decades this process was assumed to be unstoppable, and archives routinely copied their nitrate holdings onto newer stock and then destroyed the originals as a fire risk.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That assumption has been challenged by Annika Ostergren, a conservation scientist at the Nordic Film Conservation Laboratory. By monitoring reels held in different conditions over a period of twenty years, her group demonstrated that nitrate kept at low temperatures and low humidity deteriorates so slowly that many prints could survive for several centuries. Ostergren concludes that the wholesale destruction of nitrate originals after copying was a serious error, since the copies were often of poorer quality and sometimes omitted material altogether. Given her data, this conclusion is hard to dispute.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The irony is that the material introduced to replace nitrate has proved less reliable than expected. Cellulose acetate, or 'safety film', was welcomed in the 1950s as a lasting solution, being far less flammable. Within a few decades, however, archivists began to notice reels giving off a sharp smell of vinegar, a sign that the acetate was breaking down chemically. Once this so-called vinegar syndrome begins, the film shrinks and buckles, and in poorly controlled vaults some acetate prints are now in worse condition than nitrate prints several decades older. Archives in hot and humid climates have been especially badly affected, and some have lost much of their mid-century output to the condition.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Today the debate centres on digitisation. Federica Pazienza, director of the Piedmont Audiovisual Heritage Foundation, argues that high-resolution scanning is the only realistic way to make archival films available to scholars and the public. A film locked in a refrigerated vault, she points out, is safe but invisible, and a work that nobody can watch has, for practical purposes, no cultural existence at all. Her foundation has scanned several thousand titles and made many of them freely available online, which has led to a surge of interest in productions that had not been screened for generations. Pazienza accepts that scanning is costly, but she insists that the expense must be weighed against the public benefit of access.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Others warn that digital files are a poor substitute for film as a means of long-term preservation. Batbayar Gansukh, who researches digital preservation at the Ulaanbaatar Institute of Information Science, notes that storage media and file formats become obsolete within a few years, so that digital collections must be continually copied onto new systems and checked for corruption. A reel of film in a cold vault, by contrast, needs little more than stable conditions and occasional inspection. Over the long term, Gansukh calculates, maintaining a digital master costs considerably more than keeping the equivalent film, and a single interruption in funding could render a digital collection unreadable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from the film historian Rosalind Harrowgate, who stresses that a print is a historical object as well as a carrier of images. Original reels bear splices that reveal where censors removed scenes, handwritten notes from projectionists and manufacturers' codes along the edges that allow a copy to be dated. None of this, she observes, survives in a scan, which records the picture but discards the physical evidence surrounding it. Harrowgate's point is important, but it cannot be applied without limit: no archive has the space or money to keep every print it receives, and decisions about which objects to retain are unavoidable.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The most sensible policy combines these views, using cold storage to preserve film masters while digital copies provide access. Such an arrangement is unglamorous, and it struggles to attract funding, since sponsors tend to favour digitisation projects that produce visible results rather than the quiet maintenance of refrigerated vaults. But the history of nitrate suggests that the greatest threat to film has always been human judgement about what deserves to be kept. Archivists today are deciding whether to preserve advertisements, amateur footage and regional productions, and future historians may regret some of those choices as deeply as we regret the decisions of the past.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: the transition from silent film to synchronised sound: live cinema music, displaced musicians, static early talkies, Japanese live narrators and language barriers
title: When the Pictures Learned to Talk
subtitle: The coming of sound is remembered as the sudden death of an art form, but the real story was slower, stranger and more varied

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The arrival of synchronised sound in the late 1920s is usually told as a story of sudden and brutal change. Within three years, the familiar account runs, an entire art form was swept away: stars whose voices did not suit the microphone were discarded, directors who had perfected visual storytelling found themselves filming static conversations, and the silent film, at the height of its sophistication, simply died. Like many dramatic narratives, this one contains elements of truth. But it rests on a misleading premise, for the silent cinema was never silent, and the changes brought by sound were neither as abrupt nor as uniform as the legend suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Audiences of the 1920s rarely watched films in quiet. Large urban cinemas employed orchestras of thirty or more players, while smaller halls relied on a pianist or organist who improvised to the action on screen. Sound-effects operators produced galloping hooves, thunder and gunfire from behind the screen, and in many countries a lecturer or narrator stood beside it to explain the plot. What synchronised sound eliminated, therefore, was not silence but live performance. The music that accompanied a film was no longer created afresh in each cinema but fixed on the film itself, identical at every screening.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This shift had consequences that were economic before they were artistic. Rafael Cardenal, an economic historian at the Valencia Institute of Social Research, has traced the fortunes of cinema musicians in Europe and North America during the transition. He estimates that tens of thousands of performers lost their livelihoods within five years, making them one of the largest groups of workers displaced by a single technology in the interwar period. Some found work in radio or in the studios that recorded film soundtracks, but these openings were few compared with the positions that had disappeared. Cardenal also points out that the cost of installing sound equipment drove many small independent cinemas out of business, accelerating the concentration of exhibition in the hands of a few large chains. In his account, sound was less an artistic revolution than a reorganisation of the industry.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics of the period, however, focused on the screen, and many were dismayed by what they saw. Early sound cameras were so noisy that they had to be enclosed in soundproof booths, which made movement almost impossible, while actors were obliged to stay close to microphones hidden in flower vases and telephones. Yelena Bystrova, a film historian at the Kazan Academy of Screen Arts, argues that the result was a genuine artistic regression: films of 1929 are, in her view, visually poorer than those of 1927, with long static takes resembling recorded stage plays. Yet Bystrova also emphasises how short-lived this phase was. Within a few years, booms that suspended the microphone above the actors, together with quieter cameras, had restored much of the lost mobility. Her description of the early sound film is accurate, but to call it a regression is to judge it by the standards of the medium it replaced. Film-makers were learning a new grammar, and some of the most inventive uses of sound date precisely from these awkward years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The legend of sudden death also ignores geography. Haruki Ichikura, who studies Japanese film history at the Sendai Centre for Media Studies, notes that in Japan silent films continued to be made in large numbers until the mid-1930s. The reason lay partly in the popularity of benshi, the live narrators who performed alongside each screening, voicing characters and commenting on the action. Many audiences went to the cinema as much to hear a favourite narrator as to see a particular film, and the narrators' professional associations resisted the new technology. The most celebrated narrators commanded fees higher than those of leading actors, and their names appeared prominently on posters. For Ichikura, the Japanese case shows that the speed of the transition was determined by local cultural and commercial conditions, not by the technology itself.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most far-reaching effect of sound, and the least appreciated, concerned language. Silent films travelled across borders with remarkable ease, since only the intertitles, the printed cards that conveyed dialogue and narration, needed to be translated. Imogen Ravensdale, a cultural historian at the Exeter Institute of Cultural History, describes how studios initially responded to the problem by shooting the same film several times in different languages, using different casts on the same sets. Performers whose fame had crossed many frontiers suddenly found their appeal confined to a single language.The practice proved too expensive and was soon replaced by dubbing and subtitling, but Ravensdale argues that the international film culture of the silent era, in which a single film could be understood almost anywhere, was never fully recovered.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is to deny that sound transformed cinema. It did, and in ways that brought new possibilities as well as losses. But the familiar story of overnight extinction obscures more than it reveals. It overlooks the musicians whose work vanished, the countries where silent film persisted, and the audiences abroad for whom sound erected a new barrier. A history of the transition that gave these figures their due would be less dramatic, but considerably more accurate. Accuracy matters here, because the episode is regularly cited as a warning whenever a new technology appears to threaten an established art.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: astronomical photographic glass plates: a century of sky photography, the assistants who measured them, their abandonment and their revival as historical data
title: Starlight on Glass
subtitle: Millions of photographic plates once used by astronomers are being rediscovered as a record of the changing sky

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly a century, from the 1880s until the closing decades of the twentieth century, the principal instrument of astronomy was not the telescope alone but the photographic plate attached to it. These sheets of glass, coated with a light-sensitive emulsion, could be exposed for an hour or more, steadily accumulating the faint light of stars and nebulae that no observer could ever detect by looking through an eyepiece. Observatories around the world produced them in enormous numbers, and it has been estimated that more than two million plates survive in institutional collections. Photography, it is fair to say, altered the practice of astronomy more profoundly than any increase in the size of telescopes: it replaced the fleeting impressions of the human eye with a permanent record that could be examined, measured and compared at leisure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That record had to be read, however, and the reading was done largely by hand. Many observatories employed teams of assistants, very often young women, who spent their days peering at plates through magnifying lenses, measuring the positions of stars and estimating their brightness from the size and darkness of each image. The work demanded intense concentration, and a single crowded plate could take days to measure completely.These workers were typically paid a fraction of the salary received by the astronomers who directed them, and their names rarely appeared on the publications that their measurements made possible. Some developed classification systems that remain in use today. Their contribution has only recently begun to receive the acknowledgement it deserved, and much of the story is still to be recovered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: By the 1990s, the plate had been almost entirely displaced by electronic detectors, which were many times more sensitive and produced data that could be fed directly into computers. Plate collections, once the pride of their institutions, became an awkward burden, and within a few years the last manufacturer of emulsions designed for astronomy had ceased production.Some were moved to basements and outbuildings where damp and fluctuating temperatures caused the emulsion to deteriorate; a number of observatories, short of space, discarded parts of their archives altogether. For several decades the prevailing assumption was that the plates had been superseded and held nothing of scientific value that modern instruments could not obtain more easily.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That assumption has been overturned, at least in part. Eero Sihvonen, who leads a digitisation project at the Finnish Centre for Astronomical Archives, argues that the plates contain something no modern telescope can provide: a record of how the sky looked over the course of a hundred years. Using purpose-built scanners capable of capturing the position and density of every star image, his team has converted tens of thousands of plates into digital form. By comparing the brightness of the same stars across decades, they have identified objects that slowly faded or brightened, as well as rare outbursts that were recorded on the glass but never noticed by the assistants who examined it at the time. A few of these stars, when observed again with modern equipment, have turned out to be behaving unusually still.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares Sihvonen's confidence. Alastair Morcombe, a specialist in photographic imaging at the Leeds Institute of Imaging Science, points out that photographic emulsion does not respond to light in a simple, proportional way, and that its sensitivity varied from one batch of plates to another and with the conditions in which each was developed. Weather, the age of the plate and the skill of the photographer all left their mark. Worse still, defects such as dust, scratches and spots of mould can produce marks almost indistinguishable from faint stars. Morcombe argues that apparent changes in brightness may therefore reflect the behaviour of the plates rather than that of the stars, and that any claim of a dramatic celestial event based on archival plates should be confirmed by independent evidence before it is accepted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from Dimitrina Tchakarova, a historian of science at the Sofia Institute for the History of Science, who urges archives not to treat the plates merely as sources of measurements. Each plate was usually stored in a paper envelope on which the photographer had written remarks recording the date, the exposure time, the state of the sky and any mishaps during the night. These envelopes, together with observatory logbooks, explain how and why each image was made, and they also reveal a great deal about the routines and hierarchies of scientific work. Tchakarova recommends that digitisation projects photograph this accompanying material alongside the plates themselves, since a scan stripped of its context loses much of its historical and even scientific value.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Morcombe is right to insist on caution, but his conclusions are arguably too pessimistic. Many of the distortions he describes are systematic, affecting all the stars on a plate in similar ways, and modern statistical techniques can correct for them with considerable success; spurious marks, meanwhile, can usually be identified by comparing several plates of the same region. More importantly, the plates are irreplaceable in a way that few scientific records are. A modern telescope can observe the sky of today with extraordinary precision, but it cannot return to the sky of 1910. Whatever their imperfections, these fragile sheets of glass are the only witnesses we have, and the cost of preserving and scanning them is small compared with the cost of losing them for good.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: manipulated photographs in the nineteenth century: portrait retouching, spirit photography, fraud trials and the origins of trust in photographic evidence
title: The Camera Cannot Lie?
subtitle: Anxiety about doctored images is often treated as a product of the digital age, but its roots lie in the earliest years of photography

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: From the moment of its invention, photography was promoted as a medium that recorded the world without human interference. Early enthusiasts described the photograph as an image made by light itself, free from the errors and flattery of the painter's hand, and the idea that 'the camera cannot lie' became a commonplace within a generation. Photographs were soon being used to record the faces of criminals, to catalogue museum collections and to persuade newspaper readers that distant events had occurred as described.Yet the history of the medium suggests that this confidence was never as natural as it now appears. Manipulation began almost as soon as photography did, and the belief in photographic truth was, to a considerable degree, cultivated by those who had an interest in promoting it rather than arising spontaneously from the technology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider the ordinary studio portrait. By the 1870s, retouching negatives had become a routine part of commercial practice. Skilled workers, often employed specifically for the task, used fine pencils and etching knives to soften wrinkles, remove blemishes and slim the outline of a waist or jaw. Manuals for professional photographers devoted whole chapters to the technique, and a studio that failed to offer it risked losing customers to its rivals. Far from being regarded as deception, the improvement of the sitter's appearance was simply part of what a client paid for. Meanwhile, landscape photographers frequently combined several negatives into a single print, adding dramatic clouds to skies that their slow plates had rendered blank and white. Few viewers objected, since the result was thought to be closer to what the eye had actually seen than a single plate could ever record.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most notorious form of manipulation, however, was spirit photography. From the 1860s onwards, certain photographers offered portraits in which a faint, ghostly figure appeared beside the sitter, identified as the spirit of a dead relative. The effect was usually achieved by double exposure or by the use of a prepared plate, and the practice flourished particularly after major wars, when demand from the bereaved was greatest. Some practitioners claimed that the spirits would appear only in the presence of a sympathetic sitter, a condition that conveniently discouraged sceptical investigation.Aino Vainio, a historian of popular culture at the Tampere Institute of Cultural History, has studied letters written by customers of spirit photographers. She argues that many of them suspected, or even knew, how the images were produced, but valued them nonetheless as a form of consolation and a focus for mourning. This seems a far more convincing account than the traditional picture of customers as simply credulous, and it helps to explain why the trade survived repeated public exposures of fraud.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Those exposures had consequences that extended well beyond the spiritualist movement. Selin Ozdemiroglu, a legal historian at the Ankara Centre for Legal History, has examined a series of trials in which spirit photographers were prosecuted for obtaining money by deception. In court, expert witnesses demonstrated step by step how the ghostly figures could be created, and judges were obliged to consider what conditions would have to be met before a photograph could be accepted as reliable. Newspapers followed the proceedings closely, and some printed diagrams explaining the methods to their readers.Ozdemiroglu argues that these cases contributed to the development of rules for photographic evidence, including the requirement that the original negatives be produced and examined. Paradoxically, then, the scandals strengthened the authority of photography: by defining when an image could be trusted, they gave that trust a firmer foundation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This history has obvious relevance today, when software allows almost any image to be altered. Julian Penhaligon, a curator at the Plymouth Gallery of Photography, maintains that current fears about digital manipulation largely repeat anxieties that are as old as the medium itself. The claim that digital editing has destroyed photographic truth, he argues, rests on a myth, since photographs never possessed an inherent truthfulness that could be lost. There is much to be said for this view, which usefully punctures the nostalgia surrounding pre-digital photography. But Penhaligon underestimates what has changed. A nineteenth-century spirit photograph required technical skill and specialised equipment, and its methods could be demonstrated by experts examining the negative. Today convincing alterations can be made in seconds by people with no training at all, and the evidence of tampering is far harder to detect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What the history of manipulation reveals most clearly is that trust in photographs has never rested on the technology alone. It has depended on institutions and conventions: on courts that set standards of evidence, on newspapers that adopted rules about what could and could not be altered, and on the shared expectations of the people who made and viewed images. Those arrangements took decades to develop in the nineteenth century, and new ones will be needed now. Captions, credits and published codes of practice may well matter more in the coming decades than any technical method of detecting alterations, although such methods will undoubtedly play their part.The question is not whether photographs can be believed, but under what conditions, and on whose authority, they deserve to be.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: the myth of panicking first film audiences: contemporary reports, perception and the looming reflex, showmanship, and condescending accounts of first-time viewers
title: The Train That Never Was
subtitle: A famous story about the first cinema audiences says more about later generations than about the spectators of the 1890s

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few anecdotes in the history of cinema are repeated as often as the tale of the runaway train. At one of the earliest public film screenings in the mid-1890s, so the story goes, the audience watched a locomotive steam into a station towards the camera and, convinced that it was about to burst through the screen, leapt from their seats and fled in terror. The anecdote appears in textbooks, documentaries and popular histories, usually as proof of the overwhelming novelty of moving pictures. It is almost certainly untrue, at least in the form in which it is normally told. Yet its persistence is revealing, and the question of why so many people have wanted to believe it is more interesting than the question of whether it happened.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most thorough attempt to trace the story has been made by Zsofia Winterbourne, a film historian at the Debrecen Institute for Media History. She and her colleagues examined several hundred newspaper and magazine reports of film screenings published between 1895 and 1898 in five European languages. Reviewers described audiences as astonished, delighted and occasionally unsettled, and many remarked on the vividness of the moving images. Several singled out the trembling of leaves in the wind or the steam drifting from an engine, rather than the approach of the train, as the most striking sight.But not one report described spectators running from the hall. According to Winterbourne, the dramatic version of the story emerges only in the 1920s and 1930s, in the memoirs of people recalling their childhoods and in journalism celebrating the achievements of the film industry.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Psychological research suggests why the legend is implausible and also why it may contain a grain of truth. Kenji Hoshiyama, who studies visual perception at the Kyoto Laboratory for Perceptual Science, points out that audiences of the 1890s were thoroughly familiar with projected images. Magic lantern shows, panoramas and photographs were common forms of entertainment, and the early films themselves were silent, grey and small, hardly capable of being mistaken for reality. However, Hoshiyama also notes that an object appearing to approach rapidly triggers an automatic defensive reaction, a flinch or a turn of the head, even in viewers who know perfectly well that they are looking at an image. He has recorded the same reflex in volunteers watching modern footage on large screens. Some spectators probably did recoil when the train advanced, and later storytellers may have inflated this involuntary movement into a stampede.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why was the inflated version so appealing? Thomas Brockhurst, a cultural historian at the Norwich Centre for the Study of Popular Media, argues that the myth served the interests of those who told it. For later audiences, it offered a flattering contrast between their own sophistication and the supposed naivety of their grandparents. For the film industry, it was a convenient way of advertising the extraordinary power of its product: if the earliest films could make people run, what might modern cinema achieve? Brockhurst's argument is convincing as far as it goes, but it does not explain why the story was eagerly repeated by people with no connection to the industry and nothing obvious to gain from it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from Eleni Anagnostaki, who studies the history of popular entertainment at the Thessaloniki School of Performing Arts. She emphasises that early films were rarely shown in quiet, darkened theatres. They appeared in fairground booths, music halls and shopfronts, often introduced by a lecturer or showman who urged the crowd to gasp and cheer. In these settings, Anagnostaki argues, the line between genuine reaction and performance was blurred. Showmen had every reason to cultivate noisy behaviour, since a lively crowd attracted paying customers from the street outside.Spectators who shrieked or ducked when the train appeared may have been playing their part in a shared amusement, much as audiences at a ghost story enjoy pretending to be frightened.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Accounts of strong reactions do become more common later, when travelling exhibitors took films to rural regions and to parts of the world where cinema had not yet arrived. Here the sociologist Ingrid Haugsvold, of the Bergen Institute of Social Research, urges particular caution. Many of these descriptions, she observes, were written by colonial officials, missionaries and visiting journalists who were inclined to portray local audiences as childlike and easily deceived, and some described scenes they had not witnessed themselves, relying instead on anecdotes passed on by others.Such reports, in Haugsvold's view, often reveal more about the attitudes of the observers than about the experiences of the people they claimed to describe, and they should not be read as straightforward evidence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the story of the runaway train belongs less to the history of early cinema than to the history of how each generation imagines its relationship with new media. Similar tales circulate today: of users who mistake virtual reality for the real world, or of elderly people baffled by video calls. Such stories may sometimes be true, but they deserve the same scepticism that historians have applied to the panicking spectators of the 1890s. More often than not, they flatter the teller and diminish the people they describe, who were, in all likelihood, considerably less gullible than we would like to think.
