area: the history of photography and film
topic: staging and re-enactment in early documentary film: technical constraints, period conventions, ethnographic misrepresentation, faked newsreels and observational cinema
title: Staging the Real
subtitle: Early documentary makers routinely reconstructed the events they claimed to record. Were they deceiving their audiences?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Documentary film presents itself as a record of reality, yet for much of its early history it relied heavily on staging. Expedition films of the 1910s and 1920s showed hunts that had been arranged for the camera; families were asked to perform daily tasks in front of carefully positioned lights; and cinema newsreels sometimes recreated battles using actors and model ships. When modern viewers learn of these practices, their first reaction is often to condemn the films as frauds. Even some of the most admired works of the era, long praised for their intimacy and authenticity, are now known to have been substantially arranged.That reaction is understandable, but it is largely anachronistic, since it applies to the past a set of expectations that took shape only later in the century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the explanation is technical. Cameras of the period were heavy, usually mounted on tripods, and loaded with film that required strong light. The length of a single shot was also limited by the amount of film a camera could hold, often little more than ten minutes.Recording synchronised sound away from a studio was impractical until lightweight equipment became available in the 1960s, so conversations had to be scripted and filmed later or simply left out. A film-maker who wished to show the inside of a home, a conversation between neighbours or an event that happened at night had little choice but to arrange it. In this sense reconstruction was less a matter of dishonesty than of necessity: without it, many aspects of everyday life could not have been filmed at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some historians go further and argue that staging was an accepted convention. Klaus Gruenfeld, a film historian at the Leipzig Documentary Archive, points out that early definitions of documentary described it as the creative treatment of actuality, a phrase that openly allowed for arrangement and dramatisation. Audiences, he contends, understood that a documentary shaped its material much as a novel shapes experience, and did not expect every scene to have occurred spontaneously. He adds that film-makers rarely concealed their methods from the critics who reviewed their work, which suggests that they did not regard them as shameful. On this view, the films should be judged by the standards of their own time, and those standards permitted a considerable degree of reconstruction.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that period conventions settle the matter. Odile Mirabeau, an anthropologist at the Marseille Institute of Visual Anthropology, has studied ethnographic films made among indigenous communities between the wars. Directors frequently asked their subjects to wear clothing that had been abandoned decades earlier, to use tools that had long been replaced by manufactured goods, and to perform ceremonies out of season. The resulting films portrayed living societies as if they existed in an unchanging past, untouched by trade or modern life. Mirabeau stresses that the damage was not confined to the period in which the films were made: the same images have been reused for decades in schools and museums, shaping how generations of viewers imagine these communities. Here her objections are surely justified, for whatever the conventions of the day, the people being filmed were misrepresented, and they bear the consequences still.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Research on newsreels also complicates Gruenfeld's argument. Mariko Ishimoto, a media historian at the Nagoya Institute of Film and Media, examined the letters that cinema-goers sent to newsreel companies and newspapers during the First World War. Reconstructed battle scenes were common in this period and were usually presented with no indication that they had been staged. Ishimoto found that when viewers discovered the truth, many wrote to complain that they had been misled. Several companies responded by adding brief notices to later releases, although the practice was never applied consistently.Their anger, she argues, shows that ordinary audiences expected newsreels to show what had actually happened, whatever more sophisticated critics may have believed about the creative nature of documentary.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The arrival of portable cameras and sound recorders in the 1960s gave rise to a new style of film-making that rejected staging altogether. Its practitioners aimed to observe events as they unfolded, with no interviews, no commentary and no requests to repeat an action. This observational approach was often promoted as a purer form of documentary, but it had distortions of its own. People behave differently when they know that a camera is present, and the editing process, which might reduce hundreds of hours of footage to ninety minutes, inevitably imposed a structure and a point of view that viewers did not always recognise. Some practitioners acknowledged these problems openly; others insisted that their subjects soon forgot the camera was there.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson of this history is that the crucial question is not whether a documentary contains staged material, but whether its makers are honest with audiences about how it was produced. Many contemporary documentaries use reconstruction openly, signalling it through captions, distinctive visual styles or the presence of actors, and few viewers object. What remains unacceptable, now as in the past, is reconstruction presented as if it were a direct record, particularly when the people depicted have no say in how they appear. Viewers, for their part, may need to become more alert to the many ways in which even unstaged footage is shaped.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: amateur home movies on small-gauge film as historical sources: reversal film, archive collecting, class bias, gender and the camera, and incidental background detail
title: History in the Family Reels
subtitle: For decades, archives ignored the films that ordinary families made of themselves. Historians are now discovering what they missed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1920s, manufacturers began to market cameras and film designed not for professionals but for families. Using narrower film than the cinema industry and selling equipment at a fraction of the price, they made it possible for the first time for ordinary households, or at least prosperous ones, to film their own lives. Over the following half-century, millions of reels were shot: birthdays and weddings, seaside holidays, children taking their first steps. For most of that time, archives regarded these films as trivial, private mementoes of no interest to anyone beyond the family concerned. That judgement now looks like a serious error. Home movies are arguably among the richest visual sources we possess for everyday life in the twentieth century, and a great many of them have already been lost.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technology itself helps to explain both their value and their fragility. Most amateur formats used reversal film, which was processed directly into a positive image rather than producing a negative from which prints could be made. This reduced costs, but it meant that each reel was usually unique: the film that ran through the camera was the same film that was later projected in the living room, scratched and worn with every showing. Early cameras were wound by hand and held only a few minutes of film, which encouraged short, fragmentary shots. Later formats, including one introduced in 1965 that came in cartridges which could be dropped into the camera without threading, made filming easier still and greatly expanded the number of people who did it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Among those who have campaigned to rescue these films is Vesna Cvetkovic, founder of the Zagreb Amateur Film Archive. Over two decades her organisation has gathered more than forty thousand reels, many of them retrieved from attics, flea markets and house clearances after the death of their owners. Each reel is catalogued with whatever information its donors can provide, however fragmentary.Cvetkovic argues that home movies record precisely what professional film-makers tended to ignore: the interiors of ordinary homes, the clothes people wore when they were not dressed for an occasion, children's games, and the appearance of streets and villages that no newsreel crew ever visited. In her view, a collection of family films can tell historians more about how people lived than any number of carefully composed documentaries.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The historian Gérard Bellcourt, of the Lille Centre for Twentieth-Century Studies, is more cautious. He points out that home movies are highly selective. Families filmed celebrations and leisure, not quarrels, illness, housework or paid employment, and the result is a relentlessly cheerful picture of domestic life. More importantly, Bellcourt notes, the equipment remained expensive for decades, so the families who filmed themselves were disproportionately wealthy, urban and, in many countries, drawn from particular ethnic groups. Treating their films as a portrait of society as a whole risks producing a nostalgic and distorted history. Bellcourt's warning about social class deserves to be taken seriously. Yet the selectivity he describes is not simply a weakness, since what families chose to film, and what they chose to leave out, is itself evidence of what they valued and how they wished to be seen.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This point has been developed by Aleksi Silvennoinen, a sociologist at the Helsinki Institute for Family Studies, who has analysed several hundred hours of amateur footage from the 1950s and 1960s. In the great majority of films, he found, the camera was operated by the father, while mothers and children appeared in front of it, often directed to wave, smile or walk towards the lens. Many families filmed the same scenes year after year, such as the cutting of a birthday cake or a departure for the holidays, turning the camera into part of a domestic ritual.For Silvennoinen, home movies are therefore not neutral records but performances of an ideal family, and the question of who held the camera reveals much about the distribution of authority within the household. His conclusions are persuasive, although the reasons why so few women filmed remain a matter for further research.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A rather different use of the material is made by Fiona Ogilvane, an urban historian at the Dundee School of Architecture and Planning. Ogilvane is less interested in the families than in what happens behind them. By comparing amateur footage of the same streets filmed over several decades, she has traced changes in buildings, traffic and shop signs that official photographs rarely captured. She argues that these incidental details are the most valuable content of all, precisely because the people holding the cameras had no intention of recording them and therefore did nothing to arrange or conceal them. Her findings have been used by planning authorities seeking to restore historic shopfronts, and they have documented whole neighbourhoods that were demolished before any systematic photographic survey was made.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever their differences, these researchers agree that time is short. Many surviving reels are deteriorating, and commercial services that transfer family films to digital formats often return the files to their owners and discard the originals. Equally damaging is the loss of information about the footage itself. A reel showing an unidentified wedding in an unidentified town is of limited use to a historian, whereas the same reel accompanied by names, dates and places can become a valuable document. Archives would therefore be wise to combine the collection of films with interviews with surviving family members, before the memories that give the images their meaning disappear along with the people who hold them.

area: the history of photography and film
topic: the rise and fall of the picture magazine and the photo-essay: small cameras, editors versus photographers as authors, competition from television, and the form's legacy
title: The Age of the Photo-Essay
subtitle: For four decades, weekly picture magazines shaped how millions of readers saw the world. Who really made them, and why did they disappear?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the mid-1930s and the early 1970s, illustrated weekly magazines were among the most widely read publications in the world. Their pages were dominated not by text but by large photographs, frequently arranged as a photo-essay: a sequence of pictures, linked by brief captions, that told the story of an event, a place or a single person's working life. At their peak, the leading titles sold several million copies a week, and each copy was typically passed among family members, neighbours and the customers of barber shops and waiting rooms. The photo-essay was arguably the most influential form of visual journalism ever devised, and for a generation of readers it defined what the wider world looked like.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two technical developments made the form possible. The first was the compact camera using 35-millimetre film, which, combined with lenses that admitted far more light than earlier designs, allowed photographers to work quickly and unobtrusively without flash, capturing people who were barely aware that they were being photographed. A photographer could now carry two or three cameras at once and change film in seconds, moving freely through crowds, homes and battlefields.The second was the improvement of high-speed printing methods that could reproduce photographs in rich tones on relatively cheap paper. Together these innovations produced a new kind of image, informal and immediate, and a means of distributing it on an unprecedented scale.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Popular memory tends to credit the photo-essay to the photographers whose names appeared beside it. Henrik Lagerholm, a media historian at the Malmö Institute for Press History, argues that this is misleading. Having studied the surviving editorial records of several magazines, he has shown that a photographer might expose hundreds of frames for a single story, of which perhaps a dozen were published. He also found memoranda in which editors specified the shots they required before the photographer had even left the office.The selection was made by picture editors, the sequence was determined by layout designers and the captions, which often told readers how to interpret each image, were written by staff writers who had never visited the location. In Lagerholm's account, the meaning of a photo-essay was produced largely in the editorial office, and photographers frequently complained that their work had been distorted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lucía Tavera, a historian of photography at the Seville Centre for Visual History, offers a different emphasis. She accepts that editors exercised great power, but points out that photographers did not simply accept it. In the years after the Second World War, a number of leading photographers established cooperative agencies that retained ownership of their pictures and insisted on approving captions before publication. For Tavera, this struggle demonstrates that the finest photo-essays bore the stamp of an individual vision, and that the photographers deserve to be regarded as their principal authors. Both historians capture part of the truth. The photo-essay was a collaborative product, and its strengths and weaknesses alike arose from the tension between the people who took the pictures and those who arranged them on the page.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The decline of the picture magazines was swift. During the 1950s and 1960s television took over the immediacy of news, bringing moving images of events into the home on the day they occurred, and the great weeklies closed or were converted into monthlies in the early 1970s. It is often assumed that readers simply lost interest. Dragan Kovacevski, an economist at the Skopje Institute of Economics who has reconstructed the finances of several titles, rejects this explanation. Circulation, he notes, remained remarkably high until the very end. The difficulty was that advertisers, who supplied most of the magazines' revenue, could reach audiences more cheaply through television, and the magazines' large readerships became a burden rather than an asset when sharp increases in postage costs raised the expense of delivering each copy to subscribers. Some titles tried to survive by reducing their page size or publishing fewer issues, but these measures came too late.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some commentators believe that the photo-essay has not so much died as migrated. Kaisa Ruusmann, a cultural critic at the Tartu School of Media, argues that its legacy lives on in the long-form multimedia features published by news websites, which combine photographs, text and video in carefully designed sequences. She adds that digital publication allows far more pictures to be shown than a magazine's limited number of pages ever permitted.There is something in this, as many such features are clearly influenced by the magazine tradition. But they lack an essential element of the original. A picture magazine was read by millions of people in the same week, and its images became a shared point of reference across a whole society, whereas an online feature is consumed by scattered individuals at different times and quickly displaced by the next.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The picture magazines left a profound mark on how a generation imagined the events of its time; for many readers, the memory of a war, a famine or a coronation is inseparable from a particular photograph they first saw on a magazine page. Yet that influence was not without its costs. The leading magazines employed few women photographers, and their coverage of distant countries was shaped almost entirely by visitors whose assumptions they seldom questioned. Their vision of the world was vivid and memorable, but it was also a narrow one.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: the British canal mania of the 1790s: local investors, cost overruns, water supply miscalculations and the legacy of failed canal companies
title: The Waterway Fever
subtitle: Was the canal boom of the 1790s a speculative folly, or something more rational than its reputation suggests?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 1790s Britain was gripped by a sudden enthusiasm for building canals. Within the space of a few years, Parliament authorised dozens of new canal companies, shares in proposed waterways changed hands at large premiums, and meetings held in provincial inns to raise capital were sometimes oversubscribed within hours. Later commentators gave the episode a dismissive label, 'canal mania', and placed it alongside earlier financial bubbles as a cautionary tale of collective credulity. That interpretation has the merit of simplicity, but it fails to explain why so many sober and otherwise cautious people chose to put their savings into ditches that had not yet been dug.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the answer lies in the record of the canals that came first. The waterways opened between the 1760s and the 1780s were built mainly to carry coal, and several of them delivered handsome dividends while dramatically reducing the price of fuel in the towns they served. These visible successes shaped expectations for the next generation of schemes. Crucially, the people who subscribed were not, for the most part, metropolitan financiers. Dr Lucjan Wawrzak, an economic historian at the Institute of Regional History in Gdansk, has analysed the surviving subscription lists of sixty canal companies and found that more than two-thirds of shareholders lived within twenty miles of the proposed route. Landowners, merchants, clergymen and widows dominate the lists; names from London are comparatively rare.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Wawrzak draws a bold conclusion from this geographical pattern. Local investors, he argues, were motivated less by the prospect of dividends than by the indirect benefits a canal would bring: cheaper coal and lime, access to wider markets for farm produce, and a rise in the value of nearby land. On this reading, a canal that never paid its shareholders a penny might still have been a perfectly sensible investment for those who lived beside it. The argument is persuasive as far as landowners are concerned, since they could expect their estates to appreciate whatever the fortunes of the company. It is far less convincing for the many small investors who bought shares late, at inflated prices, and who owned no land at all. For them, dividends were the only conceivable reward, and many were bitterly disappointed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Nell Hathersage of Pendlebury College takes a considerably sterner view of the period. She points out that many of the schemes promoted in the mid-1790s were planned through difficult upland country, where tunnels, long flights of locks and extensive embankments were unavoidable and where there were few industrial towns to generate traffic. Construction costs routinely ran to double the original estimates, forcing companies to make repeated calls on shareholders for additional capital. The outbreak of war with France in 1793 made matters worse by pushing up interest rates and drawing labourers away into the army and navy. Hathersage maintains that promoters knowingly understated costs in order to attract subscribers. Such deliberate deception, however, is difficult to demonstrate. Methods of estimating engineering costs were still primitive, and the surveying of hill country was notoriously unreliable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A less obvious difficulty concerned water. A canal that crosses high ground must be supplied at its summit, usually from reservoirs, because every boat that passes through a lock draws water down from the top level. Dr Tobiah Kettleborough, a hydraulic engineer who turned to history after retirement, has reconstructed the water budgets of twelve summit canals from the period. He calculates that nine of them could not have operated with fully loaded boats through an average summer using the reservoirs that were originally planned. In dry years, boatmen were indeed forced to carry partial cargoes, and some canals closed entirely for weeks. Kettleborough does not regard these shortcomings as evidence of dishonesty. In his view they reflect genuine ignorance, since the measurement of rainfall, evaporation and seepage was then in its infancy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The financial outcomes of the boom were undeniably mixed. A number of canals authorised during these years were never completed, others opened decades behind schedule, and only a minority ever paid regular dividends. Yet even the failures left a lasting legacy. They trained a generation of engineers, surveyors and contractors, and they created a mobile workforce experienced in excavation that would later be employed on the railways. It has also been suggested that the canal boom accustomed provincial investors to the idea of buying shares in joint-stock companies, and so prepared the ground for railway finance. This claim should not be pushed too far: the railway boom of the 1840s drew on a broader, more national investing public, and its shares were traded through new provincial stock exchanges that simply did not exist half a century earlier.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should we make of the waterway fever? The word 'mania' obscures the sheer variety of the schemes it describes, from sound projects linking coalfields to growing towns to optimistic ventures through thinly populated hills. Judged by the returns paid to shareholders, many canals were plainly failures. Judged by their effect on the regions through which they passed, the picture is considerably more favourable. Historians who wish to understand the episode would do better to ask what a canal did for its surrounding district than to ask only whether its investors were repaid.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: eighteenth-century turnpike trusts: toll finance, faster coaching, fragmentation, the burden on farmers and decline after the railways
title: Paying at the Gate
subtitle: The turnpike trusts transformed travel in eighteenth-century England, but historians still disagree about how much credit they deserve

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Travellers in early eighteenth-century England complained endlessly about the state of the roads. Responsibility for highways lay with the parishes through which they passed, and every able-bodied householder was obliged to contribute several days of unpaid labour each year under the direction of a local surveyor, who was himself unpaid, elected annually and frequently reluctant to serve. Unsurprisingly, the work was often done badly or not at all. Yet the deeper flaw of the system was not idleness but injustice. A parish that happened to lie on a major route between two cities was expected to maintain a road worn out by coaches and wagons whose passengers and owners contributed nothing to its upkeep and brought the parish little benefit in return.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The turnpike trust offered a way out of this impasse. A group of local landowners, merchants and manufacturers would petition Parliament for an Act establishing a trust with the power to erect gates across a defined stretch of road, to charge tolls on those who used it, and to spend the proceeds on repair and improvement. The first such bodies appeared at the end of the seventeenth century, but the real expansion came between the 1750s and the 1770s, when hundreds of new trusts were created. By the 1830s more than a thousand of them administered around twenty thousand miles of road, and a traveller on a main route might expect to stop and pay every few miles.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Improving a road cost money long before any tolls could be collected, so trusts borrowed in advance, issuing bonds that were secured on their future toll revenue. The interest they could pay was capped by the usury laws at five per cent, which might have been expected to deter lenders. Dr Ifeoma Strudwick, who has examined the accounts of some two hundred trusts, found that it did not. Those who lent were overwhelmingly local people, such as innkeepers, farmers, carriers and attorneys, whose businesses stood to gain from better communications. For Strudwick, the turnpike was an ingenious device for converting private, local self-interest into public infrastructure without placing any burden on central government, which at that time had neither the means nor the inclination to build roads itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The effects on travel were striking. Between 1750 and 1800, scheduled journey times between London and the major provincial cities fell by roughly half, and the number of regular coach services multiplied. Strudwick attributes most of this acceleration to the physical works carried out by the trusts: wider carriageways, firmer surfaces and the easing of steep gradients. Professor Henrik Dalvang of the Centre for Economic History in Bergen disagrees. In his view the greater part of the gain came from the coaching business itself, through lighter, better-sprung vehicles, improved breeds of horse and, above all, the organisation of frequent changes of team at staging inns. This distinction seems to me too sharp. Operators would hardly have invested in fast services and teams of fresh horses unless the roads had first become reliable enough to permit rapid running throughout the year. The vehicles and the roads improved together, each making the other worthwhile.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An older generation of historians took a far dimmer view of the trusts. They emphasised the fragmentation of the system: a journey of a hundred miles might pass through a dozen separate trusts, each with its own scale of charges and its own standard of maintenance, and trustees were regularly accused of negligence or of diverting funds to their own purposes. There is some truth in these charges, but the damage caused by fragmentation has been exaggerated. Neighbouring trusts frequently employed the same surveyor and coordinated their repairs, and in the early nineteenth century new methods of surfacing with compacted layers of small broken stones spread from one trust to the next with remarkable speed. A decentralised system, it turns out, could still learn.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different objection concerns who actually paid. Dr Amalia Querejeta, a social historian at the Andean Centre for Social History, notes that tolls were levied per animal and per vehicle rather than per mile. As a result, the heaviest burden fell on farmers carting bulky, low-value goods such as lime or manure over short distances, who might pass through a gate several times a week, while wealthy passengers making long journeys by coach paid comparatively little for each mile travelled. Resentment sometimes erupted into violence, most famously in south-west Wales in the late 1830s and early 1840s, when toll gates were attacked and destroyed at night. Querejeta concludes that the benefits of the trusts flowed disproportionately to the prosperous. Her case is weakened somewhat by the exemptions that many Acts granted to agricultural traffic, although where such exemptions were absent the grievances were undoubtedly genuine.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The decline of the trusts came swiftly. Once railways began to carry long-distance passengers and goods in the 1830s and 1840s, toll income on the main routes collapsed. Many trusts could no longer pay interest on their bonds, and those who had lent to them lost much of their money. From the 1860s onwards Parliament gradually wound the trusts up, and responsibility for the roads passed to new county authorities. It is now fashionable to cite the turnpikes as a precedent for modern road charging, but the comparison is less helpful than it appears. Today's drivers have grown up expecting roads to be free at the point of use, and no government could rely on the local enthusiasm that once filled the trusts' coffers. The turnpikes are better understood as a successful transitional institution, one that bridged the gap between parish labour and public funding, than as a model to be revived.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: the nineteenth-century railway gauge war: broad versus standard gauge, lock-in, break-of-gauge costs and the timing of state intervention
title: A Matter of Inches
subtitle: How Britain's railways came to run on a single width of track, and what the battle over gauges reveals about technical standards

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1840s, travellers passing through certain junction towns in the west of England witnessed a peculiar kind of chaos. At these points two railway systems met, but their tracks were of different widths, so no train could continue from one to the other. Passengers changed carriages with their luggage, while goods of every description, from coal and grain to furniture and crates of pottery, were transferred by hand from one set of wagons to another. The cause was a disagreement over gauge, the distance between the rails. Most companies used a gauge of four feet eight and a half inches, a measurement inherited from the horse-drawn wagonways of the northern coalfields. One major company, however, had adopted a gauge of seven feet, arguing that it would allow faster and steadier running. For a time it seemed possible that the country would be divided permanently between two incompatible networks, each expanding into territory the other regarded as its own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The conventional account of what followed is a story of accident triumphing over merit. Dr Bartholomew Doorewaard, an economic historian at the Rhineland Institute for Economic History, describes the gauge war as a textbook case of 'lock-in'. By 1845 the narrower gauge already accounted for roughly eight times as much track as its rival, and every new line that wished to exchange traffic with its neighbours had a strong incentive to follow the majority. In Doorewaard's view, the eventual standard was decided not by any engineering comparison but by the simple fact that it had spread first, in much the same way that certain keyboard layouts became fixed long after the reasons for them had disappeared.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some historians go further and claim that Britain chose the worse option, and that the country paid for its haste for decades afterwards. Professor Itzel Marroquín of the Colegio de Ingeniería Histórica in Mexico City has re-examined the official trials of 1845 and points out that broad-gauge locomotives consistently reached higher speeds while hauling heavier loads. The wider track, she explains, allowed larger boilers to be placed between the wheels, producing more powerful engines with a lower centre of gravity. Her technical points are sound, but the conclusion that the nation adopted an inferior standard does not follow. Within two decades, designers had learned to mount boilers above the wheels, and narrow-gauge engines were matching the speeds that had once seemed the preserve of the broad gauge. The advantage was real, but it was temporary.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further question concerns the costs of the break of gauge itself. Dr Eero Valkeapää, who studies transport archives at the Nordic Railway History Centre, argues that these costs were deliberately exaggerated. He has found evidence that companies favouring the narrow gauge arranged scenes of spectacular confusion at junction stations when government commissioners came to inspect them. His analysis of surviving goods records suggests that transfers normally took hours rather than days, and that losses through breakage were small. This may well be true for durable goods. For perishable produce and livestock, however, even short delays mattered, and the mere uncertainty of transfer probably discouraged merchants from sending goods long distances at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The matter was eventually settled by the state. A commission appointed in 1845 recommended the narrower gauge as the national standard, and an Act of the following year required new passenger lines to be built to that width unless they were specifically authorised otherwise. The broad gauge did not vanish overnight. For several decades, many routes were laid with a third rail, so that trains of either width could use the same track. The final conversion took place in 1892, when thousands of workers relaid the remaining broad-gauge lines in the west of England over a single weekend. Contemporary accounts describe gangs working through the night by lamplight, and the operation was planned with such care that services resumed on the Monday morning almost as normal.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Comparisons with other countries suggest how fortunate Britain was. Researchers in the Network History Group at the Antipodean Institute of Transport Studies have traced the consequences of different gauges in Australia, where separate colonies built their railways to different widths in the nineteenth century. Breaks of gauge at the borders between states persisted for more than a hundred years, and the group estimates that the accumulated costs of transferring goods and maintaining incompatible rolling stock far exceeded what early standardisation would have cost. Their conclusion, which seems to me entirely justified, is that the decisive factor in Britain was not the choice of gauge but the timing of intervention: Parliament acted while the network was still small enough to be unified at reasonable expense.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The gauge war is often cited as a lesson for modern technical standards, from electrical plugs to mobile telephone networks, and the usual moral drawn is that a common standard adopted early matters more than the best possible one. That moral is broadly correct, but it needs qualifying. It does not mean that any standard will do. The narrower gauge proved adequate for the demands later placed on it; had it been seriously deficient, the lock-in that Doorewaard describes would have imposed a heavy and lasting penalty. What Britain enjoyed in the end was not merely an early decision but a reasonably good one.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: how Roman roads were really built and used: the myth of standard layered construction, straight alignments, state versus local traffic and the fate of the roads after Rome
title: Beneath the Paving Stones
subtitle: Excavation and aerial survey are overturning long-held assumptions about how Roman roads were built and what they were for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few images of the ancient world are as familiar as the Roman road: ruler-straight, solidly paved and built to a standard recipe of four distinct layers. According to the textbook version, engineers first laid a foundation of large stones, then a bed of rubble bound with lime, then a layer of fine concrete, and finally a surface of closely fitted paving slabs. This description has been repeated in schoolbooks and museum displays for more than two centuries. Its source, however, is surprising. It derives largely from an ancient architectural treatise that describes how to construct floors, not roads, and it was applied to highways by eighteenth-century antiquarians who had excavated very few of them. The picture is seductive, but as a general account of Roman road building it is seriously misleading.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Ottilie Brandreth, a field archaeologist at the Northumbrian Institute of Archaeology, has spent two decades cutting cross-sections through Roman roads in what was once a northern frontier province. Of more than forty roads she has examined, only three bear any resemblance to the textbook model. The great majority consist of successive layers of gravel and whatever stone was available nearby, laid on a raised embankment known as an agger and flanked by drainage ditches. Stone paving, she found, was largely confined to towns and the roads immediately approaching them. Brandreth concludes that Roman engineers were thoroughly pragmatic, adapting their methods to local materials rather than following a fixed formula. This is surely right, yet it does not mean that there were no standards at all. What appears to have been consistent was the design rather than the materials: the width of the carriageway, the limits placed on gradients and, above all, the provision for drainage.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The famous straightness of the roads has attracted its own theories. Some scholars have read it as a statement of power, an imperial geometry imposed on conquered landscapes. Dr Femke Hoogstraten, a landscape historian based in Groningen, offers a more practical explanation. Surveyors, she argues, laid out long alignments by sighting between beacons or poles placed on high ground, and this is why changes of direction typically occur on summits, from which the next stretch could be seen and marked. Where terrain made a direct line impractical, roads did deviate, zigzagging up steep slopes or following valleys around obstacles. Hoogstraten therefore sees straightness as a by-product of surveying technique. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, however: a method adopted for convenience could still come to carry symbolic meaning.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental question is what the roads were for. Professor Davit Kharazishvili of the Caucasus Institute of Classical Studies argues that the major highways existed primarily to serve the state. They carried officials, messages and, when necessary, troops, and they were punctuated at regular intervals by relay stations of the imperial post, where travellers carrying an official permit could obtain fresh animals and lodging. Ordinary commerce, in his view, made relatively little use of them. Moving bulky goods overland by ox-cart was slow and costly, and an edict on maximum prices issued in the early fourth century implies that carrying grain by land was many times more expensive than shipping it by sea. Wherever possible, therefore, merchants sent heavy goods by water.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Recent aerial survey has complicated this picture considerably. Using lidar, a laser-scanning technique that can reveal earthworks beneath woodland and ploughed fields, researchers on the Sava Valley Roads Survey have mapped dense networks of minor roads linking farms, villas, quarries and market centres. Most of these routes were unpaved, and almost none of them appears in the ancient itineraries that list stations and distances along the main highways. The project team argues that it was this local network, rather than the trunk roads, that carried the bulk of everyday traffic and sustained the regional economy. Their findings do not refute Kharazishvili so much as reveal how narrow the debate had become. By concentrating on the famous highways, historians had mistaken one part of the system for the whole.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The afterlife of the roads is equally instructive. When the Roman administration in the western provinces collapsed during the fifth century, systematic maintenance ceased. Many routes nevertheless remained in use for hundreds of years, even as their stone was quarried for churches, walls and houses. In some regions, medieval roads continued to follow the Roman alignments for long distances; in others, they were abandoned altogether as settlement patterns shifted and new centres of population emerged away from the old towns. The evidence suggests that whether a road survived had less to do with the quality of its construction than with whether it still linked places that people wanted to reach.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the scale of the Roman achievement, but it relocates it. What distinguished the Roman road network was not a single, miraculous method of construction but an administrative system capable of surveying routes across entire provinces, of placing obligations for repair on local communities and of recording distances with milestones that travellers could rely on. The myth of the four-layered road, by focusing attention on the stones themselves, has tended to obscure the organisation that put them there.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: the navvies who dug Britain's railways: the stereotype of the wild itinerant labourer, local recruitment, the truck payment system, accidents and late mechanisation
title: The Men with the Shovels
subtitle: Victorian observers saw the railway labourer as a menace; historians are now asking who he really was

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the 1830s and the 1870s, the greater part of Britain's railway network was excavated, embanked and tunnelled by hand. The men who did this work were known as navvies, a name derived from the 'navigators' who had dug the canals of the previous century, and at the height of construction in the late 1840s they may have numbered a quarter of a million. To many of their contemporaries they were an alarming presence: rough, hard-drinking wanderers who descended on quiet villages, fought among themselves and moved on, leaving debts and disorder behind them. This image has proved remarkably durable. It is also, I would argue, more revealing about the anxieties of the people who created it than about the labourers it claimed to describe.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The problem begins with the sources. Most of what was written about navvies at the time came from clergymen, missionaries and journalists, few of whom spent long among the men they described. Missionary societies, in particular, depended on public donations, and an account of souls in moral peril was a far more effective appeal than a description of ordinary working men going quietly about their business. When a parliamentary committee investigated conditions on the railway works in 1846, it heard extensively from contractors, engineers and clergy, but scarcely at all from the labourers themselves. The navvy, in other words, was almost always spoken about and rarely allowed to speak.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Hester Rosewarne, a social historian at the Westcountry Institute of Labour History, has tried to recover a more representative picture by tracing railway workers through the census returns of 1851 and 1861. In the construction camps she studied, roughly sixty per cent of the labourers had been born in the same county as the works, and many had previously been agricultural labourers. Her interpretation is that most men took railway work for a season or two, attracted by wages well above those available on farms, and then returned to the land. The professional navvy who travelled from contract to contract across the country was, on her figures, a minority of perhaps a quarter, though he was by far the most visible and the most written about. Rosewarne's research is valuable, but it has a limitation she herself acknowledges. A census records where people slept on a single night, and the most mobile men, who often slept in barns or in the open, are precisely those most likely to have been missed. The itinerant share may therefore be larger than her figures suggest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If the navvies were not quite the race apart that Victorian writers imagined, why did disorder so often accompany the works? Professor Anselm Wolfsteiner of the Hanseatic School of Economic History locates the explanation in the way labour was organised and paid. Large contractors divided their lines into sections and let them to subcontractors, who in turn employed gangers to supervise small groups of men. Wages were frequently paid only at long intervals, sometimes as rarely as once a month. In the meantime, workers had little choice but to buy food and other necessities on credit from shops owned by the contractors, where goods were sold at inflated prices. When pay day finally came, much of it was already owed, and what remained was often spent in a single burst of drinking. Wolfsteiner concludes that the much-reported disorder was the predictable product of this system rather than a reflection of the men's character, and the evidence he assembles is difficult to dispute.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The work was also extraordinarily dangerous. Men were crushed by falls of earth in deep cuttings, struck by runaway wagons on temporary tracks and killed in explosions while blasting rock in tunnels. On some of the longest tunnels, the proportion of the workforce killed or seriously injured was comparable to the casualty rates of military campaigns. Compensation for injured men or for widows was rare and depended largely on the goodwill of individual contractors. It is a curious feature of railway history that these losses have so often been treated as a footnote. The great engineers are commemorated in statues and biographies; the men who died carrying out their designs are, for the most part, unnamed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The quantity of work achieved by hand is still astonishing. Dr Chidinma Orakwue, an economic historian who has reconstructed output from contractors' ledgers, estimates that an experienced navvy could shift up to twenty tons of earth in a day. She argues that this abundance of cheap and productive labour explains why British contractors were so slow to adopt the steam excavators that were already in use on some American lines by the 1840s: there was simply no financial reason to invest in them. The argument is persuasive up to a point. Early excavators, however, were heavy, unreliable and poorly suited to the wet clay found in many British cuttings, and their limited adoption owed something to these practical drawbacks as well as to the price of labour.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Much of the network the navvies built is still in daily use, its cuttings and embankments carrying trains that their builders could scarcely have imagined. They deserve to be remembered not through the caricature of the drunken wanderer, nor through sentimental celebration, but as what they mostly were: a skilled and physically formidable workforce whose behaviour was shaped, for better and worse, by the economic arrangements under which they laboured.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: were railways indispensable to nineteenth-century economic growth? The social-savings method, its critics, dynamic effects and market-access models
title: Counting the Difference
subtitle: Economic historians have spent sixty years trying to measure what the railways were really worth

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century it was taken for granted that the railways had been indispensable to the economic growth of the nineteenth. They appeared in textbooks as the engine of industrialisation, the innovation without which factories could not have been supplied, cities fed or national markets formed. In the 1960s, however, a new and deliberately provocative method challenged this assumption. Instead of describing what the railways had done, economic historians began to ask what would have happened without them. The resulting measure, known as the 'social saving', estimates how much more it would have cost in a given year to move the same goods by the next best alternative, usually a combination of canals, rivers and roads, and expresses that extra cost as a share of national income.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The figures produced by this approach were far smaller than the traditional story implied. Professor Aurelio Sbarbaro of the Institute for Quantitative History in Turin has recently re-estimated the social saving on freight for several European economies in the 1860s and arrives at figures of between four and six per cent of national income. That is a substantial sum, but it hardly suggests that growth depended on the railways for its very existence. On Sbarbaro's calculations, an economy without railways would have reached the same level of income only two or three years later than it actually did. Whatever its limitations, the method has one indisputable virtue: it obliges anyone who claims that a technology was essential to say precisely how essential, and to put a number on it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics of the social saving have attacked its assumptions from several directions. Dr Margit Brekkelund, a transport economist at the University College of Tromsø, points out that the calculation assumes that canals and roads could have absorbed all the traffic actually carried by rail at roughly their existing costs. In reality, she argues, waterways would have become badly congested, many would have run short of water in dry summers, and in northern climates a significant number froze for weeks each winter. Moreover, the method values only the lower price of transport, ignoring the speed and reliability that allowed perishable goods to reach distant markets and manufacturers to hold smaller stocks. Brekkelund concludes that the social saving systematically understates the railways' contribution. On the first point she is surely correct; on the second, the problem is real but its scale is harder to establish, since reliability is difficult to price.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious critique comes from Dr Tafadzwa Chinyanganya of the Centre for Economic Geography in Harare, who argues that the calculation captures only the static effect of cheaper transport in a single year. Its real limitation, in her view, is that it ignores the ways in which railways transformed the shape of economies over decades. They allowed cities to grow far from navigable water, opened up interior farmland that would otherwise have remained uncultivated, and integrated scattered regional markets into national ones. Their construction also generated enormous demand for iron, coal and engineering products, stimulating the growth of these industries in turn. All of this is plausible, and some of it is undoubtedly true. Yet these effects are extremely difficult to quantify, and an argument built on them risks drifting back towards precisely the kind of confident but unprovable assertion that the social saving was designed to discipline.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most recent contribution attempts to bridge this gap. Researchers in the Spatial History Group at the Institute for Quantitative History have used digitised maps of every railway, canal and navigable river to calculate, for each county in a large national economy, how far the railways reduced the cost of trading with all other markets. They then relate this 'market access' to changes in the value of agricultural land. Their models suggest that removing the railways entirely would have reduced farmland values by more than half, although the loss would have been partly offset if the canal network had been extended to compensate. The work is technically impressive, and it captures some of the geographical effects that Chinyanganya emphasises. Its conclusions, however, depend heavily on assumptions about how lower trading costs are translated into higher land values, assumptions which the data themselves cannot test.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One feature of the debate that has received surprisingly little attention is the carriage of passengers. The pioneering studies concentrated almost entirely on freight, partly because goods traffic was better documented and partly because economists were primarily interested in industrial costs. Yet when the time saved by travellers is valued, even conservatively, the social saving on passenger traffic in some countries turns out to be larger than that on goods. The early neglect of passengers was a significant omission, and it probably led an entire generation of historians to underestimate what the railways had achieved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, has sixty years of argument established? Few historians now believe that the railways were indispensable in the strict sense that economic growth would have been impossible without them. Equally, few would accept that their contribution was trivial. The most useful legacy of the controversy may be a change in the question itself. Asking whether a technology was indispensable invites a yes-or-no answer that the evidence can rarely support. Asking how much difference it made, and to whom, invites careful measurement, and it is a question that those who appraise new infrastructure today would do well to keep in mind.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: the slow decline of British canal carrying after the railways: railway-owned canals, short-haul industrial traffic, rate wars and the rise of the family boat
title: Slow Water
subtitle: The canals did not die when the railways arrived; their long retreat tells a more interesting story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The usual account of Britain's canals is brief and melancholy. Built in a burst of enthusiasm in the late eighteenth century, they are said to have been overwhelmed within a few years by the railways of the 1840s, after which they lingered as weed-choked relics until rescued by leisure boaters a century later. The real history is considerably more complicated. On several networks, the total tonnage carried at the end of the nineteenth century was little lower than at its peak, and commercial traffic on some routes continued well into the 1960s. The decline of the canals was real, but it was slower, more uneven and more interesting than the familiar story allows.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One element of that story concerns the railway companies themselves, which by the 1860s owned or leased roughly a third of the canal mileage in the country. It has often been assumed that they acquired these waterways in order to strangle a competitor. Dr Isadora Quilliam, who has worked through the board minutes of more than twenty railway companies, has found little evidence of such a strategy. Many purchases, she argues, were forced on the railways by canal proprietors, who demanded that their undertakings be bought as the price of withdrawing opposition to new railway bills in Parliament. Having acquired canals they had never wanted, the railway companies then spent as little on them as possible, so that the waterways deteriorated through neglect rather than deliberate sabotage. To the boatmen whose livelihoods suffered, the distinction may have seemed academic. For historians trying to understand the motives of the railway companies, however, it is fundamental.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why did some canals keep their traffic while others lost it? Professor Bogumił Kryspin, an economic geographer at the Katowice Centre for Industrial Landscapes, points to the location of industry. In districts such as the Black Country, hundreds of collieries, ironworks and factories had been built directly on the canal bank, often with their own private wharves and basins. For short journeys between such premises, moving coal by boat remained cheaper than carting it to a railway yard, loading it into wagons and unloading it again at the other end. Kryspin argues that the investment already sunk in canal-side sites tied these firms to the water for decades, and the evidence of surviving traffic records supports him. Where industry had instead grown up around railway stations, or where canals served mainly long-distance through traffic, boats lost their custom far more rapidly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Survival came at a price, however. To compete with the railways, canal companies cut their tolls and carrying firms cut their charges, and much of the burden was passed on to the boatmen in the form of lower wages. Unable to afford a house on land as well as hired help on the boat, many boatmen took their wives and children aboard to work as unpaid crew. Dr Akosua Odoom-Ashworth, who has studied the registers of canal boats introduced in the late 1870s, has shown that the proportion of boats carrying whole families rose markedly in the decades after 1840. She concludes that the family boat, often presented in later romantic accounts as an ancient way of life, was in fact a relatively recent adaptation to economic pressure.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Life aboard these boats alarmed Victorian reformers. Campaigners described families of six or seven crammed into cabins barely ten feet long, and children who grew up without any schooling because they never stayed in one place long enough to attend. Laws passed in 1877 and 1884 required boats to be registered, limited the number of people permitted to sleep in each cabin and provided for inspection. The reformers' concern was undoubtedly genuine, but their descriptions were frequently exaggerated for effect, and they rarely consulted the families themselves. In any case, the legislation had limited practical impact, because only a handful of inspectors were appointed to cover thousands of boats.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It was not the railways but the motor lorry that finally ended most commercial carrying. After the First World War, large numbers of surplus military vehicles were sold off cheaply, and road haulage offered a flexibility that neither boats nor trains could match. Road transport completed the decline that the railways had begun, and by the time the canals were nationalised in 1948, much of the remaining traffic was already in terminal decline. Paradoxically, the very slowness of this decline helped to preserve the network. Had the canals been abandoned in the 1850s, most would have been drained, filled in and built over long before anyone thought them worth saving. Because a thin stream of traffic kept them open into the twentieth century, they survived long enough to be rediscovered by volunteers and holidaymakers. Many of the locks, aqueducts and towpaths that now attract visitors owe their existence to coal barges that went on working when the canals' commercial prospects had long since faded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of the canals after the coming of the railways holds a lesson that extends well beyond transport. Established technologies rarely disappear at the moment something better is invented. More often they retreat into the niches where they retain an advantage, survive there for longer than anyone expects, and decline only when the economic arrangements that sustained them finally give way.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: who remade the roads before and after the motor car: cyclists' campaigns for better roads, rural pressure, the dust problem, tar surfacing and motor taxation
title: Before the Car Came
subtitle: The smooth, sealed road is usually credited to the motorist, but the story begins with the bicycle

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is natural to assume that the modern road was created by and for the motor car. The assumption is understandable but largely mistaken. By the 1880s the roads of rural Britain and North America were in a sorry state. The railways had drawn away most long-distance traffic, the turnpike trusts that had once maintained the main routes had been wound up, and local authorities, responsible for highways that now served mainly farm carts, spent as little on them as they could. The first sustained campaign to reverse this neglect came not from motorists, who scarcely existed, but from a far humbler constituency: the cyclists.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The bicycle boom of the 1890s brought hundreds of thousands of new travellers onto country roads, and they quickly organised. Cycling clubs and touring associations published maps, erected warning signs at the top of dangerous hills, lobbied local councils and paid for pamphlets explaining the principles of road construction to the officials who were supposed to apply them. Dr Philippa Ormsworth, a historian of technology at the Midland Institute of Social History, regards the cyclists as the indispensable pioneers of road reform. In her account, they created both the political arguments and the technical expertise that motorists would later inherit, so that the early motoring organisations stepped into a campaign that was already well under way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Lorcan Ditchburn of the Atlantic Centre for Rural Studies thinks this account gives the cyclists too much credit. In the United States, he argues, the decisive pressure for better roads came from farmers, who needed to haul their produce to railway stations in all weathers, and from the expansion of free postal delivery to rural households, which required passable roads to every farm gate. The cycling organisations, by contrast, were small, urban and largely middle-class, and their membership collapsed when the craze for cycling faded around the turn of the century. Ditchburn is right about the collapse, but that does not settle the matter. The cyclists' importance lay not in their numbers but in the arguments, standards and expertise they established, much of which outlived the organisations themselves.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever the cyclists achieved, the arrival of the motor car created a problem that no one had anticipated. Most roads of the period were surfaced with layers of broken stone bound together by fine dust and water, a method that worked adequately for horse-drawn traffic. Fast motor vehicles, however, tore these surfaces apart: their rubber tyres sucked out the binding material, and their speed raised dense clouds of dust that settled on houses, gardens and fields. Rural residents complained of ruined crops, damaged health and roads that disintegrated within months of being repaired. Engineers responded by experimenting with ways of sealing the surface, spraying roads with tar, oil or calcium chloride, and eventually by mixing tar into the stone itself before it was laid.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Sushila Ramdewar, who has examined the correspondence of county engineers in the decade before the First World War, argues that this transformation was driven less by motorists than by the people who lived beside the roads. Motorists, she points out, were often content to drive through the dust they created; it was the letters, petitions and lawsuits of householders and farmers that forced councils to act. This is a valuable corrective to the idea that the car simply demanded, and received, the roads it needed. Yet it should not be pushed to the point of making motorists irrelevant, since without their vehicles there would have been no dust problem to complain about.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question of who should pay for the new surfaces proved equally contentious. In Britain, taxes on vehicles and fuel were introduced in 1909, and the revenue was at first set aside for road improvement, on the principle that those who damaged the roads should pay to repair them. Within two decades governments were diverting much of this money to other purposes. Motoring organisations denounced the change as a breach of faith, and the complaint is still heard today. It is not obvious, though, that the principle deserved to survive. Roads serve the whole community, not only those who drive on them, and there is no compelling reason why one tax should be permanently tied to one category of spending.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Physical evidence is now adding to the documentary record. The Highways Archaeology Unit, a research team that cuts sections through old road surfaces during modern repairs, has found striking local variation in the materials and methods used well into the twentieth century. Standard specifications issued by central authorities, the team concludes, were adopted only slowly, as county surveyors continued to experiment with whatever stone, slag or tar they could obtain cheaply. The modern road, in other words, was not the product of a single invention but of countless small trials.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the car was unimportant. The cyclists may have revived the cause of better roads, and rural residents may have forced the first sealed surfaces, but it was the motor vehicle, with its weight, its speed and eventually its sheer numbers, that determined what the modern road would become. The car did not create the demand for good roads; it did, however, decide their form.

area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: the horse-drawn city of the late nineteenth century: the manure-crisis myth, manure as a commodity, the costs of horse traction and the electric tram
title: The Horse-Powered City
subtitle: Why did the horse vanish from city streets, and why is the most famous story about its disappearance probably untrue?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the end of the nineteenth century, the great cities of Europe and North America ran on horses. Omnibuses, cabs and horse-drawn trams carried millions of passengers every day, while carts and vans delivered coal, milk, bread, beer and parcels to every street. London is thought to have depended on around three hundred thousand horses, and the largest American cities on well over a hundred thousand each. Within forty years almost all of them had gone, replaced first by electric trams and then by motor vehicles. Few transformations of urban life have been so rapid or so complete, and few have attracted so many misleading explanations.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely repeated of these is the tale of the 'great manure crisis'. According to this story, a leading London newspaper predicted in 1894 that within fifty years every street in the capital would lie buried under nine feet of manure, and the prediction was overturned only by the timely arrival of the motor car. Dr Wilhelmina Kinnersley, a historian at the Bow Creek Institute of Urban History, has searched the newspaper archives of the period and found no trace of any such article. As far as she can establish, the anecdote first appeared in print around the end of the twentieth century. She suggests that its popularity owes less to its accuracy than to its usefulness, since it neatly illustrates the argument that problems which seem insoluble are often solved by unexpected technological change. Whatever the merits of that argument, a story with no traceable source cannot be used to support it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This does not mean that horses created no problems. Their manure and urine fouled the streets, the noise of iron-shod hooves and wheels on stone was deafening, flies bred in vast numbers, and the carcasses of horses that collapsed in harness had to be removed from public roads. Professor Chukwudi Ezeilo of the Centre for Environmental History in Enugu argues, however, that contemporaries were less troubled by these nuisances than we might imagine. Manure, he points out, was a valuable commodity, collected from city stables and sold to the market gardens that surrounded every large town, so that the urban horse formed part of a cycle linking city and countryside. Ezeilo's picture is accurate for the middle decades of the century. By the 1890s, however, cities had grown so large that the market gardens had moved far beyond their edges, supply greatly exceeded demand, and some stable owners were obliged to pay to have manure taken away.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In the view of the economic historian Dr Inés Larramendi, it was cost rather than cleanliness that sealed the horse's fate. Her analysis of tramway company accounts shows how expensive animal traction had become. Horses on tram routes typically worked for only about four hours a day, so that keeping a single tram in service required a team of ten to twelve animals. A horse might last no more than four or five years in such work before it was worn out, and the price of feed was rising steadily. Companies were also vulnerable to disease: in 1872 an epidemic of equine influenza swept across North America and brought transport in many cities to a standstill for weeks. Larramendi concludes that tramway operators adopted electricity because it cut their running costs dramatically, and that public health concerns played only a minor part in the decision.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Electric trams spread rapidly from the late 1880s onwards, and the effects went far beyond the companies' balance sheets. Lower operating costs allowed lower fares, and for the first time large numbers of clerks and skilled workers could afford to live several miles from their workplaces and travel in daily. New suburbs grew up along the tram lines, and the shape of the modern city began to emerge. It would be a mistake, though, to imagine that horses disappeared from the streets as soon as the trams arrived. For local deliveries, horses survived for decades. A milkman or baker making frequent stops found that a horse would walk on to the next house by itself, saving time that no early motor van could match, and in some cities horse-drawn delivery rounds continued until the 1950s.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is a certain irony in the way the motor car was received. When the first automobiles appeared on city streets, many reformers welcomed them precisely because they promised cleaner, quieter and healthier cities, free from manure, flies and the cruelty inflicted on overworked animals. Few anticipated that the new machines would bring problems of their own, from road deaths to exhaust fumes, on a scale that would eventually dwarf those of the horse-drawn city.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The real story of the horse's disappearance is therefore less dramatic than the legend, but more instructive. It was not a single invention arriving just in time to avert catastrophe, but a gradual process, driven largely by economics, in which different kinds of traffic changed at very different speeds. That pattern, rather than the myth of a city rescued from drowning in manure, is the one most worth remembering.
