area: the history of transport (canals, railways, roads)
topic: the Suez Canal and trade between Europe and Asia after 1869: complementarity with the compound steam engine, uneven effects by cargo type, the persistence of sail and the decline of London's warehouse role
title: The Short Way East
subtitle: The Suez Canal is remembered as a revolution in world trade, but its effects were slower, narrower and more entangled than legend suggests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the Suez Canal opened in 1869, it shortened the sea voyage between London and Bombay by roughly forty per cent, eliminating the long passage around the southern tip of Africa. Contemporaries hailed it as one of the great engineering achievements of the age, and it is still commonly described as having transformed commerce between Europe and Asia almost overnight. The reality was rather different. In its first years the canal carried far less traffic than its promoters had forecast, and the company that operated it struggled to meet its obligations. The transformation, when it came, owed as much to developments elsewhere as to the canal itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The chief obstacle was that the canal was of little use to sailing ships, which still carried most of the world's long-distance cargo. Contrary winds in the Red Sea made the approach slow and hazardous for vessels under sail, and towing them through the canal was expensive. Steamships faced a different difficulty: early marine engines consumed so much coal that a large part of a ship's capacity had to be devoted to fuel, leaving little room for paying cargo. Dr Ottavio Pellandini, a maritime historian at the Ligurian Institute of Naval History, argues that the canal became commercially decisive only in combination with the compound engine, which reused steam in a second cylinder and greatly reduced coal consumption. In his view, the two innovations were complementary: the canal shortened the route enough to make steam voyages to Asia feasible, and the new engine made the remaining fuel costs affordable. Neither, he insists, would have shifted the Asian trade to steam on its own.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How much did the canal actually increase trade? Professor Shirin Shahbazian, an economist at the Caspian School of Economics, has compared the growth of trade between European and Asian ports whose sailing distances were cut by different amounts. Those that gained the most from the shorter route, she finds, saw their trade grow markedly faster than the rest. But the effect was highly uneven. It was concentrated on goods whose value was high in relation to their weight, or which lost value with delay, such as tea, silk and the mails, while bulk cargoes such as rice and jute continued to travel around the Cape by sail for decades. Shahbazian's study is careful and persuasive. Even so, the ports whose distances fell most were not identical to the others in every other respect, and some also benefited from heavy colonial investment in railways and harbours during the same period, which makes it difficult to attribute all of the difference to the canal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The persistence of sail is itself revealing. Far from disappearing, sailing ships were redeployed to routes where speed mattered less than cheapness, carrying grain from Australia and nitrates from South America, and their design improved remarkably in the late nineteenth century. Some historians have described this as a competitive response, in which the threat posed by steam spurred builders of sailing ships to innovate. Dr Mbali Zondo of the Cape Maritime Research Centre is sceptical. She attributes most of the improvement to the falling price of iron and then steel, which allowed larger, stronger and more economical hulls regardless of any competition from steam. Her emphasis on materials is well founded, but it seems unlikely that competition played no role at all: the most striking innovations, in rigging that allowed smaller crews to handle larger ships, addressed exactly the costs on which sail was losing ground.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The canal also had consequences for the organisation of trade that are less often noticed. Researchers working on the Maritime Trade Database, a project that has digitised the records of several hundred trading firms, have shown that the combination of a faster sea route and the newly laid submarine telegraph to India changed how merchants did business. Before 1869, European firms had held large stocks of Asian goods in London warehouses, buying in bulk months in advance. Afterwards, a merchant in Manchester could telegraph an order to Calcutta and expect delivery within weeks, so the need for large stockpiles diminished, and London's role as the great storehouse of Asian produce began to decline. This reorganisation has been remarkably neglected in a literature preoccupied with volumes of trade, and it may in the long run have mattered as much as any increase in tonnage.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The canal's strategic significance was apparent from the start. In 1875 the British government bought a large block of shares in the canal company, and critics at the time warned that the purchase would bind Britain ever more tightly to the defence of Egypt, a prediction that subsequent events would largely confirm. For Asian economies, the consequences were mixed. Cheaper and faster shipping brought European manufactured goods into competition with local handicraft producers, many of whom were ruined, while exporters of raw materials and some cash crops prospered. Whether the canal was beneficial to Asia as a whole is a question that aggregate trade statistics simply cannot answer, since they reveal nothing about who gained and who lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the canal's importance, but it does suggest that the habit of attributing large historical changes to a single piece of infrastructure is misleading. The Suez Canal mattered because it arrived alongside more efficient engines, a chain of coaling stations and a telegraph network, and because merchants learned to use all of them together. Its history is best understood as part of a system rather than as a solitary triumph of engineering.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: why the first coins were made in seventh-century BCE western Anatolia: the trade theory, variable electrum, mercenary payment and temple offerings
title: The Promise in the Metal
subtitle: Historians still disagree about why the first coins were struck, and the answer reveals what money really rests on

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few objects are as familiar as the coin. Yet the round, stamped pieces of metal that most people handle without a second thought had a surprisingly late and localised beginning. The earliest known examples were produced in western Anatolia, in what is now Turkey, at some point in the late seventh century BCE. They were small, irregular lumps of electrum, a naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver, marked on one face with a design such as a lion's head and on the other with simple punch marks. Why anyone should have gone to the trouble of making them is a question that has occupied historians for more than a century. How coins began says a great deal about what money actually is, and the answer that has dominated textbooks for most of that time is, in my view, almost certainly wrong.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The traditional explanation holds that coinage was invented to make trade easier. Merchants, so the argument runs, grew tired of weighing and testing metal at every transaction and welcomed pieces whose value was guaranteed in advance. The theory has an appealing simplicity, but it fits the evidence poorly. The earliest coins were of extremely high value: a single piece of the largest denomination may have been worth several weeks of a labourer's earnings, far too much for buying bread or oil. Moreover, finds of the earliest issues are concentrated close to where they were made, rather than scattered along the routes that traders used. Most tellingly, the great economies of Mesopotamia and Egypt had conducted long-distance commerce for two thousand years using silver measured by weight, without ever feeling the need to stamp it. Whatever problem coins solved, it does not seem to have been one that merchants found pressing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more promising line of enquiry begins with the metal itself. Electrum collected from the rivers of the region varied greatly in composition, with gold making up anything from about seventy to well under fifty per cent of a nugget's weight. Since gold was worth far more than silver, two lumps of identical weight could differ considerably in value, and there was no simple way to tell them apart by eye. Laboratory analyses of early coins carried out by Ayumi Haraguchi of the Kansai Centre for Ancient Metallurgy show something striking: their gold content is remarkably uniform, and consistently lower than that of typical natural electrum. Haraguchi concludes that the issuing authority deliberately mixed in extra silver and then used the stamp to insist that every piece be accepted at a fixed value, pocketing the difference. Her findings are difficult to dispute, but her interpretation seems to me too narrow. A guaranteed value would have removed a genuine obstacle to using electrum at all, and the profit motive and the desire for convenience are hardly mutually exclusive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Who, then, were the first users? Orsolya Dimény, a numismatist at the Pannonian Institute of Economic History, argues that the answer lies in the army. The kings of Lydia, the dominant power in the region, are known to have employed large numbers of foreign soldiers, and paying hundreds of men in standardised pieces would have been far quicker than weighing out metal for each of them. The coins, Dimény suggests, would then have flowed back to the treasury as taxes and fees, creating a closed circuit that the state itself controlled. Her account explains why the earliest denominations were so valuable, since a soldier's pay for a season was a substantial sum. Its weakness is that no surviving document directly records mercenaries being paid in coin during this period, and the theory therefore rests on inference rather than testimony.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A quite different proposal comes from archaeologists working at the sanctuary of a goddess on the coast. A team led by Luiz Ferreira-Amado of the Coastal Anatolia Excavation Project uncovered what remains the largest single group of early coins, buried in the foundations of the temple. Ferreira-Amado contends that coins originated as offerings, or as a means by which temple authorities recorded and stored wealth, and that their economic role developed only later. The discovery is undeniably important, yet the conclusion drawn from it does not follow. A foundation deposit tells us where coins ended up, not why they were made, and valuable objects of every kind were routinely dedicated to the gods in the ancient world.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What is clear is that coinage spread with remarkable speed once it appeared. Within a few generations, Greek cities across the Aegean were minting their own coins, now generally in pure silver rather than electrum, and in an expanding range of denominations. By the fifth century BCE some cities were issuing fractions so tiny that they could be carried in the mouth. It was at this stage, and not before, that coins became the ordinary means of buying food and paying for small services. The everyday market use that the traditional theory places at the beginning of the story was, in fact, one of its later consequences.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate is unlikely ever to be settled conclusively, since the surviving evidence is fragmentary and the motives of seventh-century rulers left no written trace. Nevertheless, the competing theories share one significant feature: in each of them, coins depend on an authority that stands behind them, whether a king, a city or a temple. The material from which they were made mattered less than the promise stamped upon it. That insight remains relevant today, when discussions of new forms of digital currency often focus on technology while neglecting the more fundamental question of who guarantees that a token will be accepted tomorrow.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: the medieval bill of exchange in Italian merchant banking: fund transfer, concealed interest, theological tolerance of exchange risk and 'dry exchange'
title: Paper Across the Alps
subtitle: How medieval Italian bankers lent money at a profit in an age that condemned interest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Throughout the Middle Ages, the Christian Church taught that charging interest on a loan was a sin. Usury, as it was called, was condemned by councils, denounced from the pulpit and, in principle, punishable in the church courts. Yet in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, Italian merchant banks grew into some of the wealthiest enterprises in Europe, with branches stretching from Bruges and London to Avignon and Geneva. At the heart of their business lay a modest-looking document: the bill of exchange. Popular histories often present it as an ingenious trick for evading the usury laws. That description is not exactly false, but it leaves out most of what made the instrument so important.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A typical bill worked as follows. A merchant in Florence handed a sum in florins to a local banker and received in return a written order instructing the banker's agent in Bruges to pay an equivalent amount in Flemish currency at a later date. The interval between issue and payment, known as usance, was fixed by custom for each pair of cities: around two months between Florence and Bruges, and three between Florence and London. Rates were quoted on the exchanges of the great commercial cities, where brokers brought together those who wished to remit funds abroad and those who had money waiting to be collected there. Every bill therefore involved two currencies, two places and a delay, and it was within this combination that profit could be made without anything being labelled as a loan.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Just how that profit arose has been reconstructed by Tadeusz Gołębiowski of the Vistula School of Economics, who has compiled many thousands of exchange rates quoted in surviving merchant correspondence. Because the rate in each city tended to favour the holder of local money, a banker who sent funds abroad and then had them sent back almost always ended up with more florins than he had started with. Gołębiowski calculates that such a round trip yielded an average return of roughly twelve per cent a year, a figure close to the interest charged on openly declared loans where these were permitted. His conclusion is that the bill of exchange was, above all, a credit instrument in which interest had been concealed. Given the sheer quantity of data on which it rests, this argument is very hard to resist.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that concealment was the point, however. Henrik Aasgaard, a historian of trade at the Bergen Institute for Commercial History, emphasises the practical problem that bills solved. Carrying coin over the Alps or along pirate-infested coasts was slow, costly and dangerous, and the volume of payments flowing across Europe was enormous, not least because of the church revenues that were collected in every diocese and had to reach Rome. In Aasgaard's view, merchants used bills chiefly to avoid shipping heavy chests of silver, and the opportunity to earn hidden interest was a convenient by-product. Both positions, it seems to me, capture part of the truth. The profit Gołębiowski measures was certainly real, but it was the need to move money that made bills indispensable in the first place.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, did the Church tolerate them? Mariam Al-Sabbagh, who has studied the treatises of late medieval theologians, argues that the tolerance was principled rather than hypocritical. The theologians drew a distinction between a loan, in which the lender's gain was certain, and an exchange, in which rates might move unexpectedly and leave the banker out of pocket. Risk, they reasoned, justified reward. Some went further, arguing that the banker also provided a genuine service by delivering money in a distant place, and was entitled to payment for it. Al-Sabbagh is right that this was a serious intellectual position and not merely an excuse. Nonetheless, Gołębiowski's figures suggest that in practice the risk was slight, since losses on round trips were rare. The theory was sincere; the danger it relied upon was largely imaginary.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Merchants themselves seem to have understood where the limits lay. Lorenza Pichetti, working through the account books of a Florentine company, has identified numerous examples of so-called dry exchange: bills that were drawn on a foreign city and immediately redrawn, without any money actually changing hands abroad. These were loans in all but name, and theologians condemned them explicitly. Tellingly, the company's clerks did not record such transactions openly but entered them under deliberately vague headings. Such caution indicates that bankers were well aware of the boundary between acceptable and unacceptable practice, even when they chose to cross it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The bill of exchange outlived the usury debate. By the sixteenth century, bills could be transferred to a third party by endorsement, so that a single document might settle several debts as it passed from hand to hand, and in this form it became an ancestor of both the banknote and the cheque. It is tempting to draw a modern moral from the story, namely that strict regulation simply drives financial ingenuity into new and less visible forms. There is something in this, but the parallel should not be pushed too far. Medieval bankers operated within a shared moral framework that they broadly accepted, which is rather different from the relationship between regulators and financial firms today.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: paper money in imperial China from the Sichuan deposit receipts to the Ming collapse: iron coinage, fiscal motives, early issuing discipline and over-issue
title: The First Paper Promise
subtitle: China used paper money for four centuries before abandoning it. What went wrong is not what is usually assumed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When European travellers reached China in the thirteenth century, few things astonished them more than the sight of people buying and selling goods with sheets of printed paper. To visitors from a continent where money meant gold and silver coins, the idea that a piece of mulberry-bark paper could be exchanged for silk or grain seemed close to magic. China had in fact been using paper money for more than two centuries by then, and its long experiment with the new form of currency, which ended in a spectacular collapse, remains one of the most instructive episodes in monetary history. It is also, I would argue, widely misunderstood: the collapse is often taken to prove that paper money is inherently unstable, when the record actually shows something more interesting.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The story begins in Sichuan, a prosperous but mountainous province in the south-west. For reasons of state policy, the region was largely cut off from the bronze coinage used elsewhere in the empire and relied instead on coins of iron, which were bulky and of low value. A string of iron coins sufficient for a modest purchase could weigh several kilograms, making large transactions extremely cumbersome. Merchants responded by leaving their coins with deposit shops, which issued handwritten receipts that soon began to change hands in place of the coins themselves. In the early eleventh century the authorities granted the right to issue these receipts to a group of sixteen wealthy merchant houses. When several of them proved unable to honour their notes, the state stepped in, and in 1023 it established an official agency with a monopoly over issue. Saskia Lervåg, an economic historian at the Nordmark Institute of Economic History, regards the iron coinage as decisive: without its extraordinary inconvenience, she contends, there would have been no pressure to experiment.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ouyang Mingde of the Lingnan Academy of Social Sciences offers a different emphasis. Paper money, he observes, spread well beyond Sichuan once the state discovered how useful it could be in financing its armies on the northern frontier, where enormous quantities of grain and horses had to be purchased. On this reading, the government's interest was fiscal rather than commercial: notes allowed it to command resources it could not otherwise afford. These two accounts are less opposed than they first appear. Lervåg explains why the experiment started where it did; Ouyang explains why the state was so eager to continue it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The officials who took over the system initially managed it with considerable restraint. Each issue was limited to a fixed quota, and notes were valid only for a set term of about three years, after which they had to be exchanged for new ones on payment of a small fee. The issue was supported by a reserve of coin equivalent to roughly a quarter of the notes in circulation, and the notes themselves were printed from several blocks in different colours, a technique intended to defeat forgers. For several decades this discipline held, and the notes circulated at or close to their face value.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The discipline did not survive the pressures of war. Faced with prolonged conflicts in the twelfth century, both the Song and their northern rivals, the Jin, printed notes in quantities far exceeding any reserve, and their value collapsed. The Mongol Yuan dynasty, which conquered all of China in the thirteenth century, created the first paper currency valid throughout an entire empire, and for a time managed it competently, backing the notes with silver and restricting their supply. By the mid-fourteenth century, however, the dynasty was printing money to pay for rebellions and natural disasters, and inflation once again spiralled. Efua Dompreh, who compares monetary systems across pre-modern Eurasia, insists that these failures were political rather than technical. Paper money did not fail because it was paper, she argues, but because rulers in crisis could not resist the temptation to print more of it. I find her case largely convincing, though it perhaps underplays how much easier paper made that temptation to indulge than coins ever had.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The final chapter came under the Ming dynasty, founded in 1368. Its early rulers issued notes that could never be redeemed for metal and printed them without limit. By the middle of the fifteenth century they had become virtually worthless, and commerce moved instead to uncoined silver, weighed out at each transaction. A research group led by Pieter Oostervink at the Zuiderzee Institute for Global History has argued that this shift was so large that it reshaped the world economy, since China's demand for silver drew in metal first from Japan and later from the mines of Spanish America. The scale of the silver flows is not in doubt, but to attribute them chiefly to the failure of Chinese paper money is to overstate the case: population growth and the commercialisation of the Chinese economy would have generated enormous demand for silver in any event.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, does the Chinese experience teach? Not that paper money is doomed, for it functioned well for long periods under careful management. The lesson, rather, is that a currency with no intrinsic value depends entirely on the self-restraint of whoever issues it, and that this restraint is most likely to give way precisely when it is most needed. Modern arrangements that place the issue of money at some distance from day-to-day political pressures are, in this light, less a modern invention than a response to a very old problem.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: the goldsmith-bankers of seventeenth-century London: deposit receipts, early lending, loans to the Crown and the origins of fractional-reserve banking
title: From Strongroom to Bank
subtitle: The London goldsmiths are often credited with inventing modern banking. The real story is less tidy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1640, short of money and in conflict with Parliament, King Charles I seized the bullion that London merchants had stored for safety at the Royal Mint in the Tower of London. The metal was eventually returned, but the episode destroyed the merchants' confidence in the Mint, and many turned instead to the city's goldsmiths, whose trade required them to keep secure vaults. The goldsmiths accepted coin and bullion for safekeeping and handed depositors written receipts in exchange. Before long, these receipts were being passed from one merchant to another in settlement of debts, and depositors began to write instructions directing a goldsmith to pay a named person out of their account, a practice that foreshadowed the modern cheque.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The textbook account of what happened next is familiar. The goldsmiths, it is said, gradually noticed that only a small proportion of the money left with them was ever reclaimed at any one time, and began lending out the remainder at interest. Modern fractional-reserve banking, in which banks hold only a fraction of their deposits as cash, was thus born of a discovery. This story is broadly right, but it is considerably tidier than the evidence allows, and it obscures what was most distinctive about the goldsmiths' business.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Wilhelmina Ruskamp, of the Amstel Centre for Financial History, has examined the few surviving goldsmiths' ledgers from the period, and her findings undermine the idea of a gradual discovery. Lending appears in the accounts almost from the moment deposits do. Many goldsmiths, Ruskamp points out, had already been extending credit to customers as part of their ordinary trade, selling plate on deferred payment or advancing money against pawned jewellery. Deposits simply gave them more to lend. In her words, they were lenders who acquired deposits, not custodians who stumbled upon lending. The ratio of cash to deposits that they maintained varied greatly, from about a third in cautious houses to well under a tenth in the most adventurous.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The goldsmiths' most important borrower was the Crown. After the restoration of the monarchy in 1660, Charles II borrowed heavily from them against the security of future tax revenues, and some leading goldsmiths lent far more to the government than to all their private customers combined. In 1672, under the strain of war, the Exchequer suspended repayments. The so-called Stop of the Exchequer ruined several prominent goldsmiths and inflicted heavy losses on the people whose deposits they had lent to the king. Arvo Tiilikainen, an economic historian at the Lapland Institute of Social Research, argues that the episode reveals where the real weakness of the system lay. The danger, he maintains, came less from keeping small reserves than from concentrating loans on a single borrower who could not be compelled to pay. This seems to me largely correct, although small reserves certainly made the consequences of the Stop worse than they would otherwise have been.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different emphasis comes from Rhiannon Torrance-Bell, who studies the history of payment. For her, the decisive innovation was not lending at all but the transferability of the goldsmiths' paper. Once receipts made out to the bearer circulated freely, she argues, they ceased to be mere evidence of a deposit and became a form of money in their own right, a development that led directly to the banknote. There is much to be said for this view, since a bank that only lent its depositors' coin would hardly have transformed the economy. But transferability and lending were intimately connected: it was precisely because receipts circulated instead of being cashed that goldsmiths could safely lend so much.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The goldsmiths' position was challenged in 1694, when the Bank of England was founded. Zeynep Altınsoy, who has written extensively on the Bank's early decades, interprets its creation partly as a reaction to the failures of the goldsmiths, which had left the government without a reliable source of credit. Others see it more simply as a device for financing the long and expensive war with France, since the Bank's entire initial capital was lent to the government in return for its charter. The second explanation strikes me as the stronger: whatever the merchants who subscribed hoped for, the state's motive was plainly the war. Over the following century, many goldsmiths withdrew from banking altogether, while a minority abandoned the working of precious metals and became private banks, some of which survive under other names to this day.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, did the goldsmiths contribute? They did not discover that deposits could be lent; that idea was implicit in their existing trade. What they demonstrated was that paper promises could circulate as money, provided that holders trusted the issuer to pay. They also demonstrated, more painfully, how quickly that trust could vanish. When a Dutch fleet raided the River Medway in 1667, panicked depositors rushed to withdraw their money, and several goldsmiths were forced to close their doors. Bank runs, in other words, are as old as banking itself, and the lessons of the seventeenth century were available long before modern regulators set out to learn them.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: the barter myth and the origins of money: Mesopotamian units of account, ethnographic evidence on barter, the textbook model and pre-coinage weighed silver
title: Before the Coin, the Debt
subtitle: Did money really emerge to replace barter? Historians and anthropologists have increasingly come to doubt it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than two centuries, introductory economics has told the same story about the origins of money. In the beginning, it runs, people exchanged goods directly: the farmer with surplus grain traded it for the shoemaker's boots. Such barter, however, required what economists call a double coincidence of wants. The farmer had to find a shoemaker who happened to want grain, at the very moment the farmer wanted boots. To escape this inconvenience, communities gradually settled on a single commodity, often a metal, which everyone would accept, and money was born. The tale is elegant and intuitively plausible. Its difficulty is that anthropologists, having looked for well over a century, have never found a society in which barter was the principal means by which neighbours exchanged goods. The story endures, I would suggest, because its logic is so neat, not because anyone has demonstrated that it happened.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the earliest written evidence about economic life points in a different direction. In the temples and palaces of southern Mesopotamia during the third millennium BCE, administrators recorded obligations on clay tablets in standard units of silver and barley. Silver rarely changed hands in these records; rather, it served as a yardstick for comparing the value of quite different things, from wool to labour. Most transactions appear to have taken place on credit, with debts accumulating through the year and settled after the harvest. Gunnhild Ekerholt of the Fjordland Institute of Near Eastern Studies argues that money originated in exactly this way, as a unit of account fixed by administrators to manage the flow of goods through large institutions. Her reading of the tablets is compelling. It is less clear, however, that what was true of Mesopotamia, with its exceptionally powerful temple bureaucracies, can be assumed to hold for every early society.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ethnographic research adds a further complication. The anthropologist Mariama Tounkara, who has spent many years studying exchange in rural West Africa and comparing her findings with published accounts from elsewhere, observes that barter certainly exists, but in particular circumstances. It tends to occur between strangers, or between communities that meet only occasionally and have no continuing relationship. Within a village, by contrast, goods and services circulate through gifts, favours and obligations that are remembered rather than settled on the spot. Tounkara also notes that many of the best-documented cases of barter, such as the use of cigarettes in prison camps or the swapping of goods after a currency has collapsed, involve people who are already thoroughly familiar with money. Barter, on this evidence, is less the ancestor of money than what people fall back on when money or trust is unavailable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the conventional account are not without a reply. Kenji Sasamori, an economist at the Hokuriku Graduate School of Policy, contends that the barter story was never intended as history. It is, he argues, a thought experiment designed to show why a generally accepted medium of exchange is so useful, and it should be judged on those terms. To attack it with archaeological evidence is, in his view, to misunderstand its purpose. There is something to this defence, and the logical point about the usefulness of money survives the historical objections. Yet Sasamori's claim does not describe how the story is actually told. Many textbooks present the progression from barter to money explicitly as a sequence of real events, and generations of students have understandably taken it as such.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the credit theory has been gaining ground, it has not gone entirely unchallenged. Ilse Kronvall, an archaeologist at the Baltic Centre for Material Culture, points to hoards of so-called hack-silver, fragments of cut and broken metal, found across the eastern Mediterranean and dating from centuries before the first coins. Many fragments bear marks of having been tested and weighed repeatedly, which suggests they passed from hand to hand in actual payments rather than merely serving as an abstract measure. Kronvall concludes that credit and physical money existed side by side from an early date, each suited to different kinds of transaction: credit among people who knew one another, weighed metal among those who did not. This position seems to me the most sensible available, since it accommodates both the Mesopotamian tablets and the material evidence without forcing either into a single scheme.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The debate is not merely of antiquarian interest. If money is fundamentally a record of obligations rather than a commodity, then the institutions that keep and enforce that record, above all the state, are central to its existence. This view has been invoked in modern arguments about how money is created, particularly the observation that commercial banks create new deposits whenever they make loans. Some enthusiasts have gone further, concluding that governments able to issue their own currency need never worry about the quantity they create. That conclusion does not follow. Understanding money as credit explains where it comes from; it does not abolish the possibility that too much of it will be issued.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the textbook story should simply be deleted. Its account of the inconvenience of barter remains a useful illustration, and it would be a mistake to replace one tidy myth with another. What the evidence demands is greater modesty about origins. Money appears to have arisen in different ways in different places, sometimes as an administrator's unit of account, sometimes as a metal weighed at a market, and most often, perhaps, as a shifting combination of the two.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: how the Bank of England reluctantly became a lender of last resort in nineteenth-century financial panics (1825, 1847, 1857, 1866) and the moral hazard debate
title: The Reluctant Rescuer
subtitle: How a private company with shareholders came to stand behind an entire financial system

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Financial panics were a recurring feature of nineteenth-century Britain. In 1825, 1847, 1857 and 1866, a sudden loss of confidence sent depositors and creditors rushing to turn their claims into cash, and banks that were perfectly sound found themselves unable to meet the demand. Since every bank kept only a fraction of its liabilities in cash, a run on one institution could quickly spread to others as frightened customers assumed the worst. Out of these crises emerged the principle that, in a panic, a central institution should lend freely to any bank able to offer good security, so that solvent firms are not destroyed simply because cash has temporarily become scarce. Today this role, known as the lender of last resort, is regarded as one of the defining functions of a central bank. It is often described as though it had been deliberately designed. In reality, the institution that performed it accepted the role slowly, inconsistently and with considerable reluctance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That reluctance is easy to understand. Throughout this period the Bank of England was a private company owned by shareholders, and its directors naturally regarded their first duty as being to those owners. During the crisis of 1825, the Bank initially restricted its lending in order to protect its own reserves, behaving exactly as any prudent commercial bank would. Only when the panic threatened to engulf the entire City did it reverse course and begin lending on an unprecedented scale. Tomasz Rybarczyk, a historian at the Silesian Institute of Economic Thought, regards this reversal as the real starting point. In his view, the Bank was acting as a lender of last resort in practice several decades before anyone set out the doctrine in writing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The crises of 1847 and 1857 added a further twist. Under legislation passed in 1844, the Bank's issue of banknotes was strictly limited, and in both years the government sent the Bank a letter promising to seek retrospective approval if it exceeded that limit. Camila Ortúzar, who has studied the correspondence surrounding these episodes, points out that in 1847 the letter alone was enough to calm the markets; very few additional notes were actually issued. For Ortúzar, this shows that what mattered was the guarantee rather than the money. Her interpretation fits 1847 well, but it is harder to apply to 1857, when the Bank did in fact issue notes beyond the legal limit and lent heavily to firms in difficulty. Confidence was certainly part of the story, but so was cash.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most celebrated episode came in 1866, when Overend, Gurney and Company, a giant of the London money market, collapsed. The Bank refused to rescue it, yet in the days that followed it lent enormous sums to other banks and discount houses. Fergus Strachan of the Clydebank School of Finance argues that this combination was crucial. By allowing a firm that was genuinely insolvent to fail while supporting those that were merely short of cash, the Bank established a rule for deciding who deserved help. The distinction is clear enough in principle. In the middle of a panic, however, when the value of every asset is uncertain and rumours spread by the hour, telling an insolvent firm from a temporarily illiquid one is very much harder than Strachan's account implies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Then, as now, critics warned of what is today called moral hazard: if banks know they will be rescued, they may take greater risks. Bertil Engqvist, an economist at the Malaren Institute for Monetary Studies, argues that the Bank kept this danger in check by charging a high rate of interest on emergency loans, so that help was available but never cheap. He points out that after 1866 Britain experienced no comparable panic for almost half a century; even the Baring crisis of 1890 was contained by a guarantee fund that the Bank organised among the leading banks. The record is impressive, but attributing it chiefly to interest-rate policy seems doubtful. The same decades saw small local banks merge into large national companies with extensive branch networks, which were far less vulnerable to local runs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These nineteenth-century debates are frequently invoked when central banks intervene in modern crises, and the classical principle of lending freely at a high rate against good security is still treated as a benchmark. Yet the resemblance is often superficial. Modern central banks lend against a much wider range of assets, frequently at low rather than penalty rates, and sometimes to institutions that are not banks at all. There may be good reasons for these changes, given the scale and complexity of today's financial system. But it would be more honest to acknowledge that current practice has moved further from the Victorian rule than its defenders usually admit.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the achievement of the Victorian Bank. Its directors, caught between their obligations to shareholders and the mounting expectations of the City and the government, gradually worked out a set of practices that turned recurrent disasters into manageable episodes. They did so without a clear mandate and often against their own instincts. Perhaps the most enduring lesson of their experience is that the responsibilities of a central bank are rarely assigned in advance; more often, they are discovered in the middle of a crisis and only later written into law.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: the classical gold standard of 1870-1914: how adjustment really worked, London's central role, deflation and its costs, political foundations and the luck of new gold supplies
title: A Golden Age Reconsidered
subtitle: The international gold standard is often remembered as a model of stability. Was it really so stable, and why did it work at all?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the 1870s and the outbreak of the First World War, most of the world's major economies fixed the value of their currencies to a set weight of gold. Britain had effectively done so since early in the century; Germany, France, the United States and many others followed in the decades after 1870. The result was a system of fixed exchange rates within which goods and capital moved across borders with remarkable freedom. In retrospect, the period has acquired an almost legendary reputation as an era of monetary order, and some modern commentators speak of it with open nostalgia. That reputation, in my view, is considerably inflated. The gold standard did work, after a fashion, but for reasons rather different from those usually given, and at a cost that was borne very unevenly.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The textbook explanation of how the system corrected itself is elegant. A country that imported more than it exported would pay for the difference by shipping gold abroad. Its money supply would therefore shrink, its prices would fall, its goods would become cheaper for foreigners, and the trade imbalance would gradually disappear. Anneliese Vortmann, an economic historian at the Weser Institute of Monetary History, has tested this account against the records of actual gold shipments and found that they were far too small to have performed the work attributed to them. Instead, she argues, imbalances were corrected chiefly by central banks raising their interest rates, which drew short-term funds from abroad within days and spared the need to move much metal at all. Her evidence is persuasive, and it changes our picture of the system substantially: the gold standard was managed by bankers far more than it was governed by the automatic movement of gold.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Which bankers mattered most? Meenakshi Thirunavukkarasu, of the Coromandel School of International Finance, places London at the centre of everything. Much of the world's trade, she notes, was financed by sterling bills drawn on London banks, so that when the Bank of England raised its rate, funds flowed towards Britain from every corner of the globe. The system, she concludes, was in effect a sterling standard dressed in gold clothing. This argument is largely convincing, but it understates the extent to which London itself depended on others. During the Baring crisis of 1890, for example, the Bank of England was able to defend its reserves only because the Bank of France lent it gold. Cooperation, in other words, was occasionally as important as dominance.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The costs of the system fell most heavily on those at its edges. Countries in Latin America and southern Europe repeatedly found themselves unable to maintain convertibility and were forced off gold, often amid severe financial distress. Even at the centre, the period from 1873 to 1896 saw prices fall steadily, as the supply of gold failed to keep pace with economic growth. Dmitri Volodarsky, an economist at the Kama Institute of Applied Economics, argues that this deflation has been overdramatised, pointing out that total output continued to grow throughout. The aggregate figures, however, conceal a great deal. Falling prices increased the real burden of debts, and indebted farmers in the United States campaigned so bitterly against gold that the use of silver alongside it became the central issue of a presidential election. Growth in the national accounts was little comfort to a farmer who lost his land.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A deeper question is why governments were prepared to accept such costs at all. Yasmin Bourkadi of the Maghreb Centre for Political Economy offers a political answer. Before 1914, she points out, the right to vote was restricted in most countries, trade unions were weak, and there was little expectation that governments should prevent unemployment. Authorities could therefore raise interest rates and allow wages and employment to fall without serious political consequences. Once mass democracy and organised labour arrived, that freedom disappeared. Of all the explanations on offer, this seems to me the most illuminating, particularly in accounting for why the attempt to restore the gold standard in the 1920s collapsed so quickly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Finally, the system enjoyed a good deal of luck. The long deflation came to an end not because of any change in policy but because of a series of gold discoveries, most notably in South Africa from 1886 and later in the Yukon, together with a new chemical technique, the cyanide process, which made it possible to extract gold profitably from low-grade ore. World gold output rose sharply, and prices began to climb again after 1896. Had these discoveries not occurred, the deflationary pressures of the 1880s might well have continued, with unpredictable political results.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the gold standard was a failure. It provided a framework of predictable exchange rates during a remarkable expansion of world trade and investment. But it was neither automatic nor costless, and it rested on political and geological conditions that no longer exist. Those who propose a return to gold as a cure for modern monetary problems would do well to remember that the system they admire depended on bankers' discretion, on London's peculiar position and on a succession of fortunate discoveries in distant mines.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: cowrie shells as currency from the Maldives to Bengal and West Africa: small-change function, supply routes, links to the Atlantic trade, nineteenth-century inflation and colonial replacement
title: Small Change from the Lagoons
subtitle: For centuries, a tiny shell from the Indian Ocean served as money across two continents

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the many objects that have served as money, few travelled as far or lasted as long as the cowrie, the small, glossy shell of a sea snail found in the warm waters of the Indian Ocean. From at least the thirteenth century until the early twentieth, cowries circulated as currency in Bengal, in parts of south-western China and, above all, across a broad belt of West Africa. European observers of the colonial era frequently dismissed them as 'primitive money', a curiosity that proved the backwardness of the societies that used it. That judgement says more about the observers than about the shells. Cowries met real economic needs with considerable efficiency, and their eventual disappearance owed little to any failing of their own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physical qualities of the shell go some way towards explaining its success. Cowries are durable, of fairly uniform size and almost impossible to imitate, and because they could be counted rather than weighed, transactions were quick and straightforward. Ksenia Tarabrina, a historian of Indian Ocean trade at the Kazan Centre for Oriental Studies, nonetheless argues that their most important characteristic was their very low value. A single shell was worth only a tiny fraction of the smallest copper coin, which meant that cowries could be used for the countless minor purchases of everyday life, such as a handful of vegetables or a cup of water, for which metal coinage was simply too valuable. Producing coins of such small denominations would have cost more than the coins themselves were worth. Cowries, in Tarabrina's view, solved the problem of small change that troubled monetary systems everywhere. This seems to me exactly right.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Almost the entire supply came from a single source, the Maldive Islands. Islanders gathered the shells by laying bundles of coconut palm leaves in the shallow lagoons, waiting for the snails to attach themselves, and then leaving the creatures to die and decay in the sun. The cleaned shells were shipped to Bengal, where they were used both as local currency and as ballast in the holds of ships sailing westward. From the sixteenth century onwards, European traders, first the Portuguese and later the Dutch and English, bought cowries in vast quantities and carried them to West Africa, where many were used to purchase captives for the Atlantic slave trade. Wanjiru Nyabuto-Ashby of the Rift Valley Institute of African History insists that the cowrie currency of West Africa cannot be understood apart from that trade. She is right to stress the connection, which was for a long time politely ignored. Yet cowries also circulated in local markets far from the coast, among people who had no direct involvement with European commerce, and their monetary role was not simply an extension of the slave trade.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In the nineteenth century the system came under severe strain. German and French merchants discovered that a larger related species could be gathered cheaply along the coast of East Africa, and they began shipping it to West Africa in quantities that dwarfed earlier imports. The consequences were predictable. Ilari Pöyhönen, an economic historian at the Saimaa Institute of Economic Research, has reconstructed cowrie prices from merchants' records and estimates that in some West African markets the value of the shell fell by more than four-fifths over the second half of the century. Ordinary transactions came to require such enormous numbers of shells that porters had to be hired simply to carry the money needed for a large purchase. Pöyhönen is careful to note that the decline was uneven, being steepest near the ports where the new shells arrived and much gentler in inland markets, which were supplied more slowly and continued to prefer the smaller, traditional variety.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How did African societies manage a currency over which they had no control of supply? Duarte Coutinho-Vale, of the Atlantic Centre for Economic Anthropology, argues that local rulers regulated its use with some sophistication. He points to standard counting units, in which shells were threaded on strings of forty and grouped into larger bundles of fixed size, and to evidence that some kingdoms set official exchange rates between cowries and other goods. It is an attractive argument, but the documentary basis for it remains slender, consisting largely of the reports of a handful of European visitors who may not have understood what they saw. Until more evidence is found, his conclusions are best treated as a promising hypothesis rather than an established fact.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The final blow came from colonial governments in the early twentieth century. Determined to integrate their territories into imperial economies, they introduced metal coins and, crucially, required taxes to be paid in the new currency rather than in shells. Even so, cowries survived in rural markets for decades, a sign of how deeply they were embedded in daily life. Their replacement was therefore a political decision imposed from outside, not the natural triumph of a superior form of money. The history of the cowrie is a reminder that a currency does not need to be made of precious metal to function well; what it needs is acceptance, and acceptance can be withdrawn by those with the power to do so.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: English Exchequer tally sticks (twelfth century to 1826): split-stick security, tallies of assignment, whether tallies circulated as money, and why the system lasted so long
title: Notches of Account
subtitle: For six centuries the English state kept its accounts on split wooden sticks. Were they also a form of money?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On an October evening in 1834, workmen disposing of a great quantity of old wooden sticks in a furnace beneath the House of Lords overloaded the flues, and by nightfall most of the medieval Palace of Westminster was in flames. The sticks were Exchequer tallies, the device by which the English state had recorded payments for more than six hundred years before finally abandoning them in 1826. The irony of the episode, in which the obsolete records of royal finance burned down the seat of government, has ensured that the tally is remembered chiefly as an anecdote. That is a pity, because the humble stick raises questions about the nature of money that are anything but trivial.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle was simple. When a sum was paid into the Exchequer, notches were cut across a squared stick of hazel or willow, their width indicating the amount: a cut as broad as the palm of a hand stood for a thousand pounds, one the width of a thumb for a hundred, and progressively narrower cuts for smaller sums. The stick was then split lengthwise through the notches. The longer piece, the stock, went to the payer as a receipt, while the shorter foil was retained by the Exchequer. Hrafnhildur Sveinsdóttir, a historian of administrative technology at the Reykjavik School of Archival Studies, emphasises the security this provided. Because no two pieces of wood share the same grain, the halves could be matched only with each other, and any attempt to add or alter a notch on one half would be exposed at once. For Sveinsdóttir, this explains the system's extraordinary longevity. Her account of the security is undoubtedly correct, but a technique that worked well is not in itself enough to explain why it survived for so long after better alternatives had become available.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The more intriguing chapter in the tally's history concerns what were known as tallies of assignment. Medieval kings were chronically short of cash, and rather than paying suppliers and soldiers in coin, the Exchequer often handed them a tally that entitled the holder to collect the sum from a particular sheriff or customs officer when the revenue came in. Rangimarie Tawhai of the Aotearoa Institute of Fiscal History argues that these instruments functioned as a kind of money. Creditors who could not afford to wait, she points out, frequently sold their tallies to merchants or financiers at a discount, and the buyers then collected the full amount at a later date. A market in royal debt, on this view, existed centuries before the creation of government bonds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ruben Kalmthout, an economic historian at the Lowlands Centre for Public Finance, is unconvinced. The surviving records, he notes, show relatively few transfers of tallies from one holder to another, and a striking number of tallies of assignment proved impossible to collect at all, because the revenue they were drawn on had already been spent; such tallies were returned to the Exchequer and replaced, sometimes repeatedly. To call them money, Kalmthout maintains, is to project a modern concept onto a medieval practice. Each side, it seems to me, is describing a different period. In much of the Middle Ages, Kalmthout's caution is justified. But in the later seventeenth century, when legislation made certain Exchequer orders formally transferable, a lively trade in such paper undoubtedly developed. Whether tallies behaved like money depended on when one looks.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, did the system survive into the nineteenth century? Nikolai Zhdanovich, of the Volga Institute of Institutional History, finds the answer in the Exchequer's own staff. Many of its offices had become hereditary or purchased positions whose holders earned fees for each stage of the ancient procedure, and they had every reason to resist reform. Only when the last of these office-holders died could the tallies be abolished. This account is persuasive as far as it goes, but it should be added that tallies were extremely cheap to produce and, as Sveinsdóttir rightly observes, almost impossible to forge. Self-interest and genuine practical merit probably worked together.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What makes the tally more than an antiquarian curiosity is the light it casts on the relationship between money and debt. A tally was, at bottom, a record of an obligation, yet in the right circumstances it could pass from hand to hand and settle other obligations, which is precisely what money does. The point was not lost on contemporaries. When the Bank of England enlarged its capital in 1697, subscribers were permitted to pay for a substantial part of their new shares with tallies rather than coin, a clear indication that these wooden records had come to be treated as financial assets in their own right. The line between a debt and a means of payment was, and perhaps still is, far less sharp than we tend to assume.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The tallies that fed the furnace in 1834 were, by then, nothing more than surplus firewood. Yet for most of their long history they had been at the centre of the state's finances, recording what it was owed, promising what it would pay and, at times, serving as a currency of sorts among those who traded in its debts.

area: the history of money and banking
topic: competitive note issue without a central bank: Scottish free banking (1716-1845) compared with the American free banking era (1837-1863)
title: Banks Without a Master
subtitle: Two historical experiments with competing private banknotes still divide economists

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Today it is taken for granted that the banknotes in a country's pockets are issued by a single central authority. For long stretches of history, however, this was not the case. From the early eighteenth century until 1845, Scotland had no central bank at all; instead, a number of private banks issued their own notes and competed openly for customers. Across the Atlantic, between 1837 and 1863, many American states adopted so-called free banking laws, under which anyone who met certain conditions could open a bank and print money. These two episodes are regularly cited in arguments over whether money can safely be left to competition: Scotland as proof that it can, the United States as a warning that it cannot. Both cases, I would argue, are routinely misrepresented by the people who invoke them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Scottish system was undeniably successful. Notes from the leading banks were widely trusted, failures were rare, and losses to noteholders were small. A key mechanism was the regular note exchange, at which banks swapped the notes of their rivals that had come into their hands and settled the balances in gold or in claims on London. A bank that issued more notes than the public wished to hold would soon find them presented for payment by its competitors and would have to pull back. Ciprian Moldovanu, an economic historian at the Carpathian Institute of Monetary Studies, regards this as conclusive evidence that competition itself produced stability, without any need for a central authority. It is an impressive argument, but it passes over an important advantage. Scottish banks were closely tied to the London money market and could, in an emergency, obtain funds there, which meant that the Bank of England stood in the background as an indirect source of support.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Elif Karataşlı, of the Bosphorus School of Economic History, points to a different feature of Scottish banking: unlimited liability. The partners of most Scottish banks were personally responsible for its debts to the full extent of their private fortunes. Since these partners were often landowners of considerable wealth, they had every reason to insist on cautious management. The fate of the Ayr Bank, which collapsed spectacularly in 1772, illustrates the point. Although the bank failed, its noteholders were eventually paid in full, because the estates of its partners were sold to meet its obligations. The partners were ruined; the public was protected. Karataşlı's emphasis seems to me entirely reasonable, and it suggests that the Scottish achievement owed as much to legal rules as to market competition.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The American experience has a far worse reputation. The term 'wildcat bank' evokes institutions set up in remote places, where it was supposedly so difficult to find them that noteholders could never redeem their notes, and whose owners vanished once the notes had been spent. Ugnė Petrauskaitė, who has examined the surviving records of banks in several states, has found little evidence of such widespread fraud. Average losses to noteholders, she reports, were modest, and most failures were caused not by dishonesty but by a fall in the market value of the state government bonds that banks were required to hold as security for their notes. When those bonds lost value, as many did at the outbreak of the Civil War, banks that had behaved perfectly properly could no longer cover their issue. Her work is convincing, and it suggests that the image of the wildcat banker owes more to folklore than to the historical record.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This does not mean the American system was without serious flaws. Joseph Kuoh, an economist at the Wouri Institute of Development Finance, draws attention to a cost that is easy to overlook. By the 1850s, thousands of different notes were in circulation, each accepted at a discount that varied with the distance from the issuing bank and its reputation. Merchants relied on regularly published guides listing the current value of every note and describing known forgeries. The result, Kuoh argues, was a substantial burden on everyday trade, since every transaction involving an unfamiliar note required checking and bargaining. The point is well made. Markets adapted with considerable ingenuity, but the sheer inconvenience of the system was a real cost, even if it rarely appears in statistics of bank failures.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Neither experiment ended because it had been shown to fail. In Scotland, legislation in 1845 restricted the issue of new notes as part of a wider effort by the British government to centralise control over money. In the United States, the free banking era was brought to a close by the National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864, passed in the middle of the Civil War largely to create a market for federal government debt. In both cases, political and fiscal priorities, rather than any clear verdict on the merits of competition, determined the outcome.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Advocates of privately issued digital currencies sometimes point to Scotland as evidence that money does not require a central bank. The comparison deserves caution. Scottish banks operated with unlimited liability, close links to a powerful financial centre and a small, tightly knit community of bankers who watched each other closely. Few of those conditions apply to the issuers of digital tokens today, and drawing simple lessons from either historical case is likely to mislead.

topic: the radiocarbon calibration plateau of the first millennium BC and strategies for dating sites that fall within it
title: The Fog Over Four Centuries
subtitle: Why radiocarbon dates become frustratingly vague for part of prehistory, and what archaeologists are doing about it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since its development in the mid-twentieth century, radiocarbon dating has become the most widely used tool for placing archaeological remains in time. The principle is straightforward. Living organisms absorb carbon from the atmosphere, including a tiny proportion of the radioactive isotope carbon-14, and when they die this isotope decays at a known rate, halving roughly every 5,730 years. By measuring how much remains in a fragment of charcoal, bone or seed, a laboratory can estimate how long ago the organism died. What is less widely appreciated outside the discipline is that the raw measurement is not, in itself, a calendar date. It must first be converted, or 'calibrated', and it is in this conversion that some of the most stubborn problems in archaeological chronology arise.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Calibration is necessary because the concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has never been constant. It has fluctuated with changes in solar activity, in the strength of the earth's magnetic field and in the exchange of carbon between the air and the oceans. To correct for this, scientists have built calibration curves from materials whose calendar ages are independently known, above all tree rings, which can be counted year by year. The curve allows a radiocarbon measurement to be translated into a range of possible calendar years. Where the curve slopes steeply, a measurement corresponds to a narrow range; where it wiggles or flattens, a single measurement may be consistent with several centuries.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most notorious of these flat sections, known as a plateau, spans roughly 800 to 400 BC, a period of great importance for European prehistory. Samples from anywhere within this interval tend to yield almost identical radiocarbon ages, so that a hearth lit in 750 BC can be indistinguishable from one lit three hundred years later. Dr Ilinca Ardeleanu of the Carpathian Institute for Archaeometry has described the plateau as 'a fog that settles over four centuries'. Her survey of more than two hundred excavation reports found that sites falling within it were routinely assigned date ranges so wide that they could not show whether neighbouring settlements had been occupied at the same time. As a result, she argues, models of population growth have been quietly distorted, because sites that may have been occupied in succession are counted as contemporary. Her concern seems well founded, since estimates of past population often depend on counting how many settlements existed at any one moment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One response has been to look for help elsewhere. Professor Hideo Kobayakawa, who directs a tree-ring laboratory in northern Japan, argues that the only dependable route through the plateau is to abandon radiocarbon wherever possible and to date timbers directly from their ring patterns, which can identify the exact year in which a tree was felled. His laboratory's work on waterlogged wooden structures has produced some striking results, including felling dates for lakeside platforms that had previously been placed only within a broad two-hundred-year window. The limitation, as Kobayakawa himself acknowledges, is that suitable timber survives only in exceptional conditions, and the great majority of sites yield nothing more than scattered charcoal.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second approach, championed by Marisol Antequera's group at the Andean Centre for Chronometric Studies, relies on a technique known as wiggle-matching. When a piece of wood contains many rings, a sequence of radiocarbon measurements taken at known intervals across it produces a pattern of rises and falls that can be fitted against the shape of the calibration curve, much as one might match a fragment of a torn page to the rest of the document. Antequera's team has shown that even on the plateau, the small irregularities in the curve can sometimes be exploited in this way to narrow a date to within a few decades. The method is costly, however, requiring a dozen or more measurements for a single object. Its expense means that, for the foreseeable future, it is likely to remain a specialist tool reserved for key objects rather than a routine procedure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that technical refinements are the answer. Dr Konrad Falkenrath, an archaeologist who has written extensively on Iron Age Europe, contends that the plateau is as much an intellectual problem as a scientific one. Researchers, he claims, have grown so reliant on laboratory dates that they have neglected older forms of evidence, such as the sequence of layers on a site and the gradual change in the styles of pottery and metalwork. Combined carefully, he believes, such evidence can place events in order even where absolute dates are unavailable. This argument contains an important truth, but it can be pushed too far. Stylistic sequences were themselves anchored, in many cases, to radiocarbon dates, and treating them as an independent check risks a circular argument.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What seems clear is that no single solution will lift the fog. The most promising work combines several lines of evidence within statistical frameworks that take account of the sequence in which samples were deposited, so that the layering of a site can constrain otherwise vague measurements. It would be a mistake, though, to regard the plateau purely as a nuisance. By forcing archaeologists to be explicit about the uncertainty in their chronologies, it has arguably encouraged more honest scholarship than the deceptively precise dates of earlier decades. The real danger lies not in imprecise dates but in imprecise dates presented as if they were exact.

topic: cosmic-ray radiocarbon spikes in tree rings (Miyake-type events) as markers for exact-year dating of wood
title: Fixed Points in the Rings
subtitle: Sudden bursts of radiation from space have left traces in ancient wood that may allow archaeologists to date some objects to a single year

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of archaeological science, the phrase 'exact date' has been reserved for a small and privileged class of objects: coins stamped with a ruler's name, inscriptions recording a reign, or timbers whose ring patterns can be matched against a master tree-ring sequence. Everything else has been assigned a range, often a generous one, of possible years. In the past decade, however, a discovery made almost by accident in the rings of ancient trees has begun to blur this distinction. Short, sharp spikes in the amount of radiocarbon trapped in wood, apparently caused by bursts of cosmic radiation, can serve as markers that fix a sample to a single calendar year, even when the sample has no other connection to a known chronology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first such spike was identified when a team analysing individual annual rings from old cedar trees found that the carbon-14 content rose abruptly between one year and the next, by an amount roughly twenty times larger than the normal year-to-year variation. Similar jumps were subsequently found in trees from several continents, all in the ring for the same year, which ruled out a local explanation. A handful of further events have since been detected, the oldest more than nine thousand years ago. Their cause is still disputed. The prevailing view links them to extreme storms of particles from the sun, far larger than any recorded in the era of scientific instruments, though other explanations, including distant stellar explosions, have not been entirely excluded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For archaeologists, the cause matters less than the consequence. Because every tree alive at the time of an event recorded the spike in the ring it formed that year, any piece of wood containing enough rings, together with some bark or the outermost growth ring, can in principle be dated precisely. One locates the ring with the spike, then counts outward to the last ring formed before the tree was cut down. Dr Sigrun Hrafnsson, whose laboratory pioneered the archaeological use of the method, describes it as 'turning a radiocarbon problem into a counting exercise'. Her team used it to show that the timbers of a North Atlantic trading post had all been felled in a single winter, a finding that overturned an earlier interpretation of the site as a settlement built up gradually over several generations.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The approach has obvious attractions in regions where conventional tree-ring dating is impossible. Building a master chronology requires long runs of overlapping timbers from a single area, and in much of Africa, South America and the tropics such sequences either do not exist or cannot be constructed, often because tropical trees do not lay down clear annual rings. Professor Ousmane Hamadou of the Sahel Institute of Earth Sciences has argued that cosmic-ray markers could finally give these regions access to the kind of precision that European archaeology has enjoyed for decades. His own pilot study of wooden granary posts from the Niger bend, though limited to a few samples, produced dates that matched oral histories of the granaries' construction to within a generation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet the method's usefulness is constrained by the rarity of the events themselves. Only a few spikes are firmly established across the past twelve thousand years, separated by intervals of many centuries. A timber can be pinned to one of them only if its rings happen to span the relevant year, and few archaeological samples are so fortunate. Dr Taras Ostapchuk, a radiocarbon specialist based in Lviv, has calculated that fewer than one in twenty of the timbers in his institute's collection could be dated in this way. He also warns that the search for a spike is expensive: because the signal is visible only in individual annual rings, dozens of separate measurements may be needed to locate it, each requiring the painstaking separation of rings that may be less than a millimetre thick.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty concerns the reliability of the markers. Bettina Leutwiler, who leads an atmospheric physics group in Bern, has drawn attention to evidence that the spikes do not appear with equal clarity everywhere. In trees from some southern latitudes the increase seems to have been smaller, and in a few cases it appears to have arrived a year later, perhaps because of the time taken for carbon to mix through the atmosphere. Leutwiler does not dispute the value of the method, but she insists that archaeologists should not treat the spike as an infallible stamp, particularly when dating wood from regions where its behaviour has not been checked against independently dated trees.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These cautions are important, and enthusiasm for the technique has sometimes run ahead of the evidence. Several published claims of exact-year dates have relied on a single tree, without the replication that tree-ring scientists would normally demand. Nonetheless, the significance of the discovery is hard to overstate. It has shown that the radiocarbon record, long regarded as a source of smooth and blurred information, contains sharp features of extraordinary precision. More events will almost certainly be found as annual-ring measurements become cheaper, and each one will add another fixed point to which the past can be anchored.
