topic: optically stimulated luminescence dating of sediments: partial bleaching, single-grain measurement and the problem of artefacts moving between layers
title: When the Sand Last Saw the Sun
subtitle: Luminescence dating has pushed archaeological chronologies far beyond the reach of radiocarbon, but its results depend on knowing exactly what is being dated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Many of the most important questions in human prehistory concern sites where nothing organic survives. Bone dissolves in acidic soils, charcoal is washed away, and in any case radiocarbon dating cannot reach much beyond fifty thousand years, after which too little carbon-14 remains to be measured. For deposits older than this, or for sites consisting of little more than stone tools embedded in sand, archaeologists increasingly turn to a technique known as optically stimulated luminescence, or OSL. Rather than dating the remains of a living thing, OSL dates the moment at which grains of sediment were last exposed to daylight, which, for an archaeologist, usually means the moment they were buried.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physics behind the method is elegant. Minerals such as quartz and feldspar contain tiny defects in their crystal structure which can trap electrons. Once a grain is buried, natural radiation from the surrounding sediment gradually fills these traps, so that the longer the grain remains underground, the more energy it stores. Exposure to sunlight empties the traps within minutes, setting the clock back to zero. In the laboratory, grains are stimulated with light under controlled conditions, and the luminescence they emit reveals the total radiation dose received since burial. Dividing this figure by the annual dose rate gives an age. The dose rate, however, must be estimated from the concentrations of radioactive elements in the surrounding soil, and it is also affected by water held in that soil, which absorbs part of the radiation before it reaches the grains.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first complication is that not every grain enters the ground with its clock properly reset. Sediment carried by murky floodwater, or dumped suddenly by the collapse of a riverbank, may receive too little light for all its traps to empty. Such grains retain an inherited signal, and a sample containing many of them will appear older than it really is. For decades the problem was difficult to detect, because measurements were made on aliquots containing hundreds or thousands of grains at once, so that a few poorly reset grains could distort the average without anyone noticing. The solution, developed largely by Dr Nirosha Dassanayake and her colleagues at the Institute of Quaternary Geochronology, was to measure grains one at a time. Single-grain analysis allows researchers to plot the full distribution of ages within a sample and to identify, and exclude, grains whose signals were never fully cleared. It is no exaggeration to say that this innovation has transformed the reliability of the method.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second complication is subtler and has generated fiercer debate. Sediments do not necessarily stay where they were deposited. Burrowing animals, plant roots and the feet of later occupants can all move grains, and the artefacts among them, up or down through a sequence. Dr Milan Sarvanovic, a geoarchaeologist who has studied termite activity in tropical soils, argues that at several sites claimed as evidence of very early human arrival, stone tools may have worked their way downwards through loose sand over thousands of years. If so, the sediment surrounding the tools would be older than the tools themselves, and the impressive ages reported would date the sand rather than the human presence. Sarvanovic does not claim to have proved that this happened, only that the possibility has not been adequately ruled out.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The researchers responsible for one of the most contested of these sites, a team led by Annika Lorentzen, have responded in detail. They point out that single-grain measurements, besides revealing poorly reset grains, can also expose mixing: if grains had moved freely between layers, the age distributions of neighbouring samples would overlap heavily, yet their data show distinct, well-separated groups. They also report that broken stone flakes found in the same layer can often be fitted back together, which would be unlikely if the pieces had migrated independently through the deposit. On this particular site, Lorentzen's evidence seems to me considerably stronger than her critics allow. Sarvanovic's general warning, though, remains valuable, since many older OSL studies were carried out before such checks were routine.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third source of uncertainty receives far less public attention, although specialists regard it as equally significant. Because the dose rate depends on the moisture content of the sediment, any change in that content over time alters the calculation. A deposit that is dry today may have been waterlogged for long periods in the past, and vice versa. Researchers must therefore estimate an average water content across the entire period of burial, a figure that can rarely be checked directly. Errors of this kind typically add five to ten per cent to the uncertainty of an OSL date, which for a sample sixty thousand years old amounts to several thousand years. Popular accounts that report such ages as if they were precise to the century are, at best, misleading.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this undermines the value of luminescence dating, which has opened periods of prehistory that were once almost entirely inaccessible. What it does underline is that an OSL age is a measurement of when sediment was buried, not of when a person dropped a tool, and that the connection between the two must always be argued rather than assumed. The most convincing studies are those that publish their full single-grain data alongside their conclusions, allowing others to examine the evidence for themselves. That practice ought to become a standard expectation rather than an admirable exception.

topic: Bayesian statistical modelling of radiocarbon dates and the debate over priors, outliers and generation-scale prehistory
title: Prehistory at the Scale of a Lifetime
subtitle: Statistical modelling promises to date ancient events to within a few decades. How far should archaeologists trust it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A single radiocarbon date, once calibrated, rarely tells an archaeologist when something happened with any real precision. More often it yields a span of one or two centuries within which the event probably occurred. For many purposes this is adequate, but it makes it almost impossible to distinguish between developments that took place within a few generations of one another. Two houses with overlapping date ranges might have been lived in simultaneously, or a hundred years apart; a monument might have been built in a single campaign or extended piecemeal over centuries. The raw dates alone cannot settle the matter.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the past thirty years, a statistical approach derived from the work of the eighteenth-century mathematician Thomas Bayes has been applied to this problem with increasing confidence. Its central idea is that radiocarbon results should not be interpreted in isolation but combined with other things the excavator knows. The most common form of such 'prior' information is the order of layers on a site: if one deposit lies sealed beneath another, its contents must be older. By building this knowledge into a formal model, researchers can exclude portions of each date range that are incompatible with the sequence, often reducing uncertainties from centuries to decades. In my view, this represents one of the most significant advances in archaeological method since radiocarbon itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Its enthusiasts have made striking claims. Professor Nino Abuladze, whose team has modelled hundreds of dates from Neolithic enclosures, argues that the approach has finally allowed archaeologists to write histories at the scale of human lives rather than vague epochs. Her models suggest that many enclosures once thought to have been used for centuries were in fact constructed, used and abandoned within the span of two or three generations. Prehistory, on this view, was not a slow, uniform drift but a sequence of short-lived episodes, bursts of building separated by long intervals of relative inactivity. Abuladze also maintains that this pattern has implications well beyond chronology: if communities invested enormous effort in monuments that were used only briefly, the motives behind their construction may have had more to do with the shared act of building than with the long-term use of the finished structure.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others are more cautious. Dr Yonas Tsegai, a statistician who has collaborated on numerous excavation projects, points out that a model's output can be highly sensitive to the assumptions put into it. Researchers must decide, for instance, whether the dated events within a phase are spread evenly through time or clustered towards its beginning. Such choices are seldom determined by the evidence, and Tsegai has shown that two models, each perfectly reasonable, can produce estimates for the same event that differ by more than a century. His criticism is important, but it is sometimes taken further than he intends. Sensitivity can itself be tested, by running alternative models and reporting how far the conclusions change, and the best studies now do exactly that.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different concern is raised by Dr Lucía Cabrejos, who specialises in the formation of archaeological deposits. Not every sample found in a layer belongs to the moment that layer was laid down. Charcoal may come from the heartwood of a tree that was already centuries old when burnt, and fragments of bone may have been disturbed and redeposited from earlier levels. Modelling software includes procedures for identifying such 'outliers', but Cabrejos warns that these can be used, consciously or not, to discard dates that do not fit a favoured interpretation. Her solution is to select samples far more rigorously in the first place, favouring short-lived material such as cereal grains or animal bones still joined at the joint, which are likely to have entered the deposit soon after death. On this point I agree with her entirely: no statistical technique can rescue a model built on poorly chosen samples.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Daniyar Ermekov approaches the debate from yet another angle. His concern is less with the models themselves than with their transparency. Many published studies, he notes, describe their conclusions in detail but provide too little information about the code and assumptions behind them for anyone else to repeat the analysis. Ermekov has called for all models to be published in full, so that other researchers can test alternative assumptions against the same data. He argues that, in a field where a handful of laboratories produce most of the models, independent checking is the only real safeguard against shared blind spots. A number of journals have begun to adopt this requirement, although whether it will become universal remains to be seen.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The greatest risk, perhaps, lies beyond the specialist literature. Modelled dates are typically expressed as ranges with stated probabilities, yet when they reach textbooks, museum labels and popular articles the qualifications tend to disappear, and an estimate of 'between 3640 and 3620 BC, at 68 per cent probability' becomes simply '3630 BC'. The vivid narratives of rapid construction and abandonment that Bayesian modelling has generated are genuinely illuminating, but they remain interpretations built on chains of assumptions. They deserve to be treated as well-supported hypotheses, not as settled fact.

topic: archaeomagnetic dating of kilns, hearths and burnt houses: reference curves, intensity measurements on pottery and evidence of synchronous burning
title: The Memory of Fired Clay
subtitle: Burnt hearths and pottery preserve a record of the earth's shifting magnetic field, and archaeologists are learning to read it as a clock

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every fired kiln, hearth and burnt house floor holds a faint memory of the earth's magnetic field at the moment it last cooled. Clay and soil contain small quantities of iron oxide minerals, and when these are heated above a few hundred degrees they lose their existing magnetisation. As they cool, they acquire a new one aligned with the field prevailing at that time and place, and this alignment is then locked in, often for thousands of years. Because the field itself wanders, its direction and strength changing continuously over decades and centuries, the magnetic record preserved in burnt material can be used as a clock. The technique, known as archaeomagnetic dating, is less familiar than radiocarbon, but in certain circumstances it can be considerably more precise.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle is simple, but the practice is demanding. To determine the direction of the ancient field, investigators must take samples from material that has not moved since it cooled, recording their orientation with great care, usually by encasing small pieces of baked clay in plaster and marking them with a compass and level before removal. In the laboratory, the direction of magnetisation in each sample is measured, and the average for the feature is compared with a reference curve showing how the field direction in that region has changed over time. Where the two match, a date can be read off. Because the final firing of a kiln is precisely the event an archaeologist usually wishes to know about, the method dates exactly the right moment, a claim that radiocarbon dating of associated charcoal cannot always make.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The reference curves, however, are a weak point that the method's advocates do not always acknowledge. Professor Pieter Bisschop, who spent two decades assembling the curve for one part of north-western Europe, points out that such curves are themselves constructed from archaeological features dated by other means, chiefly radiocarbon, historical documents and pottery styles. Errors in those dates are therefore built into the curve. Bisschop has also stressed that a curve is valid only within a limited radius, perhaps a thousand kilometres, since the field's direction differs from place to place. In regions such as much of Africa and Central Asia, where few well-dated burnt features have been studied, no reliable curve yet exists. There is a further complication: the field occasionally returns to a direction it occupied centuries earlier, so a single measurement may match the curve at two or more points.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A partial solution comes from measuring the strength of the ancient field rather than its direction. Intensity, unlike direction, does not require the sample to remain in its original position, and so it can be measured on ordinary pottery fragments, which survive in vast quantities. Dr Rosalind Sephton, whose laboratory specialises in such measurements, argues that this opens up museum collections that have lain unstudied for a century. The process is slow, however: each fragment must be repeatedly heated and cooled in a controlled field, and a high proportion of samples fail tests of reliability because their minerals altered chemically during the laboratory heating. Sephton estimates that fewer than half of the sherds she analyses yield usable results.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Intriguingly, the flow of information has begun to run in both directions. Dr Keiko Yamanouchi, a geophysicist rather than an archaeologist, contends that archaeological materials now provide the best available record of how the earth's field behaved before the invention of scientific instruments. Some of the intensity data have revealed episodes in which the field strengthened far more rapidly than geophysical models had predicted, rising and falling within a few decades. Archaeology, long a borrower of techniques from the physical sciences, is thus repaying its debt. This is a welcome development, though one with an awkward implication: if the field can change more abruptly than was assumed, the smooth reference curves used for dating may conceal fluctuations that could mislead.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Archaeomagnetism can also answer questions other than 'when?'. Dr Mekonnen Tafari has studied burnt settlements in which dozens of houses were destroyed by fire. By comparing the magnetic directions recorded in the floors of different houses, he has been able to establish whether they burned at the same moment or in separate episodes, since a gap of even a few decades would leave a detectable difference. His results suggest that in several villages the houses burned simultaneously, which he interprets as evidence that the fires were set deliberately, perhaps as part of a ritual of abandonment, rather than spreading by accident. The interpretation is plausible, but the magnetic evidence alone cannot distinguish deliberate burning from a single catastrophic accident, and Tafari's conclusion rests on other evidence, such as the careful emptying of houses before they burned.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong to present archaeomagnetic dating as a rival to radiocarbon. Its precision depends entirely on the quality of local reference data, and it can be applied only to material that was strongly heated. Yet where those conditions are met, it offers something few other methods can: a date tied directly to a human action. As reference curves improve, its contribution is likely to grow considerably, particularly in regions that have so far been neglected.

topic: obsidian hydration dating: early enthusiasm, the collapse of confidence, mass-spectrometry revival and the problem of accelerated hydration experiments
title: A Clock in Volcanic Glass
subtitle: Obsidian hydration dating was once hailed as a cheap way to date stone tools, then almost abandoned. Is it due a second chance?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Obsidian, the glassy black rock formed when lava cools too quickly to crystallise, was prized by toolmakers across the ancient world for the razor-sharp edges it produces when struck. It also possesses a property that, in 1960, a pair of geologists proposed could turn every obsidian flake into a clock. A freshly broken surface of obsidian begins at once to absorb water from its surroundings, and the water penetrates the glass slowly, forming a thin layer, or hydration rim, that thickens over time. If the rate of thickening were known, measuring the rim would reveal how long ago the flake was struck. No other dating method so directly records the moment at which a stone tool was made.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea was received with an enthusiasm that is easy to understand. Radiocarbon dating was then expensive and slow, while preparing a thin slice of obsidian and measuring its rim under an optical microscope cost very little. Moreover, obsidian is abundant at many sites in the Americas, the Mediterranean, East Africa and the Pacific, frequently in layers where no charcoal survives. During the 1970s, laboratories produced tens of thousands of hydration dates, and in some areas entire regional chronologies came to rest on them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The disillusionment, when it came, was severe. As more hydration dates were checked against radiocarbon, discrepancies of hundreds or even thousands of years emerged. Dr Ingrid Kjellberg, whose re-examination of collections from the Mexican highlands proved especially influential, showed that flakes recovered from a single sealed layer, and therefore presumably of similar age, could display rims of widely differing thickness. The explanation lay in the variables that govern hydration. The rate depends strongly on temperature, so that a flake buried near the surface, where the soil warms in summer, hydrates faster than one buried deeper. It also varies with humidity and with the chemistry of the glass itself, particularly its original water content, which differs not only between volcanic sources but even within a single lava flow. By the 1990s, many archaeologists had concluded that the method was too unreliable to be worth pursuing. In retrospect, this verdict was arguably an overreaction. The method had not failed; it had been applied without the controls its complexity demanded.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A revival has been led by researchers who believe those controls are now available. Professor Bishnu Pradhananga's laboratory replaced the microscope with secondary ion mass spectrometry, which measures the concentration of hydrogen at successive depths below the surface and so produces a detailed profile of the hydration layer rather than a single, sometimes blurred, boundary. Combined with burial temperatures recorded by sensors left in the ground for a full year, and with chemical analysis of each specimen's water content, the technique has, Pradhananga claims, achieved accuracy comparable to that of radiocarbon dating. Such a claim seems premature. The published tests involve a limited number of sites, most of them in a single arid region, and it is not yet clear whether the same success can be achieved in wetter or more variable environments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns how hydration rates are established in the first place. Because natural hydration is far too slow to observe directly, rates are usually determined by heating samples in water to temperatures of 150 degrees or more, which compresses thousands of years of hydration into a few weeks, and the results are then extrapolated to the temperatures of ordinary soil. Dr Chiara Sabatini, an experimental petrologist, has questioned whether glass behaves in the same way under such contrasting conditions. Her experiments suggest that at high temperatures additional chemical reactions take place which are negligible in cool soil, so that rates derived from accelerated experiments may be systematically misleading. Of all the criticisms the method faces, this is surely the most serious, because it calls into question the foundation on which every calibrated date rests.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone believes that the method must produce calendar dates to be useful. Dr Alexandros Koutsoukis argues that hydration measurements are most valuable as a means of comparing artefacts from the same site, where burial conditions and obsidian sources are often similar enough for differences in rim thickness to indicate which objects are older. He has also shown that the method can detect the recycling of artefacts: a tool that was abandoned and later picked up and reworked by a subsequent occupant may carry two rims of different thickness, one on its original surfaces and another on the newly flaked edges. Such evidence of reuse would be almost impossible to obtain in any other way.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Koutsoukis's position seems to me the most realistic. Obsidian hydration is unlikely ever to rival radiocarbon as a source of absolute dates, given the number of environmental variables that must be controlled. But as a cheap, widely applicable tool for placing finds in sequence and tracing the life histories of individual objects, it still has a great deal to offer, and its near-abandonment in the 1990s cost archaeology a valuable source of evidence.

topic: amino acid racemization dating: the failure of early bone dates and the revival using closed-system proteins in snail opercula and ostrich eggshell
title: Left Hand, Right Hand
subtitle: A dating method once dismissed as an embarrassment has quietly returned to archaeology, thanks to proteins sealed inside shells

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the techniques available for dating the remote past, few have travelled so far from disgrace to respectability as amino acid racemization. In the early 1970s it was hailed as a means of dating bones far beyond the range of radiocarbon, and a series of human skeletons from the Americas were assigned startling ages of up to fifty thousand years, which, had they been correct, would have meant that people reached the continent far earlier than most specialists believed. Within a decade those ages had collapsed: when the same bones were dated by improved radiocarbon methods, they proved to be only a few thousand years old. For many archaeologists the episode became a byword for scientific overconfidence, and the method was quietly set aside. Its recent return deserves to be far better known.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle rests on a peculiar feature of biological chemistry. Most amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other, conventionally labelled L and D, much as a left hand mirrors a right. Living organisms build their proteins almost exclusively from the L form. After death, however, the amino acids begin to convert spontaneously into the D form, a process called racemization, which continues until the two forms are present in roughly equal amounts. In principle, therefore, the ratio of D to L in a fossil reveals how much time has passed since the organism died. The catch is that the speed of conversion depends heavily on temperature: a bone lying in tropical soil will racemize many times faster than one buried in a cool cave.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Temperature was one source of the 1970s errors, but not the most important. Professor Haruki Tsuchiya, a geochemist who has reanalysed much of the early work, argues that the decisive problem was that bone is an 'open system'. Its porous structure allows amino acids to leach out into the surrounding ground water and allows foreign amino acids, from bacteria, roots and the soil itself, to seep in. Since these newcomers can have very different ratios, the value measured in a bone may bear little relation to its true age. Tsuchiya's diagnosis is, in my view, persuasive, and it explains why careful attention to temperature alone could never have rescued the method in its original form.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The revival began with the search for materials that behave as closed systems. Dr Beatriz Nascimento of the Laboratory of Quaternary Biochemistry turned to the small calcite plates with which certain freshwater snails seal the opening of their shells. Within the crystals of these plates is a fraction of protein that is physically trapped, isolated from the outside world for as long as the crystal survives. By chemically removing everything outside the crystals before analysis, Nascimento's team obtained ratios that increased consistently with the depth of deposits and agreed well with independently dated sequences. Her laboratory has since used such measurements to distinguish between deposits laid down in separate warm periods hundreds of thousands of years apart, an achievement that no other inexpensive method has matched.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even closed-system proteins, however, cannot escape the influence of temperature, and this is where the debate now lies. Dr Lerato Ramaphala, who works with fragments of ostrich eggshell from archaeological sites in southern Africa, points out that converting a ratio into a calendar age requires knowledge of the temperatures a sample has experienced throughout its burial, a history that spans several glacial cycles and can only be estimated from climate models. An error of a single degree in the assumed average temperature can shift a calculated age by as much as fifteen per cent. Ramaphala therefore treats racemization results primarily as a way of ranking samples within a region whose climatic history they share, and she is cautious about any figure expressed in years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nascimento, by contrast, believes that the temperature problem can be overcome by calibrating each regional framework against a small number of sites dated by other methods, such as layers of volcanic ash or uranium-series measurements on cave formations. Once anchored at a few points, she argues, the framework can be used to assign approximate ages to the many sites in between. Both positions have merit, but it is worth noting that the dispute is narrower than it might appear: neither researcher claims that racemization can produce dates as precise as those of radiocarbon, and both agree that its greatest value lies in periods that radiocarbon cannot reach.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The method's history offers a lesson that extends well beyond chemistry. The original failure did not arise because the underlying principle was wrong, but because a sound principle was applied to an unsuitable material, and the resulting errors were then taken as a verdict on the principle itself. Had the method been abandoned entirely, archaeology would have lost one of its few affordable tools for the immense stretch of time between roughly fifty thousand and two million years ago. Scientific techniques, like the samples they measure, should be judged on their best evidence rather than their worst.

topic: uranium-series dating of calcite crusts over cave paintings and the controversy over claims of Neanderthal cave art
title: Beneath the Calcite Veil
subtitle: Dating the mineral crusts that form over cave paintings has produced startling claims about who the first artists were. How secure are they?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, the painted caves of western Europe have been regarded as the work of our own species, Homo sapiens, and as some of the earliest evidence of a distinctively human imagination. Establishing when the paintings were made, however, has always been difficult. Most were produced with mineral pigments such as red ochre, which contain no carbon, so radiocarbon dating can be applied directly only to the minority of images drawn in charcoal. In the past two decades a different technique, uranium-series dating, has offered a way around this obstacle. It dates not the paint itself but the thin, translucent crusts of calcite that sometimes form over it as water trickles down the walls of a cave.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method exploits a chemical contrast between two elements. Water percolating through limestone carries dissolved uranium but almost no thorium, because thorium is virtually insoluble. When calcite crystallises from that water, it therefore locks in uranium while starting with essentially no thorium. The uranium then decays at a known rate into thorium-230, and by measuring the ratio of the two, a laboratory can calculate how long ago the crust formed. Since the crust lies on top of the paint, the painting must be older than the crust, so the result is a minimum age. The method can reach back several hundred thousand years, and it requires only tiny samples scraped from the surface with a scalpel, so the damage to the art itself is minimal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The results have been dramatic. Teams have reported ages greater than sixty thousand years for red lines, dots and hand stencils in caves on the Iberian Peninsula, well before modern humans are thought to have reached Europe, which would mean that the artists were Neanderthals. Dr Chukwuemeka Ibekwe, whose laboratory produced several of these dates, stresses that because they are minimum ages, the paintings could be considerably older still. He also points out that his team removes successive thin layers from each crust, working from the outer surface inwards, and that the ages increase consistently towards the paint, as would be expected if the crust had grown steadily and remained chemically undisturbed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this reasoning. Dr Freja Skogheim, a geochemist, argues that calcite crusts on cave walls are frequently exposed to fresh water long after they form. Because uranium dissolves easily, such water can strip some of it away while leaving thorium behind, which makes the crust appear older than it really is. A consistent sequence from outer to inner layers, she maintains, does not rule this out, since leaching tends to affect the outer layers most and could produce the very pattern that Ibekwe cites as evidence of reliability. Skogheim's point is a valid one, and it has been underestimated by some advocates of the method. Her proposed safeguard is to date, wherever possible, crusts lying both above and beneath a painted layer, which would bracket the painting between a maximum and a minimum age.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of criticism focuses not on the chemistry but on what exactly has been dated. Professor Ryo Matsunaga, who has spent thirty years recording rock art, notes that several of the marks attributed to Neanderthals are simple red smears or stains on flowstone. Iron oxides occur naturally in many caves and can be deposited by water, producing patches of colour that resemble deliberately applied pigment. Until such marks have been shown by microscopic and chemical analysis to have been applied by human hands, he argues, their age, however secure, tells us nothing about artistic behaviour. Matsunaga's objection does not apply to the hand stencils, which are unmistakably human in origin, but it is a useful reminder that the most ancient claims tend to rest on the most ambiguous images.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Hendrik Oberholster, a historian of scientific dating, takes a broader view. In his judgement, the controversy has been prolonged by the fact that almost all of the earliest dates come from a small number of laboratories using similar procedures. He has called for samples from the disputed caves to be divided and analysed independently in several laboratories, and ideally cross-checked against other methods applied to the same crusts. Whatever the outcome, he suggests, such replication would carry more weight than any amount of further argument over the existing figures.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to portray this debate as a contest between those eager to promote the Neanderthals and those reluctant to credit them with art. That would be a mistake. Most participants agree on the principles of uranium-series dating and differ chiefly on how confidently those principles can be applied to particular samples. Nor does the question of Neanderthal symbolic behaviour stand or fall on a few cave walls: perforated shells and carefully processed pigments found at Neanderthal sites point in the same direction. Nonetheless, until the chemical concerns raised by critics have been resolved, the cave dates should be regarded as intriguing rather than conclusive.

topic: typology and seriation as relative dating methods: their eclipse by radiocarbon, computer-based revival and regional time lags in changing styles
title: The Order of Things
subtitle: Long overshadowed by laboratory methods, the old art of dating objects by their style is enjoying an unexpected revival

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before physicists gave archaeologists radiocarbon, the discipline had developed its own ways of putting the past in order. The most important rested on a simple observation: manufactured objects change over time. The shape of a pot, the decoration on a brooch and the form of a sword hilt all follow fashions that emerge, spread and eventually fade. By arranging objects according to such changes, archaeologists could construct sequences showing which came before which, even if they could not say how many years separated them. These methods, known as typology and seriation, dominated chronological research for the best part of a century, and despite their reputation as outdated, they are still quietly relied upon on almost every excavation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Seriation in its classic form was devised at the end of the nineteenth century by an Egyptologist faced with several thousand graves and no means of dating them. He recorded the types of pottery in each grave and arranged the graves so that each type appeared in an unbroken run, on the assumption that a style, once abandoned, was rarely revived. Later researchers refined the approach by counting the proportions of different styles within groups of finds. When graphed, the popularity of each style tends to follow a characteristic shape: rare at first, gradually more common, dominant for a time and then in decline. Arranging the groups so that every style traces this pattern as smoothly as possible yields a relative chronology. The procedure demands little more than careful observation and patience, which partly explains its long survival.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The arrival of radiocarbon dating in the 1950s and 1960s exposed the weaknesses of this approach when it was stretched too far. Typological sequences had been linked across great distances on the assumption that similar objects must be of similar age, and that innovations had travelled outwards from a few centres of civilisation in the eastern Mediterranean. Radiocarbon showed that many monuments in western Europe were centuries older than the supposed sources of their inspiration. The resulting upheaval was healthy; assumptions that had passed for facts were rightly discarded. But the reaction went further than the evidence justified, and for a generation typological expertise was widely regarded as old-fashioned, with the result that fewer students were trained to recognise and classify artefacts in detail. That decline is now being felt.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some researchers argue that seriation deserves a far more prominent place. Dr Agnieszka Szymanek, who applies statistical techniques to large databases of excavated pottery, maintains that computer-based seriation can order hundreds of assemblages with a consistency no individual specialist could achieve, and at a fraction of the price of laboratory dating. For the last five centuries, a period in which radiocarbon dating is hampered by irregularities in the calibration curve, she argues that well-studied artefacts such as glass bottles and clay tobacco pipes, whose features changed rapidly and are often documented in manufacturers' records, can provide dates accurate to within a decade or two. In this narrow context her claim is convincing; whether it can be extended to prehistory, where no written records exist to anchor sequences, is far less clear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Professor Lars Malmquist has drawn attention to a hidden assumption behind seriation: that a style rises and falls at the same pace wherever it is found. In practice, he points out, a fashion may reach a remote valley a generation after it appeared in a busy port, and conservative communities may continue making a traditional style long after others have abandoned it. His own study of grave goods from northern Scandinavia found brooch styles persisting in inland districts for up to sixty years after they had disappeared from coastal trading centres. Two groups of finds with identical proportions of styles may therefore be of quite different ages. This point is fundamental, and it explains why seriations are most trustworthy when confined to a small area.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Dr Kenji Shibasaki's work on the elaborately decorated pottery of prehistoric Japan illustrates both the power and the limits of typology. Because potters there altered decorative motifs frequently, and because the tradition lasted for thousands of years, specialists have been able to divide it into more than seventy successive phases, some apparently lasting only a few decades. Shibasaki has nonetheless found that when phases defined in one region are compared with radiocarbon dates from another, supposed contemporaries sometimes differ by a century or more, confirming Malmquist's warning on a large scale. He concludes that finely divided phases are a powerful tool within a single region but a treacherous one when used to link distant areas.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Dr Giulia Pellerano, a specialist in Bronze Age metalwork, argues that the old opposition between 'scientific' and 'traditional' dating is misleading. A seriation reveals the order of things but not the direction of time, whether the sequence runs forwards or backwards, nor the length of the intervals involved; radiocarbon supplies these but is often too imprecise to separate closely spaced events. Used together, she suggests, each can compensate for the other's weaknesses. She is surely right, and it is to be hoped that renewed interest in combining the two will also revive the training of the specialists on whom typology depends.

topic: marine and freshwater reservoir effects in radiocarbon dating, fish-eating populations and the correction of human bone dates
title: Borrowed Time from the Water
subtitle: Why people who ate fish can appear centuries older than they really were, and how archaeologists are trying to correct the error

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dating rests on an assumption so basic that it is rarely stated: that the organism being dated drew its carbon from the atmosphere of its own time. For a tree, a cereal plant or a grazing sheep, this is essentially true. But not every living thing feeds, directly or indirectly, on the air. Creatures of the sea, rivers and lakes take up carbon dissolved in water, and that carbon may be considerably older than the carbon in the atmosphere. When such organisms, or the humans who ate them, are radiocarbon dated, they appear older than they really are. The phenomenon, known as the reservoir effect, has quietly distorted a surprising number of archaeological chronologies.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the oceans, the cause lies in the slow circulation of water. Surface water exchanges carbon with the atmosphere fairly readily, but deep water may remain isolated from the air for many centuries, during which its carbon-14 steadily decays. Where deep water wells up to the surface, it brings this 'old' carbon with it. On average, marine organisms appear about four hundred years older than land organisms of the same age, but the global average conceals substantial local variation. Dr Maarten Hoekstra has radiocarbon dated hundreds of mollusc shells that were collected alive by naturalists before 1950, and whose true ages are therefore known. He has found that the offset can vary by several centuries between sites only a few dozen kilometres apart, particularly near estuaries and zones of upwelling. His approach is ingenious, and its results are a sobering corrective to the routine application of a single regional figure.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Freshwater environments can be even more unpredictable. Where rivers and lakes drain landscapes of limestone or chalk, the water dissolves carbonate rock that is millions of years old and therefore contains no carbon-14 at all. Aquatic plants incorporate this 'dead' carbon, and it passes up the food chain to fish, waterfowl and, ultimately, people. Dr Elif Feyzioglu, who has studied lakes on the Anatolian plateau, has recorded offsets of up to two thousand years in fish from a single lake, and found that the offset changed with the seasons as the balance between rainwater and spring water shifted. In such settings, she concludes, no fixed correction can be applied with confidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For archaeologists, the most troubling consequence concerns human remains. A person whose diet included a great deal of fish will carry part of the reservoir offset in their bones, so that their skeleton may appear several centuries older than that of a contemporary who ate only meat and grain. This has generated some notable puzzles: burials that seemed to predate the settlements beside them, or cemeteries that appeared to have been in use for implausibly long periods. Professor Ainhoa Garaycochea, who has re-examined several such cases along major European rivers, argues that many of these anomalies disappear once the diets of the dead are taken into account, and that some theories about the movements of populations were built on dates that were simply too old.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The difficulty lies in knowing how much aquatic food a person actually ate. The standard approach measures stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen in bone collagen, which differ between marine, freshwater and terrestrial food chains, and then uses a mathematical model to estimate the proportion of each in the diet. Dr Sipho Mbathane, who specialises in such reconstructions, warns that the uncertainties are large. Nitrogen values rise not only with fish consumption but also with the use of manure on crops, and freshwater and land-based foods can have overlapping signatures. A correction based on an uncertain dietary estimate, he points out, can introduce errors as great as the one it is meant to remove. His preferred solution is to date, wherever possible, a terrestrial object buried with the individual, such as an antler tool or an offering of grain, alongside the bone itself, so that the offset can be measured directly rather than inferred. This is admittedly not always feasible, but it seems to me far preferable to stacking one model upon another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Garaycochea has also raised a less obvious concern. Now that the reservoir effect is widely understood, she suggests, there is a temptation to invoke it whenever a date conflicts with expectations, even in the absence of any evidence that the individual ate fish. In her view, the effect has become, for some researchers, a convenient means of explaining away inconvenient results. The criticism is fair, though it applies to only a minority of studies; most researchers who apply corrections do so on the basis of isotopic evidence rather than assumption.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The reservoir effect is a reminder that radiocarbon dating measures a chemical property rather than time itself, and that the link between the two depends on where an organism obtained its carbon. Far from undermining the method, recognising this has made it more reliable, because it has forced archaeologists to think carefully about what they sample. The safest policy remains to date short-lived land plants and plant-eating animals wherever they are available, and to treat dates from aquatic creatures, and from the people who ate them, with appropriate caution.

topic: the beer-before-bread hypothesis: brewing, feasting and the motive for cultivating wild cereals
title: Thirst Before Hunger?
subtitle: Some archaeologists argue that the first cereal farmers were brewers rather than bakers, but the evidence remains fiercely contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the standard account of how farming began was a story about calories. Hunter-gatherers in south-west Asia, faced with growing populations or a deteriorating climate, were thought to have turned to wild cereals out of necessity, eventually learning to sow and harvest them so that bread could become a dependable staple. In the 1950s, however, a botanist at a provincial American university put forward a deliberately provocative alternative: perhaps the first cereal farmers were motivated not by hunger but by thirst, and the grain they tended so carefully was destined for brewing rather than baking. The suggestion was greeted with polite amusement and largely forgotten. Over the past two decades it has returned, armed with new evidence, and it now divides specialists more sharply than its original author could have imagined.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for brewing rests partly on the economics of early cereal use. Wild wheat and barley yield small, hard seeds that must be threshed, dehusked and ground before they can be eaten, and the effort involved is considerable for a modest return in energy. Professor Aino Haavisto of the Institute for Prehistoric Food Studies argues that such an investment makes more sense if the product had a social value out of all proportion to its nutritional content. Fermented drinks, she points out, are central to hospitality in a great many traditional societies, where they are consumed at work parties, weddings and other gatherings that bind communities together. In her view, a group able to host such events would gain allies and labour, so the incentive to secure a reliable supply of grain may have been political as much as dietary.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporting evidence has come from residue analysis. At several cave sites in the eastern Mediterranean associated with the Natufian culture, which flourished roughly 15,000 to 11,500 years ago, a team led by Dr Femi Makinwa examined stone mortars cut into the bedrock. Microscopic starch grains recovered from these hollows show the swelling and pitting typical of malting and mashing, the first stages of brewing. Makinwa's group dates the residues to around 13,000 years ago, several millennia before the earliest firm evidence of domesticated cereals. If the interpretation is correct, people were making a beer-like gruel long before anyone was farming in the full sense. Makinwa himself is careful to describe this drink as thin and only mildly alcoholic, quite unlike modern beer, and he concedes that the same mortars were probably also used to process other plants.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics have not been slow to respond. The archaeobotanist Lucien Duvalcourt doubts that starch damage can reliably distinguish malting from other forms of processing, noting that grains soaked in water before cooking, or simply left damp, can display similar alterations. He also questions the chronology. Charred remains of flatbread found at a hearth in north-eastern Jordan have been dated to about 14,400 years ago, which, in his view, means that baking is at least as old as brewing and cannot be dismissed as a later development. Duvalcourt accepts that fermented drinks existed but sees no reason to treat them as the driving force. 'People who are hungry will process grain whatever the eventual product,' he argues, 'and the archaeological record cannot tell us which use they valued more.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The feasting dimension of the argument has received support from an unexpected quarter: monumental architecture. At hilltop sites in what is now south-eastern Turkey, massive carved stone pillars arranged in circular enclosures were erected by people who had not yet domesticated any plant or animal. Large stone vessels found at such sites, some capable of holding around 160 litres, have been interpreted as containers for fermenting liquids, and traces of oxalate, a by-product of brewing, have reportedly been identified on their inner surfaces. For Giulia Paltrinieri, an anthropologist who studies ritual and food, these discoveries suggest that collective work on monuments was rewarded with food and drink on a large scale, and that the demand created by such feasts encouraged the intensive harvesting that eventually turned wild cereals into crops.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Each piece of this argument is plausible, yet the overall case is weaker than its supporters sometimes suggest. Chemical traces of oxalate are notoriously difficult to interpret, since the compound also forms naturally in many plants, and no single site has yet produced a combination of residues, tools and containers that would satisfy a sceptic. More fundamentally, the hypothesis tends to assume that early farmers had one dominant motive. It seems far more likely that wild cereals were valued for several reasons at once: as porridge in lean seasons, as bread on occasion and, at certain moments, as the basis of a drink that made gatherings memorable. Separating these uses after more than ten thousand years may simply be beyond what the evidence allows.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means the debate has been unproductive. By forcing researchers to consider why people would invest heavily in an unpromising food, the brewing hypothesis has drawn attention to the social life of early communities, which older accounts based purely on population pressure and climate tended to ignore. The more valuable legacy of the controversy may therefore lie not in settling which came first, beer or bread, but in establishing that the origins of agriculture cannot be understood without considering feasting, status and cooperation alongside the simpler question of how people avoided starvation.

topic: the health of the first farmers: skeletal stature, tooth decay, disease and the osteological paradox
title: Bones of the First Farmers
subtitle: Skeletons suggest that the switch to agriculture made people less healthy. Why, then, did farming spread across the world?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is one of the more uncomfortable findings of modern archaeology. When the skeletons of the earliest farmers are compared with those of the hunter-gatherers who preceded them in the same regions, the farmers frequently appear to have been worse off. They were, on average, shorter; their teeth show more decay; and their bones carry more frequent signs of childhood stress and infectious disease. Many also display the distinctive wear on the spine, knees and toes that results from long hours spent kneeling at grinding stones. A widely read essay of the 1980s went so far as to call agriculture the worst mistake in human history. That verdict was too sweeping, but the evidence behind it has proved remarkably durable, and explaining it remains one of the central puzzles in the study of how farming began.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the data comes from careful measurement of skeletal remains. Dr Selim Kizilbash, a bioarchaeologist at the Anatolian Centre for Human Osteology, has compiled records from more than 2,000 individuals buried in the eastern Mediterranean region between roughly 12,000 and 7,000 years ago. His analysis indicates that average adult height fell by several centimetres in the millennia following the adoption of cereal farming, and recovered only slowly. He also records a marked rise in enamel hypoplasia, horizontal lines in tooth enamel that form when a child's growth is interrupted by illness or malnutrition. Kizilbash attributes these changes chiefly to diet: a menu dominated by a few starchy crops, he argues, lacked the variety of the wild foods that foragers had gathered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dental evidence points in a similar direction. Cereals are rich in carbohydrates that oral bacteria convert into acids, and rates of tooth decay rise steeply in many farming populations. Yet Marjatta Lehtinen of the Baltic Institute of Archaeological Science warns against treating teeth as a simple index of overall wellbeing. Some foraging groups that relied heavily on wild acorns and other starchy plants show levels of decay as high as those of any early farmers, and in her view the shift in dental health reflects the type of carbohydrate eaten rather than the arrival of agriculture as such. Her work is a reminder that the familiar contrast between 'healthy foragers' and 'sickly farmers' conceals considerable variety on both sides.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second explanation focuses on disease rather than food. Settled villages brought people into close and permanent contact with one another, with their refuse and, in time, with domestic animals. Professor Andrés Ricaurte, an epidemiologist who has turned his attention to prehistory, argues that these conditions allowed infections to circulate in ways that would have been impossible among small, mobile bands. Contaminated water, accumulating waste and the presence of rodents attracted by stored grain may all have contributed. Ricaurte believes that this disease burden, more than any nutritional deficiency, explains why so many early farmers died young. He points to genetic material recovered from village burials, which has identified bacterial infections rarely detected among earlier foragers, although he acknowledges that the number of samples analysed so far remains small.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is, however, a statistical trap in such arguments, first described in the 1990s and known as the osteological paradox. Skeletons in a cemetery represent people who died, not the living population, and a skeleton without visible damage does not necessarily belong to a healthy person. Lesions on bone take time to form; an individual who succumbed quickly to an acute infection may leave no trace at all, whereas someone who survived repeated illnesses will carry their marks. Paradoxically, then, a population showing more skeletal lesions might have been more resilient, not less. Thandiwe Gwala, a palaeodemographer, has argued that this problem has been underestimated in studies of early farming, and that some apparent declines in health may partly reflect improved survival from illness.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Gwala's point is important, but it should not be pushed too far. The fall in stature, in particular, is difficult to explain away, since height is a cumulative record of growth throughout childhood and does not depend on whether an individual died suddenly or slowly. Moreover, the pattern is repeated across regions as distant as China, Mesoamerica and the Indus valley, which makes it unlikely to be an artefact of a few unusual cemeteries. The balance of the evidence still suggests that the first generations of farmers paid a real price in health for their new way of life.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Why, then, did farming spread? The answer appears to lie in numbers rather than individual wellbeing. Farming populations, even if less healthy, grew faster than foraging ones, because settled women could raise children at shorter intervals and a cultivated field could feed far more people than the same area of wild land. Mobile foragers, by contrast, had to carry infants from one camp to the next, which limited how many young children a mother could care for at once. Over centuries, communities of farmers simply outnumbered and absorbed their neighbours. This conclusion carries an uncomfortable implication: that a way of life can succeed and expand while making those who practise it, at least at first, measurably worse off.

topic: rapid versus protracted domestication of cereals: non-shattering ears, harvesting experiments and the tempo of change
title: A Revolution in Slow Motion
subtitle: Did wild grasses become crops in a few generations, or over thousands of years?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When wild wheat ripens, its ears shatter: the brittle stalk that holds the seeds breaks apart, scattering grain onto the ground where it can germinate. In domesticated wheat and barley, by contrast, a mutation keeps the ear intact until it is harvested, so that the plant depends entirely on human beings to sow its seed. This non-shattering trait is the single most important marker of cereal domestication, and how quickly it spread through early fields has become the focus of one of the liveliest debates in archaeobotany. Was the transformation of wild grasses into crops a swift event, accomplished within a few human lifetimes, or a slow drift lasting thousands of years?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for speed was set out in the 1970s and 1980s through a series of harvesting experiments. Researchers cut stands of wild einkorn with replica flint sickles and found that the technique favoured non-shattering mutants, because plants that kept their seeds were more likely to be gathered and resown the following season. Building on such work, the agronomist Pavel Hrabánek calculated that, under steady selection, a field of wild cereals could become predominantly domesticated in as little as twenty to two hundred years. For Hrabánek, the implication was clear: once people began sowing harvested seed deliberately, domestication would follow almost automatically, and archaeologists should expect to find it appearing abruptly in the record.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The archaeological evidence has not cooperated. Over the past twenty years, teams examining charred plant remains from sites across south-west Asia have measured the proportion of non-shattering ears in successive layers. Dr Lerato Moerane of the Institute of Archaeobotany, who led several of these studies, found that the proportion rose only gradually, from around ten per cent to more than ninety per cent over a period of roughly two to three thousand years. Grain size increased at a similarly leisurely pace, and in some places the trend even reversed for several centuries. In Moerane's view, these figures leave little room for a rapid model; domestication, she argues, was a protracted process, more comparable to the slow emergence of a dialect than to an invention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should selection have been so weak? One answer concerns how early cultivators actually harvested their crops. Kyriakos Anastasiou, an ethnographer who has documented traditional farming in the eastern Mediterranean, observes that sickles are not the only option. Grain can be beaten into baskets, uprooted by hand or gathered while still slightly unripe, before shattering begins. Each of these techniques reduces or removes the advantage enjoyed by non-shattering plants. Anastasiou also notes that if early cultivators collected fresh seed from wild stands each year, rather than resowing their own, any progress towards domestication would have been continually diluted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from the geneticist Itziar Gorostiza, whose work on the genomes of modern and ancient cereals suggests that domestication did not occur in a single place. Instead, she argues, genes associated with domestic traits appear in populations from several regions, implying that cultivation was taking place in many communities simultaneously, with seed exchanged between them. Gorostiza believes that this mosaic pattern helps explain the slow tempo: domestic traits arose in different places at different times and only gradually came together in the crops we know today.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the record has been read correctly. Professor Ville Talvela, a specialist in the chronology of early farming sites, points out that charred remains are a highly selective sample. Grain is preserved only when it is accidentally burnt, and the material that ends up in a hearth may come disproportionately from wild plants gathered alongside crops, or from weeds. If so, the apparent persistence of wild-type ears might partly reflect what was thrown into fires rather than what was grown in fields. Talvela does not claim that domestication was rapid, but he insists that the case for a very slow transition has been stated with more confidence than the evidence permits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Talvela's caution deserves to be taken seriously, but it does not overturn the broad picture. The gradual pattern has now been documented at so many sites, and for so many different crops, including barley, lentils and rice, that sampling bias alone is unlikely to account for it. What the debate has done, however, is to change the questions researchers ask. If domestication was slow, then it cannot have been the result of a deliberate plan to create better crops, since no single generation would have noticed much difference. The first farmers did not set out to domesticate anything. They were simply managing wild plants in ways that, over a hundred generations, reshaped them.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: This interpretation has a wider significance. A rapid model encouraged the idea of an agricultural revolution: a turning point at which human beings suddenly took control of nature. The protracted model replaces that image with a long period of experimentation, in which communities moved back and forth between foraging and cultivation as circumstances changed. It is a less dramatic story, but in all likelihood a more accurate one.

topic: the Neolithic demographic transition: cemetery age ratios, radiocarbon booms and busts, and the reliability of prehistoric population estimates
title: Numbers from the Grave
subtitle: Cemetery evidence points to a population explosion when farming began, but how much can the dead tell us about the living?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Around the world, the arrival of farming appears to have been followed by a surge in human numbers. Archaeologists refer to this as the Neolithic demographic transition, and the idea has become central to explanations of how agriculture spread so widely. Yet the populations concerned left no written records, no censuses and no tax rolls. Everything we believe about their growth has been inferred indirectly, from the bones they left behind, the settlements they built and, more recently, the DNA of their descendants. How far such indirect methods can be trusted is a question that deserves more attention than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential approach was pioneered by the palaeodemographer Eleni Vasilakis, who compiled data from several hundred prehistoric cemeteries in Europe and North Africa. Vasilakis focused on a single ratio: the proportion of skeletons belonging to individuals aged between five and nineteen, relative to all those older than five. Because young people make up a larger share of the dead in a population that is growing quickly, a high value of this ratio indicates high fertility. Her results showed a sharp increase in the ratio within a few centuries of the local adoption of farming, followed by a plateau or slight decline. She interpreted this as evidence that birth rates rose abruptly when people began to cultivate crops. Remarkably, the same pattern appeared in regions as different as the Nile valley, the Balkans and the Atlantic coast, despite the fact that farming reached these areas at very different times.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The explanation for this rise is generally sought in the changed circumstances of women. Among mobile foragers, a mother must carry a young child over long distances, and births tend to be spaced three or four years apart. Settled life removed much of this constraint. In addition, soft foods such as cereal porridge and, later, animal milk allowed infants to be weaned earlier, which shortened the interval before a mother could conceive again. Professor Wanjiru Mbugua, a biological anthropologist, has added a further factor: a diet richer in carbohydrates, she argues, may have increased women's energy reserves and hence their fertility, even if the diet was poorer in other respects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Higher fertility was not, however, the whole story. The same cemeteries suggest that mortality also rose, particularly among infants and young children, as infections spread in crowded villages. The result was a population that grew rapidly but also experienced frequent crises. Héctor Lozoya, an archaeologist who studies settlement patterns, has used the dates of thousands of radiocarbon samples as a rough measure of human activity through time. His results reveal not steady growth but a series of booms and busts, in which population rose for several centuries after farming arrived in a region and then fell sharply, sometimes by half, before recovering. Lozoya suggests that early farming communities repeatedly outgrew the capacity of their land, or were devastated by epidemics.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These approaches have attracted serious criticism. Radiocarbon dates, sceptics note, reflect not only how many people lived at a given time but also how many sites have survived and been excavated, and how much money archaeologists have spent on dating them. Cemetery data present different problems. Children's bones are fragile and decay more readily than those of adults, so the proportion of young people in a burial ground may depend on soil conditions as much as on fertility. Dr Kaisa Suvanto has gone further, arguing that the age estimates on which the ratio depends are themselves unreliable, since standard methods systematically underestimate the age of older adults.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such objections are valid, but they are often presented as if they invalidated the entire field, and that conclusion does not follow. The various methods have different weaknesses, yet they point in the same direction: cemetery ratios, radiocarbon dates and the size of settlements all suggest rapid growth after the adoption of farming. When independent lines of evidence converge in this way, it is reasonable to accept the general trend, even if the precise figures remain uncertain. Ancient DNA, which can reveal changes in effective population size, has so far tended to support rather than contradict this picture.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is less certain is the meaning of the boom-and-bust pattern. If Lozoya is right, the history of early farming was far less of a smooth progression than textbooks imply, and periods of collapse may have been as important as periods of expansion in driving farmers into new territories. This is a possibility that deserves further investigation, though it is too early to treat it as established. A population crash can result from many causes, including climate change, conflict and disease, and the evidence currently available rarely allows these to be distinguished.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The study of prehistoric populations will always involve a degree of uncertainty. Nevertheless, the demographic transition is one of the few aspects of the origins of farming on which a broad consensus has emerged, and its implications are profound. It helps to explain why farming languages, genes and customs so often replaced those of foragers rather than merely mixing with them, and why the expansion of agriculture, once under way, proved so difficult to reverse. The world's population today, numbering in the billions, is the distant outcome of a change that began when a few communities in a handful of regions settled down and started to plant their food.

topic: the spread of farming into Europe: demic versus cultural diffusion and the evidence of ancient DNA
title: Migrants or Imitators?
subtitle: Was farming brought to Europe by incoming settlers, or adopted by the people already living there?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some nine thousand years ago, farming began to appear in south-eastern Europe, and over the following three millennia it spread as far as Britain, Scandinavia and the Atlantic coast of Iberia. For most of the twentieth century, archaeologists argued about how this happened. One school held that farming was carried by people: colonists from Anatolia and the Aegean who moved gradually northwards and westwards, bringing their crops, livestock and pottery with them. Another maintained that it was ideas, not populations, that travelled, and that native hunter-gatherers adopted cultivation from their neighbours, much as later societies adopted writing or metalworking. The first view is usually called demic diffusion; the second, cultural diffusion. The distinction might sound academic, but it bears on questions that matter well beyond archaeology, including the origins of Europe's languages and the extent to which its modern inhabitants descend from its earliest settlers.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s, a mathematical model gave the demic view a powerful boost. Treating the expansion of farmers as a wave, rather like the spread of a gene through a population, researchers calculated that a modest rate of population growth combined with short-distance movement in each generation would produce an advance of roughly one kilometre per year. Remarkably, radiocarbon dates from early farming sites suggested a similar average speed. The physicist-turned-archaeologist Dragan Yarrowby, who refined the model in later decades, argues that this agreement is no coincidence: in his view, the steady pace of the expansion is precisely what one would expect if farmers were reproducing and occupying new land, and is difficult to explain if the process depended on the uneven willingness of foragers to change their way of life.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters of cultural diffusion were never fully persuaded. Dr Paloma Benavente, who has excavated coastal shell middens in Portugal, points out that the advance was anything but steady at a local scale. Farming reached some regions with startling speed (along the Mediterranean coast it may have travelled more than ten times faster than the average) and then stalled for centuries at the edges of the North European Plain and in Scandinavia, where foragers enjoyed rich marine and freshwater resources. For Benavente, these pauses show that local people were making choices, and that farming was adopted only when its advantages outweighed those of the existing economy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The debate was transformed by ancient DNA. Over the past fifteen years, genomes recovered from hundreds of prehistoric skeletons have shown that the earliest farmers of central and western Europe were, for the most part, genetically distinct from the hunter-gatherers who preceded them, and closely related to populations in Anatolia. The geneticist Antti Koskela, who has led several of these studies, describes the result as decisive. 'Whatever role local people played,' he says, 'the bulk of the first farming population in Europe was descended from migrants.' The arrival of agriculture, in this account, was above all a movement of people. Koskela's team has also traced distinct migration routes, one following the Danube into the heart of the continent and another hugging the Mediterranean shore, apparently by boat, as far as southern France and Iberia.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That conclusion is broadly justified, but it is also more complicated than headlines have suggested. The same genetic studies reveal that hunter-gatherer ancestry did not disappear. In many regions it increased over time within farming communities, rising from a few per cent in the earliest generations to a quarter or more two thousand years later. This implies sustained contact, intermarriage and, presumably, the exchange of knowledge between the two groups. Kwame Osei-Bonsu, an anthropologist who studies frontier societies, argues that the long coexistence of farmers and foragers, sometimes within a few kilometres of each other, has been neglected because it fits neither of the traditional models.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also regional exceptions. In parts of the Baltic and in the western steppe, genetic evidence suggests that local foragers took up pottery, and in some cases livestock, without any significant influx of newcomers. Here cultural diffusion seems to describe what happened rather well. In these communities, hunting, fishing and gathering continued to supply most of the diet for many centuries, and cereals appear to have been a minor addition rather than a new foundation. Professor Mila Kolarova has argued that these cases should not be treated as marginal curiosities. In her view, the mixture of mechanisms varied so widely from one region to another that any single label for the spread of farming across the continent is misleading.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Kolarova's position is, in my view, the most defensible one, although it is sometimes misread as a claim that the old dispute was meaningless. It was not. The genetic data have shown beyond reasonable doubt that migration was the dominant force in most of Europe, and those who argued for an almost entirely local adoption of farming were mistaken. What the evidence does not support is the image of a uniform wave sweeping over passive foragers. The frontier was a place of negotiation as well as replacement.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most useful lesson of this long argument concerns the relationship between disciplines. For decades, archaeologists debated the spread of farming on the basis of pots, tools and radiocarbon dates, and the evidence was too ambiguous to settle the question. Genetics did not make archaeology redundant; it answered one question cleanly and, in doing so, raised several more that only careful excavation can address. Who lived at the frontier, how farmers and foragers divided the landscape between them, and what each group learned from the other are matters that genomes alone cannot reveal.
