topic: independent early agriculture in the New Guinea highlands: wetland drainage, bananas and taro, and the definition of farming
title: Gardens Above the Clouds
subtitle: A wetland in the highlands of New Guinea has forced archaeologists to rethink where, and how, farming began

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For a long time, the story of agriculture's origins was told almost entirely from the perspective of a few celebrated centres: south-west Asia with its wheat and barley, China with its rice and millet, Mesoamerica with its maize. Other regions were assumed to have received farming from outside, usually much later. The highlands of New Guinea, the rugged island to the north of Australia, seemed an especially unlikely candidate for independent invention. Its interior was not even visited by Europeans until the 1930s, when explorers were astonished to find densely populated valleys covered in neatly drained gardens. That those gardens might have a history stretching back thousands of years was not seriously considered until much later.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The decisive evidence came from a wetland site in the upper Wahgi valley, more than 1,500 metres above sea level. Excavations there, carried out over several decades, uncovered a sequence of ditches, pits and stake holes cut into the swamp margin. The oldest features, dated to around 10,000 years ago, appear to be planting holes and channels associated with the cultivation of plants on better-drained ground. By about 6,500 years ago, people had built mounds of soil, which improve drainage and warm the roots of plants, and by 4,000 years ago they were digging extensive networks of ditches to drain the wetland itself. Dr Hinemoa Tepaeru, an archaeobotanist who has re-examined much of the plant material, has identified starch grains and microscopic silica bodies from bananas and taro on stone tools from the earliest levels.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that New Guinea was one of the places where agriculture developed independently, at roughly the same period as in south-west Asia. Yet the nature of that agriculture was very different. Its staple crops, among them taro, yams, bananas and sugarcane, are propagated not from seed but from cuttings, suckers or tubers. Such plants show few of the obvious physical changes, such as larger seeds, that allow archaeologists to recognise domestication in cereals. For this reason, Professor Joost Aukema argues that the conventional criteria for identifying early farming are biased towards grain crops and have led researchers to overlook vegetative agriculture elsewhere in the tropics. In his opinion, many other regions may have independent agricultural origins that remain undetected simply because the evidence does not look the way archaeologists expect.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that the earliest features at the site represent farming at all. The palaeoecologist Mateo Pazmiño accepts that people were exploiting bananas and taro 10,000 years ago, but suggests that the planting holes may reflect the tending of wild stands rather than true cultivation. He notes that both plants grow naturally in the lowland forests of the region and that, in the warmer climate of the early Holocene, they could have extended to higher altitudes without human help. Pazmiño does not dispute the later mounds and ditches, which he regards as clear evidence of agriculture, but he believes that the claim of a 10,000-year-old origin goes beyond what the data can show. He also warns that features dug into soft swamp sediments are notoriously difficult to date, because material from older or younger layers can easily be displaced into them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This disagreement is partly about definitions. If farming means the deliberate planting and care of chosen species, then the early inhabitants of the Wahgi valley were almost certainly farmers. If it requires plants that have been genetically altered by cultivation, the case is weaker, since it is difficult to show that bananas and taro had changed much by then. Neither definition is obviously correct, and the second has the disadvantage of excluding precisely the kinds of crops on which New Guinea's farmers depended. On balance, the broader definition seems more useful, provided it is applied consistently to other regions as well.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The environmental record adds a further dimension. Pollen and charcoal from cores taken in the valley indicate that forest was cleared repeatedly from about 7,000 years ago, and that grassland expanded as cultivation intensified. Layers of eroded soil washed down from the surrounding hills also appear in the swamp at about this time, suggesting that the cleared slopes were becoming unstable. Dr Sigrún Bjarnadóttir, who analysed these cores, argues that the ditch networks were partly a response to this degradation: as soils on the slopes became exhausted, farmers turned to the more difficult but more fertile wetland. If she is right, the history of agriculture in the highlands was driven not only by innovation but also by the need to cope with damage that farming itself had caused.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The site has now been recognised as being of global importance, and it is easy to see why. It challenges the assumption that agriculture was the achievement of a few favoured regions, from which it was later passed on to less inventive peoples. It also reminds us that farming took many forms, and that a focus on seeds and grains can distort our picture of the past. The highland gardens of New Guinea, with their mounds, tubers and drains, represent a tradition every bit as sophisticated as the wheat fields of the Fertile Crescent, and one that continues, in recognisable form, to the present day.

topic: climate and the origins of agriculture: Holocene stability, the Younger Dryas crisis, rising carbon dioxide and cultural choice
title: Did the Weather Make Farmers?
subtitle: Agriculture arose on several continents soon after the last ice age ended. How much of that was down to the climate?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Human beings have been anatomically modern for perhaps 300,000 years, yet farming appeared independently in several parts of the world only within the last 12,000. The coincidence in timing is striking. Within a few thousand years of one another, people in south-west Asia, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes and New Guinea began to cultivate plants. Such a pattern seems to demand a global explanation, and the most obvious candidate is climate: the end of the last ice age and the beginning of the Holocene, the relatively warm and stable period in which we still live.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One influential version of this argument emphasises stability rather than warmth. Professor Yonas Gebremedhin, a palaeoclimatologist, has pointed out that ice-age climates were not only colder but also far more variable than today's, with large swings in temperature and rainfall occurring within a single human lifetime. Under such conditions, he argues, any investment in cultivating a particular plant in a particular place would frequently have been wiped out. Only when the climate settled down after about 11,700 years ago did agriculture become a reasonable gamble. Gebremedhin goes further, suggesting that farming was 'mandatory' in the Holocene: once conditions allowed it, competition between groups made its eventual adoption all but inevitable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A rival account focuses on a specific event. Around 12,900 years ago, after several millennia of warming, the northern hemisphere was plunged back into near-glacial conditions for roughly 1,200 years, a period known as the Younger Dryas. The archaeologist Chiara Fiorentino has argued that this cold, dry interval placed severe pressure on communities in the Levant that had come to rely on dense stands of wild cereals. As those stands shrank, people began to cultivate cereals deliberately in order to maintain their supply. In this view, agriculture was a response not to favourable conditions but to a crisis.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The Younger Dryas hypothesis has had a mixed reception. Its great attraction is that it explains why cultivation began in one particular region at one particular time. However, Dr Eero Ylikoski, who has compiled radiocarbon dates from sites across the Levant, notes that the clearest evidence for cultivation appears towards the end of the cold period or after it, not at its height. He also points out that some communities appear to have responded to the cold by becoming more mobile, not by settling down to farm. For Ylikoski, the Younger Dryas may have shaped how people lived, but the timing makes it a weak candidate for the trigger of agriculture.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective concerns the atmosphere itself. During the last glacial maximum, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air was roughly a third lower than in the early Holocene. Experiments by the plant physiologist Haruto Kawashima, in which wild wheat and barley were grown under carbon dioxide levels typical of the ice age, showed sharply reduced growth and seed production. Kawashima concludes that cultivation would have been barely worthwhile before the rise in carbon dioxide, which acted, in his words, as 'an invisible fertiliser' for the first farmers. The finding is elegant, though it is less clear how it applies to crops such as taro or squash that were not included in his experiments.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These climate-based explanations share a weakness. Each identifies conditions that made farming possible, but none explains why particular communities chose to farm while others, living in similar environments, did not. Hunter-gatherers continued to thrive in many regions with suitable climates and plants for thousands of years after the Holocene began. The anthropologist Zuzana Brezina insists that these cases deserve as much attention as the famous centres of domestication. Drawing on her research among the historical records of foragers in California and the archaeology of the eastern Mediterranean, she argues that cultural factors, including systems of land ownership, ritual obligations and attitudes to storage, were at least as important as climate in deciding whether people took up cultivation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Brezina's emphasis on choice is a valuable corrective, but it would be wrong to conclude that climate does not matter. The near-simultaneous appearance of agriculture on several continents is hard to explain by local cultural factors alone, and there is no record of farming emerging anywhere during the long, unstable glacial period. The most persuasive position, I believe, is that the Holocene climate was a necessary but not a sufficient condition: it opened a door that human societies could pass through, but it did not push them. That framing has the advantage of explaining both the global timing and the long delays and local variations that the climate argument on its own cannot account for.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: There is a contemporary resonance to this debate. If agriculture was made possible by an unusually stable climate, then the rapid changes now under way raise uncomfortable questions about the security of the system that has supported human civilisation ever since. It would be unwise to push the parallel too far, since modern farming has tools and knowledge that its Neolithic predecessors lacked, but the lesson that agriculture depends on a predictable environment is one that today's societies can hardly afford to forget.

topic: the domestication of sheep and goats: kill-off age and sex profiles, dung and isotope evidence, and multiple wild lineages
title: Reading the Herd
subtitle: How can archaeologists tell when people stopped hunting wild sheep and goats and started keeping them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the animals that human beings have domesticated, sheep and goats were among the first, and they remain among the most important. Today they number well over two billion, providing meat, milk, wool and leather across almost every inhabited region of the world. Yet the process by which wild mouflon and bezoar goats in the mountains of south-west Asia became the docile animals of the farmyard left remarkably little trace. Unlike plants, whose seeds and fruits change shape under cultivation, early domestic animals often looked almost identical to their wild relatives. Identifying the moment when people stopped hunting these animals and started herding them has therefore required considerable ingenuity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years, the principal clue was size. Domestic sheep and goats are generally smaller than their wild ancestors, and archaeologists treated a reduction in bone size as a sign of domestication. This approach has now largely fallen out of favour. Dr Rania Arnaout, a zooarchaeologist who has analysed bones from more than forty sites in the Zagros Mountains, points out that body size in wild animals varies with climate, altitude and sex, and that a change in the proportion of males and females in a sample can produce an apparent reduction without any change in the animals themselves. Size, in her view, is a lagging indicator: it changed only after centuries of herding, and therefore cannot tell us when management began.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Arnaout's own approach relies instead on demographic profiles. Hunters and herders make different decisions about which animals to kill. A hunter tends to target large adults, especially males, because they provide the most meat per kill. A herder, by contrast, needs to keep breeding females alive for as long as possible, and so typically slaughters most young males before they reach full size, retaining only a few for breeding. By estimating the age and sex of each animal from its bones and teeth, it is possible to reconstruct these patterns. At a site in the Zagros dated to around 10,000 years ago, Arnaout found that most male goats had been killed at about two years old while females survived well into adulthood, a pattern she interprets as clear evidence of herd management.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The method has been widely adopted, but it has critics. Professor Erlend Tønnessen notes that some hunters also select animals by age and sex, particularly when they are able to drive whole groups into enclosures or traps. Under such circumstances, he argues, hunters might deliberately spare pregnant females to protect future supplies, producing a profile that resembles herding. Tønnessen does not reject the method, but he believes that demographic profiles should be combined with other evidence before firm conclusions are drawn.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One such source of evidence is chemical. Animals that are kept in pens and fed by people often eat a different diet from wild animals, and this is recorded in the isotopes preserved in their bones. Dr Inés Narváez has also examined deposits of dung that accumulated inside early settlements, which provide direct proof that animals were being kept within the village. At one site in central Anatolia, layers of burnt dung suggest that young sheep were penned inside the settlement as early as 10,400 years ago, probably for short periods during the lambing season. For Narváez, this indicates that the earliest stage of management involved keeping a few animals close at hand rather than large herds on open pasture.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Genetics has added a further layer of complexity. Studies of modern and ancient DNA show that domestic sheep and goats are descended from several distinct wild lineages, suggesting that they were brought under human control in more than one place. The geneticist Floor Huitema argues that management began across a wide area of south-west Asia, from the Taurus Mountains to the Zagros, and that domestic stock was then exchanged and mixed. In her view, the search for a single centre of animal domestication is misguided.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Each of these techniques has its limitations, and it is tempting to regard their disagreements as evidence that the question cannot be answered. That would be a mistake. Where demographic, chemical and genetic evidence are available from the same region, they increasingly tell a consistent story: people began managing wild goats and sheep around 11,000 to 10,000 years ago, at several locations at once, and the physical changes associated with domestication followed slowly over the next two thousand years. What remains genuinely uncertain is how deliberate the process was. It seems unlikely that the first herders saw themselves as creating a new kind of animal; more probably, they were trying to secure a reliable supply of meat at a time when hunting pressure had reduced wild populations.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: This conclusion matters beyond archaeology. Animal domestication is often imagined as an event, a moment of capture and taming, but the evidence suggests a gradual change in the relationship between people and animals. Understanding that relationship, rather than searching for a single moment of transformation, is what the next generation of research should aim to do.

topic: behavioural ecology (diet-breadth model) versus niche construction theory as explanations of why foragers began to cultivate plants
title: Engineers or Economists?
subtitle: Two rival theories offer competing accounts of why foragers began to cultivate plants, and neither may be sufficient on its own

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, attempts to explain why people abandoned a purely foraging way of life searched for a single decisive trigger: a drying climate, a growing population, or the extinction of the large animals on which hunters had depended. Few archaeologists now believe that any one of these factors will suffice. Instead, the debate has increasingly crystallised around two broad theoretical frameworks. The first, drawn from behavioural ecology, treats early cultivators as practical decision-makers who weighed the costs and benefits of the foods available to them. The second, known as niche construction theory, portrays them as engineers who gradually remodelled their surroundings over many generations. The contest between the two is frequently presented as a clash of incompatible worldviews, but in my view that framing has done more to entrench rival camps than to clarify what the evidence actually shows.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The behavioural ecology position is most forcefully argued by Halvard Ostrømsvik of the University of Tromsdal. His work rests on what is known as the diet-breadth model. Foragers, according to this model, rank potential foods by the energy they yield for each hour spent searching for, catching and processing them. Large animals, which provide a great deal of meat for relatively little handling, sit at the top of the list; the tiny seeds of wild grasses, which must be gathered, threshed, winnowed and ground, sit near the bottom. Such low-ranked foods, Ostrømsvik argues, would be added to the diet only when higher-ranked resources became scarce. Cultivation was therefore not an innovation eagerly embraced but a reluctant response to falling returns. In support, he cites sites in several regions where the bones of large mammals become rarer in refuse deposits at roughly the time that grass seeds become more common.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Amaru Quelcca, of the Andean Institute of Human Ecology, rejects this account almost entirely. The earliest evidence of cultivation, he observes, tends to come not from impoverished landscapes but from rich ones: lake margins, river valleys and coastal wetlands, where fish, waterfowl and wild plants were plentiful. People in these places, Quelcca maintains, were not driven by hunger but deliberately enhanced the productivity of their environment, burning undergrowth to encourage fresh growth, transplanting useful species closer to camp and removing competing weeds. Domestication, on this view, was the cumulative outcome of practices handed down from one generation to the next. Quelcca's central complaint about diet-breadth models is that they treat the environment as a fixed backdrop against which choices are made, when in reality people were continually altering it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ostrømsvik's reply is twofold. First, he points out that abundance and stress are not mutually exclusive: a resource-rich valley might attract and sustain a growing population, which would in time deplete the very animals that drew people there. Second, and more pointedly, he argues that niche construction describes what early cultivators did without explaining why they did it. Because it makes no prediction that could turn out to be wrong, he contends, it amounts to a narrative rather than a theory. This criticism has real force. A framework that can accommodate any outcome is difficult to test, and Quelcca's supporters have yet to specify what kind of evidence would count against their position.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet behavioural ecology has weaknesses of its own, and these have been exposed most clearly by experimental work. The archaeobotanist Delphine Rocaserra, at the Mediterranean Centre for Archaeobotany, has spent several seasons harvesting and processing stands of wild wheat and barley using replica tools. Her results show that return rates vary enormously. A dense stand cut with a flint sickle at the right stage of ripeness can provide calories at a rate comparable to hunting small game, whereas the same stand harvested a fortnight too late, after most of the grain has fallen, may yield almost nothing. Depending on the conditions, the figures she obtained differed by a factor of ten. This does not invalidate the diet-breadth model, but it does mean that the model's predictions are only as reliable as the numbers fed into it, and for the distant past those numbers are often little more than educated guesses.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An attempt to reconcile the two approaches has come from Yusra Al-Hakimawi and her colleagues at the Levant Modelling Group. Using computer simulations of foraging communities, they found that cultivation emerged most readily where two conditions coincided: people had already modified their habitat in ways that made useful plants more accessible, and they periodically experienced shortages of preferred foods. Al-Hakimawi suggests that niche construction lowers the cost of obtaining plant foods and thereby raises their position in the rankings that behavioural ecologists describe. On this interpretation, the two frameworks are not competitors at all but accounts of different stages in a single process. Her proposal is, to my mind, the most promising contribution to the debate so far, although simulations inevitably inherit the assumptions of those who design them, and a model with enough adjustable settings can be made to produce almost any result.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Part of the disagreement, I suspect, arises from a difference of scale. Behavioural ecology concerns the decisions of individuals over a season or a lifetime, while niche construction deals with processes that unfold across centuries. Neither is wrong to focus where it does. What seems certain is that the controversy has been productive, prompting archaeologists to collect far more detailed evidence about plant processing and the use of fire in prehistoric landscapes. Agriculture arose independently in perhaps a dozen regions, from south-west Asia to Mesoamerica and New Guinea, under very different circumstances. To expect any single model to account for all of them would be a mistake.

topic: sedentism before farming: evidence for year-round forager settlement (architecture, house mice, seasonal plants), food storage and whether settling down caused agriculture
title: Settled Before Sowing
subtitle: Did people stop moving before they began to farm, and does it matter which came first?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the traditional account of human prehistory, farming came first and villages followed. Only once people could grow their own food, the argument ran, were they able to give up a wandering life and settle in one place. Over the past few decades, however, excavations in south-west Asia and elsewhere have revealed substantial settlements built by people who still lived entirely by hunting and gathering, sometimes centuries before any crops were domesticated. This reversal of the expected order is, I believe, one of the most significant changes in our understanding of how agriculture began. It must be said, though, that the word 'permanent', which is often used to describe these communities, can be misleading, since few of them appear to have been occupied continuously for long.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: How can archaeologists tell whether a site was lived in all year round? Some indicators are architectural: round houses with stone foundations represent a considerable investment of labour, and large grinding stones, some weighing more than fifty kilograms, are too heavy to have been carried from camp to camp. Cemeteries placed beneath or beside dwellings also suggest an enduring attachment to place. A more unusual line of evidence comes from Haruki Tsuzumida of the Kansai Institute of Zooarchaeology, who studies the teeth of mice. Where humans remain in one spot throughout the year, he explains, the house mouse, which thrives on human food and shelter, tends to outcompete its wild relatives. At sites where house mouse teeth predominate, people were probably present for most of the year; where wild species return, occupation had probably become seasonal again. For Tsuzumida, the mouse is a kind of living gauge of how long people stayed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The significance of early settlement is the subject of considerable disagreement. Ileana Brâncuşanu, an archaeologist at the Danube Institute of Prehistory, argues that sedentism was the cause of agriculture rather than its consequence. A community that has invested in houses and stores cannot simply move on when local resources run low. Having exhausted the most accessible game and wild plants nearby, such groups were, in her view, trapped with the shortages they had created, and cultivation offered a way of extracting more food from the same territory. She adds that settled life may have increased birth rates, because mothers no longer needed to carry young children over long distances, which would have intensified the pressure still further.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The anthropologist Kofi Adjeibuor, of the West African Centre for Comparative Ethnography, believes that this argument relies on too sharp a distinction between mobile and settled peoples. Drawing on studies of recent foraging societies, he notes that many groups shift between the two over a span of years, staying in one location when conditions are good and dispersing when they are poor. Sedentism, he argues, should be thought of as a sliding scale rather than a fixed condition. Adjeibuor also maintains that the decisive development was not cultivation but food storage: once a community had accumulated reserves of nuts or wild grain, it had a strong reason to remain near them, whether or not it grew any crops.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even the evidence for year-round occupation is less straightforward than it seems. The archaeobotanist Mirela Zacharewicz has pointed out that the remains of plants that ripen in different seasons are often taken as proof that a site was inhabited throughout the year. Yet if those plants were gathered in autumn and kept for later use, their remains could accumulate in a site that was occupied only during the winter months. Storage, in other words, can mimic continuous occupation. Zacharewicz's warning deserves to be taken seriously, and it suggests that no single kind of evidence should be relied upon on its own.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Brâncuşanu's model is persuasive for parts of south-west Asia, but I do not accept that it can be applied universally. In several regions the sequence appears to have run the other way. In parts of the Americas, for instance, communities cultivated squash and other plants for thousands of years while continuing to spend part of each year at distant hunting camps; full-time village life came much later. Similar patterns have been proposed for parts of Africa, where herding and the tending of wild cereals seem to have coexisted with considerable mobility for long periods. If farming could begin without settlement, then settlement cannot have been a necessary precondition for it, however important it may have been in particular places.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is clear is that settling down carried real costs. Living in one place meant accumulating waste, sharing space with disease-carrying animals and competing with neighbours for land. The more interesting question, therefore, may be why people were willing to tolerate these drawbacks at all. Some researchers point to social motives, such as the prestige associated with hosting large gatherings and feasts, while others suggest that defending valuable stores against rival groups simply made departure too risky. Whatever the answer, the long-running argument over which came first, the village or the field, seems to me less illuminating than an investigation of how each made the other more likely.

topic: the Beringian standstill hypothesis: whether the ancestors of Native Americans spent thousands of years isolated before entering the Americas, and where and for how long
title: Waiting at the Threshold
subtitle: Did the ancestors of the first Americans pause for thousands of years on a land bridge that has since vanished beneath the sea?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some twenty thousand years ago, at the height of the last ice age, so much water was locked in glaciers that the sea stood roughly 120 metres lower than it does today. Between north-east Siberia and Alaska, the retreating ocean exposed a vast plain which geologists call Beringia. For much of the twentieth century, the story of how humans reached the Americas across this land was told with satisfying simplicity: big-game hunters, following herds of mammoth and bison, crossed swiftly from Asia around 13,000 years ago and spread south within a few centuries. That account has since collapsed under the weight of sites in both North and South America that are older than it allows. In its place, geneticists have proposed something stranger: that the ancestors of the first Americans did not hurry across at all, but waited, for many thousands of years, at the threshold of a continent.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The so-called standstill hypothesis grew out of a puzzle in the DNA of living Indigenous peoples. Comparisons with East Asian populations indicate that the lineages leading to Native Americans began to diverge from their Asian relatives perhaps 25,000 years ago, yet the earliest secure evidence of people south of the ice sheets dates to around 16,000 years ago. Something, it seemed, had to fill the gap. Saule Kurmangaliyeva, a population geneticist at the Steppe Institute of Genomic History, drew attention to a further clue. A number of maternal lineages that are widespread among Native Americans are entirely absent from present-day Siberia. Such lineages, she argues, could only have arisen in a population cut off from its Asian neighbours for a very long time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most popular answer to the question of where this population lived has been Beringia itself. The palaeoecologist Kasimir Brzezinka has reconstructed the region's vegetation from pollen preserved in lake sediments and in cores drilled from the floor of the Bering Sea. His results suggest that, while the surrounding uplands were cold and largely treeless, the low-lying centre of the land bridge supported shrub tundra with dwarf birch and willow, providing fuel for fires and shelter for game. Such a refuge, Brzezinka argues, could have sustained a small human population through the harshest millennia of the glaciation. The idea has obvious appeal, not least because it explains why archaeologists have found so little: the supposed homeland now lies beneath the sea. Yet that is precisely what makes it awkward. A hypothesis whose decisive evidence is out of reach is difficult either to confirm or to refute, and its supporters have sometimes treated this inconvenience as if it were a strength.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the waiting took place on the land bridge. The archaeologist Fenella Draycott points out that no site in Alaska or the Yukon, the still-dry eastern part of Beringia, has been reliably dated to earlier than about 14,500 years ago. If people had lived nearby for eight or nine thousand years, she reasons, some trace of them ought to have survived on higher ground. Draycott proposes instead that the isolated population lived in north-east Asia, perhaps in the Amur basin, separated from other groups by the severity of the climate rather than by distance or water. The genetic data, she stresses, reveal when populations separated but say nothing about where they were living. This is an important corrective, and one that enthusiasts for a Beringian homeland have been too quick to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different challenge concerns the duration of the standstill. Wayra Achahui, a computational geneticist at the Andean Centre for Population Studies, argues that the long pause may be partly an artefact of method. Estimates of when two populations split depend on assumptions about the rate at which mutations accumulate, and recent studies of family pedigrees suggest that this rate may be faster than older calculations assumed. Achahui also notes that if small numbers of people continued to move back and forth between Asia and the ancestral American population, the resulting gene flow would make the original separation appear earlier than it really was. Allowing for both effects, her models reduce the standstill to perhaps two or three thousand years. This argument has received less attention than it deserves, since a pause of that length would turn a people suspended in isolation into one moving gradually eastward.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ancient DNA has added evidence without settling the matter. The genome of an infant buried in central Alaska roughly 11,500 years ago revealed a previously unknown population, the Ancient Beringians, which appears to have separated from the ancestors of all other Native Americans around 20,000 years ago. Hallvard Leirvag, who led part of the analysis at the Nordkapp Laboratory for Archaic Genomes, regards this as strong support for a long residence in the north. Draycott counters that the split could equally have occurred in Asia. The same genome, in other words, has been recruited by both sides.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most reasonable verdict is that the standstill hypothesis is probably correct in outline, but the image it has popularised, of a single community frozen in place on a lost plain, is almost certainly too neat. A more realistic picture would involve several loosely connected groups in north-east Asia and Beringia, exchanging marriage partners as conditions allowed. Nor is it likely that further sampling of living populations will resolve the remaining questions, since modern genomes have already yielded most of what they can. The decisive evidence will come, if at all, from ancient remains recovered in Siberia or from surveys of the drowned landscape itself. Meanwhile, the hypothesis has already performed a valuable service: it has obliged geneticists and archaeologists, who long worked in parallel, to test their conclusions against each other.

topic: the 'pots versus people' debate: how ancient DNA revived migration as an explanation for archaeological change, and the risks of equating artefacts with populations
title: Pots, People and Genomes
subtitle: Ancient DNA has brought migration back to the centre of archaeology, but not everyone welcomes its return

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the early twentieth century, archaeologists explained change in the past in a straightforward way. When a new style of pottery, a new kind of burial or an unfamiliar type of house appeared in a region, it was taken as evidence that a new people had arrived, bringing their customs with them. Textbooks were filled with maps on which bold arrows traced the movements of tribes across continents. By the 1960s, however, a younger generation had grown impatient with this approach. Change, they argued, could just as easily result from local invention or from ideas passed between neighbours through trade and imitation. Their slogan, 'pots are not people', captured a mood that dominated the discipline for decades, during which any archaeologist who proposed a migration risked being thought naive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The analysis of ancient DNA has overturned that consensus with remarkable speed. Since around 2010, genomes recovered from thousands of skeletons have revealed that many regions experienced dramatic shifts in ancestry. The first farmers of Europe, for example, were not local hunter-gatherers who had adopted agriculture, but largely the descendants of migrants from Anatolia. Nikos Hadjikyriacou, a geneticist at the Aegean Centre for Ancient Genomics, goes further, maintaining that large-scale movement was not the exception in prehistory but its normal condition, and that archaeologists' reluctance to accept this delayed progress by a generation. There is truth in his complaint, but it is overstated: the sceptics of the 1960s were reacting against genuinely careless reasoning, and their insistence on evidence was not misplaced.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Indeed, some archaeologists fear that the pendulum has swung too far. Itziar Zapiain, who directs excavations for the University of the Basque Coast, objects to the habit of naming genetic clusters after archaeological cultures, a practice which implies that a style of pottery corresponds neatly to a biological population. Her own work at a Bronze Age cemetery in the western Pyrenees illustrates the danger. Individuals with very different ancestries were buried there side by side, with identical grave goods and in identical positions. Whatever their origins, the newcomers had evidently embraced the customs of the community they joined. Zapiain's warning deserves to be taken seriously, since the old equation of objects with ethnic groups has a troubling history of political misuse.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The case of the so-called Bell Beaker phenomenon shows why simple formulas fail. Around 4,500 years ago, distinctive bell-shaped drinking vessels spread across much of western Europe. In Iberia, genetic studies have found that the beakers were adopted with little change in the local population. In Britain, by contrast, their arrival coincided with a turnover so profound that, within a few centuries, most of the island's earlier ancestry had disappeared. The same objects, in other words, travelled by entirely different means in different places. Neither the old assumption that pots are people nor the later insistence that they are not can account for both outcomes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different set of concerns relates to who is being studied, and by whom. The anthropologist Josiane Mukabalisa points out that ancient DNA survives best in cold, dry conditions and degrades rapidly in heat and humidity. As a result, the published record is dominated by samples from Europe and northern Asia, while much of Africa and South-East Asia remains almost unrepresented. The emerging picture of human prehistory, she argues, is therefore shaped as much by climate and research funding as by the past itself. Mukabalisa also notes that communities descended from the people whose remains are analysed have rarely been consulted. This second criticism is, if anything, more pressing than the profession has yet acknowledged.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even where samples are plentiful, genetic data have limits. DNA can reveal that a population's ancestry changed, but not why people moved or how the newcomers came to predominate. The demographer Rémi Laforgue has used computer simulations to show that near-total replacement need not involve conquest. A modest advantage in birth rates, or greater resistance to an epidemic disease, can transform the ancestry of a region over twenty or thirty generations without a single battle. Such models are a valuable corrective to the dramatic narratives of invasion that sometimes accompany genetic papers. They should not, however, be taken to imply that prehistoric migrations were peaceful; mass graves from several periods make clear that violence sometimes accompanied them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most promising research now combines several kinds of evidence. Chemical isotopes in teeth can show where an individual spent their childhood; DNA can reveal their ancestry and family relationships; artefacts and burial practices indicate how they wished to be seen. Studied together at the scale of a single village or household, these sources can reveal how migrants and locals actually lived alongside one another. There is a certain irony in the fact that the continental maps produced by some genetic studies, with their sweeping arrows, look remarkably like those the archaeologists of the 1960s rejected. The challenge for the next generation is to ensure that the new science produces not merely a revival of old stories, but better ones.

topic: early dispersals of Homo sapiens out of Africa that left no living descendants: the Levant, European pioneers, volcanic and demographic explanations
title: Pioneers Without Heirs
subtitle: Several early groups of modern humans reached Europe and Asia long before the migration that peopled the world. Why did they vanish?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The textbook account of how modern humans populated the world has long been admirably simple. Our species, it holds, evolved in Africa and then, around 60,000 years ago, a single wave of migrants crossed into Asia and spread rapidly across the rest of the globe. Recent discoveries have made that story harder to sustain. Fossils of Homo sapiens have turned up outside Africa in deposits far older than 60,000 years, and ancient genomes show that several populations which did reach Europe and Asia contributed little or nothing to people alive today. These lost pioneers are often treated as curiosities, but they deserve a more central place in the story, since they reveal how precarious the expansion of our species actually was.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest of them may be represented by a partial skull from a cave in southern Greece, dated to more than 200,000 years ago, although its identification as Homo sapiens remains disputed. Firmer evidence comes from burials in caves in the Levant, where anatomically modern people lived between roughly 130,000 and 90,000 years ago. Genetic studies indicate that today's non-Africans descend overwhelmingly from a later dispersal, so these early Levantine groups appear to have vanished. Teimuraz Vashakmadze of the Caucasus Institute of Human Origins argues that they retreated or died out when the region became colder and drier, after which Neanderthals moved back into the caves. This explanation is plausible, but the dating of the Levantine sites is still too imprecise to confirm it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much more is known about pioneers in Europe, thanks to ancient DNA. Remains from a cave in Bulgaria, around 45,000 years old, have yielded genomes from individuals belonging to a population that left almost no trace in later Europeans. Strikingly, one of them had a Neanderthal ancestor only about six generations earlier, a sign that the two kinds of human were mixing freely. The geneticist Ifeoma Okonkwo-Bassey attributes the disappearance of such groups to what she calls demographic fragility. Small bands, scattered across vast territories, were vulnerable to inbreeding, to the loss of a few key individuals and to sheer bad luck. Her account is more persuasive than older suggestions that the pioneers were somehow less capable than the people who followed them, an idea for which there has never been good evidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others look to a more dramatic cause. Around 39,000 years ago, a massive eruption near present-day Naples spread volcanic ash across much of eastern Europe. Lidia Zvereva, a specialist in volcanic deposits, has found that layers of this ash in several caves sit directly above the last traces of early modern occupation, and she proposes that the years of cold and darkness which followed the eruption destroyed the remaining pioneer groups. The coincidence in timing is certainly suggestive, and Zvereva has strengthened her case by showing that in some valleys the ash fell thickly enough to smother vegetation for several seasons. However, genetic evidence shows that some pioneer populations had already disappeared thousands of years before the eruption, so it cannot be the whole explanation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further possibility is that the pioneers vanished biologically while leaving a cultural legacy. Stone-tool industries associated with the earliest modern humans in Europe and Asia share features across enormous distances, and some of these features reappear in assemblages made by later groups, or even by Neanderthals. The archaeologist Callum Abernethy-Lowe suggests that techniques may have passed from the pioneers to their neighbours before the pioneers themselves disappeared. He points in particular to a distinctive way of striking long, narrow blades from a carefully prepared core, which appears at sites thousands of kilometres apart within a few millennia. The idea is attractive, but it is hard to demonstrate, since similar methods of shaping stone could easily have been invented independently by different groups.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ecologists offer a broader perspective. Josephine Kimbugwe, who studies biological invasions, notes that when plants or animals are introduced to a new region, most introductions fail; colonising species usually succeed only after repeated arrivals have built up a sufficient population. If human dispersal followed the same pattern, the expansion of Homo sapiens should be understood not as a single journey but as a series of waves, most of which ended in local extinction. The famous exodus of around 60,000 years ago would then simply be the wave that happened to succeed. Such a view would also explain why the pioneers left so few remains: groups that survived only a few centuries in a new region would rarely produce the dense accumulations of bones and tools that archaeologists are most likely to find.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even the word 'failure' may be misleading. The pioneers lived for many generations in their new homelands, and some of their DNA survives in the genomes of Neanderthals with whom they interbred. That we tend to overlook them reflects a bias built into genetic research: present-day genomes record only the ancestors of the living, not the full range of people who once existed. Filling the gaps will depend on ancient samples from Arabia and South Asia, regions that lay on the likely routes out of Africa but where the warm climate rapidly destroys genetic material. Until such samples are found, any account of how our species spread will remain, in an important sense, a history written by the survivors.

topic: humid phases in the Sahara and Arabia as climate windows for human dispersal out of Africa: the 'pump' model, dating problems and human adaptation to aridity
title: Corridors of Rain
subtitle: Did changes in climate open and close the routes by which early humans left Africa?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Today the Sahara and the deserts of Arabia form one of the most formidable barriers on Earth: thousands of kilometres of sand, gravel and bare rock separating the well-watered regions of Africa from the rest of Eurasia. Any account of how our species spread across the world must explain how people managed to cross this expanse. Over the past two decades, a growing number of researchers have found the answer in climate. At intervals during the last few hundred thousand years, they argue, the deserts turned green, and for a while the barrier became a bridge. This idea represents one of the most significant shifts in thinking about human origins in recent times, although, as is often the case with powerful ideas, it has sometimes been pushed further than the evidence allows.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physical evidence for wetter periods is now difficult to dispute. Satellite radar, which can penetrate a thin layer of dry sand, has revealed networks of ancient river channels buried beneath the Sahara. In the interior of Arabia, Salim Al-Mahrouqi, a geomorphologist at the Institute of Arid Lands in Muscat, has spent a decade mapping the shorelines of vanished lakes. He dates them using luminescence, a technique that measures how long ago grains of sand were last exposed to sunlight. His results point to at least five humid phases in the past 400,000 years, each lasting a few thousand years, during which lakes held fresh water for long periods and grassland stretched between them. The bones of hippopotamuses, found in what is now among the driest terrain on the planet, offer a vivid confirmation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should the deserts have flourished in this way? According to the climate modeller Ingrid Solheimsnes, the cause lies in small, regular variations in the Earth's orbit, which periodically intensify summer sunshine in the northern hemisphere and draw the monsoon rains northwards. Her simulations underpin what has become known as the 'Sahara pump'. In each green phase, animals and the humans who hunted them would have moved into the newly habitable land; when aridity returned, they would have been forced out again, some retreating south, others pushing on towards the Levant or Arabia. Part of the model's appeal is that it can be tested, since it predicts that evidence of dispersal should cluster within humid periods rather than being spread evenly through time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the image of a pump, however memorable, carries a hidden assumption: that human beings were moved about by climate much as particles are moved by a current. The archaeologist Farid Benyoucef has challenged this picture. At several sites in eastern Arabia he has found stone tools in layers laid down during dry phases, suggesting that people did not simply abandon the region when the rains failed. Instead, he argues, they concentrated around springs and moved seasonally between them. On this view, crossing the desert did not require a continuous green corridor, only a chain of dependable water sources and the knowledge of where to find them. The pump model, attractive as it is, leaves too little room for this kind of human decision-making.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more technical objection concerns dating. Camila Sarmiento-Ruiz, a geochronologist who has re-examined many of the published dates, points out that luminescence ages frequently carry uncertainties of several thousand years, a margin as long as some of the humid phases themselves. It is therefore often impossible to say whether a particular archaeological layer belongs to a wet period or a dry one. Worse, she suggests, researchers who expect sites to fall within humid phases may unconsciously interpret ambiguous dates in that light, producing a pattern that partly reflects their own assumptions. This is a sobering point. It does not mean that climate was irrelevant, but it does mean that many of the neat correlations reported so far should be treated as provisional.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a problem of presentation. Popular reconstructions frequently show broad green bands sweeping across North Africa and Arabia, implying a continuous belt of savannah. The reality, even in the wettest phases, was almost certainly more varied: lakes and rivers separated by stretches of dry scrub, with conditions shifting from one decade to the next. To speak of 'corridors' in such circumstances risks creating a false impression of a landscape through which people could stroll from one continent to another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most balanced conclusion is that climate set the stage without writing the script. Humid phases determined when crossing the deserts was easiest, but whether and how particular groups made the journey depended on their skills, their numbers and, no doubt, on circumstances that leave no trace. Progress will come from better dating. Mineral deposits that grow in caves, known as speleothems, form only when water drips through the rock, and they can be dated with far greater precision by measuring the decay of uranium. Combined with more securely dated archaeological sites, they may eventually show that the deserts were not merely obstacles crossed during rare green interludes but, for some populations at least, a homeland in their own right.

topic: the first sea crossings to Sahul (Pleistocene Australia-New Guinea) through Wallacea: accidental drift versus planned voyages, founding-population models, intervisibility of islands and indirect evidence for seafaring
title: Beyond the Last Shoreline
subtitle: How did the first Australians cross a sea that no land bridge ever spanned, and did they mean to?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: During the colder phases of the last ice age, sea levels fell far enough to join Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into a single continent that archaeologists call Sahul. Java, Sumatra and Borneo were likewise joined to Asia as Sunda. What never appeared, however low the sea fell, was a land bridge between the two. Between them lay Wallacea, a scatter of islands divided by deep channels, and anyone travelling from Asia to Australia had to make at least eight separate sea crossings, the longest of which may have exceeded seventy kilometres. Since people were living in Sahul at least 50,000 years ago, these journeys rank among the earliest known passages across open water by any human population. It is remarkable, then, that for most of the twentieth century they were treated as a curiosity rather than as one of the defining achievements of prehistory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The traditional explanation was that no one intended to make the journey at all. Small groups foraging along the shore, it was supposed, were occasionally swept out to sea on mats of floating vegetation torn loose by storms or tsunamis, and a few fortunate castaways eventually washed up on the far side. This scenario has been badly damaged by demographic modelling. Annelie Brouwersma, who simulates the fortunes of small populations at the Delta Institute for Quantitative Prehistory, has calculated that a colonising group would need to number several hundred people, including a substantial proportion of women of child-bearing age, if it were to avoid extinction through chance fluctuations in births and deaths. Such numbers, she argues, could only have arrived through repeated and organised voyages, not through a handful of accidents.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Two routes have been proposed: a northern one, through Sulawesi and the Moluccas to New Guinea, and a southern one, by way of Timor to the now-submerged continental shelf off north-western Australia. Dewi Kusumawardhani, a geographer at the Institute of Archipelago Studies, has used digital elevation models to work out which islands would have been visible from which. On the northern route, her analysis shows, travellers could almost always see their next landfall before setting out, either directly or as a bank of cloud gathering over distant mountains. On this view, the first voyagers were not launching themselves into the unknown but heading for a destination already in sight. The finding is valuable, but it explains less than its admirers sometimes suggest. Knowing that land exists on the horizon is one thing; possessing a craft able to carry families and supplies across a powerful current is quite another.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A challenge to the planned-voyage consensus has come from oceanography. Joaquim Saldanha-Ferro and colleagues at the Southern Ocean Modelling Group reconstructed ice-age currents in the Timor Sea and released thousands of virtual rafts into them. A small but consistent fraction reached Sahul within a fortnight, and over several thousand years, he points out, such arrivals would have mounted up. Saldanha-Ferro does not claim that every landing was accidental, only that the demographic argument has been pressed too hard: chance arrivals, repeated often enough, could have supplied a founding population after all. His critics respond that a trickle of castaways spread over millennia is not the same as a group large enough to survive at a single moment. The two positions are, I would suggest, less opposed than their proponents imagine, since deliberate and accidental crossings were probably both taking place.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Direct evidence is scarce, since the vessels, probably of bamboo or lashed logs, have long since rotted. Archaeologists have therefore looked for indirect signs of seafaring skill. Teuila Afamasaga, a zooarchaeologist at the Pacific Faunal Research Unit, has studied fish remains from a cave on Timor, where the bones of tuna and other species that live far from the coast appear in layers dated to around 42,000 years ago, alongside hooks carved from shell. Catching such fish, she argues, would have required seaworthy craft and detailed knowledge of the open ocean. The evidence is persuasive as far as it goes, but it should be noted that the Timor deposits are several thousand years younger than the earliest occupation of Sahul. They show that maritime expertise existed in the region; they cannot show that it existed when the first crossings were made.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In one experiment, a team led by the archaeologist Fionnuala Ó Ceallacháin built a bamboo raft using only stone tools of the kind found at Pleistocene sites and, with a crew of six, paddled it from Timor into the open sea, covering more than fifty kilometres before rough weather forced them to abandon the attempt. Ó Ceallacháin regards the voyage as proof that such craft were capable of the crossing. That is a stronger conclusion than the experiment supports. A modern crew equipped with weather forecasts, navigational training and a support vessel is not a reliable guide to what was possible for people 50,000 years ago, and an attempt that ended prematurely demonstrates the difficulty of the passage at least as much as its feasibility.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The case for deliberate voyaging is, on balance, the stronger one, but it rests more on the implausibility of the alternatives than on direct proof. The settlement of Sahul ought nonetheless to change how early modern humans are imagined. A population that could build vessels, transport enough people to found a viable community and act on the expectation of land beyond the horizon was capable of planning and cooperation on a considerable scale. It would be a mistake, though, to recast the first Australians as heroic explorers in a modern mould. They were probably moving in modest steps, island by island, over many generations, each crossing only slightly more ambitious than the last.

topic: the Pacific coastal ('kelp highway') route versus the inland ice-free corridor as the path of the first people into the Americas: drowned shorelines, deglaciation dating, sediment DNA and the speed of southward dispersal
title: The Road by the Sea
subtitle: The first Americans may have reached the continent's interior not by walking between glaciers but by following the shoreline

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the peopling of the Americas was explained by a single, tidy story. Around 13,000 years ago, hunters carrying distinctive fluted spear points walked south from Alaska through a narrow gap that had opened between the two great ice sheets covering Canada, and from there spread across both continents within a few centuries. This 'ice-free corridor' model had the virtue of simplicity, but two discoveries undermined it. First, excavations at a waterlogged site in southern Chile produced convincing evidence of human occupation at least 14,500 years ago, long before the corridor is supposed to have been passable. Second, studies of pollen and animal remains suggested that, even after the ice had parted, the corridor remained a barren landscape of meltwater lakes and bare gravel, offering neither game nor firewood for perhaps a thousand years.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Attention therefore shifted west, to the Pacific coast. According to what has become known as the kelp highway hypothesis, the first Americans travelled not overland but along the shoreline, probably in boats, exploiting the dense forests of giant seaweed that fringe the northern Pacific. Marisol Chacaltana, a coastal archaeologist at the Institute of Littoral Studies, has been among its most energetic advocates. Kelp forests, she points out, support an extraordinary concentration of food: fish, shellfish, sea urchins, seals and seabirds. Because this ecosystem stretched more or less continuously from Japan to Baja California, people already skilled at harvesting it in north-east Asia could have moved thousands of kilometres without needing to learn a new way of life. In her view, the coast offered not merely an alternative route but an easier one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The obvious difficulty is that the evidence, if it exists, lies underwater. Since the end of the ice age, the sea has risen by more than a hundred metres, drowning the shorelines along which the earliest migrants would have travelled. Chacaltana argues that the scarcity of early coastal sites is therefore exactly what the hypothesis predicts. This is true, but it is also a little too convenient. A theory that explains away the absence of its own evidence deserves to be treated with caution until that evidence begins to appear, and its supporters have sometimes been slow to acknowledge as much. Encouragingly, sonar mapping of the continental shelf off British Columbia has begun to identify drowned river channels and former lake shores where submerged sites might yet be found.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second objection was that the coast itself had been buried under glaciers flowing into the sea. Here the evidence has moved decisively in the hypothesis's favour. Henrik Harjunpää, a glacial geologist at the Northern Quaternary Laboratory, has dated boulders left behind by retreating ice along the coasts of south-east Alaska and British Columbia, measuring the tiny quantities of rare isotopes that accumulate in rock once it is exposed to cosmic rays. His results indicate that substantial stretches of shoreline were free of ice by around 17,000 years ago, and that some offshore islands had served as refuges for bears and other mammals throughout the coldest period. If animals could survive there, Harjunpää argues, so could people.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the corridor have not given up. Lucas Wojtaszczyk, who analyses ancient DNA preserved in lake sediments at the Centre for Environmental Genomics, has found traces of grasses, bison and mammoth in the corridor dating from about 12,600 years ago. He accepts that this is too late for the first arrivals, but maintains that the corridor became an important route shortly afterwards, especially for groups who hunted large animals on the plains. This seems entirely reasonable. Much of the debate has been framed as a contest in which only one route can win, yet there is no reason why different groups should not have used different paths at different times.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Genetics has added a further dimension. Studies of ancient and modern genomes suggest that, soon after entering the continent, the founding population split into northern and southern branches, and that the southern branch reached South America with remarkable speed. Sigrún Hallbjörnsdóttir, a population geneticist at the Reykjanes Institute of Human Evolution, considers such rapid movement much easier to explain along a coast than through the interior, where every river valley and mountain range would have demanded new skills. However, she is careful to note that DNA can reveal when populations separated and how quickly they spread, but not the path they took. Archaeologists, in other words, cannot expect geneticists to settle the question for them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: On balance, the coastal route now offers the most convincing explanation for the earliest entry into the Americas. Yet the image of a 'highway' is misleading. It suggests a smooth and rapid journey along an unbroken shoreline, when the reality must have involved glaciers, estuaries and exposed headlands that could be passed only with difficulty. The first migrants probably advanced in fits and starts, settling for generations in favourable places before moving on. Until underwater archaeology receives the investment it requires, however, the hypothesis will remain more plausible than proven.

topic: the Bantu expansion across sub-Saharan Africa: reconstructed vocabulary and the role of iron, early- versus late-split routes, the rainforest corridor, genetic admixture with foragers
title: Words, Genes and Forests
subtitle: How linguists, geneticists and ecologists are rewriting the story of one of Africa's great population movements

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: More than five hundred closely related languages, collectively known as Bantu, are spoken today across an immense area stretching from Cameroon in the west to Kenya in the east and South Africa in the south. Their similarity is unmistakable: words for 'person', 'water' or 'three' are often recognisably alike in languages whose speakers live thousands of kilometres apart. Linguists have long agreed that this family must have spread from a homeland near the present border of Nigeria and Cameroon within the last five thousand years. The movement that carried it across roughly half a continent was one of the most consequential population events of the past few millennia, and it is curious that it remains far less familiar to the general public than the settlement of the Pacific or the spread of farming into Europe.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the expansion was explained in terms of technological superiority. Bantu-speaking farmers, equipped with iron tools, were thought to have cleared forest and cultivated land more efficiently than anyone before them, multiplying rapidly and pushing older populations aside. That interpretation has been substantially revised. Kalombo Mwanangombe, a historical linguist at the Centre for Comparative African Languages, has reconstructed the vocabulary of the ancestral language by comparing words that survive across the family. The reconstructed lexicon includes terms for yams, oil palms, goats, fish traps and pottery, but no shared vocabulary for smelting or forging metal. Mwanangombe concludes that the expansion was well under way before iron came into use, and that metallurgy was adopted later and independently by different branches. His argument is convincing, and it removes iron from the role of prime mover that it occupied for so long.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The routes taken by the migrants have proved harder to establish. Linguists have debated whether the eastern languages, now spoken from Uganda to Mozambique, branched off early and travelled around the northern edge of the equatorial rainforest, or whether they emerged much later from groups that had already passed through the forest. A team led by Ottoline Verbrugghen at the Scheldt Laboratory for Language Evolution applied methods borrowed from evolutionary biology to several hundred Bantu languages and produced family trees that favour the second scenario. Such analyses are impressive, but their results are only as reliable as the data fed into them. Neighbouring languages borrow words from one another continually, and where borrowing is mistaken for shared descent, the resulting trees can mislead with considerable confidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The rainforest itself was long regarded as a formidable obstacle to farmers whose crops required abundant sunlight. Ifeoluwa Adegbesan, a palynologist at the Institute of Tropical Palaeoecology, has examined pollen preserved in lake sediments from the western Congo basin. Her cores show that, around 2,500 years ago, a drier climate caused the forest to retreat and allowed savanna grasses to spread along a north-south corridor through its heart. Adegbesan suggests that this opening enabled farming communities to move south far more rapidly than before. The argument is attractive, yet it may attribute too much to climate. Archaeological sites show that pottery-using communities had already been living within the forest for several centuries before the dry phase began, which suggests that the environmental change accelerated a movement that was already in progress rather than setting it in motion.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Genetic research has resolved one long-standing question. It was once possible to argue that Bantu languages had spread largely through adoption, with local populations taking up a prestigious new language without any significant movement of people. Analyses directed by Jean-Baptiste Mabiala-Koffi at the Congo Basin Genome Initiative indicate otherwise: Bantu-speaking populations across central, eastern and southern Africa share a substantial component of ancestry traceable to west-central Africa. At the same time, the proportion of ancestry derived from earlier hunter-gatherer populations increases with distance from the homeland, and much of it entered through the maternal line. The migrants, in other words, did not simply replace those they encountered; over many generations they married into local communities.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This finding has encouraged a more nuanced view of relations between farmers and foragers. The traditional image of an advancing frontier sweeping all before it now looks too crude. In parts of the central African forest, hunter-gatherer communities adopted the languages of their farming neighbours while retaining a distinct way of life, and the two groups have exchanged honey, game, labour and crops for centuries. Such relationships were not always equal, and in some regions farmers came to dominate the exchange, but they were rarely as one-sided as older accounts implied. Indeed, it is likely that the migrants depended heavily on local knowledge of forest plants and animals during the early stages of settlement.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges is a picture far removed from the image of a single wave rolling southwards. The expansion seems to have unfolded over roughly three thousand years, in a series of movements punctuated by long pauses, shaped by climate, local negotiation and the choices of individual communities. It also offers a lesson for the study of other dispersals: neither linguistics nor genetics nor archaeology could have produced this account on its own. The greatest weakness remains archaeological. Central Africa is among the least excavated regions on earth, and until that changes, many of the dates on which the debate depends will continue to rest on a handful of sites.

topic: the settlement of Madagascar by Austronesian and African populations: early cut-marked bones, Malagasy's Bornean linguistic links, the small founding population, direct versus coastal voyaging routes and later admixture
title: An Island Between Two Oceans
subtitle: Why do the people of an island off the African coast speak a language from Borneo?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Madagascar, the fourth-largest island in the world, lies only about four hundred kilometres off the coast of Mozambique, yet its people speak a language whose closest relatives are found not in Africa but on the island of Borneo, more than six thousand kilometres to the east. Malagasy belongs to the Austronesian family, which also includes the languages of Indonesia, the Philippines and the Pacific islands. Equally striking is the genetic make-up of the population: almost every Malagasy carries a mixture of ancestry from Island South-East Asia and from eastern Africa. How a population with roots on opposite sides of the Indian Ocean came to occupy one of the last large landmasses settled by humans is among the most intriguing puzzles in the study of migration.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first question is when people arrived. For many years, the accepted answer was that the island was uninhabited until roughly 1,500 years ago. That consensus was disturbed when Henrique Nhantumbo, an archaeologist at the Mozambique Channel Research Centre, re-examined animal bones held in museum collections and reported cut marks on the remains of extinct giant birds that appeared to be several thousand years older. If correct, his findings would place the first visitors on the island long before any Austronesian could have arrived. The claim deserves to be taken seriously, but it has not yet been matched by stone tools, hearths or other traces of occupation, and marks on bone can be produced by trampling or by scavenging animals. At most, these early visits seem to have been brief, perhaps by foragers who never established a permanent presence.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Linguistic evidence offers a clearer picture of the Asian contribution. Voahangy Ravelonjanahary, a historical linguist at the Institute of Indian Ocean Languages, has shown that Malagasy shares a particularly large stock of vocabulary with Ma'anyan, a language spoken along a river in southern Borneo. Yet Malagasy also contains words borrowed from Malay and Javanese, especially terms connected with navigation and trade. Ravelonjanahary concludes that the settlers were not a single group from one river valley but a mixed company assembled through the maritime trading networks of the region, in which Malay sailors played a leading role. Her interpretation is persuasive, and it helps to explain why voyages of this length should have been undertaken at all: they were an extension of commerce, not a leap into the unknown.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Genetic research has added striking detail. A team led by Tsiry Andrianjafy at the Antananarivo Centre for Human Genomics has modelled the history of the Asian lineages found in present-day Malagasy and estimates that they may descend from as few as thirty women. Andrianjafy acknowledges that the figure is uncertain, but argues that a founding group of this size points to a small number of voyages rather than a sustained colonisation. The estimate has been widely publicised, and it is easy to see why. Nevertheless, it should not be read as a head count of the original settlers. Genetic models of this kind describe the women whose lineages happened to survive, and many others may have arrived without leaving descendants in the modern population.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The route of these voyages remains disputed. One possibility is that sailors crossed the open Indian Ocean directly, carried by the equatorial current and the seasonal monsoon winds. Dwi Purnomosidi, a maritime historian at the Archipelago Seafaring Archive, rejects this as unnecessarily heroic. He points to the trading ports that already linked South-East Asia with India, Arabia and the East African coast, and suggests that the ancestors of the Malagasy reached the island in stages, along the rim of the ocean. A coastal route, he argues, might also explain the presence of Asian crops such as bananas and rice on the African mainland. Of the two views, his is probably the more realistic, although it is fair to say that the evidence for neither is conclusive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The African side of the story has received less attention, and that imbalance is unfortunate. Bantu-speaking communities from the mainland contributed roughly half of the island's ancestry, as well as cattle, many agricultural practices and a substantial part of the Malagasy vocabulary for animals. Andrianjafy's data suggest that African and Asian groups began to mix around a thousand years ago, on the island itself, rather than arriving already combined. This implies that, for some time, Madagascar was home to distinct communities who later merged, a process that ancient DNA, if it can be recovered from the island's humid soils, may one day reveal in detail.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Madagascar is sometimes presented as a curiosity, an exception to the general pattern of human dispersal. In fact, it illustrates a theme common to many migrations: that movement across great distances is usually made possible by existing networks of exchange, rather than by isolated acts of daring. Seen in this light, the peopling of Madagascar belongs less to the history of exploration than to the history of trade, and the sailors who reached it were probably following routes that merchants had used for generations. What makes the island unusual is not the length of the voyages but the clarity with which language, genes and archaeology together preserve the memory of them.
