topic: the human occupation of the Tibetan Plateau: Denisovans at high altitude, seasonal forays by modern hunters, barley farming and year-round settlement, and the Denisovan-derived EPAS1 adaptation to low oxygen
title: Settlers of the Roof of the World
subtitle: When did people first make their homes on the Tibetan Plateau, and what does it mean to live somewhere so high?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest elevated region on earth. Its average altitude exceeds 4,000 metres, and at that height each breath contains only around sixty per cent of the oxygen available at sea level. Winters are long and bitterly cold, the growing season is short, and firewood is scarce over much of the surface. For these reasons, the plateau was long assumed to have been one of the last habitable regions to be occupied, settled only after the invention of farming made permanent residence possible. Over the past two decades, however, a series of discoveries has pushed the human story on the plateau far deeper into the past, and has raised the question of what, exactly, counts as living there.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest evidence does not come from our own species at all. A jawbone recovered from a limestone cave at about 3,300 metres on the north-eastern margin of the plateau has been identified, from the proteins preserved in its teeth, as belonging to a Denisovan, a member of an archaic human group known otherwise mainly from fragments found in Siberia. The jaw is at least 160,000 years old. Sediments from the same cave contain Denisovan DNA in layers that are far younger, suggesting that these people used the site repeatedly over a long period. Ewa Laszkiewicz, who led the sediment analysis at the Carpathian Institute of Molecular Archaeology, argues that Denisovans were therefore at least partly adapted to the cold and low-oxygen conditions of high altitude. This is a reasonable inference, although 3,300 metres is a modest elevation by the standards of the plateau, and the cave lies close to lower valleys into which its occupants could have retreated in winter.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Modern humans appear much later. At a site at about 4,600 metres in the central plateau, archaeologists have recovered several thousand stone artefacts, including large blades, dating to between 30,000 and 40,000 years ago. No hearths or animal bones have been found there, and Pema Yangzom, an archaeologist at the Highland Heritage Institute who has worked at the site, believes that it was probably a place to which hunting parties returned to make tools from good-quality local stone. In her view, the site shows that people were capable of reaching very high altitudes long before farming, but not that they stayed. The distinction matters, because occupation by short-term visitors and year-round residence are quite different achievements.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: On the question of permanent settlement, Rinchen Wangmo, an archaeobotanist at the Lhasa Valley Research Station, has been the most influential voice. From charred plant remains, she has shown that barley, a crop originally domesticated in south-west Asia, appeared on the plateau around 3,600 years ago. Unlike millet, the crop grown by earlier farmers in the lower valleys to the east, barley tolerates frost and can ripen in a short summer, and it allowed farming communities to establish villages above 3,000 metres for the first time. Wangmo argues that, combined with the herding of yak and sheep, barley cultivation was the decisive development that made year-round life on the high plateau possible. Her account is well supported, but it may underestimate the foragers who preceded the farmers. Footprints and handprints preserved in hardened deposits around hot springs at over 4,000 metres suggest that some groups may have wintered at sites where warm water offered shelter from the worst of the cold.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Genetics has added an unexpected twist. Most Tibetans carry a version of a gene called EPAS1 that helps the body respond to low oxygen without overproducing red blood cells, a reaction that thickens the blood and causes illness in many lowland visitors. Haruki Sonobe, a geneticist at the Kansai Centre for Evolutionary Medicine, has shown that this variant closely matches a sequence found in the Denisovan genome, and was probably acquired when the ancestors of Tibetans interbred with Denisovans. He estimates that the variant spread rapidly through the population within roughly the last ten thousand years. Andean highlanders, by contrast, have adapted to similar altitudes through different genetic changes, which suggests that there is more than one biological solution to life in thin air.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that genetic adaptation was required for early occupation. Anselm Kreutzträger, a physiologist at the Alpine Research Institute for Human Performance, points out that lowlanders acclimatise substantially within weeks, and that small groups of hunters could have made seasonal journeys to high altitude without any inherited advantage. In his view, genetic adaptation was a consequence of permanent settlement rather than a precondition for it. The argument is persuasive, and it shifts attention from biology back to culture: clothing, shelter and knowledge of the landscape.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges is not a single moment of colonisation but a long sequence of episodes: archaic humans on the plateau's edge, seasonal forays by modern hunters, perhaps winter camps at hot springs, and finally villages supported by barley and livestock. The high pastures, passes and springs were almost certainly known and used by many generations of visitors long before anyone built a permanent house among them. Asking when the plateau was first settled is therefore less helpful than asking what kinds of occupation were possible at different times, and why.

topic: the dual-structure model of Japanese population history: Jomon foragers and Yayoi rice-farming migrants from the Korean peninsula, revised radiocarbon chronology, a third Kofun-period ancestry component and Jomon responses to farming
title: Two Peoples, One Archipelago
subtitle: New dates and ancient genomes are complicating a long-established account of how the population of Japan was formed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the past century, the population history of Japan has been told through a model of elegant simplicity. According to the so-called dual-structure hypothesis, the people of the modern archipelago descend from two sources. The first were the Jomon, hunter-gatherers who had lived on the islands for more than fifteen thousand years and who produced some of the oldest pottery known anywhere in the world. The second were migrants from the Asian mainland who, during what archaeologists call the Yayoi period, brought wet-rice agriculture and metal tools to the southern island of Kyushu and gradually spread north-eastwards. The model explains why the Ainu of the far north and the people of the Ryukyu Islands in the far south, regions the newcomers reached late or not at all, differ in appearance and genetic make-up from the population of the main islands. It has endured, in large part, because it accounts for so much evidence of so many different kinds.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest support for the hypothesis came from skeletons. Sayaka Imaizumi, a physical anthropologist at the Kyushu Institute of Human Remains, has compared hundreds of skulls from burial sites on the northern coast of Kyushu. Individuals from Yayoi-period cemeteries were, on average, several centimetres taller than their Jomon predecessors and had longer, flatter faces. Imaizumi interprets these differences as evidence of large-scale immigration, and has argued that the migrants soon came to outnumber the local population because farming supported much higher birth rates than foraging. Her measurements are not in dispute, but her interpretation deserves a degree of caution. Stature and facial shape respond to diet and to patterns of chewing as well as to ancestry, and a sudden change in the food people ate could account for some of the contrast.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental revision has concerned chronology. Textbooks long placed the beginning of the Yayoi period around 2,400 years ago. Daisuke Kuwabara, of the Laboratory for Archaeological Chronometry, has radiocarbon-dated food residues charred onto the inner surfaces of early Yayoi cooking pots and concluded that rice paddies were already being cultivated in northern Kyushu about 3,000 years ago, roughly five centuries earlier than previously believed. Since the dates for the arrival of farming in eastern Japan changed little, his results imply that agriculture took far longer to spread across the archipelago than had been assumed. This is arguably the most important change to the model in decades. A slow spread over several centuries is difficult to reconcile with the image of incoming farmers rapidly overwhelming the existing population, and much easier to reconcile with a long period of coexistence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Where did the migrants come from, and why did they leave? Eom Seo-yeon, an archaeologist at the Institute of Korean Prehistory, points to striking similarities between early Yayoi sites and settlements of the same date in the southern Korean peninsula, including the layout of rice paddies, the form of stone reaping knives and the design of defensive ditches. She believes the movement took the form of a steady trickle of small groups across the strait over many generations, rather than a single organised migration. Some have connected the departures with a period of cooler climate, others with growing competition for farmland. Both explanations are plausible, but neither has yet been supported by firm evidence, and the motives of the migrants remain largely a matter of speculation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ancient DNA has introduced a further complication. A team led by Tomasz Wrzesniewski at the Baltic Centre for Palaeogenomics has sequenced genomes from Jomon, Yayoi and later burials, and argues that a substantial part of the ancestry of present-day mainland Japanese arrived not in the Yayoi period but several centuries afterwards, during the Kofun period, when large burial mounds were constructed and the first centralised states emerged. On this view, the population was formed from three components rather than two. The finding refines the dual-structure model rather than overturning it, though the number of ancient genomes analysed so far remains small, and conclusions drawn from a few dozen individuals should be regarded as provisional.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Lost in many accounts is the role of the Jomon themselves. They are often portrayed as passive recipients of a superior way of life, yet the evidence suggests otherwise. Many Jomon communities adopted rice cultivation selectively, combining it with fishing, nut gathering and hunting rather than giving up their established economy. In the far north of the main island of Honshu, paddy fields were constructed within a few centuries of their appearance in Kyushu, only to be abandoned when a cooler climate made rice unreliable, after which the inhabitants returned to foraging for several hundred years. The spread of farming, in other words, was neither inevitable nor irreversible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has implications beyond archaeology. Ideas about the origins of the Japanese have long been entangled with questions of national identity, and claims of a single, homogeneous population have sometimes drawn on selective readings of the evidence. What the research actually shows is a population formed through repeated episodes of migration and mixing. The danger now is that a new and equally tidy story, this time with three ingredients instead of two, will harden into orthodoxy before the evidence for it is secure.

topic: the Trypillia mega-sites of prehistoric Ukraine: whether they were cities, population size, the seasonal-gathering hypothesis, assembly houses, house burning and abandonment
title: Cities Without Kings
subtitle: The vast prehistoric settlements of the Ukrainian forest-steppe challenge the familiar story of how urban life began

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s, aerial photographs taken over the farmland of central Ukraine revealed something that archaeologists at first struggled to believe. Arranged in vast concentric ovals, the faint outlines of thousands of burnt houses marked settlements of the Trypillia culture, which had flourished between roughly 4100 and 3600 BC. The largest of them covered more than three square kilometres, making them bigger than any contemporary site in Mesopotamia, the region conventionally credited with inventing the city. Yet for decades these so-called mega-sites received little attention outside eastern Europe, partly because of language barriers and partly, I suspect, because they did not fit the familiar story of how urban life began.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That story, shaped largely by excavations in southern Iraq, holds that cities emerged alongside kings, temples, writing and a sharply stratified society. The Trypillia settlements possess none of these features. There are no palaces, no monumental tombs and no obvious storehouses under elite control; the houses are strikingly similar in size and contents. For some scholars, this absence is sufficient reason to deny the mega-sites urban status altogether and to describe them instead as overgrown villages. Such a conclusion seems to me premature. A definition of the city built on a single region's history is bound to treat any departure from that history as a failure, when it may simply be a different solution to the problem of living together in large numbers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The scale of that problem depends, of course, on how many people actually lived there, and here the evidence is contested. Mykola Ivashchenko, whose team has carried out magnetometer surveys across several sites, has mapped close to three thousand houses at the largest of them. Assuming that most houses stood at the same time, he estimates a population of between ten and fifteen thousand. Critics point out that radiocarbon dates from individual houses span more than a century, raising the possibility that the settlement grew and shifted gradually, with only a fraction of buildings occupied at any one moment. Ivashchenko accepts that some houses were abandoned before others were built, but he argues that the regular layout of the ovals implies a plan conceived and largely realised within a few generations.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical alternative has been proposed by Helen Brokenshire of the Centre for Prehistoric Landscapes. She suggests that the mega-sites were not permanent towns at all but gathering places, filled for some months of the year when dispersed farming communities came together for ritual, exchange and the arrangement of marriages. In support, she notes that pollen cores from nearby lakes show surprisingly modest clearance of woodland, which seems inconsistent with year-round cultivation by many thousands of people. The hypothesis is ingenious, but it struggles to explain why households would invest in substantial two-storey clay buildings, complete with ovens and storage vessels, merely for seasonal use. Moreover, soil chemistry studies have found the kind of dense domestic waste that normally accumulates only through continuous occupation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the mega-sites were indeed home to thousands of people, the question of how decisions were made becomes pressing. Lars Tjernagel, of the Institute for Settlement Archaeology in Trondheim, has focused on a distinctive category of building known as the assembly house: structures considerably larger than ordinary dwellings, spaced at intervals around the ovals and often containing few domestic finds. Tjernagel interprets them as meeting halls where representatives of neighbourhoods gathered, arguing that the settlements were governed from the bottom up through a nested system of councils rather than by a ruling family. The interpretation is attractive and fits the uniformity of the housing, although it should be remembered that political arrangements leave only indirect traces, and a meeting hall could equally have served a religious purpose.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most puzzling aspect of the Trypillia record is the fate of the houses themselves. Almost every dwelling appears to have been burned, and experiments in which replica houses were set alight suggest that the fires reached temperatures which could only have been achieved deliberately, by packing the buildings with fuel. Explanations range from warfare to the ritual 'killing' of a house at the end of its owners' lives. None has yet commanded general agreement, and it would be unwise to assume that a single motive applied across every site and century.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What does seem clear is that the experiment did not last. Within two or three centuries the largest settlements were abandoned, and their populations dispersed into smaller villages. Adewale Odunlami, who studies low-density urbanism in a comparative framework, sees in this decline evidence that consensus-based government becomes increasingly fragile as numbers grow, since disputes multiply faster than the institutions designed to resolve them. It is a plausible argument, though perhaps too neat: soil exhaustion and climatic change may have played as large a part. Nevertheless, Odunlami is surely right that the mega-sites deserve a central place in any history of urbanism. They show that people could live together at an unprecedented scale without first submitting to kings, even if the arrangement proved, in the end, to be temporary.

title: The Faceless Metropolis
subtitle: Who ruled Teotihuacan, the greatest city of the ancient Americas, remains one of archaeology's most stubborn puzzles

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the Aztecs came upon the ruins of Teotihuacan in the fourteenth century, the city had been deserted for some seven hundred years, yet its scale so impressed them that they called it the place where the gods were born. At its height, around AD 400, it covered roughly twenty square kilometres of the Basin of Mexico and housed perhaps a hundred thousand people. Its core was laid out along a broad ceremonial way, now known as the Avenue of the Dead, flanked by two colossal pyramids, and the entire grid followed a single orientation to which even the course of a river was made to conform. Planning on this scale implies an authority capable of commanding enormous labour. What is remarkable is how difficult it has proved to identify that authority.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In most early Mesoamerican states, rulers ensured that they would not be forgotten, commissioning stone monuments that proclaimed their names, ancestry and victories. Teotihuacan offers nothing comparable. Its murals depict processions of richly dressed figures, but these are anonymous, often masked, and repeated in identical rows, as if the office mattered more than the individual. No royal tomb has been securely identified, and no inscription records the name of a ruler. For Elena Ocaranza of the Institute of Highland Archaeology, this silence is itself the evidence. She argues that the city was governed by a council drawn from its leading lineages, which deliberately suppressed displays of personal glory in order to preserve a balance of power among them. To my mind, the argument is stronger than a mere appeal to absence, since the pattern holds across thousands of images; it is hard to believe that a dynasty would so thoroughly have refused to commemorate itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this picture. Søren Berthelsen, who has worked for many years on the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, points to the more than two hundred individuals sacrificed and buried beneath that monument at its dedication in the early third century. Many were young men equipped as warriors and adorned with necklaces of imitation human jaws. Such a spectacle, Berthelsen contends, is the work of a ruler dramatising his power, not of a council seeking consensus. He also notes that, some generations later, the temple's facade was partly hidden behind a new platform and its sculptures defaced. In his view, the city experimented with one-man rule and then decisively turned against it. The interpretation has the merit of reconciling both bodies of evidence, although it rests on a single monument, and the defacement could have had religious rather than political motives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The everyday fabric of the city may say more about its government than its monuments do. Most Teotihuacanos lived not in individual houses but in some two thousand walled apartment compounds, each accommodating between sixty and a hundred people organised into several households with shared courtyards and shrines. Kenji Kiyonaga, who has compared floor areas, building materials and grave goods across more than forty excavated compounds, finds that differences in living standards were real but modest; even the poorer compounds had plastered floors and drainage. He argues that a city which housed its ordinary inhabitants this well is unlikely to have been run for the benefit of a narrow elite. This seems a fair inference, though it should not be pressed too far, since comfortable housing can equally be a means by which rulers secure the loyalty of their subjects.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The compounds also reveal the city's diversity. Analysis of strontium and oxygen isotopes in tooth enamel, which preserve a chemical signature of the place where a person grew up, shows that a substantial proportion of residents in some districts were born elsewhere. One neighbourhood on the western edge was home to people from the Oaxaca valley, who for centuries continued to bury their dead according to their own customs and to make their own style of pottery. A city that accommodated such communities without forcing them to assimilate was arguably held together less by coercion than by negotiated arrangements between groups.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The end of Teotihuacan has been read in the same light. Around AD 550, the buildings along the Avenue of the Dead were burned and their sculptures smashed. Agata Kasprowicz, who has catalogued the destruction in detail, observes that the fires were concentrated on the ceremonial centre and on elite residences, while most ordinary compounds were left largely untouched. She concludes that the city was not overrun by outsiders, as was once assumed, but brought down by its own inhabitants in a revolt against those who governed them. The selective pattern of burning makes this the most convincing explanation yet offered, but whether the uprising was a cause of decline or merely a symptom of it, following decades of drought and failing harvests, remains unresolved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is less a single answer than a warning about the assumptions that archaeologists bring to the past. Because the best-known early cities were ruled by kings, it has been tempting to treat monarchy as the natural form of urban government and every alternative as an anomaly requiring special explanation. Teotihuacan suggests that large populations could be organised through collective institutions, which might under pressure give way to more autocratic forms, and later recover.

topic: Angkor as a low-density city revealed by lidar: the extent of the settlement, the purpose of the reservoirs and competing explanations of its abandonment
title: The Forest That Hid a City
subtitle: Airborne laser scanning has transformed what is known about Angkor, and reopened the question of why it was abandoned

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century after European visitors publicised its temples, Angkor was understood primarily as a religious complex: a cluster of magnificent stone monuments, Angkor Wat foremost among them, set in the forests of northern Cambodia. The people who had built and served those temples were largely invisible, because their homes, made of timber and thatch, had long since rotted away. Scholars knew from inscriptions that the Khmer capital had once supported a substantial population, but estimates varied enormously, and the physical extent of the settlement was a matter of guesswork.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That situation changed dramatically with the arrival of lidar, a technique in which an aircraft fires millions of laser pulses at the ground and records the time each takes to return. Because some pulses pass through gaps in the vegetation, the data can be processed to strip away the forest canopy and expose subtle variations in the land surface beneath. Surveys carried out over the past fifteen years by a team led by Dara Sovannara have revealed an extraordinary landscape: a dense grid of earthen embankments, roads, small ponds and raised mounds on which houses once stood, extending far beyond the temple enclosures. Sovannara argues that Angkor was not a ceremonial centre ringed by scattered villages but a single urban complex covering more than a thousand square kilometres, which at its height in the twelfth century may have housed several hundred thousand people. It is difficult to overstate the significance of these findings; few technologies have altered our picture of an ancient society so rapidly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The city revealed by lidar, however, looks quite unlike the compact walled towns of medieval Europe. Its population was spread thinly across a landscape in which homes, rice fields, fish ponds and orchards were interwoven, an arrangement that archaeologists now describe as low-density urbanism. Holding this sprawling settlement together was an immense network of water infrastructure: canals, dykes and vast rectangular reservoirs known as barays, the largest of which measures eight kilometres by two. How this network functioned has long been disputed. An earlier generation of scholars regarded the barays as the heart of a centrally managed irrigation system that allowed several rice harvests a year. Mathilde Rouvillois, a historian of Khmer religion, rejects that view, pointing out that the reservoirs held too little water to irrigate more than a fraction of the surrounding fields, and that inscriptions describe them chiefly as earthly representations of the oceans encircling the mythical Mount Meru. In her account, they were monuments first and practical works only incidentally.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Rouvillois is right to challenge the image of Angkor as a 'hydraulic state' whose kings derived their power from controlling water. Yet her argument underestimates the evidence, also produced by lidar, of channels that carried water from the barays to the fields and of modifications made over centuries to manage flooding. It seems more reasonable to conclude that the reservoirs served several purposes at once, and that religious symbolism and practical engineering were not, for the Khmer, separate categories.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The importance of the network becomes clearest when one considers the city's decline. Traditional histories attributed the abandonment of Angkor to the sack of the city by the neighbouring kingdom of Ayutthaya in 1431. Owen Tregenza, a geoarchaeologist, considers this explanation insufficient. Tree-ring records from the region show that the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries were marked by decades-long droughts interrupted by exceptionally intense monsoons. Tregenza's excavations of canal beds reveal thick layers of sand deposited by floods, as well as places where embankments were breached and never repaired. He argues that the water system, already overstretched and silting up, was pushed beyond its limits, and that because its components were interdependent, a failure in one place could cascade through the entire network.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all specialists accept that Angkor collapsed at all. Lakshmi Sheshadri, an economic historian, notes that the royal court moved south towards the region of present-day Phnom Penh, where it could profit from expanding maritime trade with China. For her, the abandonment of Angkor was a gradual reorientation of the Khmer state rather than a catastrophe, and many ordinary inhabitants probably remained in the area for generations. This is a valuable corrective, and the word 'collapse' does conjure up an image of sudden disaster that the evidence scarcely supports. Even so, a move that coincided with the breakdown of the city's infrastructure can hardly be explained by commercial opportunity alone.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It has become fashionable to present Angkor as a warning to the sprawling cities of today, which likewise depend on vast, interconnected infrastructure. The comparison has some value, but it should be drawn with care. Angkor's inhabitants lacked the engineering knowledge and the climate forecasts now available, and their fate tells us less about the inevitability of urban decline than about the dangers of building systems that cannot easily be adapted when conditions change.

topic: Neolithic Çatalhöyük: whether it was a city, egalitarianism versus ritual prestige in 'history houses', the social reasons for aggregation and its costs, and late changes before the move to the West Mound
title: The Town Without Streets
subtitle: Nine thousand years ago thousands of people lived side by side on the Anatolian plain. Archaeologists still disagree about what kind of place they had created

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some nine thousand years ago, on the Konya plain in central Anatolia, several thousand people lived in a settlement whose layout would baffle a modern visitor. Çatalhöyük had no streets. Its rectangular mud-brick houses were built wall against wall, and residents moved across the rooftops, entering their homes by ladder through an opening in the ceiling. Occupied for well over a thousand years, from roughly 7100 to 6000 BCE, the site covers some thirteen hectares, and estimates of its population at its height range from three thousand to eight thousand. When excavations first revealed its scale in the 1960s, it was hailed as the world's earliest city. That description has proved remarkably durable, but it is, in my view, more misleading than illuminating, because it encourages us to look for features that were never there.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most conspicuous absence is that of any building that might have housed a ruler or a central institution. There is no palace, no temple precinct and no granary large enough to have served the community as a whole. The houses themselves are strikingly similar in size and layout. For the archaeologist Anders Gjerdrum, this uniformity is the key to the settlement. He argues that Çatalhöyük was organised on deliberately egalitarian lines, and he points to chemical analyses of skeletons which indicate that men and women ate much the same food, as well as to patterns of bone wear suggesting that both sexes performed similar daily labour. Gjerdrum's interpretation has been enormously influential, and the evidence he cites is real. Nevertheless, equality of diet and workload is not the same as equality of standing, and it would be rash to conclude that the community lacked hierarchy of any kind.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That point is developed by Selin Sorgucu, whose work focuses on a small number of buildings that were rebuilt again and again on precisely the same footprint. These so-called history houses contain far more burials beneath their floors than ordinary dwellings — in one case over sixty individuals — together with plastered bull horns and painted walls. Sorgucu contends that the households associated with them did not accumulate more goods than their neighbours but did accumulate something else: ritual authority, derived from their long connection with the ancestors buried in them. This seems to me a more persuasive reading than either strict equality or conventional hierarchy, since it recognises that prestige in early societies need not have taken a material form.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further question is why so many people chose to live together at all. Classic accounts of urban origins assume that cities grew from agricultural surplus and long-distance trade, which supported specialist craftsmen and administrators. Çatalhöyük fits that model poorly. Each house seems to have stored its own grain, butchered its own animals and worked its own obsidian, the volcanic glass used for blades, and there is little sign of districts devoted to particular crafts. Marta Vodanović, a bioarchaeologist, proposes that the attraction was primarily social: shared ceremonies, marriage alliances and the support of extended kin. Yet she is equally clear that the arrangement came at a price. Her studies of the skeletal remains reveal high rates of infection, consistent with crowded and unsanitary living, and a surprising number of healed head wounds, many of them on the back of the skull, which she interprets as evidence of conflict within the community rather than attack from outside.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Vodanović's findings are a useful corrective to the image of Çatalhöyük as a peaceful idyll, which has become popular in some writing about the site. They do not, however, undermine the broader conclusion that a large population could live together for centuries without anything resembling a state. Whatever tensions existed were evidently managed, since the settlement was not abandoned in the face of them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The later centuries of occupation tell a different story. Houses began to be built further apart, with open spaces between them, and the variation in their size increased. Imported materials became more common, and the elaborate wall paintings of earlier levels largely disappeared. Ibrahim Ouattara, who has studied these upper layers, sees in them the gradual weakening of the communal bonds that had held the settlement together, as individual households turned increasingly towards their own economic interests and towards exchange with distant partners. Around 6000 BCE, the population shifted to a new mound on the opposite bank of the river, and the original site was left to decay. Ouattara believes that environmental change played at most a minor role in this move, although others consider drier conditions a likely contributor.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should Çatalhöyük be called? Terms such as "mega-village" or "proto-town" have been suggested, and although none is entirely satisfactory, each is preferable to "city", which implies a degree of economic specialisation and political centralisation that the site simply does not display. The more important lesson, perhaps, is that the path from village to city was not a single road. Çatalhöyük demonstrates that dense settlement could be achieved and sustained by means quite different from those of later urban centres, and that it could also, in time, come apart.

topic: governance and urban planning in the Indus cities: standardised bricks and drains, the missing palaces, rival theories of central state versus councils, neighbourhood management of drainage, and gradual decline
title: Bricks, Drains and Silence
subtitle: The cities of the Indus valley were planned with astonishing consistency, yet they have left no trace of the people who ran them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Around 2500 BCE, on the floodplain of the Indus river in what is now Pakistan, the city of Mohenjo-daro was home to perhaps forty thousand people. Its streets ran roughly north–south and east–west, its houses were built of baked brick, and hundreds of wells supplied fresh water to individual households and public spaces. Yet what is most striking about the Indus cities is not their size, which was matched by several centres elsewhere, but their regularity. Bricks at Mohenjo-daro, at Harappa several hundred kilometres upstream and at dozens of smaller settlements were made in the same proportions, with a thickness, width and length in the ratio of one to two to four. How such uniformity was achieved, and by whom, remains the central puzzle of Indus archaeology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The answer once seemed obvious. Uniformity on this scale, it was assumed, could only have been imposed by a powerful central authority, and early excavators duly christened a small carved figure of a bearded man the "priest-king", although nothing about the statue itself identified him as either. The difficulty is that the expected evidence of such rulers has never appeared. Unlike contemporary Mesopotamian cities, with their palaces, royal tombs and inscriptions celebrating military victories, the Indus settlements have yielded no building that can confidently be called a palace, no lavish burials and no images of kings. Dr Rasa Brazauskienė maintains that a centralised state existed nonetheless. In her view, Indus rulers simply chose to express their power through control of administrative tools, such as the standardised weights and the carved stone seals found across the region, rather than through monuments. The argument is ingenious, but an argument from absence cuts both ways: the lack of palaces can be explained away, but it can equally be taken at face value.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Taking it at face value is the approach of Professor Juhani Saarikoski, who suggests that the cities were governed by councils drawn from leading merchant and craft families. Uniform bricks and weights, he argues, need not reflect decrees issued from above; they could have spread through networks of builders and traders who found common standards convenient, in much the same way that shared conventions emerge in any large trading community. The seals, which often bear animal motifs, may have identified the corporate groups to which their owners belonged. Saarikoski's model has the merit of fitting what has been found rather than what has not, but it should be acknowledged that direct evidence for councils of any kind is thin.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More revealing, perhaps, is the drainage system. Most houses at Mohenjo-daro had a bathing platform and many had toilets, connected by sloping channels to covered brick drains running along the streets. At intervals the drains were fitted with openings and small pits where solid waste could collect, an arrangement that would have worked only if someone removed that waste regularly. Dr Lindiwe Hlatshwayo, who has surveyed long stretches of the network, has found that its quality varies considerably from one district to another: some sections were carefully laid and well maintained, while others were patched and poorly aligned. She concludes that drains were the responsibility of individual neighbourhoods rather than of a single civic authority. To my mind, this is the most valuable evidence of all, precisely because it concerns everyday practice rather than the grand display that archaeologists have been searching for in vain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: On the raised mound at the western edge of Mohenjo-daro stands the structure known as the Great Bath, a rectangular tank sealed with a layer of bitumen to keep it watertight and reached by steps at either end. It is widely believed to have been used for rituals of purification, and some have seen it as proof of a dominant priesthood. That conclusion goes further than the evidence allows. A bath designed for communal ceremonies implies shared religious practice; it does not by itself imply a ruler.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: From around 1900 BCE the Indus cities gradually emptied. The old idea that they were destroyed by invaders has been abandoned, since there is no sign of widespread violence. Dr Kaveh Eskandari attributes the decline instead to a weakening of the summer monsoon and to shifts in the courses of rivers, which would have undermined the farming on which the cities depended. In the final phases of occupation, however, the archaeological record shows that standards were already slipping: old bricks were reused, drains were left blocked and large houses were subdivided into smaller units. These signs suggest that the institutions which had sustained urban life were weakening at the same time as the environment was changing, and it is unlikely that either factor alone tells the whole story.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Indus cities thus present a challenge to the familiar assumption that complex urban life requires visible kings. It would be unwise to equate a lack of display with a lack of power, since authority can take many forms. Nevertheless, after a century of excavation, the burden of proof surely lies with those who insist that a hidden state must have existed, not with those who accept that the Indus people may have organised themselves differently.

topic: Great Zimbabwe: the legacy of colonial denial, re-dating of the hill and valley zones, gold trade versus cattle as the basis of wealth, the purpose of the stone walls, and dispersal rather than collapse
title: Walls of Granite, Questions of Power
subtitle: Freed at last from arguments about who built it, Great Zimbabwe is now the subject of a richer debate about how it worked

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a granite plateau in the south of present-day Zimbabwe stand the remains of the largest pre-colonial stone settlement in sub-Saharan Africa. Between roughly the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, Great Zimbabwe grew from a modest hilltop community into a centre whose population has been estimated at anything from ten to eighteen thousand. For much of the colonial era, European writers refused to accept that such a place could have been built by local people, and attributed it instead to a succession of imagined foreign builders. Those claims were discredited decades ago: the city was the work of the ancestors of today's Shona-speaking communities. Yet the controversy left a damaging legacy. Because so much energy was spent establishing who had built Great Zimbabwe, remarkably little was devoted until recently to the more interesting question of how it actually functioned.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The account that dominated the later twentieth century was elegantly simple. The ruler, it was argued, lived first on the rocky hill that overlooks the site, and the royal seat later moved down to the Great Enclosure in the valley below, followed by the homes of lesser officials. Dr Grace Tumwesigye has challenged this sequence using a new series of radiocarbon dates obtained from carefully excavated floors. Her results indicate that parts of the valley were occupied far earlier than had been believed, and that the hill and valley were inhabited at the same time for much of the city's history. She concludes that Great Zimbabwe contained several competing centres of authority rather than a single court that relocated. The more precise dating is a genuine advance. However, the fact that two areas were occupied simultaneously does not in itself demonstrate rivalry between them; it is equally consistent with a single ruling family whose members lived in different quarters.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Equally contested is the source of the city's prosperity. Gold was mined on the plateau, and excavations have uncovered glass beads from the Indian Ocean, fragments of Chinese porcelain and pottery from Persia, all of which must have arrived through the trading towns of the Swahili coast. Professor Henrik Kittelsen regards control over the export of gold as the foundation of royal power. In his view, rulers who could command the flow of precious metal to the coast were able to acquire exotic goods and redistribute them to loyal followers, thereby binding a large population to the capital.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others are unconvinced. Dr Amadou Moreau-Diallo points out that the imported objects recovered from the site are few in number when spread across several centuries, and argues that the real basis of wealth was cattle. Herds could be lent to dependants, given in marriage payments and used to build networks of obligation that extended far beyond the city. There is something to this objection. Imported porcelain and beads attract attention partly because they survive well and are easy to recognise, whereas wealth held in livestock leaves only scattered bones. It would nevertheless be a mistake to swing to the opposite extreme: the most plausible picture is one in which both herds and trade contributed to the city's rise.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The walls themselves raise further questions. The outer wall of the Great Enclosure, more than ten metres high in places and around five metres thick at its base, was built of granite blocks split from the surrounding outcrops and laid in neat courses without mortar of any kind. Along part of its upper section runs a decorative chevron pattern. Early observers assumed that such walls must have been fortifications, but they lack the platforms, ditches and easily defended gateways typical of military architecture, and inside them were houses and courtyards. Dr Nadia Wolanski, who has studied the masonry in detail, argues that the walls served chiefly to set the ruling household apart from commoners, screening elite life from public view. She further proposes that they were raised in stages over several generations, not by captives or by paid specialists, but by allied lineages fulfilling their obligations to the ruling family. The proposal is plausible, though it is hard to see what kind of evidence could ever confirm it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: By the middle of the fifteenth century, Great Zimbabwe was largely deserted. Kittelsen links its decline to a shift in the gold trade towards the Zambezi valley to the north, which would have deprived the city's rulers of the goods on which their authority depended. Tumwesigye, by contrast, emphasises environmental strain: a population of many thousands would have required vast quantities of firewood and pasture, and the surrounding land may simply have been exhausted. Both explanations have merit, but the word "decline" is itself misleading. The people did not vanish; they moved, and successor states to the north and west continued to build in stone and to observe many of the same political customs.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable outcome of recent research is that Great Zimbabwe is no longer measured against the cities of the Mediterranean or the Near East, and found either surprisingly similar or disappointingly different. It is increasingly studied as a city in its own right, shaped by the resources, values and political traditions of the African interior. That shift in perspective was long overdue, and it is likely to prove more productive than any single new excavation.

topic: Cahokia on the Mississippi: its sudden rise, population estimates from lake sediments, immigrants and pilgrimage, sacrifice and elite power, the palisade, and competing explanations of abandonment
title: The City of Earthen Mounds
subtitle: A thousand years ago a settlement on the Mississippi floodplain grew into North America's largest town. Why it appeared so quickly, and why it emptied, are still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Shortly after 1050 CE, on the broad floodplain where the Missouri and Illinois rivers join the Mississippi, a cluster of farming villages was transformed with extraordinary speed. Within a generation, the inhabitants of the place now called Cahokia had levelled an open space of some twenty hectares, known today as the Grand Plaza, and begun raising earthen platforms around it. The largest, Monks Mound, eventually rose about thirty metres and covered an area greater than that of the Great Pyramid of Giza; well over a hundred smaller mounds were built across the surrounding landscape. At its height Cahokia may have housed between ten and twenty thousand people, making it the largest settlement north of Mexico before the eighteenth century. Its size alone justifies calling it a city, but what is most puzzling about Cahokia is not how large it became so much as how suddenly it did so.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Estimating Cahokia's population has always been difficult, since counts of excavated houses vary greatly depending on how long each house is assumed to have been occupied. Dr Elena Kovalyova has approached the problem from an unexpected direction. Human waste contains distinctive chemical compounds that wash into nearby lakes and settle in their sediments, and by measuring these compounds in cores taken from a lake close to the site, she has traced how the number of people in the area changed over several centuries. Her results show a sharp increase in the eleventh century and a steady fall after about 1200. The method is ingenious, but it depends on assumptions about how efficiently such compounds reach and survive in lake beds, and it is therefore better suited to revealing trends than to producing exact figures.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Where did all these people come from? Analysis of strontium, a chemical element that is absorbed into teeth during childhood and varies with local geology, indicates that perhaps a third of those buried at Cahokia had grown up somewhere else. Professor Teodor Ormsgaard interprets this influx as evidence that Cahokia was above all a religious centre. In his view, a new set of beliefs and ceremonies, staged on the plaza and the great mounds, attracted migrants from a wide region, who came voluntarily rather than under compulsion. The scale of migration revealed by the isotope evidence is remarkable, and it makes it difficult to regard Cahokia as a place that simply grew out of local villages.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everything about the city, however, suggests willing participation. Excavations of one modest-looking mound uncovered the burial of a high-status man laid on a platform of thousands of shell beads, surrounded by the remains of more than two hundred other people, many of them young women who appear to have been killed at the same time. Dr Dilnoza Iskandarova argues that such deaths reveal an elite with the power to take lives on a large scale, and she describes Cahokia as an early state. That the people buried there were sacrificed seems hard to dispute, and it certainly implies considerable authority. To call Cahokia a state on this basis, however, is premature: ritual killing has been practised by many societies that lacked permanent administrative institutions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Around 1175, the inhabitants enclosed the central precinct within a wooden wall almost three kilometres long, built from an estimated twenty thousand posts and fitted with projecting towers at regular intervals. It was rebuilt at least three times over the following century, each time requiring the felling and transport of a vast quantity of timber. Whether it was intended to keep out external enemies or to separate an increasingly exclusive elite from the rest of the population remains uncertain. What is clear is that the wall represented an enormous investment of labour, and that it was built during a period when the population was already beginning to decline.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: By about 1350, Cahokia had been almost entirely abandoned. Several explanations have been put forward. Sediment cores reveal a thick layer of silt deposited around 1200, evidence of a major flood that would have destroyed crops and stores in the low-lying fields. Some researchers have argued that such floods were made worse by the clearing of forests upstream to supply fuel and building timber. Dr Marisol Anaya-Pinto has tested that idea by examining soil profiles near the site, and reports no sign of the erosion that widespread deforestation would have caused; she therefore rejects it. Others point to droughts in the thirteenth century that would have reduced harvests of maize. It seems to me unlikely that any single environmental cause will account for the city's end, because the population was falling before the most severe droughts began, which suggests that political and social divisions were already weakening the community.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Cahokia's abandonment should not be mistaken for the disappearance of its people. Many of the beliefs, symbols and forms of social organisation that flourished there were carried to other towns throughout the Mississippi valley and survived for centuries. For too long, discussions of early urbanism have concentrated on Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. Cahokia deserves a place in those discussions, not as a curiosity but as a case that tests our assumptions about how, and how quickly, cities can come into being.

topic: Jenne-jeno in the Inland Niger Delta: urbanism before trans-Saharan trade, the clustered-settlement model of specialist communities, ecological explanations, evidence of hierarchy, and the shift to Djenné
title: A City of Many Mounds
subtitle: Excavations on the middle Niger have overturned the belief that towns in West Africa were a foreign import, and raised the possibility that a city can function without a centre

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, it was taken for granted that urban life in West Africa south of the Sahara had been stimulated from outside. According to this view, towns appeared only after Arab and Berber merchants began leading regular camel caravans across the desert in the eighth and ninth centuries CE, bringing with them the demand for gold, the techniques of long-distance commerce and, eventually, Islam. Excavations begun in the late 1970s at Jenne-jeno, a large mound on the floodplain of the Inland Niger Delta in present-day Mali, made that view untenable. Radiocarbon dates showed that the site had been settled around 250 BCE, and that by the time the caravan trade became established it was already a substantial town with a population estimated at several thousand. In other words, the settlement had existed for the best part of a millennium before the traders who were supposed to have created it ever arrived.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What makes Jenne-jeno particularly significant, however, is not its age but its form. At its height, around 800 CE, the main mound covered some thirty-three hectares, but it was only the largest of about forty settlements located within four kilometres of it. Surface surveys suggest that several of these smaller mounds were associated with particular activities: iron slag is concentrated on some, fishing equipment on others, and pottery production on others again. No palace, temple or monumental building has been identified anywhere in the complex. Professor Liv Rognstad has argued that this arrangement represents a distinctive kind of city, in which specialist groups lived apart in order to preserve their separate identities while remaining bound together by exchange. Power, in her model, was spread among many groups rather than concentrated in a ruler. The model is elegant and has been widely adopted, yet it rests heavily on material collected from the surface; only a handful of the satellite mounds have actually been excavated, and it is possible that their apparent specialisation is less clear-cut below ground.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The floodplain itself offered neither stone nor iron ore. Both had to be brought in, the ore from deposits at least fifty kilometres away and grinding stones from even further. Copper, which does not occur in the region at all, appears in layers dating from the middle of the first millennium CE, and gold somewhat later. Such materials demonstrate that Jenne-jeno was connected to exchange networks of considerable range long before the trans-Saharan routes became important. The town, it seems, was not a product of long-distance trade but one of the nodes from which such trade was built.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why the inhabitants should have organised themselves in this way is a matter of debate. Dr Hamid Bazargan emphasises the environment of the delta, where the annual flood creates a patchwork of habitats — open water, seasonally flooded grassland, dry levees and rice-growing basins — each of which rewards different skills. On his account, specialisation was an adaptation to this diversity, and Jenne-jeno grew as the place where fishers, herders, farmers and smiths exchanged what they produced. The explanation is persuasive as far as it goes, but it accounts more readily for specialisation than for the decision of specialists to live in separate clusters rather than mixing together in a single settlement.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Petra Jovanoska questions whether Jenne-jeno was as free of hierarchy as Rognstad's model implies. She notes that around 800 CE the main mound was surrounded by a mud-brick wall some two kilometres in circumference, and that certain burials within it contained more grave goods than others. A project on that scale, she argues, required someone with the authority to organise it. The wall undoubtedly demanded coordinated effort; whether that coordination came from a ruler or from agreement among the various groups that benefited from it is a question the evidence cannot yet settle.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: From around 1100 CE the outlying mounds began to be abandoned one after another, and by about 1400 Jenne-jeno itself was deserted. Its role passed to Djenné, three kilometres away, which became one of the great commercial and religious centres of the West African interior, although whether its first inhabitants came from Jenne-jeno is not known. An older explanation held that the conversion of the town's rulers to Islam in the thirteenth century led residents to leave a site associated with earlier beliefs. Dr Boubacar Kanouté finds this too simple. Changes in burial practice show that new religious customs were indeed spreading, but he argues that the decisive factor was economic: as merchant networks linked to the trans-Saharan trade expanded, they favoured a single, more compact centre in which visiting traders could be accommodated, supervised and taxed. A gradual drying of the climate, which reduced the extent of the annual flood, may also have played a part.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Jenne-jeno does not prove that all early cities were decentralised, and enthusiasm for the clustered model should not be allowed to outrun the evidence. Nevertheless, it shows that a large, long-lived and economically complex settlement could exist without the monuments by which archaeologists have traditionally recognised urban power. That alone is reason enough to reconsider definitions of the city that were derived almost entirely from the experience of Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean.

topic: Caral and the Norte Chico sites of Peru: urbanism without pottery, the maritime-foundations hypothesis and coast–inland exchange, the role of crops, shicra construction and labour, and religious authority
title: Fish, Cotton and Stone
subtitle: Five thousand years ago, communities in a dry Peruvian valley built monumental centres without pottery, writing or, apparently, war. How did they manage it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the Supe valley, some two hundred kilometres north of Lima, lie the remains of a settlement that has forced archaeologists to rewrite the early history of the Americas. Caral, situated about twenty-three kilometres inland, where the valley begins to narrow towards the Andean foothills, contains six large platform mounds, sunken circular plazas and extensive residential quarters. Radiocarbon dates place its main period of construction between about 2600 and 2000 BCE, making it broadly contemporary with the pyramids of Egypt. It is also only one of some thirty comparable sites in the region now known as Norte Chico. Until these sites were properly dated, it had been assumed that monumental architecture in the Andes appeared much later, alongside pottery and intensive farming. Caral had neither pottery nor, so far as can be seen, any significant fortifications or weapons.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Caral has frequently been promoted as the oldest city in the Americas. The description is understandable, given the scale of the remains, but it is not especially helpful. It turns a genuinely interesting question about how these communities worked into a race for a record, and it obscures the fact that Caral was one part of a regional network rather than an isolated capital. The more fruitful approach is to ask what sustained the network as a whole.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One long-standing answer is that the foundations of Andean civilisation were maritime rather than agricultural. The cold Pacific current off Peru supports enormous shoals of anchovies and sardines, which could have provided a reliable source of protein without the need for farming on a large scale. Professor Jakub Moczulski has developed this idea into a model of exchange between coast and interior. In his view, fishing communities such as the coastal site of Áspero supplied fish, while inland settlements like Caral used irrigation channels fed by the Supe river to grow cotton, from which fishing nets were made, and gourds, which served as floats to hold the nets at the surface. Each group therefore depended on the other. The strongest support for his model comes from the large quantities of anchovy and sardine bones found at Caral itself, far from the sea, together with fragments of cotton netting.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that fish played so central a role. Dr Aigerim Arslanbek has analysed microscopic starch grains preserved on grinding stones and in cooking residues, and reports traces of maize, sweet potato and beans. She argues that crops made a greater contribution to the diet than the maritime model allows, and that the agricultural base of these communities has been underestimated. Her findings are important, because they show that plant foods were certainly being consumed. However, the quantities involved remain disputed: starch grains can survive in large numbers from a small amount of food, and they do not by themselves indicate how much of the diet a particular crop provided.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The mounds raise questions of a different kind. Much of their interior fill consists of shicras, bags woven from plant fibre and packed with stones, which were stacked in layers behind retaining walls. Engineers have pointed out that this technique gave the structures a degree of flexibility, allowing them to absorb the shocks of the earthquakes that frequently strike the region. Dr Tobias Vellacourt has gone further, suggesting that each bag represents a single unit of work contributed to the project, perhaps by one household or work party, so that the mounds were built through the pooled contributions of many families rather than by a labour force under compulsion. It is an intriguing interpretation. Yet counting bags can establish how much work was done; it cannot reveal the social relationships between the people who did it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are, nonetheless, clear signs of social difference. Larger and more carefully built houses stand close to the mounds, while smaller dwellings of cane and mud occupy the edges of the site. Dr Rosalía Ayquipa believes that the leaders who lived in these larger houses derived their authority from ceremony and specialised knowledge, including knowledge of the calendar, rather than from force. The discovery of more than thirty flutes made from the wing bones of pelicans and condors, buried together in one of the plazas, suggests that music played an important part in public ritual. Her emphasis on religious authority is convincing as far as it goes. Caution is needed, however, before describing Caral as a peaceful society: the absence of evidence for warfare is not the same thing as evidence for its absence, and little of the wider valley has been excavated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Around 1800 BCE, construction at Caral ceased and the site was gradually abandoned. Moczulski attributes this to a sequence of natural disasters, in which powerful earthquakes destabilised the valley slopes and heavy rains associated with El Niño washed debris down to the coast, where it formed sand dunes that were then blown inland across the fields. The scenario is plausible, though it does not explain why new ceremonial centres soon began to flourish in neighbouring valleys.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What Caral ultimately demonstrates is that complex society did not have to follow a single sequence, in which farming came first, pottery and villages next, and cities only at the end. Communities on the Peruvian coast assembled large populations and impressive monuments on the basis of fishing, exchange and modest cultivation. That conclusion is significant enough on its own; it does not need to be inflated by claims that Caral was the first or the greatest of anything.

topic: Liangzhu in the lower Yangtze: the walled city and palace platform, the early dam system and its purpose, jade imagery and religious authority, stored rice, whether a society without writing was a state, and its end
title: A State Built on Water
subtitle: Five thousand years ago a society in the Yangtze delta raised walls, palaces and dams. Whether it deserves to be called a state depends on what we think a state is

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the story of Chinese civilisation began in the north, on the plains of the Yellow River, with the Bronze Age dynasties of the second millennium BCE. Excavations near Hangzhou, in the delta of the lower Yangtze, have made that story increasingly difficult to sustain. Between roughly 3300 and 2300 BCE, a society now known as Liangzhu, after the modern town at the centre of its territory, built a walled settlement of some three hundred hectares, a massive raised platform for elite buildings and an extensive system of dams in the surrounding hills. These achievements predate the northern dynasties by more than a thousand years, and they oblige historians to reconsider when, and where, the first states in East Asia took shape.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The city walls, about six kilometres in circuit, were laid on a foundation of quarried stone and topped with rammed earth. They were pierced not only by land entrances but by water gates, and within them a network of canals connected residential areas, workshops and the central platform, suggesting that the settlement was planned around waterways and that boats rather than roads carried most of its traffic. The platform itself, known as Mojiaoshan, was raised artificially by as much as ten metres over an area of about thirty hectares, and supported large timber buildings. Dr Elchin Sardarov has calculated the volume of earth moved for the walls, the platform and associated works, and estimates that it represents millions of days of labour. In his view, effort on such a scale could only have been directed by a central authority capable of planning over decades and of compelling or persuading thousands of workers to take part.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even more striking is the hydraulic system to the north and west of the city. Eleven earthen dams, some built high in narrow valleys and others lower down on the plain, held back reservoirs covering several square kilometres. Their builders reinforced the earth with bundles of grass wrapped around clay, a technique that gave the structures considerable strength, and radiocarbon dates suggest that construction began around 3100 BCE, which would make this one of the oldest large-scale water-control systems known anywhere. The purpose of the dams is contested. Flood protection and irrigation are obvious possibilities, but Dr Annelie Pieterse argues that their main function was transport: the reservoirs, she suggests, allowed timber and stone to be floated down from the hills to the building sites of the city. Her argument draws attention to an aspect that earlier studies overlooked. Nevertheless, it seems to me a mistake to search for a single purpose. Structures of this size almost certainly served several needs at once, and the balance between them may well have changed over the centuries.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Liangzhu is also famous for its jade. Elite graves contain tubes with a square outer section and a round interior, flat perforated discs and ornaments, many carved with the same distinctive motif: a figure with a human face, wearing a feathered headdress, combined with the staring eyes and claws of an animal. Versions of this image have been found at sites spread across the delta. Dr Shangguan Mei interprets its consistency as evidence of a shared religious ideology that was defined and controlled from Liangzhu itself, and argues that religion supplied the foundation of political authority. The argument is attractive, but the spread of a common image does not in itself demonstrate political control; elites in neighbouring communities may simply have imitated the symbols of a prestigious centre without being subject to it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Beneath the city's economy lay rice. Paddy fields with banks and channels have been identified outside the walls, and near the central platform excavators found a deposit of charred rice estimated to have weighed many tonnes, apparently the remains of a large store destroyed by fire. Dr Kenta Hirabayashi believes that the grain had been brought in from surrounding villages as tribute, and that the ability to collect and redistribute food was a key instrument of the elite's power. Given the size of the deposit and its position beside the most important buildings in the city, this seems a reasonable reading of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Was Liangzhu, then, a state? Many scholars hesitate, chiefly because no writing has been found there, only isolated symbols scratched on pottery and jade. The objection is understandable, since writing has often been treated as a defining feature of early states. Yet that criterion was derived largely from the cases of Mesopotamia and Egypt, where writing happened to develop alongside centralised government, and there is no obvious reason why it should be applied universally. Liangzhu possessed a capital, a clear social hierarchy, monumental public works, specialised craft production and the capacity to collect resources from a wide territory. If these are not the characteristics of a state, it is hard to know what would be.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Around 2300 BCE, Liangzhu declined rapidly. Layers of silt over parts of the city indicate serious flooding, possibly linked to a period of heavier rainfall and rising water levels in the delta. There is a certain irony in the idea that a society which had invested so heavily in controlling water should have been overwhelmed by it. It is likely, however, that floods alone do not explain the collapse; the costs of maintaining walls, canals and dams may already have placed severe strain on the society, so that the floods delivered the final blow to a system that was already struggling.

topic: shipwreck site formation processes and the decline of the 'time capsule' view of wrecks
title: Not Quite a Moment Frozen in Time
subtitle: Archaeologists once treated shipwrecks as sealed snapshots of a single day. The reality, it now appears, is considerably messier

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, shipwrecks enjoyed a special reputation among archaeologists. A town or a cemetery accumulates material over many generations, whereas a ship that sinks carries a single collection of objects, all of which were in use at the same moment. This idea, often summarised in the phrase 'time capsule', made wrecks seem uniquely valuable for dating pottery styles, reconstructing patterns of trade and studying the everyday possessions of sailors. It also encouraged a particular kind of fieldwork, in which the main task was simply to recover the contents of the hull and catalogue them. The appeal of the notion is easy to understand, but it has always rested on an assumption that was rarely tested: that whatever reaches the seabed remains there, undisturbed, until a diver arrives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first systematic challenge came from Halvard Skjelbreid, a maritime archaeologist at the Skagerrak Centre for Underwater Research, who argued in the 1980s that a wreck should be understood as a sequence of processes rather than a single event. In his account, the moment of sinking is merely the beginning. As the vessel breaks up, buoyant objects such as barrels, loose timbers and wooden chests float away, sometimes travelling many kilometres before they come ashore. Later, storms, currents and the burrowing of marine animals shift the heavier items that remain, so that objects originally stored together may end up metres apart. Skjelbreid compared the archaeologist arriving at a wreck to a detective reaching a crime scene several centuries late, after the room has been repeatedly searched by people who kept no record of what they took.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That last point concerns human interference, which is, if anything, more destructive than the natural forces. Many vessels that sank in shallow water were salvaged almost immediately, either by their owners or by local communities, who removed guns, anchors and valuable cargo. Marisol Caravajal, whose work on colonial-era wrecks in the Caribbean draws on surviving salvage contracts and court records, found that at more than half of the sites she studied, the most valuable portion of the cargo had been recovered within a year of the loss. The material left for archaeologists, she concludes, is biased towards objects of low value, which means that a simple inventory of finds will tend to understate the wealth a ship was carrying. I find her argument compelling, although she perhaps underestimates how often salvors failed: diving equipment before the nineteenth century was crude, and much of what was lost in deeper water was simply beyond reach.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Natural processes, too, can be studied far more precisely than early critics assumed. A group led by Kwabena Amankwah-Sarpong at the Gulf of Guinea Marine Heritage Project has spent a decade monitoring experimental wrecks, small wooden boats deliberately sunk at measured depths, and recording how they deteriorate. Their results suggest that the decisive factor is neither depth nor water temperature but the type of seabed. Hulls that settle into soft mud are quickly covered and protected from wood-boring organisms, while those resting on rock or coarse sand may disappear almost entirely within a few decades. Amankwah-Sarpong argues that findings of this kind allow archaeologists to predict, before any excavation begins, which parts of a site are likely to have survived and which have probably been lost.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the time capsule idea should be abandoned altogether. Ilse Thuringer, a historian of ceramics, points out that even a badly scattered wreck still contains objects that were all aboard at once, which is more than can be said of almost any site on land. For her purposes, establishing which types of pottery were manufactured and traded at the same time, the precise position of a jar on the seabed matters far less than the fact that it was on the ship. In this narrow sense, she maintains, the old concept remains useful. Her defence is reasonable as far as it goes, but it overlooks the problem of intrusive material: later objects dropped from passing vessels, or carried in by currents, can settle among the remains of an earlier wreck and be mistaken for part of its cargo.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The practical consequence of this debate has been a change in how wreck sites are recorded. Where earlier projects concentrated on raising objects, modern teams devote much of their time to mapping the distribution of finds and sampling the sediments around them, in the hope of reconstructing how the site came to look as it does today. This is slower and more expensive, and some funding bodies have questioned whether it represents value for money. The criticism is misplaced. Without an understanding of how a wreck was formed, the objects recovered from it cannot be reliably interpreted, however carefully they are conserved afterwards.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, however, to conclude that a wreck is merely a disorderly heap of debris. What the newer approach reveals is that the disorder itself contains information about storms, about salvage and about the habits of marine creatures, information that the time capsule model treated as mere noise to be filtered out. A shipwreck, in other words, records not only the final day of a voyage but much of what has happened on that patch of seabed ever since. That is a less romantic idea than the one it replaces, but it is arguably a richer one.
