topic: commercial treasure salvage of historic shipwrecks versus archaeological protection
title: The Price of Sunken Silver
subtitle: Should the cargoes of historic wrecks ever be raised and sold? The argument between salvors and archaeologists shows little sign of ending

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Not long ago, a private company announced that it had located a seventeenth-century merchant vessel in deep water off the Atlantic coast, together with what it described as several tonnes of silver coins. Within weeks, the discovery had become the subject of a legal dispute involving the company, the government of the country under whose flag the ship had sailed, and the coastal state in whose waters it lay. Episodes of this kind have become familiar, and they expose a disagreement that goes to the heart of underwater archaeology: whether the contents of historic wrecks may legitimately be recovered and sold. The question is not new, but it has acquired fresh urgency as diving robots and sonar mapping have brought wrecks at depths of several thousand metres within reach for the first time.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The commercial case is put most forcefully by Lucio Bertolazzi, who has directed recovery operations for a salvage firm for more than twenty years. Locating and excavating a deep-water wreck, he points out, can cost tens of millions, a sum that no university department or museum could hope to raise. Without private investment, Bertolazzi argues, most such wrecks would never be found at all, and would gradually be destroyed by trawling and natural decay. He insists that his teams record sites to professional standards and that selling duplicate coins, of which a single cargo may contain many thousands, deprives scholarship of nothing. In his view, the revenue from such sales is simply what makes the expensive scientific work on the rest of the site possible, and critics who object to it rarely suggest where else the money might come from.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Archaeologists have generally been unconvinced. Sunil Arambepola, who spent ten years as a field director with a national maritime museum, maintains that the profit motive inevitably distorts priorities. A commercial expedition must recover saleable material within the time its investors are prepared to wait, he observes, and this creates pressure to concentrate on the cargo hold while neglecting the hull, the crew's personal possessions and the surrounding sediments that hold evidence of how the site formed. Even where recording is careful, the dispersal of objects into private collections makes it impossible for later researchers to re-examine them with methods that have not yet been invented. A pot in a public museum can be sampled again in fifty years; one sold at auction to an anonymous buyer is, for scientific purposes, effectively lost.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of so-called duplicates is more complicated than either side tends to admit. Coins struck from the same die may appear identical, but Arambepola notes that analysis of their metal content, wear and corrosion can reveal where the silver was mined and how long the coins had circulated before the voyage. A large hoard, in this sense, is a dataset rather than a pile of repeats, and its value lies partly in its completeness. That said, it seems unrealistic to expect every coin from a vast cargo to be kept in public hands indefinitely; few museums have the space or the funds to store tens of thousands of nearly indistinguishable items.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The law has struggled to keep pace with the technology that makes deep-water recovery possible. Traditional salvage law, developed to reward those who rescued ships and cargoes in distress, was never intended to apply to vessels lost centuries ago. Nadia Bouchareb, a specialist in maritime law at the Mediterranean Institute for Ocean Governance, has documented how an international convention adopted in the early 2000s established the principle that underwater heritage should preferably be preserved where it lies and should not be commercially exploited. However, many of the states with the most active salvage industries have not ratified it, and wrecks lying beyond national waters occupy a legal grey area in which enforcement is extremely difficult. Claims by the original flag state, Bouchareb adds, further complicate matters, since a government may assert ownership of a sunken warship or state cargo regardless of where it now lies.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A middle course has been proposed by the heritage economist Corentin Duvauchelle, who suggests that governments should license commercial firms to work on wrecks under archaeological supervision, with the proceeds shared between the company and a public fund for maritime research. Arrangements of this kind have been tried in a handful of countries, with mixed results. In one case, Duvauchelle reports, the state's portion of the proceeds paid for the survey of dozens of other sites along the coast; in another, the supervising archaeologists complained that they had been overruled whenever their demands threatened the project's schedule.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In my view, the licensing model deserves more serious consideration than archaeologists have usually given it, but only if supervision carries real authority. The chief weakness of the purist position is not ethical but practical: insisting that wrecks remain untouched does nothing to protect them from bottom trawlers, which have damaged far more sites than any treasure hunter. Equally, the claim that only commercial money can fund deep-water work is less persuasive than it once was, since the cost of remotely operated vehicles has fallen sharply over the past two decades. The future of these wrecks will depend less on who pays for the work than on who decides how it is done.

topic: preservation in situ versus excavation of deteriorating wreck sites (reburial, shipworm, 'preservation by record')
title: Leave It Where It Lies?
subtitle: Underwater archaeologists have long preferred to keep wrecks on the seabed. But the seabed is not always the safe place it was assumed to be

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the late twentieth century, the guiding principle of underwater heritage management has been that wrecks should, wherever possible, be left on the seabed. This preference for preservation in situ, as it is known, reflects hard experience. Excavation is not only expensive but also destructive, since a site that has been dug can never be dug again, and every object raised from the sea becomes the responsibility of a conservation laboratory for decades, sometimes indefinitely. Many museums still hold waterlogged timbers and corroded iron raised in the 1960s and 1970s that have never been fully treated, and some of these have deteriorated further in storage than they ever did underwater. Against this background, leaving wrecks alone appears both prudent and economical. Yet the principle has come under increasing scrutiny in recent years, and the case against it deserves a fair hearing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential defence of the approach comes from Sigrid Strandvik, a conservator who has spent much of her career dealing with the consequences of hasty excavation. She argues that a wreck which has survived for centuries has, almost by definition, reached a kind of equilibrium with its surroundings, and that disturbing it, whether by removing sediment or by lifting objects, is what usually triggers rapid decay. In her view, the archaeologist's first duty is to future generations, who will possess techniques for studying sites that cannot yet be imagined. Leaving a wreck undisturbed, she says, is not a refusal to investigate it but a decision to postpone investigation until it can be done better.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty, as the marine microbiologist Hamid Ebrahimzadeh has shown, is that the equilibrium Strandvik describes is often an illusion. Sediments shift constantly, and a wreck that was fully buried twenty years ago may now lie partly exposed. Once bare timber comes into contact with oxygenated water, it is colonised within months by shipworm and other boring organisms, which can reduce a solid oak beam to a fragile shell honeycombed with tunnels. Ebrahimzadeh's monitoring of several wrecks in a sheltered estuary found that more than a third of their exposed wooden structure had been lost over a period of only fifteen years. Warming seas, he adds, are likely to extend the range of wood-boring species into cooler waters where they were previously rare, placing at risk wrecks that have hitherto been considered secure.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Heritage managers have responded by trying to make preservation in situ more active. Exposed sections of hull may be covered with sandbags, with geotextile sheets or with artificial seagrass mats designed to trap moving sediment; in some cases, entire sites have been reburied under imported sand. Meron Tsegaye-Alemu, who coordinates a regional programme for protected wrecks, reports that these measures can be highly effective when they are carefully maintained. However, she acknowledges that they require regular inspection by divers, and that a covering which is neglected after a severe storm can fail within a single winter. Reburial, in other words, is not a single act but an ongoing commitment, and its long-term costs are rarely included when it is compared with excavation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This is the point pressed most firmly by Adebayo Afolabi-Coker, a field archaeologist who argues that the profession has turned a sensible preference into an unexamined rule. He contends that when a site is known to be deteriorating and cannot be effectively protected, the responsible course is to excavate and document it fully before it disappears, a policy he calls 'preservation by record'. He accepts that this is destructive, but maintains that controlled destruction accompanied by thorough documentation is preferable to uncontrolled destruction with none. Strandvik's appeal to future generations, he remarks, means little if the sites those generations inherit have already been eaten away.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: I find Afolabi-Coker's argument largely persuasive, although his phrase 'preservation by record' is somewhat misleading. A record, however detailed, preserves only the answers to the questions that its makers thought to ask; it cannot be re-examined in the way that a physical object can. The real choice is therefore not between preserving a site and destroying it, but between two different kinds of loss. Which is preferable will depend on circumstances that vary from one wreck to another: the stability of the seabed, the significance of the remains and, not least, whether any conservation laboratory is in a position to accept what is raised.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What seems clear is that neither policy can be applied mechanically. The weakness of the in situ principle has never been its logic, which is sound, but the assumption that leaving a site alone costs nothing. Monitoring, maintenance and periodic reassessment are all expensive, and few heritage agencies have budgets that match the number of wrecks under their protection. Some have begun to rank sites according to their vulnerability and importance, so that limited resources can be directed where they will do most good. Until such systems become routine, however, the decision about whether to excavate will often be made not by archaeologists weighing the evidence but by the sea itself.

topic: drowned prehistoric landscapes on continental shelves and the search for submerged Stone Age sites
title: Lost Lands Beneath the Shelf
subtitle: When the ice sheets melted, rising seas swallowed plains where people had lived for thousands of years. Can archaeologists ever find them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Around twenty thousand years ago, at the height of the last glaciation, so much of the world's water was locked up in ice that the oceans stood roughly 120 metres lower than they do today. Broad continental shelves lay exposed as grassland, marsh and forest, crossed by rivers. This vanished territory covered an area comparable to that of a continent. As the ice retreated, the sea crept back over it, sometimes by a few metres in a lifetime, sometimes far faster. Because archaeology developed as a discipline practised on dry land, the study of human prehistory has been, almost by default, a study of what happened inland. That emphasis is hardly surprising, but it has arguably distorted our picture of how early people lived, since many of the places they found most attractive now lie beneath the waves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Coastal plains offered a great deal to hunter-gatherers: shellfish and fish, migrating birds, freshwater springs emerging at the foot of cliffs, and level routes along which groups could travel. Thabo Makhubela, an archaeologist at the Southern Cape Coastal Research Unit, has spent much of his career in caves on the South African coast that are famous for early evidence of shellfish gathering and symbolic behaviour. Today these caves sit on the edge of the sea. During colder periods, however, the shoreline lay as much as ninety kilometres away, across a now drowned lowland rich in grazing animals. Makhubela contends that the caves were therefore occupied by people whose main territory was the plain below, and that what survives on land represents the margins of their world rather than its centre. The idea is persuasive, yet as matters stand it remains largely untested, because almost no fieldwork has been carried out on the submerged plain itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Finding sites under tens of metres of water and sediment is not a matter of simply sending down divers. The first step is to reconstruct the former landscape. Anneliese Kaltenecker, a marine geophysicist at the Baltic Institute for Seabed Studies, uses seismic reflection surveys, which send pulses of sound into the seabed and record the echoes from buried layers, to trace ancient river channels, lake basins and shorelines. Much of her data was collected by companies planning offshore wind farms and pipelines. Kaltenecker argues that, once the old terrain is mapped, archaeologists can predict where people would most probably have camped, such as the points where rivers entered lakes. This commercial information has been something of a windfall for the field. It should nevertheless be used with caution: it was gathered for engineering purposes, and its resolution is often too coarse to reveal anything as small as a hearth or a scatter of stone tools.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more basic question is whether anything could have survived at all. When the sea advances across a landscape, the zone of breaking waves passes over every point in turn, and many specialists long assumed that this would grind any archaeological deposits to nothing. Ryo Ohtsubo, a coastal geomorphologist at Hakodate Marine University, disagrees. In his view, the outcome depends chiefly on two conditions: how rapidly the water rose and how well a particular spot was protected from wave energy. Where sea level climbed quickly, or where a site lay in a sheltered inlet or was already buried beneath lake mud, the surf could pass over without destroying it. The evidence supports his position. Trawlers working in the North Sea and elsewhere have for decades brought up worked flint, animal bones and even carved antler, proving that material does survive submersion, although finds hauled up in nets have lost any record of where exactly they lay.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Mirela Purcarea, who coordinates a heritage programme at the Black Sea Institute of Archaeology, believes the field cannot afford to wait for ideal conditions. Dredging for sand and gravel, the laying of cables and the construction of foundations for turbines are already disturbing large areas of seabed, and she argues that sites will be destroyed long before carefully designed research surveys reach them. Her programme therefore works with fishing crews and dredging companies, asking them to log the position of anything unusual that comes up. This pragmatic approach deserves credit, and it has produced a valuable stream of finds. Its weakness is that the resulting distribution maps show where trawling and dredging take place at least as much as where people once lived, so they cannot simply be read as evidence of ancient settlement patterns.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Cost is the reason most often given for the neglect of drowned landscapes. Excavating at depths of twenty or thirty metres requires boats, specialist divers and decompression schedules that allow only short periods of work each day, and a single season can cost many times as much as a comparable dig on land. These difficulties are real, but they are frequently exaggerated as an excuse for inaction. Where archaeologists have been involved from the outset in offshore development projects, the expensive work of surveying the seabed has largely been paid for already, and the additional cost of examining promising locations has proved modest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is at stake is more than a handful of additional sites. Several influential accounts of human prehistory hold that people turned to marine resources such as shellfish relatively late, and that coastal routes played only a minor part in the spread of our species. If the earliest coastal camps were all drowned, however, this apparent lateness may be nothing more than an illusion created by rising seas. Until the continental shelves have been investigated far more thoroughly, any conclusions about when and how humans first came to depend on the sea should be regarded as provisional.

topic: conserving waterlogged wooden ship hulls after recovery: polyethylene glycol, sulphur-iron acid formation and museum climate control
title: Drying Out the Past
subtitle: Raising a wooden ship from the seabed is a triumph of engineering. Keeping it intact afterwards has proved a far harder problem

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few moments in archaeology attract as much attention as the lifting of a historic hull from the water. Television crews gather, the timbers break the surface, and the operation is reported as the culmination of years of work. In reality it marks the beginning of a far longer and less visible struggle. Wood that has lain on the seabed for centuries may look sound, but its structure has been profoundly altered. Bacteria and fungi slowly consume the cellulose that gives timber its strength, and the space they leave behind fills with water. In many cases it is this water, more than the remaining wood, that holds the object in shape. If such timber were simply left to dry in the open air, the cell walls would collapse, and a plank could shrink and twist into something barely recognisable within weeks.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Since the 1960s, the standard answer to this problem has been to replace the water with a substance that can support the weakened cells. The most widely used is polyethylene glycol, a synthetic wax-like compound that is sprayed onto large hulls, or in which smaller objects are soaked, over periods that can stretch to two decades. Once the wood is saturated with it, the object is dried slowly under controlled conditions. Hiroko Takenouchi of the Kansai Institute for Cultural Property Conservation has refined a variation in which treated objects are freeze-dried, so that the water passes directly from ice to vapour without the surface tension that pulls cell walls inwards. Her results with bowls, tools and individual timbers are excellent, but the size of the vacuum chambers involved means the technique cannot be applied to an entire ship. For whole hulls, slow drying in a controlled atmosphere remains the only practical option.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For some years these methods appeared to have solved the problem. Then, around the turn of the millennium, conservators began to notice powdery yellow and white salts blooming on the surfaces of several celebrated museum ships. Analysis traced the cause to the seabed. In sediments where oxygen is absent, certain bacteria generate sulphur compounds, which gradually accumulate in waterlogged timber. Once a hull is raised and exposed to the air of a museum, these compounds slowly oxidise, and the reaction is greatly accelerated by iron leaching from corroded bolts and nails. The product is acid, which attacks the wood from within. It would be unfair to blame the conservators who treated these vessels decades earlier; the chemistry involved was simply not understood at the time, and nothing in their training could have alerted them to it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dragan Zlatarovski, who leads the wood research group at the Adriatic Centre for Maritime Conservation, regards acid formation as the gravest long-term threat facing recovered hulls, more serious than shrinkage or biological attack. He has championed treatments that bind and extract iron from the timber, using solutions that are applied repeatedly over months. The alarm Zlatarovski has raised is justified, and his work has drawn attention to a danger that many museums had underestimated. Yet extraction is not without risk. Repeated wetting of fragile, already treated wood may wash out some of the consolidant, and nobody yet knows what the cumulative effect of such interventions will be over a century.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more radical critique comes from Lourdes Abarquez, a materials chemist at the Visayas Polymer Laboratory. Her research indicates that polyethylene glycol itself is less stable than was assumed, and that over time it breaks down into acidic by-products of its own. On this view the treatment that saved many hulls is now contributing to their decay. Abarquez and her colleagues are testing alternatives derived from plant materials, including modified sugars and compounds based on lignin, which are intended to strengthen wood while remaining chemically inert. The early results are encouraging, but they come from small samples observed for only a few years. A consolidant introduced into a ship must perform for centuries, and laboratory success is a weak guide to behaviour on that timescale.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Given these uncertainties, some specialists argue that the most effective intervention is to change the surroundings rather than the wood. Adebayo Bamgbose, an engineer who advises museums on environmental systems, points out that the chemical reactions involved slow down considerably at lower temperatures and in stable, moderate humidity. Holding a large exhibition hall at such conditions is not cheap, and its energy demands sit awkwardly with institutions' climate commitments. Bamgbose nevertheless maintains that, over the lifetime of an object, careful climate control costs less and carries fewer risks than successive rounds of chemical treatment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is that a raised hull is never finished. It requires monitoring, adjustment and funding indefinitely, much like a living collection in a zoo or botanical garden. This has implications for future projects. Decisions to lift a wreck are still too often taken on the strength of the excitement the event will generate, with the costs of conservation left for later. No hull should be raised unless the resources to look after it in the long term have been secured in advance. Where they cannot be, leaving the vessel on the seabed may be the more responsible choice.

topic: digital recording of wreck sites: underwater photogrammetry, robotic survey vehicles and the limits of 3D models
title: Wrecks in the Machine
subtitle: Cameras, software and underwater robots are transforming how shipwrecks are recorded. But a perfect-looking model is not the same as understanding

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of underwater archaeology, recording a wreck was a slow and physically exhausting business. Divers stretched tape measures between fixed points on the seabed, noted the readings with pencils on sheets of frosted plastic film, and returned to the surface when their air or their permitted time ran out. A large site could take several seasons to plan, and errors crept in whenever visibility was poor or the measuring tapes drifted in the current. Over the past fifteen years this has changed dramatically. Using photogrammetry, a technique in which thousands of overlapping photographs are processed by software into a three-dimensional model, a team can now document a wreck with an accuracy of a few millimetres. This is, in my view, the most important development in the discipline since the invention of the aqualung, and it has altered not only the speed of fieldwork but the kinds of questions archaeologists can ask.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Few have exploited the technique more thoroughly than Aino Hirvonsalo of the Gulf of Bothnia Wreck Survey. The cold, low-salinity waters of the northern Baltic preserve wooden ships unusually well, and Hirvonsalo's team recently produced a complete model of an eighteenth-century merchant vessel after just two days of diving, a task she estimates would previously have required two full seasons. For her, however, speed is not the main benefit. Because the model can be shared, specialists who will never dive, such as historians of shipbuilding or experts in rigging, are able to examine the vessel in detail from their desks, measuring timbers and checking construction methods as often as they wish. Several of her models have since been used in university teaching, and one has prompted a reassessment of the date at which a particular style of hull construction reached the region.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In deep water the transformation is even more striking. Autonomous underwater vehicles, carrying multibeam sonar and high-resolution cameras, can now survey wrecks lying a thousand metres or more below the surface, far beyond the reach of any diver. Krit Pongsapipat, who directs the Andaman Sea Marine Robotics Laboratory, predicts that within a generation human divers will be needed only on comparatively shallow sites, with machines taking over everywhere else. His enthusiasm is understandable, but the prediction goes too far. Present-day robots record surfaces; they cannot yet excavate with the delicacy that fragile organic material demands, and the few attempts at robotic digging have been, by the admission of their own designers, crude.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection has been raised by Shirin Karamandi, a theorist of archaeological method at the Caspian Institute of Heritage Science. She argues that 3D models possess a seductive precision that conceals the decisions behind them. Which parts of a site were photographed, how they were lit, and how the processing algorithms smooth out small irregularities are all choices made by people, yet the finished model appears neutral and complete. Moreover, a model shows only what was visible on the day; anything buried beneath sediment is simply absent. Karamandi also warns that digital records are surprisingly fragile, since file formats and software become obsolete. On this last point she is undoubtedly right: a considerable proportion of the digital survey data produced in the early 1990s can no longer be opened by anyone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Others emphasise what digital recording offers the wider public. Kagiso Sekgoma, who manages a maritime heritage programme along the southern African coast, has used photogrammetric models to create virtual dive trails, allowing museum visitors and schoolchildren to explore wrecks they could never see in person. She argues that this public value is itself a strong justification for the cost of survey work. Sekgoma is also alert to a less welcome consequence. A highly detailed model, combined with accurate coordinates, could serve as a guide for looters, and her programme therefore publishes its models with the precise locations of the wrecks withheld.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that traditional skills have become redundant. Drawing a site by hand forces the archaeologist to look closely at every timber, and divers who draw often notice features such as tool marks, repairs or reused wood that a camera captures but nobody subsequently examines. Abandoning such practices entirely would be a mistake. The most productive projects I have encountered combine the two approaches, using photogrammetry for overall geometry and hand recording to direct attention to details that matter. Hand drawing also produces an interpretation rather than a mere copy: the person drawing must decide where one plank ends and the next begins, and those decisions are set down openly on the page, where later researchers can challenge them in a way they rarely can with the hidden settings of a software package.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable use of the new tools, however, is one their early advocates scarcely anticipated. Because a wreck can be modelled quickly and cheaply, the same site can be surveyed again after a storm, or every year for a decade, and the models compared. Such repeated surveys reveal where timbers are being exposed, where sediment is accumulating and how fast deterioration is proceeding. A single record, however accurate, captures one moment; a sequence of records shows a wreck changing, and that is what managers need if they are to decide where protection is most urgently required.

topic: geoarchaeological coring of silted-up ancient harbours: harbour sediment signatures, ancient dredging gaps, lead pollution records and tsunami layers
title: Harbours Under the Fields
subtitle: Many of the great ports of antiquity now lie far from the sea. Drilling into the mud that buried them is revealing how they worked

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A visitor to the remains of several celebrated ancient ports around the Mediterranean may be surprised to find no sea in sight. Over the past two or three thousand years, rivers have carried enormous quantities of silt to the coast, and in many places the shoreline has advanced by several kilometres, leaving former harbours stranded beneath farmland, marshes or modern suburbs. For generations, locating these harbours was largely a matter of interpreting ambiguous passages in ancient authors and making educated guesses from the shape of the land. Excavation could occasionally confirm a guess, but digging below the water table is difficult and expensive. Since the 1990s, however, a different approach has spread rapidly: rather than excavating, researchers drill.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technique, borrowed from sedimentary geology, involves driving hollow tubes several metres into the ground to extract continuous cylinders of sediment, known as cores. Each core is a vertical archive in which the oldest deposits lie at the bottom. Eleni Tsoukalidou, who heads the Aegean Geoarchaeology Unit, was among the first to show that harbours leave a distinctive signature in this archive. Along an open coast, waves keep the sea floor covered with coarse sand and gravel. When a basin was enclosed by stone breakwaters, however, the water became calm, and fine silts and clays began to settle instead. A sharp change from coarse to fine sediment therefore marks the moment a harbour was built. Shells and fragments of plants within these layers can be dated by radiocarbon, and Tsoukalidou argues that a harbour's position and approximate date of construction can be established from cores alone, even where every trace of its masonry has been removed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The same calm conditions that make harbour mud so informative also created a practical problem for those who used the port: the basin steadily filled up. Mathilde Lebrunet of the Mediterranean Coastal Archaeology Centre has examined cores from more than a dozen harbours and found that, in a number of them, the sedimentary sequence is interrupted. Layers that ought to represent several centuries are missing altogether, so that deposits from, say, the second century BC lie directly on top of those from the sixth. Lebrunet interprets these gaps as the work of ancient dredging crews, who periodically scooped out the accumulated mud to keep the harbour navigable. If she is right, the most telling evidence of harbour maintenance is, paradoxically, an absence. The remains of flat-bottomed boats with openings in their hulls, recovered at one site, have been tentatively identified as dredging vessels, though their function is still debated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Harbour sediments also preserve a chemical record of the cities around them. Because the basins were sheltered, contaminants washed in from the town tended to settle rather than disperse. Ignacio Alzamora, an environmental geochemist at the Iberian Institute of Coastal Studies, has measured lead concentrations in harbour cores from several sites and found that they rise sharply during periods of urban growth, a pattern he links to the expansion of lead water pipes and metalworking. Alzamora suggests that these lead curves can serve as an index of a city's prosperity, rising and falling with its fortunes. His critics accept the measurements but question the interpretation, pointing out that lead may also have been carried down rivers from mining districts far inland, in which case the curves would reflect activity upstream rather than in the port itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every coastline produces the kind of evidence found in the Mediterranean. Devika Ramsundar of the Western Ghats Maritime Research Programme studies Early Historic trading ports on the south-west coast of India, where the annual monsoon dominates conditions at sea. Many of these ports, she notes, possessed no constructed breakwaters. Large ships anchored in river mouths or in the open roadstead during the sailing season, and cargo was ferried to and from the shore in smaller boats. Since no artificial basin was created, the change from coarse to fine sediment that Tsoukalidou identified may never appear in the cores. Ramsundar warns that applying the Mediterranean model uncritically could lead researchers to conclude that a port did not exist when it simply operated in a different way.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One of the more unexpected uses of harbour cores concerns natural disasters. In several basins, the fine silts are interrupted by thin layers of coarse sand containing broken marine shells and pebbles, material that could only have been thrown in from the open sea by a violent event. Some researchers interpret these layers as the deposits of ancient tsunamis and have attempted to correlate them with earthquakes recorded in historical sources. Others maintain that exceptional storms could produce very similar deposits, and the question of how to distinguish the two remains unresolved. Even so, because harbours acted as traps for such material, they may hold one of the best available records of coastal hazards over the past three millennia.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies have turned harbour mud from an obstacle into a resource. The cores cannot reveal everything; they sample only a few centimetres of a basin at each point, and the story they tell depends heavily on how many are drilled and where. Nonetheless, they have made it possible to study the working life of ports, including their construction, their upkeep and the environmental pressures upon them, in places where conventional excavation would be impractical.

topic: twentieth-century warship wrecks as war graves: illegal metal salvage, legal ownership, leaking fuel and diver access
title: Graves Beneath the Waves
subtitle: The wrecks of the two world wars are memorials, archaeological sites, pollution hazards and, for some, a source of profit. Can they be all of these at once?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The two world wars of the twentieth century sent many thousands of warships, merchant vessels, submarines and aircraft to the bottom of the sea. Many of them still contain the remains of the people who served on board. Until fairly recently these wrecks attracted little attention from archaeologists, who tended to regard anything less than a century old as recent history rather than heritage. Such wrecks were also assumed to hold little that could not already be learned from official records, logbooks and the testimony of survivors. That view has changed, and the change has brought with it a series of awkward dilemmas. A wartime wreck may simultaneously be a grave, a historical monument, a threat to the marine environment and a store of valuable metal. Of all the sites that underwater archaeologists deal with, none, I would argue, raises more difficult questions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most immediate danger is commercial. Over the past two decades, a number of large warships sunk in Asian waters during the Second World War have been almost entirely dismantled by unlicensed salvage operations, leaving little more than scars on the seabed. For a time, part of the attraction lay in the steel. Metal made before 1945 was free of the radioactive contamination that nuclear testing later introduced into the atmosphere, and it was therefore sought after for highly sensitive scientific instruments. Now that suitable steel can be manufactured in other ways, that market has shrunk, and salvagers mostly target copper, brass and bronze, particularly the large propellers that can be cut up and sold for scrap.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In principle, the law offers protection. Bjørnar Thorvik, a specialist in maritime law at the Bergen Centre for Ocean Governance, explains that warships generally remain the property of the state under whose flag they sailed, however long ago they sank. The difficulty, he observes, is that many of these vessels lie in the territorial waters of other countries, whose authorities may have neither the resources nor the inclination to patrol them. Thorvik's analysis is accurate, and it exposes an uncomfortable truth: ownership that cannot be enforced offers a wreck no real protection at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Archaeologists themselves are divided over how such sites should be treated. Lorenza Marchetto, who has surveyed submarine wrecks in the central Mediterranean, argues that their status as graves should not place them beyond study. Using non-invasive techniques such as sonar and photography, her team has been able to identify vessels whose fate had been uncertain for decades, and in several cases to tell families for the first time where their relatives died. This is valuable work, and it shows that respect and research need not be opposed. There is, however, a clear line that ought not to be crossed. Recording a wreck is one thing; disturbing the human remains within it without the agreement of the state concerned and, where possible, of relatives is quite another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different set of priorities is advanced by Hery Razafimahefa, a marine pollution scientist at the Indian Ocean Environmental Observatory. Many wartime wrecks still hold fuel oil, and some contain unexploded munitions. Razafimahefa has studied the corrosion of steel hulls and argues that, after seventy or eighty years on the seabed, many of them are approaching a point at which deterioration accelerates and structural collapse becomes likely, releasing whatever remains inside. In his view, removing fuel is urgent and should not be delayed by concerns about grave sites. The conflict he describes is real, but it can be exaggerated. Oil can often be extracted by drilling into a tank from the outside, an operation that need not disturb any part of the vessel where remains are likely to lie.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many war wrecks are also popular destinations for recreational divers, and some visitors have removed portholes, bells and personal items as souvenirs. One response has been to prohibit diving altogether. Agnieszka Golebiewska, who manages wreck sites for a Baltic heritage agency, believes this is counterproductive. Bans are almost impossible to enforce at sea, she argues, and they alienate the divers who are often the first to notice and report illegal salvage. She favours a system of licensed access combined with a code of conduct. Her reasoning seems sound for accessible sites in busy coastal waters, though it may be less suitable for remote wrecks, where any visitor would be difficult to monitor.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Behind all these arguments lies the question of whose wishes should count most. As the last survivors of the wars die, the wrecks are becoming the principal physical link between later generations and those who were lost. The views of descendants deserve to be sought and taken seriously. They cannot, however, be the only consideration, since many crews have no traceable relatives, and the obligations to protect the environment and to preserve the historical record extend well beyond any single family. Striking that balance will require the states that sent these ships to sea to accept a continuing responsibility for them, rather than treating the moment of sinking as the end of their involvement.

topic: counting dated Mediterranean shipwrecks as a proxy for the scale of Roman maritime trade, and the biases in the wreck record
title: Counting the Wrecks
subtitle: Can the number of ships that sank tell us how much the ancient world traded? An ingenious statistical idea, and the arguments it has provoked

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Historians of the ancient economy face a problem that their colleagues working on later periods rarely encounter: there are almost no figures. No Roman official recorded the total tonnage of goods shipped across the Mediterranean, and the scattered numbers that survive in literary texts are often exaggerated or impossible to verify. For much of the twentieth century, debates about whether the Roman economy was primitive and largely self-sufficient or sophisticated and highly integrated were therefore conducted with very little hard evidence. Then, towards the end of the century, a simple idea gained currency. Divers had by then located and dated well over a thousand ancient wrecks in the Mediterranean. If these were plotted century by century, the resulting graph might serve as a rough measure of the volume of seaborne trade. When the exercise was carried out, the curve rose steeply in the last centuries BC, peaked in the first century BC and the first century AD, and then fell away sharply, never recovering to the same level in antiquity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Among the most prominent advocates of this approach is Maarten Achterhof, an economic historian at the Leiden Centre for Ancient Economies, who spent several years assembling and cleaning the wreck database on which many later studies rely. Achterhof acknowledges that the record is imperfect, but he points out that the shape of the curve closely resembles that of an entirely independent source: the concentration of lead pollution preserved in layers of Arctic ice, which reflects the intensity of silver and lead mining in the Roman world. Two such different kinds of evidence, he argues, would be unlikely to coincide unless both were tracking a genuine rise and fall in economic activity. The convergence is indeed striking, and critics have yet to offer a convincing explanation for it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, the wreck record contains biases that are now widely recognised. The first concerns how ships become visible to archaeologists. Ozan Koyunoglu, who directs survey work along the Anatolian coast, has shown that most ancient wrecks are discovered because of their cargo of amphorae, the large ceramic jars used to transport wine, oil and fish sauce. A heap of amphorae survives for millennia and is easily spotted by divers. From around the third century AD, however, merchants increasingly shipped goods in wooden barrels and sacks, which decay and leave little trace. Koyunoglu contends that a ship carrying barrels is far less likely to be found than one carrying jars, so part of the apparent decline in trade may be nothing more than a change in packaging.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second problem lies in what the numbers actually measure. Lusine Abrahamyan, a statistician who has worked extensively with archaeological data, observes that a wreck is the product of two factors: the number of voyages undertaken and the probability that any one of them ended in disaster. If ships became more seaworthy, or if captains became more cautious about sailing in winter, the number of wrecks could fall even while trade was growing. Abrahamyan has also drawn attention to the way dates are assigned. Many wrecks can be placed only within a span of two or three hundred years, and the convention of dividing such a wreck equally among the centuries in its range tends to flatten peaks and spread losses into periods where they may not belong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The third bias is geographical. Rémi Lachapelle, who has compiled records of underwater surveys since the 1950s, notes that the coasts of southern France and Italy have been explored intensively by sport divers and professional teams for decades, whereas large stretches of the North African and eastern Mediterranean seabed have scarcely been examined. In his view, the distribution map of known wrecks is to a considerable degree a map of where people have chosen to dive. He has proposed weighting the figures for each region according to the amount of survey work carried out there, though the necessary information on survey effort is itself patchy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How damaging are these criticisms? Taken together, they are serious, but they do not demolish the original argument. The rise towards a peak around the turn of the millennium is consistent with several other lines of evidence and survives most attempts at statistical correction. The subsequent collapse is a different matter. It is precisely in the later centuries that the shift from amphorae to barrels, the uncertainty of dating and the uneven geography of research combine to depress the figures, and the decline is therefore much less secure than the peak. More generally, wreck counts are best used to compare broad trends over time; treating them as a means of calculating how much was actually traded asks more of the data than they can provide.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The dataset itself is also changing. Remotely operated vehicles, often deployed during surveys for pipelines and cables, have begun to locate ancient wrecks at depths of more than a thousand metres. These ships evidently sailed directly across open water rather than hugging the coast, and their cargoes do not always resemble those found in the shallows. Because the existing database consists almost entirely of coastal wrecks, such discoveries could alter the picture considerably. Whether they will strengthen the familiar curve or complicate it remains to be seen.

topic: prehistoric lake-shore settlements around the Alps: the stilt-house controversy, tree-ring dating of piles, erosion and public reconstructions
title: Villages on the Water
subtitle: For over a century and a half, the prehistoric settlements preserved in Alpine lakes have fascinated scholars and the public alike. What exactly were they?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the unusually dry winter of 1854, the water level of several lakes on the northern side of the Alps fell to a point that nobody living could remember. Along the exposed shores, local people noticed rows of blackened wooden posts protruding from the mud, surrounded by pottery, stone axes and the remains of food. Within a few years, scholars had developed a vivid interpretation of these finds: prehistoric communities, they proposed, had lived in villages of wooden houses raised on platforms above the open water, safe from wild animals and enemies. The image spread rapidly through books, paintings and school textbooks, and the so-called lake dwellers came to be celebrated as the honest, hard-working ancestors of the modern population. It is hard not to see in this enthusiasm a reflection of the nation-building preoccupations of the period, which sought a shared and respectable past.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: From the 1920s onwards, however, the picture was challenged. A number of researchers argued that the houses had in fact been built on dry land along the shore, with floors resting directly on the ground, and that they had only later been submerged as lake levels rose. For several decades the argument was conducted as a straightforward contest between two models, houses over water or houses on land. Giulia Bergamasco, a wetland archaeologist at the Insubrian Institute for Prehistory, has done much to move the debate beyond this opposition. Her excavations suggest that many houses stood on the shoreline itself, with floors raised a little above the ground on short posts, precisely because the area was flooded from time to time. The old dispute, in other words, was based on a false choice, and the reality varied from lake to lake and even from one century to the next.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The settlements have also become a showcase for dendrochronology, the dating of wood by its pattern of annual growth rings. Because tens of thousands of piles survive, and because the outermost ring is often preserved, specialists can frequently determine not merely the century but the year, and sometimes the season, in which a tree was cut down. Tomas Vaitkunas, who runs a tree-ring laboratory that has analysed piles from more than a hundred sites, has used this evidence to reconstruct the building history of individual villages house by house. His conclusion is that most settlements were remarkably short-lived, often occupied for only ten to twenty years before the community moved elsewhere. The precision of his work is extraordinary. Yet a felling date tells us when a tree was cut, not how long the building it supported continued to be used, and timber may have been reused or houses repaired with wood that leaves no trace. His estimates of occupation may therefore be on the short side.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What makes these sites so valuable is the quality of preservation. In the waterlogged, oxygen-poor sediments of the lake floor, materials that normally vanish within a few years have survived for five thousand years or more: seeds, textiles, wooden containers, fishing nets, even loaves of bread. Such conditions are, however, increasingly under threat. Paula Inchauspe, who coordinates monitoring work for a regional lake conservation authority, has documented the erosion of numerous sites, which she attributes mainly to two causes: the regulation of lakes for hydroelectric power and flood control, which has lowered average water levels, and the waves produced by motorboats. Where erosion has exposed archaeological layers, her team has covered them with synthetic fabric and a protective layer of gravel. Monitoring shows that this has proved effective in slowing the damage. The method is not cheap, though, and with hundreds of sites at risk it cannot be applied everywhere.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The lake villages remain enormously popular with the public, and several open-air museums have built life-size reconstructions. Agata Wisniowiecka, who studies the presentation of archaeology in museums, has criticised many of them for presenting houses perched on tall stilts above the water, an interpretation that few specialists would now defend. A reconstruction, she argues, is so persuasive physically that it tends to fix a single interpretation in visitors' minds long after researchers have abandoned it. I share some of her concern, but reconstructions also give people an experience no text can match, and the answer is surely not to dismantle them but to explain openly that they represent one possibility among several.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In recent years, a large group of these sites has been granted international heritage status, a decision that has brought welcome publicity. Yet the effect should not be overstated. Most of the sites are invisible beneath water or mud, and their survival depends far less on international recognition than on decisions taken by local authorities about the construction of marinas, the dredging of channels and the routes of boat traffic. Protection, in practice, is decided at the level of the town council rather than that of the international committee.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Over a century and a half, then, the lake dwellings have been transformed from a romantic emblem of national origins into a sophisticated laboratory for studying prehistoric life year by year. The questions have become more precise, but the underlying fragility of the evidence has not changed, and it is now arguably greater than at any time since the posts first emerged from the mud.

topic: who made Palaeolithic hand stencils: digit-ratio sexing, hand size, children's finger flutings and the missing-finger puzzle
title: Hands on the Rock
subtitle: Prehistoric hand stencils seem to record individual visitors to the caves, but identifying those visitors has proved far harder than it first appeared

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the images left on cave walls during the last Ice Age, few feel as personal as the hand stencil. To make one, a person pressed a hand flat against the rock and sprayed pigment around it, either directly from the mouth or through a hollow tube of bone or reed. When the hand was withdrawn, a negative outline remained: a pale palm and fingers framed by a halo of red or black. Such stencils occur in caves in western Europe, on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, in Patagonia and across northern Australia. Unlike the bison and horses painted nearby, they appear to record not an idea but a particular body at a particular moment. For most of the twentieth century, specialists assumed without much discussion that the hands belonged to adult men, largely because the animal imagery around them was taken to be the work of hunters. That assumption, it now seems clear, revealed more about the expectations of modern scholars than about the people of the Palaeolithic.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious attempt to test it came from the physical anthropologist Iolanda Strzelczyk of the Danubian Institute for Human Origins. Her method relied on a well-documented pattern in living populations: on average, women's index fingers are almost as long as their ring fingers, whereas men's index fingers tend to be noticeably shorter. By measuring these proportions on stencils from eight European caves, Strzelczyk concluded that roughly three quarters of the hands had been made by women. The finding attracted wide attention beyond academic circles, appearing in newspapers under headlines announcing that the first artists had been female.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Other researchers were less impressed. Kaito Morishige, a biostatistician at the Pacific Centre for Quantitative Archaeology, has pointed out that the difference between the sexes is a difference of averages. The ranges for men and women overlap so extensively that a single hand cannot be classified with any confidence, and a misclassification rate of one in three is not unusual even with living subjects. Morishige also notes that stencils are imperfect records. Because the pigment is blown rather than painted, the edges of the image are often blurred, and a slight change in the angle at which the hand was held can alter the apparent length of each finger. Finally, finger proportions vary between modern populations, and there are no comparative data from Ice Age people against which the stencils could be checked. These objections are serious, but they do not, in my view, make the method worthless; they show that its results should be expressed as broad probabilities rather than as confident headcounts.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different approach was taken by a team under Ngozi Eluwa at the West African School of Archaeological Science. Rather than examining the ratio between fingers, Eluwa's group concentrated on the overall size of each hand, comparing the stencils with measurements gathered from present-day foraging communities. They found that a substantial share of the hands were too small to belong to fully grown adults of either sex and were most consistent with adolescents. The implication is that the caves were visited by mixed groups that included young people, perhaps as part of some form of instruction or initiation. Whatever the precise figures, this change of emphasis, from asking whether the makers were men or women to asking who was present and why, strikes me as considerably more productive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The presence of the young is confirmed by a quite different kind of trace. In several French caves, the soft clay coating of the walls is covered with finger flutings, lines drawn by running the fingertips across the surface. Rhiannon Cadwgan, an archaeologist who has spent more than a decade recording these marks, measures the width of the fluted lines to estimate the size of the fingers that produced them. Some sets of lines are so narrow that they must have been made by children of two or three years old, and their height on the wall indicates that these children were lifted up by an adult. Here, at least, the evidence is difficult to dispute: very young children were taken hundreds of metres into dark, difficult cave passages.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even more puzzling are stencils in which one or more fingers appear to be missing. In one Pyrenean cave, the majority of the hands show shortened digits. Early commentators proposed that fingers had been lost to frostbite or removed in sacrificial rituals. A more recent suggestion is that the fingers were simply folded down, and that the different combinations formed a code, perhaps comparable to the silent signals used by some hunters when approaching prey. The amputation theory seems improbable to me, since the same few patterns recur with a regularity that injury or ritual would hardly produce. The idea of a gestural code is attractive, but it is difficult to see what evidence could ever confirm it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It should be acknowledged, too, that knowing who made a stencil would not tell us why it was made. Some researchers have argued that the act of touching the rock mattered more than the image left behind, and that the cave wall was regarded as a boundary between the human world and another realm. Such interpretations are impossible to verify, yet they are a useful reminder that the stencils may have had nothing to do with self-portraiture. The most lasting contribution of the debate may therefore be a negative one. It has not produced a reliable census of Palaeolithic artists, and probably never will, but it has dismantled the comfortable belief that the making of images was the business of grown men alone.

area: rock art and early symbolic behaviour
topic: Middle Stone Age red ochre: symbolic colour preference versus practical uses as adhesive and sun protection, sourcing and processing kits
title: Red Earth
subtitle: Was ochre the first medium of symbolic expression, or simply a useful mineral? The answer may depend on what we think the question means

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the debris left at African sites occupied during the Middle Stone Age, archaeologists repeatedly encounter lumps of ochre, an earth coloured by iron oxides that ranges in hue from yellow and brown to a deep, saturated red. Many pieces bear the facets and striations produced by grinding, and a handful carry deliberately incised lines. For several decades these finds were treated as one of the clearest indications that the humans of the period possessed fully modern minds. Red pigment, it was reasoned, could only have been wanted for painting bodies or objects, and such painting implies the use of colour to communicate identity, status or belief. The argument has an appealing simplicity, but the leap from a ground lump of mineral to a system of shared meanings was, I believe, made far too readily, and the discipline is still dealing with the consequences.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest case for a symbolic reading has been made by Khumbulani Zwelethu of the Highveld Centre for Palaeoanthropology. Zwelethu has mapped the pigment deposits within walking distance of several cave sites and compared them with the material actually recovered from the excavated layers. Again and again, he reports, the occupants ignored nearby sources of yellow and brown earth and carried home pieces of the brightest red available, sometimes from considerably further away. A purely practical motive, he argues, would not produce such a consistent preference for one particular shade. He also points to engraved fragments bearing cross-hatched patterns, which seem to have been made to be looked at rather than used.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The practical alternative has been developed most fully through experiment. Margaux Duquesne, an archaeological chemist at the Laboratoire des Matériaux Anciens, has reconstructed the adhesives with which stone points were fixed to wooden shafts. Glues made from plant gum alone, she found, tend to crack when dry, whereas the same gum mixed with powdered ochre forms a bond that withstands repeated impact. Emil Kerreth, an ethnographer at the Baltic Institute of Human Ecology, has proposed a further use. Drawing on accounts of present-day herding peoples who coat their skin with mixtures of ochre and animal fat, he suggests that the pigment protected early humans from intense sun and from biting insects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Debates of this kind are often framed as a choice between symbol and tool, but the dichotomy is a false one. A substance that is valued for practical reasons can easily acquire additional meanings, and the fact that ochre strengthened glue does not prevent it from also having been used to decorate a body. That said, the functional findings do not explain everything. Duquesne's results show that what improves an adhesive is the iron content of the mineral, which is not closely linked to how red it looks; a dull brown earth with plenty of iron serves just as well. The preference for vivid red documented by Zwelethu therefore remains unaccounted for, and it is, to my mind, the most persuasive evidence that colour itself mattered to these people.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third line of inquiry concerns where the ochre came from. Aroha Taupaki, a geochemist at the Southern Pacific Archaeometry Unit, analyses the trace elements in archaeological pigment and matches them with the chemical signatures of known deposits. Some of the pieces she has examined were obtained from sources well over a hundred kilometres from the sites in which they were found, a distance that suggests either long seasonal journeys or exchange between neighbouring groups. Taupaki interprets these networks as evidence of social ties extending across large territories. This is plausible, yet it needs to be stated plainly that exchange alone proves very little about symbolism, since people have always traded things simply because they are useful.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most revealing evidence of all comes not from the ochre itself but from the way it was prepared. At one coastal cave, excavators recovered two large shells that had served as containers for a liquid mixture of ground ochre, crushed bone, charcoal and quartz grains. Paloma Ferreiro, who led the analysis of the find for the Iberian Society for Prehistoric Research, argues that producing such a compound required a sequence of steps carried out in a fixed order, along with the collection of ingredients from several locations in advance. In her view, the question of whether the result was used as paint or as a preservative is secondary. What the containers demonstrate is the capacity to plan, to follow a recipe and to anticipate a future need.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ferreiro's approach strikes me as the most promising route out of a long and repetitive argument. Symbolic behaviour, by its nature, leaves no unambiguous trace: a line scratched on a piece of ochre may be a sign, a tally or idle doodling, and no amount of excavation can recover the intention behind it. The cognitive abilities required to locate, transport and process a material, by contrast, can be inferred with reasonable confidence from the physical evidence. Researchers who insist on proving that ochre carried meaning may be asking a question that the archaeological record is simply unable to answer, however much new material is uncovered.

area: rock art and early symbolic behaviour
topic: archaeoacoustics of decorated caves: whether Palaeolithic artists placed images at points of strong resonance, measurement methods, lithophones and altered cave acoustics
title: Echoes in the Dark
subtitle: Did the makers of Ice Age cave paintings choose their walls by ear as well as by eye?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, explanations of Palaeolithic cave art have concentrated almost entirely on what can be seen. Researchers have catalogued the animals depicted, measured the proportions of horses and bison, and debated whether the images record hunting magic, seasonal gatherings or the visions of ritual specialists. Yet the caves in which these images were made are not silent places. A voice raised in a narrow passage may die away almost instantly, while a single clap in a broad chamber can return as a series of overlapping echoes lasting several seconds. Over the past three decades a small field known as archaeoacoustics has asked whether the people who painted these walls were responding to such effects, and whether sound, as much as light, shaped where art was placed. It is a question worth asking, although, as this article will suggest, it has so far proved easier to pose than to answer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea first gained attention through the work of Aino Saarenpää, an acoustician at the Turku Institute of Sound and Space, who in the late 1990s carried a portable loudspeaker and microphone through several decorated caves in southern Europe. Saarenpää sang and played short tones at intervals along each passage and recorded how long the sound took to fade. Her conclusion was striking: the points of strongest resonance coincided, far more often than chance would predict, with concentrations of painted images. In narrow tunnels where no animals were drawn, she reported, red dots or short lines frequently marked places where the echo was unusually rich. She proposed that early artists had, in effect, mapped the acoustic landscape of the caves, and that ceremonies in front of the paintings were accompanied by chanting or rhythmic sound.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Saarenpää's findings were widely reported, and it is easy to see why. They offered a vivid picture of Ice Age ritual that went beyond the familiar image of a lone artist working by lamplight. Her method, however, was criticised almost at once. Dimitris Zervoudakis, an archaeologist at the Aegean Institute of Prehistory, pointed out that Saarenpää had chosen her measuring points herself, often by moving towards the paintings, and that the human voice is an imprecise instrument for testing resonance. More importantly, painted panels are often found in large chambers, and large chambers tend to produce long echoes for purely physical reasons. If both the art and the resonance simply reflect the size of the space, Zervoudakis argued, the correlation between them says little about the intentions of the artists.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second generation of studies attempted to address these problems. A team led by Mariam Qorbani, a statistician at the Centre for Quantitative Archaeology in Montpellier, used computer-controlled sweeps of sound rather than singing, and took measurements every two metres throughout five caves, regardless of whether art was present. Once the size of each chamber was taken into account, the link between resonance and painted animals largely disappeared. A weaker association survived, however, for the small dots and lines, which remained more common at acoustically lively points in narrow passages. Qorbani is cautious about interpreting even this result. She notes that such points are often where passages bend or narrow, places that a traveller moving in near darkness might well mark simply to avoid getting lost.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In my view, Qorbani's work represents a genuine advance, because it treats the absence of art as evidence rather than ignoring it. Too many earlier studies sampled only decorated walls and then expressed surprise that the decorated walls were acoustically interesting. Still, it would be wrong to conclude that the acoustic hypothesis has been refuted. Statistical methods can only detect patterns that are consistent across many sites, and there is no reason to assume that every Palaeolithic community responded to sound in the same way, or at all. A practice that mattered greatly in one valley may simply vanish from view when results from several regions are combined.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers believe the more promising evidence lies elsewhere. Tomasz Brzezicki, an ethnomusicologist at the Kraków Academy of Music and Archaeology, has drawn attention to stalactites and curtain-like calcite formations that ring like bells when struck. In several decorated caves these formations carry chips and polished patches consistent with repeated striking, and a few are themselves painted. Fragments of bird-bone flutes have also been recovered from cave sites, though rarely close to the art. Brzezicki argues that the worn formations are more persuasive than any echo survey, since they record something people did rather than a property of the rock. Sceptics respond that similar damage could have been caused by cave bears or by later visitors, and that dating the marks is almost impossible. The objection is fair, but it applies with equal force to many interpretations of Palaeolithic sites that are widely accepted, and it should not be used selectively.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that the caves themselves have changed. Entrances have been widened, floors lowered for tourist walkways and sediment removed by excavators, so measurements taken today may describe spaces quite unlike those the artists knew. Ewa Sokolnicka, a specialist in digital modelling, has begun using laser scans to rebuild the original floor levels of two caves in a computer and simulate how sound would have travelled through them. Her early results suggest that some chambers were considerably less resonant in the Ice Age than they are now. The archaeoacoustic question, then, will probably never be settled by measurement alone. Its most valuable contribution may be less any particular finding than a change of perspective: a reminder that caves were experienced through every sense, and not merely viewed.

topic: perforated marine shell beads as the earliest personal ornaments: deliberate versus natural perforation, use-wear experiments, symbolic cognition versus social-network explanations and gaps in the record
title: Small Shells, Large Claims
subtitle: Tiny pierced shells are among the oldest known ornaments, but what they reveal about the minds of their wearers is fiercely disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the most unassuming objects in any museum of prehistory are small marine shells, each no larger than a fingernail, pierced by a single hole. Shells of this kind, many belonging to a family of sea snails known as nassariids, have been recovered from sites in North Africa, the Levant and southern Africa, some of them dated to more than 100,000 years ago. To many archaeologists they represent something of far greater significance than their size suggests: the earliest firm evidence that humans adorned their bodies with objects whose value was social rather than practical. If that interpretation is correct, the beads mark a threshold in the history of the human mind. Whether it is correct, however, depends on a chain of inferences, every link of which has at some point been challenged.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first link concerns whether the holes were made deliberately. Shells washed up on beaches are frequently perforated by natural processes: predatory snails bore into their prey, and waves grind thin areas of shell until they break. Thandeka Makhubedu, a malacologist at the Eastern Cape Coastal Research Unit, collected several thousand modern shells from beaches and compared their holes with those on archaeological specimens. Natural perforations, she found, are scattered across the shell surface, whereas the ancient examples are overwhelmingly concentrated in one spot near the opening, where the shell is thinnest and a hole would allow it to hang neatly on a cord. Makhubedu concedes that some ancient collectors may have picked out shells that were already holed, but argues that even such selection implies a purpose.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The second link concerns use. Rodrigo Inostroza, an experimental archaeologist at the Valparaíso Laboratory of Prehistoric Technology, threaded modern shells onto cords of plant fibre and leather and asked volunteers to wear them for several weeks. The friction of cord and neighbouring shells produced distinctive smooth, shiny facets around the holes, closely matching the wear on many archaeological beads. Some ancient shells also carry traces of red pigment, which Inostroza attributes either to deliberate colouring or to contact with skin and clothing that had been treated with ochre. The wear studies are, to my mind, the most persuasive evidence in this whole debate, because they rest on direct observation rather than on assumptions about what early humans were likely to have wanted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Interpretation is far less secure. Gulnara Amanzholova, a cognitive archaeologist at the Almaty Centre for Human Origins, maintains that wearing beads requires a capacity for symbolic thought equivalent to that of living people: the wearer must understand that an object can stand for something else, such as membership of a group, marital status or rank, and that others will read it in the same way. On this view, the beads are evidence of fully modern language, since only shared language could sustain such conventions. Many researchers find this reasoning attractive, but it asks a great deal of a handful of shells. A string of beads might equally have been worn because it was pleasing to look at, or because it rattled agreeably, without encoding any message at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more modest alternative comes from Pieter Uyttenhove, an anthropologist at the Ghent Institute for Social Evolution, who regards ornaments as a response to changing social conditions rather than as a sign of new mental abilities. Beads, he points out, are most useful when people regularly meet strangers, since kin and close neighbours already know who one is. Their appearance might therefore reflect growing populations or wider networks of exchange, not a change in the brain. This would also explain a puzzling feature of the record: after the early examples, shell beads seem to disappear from many regions for tens of thousands of years before becoming common again. If ornaments signalled a permanent cognitive change, such a gap is hard to account for; if they responded to social circumstances, it is much less surprising.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Uyttenhove's model is appealing, but it has difficulties of its own. Estimating population size from Middle Stone Age sites is notoriously uncertain, and the argument risks becoming circular if the presence of beads is then used as evidence of larger populations. Moreover, the apparent gap in the record may partly reflect rising sea levels, which have submerged many of the coastlines where shell-using communities would have lived. The absence of beads from the surviving inland sites is not necessarily evidence that they were no longer being made.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One further observation complicates every account. Some of the shells have been found more than a hundred kilometres from the nearest ancient shoreline, implying either exchange between groups or deliberate journeys to the coast. Either way, people were prepared to invest considerable effort in obtaining them. What the debate shows, perhaps, is that the beads cannot by themselves settle the question of when humans became 'modern', a concept which, I would argue, has outlived its usefulness, since it implies a single moment of transformation that the evidence does not support. The shells do demonstrate that, far earlier than was once believed, people spent time modifying objects in order to wear them. That alone is remarkable, even if the meanings attached to them are now beyond recovery.
