area: rock art and early symbolic behaviour
topic: engraved ostrich eggshell water flasks in southern Africa: stable motif traditions, group identity versus ownership marks, ethnographic analogy, engraving skill and abrupt changes in design
title: Lines of Intent
subtitle: Engraved eggshell flasks from southern Africa offer a rare chance to trace how a pattern was passed between generations

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the dry interior of southern Africa, water has always been the first condition of survival, and for tens of thousands of years one of the most effective ways of carrying it has been the shell of an ostrich egg. Emptied through a small hole and sealed with a plug of grass, a single shell holds about a litre, weighs very little and is remarkably robust. Hunter-gatherers in the Kalahari were still using such flasks in the twentieth century, burying full ones in the sand along their seasonal routes as reserves for the driest months. What has turned these humble containers into a subject of intense archaeological interest is the discovery, at several rock shelters near the western coast, of fragments bearing deliberately engraved geometric patterns that are more than 60,000 years old.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The largest collection comes from a shelter excavated over a decade by a team under Lerato Mfundisi of the Western Cape Heritage Institute, which recovered more than three hundred engraved fragments from a sequence of layers spanning several thousand years. What makes the assemblage remarkable is not the complexity of the designs, which are simple, consisting of bands of parallel lines sometimes crossed by shorter strokes, but their regularity. In the lower layers, one motif, a band filled with closely spaced hatching, dominates almost completely. Higher up, it gives way rather abruptly to a design of parallel lines that never cross. Mfundisi interprets these as two successive traditions, each a set of rules for decoration that people learned from one another and maintained over many generations. In her view, the patterns functioned as markers of collective identity, signalling that a flask, and perhaps the person carrying it, belonged to a particular community.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This is a bold reading, and the evidence for its first part is strong. A pattern that remains stable for thousands of years cannot plausibly be the product of individual whim; it must have been taught, copied and, to some degree, enforced. Whether the second part follows is far less certain. The fact that a design was shared within a group does not mean that it was intended to distinguish that group from others. Many conventions, from the shape of a spoon to the way a basket is woven, persist simply because that is how things are done, and are noticed by outsiders, if at all, only by accident.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different perspective comes from Ilka Kerekes-Tóth, an anthropologist at the Budapest Centre for Comparative Ethnography, who spent two years recording how flasks are decorated in present-day Kalahari communities. She found that decoration was largely personal: owners engraved their flasks with designs of their own choosing, and a person could often pick out his or her own flask at a glance from dozens stored together. On this evidence, the ancient patterns might indicate ownership rather than group membership. Kerekes-Tóth herself, however, is careful to stress that sixty millennia separate her informants from the makers of the archaeological fragments, and that the striking uniformity of the ancient designs sits uneasily with the variety she observed. Analogy of this kind is valuable for suggesting possibilities, but it cannot, on its own, decide between them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have turned their attention from meaning to manufacture. Haja Ravelonarivo, a materials scientist at the Antananarivo Laboratory of Archaeological Materials, made replicas of the stone points found at the shelter, used them to engrave fresh eggshell, and compared the resulting grooves under a microscope with the ancient ones. Many of the archaeological lines, he found, were cut in several strokes along the same path, gradually deepening the groove, and their depth is strikingly consistent. Ravelonarivo concludes that the engravers were practised hands, and suggests that decoration may have been the task of a few skilled individuals rather than of every flask owner. That conclusion seems to me to go somewhat further than the microscope can take us: uniform grooves show that the engravers were skilled, but not how many of them there were.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The abrupt change between motifs has attracted its own explanation. Bolormaa Altankhuyag, an archaeologist at the Ulaanbaatar School of Quantitative Prehistory, used statistical models to test whether the shift was gradual or sudden. Her analysis indicates that the hatched design disappeared within a few centuries, an instant in archaeological terms, and that the change coincided with a period of increasing aridity recorded in pollen from nearby lake sediments. She proposes that harsher conditions forced people to range more widely and to mix with neighbouring groups, and that the new motif may reflect the merging of formerly separate populations. The hypothesis is ingenious, but the dating of the shelter layers is too imprecise to establish that the two events truly overlapped.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the flasks show most clearly, I would argue, is that symbolic behaviour was woven into the most practical activities of daily life. These were not objects made for ceremony or display but containers for water, the most ordinary of necessities. That people took the trouble to decorate them, and to do so according to shared rules over thousands of years, reveals as much about early human societies as any painted cave wall. Excavators have sometimes been tempted to look for the origins of art in spectacular settings; the eggshell fragments suggest that it may be found just as readily in the contents of a hunter's bag. Even if the precise meaning of the lines is lost, their persistence is itself a kind of message.

area: rock art and early symbolic behaviour
topic: conserving painted Palaeolithic caves versus public access: visitor effects on cave climate, microbial outbreaks caused by interventions, visitor capacity limits and full-scale replica caves
title: The Price of a Glimpse
subtitle: Painted caves survived for millennia in darkness; a few decades of visitors have put some of them at risk

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The paintings of the Ice Age owe their survival less to the skill of their makers than to the conditions in which they were left. Deep inside a limestone cave, temperature varies by a fraction of a degree across the year, the air is close to saturation, light is absent and the exchange of air with the outside world is slow. In such an environment pigments bound to the rock can remain stable for tens of thousands of years. The opening of decorated caves to the public in the middle of the twentieth century disturbed this equilibrium almost overnight. Each visitor exhales carbon dioxide and water vapour and gives off heat equivalent to a small electric bulb, and when visitors arrive in their thousands each day the cumulative effect is considerable. Electric lighting, installed so that the paintings could be admired, allowed green films of algae to colonise walls that had never before seen light. Several celebrated caves were closed within two decades of opening, although by then some of the damage was already irreversible.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Closure, however, did not bring the problems to an end, and in some cases it ushered in new ones. Marta Palomeque, a microbiologist at the Institute for Subterranean Conservation in Bilbao, has reconstructed the history of the Grotte de Vérane, a cave in south-western France that was sealed to tourists in 1968. In 2001 its ageing air-conditioning plant was replaced with a more powerful system, and within months white fungal filaments had spread across the floor and the lower parts of the walls. Conservators responded with biocides and quicklime. The fungus retreated, but the chemicals provided nutrients for bacteria, which flourished in its place, and dark stains subsequently appeared close to several of the paintings. Palomeque's conclusion is uncomfortable: in Vérane, at least, well-intentioned interventions by specialists have done more harm than the visitors they were designed to replace. She argues that the safest policy is to do as little as possible, accepting slow natural change rather than attempting to control it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more technical approach has been taken by Riikka Keskitalo, an environmental engineer at the Oulu Centre for Cave Climate Studies, who has installed networks of sensors in three caves in northern Spain. Her measurements show that even a single person standing in a chamber for twenty minutes raises its temperature measurably, and that the cave may take several hours to return to its previous state. From such data she has calculated what she calls a visitor capacity: the number of people a cave can receive without its climate drifting beyond its natural range. For the Cueva de Ollaberri the figure is strikingly low, around five people for half an hour once a week. Since 2014 the cave has admitted exactly that number, chosen each week by lottery from among visitors to the local museum.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the great majority of people, the only way of seeing such paintings is now through copies. Full-scale replicas, built close to the original caves, have become major attractions. The first, completed in 1983, was produced by a team of sculptors and painters who reproduced the contours of the rock from survey drawings and photographs. The latest generation uses laser scanning and three-dimensional printing to reproduce the walls to within a millimetre, after which artists apply pigments by hand using the same techniques as the original painters. Jonas Kirschbaumer, a heritage economist at the University of Graz, has studied the finances of four such sites. He found that ticket revenue from the replicas not only covers their running costs but in several cases funds monitoring of the original caves, and that surrounding towns depend heavily on the visitors they attract. In surveys, he notes, most visitors describe themselves as satisfied, and many are unaware until told that they have not entered the original cave.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The replicas are, without question, an impressive technical achievement, and the economic argument for them is hard to dispute. Yet it would be a mistake to regard them as a complete solution. A copy can reproduce the appearance of a painted wall, but not the experience of descending into the earth to reach it, nor the knowledge that the marks before one's eyes were made by human hands some twenty thousand years ago. There is also a subtler danger. Once a perfect digital record exists, the temptation is to treat the original as a mere source of data, whose survival matters less because its image has been secured. That attitude, in my view, would represent a quiet but real loss.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Palomeque and Keskitalo disagree sharply over what should follow. Palomeque believes that any human presence, however brief, risks introducing microbes on clothing and footwear, and that no visitor capacity can be considered safe while the microbial ecology of caves is so poorly understood. Keskitalo replies that her limits are deliberately cautious and that a small, carefully controlled stream of visitors helps to sustain the public interest on which conservation budgets ultimately depend. Both positions have merit, but Keskitalo's seems to me the more realistic. Caves that disappear entirely from public experience risk disappearing from public concern as well.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the history of these sites teaches, above all, is humility. Every generation of custodians has believed that it understood the cave environment well enough to manage it, and each has been proved at least partly wrong. Sensors, lotteries and replicas are useful tools, but none of them removes the fundamental uncertainty. The paintings have outlasted ice sheets and rising seas; it would be a bitter irony if they were lost within a single century of human admiration.

area: rock art and early symbolic behaviour
topic: the trance or neuropsychological theory of rock art: San ethnography, laboratory stages of altered consciousness, extension to Palaeolithic Europe and objections from archaeology, neuroscience and ethnography
title: Visions on the Wall?
subtitle: A bold theory links some of the world's oldest images to altered states of mind. How far can it be stretched?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Alongside the animals and human figures that fill the world's rock art, there are countless images of a different kind: grids, zigzags, rows of dots, nested curves and spirals. For much of the twentieth century these geometric forms were treated as an embarrassment, too abstract to be explained and too common to be ignored. In the 1980s an ambitious proposal offered a way out. Many of these marks, it was suggested, depict images seen in altered states of consciousness, and a good deal of rock art is a record of the visions experienced by ritual specialists. Within a generation the idea had become the most influential explanation of rock art in existence. It has also become one of the most fiercely disputed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theory is most closely associated with Sizwe Mahlangu-Dube, then a researcher at the Drakensberg Rock Art Archive. His starting point was a collection of nineteenth-century interviews with San people of southern Africa, in which informants described healers who entered a trance through hours of rhythmic dancing and clapping. In this state, healers reported bleeding from the nose, feeling as though they were underwater and turning into animals. Mahlangu-Dube noticed that the region's paintings included figures with lines running from their noses, figures bent forward at the waist as dancers were said to be, and beings that were part human and part antelope. He then turned to laboratory studies of altered consciousness. These suggested three broad stages: in the first, people see bright geometric shapes generated by the nervous system itself; in the second, they try to make sense of these shapes as familiar objects; and in the third, they experience full hallucinations, often preceded by a sensation of being drawn through a tunnel. Since the nervous system is common to all humans, Mahlangu-Dube argued, the model might also apply to the painted caves of Ice Age Europe.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In southern Africa, the case is strong. The link between painted images and recorded testimony is direct, and few specialists now doubt that some San art refers to the experiences of healers in trance. The difficulty lies in the leap to Europe, where no informants survive and the paintings are four or five times older. Here the argument rests not on what painters said but on what their brains are presumed to have done, and that is a considerably weaker foundation. Nothing guarantees that the European painters danced, fasted or sang in the way that nineteenth-century San healers did, or that they valued visions at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most persistent critic of the extension has been Henrik Lundevall, an archaeologist at the Uppsala Institute of Prehistoric Studies. He observes that grids, dots and zigzags are so simple that they could arise from almost any activity, whether counting, decorating the body or imitating the patterns of woven fibres. More seriously, he argues that the model is constructed in a way that makes it impossible to test. If a cave contains geometric signs, they are attributed to the first stage; if it contains animals, these are taken to be third-stage hallucinations; and if it contains few signs of either, the visions are said to have gone unrecorded. A theory that can accommodate any evidence whatsoever, Lundevall concludes, explains nothing.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Objections have also come from neuroscience. Achieng Odhiambo-Kuria, who studies visual perception at the Nairobi Institute of Brain Sciences, points out that most of the laboratory work on which the three-stage model depends was carried out on Western volunteers in the mid-twentieth century, many of them under the influence of drugs. She does not dispute that the visual system can generate geometric patterns spontaneously. However, she notes that what people report seeing, and how they describe it, is heavily shaped by their expectations and their cultural background. The sense of passing through a tunnel, for example, may be far less universal than the model assumes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third line of criticism concerns the vocabulary of the debate. Mayumi Okazawa, an anthropologist at the Sapporo Centre for Comparative Ethnography, argues that the term 'shaman', originally borrowed from Siberia, has been stretched to cover healers, diviners and ritual leaders in societies that have little else in common. Moreover, ethnographic records from Australia and North America show that rock art was frequently produced by ordinary members of a community, during initiation, for instance, or to mark a route, rather than by specialists of any kind. Okazawa does not deny that trance played a part in some traditions, but she warns that a single label can create the impression of a worldwide religion where none existed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, though, to dismiss the theory entirely, as some critics now appear inclined to do. Its great achievement was to insist that rock art meant something specific to the people who made it and to connect images with bodily experience in a way that earlier interpretations had not. The appropriate response to its weaknesses is not to reject it but to restrict it: to treat altered states as one possible explanation among several, to be applied where independent evidence supports it, rather than as a key that will open every cave. Used in that way, it still has much to offer.

area: rock art and early symbolic behaviour
topic: where figurative art began: early cave paintings in island Southeast Asia, the decline of the European 'human revolution' model, preservation and research-intensity biases, and demographic explanations
title: A Revolution Revisited
subtitle: Discoveries far from Europe have unsettled a long-standing story about the birth of art

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, textbooks told a confident story about the origins of art. Around 40,000 years ago, shortly after modern humans arrived in Europe, there was a sudden flowering of creativity: painted caves, carved figurines, bone flutes and elaborate personal ornaments appeared within a few thousand years of one another. Supporters of what became known as the 'human revolution' model concluded that something fundamental had changed, perhaps a genetic mutation affecting the brain, perhaps the emergence of fully developed language, and that Europe was where the consequences first became visible. The story was understandable given what was known at the time. Most of the evidence had been excavated by European scholars working within reach of their own universities, and the spectacular painted caves of France and Spain seemed to have no rivals anywhere else.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That picture has been shaken by work at the other end of Eurasia. A team led by Prasert Kaewkhao of the Mekong Institute of Prehistory spent a decade recording paintings in the limestone caves of islands in eastern Indonesia. By dating thin mineral crusts that had formed over the pigment, the team showed that images of wild pigs and other animals, together with numerous hand stencils, were at least as old as the earliest figurative art in Europe, and in some cases older. One panel shows small figures with apparently animal features confronting much larger animals, and has been widely described as the oldest known depiction of a story. Kaewkhao argues that figurative art must therefore either have been invented independently at both ends of the continent or have formed part of the cultural repertoire carried by people dispersing out of Africa.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts the more dramatic readings of these finds. Yelena Ostrovskaya, a specialist in dating methods at the Siberian Centre for Archaeometry, points out that dates obtained from crusts are minimum ages: the crust must have formed after the painting, so the image itself could be considerably older than the figure reported. This, if anything, strengthens the claim for early art. Her reservations concern interpretation. The figures on the celebrated panel, she observes, may have been added over many centuries by different hands, in which case they were never intended to be read together as a single scene. I share her caution. To call the panel a story is to assume that its makers composed images as modern illustrators do, and that is precisely what needs to be demonstrated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If art was not born in Europe, where did the capacity for it come from? Grace Wanjugu, an archaeologist at the Kampala Centre for Human Evolution, believes that it was present in African populations well before any of them left the continent, a conclusion supported by engraved and pigment-stained objects from African sites that are far older than any cave painting. What varied, in her view, was not ability but opportunity. Skills such as painting are easily lost unless enough people are in regular contact to learn them from one another, so art should appear wherever populations became large and well connected, and fade where they did not. Its emergence in Europe and Southeast Asia would then reflect demographic conditions rather than any change in the brain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Two further researchers argue that the geography of early art says more about modern archaeology than about ancient people. Gábor Székelyhidi, a geomorphologist at the Debrecen Institute of Rock Weathering, has shown experimentally that pigment on exposed rock faces typically fades beyond recognition within a few thousand years; only in deep caves, or where mineral layers have sealed the surface, does it survive for tens of millennia. Andrés Jaramillo-Pinto, of the Bogotá Laboratory for Archaeological Survey, has compiled data on the number of excavations carried out in different regions over the past century. In parts of south-western France, he found, the density of investigation exceeds that of most of Africa and Asia by a factor of several hundred. On his account, the apparent centres of early art are largely a map of where archaeologists have chosen to dig.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these arguments leave the old European revolution looking less like an event in human history than a product of the history of research. Yet the critics should be wary of replacing one simplification with another. It would be wrong to assume that every gap in the record is the result of bias. Several African regions have now been studied intensively, and figurative painting there still appears later than in Europe or Indonesia. Preservation and research effort can explain a great deal, but not everything, and the uneven appearance of art may reflect genuine differences between societies that deserve explanation in their own right.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the deepest lesson is that the search for a single birthplace of art was misguided from the start. The emerging picture is of a capacity that was widely shared, expressed in different ways and at different times, appearing and disappearing as circumstances changed. If that is so, the next surprises are likely to come not from the well-trodden caves of western Europe but from regions where few archaeologists have yet looked, such as the Arabian Peninsula, the interior of Australia and much of South Asia. The story of art's origins, in other words, is far from finished, and its next chapter will probably be written a long way from the places that dominated the first.

topic: lighting and cave art: fat lamps, torches and hearths in Palaeolithic caves, experimental replicas, apparent movement of images in flickering light and the limits of experimental archaeology
title: By the Light of the Flame
subtitle: How Ice Age cave art looked depended on the light by which it was seen, and that light was nothing like ours

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who visits a painted cave today sees its images under electric light: steady, white and evenly spread across the walls. The people who made the paintings saw them very differently. Their light came from flames, which flicker, cast moving shadows and illuminate only a small area at a time, leaving the rest of the cave in absolute darkness. For a long time this difference was regarded as a practical detail of little interest to anyone trying to understand the art. Over the past two decades, however, a growing number of researchers have argued that light shaped not only how the images were seen but also where and how they were made, and perhaps even what they were meant to do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The archaeological evidence for lighting is more abundant than might be expected. Deepa Kunnumpurath, an archaeobotanist at the Kerala Institute of Archaeological Science, has analysed residues in hollowed stones found in several French and Spanish caves and identified them as lamps that burned animal fat, with twigs of juniper serving as wicks. Scattered fragments of pine charcoal on cave floors show where torches were carried, and black smudges on the walls mark places where people struck burning torches against the rock to remove the charred ends and revive a fading flame. Kunnumpurath's conclusion is that cave visitors did not rely on a single kind of light but chose among several according to the task in hand: torches for moving through passages, lamps for remaining in one place, and occasional fires for lighting larger chambers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How these sources actually performed has been tested by Lucía Benavídez-Cruz, an experimental archaeologist at the Salamanca Laboratory of Prehistoric Technology. Working with replicas built from the same materials, she found that torches gave a bright, wide light and coped well with draughts, but produced a great deal of smoke and lasted only around half an hour. Fat lamps, by contrast, burned steadily for over an hour with little smoke, but were dim, giving roughly the light of a modern candle. Fires lit up a whole chamber, but consumed large amounts of fuel that had to be carried in from outside. On this basis Benavídez-Cruz suggests that painters most likely worked by lamplight, close to the wall, and that larger groups may later have viewed the finished images by the stronger but less stable light of torches.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It is that instability which has attracted the most attention. Arnaud Tchoumba, a psychologist who studies visual perception at the Yaoundé Centre for Cognitive Science, has filmed painted panels lit by moving flames. Animals drawn with several sets of legs or with heads in more than one position, he reports, appear to run, turn or toss their heads as the light shifts, while figures painted over natural bulges in the rock seem to swell outwards from the wall. Tchoumba argues that some artists deliberately exploited these effects, and has described the results, provocatively, as a kind of prehistoric cinema.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The idea is an appealing one, and Tchoumba's recordings leave little doubt that the effect itself is real: anyone who has watched a panel under flickering light can see the animals move. Whether the artists intended it is another matter. A figure with extra legs may have been designed to suggest motion, but it may equally record a correction, or the work of a later painter who added to an earlier image. I also find the language of cinema unhelpful. It invites us to see the caves through the lens of a modern technology, and suggests a passive audience watching a screen, when the people inside the cave were themselves holding and moving the lights.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A broader caution has been voiced by Ivan Prskalo, an art historian at the University of Split who has written extensively on the methods of experimental archaeology. Modern volunteers who take part in lighting experiments, he points out, bring with them a lifetime of exposure to film, television and electric light, and what they notice in the flickering shadows may tell us more about their own expectations than about the perceptions of Ice Age viewers. Replicas, moreover, can never exactly match the fuels, the humidity and the soot-blackened walls of the past. These objections are fair, but they do not make the experiments worthless. Even imperfect tests can rule certain possibilities out; they have shown, for example, that the paintings in deep chambers cannot have been seen without artificial light, and that a single lamp is quite inadequate for viewing a large panel as a whole.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable outcome of this research is a renewed attention to the placement of images. Many paintings are found close to natural ledges where a lamp could be set down, or at bends in a passage where a torch-bearer would pause. Viewing, in other words, was an event, something that took place in time and depended on the movements of the people present. Seen in this light, the bright, even illumination provided for modern visitors is not a neutral window onto the art. It is itself an interpretation, and one that the original artists would probably not have recognised.

topic: rock art of the central Sahara: the traditional stylistic sequence of periods, direct dating showing overlapping styles, the art as an environmental record and herders' readings of cattle paintings
title: Painted Pastures
subtitle: The rock art of the central Sahara records a vanished green landscape, but how faithfully?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The central Sahara is today among the driest places on earth, yet its cliffs and rock shelters carry tens of thousands of paintings and engravings of hippopotamuses, elephants and giraffes, and of great herds of cattle tended by human figures. Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago the region was far wetter than it is now, with permanent lakes, rivers and extensive grasslands. The art produced during and after that period has received only a fraction of the attention devoted to the painted caves of Europe, partly because of the remoteness of the sites and partly because of decades of political instability. This neglect is regrettable, since the Saharan images offer something that European cave art cannot: a visual record spanning both the shift from hunting to herding and the slow drying of an entire landscape.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Early twentieth-century scholars divided the art into a series of successive periods according to its style and subject matter. The oldest, consisting of large engravings of wild animals, was named after an extinct giant buffalo that features prominently in it. It was thought to be followed by paintings of human figures with large, rounded heads, then by a pastoral period dominated by cattle, then by images of horses and chariots, and finally by camels, which were introduced to the region only around two thousand years ago. Moussa Bonaventura-Sy, of the Dakar Institute of Saharan Studies, maintains that this sequence remains broadly correct. Where one image has been painted over another, he points out, the order is remarkably consistent: cattle over round-headed figures, horses over cattle, and never the reverse. The sequence was a reasonable hypothesis when it was first proposed. The difficulty is that it gradually hardened into an established fact and was then used to date individual sites without any independent evidence.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Independent evidence has recently begun to appear. Liam Lomasney, a chemist at the Galway Laboratory for Archaeological Chemistry, has identified traces of milk that were mixed with pigments as a binder in a number of paintings, and has obtained radiocarbon dates from them. His results indicate that some round-headed figures and some cattle scenes were painted within the same few centuries. The styles, in other words, appear to have overlapped rather than succeeding one another neatly, which suggests that groups with different artistic traditions, perhaps foragers and herders, may have lived alongside each other. Bonaventura-Sy has responded that the number of dated paintings is small and that contamination cannot be ruled out. The objection is reasonable as far as it goes, but samples will grow, and the existing results are already enough to show that stylistic labels cannot be treated as a clock.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns what the art can tell us about past environments. Hana Hrubešová, a palaeoecologist at the Brno Centre for Palaeoecology, has compared the animals depicted at more than two hundred sites with pollen preserved in nearby lake sediments and with animal bones recovered by excavation. In broad terms, the evidence agrees: hippopotamuses and crocodiles appear mainly in areas where the lake records confirm the presence of permanent water. The mismatches, however, are revealing. Small antelopes and hares, abundant among the excavated bones, are rarely depicted, while giraffes appear far more often than their remains would lead one to expect. Hrubešová concludes that artists chose their subjects for reasons that had little to do with how common an animal was, and that the images cannot be read as a kind of census.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This finding should give pause to anyone inclined to treat the art as a straightforward environmental archive. A painting of a hippopotamus shows that its maker knew what a hippopotamus looked like, perhaps from travel or from stories, but not necessarily that one lived close by. That does not make the images worthless as evidence. Combined with independent records, they can add a kind of detail that no sediment core will ever supply, namely an indication of how people regarded the animals around them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That question has been taken up by Kemal Özkaraman, an ethnoarchaeologist at the Ankara Institute for Ethnoarchaeology, who spent several seasons showing photographs of the paintings to present-day herding communities in the central Sahara. Elders recognised details that outsiders had overlooked: particular coat patterns which, in their own herds, mark descent from specific animal lineages, and horn shapes that are produced deliberately by training the horns of young animals. Özkaraman argues that the cattle scenes are less records of an economy than expressions of social values such as wealth, kinship and prestige. I find this argument persuasive. Analogies across thousands of years always require caution, but the long continuity of herding in the region makes this one considerably more plausible than most.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: As the Sahara dried after about five thousand years ago, its inhabitants gradually moved towards the Nile valley and the better-watered lands to the south, and the art of the later periods records a world of shrinking pastures and new animals. Its greatest value, I would suggest, lies not in dating changes of climate, which other methods can do more precisely, but in showing how people experienced, and gave meaning to, a landscape that was transforming around them. That is a question of more than historical interest at a time when many societies face environmental change of their own.

topic: the 'original affluent society' debate: how much hunter-gatherers really worked, processing time, seasonal hardship and the meaning of work
title: The Leisure Question
subtitle: Did foragers once enjoy more free time than anyone since? Half a century of argument has produced a more complicated answer

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1960s a provocative idea began to circulate among anthropologists. Hunter-gatherers, it was suggested, were not the half-starved wanderers of popular imagination but the members of an 'original affluent society', people who satisfied their needs with a few hours of effort each day and spent the remainder resting, visiting and talking. The argument drew on a handful of time studies conducted in the Kalahari and in northern Australia, which appeared to show adults devoting between two and five hours daily to obtaining food. Its appeal was obvious. At a time when many in industrial nations were questioning the value of economic growth, foragers offered living proof that a satisfying life did not require ever-increasing production. Half a century later, the idea remains one of the most quoted in anthropology, and one of the most fiercely contested.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious challenge concerned what had been counted. Tomasz Zaborowski, an economic anthropologist at the Institute for Comparative Livelihoods in Kraków, has argued that the original studies measured only the time spent hunting and gathering, while ignoring the labour needed to turn raw resources into something edible or usable. Nuts must be cracked, carcasses butchered, tubers roasted, water carried and firewood collected, and tools and containers must be constantly repaired or replaced. When Zaborowski and his colleagues added these tasks to the totals for three foraging communities, the average working week rose to a figure not far below that of a full-time factory employee. In his view, the image of leisurely foragers arose from an accounting error rather than from any genuine difference in how hard people worked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Folake Akinola, who directs a long-term field project for the West African Institute of Human Ecology, has drawn attention to a different weakness: the reliance on averages. Her team recorded what members of a forest-dwelling community were doing at randomly chosen moments over four years, a technique known as spot sampling. During the months when fruit and honey were abundant, adults did indeed spend much of the day at rest. In the dry season, however, the hours devoted to food collection more than doubled, and weight loss among adults was common. Akinola does not deny that foragers enjoy periods of considerable ease, but she insists that an annual average conceals the stretches of hardship which, for the people concerned, may matter far more.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical objection has come from Anders Skovgaard of the Aarhus Centre for Cultural Anthropology, who questions whether the distinction between work and leisure can be applied to foraging peoples at all. A day spent collecting shellfish, he notes, may involve singing, joking, swimming and the instruction of children, and those who take part rarely describe it as a burden to be endured. To ask how many hours foragers 'work', therefore, is to impose a category that belongs to wage labour. There is considerable force in this argument, since it reminds researchers that the experience of an activity cannot be read off from a stopwatch. Taken to its logical conclusion, though, it would rule out any comparison between societies whatsoever, and that seems too high a price to pay. Energy expended and food obtained can be measured, and such measures, whatever their limitations, tell us something real.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nutritional evidence complicates the picture further. Lucía Villarroel, a human biologist at the Andean Institute of Health Sciences, has compiled data on energy intake and body composition from more than a dozen foraging populations. Many, she found, live close to the margins of energy balance, with children growing more slowly than their counterparts in well-fed populations. For Villarroel, the notion that foragers were affluent because their wants were few comes uncomfortably close to suggesting that people who had little did not mind. Her data are a valuable corrective, but they do not establish that foragers were worse off than the farmers who succeeded them: skeletal evidence from many regions indicates that early agricultural populations were shorter and suffered more dental disease and infection than the hunter-gatherers before them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty is that the foragers studied by twentieth-century researchers were hardly representative of their ancestors. Aigerim Kurmanova, an archaeologist at the Steppe Heritage Institute in Almaty, points out that most surviving hunter-gatherers had been pushed by farmers and herders into deserts, dense forests and Arctic coasts, environments that no one else wanted. Before the spread of agriculture, foragers occupied fertile river valleys and rich coastlines as well. Kurmanova therefore suspects that workloads recorded in marginal habitats overstate the effort required in the past. It is a plausible suggestion, although it is equally possible that the richest environments supported denser populations and therefore more intense competition for food.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, survives of the original claim? Certainly not the picture of a leisured paradise, which owed as much to the anxieties of industrial society as to observation. Yet the debate it provoked has been enormously productive. It forced anthropologists to define what they meant by work, to measure seasonal variation rather than relying on brief visits, and to examine the assumption that the shift to farming represented straightforward progress. On that last point, the critics of the affluence thesis and its defenders now largely agree: agriculture allowed far more people to be fed from the same land, but it seldom made individual lives easier.

topic: demand sharing of meat among hunter-gatherers: insurance, tolerated theft, costly signalling and sharing norms in a cash economy
title: Asking for a Share
subtitle: Why do hunters give away most of what they kill? The answer may say less about generosity than we like to think

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A hunter walks back into camp late in the afternoon carrying an antelope across his shoulders. Within an hour, almost nothing of it belongs to him. Neighbours, cousins and in-laws arrive one after another, and each leaves with a portion. What surprises many outside observers is not the scale of the distribution but its manner. The hunter rarely offers the meat; instead, others ask for it, sometimes quite bluntly, and he is expected to comply. Anthropologists call this pattern demand sharing, and it turns upside down the familiar Western picture in which generosity is something the giver decides to display. Among many foraging peoples, it seems, the responsibility for a gift lies at least as much with the person who requests it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest explanation treats sharing as a form of insurance. Hunting is notoriously unreliable: a skilled man may return empty-handed for days, then kill an animal far too large for his own family to eat before it spoils. By handing out meat when he is lucky, he earns a claim on the meat of others when he is not. Petros Ikonomou, of the Aegean Institute for Evolutionary Studies, has tested this idea with mathematical models built on records of what different households brought into camp over several years. His results suggest that the larger and less predictable a type of food is, the more widely it is distributed. Wild plant foods, which are gathered in modest quantities and on most days, typically stay within the family that collected them, whereas a giraffe or a buffalo may be divided among an entire settlement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Genet Demissew, an anthropologist at the Highland Centre for Social Research in Addis Ababa, finds the insurance account too tidy. In her view, much of what is described as sharing is better understood as tolerated theft. A hunter standing beside a large carcass, surrounded by hungry and insistent relatives, would gain little by refusing them: defending the last portions would cost him more in conflict and resentment than the meat itself is worth. Demissew points to two observations in support. First, hunters often have remarkably little say over who receives what. Second, and more damaging for the insurance theory, the most productive hunters do not, over time, receive as much meat from others as they give away.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That imbalance has encouraged a third explanation. Rūta Kalinauskaitė, who studies the evolution of cooperation at the Baltic Institute of Anthropology, argues that the pursuit of big game is partly a form of display. Bringing down a large animal advertises strength, patience and skill to everyone in the camp, and a man who does so repeatedly may be rewarded with influence, loyal allies and desirable marriage partners. On this view, the meat is less a payment than an advertisement. The theory is ingenious, and it explains why men sometimes hunt dangerous animals when safer prey would provide more food. The evidence that good hunters actually leave more descendants, however, is mixed: in some communities they have more surviving children, while in others no such advantage can be detected.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Hiroshi Yoshinaga, an ecological anthropologist based in Kyoto, believes that the three accounts have been presented as rivals for too long. Different foods, he suggests, are shared for different reasons, and the same act may be insurance, concession and display all at once. More importantly, he stresses that sharing among foragers does not rest on individual calculation alone. Communities maintain strong expectations about distribution, and those who fall short are teased, gossiped about and, in extreme cases, avoided. A boastful hunter may find his kill described as scrawny and worthless, a ritual of mockery designed to keep successful men from thinking too highly of themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The argument matters beyond anthropology, because foragers are frequently recruited as witnesses in wider debates about human nature. Some writers present them as proof that people are naturally generous and that selfishness is a product of markets and property. Others cite the grumbling and pressure that accompany demand sharing as evidence that humans give only when compelled. Both readings, in my view, misuse the ethnographic record. What demand sharing actually demonstrates is that sharing can be obligatory and grudging at the same time, and that a society can be remarkably equal without its members being especially kind.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The practice has also proved surprisingly durable. In communities where foragers now earn wages or sell crafts, relatives commonly ask for money in exactly the way they would once have asked for meat. Some earners respond by spending their income quickly on goods that are harder to claim, and some keep their earnings out of sight altogether. The persistence of demand sharing shows how deeply the norm is rooted, but it would be wrong to romanticise it. For a young person hoping to save for education or a business, the obligation to hand over money on request can be a source of real friction and frustration, and it is far from clear that such tensions will resolve themselves.

topic: complex hunter-gatherers of the North Pacific coast: salmon storage, labour, ownership of fishing sites, ceremonial feasts and the origins of inequality without farming
title: Wealth Without Fields
subtitle: Some foraging societies built villages, ranked their members and kept slaves without ever planting a crop. What made them possible?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, textbooks told a tidy story about the origins of social inequality. Hunter-gatherers, it was assumed, lived in small, mobile and broadly equal bands; only when people began to farm did they settle in permanent villages, accumulate property and divide themselves into chiefs, commoners and slaves. Along the northern Pacific coast of North America, however, that sequence breaks down completely. Here, peoples who never cultivated a single crop lived in villages of massive cedar-plank houses, inherited their rank at birth, held captives as slaves and carved monumental wooden sculptures. Societies of this kind, often called complex hunter-gatherers, have been identified elsewhere too, from the shores of ancient Japan to the coastal marshes of Florida. They should not be treated as curiosities to be set aside, but as a direct challenge to the theory they appear to contradict.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The traditional explanation was simple abundance. The rivers of the region carried enormous runs of salmon, and a people so well supplied, it was argued, could afford to stay in one place and support specialists and chiefs. Hendrik Tjalsma, an archaeologist at the Low Countries Institute for Prehistory, regards this account as incomplete. The salmon runs, he observes, arrived reliably but lasted only a few weeks each year, and the catch had to be dried or smoked if it was to feed anyone through the winter. In Tjalsma's view, the decisive factor was therefore not abundance but storage. Fresh meat from a large animal spoils within days and must be shared before it is wasted; a house full of dried fish, by contrast, can be guarded, counted and passed on, and so becomes something that a family can own.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Adewale Oyebanji, of the Institute of Comparative Social History in Lagos, accepts the importance of storage but draws attention to the work it required. Cleaning, splitting and drying thousands of fish had to be completed in a narrow window before the flesh decayed, and the amount a household could preserve depended less on how many fish were available than on how many hands it could command. Households therefore competed to attract relatives, dependants and in-laws, and, Oyebanji argues, the same pressure explains the taking of captives in raids on neighbouring villages. On this reading, inequality grew out of rivalry over workers rather than over food itself, a conclusion that helps to explain why slavery was so widespread in a society that had no fields to tend.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Archaeology allows such ideas to be tested against the sequence of events. Darius Petrauskas, who has spent two decades dating house floors and storage pits at coastal sites, has found that large dwellings and substantial food stores appear several centuries before the first clear signs of rank, such as burials in which a few individuals were accompanied by elaborate ornaments while most received nothing. At some settlements, indeed, extensive storage persisted for long periods without any detectable division into rich and poor. The most reasonable interpretation of these findings is that storage made inequality possible without making it unavoidable. Something else, whether population growth, warfare or the ambitions of particular families, seems to have been needed to turn that possibility into a lasting hierarchy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nadeesha Amarasekara, an economic anthropologist at the Colombo Centre for Development Studies, locates that additional factor in geography. Salmon cannot be caught equally well everywhere along a river; the best sites are narrow channels and rapids where fish crowd together and can be trapped in large numbers. Families that controlled such places, she argues, possessed something closely resembling a productive field, and their hereditary claims to particular stretches of water laid the foundation for hereditary rank. The argument is attractive, but it may reverse cause and effect. Exclusive rights to fishing sites are well documented in later centuries, yet it is at least as likely that families who had already grown wealthy through storage and labour used their influence to secure the best locations as that ownership of those locations made them wealthy in the first place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: No account of these societies can ignore their great ceremonial feasts, at which chiefs gave away blankets, food and other valuables to hundreds of guests and occasionally destroyed them in public. Early European observers regarded such events as irrational squandering, evidence of a people who did not understand the value of their own property. Most researchers now see them quite differently, as occasions on which surplus food and goods were converted into prestige and alliances. They may also have served a practical purpose. Because salmon runs could fail on one river while remaining strong on another, the obligations created by feasting gave each village a claim on the resources of others in bad years. What these ceremonies reveal, perhaps above all, is that wealth was prized less for its own sake than for what it allowed its owner to give away.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The wider lesson concerns the place of farming in human history. Agriculture now appears to be one route to social complexity rather than the only one; what mattered, on the coast at least, was the ability to store resources, to control labour and to make claims on the future. Seen in this light, the real puzzle may be not why inequality appeared among some foragers, but why it appeared so rarely among the many others who could, in principle, have stored food too. Caution is nonetheless required. The northern Pacific coast combined exceptionally rich fisheries with a climate that made preservation essential, and conclusions drawn from so unusual a setting cannot simply be transferred to foraging peoples everywhere.

topic: women as hunters: challenging the 'man the hunter' model with ethnographic databases, weapon burials, physiology and childcare constraints
title: Who Brought Home the Meat?
subtitle: The long-standing belief that hunting was always men's work is being questioned, but the alternatives have their own weaknesses

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than half a century, a single image has dominated popular and academic accounts of foraging life. Men, it was said, went out to hunt, while women stayed closer to camp, gathering plants and caring for children. This arrangement was presented not merely as common but as ancient and almost universal, and it carried a heavy theoretical load. Influential theories of human evolution, from the origins of tool use to the formation of lasting pair bonds, rested on the assumption that males provided meat and females depended on them for it. In recent years, however, that assumption has been attacked from several directions at once.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely publicised challenge came from Ifeoma Feyisetan, an anthropologist at the Lagoon Institute of Social Research, who assembled an ethnographic database covering some sixty foraging societies. In a clear majority, she reported, women took part in hunting of some kind. Most commonly they pursued small animals, often trapping them with nets, but in a number of societies women also hunted larger game, usually with the help of dogs. Feyisetan believes that the supposed universality of male hunting was largely produced by the conditions of fieldwork itself. Most early ethnographers were men, she points out, and they generally accompanied other men on their expeditions, so that what women did beyond the camp was rarely observed and still more rarely recorded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kristoffer Lomholt, a behavioural ecologist at the Jutland Centre for Human Evolution, has been sharply critical of these conclusions. He argues that the database counted almost any female involvement as hunting, including occasional assistance such as driving animals towards waiting men or carrying home a carcass. When attention is restricted to who actually kills large animals, he maintains, men are responsible for the overwhelming majority of kills in nearly every society on record. It seems to me that both researchers have a point, and that their quarrel is partly a disagreement about definitions. If hunting means the whole cooperative business of finding, driving, killing and transporting prey, women were often central to it; if it means the final act of killing a large animal, the old picture holds up rather better.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Archaeology has supplied a second line of attack. A team led by Giulia Castellnuovo at the Apennine School of Archaeology re-examined a high-altitude burial in which a young adult had been laid to rest with a complete hunting toolkit, including projectile points and tools for preparing hides. Analysis of proteins in the tooth enamel showed that the individual was female. Encouraged by this, Castellnuovo has called for a systematic review of other burials that were once classified as male simply because weapons were present. Critics respond that objects placed in a grave do not necessarily reveal the occupation of the person buried; they may instead express the feelings of the mourners or the status of a family. In my view, this is the weakest strand of the new evidence, since a single burial, however striking, cannot establish a general pattern.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third argument concerns the body itself. Researchers at the Pacific Institute of Human Performance have suggested that women may in some respects be better suited to long-distance pursuit than men, because female physiology appears to rely more heavily on fat as a fuel during prolonged exercise. This claim has attracted considerable attention, but it goes well beyond what the evidence can support. The physiological studies concerned were small, they were carried out on modern athletes rather than foragers, and they say nothing about the strength needed to kill and butcher a large animal. Replacing one sweeping generalisation with another does little to advance understanding.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more promising approach looks at the practical constraints on women's time. Meron Gebrekidan, who has carried out fieldwork with forest foragers in central Africa for the Horn of Africa Research Network, argues that responsibility for young children shapes who joins which hunts. Pursuing large game often requires long, silent journeys over difficult ground, which are hard to combine with carrying an infant who needs to be fed every few hours. Short trips close to camp, by contrast, fit easily around childcare. Gebrekidan has found that in communities where infants can be left with grandmothers or older siblings, women hunt considerably more often than in those where such help is unavailable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is a picture of flexibility rather than fixed roles. The division of labour between men and women in foraging societies was real, but it was a tendency that varied with ecology, the type of prey and the availability of help with children, not a rule laid down by biology. The debate has also been a reminder of how strongly the expectations of researchers can shape the evidence they collect. Correcting the old picture is overdue; the danger now is that enthusiasm for a new one will lead scholars to make the same mistake in reverse.

topic: landscape burning by Aboriginal Australian foragers: patch burning, the charcoal record, megafaunal extinction, small mammals and modern ranger fire programmes
title: Fire as a Tool
subtitle: For tens of thousands of years, foragers in Australia shaped their land with flame. Scientists are still arguing over how far they changed it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the first European colonists travelled inland from the Australian coast, many of them recorded the same two impressions. The woodlands they passed through were strikingly open, with grassy ground beneath widely spaced trees, and the horizon was frequently marked by columns of smoke. Both observations had a single cause. Aboriginal Australians set fire to the country deliberately and routinely, and they did so with considerable skill. Most of these fires were lit early in the dry season, while grasses still held moisture from the preceding rains, so that they burned slowly and at low temperatures, often going out of their own accord by nightfall. Repeated year after year, such burning produced a fine-grained mosaic of patches burnt at different times, each at a different stage of regrowth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Accounts gathered by ethnographers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries attribute many purposes to this practice. Fire cleared paths for travel and made it easier to spot snakes. It drove small animals from cover so that they could be caught, and the tender green shoots that appeared after rain drew kangaroos and wallabies to recently burnt ground, where hunters waited for them. Certain food plants, including several kinds of yam, were said to grow more vigorously in burnt areas. Not least, regular light burning removed the dry grass and leaf litter that would otherwise accumulate and feed far larger fires later in the year.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How far back such management extends, and how much it altered the continent, is less clear. People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and if their burning transformed the landscape, the change ought to be visible in the charcoal that accumulates in lake beds and swamps. Linnea Ekberg, a palaeoecologist at the Uppsala Institute for Quaternary Studies, examined more than two hundred sediment cores from across the continent and found no consistent rise in charcoal at the time of human arrival. Instead, she concluded, the long-term record of fire follows changes in climate, increasing in warm periods and declining in cold, dry ones. Hanna Wieczorkowska of the Kraków Centre for Environmental History has questioned this interpretation. People, she argues, may have changed the pattern of burning rather than its amount: many small, cool fires leave far less charcoal than a few large, intense ones, so a landscape intensively managed by people could appear in the cores as one in which fire had actually become less important.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question is bound up with another long-running controversy, the disappearance of Australia's giant animals, including marsupials the size of a rhinoceros, some 40,000 years ago. One hypothesis holds that human burning replaced nutritious shrubs with fire-tolerant grasses and so starved the large browsing herbivores. Jean-Aimé Razafimbelo, who works at the Indian Ocean Institute of Palaeobiology, has tested this idea using the spores of fungi that grow on the dung of large plant-eaters, which fall into lake sediments along with charcoal. At several sites, he found that the spores declined sharply before charcoal began to increase. His interpretation is that burning was a consequence rather than a cause of the extinctions: once the great browsers had gone, vegetation that they would have eaten built up as fuel, and fires became more frequent.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Studies of the more recent past are less ambiguous. In the tropical savannas of the north, the decline of traditional burning after colonisation was followed by a shift towards large wildfires late in the dry season, which can sweep across thousands of square kilometres in a few days. Somchai Kittikun, an ecologist at the Northern Savanna Research Station, has compared areas with different fire histories and found that several species of small mammal have declined markedly where late fires dominate. In patchily burnt country, by contrast, animals fleeing a fire can usually find unburnt ground nearby, which provides both shelter from predators and food while the burnt area recovers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings have helped to inspire one of the more successful environmental programmes of recent decades. Teams of Aboriginal rangers across northern Australia have reintroduced early dry-season burning on a large scale, combining long-held knowledge of country with modern tools such as satellite mapping and incendiaries dropped from helicopters. In the regions where such programmes operate, the area burnt by late-season fires has fallen by roughly half. Because early fires burn less fuel and less intensely, they also release smaller quantities of greenhouse gases, and the resulting reductions have been sold as carbon credits, providing a source of income for remote communities.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to conclude that traditional burning offers a ready-made answer to the destructive fires that increasingly afflict Australia and other parts of the world. That conclusion would be premature. The northern savannas have a predictable cycle of wet and dry seasons that makes early burning relatively safe, whereas the forests of the temperate south burn differently and have, in many places, been reshaped by two centuries of clearing, grazing and fire suppression. Traditional knowledge is best understood not as a fixed recipe but as a way of reading local conditions, and applying it elsewhere will require the same careful attention to place that made it effective in the first place.

topic: how children in foraging societies learn to forage: the long-childhood learning hypothesis, skill versus strength, subtle teaching and children's own food production
title: Learning the Bush
subtitle: Why does it take so long to become a competent forager, and how do children in foraging societies acquire the skills they need?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visitors to foraging communities are often struck by how little children are supervised. From the time they can walk confidently, boys and girls spend much of the day in noisy playgroups that mix children of different ages, wandering around the edges of camp, climbing trees, digging, and only occasionally returning to an adult for food or comfort. Yet these same children will eventually need to master an extraordinary range of skills, from tracking animals to identifying hundreds of plants. One influential theory links these two observations. Human childhood, it proposes, is unusually prolonged precisely because the ways in which our species obtains food are so difficult to learn. A young forager is a poor provider, but the years spent practising are an investment that pays off in adulthood, when food returns finally reach their peak, often not until a person's thirties.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Support for this view came from Eero Pohjola, an anthropologist at the Helsinki Centre for Evolutionary Anthropology, who spent several years weighing the food brought into camp by members of a savanna-dwelling community. His figures showed that hunters became steadily more productive throughout their twenties and did not achieve their highest returns until well into their thirties, long after they had reached full physical size. For Pohjola, the only plausible explanation was that hunting depends on knowledge and judgement that accumulate slowly through experience, such as reading tracks, anticipating the movement of animals and choosing the right moment to pursue them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Abosede Ayoade, of the Institute of Human Development Studies in Ibadan, has offered a different reading of such data. In her own fieldwork, she compared the efficiency of children and adults when collecting resources that demand little strength, such as fruit, shellfish and small tubers close to the surface. By the age of ten, she found, children gathered these foods almost as efficiently as adults. Where they fell behind was in tasks requiring size and power: digging deep roots from hard ground, carrying heavy loads or drawing a powerful bow. Ayoade concludes that the slow improvement in adult hunting returns may reflect continued gains in strength and endurance rather than learning. The difficulty, of course, is that skill and strength develop together and are extremely hard to separate, and neither side of the argument has yet found a convincing way of doing so.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Equally contested is the question of how children learn. Petya Vankova, a developmental psychologist at the Sofia Institute for Cultural Psychology, reports that in the communities she has studied, adults almost never give explicit instruction. Children watch, imitate and practise in play, using small bows, toy digging sticks and miniature baskets, and they are rarely corrected. Marisa Ollero, an anthropologist based in Seville, accepts that formal lessons are absent but argues that teaching nevertheless takes place in less obvious forms. Filming everyday activities, she recorded hundreds of brief episodes in which an adult handed a child a suitable tool, adjusted a child's grip or deliberately slowed down a task so that it could be observed. Such moments last only a few seconds and are easily overlooked. It would be a mistake, then, to conclude that foraging children are never taught; what differs is the form that teaching takes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Children are not merely learners, however; in many communities they are also producers. Groups of children foraging on their own near camp may collect a significant share of the food they eat, particularly in seasons when fruit is plentiful. How much they contribute depends heavily on their surroundings. Where the landscape is open and relatively safe, children range freely and feed themselves to a considerable degree. Where there are dangerous animals, fast rivers or dense forest in which it is easy to become lost, parents keep them closer to camp, and their contribution falls accordingly. Differences between societies in children's productivity, in other words, may say more about environmental risk than about the abilities of the children themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Much of what children learn is not practical technique but knowledge of the living world. Studies in several foraging communities have found that by early adolescence most children can name and describe the uses of the majority of the plants and animals that adults recognise. Vankova's research suggests that a good deal of this knowledge passes between children rather than from parents, as older members of a playgroup point out edible berries or explain which insects sting. This finding has implications for the survival of such knowledge, since it means that when children's groups are broken up, for example by the demands of formal schooling, an important channel of transmission may be lost even if parents remain knowledgeable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some educational reformers have seized on research of this kind as evidence that modern schools are fundamentally misguided and should imitate the self-directed learning of forager children. This goes too far. Foraging skills are acquired in a setting where every piece of knowledge has an immediate use and can be observed in action, whereas much of what schools teach, such as reading or mathematics, is abstract and has no natural place in children's play. That said, the autonomy granted to forager children and the value of mixed-age groups, in which younger children learn from slightly older ones, may well offer lessons worth considering.

topic: political egalitarianism among foragers: reverse dominance and sanctions against would-be leaders, cultural learning, mobility, projectile weapons and the limits of equality
title: The Politics of Equality
subtitle: Most mobile foragers have managed without chiefs. Explaining how they did so has proved far harder than describing it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among most mobile hunter-gatherers documented by anthropologists, nobody gives orders. There are no chiefs with the right to command, decisions affecting the group are reached through lengthy discussion, and anyone who tries to boss others around is likely to find themselves laughed at. This arrangement is more remarkable than it may first appear. Our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and gorillas, live in societies organised around dominance, and so do the great majority of human societies that have emerged since the spread of farming. The equality of foragers therefore requires explanation. It would be a mistake to treat it as a mere absence of politics, as though people with few possessions simply had nothing worth fighting over. On the contrary, it is a political achievement, and one that has to be actively maintained.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential account of how it is maintained comes from Halldór Hrafnkelsson, an evolutionary anthropologist at the Reykjavík Institute of Human Behaviour. Having worked through hundreds of ethnographic reports, he argues that foragers live in a reversed hierarchy: instead of the strong dominating the weak, the weak combine to dominate anyone who becomes too strong. The sanctions they use rise in severity according to the seriousness of the offence. A boaster may be gossiped about or mocked; a persistent bully may be ignored or driven out; and in the rare cases where a man uses violence to impose his will, the group may eventually kill him. Hrafnkelsson goes further, suggesting that over many thousands of years such collective punishment shaped our moral instincts, because individuals with an unrestrained urge to dominate were steadily removed from the population.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Zeynep Yurtsever, who teaches social anthropology in Ankara, accepts the description but not the evolutionary conclusion. The supposed selection against aggressive individuals, she points out, cannot be observed directly, and the reported executions on which the argument partly rests are few in number and often known only from hearsay. In her view, equality among foragers is better understood as a cultural institution that each generation must learn anew, which would explain why groups that settled down and began storing food sometimes became hierarchical within a few generations. Yurtsever is surely right that the claim about natural selection is speculative. The speed with which settled groups became unequal, though, does not settle the matter, since an inherited dislike of being dominated could easily be overridden when circumstances changed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third explanation focuses less on punishment than on the freedom to leave. Thandiwe Xaba, an ecological anthropologist at the Southern African Centre for Human Ecology, notes that foraging bands are rarely fixed units. Families move between camps for all kinds of reasons, including visits to relatives, the availability of food and personal quarrels, so that the membership of any one band may change several times in a year. Under such conditions, a would-be leader who becomes too demanding soon finds that his followers have quietly drifted away to join other groups. Xaba argues that this constant option of departure, rather than active resistance, is what has most effectively prevented the accumulation of power.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Bogdan Ceaușu, a palaeoanthropologist at the Carpathian Institute of Archaeology, looks instead to technology. Before projectile weapons, he suggests, a physically powerful individual could intimidate others much as a dominant chimpanzee does. Once spear-throwers and bows allowed even a weaker person to kill from a distance, sheer size lost much of its advantage; a bully, after all, has to sleep. The idea is elegant, but its chronology is uncertain. The dates at which projectile weapons first appeared are still disputed, and there are hints that egalitarian behaviour may be considerably older than the earliest firm evidence for such weapons. Ceaușu acknowledges the difficulty, but maintains that even simple thrusting spears, which are far older, would have gone some way towards evening out contests between the strong and the weak.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever its origins, forager equality has limits that are easily overlooked. It typically applies most fully to relations among adult men; relations between men and women, and between the old and the young, are often far less balanced. In some communities, for example, women are excluded from important ritual knowledge, and young men are expected to defer to their elders on questions of marriage. Nor are all individuals regarded equally. Skilled hunters, healers and gifted storytellers enjoy considerable prestige, and their opinions carry particular weight in discussions. What they lack is authority: they can persuade but cannot compel, and their influence lasts only as long as others choose to listen. To describe foraging societies as egalitarian without these qualifications is to present an idealised picture that the evidence does not support.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It has become fashionable to cite foragers as proof that human beings are naturally equal and that hierarchy is a recent corruption. The record suggests something rather different. Foragers did not live without the desire for dominance; they lived with it, and devised ways of keeping it in check through ridicule, collective action and the simple possibility of walking away. If there is a lesson for larger societies, it is not that equality comes naturally, but that it survives only when ordinary people remain alert to those who would undermine it.
