topic: persistence hunting and the endurance-running hypothesis: anatomical evidence, the rarity of recorded chases, archival accounts, tracking and scavenging
title: Running Them Down
subtitle: Were early humans built to chase their prey to exhaustion? The evidence for one of palaeoanthropology's most appealing ideas is more tangled than it looks

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Compared with most four-legged animals, human beings are unimpressive sprinters. A cheetah, a horse or even a domestic dog would leave the fastest athlete far behind over a hundred metres. Over a marathon distance, however, the picture changes dramatically, particularly in hot weather. Humans can shed heat by sweating over almost the entire surface of a largely hairless body, whereas many mammals must stop and pant in order to cool down. This observation lies behind the persistence hunting hypothesis, which proposes that early members of our genus obtained meat by pursuing antelope and other game through the midday heat, keeping them on the move until they collapsed from overheating. If the hypothesis is correct, the ability to run long distances was not an incidental talent but one of the forces that shaped the human body.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The anatomical case has been most fully developed by Mikkel Lauritzen, a biomechanist at the Copenhagen Institute of Movement Science. He lists more than two dozen features that, in his view, make sense only in the context of running. Long, springy tendons in the lower leg store and release energy with each stride; a ligament at the back of the neck keeps the head steady when the body is bouncing; and the large muscles of the buttocks, which are barely used in walking, fire strongly when we run. Since none of these traits offers much advantage to a creature that only walks, Lauritzen concludes that they must have evolved because running mattered to survival. His list is impressive, but it is not entirely persuasive. Several of the features could plausibly have served other purposes, such as throwing or carrying heavy loads, and anatomy alone cannot tell us which activity drove their evolution.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection comes from Selam Tefera, an anthropologist at the Addis Ababa Centre for Human Origins. Tefera points out that recorded examples of persistence hunting are strikingly scarce. Among the foraging peoples described by twentieth-century ethnographers, the great majority of hunters relied on bows, spears, snares and pit traps, and running an animal down appears only as an occasional and opportunistic technique. She also notes a practical problem. A chase lasting several hours in extreme heat would have caused serious dehydration, yet the earliest members of our genus almost certainly lacked containers in which to carry water. In her view, an activity so rarely observed and so physically risky is unlikely to have been important enough to reshape the body.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dinara Elkanova, a historian of anthropology at the Almaty Institute of Social Research, believes that the scarcity is partly an illusion. Searching through the journals of missionaries, traders and early travellers, she has identified several hundred descriptions of hunters chasing animals on foot until they were exhausted, drawn from six continents. Some of these accounts describe pursuits in the heat of the day, but a surprising number describe hunters running down deer or elk in deep snow, where the heavy animals sank and tired quickly. Elkanova argues that professional ethnographers seldom witnessed such hunts because, by the time they arrived, firearms and horses had already made running unnecessary in many of the communities they studied.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For Luca Zanardelli, a cognitive archaeologist at the Emilia Centre for Prehistoric Cognition, the debate has focused too narrowly on the body. In the few persistence hunts that have been observed in detail, he notes, the decisive skill was not stamina but tracking. A hunter following an animal for hours over hard ground must read faint signs, lose and recover the trail, and anticipate where the animal is likely to go next. Zanardelli suggests that successful pursuits depended as much on reasoning as on endurance, and that the demands of tracking may have encouraged the evolution of the capacity to form and test hypotheses. The suggestion is intriguing, but at present it rests on very little direct evidence, and it is hard to imagine what such evidence would look like.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not all supporters of the endurance-running idea are convinced that hunting was its main purpose. Annelie Niederhauser of the Bern Institute of Evolutionary Ecology argues that running may have been more useful in scavenging. Early humans watching the sky for circling vultures, she proposes, could have run several kilometres to reach a fresh carcass before hyenas or other competitors arrived. There is no need, however, to treat scavenging and persistence hunting as alternatives. A body capable of covering long distances at a steady pace would have been valuable in both activities, and early humans who obtained meat in more than one way would have been better placed to survive lean periods.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The controversy illustrates a wider difficulty in the study of human evolution. Recent hunter-gatherers lived in a world already transformed by agriculture, trade and modern technology, and their behaviour can offer only indirect clues about the lives of people who lived nearly two million years ago. Persistence hunting remains plausible, but it is not proven, and it may never be. What is far less open to doubt is the underlying anatomical finding: whatever the reason, the human body bears unmistakable signs of having been adapted for travelling long distances on foot.

topic: violence and warfare among hunter-gatherers: ethnographic death rates, homicide versus organised war, a prehistoric massacre site, rock art and climate stress
title: Before the Battlefield
subtitle: Did war begin with farming and states, or is it as old as humanity? The evidence from foragers has been read in strikingly different ways

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Two images of early humanity have competed for public attention for centuries. In one, life before civilisation was a ceaseless struggle in which every band was at war with its neighbours; in the other, our ancestors lived in peaceful harmony until agriculture, property and the state taught them to fight. Both images, it must be said, owe far more to philosophical speculation than to evidence. Over the past few decades, however, anthropologists and archaeologists have tried to settle the question empirically, using studies of recent hunter-gatherers and the remains of prehistoric ones. The results have not ended the argument, but they have changed its terms considerably.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for ancient warfare was set out most forcefully by Stavros Ignatiadis, an anthropologist at the Aegean Centre for the Study of Conflict. Drawing on field studies of some thirty societies classified as hunter-gatherers, he calculated the proportion of all deaths that resulted from violence. In several groups the figure exceeded fifteen per cent, and the average was many times higher than the share of deaths caused by war in modern industrial nations, even when the two world wars are included. Ignatiadis concluded that warfare is not a recent invention but a deep-rooted feature of human life, and that the growth of states has, on balance, made people safer rather than more endangered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These figures were soon challenged. Hilde Ibarrondo, of the Bergen Institute for Social Anthropology, re-examined the societies in Ignatiadis's sample and found that a number of them were not mobile foragers at all but settled communities that also grew crops or depended on rich stored resources. Others had been studied after they had been disrupted by contact with outsiders, through displacement, epidemics or the arrival of firearms. When Ibarrondo restricted the analysis to mobile foragers, the picture changed. Lethal violence still occurred, but most killings arose from personal disputes, often over marriage partners, and from revenge, rather than from organised raids by one group on another. The distinction between homicide and war matters a great deal for any theory of where war came from, and Ibarrondo is right to insist on it. For the victims, though, it made little difference, and even her revised figures suggest that the risk of a violent death in such societies was far from trivial.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Archaeology offers evidence of a different kind. Nkechi Chibuzor, of the Lake Basin Archaeological Project, led the excavation of a site on the former shore of an inland lake where the remains of at least twenty-seven people were found, dated to roughly ten thousand years ago. Many of the skeletons bore injuries to the skull and ribs, and several had fragments of stone points lodged in bone. None had been buried with care. Chibuzor interprets the site as the result of an attack by one group of foragers upon another, perhaps the earliest clear evidence of inter-group violence before farming. Critics accept that a massacre took place but point out that the victims lived beside a lake rich in fish, where people may have stayed in one place for much of the year and had valuable territory to defend. A single site, however dramatic, cannot establish that war was common among all foragers; what it does show is that organised violence between groups did not have to wait for agriculture.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third line of evidence comes from rock art. Armen Tchividjian, a specialist in prehistoric imagery at the Caucasus Institute of Archaeology, has catalogued thousands of paintings from a mountainous region of the Mediterranean. The oldest images, he reports, depict hunting and dancing, with no scenes of fighting at all. Later paintings, by contrast, show lines of archers confronting one another and figures pierced by arrows. Tchividjian links the change to a period of drying climate, when water sources became scarcer and groups were forced into closer contact. In his view, inter-group fighting among foragers was a response to particular pressures rather than a constant feature of their lives.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies point towards a conclusion that neither of the traditional images can accommodate. Violence among foragers was neither absent nor uniform. It seems to have been most common where populations were dense, where people stayed in one place, and where there were fixed and valuable resources, such as fishing grounds or springs, that could be seized and defended. Small, mobile groups with few possessions were in a different position: when tensions rose, the simplest solution was often to move away, and that option must have prevented many conflicts from escalating into fighting between groups.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Why does this matter beyond academic circles? Claims about the origins of war are frequently enlisted in political arguments, whether to suggest that conflict is an unchangeable part of human nature or to portray modern institutions as the source of all violence. The evidence from foragers supports neither position. What it reveals instead is a species capable of both cooperation and cruelty, whose behaviour depends heavily on circumstances, and that, perhaps, is a more hopeful conclusion than either of the alternatives.

topic: cooperation between honey-hunting foragers and wild honeyguide birds: signalling calls, how the birds learn, the age of the partnership and its decline
title: The Bird That Leads the Way
subtitle: In parts of Africa, honey hunters and a small wild bird have worked together for generations. Scientists are only beginning to understand how the partnership works and how long it has lasted

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the woodlands of eastern and southern Africa, a honey hunter setting out in the morning may be approached by a small, rather drab bird that perches nearby and chatters insistently. When the hunter responds, the bird flies a short distance, stops, calls again and waits for him to catch up. Over the next half hour or so, it leads him in a series of stages to a tree containing a nest of wild bees. The hunter subdues the bees with smoke, cuts open the tree and removes the honeycomb, leaving behind fragments of wax and bee larvae, which the bird then eats. What makes this arrangement so remarkable is that the bird, a species known as the greater honeyguide, is entirely wild. Nobody trains it, feeds it or keeps it, and yet it cooperates with people in a way that benefits both sides.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For a long time, accounts of this partnership were largely anecdotal. The first systematic experiments were carried out by Ingrid Aamodt, an ornithologist at the Trondheim Centre for Behavioural Ecology, working with honey hunters in a forest reserve. Hunters in the area traditionally attract honeyguides with a distinctive trill followed by a grunt. Aamodt played recordings of this call, of a different human sound and of an ordinary bird song while walking through the forest, and compared the results. The traditional call more than doubled the probability that a honeyguide would begin guiding, and roughly tripled the chances of the walk ending at a bees' nest. Hunters in other regions use quite different calls, and the birds there respond most strongly to the local version. This suggests that honeyguides have learned conventions that are specific to particular human cultures, which, to my mind, is the most striking finding in the field so far.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How the birds acquire such knowledge is a puzzle, because honeyguides never meet their parents. Like cuckoos, they lay their eggs in the nests of other, unrelated species, such as bee-eaters and barbets, and the chicks are raised entirely by their foster parents. Learning to guide by watching an adult honeyguide is therefore impossible, at least in the early stages of life. Matti Heikkilä, a zoologist at the Lapland Institute of Animal Cognition, argues that the tendency to lead large mammals towards bees' nests must be inherited. Young birds start to guide within a few weeks of leaving the nest, he points out, which is too short a period for such complex behaviour to be learned from scratch. What they do learn, in his view, is the response to particular human calls, which they acquire through contact with older honeyguides and repeated encounters with people.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How old the partnership might be is even harder to determine. Rosalind Murgatroyd, a palaeoanthropologist at the Pennine Institute of Human Origins, has suggested that it may extend back more than a million years, to the time when our ancestors first learned to control fire. Smoke is essential for subduing bees, so the birds could only have benefited from human help once people were able to produce it at will. If Murgatroyd is right, this would be among the oldest relationships between humans and any other animal, older by far than the domestication of the dog. The idea is attractive, but there is no way of demonstrating it at present, not least because the date at which people gained control of fire is itself fiercely disputed. It is also frequently claimed that honeyguides once led honey badgers to bees' nests before humans came along, but this story, though endlessly repeated, rests on remarkably little reliable observation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever its age, the relationship appears to be in decline. Ana Lukačević, an anthropologist at the Dalmatian Institute for Human Ecology, has surveyed villages across several countries and found that in areas where people can now buy sugar, and where honey hunting has therefore become less common, honeyguides rarely guide at all. Traditions also vary in ways that may affect the birds. In some communities, hunters deliberately leave a generous portion of wax for their guide as a reward. In others, they bury or burn the wax, in the belief that a hungry bird will guide again sooner. Whether either practice actually changes the birds' behaviour has not yet been tested.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Lukačević argues that the partnership should be recognised as a form of cultural heritage that deserves protection, and she has proposed recording the calls used in different regions and supporting honey hunting as a livelihood. Documenting the calls is plainly worthwhile, since once they disappear they cannot be reconstructed. It would be quite another matter, however, to expect communities to continue a demanding and sometimes dangerous form of food gathering simply because outsiders find it fascinating. If young people prefer other ways of making a living, the decision should be theirs, and conservationists would do better to ensure that the knowledge is preserved than to insist that the practice itself must continue.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The honeyguide is not entirely alone. In a few coastal areas, for instance, wild dolphins have been reported to drive fish towards fishermen's nets and take a share of the catch. Such cases remain rare, however, and they challenge the common assumption that relationships between humans and animals are either those of predator and prey or those of owner and domesticated animal. The partnership between foragers and honeyguides shows that a third possibility exists: cooperation between free-living partners, each pursuing its own interests, sustained by signals that both sides have learned to understand. That it may be disappearing before it has been fully studied is a loss for science as well as for the communities concerned.

topic: how the moai of Rapa Nui were moved: sledges versus the upright 'walking' hypothesis, evidence from road statues and the deforestation narrative
title: Did the Statues Walk?
subtitle: A dispute over how Rapa Nui's giant figures were moved has become a dispute about the island's whole history

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On Rapa Nui, the remote Pacific island also known as Easter Island, nearly a thousand stone statues, or moai, stand, lie or remain half-buried across the landscape. Almost all were carved from the soft volcanic tuff of a single quarry, Rano Raraku, and many were then transported as far as eighteen kilometres to the stone platforms on which they were erected. The average statue is around four metres tall and weighs perhaps twelve tonnes; the largest ever successfully raised is roughly twice that height. How a population without draught animals, metal tools or the wheel achieved this has puzzled visitors since the eighteenth century. The question is not merely technical. For several decades the answer most commonly given has been bound up with a larger story about the island's history, and it is this story, rather than the engineering alone, that gives the debate its intensity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: According to that story, the moai were laid on their backs on wooden sledges and dragged over rails or rollers made from tree trunks. Rapa Nui was once covered by forests of a giant palm, yet by the time Europeans arrived in 1722 it was almost treeless. Professor Lorenzo Valdeorras of the Pacific Archaeology Institute in Valparaíso was among the first to link the two observations explicitly, arguing in the 1980s that competition between clans to build ever larger statues consumed the timber on which the islanders' fishing canoes and soil fertility depended. The account has since become a staple of textbooks and environmental writing, a warning of what happens when a society exhausts a finite resource. Its popularity, in my view, owes more to its moral clarity than to the strength of the evidence behind it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That is not to say horizontal transport was impossible. In the 1990s a team led by Ilse Fjeldbo, then at the Nordic Centre for Experimental Archaeology, placed a concrete replica weighing about ten tonnes on a wooden sledge and hauled it along greased timber rails with a crew of around forty people. The replica moved steadily, and Fjeldbo concluded that the method was entirely within the islanders' capabilities. What the experiment could not show was that the method had actually been used, and here the statues themselves offer awkward evidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Scattered along the ancient roads that lead away from the quarry are dozens of moai that never reached a platform. The archaeologist Tavita Haereroa, who spent six seasons recording these abandoned figures, noticed that they differ in consistent ways from statues that were successfully erected. Their bases are wider and rounded at the front, giving them a D-shaped outline, and their bodies lean forward when stood upright, so that the centre of gravity falls ahead of the base. Statues on platforms, by contrast, have flat bases and stand vertically, and there are traces showing that their bases were trimmed after arrival. Haereroa also observed that fallen road statues tend to lie face down when found on a downhill slope and on their backs when found going uphill, a pattern that is difficult to explain if they had been carried lying down. The roads themselves are slightly concave in cross-section, a shape that would help to keep an upright object centred.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These observations led an engineering group at the Coastal Mechanics Laboratory, directed by Bogumił Wyrzykowski, to test a possibility long dismissed as folklore. Island oral traditions insist that the statues 'walked' to their platforms, moved by a supernatural power. Wyrzykowski's team built a five-tonne replica with the forward lean and rounded base Haereroa had described, attached three ropes to its head, and asked eighteen volunteers to rock it from side to side while pulling it forward. With each rock the statue pivoted on one edge of its base and shuffled ahead, covering a hundred metres in less than an hour. The result is genuinely striking, and it accounts for features of the abandoned statues that the sledge hypothesis leaves unexplained. Even so, the replica weighed less than half as much as an average moai, and it was moved across firm, level ground, so its success should not be taken as proof that the largest figures could have travelled in the same way.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Fjeldbo remains unpersuaded. She points out that an upright statue moved by rocking would be extremely vulnerable on slopes, and she suggests that the road statues may not be failed deliveries at all but figures deliberately set up beside the roads to mark a ceremonial route. Some excavations support part of her argument: a few roadside statues appear to have stood in shallow pits for some time. Yet her interpretation struggles to explain why so many of these figures are broken in ways consistent with a fall, or why their bases were never trimmed as platform statues' were. The more economical reading is that most were simply dropped in transit.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If the walking hypothesis is broadly correct, the consequences extend well beyond engineering. Moving statues upright would have required ropes, made from plant fibre, but very little timber, which weakens the claim that monument building stripped the island of its forests. Researchers have proposed other contributors to deforestation, notably the Polynesian rat, which arrived with the first settlers and is known to eat palm nuts. None of this means the islanders had no effect on their environment; clearing land for gardens certainly played a part. But the image of a society destroying itself for the sake of statues now looks considerably less secure, and the catastrophic decline in the population appears to have followed, rather than preceded, the arrival of Europeans and the diseases they carried. Read this way, the moai are a record of ingenuity under constraint rather than a monument to folly.

topic: how the blocks of the Great Pyramid were raised: straight, spiral and internal ramp theories, a steep quarry ramp with post holes, wetted sand and the case for mixed methods
title: The Ramp Problem
subtitle: After two centuries of theorising, the question of how the Great Pyramid rose may have been framed the wrong way

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Great Pyramid of Khufu, completed around 2560 BCE, originally stood some 146 metres high and contains an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone, many weighing more than two tonnes. If it was built within the king's reign of roughly twenty years, as most Egyptologists accept, a block must have been set in place every two or three minutes throughout each working day. No contemporary text explains how this was done. The Greek historian Herodotus, who wrote of wooden machines lifting stones from one level to the next, was describing the monument some two thousand years after its completion, and his account tells us more about what visitors of his own day were told than about the methods of the builders. Almost every modern reconstruction relies instead on ramps; the disagreement concerns what form they took.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The simplest proposal is a single straight ramp running up to one face of the pyramid. Its weakness has long been recognised: to reach the summit at a gradient gentle enough for teams hauling sledges, such a ramp would have to be well over a kilometre long and would contain almost as much material as the pyramid itself. Dr Margarethe Hollweck, an engineer at the Institute for Historical Construction in Graz, has argued that this objection rests on a misunderstanding of geometry. Because a pyramid narrows as it rises, the lowest third of its height accounts for roughly seventy per cent of its volume. A straight ramp, Hollweck maintains, needed to serve only that lower portion, where the great majority of blocks were laid. This simple observation is, to my mind, the most important corrective in the entire debate, and it is surprising how rarely it features in popular accounts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For the upper levels, other solutions have been sought. Ramps spiralling around the outside of the structure would have been shorter, but they would have covered the corners and edges, preventing surveyors from checking that the faces were rising at the correct angle. Professor Anouar Zerhouni of the Maghreb School of Architecture has therefore proposed that a spiral ramp was built inside the pyramid, just beneath its outer casing, with openings at each corner where blocks could be turned. He points to a notch high on one edge of the monument and to a density survey which, he claims, reveals a lower-density band following a spiral path. The idea is ingenious, yet the evidence for it is slender. The notch may have had other purposes, and density surveys of a structure built from stone of variable quality are notoriously open to interpretation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more concrete clue emerged from an ancient alabaster quarry in the Eastern Desert, where a team led by Dr Ryōta Hanamaki uncovered a ramp dating from roughly the same period. It is remarkably steep, with a gradient of about twenty per cent, and is flanked on both sides by staircases lined with post holes. Hanamaki interprets the posts as anchors around which ropes were passed, so that a team pulling downhill on the stairs could help to haul a loaded sledge up the slope. If such a system was used at Giza, ramps could have been far shorter and steeper than most reconstructions assume. The discovery is important, although a ramp designed to remove stone from a quarry need not resemble one used to build a monument, and caution about transferring the technique directly is warranted.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever their form, ramps were only part of the solution: the sledges themselves had to be moved with as little effort as possible. Laboratory work by a group under Dr Galina Ostrovsky, a physicist specialising in granular materials, has shed light on one method. When a sledge is pulled across dry sand, the sand piles up into a small mound ahead of the runners, greatly increasing resistance. Adding a carefully judged quantity of water binds the grains together and makes the surface considerably stiffer, roughly halving the pulling force required. Beyond a certain point, however, the advantage disappears as the sand turns into a slippery slurry. The finding casts new light on an Egyptian tomb painting in which a figure pours liquid in front of a sledge carrying a colossal statue, an action long read as a ritual of purification rather than a practical technique.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is not a winner but a pattern. Each hypothesis solves part of the problem and creates difficulties elsewhere, which is precisely what one would expect if the builders did not rely on any single system. A broad straight ramp may have carried most of the stone for the lower courses, to be replaced by steeper ramps, perhaps of the kind found in the quarry, as the working platform shrank, while levers or small lifting devices may have been used for the final few metres. The persistent search for one method that explains everything has, in my view, been the central weakness of pyramid research.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is also worth remembering that construction began long before stone reached the site. Papyri recovered from an ancient harbour on the Red Sea coast include the logbook of an official whose team spent months shipping limestone along the Nile and its canals to Giza. Records of this kind, along with evidence from the workers' settlement near the pyramids, suggest that the project depended on rotating gangs of skilled labourers, fed and housed by the state. Seen in this light, the Great Pyramid is as much a monument to administration as to engineering, and the ramps, however they were arranged, were merely the final stage in a chain of organisation that stretched across the entire country.

topic: how Gothic master masons designed cathedrals without structural theory: geometric proportion rules, learning from collapses, tracing floors and lessons for conservation
title: Building by the Rule
subtitle: Medieval masons raised some of the most daring structures in history without any theory of forces. How did they know their cathedrals would stand?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the middle of the twelfth century and the end of the thirteenth, the builders of northern France transformed European architecture. Their cathedrals rose to heights never before attempted in stone, while their walls became thinner and were opened up into vast expanses of stained glass. Much of the load that walls had once carried was transferred instead to external flying buttresses, half-arches that carry the outward thrust of the vaults across to massive piers. All of this was achieved by men who had no mathematical theory of structures, which would not be developed for another five hundred years. How, then, did they decide how thick a pier should be, or how far a buttress should project? Historians have offered competing answers, and the disagreement reveals a good deal about how practical knowledge is created and preserved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One answer looks to the documents that survive. A handful of late-medieval booklets written for masons set out rules of proportion: the depth of a buttress, for example, is given as a fixed fraction of the span of the vault it supports. Professor Hildegard Kassenbrock of the Institute for Building History in Cologne argues that rules of this kind were the core of Gothic design. Masons, in her view, worked almost entirely through numerical relationships between the parts of a building, with no conception of the forces involved. That such rules could succeed is less surprising than it might seem. As engineers now generally accept, a masonry structure stands or falls by its shape rather than by the strength of its stone, which is rarely stressed to more than a small fraction of its capacity. A rule that preserves good proportions will therefore work at any scale.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Émile Rouquerolle, a historian at the University of Lyon, places greater weight on experience. Gothic builders, he argues, learned by pushing their designs ever further and watching what happened, and failures taught them as much as successes. The most famous example is the choir of Beauvais Cathedral, the tallest ever built, part of whose vaults collapsed in 1284 only a few years after completion; it was later rebuilt with additional piers between the original ones. The cause of the collapse is still debated. Rouquerolle's emphasis on trial and error is persuasive, but it carries a hidden difficulty. The cathedrals we admire today are, by definition, those that survived, and the many towers and vaults that cracked or fell during construction have largely vanished from the record. Our picture of medieval competence is therefore inevitably flattering.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Modern analysis has added a further complication. Using computer models of the kind applied to present-day buildings, the engineer Ivo Strnadel has examined the buttresses of several French cathedrals. He found that some were far larger than they needed to be, while others were working close to their limit. The heavy stone pinnacles that crown many buttresses, often regarded as purely ornamental, turn out to add weight that helps to direct the thrust of the vaults safely down into the foundations. Whether the masons intended this effect, or simply found that buttresses with pinnacles performed better, is impossible to determine. Strnadel himself leans towards the second explanation, noting that pinnacles become common only after several decades of experiment with plainer forms.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to treat these positions as rivals, with rules on one side and intuition on the other. In my view, this is a false choice. A proportional rule is not an alternative to experience but a way of storing it: each fraction recorded in a mason's booklet is the residue of generations of building, some of it successful and some of it disastrous. What the rules lacked was not knowledge but explanation. A mason could know that a buttress of a certain depth would stand without being able to say why, and that limitation mattered only when builders attempted something genuinely new.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How such knowledge was passed on is the subject of research by Dr Maren Iversholt, who studies the workshops, or lodges, attached to major building sites. Full-size drawings of windows, arches and mouldings were incised into plaster floors, and from these the masons made wooden templates, from which the stone was cut. Iversholt argues that these drawings served as the principal means of communicating a design to the workers, far more than any written instruction. Lodge regulations from the fifteenth century forbade members from teaching the methods of the craft to outsiders, which helps to explain why so little was ever written down.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These debates are not merely academic. During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, engineers charged with saving medieval buildings sometimes inserted steel ties or concrete beams, assuming that the old structures were weak and needed reinforcing. In several cases such interventions altered the way loads travelled through the building and caused new cracking. Conservation is more successful when it begins from an understanding of the geometric logic the original builders followed, and it is a sign of progress that this principle is now widely taught. Restorers who once saw their task as correcting medieval errors increasingly regard the original builders as guides whose reasoning deserves to be recovered.

topic: Inca fitted stone masonry and earthquakes: deliberate seismic design versus prestige building, shaking-table tests, hammerstone shaping and the evidence of the 1950 Cusco earthquake
title: Walls That Would Not Fall
subtitle: Were the famous stone walls of the Inca designed to withstand earthquakes, or did they simply turn out that way?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visitors to Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire in the Peruvian Andes, are routinely told the same story. The great walls of the city, built from blocks of stone so precisely fitted that not even a knife blade can be slipped between them, have survived centuries of earthquakes that brought down the churches and mansions the Spanish erected on top of them. The walls, it is said, were designed to move with the ground and settle back into place. The story contains a good deal of truth, but it also simplifies a more complicated picture. Precisely fitted masonry was in fact the exception rather than the rule in Inca building. The great majority of Inca walls, including those of most houses, storehouses and agricultural terraces, were made from roughly shaped fieldstones bedded in mud mortar, and it is only the finest structures that have given rise to the legend.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Among those who believe the legend is essentially correct is Professor Ayelén Huallpamayta, an architect at the National University of the Andes. She points to a group of features that recur in Inca fine masonry. Walls lean inwards slightly as they rise, typically by around five degrees. Doorways, windows and wall niches are trapezoidal, narrower at the top than at the base. Blocks are cut into irregular polygons that interlock with their neighbours, and corner stones are often shaped like the letter L so that they bind two walls together. Each of these features, Huallpamayta argues, reduces the danger posed by violent shaking, and their consistent use across the empire shows that Inca builders were deliberately designing against earthquakes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The architectural historian Corentin Malbrouck is unconvinced that the motive was seismic. He observes that fine masonry was reserved almost exclusively for temples, royal residences and other buildings of high status, and that its extraordinary cost in labour was itself the point: a wall that had obviously consumed thousands of working days announced the power of the ruler who commissioned it. The polygonal joints, in his account, reflect a method of work rather than an engineering principle, since each block was shaped to fit the stones already in place by repeatedly lowering it, inspecting the points of contact and trimming them. Earthquake resistance, Malbrouck concludes, was a fortunate by-product of building for display.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Laboratory work has clarified what the walls can do, if not why they were built. A team led by the structural engineer Raffaella Sciacchitano tested scaled models of different Inca wall types on a shaking table, a platform that reproduces the motion of an earthquake. Walls of fitted stone built without mortar proved remarkably resilient: individual blocks shifted slightly during shaking, absorbing energy through friction, and then settled back close to their original positions. The inward lean and trapezoidal openings further reduced the stresses that cause collapse. Fieldstone walls set in mud, by contrast, cracked and lost material early in the tests. The results confirm that the finest Inca walls are genuinely earthquake-resistant, but they say nothing about whether this property was the reason for building them as they were.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How the blocks were shaped is no longer much in doubt. Iron was unknown in the Andes, and bronze, which the Inca did possess, was too soft to cut the hard volcanic rocks they favoured. Instead, masons pounded the stone with hammerstones of an even harder rock, crushing the surface a few grains at a time. When the archaeologist Fermín Achacollo reproduced the technique, he found that it allowed a surprising degree of accuracy and that the chief constraint was time: fitting a single medium-sized block took a team of four several weeks. The largest blocks were dragged from the quarries on sledges up earthen ramps, and several massive stones still lie abandoned along the route from one quarry, known locally as 'tired stones'. Finished surfaces were then polished with sand and water.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most celebrated piece of evidence for the legend comes from 1950, when an earthquake struck Cusco and badly damaged a colonial monastery built on the site of the principal Inca temple. As the later additions fell away, they exposed the curved temple wall beneath, which had survived almost undamaged. The image is a powerful one, but it should be treated with some caution. The Inca walls that can be seen today are, by definition, those that survived; surveys carried out after the earthquake recorded damage to Inca structures as well, although this was largely confined to walls of the cruder type.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whether the Inca set out to defeat earthquakes may never be settled, since they left no written explanation of their methods. Yet the choice between deliberate design and happy accident may itself be too sharp. Builders working for generations in one of the most seismically active regions on Earth would have seen which walls stood and which fell after each major tremor, and the features that survived such tests would naturally have been repeated. A technique can be refined by experience without its users ever formulating the principle behind it. In that sense the walls of Cusco record not a single act of engineering foresight but a long, largely unrecorded process of learning, and it is that process, rather than any single ingenious builder, which deserves the credit that the legend usually bestows.

topic: how Stonehenge's bluestones reached Salisbury Plain: glacial transport versus human haulage, Welsh quarry evidence, the dismantled-circle idea, sledge experiments and the distant origin of the Altar Stone
title: Stones on the Move
subtitle: The smaller stones of Stonehenge travelled more than two hundred kilometres to reach it. Explaining how has divided archaeologists for a century

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Stonehenge is usually pictured as a ring of huge grey sarsens, the sandstone blocks that form its famous archways. These were brought from about twenty-five kilometres away, a considerable feat in itself. Less conspicuous, but in many ways more remarkable, are the so-called bluestones, some eighty smaller pillars weighing up to three tonnes each. Early in the twentieth century geologists traced most of them to the Preseli Hills of west Wales, roughly 225 kilometres from Salisbury Plain. Ever since, the central puzzle has been not where the stones came from but how they made the journey, and the answers proposed say as much about changing views of prehistoric societies as they do about the stones.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One school of thought holds that people did not move the bluestones at all. Professor Sigrún Brynjólfsdóttir, a glacial geologist, argues that ice sheets advancing across Wales and into southern England during an earlier cold period carried boulders of Preseli rock eastwards and left them scattered across the landscape, where the builders of Stonehenge simply gathered them. The theory has an obvious appeal: it removes the need to imagine an enormous and seemingly irrational human undertaking. Its difficulties, however, are serious. Few if any other fragments of Preseli rock have been found on Salisbury Plain, as one would expect had ice deposited them there, and there is little to suggest that the glaciers of that period ever extended so far south.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence against the glacial theory comes from the Preseli Hills themselves. Excavations directed by Dr Eluned Cadwaladr at two rocky outcrops have revealed the remains of prehistoric quarries. The rock there forms natural vertical pillars, and at the foot of the outcrops her team found stone wedges, artificial platforms on which detached pillars could be lowered, and the remains of hearths. Charcoal from these hearths dates the quarrying to several centuries before the first stones were raised at Stonehenge. Recesses in the outcrops correspond closely in size and shape to some of the bluestones on Salisbury Plain. In my view this evidence is decisive: the stones were extracted by people, not plucked from the ground by ice.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The gap between quarrying and construction has encouraged a bolder suggestion. Cadwaladr has proposed that the bluestones first stood in a stone circle in Wales, which was later dismantled and carried east, perhaps by a community migrating to Salisbury Plain and taking its ancestral monument with it. A partly excavated circle near the quarries is her preferred candidate. The archaeologist Morwenna Trethowan has questioned the interpretation, noting that several of the empty stone holes in that circle do not match the bases of any known bluestone and that its dating remains uncertain. The idea is an attractive one, and it may yet prove correct, but at present it rests more on imagination than on evidence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: However the stones began their journey, they must at some point have been moved by human effort. Wheeled vehicles were unknown in Britain at the time, so most reconstructions assume that each pillar was strapped to a wooden sledge and pulled over a track of timber rails greased with animal fat. When a team led by the engineer Kojo Ofosu-Ampem tested this method with a two-tonne replica, they found that a crew of only ten people could keep it moving at walking pace on level ground, far fewer than earlier estimates had assumed. A sea route, with the stones carried on rafts along the coast of Wales and southern England, was once widely favoured, but most researchers now consider it improbable because of the treacherous tidal currents off the rocky headlands that a raft would have had to pass. An overland route, following valleys that offer a natural corridor eastwards, now seems the more plausible option.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Any temptation to regard the bluestones as the most extreme case has recently been overturned. The Altar Stone, a six-tonne slab lying at the centre of the monument, was long assumed to come from south Wales as well. Analysis of tiny mineral grains within it has now shown that it originated in the far north-east of Scotland, some seven hundred kilometres away. How it travelled such a distance, and by land or by sea, is unknown. The discovery has also raised fresh questions about who in Neolithic Britain possessed the knowledge and authority to organise such a journey, and why a stone from so remote a source should have been given the central place in the monument.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Such distances force a reconsideration of what Stonehenge was for. If local stone was available, as the sarsens demonstrate, then the decision to bring material from Wales and Scotland must have been deliberate, and the effort of transport cannot have been a regrettable cost to be minimised. It may instead have been the point. Hauling a stone across the country would have required the cooperation, or at least the consent, of the many communities along the route, and the finished monument would have embodied those relationships. The stones, in other words, may have mattered precisely because of where they had come from. Stonehenge is best understood not as the achievement of a single local group but as a monument to connections that stretched across much of Britain.

topic: the optical refinements of the Parthenon: Vitruvius's illusion-correction theory, perception experiments, drainage, aesthetic vitality, display of craft skill and lessons from restoration
title: No Straight Lines
subtitle: The Parthenon is full of deliberate curves and tilts that most visitors never notice. Why did its builders go to such trouble?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: To the casual eye, the Parthenon in Athens, completed in the 430s BCE, is a model of geometric regularity: a rectangular platform carrying rows of identical columns beneath a horizontal roof. Careful measurement tells a different story. The platform is not flat but rises gently towards the middle of each side, by around eleven centimetres along the longer flanks. The columns swell slightly before tapering towards the top, a feature known as entasis, and they lean inwards, so that if their axes were extended upwards they would meet more than a kilometre above the building. The corner columns are thicker than the rest and stand closer to their neighbours. Scarcely a single line in the building is truly straight, and these so-called refinements are so subtle that most visitors never notice them. Their purpose has been argued over for two thousand years.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest explanation comes from the Roman architect Vitruvius, writing some four centuries after the temple was built. Straight horizontal lines, he claimed, appear to sag when seen from below, and columns seen against the bright sky appear thinner than they are; the refinements were corrections designed to make the building look straight. Vitruvius's account has dominated discussion ever since, but largely, I suspect, because it is the only ancient explanation to have survived rather than because it has been shown to be true. The perception psychologist Eleni Tsakiridou has tested the supposed illusions directly, showing volunteers images of temple facades with and without curvature. She found that a sagging effect was reported by only a minority of viewers, and inconsistently even by them. If the illusion is so unreliable, it is hard to believe that it alone justified so much effort.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more practical explanation has been offered by the structural engineer Chidinma Nwachukwu-Bello, who suggests that the rising platform helped rainwater to run off and spread the weight of the columns more evenly across the foundations. The drainage argument, however, is weak. A rise of a few centimetres over a length of nearly seventy metres would scarcely affect the flow of water, and Greek builders had far simpler means of directing rain away from a platform. Nwachukwu-Bello herself concedes that any effect on the loading of the foundations would have been small, although she maintains that the builders may have believed it to be significant. Nor does a structural motive explain the swelling of the columns or the thickening of those at the corners.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others look for the answer in aesthetics rather than in either correction or function. The architect Matteo Ferrandino argues that the refinements were intended not to make the building look straight but to prevent it from looking mechanical. A structure composed entirely of perfect straight lines, in his view, would appear rigid and lifeless, whereas the barely perceptible curves give it a sense of tension, as if the columns were bearing a living load. The historian of craft Ingrid Rekdalen draws attention instead to what the refinements demanded of the workforce. Because the platform curves and the columns lean, almost no two blocks in the building are identical, and each had to be cut for one particular position. The cost must have been considerable, and Rekdalen argues that this was precisely the point: the refinements displayed the skill of the city's craftsmen and the wealth of the city that could afford them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How such precision was achieved has become clearer in recent decades. Faint construction drawings discovered on the walls of an unfinished temple at Didyma, in present-day Turkey, show the profile of a column with entasis drawn at full size, demonstrating that the builders of later Greek temples planned their curves in advance rather than shaping them by eye. Engineers working on the restoration of the Acropolis, led by Stavros Mavrommatis, have also shown how the curvature of the Parthenon's platform could have been laid out using a straightforward method of adjusting the height of each block against a graded set of measurements, without any advanced mathematics.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The restoration has revealed the practical consequences of the refinements in another way too. Blocks removed during earlier, poorly executed repairs cannot simply be returned to any vacant position, since each fits only the place for which it was cut. Mavrommatis's team has spent years identifying the original location of scattered fragments, using the angle of each joint and the curvature of each surface as a kind of fingerprint. Progress is slow, but the work has produced the most detailed record of the building's geometry ever assembled. It has also allowed the team to correct a number of errors made by restorers in the early twentieth century, who assumed that blocks of similar size were interchangeable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be satisfying to declare one of these explanations correct, but the evidence does not permit it, and the attempt may itself be mistaken. The refinements are better understood as serving several purposes at once: they may have corrected minor visual effects, enlivened the building and advertised the skill of those who made it, without any one motive excluding the others. What the long debate reveals most clearly is a modern habit of mind. We tend to assume that every feature of a building must have one function, and that beauty is something added once practical needs have been met. The builders of the Parthenon, it seems, recognised no such division.

topic: surveying the gradients of Roman aqueducts: the chorobates versus the dioptra, error correction near the Pont du Gard, carbonate deposits as a record of flow, and what the water was for
title: A Fall of Twelve Metres
subtitle: The arches of Roman aqueducts draw the crowds, but the real achievement lies in a slope too gentle for the eye to see

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Roman aqueducts are remembered chiefly for their arches, and the most famous of them, the three-tiered bridge known as the Pont du Gard in southern France, attracts close to a million visitors a year. Yet the arches are, in a sense, the least remarkable part of these systems. Most of the channel that supplied the city of Nemausus, modern Nîmes, ran at or below ground level, winding for some fifty kilometres around hillsides and valleys. Over that entire distance, the water descended by only about twelve metres, an average fall of roughly twenty-five centimetres in every kilometre, and in some stretches considerably less. Water flowed through the channel by gravity alone, so a section laid even slightly too flat would have caused it to stagnate or overflow. That such a gradient could be laid out at all, with the instruments available two thousand years ago, is the real puzzle the aqueduct poses.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Roman writer Vitruvius describes a surveying instrument called the chorobates, a wooden table about six metres long with plumb lines hanging against marks on its legs and a groove along its top that could be filled with water to check that it was level. A surveyor sighted along the top of the table to a graduated staff held some distance away. The historian of science Benedikt Auracher built a full-size replica and used it to survey a test course. A single sighting, he found, could be wrong by several centimetres, an error far too large for an aqueduct. But when he repeated each measurement many times and sighted in both directions along the route, the errors largely cancelled out. Used patiently in this way, Auracher argues, the chorobates was capable of the accuracy the aqueducts required.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the chorobates was the instrument actually used. Dr Inès Calvet-Ruiz, a specialist in ancient technology, points out that a six-metre table would have been extremely awkward to carry across broken country, and that wind ruffling the water and swinging the plumb lines would have made it usable only on still days. She considers it more likely that surveyors relied on the dioptra, a smaller sighting instrument mounted on a stand. The disagreement is interesting, but in my view it is somewhat misplaced. No ancient instrument was accurate enough on its own; what mattered was a working method of repeated readings, cross-checks and corrections, and that method could have been applied to either device.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some of the best evidence about how the Nîmes aqueduct actually functioned comes not from instruments at all but from the channel walls. Water from the springs that fed it was rich in dissolved calcium carbonate, which gradually built up as a hard, layered crust on the inside of the channel, in places some forty centimetres thick. A team of hydraulic engineers under Dr Adaeze Akinkugbe has analysed these deposits, which form distinct seasonal bands rather like the rings of a tree. From their thickness and position, the team has estimated the depth of water in the channel at different periods, identified intervals when the aqueduct was shut down for cleaning, and traced how the deposits steadily narrowed the channel until its capacity was reduced by more than half. Few archaeological sources offer so continuous a record, and these deposits deserve far more attention than they have generally received.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The deposits have also helped to shed light on a curious feature of the route. Upstream of the Pont du Gard, the gradient is relatively steep, but close to the bridge it becomes almost flat before steepening again further on. The archaeologist Mattias Rosengaard interprets this as evidence that the builders discovered, part of the way through construction, that an earlier section had been set too high or too low, and corrected the problem by adjusting the slope of the remaining stretch. Others have argued that the flat section was deliberate, intended to keep the bridge from becoming even taller. Rosengaard's explanation seems the more convincing, since the change is too abrupt to have been part of an original plan.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why go to such lengths? The common assumption is that aqueducts were built to provide drinking water, but most Roman towns, Nîmes among them, already had wells, cisterns and springs adequate for everyday needs. Water brought by aqueduct flowed continuously and was used above all for public baths, ornamental fountains and the private houses of the wealthy, with the surplus flushing the drains. An aqueduct was, in large part, a declaration that a town was prosperous and properly Roman, and its bridges, placed where everyone could see them, were as much advertisements as engineering.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the skill of the people who built them. If anything, the evidence from Nîmes suggests that their real expertise lay less in avoiding mistakes than in noticing and correcting them before they became disastrous. Modern engineering, which depends heavily on monitoring and adjustment during construction, has more in common with that approach than is often appreciated. The image of the Roman engineer as a flawless calculator is, in the end, less impressive than the reality: a team of surveyors and labourers who expected to be wrong and organised their work so that they would find out in time.

topic: Göbekli Tepe and monumental building by hunter-gatherers: sanctuary versus settlement, feasting and the origins of farming, how the enclosures were buried and how the pillars were quarried and raised
title: Pillars Before Ploughs
subtitle: A hilltop in south-eastern Turkey once seemed to prove that monuments came before farming. The story is turning out to be more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When excavation began in the 1990s on a low hill near the city of Şanlıurfa, in south-eastern Turkey, few archaeologists expected it to overturn established ideas about the human past. Yet the site of Göbekli Tepe proved to contain a series of circular enclosures, each ringed by massive T-shaped limestone pillars, some more than five metres tall and weighing as much as ten tonnes. Many are carved in relief with foxes, snakes, wild boar and vultures. Radiocarbon dates placed the oldest enclosures at around 9500 BCE, before the appearance of domesticated plants or animals in the region and some six thousand years before the first stones were raised at Stonehenge. The people who built them were, as far as anyone could tell, hunter-gatherers, and the long-held assumption that only settled farming societies could organise monumental construction was difficult to sustain once the site had been dated.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first interpretation was bold. The enclosures, it was argued, were not dwellings but sanctuaries, built by scattered bands of foragers who gathered at the hill for ceremonies and then dispersed. The phrase 'first came the temple, then the city' captured the idea neatly, suggesting that religion rather than economics had driven people towards a settled way of life. Such a reversal of the conventional sequence was bound to attract attention, and for a time it became the accepted view. More recent fieldwork, however, has made it hard to defend in its original form.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of that fieldwork has been led by Dr Rüya Çakırgöz, whose team has excavated areas between and around the great enclosures. They have found the remains of smaller rectangular buildings with domestic hearths, rock-cut cisterns capable of storing large volumes of rainwater, and tens of thousands of grinding stones used to process wild cereals. Çakırgöz concludes that people lived at Göbekli Tepe for long periods, perhaps all year round, and that the monumental enclosures stood within a substantial settlement. Her evidence is convincing, and the picture of a lonely hilltop sanctuary visited only for rituals must now be abandoned. It would be a mistake, though, to swing to the opposite extreme and treat the site as merely a village with unusually elaborate buildings; nothing comparable in scale is known from anywhere else at this date.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of why the enclosures were built remains open. Professor Gerlinde Hufnagl, an archaeologist specialising in the origins of agriculture, argues that construction on this scale required large gatherings of workers, and that these were attracted and rewarded with feasts. Residues in large stone vessels at the site, she suggests, may indicate that grain was fermented to produce a kind of beer. The need to supply such feasts repeatedly could have encouraged people to tend stands of wild cereals more intensively, setting in motion the process that eventually led to cultivation. It is an elegant hypothesis, and it has the merit of linking the monuments to the economic transformation that followed them. At present, however, it remains speculative: the residues are open to other interpretations, and the earliest domesticated cereals in the region cannot yet be connected directly to activity at the site.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How the pillars themselves were produced is somewhat better understood. They were quarried from the limestone plateau on which the site stands, using flint tools, and one abandoned pillar, almost seven metres long, still lies partly attached to the bedrock. Dr Savaş Kılıçarslan, an engineer who has studied the enclosures, has estimated that moving and raising the largest pillars would have required several hundred people working together, using wooden levers, ropes and timber tracks. The central pillars were set into sockets cut in the bedrock, but Kılıçarslan has found that several began to tilt not long after being erected and had to be propped up with stone benches and additional walls. To some observers, a workforce of this size implies a society ruled by powerful chiefs. That conclusion does not follow. Large communal projects can be organised through custom, obligation and shared belief, and nothing found so far at the site points clearly to individuals of exceptional rank.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further debate concerns how the enclosures came to be buried. For many years it was believed that they had been deliberately filled in with rubble when they went out of use, perhaps in a ritual act of closure. The geoarchaeologist Tamar Ben-Haroush has challenged this interpretation. Her analysis of the layers within the fill shows that it built up over long periods, through slope collapses, erosion and debris from repeated repairs to the surrounding buildings, rather than in a single episode. If she is right, the enclosures were not ceremonially buried but slowly overwhelmed by the activity of a living settlement.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Göbekli Tepe is no longer unique. Surveys across the surrounding region have identified a dozen or more sites with similar T-shaped pillars, several of which are now under excavation. Rather than an isolated wonder, it appears to have been part of a wider cultural world whose inhabitants shared symbols, building practices and, presumably, beliefs. That makes the site less mysterious but in some ways more important. The slogan that the temple came before the city was too simple, yet the core insight survives: people who did not yet farm were capable of organising work on a monumental scale, and the social bonds created by such work may well have shaped what came next.

topic: how ancient Egyptian obelisks were quarried, shipped and raised: the unfinished obelisk at Aswan, pounding experiments, river barges, the sand-pit and lever theories and the limits of small-scale experiments
title: Needles of Stone
subtitle: Egypt's obelisks were cut from single blocks of granite weighing hundreds of tonnes. Raising them upright remains one of the great puzzles of ancient engineering

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few objects from the ancient world have travelled as widely as the obelisks of Egypt. Tall, tapering shafts of granite crowned with a small pyramid, they were erected in pairs before the gateways of temples, where their gilded tips caught the first light of the sun. Later conquerors found them irresistible: Roman emperors shipped more than a dozen to Rome, and in the nineteenth century others were taken to Paris, London and New York. Each removal was celebrated as a triumph of modern engineering. What makes the obelisks so remarkable, however, is not that they could be moved with the steam engines and iron cranes of the industrial age, but that they were quarried, transported and raised more than three thousand years earlier by people who had neither.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best evidence for the first stage lies in the granite quarries at Aswan, in the far south of Egypt. There, still attached to the bedrock, lies an obelisk that was never finished. Had it been completed it would have stood around forty-two metres high and weighed more than a thousand tonnes, far larger than any obelisk actually erected. Its sides are surrounded by narrow trenches, and the rock surfaces bear the marks of pounding rather than cutting: iron tools were not available, and the granite was crushed away by workers striking it with balls of dolerite, an even harder stone. The archaeologist Hamid Ait-Lahcen has reproduced the method and found that a single worker lowers the surface by only about five millimetres an hour. Slow as that is, the technique allowed hundreds of people to work at the same time, kneeling side by side in the trenches, so that the overall rate of progress was considerable. The project was eventually abandoned when cracks appeared in the stone. To my mind, this failed obelisk is more instructive than any of the finished ones, because it preserves every stage of a process that successful monuments conceal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Once freed, an obelisk had to travel north along the Nile, sometimes for hundreds of kilometres. A relief carved in a royal temple at Thebes shows two obelisks lying end to end on an enormous barge towed by a fleet of smaller boats. Dr Yasmin Abouelnaga, a specialist in ancient ships, has calculated that such a vessel must have been at least sixty metres long. She proposes that the barge was loaded by digging a channel from the river to the quarry and floating it beneath the obelisk while the water level was low, so that the rising floodwaters lifted it with its cargo. The idea is ingenious and entirely possible, but no trace of such a channel has yet been identified at Aswan.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The final and most debated stage was raising the obelisk onto its pedestal. Professor Rainer Gutzeit has championed what is known as the sand-pit method. In his reconstruction, the obelisk was hauled base first up an earth ramp until its lower end hung over a deep pit filled with sand. Workers then removed sand from the bottom of the pit through side tunnels, allowing the obelisk to sink gradually and tilt until its base rested on the pedestal, after which teams with ropes pulled it upright. The strongest support for this view comes from the pedestals themselves, several of which have a shallow groove along one edge that could have acted as a pivot, preventing the base from sliding as it came down.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Branko Stojaković prefers a different solution. He argues that the obelisk was raised little by little with wooden levers, its upper end lifted a few centimetres at a time while stacks of timber were packed underneath, until it was steep enough to be pulled vertical. Levers were certainly familiar to Egyptian builders, and the method requires no elaborate earthworks. Its main difficulty is the sheer quantity of large timber it would have demanded. Egypt had few trees suitable for such work, and long beams of cedar had to be imported at great expense from the eastern Mediterranean coast.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Experiments have been used to test both approaches. A team of engineers and volunteers once raised a granite replica weighing about twenty-five tonnes using a version of the sand-pit method combined with ropes and a timber frame. They succeeded, but only after several failed attempts in which the obelisk jammed or threatened to slip. The achievement is real, yet it should be interpreted with care. The heaviest obelisks ever erected weighed fifteen or more times as much as the replica, and the forces involved do not increase in simple proportion to weight. A method that works at modest scale may face entirely new problems, such as the crushing of the edges of the stone, when applied to a monument of several hundred tonnes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The obelisks were, above all, statements of royal power. A pharaoh who could command the labour of thousands, cut a flawless shaft of granite and set it upright before a temple was demonstrating his favour with the gods as much as his wealth. That is why the unfinished obelisk at Aswan is such a revealing object. It shows that even rulers able to mobilise the resources of an entire kingdom were constrained by the stone itself, and that ambition sometimes outran what the material would allow.

topic: why the first dome of Hagia Sophia collapsed and how the building survived: theoretical designers, rushed construction and slow-curing mortar, earthquakes, the steeper rebuilt dome and Ottoman buttresses
title: A Dome on Borrowed Time
subtitle: For nearly fifteen centuries the great dome of Hagia Sophia has defied gravity and earthquakes, but its survival has never been as secure as it appears

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the emperor Justinian dedicated the church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople in 537, its dome was unlike anything seen before. Some thirty-one metres across and rising more than fifty metres above the floor, it was supported not on a continuous circular wall, as earlier great domes had been, but on four massive piers, with curved triangular sections of masonry known as pendentives carrying the load from the round base of the dome down to the corners of a square plan. A ring of forty windows at its base flooded the interior with light, and the contemporary historian Procopius wrote that the dome seemed not to rest on solid masonry at all but to hang from heaven by a golden chain. It was not the largest dome of antiquity; that of the Pantheon in Rome, built four centuries earlier, is wider. Its originality lay in the boldness of placing so vast a dome over a square space open on several sides, and that boldness came close to costing the building its life.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The church was designed by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, men known to their contemporaries chiefly as mathematicians and authorities on geometry rather than as experienced builders. Dr Konstantinos Kouroupakis, an architectural historian, argues that this background was a weakness as well as a strength. Confident in the elegance of their geometry, he suggests, they gave the first dome too shallow a profile, so that it pressed outwards on its supports with great force, and they paid too little attention to how the structure would behave in practice. The charge has some substance, but it is also somewhat unfair. No one had attempted a structure of this kind before, and there was no body of practical experience from which the designers could have learned.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more important factor, in my judgement, was speed. Hagia Sophia was completed in less than six years, an astonishingly short time for a building of its size. Its walls and piers were built of brick laid in beds of mortar almost as thick as the bricks themselves, and lime mortar of this kind hardens slowly, over months or even years. Professor Desislava Zlatarska, a specialist in historic building materials, has studied the distortions recorded in the fabric and concludes that the piers had already begun to lean outwards before the dome was finished, as the fresh mortar was squeezed under the growing weight above it. The emperor's eagerness to see his church completed, in other words, built a weakness into the structure from the beginning.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The immediate trigger for disaster was natural. Severe earthquakes struck Constantinople in 553 and again in 557, and in May 558 the eastern part of the dome fell. A team of seismologists led by Dr Emre Sağlamtimur has modelled the effect of these events on the building, and argues that the soft ground beneath parts of the city would have amplified the shaking, so that each tremor added to cracks left by the one before. The collapse, on this view, was the result of accumulated damage rather than a single blow. Yet earthquakes alone cannot account for what happened. Other large buildings in the city survived the same tremors, and the dome of Hagia Sophia came down because the shaking found a structure already weakened by its design and by the haste of its construction.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The rebuilding was entrusted to Isidore the Younger, a nephew of one of the original architects, who raised the new dome by around six metres and gave it a steeper profile, strengthened by forty ribs between the windows. An engineering group led by Dr Paloma Urquijo has examined the two designs using computer models of the forces acting on the structure. Their analysis indicates that the taller dome directs more of its weight downwards and exerts considerably less outward thrust on the piers than its flatter predecessor. The second dome, completed in 562, is therefore best seen not as a replica of the first but as a deliberate correction, an early instance of builders learning from a failure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even the corrected dome was not invulnerable. Parts of it collapsed again after earthquakes in 989 and 1346, and each time they were rebuilt with materials and methods that differed from those used before. After the Ottoman conquest of the city in 1453, the building became a mosque, and in the sixteenth century the architect Sinan added massive external buttresses to restrain the walls. Dr Oskar Lindvreten, a structural engineer who has surveyed these additions, maintains that the building owes its survival to them more than to any feature of the original design. One consequence of this long history of repair is that the dome today is a patchwork, and distinguishing what belongs to the sixth-century structure from what was added later has become extremely difficult.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Istanbul remains one of the most earthquake-prone cities in Europe, and engineers continue to debate how Hagia Sophia might best be protected against the next major tremor. The building's history offers a sobering lesson. Its survival has never depended on the perfection of its original design, which was flawed, but on the willingness of successive generations to monitor, repair and reinforce it. Any proposal that promises to make the dome safe once and for all should therefore be treated with suspicion.
