area: automation and the future of work
topic: why estimates of jobs at risk from automation differ: occupation-based versus task-based methods, workplace reorganisation, adoption lags and uncounted new jobs
title: Counting the Vulnerable Jobs
subtitle: Forecasts of how much work machines will take over range from alarming to reassuring. The reasons tell us more than the numbers.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Little more than a decade ago, a widely circulated study concluded that almost half of all employment in one advanced economy was at high risk of being automated within twenty years. The figure travelled quickly, appearing in newspaper headlines, government reports and the speeches of company executives. Several later studies, using the same national data but different methods, arrived at estimates of less than one in ten. A gap of this size cannot be explained by rounding errors or by the choice of one statistical package over another. It reflects deeply different assumptions about what a job actually is, and for that reason the disagreement between the forecasters is arguably more illuminating than any single number they have produced.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earlier and more pessimistic approach treated the occupation as the basic unit of analysis. A panel of engineers and computer scientists was asked to judge whether a small sample of occupations, around seventy in all, could be fully performed by machines given foreseeable advances in technology. A statistical model then linked these judgements to the skills each occupation was said to require, such as fine manual dexterity, creative problem-solving and the capacity to negotiate or persuade, and used those links to assign a probability of automation to several hundred further occupations. Dr Sunniva Grönholt, a labour economist at the Bergen Institute for Work Studies, defends the method on the grounds that it was deliberately forward-looking: it asked what machines would soon be able to do, rather than what they were doing at the time, and in her view it anticipated progress in pattern recognition that many economists had dismissed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The more optimistic estimates came from a team led by Professor Vikram Anandakrishnan at the Centre for Employment Analytics, which questioned the idea that everyone holding the same job title does the same work. Using surveys in which employees reported how they actually spent their working day, the team found striking variation within occupations. One accounts clerk might devote most of her time to keying figures into a database; another, with an identical title, might spend hours resolving disputes with suppliers and explaining decisions to managers. When automation risk was calculated task by task and worker by worker, the proportion of people whose jobs consisted mainly of automatable activities fell to around nine per cent. This approach seems to me the more convincing of the two, because job titles are crude administrative labels that reveal little about the content of anyone's working life.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the task-based method has a blind spot of its own. It assumes that the list of tasks making up a job will remain broadly the same, and that machines will simply take over some items on that list. In practice, firms frequently redesign work around a new technology instead. Self-service checkouts did not automate the cashier's duties one at a time; they transferred the scanning of goods to the customer and left a single employee to supervise several machines. Dr Halima Mwenda, a sociologist at the Institute for Labour and Technology in Nairobi, calls this the reorganisation effect, and argues that it leads task-based studies to understate future displacement, since today's task lists describe workflows that may not exist in a decade. Her point is well made, although reorganisation can also generate new tasks, such as maintaining the equipment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Both approaches share a more basic limitation: they measure what is technically possible, not what will actually happen. Whether a firm replaces workers with machines depends on the level of wages, the cost of the equipment, regulation and the willingness of customers to accept the change. Tomasz Kozakiewicz, an economic historian, points out that even transformative technologies have tended to spread slowly. When electric motors first became available, factories gained little from them until buildings were redesigned around individual machines rather than a single central power source, and the full productivity benefits arrived roughly four decades later. Kozakiewicz therefore argues that any forecast with a twenty-year horizon is almost bound to overstate the pace of change. The historical analogy is instructive, but it should not be pushed too far. Software can be copied and distributed across the world in days, which was never true of heavy machinery.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further weakness is that most estimates count only the jobs that might disappear. They say nothing about the occupations that new technologies will bring into being, even though a considerable share of today's job titles did not exist half a century ago. The asymmetry is understandable: it is far easier to examine an existing job and ask whether a machine could do it than to imagine work that nobody has yet thought of. But it means that a pessimistic bias is built into the exercise from the start. Grönholt accepts that her model is blind to new occupations, but she insists that this does not make the losses it identifies any less real. Overall employment may recover, she observes, yet a fifty-year-old warehouse supervisor whose post disappears is not easily reborn as a software developer, and the costs of that transition fall on individuals and their communities.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done with numbers that vary so widely? The most sensible conclusion is that single headline figures ought to be abandoned. Policymakers would be better served by ranges of estimates, each with its assumptions stated, and by research into which workers are most exposed and how soon change will reach them. Ultimately, the question of how many jobs machines will take matters less than the question of what happens to the people who currently do them, a question on which the forecasting debate has said remarkably little.

topic: algorithmic management of warehouse pickers and delivery couriers: opaque targets, consistency versus fairness, workers' collective tactics, monitoring and health, and regulation
title: The Manager in the Machine
subtitle: In warehouses and on delivery platforms, software now gives the orders. Is it a better boss or simply a more relentless one?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of industrial history, the authority of a supervisor was personal. A foreman walked the factory floor, decided who worked which shift and judged, often on instinct, who deserved promotion and who deserved a warning. In a growing number of workplaces, these functions have passed to software. Instructions, schedules, performance ratings and even dismissals are increasingly generated automatically from streams of data, a development that researchers have labelled algorithmic management. It is tempting to regard this as a revolution in the way work is controlled. In my view, however, the change lies less in the invention of new forms of control than in the scale and precision with which very old ones can now be exercised.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanics vary from one sector to another. In large distribution centres, pickers carry handheld scanners that tell them which aisle to visit next and display a countdown for each item they must collect. On delivery platforms, couriers receive orders through a smartphone application that sets their routes and scores them on punctuality and on the proportion of jobs they accept. In both settings the data are used to rank workers against one another, and those with the lowest scores may be deactivated without ever speaking to a human being. Dr Adaeze Ogunbiyi, an organisational psychologist at the Lagos Institute for Business and Society, spent eighteen months interviewing staff at three distribution centres. She expected the speed of the work to be their main grievance. Instead, the complaint she heard most often concerned opacity: workers had no idea how their targets were calculated or why they changed from week to week.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the new systems argue that they remove a long-standing source of injustice. Professor Lauri Riihimäki, an operations researcher at the Tampere School of Logistics, points out that human supervisors have always had favourites, and that decisions about overtime or discipline were frequently coloured by friendship, prejudice or simple mood. An algorithm, he contends, applies the same rules to everyone. There is something in this argument, but consistency should not be confused with fairness. A target designed around the performance of an average worker will be applied, with perfect consistency, to an older employee or to someone with a minor disability, and it will penalise them every single time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Workers have not simply accepted these arrangements. Couriers in particular have developed tactics for influencing the systems that manage them. Inés Villafañe, a sociologist at the Southern Cone Labour Observatory, documented a practice in two South American cities in which riders waiting in a poorly paid district agreed through messaging groups to switch off the application at the same moment. The sudden shortage of available couriers triggered surge pricing, raising the fee for every delivery in the area. Villafañe interprets such episodes as a new kind of solidarity, one that flourishes even though the participants seldom meet face to face. Her account is valuable, but it may be somewhat romantic. Tactics of this kind tend to be fragile, and platforms can neutralise them with a minor change to their pricing rules.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The effects on health are harder to establish. Several surveys have associated intensive electronic monitoring with higher levels of reported stress, and injury rates in some heavily monitored warehouses appear to exceed those in the logistics industry as a whole. Caution is needed here, since the sites with the most sophisticated monitoring are also those handling the largest volumes of goods, and it may be the volume rather than the monitoring that causes harm. Nevertheless, the association is consistent enough to give legitimate grounds for concern, and it would be unwise to wait for conclusive proof before acting.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Legislators have started to respond. A number of jurisdictions now require employers to tell workers what data are being collected about them, and some insist that significant decisions, such as dismissal, must be reviewed by a person rather than taken automatically. Armen Hovhannisyan, an employment lawyer who advises a European forum on digital labour, doubts that the second requirement achieves much. A manager asked to review several hundred automated decisions a day, he argues, will inevitably approve almost all of them, so that the human check becomes a formality. He proposes instead that workers be given an enforceable right to an explanation, written in plain language, of any decision that affects their pay or employment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that algorithmic management is harmful by its very nature. The same streams of data that are now used to rank and discipline workers could just as easily be used to identify people who are being overworked, to spread demanding tasks more evenly or to detect unsafe patterns before an accident occurs. The decisive question is not whether software manages work, but who designs it and whose interests it is built to serve. If workers had a genuine voice in choosing the measures by which they are judged, the manager in the machine might turn out to be a considerable improvement on the foreman it replaced.

title: The Gentlest Grip
subtitle: Machines took over the grain harvest generations ago. Why has picking fruit proved so much harder to automate?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every summer, the orchards and berry fields of wealthy countries depend on an army of seasonal workers, many of whom travel across borders for a few months of intensive labour. In recent years that army has been shrinking. Tighter immigration rules, rising wages in the workers' home countries and an ageing rural population have left growers struggling to bring in their crops, and some have watched fruit rot on the branch for want of hands to pick it. It is hardly surprising that many now look to robots. Cereal farming offers a tempting precedent: the combine harvester mechanised the grain harvest more than a century ago, transforming a task that once occupied entire villages. Yet the picking of fresh fruit remains one of the last major agricultural operations still performed largely by hand. This is not, as is sometimes implied, because engineers have neglected the problem. It is because the problem is extraordinarily difficult.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A grain crop can be cut indiscriminately; an apple must be found, judged and detached individually. Fruit varies in size, colour and position, is often hidden behind leaves and is easily bruised, and a bruised apple may lose most of its market value. A picking robot must therefore locate each fruit with cameras, decide whether it is ripe, plan a route for its arm through a tangle of branches and grip the fruit firmly enough to remove it without damaging it. The earliest experimental machines, built in the 1980s to harvest oranges, could manage only a small fraction of a human picker's rate. Modern systems use machine-learning software to recognise fruit and soft rubber fingers or vacuum tubes to detach it. Dr Keiko Yamazato, an agricultural engineer at the Shizuoka Institute for Field Robotics, argues that recognising the fruit is no longer the main obstacle. The real bottleneck, she says, is cycle time: the seconds required to move the arm, separate the fruit and deposit it safely. An experienced worker can pick an apple in around two seconds, whereas even the best robots take several times as long for each fruit.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One response has been to change the orchard rather than the machine. In so-called fruiting walls, trees are trained into flat, narrow planes so that almost every apple is visible from one side, while strawberries are increasingly grown on raised tabletop structures instead of in the soil. Rodrigo Abarca, a horticulturalist at the Valle Central Fruit Research Station, maintains that these changes in cultivation have done more to make robotic harvesting feasible than any recent improvement in the robots themselves. The difficulty is that redesigning an orchard means replanting it, and a newly planted apple orchard takes several years to reach full production. The spread of picking robots will therefore be tied to the slow cycle of orchard renewal, which suggests that their adoption will be measured in decades rather than years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Then there is the matter of cost. A picking robot is an expensive piece of equipment, yet the harvest of any single crop may last only a few weeks. According to Maja Lindvall, an economist at the Nordic Centre for Agricultural Economics, a harvesting robot pays for itself only if it can be kept busy for well over a thousand hours a year, which in practice means that it must also be capable of pruning, thinning blossom or spraying. Large growers with several crops ripening at different times are best placed to reach that threshold. Smaller farms might instead hire machines from specialist contractors, much as many farmers once paid contractors to bring a combine harvester to their fields rather than buying one outright.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Less attention has been paid to the views of the pickers themselves. Chinedu Uzoigwe, who studies labour migration at the Centre for Mobility Research in Accra, interviewed seasonal workers on farms in three countries. Most welcomed machines that relieved them of heavy lifting, such as self-driving trolleys that follow a picker along the row and carry full trays to the packing shed, but they were far more suspicious of robots designed to do the picking. Uzoigwe notes that the first wave of field automation has in fact been mainly assistive: on the farms he visited, trolleys of this kind raised each picker's output by roughly a fifth, because workers no longer had to walk back and forth with loaded trays.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: His findings suggest that, for the foreseeable future, the typical arrangement in the field will be one of collaboration between people and machines rather than straightforward replacement. They should also make us sceptical of the claim that robots will simply solve the labour shortage. Machines need technicians to maintain and repair them, and skilled technicians are, if anything, even harder to recruit in rural areas than pickers. Moreover, where shortages arise mainly from low pay and poor living conditions, improving those conditions may be a quicker and cheaper remedy than an expensive and uncertain technology.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Robotic harvesting, then, is likely to arrive gradually and unevenly, crop by crop. It will come first to high-value produce grown in controlled settings, such as greenhouse tomatoes and tabletop strawberries, where conditions are predictable and the machine can work day and night. For crops scattered across irregular trees on steep hillsides, the human hand, with its remarkable combination of sensitivity and speed, may remain indispensable for a long time to come.

topic: universal basic income as a proposed response to automation: the case against means-tested welfare, what cash-transfer pilots can and cannot show, cost, the job guarantee alternative and insecure earnings
title: A Wage Without Work
subtitle: Fears that machines will take our jobs have revived interest in giving everyone a regular income. But are the two debates really connected?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As anxiety about automation has grown, so has enthusiasm for an idea that was once confined to the fringes of economic debate. A universal basic income is a regular cash payment made to every adult, regardless of whether they work or how much they already earn. Proposals of this kind have been championed by technology entrepreneurs, discussed in parliaments and tested in small-scale experiments on several continents. The connection usually drawn is straightforward: if machines are about to take over much of the work that people do, society will need a new way of distributing income. Yet the link between automation and basic income is, I believe, considerably weaker than is generally assumed, and the case for or against such a payment stands largely on its own merits.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The automation argument runs as follows. For two centuries, wages have been the main channel through which the wealth generated by an economy reaches ordinary households. If robots and software were to eliminate jobs faster than new ones could be created, that channel would narrow, and the gains from rising productivity would flow increasingly to the owners of machines. One of the most persuasive advocates of a basic income, the economist Halina Strzelecka of the Institute for Social Futures in Warsaw, adds a second argument that has nothing to do with robots. Existing welfare systems, she observes, were designed for a world of stable, full-time employment interrupted by occasional spells without work. Their reliance on means-testing, in which benefits are withdrawn as earnings rise, can leave claimants who take on extra hours scarcely better off than before. A payment that does not shrink when income increases would remove this disincentive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Evidence from pilot schemes has been encouraging, if limited. In one widely reported experiment in northern Europe, two thousand unemployed people received a modest monthly payment for two years with no conditions attached. Compared with a control group, they reported better health, lower stress and greater confidence in their future. Crucially for the scheme's supporters, their employment did not fall; if anything, it rose slightly. Professor Arjun Ravindran, a specialist in policy evaluation at the Bangalore Centre for Public Economics, nonetheless warns against reading too much into such results. Participants knew that the payments would end, he points out; they were drawn only from the unemployed rather than from the whole population; and nobody had to pay higher taxes to fund them. On the last point in particular he is surely right. No pilot, however carefully designed, can show how a country would respond to the tax increases that a national scheme would require.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of cost lies at the heart of the debate. A payment large enough to live on, given to every adult, would appear to consume a very large share of national income. Critics conclude that any affordable basic income would be too small to make a real difference, while one generous enough to matter would demand politically impossible tax rises. Supporters reply that the headline figure is misleading, because most of the money paid to people on comfortable incomes would be recovered through the taxes they pay. That reply is correct as far as it goes. The net cost of a basic income is certainly lower than the gross figure suggests, but it remains substantial, and advocates do their cause no favours by implying otherwise.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection comes from the sociologist Erik Söderholm, who argues that the case for basic income misunderstands why work matters. Employment provides not only money but also a daily structure, social contact, a recognised status and a sense of contributing to something larger than oneself. A cash payment, in his view, cannot supply any of these. Söderholm therefore prefers a job guarantee, under which the state would offer paid employment to anyone willing to take it. His concern for the non-financial value of work is legitimate. However, he gives too little weight to the vast amount of meaningful activity that already takes place outside paid employment, from caring for children and elderly relatives to volunteering in the community, much of which a basic income might make easier to sustain.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, finally, of the automation that supposedly makes all this urgent? So far, evidence of mass technological unemployment is thin: in many advanced economies, the proportion of adults in work has recently reached record levels. A more immediate problem is the spread of irregular and unpredictable earnings, particularly among people who find work through online platforms and may not know from one week to the next how much they will be paid. It is here, I would suggest, that the strongest case for a basic income lies, not as a substitute for work but as a stable floor beneath incomes that fluctuate.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate would therefore benefit from being separated from predictions about robots. If a basic income is a good idea, it should be adopted because it reduces poverty, removes disincentives and gives people security, whatever happens to employment. If it is a bad idea, fears about automation will not turn it into a good one.

topic: robot taxes: lost labour-tax revenue, the problem of defining a robot, effects on productivity and wages, the existing tax bias towards machines, taxing capital instead, and funding retraining
title: Taxing the Tireless Worker
subtitle: Should machines that replace people pay tax as people do? The proposal is simple to state and surprisingly hard to defend, or to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In most wealthy countries, the largest share of public revenue is raised, directly or indirectly, from work. Income tax is deducted from wages, and employers and employees together pay social insurance contributions that fund pensions and healthcare. When a machine takes over a job, therefore, the state loses more than a taxpayer: the firm that installed the machine no longer pays the employment taxes attached to the worker it has replaced. From this observation has grown the proposal for a robot tax, a levy on automation intended to recover the lost revenue and perhaps to slow the pace at which jobs disappear. Only one country has taken a step in this direction, and a cautious one, by reducing the tax relief that companies could claim when investing in automated equipment. The idea has obvious intuitive appeal. Most economists, however, regard it with considerable scepticism, and I share much of that scepticism, though not all of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty is one of definition. Dr Corina Pirvulescu, a tax lawyer at the Bucharest School of Fiscal Studies, points out that no country has yet produced a workable legal definition of a robot. An industrial arm welding car bodies obviously qualifies, but what about accounting software that eliminates a clerical post, a self-service kiosk in a restaurant or, for that matter, a dishwasher? Wherever the line is drawn, Pirvulescu argues, firms will redesign or relabel their equipment so that it falls on the untaxed side, and the revenue raised will be a fraction of what was forecast. The problem is genuine, but it is hardly unique to robots. Tax systems draw arbitrary lines all the time, between food and confectionery, for instance, or between employees and the self-employed, and they manage to function nonetheless.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more serious objection concerns the economic consequences. Professor Hiroshi Nakagami of the Kansai Institute of Public Finance argues that taxing investment in machinery discourages precisely the kind of productivity growth that has historically raised living standards. In most industries, he contends, automation complements human labour more than it replaces it, making the remaining workers more productive and therefore better paid. In the models he has constructed, a robot tax ultimately lowers the wages of the very workers it was designed to protect. Nakagami also observes that the countries with the highest number of industrial robots per manufacturing employee have not, on the whole, suffered from unusually high unemployment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most interesting defence of the idea starts from a different premise. Dr Obinna Ndiokwere, an economist at the Abuja Centre for Inclusive Growth, argues that the existing tax system is not neutral between people and machines. A company that hires a worker must pay employment taxes for as long as that worker remains on the payroll, whereas a company that buys a machine can often deduct its cost from taxable profits within a few years. The tax code, in other words, already gives employers a financial incentive to automate, even where a human being would do the job equally well. Seen in this light, a modest tax on automation would not penalise technology but would merely remove an existing bias. This argument seems to me to be the strongest in the proposal's favour, because it shifts the question from whether automation should be discouraged to whether it should continue to be subsidised.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet if the problem is that capital is taxed too lightly relative to labour, there may be better solutions than a tax aimed at robots. Elin Wahlqvist, a researcher at the Stockholm Policy Forum, proposes shifting the overall burden of taxation away from work and towards capital, by raising taxes on company profits and investment gains while cutting employment taxes for low-paid workers. Such a reform would leave firms free to choose the most productive technology without requiring anyone to decide what counts as a robot. The main obstacle is that capital, unlike most workers, can move easily across borders, so that any country acting alone risks driving investment elsewhere. The recent international agreement on a minimum rate of corporate tax suggests, though, that coordination between countries is not beyond reach.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many proposals for a robot tax specify that its revenue should pay for retraining workers whose jobs have been automated. Here the evidence counsels caution. Aino Kuusela, a labour economist at the Finnish Labour Research Unit, has reviewed the results of several dozen retraining programmes. Those designed in partnership with particular employers who had vacancies to fill generally led to stable jobs and higher earnings. By contrast, general classroom courses, unconnected to any specific opening, produced little measurable improvement in participants' earnings. Money, in short, is a necessary but far from sufficient condition for helping displaced workers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The robot tax, then, is probably a crude instrument aimed at a real problem. Tax systems were built for economies in which most income took the form of wages; if a growing share of income is earned by the owners of machines and software, those systems will eventually have to adapt. A narrow levy on a loosely defined category of equipment is unlikely to be the right adaptation. But the question that the proposal raises, namely how societies should pay for public services when work generates less of their income, is one that governments cannot avoid indefinitely.

title: The Missing Middle
subtitle: For four decades, jobs paying middling wages have been disappearing in many rich economies. Economists agree on the pattern far more than on its causes.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the early 1980s, the structure of employment in many advanced economies has changed shape. Jobs at the top of the wage scale, in the professions and management, have multiplied. So, perhaps more surprisingly, have jobs at the bottom, in care homes, restaurants, cleaning and security. What has shrunk is the middle: the clerical posts, machine-operating jobs and skilled production work that once offered people without university degrees a reasonably secure and well-paid living. Economists call this process job polarisation. The pattern itself is now well documented across dozens of countries. Its explanation, however, and its meaning for the people affected, are considerably more contested than popular accounts tend to acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation focuses on the nature of tasks rather than on jobs as a whole. Computers are extremely good at carrying out activities that can be reduced to explicit rules, such as calculating a payroll, filing records or repeating the same movement on an assembly line. Such routine tasks happened to be concentrated in middle-wage occupations. At the top of the scale, by contrast, work tends to involve judgement, persuasion and the solving of unfamiliar problems, while much low-paid work requires physical adaptability in unpredictable surroundings. Cleaning a hotel room, with its varied furniture and scattered belongings, remains far beyond the capabilities of current machines, even though most people find it undemanding. What is easy for humans, it turns out, is often difficult for computers, and the reverse.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Mira Tsvetkova, an economist at the Sofia Institute for Labour Market Studies, has assembled data from sixteen countries that lend this explanation considerable support. In her figures, the decline of middle-wage jobs began earlier and went further in countries that adopted computers more rapidly. Tsvetkova is careful, however, to distinguish between the polarisation of employment and the polarisation of pay. In several countries, she found, the number of low-wage service jobs grew strongly, yet the wages attached to them barely moved, so that the expansion at the bottom brought more work but not better rewards.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that technology is the main culprit. Professor Suman Manandhar, a sociologist at the Centre for Comparative Labour Studies, argues that two other developments account for much of the change. The first is offshoring, the transfer of manufacturing and later of back-office work to countries with lower labour costs. The second is the decline of trade unions, which had protected the wages and conditions of precisely those middle-ranking jobs. Manandhar points out that polarisation was noticeably weaker in countries where collective bargaining remained strong, even when their rate of computer adoption was similar. In my view, the two accounts are less opposed than they first appear. Communication technology was itself one of the things that made offshoring practical, and it is likely that technological and institutional forces reinforced one another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A separate question is what happened to the workers whose jobs vanished. The common assumption is that clerks and machine operators were pushed down into low-wage service work. Dr Kasper Lindeskov, a researcher at the Danish Centre for Register Research, tested this by following individual workers through national records over twenty years. He found that most of the shrinkage in routine employment came not from existing workers being displaced but from fewer young people entering such jobs in the first place. Older routine workers mostly remained in their posts until they retired, while new entrants to the labour market increasingly went either upwards, through further education, or downwards into service work. This finding is reassuring in one respect, since it suggests that relatively few mid-career workers suffered sudden displacement. It is troubling in another, because it implies that young people without degrees now enter a labour market with fewer ladders to climb.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recent advances in artificial intelligence complicate the picture further. Software that can draft documents, summarise reports and write computer code is beginning to perform tasks that were long regarded as non-routine and cognitive, and therefore safe. If these tools spread widely, the routine and non-routine distinction that explained the past forty years may prove a poor guide to the next twenty, and the professions at the top of the scale may discover that they, too, are exposed. It is sometimes argued that such systems still make errors which only an experienced specialist can detect, and that demand for senior professionals will therefore hold up. That may well be true, but it offers little comfort to those starting out, since the junior posts in which lawyers, analysts and programmers have traditionally learned their trade are exactly the ones these tools are best equipped to perform.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The standard policy response to polarisation has been to expand higher education, so that more people can move into the growing jobs at the top. That remains sensible, but it is not enough. Not everyone can obtain a degree, and not everyone wants one. Far more attention should be paid to the quality of the expanding jobs at the bottom, particularly in care work, which is difficult to automate and for which demand will rise as populations age. If the missing middle cannot easily be restored, the least that societies can do is to build a new one.

topic: collaborative robots (cobots) in small and medium-sized manufacturers: what they are used for, the meaning of 'collaborative' safety, underused machines, operators' experience and effects on jobs
title: Working Side by Side
subtitle: Lightweight 'collaborative' robots were supposed to bring automation within reach of the small workshop. The reality has been more interesting than the sales brochures.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of their history, industrial robots have been powerful, fast and dangerous. In car plants and electronics factories they are kept behind safety fences, and anyone who steps inside the enclosure while a robot is running risks serious injury. Such machines are expensive to install and must be programmed by specialists, which means they have generally made economic sense only for large manufacturers producing identical items in enormous quantities. Over the past fifteen years, however, a different kind of machine has appeared. Collaborative robots, or cobots, are lighter and slower, and are fitted with sensors that bring them to a halt if they touch an obstacle, so that in principle they can work alongside people without a cage. Many can be taught a new task simply by an operator guiding the arm through the required movements by hand. Their manufacturers have promoted them as the technology that will finally make automation affordable for small and medium-sized firms. That promise has been partly fulfilled, but in a more modest and more complicated way than the marketing suggested.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Small firms account for a large proportion of manufacturing employment in many countries, yet they have consistently lagged behind larger companies in adopting automation. Dr Paweł Kaszuba, an industrial engineer at the Baltic Institute of Manufacturing, surveyed some four hundred small manufacturers to find out how those that had bought cobots were actually using them. The great majority employed them for machine tending, the loading and unloading of parts from machine tools, or for packing finished goods into boxes; very few used them for the intricate assembly work that features prominently in promotional videos. Strikingly, when asked why they had invested, most owners did not mention reducing labour costs. Their main reason was that they could no longer find people willing to do monotonous, repetitive jobs.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question of safety turns out to be less straightforward than the term collaborative implies. A cobot is designed to limit the force and speed with which it can strike a person, but the danger it poses depends heavily on what it is holding. An arm that is harmless when moving a cardboard box becomes hazardous when it carries a sharp blade or a component that has just left a furnace. Neema Mbokani, a safety engineer at the Dar es Salaam Institute of Occupational Health, argues that it is therefore misleading to describe a robot as collaborative at all: only a particular application, the combination of robot, tool and task, can be judged safe or unsafe for people to work beside. She notes that many cobot installations end up enclosed by guards after a formal risk assessment, just like their traditional predecessors. Her point is well taken. True side-by-side working, with a person and a machine sharing a task at the same moment, is far rarer than the label suggests.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Because their speed is restricted for safety reasons, cobots are usually slower than conventional robots, and their benefits must come from elsewhere: from running unattended through the night, for example, or from freeing skilled staff for more demanding work. Professor Einar Kristjánsson, a production economist in Reykjavík, studied sixty firms in detail and found that the results depended less on the robot than on the organisation around it. Companies that redesigned the flow of work around their new machine achieved substantial gains in output. Those that simply placed a cobot at an existing workstation and expected it to replace a person saw little improvement. Kristjánsson estimates that roughly a quarter of the cobots in his sample were seriously underused, and some had been switched off altogether, becoming what one manager wryly called shelfware.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The experience of the people who work with cobots has received less attention. Dr Harleen Ahluwalia, an occupational psychologist at the Midlands Centre for Work and Wellbeing, interviewed operators in a range of factories. Many valued the relief from repetitive strain that came from handing awkward lifting and twisting movements to a machine. Others, however, complained of losing the rhythm of their work and of having to adjust their own pace to that of the robot beside them. The most consistent finding concerned involvement. Operators who had helped to teach the cobot its tasks reported far greater satisfaction than those whose machines had been installed and programmed by outside contractors. This suggests that how a robot is introduced shapes workers' attitudes at least as much as the technology itself.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What of the effect on jobs? In Kaszuba's survey, very few firms reported dismissing staff after buying a cobot; most said that workers had been moved to other duties. Such findings should be treated with some caution. Surveys of this kind rely on managers' own accounts, which may understate job losses, and a firm that dismisses nobody may still quietly decide not to replace employees who leave or retire. The absence of redundancies is not the same as the absence of an effect on employment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Cobots, then, are perhaps best understood not as robots that work hand in hand with people, but as a cheaper and more flexible way of automating simple, repetitive tasks. For small manufacturers, their greatest value may lie less in the work they perform than in what they teach: a firm that learns to install, program and adapt one modest machine acquires expertise on which more ambitious automation can later be built.

title: The Great Leveller?
subtitle: Early studies of AI assistants at work suggest they help beginners far more than experts. What that means for careers is another matter.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When software capable of drafting text and answering questions first became widely available, many commentators predicted that it would widen the gap between the most and least skilled employees. Highly educated professionals, it was assumed, would be best placed to exploit the new tools, just as they had gained most from earlier waves of computing. The first studies of these assistants in real workplaces have pointed, at least in some settings, in the opposite direction: it is the least experienced workers who appear to benefit most. This is an important finding, but its interpretation calls for more care than it has usually received.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most detailed evidence comes from a study by Dr Yelena Gerasimova, an economist at the Institute for Digital Economy Research, of a customer support company employing several thousand agents. The firm introduced an AI tool that suggested replies to agents while they were dealing with customers' queries, and because it was rolled out to different teams in stages, Gerasimova was able to compare agents with and without access. On average, the number of problems resolved per hour rose by around fourteen per cent. The gains, however, were very unevenly distributed. The newest agents improved by more than a third, reaching within two months a level of performance that had previously taken over half a year to attain. The most experienced agents, by contrast, gained almost nothing, and the quality of their conversations, as rated by customers, declined slightly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The explanation, Gerasimova suggests, lies in how the tool was built. It had been trained on thousands of conversations conducted by the company's most successful agents, so that its suggestions embodied the phrases, sequences and small tactics that distinguished the best performers from the rest. In effect, the tool captured the tacit knowledge of a few experts and made it available to everyone, a process Gerasimova describes as bottling expertise. It is worth pausing on what this implies. The knowledge of the top agents, for which they received no additional payment, was extracted and distributed to their colleagues, raising the productivity of the whole firm. Whether those agents ought to share in the resulting gains is a question that, in my view, deserves far more attention than it has so far received.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Similar results have emerged from controlled experiments. Professor Obiageli Chukwudebe, a cognitive psychologist at the Lagos Institute for Human-Computer Studies, asked several hundred professionals to complete realistic writing tasks such as reports and briefing notes. Those given access to an AI assistant finished roughly forty per cent faster, and the participants whose work had initially been rated weakest improved the most. Chukwudebe's study, however, contained an instructive twist. One of the tasks required careful analysis of a table of figures, a kind of problem at which the assistant was known to be unreliable. On that task, participants using the assistant performed worse than those working without it, apparently because they accepted plausible but mistaken suggestions. The effect was strongest among the less experienced participants, who were least able to recognise when the tool had gone wrong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This points to a broader worry. Lars Satterlund, a sociologist who studies professional training, argues that novices who rely on a stream of ready-made suggestions may never acquire the understanding that experienced workers built up through years of trial and error. Like drivers who follow satellite navigation without ever learning the layout of their city, they may perform well while the system works but find themselves helpless when it fails. Satterlund's argument is plausible, and it would be foolish to dismiss it. But it has not yet been demonstrated. The studies conducted so far have lasted months rather than years, and they offer no evidence, in either direction, about what happens to workers' skills over the course of a career.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also consequences for pay. If an assistant allows a recruit of two months to perform almost as well as a colleague of several years, employers may come to place less value on experience, and the wage premium that has traditionally rewarded seniority could shrink. Optimists point out that the same development could make it easier for newcomers to enter skilled occupations. Which of these outcomes prevails, however, will not be decided by the technology. Whether narrowing the gap in performance leads to higher pay for beginners or merely to lower pay for experienced staff depends on how wages are negotiated and on the state of the labour market, not on the software itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: AI assistants, then, are levelling devices in a narrow sense: they compress differences in measured output between workers. Their longer-term effects on careers remain genuinely uncertain. It is entirely possible that the same tool which helps a beginner through a difficult first month will, if relied upon for years, leave that person less capable than a colleague trained in the traditional way; it is equally possible that freeing novices from routine drafting will give them more time to learn what matters. Organisations adopting them would be wise to monitor not only how much their staff produce, but also whether those staff are still learning.

topic: the modern productivity paradox: why rapid advances in automation and AI have coincided with slow productivity growth (mismeasurement, implementation lags, a widening gap between leading and lagging firms, less transformative inventions)
title: The Vanishing Dividend
subtitle: Machines are cleverer than ever, yet output per worker in rich countries is growing more slowly than it did half a century ago. Economists are divided over why.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By almost any technical measure, the past two decades have been a period of extraordinary progress. Computing power has continued to multiply, robots have become cheaper and more capable, and software can now recognise speech, translate languages and write fluent prose. One might expect such advances to show up in the most basic indicator of economic progress, the amount produced per hour of work. Instead, productivity growth in most advanced economies has been markedly slower over the past fifteen years than in the decades that preceded them. A similar puzzle troubled economists in the 1980s, when computers were spreading rapidly through offices without any apparent effect on output, and it was eventually resolved in the late 1990s by a burst of productivity growth. It is tempting to assume that history will simply repeat itself. That assumption, however comforting, is not a safe one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first and simplest explanation is that the gains are real but are not being counted. Dr Anatoly Lukashevich, a statistician at the Institute for Economic Measurement, points out that many of the most widely used digital services, such as search engines, online maps and messaging applications, are provided to users free of charge. Because national accounts measure output largely through what people pay, the enormous value that consumers derive from these services is almost invisible in official figures. Improvements in quality, he adds, are also systematically underestimated. There is undoubtedly something in this argument. Yet the slowdown appears to be far too large to be explained by measurement errors alone, and it has affected countries and industries in which digital products play only a minor role. Moreover, statisticians faced similar difficulties in earlier decades, when productivity was nonetheless recorded as growing briskly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second explanation emphasises time. Professor Lilit Hakobjanyan, an economist at the Caucasus Institute for Innovation Studies, argues that technologies with wide applications require large complementary investments before they pay off. Firms must reorganise their operations, retrain their staff, redesign products and develop new ways of working, and much of this effort produces nothing that appears in measured output for several years. During this phase, Hakobjanyan maintains, productivity may actually seem to fall, since firms are devoting labour and money to building capabilities rather than producing goods. Only later, once these investments mature, does growth accelerate. On this view, the present slowdown is the quiet before a boom.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third account focuses not on the economy as a whole but on the differences between firms. Dr Rina Mukherjea, who directs the Centre for Firm Dynamics in Kolkata, has analysed data on tens of thousands of companies across a dozen countries. At the most advanced firms in each industry, she finds, productivity has continued to grow rapidly. The problem is that the rest have failed to keep up, so that the gap between leaders and laggards has widened considerably. New technologies, in other words, are not spreading. Mukherjea attributes this partly to the fact that the benefits of modern digital tools depend on large quantities of data, specialised skills and sheer scale, all of which smaller firms tend to lack. Of the explanations on offer, this seems to me the most persuasive, not least because it is consistent with what the data show at the level of individual companies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most pessimistic view comes from the economic historian Håkon Sørbøe of the Trondheim School of Economics. Sørbøe argues that today's innovations are simply less transformative than those of the century between 1870 and 1970. Electricity, the internal combustion engine, piped water and the telephone, he suggests, changed the conditions of daily life far more profoundly than any smartphone application. This is a stimulating argument, but it risks judging new technologies before their most important uses have been discovered. Those who lived through the first decades of electric power also struggled to imagine what it would eventually make possible, and many dismissed it as a luxury for the wealthy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The paradox has an awkward implication for debates about employment. Commentators frequently predict both that automation will eliminate vast numbers of jobs and that productivity growth will remain weak. These two forecasts are hard to reconcile, since if machines were replacing workers on a large scale, output per worker ought to be rising quickly. One possible resolution is that some automation is only marginally better than the people it replaces. A self-service kiosk may allow a restaurant to employ fewer staff, but if it is slower than a cashier and shifts work onto customers, the gain to the economy is small. Technologies of this kind can displace workers while contributing very little to growth, which is arguably the worst of both worlds.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The paradox probably has several causes rather than one, and the policy implications depend on which predominate. If the problem is mainly one of measurement, little needs to be done. If it is one of delay, patience may be enough. But if, as seems likely, the main difficulty is that new technologies are failing to spread beyond a small group of leading firms, then governments will need to look more closely at competition and at the support available to smaller companies.

title: The Hands Behind the Machine
subtitle: Behind many apparently automatic systems lies a large and largely unseen workforce. Will it fade away as artificial intelligence improves, or is it here to stay?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Artificial intelligence is usually presented to the public as a feat of autonomy: software that recognises faces, filters out offensive posts and answers questions without any human involvement. The reality is rather different. Behind many such systems stands a large workforce whose members label images so that programs can learn to identify objects, transcribe snippets of recorded speech, rate the quality of machine-generated answers and remove violent or abusive material that automated filters have missed. Some are even called upon to take over, remotely and without the user's knowledge, when an automated service encounters a situation it cannot handle. Technology companies often describe this labour as temporary scaffolding, needed only until the machines are clever enough to stand on their own. I believe this description is mistaken. Human work of this kind is likely to remain a lasting feature of artificial intelligence rather than a passing stage in its development.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the work is divided into tiny units, or microtasks, which are distributed through online platforms and paid for individually. A worker might be offered a few cents to draw boxes around the pedestrians in a street photograph or to decide whether a sentence expresses a positive or negative opinion. Dr Ioana Dumitrescu, a sociologist at the Cluj Centre for Digital Labour, surveyed some two thousand such workers in thirty countries. Many were university graduates living in places where suitable local employment was scarce. Once she included the time spent searching for tasks, waiting for them to appear and completing work that was later rejected without payment, median hourly earnings fell below the local minimum wage in most of the countries studied; roughly a third of all working time, she calculated, went unpaid. Nevertheless, a majority of respondents said they valued the freedom to decide when and where they worked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Will the demand for such labour decline? Professor Marko Arapović, a computer scientist at the Zagreb Institute of Machine Learning, believes it will. Newer techniques, he argues, allow systems to learn from vast quantities of unlabelled data, and models are increasingly able to generate examples on which to train themselves, so that the need for human labelling will steadily shrink. There is some truth in this, but I find the conclusion unconvincing. Each new application, each additional language and each change in the world that a system must understand creates fresh demand for human judgement. Moreover, systems trained largely on their own outputs tend to become less reliable over time, which makes human checking more important, not less. What seems to be happening is not that the work is disappearing but that its character is changing, from simple labelling towards more skilled evaluation of what machines produce.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most troubling form of this hidden labour is content moderation. Moderators may spend entire shifts viewing images and videos of violence and cruelty, and a number of studies have reported symptoms among them resembling those of post-traumatic stress. Dr Olena Prokopenko, a clinical psychologist at the Lviv Centre for Occupational Mental Health, compared moderators working for several different contractors. She found that the severity of their symptoms was related less to the total quantity of disturbing material they had seen than to the degree of control they had over their work. Strict quotas, being unable to pause after a particularly distressing item and a lack of access to counselling were all associated with worse outcomes. Contractors that permitted regular breaks and rotated staff between disturbing and routine tasks reported markedly lower levels of psychological harm among their employees.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why does this workforce remain so little known? Thandiwe Ndlovu-Kerr, an anthropologist at the Johannesburg Institute for Social Research, argues that its invisibility is partly deliberate. Investors and customers, she suggests, are attracted to the idea of fully automatic products, and acknowledging the human effort involved would undermine the impression of technological magic on which much of the industry's value depends. In addition, workers are usually classified as independent contractors and are spread across many intermediary firms, so that no single company appears responsible for them. Concealment may indeed be deliberate in some cases. In many others, however, it seems to be an accidental by-product of long chains of subcontracting, in which each firm knows little about the next, rather than the result of any conscious decision to hide.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A range of reforms has been proposed. These include a minimum rate of pay calculated per hour rather than per task, collective bargaining for platform workers and requirements for companies to disclose which of their products depend on human input. Of these, transparency seems the most important first step, since neither consumers nor regulators can address a problem they cannot see. Raising pay is clearly desirable, but it has to be pursued with care. Because the work can be performed from almost anywhere, a sharp increase in rates in one country might simply cause it to be moved to another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The story of this hidden workforce suggests that automation is often less the elimination of human labour than its relocation, to places where it is cheaper and harder to see. Any serious discussion of the future of work needs to include the people who make supposedly automatic systems function.

topic: predictive policing software, feedback loops in recorded crime data, weak evidence of effectiveness and transparency
title: The Map That Draws Itself
subtitle: Predictive policing promised to send officers where crime would happen next. Its critics argue that it mostly sent them back to where they had already been

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 2010s, a number of police forces began to experiment with software that claimed to forecast where crimes were likely to occur. The systems varied in design, but most worked on a similar principle: historical records of reported offences were fed into a statistical model, which then divided a city into small cells, often no larger than a few hundred metres across, and assigned each one a risk score for the coming shift. Officers were encouraged to spend any spare time patrolling the highest-scoring cells. The appeal was obvious. Forces facing budget cuts were told that a limited number of patrols could be deployed more efficiently, and the language of data seemed to offer an escape from accusations that decisions about where to patrol rested on prejudice or habit. It is worth remembering, however, that the promise of neutrality was a marketing claim long before it was ever a research finding.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential criticism concerns what has become known as the feedback loop. Dr Ingrid Brekkevold, a criminologist at the Skarvik Institute for Justice Studies, points out that police records are not a census of crime but a record of the crimes that happened to come to official attention. Offences such as drug possession are discovered largely when officers are present to observe them. If a model directs more patrols to a neighbourhood, more such offences will be recorded there, and the next round of predictions will rank that neighbourhood higher still. In Brekkevold's simulations, a slight initial difference in patrol intensity between two otherwise identical districts grew, within a few cycles, into a large and self-sustaining gap in recorded crime. The model, in her phrase, 'learns the shape of policing and mistakes it for the shape of crime'.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the loop is inevitable. Professor Chukwudi Nwokolo, a statistician who has advised several forces, argues that the problem depends heavily on which data are used. Burglary and vehicle theft are usually reported by victims, regardless of whether officers are nearby, and so are far less sensitive to where patrols have been sent. Models restricted to such victim-reported offences, he maintains, can be reasonably accurate without amplifying existing patterns of enforcement. This is a fair point, and it is consistent with the observation that the most controversial systems were those that included arrests for minor offences among their inputs. Yet the distinction is less clean than Nwokolo implies. Reporting rates themselves differ between communities: residents who distrust the police are less likely to report a burglary, which means that even victim-reported data partly reflect relationships with the police rather than crime alone.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A separate question is whether the systems reduced crime at all. Here the evidence is surprisingly thin. A review by the Civic Data Collective, an independent group of academic researchers and former crime analysts, examined published evaluations and found that most had been conducted by the software vendors themselves or by forces that had already purchased the product. Of the handful of controlled trials, the majority reported effects too small to distinguish from chance. The Collective's conclusion was that predictive policing had been adopted on the strength of its plausibility rather than its results, a verdict that seems, if anything, generous. Several forces quietly abandoned the tools when their contracts expired, citing cost rather than ethics.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the approach note that the alternative is rarely no prediction at all. Dr Aiko Matsuzaki, a former police analyst who now lectures on public administration, observes that patrol decisions have always rested on some form of forecast, whether the intuition of experienced sergeants or a pin map on the station wall. In her view, an explicit algorithm at least has the advantage that its assumptions can be written down, inspected and challenged, whereas the judgement of an individual officer cannot be audited in the same way. This is perhaps the strongest argument in the software's favour, but it holds only if forces actually allow outsiders to examine their models. In practice, many contracts treated the underlying code as a commercial secret.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The legal dimension adds further complications. Tomasz Krzemieniec, who researches administrative law, notes that a person stopped by police in a high-risk cell typically has no way of knowing that the decision to patrol there was influenced by software. Because the prediction concerns a place rather than an individual, existing protections against automated decision-making, which were mostly drafted with individual profiling in mind, may not apply. Krzemieniec proposes that forces be required to publish the inputs and the evaluation results of any forecasting tool before it is deployed, a requirement that would, he argues, cost little and deter the use of untested products.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be concluded? It would be a mistake to treat predictive policing as uniquely sinister; the patterns it reproduces were present in policing long before any software arrived. But the tools gave those patterns a new authority, presenting the outcomes of past decisions as if they were objective facts about the world. The more useful lesson may be a general one about data-driven decision-making: a model can only be as fair as the process that generated its training data, and when that process is itself shaped by the decisions the model is meant to guide, the risk of circularity is acute.

topic: demographic differences in the error rates of automated face recognition: training data, camera exposure, match thresholds and human review
title: Uneven Recognition
subtitle: Automated face-matching systems do not make mistakes equally often for everyone. Explaining why has turned out to be far from simple

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Automated face recognition works by converting an image of a face into a numerical template, a compact description of the proportions and textures that distinguish one face from another, and comparing it with templates already stored. Two broad tasks are usually distinguished. In verification, the system checks a single claim of identity, as when a traveller's face is compared with the photograph held on the chip of a passport. In identification, a probe image is searched against an entire database in the hope of finding a match. Both tasks can go wrong in two ways. A false non-match occurs when the system fails to recognise a person who is genuinely in its records; a false match occurs when it links a face to someone else. The consequences of these errors are far from equal. At an airport gate, a false non-match typically means a short delay and a conversation with an official, whereas a false match in a police search may lead to an innocent person being questioned or even detained.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For years, developers reported overall accuracy figures that were impressively high. It was only when independent evaluators began to break those figures down by demographic group that a less flattering picture emerged. In a large benchmarking exercise run by the International Biometrics Testing Office, more than 180 algorithms submitted by commercial and academic developers were tested on several million images. For the majority of algorithms, false match rates varied by a factor of ten or more between the groups with the lowest and highest rates, with women, the elderly and people with darker skin generally faring worst. Two qualifications were, however, emphasised in the report. First, the differences were far smaller among the most accurate algorithms, some of which showed almost no measurable disparity. Second, the direction of the bias was not fixed: several algorithms produced by developers in East Asia performed better on East Asian faces than on European ones, suggesting that the effect was a product of development choices rather than of anything inherent in particular faces.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This finding lent support to researchers who locate the problem primarily in training data. Dr Mirela Vrbanic, a computer vision specialist at the Kvarner Polytechnic Institute, notes that many early training sets were assembled by collecting photographs of public figures from the internet, a method that produced collections dominated by lighter-skinned men between the ages of twenty and fifty. In her experiments, retraining a model on a dataset balanced by age, sex and skin tone roughly halved the gap in false match rates between the best-served and worst-served groups. She concedes, though, that balancing could not close the gap entirely, and that gathering large numbers of images of under-represented groups raises its own difficult questions about consent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lars Hallqvist, an imaging engineer, believes that too much attention has been paid to algorithms and too little to cameras. The automatic exposure settings of many devices, he argues, were historically tuned to lighter skin, so that darker faces are more often underexposed and lose precisely the fine detail on which matching depends. In his laboratory, adjusting exposure for each individual face before matching narrowed demographic differences more than rebalancing the training data did. Hallqvist's results have yet to be replicated outside controlled conditions, however, and critics point out that surveillance cameras in streets and stations, unlike passport kiosks, offer little opportunity to control lighting at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective shifts attention from the system itself to the way it is operated. Every face recognition system reports a similarity score for each comparison, and an operator must decide on a threshold above which two images are declared to belong to the same person. The sociologist Nadège Ateba observes that operators normally apply a single threshold to everyone. Because some groups have higher underlying false match rates, the same threshold produces more wrongful matches for them. Some vendors have proposed setting different thresholds for different groups in order to equalise error rates. Ateba regards this as technically sensible but legally precarious, since in a number of jurisdictions it would amount to explicit differential treatment on the basis of race, which is precisely what anti-discrimination law is designed to prevent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many authorities have responded to these concerns by insisting that no match be acted upon until it has been confirmed by a trained human examiner. Yet a study led by Beatriz Lisboa-Prates suggests that this safeguard is weaker than it appears. When reviewers were shown a ranked list of candidates generated by an algorithm, they selected the top-ranked candidate in roughly four out of five cases, including many in which the true match was further down the list or absent altogether. Reviewers who had received specialist training performed better, but only modestly. The human check, in other words, frequently ratified the machine's judgement rather than testing it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to look for a single cause and a single remedy. The evidence suggests instead that disparities in face recognition arise at several points at once: in the composition of training data, in the behaviour of cameras, in the thresholds chosen by operators and in the habits of the people asked to check the results. Improvements at any one of these points are worthwhile, but none is likely to be sufficient on its own, and evaluations that report a single headline accuracy figure will continue to conceal more than they reveal.

topic: explaining automated decisions to the people affected: interpretable models, post-hoc explanation tools, counterfactual explanations and contestability
title: Reasons on Request
subtitle: When an algorithm turns down an application, what does the applicant deserve to be told?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Suppose that an application for a small business loan is rejected within seconds by an automated system. The applicant, understandably, wants to know why. In a growing number of jurisdictions, people subject to significant automated decisions now have some legal entitlement to information about the logic involved, and few would argue that this is unreasonable. The difficulty lies elsewhere. The word 'explanation' means quite different things to the engineers who build such systems, to the lawyers who draft the regulations and to the people on the receiving end of a decision, and much of the current debate consists of these groups talking past one another.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For one school of thought, the answer is to avoid the problem at its source. Professor Helka Kuusinen, a computer scientist who has worked extensively with banks and public agencies, argues that high-stakes decisions should be made only by models that are interpretable in themselves: scoring rules with a handful of weighted factors, or short lists of if-then conditions that a non-specialist can follow. Opaque systems, she maintains, are frequently adopted out of habit rather than necessity. In her comparisons across dozens of datasets drawn from lending, insurance and criminal justice, simple models typically came within one or two percentage points of the accuracy achieved by far more complex ones. Her case is persuasive where the data are structured, as credit records are, but it is weaker for tasks involving images or free text, where the advantage of complex models remains considerable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second family of techniques leaves the complex model untouched and instead generates explanations after the event. These post-hoc methods work by building a simplified approximation of how the model behaves in the neighbourhood of a single decision, and then reporting which input features carried the most weight. They are now widely offered by software providers, but Dr Ferenc Szilvassy, who studies the security of machine learning systems, has cast doubt on their reliability. In his tests, small and seemingly irrelevant changes to an applicant's details, such as rounding an income figure, could produce markedly different explanations for essentially the same decision. More troubling still, Szilvassy demonstrated that a model could be deliberately constructed so that standard explanation tools highlighted innocuous factors, such as length of employment, while its decisions in fact depended heavily on postcode, a variable that in many cities serves as a proxy for ethnicity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The legal scholar Yaw Anokye-Mensah has championed a different approach altogether. Rather than attempting to describe what happens inside the model, a counterfactual explanation tells applicants what would have had to be different for the outcome to change: had your annual income been a certain amount higher, or your existing debt a certain amount lower, the loan would have been approved. Anokye-Mensah points out that such statements can be generated without disclosing how the model works, which reassures companies anxious about trade secrets, and that they give applicants something they can act upon. The idea is an attractive one, but it is not as neutral as it first appears. For any rejected application there are usually many possible counterfactuals, and deciding which to present is itself a consequential choice. Some, moreover, point to characteristics that an applicant cannot realistically alter, such as age or the length of a credit history.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Research on how people actually respond to explanations complicates matters further. In a series of experiments, a group led by the psychologist Parisa Moaveni presented participants with automated decisions accompanied by explanations of varying quality. Explanations of any kind made participants more willing to accept the outcome, and the effect barely depended on whether the explanation was accurate. Even a statement that conveyed no real information, such as a note that the decision 'reflected the applicant's overall profile', increased acceptance compared with no explanation at all. Moaveni concludes that explanations can function less as a means of informing people than as a means of reconciling them to decisions they might otherwise question.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings point towards a conclusion that the debate has been slow to reach: explanation is a means, not an end. What a rejected applicant ultimately needs is not a description of a model but a realistic opportunity to contest the decision, to correct errors in the data on which it was based and to have the case reconsidered by someone with the authority to change the outcome. An explanation offered without any route to appeal is of limited value, however accurate it may be. It would also be sensible to shift part of the burden from individual decisions to the systems themselves, requiring organisations to justify in advance why an automated tool is appropriate for a particular purpose and to publish evidence of how it performs across different groups of applicants.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the technical work on explanation has been wasted. Interpretable models, post-hoc tools and counterfactuals each have legitimate uses, and engineers who can understand their own systems are better placed to detect errors before they cause harm. But the question of what people are owed when an algorithm decides their fate is not, in the end, a purely technical question, and it is unlikely to be settled by better software alone.
