topic: competing statistical definitions of fairness and the impossibility of satisfying them all, illustrated by risk scores used to screen child welfare referrals
title: Fair by Which Measure?
subtitle: Mathematics has shown that an algorithm cannot be fair in every sense at once. The harder question is who should decide which sense matters

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Agencies responsible for the protection of children receive far more referrals than they can investigate. A neighbour reports shouting, a teacher notices bruises, a doctor is concerned about a missed appointment; each call must be assessed, often within hours, by a screener who decides whether it warrants a visit. Several agencies now support these decisions with a statistical risk score, calculated from administrative records, which estimates how likely it is that a child will be placed in care within the following two years. The score does not make the decision, but it is intended to draw attention to cases that a busy screener might otherwise underrate. Almost as soon as such tools were introduced, they were accused of treating families from different ethnic and economic backgrounds unequally, and the attempt to settle that accusation has exposed a difficulty that runs through every debate about algorithmic fairness.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that 'fair' can be defined statistically in several reasonable ways, and the definitions conflict. A score may be calibrated, meaning that a given score corresponds to the same actual level of risk whatever group a family belongs to. Alternatively, it may produce equal error rates, meaning that the proportion of families wrongly flagged as high-risk, and the proportion wrongly passed over, are the same in every group. Dr Signe Ebbesen, a statistician, was among several researchers who proved that whenever two groups differ in the underlying frequency of the outcome being predicted, no score can satisfy both criteria simultaneously, except in the trivial case of a perfect predictor. The conflict is therefore not a flaw of any particular model but a matter of arithmetic.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ebbesen draws a political conclusion from this mathematical one. Since some form of unfairness, by at least one definition, is unavoidable, the choice of which definition to prioritise is a value judgement, and in her view it should be made openly by bodies that are accountable to the public rather than by the technical staff who happen to build the system. This seems to me entirely right. In practice the choice has usually been made by engineers, often without being recognised as a choice at all, simply because one fairness measure was the default in the software they were using.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers regard the competing definitions as equally weighty. Dr Moses Walusimbi, who studies decision-making in social work, argues that calibration matters most in this setting. If a score of eight indicated a higher real risk for one group than for another, he reasons, experienced screeners would soon learn to adjust the numbers mentally according to a family's background, quietly reintroducing the very discretion the tool was meant to discipline. The argument is reasonable as far as it goes. Calibration, however, guarantees only that a score predicts the recorded outcome equally well for every group, and that guarantee is worth having only if the recorded outcome is itself a fair measure of what the agency actually cares about.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It is precisely this assumption that Dr Inés Garcilaso challenges. Placement in care, she notes, is not a natural event but the result of decisions taken by the same agencies that use the score. Families on low incomes are in contact with public services far more often than wealthier ones, through benefit offices, public hospitals and subsidised housing, and each contact is an opportunity for a concern to be reported. Comparable difficulties in affluent households are more often handled privately and never reach official records. A model that predicts placement with perfect calibration may therefore faithfully reproduce differences in how closely families are observed. Garcilaso has proposed training models on outcomes less shaped by agency activity, such as hospital admissions for serious injury, though she acknowledges that these too are recorded unevenly.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different objection comes from the economist Henrik Westerdahl, who contends that debates about the statistical properties of scores neglect the relevant comparison. The alternative to an imperfect algorithm, he points out, is not perfect fairness but human judgement, which has its own well-documented disparities. In an evaluation he led in one regional agency, the gap between groups in the proportion of referrals screened in for investigation narrowed after the score was introduced. This deserves to be taken seriously, but it is a single study, and its results depended heavily on how screeners used the tool. Westerdahl's own data show that screeners overrode the score far more often for some families than for others, so that the narrowing may owe as much to human choices as to the algorithm.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The philosopher Alena Hroch has argued that the fairness of a prediction cannot be judged apart from what is done with it. If a high score leads to an offer of voluntary support, such as help with childcare or housing, then wrongly flagging a family carries a modest cost. If the same score triggers a formal investigation, with the fear and stigma that accompany it, the identical error becomes a serious harm. Two tools with the same error rates may thus differ greatly in their moral significance. This is, I believe, the most important point to emerge from the entire debate, because it moves attention from the properties of the algorithm to the institutions that act upon it, which is where the consequences for families are actually determined.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a company publishes its annual accounts, investors expect them to have been checked by an independent auditor. In recent years it has become common to argue that the algorithms which rank job applicants, set insurance premiums or decide which advertisements people see should be subject to something similar, and in a few places the idea has already been written into law: one major city now requires employers who use automated hiring tools to commission an annual 'bias audit' and publish a summary of the results. The comparison with financial auditing is a useful one, but it is misleading in one crucial respect. Financial audits rest on accounting standards that have been negotiated and refined over more than a century, so that an auditor's opinion has a widely understood meaning. No equivalent consensus yet exists for algorithms, and in its absence the word 'audit' can be attached to almost anything.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most revealing audits have been carried out without the cooperation of the companies concerned. In a 'sock-puppet' audit, researchers create artificial user accounts that are identical except for a single characteristic and then compare how a system treats them. A team led by Darius Rezvani, a computational social scientist, set up several thousand fictitious job-seeker profiles on a large recruitment platform, varying only whether the name on each profile was typically male or typically female. Over six months, advertisements for engineering and software vacancies were displayed to the female-named profiles substantially less often. The platform responded that its system did not use gender at all, and that the pattern arose because advertisers competing for the attention of younger women, a valuable audience for retailers, pushed up the price of reaching them, so that employers with fixed budgets reached fewer of them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The episode illustrates both the power and the limits of the method. External audits of this kind can establish that people are treated differently, but they rarely reveal why, since the researchers cannot see inside the system. They also expose auditors to considerable risk. Most platforms prohibit fictitious accounts in their terms of service, and several research groups have received warnings from lawyers threatening legal action. Marek Sokolinski, who specialises in technology law, argues that this situation is untenable and proposes a statutory safe harbour that would protect researchers conducting audits in the public interest from being sued, provided that they follow ethical guidelines and do not harm real users.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Audits commissioned by the companies themselves face a different problem. The organisational sociologist Rosario Lechuga examined thirty summaries published under the city's hiring-tool law. Most, she found, reported a single statistic: the ratio between the rates at which candidates of different sexes and ethnic groups were selected. Many relied entirely on data supplied by the vendor of the tool, and not one examined whether the tool actually predicted how well candidates would perform once employed. Lechuga describes the result as 'audit-washing', in which the language of independent scrutiny lends credibility to systems that have barely been examined. Her concern is justified. An audit paid for by the organisation under examination is never entirely free from pressure, as the history of financial scandals amply demonstrates.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Financial auditing, however, has developed safeguards against such pressure, including professional bodies, licensing examinations and legal liability for negligent work. Kaisa Eskelinen, a researcher in public administration, believes that algorithmic auditors need an equivalent professional structure, with recognised qualifications and a code of practice. Her critics respond that the field is changing too quickly for fixed standards, which might become rigid and obsolete long before they could be revised. There is something in this objection, but it argues for a particular kind of standard rather than for none. Rules that specify the procedures an audit must follow, such as which data must be independently obtained and which questions must be asked, are far less likely to date than rules that lay down precise numerical thresholds for acceptable disparity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the object of an audit. A financial audit examines a fixed period that has already ended, whereas many algorithms are retrained or adjusted every few weeks. An audit that is accurate on the day it is completed may, by the time it is published, describe a system that is no longer in use. For this reason, some regulators have begun to argue for continuous monitoring, under which companies would be obliged to give an official body ongoing access to anonymised data about the decisions their systems make. Such schemes are still at an early stage, and it remains unclear how they would be funded or staffed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these difficulties is a reason to abandon auditing. On the contrary, without some means of independent examination, claims that an algorithm is fair can be neither confirmed nor refuted. But it would be naive to regard auditing as sufficient on its own. An audit can tell us whether a system behaves as its owners say it does; it cannot tell us whether that system should have been built at all, and that question is one for public debate rather than for technical inspection.

topic: label choice bias in healthcare algorithms: predicting medical spending as a stand-in for health need, and the problem of choosing what a model should predict
title: The Wrong Target
subtitle: Some of the most consequential biases in medical algorithms arise not from the data a model learns from but from what it is asked to predict

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Many health systems run so-called care management programmes for patients with complex, long-term conditions. Those enrolled may receive additional home visits from nurses, help in organising their medication and a named coordinator who can be telephoned when problems arise. Places are limited, and in order to decide who should be offered one, hospitals and insurers increasingly rely on algorithms that predict which patients will require the most care in the coming year. Because 'need for care' is not something that is directly recorded anywhere, the developers of several widely used tools trained their models on a convenient substitute: the amount of money that would be spent on each patient's healthcare over the following twelve months. The choice appeared entirely sensible. Sicker people, after all, generally cost more to treat, and spending data are complete, standardised and readily available.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The weakness of that reasoning was exposed by a team led by the health economist Grace Mukasa-Ochola, which examined one commercial tool used across a large hospital network. The researchers found that, at any given risk score, patients from a disadvantaged minority group had considerably more active chronic illnesses than majority-group patients with an identical score. In other words, they had to be much sicker before the algorithm ranked them as highly. The explanation lay not in any mathematical error, for the tool predicted costs rather well, but in the fact that less money was spent on minority patients at the same level of illness. Distance from clinics, difficulty taking time off work and a well-founded mistrust of medical institutions all reduced the care they received. When the team retrained the model to predict a measure combining the number of active chronic conditions with avoidable emergency visits, the proportion of minority patients selected for the programme almost doubled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What makes this case especially instructive is that the tool never used ethnicity as an input. Its designers might reasonably have believed that, having excluded the variable, they had excluded the bias. The episode shows how little protection such exclusion offers. When the quantity a model is trained to predict already reflects unequal treatment, the model will reproduce that inequality through whatever other variables are available to it, and no amount of care in selecting inputs will prevent it from doing so.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It would be comforting to conclude that the solution is simply to choose a better target, but Professor Teodor Tomescu, a clinical informatician, warns that there is no perfectly neutral alternative. The number of diagnosed conditions, he points out, depends on patients having seen a doctor who recorded those diagnoses; an illness that has never been diagnosed is invisible to the data. Even emergency admissions depend on how close a patient lives to a hospital. 'Every label', Tomescu argues, 'is ultimately a record of contact with the health system.' He recommends that developers train models on several different labels and examine where their rankings diverge, since disagreement between them is often the clearest signal that one group is being misjudged. This is sound advice, though it would place a considerable burden on smaller hospitals, which rarely employ the analysts that such comparisons require.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A related controversy concerns the deliberate inclusion of group membership in clinical formulae. Some long-established prediction rules adjust their results according to a patient's recorded ethnicity, on the grounds that average physiological measurements differ between populations. The epidemiologist Liisa Paikkari argues that many such adjustments were based on small and unrepresentative studies, and that they routinely confuse biological differences with the social conditions in which different groups live. She nonetheless cautions against removing them hastily: unless a correction is replaced with better measurements, its removal may simply move errors from one group of patients to another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The ethicist Hanna Riegelhof approaches the problem from a different direction. Ranking patients by predicted spending, she contends, reflects the financial interest of the organisation, which hopes to reduce its future costs, rather than the interests of patients. The question a care programme ought to answer is not which patients will be most ill, nor which will be most expensive, but which would gain the most from the help on offer, and these need not be the same people: some of the sickest patients may benefit little from extra coordination, while others with moderate needs may benefit greatly. This is, to my mind, the deepest point in the whole debate, although it is also the hardest to act upon, since reliable evidence about who benefits from an intervention can usually be obtained only through carefully controlled trials.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What should follow in practice? At present, when vendors validate their products, they typically report how accurately the tool predicts the outcome it was built to predict. That is necessary, but it answers the wrong question if the outcome itself is a poor reflection of what matters. Regulators and purchasers should insist that developers state explicitly what their models are designed to predict and justify why that quantity is an appropriate guide to the decision being made. Such a requirement would cost little, and it would bring into the open a choice that has too often been treated as a technical detail.

topic: stereotyped associations in word embeddings and language models: measuring them, the limits of debiasing, data filtering and whether models mirror or amplify bias
title: Words That Carry Weight
subtitle: Computers that learn language from human writing also learn its prejudices. Removing them is proving harder than expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Modern language technologies do not learn the meanings of words from dictionaries. Instead, they analyse vast collections of text and represent each word as a list of several hundred numbers, calculated from the company that the word keeps. Words that tend to appear in the same kinds of surroundings, such as 'river' and 'stream', end up with closely matching lists. The results can be striking: by simple addition and subtraction of these lists, a system can complete analogies such as 'Paris is to France as Tokyo is to …' without ever having been told anything about geography. Yet the same process that captures useful regularities also captures less welcome ones. Because the system learns from patterns of use, it inevitably absorbs the habitual pairings found in human writing, including those that link particular occupations with one sex or particular names with negative words.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the first systematic attempts to measure these pairings was made by Dr Kadri Sarapuu, a computational linguist, who borrowed her method from social psychology. Psychologists have long used reaction-time tests to detect implicit associations in people, measuring, for instance, how quickly participants link certain names with pleasant or unpleasant words. Sarapuu calculated the equivalent distances within the numerical representations and found a pattern that closely mirrored the human results. For Sarapuu, the finding demonstrates that such systems function as mirrors: the prejudice they display is not created by the algorithm but inherited from the texts on which it was trained. In her view, this makes language models valuable instruments for studying society, even as it makes them hazardous to deploy uncritically.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The obvious response was to try to remove the offending associations. An influential early technique identified a 'gender direction' within the mathematical space, essentially the difference between pairs such as 'he' and 'she', and then erased that component from words that ought to be neutral, such as 'engineer' or 'nurse'. At first the method appeared successful, since the cleaned system no longer completed analogies with stereotyped answers. However, a group led by Patrice Ilunga-Mbaya then showed that words previously associated with women still clustered together after the treatment, and that a simple classifier could recover their original gender association with around ninety per cent accuracy. The bias had not been removed; it had merely been made less visible. It is hard to avoid the conclusion that these early efforts were largely cosmetic.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Today's large language models, which generate entire passages of text, present the same problem on a larger scale. Developers now attempt to reduce bias in two main ways: by filtering out objectionable material before training, and by adjusting a model afterwards on the basis of human ratings of its responses. The sociolinguist Eleni Lavrentiou has drawn attention to an unintended consequence of the first approach. Automated filters designed to remove offensive language, she found, disproportionately flagged writing that contained features of certain regional and minority dialects, apparently because such features rarely appeared in the 'clean' examples used to build the filters. The result was that texts produced by these communities were removed in disproportionate numbers, leaving the model even less familiar with their ways of speaking. This is an important finding, because it shows how an effort to reduce one kind of unfairness can quietly create another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sarapuu's image of the mirror has itself been challenged. Dr Anders Bergsland, a data scientist, argues that it is too comfortable, since it implies that models merely reflect society as it is. The text collections used to train them are far from representative of human language use: they over-represent material from a small number of wealthy countries, from online forums and from the kinds of people who write most prolifically on the internet. Moreover, Bergsland's measurements suggest that models can intensify associations as well as reproduce them; for several occupational categories, the gender skew in a model's outputs exceeded the skew in the text it had been trained on. Both researchers are, I think, partly right. Language models do inherit their biases from human writing, but from a narrow and distorted sample of it, and the process of learning can exaggerate what it inherits.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Underlying the technical debate is a question that engineers cannot settle alone: should a language system reflect the world as it is, or as it ought to be? If most nurses in a given country are women, is a model that assumes a nurse is female simply accurate, or is it perpetuating an injustice? The answer, it seems to me, depends on the purpose to which the system is put. A tool designed to help historians search nineteenth-century newspapers should preserve the associations of its period, since those associations are part of what is being studied. A system that drafts job advertisements or screens applications, by contrast, has no business reproducing them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the experience of the past decade suggests, then, is that bias in language technology cannot be removed by a single technical fix applied at the end of development. It has to be considered at every stage, from the choice of training texts to the decision about where and how the finished system will be used.

topic: disagreement among human data labellers in training AI systems: majority voting, systematic perspective differences, soft labels, annotators' working conditions and dataset documentation
title: Whose Ground Truth?
subtitle: Machine learning depends on human beings labelling examples correctly. But what if there is no single correct label to give?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of the artificial intelligence systems in everyday use learn from examples that people have labelled by hand: this photograph contains a dog, that email is spam, this comment is abusive. Engineers refer to such labels as 'ground truth', a phrase borrowed from the practice of remote sensing, in which readings taken from aircraft or satellites were checked against observations made at the site itself. The metaphor implies that a label is a fact waiting to be recorded. For many tasks this is reasonable enough, since almost everyone agrees about whether an image shows a dog. For others, such as deciding whether a remark is offensive, sarcastic or threatening, agreement among labellers is often strikingly low. The standard response has been to collect several judgements for each item, adopt the majority verdict and treat the remaining opinions as noise to be discarded. This practice, so routine that it is rarely even described in research papers, deserves considerably more scrutiny than it has received.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Evidence that the discarded opinions are not merely noise comes from a study by the sociologist Awa Sangare-Diallo. Her team asked annotators from a range of backgrounds to rate the same set of online comments for offensiveness. Comments in which members of a community used terms or dialect features characteristic of that community were judged offensive far more often by annotators from outside it, who did not recognise the usage as affectionate or ironic. Conversely, annotators who belonged to groups targeted by certain kinds of remark frequently rated as offensive comments that others regarded as harmless. The disagreement, in other words, was systematic: it followed the lines of annotators' experience. Under majority voting, the perspective that prevails is simply that of whichever group happens to supply the most labellers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One proposed remedy is to stop forcing a single answer. Mikko Ylitalo, a machine learning researcher, has trained models to predict the full distribution of annotators' judgements, so that a comment might be represented as, say, sixty per cent offensive rather than simply offensive or not. In his experiments, such models were no less accurate than conventional ones and gave a more honest indication of their own uncertainty. The approach is promising, but it does not dissolve the underlying difficulty. A platform must still decide whether to remove a given comment, and that decision is binary. Preserving disagreement within the model merely postpones the moment at which someone must choose whose view counts.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The conditions under which labelling is done add a further layer of complication. Tendai Dzamba, who studies digital labour, has documented how annotation is commonly outsourced to workers in lower-income countries who are paid per item and must work quickly to earn a reasonable wage. They are frequently asked to judge material from cultural contexts quite unlike their own, following guidelines written in a second language. Quality control is often carried out by comparing each worker's answers with those of the majority, and workers whose answers diverge too often are removed from the project. Dzamba argues that this arrangement teaches annotators to predict what other annotators will say rather than to report their own judgement, which manufactures an appearance of consensus where none exists.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, however, to conclude that every disagreement reflects a meaningful difference of perspective. The psychologist Ioana Ghiorghiu presented annotators with items they had already labelled several weeks earlier and found that they changed their own verdict in roughly one case in five. Their ratings were also affected by the order in which material appeared: a comment seen immediately after a series of extremely abusive ones was judged noticeably milder than the same comment seen in isolation. Some of what is discarded as noise, then, really is noise, and any approach that treats all variation as valuable information risks enshrining inconsistency.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most practical proposal may be the least glamorous. Rui Ferraz-Lobo, a specialist in data management, argues that every labelled dataset should be accompanied by documentation describing who produced the labels, what instructions they were given, how they were paid and how disagreements were resolved. Without such information, he contends, users of a dataset cannot judge whose perspective it embodies. Some critics object that collecting details of annotators' backgrounds would intrude on the privacy of workers who are already poorly protected. The objection is a fair one, but it can be met by reporting such information only in aggregate, so that no individual can be identified.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these measures will produce labels that are objectively correct, because for many of the tasks now delegated to machines no such labels exist. What they can do is make visible the judgements that have been built into a system, and the people who made them. A label, on this view, is not a fact about the world but a decision about it, and decisions, unlike facts, can and should be open to question.

topic: algorithmic credit scoring with alternative data such as mobile phone records: financial inclusion, debt cycles, proxies for disadvantage, gaming and regulation of loan terms
title: Credit from the Call Log
subtitle: Lenders are using mobile phone data to judge people who have never had a bank loan. Is this inclusion, or a new kind of exclusion?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Around the world, well over a billion adults have never borrowed from a bank, and for most of them the obstacle is not a poor repayment record but the absence of any record at all. A conventional credit score is built from a history of loans, card payments and bank accounts; someone who has never had these is, from a lender's point of view, simply invisible. Over the past fifteen years, a new generation of digital lenders has set out to solve this 'thin file' problem by drawing on what is known as alternative data. With an applicant's permission, their software may examine how often a mobile phone is topped up with credit, the regularity of utility payments, the number and pattern of calls and messages, and even the way the application form itself is completed, including the time of day and the speed of typing. In several countries, small loans assessed in this way are now approved within minutes and paid directly into a mobile money account.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the approach point to impressive results. Adnan Jusufovic, a development economist, studied a digital lender operating across several low-income countries and found that its phone-based scores predicted repayment almost as accurately as conventional bank scores did for applicants who possessed both. More importantly, the lender extended credit to several hundred thousand people who had never previously borrowed from a formal institution. For market traders who need to buy stock, or farmers waiting for a harvest, such loans can make a real difference, and there is little doubt that alternative data have opened doors that were previously closed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Access to credit, however, is not the same thing as benefiting from it. Digital loans of this kind are typically small, short and expensive: when fees are taken into account, annual interest rates frequently run into the hundreds of per cent. Fatmata Sesay-Koroma, who has researched microfinance for two decades, surveyed borrowers in three cities and found that a substantial minority had taken loans from several different apps, using new borrowing to repay old debts. Many described receiving repeated and sometimes threatening messages from collectors. It would be a mistake to assume that every additional borrower represents a gain; for some, easy credit has been the start of a cycle of debt that is difficult to escape.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Questions of fairness arise as well. Sigrid Amundrud, a specialist in consumer law, argues that many alternative indicators act as hidden proxies for disadvantage. Irregular phone top-ups, for example, often reflect irregular wages rather than irresponsibility, and some models have lowered an applicant's score if people in their list of contacts had previously defaulted, a practice critics describe as 'guilt by association' that inevitably penalises residents of poor neighbourhoods. Amundrud also notes that legal safeguards have failed to keep pace. In many jurisdictions, applicants who are refused credit are entitled to be told the main reasons, but these rights were framed when credit decisions relied on loans and repayment histories. Moreover, an applicant can dispute an inaccurate entry in a bank record, whereas there is no obvious way to contest a judgement based on typing speed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Joseph Lumbwe, a data scientist who has built scoring models for a digital lender, accepts some of these criticisms but insists that they can be addressed. When his company removed all variables derived from applicants' contacts, he reports, the accuracy of its predictions declined only slightly, suggesting that the most objectionable features were also among the least necessary. Lumbwe further argues that alternative lending should be evaluated against the options borrowers actually have, which in many places means informal moneylenders whose charges are even higher and whose methods of collection are considerably harsher.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A subtler difficulty concerns the stability of the signals themselves. Once borrowers learn which behaviours raise their scores, they can be expected to adjust them, topping up their phones in a regular pattern or filling in forms at particular times of day. Whether such indicators would remain informative once they become widely known seems to me highly doubtful, since a measure that people deliberately manage ceases to reveal what it once did. There are also serious concerns about privacy. The consent that applicants give is usually obtained through lengthy agreements on a small screen, written in technical language, which few people read and fewer still could reasonably be expected to understand.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Much of the debate about alternative data has concentrated on the data: which variables are acceptable, how accurate the models are and how applicants can challenge them. These questions matter, but they are not the whole story. The harm suffered by over-indebted borrowers arises chiefly from the cost of loans and the conduct of those who collect them, and regulators would do well to give these matters at least as much attention as the algorithms. Financial inclusion is a worthwhile goal, but only if the credit on offer is affordable for those who receive it.

topic: human oversight of algorithmic decisions: automation bias, algorithm aversion, alert fatigue and 'rubber-stamp' review in public agencies
title: A Signature on the Machine's Verdict
subtitle: Laws increasingly demand that a human being review important automated decisions. Whether that review achieves anything is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As algorithms have taken on a larger role in decisions about welfare benefits, medical treatment and criminal justice, legislators have reached for a reassuring formula: significant automated decisions must be subject to meaningful human oversight. The principle has obvious appeal. It promises to combine the consistency and speed of a computer with the contextual understanding and moral responsibility of a person, and it ensures that someone can be held to account when things go wrong. Yet the assumption that placing a human being between an algorithm and the people it affects automatically adds a safeguard rests on surprisingly little evidence. Indeed, a growing body of research suggests that in many settings the human reviewer contributes much less than the law presumes, and occasionally makes matters worse.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-documented problem is what psychologists call automation bias. In a series of experiments conducted by the cognitive psychologist Bruno Tchakounte, participants were asked to review applications for welfare benefits, each accompanied by the system's suggested outcome. When that suggestion was deliberately made incorrect, participants went along with it in roughly three-quarters of cases. They also frequently failed to notice problems that the system had not drawn attention to, as though the absence of a warning were proof that none was needed. The tendency became stronger as the number of cases to be processed increased and the time allowed for each one shrank. Strikingly, when the underlying system was highly accurate, the combination of human and machine performed slightly worse than the machine on its own, because reviewers overturned some correct recommendations while accepting most of the incorrect ones.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A quite different pattern has been reported by the behavioural economist Maren Hemmingsen. In her studies, participants who watched an algorithm make a single conspicuous error lost confidence in it far more sharply than they did after watching a human adviser make the same mistake, and they subsequently ignored the algorithm even when it was demonstrably more accurate than their own judgement. Hemmingsen found, however, that this aversion largely disappeared when participants were permitted to adjust the algorithm's forecasts, even by a small amount; a modest degree of control was enough to restore their willingness to use it. At first sight, these findings appear to contradict those of Tchakounte. In fact they are two sides of the same coin. Human trust in algorithms is poorly calibrated in both directions, too generous in some circumstances and too grudging in others, and in neither case does it closely track how reliable the system actually is.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The design of the systems themselves can make matters better or worse. Sofia Kalaitzaki, a clinical researcher, studied an automated warning system intended to alert hospital staff to the early signs of a dangerous infection. Because the system was set to err on the side of caution, it generated alerts so frequently that most turned out to be unfounded. On the wards she observed, more than four in five alerts were dismissed within a few seconds, including many that later proved to be correct. When the hospital raised the threshold at which an alert was triggered, so that fewer were issued, the proportion that staff investigated rose sharply. Oversight, Kalaitzaki concludes, is not a quality that individuals possess but one that systems either support or undermine.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The institutional setting matters as much as the interface. Danica Kovacevic, a scholar of administrative law, examined one public agency in which caseworkers were required to approve the recommendations of a benefits algorithm. They had, on average, less than two minutes per case, and they were obliged to write a justification only when they disagreed with the system. Agreement thus cost nothing, while disagreement demanded time that caseworkers did not have. Kovacevic describes the result as 'rubber-stamp oversight' and argues that it functions chiefly as a legal device, allowing organisations to claim that decisions are made by people and thereby escape the stricter rules that apply to fully automated decision-making. I find her argument entirely convincing; a review that is designed to be completed in under two minutes is a review in name only.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What, then, would genuinely meaningful oversight require? At a minimum, reviewers would need relevant expertise, enough time to consider each case, access to the evidence on which a recommendation was based, and an obligation to justify agreement as well as disagreement. Organisations should also monitor how often reviewers depart from the system's advice. An override rate close to zero is a strong indication that reviewers are not exercising independent judgement. Even so, a high rate of override is not automatically a good sign, since, as Tchakounte's results show, reviewers may reject correct recommendations as readily as incorrect ones.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The underlying lesson is that human oversight is itself part of the system, and like any other part it can be well or badly designed. Whether adding a human reviewer improves outcomes is an empirical question, and it should be tested with the same rigour that is applied to the algorithm, rather than simply assumed because it sounds reassuring.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: human computers: the people employed to calculate by hand before electronic machines, the division of labour, skill, gender and the transition to programming
title: When Computers Were People
subtitle: For more than a century 'computer' was a job title, and historians still disagree about what the people who held it can teach us

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the period between the late eighteenth century and the 1950s, the word "computer" did not describe a machine at all. It was a job title, held by people who spent their working days carrying out long sequences of arithmetic by hand or with the help of mechanical desk calculators. Observatories employed them to reduce astronomical observations; insurance firms used them to compile mortality tables; and military agencies relied on them to produce the firing tables that told artillery crews how to aim. Because such work was rarely glamorous and almost never credited by name, the people who did it were largely forgotten once electronic machines took over their tasks. Over the past three decades, however, historians have begun to reconstruct their world, and in doing so they have reopened questions about skill, gender and the nature of computation itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The organising principle of most large computing offices was the division of labour. A senior mathematician, sometimes called the planner, would break a difficult problem into a series of elementary steps and record them on printed worksheets. Junior staff then worked through the sheets column by column, rarely needing to understand the purpose of the calculation as a whole. Errors were caught not by insight but by duplication: two computers would often perform the same calculation independently, and a third would compare the results. The historian Tamar Abashidze of the Institute for the History of Calculation describes this arrangement as "a factory for numbers", and argues that it anticipated the logic of the stored-program computer, which likewise executes simple instructions without grasping their meaning.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That comparison has proved influential, but it has also been contested. Dr Ezequiel Bolsonello, who has studied the surviving payroll records and correspondence of several European observatories, contends that the factory image exaggerates how mechanical the work actually was. Experienced computers, he found, routinely noticed when a figure 'looked wrong' long before the formal checking stage, and some devised shortcuts that their supervisors later adopted as standard practice. In his view, the worksheets recorded an idealised procedure, while the real work depended on a form of numerical judgement that was never written down. The evidence he presents is persuasive as far as it goes, although it comes overwhelmingly from the most prestigious institutions, where staff tended to stay for many years; whether the same was true of the large temporary offices established during wartime is far less certain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The gender composition of computing work has attracted particular attention. From the late nineteenth century onwards, an increasing proportion of computers were women, many of them graduates who had been excluded from academic posts. Employers frequently justified hiring them on the grounds that women were naturally patient and careful, qualities supposedly suited to repetitive tasks; they were also, not coincidentally, paid considerably less than men with comparable qualifications. Some commentators have presented the computing office as an early route into scientific careers for women. The sociologist Nadège Lapointe takes a more sceptical line, pointing out that very few computers were ever promoted to the role of planner, and that the classification of their work as clerical rather than scientific was precisely what allowed it to be poorly rewarded.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, though, to treat these two positions as entirely incompatible. A job can be both exploitative and an opportunity, and the letters of former computers frequently express pride in their competence alongside frustration at their prospects. What seems clear is that the label "clerical" was a choice rather than a description: identical work performed by men in university departments was commonly described as research assistance. Recognising this does not settle the debate, but it does suggest that the low status of computing work was not an inevitable consequence of the tasks themselves, and that it might have been arranged quite differently.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Human computing did not disappear overnight when electronic machines arrived. Early electronic computers were expensive, unreliable and available only to a handful of organisations, and many offices continued to operate well into the 1960s. Indeed, several of the first programmers were recruited directly from the ranks of human computers, since they were among the few people who understood how a large calculation could be broken into steps. Kazimierz Tvardovski, an economic historian, argues that this continuity has been obscured by accounts that present the electronic computer as a sudden break with the past. He suggests that the transition is better understood as a gradual transfer of established procedures from paper to machine, carried out by people who brought their old habits of checking and dividing work with them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Tvardovski's argument is a useful corrective, but it can be pushed too far. The speed of electronic machines did not merely accelerate existing calculations; it made feasible kinds of problem, such as large-scale numerical weather prediction, that no office of human computers could have completed in time to be of use. Continuity of method, in other words, did not mean continuity of possibility. What the history of human computing does demonstrate is that the boundary between "mechanical" and "intellectual" labour has always been drawn partly by social convention, and the decision about which side of that line a task falls on has consequences for who performs it and how they are valued.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: packet switching and the myth that the early internet was designed to survive a nuclear attack
title: The Network That Was Never Built for War
subtitle: A popular story holds that the internet was designed to survive a nuclear attack, but historians of computing are not so sure

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few origin stories in the history of technology are repeated as often as the claim that the internet was designed to withstand a nuclear war. In its usual form, the story runs as follows: during the Cold War, military planners feared that a single strike on a central telephone exchange could cut off communication across an entire country, and they therefore commissioned a network with no centre at all, in which messages could find their own way around damaged sections. The account is tidy and dramatic, and it neatly explains one of the internet's most distinctive features. The trouble is that, according to a growing number of historians, it is at best a half-truth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technical idea at the heart of the story is packet switching. In a conventional telephone system, a call reserves a continuous circuit between two parties for as long as the conversation lasts, whether or not anyone is speaking. Packet switching instead divides a message into small blocks of data, each labelled with its destination, which travel independently through the network and are reassembled on arrival. Because no line is reserved, many users can share the same links, and if one route is blocked, packets can in principle be sent along another. In the early 1960s, the concept was proposed more or less independently by researchers on both sides of the Atlantic, and their motives were by no means identical.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Grace Tapsell, a historian of telecommunications, has examined the internal reports of several of the organisations involved. She acknowledges that one strand of early research was indeed concerned with keeping military command links functioning after an attack, and that its authors wrote explicitly about redundancy and survivability. But she points out that this work was largely shelved, partly because the national telephone monopoly of the day showed little interest in building it. The network that was eventually constructed at the end of the decade, which connected a handful of university and government laboratories, was funded for a much more mundane reason: computers were extremely expensive, and the agency paying for them wanted researchers in different places to share them rather than each demanding their own.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Dragan Tanaskovic, an engineer who has written extensively on the design of early networks, goes further. In his view, the survivability narrative was largely constructed after the event. Its popularity, he suggests, owes something to the fact that it allowed later commentators to present a project funded by a defence agency as either sinister or heroic, depending on their politics, when in practice most of the people who built it were academics pursuing problems they found intellectually interesting. He also notes that the early network was in fact rather fragile: it depended on a small number of leased telephone lines and frequently failed when a single node broke down. A system designed above all to survive the destruction of its parts, he argues, would hardly have been built in such a vulnerable way.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the myth should simply be discarded. Folake Olabode, a sociologist who studies how engineering communities remember their own past, argues that the survivability story contains an important truth about design philosophy even if it is wrong about motives. The engineers who built the network, she observes, chose to place intelligence at the edges, in the computers that sent and received data, rather than in the network itself, which was kept deliberately simple. That decision, whatever its origins, is what later allowed the system to grow without central planning, and it is also, in her account, what makes the network so robust today. On this reading, the legend survives because it points, however clumsily, to something real about how the system behaves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Olabode's point is a fair one, and it is worth keeping separate the question of why something was built from the question of what properties it turned out to have. Yet it seems to me that the persistence of the nuclear story has done some harm. By attributing the internet's character to a single military requirement, it obscures the contribution of the many civilian groups, in Europe as well as in North America, whose ideas about sharing resources shaped its architecture. It also encourages a misleading belief that resilience was guaranteed from the beginning, rather than being an achievement that had to be worked at and that still requires constant maintenance by engineers whom the public never sees.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is, moreover, a broader lesson here about the way origin stories function. A good story compresses a messy, collective process into a single purpose and, often, a single moment of invention. Such compression is understandable, since few people have the patience for the detailed history of committee meetings, funding applications and incremental technical standards. But the internet, perhaps more than most technologies, was the product of gradual agreement rather than heroic vision, and its history deserves to be told in a way that reflects this. The real story may be less thrilling than the legend, but it is also more instructive, because it shows how a technology of global significance can emerge from modest and essentially practical goals.

topic: punched-card tabulating machines in population censuses: reusable data, uneven adoption, coding constraints on categories and the labour of card punching
title: Counting by Holes
subtitle: The punched-card machines built for population censuses transformed the business of government, but historians disagree about how far, and in what direction

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the end of the nineteenth century, the national census had become a victim of its own ambition. As populations grew and governments asked ever more questions about age, birthplace, occupation and household, the task of turning millions of completed forms into tables of statistics stretched clerical offices to breaking point. In one widely cited case, the processing of a census was still unfinished when preparations for the next one were due to begin. It was against this background that electrically operated tabulating machines, which read information recorded as holes punched in stiff paper cards, were first adopted by statistical offices. Within a few decades they had spread to railways, insurance companies and large manufacturers, and the firms that supplied them became the forerunners of the twentieth-century computer industry.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle was straightforward. Each individual's answers were translated into a pattern of holes in a card, with each position on the card standing for a particular answer. When a card was placed in the reading device, metal pins passed through the holes and completed electrical circuits, advancing counters on a dial. Later machines could also sort cards automatically into groups, so that a clerk could, for instance, separate all the cards for married women born abroad and then count them by occupation. What had previously required weeks of tallying by hand could now be done in hours, and, crucially, the same set of cards could be re-sorted to answer questions that had not been anticipated when the census was designed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For the economic historian Ifeoma Ekwuribe, this last capacity was the real revolution. Hand tabulation, she argues, forced statisticians to decide in advance which cross-classifications they wanted, since each additional table meant another laborious pass through the forms. Punched cards turned the census from a fixed set of answers into a reusable store of data, and in doing so they changed what officials thought it was possible to know about a population. Ekwuribe traces a direct line from this shift to the growth of social insurance schemes, which relied on detailed statistics about employment, illness and mortality.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Halina Szymanowska, who has studied the records of several European statistical bureaux, is more cautious. She points out that the machines were expensive to rent, and that many offices continued to use them only for the handful of tables they had always produced, simply producing those tables faster. In her reading, the impact of the technology depended less on its capabilities than on the willingness of senior statisticians to rethink their methods, and that willingness was uneven. Some bureaux experimented boldly; others treated the new machines as nothing more than quicker clerks. A history that focuses only on the most adventurous offices, she warns, will inevitably exaggerate how quickly statistical practice changed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of criticism concerns the cards themselves. A card had a fixed number of columns, and every answer had to be squeezed into a code that fitted. Renzo Albertazzi, a historian of statistics, has shown how this constraint shaped the categories that censuses recorded. Occupations had to be grouped into a limited list; complex household arrangements were reduced to a few standard types; and people whose circumstances did not fit the available codes were assigned to whichever category was closest. In his view, the technology did not merely count the population but helped to define it, and some of the simplified categories it encouraged persisted in official statistics long after the cards themselves had disappeared.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This argument is important, but it should not be overstated. Census categories were simplified long before punched cards existed, since printed forms with tick boxes impose limits of their own, and handwritten tally sheets were hardly more accommodating. What the cards did was make such simplification more systematic and harder to undo, because a code, once fixed in thousands of machines and procedures, became costly to change. That is a significant point, but it concerns the rigidity of the categories rather than their origin.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The labour history of the punched card has received far less attention. Amos Matumbe, who has examined the employment records of one large statistical office, found that the introduction of tabulating machines created a new class of workers, mostly young women, whose job was to punch cards from completed forms at high speed. Their pay was tied to the number of cards they completed, and errors were penalised. Matumbe argues that this marked an early instance of the close monitoring of individual productivity that later became common in data-processing work. It is a claim that deserves wider recognition, because it reminds us that the efficiency of the machines rested on a great deal of repetitive human effort.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the punched card was neither a simple labour-saving device nor a sudden revolution in government. It was a technology whose consequences depended on the institutions that adopted it, and which, in the process, quietly reshaped both the way states saw their citizens and the kinds of work that counting required. Its history is worth remembering at a time when much larger systems for gathering and classifying information about people are being built, often with as little public discussion as the tabulating machines once received.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: time-sharing computers of the 1960s and the failed vision of a public 'computer utility', compared with today's cloud services
title: Computing on Tap
subtitle: In the 1960s many experts expected computing power to be piped into homes like water or electricity; why it did not happen remains a matter of dispute

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1950s, using a computer was an exercise in patience. Programs were typically written out by hand, transferred onto punched cards and handed over a counter to an operator, who would add them to a queue of other jobs to be run in sequence. Hours or even days later, the programmer received a printout, which all too often revealed that a single misplaced character had caused the whole job to fail. This arrangement, known as batch processing, made efficient use of extremely expensive machines, but it made very poor use of the people who programmed them, and it is hard to read accounts from the period without sympathising with their frustration.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Time-sharing offered a radical alternative. Instead of running one job at a time, a computer would switch its attention rapidly between many users, each seated at a terminal typing commands. Because the machine moved between them in fractions of a second, every user had the impression of having it entirely to themselves. Errors could be spotted and corrected immediately, and programming became something closer to a conversation with the machine than a correspondence conducted by post. Several experimental systems were running at universities by the mid-1960s, and they generated considerable excitement among researchers and funding bodies alike.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of that excitement concerned not the technique itself but what it seemed to make possible. If one computer could serve dozens of users in the same building, it was argued, a sufficiently large one could serve thousands of customers through the telephone network. Computing would then become a public utility, supplied like electricity or water to homes and businesses that would no longer need machines of their own. Commercial time-sharing bureaux appeared in many countries towards the end of the decade, selling access to their computers by the hour. Yet within twenty years most had disappeared or turned to other lines of business, and the computer utility had become a curiosity in the history of forecasting.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why the vision failed has been debated ever since. The historian Esther Fairbrass argues that the explanation is essentially economic. The utility model assumed that computers would remain so costly that only centralised sharing could make them affordable. In fact, the price of processing power fell far more rapidly than the price of telephone connections, so that for many organisations it soon became cheaper to buy a small computer outright than to rent time on a distant one. On this view, the utility was undermined not by any flaw in its logic but by a change in the costs on which that logic depended.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nikhil Chakravorty, a computer scientist who has written about the operating systems of the period, places more weight on technical difficulties. The software required to share a machine safely among hundreds of users was enormously complex, and the most ambitious projects ran years behind schedule and proved unreliable in service. Customers who lost hours of work to a system crash were understandably reluctant to entrust their businesses to a remote computer. Chakravorty nevertheless insists that time-sharing should not be judged a failure, since its most lasting legacy was cultural rather than commercial: users of shared machines began leaving messages and files for one another, creating some of the earliest online communities.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: I find Chakravorty's emphasis on this social dimension persuasive. The habits of interactive computing, and the expectation that a computer is a place where people meet as well as a tool for calculation, owe more to the time-sharing era than to almost any other period. It is worth noting, however, that these communities were small and largely confined to universities and research laboratories, so their influence was felt mainly through the people who later went on to build wider networks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A third position is taken by the economist Bernadette Oyono, who contends that the computer utility did not fail at all but merely arrived several decades early. Today, she points out, businesses and individuals routinely rent processing power and storage from vast data centres, paying according to use, much as the early enthusiasts predicted. The resemblance is real, but I think the comparison can mislead. Electricity and water utilities have traditionally been subject to public regulation, with obligations to serve everyone at controlled prices. Commercial cloud services carry no such obligations, and the market for them is concentrated in the hands of a few very large firms. To call this the fulfilment of the utility dream is to forget that the original vision was as much about public access as about technical arrangements.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most useful lesson of the episode is that predictions about technology often reveal more about the period in which they are made than about the future. Engineers in the 1960s imagined computing as a scarce resource to be rationed and distributed, because that was their own experience of it. The personal computer, which turned the scarce resource into an ordinary household object, lay almost entirely outside their imagination. Today's confident forecasts about computing deserve to be read with the same awareness, since they too are shaped by the circumstances of those who make them, and future historians may find them just as revealing and just as mistaken.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: the 'software crisis' of the late 1960s and the birth of software engineering: the sequential development model, crisis rhetoric and the engineering metaphor
title: A Crisis That Never Ended?
subtitle: Half a century after programmers declared their craft to be in trouble, historians are still arguing about what the trouble was

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the autumn of 1968, a group of computer scientists, industrial programmers and managers met at a conference to discuss what several of them were already calling a crisis. Computer hardware had become dramatically faster and cheaper over the previous decade, yet the programs that ran on it were another matter. Large software projects were routinely delivered years late, far over budget and full of errors; some were abandoned altogether. The organisers chose a deliberately provocative title for the meeting: "software engineering". The phrase implied that writing programs ought to be governed by the same disciplined methods, theoretical foundations and professional standards as building bridges or power stations, something that, by general agreement, it was not.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulties were most acute in very large systems, such as operating systems for mainframe computers, airline reservation networks and military command systems, each of which might involve hundreds of programmers. Experience showed that such projects behaved in counter-intuitive ways. When a project fell behind schedule, the obvious response was to recruit more staff, but newcomers had to be trained, and every additional person multiplied the number of conversations required to keep the team coordinated. As a result, adding programmers to a late project frequently made it later still. Programming at the time was widely regarded as a craft, learned on the job and practised according to individual style, and few organisations had any reliable way of estimating how long a piece of software would take to write.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The decade that followed produced a series of proposed remedies, from new programming languages to mathematical methods for proving that a program met its specification. The most influential in management terms was the idea that software should be developed in a fixed sequence of stages: requirements would be agreed, a design produced, the code written and finally the whole tested, with each phase completed and signed off before the next began. Dr Lars Zetterlund, who has traced the history of this model, argues that it was widely misunderstood. The early descriptions on which it was based, he notes, warned that a single pass through the stages was risky and recommended repeating the cycle. Managers nonetheless adopted the strictly sequential version, in his view because it resembled the construction contracts with which they were already familiar and allowed progress to be measured by documents rather than working programs.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all historians accept that the crisis was what it claimed to be. Professor Adaeze Okeowo points out that complaints about late and faulty programs predated 1968 by many years, and that cost overruns of a similar scale were common in large civil engineering and aerospace projects of the period. What changed in the late 1960s, she suggests, was not the frequency of failure but the willingness of an emerging academic discipline to describe it as a crisis. Talk of crisis helped computer scientists to argue for research funding, university departments and professional recognition. A field that could present itself as the solution to an urgent national problem, Okeowo observes, was far more likely to be taken seriously by governments and by older academic disciplines that had previously regarded programming as a merely technical skill.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Okeowo's analysis is valuable, and there is little doubt that crisis language served professional interests. But it does not follow that the problem was invented. For the airlines, banks and government agencies that depended on large programs, failures had real and sometimes serious consequences, and the fact that a crisis is useful to someone does not make it imaginary. Rhetoric and reality, in this case, reinforced each other.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns the engineering metaphor itself. The philosopher of technology Mariela Ribadeneira argues that it has led the discipline astray. Software, she observes, does not wear out, and it is not manufactured in the sense that a bridge is; almost all of its cost lies in design and, above all, in subsequent change. Treating programs like physical structures encouraged organisations to fix requirements in advance and to regard later changes as failures of planning, when in practice the needs that software serves are constantly shifting.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Thabo Moalosi, a software practitioner turned historian, goes further still, proposing that the crisis never ended. Every improvement in methods, he argues, has simply allowed organisations to attempt more complex systems, which then fail at the limits of the new methods just as the old systems failed at the limits of the old ones. On this view, the software crisis is better understood as a permanent condition than as an episode with a beginning and an end. He cites the continuing stream of abandoned government computer projects as evidence that the basic pattern has hardly changed in fifty years.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: There is truth in both arguments, but each can be pushed too far. Ribadeneira is right that software differs from bridges, yet in safety-critical fields such as aviation and medical devices, the engineering ideal of rigorous specification and independent checking has demonstrably saved lives. And while Moalosi's account captures something real about the escalation of ambition, it risks a kind of fatalism that overlooks how much more reliable ordinary software has become. The term coined in 1968 may still describe an aspiration rather than an achievement, but it is an aspiration worth keeping.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: dial-up bulletin board systems (BBSs) of the 1980s and early 1990s: local communities, overnight message networks, sysop governance and lost records
title: Communities Before the Web
subtitle: Dial-up bulletin boards gave many people their first taste of life online, yet most of what happened on them has already been lost

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before the World Wide Web made going online an everyday activity, a few hundred thousand enthusiasts were already doing so by a different route. From the late 1970s until the mid-1990s, anyone with a home computer, a modem and a telephone line could dial into a bulletin board system, or BBS: a computer, usually in someone's spare bedroom, that stored messages and files for callers to read and download. At their peak, tens of thousands of such boards were operating around the world. Almost all of them have since vanished, and with them much of the record of what was, for many participants, their first experience of online community.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technology imposed severe limits. A typical board had a single telephone line, so only one person could be connected at a time; callers who found the line engaged simply tried again later. Conversations therefore unfolded slowly, with users posting replies that others would read hours or days afterwards. Because local telephone calls were cheap or even free in many countries, whereas long-distance calls were expensive, most callers used boards in their own area. To connect these local communities, operators developed networks that collected messages during the day and passed them from board to board in batches late at night, when call charges were lowest. A message might take several days to cross a continent, but it would eventually arrive at a fraction of the cost of a direct call.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Owain Pemberthy, a historian of communications, argues that this economic geography made BBS culture fundamentally local. Users of a board often lived within a few kilometres of one another, and many boards organised regular meetings in cafés or parks where callers could put faces to usernames. In Pemberthy's view, the boards resembled neighbourhood clubs more closely than the global networks that replaced them, and the familiar description of them as an early version of the internet obscures this difference. He points to the many friendships, business partnerships and even marriages that began on local boards and continued offline, arguing that for most participants the screen was a means of meeting people nearby rather than a window onto a distant world. Communities of this kind, he suggests, had more in common with the amateur radio clubs of earlier decades than with anything that came afterwards.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Each board was controlled by its operator, known as the sysop, who paid for the equipment and the telephone line and could delete messages, ban users or close the board entirely at will. Anahit Gabrielyan, who studies online governance, describes the result as "thousands of tiny monarchies". Rather than regarding this as a weakness, however, she sees it as a source of variety: because each sysop set their own rules, boards experimented with everything from elected moderators to formal written constitutions, and users who disliked one regime could simply call another. Gabrielyan suggests that today's large social media platforms, which apply a single set of rules to hundreds of millions of people, could learn from this diversity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It is an appealing suggestion, but I am not convinced that it can be applied as directly as she implies. The ease with which a dissatisfied user could move to another board depended on there being many boards of roughly similar size, none of which dominated. Today's platforms are valuable to their users precisely because everyone else is on them, which makes leaving far more costly. The lessons of the BBS era may concern the benefits of small scale itself rather than any particular set of rules, and small scale is precisely what the dominant platforms cannot offer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some caution is also needed about the nostalgia that surrounds these systems. Taking part required equipment that was expensive at the time, as well as considerable technical patience, and surveys of the period suggest that callers were overwhelmingly young, male and relatively affluent. Boards could be welcoming places, but they could also be hostile to newcomers who did not share the prevailing culture. To present them as open, egalitarian spaces, as some accounts do, is to read the present's disappointments back into the past.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most serious obstacle to understanding the BBS era, however, is the poverty of the surviving evidence. Tolga Sezgin, who has spent a decade collecting disks and printouts from former sysops, estimates that only a tiny proportion of the messages ever posted has been preserved. What survives is skewed towards technical files, which were copied widely, rather than the everyday conversations that made up most of the traffic, and towards boards in North America, which have attracted the most attention from collectors. Sezgin points out that boards flourished in many other places, including parts of Eastern Europe, South America and Africa, where they sometimes offered the only means of exchanging information outside official channels.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: If Sezgin is right, the history of the BBS is still largely unwritten. That matters, because the period offers one of the few cases in which large numbers of people built online communities without the involvement of large companies, and its successes and failures deserve to be understood on their own terms rather than merely as a prelude to what followed. The former sysops who still keep boxes of disks in their attics may hold the key to that history, but they will not do so for ever.
