area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: web archiving and the impermanence of the web: lost early websites, crawling limits, broad versus curated collecting, geographical bias and legal deposit
title: The Vanishing Web
subtitle: Libraries and archives have spent three decades trying to preserve the internet, but they disagree about what preserving it should mean

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has followed an old link only to be greeted by an error message has encountered one of the defining features of the web: its impermanence. Studies of web citations in academic journals and court judgments have repeatedly found that a substantial proportion of links stop working within a few years, and that even when a link still functions, the content it leads to has often been altered. For a medium that now carries much of the world's public record, from government announcements to scientific data, this instability poses a problem that earlier archivists, dealing with paper, never had to face. A letter in a box may be damaged by damp or fire, but it does not quietly rewrite itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The problem is most acute for the web's earliest years. The first websites appeared in the early 1990s, but systematic attempts to preserve them did not begin until several years later, by which time much of the original material had already been deleted or overwritten. Unlike a book, which survives as long as at least one copy is kept somewhere, a web page usually exists in only one place, on a server maintained by its author. When the author lost interest, changed jobs or stopped paying for hosting, the page simply ceased to exist. It seems to me that the near-total loss of these early pages, which recorded the first experiments of a new form of public expression, is a genuine cultural loss, even if few people at the time thought them worth keeping.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The main technique used by web archives is crawling: automated programs follow links from one page to the next, copying everything they find. Crawling has preserved billions of pages, but it has well-known limitations. Crawlers struggle with pages that are generated on demand from databases, with content that requires a login, and with interactive features that depend on programs running in the user's browser. Material on social media platforms is particularly difficult to capture, and much of it is also restricted by the platforms' terms of service. As a result, a growing proportion of online life falls outside what crawlers can reach. Even where a page is captured successfully, the archive preserves only a series of snapshots taken at intervals, so changes made between visits are lost, and a reader may have no way of knowing which version of a page was seen by the public on any particular day.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Among archivists, a long-running debate concerns how much should be collected. Dr Yusuf Kohistani, a digital preservation specialist, argues for collecting as broadly as possible. Archivists, he points out, have a poor record of predicting what future researchers will want; material dismissed as trivial in one generation, such as advertisements or fan publications, has repeatedly become valuable to the next. Any process of selection, in his view, inevitably reflects the priorities and blind spots of those doing the selecting. Professor Ingrid Bembridge disagrees. Broad crawls, she argues, produce enormous quantities of shallow captures, many of them broken, in which images are missing, links lead nowhere and the context needed to interpret a page has been lost. She advocates smaller, curated collections in which selected sites are captured completely and repeatedly, accompanied by documentation explaining who created them and why.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Funmilayo Sowande, who has studied the composition of several major web archives, raises a different concern. Crawls typically begin from lists of starting addresses compiled by archivists, and these lists, she has found, are heavily weighted towards websites in a small number of languages and countries. Content from much of Africa, South Asia and Latin America is consequently thin. Sowande does not believe that large institutions in wealthy countries can correct this imbalance on their own, and argues that communities whose online history is at risk should be given the means to build and control their own archives. Such projects, she accepts, are harder to sustain than national programmes, but they are more likely to capture material that outsiders would not recognise as significant.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares the sense of alarm. Pavel Andrianov, a historian of information, has criticised the popular warning that we are entering a "digital dark age" in which the records of our era will be lost. He notes that far more material from the present period is likely to survive than from any previous one, and that the real difficulty facing future historians will be finding relevant sources among the vast quantities that remain. Andrianov is right that abundance, not scarcity, is the more typical condition of the digital record. But his argument offers little comfort to those whose records happen to fall into the gaps, and the gaps, as Sowande shows, are not randomly distributed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In practice, the choice between broad and selective collecting is a false one; the two approaches complement each other, and the most effective archives already combine them. What has changed in recent years is the legal framework. A number of countries have extended legal deposit, the long-established requirement for publishers to give copies of printed works to a national library, to cover websites published within their borders. This is perhaps the most promising development of all, since it gives archives a clear right to collect, rather than relying on the tolerance of website owners. It does not solve every problem, but it treats the web, at last, as part of the published record that a society has a duty to keep.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: the Y2K millennium bug: origins of two-digit dates, whether remediation prevented disaster or the threat was exaggerated, international spending comparisons and the legacy of the episode
title: The Disaster That Didn't Happen
subtitle: More than two decades on, historians still disagree about whether the millennium bug was a genuine threat or an expensive false alarm

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the clocks struck midnight on 1 January 2000, the catastrophe that many had predicted failed to arrive. Aircraft did not fall from the sky, power grids continued to hum, and bank accounts, by and large, held the same balances they had held the previous evening. For a few days the absence of disaster was greeted with relief; within weeks, however, it had become a source of suspicion. Newspapers that had spent months warning of chaos began to ask whether the public had been misled, and whether the vast sums spent on preparation – estimates of global expenditure range from 300 to 600 billion US dollars – had been squandered on a problem that was never as serious as claimed. That question has never been entirely settled, and it deserves more careful treatment than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The origins of the so-called millennium bug are not in dispute. In the 1960s and 1970s, computer memory was extraordinarily expensive, and programmers routinely stored years as two digits rather than four, so that 1968 became simply '68'. The saving on each record was tiny, but across millions of records it was considerable. Few of those programmers expected their software to remain in use for three decades; most assumed it would be replaced long before the century turned. Instead, much of it was patched, extended and built upon, until the original code lay buried beneath layers of later additions that nobody fully understood. When the year 2000 arrived, a system reading '00' might interpret it as 1900, miscalculating ages, interest payments or maintenance schedules, or simply halting altogether.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The orthodox account, defended most vigorously by Dr Teodora Brânzei of the Institute for the History of Information Technology, holds that the smooth transition was the direct result of the remediation effort. Brânzei has examined internal records from more than sixty organisations and found that testing repeatedly uncovered faults that would have caused serious failures. In one utility company, a simulation in which the system clock was advanced to January 2000 shut down the control system of a water treatment plant. In her view, the quiet New Year was not evidence that the danger had been exaggerated but proof that the work had succeeded. She compares the situation to vaccination: when a programme is effective, the illness it prevents becomes invisible, and people begin to doubt that it was ever a threat.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics point to an awkward fact. Several countries were widely reported to have spent far less per head on preparation than the United States or Britain, yet they suffered no greater disruption. The economist Haruto Kiyomizu has argued that this comparison undermines the orthodox account. If the problem had been as severe as claimed, he reasons, the countries that did least should have suffered most. Kiyomizu does not deny that faults existed; his contention is that most of them would have produced minor inconveniences, easily corrected after the event, rather than the cascading failures that consultants predicted. He also notes that those consultants had a strong financial interest in describing the threat in the most alarming terms available.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Kiyomizu's argument is attractive, but it rests on a weaker foundation than it first appears. The low-spending countries were not unprepared; many relied on software and hardware imported from nations that had already corrected it, and they were therefore able to benefit from remediation paid for elsewhere. Moreover, a nation's total spending says little about how that money was used. A country that concentrated its limited funds on electricity, telecommunications and banking might well have protected itself more effectively than one that spread a larger budget evenly across every government department. The international comparison, in short, cannot bear the weight that sceptics place on it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third position, associated with the sociologist Paloma Sarrazin, shifts attention away from the question of whether the threat was real. Sarrazin is interested in what the episode revealed about the relationship between modern societies and the technology on which they depend. Before 1998, she observes, few senior executives or politicians had any clear idea which of their operations relied on computers, or how those computers were connected to one another. The process of compiling inventories forced organisations to map their own systems for the first time, and many discovered dependencies they had never suspected. For Sarrazin, this accidental audit was the most valuable outcome of the whole affair, and one that later helped organisations respond to quite different threats, from computer viruses to floods.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to conclude that the truth lies somewhere between the two camps, and in a sense it does. Some money was undoubtedly wasted, particularly on the replacement of equipment that would have continued to work perfectly well, and some warnings were exaggerated beyond anything the evidence supported. Yet the lesson most often drawn from the episode – that experts cannot be trusted to assess risk – is precisely the wrong one. The more troubling legacy of the millennium bug may be that its very success has made similar efforts harder to justify. When the next slow-moving technological hazard emerges, those who argue for costly precautions are likely to be reminded of the year 2000, and told that last time nothing happened.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: the electronic spreadsheet: automatic recalculation and 'what if' planning, the disputed 'killer application' story of personal computer sales, end-user computing and the hidden prevalence of spreadsheet errors
title: Thinking in Cells
subtitle: The electronic spreadsheet is usually remembered as the program that sold the personal computer, but its deeper influence may lie in how it changed the way organisations reason

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Histories of the personal computer often turn on a single program. In 1979 an electronic spreadsheet appeared for one of the first mass-market microcomputers, and within a few years, the story goes, accountants and financial planners were buying machines costing several thousand dollars simply in order to run it. The program, according to this account, was the first 'killer application': software so useful that it justified the purchase of the hardware on which it ran. The story has been retold so often that it has acquired the status of a founding myth. Like most founding myths, it contains a good deal of truth, but it also conceals as much as it reveals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What the electronic spreadsheet did was not new in principle. Accountants had long worked with paper ledgers ruled into rows and columns, and large firms employed clerks whose job was to recalculate totals whenever a single figure changed. The innovation lay in automatic recalculation: alter one cell, and every figure that depended on it was updated instantly. A task that had occupied a clerk for an afternoon could now be completed in seconds and, more significantly, it could be repeated as many times as the user wished. The economic historian Femke Rozendaal argues that this transformed the purpose of financial calculation. Where a paper budget had been a record of decisions already taken, the electronic version became a tool for exploring decisions not yet made – the 'what if' question that managers had previously been unable to ask in any systematic way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Rozendaal's account of the spreadsheet as a catalyst for computer sales has been challenged by Tadeusz Wiśniowiecki, whose study of retailers' records from the early 1980s suggests a more complicated picture. In the shops he examined, word-processing software was sold alongside computers at least as often as spreadsheets, and in households, games and educational programs dominated. Wiśniowiecki concludes that no single application drove adoption; rather, the spread of microcomputers depended on a broad range of uses, each attracting a different group of buyers. His evidence is valuable, but his conclusion goes further than it can support. Retail records show what was bought, not why: a business that acquired a word processor together with its first computer may still have been persuaded to buy the machine by the prospect of financial modelling.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is less disagreement about the spreadsheet's effects inside organisations. Because the software required no knowledge of programming, it allowed managers, analysts and administrators to build their own calculating tools without waiting for the specialist data-processing departments which had previously controlled access to computing. This shift is often celebrated as a democratisation of computing, and in many respects it was. However, it also meant that models on which significant financial decisions rested were increasingly constructed by people with no training in testing or documenting what they had built.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences of that shift are the focus of work by Anahera Pōtiki, a researcher in information systems who has spent much of her career auditing spreadsheets used in business and government. In a sample of several hundred operational spreadsheets, her team found that the large majority contained at least one error, and that the probability of error rose with the size and complexity of the file. Most of the mistakes were trivial, but a minority affected figures that informed investment and staffing decisions. Pōtiki is careful to emphasise that people are not more careless with spreadsheets than with other tools. The difficulty, she argues, is that the grid presents its results with a uniform air of precision: a figure produced by a faulty formula looks exactly like one produced by a correct one, and nothing on the screen invites the user to doubt it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Pōtiki's proposed remedies are modest – peer review of important models, clear separation of inputs from calculations, and written records of assumptions – and they have been adopted by some financial regulators. Yet it would be wrong to treat the problem as purely technical. The spreadsheet's appeal has always lain in the speed with which it allows an individual to construct an argument in numerical form, and that same speed discourages the slow, critical scrutiny that numerical arguments require. Procedures can reduce errors, but they cannot easily alter the habits of mind that the tool itself encourages.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most enduring effect of the spreadsheet, then, is not economic but cultural. It has made a particular style of reasoning – breaking a problem into quantities, linking them by formulae and adjusting the inputs until the outcome looks acceptable – so familiar that it is rarely recognised as a style at all. Whether that has improved the quality of decisions in business and government is a question that no one has yet found a convincing way to answer. What seems clear is that the history of the spreadsheet is not simply a story about how computers came into offices; it is also a story about how offices came to think like computers.

area: the history of computing and the internet
topic: character encoding in computing: the seven-bit code and its English-language bias, incompatible code pages and garbled text, the universal character set, the merging of East Asian characters and the role of emoji
title: Every Letter Counted
subtitle: How computers learned, slowly and unevenly, to write the world's languages

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of electronic computing, the question of which letters a machine could display was settled not by linguists but by engineers working under severe constraints. Every character a computer stores must be represented by a number, and the range of numbers available depends on how many binary digits are allotted to each character. The early decisions about that allocation were made quickly and, for the most part, by people who wrote in English. Their consequences have proved remarkably durable, and it is no exaggeration to say that they shaped which communities could participate in the digital world, and on what terms.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential of these early schemes, a seven-bit code standardised in the United States in the 1960s, offered room for only 128 characters. Once space had been reserved for control signals inherited from teleprinters, around 95 printable characters remained: the unaccented Latin alphabet in upper and lower case, the digits, and a selection of punctuation marks. The historian of technology Søren Kvistgaard has shown that the committee responsible considered a larger code but rejected it, partly because transmission over telephone lines was costly and every additional bit added to the price. Kvistgaard does not regard the outcome as the product of indifference to other languages; in his reading, the committee members simply assumed that other countries would adapt the code to suit their own needs, as indeed they did.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That adaptation, however, created its own problems. National variants replaced little-used symbols such as brackets with accented letters, so that a single numeric value might represent a bracket in one country and an umlauted vowel in another. When eight-bit systems later doubled the available space to 256 characters, manufacturers and national bodies filled the upper half in incompatible ways, producing dozens of so-called code pages. A document written on one system could appear on another as a meaningless jumble of symbols – a phenomenon that Japanese users named mojibake, or 'character transformation'. The linguist Mei Tsuchida, who has studied business and personal correspondence from the period, argues that the burden of this confusion fell most heavily on writers of languages other than English, who learned to avoid accented characters altogether or to transliterate their own names into an approximate Latin form. It is difficult to disagree with her conclusion that, for two decades, computers quietly penalised linguistic diversity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For languages written with thousands of characters, the obstacles were greater still. Chinese, Japanese and Korean required at least two bytes for each character, and each language developed several competing encodings. Engineers in East Asia devised ingenious methods of entering characters through a standard keyboard, typing a pronunciation and then selecting the intended symbol from a list, but the lack of a common standard meant that exchanging text across borders, or even between companies in the same country, remained unreliable well into the 1990s.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The solution eventually adopted was a universal character set, developed from the late 1980s onwards, which aimed to assign a unique number to every character in every writing system, past and present. Its first version contained around 7,000 characters; current versions include well over 140,000, covering scripts that range from ancient cuneiform to recently devised alphabets for minority languages. The economist Nnamdi Oparaocha argues that the standard's success owed less to its technical merits than to the decision of major software firms to adopt it, which created network effects that rival systems could not match. This is plausible, but it underplays the patient work of the scholars who documented hundreds of scripts, often without payment, so that they could be included.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomed the universal approach. One of its most contested features was the merging of Chinese characters used in China, Japan and Korea into a single set wherever their forms were judged to be historically identical, even when they are written slightly differently in each country. Ludmila Karpenkova, who studies the politics of technical standards, has documented the objections raised by Japanese specialists, who argued that the decision treated distinct national traditions as mere variations in typeface. Supporters replied that without such merging the character set would have grown unmanageably large. The dispute has subsided rather than been resolved, and in practice users depend on fonts that display the appropriate regional form.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: More recently, the universal standard has attracted attention for a less expected reason: the addition of emoji, the small pictorial symbols now used in billions of messages each day. Some commentators complain that the organisation responsible devotes disproportionate time to debating new emoji while proposals for historic scripts wait for years. The complaint is understandable, but somewhat misplaced. The popularity of emoji has given software companies a commercial reason to support the standard fully, and the technical improvements made in order to display them have benefited lesser-used scripts too. Whether this happy coincidence will continue is uncertain, but for now the smiling face and the ancient alphabet appear to be allies rather than rivals.

topic: gecko-inspired dry adhesives: setae and molecular attraction, controllable release, wild climbing behaviour, robotic grippers and the limits of the gecko analogy
title: Sticking Without Glue
subtitle: The gecko's foot has inspired two decades of research into dry adhesives, but turning a biological trick into a reliable product has proved harder than expected

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Geckos can sprint up a pane of glass and hang from a ceiling by a single toe, a feat that puzzled naturalists for well over two thousand years. Suction, microscopic hooks and sticky secretions were all proposed as explanations, and all were eventually rejected. It is now accepted that the grip arises from millions of tiny hairs, known as setae, on the underside of each toe. Every seta branches into hundreds of still finer tips, and these come so close to a surface that weak attractions between molecules, which would be negligible on their own, add up to a remarkably firm hold. The discovery that a lizard sticks by physics rather than chemistry made the gecko a favourite of engineers. If adhesion depended on geometry alone, the reasoning went, then it ought to be possible to reproduce it in almost any suitable material. That expectation, in my view, has been fulfilled only in part, and the reasons for the shortfall are more instructive than the successes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The early years of research were marked by considerable optimism. Laboratories around the world fabricated arrays of synthetic hairs from polymers and carbon nanotubes, and the first prototypes could support surprising loads on clean glass. Takeshi Oyamada, a surface engineer at the Kansai Institute of Applied Mechanics, predicted in an influential paper that within ten years so-called gecko tape would displace conventional adhesive tapes and even screws in many household applications. The reality proved less obliging. Prototypes lost much of their grip after a few dozen uses, gathered dust rapidly and performed poorly on surfaces that were anything other than smooth. Oyamada now concedes that his forecast was premature, but he insists that the delay reflects the difficulty of manufacturing such fine structures cheaply and at scale, not any weakness in the underlying principle.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What makes the gecko genuinely remarkable, however, is not how strongly it sticks but how easily it lets go. A running gecko attaches and detaches each foot many times per second. It does so by peeling its toes away from the surface, beginning at the tip, which alters the angle of the setae and switches the adhesion off almost instantly. The attachment is also directional: it is strong when the foot is dragged in one direction and almost absent when it is pushed in the other. Ordinary glue offers nothing comparable, since a bond that is strong is also, as a rule, difficult to undo. Much of the early engineering work judged its prototypes by the maximum weight they could bear, and this was, I would argue, a misplaced emphasis. Controllability, rather than raw strength, is the gecko's real lesson.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Field biologists have added a further complication. Adaeze Umeasiegbu, a zoologist at the Coastal Institute of Tropical Ecology, has filmed several species of gecko in their natural habitats, climbing tree bark, rock faces and leaves. She found that on rough surfaces the animals rely heavily on their claws, using the setae mainly on smooth ones, and that many species switch between the two methods within a single stride. In her view, engineers have been studying an idealised animal, defined by its performance on laboratory glass, rather than the versatile climber that actually exists. The implication is that the most effective artificial systems may need to combine adhesive pads with mechanical grips of some kind.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Where gecko-inspired adhesives have succeeded, it has largely been in robotics. A team at the Tagus Institute of Robotics has developed grippers that can lift a sheet of glass and a ripe tomato using the same pad, without damaging either. Similar devices have been proposed for capturing debris in orbit, where suction is useless in a vacuum and chemical adhesives become unreliable at extreme temperatures. Wall-climbing robots for inspecting storage tanks and ship hulls are another promising use. The Tagus researchers argue that dry adhesives are best suited to specialised settings of this kind, in which their high cost is outweighed by the absence of any practical alternative, rather than to mass-market consumer goods.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical scepticism comes from Rasmus Høyrup, a materials scientist at the Nordic Centre for Polymer Research. Høyrup points out that many products marketed as 'gecko-inspired' owe little to the gecko at all: they consist of simple elastomer surfaces covered in mushroom-shaped tips, a design that resembles the feet of certain beetles more closely than those of any lizard. He argues that the gecko analogy has become largely a marketing label and that biology should be treated as a loose source of ideas rather than a set of blueprints. Høyrup is right that the term is often applied carelessly. Yet he underestimates the value of the biological model as a benchmark. Before the gecko's setae were understood, few engineers believed that a dry, reusable and residue-free adhesive was physically possible; the animal demonstrated that it was, and gave researchers a target against which to measure their progress.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The gecko story illustrates a wider truth about biomimicry: copying a structure is rarely sufficient without an understanding of the conditions under which it evolved. One of those conditions is easily overlooked. A gecko does not need its setae to last indefinitely, because it replaces them every time it sheds its skin, which may happen every few weeks. Synthetic hairs, by contrast, are expected to survive thousands of cycles without regrowing. Perhaps the most useful thing engineers could borrow from the animal is therefore not its hairs but its habit of renewal: designing adhesive pads as inexpensive components that are meant to be replaced, rather than as permanent surfaces that are bound to wear out.

topic: swarm robotics inspired by social insects: stigmergy and collective construction, the simulation-to-reality gap, harmful failures, centralised versus decentralised control and the cost of redundancy
title: Many Small Minds
subtitle: Engineers have long hoped to coordinate robots the way insects coordinate colonies, but the comparison may conceal as much as it reveals

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: An ant colony has no architect, no manager and no plan. Yet tens of thousands of workers, each responding only to what is immediately around it, manage to forage across large territories, defend their nest and, in some species, build structures many times larger than themselves. Since the late 1980s, this apparent paradox has inspired a branch of engineering known as swarm robotics, which aims to coordinate large numbers of simple machines without any central controller. Its advocates point to three advantages. A swarm should be robust, since the loss of a few members makes little difference; scalable, since adding more robots requires no redesign; and flexible, since the same rules can produce different results in different circumstances. These are attractive promises. They have, however, been tested far less rigorously than the enthusiasm surrounding the field would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The insect principle that has proved most fruitful for engineers is stigmergy, a term coined to describe how termites coordinate their building. Rather than communicating directly, each termite responds to the state of the structure itself: a pellet of mud deposited by one worker makes it more likely that others will add pellets at the same spot. Ingvild Haugsbakk, who directs the Collective Construction Laboratory at the Bergen Institute of Technology, has built robots that work in a similar way. Each robot carries a block, inspects the partly completed structure in front of it and decides where to place its load according to a short list of rules. None of the robots holds a picture of the finished building, yet walls, ramps and towers emerge reliably. Haugsbakk argues that stigmergy is the most transferable lesson the insects offer, because it allows coordination without radio links or shared maps, both of which tend to fail in exactly the environments where robots are most needed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ferhat Tekinalp, a roboticist at the Anatolian Technical University, is less impressed by such demonstrations. His concern is what engineers call the reality gap. In computer simulations, swarms of thousands of virtual robots perform elegantly; in the laboratory, physical robots suffer from flat batteries, wheels that slip, sensors that misread and collisions that no model anticipated. Tekinalp reviewed several hundred published studies and found that fewer than one in ten had involved real machines at all, and that those which did rarely used more than a few dozen. In his view, the field has allowed simulated success to stand in for practical achievement, and claims about scalability in particular should be treated with caution until they are demonstrated with hardware.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even the claim of robustness may need qualifying. Lucía Goicoechea, at the Montevideo Centre for Complex Systems, has studied what happens when individual robots fail in different ways. Robots that simply stop moving, she found, are absorbed by the swarm with little effect. Robots that continue to act on faulty information are another matter: a single machine with a damaged sensor, laying down misleading signals, can lead dozens of others astray. Insect colonies are not immune to such failures either. Army ants that lose the chemical trail sometimes begin following one another in a circle, a so-called ant mill, and may continue until they die of exhaustion. Goicoechea's results seem to me to be among the most important in the field. A swarm, it appears, is robust against the absence of its members, but not necessarily against their misbehaviour.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Practical applications so far are modest. Proposals include fleets of small drones that monitor crops, floating robots that track oil spills and miniature machines that search collapsed buildings for survivors. It is worth noting, though, that many commercial systems described as swarms, such as the robots that move shelves in large warehouses, are in fact directed by a central computer. Prapaporn Siriwattanakul, whose group at the Chao Phraya Robotics Institute designs agricultural robots, argues that this is no failure. In her view, the insistence on complete decentralisation reflects an attachment to an attractive idea rather than an engineering requirement, and the most effective systems are likely to be hybrids in which a central planner sets broad goals while local rules deal with the details. I find this persuasive, although it raises the question of whether such hybrids still deserve to be described as swarms.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty lies in designing the rules themselves. Predicting the collective behaviour that will emerge from a given set of local rules is hard; working backwards from a desired outcome to the rules that will produce it is harder still. Many researchers now use evolutionary algorithms, which generate thousands of candidate rule sets, test them in simulation and retain the most successful. The method works, but the rules it produces are often impossible for a human to interpret. That creates a serious obstacle for any regulator asked to certify that a swarm operating near people will behave safely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means the insect analogy has been a mistake. It is worth remembering, however, that colonies are the product of millions of years of selection, and that their resilience is bought at a price. A large proportion of the workers in many ant colonies appear to do almost nothing at any given moment, and foragers are lost in great numbers. Engineers, who must account for the cost of every machine, may be unwilling to tolerate this kind of waste, even though it may be precisely what makes a colony so hard to disrupt. Swarm robots are therefore likely to succeed first in settings where individual units are cheap and redundancy is affordable.

topic: fish-inspired underwater robots: undulating propulsion versus propellers, vortex use, efficiency versus manoeuvrability, quiet robots for reef observation and partial biomimicry
title: Swimming Lessons
subtitle: Engineers have spent decades trying to build machines that swim like fish. What have they actually learned?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every vehicle that travels beneath the sea, from submarines to small survey drones, is driven by a propeller. Fish, by contrast, move by bending their bodies and sweeping their tails from side to side, and engineers have long wondered whether copying them might produce vehicles that are faster, more efficient or more agile. Much of this curiosity can be traced to a puzzle first raised in the 1930s, when calculations appeared to show that a dolphin would need muscles several times more powerful than any known to science in order to reach the speeds it was observed to achieve. The calculations were later shown to rest on flawed assumptions about the resistance of water flowing over the animal's skin. Nevertheless, the notion that swimming animals possess some hidden secret has proved remarkably durable, and in my view it has not always been a helpful one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first robotic fish, built in the 1990s, were elaborate machines with dozens of linked segments driven by cables and pulleys. Since then the emphasis has shifted from imitating the appearance of fish to understanding how they interact with the water around them. Siddhartha Barooah, a fluid dynamicist at the Hooghly Institute of Marine Engineering, has shown that a beating tail leaves behind a regular pattern of swirling eddies, and that the arrangement of these eddies largely determines how much thrust is produced. Fish also appear able to draw energy from eddies created by other objects. Trout holding position behind a rock in a fast stream, for instance, use remarkably little muscular effort, because they adjust their bodies to slip between the swirls shed by the rock. Barooah believes that robots could one day exploit disturbed water in the same way, travelling through rough conditions while consuming less power than they would in calm ones.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whether robotic fish are more efficient than propeller-driven vehicles in ordinary conditions is a separate question, and here the evidence is less encouraging. Marta Dąbkowska, at the Baltic Polytechnic in Gdynia, compared a fish-like robot with a conventional vehicle of similar size and weight. At a steady cruising speed, the propeller consumed less energy over the same distance. The fish-like robot's advantage appeared only during manoeuvres, when it accelerated from rest or turned sharply. Dąbkowska concludes that the widely repeated claim that fish-like propulsion is inherently more efficient is a myth, and that its real benefit is agility. Her experiments were carefully designed, but they involved a single robot of one particular shape, and it would be premature to treat the question as closed on that basis.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Agility, at least, is not in dispute. Many fish can reverse direction within a fraction of their own body length, whereas vehicles driven by propellers generally need a wide arc in order to turn. In open water this hardly matters. In cluttered environments, however, such as coral reefs, the interiors of shipwrecks or the forests of pillars that support harbours and offshore platforms, the ability to turn on the spot can determine whether an inspection is possible at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A less expected application has emerged in marine biology. Kalani Mahoe, who leads a monitoring programme at the Pacific Reef Observatory, has found that reef fish usually scatter when a propeller-driven survey vehicle approaches, but largely ignore a robot that looks and moves like a fish and makes little noise. On some occasions, small fish have even joined the robot as it swam. Mahoe argues that such machines allow researchers to watch natural behaviour at close range in a way that has never previously been possible. This may well prove true, but some caution is needed. The fact that animals do not flee from a machine does not guarantee that they behave exactly as they would in its absence, and tolerance of an unfamiliar object may fade, or change in character, over time.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical obstacles remain considerable. A flexible body requires a waterproof skin that can withstand being bent thousands of times a day, and the materials currently available tend to crack within months. Salt water corrodes joints, and marine organisms colonise any surface that stays submerged for long. Eero Ojanperä, an engineer who designs inspection vehicles for offshore wind farms, argues that the most promising approach is not to imitate an entire fish but to borrow particular features and attach them to conventional designs: a flexible fin that improves steering, for example, mounted on an otherwise ordinary hull. In his experience, partial imitation of this kind is far easier to make reliable than a complete artificial animal.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Measured against the propeller on the propeller's own terms, then, the robotic fish has seldom won. Yet asking which of the two is superior is, I would suggest, the wrong question, since each is suited to different tasks. The long search for the fish's supposed secret has produced something of more lasting value than a faster submarine: a detailed understanding of how flexible bodies and moving water act upon one another. That knowledge is already informing the design of underwater turbines and even artificial heart valves, fields that have nothing to do with swimming at all.

topic: soft robotics inspired by boneless animals: compliance and 'intelligence in the material', the tether and power problem, distributed versus learned control, self-healing materials and medical uses
title: Without a Skeleton
subtitle: Robots modelled on octopuses and caterpillars promise to be safer and gentler than their rigid predecessors, but softness brings problems of its own

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of their history, robots have been built like machines rather than animals: rigid links of metal joined by motorised joints, each movement calculated in advance. Such robots are precise and powerful, but they are also dangerous to work beside and clumsy with anything delicate or irregular in shape. Soft robotics takes a different model. Its inspiration comes from creatures with no rigid skeleton at all, such as the octopus, the caterpillar and the earthworm, or from boneless structures like the elephant's trunk. Typical soft robots have bodies made of silicone rubber and are moved by pumping air or liquid into chambers inside them, which then swell and bend. Over the past fifteen years the field has, in my view, advanced faster than almost any other branch of robotics. Its practical successes, however, have been confined to a surprisingly narrow range of tasks.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central attraction of softness is compliance. A soft gripper closing around an object conforms to its shape, so it can pick up a raw egg, a strawberry or an irregular machine part without the elaborate sensing and calculation a rigid hand would need. Johan Wennerbom, of the Mälardalen Robotics Centre, describes this as placing intelligence in the material: the body itself performs part of the work that would otherwise have to be done by a computer. It is an elegant idea, but it is sometimes pressed too far. A gripper that adapts itself to any shape cannot, for that very reason, hold an object in a precisely known position, and many industrial tasks depend on exactly that.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more stubborn difficulty concerns power. An octopus carries its own energy supply; most soft robots do not. They are typically tethered, connected by tubes to compressors or pumps that sit beside them on the laboratory bench. Varvara Lyubimtseva, a materials engineer at the Volga Institute of Applied Physics, has calculated that the pumps, valves and batteries needed to free a soft robot from its tether usually weigh several times as much as the soft body itself, and are themselves rigid. Adding them, she argues, largely defeats the purpose. In her view, unless new power sources are developed, such as chemical reactions that release gas inside the robot's body, most soft robots will remain tethered and confined to factories and laboratories.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Control presents a different kind of challenge. A conventional robot arm with six joints has six quantities to manage. A soft arm can bend at every point along its length, which in principle gives it an unlimited number of ways to move. Aiko Tsuchimochi, who studies octopus neurology at the Hokuriku Marine Laboratory, points out that around two-thirds of the animal's nerve cells lie not in its brain but in its arms, which appear to make many decisions locally. She argues that soft robots will need similarly distributed control, with each section processing information for itself rather than waiting for instructions from a central computer. Sipho Ngwenyama, of the Highveld Institute of Technology, takes the opposite view. His group allowed a soft arm to move at random for several hours while a learning algorithm built up a model of its behaviour; the trained system then controlled the arm with considerable accuracy. These results are impressive. Yet rubber stiffens as it ages, and a model learned from a new arm may gradually cease to describe the arm it is meant to control.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Durability is a further concern, since soft materials are easily punctured and tend to tire with repeated bending. Rosa Condori-Mamani, at the Andean Polytechnic University, is developing polymers that repair cuts in their own surface when heated. Healing takes several hours, and the repaired material recovers only part of its original strength. Condori-Mamani maintains that this is acceptable for robots working in agriculture, where a machine can be withdrawn overnight without serious loss.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: So far the greatest commercial success has come in food packing, where soft grippers handle fruit, vegetables and baked goods that vary too much in shape for rigid hands. Rehabilitation gloves that help patients recovering from strokes to move their fingers are also in clinical trials. It is in medicine, I believe, that softness offers the greatest advantage, for the simple reason that the human body is itself soft. Flexible instruments that can follow the curves of blood vessels or the gut without damaging tissue could transform certain forms of surgery, although the process of approving such devices is, rightly, a slow one.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important lesson is that the label 'soft robot' may itself be misleading. Even the octopus, the field's favourite example, possesses a hard beak, and most animals combine soft tissue with rigid structures, using each where it is most useful. The most successful machines of the coming decades are likely to follow the same principle. They will not be entirely soft but will have soft parts wherever contact with fragile objects or people demands them.

topic: bird-inspired flight robotics: morphing wings, passive gust absorption by feathers, feathered prototype wings, perching drones with tendon-locking feet and the relevance to large aircraft
title: Lessons from the Living Wing
subtitle: Engineers who once dismissed bird flight as too complicated to imitate are now borrowing its secrets for a new generation of small aircraft

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, aircraft designers have treated the wing as a fixed object. The wing of an airliner keeps the same shape from take-off to landing, and its performance is optimised for a single cruising condition. Birds work on an entirely different principle. A swift or a gull continuously reshapes its wings in the air, sweeping them back to dive, spreading its feathers to slow down and twisting individual sections to correct for sudden gusts. The idea of building aircraft that can do the same, known as morphing, has been discussed since the earliest days of aviation, but for most of that time it remained a laboratory curiosity. It is fair to say that the field promised far more than it delivered. In the last decade, however, cheaper sensors, lighter materials and a better understanding of how birds actually fly have begun to turn speculation into working prototypes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Ottilie Grønnevik, who studies animal locomotion at the Bergen Institute of Comparative Biomechanics, spent several years filming pigeons as they flew through a wind tunnel in which turbulence could be generated on demand. Her high-speed recordings showed that the birds' bodies and heads stayed remarkably steady even when the air around them was violently disturbed. Surprisingly, this stability was not achieved mainly through rapid muscular corrections. Instead, the outer feathers bent and rotated under the pressure of each gust and then sprang back, absorbing much of the disturbance before it reached the body. Grønnevik concludes that a large share of a bird's wing control is passive, built into the structure of the feathers themselves rather than issued as commands by the nervous system. For engineers, this was an encouraging message, since passive mechanisms require neither sensors nor processing power.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ruslan Abdykadyrov and his colleagues at the Almaty Polytechnic Flight Laboratory took this insight literally. Their experimental wing consists of real pigeon feathers mounted on an artificial skeleton and linked by elastic bands, so that the feathers slide over one another and fan out as the wing is extended. Fitted to a small remote-controlled aircraft, the wing allowed tighter turns and steadier flight in gusty conditions than a rigid wing of similar size. The achievement is genuine, but it should be seen as a demonstration rather than a product. Natural feathers wear out, absorb moisture and cannot be manufactured to order, and the synthetic substitutes tested so far lack the subtle combination of stiffness and flexibility that makes the real thing so effective. Until that problem is solved, the feathered wing will remain a scientific instrument.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns not flight itself but what happens at the end of it. Small battery-powered drones can typically stay airborne for less than half an hour, which severely limits their usefulness for tasks such as monitoring wildlife or inspecting bridges. Tamsin Pellow, a roboticist at the Coastal Autonomous Systems Group, argues that the solution is to let drones behave like birds and perch. Her team has built a quadcopter fitted with a pair of grasping feet modelled on those of songbirds. In many perching birds, a tendon running down the back of the leg automatically tightens the toes when the bird crouches, so that it can grip a branch while asleep without using any energy. Pellow's drone exploits the same mechanism: the impact of landing closes the feet around a branch or railing, after which the motors can be switched off entirely. In field trials the drone stayed put for several hours, recording images, before flying on.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that such ideas will spread beyond small machines. Itzel Huitrón, an aerospace engineer who has worked on the certification of commercial aircraft, points out that every additional moving part is a potential point of failure, and that the regulators who approve passenger aircraft are, with good reason, deeply suspicious of complexity. A morphing wing would also be heavier than a conventional one, and the fuel saved by its adaptability could easily be cancelled out by the extra weight. In her view, biomimetic flight will remain confined to drones. This argument is sensible as far as it goes, but it underestimates how gradually aviation adopts new ideas. Large aircraft are unlikely ever to have feathered wings, yet flexible trailing edges, which change their curvature smoothly instead of hinging, have already been tested on full-sized aircraft and appear to reduce drag measurably.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is nonetheless at the small scale that the lessons of bird flight matter most. An airliner cruising at high altitude barely notices a gust that would throw a small drone off course, because the forces involved are tiny in comparison with its weight and speed. Drones, like birds, operate close to the ground, where the air is constantly churned into eddies. If delivery drones are ever to become a routine feature of city life, they will need exactly the kind of gust tolerance that pigeons display every day.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The broader lesson of this research concerns what imitation should mean. Early attempts at bird-like flight failed largely because they copied appearance rather than function. The current generation of researchers has been more successful precisely because it asks why a bird's wing works before deciding which features to reproduce. A drone need not look anything like a pigeon in order to benefit from the principle that a flexible structure can absorb disturbances on its own. The most useful thing biology offers engineering, I would suggest, is not a set of blueprints but a set of questions.

topic: shark-skin-inspired surfaces: denticles and riblets, the narrow conditions for drag reduction, denticles and thrust in swimming, the competitive swimsuit claims, riblet films on aircraft and antibacterial microtextures
title: The Shark's Rough Edge
subtitle: Shark skin has become one of the best-known examples of nature inspiring engineering, but the science behind it is less settled than the stories suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Run a hand from a shark's head towards its tail and the skin feels smooth; run it the other way and it rasps like sandpaper. The roughness comes from dermal denticles, tiny tooth-like scales, each carrying fine ridges aligned with the direction in which the animal swims. Since the 1980s these ridges have been credited with reducing the resistance of the water flowing over the shark's body, and the idea has inspired grooved films for aircraft, coatings for ship hulls and, most famously, racing swimsuits. It is an appealing narrative: an animal refined by hundreds of millions of years of evolution hands engineers a ready-made solution. Yet the evidence that denticles exist chiefly to reduce drag is considerably thinner than its popularity would suggest, and the history of the idea is as much a lesson in the hazards of biomimicry as in its rewards.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The engineering principle, at least, is well understood. Close to any surface moving through a fluid, the flow breaks up into small, swirling eddies that drift sideways and transfer momentum to the surface, producing friction. Microscopic grooves, known as riblets, can restrict this sideways motion, keeping the eddies further from the surface and reducing friction. Lucía Arambarri, a fluid dynamicist at the Cantabrian Institute of Fluid Mechanics, has measured reductions of up to eight per cent on riblet plates in water channels. Her experiments also reveal a less advertised fact: the benefit appears only when the spacing of the grooves is matched to the speed of the flow. If the flow is too slow or too fast for a given spacing, the riblets cease to help and may actually increase drag, since they add to the area of surface in contact with the water.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This sensitivity is a problem for the standard account, because a shark does not swim at one fixed speed. Soraya Mehrabadi, who leads a biomechanics group at the Caspian University of Marine Science, decided to test real skin rather than idealised plates. Her team attached strips of shark skin to flexible foils that could be made to flap like a swimming tail. When the foils were held rigid, the skin produced slightly more drag than a smooth surface. When they flapped, however, the skinned foils swam measurably faster, and flow visualisation suggested that the denticles strengthened a swirl of water along the leading edge of the foil, which increased thrust. If Mehrabadi is right, the shark's skin is better understood as an aid to propulsion than as a means of reducing friction, and engineers who copied the ridges in the hope of making surfaces slippery may have taken the wrong lesson from the animal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Nowhere was the gap between science and publicity wider than in competitive swimming. During the 2000s, full-body suits marketed as imitating shark skin coincided with an extraordinary run of world records, and they were eventually banned from elite competition. Vahagn Ter-Sargsyan, a sports engineer who analysed the suits after the ban, concluded that their textured surfaces contributed almost nothing. The real advantages, he argues, lay in the compression of the swimmer's body into a more streamlined shape and in the buoyancy provided by air trapped in the fabric. The episode does not show that riblets are useless, but it does show how readily a striking biological story can be attached to a product whose benefits come from somewhere else entirely.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Aviation offers a more sober test. Riblet films applied to the wings and fuselage of passenger aircraft have been found to reduce fuel consumption by roughly one per cent. Snorri Ásbjarnarson, an engineer who has advised several airlines on fuel efficiency, insists that the figure should not be dismissed: across a large fleet operating for decades, one per cent represents enormous sums of money and substantial reductions in emissions, enough to justify a considerable outlay on the technology. The difficulty, in his view, is durability. Adhesive films are scratched by dust and ice, degraded by cleaning fluids and must be removed whenever an aircraft is repainted. He expects that textures etched directly into paint by lasers will eventually replace them, though this has yet to be demonstrated on a commercial scale.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most promising applications have little to do with drag at all. Chidimma Ezeokonkwo, a microbiologist at the Lagos Centre for Surface Hygiene, has shown that plastics patterned with denticle-like textures are colonised by bacteria far more slowly than smooth ones, apparently because the ridges make it harder for microbes to establish themselves. She is particularly interested in hospital surfaces such as bed rails and door handles, where a texture that discourages bacteria without chemical agents would avoid contributing to antibiotic resistance. The results are encouraging, but they come from controlled laboratory conditions. In a busy ward, grease and cleaning residues could quickly fill the microscopic grooves, and I suspect the protection would prove far weaker than the trials imply.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, does the shark really teach? Perhaps that biological structures rarely do only one thing. Denticles protect the skin from abrasion and parasites, may assist propulsion and possibly reduce friction under certain conditions, all at once. Engineers, by contrast, tend to isolate a single function and optimise for it. There is nothing wrong with that, provided that we do not assume a structure evolved for the purpose that happens to interest us. The most valuable habit biomimicry can cultivate is the patience to ask what a feature actually does before deciding what it is for.

topic: animal-inspired legged locomotion: passive dynamic walkers, self-stabilising springy insect legs, limits of passive mechanics, learned controllers in quadruped robots and spring-based prostheses
title: Legs That Think for Themselves
subtitle: Why some roboticists believe the secret of walking lies less in the brain than in the body

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walking looks effortless when animals do it, which is precisely why it proved so difficult for robots. The first generation of walking machines treated every step as a problem of calculation. Sensors measured the angle of each joint many times a second, and a central computer issued corrections to motors at the hip, knee and ankle so that the robot's weight never strayed outside a carefully defined zone. The results were impressive in a laboratory but painfully slow, and such robots consumed perhaps fifteen times as much energy as a human covering the same distance. In my view, the approach was mistaken in principle, not merely in execution: it assumed that a body is a passive load to be pushed around by an intelligent controller, when in animals the body itself does much of the work.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The clearest demonstration of this comes from a strange family of machines known as passive dynamic walkers. These are pairs of legs with no motors, no sensors and no computer at all. Placed at the top of a gentle slope, they stroll down it, each leg swinging forward like a pendulum under gravity and landing in time to catch the falling body. Wouter Kloosterhuis, an engineer at the Lowlands Institute of Mechatronics, built one such walker and then added small motors at the ankles, just enough to replace the energy that the slope would otherwise supply. The result could walk on level ground using roughly the same energy per kilogram as a person. For Kloosterhuis, the lesson is that a well-designed leg already knows how to walk; the controller's task is merely to keep it going.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Insects suggest that the same principle applies to running. A cockroach can cross rough ground at a speed that leaves almost no time for its nervous system to react to each obstacle. Dilnoza Tursunbaeva, a zoologist at the Samarkand Institute of Comparative Physiology, investigated how this is possible by fitting running cockroaches with a tiny device that delivered a sudden sideways jolt. The insects recovered their course within a single stride, faster than any signal could travel from their legs to their brain and back. Their springy legs, she concluded, absorb and redirect disturbances automatically. Engineers have since built six-legged robots with flexible legs that scramble over rubble while relying on very little sensory information, something that rigid-legged machines with far more sophisticated sensors struggled to manage.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every researcher thinks passive mechanics can carry robots very far. Gideon Ntimbwa, who designs inspection robots at the Kilimanjaro Robotics Centre, points out that the tasks which matter most in practical settings, such as climbing stairs, stepping across gaps or balancing on narrow beams, require each foot to be placed in a particular spot. A springy leg cannot decide where to land. Animals, he notes, also use their eyes when the ground becomes treacherous. He is surely right that mechanics alone will not suffice, although his argument applies more to difficult terrain than to the ordinary walking that makes up most of what a legged robot does.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most visible recent progress has come from a quite different direction. Four-legged commercial robots now trot, climb and even recover from being kicked, guided by controllers trained through millions of trials in computer simulation. Some commentators have concluded that clever software has made the study of passive dynamics obsolete. Anahí Ruiz-Tagle, a biomechanist at the Valparaíso School of Engineering, disagrees strongly. Learned controllers, she argues, often compensate for poorly designed bodies by applying constant small corrections, and those corrections are paid for in battery power; many such robots can operate for only about ninety minutes before recharging. Her criticism is somewhat overstated, since these machines perform tasks no passive walker could attempt, but the energy problem she identifies is real. Far from being obsolete, the study of how bodies move without assistance has arguably become more urgent as legged robots leave the laboratory.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is in devices worn by people that passive principles have so far had their greatest practical influence. Modern prosthetic ankles often contain carbon-fibre springs that compress as the wearer's weight comes onto the foot and release that stored energy as the foot pushes off, giving a more natural gait with less effort. Lightweight exoskeletons that help factory workers lift loads increasingly use springs rather than motors for the same reason. Ruiz-Tagle's own group has shown that a spring-loaded knee can halve the demands a powered exoskeleton makes on its battery. Such devices must work alongside a human nervous system rather than a computer, and a design that behaves predictably without constant adjustment is easier for a wearer to trust. Here, at least, the argument for letting the mechanics do the work has already been won.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The emerging consensus, which I find persuasive, is that the old division between body and brain was artificial. Animals are not either well built or well controlled; they are both, and each quality makes the other possible. A good legged robot will neither leave everything to its mechanics nor attempt to control everything through computation. The most capable machines of the coming decades are likely to be those whose legs and control systems are designed together from the start, so that each does what it does best.

topic: bat-inspired sonar for robots: the limits of engineered ultrasonic sensing, moving ear shapes in horseshoe bats, robotic bat heads, echo-based place recognition in clutter, sonar versus cameras and lidar, and human echolocation
title: Seeing with Sound
subtitle: Bats find their way through dark and crowded spaces using echoes alone. Can robots learn to do the same?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A bat hunting at night can detect an insect the width of a human hair, distinguish it from the leaves around it and seize it in mid-air, all by interpreting the echoes of its own calls. Robots, by comparison, depend overwhelmingly on light. Cameras and laser scanners, known as lidar, give machines a detailed picture of their surroundings, but both fail in smoke, thick fog or dense dust, precisely the conditions in which robots might be most useful. Ultrasonic sensors do exist, and every car fitted with parking aids carries several, yet they are remarkably crude: each reports little more than the distance to the nearest solid object. Of all the areas in which engineers have attempted to borrow from nature, I would argue that none reveals a wider gap between the biological original and its imitation than sonar.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the explanation lies in the bat's ears. Many species possess elaborately folded outer ears that filter returning echoes differently according to the direction from which they arrive, so that a sound coming from above and to the left acquires a slightly different character from one arriving from straight ahead. Fenna Wiersma, a sensory ecologist at the Wadden Institute of Sensory Ecology, used high-speed cameras to film horseshoe bats in flight and discovered that they do not hold their ears still. Within a tenth of a second during each call, muscles bend and twist the outer ear into a different shape, altering the direction in which it is most sensitive. Wiersma interprets this as a way of extracting more information from every call: by listening to the same echo through a changing filter, the bat effectively samples its surroundings from several angles at once.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yerlan Kenzhebulatov and his colleagues at the Steppe Polytechnic University set out to test whether a machine could benefit in the same way. Their robotic bat head consists of a single ultrasonic emitter flanked by two soft, ear-shaped receivers whose form is altered by small motors. When the ears were kept rigid, the head could estimate the direction of a target only roughly; when they deformed during each pulse, its accuracy improved several-fold. Conventional sonar arrays that achieve comparable precision use dozens of microphones. The result is elegant, but it was obtained in an echo-free laboratory chamber containing one target at a time, which is about as far from a bat's world as it is possible to get.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That world is cluttered. A bat flying through a forest receives thousands of overlapping echoes from trunks, branches and leaves with every call, and no amount of clever ear design can, on its own, untangle them. Kwabena Adjei-Brenya, a roboticist who has spent years trying to make sonar work in agricultural settings, believes that bats solve the problem not by processing each echo from scratch but by memory. Field studies show that bats return night after night along the same routes, and Adjei-Brenya suggests that they recognise familiar places by their characteristic patterns of echoes, much as we might recognise a street by its outline. He has trained a robot to identify its position in a large greenhouse from such acoustic fingerprints, and reports that it located itself correctly more than nine times in ten without any camera.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sceptics question whether any of this will matter commercially. Sione Fonokalafi, who develops navigation systems for warehouse robots, points out that cameras and lidar are becoming cheaper and more capable every year, while the processing power that makes the bat's achievement possible resides in a brain that no one knows how to copy. At best, he concludes, sonar will serve as a backup for when the primary sensors fail. This is a fair assessment of the commercial picture, but it misses the point. The occasions on which cameras and lidar fail, such as a burning building or a mine filled with dust, are exactly those in which a rescue robot is needed most, and a backup that works when nothing else does is hardly a minor contribution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Further support for the importance of the brain comes from an unexpected source. Some blind people teach themselves to echolocate by making clicking sounds with their tongues and listening to the echoes, and the most skilled can identify the size and position of objects several metres away. Their hearing is usually no better than anyone else's; what changes, according to brain-imaging studies, is that regions normally devoted to vision begin to process the echoes. If human beings can acquire this skill as adults, it suggests that effective sonar depends less on specialised hardware than on learning how to interpret what returns.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the deepest lesson bats offer is that sensing is something an animal does, not merely something it receives. As a bat closes on an insect, it calls more rapidly and shortens each call, ending in a rapid burst that gives it continuous updates in the final moments of the chase. Robotic sonar, by contrast, usually emits the same pulse at the same rate regardless of circumstances. Machines that adapted their signals to the task in hand, calling differently when exploring than when approaching an obstacle, would be closer to the bat in spirit than any number of carefully sculpted artificial ears.

topic: whisker-inspired tactile sensing: active whisking in rats, tapered artificial whiskers, seal whiskers and wake tracking, fragility and practical niches, and whiskered robots as tools for neuroscience
title: Feeling the Way
subtitle: The whiskers of rats and seals are inspiring a new kind of robotic sense

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A rat moving through a dark tunnel does not need to see where it is going. Sweeping its whiskers forward and back several times a second, it builds up a detailed impression of the walls, the floor and any obstacles ahead, often deciding whether a gap is wide enough to squeeze through before its nose has reached it. Remarkably, a whisker itself is little more than a hair: its shaft contains no nerves, and all the sensing takes place at the base, where the follicle is packed with receptors that respond to the slightest bending. For robot designers, who have lavished attention on cameras and microphones, this offers an intriguing model. Touch is, in my view, the most neglected of the senses in robotics, and whiskers suggest a way of giving machines a sense of touch that operates before, rather than at, the moment of collision.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most revealing discoveries about whiskers concerns not their structure but the way they are moved. Elif Çelikbilek, a neuroscientist at the Anatolian Institute of Neuroscience, filmed rats exploring objects and measured the force of every contact. She found that once a whisker touched a surface, the rat reduced the force of the following sweep, so that the whisker brushed the object lightly instead of pressing against it. Çelikbilek argues that light contact produces cleaner signals, since a whisker that is bent too far gives information mainly about its own stiffness rather than about the object. Her interpretation strikes me as convincing, and it carries a broader message: how well an animal senses depends as much on how it controls its movements as on the quality of its sensory organs.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Engineers were quick to take note. Mateus Quintal, who leads a robotics group at the Atlantic Institute of Technology in the Azores, has built a mobile robot carrying an array of artificial whiskers made from tapered plastic, each mounted on magnetic sensors that record exactly how far and in which direction it bends. The robot can distinguish rough surfaces from smooth ones and identify simple shapes in complete darkness. Quintal's most interesting finding concerns the whiskers' shape. Tapered whiskers, like real ones, bend smoothly along their length when they meet an object, whereas cylindrical whiskers tend to snap suddenly from straight to bent. As a result, tapered whiskers deliver a richer and more continuous signal, which suggests that the natural form is not an accident of growth but an important part of the sensing mechanism.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Seals use their whiskers in a quite different way. Nomvula Ndlela, a marine biologist at the Benguela Marine Laboratory, trained harbour seals wearing blindfolds and ear covers to follow the trail left by a small submarine. The animals could track the swirling wake more than half a minute after the vessel had passed, detecting the faint water movements through their whiskers alone. This is all the more surprising because a swimming seal's whiskers might be expected to vibrate constantly in the current it creates. Ndlela's team found the explanation in their surface, which has a wavy profile that breaks up the eddies forming behind each whisker and so suppresses vibration caused by the seal's own motion. Engineers have since copied this profile for underwater flow sensors and, in an unexpected spin-off, for bridge cables, where it reduces the vibration caused by wind.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares the enthusiasm. Aleksander Wróblewicz, an industrial engineer who evaluates sensing systems for manufacturers, points out that whiskers protrude, catch on things and break, and that replacing them would add to the cost of running any robot. He believes that most robots will be better served by cameras combined with soft, sensitive skins that register contact over a wide area. For robots in tidy, well-lit factories, I suspect he is correct. But in drains, collapsed buildings or murky harbours, where cameras see little and contact is unavoidable, the ability to feel an obstacle before striking it could prove decisive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a benefit that has nothing to do with commercial products. Building whiskered robots has given neuroscientists a way of testing ideas about how the brain handles touch. Çelikbilek, for example, used one of Quintal's robots to examine whether her account of light contact actually improved recognition, programming it to whisk with and without the adjustment and comparing the results. The exchange of ideas between biology and engineering is often presented as running in one direction only, from nature to machines, but in this field it plainly flows both ways.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whisker sensors remain largely confined to laboratories, and it would be rash to predict when they will become common. My own expectation is that they will appear first in underwater inspection, where vision is often useless and the seal has already shown what is possible. Whatever their commercial future, whiskers have already reminded robot designers that sensing is something to be performed, not simply something to be installed.
