topic: biohybrid robots powered by living muscle: how muscle-driven devices are built and trained, survival and the nutrient-diffusion limit on size, use as medical test platforms, biodegradable environmental robots and ethical questions raised by adding neurons
title: Living Engines
subtitle: A small community of researchers is building robots that move with real muscle. What, if anything, are such machines for?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most attempts to imitate nature in robotics borrow a shape or a principle: the profile of a fin, the grip of a gecko's foot. Biohybrid robotics goes further, building living tissue directly into the machine. Its best-known products are tiny and slightly unsettling. One is a swimming device, smaller than a coin and shaped like a stingray, whose body is driven by a layer of heart muscle cells and which can be steered by flashes of light. Others are walkers a few millimetres long, propelled by strips of skeletal muscle. The attraction of muscle is easy to understand. It converts chemical energy into motion efficiently, it is soft and quiet, it can repair minor damage, and it grows stronger with use, which no electric motor can do. The field is genuinely original, but it has attracted a degree of excitement that its achievements so far do not justify, and it deserves a more sober assessment than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Building such a device begins in the culture dish. Muscle cells, obtained either from animal tissue or from stem cells, are grown on a scaffold of soft gel, where they fuse into fibres capable of contracting. They can then be triggered in one of two ways: by pulses of electric current, or, if the cells have been genetically modified to carry light-sensitive proteins, by light. Bagus Wiratmaja and his colleagues at the Java Institute of Bioengineering have built a walker seven millimetres long that moves at roughly one body length per minute, a pace that would embarrass a snail. More interesting than its speed is its response to training. After a week in which the muscle was stimulated electrically at regular intervals, a form of exercise, the force it produced rose by about a third, much as a human muscle strengthens with repeated use.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Keeping the tissue alive is another matter. Biohybrid robots must be kept in a warm, sterile liquid containing nutrients, they cannot operate in air, and even under ideal laboratory conditions most stop working within about two weeks. Folasade Akinbiyi, who studies engineered tissue at the Ibadan Centre for Tissue Engineering, insists that these are not engineering problems awaiting clever solutions but consequences of basic biology. In the body, muscle is threaded with blood vessels that carry oxygen and nutrients to every cell. In a culture dish there are none, and nutrients must simply seep in from the surrounding liquid. In tissue thicker than about a fifth of a millimetre, cells in the interior starve and die, so a larger robot cannot be made merely by adding more muscle. Her group is experimenting with networks of fine channels inside the gel to deliver nutrients, a promising approach that remains far from the complexity of a real circulatory system. I would argue that this limit on size, rather than any shortage of ingenuity, is the central obstacle the field faces.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Given these constraints, it is worth asking what biohybrid devices are actually for. Eilidh MacAskill, a pharmacologist at the Firth Institute of Biomedical Research, believes their greatest value has little to do with robotics at all. A muscle-powered walker, she points out, is in effect a miniature laboratory for observing how living muscle behaves under load. Drugs intended to strengthen weakened muscles could be tested on such devices before being given to patients, and tissue grown from the cells of people with inherited muscle diseases could reveal how those conditions develop. This seems to me the most compelling case yet made for the field, precisely because it turns the fragility of living tissue from a defect into an object of study.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Others still dream of machines that operate outside the laboratory. Leilani Nāone, an environmental engineer at the Pacific Institute of Ocean Technology, envisages swarms of biodegradable robots released into the sea to monitor pollution. Because they would be made largely of living tissue and gel, any devices that were lost would simply decompose, leaving no plastic or batteries behind. Some cells might even be modified to change colour or behaviour in the presence of particular chemicals. The idea is imaginative, but the obstacles described above make it a distant prospect at best: the open sea is cold, salty and teeming with microbes, almost the opposite of the conditions that cultured muscle requires.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The field also raises ethical questions that have received surprisingly little attention. Muscle tissue on its own has no nerves and cannot feel anything, so the devices built so far pose no obvious moral difficulty. However, several groups have already combined muscle with motor neurons, the nerve cells that normally instruct muscles to contract, in order to achieve finer control. No one suggests that such devices are remotely capable of sensation. Yet as the networks of neurons grow larger and more complex, the question of where to draw a line will become harder to avoid, and it would be wise to establish guidelines before rather than after it becomes urgent.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Biohybrid robots will not replace electric motors, and claims that they herald a new generation of living machines should be treated with caution. Their importance lies elsewhere. By trying to put muscle to work outside the body, researchers are learning, often through failure, exactly how much living tissue depends on the systems that surround it. That knowledge may well prove more valuable than any robot.

topic: re-identification of 'anonymised' smartphone location data: uniqueness of mobility traces, coarsening, auxiliary information, noise in aggregates and controlled research access
title: The Trail That Names You
subtitle: Location records stripped of names are sold and shared as if they were anonymous. A growing body of research suggests that the label is misleading

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every smartphone continuously reports where it is, and much of that information ends up in the hands of data brokers, advertising firms and researchers. Before it is passed on, it is usually described as anonymised: names and telephone numbers are removed and replaced with random codes, so that the record shows only that a device labelled with a meaningless string was at a particular place at a particular time. The reassurance offered to the public is that, once the name has gone, so has the person. That reassurance, however, rests on a misunderstanding of what makes information identifying. A name is merely one convenient label among many, and it is by no means the most revealing thing about us.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The point was made forcefully by a study led by Ewa Szymańczak at the Baltic Institute for Computational Social Science. Her team examined fifteen months of hourly location records for roughly 1.2 million mobile phone users and asked a simple question: how many points in a person's trace are needed to distinguish that person from everyone else in the dataset? The answer was startlingly small. Four observations, each giving an approximate place and hour, were enough to single out more than nine in ten individuals. The pairing of the place where a device spends its nights with the place where it spends its working days was, on its own, shared by very few people. As Szymańczak put it, the removal of names had changed the format of the data but not its meaning, because the trajectory itself does the work that a name would otherwise do.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The industry's standard response has been to coarsen the data, rounding locations to districts rather than street corners and times to the nearest few hours. Szymańczak tested this too, and found that uniqueness declined only gradually: each reduction in precision bought a modest gain in protection, and the data had to be made extremely crude before most people blended into the crowd. By that stage it was of little value to the transport planners and epidemiologists who wanted it. Critics of the data trade sometimes treat this trade-off as a convenient excuse invented by companies reluctant to change their practices. That is unfair. The tension between precision and privacy is real, and any honest policy must begin by admitting that it cannot be wished away.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that uniqueness is the right measure of danger. Hiroshi Takamatsu, a legal scholar at the Osaka Centre for Information Law, argues that being distinguishable is not the same as being named. A trace may be unlike any other, but to attach it to a real individual an intruder needs some outside knowledge that connects the two, and Takamatsu believes the risk has therefore been overstated. Regulation, in his view, should target the actual misuse of data rather than its mere circulation. The distinction he draws is logically sound, but in practice it offers less comfort than he supposes. The supplementary knowledge required is rarely difficult to come by: a geotagged photograph, a public post about a favourite café or a colleague who knows roughly where someone lives may be all that is needed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nor is the danger purely hypothetical. Journalists in several countries have purchased commercially available location files and, using nothing more sophisticated than public records, matched individual traces to named officials, recording their visits to clinics and private addresses. Faced with such cases, some organisations have stopped releasing individual records altogether and publish only totals, such as the number of devices present in a neighbourhood each hour. Abena Odhiambo-Kerr, a statistician at the Accra School of Data Science, warns that this is less safe than it appears. When counts are very small, or when overlapping tables can be subtracted from one another, the presence of a single person can be inferred. She recommends adding carefully calibrated random noise to published figures. The method is mathematically elegant, yet its cost falls disproportionately on sparsely populated rural districts, whose small numbers are distorted most, a consequence that its advocates rarely acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Regulators have begun to respond. A working group of European data protection authorities, chaired by Lorenzo Murgia, has proposed that location histories be treated as personal information whatever technical treatment they have received, so that their sale would require the explicit agreement of the people concerned. Data companies object that such a rule would halt research of real public value, from modelling the spread of infectious disease to redesigning bus networks. Both positions contain some truth, but neither unrestricted sale nor outright prohibition is the right answer. A more promising compromise is controlled access, in which approved researchers analyse sensitive records inside secure computing environments and may remove only aggregated results that have been checked before release.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the debate shows above all is that the vocabulary of privacy has fallen behind the technology. To call a dataset anonymous suggests a permanent state, as though identity, once removed, could never return. In reality the risk of re-identification depends on what else is known, by whom and at what point in the future, and it can grow as more information becomes available elsewhere. Technical safeguards will matter, but it may be that the single most useful reform is linguistic: abandoning a word that promises more than it can deliver, and describing data instead in terms of the level of risk it carries.

topic: the 'privacy paradox': why people say they value privacy yet disclose data cheaply — present bias, the cost of reading policies, digital resignation and survey measurement
title: Saying One Thing, Clicking Another
subtitle: Why do people who claim to care about their personal information give it away so readily?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Opinion surveys in many countries tell a consistent story: large majorities of people say they are worried about how companies collect and use their personal information. Yet the same people install applications that track their location, accept every cookie on a website without reading a word, and hand over their phone numbers at supermarket tills in exchange for a voucher worth less than a cup of coffee. Researchers have named this mismatch the privacy paradox. The name has proved popular, but it carries an assumption that deserves closer examination, namely that people's behaviour is inconsistent with their real preferences and that one of the two must therefore be mistaken.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most familiar explanation comes from behavioural economics. Liisa Soininen of the Helsinki Institute for Behavioural Economics argues that disclosure decisions suffer from what economists call present bias. The rewards for sharing information, whether a discount or a more convenient service, arrive immediately, whereas the costs are distant, uncertain and often invisible. Faced with such a choice, people consistently give too little weight to what might happen later. Soininen's experiments also reveal how unstable privacy valuations are. Participants who were told that their data was already protected demanded around five times as much money to give up that protection as other participants were willing to pay to obtain it. The value people place on privacy, she concludes, is not a fixed quantity waiting to be measured but something that changes according to how the question is framed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second account focuses less on psychology than on arithmetic. Dmytro Prokopenko, an information economist at the Kharkiv School of Economics, has estimated that an ordinary internet user who read the privacy policy of every service they used would need to set aside more than two hundred hours a year for the task. Under these conditions, he argues, ignoring the policies is not foolish but perfectly rational. People are not failing to protect their interests; they are declining to pay an absurdly high price in time for information that would rarely change their decisions. Once the hours are counted, Prokopenko suggests, much of the paradox simply dissolves. The argument is elegant, though its reach is limited: it explains why policies go unread, but says rather less about why people continue to use services whose intrusive habits they already know about from news reports or personal experience.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The sociologist Nirmala Gunawardane offers a darker interpretation. Her interviews with more than three hundred adults found that many participants regarded data collection as unavoidable, describing it as part of the price of taking part in modern life. They disclosed information not because they did not care, but because they believed that refusing would make no difference. Gunawardane calls this condition digital resignation. Of the explanations on offer, hers seems the most convincing for a large part of the population, since it accounts for both the concern people express and their apparent passivity. It cannot, however, explain everything. Many young people share details of their lives online not with weary reluctance but with obvious enthusiasm, and resignation is hardly the word for that.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers doubt that the paradox is as large as it appears. Ignacio Brizuela, a psychologist at the University of Rosario, points out that surveys typically ask about attitudes in very general terms, such as whether privacy matters, while behaviour is observed in highly specific situations. Broad attitudes are poor predictors of specific actions in almost every area of life, and there is no reason why privacy should be an exception. When Brizuela asked people about particular kinds of information in particular settings, their stated preferences matched their behaviour much more closely. His work is an important corrective, but it does not make the gap disappear entirely; a substantial difference between what people say and what they do remains even under the most careful measurement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These debates matter because the paradox is often used as an argument. If people freely give their data away, some technology firms reason, then their behaviour reveals what they truly want, and claims that the public needs stronger protection are exaggerated. This reasoning is deeply flawed. Choices made when every available service demands the same terms, and when the alternative is to abandon tools that are essential for work or study, tell us very little about genuine preferences. A shopper who buys the only loaf of bread on the shelf has not demonstrated a love of that particular loaf.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the research suggests that the privacy paradox may not be a paradox at all, but the predictable outcome of choices structured in ways that make protection costly and disclosure easy. If so, the responsibility for protecting personal information should shift away from individuals and towards the organisations that design these choices, through measures such as privacy-protective default settings and limits on how much data may be collected in the first place. Such measures would not remove individual choice altogether, but they would ensure that the easiest option available to a busy person was also the safer one. Further surveys of public attitudes are unlikely to add much to what is already known.

topic: the chilling effect of surveillance on lawful behaviour: natural experiments with encyclopaedia page views after surveillance disclosures, confounds in aggregate data, self-censorship by journalists and writers, and the burden of proof
title: The Silence That Watching Makes
subtitle: Does the knowledge of being observed change what people read, write and say, and can such an effect ever be measured?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The idea that surveillance alters behaviour even when nobody is actually watching has a long pedigree. Eighteenth-century designs for an ideal prison placed a single inspector at the centre of a ring of cells, so that inmates, unable to tell whether they were being observed at any given moment, would learn to behave as though they always were. Lawyers later gave the phenomenon a less architectural name: the chilling effect, meaning the tendency of people to refrain from perfectly lawful activities, such as reading controversial material or joining a protest, because they fear the consequences of being seen to do so. The concept is now invoked in almost every argument about state and corporate monitoring. Yet for most of its history it rested on intuition rather than evidence, and its popularity as a slogan has arguably run well ahead of what researchers can demonstrate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is fundamentally one of measurement. A chilling effect, by definition, consists of things that do not happen: the article left unread, the search never typed, the opinion never posted. Self-reports are of limited value, since people may be unaware of the ways in which they have adjusted their behaviour, or unwilling to admit that they have been intimidated. Laboratory studies, in which participants are told that their keystrokes are being logged, can show that people become more cautious, but such settings bear little resemblance to the diffuse and largely invisible monitoring of everyday life. For these reasons, the most influential recent work has relied on natural experiments: sudden public disclosures about surveillance programmes, after which researchers compare behaviour before and after the news broke.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One such study was carried out by Dragana Kovačina, a legal scholar at the University of Zagreb, who examined page views for several hundred encyclopaedia articles on subjects that a government might plausibly regard as sensitive, among them extremist organisations, explosives and certain infectious diseases. In the months following widely reported revelations about the scale of online monitoring by intelligence agencies, traffic to these articles fell by roughly a fifth and, crucially, did not recover to its previous trend. Articles on neutral subjects showed no comparable decline. Kovačina interprets the result as direct evidence that ordinary readers had begun to avoid information they feared might mark them out. Her design is ingenious, and the absence of any fall for the neutral articles makes the most obvious alternative explanation, a general decline in the use of online encyclopaedias, hard to sustain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Tharindu Ranasooriya, a statistician at the Colombo Institute of Social Data, has reanalysed similar datasets and argues that page-view figures are vulnerable to influences that have nothing to do with fear. Changes in the way search engines rank results, the growth of mobile browsing, and the fading of news stories that had temporarily inflated interest in a topic can all produce declines of comparable size. Ranasooriya does not deny that chilling effects exist; his objection is that aggregate data cannot distinguish them from routine fluctuations in online attention. The criticism is a fair one, although it applies with equal force to almost any study based on observational data, and if pressed too far it would rule out investigation of the question altogether.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different approach has been taken by Mateo Huidobro and his colleagues at the Valparaíso Centre for Media Studies, who surveyed journalists, novelists and academics in five countries. Large proportions reported having avoided certain topics in their work, steered clear of particular sources in telephone or email conversations, or deliberately declined to research a subject online. Huidobro argues that the most significant consequences of surveillance fall not on the general public but on these professional groups, whose self-restraint ultimately deprives everyone else of information. This is an important point, and one that debates framed around the privacy of the individual tend to overlook: the harm done by a chilling effect may be collective rather than personal, a loss to public knowledge rather than to any one citizen.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most sceptical voice is that of Agnes Mattsdotter, a sociologist at the Northern Institute for Digital Society, who questions whether the concept is coherent at all. Mattsdotter points out that much behaviour described as chilled could equally be described as prudence, and that surveillance is only one of many pressures, including social disapproval, employers' expectations and the permanence of online records, that encourage people to be careful about what they say. Attributing self-restraint specifically to government monitoring, she argues, requires a precision that current methods cannot achieve. Her point about competing pressures is well taken, but it does not follow that the concept should be abandoned. That a phenomenon has several causes is a reason to study it more carefully, not to deny that it exists.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, can reasonably be concluded? The evidence for a chilling effect is suggestive rather than conclusive, and advocates of privacy would do well to avoid overstating it. At the same time, the burden of proof deserves reconsideration. Because the effect is inherently hard to observe, demanding decisive evidence before taking it seriously is, in practice, a way of guaranteeing that it will never be taken seriously at all. Courts in several jurisdictions have begun to accept that a reasonable fear of monitoring may be sufficient to justify a legal challenge, even where no individual can show that they personally were watched. Perhaps the most valuable lesson of the research so far is that the costs of surveillance cannot be calculated simply by counting the people who have been monitored; they must also include those who, fearing that they might be, quietly changed what they did.

topic: investigative genetic genealogy: police use of consumer ancestry DNA databases to identify suspects through relatives, shared genetic information and consent, opt-in rules, accuracy and unrepresentative databases
title: Relatives in the Database
subtitle: Consumer DNA services have given detectives a powerful new tool, but at the price of exposing people who never chose to take part

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of forensic DNA analysis, a genetic profile recovered from a crime scene was useful only if it matched one already held in a police database, which typically contained samples from people who had been arrested or convicted. If the offender had never come into contact with the police, the trail went cold. In the past decade, that limitation has been dramatically loosened. Millions of people have sent saliva samples to commercial companies in order to learn about their ancestry or to trace distant relatives, and some of the resulting genetic data has been uploaded to openly searchable genealogy websites. Investigators have discovered that by comparing crime-scene DNA with these collections they can identify not the suspect but his or her cousins, and from there reconstruct family trees until a likely individual emerges. The first widely publicised success came in a case that had defeated detectives for more than forty years, and within months police forces in several countries had begun to experiment with the approach.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technique, known as investigative genetic genealogy, has been credited with resolving hundreds of cases that had remained unsolved for decades, including murders and assaults dating back to the 1970s. Its advocates are understandably enthusiastic. Pieter Aalderink, a former detective who now trains forensic genealogists in the Netherlands, argues that the method is not fundamentally different from asking a suspect's neighbours questions: investigators are simply following leads provided by relatives' publicly available information. He also stresses that a genealogical match never constitutes proof. It merely narrows the field, after which a conventional DNA comparison with the suspect is required before any charge can be brought. Aalderink adds that genealogists working with the police are bound by professional codes that forbid them to contact relatives without authorisation, and that most of their work consists of patient research in public archives rather than anything resembling covert surveillance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics see the matter differently. The central problem, according to the bioethicist Chiamaka Ebuehi of the Lagos Centre for Health Law, is that genetic information is inherently shared. A person who uploads her DNA profile discloses something about her parents, siblings and cousins, none of whom were consulted and many of whom may not even know she has done so. Ebuehi calculates that once around two per cent of a population has contributed to a searchable database, almost everyone in that population will have at least a third cousin within it, making nearly all of them identifiable. In her view, consent given by one individual cannot reasonably be stretched to cover a whole extended family. This is surely the most serious objection to the practice, and Aalderink's comparison with questioning neighbours does not answer it, since neighbours choose what they say, whereas relatives' genes speak whether their owners wish them to or not.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The early years of the technique were marked by considerable confusion over the rules. Several genealogy websites initially allowed police searches without informing their users, and when this became known there was a public outcry. One platform lost a large share of its members within weeks, a reminder that the cooperation of ordinary users cannot be taken for granted.Most platforms now require users to opt in before their profiles can be compared with crime-scene samples, and the proportion who do so has been lower than investigators had hoped. Some jurisdictions have gone further, restricting the method to serious violent crimes and requiring judicial approval before a search is carried out. These safeguards are welcome, but they rely heavily on the policies of private companies, which can change overnight when a firm is sold or its commercial priorities shift.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also questions about accuracy. Family-tree reconstruction depends on birth, marriage and death records, which may be incomplete, and on assumptions about biological relationships that are not always correct; adoptions, undisclosed parentage and donor conception can all lead investigators towards the wrong branch of a family. Irina Sarkissova, a population geneticist at the Yerevan Institute of Molecular Biology, points out that the databases themselves are far from representative. Because customers of ancestry services have been disproportionately of European descent, the method works much better for some communities than for others, and suspects from under-represented groups are less likely to be identified. Sarkissova regards this as a matter of fairness: if the technique is to be used at all, she suggests, its benefits and burdens ought to be distributed equally across society.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would nevertheless be a mistake to conclude that the method should be abandoned. The families of victims in long-unsolved cases have obtained answers that no other technique could have provided, and in a number of instances genealogical evidence has led to the release of people who had been wrongly convicted. What is needed is a framework that treats genetic data as a family resource rather than as individual property, perhaps by limiting how long crime-scene profiles may be retained and by prohibiting the use of the method for minor offences. The real danger lies not in the technique itself but in allowing its scope to expand gradually, case by case, without any genuine public debate about where its limits should be drawn.

topic: networked doorbell and home security cameras: weak evidence of crime deterrence, value for investigations, police requests for residents' footage, bias in neighbourhood-app posts, disputes between neighbours and regulating household surveillance
title: Every Doorstep a Lens
subtitle: Networked home cameras promise safer streets, but they are quietly changing who watches whom in residential neighbourhoods

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Not long ago, a camera trained on a public street was almost always the property of a government or a large business. Today, in many suburbs, the most extensive surveillance network belongs to no one in particular. Video doorbells and inexpensive security cameras, connected to the internet and often linked to smartphone applications that let owners share clips with neighbours, have spread with remarkable speed. A single residential road may now be covered from a dozen angles, with footage stored for weeks on remote servers. This network was never planned, debated or approved by anyone; it has simply accumulated, one purchase at a time, and that is precisely what makes it so difficult to govern.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Manufacturers market the devices chiefly as tools for deterring burglary and the theft of parcels left on doorsteps. The evidence that they achieve this is surprisingly thin. Sigrid Ellingsæter, a criminologist at the University of Bergen, compared reported property crime in neighbourhoods with high and low densities of doorbell cameras over a five-year period and found no statistically meaningful difference. She suggests that offenders quickly learn to conceal their faces, and that recordings of hooded or masked figures are of little use to investigators. The devices, in her account, mainly change how safe residents feel rather than how safe they actually are. Ellingsæter's study is careful, though a single comparison of this kind can hardly settle the matter, since neighbourhoods that buy more cameras may differ from others in ways that her data could not capture.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others are more positive. Nattapong Kittichai, who studies policing at the Bangkok Institute of Urban Affairs, has examined cases in which officers requested footage from residents, and reports that private recordings were frequently decisive in identifying vehicles involved in hit-and-run collisions and in establishing timelines for more serious offences. For Kittichai, the value of the cameras lies less in prevention than in investigation after the event. He sees the voluntary sharing of footage as a modern version of the traditional witness statement, and argues that it allows communities to cooperate with the police on their own terms.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That phrase, 'on their own terms', is where much of the controversy lies. In several countries, technology companies have established programmes through which police can ask camera owners in a given area to hand over recordings, sometimes without a warrant. Residents who agree may not realise that they are also supplying images of passers-by, delivery workers and neighbours who have consented to nothing. Daniela Landázuri, a legal scholar at the Central University of Quito, argues that such arrangements allow the state to obtain, through private intermediaries, a degree of surveillance that it could never lawfully build for itself. The camera owner's consent, she points out, does not extend to the people who happen to walk past. Her argument deserves more attention than it has received, because it shows that the familiar distinction between public and private surveillance is rapidly breaking down.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further concern relates to who comes to be regarded as suspicious, and why. Clips shared on neighbourhood apps are typically accompanied by comments, and Aram Gasparyan, a sociologist at the Caucasus Research Centre, has analysed thousands of such posts. He found that people were flagged as suspicious far more often on the basis of their appearance than of anything they were doing, and that delivery drivers, teenagers and members of ethnic minorities were disproportionately singled out. Gasparyan argues that the apps do not merely record existing prejudices but amplify them, since each post invites further comments and encourages others to watch for the same people. There is a risk of overstating this point, since many posts are entirely mundane, concerning lost pets or parcels delivered to the wrong address. Still, the pattern he identifies is too consistent to be dismissed as the product of a few unpleasant individuals.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of relations between neighbours themselves. A camera that covers a front door may also capture a neighbour's garden, windows or driveway, and disputes of this kind have begun to reach the courts. In one widely reported case, a judge ruled that a homeowner had breached data protection law by recording the property next door, though such rulings remain rare and the law in most places is unclear. It is striking that the legal obligations devised for organisations, which require them to justify recording, to limit how long footage is kept and to tell people they are being filmed, have scarcely been applied to private households, even though households now operate cameras on a comparable scale.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that home cameras should be prohibited. For people who live alone or who have previously been victims of crime, they can offer a reassurance that is not easily dismissed. The more modest and more realistic goal is to bring them within the same principles that govern other forms of surveillance. Simple measures, such as default settings that blur areas beyond the owner's property, short automatic deletion periods, and a requirement that police requests be routed through courts rather than companies, would go a long way. The deeper lesson is that surveillance need not be imposed from above to be pervasive. It can be assembled from below, through millions of individually reasonable decisions, none of which was intended to create the network that results.

topic: parental monitoring software for teenagers: location tracking and message reading, parental knowledge as a product of trust, covert versus agreed monitoring, online risks, effects on attitudes to privacy and false reassurance
title: Watching Over or Watching Too Closely?
subtitle: Monitoring software lets parents follow their children's every move, but researchers disagree about whether it makes young people any safer

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Generations of parents have worried about where their teenage children were and whom they were with. What has changed is the means available to find out. Applications that display a child's location on a map in real time, report which websites have been visited and, in some cases, allow parents to read text messages are now widely sold, often advertised with images of anxious mothers and fathers sleeping soundly once the software has been installed. Surveys in several countries suggest that a substantial minority of parents of children aged eleven to sixteen use at least one such tool. Whether these products deliver what they promise is surprisingly hard to establish, and the question is complicated by the fact that their most important effects may be on family relationships rather than on safety.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Developmental psychologists have long held that adolescence is a period in which young people must gradually take responsibility for their own decisions. Older research on parenting found that teenagers whose parents knew a great deal about their activities tended to be less involved in risky behaviour, and for many years this was interpreted as evidence that close supervision works. The conclusion seemed intuitive, and it was widely repeated in advice offered to parents. However, Henrik Brodersen, a psychologist at Aarhus University, revisited these studies and concluded that parental knowledge came mainly not from tracking or questioning but from children's willingness to tell their parents what they were doing. Knowledge, in other words, was a product of trust rather than of surveillance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This distinction matters a great deal when it comes to monitoring software. If what protects teenagers is an open relationship in which they choose to confide in their parents, then covert tracking may actually undermine the very thing that keeps them safe. Brodersen's later studies found that adolescents who discovered they were being secretly monitored reported lower trust in their parents and were more likely to conceal information in other ways, for instance by borrowing a friend's phone or creating second accounts on social media. These findings are persuasive, though they concern secret monitoring specifically; arrangements that children know about and have agreed to may produce quite different results.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Sunita Bajracharya, who researches child online safety at the Kathmandu Institute of Social Research, takes a more sympathetic view of parents. She points out that the dangers young people face online, from contact with adults seeking to exploit them to exposure to material promoting self-harm, are real, and that children are often reluctant to report them precisely because they fear having their devices taken away. In her interviews with families, some parents described monitoring tools as the only way they had discovered that their child was at risk. Bajracharya argues that the debate is too often conducted as if all monitoring were the same, when a location-sharing arrangement agreed between parent and child differs fundamentally from the secret reading of private messages. She adds that many parents lack the technical knowledge to recognise warning signs without some form of assistance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Elena Lazarevska, a sociologist at the Skopje Centre for Family Studies, draws attention to a different issue: what children learn about privacy from being monitored. In her view, young people who grow up under constant observation may come to regard surveillance as a normal feature of close relationships, and may later accept similar behaviour from partners or employers without question. This is a speculative claim, as Lazarevska herself acknowledges, since the first generation raised with monitoring apps has only recently reached adulthood and long-term evidence does not yet exist. It is nevertheless a possibility that deserves to be taken seriously, because habits of mind formed in childhood are notoriously difficult to change later.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Monitoring tools are not only potentially harmful; they are also less effective than their marketing implies. Technically capable teenagers frequently find ways around them, and many products can be disabled by anyone prepared to search for instructions online. Location data, moreover, can provide false reassurance: knowing that a child's phone is at a friend's house reveals nothing about what is happening there, or indeed whether the child is with the phone at all. Parents who rely on such tools may therefore feel better informed while in fact knowing little more than they did before.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should parents do? The research points less towards prohibition than towards transparency and gradual withdrawal. Monitoring that is discussed openly, agreed in advance and reduced as a child grows older seems far less likely to damage trust than secret surveillance that continues indefinitely. Children who are invited to help set the rules that apply to them also tend to regard those rules as fairer, and are therefore more inclined to keep to them. Ultimately, no software can substitute for the slow work of building a relationship in which children actually want to tell their parents where they are going. Manufacturers, for their part, could help by designing products that make monitoring visible to the child by default, though at present there is little commercial incentive for them to do so.

topic: the 'black chambers' of early modern Europe: secret state offices that opened and copied letters, their techniques and efficiency, doubts about their usefulness, self-censorship by letter-writers, protests and the history of the idea of privacy
title: Reading Other People's Letters
subtitle: Early modern states built elaborate systems for intercepting the post; historians disagree about what these secret offices achieved and what they reveal about privacy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before the telegraph or the telephone, governments faced a problem familiar to modern intelligence agencies: the communications they most wanted to read were precisely the ones their authors most wanted to keep private. From the seventeenth century onwards, as postal networks expanded across Europe and letters came to be carried in large numbers by state-run services, several governments established secret offices whose task was to open, copy and reseal correspondence before sending it on its way. These 'black chambers', as they were later called, operated in great secrecy, often in rooms adjoining the main post office, so that letters could be diverted and returned without causing any delay that might arouse suspicion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The work demanded remarkable technical skill. Clerks learned to soften wax seals with heated blades, to forge the impressions left by signet rings, and to refold paper along its original creases. Where letters were written in cipher, specialists attempted to break the codes, and some offices employed mathematicians and linguists for this purpose. According to Klaus Wolfsteller, a historian of communications at the University of Leipzig, the most efficient offices could process several hundred letters in a few hours, returning them to the mail so quickly that the interruption was rarely detected. Wolfsteller regards these offices as early examples of bureaucratic rationalisation, with fixed procedures, specialised staff and meticulous record-keeping that anticipated the intelligence agencies of the twentieth century.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet the scale of the operation should not be confused with its effectiveness. Isobel Ruthven, who has studied the surviving copies of intercepted letters held in several archives, argues that the offices gathered far more material than anyone could sensibly use. Ministers received thick bundles of transcripts, much of them diplomatic gossip of little value, and there is scant evidence that interceptions changed major decisions. Ruthven suggests that the chambers persisted less because of what they revealed than because no ruler wished to be the first to give up an advantage that rivals were assumed to possess. This argument is plausible, though it may underestimate the value of intelligence that merely confirmed what governments already suspected; knowing that a suspicion is correct can be as useful as discovering something entirely new.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Correspondents, for their part, were rarely naive. Diplomats, merchants and scholars widely assumed that their letters might be read, and they adapted accordingly. Some wrote in cipher or entrusted sensitive material to private couriers; others resorted to deliberately bland language, or adopted codes based on references that only the recipient would understand, such as nicknames for public figures. Pilar Ferreirós, of the Galician Institute of Historical Studies, has argued that this habit of self-censorship shaped the very style of early modern letter-writing, and that historians who read such letters at face value risk mistaking caution for sincerity. Her warning is an important one, and its implications extend well beyond the history of espionage to any study that relies on private correspondence as evidence of what people really thought.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Interception also generated political controversy whenever it was exposed. In several countries, revelations that the post had been opened prompted protests in which critics insisted that the secrecy of correspondence was a fundamental right. Such protests are sometimes cited as evidence that a modern concept of privacy existed long before the word was widely used in that sense. Edgars Ozoliņš, a legal historian at the Riga School of Law, rejects this interpretation. In his view, the complaints concerned mainly the honour of the writer and the confidentiality of commercial information, not an individual's right to a protected personal sphere, and to read them as early declarations of privacy rights is anachronistic.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ozoliņš is right to warn against projecting present concerns onto the past, but he arguably draws the line too sharply. Whatever vocabulary they used, those who protested were objecting to the idea that the state might read their thoughts without their knowledge, and that objection is not far removed from what privacy means today. Concepts often exist in practice long before they acquire a settled name.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Several states eventually enshrined the secrecy of letters in law, and in the nineteenth century some publicly announced the closure of their secret offices. Abolition, however, was not always what it seemed. In more than one case, interception simply moved to other departments and continued with less oversight than before, while official declarations that the post was inviolable coexisted with quiet exceptions for matters of state security.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The history of the black chambers offers a corrective to the common belief that mass surveillance is a product of the digital age. The tools were different, but many of the dilemmas are recognisably the same: the temptation to collect more than can be analysed, the adaptation of those who suspect they are being watched, and the gap between legal protections and actual practice. It would be a mistake, though, to push the comparison too far. The labour of opening each letter by hand placed natural limits on what even the most determined government could achieve, and such limits scarcely exist when communications can be copied automatically and stored indefinitely.

topic: smartphone contact-tracing apps during an epidemic: centralised versus decentralised designs, public trust and mission creep, uneven effectiveness dependent on testing and support, and whether technical fixes diverted resources
title: Tracing Without Tracking
subtitle: Smartphone apps that alerted people exposed to infection promised to control an epidemic without sacrificing privacy; the results were more mixed than either supporters or critics predicted

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Contact tracing, which involves identifying the people with whom an infected person has been in close contact and advising them to isolate, is one of the oldest tools of public health. Traditionally it has been carried out by trained staff who interview patients and telephone their contacts, a process that is effective but slow and labour-intensive. When a fast-spreading respiratory virus began circulating internationally, many governments turned to smartphones in the hope of doing the same work automatically. Phones would exchange short-range radio signals with other nearby phones, and if a user later tested positive, everyone whose device had been close enough for long enough could be alerted within minutes rather than days.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The design of these apps quickly became the subject of intense dispute. In a centralised system, the records of which phones had been near each other were uploaded to a server run by health authorities, who could then analyse the data and contact people directly. In a decentralised system, the matching took place on each user's own phone: devices broadcast anonymous identifiers that changed every few minutes, and the server merely distributed the identifiers of those who had tested positive, so that each phone could check privately whether it had encountered any of them. Under the decentralised model, the authorities never learned who had met whom. Each approach had passionate advocates among scientists, engineers and civil liberties groups, and the arguments were conducted with unusual urgency, since every week of delay in launching an app was expected to mean thousands of additional infections.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Hiroko Matsubayashi, an epidemiologist at the Osaka Centre for Infectious Disease Modelling, was among those who initially favoured centralised designs. She argued that access to the network of contacts would allow health officials to identify clusters of cases, understand how the virus was spreading and refine the criteria for sending alerts. Without such data, she warned, the apps would be operating blind. Matsubayashi's argument had considerable scientific merit, but it underestimated the importance of public trust. An app of this kind depends on voluntary installation by millions of people, and any design that appeared to hand the state a map of citizens' social lives was likely to deter precisely the people whose participation was needed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That concern was central to the work of Trond Steinsland, a computer scientist at the Nordic Institute for Secure Computing who helped to develop one of the decentralised protocols. Steinsland argued that any system storing contact data centrally would inevitably attract demands for its use beyond public health, by police investigators, for instance, or immigration officials. Such fears were not entirely hypothetical: in at least one country, information gathered for disease control was later obtained by detectives working on a criminal case, prompting a public outcry. In the event, most countries adopted decentralised designs, partly because the companies that controlled the major smartphone operating systems would support only that approach.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How much did the apps actually achieve? Efua Opoku-Mensah, a public health researcher at the Accra School of Population Health, has reviewed evaluations from more than a dozen countries and concludes that the results varied enormously. Where large proportions of the population installed the app and acted on its alerts, the technology appears to have prevented a meaningful number of infections. Elsewhere, low uptake, delays in testing and the reluctance of alerted users to isolate, particularly those who could not afford to miss work, meant that the effect was negligible. Opoku-Mensah stresses that the apps were only ever as effective as the testing and support systems around them. This is surely the central lesson of the whole experience, and one that the early debate over app design, absorbed as it was in technical questions of architecture, largely overlooked.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Luca Ventimiglia, a sociologist at the Turin Institute for Technology and Society, takes a more critical view of the episode. He argues that the enthusiasm for apps reflected a broader tendency to seek technical solutions to what are essentially social problems, and that the resources devoted to them might have been better spent on employing human contact tracers and providing financial support for people asked to stay at home. Ventimiglia's criticism has force, though it relies partly on hindsight. At the time, nobody could be certain how the epidemic would develop, and trying several approaches at once was a reasonable response to that uncertainty. It is also worth remembering that in several places human tracers and apps were used side by side, with the apps reaching contacts, such as strangers on public transport, whom no interview could ever have identified.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most encouraging aspect of the experience is that it demonstrated that privacy and public health need not be opposed. The decentralised apps showed that a useful service could be delivered without the authorities collecting sensitive data about individuals, something many experts had doubted was possible. Engineers and health officials who had begun the debate as opponents ended it, in many cases, as collaborators. Whether that lesson will survive the next emergency is another matter. Crises tend to weaken resistance to surveillance, and measures adopted in haste have a habit of outlasting the circumstances that were used to justify them.

topic: the right to be forgotten and search-engine delisting: how removal requests work, who makes them and which succeed, delegation of decisions to private companies, spent convictions and rehabilitation, unintended consequences and geographical scope
title: The Right to Fade Away
subtitle: Laws that let people have old information about them removed from search results set personal privacy against the public's right to know

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before the internet, embarrassing information about ordinary people tended to fade naturally. A newspaper report of a minor court case or a business failure would be read, discussed and then filed away in archives that few people ever consulted. Search engines changed this. An article published decades ago can now appear at the top of the results whenever someone types a person's name, presenting a youthful mistake or a long-settled debt as if it were current news. It was in response to this situation that courts and legislators in a number of jurisdictions began to recognise what has come to be called the right to be forgotten: a right, under certain conditions, to have links to outdated or irrelevant personal information removed from search results.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The right is considerably narrower than its name suggests. In most systems where it applies, the original article is not deleted; it remains on the publisher's website and can still be found by searching the site directly or by using terms other than the person's name. What disappears is only the link that appears when the individual's name is entered into a search engine. Requests are submitted first to the search company itself, which must weigh the person's privacy against the public interest in access to the information. Only if the request is refused can the individual appeal to a data protection authority or a court.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The volume of requests has been considerable. Within the first five years of the right being established in Europe, the largest search company reported receiving requests concerning more than three million web addresses, of which it agreed to delist slightly under half. Ruslan Bekmukhamedov, an information lawyer at the Almaty Institute of Digital Law, analysed a sample of several thousand decisions and found that the great majority of requests came from private individuals rather than from politicians or celebrities, and that the most common category concerned professional information, such as old reports of business disputes. Requests relating to serious crimes were rarely granted, he found, whereas those concerning minor offences committed many years earlier usually were.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics, particularly in the news media, regard the arrangement with deep suspicion. Their chief objection is that decisions about what the public may easily find have effectively been delegated to private companies, which possess neither the expertise nor the democratic legitimacy to make them, and which may be tempted to grant requests simply to avoid the cost of disputes. Astrid Prebensen, a media scholar at the Oslo School of Journalism, has documented cases in which links to accurate reports about professionals, including a doctor disciplined for negligence, were removed. She argues that patients choosing a doctor have a legitimate interest in such information, and that a professional's record should not cease to matter merely because time has passed. Such cases are troubling, although Prebensen's sample was drawn largely from complaints submitted by publishers and is therefore likely to overrepresent the most controversial decisions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the right respond that the alternative, a world in which every past mistake remains permanently attached to a person's name, has serious costs of its own. Emir Hadžiomerović, a sociologist at the Sarajevo Centre for Social Research, has interviewed people whose old convictions or debts continued to appear in search results years after they had been resolved. Many reported difficulties in finding employment or housing, and some said they had abandoned attempts to rebuild their lives. Hadžiomerović points out that legal systems have long recognised that people can change, through rules that allow minor convictions to be treated as spent after a set period, and he argues that search engines had quietly undermined those rules without anyone deciding that they should.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: His point about spent convictions is perhaps the strongest argument for the right, because it shows that forgetting is not a novel invention but a principle that societies had already accepted long before the internet existed. Yet the right has also generated problems that its designers did not foresee. Search engines usually notify publishers when a link to one of their articles has been removed, and some newspapers have responded by publishing lists of delisted articles, thereby drawing renewed attention to the very stories that individuals had wanted to fade. There are also disputes about geography: a link removed from search results in one country may still appear when the same search is made from elsewhere, and courts have disagreed about whether delisting ought to apply worldwide.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Several countries outside Europe have adopted versions of the right, while others, particularly those with strong constitutional protections for free expression, have rejected it outright. The divergence reflects genuine differences in how societies balance competing values, and no single model is likely to be adopted everywhere. Some legal scholars have proposed that delisting should become automatic for certain categories of information after a fixed number of years, which would relieve companies of the burden of case-by-case judgement. What seems clear is that the underlying problem, the way search technology collapses the distinction between past and present, will not disappear. If anything, it will intensify as more archives are digitised, and the debate would benefit from less talk of censorship on one side and of absolute privacy on the other.

topic: end-to-end encrypted messaging and law enforcement: demands for exceptional access by warrant, cryptographers' objections that any access mechanism weakens security, the political nature of the risk judgement, the abundance of other digital evidence, and on-device scanning
title: Locked Out
subtitle: Should the police be able to read encrypted messages? A long-running dispute between security agencies and cryptographers shows little sign of being resolved

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Encryption, the mathematical scrambling of information so that only those holding the correct key can read it, was once largely the preserve of governments and armed forces. Today it is built into the messaging applications used by billions of people. In many of these services, messages are encrypted on the sender's device and decrypted only on the recipient's, so that even the company operating the service cannot read them. For users, this offers protection against criminals, hostile governments and the company itself. For police and intelligence agencies, however, it presents what some officials describe as a growing blind spot: communications that could once be intercepted with a warrant are now, in practice, unreadable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Law enforcement agencies have therefore argued for some form of 'exceptional access', a mechanism allowing authorised officials to read specific messages when a court permits it. Ingrid Grimsrud, a former prosecutor who now researches criminal justice policy at the Stavanger Institute for Security Studies, maintains that the inability to read messages has hampered investigations into child exploitation, terrorism and organised crime. She emphasises that agencies are not seeking unrestricted access, only the ability to do what they have long done with telephone calls and letters: examine the communications of a particular suspect when a judge is satisfied that there is good reason to do so. In her view, a space in which no warrant can ever be executed is incompatible with the rule of law.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cryptographers have been almost unanimous in their opposition. Their central argument, set out forcefully by Kerem Aksoyoğlu of the Ankara Centre for Applied Cryptography, is that there is no way to build a door that only the right people can open. Any mechanism that allows officials to decrypt messages must involve keys or deliberate weaknesses that could also be discovered, stolen or abused by others, whether criminal gangs or foreign intelligence services. Aksoyoğlu points to cases in which hacking tools developed for government use later leaked and were exploited in large-scale attacks on hospitals and businesses. Weakening encryption in order to catch a minority of offenders would, he argues, expose the far larger number of ordinary users, companies and public institutions that depend on it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The technical argument is strong, and officials have too often dismissed it as mere obstruction. It is not simply that experts have failed to try hard enough: every detailed proposal published so far has, on close examination, introduced serious vulnerabilities. At the same time, the cryptographers' case is sometimes presented as if it settled the matter, when in fact it leaves an important question open. Even if exceptional access cannot be made perfectly safe, a society might reasonably decide that a certain level of risk is worth accepting in exchange for the ability to investigate serious crimes. That is a political judgement rather than a mathematical one, and it ought to be made openly by elected representatives rather than left to engineers or security agencies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers question whether the problem is as severe as officials claim. Paweł Lisowiec, a criminologist at the Silesian Institute for Crime Research, argues that the shift to encrypted messaging has coincided with an enormous expansion in other kinds of data available to investigators: location records, metadata showing who contacted whom and when, cloud backups, and information stored on seized devices. Far from being left in the dark, he suggests, police now operate in what may be the richest environment for evidence in history. Lisowiec acknowledges that the content of encrypted messages is sometimes crucial, but argues that agencies have provided little systematic evidence of how often investigations have actually failed for this reason.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further proposal has attracted particular controversy: scanning messages on users' own devices before they are encrypted, in order to detect known illegal images. Supporters argue that this leaves encryption itself untouched. Hanna Kinnunen, who studies technology policy at the Helsinki Centre for Digital Rights, rejects this reasoning. A system capable of checking messages against a list of prohibited images, she observes, could be extended to search for other content, such as political material, simply by changing the list, and users would have no reliable way of knowing that this had happened. Her concern is far from merely theoretical, since the history of surveillance is full of systems that expanded well beyond their original purpose.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has frequently been framed as a choice between privacy and security, but this framing is misleading, because encryption is itself a security technology. It protects banking transactions, medical records and, not least, the communications of governments themselves. The real choice is between different kinds of security, and between different groups whose safety is at stake. A more productive approach might concentrate on improving investigators' ability to use the large quantities of data already available to them, while continuing to examine, without prejudging the outcome, whether any narrowly targeted form of access could meet acceptable standards of safety.

topic: orbital debris removal: the runaway collision threshold, capture technologies, orbital use fees versus the liability regime, and jurisdiction over defunct satellites
title: Clearing the Orbital Commons
subtitle: Everyone agrees that the space around the earth has become dangerously cluttered; far fewer agree on who should pay to tidy it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the first artificial satellite was launched in 1957, the region of space immediately surrounding the earth has gradually filled with the remnants of human activity. Spent rocket stages, defunct satellites, fragments from explosions and collisions, and even flecks of paint now circle the planet at speeds of several kilometres per second. Tracking networks follow tens of thousands of objects larger than a cricket ball, but models suggest that the number of smaller pieces, each capable of disabling a spacecraft, runs into the millions. For decades this accumulation was treated as a minor nuisance, a cost of doing business in orbit. That complacency is no longer tenable, and the question that now preoccupies engineers, lawyers and diplomats alike is not whether the problem should be addressed but who should bear the expense of doing so.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The urgency stems from a mechanism first described in theoretical terms several decades ago. Once the density of objects in a given orbital band passes a critical threshold, collisions generate fragments faster than the thin upper atmosphere can drag them down, and each new collision raises the probability of the next. Dr Aleksandra Drabczyk, who models debris populations at the Baltic Institute for Orbital Studies, believes that certain altitudes between 750 and 1,000 kilometres may already have crossed this threshold. Even if every launch were halted tomorrow, she argues, the number of fragments in these bands would continue to grow for at least a century. Her conclusion is that preventing new debris, although essential, is no longer sufficient; some of the largest existing objects must be physically removed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Removal, however, is formidably difficult. A defunct satellite is not a cooperative target: it may be tumbling, it has no handles or docking ports designed for capture, and its fuel tanks may still contain propellant. Proposed techniques range from robotic arms and nets to harpoons and magnetic plates fitted to future satellites in anticipation of their eventual retrieval. Several demonstration missions have succeeded in capturing purpose-built targets released for the occasion, but none has yet removed a large, uncooperative object of the kind Drabczyk considers most dangerous. Each mission, moreover, is costly, with estimates for removing a single large rocket body running to tens of millions of dollars.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It is at this point that the economic dimension becomes decisive. The economist Joseph Masamba, of the Centre for Space Governance in Nairobi, describes low earth orbit as a classic commons: every operator benefits from a clean environment, but no individual operator has an incentive to pay for cleaning it, since the benefits would be shared by competitors who contributed nothing. Masamba proposes an orbital use fee, an annual charge levied on each satellite in proportion to the collision risk it imposes on others. Such a fee, he contends, would both fund removal missions and encourage operators to design satellites that leave orbit promptly at the end of their working lives. The logic of this proposal is hard to fault, although it rests on an assumption that every launching state would agree to the same charges, which seems optimistic.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A rather different view is taken by the legal scholar Camille Henaff, who points out that existing international law already assigns liability for damage caused by space objects to the state that launched them. In her view, the priority is not to invent new taxes but to make the existing liability regime function, by clarifying how fault should be established when a collision involves fragments whose origin is uncertain. Henaff also draws attention to a less obvious obstacle: under current law, a state retains jurisdiction over its space objects indefinitely, even when they have become useless. A commercial company wishing to remove a defunct satellite would therefore need the permission of the state that registered it, and some governments are reluctant to allow foreign spacecraft to approach hardware that may once have had military functions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This last point deserves more attention than it usually receives. Discussions of debris tend to concentrate on technology and money, as if the only barriers to a cleaner orbit were engineering ingenuity and adequate funding. Yet the technology that allows one spacecraft to grapple with another could equally be used to disable a rival's satellite, and this dual-use character makes many governments wary. Without agreements that build confidence between the major spacefaring nations, removal missions are likely to remain confined to each country's own hardware, which would leave much of the most hazardous material untouched.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that progress is impossible. International guidelines now recommend that satellites in low orbit be removed within a set period after the end of their missions, and some national regulators have shortened that period considerably. Compliance has improved, particularly among large commercial operators whose business depends on a usable orbital environment. Still, guidelines are voluntary, and enforcement varies widely between countries. A durable solution will probably require all three of the approaches described here: a reliable means of removal, a fair method of paying for it, and a legal framework that allows it to happen. The orbital environment took six decades to degrade; repairing it is likely to demand at least as long, and a degree of international cooperation that has so far proved elusive.
