topic: ownership of space resources: the non-appropriation principle, the high-seas fishing analogy, profit-sharing proposals and safety zones around lunar mining sites
title: Claims Without Borders
subtitle: A treaty written before anyone could mine the Moon is now being asked to decide who may keep what is taken from it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The treaty that has governed activity in space since 1967 contains a deceptively simple provision: outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means. For half a century this principle provoked little controversy, largely because nobody possessed the means to extract anything of value from another world. That is beginning to change. Water ice detected in permanently shadowed craters near the lunar poles could, in principle, be split into hydrogen and oxygen to make rocket propellant, and several near-earth asteroids are believed to contain metals in concentrations far higher than those found in terrestrial ores. The prospect of actually harvesting these materials has turned an abstract clause into a matter of practical urgency.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central question is whether a ban on appropriating territory also prohibits the ownership of resources removed from it. Several countries have recently passed domestic laws stating that companies which extract materials in space are entitled to own and sell them. Their position, articulated most forcefully by the legal theorist Dr Per Lorentzon of the Nordic Centre for Commercial Space Law, draws an analogy with the high seas. No nation owns the open ocean, Lorentzon observes, yet fishing fleets have always been permitted to keep the fish they catch. By the same reasoning, extracting ice from a lunar crater no more amounts to claiming the Moon than landing a tuna amounts to claiming the Pacific.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The analogy is elegant, but it is less secure than its advocates suppose. Fish are a renewable resource distributed across vast areas, whereas the ice deposits that matter most are concentrated in a small number of craters, some only a few kilometres across. Whoever operates first in such a crater may, in practice, exclude everyone else, not by asserting sovereignty but simply by being there. Ivana Strakova, an international lawyer at the Central European Institute of Air and Space Law, argues that this is precisely the kind of de facto appropriation that the 1967 treaty was intended to prevent. In her view, the domestic laws passed so far amount to unilateral reinterpretations of a multilateral agreement, and they set a precedent that less scrupulous actors may later exploit.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Strakova's critique has gained support from a group of states that were not yet capable of space activity when the treaty was drafted. Their concern, expressed through a working group coordinated by the diplomat Folake Odukoya, is that a first-come, first-served regime would allow a handful of technologically advanced nations to lock up the most valuable sites for generations. Odukoya's group has proposed that a share of any profits from space mining should be paid into an international fund, an idea modelled on arrangements already in place for minerals on the deep seabed. Opponents reply that the seabed regime has deterred investment so effectively that commercial mining there has scarcely begun, and that a similar system would stifle space enterprise before it could get started.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Both sides, it seems to me, overstate their case. The seabed comparison is not as damning as critics suggest, since the slow pace of ocean mining owes as much to low metal prices and environmental objections as to the sharing of revenues. Equally, the fear that a few nations will monopolise space resources sits uneasily with the reality that most proposed mining ventures remain unfunded and technically unproven. What both arguments neglect is the question of coordination, which is likely to become pressing long before profits do.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This is the focus of work by the engineer Dr Vikram Ramanathapura, who has studied how multiple missions might operate within a single lunar crater. His simulations show that the exhaust from a landing spacecraft can scatter dust and fine particles for several kilometres, contaminating equipment and potentially degrading the ice itself. Ramanathapura therefore argues for safety zones around active operations, inside which other missions would need to give notice before approaching. Such zones are already provided for in some bilateral agreements on lunar exploration. Critics, Strakova among them, worry that safety zones could become a form of territorial claim by another name, particularly if they are drawn generously and maintained indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Her worry is reasonable, but it should not be allowed to obstruct an idea that is fundamentally sensible. The difference between a temporary zone justified by physical risk and a permanent claim justified by priority is real, and it can be written into rules: zones could be limited in size, tied to specific activities and required to lapse when those activities end. What matters is that such rules be agreed multilaterally rather than accumulated through a patchwork of national laws and bilateral deals, each reflecting the interests of whoever happened to negotiate it.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The history of other shared resources, from ocean fisheries to radio frequencies, suggests that rules are easiest to establish before valuable activity begins and hardest to change once it has. Those already profiting from an arrangement rarely volunteer to give up their advantages. If that pattern holds, the next decade may matter more for the governance of space resources than the century that follows, and the opportunity to set fair terms will not remain open for long.

topic: planetary protection: sterilising spacecraft, the debate over relaxing Mars rules versus tightening rules for icy moons, private missions and the problem of crewed landings
title: Keeping Other Worlds Clean
subtitle: As missions to Mars and the icy moons multiply, the rules designed to stop earthly microbes hitching a ride are being questioned from two directions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every spacecraft that leaves the earth carries passengers that no one intended to send. Despite the elaborate cleaning procedures used in assembly facilities, the surfaces of landers and rovers harbour hardy bacterial spores, some of which can survive vacuum, extreme cold and intense ultraviolet radiation for long periods. Since the earliest days of space exploration, scientists have worried that such stowaways might contaminate other worlds, either by establishing themselves in a suitable niche or simply by leaving behind organic traces that future instruments could mistake for evidence of native life. The body of rules intended to prevent this, known collectively as planetary protection, has been in place for more than half a century. It is, in my view, one of the quieter successes of international cooperation in space, but it was designed for an era of occasional government missions, and that era is ending.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The system works by sorting destinations into categories according to how likely they are to harbour life and how interesting they are for the study of its origins. A flyby of a barren moon attracts almost no requirements, whereas a lander bound for a region of Mars where liquid water may occasionally appear must meet stringent limits on the number of spores it carries, often achieved by baking components at high temperatures for many hours. Dr Ilse Brekkenes, a microbiologist at the Tromsø Centre for Astrobiology, has spent much of her career counting organisms in spacecraft clean rooms. She reports that the rooms themselves select for unusually resilient species: by eliminating ordinary microbes, cleaning regimes leave behind those best equipped to endure the journey. 'We are, in effect, breeding the very travellers we are trying to exclude,' she remarks, although she stresses that the absolute numbers remain very small.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics of the current rules come from two opposite directions. One camp, represented most forcefully by the astrobiologist Tudor Costache of the Carpathian Institute for Space Science, argues that the requirements for Mars are now too restrictive. Decades of exploration, he points out, have revealed a planet whose surface is bathed in radiation and laced with chemicals that destroy organic molecules. In his view, the probability that an earthly microbe could grow there is so remote that the expense of sterilising every lander is no longer justified, and the money would be better spent on additional missions. Costache also notes that meteorites have carried material between the earth and Mars for billions of years, so that the two planets may never have been biologically isolated in the first place.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This argument has some force, but it overlooks a crucial distinction. The concern is not only that microbes might flourish but that their remains might confuse the search for life. An instrument capable of detecting traces of ancient Martian biology is, by the same token, capable of detecting contamination from the earth, and a single false positive could undermine confidence in an entire programme of research. The cost of thorough cleaning is real, yet it is modest compared with the cost of an ambiguous result that no subsequent mission could fully resolve.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The second camp worries that the rules are not strict enough, particularly for the ice-covered moons of the outer solar system. Beneath the frozen crusts of several of these bodies lie oceans of liquid water that may have persisted for billions of years. Rana Khaddour, who advises on space policy at the Levant Science Policy Forum, argues that these oceans represent the most promising places to look for an independent origin of life, and that a single careless mission could compromise them permanently. Unlike the Martian surface, she observes, a subsurface ocean offers no radiation to sterilise intruders, so any organism that reached it might survive indefinitely.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Underlying both debates is an institutional weakness. The planetary protection guidelines are drawn up by a scientific committee rather than by governments, and they become binding only when national agencies choose to adopt them. For most of the space age this arrangement caused few problems, because almost all missions beyond earth orbit were conducted by a handful of state agencies with a shared culture of compliance. The arrival of private companies with ambitions to land on the Moon and Mars has changed the picture. Daniel Lethbridge, a legal scholar at the Southern Cross School of Law, points out that international treaty law makes states responsible for the activities of their citizens and companies in space, but leaves it to each state to decide how that responsibility is exercised. Some countries have written planetary protection into their licensing procedures; others have no procedure at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most difficult question concerns human missions. Astronauts cannot be baked, and every crewed landing will inevitably release vast numbers of microbes into its surroundings. Some planners argue that this makes planetary protection for Mars a temporary concern, to be relaxed once people arrive. I would draw the opposite conclusion. If contamination is unavoidable once humans land, then the period before that moment is precisely when the most careful robotic searches for life must be completed. Far from being made obsolete by human exploration, planetary protection is what gives the robotic missions that precede it their scientific value.

topic: space procurement models: cost-plus contracts versus fixed-price commercial services, hidden public subsidies, one-off science missions and the implicit duty to rescue key suppliers
title: Who Carries the Risk?
subtitle: Space agencies are moving away from the contracts that built the first rockets, but whether the new model saves money or merely relocates the risk is fiercely disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, governments that wanted to reach space paid contractors to build the necessary machinery under arrangements in which the state owned the design and covered whatever the work turned out to cost. Under these 'cost-plus' contracts, the agency reimbursed every legitimate expense and added a fee, typically a percentage of the total, as the contractor's profit. The arrangement made sense when no one knew how to build a rocket capable of carrying people, and when national prestige depended on success at almost any price. It also produced, critics argue, a culture in which overruns were routine and the incentive to economise was weak, since a contractor whose costs rose saw its fee rise with them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the past two decades, a number of agencies have experimented with a different model. Instead of specifying a design and paying for its construction, the agency defines a service, such as delivering cargo to an orbiting station, and invites companies to provide it at a fixed price. The company owns the vehicle, bears the cost of any overruns, and is free to sell the same service to other customers. Advocates point to striking reductions in the price of reaching orbit as evidence that the approach works. The economist Margarethe Kaltenbrunner, of the Graz Institute for Public Finance, estimates that a cargo service purchased in this way cost the commissioning agency roughly a third of what a traditionally procured equivalent would have required. Her analysis has been widely cited, and with reason: it is one of the few attempts to compare the two models using consistent accounting.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet the comparison is less straightforward than such figures imply. Dr Nalin Abeykoon, who studies industrial policy at the Colombo School of Economics, observes that the companies which succeeded under fixed-price arrangements had often benefited from decades of publicly funded research, as well as from engineers trained in government programmes. In his view, the savings attributed to the commercial model partly reflect investments made long before under the old one. A fair accounting, he argues, would treat the two systems not as rivals but as successive stages, the second building on knowledge that only the first could have produced.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others question whether fixed-price contracts suit every kind of mission. Anna Grabarczyk, a former programme manager now at the Warsaw Centre for Technology Policy, distinguishes between services for which a commercial market exists and one-off scientific projects for which it does not. A company delivering cargo can spread its development costs across many customers; a company building a unique probe to an outer planet has only one buyer. In the latter case, Grabarczyk maintains, a fixed price simply encourages bidders to underestimate costs in order to win the contract, after which they either demand renegotiation or cut corners. She has documented several instances in which firms bidding for one-off projects withdrew or sought additional funds once technical difficulties emerged.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This seems to me the most important qualification in the entire debate. The success of the service model has encouraged some policymakers to treat it as a universal remedy, but its advantages depend on conditions, namely competition and multiple customers, that are absent for much of what space agencies actually do. To apply it indiscriminately would be to repeat, in reverse, the error of the earlier era, when a single contracting method was used regardless of the task.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further concern relates to who ultimately bears the risk. The legal scholar Rohit Kanjilal, of the Calcutta Institute of Contract Law, points out that fixed-price contracts transfer financial risk to the contractor only on paper. If a company that provides an essential service, such as the sole means of transporting crew to a station, faces bankruptcy, the government that relies on it can hardly allow it to fail. Kanjilal argues that agencies have, in effect, acquired an implicit obligation to rescue their key suppliers, an obligation that appears in no budget and is therefore never debated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Not all commentators share this pessimism. Henrik Ivarsson, who advises the Nordic Space Council on procurement, contends that the danger of dependence can be managed by deliberately funding at least two competing providers for every essential service. Redundancy is expensive, he concedes, but it preserves the agency's bargaining power and ensures that no single failure can halt a programme. The proposal is sensible, although it sits awkwardly with the claim that the commercial model is cheaper: paying two companies to maintain capabilities that only one is needed to provide erodes precisely the savings that justified the change.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this debate is not a verdict in favour of either system but a case for choosing contract types with far greater care. The old model was not as wasteful as its critics suggest, and the new one is not as cheap as its champions claim. Agencies that match the form of contract to the nature of the task, and that are honest about the hidden obligations each form creates, are likely to spend public money more wisely than those that adopt either model as an article of faith.

topic: satellite mega-constellations and astronomy: satellite streaks on wide-field images, radio interference, voluntary dimming by operators and the absence of authority over night-sky brightness
title: Streaks Across the Sky
subtitle: Vast fleets of communications satellites promise internet access everywhere; astronomers fear they will cost humanity its clearest view of the universe

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a clear night in the high desert, an astronomer reviewing the previous evening's images may now find them crossed by a series of bright parallel lines, each the trail of a satellite catching sunlight as it passes overhead. A decade ago such streaks were occasional curiosities. Today, as private companies place thousands of small communications satellites into low orbit, with plans for tens of thousands more, they have become a routine feature of observations from some of the world's most important telescopes. The companies argue that their constellations will bring fast internet to remote regions that cables will never reach, and that benefit is not trivial. But the night sky has never before been altered on this scale by the decisions of a few commercial firms, and it is reasonable to ask whether anyone gave permission.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the effect depends heavily on the type of observation. Dr Eleni Mavrokordatou, who leads a survey programme at the Aegean Observatory, explains that wide-field telescopes, designed to photograph large areas of sky repeatedly in search of faint or fleeting objects, are especially vulnerable. Because each exposure covers a broad patch of sky and lasts many seconds, the chance that a satellite will cross it is high, particularly in the hours after dusk and before dawn, when satellites are illuminated by the sun while the ground below is dark. Her team estimates that, if current deployment plans are fulfilled, a substantial share of twilight images from such instruments will contain at least one streak. Software can remove some trails, she notes, but it cannot recover information about objects hidden beneath them, and brighter trails can saturate detectors entirely.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Optical astronomy is not the only discipline affected. Radio astronomers, who detect extremely weak signals from distant galaxies, worry that transmissions from satellites will leak into frequency bands traditionally kept quiet for scientific use. Professor Lars Ekholm of the Uppsala Radio Observatory points out that radio telescopes are often built in remote valleys precisely to escape terrestrial interference; a satellite overhead, however, cannot be escaped by geography. Ekholm has called for binding limits on unintended emissions, arguing that voluntary measures have historically been ignored once commercial pressures mount. He adds that, unlike a streak across a photograph, radio interference is not always obvious: a contaminated signal can resemble a genuine astronomical source, so the danger lies as much in false discoveries as in lost data.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The companies, for their part, have responded more constructively than many expected. Some have tested darker coatings and sunshades designed to reduce the amount of light their satellites reflect, and they have shared orbital data so that observatories can schedule exposures to avoid known passes. Somchai Tiwaripong, an engineer who has acted as a liaison between operators and the astronomical community, believes that cooperation of this kind can resolve most of the conflict. In his experience, operators are willing to adjust designs when astronomers explain precisely what they need, and regulation, which is slow to draft and difficult to enforce across borders, would add little. This optimism is understandable, but it rests on the goodwill of a small number of firms whose priorities might change. A dimming measure that is adopted voluntarily can just as easily be abandoned when it proves costly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The deeper difficulty is that no institution currently has clear authority over the appearance of the night sky. Launch licences are granted by national regulators, who consider safety, radio frequencies and, increasingly, debris; brightness is rarely among their criteria. The environmental lawyer Ximena Bustamante-Ruelas, based at the Andean Centre for Environmental Law, has argued that the dark sky should be treated as a shared environmental resource, comparable to clean air, so that its degradation would trigger the kind of impact assessment required for a new mine or motorway. Her proposal has attracted support among astronomers but faces an obvious objection: assessments of this sort are designed for activities on a state's own territory, while satellites pass over every country without asking.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is worth noting that the people most affected are not only professional scientists. Many cultures have long traditions of reading the stars for navigation, timekeeping and storytelling, and amateur observers vastly outnumber professionals. Some indigenous communities regard particular star patterns as part of their cultural inheritance, and what they stand to lose cannot be measured in data points. Yet the debate has been conducted almost entirely between operators, regulators and large observatories, with little opportunity for these wider groups to be heard. That exclusion is, in my judgement, a mistake, because a resource that belongs to everyone ought not to be governed solely by those with the technical expertise to measure it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that constellations should be prohibited; the benefits of connectivity are real, and astronomy has adapted to earlier intrusions, from city lighting to aircraft. What it does mean is that the costs should be acknowledged and shared fairly. Requiring operators to meet brightness standards as a condition of their licences would hardly be an excessive demand, and it would convert today's welcome but fragile cooperation into something more durable. Operators that already dim their satellites would face little additional expense, while those that do not would lose an advantage they were never entitled to.

topic: planetary defence governance: the incomplete census of medium-sized asteroids, deciding under uncertain impact probabilities, liability for shifting the impact point and the nuclear deflection dilemma
title: The Politics of the Nudge
subtitle: Humanity can now, in principle, push a dangerous asteroid off course; deciding who should give the order is proving a far harder problem

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the hazards that confront human civilisation, the impact of a large asteroid is perhaps unique in being both catastrophic and, in principle, preventable. Unlike earthquakes or volcanic eruptions, an approaching asteroid can be detected years or even decades before it arrives, and its trajectory calculated with growing precision. A recent demonstration, in which a spacecraft deliberately struck a small asteroid and measurably altered its orbit, has shown that the basic technique of deflection by collision works. Planetary defence, once the preserve of speculative fiction, has therefore become a matter of practical policy. Yet the technical success has outpaced the institutional arrangements, and it is these, rather than the engineering, that now represent the weakest link.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty is detection. Most asteroids large enough to destroy a continent have already been found, but the census of medium-sized objects, those capable of devastating a city or a region, remains far from complete. Dr Parisa Saberi, who directs a survey programme at the Zagros Observatory, estimates that fewer than half of these objects have been catalogued, largely because they are dark and faint and many approach from the direction of the sun, where ground-based telescopes cannot look. She argues that a dedicated space telescope observing in infrared light, in which asteroids glow by virtue of their warmth, would find most of the remainder within a decade. Such an instrument would cost a fraction of what a single deflection mission would require, and it seems to me the most cost-effective investment in planetary defence that governments could currently make.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Detection, however, raises a second problem: uncertainty. When an asteroid is first discovered, its orbit is known only approximately, and the probability that it will strike the earth may be calculated at one in several thousand. As further observations accumulate, that figure typically falls to zero, but occasionally it rises. The astronomer Darius Jankauskas, of the Vilnius Centre for Celestial Mechanics, has studied how such probabilities are communicated and concludes that the public, and many politicians, interpret them poorly. A rising probability may provoke alarm, while a small but persistent risk may be dismissed. Because a deflection mission must be launched years before impact to have any effect, Jankauskas argues, decisions will almost certainly have to be taken while the threat remains uncertain, perhaps at a probability of one in ten or lower.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This is where the questions become political. Deflecting an asteroid does not make it vanish; it shifts the point at which it would strike. During the course of a deflection, the projected impact site moves across the surface of the earth, and a partially successful mission could transfer the danger from one country to another. Shanika Gunawardhana, an international lawyer at the Kandy Institute for Global Governance, points out that no treaty specifies who has the authority to undertake such a mission, or who would be liable if it went wrong. Under existing space law, a state that launched a deflection spacecraft might be held responsible for damage caused by the redirected object, a prospect that could deter precisely the action that is needed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Gunawardhana proposes that decisions be delegated in advance to an international body, which would assess threats, authorise missions and share liability among participating states. The proposal has obvious merits, but I doubt that it is realistic. Governments with the capability to launch deflection missions are unlikely to surrender that capability to a committee, particularly when their own populations are at risk. A more achievable goal might be a set of agreed procedures, binding in principle if not in law, that would govern consultation between states once a threat is identified.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns the methods themselves. Kinetic impactors, which simply ram the asteroid, are the best-tested option, but for very large objects or very short warning times some scientists have suggested using nuclear explosions to vaporise part of the surface and push the asteroid aside. Professor Eirik Solhaug of the Bergen Institute for Space Physics regards this as the only credible option for the most extreme scenarios and believes that the technique should be studied openly. Others fear that research into nuclear deflection could provide cover for weapons development and undermine treaties that prohibit nuclear devices in space. Solhaug acknowledges the concern but argues that refusing to study the method would leave the world defenceless against precisely the threats most likely to cause mass casualties.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be easy to conclude from all this that planetary defence is hopelessly entangled in politics. That conclusion would be premature. The international warning network that coordinates asteroid observations has functioned smoothly for years, sharing data among observatories in countries that agree on little else. Cooperation is evidently possible when the threat is recognised as common to all.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The real danger, then, is not that nations will fail to cooperate in a crisis, but that the preparation required to make cooperation effective will be postponed until a crisis arrives. Because the probability of a damaging impact in any given year is low, planetary defence competes poorly for funds against more immediate concerns. The decades of warning that make asteroids uniquely preventable are of value only if they are used.

topic: preserving historic lunar landing sites: archaeological context, the non-sovereignty obstacle to heritage law, voluntary keep-out guidelines and the debate over scientific sampling of abandoned equipment
title: Footprints Worth Keeping
subtitle: The places where people first walked on the Moon are protected by no law, and as new missions head there, archaeologists want that to change

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere on the dusty plain where the first astronauts landed in 1969, their footprints remain almost exactly as they were left. With no wind or rain to erode them, the impressions in the lunar soil could survive for millions of years, disturbed only by the slow rain of micrometeorites. Around them lie the objects the astronauts abandoned: the descent stage of the landing craft, scientific instruments, discarded tools, even boots and bags of waste. For half a century these remnants were safe simply because no one could reach them. That protection by inaccessibility is now ending, as a growing number of government agencies and private companies plan missions to the lunar surface, and the question of whether the earliest landing sites should be legally preserved has moved from the seminar room into the realm of policy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Advocates of preservation begin from an archaeological premise. Dr Aroha Pōtae, who specialises in the archaeology of the recent past at the Aotearoa Heritage Institute, argues that the landing sites are not merely collections of hardware but places where a defining moment in human history can be studied in its original context. The arrangement of objects, the pattern of footprints and the paths the astronauts walked reveal how they actually worked, sometimes contradicting the official accounts recorded at the time. Once disturbed, Pōtae insists, this context cannot be reconstructed, however carefully individual artefacts are retrieved. I find this argument compelling, not least because the archaeology of earth is full of sites whose meaning was lost when well-intentioned collectors removed objects without recording where they lay.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The legal obstacles, however, are considerable. International space law forbids any nation from claiming sovereignty over the Moon or any part of it. This principle, intended to prevent territorial competition, has the unintended effect of making conventional heritage protection impossible, since such protection normally depends on a state designating and policing sites within its own territory. Tomasz Jędrzejczyk, a specialist in international law at the Kraków Institute of Legal Studies, observes that the country which launched the missions retains ownership of the objects it left behind, but not of the ground on which they rest. It could object if its equipment were removed, but it has no clear authority to stop another party from landing nearby or driving over the footprints.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One proposed solution is to designate the sites through an international agreement modelled on the convention that protects places of outstanding universal value on earth. Jędrzejczyk regards this as the most promising route but warns that negotiations would be slow and that existing heritage conventions explicitly apply only to the territory of member states. Some countries have instead issued voluntary guidelines recommending that visiting spacecraft keep a set distance from historic sites and avoid flying directly over them, since the exhaust from a landing engine can scatter dust and debris at high velocity across a wide area. These recommendations have been welcomed by archaeologists, but they carry no penalties, and a company in a hurry, or one registered in a country that has not endorsed them, is under no obligation to follow them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that special protection is warranted. Behrouz Zarrabi, an economist at the Isfahan Centre for Space Economics, contends that preserving a handful of sites from a single country's programme privileges one national narrative over others. If the first crewed landings deserve protection, he asks, why not the first robotic landers, which were sent by a different nation years earlier? More fundamentally, Zarrabi doubts that preservation zones would be respected once lunar resources acquire commercial value. Rules that cannot be enforced, he argues, may do more harm than good by creating an illusion of protection.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Zarrabi's first point is fair, and any regime worth having should cover robotic as well as human landings, regardless of the nation responsible. His second point is weaker. It is true that heritage rules on earth are frequently broken, yet no one concludes from this that they should be abandoned; their value lies partly in establishing a standard against which conduct can be judged. A visitor who damages a protected lunar site would at least be seen to have done something wrong, which is more than can be said under the present arrangements.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A rather different perspective comes from Anahit Ghazaryan, a planetary scientist at the Yerevan Space Research Laboratory. She points out that the landing sites are scientifically, as well as historically, valuable. The equipment has now been exposed to the lunar environment for more than fifty years, and samples taken from it could reveal how materials degrade under prolonged radiation and extreme temperature change, information that would be invaluable for designing future bases. Ghazaryan therefore proposes that small, carefully documented samples be permitted under strict supervision. Her colleague Rūta Morkūnaitė, a conservator at the same laboratory, disagrees, arguing that even minimal sampling sets a precedent that commercial visitors would soon exploit.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What seems beyond dispute is that a decision must be taken before the first uncontrolled visit rather than after it. Heritage protection on earth has usually arrived too late, after the damage it was meant to prevent had already been done. The footprints have survived half a century of neglect; whether they survive the next decade of attention will depend on choices being made now.

topic: astronaut radiation limits for a Mars mission: career cancer-risk standards, uncertainty in accelerator-based risk models, possible cognitive effects, informed-consent waivers and shielding versus faster transit
title: The Dose Problem
subtitle: A voyage to Mars would expose its crew to more radiation than any space agency's rules currently permit; the question is whether the rules should bend or the mission should wait

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every space agency that sends people into orbit sets limits on the radiation they may receive over the course of a career. These limits are expressed as a maximum acceptable increase in the astronaut's lifetime risk of dying from cancer, and for decades they were set at a level, roughly a three per cent increase, that few missions came close to reaching. Astronauts on the international space station, which orbits within the protective shield of the earth's magnetic field, accumulate doses far higher than those received on the ground but generally well within their career allowances. A mission to Mars would be a different matter. Outside the magnetic field, a crew would be exposed throughout a voyage of two to three years to galactic cosmic rays, energetic particles originating beyond the solar system that pass through spacecraft walls with ease.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Estimates of the total dose for such a mission vary, but most suggest that it would approach or exceed the career limits of every agency, particularly for younger astronauts and, under some older models, for women, whose limits were set lower because of differences in calculated cancer risk. One agency recently replaced its sex- and age-specific limits with a single universal standard, a change welcomed as fairer, although critics noted that the new figure was lower for some astronauts than the one it replaced. In either case, the uncomfortable fact remains that a Mars mission conducted with existing technology would almost certainly breach the rules.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How much the breach matters depends on how much confidence one places in the risk models themselves. Dr Selin Esenbel, a radiation biologist at the Anatolian Institute of Space Medicine, points out that the biological effects of cosmic rays are known largely from experiments in which cells and animals are exposed to particle beams at ground-based accelerators. These experiments deliver in minutes or hours a dose that astronauts would receive over years, and the heavy ions that make up a small fraction of cosmic radiation, but cause disproportionate damage, are difficult to reproduce. As a result, Esenbel argues, the uncertainty in current estimates of cancer risk spans a factor of three or more in either direction. A mission could be considerably safer than the models predict, or considerably more dangerous.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cancer is not the only concern. Experiments on rodents have suggested that heavy ions can damage the central nervous system, impairing memory and decision-making at doses comparable to those expected on a Mars voyage. Wojciech Kondratowicz, a neuroscientist at the Gdańsk Centre for Aerospace Health, regards these findings as potentially more significant than the long-term cancer risk, because cognitive effects could appear during the mission itself, when a crew far from earth would depend on clear thinking to survive. He cautions, however, that the rodent studies used doses delivered far more rapidly than in space, and that no comparable effect has yet been observed in astronauts.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Faced with these uncertainties, some have proposed that astronauts should be allowed to accept higher risks voluntarily, provided they are fully informed. Professor Ulrike Haslinger, a bioethicist at the Salzburg Centre for Medical Ethics, argues that astronauts are highly educated adults who already accept considerable dangers, from launch accidents to the hazards of spacewalks, and that preventing them from volunteering for a Mars mission is paternalistic. In her view, an agency could legitimately grant a waiver to an individual who understood and accepted the additional risk.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The argument is attractive, but it underestimates the peculiar position of an astronaut. Unlike a mountaineer who chooses to attempt a dangerous peak, an astronaut is an employee whose career depends on being selected, and the pressure to accept whatever conditions are offered is considerable. Consent obtained in such circumstances is not worthless, but it is hardly the free choice that the language of autonomy implies. Moreover, the risks cannot be fully explained when, as Esenbel's work shows, they are not fully known.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further perspective is offered by Jussi Mäkiranta, an engineer at the Oulu Space Systems Laboratory, who argues that the debate over limits distracts from the more productive question of how to reduce exposure. Thicker shielding made from hydrogen-rich materials such as polyethylene or water can absorb some radiation, although adding mass is expensive, and against the most energetic particles shielding can even generate secondary radiation. Faster propulsion would shorten the journey and hence the dose; Mäkiranta estimates that halving the transit time would cut total exposure by around a third, since the time spent on the Martian surface, partly shielded by the planet itself, would remain unchanged.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: There is merit in all of these positions, yet none on its own resolves the dilemma. Engineering may reduce the dose but is unlikely to eliminate it; better biology may narrow the uncertainty but will take years. In the meantime, agencies will face pressure, from governments and from their own astronauts, to set the rules aside. If they do so, they should at least say so openly, rather than quietly revising the models until the mission appears to comply.

topic: space programmes in emerging economies: buying satellite data versus national ownership, dependence on foreign providers, skills transfer versus turnkey purchases, and prestige as a route to influence over space rules
title: A Ladder to Orbit
subtitle: More and more lower-income countries are founding space agencies, and the reasons they give deserve a closer look than either supporters or critics usually offer

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the space of two decades, the number of countries with a national space agency has more than doubled. Many of the newcomers are not wealthy industrial powers but middle- and lower-income states in Africa, Asia and Latin America, some of which face pressing needs in health, education and infrastructure. Their programmes are usually modest: a small earth-observation satellite built with foreign assistance, a ground station, perhaps a training scheme for engineers. Even so, the decision to spend public money on space in countries where many citizens lack reliable electricity provokes predictable criticism, and the justifications offered by governments deserve closer scrutiny than they usually receive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most common defence is practical. Satellites, supporters argue, provide services that poorer countries need more urgently than rich ones: images that track crop health and deforestation, data for weather forecasting, and communications for remote regions beyond the reach of cables. Thabo Ntombela, an economist at the Highveld Institute for Development Studies, has examined the case for national ownership of such capabilities. He concludes that the services themselves are indeed valuable, but that most could be obtained far more cheaply by purchasing data from existing commercial or foreign providers. Imagery of adequate resolution, he notes, is now often available free of charge. In his view, a country that builds its own observation satellite primarily to obtain images is paying a premium for something it could largely have had for nothing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Advocates have responded that the purchase of data creates dependence. Chiamaka Ezeagu, who studies technology policy at the Lagos Centre for Science Diplomacy, points to occasions on which foreign providers restricted access to imagery during political disputes or prioritised the needs of their own governments during emergencies. A country without its own capability, she argues, cannot be certain of receiving the data it needs at the moment it needs it most. There is something to this argument, but it should not be overstated. Most of the services in question are now supplied by numerous competing companies in many countries, and the likelihood that all of them would refuse to sell at once seems remote.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second justification concerns skills rather than services. Building and operating even a small satellite requires expertise in electronics, software, materials and project management, and governments often present space programmes as a means of training a generation of engineers whose abilities will spill over into other industries. Ganbold Ochirbat, an engineer who helped establish a satellite programme at the Mongolian University of Technology, believes this effect is real but depends heavily on how the programme is organised. Where satellites are bought complete from foreign manufacturers, with local staff merely observing, little knowledge is transferred. Where local engineers are given responsibility for design and assembly, even at the cost of delays and failures, the gains can be considerable. Ochirbat's own team lost its first satellite shortly after launch, an experience he describes as the most instructive of his career.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This seems to me the strongest argument for national programmes, and also the one most often undermined in practice. Governments under pressure to show quick results tend to favour turnkey purchases, which produce a satellite in orbit and a celebratory launch but leave little behind in domestic industry. The prestige that attaches to a launch can thus work against the very capabilities that justify the expense.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Prestige itself is the third and least openly discussed motive. Luísa Pinheiro-Lago, a political scientist at the São Paulo Institute of International Relations, argues that space programmes allow emerging states to signal technological competence to investors, neighbours and their own citizens, and to claim a seat in international forums where the rules of space are made. She regards this motive as entirely legitimate. Countries that have no presence in space, she observes, have little influence over decisions about orbital slots, radio frequencies and debris that will shape their future access. Critics who dismiss national programmes as vanity projects, Pinheiro-Lago contends, overlook the fact that the established space powers built their own programmes for reasons that were at least as symbolic.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Her point about the inconsistency of some criticism is well made. It is difficult for countries that spent heavily on space during the twentieth century, often for reasons of national pride, to lecture others on the virtues of restraint. Yet legitimacy is not the same as value for money, and the question for any government remains whether a given programme delivers benefits commensurate with its cost.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The most useful conclusion may be that the decision is less about whether to invest in space than about how. A programme designed to build domestic skills, with realistic expectations and a willingness to tolerate early failure, may justify its cost many times over. One designed chiefly to place a flag in orbit, purchased complete and operated by foreign contractors, probably will not. Regional cooperation, in which neighbouring states pool resources to share satellites and training facilities, offers a further way of spreading costs, although it requires a degree of trust that is not always present.

topic: robotic versus crewed exploration: scientific return per unit of cost, human field judgement versus improving rover autonomy, inspiration as a public good and the risk that combined programmes starve robotic science
title: Machines or Minds?
subtitle: For half a century robots have done almost all of humanity's exploring beyond the Moon; as crewed missions return to the agenda, the old argument over who should go has revived

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since the last crewed landing on the Moon in 1972, every surface of another world that humans have studied at close quarters has been explored by machines. Robotic landers and rovers have drilled into Martian rock, sampled the surface of comets and photographed the methane lakes of a distant moon, all at a fraction of the cost of sending people. Yet the ambition to send astronauts beyond earth orbit has never disappeared, and several space agencies are again planning crewed missions to the Moon, with Mars as a declared long-term goal. The question of whether such missions are worth their enormous expense has divided scientists for decades, and the arguments on both sides are more subtle than the familiar slogans suggest. Much of that subtlety is lost when the debate is reduced, as it often is, to a contest between romance and accountancy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for machines rests chiefly on cost. A crewed mission must carry air, water, food and shielding, and above all it must bring its passengers home, requirements that multiply the mass of the spacecraft and hence the price. Professor Imre Vereckei, a planetary scientist at the Pannonian Institute of Astronomy, has calculated that the budget of a single crewed lunar programme could fund between twenty and thirty sophisticated robotic missions to destinations throughout the solar system. In his view, the scientific return per unit of expenditure is so heavily weighted towards robots that the continued pursuit of human exploration can be explained only by political motives, not scientific ones.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of human spaceflight dispute this arithmetic. Dr Agnieszka Kubiszyn, a field geologist who has trained astronauts at the Silesian Centre for Planetary Science, argues that robots, for all their durability, are painfully slow. A rover on Mars, controlled from earth with signal delays of up to twenty minutes in each direction, may take a week to reach and examine a rock that a trained geologist could assess in minutes. More importantly, she contends, human beings excel at recognising the unexpected: a scientist on the surface can notice an unusual colour or texture and change plans immediately, whereas a robot does only what its operators have anticipated. On this view, the higher cost of human missions is offset by a vastly greater rate of discovery.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kubiszyn's point about speed is well supported by experience; the six crewed lunar landings returned more material, and more varied material, than all robotic sample-return missions combined. But it does not follow that the same advantage will hold indefinitely. Robotic autonomy has improved markedly, and rovers can now select targets and navigate around obstacles without waiting for instructions from earth. The gap between human and machine is narrowing, and any comparison based on the technology of the 1970s is bound to overstate it. Software, moreover, can be upgraded between missions at little additional cost, whereas human abilities cannot.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third position shifts the debate away from science altogether. Rustam Umarov, a historian of technology at the Tashkent Institute for the History of Science, argues that the value of human exploration has never been primarily scientific. The crewed lunar landings, he notes, inspired a generation to pursue careers in science and engineering, and few robotic missions have captured public imagination in the same way. Photographs of astronauts on the lunar surface, he observes, remain among the most widely reproduced images ever made, whereas few members of the public could name a single robotic rover. Umarov regards this inspirational effect as a legitimate public good, comparable to the cultural value of museums or national parks, which no one expects to justify themselves in purely economic terms.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This argument is harder to dismiss than critics suppose, but it is also harder to measure than its advocates admit. The surge of interest in science that followed the lunar landings coincided with heavy government investment in education and research, and disentangling the effect of the missions themselves from these wider policies is extremely difficult. Moreover, the public enthusiasm that greeted the first landing faded remarkably quickly; television audiences for later missions were a fraction of those for the first. If inspiration is the justification, it appears to be a benefit that diminishes with repetition.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most promising contribution to the debate may be the one that rejects the choice altogether. Wairimu Wangeci, an engineer who plans mission architectures at the East African Space Systems Institute, argues that robots and humans are complementary rather than competing. In her scheme, robotic missions would survey a destination in advance, identifying the most promising sites, while astronauts would follow to conduct detailed investigations that machines cannot. Astronauts orbiting a planet could also control robots on its surface without the long delay that hampers operators on earth, combining human judgement with robotic endurance and avoiding the expense and danger of landing at every site of interest.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Not everyone finds this compromise convincing. Hery Rakotonirina, an economist at the Antananarivo School of Public Policy, warns that in practice combined programmes tend to be dominated by their crewed component, which absorbs the largest share of the budget and is the first to be protected when costs rise. Robotic science, he argues, has repeatedly been sacrificed to keep human programmes on schedule, with probes cancelled or postponed so that launch dates for astronauts could be met. Whether this pattern is inevitable or merely the result of past management decisions remains, for the moment, an open question, but it is one that any agency planning a return to the Moon would do well to take seriously.

topic: the supervision problem in partially automated cars: vigilance decrement, takeover time and situation awareness, driver monitoring, insurers' crash data, skill loss and the case for skipping partial automation
title: Hands Off, Eyes On?
subtitle: Partly automated cars ask drivers to supervise a machine that rarely needs them, and psychology suggests that this is exactly where the danger lies

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a decade, many new cars have been sold with systems that can steer, accelerate and brake by themselves on major roads. Under the rules that govern them, however, the person in the driver's seat remains legally responsible at every moment and must watch the road continuously, ready to intervene if the system makes a mistake. Manufacturers describe such features as driver assistance, a term meant to reassure: the human is still in charge, merely relieved of some tedious work. Yet the arrangement rests on an assumption that deserves far closer scrutiny than it has received, namely that ordinary people can supervise an automated process for long periods and take over within seconds when required. Half a century of psychological research suggests that this capacity is considerably weaker than the advertising implies.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty was first documented in military control rooms. Studies of radar operators in the 1940s found that their ability to detect rare signals on a screen fell noticeably after roughly thirty minutes on watch, a pattern later termed the vigilance decrement. Crucially, the decline is steepest when signals are infrequent. This creates an awkward paradox for vehicle automation: the better a system performs, the fewer occasions the supervising driver has to respond, and the faster attention drains away. Solveig Hammerfjeld, a human factors specialist at the Bergen Institute for Applied Psychology, demonstrated the effect in a driving simulator. Participants whose automated system was almost flawless reacted far more slowly to its eventual failure than those whose system had made occasional minor errors during the session. Hammerfjeld does not recommend building unreliable cars, but she believes designers must stop treating greater reliability as an unqualified gain for safety.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second problem concerns what taking over actually involves. Takumi Nagasebe of the Kansai Mobility Laboratory points out that most regulatory standards measure the interval between an alert and the moment the driver's hands return to the wheel, which is typically a second or two. In his own experiments, however, drivers who had been disengaged for some time needed as long as fifteen seconds before their steering and speed control were as stable as those of people who had been driving manually throughout. The delay, Nagasebe argues, reflects the time required to rebuild situation awareness: an understanding of where surrounding vehicles are, how fast they are moving and what the road ahead is likely to do. His conclusion seems to me difficult to resist. A hand on the wheel shows that a driver is physically present, not that he or she is mentally prepared to drive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Manufacturers have responded by monitoring drivers more closely. Early systems relied on torque sensors that detect slight pressure on the steering wheel, but these are easily fooled, and some owners hang weights from the wheel precisely to silence the warnings. Newer vehicles use small cameras to track the direction of the driver's gaze. Duarte Ramalhoso, an engineer at the Atlantic Road Safety Institute in Porto, regards gaze tracking as the decisive improvement. In the design he advocates, if a driver's eyes leave the road for more than a few seconds, the system first issues warnings and then reduces its assistance step by step, obliging the driver to re-engage. This is undoubtedly an advance, but it does not entirely solve the problem. Accident investigators have long recorded cases in which drivers looked straight at a hazard and still failed to register it; gaze direction reveals where the eyes are pointing, not whether the mind is following.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the risks are as serious as these studies suggest. Ilinca Ciobotaru, who leads the research unit of a large European motor insurer, cites claims data showing that cars fitted with assistance systems are involved in substantially fewer rear-end collisions than comparable vehicles without them. In her view, the occasional crash caused by an inattentive supervisor is outweighed many times over by the accidents prevented. Her figures are genuine, but their interpretation is less straightforward than it appears. The systems have mostly been installed in expensive new models, whose owners tend to be older and more cautious than the average motorist, and they are used largely on motorways, which are already the safest roads in any national network. Some of the apparent benefit may therefore belong to the drivers and the roads rather than to the technology.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a longer-term concern. Hammerfjeld has drawn attention to research in commercial aviation, where pilots who rely heavily on the autopilot have been found to lose some of their proficiency in manual flying. If the same happens to motorists, the people asked to rescue a failing system may be precisely those least practised at doing so. She has proposed that assisted vehicles should periodically require their owners to drive unaided, although she concedes that few customers would welcome such a car.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For some engineers, these difficulties point towards a more radical conclusion. Marisol Leizaola, a former developer of automated vehicles, argues that partial automation is a dead end and that the industry should move directly to systems which need no human supervision at all, even if they can operate only within carefully mapped zones and in good weather. Such vehicles would bring themselves to a safe stop when conditions exceeded their competence, rather than handing control to an unprepared occupant. This position strikes me as the most coherent one available, since it removes the human supervisor instead of assigning that person a task for which human attention is poorly suited. It does, however, carry an uncomfortable implication: that a generation of products sold as stepping stones towards full automation may in fact have been a detour.

topic: truck platooning on motorways: aerodynamic fuel savings, matching vehicles from different firms, road and bridge wear, drivers' concerns and the shift towards driverless lorries
title: Convoys Without Couplings
subtitle: Electronically linked lorries were supposed to make road freight cheaper and cleaner. A decade of trials has produced a more complicated picture

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The idea behind truck platooning is simple. Two or more lorries travel in close formation along a motorway, connected not by physical couplings but by a wireless link. When the lead vehicle brakes or accelerates, the ones behind respond within a fraction of a second, far faster than any human driver could, which allows them to follow at gaps of ten or fifteen metres instead of the fifty or more normally required for safety. Travelling so close together reduces air resistance and therefore fuel consumption. Around 2015, trials were under way in Europe, North America and Japan, and industry forecasts confidently predicted that platoons would be a familiar sight on major roads within a decade. That has not happened, and the reasons are instructive, because most of them have little to do with whether the technology works.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The aerodynamic case, at least, is well established. Henrik Brannvoll of the Nordic Vehicle Aerodynamics Centre has measured fuel use in wind tunnels and on closed test tracks, and found that following lorries can save up to ten per cent. Even the leader gains slightly, by two to four per cent, because the vehicle behind fills the region of low pressure that would otherwise form in its wake and hold it back. On public roads, however, the figures shrink. Cars cut into the gaps, breaking up the convoy; on hills, heavily and lightly loaded lorries cannot keep the same speed; and once the gap widens beyond about twenty metres, most of the benefit disappears. Average savings in real traffic have been closer to four per cent. In an industry where fuel can account for a third of operating costs, that is still worth having, but it is far from the transformation that was promised.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of who gains. Because the vehicles at the back save more than the one in front, platooning between lorries from different companies raises an awkward issue of fairness, and several schemes have proposed payments from followers to leaders, arranged through matching apps. Oksana Sorokolat, a logistics economist at the Vienna Institute for Freight Studies, doubts that such arrangements will ever be widely used. Her analysis of journey records shows that lorries, even those belonging to the same operator, rarely travel the same route at the same moment, and that waiting at a service station for a partner to arrive typically costs more in driver time than the convoy saves in fuel. In her view, platooning makes commercial sense only on a handful of very busy corridors linking major ports and distribution centres.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Road engineers have raised a different set of concerns. Priyanka Bellamkonda, who studies pavement durability, notes that automated steering holds each lorry in precisely the same lane position, so the tyres of every vehicle in a platoon pass over the same narrow strips of asphalt. Over time this accelerates rutting. Bridges present a further difficulty, since several heavy vehicles travelling close together place a greater load on a span than its designers anticipated when they assumed normal spacing. Bellamkonda proposes that steering systems be programmed to introduce a small, deliberate variation in each lorry's position within the lane, spreading the wear. It is a sensible suggestion, and a useful reminder that new technology must be fitted to the roads we already have rather than the reverse.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other road users must also be considered. A long convoy can form a moving wall that prevents cars from reaching motorway exits, which is why most countries that permit platooning limit it to two or three vehicles. Drivers' unions, meanwhile, have objected that the person in a following lorry, a few metres behind a large trailer, cannot see the road ahead, and that hours spent in this position are both stressful and monotonous. More fundamentally, they suspect that platooning is the first step towards removing drivers from following vehicles altogether. This fear is not unfounded: several developers now describe the follower lorry openly as a vehicle that will ultimately need no one at the wheel.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Indeed, by the early 2020s a number of large manufacturers had quietly paused their platooning programmes and redirected investment towards fully autonomous lorries. The explanation they gave was that the fuel savings were too small to justify the cost of the equipment while every vehicle still carried a driver; the figures only worked if the follower had none. Some critics have concluded that platooning was always a labour-saving technology presented in environmental clothing. That judgement seems to me too cynical. The emissions benefits were real, and they were what motivated many of the engineers involved. But it is fair to say that the commercial calculation depended on wages as much as on fuel.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Platooning may yet return in modified forms, perhaps on dedicated freight lanes or as looser coordination between lorries that do not follow so closely. Its story so far, though, carries a broader lesson. A technology evaluated on a single measure, in this case litres of diesel saved, can look compelling in a test facility and still struggle once it meets the economics, infrastructure and people of the real world.

topic: proving that autonomous vehicles are safer than human drivers: the statistics of rare fatal crashes, disengagement reports, simulation testing, standardised scenario catalogues and the choice of human baseline
title: Counting the Miles That Matter
subtitle: How could anyone actually demonstrate that a self-driving car is safer than a human being at the wheel?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every company developing self-driving cars says that its vehicles will be safer than those driven by people, and many point to millions of miles of testing as proof. Yet the question of how such a claim could actually be demonstrated has received far less attention than the sensors and software themselves. In much of the industrialised world, a fatal road crash occurs roughly once for every hundred million miles driven by humans. Fatalities are therefore, in statistical terms, rare events, and showing that a machine produces fewer of them requires an enormous quantity of driving. In this sense, the real obstacle facing the industry is less an engineering problem than a statistical one, and it is one that no amount of clever programming can make disappear.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the difficulty was set out most starkly by Einar Kolbeinsson, a statistician at the Institute for Applied Risk Analysis in Reykjavik. His calculations suggest that, to demonstrate with reasonable confidence that an autonomous fleet causes twenty per cent fewer deaths than human drivers, the vehicles would need to cover several billion miles. A fleet of one hundred cars operating around the clock would take several centuries to accumulate that distance. Kolbeinsson's conclusion is that road testing, however extensive, can never by itself settle the question. His arithmetic is difficult to dispute, but it rests on the assumption that deaths are the only outcome worth counting. Injuries and minor collisions are far more frequent, and would therefore yield a statistical signal much sooner, although the way such incidents are recorded varies so widely between police forces and insurers that they are an imperfect substitute.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some regulators have tried to fill the gap by requiring companies to report 'disengagements': occasions on which a human safety driver takes over from the automated system. Ingrid Sahlstrom, a transport policy analyst at the Baltic Mobility Observatory, regards these figures as close to meaningless. Firms define a disengagement differently: some log every precautionary intervention, while others record only those made when a collision was imminent. Moreover, a company testing in congested city centres will inevitably register more takeovers than one operating on quiet suburban streets, even if its software is superior. Sahlstrom's objections seem to me entirely justified, and it is regrettable that the annual figures have nevertheless been presented in the press as a kind of league table, with firms ranked as though they were competing on equal terms.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more promising route, according to Hana Tanimura of the Kansai Institute of Mobility Engineering, lies in simulation. In a virtual environment, millions of miles can be driven in a single day, and rare hazards, such as a child stepping out between parked vans or a tyre bursting on a vehicle ahead, can be replayed thousands of times with slight variations in speed, lighting and position. Tanimura's group reports that simulated testing uncovered faults in perception software that had gone unnoticed during months on public roads. Critics respond that a simulation is only as faithful as its model of the world: cameras and radar behave differently in heavy rain or low sunlight, and the situations that cause real crashes are often precisely those that nobody thought to programme. Simulation is clearly indispensable, but a method that can only test what its designers have imagined cannot be allowed to certify itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach, championed by Daudi Mwakilema of the East African Vehicle Standards Council, borrows from the driving test. Regulators, he proposes, should compile a catalogue of standard scenarios drawn from national crash databases and require every automated vehicle to negotiate them, on test tracks and in simulation, before being licensed. The great advantage of this scheme is that results would be comparable across manufacturers. The obvious objection is that companies might tune their systems to pass the catalogue while performing less well elsewhere, much as some car engines were once engineered to behave differently during emissions tests. Mwakilema's answer is that part of the catalogue should be kept confidential and the scenarios selected at random on the day. This is a sensible refinement, yet it presupposes that regulators possess a depth of technical expertise which, at present, few of them can claim.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even if the measurement problems were solved, there would remain the question of what autonomous vehicles should be compared with. Selin Ozkaynak, an economist at the Ankara Centre for Transport Studies, points out that the familiar figure for human drivers is an average which includes those who are drunk, exhausted or newly qualified, and covers night-time journeys on unlit rural roads. Most automated fleets, by contrast, operate in daylight, in good weather and within carefully mapped urban districts. Measured against a sober, attentive and experienced motorist under the same conditions, she argues, their apparent advantage might shrink considerably or disappear altogether. Yet her point cuts both ways. If driverless cars need only outperform the minority of drivers who cause a disproportionate share of crashes, they could save lives even while falling short of the most careful human.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No single method, then, can deliver the proof that the industry promises and the public expects. Road miles, simulation and standardised scenarios each answer part of the question, and only in combination are they likely to command confidence. It should also be acknowledged that public opinion is shaped less by statistics than by individual events: a single widely reported crash can undo the reassurance of many millions of uneventful miles. For that reason, the most useful step companies could take would be to release their raw driving and incident data, so that researchers with no commercial stake in the outcome could reach their own conclusions.
