topic: pavement delivery robots: last-mile delivery costs, remote supervision ratios, who actually uses them, obstruction of disabled pedestrians, municipal permits and charging for footway space
title: Small Wheels on the Pavement
subtitle: Six-wheeled delivery robots are spreading through suburbs and campuses, raising the question of who the footway is really for

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: They are roughly the size of a picnic cooler, travel at walking pace on six small wheels and carry groceries, parcels or takeaway meals over distances of a few kilometres. Unlike the driverless cars that attract most of the publicity, delivery robots of this kind travel not on the road but on the pavement, pausing at kerbs and crossings while a remote supervisor, who may be watching several machines at once, intervenes if one becomes stuck. They first appeared on university campuses and in newly built suburbs, where paths are wide and residents tend to be enthusiastic about new technology. Their modest, almost toy-like appearance is deceptive, however. Behind it lies a significant question about who controls public space, and it is one that most cities have so far preferred not to answer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The commercial case rests on the cost of the so-called last mile, the final stage of a delivery from a local depot or shop to the customer's door, which is often estimated to account for more than forty per cent of total delivery costs. Taras Vlasenko, an urban economist at the Black Sea School of Spatial Economics, has modelled the conditions under which robots could undercut human couriers. His figures suggest that they become cheaper only when a single supervisor can oversee at least eight machines and when orders are densely clustered in a small area. Few current schemes meet both conditions, and Vlasenko concludes that most are best understood as subsidised demonstrations rather than viable businesses. His analysis is persuasive as a snapshot, but the cost of sensors and batteries has fallen sharply in recent years, and it would be premature to dismiss the robots on the basis of today's prices.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Who actually uses the machines has turned out to be more surprising than their economics. Over two years, Aino Pellikka of the Lakeland University of Applied Sciences followed a robot delivery service in a small Finnish town. The operator had expected its main customers to be busy young professionals ordering lunch. In practice, the heaviest users were older residents and people with limited mobility, who relied on the robots to bring bulky or heavy shopping such as bottled water and potatoes. Pellikka also recorded a modest fall in short car journeys to the local supermarket among participating households. She is careful to stress, however, that her sample was small and that the town is flat, with unusually broad pavements, so that her findings may not apply to places with narrower or hillier streets.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For other pedestrians, the arrival of the robots has been less welcome. Folake Okubadejo, who researches street accessibility at the Centre for Inclusive Mobility, has collected hundreds of reports of machines blocking the dropped kerbs that wheelchair users need in order to cross, or stalling in narrow stretches of footway so that people are forced to step into the road. Blind and partially sighted pedestrians, she notes, may be unable to detect a nearly silent robot until they collide with it. In her view, the pavement is the one part of the street that was designed for its slowest and most vulnerable users, and any machine that shares it should always give way to them. On that principle she is surely right. Where I part company with her is over her call for an outright ban, since the problems she documents seem to arise from poor design and weak regulation rather than from the robots themselves.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What regulation might look like has been explored by Mateus Barreiro, a transport planner who has advised several Iberian municipalities. He proposes that operators should require permits that cap the number of robots in each district, that the machines be limited to six kilometres per hour, and that companies share data on every incident involving a pedestrian. He also suggests that operators pay a fee for each robot, with the money used to repair and widen footways. At present, some cities have banned the robots entirely while others have allowed them to operate without any rules at all. Barreiro argues that the second approach is the more damaging, because firms that occupy public space informally for several years acquire what amount to customary rights, which later prove very difficult for a city to withdraw.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is worth remembering that the pavement was never empty before the robots arrived. Wheelie bins, hired scooters, café tables and advertising boards already compete for the same narrow strip of tarmac, and pedestrians have rarely been consulted about any of them. Delivery robots are therefore best seen as a test case for a much broader issue: the terms on which private companies may use shared public space for commercial gain. A city that charges for kerbside parking but allows robots onto its footways free of charge is sending a confused message. Whether the machines become a familiar sight is likely to depend less on advances in their technology than on whether operators are willing to pay a fair price for the space they occupy.

topic: electric vertical take-off air taxis in cities: battery energy limits and range, the character of rotor noise, rooftop landing sites as bottlenecks, who benefits, pilotless operation and the claim of relieving road congestion
title: The Rooftop Commute
subtitle: Battery-powered air taxis promise to lift city travellers above the traffic. The obstacles are more down to earth

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The vision is seductive: small electric aircraft with clusters of rotors rising vertically from rooftops and carrying two to five passengers across a congested city in minutes rather than hours. Supporters argue that electric propulsion transforms the economics of short-distance flight. Electric motors have far fewer moving parts than turbine engines, so maintenance should be cheaper, and distributing thrust across many small rotors is said to make the aircraft quieter and more resilient to the failure of any single one. Yet the idea of hopping over traffic by air is hardly new. Scheduled helicopter shuttles between airports and city centres were launched with great fanfare in several countries during the 1950s and 1960s, and almost all of them closed within a few years, defeated by high costs, noise complaints and accidents. What is new is the scale of private investment, and the fate of those earlier services ought to make even enthusiasts more cautious than they currently appear.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first constraint is chemical. According to Sigrid Gulbrandsen, a battery engineer at the Trondheim Laboratory for Energy Storage, even the best lithium cells store only a small fraction of the energy contained in an equivalent weight of aviation fuel. The problem is aggravated by the fact that hovering during take-off and landing consumes far more power than cruising, and by aviation rules that require every aircraft to carry enough reserve energy to divert to an alternative landing site. Once these demands are accounted for, Gulbrandsen calculates that the practical range of most designs is considerably shorter than the figures advertised, and that frequent rapid charging between flights will shorten the life of the batteries themselves. She concludes that the aircraft will be suitable only for short hops. This need not be a fatal weakness, however, since short urban journeys are precisely those on which road congestion imposes the heaviest delays.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Noise poses a subtler difficulty. Manufacturers routinely point out that their aircraft are measurably quieter than helicopters, and in terms of decibels this is often true. But Kenji Hiroshige, who studies community responses to sound at the Institute of Environmental Acoustics, has found that loudness is a poor guide to annoyance. In listening experiments, volunteers rated the high-pitched, tonal whine produced by many small rotors as more irritating than the deeper thud of a helicopter of comparable volume. Annoyance also rose steeply with the frequency of overflights, which matters because commercial services would concentrate dozens of flights a day along a few fixed corridors. If Hiroshige is right, and his results have since been replicated by other laboratories, then the decibel comparisons favoured by the industry give a misleadingly reassuring picture.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even if the aircraft perform as promised, they will need somewhere to land. Planners envisage 'vertiports' on the roofs of office blocks and on the upper decks of multi-storey car parks, each equipped with high-power chargers for recharging aircraft between flights and with space for screening passengers and their luggage. Few existing roofs were built to bear the weight of a loaded aircraft, however, and strengthening them is costly. More fundamentally, the number of take-offs and landings a vertiport can handle in an hour is governed largely by its size, since each landing pad can accommodate only one aircraft at a time and must be cleared before the next arrives. A small rooftop site may manage only a handful of movements per hour, a constraint that could limit the capacity of a whole network far more than the aircraft themselves.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of who would benefit. Voahangy Raharimanana, an urban geographer at the Indian Ocean Institute of Regional Studies, predicts that the first services will link international airports with central business districts at fares affordable only to executives and wealthy travellers, while the noise is borne by residents of the neighbourhoods below, most of whom will never board an aircraft. Her concern is legitimate. It is worth recalling, though, that many forms of transport, from the private car to commercial aviation, began as luxuries before falling prices brought them within reach of ordinary people. Whether air taxis will follow the same path is impossible to predict, but their early exclusivity is not, in itself, evidence that they will remain exclusive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Safety regulation adds a further layer of uncertainty. Aircraft with novel configurations must be certified from first principles, a process that Rokas Juskevicius, a former adviser to a European aviation authority, describes as necessarily slow. Most operators, moreover, regard the pilot as a temporary feature. A pilot occupies a seat that could otherwise be sold and draws a salary that a small aircraft can scarcely support, so business plans typically assume that flights will eventually be remotely supervised or fully autonomous. Juskevicius doubts this timetable. In his view, regulators will insist on years of data from piloted operations before approving pilotless passenger flights, and the travelling public is likely to take considerably longer to accept such flights than companies currently assume.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that air taxis have no future. They seem well suited to particular niches: airport transfers, the urgent transport of medical supplies and organs, and routes across water or mountainous terrain where ground transport is slow. What appears much less plausible is the claim, repeated in many promotional campaigns, that they will relieve road congestion. Even an optimistic network of rooftop sites would move only a few hundred passengers an hour, a figure that a single dedicated bus lane can comfortably exceed. Air taxis may well become a useful addition to urban transport, but they are a remedy for the inconvenience of a few rather than for the traffic endured by many.

topic: high-definition maps for self-driving cars: maps as stored prior knowledge, the cost of keeping maps current and geofenced services, map-light driving from sensors alone, publishing road works data, and roads without clear markings
title: The Map Beneath the Machine
subtitle: Most self-driving cars rely on detailed digital maps. Whether they should is one of the quieter arguments in the industry

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a self-driving car moves along a city street, it is not simply reacting to what its cameras and laser scanners can see. Most such vehicles also carry a high-definition map, a three-dimensional record of the road accurate to within a few centimetres. Such maps record the exact position of lane markings and pedestrian crossings, the precise height of kerbs and the location of every traffic light and road sign. By constantly comparing what its sensors detect with this stored model, the car can work out where it is far more accurately than satellite positioning alone would allow. The map is therefore as much a part of the driving system as the sensors themselves, yet in public discussion of autonomous vehicles it is rarely mentioned at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For Pieter Moerdijk, a geospatial engineer at the Lowlands Institute of Mapping Science, the advantages are decisive. A map, he argues, functions as a kind of memory. Because the vehicle already knows where the permanent features of the road are, it can devote its limited computing power to the things that move: pedestrians, cyclists and other vehicles. The map also allows the car to anticipate what it cannot yet see, such as a stop line hidden beyond the crest of a hill or a sharp bend after a bridge. Without one, Moerdijk maintains, a vehicle would be obliged to interpret every junction afresh each time it approached, much as a visitor does in an unfamiliar town.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that roads do not stay the same. Lanes are repainted, junctions redesigned and temporary road works appear overnight. Larisa Sevastyanova, a transport economist at the Volga Centre for Infrastructure Studies, has estimated that in a large city a small but significant share of road segments changes in some way every month, so that a map surveyed at great expense begins to go out of date almost as soon as it is completed. This, she argues, explains why commercial robotaxi services operate only within carefully defined zones, a practice known as geofencing, and why their expansion into new districts has been so slow and costly. Her figures may well overstate the problem, however. Vehicles in a fleet can detect changes as they drive and report them, allowing the map to be updated continuously, although this raises the awkward question of who checks that the updates are correct.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A rival school of thought holds that detailed maps are a crutch that the industry should learn to do without. Goran Obradovic, who works on machine learning at the Adriatic Institute of Technology, argues that vehicles should be trained to read the road directly from sensor data, as human drivers do, using conventional navigation maps only to plan their route. Such a car could in principle drive anywhere, not merely in places that have been surveyed. Critics point out that systems of this kind still make occasional errors at unusual junctions and are harder to test, because their behaviour depends on patterns learned from data rather than on explicit rules. Supporters often observe that people drive perfectly well on roads they have never seen. The comparison is less convincing than it sounds, since human drivers bring to every new road a store of common sense about the world that no machine yet possesses.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Part of the problem lies with public authorities rather than with the vehicles. Leilani Kamakau, a data officer with the Pacific Cities Data Collaborative, points out that municipalities already know where most road works and lane closures will be, because contractors must apply for permits in advance. In many cities, however, this information exists only as paper forms or scanned documents that no vehicle can read. Kamakau proposes that cities publish it in a standard digital format, so that automated vehicles, and ordinary navigation apps, are warned of changes before they reach them. This seems to me one of the most sensible proposals in the whole debate, and one that would cost cities very little to implement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further concern is raised by Chinedu Udeh of the West African Road Research Centre. Across much of the world, he notes, roads lack clear lane markings, many are unpaved, and traffic includes handcarts, livestock and informal minibuses that stop wherever passengers wave them down. A technology built around centimetre-accurate maps of orderly streets is, in his view, a technology designed for the wealthiest cities. If it becomes the industry standard, Udeh warns, the benefits of automation may be confined to places that are already well served, while poorer regions are left behind.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most likely outcome is neither of the extremes. Maps will probably continue to serve as a valuable source of prior knowledge, but vehicles will increasingly be expected to drive safely when that knowledge turns out to be wrong. Indeed, the most important design question may not be whether a car uses a map at all, but how it behaves at the moment when the map and reality disagree. A vehicle that slows down and proceeds with caution in such circumstances is far safer than one that trusts its stored record over the evidence of its own sensors.

topic: driverless metro trains: grades of automation, shorter intervals between trains and energy recovery, platform screen doors, the cost of converting existing lines, redeployed station staff, and what automated rail does and does not show about driverless cars
title: Nobody in the Cab
subtitle: Fully automated metro lines carry millions of passengers a day with little fuss. Their quiet success is more revealing than it seems

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each day, millions of urban passengers board trains that have no driver, and many of them never notice. The first fully automated urban rail lines opened in the early 1980s, initially as small shuttles linking airport terminals or serving new suburban developments, and the technology has since spread to dozens of cities on several continents. What is remarkable is not so much the engineering as the absence of controversy. While driverless cars remain the subject of intense public anxiety, the automation of metro systems has proceeded with scarcely any debate, and the reasons for this contrast deserve closer attention than they usually receive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious reason is that a train is a far easier machine to automate. It runs on a fixed track, cannot steer, and on most metro lines operates in tunnels or on viaducts from which pedestrians and other vehicles are excluded. Engineers describe automation in terms of grades. At the second grade, which is common on older lines, a computer controls the train's speed and braking, but a staff member on board opens and closes the doors and starts the train from each station. At the fourth and highest grade, there is no member of staff on the train at all. Advocates of driverless cars often cite the safety record of automated metros as evidence for their own case, but the comparison is largely misleading: a system that has removed almost every source of unpredictability tells us very little about one that must cope with all of them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The benefits for operators are nonetheless considerable. Ilker Arslanoglu, who studies rail operations at the Bosphorus Institute of Rail Systems, has analysed lines before and after conversion and found that the interval between trains could be shortened substantially, increasing capacity by as much as a fifth. Computers accelerate and brake more consistently than human drivers, allowing trains to run closer together safely, and additional trains can be dispatched within minutes when, for instance, a stadium empties after a match. Automation also makes it possible to coordinate the movements of trains so that the electricity generated by one train as it brakes is used by another that is accelerating nearby. These results are impressive, though it should be noted that part of the capacity gain comes from the modern signalling that accompanies automation, which could in principle be installed while keeping drivers in the cab.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Removing staff from trains entirely brings its own requirements, of which the most visible is the platform screen door, a glass barrier along the platform edge whose doors open only when a train is in the station. Beatriz Zamorano, a railway engineer at the Andean Polytechnic University, regards such barriers as essential at the highest grade of automation, since there is no driver to spot a person or object on the track. The doors have additional benefits: they reduce suicides and prevent the delays caused by litter or dropped belongings falling onto the rails. But they demand that every train stops with great precision, so that its doors align with those on the platform, and Zamorano points out that this becomes complicated on lines that use several types of train with doors in different positions. Installing barriers in old stations, where platforms may be curved or structurally weak, is also expensive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Converting an existing line is a different matter from automating a new one. Mikhail Yakubovich, a transport economist at the Ural Institute of Public Investment, has compared conversions in several cities and found that they consistently cost more, relative to the length of line involved, than automating lines built from scratch. Because passenger services must keep running during the day, most of the work has to be carried out overnight, in windows of three or four hours, and projects frequently take a decade. The entire signalling system must be replaced with a computer-based one, and trains must be refitted or replaced. Since the main financial return comes from reduced staff costs, Yakubovich calculates that the investment is typically recovered only after twenty years or more. He therefore recommends that every new line be automated from the outset, but that proposals to convert existing lines be judged individually rather than adopted as a general policy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The effect on employment has been more complex than either supporters or opponents predicted. Trade unions resisted automation in several cities, fearing large-scale job losses. Awa Doumbia, a sociologist of work at the Sahel Institute for Labour Studies, has found that on many converted lines former drivers were retrained as roving attendants who travel on trains and patrol stations, helping passengers and responding to incidents. Surveys of passengers consistently show that most prefer some staff to be present, particularly late at night, and very few say they would rather travel with no staff in sight. Doumbia concludes that automation initially transformed jobs rather than abolishing them. She warns, however, that several operators quietly reduced the number of attendants a few years later, once public attention had moved elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson of the automated metro, then, is not that machines have become clever enough to replace human drivers in general. Rather, it is that automation succeeds when the environment has been redesigned to suit it: segregated tracks, protected platforms and centralised control. If driverless cars are ever to achieve comparable reliability, it may be that changes to the roads themselves, such as dedicated lanes, will matter as much as improvements to the vehicles.

topic: moral dilemmas and self-driving cars: large online dilemma surveys, why genuine crash dilemmas almost never arise, everyday distribution of risk, legal limits on programming preferences and publishing driving policies
title: The Trolley in the Traffic
subtitle: Debates about the ethics of driverless cars have focused on rare and dramatic dilemmas. The everyday choices may matter far more

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Should a self-driving car that cannot stop in time swerve to hit one pedestrian rather than five? Should it sacrifice its own passenger to save a group of children? Over the past decade, questions of this kind, modelled on a famous philosophical puzzle about a runaway railway trolley, have dominated public discussion of the ethics of autonomous vehicles. They feature in newspaper articles, school debates and television documentaries, and they are often the first thing a lay audience raises when the subject of driverless cars comes up. Their appeal is easy to understand: they are vivid, they seem to admit of a clear answer, and they flatter the sense that a machine might be made more principled than a panicking human. Yet these thought experiments have attracted attention out of all proportion to their practical importance, and in doing so they have arguably diverted attention from the ethical choices that engineers actually face.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the interest was stimulated by a large online survey organised by Rania Mahfouz and colleagues at the Mediterranean Centre for Social Data. Several hundred thousand respondents in more than a hundred countries were shown pairs of unavoidable crash scenarios and asked which outcome the car should choose. Broad preferences emerged: most people wanted to spare more lives rather than fewer, and the young rather than the old. There were also striking regional differences in how strongly these preferences were held. Perhaps the most widely reported finding was a paradox: respondents approved of cars programmed to sacrifice their passengers for the sake of a larger number of pedestrians, but said they would not buy such a car themselves. As a contribution to social psychology the study is fascinating. As a guide to how vehicles should be regulated, it is close to worthless, since the moral intuitions of survey participants are not the same as principles that could be defended in law.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Engineers, for their part, tend to regard the whole debate with some impatience. Halvard Trondsen, who designs collision-avoidance software at the Nordic Automotive Research Group, argues that genuine dilemmas of the trolley type practically never arise on real roads. A vehicle facing an unavoidable collision typically has only a fraction of a second in which to act, and its knowledge of the situation is incomplete: it cannot know the ages of the people ahead, or even be certain how many there are. In almost every case, Trondsen maintains, the safest course is to brake as hard as possible in a straight line, because swerving makes the car's movements less predictable for other road users and may create new hazards. The real ethical questions, in his view, are mundane: how fast to travel past a school, how much room to leave when overtaking a cyclist, how cautiously to approach a blind corner.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the dilemmas are irrelevant. Ermira Hoxha, a moral philosopher at the Balkan Institute for Applied Ethics, contends that Trondsen's mundane decisions involve exactly the trade-offs that the thought experiments dramatise. A car that gives a cyclist a wide berth moves closer to oncoming traffic; a car that drives slowly on a busy road may provoke dangerous overtaking by impatient drivers behind. Each such choice shifts a small amount of risk from one group of people to another, and repeated across millions of journeys, these small shifts add up. The dilemmas, she suggests, simply make this distribution of risk visible. Hoxha is right that the distribution of risk is the central ethical issue. But the trolley framing misleads in one important respect: it presents outcomes as certain, when every real driving decision is a matter of probabilities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also legal constraints. Joaquin Mendieta, a specialist in technology law at the Pampas University School of Law, points out that the legal systems of many countries forbid discrimination between individuals on the basis of age, sex or other personal characteristics. Even if the public expressed a clear preference for sparing the young, such a rule could not lawfully be built into a vehicle. An ethics committee convened by one European government reached a similar conclusion, recommending that personal features should play no part in any decision taken by an automated system. Mendieta adds that manufacturers, anxious to avoid expensive lawsuits, are likely to programme their vehicles to behave in ways that are easy to justify in court rather than in ways that minimise harm overall.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that public debate about the ethics of driverless cars is pointless. It does mean that the debate should shift from improbable catastrophes to the ordinary settings that determine how risk is shared on the road every day. The most useful step would be for manufacturers to publish the policies that govern their vehicles' behaviour, including the speeds they choose in different conditions and the distances they keep from pedestrians and cyclists. Such disclosures would be less dramatic than a debate about runaway trolleys, but far more consequential. Only then could citizens, rather than software engineers alone, decide whether those choices are acceptable.

topic: autonomous and remotely operated cargo ships: the human-error argument, where crew savings matter most, designing ships without accommodation, collision rules written for human lookouts, shore-based operators' missing sensory cues and the future pipeline of seafaring skills
title: Empty Bridges
subtitle: Ships that sail with few or no crew on board are moving from the drawing board to coastal waters. The hardest questions are not about the technology

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Merchant shipping has a reputation as one of the most conservative of industries, yet it has become an unlikely testing ground for automation. Small coastal cargo vessels have completed voyages with their bridges unattended, and several ferry routes are now partly supervised from control rooms on shore. The case made by proponents is simple: since the great majority of maritime accidents are attributed to human error, removing people from ships should make them both safer and cheaper to operate. The statistic on which this argument rests is, however, frequently misused. Accident investigations tend to record as 'human error' failures that originated in poor ship design, inadequate training or commercial pressure to keep to schedule, simply because a person on the bridge was the last to act before the disaster.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economics are also less straightforward than often assumed. Wiktor Tomczewski, a shipping economist at the Gdansk School of Maritime Commerce, points out that for a large ocean-going container ship, crew wages amount to only a small fraction of operating costs, far less than fuel, insurance and the cost of the vessel itself. Removing twenty seafarers from a ship worth many millions would make little difference to its profitability. The proportion is very different on small vessels making short voyages, such as coastal feeders and ferries, where crew costs loom much larger and where shore stations are never far away. It is on such routes, in Tomczewski's view, that removing the crew offers the largest savings. His analysis seems to me convincing, and it suggests that the popular image of giant crewless container ships ploughing across the Pacific is, for the present, premature.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Removing the crew would also change the ship itself. Petter Kallistrom, a naval architect at the Baltic Institute of Ship Design, notes that a vessel without people needs no cabins, galley, lifeboats or living-quarters air conditioning, freeing space and weight for cargo and allowing a more streamlined superstructure. The difficulty lies in the engine room. On a conventional ship, engineers spend much of their time keeping machinery running, cleaning filters, repairing pumps and responding to leaks while at sea. An uncrewed vessel would therefore require machinery that is far more dependable and duplicated throughout, perhaps using electric propulsion with fewer moving parts. Kallistrom expects a long transitional phase in which ships carry reduced crews and the bridge is left unattended at night, much as engine rooms have been permitted to operate unmanned overnight for several decades.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The legal framework poses a different kind of obstacle. The international rules for preventing collisions at sea require every vessel to maintain a proper look-out 'by sight and hearing', wording drafted at a time when no one imagined that the look-out might be a camera or an operator hundreds of kilometres away. Laima Grigaliunas, who specialises in maritime law at the Klaipeda Centre for Ocean Governance, argues that existing rules should be reinterpreted to accommodate new technology rather than rewritten, since renegotiating international conventions can take decades. This is a pragmatic position, but it carries a risk. If ambiguities are left unresolved, the meaning of the rules may in practice be decided by courts only after a serious accident has occurred.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Supervising ships from shore raises questions of human performance. Jana Ruzickova, who studies human factors at the Central European Institute of Transport Psychology, observes that seafarers rely heavily on cues that a remote operator cannot perceive: the roll of the hull in a rising swell, a change in the vibration of the engine, the smell of overheating equipment. In her simulator studies, operators working from a shore centre took noticeably longer than crews on board to detect problems as they developed, and those responsible for several vessels at once sometimes faced alarms from different ships simultaneously. She recommends interfaces that convey motion and sound as well as visual data. These findings deserve attention, though we should not romanticise the alternative: exhausted officers on long night watches have also been known to miss the most obvious warning signs.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A longer-term concern is raised by Folasade Olawale of the West African Seafarers' Welfare Institute. Today's ship's officers, she notes, develop their judgement over years at sea, learning how vessels behave in heavy weather and congested ports. If fewer people go to sea, it is unclear where the next generation of shore-based operators will acquire that experience. Olawale fears that the supply of skilled mariners could dwindle just as the industry comes to depend on their expertise in remote centres, and she proposes training programmes in which cadets alternate between periods at sea and placements in control rooms.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Autonomy is therefore likely to arrive gradually and unevenly, first on short sea crossings, inland waterways and specialised survey vessels, and only much later, if ever, on the great ocean routes. Indeed, the most consequential change of the coming decades may not be the crewless ship at all, but the spread of systems that warn crews of collision risks, monitor machinery and suggest safer routes. Technology of this kind assists the people on board rather than replacing them, and it may achieve much of the safety benefit that autonomy promises at a fraction of the social and legal cost.

topic: whether self-driving cars will increase total travel: the falling cost of time spent travelling and urban sprawl, a chauffeur experiment simulating car autonomy, empty zero-occupancy journeys and road pricing, freed parking land, shared versus private ownership and lessons from ride-hailing
title: More Miles, Fewer Drivers
subtitle: Driverless cars are often promised as a cure for congestion. They may instead encourage us to travel more than ever

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Forecasts of the driverless future tend to be strikingly optimistic. Automated vehicles, it is said, will travel closer together and more smoothly than human drivers, eliminating the stop-start waves that clog motorways. Crashes, a major cause of delays, will become rare. Fleets of shared vehicles will reduce the need to own a car, and the vast car parks that occupy city centres will give way to housing and green space. Each of these predictions may contain some truth. Yet together they rest on assumptions about human behaviour that deserve far closer scrutiny than they usually receive, for the history of transport suggests that technologies which make travel easier almost always generate more of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central issue concerns the way people value their time. Transport economists have long treated time spent driving as a cost, because a driver must concentrate on the road and can do little else. Magnus Hornqvist, a transport modeller at the Uppsala Centre for Mobility Analysis, points out that if passengers in an automated car can read, work or sleep, the perceived cost of each hour on the road will fall sharply. His models indicate that commuters would then tolerate considerably longer journeys, making it attractive to live much further from city centres and potentially triggering a new wave of suburban sprawl. The logic is plausible, but the scale of the effect may be overstated. Rail commuters have long been able to work during their journeys, and train commutes have not lengthened without limit as a result.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Direct evidence about how people would use automated cars is inevitably scarce, since few such vehicles are yet available to private owners. Anastasia Sorokina, a behavioural researcher at the Neva Institute of Urban Studies, devised an ingenious substitute. She provided a sample of households with a free car and a professional driver for one week, on the reasoning that a chauffeur offers much the same convenience as an automated vehicle. On average, the distance households travelled by car rose by more than half. The largest increases were among older people and those who did not normally drive, and many of the additional trips were made for leisure in the evening. Some journeys were made with no passenger at all, as households sent the car to collect shopping or to fetch a child from school. Sorokina is careful to note that the novelty of a free week may have inflated these figures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Those empty journeys point to a problem that has received surprisingly little attention. Rodrigo Anzaldua, an urban economist at the Sonoran School of Public Policy, observes that in dense city centres, where parking is expensive, the owner of an automated car might find it cheaper to send the vehicle home empty, or simply to let it circle the block, than to pay for a parking space. Such zero-occupancy journeys would add traffic without moving anyone. Anzaldua argues that roads should be priced by the kilometre, with higher charges for vehicles travelling without passengers. Charges of this kind would undoubtedly be unpopular with voters, but without them the empty car could become one of the defining nuisances of the automated city.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The prospect of freeing land from parking is perhaps the most attractive part of the optimistic vision. Wairimu Gakuru, an urban planner at the East African Institute of Cities, estimates that in some city centres a fifth or more of the land is devoted to parking, and believes that much of it could be converted into homes and parks if shared fleets reduce demand. She stresses, however, that this will happen only if planners intervene deliberately. Without such intervention, released land may simply be absorbed by wider roads, while the kerb space needed for picking up and dropping off passengers could become a new source of congestion.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Much depends, in the end, on whether automated vehicles are shared or privately owned. Pooled services, in which strangers travelling in the same direction share a vehicle, are likely to reduce the number of vehicles on the road; private ownership of automated cars is likely to increase the distance driven. Here the recent history of app-based ride-hailing offers a warning. Introduced with promises of reducing car ownership and easing congestion, such services appear in many cities to have added to traffic, partly by attracting passengers away from buses and trains and partly because their vehicles spend much of their time driving empty between fares. There is little reason to assume that automated fleets would behave very differently unless policy obliges them to.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Driverless cars, then, are neither inherently good nor inherently bad for cities. Whether they ease congestion or worsen it will depend on decisions about pricing, the integration of automated vehicles with public transport, and the planning of land released from parking. Crucially, those decisions should be taken before the technology becomes widespread. Once people have moved to distant suburbs and new habits of travel have formed, the pattern will be extremely difficult to reverse.

topic: traditional windcatchers (wind towers) and their revival for passive cooling and school ventilation
title: Catching the Wind
subtitle: Traditional wind towers are being studied again by engineers who want to cool and ventilate buildings without machines

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Approach the old quarter of Yazd, in central Iran, and the skyline is defined not by domes or minarets but by rows of tall rectangular towers. These are badgirs, or windcatchers, and for several centuries they kept the houses beneath them habitable through summers in which outdoor temperatures routinely exceeded forty degrees. Similar structures appeared across the Gulf, Egypt and parts of South Asia. With the arrival of cheap electricity and mechanical air conditioning in the twentieth century, most fell into disuse, surviving as ornaments or as emblems on tourist brochures. Today, with global demand for cooling forecast to triple by the middle of the century, architects and engineers are looking at them again. The renewed attention is welcome, but it carries a risk: affection for a picturesque tradition is no substitute for careful measurement, and claims about what windcatchers can achieve have often run well ahead of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic principle is straightforward. A windcatcher is a vertical shaft rising above the roofline, with openings near its top. When the breeze blows, air enters through the openings facing the prevailing wind and is forced down the shaft into the rooms below, while the openings on the sheltered side, where pressure is lower, draw stale air out. On still days, the tower can work in a different way. Sunlight heats its walls, the warm air inside rises because it is lighter than the surrounding air, and cooler air is pulled in from a shaded courtyard to replace it, an effect engineers call stack ventilation. In many traditional buildings the incoming air was also passed over a pool of water or through porous clay jars, so that evaporation lowered its temperature further before it reached the occupants.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Shirin Haghshenas, a building physicist at the Plateau Institute of Vernacular Architecture, has spent a decade placing sensors inside historic towers. Her data show that when the wind exceeds a modest speed, rooms connected to a tower can be several degrees cooler than the air outside. On the calm afternoons that are typically the hottest of all, however, performance drops sharply, and in some cases the shaft actually delivers warm air into the house. Haghshenas does not regard this as a failing. The towers, she argues, were never intended to work alone; they belonged to a system that included thick earthen walls, deep courtyards and a household routine in which families moved to cool basements during the summer and to upper rooms in winter. Judging a windcatcher in isolation, in other words, is rather like judging a sail without the hull it was built to drive, and it is hard to disagree with her.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Paradoxically, the most commercially successful modern windcatchers have appeared not in deserts but in the cool, damp climate of northern Europe. Luc Duvivier, an engineer with the Brussels-based consultancy Aeraulis, has fitted roof-mounted wind towers to more than two hundred schools. Their purpose is ventilation rather than cooling: they replace the stale, carbon dioxide-rich air of crowded classrooms with fresh air from outside, without the electricity consumed by fans. Duvivier reports measurable improvements in air quality, but he concedes that early installations produced uncomfortable cold draughts in winter, a problem that has required the addition of adjustable dampers and, in some designs, heat-recovery units. Even so, it may well be here, in ordinary public buildings far from the places where windcatchers originated, that the technology has its most significant future.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is enthusiastic. The architectural historian Amara Kazembe has criticised what she calls the 'romance of the badgir'. Historic towers, she points out, were expensive to build and largely confined to the houses of wealthy merchants; most households had to manage without one. They also admitted sand, dust, insects and birds, and their timber and plaster required constant repair. Kazembe's corrective is valuable, since the image of an egalitarian, maintenance-free traditional technology is plainly false. Yet her objections concern the social history of the towers rather than their physics. That only the rich could afford them says nothing about whether the principle works.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more serious limitation is climatic. Evaporative cooling depends on dry air, which can absorb moisture readily; in humid coastal cities such as those of the Gulf shoreline, air that is already laden with moisture can take up very little more, and so evaporation achieves almost nothing. Towers in these places cooled people chiefly by moving air across their skin, not by lowering its temperature. Some researchers have therefore proposed hybrid systems, in which the shaft houses chilled-water coils or small solar-powered fans. Critics such as Kazembe dismiss these as conventional ventilation ducts dressed in heritage styling, but this seems unduly harsh: a tower that does most of the work passively and calls on machinery only at the hottest hours still saves a great deal of energy.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be learned from the windcatcher? It would be unrealistic to imagine that towers could replace air conditioning in the hottest cities at the height of summer. Their real lesson is a way of thinking, in which a building is shaped around the climate it occupies rather than equipped to overpower it with energy. If that principle reduces the number of hours for which machines must run, the old towers of Yazd will have earned their second life.

topic: the revival of rammed earth construction: cement stabilisation, weather detailing, thermal performance in cold climates, prefabrication and cultural perceptions of earth
title: Good Boots and a Good Hat
subtitle: Rammed earth is enjoying a revival among architects, but its modern form raises awkward questions about what makes the material worth using

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few building techniques are as old, or as easily overlooked, as rammed earth. Damp subsoil, containing a suitable balance of gravel, sand and clay, is poured into a temporary frame in shallow layers and compacted with heavy rammers. When the frame is removed, what remains is a dense wall with a distinctive striped appearance, each band recording a separate episode of compaction. Such walls survive in ancient fortifications in China and in farmhouses in southern France, some of them centuries old. Recently, architects in Australia, Europe and North America have rediscovered the technique, attracted by its low environmental impact and the warm, geological quality of the finished surface. Yet the revival has exposed a set of disagreements about what rammed earth is for, and about whether its modern form remains true to the qualities that made it attractive in the first place.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental argument rests largely on what the material does not require. Subsoil is often dug on the site itself, and unlike fired brick it needs no kiln. At the end of a building's life, an unstabilised wall can in principle be broken down and rammed again, or simply returned to the ground. However, much contemporary rammed earth contains between five and ten per cent cement, added to increase strength and resistance to rain. Sunethra Ratnayake, a structural engineer who advises local authorities, defends the practice. Inspectors, she points out, assess materials against numerical standards, and insurers are reluctant to cover walls whose performance is unpredictable; a little cement makes an unfamiliar material measurable. In her view, a modestly stabilised earth building that is actually constructed is preferable to an unstabilised one that never gets beyond the planning stage.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This argument has force, but at a price seldom acknowledged. Cement manufacture is a major source of construction emissions, and once cement has been added, the soil can no longer be recycled as earth; it becomes, in effect, a weak form of concrete. Stabilisation therefore removes two of the very qualities that justify choosing rammed earth over the alternatives. It is also often unnecessary. Dr Navid Bazargani, who has spent a decade exposing test walls to driving rain near the Caspian coast, reports that unstabilised walls with adequate protection lost only a few millimetres of their surface over that period. What matters, he argues, is not the chemistry of the wall but its detailing: a raised plinth of stone to keep the base clear of splashing water, and generous roof overhangs to shelter the face. Earlier builders put it more simply: an earth wall needs 'good boots and a good hat'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second dispute concerns comfort. Rammed earth is often promoted for its thermal mass: thick walls absorb heat by day and release it at night, smoothing out indoor temperatures. In hot, dry regions this is genuinely valuable. A group led by the building physicist Eirik Skarpengland in Norway, however, has shown that the same walls perform poorly where winters are long and cold, since earth conducts heat relatively well. Skarpengland's group concludes that in such climates rammed earth must be combined with an insulating layer, typically placed between two leaves of compacted soil. This is awkward for enthusiasts who call earth naturally efficient, and it is right that such claims should be tied to particular climates rather than made universally. It does not, though, undermine the case for earth altogether; it simply means that the material should be specified with the same care as any other.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most stubborn obstacle is economic. Ramming is labour-intensive, and where wages are high an earth wall can cost far more than a conventional one. Dr Ines Faltermeier, an architect in western Austria, believes the answer lies in moving production off site. Her firm compacts wall sections in a heated workshop, dries them under controlled conditions and transports them to the site, where a crane sets them in place. Faltermeier claims that this approach removes the dependence on dry weather, which has traditionally limited the construction season to a few summer months. Critics reply that heavy prefabricated elements erode the local character of the technique. Faltermeier accepts the trade-off, arguing that a material which remains a luxury for a handful of wealthy clients cannot make any meaningful contribution to reducing emissions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Professor Kwame Kyekyeku, who directs a research programme on earthen architecture in Accra, draws attention to an irony in the material's revival. In much of West Africa, families who can afford it are replacing earth houses with cement block, a symbol of prosperity, while in Europe the same material has become fashionable for expensive homes. For Kyekyeku, the decisive barriers are cultural rather than technical: as long as earth is regarded as the material of the poor in the places where it is most needed, improvements in engineering will make little difference. This is an important corrective to the assumption that better engineering alone will drive adoption, though it may underestimate the extent to which perceptions follow regulation. Where building codes include clear provisions for earth, as in New Zealand, the material has acquired a legitimacy that promotion alone could not provide.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The real danger is that, in seeking to make earth acceptable to inspectors, insurers and clients, its advocates gradually turn it into something else: a cement-rich, factory-made, heavily insulated product that retains the striped appearance of rammed earth but few of its environmental advantages. The more promising path is to invest in the long-term testing and published standards that would allow unstabilised walls to be approved with confidence. Such work is unglamorous, but without it the most sustainable version of an ancient technique is likely to remain the exception rather than the rule.

topic: 3D-printed concrete housing: speed and cost claims, cement-rich printable mixes, reinforcement and layer bonding, design freedom and the effect on construction labour
title: Houses from a Nozzle
subtitle: Printing buildings in concrete has captured the public imagination, but the technology's real strengths may lie somewhere other than where its promoters suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few construction technologies have attracted as much publicity as the printing of houses. Images of a robotic arm or gantry moving steadily across a site, laying down a ribbon of grey mortar that rises layer by layer into a curving wall, have become a fixture of news reports, usually accompanied by claims that a home can now be produced in a single day for a fraction of the usual cost. The process itself is genuinely ingenious: because the material is extruded directly from a nozzle, no timber or steel formwork is needed to hold it in place while it hardens. Yet the headlines have created an impression of a revolution that the evidence so far does not support, and the technology deserves a more careful assessment.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider first the question of speed. Dr Valentina Ardila, who studies low-cost housing at a university in Bogotá, points out that the celebrated figure of twenty-four hours almost always refers to the time the printer spends extruding the walls, and that this time is usually spread over several days. Foundations, roofs, windows, plumbing and electrical wiring are still installed by conventional means, and together they account for most of the time and money a house requires. In Ardila's estimate, the walls of a typical single-storey dwelling represent no more than a fifth of its construction cost. The greatest expenses facing families in need of housing, she argues, are not walls at all but land and the connection of a plot to water, drainage and power.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The material raises further doubts. Professor Tamar Lomidze, a materials scientist in Tbilisi, explains that a printable mortar must satisfy two conflicting demands: it has to be fluid enough to be pumped through a hose, yet stiff enough to support the layers placed on top of it within minutes. Manufacturers usually achieve this by leaving out the coarse stones found in ordinary concrete and raising the proportion of cement, the most carbon-intensive ingredient. Supporters reply that printed walls are often hollow and that no formwork is thrown away. This is true, but in most of the projects Lomidze has examined, the material saved in this way rarely compensates for the additional cement, and claims that printing is inherently a low-carbon method should be treated with caution.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Structural performance presents a third challenge. Mikko Hartikainen, a structural engineer based in Finland, notes that steel reinforcement, which gives concrete its ability to resist bending and cracking, cannot easily be placed while the nozzle is moving. Many printed houses therefore rely on vertical bars inserted afterwards into cavities, an arrangement whose behaviour under earthquake loading is still poorly understood. Hartikainen also warns about the bond between layers. If the printer pauses for too long, perhaps because of a blockage, the lower layer begins to harden before the next one is placed, and the joint between them can become a plane of weakness. Since few national building codes yet contain rules for printed walls, each project tends to be approved individually, which adds time and expense.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For the architect Chinedu Igwebuike, all of this misses the point. The real advantage of printing, he argues, is geometric freedom: once a printer is on site, a curved or tapering wall costs no more to produce than a straight one, and walls can be given internal cavities for insulation or shaped to use material only where it is structurally needed. This is a persuasive argument in principle. It is striking, however, that the great majority of printed houses built so far are ordinary rectangular boxes, which suggests that the promise of new forms remains largely unrealised. Curved walls also bring practical drawbacks that enthusiasts seldom mention: standard windows, kitchen units and wardrobes are designed for straight surfaces, so a curving room can be surprisingly difficult to furnish.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The effect on labour is similarly mixed. Advocates point to a shortage of skilled bricklayers and carpenters in many countries, and suggest that printing could allow homes to be built in remote regions with only a small team of operators. The printer, however, still has to be transported, assembled, calibrated and maintained, and the work that remains after printing calls for the same trades as before. Labour, in other words, is not eliminated but redistributed, from manual workers towards technicians who understand software and machinery. Whether that shift benefits the communities where the houses are built depends largely on whether local people are trained to run the equipment, or whether specialist crews arrive for each project and leave once the walls are finished.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that printed construction lacks value. In settings where unusual forms are wanted, where formwork would be costly, or where a series of near-identical structures must be produced quickly, the technology may well prove its worth. What it is unlikely to do, on its own, is resolve shortages of affordable housing, whose causes lie largely in the price of land, the availability of finance and the slow pace of planning decisions. Treating printing as a specialised tool rather than a universal solution would allow its genuine strengths to be developed without the disappointment that inflated expectations tend to bring.

topic: the energy performance gap in buildings: compliance modelling, construction quality, occupant behaviour, the prebound effect in older homes and the lack of post-occupancy feedback
title: Between the Drawing and the Meter
subtitle: Why do so many energy-efficient buildings consume far more energy than their designers predicted?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past three decades, building regulations in many countries have demanded steadily higher standards of energy efficiency. On paper, the results are impressive: new offices, schools and homes are calculated to need a fraction of the heating energy of their predecessors. When the meters are read, however, the picture is often different. Studies of completed buildings have repeatedly found that actual consumption exceeds the predicted figure, sometimes by a factor of two or more. This discrepancy, known as the performance gap, is not merely an embarrassment for designers. National carbon budgets assume that efficiency standards will deliver the savings promised in calculations, and if those savings fail to appear, the gap between policy and reality will widen in a way that is difficult to correct later.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the explanation lies in the calculations themselves. Dr Fiona Cairncross, an energy consultant who has reviewed hundreds of design assessments, argues that the models used to demonstrate compliance with regulations were never intended to forecast real consumption. Their purpose is to compare a proposed design against a standard, and to do so they assume fixed occupancy patterns, uniform thermostat settings and a notional climate. They also usually exclude the electricity used by computers, kitchen appliances and other equipment brought in by occupants. To set the output of such a model beside a meter reading, Cairncross contends, is to compare two quite different things. Her point is valid, but it explains only part of the problem: even when models are adjusted to reflect actual use, a substantial shortfall frequently remains.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second explanation concerns the quality of construction. Professor Haruto Moriyasu and his colleagues used thermal cameras and pressure tests to examine more than a hundred newly completed dwellings. In the majority, air leaked through the building envelope at rates well above those specified in the design, typically around poorly sealed windows, service pipes and junctions between walls and roofs. Insulation was sometimes missing altogether from sections that were hidden once the building was finished. Moriyasu attributes these faults less to negligence than to fragmentation: dozens of subcontractors work on a single site, each responsible for one element, and no one is charged with ensuring that the parts fit together as a continuous thermal barrier. He recommends that airtightness testing be required on every new building rather than on a small sample.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Occupants are a third and more controversial factor. Designers commonly attribute excess consumption to residents who open windows in winter, override automatic controls or set thermostats too high. Dr Hery Andriamihaja, a social scientist who interviews people in low-energy buildings, finds that such behaviour usually has a rational basis. Controls are often unlabelled or counter-intuitive, ventilation systems are noisy, and rooms designed to be sealed become stuffy, so occupants respond in the only ways available to them. In Andriamihaja's view, a building that performs well only if its users behave as the model expects has simply been badly designed. The criticism is fair, and it is hard to avoid the suspicion that blaming occupants has at times served as a convenient way for the building industry to deflect attention from its own failings.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The gap does not always run in the same direction. Dr Klara Wintersteller, who compared calculated and measured consumption in several thousand older houses, found that poorly insulated homes typically use considerably less energy than their ratings suggest. The reason is that residents of cold, expensive-to-heat houses economise, heating only one or two rooms and tolerating lower temperatures. Wintersteller calls this the prebound effect, and it has an important consequence: when such homes are renovated, the savings actually achieved are smaller than those predicted, because the original consumption was overestimated. Subsidy schemes that justify spending on the basis of calculated savings may therefore promise more than they deliver. That does not make renovation worthless. Warmer, drier homes bring benefits to health and comfort that conventional calculations simply ignore.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most fundamental cause, however, is the absence of feedback. Modern buildings increasingly depend on sophisticated mechanical systems for heating, cooling and ventilation, and these are frequently not adjusted correctly before handover. Investigations have found heating and cooling equipment operating at the same time in a single space, each working against the other. Detailed studies of how buildings perform once occupied remain unusual, chiefly because nobody is paid to carry them out: the architect's contractual obligations normally end on the day the keys are handed over. As a result, designers rarely discover whether their buildings work as intended, and the same mistakes are repeated from one project to the next.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Several remedies have been proposed. Some cities now require large buildings to publish their measured annual energy use, exposing poor performers to public scrutiny. Others have experimented with contracts in which designers and builders guarantee a level of consumption and pay penalties if it is exceeded. Critics object that such guarantees will increase construction costs, since firms will charge for the risk they assume. They probably will, at least at first. But a modest rise in initial cost seems a reasonable price for closing a gap that otherwise undermines the credibility of efficiency standards themselves.

topic: embodied carbon and the case against demolition: carbon payback of new buildings, limits of retrofitting, reuse of structural steel, retrofit-first planning rules and tax incentives that favour new construction
title: The Carbon in the Walls
subtitle: As new buildings grow more efficient to run, attention is shifting to the emissions released before anyone moves in

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the past half-century, efforts to reduce the climate impact of buildings concentrated on the energy used to heat, cool and light them once they were occupied. That focus made sense when buildings were poorly insulated and their running costs dwarfed everything else. As operational efficiency has improved, however, a different source of emissions has come into view: the carbon released in extracting, manufacturing and transporting materials and in the construction process itself. This is known as embodied carbon, and in a modern, well-insulated building it can account for half or more of the emissions associated with the structure over its entire life. It is remarkable how long the construction industry overlooked this figure, and the oversight has had a predictable result: perfectly serviceable buildings have been demolished and replaced in the name of energy efficiency.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Dr Eleni Sakellaridou, who carries out life-cycle assessments for public bodies, has tried to quantify the trade-off. When an old building is demolished and replaced by a more efficient one, the new structure begins its life with a large carbon debt, created by the concrete, steel and glass needed to build it. Only gradually do the savings from lower energy use repay that debt. In many of the cases Sakellaridou has analysed, the payback period runs to several decades, and in some it exceeds the expected lifespan of the new building. Such figures should be treated with care, since the results change considerably depending on assumptions about future energy supplies and how long a building will stand. But the general direction of her findings is difficult to dispute.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that refurbishment is the obvious answer. Obinna Nnadozie, a structural engineer who advises property developers, points out that many buildings from the 1960s and 1970s were designed with low ceilings, closely spaced columns and floors that cannot carry heavy loads. Adapting them for modern use, he argues, can cost more than building anew and still leave the owner with a mediocre building that tenants do not want. Nnadozie favours demolition accompanied by systematic recovery of materials. His objections are legitimate for certain structures, and it would be unwise to insist that every building be preserved regardless of its condition. Yet they are sometimes deployed too readily, by owners whose real motive is to increase the floor area of a valuable site.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Material recovery itself is less straightforward than it sounds. Steel is frequently described as infinitely recyclable, but recycling involves melting it down, which consumes considerable energy. Dr Marek Dobrzanski, who studies the circular use of construction materials, argues that a far greater saving comes from reusing beams and columns in their existing form. The obstacles, though, are practical. Each reclaimed beam must undergo load testing before it can be certified for a new structure, and many beams are damaged during demolition because they were welded rather than bolted in place. Dobrzanski therefore urges designers of new buildings to use connections that can easily be undone, so that future generations can dismantle the structure rather than destroy it. Reuse, in short, is a sound principle, but it is not yet a simple one to apply.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some city governments have begun to translate these arguments into regulation. Under so-called retrofit-first policies, owners who wish to demolish a building must first demonstrate that refurbishment is not a reasonable option. Signe Engebretsen, a planner who helped to draft one such policy, proposes going further by making a whole-life carbon assessment a condition of receiving a demolition permit. Developers complain that this adds another layer of bureaucracy to an already slow approval process. The complaint is understandable, but it is hardly unreasonable to ask those who intend to destroy a building to show that they have considered the consequences.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An economic factor that receives far less attention has been identified by Aigerim Toleubay, an economist who studies the property market. In a number of countries, she notes, the construction of new homes is exempt from value-added tax, whereas repair and renovation work is taxed at the full rate. The result is a system that quietly rewards demolition and penalises the reuse of existing buildings, whatever the stated aims of environmental policy. Toleubay argues that equalising the treatment of new and old would do more to change developers' behaviour than any amount of exhortation. Whether such a change would be politically achievable is another matter, since it would reduce government revenue at a time when public finances are under strain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Campaigners for conservation have adopted the slogan that the greenest building is the one that already exists. As a starting point, the phrase is valuable, because it reverses the long-standing assumption that new construction represents progress. As a universal rule, however, it goes too far: some buildings are so inefficient, unsafe or unsuited to any foreseeable use that replacing them is the better choice. What is needed is not a ban on demolition but a shift in the burden of proof, so that a building's survival becomes the default and its destruction the exception that has to be justified.

topic: wind engineering of tall slender towers: vortex shedding, aerodynamic shaping, tuned mass dampers, human perception of building motion, wind tunnels versus computer simulation and pedestrian-level winds
title: Taming the Wind at Height
subtitle: For the designers of very tall buildings, the greatest challenge is not keeping a tower standing but keeping its occupants from noticing that it moves

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As towers have grown taller and, crucially, more slender, the forces that shape their design have changed. For a squat office block, the main concerns are the weight of the structure and, in some regions, the shaking caused by earthquakes. For a residential tower whose height is fifteen or twenty times its width, it is wind that governs almost every structural decision. Remarkably, the danger is rarely that the building will collapse; modern towers are designed with large margins of strength. The difficulty is motion. A tall building sways constantly, and if the accelerations at its upper floors exceed certain thresholds, occupants begin to experience discomfort, anxiety and, in severe cases, symptoms resembling seasickness. A tower that is perfectly safe may therefore still be a commercial failure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most troublesome movement is not caused by the wind pushing directly against a building. When air flows past a tall, blunt object, it separates from the sides and forms swirling eddies, or vortices, which detach alternately from one side and then the other. Each time a vortex breaks away, it exerts a small sideways force, so that the building is pushed back and forth at right angles to the wind. If the rhythm at which vortices are shed happens to coincide with the natural frequency at which the tower sways, the motion builds up in the same way that a child on a swing goes higher with each well-timed push. Predicting this behaviour has long depended on testing scale models in wind tunnels.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One response is to design the vortices away. Dr Ingrid Henningsmoen, a wind engineer who has tested more than sixty tower designs, has shown that tapering a building, introducing setbacks at intervals up its height or softening its corners can disrupt the regular formation of vortices and roughly halve the crosswind response. Such measures, she argues, are cheapest when adopted at the earliest stage, before the floor plans have been fixed, and far more expensive to retrofit. Her case is a strong one, and there is a certain elegance in a building whose form itself solves the problem. It should be acknowledged, however, that on crowded urban plots, where developers seek to maximise every square metre of floor space, aggressive tapering is not always a realistic option.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Where shaping alone is insufficient, engineers often install a tuned mass damper: a heavy block of steel or concrete, or a large tank of water, placed near the top of the building and allowed to move. Its motion is tuned to the frequency of the tower, so that when the building sways one way, the damper moves the other, absorbing energy and reducing the amplitude of the sway. In a few towers, the damper has become a tourist attraction, with a viewing gallery from which visitors can watch a giant pendulum swing. Dr Armen Danielyan, who monitors completed buildings, cautions that dampers work well only within a narrow range of frequencies. A finished tower rarely behaves exactly as calculated, and a damper tuned to the predicted frequency may perform disappointingly until it is adjusted on site.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How much motion is acceptable is a question about people rather than structures. Dr Zoran Vukovljak has spent a decade studying volunteers in a motion simulator built to resemble an apartment. His experiments show that sensitivity varies widely between individuals, and that people detect movement at much lower levels when they also have visual or acoustic cues, such as a swinging lamp, rippling water in a glass or the creaking of partitions. For this reason, design guidelines in several countries set stricter limits for residential towers than for offices: residents are present at night, often lying still, and are less tolerant of motion in their own homes than in a workplace.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The tools used to predict wind effects are also evolving. Computational fluid dynamics, which simulates airflow numerically, is far cheaper and quicker than building a physical model. Eero Laaksonen, who directs a commercial wind tunnel, accepts that simulation is valuable for comparing alternative shapes early in the design process. He maintains, though, that it cannot yet reproduce the turbulent, gusty flow of real wind reliably enough to replace physical testing for a building's final design. Given what is at stake, his caution seems justified, even if commercial self-interest is not entirely absent from it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Tall buildings also affect conditions at their feet. A tower intercepts faster-moving air at height and deflects part of it downwards, so that strong gusts sweep across the pavement at its base. In some cities, pedestrians have been knocked over, and plazas intended as public gathering places have remained deserted because they are too windy to sit in. Remedies include a broad podium at the base to catch the descending air, canopies over entrances, and trees, although the last offer little protection in winter once deciduous species lose their leaves.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It is striking that this street-level problem received so little attention for so long, when the movement of upper floors has been studied for decades. The explanation is probably commercial: discomfort at the top of a tower affects the value of its most expensive apartments, whereas wind at the base affects mainly passers-by, who are not the developer's customers. Several planning authorities now require wind assessments at street level before permission is granted, a welcome sign that the public realm is beginning to count.
