topic: the passenger lift and vertical living: how lifts reversed the social value of upper floors, safety and public trust, cable limits and ropeless systems, destination dispatch and perceived waiting, and lift breakdowns in social housing
title: Rising Without Effort
subtitle: The passenger lift is so familiar that it is easy to forget how thoroughly it has reshaped buildings, cities and the way people live

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before the arrival of the passenger lift, the most desirable rooms in a city building were usually those closest to the street. Climbing five or six flights of stairs was tiring and time-consuming, so the upper floors of apartment blocks were let at the lowest rents, often to servants, students and the poor. The lift reversed this order. Once height could be reached without effort, the top floors, with their light, views and distance from the noise of the street, became the most prestigious, and the penthouse was born. Histories of the skyscraper tend to dwell on the steel frame, which allowed buildings to rise without enormously thick walls, but the social revolution brought about by the lift has received far less attention than it deserves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Hoists for raising goods had existed for centuries, but they were not trusted to carry people, because a broken rope meant a fatal fall. The decisive invention of the mid-nineteenth century was a safety brake that gripped the guide rails automatically if the rope failed. Yet Dr Walter Grünberger, a historian of technology, argues that the device alone did not persuade the public. In his reading of contemporary newspapers and hotel advertisements, acceptance spread slowly over several decades, as people saw lifts operated daily without incident and as uniformed attendants reassured nervous passengers. On this view, the lift's success depended as much on the gradual accumulation of trust as on engineering. The argument is persuasive, though it perhaps underplays the importance of the electric motor, which later made lifts faster, smoother and far cheaper to run.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Today the lift imposes its own limits on how tall a building can practically be. Conventional lifts hang from steel cables, and beyond a certain height the cables become so heavy that much of the machine's power is spent lifting the cable itself. In the tallest towers, passengers therefore travel to an intermediate floor, known as a sky lobby, and change to a second lift. Shafts also consume a substantial share of every floor, space that cannot be rented. Dr Haruka Kitaoka, an engineer who develops lift systems, is working on two remedies: cables made of lightweight carbon fibre, and ropeless cars driven by magnetic motors, several of which could share a single shaft and even move sideways between shafts. Such systems are promising, but none has yet been proven over years of heavy use in a large building.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other improvements concern how lifts are managed rather than how they are built. In a destination dispatch system, passengers enter their floor on a keypad in the lobby before boarding, and a computer assigns them to a particular car, grouping people who are travelling to the same or neighbouring floors. Each car therefore makes fewer stops, and the building can move more people with the same number of shafts. Manufacturers report significant gains in capacity. Users, however, are not always pleased: there are no floor buttons inside the cars, and visitors unfamiliar with the system sometimes board the wrong lift or find themselves unable to change their minds once inside.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such reactions interest Dr Irina Zolotareva, a psychologist who studies how people experience waiting. Her research suggests that the frustration lift users feel depends less on the actual length of the wait than on how long it seems and whether they feel in control. People routinely overestimate the time they have spent waiting, especially when they have nothing to occupy them. This is why mirrors are so common in lift lobbies: watching themselves and others, people become less aware of the passing seconds. Zolotareva found that displays indicating which car will arrive, and when, reduced complaints even where they did nothing to shorten waits. It follows that the efficiency of a lift system cannot be judged by engineering measurements alone.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For some residents, the problem is not a slow lift but no lift at all. Dr Paolo Aguinaldo, an urban sociologist in Manila, has documented the effects of breakdowns in high-rise housing. When a lift fails, the consequences fall unequally. Younger residents can climb the stairs, but elderly and disabled people on upper floors may be confined to their flats for days or even weeks. In public housing, where maintenance budgets are frequently cut, such failures are common. Aguinaldo argues that lifts should be classed as essential infrastructure, like water or electricity, with legally enforceable standards for repair times. It is difficult to disagree. A tower whose lifts cannot be relied upon is not merely inconvenient; for many of its occupants it is a place of isolation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lift, then, is more than a mechanical device. It determines which floors are valued, how much of a building can be used and who can reach their own front door. Engineers understandably measure progress in speed, capacity and the height a single car can travel, but these are not the only measures that matter to the people who depend on lifts every day. As cities build ever higher in response to growing populations, the future of vertical living will depend at least as much on reliable maintenance and fair management as on faster cars and lighter cables.

topic: bio-based building materials (hemp-lime and mycelium composites): carbon storage claims, drying and prefabrication, durability and moisture, crop supply and the role of public procurement
title: Growing a Building
subtitle: Materials made from plants and fungi promise to turn buildings into stores of carbon, but the evidence is more mixed than their champions admit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Modern construction depends overwhelmingly on concrete, steel and fired brick, all of which require large quantities of energy to produce. A growing number of architects and researchers believe that part of the answer lies in materials derived from living organisms. The attraction is simple: plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as they grow, and if their fibres are locked into the fabric of a building, that carbon remains out of the atmosphere for as long as the building stands. Two materials have attracted particular interest. Hemp-lime is made by mixing the chopped woody core of the hemp plant with a lime-based binder, while mycelium composites are produced by allowing the root-like threads of fungi to grow through agricultural waste packed into moulds, after which the material is heated to stop further growth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Promoters of both materials frequently describe them as carbon-negative, meaning that they store more carbon than is released in making them. Dr Liv Sørbye, who carries out environmental assessments of building products, regards such statements with some suspicion. Hemp certainly absorbs carbon during cultivation, and lime gradually reabsorbs carbon dioxide from the air as it hardens. But the manufacture of lime itself releases a substantial amount of carbon, and Sørbye's calculations show that the overall balance depends heavily on the proportion of binder in the mix and on how the material is transported and dried. Some formulations do indeed store more than they emit; others do not. The label, it seems, has spread faster than the evidence, and its popularity owes at least as much to marketing as to measurement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Hemp-lime has genuine strengths. It insulates well, it absorbs and releases moisture in a way that helps to stabilise indoor humidity, and it is resistant to fire and pests. It is not, however, strong enough to carry the weight of floors and roofs, so it is normally cast around a timber frame that does the structural work. Traditionally it has been mixed and placed wet on site, and in cool, damp weather a thick wall may take several months to dry, holding up the installation of finishes. Josef Kirchmayr, a builder who has worked with the material for twenty years, now produces hemp-lime panels in a heated factory, where they dry in a matter of days before being delivered to site. In his experience, this has removed the delays that once deterred contractors from using the material at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Mycelium composites are at a much earlier stage. Dr Ayu Soetomo, who leads a laboratory developing fungal materials in Yogyakarta, grows them on rice husks and sawdust, wastes that are abundant in the region and otherwise often burned. The process requires little energy, takes place at room temperature and produces a lightweight material that can be composted at the end of its life. Its compressive strength, though, is a small fraction of that of concrete, and for the present Soetomo sees its main uses in insulation boards, acoustic panels and temporary exhibition structures. She is optimistic that mycelium boards could eventually displace the plastic foams that dominate the insulation market.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Others are more cautious. Dr Tomas Pilkauskas, who tests the durability of construction materials, has exposed mycelium samples to cycles of wetting and drying. He found that the material readily absorbs water and can lose much of its strength when it does, and that its resistance to fire varies considerably from one batch to another. Unless these weaknesses can be overcome, Pilkauskas argues, mycelium will remain confined to dry interiors and short-lived installations. His concerns are legitimate, and they deserve to be taken seriously by designers. It is worth recalling, however, that very similar doubts were once raised about engineered timber, which is now used in multi-storey buildings in many countries.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even if the technical questions are settled, a practical obstacle remains: supply. Bálint Csordás, an agricultural economist, points out that hemp is still grown on a very small scale in most countries, partly because its cultivation has long been restricted by laws aimed at varieties used as drugs. Farmers are reluctant to plant a crop for which there is no reliable market, while manufacturers hesitate to build processing plants without a dependable supply of raw material. Each side, in Csordás's analysis, is waiting for the other to commit first. It is here that governments could play a decisive role. If public bodies, which commission a large share of all construction, were to specify bio-based materials in schools, offices and housing, the resulting demand could give farmers and manufacturers the confidence to invest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this suggests that buildings of the near future will be grown rather than built. Concrete and steel will remain indispensable for foundations and structural frames for the foreseeable future. The realistic prospect is a more modest one: that bio-based materials will gradually replace synthetic products in insulation, partitions and interior finishes, where their limitations matter least and their benefits are greatest. Such a change would attract fewer headlines than the vision of a living building, but it would be considerably more likely to happen.

topic: concert hall acoustics: reverberation time and its limits, shoebox versus vineyard halls and lateral reflections, bias in listener surveys and auralisation, stage acoustics for musicians and variable or electronic acoustics
title: The Sound of the Room
subtitle: More than a century after acoustics became a science, designing a concert hall that musicians and audiences love remains surprisingly difficult

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some of the most admired concert halls in the world were built in the nineteenth century, long before anyone could calculate how sound would behave inside them. Their designers worked from precedent and intuition, and their success arguably owed a good deal to fortunate accident, as well as to the fact that the halls which sounded poor were eventually altered or demolished and are now forgotten. One might expect that modern science would have made such uncertainty a thing of the past. Yet several expensive halls opened in the twentieth century disappointed critics and performers so badly that they required major reconstruction within a few years. Acoustic design, it seems, remains part science and part art.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first scientific measure of a room's acoustics was reverberation time: the period it takes for a sound to fade to inaudibility after its source stops. Early researchers showed that this depends on the volume of the room and on how much sound its surfaces absorb, and for orchestral music a reverberation time of around two seconds came to be regarded as ideal. The measure was a genuine breakthrough, and it remains in use today. On its own, however, it is a blunt instrument. Two halls with almost identical reverberation times can sound remarkably different, because the figure says nothing about the direction from which reflected sound reaches the listener or about the timing of the earliest reflections.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These factors lie at the heart of a long-running debate about the shape of halls. The traditional 'shoebox' is tall, narrow and rectangular, while the 'vineyard' design, which became fashionable in the later twentieth century, arranges the audience on terraces surrounding the stage, giving more listeners a close view of the performers. Dr Katrin Haberland, an acoustician who has measured more than forty halls, argues that the shoebox owes its reputation to its side walls. Sound reflected from these walls reaches listeners from the side within a few hundredths of a second of the direct sound, and it is these lateral reflections, she maintains, that create the sense of being enveloped by music. In listener surveys, she notes, shoebox halls consistently receive the highest ratings. Designers of vineyard halls have tried to compensate by using the low walls that separate the terraces as reflecting surfaces, though with varying degrees of success.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Henrik Malmqvist, a researcher in auditory perception, doubts that such surveys can settle the matter. Listeners' judgements, he points out, are shaped by a hall's fame, its history and its visual appearance as much as by what they actually hear. To remove these influences, Malmqvist uses a technique called auralisation: performances are recorded in different halls with special microphones, and listeners compare them through headphones without knowing which hall they are hearing. His results suggest that preferences vary with the listener's musical training and with the music being played, and that no single shape is best for everyone. His methodological point is an important one. Headphones, though, cannot convey the physical sensation of deep bass felt through the body, so auralisation captures only part of the experience of attending a concert.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The audience, moreover, is not the only group whose needs must be met. Dr Agnieszka Kołodziej, a former orchestral violinist who now studies stage acoustics, has interviewed players in a number of recently built halls. A recurring complaint is that musicians cannot hear one another clearly, which makes it difficult to play precisely together; in one new hall, members of the string section reported that they could barely hear the woodwind only a few metres away, and the orchestra spent several seasons experimenting with different seating arrangements before settling on one that worked. Kołodziej attributes the problem to designs optimised for the seats rather than the stage, and she recommends suspended reflectors above the platform, which return sound to the players and help them maintain their ensemble.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that few halls today host only orchestral concerts. To accommodate chamber music, opera, jazz and amplified performances, many incorporate variable acoustics: curtains that can be drawn across walls, movable ceiling panels and chambers that can be opened to add reverberation. Emre Rüzgar, an engineer who designs electronic enhancement systems, goes further. Arrays of microphones and loudspeakers, he argues, can now alter the apparent acoustics of a room at the touch of a button, allowing a single hall to suit many kinds of performance. Purists object that such systems produce an artificial sound. Their resistance is not purely a matter of sound quality, however; in part it reflects a reluctance to accept that technology might achieve what architecture alone has struggled to deliver.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Acoustic science has undoubtedly reduced the risk of failure, and few new halls today are outright disasters. But the experience of a concert is not merely acoustic. The appearance of a room, the comfort of its seats, the closeness of the audience to the stage and the sense of occasion all influence how music is perceived. A hall that performs well in measurements but feels cold or remote may never win the affection of its audience, and designers would do well to remember that they are creating places, not simply instruments.

topic: facadism in historic cities: keeping street fronts while demolishing the buildings behind them, planning rules that protect appearance, engineering risks of retained facades, defences based on streetscape, and design guidelines
title: Only Skin Deep?
subtitle: Keeping the historic front of a building while replacing everything behind it has become routine in many cities. Is it conservation or deception?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk along the main streets of many European, North American or Australian cities and you will pass buildings that are not quite what they seem. Behind a nineteenth-century frontage of carved stone and tall sash windows stands a structure of steel and concrete completed only a few years ago, often rising several storeys above the old roofline. The practice of retaining a historic façade while demolishing everything behind it is known as facadism, and it has attracted fierce criticism. Opponents have called it architectural taxidermy, the preservation of an empty skin from which the living animal has been removed. The term is now almost always used as an insult. Yet the practice is more varied than its critics allow, and it deserves a more careful assessment than it usually receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The spread of facadism owes much to the way historic buildings are protected. In many cities, planning rules concentrate on the character of the street, judging a proposal largely by what can be seen from the pavement. A developer who keeps the frontage intact can therefore often obtain permission for a far larger building than would otherwise be allowed. Such rules, intended to protect the townscape, have arguably done more to promote facadism than any other single factor. Dr Nino Beridze, a conservation architect, argues that this approach rests on a misunderstanding of what a historic building is. Its value, she contends, lies in the whole: the plan, the staircases, the structure and the craftsmanship of its interiors. A façade on its own is little more than a mask, and by preserving it, cities risk persuading the public that their history has been saved when most of it has been discarded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Retaining a façade is also far from straightforward in engineering terms. Rafael Sagastume, a structural engineer who has worked on many such projects, explains that once the floors and rear walls are removed, a tall masonry frontage loses the support that kept it upright. It must be held in place by temporary steel frames, sometimes for years, while the new building is constructed behind it. These frames occupy pavements, add considerably to construction costs and consume large quantities of material. Façades have occasionally collapsed during the works. In Sagastume's experience, keeping a frontage standing can cost more than demolishing it and building an accurate replica, an outcome that surprises many clients.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the practice see it differently. Lukas Draxler, who advises developers on historic sites, points out that many buildings now subject to facadism had already lost their original interiors through decades of alteration, fire or neglect. Their floor plans, moreover, are often unsuited to modern offices or apartments, and without the compromise that facadism offers, owners would simply have sought permission to demolish the whole building. In Draxler's view, retaining the frontage is the only realistic way of keeping old streets intact. His argument has real force where little of historic value survives behind the façade. It is far weaker, however, when it is used to justify the destruction of interiors that remain largely intact, as it frequently is.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different defence comes from Sanna Pukkila, an urban historian who studies how residents experience their cities. For most people, she observes, a building is something encountered from the street; the interiors of offices and private homes are seen only by those who work or live in them. Surveys she has conducted suggest that residents attach great importance to the continuity of historic street frontages and relatively little to interiors they will never enter. This is a valid point, and it helps to explain why facadism has proved politically acceptable. Taken to its conclusion, though, it leads to a city of stage sets, and it overlooks the effect of the new structure itself. A large modern block looming over a delicate frontage frequently diminishes the very streetscape that the façade was kept to protect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The quality of execution varies enormously. In the crudest examples, windows open onto nothing, or new floor slabs can be seen crossing old windows halfway up, betraying the fact that the façade bears no relation to what lies behind it. Thandiwe Mavuso, a city planner who has drafted guidance on the subject, believes such failures can be prevented. Her proposals would require developers to retain at least the front rooms of the original building, so that the façade retains some depth, to align new floors with the existing windows, and to set back any additional storeys from the frontage so that they are less visible from the street. These are sensible measures that would eliminate the worst abuses without forbidding the practice altogether.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this amounts to a case for banning facadism. There are situations in which it is the least bad option available, particularly where a building's interior has already been lost. But it should be treated as a last resort rather than as a routine means of securing planning permission. The deeper problem lies in protection rules that value the appearance of a building above its substance. Until those rules are reformed, facadism will continue to flourish, not because it is the best way of conserving the past, but because it is the most profitable way of appearing to do so.

topic: the restitution of objects taken during the colonial period: the universal museum argument, coercive acquisition, provenance research, long-term loans and digital replicas
title: The Long Road Home
subtitle: Museums that once treated their collections as beyond question are now being asked how, and from whom, their treasures were obtained

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the great encyclopaedic museums of Europe and North America regarded the contents of their galleries as settled. Objects acquired during the colonial period, whether purchased, presented as diplomatic gifts or seized during military campaigns, were catalogued, displayed and studied as part of a shared human inheritance. Requests for their return, when they came, were usually answered with polite refusals or ignored altogether. Over the past two decades, however, that confidence has eroded remarkably quickly. Several national governments have passed legislation permitting the transfer of objects out of state collections, and directors who once dismissed restitution as unthinkable now speak of it as a matter of when rather than whether. The speed of this shift deserves explanation, because it cannot be attributed to any single campaign or court ruling.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against return has traditionally rested on the idea of the 'universal museum'. Its most articulate recent defender, the cultural historian Professor Dieter Harbrecht of the Institute for Comparative Collections, argues that great collections allow visitors to see the achievements of many civilisations side by side, encouraging comparison and a sense of common humanity that no single national museum could provide. Dispersing such collections, he warns, would replace a cosmopolitan ideal with a narrow, nationalist one in which every object is assumed to belong to a particular modern state. There is something attractive in this vision, and it would be wrong to dismiss it as mere self-interest. Yet it sits awkwardly with the fact that the visitors able to enjoy these side-by-side comparisons are overwhelmingly those who live in, or can afford to travel to, a handful of wealthy cities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters of restitution make a different kind of argument. For Dr Adaeze Faleti, an anthropologist at the West African Heritage Research Centre, the central question is not where objects can best be seen but how they were obtained. Faleti distinguishes between items acquired through what she calls 'consensual exchange' and those removed under conditions of coercion, whether through outright looting or through transactions in which one side had no real freedom to refuse. In her view, the first category may legitimately remain where it is, while the second carries a moral debt that the passage of time does not cancel. This distinction is useful, because it shifts attention away from sweeping claims about entire collections and towards the history of individual objects. The difficulty is that such histories are frequently incomplete.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Provenance research, the reconstruction of an object's ownership history, has therefore moved to the centre of the debate. It is painstaking work. Acquisition records from the nineteenth century are often vague, recording only that an item was 'obtained' on a particular expedition, and the names of the original owners were seldom written down at all. Researchers must piece together evidence from military dispatches, private letters, auction catalogues and, increasingly, the oral histories of the communities from which objects came. A study led by the historian Haingo Rakotondrabe for the Indian Ocean Collections Project found that, for nearly half of the objects examined, no reliable account of acquisition could be established. Rakotondrabe argues that, in such cases, uncertainty should count in favour of the claimant community rather than the museum, since it was the collectors who failed to keep proper records in the first place.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some museums have sought a middle path through long-term loans, under which objects travel to their place of origin while legal ownership remains unchanged. Defenders of this approach point out that it allows objects to be seen by the communities most connected to them without requiring complex changes to the law. Critics, however, regard such arrangements as a way of conceding the substance of a claim while retaining its symbolic victory. To lend someone an object that they believe was taken from their ancestors, they argue, is to insist that it remains yours. On this point the critics are surely correct: a loan may be a practical first step, but it cannot be presented as a resolution.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Digital technology offers another proposed compromise. High-resolution scanning and three-dimensional printing now make it possible to produce replicas of remarkable accuracy, and some commentators have suggested that these could be offered either to source communities or to the museums that give up the originals. Such proposals tend to misunderstand what is at stake. For many communities, objects are not simply visual records but participants in ceremonies, or the physical embodiment of ancestors, and a copy, however faithful, cannot perform these roles. Replicas can certainly enrich education and research, but treating them as a substitute for return confuses the information an object contains with the relationships it sustains.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that restitution is straightforward. Questions remain about who should receive an object when the community that produced it no longer exists in recognisable form, or when a modern state and a local group both claim to represent it. Returned objects also require suitable conditions for their care, although concerns on this score are sometimes raised in a manner that implies museums in the global South are inherently less capable, an assumption that recent investment in new institutions in several African countries has done much to undermine. What seems clear is that the old position, in which possession was treated as its own justification, can no longer be sustained.

topic: deaccessioning: when and why museums should dispose of objects from their collections, restrictions on the use of sale proceeds, and transparency in disposal decisions
title: Letting Go of the Collection
subtitle: Museums dispose of objects far more often than the public realises; the argument is about why, and on whose authority

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Not long ago, a regional art museum announced that it would sell three paintings from its collection to pay for repairs to its leaking roof. The outcry was immediate. Professional associations threatened sanctions, former donors demanded that their gifts be returned, and the director resigned within months. The episode was hardly unique, but it illustrated with unusual clarity a question that museums have long preferred to avoid: under what circumstances, if any, should an institution dispose of objects it has been entrusted to keep? The practice, known as deaccessioning, is far more common than public controversy suggests; most large museums quietly remove hundreds of items from their registers each year. What provokes anger is not disposal itself but disposal for money, and specifically for money spent on anything other than new acquisitions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The professional codes that govern this area typically allow objects to be sold only if the proceeds are used to buy further items for the collection or, in some versions, for the direct care of existing ones. The logic is that a collection is held in trust for the public and must not be treated as a financial reserve to be drawn upon whenever budgets are tight. Professor Ruth Lindebaum, who has written extensively on museum ethics, defends this rule vigorously. Once sales are permitted to cover running costs, she argues, governments and other funders will begin to regard collections as a substitute for public subsidy, and the pressure to sell will become self-perpetuating. Her concern is not hypothetical: in at least two countries, local authorities facing budget cuts have already instructed the museums they run to identify items that could be sold.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet the rule has its critics, and not all of them are cynical administrators looking for easy money. The economist Murat Kaptanoglu points out that the restriction on how proceeds may be used treats the purchase of an object as inherently more valuable than, say, the employment of a conservator or the funding of an education programme for local schools. This hierarchy, in his view, reflects the priorities of a period when museums defined themselves almost entirely through what they owned. He further notes that many institutions hold vast reserves of objects that have not been displayed for decades and, in some cases, have never been examined by a specialist. A painting that hangs in a storeroom serves no public purpose, he contends, and its sale might do more good than its continued retention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kaptanoglu's argument is more persuasive than its opponents tend to admit, but it underestimates how difficult it is to judge in advance which objects will matter to future generations. The history of collecting is full of items dismissed as worthless in one era and treasured in the next. Ethnographic material, folk art and the work of women artists were all, at various times, relegated to storage or quietly disposed of, only to be reassessed later as significant. A sale is irreversible in a way that most other management decisions are not; an exhibition can be redesigned and a programme revived, but an object sold to a private buyer may disappear from public view permanently.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from Dr Lucia Dellamonica, who has studied disposal practices in more than sixty institutions. She argues that the focus on sales has distorted the debate, since the majority of deaccessioned objects are not sold at all but transferred to other museums, returned to donors' families, or destroyed because they are damaged beyond repair or pose a hazard, as some specimens preserved with toxic chemicals do. In her view, the real weakness lies in the process rather than the principle. Decisions are often made by small groups of staff, recorded inadequately, and communicated to the public only after the event. Dellamonica proposes that every planned disposal be published in advance, with a fixed period during which other institutions and members of the public can raise objections or offer to take the object.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such transparency would certainly be an improvement, although it would be naive to imagine that it could settle the matter. Publishing a list of proposed disposals tells the public what a museum intends to do; it does not tell anyone whether the intention is wise. Moreover, smaller institutions, which are most likely to face financial pressure, are also least likely to have the staff needed to manage an elaborate consultation process. There is a real risk that rules designed to prevent hasty sales would, in practice, make responsible disposal so burdensome that unwanted collections simply continue to accumulate, consuming storage space and conservation budgets that might be better spent elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the debate reveals, ultimately, is an unresolved tension in the idea of a museum itself. If a collection exists to be preserved for its own sake, then any disposal is a kind of failure. If, on the other hand, it exists to serve the public, then holding objects that no one sees and no one studies is difficult to justify. Most institutions would claim to believe both things at once, and in ordinary circumstances the contradiction can be left unexamined. Until museums decide, more explicitly than they have so far, which of these purposes takes priority when the two conflict, controversies like the one over the leaking roof will continue to recur.

topic: museum fatigue: tracking studies of declining visitor attention, physical versus cognitive explanations, restorative spaces, visitor agendas and reducing the number of objects on display
title: The Weary Visitor
subtitle: Why do museum-goers stop looking long before they reach the exit, and should museums try to change this?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has spent an afternoon in a large museum will recognise the feeling. After an hour or so of attentive looking, the eyes begin to glide over display cases, labels go unread, and the visitor's main interest shifts to the location of the café. Curators described the phenomenon more than a century ago, when an early study photographed visitors bending and stretching to examine poorly positioned exhibits and concluded that the galleries themselves were exhausting their public. The term 'museum fatigue' has been in use ever since. What has changed is the sophistication of the methods used to study it and, more recently, a growing doubt about whether fatigue is the right word at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Modern research relies heavily on tracking: observers, or increasingly sensors and smartphone signals, record where visitors go and how long they stop. The findings are remarkably consistent across institutions and countries. Visitors typically spend less than half a minute at any single exhibit, and many items receive no attention whatsoever. Time spent per exhibit is highest in the opening galleries and declines steadily thereafter, regardless of what the later galleries contain. In one widely cited analysis, the proportion of visitors stopping at exhibits fell by more than half between the first and final rooms of a natural history museum, even though the final rooms held some of its most celebrated specimens.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The traditional explanation is physical. Dr Owen Brucknell, a specialist in ergonomics, has measured the strain imposed by what he calls 'museum walking', a stop-start shuffle that is, he argues, more tiring than a brisk walk of the same duration. Combined with prolonged standing and the hard floors common in historic buildings, this produces genuine bodily fatigue within an hour. Brucknell's evidence is convincing as far as it goes, but bodily tiredness cannot account for everything. Visitors who are offered seats at regular intervals still show the same decline in attention, if somewhat later, and the decline appears in short visits as well as long ones.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An alternative account treats the problem as one of attention rather than muscle. The psychologist Mila Veselinova describes a process of 'object satiation', in which each new item becomes less interesting simply because so many similar ones have been seen already. In her experiments, participants viewing a sequence of ceramic vessels rated later items as less appealing even when the order was reversed, suggesting that the decline depended on position rather than on the objects themselves. A related line of research, led by Haruki Mizoguchi, draws on theories of mental restoration. Mizoguchi found that visitors who passed through a quiet, sparsely furnished space, such as a garden court or a room containing a single large work, recovered much of their earlier attentiveness, and he recommends that museums deliberately design such pauses into their layouts.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that declining attention is a problem to be solved. Dr Itziar Gorrochategui, who interviews visitors before and after their visits, argues that most people arrive with a clear, if unspoken, agenda: to see a particular object, to entertain a child, or simply to spend a pleasant hour with a friend. Measured against such goals, a visitor who walks briskly past nine-tenths of the collection may have had an entirely successful visit. In her view, researchers have imported an unrealistic ideal of the diligent visitor who examines everything, and then labelled ordinary behaviour as a failure. There is much to be said for this argument, although it risks becoming an excuse for complacency about galleries that are genuinely badly designed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Designers have responded in various ways, from improved lighting to shorter labels, but the most radical response is simply to show less. In an experiment described by the curator Ewa Lewandowicz, a gallery of decorative arts was rehung with roughly a third fewer objects. The time visitors spent on each remaining object increased substantially, but the total length of time they stayed in the gallery hardly changed. Lewandowicz interprets this as evidence that visitors have a fixed 'attention budget', which museums can either spread thinly or concentrate. It is a tidy conclusion, but a single gallery provides too slender a basis for it, and the result might well differ in a museum of science or history, where objects are not primarily viewed for their beauty.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important lesson of this research is that the time visitors spend in front of an exhibit is a poor measure of what they gain from it. A glance at a familiar painting can be deeply moving; a long pause in front of a confusing diagram may reflect nothing more than bewilderment. Museums that judge their galleries solely by tracking data therefore risk designing for the wrong goal. Yet it would be equally mistaken to dismiss the evidence of declining attention. The pattern is too consistent to be ignored, and it suggests that the order in which a collection is presented matters a great deal more than curators have traditionally assumed.

topic: intangible cultural heritage: international listing of living traditions, community consent, the 'fossilising' effect of nomination files, strategic use of recognition and tourism pressures
title: Heritage That Will Not Stand Still
subtitle: Efforts to protect songs, rituals and crafts have raised an awkward question: can a living tradition be safeguarded without being frozen?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Heritage was long understood as something solid: a cathedral, a fortress, a painted manuscript. Over the second half of the twentieth century, however, scholars and officials in many parts of the world began to argue that this definition reflected a distinctly European preoccupation with monuments, and that it ignored forms of culture which exist only in being performed or practised, such as songs, rituals, crafts, culinary traditions and ways of navigating by the stars. The response was the notion of intangible cultural heritage, given formal international recognition in a convention adopted in 2003. States that ratify it undertake to draw up inventories of the living traditions within their territories, and may nominate particular practices for inclusion on international lists. More than five hundred elements have now been inscribed on these lists, ranging from forms of epic singing to techniques of boat-building.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The convention differs from earlier heritage instruments in one crucial respect. Whereas a monument can be conserved by experts with little reference to the people who live near it, an intangible practice survives only if people continue to perform it, so the convention places great emphasis on the participation of the communities concerned. Nominations must, in principle, demonstrate that those communities have given their free and informed consent. In practice, however, nominations are submitted by national governments, and the extent of genuine consultation varies widely. This is not a minor procedural detail. Since a nomination file describes a practice in a particular way, it inevitably privileges some versions of that practice, and some of its practitioners, over others.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The anthropologist Dr Sunita Ramkhelawan has documented what she calls the 'fossilising effect' of listing. In her fieldwork with a mask-dance tradition, she found that the description submitted in the nomination file, which was based largely on the recollections of a few senior performers, quickly became treated as the authentic form of the dance. Variations that had previously been common, including regional differences in costume and the participation of women in certain roles, came to be regarded as departures from the correct version. Within a decade, Ramkhelawan reports, a tradition that had always been fluid had acquired something close to an official script. Her conclusion is that the very act of describing a living practice for administrative purposes tends to arrest the changes that kept it alive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Dilnoza Yuldasheva, who has studied the effects of listing across a wider range of cases, offers a more positive assessment. In a survey of forty inscribed elements, she found that in twenty-eight cases practitioners reported increased interest among young people following inscription, and in thirty cases new sources of public funding had become available. Yuldasheva acknowledges that inscription can alter a tradition, but she points out that communities are far from passive in this process. Many, she argues, use international recognition strategically, to gain leverage over national governments or to resist pressures, such as land development, that threaten the conditions on which their practices depend.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third concern relates to tourism. Dr Bence Csengeri, an economist who studies cultural tourism, has found that inscription is frequently followed by a marked increase in visitor numbers, particularly where the practice involves public performance or food. In one coastal region he studied, attendance at an annual festival roughly tripled in the five years after inscription. The economic benefits were considerable, but Csengeri also observed that performances were shortened, rescheduled to suit tour itineraries and, in some cases, staged outside their customary season. He does not argue that such changes are necessarily harmful; rather, he notes that the decisions about them were taken mainly by tourism agencies and local authorities rather than by practitioners themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the problem lies less with the idea of intangible heritage than with the administrative tools used to protect it. Inventories and nomination files are designed to identify and fix, which is appropriate for a building but sits uneasily with practices whose vitality depends on adaptation. Ramkhelawan's account of fossilisation is compelling, yet her evidence comes largely from a single tradition, and Yuldasheva's broader survey makes it difficult to treat her findings as typical. On the other hand, Yuldasheva's reliance on practitioners' own reports may overstate the benefits, since those who responded were often the individuals who had gained most from inscription.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What these debates expose is a question the convention has never fully resolved: who speaks for a tradition? A practice shared by thousands of people across several regions is unlikely to have a single authoritative voice, and any process that requires one will inevitably elevate some practitioners while marginalising others. The most promising recent initiatives have tried to address this by allowing inventories to record disagreement and variation rather than a single standard description. Such approaches are messier and harder to administer, and they will not satisfy officials who want clear criteria for funding decisions. But they come considerably closer to reflecting the nature of the thing being protected, which is, after all, not an object but a set of relationships between people.

topic: museum storage and the unseen majority of collections: research value of stored material, overcrowded and uncatalogued stores, visible storage, shared storage centres and digitisation
title: Behind the Storeroom Door
subtitle: Most of what museums own is never on display. Is that a scandal, or simply what museums are for?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk through the galleries of almost any major museum and you will see only a small fraction of what it owns. Estimates vary between institutions, but it is commonly suggested that large museums display no more than five to ten per cent of their holdings at any one time; for natural history and archaeological collections, which may contain millions of specimens and fragments, the proportion can be far lower. The remainder sits in storerooms, basements and, increasingly, purpose-built warehouses on the edges of cities. To many members of the public, this seems a scandal. Newspaper articles regularly describe 'hidden treasures' locked away from view, and politicians occasionally demand to know why taxpayers should fund the care of objects that nobody is allowed to see.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Such criticism rests on a misunderstanding of what museum storage is for. A collection is not simply a stock of exhibits waiting their turn on display; it is also a research resource, and much of its value lies in its completeness. A single beetle specimen may be of little interest to a casual visitor, but a drawer containing several hundred individuals of the same species, collected over a century from many locations, can reveal how its range and body size have changed in response to a warming climate. Such material would make a dull exhibition, yet it is precisely the kind of evidence on which researchers increasingly rely. To judge stored collections by their suitability for display is to apply the wrong standard entirely.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That said, the scale of what museums hold has become a genuine problem. Dr Paola Galeazzi, a collections manager who has surveyed storage conditions in over a hundred institutions, reports that around a third of them describe their stores as full or overcrowded, and that many lack adequate records of what those stores contain. In some cases, she found, objects had been acquired decades ago and never catalogued at all, so that the museum could not say with confidence whether a particular item was in its possession. Galeazzi argues that the priority should be documentation rather than display: until a museum knows what it holds, debates about how much of it the public should see are premature.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One response to public criticism has been 'visible storage', in which stored objects are arranged in glass-fronted cabinets or on open shelving that visitors can walk among. Supporters claim that this allows thousands of items to be seen without the cost of designing conventional exhibitions, and that visitors enjoy the sense of glimpsing a museum's inner workings. Dr Chidi Ukaegbu, who has evaluated several such schemes, is unconvinced. Her observations suggest that visitors spend even less time per object in visible storage than in ordinary galleries, largely because the objects are presented with minimal interpretation. In her view, visible storage satisfies a demand for transparency without greatly increasing understanding.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ukaegbu's findings are a useful corrective, but they may set the bar unreasonably high. Not every museum experience needs to be measured by how much visitors learn; the simple experience of abundance, of seeing three hundred teapots or a wall of carved doors, can itself convey something about the scale of human making that no carefully selected display could. The more serious objection to visible storage is practical: open arrangements expose objects to dust, light and handling, and some materials simply cannot be kept safely in such conditions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different approach looks beyond the individual museum altogether. In several countries, groups of institutions have begun to pool their resources in shared storage centres, where collections from a number of museums are kept under a single roof with common environmental controls and specialist staff. The architect Henrik Sørbråten, who has designed two such facilities, argues that consolidation not only reduces costs but also makes collections easier for researchers to use, since related material from different institutions can be studied side by side. Critics worry that removing objects from local museums weakens the connection between communities and their heritage, though Sørbråten counters that most of the items concerned were never on local display in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Digitisation offers a further way to open stores to the public, and many museums now publish online catalogues containing images of objects that have never been exhibited. The benefits are real but often exaggerated. Photographing and describing millions of items is enormously expensive, and online catalogues are used far less than their creators hope; one museum found that more than half of the records it had placed online had not been viewed even once in the following year. Digital access can supplement physical access, but it would be unwise to treat it as a solution to the storage problem rather than as an addition to the work involved.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The debate over storage, then, is really a debate about what museums are for. If they are primarily places of display, then vast reserves of unseen objects are hard to defend. If they are also archives of material evidence, held for purposes that cannot always be foreseen, then storage is not a failure but a core function, and one that deserves far more public explanation, and far more funding, than it currently receives. Museums have been slow to make this case, perhaps because storerooms lack the glamour of new galleries; they will need to make it more confidently if the criticism is to be answered.

topic: rebuilding monuments destroyed in war: conservation doctrine against replicas, community meaning, donor-driven reconstruction, 3D scanning and the reuse of surviving fragments
title: Out of the Rubble
subtitle: When war destroys a cherished monument, should it be rebuilt exactly, preserved as a ruin, or something in between?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a monument is destroyed in war, the question of what to do next arrives with unusual urgency. The rubble of a mosque, a cathedral or an ancient bridge is not merely a heap of stone; it is evidence of a deliberate attack on a community's memory, and the decision about whether and how to rebuild becomes a statement about the future as much as the past. Over the past three decades, conflicts in several regions have destroyed or badly damaged hundreds of historic structures, many of them targeted precisely because of what they symbolised. The international response has generated an intense, and sometimes bitter, debate among the professionals responsible for heritage.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the dominant view in conservation was hostile to reconstruction. Influential charters drafted by heritage professionals insisted that historic buildings should be repaired with as little intervention as possible, and that new work should always be distinguishable from old. Rebuilding a vanished structure from scratch was regarded as a kind of forgery. The conservation theorist Pieter Hendrikse remains a forceful advocate of this position. A replica, he argues, can reproduce a building's appearance but not its history; it presents the visitor with a falsely seamless past and, worse, conceals the very violence that destroyed the original. In his view, damaged monuments should be stabilised and preserved as ruins, so that they continue to bear witness to what happened.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet this doctrine has always sat uneasily with practice. After the Second World War, the historic centre of one European capital was rebuilt almost entirely, using eighteenth-century paintings and pre-war architectural drawings as guides, and the result was later recognised as a heritage site in its own right. The architectural historian Yasmin Mazrouei sees in such cases evidence that the value of a monument resides less in its original materials than in the meanings people attach to it. For a community that has lost a building central to its identity, she contends, a faithful reconstruction is not a forgery but an act of recovery; insisting on ruins may simply prolong the injury. Mazrouei's argument is powerful, and Hendrikse's position, whatever its intellectual consistency, seems to assume that experts rather than residents should decide what a monument means.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That is not to say that reconstruction is always welcomed by the people it is meant to serve. The sociologist Mirela Perendić has interviewed residents of several war-damaged towns and found that their priorities were frequently housing, employment and the return of displaced relatives, with the restoration of monuments ranked well below these. Because major reconstruction projects are often paid for by foreign governments or international organisations, Perendić argues, they can end up reflecting the preferences of donors, for whom a rebuilt landmark offers a highly visible symbol of their generosity, rather than those of local people. Her findings should give pause to anyone who assumes that rebuilding a famous structure is automatically an act of healing.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Technology has added a new dimension to the debate. Detailed three-dimensional scans of many vulnerable sites were made in the years before they were damaged, and the engineer Karim Aldabagh has argued that these records make it possible to reconstruct lost structures with a precision unimaginable a generation ago. The claim is true as far as it goes, but scans record surfaces, not the methods by which a building was made. A digitally guided reconstruction may reproduce every carved detail while using concrete cores and steel reinforcement in place of traditional masonry, producing something that looks identical to the original but behaves quite differently and contains none of the knowledge embodied in it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The archaeologist Ana Vintilescu proposes a middle course. In the projects she has advised on, surviving fragments are reincorporated into the rebuilt structure, but in a way that leaves them visibly distinct from the new stone, so that the building tells the story of both its creation and its destruction. She also insists that reconstruction should, wherever possible, use traditional techniques and employ local craftspeople, arguing that the training of a new generation of masons is as important a form of heritage as the building itself. This approach has much to recommend it, though it is slower and more expensive than either leaving a ruin or erecting a precise replica, and it may not satisfy communities who want their monument back exactly as it was.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these competing views is that no single principle can settle every case. A rule against reconstruction protects the integrity of the historical record but may deny communities something they deeply value; a presumption in favour of rebuilding risks turning heritage into a stage set designed to please donors and attract visitors. The most defensible decisions are likely to be those in which the people who live alongside a monument have a genuine say, and in which the reasons for choosing one approach over another are made explicit rather than assumed. That will rarely produce quick results, but haste has seldom served damaged heritage well.

topic: touch in museums: the history of the 'do not touch' rule, research on handling and memory, cumulative damage from handling, tactile access for visually impaired visitors, handling collections, 3D-printed replicas and gloves
title: Please Do Not Touch?
subtitle: The ban on handling museum objects is younger than most people think, and it is being questioned as never before

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visitors to the earliest public museums in Europe expected to touch what they saw. Accounts written in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries describe guests lifting vessels to feel their weight, running their fingers over carved surfaces and even, on occasion, tasting mineral specimens in order to identify them. Handling was regarded as a natural part of polite curiosity, and a host who refused it would have been thought ungracious. It was only during the nineteenth century, as museums opened their doors to much larger and socially broader audiences, that the familiar rule of 'look but do not touch' became firmly established. The prohibition, in other words, is not a timeless principle of museum practice but a relatively recent convention, shaped as much by anxieties about crowds as by concern for the objects themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In recent years, that convention has come under pressure from several directions. The most influential has been psychological research suggesting that touch plays a significant role in how people learn about and remember objects. In a series of studies by the cognitive psychologist Dr Aino Vainikka, participants who handled replica artefacts were able to recall considerably more about them a week later than those who had only looked at the same items through glass. Vainikka argues that touch supplies information about weight, temperature and texture that vision cannot, and that it also creates a stronger sense of personal connection with the past, which in turn makes the experience more memorable. She also reports that the effect is strongest for objects whose purpose is not obvious from their appearance, such as tools and scientific instruments, where the hand seems to grasp what the eye alone misses.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These findings are intriguing, though they should not be overstated. Most of Vainikka's participants were university students tested under laboratory conditions, and it is not obvious that the effect would be as large among, say, families with young children moving quickly through a busy gallery. Nor is it clear how much of the benefit comes from touch itself and how much from the novelty of being allowed to do something normally forbidden; if handling became routine, its advantage might diminish. None of this undermines the case for touch, but it suggests that the claims made for it in some museum publicity have run ahead of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Against these potential benefits must be set the risks. The conservator Dr Helen Lockridge has spent much of her career measuring the cumulative effects of handling, and her conclusions are sobering. Even clean hands deposit oils, salts and moisture, which over time can stain metals, discolour stone and weaken textiles. A single touch does negligible harm, but popular objects in a busy museum may be touched hundreds of thousands of times a year. Lockridge points to bronze sculptures whose feet have been polished bright by generations of admirers, and to stone steps hollowed by centuries of footfall, as reminders that small acts repeated endlessly produce dramatic change. Her conclusion is not that touch should be banned entirely, but that it must be confined to objects chosen specifically because they can tolerate it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The debate has also been reframed by campaigners for visitors with disabilities. Dr Rania Raffoul, a researcher in disability studies who is herself partially sighted, argues that for blind and visually impaired people the ban on touch is not a minor inconvenience but an almost total exclusion from the experience museums offer. Audio guides and large-print labels, she points out, describe objects at second hand, whereas touch allows a visitor to form an independent judgement of an object's form and craftsmanship. Many institutions now run occasional 'touch tours', but Raffoul regards these as inadequate, since they typically require advance booking, take place only a few times a year and cover a handful of objects selected for their durability rather than their importance. In her view, access through touch should be treated as a right, comparable to wheelchair access, rather than as a special favour.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Museums have responded with a range of compromises. Many maintain handling collections made up of duplicate items, minor pieces or objects already damaged, which can be touched freely without endangering anything of significance. Others have begun to produce three-dimensional printed copies of important works specifically for tactile exploration, sometimes placing them in the galleries beside the originals so that touch becomes part of an ordinary visit rather than a separate activity. The second approach seems particularly promising, because in this context the information conveyed through touch, the shape, proportions and surface of an object, is exactly what a good copy can reproduce. Handling collections, by contrast, risk creating a two-tier system in which visitors who rely on touch are offered only the objects nobody else much wants to see.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question of gloves illustrates how unsettled the field remains. For decades, cotton gloves were regarded as essential whenever an object was handled, even by experienced staff. Many conservators now argue that gloves can be counter-productive, reducing grip and sensitivity so that objects are more likely to be dropped, and that for many materials clean, dry hands are actually safer. Close-fitting synthetic gloves have replaced cotton in some institutions, but the underlying disagreement has not gone away. If professionals themselves are reconsidering such a basic rule, it seems reasonable to expect that museums will continue to revise their policies on visitor touch, and that the boundaries of what may be handled will shift again in the coming decades.

topic: overtourism at heritage sites: the effect of international listing on visitor numbers, depopulation of historic town centres, visitor caps and timed tickets, entrance pricing, dispersal to lesser-known sites and mobile-phone data on day visitors
title: Loved to Death
subtitle: Crowds are threatening some of the world's most treasured historic places, but the familiar diagnosis of 'too many tourists' may be too simple

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few phrases have entered the vocabulary of heritage management as rapidly as 'overtourism'. Barely heard fifteen years ago, it now appears routinely in newspaper headlines, municipal strategies and academic conferences, usually accompanied by images of narrow medieval streets packed shoulder to shoulder with visitors. The concern is real enough. Between the early 1990s and the late 2010s, international tourist arrivals worldwide more than doubled, and a disproportionate share of that growth was absorbed by a relatively small number of famous historic cities and archaeological sites. Yet the term itself is less helpful than its popularity suggests. It implies that the problem is simply one of excessive numbers, when the evidence points to something more complicated: a question of when, where and how visitors arrive, and of who benefits from their presence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider the effect of international recognition. Inscription on a prestigious heritage list is often sought by governments in the expectation that it will attract visitors and investment, and it frequently does. The tourism economist Professor Sigrid Kjeldsen has calculated that, for sites that were not already well known, visitor numbers rose by an average of around thirty per cent in the five years following inscription. For sites that were already famous, the effect was negligible. Kjeldsen's work therefore suggests that this 'label effect' matters most for precisely the places least equipped to cope with a sudden influx, since lesser-known sites rarely have the visitor facilities, staff or management plans that established ones possess.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The pressures on living historic towns are of a different order from those on archaeological sites. The urban geographer Dr Marco Pandolfini has tracked population change in several historic centres over three decades, and found that in the most visited of them the number of permanent residents fell by between a quarter and a half. The principal cause, in his analysis, was the conversion of housing into short-term holiday rentals, which pushed up rents and replaced shops serving residents, such as bakers and hardware stores, with souvenir outlets and cafés. Pandolfini describes the result as 'museumification': a town that continues to look historic but has lost the everyday life that once gave it meaning. It is hard to disagree with his diagnosis, although the term risks implying that museums themselves are lifeless, which is hardly fair to them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: At archaeological sites, where nobody lives, managers have more freedom to act. Dr Patrice Tshimanga, who directs a large site of ancient ruins, introduced timed tickets and a daily cap on visitor numbers after years of damage to fragile paving and wall paintings. In the first three years, he reports, measurable erosion along the main routes fell by more than half, and surveys indicated that visitors were more satisfied with their experience, even though some had to book weeks in advance. Tshimanga's results are impressive, but they cannot simply be transferred to cities. A ruined town can be closed at the gate; a living one cannot, and attempts to limit entry to historic districts raise awkward questions about the rights of residents and their guests.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Pricing is another commonly proposed tool. Kjeldsen argues that significantly higher entrance charges at the most popular sites would reduce crowding while raising revenue for conservation. There is a logic to this, but it is not without cost. High fees fall most heavily on those with least money, including, in many cases, citizens of the very country to which the heritage belongs. Some sites have attempted to address this by offering reduced prices to local residents, though such schemes can be difficult to administer and occasionally provoke accusations of discrimination from foreign visitors.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An alternative strategy aims not to reduce numbers but to spread them. The sociologist Dr Élodie Bourdonnais points out that, in most countries she has studied, the great majority of heritage visitors go to a tiny fraction of available sites, while hundreds of others of comparable interest receive few visitors at all. Promoting these neglected places, she argues, would ease pressure on the famous ones and bring economic benefits to regions that currently see little of the tourist trade. The idea is attractive, but it rests on the assumption that visitors are willing to substitute one site for another, and there is little evidence that this is so. A traveller who has crossed the world to see one celebrated monument is unlikely to be satisfied with a less famous alternative, however worthy.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Better information may at least help managers understand what they face. The data scientist Lev Arkhipenko has used anonymised mobile phone records to map the movements of visitors in several historic cities. His findings show that the most intense crowding is often caused not by overnight tourists but by day visitors, particularly passengers from cruise ships, who arrive in large groups, concentrate on a few streets for a few hours and spend relatively little money locally. Such evidence makes it possible to target measures much more precisely, for instance by staggering the arrival times of ships rather than restricting tourism as a whole.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of these approaches offers a complete solution, and each carries trade-offs that are ultimately political rather than technical. Whose interests should prevail when residents, visitors, businesses and conservators want different things? There is no formula that can answer that question once and for all. The places that seem to have managed best, however, are those in which residents have had a real voice in setting limits, rather than having decisions imposed by national authorities or simply left to the market.

topic: ecomuseums and community-run 'museums without walls': defining criteria, whose voices community participation represents, nostalgia in post-industrial areas, financial sustainability and influence on mainstream museums
title: Museums Without Walls
subtitle: Fifty years ago, a radical idea proposed that a whole landscape and its people could become a museum. How has it fared?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 1970s, a small group of French museum professionals coined a new word to describe an institution that did not yet exist. The 'ecomuseum', as they imagined it, would have no single building and no permanent collection in the conventional sense. Instead, it would encompass an entire territory, such as a valley, an island or an industrial district, and treat its landscapes, buildings, skills and memories as heritage to be interpreted where they stood. Its 'exhibits' might include a working farm, a chapel, a disused railway station or the knowledge of an elderly basket-maker, each understood in its original setting rather than removed to a display case. Above all, it would be run not by curators for visitors but by local inhabitants for themselves. Half a century later, several hundred institutions around the world describe themselves as ecomuseums, from former mining regions in Europe to rice-growing villages in East Asia. Whether they have lived up to the original vision is a matter of considerable debate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The museologist Professor Tomasz Gwiazdowski has proposed a widely used way of identifying a genuine ecomuseum. In his account, it involves three shifts away from the traditional museum: from a building to a territory, from a collection to a broader notion of heritage, and from an audience of visitors to a community of participants. By this standard, he argues, many institutions that carry the label are ecomuseums in name only. Some are conventional local history museums that have adopted a fashionable title; others are heritage trails designed by regional tourist boards, with little involvement from the people whose lives they depict. Gwiazdowski's criteria are useful as an ideal, but applied strictly they would exclude almost every existing example, which suggests that the definition may be too demanding to guide practice.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The third of his shifts, the idea of community participation, has proved both the most attractive and the most problematic. The anthropologist Dr Funmilayo Oloruntoba spent two years studying an ecomuseum in a former coal-mining valley, where local volunteers had restored a pithead, recorded interviews with retired miners and organised an annual festival celebrating the industry. The project was widely praised. Yet Oloruntoba found that the history it presented was overwhelmingly that of the men who had worked underground. The experiences of women, who had run households on uncertain wages and organised support during strikes, received little attention, and the families of migrants who had arrived after the mines closed were almost entirely absent. 'Community', she concludes, is too often treated as a single voice, when in practice it is the most confident and established residents who speak.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This is an important corrective, though it applies to heritage projects of many kinds and not to ecomuseums alone. Any account of the past selects and omits; what distinguishes the ecomuseum is that its omissions are made by residents rather than by outside experts, which at least makes them open to challenge by neighbours. There is also a risk, which Oloruntoba's study illustrates, that ecomuseums in declining industrial areas become exercises in nostalgia, celebrating a vanished way of life while saying little about the problems that the community faces now. An ecomuseum that helps people understand why their mine closed seems more valuable than one that merely mourns it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The economic dimension adds further complications. Many ecomuseums were established in the hope that they would contribute to the regeneration of struggling regions, attracting visitors and creating jobs. Supporters pointed to the success of large open-air museums elsewhere as proof that heritage could draw tourists to remote areas. The regional economist Dr Inês Carrapiço surveyed twenty-five such institutions and found that, in most cases, visitor income was modest and rarely covered running costs. Nearly all depended heavily on public grants and on volunteers, and several had closed when a key volunteer moved away or a grant was not renewed. The institutions that had survived longest, Carrapiço observed, almost all employed at least one paid coordinator, whose role was not to direct the project but to sustain it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Carrapiço's findings undermine a romantic assumption that sometimes surrounds the ecomuseum: that enthusiasm alone can sustain a cultural institution indefinitely. Volunteers can achieve remarkable things, but asking a small number of residents to maintain buildings, guide visitors and raise funds year after year is a recipe for exhaustion. If ecomuseums are to be treated as genuine public institutions, they will need a modest but reliable level of public support, of the kind that conventional museums take for granted. This need not mean surrendering control to officials; the paid coordinators in Carrapiço's study served the volunteers rather than replacing them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most lasting influence of the ecomuseum, however, has been on museums that never adopted the name. Ideas that once seemed radical, such as collecting oral testimony, involving local people in deciding what to display, and interpreting heritage in the landscape rather than only in galleries, are now commonplace in mainstream institutions. Even large national museums routinely invite community groups to help shape displays about their own histories. In this sense, the movement may have succeeded less by multiplying ecomuseums than by changing what all museums regard as part of their work. That is a quieter achievement than its founders hoped for, but it is by no means a small one.
