topic: museum climate-control standards: the origins of the fixed 50 per cent humidity rule, laboratory evidence for wider tolerances, energy costs of air conditioning, risks to composite objects, and loan agreements as a barrier to change
title: The Fifty Per Cent Rule
subtitle: For decades, museums have held their galleries at fixed temperature and humidity. The scientific basis for doing so is weaker than many assumed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the past seventy years, the inside of a major museum has been one of the most tightly controlled environments that ordinary people are likely to encounter. Galleries and storerooms were kept, day and night and throughout the year, at a temperature of around twenty degrees Celsius and a relative humidity close to fifty per cent, with permitted variations of only a few percentage points. These figures came to be treated almost as laws of nature. They were written into building specifications, insurance policies and, crucially, the agreements under which museums lend objects to one another. Over the past fifteen years, however, they have been questioned with increasing force, partly because of new scientific evidence and partly because maintaining them consumes enormous quantities of energy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The historian of conservation Dr Konrad Barthelmess has traced the origins of the standard and found them surprisingly casual. During the Second World War, the paintings of one national collection were evacuated to an underground quarry, where conditions happened to remain stable at roughly the levels later adopted as the norm. When the paintings emerged in good condition, curators concluded that those particular conditions were ideal. The early air-conditioning equipment installed in museums after the war could, moreover, hold conditions around those values more easily than others. In Barthelmess's view, the fifty per cent figure was therefore less a scientific finding than a convenient compromise that later acquired the authority of science. His account is persuasive, and it helps to explain why the standard proved so resistant to challenge: its status depended on habit rather than on evidence that could be re-examined.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The scientific case for relaxation rests largely on laboratory work. The conservation scientist Dr Willem Osterhout has subjected samples of wood, canvas, paint layers and other materials to controlled cycles of humidity change, measuring the point at which they begin to crack, warp or separate into layers. His results indicate that most materials can tolerate fluctuations within a band of roughly forty to sixty per cent relative humidity without measurable damage, provided that changes occur gradually. On this basis, he argues that the tight tolerances of the traditional standard offer little additional protection while imposing very large costs.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Those costs are considerable. The energy engineer Dr Camila Fajardo has calculated that climate control can account for more than half of the total energy consumption of a large museum. In a study of twelve institutions that adopted wider humidity and temperature bands, she found that energy use for heating, cooling and humidity control fell by about a third on average, with no increase in recorded damage to collections over the following five years. Fajardo cautions that five years is a short period in the life of an object, but she points out that museums which cling to the old figures are spending a great deal of money, and generating substantial emissions, to guard against risks that may be largely imaginary.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is reassured. The conservator Dr Saara Rehunen accepts that many objects can safely experience wider fluctuations, but she warns against treating laboratory samples as representative of real collections. Historic objects are rarely made of a single material; a painted panel, an inlaid cabinet or a musical instrument combines materials that respond to moisture at different rates, and old repairs may introduce further weaknesses. Rehunen also questions the widely held belief that objects which have survived centuries of fluctuating conditions are thereby 'proofed' against future change. An object that has spent the last fifty years in a tightly controlled museum may have lost whatever resilience it once had. She favours assessing the risks for each object or group of objects individually rather than adopting a new universal rule.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Rehunen's caution is well founded, and it points to a danger in the current debate. Having discovered that the old standard was arbitrary, the profession should be wary of simply replacing it with a new set of numbers, however much better supported. A wider band is still a band, and if it is applied without regard to the needs of particular objects, it may protect some items too much and others too little. The real lesson of the past seventy years is not that fifty per cent was the wrong figure, but that any single figure is a poor substitute for informed judgement.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most stubborn obstacle to change, however, may be institutional rather than scientific. Professor Astrid Nygaard, who has studied loan agreements between museums, notes that lenders routinely require borrowers to maintain the traditional conditions, and that insurers often insist on these clauses. A museum that relaxes its own standards may therefore find itself unable to borrow important works for exhibitions, which are often its most effective means of attracting visitors. Nygaard argues that no individual institution can afford to break ranks, and that change will come only if major museums agree collectively to revise the conditions they demand of one another.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Climate change gives the question added urgency. As summers grow hotter and energy prices more volatile, the cost of holding galleries at fixed conditions will rise, and museums that present themselves as guardians of the future can hardly ignore the emissions their buildings produce. The evidence now available suggests that caring for collections and limiting environmental harm need not be in conflict, provided that the old certainties are replaced by careful, object-centred assessment rather than by new dogma. That is a more demanding approach than following a number, but it is the only one consistent with what is now known.

topic: inclusionary zoning: requiring developers to provide below-market homes, who bears the cost, density bonuses and 'poor doors', scale and the duration of affordability
title: Affordable by Obligation
subtitle: Cities increasingly require developers to build cheaper homes alongside expensive ones, but the policy promises more than it can deliver

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few housing policies have spread as rapidly in recent decades as inclusionary zoning. The principle is simple: when a developer applies for permission to build homes, the local authority makes approval conditional on a proportion of the new units, typically between ten and thirty per cent, being offered at rents or prices below the market rate. To politicians, the attraction is obvious. Affordable homes appear to materialise without any call on public budgets, and the burden seems to fall on an industry that rarely commands much public sympathy. That impression, however, is misleading. Somebody always pays for a below-market home, and the central question in the debate is not whether inclusionary zoning has costs but who ends up bearing them and whether the benefits justify them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most sustained critique has come from economists who treat the requirement as a form of tax on construction. Signe Lindgård, an urban economist at the Øresund Institute for Urban Economics, argues that a developer faced with the obligation has only three options: to pay less for land, to charge more for the market-rate units in the same scheme, or to abandon marginal projects altogether. Each of these, she contends, works against affordability in the wider market. Her study of thirty-seven municipalities that introduced mandatory schemes found that applications for residential permits fell by around eight per cent over the following three years. Lindgård herself concedes that the figure needs careful interpretation, since part of the decline reflects developers hurrying to submit applications before the rules came into force, which artificially inflated the earlier numbers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the policy dispute where the burden ultimately lands. Rustam Abakarov, a planning lawyer who has advised several city governments, maintains that if the requirement is known well in advance, it is absorbed largely by landowners, because developers simply bid less for sites. In his view, the damage Lindgård identifies is caused not by inclusionary zoning itself but by its sudden imposition on projects whose land was bought under the old rules. The remedy, he suggests, is to announce requirements years before they take effect and to phase them in gradually. There is much to be said for this argument, and transitional arrangements clearly matter. Yet it rests on the assumption that landowners will accept lower offers, when many of them, particularly those under no pressure to sell, may simply keep their land off the market and wait for the policy to change.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second strand of the debate concerns design. Many cities avoid outright mandates and instead offer density bonuses, allowing developers to build additional floors in return for providing affordable units. Elena Salgueiro, who coordinates research for the National Federation of Tenants' Associations, has documented the results in a dozen cities and is unimpressed. Voluntary schemes, she reports, generate far fewer homes than mandatory ones, and the units they do produce are often located in a separate building or reached through a separate entrance, an arrangement critics have labelled the 'poor door'. Such arrangements deserve more criticism than they usually receive. The standard justification for inclusionary zoning is that it creates mixed communities in which households of different incomes share streets and services; a building that divides its residents by entrance undermines the very purpose the policy is meant to serve.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even well-designed programmes, however, operate on a modest scale. Because affordable units are produced only when market housing is built, output rises and falls with the property cycle, and it shrinks precisely when a downturn makes affordable homes most needed. One of the longest-running schemes, in a large North American city, has been in place for a quarter of a century and has yielded several thousand homes, an achievement that sounds considerable until one learns that it represents roughly four per cent of the city's affordable stock. It would be unreasonable to expect inclusionary zoning to replace direct public investment in housing. At best it is a supplement, and governments that present it as a substitute are avoiding a more expensive commitment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further problem, long overlooked, is how long affordability lasts. Early schemes commonly required units to remain below market price for only fifteen or twenty years, after which they could be sold or let at full value. Researchers at the Westbourne Housing Observatory traced the units produced in the 1980s across six cities and found that more than half had since passed into the open market. Most recent programmes therefore impose permanent restrictions, recorded in legal covenants attached to the property. This solves one problem but creates another: owner-occupiers of permanently restricted homes can sell only at a capped price, so they accumulate little wealth from their property, which some households regard as a significant disadvantage compared with ordinary ownership.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be expected of inclusionary zoning? Judged as a solution to the affordability crisis, it inevitably disappoints, but that is arguably the wrong test. Its more important contribution may be to establish a principle: that when public decisions about land use create private wealth, some of that wealth should be returned to the community. That principle is worth defending, provided that its advocates are honest about the limited number of homes it can deliver and do not allow it to become an excuse for inaction elsewhere.

topic: superblocks: closing interior streets to through traffic, traffic evaporation versus displacement, noise and health, effects on local shops, rising rents and tactical urbanism
title: Reclaiming the Grid
subtitle: Superblocks promise quieter, greener neighbourhoods by pushing traffic to the edges, but the evidence for their benefits is still being assembled

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the street was treated primarily as a channel for moving vehicles. Pavements narrowed, junctions were widened and children's play was pushed indoors or into designated parks. The superblock reverses this logic. A group of city blocks, typically arranged in a three-by-three square, is treated as a single unit: through traffic is diverted to the roads around its edge, while the interior streets are restricted to residents, deliveries and emergency vehicles travelling at walking pace. The space released is given over to benches, trees and play equipment. Few recent experiments in urban planning have attracted so much international attention, and the enthusiasm is understandable. Nevertheless, it has run some way ahead of the evidence, and several of the claims made on behalf of superblocks deserve closer scrutiny.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most fundamental question is what happens to the traffic. Supporters often invoke the phenomenon known as traffic evaporation, in which a proportion of car journeys simply cease when road space is removed, as drivers switch to other modes, combine trips or travel less. Luca Montagnani, a transport engineer at the Ligurian Polytechnic, accepts that evaporation is real but believes its scale is routinely exaggerated. His modelling of a medium-sized city suggests that perhaps one journey in five would disappear if a network of superblocks were introduced; the remainder would be redistributed onto the perimeter roads, where congestion and pollution would rise. Montagnani does not regard this as a reason to abandon the idea, but he argues that schemes should be judged by their effects on the whole district rather than on the pleasant interior streets that visitors photograph.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This point has a direct bearing on the health benefits that are often cited. Agnieszka Kwiatkowska, an environmental epidemiologist, has estimated that a citywide programme could prevent a substantial number of premature deaths each year, mainly through reductions in traffic noise and, to a lesser degree, in nitrogen dioxide. Her emphasis on noise is unusual, since public debate tends to focus on air quality, but she points out that chronic exposure to road noise is associated with disturbed sleep and raised blood pressure, and that noise falls very sharply once vehicles are removed from a street. Her figures are carefully derived, yet they assume that pollution displaced to the perimeter will be modest. If Montagnani's modelling is correct, the net gain may be considerably smaller than her projections imply, at least for people who live on the boundary roads.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Local businesses have been among the most vocal opponents of superblocks, and their anxieties are not difficult to understand. Shopkeepers fear that once cars are excluded they will lose passing trade, and that deliveries will become slow and expensive. Research by the retail economist Hugh Ockenden offers some reassurance. Comparing sales data from shops inside and outside several pilot schemes, he found that turnover on the interior streets typically dipped during the first year but recovered and then exceeded previous levels, as more people walked and lingered. He also found that shopkeepers consistently overestimated the proportion of their customers who arrived by car, in some cases believing it to be twice the true figure. Deliveries, however, did become more difficult, and Ockenden recommends designated loading hours rather than unrestricted access.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more troubling objection concerns who ultimately benefits. The sociologist Oyuna Baatarkhuu has tracked residential rents in neighbourhoods where superblocks were installed and reports that within five years they rose noticeably faster than in comparable areas. In her view, a quieter, greener street is precisely the kind of amenity that is quickly reflected in property prices, so that the long-standing tenants for whom such schemes are supposedly designed may eventually be unable to afford to stay. The danger is real, but it does not follow that superblocks should be avoided. Rising rents near any improvement are an argument for stronger protections for tenants, not for keeping poorer neighbourhoods noisy and polluted; otherwise, the same logic would condemn every public investment in such areas.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One feature of the superblock model that is often overlooked is the way it is implemented. Rather than rebuilding streets from scratch, many cities begin with what is sometimes called tactical urbanism: road markings are repainted, large planters block vehicle access and movable furniture is placed in the roadway. Critics complain that the results can look improvised and untidy. That is, however, a strength rather than a weakness. Inexpensive, temporary measures allow a city to test a layout, observe how residents respond and adjust or reverse it before committing to costly permanent works. They also make it far easier to win public consent, because residents are being asked to accept an experiment rather than an irreversible decision.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, finally, to assume that the model can be transplanted unchanged to any city. Superblocks were conceived for a regular grid of streets, and in older cities with irregular, winding networks it is much harder to identify coherent units or to find suitable alternative routes for through traffic. Even so, the underlying principle, that streets in residential areas should serve the people who live on them before the vehicles passing through, is sound and widely applicable. What is needed now is not more advocacy but systematic monitoring of the schemes already in place, so that the next generation can be designed on firmer ground.

topic: rent control: first-generation freezes versus second-generation rent stabilisation, effects on rental supply and tenant stability, scheme design loopholes and housing allowances
title: The Ceiling on Rents
subtitle: Economists have long condemned rent control, but the modern version of the policy is a different creature from the one they first attacked

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few policies divide economists and the public as sharply as rent control. Polls in many cities show that capping rents is consistently popular with voters, while surveys of professional economists have for decades recorded something close to unanimous opposition. The policy itself has a long history. Many governments first imposed restrictions on rents during the First World War, when munitions workers flooding into industrial towns drove housing costs sharply upwards, and in a number of countries the controls were never fully removed. It is worth noting, however, that the economic consensus against rent control was formed largely in response to the blunt rent freezes of that era. Whether it applies with equal force to the more sophisticated systems that have since replaced them is a separate question, and one that has received less attention than it deserves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic case against rent control rests on three arguments. First, if rents are held below the level the market would set, investors will build fewer rental homes, worsening the very shortage that controls were meant to relieve. Second, landlords receiving a fixed income have little incentive to maintain their properties, so that controlled buildings gradually deteriorate; the decaying apartment blocks of several post-war European cities are frequently cited as evidence. Third, controls discourage mobility. Tenants who pay far less than the market rate are reluctant to move, even when their flat no longer matches their needs, with the result that elderly couples remain in large family apartments while young families crowd into small ones. Economists sometimes describe this as a mismatch between households and dwellings.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Most modern schemes are of a different kind, often described as second-generation controls or rent stabilisation. Rather than freezing rents, they permit annual increases, usually linked to inflation, while preventing the sudden rises that can force tenants out. Crucially, many allow the rent to return to the market level when a tenancy ends, and buildings completed after a certain date are frequently exempt. The most detailed recent evidence on such a system comes from Ilona Szalóki, an economist at the Pannonian Housing Research Unit, who studied a city that extended stabilisation to smaller buildings that had previously been unregulated. Tenants who benefited were markedly more likely to be living at the same address a decade later. However, the owners of affected buildings responded by converting units into flats for sale or redeveloping them, so that the stock of rental housing in those buildings shrank by roughly fifteen per cent, and rents in the unregulated part of the market rose as a result.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How these findings should be interpreted is disputed. For Felix Lichtblau, a housing policy analyst, the stability that tenants gained is not a side effect but a legitimate goal in its own right. Children who do not have to change schools, elderly residents who keep their networks of neighbours and shops, and workers who remain close to their jobs all derive benefits that a market price cannot capture. Szalóki does not deny this, but she points out that the gains of protected tenants were financed, in effect, by those who came later and faced higher rents in a smaller market. Both positions contain some truth. The difficulty is that the beneficiaries of control are visible and organised, whereas those who lose out, future tenants who have not yet arrived in the city, have no voice in the debate at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The detailed design of a scheme matters a great deal. Allowing rents to reset between tenancies limits the damage to supply, but it also gives landlords a strong financial reason to see tenants leave, and tenant organisations have documented cases of owners using intimidation or neglect to encourage departures. Exemptions for new buildings raise a different problem. Rohini Sengupta, an urban planner who has compared construction rates across several regulated cities, found that such exemptions prevented the fall in building that might otherwise have been expected, but only where developers believed they would last. In cities where governments had previously moved the cut-off date to bring newer buildings under control, developers remained cautious for many years, regardless of what current rules promised.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some economists argue that tenants would be better served by housing allowances, cash payments that help low-income households meet their rent, which have been used in parts of Europe for more than half a century. These target help at those in need without discouraging investment. Yet critics claim that allowances are partly absorbed by landlords in the form of higher rents. In truth, neither instrument tackles the underlying problem. Where rents are high because too few homes have been built, any measure that leaves supply unchanged will only redistribute scarcity.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps rent regulation is best understood not as a means of making housing affordable, which it cannot achieve on its own, but as a form of insurance against sudden and unpredictable increases. Judged in this more modest way, well-designed stabilisation can be defended, provided that it is accompanied by vigorous efforts to expand the supply of housing.

topic: volumetric modular housing built in factories: precision and airtightness, transport limits, why modular factories fail, monotony fears, labour and government demand
title: Homes from the Factory Floor
subtitle: Building houses in factories has been tried before and failed; its supporters insist that this time will be different

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the years after the Second World War, Britain erected more than 150,000 prefabricated bungalows to house families whose homes had been destroyed by bombing. Assembled from factory-made panels in a matter of days, they were intended to last for no more than a decade, yet some were still occupied half a century later, and many of their residents remembered them with affection. The reputation of factory-built housing has since had a more troubled history. The concrete-panel tower blocks of the 1960s, hurriedly erected with poorly sealed joints, became associated with damp, condensation and, in the worst cases, structural failure. For many people, the word 'prefabricated' still suggests something cheap and temporary. That association is understandable, but it is increasingly out of date.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious current form of off-site construction is volumetric modular building, in which complete three-dimensional units, often whole rooms with plumbing, wiring and finishes already installed, are manufactured in a factory, transported by road and lifted into position by crane. Its advocates make a number of claims. Construction times, they say, can be cut by up to half, because site preparation and manufacturing take place simultaneously rather than one after the other. Waste is reduced, since materials are cut to order and offcuts can be reused. And workers are spared the hazards of working at height in poor weather. Some of these claims are better supported than others, but taken together they explain why governments facing housing shortages have shown such interest in the approach.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kenji Uchimaru, a construction engineer who has tested homes produced by several manufacturers, argues that the greatest advantage is not speed but precision. On a conventional site, he notes, quality depends heavily on the weather and on the skill of individual tradespeople, many of them working under pressure to finish quickly. In a factory, components are assembled on jigs under controlled conditions and checked at each stage. His measurements show that modular homes are, on average, considerably more airtight than comparable homes built on site, which means they lose less heat. Such tests also reveal fewer of the small gaps around windows and service pipes that, on conventional sites, are often discovered only after residents complain of draughts. Uchimaru is careful to add that the method has its own constraints: because modules must travel on public roads, their width is restricted, and this can produce narrow rooms and awkward floor plans unless designers plan around the limitation from the outset.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If the technology works, why has the industry struggled? Over the past decade, several heavily publicised modular factories have closed within a few years of opening, despite generous investment. Dragana Ivanišević, a construction economist, believes the explanation lies in the structure of costs. A factory carries large fixed expenses, such as buildings, machinery and a permanent workforce, and can only cover them if orders arrive in a steady stream. Housebuilding, however, is notoriously cyclical. A conventional builder facing a downturn can simply stop hiring subcontractors, whereas a factory must keep paying for idle equipment. This analysis is convincing, and it suggests that the industry's difficulties have less to do with engineering than with finance. A method that is technically superior can still fail if its business model cannot survive an ordinary property slump.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other obstacles are cultural. Mortgage lenders and insurers have sometimes hesitated to finance homes built by unfamiliar methods, fearing that they will prove hard to value or resell. There is also a widespread fear that factory production will lead to monotonous, identical streets. The architect Siobhan Quigley rejects this concern, arguing that a limited set of standard modules can be combined in a vast number of arrangements and finished with a wide variety of facades and roofs. Her own schemes certainly demonstrate what is possible. Yet it would be naive to ignore the economic pressure in the opposite direction: factory production becomes cheaper the more often the same design is repeated, so every additional variation adds to cost. Variety is achievable, but it is not free.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Modular construction is also sometimes presented as an answer to the shortage of skilled building workers. Factory employment, with regular hours and indoor conditions, appeals to people who would never consider working on a site, and some manufacturers report recruiting a far higher proportion of women than the construction industry as a whole. It should be remembered, though, that a substantial share of the work still takes place on site: foundations must be laid, utilities connected and modules joined and sealed, tasks that can account for a third of the total cost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that factories will replace building sites. A more realistic ambition is for modular methods to take a significant and stable share of new housing. Since the main weakness is unpredictable demand, the most useful step governments could take is to provide that demand themselves, for instance by committing to long-term orders for social housing. Such commitments would cost the public relatively little and could give manufacturers the stability they have so far lacked.

topic: Housing First for homeless people: the staircase model, tenancy retention versus health outcomes, the 'pays for itself' claim, fidelity when scaled up, isolation in cheap districts and the Finnish case
title: A Key Before Conditions
subtitle: Giving homeless people a permanent home first, and support afterwards, has transformed policy in several countries, but its success depends on more than the idea itself

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, services for homeless people in Europe and North America were organised around what has been called the staircase model. A person sleeping rough would move first to an emergency shelter, then to a hostel, and then perhaps to transitional accommodation, earning each step by demonstrating progress: abstaining from alcohol and drugs, accepting psychiatric treatment, keeping appointments. Only at the top of the staircase was a permanent home offered. Housing First turns this sequence upside down. Participants are given a self-contained flat with an ordinary tenancy at the outset, and support with health, addiction and finances is offered but not imposed as a condition of keeping the home. Since its development in the 1990s, the approach has spread from a handful of pilot projects to national policy in several countries, and it is now widely described as best practice.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its central claim rests on unusually strong evidence. Milica Vukmirović, a social policy researcher who led a randomised trial across five cities, found that more than four in five participants remained housed after two years, compared with fewer than a third of those receiving conventional services. Her trial also measured a range of other outcomes, and here the results were less striking: participants' use of alcohol and drugs, and their reported mental health, differed little from those of the comparison group. Some critics have seized on these findings as evidence that the model merely moves problems indoors. To treat them as a failure, however, is to misunderstand what Housing First sets out to do. Its aim is to end homelessness, and on that measure the evidence is about as convincing as social policy research ever becomes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More contentious is the claim, made by many early advocates, that Housing First pays for itself. The argument was that people living on the streets make heavy use of expensive emergency services, from hospital accident departments to police cells, and that housing them would reduce these costs by more than the price of the programme. Arohanui Whaanga, a health economist, re-examined the cost data from several trials and concluded that full savings were achieved only for the small group of participants with the very highest previous use of emergency services. For the typical participant, reduced spending elsewhere covered roughly half the cost. This claim of self-financing has, in my view, done the model a disservice. It invited governments to judge Housing First by a financial test it was never likely to pass, when the stronger case for it is a moral one: that a person should not have to earn the right to a home.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different problem emerges when programmes are expanded. The original model specified small caseloads for support workers, rapid access to housing and an absence of treatment conditions, but as services are scaled up under budget pressures, these features tend to erode. Graham Hazelgrove, who has evaluated programmes in more than twenty local authorities, developed a scale for measuring how closely each followed the original design. Those scoring lowest, he found, kept people housed at rates barely distinguishable from the traditional services they had replaced. His conclusion, that the label 'Housing First' is no guarantee of results, is hard to dispute, and it suggests that funders should monitor how programmes operate rather than simply counting how many have been established.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even a faithful programme depends on something it cannot create: available housing. Where cheap rental flats are scarce, participants may wait months for a tenancy, and the promise of immediate housing becomes empty. The urban geographer Hery Razafimahatratra has drawn attention to a subtler consequence. Because programmes must work within tight rent limits, participants are frequently placed in the cheapest districts, often far from the neighbourhoods where they had friends, family or familiar services. In his interviews with former participants, loneliness was among the most common reasons given for abandoning a tenancy. This danger has received too little attention. A flat on the edge of a city, reached by two bus journeys from anyone the tenant knows, may solve the problem of shelter while creating a different kind of hardship.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters frequently point to Finland, where homelessness has fallen steadily since the government adopted the approach as national policy and converted many of its shelters into permanent supported apartments. The Finnish case is impressive, but it is often misread. Finland already possessed a large stock of publicly owned and non-profit housing, and it continued to build more. Its success therefore owes at least as much to that supply as to Housing First itself, and countries hoping to copy the results without investing in homes are likely to be disappointed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these reservations undermines the basic insight on which Housing First rests: that stability is more often a foundation for recovery than a reward for it. But the model is not a technique that can be adopted cheaply and applied anywhere. It works best where its principles are respected and where homes are available to put people in, and policymakers who ignore either condition should not be surprised when results fall short.

topic: the fifteen-minute city: its roots in the neighbourhood unit, measuring accessibility, the problem of employment, equity concerns, the backlash against traffic filters and the density needed to support local shops
title: Everything Within Reach
subtitle: The idea that daily needs should lie a short walk from home has captured the imagination of mayors, but turning it into reality is harder than the slogan implies

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few planning ideas of recent years have travelled as quickly as the fifteen-minute city. Its premise is easy to grasp: residents should be able to reach most of the things they need in daily life, including shops, schools, doctors, parks and, ideally, their workplace, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. The idea gained enormous attention around 2020, when restrictions on travel forced millions of people to rediscover their immediate surroundings, and within a few years mayors on several continents had adopted it as an official goal. Yet the concept is less novel than its presentation suggests. Planners in the early twentieth century promoted the 'neighbourhood unit', a district organised around a primary school within walking distance of every home, and many of the arguments now made for the fifteen-minute city were rehearsed then. Recognising this lineage is useful, because the earlier experiments reveal both what the idea can achieve and where it tends to fall short.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first practical question is how to measure whether a neighbourhood meets the standard. Algis Sventickas, a geographer who has mapped access to services across eleven cities, found that the results depend heavily on the method chosen. Most residents of central districts already lived within fifteen minutes of nearly every category of service, whereas in outer suburbs the figure fell sharply. More importantly, he argues, simply recording the distance to the nearest example of each service is misleading. A neighbourhood with a single supermarket ten minutes away scores as well as one with a dozen food shops of different kinds, though residents of the second clearly enjoy far greater choice. Sventickas therefore proposes that accessibility should be judged by the variety of destinations within reach rather than by proximity to one of each type.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Work presents the greatest difficulty. Whereas groceries and primary schools can be distributed fairly evenly across a city, employment tends to cluster in particular districts, and specialised jobs are found in only a few places. Most people cannot realistically choose a job because it happens to be close to home, and households with two working adults face the problem twice over. It follows that claims that the fifteen-minute city will make commuting a thing of the past are exaggerated. A more realistic version of the concept would concentrate on the everyday trips that make up a large share of journeys, such as shopping, schooling and leisure, while treating access to employment as a separate question to be addressed through public transport.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Questions of fairness have also been raised. Lucía Ballesteros, an urban sociologist, points out that the neighbourhoods which already come closest to the ideal are generally prosperous inner districts, and that investment in the concept risks being concentrated where it is least needed. Meanwhile, lower-income households pushed to the urban fringe by high housing costs may continue to face long journeys to almost everything. Ballesteros also worries that an emphasis on self-contained districts could deepen social segregation, if people of different backgrounds rarely have reason to leave their own area. The first of these concerns deserves serious attention. The second, however, seems overstated: no serious proposal restricts where people may travel, and making local services convenient does not prevent anyone from going further afield.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, a fear of restriction has driven a surprisingly fierce backlash. In several cities, the introduction of traffic filters, which close certain roads to through traffic and fine drivers who pass through them, was widely interpreted as the first step in a plan to confine residents to their districts. Such claims are unfounded, but dismissing them as mere misinformation would be a mistake. In many cases, measures were introduced with little consultation and presented as decisions already taken, and residents who felt excluded from the process were understandably receptive to the suggestion that something was being hidden from them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The economics of the idea receive less attention than they deserve. Einar Thorarensen, an economist who studies retail location, observes that a local bakery, pharmacy or café can survive only if enough customers live within walking distance. By his estimates, the population densities required are roughly those found in older European districts built before mass car ownership; typical low-density suburbs fall well short. Making such suburbs into fifteen-minute neighbourhoods would therefore require substantial numbers of new homes to be built in them, a prospect that existing residents frequently resist. The slogan, in other words, conceals a demanding and politically difficult programme of densification.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the concept should be abandoned. Its value lies less in the precise figure of fifteen minutes than in the question it encourages planners to ask of every decision: does this make daily life easier to conduct close to home? Treated as a rigid rule to be met in every neighbourhood, the standard would be unattainable in many places and largely irrelevant in others. Treated as a direction of travel, it offers a useful corrective to decades of planning that assumed every journey would be made by car.

topic: upgrading informal settlements in place versus relocation: the importance of location, land titling and tenure security, re-blocking for infrastructure, resident enumerations and participation, and rising rents for tenants
title: Upgrading in Place
subtitle: Improving informal settlements rather than clearing them has become the accepted wisdom, but its limits are rarely acknowledged

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere close to a billion people, by most estimates, live in informal settlements: neighbourhoods built without planning permission, often on land the residents do not legally own, and typically lacking piped water, sewers, paved roads or street lighting. For much of the twentieth century, governments regarded such settlements as an embarrassment to be removed. Bulldozers cleared them, sometimes with only days of warning, and residents were either left to find shelter elsewhere or moved to purpose-built estates. Over recent decades, however, opinion among planners and international agencies has shifted decisively towards upgrading in place: improving infrastructure and services while allowing residents to remain where they are. This shift is, on the whole, a welcome one. But upgrading has sometimes been presented as a comprehensive answer to urban poverty, and that claim deserves far more scepticism than it has received.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against relocation is well established. Resettlement estates have usually been built where land is cheap, which in practice means on the urban periphery, far from jobs, markets and the informal networks on which poor households depend. Rosa Cárdenas-Llosa, an urban anthropologist, followed several hundred families moved from central settlements into new apartment blocks on the edge of a large Latin American city. Within five years, almost half had left, many of them renting or selling their apartments and returning to informal neighbourhoods closer to the centre. Their new homes were, by any physical standard, superior to those they had abandoned. What mattered more, Cárdenas-Llosa concludes, was where a dwelling stood rather than how well it was built, since a sound flat two hours from work was of little use to a street vendor or a domestic cleaner.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Advocates of upgrading have often linked it to the granting of formal land titles. The argument, influential since the 1990s, holds that residents of informal settlements possess substantial assets but cannot use them, because without legal documents their homes cannot serve as security for a loan. Give them titles, the reasoning goes, and capital will be released for investment in businesses and education. Jean-Paul Gatabazi, a development economist, has evaluated titling programmes in several countries and found a more mixed picture. Households that received titles did spend noticeably more on housing improvements, apparently because they no longer feared eviction. Yet titles did little to improve access to credit, since banks remained reluctant to make small loans to people with irregular incomes. The lesson, surely, is that security of tenure is what counts, and that formal ownership is only one way of providing it. Residents who believe they will not be evicted, perhaps because a municipality has publicly recognised their settlement, may invest just as readily without a title deed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Physical improvements raise their own difficulties. Of all the interventions available, piped water and sanitation tend to bring the largest gains in health, particularly for young children. But installing them in settlements whose lanes are narrow, winding and unevenly built is technically demanding and expensive, and the new pipes must be connected to the city's main networks, which may themselves be overloaded. In some projects, a number of houses are demolished so that lanes can be widened and straightened, a process known as re-blocking. Critics see this as eviction by another name. That objection is understandable but too absolute: where the households affected are rehoused nearby and the plan has been agreed by the community as a whole, removing a handful of dwellings may be a price worth paying for drains and access for emergency vehicles.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is broad agreement that residents should take part in designing upgrading schemes, though less agreement about what participation means. Funmilayo Oyinlola, a planner who has worked with federations of slum dwellers, argues that the most successful projects begin with enumerations, surveys in which residents themselves map every plot and record every household. In her experience, the information they produce is more accurate than official data and gives communities a strong sense of ownership over the project that follows. Her argument is persuasive as far as it goes. However, participation is rarely as inclusive as its champions imply. Meetings tend to be dominated by long-standing residents and by those who own structures, while tenants, who in many settlements make up the majority, are easily overlooked.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That omission matters, because tenants are the group most exposed to one of upgrading's least discussed effects. Improvements in water, drainage and security make a settlement more attractive, and rents respond accordingly. Desislava Ilieva, a housing researcher, compared rents in upgraded and unimproved settlements in three cities and found that in upgraded areas they rose by roughly thirty per cent within three years, while tenants' incomes barely changed. Some tenants moved to settlements that had not yet been improved, taking their problems with them. This is the hidden cost of upgrading, and it is seldom recognised, partly because programmes typically record benefits to the structures and owners on site rather than following the people who leave.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, upgrading addresses the settlements that already exist, not those that will form in the future. Cities in many regions are expected to grow rapidly for decades, and unless serviced land is made available in advance for newcomers, new informal neighbourhoods will continue to appear. Upgrading is therefore necessary but insufficient. A credible urban strategy must combine it with planning for the growth still to come.

topic: cohousing communities: shared common houses, layout and casual encounters, evidence on loneliness, senior cohousing, the limits of affordability claims and the burden of consensus governance
title: Private Homes, Shared Lives
subtitle: Cohousing combines self-contained dwellings with communal facilities, and governments increasingly see it as a remedy for several social problems at once

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 1960s, a group of Danish families frustrated by the isolation of suburban life set out to design a different kind of neighbourhood. Each household would have its own self-contained home, but the homes would be clustered around a common house containing a large kitchen, a dining room and space for children to play, and the residents themselves would plan, run and maintain the whole development. The model, known in English as cohousing, has since spread across northern Europe and North America, and there are now several hundred such communities in operation. In recent years it has attracted interest well beyond its traditional supporters. Governments concerned about loneliness, ageing populations and the cost of housing have all, at various times, presented cohousing as part of the answer. It is a valuable model, but it is being asked to carry more expectations than it can bear.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the appeal of cohousing lies in its physical layout. Cars are typically kept in a car park at the edge of the site, so that homes face onto shared pedestrian paths, and kitchens are often placed at the front of each dwelling, overlooking the common space. Residents usually eat together in the common house several times a week, taking turns to cook. Chiara Lusardi, an architect who has designed a number of cohousing schemes, argues that such details have a decisive influence on how residents behave. In her observations, communities in which front doors face one another across a narrow path generate far more casual conversations than those in which homes are arranged in parallel rows. There is no reason to doubt her findings, but it is important not to draw too much from them. Design can make encounters more likely; it cannot by itself turn neighbours into a community. That depends on the willingness of residents to invest time and effort in one another.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Is there evidence that cohousing delivers the social benefits claimed for it? Kadri Vaher, a sociologist, surveyed residents of forty communities and found that they reported considerably lower levels of loneliness than the population as a whole, together with unusually high satisfaction with their housing. The obvious objection is that people who choose to live this way are likely to be more sociable than average to begin with. Vaher accepts the point and has attempted to address it by following new residents over several years. Their reported loneliness fell after the move, which suggests a genuine effect, though she is careful to note that the number of people she was able to follow was small and that most of them had moved from living alone.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The fastest-growing form of the model in recent years has been senior cohousing, in which membership is restricted to people over a certain age, often fifty-five. Residents offer one another everyday assistance, from doing the shopping to giving lifts to medical appointments and checking on neighbours who are unwell, and some studies suggest that such mutual support allows people to postpone a move into residential care. The arrangement has an inherent weakness, however. Because members grow old together, a community founded by energetic sixty-year-olds may find, two decades later, that many residents need help and few are able to give it. Mixed-age communities, despite the frictions that children and teenagers can cause, are in my view a more robust arrangement over the long term.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The claim that cohousing can make housing more affordable is harder to sustain. Pieter Hanssens, a housing economist, has calculated that because residents share a common house, laundry and guest rooms, each private dwelling can be smaller, reducing the cost per household by perhaps ten to fifteen per cent. He stresses, however, that these savings materialise only if the group acquires land at a reasonable price and completes the project without long delays. In practice, groups often spend five years or more searching for a site, negotiating with planning authorities and persuading banks, which tend to be wary of lending to collectives. Many groups dissolve before a single home is built, and those that succeed are dominated by well-educated, middle-income households with savings to contribute. Without public help, cohousing is more likely to remain a choice for the comfortable than a route into housing for those on low incomes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Daily life in a cohousing community also places demands on residents that are rarely discussed in promotional material. Most communities take decisions by consensus, which requires frequent and sometimes lengthy meetings, and residents are expected to sit on committees, cook communal meals and take part in maintenance days. For many members these obligations are part of the attraction. For people working long hours or caring for relatives, they can be a serious burden, and the model may quietly exclude precisely those who might benefit most from a supportive neighbourhood.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these limitations is a reason to dismiss cohousing. It offers a form of neighbourhood life that conventional housing markets rarely provide, and its residents are, on the evidence available, generally content. What it requires from governments is not enthusiastic rhetoric but practical support, such as reserving suitable public land for groups and offering guaranteed loans. With such help it could become a significant option for many more households, even if it will never be a solution to the housing crisis as a whole.

topic: minimum parking requirements in zoning codes: their weak evidential origins, costs to housing, effects on urban form, kerbside spillover, shift workers' car dependence and abolition
title: The Space Reserved for Cars
subtitle: Rules requiring new buildings to provide parking have quietly reshaped cities for decades; a growing movement now wants them scrapped

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every city zoning code in North America, and many elsewhere, contains a table that few residents have ever read. It specifies how many parking spaces must accompany each type of building: perhaps one and a half spaces for every flat, four for every hundred square metres of shop floor, one for every three seats in a restaurant or place of worship. These parking minimums were introduced, mostly in the decades after the Second World War, with the reasonable aim of preventing new buildings from overwhelming the streets around them with parked cars. Their consequences, however, have been far-reaching. Few regulations have done as much to shape the physical form of modern cities, and few have attracted so little public scrutiny in proportion to their effects.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The origins of the figures are surprisingly obscure. Thomas Ferraby, a transport planner who has traced the requirements in dozens of codes back to their sources, found that many were derived from counts of parked cars at a small number of suburban sites, sometimes fewer than five, with no public transport nearby. Planners typically recorded demand at the busiest hour of the busiest day of the year, such as a Saturday shortly before a major holiday, and set the requirement to match it, ensuring that spaces would stand empty for most of the remaining time. Once published in professional manuals, these ratios were copied from one city to the next, often to the decimal point, regardless of local conditions. The apparent precision of the numbers lent them an authority that the underlying evidence never justified.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The costs of such requirements fall largely on housing. A space in a multi-storey car park can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space considerably more, and these costs are inevitably passed on to buyers and tenants. Nurlan Dzhaparov, a housing economist, estimates that a requirement of one space per flat adds between twelve and seventeen per cent to the cost of a typical apartment in a dense urban neighbourhood. On small, irregular plots, where there is no room for a ramp, the requirement can make a project impossible altogether. Dzhaparov has also examined what happened in districts where minimums were lifted. Developers built fewer spaces and more homes, but they did not stop providing parking: where buyers wanted spaces and were prepared to pay for them, the market continued to supply them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The effects on the wider city are equally significant. Because surface car parks occupy large areas of land, they push buildings apart, lengthening the distances between homes, shops and workplaces. A walk that might take five minutes along a street of shopfronts can take fifteen across a succession of car parks, which makes walking less attractive and so reinforces the very dependence on cars that generous parking was intended to accommodate. Extensive paved surfaces also increase the volume of rainwater running off into drains and absorb heat during the day, contributing to higher temperatures at night. It is no exaggeration to say that, in many suburbs, the car park rather than the building has become the dominant element of the landscape.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most common objection to removing minimums comes from existing residents, who fear that newcomers without off-street spaces will compete with them for places on the street. Claire Hennequin, a planner responsible for kerbside policy in a large city, accepts that this spillover is real but argues that it can be managed: residential permit schemes, time limits and, above all, charging an appropriate price for kerbside space can ensure that spaces remain available. Her argument is sound in principle. The difficulty is that charging for street parking, which motorists have long regarded as free, is one of the least popular measures a local politician can propose. Cities that abolish minimums without also managing the kerb therefore risk a backlash that could reverse the reform.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different concern has been raised by Kwame Yeboah-Asante, a sociologist who studies low-paid work. He points out that many cleaners, care workers and warehouse staff work shifts that begin or end at times when public transport is infrequent or absent, and that for them a car is a necessity rather than a choice. Reducing the supply of parking, he argues, could make their lives harder. The concern is legitimate, but it overlooks a countervailing consideration. Under the present system, the cost of parking is bundled into the price of every home, so that households without cars, which on average have lower incomes than those with them, help to pay for spaces they do not use.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A growing number of cities have now abolished parking minimums entirely, and the reform is long overdue. It should be understood, though, for what it is: the removal of an obligation, not a prohibition. Developers remain free to build as much parking as their customers want. What changes is that the decision is made according to actual demand rather than by figures inherited from a handful of suburban car parks decades ago. For the reform to succeed, it must be accompanied by sensible management of street parking and by investment in alternatives to driving.

topic: demolishing versus refurbishing post-war tower blocks: embodied carbon, external retrofits with winter gardens, structurally unsound blocks, displacement of tenants, stigma and management, and tax rules favouring new build
title: Knock Down or Make Good?
subtitle: Demolition has long been the standard fate of ageing tower blocks, but environmental and social arguments are shifting the balance towards renovation

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between the 1950s and the late 1970s, governments across Europe built hundreds of thousands of flats in high-rise blocks. Constructed quickly to replace bomb-damaged housing and overcrowded slums, many of these towers were welcomed at first by tenants who had never before had indoor bathrooms or central heating. Half a century later, a large number are in poor condition, with failing windows, inadequate insulation and lifts that frequently break down. For the past few decades, the standard response has been demolition: clear the site and build something new, usually lower in height and with a larger share of private homes. That approach is now being questioned on environmental, social and financial grounds. The case for refurbishing existing blocks is considerably stronger than its critics allow, although it would be a mistake to treat it as applicable to every building.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental argument centres on what is called embodied carbon: the emissions released in producing, transporting and assembling building materials. Concrete and steel, the main components of most towers, are among the most carbon-intensive materials in use. Kateřina Doubravová, a building scientist, has carried out life-cycle assessments comparing the demolition and replacement of residential blocks with deep retrofits that bring the existing structures up to high standards of energy efficiency. Her results indicate that, once the emissions from demolition and new construction are included, a replacement building may take between thirty and sixty years to make up for its carbon debt through lower heating requirements, and in some cases longer than the building's expected lifespan. This turns a widespread assumption on its head. A new building may consume less energy once occupied, but that is not the same as being better for the climate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Retrofitting has also become far more ambitious than the cosmetic recladding of earlier decades. In one widely admired approach, prefabricated structures are attached to the outside of a block, adding glazed winter gardens and balconies that extend each flat by several square metres. The new layer improves insulation, admits more daylight and gives residents space that their original homes lacked. Because the work takes place largely from the outside, tenants can usually remain in their homes while it is carried out, and project costs have often been well below those of demolition and rebuilding. Such schemes demonstrate that the choice is not between a tired tower and a new building but between two very different kinds of renewal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every block, however, is a candidate for this treatment. Martin Aldred, a structural engineer who has inspected towers in several countries, warns that some were built using large concrete panels joined by connections that were poorly designed or badly executed, and that hidden defects can make them vulnerable to progressive collapse if one part fails. Others contain extensive asbestos or have foundations unable to carry additional loads. In such cases, he argues, the cost of making a building safe may exceed that of replacing it, and even an expensive refurbishment may not achieve the standards expected of new construction. Aldred is right to insist on this. Advocates of retrofit do their cause no favours if they imply that every tower can be saved, and decisions ought to rest on careful surveys of each building rather than on general principles.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The social consequences of demolition are often underestimated. Regeneration schemes typically promise residents that they will be able to return, but the replacement developments frequently contain fewer homes at social rents, and the years of construction scatter communities that took decades to form. Liisa Pihlakas, a sociologist, followed tenants from six demolished estates and found that only around one in five eventually moved back. Her research also revealed a complication. On several estates, a majority of residents had actively wanted demolition, associating the towers with crime, neglect and the stigma attached to their address. Their wishes deserve respect. Whatever the technical and environmental arguments, the people who live in a building should have a decisive voice in its future.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That stigma, however, tells us more about how towers were managed than about how they were designed. Many blocks declined because maintenance budgets were cut, caretakers were withdrawn and the poorest households were concentrated in them by allocation policies. In cities where high-rise public housing has been well maintained and occupied by a broad social mix, it has remained popular for generations. To blame the form of the buildings for problems that arose largely from neglect is to draw the wrong lesson, and it risks repeating the same mistakes in whatever replaces them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If refurbishment is so often the better option, why is demolition still so common? Part of the answer lies in financial rules that favour new construction. In some countries, building new homes attracts no sales tax, while repair and renovation are taxed at the full rate, so that the cheaper option on paper can be the more wasteful one in practice. Removing that imbalance would cost relatively little and would allow each decision to be judged on its merits. Demolition will sometimes be the right answer, but it should be a conclusion reached after careful assessment, not the default from which every alternative must depart.

topic: psychological safety in work teams: error reporting, speaking up, survey measurement, accountability and job insecurity
title: Counting Mistakes
subtitle: Why the teams that report the most errors may be the ones learning fastest, and why that idea needs careful handling

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the mid-1990s a study of hospital nursing units produced a result that at first seemed to make no sense. The researchers had expected that units with better leadership and stronger working relationships would record fewer medication errors. Instead, the best-functioning units reported considerably more. The explanation eventually proposed was not that these teams were more careless but that their members felt able to admit mistakes, whereas in poorly led units errors were concealed for fear of punishment. The finding has since become a founding story for the concept now known as psychological safety: a shared belief within a group that it is acceptable to speak up, ask questions or confess errors without being humiliated. It is a powerful idea, and in my view a largely correct one, but its popularity has run well ahead of the evidence in several respects.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest support comes from the work of Dr Thandiwe Ngubane, an organisational psychologist at the Southern Institute for Workplace Studies, who spent four years observing surgical, engineering and software teams. Ngubane found that what distinguished teams that improved over time was not the number of mistakes they made but the speed with which problems surfaced. In teams where junior members hesitated to contradict senior colleagues, minor faults went unmentioned until they had grown into serious failures. She argues that silence, rather than error itself, is the true enemy of organisational learning, and that managers who punish the messenger effectively purchase short-term calm at the price of long-term blindness.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ngubane's conclusions have been widely adopted, but not always in the form she intended. Many organisations now run workshops on 'speaking up' and measure psychological safety through annual staff surveys. Dr Paolo Castiglioni of the Lombardy School of Management is sceptical of this approach. In a comparison of thirty manufacturing firms, he found that survey scores bore only a weak relationship to the number of safety concerns that staff actually raised. Employees, he suggests, quickly learn which answers are expected and supply them, particularly when the results are linked to managers' bonuses. Castiglioni does not dispute that openness matters; his objection is to the assumption that it can be captured in a questionnaire. On this point I think he is right: a climate is something that has to be observed in behaviour, not declared on a form.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different reservation concerns the relationship between safety and standards. Critics sometimes caricature psychological safety as a recipe for complacency, in which nobody is held responsible for anything. Ngubane rejects this reading, insisting that the most effective teams combine high openness with demanding expectations; it is the combination of low expectations and high comfort, she says, that produces a workplace which is pleasant but unproductive. Professor Reza Hakimzadeh, who studies accountability systems at the Caspian Business School, broadly agrees but adds a qualification. In his view, organisations must distinguish clearly between honest errors, risky shortcuts and deliberate violations of rules, because treating all three identically, whether leniently or harshly, undermines trust. A nurse who misreads a poorly printed label and one who ignores a checklist to save time should not, he argues, receive the same response.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of where psychological safety comes from. Much of the popular literature places the burden on the team leader, whose reactions to bad news are said to set the tone for everyone else. The sociologist Aino Puhakka, of the Baltic Centre for Labour Research, considers this emphasis misplaced. Her fieldwork in shipyards and call centres suggests that job insecurity can override even the most encouraging leadership: where workers fear redundancy, they keep quiet regardless of how their supervisor behaves. Openness, on this account, is shaped as much by contracts and labour markets as by interpersonal skill, and training managers to respond warmly to bad news will achieve little if employees believe their positions are at risk.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that leaders are irrelevant. What Puhakka's evidence shows is that good leadership is necessary but not sufficient, and that organisations which cut staff while urging employees to speak up are sending contradictory signals. Nor is it clear that every team benefits equally. Ngubane's own data indicate that the advantages are greatest where work is complex and uncertain; in highly routine tasks, where the correct procedure is already known and rarely changes, the gains from open discussion appear to be modest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The original hospital finding contains a lesson that is easily overlooked. A rising count of reported errors may signal a healthier organisation, but it may equally signal a deteriorating one, and the number alone cannot tell the two apart. Anyone who interprets error statistics must therefore ask how the figures were generated before deciding what they mean. That is less satisfying than a simple rule of thumb, but it is considerably more honest, and it is a discipline that the enthusiasts for psychological safety would do well to apply to their own favourite measures.

area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: the 'fail fast' culture among start-up founders: whether failed ventures teach entrepreneurs anything, self-serving explanations, cheap early experiments and who can afford to fail
title: The Cult of the Quick Collapse
subtitle: Entrepreneurial culture has learned to celebrate failure. Whether failure actually teaches founders anything is far less certain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past two decades, a distinctive vocabulary has spread from technology start-ups into boardrooms, government departments and even schools. Founders are urged to 'fail fast', to 'pivot' and to treat each collapsed venture as a lesson. Conferences devoted entirely to failure invite entrepreneurs to recount their most expensive mistakes before audiences of several hundred, and some investment firms say they look favourably on applicants whose previous companies have folded. The rhetoric has an obvious appeal. In a sector where most new firms do not survive their first decade, it offers consolation to the many and a sense of daring to the few. What it does not offer, unfortunately, is much evidence that failure, in itself, makes people better at business.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most systematic attempt to test the claim was carried out by the economist Dr Ioanna Kazantzidis and colleagues at the Aegean Institute for Enterprise Research, who tracked roughly eleven thousand founders across three countries over fifteen years. Their question was simple: are entrepreneurs whose first venture failed more likely to succeed with a second? The answer was no. Once differences in industry, age and access to capital were taken into account, a previous failure predicted success neither better nor worse than having no prior experience at all. Founders whose first company had prospered, by contrast, were substantially more likely to succeed again. Kazantzidis interprets this as evidence that what carries over between ventures is not wisdom acquired from disaster but skill, reputation and contacts, all of which success supplies more abundantly than failure does.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should failure teach so little? One answer comes from research on how people explain their own setbacks. Dr Mateo Lomeli, a psychologist at the Pacific Coast Business School, interviewed more than two hundred founders within a year of their companies closing. The great majority attributed the collapse mainly to external causes: a sudden change in the market, an unreliable investor, a competitor with deeper pockets. Relatively few identified decisions of their own that they would now make differently. Lomeli does not regard this as dishonesty; attributing blame outward, he notes, protects the self-esteem that a founder needs in order to try again. But it also means that the lesson the culture of failure promises is often never drawn. In a follow-up laboratory study, participants who were told they had failed a business simulation spent less time reviewing their results than those told they had succeeded, even though both groups were allowed exactly the same amount of time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lomeli's findings complicate a further assumption, namely that the problem is merely one of stigma. Advocates of failure culture often argue that, if only the shame attached to bankruptcy were removed, entrepreneurs would reflect openly and learn. Yet many of the founders Lomeli interviewed had been operating in an environment that already celebrated failure, and they reflected no more deeply than the rest. Removing shame, it seems, may be necessary for honest reflection, but it does not guarantee it. Indeed, there is a risk that a culture which treats failure as a badge of honour makes careful self-examination less likely, not more, since a founder who has been applauded for failing has little reason to ask what, specifically, went wrong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the 'fail fast' idea is worthless. Dr Anjali Raveendran, who studies product development at the Deccan School of Technology Management, argues that the phrase originally had a narrow and sensible meaning: test assumptions cheaply and early, so that a flawed product is abandoned before large sums have been committed. Her study of 140 software projects found that teams which ran small, inexpensive experiments in the first months were considerably less likely to suffer a costly late-stage collapse. The value here lay not in failure as an experience but in the deliberate design of small tests whose results were recorded and examined. What has happened since, Raveendran contends, is that the slogan has detached itself from the method, so that failing has come to be seen as admirable in its own right.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: That detachment carries real costs, and they are not evenly distributed. A failed venture is a tolerable setback for a founder with savings, family wealth or a well-paid job to return to; for others it can mean years of debt. Studies of start-up founders consistently show that they come disproportionately from affluent backgrounds, and it would be naive to imagine that celebrating failure does anything to change this. If anything, a culture that encourages repeated risk-taking rewards those who can most easily afford to lose, while presenting their good fortune as a kind of courage.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The more useful lesson, then, may be that organisations should take failure seriously rather than romantically. That means distinguishing between failures that produce information, such as a well-designed experiment that disproves a hypothesis, and failures that merely consume resources. It means building routines for examining what went wrong, since Lomeli's work suggests that reflection will not happen spontaneously. And it means being honest that, for most people most of the time, success remains the better teacher. Failure can certainly be instructive, but only when someone has gone to the trouble of extracting the instruction.
