area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: blameless post-incident reviews in technology organisations: candour, hindsight bias, shielding of managerial decisions and failure to follow up recommendations
title: After the Outage
subtitle: The 'blameless review' has become standard practice in many technical organisations. Its critics say it has quietly abolished responsibility

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a large online service fails, whether a payment system freezes or a hospital's records become unreachable, the engineers responsible are increasingly expected to write a document known as a post-incident review. Its purpose is to reconstruct what happened, minute by minute, and to identify changes that would prevent a recurrence. Over the past fifteen years, many technology companies have adopted a particular version of this practice, the so-called blameless review, in which participants agree in advance that no individual will be punished for actions described in the report. The approach borrows heavily from aviation and from accident investigation in the rail and chemical industries, and its spread has been remarkably rapid. In my judgement, it represents one of the more genuine advances in management practice of recent decades, though not for all the reasons its advocates give.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for blamelessness rests on an argument about information. Dr Marek Wojcicki, who studied incident reviews at twelve software firms for the Vistula Institute of Systems Safety, found that when engineers expected to be disciplined, their accounts of an incident became shorter, vaguer and noticeably more defensive. Crucial details were omitted: that a warning had been ignored because it fired dozens of times a day, for instance, or that a risky change had been rushed through to meet a deadline. In firms with blameless policies, by contrast, reports routinely described such details, and the remedies proposed addressed the conditions that made mistakes likely rather than the individuals who made them. Wojcicki's central point is that the people closest to a failure hold knowledge that nobody else possesses, and that punishment is the most efficient way to ensure that this knowledge stays hidden.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is a second, subtler argument. Accident investigators have long warned of hindsight bias: once the outcome of a sequence of events is known, the decisions that led to it appear far more obviously wrong than they did at the time. An engineer who restarted a server that later crashed looks negligent in retrospect, yet the same action, in the same circumstances, may have been taken successfully a hundred times before. Blameless reviews, at their best, ask not 'Who made the error?' but 'Why did this action make sense to the person who took it?' This is a harder question to answer, but it produces far more useful answers. It directs attention towards the confusing displays, ambiguous instructions and competing pressures that shaped the decision, all of which will still be present when the next engineer faces a similar situation. Dismissing the original engineer, by contrast, removes one person while leaving every one of those traps in place.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics have not been silent. Professor Lindiwe Ntsebeza, who teaches professional ethics at the Highveld School of Engineering, argues that the blameless review has been stretched well beyond its original purpose. In some organisations, she contends, the term is now used to shield managers from criticism for decisions, such as chronic understaffing or the repeated postponement of maintenance, that made failures almost inevitable. Because the review focuses on the technical sequence of events, those structural choices are rarely examined, and the engineers who were on duty end up feeling that the system has been judged while the people who designed it have not. Ntsebeza does not want individual engineers punished; her complaint is that blamelessness has been applied downwards but not upwards.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This criticism seems to me largely justified, but it is an argument for applying the principle more consistently, not for abandoning it. A review that asks why an action made sense must, if it is honest, eventually ask why the conditions were as they were, and that inevitably leads to budgets, staffing levels and priorities set far above the engineer's desk. The difficulty is less conceptual than political: few managers commission investigations into their own decisions, and fewer still publish the results. Some organisations have responded by asking an independent team, drawn from outside the department concerned, to conduct reviews of major incidents, an arrangement that at least makes it harder for awkward questions to be avoided.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different objection concerns what happens after the report is written. Dr Francesca Graziadei of the Ligurian Centre for Organisational Research examined more than four hundred reviews produced by three large firms and found that fewer than half of the recommended actions had been completed a year later. Many were quietly dropped when the teams responsible were reorganised; others were marked as complete when only part of the work had been done. In Graziadei's view, organisations have become skilled at the ritual of investigation while neglecting the duller work of follow-up. She suggests that a review whose recommendations are not tracked may do more harm than good, since it creates the appearance of learning without the substance, and reassures senior staff that a problem has been dealt with when it has merely been described.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that the blameless review is valuable but fragile. It works when engineers trust that candour will not be used against them, when its gaze extends to managerial decisions as well as technical ones, and when someone remains responsible for ensuring that its recommendations are carried out. Remove any of these conditions and the practice degenerates into paperwork. The irony is that a method designed to remove blame from individuals depends, in the end, on someone accepting responsibility for the organisation as a whole.

area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: near-miss reporting systems: the safety pyramid assumption, the aviation confidential reporting model, hospital and construction evidence, and the influence of leaders on reporting
title: Lucky Escapes
subtitle: Organisations are urged to collect reports of near misses, but what exactly a near miss reveals is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For almost a century, safety managers have been taught a simple diagram. At its base lie hundreds of minor incidents and near misses; above them, a smaller number of injuries; at the apex, a single fatality. The so-called safety pyramid, derived from insurance records compiled in the 1930s, implies that serious accidents and trivial ones share common causes, so that reducing the latter will inevitably reduce the former. It is on this assumption that thousands of organisations now invest in systems for reporting near misses: events in which something went wrong but, through luck or last-minute intervention, nobody was hurt. The assumption is attractive, and in some industries it appears to have been vindicated. It is, however, considerably weaker than its popularity would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The model most often cited is civil aviation, where pilots and air traffic controllers have for decades been able to submit confidential accounts of incidents to an independent body, usually with a guarantee of immunity from disciplinary action unless the event involved criminal conduct or deliberate recklessness. Dr Haruki Sakuraba, who has analysed aviation reporting schemes for the Pacific Transport Safety Foundation, attributes their success to three features: reports are received by an organisation with no power to punish, identifying details are removed before analysis, and reporters receive feedback showing what was done with their information. Remove the third feature, he argues, and reporting rates collapse within a few years, because people quickly conclude that nobody is listening.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Attempts to transplant this model have had mixed results. Aviation enjoys unusual advantages: its accidents are rare, highly visible and investigated by well-funded national agencies, and its workforce shares a strong professional identity built around procedures and checklists. Few other sectors possess all of these conditions at once. In hospitals, reporting systems have generated enormous quantities of data, with one national scheme receiving more than two million reports a year, but there is little evidence that the volume has translated into fewer patients being harmed. Dr Elin Ahlquist, a health services researcher at the Nordic Patient Safety Institute, believes the problem lies in what is reported. Because the systems are designed to capture everything, staff tend to report the events that are easiest to describe, such as falls and medication slips, while the slow, diffuse failures that cause the most serious harm, such as a diagnosis delayed by poor communication between departments, rarely appear at all. A system that counts what is countable, she observes, risks directing attention to precisely the wrong places.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical challenge comes from the construction industry. Dr Kibet Barasa, of the East African Institute of Building Research, examined injury records from over two hundred building sites and found that the causes of minor injuries, such as cuts and sprains, were largely different from those of fatal accidents, which more often involved falls from height, collapsing structures and heavy machinery. Sites that had sharply reduced their minor injury rates showed no corresponding decline in fatalities. Barasa concludes that the safety pyramid is misleading in industries where serious hazards are physically distinct from everyday ones, and that firms which celebrate falling injury counts may be lulled into complacency about the risks that actually kill.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Barasa's findings are persuasive within their domain, but it would be wrong to treat them as a refutation of near-miss reporting itself. What his data undermine is the idea that all incidents are interchangeable, not the value of studying the right incidents. A near miss in which a crane load swings over a crowded walkway is highly informative about fatal risk; a worker stubbing a toe on a stray brick is not. The lesson, surely, is that reporting systems need to be selective, focusing on events with the potential for serious harm rather than on events that are merely frequent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further complication is cultural. Professor Dimitra Vlahos, who studies organisational behaviour at the Aegean School of Management, compared near-miss reporting in shipping companies registered in eleven countries. She found that reporting rates varied more with the attitudes of individual ship captains than with formal company policies: crews reported freely under captains who acknowledged their own mistakes, and scarcely at all under those who did not. Formal guarantees of confidentiality, in her view, count for little if the person at the top of a small, isolated hierarchy signals disapproval. This finding is consistent with Sakuraba's emphasis on trust, although Vlahos is more doubtful than he is that well-designed rules can ever substitute for it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the effort to learn from near misses is misguided. It suggests rather that the practice has been sold on a promise that it cannot keep: that a single system, gathering every minor mishap, will automatically protect against catastrophe. The more modest claim, that carefully chosen near misses, analysed by people who are trusted and who report back, can reveal hazards before they cause harm, is less exciting. It is also, I would argue, the only version of the idea that the evidence supports, and organisations would be wiser to build their reporting systems around it than around a diagram drawn from insurance files compiled nearly a century ago.

area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: the pre-mortem technique in project planning: prospective hindsight, laboratory and field evidence, exercises without consequence and the influence of hierarchy
title: Imagining the Wreckage
subtitle: A planning technique asks teams to picture their project's failure before it begins. Does it work as well as its admirers claim?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most organisations that launch a new project hold some form of risk assessment. A team gathers, lists what might go wrong, assigns each danger a probability and a cost, and files the result. The exercise is so familiar that its weaknesses are rarely discussed. Yet anyone who has sat through such a meeting will recognise the pattern: once a plan has been approved and its sponsor is in the room, the risks named tend to be modest, external and easily managed, while the possibility that the plan itself is fundamentally flawed is left unspoken. A technique known as the pre-mortem was devised to break this silence, and over the past two decades it has moved from the margins of management consultancy into mainstream practice in engineering, healthcare and government.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method is simple. Before a project begins, participants are asked to imagine that it is a year later and the project has failed completely. Each person then writes down, independently and within a few minutes, the most plausible reasons for that failure. The reasons are read aloud and discussed, and the plan is revised accordingly. The crucial shift is from asking 'What could go wrong?' to stating 'It has gone wrong; explain why.' Its proponents claim that this framing, sometimes called prospective hindsight, frees people to voice doubts that would otherwise seem disloyal: one is no longer criticising the plan but completing an assigned exercise in storytelling. The whole procedure can be completed in under an hour, which partly explains its appeal to busy managers who are wary of elaborate planning methods requiring outside consultants and weeks of analysis.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The psychological basis for this claim comes largely from experiments conducted by Dr Zofia Jankowska at the Tatra Institute of Cognitive Science. She found that participants who were told that an event had definitely occurred generated about thirty per cent more explanations for it, and more specific ones, than participants who were asked merely whether it might occur. Jankowska attributes the effect to the way certainty changes the task: explaining a known outcome is a familiar mental activity, whereas estimating possibilities invites vagueness. She is careful, however, to note that her experiments involved everyday events, such as a friend missing a train, rather than complex organisational projects, and that the transfer from laboratory to boardroom remains largely untested.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Field evidence is thinner than the technique's popularity might lead one to expect. Dr Faly Ratsimbazafy, of the Indian Ocean Business School, compared forty infrastructure projects in which teams had conducted pre-mortems with forty similar projects in which they had not. The pre-mortem teams identified more risks at the planning stage, and their projects were somewhat less likely to exceed their budgets by large margins. But Ratsimbazafy found no difference in the rate at which projects were abandoned, and he cautions that teams which chose to use the technique may already have been more reflective than others, so that the method may be receiving credit for qualities its users already possessed. This seems to me a serious objection, and one that only a properly randomised trial could settle.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second concern is that the exercise can be performed without consequence. Professor Hélène Lemoyne, who studies decision-making in public administration at the Saône Institute of Public Policy, observed pre-mortems in several government ministries and found that many generated long lists of risks that were then filed and forgotten. In her account, the problem was not that participants were unwilling to speak, but that the meeting had no authority to change the plan; the decision to proceed had effectively been made before anyone imagined its failure. Lemoyne argues that a pre-mortem is worthless unless it is held early enough for its findings to alter what is done, and unless someone is obliged to respond in writing to each serious concern that is raised. Without these conditions, she suggests, the exercise may even be counterproductive, since it allows an organisation to claim that risks were considered when in practice they were merely listed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also those who doubt whether the technique really escapes the hierarchy it is meant to bypass. Junior staff, it is suggested, still read the room; if the senior sponsor's own list of reasons for failure is mild, others will follow. Some facilitators therefore insist that written lists be collected anonymously before any discussion begins. Jankowska's research offers indirect support for this precaution: in her group experiments, explanations offered aloud converged quickly on the first idea mentioned, whereas those written privately were far more varied. Whether anonymity survives in small teams, where colleagues can often recognise one another's concerns and handwriting, is another matter.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should organisations make of the pre-mortem? It would be a mistake to treat it as a cure for overconfidence, as some enthusiastic accounts do. Its benefits appear real but modest, and they depend heavily on how and when it is carried out. Yet the alternative, a conventional risk meeting in which the most important risks remain unspoken, is hardly reassuring. At the very least, the pre-mortem acknowledges a truth that formal planning procedures tend to obscure: that the people who know most about why a project might fail are often the least able to say so.

area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: red teams and institutionalised dissent in organisations: assigned versus authentic dissent, independence of critics, review fatigue and the personal cost to challengers
title: Paid to Disagree
subtitle: Organisations increasingly appoint people whose job is to attack their own plans. Whether this works depends on far more than the appointment

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For centuries, when the Catholic Church considered a candidate for sainthood, it appointed an official, popularly known as the devil's advocate, whose task was to argue against the case. The office has long since lost most of its importance, but the idea behind it has enjoyed a remarkable revival in secular organisations. Military planners, intelligence agencies, banks and technology firms now commonly establish 'red teams', groups instructed to find the weaknesses in a plan, a security system or a strategic forecast before an adversary or a competitor does. The practice rests on a plausible premise: that groups which agree too readily make worse decisions, and that dissent, if it does not arise naturally, can be manufactured.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Whether manufactured dissent works as well as the genuine article is the central question, and on this the evidence is less encouraging than its advocates suppose. Laboratory studies conducted by Dr Eleni Zografos at the Ionian Centre for Decision Research compared groups containing a member who sincerely held a minority view with groups in which a member had merely been assigned to argue that view. Authentic dissenters prompted the majority to search more widely for information and to consider options that neither side had initially proposed. Assigned dissenters, by contrast, tended to provoke the majority into defending its original position more vigorously, so that the group ended up more confident in its first choice than it had been at the start. Zografos's explanation is that people discount arguments they know to be performed: a role, however skilfully played, lacks the credibility of conviction.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This is a striking result, but it would be premature to conclude that institutionalised dissent is useless. Laboratory groups typically meet for an hour to resolve an artificial problem; red teams in organisations often work for weeks, gather their own evidence and present findings that can be tested against reality. Professor Thabo Lekgotla, who spent three years observing red teams at a financial regulator and two defence agencies, argues that the decisive variable is not sincerity but independence. Teams drawn from the same department as the planners, and reporting to the same superior, produced critiques that were cautious and largely cosmetic. Teams composed of outsiders, with guaranteed access to senior decision-makers and protection from career consequences, frequently identified flaws that led to substantial revisions. Lekgotla's findings seem to me the more relevant for practical purposes, although they do not refute those of Zografos: an independent team may be persuasive precisely because its members come to believe their own criticisms.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A recurring difficulty is what Lekgotla calls 'red team fatigue'. When a critical review becomes a compulsory step in every project, planners learn to anticipate its objections and to present proposals already armoured against them. The red team, meanwhile, comes under pressure to find something to criticise in order to justify its existence, and its reports drift towards minor technical issues while the strategic assumptions behind a plan pass unexamined. Dr Nadia Tchoubar, an organisational sociologist at the Maghreb Institute of Management Studies, has documented this pattern in large engineering firms. In her view, the most effective arrangement is not a permanent red team but a temporary one, convened for decisions that are both important and difficult to reverse, and then disbanded.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Tchoubar's proposal has obvious merits, but it raises the question of who decides which decisions deserve scrutiny. If that judgement rests with the senior figures whose plans will be examined, the choice is likely to fall on projects they already have doubts about, leaving their favourite schemes untouched. This is not a hypothetical concern: several of the most costly corporate failures of recent decades involved strategies that had been explicitly exempted from internal challenge because of their importance to the organisation's leaders. One partial remedy, adopted by a handful of public bodies, is to give the authority to commission a review to a board or committee that has no stake in the outcome. Another is to subject a random sample of major decisions to challenge each year, so that no project can be confident of escaping attention. Neither solution is perfect, but both are preferable to leaving the choice entirely in the hands of those with most to lose.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further strand of research focuses on the people who do the challenging. Dr Ilmari Pirttilä of the Karelian School of Business surveyed more than six hundred employees who had served on red teams and found that a substantial minority reported damage to their working relationships afterwards, particularly when their critiques had led to the cancellation of a colleague's project. Those who had served on teams drawn from outside their own division reported such damage far less often. Pirttilä suggests that organisations which rely on internal critics without protecting them are, in effect, asking individuals to bear the cost of a benefit that the whole organisation enjoys, an arrangement unlikely to persuade many talented people to volunteer.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lesson that emerges is that dissent cannot simply be ordered into existence. A red team works best when it is genuinely independent, when it is deployed selectively and when its members are shielded from the consequences of doing their job well. These are demanding conditions, and many organisations that claim to welcome challenge meet none of them. What they possess instead is the outward form of dissent, a team with an impressive name and a place on the organisational chart, without the substance that would make it uncomfortable. Appointing a devil's advocate is easy; listening to one is considerably harder.

area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: learning from other organisations' failures: launch-failure evidence, the decay of lessons over time, distancing from competitors' disasters and preserving the stories behind safety rules
title: Other People's Disasters
subtitle: Organisations are supposed to learn from the failures of their rivals. The evidence suggests they do so reluctantly, and forget quickly

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When an aircraft crashes or a bridge collapses, the organisation responsible is not the only one with something to learn. Competitors operating similar equipment, regulators overseeing the sector and firms in entirely different industries may all draw lessons from the investigation that follows. In principle, this ought to make learning remarkably efficient: one organisation pays the price of failure and many benefit. In practice, a growing body of research suggests that organisations learn from other people's disasters far less reliably than they learn from their own, and that what they do learn tends to fade with surprising speed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most detailed evidence comes from the space industry. Dr Callum Ballantyne, an economist at the Clyde Institute for Technology Studies, assembled records of several thousand orbital launch attempts made by dozens of organisations over half a century. He found that a launch failure substantially reduced the probability that the same organisation would fail again on its next few attempts, an effect he attributes to the intense scrutiny that follows a public and expensive loss. Failures by other organisations also reduced the likelihood of subsequent failure, but the effect was smaller and depended heavily on how similar the rockets involved were. Most strikingly, Ballantyne found that the learning from failure decayed: the protective effect of a failure, whether one's own or a competitor's, had largely disappeared within a few years. Successes, by contrast, produced almost no measurable learning at all. Because launch records are unusually complete and failures are impossible to conceal, Ballantyne argues that the industry offers something close to a natural laboratory for studying how organisations respond to setbacks, and his findings have since been cited in fields as distant from rocketry as banking and surgery.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ballantyne's interpretation of this last finding is that success breeds complacency, a conclusion that has been widely quoted. I think it goes slightly too far. A successful launch may simply provide less information than a failed one; there is nothing to investigate when everything works as intended. To describe this as complacency is to attribute an attitude to organisations when the data reveal only an absence of evidence. The distinction matters, because the remedies differ: complacency calls for a change in culture, whereas a shortage of information calls for better ways of examining near misses and small anomalies within apparently successful operations.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should learning from others be weaker than learning from oneself? Professor Ariadne Spyridaki, who studies organisational memory at the Aegean Institute of Social Research, identifies two obstacles. The first is what she calls 'distancing': on learning of a competitor's failure, managers search for differences that make it irrelevant to their own operations, such as the other firm's poor management, its outdated equipment or its unusual circumstances. Such differences can almost always be found, and they provide a comfortable reason to change nothing. The second obstacle is practical: the detailed knowledge needed to apply a lesson is often held by the failed organisation's own engineers and is lost when official reports are condensed into a short list of recommendations. Spyridaki found that hospitals which sent staff to visit institutions where serious errors had occurred adopted far more of the resulting reforms than hospitals which merely read the published reports. Conversations with the people involved, she suggests, conveyed both the practical detail and the emotional weight of the event in a way that no written document could.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The decay that Ballantyne observed has also attracted attention. Dr Lucía Rendón, of the Cordillera School of Management, examined how lessons from major accidents were retained in chemical plants over two decades. She found that procedures introduced in response to an accident were frequently weakened or abandoned once the staff who had experienced it retired or moved on. New employees, unaware of the event that had prompted a rule, regarded it as needless bureaucracy and found ways around it. Rendón argues that organisations must preserve not only rules but the stories behind them, so that each generation of workers understands why a procedure exists. Some of the plants she studied had begun to include detailed accounts of historical accidents, including those at other companies, in their induction training, and reported that new staff were noticeably more willing to follow the procedures concerned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Rendón's emphasis on narrative is persuasive, but it should not be overstated. Stories are vivid, and vividness can distort as well as inform: a dramatic accident may dominate an organisation's memory long after the risk it illustrates has been brought under control, crowding out attention to newer and less spectacular hazards. Memory needs to be curated, not merely preserved. Deciding which stories still deserve retelling is itself a judgement that requires expertise, and it is one that few organisations have assigned to anybody in particular.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, this research suggests that learning from failure, particularly the failures of others, is neither automatic nor permanent. It requires organisations to resist the comfortable conclusion that someone else's disaster could never happen to them, to seek out the detailed knowledge that official reports leave out and to keep lessons alive after the people who learned them have gone. None of this is glamorous work, and it rarely features in the strategies that senior executives present to their boards, which may be precisely why it is so often neglected until the next disaster arrives.

topic: why managers avoid risky projects: outcome-based evaluation, judging decisions by process, career stage and risk-taking, and whether managerial caution protects firms
title: The Safe Bet
subtitle: Managers often turn down ambitious projects that their employers would gladly accept. Researchers disagree about why, and about whether it matters

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine a manager offered a choice between two projects. The first is almost certain to produce a modest return. The second has a good chance of producing a far larger one, but also a real possibility of failing outright. For the company as a whole, which runs dozens of such projects at once and can absorb the occasional loss, the second option may be clearly preferable. For the individual manager, however, the calculation looks very different: a failure will be attached to her name and may end her prospects of promotion, while a spectacular success will be credited partly to colleagues, partly to luck and partly to the market. Economists have long suspected that this mismatch makes managers more cautious than their employers would wish, and a body of evidence now suggests that the suspicion is well founded.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The clearest demonstration comes from experiments run by Dr Grace Wachira at the Great Lakes Institute of Economic Research. Wachira asked several hundred practising managers to choose between investment proposals, varying only the information they were given about how outcomes would be judged. When told that decisions would be evaluated on results alone, managers overwhelmingly preferred the safe option, even when the risky one had a substantially higher expected value. When told instead that evaluators would assess the quality of the reasoning behind a decision, regardless of how it turned out, the proportion choosing the risky option nearly doubled. Wachira concludes that much of what passes for managerial caution is a rational response to the way performance is judged rather than a fixed personality trait.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Wachira's result suggests an apparently simple remedy: judge decisions by their process rather than their outcomes. Professor Ekaterina Kamenova, an organisational economist at the Rila School of Business, is unconvinced that this can work in practice. Evaluating the quality of a decision without reference to its outcome, she argues, requires information that superiors rarely possess and a degree of discipline that few can sustain. Once a project has failed, the reasoning behind it inevitably looks weaker than it did beforehand; once it has succeeded, flaws in the original analysis are forgotten. In her studies of annual appraisals at three large firms, Kamenova found that managers' written assessments of a decision's quality shifted sharply depending on whether its result was already known. Process evaluation, she concludes, is an ideal that collapses on contact with hindsight.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kamenova's scepticism is well grounded, but it seems to me to underestimate what can be achieved by recording reasoning before outcomes are known. Some investment firms now require analysts to document their expectations, including the probability they attach to failure, at the moment a decision is made, and to have those documents reviewed later alongside the results. Such records do not abolish hindsight bias, but they make it harder to rewrite history, and they allow an organisation to distinguish, over many decisions, between a manager who is unlucky and one who is simply careless.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of research examines the role of careers. Dr Nikola Dimitrijević of the Morava Institute for Labour Studies analysed the decisions of more than two thousand managers over fifteen years and found that caution was greatest among those in the middle of their careers, who had much to lose and limited time to recover from a setback. Younger managers, with many years ahead of them in which to rebuild a damaged reputation, took more risks, as did those close to retirement, who had little left to protect. Dimitrijević suggests that organisations wishing to encourage bold projects might deliberately assign them to people at either end of the career ladder, though he acknowledges that this raises obvious questions about experience and judgement. A less drastic option, he proposes, is to soften the career consequences of failure for mid-career staff, for instance by guaranteeing that a manager whose well-reasoned project collapses will be offered a comparable position rather than being quietly sidelined. Several engineering firms have experimented with such guarantees, although none has yet published evidence of their effects.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that managerial caution is a problem to be solved. Dr Anneliese Wendling, of the Moselle Centre for Corporate Governance, argues that much of the literature underestimates the damage that a single catastrophic failure can do, particularly in sectors such as banking or pharmaceuticals, where one disastrous decision can threaten the survival of the entire firm. In her view, the caution of middle managers acts as a useful brake on the ambitions of senior executives, who are often protected by generous severance terms and therefore face little personal risk. On this account, the mismatch between individual and organisational interests sometimes works in the organisation's favour, supplying a check that formal governance structures often fail to provide.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Wendling's argument is a useful corrective, though I am not persuaded that it applies outside the high-stakes sectors she describes. In most organisations, the cost of excessive caution is not a dramatic collapse but a slow accumulation of opportunities missed: products never developed, markets never entered, improvements never tried. Such losses rarely appear in any report, because nobody records the projects that were never proposed. That invisibility is precisely what makes them so easy to ignore, and it helps to explain why organisations that loudly profess a love of innovation so often reward the people who avoid it.

title: The Slow Slide
subtitle: Organisational disasters rarely arrive without warning. The difficulty is that the warnings stop looking like warnings

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Major organisational disasters are often described as sudden: a dam bursts, a refinery explodes, a hospital ward is found to have been harming patients for years. Investigations, however, typically reveal a different story. Long before the catastrophe, there were warning signs: small departures from procedure, equipment operating outside its intended limits, alarms that sounded and were silenced. What is striking is not that these signs existed but that, at the time, they did not seem alarming to the people who saw them. Each deviation, once it had occurred without consequence, became a little more acceptable, until conditions that would once have halted operations were regarded as routine. This process, sometimes called the normalisation of deviance, has become one of the most influential ideas in the study of organisational failure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its appeal lies partly in its refusal to blame individuals. Professor Ruth Abernathy, a sociologist at the Appalachian Centre for Risk Studies, has reconstructed the histories of more than thirty industrial accidents and argues that in almost every case the decisions which, in retrospect, appear reckless were reasonable given what the decision-makers knew and the pressures they faced. A seal that had leaked slightly on previous occasions without causing harm was, quite logically, treated as a minor issue; a maintenance interval extended once without incident became the basis for extending it again. Abernathy insists that the drift was produced not by careless people but by an organisational system that rewarded production and treated each successful deviation as evidence of safety.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This account has an obvious attraction, and I believe it is broadly correct, but it carries a risk of its own. If every disaster can be explained as the product of gradual, invisible drift, the concept begins to explain too much, and with it the possibility of holding anyone responsible disappears. Dr Ixchel Xiloj, who studies regulation at the Mesoamerican Institute of Public Affairs, makes a related criticism. In her examination of accident inquiries, she found that the phrase 'normalisation of deviance' was increasingly used by companies themselves, often in public statements issued shortly after an accident, to suggest that a failure was nobody's fault. A concept intended to illuminate how organisations go wrong, she argues, has been adopted as a way of avoiding accountability. Xiloj does not reject the idea itself; she proposes instead that inquiries should identify who had the authority to halt the drift at each stage, and why they did not use it. Drift, on this view, may be gradual, but the decisions that permit it are still taken by identifiable people occupying identifiable positions.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further question is whether drift can be detected while it is happening, rather than only afterwards. Dr Tomasz Drozdowski, an engineer at the Oder Institute of Industrial Safety, believes it can. He has developed methods for tracking how far actual operating practices diverge from written procedures over time, using maintenance logs, equipment data and anonymous staff surveys. In a study of nine power stations, the plants whose practices had diverged furthest from their procedures experienced significantly more serious incidents in the following three years. Drozdowski accepts that some divergence is healthy, since written procedures are often outdated and workers adapt them sensibly, but he argues that the rate of change, rather than its direction, provides the earliest warning.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares this optimism. Professor Gulnora Rasulova, an organisational psychologist at the Samarkand School of Management, points out that the people inside an organisation are least able to see drift precisely because they have adapted to it, and that measurements designed by insiders will reflect insiders' assumptions about what counts as normal. In her studies of hospital wards, she found that newly arrived staff identified unsafe practices far more readily than their experienced colleagues, but that within about six months their judgements had converged with those of everyone else. Rasulova concludes that fresh eyes are a perishable resource, and that organisations should systematically gather the observations of newcomers before they too become accustomed to local habits.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Rasulova's finding seems to me among the most practically useful in this field, and one that is easy to act upon. Many organisations already ask new employees for feedback, but they typically do so through general satisfaction surveys that are not designed to capture concerns about safety. A brief structured interview conducted within a new employee's first weeks, asking specifically what has surprised or worried them, would cost little and might reveal more than many expensive audits. The same logic applies to staff who transfer between sites, and to contractors who visit many organisations in the same industry: each carries a standard of comparison that permanent employees have lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these approaches can eliminate drift entirely, and it would be unwise to pretend otherwise. Organisations operate under constant pressure to do more with less, and some adaptation of procedures is both inevitable and desirable. The aim should not be to prevent all deviation but to ensure that deviations are noticed, discussed and deliberately accepted or rejected, rather than slipping silently into the category of things that are simply done. That is a modest ambition, but it is one that most of the disasters described in accident reports suggest was not achieved.

area: attitudes to failure and risk in organisations
topic: tolerance of failure in research funding: whether grant panels penalise novel proposals, high-risk funding schemes, political pressure on funders and career incentives for scientists
title: Permission to Fail
subtitle: Research funders say they want bold science. Their own procedures, and those of universities, may be the main obstacle

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every major research funder now claims to support 'high-risk, high-reward' science: projects that will probably fail but that, if they succeed, could transform a field. The rhetoric reflects a widespread anxiety that the conventional system of grant review has become too cautious. Panels of experts, asked to rank hundreds of proposals against limited budgets, are thought to favour projects that extend existing knowledge in predictable ways, while ideas that challenge prevailing assumptions are marked down as speculative. If this is true, the consequences are serious, since many of the discoveries that later proved most valuable were initially regarded as unpromising. Yet the evidence that review panels systematically penalise risk is less clear-cut than is often assumed, and the remedies proposed raise difficulties of their own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against conventional review has been made most forcefully by Dr Tamar Orbeliani, a sociologist of science at the Kartli Institute for Science Policy. Orbeliani analysed the scores awarded to more than eight thousand proposals by a national funding body and found that proposals judged by independent assessors to be highly novel received lower scores on average than conventional ones, even after the applicants' track records had been taken into account. The penalty was largest, she found, for proposals that combined ideas from fields rarely brought together. Orbeliani attributes this to the composition of panels: reviewers are experts in established fields, and they are understandably more confident judging work that resembles their own.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone reads the evidence in the same way. Professor Dieter Lautenbach, a statistician at the Weser Centre for Research Evaluation, points out that novelty and quality are difficult to separate. Highly novel proposals, he suggests, are also more likely to be poorly specified, because their authors are venturing into territory where methods are untested and preliminary data are scarce. Lower scores might therefore reflect genuine weaknesses rather than prejudice. In a re-analysis of a smaller dataset, Lautenbach found that the novelty penalty shrank considerably once the clarity of each proposal's methods had been taken into account. His work does not show that panels are entirely fair to unconventional ideas, but it should make us cautious about assuming that every low score for a bold proposal is evidence of timidity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever the cause, many funders have introduced dedicated schemes intended to reward risk. Typically, these offer longer grants, require less preliminary data and instruct reviewers explicitly to value ambition over feasibility. Dr Valeria Quiñonez, who evaluates research programmes at the Río de la Plata Institute of Public Policy, compared the subsequent output of researchers funded through such schemes with that of similar researchers funded through conventional grants. The risk-tolerant schemes produced more papers that were later among the most cited in their fields, but also more papers that were rarely cited at all; their results, in other words, were more variable. Quiñonez regards this as exactly what a successful high-risk programme should look like, since a scheme whose projects all succeed is, almost by definition, not taking real risks. She also notes that the most highly cited papers often appeared many years after the grant had ended, which means that evaluations conducted at the close of a project are likely to underestimate its value.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: I find this argument convincing as far as it goes, but it leaves aside a practical problem. Funders answer to governments, and governments answer to taxpayers, few of whom are likely to be reassured by the news that a programme's failures prove its boldness. When a high-profile project collapses, the pressure to tighten selection criteria is considerable, and risk-tolerant schemes tend gradually to drift back towards conventional standards. A tolerance for failure that depends on the courage of individual programme managers is unlikely to survive their departure. If funders are serious, they will need to explain in advance, and in public, what proportion of projects they expect to fail, so that a collapse can be presented as part of the plan rather than as a scandal. A few have begun to publish such figures, but the practice remains rare, perhaps because few organisations relish the prospect of announcing that most of the money they spend will produce nothing of immediate use.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers argue that the problem lies less in how proposals are judged than in how researchers are judged afterwards. Dr Signe Frølund of the Øresund Institute for Higher Education surveyed nearly three thousand early-career scientists and found that the main reason most gave for avoiding ambitious projects was not fear of rejection by funders but fear of producing too few publications to secure a permanent position. Even scientists who held risk-tolerant grants frequently reported pursuing a safer side project alongside their main work in order to guarantee a steady flow of papers. On this view, dedicated funding schemes treat the symptom rather than the disease; as long as careers are assessed by publication counts over short periods, researchers will hedge their bets whatever funders say.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Frølund's point seems to me decisive, and it suggests that the debate about grant review, while not irrelevant, has been somewhat misdirected. A funder can tell reviewers to value ambition, but it cannot alter the hiring decisions of universities, which remain heavily influenced by short-term output. Genuine tolerance for failure would require the institutions that employ scientists, not just those that fund them, to accept that a few years without a significant result may be the price of attempting something difficult. Until that happens, the language of high-risk research will continue to promise considerably more than it delivers.

topic: mental accounting and the fungibility of money: savings held alongside debt, labelled cash transfers, fading label effects and fairness
title: Money with Labels
subtitle: Economists have long insisted that a pound is a pound, wherever it comes from. Ordinary spending behaviour suggests otherwise

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Standard economic theory treats money as fungible: any unit of currency can be substituted for any other, so the source of a sum, or the purpose a household assigns to it, should make no difference to how it is spent. A family that receives an unexpected tax refund ought, by this reasoning, to treat it exactly as it would an equivalent rise in salary. Yet anyone who has kept a jar of coins for holidays, or refused to touch a savings account while paying interest on a credit card, knows that people rarely behave this way. Since the 1980s, the habit of sorting money into separate mental categories, each governed by its own rules, has been known as mental accounting, and it has proved one of the more durable ideas in behavioural economics.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The concept explains several puzzles that conventional models struggle with. People who win a modest sum at a casino are often noticeably more willing to gamble it away than they would be with money from their wages, as though winnings were not quite their own. Shoppers who have just saved on a planned purchase frequently spend the difference on something they had not intended to buy. Perhaps most strikingly, many households simultaneously hold low-interest savings and high-interest debt, a combination that costs them money every month. Grace Quagraine, an economist at the Accra Institute for Household Finance, has documented this pattern among salaried workers in five West African cities and found it to be most common among those who describe their savings as being 'for the children'. To her, such accounts function less as a store of wealth than as a promise, and breaking a promise carries a psychological cost that the interest rate does not capture.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not every economist accepts that labels genuinely change behaviour. Dieter Fahrenkrug of the Rhineland Centre for Economic Analysis argues that many apparent examples of mental accounting dissolve once the full circumstances of a household are considered. A family that keeps its savings untouched while borrowing may simply be insuring itself against the risk that a credit line will be withdrawn in a crisis, which is a rational precaution rather than a cognitive error. Fahrenkrug's objection deserves to be taken seriously, since behavioural economists have sometimes been too quick to label any departure from textbook behaviour as a mistake. It does not, however, account for the most persuasive evidence, which comes not from surveys of existing habits but from experiments in which the label on money is the only thing that varies.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The best known of these concern cash transfers to poor households. In one programme studied by Marisol Ilagan and colleagues at the Manila School of Development Studies, families received identical monthly payments, but half were told that the money was intended for their children's schooling while the other half were given no guidance at all. No conditions were attached, and no one checked how the money was used. Even so, the households told about schooling spent markedly more on uniforms, books and fees. Ilagan interprets this as clear evidence that a label can shape spending without any enforcement. A comparable result has been observed with winter fuel payments in northern Europe, where a benefit given to all older people was spent disproportionately on heating, even though recipients were free to use it however they wished.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The policy implications seem obvious, yet they are less straightforward than enthusiasts suggest. If a label alone can steer spending, governments might be tempted to replace costly systems of monitoring with simple naming. Henrik Tjernberg, who advises the Swedish social insurance agency, warns that the effect may fade as recipients become accustomed to the payments. In his agency's data, the bias towards labelled spending was strongest in the first year of a new benefit and had largely disappeared by the third. Tjernberg's finding is drawn from a single country, and it would be unwise to generalise from it too readily; nonetheless, it suggests that labelling is better understood as a way of encouraging a new habit than as a permanent instrument of control.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also questions of fairness. Mental accounting may help disciplined individuals, but it can trap less fortunate ones. A household that rigidly reserves money for rent may go hungry rather than dip into that fund, while one that treats a windfall as 'free money' may spend it before considering its debts. Quagraine has argued that financial education should aim not to eliminate mental accounts, which she regards as an unavoidable feature of human cognition, but to help people design accounts that serve their own goals. This is an attractive idea, although it presumes a degree of planning that many people under financial strain may find difficult to achieve.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be made of the claim that money is fungible? It remains true in the narrow sense that a coin buys the same goods whichever pocket it comes from. But the evidence of the past four decades makes clear that people do not experience their money in that way, and an account of economic behaviour that ignores this is incomplete. The challenge now is less to prove that mental accounting exists than to understand when it helps people and when it harms them.

topic: measuring present bias: preference reversals in money-choice experiments, trust and liquidity confounds, effort-based tasks and payday borrowing
title: Sooner or Later
subtitle: The idea that people overvalue the present is central to modern economics, but measuring it has proved surprisingly difficult

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Offer someone a choice between £100 today and £110 in a month, and many will take the smaller sum now. Offer the same person £100 in twelve months or £110 in thirteen, and most will happily wait the extra month. To economists, this reversal is revealing. If people discounted the future at a constant rate, a one-month delay should matter equally whether it begins today or a year from now. That it does not has been taken as evidence of 'present bias': a disproportionate preference for rewards that are immediate. The idea underpins a great deal of policy thinking, from pension design to the regulation of short-term loans. Yet the methods used to measure present bias are more fragile than the confidence placed in them would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The classic approach is the monetary choice experiment, in which participants make a series of decisions between smaller-sooner and larger-later payments. From these choices, researchers estimate how steeply each person discounts the future. Early studies produced startling numbers: some implied annual discount rates of several hundred per cent, figures that would make almost any long-term investment unappealing. Aino Saarnivaara, a behavioural economist at the Baltic Institute for Experimental Economics, has spent a decade re-examining such estimates. She points out that participants in these experiments often have good reasons to prefer payment today that have nothing to do with impatience. They may doubt that the researchers will actually pay them later, or they may need cash urgently to cover a bill. Both factors would make people appear impatient even if their underlying preferences were perfectly consistent.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Saarnivaara's own studies attempted to remove these confounding influences. Payments were made by automatic bank transfer, both the sooner and the later amounts were guaranteed in writing, and even the 'immediate' option was paid a day after the session so that neither choice offered instant cash. Under these conditions, the reversal of preferences shrank considerably, and in some groups it vanished altogether. Her conclusion is that much of the apparent present bias in money is an artefact of trust and liquidity rather than a fundamental feature of human preference. This is a valuable corrective, but it goes further than the evidence allows. A preference that appears only when cash is truly immediate is still a preference, and many real decisions, such as whether to borrow at a high rate shortly before payday, involve precisely that kind of immediacy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of criticism concerns what money can tell us at all. Kwabena Kpodo of the Kumasi Centre for Applied Economics argues that money is a poor measure of time preference because it is not consumed at the moment it is received. A person who accepts £100 today may not spend it until next month, so the choice says little about when they wish to enjoy anything. Kpodo has instead studied choices involving effort, asking participants to decide how many tedious transcription tasks they will complete today or next week. Here present bias appears clearly and consistently: people commit to heavy workloads in the future, then ask to reduce them when the day arrives. Kpodo's design has been widely praised, and rightly so, since effort, unlike money, cannot be stored for later use.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even if present bias is real, its practical significance is debated. Paula Larrondo, who has studied payday lending for the Santiago Consumer Finance Observatory, found that borrowers who scored as most present-biased in laboratory tasks were indeed more likely to take out expensive short-term loans. However, the relationship was weak, and the strongest predictor of borrowing was simply an unexpected expense such as a medical bill or a car repair. Larrondo is careful not to dismiss behavioural explanations, but she warns that policy built on the assumption that borrowers are impatient may overlook the more mundane problem that they lack the savings to absorb shocks.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that a single number cannot capture an attitude to time. People who are impatient about food may be patient about money; those who procrastinate over exercise may plan their finances meticulously. Measures obtained in one domain frequently fail to predict behaviour in another, and the same person may give quite different answers on different days. Researchers who speak of an individual's 'discount rate' as though it were a stable trait, like height, are relying on a convenient simplification that has gradually hardened into an assumption.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that present bias should be abandoned as a concept. The tendency to favour the immediate over the delayed is too widely observed, in too many settings, to be explained away. But the history of its measurement offers a cautionary lesson. The most dramatic early findings depended partly on features of experimental design, and the effect became clearer, not weaker, once researchers moved from money to effort. Economists would do well to treat their estimates as descriptions of behaviour in particular circumstances, rather than as windows onto a fixed human nature. Doing so would make the concept less tidy, but it would also make it considerably more useful to those who design pensions, loans and savings schemes for real people.

topic: the endowment effect: the gap between buying and selling prices, loss aversion versus procedural confusion, trader experience, cultural variation and policy relevance
title: Mine Is Worth More
subtitle: Why do people demand more to give up an object than they would pay to acquire it? The answer is less settled than textbooks imply

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a now-familiar kind of classroom experiment, half the students in a room are given a coffee mug and the other half are given nothing. Those with mugs are asked the lowest price at which they would sell; those without are asked the most they would pay. Since the mugs were handed out at random, the two groups should value them roughly equally, and about half the mugs ought to change hands. In practice, far fewer trades take place, because owners typically demand around twice as much as buyers are prepared to offer. This gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay has become known as the endowment effect, and it is commonly cited as one of the clearest demonstrations that people do not behave as standard economic theory predicts.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The usual explanation draws on loss aversion, the idea that losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Giving up a mug feels like a loss to its owner, while acquiring one is merely a gain to the buyer, so owners require more compensation. Rustam Bekmurzaev, of the Tashkent Laboratory for Decision Research, has defended this account for many years. He argues that the endowment effect appears almost instantly, with students valuing a mug more within minutes of receiving it, and that this speed is hard to explain except as a deep-seated reaction to the prospect of loss. Bekmurzaev's evidence on timing is impressive. Even so, the speed of an effect tells us little about its cause, and other explanations predict an equally rapid response.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of these concerns the way experiments are conducted. Shirin Varzaneh, an experimental economist at the Caspian School of Economics, has shown that the size of the gap depends heavily on the procedures used to elicit valuations. When participants are given practice rounds, detailed explanations of how prices are determined and an assurance that stating their true value is in their interest, the difference between buying and selling prices narrows sharply, and in some of her studies it disappears. Varzaneh does not claim that the effect is purely an illusion, but she believes that much of it reflects participants' uncertainty about unfamiliar selling procedures, which leads them to adopt the cautious strategy of asking a high price. Her critics reply that confusion cannot explain why the same pattern appears outside the laboratory, in housing markets for example, where sellers often refuse offers that would have seemed fair to them before they owned the property.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third line of research asks who displays the effect. Mads Dalgaard of the North Sea Institute of Market Studies studied traders at sports-memorabilia fairs and found that experienced dealers, who buy and sell collectables as a matter of routine, showed little or no endowment effect, whereas inexperienced collectors showed a substantial one. In follow-up work, he found that the gap shrank among novices who were encouraged to make several trades over a period of months. To Dalgaard, this suggests that the effect is learned behaviour, or at least behaviour that experience can unlearn. The finding is often presented as a refutation of the loss-aversion account, but that interpretation seems premature. Dealers may simply think of their stock as goods held for exchange rather than as possessions, in which case no loss is felt on selling, and the underlying aversion to loss remains intact.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Cultural comparisons have complicated matters further. Esther Mumbere and colleagues at the Kampala Centre for Behavioural Studies ran mug-style experiments in several communities, including a group of pastoralists who trade livestock and household goods regularly and have relatively few private possessions. Among these participants, owners and buyers placed almost identical values on the objects offered. Mumbere argues that the endowment effect may be strongest in societies in which personal ownership of goods is highly prized and market exchange is comparatively rare in daily life. This is an intriguing hypothesis, although it rests so far on a small number of communities and should be tested more widely before it is accepted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What would follow if the effect turned out to be less universal than once assumed? The answer matters beyond academic economics. The endowment effect has been used to justify a range of policy recommendations, from the design of default options in pensions to the allocation of legal rights over land and pollution. Where owners value what they hold more highly than others would, the initial allocation of a right matters, since it may never be traded to the person who would value it most. If the effect is largely a product of inexperience or of experimental procedure, that argument is considerably weakened.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most reasonable conclusion, it seems to me, lies between the extremes. The gap between buying and selling prices is real, and it appears in markets as well as classrooms. But it is neither as large nor as fixed as early studies suggested, and it varies with experience, culture and context. Rather than treating it as a universal law of human behaviour, economists should regard it as a tendency whose strength depends on how people understand the objects they own and the transactions they are asked to make.

topic: scarcity theory and cognitive bandwidth: financial worry and reasoning scores, pre-harvest testing of farmers, replication of smaller effects, anthropological objections and the paperwork burden of welfare
title: The Mental Tax of Want
subtitle: Does financial pressure itself make decisions harder? A popular theory of poverty faces its first serious tests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, discussions of poverty tended to fall into two camps. One emphasised structural causes such as low wages and lack of opportunity; the other pointed to the choices poor people made, from borrowing at ruinous rates to neglecting preventive health care. In the past fifteen years, a third position has gained influence. According to what is often called scarcity theory, the experience of not having enough, whether of money, time or food, captures attention and consumes mental resources, leaving less capacity for everything else. Poor decisions, on this view, are not the cause of poverty but one of its consequences: anyone placed under persistent financial pressure would begin to make them. The idea was not entirely new, since psychologists had long known that stress narrows attention, but it had rarely been applied so directly to economic behaviour.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theory's appeal rests largely on a handful of striking studies. In one, conducted by Leila Tamaddon at the Levant Institute for Economic Hardship, shoppers at a city market were first asked to think about how they would pay for an expensive car repair and were then given a set of reasoning puzzles. Among lower-income participants, merely contemplating the bill reduced scores substantially, by an amount Tamaddon compared to losing a full night's sleep; among higher-income participants, scores barely changed. A second study followed sugar-cane farmers who receive most of their annual income at harvest. The same farmers performed noticeably worse on cognitive tests in the weeks before the harvest, when money was tight, than in the weeks after it, which suggests that the difference reflected their circumstances rather than any fixed personal trait. Because the comparison involved the same people, differences in education or upbringing could not account for the result.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These findings attracted enormous attention, not least because of their implications for policy. If financial strain impairs judgement, then programmes that demand complex paperwork from people in poverty are not merely inconvenient; they may be setting tests that applicants are least able to pass at the very moment they most need help. Tamaddon has argued that welfare systems should therefore be redesigned to minimise the number of decisions and forms they require. This seems to me one of the most valuable practical contributions of the theory, and it does not depend on every detail of the original studies being correct: simplifying access to support is sensible whether or not scarcity reduces mental capacity. Some governments have already experimented with enrolling eligible families in benefits automatically, removing the need to apply at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The details, however, have come under scrutiny. When Jussi Keskinen and colleagues at the Nordic Centre for Replication in Social Science repeated the car-repair experiment with a much larger and more varied sample, they found an effect less than half the size originally reported, and in some groups none at all. Keskinen does not regard this as a refutation, but he suggests that the early studies, which were small, may have exaggerated the strength of the phenomenon, as small studies often do. Re-analyses of the harvest data have also produced mixed results; in one, the apparent drop in performance before harvest could be largely explained by participants becoming more familiar with the tests over successive sessions. Keskinen's caution is entirely justified, though it would be a mistake to conclude from the smaller effects that the underlying idea has been discredited.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different objection comes from Nomvula Siwela, an anthropologist at the Institute for Southern African Social Research, who has spent several years living in low-income communities. Siwela does not dispute that money worries are mentally exhausting, but she is uneasy with the way scarcity theory portrays poor people as cognitively depleted. In her fieldwork, she observed households managing irregular incomes with considerable skill, juggling informal loans, rotating savings groups and complex obligations to relatives. Many were planning months ahead, setting money aside for school fees and funerals, which hardly fits the image of minds absorbed by immediate needs.To describe such people chiefly in terms of what their minds lack, she argues, risks reviving older stereotypes in a more scientific vocabulary. Her concern is understandable, but it rests partly on a misreading: the theory claims that anyone under scarcity would behave similarly, which is a statement about situations, not about poor people as a group.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the debate? The more extravagant claims made for scarcity theory, notably that it can explain persistent poverty on its own, are unlikely to survive. The effects found in recent replications are real but modest, and they are only one of many factors shaping the lives of people on low incomes. Yet the central insight remains important. Policies that assume people in poverty have unlimited time and attention to devote to forms, deadlines and eligibility rules are poorly designed, whatever the precise size of the cognitive cost. A form that takes an hour to complete, or a benefit that lapses if a single letter goes unanswered, imposes costs that fall most heavily on those with the least room for error. Reducing such burdens is cheap compared with most anti-poverty measures, and it is a reform that supporters and critics of the theory alike ought to be able to endorse.The theory's lasting contribution may lie less in its laboratory measurements than in having obliged policy-makers to consider the mental burden that their own systems create.
