topic: automatic enrolment in workplace pensions: default contribution rates, drift to low defaults, offsetting borrowing, automatic escalation and active choice as an alternative
title: Saving Without Deciding
subtitle: Automatic enrolment has transformed pension participation. Its critics ask what else it has changed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When employees are left to decide for themselves whether to join a workplace pension, many never get round to it. They intend to enrol, perhaps next month or after a pay rise, but the moment never seems right, and years pass without a single contribution being made. Automatic enrolment reverses this arrangement. Workers are placed in a pension scheme from their first day unless they actively choose to leave, and the contribution rate and investment fund are set in advance. Since the approach was adopted at national level by several countries in the 2010s, participation among eligible employees has in some cases risen from around half to nine in ten. Few policies derived from behavioural economics can claim such dramatic results, and it is not surprising that automatic enrolment is frequently held up as the field's greatest practical success.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanism appears straightforward. Changing from the default requires effort, attention and a decision, and many people prefer to avoid all three. Default options may also be interpreted as a recommendation: if an employer has chosen a particular contribution rate, employees may assume it is the sensible amount. Onni Kauhanen, an economist at the Baltic Pensions Research Centre, has studied the records of more than two hundred employers and found that the proportion of staff remaining at the default rate was remarkably similar whatever that rate happened to be. Kauhanen concludes that most employees treat the default not as a starting point for deliberation but as the answer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This is where the difficulties begin. If people simply accept whatever rate is chosen for them, the rate must be set wisely, and early schemes set it low to avoid provoking large numbers of people to opt out. Kauhanen's data suggest that, in some firms, the introduction of automatic enrolment actually reduced the average contribution, because employees who would previously have chosen a generous rate drifted towards the lower default. The overall effect on retirement savings was still positive, since so many more people were saving, but the gain was smaller than headline participation figures implied. This seems to me a genuine weakness of early policy, and one that has received too little attention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second concern is what happens to the rest of a household's finances. Begoña Cuadrado, of the Iberian Institute for Household Economics, has linked pension records to data on credit-card borrowing and overdrafts. Her analysis indicates that some automatically enrolled workers, especially those on modest incomes, borrowed more in the years after enrolment, as though the money diverted to pensions had to be replaced from somewhere. For these workers, part of the apparent increase in saving was offset by higher-cost debt. Cuadrado stresses that the effect was concentrated in a minority and that most enrolled employees did not increase their borrowing. Even so, her work is a useful reminder that a pension balance is not the same thing as overall wealth.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of automatic enrolment have an answer to both objections. Kofi Amuzu, who led the design of the scheme operated by the West African Retirement Savings Authority, argues that low defaults were a deliberate compromise, accepted in order to keep opt-out rates low while workers grew accustomed to saving. Under the scheme he designed, the default rate rises automatically by a small amount each year, usually timed to coincide with annual pay increases so that take-home pay never falls. Participation has remained high as rates have risen, which Amuzu takes as evidence that inertia can be harnessed not only to start saving but to increase it. The design is an elegant one, though it remains to be seen whether workers will tolerate escalation indefinitely once contributions reach levels they notice.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more philosophical objection concerns the ethics of steering people at all. Critics argue that automatic enrolment exploits the very inattention that economists once regarded as irrational, and that a policy which works because people fail to think about it is difficult to reconcile with respect for individual choice. Ekaterina Pirogova, a political philosopher at the Institute for Public Reason, has proposed an alternative known as active choice, in which employees must tick a box indicating whether they wish to join, with no default at all. In trials, active choice produced participation nearly as high as automatic enrolment, while ensuring that every saver had made a decision. Pirogova's proposal deserves more attention from policy-makers than it has so far received.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Yet active choice is not free of drawbacks. Forcing a decision at the moment of starting a new job, when employees are already overwhelmed with paperwork, may produce choices that are rushed rather than considered. And for many people, particularly those with little financial knowledge, a requirement to choose may feel less like respect than like a burden. Some of the trials that produced encouraging results also involved well-educated office staff, and it is not yet clear whether the same participation would be achieved among shift workers or those employed through agencies.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Automatic enrolment, then, is neither the triumph its admirers describe nor the manipulation its critics fear. It has undoubtedly brought millions of people into pension saving who would otherwise have had nothing. But its success has depended on careful design, and defaults chosen carelessly can quietly shape outcomes for the worse. The lesson for policy-makers is that a default is never neutral: whoever sets it bears responsibility for where people end up.

topic: how robust is loss aversion: small versus large stakes, hypothetical versus real money, field evidence from sport and taxi drivers, and loss-framed bonuses for teachers
title: Do Losses Really Loom Larger?
subtitle: One of behavioural economics' best-known findings is being re-examined, and the famous ratio behind it looks less fixed than once believed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas in behavioural economics have travelled as far as loss aversion: the claim that the pain of losing something is roughly twice as intense as the pleasure of gaining the same thing. It has been invoked to explain why investors hold on to falling shares, why shoppers resist price rises more than they welcome price cuts, and why people turn down bets that offer a fair chance of winning more than they could lose. A ratio of about two to one, derived from early laboratory studies, has been repeated so often in textbooks and policy reports that it is sometimes treated as a constant of human nature. Over the past decade, however, a growing number of researchers have begun to ask how robust the evidence really is.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The challenge is not that losses never matter more than gains, and few critics would go so far as to say so. Rather, critics argue that the effect is far more variable than the famous ratio suggests. Nino Laoshvili, a psychologist at the Caucasus Centre for Decision Science, has reviewed hundreds of experiments in which participants accepted or rejected gambles. She found that when stakes were small, such as a coin toss for a few coins, many people showed no loss aversion at all, and some even appeared to seek risk. The asymmetry became pronounced only when the potential losses were large relative to the participant's income. Laoshvili argues that what has been called loss aversion may often be nothing more than sensible caution about outcomes that could genuinely hurt.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others have questioned how the effect has been measured. Many classic demonstrations asked people to imagine hypothetical gains and losses rather than risking real money. Tomas Sakalauskas, an economist at the Baltic School of Applied Economics, has compared studies using imaginary and real stakes and found that the asymmetry was consistently weaker when participants had actual money at risk. He also notes that the wording of experimental questions often draws attention to losses, which may encourage participants to weigh them more heavily. Sakalauskas does not dismiss loss aversion, but he believes the size commonly quoted owes much to the conventions of the laboratory. His point about hypothetical stakes is well taken, although real-money experiments have their own limitations, since ethical rules generally prevent researchers from imposing losses large enough to matter.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the concept point to evidence from outside the laboratory. Professional golfers, for example, are reported to putt more accurately when attempting to avoid a score above par than when trying to score below it, as though avoiding a loss relative to a reference point motivates them more than achieving an equivalent gain. Similar patterns appear in the behaviour of taxi drivers, who seem to work harder on days when they are short of a daily earnings target. Such findings suggest that loss aversion is not simply an artefact of the way experiments are designed, and they are difficult to explain as sensible caution, since nothing of great value is at risk on a single putt.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious attempt to put the idea to practical use concerns incentives for teachers. Marie-Claire Tchoumi, an education economist at the Central African Institute for Education Policy, ran a trial in which some teachers received a bonus at the end of the school year if their pupils' test scores improved, while others were given the same bonus at the start of the year and told they would have to repay it if scores did not rise. The second group, who stood to lose money they already held, produced noticeably larger gains in pupil performance. Tchoumi interprets the result as strong confirmation that loss aversion can be harnessed to improve public services. It is a striking finding, but the approach raises questions that the trial alone cannot answer. Teachers asked to return money they have already spent may face real hardship, and it is doubtful whether such schemes would remain acceptable to staff, or to the unions that represent them, if they were used routinely.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also reason to doubt whether the effect would persist. Several attempts to repeat loss-framed incentive schemes in other settings have produced smaller benefits, and in some cases none. It is possible that the novelty of the arrangement, rather than loss aversion itself, accounted for part of the original improvement. If so, the effect might fade as teachers grew used to receiving, and potentially returning, money. Only trials that run for several years, with the same staff, are likely to settle the question, and few such trials have yet been attempted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these debates is not the collapse of loss aversion but its refinement. Losses do seem to matter more than gains in many circumstances, particularly when the stakes are high and the reference point is clear. But the idea that people everywhere feel losses twice as strongly as gains is an oversimplification that has outlived its usefulness. Policy-makers who rely on a fixed ratio to design incentives or predict behaviour risk building on foundations that are considerably less solid than they appear.

topic: the decoy effect (asymmetric dominance): laboratory evidence, failure under realistic presentation, online pricing pages, shortlists of candidates and implications for regulation
title: The Option Nobody Chooses
subtitle: An unwanted alternative can change what people buy. The harder question is how often it really does

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine a cinema that sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub for three pounds and a large one for seven. Many customers settle for the small tub. Now add a medium tub priced at six pounds fifty. Almost nobody buys it, yet its presence appears to push a sizeable share of customers towards the large tub, which suddenly looks like a bargain. This phenomenon, known to researchers as the decoy effect or, more technically, asymmetric dominance, occurs when an option that is clearly inferior to one alternative, but not to another, shifts preferences towards the option that beats it. It sits awkwardly with a foundational assumption of classical economics: that adding an option to a set should never increase the share of an option already available. That such an apparently trivial manipulation could violate this principle has made the decoy a favourite illustration of the claim that preferences are constructed rather than simply revealed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The early experimental evidence was striking. In a series of laboratory studies at the Lakeshore School of Management, Solveig Gjerstadli presented participants with choices between products described on two dimensions, such as the price and quality of a beer. When a decoy was introduced that was slightly worse than one target on both attributes, the proportion of participants choosing that target rose by between ten and twenty percentage points. Gjerstadli interpreted the effect as evidence that people find it difficult to evaluate options in absolute terms and instead rely on comparisons that are easy to make. A dominated option offers precisely such a comparison: it supplies an obvious reason for preferring the target, and reasons, she argued, are what people look for when they must defend a decision to themselves or to others.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Commercial applications followed swiftly, and the decoy is now routinely presented in marketing textbooks as a pricing tool. A publisher, for example, might offer a print-only subscription at the same price as a bundle that includes both print and digital access, in the expectation that the bundle will look irresistible. Yet the leap from laboratory to marketplace was made with less caution than it deserved. Most of the original studies used stimuli that were deliberately stripped down: products described by two numbers in a table, with no brand names, no images and no opportunity to consult other sources. Real purchasing decisions are rarely so tidy, and it would be surprising if an effect generated under such controlled conditions survived intact in a noisy commercial environment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This concern was put to the test by Chukwudi Ezeogwu and colleagues at the Institute for Applied Choice Research, who attempted to reproduce several classic decoy experiments using more realistic presentation. When options were shown as pictures rather than as numerical attributes, the effect largely disappeared; in some conditions it even reversed, with the decoy appearing to draw attention to the weaknesses of the target. Ezeogwu suggests that the effect depends on the decoy's inferiority being instantly visible. Where attributes must be inferred from images or descriptions, consumers may never notice that one option is dominated at all, and the comparison that drives the effect simply does not take place. In his view, the decoy is real but fragile, a phenomenon of spreadsheets rather than shop floors.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this conclusion. Marisol Echegaray, an economist who has worked with several online retailers, points out that a great deal of modern shopping does in fact resemble the laboratory: comparison websites display products in tables, and subscription pages list plans side by side with their features ticked or crossed. Analysing data from a software company that varied its pricing page over eighteen months, Echegaray found that introducing a deliberately unattractive mid-priced plan raised sales of the premium plan by around six per cent, a smaller effect than laboratory studies would predict but far from negligible. Her findings imply that the question is not whether the decoy works outside the laboratory but where it does so. That reframing strikes me as the most productive contribution to the debate so far.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more unsettling line of research concerns the decoy's influence beyond consumer markets. Lenka Prochazkova, a political psychologist at the Central European Decision Laboratory, has examined whether similar effects shape choices between job applicants, medical treatments and even candidates for public office. Her experiments suggest that introducing a weak candidate who resembles one of two front-runners can tilt support towards that front-runner, although the results were inconsistent across studies and the effect shrank when participants already knew a good deal about the people involved. Prochazkova is careful not to claim that any election has been decided by a decoy, and rightly so; voters arrive with loyalties and information that laboratory participants lack. Nevertheless, her work raises an uncomfortable possibility: that the composition of a shortlist may influence the outcome as much as the merits of those on it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be concluded? It would be a mistake to treat the decoy effect as either a universal law of choice or a mere laboratory curiosity. The evidence points to an effect that is real under particular conditions, namely when attributes are numerical, comparisons are easy and choosers lack strong prior preferences, and weak or absent elsewhere. For regulators, this suggests that scrutiny should be directed not at decoys in general but at the specific formats, such as comparison tables, in which they are most potent. For economists, the lesson is subtler. Even a fragile effect shows that preferences can depend on context in ways that classical theory did not anticipate, and that conclusion does not require the decoy to be large.

topic: the identifiable victim effect in charitable giving: named individuals versus statistics, proportion dominance, weaker replications, the ethics of appeals and the misallocation of donations
title: The Face in the Appeal
subtitle: Why does one named child raise more money than a million anonymous ones, and what should charities do about it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Charities have long known that a single photograph of a named child raises more money than a page of statistics. Behavioural economists call this the identifiable victim effect: people give more generously to help one specific, identified person than to help a larger number of people described only in aggregate. The pattern has been documented in donation experiments, in public responses to news coverage of disasters and in the fundraising records of aid organisations. It poses an awkward puzzle. If giving were driven by a rational assessment of how much good a donation could do, a statistic describing thousands in need ought to be more persuasive than the story of one. That it is usually less persuasive suggests that charitable decisions are guided as much by feeling as by calculation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Among the most frequently cited studies is one conducted by Agnieszka Mrozowiak at the Vistula Centre for Experimental Economics. Participants who had just earned a small payment were invited to donate part of it to a food charity. Some read a short profile of a seven-year-old girl, including her name and photograph; others read figures on the millions affected by food shortages in the same region; a third group received both. Those who read only the profile gave roughly twice as much as those who saw only statistics. More surprisingly, the group that received both gave less than the profile-only group, as though the numbers had diluted the emotional impact of the individual story. Mrozowiak concluded that adding statistical information to a personal appeal can be counterproductive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should a single face move people more than a crowd? Parisa Dehkordi, a psychologist at the Caspian Institute of Social Cognition, argues that the explanation lies in the way attention and emotion work. A named individual can be imagined vividly, and that vividness triggers sympathy; a large number, by contrast, is abstract and produces little feeling at all. Dehkordi has also documented what she calls 'proportion dominance': people are more willing to help when their contribution would rescue a large share of a small group than when it would rescue the same number of people from a much larger one. On this view, donors respond less to the absolute good achieved than to the sense of making a visible difference.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers accept that the effect is as robust as early studies implied. Eleni Vasilakou, of the Aegean School of Economics, has analysed several attempts to replicate the original experiments and found that the advantage of identified victims was considerably smaller in larger samples, and in some cases absent altogether. She notes that many early studies relied on university students donating small sums in artificial settings. In real fundraising campaigns, where potential donors encounter dozens of appeals every week, a single photograph may be far less distinctive than it was in a quiet laboratory. Vasilakou does not deny that identification can increase giving, but she argues that its typical effect is modest. Her caution seems justified, though it would be wrong to conclude from it that the effect is negligible: even a modest increase, multiplied across millions of appeals, represents a substantial sum.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The effect also raises ethical questions for the organisations that exploit it. Kwame Amponsah-Ofori, who has advised several international aid agencies, points out that appeals featuring individual children can reinforce stereotypes of helplessness and distort public understanding of the causes of poverty. A donor who sees only a hungry child, he observes, learns nothing about failed harvests, debt or conflict. He argues that charities have an obligation to present beneficiaries with dignity, even if this reduces donations in the short term. Some agencies have responded by portraying people as active agents in improving their own lives rather than as passive recipients of aid, and early evidence suggests that such appeals need not raise less money.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is a further problem, which concerns how donations are allocated rather than how much is given. If donors are drawn to vivid individual stories, money may flow towards causes that are easily photographed, such as sudden earthquakes or floods, while chronic problems like poor sanitation, which kill far more people but lack dramatic images, remain underfunded. This seems to me the most serious consequence of the identifiable victim effect, and one that charities alone cannot correct. Governments and large foundations, which can base their decisions on evidence rather than emotion, have a particular responsibility to fill the gaps left by private generosity.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that personal stories should be abandoned. They remain one of the few tools capable of overcoming the indifference that large numbers tend to produce, and a fundraising culture that relied on statistics alone would probably raise far less for everyone. The challenge is to use such stories in ways that are honest and respectful, to avoid reducing the people they depict to symbols of suffering, and to combine them with institutions designed to ensure that the needs which move the public least are not neglected altogether.

topic: behaviourally designed tax reminder letters: social norm messages, deterrence versus persuasion, fading and displaced effects, cross-country transfer and simplification
title: A Polite Reminder
subtitle: Tax authorities have rewritten their letters with the help of behavioural science. The results are real, but more modest and more varied than the headlines suggest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, tax authorities send millions of letters to citizens who have failed to pay what they owe. For most of the twentieth century these letters were written in the language of threat: they cited the relevant legislation, listed the penalties for continued non-payment and were signed, if at all, by an anonymous department. Over the past fifteen years, however, a growing number of authorities have begun to rewrite them with the help of behavioural scientists. The new letters might tell recipients that most people in their town have already paid, emphasise the public services that taxes fund, or simply make the amount owed and the method of payment easier to find. The results of these experiments have been widely publicised, and they are frequently presented as evidence that small changes in wording can raise substantial sums at almost no cost.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-known findings concern so-called social norm messages. In a large trial conducted with a national revenue agency, Femke Oosterwijk of the Rhineland Institute for Public Economics randomly assigned overdue taxpayers to receive either a standard reminder or one stating that nine out of ten people in their area paid on time. Those who received the norm message were around five percentage points more likely to pay within a month. Oosterwijk attributes the effect to a desire to conform: people who learn that non-payment is unusual feel uncomfortable being in the minority. Interestingly, the effect was stronger when the comparison group was local rather than national, which she takes to show that people care most about the behaviour of those they regard as similar to themselves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second strand of research has examined deterrence. Nurlan Sarsenbayev, an economist at the Steppe Centre for Fiscal Research, compared letters that stressed social norms with letters that described, in plain terms, the penalties for non-payment and the likelihood of an audit. In his trials, the deterrence letters produced larger and more durable increases in payment than the norm messages, particularly among self-employed taxpayers with substantial incomes, a group whose tax affairs are harder for authorities to monitor. Sarsenbayev argues that the enthusiasm for gentle persuasion has obscured an older lesson: that the credible threat of enforcement remains the most powerful influence on compliance. The point is well made. It is a curious feature of the behavioural literature that the messages most often celebrated are rarely the ones that perform best.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even where letters succeed, there is the question of how long their effects last. Most trials measure payments over a few weeks or months, and few follow taxpayers into the following year. Ilze Kalnciema, who has re-examined data from several European trials, found that the extra payments prompted by a letter were partly offset by lower payments later: some recipients appear simply to have paid earlier than they otherwise would have. In her estimate, roughly a third of the apparent gain disappears once a full year is considered. This does not make the letters worthless, since earlier payment has genuine value to a government managing its cash flow, but it does suggest that the headline figures overstate what has been achieved.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also reasons to doubt whether findings transfer readily from one country to another. Trust in government varies enormously, and a message emphasising that taxes fund hospitals and schools may be persuasive where public services are visibly good and merely irritating where they are not. Kalnciema reports that a public-services message which raised payments in one Nordic country had no measurable effect in a southern European trial, and a slightly negative one among taxpayers who had previously disputed an assessment. It is easy to see why: a citizen who already feels unfairly treated is unlikely to welcome a lecture on civic duty. Behavioural interventions, it seems, interact with the relationship between citizens and the state rather than operating independently of it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most practically useful finding is also the least glamorous. Gustav Lindskog, who led a programme of trials within a Scandinavian tax administration, found that simplification alone, that is, placing the amount owed and the deadline at the top of the letter and including a direct payment link, raised payment rates by almost as much as any persuasive message. Lindskog argues that a good deal of non-payment reflects confusion or disorganisation rather than deliberate evasion, and that authorities should remove obstacles before attempting to change attitudes. His conclusion seems to me entirely sound, although it has received far less attention than the more psychologically intriguing results.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this undermines the case for testing letters rigorously; indeed, the trials themselves are a model of how public administration can learn from evidence rather than habit. But the lessons are more modest and more varied than early publicity suggested. Different taxpayers respond to different messages, effects can fade or merely shift payments in time, and the wider political context matters a great deal. Behavioural letters are best seen as one useful instrument among many, not as a substitute for effective enforcement or for a tax system that people regard as fair.

topic: drip pricing and shrouded fees: why hidden add-on charges survive competition, consumer underweighting of late charges, unbundling as choice, all-inclusive price rules and evasion of regulation
title: The Price You Did Not See
subtitle: Hidden charges that appear only at the final screen should, in theory, be driven out by competition. Behavioural economists explain why they are not

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has booked a cheap flight online will recognise the experience. The fare advertised on the first screen is attractive, but as the booking proceeds, further charges appear: a fee for choosing a seat, another for a checked bag, a third for paying by card. By the time the final page is reached, the total may be half as much again as the price that first caught the eye. Economists call this practice drip pricing, and it belongs to a broader family of strategies in which part of a product's cost is 'shrouded', or hidden from consumers until it is too late, or too inconvenient, to look elsewhere. Similar techniques are found in hotel resort fees, service charges on concert tickets and the supplies sold for printers, whose ink cartridges are often expensive relative to the machines themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why do such practices persist in markets that are supposedly competitive? The standard economic answer is that if some firms hide fees, their rivals should advertise honest all-inclusive prices and win customers. Margarida Fontoura, an industrial economist at the Lusitanian Centre for Competition Studies, has developed an influential model showing why this rarely happens. If a significant share of consumers fails to anticipate add-on charges, a firm that reveals its true prices merely looks more expensive than its rivals at the first stage. Meanwhile, the better-informed consumers it might hope to attract can simply buy from the cheapest-looking competitor and avoid the add-ons themselves. Under these conditions, Fontoura argues, transparency goes unrewarded, and hidden fees can survive indefinitely even when many firms compete.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Laboratory and field evidence suggests that consumers do indeed give too little weight to charges revealed late. Bence Hegedüs, of the Danube Institute of Behavioural Research, ran an experiment in which participants bought items in an online auction where the shipping cost was either included in the price or added at checkout. When shipping was added separately, participants paid more in total and were less likely to remember the overall cost afterwards. Hegedüs attributes the effect partly to limited attention and partly to a sense of commitment: once people have mentally decided to buy and invested time in the process, they are reluctant to abandon it, even when the final price would have deterred them at the outset. The longer the process, he notes, the stronger this reluctance becomes, which may explain why so many booking sites spread their charges across several screens.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards the evidence as a case for intervention. Dilshod Rahmatullaev, an economist who has advised airline regulators, points out that unbundling fees allows passengers who travel without luggage, or who do not mind where they sit, to pay less than they would under an all-inclusive fare. In his view, much of what is described as hidden pricing is really a form of choice, and banning it could raise prices for the most cost-conscious travellers. This argument has some force, but it conflates two separate issues. Offering optional extras is one thing; concealing compulsory charges until the final screen is quite another, and it is the latter that does the damage.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Regulators in several jurisdictions have now acted. Some require that compulsory fees be included in the first price displayed; others have restricted the way optional extras are presented, for example by prohibiting pre-ticked boxes. Auma Odhiambo-Were, who evaluated a reform requiring ticket platforms to show all-inclusive prices from the outset, found that consumers spent slightly less per transaction and were noticeably more satisfied with their purchases. Interestingly, the platforms' total revenues fell only modestly, because consumers who saw honest prices were more willing to buy at all. Odhiambo-Were suggests that the firms had overestimated how much they gained from shrouding, a conclusion that, if confirmed elsewhere, would greatly strengthen the case for reform.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, rules on price display are not a complete solution. Firms are inventive, and each new regulation tends to provoke fresh tactics: compulsory fees renamed as optional ones, charges moved to the point of collection, or prices that are technically all-inclusive but presented in small print beneath a more prominent headline figure. Enforcement therefore requires constant vigilance, and regulators with limited budgets may struggle to keep pace with an industry that can redesign a web page overnight. I suspect, too, that some consumers will continue to choose the cheapest-looking option whatever the rules, because a low headline price is simply more memorable than a footnote. Regulation can make the true price available; it cannot oblige anyone to read it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What drip pricing reveals, in the end, is a weakness in a familiar argument. It is often claimed that competition protects consumers from exploitation, since any firm that treats its customers badly will lose them to rivals. Fontoura's work shows that this reasoning holds only when consumers can compare like with like. Where the information that matters is deliberately withheld, competition may intensify the problem rather than cure it, rewarding the firms that are cleverest at concealment rather than those that offer the best value. Ensuring that prices are visible is therefore not an interference with the market but a condition of its working at all.

topic: street vending and urban policy: vendors' choice of location, eviction campaigns, relocation markets, licensing and vendor associations
title: Trading on the Kerb
subtitle: Street vendors are often treated as a problem to be cleared away, but research suggests that cities misunderstand what they are dealing with

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late afternoon, as office workers stream towards bus terminals in cities across Africa, Asia and Latin America, the pavements fill with traders selling cooked food, phone credit, fruit, umbrellas and second-hand clothing. Street vending is among the most visible forms of informal work, and in many low- and middle-income countries it accounts for a substantial share of urban employment, particularly among women and recent migrants. Yet municipal authorities have tended to regard vendors as an obstruction: a source of congestion, litter and lost tax revenue that modern planning should eliminate. This view, though understandable, rests on a misreading of how street trade actually functions, and policies built upon it have frequently produced the opposite of what they intended.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first point that critics overlook is that vendors are not randomly scattered. Ruth Lukwago, an urban geographer at the Institute for Livelihood Studies in Kampala, has mapped the positions of several thousand traders over a period of six years. Her central finding is that vendors cluster with remarkable precision at points where pedestrian flows are densest and slowest: around transport interchanges, at the gates of hospitals and schools, and beside the narrow crossings where crowds are forced to pause. Location, in other words, is the vendor's principal asset, and the ability to intercept passers-by matters far more than the size or quality of a stall. Lukwago also notes that customers rely on this arrangement. For low-income commuters, buying a meal or a single sachet of soap on the way home saves both a separate journey and the cost of buying in bulk.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Seen in this light, the recurrent 'clean-up' campaigns that sweep vendors from city centres appear considerably less rational than their supporters claim. Such operations, often launched before an international summit or a sporting event, involve the confiscation of goods and the demolition of stalls. Their effects are seldom lasting: within weeks, and sometimes within days, most traders have returned to the same spots, having lost their stock and, in many cases, borrowed money to replace it. The financial damage falls hardest on the poorest sellers, who lack savings to absorb the loss. It would be an exaggeration to say that evictions achieve nothing at all, since they may temporarily ease congestion, but the costs they impose are out of all proportion to these modest and short-lived gains.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more considered response has been to relocate vendors to purpose-built markets. Here too, the results have often disappointed. Mateo Ferreyros, an economist at the Andean Centre for Urban Policy, examined eleven relocation schemes and found that, on average, fewer than half of the allocated stalls were still occupied three years after opening. The usual explanation offered by officials is that vendors are unwilling to accept regulation. Ferreyros rejects this interpretation. In his view, the markets failed because they were built where land was cheap, typically at the edge of the city, far from the crowds on which traders depend. Vendors who abandoned them were making a sound commercial calculation, not displaying hostility to order. His evidence is convincing, although it should be added that some relocated markets have succeeded, notably those built directly above or beside busy transport hubs.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Licensing offers a third approach. Under such systems, vendors pay a fee in return for the right to trade in a designated zone or during specified hours. Kwabena Amponsah-Dei, a legal scholar who has advised several West African municipalities, argues that licences give traders a measure of security that encourages them to invest in better equipment and to observe hygiene rules. The difficulty lies in the number of permits issued. Where authorities cap licences far below actual demand, a secondary trade in permits tends to emerge, with licence holders renting out their pitches to unlicensed sellers at inflated prices. Amponsah-Dei acknowledges this risk but believes it can be managed through regular reviews of quotas. That may be true in principle, but it assumes a degree of administrative capacity that many city governments plainly lack.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further strand of research concerns the organisations that vendors build for themselves. Somphone Phommachanh, a sociologist at the Mekong Institute of Social Research, has studied vendor associations in four Southeast Asian cities. She finds that well-organised associations can negotiate trading hours with police, settle disputes between members and collect small contributions to support traders who fall ill. At the same time, she warns that such bodies can become exclusive, restricting entry to protect established members and sometimes charging newcomers informal fees. Associations, she concludes, are neither a simple solution nor a threat, but a form of local governance whose character depends heavily on who controls it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this work is the need to treat the street as a shared resource rather than as space that belongs either to traffic or to trade. Several cities have experimented with time-based arrangements in which the same pavement serves pedestrians in the morning and becomes a market in the evening. Such compromises are untidy, and they will not satisfy those who measure urban progress by the absence of visible poverty. They do, however, reflect the reality that millions of households depend on the pavement for their income, and that policies which ignore this dependence are unlikely to succeed for long.

title: The Pot That Goes Round
subtitle: Rotating savings groups seem to offer their members almost nothing that a tin box could not. Why, then, do millions of people belong to them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a market town in coastal Ghana, twelve cloth traders meet every Friday afternoon. Each hands over the same sum to the group's treasurer, and the entire pot is then given to one of them. The following week the process is repeated, and so on until every member has received the pot exactly once, at which point the cycle can begin again. Arrangements of this kind, known to economists as rotating savings and credit associations, or ROSCAs, go by dozens of local names, among them susu in West Africa, tanda in Mexico, hui among Chinese communities and chit funds in India, and they flourish not only in villages but also among migrant workers in London, Toronto and New York. Their very popularity has long puzzled economists. Members earn no interest, carry the risk that others will stop paying once they have collected, and could, in principle, achieve much the same result by putting money aside at home.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential attempt to resolve this puzzle was put forward by Ignacio Cuaresma, an economist at the Universidad del Litoral Austral. Cuaresma pointed out that many members save towards a single costly item, such as a sewing machine, a set of roofing sheets or a bicycle, that cannot be bought in instalments. A person saving alone must wait until the full price has been accumulated. In a group of twelve, by contrast, all but the final recipient obtain the pot, and therefore the item, earlier than they would have done by saving independently, while the last member is no worse off than a solitary saver. The model is elegant, and it explains why ROSCAs are associated with purchases of durable goods. Yet it leaves a great deal unexplained, not least because it assumes that members are capable of saving on their own and merely wish to do so faster.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That assumption has been directly challenged by Halima Rwegasira, a behavioural economist at the Eastern Africa Institute for Household Finance. In interviews with more than eight hundred members of savings groups, she found that the reason most frequently given for joining was the difficulty of keeping cash at home. Money held in a tin or under a mattress, respondents explained, is spent on small temptations or handed over to relatives who ask for help, requests that are socially difficult to refuse. A contribution owed to the group, on the other hand, is a commitment that can be cited as an excuse. Most strikingly, when Rwegasira asked members which position in the rotation they would choose if given the option, a considerable proportion named the last one. For such people, the point of the group is plainly not to obtain money early but to be prevented from spending it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A related but distinct explanation focuses on relations within the household. Farzana Khondker, a sociologist at the Centre for Gender and Livelihoods in Dhaka, observes that in many regions the great majority of ROSCA members are women. In her account, membership allows a wife to remove part of her earnings from the household budget, where it might otherwise be claimed by her husband, and to accumulate a sum over which she has greater control. Because the contribution is framed as an obligation to neighbours rather than as a personal choice, it is harder for a spouse to object. Khondker's analysis is persuasive for the communities she has studied, but it cannot be extended to every case: the large commercial chit funds of southern India, for example, are dominated by male businessmen and serve quite different purposes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of these accounts, however, explains why members who have already collected the pot continue to contribute. Teodoro Lacsamana, an anthropologist at the Visayas Institute of Social Research, argues that the answer lies in the way groups are formed. Members are almost always recruited from dense networks of kin, neighbours or co-workers, in which information travels quickly. A defaulter faces not only gossip but exclusion from every future group in the area, a penalty that in most cases far outweighs the value of a single pot. This mechanism works remarkably well, yet it carries a cost that enthusiastic accounts of ROSCAs tend to neglect. People without established connections, such as newcomers to a town, are often refused entry, so the institution may be least accessible to those who need it most.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For several decades, development agencies assumed that ROSCAs were a primitive substitute for banking that would fade once formal financial services became available. The evidence has not been kind to this prediction. Adebola Bamigboye, a development economist who has tracked households in southwestern Nigeria for over a decade, found that people who opened bank accounts were more, not less, likely to join a savings group afterwards. The two, it seems, serve different needs: the bank offers safe storage, while the group supplies the discipline and the social obligation that a bank account cannot.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The newest development is the appearance of mobile applications that organise rotating savings among people who have never met. Their promoters present them as a modern version of an ancient practice. This claim deserves scepticism. If the analysis above is correct, the strength of the traditional ROSCA lies precisely in the relationships between its members, which provide both the pressure to save and the guarantee of repayment. An app that removes these relationships must replace them with deposits, credit checks or penalty fees, and at that point it has become something much closer to an ordinary loan product. The enduring appeal of the ROSCA, in short, says less about the mechanics of finance than about the value people place on saving alongside others.

topic: measuring the size of the informal economy: household surveys, the electricity-consumption method, currency-demand estimates, MIMIC models and night-time satellite light
title: Weighing a Shadow
subtitle: How large is the informal economy? The answer depends, to an uncomfortable degree, on who is doing the counting and how

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few statistics about developing economies are quoted as often, or with as much confidence, as estimates of the size of the informal sector. Reports routinely state that unregistered activity accounts for a third, a half or even two-thirds of a country's output, and such figures are used to justify tax reforms, aid programmes and campaigns to bring small businesses into the formal system. Yet the informal economy is, by definition, the part of economic life that escapes official records, and measuring it is rather like weighing a shadow. For a single country, credible studies have produced estimates ranging from under a fifth of national output to well over half, depending on the method used. Such discrepancies ought to make anyone wary of the apparent precision with which these numbers are usually reported.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most direct approach is simply to ask. Labour force and household surveys question people about where and how they work: whether their employer is registered, whether they have a written contract, whether they pay into a pension scheme. Neema Mbilinyi, who heads the methods unit at the Lake Zone Statistical Research Bureau, regards such surveys as the most trustworthy source available, chiefly because they measure people rather than money. A street trader may be reluctant to reveal her income, she notes, but she is rarely unwilling to say that she sells vegetables at a roadside stall. Mbilinyi readily concedes that the earnings figures collected in surveys are far weaker, since respondents underreport income for fear of tax officials or simply because they do not keep accounts. Surveys, in other words, are good at telling us how many people work informally but much less reliable as a guide to how much they produce.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Because of this weakness, economists have developed indirect methods that infer hidden activity from visible traces. One of the earliest relies on electricity. If power consumption is assumed to track total economic output closely, then any gap between the growth of electricity use and the growth of officially recorded output can be attributed to activity that the statistics miss. The logic is appealing, but its flaws are considerable. Improvements in energy efficiency mean that the same output may require less power over time, and many informal activities, from hairdressing under a tree to small-scale farming, consume almost no electricity at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second indirect method examines the demand for cash. Since informal transactions are overwhelmingly conducted in banknotes, it is argued, holdings of currency above the level predicted by incomes and interest rates indicate the scale of the hidden economy. Rodrigo Ochoa-Zelaya, an economist at the Instituto de Estudios Monetarios in Quito, has been among its most forceful critics. People hold cash, he points out, for many reasons unrelated to informality, including distrust of banks, the receipt of remittances and memories of past banking crises. More fundamentally, the method requires the analyst to choose a base year in which the informal economy is assumed to have been zero, an assumption that he describes as absurd for almost any country. On this point his criticism is entirely justified: an estimate that depends on so implausible a premise cannot carry much weight.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The estimates most frequently cited in international comparisons, however, come from a third family of techniques known as MIMIC models, which combine supposed causes of informality, such as the tax burden and the extent of regulation, with supposed indicators of it, such as cash holdings and labour force participation. These models generate tidy rankings of countries, which is no doubt why they are popular. Their difficulty is that they are largely circular. A model that assumes high taxes cause informality will inevitably find more informality where taxes are high, and the results are then presented as though they confirmed the original assumption. To make matters worse, the models produce only relative values, which must be converted into percentages using figures borrowed from other methods.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most recent innovation draws on satellite images of the earth at night. Parisa Tabrizian, a specialist in remote sensing at the Caspian Centre for Spatial Economics, has compared the intensity of artificial light with official output data and argues that regions which appear brighter than their recorded incomes would predict are likely to contain substantial unrecorded activity. The approach is particularly promising for countries whose official statistics are weak or out of date. To her credit, Tabrizian is the first to acknowledge its limits. Light reflects access to electricity as well as economic activity, so poor districts may remain dim however busy they are, and the method measures total activity rather than the informal share of it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What this survey of methods suggests is not that one technique is right and the others wrong, but that each is measuring something different. The term 'informal economy' is used for unregistered small firms, for workers without legal protection, and for tax evasion by large companies, and there is no reason to expect a single number to capture all three. Policymakers would be better served by first deciding which of these they actually need to know about, and then choosing a method accordingly. A frank range of estimates may be less satisfying than a single headline figure, but it is considerably more useful.

topic: informal apprenticeship in West African workshops: entry fees and cost-sharing, exploitation and delayed graduation, earnings of former apprentices, dual-system certification and reform through trade associations
title: Learning at the Master's Bench
subtitle: Informal apprenticeship trains more young people in West Africa than all its vocational colleges, yet economists disagree about whether it should be reformed, regulated or left alone

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the roadside workshops of cities such as Kumasi, Cotonou and Ouagadougou, young people learn to repair engines, sew garments, weld gates and cut hair under the eye of a master craftsperson. No government ministry designs the curriculum and few of the arrangements are written down, yet informal apprenticeship is by a wide margin the largest source of vocational skills in much of West Africa. In some countries it is estimated to train several times as many young people as all public technical colleges together. For decades, policy-makers treated this system as a relic that would fade once modern schooling expanded. That expectation has proved mistaken, and it should now be accepted that any serious attempt to improve the skills of the workforce must start from the workshops rather than from the classroom.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The arrangements follow a broadly similar pattern across the region. A young person, often introduced by a relative, agrees to work for a master for a period that may range from two to five years. In many trades the apprentice, or the apprentice's family, pays an entry fee, sometimes accompanied by gifts such as drinks or cloth, and a further payment may be due at a graduation ceremony when the master formally releases the trainee. During the apprenticeship the young person receives little or no wage, although masters commonly provide food or a small allowance. Skills are acquired by observation and gradual participation: a newcomer sweeps the floor and fetches tools before being trusted with a customer's vehicle or fabric.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To Kofi Ossei-Bampoe, a labour economist at the Coastal Institute for Employment Studies, the persistence of this model reflects its underlying efficiency rather than any lack of alternatives. Training, he points out, is expensive for whoever provides it, and a master who invests years in a young worker risks seeing that worker leave to open a competing business. The entry fee and the low wage are the means by which the trainee shares this cost, which is precisely what economic theory predicts should happen when the skills being taught are useful to many employers rather than one. Ossei-Bampoe also stresses that apprentices learn in a setting identical to the one in which they will later earn a living, dealing with real customers and with the scarcity of spare parts. No college workshop, he argues, can reproduce that environment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others regard the same features with far less enthusiasm. Rosine Houngbedji, who has interviewed several hundred apprentices in Benin for the Sahel Youth Observatory, reports that many spend the first year or more running errands with only a loose connection to the trade they hope to learn. Some masters, she found, delay graduation in order to retain unpaid help, particularly during busy seasons, and the cost of the final ceremony keeps some trainees in workshops long after they have mastered the necessary skills. Houngbedji does not dispute that the system transmits real competence. Her objection is that bargaining power lies overwhelmingly with the master, and that young women, who are concentrated in a small number of trades such as hairdressing and dressmaking, are especially poorly placed to negotiate. This is a fair criticism, although it applies to much of the labour market in which these workshops operate, not to apprenticeship alone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Evidence on outcomes is mixed. A tracer study directed by Tsegaye Kebede of the Regional Skills Policy Unit followed some two thousand former apprentices for six years after graduation. Those who had completed an apprenticeship earned noticeably more than young people of similar background who had not, but the gains were concentrated among graduates who went on to open their own workshops; former apprentices who became employees elsewhere earned little more than their untrained peers. Kebede interprets this as evidence that what apprenticeship chiefly supplies is not technical knowledge alone but access to customers, suppliers and reputation, assets that are difficult to carry into a different workplace.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Reformers have tried in various ways to raise standards. The most ambitious proposals, championed by the vocational education consultant Annelies Marrevelde, envisage a 'dual' arrangement in which apprentices spend one or two days a week at a technical college while continuing to work in a workshop, and finish with a nationally recognised examination. Marrevelde argues that certification would allow skilled young people to move between employers and regions, and would give banks and customers a reliable signal of competence. Pilot schemes have produced some encouraging results, particularly in electrical trades, where knowledge of safety regulations matters. Yet participation has been patchy. Many masters, themselves lacking formal qualifications, are reluctant to release apprentices during working hours, and some fear that an external examination will undermine their own authority.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The difficulty with importing a dual model is that the German and Swiss systems on which it is based rest on large firms, employers' chambers and a long tradition of public funding, none of which exists in a market of tiny, cash-strapped workshops. A more realistic route, it seems to me, is to build on institutions that already exist. Many trades in the region have associations of master craftspeople that set fees and settle disputes; strengthening these bodies, rather than bypassing them, would give reform a better chance of being accepted. Modest measures, such as written contracts specifying the length of training, or short courses for masters in teaching and bookkeeping, may well achieve more than ambitious certification programmes. The workshops have survived precisely because they adapt to local conditions, and reform that ignores this is unlikely to last.

topic: informal minibus transport (paratransit) in fast-growing cities: daily-rental 'target' contracts, route associations, responsiveness to new settlements, road safety, bus rapid transit replacement, route mapping and distance-based payment reforms
title: The Fleet Nobody Planned
subtitle: Privately run minibuses carry most commuters in many growing cities, and the question of what to do about them divides planners and economists

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every weekday morning, millions of commuters in cities such as Lagos, Nairobi, Kinshasa and Jakarta squeeze into privately owned minibuses that follow no published timetable and appear on few official maps. Known by local names such as danfo, matatu and angkot, these vehicles carry, by most estimates, a majority of public transport passengers in many of the world's fastest-growing cities. Yet transport authorities have long regarded them as an embarrassment: noisy, dangerous and a symptom of the state's failure to provide proper buses. That attitude is understandable but, in my view, misguided. Whatever their faults, these minibuses are the public transport system of these cities, and policy that begins by wishing them away is bound to fail.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economics of the trade are simple. Most vehicles are owned not by the people who drive them but by small investors, among them civil servants, traders and police officers, who rent them to drivers for a fixed daily sum, known in several countries as the 'target'. Whatever the driver collects beyond this sum, after paying for fuel, is his to keep; if takings fall short, he bears the loss. Access to routes is regulated not by the city but by drivers' and owners' associations, which control the terminals and decide which vehicles may load there. A minibus generally leaves only when every seat is taken, so that passengers on quieter routes or at off-peak hours may wait an hour or more, which makes journey times extremely hard to predict.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For Chidinma Mbakwe, a transport geographer at the Gulf of Guinea Urban Mobility Centre, this arrangement has virtues that planners routinely overlook. When a new settlement appears on the edge of a city, she notes, minibus operators typically begin serving it within weeks, whereas a municipal bus company may take years to approve a new route, if it ever does. The system also receives no public subsidy: fares cover the full cost of the vehicles, fuel and labour. Mbakwe compares the network to a living organism, constantly redrawing itself in response to where people actually want to go, and she argues that cities should study how routes emerge before trying to replace them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The darker side of the trade is equally well documented. Road safety researchers have long linked minibuses to a disproportionate share of traffic accidents, and the economist Hendra Lumbantobing has traced much of this to the rental contract itself. Because a driver earns nothing until the daily target has been met, he has every incentive to drive fast, overload the vehicle, stop wherever a passenger waves and work shifts of fourteen hours or more. Lumbantobing insists that reckless driving is a rational response to the way risk is distributed, rather than a matter of individual character, and that lectures and fines aimed at drivers will achieve little while the contract remains unchanged. His analysis is convincing as far as it goes, but it leaves out the associations, whose loading fees and informal levies add considerably to the sum a driver must earn before he sees any income.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Many governments have responded by building bus rapid transit (BRT) systems, in which large buses run on dedicated lanes between enclosed stations. The urban planner Lucía Ocharan, who has advised several African and Latin American cities, has been a prominent advocate, arguing that BRT can deliver the speed and reliability of a metro at a fraction of the cost. Results have been mixed. On one corridor she studied, average journey times fell by about a third, but minibus operators who lost the route organised strikes, and passenger numbers stayed well below forecasts because many commuters still needed a minibus to reach the nearest station. The lesson seems clear: rapid transit lines succeed only when they are planned as part of a network that includes the minibuses, not as a replacement for them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A quieter innovation has come from mapping. Until recently, few cities had any record of where their minibuses actually went. A project co-ordinated by the data scientist Mikko Haukilahti recruited students to ride every route they could find, carrying smartphones that logged their position, and the resulting maps showed a network far denser and more extensive than transport officials had assumed; in one city, more than a hundred routes did not appear in any government document. Such maps have since been used to plan new feeder services and to choose sites for terminals. They are a valuable tool, although knowing where minibuses run does nothing in itself to make them safer.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most promising reforms try to change the incentives rather than the vehicles. In a handful of cities, owners have been encouraged to pool their minibuses into companies that are paid by the city according to the distance they cover, instead of keeping whatever fares their drivers can collect. Drivers become salaried employees, and the race for passengers loses its point. Such schemes are slow to arrange and some owners resist the loss of independent income, but where they have taken hold, accident rates appear to have fallen. If there is a general lesson, it is that reform works best when existing operators are brought inside it; attempts to sweep them aside have tended to produce strikes and empty stations.

topic: informal remittance systems such as hawala: how brokers settle balances, low costs and remote reach, trust and closed networks, anti-money-laundering rules and bank de-risking, mobile money as a rival or partner, and proportionate regulation
title: Money That Travels on Trust
subtitle: Informal transfer networks move billions across borders every year with barely a paper record, and regulators, economists and anthropologists cannot agree on what should be done about them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The money that migrants send home now exceeds the combined value of foreign aid to low- and middle-income countries, and a substantial share of it never passes through a bank. In the Horn of Africa, South Asia and parts of the Middle East, families rely on brokers operating systems known as hawala or hundi, which can deliver funds across continents within hours. Because these systems leave few records, estimates of their size vary enormously, from a tenth to well over half of all remittances on some routes. They are frequently described in the press as shadowy or archaic. Such descriptions are, I believe, profoundly misleading: informal transfer networks are better understood as a sophisticated piece of financial infrastructure, one that has flourished precisely where formal institutions have failed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanics are deceptively simple. A worker in London hands cash to a local broker, who telephones or messages a counterpart in, say, Hargeisa; the counterpart then pays the equivalent sum to the worker's relatives, minus a small commission, often the same day. No money crosses the border at the moment of the transfer. Instead, the two brokers accumulate a balance, which they settle later, sometimes through an occasional bank payment but more often through trade, for instance by over- or under-invoicing shipments of rice, textiles or electronics. Records are kept, but they tend to be brief, and they are rarely shared with anyone outside the network.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The economist Yonatan Abuye, who leads the Horn of Africa Remittance Research Group, has compared prices along several corridors. On the routes he studied, hawala brokers typically charged between two and four per cent of the sum sent, whereas licensed money-transfer companies sometimes charged more than ten. Price, however, is only part of the explanation for the system's popularity. Abuye emphasises that brokers routinely deliver money to remote villages, pastoral areas and refugee camps where no bank has ever opened a branch, and that in times of drought these transfers can determine whether a household is able to buy food.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should anyone hand over their savings to a broker with no licence and no written contract? The anthropologist Meera Selvanathan, who has spent several years among brokers in East Africa and the Gulf, argues that the answer lies in the social organisation of the trade. Brokers usually belong to the same clan, caste or home district as their counterparts and many of their customers, and their reputations are common knowledge within these communities. Defaults are rare, in her account, because a broker who cheated a partner would be shut out of the only business network open to him. Selvanathan is careful to add that these closed circles have a cost: migrants who do not share the brokers' background may find themselves charged higher fees, or refused service altogether.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Since the early 2000s, informal transfers have attracted intense scrutiny from regulators concerned about money laundering and the financing of terrorism. Many countries now require brokers to register and to identify their customers, and numerous Western banks, fearing heavy penalties, have closed the accounts of remittance companies altogether, a practice known as de-risking. Lars Ostergaard, a researcher at the Institute for Financial Integrity, defends the principle behind these rules, pointing out that anonymous cross-border payments are inherently attractive to criminals. Yet he concedes that, by depriving legitimate operators of banking services, de-risking has driven some transfers into channels that are even harder to observe. The irony is striking, and it suggests that enforcement pursued without regard to its consequences may weaken the very transparency it is meant to secure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The arrival of mobile money has added a new element to this picture. In parts of East and West Africa, people can now send small sums from one phone to another and withdraw them as cash from local agents. Aminata Coulibaly of the Sahelian Household Finance Project surveyed rural families over several years and found that those with mobile money accounts maintained their spending on food and schooling after harvest failures, largely because relatives in towns could send many small amounts quickly rather than a single sum after a long delay. Mobile money has limits, however. International transfers by phone remain relatively costly on many routes, and village agents frequently run out of the cash needed to pay recipients, particularly at the end of the month.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to assume that digital wallets will eventually make hawala obsolete. The evidence so far points in a different direction. Many brokers have adopted mobile money themselves, using it to pay recipients in distant areas while continuing to settle balances with partners abroad in the traditional way. In my view, the likeliest future is one of convergence, in which the trust networks of the old system are carried over into the technology of the new, rather than one in which a single method simply displaces its rival.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What, then, should governments do? Attempts to suppress informal transfers have generally failed, since demand for cheap and rapid delivery does not disappear when brokers are prosecuted. A more productive approach would be to make registration simple and inexpensive, so that brokers gain more from being visible than from staying hidden, and to require banks to judge remittance companies individually rather than closing their accounts wholesale. Such proportionate regulation will not eliminate every risk. But it offers a better prospect than outright prohibition of bringing these networks into view, and of protecting the families who depend on them.

topic: why small firms stay unregistered and whether formalisation pays: registration costs and one-stop shops, field experiments paying firms to register, survival enterprises versus growth firms, subcontracting by formal companies, and tax inspections
title: Registering the Unregistered
subtitle: For thirty years, governments have tried to coax small businesses into the formal economy. The results have forced economists to rethink why those businesses stay outside it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In much of Africa, South Asia and Latin America, the majority of businesses are not registered with any authority. They pay no corporate tax, hold no licence and appear in no official statistics, yet they employ most of the working population. For several decades the dominant response among governments and international lenders was to treat this as a problem of access: if registering a business could be made cheaper and quicker, it was assumed, informal firms would come forward in large numbers and would grow once they enjoyed the protections of the law. The idea was attractive, and it was widely adopted. Looking back, however, it is hard to avoid the conclusion that enthusiasm for formalisation ran well ahead of the evidence supporting it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The intellectual case was set out most forcefully by the economist Kwabena Agyekum-Dua, who in the 1990s led a team that attempted to register an imaginary garment workshop in a number of capital cities. In the worst cases the process involved more than twenty separate steps, took several months and required fees that exceeded the annual earnings of a typical small business. Faced with such obstacles, Agyekum-Dua argued, entrepreneurs were behaving entirely rationally by staying informal. His findings inspired a wave of reforms. Many countries created so-called one-stop shops, where all the paperwork could be completed in a single office, and in several of them the time required to register fell from around two months to less than a week.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The impact of these reforms proved disappointing. Registrations did rise, but only modestly, and closer analysis suggested that most of the additional firms were newly created businesses, or businesses that would probably have registered in any case. Very few established informal enterprises converted. This does not mean that the reforms were pointless: cutting needless bureaucracy is worthwhile in its own right, and it may have helped some new firms to start life on the right side of the law. But it did suggest that the cost of registration was not, for most informal businesses, the main reason they had stayed outside the system.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A series of field experiments sharpened the puzzle. In one, designed by the development economist Noa Tlalim, several thousand informal shops and workshops were randomly offered free registration, help with the forms and, in some cases, a cash payment roughly equal to a month's profit. Take-up was low among firms offered information and assistance alone; only the cash payment persuaded substantial numbers to register. When Tlalim's team returned two years later, the average firm that had formalised was earning little more than before. A minority of larger businesses had benefited, chiefly by gaining access to bank loans and government contracts, but for most owners registration had brought costs, such as taxes and inspections, without obvious rewards.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: To Hélène Hurtubise, a labour economist who has studied informal work for over twenty years, these results are unsurprising. In her view, most informal enterprises are not small companies waiting to grow but survival activities: one-person operations with little capital, run by people who would gladly accept a stable wage job if one were available. Formalisation offers such people almost nothing, and the real policy challenge lies in creating productive employment rather than in registering market stalls. Her account is largely persuasive, but it risks treating the informal sector as uniformly static. Surveys repeatedly identify a small group of informal firms that grow quickly, hire workers and invest in equipment, and it is precisely these firms for which the advantages of formality are greatest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third perspective, associated with the sociologist Marc Arceneaux, rejects the very idea of a separate informal sector. Arceneaux points out that many unregistered workshops produce goods on contract for large registered companies, which pass on orders precisely in order to avoid labour regulations, social security contributions and taxes. On this view, informality is not a leftover from an earlier stage of development but something that the formal economy actively generates. The argument carries considerable weight in industries such as clothing and footwear, where subcontracting chains are well documented. It is much less convincing as an account of the street traders, small farmers and domestic workers who make up most of the informal workforce.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave policy? One striking result came from an experiment in which tax inspectors made unannounced visits to informal businesses: these visits produced more registrations than any of the incentive schemes had, although they raise obvious concerns about harassment and bribery. Persuasion and pressure can both raise the numbers, yet neither guarantees that firms will be better off. The most sensible course, it seems to me, is to abandon the goal of blanket formalisation and to concentrate instead on the minority of firms with the capacity to grow. For them, the benefits of formal status, from credit to public contracts, must be real and accessible; without such benefits, registration will remain a cost that rational owners prefer to avoid.
