topic: artisanal and small-scale gold mining: mercury amalgamation and exposure in towns, mercury bans, seasonal miners versus gold rushes, sponsors' pre-financing of pits, licensing and land concessions, ethical gold certification
title: The Diggers' Dilemma
subtitle: Millions of people mine gold by hand, outside the law and often with toxic methods. Is this a livelihood to be supported or a problem to be stamped out?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere between fifteen and twenty million people around the world earn their living by digging for gold with picks, shovels and simple pumps. Working in shallow pits and riverbeds from Ghana to Indonesia and from Peru to Tanzania, these artisanal miners are thought to produce as much as a fifth of the world's newly mined gold, and most of them do so without a licence. Public debate tends to offer two competing images of them. In one, they are desperate people scraping a living from the ground; in the other, they are environmental criminals poisoning rivers and destroying forests. Each image contains some truth, but neither, in my view, is of much help to anyone trying to design sensible policy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental case against the trade centres on mercury. Once miners have crushed gold-bearing ore, they mix it with liquid mercury, which binds to the fine particles of gold to form a soft lump known as an amalgam. The lump is then heated, often over an open flame, so that the mercury evaporates and leaves the gold behind. Artisanal mining is now considered the largest single source of mercury released into the air by human activity. Ingrid Bergvold, an environmental chemist at the Nordic Institute for Toxicology, has measured concentrations of mercury vapour in mining districts for over a decade. Her most troubling finding is that the highest readings are often recorded not at the pits but in the gold-buying shops of nearby towns, where traders reheat amalgam to purify it, exposing families who have no connection with mining at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why does a substance with such well-known dangers remain so widely used? Mercury is cheap, easy to carry and requires no training, and it allows a miner to turn ore into saleable gold within hours. Alternative methods, such as gravity concentration using sluices and shaking tables, can recover gold without chemicals, but they require an initial investment in equipment that few miners can afford. Bergvold argues that outright bans on mercury have proved counterproductive: in several countries they have simply pushed the trade into smuggling networks, raising the price of mercury without greatly reducing its use. Her conclusion is difficult to dispute, and it suggests that prohibition without practical alternatives achieves little beyond criminalising the poor.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The geographer Ifeoma Okoronkwo has challenged a different assumption: that artisanal mining is a last resort for those with no other options. Her surveys in West Africa found that many miners are farmers who dig for a few months each year, after the harvest, and who earn several times more from mining than from their crops. For such households, mining is a deliberate strategy for raising cash, often to pay school fees or invest in livestock, rather than a sign of destitution. Okoronkwo's research is a valuable corrective, but it does not describe every site. When a rich deposit is discovered, rushes can draw thousands of migrants with no land to return to, and in these camps the picture of poverty and insecurity is considerably closer to the popular image.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Mining also depends on finance. Digging a deep pit requires fuel, pumps, timber and food for weeks before any gold is found, and banks do not lend for such ventures. The gap is filled by local sponsors, typically gold traders or wealthy residents, who pay these costs in exchange for the right to buy the pit's output, usually at a price below the market rate. The economist Daudi Kisanga has studied hundreds of such arrangements in Tanzania. Critics often describe them as a form of debt bondage, but Kisanga maintains that they are better understood as partnerships for sharing risk, since a sponsor who backs a pit that yields nothing loses the entire investment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many governments now offer small-scale mining licences, in theory allowing miners to operate legally. In practice, few obtain them. Applications commonly require geological surveys and environmental impact assessments that cost more than most miners earn in a year. A still greater obstacle is that the most promising land has frequently already been allocated as concessions to large mining companies, many of which do not intend to develop it for years. Miners working on such land are trespassers by definition, regardless of how carefully they work.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A different approach has come from the market. Certification schemes promise jewellers and consumers gold produced without mercury or child labour, and pay participating mines a premium above the world price. Paula Moyano, who has evaluated several such schemes for the Andean Mining Policy Forum, acknowledges that only a few dozen mines have been certified and that their output represents a tiny fraction of artisanal production. She insists, however, that their value lies in showing what responsible mining looks like. That may be so, yet the standards are so demanding that they exclude precisely the poorest miners, and there is a danger that such schemes do more to ease the consciences of wealthy buyers than to improve conditions in the pits.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: A more effective strategy would begin with land. If governments set aside areas specifically for artisanal miners, simplified licences to match the scale of their operations and offered technical support for mercury-free processing, they would give miners a reason to work within the law rather than outside it. Such measures would not resolve every problem, and enforcement against the worst environmental damage would still be needed. But for a trade that supports so many families, the aim should be to make legality achievable before demanding it.

topic: informal cross-border trade by small traders: scale revealed by border monitoring, women traders and harassment, food price stabilisation and export bans, simplified trade regimes, and improving conditions at border posts
title: Trade on Foot
subtitle: At land borders across Africa, small traders carry goods worth billions each year without appearing in official figures. Researchers are now asking what that hidden commerce achieves

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At busy land crossings in southern and eastern Africa, a steady stream of people passes the customs post each morning carrying sacks of maize, bales of second-hand clothing, crates of tomatoes and boxes of soap, on their heads, on bicycles or in the backs of shared taxis. Much of this commerce goes unrecorded, and for many years officials referred to it simply as smuggling. That label is, I would argue, largely inaccurate. Most of the goods involved are perfectly legal and most of them travel through official crossings; what makes the trade informal is that individual consignments are too small, or the paperwork too complicated, for them to be properly declared.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of this activity was long a matter of guesswork. In the early 2000s, a team led by the economist Grace Chirwa stationed monitors at dozens of border posts, where they counted and estimated the value of goods carried by small traders. Their results surprised many policy-makers: for some staple foods, notably maize, rice and beans, the value of unrecorded trade exceeded that of recorded trade across the same borders. If these figures are even approximately correct, national statistics substantially understate how closely the economies of neighbouring countries are already connected, and regional trade agreements ought to be judged with this hidden integration in mind. Chirwa herself is cautious about the precision of her estimates, noting that monitors could not cover every crossing at every hour of the day, and that bush paths away from official posts were excluded entirely. The true figures, she suggests, are therefore more likely to be higher than lower.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: On many routes, the majority of informal traders are women. The sociologist Samira Halloumi, who interviewed several hundred traders at four crossings, found that many had chosen the work because it required little starting capital and could be combined with childcare. Traders frequently travel in groups, pool their transport and share information about prices and officials. Yet the border can be a hostile place. Women described having goods confiscated, being asked for unofficial payments and, in some cases, suffering sexual harassment. Halloumi's most significant finding is that the formal duties themselves are rarely the main burden; what traders fear most is the arbitrary nature of the demands made by officials, which can turn a profitable journey into a loss without warning.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Informal trade also plays a part in feeding the region. The food security specialist Anjali Banerjee-Roth has tracked the movement of maize between areas with surplus harvests and those facing shortages. In her analysis, small traders respond to price differences far faster than government agencies, moving grain into deficit areas and so limiting the sharp price rises that would otherwise follow a poor harvest. She also observes that when governments impose export bans during shortages, informal trade continues across the border, and she concludes that such bans are largely ineffective. This is broadly right, but it understates their cost: traders who keep moving grain during a ban must pay larger bribes and take longer routes, and these expenses are passed on to the people buying food.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Governments have attempted to bring some of this trade into official channels. Several regional economic communities have introduced simplified trade regimes, under which goods on an agreed list and below a set value can cross duty-free with only a simple certificate of origin. Tafadzwa Matongo, a former customs officer who now researches border policy, has evaluated these schemes and found that use of them remains limited. The lists of eligible goods are often out of date, many traders have never heard of the regimes, and even officials at the border are sometimes unaware of the rules. Matongo also points out that the value limits, fixed when the schemes were launched, have rarely been adjusted for inflation, so that an ordinary trader's load now often exceeds them. Where trader associations have staffed information desks at crossings, however, Matongo found that use of the simplified procedures rose considerably.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake to conclude that every small trader should be brought into the formal system. The administrative cost of processing thousands of tiny consignments would be considerable, and the attempt might simply create new opportunities for officials to demand payments. Many traders, moreover, value the flexibility that informality allows them. Some recording of informal trade is clearly valuable, if only to improve statistics, and declarations made by mobile phone might eventually offer a low-cost way of achieving it. But insisting on full formalisation would be both impractical and, for the traders themselves, of doubtful benefit.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The more urgent priority is to make the border a safer and more predictable place. Clearly displayed lists of duties, complaint procedures that traders can use without fear and better training for officials would reduce the arbitrary treatment that Halloumi documented. Modest physical improvements, such as lighting, toilets and separate inspection areas for women, would cost relatively little and would make a real difference to people who cross the border several times a week. Informal traders are not a problem to be eliminated; they are, in many places, the most active participants in regional trade, and policy should begin by treating them as such.

topic: pensions for informal workers: why payroll-based schemes exclude them, matched micro-pension savings via mobile phone, automatic deductions and irregular income, universal tax-funded social pensions, fiscal cost and means-testing, and the political voice of informal workers
title: Old Age Without a Payslip
subtitle: Most of the world's informal workers will reach old age with no pension at all. Economists are divided over how, and whether, that can be changed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many low- and middle-income countries, fewer than one worker in five contributes to any kind of pension scheme. The reason is structural. Social insurance systems were designed around the salaried employee, whose contributions are deducted from wages and matched by an employer; the street vendor, the smallholder and the domestic worker, who together make up most of the labour force, fall outside them. For generations this gap was filled by the family, with adult children supporting their parents. Urbanisation, migration and smaller families are steadily weakening that arrangement, and it would be unwise, I believe, to go on assuming that relatives will provide for the growing number of people who will reach old age over the coming decades.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Extending conventional contributory schemes to informal workers has rarely succeeded. Without an employer, the worker must bear the whole contribution alone. Incomes in informal work rise and fall from week to week, yet most schemes require a fixed sum every month and impose penalties when payments are missed. Many potential members are also wary of handing savings to institutions that, within living memory, saw pension funds wiped out by inflation or mismanagement. In these circumstances, low participation reflects sensible caution rather than ignorance or indifference.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One response has been the micro-pension: a voluntary savings account designed around the realities of informal work. The pension economist Bahati Kazungu evaluated a pilot scheme for market traders in an East African port city, in which members could deposit any amount, at any time, using their mobile phones. For the first year, participation remained low, at around four per cent of eligible traders. When the government began adding fifty cents for every dollar saved, up to an annual limit, enrolment climbed to nineteen per cent within two years. Kazungu regards the matching contribution as decisive, but he acknowledges a sobering limitation: the average balance accumulated by members would fund only a few months of retirement income.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The behavioural economist Phonsavanh Sisouphanh has focused less on incentives than on the timing of saving. People with irregular incomes, she argues, are most likely to save at the moment money arrives, before it is absorbed by daily needs and requests from relatives. In a trial she conducted with a mobile payment provider, traders who agreed to have two per cent of every incoming payment transferred automatically into a pension account saved considerably more than those who received regular text-message reminders. Automatic deduction was not a complete solution, however. During lean seasons, a substantial proportion of participants switched the deductions off, and not all of them switched them back on afterwards. Sisouphanh nevertheless concludes that the design of a scheme matters at least as much as the financial rewards attached to it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: To the social policy scholar Ricardo Vasquez-Lira, such experiments, however ingenious, address the wrong question. Any scheme that depends on contributions, he contends, will inevitably leave out the poorest, who have nothing left over to save. He advocates instead universal social pensions: modest payments, financed through taxation, made to every resident above a certain age regardless of their work history. A number of countries in Latin America and southern Africa already operate such schemes, typically at a cost of around one per cent of national income. Studies of these programmes have recorded significant falls in old-age poverty, and have found that pensioners frequently use part of the money to pay for their grandchildren's schooling.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. The actuary Lindiwe Mhlongo has projected the cost of universal pensions under different demographic scenarios and warns that, as populations age, the expense could roughly triple by the middle of the century. She recommends that payments be restricted through a means test to those with little other income. The fiscal concern is legitimate, but means testing has its own drawbacks. Experience in several countries shows that complex eligibility rules and demands for documents deter many of the people the schemes are intended to reach, while the administrative cost of assessing applicants consumes resources that could otherwise be paid out. Raising the qualifying age gradually as life expectancy increases would seem a less damaging way of controlling costs.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate is often framed as a choice between contributory and universal approaches, but this seems to me a false opposition. A modest universal pension would provide a floor beneath which no older person could fall, while matched voluntary savings would allow those who are able to save to build something more on top of it. Each approach compensates for the weaknesses of the other: the universal pension reaches those who could never save, and the savings scheme rewards effort without placing the entire burden on public finances.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Whether any of this happens is ultimately a political question. Informal workers have traditionally had little organised influence over pension policy, which has been shaped mainly by trade unions representing formal employees. That is beginning to change. Associations of domestic workers, street vendors and waste collectors have started to campaign for social protection in several countries, and some have been invited to take part in national consultations. Their involvement is likely to be crucial, since schemes designed without the participation of those they are meant to serve have a long history of failure.

area: the economics of happiness and alternatives to GDP
topic: the non-monetary costs of unemployment: life satisfaction losses beyond lost income, scarring after re-employment, the social norm effect, spillovers to households and the nation, and job guarantees versus faster re-employment
title: More Than a Wage
subtitle: Surveys of life satisfaction suggest that losing a job costs people far more than their pay packet

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, economists counted the cost of unemployment in a fairly narrow way. A person who lost a job lost an income, but in the standard model of the labour market they also gained something in return: time. Since leisure was assumed to be valued, the true loss suffered by a jobless worker was taken to be somewhat smaller than the wage that had disappeared, and adequate benefits could, in principle, close most of the gap. Over the past three decades, large surveys asking people how satisfied they are with their lives have made this reasoning very difficult to sustain. The textbook account, it now seems clear, is not merely incomplete but misleading, because it treats work as a burden endured only for the sake of pay.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the discrepancy is illustrated by the work of Dr Ewa Zubrycki of the Baltic Institute for Labour Studies, who has analysed a panel survey that has followed the same households for more than twenty years. Zubrycki finds that the drop in life satisfaction following job loss is several times larger than the fall in household income alone would predict. By her calculations, restoring an unemployed person to their previous level of contentment through money alone would require a sum far exceeding the salary they used to earn. She attributes the remainder of the damage to things that a job supplies almost incidentally: a daily routine, regular contact with colleagues and a recognised place in society. These figures are arresting, although monetary equivalents of this kind should be handled cautiously, since they depend heavily on how the relationship between income and satisfaction is modelled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Equally troubling is what happens afterwards. Professor Henrik Sorhaug, of the Nordic Centre for Welfare Research, has shown that people who have experienced a spell of unemployment continue to report lower satisfaction for years after they find new work, an effect he calls 'scarring'. Part of the explanation, he suggests, is a persistent fear that the experience will be repeated; part is that many people return to jobs that are less secure or less well paid than the ones they lost. Sorhaug also draws attention to a contrast with other adverse events. Following bereavement or serious injury, life satisfaction typically recovers, if slowly and incompletely. Among the long-term unemployed, by contrast, there is remarkably little sign of adjustment: satisfaction remains depressed for as long as the spell lasts.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone, however, suffers to the same degree. Dr Mirela Paleologu, an economist at the Danube School of Economics, has compared regions with very different rates of joblessness and found that unemployed people living where unemployment is widespread report noticeably less distress than those in areas where it is rare. Her interpretation is that the stigma of being without work weakens when it becomes a common experience. Paleologu draws a cautious policy conclusion from this. If the psychological penalty of unemployment is softened in such places, she argues, there is a danger that entire communities may come to regard worklessness as normal and that the pressure to look for jobs may fade. This possibility deserves attention, but the evidence that reduced distress actually leads people to search less is, so far, thin. It would certainly be perverse to conclude that the unemployed should be made to feel worse in order to keep them motivated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The harm also spreads well beyond those directly affected. A research group led by Anjali Neupane at the Centre for Household Economics has found that the partners of people who lose their jobs experience a significant decline in wellbeing themselves. At the national level, Neupane's team estimates that a one-percentage-point rise in the unemployment rate reduces the average wellbeing of the whole population considerably more than a one-point rise in inflation, partly because those still in work begin to fear for their own positions. Such estimates have obvious implications for central banks, which have often been criticised for treating price stability as their overriding objective. Nevertheless, comparisons of this kind are sensitive to when surveys happen to be conducted and should not be treated as precise exchange rates.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If the most serious damage caused by unemployment is not financial, then income support, however generous, cannot by itself repair it. This has encouraged interest in job guarantee schemes, under which the state offers work to anyone who wants it. Zubrycki is doubtful about such proposals. Positions created simply to occupy people, she warns, may carry a stigma of their own and fail to supply the sense of identity that genuine employment provides. A stronger case can be made for measures that shorten spells of unemployment, such as intensive help with job searching and retraining, rather than measures that merely make those spells more bearable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the life-satisfaction evidence is beyond criticism. It has been objected that unhappy people may be more likely to lose their jobs in the first place, which would exaggerate the apparent effect of unemployment. Researchers have addressed this by studying workers who were dismissed when entire factories closed, an event unrelated to individual temperament, and the large effects persist. The broader lesson is that official unemployment figures ought to be read not simply as a measure of unused productive capacity but as an indicator of human suffering, and that accounts of a recession which focus only on lost output will always understate its true cost.

topic: the Genuine Progress Indicator: adjusting consumption for defensive expenditures, unpaid work, resource depletion and inequality, the 'threshold' pattern and why regional governments rarely act on it
title: Subtracting the Damage
subtitle: An alternative to GDP promises to separate the costs of growth from its benefits, but its own arithmetic is open to dispute

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Gross domestic product records every market transaction, whether or not it leaves anyone better off. When two cars collide on a motorway, the tow truck, the repairs to the vehicles, the hospital treatment of the drivers and the fees of the lawyers who settle the insurance claims are all counted as output, so that the accident itself appears in the national accounts as a small contribution to growth. The Genuine Progress Indicator, or GPI, was designed to correct this kind of distortion. It begins with personal consumption and then makes a series of adjustments: it adds the value of work that is never paid for, such as caring for children or volunteering, and subtracts the costs of crime, pollution, long commutes and the exhaustion of natural resources. The idea is appealing in its simplicity, but that simplicity is, to a considerable degree, an illusion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest argument for the GPI has come from long-run reconstructions of it. Dr Ilona Takacsova of the Bratislava Institute for Social Accounting has calculated the indicator for seventeen countries. In almost every case, she reports, the GPI rose in step with GDP for a period and then levelled off or even declined while GDP continued to climb. This has come to be known as the threshold pattern: beyond a certain level of prosperity, the social and environmental costs of further growth increase faster than its benefits. Takacsova is careful, however, not to treat the threshold as a fixed income level. In her data it arrives earlier in some countries than in others, and she suspects that the point at which it occurs depends heavily on national policy choices rather than on wealth alone.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Central to the GPI is the notion of defensive expenditure: spending that merely protects people against a deterioration in their circumstances. Burglar alarms, water filters and the cost of travelling to work are standard examples. Marco Gaudenzi, an economist at the Turin Institute of Applied Statistics, has argued that the boundary between defensive and ordinary spending cannot be drawn in any principled way. Food, he notes, defends against hunger, and clothing against the cold; by the same logic almost all consumption could be reclassified as defensive. The objection is ingenious but overstated. Some categories, such as the expense of cleaning up an oil spill, are plainly a response to damage rather than a gain in welfare. Nevertheless, Gaudenzi is right that the doubtful cases matter, because several of them, commuting in particular, are large enough to shift the overall result.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even greater difficulties arise when items that have no market price must be given one. Unpaid household work is usually valued at the wage that would have to be paid to a hired housekeeper. The depletion of oil, gas and minerals is often priced at what it would cost to replace them with a renewable source of the same energy or material. Most contentious of all is the treatment of long-term environmental harm. Several versions of the GPI subtract not just the damage caused by each year's carbon emissions but the accumulated cost of all past emissions, a figure which by its nature grows every year. Professor Jeptoo Toroitich of the East African Centre for Green Accounting has shown that this cumulative entry alone accounts for much of the apparent decline in the indicator in wealthy countries. Of all the criticisms the GPI faces, hers is the most damaging, since it implies that its best-known finding may owe as much to accounting conventions as to any real change in welfare.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The adjustment for inequality has provoked a different kind of argument. In most versions, personal consumption is weighted by an index of income distribution, so that if inequality widens the GPI falls, even if every household's income is rising. Its defenders appeal to the principle of diminishing marginal utility: an extra unit of income, they argue, adds more to the welfare of a poor family than to that of a rich one. Critics reply that this smuggles a political value judgement into what claims to be a statistical measure. That is true, but it is hardly a decisive objection. Every measure of national performance rests on judgements about what counts. GDP itself embodies the judgement that a pound spent on cigarettes is worth exactly as much as a pound spent on medicine; it is simply that this assumption is rarely noticed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In practice, the GPI has had a modest career in government. A handful of regional administrations have published it alongside conventional economic statistics. Dr Annika Brolund of the Nordic Institute for Policy Evaluation interviewed officials in several of these regions and found that the figures had almost never influenced a budget decision. They appeared in annual reports and were then set aside. The difficulty, Brolund concluded, lies in the form of the indicator. A single number that combines pollution, inequality, housework and crime cannot tell a minister which department deserves more money. She recommends that governments publish the component accounts separately.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means the GPI should be abandoned. Its real contribution lies less in its headline figure than in the questions it forces into the open: how the future should be weighed against the present, and whether the distribution of income matters as well as its total. It is better understood as a structured argument about welfare than as a neutral measurement of it. If it is to become more than that, the most useful step would be agreement on a common method, so that figures from different places could be compared with confidence. Whether governments will agree to such a standard is far from certain.

topic: counting unpaid household and care work in national accounts: replacement-cost versus opportunity-cost valuation, output-based measurement, water collection in poorer countries, satellite accounts versus inclusion in GDP, and the circularity of low care wages
title: The Unpriced Shift
subtitle: Most of the work done in homes never reaches the national accounts. Statisticians disagree about whether it should, and how

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Cooking a meal at home adds nothing to gross domestic product; buying the same meal in a restaurant does. Since the first national accounts were compiled in the mid-twentieth century, the cooking, cleaning, shopping and caring that households do for themselves have been left out, on the grounds that such activities have no market price and would be difficult to measure. Yet the quantities involved are enormous. Time-use surveys, in which participants record their activities through a sample day, show that in many countries the hours devoted to unpaid domestic work are roughly equal to, and sometimes greater than, the hours spent in paid employment. Excluding this work is often presented as a neutral technical convention. It is nothing of the kind: what a society counts shapes its sense of who contributes to the economy, and for decades the omission has rendered much of the work done by women invisible in official figures.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Statisticians who want to measure household production face an immediate choice of method. The replacement-cost approach asks what it would cost to pay someone else to do the work, using either the wage of a general housekeeper or, in a more detailed version, the separate wages of cooks, cleaners and childminders. The opportunity-cost approach instead values each hour at the wage the person doing the work could have earned in the labour market. The second method leads to conclusions that are difficult to defend: an hour spent ironing shirts becomes several times more valuable when performed by a surgeon than by a shop assistant, although the shirts are no smoother. Depending on which method is chosen, published estimates of the value of unpaid work vary from around fifteen per cent of GDP to well over half.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Zuzana Rusnakova of the Central European Office for Time-Use Research argues that both approaches share a deeper flaw: they measure inputs rather than outputs. A better method, she proposes, would count what households actually produce, such as meals prepared, garments washed and hours of supervised childcare, rather than the hours spent producing them, and price each at its market equivalent. Her reasoning is that input methods misread technological change. When washing machines became common, the time spent on laundry fell sharply, while the amount of clean clothing did not; an hours-based account therefore records a decline in household production at precisely the moment it became more efficient. The argument is conceptually compelling, but its data demands are formidable, and at present very few national statistical offices collect anything resembling output information for households.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In lower-income countries the case for measurement takes a more practical form. Professor Arulmozhi Thangaraj of the Coromandel Institute of Development Studies points out that unpaid work there includes hours of carrying water and gathering firewood, tasks that fall overwhelmingly on women and girls. When a village is connected to a piped water supply, she notes, GDP registers the project only as construction spending, while the hours released for schooling, rest or paid work go entirely unrecorded. Infrastructure that transforms daily life can therefore look, in the official statistics, no more valuable than any other building contract. Of all the arguments for household accounts, this seems to me the one with the most direct consequences for policy, since it bears on which projects governments and aid agencies choose to finance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone who supports measurement wants the results added to GDP. Dr Lucía Esquivias, a national accounts specialist at the Ibero-American Statistical Commission, warns that merging imputed household values into the headline figure would undermine its original purpose, which is to track market activity. Imputed values, she observes, cannot be taxed, saved or spent in the way that wages and profits can, and including them would make GDP a poorer guide to short-term economic fluctuations. Esquivias favours publishing separate satellite accounts but regards these as chiefly of interest to specialists. On the first point she is persuasive; on the second, less so. Regular household accounts could inform practical decisions, for example on the level of childcare subsidies or the design of pension credits for people who leave employment to care for relatives.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more unsettling objection comes from the sociologist Babatunde Ogundipe of the Lagos Centre for Gender and Labour. Replacement-cost estimates, he observes, rely on the wages of domestic workers, and those wages are themselves depressed by the low status that societies attach to care. Valuing unpaid care at market rates therefore reproduces the very undervaluation that the exercise was meant to expose. Ogundipe adds that attaching a price to looking after children or elderly parents may encourage policymakers to treat care as a cost to be minimised rather than as a relationship. The first part of this criticism is difficult to answer, although it argues for better valuation rather than none at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most revealing consequence of the exclusion concerns economic history. When women entered paid work in large numbers during the second half of the twentieth century, many tasks once performed at home, from childcare to food preparation, moved into the market, where they were counted for the first time. Part of the growth recorded in those decades was therefore not new production at all, but the transfer of existing work from an unmeasured sphere to a measured one. Counting household labour will not lighten it, but it would at least allow such shifts to be seen for what they are.

area: the economics of happiness and alternatives to GDP
topic: lottery prizes as natural experiments on money and happiness: early small studies, registry-based evidence on life satisfaction versus daily mood, whether windfalls resemble earned income, effects on neighbours, and relief from financial worry
title: Fortune by Chance
subtitle: Lottery winners have become an unlikely source of evidence on one of the oldest questions in economics

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Wealthier people report, on average, greater satisfaction with their lives than poorer people do. What this pattern cannot reveal is which way the influence runs. Money may make people happier, but it is equally possible that cheerful, healthy and energetic people are better at earning it, or that some third factor, such as a stable childhood, produces both. To separate these explanations, researchers would ideally hand out large sums of money at random and observe what follows, an experiment no ethics committee would fund. Lotteries, however, perform it for them. Prizes are allocated purely by chance, so a winner is, in principle, no different from an unlucky player except for the money. For this reason, lottery data are arguably the nearest thing economists possess to a controlled trial of wealth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years, the received wisdom was that winning made little lasting difference. This belief rested partly on a handful of early studies that interviewed a few dozen winners and found them no happier than comparison groups, and partly on newspaper accounts of winners who squandered their fortunes, quarrelled with their families or fell into debt. Neither source deserved the influence it acquired. Samples of that size could not support firm conclusions, and the stories of ruin were widely reported precisely because they were unusual; the far larger number of winners whose lives simply became more comfortable did not make headlines.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The picture changed when researchers gained access to national registers that link lottery records to tax data. Dr Sigrun Hjaltested of the Reykjavik Centre for Household Finance has followed several thousand winners in northern Europe, some for more than twenty years. Her results show that substantial prizes produce a clear increase in life satisfaction, measured by asking people to rate their lives as a whole, and that this improvement remains visible a decade or more after the win. Yet when the same people are asked how much enjoyment, worry or sadness they felt on the previous day, the differences between winners and others are small. Money, it appears, changes how people judge their lives far more than how their days feel.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Such studies take care over whom winners are compared with. Since people who buy many tickets may differ systematically from those who buy none, the usual approach is to compare large winners with players who won only small prizes, so that both groups share whatever traits lead people to gamble. Even so, Professor Kenji Nakagiri of the Osaka Institute of Behavioural Economics doubts that the findings can be applied to income in general. Regular lottery players, he notes, are not a representative group, and a sudden windfall differs from a salary in an important respect: it arrives without the effort, recognition and social standing that accompany earned income. His caution is reasonable, but it does not render lottery research worthless. If anything, the absence of those benefits suggests that lottery studies may understate, rather than exaggerate, the effect of money earned through work.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Lotteries also reveal how one person's good fortune affects others. In a number of countries, postcode lotteries award prizes to every participating household in a winning street, which allows researchers to study neighbours who did not take part. A team led by Dr Ramiro Barranquero at the Levante Institute of Applied Economics found that non-participating households on winning streets bought new cars more often in the following months than comparable households elsewhere, and reported slightly lower satisfaction with their own finances. The findings support the long-standing idea that people judge their income partly by comparison with those around them, and that visible spending by neighbours can prompt imitation. Barranquero himself is cautious about the size of the effect, noting that it was concentrated among households whose incomes were closest to those of the winners.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What do winners actually do with their money? Contrary to popular belief, few give up work entirely; most reduce their hours modestly or change jobs. Physical health improves only slightly, and there is little evidence that winners adopt healthier habits such as exercising more or giving up smoking. The most consistent change is psychological: winners report far fewer financial worries and score better on standard measures of mental distress. This suggests that the main benefit of additional money lies less in the pleasures it can buy than in the anxiety it removes, a conclusion with obvious relevance to households living close to the margin.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, though, to read lottery results directly into policy. A lottery prize is a single lump sum, often very large, while most government transfers provide modest amounts at regular intervals, and there is little reason to assume that the two have identical effects. Nor do lottery studies settle how much money matters at different levels of income, since most winners are neither very poor nor very rich before their win. What the evidence does establish is that the popular saying that money cannot buy happiness is, at best, half true. Money appears to buy a particular kind of happiness: a more favourable verdict on one's life as a whole, rather than greater joy from one day to the next.

area: the economics of happiness and alternatives to GDP
topic: wellbeing-adjusted life years (WELLBYs) in policy appraisal: comparing programmes in units of life satisfaction, the bias of willingness to pay, whether rating scales can bear arithmetic, the neutral point for valuing lives, borrowed estimates and distributional weights
title: The Currency of Contentment
subtitle: Some economists want every government policy to be judged by a single unit of life satisfaction. The idea is bold, and its difficulties are instructive

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a government decides whether to build a bypass, fund a cancer drug or expand an apprenticeship scheme, it typically translates the expected benefits into money. Travel time saved is priced at an hourly rate, a reduced risk of death at a figure known as the value of a statistical life, and improvements in health through quality-adjusted life years. A growing group of economists proposes a different common unit: the wellbeing-adjusted life year, or WELLBY, defined as a one-point rise in life satisfaction, on a scale from zero to ten, enjoyed by one person for one year. In principle, this would allow a programme of talking therapy to be compared directly with a road scheme or a tax credit. The ambition of placing such different policies on a single scale is admirable. Yet every unit of measurement carries assumptions, and those built into the WELLBY deserve closer scrutiny than they have generally received.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its advocates point to striking results. Dr Mateja Cvitanic of the Zagreb Centre for Wellbeing Policy has calculated that psychological treatment for depression yields many more WELLBYs per unit of public spending than a wide range of conventional programmes, including several transport and housing schemes. Money-based appraisal, she argues, systematically undervalues such treatment, because it relies heavily on willingness to pay, and what people are willing to pay depends on what they are able to pay. Those who would benefit most from mental health care are disproportionately poor, so their gains shrink when expressed in currency. This is, in my view, the most compelling case for the new approach: an appraisal method that counts the preferences of the rich more heavily than those of the poor can hardly claim to be neutral.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more technical worry concerns the scale itself. Adding and subtracting WELLBYs assumes that a move from two to three on the satisfaction scale is worth exactly as much as a move from eight to nine, and that different people mean the same thing by the same number. Dr Oyunbileg Lhamsuren of the Ulaanbaatar Institute of Social Measurement has found evidence that neither assumption holds perfectly. Respondents interpret the endpoints of the scale in different ways, and, more troublingly, they appear to redefine what a ten means as their circumstances improve, so that real gains are partly absorbed by rising standards. Lhamsuren concludes that WELLBYs are dependable for ranking policies from more to less beneficial, but not for the precise arithmetic on which budget decisions are often based.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The deepest difficulty arises when policies affect how long people live. Because a WELLBY combines satisfaction with duration, saving a life adds years to the total, but only if those years are counted from some neutral level of wellbeing below which a life would add nothing. Whether that point is placed at one, two or four on the scale makes an enormous difference to the relative value of extending lives as opposed to improving them. Professor Livia Ambrogetti of the Adriatic Centre for Ethics and Public Policy insists that choosing the neutral point is a moral decision that no survey can settle, and warns that it also carries uncomfortable implications for decisions about population. She is right that the choice is ethical rather than empirical. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that monetary appraisal escapes such dilemmas; the value of a statistical life rests on equally contestable judgements, which are simply less frequently debated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also the matter of evidence. For most policies, the effect on life satisfaction has never been measured, because trials and evaluations have tracked outcomes such as income, employment or hospital admissions instead. Dr Eero Pelkonen, formerly an appraisal adviser at the Helsinki Public Appraisal Unit, observes that analysts often fill these gaps by borrowing estimates from studies conducted in other countries or on quite different programmes, producing figures whose apparent precision is unwarranted. He recommends that WELLBYs be used as a supplementary measure, reported alongside conventional monetary analysis rather than replacing it. This is a sensible precaution, but it carries a risk of its own: methods that are always presented as supplementary are seldom allowed to change a decision, and the approach could remain permanently on the margins.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One respect in which the WELLBY performs well is the treatment of distribution. In its basic form, a point of satisfaction counts the same whoever receives it. Some researchers argue that gains to people who are struggling should count for more, and propose explicit weights to achieve this. Whatever one thinks of such weighting, it has the merit of being visible and open to argument, whereas the distributional assumptions hidden in willingness-to-pay methods are rarely stated at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is unlikely that the WELLBY will displace monetary appraisal altogether, and perhaps it should not. Its greatest value may lie in areas where markets offer no meaningful prices, such as mental illness, loneliness or the quality of community life, and where conventional methods have consequently tended to assign little or no value. In those fields, a rough measure of what matters may be preferable to a precise measure of something else.

area: the economics of happiness and alternatives to GDP
topic: positional consumption and status competition: relative-standing survey experiments, expenditure cascades from rising inequality, the case for a progressive consumption tax, administrative objections and luxury taxes, and modest alternative reforms
title: Keeping Up, Paying More
subtitle: If much of what people buy matters only in comparison with what others own, should spending itself be taxed?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Economists draw a distinction between two kinds of goods. Some, such as safety at work, clean air or time with friends, are valued largely for what they are. Others, known as positional goods, are valued for how they compare with what other people possess: the largest house on the street, a place at the most selective school, a car that is newer than the neighbours'. Spending on positional goods can resemble an arms race. If everyone buys a bigger house in order to stand out, nobody stands out any more, and the resources consumed in the attempt are lost to other uses. The image often used to illustrate this is a crowd at a football match in which one spectator stands to get a better view, forcing everyone behind to stand as well, until all are on their feet and no one sees any better. The comparison is vivid, but it has been stretched to cover situations in which it hardly applies, since much spending that looks competitive is in fact driven by ordinary needs.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Evidence for positional concern comes partly from survey experiments. Respondents are asked, for instance, whether they would rather earn a certain salary in a society where others earn half as much, or double that salary where others earn four times as much. Dr Tomasz Strzelbicki of the Kraków School of Consumer Research has posed such questions in eleven countries. A clear majority, he reports, prefer the lower but relatively higher income, whereas when the same choice is framed in terms of weeks of holiday, most opt for the larger absolute amount. Concern with relative standing, in other words, is strong for income, housing and cars but weak for leisure. Strzelbicki argues that this asymmetry pushes societies towards working longer hours than their members would collectively choose. The reasoning is plausible, though hypothetical survey answers cost respondents nothing, and real decisions may follow a different pattern.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Behavioural data offer a firmer foundation. Dr Ratna Tambunan of the Bandung Institute for Economic Studies has examined household budgets across districts in which income inequality rose at different rates. Where the incomes of the richest grew fastest, she found, middle-income families spent a larger share of their earnings on housing, travelled further to work and were more likely to report financial distress. Tambunan describes this as an expenditure cascade: when those at the top spend more, those just beneath them adjust their own standards upwards, and the pressure passes down the income scale. The pattern is striking, although it falls short of proving that envy is the cause; rising house prices in prosperous districts could produce similar results without any desire to imitate.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If positional spending is partly wasteful, one remedy is to tax it. The proposal most often discussed is a progressive consumption tax. Instead of taxing income, the government would tax what each household spends in a year, calculated as income minus savings. A generous allowance would leave basic spending untaxed, but the marginal rate would rise steeply as consumption increased. Supporters argue that this would dampen competition at the top of the income scale and encourage saving, while leaving relative positions largely unchanged; if every wealthy household spent somewhat less on houses and cars, none would lose status in comparison with the others.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Inés Madurga of the Basque Institute for Fiscal Studies is unconvinced. Measuring consumption as income minus savings, she points out, requires households to report every change in their savings, and it would be easy to disguise spending by buying assets, such as works of art, that could be enjoyed and later resold. She adds that the tax would fall on all spending above the allowance, including spending on medical care or on supporting relatives, which is hardly positional. Madurga prefers targeted taxes on particular luxury goods. Yet such taxes have a poor record: because they cover only a narrow range of items, buyers have repeatedly avoided them by purchasing abroad or switching to untaxed alternatives. The breadth of a consumption tax, which Madurga regards as a weakness, is in this respect its principal strength.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It should also be acknowledged that competition for status is not wholly destructive. The desire to own the newest or best product has financed a great deal of innovation, and the wish for public esteem has funded hospitals, libraries and concert halls. A theory that treats all positional spending as waste ignores these benefits. Still, the question is one of scale, and few would argue that the benefits of status competition come close to justifying the debt and long working hours associated with it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A progressive consumption tax is unlikely to be enacted soon. It would require a wholesale redesign of tax administration, and it challenges deeply held assumptions about the right to spend one's own money. More modest measures, however, could capture part of its benefit. Limiting tax relief on very large mortgages, for example, would reduce the public subsidy currently given to the competition for housing, and could be introduced without any major reform of the tax system.

topic: does income inequality itself lower happiness? Mixed cross-country evidence, the 'tunnel' signal of opportunity in transition economies, perceived versus measured inequality, fairness and mobility beliefs, trust as a channel, and the dispersion of happiness as an indicator
title: The Shape of the Ladder
subtitle: Whether unequal societies are unhappy societies turns out to depend on what people believe about how the gaps arose

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It seems almost self-evident that people living in highly unequal societies should be less content than those in more equal ones. The statistical record, however, is remarkably untidy. Comparisons across European countries tend to find that wider income gaps go together with lower average life satisfaction, but similar studies in Latin America and East Asia frequently find no relationship at all, and a few report a positive one. Part of the difficulty is technical: income gaps are measured in different ways in different countries, and survey questions about satisfaction are not always worded identically. It would be a mistake to conclude from this inconsistency that inequality is irrelevant to wellbeing. A more reasonable interpretation is that inequality affects people through several channels at once, some of which push in opposite directions, and that their balance differs from one society to another.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One such channel was described decades ago with the image of a traffic jam. Imagine drivers stuck in both lanes of a two-lane tunnel. If the adjacent lane starts to move, those still stationary initially feel encouraged, taking the movement as a sign that their own turn is coming. Should their lane remain at a standstill, though, encouragement gives way to frustration and, eventually, anger. Dr Joost Gerritzen of the Twente Institute for Comparative Social Research has found a similar sequence in the economies of central and eastern Europe after the end of central planning. In the early years of the transition, he reports, rising inequality was accompanied by growing optimism, even among people whose own incomes had not improved. After roughly a decade, however, the relationship reversed, and greater inequality became associated with lower satisfaction as expectations of catching up faded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second complication is that people's sense of inequality may bear little resemblance to official measures. Dr Feruza Salimova of the Fergana Centre for Survey Methodology asked respondents in several countries to estimate how incomes were distributed and compared their answers with the actual figures. Estimates varied widely, and it was perceived inequality, not the measured kind, that predicted life satisfaction most closely. In follow-up experiments, giving participants accurate information altered their satisfaction only modestly. Salimova suggests that perceptions are shaped less by national statistics than by what people see in their own neighbourhoods and workplaces, which may explain why aggregate data produce such inconsistent results. She also found that respondents almost everywhere underestimated the incomes of the very richest, often by a wide margin.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most influential explanation concerns fairness. Professor Giacomo Ricardi of the Piedmont School of Political Economy argues that inequality damages wellbeing chiefly where people believe that success depends on luck, inheritance or personal connections. Where they believe that effort is rewarded and that children can rise above their parents' station, large disparities are tolerated with little apparent cost to happiness. The evidence for this view is substantial. Yet it is less reassuring than it may appear. Beliefs about social mobility are frequently out of date, and the societies whose citizens are most confident that hard work pays are not always those in which movement up the ladder is most common. If acceptance of inequality rests on a misunderstanding, its apparent harmlessness offers little comfort.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other researchers emphasise social relationships. Dr Alina Tokareva of the Volga Institute for Health and Society has followed households over fifteen years and finds that inequality is linked to lower wellbeing mainly because it erodes trust, both in other people and in public institutions. Once levels of trust are taken into account, the direct association between inequality and satisfaction in her data largely disappears. Her sample, drawn mainly from medium-sized towns, may not reflect conditions in large cities, as she herself acknowledges. Tokareva infers that policies designed to rebuild trust, such as improving the transparency of public services, might offset some of the harm. The logic is sound as far as it goes, but it is doubtful that trust can be restored while the disparities that undermined it remain untouched.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical suggestion is to measure the inequality of happiness itself. Rather than asking how income is distributed, statisticians would track how widely life satisfaction scores are spread across a population. Interestingly, in several wealthy countries this dispersion has narrowed in recent decades even as income gaps have widened, perhaps because public services have cushioned the effects of low income. It is also possible that people on low incomes have lowered their expectations, which would narrow the spread of scores without any genuine improvement in their lives. The proposal is intriguing, but it has a peculiar weakness: a society in which almost everyone was equally dissatisfied would score very well, and no one would wish to live there.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that the question of whether inequality makes people unhappy has been posed too simply, and few social scientists now expect a single figure to capture the relationship. The answer depends on how gaps are perceived, how they are thought to have arisen and what they do to the bonds between citizens. For policymakers, the implication is that the fairness of processes, such as access to good schools and to secure jobs, deserves attention alongside the distribution of income, since it is often the sense that the game is rigged, rather than the size of the gap, that does the damage.

title: How Things Are Decided
subtitle: People appear to care not only about what they receive but about the way in which it is decided, and that has consequences for how progress is measured

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Conventional economics assumes that people judge their circumstances by outcomes: the income they earn, the goods they consume, the services they receive. How those outcomes come about is treated as a matter of indifference. A growing body of research challenges this assumption. It suggests that people also derive satisfaction, or dissatisfaction, from processes, valuing the chance to be heard, the freedom to make their own choices and the experience of being treated fairly, quite apart from what they eventually obtain. Economists call this procedural utility. The idea strikes at one of the foundations of their discipline, and it has been given far less attention than its implications deserve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence comes from the world of work. Self-employed people consistently report higher job satisfaction than employees, despite lower average earnings, longer hours and greater financial risk. Dr Besnik Krasniqi of the Balkan Institute for Labour Studies attributes the difference largely to autonomy: the freedom to decide what to do, how to do it and when. To rule out the possibility that naturally contented people are simply more likely to work for themselves, he followed the same individuals before and after they switched between employment and self-employment, and found that satisfaction rose after the move and fell when people returned to employment. The finding is persuasive. It should be added, however, that much recent self-employment, particularly in delivery and transport work arranged through apps, is taken up for lack of other options, and in such cases the freedom on offer may be more apparent than real.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Politics offers a second test. Dr Ornella Vaccarezza of the Ticino Centre for Democratic Studies has compared regions within a federal Alpine country that grant their residents very different rights to propose laws and call referendums. Residents of regions with more extensive participation rights reported higher life satisfaction, even after differences in income and public services had been accounted for. Her most telling observation concerned residents without citizenship, who live under the same policies but cannot vote: they gained considerably less from living in a region with strong participation rights. This suggests that the benefit flows partly from the right to take part, rather than only from the better policies that participation may produce. The design is elegant, although non-citizens differ from citizens in many ways besides voting rights, and these differences cannot all be measured.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Encounters with public authorities provide a third source of evidence. Professor Torunn Fonsdal of the Western Norway Institute of Public Administration studied applicants for disability benefits. Those whose claims were rejected after a face-to-face hearing, at which they could explain their circumstances, expressed almost as much confidence in the system as applicants who had been approved through a purely written procedure. Fonsdal concludes that people's willingness to accept an unwelcome decision depends heavily on whether they feel they were given an opportunity to state their case. Her result echoes a long tradition of research on courts and policing, where perceptions of fair treatment predict compliance with the law better than the severity of penalties does.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These findings acquire new urgency as governments automate their decisions. Algorithms now assess applications for benefits, screen tax returns and allocate school places, often far more quickly and cheaply than human officials. Dr Halina Dabrowska of the Gdańsk Centre for Digital Governance warns that the efficiency gains from such systems may be partly offset by procedural losses, since those affected no longer have anyone to whom they can explain themselves, and these losses never appear in the cost-benefit studies used to justify automation. She proposes a legal right to human review of automated decisions. The proposal is a sensible one, but there is a danger that review becomes a formality in which an official simply confirms what the machine has already decided.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Procedural utility has its critics. It is difficult to measure directly, and it is easily confused with satisfaction about outcomes, since people who receive what they want tend to describe the process as fair. There is also a political hazard. Governments that learn that participation makes citizens happier may be tempted to offer its appearance without its substance, holding consultations whose results are ignored. Such exercises may well be counterproductive. In my view, consultation that has no effect on decisions is worse than no consultation at all, because people who discover that their views were never going to count are likely to become more cynical than if they had not been asked.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate has implications for the search for measures of progress beyond GDP. Most of the alternatives proposed so far, such as indices combining income, health and education, remain focused on outcomes. Some researchers have suggested adding indicators of voice and autonomy, drawn from questions about whether people feel able to influence decisions that affect them at work, in public services and in politics. Constructing such indicators would not be straightforward, but leaving process out entirely means that official statistics may show a society to be thriving when its members feel increasingly powerless.

title: Pricing the Quiet
subtitle: Economists have found a new way to put a value on clean air, green space and silence: asking people how satisfied they are with their lives

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Nobody buys peace and quiet in a shop, yet decisions about airports, motorways and urban parks constantly require it to be given a price. Economists have traditionally relied on two techniques. The first, known as stated preference, simply asks people how much they would pay for, say, a reduction in traffic noise; its weakness is that answers to hypothetical questions cost nothing and may bear little relation to real behaviour. The second infers values from house prices, on the reasoning that if homes in quiet streets sell for more than otherwise identical homes on busy roads, the difference reveals what buyers will pay for quiet. This method assumes, however, that housing markets operate smoothly and that buyers are fully informed about the places they move to. A third technique, first proposed around the turn of the century, takes a different route. Known as the life satisfaction approach, it estimates how much an environmental nuisance lowers people's reported satisfaction with life, and how much additional income raises it; the ratio of the two gives the sum of money that would compensate for the nuisance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most cited applications concerns aircraft noise. When the flight paths into a large European airport were redrawn, thousands of households found themselves under aircraft for the first time, while others were relieved of noise they had long endured. Dr Yacine Bouzidi of the Mediterranean Institute for Environmental Economics surveyed residents before and after the change. Among the newly affected, life satisfaction fell by an amount equivalent to a loss of roughly fifteen per cent of household income, and three years later there was no sign that they had grown used to the noise. House prices in the same streets, by contrast, fell by only about three per cent. Bouzidi suggests that buyers tend to view properties at weekends or at quiet times of day, and that they underestimate how much the noise will continue to bother them, so that the housing market captures only a fraction of its true cost.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Similar studies have linked daily readings of air pollution to responses in national wellbeing surveys, and several have detected a negative effect on satisfaction even when concentrations were below the limits set by regulators. The method has a significant technical weakness, however, which Dr Jurgita Rimkute of the Baltic Centre for Applied Wellbeing Research has examined in detail. Because income has only a modest effect on reported satisfaction, the income term in the calculation is small, and dividing by a small number produces a large result. Some published estimates imply that people would need compensation exceeding their entire annual income to accept a moderate increase in pollution, a conclusion that is plainly implausible. Rimkute recommends estimating the effect of income from sudden, externally caused changes, such as tax reforms or inheritances, which tend to yield larger and more credible figures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Applied to urban green space, the approach generally finds that living close to a park raises satisfaction, with the effect larger for older residents and for families with young children than for other groups. Professor Myroslav Gavrilenko of the Dnipro Institute of Urban Studies cautions that such estimates are complicated by the fact that people choose where to live. Those who particularly value parks will tend to move near them, so comparisons between residents near and far from green space may overstate the benefit that a new park would bring to a typical household. The same process works in reverse for nuisances: people who are especially sensitive to noise are likely to move away from it, leaving behind residents who mind it less, which would cause the harm to be underestimated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Governments have been cautious. Only a handful of environment ministries have used the life satisfaction approach in official appraisals, and generally as a supplement to conventional methods rather than a replacement. Its most prominent use proved controversial. In the appraisal of a proposed new runway, a noise cost derived from wellbeing data was several times larger than the figure produced by house-price methods, and opponents and supporters of the scheme spent months disputing which number should be believed. To my mind, this dispute illustrates the method's value rather than its failure, since it exposed how much the conventional estimate depended on assumptions about the housing market that few had previously questioned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The approach has genuine advantages. It does not require people to be aware of how pollution affects them, as stated preference does, since it records how their lives actually go rather than what they believe; nor does it depend on the efficient functioning of the housing market. Its limitations are equally real. It captures only those effects that people experience consciously, so damage to health that has not yet appeared, such as a raised risk of heart disease decades in the future, falls entirely outside its scope.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would therefore be unwise to treat the life satisfaction approach as a replacement for older methods. It is best regarded as a check on them. Where all three techniques produce similar values, decision-makers can proceed with some confidence; where they diverge sharply, as in the case of aircraft noise, the divergence is itself informative, pointing to a market that is failing or a public that is poorly informed.
