title: Prosperity Without More?
subtitle: As doubts grow about endless economic expansion, economists are divided over whether wealthy nations can do well without it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the past century, economic growth has been the organising aim of government policy in almost every country. Rising GDP was expected to bring higher living standards, fuller employment and the tax revenue needed for public services. In recent decades, however, that consensus has come under pressure from two directions: evidence that further growth in rich countries adds little to average wellbeing, and concern that the environmental cost of expansion is becoming unsustainable. The resulting debate is often presented as a contest between two camps, one confident that growth can be made environmentally benign, the other convinced that wealthy economies must deliberately shrink. This framing is unhelpful, because it has left the more promising positions between the two largely unexamined.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Advocates of green growth rest their case on decoupling: the possibility that output can continue to rise while emissions and resource use fall. They can point to genuine successes. A number of wealthy countries have reduced their carbon emissions in absolute terms over the past two decades while their economies have expanded. Dr Pavel Sevcik of the Brno Institute for Environmental Economics accepts that such decoupling is real but argues that its pace is the problem. On his calculations, emissions would need to fall several times faster than in even the best-performing countries for international climate targets to be met. He adds that material use presents a bleaker picture than carbon: once the raw materials embodied in imported goods are counted, the consumption of minerals and biomass in rich countries has continued to rise more or less in step with income.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Degrowth advocates draw a more radical conclusion. Dr Zarina Hamidova of the Almaty Institute for Ecological Economics argues that rich countries should plan a gradual reduction in the production of goods that contribute little to wellbeing, combined with shorter working hours and free access to essential services such as transport, healthcare and housing. Her case relies heavily on international comparisons. Several middle-income countries, she notes, achieve levels of life expectancy and life satisfaction close to those of far richer nations while using a fraction of the energy per person. The comparison is instructive, since it shows that a good life does not require the levels of consumption now typical of the wealthiest societies. It does not follow, however, that reducing consumption in a rich country would be painless. A society that has organised itself around high consumption cannot simply adopt the habits of one that never did.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that modern economies are, in important ways, structurally dependent on growth. Pension systems assume rising wages; the servicing of public and private debt is far easier when incomes are increasing; and because productivity rises each year, output must grow merely to keep employment stable. The experience of recessions, which are in effect episodes of unplanned degrowth, is not encouraging: unemployment rises, public finances deteriorate and reported wellbeing falls sharply. Professor Lucas Moraga of the Valparaíso Institute of Political Economy adds a political dimension. Growth, he argues, has historically allowed governments to improve the position of poorer groups without making anyone worse off in absolute terms. In a stationary economy, any gain for one group must come at another's expense, and politics risks becoming a zero-sum struggle. This is the most serious objection to degrowth, but it is an argument for reforming institutions so that they depend less on expansion, not a justification for pursuing growth whatever the cost.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Between these positions lies what has been called an agnostic view. Its proponents argue that governments should stop treating GDP growth as a goal in itself and should instead pursue environmental and social objectives directly, through carbon pricing, regulation and investment in public services, accepting whatever rate of growth, positive or negative, results. Critics complain that this position is evasive, avoiding the hard question of whether growth and environmental limits can be reconciled. The charge has some force, but it misses the point. The agnostic view does not deny that the question matters; it holds that no government needs to answer it in advance in order to act. Simply removing growth from the list of official targets would be a modest but sensible step.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some practical measures follow naturally from this view. Pension and welfare systems could be redesigned so that their solvency does not rely on continuous expansion, for instance by linking benefits more closely to available revenue. Budget documents could report progress on emissions, health and wellbeing as prominently as the growth forecast. None of these reforms would require a government to declare itself for or against growth.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question of whether wealthy societies can thrive without growth may not be settled for decades, and perhaps it never will be in the abstract. What can be said is that the institutions of rich countries have been built on the assumption of perpetual expansion, and that this assumption leaves them fragile. Making them robust to slower growth, whatever its cause, is worthwhile regardless of which side of the debate turns out to be right.

topic: earworms (involuntary musical imagery): diary studies, what makes tunes sticky, personality, competing functional accounts and remedies
title: The Tune That Will Not Leave
subtitle: Why do fragments of music replay themselves in our heads, and should we be trying to stop them?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost everyone knows the experience: a few bars of a song, often one the listener does not even like, begin to play in the mind and refuse to stop. Surveys in several countries suggest that more than ninety per cent of adults experience this at least once a week, and around a quarter report it several times a day. The popular term 'earworm' is a loan translation of the German Ohrwurm, but psychologists increasingly prefer the more cumbersome label 'involuntary musical imagery'. For decades the phenomenon was treated as a curiosity, too trivial and too private to merit laboratory attention. That neglect was a mistake. Because earworms arrive uninvited, they offer one of the few windows researchers have onto the mind's spontaneous activity, the thoughts and images that surface when nobody has asked for them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first systematic portrait came from diary studies. Ingrid Halsnes, a cognitive psychologist at the Vestland Institute for Cognitive Science, asked more than four hundred volunteers to log every episode over a fortnight, noting what they had been doing, how long the tune lasted and how they felt about it. The results contradicted the image of the earworm as a form of mental torture. The great majority of episodes ended within thirty minutes, and most were rated as neutral or even pleasant. What returned was almost never a complete song but a fragment, usually the chorus, lasting perhaps fifteen to twenty seconds and looping repeatedly. Recent exposure was the most common trigger, but many episodes were prompted by associations, such as a word in conversation that echoed a lyric. Episodes were also most likely to start during undemanding activities such as walking, showering or household chores.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If certain tunes are especially prone to return, it is natural to ask what distinguishes them. Ren Okafuji, a music theorist at Seto University, compared the melodies most frequently named in earworm surveys with others of similar popularity that were rarely mentioned. The frequently reported tunes tended to be relatively fast and to follow a common melodic contour, rising and then falling, yet they also contained some unusual feature, such as an unexpected leap or an odd pattern of repeated notes. In Okafuji's phrase, the recipe is 'a familiar shape with a distinctive twist'. Advertisers have predictably seized on such findings. However, the idea that a guaranteed earworm can be manufactured is fanciful. Okafuji's melodic features explain only a modest share of the variation between songs, and the single best predictor of whether a tune lodges in the mind remains how often people have recently heard it, whether on the radio, in shops or through streaming services.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Individual differences matter too. Grace Mwamburi, at the Rift Valley Centre for Behavioural Research, found that people scoring highly on measures of obsessive thinking reported episodes that were more frequent, longer and more upsetting. Mwamburi is careful not to conclude that earworms are a symptom of anything. In her view, the unpleasantness arises less from the music itself than from the struggle to get rid of it: those who tried hardest to banish a tune were the most likely to describe it as intrusive. Professional musicians, interestingly, report more earworms than non-musicians but appear to be less troubled by them, perhaps because, for them, a melody running through the head is an ordinary part of working life.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why the brain should behave this way at all is disputed. Duarte Cerqueira, a neuroscientist at the Atlantic Institute of Memory, argues that earworms are a by-product of the memory system rehearsing material it has recently encoded, in the same way that a newly learned telephone number may repeat itself unbidden. On this account, the replaying fragment is part of a process of consolidation. Petra Hlavacek, who studies mind-wandering, regards this as an elaborate answer to a simple question. She contends that earworms have no function at all: they occupy attentional capacity that happens to be idle, which is why they flourish during routine tasks and fade when the mind is fully engaged. Cerqueira's hypothesis is elegant, but the evidence for it remains thin, and the way episodes cluster in moments of low mental demand fits Hlavacek's more modest explanation rather better.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For those who simply want the music to stop, research offers some practical guidance. In one laboratory study, chewing gum reduced the number of unwanted tunes, presumably because it engages the muscles used in silent rehearsal of speech and song. Other work suggests that absorbing tasks help, but only up to a point: anagrams of moderate difficulty seemed most effective, whereas puzzles that were too easy left the mind free to wander and those that were too hard caused people to give up. Some sufferers swear by listening to the whole song through, on the theory that an unfinished fragment nags at the mind. Halsnes's diaries, meanwhile, showed that deliberate attempts at suppression tended to prolong episodes rather than shorten them. The familiar advice simply to ignore the tune can sound glib, but on this evidence it is sounder than it seems.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this should be confused with genuine musical hallucinations, in which people, often older adults with hearing loss, perceive music as though it were coming from outside the head. These are a distinct clinical condition, and conflating them with ordinary earworms does a disservice to both fields of research. The everyday earworm is not a malfunction. It is better understood as a vivid demonstration of how much music the brain retains, and of how readily that store is reactivated. Its greatest value to science may lie less in finding a cure than in what it reveals about the stream of thought that runs, largely unnoticed, beneath our deliberate intentions.

topic: absolute pitch: early training versus genetics, the tone-language link, drawbacks for musicians and whether adults can learn it
title: The Note Without a Reference
subtitle: Absolute pitch has long been treated as a gift of the musically elect, but research suggests a more ordinary and more interesting story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask most people to sing a familiar melody and they will reproduce its shape faithfully, rising and falling in the right places, yet they will rarely begin on any particular note. A small minority, however, can name a pitch the moment they hear it, or sing a requested note without first hearing another for comparison. This capacity, known as absolute pitch, is thought to occur in fewer than one person in ten thousand in Europe and North America. Because several celebrated composers are said to have possessed it, absolute pitch has acquired an almost mythical reputation as a hallmark of musical genius. That reputation is, in my view, badly misplaced. Many outstanding performers lack the ability entirely, and plenty of people who have it never become notable musicians at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential explanation for absolute pitch emphasises the timing of musical experience. Tomoko Hirasaki, a psychologist at the Kansai Institute of Music Psychology, surveyed more than two thousand conservatoire students and found that those who had started formal lessons before the age of six were far more likely to have the ability than those who had started later; among students who began after the age of nine, it was almost unknown. Hirasaki argues that there is a critical period for acquiring absolute pitch, comparable to the window in which young children absorb the sounds of their first language with apparently little effort. The pattern she identified is striking, but it does not settle the matter. Children who begin lessons very young are likely to differ from their peers in other respects, not least in growing up in households where music is played, discussed and valued.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of those other respects may be genetic. Benedek Tarjanyi, who studies behavioural genetics at the Danube Centre for Human Development, has shown that absolute pitch clusters in families. The brothers and sisters of people who possess it are many times more likely to possess it themselves, and this remains true even when Tarjanyi compares only siblings who started lessons at the same age. He concludes that early training is necessary but insufficient: without some inherited predisposition, even a child given lessons at three will not develop the skill. Tarjanyi concedes, though, that the twin studies which might confirm his account remain few and small, and that no specific gene has yet been convincingly linked to the trait.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third line of research complicates both positions. A team led by Adaeze Ikwuemesi compared music students who spoke tone languages, such as Mandarin, Cantonese and Vietnamese, in which the pitch of a syllable can change its meaning, with students who spoke non-tonal languages and had begun lessons at the same age. The proportion with absolute pitch was dramatically higher among the tone-language speakers. Ikwuemesi suggests that learning, in infancy, to treat pitch as meaningful prepares the brain to attach stable labels to notes later. Critics objected that the tonal speakers had often been taught by different methods, but Ikwuemesi points out that the gap persisted even among students trained side by side in a single conservatoire.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever its origins, absolute pitch is not an unmixed blessing. Lars Ottervik, a music educator at the Western Norway Academy of Music, has documented a range of difficulties that its possessors report. Some find it disturbing to hear a familiar piece transposed into another key, or played on instruments tuned to the lower pitch standards used in earlier centuries. More surprisingly, in Ottervik's experiments students with absolute pitch were slower than their classmates at recognising a melody once it had been shifted away from its usual key, apparently because they relied on note names rather than on the intervals between notes. Ottervik's findings deserve far wider attention than they have received, although it should be said that the problems he describes seem to affect only a minority of those with the ability.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If absolute pitch depends on a childhood window, adults should be unable to acquire it, and for decades experiments appeared to confirm this. Commercial courses promising to teach the skill have nonetheless flourished. Recently, however, several laboratories have reported that adults who undertake intensive daily practice over about eight weeks can improve dramatically, with a few reaching near-perfect accuracy on a restricted set of notes. Hirasaki dismisses such results as the rote memorisation of a handful of tones rather than genuine absolute pitch. She is partly right: the gains tend to fade within months once practice stops. Even so, the studies show that the line between those who have the ability and those who lack it is far less sharp than the label implies, and it may be better to think of absolute pitch as lying at one end of a continuum.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That idea is reinforced by an unexpected finding. When people with no musical training are asked to sing a favourite pop song from memory, a large proportion begin within a semitone or two of the key in which the recording was made. Memory for pitch, it seems, is widespread; what is rare is the ability to attach a name to it. If that is correct, the scarcity of absolute pitch may reveal more about how, and when, we are taught to label notes than about any special quality of the ear.

topic: musical chills (frisson): triggers, expectation, reward and dopamine, separation-call theory, individual differences and measurement problems
title: A Shiver Down the Spine
subtitle: Why do some passages of music raise the hairs on our arms, and what can a fleeting bodily reaction tell us about aesthetic pleasure?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most listeners will recognise the experience: a voice enters, an orchestra swells, and a tingling sensation spreads across the scalp and down the back, sometimes accompanied by goosebumps. Surveys suggest that somewhere between half and two-thirds of adults have felt these so-called musical chills at least once, while a sizeable minority insist they never have. The reaction lasts only a few seconds and serves no obvious purpose, so it might easily be dismissed as a curiosity. I would argue the opposite. Precisely because chills are brief, physical and reasonably easy to detect, they offer researchers one of the few reliable footholds in the otherwise slippery question of why organised sound should move us at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Jovan Radenkovic, a music theorist at the Adriatic Centre for Auditory Research, began by asking several hundred volunteers to nominate passages that reliably gave them chills and then analysing what those passages had in common. Certain features recurred with remarkable regularity: a sudden increase in loudness, the entry of a solo instrument or voice, and harmonies that briefly clash before resolving. Radenkovic interprets these as moments at which the music departs from what the listener has been led to predict. In his account, chills are the body's response to a violated expectation that is swiftly and satisfyingly corrected. The explanation is elegant, but it cannot be the whole story. Many people report chills most reliably in pieces they have heard dozens of times, where nothing could possibly come as a surprise.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A partial answer to that puzzle has come from brain imaging. Haruki Kagemori and his colleagues scanned listeners while they heard self-selected music and found that, at the peak of a chill, regions of the brain associated with reward became highly active, much as they do in response to food or money. More intriguingly, a chemical signal linked to pleasure was released not only at the peak itself but in the seconds leading up to it, in a separate region associated with wanting rather than liking. Kagemori describes music as having found a way into some of the oldest reward machinery in the brain. To my mind, the anticipation result is the most important finding in the field, since it explains how a familiar piece can still thrill: the listener knows the moment is coming, and the knowing is itself rewarding.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A quite different explanation has been proposed by the biopsychologist Marisol Uzkudun. She notes that many young mammals emit high, sustained cries when separated from their mothers, and that hearing such cries produces a sensation of cold and an urge to seek contact. Music that resembles these calls, such as a lone soprano or violin climbing above a quiet accompaniment, may, she suggests, trigger the same ancient response, which would explain why chills so often feel tinged with melancholy. In support, Uzkudun found that volunteers who experienced chills frequently were also more likely to describe the music that caused them as sad or bittersweet. The theory is intriguing, but questionnaires about present-day listening can say little about the origins of a response in our evolutionary past.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, do some people never feel chills? Folake Oduwole, a personality psychologist, has found that the best predictor is not musical training, which appears to make little difference, but a trait psychologists call openness to experience, a tendency to be curious, imaginative and receptive to new ideas and sensations. More strikingly, she has identified a small group of people who enjoy food, company and financial rewards in the normal way but feel almost nothing in response to music. Scans of these individuals revealed weaker connections between the areas that process sound and those that generate pleasure, suggesting that their indifference has a neurological basis rather than reflecting a lack of exposure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that the phenomenon is being measured correctly. Sigrun Aasebo, who studies psychophysiology, points out that most studies depend on participants pressing a button whenever they feel a chill. When she recorded skin conductance and the tiny muscle contractions that raise body hair at the same time, she found that button presses and physical signs coincided only around sixty per cent of the time. Some listeners, she suspects, report chills because they know the music is supposed to produce them. Her concern is legitimate, yet it is somewhat overstated, since the physical measures she favours are themselves imperfect and can be triggered by changes in temperature or simple surprise.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Enthusiasm for the research has already prompted suggestions that chill-inducing playlists might be used to lift the mood of people with depression. Such applications seem to me premature; the studies to date involve small numbers of mostly young, musically engaged volunteers, and their findings may not transfer to people for whom pleasure itself has become elusive. What the work has achieved, however, is to demonstrate that talk of music being moving is far more than a figure of speech. A passage of sound, arranged in the right way, can reach into the same systems that keep us alive and attached to one another.

topic: beat synchronisation in non-human animals: the vocal-learning hypothesis, parrot and sea lion experiments, primate timing and the gradual-evolution alternative
title: Keeping Time
subtitle: Can animals other than humans move to a musical beat, and if so, what does that reveal about the origins of rhythm?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some years ago, a short home video of a crested cockatoo bobbing its head and lifting its feet to a pop song was watched by millions of people. For scientists, the clip raised a serious question. Moving in time to a regular pulse, an ability known as beat synchronisation, comes so naturally to humans that toddlers do it without instruction, yet it had rarely been documented in any other species. Researchers were initially sceptical of the video, chiefly because the bird's owner might have been dancing out of shot, giving the cockatoo visual cues to copy rather than a rhythm to follow.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The leading theory of why beat synchronisation should be so rare was developed by Cian Ó Maoilmhichíl, a comparative neuroscientist at the Western Isles Institute for Comparative Cognition. He argues that keeping time requires an unusually tight link between the brain regions that process sound and those that control movement, and that such a link exists only in species capable of vocal learning, the ability to imitate new sounds. This would restrict the skill to a handful of groups: humans, parrots, some songbirds, elephants, certain whales and dolphins, and a few seals. It would also explain a curious fact. Dogs, cats and horses have lived alongside human music for thousands of years, but none has been shown to move reliably to a beat, and none of them can learn new vocalisations.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The cockatoo offered a chance to test the idea under controlled conditions. A team led by Ilse Dorrestijn played the bird's favourite song at a range of speeds, using software that altered the tempo without raising or lowering the pitch, and filmed it with no human dancing in view. The bird adjusted its movements to the new tempos, but only in bursts; it stayed in time for a few seconds, drifted away and then caught the beat again. Some commentators took this inconsistency as a reason to dismiss the results. That seems to me mistaken. Human children under the age of about five synchronise in exactly the same intermittent way, and nobody concludes from this that they lack a sense of rhythm.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The vocal-learning hypothesis soon faced a more direct challenge. Rahim Chakladar and his colleagues spent many months training a California sea lion, a species then thought incapable of vocal learning, to nod its head in time to simple rhythms, rewarding it with fish whenever it matched the beat. Remarkably, the animal went on to synchronise with tempos and pieces of music it had never encountered in training. Chakladar argues that beat-keeping need not depend on specialised vocal circuitry at all; given enough practice, it can emerge from the general learning mechanisms found in many mammals. Supporters of the original theory were not persuaded, replying that related seal species do show a limited ability to imitate sounds, so the sea lion may not be the exception it appears.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Evidence from our closest relatives has added a further complication. Monkeys can be trained to tap along with a metronome, but their taps tend to fall just after each beat, as if they are reacting to the sound rather than predicting it; human tappers, by contrast, typically land slightly ahead of the beat. Chimpanzees, meanwhile, have occasionally been observed swaying spontaneously to repetitive piano notes. On the basis of such findings, the primatologist Valentina Lanzavecchia proposes that the ability to perceive and anticipate a beat was assembled gradually over millions of years of primate evolution, reaching its fullest form in humans, rather than appearing suddenly as a by-product of vocal learning.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These accounts are usually presented as rivals, but I suspect they are less opposed than their advocates imply. Vocal learning may well sharpen the connection between hearing and movement, while a gradual primate inheritance supplies the capacity to predict. More importantly, the debate has tended to focus on whether a species can synchronise at all, when the more revealing question is how flexibly and how spontaneously it does so. Here, Chakladar's study is less decisive than it first appears. It shows convincingly that the capacity can be trained, but it tells us very little about why human beings, unprompted, get up and dance.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That question matters because rhythm may lie close to the origins of music itself. In experiments with human volunteers, people who have just walked, clapped or sung in synchrony with others are subsequently more generous and more cooperative towards them than those who have performed the same actions out of step. If other animals keep time only when trained to do so, this social dimension of shared rhythm may be a distinctively human development. It is also worth sounding a note of caution about popular claims that animals enjoy music. There is, as yet, no good evidence for this; a parrot that bobs its head to a song may be seeking its owner's attention as much as responding to the melody.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Nearly two decades after the cockatoo first appeared online, then, the question it raised has not been settled so much as transformed. The issue is no longer whether a few animals can follow a beat, since several clearly can, but what kind of mind turns that ability into music.

topic: whether musical training improves general cognition: the listening effect, self-selection in correlational studies, near versus far transfer, randomised trials with active controls and meta-analysis
title: Does Music Make Us Cleverer?
subtitle: The belief that learning an instrument sharpens the mind is widely held, but the evidence for it has proved surprisingly fragile

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few educational claims have proved as durable as the idea that music lessons make children more intelligent. It is repeated by parents choosing after-school activities, by head teachers defending their timetables and by charities appealing for donations. The modern version of the claim can be traced to a widely publicised laboratory study in the 1990s, which reported that students who had listened to ten minutes of a classical sonata performed better on a spatial reasoning task than those who had sat in silence. The effect lasted only a quarter of an hour, and later work suggested that it reflected nothing more than a temporary lift in mood and alertness: upbeat pop music or an exciting story produced similar gains. Attention then shifted from listening to music to the more demanding business of learning to play it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At first sight, the evidence for this second claim looks impressive. Nkechi Ezeanya, an educational psychologist who has followed some four thousand children from the age of five, found that those who took instrumental lessons scored several points higher on intelligence tests in adolescence than those who did not. Yet children who learn instruments differ from their classmates in many ways. Their families tend to be wealthier and their parents better educated, and they often show higher ability and greater persistence before their first lesson. When Ezeanya adjusted for these factors, the gap shrank by around two-thirds. It is the residual difference that tends to be quoted, but it is more plausibly explained by self-selection. Lessons are demanding, and the children who persist with them for years are likely to be those who were already unusually disciplined.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Researchers in the field distinguish between near transfer, in which training improves skills closely related to those practised, and far transfer, in which it improves quite different abilities. Piotr Chmielarz, a cognitive neuroscientist, emphasises that near transfer from music is well established. Trained musicians are better than non-musicians at discriminating small differences in pitch, detecting changes in the intonation of speech and, according to some studies, following a conversation against background noise. Evidence for far transfer to mathematics, memory or general intelligence is much weaker. Chmielarz believes that if far transfer occurs at all, it most probably operates through hearing: sharper processing of sound may help children to break words into their component sounds, which in turn supports learning to read. His own studies have found modest reading gains among young children judged to be at risk of reading difficulties.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Correlational studies cannot establish cause, so the most informative evidence comes from randomised trials. Mireille Castagnoux and her team assigned children in thirty primary schools by lottery to one of three groups: two years of weekly music lessons, two years of drama lessons, or no additional lessons. At the end of the trial, the music group performed no better than the drama group in intelligence or mathematics, although both scored slightly higher than children who had received no extra lessons. The most natural reading is that any benefit arose from additional structured activity and adult attention rather than from music in particular. The inclusion of an active comparison group of this kind is, in my view, the single most valuable feature of Castagnoux's design, because it is precisely what most earlier studies lacked.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The wider literature points in the same direction. Hemi Paraone, a statistician specialising in research synthesis, combined the results of around fifty studies of musical training in children. The overall effect on non-musical cognitive skills was small, and it fell almost to zero when he considered only studies in which children had been randomly allocated to groups and compared with others engaged in some alternative activity. In other words, the more rigorous the study, the weaker the effect. Paraone also found signs that studies with positive results were more likely to have been published than those finding nothing. He concludes that the claim of far transfer should be abandoned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Chmielarz has objected that such syntheses treat programmes lasting a few weeks as equivalent to years of serious training, whereas skilled musicians typically accumulate thousands of hours of practice, an intensity no school trial can reproduce. The objection has some force, but it cuts both ways. If benefits emerge only after many years of dedicated practice, they cannot justify the short, low-intensity programmes that schools are actually able to fund. There is also a strategic danger here. By resting their case on claims about intelligence and test scores, advocates of music education leave it vulnerable: should those claims collapse, as they increasingly appear to be doing, the case for music collapses with them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that music lessons are without value. Learning an instrument develops a demanding skill, opens access to a vast cultural inheritance and provides opportunities for collaboration and performance that few other school subjects offer. Nobody argues that history should be taught because it improves arithmetic, and music should not have to meet a test that other subjects are spared. The weakness of the evidence for far transfer tells us only that music is not a shortcut to general intelligence. It is not evidence that music education is worthless, and it would be a serious mistake to treat it as such.

topic: congenital amusia (true tone deafness): diagnosis, pitch perception without awareness, effects on speech, heritability and training
title: Deaf to the Tune
subtitle: For a small number of people, music never makes sense. Their condition is helping scientists understand how the brain hears melody

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Plenty of people describe themselves as tone-deaf, usually by way of apology before they are persuaded to sing. In the great majority of cases the description is inaccurate. When such people are tested, they turn out to hear differences in pitch perfectly well; their difficulty lies in controlling their voices, not in perceiving sound. There is, however, a genuine condition that the casual label obscures. Congenital amusia, which is thought to affect somewhere between one and a half and four per cent of the population, leaves people unable to recognise a familiar tune without its words, to notice when a singer is badly out of tune, or to tell one melody from another. It is present from birth, occurs in people with normal hearing and intelligence, and persists despite ordinary exposure to music throughout childhood.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years the condition was hard to study because there was no simple way of identifying those who had it. That changed when Eluned Pryderi, a neuropsychologist at the Cambrian Institute for Hearing Research, developed a series of short listening tests that can be completed online. In the most revealing of them, participants hear an unfamiliar melody twice and must say whether one note has been altered. Most listeners notice changes far smaller than a semitone, the smallest step on a piano keyboard; people with amusia frequently miss changes of a semitone or more. Interestingly, many of them perform normally on tests of rhythm, which leads Pryderi to argue that amusia is essentially a disorder of pitch. Her tests have made studies involving thousands of participants possible, although online testing inevitably sacrifices some control: researchers cannot check the quality of the headphones people use or the noise in the rooms around them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most unexpected finding in this field concerns what amusic people hear without knowing it. Chidera Okeagu recorded the electrical activity of the brain while volunteers listened to melodies containing occasional wrong notes. In people with amusia, the auditory regions produced a clear response to the errors, even though the listeners themselves insisted they had noticed nothing. Okeagu concludes that the brain registers the pitch information but that it fails to reach conscious awareness. Imaging studies appear to support her: they reveal weaker connections in a pathway in the right hemisphere that links areas processing sound with frontal regions involved in attention and decision-making. The problem, in other words, may lie less in hearing than in the communication between parts of the brain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If amusia impairs the processing of pitch, one might expect it to affect language as well, since pitch carries meaning in speech. Matthias Brunnhuber, a phonetician, has found that most people with amusia understand speech without apparent difficulty, probably because the pitch movements of speech are far larger than those that distinguish musical notes. Under careful testing, however, some struggle to tell whether a short sentence is a question or a statement when intonation is the only clue, and some find it hard to judge a speaker's emotional tone. Brunnhuber has also studied speakers of Mandarin, a language in which pitch distinguishes one word from another, and found that amusic speakers make more errors in identifying these tones in isolation but rely on the surrounding context to resolve ambiguity in conversation. These difficulties are real, but they are usually mild, and it would be wrong to present amusia as a language disorder.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Where does the condition come from? Shirin Zarrinkelk, a geneticist, studied the families of people diagnosed with amusia and found that close relatives were many times more likely to have the condition than members of the general population. This pattern strongly suggests an inherited component, although Zarrinkelk is careful to note that families share environments as well as genes, and that a household in which little music is heard might also contribute. No single gene responsible for the condition has been found, and she expects that many genes, each with a small effect, are involved.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whether amusia can be treated is less clear. Kenji Mizukoshi gave a small group of amusic children several weeks of computer games in which they had to distinguish between rising and falling tones, and found that some improved substantially, while a comparable group of adults showed little change. He argues that intervention is likely to work best early in childhood, when the brain is most adaptable. The results are encouraging, yet with fewer than twenty children involved they hardly amount to proof. It is also fair to ask whether treatment is wanted. Many amusic adults live entirely contented lives, some describing a symphony as sounding like traffic noise, and their main complaint is social: the awkwardness of being expected to sing at birthdays or to enjoy a concert with friends.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Beyond its importance for those who have it, amusia offers researchers a natural experiment. It shows that music depends on particular neural machinery which can fail while language, intelligence and ordinary hearing remain largely intact. Some commentators have gone further, treating amusia as proof that the brain contains a module dedicated exclusively to music. That conclusion seems to me too hasty. The core deficit concerns fine distinctions of pitch, which music happens to demand far more than speech does. Amusia tells us that music makes unusual demands on the brain, not necessarily that the brain has set aside a special place for it.

topic: musical universals across cultures: identifying song function in unfamiliar cultures, objections from ethnomusicology, consonance preference in a remote community and statistical universals
title: Is Music a Universal Language?
subtitle: After decades in which scholars stressed the diversity of the world's music, the search for what all musical traditions share has returned

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The phrase 'music is a universal language' is so familiar that it has become a cliché. For much of the twentieth century, however, the scholars best placed to judge it, the ethnomusicologists who study music in its cultural setting, regarded it with deep suspicion. Their fieldwork had revealed an astonishing variety of scales, rhythms, instruments and ideas about what music is for, and they saw talk of universals as a disguised way of measuring other traditions against European norms. The emphasis fell firmly on difference, and the search for common ground was left largely to psychologists, whose experiments were usually conducted with Western students.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the past decade, that division has begun to break down. A team led by the cognitive scientist Teodora Rusnac assembled a collection of vocal recordings from sixty small-scale societies across the world, chosen to represent four common song types: lullabies, dance songs, healing songs and love songs. They then played short excerpts online to around twenty-nine thousand listeners in more than fifty countries, most of whom had no formal musical training, and asked them to guess what each song was used for. None of the listeners was familiar with the cultures concerned, and the songs were in languages they did not speak.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The listeners guessed correctly far more often than chance would predict. Lullabies were the easiest to identify, followed by dance songs, while love songs proved hardest. Analysis of the recordings showed why: across cultures, lullabies tended to be slow, quiet and smooth, with a narrow range of pitch, whereas dance songs were faster, louder and more rhythmically regular. Rusnac concludes that the link between a song's form and its function is shared across human societies, which suggests that at least some aspects of musical meaning do not depend on cultural familiarity. It is worth stressing, though, that 'above chance' is not the same as 'easily': even the lullabies were misidentified a considerable proportion of the time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all ethnomusicologists have welcomed this work. Kwabena Agyemfra argues that it rests on two questionable foundations. First, archive recordings were for the most part made by visiting outsiders, who may have preferred performances that already sounded coherent to their own ears. Second, the four categories themselves reflect the assumptions of Western researchers; in many societies, singing is inseparable from dance, ritual and social obligation, and a single performance may soothe a child, mark a ceremony and entertain a crowd at once. To ask listeners which of four functions a song serves, Agyemfra suggests, is to build the conclusion into the question.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The first of these objections is less damaging than it might appear. Rusnac's team deliberately included recordings made by researchers from the communities themselves, and found the same pattern of results in that subset. The second is more serious, and it has not yet been satisfactorily answered. Even so, the finding that a lullaby from one continent can be recognised as such by a listener on another is difficult to explain away entirely, whatever reservations one has about the categories.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other apparent universals have fared less well. It has long been assumed that people everywhere prefer consonant combinations of notes, such as those in a major chord, to dissonant ones that sound harsh to Western ears. To test this, the anthropologist Ximena Llactahuaman worked with a community in the Amazon basin whose members had very limited exposure to Western music. They could distinguish consonant from dissonant chords as reliably as a comparison group in Lima, but they rated both types as equally pleasant. The comparison group, by contrast, strongly preferred consonance. Llactahuaman concludes that the preference, often treated as a fact of human biology, is largely acquired through listening.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Such findings have encouraged a more modest conception of universals. The musicologist Bjorn Haugsvaer, who analysed transcriptions of more than three hundred recordings from around the world, argues for what he calls statistical universals, strong tendencies rather than laws. Almost all the traditions in his sample build melodies from a limited set of discrete pitches rather than gliding continuously between them, and very few use scales of more than seven notes. Melodies overwhelmingly move by small intervals, and most music is organised around a regular beat, although some funeral laments in his sample have no steady pulse at all. Haugsvaer argues that these regularities reflect constraints of human memory and movement, which make certain structures easier to learn and to perform together.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The debate is often caricatured as a contest between nature and culture, but this framing seems to me unhelpful. The most persuasive picture to emerge from recent work is one in which biology does not dictate what music sounds like but marks out a broad space of possibilities, within which cultures have developed their own remarkably varied traditions. Music may not be a universal language, then, but neither is it a set of wholly unrelated dialects. Ethnomusicologists were right to resist the idea that all music should be judged by a single standard; they were wrong, perhaps, to assume that recognising shared foundations would require any such judgement.

topic: rhythm and music in neurological rehabilitation: rhythmic cueing for walking in Parkinson's disease, music versus metronome, individual beat-perception differences, singing in stroke recovery and wearable devices
title: Walking to the Beat
subtitle: A regular rhythm can help people with movement disorders regain control of their steps, but the reasons, and the limits, are only now becoming clear

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: One of the most distressing symptoms of Parkinson's disease is a phenomenon known as freezing. A person may be walking normally when, without warning, their feet seem glued to the floor; they want to move forward but cannot. Yet clinicians have noticed for decades that the same person may be able to stride across a room quite fluently when a march is played, or when stripes are painted across the floor for them to step over. This observation, long treated as a curiosity, has become the basis of a family of therapies. In my view, it is among the most practically valuable discoveries to have emerged from the study of music and the brain, precisely because it costs so little to apply and can be used in the home.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation most researchers accept concerns the basal ganglia, a group of structures deep in the brain that help to produce the internal timing signals needed for smooth, automatic movement. In Parkinson's disease these structures are progressively damaged, and the internal rhythm falters. An external beat appears to supply the missing timing, allowing movement to be organised through alternative pathways that are less affected by the disease. Agnieszka Pruszynska, a physiotherapist and researcher, tested this approach in a twelve-week trial in which patients practised walking to a metronome or to music set about ten per cent faster than their natural pace. By the end of the programme, they were taking longer strides, walking faster and reporting fewer falls. Encouragingly, a substantial part of the improvement was still evident when they were assessed again a month after the training had ended.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Is music any better than the simple tick of a metronome? Siosaia Fusitua, who studies motor rehabilitation, believes that it is, although not because it provides a superior beat. Exercises that must be repeated daily for months are tedious, and many patients abandon them. Fusitua found that those who walked to music they knew and liked kept up their exercises for far longer than those given a metronome, and that this persistence, rather than any difference in the cue itself, accounted for their better results. He cautions, however, that music is not suitable for everyone. For patients whose mental abilities have begun to decline, attending to a song while walking can become a second task competing for limited attention, making walking worse rather than better. Fusitua therefore recommends that music be chosen individually, with a metronome kept as an alternative.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication has been identified by the neuropsychologist Hélène Vaucouleurs. People differ considerably in how easily they can detect a beat, and Vaucouleurs found that this ability, measured before treatment began, predicted how patients responded to rhythmic cueing. Strong beat perceivers benefited markedly. Weak beat perceivers, by contrast, sometimes developed a less stable gait when music was played, apparently because their efforts to find the beat disrupted their steps. This finding has received far less attention than it deserves. It implies that offering the same cueing programme to every patient may actually harm a minority, and that a brief test of beat perception should be part of routine assessment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Music has also been used in recovery from stroke, particularly for aphasia, the loss of language that can follow damage to the left side of the brain. Some patients who cannot speak a phrase can nevertheless sing it, and therapies have been developed in which patients learn to intone short phrases before gradually returning to ordinary speech. Dumisani Dlamvuza, a speech scientist, is sceptical. He notes that the gains reported in trials are often small and that, when singing-based therapy is compared with conventional speech therapy given for the same number of hours, the difference largely disappears. In his view, the benefit comes from the sheer quantity of practice rather than from melody. The point is well made, but it is not the whole story. If patients are willing to practise for longer when they sing, then the motivating effect of music is itself part of how the therapy works.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The newest development is technological. Several research groups have built wearable devices that detect a patient's steps through sensors in the shoes and adjust the tempo of the music in real time, speeding up gradually to draw the walker into a longer stride or slowing when the person tires. Early results are promising, and patients describe the experience as less mechanical than walking to a fixed beat. Nevertheless, most studies so far have lasted a few days or weeks and have taken place in laboratories or clinics. Whether people will continue to use such devices at home, month after month, remains largely untested.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Music therapy has sometimes been regarded by other health professionals as a pleasant extra rather than a serious treatment. Work on rhythmic cueing has done much to change that perception, showing that sound can be used with something approaching clinical precision. It is important, though, not to claim too much. Rhythmic cueing can help people move more safely and confidently, but there is no evidence that it slows the underlying progression of Parkinson's disease, and patients should not be led to believe otherwise.

topic: historically informed performance of early music: period instruments, unreliable treatises, authenticity as modern taste, the problem of composers' intentions, early recordings and vibrato, and historical listening
title: Playing the Past
subtitle: The movement to perform old music as it was first heard has changed concert life, but can it ever achieve what it set out to do?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1960s and 1970s, a small number of musicians began to perform music of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in a strikingly unfamiliar way. They played on instruments built, or rebuilt, to old designs: violins strung with gut rather than steel, horns without valves, keyboard instruments whose strings were plucked rather than struck. They tuned lower than modern orchestras, chose brisker speeds and used far less of the continuous wavering of pitch, known as vibrato, that had become standard in the twentieth century. Once dismissed as the eccentric pursuit of a few enthusiasts, historically informed performance, as it came to be called, is now thoroughly mainstream. Its founding promise was to let audiences hear music as its composers had intended. That promise was always more problematic than its advocates admitted, yet the movement has, in my judgement, transformed musical life decisively for the better.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulties begin with the evidence. Ottavio Scarampi, a specialist in the history of instruments, points out that most so-called original instruments did not survive in their original form. Large numbers of eighteenth-century violins, for example, were fitted with longer necks and heavier internal supports in the nineteenth century so that they could produce the greater volume demanded by larger concert halls. Reconstructing their earlier state involves a good deal of informed conjecture, and many period instruments heard today are modern copies based on that conjecture. Written sources pose problems of their own. The instruction manuals on which performers rely were often aimed at amateurs, and Scarampi warns that their authors frequently described how music ought to be played rather than how it actually was.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection has come from the musicologist Wilhelmina Kortmulder. In her view, the pursuit of authenticity is less a recovery of the past than an expression of the present. The clean textures, light articulation and quick tempos associated with historical performance, she argues, closely match the tastes of the late twentieth century, which favoured clarity and restraint over grandeur and emotional excess; performers have, without realising it, created a modern style and labelled it historical. Kortmulder's argument is largely persuasive, but she goes too far when she implies that historical evidence is therefore irrelevant. Evidence may not determine how a piece should be played, but it can rule out many possibilities, and that is no small achievement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of what composers actually intended. Ferenc Bodrogi, who has studied the working practices of eighteenth-century court and church musicians, notes that composers routinely adapted their works to circumstances. A part written for an oboe might be given to a violin if no oboist was available; an aria might be rewritten for a new singer with a different range; a piece performed in a large church might be taken more slowly than in a small room. In many cases, Bodrogi argues, there was no single intended version to be faithful to. He proposes that performers should abandon the search for the composer's wishes and aim instead to work within the range of practices that would have been familiar at the time.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In recent decades the movement has extended its reach to music of the nineteenth century, and here a new kind of evidence becomes available. Ama Kwakyewaa has examined the earliest orchestral recordings, made in the first decades of the twentieth century, and found that string players at that time used vibrato sparingly, as an occasional ornament rather than a constant feature of the sound. If so, the rich, continuously vibrating string tone now associated with Romantic symphonies may be a later development. Kwakyewaa regards recordings as the most trustworthy evidence there is, since they capture what performers did rather than what theorists recommended, although she acknowledges that early recording equipment distorted the sound in ways that are hard to correct for. Audiences have not always welcomed the results, and some listeners find vibrato-free strings thin and cold.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most radical challenge concerns not performers but listeners. Lucien Marcheval, a philosopher of music, argues that even a perfect reproduction of an eighteenth-century performance would not be heard as eighteenth-century listeners heard it, because modern audiences bring with them everything they have heard since. A harmony that shocked its first listeners may now pass almost unnoticed. Marcheval therefore suggests that performers should seek to recreate the effect of the music rather than its sound, exaggerating a dissonance, perhaps, so that it disturbs a modern audience as it once disturbed an older one. The proposal is ingenious, but it is also dangerous, since almost any interpretation could be defended on the grounds that it recreates an original effect.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Where, then, does this leave the movement? Its lasting value, I would suggest, lies less in any recovery of the past than in the questions it has forced performers to ask. Musicians who once played every piece in much the same way now think carefully about speed, sound and phrasing, and mainstream symphony orchestras have adopted many of the movement's habits, playing earlier music with lighter textures and less vibrato. Historically informed performance is best understood not as a restoration project, which could never be completed, but as a creative tradition in its own right, one that uses the past as a source of ideas rather than as a set of rules.

topic: why minor keys sound sad: child development, resemblance to sad speech, cross-cultural counter-evidence, acoustic roughness and the history of modes
title: The Sadness of the Minor Key
subtitle: Is the link between minor keys and melancholy written into our biology, or is it a habit learned from the music around us?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Play a simple melody in a major key and then repeat it in a minor key, and most listeners raised on Western music will say that the first sounds cheerful and the second sad. The association is so strong that film composers rely on it, and so familiar that it seems almost self-evident. Yet the difference between the two versions can be remarkably slight, often a matter of lowering one or two notes by the smallest interval a piano can produce. Why such a small change should have such a large emotional effect has puzzled scholars for centuries. The question matters beyond music, I believe, because it bears directly on a larger issue: whether the emotional meaning we hear in sound is rooted in human biology or constructed by culture.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One approach has been to ask when children acquire the association. Inés Larrinaga, a developmental psychologist, played short melodies to children aged between three and eight and asked them to point to a happy or a sad face. The youngest children based their judgements almost entirely on speed, describing fast pieces as happy and slow ones as sad regardless of key. Sensitivity to mode did not appear reliably until around the age of five or six, after several years of exposure to the music of their surroundings. Larrinaga interprets this as evidence that the link is learned. The finding is suggestive, but it falls short of proof. Many capacities, from abstract reasoning to the perception of depth in pictures, emerge late in childhood without being taught, simply because the brain takes time to mature.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A different line of argument looks for the origin of the association in speech. Yuval Ben-Shoshan, an acoustician, analysed recordings of actors speaking in several languages, including Hebrew, Tamil and Spanish, while portraying different emotions. When speakers sounded sad, their voices were lower and quieter and moved between pitches in smaller steps than when they sounded happy. Ben-Shoshan points out that the characteristic interval of a minor key, the minor third, is smaller than its major equivalent, and he argues that minor melodies therefore echo the patterns of sorrowful speech. Of the explanations currently on offer, this seems to me the most promising, not least because it links music to a form of emotional expression that all human societies share.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Any purely biological explanation, however, must confront evidence from other musical traditions. The ethnomusicologist Taavi Roomusaar has spent many years recording village music in north-eastern Europe and Central Asia, where scales resembling the Western minor are commonly used for wedding songs and lively dances. When he played Western major and minor melodies to listeners in an isolated mountain community with little exposure to Western harmony, they showed no tendency to hear the minor versions as sadder. Roomusaar concludes that the connection between mode and emotion is acquired through cultural experience. His findings demonstrate convincingly that the association is not inevitable, but they do not show that biology plays no part at all; a weak natural tendency could easily be overridden by a strong local tradition.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third approach concerns the physical properties of chords. The music psychologist Lerato Sefotlhelo has measured the acoustic roughness of different combinations of notes, a kind of rapid fluctuation produced when frequencies that are close together interact. Minor chords, she found, contain slightly more roughness than major ones, which might make them sound marginally more tense. Yet in her experiments, the preference for major chords was much weaker among listeners with little exposure to Western music than among those who had grown up with it. Sefotlhelo proposes that a small perceptual difference, present in everyone, has been magnified over centuries by cultural convention into the powerful association that Western listeners now take for granted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: History supports this view of gradual amplification. Anahera Rangiita, a historian of music theory, has traced how writers in Europe described the emotional character of different scales. Before about 1600, European music was organised not around two modes but around a larger family of eight or more, each credited with its own mood in the theoretical writings of the period. Several of the modes that a modern listener would hear as minor were described by these writers as cheerful, devout or warlike rather than sad. Only as the major–minor system came to dominate, during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, did the sharp opposition between happy major and sad minor become firmly established.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The evidence, taken together, points neither to pure biology nor to pure culture. A modest natural link, perhaps derived from the sound of sad speech, seems to have been developed by Western tradition into a strong and widely understood convention. Some commentators have concluded that the association is therefore entirely arbitrary, like the relationship between a word and the object it names. That conclusion strikes me as mistaken, since it ignores the evidence of a natural starting point. It is also worth remembering that mode is only one of many emotional cues in music, and frequently not the strongest. In popular music, a great many melancholy songs are written in major keys, and a slow tempo, a soft dynamic or a low register will often convey sadness more powerfully than any choice of scale.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: the varnish-removal (cleaning) controversy in the conservation of old paintings: yellowed resin coatings, original toning glazes, solvent gels, partial versus total cleaning and the unattainable original appearance
title: The Varnish Wars
subtitle: Removing the yellowed coatings from old paintings can reveal astonishing colour, but critics fear that something of the artist goes with them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For several centuries, European painters protected their finished pictures with varnishes made from natural tree resins dissolved in oil or spirit. These coatings gave the paint surface depth and gloss, but they had a serious drawback: over decades they turned yellow, then brown, and gradually became cloudy as fine cracks spread through them. As a result, many of the most celebrated works in public collections were, for generations, seen through what amounted to a tinted window. Removing such varnish with carefully chosen solvents has been a routine part of conservation for about two hundred years, yet almost every high-profile cleaning provokes an outcry. When one gallery recently revealed a freshly cleaned landscape, several visitors complained that it now resembled a cheap reproduction. It would be easy to dismiss such reactions as nostalgia, but these quarrels are about more than taste. At their heart lies a genuinely difficult question: which layers of an old painting actually belong to the work of art?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Those who favour thorough cleaning have a clear answer. Dr Samira Elmasry, a conservator at the Rhine Valley Conservation Institute, argues that discoloured varnish is simply an accident of time, no more part of the painting than the dust that settles on its frame. The warm 'golden glow' prized by nineteenth-century collectors, she maintains, was a taste learned from looking at pictures that were already dirty, and it was then mistakenly projected back onto the artists themselves. Pigment analysis supports her in one important respect: many painters of earlier centuries used intensely saturated blues, greens and reds, colours that a brown film would have made unrecognisable. Her position is persuasive in principle. If the purpose of conservation is to serve the artist rather than later fashions, there seems little justification for preserving a coating that the painter would never have wished to see darken.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The opposing case is put most forcefully by the art historian Lorenzo Tonelli. He points out that some painters finished their work with thin, semi-transparent glazes or tinted varnishes intended to soften contrasts and unify the composition. Because these final touches were made from resins chemically similar to those in later protective coatings, the solvents that remove one can also dissolve the other. Tonelli cites workshop manuals that recommend toning a picture before delivery, and he warns that such layers, once lost, can never be recovered. On the first point his evidence is rather limited, since the manuals he quotes come from only a handful of regions and decades, and it would be unwise to generalise from them. On the second point, however, he is surely right. Cleaning cannot be undone, and an intervention that is irreversible deserves a correspondingly high standard of caution.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Science has done much to make cleaning safer. Under ultraviolet light, aged natural varnish fluoresces with a characteristic greenish glow, allowing conservators to map where it lies and how thick it is. Microscopic cross-sections taken from the edges of a painting reveal the sequence of layers like the strata in a cliff face. A team led by the chemist Wanjiru Okoth has developed solvent gels that hold the liquid against the surface so that it acts only on the uppermost coating instead of soaking into the paint beneath, where it might weaken the binding medium. Yet Okoth herself acknowledges a limitation. When an original glaze and a later varnish are both natural resins of considerable age, current techniques cannot always tell them apart. Technology, in other words, has narrowed the area of disagreement without removing it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One response to this uncertainty is partial cleaning, in which the restorer thins the old varnish rather than removing it completely, leaving a faint tone that holds the colours together. This approach has long been favoured in some national traditions, while others have tended towards total removal. Konrad Haupenthal, director of a regional gallery that has adopted the partial method, describes it as an act of humility: by stopping short, the restorer leaves room for future specialists with better tools. Critics reply that the method merely replaces one subjective judgement with another. Deciding how much varnish to leave, and where, is itself an aesthetic choice, and an uneven residue may distort the balance of a picture as seriously as a heavy brown film.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The argument is further complicated by a fact that both sides sometimes overlook: the paint itself has changed. Certain pigments fade when exposed to light, others darken, and the oil in which they are bound becomes more transparent with age, so that underdrawings and earlier compositions can begin to show through. Even a perfectly cleaned painting, therefore, does not look as it did on the day it left the studio. The 'original appearance' that cleaning claims to recover is, strictly speaking, beyond reach. It follows that the aim of conservation ought to be modest and honest interventions that are carefully documented, rather than the pursuit of a pristine state that no longer exists.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the cleaning debate is futile. On the contrary, the periodic controversies have forced museums to justify decisions that were once taken behind closed doors, and the standard of practice has risen as a result. What remains unacceptable is secrecy. Galleries should publish photographs taken before, during and after treatment, together with a clear account of the reasoning behind each choice. Visitors may still disagree about whether a cleaned painting looks better or worse, but they will at least be able to judge what has been done in their name.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: the optical devices hypothesis: whether late medieval and Renaissance painters used concave mirrors or lenses to project and trace images, and the evidence from paintings, optics experiments, documents, underdrawings and drawing studies
title: Painting with Light?
subtitle: Did the masters of early naturalism rely on mirrors and lenses? A long-running dispute says as much about our idea of genius as about the history of optics

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Somewhere around the second quarter of the fifteenth century, portrait painting in parts of northern Europe underwent a startling change. Within a generation, artists were rendering the nap of velvet, the soft gleam of pearls and the distorted reflections in a brass chandelier with a fidelity that earlier painters had seldom attempted. The conventional explanation credits a combination of individual talent, patient observation and the new possibilities of oil paint. Over the past few decades, however, a more provocative account has gained ground: that some painters used concave mirrors or glass lenses to project an image of their subject onto a surface, and then traced or closely followed what they saw. Few questions in art history generate as much heat. My own view is that the hypothesis has been dismissed too briskly by some scholars and embraced too uncritically by others, and that both reactions have obscured what the evidence can and cannot show.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for optical assistance was first argued in detail by Dragan Vukadinović, a painter who later turned to research at the Adriatic Academy of Fine Arts. Studying enlarged reproductions, he noticed that in certain pictures a patterned tablecloth or carpet appears to have several slightly different vanishing points, as if the artist had refocused an instrument with a shallow depth of field on successive sections of the scene. He also drew attention to the surprising number of sitters who hold cups or swords in their left hands, which he interprets as the result of an image reversed by a mirror. These anomalies, Vukadinović contends, amount to optical fingerprints that no unaided eye would have produced.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Claims of this kind invite experimental testing, and the most careful tests so far have been carried out by the optical physicist Emiko Nakatsuji. Using reconstructions of mirrors of the size and curvature that craftsmen of the period could plausibly have made, she found that a usable projection could indeed be obtained, but only in strong direct sunlight and only at a modest scale, roughly that of an outstretched hand. A small portrait head might therefore have been produced in this way. A large group scene, by contrast, would have required the apparatus to be repositioned dozens of times, with every section painstakingly joined to the next. Nakatsuji concludes that the method was physically feasible yet so laborious that feasibility alone tells us little about whether anyone actually adopted it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The sharpest objection comes from the historian Aminata Leclercq-Thiam, who emphasises the silence of the written record. Guild regulations, contracts, painters' handbooks and private letters from the period contain, she notes, no unambiguous reference to projecting images for painting. Supporters of the hypothesis reply that a technique giving one workshop an advantage over its rivals would naturally have been kept secret. Leclercq-Thiam answers that no secret could have been preserved across hundreds of workshops for two centuries. Her argument is weaker than she supposes. A great deal of studio practice went unrecorded; the recipes for many preparatory grounds, for instance, are known to us only through laboratory analysis of the paintings themselves. Absence of evidence, in a craft transmitted largely by example rather than by text, is a fragile foundation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Physical examination of the pictures offers another line of enquiry. The conservator Helmut Ostermeier has used infrared reflectography, which can reveal the preparatory drawing beneath layers of paint, to study more than sixty panels from the relevant period. In some, the underdrawing is hesitant and exploratory, with outlines redrawn several times before the artist settled on a final position, a pattern hard to reconcile with tracing. In others, however, the contours are fluent and decisive, set down without visible searching, which is at least consistent with an artist following a projected outline. Ostermeier is careful to point out that confident drawing may simply indicate a confident draughtsman, and that his findings neither confirm nor exclude the use of optics.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different challenge has emerged from cognitive science. Ingrid Lindeberg asked students trained in traditional observational drawing to copy complex still-life arrangements without any optical aid. Given enough time, several achieved levels of accuracy comparable to those found in the disputed paintings, including convincing reflections on curved metal. Lindeberg suggests that the fifteenth-century leap may owe more to changes in training and to the slow drying of oil paint, which allowed prolonged revision, than to any instrument. Her experiments are illuminating, but they share a logical weakness with Nakatsuji's: demonstrating that something could have been done is not the same as showing that it was done.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is most revealing about the controversy is the assumption, shared by many on both sides, that the use of an optical aid would somehow diminish the artist's achievement. I do not believe it would. A projected image is faint, unstable and fleeting; selecting a viewpoint, composing figures and translating shifting patches of light into durable layers of pigment would still demand extraordinary skill. Much of the indignation that greets the optical hypothesis seems to spring from an anxiety about cheating rather than from a dispassionate reading of the evidence. A more fruitful question than whether painters used lenses would be how far, and for which particular tasks, they might have done so.
