area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: painted ancient sculpture (polychromy): the white marble ideal, scientific detection of lost pigments, full-colour reconstructions and their critics, and how museums should present colour
title: The Myth of the White Statue
subtitle: Classical sculpture was once brightly painted. Why has the image of pure white marble proved so hard to give up?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than five hundred years, the gleaming white statues of ancient Greece and Rome have served as a model of ideal beauty. When Renaissance collectors began to excavate sculptures from the ruins of Italian cities, the figures they unearthed had spent many centuries underground, and burial, damp and weathering had stripped away almost all of their original surface colour. Artists who studied these works assumed that bare marble was what the ancients had intended, and later sculptors working in the classical manner carved their figures in flawless white stone. Eighteenth-century critics went further, praising whiteness itself as an essential element of beauty. Yet the statues of antiquity were, in fact, painted, often vividly. This has been known to specialists for well over a century, but it is a fact that has rarely been conveyed beyond them, and the public image of classical art remains stubbornly colourless.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The evidence for ancient colour has grown considerably more detailed in recent decades. Under magnification, minute particles of pigment can often be detected in the crevices of drapery or hair. More striking is a technique refined by the archaeometrist Tatiana Prokofieva and her colleagues at the Black Sea Institute of Archaeometry. Egyptian blue, one of the most widely used pigments in the ancient Mediterranean, emits a faint infrared glow when illuminated with ordinary light. Photographed with a suitable camera, even traces too small to be seen by the naked eye shine brightly, allowing whole patterns of decoration to be mapped. Other clues are subtler still. Where paint once covered marble, it protected the surface from weathering, so that a raking light can reveal so-called weathering shadows: the faint outlines of borders, eyes and ornament long after the colour itself has vanished.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such findings have inspired a series of full-scale painted reconstructions. The best known were produced by a team under the direction of Nimal Siriwardane, which casts replicas of famous statues and paints them according to the pigments identified on the originals. Touring exhibitions of these replicas have attracted very large crowds, but they have also provoked ridicule. Critics have compared the brightly coloured warriors and goddesses to fairground figures or children's toys. Siriwardane defends the flat, intense colours as a faithful reflection of the evidence. What survives on the stone, he explains, is chiefly the lowest layer of paint, and he prefers to show only what can be demonstrated rather than invent details for which there is no proof.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It is precisely this restraint that troubles the art historian Paola Delvecchio. Ancient painters, she argues, did not stop at a base coat. Literary sources and the better-preserved examples suggest that they modelled flesh with gradual shading, applied translucent glazes and added gilding and wax, all materials that are the first to deteriorate. A reconstruction based only on the surviving base layers will therefore systematically understate the subtlety of the original, and to present it as a view of how the statue actually looked is to mislead. Delvecchio has a point, and reconstructions should be clearly labelled as hypotheses rather than offered as certainties. But her criticism should not become an excuse for continuing to display unpainted marble as though it were the authentic appearance of ancient sculpture. A cautious reconstruction may be incomplete; a white statue is simply wrong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why did the white ideal last so long? Ignorance is only part of the answer. Some nineteenth-century scholars who found clear traces of paint on newly excavated sculpture dismissed them as later additions by people of supposedly lesser taste. Whiteness had become associated with purity, restraint and rationality, and in certain writings of the period it was even bound up with theories of racial hierarchy. This history matters. It means that the question of ancient colour is not merely a technical matter for archaeologists but bears on assumptions about culture and identity that extended far beyond the study of antiquity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Museums face practical choices about how to share this knowledge. The museum educator Folake Olaniyan observed visitors in galleries where a painted replica was displayed beside the original. Those who saw both spent noticeably longer at the display and asked more questions of the staff than visitors who saw the original alone. A sizeable minority, however, told her they felt deceived that museums had not explained the matter much earlier. Some institutions have begun experimenting with digital projection, casting coloured light directly onto original sculptures. The method leaves the stone untouched, can be switched off at will and can be altered whenever new evidence comes to light.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Of the options now available, projection seems to me the most promising, because it allows several competing interpretations to be shown on the same object and makes the provisional nature of each one obvious to the viewer. Painted replicas will remain valuable, but they tend to fix a single version of the past in solid form. Ultimately, the strongest argument for showing colour is not that it makes ancient art more attractive; to many modern eyes it does not. It is that museums owe their visitors an honest account of the evidence, and the evidence no longer allows white marble to be presented as the natural condition of classical sculpture.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: attributing Old Master paintings produced in busy workshops: collaborative studio practice, connoisseurship versus technical analysis (dendrochronology, thread counts), market pressure on attribution committees and proposals for descriptive labels
title: The Master and His Many Assistants
subtitle: Old Master paintings were often produced by teams, yet museums and the art market still demand a single name on the label

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some years ago, a large altarpiece that had hung for decades in a provincial museum as a celebrated work by a renowned seventeenth-century master was quietly reclassified. After a fresh examination, specialists concluded that it had been painted largely by assistants in his studio, and the label was changed to read 'workshop of'. Its estimated value fell by around ninety per cent, and the museum's own records show that the number of visitors pausing in front of it declined noticeably in the following year. Not a single brushstroke had altered. Episodes like this reveal how much weight a name can bear, and they raise an uncomfortable question about whether we are looking at paintings at all, or merely reading the labels beside them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty lies in the way many paintings were made. Petra Ruzicka-Maier, a historian of artistic practice, has spent years reconstructing the operations of large European studios from inventories, account books and contracts. Successful masters, she shows, often ran sizeable enterprises in which assistants and apprentices prepared panels, ground pigments, painted landscape backgrounds and drapery, and sometimes produced complete replicas of popular compositions. Revealingly, some contracts stipulated that the master must paint the faces and hands himself, a clause that would have been unnecessary had clients not known that much of the remaining work was delegated. Ruzicka-Maier concludes that the ideal of the wholly 'autograph' painting, executed from start to finish by one individual, owes more to the priorities of later collectors than to the realities of the workshop.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Traditionally, the task of separating master from assistant has fallen to the connoisseur. Bence Szolnoki, one of the most respected practitioners, argues that every painter has a kind of handwriting, visible in the way an ear is shaped, a fold of cloth is described or a highlight is placed on an eye, and that decades of close looking allow an expert to recognise it. To those who accuse connoisseurship of subjectivity, he replies that it resembles the diagnosis of an experienced physician: a judgement grounded in accumulated knowledge that cannot always be reduced to explicit rules. The analogy is apt, but only up to a point. A physician's diagnosis is eventually checked against the course of the illness, whereas a connoisseur's verdict can seldom be tested in any comparable way, and history records misattributions that went unchallenged for generations.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Scientific methods promise a more objective footing. The dendrochronologist Aigerim Kemelbekova measures the growth rings of the oak panels on which many northern European pictures were painted; by matching the pattern of rings against reference sequences, she can establish when the tree was felled and therefore the earliest date at which the painting could have been made, once allowance is made for the years the timber spent seasoning. Canvases can be analysed in a similar spirit, since the density of threads may show that two pictures were cut from the same roll of cloth. Pigment analysis adds further evidence. Yet Kemelbekova is frank about the limits of these techniques. They are powerful in excluding an attribution, as when a panel proves to come from a tree felled after the supposed artist's death, but they rarely confirm one, because a master and his assistants drew on precisely the same stock of materials.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Overshadowing all of this is the market. The economist Mathilde Quesnel has calculated that a full attribution to a famous master can be worth many times the price of an otherwise comparable 'workshop' picture. Such sums create intense pressure. Owners and dealers lobby scholars, and experts who sit on attribution committees have faced lawsuits from collectors whose paintings they declined to authenticate; several committees have disbanded rather than continue to run that risk. Quesnel regards the gap in prices as irrational, given that buyers frequently cannot distinguish the two categories by eye, and suggests that what they are really purchasing is a story. That verdict seems to me too harsh. A name connects a painting to a documented life and to a particular moment in history, and it is not foolish to value that connection. What is indefensible is allowing commercial interests to determine what scholars are prepared to say.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Several museums have begun to experiment with an alternative. Instead of a single name, their labels describe the process of production, indicating, for example, that the principal figures appear to be by the master while the landscape and secondary figures were executed in his studio. Sceptics object that such precision is largely illusory, since in most cases the division of labour cannot be reconstructed with any confidence. The objection has force, yet even an approximate account of collaboration is arguably more truthful than a label that implies a solitary genius where none existed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is to suggest that attribution is a worthless pursuit. Knowing who made what, and how, remains a legitimate and often fascinating historical question, and the techniques now available have answered many puzzles that once seemed insoluble. But the quality of a painting is not altered by a change to the card on the wall beside it. If the debates of recent decades encourage visitors to spend a little more time studying the surface of the canvas and a little less time searching for a famous name, they will have achieved something worthwhile.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: whether street art should be preserved: detaching murals from walls, ownership and artists' rights, protective panels, murals and gentrification ('artwashing'), artists' acceptance of impermanence and photographic documentation
title: Saving the Writing on the Wall
subtitle: Street art has moved from criminal nuisance to cultural asset. Should we now try to make it last?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Within a single generation, painting on the walls of cities has undergone a remarkable change in status. Work that was once prosecuted as vandalism is now celebrated in municipal festivals, promoted in tourist guides and studied in universities. Guided walks lead visitors past the most admired murals, and pieces by a few celebrated anonymous artists have been cut out of buildings and sold at auction for very large sums. This new respectability has created a dilemma that hardly existed before: should street art be preserved, and if so, how? The question is less straightforward than it appears. Unlike a painting on canvas, a work sprayed onto a wall was usually made in the knowledge that it would fade, be painted over or disappear with the building. That impermanence is not an unfortunate side effect of the form; it is part of what the form means.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Preservation in the most literal sense has become technically possible. The conservator Owen Trelawny has adapted a method first devised for removing medieval frescoes, in which a fabric facing is glued to the surface and the paint layer is then peeled away from the masonry and transferred to a new support. Trelawny presents his work as a form of rescue. Many of the walls on which important pieces appear, he notes, are scheduled for demolition, and without intervention the paintings would be lost entirely. There are occasions when such rescue is clearly justified, but critics are right to observe that a mural detached from its wall is no longer quite the same work. Street art frequently responds to a particular site, whether a neglected corner, a political slogan nearby or the history of a neighbourhood, and much of its meaning is left behind when the paint is carried away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Removal also raises awkward legal questions. According to the legal scholar Tiago Maranhão, the owner of a building generally owns whatever is painted on it, and may sell, conceal or destroy it at will. In some countries, artists retain moral rights that protect their work from distortion and allow them to object to certain uses, but these rights are difficult to assert when the work was painted without permission in the first place. Maranhão does not argue that street artists should be able to prevent owners from doing as they wish with their property. He proposes instead that artists, where they can be identified, should at least be consulted before a work is taken down, particularly when it is to be sold.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Less drastic forms of protection have their own drawbacks. Some cities have fixed transparent acrylic sheets over admired murals, while others apply clear coatings that allow paint added later to be washed off. Ewa Wojtyniak, a heritage officer responsible for public art in a large port city, has found that protective panels often attract more tagging, as if the barrier itself were an invitation, and that reflections and condensation alter the appearance of the work beneath. A few cities have gone further and given individual murals formal heritage status. Wojtyniak supports such listings in exceptional cases but warns that they can freeze a living tradition into a set of approved monuments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns who benefits when street art is valued. The sociologist Kavita Mirchandani has studied several districts where mural festivals coincided with rising property prices. Developers, she shows, have sometimes sponsored large commissioned murals to give run-down areas an image of creativity, after which rents climbed and long-standing residents were forced to move away. She calls this process 'artwashing'. Her findings are important and deserve wider attention, but they cannot be applied to every painted wall. Many community murals are commissioned and designed by residents themselves, and in such cases the art may strengthen local identity rather than serve as a prelude to displacement.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Strikingly, the people whose work is at stake are often the least enthusiastic about preserving it. The urban geographer Milena Radovanović interviewed one hundred and twenty street artists in four countries. Most told her that they fully expected their pieces to be painted over, and several described this as a healthy process in which a wall passes from one artist to the next. What angered them was not disappearance but extraction: the removal of a work from the street so that it could be bought and sold. In the view of many artists, a mural that has been cut out and hung in a private collection has been taken away from the public for whom it was made.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These arguments suggest that physical preservation should be the exception rather than the rule. In most cases, the better course is careful documentation. Photographic archives, some built by enthusiasts who record new works every week, already capture far more of the history of street art than any museum could hold, and they do so without removing anything from the places where it was made. Walls will continue to change, as they always have. Our responsibility is not to halt that process but to ensure that what passes through it is remembered.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: Renaissance linear perspective: optical discovery or cultural convention, perception experiments, East Asian and Persian alternatives, mercantile mathematics and painters' departures from strict geometry
title: The Vanishing Point
subtitle: Was linear perspective the discovery of how we really see, or simply one convention among many?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Early in the fifteenth century, according to an account written some decades later, a Florentine craftsman painted a small panel of a famous building, drilled a hole through it and invited spectators to look through the back of the panel at a mirror held in front of it. Seen in this way, the painted image appeared to merge almost seamlessly with the real building behind. Within a generation the method underlying the experiment had been set out in a written treatise: parallel lines receding from the viewer were to be drawn so that they met at a single vanishing point, and objects were to diminish in size in strict proportion to their distance. For centuries this geometric system was celebrated as a discovery that at last allowed painting to show the world exactly as the eye perceives it. Since the early twentieth century, however, that confident view has been vigorously challenged.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most radical challenge treats perspective as a convention. The philosopher Gábor Lukácsy argues that the system rests on a highly artificial assumption: a single, motionless eye fixed at one point in space. Human beings, by contrast, see with two eyes that move constantly, and the retina on which images fall is curved rather than flat. A perspective picture, Lukácsy contends, looks convincing not because it reproduces vision but because people raised among such pictures have learned to read them. In support, he points to reports that people unfamiliar with pictures sometimes fail to interpret perspective drawings as scenes in depth. Lukácsy has not gathered such evidence himself; he relies on accounts collected by earlier travellers and anthropologists, many of them anecdotal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experimental psychology has supplied a different picture. Sigrid Aarsheim tested adults from a range of cultural backgrounds, including some with very limited exposure to printed images. Once participants understood that a drawing was intended to represent something, most identified depth in perspective scenes fairly readily, without extended instruction. Aarsheim also draws attention to a curious fact: a perspective painting viewed from well to one side, rather than from the single correct position, still looks broadly acceptable, even though its geometry is now wrong for the viewer. She interprets this as evidence that the visual system actively compensates for the viewing angle, and therefore that the effectiveness of perspective rests on robust features of perception rather than on learned habit. Her results make it difficult to maintain that perspective is arbitrary. Yet the compensation she describes cuts both ways, for it suggests that exact geometrical correctness is not what makes a picture look right.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further perspective, so to speak, comes from outside Europe. The art historian Preecha Thanomsak has studied pictorial systems in which receding lines remain parallel instead of converging, or in which the viewpoint shifts across a single work. In Chinese handscrolls, which are unrolled section by section, the observer travels through a landscape rather than surveying it from a fixed spot, and in many Persian miniatures distant figures are placed higher on the page rather than made smaller. Thanomsak insists that these were not failed attempts to discover perspective. European methods reached several East Asian courts in the eighteenth century through missionaries, and court painters studied them closely, yet they generally confined the technique to particular subjects, such as architectural views, and rejected it as a general method because a single fixed standpoint was ill suited to scrolls meant to be viewed in sequence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other historians have asked why perspective emerged where and when it did. Jana Hrabalová, a historian of mathematics, links it to the practical geometry taught in the so-called abacus schools attended by the sons of merchants in Italian commercial cities. Pupils learned to calculate proportions, gauge the volume of barrels and survey plots of land, and Hrabalová argues that a clientele trained in such skills was especially receptive to pictures built on measurable proportion. In her account, perspective owes its rapid spread less to a breakthrough in understanding vision than to the commercial culture of the cities in which it flourished.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What artists actually did complicates matters further. Close analysis of Renaissance paintings shows that perspective rules were rarely applied strictly. Painters frequently drew lines converging on several different points within the same picture and enlarged important figures for emphasis, regardless of where they stood in the imagined space. Moreover, a rigorously constructed perspective produces visible distortions near the edges of a wide composition, where spheres turn into ovals and figures appear stretched, and painters routinely corrected these shapes by eye. The geometry, in other words, was treated as a useful scaffold rather than an inviolable law, and this alone undermines both the claim that it captures vision perfectly and the claim that it is a mere arbitrary code.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most defensible conclusion lies between the two extremes. Linear perspective exploits real properties of light and of the human visual system, which is why it can be understood with so little training. But it was selected, refined and promoted within a particular culture for particular purposes, and other traditions had sound reasons for preferring alternatives. To describe it as the correct way to depict space is untenable; to dismiss it as an arbitrary habit is equally mistaken. It is best understood as a powerful tool, whose authority owes as much to history as to optics.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: the rediscovery of historical women painters and the art-historical canon: exclusion from academies and guilds, misattribution to male relatives, posthumous neglect, museum acquisition policies and the hierarchy of genres
title: Restoring the Missing Names
subtitle: Exhibitions of long-forgotten women painters now draw large crowds. But is adding names enough to change the story of art?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In recent years, a striking number of major museums have staged retrospectives devoted to women painters of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries whose names were, until recently, familiar only to specialists. Some of these exhibitions have attracted record attendances, and paintings by artists who were scarcely mentioned in standard textbooks a generation ago have achieved high prices at auction. This revival raises two questions that are related but distinct. Why were these artists overlooked for so long? And what should the discipline of art history do now that they have been found? The answers given to the first question tend to shape the answers given to the second, and it is worth examining them with some care.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious explanation lies in the obstacles women faced. The historian Lucía Benavides, who has worked for many years in European municipal and church archives, emphasises that most academies refused to admit women to classes in which students drew from live models, a training regarded as essential for the prestigious genre of large figure painting. Membership of painters' guilds was often restricted too. As a result, many women learned their craft in the workshops of their fathers or husbands, and some of their works left the studio bearing the signature of the male head of the household. Benavides has traced dozens of pictures listed in old inventories under a woman's name that were later catalogued as the work of a male relative, or of an unidentified man.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet exclusion is only part of the story. Pieter Vandoorne, a historian of the art trade, has shown that a number of women painters were prosperous and well known during their own lifetimes, receiving commissions from courts and wealthy merchants and charging fees comparable to those of their male contemporaries. Their eclipse came later. Many of the general histories of art written in the nineteenth century were organised around a small number of heroic masters, and artists who did not fit that narrative were quietly omitted. Vandoorne also found cases in which dealers replaced a woman's name with that of a more famous man in order to obtain a better price. His research is an important corrective. It shows that the neglect of these artists was not an inevitable consequence of the attitudes of their time, but the result of choices made by later writers and traders.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Museums have responded in different ways. The curator Chiara Imbriani argues that temporary exhibitions, however successful, do little to alter the long-term picture, since borrowed works return to their owners when the show closes and visitors who come afterwards find galleries much as they were before. She urges institutions to buy works by women for their permanent collections, noting that such purchases still make up only a small share of acquisitions at many major museums. Some have gone further and set targets for the proportion of acquisitions by women. This policy has obvious appeal, but it carries a risk: under pressure to meet a quota, a museum might acquire weaker pieces simply because they are available. Then again, the judgement of what counts as 'weaker' has itself been shaped by the very canon now under question.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That point is pressed most forcefully by the critic Agnieszka Szczepanek. In her view, inserting a handful of women into the established sequence of great artists leaves untouched the criteria by which greatness has been measured: originality, ambition and, above all, achievement in large-scale history painting. Because women were largely excluded from that genre, they were channelled towards still life, portrait miniatures, flower painting and textile design, forms that the traditional hierarchy ranked as minor. Unless that hierarchy is reconsidered, Szczepanek argues, women will be admitted to the canon only as exceptions. There is much to be said for this argument. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that every rediscovered artist is a neglected genius. Some were accomplished but unremarkable, as were the great majority of their male contemporaries, and honest scholarship must be able to say so.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Indeed, the popular narrative of the rediscovered genius carries dangers of its own. It makes for compelling exhibition publicity and attractive book titles, and it gives audiences a satisfying story of injustice put right. But it tends to reproduce the very model of art history that critics such as Szczepanek reject, one built around exceptional individuals rather than networks of training, patronage and collaboration. A more informative approach would ask how workshops actually functioned, who bought which kinds of picture and why some reputations endured while others faded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The canon, in short, was never a fixed list handed down from the past; it was assembled by particular people for particular purposes, and it can be revised. The recovery of forgotten women artists is a valuable part of that revision, but it should be the beginning of a broader reassessment rather than its conclusion. The goal is not simply a longer list of famous names. It is a more accurate account of how art was made, valued and remembered.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: the aesthetics of forgery: why an exposed fake loses value, formalist versus achievement theories of art, dated forgeries, neuroimaging of authenticity labels, the market for forgers' works and forgery exhibitions
title: The Perfect Fake
subtitle: If no one can tell a forgery from the original, why does its exposure change everything?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few events in the art world are as dramatic as the unmasking of a forgery. A painting that has hung for decades in an important collection, praised by critics for its luminous colour and subtle handling, is revealed to be the work of a twentieth-century imitator. Almost at once, the critics who admired it begin to discover clumsy passages and lifeless faces, and the picture is removed from the gallery walls. Yet the canvas itself is exactly as it was the day before. Why, then, should its value, both financial and aesthetic, collapse so completely? The question is sometimes treated as a mere curiosity, but it is far from trivial. How we answer it reveals what we believe we are responding to when we admire a work of art.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One answer is that we should not respond differently at all. The philosopher Lars Tengbom defends a strict form of what is usually called formalism: the aesthetic value of a painting, he maintains, lies wholly in its perceptible qualities, in colour, line, composition and texture. If a forgery is genuinely indistinguishable from an authentic work, then it possesses the same aesthetic value, and to reject it once its origin is known is a form of snobbery. For Tengbom, the sudden reversal of critical opinion that follows every exposure is evidence that much of what passes for appreciation is driven by social prestige rather than by looking.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most influential reply comes from Chidi Ojukwu-Hale, who argues that artworks are best understood as the products of performances. Just as we admire an athlete not merely for crossing a finishing line but for the effort, training and skill that the crossing represents, so we admire a painting partly as the record of an artist solving a problem for the first time. A forger may reproduce the result with great technical skill, but cannot reproduce the achievement of having invented it; a race won with a concealed motor is not the same feat, however similar it looks. This account is persuasive, and it captures why originality matters so much to us. It is less comfortable with paintings largely executed by studio assistants, whose achievement is hard to separate from the master's. And it seems to imply that a forger who devises an entirely new composition in an earlier artist's manner shows a degree of the very inventiveness the theory reserves for authentic works.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is, moreover, a factual difficulty with the notion of a perfect fake. History suggests that forgeries are rarely indistinguishable for long. Forgers, however gifted, cannot help absorbing the tastes of their own period, and these betray them as the years pass. A forger working in the 1930s might give the women in his supposedly seventeenth-century scenes the heavy-lidded eyes and pencilled brows fashionable in the cinema of his day; to his contemporaries such details looked natural, but to later viewers they appear unmistakably modern. If this is right, then the critics who suddenly see flaws in an exposed forgery are not always deceiving themselves. Differences of perception do exist; it is simply that they become visible only with time, which considerably weakens Tengbom's position.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Experimental work suggests that knowledge of origin affects not only our judgements but our experience itself. The neuroscientist Haingo Andrianarivo showed volunteers a series of images while they lay in a brain scanner, telling them that some were authentic works and others copies, although in fact the labels were assigned at random. When participants believed they were looking at an original, regions of the brain associated with reward were noticeably more active, and they rated the images more highly. Andrianarivo concludes that context shapes the pleasure we take in art at a basic level. Her findings demonstrate that the label matters, but they cannot tell us whether it ought to; a placebo also changes experience, without becoming a medicine.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the forgeries themselves have acquired a curious afterlife. The economist Dieter Uhlenbrock has traced the sales of works by several notorious forgers, which, once exposed, briefly became almost worthless but now change hands among collectors for substantial sums as objects of interest in their own right. Museums have also begun to treat fakes as instructive. Marta Pozzebon, director of a regional gallery, mounted an exhibition in which exposed forgeries were hung beside authentic works by the artists they imitated, inviting visitors to judge for themselves. The show drew far larger crowds than the gallery's usual exhibitions, and Pozzebon argues that forgeries, by forcing people to compare, are among the best tools available for teaching visitors to look closely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, does the forgery problem teach us? We value paintings in two ways at once: as objects that reward looking and as historical documents of human achievement. A forgery may satisfy the first demand, at least for a time, while falsifying the second. That is why exposure feels like a betrayal. But we should be careful to locate the offence correctly. The moral objection to forgery, that it deceives buyers and distorts the historical record, is a separate matter from the aesthetic quality of the forged object. The real wrong lies in the lie, not in the paint.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: Japonisme and the supposed influence of Japanese woodblock prints on nineteenth-century European painting: the packing-paper legend, evidence for direct borrowing, parallel European sources such as photography, European misreadings of Japan and export production
title: Pictures from the Floating World
subtitle: Did Japanese prints transform European painting, or did Europeans see in them only what they were already looking for?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: After Japan reopened its ports to Western trade in the 1850s, goods from the country began to reach Europe in remarkable quantities. Lacquerware, fans, ceramics and, above all, colour woodblock prints appeared in the shops of Paris and London, and within a few years they had become fashionable among artists and collectors. The episode is usually summarised by a familiar story. According to this account, the prints liberated European painters from centuries of academic convention, teaching them to use flat areas of bright colour, bold outlines, unusual high viewpoints and compositions in which figures are abruptly cut off by the edge of the frame. There is truth in this story. But it is also a considerable simplification, and in some respects a misleading one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider first the way the prints arrived. A widely repeated legend holds that European artists first encountered them as scraps of paper used to wrap porcelain shipped from Japan. The historian Siobhan Murtagh has examined customs records and the account books of import firms, and finds that the great majority of prints entered Europe through specialist dealers who bought them in bulk and sold them, often very cheaply, by the thousand. The packing-paper story is not impossible in individual cases, but it is clearly a misleading guide to how prints reached European hands. Its appeal lies in the romance of accidental discovery, which obscures the fact that Japonisme was, from the start, a commercial phenomenon. Dealers, not accident, determined which prints were available, at what price and to whom.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The case for direct influence has been made most rigorously by the art historian Rafael Dorantes. Rather than relying on general impressions, he has matched specific prints, documented in the inventories and letters of particular painters, against works those painters produced shortly after acquiring them. In a number of cases, a distinctive motif, such as a bridge seen from below, a tree trunk slicing vertically through the foreground or a figure viewed from directly above, appears in a painting within months of the corresponding print entering the artist's collection. Dorantes argues that such close sequences of acquisition and adaptation leave little room for coincidence. He accepts that painters looked at many kinds of image, but insists that the burden of proof should fall on those who would explain away such precise correspondences, not on those who take them at face value.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others urge caution. Yelena Aurelova points out that several of the devices attributed to Japanese example were already circulating in Europe by other routes. Photography, in particular, had accustomed viewers to images in which figures were arbitrarily cropped and viewpoints were unconventional, while illustrated magazines and popular posters made frequent use of flat colour and strong outlines. In Aurelova's view, the prints confirmed and accelerated tendencies that were already present rather than creating them, and many claims of influence rest on nothing more than resemblance. Both scholars are partly right. Some paintings unmistakably borrow from identifiable prints, and to deny this would be perverse. Yet the broader assertion that Japanese art was responsible for the emergence of modern painting in Europe is greatly overstated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further problem concerns what Europeans thought they were seeing. As the historian Kanya Saetang emphasises, the prints that Parisian collectors treated with reverence were, in Japan, inexpensive commercial products, bought as souvenirs, theatre posters or illustrations of fashionable beauties, and generally regarded as being of low status compared with painting. European enthusiasts, moreover, tended to imagine Japan as a timeless land untouched by modernity, at the very moment when the country was industrialising at great speed. Nor was the exchange one-directional. Japanese artists of the same decades were eagerly studying Western techniques, adopting linear perspective and the use of light and shade to suggest depth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The economic dimension also deserves attention. The economic historian Helga Sandvoss has shown that the surge in European demand altered production in Japan itself. Publishers began to issue prints designed specifically to suit Western tastes, and some of the works now displayed in European and American museums as examples of traditional Japanese art were in fact made for export. At the same time, the readiness of Japanese owners to part with prints they did not especially value allowed Western collections to grow rapidly and cheaply, a process that later generations in Japan came to regret. Sandvoss estimates that by the end of the century tens of thousands of prints had left the country, many of them acquired for sums that the collectors who bought them would have considered trivial.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that 'influence' is the wrong word for what took place, or at least an incomplete one. The term implies an active recipient and a passive source, flattering the originality of European painters while reducing Japanese artists to suppliers of raw material. A more accurate description would speak of exchange: a complex traffic of objects, techniques and misunderstandings moving in both directions, shaped throughout by commerce. None of this diminishes the paintings that resulted, many of which remain among the most admired works of their era. It simply places them within a wider history in which Japanese makers, merchants and buyers were participants rather than spectators. The story is less tidy than the familiar one, but it is considerably more interesting.

area: debates in art history and visual arts
topic: authorship and fabrication in contemporary art: artists who design but do not make their works, historical precedents, the hidden role of professional fabricators, co-authorship in law, certificate and instruction works, market prices and the value of making by hand
title: Made by Other Hands
subtitle: Many celebrated contemporary artworks are produced by teams of specialists the public never hears about. Does it matter who actually makes art?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the centre of a European city stands an enormous sculpture of polished stainless steel, admired by thousands of visitors every day. The artist whose name appears on the plaque never touched it. The work was engineered and assembled by a specialist fabrication firm, working from digital files supplied by the artist's studio, and the finishing of its mirror-like surface took a team of metalworkers several months. Such arrangements are now routine at the upper levels of the art world, and they regularly provoke accusations of outsourcing and even fraud. Defenders reply that what matters is the idea, not the labour. The quarrel is not a new one, but the scale of the practice, and the degree to which it is concealed from the public, have no real precedent.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Historians are quick to point out that collaboration is the norm rather than the exception. Giulia Cavazzoni, who has written extensively on the organisation of artists' studios, reminds us that Renaissance masters employed teams of assistants, and that in the twentieth century many conceptual artists dispensed with making altogether, issuing written instructions or a signed certificate that allows a work to be remade whenever it is exhibited. In her view, the belief that a genuine work of art must be made by the artist's own hand is largely a nineteenth-century invention, a product of the Romantic cult of personal expression. Cavazzoni is largely right, but her parallel overlooks an important difference. The patrons of Renaissance workshops generally knew that assistants were involved; many buyers of contemporary art have only the vaguest idea of how much of their purchase the artist personally produced.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The people who do the making have only recently attracted serious study. The sociologist Femke Tamminga spent two years observing the daily work of three fabrication workshops. She found that fabricators frequently make decisions with significant aesthetic consequences: choosing among surface finishes, resolving structural problems in ways that alter a work's proportions, or proposing materials the artist had not considered. Yet they remain almost entirely anonymous, and many sign agreements that prevent them from discussing their contribution in public. Tamminga argues that the conventions of the art world systematically erase this labour, and that credit should be shared far more openly than it is at present.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Such questions are not merely matters of etiquette; they can end up in court. The legal scholar Tomasz Morawiec has analysed disputes in which fabricators claimed to be co-authors of works they had built. Copyright law generally assigns authorship to the person whose creative choices are expressed in a work, and courts have tended to side with artists who supervised the making of the work closely. Where an artist's instructions were vague, however, and the fabricator effectively determined the final form, the outcome has been far less predictable. Certificate-based works raise their own puzzles. Morawiec describes a case in which a collector lost the certificate for an installation and was told by the artist's estate that, without it, the work no longer officially existed, although the materials remained in the collector's possession.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The market, it seems, is untroubled by these complexities. The economist Dinara Bakhtiyarova compared auction results for works whose fabrication had been publicly disclosed with those of similar works by the same artists, and found no measurable difference in price. Buyers, she concludes, pay for the artist's name and concept rather than for evidence of personal craftsmanship, although she notes that a minority of collectors still refuse to acquire works consisting only of written instructions. Her findings show that commercial acceptance of fabrication is widespread. But acceptance by the market cannot settle whether the practice is ethically sound; markets have tolerated many arrangements that later came to seem indefensible.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The strongest case for the artist's hand comes from the critic and former sculptor Alasdair Ochiltree. Making, he argues, is itself a form of thinking. In carving, casting or painting, an artist responds to the resistance of the material, and many of the decisions that give a work its character are discovered in the course of production rather than planned in advance. An artist who hands a design to a fabricator forfeits those discoveries. There is real insight in this argument, and anyone who has worked with materials will recognise it. Yet it does not follow that the discoveries are lost; Tamminga's research suggests that they are often made by the fabricators instead. The real question, then, is not whether such decisions are made but who receives recognition for them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Seen in this light, the controversy over fabrication is less about authenticity than about honesty. There is nothing inherently wrong with an artist conceiving a work that others produce, any more than with an architect designing a building that others construct. What is harder to defend is the silence that surrounds the practice. Exhibition labels and catalogues should name the workshops and individuals who made a work, as film credits name everyone from the director to the electricians. That galleries so rarely do so suggests that the art world remains more attached to the myth of the solitary creator than it cares to admit.

topic: altitude training for endurance athletes: the haemoglobin mechanism, 'live high, train low', individual responders, blinded hypoxic-room trials and East African running success
title: Thin Air, Thick Blood?
subtitle: Altitude training has been a fixture of endurance sport for half a century, but the evidence for it is less solid than its popularity suggests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the Olympic Games were held in Mexico City in 1968, at an elevation of some 2,240 metres, the results of the endurance events startled observers. Runners from lowland nations, many of them favourites, faded badly in the thin air, while athletes who had grown up in the highlands of East Africa collected medal after medal. Coaches drew what seemed an obvious lesson: if living at altitude conferred such an advantage, then deliberately training there might give lowland athletes a similar boost when they returned to compete near sea level. Within a generation, mountain training camps had become a standard feature of the elite calendar. Yet the popularity of a practice is a poor guide to its effectiveness, and altitude training is a case in point.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The theory itself is straightforward. At high elevations the pressure of oxygen in the air is lower, and the kidneys respond by releasing a hormone, erythropoietin, which stimulates the production of red blood cells. More red cells mean more haemoglobin, and therefore more oxygen delivered to working muscles. The difficulty is that athletes in thin air cannot train as hard as they can at sea level, so the gains in the blood may be offset by a loss of fitness. The so-called 'live high, train low' model, which became fashionable in the 1990s, was designed to resolve this dilemma: athletes sleep at altitude but descend each day to complete their most demanding sessions. Kristjana Eldjárnsdóttir, a physiologist at the Nordic Endurance Laboratory, has measured haemoglobin mass in hundreds of athletes. On average, she reports, four weeks at around 2,500 metres raises it by three to four per cent. But the average hides enormous variation: some individuals show no change at all, while others improve by more than ten per cent. Eldjárnsdóttir therefore argues that athletes should be screened for their likely response before being sent on costly expeditions to the mountains.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental challenge came from a study led by Toshiro Habukawa at the Hokkaido Centre for Sports Medicine. Habukawa was troubled by a weakness common to almost all earlier research: athletes always knew when they were at altitude, and their expectations might influence how they performed. His team therefore used specially built rooms in which the oxygen content of the air could be lowered without the occupants being aware of it. For four weeks, well-trained cyclists slept in these rooms; half breathed air with reduced oxygen and half breathed normal air, and neither the riders nor their supervisors knew who was in which group. As expected, haemoglobin mass rose only in the low-oxygen group. Performance in time trials, however, improved by a similar amount in both. Habukawa concluded that much of the benefit traditionally credited to altitude may in fact derive from the camp itself: concentrated training, freedom from everyday distractions and, not least, the athletes' belief that they are getting stronger.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This is, to my mind, the most rigorous investigation of the subject to date, and it deserves far more attention than it has so far received from coaches and sporting federations. Even so, it would be premature to conclude that altitude training is worthless. The cyclists in Habukawa's study were fit but not world-class, and the experiment lasted only a month. At the very top of a sport, races are often decided by margins of less than one per cent, and an effect of that size could easily escape detection in a trial involving a few dozen participants. A failure to find a benefit in a small sample is not the same as proof that no benefit exists.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Matías Ticona, of the Andean Institute of Sport Physiology in La Paz, takes a different line again. In his view, researchers have concentrated too narrowly on the blood, and any advantage from altitude may lie elsewhere, for instance in the muscles' ability to tolerate acid or in improved efficiency of movement. He is equally concerned with the costs. Time spent at altitude frequently disturbs sleep, suppresses the immune system and reduces the quality of training, and Ticona believes that for some athletes these drawbacks outweigh whatever is gained. His prescription is a carefully measured dose: an elevation of between 2,200 and 2,500 metres, at least twelve hours a day, for a minimum of three weeks.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The sociologist Njeri Nyakundi approaches the question from another angle altogether. The extraordinary success of Kenyan and Ethiopian distance runners, she observes, is routinely attributed to the altitude at which they live. Nyakundi regards this explanation as suspiciously convenient, since it ignores the economic incentives that draw young people into running, the distances many children cover on foot each day and the culture of large training groups. Western athletes who spend months in the Kenyan highlands, she points out, do not return as champions. Her argument is a valuable corrective, but she goes too far in dismissing altitude entirely: physiological measurements consistently show that lifelong highland residents carry a greater mass of haemoglobin than lowlanders of comparable fitness.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should a coach conclude? Altitude training is neither the miracle its enthusiasts proclaim nor the myth its sternest critics allege. Its costs, however, are rarely trivial, in money, in time away from families and in the risk of illness. The most useful change would be for teams to measure each athlete's response as a matter of routine rather than relying on tradition and anecdote. Beyond that, governing bodies that spend heavily on mountain camps would do well to fund blinded trials involving genuinely elite competitors, so that the question raised in Mexico City more than half a century ago might at last receive a reliable answer.

topic: carbon-plated 'super shoes' in distance running: energy return and running economy, individual variation in benefit, footwear regulations, comparing records across eras and injury concerns
title: A Spring in the Step
subtitle: A new generation of running shoes has rewritten the record books and raised awkward questions about what races are really measuring

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the ideal racing shoe was thought to be as light and as thin as possible. Then, in the late 2010s, a radically different design appeared: a thick sole of soft, highly resilient foam with a stiff carbon-fibre plate embedded inside it. Within a few years, records at almost every distance from five kilometres to the marathon had fallen, many of them by margins that would once have been considered unthinkable. The change was most striking in road racing, where a cluster of world-best marathon performances arrived within a short period and the finishing times of ordinary club runners also began to improve. It is no exaggeration to say that these shoes have done more to transform distance running than any development in training methods over the past several decades.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two features account for most of the effect. The first is the foam, which returns around 85 per cent of the energy put into it when it is compressed, compared with roughly 65 per cent for the materials used in older racing shoes. The second is the plate, which stiffens the front of the shoe so that it behaves somewhat like a lever, reducing the work that the ankle and the joints of the toes must do as the runner pushes off. Ayumu Kurosaki, who directs a laboratory at the Kansai Institute of Human Movement, measured the oxygen consumed by trained athletes running on a treadmill in different shoes. On average, his subjects required about four per cent less energy to maintain a given pace in the new designs, an improvement in what physiologists call running economy that translates into race times roughly two to three per cent faster.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Averages, however, can mislead. The biomechanist Sigrun Tørresdal repeated similar tests with a much broader range of runners and found that the gains varied considerably, from close to ten per cent in some individuals to almost nothing in others. The benefit also appeared to shrink at slower speeds, probably because recreational joggers land with less force and so compress the foam less. Tørresdal therefore cautions that many amateurs who pay premium prices for the shoes may receive only a modest return. It seems clear, then, that advertising which implies every buyer will enjoy the gains seen in elite athletes is misleading.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The shoes also provoked a crisis of fairness at the elite level. For a time, only athletes sponsored by one manufacturer had access to the most advanced models, while rivals bound by contracts to other companies were left at a disadvantage. In 2020 the sport's governing body responded with new rules: soles could be no more than 40 millimetres thick, could contain only one plate, and any shoe had to be on general sale for a set period before it could be worn in competition. Lindiwe Khumalo-Ndaba, a philosopher of sport, argued at the time that these rules missed the central point, since they did nothing for athletes whose contracts prevented them from wearing a competitor's product. Her objection was reasonable in 2020, but it has lost much of its force: almost every major brand now produces a comparable shoe.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different set of concerns surrounds the record books. A group of sports statisticians led by Ramón Aldunate has argued that performances achieved before and after the new shoes simply cannot be compared, and has proposed that records be kept in separate lists according to the footwear used. I find this proposal unconvincing. Athletics has always evolved alongside its equipment: cinder tracks gave way to synthetic surfaces, and spikes have changed beyond recognition since the early Olympic Games. Swimming offers a useful parallel: when high-technology bodysuits were outlawed, the records set while wearing them were allowed to stand rather than being placed on a separate list. If every technological change required a new set of records, the history of the sport would dissolve into countless incompatible eras.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also questions about the effect of the shoes on the body. Their thick, soft soles are less stable than traditional designs, and some coaches have reported a rise in stress fractures in the bones of the foot among athletes who adopted them. Tørresdal points out that these reports are anecdotal and that no controlled study has yet confirmed a link. Even so, it would seem prudent for runners to introduce the shoes gradually, using them at first only for occasional sessions rather than for every run.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Underlying all of these debates is a more basic question about what a race is supposed to measure. Purists argue that it should test the athlete alone, but no race has ever been run without some contribution from technology, from the design of tracks to the fabric of clothing. My own view is that a technology is legitimate provided it is available to every competitor and its limits are clearly defined. What the episode has revealed above all is the danger of regulating too late. When the next innovation arrives, the authorities should establish the boundaries before records begin to fall, not scramble to draw them afterwards.

topic: the rehabilitation of lactate in exercise physiology: the lactate shuttle, whether acidity causes muscle fatigue, lactate and delayed muscle soreness, and the continued use of lactate-threshold testing
title: Clearing the Name of Lactate
subtitle: For decades a molecule produced by working muscles was blamed for fatigue, pain and stiffness. The evidence now tells a very different story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few substances in sport have been as thoroughly demonised as lactic acid. Generations of athletes were taught that it accumulated in their muscles during hard exercise, producing the burning sensation of a sprint finish, forcing them to slow down and leaving them stiff and sore the following morning. The idea had respectable origins. Early in the twentieth century, a series of influential experiments showed that isolated frog muscles, stimulated repeatedly until they could no longer contract, built up large quantities of lactic acid when they were deprived of oxygen. From this it seemed natural to conclude that lactate was the waste product of a muscle working beyond its oxygen supply, and that its accumulation was the cause of exhaustion. The conclusion entered textbooks, coaching manuals and popular belief, where it remained largely unchallenged for the best part of a century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious cracks appeared when researchers began to trace what actually happened to lactate inside the living body. Benedek Sztojka, a physiologist at the Pannonian University of Sport Sciences, used chemically labelled forms of the molecule to follow its movements during exercise. His results showed that lactate is produced continuously, even when oxygen is plentiful, and that much of it does not remain where it is made. Instead it is exported from fast-contracting muscle fibres and carried to slower fibres, to the heart and even to the brain, where it is burned as fuel. During moderate exercise, Sztojka found, the great majority of the lactate produced is consumed in this way rather than accumulating. This 'shuttle', as it came to be called, transformed lactate from a metabolic dead end into a central currency of energy exchange, and it represents one of the most significant reversals in modern physiology.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If lactate is a fuel, what of the acidity that accompanies intense effort? The biochemist Chiamaka Uchenwa has argued that the traditional account gets the chemistry backwards. The hydrogen ions that make a muscle more acidic, she points out, are released mainly when the cell breaks down its immediate energy supply, not when lactate is formed; indeed, the reaction that produces lactate actually absorbs hydrogen ions and therefore slows the rise in acidity rather than causing it. Uchenwa also cites experiments on single muscle fibres kept at body temperature, in which artificially increasing acidity had surprisingly little effect on the force the fibres could generate. On this view, fatigue is more plausibly explained by other changes, such as the build-up of phosphate within the cell or the leakage of potassium across its membrane.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Uchenwa's chemistry is difficult to dispute, but her conclusion that acidity is irrelevant to fatigue goes further than the evidence allows. A single fibre in a laboratory dish is a long way from a runner in the final stages of a race, with intact blood vessels, nerves and a brain interpreting signals from the whole body. Specialised nerve endings in muscle respond to the combined presence of lactate, hydrogen ions and other by-products of exertion, and it is these receptors that generate the familiar burning sensation. Even if acidity does little to weaken muscle fibres directly, the discomfort it contributes to may well persuade an athlete to ease off. Perception, in other words, can limit performance just as surely as chemistry.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The case against lactate as the cause of next-day soreness is more clear-cut. Delayed muscle soreness typically peaks between 24 and 72 hours after unaccustomed exercise, whereas blood lactate returns to resting levels within an hour of stopping. A substance that has already been cleared cannot plausibly be responsible for pain that arrives a day or two later. The soreness is now attributed instead to microscopic damage to muscle fibres and the surrounding connective tissue, caused above all by contractions in which a muscle lengthens while resisting a load, as the thigh muscles do when a runner descends a steep hill. What is remarkable is how stubbornly the older explanation survives in gyms and changing rooms, decades after it was abandoned in the laboratory.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that measuring lactate has lost its value. Coaches routinely take small blood samples during graded exercise tests to identify the 'lactate threshold', the intensity at which lactate begins to rise sharply, and use it to set training zones. Corinna Ressegatti, who trains coaches for a national endurance programme, argues that the threshold remains an excellent guide even though the theory originally used to justify it was mistaken. In her analogy, the threshold works like a smoke alarm: it does not explain the fire, but it reliably signals the point at which lactate production begins to outpace the body's capacity to clear it. This seems to me exactly right. A measurement can retain its practical worth long after the story told about it has been discarded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The rehabilitation of lactate has also opened unexpected avenues in medicine, where infusions of the molecule are being investigated as a source of fuel for injured brains and failing hearts. Yet perhaps the most instructive aspect of the episode concerns the way scientific ideas persist. The notion of lactic acid as a poison endured not because it was well supported but because it was intuitive: it offered a vivid, simple villain for an experience every athlete recognised. Textbooks have been slow to catch up, and they should now be revised without further delay. More generally, the story is a warning against casting any single molecule as the sole culprit in a process as complex as human fatigue.

topic: the brain's role in exercise fatigue: the end spurt, the central governor theory, peripheral muscle fatigue, the psychobiological model of perceived effort, deception trials and carbohydrate mouth rinsing
title: The Governor in the Head
subtitle: Is exhaustion a failure of the muscles or a decision made by the brain? Sport scientists remain divided

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Watch almost any long-distance race and a curious pattern emerges. Runners set off quickly, settle into a steady pace that gradually slows as fatigue sets in, and then, in the final few hundred metres, somehow find the strength to accelerate. This 'end spurt' is so familiar that spectators rarely remark on it. Yet it poses a serious problem for the traditional view of fatigue, according to which athletes slow down because their muscles have run short of oxygen or fuel and can no longer contract with the same force. If that were the whole story, a sudden burst of speed at the very end of a race ought to be impossible. In my view, no single observation is more awkward for the conventional model than this one.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most radical alternative was put forward by Lisandro Etchepare, a physiologist at the Patagonian Institute of Human Performance. He proposed that the brain acts as a 'central governor', continuously monitoring signals from the body and adjusting the number of muscle fibres it recruits so that exercise never reaches the point of genuine physical danger. Even at the moment of apparent exhaustion, Etchepare argues, only a proportion of the available muscle fibres are active. The sensation of fatigue, on this account, is not a direct report of the state of the muscles but a feeling generated by the brain to make the athlete slow down. Among his evidence is the finding that athletes competing in hot conditions run more slowly from the very outset of a race, long before their body temperature has had time to rise, which suggests that the brain anticipates trouble rather than merely reacting to it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Paavo Kähkönen, a muscle physiologist, is among the theory's sharpest critics. He points to experiments in which the nerves supplying a muscle are stimulated electrically, bypassing the brain entirely; under these conditions the force the muscle can produce still declines steadily with repeated contractions, demonstrating that fatigue within the muscle itself is real. Kähkönen's more fundamental objection is that the governor theory is impossible to test, since any result, whether an athlete speeds up, slows down or collapses, can be explained after the event as the brain's decision. There is some force in this complaint. A theory capable of accounting for every outcome is in danger of explaining none of them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ayşe Gülbaharoğlu, a psychologist who studies endurance, offers a third position. She sees no need for a hidden governor operating below the level of consciousness. Instead, she argues, athletes stop or slow down when their perception of effort reaches the maximum they are prepared to tolerate, or when they come to believe that continuing is impossible. Crucially, that perception can be altered by factors unrelated to the muscles. In one of her studies, volunteers who had spent ninety minutes on a demanding computer task before a cycling test gave up about fifteen per cent sooner than those who had watched a relaxing film, even though their heart rates and other physical measurements were no different. It is an elegant experiment, and its implication is striking: tiredness of the mind can shorten the endurance of the body.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A research team led by Marit Søbstad has tried to measure how much reserve an athlete actually holds back. Cyclists rode a time trial against an on-screen avatar which, they were told, reproduced their own best performance. In reality, the avatar had been set to ride two per cent faster, and most riders kept pace with it, beating their previous best. When the deception was increased to five per cent, however, they fell behind. Søbstad concludes that a reserve does exist, but that it is modest and cannot be released by belief alone.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If the brain plays a part in setting limits, it might be possible to train it. Some researchers have experimented with mental exercises designed to make demanding tasks feel easier, while others have studied the curious effect of rinsing the mouth with a carbohydrate drink and spitting it out. In events lasting around an hour, this simple procedure has been shown to improve performance, apparently because receptors in the mouth signal to the brain that energy is on its way. Such findings are intriguing, but the commercial enthusiasm they have generated has run well ahead of the evidence. Several companies now market brain-training programmes to endurance athletes, and the benefits reported in independent studies have been small and inconsistent.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Over the past decade, the debate has become less polarised, and most researchers now accept that both the brain and the muscles contribute to fatigue. The popular slogan that fatigue is 'all in the mind', however, is seriously misleading. Exhaustion arises in the mind and the body together, and the most productive question is no longer which of them is in charge, but how the signals passing between them combine to determine when an athlete finally slows down. Answering it will not be easy, since it requires recording the activity of the brain in people who are moving vigorously, a task for which most current imaging equipment is poorly suited.

topic: endurance sport in hot conditions: how the body sheds heat, heat acclimatisation and its decay, heat training as a performance booster in cool weather, pre-cooling with ice slurry, neck cooling risks and event scheduling
title: Racing the Thermometer
subtitle: As major sporting events move to ever hotter venues, scientists are asking how far athletes can prepare their bodies for the heat

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Human muscles are remarkably inefficient engines. Of the chemical energy they consume during exercise, only around a quarter is converted into movement; the rest is released as heat. At rest, the body keeps its core temperature close to 37°C, but during prolonged hard exercise it can climb rapidly, and once it approaches 40°C performance deteriorates sharply and the risk of serious heat illness rises. The body's principal defence is the evaporation of sweat from the skin, which carries heat away. In humid air, however, sweat evaporates far less readily, so that it simply drips from the body without providing much cooling. As commercial pressures increasingly bring international championships to hot and humid locations, the question of how athletes should cope with such conditions has moved from the margins of sport science to its centre.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most reliable answer remains acclimatisation. When athletes exercise in the heat for ten to fourteen consecutive days, their bodies undergo a series of well-documented changes. The volume of blood plasma expands, sweating begins earlier and becomes more profuse, the sweat itself becomes more dilute so that less salt is lost, and the heart beats more slowly at any given workload. Most of these adaptations are established within the first week. They do not, however, last indefinitely. Hamid Zarghami, of the Caspian Centre for Environmental Physiology, has tracked athletes after they return to cooler climates and estimates that the benefits fade by roughly two and a half per cent for each day without heat exposure. He therefore recommends brief 'top-up' sessions in a heat chamber for athletes who must travel some time before competing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More controversial is the claim that heat training can improve performance even in cool conditions. In a widely publicised study, Kaito Nishiyama had cyclists train for ten days in a chamber heated to 40°C and found that their time-trial performance in mild conditions improved by around six per cent, while that of a control group training in normal temperatures did not change. Nishiyama attributed the gain to the expansion of plasma volume, which allows the heart to pump more blood with each beat, and the method was soon promoted as an inexpensive substitute for altitude camps. Subsequent research has been less encouraging. Liv Sundqvist-Ebbe repeated the experiment with closely matched training loads and found no benefit at all in cool conditions; she suggests that the control group in the original study had simply trained less than the heat group. On present evidence, the case for heat training as a general performance booster remains unproven, although for athletes who will actually compete in the heat its value is beyond question.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Alongside long-term adaptation, athletes now use a range of short-term cooling methods. The principle behind 'pre-cooling' is that lowering core temperature before the start increases the quantity of heat the body can absorb before it reaches a critical level. Ice vests and cold-water baths are common, but the most popular technique is to drink a slurry of finely crushed ice, typically around 7.5 grams per kilogram of body weight, roughly thirty minutes before the race begins. Because ice absorbs a large amount of heat as it melts, the slurry cools the body more effectively than the same volume of cold water. During competition, some athletes also wear cooling collars or drape cold towels around the neck.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Esperanza Rubalcava, a physician who provides medical cover at endurance events, has raised concerns about this last practice. The neck contains a dense concentration of temperature receptors, she explains, so cooling it can make an athlete feel considerably cooler without having any meaningful effect on core temperature. An athlete who feels comfortable may then push harder, generating more heat and moving closer to danger. The risk Rubalcava describes is genuine, but it should be kept in proportion. Cases of heatstroke among elite competitors, who are closely monitored and usually well acclimatised, remain rare; the great majority occur among less experienced participants in mass-participation races.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Individual differences also matter. It was once widely assumed that women tolerate heat less well than men, but more recent studies indicate that most of the apparent difference disappears once body size and fitness are taken into account. Larger, heavier athletes are at a disadvantage because they produce more heat relative to the surface area of skin available to lose it, which may help to explain why the most successful marathon runners tend to be light and slender. Fitness itself offers considerable protection, since trained individuals begin sweating sooner and have larger plasma volumes even before any deliberate acclimatisation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, though, the burden should not fall on athletes alone. Heat stress is now commonly assessed using the wet bulb globe temperature, a composite index that takes into account air temperature, humidity, solar radiation and wind. Many medical guidelines recommend that mass-participation races be postponed or cancelled when this index exceeds about 28°C. Organisers frequently resist such measures because of television schedules and the cost of road closures. Yet moving start times to the early morning would do more to protect competitors than any cooling vest or ice drink, and governing bodies ought to make such scheduling a condition of awarding their events.
