topic: stretching and the pre-exercise warm-up: whether static stretching weakens muscles, stretch duration, stretching and injury prevention in recruits, structured dynamic warm-up programmes for youth football and the psychology of routines
title: Before the Whistle
subtitle: The humble warm-up stretch has been praised, condemned and partly rehabilitated. What does the evidence actually support?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, few rules of exercise seemed more secure than the instruction to stretch before playing sport. Schoolchildren were lined up to touch their toes and hold the position, and professional athletes performed long sequences of static stretches, in which a muscle is lengthened and held still, in the belief that this would protect them from injury and help them perform. Then, around the turn of the millennium, a wave of laboratory studies suggested that stretching before activity might actually weaken muscles, and the message changed abruptly. Newspaper articles warned readers that their pre-run routine was doing them harm. In hindsight, both the old orthodoxy and the sudden backlash against it went well beyond what the evidence could support.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against stretching rested on a plausible mechanism. Muscles and tendons behave partly like springs: a relatively stiff tendon transmits the force of a contracting muscle to the bone efficiently, and stores and returns elastic energy during movements such as running and jumping. Holding a muscle in a lengthened position appears to reduce this stiffness temporarily, and may also dampen the nerve signals that activate the muscle. In theory, then, a stretched muscle should be a slightly less powerful one. Sprinters and jumpers, whose events depend heavily on this elastic recoil, were consequently thought to be the athletes with most to lose.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question is how large the effect really is. Dagny Øverli, a sports scientist who reviewed more than one hundred experiments, found that the answer depends heavily on the duration of the stretch. When each muscle was held for more than sixty seconds, strength and jumping height fell by around four or five per cent. When stretches lasted under thirty seconds, however, the loss was close to one per cent, and when stretching was followed by a few minutes of vigorous dynamic activity, even that small effect largely disappeared. Many of the early studies, Øverli noted, had asked volunteers to hold stretches for several minutes at a time, far longer than athletes typically do in practice. The initial alarm, it seems, was to a considerable extent a product of unrealistic laboratory procedures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The supposed protective effect of stretching has fared no better. Tendai Kanaventi led one of the largest trials on the subject, assigning some two thousand military recruits either to stretch before each training session or not to stretch at all. Over twelve weeks, the overall rate of injury in the two groups was almost identical, although there was a slight and statistically uncertain reduction in muscle strains among those who stretched. Kanaventi concluded that stretching is of little value in preventing injury. That conclusion may be too sweeping. Recruits spend much of their time marching and running at moderate speeds, whereas many sports involve sprinting, kicking and sudden changes of direction, precisely the actions in which muscle strains are most common. A finding from the parade ground may not transfer straightforwardly to the football pitch.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What does appear to reduce injuries is a different kind of warm-up altogether. Halina Śliwińska designed a fifteen-minute routine for youth football clubs combining jogging, balance exercises, jumps, practice in landing safely and simple strength work. In a large trial, teams using the routine suffered about a third fewer injuries than teams following their usual warm-up, with the largest reduction in serious knee injuries among girls. The benefit, however, depended on commitment: it was clear only in teams that performed the routine at least twice a week, and Śliwińska found that many coaches abandoned it within a few weeks, often because players found it repetitive. A revised version, with shorter exercises and added competitive games, was taken up more enthusiastically, suggesting that the way such programmes are packaged matters almost as much as what they contain.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The psychologist Efemena Ekong-Bassey draws attention to an aspect of warming up that physiological studies tend to ignore. Athletes who believe that stretching benefits them, she has found, perform worse when they are prevented from carrying out their usual routine, apparently because familiar rituals reduce anxiety and increase confidence before competition. This is an underrated consideration, and coaches who abruptly ban long-established habits may lose more than they gain. Even so, it cannot justify routines that genuinely impair performance; an athlete who holds long static stretches moments before a sprint is still handicapping himself, however reassuring the ritual feels.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: From this tangle of findings a reasonably clear picture emerges. A sensible warm-up begins with general aerobic activity to raise muscle temperature, moves on to dynamic movements and sport-specific drills, and may include brief static stretches of under thirty seconds for athletes who find them helpful. Sports that demand an exceptional range of movement, such as gymnastics and dance, are a partial exception, since performers may need longer stretching to reach the positions their discipline requires. None of this calls for expensive equipment or specialist staff, which makes the persistence of outdated routines at many amateur clubs all the more surprising. More broadly, the history of stretching research illustrates how readily a qualified scientific finding can be converted into a simple rule, and how the simple rule then outlives the evidence on which it was based.

topic: early specialisation versus multi-sport childhoods in athlete development: retrospective studies of elite athletes, early-peaking sports, overuse injury, burnout and autonomy, and the incentives of youth academies
title: One Sport or Many?
subtitle: Parents of talented children are often told that the road to the top begins early and admits no detours. The research suggests otherwise

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The idea that sporting excellence demands an early start has an appealing logic. If world-class performance depends on accumulating thousands of hours of focused practice, then the child who begins at six and concentrates on a single sport will surely outstrip the one who dabbles in several until her teens. Much of the intellectual support for this view came from research on musicians, which found that the most accomplished violinists had practised far more, and from a younger age, than their less successful peers. Sports academies, many of which now recruit children before they have finished primary school, have embraced the principle enthusiastically. Yet the transfer of conclusions from the concert hall to the playing field was made with remarkably little scrutiny, and the evidence from sport itself points in a rather different direction.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Kwabena Asante-Ofori, who studies talent development, has collected detailed training histories from several thousand athletes across more than twenty sports. His most consistent finding is that those who went on to reach the very highest level as adults had, on average, specialised later than athletes who peaked at national level. As children, the eventual world-class performers had typically played a variety of sports and accumulated less practice in their main discipline before the age of fifteen. Once they did commit to a single sport, however, they improved faster than their early-specialising counterparts, as though the broad base of movement skills acquired in childhood allowed them to learn more efficiently. Asante-Ofori is careful to present this as a statistical tendency rather than a law: a minority of world champions did commit to their sport very young, and in some disciplines that minority is far from small.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These findings deserve to be taken seriously, but they are not without weaknesses. They rely on athletes' recollections of training undertaken many years earlier, and memory is an imperfect record. More importantly, sports differ enormously in the age at which performance peaks. In gymnastics, figure skating and diving, competitors often reach their best in their mid-teens, when the body is still small and light, and a child who delays specialisation until fifteen will have missed the window altogether. In such disciplines, an early start may be unavoidable. Any single rule intended to apply to every sport is therefore bound to mislead.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Physical health provides a second line of argument. Tomoko Ishizaki, a specialist in paediatric sports medicine, has documented the rising incidence of overuse injuries among young athletes, including stress fractures and damage to the growth plates, the areas of developing cartilage near the ends of children's bones. Such injuries arise from repetitive loading of the same tissues, and they are concentrated among children who train intensively in a single sport. Ishizaki proposes a simple guideline: a child should not spend more hours per week in organised training for one sport than his or her age in years. The rule has the merit of being easy to remember and apply, even if the precision it implies is somewhat artificial.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The psychologist Yevheniia Stasiuk has focused on a different risk: that children who specialise early are more likely to abandon sport altogether by their mid-teens. She attributes this partly to the way intensive programmes change the meaning of sport for the child. What began as play becomes an obligation, organised and evaluated by adults, and the enjoyment that originally sustained participation gradually wears away. Significantly, however, Stasiuk found that children who had chosen to concentrate on one sport themselves showed no greater tendency to drop out than those who played several. The crucial factor, in other words, appears to be autonomy rather than specialisation as such. It is a distinction of real importance, and one that is all too often lost in public discussion of the issue.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mehrnaz Jahanbani, an economist who studies sporting institutions, argues that the pressure to specialise is driven less by evidence than by incentives. Professional clubs and academies gain a commercial advantage by identifying and securing promising players before their rivals do, and they bear few of the costs when those players fail to progress. In some football academies, she calculates, several hundred boys are released for every one who goes on to earn a professional contract. Many of those released are fourteen or fifteen, having devoted most of their childhood to a single ambition, and some struggle to find a place for themselves outside the game. Jahanbani proposes prohibiting formal academy registration before the age of twelve. I have some sympathy with her diagnosis, but less with her remedy. A ban of this kind would be likely to push early selection into private coaching schemes, which are subject to even less oversight than the academies themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For parents, the practical implications are nonetheless reasonably clear. In most sports, a childhood spent sampling a range of activities appears to be the wiser default, offering better protection against injury and loss of interest without sacrificing long-term potential. Where early specialisation is genuinely required by the nature of the sport, the priority should be to limit training volume and preserve the child's sense of ownership. Perhaps the most useful lesson of this research is that the timing of specialisation matters less than is commonly supposed, and that the more important questions are who makes the decision and how much is asked of the child once it has been made.

topic: sleep and athletic performance: why elite athletes sleep poorly, sleep-extension studies, sleep and injury in adolescents, chronotype and training time, eastward travel across time zones, and wearable sleep monitoring in teams
title: Resting to Win
subtitle: Athletes will spend a fortune on equipment and nutrition, yet the most powerful aid to performance may be one they neglect every night

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Elite sport has become an industry of marginal gains. Teams employ nutritionists, analysts and engineers in pursuit of improvements measured in fractions of a second, and athletes will pay large sums for lighter equipment or a more sophisticated recovery garment. Sleep, by contrast, has until recently received remarkably little attention. Surveys consistently find that elite athletes sleep less, and less well, than people of the same age in the general population. Early-morning training sessions, competitions that finish late in the evening, frequent travel and anxiety before important events all take their toll. It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that sleep is the most underused means of improving performance available to athletes today, not least because it costs nothing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study most often cited in support of this view was conducted by Liesbeth Verbruggen, a sleep researcher who asked members of a university basketball squad to spend at least ten hours in bed every night for six weeks. By the end of the period, the players were sprinting faster, their shooting accuracy had risen by around nine per cent, their reaction times had shortened and they reported feeling more alert and in better spirits. The results have been repeated in countless articles and coaching presentations. Yet the study involved only eleven players, there was no comparison group, and the participants knew perfectly well what the researchers hoped to find. Its findings are plausible, but they should be regarded as a promising starting point rather than settled fact.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sleep may also influence an athlete's vulnerability to injury. Citlali Ameyalli followed several hundred adolescent athletes over a competitive season and found that those who regularly slept for fewer than eight hours were about one and a half times as likely to be injured as those who slept longer. Ameyalli is cautious about interpreting this result, however. Young athletes with the heaviest training and competition schedules may well be the ones who both sleep least and get injured most, in which case the association need not mean that lack of sleep is itself the cause. Similar uncertainty surrounds reports that athletes who sleep badly before major championships catch more colds and other respiratory infections, since the stress of competing may disturb sleep and weaken resistance at the same time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: When athletes train may matter as well as how long they sleep. For most people, physical performance peaks in the late afternoon or early evening, when body temperature is at its highest. But individuals differ in their 'chronotype', their natural tendency to be active earlier or later in the day. Radosław Szulc, who studies biological rhythms in sport, tested swimmers at different times of day and found that those with a pronounced late chronotype performed up to ten per cent worse in early-morning trials than in the evening, whereas early types showed a much smaller variation. The late types were not slower swimmers overall: in the evening, their times were as good as anyone's. Szulc suggests that, where possible, training should be timed to suit each athlete's rhythm, although he acknowledges that competition times are usually fixed by organisers and broadcasters.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Travel across time zones presents a further challenge. The body's internal clock naturally runs on a cycle slightly longer than twenty-four hours, which means it adapts more readily to a lengthened day than to a shortened one. Journeys eastward, which shorten the day, are therefore generally harder to recover from than journeys westward. An analysis of results from a professional league whose teams are spread across several time zones found that visiting teams which had travelled east lost noticeably more often than those which had travelled west. Carefully timed exposure to bright light can help to shift the internal clock, as can the hormone melatonin, which is now widely available as a supplement. Its use, however, ought to be supervised by medical staff, since the timing and dose determine whether it advances or delays the clock.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many professional teams now ask their athletes to wear devices that record sleep every night. A group at the Tarragona Sport Sleep Unit has warned that such devices often overestimate total sleep and misclassify its stages, and that some athletes become so preoccupied with their nightly scores that their sleep actually deteriorates. Wearable monitoring certainly has a place, but the information it produces should serve as the starting point for a conversation between athlete and coach, not as an instruction that determines the following day's training.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these findings will make much difference unless the culture of sport changes. In many teams, early starts and the ability to function on little rest are still treated as evidence of dedication and toughness. Some clubs have begun to move morning sessions later, to schedule short afternoon naps and to teach young athletes about the importance of a regular bedtime. These are welcome developments. Ultimately, sleep needs to be understood not as time taken away from training but as an essential part of it, the period in which the body actually absorbs the work that has been done.

topic: cold-water immersion and cryotherapy for athletic recovery: effects on soreness, placebo, blunting of strength-training adaptation, endurance training, whole-body cryotherapy chambers and periodised recovery
title: Cold Comfort
subtitle: Ice baths have become a ritual of modern sport. New research suggests that the relief they bring may come at a hidden price

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few images capture the professionalism of modern sport quite like that of exhausted athletes lowering themselves, grimacing, into tubs of icy water after a match. Cold-water immersion has become a routine part of recovery in sports ranging from football to cycling, and at the more extravagant end of the market, athletes now step into 'cryotherapy' chambers in which the air is cooled to more than a hundred degrees below zero. Professional clubs have installed purpose-built cold pools at their training grounds, and portable inflatable tubs are now marketed to amateur runners. The appeal is easy to understand: cold is believed to reduce soreness and inflammation and to help the body recover more quickly between demanding sessions. But the popularity of these practices has run considerably ahead of the scientific understanding of what they actually do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The rationale is straightforward enough. Cold causes blood vessels to narrow, which is thought to limit swelling in damaged tissue, and it slows the conduction of signals along nerves, which dulls the sensation of pain. Pernille Kjærgaard, a sports scientist who has pooled the results of dozens of trials, concludes that immersion in water at ten to fifteen degrees for ten to fifteen minutes does reduce muscle soreness over the following four days, although the effect is modest. Its influence on the recovery of strength and power is smaller and far less consistent, and water colder than ten degrees appears to bring no additional benefit while being considerably more unpleasant. Kjærgaard also draws attention to a problem that runs through the entire field: it is impossible to disguise cold water from those who sit in it. In one study she cites, athletes who drank what they were told was a powerful recovery drink, but was in fact flavoured water, reported recovering just as well as those who took ice baths.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more troubling possibility was raised by Aigerim Tulegenova, who studies how muscles adapt to training. Over twelve weeks, she had one group of volunteers sit in cold water after each strength-training session, while a second group performed ten minutes of gentle cycling instead. At the end of the period, the cold-water group had gained noticeably less muscle size and strength. Muscle biopsies, small samples of tissue taken through a needle, revealed why: cold had suppressed the activity of the molecular signals that instruct muscle cells to build new protein. The inflammation that athletes are so eager to eliminate, it appears, is not merely a nuisance but part of the message that tells the body to adapt.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This finding is, in my view, among the most important in recent sports science, but it does not mean that athletes should abandon the ice bath. What it calls for is a more discriminating use of cold. In a tournament where matches follow one another on successive days, the need to feel fresh for the next game clearly outweighs any small loss of long-term adaptation, and cold-water immersion is entirely sensible. During a block of training designed to build strength, by contrast, routinely plunging into cold water after every session may undermine the very purpose of the work.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whether the same caution applies to endurance athletes is less clear. Delroy Ashpitel, an endurance physiologist, points out that the evidence of blunted adaptation comes almost entirely from strength training. Indeed, some laboratory studies have found that cold exposure increases signals associated with the formation of new mitochondria, the structures that generate energy within muscle cells, a key adaptation to endurance work. Ashpitel therefore believes that runners and cyclists have little reason for concern. His optimism may prove justified, but it is premature: the studies he relies on are few in number, involved small groups and lasted only a matter of weeks. None followed trained athletes through a full competitive season, which is precisely the situation in which the question matters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The case for whole-body cryotherapy is weaker still. Sessions typically last only two or three minutes, and because air conducts heat far less effectively than water, the skin cools dramatically while the temperature of the underlying muscle barely changes. A research team led by Haruki Somekawa compared the two methods directly and found that cryotherapy was no more effective than cold-water immersion in reducing soreness, and on some measures of recovery it performed worse. Given that a single session can cost many times the price of a bath of cold water, and that cases of frostbite and other injuries have been reported, the expense is very difficult to justify.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Coaches increasingly speak of 'periodised recovery', meaning that methods of recovery, like training itself, should be matched to the goals of each phase of the season. It is a sensible principle, and it reflects a wider shift in thinking. For decades, recovery was treated as a matter of making athletes feel better as quickly as possible, on the assumption that soreness and fatigue were simply obstacles to be removed. The research on cold suggests a more complicated picture, in which some of the discomfort that follows hard training may be an essential part of the process by which the body grows stronger. Athletes who suppress every sign of strain may, without realising it, be throwing away part of what their training was meant to achieve.

topic: tapering before competition: the fitness-fatigue balance, reducing volume while keeping intensity, individualised tapers and monitoring, 'taper madness', tapering in team sports and deliberate overreaching before a taper
title: The Art of Doing Less
subtitle: Why do athletes perform best after they have cut back their training, and how much should they cut?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: After months of gruelling preparation, the final weeks before a major championship present athletes with a curious paradox: the best way to improve is to train less. This reduction in workload, known as the taper, is practised in almost every endurance sport and in many others besides. Swimmers, runners, rowers and cyclists typically find that a well-judged taper improves their competition performance by around two to three per cent, a margin that frequently separates a medal from fourth place. Few interventions in sport offer such a dependable return. Yet, surprisingly, the taper remains more a matter of craft and tradition than of precise science, and coaches who agree on its value often disagree sharply about how it should be done.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic principle is reasonably well understood. Hard training produces two effects at once: it builds fitness, but it also generates fatigue, and while the athlete is training heavily, the fatigue conceals much of the fitness that has been acquired. When the training load is reduced, fatigue dissipates within days, whereas fitness declines far more slowly. For a brief period, therefore, the athlete retains most of the benefits of training without the accumulated tiredness. The difficulty lies in timing: reduce the load too little and fatigue remains; reduce it too much or for too long and fitness itself begins to erode.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Miriam Grünbaum, a sports scientist who has analysed the results of dozens of tapering studies, has attempted to identify the most effective formula. Her analysis suggests that athletes should cut the total volume of their training by between forty and sixty per cent over roughly two weeks, while maintaining both the intensity of their sessions and the number of sessions they complete each week. The most common mistake, she argues, is to reduce intensity along with volume: athletes who replace their hard sessions with gentle ones tend to lose some of the sharpness they have worked so hard to develop.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Duarte Vasconcelos-Pinto, a coach and researcher who works with international rowers, is wary of any general prescription. In his experience, some athletes reach their peak after a single week of reduced training, while others need three or more, and the same athlete may respond differently from one season to the next. He therefore monitors his rowers daily, using measures such as the variation in their resting heart rate and the height they can jump, and adjusts each taper according to the results. The approach is promising, but it is not as precise as it may appear. Such measurements fluctuate considerably from day to day for reasons that have nothing to do with training, and distinguishing a genuine trend from random variation is far from easy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The taper also has a psychological dimension, and the sport psychologist Selin Aksoylu has studied it closely. Athletes accustomed to long hours of hard training often find the reduced workload deeply unsettling. Many report feeling sluggish and restless, notice aches they had never felt before and begin to doubt whether their preparation has been sufficient, a state that some swimmers call 'taper madness'. A few respond by secretly adding extra sessions. Aksoylu recommends warning athletes in advance about these feelings and filling the spare time with structured activities such as mental rehearsal of the race. This side of tapering is too often underestimated: a reduction in training that is perfectly judged in physical terms can still be undone by an anxious mind.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Team sports raise different problems. In football or basketball, where matches are played every week over a season lasting many months, it is plainly impossible to taper before every game. A research group led by Anjali Mohapatra-Senn used tracking data from professional football clubs to examine how training loads were managed, and found that most teams reduced training only modestly in the days before important matches. Whether even this modest reduction affects results is unclear. Outside short tournaments, it seems likely that tapering offers team players considerably less benefit than it does athletes in individual sports, where performance can be planned around a handful of key events.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some coaches attempt to amplify the effect of the taper by deliberately overloading their athletes in the weeks immediately before it, in the hope that a period of extreme fatigue will be followed by an even larger rebound in performance. Grünbaum regards this strategy as hazardous. If the overload goes too far, athletes may enter a state of prolonged exhaustion from which they cannot recover before the competition, and the potential gains appear to be small. Her caution seems well founded. The margin between productive overload and harmful exhaustion is narrow, and the cost of misjudging it is a wasted season.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What, then, should coaches do? Rather than searching for a universal formula, they would be better advised to keep careful records of each athlete's tapers, noting what was done and how the athlete performed, and to refine their approach over successive seasons. More broadly, the taper illustrates a truth that applies far beyond the final weeks before competition: athletes do not improve while they are training, but while they are recovering from it.

topic: taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages: volumetric versus tiered designs, reformulation, price pass-through and substitution, regressivity, measuring health effects and the use of revenue
title: Taxing the Fizz
subtitle: Levies on sugary drinks have spread rapidly around the world, but there is little agreement about what they should be expected to achieve

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past decade, more than fifty countries, states and cities have introduced taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages, making them one of the most rapidly adopted public health measures of recent times. The case for singling out such drinks rests on a distinctive feature of liquid sugar: it supplies large amounts of energy without producing the sense of fullness that accompanies solid food, so its calories tend to be added to those eaten at meals rather than replacing them. Consumption is also concentrated among adolescents and lower-income households, the groups in which obesity and dental disease are most common. Yet the enthusiasm with which governments have embraced these levies has run well ahead of the evidence about what they actually accomplish. That said, the objections most frequently raised against them are often misplaced, and the more interesting questions lie elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Not all sugar taxes are designed in the same way. The simplest charge a fixed amount per litre of any sweetened drink, regardless of how much sugar it contains. Such volumetric schemes raise prices, but they give manufacturers no incentive to alter their recipes, since a slightly less sweet product is taxed at exactly the same rate. Tiered levies, by contrast, impose higher charges above particular sugar thresholds, and their effects can be dramatic. In one widely studied case, manufacturers reformulated many of their products in the two years between the announcement of the levy and its introduction, so that the revenue eventually collected fell far short of forecasts. Finance ministry officials described the shortfall as disappointing; health officials regarded it as proof that the policy had worked. The episode illustrates a point that is too often overlooked: a health tax that is assessed by how much money it raises is being measured against the wrong standard.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What happens to prices and purchases once a tax is in place has been examined by Lucia Tamburelli, a health economist at the Adriatic Centre for Fiscal Health Research. Using shopping data recorded by thousands of households, her team found that large supermarkets generally passed the tax on to customers in full, while small convenience stores frequently raised prices by more than the tax itself. Purchases of taxed drinks fell by roughly a fifth over two years. Tamburelli stresses, however, what this headline figure conceals. A significant share of the decline was offset by increased buying of untaxed products with comparable sugar content, notably fruit juices and milk-based drinks, which most schemes exempt because they contain other nutrients.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most persistent criticism of sugar taxes is that they are regressive. Tunde Ogunmola, an economist at the West African Institute for Social Policy, has calculated that the poorest fifth of households pay almost three times as much of their income in levies as the richest fifth. His arithmetic is not in dispute, but it tells only part of the story. Because poorer households drink more sugary beverages to begin with, they also stand to gain most if they cut back, through lower medical costs and, eventually, longer lives. It must be conceded, though, that for a household which carries on buying exactly as before, the tax is nothing more than a loss of income, which is why the question of how the revenue is spent cannot be treated as an afterthought.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Demonstrating that the taxes improve health is harder still. Body weight changes slowly and is influenced by countless other factors, from working hours to the price of vegetables, so isolating the effect of a single levy is extraordinarily difficult. The epidemiologist Aino Rantanen, who has reviewed evaluations from several countries, suggests that researchers have been looking in the wrong place. The first measurable benefits, she argues, are more likely to appear in children's teeth than in their waistlines, and she points to falling hospital admissions for tooth extraction as an early indicator. Rantanen is also critical of modelling studies that project large reductions in diabetes from modest falls in sugar intake. Such projections, she notes, typically assume that calories removed from the diet stay removed, whereas people tend to make up at least part of the difference by eating more of something else.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The response of the drinks industry has been varied. Some manufacturers shrank bottle and can sizes so that the price of a single serving remained familiar; others shifted their advertising towards sugar-free versions of established brands. Retail associations have argued that the levies damage small shops, although studies of employment in the sector have so far found little evidence of job losses. Meanwhile, a research network led by Nino Kobiashvili has examined why some taxes survive changes of government while others are quickly repealed. Its conclusion is that public support depends heavily on what happens to the money. Where revenue is visibly linked to local benefits, such as drinking fountains in schools, opposition tends to fade; where it disappears into general budgets, the tax is easily portrayed as a cynical revenue-raising device.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that sugar taxes are a solution to obesity, and their more ardent supporters do the policy no favours by presenting them as one. But neither should the taxes be written off as failures simply because obesity rates have not fallen within a few years of their introduction. Their most important effects may be indirect: prompting manufacturers to change their recipes, and signalling, in a way that leaflets rarely manage, that a once-unremarkable product carries real costs. Judged by those criteria, the evidence so far is more encouraging than many critics allow.

topic: standardised (plain) tobacco packaging: the pack as the last advertising space, attention studies, separating its effect from existing trends, illicit-trade claims, smokers' social rituals, legal challenges and extension to other products
title: The Uniform Pack
subtitle: Stripping cigarette packets of their branding was meant to be the final blow to tobacco marketing. Has it lived up to the expectations?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By the early years of this century, tobacco companies in most wealthy countries had lost almost every conventional means of promoting their products. Television and radio advertising had long been prohibited, billboards and magazine campaigns followed, and the sponsorship of sporting events was gradually outlawed. What remained was the packet itself. Marketing executives had a name for it, the 'silent salesman', and its value was considerable: a regular smoker might take a pack out twenty times a day, placing it on tables, desks and bar counters in full view of others. Standardised packaging, first introduced nationally in the early 2010s and since adopted by more than two dozen countries, removes logos, distinctive colours and decorative features. Every pack is a uniform dark olive-brown, a shade chosen after consumer testing identified it as the least attractive available, with the brand name printed in a regulated typeface beneath large graphic health warnings.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the measure proposed that it would work through three mechanisms: by reducing the appeal of smoking, particularly to the young; by making health warnings more noticeable; and by preventing packaging from creating false impressions, as when pale colours or silver trim imply that one brand is less harmful than another. Some of the most frequently cited evidence comes from the laboratory of the psychologist Halla Sigurgeirsdottir, whose eye-tracking experiments found that adolescents who did not smoke looked first at the brand imagery on conventional packs but at the health warning on standardised ones. These studies are elegant, but their limitation is easily overlooked: they reveal where people direct their gaze, not whether anyone smokes less as a result.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Establishing real-world effects has proved more contentious. In most countries, the new packaging was introduced alongside tax increases and enlarged warnings, and smoking rates were already falling. Ramya Palakodeti, a statistician who has analysed national survey data, used a method that compares the trend after a policy change with the trend that would have been expected had the previous pattern continued. She estimated that plain packaging accounted for a further decline in adult smoking prevalence of around half a percentage point. Owen Brassington, an economist who has frequently been critical of the policy, argued that a change of this size lies within the normal year-to-year fluctuation of survey estimates, and he drew attention to claims that the illicit trade in counterfeit cigarettes had expanded. The second objection, at least, has not withstood examination: customs seizure data showed no sustained increase in counterfeit products after the change.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Brassington's first point deserves a more careful answer. Half a percentage point does indeed sound trivial, but applied to an adult population of twenty million it represents roughly a hundred thousand fewer smokers, each with a substantially reduced risk of premature death. Moreover, the people whom the policy was principally designed to influence are those who have not yet started to smoke. Its effect on them can only become fully visible over a generation, and to dismiss the measure on the basis of short-term adult prevalence figures is to evaluate it against a goal it was never primarily intended to achieve.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different kind of evidence comes from the sociologist Ngozi Ezenwaka, who conducted repeated interviews with smokers before and after the change. Many reported that they were now reluctant to leave their packs on café tables, and some had begun transferring their cigarettes into metal tins or cases, which suggests that the branded packet had functioned as a statement of identity in a way smokers themselves had rarely acknowledged. Ezenwaka is careful, however, not to overstate her findings. Long-term heavy smokers were, for the most part, indifferent to the appearance of the packet, and she concludes that its influence on those already dependent on nicotine is slight.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most dramatic chapter in the story has been legal. Tobacco manufacturers argued in domestic courts and international tribunals that the measure amounted to the confiscation of their trademarks and breached investment treaties. These challenges were, almost without exception, rejected. Judges and arbitrators generally accepted that a state may restrict how a trademark is used without taking ownership of it, and that a measure supported by a reasonable body of public health evidence does not become unlawful merely because its effects are difficult to quantify. It could reasonably be argued that this outcome mattered more than any change in smoking rates, since governments that had hesitated for fear of costly litigation now had a tested legal model to follow, and a wave of countries duly introduced similar laws.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Encouraged by this record, some public health advocates now propose extending standardised packaging to alcohol, confectionery and other foods high in sugar or fat. The proposal is understandable, but the analogy is weaker than it first appears. Tobacco is unusual in that no level of consumption is considered safe, which made it politically and legally possible to treat its marketing as illegitimate in itself. Most foods, by contrast, are harmless in moderation, and stripping their packaging of identity would be far harder to justify. A more defensible course might be to concentrate on the ways such products are marketed to children, where the case for restriction is considerably stronger.

topic: community water fluoridation: its origins, declining benefit in the toothpaste era, neurodevelopmental safety concerns, consent and the ethics of mass medication, and evidence from cities that stopped fluoridating
title: Something in the Water
subtitle: For eighty years, adding fluoride to drinking water has been praised as a public health triumph and condemned as mass medication. The truth is less dramatic than either side suggests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The story of water fluoridation began with a puzzle. In the early twentieth century, a young dentist working in a small mountain town noticed that many of his patients had teeth disfigured by brown stains, yet were strikingly resistant to decay. It took him decades, and the help of chemists, to trace both effects to unusually high concentrations of fluoride occurring naturally in the local water. If too much fluoride stained the teeth, researchers reasoned, a smaller amount might protect them without causing visible damage. In the 1940s, one city began adding fluoride to its supply at roughly one part per million, while a similar city nearby served as a comparison. After a decade, decay among children in the fluoridated city had fallen dramatically, and the practice spread rapidly across several countries.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Today the picture is far more varied. Some nations fluoridate the water supplied to most of their population, while much of continental Europe has never done so, relying instead on fluoride added to table salt or simply on toothpaste. Fluoridated salt has the advantage of leaving consumers free to buy an alternative, although it reaches households far less evenly than water does. This divergence has produced what is perhaps the most uncomfortable fact for supporters of the policy: over the past half century, tooth decay among children has declined just as steeply in many countries that do not fluoridate their water as in those that do. It does not follow that fluoridation is useless, but it does mean that the dramatic results of the early trials cannot simply be assumed to hold today.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Marta Zoltanski, a dental epidemiologist who has reviewed several decades of studies, argues that the explanation lies in the arrival of fluoride toothpaste, which became almost universal from the 1970s onwards. Most of the original trials, she points out, were conducted before such toothpaste existed, and the additional benefit of fluoridated water for a child who already brushes twice a day is considerably smaller, perhaps a quarter of the original estimates. Yet Zoltanski insists that this average conceals an important pattern. The remaining benefit falls overwhelmingly on children from poorer households, who are less likely to brush regularly or visit a dentist. In her words, fluoridation is the only dental intervention that requires no effort whatsoever from the people it protects.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Opponents have long raised concerns about safety, and in recent years these have focused on the developing brain. Kenji Nakashiro, a toxicologist, has drawn attention to studies from regions with naturally high fluoride levels that report lower average scores on children's cognitive tests. He maintains that the margin between a beneficial dose and a harmful one was never rigorously established, and that pregnant women and infants fed on formula made with tap water deserve particular attention. His call for better research is entirely reasonable. However, most of the studies he cites come from areas where concentrations are several times higher than those used in fluoridation schemes, and to apply their findings directly to controlled supplies is a leap the evidence does not support. Several of those studies also failed to account for other contaminants, such as arsenic, that frequently occur in the same groundwater.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most enduring objection, though, is ethical rather than scientific. Adaeze Okpanachi, a bioethicist, describes fluoridation as a medical intervention delivered without individual consent. Unlike vaccination, where parents may at least decline, fluoridated water can be avoided only by purchasing bottled water or filtration equipment, options which many low-income families cannot afford. Defenders of fluoridation respond that the same could be said of chlorination, which is equally imposed on everyone. The comparison is less convincing than it seems. Chlorine is added to make water safe to drink, whereas fluoride is added to produce a health effect in the people who drink it, and that distinction, though often dismissed as a technicality, is a genuine one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most revealing recent evidence has come from cities that have chosen to stop. Lionel Vanterpool, a health economist, examined one city that ended fluoridation after a public vote and found that, within five years, the number of children requiring dental treatment under general anaesthetic had risen substantially. Yet in a second city that stopped at around the same time, he detected no measurable change. Vanterpool's cost calculations help to explain the difference. Fluoridation costs very little per person each year, and in deprived districts the savings in dental treatment exceed this cost many times over; in affluent areas, where decay is already uncommon, the financial return is marginal.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the evidence points away from the polarised positions that have dominated public debate. Fluoridation is neither the miracle once claimed nor the poison its fiercest critics allege. Its value now depends heavily on local circumstances, particularly the level of childhood decay and the degree of deprivation in a community. Decisions about it would therefore be better taken area by area, on the basis of local data, than through national mandates or national bans. Such an approach lacks the simplicity that both campaigns have found useful, but it has the considerable merit of matching the policy to the people it is supposed to serve.

topic: minimum unit pricing for alcohol: targeting cheap strong drinks, modelled effects by drinking level and income, sales and mortality outcomes, dependent drinkers, the retailer windfall, erosion by inflation and cross-border buying
title: A Floor Under the Price
subtitle: Setting a minimum price for every unit of alcohol was once dismissed as unworkable. Its first years in operation have complicated the arguments on both sides

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The harm caused by alcohol is distributed very unevenly. A relatively small proportion of drinkers consume a large share of all the alcohol sold, and they account for a disproportionate number of the deaths and hospital admissions linked to it. Many of these heavy drinkers rely on the cheapest products available: large bottles of strong cider and own-brand spirits sold in supermarkets, which can deliver a day's recommended limit for less than the price of a cup of coffee. Minimum unit pricing is designed to address precisely this market. Instead of raising the price of all alcohol, as a conventional tax does, it sets a legal floor below which a given quantity of pure alcohol cannot be sold. The price of a glass of wine in a restaurant or a pint of beer in a pub, already well above that floor, is left largely untouched. The first national scheme came into force only after a legal challenge by drinks producers that dragged on for six years, eventually ending in the country's highest court.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the case for the policy rested on computer modelling. A research group led by Camille Delacombe built a simulation of how drinkers in different income and consumption bands would respond to various minimum prices. The model predicted that moderate drinkers would barely notice the change, paying only a few pounds more each year, whereas heavy drinkers on low incomes, who purchase the cheapest alcohol in the greatest quantities, would experience the largest price rises and, the team expected, the largest reductions in consumption. Because these are also the people at greatest risk of alcohol-related illness, the model forecast substantial health gains for a modest overall effect on the drinking population.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first evaluations have broadly supported these predictions, although the effects are smaller than some advocates had hoped. Alcohol sales per adult fell by around three per cent relative to a neighbouring jurisdiction where no minimum price applied. More strikingly, deaths wholly attributable to alcohol, such as those from alcoholic liver disease, fell by roughly thirteen per cent, with hospital admissions declining by a smaller amount. The largest falls in both measures occurred in the most deprived areas, which is exactly where the policy's designers had hoped it would make a difference. For a measure that costs the government almost nothing to implement, these are significant results.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that they tell the whole story. Somchai Thammasorn, an economist who studies addiction, warns that for drinkers who are physically dependent on alcohol, higher prices may not reduce consumption so much as redirect spending. Small interview studies have found that some dependent drinkers maintained their intake by cutting back on food or heating, or by borrowing money, and Thammasorn argues that such hardship is invisible in aggregate statistics. His concern deserves to be taken seriously, but it should not be overstated: the fall in deaths suggests that, across the population of heavy drinkers as a whole, the health benefits have outweighed the harms. What it does demonstrate is that a pricing policy is no substitute for accessible treatment services, and that the two must be funded together.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Here the scheme runs into an awkward difficulty of its own making. Because a minimum price is not a tax, the additional money that consumers pay goes not to the government but to retailers and producers. Petra Grunwaldt, a specialist in public finance, has estimated that supermarkets gained tens of millions in extra revenue in the first years alone. She describes this as a perverse outcome, since a targeted levy on cheap, strong drinks could have raised the same sum for treatment and prevention. Defenders of the scheme reply that trade rules and existing tax law made such a levy legally impossible at the time. That may be true, but it makes the policy a compromise forced by legal circumstance rather than an ideal design, and its supporters would do well to acknowledge this.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further weakness has been the treatment of inflation. The minimum price was fixed in law at the level proposed many years before it finally took effect, and no mechanism was included for raising it automatically. By the time it was first increased, general price rises had reduced its real value by about a fifth, gradually weakening the very effect the policy was designed to produce. Linking the floor price to an index of inflation, as is routinely done with many benefits and taxes, would avoid the need for repeated political decisions and would protect the policy from quiet erosion.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, sceptics predicted that drinkers would simply cross the border or shop online to avoid the higher prices. Ketevan Tsitsishvili, a geographer, examined retail data and found that cross-border purchasing increased only in towns within a short drive of the border, and that its overall effect on consumption was negligible. Online sales, which must comply with the same rules when delivered within the country, have proved harder to monitor. Taken as a whole, the evidence suggests that minimum pricing is neither the decisive solution its champions proclaimed nor the futile gesture its critics expected. It is a useful but limited instrument, and its value will depend on whether governments are prepared to maintain it and to invest in the services that must accompany it.

topic: calorie labelling on restaurant menus: informed choice, small effects on what customers buy, misjudging portion energy, restaurant reformulation, eating-disorder concerns, accuracy of stated values and exemptions for small businesses
title: Counting at the Counter
subtitle: Laws requiring restaurants to print calorie figures on their menus have changed less about what diners eat than expected, but they may have changed something else

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many wealthy countries, food eaten outside the home now supplies around a quarter of the energy in the average adult diet, and restaurant portions have grown considerably over the past forty years. Partly in response, a number of governments have obliged large restaurant chains to display the calorie content of every item on their menus and menu boards. The principal justification offered for these laws is not paternalistic but informational. Diners, it is argued, cannot be expected to make sensible decisions about what they eat if the most basic fact about a meal is hidden from them, and a market functions properly only when buyers know what they are buying. On this view, the labels would be worthwhile even if nobody changed their order as a result.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, most people expected that customers would change their orders, and the early evidence was a disappointment. Grace Mukanzi, a nutrition scientist, collected thousands of till receipts from chain outlets before and after labelling became compulsory in one large city. The average number of calories purchased per transaction fell by only about four per cent. Because she also collected receipts in a comparison city with no such law, she could rule out the possibility that even this small decline simply reflected a general change in eating habits. Moreover, almost all of that reduction came from customers who, in follow-up questionnaires, described themselves as already trying to eat healthily. More than half of those surveyed said they had not noticed the figures at all, despite their prominent position beside the prices.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Mukanzi's subsequent research has, however, painted a slightly more encouraging picture. When she tracked purchases over three years, the small reduction did not fade, as many effects of health information do, and it was noticeably larger for side dishes and sweetened drinks than for main courses, perhaps because these are the items customers regard as optional. She also found that, before labels were introduced, diners systematically underestimated the energy content of large meals, often by a third or more, while judging small snacks with reasonable accuracy. The labels appear to correct the very errors that matter most.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet the most important consequences of labelling may lie on the other side of the counter. Emre Kuyumcu, an economist who studies the food industry, compared the nutritional content of dishes launched by restaurant chains in the years before and after labelling laws were passed. New items introduced after the laws took effect contained, on average, roughly a tenth fewer calories than those they replaced, while long-established items were rarely altered. Kuyumcu's interpretation is that companies are reluctant to place a conspicuously large number on a newly advertised product. This quiet reformulation affects every customer, including those who never glance at the figures, and it is remarkable how seldom it features in public discussion of the policy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all the consequences have been welcome. Liisa Tauvela, a clinical psychologist who treats patients with eating disorders, reports that many of them find calorie-labelled menus distressing, and that some avoid restaurants altogether as a result. She argues that a policy designed for the general population may inflict real harm on a vulnerable minority, particularly adolescents, who are both especially susceptible to such disorders and frequent customers of the fast-food outlets covered by the laws. Her concern is a legitimate one, although the research on this question remains sparse. It hardly justifies abandoning labels altogether, but it does strengthen the case for a simple compromise already adopted in some places: offering, on request, a version of the menu without the numbers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other critics object that calories are a crude measure of a meal's value, saying nothing about fibre, salt or the quality of fat. A grilled fish dish and a plate of fried snacks may carry similar figures while differing greatly in their effects on health. This is true, but proposals to add further information, such as colour-coded ratings for several nutrients, risk overloading customers who must decide what to order within a few seconds at a busy counter. A more pressing problem is accuracy. When independent investigators sent restaurant meals to laboratories for analysis, some dishes differed from their stated calorie values by more than a fifth, and those marketed as light or healthy options were the most likely to contain more energy than the menu claimed. A figure that is printed with precision is easily mistaken for one that has been measured with precision.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Most labelling laws apply only to chains with a minimum number of outlets, on the grounds that laboratory analysis of every dish is expensive and that small independent restaurants change their menus frequently. Given these costs, the exemption is sensible, even if it means that labels are absent from many of the places where people eat. Some governments have tried to reduce the burden on chains by allowing values to be calculated from recipe databases rather than measured directly, although this inevitably makes errors more likely. Taken as a whole, menu labelling is best understood as an inexpensive policy with modest direct effects and potentially larger indirect ones. It will not by itself reverse the growth of restaurant portions, but as one element of a broader strategy it has earned its place.

topic: supervised drug consumption facilities: overdose deaths at neighbourhood level, public injecting and residents' perceptions, contact with treatment and self-selection, cost-effectiveness compared with naloxone, opening hours and adapting to smoked synthetic drugs
title: Behind the Unmarked Door
subtitle: Facilities where people can use illegal drugs under medical supervision remain among the most contested ideas in public health. What does the evidence actually show?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: From the street, the building looks like any other converted shopfront. Inside, however, people bring drugs they have bought elsewhere and inject them in individual booths, using sterile equipment and watched over by nurses who are trained to reverse an overdose. The staff are forbidden by law from supplying or handling the drugs themselves, and nobody is required to give their name. There are now more than a hundred such facilities in over a dozen countries, and few public health measures provoke such sharply divided reactions. Supporters regard them as a pragmatic way of keeping alive people who would otherwise inject alone in alleys and stairwells. Opponents see them as an official endorsement of illegal behaviour that will draw dealers and drug users into neighbourhoods which are already struggling.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The figure most often cited in their defence is that, across decades of operation and millions of supervised injections, almost no one has died of an overdose inside a facility. The statistic is genuine, but it is weaker evidence than it appears, since the great majority of overdoses occur elsewhere, and a facility could prevent every death within its walls while making little difference to the city as a whole. More persuasive is work by the epidemiologist Arpine Sarkissian, who compared overdose deaths in the streets within five hundred metres of one facility with those in the rest of the same city. In the two years after it opened, deaths in the surrounding blocks fell by about a third, compared with a fall of less than a tenth elsewhere. The numbers involved are small, as Sarkissian acknowledges, but the pattern has since been reported in several other cities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Concerns about public order have been examined by the criminologist Tama Ahuriri, who counted discarded syringes and recorded instances of public injecting in the streets around facilities before and after they opened. Both declined by roughly half, and police records showed no increase in drug-related theft or assault. Ahuriri found, however, that surveys of local residents told a different story. Many continued to describe their neighbourhood as less safe than before, even where the measurable indicators had improved, and their hostility to the facility showed little sign of softening over several years. Public perception, in other words, does not necessarily follow the evidence, and policymakers who assume otherwise are likely to be disappointed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Reinhold Oberhauser, a specialist in addiction medicine, argues that the most valuable function of these facilities is not the supervision of drug use at all but the contact they create. People who rarely see a doctor visit regularly, and staff can offer wound care, testing for infections and referral to treatment. Oberhauser's data indicate that frequent attenders are around thirty per cent more likely to enter a detoxification programme than infrequent ones. The finding is plausible, yet it is vulnerable to an obvious objection: those who choose to attend often may already be more motivated to change, so the facility may be identifying such people rather than creating them. Fortunately, the case for supervised facilities does not depend on this claim; the reductions in deaths and public injecting would justify them on their own.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most substantial criticism comes from those who accept the evidence but question the priorities. Bogusława Dziobak, a health economist, has calculated that the cost of each death prevented is considerably higher for a supervised facility than for programmes that distribute naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose, to users and their families. She also notes that most facilities open only during the day, while a large proportion of fatal overdoses occur at night. Her point about opening hours is well made and identifies a genuine weakness. Her broader comparison, though, presents as alternatives two measures that serve different purposes, and a city that can afford both is under no obligation to choose.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A newer challenge arises from changes in the drugs themselves. In many regions, heroin has been partly replaced by far more potent synthetic opioids, often mixed unpredictably into other substances, and a growing number of users smoke rather than inject them. Irina Petrossova, a public health researcher, points out that many facilities were designed and licensed solely for injection, with no ventilated spaces for inhalation. She argues that they must adapt by adding smoking rooms and services that allow users to have their drugs chemically tested before use. Such changes, however, frequently require new legislation, and the laws governing these facilities have so far lagged well behind the drug markets they are meant to address.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from the research is a picture of real but local benefits: fewer deaths in the immediate area, fewer needles in the street and more contact with health services for a population that is otherwise hard to reach. These achievements are worth having, but they are modest, and the political debate has tended to load the facilities with a symbolic significance that the evidence cannot support. They should be judged by what they can realistically deliver, not condemned for failing to resolve a city's drug problem, which no single service could ever be expected to do.

topic: mandatory folic acid fortification of flour to prevent neural tube defects: limits of supplement advice, international adoption and European reluctance, vitamin B12 masking, cancer concerns, freedom of choice, gaps in coverage and monitoring
title: The Vitamin in the Loaf
subtitle: Adding folic acid to flour has prevented thousands of serious birth defects. Why have so many countries hesitated to do it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among the most serious birth defects are those of the neural tube, the structure in the embryo that develops into the brain and spinal cord. When it fails to close properly, the result may be spina bifida, which can cause lifelong paralysis, or anencephaly, which is invariably fatal. The neural tube forms within the first four weeks of pregnancy, often before a woman is aware that she has conceived. In the early 1990s, large randomised trials demonstrated that taking supplements of folic acid, a synthetic form of one of the B vitamins, before conception and in early pregnancy reduced the risk of these defects by up to seventy per cent. Health authorities duly advised all women who might become pregnant to take daily tablets. The advice, however, ran into an obvious difficulty: around half of all pregnancies are unplanned, and the women least likely to follow it are typically younger and poorer, precisely those who are least likely to be in contact with health services before pregnancy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The alternative was to add the vitamin to a food that almost everyone eats. In the late 1990s, several countries in the Americas began requiring millers to fortify wheat flour with folic acid, and more than sixty nations have since followed. In those countries, rates of neural tube defects have fallen by between a fifth and a half, with the largest reductions in populations where they had previously been highest. Yet for more than two decades, most European governments declined to act, preferring to rely on supplement advice that the evidence showed to be failing. Given the severity of the conditions involved and the low cost of fortification, this prolonged hesitation is difficult to justify.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of the hesitation stemmed from a specific medical worry. Folic acid can correct the anaemia caused by a deficiency of vitamin B12, which is common among older people, while leaving untreated the nerve damage that the same deficiency produces. Fortification, critics feared, might therefore conceal the warning sign that leads doctors to diagnose the condition. Inês Soares-Bento, a haematologist, has traced this concern to a handful of case reports from the 1940s, in which patients had been given doses of folic acid many times greater than any fortified diet could supply. Large studies conducted in countries that fortify have found no increase in undiagnosed B12 deficiency among the elderly, and the fear that fortification at current levels endangers older people now appears to have little foundation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more recent concern relates to cancer. Tadeusz Mazurkiewski, an oncologist, points out that folate is needed for cell division, and that it may therefore accelerate the growth of pre-cancerous lesions that already exist in the bowel. He cites a trial in which participants given high-dose folic acid developed more advanced polyps than those given a placebo. The doses in that trial, however, were several times higher than those obtained from fortified flour, and surveillance in countries that fortify has not revealed any rise in bowel cancer that could be attributed to the policy. Mazurkiewski's argument is not a reason to halt fortification, but it is a reason to monitor its effects carefully rather than assuming that more is always better.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other objections are philosophical. Freya Kaunitzer, a political philosopher, argues that mandatory fortification removes a choice from the whole population in order to benefit a small group. Men, children and older women gain nothing from it in terms of birth defects, yet they consume the vitamin whenever they eat bread. Kaunitzer favours voluntary fortification, under which manufacturers may add folic acid to selected products such as breakfast cereals. The difficulty is that voluntarily fortified products tend to be more expensive and are bought disproportionately by better-off households, leaving the women at greatest risk unprotected. Moreover, unfortified flour remains available to anyone who wishes to avoid the vitamin, so the burden placed on those who object is, in practice, a small one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even where fortification is mandatory, its reach is incomplete. Wholemeal and specialist flours are frequently exempt, and the growing popularity of gluten-free diets means that some women of child-bearing age consume little wheat flour at all. In parts of the world where rice rather than wheat is the staple, the problem is more fundamental. Flour can be fortified simply by mixing in a powder, but rice is eaten as whole grains, and fortifying it requires the manufacture of artificial kernels containing the vitamin, which must then be blended with ordinary rice in the correct proportion. This process is considerably more complicated and costly, and it remains uncommon.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these limitations alters the central conclusion. Folic acid fortification is among the clearest successes in modern public health: an inexpensive intervention, requiring no change in individual behaviour, that has prevented many thousands of devastating birth defects. Its success, however, should not be taken as a reason for complacency. Diets change, and the level of fortification set a generation ago may no longer be the right one. Regular measurement of folate levels in the blood of women of reproductive age, and of older adults, would allow governments to review that level in the light of evidence rather than leaving it fixed indefinitely.
