topic: financial incentives for vaccination: prize lotteries and their disputed effect, overweighting small probabilities, payment as a warning signal to distrustful people, guaranteed cash for procrastinators, fairness and future expectations, practical access barriers and building evaluation into policy
title: Paying People to Roll Up Their Sleeves
subtitle: When governments offered cash and prize draws to the vaccinated, they also created an unplanned experiment in how incentives work, and how easily their effects are misjudged

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the months after vaccines against a new respiratory virus became widely available, vaccination rates in many regions stalled well short of official targets. Governments responded with a remarkable variety of rewards. Some offered guaranteed cash payments; others promised free sports tickets, public transport passes or meals; and several staged lotteries in which every vaccinated resident was entered into a draw for prizes worth a million dollars or more. Paying people to adopt healthier behaviour was not in itself a new idea. Health services had for years experimented with modest rewards for attending screening appointments, completing courses of treatment or giving up smoking. What was new was the scale and the publicity, and the episode turned out to be at least as instructive about how such policies are evaluated as about vaccination itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first lottery to be announced appeared to be a spectacular success. In the fortnight that followed, vaccinations in the region rose by around forty per cent, and politicians elsewhere hurried to copy the scheme. Giulia Bacigalupo, an economist, was among the first to question the claim. She noted that the announcement coincided almost exactly with a decision to extend vaccine eligibility to adolescents, which would have increased the numbers regardless of any prize. Using a technique known as a synthetic control, in which the region's actual vaccination rate is compared with that of a weighted combination of similar regions that held no lottery, she found no statistically significant effect. Later analyses of other lotteries have mostly reached similar conclusions, which suggests that the early declarations of victory were, to say the least, premature.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should lotteries have been expected to work at all? The theory draws on a well-established finding in behavioural economics: people tend to give too much weight to small probabilities, which is why lottery tickets sell even though the expected return is poor. A large prize, it was reasoned, would therefore motivate far more people than the same money distributed in small payments. Andrés Viteri, a social psychologist, argues that this reasoning overlooked the nature of vaccine hesitancy. Many unvaccinated people were not merely inert but actively distrustful, and for them, he suggests, an offer of payment may even act as a warning: if the authorities need to pay people to take a vaccine, perhaps there is something wrong with it. The idea is plausible, though the evidence for such a backfire effect so far remains mixed rather than conclusive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Guaranteed rewards have produced clearer results. Hemi Rewiti, a health economist, conducted a randomised trial in which residents were offered a modest cash sum on receiving their first dose, while a comparison group received only reminders. The payment raised vaccination by about four percentage points, a small but reliable effect. Importantly, those who were paid were no less likely than others to return for a second dose without further reward, suggesting that the incentive had not undermined their own motivation. Rewiti emphasises, however, that the effect was concentrated almost entirely among people who had intended to be vaccinated but had not yet got round to it. Those who had firmly decided against vaccination were unmoved by the money.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Incentives also raise questions of fairness. The bioethicist Corina Moldoveanu does not regard small payments as coercive, as some critics have claimed, since a modest sum hardly overrides anyone's free choice. Her objection is different. Rewarding those who delayed, she argues, is unfair to the many who were vaccinated promptly and received nothing, and it may teach the public to expect payment in the future, making the next vaccination campaign more expensive and more difficult. This concern about expectations has received surprisingly little attention, and it deserves systematic investigation, although evidence from blood donation, where payments have been studied for decades, points in no single direction.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, a less glamorous explanation for low vaccination rates was often neglected. Surveys in several countries found that a substantial share of unvaccinated adults were not hesitant at all but faced practical obstacles: they could not take time off work, lacked transport to a clinic or had nobody to look after their children. In districts where authorities sent mobile clinics to workplaces and estates, or required employers to provide paid leave on the day of vaccination and the day after, the gains frequently exceeded those attributed to any lottery. Removing such barriers may not attract headlines, but it is a considerably more reliable way of raising uptake than offering the chance of sudden wealth.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the evidence suggests that financial incentives are a useful tool for a particular group, those who are willing but have not yet acted, rather than a means of persuading the determined sceptic. Neither the enthusiasm with which lotteries were launched nor the outrage they provoked in some quarters was justified by the results. The more lasting lesson concerns evaluation. Had the schemes been introduced through a staggered rollout, with regions or districts starting at different, randomly chosen times, their effects could have been measured with confidence, instead of being inferred from statistics that were open to many interpretations.

topic: compulsory bicycle helmet laws: individual protection versus population health, falls in cycling after legislation, health benefits of cycling against injury risk, safety in numbers, risk compensation and its replication, effects on public bike-share schemes
title: The Helmet Question
subtitle: Few people dispute that a helmet protects a cyclist's head. Whether the law should require one is a very different matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Head injuries are among the most serious consequences of cycling accidents, and studies comparing injured cyclists who were and were not wearing helmets consistently find that a helmet roughly halves the risk of serious head injury in a crash. On the strength of such evidence, a small number of countries and states made helmets compulsory for all cyclists in the 1990s, and campaigners in many other places have urged their governments to do the same. Yet most of the countries where cycling is most common, including those in which a large share of all journeys are made by bicycle, have never introduced such laws. The disagreement is often presented as a dispute about whether helmets work. It is better understood as a dispute about something else: whether compelling adults to wear them improves the health of the population as a whole.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most striking evidence concerns what happened to cycling itself. In the year after one national law came into force, counts of cyclists on city streets fell by around a third, with the steepest declines among teenagers and people who rode only occasionally. Paola Ingrisani, a transport researcher who analysed hospital records from the same period, found that the number of cyclists admitted with head injuries did fall, but almost in proportion to the fall in the number of people cycling. The rate of head injury per cyclist, in other words, barely changed. Critics of these findings have pointed out that the cycle counts were collected irregularly and at a limited number of sites. The objection has some force, but a decline of this magnitude, recorded in several cities at once, is too large to be dismissed as a statistical artefact.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should fewer cyclists matter for public health? Marek Szczurek, a health economist, has estimated that the benefits of regular cycling, chiefly reduced rates of heart disease, diabetes and some cancers, outweigh the risks of injury by a factor of around twenty. If so, a law that discourages even a modest number of people from cycling could cost more years of healthy life than it saves through prevented head injuries. Szczurek's calculation has been challenged on the grounds that it assumes people who stop cycling become inactive, when some will walk, swim or go to the gym instead. This is a fair criticism, and it means his figures probably overstate the cost of the law. It does not, however, reverse the direction of his argument, since the gap between benefits and risks is wide enough to survive considerable adjustment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further consideration is what is sometimes called 'safety in numbers'. In cities where cycling is common, the risk of injury for each individual cyclist tends to be lower, apparently because drivers grow used to looking out for bicycles. Shirin Tavakolian, a traffic engineer, argues that by reducing the number of cyclists, helmet laws may therefore make cycling more dangerous for those who continue. She also contends that physically separated cycle lanes do far more to prevent injuries than any item of protective clothing. The safety-in-numbers relationship is less straightforward than it is often presented, however. It is at least as likely that safe streets attract cyclists as that large numbers of cyclists make streets safe, and the two effects are extremely difficult to disentangle.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Opponents of helmet laws have also appealed to risk compensation, the idea that people who feel protected take greater risks. Helmeted cyclists, it has been suggested, ride faster, and a widely publicised early experiment, in which a single researcher rode an instrumented bicycle along ordinary roads, found that drivers passed noticeably closer when he wore a helmet. Keoni Hokulani, a psychologist, repeated the experiment with a large sample of riders of different ages and both sexes, and found almost no difference in passing distance. Risk compensation is a real phenomenon in some settings, but in debates about cycling it has frequently been given more weight than the evidence can bear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most recent dimension of the debate concerns public bicycle-sharing schemes, which allow people to hire a bicycle for a short trip and leave it at another docking station. Such schemes depend on spontaneous use by people who did not plan to cycle when they left home, and who are therefore unlikely to be carrying a helmet. Cities with compulsory helmet laws have generally recorded far lower use of their shared bicycles than comparable cities without them. Some operators have tried supplying helmets with each bicycle, but these are frequently stolen or left unused because of concerns about hygiene.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this amounts to an argument against helmets. Wearing one is a sensible precaution, particularly for children and for those who ride fast on open roads, and encouraging their use through education is entirely reasonable. The case against compulsion for adults rests instead on the evidence that, where cycling is not already an established habit, such laws deter people from riding while doing little to reduce the rate of injury. Governments seeking to make cycling safer would achieve more by building protected lanes and lowering traffic speeds, measures that make cyclists safer and encourage more people to cycle, rather than placing the responsibility for safety on the cyclists themselves.

topic: universal versus means-tested free school meals: under-claiming and stigma, diet and obesity effects dependent on food standards, disputed attainment gains, targeting and political durability, families just above the eligibility threshold, and kitchen capacity
title: Lunch for Everyone
subtitle: Should free school meals be reserved for the poorest children, or offered to every pupil? The answer depends on what such meals are expected to achieve

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many countries, a free midday meal at school has long been available only to children whose families fall below a specified income threshold. A smaller group of countries, several of them in northern Europe, have for decades provided lunch to every pupil regardless of family income, treating it as a normal part of the school day in the same way as textbooks or heating. In recent years, a growing number of cities and regional governments elsewhere have moved from the first model to the second, often amid fierce argument. Universal provision is expensive, and its opponents ask why public money should pay for the lunches of children whose parents could easily afford them. Its supporters reply that the targeted system has never worked as well as it appears to on paper.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious weakness of means-tested schemes is that many of the children they are intended for never benefit. Families must apply, often by completing lengthy forms and providing evidence of income, and official estimates in several countries suggest that between one in ten and one in five eligible children are not registered. That so many miss out through a process designed to help them is, in itself, a serious indictment of the targeted approach. Even registration does not guarantee that children eat. The sociologist Ewan Maclachlan interviewed pupils in schools where those receiving free meals had once queued separately or handed over coloured tokens, and found that some had preferred to go hungry rather than be identified as poor. Many schools have since introduced cashless payment cards so that nobody can tell who is paying. Maclachlan found, however, that among teenagers the sense of being marked out often persisted, because pupils learned in other ways which of their classmates were eligible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters of universal meals also point to their effect on diet. Siriporn Krisanaphan, a nutritional epidemiologist, evaluated a pilot programme in which every primary school pupil in two districts received a free lunch, comparing them with children in similar districts where the targeted system continued. Children in the pilot districts ate more vegetables and fewer of the crisps and sweets that are common in packed lunches brought from home, and the prevalence of obesity among the youngest pupils fell slightly relative to the comparison districts. Krisanaphan stresses, though, that these improvements depended on strict nutritional standards for the food served. Where schools were free to offer whatever pupils preferred, the gains largely vanished. This point is crucial: free meals of poor quality would simply be a costly way of spreading poor diets more widely.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Claims about learning are more contentious. Aleksi Pyykonen, an economist, examined test results from the same pilot and reported modest gains in reading and mathematics, which were largest among disadvantaged pupils. Intriguingly, these gains were greater even than those of poorer children who had already been receiving free meals under the old system. Pyykonen attributes this to the effect of an entire class eating together, which teachers described as producing calmer and more attentive afternoons. Other researchers have noted that the pilot was small, and attempts to find similar gains elsewhere have produced inconsistent results. Improvements in attainment, if they occur, are a welcome bonus, but they are too uncertain to serve as the principal justification for the policy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The strongest objection to universal provision comes from those concerned with value for money. Giacomo Balestrieri, a public finance economist, calculates that more than half the additional spending required for universal meals goes to families who are not poor and who would otherwise have paid for lunch themselves. The same sum, he argues, could instead be used to double the cash support available to the poorest households. His arithmetic is difficult to dispute. Yet it overlooks a political reality that history repeatedly confirms: services used by everyone attract broad public support and are far less vulnerable to cuts than those reserved for the poor, which can easily become stigmatised and starved of funds. A narrowly targeted programme that is efficient in theory but steadily eroded in practice may in the end deliver less to the families it was designed to help.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nadia Ravindranathan, who studies household budgets, draws attention to another group. Families whose income lies just above the eligibility threshold receive no help under a means-tested system, yet they often have less money left over each week than families just below it, who also qualify for other forms of assistance. For these households, the cost of school lunches for two or three children can amount to a significant share of their food spending. Ravindranathan's research suggests that it is this group, rather than the very poorest, who gain most when meals become universal, and that rates of food insecurity among them fall noticeably as a result.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Practical obstacles should not be underestimated. Many schools built in recent decades were designed without full kitchens, on the assumption that most pupils would bring food from home, and expanding provision has required substantial investment in equipment and staff. Some authorities have used the expansion to buy more food from local producers, which has been popular with parents. Taken as a whole, the evidence suggests that universal free meals are a defensible use of public money, provided that the food is of genuinely high quality and that the policy is not used as an excuse to reduce other forms of support for families in poverty.

topic: why working hours stopped falling in rich economies despite rising productivity: individual choice, employers' fixed costs per worker, inequality and status competition, individual versus household measurement, and the role of collective institutions
title: The Hours That Never Shrank
subtitle: Productivity has soared for a century, so why has the promised age of leisure failed to arrive?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1930, a celebrated British economist made a forecast that has since become one of the most frequently quoted predictions in the social sciences. Within a century, he suggested, technical progress would raise living standards so far that his grandchildren's generation would need to work no more than fifteen hours a week. On the first half of the prediction he was broadly right: average incomes in the wealthy economies have grown roughly as fast as he expected. On the second half he was spectacularly wrong. Although annual hours fell steadily for much of the twentieth century, the decline slowed sharply after about 1980, and in several countries full-time employees today work much the same week as their parents did. Explaining why the dividend of growth has been taken almost entirely as goods rather than as time is arguably one of the most important unresolved questions in economics.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most familiar explanation treats working hours as the outcome of individual choice. Dimitra Varvarigos of the Aegean Institute of Labour Economics points out that rising wages pull people in two directions at once. Higher pay means that a household can maintain the same standard of living with fewer hours, which encourages it to work less; but it also raises the price of every hour not spent working, since each hour of leisure now means sacrificing more income. According to Varvarigos, the first effect dominated for most of the twentieth century, whereas in recent decades the two have roughly cancelled each other out. The model is elegant, and it fits the historical pattern neatly. Its weakness is the assumption on which it rests: that employees are free to select the number of hours they work, rather like shoppers deciding how many apples to buy. For the majority of the workforce, this is simply not the case.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That objection is central to the work of Kenji Tamanaha, a sociologist at the Pacific Centre for Employment Research, who argues that hours are determined largely on the employer's side of the bargain. Many of the costs of taking on a worker, including recruitment, induction and benefits such as health insurance, are incurred per person rather than per hour. As a result, it is usually cheaper for a firm to employ a compact team working long weeks than a larger team working short ones. Tamanaha supports his case with surveys in which a substantial minority of full-time staff say they would willingly give up part of their salary in exchange for shorter hours, if only such an arrangement were available. The argument about recruitment costs is convincing. The survey evidence, however, is weaker than it appears: when firms have actually offered reduced hours at reduced pay, the proportion of employees accepting has typically been far smaller than questionnaires predicted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third account shifts attention from the workplace to society as a whole. Wairimu Gacheru, an economist at the East African Policy Institute, links the stalling of working hours to the growth of inequality since 1980. Where the rewards at the top are very large, the incentive to compete for promotion through visible effort becomes intense, and long hours become a signal of commitment. Her comparison of twenty countries finds that those in which inequality rose most steeply also saw the smallest reductions in working time. As she notes, the best-paid professionals now work longer weeks than the lowest paid, overturning a nineteenth-century pattern in which leisure was the privilege of the wealthy. Gacheru's correlation is suggestive, but it cannot by itself establish which way the influence runs; it is at least as plausible that industries demanding long hours have also generated unequal pay.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers question whether the puzzle has even been framed correctly. A group led by the demographer Anneliese Felsberg at the Hanseatic Centre for Time-Use Studies contends that the answer depends heavily on the unit of measurement. Average hours per employed person have in fact continued to fall in many countries, largely because of the spread of part-time work. Yet over the same period the number of hours supplied by a typical household has risen, because many more women have entered paid employment while domestic responsibilities have not diminished correspondingly. A couple who together sell seventy or eighty hours of labour a week may well feel more pressed for time than a single-earner household of the 1950s, even if each partner works fewer hours than the breadwinner of that era. This is a valuable corrective, and it suggests that much of the debate has been conducted at the wrong level.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Official figures may also miss changes in the character of time itself. Measured hours record when people are formally at work, not when they are answering messages on a train or reading reports after their children have gone to bed. More importantly, perhaps, the leisure that remains has become fragmented into short, interrupted intervals, and there are good reasons to think that scattered free minutes do not offer the same benefits as an uninterrupted evening.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, became of the age of leisure? The countries that have gone furthest in converting productivity into free time did so mainly through legislation and agreements negotiated by trade unions, not through millions of individual decisions. This suggests that the forecast failed not because people prefer possessions to time, but because the institutions needed to turn rising output into shorter working weeks were never built in most economies. None of this means that a fifteen-hour week is either attainable or desirable for everyone. It does mean that working time should be treated as a question of public policy, rather than as a private matter between individual workers and their employers.

topic: four-day working week trials: self-selected participant firms, self-reported versus objective measures, eliminating workplace waste and the loss of informal contact, costs in services that require attendance, and compressed hours
title: Thirty-Two Hours
subtitle: Trials of a shorter working week have produced enthusiastic headlines, but what do they really show?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a handful of companies first announced that their staff would work four days a week for the same pay, the idea was treated as a curiosity. Within a few years, it had become a movement. Coordinated trials involving hundreds of organisations have now been conducted in several countries, most following what organisers call the 100-80-100 model: employees receive their full salary and work eighty per cent of their previous hours, on condition that they maintain their full output. The headline results have been striking. Participants report less exhaustion, employers report easier recruitment, and the large majority of firms chose to continue with the arrangement once the trial period had ended. Such enthusiasm is understandable, yet the evidence, examined closely, is a good deal less decisive than the newspaper coverage has implied.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty concerns who took part. Lusine Arakelian, a labour economist at the Caucasus Institute for Labour Market Studies, has analysed the composition of the major trials and found that participating firms were disproportionately small, office-based and concentrated in professional services such as marketing, software and consultancy. Their managers, moreover, had volunteered precisely because they already believed in the idea. 'We are watching enthusiasts confirm their own expectations,' Arakelian remarks, 'and the economy as a whole looks nothing like them.' Her point is a fair one, but it can be pushed too far. The fact that the firms were not typical does not make their experience worthless; it shows what can be achieved where conditions are favourable, which is a reasonable place for any reform to begin.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second problem is how success was judged. Few trials measured productivity directly; most relied on revenue figures supplied by the companies themselves and on questionnaires in which employees rated their own well-being. Thandeka Mpofana, an occupational psychologist at the Southern Institute of Work Psychology, set out to address this weakness by tracking objective indicators instead. In a trial involving some forty firms, she recorded sickness absence and staff turnover, and asked volunteers to use wearable monitors that measured their sleep. Absence fell by roughly a third, and sleep on working nights lengthened by around half an hour. Mpofana is careful to add, however, that the improvements were largest in the first six months and partly faded thereafter, although a significant effect was still visible after a year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How did firms produce the same output in less time? According to Eero Vihavainen, who studies organisational change at the Lakeland Institute of Organisational Studies, the answer lies mainly in eliminating waste. Meetings were shortened or abolished, email was dealt with in batches, and many companies introduced 'quiet hours' during which interruptions were forbidden. In Vihavainen's view, the shorter week functions less as a reward than as a forcing device that compels organisations to confront inefficiencies they had tolerated for years. Yet he also found that in some firms the working day had become noticeably more intense, and that employees missed the casual conversations which had once filled the gaps between tasks. This social cost has been almost entirely ignored in public debate, and it deserves far more attention: informal contact is how newcomers learn and how colleagues come to trust one another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The arrangement is hardest to apply where work cannot be compressed. Hospitals, care homes, schools and shops must be staffed for set periods, and a nurse cannot treat patients more quickly simply because her week has been shortened. Marek Zubrzycki, a public finance economist at the Vistula School of Economics, estimates that in services of this kind, where output depends on hours of attendance, a four-day week on full pay would raise labour costs by up to a quarter. His arithmetic is sound as far as it goes, but it leaves out an important consideration. When one city council introduced the scheme for its administrative and care staff, vacancies in hard-to-fill roles fell sharply, and the savings on agency workers covered a substantial part of the additional cost.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is also worth distinguishing between different versions of the idea. Some employers have simply squeezed a five-day week into four longer days. This retains the three-day weekend but does not reduce total hours, and studies of shift workers suggest that fatigue accumulates towards the end of a ten-hour day, raising the risk of errors. Compressed schedules of this kind should not be confused with a genuine reduction in working time; they redistribute effort rather than lessening it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the trials have shifted the debate from whether a shorter week is possible to how and where it might work. That is real progress, though it hardly justifies calls for a universal four-day week imposed by law. A more lasting contribution may lie elsewhere. By showing how much of the ordinary working week was being lost to unnecessary meetings and constant interruption, the experiments have raised a question that applies to every organisation, whatever the length of its week.

topic: time-use diaries as a research method: overstated working hours in survey questions, falling response rates and weighting, recording simultaneous activities and valuing unpaid work, and smartphone and sensor alternatives
title: Accounting for Every Minute
subtitle: How researchers learned to measure the way people spend their days, and why the numbers remain contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask people how many hours they worked last week and most will give an answer without hesitation. Ask the same people to write down, slot by slot, everything they did over a single day, and a rather different picture tends to emerge. The second technique, known as the time-use diary, has a longer history than is often realised. The first large-scale diary surveys were carried out in the 1920s by planners who wanted to know how factory workers divided their time between labour, rest and political activity, and in the 1960s a multinational study spanning twelve countries established the method as a standard tool of social science. Today, national statistical offices in dozens of countries collect diaries in which respondents record their activities over twenty-four hours, typically in ten-minute slots. The method is laborious and far from flawless, but it remains the most dependable means yet devised of finding out how people actually spend their time.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its superiority is clearest when diary records are set against the answers people give to direct questions. Guðrún Kristjánsdóttir, a sociologist at the North Atlantic Institute for Social Research, compared the two for several thousand employees and found that estimates of weekly working hours were consistently higher than the totals implied by diaries. The discrepancy was modest for those reporting ordinary weeks, but it grew steadily with the hours claimed: respondents who said they worked more than sixty hours overstated their total by an average of around twelve. Kristjánsdóttir attributes this pattern less to faulty memory than to identity. People who regard themselves as hard-working, she suggests, report the week that corresponds to their image of themselves rather than the week they lived. The explanation is persuasive, although simple difficulty in recalling irregular hours probably plays a part as well.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The diary has weaknesses of its own, the most serious of which is the burden it places on respondents. Completing a detailed record of one's day is tedious, and participation has fallen sharply: some early national surveys achieved response rates of around seventy per cent, whereas several recent ones have struggled to reach forty. Those who decline are not a random group. People with the most demanding schedules are the least likely to find time for a diary, so the surveys may systematically understate how busy the population is. Budi Dewantara, a statistician at the Java Centre for Survey Methodology, argues that careful weighting, which gives extra importance to the responses of under-represented groups, can correct much of this bias. His confidence is not entirely misplaced, but weighting can only adjust for characteristics that are recorded, such as age, sex and occupation. If busy people within each of those groups are the ones who fail to respond, no amount of weighting will reveal it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication is that people often do two things at once. Most diaries therefore ask respondents to record a main activity and, separately, anything else they were doing at the same time. The choice of which to count makes an enormous difference. Much childcare, for example, takes place while parents are cooking, cleaning or travelling, and is therefore recorded only as a secondary activity; including such episodes can double estimates of the time parents spend with their children. Chiara Pellicciotti, an economist at the Tyrrhenian Institute of Applied Economics, has used diary data to argue that unpaid domestic work should be incorporated into national economic statistics, from which it is currently excluded. By her calculations, cooking, cleaning and caring would be worth more than a third of national output in some countries. The principle is sound, but the figure depends heavily on the wage chosen to value each hour: that of a paid housekeeper produces a far lower total than the earnings the person doing the work could have obtained elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Technology promises to lighten the burden on respondents. Smartphone applications can prompt participants at random moments to report what they are doing, while location tracking and wearable sensors record movement without any effort on the participant's part. A team led by Mikkel Rosbjerg at the Øresund Digital Behaviour Laboratory has compared these passive measurements with conventional diaries and found them considerably more accurate about where people were and when they travelled. What sensors cannot reveal, Rosbjerg concedes, is the meaning of an activity: a person seated at a desk may be preparing a report, paying household bills or simply browsing. For this reason, new tools seem likely to complement the diary rather than replace it, at least until the serious questions they raise about privacy have been resolved.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most intriguing finding to emerge from decades of diary research concerns the widespread sense of being short of time. In many wealthy countries, diaries show that the total amount of free time has not fallen since the 1960s and in some groups has actually risen, yet surveys reveal that people feel more rushed than ever. Kristjánsdóttir argues that the explanation lies partly in the fragmentation of leisure into brief, scattered intervals and partly in the growing number of households in which both adults are employed, making coordination of family life more difficult. Whatever the cause, the gap between measured and perceived time is itself an important social fact, and it would be a mistake to dismiss feelings of time pressure simply because the diaries fail to confirm them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of the method contains a broader lesson. Every number derived from a diary reflects a series of choices about what to count, whom to ask and how to classify what they report. Such choices are unavoidable, and acknowledging them openly is a strength rather than a weakness of the research.

topic: serious leisure: demanding amateur hobbies and volunteering as 'leisure careers', harmonious versus obsessive commitment, whether demanding jobs spill over into demanding hobbies, hobbies and adjustment to retirement, and volunteer organisations
title: The Pleasures of Effort
subtitle: Why do so many people spend their free time on pursuits that look remarkably like hard work?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a cold Saturday morning, a group of volunteers gathers in a railway shed to spend nine hours scraping rust from the boiler of a steam locomotive. Elsewhere, an amateur choir is preparing for its third rehearsal of the week, and a retired teacher is recording the brightness of a distant star for the fourth year running. None of these people is paid, and few would describe what they are doing as relaxing. Researchers have a name for such activities: serious leisure, defined as the systematic pursuit of an amateur, hobbyist or volunteer activity that demands considerable skill, knowledge and perseverance. It is usually contrasted with casual leisure, such as watching television or chatting with friends, which is immediately enjoyable and requires little training. The distinction is not new, but it deserves far more attention than it receives from policymakers, who tend to treat free time simply as the hours left over when work is done.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most detailed evidence comes from Yasmina Elbazzi, a sociologist at the Maghreb Centre for Social Studies, who spent four years observing amateur archaeologists and model engineers. She found that participants consistently described their involvement in terms borrowed from working life. They spoke of starting as novices, gradually acquiring expertise and eventually becoming respected figures who trained newcomers, a progression Elbazzi calls a 'leisure career'. Each pursuit formed a distinct social world, with its own specialised language, its own heroes and its own standards of good work. The rewards participants valued most were not momentary enjoyment but self-esteem, a lasting sense of identity and the feeling of belonging to a community. These, Elbazzi argues, are more durable than the pleasures of casual leisure, which tend to fade as soon as the activity ends.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, however, to present serious leisure as an unmixed blessing. Elbazzi's participants also reported frustration, disappointment and considerable expense, and several described tensions with partners who resented the hours spent in the workshop or at the excavation site. Zuzana Kelemenova, a psychologist at the Danube Institute of Behavioural Science, has refined this picture by distinguishing between two forms of commitment. Where a passion is harmonious, the person chooses freely when to engage in it and can set it aside without distress. Where it is obsessive, the activity seems to control the person rather than the reverse, and Kelemenova's surveys link this second form to conflict at home, neglect of other interests and, eventually, a kind of burnout familiar from studies of overworked employees. Accounts that celebrate dedicated hobbyists without acknowledging this darker side are telling only half the story.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How does serious leisure relate to paid employment? One long-standing view holds that people seek in their free time what their jobs fail to provide, so that those in dull, routine work should be drawn to absorbing and challenging hobbies. Thomas Brightwater, an economist at Pennine University, tested this idea using data that followed several thousand adults over two decades. He found little support for it. People in jobs offering variety and independence were considerably more likely to take up demanding pastimes, whereas those in repetitive, closely supervised work tended to favour casual leisure. Brightwater concludes that the skills and confidence developed at work spill over into free time. If he is right, inequality at work is reproduced in leisure as well. Yet his figures describe averages, and they should not be read as a rule: the long tradition of brass bands and choirs founded by miners and mill workers shows that demanding pastimes have flourished among people whose jobs offered very little independence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Serious leisure appears to matter most when paid work ends. Rosario Cordovilla, who studies ageing at the Iberian Observatory of Later Life, interviewed several hundred people in the years after retirement. Those who had established a demanding pursuit well before leaving work adjusted more successfully than those who had not, reporting greater satisfaction and a stronger sense of purpose. By contrast, retirees who took up a new hobby specifically to fill the gap seldom achieved the same benefits, perhaps because they lacked the skills and social connections that long involvement provides. The practical implication is that preparation for retirement should begin many years before it, and should concern time as much as money.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many organisations now depend on people engaged in serious leisure. Heritage railways, museums and conservation charities rely heavily on volunteers, and citizen science projects draw on the expertise of skilled amateurs. Such organisations, however, face a delicate balance. As they grow, they are often tempted to manage volunteers like employees, introducing targets, rotas and formal appraisals. Volunteers who joined for the satisfaction of self-directed work frequently respond by leaving. Organisations that wish to keep them must accept that the freedom to choose what to do, and when, is precisely what makes the activity attractive.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this implies that everyone ought to adopt a demanding hobby, or that casual leisure is worthless: rest and simple enjoyment are genuine goods in their own right. But public spending on leisure has traditionally concentrated on facilities for passive entertainment. A stronger case can be made for supporting the infrastructure that serious pursuits require, from community workshops and rehearsal spaces to local clubs and societies.

topic: busyness as a status symbol: the reversal of leisure as a sign of rank, cultural differences in how busy people are judged, scarcity and earned income, busyness as a claim to respectability, workload complaints on social media, and leisure turned into self-improvement
title: The Badge of Busyness
subtitle: Once a mark of low rank, being overstretched has become something to boast about. But who is boasting, and why?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the end of the nineteenth century, an influential critique of the wealthy argued that the upper classes displayed their position chiefly through idleness. Elaborate dinners, long country weekends and the cultivation of skills with no practical use all advertised the fact that their owners had no need to work. Anyone who visits a modern office, or scrolls through professional networking sites, will notice that this logic seems to have been turned on its head. 'I'm absolutely swamped' has become one of the commonest replies to a polite enquiry, and it is delivered with an unmistakable note of pride. The reversal is real and deserves explanation, but popular commentary has tended to exaggerate it, treating a pattern found mainly among certain groups in certain countries as though it were universal.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best evidence that busyness can confer prestige comes from a series of experiments by Agnieszka Sorokowska, a consumer researcher at the Silesian School of Marketing. Participants read short descriptions of an imaginary person and were asked to estimate that person's social standing. When the individual was described as working long hours with little time to spare, American participants rated them as higher in status than an otherwise identical person who enjoyed plenty of leisure. Among Italian participants, however, the result was reversed: the person with a relaxed schedule was judged the more successful. Sorokowska links the difference to beliefs about social mobility. Where people believe that effort is the main route to advancement, she argues, a crowded diary becomes evidence of ambition and worth; where success is seen as depending more on family background or connections, it carries no such meaning.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Femi Anjorin, an economist at the Lagos Institute of Economic Research, offers an explanation grounded in labour markets. In the past, he observes, the richest members of society typically lived on inherited land or investments, so their time had little market value. Today, a far larger share of top incomes comes from salaries and fees, and the hours of a senior lawyer or surgeon command a very high price. For such people, a schedule that is permanently full signals that their time is scarce and therefore valuable, in much the same way that a waiting list signals the desirability of a restaurant. The theory is elegant, but it has a conspicuous gap. People on modest wages, whose hours command no such premium, are often just as eager to tell others how hard-pressed they are, and Anjorin's account cannot explain why.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That gap is addressed by Lorenzo Sepulcri, a cultural sociologist at the Emilia Centre for Social Research, who has interviewed cleaners, delivery drivers and care workers about how they describe their days. For these workers, Sepulcri found, talk of exhaustion and long shifts functioned less as a boast than as a defence. In societies where idleness is associated with dependence on welfare, emphasising one's busyness is a way of asserting respectability and moral worth. This seems to me an important insight, because it suggests that the display of busyness is not merely a game played by elites but a response to the stigma that attaches to apparent inactivity at every level of society.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Digital media have given these displays a new stage. Ingrid Mortensrud, who studies online communication at the Bergen Media Laboratory, analysed thousands of social media posts in which users complained about their workload, often while mentioning an impressive project or an important client in passing. Such posts reliably attracted sympathetic and admiring replies. Yet in follow-up experiments Mortensrud found that readers who recognised the complaint as a disguised boast rated its author as less likeable and less sincere than someone who had simply stated their achievement. The strategy, in other words, works only for as long as nobody notices it, and as audiences become more alert to it, it may well do more harm than good.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The consequences extend beyond questions of image. Haruto Kaihara, a psychologist at the Kansai Institute of Occupational Health, has documented what happens when being busy becomes a source of esteem. In workplaces where long hours are admired, employees are reluctant to admit that they have any free time at all, and many leave part of their annual holiday entitlement untaken. Leisure itself, meanwhile, is increasingly justified by its usefulness: hobbies are reframed as opportunities for self-improvement, exercise is recorded and analysed, and even reading becomes a means of professional development. Of all the effects of the cult of busyness, this colonisation of free time by the values of work is the most troubling, since it deprives people of the one kind of time in which nothing needs to be achieved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What can be done? It is important to remember that the display of busyness and actual busyness are not the same thing. What has changed most is not necessarily how much people do but the story they feel obliged to tell about it, and stories, unlike working hours, can shift relatively quickly. Managers who openly take breaks and leave at a reasonable hour may do more to alter workplace norms than any official policy on well-being. Whether the prestige of the overstretched life will fade remains uncertain, but there is little reason to regard it as permanent.

topic: the right to disconnect from work messages outside working hours: expectations of availability and stress, overnight email shutdowns versus flexible hours, laws without enforcement, response-time agreements across time zones, and who the laws leave out
title: The Inbox That Never Closes
subtitle: Laws giving employees the right to ignore work messages after hours are spreading. Will they make any difference?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the end of the working day was marked by a physical event: the factory gate closed, the office emptied and the employee went home, beyond the reach of the employer until the following morning. The smartphone has dissolved that boundary. Messages now arrive at the dinner table, on the sofa and on holiday, and many employees feel obliged to answer them. In response, a growing number of governments have introduced what is usually called a right to disconnect. The details vary, but most such laws require employers above a certain size to agree with staff on rules governing contact outside working hours. The principle behind these measures is sound. Legislation, however, is a blunt instrument for regulating something as subtle as the expectations that colleagues hold of one another, and its effects so far have been modest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That the problem is real is not seriously in doubt. Paola Ubaldini, an organisational psychologist at the Turin Institute for Work and Health, followed several hundred office employees over two years and made a surprising discovery. The amount of time people actually spent dealing with messages in the evening was only weakly related to their levels of exhaustion. What mattered far more was whether they believed they were expected to remain available. Employees who felt they had to keep checking their phones reported greater fatigue even in weeks when very few messages arrived, a phenomenon Ubaldini describes as anticipatory stress. More strikingly still, the partners of these employees also reported lower well-being, suggesting that the costs of constant availability spread well beyond the workplace.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some companies have responded with technical solutions, configuring their servers so that emails are not delivered to staff between, say, eight in the evening and seven in the morning. Reza Bakhshandeh, an economist at the Caspian School of Business, evaluated several such schemes and found that they did reduce evening email traffic considerably. But they also produced unwelcome side effects. Messages that had been held back overnight arrived all at once, so that employees began each day facing a backlog. Moreover, the shutdowns penalised staff who deliberately chose unconventional hours, such as parents who left early to collect their children and preferred to finish their work once the children were asleep. Bakhshandeh's findings point to a genuine tension: protection from out-of-hours contact and freedom to choose when to work are both desirable, but they cannot always be pursued at the same time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Legal scholars have raised a different concern. Selam Eshetu, who specialises in employment law at the Addis Institute of Labour Studies, has examined how firms have complied with right-to-disconnect legislation in three countries. Since most of the laws oblige companies only to negotiate a policy, rather than imposing specific limits or penalties, compliance often amounts to little more than a document that few employees have read. Eshetu nevertheless resists the conclusion that such laws are pointless. Legislation, she argues, can gradually change what is considered normal, much as early laws on workplace smoking did before they were strictly enforced. The comparison is apt, though it should be remembered that smoking bans eventually succeeded because they were backed by clear rules that anyone could observe being broken; an unanswered email is far harder to police.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: International organisations face an additional complication, since one employee's evening is another's morning. Tomasz Drozdzik, a management researcher at the Baltic Business School, argues that the solution lies not in blocking messages but in changing what their arrival is taken to mean. In his trials with multinational firms, teams adopted explicit response-time agreements specifying that anything sent outside the recipient's working hours required no reply until the following working day, and senders were encouraged to use the scheduled-delivery functions built into most email software. After six months, the proportion of employees reading work messages in the evening had fallen by around forty per cent. This approach seems to me the most promising of those so far attempted, precisely because it addresses expectations directly rather than relying on technology to override them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further question is who the laws actually protect. Most exclude senior managers, whose contracts typically assume unlimited availability, and none apply to the self-employed. Gig workers, whose income depends on accepting tasks the moment they are offered, gain almost nothing from rules framed around a conventional employer and a fixed working day. There is a risk, then, that the right to disconnect will be enjoyed mainly by salaried employees who already have relatively secure conditions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the legislation should be abandoned. It does mean that its supporters should be realistic about what it can achieve on its own. The habits that keep employees tethered to their phones are formed by countless small signals, above all by the behaviour of managers, who need only send a single message at midnight to remind everyone that the working day has no clear end.

topic: time poverty and the gender gap in free time: defining a time-poverty threshold, how lack of money and lack of time compound, leisure shared with childcare, the 'mental load' of household planning, equal total workloads, and leave reserved for fathers
title: Whose Free Time?
subtitle: Researchers agree that some people are chronically short of time. They disagree about how to measure it, and about what the measurements reveal

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Economists have long measured poverty in terms of money, defining as poor those whose income falls below a certain threshold. Over the past two decades, a growing number of researchers have argued that time deserves similar treatment. A household may have an adequate income yet so little discretionary time that its members cannot rest, maintain friendships or take part in community life. The concept of time poverty captures something real, and it has drawn attention to groups whose hardship conventional statistics overlook. Unfortunately, there is no agreement on where the threshold should lie or which activities should count as obligatory, and estimates of the proportion of people who are time-poor range from under ten per cent to more than a third of the adult population. Some of the figures that circulate in public debate are, as a result, almost meaningless.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the more rigorous approaches has been developed by Dilnoza Mirzakhanova of the Central Asian Institute for Development Studies. Her measure adds together hours of paid employment, unpaid household work and essential personal care, and classifies as time-poor anyone whose remaining hours fall below a level judged necessary for rest and recovery. Applying it to survey data from eleven countries, she found that the most severely affected groups were lone parents and women in low-paid jobs who also bore most of the responsibility for their households. Crucially, Mirzakhanova argues that shortages of time and money reinforce each other. Better-off families can purchase time by paying for childcare, cleaning or ready meals; those on low incomes cannot, and so must supply these services themselves. This is surely right, and it explains why time poverty and income poverty so often occur together.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question of whether men and women differ in their free time has proved more contentious. Diary surveys in most countries show that men enjoy more hours of leisure than women, although the size of the gap varies considerably and in some Nordic countries it is small. Nomvula Ndiwane, a sociologist at the Durban Centre for Gender and Society, contends that counting hours seriously understates the difference. In her research, a far larger share of mothers' leisure than fathers' took place while children were present and in need of supervision, so that reading a newspaper or watching a film was repeatedly interrupted. Ndiwane calls this accompanied leisure, and argues that it provides much less genuine relief than time that is entirely one's own. Her findings suggest that any comparison based solely on the number of leisure hours will be misleading.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Fabrizio Delpiano, a psychologist at the Adriatic Institute of Applied Psychology, has gone further, arguing that diaries miss an entire category of effort. Running a household, he points out, involves not only cooking and cleaning but also planning meals, remembering appointments, anticipating when supplies will run out and keeping track of children's needs. This cognitive work, often called the mental load, is largely invisible because it is carried out in the background while people are doing something else. Using a questionnaire designed to capture such tasks, Delpiano found that women in couples carried the larger share in almost every household he studied. The idea is persuasive and corresponds closely to many people's experience. It is, however, difficult to measure with any precision, and there is a danger that it becomes a catch-all term into which any form of domestic dissatisfaction can be placed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that women are more pressed for time. Kasia Wojcikowska, an economist at the Pomeranian School of Economics, has pointed out that when paid and unpaid work are added together, the total working hours of men and women in many wealthy countries are remarkably similar. Men, on average, do more paid work and women more unpaid work, but the sums come out roughly equal. The real inequality, in her view, lies in the composition of work rather than its quantity, and she warns that exaggerated claims risk undermining public confidence in the research. This is a useful corrective, yet equal totals can conceal important differences. Paid work usually occurs in predictable blocks with clear boundaries, whereas unpaid care is scattered across the day and difficult to postpone. Two people with identical working hours may therefore experience very different degrees of pressure.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If time poverty is shaped by the division of household work, can policy change that division? Jacobus Pretorius, a social policy researcher at the Cape Institute of Social Policy, has studied countries that introduced paid parental leave reserved exclusively for fathers, which is lost if it is not taken. Uptake rose sharply in each case. More significantly, fathers who had taken such leave were still doing more routine childcare five years later than comparable fathers who had not. Few family policies can demonstrate effects of such duration, and the finding deserves more attention than it has so far received.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a strong case for official statistics to report time alongside income when describing living standards. The disputes outlined above, however, suggest that no single figure can do justice to the problem. A credible account of time poverty will need to consider not only how many hours people have to themselves, but also how fragmented those hours are and how much control people have over when they occur.

topic: why employees leave paid holiday unused: workload on return and lack of cover, unlimited-leave policies and downward norms, the fade-out of holiday benefits, psychological detachment and compulsory consecutive leave, and workers with no statutory entitlement
title: The Untaken Holiday
subtitle: Every year, millions of employees fail to use the paid leave they are entitled to. Who, or what, is to blame?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Paid annual leave is one of the great achievements of twentieth-century labour movements. Yet in a number of wealthy countries, a substantial proportion of employees do not take all of it. Surveys regularly find that the average worker leaves several days unused at the end of each year, and a minority take less than half of their allowance. At first sight this is puzzling, since unused leave is, in effect, time that the employer has already paid for and the employee has chosen to give back. The explanation most often offered in the press is that a culture of overwork has persuaded people that rest is a sign of weakness. There is some truth in this, but it is far too simple an account of a pattern that turns out to have several distinct causes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Marta Galczynska, a workplace psychologist at the Carpathian Institute of Work Psychology, surveyed several thousand employees about why they had not used their full entitlement. Concern about appearing uncommitted was mentioned, particularly in organisations that had recently made staff redundant. But by a clear margin, the most frequent reason was the prospect of the work that would be waiting on their return. In many teams, Galczynska found, nobody covered an absent colleague's duties, so that a fortnight away simply meant a fortnight's tasks accumulating in the employee's absence. For such workers, a holiday is less a release from work than a postponement of it, followed by a period of intense pressure. Seen in this light, unused leave is often a symptom of understaffing rather than of individual attitudes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some employers, particularly in the technology sector, have tried a radical alternative: abolishing fixed allowances altogether and allowing staff to take as much leave as they wish, provided their work is done. Pieter Vrielink, an economist at the Rhine Delta School of Economics, compared employees' behaviour before and after such policies were introduced and found that, on average, they took fewer days off than before. Without a defined entitlement, he suggests, employees look to their colleagues to judge what is acceptable, and since nobody wishes to be the person who takes the most, the norm drifts steadily downwards. Vrielink also notes that firms with unlimited leave no longer need to pay departing staff for holiday they have accumulated but not taken. It is hard to avoid the conclusion that such policies are frequently a way of reducing costs presented as an act of generosity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental question is whether holidays do people as much good as is commonly assumed. Daniel Matzkin, a health psychologist at the Buenos Aires Centre for Behavioural Health, tracked the mood, sleep and reported stress of several hundred employees before, during and after their summer breaks. Well-being rose sharply while they were away but had returned to its pre-holiday level within two to four weeks of their return. On the basis of this fade-out effect, Matzkin recommends that people spread their leave across several short breaks rather than concentrating it in one long holiday. His data are convincing, but the rapid fading of benefits does not mean that holidays are of little value. Long-term studies have associated regular holidays with lower rates of heart disease, although such findings cannot show that the holidays themselves were responsible.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What happens during a holiday matters as much as its length. Research on recovery consistently finds that time off restores people only if they are able to detach themselves mentally from their jobs. Employees who continue to check work emails while away gain markedly less than those who switch off completely, even if the time spent on email is brief. Some organisations have recognised this. A number of banks require employees to take at least two consecutive weeks of leave each year, a rule originally intended to expose fraud, since irregularities concealed by an employee tend to come to light during a prolonged absence. Whatever its origins, the rule guarantees a break long enough to allow genuine detachment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The debate about unused leave can obscure a larger inequality. Adebayo Ogunlesi, a sociologist at the Ibadan Institute of Social Research, has compared countries with and without a legal minimum entitlement to paid holiday. Where no statutory minimum exists, he found, many low-paid workers, especially those in part-time or casual jobs, receive no paid leave whatsoever, while well-paid professionals enjoy generous allowances. From this perspective, the problem of leave left untaken is largely confined to workers who are already relatively fortunate. Ogunlesi's analysis usefully shifts the focus of the debate from the choices of individual employees to the question of who has access to paid time off in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What follows for employers? If workload on return is the principal deterrent, then encouraging staff to take their holidays is pointless unless arrangements are made to cover their duties while they are away. Leave needs to be built into the planning of work rather than treated as an interruption to it. And as in so many areas of working life, managers' example counts for more than written policy: employees whose superiors visibly take their full allowance are far more likely to do the same.

topic: how retirement reshapes time use: the post-retirement dip in satisfaction and loss of time structure, whether retirement accelerates memory decline, the 'busy ethic' among retirees, couples retiring at different times, and phased retirement through bridge jobs
title: The Long Weekend
subtitle: Retirement hands people tens of thousands of unstructured hours. What they do with that time, and what it does to them, is more contested than one might expect

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A little over a century ago, retirement was a privilege enjoyed by few; most people worked until illness or death prevented them. Today, in wealthy countries, it is an expected stage of life that may last twenty years or more. It also brings the largest change in the use of time that most adults ever experience: overnight, some forty hours a week that were previously committed to employment become available for other purposes. Given the scale of this transition, it is remarkable how little reliable knowledge exists about how best to manage it. The advice offered to those approaching retirement is frequently contradictory, urging them in one breath to slow down and enjoy a well-earned rest and in the next to keep as active as possible.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Giulia Pirozzi, a gerontologist at the Vesuvian Institute of Gerontology, followed more than two thousand people for six years after they left work. She identified a characteristic pattern: satisfaction with life typically rose in the months after retirement, fell back during the second year and then stabilised. Pirozzi attributes the dip principally to the loss of time structure. Employment, she points out, supplies a framework of fixed hours, regular contacts and deadlines, and when that framework disappears, days can lose their shape. Those who quickly established routines of their own, such as regular commitments on particular days of the week, showed little or no decline. Her explanation is plausible, but it should be noted that the average dip was small and that a substantial minority of her participants did not experience it at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others have asked whether retirement affects the mind. Rafael Fonseca-Rios, an economist at the Atlantic School of Economics, compared memory test scores among older adults in a dozen countries with different official pension ages. In countries where people could draw a pension earlier, he found, memory scores declined more steeply in the years after sixty. Simple comparisons between retired and working individuals are hard to interpret, since poor health often causes people to retire early; by relying on national pension rules, which individuals cannot choose, Fonseca-Rios hoped to avoid this difficulty. The approach is ingenious. Nevertheless, countries with early pension ages may differ from others in their education systems, diets and health services, any of which could influence memory. The popular conclusion that mental activity at work protects against cognitive decline remains, for now, premature.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Eszter Takács-Veres, a sociologist at the Pannonian Institute of Social Research, has studied the way retired people talk about their time. A striking number insist that they have never been busier, listing committees, grandchildren and voluntary work with evident satisfaction. Takács-Veres calls this the busy ethic: a continuation, in retirement, of the values that once justified paid employment. In her view it is a healthy adaptation, since it allows retirees to present their lives as purposeful and to resist stereotypes of old age as a time of decline and dependence. There is much in this argument. Yet an ethic of busyness can also become a burden, making those who would simply prefer to rest feel that they have somehow failed at retirement.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Retirement is rarely an individual event, and Astrid Lindahl-Moreau of the Scandinavian Centre for Family Research has examined what happens when partners leave work at different times. Because wives are on average younger than their husbands, it is common for a husband to retire while his wife remains employed. In such households, Lindahl-Moreau found, the husband's free time rose substantially, but his share of domestic work increased only slightly, and the wife's satisfaction with the marriage fell. Satisfaction for both partners was highest when they retired at around the same time. These findings suggest that decisions about retirement are best understood as decisions taken by households rather than by individuals.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many experts now recommend a gradual transition, in which people reduce their hours or move into less demanding 'bridge' jobs before stopping work entirely. Studies regularly find that those who retire in this way report better health and well-being than those who stop abruptly. Søren Riisager, an economist at the Jutland Institute of Labour Economics, has questioned how much of this advantage is genuine. People who obtain bridge jobs, he notes, tend to be healthier, better educated and more highly skilled than those who do not, and such characteristics would improve their well-being in any case. When one country made phased retirement available to all older employees, Riisager found that the benefits were considerably smaller than earlier studies had implied, though they did not disappear altogether. The case for gradual retirement survives, then, but in a more modest form.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is that there is no single recipe for a successful retirement. How people experience their newly available time depends on their health, their finances, their relationships and their own temperament. Governments keen to promote what is often called active ageing should therefore concentrate on widening the options available to older people, such as flexible pension arrangements and opportunities for part-time work, rather than prescribing a particular way of spending the later years.
