topic: breaks during the working day: early factory rest pauses, what very short breaks do and do not achieve, which break activities restore people, self-chosen versus scheduled breaks, guilt about leaving the desk at lunch, and the 'recharging battery' metaphor
title: The Value of a Pause
subtitle: Research on breaks at work is challenging some long-held assumptions about rest, effort and productivity

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early decades of the twentieth century, researchers studying industrial fatigue made a discovery that surprised many factory owners. When workers performing repetitive tasks were given short, scheduled rest pauses during each shift, their total output frequently rose, even though they spent less time at their machines. The finding helped to establish the rest break as a normal feature of industrial employment. A century later, the situation in many workplaces looks rather different. Office employees routinely work through the morning without stopping, and eating lunch at one's desk while answering emails has become commonplace. Against this background, the recent revival of research on breaks is welcome. Some of its findings, however, have been reported with more enthusiasm than the evidence justifies, and a careful reading suggests a more qualified picture.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the popular interest has centred on micro-breaks, pauses of a few minutes taken between tasks. Valentina Imbrogno, an occupational psychologist at the Institute of Applied Ergonomics in Bari, has combined the results of several dozen experiments on breaks lasting under ten minutes. Her analysis shows that such pauses reliably increase feelings of vigour and reduce reported fatigue. Their effect on performance, by contrast, is modest, and it appears mainly in routine clerical work and physically demanding jobs. For complex intellectual tasks, such as writing or analysis, Imbrogno found little evidence that short pauses improved results at all. This is an important qualification of the claim, often repeated in management literature, that frequent micro-breaks will make any employee more productive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What people do during a break appears to matter at least as much as how long it lasts. Jean-Baptiste Delacroix-Ayo, who studies workplace health at the Rhône Centre for Organisational Health, asked employees to record their activities during every break over several weeks, along with their energy levels before and afterwards. Walking outdoors and simple relaxation produced the greatest recovery. Breaks spent browsing on a smartphone were markedly less restorative, although Delacroix-Ayo discovered that this was partly because many participants found themselves reading work-related messages during them. Social breaks gave mixed results: conversation with colleagues whom employees had chosen to join was beneficial, while obligatory chat, particularly with a supervisor, often left people more tired than before. The lesson seems clear: a break's content, rather than its duration, largely determines whether it does any good.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Should employees decide for themselves when to stop, or should breaks be scheduled? Ondřej Palacký, a management researcher at the Brno School of Management, has found that self-chosen breaks generally bring greater benefits than fixed ones, because workers can stop at natural pauses in their tasks. But his study of call-centre staff revealed a complication. Employees who were free to choose their own breaks took fewer than they needed, repeatedly postponing them until they were already exhausted. Palacký therefore proposes what he calls prompted autonomy: software reminds employees at intervals to take a break, but they may dismiss the reminder if they are in the middle of something. This seems a sensible compromise between the rigidity of fixed timetables and the risk that unrestricted freedom will simply be used to keep working.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The lunch break deserves particular attention. Mariana Tiradentes, a sociologist at the São Paulo Institute of Work and Society, found that employees who left their desks and genuinely stopped thinking about work at lunchtime reported significantly less fatigue by the end of the afternoon. Many, however, admitted that they felt guilty about leaving their workstations, fearing that colleagues would consider them less dedicated. Workplace norms appeared to be decisive. In one department she studied, a team leader began to take her lunch away from the office every day and to mention it openly; within weeks, most of her staff were doing the same. The guilt these employees describe is misplaced. Working through lunch may look like dedication, but if afternoon performance suffers as a result, it is a false economy.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Discussion of breaks is often framed by the metaphor of a battery that drains during work and must be recharged. The image is intuitive but misleading. It implies that people possess a fixed store of energy that is used up at a steady rate, whereas research suggests that the rate at which people tire depends heavily on whether they find their work interesting: tedious tasks exhaust people far more quickly than absorbing ones of equal difficulty. Imbrogno has suggested that breaks may work as much by restoring motivation as by replenishing energy, a possibility the battery image entirely obscures.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, it is worth questioning why breaks so often need to be defended in terms of output. Employers are more likely to accept them if they can be shown to raise productivity, and researchers understandably emphasise such effects. Yet even where breaks bring no measurable gain in performance, the fact that they make employees feel less exhausted and more able to enjoy their evenings is surely reason enough to provide them.

topic: product placement in film and television: conscious recall versus implicit effects, character association, disclosure rules, children and digital insertion
title: Brands in the Background
subtitle: Product placement has moved from the margins of entertainment to its centre, but whether it actually persuades anyone is still disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The practice of weaving commercial products into stories is almost as old as broadcasting itself. Early radio serials in the United States were paid for by firms that made soap powder, which is why the genre is still known by a name that recalls its sponsors. What has changed is scale. As viewers have learned to skip, mute or block conventional advertisements, companies have shifted money into placements that cannot be avoided because they are part of the programme. Industry surveys now describe the arrangement as one of the fastest-growing forms of marketing. Yet the confidence with which producers and brand managers speak about its effects runs well ahead of what the research has actually demonstrated, and the evidence that does exist points in several directions at once.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious way to judge a placement is to ask whether audiences remember it. Studies of this kind were pioneered by Dr Anong Kaewprasert of the Institute for Media and Commerce in Chiang Mai, whose team questioned viewers immediately after screenings and again a week later. Prominent placements, in which a character names a product or handles it in close-up, were recalled far more often than items glimpsed on a shelf. But Kaewprasert also measured how much participants liked the brands, and here the picture reversed. When a placement was conspicuous enough to interrupt the story, many viewers rated the brand less favourably than viewers who had not seen it at all. She describes this as a 'prominence trap': the very features that make a placement memorable can also make audiences feel that they are being sold to, and resent it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A quite different line of work suggests that memory may be beside the point. The psychologist Owen Hollingdrake, at the Northfield School of Communication, showed participants a short film in which an unfamiliar brand of fruit drink appeared only in the background of one scene. Afterwards, as a supposed reward for taking part, each person selected one item from a refreshment trolley. Those who had watched the film chose the featured drink noticeably more often than a control group, even though fewer than one in ten could recall having seen it. Hollingdrake argues that repeated, effortless exposure makes a product feel familiar, and that familiarity is quietly mistaken for preference. His findings are elegant, but they should not be over-interpreted. The brand was invented for the experiment, and when well-known products were used instead the effect largely disappeared, which suggests that background placement may matter most where consumers know least.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of who uses the product on screen. Research led by Farida Ramadhani at the Coastal University of Dar es Salaam found that viewers' feelings about a character tend to spill over onto whatever that character drinks, drives or wears. A watch worn by an admired detective gained in appeal; the same watch worn by a cruel employer lost it. Advertisers are well aware of this, and some contracts now specify that a product must never be used by on-screen villains, or must appear only in scenes with a positive emotional tone. In my view, this is where the practice becomes genuinely troubling. Placement is no longer a matter of a can on a table; it gives commercial partners a degree of influence over plots and characters that audiences cannot see and have not agreed to.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Regulators have responded mainly by requiring disclosure. In much of Europe, programmes containing paid placements must display a symbol at the start and end of a broadcast. The assumption is that viewers who are told about a commercial arrangement will view it more critically. Work by Dr Hana Kubelkova at the Central European Media Observatory complicates this picture. Disclosure did make viewers more likely to recognise that they had been the targets of persuasion, but it also increased the number who remembered the brand afterwards, presumably because the warning drew attention to it. Only when the notice appeared before the programme, rather than after it, did attitudes towards the brand become slightly more negative. Disclosure, it seems, is a far weaker safeguard than its supporters assume, and in some cases it may even work in the advertiser's favour.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These concerns are sharper where children are concerned. Younger viewers often fail to distinguish entertainment from commercial messages even when advertisements are clearly separated from programmes, and a placement removes even that boundary. A group at the Lagos Screen Audience Project, headed by Tunde Agbaje, interviewed children aged six to eleven after they had watched a cartoon featuring branded snacks. Most of the younger children could describe the snacks in detail, but very few suggested that anyone had paid for them to be there. There is a strong case, therefore, for banning placements in programmes made primarily for children, as several countries already do.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The newest development may change the debate altogether. Software can now insert products digitally into archived episodes long after filming, and in principle different audiences could see different brands in the same scene depending on where, or even who, they are. For advertisers, this promises the flexibility of conventional commercials combined with the unavoidability of placement. For writers and directors, it raises awkward questions about who controls the finished work. The real difficulty with product placement, perhaps, is not that it is irresistibly powerful, but that its effects are so varied and so hard to observe that neither viewers nor regulators can easily tell when it is working.

topic: neuromarketing (consumer neuroscience): brain imaging of responses to brands and advertisements, neural forecasting, the reverse-inference problem and the reliability of commercial services
title: Scanning the Shopper
subtitle: Neuromarketing promised to reveal what consumers really think of advertisements. Two decades on, its record is decidedly mixed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Advertisers have never entirely trusted what consumers tell them. People in focus groups praise commercials that later fail to shift a single product, claim they would pay more for ethically produced goods and then buy the cheapest option, and frequently cannot explain why they prefer one brand to another. In the early 2000s a new discipline offered a way around this problem. Neuromarketing, or consumer neuroscience as its academic practitioners prefer to call it, proposed to bypass self-report altogether by measuring the responses of the brain directly. Its tools range from functional magnetic resonance imaging, which tracks changes in blood flow deep inside the brain, to electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical activity at the scalp, along with cheaper measures such as eye-tracking. The ambition was understandable, but the history of the field has been as much a story of overpromising as of genuine discovery.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the early findings were genuinely illuminating. At the Molde School of Economics, Professor Ragnhild Søvdeflaten gave volunteers lying in a scanner small pieces of chocolate, labelled on some occasions as a luxury product and on others as a supermarket's budget range. In reality, every piece came from the same bar. Participants not only reported enjoying the 'luxury' chocolate more but also showed greater activity in a region of the brain associated with the experience of pleasure. Søvdeflaten argues that the label had altered the experience itself, rather than simply what volunteers were prepared to say about it, a distinction that questionnaires alone could never have revealed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More ambitious claims followed. Dr Temur Ishankhodjaev, who directs the Fergana Laboratory for Decision Neuroscience, showed forty volunteers three online videos produced to persuade people to register as blood donors. The volunteers' own ratings suggested that the first video would be the most effective. Activity in a brain region linked to judgements of personal relevance, however, pointed to the third, and when the videos were released nationally, the third generated by far the largest number of new registrations. Ishankhodjaev believes such results show that the brains of a small group can anticipate the behaviour of an entire population, an approach he calls neural forecasting. If he is right, a campaign could be tested on a few dozen people before millions are spent on distributing it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Dr Florencia Etcheverrigaray, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Mendoza Institute of Brain Sciences, argues that much of the field rests on a logical error known as reverse inference. Brain regions, she points out, are rarely dedicated to a single mental process: the area that becomes active when people experience pleasure also responds to surprise, anticipation and even physical pain. To observe activity there and conclude that a viewer likes an advertisement is therefore to reason backwards from an ambiguous signal. Etcheverrigaray adds that many studies use small samples and examine so many brain regions that some apparently significant results are bound to appear by chance. Her objection is, in my view, the most serious that the field faces, although it applies with almost equal force to large areas of conventional psychology.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such difficulties have not prevented a flourishing commercial industry. A number of agencies now offer EEG-based services that claim to measure a viewer's 'engagement' second by second as an advertisement plays, using algorithms that are proprietary and have rarely been published. Professor Min-jae Sagong of the Gwangju Marketing Research Centre decided to examine how consistent these services are. He sent the same twelve television commercials to three commercial providers and asked each to identify the most effective. In most cases the providers disagreed, and the level of agreement between them was no higher than would be expected if the rankings had been produced at random. Sagong notes that clients usually have no means of checking the methods for which they are paying.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that brain measures are worthless. Recent reviews combining the results of many studies suggest that adding neural data to conventional surveys improves predictions of advertising success, though only by a few percentage points. Sagong argues that for very large campaigns, where a small improvement in effectiveness can be worth millions, even this limited gain may justify the expense. Etcheverrigaray counters that less costly behavioural techniques, such as measuring how quickly people respond to a brand name, appear to capture much of the same information. Both may be right; the value of brain imaging probably depends on the size of the budget and the questions being asked.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Public anxiety about neuromarketing has tended to focus on the fear that companies will discover a 'buy button' in the brain and manipulate consumers against their will. That fear seems to me greatly exaggerated; nothing in the research so far suggests that such precise control is remotely possible. The more realistic danger is a different one: not that marketers will read minds, but that their clients will pay for the appearance of scientific certainty. Neuromarketing is best regarded as a modest supplement to traditional research, not as the window into the consumer's soul that its early promoters advertised.

topic: celebrity endorsement in advertising: the match-up hypothesis, meaning transfer, the 'vampire effect', endorser scandals and the rise of social-media influencers
title: Borrowed Glamour
subtitle: Companies pay vast sums to attach famous faces to their products. Researchers are still arguing about what, exactly, they are buying

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Using famous people to sell goods is hardly new. In the nineteenth century, stage actresses lent their names to soaps and face creams, and by the middle of the twentieth century sports stars were promoting everything from razors to breakfast cereal. Today, by some estimates, around one in five television advertisements in wealthy countries features a recognisable personality, and the largest contracts run to tens of millions of dollars. Such sums imply a confident understanding of how endorsement works. In reality, the assumptions behind them have rarely been examined with much care, and the research that has been done suggests that fame alone is a poor guide to commercial value.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Early theories were straightforward. Celebrities, it was argued, are attractive and widely trusted, and a message delivered by an attractive and trustworthy source is more persuasive than the same message delivered by a stranger. This explanation soon ran into difficulties, because some extremely popular figures proved remarkably ineffective at selling particular products. Professor Liisa Koivuniemi of the Tampere School of Economics proposed that what mattered was the degree of fit between the person and the product. In her experiments, a well-known runner was persuasive when recommending a sports drink but not when recommending a mortgage, while a lesser-known financial journalist performed better for the mortgage than the runner did. The suitability of an endorser for a given product, Koivuniemi concluded, counts for more than the size of the endorser's public profile.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious explanation was put forward by the anthropologist Femi Balogun, who studies consumer culture at the University of Ilorin. Balogun argues that celebrities are best understood as carriers of meaning. Through their roles, their public behaviour and the stories told about them, they accumulate associations such as toughness, sophistication or rebelliousness. An advertisement transfers these meanings to the product, and consumers who buy the product hope, in turn, to acquire something of them. On this account, what an advertiser is really purchasing is not fame as such but a specific bundle of associations. The theory has the considerable merit of explaining why relatively obscure figures, a respected chef or a little-known climber, can sometimes outperform global stars: they may carry exactly the meanings a brand needs, without the clutter that surrounds the very famous.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Celebrity can also work against the brand it is meant to serve. Dr Paola Castellucci, a marketing researcher at the University of Bologna, has documented what practitioners call the 'vampire effect'. In her recall tests, viewers who had watched advertisements featuring major stars frequently remembered the star in vivid detail while being unable to name the product. The more striking the celebrity, the greater the risk that attention is absorbed by the person rather than the brand. Castellucci also found that endorsers who promote many unrelated products are judged less credible by audiences, who reasonably suspect that the recommendation reflects the fee rather than any genuine enthusiasm. This finding seems to me entirely plausible, and it is surprising how often advertisers ignore it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most publicised danger is scandal. When an endorser is caught behaving badly, the brand linked to them may share the disgrace, and many contracts now contain 'morality clauses' allowing companies to withdraw. The economist Aigerim Kerimbekova examined the share prices of companies on the days after damaging news about their endorsers emerged. On average, the market value of these firms fell, but the decline was small and had usually disappeared within a few weeks. Her work suggests that the financial harm caused by scandals is considerably more modest than dramatic newspaper coverage implies. It does not follow, however, that such episodes are harmless, since share prices say little about slower changes in how ordinary customers regard a brand.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The rise of social media has complicated these debates further. So-called influencers, some with audiences of only a few thousand followers, are now paid to recommend products in posts that often resemble personal conversation rather than advertising. Koivuniemi's more recent work suggests that such figures are trusted precisely because they seem ordinary, and their recommendations are judged more authentic than those of film stars. In her surveys, followers frequently described such figures as friends or neighbours rather than as performers, and said they would be disappointed, but not especially surprised, to learn that a favourite influencer had been paid. Several countries now require paid posts to carry labels, although enforcement is patchy. The difficulty is that the line between a sincere recommendation and a paid one is becoming increasingly hard for audiences to see.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What these studies share is a rejection of the idea that celebrity is a simple commodity whose value rises with recognition. A famous face is better thought of as a tool, useful when its associations suit the product and potentially damaging when they do not, and its effects depend on the audience as much as on the person. Advertisers who choose endorsers mainly by measuring how many people know their names may be paying a great deal for the least important part of what they are buying.

topic: charm pricing (prices ending in 9): the left-digit effect, price endings as signals of value or quality, field evidence, habituation and price rounding after currency reform
title: The Power of Ninety-Nine
subtitle: Why do so many prices stop just short of a round number, and does the habit still fool anyone?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk through almost any supermarket and the same pattern repeats itself on shelf after shelf: 1.99, 4.49, 19.99. Surveys of retail prices in Europe and North America have found that a clear majority end in the digit nine, far more than would occur if prices were set purely by costs and margins. The practice, known in the trade as charm pricing, is old enough to have acquired its own folklore. One popular story holds that odd prices were introduced in the late nineteenth century to force shop assistants to open the till and give change, making it harder for them to pocket the money. It is an appealing tale, but there is no documentary evidence for it, and the far more likely explanation is that retailers simply discovered, by trial and error, that such prices seemed to sell more goods.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why they should do so remains contested. The best-known explanation concerns the way people read numbers. Because digits are processed from left to right, and because attention fades as one moves along the number, the first digit carries disproportionate weight. A price of 2.99 is therefore perceived as being much closer to two than to three. The economist Rasmus Djurhuus, working at the Copenhagen Business Academy, found a striking example of this in records of used-car auctions. Sale prices did not decline smoothly as the distance on a car's odometer increased; instead they dropped abruptly each time the reading crossed a multiple of ten thousand kilometres, so that a car with 59,900 kilometres fetched noticeably more than an otherwise identical one with 60,100. Buyers, it seems, were reacting to the leading digit rather than to the full figure.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second explanation treats the price ending as a message rather than a perceptual error. According to Dr Agne Pakalniskis of the Vilnius Institute of Consumer Studies, shoppers have learned that prices ending in nine tend to appear on discounted or economy goods, so the ending itself has come to signal a bargain. Round prices, by contrast, are associated with prestige and quality, which is why expensive restaurants and jewellers so often avoid nines. In one of her experiments, participants tasted the same wine at two prices; when it was labelled 20.00 rather than 19.99, they rated it as more refined. Neither explanation, in my view, need exclude the other. It is entirely possible that the left-digit effect first made nine-endings profitable and that, once they became widespread, they also acquired a meaning of their own.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Field evidence suggests that the effect can be large enough to override basic economics. The marketing scientist Wanjiru Wekesa collaborated with an online clothing retailer in Nairobi to test identical dresses at three different prices in randomly selected versions of its website. The dress sold best not at the lowest price but at the one ending in nine, which outsold a version priced slightly below it. Wekesa also noticed, however, that the advantage of the nine-ending shrank considerably when the item already carried a prominent 'sale' label. Her interpretation is that once a bargain has been announced in words, the price ending adds little further information, a finding that fits comfortably with the idea of the ending as a signal.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that charm pricing still works as well as it once did. The behavioural economist Mateo Villca, at the Andean University of Social Sciences, points out that consumers are now thoroughly familiar with the technique. In his surveys, a large proportion of shoppers reported that they deliberately round prices up when comparing products, so that 4.99 is mentally recorded as five. He also notes that a growing share of purchases are made by card or phone, often without the buyer studying the number at all. Villca therefore suspects that the effect is weakening. His argument is plausible, but it remains speculative: no study has yet tracked the size of the effect over a long enough period to show that it has actually declined.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Charm pricing may even have consequences beyond the individual shop. When a Pacific island nation replaced its currency with a new one some years ago, the economist Losa Matagi examined how retailers converted their prices. Rather than adopting exact equivalents, many shops rounded the converted figures up to the nearest price ending in nine, producing small increases across thousands of items. Consumers, Matagi found, widely believed that the new currency had caused a wave of inflation, and resentment of the reform persisted for years. Official figures, however, indicated that the rounding added only a fraction of a percentage point to the general price level. The episode reveals less about inflation than about perception: small and frequent changes to familiar prices are noticed far more than their economic significance would justify.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Is charm pricing a form of deception? It would be difficult to argue so with much force. The full price is displayed, nothing is hidden, and the sums involved are tiny. Compared with practices such as adding compulsory fees at the final stage of an online purchase, it is a relatively innocent device, and regulators have rightly concentrated their attention elsewhere. Its persistence is nevertheless revealing. Economic models have traditionally assumed that buyers process prices accurately; the stubborn popularity of the nine suggests that they often do not, even if, as Villca argues, they are learning to see through the trick.

topic: ambient scent in retail environments: effects on browsing and spending, congruence with products and music, simple versus complex scents, arousal, memory, habituation and staff welfare
title: Selling by the Nose
subtitle: Shops and hotels increasingly perfume the air in the hope of influencing what customers feel and buy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Step into certain clothing stores, hotel lobbies or car showrooms and you may notice a faint but distinctive smell: vanilla, perhaps, or cedar, or freshly cut grass. It is unlikely to be accidental. A specialised industry now designs 'signature scents' for businesses and installs equipment that releases them through ventilation systems. Its promotional literature speaks confidently of longer visits, stronger brand loyalty and double-digit increases in sales. The scientific literature on ambient scent is considerably more cautious, and a careful reading of it suggests that the commercial claims have been inflated well beyond what the evidence can bear.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest systematic studies concentrated on whether a pleasant scent, of any kind, changes behaviour. Dr Ragnar Bergsveinsson, then at the Reykjavik School of Business, arranged for a department store to scent one floor while leaving another unscented, and observed shoppers over several weeks. Customers on the scented floor stayed somewhat longer, and in interviews they described the merchandise as more attractive and the store as more modern. Yet when Bergsveinsson examined the till receipts, the difference in spending between the two floors was small and varied from week to week. His results, in other words, showed that scent could improve how people felt about a shop without reliably altering what they paid. They are sometimes cited as proof that scent boosts sales, but that is not what they demonstrate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Later work suggested that the type of scent matters as much as its presence. The consumer psychologist Selin Ozdogan of Bosphorus Commercial University tested scents in combination with background music during the weeks before a winter holiday. When a festive scent of cinnamon and orange was paired with seasonal music, shoppers rated the store highly; when the same scent was paired with ordinary pop music, their ratings of the store actually fell below those recorded with no scent at all. Ozdogan also compared a simple, single-note scent of lemon with a complex blend of several ingredients. Shoppers exposed to the simple scent spent more, which she attributes to the fact that it demands less mental effort to process, leaving more attention for the goods themselves. The lesson for retailers seems clear: a scent that fails to suit its surroundings may be worse than none.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A related line of research concerns stimulation. Professor Darya Rumyantseva of the St Petersburg Institute of Trade has studied how scent and music work together to raise or lower shoppers' level of arousal. Energising scents such as peppermint and fast, loud music each tend to make people more alert, but in her experiments the two combined produced a sense of being overwhelmed, and satisfaction with the visit dropped. Calming scents paired with slow music, conversely, could make a nearly empty shop feel dull. Rumyantseva argues that the right degree of stimulation is not fixed but depends on how crowded the store already is, since a busy shop supplies plenty of arousal of its own.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most intriguing findings concern memory. Smell is closely connected with the brain regions involved in emotion and recollection, and marketers have long hoped to exploit this link. In a study led by Thabo Sekgobela at the Pretoria Centre for Consumer Research, participants examined products in plain or lightly scented packaging. Two weeks later, those who had handled the scented versions recalled noticeably more details about the products, including features that had nothing to do with the smell. Interestingly, the advantage was greatest among participants who said afterwards that they had not consciously noticed any scent, which implies that the effect operates largely below the level of awareness. This suggests that the value of scent may lie less in prompting immediate purchases than in helping a brand lodge itself in the memory.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are, however, obvious limits. People differ widely in their sensitivity to smells and in the smells they enjoy, and preferences vary from one culture to another, so that a scent welcomed in one country may seem unpleasant or even medicinal in another. A minority of customers report headaches or breathing difficulties in heavily perfumed spaces. Moreover, the nose adapts quickly: within a few minutes of entering a scented shop, most people are no longer aware of the smell at all. The group least often considered is the staff, who may spend eight hours a day breathing air that customers encounter for twenty minutes. Their welfare has received remarkably little attention in either the commercial or the academic literature, and it deserves much more.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that ambient scent is useless or sinister. Its effects appear to be modest, they depend heavily on context, and they are easily cancelled out by a poor choice of fragrance. Compared with marketing techniques that exploit time pressure or hide the true cost of a purchase, perfuming the air is a mild form of influence. It may be most accurately described as one element in the overall atmosphere of a shop, comparable to lighting or music, rather than as a hidden lever that can be pulled to release spending.

topic: greenwashing in advertising: vague and irrelevant environmental claims, hidden trade-offs, the 'green halo' of packaging, spillover scepticism, offset-based carbon-neutral claims and 'greenhushing'
title: Shades of Green
subtitle: Environmental claims have become one of advertising's most popular selling points, and one of its most difficult to trust

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few marketing messages have spread as quickly in recent years as the promise that a product is good for the planet. Detergents are described as 'eco', clothing as 'conscious', airline tickets as 'carbon neutral' and almost anything in brown cardboard as 'natural'. Regulators have begun to examine these claims more closely, and the results have not been reassuring: one review of online advertising by a European consumer authority concluded that more than half of the environmental claims it examined were vague, misleading or impossible to verify. It would be a mistake, however, to imagine that the problem consists mainly of outright lies. Far more common, and far harder to police, are claims that are technically true yet leave consumers with an impression that the facts do not justify.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A useful way of classifying such claims was developed by Dr Kaisa Toivanen at the Turku School of Sustainable Business. Her team audited several thousand products sold in Nordic supermarkets and grouped misleading claims into a small number of types. Some relied on vague terms such as 'green' or 'environmentally friendly' that have no agreed definition. Others were irrelevant claims, such as announcing that an aerosol contains no substance that has in any case been prohibited for decades. The most frequent category, however, involved hidden trade-offs: emphasising a single favourable attribute, such as recycled packaging, while saying nothing about far larger impacts arising from how the product itself is made or used. Toivanen notes that this kind of claim is especially effective because every individual statement in it can be defended.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How do consumers respond to such messages? The experimental work of Professor Marco Lombardini at the Milan Institute of Consumer Behaviour suggests that they are poorly equipped to distinguish genuine information from decoration. In one study, participants were shown products carrying either labels issued by independent certification bodies or logos designed by the manufacturers themselves. As long as the company logos featured images of green leaves or globes, they were rated as almost exactly as trustworthy as the independent labels. Lombardini also found that simply printing a package in shades of green, without any written claim at all, led participants to judge the product more environmentally friendly, a phenomenon he describes as a 'green halo'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One might suppose that the remedy lies in public exposure, since highly publicised scandals should teach consumers to be more careful. The research of Dr Alsu Abdulkadirova at the Volga Institute of Marketing indicates that the lesson learned is a blunt one. After reading news reports about a company caught making false environmental claims, participants in her studies became more sceptical not only of that company but of green claims in general, including accurate ones made by firms with excellent records. She calls this effect 'spillover scepticism'. Her findings point to what is arguably the most compelling case for stricter regulation: it is not simply that consumers are misled, but that responsible companies lose the commercial reward for genuine effort when every claim is treated as suspect.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Claims of carbon neutrality raise particular difficulties. In most cases, a company that describes a product in this way has not eliminated the emissions involved in making it, but has paid for projects elsewhere, such as tree planting or forest protection, that are supposed to compensate for them. The environmental economist Claudine Nzeyimana, at the Kigali Centre for Climate Policy, has examined a sample of such projects and concluded that many deliver far smaller benefits than they claim, either because the forests concerned were never under threat or because the carbon they store may later be released by fire or logging. Her consumer surveys add a further problem: a majority of respondents believed that a carbon-neutral product had been manufactured without producing any emissions at all. Given this misunderstanding, it is difficult to see how claims based largely on such compensation schemes can be anything other than misleading, and several jurisdictions are now moving to restrict them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Paradoxically, closer scrutiny may be producing the opposite problem. Kwabena Kuwornu, a management researcher at the Accra School of Business, has drawn attention to what he calls 'greenhushing': the decision by firms to stay silent about genuine environmental achievements for fear of attracting criticism or legal challenge. In a survey of several hundred large companies, around a quarter admitted that they had chosen not to publicise sustainability targets or results in the previous year. Kuwornu warns that such silence deprives consumers and investors of useful information. His concern is legitimate, but his figures may overstate the scale of the problem, since some companies that remain silent may do so simply because their achievements would not withstand close examination.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be done? The evidence reviewed here makes one conclusion difficult to avoid. Ordinary shoppers, deciding between products in a matter of seconds, cannot reasonably be expected to investigate certification schemes or assess the quality of forest projects on the other side of the world. The burden of substantiation must lie with the companies that make the claims, supported by legally defined terms and independent verification. At the same time, rules should not be so restrictive that firms making real progress find it safer to say nothing at all. The aim is not to silence environmental advertising, but to make it mean something again.

topic: advertising repetition and wear-out: the two-factor model of liking, humorous versus informative ads, variation strategies, frequency capping online, spaced versus massed exposure and wear-in
title: How Often Is Too Often?
subtitle: Advertisers have argued for a century about how many times a message should be repeated. The answer turns out to depend on more than the number

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every advertising campaign must answer a deceptively simple question: how many times should the audience see it? Too few exposures, and the message may never register; too many, and money is wasted or, worse, viewers grow irritated. For decades the industry relied on rules of thumb, the most famous being that three exposures are enough for an advertisement to have its full effect. The rule is still quoted in training courses and media plans. Yet it rests on remarkably little evidence, and the research of the past few decades suggests that the search for a single magic number was misguided from the start.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Psychologists have long known that people tend to like things more the more often they encounter them, provided those things are neutral to begin with. Advertisers naturally hoped that the same would hold for their messages. The consumer researcher Sigrid Eskeland, at the Oslo Institute of Marketing Science, tested this by showing participants the same television commercial between one and ten times within a longer programme. Liking for the advertisement, and for the brand it promoted, rose over the first few showings but then levelled off and declined. Eskeland interprets this pattern as the result of two competing processes. Early repetitions help viewers understand and become comfortable with the message; later ones produce boredom and a sense of being pressured, which eventually outweigh the benefits.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The point at which decline sets in, known in the trade as wear-out, varies considerably between types of advertisement. In a series of studies, Dr Joaquín Samaniego of the Pacific School of Business in Lima found that humorous commercials wore out fastest of all. A joke depends on surprise, and once viewers know the punchline, much of the pleasure disappears. Advertisements that presented facts about a product, by contrast, declined far more slowly, perhaps because viewers continued to extract information from them. Samaniego also tested ways of postponing wear-out. Simply running shorter, cut-down versions of the same commercial made little difference, but producing several altered versions that conveyed the same message in different settings kept audiences responsive for much longer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Online advertising has transformed the scale of the problem. Because platforms can track individual users, an advertiser can in principle show the same person the same message dozens of times in a single day. Hery Ramanantsoa, a data scientist at the Antananarivo Centre for Digital Economics, analysed millions of impressions on a large advertising network and found that the proportion of users who clicked fell steeply after the fourth showing in one day. Many platforms now allow advertisers to set a 'frequency cap' limiting how often any individual sees a message, but such caps are optional, and Ramanantsoa found that fewer than half of the campaigns in his sample used one. More troubling was what happened next. Users who had been shown an advertisement very frequently expressed more negative opinions of the brand in follow-up surveys, and they were more likely to install software that blocks advertisements altogether. Irritation, in other words, did not stay attached to the advertisement; it spread to the brand itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every researcher accepts that wear-out is as serious as these findings imply. Professor Beata Leczycka of the Krakow University of Economics points out that most laboratory studies, including Eskeland's, compress all the exposures into a single session lasting an hour or so. In everyday life, by contrast, people usually encounter a commercial at intervals spread over days or weeks, and Leczycka's own experiments suggest that such spaced repetition produces much less boredom. She notes that some television campaigns have run successfully for many years without obvious loss of effect. Her criticism of laboratory methods is well founded. It is less clear, however, that it applies to the online world, where the practice of following users from website to website effectively recreates the concentrated exposure that she regards as artificial.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also an opposite danger. Some advertisements, particularly those that are unusual or complex, appear to need several exposures before they have any measurable effect at all, a process sometimes called wear-in. Campaigns of this kind can easily be abandoned too early. In my view, this happens more often than is generally admitted, and for a revealing reason: the people who commission and approve advertisements see them far more often than the public does, in meetings, presentations and tests, and they may grow tired of a campaign long before most consumers have properly noticed it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is not a number but a set of conditions. The effect of repetition depends on the type of message, on how varied its executions are, on the intervals between exposures and on the medium through which it is delivered. An advertisement full of facts, seen occasionally over several months, may continue to work long after a clever joke shown four times in an evening has begun to annoy. Measuring these conditions is harder than counting exposures, which may partly explain why the old rules of thumb have survived for so long. Advertisers who still plan campaigns around a fixed frequency are, in effect, applying a single answer to a question that has many.

topic: restricting the marketing of unhealthy food to children: development of persuasion knowledge, effects on snack consumption, broadcast time bans and displacement, industry self-regulation, advergames and evidence on obesity
title: Hungry Eyes
subtitle: Governments are under pressure to limit the advertising of sugary and fatty foods to children. Whether such limits work is a harder question than either side admits

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A child growing up in a wealthy country today may see thousands of food advertisements a year, on television, on packaging, in games and on video-sharing sites. Content analyses consistently show that the great majority of these promote products high in sugar, fat or salt: breakfast cereals, confectionery, fast food and soft drinks. At the same time, rates of childhood obesity have risen steeply in many countries over the past four decades. It would be simplistic to treat advertising as the principal explanation for this trend, which also reflects changes in diet, transport, family life and the price of food. But it would be equally mistaken to dismiss its contribution, and the real debate is no longer whether marketing influences children's eating, but what, if anything, can effectively be done about it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the case for treating children differently from adults rests on developmental research. Dr Maarja Kirsipuu, a developmental psychologist at the University of Tartu, has studied how children's understanding of advertising changes with age. Most children can distinguish advertisements from programmes by about the age of five, but they generally do not grasp that advertisements are designed to persuade them until around eight. Even more importantly, Kirsipuu found that older children who could explain the purpose of advertising perfectly well were no less influenced by it in practice; knowing that a message is persuasive, it seems, does not automatically lead a child to resist it. For this reason the age thresholds written into many regulations, commonly twelve or sixteen, are inevitably somewhat arbitrary, yet they are not without justification.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The food industry has often argued that advertising does not make children eat more, but merely persuades them to choose one brand rather than another. Experimental work by Professor Arben Hajdari at the Tirana Institute of Public Health challenges this claim. Children who watched a cartoon interrupted by food advertisements subsequently ate considerably more from a selection of freely available snacks than children who saw advertisements for toys, and the increase was not confined to the brands that had been advertised. If advertising raises consumption across an entire category of food, the argument that it simply redistributes sales between competitors loses much of its force.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Several governments have responded by banning advertisements for unhealthy foods during programmes made for children. The results have been instructive. Pema Dorjee, a health economist who evaluated one such scheme, found that children's exposure to the restricted advertisements during children's programmes fell sharply, as intended. However, advertisers moved much of their spending to the early evening, to family entertainment shows and sports broadcasts that large numbers of children also watch. Once these programmes were taken into account, the reduction in children's total exposure was considerably smaller than the government had anticipated. Dorjee concluded that rules defined by the type of programme are easily circumvented, and that restrictions based on the time of day are likely to be more effective.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Elsewhere, governments have preferred to rely on voluntary pledges by food and drink companies. These schemes allow firms to set their own nutritional standards and to decide which audiences count as children. Chanda Lungu, a public health researcher based in Lusaka, has audited several such pledges and found that they typically apply only to programmes in which children make up more than a third of the audience. Because most children's viewing takes place during programmes aimed at a general audience, the pledges leave untouched the majority of the advertisements that children actually see. Industry bodies point to high rates of compliance with their codes, but compliance with rules that companies have written for themselves proves very little. Self-regulation of this kind cannot reasonably be regarded as a substitute for legislation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the media landscape has moved on. Much food marketing now takes forms that broadcast regulations were never designed to address: branded online games known as advergames, cartoon characters on packaging, and videos in which young presenters unwrap and taste products. Dr Nare Melikyan of the Yerevan Centre for Media and Childhood asked children aged seven to eleven to identify the advertising in a series of online activities. While most recognised conventional banner advertisements, very few realised that a game featuring a cereal brand's mascot had been created to sell cereal. Digital platforms also allow messages to be targeted at individual children on the basis of their viewing histories, a practice that is extremely difficult for parents, let alone regulators, to observe.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Critics of restrictions often point out that no study has yet shown that an advertising ban has reduced rates of childhood obesity. This is true, but it is less damaging than it sounds. Body weight is influenced by so many factors that the effect of any single measure would be extremely difficult to isolate, and the restrictions introduced so far have been partial and easily evaded. The more reasonable conclusion is that advertising rules should be comprehensive, covering digital media as well as television, and that they should form one part of a wider set of policies on food pricing, labelling and school meals. On their own, they were never likely to reverse a problem with so many causes.

topic: comparative advertising that names rival brands: its legalisation, effects on attention and credibility, misattribution to the rival, selective information, cultural differences and legal challenges between competitors
title: Naming the Rival
subtitle: Once regarded as bad manners, advertisements that openly compare one brand with another are now commonplace. Have they delivered what their supporters promised?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, advertisers in most countries observed an unwritten rule: you could praise your own product as extravagantly as you liked, but you did not mention your competitor's. Broadcasters often refused advertisements that named rival brands, and in several European countries the practice was effectively prohibited by laws against unfair competition. Attitudes began to change in the 1970s, when consumer protection agencies in North America started to encourage comparative advertising on the grounds that it would give shoppers more information with which to judge competing products. Europe followed, more cautiously, at the end of the 1990s, permitting comparisons provided they were objective, verifiable and not misleading. Underlying these reforms was the conviction that more information makes markets work better. That conviction has turned out to be only partly justified.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first question is whether comparative advertisements actually work. Dr Henrik Brannvall of Uppsala University combined the results of more than seventy experiments in a statistical review. He found that, compared with conventional advertisements, comparative ones attracted more attention and were better remembered, but they were also judged less credible, and they sometimes left viewers with a less favourable opinion of the advertiser, who could appear aggressive or petty. The balance between these effects depended heavily on the advertiser's position in the market. For small or recently launched brands, the gains in attention generally outweighed the costs; for established market leaders, comparative advertising rarely produced any net benefit, since they had little to gain from being associated with smaller rivals.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is a further hazard, which might be called the problem of the borrowed spotlight. The marketing researcher Valentina Sepulveda, at the Santiago School of Commerce, tested viewers' memory of comparative advertisements a few days after they had seen them. A substantial minority confidently named the wrong company as the sponsor, most often crediting the well-known rival that had been mentioned rather than the challenger that had paid for the advertisement. The more familiar the rival, the more frequent the error. There is a certain irony in this: a campaign designed to take customers from the market leader may, through simple confusion, end up giving that leader free publicity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What of the informational benefits on which the reforms were based? Here the evidence is genuinely mixed. The economist Nurlan Ibraimov, at the Bishkek Institute of Market Studies, analysed the content of several thousand advertisements and found that comparative ones were indeed more likely than others to contain checkable facts, such as prices, fuel consumption or battery life. Yet the facts they contained were highly selective. Advertisers almost invariably compared their products on the attributes where they performed best and remained silent about those where they performed worse. The information supplied is therefore real but partial, and there is little reason to suppose that ordinary consumers make allowance for what has been left out. Most people, in my view, take the comparison they are shown as if it were the whole picture.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Responses also vary from one culture to another. Dr Ieva Vilkaite of the Kaunas Centre for Cross-Cultural Marketing presented the same advertisements to consumers in several countries. In societies that place a high value on social harmony and indirect communication, direct comparisons that named a rival were frequently perceived as rude, and they damaged the reputation of the advertiser. Indirect comparisons, which referred only to 'other leading brands', were received far more positively in those countries. Vilkaite's work helps to explain why international companies that run aggressive comparative campaigns in one market often adopt a much gentler style elsewhere, sometimes for exactly the same product.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Comparative advertising has had one consequence that its early advocates did not fully anticipate: a steady stream of legal disputes. Companies that feel misrepresented by a rival's advertisement frequently challenge it, either before industry review bodies or in the courts, and advertisers must be prepared to demonstrate that every claim can be substantiated. This system of mutual scrutiny has real advantages. Competitors know their own markets intimately and have every incentive to expose a misleading claim, and they are often far more effective at doing so than regulators with limited budgets. The difficulty is that litigation is expensive, and the fear of being sued may deter precisely the small and new firms that, as Brannvall's work suggests, have the most to gain from comparing themselves with larger rivals.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Today the most common comparisons are not dramatic television confrontations but routine claims about price, made by supermarkets, insurers and energy suppliers, often reinforced by independent comparison websites. These are, on the whole, more useful to consumers than the brand rivalries of earlier decades, because price is easy to verify. Taken as a whole, comparative advertising has proved neither the great informational advance that its supporters hoped for nor the descent into mudslinging that its critics feared. Like most forms of advertising, it informs a little, persuades rather more and depends for its honesty largely on the vigilance of those it targets.

topic: scarcity cues in marketing: supply-based versus demand-based scarcity, reduced deliberation, false stock warnings and countdown timers online, consumer scepticism and limited-edition releases
title: Only Three Left
subtitle: Warnings that a product is about to run out are among the oldest tools of persuasion. Online, they have become almost impossible to avoid, and frequently impossible to believe

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has booked a hotel room or bought clothes online will be familiar with the messages: 'Only three left in stock', 'Twelve people are looking at this right now', 'Offer ends in 09:59'. They draw on one of the most robust findings in the psychology of persuasion, namely that things appear more desirable when they seem to be in short supply. In a well-known early experiment, participants rated identical biscuits as more appealing when they were taken from a jar containing only two than when the jar held ten. Scarcity, it seems, is read as a sign of value. The principle itself is sound, and there is nothing inherently dishonest about telling customers that a product is running low. What has changed is the ease with which such signals can now be manufactured, and the scale on which this is being done.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Not all scarcity works in the same way. The consumer psychologist Yelena Kapoustina, of the Novosibirsk Higher School of Retail Studies, distinguishes between scarcity that arises because a product has been made in limited quantities and scarcity that arises because many people are buying it. The second kind, she argues, functions as a form of recommendation: if a product is selling fast, other buyers must have judged it worth having. In her experiments this type of message was particularly effective for everyday goods such as kitchen equipment, where shoppers wanted reassurance that they were making a sensible choice. Limited production, by contrast, signalled exclusivity, and it was most persuasive for luxury items and among shoppers who expressed a strong desire to stand out from others. For such buyers, evidence of popularity could actually reduce a product's appeal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why are scarcity messages so effective? A study by Dr Mwila Chibwe at the Copperbelt Institute of Consumer Science offers a revealing answer. Participants browsed a simulated online shop in which some products carried low-stock warnings and others did not. When a warning was displayed, participants spent less time on the product page, consulted fewer customer reviews and were more likely to buy within the first minute. Chibwe concludes that scarcity cues work less by increasing the perceived value of a product than by cutting short the process of comparison. This, in my view, is the heart of the matter. A message that encourages people to think less carefully about a purchase is in a different category from one that simply gives them useful information about availability.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The question of honesty becomes pressing once it is recognised how often such messages are false. Researchers led by Bertrand Eyenga at the University of Yaoundé Centre for Digital Commerce examined several thousand retail and travel websites using automated software. On a substantial proportion of sites, countdown timers simply started again from the beginning when the page was reloaded, and 'limited stock' notices appeared regardless of how many items were actually available. Some sites displayed claims about the number of other shoppers viewing a product that were generated at random. Eyenga's team estimates that roughly one in ten scarcity messages they recorded was demonstrably fabricated, and they stress that this figure is a minimum, since many false claims cannot be detected from outside the company.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One might expect consumers to adapt, and to some extent they do. Kristjan Saarepuu, a behavioural economist at the Tallinn School of Economics, has tracked the responses of regular online shoppers over two years. The influence of scarcity messages on purchasing declined steadily as participants encountered them more often, and shoppers who discovered that a particular site used fake timers became markedly less willing to buy from it at all. Saarepuu argues that false scarcity is therefore self-defeating in the long run, since it erodes the credibility on which honest warnings depend. This may well be true, but it offers little comfort in the short term. Learning of this kind is slow and uneven, and those who shop online least often, who are frequently older or less confident with technology, are precisely the people who have had the least opportunity to acquire it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Regulators have begun to take notice. Consumer authorities in several jurisdictions have classified fake countdown timers and invented stock warnings as unfair commercial practices, and a number of travel booking sites have been required to change the way they present availability. Enforcement, however, depends on proving that a particular claim is untrue, which is difficult when the relevant data are held by the company itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A rather different case is presented by limited-edition releases, such as trainers or collectable toys issued in deliberately small quantities on announced dates. Here the scarcity is genuine and openly declared; nobody is misled about how many items exist. Such releases have nevertheless created problems of their own, notably thriving resale markets in which much of the stock is bought within seconds by automated programmes and resold at several times the original price. Whether the manufacturers regard this as a regrettable side effect or a welcome source of publicity is not always easy to tell.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The lesson from this research is not that scarcity messages should be prohibited altogether. Accurate information about availability can genuinely help consumers, for example by warning them that a flight is nearly full. The problem lies with claims that are invented, and with designs whose purpose is to hurry people past the point at which they might reconsider. Nor can the problem safely be left to consumers themselves; as Saarepuu's own figures suggest, scepticism develops too slowly, and too unequally, to serve as adequate protection.

topic: social impact bonds (pay-for-success contracts): outcome-based payment, weak evaluation designs, transaction costs and the real distribution of risk, cream-skimming and the influence on ordinary commissioning
title: Investing in Outcomes
subtitle: Social impact bonds promised to bring the discipline of the market to public services. More than a decade on, the evidence is decidedly mixed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late 2000s a new financial instrument began to attract attention among governments, charities and investors. Under a social impact bond, private investors provide the up-front capital needed to run a social programme, such as reducing reoffending among released prisoners or keeping vulnerable children out of residential care. An independent evaluator then measures whether agreed targets have been met. If they have, the government repays the investors their capital plus a return; if not, the investors lose some or all of their money. The arrangement was hailed as a way to transfer the risk of failure away from taxpayers, while giving service providers the freedom to innovate. Several hundred such contracts have now been signed in more than thirty countries, though the total sums involved remain modest compared with conventional public spending.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The appeal of the model rests on a simple diagnosis. Governments, its supporters argue, tend to fund activities rather than achievements: they pay a charity to run a certain number of counselling sessions, regardless of whether those sessions change anyone's life. Dr Marta Wrobelski, a public finance specialist at the Institute for Contract Governance, was among the earliest advocates of the idea. In her view, the requirement to define measurable outcomes in advance forces all parties to think clearly about what a programme is meant to achieve, and this clarity is valuable even when the bond itself performs poorly. She also points to the preventive character of many projects. Because savings from prevention arrive years later and often in another department's budget, ministries rarely fund it; an outside investor willing to wait can, in principle, bridge that gap.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The early results, however, did little to settle the argument. One of the first bonds, aimed at short-sentence prisoners, recorded a fall in reconviction rates, but the fall was not large enough to trigger the full payment, and the scheme was ended early when national probation arrangements were reorganised. Elsewhere, programmes reported success against their targets, yet critics noted that the targets themselves had been set cautiously. Kenji Tsuchimoto, an evaluation methodologist who has reviewed more than sixty contracts, observes that fewer than a fifth used a randomised control group to establish what would have happened without the intervention. Most relied instead on historical baselines or comparisons with similar areas, methods that, in his words, 'cannot tell you whether the money bought the improvement or merely coincided with it'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second line of criticism concerns cost. Designing a bond requires lawyers, financial intermediaries and evaluators, and these transaction costs can be considerable for contracts that are often worth only a few million pounds. Investors, moreover, expect to be compensated for the risk they bear, so that a successful bond is generally more expensive for the government than funding the same service directly would have been. Akosua Agyemang, an economist at the Centre for Social Investment Analysis, has calculated that across a sample of completed contracts the risk actually borne by private investors was smaller than advertised, because many bonds included guarantees from philanthropic foundations that absorbed the first losses. If this is so, the central justification for the higher price, namely that taxpayers are protected from failure, is considerably weakened.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders reply that such criticisms judge the instrument by the wrong standard. Social impact bonds were never meant to be the cheapest way of delivering proven services, they argue, but a means of testing unproven ones. This defence has some force, but it sits uneasily with the way bonds have been used in practice. If the purpose is experimentation, then rigorous evaluation is essential, and as Tsuchimoto's survey shows, rigorous evaluation has been the exception rather than the rule. It is difficult to claim to be learning what works without the tools needed to find out.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also concerns about what happens to the people a programme is supposed to serve. When payment depends on hitting a numerical target, providers face an incentive to concentrate on the cases most likely to succeed, a practice known as 'cream-skimming', while neglecting those with the most complex needs. Ignacio Cifuentes, who has studied employment programmes in Chile and Spain, found evidence of this in contracts that rewarded individual job placements, though not in those that measured progress across an entire referred group. His conclusion is that the problem lies less in outcome payment itself than in careless contract design, and that it can largely be avoided if the population to be served is fixed before the programme begins.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable legacy of social impact bonds will prove to be indirect. The habit of specifying outcomes, collecting data and paying attention to results has spread into ordinary commissioning, where governments increasingly attach part of a contract's value to measured achievements without involving private investors at all. Whether this is a gain depends on the quality of the measures chosen; a poor indicator rewarded generously can do more harm than no indicator at all. What seems clear is that the original claims made for the bonds, that they would unlock vast sums of private capital and transform public services, were overstated. Their real contribution has been more modest, and it deserves to be recognised for what it is rather than for what was once promised.

topic: the degeneration thesis of worker cooperatives: hiring non-member workers, survival rates, managerial power and member democracy, and indivisible reserves as a legal safeguard
title: Do Cooperatives Grow Old?
subtitle: A century-old prediction says that firms owned by their workers must either fail or abandon their ideals. The evidence suggests a more complicated story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, a pessimistic prediction has shadowed the worker cooperative. The firm owned and governed by those who work in it, the argument runs, is doomed to one of two fates. Either it fails commercially, because democratic decision-making is slow and members are reluctant to reinvest their earnings, or it succeeds and gradually turns into an ordinary business, hiring employees who have no vote and allowing a shrinking core of founders to behave much like conventional owners. This 'degeneration thesis', first set out by early twentieth-century social reformers, remains influential, and it is not difficult to find cases that appear to confirm it. Whether it describes a general law, however, is another matter.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the thesis concerns economics. Lucien Vasquelin, an economist at the Lyon Institute for Enterprise Studies, has modelled the incentives facing members of a successful cooperative. When a firm prospers, he notes, each existing member's share of the profits is diluted every time a new member is admitted. Members therefore have a financial reason to expand by taking on hired workers instead, who are paid a wage but do not share in surpluses. Over time, Vasquelin argues, this can produce a firm in which a minority of members effectively employs a majority of non-members, an outcome that reproduces the very division between owners and workers that the cooperative was established to abolish. Vasquelin is careful to add that he is describing incentives rather than motives: many members, he acknowledges, resist the temptation for reasons of principle.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The empirical record, though, is less tidy than the model suggests. Dilani Ranaweera, who has assembled data on several thousand cooperatives in southern Europe and South Asia over four decades, finds that the proportion of hired non-members does tend to rise as firms grow, but that the trend is neither universal nor irreversible. Many cooperatives impose rules requiring that employees be offered membership after a probationary period, and where such rules exist the share of non-members typically stabilises at a low level. Ranaweera also reports that cooperatives in her sample were no more likely to close in their first ten years than conventional small firms in the same industries, a finding that sits awkwardly with the claim that democratic firms are commercially fragile.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different strand of the debate concerns governance rather than ownership. Even where almost everyone remains a member, critics argue, real power drifts towards managers, because ordinary members lack the time or expertise to scrutinise complex decisions. Henrik Nordbeck, a sociologist who spent two years observing meetings at a large engineering cooperative, describes general assemblies in which proposals prepared by managers were approved with little discussion. Yet he resists the conclusion that democracy had become empty. Members, he found, intervened forcefully on a narrow range of issues they cared about most, such as pay differentials and job security, and managers anticipated these reactions when drawing up their plans. Influence, in other words, could be real without being constant.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This seems to me the most useful corrective to the degeneration thesis. The thesis tends to measure cooperatives against an ideal of continuous, equal participation that no large organisation of any kind achieves. Judged against that standard, almost every cooperative will appear to have degenerated. Judged against realistic alternatives, the picture is different: a firm in which workers can dismiss managers and set limits on executive pay is not the same as a conventional company, even if most daily decisions are taken by a small group. Nor is it obvious that conventional firms offer more meaningful participation; in most of them, employees have no formal say over strategy at all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the pressures Vasquelin describes are imaginary. Ioana Valeanu, who studies cooperative law, points out that some of the best-known failures of the model occurred when successful cooperatives were sold to outside investors, allowing the members of the day to collect the accumulated value of the business. To guard against this, legislation in several countries requires that a portion of every cooperative's reserves be held as 'indivisible' capital, which cannot be distributed to members even if the firm is dissolved. Valeanu regards this as the single most effective protection against degeneration, although she concedes that it may also discourage some workers from forming cooperatives in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges is not a law of inevitable decline but a set of tendencies that can be strengthened or weakened by institutional design. The founders of the degeneration thesis were right to identify the forces at work, but they underestimated the capacity of cooperatives to recognise those forces and build defences against them. A number of cooperatives founded early in the last century are still trading today, and while none of them has escaped every pressure described above, their survival suggests that decline is a risk to be managed rather than a destiny.The more interesting question today is not whether cooperatives degenerate, but which rules allow them to grow without abandoning their founding principles.
