topic: perpetual philanthropic foundations versus spending down: the 'dead hand' of donors, independence and long horizons, payout rates and the claims of present generations, exit planning and the revision of founding purposes
title: The Dead Hand and the Living Gift
subtitle: Should a charitable fortune be preserved for ever, or spent while its donor's intentions still make sense?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the eighteenth century, a wealthy merchant in a provincial English town left money in his will to provide warm cloaks each winter for the town's poorest widows. Two hundred years later, the trustees were still dutifully distributing cloaks, although the town's widows by then had little need of them and considerably more need of almost anything else. Stories of this kind, which can be found in the records of charitable trusts across Europe, have long been used to illustrate the problem of the 'dead hand': the power of a donor, long after death, to bind resources to purposes that have ceased to make sense. The problem has acquired new urgency as the number of very large private foundations has grown, and with it a debate about whether philanthropic wealth should be preserved indefinitely or spent within a defined period.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for perpetuity rests chiefly on the idea of independence. A foundation that expects to exist for centuries, argues Armen Karapetyan, a historian of philanthropy at the Yerevan Centre for Civil Society Studies, can take positions that neither governments nor markets will support. It can fund unfashionable research, sustain institutions through periods of political hostility and wait decades for results. Karapetyan points to foundations that financed scientific fields long before those fields became respectable, and suggests that only an organisation confident of its own survival would have accepted such a long horizon. Perpetual endowments, in his account, are a form of insurance for civil society: a reserve that exists precisely because no one can predict which causes will need defending in fifty or a hundred years' time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics reply that this argument confuses the longevity of an institution with the value of its work. Greta Bertholdt, an economist who studies charitable finance, notes that most perpetual foundations are legally or conventionally committed to spending only a small fraction of their assets each year, commonly around five per cent, so that the capital is preserved. The remainder is invested, often in ordinary financial markets, where it may do little social good and occasionally considerable harm. Bertholdt argues that if a problem is urgent now, money held back for the distant future represents a real cost to people alive today, and that there is no reason to assume future generations, who will in all probability be richer, are more deserving of help. On her reckoning, the default rate of spending should be considerably higher than it is.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is something to be said for both positions, but Bertholdt's point about the moral weight of the present seems to me the stronger, at least where problems are well understood and solutions are known to work. A vaccine delivered this year prevents illness this year; a vaccine funded in a hundred years prevents illness that might never have occurred. Yet this logic is weaker for problems whose solutions have not yet been found. Where knowledge is the bottleneck, patient funding may be exactly what is required, and spending quickly risks wasting money on approaches that have not been properly tested.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A growing number of donors have chosen the alternative of spending down, committing their foundations to distribute all their assets and close within a fixed period, typically twenty to forty years. Mariam Sawadogo, who has interviewed the leaders of more than thirty such foundations, reports that many describe a sense of liberation: freed from the need to preserve capital, they can make larger grants and take bolder risks. She also found, however, that organisations nearing their closing date often struggled to ensure that the projects they had supported would survive their departure. Several grantees had become heavily dependent on a single funder and were left in difficulty when it withdrew. Sawadogo concludes that a spend-down foundation must plan its exit from the first day, not merely in its last few years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A third position questions whether the choice between perpetuity and spending down is the right one to focus on. Nimal Udagama, a legal scholar, argues that the real difficulty lies in the inflexibility of founding documents rather than in the lifespan of the foundation. The widows' cloaks, he points out, were a problem not because the trust was perpetual but because its purpose could not easily be revised. Courts in many jurisdictions have long had the power to redirect charitable funds whose original aims have become impossible to fulfil, but Udagama considers these powers too narrow and too slow, and would prefer that foundations be required to review their purposes formally every few decades.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Others are sceptical that formal reviews would change much. Lorna Macaraeg, who sits on the boards of several grant-making trusts, observes that the boards of established foundations tend to recruit people similar to themselves, and that a review conducted by such a board is unlikely to produce radical change. In her experience, the culture of a foundation matters more than its constitution. Whether one accepts her pessimism or not, the debate has at least made one thing clear: the decision about how long a foundation should exist is not merely technical. It expresses a judgement about whose needs count, and how much trust to place in the people who will manage wealth after its donor has gone.

topic: judging charities by overhead ratios: what the ratio leaves out, cosmetic cost allocation, the 'starvation cycle' of underfunded core costs, high ratios as warning signs and the difficulty of measuring outcomes instead
title: The Cost of Looking Cheap
subtitle: Donors have long judged charities by how little they spend on themselves. A growing body of research suggests they have been asking the wrong question

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask a potential donor what they want to know about a charity, and one answer comes up more often than almost any other: how much of each donation actually reaches the cause? The question seems entirely reasonable. Nobody wishes to see their generosity absorbed by office rents, salaries and fundraising campaigns. For several decades, charity rating agencies have responded to this concern by publishing 'overhead ratios', which express administrative and fundraising costs as a share of total spending, and many donors treat a low figure as a reliable sign of a well-run organisation. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this measure is at best uninformative and at worst actively damaging.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty begins with what the ratio leaves out. It says nothing about whether a charity's programmes achieve anything. Two organisations spending identical proportions on administration might differ enormously in effectiveness; one may transform the lives of those it serves while the other accomplishes very little. Hiroshi Matsukane, who analysed the published accounts of around four thousand charities in Japan and North America, found no meaningful relationship between overhead ratios and independent assessments of programme quality. If anything, he notes, some of the most rigorously evaluated organisations reported above-average administrative costs, partly because evaluation itself is classed as an overhead. An organisation that pays for careful monitoring of its own work is therefore penalised in the ratings, while one that never checks whether its programmes succeed looks admirably lean.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The ratio is also easy to manipulate. Accounting rules give charities considerable discretion in deciding how to classify spending: the salary of a manager who supervises field staff may be recorded as a programme cost or as administration, depending on how her time is apportioned. Carla Escandell, an auditor who has reviewed charity accounts for regulators in Spain, describes what she calls 'cosmetic allocation', in which costs are shifted between categories to produce a more attractive figure. She is careful to distinguish this from fraud, since the practice is usually within the rules. Her concern is that it renders comparisons between organisations almost meaningless. Charities that classify their costs honestly and conservatively, she adds, may end up looking worse than rivals who are simply more inventive with their bookkeeping.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: More troubling is the effect that the ratio has on behaviour. Sibusiso Nhlapo, an organisational researcher in Johannesburg, has coined the phrase 'the starvation cycle' to describe what he observed among mid-sized charities. Funders and donors, expecting low overheads, offer grants that cover little or nothing of an organisation's core costs. Charities respond by underreporting their real expenses and by underinvesting in staff training, information systems and financial management. The resulting weaknesses make the organisation less effective, which in turn makes funders more anxious about waste, and the cycle tightens. Nhlapo found that charities caught in this pattern had markedly higher staff turnover than their peers, and that experienced employees frequently cited exhaustion as a reason for leaving.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the overhead ratio should be abandoned entirely. Ilze Kalnberzins, who directs a donor advisory service in Riga, argues that extremely high ratios can still be a useful warning sign. An organisation spending most of its income on fundraising, she points out, may be engaged in practices that donors would find objectionable, and she sees no harm in flagging such cases. What she rejects is the use of the ratio to rank charities that fall within a normal range, where small differences reveal almost nothing. This seems to me a sensible compromise, although it leaves unanswered the question of what donors should look at instead.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The obvious alternative is to measure outcomes directly, but this is far more difficult than it sounds. Some kinds of charitable work, such as distributing medicines, lend themselves to measurement; others, such as campaigning for legal reform or supporting the arts, produce benefits that are diffuse, delayed or hard to attribute to any single organisation. There is a danger that a demand for measurable results will simply replace one distortion with another, steering money towards causes that are easy to count rather than those that matter most. Measurement, moreover, costs money, and that money will appear in the accounts as overhead. A small charity asked to prove its impact through a formal study may find that the study consumes a large part of its annual budget.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should a thoughtful donor do? Probably the most useful step is to change the question. Instead of asking how little a charity spends on itself, donors might ask what it is trying to achieve, how it knows whether it is succeeding, and what it would do with additional unrestricted funds. These questions are harder to answer with a single number, and they demand more effort from donors than a glance at a rating table. But the simplicity of the overhead ratio is precisely its weakness. A measure that is easy to calculate and easy to understand has, for decades, been rewarding charities for appearing frugal rather than for doing good.

topic: farmer-owned agricultural marketing cooperatives: side-selling and late payment, trust in management, the horizon problem of non-tradable shares, conversion to investor-owned firms, new-generation cooperatives and the competitive effect on traders' prices
title: Loyalty at the Farm Gate
subtitle: Farmers' marketing cooperatives promise growers a stronger hand when they sell. Why do so many of them struggle to keep their members?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For smallholder farmers, the moment of sale is often the moment of greatest weakness. A grower with a lorry-load of perishable fruit or a tank of fresh milk cannot afford to wait for a better offer, and the buyers who arrive at the farm gate know it. The agricultural marketing cooperative was conceived as a remedy. By pooling their produce and selling collectively, members could negotiate as a single large supplier, share the cost of storage and processing, and capture some of the value that would otherwise go to traders. In parts of Europe and North America, such cooperatives came to dominate entire sectors, particularly dairy. Elsewhere, their record has been far more uneven, and the reasons for this unevenness are the subject of a long-running debate.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most familiar problem is known as side-selling. When a private trader offers a slightly higher price on a particular day, individual members are tempted to sell to that trader rather than to their own cooperative, even though the cooperative's existence is often the only reason the trader's price is so high. Olga Nakhimova, an agricultural economist who has studied coffee and dairy cooperatives in East Africa and Central Asia, found that side-selling rates rose sharply whenever the cooperative paid members late. In her view, the problem is less one of disloyalty than of cash flow: a farmer facing school fees or medical bills will take immediate payment over a better price next month. Cooperatives that arranged advance payments, she reports, saw side-selling fall by as much as half.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: I find Nakhimova's account persuasive as far as it goes, but it is unlikely to be the whole story. Farmers who are paid promptly still sometimes sell elsewhere, and their reasons appear to include a lack of trust in the cooperative's management. Where members suspect that officials are mismanaging funds or favouring relatives, prompt payment alone does little to restore commitment. Suspicion of this kind is difficult to dispel once it has taken hold, because the evidence that would refute it, such as audited accounts, is often unavailable or unreadable to members with limited schooling.The cooperatives that endure seem to combine financial reliability with a degree of transparency in their accounts that private traders, for obvious reasons, never offer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second difficulty arises from the way ownership is structured. In a traditional cooperative, a member's stake cannot be sold and is usually repaid at its original value when the member leaves. Somchai Kittiwong, who has written on cooperative finance in Thailand, describes the consequence as a 'horizon problem'. Older members, expecting to retire within a few years, have little reason to support investments in processing plants or brands that will pay off only after they have gone, because they will never share in the increased value. Kittiwong argues that this bias towards the short term explains why many cooperatives remain stuck selling raw commodities while investor-owned competitors move into higher-value products.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some cooperatives have responded by converting into conventional companies, whose shares can be bought and sold. Conversion releases the accumulated value of the business to its members and makes it easier to raise outside capital. Darius Moradzadeh, who studied a series of conversions among large dairy cooperatives, found that members typically received substantial one-off payments, but that within a decade the converted firms had in several cases reduced the prices they paid to farmers, since their obligations were now to shareholders rather than suppliers. To Moradzadeh, this pattern shows that the benefits of conversion accrue mostly to the generation that votes for it. Farmers who join the industry afterwards inherit neither the payout nor the bargaining power that the cooperative once provided, and may find themselves selling to a large company on terms that the cooperative was originally founded to resist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: An alternative model, developed in the late twentieth century, attempts to solve the horizon problem without abandoning cooperative ownership. In these so-called new-generation cooperatives, membership is closed and linked to delivery rights: each share obliges its holder to supply a fixed quantity of produce and entitles them to a corresponding portion of the profits. Because the shares can be traded among farmers and rise in value as the business grows, departing members can realise the gains from investments made during their membership. Nino Anjaparidze, who has evaluated several such ventures, considers them a genuine innovation but warns that high share prices can exclude younger and poorer farmers, recreating the inequalities that cooperatives were meant to reduce. In one venture she examined, the price of a single share had risen within fifteen years to more than the annual income of a typical local household.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Finally, there is the question of whether cooperatives should be judged by their own survival at all. Issa Zongo, who has worked with cotton producers in West Africa, argues that a cooperative which forces private traders to raise their prices has succeeded even if it subsequently collapses, because farmers in the region are better off. This is an important point, and too often overlooked in assessments that count only the cooperatives still in business. It should not, however, be pushed too far. A competitive effect that depends on the cooperative's presence is likely to disappear soon after it does, and traders who have been forced to pay more will hardly hesitate to pay less once the threat has gone.

topic: community land trusts and permanently affordable housing: separating land from buildings, resale formulas, subsidy retention, the limited-equity objection, foreclosure and savings outcomes, and the problem of acquiring land at scale
title: Land Held in Common
subtitle: Community land trusts aim to keep homes affordable for ever by taking the land beneath them off the market

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In most housing markets, the price of a home reflects two quite different things: the building itself and the land on which it stands. Over time, it is usually the land that accounts for most of the increase in value, and this increase owes little to the efforts of the owner. It results instead from public investment in transport and schools, from the growth of local employment, and from the general scarcity of land in places where people want to live. The community land trust, a model that has spread from a handful of rural experiments into cities on several continents, rests on a simple proposition: if the rising value of land is created by the community, the community should be able to keep it. The idea is not new; reformers have argued for public capture of land values since at least the nineteenth century. What is new is the attempt to put the principle into practice one neighbourhood at a time, through voluntary organisations rather than national legislation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanism is straightforward in outline. A non-profit trust acquires land, often through donation, public grant or purchase at below-market prices, and holds it permanently. Homes built on the land are sold to households on modest incomes, but the buyers own only the building; the land is leased to them, typically for ninety-nine years. When owners wish to sell, a formula written into the lease limits the price they can ask, so that the home remains affordable for the next buyer. Owners usually receive back what they paid plus a share of any increase in value, commonly around a quarter, together with the value of improvements they have made.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters regard this as an elegant solution to a problem that conventional housing subsidies handle badly. When governments help a family buy a home with a grant, the subsidy often disappears at the first resale, as the family pockets the gain and the home passes into the open market. Aino Ruuskanen, an urban economist at the Helsinki Institute for Housing Research, calculates that over a period of thirty years a single subsidy invested in a land trust home can assist four or five successive households, whereas the same sum given as a conventional grant typically benefits only one. In her view, this 'subsidy retention' is the model's most important and least appreciated feature.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics question whether homeowners in such schemes are really owners at all. Jean-Baptiste Nsengiyumva, who has studied low-income housing in Belgium and Canada, argues that limiting resale gains denies families the main route by which ordinary households have accumulated wealth over the past century. A family that buys on the open market and sees its home double in value can pass that wealth on to its children or borrow against it; a land trust family cannot. Nsengiyumva does not oppose the model, but he insists that it should be presented honestly as a form of shared ownership, not as a substitute for the full ownership enjoyed by better-off households.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is force in this objection, though it rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny. The comparison Nsengiyumva draws is between a land trust home and an ordinary purchase. For most households who take up land trust homes, however, the realistic alternative is not open-market ownership, which they could not afford, but renting, which builds no wealth at all. Research by Céline Duvignaud, who followed some eight hundred land trust households over fifteen years, found that the majority accumulated modest but real savings through their equity share, and that rates of foreclosure were markedly lower than among comparable buyers on the open market. The gains are smaller than those of ordinary owners in a rising market, but they are gains nonetheless.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The more serious challenge, in my judgement, is one of scale. Land trusts depend on acquiring land cheaply, and in the very cities where they are most needed land is the scarcest and most expensive resource of all. Ramon Pangilinan, who advises municipal governments on housing policy, notes that most trusts hold only a few dozen homes, and that their growth has depended heavily on the willingness of local authorities to transfer public land to them. Where such land is available, he suggests, trusts can expand rapidly; where it is not, they remain marginal. Pangilinan also observes that the governance of trusts, which typically gives seats on the board to residents, neighbours and public representatives, can make decisions slow and contentious as organisations grow.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these difficulties is fatal, but they suggest that the community land trust is better understood as one tool among several than as a complete answer to the housing problem. Its distinctive contribution is to treat affordability as a permanent characteristic of a home rather than a temporary benefit attached to a particular household. That is a genuinely important idea, and one that policymakers could apply far more widely, whether or not they adopt the land trust model in its full form. Resale restrictions attached to publicly funded homes, for instance, could achieve something similar without requiring a separate organisation to own the land.

topic: the history of consumer retail cooperatives: the dividend on purchases, idealism versus material motives, unadulterated food and the cash-only rule, women's cooperative guilds, and explanations of decline against supermarket chains
title: The Dividend on the Shopping Basket
subtitle: Customer-owned grocery stores once counted their members in millions. Historians still disagree about why they flourished and why so many later faded

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the second half of the nineteenth century, a modest shop selling flour, butter, tea and candles became one of the most successful social institutions in industrial Europe. The consumer cooperative store was owned by its customers. Members bought shares for a small sum, elected a committee to run the business, and received, at regular intervals, a 'dividend' calculated not on the capital they had invested but on the amount they had spent. A family that bought most of its groceries at the co-op might receive a lump sum several times a year, often used to buy shoes or pay for a holiday. By the early twentieth century, cooperative societies in several countries counted their members in millions, ran their own factories and farms, and operated wholesale organisations that rivalled the largest private firms.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Historians have long debated what made the movement so attractive. The traditional explanation emphasises idealism: cooperators saw their stores as the first step towards a 'cooperative commonwealth' in which production and distribution would be organised for use rather than profit. Pieter Vermaelen, a social historian at the Flemish Institute for Labour History, questions this account. Examining the minute books of more than a hundred local societies, he found that discussion of broader social goals was largely confined to a small group of activists, while ordinary members raised questions almost exclusively about prices, quality and the size of the dividend. For Vermaelen, the movement's success rested on solid material advantages, and its rhetoric of transformation was something most members tolerated rather than embraced.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Among those material advantages, one was particularly valued. Private grocers in working-class districts were notorious for adulterating food: flour was mixed with chalk, tea with used leaves, and butter was padded out with water. Solveig Brekhus, who has studied the records of food inspectors in Norway and Scotland, argues that the cooperatives' reputation for honest weights and pure goods was at least as important as the dividend in attracting members, especially among women, who generally did the household shopping. Brekhus adds, however, that the stores' insistence on cash payment, intended to protect members from debt, effectively excluded the poorest households, who depended on credit from local shopkeepers to survive between pay days.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The role of women is the focus of work by Lucía Riveros, who has reconstructed the activities of cooperative women's guilds in Spain and Argentina. Women were often barred from holding office in the societies themselves, since membership was frequently registered in the husband's name. Through the guilds, however, they organised campaigns on issues ranging from maternity care to the minimum wage, and in some regions they were responsible for persuading societies to open branches in poorer neighbourhoods. Riveros argues that the guilds were the movement's most genuinely political element, and that historians who focus only on the stores' committees have badly underestimated women's influence. The guilds also served as informal schools, teaching members to chair meetings, keep accounts and speak in public, skills that a number of them later carried into trade unions and local government.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Riveros's case is convincing, and it complicates Vermaelen's picture in an important way. If the movement's political ambitions were sustained largely by women working outside its formal structures, then the minute books Vermaelen examined, which recorded the deliberations of male-dominated committees, would naturally give the impression that such ambitions were marginal. The absence of political discussion in the official record may tell us more about who was allowed to speak than about what members cared about.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The decline of the consumer cooperatives in many countries after the mid-twentieth century has generated its own debate. The usual explanation points to the rise of supermarket chains, which could exploit economies of scale, centralised buying and modern management in ways that federations of independent local societies found hard to match. Ruwan Jayasekera, an economic historian, accepts this account but stresses a less obvious factor: the dividend itself. As rising incomes reduced the importance of a periodic lump sum, and as supermarkets offered permanently lower prices, the dividend came to look less like a reward and more like a disguised overcharge. Societies that cut prices and abolished the dividend, he finds, generally held their market share better than those that clung to it. Abolition was rarely popular, however, since older members regarded the dividend as the very symbol of cooperation, and committees that proposed ending it sometimes faced revolts at general meetings.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Not all historians accept that decline was inevitable. Aigerim Esenova, who has compared cooperative sectors across Europe, points out that in some countries consumer cooperatives remain among the largest retailers, having merged their local societies into national organisations early enough to compete with private chains. In her view, the difference lay less in economic circumstances than in the willingness of local societies to give up their independence. This is a plausible argument, though it is perhaps too easy to read success backwards: mergers that worked are remembered as far-sighted, while those that failed are forgotten. What can be said with some confidence is that the consumer cooperative's history offers no simple lesson about whether democratic ownership can survive in a competitive market. It shows, rather, how much depends on the particular choices made at critical moments.

topic: online medical crowdfunding: unequal success linked to social networks, presentation and cues of deservingness, campaigns for unproven treatments and platform responsibility, non-financial benefits, and crowdfunding as a substitute for collective health provision
title: Appeals in Public
subtitle: Online fundraising for medical bills has become a vast informal charity. Who does it help, and at what cost?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A generation ago, a family facing a medical bill they could not pay had limited options: borrow from relatives, sell possessions, or appeal to a local newspaper or religious congregation. Today many turn instead to online crowdfunding platforms, where a short description, a few photographs and a target sum can be shared with thousands of potential donors in an afternoon. Medical appeals have become one of the largest categories of fundraising on such sites, collectively raising very large sums each year. To some observers this represents a remarkable expansion of everyday generosity, made possible by technology. To others, it is a symptom of failing health and welfare systems, and a deeply unequal way of deciding who receives help.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of giving is not in doubt, but its distribution is. Elina Jaakkola, a sociologist who analysed some twenty thousand medical campaigns, found that the great majority failed to reach their targets, and that a substantial proportion received no donations at all. Success was strongly associated with the size and wealth of the campaigner's social network: those whose friends and relatives had high incomes and large online followings raised far more than those with smaller or poorer networks, regardless of the seriousness of the illness. In effect, Jaakkola argues, crowdfunding tends to channel resources towards people who are already relatively advantaged, reproducing rather than reducing existing inequalities. The pattern was visible even within single cities, where campaigns from prosperous districts consistently outperformed those from poorer neighbourhoods a short distance away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Presentation matters as well. Campaigns that told a vivid, emotionally compelling story, accompanied by professional-quality photographs, attracted more money than those that simply described a condition and its costs. Arnab Thakuria, who studies digital communication, has shown that appeals written in fluent, polished prose outperformed otherwise similar appeals containing spelling errors, and that campaigns for children and young adults drew more support than those for older people. Thakuria interprets these patterns as evidence that donors respond to cues of 'deservingness', judgements that have little to do with medical need and much to do with the narrative skills and social characteristics of the person making the appeal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are also concerns about what is being funded. A minority of campaigns seek money for treatments that lack scientific support, such as unproven therapies offered by overseas clinics. Pilar Morcillo, a specialist in health policy, examined campaigns of this kind and found that they were, on average, no less successful than appeals for conventional treatment. She argues that platforms, by providing a means of payment, lend unproven treatments a degree of legitimacy, and that they have a responsibility to warn donors, or even to refuse such campaigns altogether. The platforms themselves have generally resisted this role, maintaining that they are neutral intermediaries and that judgements about medical treatment belong to patients and their doctors. Some have nonetheless removed campaigns for treatments that public health authorities have formally declared dangerous, an indication that the claim of complete neutrality is less firm than it first appears.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Morcillo's argument seems to me largely correct, although her proposed remedy raises difficulties of its own. Determining which treatments are unproven is not always straightforward; some therapies regarded as experimental in one country are standard in another, and patients with rare conditions may have no option except treatments with limited evidence. A blanket ban would risk excluding precisely those patients for whom conventional medicine has nothing to offer. Clear warnings, together with links to independent medical information, would seem a more proportionate response.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Defenders of crowdfunding point out that, whatever its flaws, it provides help that would otherwise not exist. Teresa Sangalang, who has interviewed campaigners in several countries, found that even unsuccessful appeals often brought benefits that were not financial: offers of practical help with transport and childcare, renewed contact with distant friends, and a sense that one's difficulties were recognised. Many recipients, she reports, described the experience as an expression of community solidarity at a time of great vulnerability. Others, though, spoke of the discomfort of exposing their private medical details to public view, and of the pressure to keep posting cheerful updates in order to sustain donors' interest.She cautions, however, against treating these benefits as a justification for leaving people to rely on the generosity of strangers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: That caution is well placed. The most troubling feature of medical crowdfunding is not that some campaigns succeed and others fail, but that it encourages us to regard access to treatment as a matter of private charity rather than collective provision. Every successful appeal is a reminder that someone fell through the gaps of the system; every failed one is a reminder that many more did so without anyone noticing. The individual stories that make such appeals compelling also make it easy to forget the policies that produced them.Crowdfunding can alleviate individual hardship, but it cannot substitute for health systems that cover people according to need, and it would be a mistake to allow its visibility to obscure that fact.

topic: charitable giving in kind versus in cash: suspicion of the poor and evidence on spending, delivery costs and local market effects, cash as a benchmark for aid programmes, the limits of cash where markets fail, and donors' preference for tangible gifts
title: Gifts in Kind, Gifts in Cash
subtitle: Should charities give people in need the things donors imagine they need, or simply give them money?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When disaster strikes, warehouses fill with donations: tins of food, blankets, bottled water, children's toys and, notoriously, clothing of every description. Aid workers have a wry name for the less useful contributions, which arrive unsorted and must be stored, transported and often discarded at considerable expense. After one major earthquake, relief agencies reportedly spent weeks clearing donated winter coats from airport runways in a country where temperatures rarely fall below twenty degrees. Behind the joke lies a serious question that has preoccupied researchers and charities for two decades. Is it better to give people in need the things that donors think they need, or simply to give them money and let them decide for themselves?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the answer seemed obvious. Charitable giving in kind, whether food parcels, school uniforms, livestock or seeds, was the norm, partly because donors could see what their money bought and partly because of a widespread suspicion that poor people given cash would waste it. That suspicion has not survived careful scrutiny. Nandini Barua, an economist who reviewed several dozen experimental studies of cash transfers in Asia, Africa and Latin America, found no evidence that recipients spent significant amounts on alcohol or tobacco. On the contrary, spending on such goods typically fell slightly, while spending on food, schooling and productive assets such as tools or livestock rose. Barua concludes that the image of the feckless poor is a prejudice rather than a finding.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cash also has practical advantages. It is cheaper to deliver, particularly now that transfers can be sent to mobile phones, and it avoids the costs of buying, shipping and storing goods. It allows recipients to buy what they actually need, which may differ greatly from one household to the next: one family may need a roof repaired, another school fees, another a sewing machine to start a small business. And it supports local traders rather than undercutting them. Joseph Lusambo, who has studied food aid in Central Africa, found that large shipments of donated grain depressed prices in local markets, harming the very farmers whose production might have relieved future shortages. Cash, by contrast, increased demand for locally produced food.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Such findings have led some researchers to propose that cash should become the standard against which all aid is judged. Under this approach, a charity proposing to deliver goods or services would have to show that its programme achieves more than an equivalent sum given directly to the same people. Matti Savolainen, who has helped design several such comparisons, reports that many programmes performed poorly against this benchmark. A scheme that distributed livestock, for example, delivered smaller gains in household income than an equal amount of cash, largely because the costs of buying and transporting the animals consumed a large share of the budget. Savolainen is quick to add that some programmes passed the test comfortably, particularly those offering training or advice that recipients could not easily have purchased for themselves.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The benchmark is a valuable discipline, and it is hard to see how any charity could object to being asked whether its work does more good than a simple cash grant. It should not, however, be mistaken for a universal verdict in favour of cash. Some goods and services cannot easily be bought, even by people with money in their pockets. Where markets are weak or absent, as in remote areas, in the immediate aftermath of a disaster or during conflict, cash may simply drive up the price of scarce goods without increasing their supply. Nor can cash readily substitute for public goods such as clean water systems or vaccination campaigns, whose benefits extend beyond the individual household.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of what donors themselves want. Ana Guerreiro, a psychologist who studies charitable motivation, has found that people are considerably more willing to give when they can picture a specific item, such as a goat, a mosquito net or a school desk, than when asked to contribute to a cash transfer. Charities that switch to cash risk losing income, she argues, and some have responded by continuing to advertise tangible gifts while quietly spending the money in more flexible ways. Guerreiro regards this practice as understandable but troubling, because it misleads donors about how their money is used and reinforces the very preferences that make cash hard to promote. A more honest approach, she suggests, would be to tell donors the stories of what recipients chose to buy, which her experiments indicate can be almost as persuasive as the picture of a single animal.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate between cash and kind is sometimes presented as a contest between respect for the poor and paternalism. That framing contains an important truth: people living in poverty are generally the best judges of their own needs, and decades of aid policy were distorted by a refusal to believe it. But it oversimplifies. The choice is better seen as an empirical question to be answered case by case, with cash as the default and the burden of proof on those who would do something else. On that view, the warehouses of unsolicited goods are not simply wasteful; they are a reminder of how often generosity is shaped more by the giver's imagination than by the recipient's circumstances.

topic: work-integration social enterprises for the long-term unemployed: real work versus classroom training, psychological gains, adjusting placement statistics for participants' backgrounds, the business-versus-mission tension, rewarding transitions, and permanent supported employment versus segregation
title: Business with a Second Purpose
subtitle: Social enterprises that employ people excluded from the job market must compete as businesses while trying to help their workers leave

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a converted warehouse on the edge of a northern European city, a team of workers repairs and resells used furniture. The business sells to the public, competes with other second-hand dealers and must cover its costs. But its real purpose lies elsewhere. Most of its employees have been out of work for years, some after prison sentences, others because of long-term illness, addiction or homelessness. The enterprise exists to give them a period of paid employment, training and support, after which, it is hoped, they will move on to jobs in the ordinary labour market. Organisations of this kind, known as work-integration social enterprises, have multiplied across Europe, Asia and the Americas, and governments increasingly fund them as an alternative to conventional employment programmes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Their advocates argue that they offer something traditional training schemes cannot: real work. A classroom course in customer service, however well designed, is no substitute for dealing with actual customers, meeting actual deadlines and earning an actual wage. Kaisa Hyvärilä, who has followed participants in work-integration enterprises in Finland for more than a decade, found that the experience of being relied upon by colleagues had a profound effect on self-confidence, particularly among people who had been told repeatedly that they were unemployable. Several of her interviewees described their first pay slip as a turning point. Hyvärilä argues that these psychological gains are a precondition for later success, even if they are rarely captured in official statistics.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Official statistics, however, are what funders tend to ask for, and here the record is more ambiguous. Studies that track whether participants find jobs after leaving have produced widely varying results, partly because the enterprises serve very different populations. Florian Oberhollenzer, a labour economist in Innsbruck, points out that comparisons are often misleading: an enterprise that works with people recently released from prison should not be expected to achieve the same placement rates as one that works with young graduates who have struggled to find a first job. Oberhollenzer has developed methods that adjust for the characteristics of participants, and finds that once this is done, the better enterprises outperform conventional programmes by a modest but meaningful margin. The weaker ones, he concedes, do no better than the schemes they are meant to replace, and some do worse, which suggests that the label 'social enterprise' guarantees very little on its own.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A deeper problem concerns the tension built into the model itself. A social enterprise must succeed as a business in order to survive, yet its social mission requires it to employ people who are, at least initially, less productive than workers it could hire on the open market. Moreover, the enterprise loses its most capable employees precisely when they become most valuable, at the point when they are ready to leave for mainstream jobs. Wanjiru Chebet, who has studied social enterprises in Kenya and the United Kingdom, describes managers who quietly delayed the departure of their best workers to protect the business, an outcome directly contrary to the enterprise's purpose. Chebet does not blame the managers, whom she regards as responding rationally to impossible pressures, but she believes funders should reward enterprises for successful transitions rather than for the number of people employed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This seems to me a sound proposal, though it is not without risks. If enterprises are paid according to the number of participants who move into mainstream jobs, they will face an incentive to select those most likely to succeed and to turn away those with the greatest needs, exactly the people the sector was created to help. Any reward system would therefore need to take account of how difficult each participant's situation was at the outset, which brings us back to the kind of adjustments Oberhollenzer has proposed. Such adjustments are technically demanding, and smaller enterprises, which often lack staff with expertise in data analysis, may struggle to supply the detailed records they require.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some critics question whether the goal of transition to mainstream work is always appropriate. Karim Medjber, a sociologist who has worked with social enterprises in France and Algeria, argues that for some participants, particularly those with severe disabilities or long histories of mental illness, a permanent place in a supportive enterprise may be a better outcome than a precarious job in the open market. Treating such placements as failures, he says, reflects a narrow view of what work is for. Rustam Qadirov, who advises governments on employment policy, takes a less sympathetic view: permanent sheltered employment, he warns, can become a form of segregation, keeping disadvantaged workers apart from the rest of the labour force and offering them lower wages and fewer rights.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Both arguments have merit, and the disagreement between them cannot be settled by evidence alone, since it reflects different judgements about what a good working life looks like. What the evidence does suggest is that work-integration enterprises are neither the miracle cure their most enthusiastic advocates proclaim nor the expensive distraction their critics allege. They work best when their goals are realistic, their funding is stable and their success is measured in ways that reflect the people they actually serve. None of these conditions is easy to secure, but each is within the reach of funders who are prepared to think beyond a single headline figure.

topic: peatlands and carbon storage
title: Waterlogged Wealth
subtitle: Long dismissed as wasteland, peatlands are now at the centre of a debate about how to keep carbon in the ground

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Peatlands cover only around three per cent of the earth's land surface, yet they are thought to store more carbon than all of the world's forests combined. This extraordinary capacity is a product of their waterlogged conditions. Where the ground remains saturated throughout the year, oxygen is scarce, and the remains of mosses, sedges and other plants decompose only partially. Instead of rotting away, this material accumulates layer upon layer over thousands of years. For most of recorded history, however, bogs and fens were seen as obstacles to progress. Across northern Europe they were drained for farmland, cut for fuel and planted with conifers, and each of these projects was celebrated as a triumph of human improvement over unproductive nature. Only in recent decades has the true price of that transformation become apparent, and the reassessment now under way is long overdue.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Once the water table is lowered, air penetrates the upper layers of peat, and organic matter that has been preserved for millennia begins to oxidise, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Dr Helena Varga, a soil scientist at the Nordic Wetland Research Centre, has spent fifteen years measuring these fluxes. Her estimates suggest that drained peatlands, although they occupy a tiny fraction of agricultural land, may account for a disproportionate share of farming's greenhouse gas output. Drainage also causes the land itself to subside as the peat shrinks and decomposes; in parts of eastern England, fields now lie several metres below the level they occupied two centuries ago. Varga points out that subsidence tends to dominate public discussion because it can be seen and photographed. Yet in her judgement it is the invisible release of carbon, rather than the sinking ground, that represents the more serious long-term threat.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The obvious remedy is to put the water back. Rewetting typically involves blocking drainage ditches with dams of peat or timber so that the water table rises towards the surface. A team led by the ecologist Tomas Brennan at the Atlantic Peatland Trust has monitored more than forty rewetted sites and reports that, within a few years, emissions of carbon dioxide fall sharply and sphagnum mosses, the principal peat-forming plants, begin to recolonise bare ground. Rewetting is not without complications, however. Waterlogged soils produce methane, a gas with a far stronger warming effect than carbon dioxide, and newly flooded sites can release substantial quantities of it. Brennan maintains that this methane pulse is temporary and is comfortably outweighed by the carbon savings achieved over several decades. His reasoning is persuasive, but critics are right to insist that the timescales behind such calculations be stated openly, since a benefit that only materialises after fifty years is of limited help in meeting targets set for the next fifteen.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Nor should restoration be regarded as a simple reversal of past damage. Peat accumulates at a rate of roughly one millimetre per year, which means that a metre of peat lost to drainage represents around a thousand years of growth. A rewetted bog may stop losing carbon relatively quickly, but it will take centuries to rebuild what has disappeared. It follows that the first priority ought to be the protection of peatlands that remain intact, rather than the repair of those already degraded. Current policy often works against this principle. Many national programmes measure success in hectares restored, a metric that rewards projects on sites which are cheap and easy to rewet while discouraging investment in the most badly damaged areas, where the gains per hectare might be greatest.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For the people who live on drained peat, the debate is far from abstract. Ines Okafor, an agricultural economist at the Centre for Rural Policy, notes that thousands of farms depend on land which would become unusable for conventional grazing or arable crops if it were rewetted. Compensation schemes exist, but Okafor argues that they are poorly designed: most offer contracts lasting five years, whereas the hydrological and ecological changes involved in restoration unfold over decades. One proposed solution is paludiculture, the cultivation of crops suited to wet conditions. Reeds can be harvested for thatching and building panels, bulrushes processed into insulation, and sphagnum grown as a sustainable substitute for the peat used in garden compost. Okafor regards these as promising options but cautions that the markets for such products remain small and largely untested.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental scepticism comes from the hydrologist Marcus Lindqvist, who doubts that rewetting can be carried out on the scale that climate targets imply. Raising the water table on one site, he observes, inevitably affects the surrounding area, and the result may be the flooding of neighbouring farmland, roads or homes. Lindqvist therefore advocates a selective approach, concentrating effort on isolated sites where water levels can be precisely controlled. His caution is understandable, but it risks becoming a justification for doing very little. The engineering difficulties he describes are genuine, yet they are hardly insurmountable: the Netherlands has managed water levels across densely populated, low-lying land for centuries.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most striking lesson of the peatland debate is how easily environmental value can go unnoticed. Forests attract public affection and generous funding, while bogs, flat and treeless, inspire little enthusiasm. This imbalance has had perverse consequences: in several countries, subsidies once encouraged landowners to plant trees on peat, a practice that dries the soil and can lead to a net loss of carbon. Whether peatlands are protected on the scale required will ultimately depend less on further scientific research than on whether societies can learn to value a landscape that, to the untrained eye, appears to contain almost nothing at all.

title: The End of the Full Course?
subtitle: One of medicine's most familiar instructions is being questioned, and the debate shows how rarely some rules were ever tested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than half a century, patients leaving a doctor's surgery with a prescription for antibiotics have been given the same instruction: finish the course, even if you feel better. The reasoning seemed straightforward. Stopping early, it was said, would leave the hardiest bacteria alive, and these survivors would multiply into a population that the drug could no longer kill. The message was repeated so often, on posters, in leaflets and in national campaigns, that it came to be regarded as one of the basic rules of responsible medicine. Yet when researchers began to look for the studies on which it rested, they found remarkably few. The advice, it now seems, owed more to habit than to experiment.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The standard durations themselves are revealing. Courses of seven, ten or fourteen days dominate prescribing guidelines, figures that correspond suspiciously well to the calendar week. Dr Ilse Brandvold, a historian at the Tromsø Institute for Medical History, has examined clinical records from the earliest days of penicillin in the 1940s, when the drug was so scarce that it was sometimes recovered from patients' urine and reused. Under those conditions, she notes, physicians gave the drug only until the patient recovered and then stopped. Fixed courses, in her account, became the norm during the following decade, when manufacturers began supplying antibiotics in standard packs, so that commercial convenience quietly shaped clinical practice. Her research is persuasive, but it arguably overstates the influence of the industry; doctors themselves had every reason to welcome a simple rule that spared them difficult judgements about individual patients.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The biological case against long courses has been made most forcefully by Kwabena Owusu-Darko, a microbiologist at the Kumasi Centre for Infection Biology. He points out that the resistance which threatens public health rarely emerges in the organism a doctor is trying to treat. Far more often it develops among the harmless bacteria that live in the gut and on the skin, which are exposed to the drug for every day that treatment continues. Each additional day favours resistant strains within these communities, and such strains can later pass their resistance genes to dangerous species. On this view, taking antibiotics for longer than necessary increases, rather than reduces, the risk of resistance. Owusu-Darko accepts that there are exceptions. In tuberculosis, for instance, the bacteria causing the disease can themselves become resistant if treatment is interrupted, which is why patients are still required to take drugs for many months.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The theory would matter less if shorter courses were known to fail, but the clinical evidence points in the opposite direction. Over the past two decades, randomised trials have compared short and conventional courses for pneumonia, urinary tract infections and skin infections, and many have found that three to five days of treatment work as well as a week or more. When the Lindgaard Clinical Trials Unit in Copenhagen pooled the results of more than forty such trials, it found no meaningful difference in cure rates for most common infections. Patients on shorter courses, moreover, reported fewer unpleasant side effects, such as diarrhoea and rashes. Individual trials can always be criticised, but the combined weight of these findings is now very hard to dismiss.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That is not to say that the question is settled. Dr Marisol Arrospide, an infectious disease specialist in Montevideo, observes that the trials mostly recruited otherwise healthy adults, while elderly people, young children and those with weakened immune systems were seldom included. In addition, trial participants were diagnosed with unusual care, whereas in an ordinary clinic a doctor may be uncertain what kind of infection is present at all. Arrospide therefore favours tailoring the length of treatment to each patient, stopping when symptoms have resolved and, where possible, using blood tests that measure markers of bacterial infection. This is a sensible approach in a well-equipped hospital, but in many community clinics such tests are simply unavailable, and a doctor must decide without them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of what patients should be told. If the familiar instruction is withdrawn and replaced with 'stop when you feel better', some people may stop too early, while others may keep the remaining tablets for future use. Dr Tavita Aumua-Pele, a behavioural scientist at the Pacific Health Behaviour Unit, surveyed households and found that leftover antibiotics were frequently taken later for colds and other viral illnesses, against which they are useless. Simple rules have value precisely because they are easy to remember and follow. The answer, however, is not to retain an inaccurate rule but to replace it with a better one, such as taking antibiotics for exactly the period a doctor specifies and returning any that remain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The story of the full course is not one of foolish doctors. Those who prescribed long courses acted reasonably on the knowledge and conventions of their time. What it demonstrates is how easily a recommendation can harden into dogma once it has been repeated often enough. In future, the burden of proof should lie with longer durations rather than shorter ones: if a fourteen-day course cannot be shown to outperform a five-day one, there is little reason to prescribe it.

topic: the revival of bacteriophage therapy as an alternative to antibiotics
title: The Enemy of My Enemy
subtitle: Viruses that kill bacteria are being rediscovered as a weapon against resistant infections, but their return raises as many questions as it answers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Bacteriophages, or phages, are viruses that infect bacteria, multiply inside them and burst them open. Discovered in the early twentieth century, they were used to treat dysentery and infected wounds as early as the 1920s, years before penicillin reached hospitals. Once antibiotics arrived, however, phage therapy was largely abandoned in western Europe and North America. The new drugs acted against a broad range of bacteria, could be produced cheaply in vast quantities and kept well on a shelf, advantages that a living virus could not match. Only in a few research centres in eastern Europe did the practice continue. Now, as resistance erodes the power of antibiotics, phages are attracting renewed interest. That revival is understandable, but public enthusiasm has run well ahead of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The defining feature of phages is their specificity. Most will attack only a narrow range of strains within a single bacterial species, leaving the body's beneficial microbes untouched, which antibiotics conspicuously fail to do. The same quality, though, creates a practical obstacle: before treatment can begin, the bacterium responsible for an infection must be isolated and tested against candidate phages, a procedure that may take days or even weeks. Professor Anzor Gelashvili, whose institute in Tbilisi maintains a collection of several thousand phages, argues that ready-made cocktails combining many phages can cover most strains of a given species. Cocktails certainly ease the matching problem, yet they do not solve it, because bacterial populations are so varied that even a well-stocked mixture will meet strains it cannot kill.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Bacteria, moreover, can become resistant to phages, sometimes within days. Dr Liesel Ostrowiak of the Hanseatic Institute of Microbial Evolution sees an opportunity in this apparent setback. Phages usually gain entry to a cell by attaching to particular structures on its surface, and bacteria often escape them by altering or discarding those structures. In several species, Ostrowiak has shown, the structures concerned include pumps that expel antibiotics from the cell or a protective coating that shields it from the immune system. A bacterium that evolves resistance to the virus may therefore become vulnerable once more to drugs that had previously failed. Ostrowiak describes this as an evolutionary trap. The idea is elegant, but so far it has been demonstrated mainly in laboratory cultures and in only a handful of patients.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Much of the clinical evidence for phage therapy consists of individual case reports, typically involving desperately ill patients for whom every available antibiotic has failed. Some of these recoveries have been dramatic and widely publicised. Dr Emeka Ezeogu-Bray, a specialist in trial design at the Lagos Institute of Clinical Evaluation, urges caution. Such patients, he notes, almost always receive phages alongside antibiotics, surgery and intensive nursing, making it impossible to say which intervention produced the improvement; moreover, cases in which phages failed are seldom written up at all. The few controlled trials completed so far have been disappointing. One study of infected burns was stopped early after it emerged that the phage preparation had lost much of its strength in storage, so that patients received a fraction of the intended dose. Such setbacks reveal more about the difficulty of manufacturing phages consistently than about the limits of the therapy itself.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Regulation presents a further difficulty. Medicines law was written for chemical compounds that can be produced identically, batch after batch, and approved once. Phages are living entities that evolve, and an effective cocktail may need to be altered as the bacteria it targets change. A treatment in which a different phage is selected for each patient fits even less comfortably into existing rules. At least one European country has responded by allowing hospital pharmacies to prepare phages for named patients on a doctor's prescription, much as they might prepare a tailored ointment. This pragmatic arrangement deserves to be copied more widely, although it can never replace the rigorous trials needed to establish whether phages work.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Commercial incentives are equally weak. Phages occur naturally in soil, rivers and sewage, and naturally occurring organisms are difficult to patent, which leaves companies with little prospect of recovering the cost of development. Some firms have responded by genetically modifying phages, broadening the range of bacteria they attack or equipping them with enzymes that break down the slimy films in which bacteria shelter. Modified phages can be protected by patents, but they introduce new questions about safety and may meet public suspicion of engineered viruses.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that phages are a false hope. It does suggest that they are unlikely to replace antibiotics, and that their most realistic role is as a complement to them: a targeted treatment for particular stubborn infections, or a partner that makes existing drugs effective again. Perhaps the most valuable consequence of the phage revival will be conceptual. By forcing doctors to think of bacteria as evolving populations rather than fixed targets, it may change how all antimicrobial treatments are designed.

topic: antibiotic use in livestock farming and its contribution to human resistance
title: Medicine on the Farm
subtitle: Most of the world's antibiotics are given not to people but to animals. How much does that matter?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many countries, more antibiotics are sold for use in animals than in human medicine, and in some the proportion is well over half. This pattern dates from the late 1940s, when researchers discovered that chickens and pigs fed small quantities of antibiotics put on weight more quickly than those that received none. Within a decade, low doses were being mixed routinely into commercial feed, and the drugs used in this way became known as growth promoters. Remarkably, the reason they worked has never been fully explained. Some scientists believe the drugs suppress minor infections that divert an animal's energy; others think they alter the gut bacteria involved in digestion. That such an enormous quantity of medicine should have been used on the strength of an effect nobody properly understood is, in retrospect, astonishing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central question is how far farm use contributes to resistant infections in people. Dr Annelies Verhoeckx of the Lowlands Institute of Veterinary Epidemiology has tracked resistant bacteria from pig units to the workers who look after the animals and to members of their households. Resistant strains also leave farms in meat, in manure spread on fields and in water running off them, and Verhoeckx regards agriculture as a major source of the problem. Professor Ingvar Holmsund, an animal scientist, disagrees about the scale. He points out that most resistant infections treated in hospitals can be traced to the use of antibiotics in people, and that genetic studies often find the strains carried by humans to be distinct from those found in livestock. In truth, both may be right, but about different organisms: the share of resistance attributable to farming varies greatly from one bacterial species to another, and arguments over a single overall figure therefore obscure more than they reveal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whatever the precise contribution, a number of governments have acted. One Scandinavian country prohibited growth promoters in the mid-1980s, and others followed over the next two decades. The immediate consequences were not entirely encouraging. Without routine doses, animals fell ill more often, particularly young pigs in the weeks following weaning, and the quantity of antibiotics prescribed by vets to treat sick animals rose. Over time, however, this increase was reversed as farmers improved hygiene and ventilation, vaccinated more widely and weaned piglets later. The experience shows that intensive livestock farming without routine antibiotics is possible, even if the transition demands money and patience.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The agricultural economist Joaquín Sotomayor-Baeza has studied what the bans cost producers. On large, modern farms, he calculates, the loss of productivity was small, perhaps one or two per cent, largely because improvements in hygiene had already reduced the growth benefit the drugs provided. He warns, though, that the same may not hold elsewhere. On small farms where animals are kept in crowded and unsanitary conditions, antibiotics may still deliver substantial gains, and a sudden prohibition could fall hardest on the producers least able to absorb it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This matters because the fastest growth in meat production is now taking place in Asia, Africa and Latin America, where rising incomes are increasing demand. Researchers from the Mekong Livestock Health Consortium interviewed several hundred small-scale farmers and found that antibiotics were commonly bought without a prescription from feed shops and mixed into rations by the farmers themselves. Many of those interviewed could not distinguish antibiotics from vitamin supplements sold in similar packaging. Rather than recommending outright bans, the consortium proposes training village animal health workers who can advise farmers on disease prevention. The proposal is pragmatic, but advice alone is unlikely to be enough unless rules on the sale of the drugs are also enforced.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some specialists argue that the most urgent task is to protect particular drugs. Dr Khadija Bouzerda, a veterinary pharmacologist, has drawn attention to colistin, an old antibiotic that had been regarded as a last resort for treating people with infections resistant to everything else, yet was used in large quantities on farms. The discovery in farm animals of a resistance gene that could pass easily between bacteria prompted several countries to restrict its agricultural use. Bouzerda argues that antibiotics of critical importance to human medicine should be reserved for people alone. It is hard to dispute the principle, although the list of drugs considered critical is not fixed; it lengthens as resistance to other treatments spreads.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Consumers, too, have begun to influence practice, as supermarkets advertise meat from animals raised without antibiotics. Such labels may encourage better husbandry, but they also carry a risk: a farmer anxious to keep a lucrative contract may hesitate to treat an animal that is genuinely sick. Animal welfare must not be the price of reducing drug use. The goal should be fewer infections on farms, not simply fewer prescriptions. Judged by that standard, progress will depend as much on the design of barns, the quality of feed and the skill of stockworkers as on any regulation governing medicines.

topic: the broken economics of antibiotic development and subscription-style 'pull' incentives
title: Paying for the Fire Engine
subtitle: Why new antibiotics so rarely make money, and what governments might do about it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the decades after the Second World War, new families of antibiotics appeared at a rate that encouraged a dangerous complacency. Between the 1940s and the early 1960s, most of the major classes still in use today were discovered, and many doctors assumed that the supply of novel drugs would continue indefinitely. It did not. Since the late 1980s, very few genuinely new classes have reached patients, and the number of large pharmaceutical companies with active antibiotic research programmes has fallen from several dozen to a handful. More troubling still, some of the small firms that did succeed in bringing a new antibiotic to market collapsed shortly afterwards. One such company, Veridane Therapeutics, filed for bankruptcy less than a year after its drug was approved, having sold only a fraction of the quantity it had forecast. The paradox is stark: at a time when resistance is rising, the commercial reward for meeting the need appears to be failure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation lies in the peculiar economics of the product. Most medicines that generate large profits are taken daily for years, often for chronic conditions such as high blood pressure. An antibiotic, by contrast, is usually prescribed for a week or two. Moreover, a new antibiotic that works against resistant bacteria is, almost by definition, one that doctors are urged not to use. To preserve its effectiveness, hospital guidelines typically hold it in reserve for patients who have exhausted older options. Tamsin Quarshie, a health economist at the Brekkestad Institute for Pharmaceutical Policy, describes this as 'a market that punishes success': the more responsibly a drug is used, the less revenue it earns. Developing a new antibiotic is estimated to cost well over a billion dollars when failed candidates are included, yet annual sales of a newly approved one have often been below fifty million.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For many years, the main response of governments was to fund the early stages of research, a so-called 'push' approach. Grants were offered to universities and small companies to identify promising compounds and to carry them through laboratory testing and initial trials. Quarshie acknowledges that such funding has enlarged the pool of candidate drugs, but she argues that it addresses the wrong end of the problem. Push funding reduces the cost of getting a drug to approval; it does nothing to change what happens afterwards. A firm that successfully completes the process still confronts a market in which its product will barely be bought, and investors, knowing this, remain reluctant to provide the capital needed for the final and most expensive stage of clinical trials.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Attention has therefore shifted to 'pull' incentives, which reward a drug's arrival rather than its development. The most discussed is the subscription model, under which a health system pays a company a predetermined annual sum for access to an antibiotic, regardless of how many doses are actually used. The approach separates income from sales volume, removing any pressure on the manufacturer to promote wider prescribing. One European health service introduced such contracts for two antibiotics in a trial lasting three years. Oluwaseun Fadipe-Lund, who evaluated the scheme for an independent research group, found that it operated smoothly in administrative terms and that prescribing of the two drugs remained appropriately restrained. However, he notes that the sums involved, although generous by national standards, were far too small on their own to influence the investment decisions of a global industry. In principle the model is sound, but unless several large economies adopt it together, it will remain a gesture rather than a solution.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Kenji Morohashi, a clinical pharmacologist at Hanazono Medical College, objects that subscription payments may reward companies for drugs that offer little real advance. Of the antibiotics approved over the past two decades, he calculates that only a minority belong to new chemical classes; most are variations on existing molecules, against which bacteria may already possess partial resistance. Morohashi proposes that only drugs meeting strict criteria of novelty, such as a new mechanism of action, should qualify for the highest payments. The concern is reasonable, yet the remedy is less straightforward than it appears. A modified version of an old drug can occasionally be the only treatment that works against a particular resistant strain, and criteria based solely on chemical novelty could exclude it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical proposal comes from the Antimicrobial Commons Network, a coalition of academics and patient groups, which argues that antibiotic development should be removed from the commercial sector altogether and carried out by publicly funded bodies, much as many countries maintain public water supplies. Its members point out that taxpayers already finance much of the early science. The idea has an obvious appeal, but it underestimates how much specialist expertise late-stage development requires. Running large clinical trials across many countries, securing regulatory approval and manufacturing drugs to consistent standards are capabilities that few public institutions currently possess. Partnerships between non-profit organisations and smaller companies, in which public money is exchanged for commitments on pricing and access, seem a more realistic path.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever mechanism is chosen, it must also address a problem that rich-country debates often neglect. In many low-income countries, more people die from a lack of access to antibiotics than from resistance to them. A reward system that secures the development of new drugs but prices them beyond the reach of most of the world's patients would solve only half the problem. Perhaps the most useful way to think about antibiotics is as a form of insurance, comparable to a fire service: society pays to keep it ready, and judges it not by how often it is called upon but by whether it works when it is needed.
