topic: antibiotic residues and resistance genes in wastewater, rivers and factory discharges
title: Downstream
subtitle: Sewage works, rivers and factory outflows may be quietly breeding resistant bacteria

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Antibiotic resistance is usually described as a medical problem, and the remedies proposed for it are correspondingly medical: doctors should prescribe fewer drugs, patients should take them properly and hospitals should control infection more strictly. All of this is sensible, but it tells only part of the story. A large proportion of every antibiotic dose, between a third and nine-tenths depending on the drug, leaves the body largely unchanged and flows into the sewers. There it meets enormous numbers of bacteria from millions of human guts, together with disinfectants and traces of heavy metals. Framing resistance purely as a clinical issue has, in my view, allowed this hidden half of the problem to be overlooked for far too long.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Wastewater treatment plants are central to this story. They were designed to remove solid waste, organic matter and disease-causing microbes from sewage, not to eliminate medicines or the genes that allow bacteria to survive them. Dr Aigerim Dzhumabaeva, an environmental microbiologist at the Steppe Institute for Water Research, has sampled twelve such plants over four years. In the tanks where sewage is broken down by bacteria, she found microbes living in dense communities while being exposed to low levels of antibiotic residues, conditions in which they readily exchange resistance genes. At several plants, the treated water released into rivers contained a higher proportion of resistant bacteria than the sewage that had entered. Dzhumabaeva describes the plants as 'unintended incubators', places where resistance is not merely passed along but actively encouraged.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers accept this interpretation. Professor Ioana Zamfirescu, a water engineer, points out that antibiotic concentrations in sewage are typically thousands of times lower than those needed to kill bacteria. She adds that many of the resistance genes detected in rivers belong to gut bacteria that survive only briefly outside the body. In her view, the ability to detect a gene in a water sample has run ahead of the ability to say whether it poses any danger. Zamfirescu is right that the presence of a gene does not prove a threat to human health. However, she underestimates what low concentrations can do. Laboratory experiments have shown that levels a hundred times below the lethal dose can still give resistant strains a competitive advantage, allowing them gradually to replace their susceptible neighbours.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If sewage works are a concern, factories that manufacture antibiotics are a far greater one. Investigators sampling rivers below production sites in several countries have recorded drug concentrations higher than those found in the blood of patients undergoing treatment. Dr Faith Kipkemboi, a health policy researcher, argues that the most effective lever is the purchasing power of governments and international agencies. Under her proposal, these buyers would refuse to sign contracts with manufacturers that could not demonstrate safe levels of discharge. The idea is attractive because it uses an existing mechanism rather than relying on new international law. Yet it has a cost that its supporters tend to pass over: cleaner production will raise prices, and the countries that can least afford more expensive medicines may be the ones that suffer most.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whether resistant bacteria in the environment actually make people ill is harder to establish. One coastal study compared regular surfers with people who rarely entered the sea and found that the surfers were noticeably more likely to carry resistant bacteria in their gut, presumably because they swallowed more seawater contaminated by sewage outflows. The finding is suggestive, but carrying a resistant organism is not the same as becoming sick, and the number of infections that can be traced to environmental exposure remains unknown. Caution is needed in both directions: the absence of proof is not proof that the risk is negligible.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Technologies to reduce the problem already exist. Treatment with ozone or ultraviolet light can destroy many antibiotic residues and damage bacterial DNA, but fitting these systems to every treatment plant would be expensive and would consume large quantities of energy. Dzhumabaeva therefore favours a targeted approach, treating wastewater at the point where it leaves hospitals, which discharge particularly concentrated mixtures of drugs and resistant organisms. This seems the more sensible priority. A modest number of installations at the most concentrated sources would achieve much of the benefit at a fraction of the cost of upgrading entire networks.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most valuable contribution of environmental research, however, lies not in cleaning water but in reading it. Sewage contains a record of the bacteria carried by everyone connected to a network, healthy and sick alike, and regular testing could reveal the spread of a new form of resistance in a community well before it appears in hospital laboratories. Very few countries currently monitor sewage or rivers in this way. Building such systems would be cheap compared with the costs of an untreatable infection, and it would finally give the environment the place it deserves in the response to resistance.

topic: rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests and the reduction of unnecessary antibiotic prescribing
title: A Test Before the Prescription
subtitle: Can fast diagnostic tools end the habit of prescribing antibiotics 'just in case'?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A patient arrives at a family doctor's surgery with a fever and a persistent cough. The cause may be a virus, in which case antibiotics will do nothing, or a bacterium, in which case they may be essential. The doctor has perhaps ten minutes to decide and, in most cases, no reliable way of telling the two apart. Faced with this dilemma, many doctors prescribe an antibiotic as a precaution. Surveys frequently blame such prescriptions on patients who demand medication, but this explanation is too convenient. The deeper cause is uncertainty: a doctor who cannot rule out a serious bacterial infection will understandably choose the option that seems to carry the smaller risk, even if, across thousands of consultations, the result is an enormous volume of unnecessary drugs.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In principle, the laboratory can resolve this uncertainty. In practice, growing bacteria from a sample and testing their response to different drugs usually takes two or three days, by which time the decision about treatment has long been made. Hence the interest in rapid tests that deliver a result during the consultation itself. The most widely used measures C-reactive protein, a substance whose level in the blood rises sharply in many bacterial infections, from a single drop of blood taken from a fingertip. Halldis Thorvaldsen, a general practitioner and researcher, led a series of trials in which family practices were given the test. Prescribing for respiratory infections fell by roughly a quarter, with no increase in complications or hospital admissions. Thorvaldsen is careful to add, however, that the benefit depended almost entirely on whether doctors believed the result; in practices where low readings were routinely disregarded, prescribing barely changed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More ambitious technologies are emerging in hospitals. The microbiologist Mathieu Duroselle has worked on molecular tests that identify both the species of bacterium in a sample and the genes it carries for resistance, producing a result in a few hours rather than days. Duroselle predicts that such tools will allow doctors to abandon the practice of starting seriously ill patients on broad-spectrum drugs, which attack many kinds of bacteria at once, and to move them almost immediately onto narrower treatments aimed at the specific organism. His enthusiasm is understandable, but it runs ahead of the evidence. The presence of a resistance gene does not always predict how a bacterium will actually respond to a drug, since genes can be present but inactive, and resistance can arise through mechanisms that current tests are not designed to detect.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Then there is the question of who pays. Priyamvada Bakshi-Rao, a health economist, has analysed the finances of diagnostic testing in primary care. Each test costs considerably more than the course of antibiotics it might replace, because most common antibiotics are now extremely cheap. The principal benefit of testing, a slower spread of resistance, is real but diffuse: it accrues to society as a whole and largely in the future, while the cost falls on the individual practice today. Bakshi-Rao concludes that few practices will adopt tests voluntarily and argues that health systems should reimburse them directly. This is surely correct. Judging a diagnostic test by the drug costs it saves is like judging a smoke alarm by the price of the matches it prevents people from striking.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An unexpected perspective comes from the Ostrava Primary Care Collaborative, a group of practices that compared the effect of rapid testing with that of training doctors to explain to patients why antibiotics might be unnecessary. Training alone reduced prescribing almost as much as testing did, and patients who received a clear explanation were as satisfied as those who left with a prescription. The group suggests that the main value of a test may lie less in informing the doctor than in giving the patient a visible, objective reason to accept a decision. The finding deserves attention, though it would be a mistake to conclude that tests are merely props; in the minority of cases where a doctor's judgement is wrong, an accurate result still matters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Experience in lower-income countries offers a sobering lesson. Koffi Thibeault, who studies health services in West Africa, has examined what happened when rapid tests for malaria were introduced in rural clinics. Previously, health workers had treated almost every fever as malaria. Once the tests showed that most patients did not have the disease, prescriptions of antimalarial drugs fell steeply, as intended. But prescriptions of antibiotics rose. Health workers faced with a feverish patient and a negative result felt obliged to offer some treatment, and an antibiotic was the obvious alternative. A negative test, Thibeault observes, removes one explanation without supplying another, and something will usually fill the gap.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Rapid diagnostics, then, are necessary but not sufficient. A test that tells a doctor what a patient does not have is of limited use unless it is accompanied by clear guidance about what to do next, whether that means a follow-up appointment, advice on managing symptoms at home or a delayed prescription to be collected only if the illness worsens. The aim should not simply be fewer prescriptions but decisions taken with confidence, by doctors who understand what a result means and patients who understand why it matters.

topic: the ancient natural origins of antibiotic resistance genes in permafrost, caves and soil
title: Older Than Medicine
subtitle: Resistance to antibiotics was not invented in the twentieth century, and recognising this changes the question we should be asking

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is widely assumed that antibiotic resistance is a modern phenomenon, a direct product of the medical revolution that began in the 1940s. According to this view, bacteria learned to withstand drugs only after humans started to use them in vast quantities. The truth is more interesting and, in some ways, more humbling. Resistance is ancient, far older than medicine and probably older than humanity itself. What people did in the twentieth century was not to bring resistance into being but to create conditions in which bacteria that already possessed it would flourish at the expense of those that did not. The distinction may sound academic, but it has practical consequences for the way the problem should be tackled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence comes from frozen ground. Larysa Velichko, a palaeomicrobiologist, extracted DNA from permafrost sediments in north-eastern Siberia that had remained frozen for roughly thirty thousand years. Among the genetic material she recovered were genes very similar to those that today protect bacteria against several classes of drugs used in hospitals. Because modern DNA is everywhere, and because a single contaminating bacterium could have produced misleading results, Velichko's team took elaborate precautions, analysing samples in sealed laboratories and checking that the ancient genes showed the chemical damage expected in material of great age. Their conclusion was unambiguous: these genes existed tens of thousands of years before anyone isolated penicillin.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An even more striking case was reported by Sayuri Ishikura, who studied bacteria living deep inside a limestone cave that had been cut off from the surface for an estimated four million years. No human, and therefore no human medicine, could have influenced these microbes. Yet when Ishikura exposed them to a range of modern antibiotics, most of the strains resisted several drugs, and some withstood compounds that had been synthesised by chemists only in recent decades. Her explanation is that many soil and rock bacteria produce antibiotic substances naturally, to suppress their neighbours, and that the neighbours in turn have evolved defences. Resistance, on this account, is one side of an arms race that has continued for millions of years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts the language of warfare. The microbial ecologist Esteban Arriagada points out that in natural environments antibiotic substances are usually present in tiny concentrations, far too low to kill anything. At such levels, he argues, they appear to act less like weapons than like signals, molecules that bacteria use to sense and respond to one another. If so, many of the genes now described as 'resistance genes' may originally have served quite different purposes, such as processing nutrients or removing toxic waste, and applying a medical label to them is a case of reading history backwards. Arriagada's interpretation is plausible and deserves to be taken seriously. It does not, however, alter the fact that these genes protect bacteria against drugs once they find their way into the wrong organisms.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That is the crucial step. A resistance gene in a harmless bacterium living in a cave or a field poses little threat to anyone. The danger arises when such a gene is transferred, often on small mobile pieces of DNA, into a species capable of causing disease in people. Several resistance genes now common in hospital infections have been traced to environmental bacteria; in one well-documented case, a gene carried by a dangerous pathogen proved to be almost identical to one found in a bacterium that lives in fresh water. Such transfers are rare events. But wherever antibiotics are used heavily, any bacterium that acquires a protective gene gains an immediate advantage, so a transfer that would otherwise have vanished is likely to persist and spread.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recognising the environment as a vast reservoir of resistance has prompted new research strategies. The Resistome Atlas Project, an international consortium of laboratories, is building a catalogue of resistance genes found in soils, rivers and sediments around the world. Its members propose that candidate drugs should be tested against this collection before they reach patients, so that likely routes to resistance can be identified while there is still time to modify the compound or plan its use carefully. This is a sensible form of early warning, although its limits should be acknowledged: the number of genes in nature is so great that any catalogue will remain incomplete, and some forms of resistance will inevitably come as a surprise.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, follows from the antiquity of resistance? Above all, it suggests that resistance cannot be defeated, only managed. Bacteria have been evolving defences against natural antibiotics for longer than complex animals have existed, and they will not be outmanoeuvred by any single new drug. The familiar talk of a 'war' against superbugs is therefore misleading, since it implies that victory is possible. A more accurate image might be that of careful husbandry, in which a precious and limited resource is used sparingly, so that the defences already present in the microbial world are given as few opportunities as possible to spread.

topic: behavioural 'nudges' such as peer-comparison letters, commitment posters and software defaults to reduce antibiotic prescribing
title: Nudging the Prescriber
subtitle: Behavioural science has produced some cheap and surprisingly effective ways of changing how doctors use antibiotics, but their limits are becoming clear

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For decades, the standard method of persuading doctors to prescribe fewer antibiotics was to tell them why they should. Guidelines were circulated, lectures delivered and leaflets printed, and although these efforts raised awareness, their effect on actual prescribing was usually modest and short-lived. Campaigns aimed at the public fared little better, since many patients who had seen them still expected a prescription whenever they felt unwell. Doctors, it turned out, already knew that antibiotics do not cure colds; what they lacked was not knowledge but a reason to act differently in the pressured setting of a busy surgery. Behavioural science offers a different approach. Rather than supplying more information, it seeks to alter the context in which decisions are made, often through changes so small that they cost almost nothing. The appeal for health systems with limited budgets is obvious.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the best-known experiments was designed by the behavioural economist Ignasi Benavent-Soler. Family doctors whose prescribing rates placed them in the top fifth of their region received a single letter informing them that they prescribed more antibiotics than four out of five of their colleagues. Crucially, the letter was signed by the country's chief physician, a figure whose authority most doctors respected. Over the following six months, prescribing among those who received the letter fell by around three per cent compared with a control group. The figure may sound trivial, but it should not be dismissed. Spread across thousands of practices, it represented tens of thousands of prescriptions avoided, at a cost of little more than paper and postage.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The question is how long such effects last. Torunn Hagelund, a health services researcher, followed the same doctors for a further two years. The difference between the two groups faded steadily after the first year, and when a second round of letters was sent, its impact was noticeably smaller than that of the first. Hagelund attributes this to habituation: a message that is surprising the first time becomes familiar, and familiar messages are easily ignored. Benavent-Soler does not dispute the data but draws a different conclusion. In his view, an intervention that costs so little need not be permanent to be worthwhile, and even a fading effect delivers a substantial return on a very small investment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other studies have targeted the moment of consultation itself. In one trial, posters were displayed in the waiting rooms of participating clinics, each carrying a photograph of the clinic's doctor and his or her signature beneath a pledge to avoid prescribing antibiotics when they were unlikely to help. Inappropriate prescriptions for respiratory infections fell by about a fifth. The researchers suggest that the posters exploit a well-established tendency: people like to remain consistent with commitments they have made publicly. A further benefit, reported by several of the doctors involved, was that the poster made conversations easier, since patients had often read the pledge before they entered the room.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is comfortable with these techniques. Farrukh Yuldashev, a medical ethicist, argues that peer comparison measures the quantity of prescriptions rather than their appropriateness. A doctor who serves an elderly or deprived population may prescribe more because her patients are genuinely more vulnerable to serious infection, and letters that imply she is behaving badly could pressure her into withholding treatment that is needed. This is a valid concern, and comparisons of prescribing ought to be adjusted for the characteristics of each practice's patients. Yet Yuldashev's warning should not be overstated: in none of the major trials so far has any rise in complications or hospital admissions been detected among the patients of doctors who received letters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The Corrib Prescribing Research Unit has argued that the most powerful behavioural tools are not messages at all but the design of the systems doctors use every day. Most prescriptions are now issued through computer software that suggests a dose and a course length. When the unit persuaded one regional health service to reduce the default duration offered by the software from seven days to five, the great majority of prescriptions changed accordingly, with almost no doctors overriding the new setting. Defaults raise their own questions, since many users may be unaware that a choice has been made on their behalf. They do, however, have one advantage over letters and posters: they place no social pressure on individual doctors.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would nevertheless be a mistake to regard nudges as a substitute for more fundamental reform. Many doctors prescribe antibiotics not because they misunderstand the evidence or are indifferent to peer opinion, but because a consultation lasting a few minutes leaves no time to examine a patient thoroughly, explain a decision or arrange a follow-up visit. In countries where doctors are allowed fifteen or twenty minutes per patient, prescribing rates tend to be lower, although so many other features of those health systems differ that the comparison is difficult to interpret. In the end, it is the length of the consultation, more than the attitudes of those conducting it, that constrains good practice. Behavioural techniques can make the best of a difficult situation; they cannot by themselves change the situation.

topic: new routes to antibiotic discovery: culturing 'unculturable' soil bacteria, insect symbionts and genome mining
title: Digging Deeper
subtitle: After decades in which the search for new antibiotics stalled, scientists are finding fresh ways to explore the microbial world

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of the antibiotics in use today were found by a remarkably simple method. In the middle of the twentieth century, scientists collected samples of soil, grew the bacteria they contained on dishes of nutrient jelly and tested whether any of them produced substances that killed disease-causing microbes. For about two decades the approach yielded discovery after discovery. Then it began to fail. Researchers screening new soil samples found the same compounds again and again, and the expense of sifting through thousands of familiar molecules for a rare novelty eventually led most companies to abandon the effort. The underlying problem, it later became clear, was not that soil had run out of antibiotics but that the method could reach only a tiny part of it. It is estimated that around ninety-nine per cent of soil bacteria refuse to grow under standard laboratory conditions, and it was from the remaining one per cent that almost every classic antibiotic had come.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One ingenious attempt to reach the missing majority was developed by the microbiologist Yaw Asantewaa-Holt. Instead of trying to reproduce soil conditions in the laboratory, his team placed diluted soil samples in a small chamber sealed between two porous membranes and then buried the device back in the ground. Nutrients and chemical signals from the surrounding soil could pass through the membranes, while the bacteria themselves remained trapped inside. Many species that had never grown on a dish formed colonies in the chamber, and some, once established, could subsequently be grown in the laboratory. Screening around ten thousand such isolates, the team identified a compound that attacks the building materials of the bacterial cell wall rather than a protein, a target that bacteria cannot easily alter through a single genetic change. In weeks of laboratory tests, no resistant mutants appeared. The discovery is undoubtedly important, but some of the claims made on its behalf, including the suggestion that it might prove resistance-proof, are premature.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The pharmacologist Kerttu Nieminen has been among the most measured commentators. She notes that the journey from a promising compound to an approved medicine typically takes between ten and fifteen years, and that most candidates are abandoned along the way because they prove toxic, are poorly absorbed or behave differently in the human body than in a dish. More fundamentally, she points out that the failure to produce resistant mutants in a laboratory says nothing about another route to resistance. The bacterium that manufactures an antibiotic must possess some means of protecting itself from it, and the genes responsible could one day be transferred to the pathogens the drug is meant to kill. Her caution is well founded, although it applies to every new antibiotic and so is not an argument against pursuing this one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have looked beyond soil altogether. Sami Belloumi, an evolutionary biologist, studies bacteria that live in partnership with insects. Certain ants, for example, cultivate fungus gardens as food and carry bacteria on their bodies that produce compounds suppressing invading moulds. Belloumi argues that such partnerships, which have persisted for millions of years, represent a natural screening programme: the compounds involved have been refined to attack harmful microbes while leaving the host animal unharmed, a property that random soil screening cannot guarantee. Searching where ecology suggests antibiotics are being used, rather than sampling at random, should in his view make discovery considerably more efficient. The argument is attractive, though it remains to be seen whether compounds that are safe for an ant will prove equally safe for a human being.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third strategy relies on computers rather than shovels. Researchers at the Chiloé Natural Products Group analyse the complete DNA sequences of thousands of bacterial species, searching for clusters of genes that resemble those known to produce antibiotics. Their work has revealed that even well-studied organisms contain many such clusters that remain silent under laboratory conditions, apparently because the environmental cues that would normally trigger them are absent. By switching these clusters on, either by altering growing conditions or by transferring the genes into more cooperative host species, the group hopes to obtain compounds that no one has ever seen. The approach offers enormous breadth, yet it does not remove the need for laboratory work. Every molecule predicted on a screen must still be made in usable quantities and tested before its value can be judged, so the bottleneck is moved rather than eliminated.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these developments justify cautious optimism. The idea that nature had been exhausted as a source of antibiotics now looks mistaken; the microbial world is far larger and more varied than mid-century scientists could have known. It would be wrong, however, to suppose that better science alone will refill the medicine cabinet. Researchers can now identify promising candidates more readily than at any time in the past half-century. Whether those candidates ever reach patients will depend chiefly on whether anyone is prepared to pay for the long and costly process of turning them into medicines.

topic: evolution-informed treatment strategies: fitness costs, combination therapy, drug cycling and collateral sensitivity
title: Thinking One Move Ahead
subtitle: Some scientists believe antibiotics should be prescribed with an eye on how bacteria will evolve, not just on whether a drug works today

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a doctor chooses an antibiotic, the decision normally rests on a single question: which drug is most likely to kill the bacteria causing this infection now? How those bacteria, or the many others in the patient's body, might evolve in response is rarely considered. Yet resistance is, at bottom, an evolutionary process, and a growing number of researchers argue that treatment should be designed to anticipate it. The proposal is hardly radical; farmers managing pests and oncologists treating tumours have long thought in such terms. That medicine has taken so long to apply the same logic to bacterial infections is, in my view, one of the more curious oversights in modern healthcare.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years, one evolutionary idea offered considerable comfort. Resistance, it was argued, usually comes at a price: a bacterium that has altered its machinery to withstand a drug often grows more slowly than its unaltered relatives. If the drug were withdrawn, susceptible strains should therefore outcompete resistant ones, and resistance should gradually disappear. The epidemiologist Dorottya Gyulai tested this prediction using records from a country that had sharply reduced its use of one common antibiotic. Over the following decade, resistance to the drug declined only slightly. Laboratory work explained why: resistant bacteria frequently acquire further mutations that restore their growth rate without sacrificing their resistance. The implication is sobering. Resistance, once established, is far more persistent than the original theory suggested, and simply resting a drug cannot be relied upon to restore its power.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more promising strategy is to deny bacteria the chance to become resistant in the first place. If two drugs that act in different ways are given together, a bacterium must acquire two independent changes at once to survive, an event far less probable than acquiring one. This principle has underpinned the treatment of tuberculosis for decades, and the microbiologist Txomin Ibarzábal argues that it should be applied to a much wider range of serious infections. His case is strong, but combinations are not universally beneficial. Some pairs of antibiotics interfere with each other, so that one drug actually weakens the effect of the other. Using two drugs also increases the likelihood of side effects and inflicts greater damage on the harmless bacteria of the gut.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Hospitals have also experimented with altering how drugs are used across whole wards. In a policy known as cycling, the antibiotic used as the first choice for a given type of infection is changed every few months, in the hope that bacteria resistant to one drug will decline while another is in use. The results of clinical trials have been largely disappointing. Mathematical modelling by the Jämtland Evolutionary Medicine Group offers an explanation. During each period of a cycle, every patient on the ward receives the same drug, creating intense and uniform pressure that favours resistance to it. Their models suggest that mixing, in which different patients receive different drugs at the same time, performs at least as well and often better.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most intriguing idea of all exploits a phenomenon called collateral sensitivity. Bacteria that become resistant to one antibiotic sometimes become more vulnerable to a second, because the change that protects them against the first drug weakens a defence that the second would otherwise have to overcome. Kalena Kaawaloa, a systems biologist, has mapped hundreds of such relationships in the laboratory. She proposes that drugs could be given in carefully planned sequences, so that each episode of resistance leaves the bacteria exposed to the next treatment. In laboratory experiments, such sequences have succeeded in keeping bacterial populations susceptible for much longer than conventional treatment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whether this success can be repeated in patients is another matter. Laboratory experiments typically involve a single strain of bacteria grown under controlled conditions, whereas an infection in a human body may involve diverse populations exposed to fluctuating drug levels. Kaawaloa herself has found that a relationship between two drugs observed in one strain is sometimes reversed in another strain of the same species. If that is the case, a sequence that traps one infection could accelerate resistance in the next. Before collateral sensitivity can guide treatment, doctors will need to know quickly and precisely which strain they are facing, something that routine laboratory testing cannot yet provide.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is also an ethical complication. Doctors are trained to choose the best treatment for the individual in front of them, whereas many evolutionary strategies appear to ask them to accept a slightly less effective option today for the sake of patients in the future. Critics have warned that this places clinicians in an impossible position. The tension is real, but it has been exaggerated. In many cases, a treatment chosen to prevent resistance also protects the patient being treated, since an infection that develops resistance during therapy is a leading cause of relapse and treatment failure.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of these approaches offers a simple solution, and some may never leave the laboratory. Taken together, however, they reflect an important change of perspective. Evolution is the reason antibiotics lose their power; it is only sensible that an understanding of evolution should shape the way they are used.

topic: classical biological control of invasive weeds and the risks of releasing specialist insect agents
title: Fighting Weeds with Insects
subtitle: Releasing a weed's natural predators can tame an invasion, but the history of biological control is not free of costly mistakes

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a plant is carried far from its native range, it frequently leaves behind the insects, fungi and mites that feed on it at home. Freed from these pressures, some newcomers spread with startling speed, smothering riverbanks, pastures and wetlands. Classical biological control attempts to restore the missing pressure by deliberately importing one or more of the plant's specialised enemies. The logic is appealingly simple, and when it works the results can be remarkable: a single beetle or weevil, once established, may suppress a weed across an entire continent at no further cost to anyone. Herbicide programmes, by contrast, must be repeated year after year and rarely reach remote or inaccessible terrain. It is unsurprising, then, that land managers faced with vast infestations have long regarded biocontrol as the most attractive option available.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method's reputation, however, has been shadowed by a handful of notorious failures. Most of these date from an era when agents were chosen with little regard for what else they might eat. Generalist predators, such as certain snails and vertebrates, were released to control pests and instead turned their attention to native species, in some cases driving them towards extinction. Critics of biocontrol still cite these episodes, and with some justification. Yet it would be misleading to treat them as representative of modern practice. The cases most often quoted involved animals released against insect or mammal pests, not the narrowly specialised herbivores now used against weeds, and the regulatory systems of most countries have changed beyond recognition since then.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Central to contemporary practice is host-specificity testing. Before any release is approved, candidate agents are confined with a list of test plants, typically including close relatives of the target weed, native species of conservation value and economically important crops. Dr Katarzyna Dobrowolny, who directs a quarantine laboratory at the Southern Hemisphere Weed Research Institute, explains that the selection of test plants follows a phylogenetic principle: the more closely related a plant is to the weed, the more likely it is to be attacked. Her laboratory routinely rejects more than half of the candidates it screens. 'Most promising insects never leave quarantine,' she notes, 'and that is precisely how the system should work.'

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is reassured. The entomologist Sipho Mabaso of the Cape Biodiversity Council argues that laboratory tests can only reveal what an insect is physiologically capable of eating, not what it will do in the field over many decades. Cage trials, he points out, last weeks rather than generations, and an agent's behaviour may change once its preferred host becomes scarce, which is exactly the condition that successful control is designed to create. Mabaso does not oppose biocontrol outright, but he favours long-term monitoring of every released agent, funded for at least twenty years after release. Few programmes currently meet this standard, since funding bodies are generally willing to pay for releases but reluctant to pay for what follows.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the method reply that the evidence from the field is, on the whole, encouraging. A review of several hundred weed biocontrol agents released worldwide over the past century, compiled by a team under Hiroshi Yanagida at the Pacific Agroecology Consortium, found that significant damage to non-target plants had been recorded in fewer than one per cent of cases, and that nearly all of those involved plants closely related to the target which had been identified as at risk before release. Yanagida concludes that the real hazard of biocontrol is not unpredictable behaviour but the willingness of regulators, under pressure, to approve agents whose risks were already known. This is a persuasive reading of the data, though it should be noted that non-target effects on plants that nobody monitors are, by definition, unlikely to appear in such a review.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different objection concerns not safety but effectiveness. Only around a third of released agents are thought to exert meaningful control over their target, and many fail to establish at all. Ana Lucía Bastidas, an economist at the Andean Institute for Environmental Policy, has calculated the returns of programmes across four continents and reports that the successful projects more than repay the cost of the failures, with benefit-to-cost ratios that often exceed those of chemical or mechanical control. Her figures are striking, but they rest on the assumption that a weed's spread would have continued unchecked without intervention, an assumption that is difficult to test.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this debate is not a verdict but a matter of proportion. Biological control is neither the reckless gamble its detractors describe nor the risk-free solution its advocates sometimes imply. Its record over the past half-century is far better than its early history suggests, and for many widespread weeds there is simply no realistic alternative. The more pressing problem lies elsewhere: a system that invests heavily in screening agents before release while neglecting to watch what they do afterwards is, in effect, conducting an experiment and declining to record the results.

topic: ballast water and hull fouling as pathways for marine invasive species, and the regulation of shipping
title: Stowaways in the Hold
subtitle: Ships carry billions of tonnes of seawater around the globe every year, and with it a hidden cargo of living organisms

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A cargo ship that has unloaded its goods rides high in the water and becomes unstable. To restore its balance, it pumps seawater into tanks within its hull, sometimes tens of thousands of tonnes, and discharges that water at the next port, where new cargo is taken on. The practice is essential to safe navigation, and it has been routine since steel hulls replaced solid ballast such as stones and sand in the late nineteenth century. Yet each tank is, in effect, a floating aquarium. Plankton, larvae, small fish and microbes drawn in at one port may be released thousands of kilometres away, in waters where they have no natural competitors. It is estimated that several thousand species are in transit in the world's ballast tanks at any given moment.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For decades it was assumed that few of these passengers could survive the voyage. Tanks are dark, oxygen levels can fall sharply, and food is scarce. Research by the marine biologist Ingrid Sørlie at the Norwegian Institute for Coastal Ecology overturned that assumption. Sampling tanks on vessels crossing the North Atlantic, her team found that while the total number of living organisms declined over the course of a journey, a substantial minority of species persisted, and some, notably certain dinoflagellates, formed resistant cysts that could remain dormant in the sediment at the bottom of a tank for months. Sørlie concluded that the length of a voyage was a poor predictor of risk; what mattered far more was the biology of the species being carried.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The consequences of a successful arrival can be dramatic. Rustam Kerimov, of the Caspian Basin Research Station, has documented the appearance of a comb jelly in the Caspian Sea, almost certainly in ballast water carried through the inland canal network. Within a few years the jelly, which consumes zooplankton and fish eggs, had contributed to a collapse in catches of the small fish on which the local fishing industry depended. Kerimov stresses that the comb jelly did not act alone, since overfishing and pollution had already weakened the ecosystem, but he regards the episode as a warning that degraded waters are especially vulnerable to newcomers. This point deserves more attention than it receives: the ports where ballast is discharged are frequently among the most polluted stretches of coast anywhere.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: International regulation has been slow to respond. A convention requiring ships to manage their ballast water was adopted in the early 2000s, but it did not come into force for well over a decade, because it required ratification by states representing a large share of global shipping tonnage. Initially, ships were asked to exchange coastal water for open-ocean water in the middle of a voyage, on the reasoning that oceanic organisms are unlikely to survive in coastal conditions, and vice versa. Exchange is now being replaced by on-board treatment systems, which filter the water and then kill the remaining organisms with ultraviolet light or chemical agents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whether these systems perform as promised is disputed. Clarisse Uwimana, an engineer who has tested treatment units for a consortium of port authorities, reports that many perform well under trial conditions but considerably worse in service. Ultraviolet treatment, for instance, depends on light penetrating the water, and in turbid estuaries laden with sediment its effectiveness can fall sharply. She advocates routine sampling of discharged water at ports, rather than reliance on the certificates issued when units are first installed. The shipping economist Felipe Navarrete counters that such inspections would delay vessels and impose costs that fall disproportionately on smaller operators. His concern is legitimate, but it is hard to see how a regulation can be credible if no one checks whether it is being obeyed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is, moreover, a growing recognition that ballast water is only part of the problem. Dewi Tjahjono, a biologist with the Java Sea Biosecurity Programme, has argued for years that the organisms attached to ships' hulls, such as barnacles, mussels, seaweeds and tubeworms, may now introduce as many species as ballast does. Hull fouling has received far less regulatory attention, partly because it is harder to measure and partly because the antifouling paints once used to prevent it were themselves banned for their toxicity to marine life. Tjahjono's position was once regarded as marginal, but recent surveys of ports in Asia and Australasia have tended to support it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the ballast convention has been a failure. It has established the principle that ships are responsible for the organisms they carry, and it has stimulated an entire industry devoted to treatment technology. But a measure that targets only one pathway, and whose results are verified largely on paper, should not be mistaken for a solution. The organisms that ships carry have no regard for the categories that regulators draw, and policy will need to treat the vessel as a whole, rather than its tanks alone, if the flow of marine invaders is to be meaningfully reduced.

topic: the accelerating spread of cane toads in Australia, spatial sorting and rapid evolution at an invasion front
title: Faster at the Front
subtitle: Australia's most notorious invader has been evolving as it spreads, and the lesson reaches well beyond one unloved amphibian

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1935, around a hundred cane toads were shipped from Hawaii to the sugar-growing districts of north-eastern Australia in the hope that they would eat the beetles that were damaging the crop. They did not noticeably control the beetles, but they did thrive. From a handful of release sites in Queensland, the toads have spread across much of the tropical north and are now established more than two thousand kilometres to the west, in the Kimberley region. Their success owes a great deal to their toxicity. Glands on the shoulders secrete a poison that kills many of the native predators which attempt to eat them, including goannas, freshwater crocodiles and the northern quoll, a small carnivorous marsupial. Because Australian animals evolved without toads, few possess any resistance to the poison.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What makes the toad of particular interest to biologists, however, is not its toxicity but its speed. In the early decades of the invasion, the front advanced by roughly ten kilometres a year. By the early 2000s, it was moving at more than fifty kilometres a year. Climate and terrain explain part of this acceleration, but Dr Marek Hrdlička, who fitted radio transmitters to toads at the invasion front in the Northern Territory, found something else. Toads at the leading edge had longer legs relative to their body size than those in long-established populations, and they moved in straighter lines, travelling further each night and on more nights of the year. Some covered more than a kilometre in a single night, a distance that would be extraordinary for an animal of their size.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The explanation proposed by the evolutionary biologist Ebere Inyang has come to be known as spatial sorting. At an expanding front, Inyang argues, the individuals that arrive first are, almost by definition, the fastest dispersers. They breed with one another, because no slower toads have yet arrived, and their offspring inherit the traits that carried their parents forward. Repeated over many generations, this process can drive dispersal ability upwards even if it brings no advantage in survival or reproduction. Indeed, toads at the front appear to pay a price: Hrdlička's team recorded higher rates of spinal injury among the longest-legged individuals, suggesting that speed comes at a physical cost. Spatial sorting is unusual in that it operates alongside natural selection rather than through it, and some theorists initially doubted that it could be strong enough to matter. The toad data have largely silenced those doubts.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The implications for management are uncomfortable. If invasions speed up as they proceed, forecasts based on early rates of spread will consistently underestimate how quickly a species will reach new areas. Inyang has suggested that this may apply to many invaders, from plants whose seeds are carried by the wind to insect pests, although data of comparable quality exist for very few of them. It is a reasonable hypothesis, but it should not yet be treated as a general law. The toad is an unusually mobile animal spreading across an unusually uniform landscape, and the conditions that allowed sorting to operate so powerfully may be rare.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Attempts to halt the toad have achieved little. Volunteer groups have collected and killed millions of adults, and fences and traps have been tried, but no method has slowed the front over any significant distance. Dr Saara Lepistö, a conservation biologist, therefore argues that resources would be better spent on reducing the toads' impact than on reducing their numbers. Her team has trained northern quolls to avoid toads by feeding them small, non-lethal pieces of toad meat treated with a chemical that induces nausea, shortly before the invasion front arrives. Trained quolls were considerably more likely to survive the toads' arrival than untrained animals. In some populations the young of trained mothers also avoided toads, although whether this behaviour was learned from the mothers remains unclear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A complementary approach has come from Indigenous ranger groups in the Kimberley. The Kimberley Ranger Collective has combined traditional knowledge of the movements of goannas and other predators with modern monitoring techniques, identifying the sites where predators are most concentrated and where aversion training is therefore likely to have the greatest effect. The rangers argue that the debate over toads has focused too heavily on the toad itself and too little on the country into which it is moving. Their emphasis on detailed knowledge of particular landscapes is arguably the most promising development of recent years, precisely because the toad's advance cannot realistically be reversed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ninety years after its introduction, the cane toad has become a textbook example in two senses. It remains the archetypal warning against introducing one species to control another. But it has also become a natural experiment in rapid evolution, revealing that invaders are not fixed entities with fixed rates of spread, but populations that change as they move. Managers who plan for the invader as it was when it arrived, rather than as it will become, are likely to find themselves repeatedly outpaced.

topic: eating invasive species: the lionfish in the western Atlantic and the limits of harvest-based control
title: Dinner as Defence
subtitle: Can turning an invasive predator into a menu item help to protect the reefs it threatens?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few marine invasions have unfolded as quickly, or as visibly, as that of the lionfish in the western Atlantic. Native to the Indo-Pacific, the striped, spine-covered fish was first recorded off the coast of Florida in the mid-1980s, probably after being released from home aquariums. Within three decades it had colonised reefs from the eastern seaboard of the United States to the northern coast of South America, reaching densities several times higher than any recorded in its native range. Lionfish are voracious generalists, consuming dozens of species of small reef fish and crustaceans, and they reproduce throughout the year, with a single female able to release tens of thousands of eggs every few days. Native Atlantic predators, unfamiliar with the newcomer, rarely attack it, and its venomous spines deter all but the most determined.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Faced with an invader that cannot be eradicated by any known method, a number of conservation organisations have adopted an unconventional strategy: encouraging people to eat it. Campaigns promoting lionfish as a sustainable delicacy have appeared in restaurants, cookery books and fishing tournaments across the Caribbean. Some governments have joined in, licensing spearfishing that would otherwise be prohibited on protected reefs and sponsoring competitions in which teams of divers try to land the largest number of fish in a single day. The approach, sometimes called invasivorism, has obvious appeal. It converts a problem into a resource, gives fishers a new source of income and offers consumers the satisfaction of contributing to conservation simply by choosing a meal. Few environmental messages are so easily communicated, and it is not difficult to understand why the idea has spread almost as rapidly as the fish itself.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters can point to some evidence of success. Rodrigo Corvalán, a fisheries ecologist at the Mesoamerican Reef Institute, studied reefs off the coast of Belize where divers removed lionfish regularly over several years. On reefs culled at least once a month, lionfish densities fell by around three-quarters, and populations of the small native fish on which they prey showed signs of recovery. Corvalán stresses, however, that the removals had to be sustained: when culling stopped, lionfish returned within months, recolonising from deeper water and from unculled reefs nearby. In his view, harvesting can protect particular reefs of high value, such as those important for tourism or as nurseries for young fish, but it cannot be expected to reduce lionfish numbers across a whole region.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The main obstacle to scaling up is depth. Lionfish thrive at depths of over a hundred metres, far beyond the reach of recreational divers armed with spears, and these deep populations are thought to act as a reservoir from which shallower reefs are restocked. Adaeze Nkemelu, a marine engineer, has been developing traps designed specifically for lionfish that can be deployed at depth without catching native species. Early trials have been encouraging, but she cautions that a trap that works well in one location may perform poorly in another, and that commercial fishers will adopt the technology only if it proves reliably profitable. Nkemelu's prototypes use an open frame rather than bait, exploiting the lionfish's habit of gathering around any structure on the seabed, and the frames are then hauled to the surface with the fish still sheltering inside.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Profitability depends in turn on demand, and here the picture is more complicated. Leyla Zarifian, an economist who studies seafood markets, argues that invasivorism contains a hidden contradiction. Creating a profitable market for lionfish gives fishers an incentive to keep the species abundant; if a fishery succeeds in reducing numbers sharply, catches decline and the market collapses. In the worst case, she suggests, fishers might even resist efforts to control the invader by other means. A similar pattern, she notes, has been observed in some freshwater fisheries built around introduced species, where local enthusiasm for control quickly faded once the catch had become a livelihood. Zarifian's argument is logically sound, but it seems to overstate the danger in the case of lionfish, whose reproductive rate is so high that the risk of fishing them into scarcity is, for the foreseeable future, extremely remote.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also concerns about the fish's safety as food. Lionfish caught on certain reefs may contain a toxin that accumulates in large predatory fish and causes illness in humans, and some islands have issued warnings against eating fish taken from particular areas. The Gulf Reef Fishers' Cooperative, which supplies lionfish to restaurants, has argued that testing should be organised by public health authorities rather than left to individual suppliers. This is a reasonable demand, given that a single well-publicised case of poisoning could undo years of patient promotion. Such testing is neither expensive nor technically demanding, but it requires a degree of coordination that small suppliers cannot provide on their own.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, should be expected of eating invaders? The lionfish case suggests that the strategy is valuable but limited. It can relieve pressure on specific reefs, generate income in coastal communities and, perhaps most importantly, keep public attention on a problem that might otherwise be forgotten. What it cannot do is substitute for preventing invasions in the first place, and it would be unfortunate if the popularity of lionfish dishes encouraged the belief that any invader can simply be eaten away. For most invasive species no such market exists, and none could plausibly be created.

topic: the nativeness debate: whether introduced species should be judged by their origin or by their impact
title: Judged by Origin
subtitle: Should a species be condemned simply because it arrived recently? A long-running dispute in ecology is far from settled

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, conservation rested on a simple principle: native species were to be protected, while species introduced by humans were, at best, tolerated and, at worst, eliminated. The distinction seemed obvious. Native species had evolved together over long periods, forming communities whose members were adjusted to one another; newcomers, arriving suddenly through human agency, disrupted those relationships. Out of this principle grew an entire discipline, invasion biology, with its own journals, its own vocabulary of aliens, invaders and exotics, and an influential body of policy dedicated to keeping newcomers out or removing them once they had arrived.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In recent years, however, the principle has come under sustained attack. The ecologist Torgeir Haraldsen, of the Nordic Institute for Applied Ecology, argued in a widely discussed essay that conservationists should judge species by their effects rather than by their origins. Many introduced species, he pointed out, cause no measurable harm, and some provide real benefits: introduced shrubs that shelter rare songbirds, for example, or non-native trees that stabilise eroding hillsides. Treating all newcomers as enemies, Haraldsen contends, wastes scarce resources on harmless species and fosters a hostility to change that is ill-suited to a century of rapid environmental transformation. His critics accused him of naivety, but much of what he said was difficult to dispute. Spending large sums to remove an introduced plant that threatens nothing is hard to justify on any grounds.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The case against Haraldsen was put most forcefully by Ileana Pîrvu, an invasion biologist at the Carpathian Ecological Research Centre. Pîrvu's objection is essentially practical. The effects of an introduced species, she argues, are often impossible to predict at the time of its arrival and may not become apparent for decades. Many species that later became destructive spent long periods at low densities, apparently harmless, before spreading explosively. By the time the harm is evident, eradication is usually no longer possible. Origin, in her view, is not a perfect guide to risk, but it is the only one available early enough to act upon. A newcomer should therefore be regarded with suspicion until there is good reason to think otherwise.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Pîrvu's argument is a strong one, and it identifies the central weakness of the impact-based approach: impacts are known reliably only in retrospect. But it does not follow that every introduced species deserves equal suspicion. Several large studies have shown that the proportion of introductions which go on to cause serious damage is small, and that those which do tend to share certain characteristics, such as rapid reproduction, a broad diet, or close relatives that are already known to be invasive elsewhere. A policy that concentrated vigilance on species with these traits would preserve the precautionary logic of Pîrvu's position while avoiding its more indiscriminate consequences.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different line of criticism has come from historians and social scientists. Nomvula Sefolosha, who studies the history of environmental ideas, has traced the language of invasion biology back to its origins and finds that metaphors of invasion, aliens and natives were borrowed freely from political debates about immigration. She does not claim that invasion biologists share the prejudices expressed in those debates, but she argues that the vocabulary shapes public perception in ways that scientists may not intend, encouraging people to view ecological change in moral terms. Sefolosha recommends that the field adopt more neutral terminology. Her historical analysis is illuminating, yet a change of vocabulary alone would do little to resolve the underlying scientific disagreement, which concerns evidence and prediction rather than words.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Climate change has added a further complication. As temperatures rise, many species are shifting their ranges towards the poles and to higher altitudes without any direct human assistance. Andreas Varnavas, a biogeographer at the Eastern Mediterranean Biodiversity Unit, points out that these range-shifting species are, under most legal definitions, native to the country they are leaving but foreign to the one they are entering. Should a butterfly that crosses a border under its own power be treated as an invader? Varnavas argues that it should not, and that policy must distinguish between species moved by people and those moving in response to a changing climate. The distinction is sensible, though it will be hard to apply in practice, since climate change is itself a human creation and many species are travelling with indirect help from roads, canals and gardens.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the debate has achieved, perhaps, is a more mature understanding of what nativeness can and cannot tell us. It is a useful indicator of risk, not a measure of worth. The most defensible position lies somewhere between Haraldsen's and Pîrvu's: treating origin as a reason for vigilance, while reserving the costly business of removal for species whose harm is either demonstrated or strongly predicted by their traits. That is less satisfying than a simple rule, but ecology rarely offers simple rules, and the history of species introductions should have taught us to be suspicious of any rule that claims otherwise.

topic: environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling for the early detection of aquatic invasive species, and how managers should act on uncertain results
title: Traces in the Water
subtitle: A genetic technique can now reveal an invader before anyone has seen it, but knowing what to do with that information is another matter

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among biologists who study invasive species, there is a widely shared rule of thumb: the earlier an introduction is noticed, the cheaper and more likely its removal becomes. A population of a few dozen individuals confined to a single pond can sometimes be eliminated within weeks; the same species, once established across a river catchment, may be impossible to remove at any price. The difficulty is that newly arrived organisms are, almost by definition, rare. Traditional surveys rely on nets, traps and trained observers, and they are good at confirming the presence of species that are already abundant but poor at finding the handful of pioneers that matter most. It is arguably this failure of detection, rather than any shortage of control methods, that has been the weakest link in the defence against biological invasions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the past fifteen years, a technique known as environmental DNA analysis, usually shortened to eDNA, has begun to change this picture. Every living organism continuously sheds genetic material into its surroundings, in the form of skin cells, mucus, scales, faeces and gametes. In aquatic habitats this material is suspended in the water, where it can be captured by passing a sample through a fine filter. Back in the laboratory, short sequences unique to a particular species are copied millions of times, so that even minute traces become measurable. Dr Ilse Tveterås, a molecular ecologist at the Hardanger Freshwater Institute, recalls the moment when her team detected the DNA of an invasive freshwater mussel in a reservoir that had been surveyed repeatedly by divers. No adult mussel was found there for another two years. For Tveterås, the episode demonstrated that the method could see what experienced field workers could not.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The attractions of the approach are considerable. Collecting a water sample requires little training, so volunteers, anglers and school groups can contribute to monitoring programmes that would otherwise depend on scarce specialists. The process does not harm the animals being sought, which matters when the same waters also contain protected native species. A more recent development, metabarcoding, allows a single sample to be screened for hundreds of species simultaneously. Tveterås argues that the cost per site has fallen so steeply that routine screening of every major port and canal in a country is now financially realistic, a claim that would have seemed fanciful a decade ago.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet a positive result is not quite the same thing as a discovery. Professor Tadeo Quispehuaman, a hydrologist at the Andean Water Sciences Institute, has spent several years tracking how genetic material moves once it enters a river. His experiments show that DNA can be carried several kilometres downstream and, in cold, shaded water, may remain detectable for weeks. A detection may therefore reflect an organism that died long ago, or one living far from the sampling point. Genetic material can also arrive by indirect routes: in the gut of a fish-eating bird, on the hull of a recreational boat, or in treated wastewater. Added to this is the ever-present risk that samples are contaminated during collection or analysis. Quispehuaman does not dispute the value of the technique, but he insists that a single positive should be read as a reason to look harder, not as proof that a population has become established. This is surely the correct reading.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How managers ought to respond to such ambiguous signals is a matter of genuine disagreement. Renske Oudejans, a policy adviser to a regional water authority in the Netherlands, has documented cases in which a lone eDNA detection prompted the closure of lakes to boating and fishing for an entire season, at considerable cost to local businesses, only for intensive follow-up surveys to find nothing. She proposes a formal confirmation protocol, under which action would be taken only after repeated positive samples or the recovery of a physical specimen. Her concern for public confidence is legitimate: authorities that raise false alarms too often may find their warnings ignored. Nevertheless, her protocol carries a hidden cost. The entire value of eDNA lies in its capacity to provide early warning, and a rule requiring a physical specimen would, in many cases, delay a response until the invader was common enough to be caught by conventional means, which is precisely the situation the technique was meant to avoid.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further question is whether eDNA can tell managers not only that a species is present but how many individuals there are. Researchers in the Pacific Biosecurity Network, led by Dr Adwoa Dankwah, have compared DNA concentrations with physical counts in small, enclosed ponds and found a reasonably close relationship: more fish generally meant more DNA. In flowing rivers, however, the correlation weakened considerably, because the rate of shedding varies with water temperature and with the age and activity of the animals. Dankwah is cautiously optimistic that statistical models incorporating these variables will eventually produce reliable estimates. For the time being, she concedes, eDNA results from rivers are better treated as a simple indication of presence or absence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: eDNA has already allowed several invasions to be identified while eradication was still feasible, and it seems likely that it will become a standard element of biosecurity surveillance. But it is a tool for deciding where to look, not a substitute for looking. The more serious obstacle now lies elsewhere. Many agencies can detect an invader within days, yet lack the funding, legal powers or agreed procedures to act on what they find. The technology, in other words, has advanced faster than the institutions that are supposed to use it, and until that gap is closed, earlier detection will not necessarily mean earlier action.

topic: invasion lag phases: why some naturalised plants remain inconspicuous for decades before spreading, and the policy implications of 'sleeper' weeds
title: The Long Sleep of Invaders
subtitle: Why do some introduced plants wait for decades before they spread, and what should be done about them in the meantime?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1874 a small evergreen shrub from the eastern Himalayas was planted in the botanic garden of a temperate southern-hemisphere city, where it was admired for its scarlet berries. For the next eighty years it behaved impeccably. A few seedlings appeared in neighbouring gardens, and occasional specimens were recorded along a nearby creek, but nobody regarded it as a threat. Then, in the late 1950s, it began to appear in pine plantations and native forest remnants tens of kilometres away, and within three decades it had become one of the most troublesome weeds in the region. Its story is far from unusual. Ecologists now recognise that a delay of this kind, known as a lag phase, is the rule rather than the exception among introduced plants, and its existence has uncomfortable implications for the way invasions are managed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most systematic attempt to measure such delays has come from the Tasman Weed Records Project, a collaboration between several herbaria that examined more than eleven thousand herbarium specimens of naturalised plants. By noting where and when each specimen had been collected, the team reconstructed the spread of over two hundred species. They found that the typical interval between the first record of a plant growing wild and the onset of rapid expansion was roughly thirty years for trees and shrubs, but considerably shorter for herbaceous species, and that a few plants had waited more than a century. These figures are striking, yet they almost certainly underestimate the true length of lags. Collectors tend to gather plants that are already conspicuous, so the earliest, sparsest phase of a population's history is the one least likely to be documented.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why should an introduced species remain quiet for so long? The simplest answer comes from Professor Itzel Cuauhtli, a population ecologist, who argues that many apparent lags require no special explanation at all. A population that grows exponentially, she points out, adds very few individuals in absolute terms during its early years: a colony that doubles every five years will still be tiny after several decades, and only later will its expansion become dramatic enough to be noticed. In her view, the lag is partly an illusion produced by human perception rather than a genuine change in the plant's behaviour. There is much to be said for this argument, and it certainly accounts for a proportion of recorded cases.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Bogdan Vrtačnik, an evolutionary biologist, offers an alternative account. Most introductions, he notes, involve only a handful of individuals, and the populations descended from them often lack the genetic variation needed to adapt to an unfamiliar climate or soil. On this view, a lag ends when something alters the population's genetic make-up, typically the arrival of further plants from a different part of the native range. Interbreeding between these separate stocks can generate new combinations of traits, such as a change in flowering time, which allow the species to thrive in conditions it previously tolerated only marginally. Genetic surveys of several notorious invaders have indeed revealed ancestry drawn from multiple source regions, which is consistent with, though not proof of, Vrtačnik's hypothesis.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third school of thought, associated with Dr Saule Zhaksybekova of the Steppe Ecology Institute, locates the cause outside the plant itself. Zhaksybekova emphasises that a species' surroundings rarely stay constant for decades. The climate may warm, livestock may be removed, or a pollinating insect may arrive independently and allow a previously sterile plant to set seed for the first time. Even infrastructure can play a role: she has shown that the verges of motorways act as corridors along which wind-dispersed seeds travel far more rapidly than through farmland. For Zhaksybekova, a lag is best understood as a period of waiting for the right environmental opportunity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These explanations are not mutually exclusive, and it would be surprising if a single mechanism accounted for every case. Indeed, the purely arithmetical account cannot explain them all. Some well-documented populations remained stable, or even shrank, for decades before expanding suddenly, a pattern that is difficult to reconcile with steady exponential growth. The distinction matters in practice. If lags were merely a matter of arithmetic, every naturalised species would be a potential future invader, and prediction would be close to impossible. If, on the other hand, specific triggers are involved, it might be possible to anticipate which species will be released by changes such as warming or new transport links.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever the mechanism, the policy lesson is clear. Most risk assessments judge a species by its current behaviour, so a plant that has been naturalised for fifty years without spreading is usually classed as harmless. That reasoning is mistaken: a long period of inactivity is not evidence that a species will remain inactive. Authorities would be better advised to maintain watch lists of naturalised plants with invasive relatives elsewhere and to remove small populations while doing so is still cheap. Such a policy will never be popular, since it involves spending money on problems that do not yet exist. But the alternative is to keep waiting until a sleeping species wakes.
