topic: estimating the economic cost of biological invasions: global cost databases, extrapolation, damage versus management spending and non-market losses
title: Pricing the Uninvited
subtitle: Global estimates of what invasive species cost the world economy make dramatic headlines, but what do the numbers really measure?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every few years a new estimate of the global cost of biological invasions makes headlines. The most recent, compiled by the Global Invasion Cost Inventory, puts the figure at well over a hundred billion dollars a year, a total that has roughly tripled each decade since 1970. Numbers on this scale are designed to command attention, and they have succeeded: they are quoted by ministers, in funding applications and at international conservation summits, and they have done much to persuade the public that invasive species are an economic problem rather than merely an ecological curiosity. Yet a single headline figure conceals a remarkable amount of uncertainty about what is being measured, and how. Before such estimates are used to guide spending, it is worth asking what exactly they represent.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Inventory, coordinated by the economist Dr Folasade Akintola, takes an unglamorous but transparent approach. Rather than modelling costs from first principles, her team gathered every published estimate they could find, from government reports, academic papers and industry surveys in more than a dozen languages, and converted them into a common currency at a fixed year's prices. Each entry is tagged according to its reliability, the region and sector affected, and whether it describes damage actually observed or a projection. Akintola is frank about the limitations of this method: costs that nobody has studied simply do not appear, which means that the database is weighted heavily towards wealthy countries with long traditions of agricultural research. Africa and much of Asia, she notes, are almost certainly under-represented.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Hamid Zarrinkafsh, a resource economist, raises a different objection. In his analysis, a substantial share of the headline total rests on extrapolation: a cost measured in one district or year is scaled up to an entire country or decade. A figure for crop losses caused by an insect pest on a few hundred farms, for instance, may be multiplied by the national area under cultivation, regardless of whether the pest is present everywhere. When Zarrinkafsh restricted his calculations to costs that had been directly observed and recorded, the annual total fell by more than half. He does not conclude that invasions are unimportant, but he argues that inflated figures risk damaging the credibility of the field if they are later shown to be exaggerated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third line of criticism concerns the kind of costs that are counted. Dr Mateus Junqueira, who works on environmental accounting, points out that the inventories combine two very different categories: damage, such as lost harvests or blocked water pipes, and management, meaning money spent on prevention, surveillance and control. The latter, he argues, is not strictly a loss at all but an investment, and a country that spends heavily on keeping invaders out will paradoxically appear to suffer greater costs than one that does nothing. This is a fair point, and the distinction ought to be made explicit in every published estimate. It would be wrong, however, to treat management spending as irrelevant, since money devoted to controlling one invader is money that cannot be spent on schools, hospitals or other conservation priorities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If some critics believe the figures are too high, there are equally strong reasons to think them too low. Almost none of the estimates include losses that have no market price: the extinction of native species, the degradation of landscapes valued for recreation, or the erosion of cultural practices that depend on particular plants and animals. A wetland choked by an invasive water weed may cost a local fishery a measurable sum, but the disappearance of the birds that once fed there will not appear in any ledger. Akintola herself acknowledges that her database captures only the fraction of impacts that someone has thought, and been able, to express in money.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these arguments suggest that the headline numbers are simultaneously inflated in some respects and incomplete in others, and there is no reason to assume that the errors cancel out. The most sensible response is not to abandon economic estimates but to report them as ranges, with observed and projected costs clearly separated. Zarrinkafsh's observed-only figure and Akintola's broader total could then be presented side by side, allowing readers to see how much of any estimate depends on assumptions. A figure of 'between forty and two hundred billion dollars' is less quotable than a single round number, but it is considerably more honest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is also a case for asking whether global totals are useful at all. Policymakers rarely decide how much to spend on invasions in general; they decide whether to fund a particular border inspection scheme or eradication campaign. For such choices, what matters is the comparison between the cost of acting and the cost of not acting for a specific species in a specific place. Several of the most successful eradication programmes, including those that removed feral goats from small oceanic islands, were justified by precisely this kind of local calculation rather than by any appeal to global statistics. Detailed studies of this kind are slow and expensive to produce, but they are far more likely than a dramatic worldwide figure to change what governments actually do.

topic: the enemy release hypothesis: whether escaping natural enemies explains the success of invasive plants, including enemy accumulation, evolution of growth over defence and soil pathogens
title: Freed from Their Foes
subtitle: Do invasive plants thrive simply because they have left their enemies behind? The answer turns out to be less straightforward than it first appears

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Plants that become invasive often behave in their new homes in ways they never do in their native range. A shrub that grows as a scattered understorey species in its homeland may form dense thickets abroad; a modest wildflower may grow twice as tall and produce many times more seed. The most widely cited explanation for this transformation is disarmingly simple. When a species is carried to a new continent, it is thought to leave behind the insects, fungi and viruses that kept it in check at home, and, freed from these natural enemies, it flourishes. Known as the enemy release hypothesis, this idea owes much of its popularity to its intuitive appeal: it requires no knowledge of genetics or soil chemistry to grasp. It also has considerable practical significance, because it supplies the rationale for classical biological control, the deliberate introduction of a plant's specialist enemies to suppress it in its new range. If the hypothesis is wrong, or right only occasionally, a great deal of public money may be spent on the wrong remedy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At first sight the evidence appears overwhelming. A survey led by Dr Thandeka Zikalala at the Highveld Plant Health Unit compared twenty-eight plant species in both their native and introduced ranges and found that, on average, each species was attacked by fewer than half as many species of fungi and viruses abroad as at home. Leaf damage from insects showed a similar pattern. Studies of this kind have been repeated on several continents with broadly consistent results, and there is little doubt that introduced plants do typically escape many of their enemies. Demonstrating that enemies are missing, however, is not the same as demonstrating that their absence is what makes a plant successful, and it is on this distinction that the debate turns.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most direct test is to remove enemies from plants in their native range and see whether they then behave like invaders. Professor Kaito Hayashida of the Kansai Ecological Research Station has carried out such experiments for over a decade, using fine mesh cages and selective pesticides to protect native-range populations of several notorious invaders. The protected plants grew somewhat larger, but the improvement was a fraction of the difference observed between native and invasive populations. Hayashida also points out that release from enemies is very widespread among introduced species, the great majority of which never become invasive at all. In his view, enemy release is a common condition of introduced plants but explains comparatively little about why only certain ones become a problem.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication concerns time. Dr Ludmila Krasnopevtseva, a plant pathologist, compiled more than a century and a half of published reports of pathogens found on introduced plants in central Europe. She found that the number of local pathogen species recorded on a plant rose steadily with the length of time since its arrival, suggesting that release is often temporary: native enemies gradually discover and adapt to the newcomer. Krasnopevtseva believes this may account for the boom-and-bust pattern seen in some invasions, in which a population expands explosively and then declines without human intervention. It is tempting to conclude that nature will eventually solve the problem on its own. That would be unwise. On her own figures, the accumulation of enemies typically unfolds over centuries, far too slowly to protect the native species being displaced today.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some researchers argue that release matters less for its immediate effects than for what it allows plants to become. If enemies are absent, a plant that invests heavily in chemical defences is wasting resources, and natural selection might favour individuals that divert that energy into growth and reproduction. To test this idea, Dr Ignacio Urquiola grew seeds collected from native and introduced populations of fourteen species side by side in a common garden, where all plants experienced identical conditions. Plants of introduced origin grew taller in roughly half of the species, but there was no consistent evidence that they had become less well defended. The evolutionary hypothesis is elegant, then, but for the moment its empirical support is decidedly mixed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A quite different perspective comes from the Baltic Grassland Network, a consortium of ecologists who study interactions below ground. Their experiments suggest that the enemies whose absence matters most may not be the insects and fungi visible on leaves, but microorganisms in the soil that attack roots. When the group grew invasive species in soil collected from their native range, growth was markedly suppressed; in sterilised soil, or in soil from the introduced range, it was not. Because such organisms are invisible and difficult to identify, the network argues, they have been neglected in most tests of the hypothesis.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is not a refutation of enemy release but a more modest picture of it. Escape from enemies is real and almost universal, but its consequences vary greatly between species, places and periods of time, and it is probably one contributing factor among several, alongside traits such as rapid growth, abundant seed production and the disturbance of habitats by people. The danger lies in treating it as a general explanation. For those designing biological control programmes, the implication is that each candidate weed should first be examined to establish whether enemies actually limit it in its native range; where they do not, introducing them abroad is unlikely to achieve much.

topic: the exotic pet and aquarium trade as a pathway for invasive species, owner releases, and the debate over whitelists, blacklists and surrender schemes
title: From Tank to Wild
subtitle: Unwanted pets released by their owners have become one of the main sources of new invasive animals, and regulators disagree about how to respond

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When people think about how invasive animals reach new countries, they tend to picture rats leaving cargo ships or insects hidden in imported timber. Far fewer think of the goldfish bowl or the reptile tank. Yet over the past half-century the trade in pets and aquarium species has become one of the leading routes by which non-native vertebrates establish themselves in the wild. Freshwater turtles now breed in ponds across southern Europe, flocks of tropical parakeets roost in the parks of northern cities, and aquarium fish compete with native species in rivers on every inhabited continent. The pathway has, I believe, been seriously underestimated, largely because each individual release seems too small to matter. A single turtle tipped into a lake hardly resembles an ecological disaster, but thousands of such acts, repeated over decades, add up to precisely that.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why do owners release their animals? A survey of more than three thousand pet keepers, conducted by Dr Marisol Itturalde of the Institute for Human-Wildlife Studies, found that roughly one in six aquarium owners had either released an animal or seriously considered doing so. The most common reasons were practical: fish and reptiles frequently grow far larger, or live much longer, than buyers had been led to expect, and owners who move house or lose interest are left with an animal they cannot rehome. Strikingly, most of those who had released a pet believed they were giving it a better life. Release, in other words, is more often an act of misplaced compassion than of carelessness, which makes it considerably harder to discourage through publicity campaigns that simply tell people it is wrong.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Governments have generally responded with what are known as blacklists: lists of species whose import or sale is prohibited because they are known to cause harm. Professor Lavinia Fotofili, an environmental lawyer, argues that this approach is fundamentally reactive. A species is usually added to a blacklist only after it has escaped, established itself and caused measurable damage, by which time eradication may no longer be possible. Fotofili advocates the opposite system, a whitelist, under which only species that have been assessed and approved as low-risk may be traded. The effect, she points out, is to transfer the burden of proof from regulators, who must currently demonstrate that a species is dangerous, to traders, who would have to show that it is safe.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not surprisingly, the trade itself takes a different view. The Federation of Ornamental Animal Traders, which represents several thousand businesses, warns that a whitelist would ban most of the species currently on sale at a stroke, ruining small specialist shops and driving demand towards unregulated online sellers and smugglers. As an alternative, it proposes more targeted blacklisting combined with compulsory licences for keepers of high-risk species. The fear of a black market is not unreasonable, and any new regulation must take it seriously. However, the experience of the few countries that have introduced whitelists suggests that the great majority of traders and owners comply with the rules, and that the predicted collapse of the industry has not occurred.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further complication is climate change. Dr Oyun Sandagdorj, an ecologist who models the potential distribution of non-native species, notes that many popular pets are tropical animals that cannot currently survive a temperate winter outdoors. This has long been regarded as a natural safeguard. Her projections, however, indicate that rising temperatures will steadily enlarge the number of traded species capable of forming wild populations in central and northern Europe over the coming decades. Risk assessments based on present-day conditions, she argues, may soon be obsolete. This seems to me an important warning: the fact that a species is harmless today offers no guarantee that it will remain so.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The internet has made the regulator's task harder still. Animals can now be ordered from sellers in other countries and delivered by post, often without passing through the inspection points that once controlled the trade. In a follow-up study, Itturalde and her colleagues monitored online advertisements over a twelve-month period and identified several hundred species offered for sale that did not appear on any national blacklist or whitelist at all, many of which had never been assessed for invasive potential. Whatever system of lists a country adopts, it can only be as effective as its ability to enforce it across borders that are increasingly virtual.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: No single measure, then, is likely to solve the problem. A well-designed whitelist addresses the risk of new introductions, but it does little for the millions of animals already in private homes, some of which will inevitably become unwanted. For these, the most effective intervention may be the simplest: giving owners somewhere to take them. Several regions now run surrender schemes and periodic amnesty days at which unwanted pets can be handed over, no questions asked, to be rehomed or humanely cared for. Such schemes cost relatively little, and they turn the compassion that currently drives release into a force that works with conservation rather than against it.

topic: the moon illusion: apparent-distance, oculomotor and size-contrast explanations of the enlarged horizon moon
title: The Giant on the Horizon
subtitle: Why does the rising moon look so large? An effect visible to anyone continues to divide perceptual scientists

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has watched a full moon rise over a city skyline will have noticed that it seems enormous, only to shrink to an unremarkable disc once it has climbed high into the sky. The effect is so compelling that many people assume it must have a physical cause. It does not. Careful measurement shows that the angle the moon subtends at the eye is essentially constant throughout the night, and if anything the horizon moon casts a fractionally smaller image on the retina, because an observer on the earth's surface is slightly further from it when it is low than when it is overhead. Cameras record no enlargement whatsoever. The moon illusion, as it is known, is therefore entirely a product of the brain, and it is perhaps the most widely experienced of all visual illusions. It is also, remarkably, one of the least satisfactorily explained.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest explanation, that the atmosphere acts as a kind of magnifying lens, can be dismissed. Refraction does alter the appearance of the low moon, but it squeezes the disc vertically into a slight oval rather than enlarging it. Most modern accounts therefore look to the way the visual system interprets distance. According to the apparent-distance theory, we perceive the sky not as a hemisphere but as a flattened dome, so that the horizon seems much further away than the point directly overhead. Since an object of fixed angular size must be physically larger if it is further away, the brain inflates the horizon moon accordingly. Solveig Aarvold of the Bergen Institute for Vision Science has offered some of the strongest support for this view. Using a planetarium in which an artificial landscape could be projected or removed, she found that the enlargement shrank dramatically whenever the simulated terrain was taken away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that the theory appears to clash with what observers actually say. Asked whether the horizon moon looks nearer or further than the overhead moon, most people reply that it looks nearer. Teodor Vrabie, who directs the perception laboratory at Cluj, regards this so-called size-distance paradox as fatal. In his view, the apparent-distance account asks us to believe that the brain unconsciously registers the horizon moon as distant, enlarges it, and then consciously judges it to be close, a sequence he describes as constructed to fit the facts rather than derived from them. Vrabie instead locates the cause in the eyes themselves. When we look upwards, he argues, small changes in focusing and in the angle between the two eyes accompany the raised gaze, and these adjustments are known to make objects appear somewhat smaller. On this account, the overhead moon is shrunk rather than the horizon moon enlarged.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third camp emphasises comparison rather than distance. Ottilie Szczerbak, a psychologist at the University of Wrocław, points out that the horizon moon is seen alongside trees, rooftops and distant hills, all of which subtend tiny angles, whereas the overhead moon floats in a vast and featureless expanse. Just as a circle surrounded by small circles looks larger than an identical one surrounded by large ones, the moon may borrow its apparent size from its neighbours. Critics reply that the illusion survives perfectly well over an open sea, where there are no objects to compare it with. Szczerbak's answer is that the textured surface of the water, with its waves receding into the distance, provides a scale of its own. This is ingenious, but it arguably moves her position closer to the distance theories it was meant to replace.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Attempts to settle the matter experimentally have produced intriguing but inconclusive results. A popular claim holds that the illusion vanishes if one bends over and views the horizon moon upside down between one's legs; controlled tests suggest the reduction is real but modest, and may owe as much to the unusual posture as to the inverted scene. More promising are studies by Rafael Ybarrondo and colleagues at the Universidad de Cuyo, who used virtual-reality headsets to separate two variables that are normally bound together in nature: the elevation of the viewer's gaze and the presence of terrain. Their participants reported a large moon whenever a landscape was visible, regardless of whether they were looking straight ahead or upwards, a finding that seems to favour distance-based accounts over Vrabie's. Yet caution is warranted. People are known to underestimate distances inside virtual environments, and an illusion that depends on perceived distance may behave quite differently in a headset than under a real night sky.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: My own view is that the search for a single cause may be misguided. It is entirely plausible that several mechanisms operate at once, with terrain cues, comparison with nearby objects and the posture of the eyes each contributing a share that varies from one observer and one setting to another. Such pluralism is less elegant than any of the rival theories, and researchers understandably find it less satisfying, but elegance is not evidence. Nor should the illusion be dismissed as a mere curiosity. It demonstrates with unusual clarity that the size we see is not read directly from the retina but constructed from assumptions about the surrounding world, and those assumptions can have consequences: pilots approaching runways at night have been known to misjudge the size and distance of lights near the horizon.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Generations of astronomers, philosophers and psychologists have examined an effect that anyone can observe on any clear night, and they have still not agreed on why it occurs. That should not be read as a failure of perceptual science. On the contrary, it shows how much interpretation is involved in even the simplest act of looking.

topic: cross-cultural differences in susceptibility to geometric illusions and the carpentered-world hypothesis
title: Lines, Corners and Cultures
subtitle: Do the surroundings we grow up in shape what we see? A decades-old claim about geometric illusions is being re-examined

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few images are reproduced in psychology textbooks as often as the Müller-Lyer figure: two horizontal lines of identical length, one capped with arrowheads pointing inwards, the other with fins splaying outwards. Almost every reader who sees it judges the second line to be longer, and for much of the twentieth century the effect was treated as a fixed property of human vision. That assumption was shaken in the 1960s, when a survey conducted across more than a dozen societies reported that susceptibility varied enormously. Students in European and North American cities showed the strongest illusion, while members of several rural and foraging communities were barely affected at all. The result is mentioned in most introductory courses and then quickly forgotten, which is a pity, because it strikes at the comfortable belief that the most basic operations of seeing are identical in everyone.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation offered by the original investigators became known as the carpentered-world hypothesis. People raised among rectangular buildings, rooms and furniture, it proposes, acquire an unconscious habit of interpreting acute and obtuse angles on a flat surface as right-angled corners seen in three dimensions. The line with outward fins resembles the inside corner of a room, whose vertical edge is further from the viewer; the line with inward arrowheads resembles the outside corner of a building, which juts towards the observer. Because the brain scales perceived size according to inferred distance, the apparently more distant line is enlarged. Eleni Kallistratou, a developmental psychologist at the University of Thessaloniki, maintains that the hypothesis remains the most convincing account available. Her longitudinal studies indicate that children growing up in towns become more susceptible to the illusion as they get older, and do so at a noticeably quicker pace than children in the surrounding countryside.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the environment is responsible. A rival proposal, first advanced soon after the original survey and recently revived by Chikondi Mbekeani of the Blantyre Vision Unit, concerns the eye itself. Denser pigmentation at the back of the eye, Mbekeani argues, slightly reduces sensitivity to contrast, so that the fine contours of the fins register less forcefully and exert a weaker pull on the perceived length of the line. In her samples, a direct measure of contrast sensitivity predicted susceptibility more accurately than any description of participants' surroundings. The difficulty is that pigmentation is far from randomly distributed across the globe; it is closely associated with geography, and therefore with the kinds of dwellings people inhabit. Separating the two influences is consequently much harder than either camp tends to admit, and there is no obvious reason why they could not both be contributing at the same time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical challenge comes from Anders Lindholt at Aarhus, who doubts that the early findings reflect perception at all. Participants in the 1960s survey, he notes, were often unfamiliar with pictures printed on paper, received instructions in translation, and may have interpreted the task quite differently from university students accustomed to being tested. When Lindholt repeated the procedure using tablets on which participants adjusted a line until it matched another, the gap between groups narrowed considerably. His critique is a valuable corrective, yet he goes too far in implying that the original differences were mere artefacts of method. His own data show that they shrank but did not disappear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The debate has acquired wider significance because of growing unease about who takes part in perception research. The overwhelming majority of experiments have recruited undergraduates in wealthy, industrialised countries, and conclusions drawn from them are routinely presented as facts about humanity. Kenji Teruya, whose group at the University of the Ryukyus studies visual attention, suggests that culture may affect not the early stages of vision but the way attention is spread across a scene. In his experiments, participants raised in communities that emphasise relationships between people tended to take in the surrounding context of an image, whereas those from more individualistic settings concentrated on the central object. Teruya believes that some apparent differences in illusion strength may be by-products of these contrasting habits of looking.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whichever explanation is correct, the opportunity to investigate the question is slipping away. Urbanisation and mass-produced housing have spread right-angled architecture to almost every region, and rectangular screens now accompany even those who live far from cities. Populations with little exposure to carpentered environments are becoming difficult to find, and future comparisons may reveal smaller differences simply because human surroundings have converged.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that if experience shapes susceptibility then perception must be arbitrary or unreliable. A visual system that adjusts its assumptions to the regularities of its environment is behaving sensibly: the shortcuts that produce the illusion on paper are the same ones that allow city dwellers to judge the depth of rooms and streets at a glance. What the cross-cultural findings really expose is a habit of thought among scientists rather than a flaw in the human eye. The version of vision described in textbooks may be just one local variety, mistaken for the universal pattern because it happened to be the one most conveniently studied.

topic: the rubber hand illusion, body ownership and multisensory integration
title: Whose Hand Is It Anyway?
subtitle: A simple trick involving a rubber limb has become one of the most powerful tools for studying how the brain decides what belongs to the body

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The procedure could hardly be simpler. A volunteer sits at a table with one arm hidden behind a screen, while a life-sized rubber hand is placed in full view where their own hand might plausibly be. An experimenter then strokes the hidden hand and the rubber one with two small paintbrushes, taking care that the touches occur at exactly the same moment and in the same place. After a minute or two, a remarkable number of people report an uncanny sensation: the touch seems to be located in the rubber hand, and the artificial limb feels, in some difficult-to-describe way, like their own. Asked to close their eyes and point to their concealed hand, they typically indicate a position shifted towards the rubber hand. If the brushing is deliberately mismatched in timing, the effect largely disappears. Since it was first described, this modest illusion has arguably been one of the most productive experimental methods in the study of the self.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The standard interpretation is that the brain continually combines information from different senses and, when they conflict, resolves the disagreement by favouring whichever source is most reliable. In the rubber hand set-up, vision reports a hand being touched in one place, touch reports a stroke arriving at the same instant, and the sense of limb position, which is comparatively imprecise, is overruled. Nino Kvitashvili, a neuroscientist at Tbilisi State Medical University, has gone further, arguing that the illusion alters ownership itself rather than merely the location of touch. In her experiments, participants whose rubber hand was suddenly threatened with a kitchen knife showed a sharp rise in skin conductance, a bodily stress response that people cannot easily fake. For Kvitashvili, such reactions demonstrate that the experience is more than a form of words that participants adopt to describe an odd situation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Joseph Opondo of the University of Nairobi has drawn attention to the questionnaires on which most studies rely, which ask participants to rate statements such as 'It felt as if the rubber hand were my hand'. Such wording, he argues, makes the expected answer obvious. Opondo found that the illusion was reported most strongly by people who scored highly on tests of hypnotic suggestibility, and that a substantial minority claimed to feel it even when the brushing was mismatched. His critique is an important one and should make researchers more careful in designing their measures. It seems unlikely, however, that suggestion accounts for the whole effect, because the shift in where people believe their hidden hand to be is measured indirectly, without asking them how they feel.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One curious feature of the illusion is that roughly a third of people never experience it at all. Lucia Pasquinelli and her colleagues at the University of Padua have explored why. Using a task in which participants were asked to count their own heartbeat without touching their pulse, they found that those who performed most accurately were the least susceptible to the rubber hand. Pasquinelli proposes that people who are attuned to signals from inside the body have a firmer anchor for their sense of self, and are therefore less easily swayed by what they see. If she is right, the illusion may offer a way of measuring a quality that has otherwise proved hard to pin down.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Virtual reality has allowed the principle to be extended from a single hand to an entire body. Participants wearing headsets who see a virtual body being touched while they feel matching touches can come to experience that body as their own, even when it differs markedly from theirs in size, age or skin colour. Some researchers have reported that inhabiting a body of a different ethnicity reduces measures of unconscious bias. Farhad Yazdani, whose laboratory in Shiraz has attempted to replicate such work, found that the reduction appeared immediately after the session but had faded within a week. The more ambitious claims about using virtual bodies to change social attitudes should therefore be treated with considerable reserve.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most promising applications lie in medicine. People who have lost a limb often describe their prosthesis as a tool rather than a part of themselves, and many abandon it. A team led by Eirik Grindheim in Trondheim fitted amputees with artificial hands containing sensors that delivered gentle vibrations to the remaining part of the arm whenever the prosthetic fingers made contact with an object. When the vibration coincided precisely with what the wearer saw, patients reported that the device felt increasingly like their own hand, and they used it more often in daily life.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the rubber hand ultimately reveals is that the feeling of owning a body is not given once and for all but is continuously inferred from the evidence available. Some commentators have drawn a more dramatic conclusion: that the self is merely an illusion. That, I think, is a step too far. A sense of ownership that is constructed by the brain is not therefore false, any more than colour is unreal because it depends on the eye; in ordinary life the inference is almost always correct.

topic: the McGurk effect: audiovisual speech integration, variability between individuals and stimuli, and its value as a research and clinical tool
title: Hearing with the Eyes
subtitle: A famous illusion seemed to prove that sight and sound merge seamlessly in speech. Its reputation is now under closer scrutiny

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s, two researchers preparing videos for a study of infant language noticed something odd. When a recording of a woman saying 'ga' was dubbed with the sound of her saying 'ba', they did not hear either syllable. Instead, they heard a third, 'da', which corresponded neither to the voice nor to the lips. The phenomenon, now called the McGurk effect after one of its discoverers, has since been demonstrated in countless lecture halls. Its most unsettling feature is that knowledge offers no protection: viewers who have been told exactly how the trick works, and who can hear 'ba' perfectly well with their eyes closed, still hear 'da' the moment they look at the screen. For decades the effect has served as the standard illustration of a broader principle, namely that the brain does not process speech as sound alone but fuses what it hears with what it sees.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Yet the effect is far less uniform than its fame suggests. Dimitra Seferis, a psycholinguist at the University of Athens, recruited more than five thousand volunteers through an online platform and showed each of them fourteen different McGurk videos recorded by different speakers. Individual susceptibility ranged across the whole spectrum: some participants reported the fused syllable on virtually every trial, while others almost never did. Even more striking was the variation between videos. Certain recordings produced the illusion in most viewers, whereas others did so in fewer than one in ten. Seferis concluded that the specific clip used in an experiment can matter as much as any characteristic of the people watching it, a finding with uncomfortable implications for the many studies that have relied on a single recording.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Her conclusion casts doubt on one of the best-known claims in the field: that speakers of some languages are less susceptible than others. Early studies reported that Japanese participants experienced the effect much less often than English speakers, and the difference was attributed to cultural conventions that discourage looking directly at a speaker's face. When Aigerim Omarova of the Kazakh National University repeated these comparisons with several hundred participants in each group, rather than the twenty or so used in the original work, and with a range of videos instead of one, the differences became small and inconsistent, sometimes even reversing direction. In retrospect, it seems clear that an elegant cultural explanation was built on far too slender a foundation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more fundamental objection concerns what the effect actually measures. Seeing a speaker's face undoubtedly helps listeners in ordinary life, particularly in noisy surroundings, where watching the lips can improve comprehension about as much as raising the volume of the voice by around fifteen decibels. Uchenna Nakpodia, who studies speech perception at the University of Ibadan, set out to discover whether people who are highly susceptible to the McGurk effect also gain most from seeing faces in noise. Testing the same participants on both tasks, she found almost no relationship between the two. Nakpodia argues that the illusion captures a peculiar response to conflicting signals, which listeners rarely encounter, and reveals little about the cooperative use of sight and sound that makes conversation in a crowded café possible.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This matters because the effect has been widely adopted as a clinical yardstick. Reduced susceptibility has been reported in groups including autistic children and adults with schizophrenia, and has been interpreted as evidence that these individuals combine information from different senses less effectively. Given the variability Seferis documented and the weak link Nakpodia found with real-world listening, such inferences seem premature. A group might differ in its response to a particular video for reasons that have nothing to do with integration, such as where its members tend to direct their gaze.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The effect still has defenders. Mateo Belaunde of the Pontifical Catholic University in Lima accepts that a mismatch between sight and sound is rare in conversation, but argues that it is precisely by creating such a mismatch that experimenters can watch the merging of the senses at work, much as engineers learn about a bridge by loading it until it strains. His longitudinal research indicates that susceptibility is weak in young children and climbs steadily until around the age of ten, even though infants only five months old already look longer at faces whose mouth movements do not match the sounds they hear. Belaunde attributes the gradual rise to the accumulating experience of watching people talk. On this view, the illusion is not a quirk but a measure of how thoroughly someone has learned the link between particular mouth shapes and particular sounds.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Belaunde's argument is reasonable as far as it goes, but it does not rescue the effect's status as a general index of audiovisual skill. The fairest conclusion is that the McGurk effect remains a vivid demonstration that perception is an act of combination rather than passive recording, while being a much blunter scientific instrument than was once assumed. Its story is also a cautionary tale about how readily a striking demonstration, repeated in textbooks for half a century, can come to be treated as a precise measurement.

topic: crossmodal correspondences and the influence of sound, shape and colour on perceived flavour ('sonic seasoning')
title: The Taste of Sound
subtitle: Music, shapes and the colour of a plate can all change how food seems to taste. But how much do these effects really matter?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people believe that they taste food with their tongues. In fact, what we call flavour is a composite experience assembled by the brain from many sources: the basic tastes detected in the mouth, the aromas that reach the nose from the back of the throat, the texture and temperature of the food, and, more surprisingly, what we see and hear while eating. Over the past twenty years, a growing body of research has documented how these influences interact. Diners have rated the same piece of toffee as sweeter while listening to high, tinkling piano music and as more bitter while listening to low, brassy tones. Such findings are among the most intriguing in the study of perception. Their practical significance, however, has often been exaggerated, not least by the companies and restaurants that have rushed to exploit them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The phenomenon underlying these effects is known as crossmodal correspondence: the consistent tendency of people to link features experienced through different senses. Asked to match tastes with sounds, most participants pair sweetness with high pitches and bitterness with low ones; asked to match tastes with shapes, they associate rounded forms with sweetness and angular forms with sourness or fizziness. High-pitched sounds are also reliably linked with objects that are small and bright. Aleksandra Kaczala, a cognitive psychologist at Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań, argues that these associations are not built into the brain from birth but acquired from the statistics of everyday experience. Small creatures, she observes, generally produce shrill calls while large ones produce deep calls, so that a link between pitch and size is a useful generalisation that any learner could extract from the world.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Jean-Pierre Ruzindana of the University of Rwanda takes a different view. His fieldwork has found many of the same taste-sound pairings among communities whose diets and musical traditions differ greatly from those of the European students who make up most research samples. This makes it hard, he suggests, to explain the correspondences purely by reference to particular environments. Ruzindana proposes instead that they are mediated by emotion: sweet tastes and high, light melodies are both pleasant, and people match them because they share a common emotional value. The idea is attractive and accounts for a good deal of the data. It struggles, though, to explain why bitterness should be associated specifically with low sounds, since many high sounds, such as a screeching brake or a dentist's drill, are at least as unpleasant.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Laboratory studies of this kind are open to an obvious objection: tasting small samples in a cubicle bears little resemblance to eating a meal. Inés Villaseñor of the Polytechnic University of Valencia therefore moved her research into a working restaurant. On different evenings, diners who ordered the same dessert heard a soundtrack that had previously been rated as either 'sweet' or 'bitter', and were later asked to evaluate their food. Those exposed to the sweet music rated the dessert roughly ten per cent sweeter. Villaseñor acknowledges that some diners may have noticed the unusual music and guessed what the study was about, which could have influenced their ratings. Her willingness to test the effect in a realistic setting is admirable, but the size of the difference she found hardly supports the claim that music can transform a meal.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Commercial interest has nevertheless been intense. Some airlines have experimented with menus designed to compensate for the effects of engine noise, which is thought to dull the perception of sweetness and saltiness. Food manufacturers, under pressure to reduce sugar and salt, have examined whether rounded packaging, particular colours or accompanying sounds might allow them to cut these ingredients without consumers noticing. This is a worthwhile aim, but there is as yet no long-term evidence on whether such strategies work outside short tasting sessions, or whether shoppers might simply respond to less sweet products by eating more of them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Concerns about the strength of the evidence have been sharpened by efforts to replicate it. Samir Qadiri, who leads a sensory science group at Mohammed V University in Rabat, points out that many early studies tested a few dozen people and relied on rating scales that are easily swayed by participants' expectations. In a study involving more than a thousand volunteers, whose methods and analyses were registered publicly before data collection began, Qadiri did find that music influenced judgements of sweetness, but the effect was only about half as large as earlier reports had suggested. Other well-publicised findings, such as the claim that a dessert tastes sweeter on a white plate than on a black one, proved even less consistent and appeared in some conditions but not in others.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the original insight was mistaken. The research has shown convincingly that flavour is constructed rather than simply detected, and that the senses are in constant conversation with one another. What it has not shown is that a well-chosen playlist or a carefully coloured plate can work dramatic changes. Crossmodal effects are best understood as gentle nudges that operate at the margins of experience. Their real value lies less in selling desserts than in what they reveal about how the brain weaves separate streams of information into a single, apparently seamless perception.

topic: the hollow-face illusion: face-specific versus general convexity explanations, and reduced susceptibility in psychosis
title: The Face That Will Not Turn Inside Out
subtitle: Why does the hollow back of a mask look like a solid face, and why do some people see through the deception?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Turn a theatrical mask around so that its hollow inner surface faces you, and something curious happens. Instead of a concave shell, you see an ordinary face bulging outwards, nose towards you, as solid as the front of the mask. If the mask is rotated slowly, the effect becomes even stranger: the illusory face appears to swivel in the opposite direction from the actual movement, following the observer around the room. Knowing perfectly well that the surface is hollow makes no difference. Only when the observer comes within a short distance and views the mask with both eyes does the true shape begin to assert itself, and even then the correction is often unstable. The hollow-face illusion is, I would argue, one of the clearest demonstrations available of how powerfully expectation can override the evidence of the senses.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The usual explanation is that the visual system brings to every scene a set of assumptions derived from past experience, and that a lifetime of seeing faces has taught it that faces are always convex. When the sensory signals, including the slight differences between the images received by the two eyes, indicate a hollow surface, this prior knowledge wins the contest. Hélène Dufrenoy, a vision scientist at the University of Lyon, holds that the illusion is specifically a product of our expertise with faces. In her studies, hollow objects of roughly similar shape but with no facial features, such as moulded bowls and abstract forms, produced a much weaker illusion. Turning the mask upside down, which is known to disrupt face recognition, also made it considerably easier for viewers to perceive its true depth.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Pavol Moravcik of Comenius University in Bratislava interprets the same evidence differently. He points out that hollow objects of many kinds, from the inside of a half-eggshell to a crumpled piece of moulded plastic, are frequently misperceived as convex when lit appropriately, a tendency that reflects a general assumption that objects bulge towards the viewer. In Moravcik's account, faces do not require a separate mechanism; they simply produce the strongest illusion because familiarity with them is added to this broader bias. The dispute has sometimes been conducted with considerable heat, yet it is difficult to see that the two positions differ much beyond the weight each gives to familiarity. Both agree that what we expect to see shapes what we do see.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The illusion took on clinical significance when researchers noticed that people with schizophrenia are much less susceptible to it. Shown a rotating hollow mask, many patients correctly report a concave surface. Similar reductions have been observed after sleep deprivation and under the influence of certain drugs. One influential interpretation is that psychosis involves a weakening of the expectations that normally guide perception, so that raw sensory input carries more weight than usual. Ragnheiður Thorvaldsdottir, a psychiatrist at the University of Iceland, has gone so far as to propose that a simple test of susceptibility could help to identify young people at risk of developing psychosis before obvious symptoms appear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That proposal deserves serious attention, but it is premature to treat the illusion as a diagnostic marker. Reduced susceptibility is not confined to schizophrenia, so a positive result would not reveal which condition, if any, a person had. Many patients in the published studies were also taking medication, whose effects on depth perception are poorly understood. At best, the test might complement established assessments rather than replace them. A further complication comes from Kwesi Twumasi-Ankrah at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Kumasi. Using eye-tracking equipment, his team found that patients tended to fixate on the edges of the mask, where cues to its hollowness are strongest, rather than on the central features of the face. Differences in the way people inspect the mask, he suggests, may explain part of what has been attributed to weakened expectations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The clinical findings expose an apparent paradox. In this particular case, the group whose perception is supposedly impaired sees the world more accurately than everyone else. The paradox dissolves once one recognises that illusions are not failures of the visual system but by-products of strategies that serve it well. Real faces are virtually never hollow, so a brain that discounts the rare contrary evidence will almost always be right, and will reach its conclusion more quickly than one that weighs every signal afresh. A strong expectation of convexity is therefore an asset, not a flaw, even if it occasionally leads us astray in front of an inverted mask.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It follows that susceptibility to illusions should not be thought of as simply good or bad. A visual system that is too easily swayed by expectation risks seeing what is not there; one that gives expectation too little weight may be slow, uncertain and overwhelmed by detail. The hollow mask offers a rare opportunity to observe this balance being struck, and it is that balance, rather than either extreme, that researchers studying perception and mental illness should seek to understand. Studies that combine eye tracking with virtual masks, whose depth, lighting and orientation can be altered at will, may at last allow the competing explanations to be separated cleanly.

topic: the science of magic: misdirection, the vanishing ball illusion and card forcing as tools for studying perception and choice
title: The Psychology of the Impossible
subtitle: Magicians have exploited the limits of human perception for centuries. Scientists are now asking what they can learn from them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before psychologists began to map the limits of attention and memory, conjurors were exploiting them nightly in front of paying audiences. A good magician knows, without needing a laboratory, that people cannot attend to everything at once, that they fill gaps in what they see with what they expect, and that they remember a performance not as it happened but as it was meant to be understood. Over the past two decades, a small but energetic field sometimes called the science of magic has tried to turn this practical wisdom into experimental evidence. The partnership between scientists and performers has obvious potential. It has not, however, fulfilled all of the hopes initially placed in it, and an honest assessment requires distinguishing its genuine contributions from its more inflated claims.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-studied technique is misdirection. Performers distinguish between overt misdirection, in which they lead the spectator's eyes towards one location while the secret action happens elsewhere, and covert misdirection, in which attention is drawn away even though the eyes remain where they are. Dragan Sarbanovic, a cognitive scientist at the University of Belgrade, recorded the eye movements of spectators watching a trick in which a magician silently drops a lighter into his lap. A large proportion of those who failed to notice the drop turned out to have been looking almost directly at it when it fell. Sarbanovic concludes that where people point their eyes is a surprisingly poor guide to what they perceive; it is the allocation of attention, not of gaze, that the magician controls.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of research concerns the so-called vanishing ball illusion. The magician tosses a ball into the air and catches it twice, then on the third throw merely mimes the action while secretly keeping the ball in his hand. A majority of spectators report seeing the ball rise and then disappear in mid-air. Marisol Esparza of the University of Guadalajara argues that this happens because the brain predicts the ball's path on the basis of the previous throws and perceives the prediction as though it were real. Crucially, she found that the illusion was far stronger when the magician followed the imaginary ball upwards with his eyes than when he looked at his hand. The performer's own gaze, it appears, acts as a social cue that shapes what the audience believes it sees.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Magicians are also adept at influencing decisions while leaving the chooser convinced of their freedom. In a typical card 'force', the performer offers a spectator what seems to be a free choice but ensures that a particular card is selected. Tatsuya Ogasawara and his colleagues at Kyoto University found that participants who had been forced rated their decision as just as free as those who had chosen without interference, and many invented reasons for their selection afterwards. Some commentators have treated such results as evidence against free will. That conclusion goes well beyond the data. What the experiments show is narrower, though still important: people frequently have little insight into the influences acting on their choices, and readily construct explanations for decisions they did not really make.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is impressed by the field's achievements. Zhanar Mukanova, a psychologist at Nazarbayev University in Astana, argues that most experiments on magic have merely confirmed phenomena already familiar from conventional research, such as the failure to notice unexpected events, and have yielded few new theories. Much of what magicians know, she adds, is tacit, acquired through years of performance and almost impossible to express in a form that can be tested scientifically. Mukanova is right about the tacit nature of the craft, and her warning against confusing publicity with progress is timely. But her dismissal is too sweeping. The discovery that the vanishing ball depends on the performer's gaze was not predicted by any existing theory of attention, and it has prompted new research on how social signals shape perception.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Magic also has practical advantages as a research tool. Laboratory tasks are often tedious, and bored participants produce unreliable data; magic tricks, by contrast, are naturally engaging, and audiences seem to enjoy the experience of being fooled. That enjoyment makes it possible to study deception and its detection under conditions that are both controlled and closer to real life than most experimental tasks. Researchers have used tricks to investigate when children begin to understand that others can hold false beliefs, and some educators have built lessons in scepticism around the question of how a trick might have been done. Studies of pickpockets and fraudsters, who use many of the same techniques as stage magicians, suggest that this knowledge could also help people protect themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Performers themselves remain divided about the enterprise. Some welcome the scientific attention as recognition of their craft, while others fear that publishing their methods will spoil the wonder on which their livelihoods depend. Yet the deepest lesson of this research concerns not the ingenuity of magicians but the nature of ordinary experience. The confident, continuous world we seem to inhabit is in large part a reconstruction, and magicians simply make visible the gaps that are always there.

topic: predictive processing: perception as the brain's best guess, evidence from two-tone images and conditioned hallucinations, and the falsifiability debate
title: Seeing What We Expect
subtitle: An influential theory holds that perception is a form of disciplined guesswork. How far can the idea be pushed before it breaks?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, perception was described as a process that runs from the bottom up. Light strikes the retina, signals pass through a series of processing stages, and at each stage simple features such as edges and colours are assembled into more complex ones until a recognisable scene emerges. Over the past three decades, an alternative account known as predictive processing has turned this picture on its head. According to this view, the brain is constantly generating predictions about the input it is about to receive, and what travels up from the senses is chiefly the mismatch between what was predicted and what actually arrived. What we perceive is therefore the brain's best current hypothesis about the causes of its sensations, a hypothesis that is continually tested and revised. Predictive processing is arguably the most ambitious theory in contemporary neuroscience, aspiring to explain not only perception but also action, attention and learning. Its ambition, however, is also the source of its greatest weakness.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of the most persuasive evidence comes from so-called two-tone images: photographs reduced to stark patches of black and white, which at first glance look like meaningless blotches. Once observers have been shown the original photograph, they immediately see the object in the two-tone version, and they find it impossible to return to their earlier state of confusion. Barbara Wieczorek, a neuroscientist at the University of Warsaw, scanned the brains of volunteers before and after they had seen the originals. She found that activity in the earliest visual areas, regions traditionally thought to register little more than lines and contrasts, came to resemble the pattern evoked by the full photograph. Prior knowledge, in other words, appears to reshape processing at the very first stages of the cortex, just as the theory proposes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If perception is guided by expectation, then sufficiently strong expectations ought to produce experiences with no external cause at all. Grace Kirabo of Makerere University in Kampala has tested this idea with a procedure in which volunteers repeatedly see a light at the same moment as they hear a faint tone. Later, when only the light is shown, many report hearing the tone. People who regularly hear voices that others cannot hear were especially prone to these conditioned hallucinations, which Kirabo interprets as evidence that psychosis can involve unusually powerful expectations. Yet other researchers have explained the reduced susceptibility of the same patients to certain visual illusions by claiming that their expectations are unusually weak. That the theory can accommodate both findings ought to be a cause for concern rather than reassurance.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This flexibility lies at the heart of the most serious criticism of predictive processing. Stepan Lukashik, a philosopher of science at Vilnius University, argues that the theory contains so many adjustable elements that it can be made to fit almost any result. In particular, the confidence the brain is assumed to place in its predictions relative to incoming signals can be set high or low after the event, depending on what the data require. For Lukashik, predictive processing is thus an unfalsifiable framework rather than a theory in the strict sense. His objection has real force when applied to the general idea. It is less damaging to the specific computational models built upon it, many of which make precise, risky predictions that could easily turn out to be wrong. Broad frameworks have frequently preceded testable theories in the history of science, and that alone is not grounds for rejecting them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One such prediction concerns the anatomy of the cortex. If predictions and errors are carried by separate populations of neurons, those populations should occupy distinct layers. Anjali Venkataraghavan and her colleagues at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru recorded from individual cells in several layers of the visual cortex in mice that had been trained to expect a particular sequence of images. Neurons in the upper layers responded vigorously when the sequence was broken, much as error signals should, while cells deeper down appeared to encode the expected image. Not every result fitted, however: a substantial number of error-like responses were found in layers where the models had not predicted them, and the team concluded that the existing models would require revision.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Much of the public enthusiasm for predictive processing has been generated by a striking slogan: that perception is a 'controlled hallucination'. The phrase captures something genuine, namely that experience is constructed by the brain rather than passively received, and it neatly explains why illusions arise when expectations that are usually reliable meet unusual circumstances. But the slogan is easily misunderstood. Many non-specialists take it to mean that what we perceive is essentially invented, when the crucial word is 'controlled'. In ordinary circumstances, the brain's guesses are tightly constrained by the senses, which is precisely why they are so seldom wrong.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It seems likely that predictive processing will survive, though perhaps in a more modest form than its most enthusiastic advocates envisage. Its real promise lies in its capacity to bring perception, movement and learning under a single explanatory roof. Whether that promise is realised will depend less on further demonstrations that expectations influence experience, which few now doubt, than on whether its supporters can produce precise models that state in advance what results would prove them wrong.

topic: susceptibility of non-human animals to visual illusions and the bowerbird's use of forced perspective
title: Do Animals Fall for Illusions?
subtitle: Testing other species with the tricks that fool human eyes is shedding light on how, and why, vision evolved

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Visual illusions are usually presented as curiosities of the human mind: entertaining demonstrations that our perception can be led astray. But if illusions arise from general solutions to problems that any visual system must solve, such as estimating the size of an object or its distance, then other animals ought to experience them too. If, on the other hand, they reflect features peculiar to human brains or human culture, they should be rare elsewhere in the animal kingdom. Over the past two decades, researchers have put this question to species ranging from chimpanzees and dogs to pigeons, chicks and fish. The resulting body of work is uneven, but in my view the comparative approach offers one of the most revealing ways of asking not merely how illusions occur but why they exist at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Animals cannot simply be asked what they see, so experimenters rely on training. In a typical study, an animal learns to choose the larger of two discs in order to obtain food. Once it performs reliably, it is shown test displays in which the discs are physically identical but placed in contexts that make one appear larger to human eyes. In the Ebbinghaus figure, for instance, a circle surrounded by small circles looks bigger than an identical circle surrounded by large ones. If the animal consistently selects the disc that humans see as larger, it is judged to be susceptible. Benedikt Harrach, a comparative psychologist at the University of Vienna, warns that this logic is less secure than it appears. Animals are adept at discovering shortcuts, and a pigeon or a fish may learn to respond to the total amount of colour in a display, or to the size of the surrounding shapes, rather than to the target itself. In Harrach's assessment, a number of early reports of susceptibility may reflect such unintended strategies rather than genuine illusions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even so, some patterns have emerged. Chimpanzees and several species of monkey appear to be fooled by many of the same figures as humans, which is hardly surprising given how closely related we are. Pigeons, by contrast, often show the reverse of the human response to the Ebbinghaus figure, choosing the circle surrounded by large circles as the bigger one. The usual explanation is that pigeons attend to local details before the overall arrangement, whereas humans tend to take in the whole configuration first and only then its parts. More unexpected are the results obtained by Ignacio Saldías at the University of Concepción, who found that guppies respond to the Ebbinghaus figure in the same direction as people when choosing between food items. Because the ancestors of fish and primates parted company hundreds of millions of years ago, Saldías interprets the finding as an example of independent evolution arriving at similar solutions. That interpretation may eventually prove correct, but with so few species tested, and with the methodological doubts Harrach has raised, it is too early to draw such a conclusion.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some animals may not merely experience illusions but create them. Male great bowerbirds of northern Australia build an avenue of sticks that opens onto a court covered with stones, bones and shells. These objects are not arranged at random: the smallest tend to be placed nearest the avenue and the largest furthest away. To a female standing in the avenue, this gradient could make the court appear more uniform in size, and perhaps make the displaying male seem larger. Claire Duchesneau of Université Laval has studied these birds in the field for over a decade. She found that males whose gradients were more regular enjoyed greater mating success, and that when her team reversed the arrangement, the males restored the original pattern within a few days. Duchesneau regards this as deliberate construction of a forced perspective. The evidence is intriguing, yet whether females actually perceive any illusion has never been tested directly. A regular gradient might impress them simply as evidence of a male's diligence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The bowerbird is not the only example of animals exploiting the perceptual biases of others. The bold patterns of many prey species seem designed to confuse a predator's judgement of speed and direction, and the markings of some fish appear to disguise the position of the eye. Such cases suggest that susceptibility to illusions is not merely an accidental by-product of how brains work but a feature that natural selection can act upon, both in the animals that are deceived and in those that do the deceiving.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What remains unclear is why species differ. One possibility is that each visual system is tuned to the demands of its environment, so that a bird searching for seeds on cluttered ground benefits from attending to fine detail, while a primate moving through a forest canopy needs to grasp spatial layouts quickly. Harrach cautions, however, that differences between individuals within a single species are often as large as those between species, which makes broad ecological stories hard to test.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the evidence suggests that illusions are best understood not as design faults but as windows onto the shortcuts that each species' brain relies on. Exploiting those windows fully will require researchers to agree on common procedures, so that results from different laboratories and different animals can be compared with confidence.

topic: distortions of subjective time: the stopped-clock illusion and the apparent slowing of time during danger
title: The Elastic Second
subtitle: Why does a clock seem to freeze when we glance at it, and why do moments of danger appear to unfold in slow motion?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Glance suddenly at an analogue clock with a moving second hand, and you may notice something odd: the hand seems to hang motionless for slightly longer than a second before resuming its regular progress. This so-called stopped-clock illusion, known to researchers as chronostasis, has a well-established explanation. During the rapid eye movement that carries our gaze to the clock, visual input is largely suppressed, so that we do not experience the world as a blur. Rather than leave a gap in experience, the brain appears to backdate the perception of the clock face to the moment the eye movement began, effectively filling the missing fraction of a second with the image of the new target. The first second we see is therefore genuinely stretched. Small as it is, the illusion is one of the most elegant demonstrations we have that our sense of time is not a direct reading of the world but something the brain actively assembles.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Haruka Matsukura, a cognitive scientist at Tohoku University, has shown that the phenomenon is not confined to the eyes. When participants shifted their attention to a new sound, such as a telephone tone in one ear, or to a vibration delivered to a fingertip, they likewise overestimated the duration of the first interval they experienced. Since no eye movement is involved in these cases, Matsukura argues that backdating cannot be the whole story. She proposes instead that the stretching of time accompanies any sudden arrival of attention at a new object, with the eye movement being merely the most common way in which attention is redirected.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more dramatic distortion is reported by people who have survived accidents, falls or assaults, many of whom insist that the event unfolded in slow motion. Itzel Cuautle of the National Autonomous University of Mexico devised an ingenious test of whether perception really speeds up in such moments. Volunteers were dropped backwards from a tall platform into a safety net, a genuinely frightening experience, while wearing a wrist display that flashed numbers too rapidly to be read under normal conditions. If time were truly being perceived more slowly, Cuautle reasoned, the falling participants should be able to read the numbers. They could not. Asked afterwards, however, they estimated that their own fall had lasted roughly a third longer than the falls of others they had watched. Cuautle concludes that the slowing is a trick of memory: frightening events are recorded in unusual detail, and a densely packed memory is later judged to have taken longer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Henrik Sigurbjörnsson of Reykjavík University is not persuaded. The ability to read rapidly changing numbers, he points out, depends on the fine timing of the visual system, and there is no reason to assume that a change in the felt passage of time must involve an improvement in that capacity. Moreover, laboratory studies show that briefly presented threatening images, such as photographs of snakes or angry faces, are judged to last longer than neutral images of identical duration, even when participants make their judgement immediately. Sigurbjörnsson attributes this to arousal accelerating an internal timing mechanism, so that more 'ticks' accumulate during a given interval. His objection to the wrist display is a fair one. Even so, it is doubtful that an angry face glimpsed on a screen and a fall towards the ground produce the same phenomenon, and the two kinds of evidence should not be treated as interchangeable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Both of these accounts assume that the brain contains something resembling a clock. Ruairí Mac Giolla Phádraig, a computational neuroscientist at Trinity College Dublin, questions that assumption. He argues that there is no dedicated timer anywhere in the brain, and that duration is instead estimated from the amount of change registered by perceptual networks. A computer model built on this principle, which judged the length of video clips solely by how much their content altered from moment to moment, reproduced several familiar human biases, including the tendency to judge busy scenes as longer than quiet ones. The approach is promising and has the virtue of not requiring any mysterious internal clock. Its models, however, have so far been tested only on calm, everyday scenes, and it remains unclear how they would account for the distortions experienced in fear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These debates have practical consequences. Witnesses to crimes are often asked how long an incident lasted, and their answers can influence judgements about intent or about whether a defendant had time to escape. Studies consistently find that witnesses overestimate the duration of stressful events, sometimes by a large margin. Whatever the underlying mechanism, testimony about the length of frightening episodes should be treated with considerable caution by investigators and courts alike.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Unlike vision or hearing, time has no sense organ of its own. Our experience of duration is inferred from other information, and like every inference it can be biased by circumstance. That flexibility, which allows a brief glance or a terrifying fall to bend our sense of time, is perhaps not a defect but a reminder that perception was shaped to serve action rather than to keep accurate records.
