area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: the potato and European population growth, 1700-1900: cause, consequence and the limits of a single crop
title: The Tuber and the Multitude
subtitle: Did the potato fuel Europe's population boom, or did a crowded continent simply turn to the potato?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the potato first reached Europe from the Andes in the second half of the sixteenth century, few observers would have predicted that it would one day sustain millions. For roughly two hundred years it remained a curiosity, grown in botanical gardens or fed to livestock, and it was only in the eighteenth century that farmers across northern and eastern Europe began to plant it on a large scale. By the middle of the nineteenth century, it had become the principal source of calories for a considerable part of the continent's rural poor. This coincided with an unprecedented rise in population: between 1750 and 1850 the number of people in Europe roughly doubled. The temptation to connect the two developments is understandable, and historians have been doing so since the eighteenth century itself. Whether the connection is one of cause and effect, however, remains one of the more stubborn questions in economic history.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most ambitious attempt to answer it was made by Professor Leopold Bjurholm and his colleagues at the Baltic Institute for Economic History. Rather than tracing the crop's diffusion through scattered local records, the team used modern agronomic data to classify every region of the Old World according to how well its soils and climate suited the potato. They then compared population and urban growth in suitable and unsuitable regions before and after the crop became available. Their conclusion was striking: the introduction of the potato, they calculated, explains around a quarter of the growth in population and urbanisation in the Old World between 1700 and 1900. The design is undeniably elegant, but it rests on an assumption that deserves closer scrutiny. A region being able to grow potatoes is not the same as its farmers actually choosing to grow them, and the gap between the two was, in many places, wide and long-lasting.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why that gap existed is itself contested. A long tradition, still repeated in popular histories, holds that Europeans distrusted the potato because it was absent from the Bible, belonged to the same botanical family as poisonous nightshades, and was rumoured to cause leprosy. Dr Inés Zabalegui, an agrarian historian, considers such explanations largely beside the point. In her view, the real obstacles were institutional. Across much of the continent, land was farmed in open fields under a rotation agreed by the whole village, and fallow land was used for communal grazing; a farmer who planted potatoes on his strip disrupted the system for his neighbours. Tithe arrangements, which often specified traditional grains, created further disincentives. I find her argument largely convincing: suspicion of a novel food may well have existed, but it is unlikely to have held back for two centuries a crop whose advantages were so evident to anyone who grew it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Those advantages were considerable. An acre of potatoes could yield several times as many calories as an acre of wheat or rye, and the tubers supplied significant quantities of vitamin C, which grain-based diets often lacked. Combined with a little milk, they provided an almost complete diet. The crop also had a less obvious merit. Because the edible part grows underground and can be left in the soil until needed, it was far harder for passing armies to requisition or destroy than a field of standing grain, a feature that some historians believe encouraged its adoption in the war-torn regions of central Europe.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that these qualities drove population growth. The demographer Dr Teodor Pietrusewicz points out that in several regions, including parts of England and Scandinavia, populations had begun to rise well before the potato was widely cultivated. He attributes this earlier phase of growth to falling mortality, as epidemic disease became less frequent and harvests less volatile. For Pietrusewicz, the direction of causation may often have run the other way: as families multiplied and holdings were subdivided among heirs, households on ever smaller plots turned to the potato because no other crop could feed them from so little land. This reversal deserves more attention than it has received. It does not refute the case for the potato, but it suggests that the crop frequently followed population pressure rather than creating it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nowhere were the consequences of that pressure clearer than in Ireland. By the 1840s, around a third of the population relied almost entirely on potatoes, and much of the crop consisted of a single high-yielding variety. When a fungus-like pathogen destroyed successive harvests from 1845, about a million people died and a further million emigrated. Dr Caoimhe Delargy argues that it is misleading to treat the potato as the cause of the catastrophe; the dependence on a single crop, she contends, was the product of a system of land tenure that left the poor with tiny plots and no security, and the scale of the mortality reflected political decisions about relief. Her emphasis on policy is necessary, though it should not obscure the biological lesson: a population that depends on one genetically uniform crop is exceptionally exposed to a single disease.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, can be concluded? It seems to me that the potato is best understood as an enabling factor rather than a determining one. It allowed more people to live on less land, but whether that capacity translated into growth depended on institutions, on mortality from other causes and on the choices of millions of farmers. This distinction matters beyond economic history. Modern advocates of new 'miracle' crops sometimes speak as though introducing a plant were enough to transform a society's prospects. The history of the potato suggests otherwise: a crop's potential is realised only when the social arrangements around it allow it to be.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: why medieval Europeans prized spices: the rotten-meat myth versus status display, humoral medicine and imagined geography
title: A Taste of Paradise
subtitle: Medieval Europe paid fortunes for pepper, cloves and nutmeg, and the most familiar explanation for its appetite does not survive scrutiny

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few claims about medieval food are repeated as often as the idea that cooks used heavy spicing to disguise the taste of meat that was on the point of going bad. It appears in school textbooks, in television documentaries and on the menus of restaurants that offer 'authentic' medieval banquets. On inspection, however, it collapses almost immediately. Imported spices were extraordinarily expensive: in fifteenth-century England, a pound of cloves might cost a skilled craftsman more than a week's wages. Anyone wealthy enough to season a dish generously could also afford meat from animals slaughtered that morning, and great households kept livestock on hand precisely for that purpose. Conversely, the poor, who were far more likely to eat food of doubtful freshness, could not have bought spices in any meaningful quantity. The real question, then, is not what spices were hiding but why they were wanted at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential answer has come from the food historian Dr Mirela Ohanessian, who sees spices primarily as instruments of social display. The cookery manuscripts produced for aristocratic kitchens, she notes, call for pepper, ginger, cinnamon and saffron in dish after dish, while the accounts of noble households show that purchases rose sharply in the weeks before feasts at which important guests were expected. Spices were not only eaten but exhibited: at the end of a banquet, sugared aniseed and candied ginger were carried in on ornate spice plates and offered to the company. In Ohanessian's reading, the value of a spice lay partly in the fact that most people could not obtain it, so that consuming it publicly was a way of announcing one's rank.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Kenji Sugimori, a historian of medicine, regards this interpretation as incomplete. Medieval dietary theory, inherited from ancient Greek physicians, classified every food according to whether it was hot or cold, moist or dry, and held that health depended on keeping these qualities in balance. Spices were considered hot and dry, and were therefore prescribed to correct foods regarded as cold and moist, such as fish, pork and many fruits. Spices were sold by apothecaries as well as grocers, and the boundary between seasoning and medication was blurred. For Sugimori, the medical rationale came first and the prestige followed. The two accounts, however, need not be set against each other. Dietary advice was written for, and largely followed by, the same wealthy patrons whose banquets Ohanessian describes, so a spice could easily be both a remedy and a badge of status at once.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third dimension is stressed by Dr Ayodele Okonjo-Bello, who studies how medieval Europeans imagined distant lands. Few people in Europe had any clear idea where pepper or nutmeg actually grew. Learned writers placed their origins near the earthly Paradise, which was believed to lie somewhere in the far East, and travellers' tales described pepper forests guarded by serpents and cinnamon gathered from the nests of enormous birds. Okonjo-Bello argues that this mystery was itself part of what buyers were paying for. Of the three interpretations, hers is the hardest to test against documentary evidence, but it helps to explain why the merchants who controlled the trade did so little to correct such stories.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What did spiced food actually taste like? Surviving recipes are frustratingly vague about quantities, often instructing the cook simply to add 'enough' or 'a good deal'. Yet they do reveal consistent patterns. Spices were frequently combined with sugar and vinegar to create sweet-and-sour sauces, and they were often added towards the end of cooking rather than at the start. Attempts to reconstruct these dishes in modern kitchens have generally produced food that is aromatic rather than fiery. The medieval palate, in other words, was neither crude nor indiscriminate; it followed principles that were as systematic as those of any later cuisine.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The decline of spicing offers a further test of these theories. After Portuguese ships reached India by sea at the end of the fifteenth century, and especially after Dutch merchants gained control of the main clove and nutmeg islands in the seventeenth, prices fell considerably. At roughly the same time, fashionable French cooking began to abandon heavy spicing in favour of herbs, butter and what its advocates called the natural taste of ingredients. The economic historian Professor Linnea Söderqvist interprets this shift as decisive support for the status thesis: once pepper became affordable to prosperous merchants and shopkeepers, the elite lost interest in it. The argument is persuasive but incomplete, since the same period saw the old medical system lose its authority among physicians. Falling prices and changing medical ideas probably reinforced one another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Why, then, does the myth of the rotten meat persist? Part of its appeal, I suspect, is that it flatters a modern sense of superiority, implying that people in the past were careless about hygiene and indifferent to flavour. The evidence points in the opposite direction, towards a culture in which food, medicine and imagination were closely intertwined. Spices are a reminder that the value of a commodity cannot be explained by its practical uses alone; historians must also ask what it meant to the people who bought it.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: how sugar became an everyday staple in Britain, 1650-1850: supply, household demand, nutrition and the abolitionist boycott
title: The Sweetening of Britain
subtitle: In two centuries, a rare luxury became part of the daily diet of the poor. Historians still disagree about why

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the seventeenth century, sugar was a scarce and costly substance in Britain. Apothecaries dispensed it as a remedy for coughs and fevers, and confectioners in wealthy households moulded it into elaborate table decorations that were admired rather than eaten. Two hundred years later, it was an ordinary item in the shopping of labouring families, stirred into tea several times a day. Estimates vary, but average consumption per person appears to have risen roughly fivefold over the course of the eighteenth century alone. Few changes in the history of diet have been so rapid or so complete. Any account of this transformation must begin by acknowledging how the sugar was produced: overwhelmingly by enslaved Africans on Caribbean plantations, under a labour regime of exceptional brutality. The question that has divided historians is not whether this system made cheap sugar possible, but whether it is enough to explain why Britons came to consume so much of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For Professor Amara Thiongo, an economic historian, the answer lies chiefly on the side of supply. As plantations multiplied across the Caribbean in the second half of the seventeenth century, output rose dramatically and the price of sugar in London fell by more than half within a few decades. Merchants, refiners and shopkeepers then had every incentive to find new customers. Refineries multiplied in London and Bristol, and by the middle of the eighteenth century village shops were selling sugar in quantities small enough for a labourer to afford. In Thiongo's view, availability created its own demand. This argument is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Many goods became cheaper during the same period, and not all of them found a place in every household. Falling prices explain how sugar came within reach of the poor; they do not explain why the poor chose it rather than something else.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Owain Hollingbrook approaches the question from the other end, by looking at how households earned and spent their money. Drawing on the inventories of possessions compiled when people died, he shows that teapots, cups and sugar bowls began to appear in the homes of artisans and labourers early in the eighteenth century. Hollingbrook argues that families during this period gradually shifted their time away from producing goods for their own use and towards work paid in money, with wives and children increasingly taking wages. Sugar, together with tea, was among the first purchases that made this extra effort seem worthwhile. It functioned, in his phrase, as a small daily reward that justified longer hours.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The nutritional consequences have been examined by Dr Priya Kapadia. By the early nineteenth century, she calculates, sugar supplied a significant proportion of the calories consumed by working families in industrial towns. Hot, sweet tea turned a cold meal of bread into something that felt like a proper meal, and it provided quick energy for people working long shifts in mills and workshops. Kapadia does not regard this as a simple improvement. In households where meat was scarce, she notes, it was usually reserved for the male wage-earner, while women and children made do with bread, tea and sugar. Sugar may therefore have displaced more nourishing foods precisely for the family members who most needed them. Her conclusion is sobering, and I think it largely justified, although the evidence from household budgets is too fragmentary to show how widespread the pattern was.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A long-standing explanation holds that ordinary people adopted sugar in imitation of their social superiors, for whom it had once been a mark of distinction. Dr Rasmus Nyberg, a cultural historian, rejects this view. The rich had displayed sugar at banquets in the form of sculptures and sweetmeats, whereas workers consumed it in tea, at work and in haste. The meaning of the substance, Nyberg argues, was not copied but transformed: what had been a symbol of leisure became a fuel for labour. His reasoning seems to me convincing, and it suggests that the notion of emulation explains rather little.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Consumers were not, however, unaware of where their sugar came from. In the early 1790s, campaigners against the slave trade urged the public to stop buying sugar grown by enslaved people, and contemporary estimates suggested that several hundred thousand families joined the boycott. Pamphlets reminded readers that every spoonful was stained with blood, and some grocers advertised sugar from India as produced without slave labour. This was among the earliest organised consumer campaigns in British history, and it demonstrates that an appetite which had seemed fixed could be reconsidered on moral grounds.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of the explanations offered by these historians is sufficient on its own. Cheap supply, new patterns of work, the needs of tired bodies and a shift in cultural meaning all played a part, and they reinforced one another. Each illuminates something that the others leave in shadow, and the temptation to crown one of them as the decisive cause should be resisted. What the history of sugar does make clear is that demand for a commodity is not a fixed feature of human nature waiting to be satisfied. It is shaped by prices, by labour, by habit and, as the boycott showed, by conscience. That lesson remains relevant for anyone who assumes that modern patterns of consumption are simply what people naturally want.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: the rapid spread of the American chilli pepper across Asia after 1500: routes, naming, economics and competing explanations
title: Fire from the New World
subtitle: Within a century of reaching Asia, an American plant had remade some of the world's great cuisines. How did it happen so fast?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is difficult to imagine the cooking of Thailand, Sichuan, Korea or southern India without the chilli pepper. Yet before the closing years of the fifteenth century, no one in Asia had ever tasted one. The plant is native to the Americas, and it crossed the oceans only after European ships began to link the continents. What is remarkable is the speed of its adoption. In Europe, the potato and the tomato took two centuries or more to move from curiosity to staple; the chilli, by contrast, appears to have been grown and eaten across large parts of southern and eastern Asia within roughly a hundred years of its arrival. Explaining why some foods travel quickly while others languish is one of the central problems of culinary history, and the chilli is perhaps its most striking case.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The conventional account traces the plant along Portuguese trading routes. Having reached the west coast of India in the early sixteenth century, the Portuguese established Goa as a commercial base, and from there chillies are thought to have spread to Bengal, Southeast Asia and the port of Macau. Dr Hélène Brisbois, a historian of economic botany, believes this picture is too tidy. She points to the considerable diversity of chilli varieties grown in parts of Central Asia and the Balkans, and to Chinese provincial records suggesting that the plant reached some inland regions from the west rather than from the coast. In her view, at least one overland route through Ottoman and Persian territory operated alongside the maritime one. Her evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive, but it seems likely that the chilli travelled by more than one path, even if the sea lanes carried most of it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Professor Daisuke Fujikawa, a historical linguist, has approached the question through vocabulary. In language after language, he observes, the newcomer was not given an entirely new name but was described as a kind of pepper, usually with a word indicating that it came from abroad. In some cases neighbouring peoples each attributed the plant to the other: early Korean texts referred to it as a Japanese spice, while certain Japanese sources called it Korean pepper. Fujikawa argues that such naming made acceptance easier, because cooks could treat the chilli as a familiar ingredient in a new form rather than as something wholly alien. This is an insightful point, although names tell us more about how a plant was perceived than about the route by which it actually arrived.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most persuasive explanation, to my mind, is economic. Black pepper had been prized across Asia for centuries, but it grew only in particular tropical regions and, once traded inland, was often heavily taxed. Dr Nurlan Dzhumabaev, an agrarian economist, emphasises that the chilli could be raised from seed in a single season, in a small plot or even a pot beside the house, and that its fruit could be dried and stored for a year. Pungency, previously something that had to be purchased, could now be produced at home. Dzhumabaev's research on rural account books shows that chilli was taken up first by peasant households and only later appeared in the kitchens of the elite. In the poorer upland districts of Sichuan, where salt was expensive, chilli made monotonous meals of grain and vegetables considerably more palatable.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A quite different hypothesis has been advanced by the food scientist Dr Marisol Escobedo. Comparing thousands of traditional recipes, she found that cuisines in hot climates use more spices than those in cool ones, and she argues that this reflects a protective function: many spices, chilli included, contain compounds that inhibit bacteria responsible for food-borne illness. I find this argument unconvincing as an explanation of the chilli's spread. Hot countries differ from cool ones in many ways, including the variety of plants available, so the correlation may have other causes. More importantly, chilli was adopted within a few decades, far too quickly for communities to have noticed any modest reduction in illness.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Medical traditions offer a more plausible supplementary explanation. Dr Sunniva Baekeland, a historian of medicine, has shown that physicians in both India and China quickly assigned the chilli a place within existing systems of classification. It was regarded as strongly heating and drying, and was recommended for expelling the dampness that was believed to cause illness. It is surely no coincidence that some of the most enthusiastic chilli-eating regions, such as Sichuan and Hunan, are notoriously humid. Medical theory, in this case, gave a new food a respectable reason to be eaten.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is that the chilli succeeded largely because it fitted into existing categories: it resembled a spice people already valued, it could be grown in gardens people already kept, and it answered to medical ideas people already held. Novelty, it seems, travels best when it does not look too new. Nevertheless, its triumph was not universal. In Japan, where the chilli was known from an early date, it remained a relatively minor seasoning for centuries, a reminder that even the most adaptable crop does not conquer every kitchen automatically.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: the slow acceptance of the tomato as food in Europe, 1540-1800: poison myth, humoral medicine, fragile early varieties and the bias of elite cookbooks
title: The Golden Apple's Long Wait
subtitle: Why did a fruit that now defines Mediterranean cooking take two centuries to reach European tables?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ingredients seem as firmly rooted in a national cuisine as the tomato in Italian cooking. It is therefore something of a surprise to learn that the fruit, which reached Europe from the Americas in the first half of the sixteenth century, spent the best part of two hundred years on the margins of European diets. An Italian herbalist described it in the 1540s, naming it the 'golden apple', and within a few decades it was being grown across the continent. Yet it was grown mostly in the gardens of the wealthy, where it was admired for its glossy colour rather than eaten, and the first printed recipe for a tomato sauce did not appear until the closing years of the seventeenth century. The most familiar explanation for this delay is that Europeans believed the fruit to be poisonous. That explanation contains some truth, but it is far too tidy to account for what actually happened.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The poison theory rests on botany. The tomato is a member of the nightshade family, and sixteenth-century naturalists, who grouped plants largely by appearance, noted its resemblance to mandrake and deadly nightshade, both notorious for their toxic properties. A further story, often repeated in popular histories, holds that wealthy diners fell ill after eating tomatoes from pewter plates, because the acidic fruit drew lead out of the metal. It is an appealing tale, yet no one has produced a contemporary document that describes such an episode, and it should probably be retired. Renata Quilisch, of the Centre for Early Modern Botany, has examined more than sixty herbals printed between 1540 and 1750. She found that, although many authors advised caution, only a handful described the tomato as deadly. Far more commonly, they complained that it was unwholesome, that it produced 'thin blood' or that it sat badly in the stomach.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Quilisch locates these complaints within the medical framework of the time. Under the humoral system, every food was assigned qualities of heat, cold, moisture and dryness, and a healthy diet kept them in balance. The tomato, like the cucumber and the melon, was judged cold and moist, and such foods were thought to cause fevers if eaten raw. In Quilisch's words, the fruit was regarded as 'a food to be managed rather than a danger to be avoided', which is why recipes, when they finally appeared, almost always cooked it with oil, salt and pepper, ingredients believed to correct its chilling effects. This is a valuable correction to the poison myth, but it cannot by itself explain the delay. Melons attracted exactly the same medical warnings and were nonetheless eaten with enthusiasm across Europe.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more practical explanation is offered by Tobiah Arkwell, an agricultural historian at the Hallam Institute. Arkwell points out that the earliest European tomatoes were small, deeply ribbed and thin-skinned. They bruised easily, rotted within days of picking and were unsuited to transport over any distance. Until gardeners had selected sturdier varieties, and until cooks had developed ways of preserving the fruit, such as reducing it to a concentrated paste and drying it in the sun, the tomato could be eaten only fresh, in a short summer season and close to where it was grown. This, Arkwell argues, explains why it established itself first in the warm south of Italy and Spain while remaining a rarity in the north. His account explains geography well, but chronology less well: the climate of Naples was ideal from the outset, yet the city waited over a century before its cooks committed the tomato to print.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most provocative contribution comes from Yusuf Demirkapi, a culinary anthropologist, who questions whether there was any real delay at all. Printed cookbooks, he observes, were written by and for the households of the nobility and the wealthy merchant class. The kitchens of labourers and peasants left almost no written trace. Demirkapi believes that the tomato was adopted by the poor long before it appeared in elite recipe collections, and that its very association with humble tables made cookery writers reluctant to acknowledge it. Tellingly, the earliest Neapolitan recipe labels its tomato sauce as being 'in the Spanish style', as though distancing the dish from local tradition. I find this argument the most important of the three, because it exposes a weakness in the sources on which the whole debate depends. Its difficulty, admittedly, is that it is hard to prove: the absence of evidence about what the poor ate is precisely the problem it seeks to explain.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these competing accounts is not a single barrier but a cluster of overlapping ones: botanical suspicion, medical theory, the limitations of early varieties and the snobbery of written sources. The original question also deserves scrutiny. To ask why the tomato was adopted so slowly is to imply that rapid adoption was the norm. In fact, it was not. Most crops transferred from the Americas spent generations being tested in gardens, fed to animals or confined to particular regions before they became everyday foods, and the tomato's slow progress was entirely typical of the period.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: By the nineteenth century, the picture had changed decisively. Improved varieties, commercial canning in northern Italy and the expansion of urban markets turned the tomato into a staple, and millions of emigrants carried tomato-based cooking across the Atlantic, returning the fruit, transformed, to the continent from which it had come. Tastes that appear timeless are often recent, and an ingredient now regarded as the very essence of a national cuisine was, for most of its European history, a foreign curiosity of uncertain value.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: the Dutch East India Company's monopoly of nutmeg and cloves, 1620-1800: extirpation of trees, hidden costs, restricted demand and whether the monopoly paid
title: Scarcity by Design
subtitle: For almost two centuries a single trading company controlled the world's supply of two spices. Was its monopoly the commercial triumph it appeared to be?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the seventeenth century, nutmeg and its lacy outer covering, mace, grew on only a handful of small volcanic islands in the Banda group of what is now eastern Indonesia, while cloves were confined to a few islands of the northern Moluccas. Few valuable commodities have ever been so geographically concentrated, and that concentration made the two spices uniquely tempting targets for monopoly. The Dutch East India Company set out to secure one. In 1621 its forces conquered Banda, killing, enslaving or deporting most of the islands' inhabitants and replacing them with plantations run by Company-licensed planters and worked by enslaved labourers brought from elsewhere. The episode is rightly remembered as one of the most brutal of the early colonial era. Less often discussed is a question that economic historians have debated for decades: whether the monopoly so ruthlessly obtained actually paid.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The mechanics of the system were straightforward, if severe. Clove cultivation was restricted to the island of Ambon and a few neighbouring districts, and each year armed fleets were sent to cut down clove trees growing anywhere else, a practice known as extirpation. Local rulers who agreed to the destruction received annual compensation payments. Nutmegs were dipped in lime before they were shipped, in the belief that this would prevent them from germinating if they fell into rival hands. In Amsterdam, meanwhile, the Company managed its stocks with great care, releasing only enough to keep prices high and steady; when supplies threatened to exceed demand, surplus nutmegs were on occasion burned rather than sold cheaply.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To Lotte Ruisdonk of the Institute for Maritime Economic History, the result was a commercial triumph. Drawing on the Company's own accounts, she calculates that for well over a century the fine spices generated a share of its European profits out of all proportion to the volume traded, at margins far higher than those on pepper, which grew across so vast an area of South and Southeast Asia that no single power could hope to control it. Ruisdonk places particular weight on the stability of prices. Because the Company knew roughly what each consignment would fetch, she argues, it could plan its shipping years in advance and offer investors the predictable returns that sustained confidence in the enterprise.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ruisdonk's figures are impressive, but they may flatter the monopoly. The accounts she relies on record the revenue earned in Amsterdam, whereas the costs of maintaining control in Asia were scattered across many separate ledgers: the garrisons and fortresses of the Moluccas, the patrol fleets that intercepted smugglers, the extirpation expeditions and the payments to local rulers. Teodora Zamfirache, an economic historian who has spent years reassembling these dispersed expenses, concludes that once military spending in the spice islands is included, the Company's margin on nutmeg and cloves shrinks dramatically, perhaps to a level little better than that of trades conducted without such violence. Her estimates are necessarily approximate, since many forts and ships served several purposes at once, yet they make Ruisdonk's figure look less like a typical result than a best case.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further difficulty concerns demand. By holding prices high, the Company ensured that nutmeg and cloves remained luxuries in Europe, consumed in modest quantities by the prosperous. Several economists have suggested that a lower price would have sold far greater volumes and might well have produced higher total revenue. The directors chose scarcity instead. That choice is easier to understand than to admire: men whose first concern was a reliable annual dividend had little reason to gamble on expansion, but by keeping the market small they also left the Company exposed should its control of supply ever be broken.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The environmental historian Haruto Sumiyoshi approaches the monopoly from a different angle. Extirpation, he points out, removed clove trees from dozens of islands, while the nutmeg trade came to depend on a small number of plantations on a few square kilometres of land. In Sumiyoshi's view, monopoly by destruction is inherently fragile, because in eliminating every alternative source it also eliminates any insurance against disaster. His argument is borne out by events: when a violent storm struck Banda in the late eighteenth century, it flattened a large proportion of the nutmeg trees, and there was nowhere else from which the losses could be made good.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The monopoly finally collapsed through the one route the Company had worked hardest to close. In the 1770s a French colonial official succeeded in smuggling seedlings to the island of Mauritius, and during the wars of the early nineteenth century British forces occupied the spice islands and transplanted thousands of young trees to their own colonies in Asia and the Caribbean. Within a few decades prices had fallen sharply. The lesson, I would suggest, is that the system endured not because it was efficient but because the trees were genuinely difficult to establish elsewhere. Once that natural barrier was overcome, a monopoly built on coercion had nothing left to protect it.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: why canned food took most of the nineteenth century to reach ordinary households: hand-made cans, ignorance of spoilage, the naval meat scandal, price and middle-class attitudes
title: Sealed and Suspect
subtitle: The tin can was invented early in the nineteenth century, yet it was decades before most families would buy food in one

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The principle of preserving food by heating it inside a sealed container was worked out in France in the first decade of the nineteenth century, when a Parisian confectioner responded to a government prize offered for a means of feeding armies on the move. Within a few years, a firm in London was sealing meat and vegetables in canisters of tinned iron rather than glass. Naval officers and polar expeditions were among the earliest and most enthusiastic customers, since the containers allowed provisions to be carried for months without spoiling. The invention looks, in retrospect, like an obvious success. Yet for roughly half a century canned food was eaten almost exclusively by sailors, soldiers and explorers, and it was only in the closing decades of the century that it became a regular item in ordinary kitchens. The delay is usually put down to the limitations of the early technology. That explanation is not wrong, but in my view the obstacles were at least as much social as they were technical.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technical problems were certainly considerable. Early cans were heavy and made entirely by hand: each body was cut, rolled and soldered individually, and a skilled tinsmith could manufacture only around sixty canisters in a day. Opening them was a further trial. Instructions on some early tins advised the user to cut round the top with a hammer and chisel, and a dedicated opening tool did not come into general use until nearly fifty years after the first cans were sold. More fundamentally, nobody understood why the method worked. Since the role of microorganisms in decay had yet to be discovered, processors relied on trial and error, heating some foods for hours and others for a fraction of that time. Aurelie Fontcuberta, a historian of technology, regards this ignorance as the decisive barrier: because manufacturers could not explain spoilage, they could not reliably prevent it, and a proportion of every batch went bad.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Those failures could be spectacular. In the early 1850s, inspectors at a naval supply yard opened a consignment of very large canisters of meat and found the contents of many to be putrid; the heat, it was later realised, had failed to penetrate to the centre of such bulky containers. The episode was reported at length in the press and debated in Parliament, where it became a symbol of official negligence. Milos Petrikovic argues that its real damage was to the reputation of the product rather than to the volume of production, since naval orders soon resumed; what lasted was an image of canned food as cheap, dubious and possibly dangerous, an image that clung to it for decades. There is something in this, although the point should not be pressed too far. Sales to private households were tiny before the scandal, so there was relatively little civilian goodwill to lose.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the economic historian Sanna Koskivaara, the most important factor was simply price. Hand production made cans expensive, and until the 1870s their contents were beyond the means of most working families. The change came with machinery that stamped out can ends, rolled bodies and eventually automated much of the soldering, multiplying the output of each worker many times over. At the same time, vast quantities of cheap meat from Australia and South America were canned for export to Britain, where tinned mutton briefly became a byword for an affordable meal. Modestly rising wages in the industrial towns added further to demand. In Koskivaara's view, it was the falling cost of cans, not any change in public opinion, that opened the mass market.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Gwilym Llewelyn, a cultural historian, places more emphasis on attitudes. He has studied the household manuals that instructed middle-class wives on the management of the home, and finds that many treated a reliance on tinned food as evidence of poor housekeeping: a capable wife, the manuals implied, cooked from fresh ingredients. Manufacturers, Llewelyn shows, worked hard to counter this view, using brightly printed labels and advertisements that presented the tin as modern, scientific and above all clean. His reading of these sources is persuasive as far as it goes. Its limitation is that the manuals were written for a comfortable minority and may reveal little about working-class homes, where long hours and limited cooking facilities could make convenience far more valuable than respectability.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Each of these accounts captures part of the story, but none is sufficient on its own. The discovery during the 1860s that microorganisms cause decay gave processors a rational basis for heating times and made failures rarer; mechanisation brought prices within reach of poorer families; and advertising gradually softened middle-class disapproval. These developments reinforced one another, and it is difficult to imagine any one of them succeeding without the others. Koskivaara is surely right that cost mattered most to the poorest households, yet a cheap product that people distrust does not sell well for long. The history of the can, then, is less a story of invention than one of the slow and uneven construction of trust, a process that took far longer than the engineering itself.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: the establishment of tea growing in British India, 1834-1890: native Assam tea, plants and experts from China, coerced labour and the myth of botanical theft
title: Leaves of Contention
subtitle: How India replaced China as Britain's tea garden is often told as a tale of daring theft. The full story is less romantic and more revealing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the start of the nineteenth century, almost all the tea drunk in Britain came from China, purchased at the single port of Canton, where foreign merchants were confined to a narrow strip of waterfront and permitted to trade only through licensed Chinese intermediaries. British officials had long been uneasy about dependence on a supplier they could not control, and in 1833, when the East India Company lost its monopoly of trade with China, the incentive to grow tea within British-ruled territory became pressing. The following year the Governor-General in Calcutta appointed a Tea Committee to investigate the possibility. Within little more than half a century, India had overtaken China as Britain's principal source of tea. Popular histories frequently present this transformation as the outcome of an audacious act of botanical theft. The reality was considerably messier, and the theft story, for all its appeal, obscures more than it reveals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of what it obscures is that tea was already growing in India. In the 1820s, chiefs of the Singpho people in the hills of Assam had shown British officers wild tea plants whose leaves they dried and brewed. When specimens reached Calcutta, however, the Committee's botanists hesitated to accept them as genuine tea, apparently because they assumed that the true plant could only be Chinese. Bhaskar Saikia, of the Brahmaputra Institute of Regional History, argues that this assumption cost the infant industry the best part of a decade, and that the expertise of Assamese communities was steadily written out of official reports as the enterprise grew.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Rather than build on local resources, the Committee sent an expedition to China in 1834 to acquire seed. Tens of thousands of seedlings were raised in the botanic garden at Calcutta and dispatched to Assam and the foothills of the Himalayas. Large numbers perished on the journey, and those that survived often fared badly in the hot, humid lowlands of Assam, where they also crossed freely with the native plants to produce a bewildering range of hybrids. In the late 1840s a Scottish plant collector, travelling in Chinese dress, penetrated the inland tea districts and shipped some twenty thousand plants and seedlings to India in Wardian cases, sealed glass boxes in which plants could survive voyages lasting months without needing to be watered. Most of this consignment went to the north-western Himalayas and to Darjeeling, whose cooler climate suited the Chinese variety far better than the Assam plains.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Haruki Watabiki contends that the plants were in fact the lesser part of what was transferred. What India lacked, he argues, was the knowledge needed to turn fresh leaves into a saleable product: the precise techniques of withering, rolling and firing that Chinese producers had refined over centuries. The same collector recruited a group of experienced Chinese tea makers, together with their tools, and Watabiki has traced pay records showing that such specialists earned several times the wages of other workers on the early plantations. Indian tea, moreover, was initially judged by London brokers according to how closely it resembled the Chinese product. Watabiki's case is convincing for the early decades. From the 1870s onwards, however, planters developed machines for rolling and drying the leaf that displaced hand methods, and Indian processing began to follow a path of its own.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The economic historian Miriam Zelenka shifts attention away from plants and techniques altogether. In her account, the decisive factors were land and labour. The colonial government made vast tracts of forest available to planters on generous terms, and the plantations were worked by hundreds of thousands of labourers recruited from central and eastern India under contracts that bound them for years, imposed criminal penalties for leaving and were associated with appalling death rates. Zelenka maintains that the image of the lone adventurer smuggling plants out of China has endured precisely because it draws attention away from the coercion on which the industry was built. This seems to me the most important correction of all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is a further irony. The tea that eventually conquered the British market came predominantly not from Chinese stock but from the Assam variety and its hybrids, which planters had at first regarded as inferior. It produced a stronger, darker and more astringent drink than most Chinese teas, well suited to the British habit of adding milk and sugar, and it could be grown on an industrial scale. In 1888, Indian tea imported into Britain exceeded Chinese tea in quantity for the first time, and the gap widened rapidly in the following decades as Ceylon joined India as a major producer.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the Chinese plants and experts were unimportant; the Darjeeling estates, in particular, were founded on them. But the familiar narrative of theft compresses a long, uneven and frequently brutal process into a single dramatic episode. It casts a European collector as the hero while leaving the Singpho chiefs, the Chinese tea makers and the indentured labourers in the background, even though, taken together, their contribution was arguably far greater. Restoring them to the story is not merely a matter of historical fairness; it also changes how we understand the movement of crops between continents, which has rarely depended on seeds and cuttings alone.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: Roman fermented fish sauce (garum): coastal salting factories, amphora distribution, regional varieties, ancient terminology and modern distaste
title: The Salt of the Empire
subtitle: Once dismissed as a foul-smelling extravagance, Roman fish sauce is now seen by archaeologists as one of the ancient world's great mass-produced foods

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few features of Roman cookery provoke as much modern distaste as garum, the sauce produced by leaving fish to ferment in salt. Ancient authors were themselves divided about it. Some praised the finest grades as worthy of the most refined tables, while satirists made fun of its pungent smell and of the prices that connoisseurs were willing to pay. For much of the twentieth century, historians took their cue from these literary sources and treated the sauce as an exotic indulgence of the wealthy, interesting chiefly as evidence of Roman decadence. Excavations over the past few decades have transformed that picture. What is emerging, in my view, is an industry that has more in common with modern food processing than with gourmet eccentricity.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physical remains of that industry are impressive. Salting works lined the coasts of southern Spain, Portugal and North Africa, as well as parts of the Black Sea. Each consisted of rows of rectangular vats, cut into rock or built of waterproof concrete, in which small fish such as anchovies and sardines, together with the entrails of larger species such as tuna, were layered with salt and left exposed to the sun. After two or three months the liquid that had collected was drawn off and bottled as sauce; the thick residue that remained, known as allec, was sold separately as a cheap paste. Some sites contained dozens of vats with a combined capacity of several hundred cubic metres. Production was concentrated in the months when migrating shoals passed close to shore, which meant that a factory might lie idle for much of the year and then work at full stretch for a few weeks.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How widely was the product consumed? Lucilla Abbondanza, of the Tyrrhenian Archaeological Institute, has catalogued the distinctive jars in which fish sauce was transported, and has found them not only in cities and wealthy villas but also in military forts on the empire's northern frontier and in modest farming settlements far from the sea. She concludes that fish sauce functioned much as salt does in modern kitchens, as a routine seasoning used at every social level. She also points to storeroom inventories scratched on walls in Pompeii, where jars of sauce appear among the provisions of quite ordinary households. Further support evidence comes from a price list issued in the early fourth century, which distinguishes several grades of sauce, the cheapest of them priced within reach of an ordinary labourer.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Joana Aboim, a zooarchaeologist, has approached the question from the contents of the vessels themselves. By identifying fish bones preserved in residues at the bottom of vats and jars, and in some cases by extracting ancient DNA from them, she has shown that the species used varied considerably from one region to another, and that sauces from particular coasts were shipped hundreds of kilometres while others were consumed close to where they were made. Her work has also revealed that individual vats were sometimes reused for different species within a single season. Aboim argues that it is misleading to speak of garum as though it were a single substance. It was, she suggests, a family of related products differing in origin, ingredients and quality, rather as wine does today.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A note of caution has been sounded by the food historian Esther Rubinfeld. The painted labels on surviving jars use a number of different names, among them garum, liquamen and muria, and Rubinfeld argues that modern scholars have been too quick to treat these as interchangeable. If, as she suspects, garum was an expensive speciality and liquamen an everyday product, then evidence for the wide distribution of one cannot simply be used to make claims about the other. Rubinfeld is right to insist on precision, but her argument assumes a consistency that the sources do not show. The labels are often contradictory, and ancient writers themselves appear to have used the terms loosely, sometimes within a single recipe.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: As for the sauce's reputation, much of the modern revulsion rests on a misunderstanding. The process was not one of rotting: the high concentration of salt prevented the growth of the bacteria responsible for putrefaction, and the fish were broken down instead by enzymes in their own tissues. Experimental archaeologists who have recreated the sauce using ancient methods report a liquid that is intensely salty and savoury rather than repellent, and comparable fermented fish sauces remain popular across Southeast Asia today. None of this means that the factories were pleasant neighbours. The smell during production must have been overwhelming, and several excavated works stand some distance from the settlements they served.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: From the fifth century onwards, production in the western Mediterranean declined, and by the early Middle Ages the sauce had largely disappeared from western European cooking. It is tempting to explain this as a change in taste, but the evidence points elsewhere. Large-scale salting depended on secure sea routes, a reliable supply of salt and an extensive network of buyers, and as these broke down with the fragmentation of the western empire, the industry lost the conditions that had sustained it. Tellingly, fish sauces survived for several more centuries in the eastern Mediterranean, where long-distance trade held up far better. The fate of garum is a reminder that what people eat depends as much on infrastructure as on preference.

area: the history of food, crops and spices
topic: how chocolate drinking passed from Mesoamerica to early modern Europe, 1520-1750: acquired colonial taste versus Europeanisation, sugar and recipes, medical and fasting debates, and cheaper cacao supplies
title: A Drink Between Two Worlds
subtitle: Did Europeans tame a bitter foreign beverage, or did a foreign beverage quietly reshape European taste?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before the arrival of Europeans, the peoples of Mesoamerica had made cacao the basis of an elaborate drinking culture. The beans were fermented, roasted and ground, then mixed with water and often with maize, chilli or aromatic flowers, and the drink was poured from a height to raise a prized layer of foam. It was served at feasts, offered in religious ceremonies and exchanged between rulers, while the beans themselves circulated as a form of currency in local markets. Spanish soldiers and missionaries encountered the drink in the 1520s, and within a century it had become fashionable at the Spanish court, from where it spread to Italy, France and, by the 1650s, England. The usual account of this journey is one of adaptation: Europeans, it is said, found the native beverage bitter and unpleasant, and made it acceptable only by sweetening it with sugar, spicing it with cinnamon and serving it hot. That account, which still dominates popular histories, is in my view largely mistaken.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential challenge to it comes from Montserrat Sabater, a historian of colonial Spanish America. Sabater points out that chocolate did not travel directly from Mesoamerican palaces to European tables. For several decades it was consumed by Spanish settlers in New Spain, who lived, traded and frequently intermarried with indigenous communities, and whose drinks were typically prepared by indigenous and mixed-ancestry women working in their households. Through this daily contact, she argues, colonists gradually acquired a taste for the beverage much as it was already made. When chocolate eventually reached Spain, the recipes and equipment that accompanied it preserved most of the Mesoamerican elements, including the frothing, the vanilla and, in some cases, the chilli. In Sabater's memorable phrase, Europeans did not transform chocolate so much as chocolate transformed Europeans.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even the changes usually cited as evidence of European adaptation look less dramatic on closer inspection. Mesoamerican drinkers sometimes sweetened cacao with honey, so the use of cane sugar is better understood as a substitution than as a revolution in taste. Similarly, while cold or room-temperature drinks seem to have been preferred in central Mexico, warm preparations were known in parts of the Maya region. The European version, in other words, selected from a range of existing practices rather than inventing new ones.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Pavel Vlasak accepts much of this but adds an important qualification. As chocolate moved beyond Spain during the seventeenth century, he observes, recipes shed their indigenous features one after another. Chilli disappeared from French and Italian preparations, flowers were replaced by cinnamon and other familiar Old World spices, and in England chocolate was increasingly mixed with milk, eggs and wine. Europeanisation, Vlasak concludes, did take place, but later, and further from the colonial setting, than the traditional story supposes. This seems to me a sensible refinement rather than a contradiction. The two positions sit together comfortably once Spain, with its direct and continuing links to New Spain, is distinguished from those parts of Europe that encountered chocolate only at second hand.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Abebe Taddesse looks instead at the institutions that shaped consumption. European physicians debated at length whether chocolate was heating or cooling according to the humoral theory of the body, and many recommended it as a remedy for weakness or poor digestion. At the same time, theologians argued over whether drinking chocolate broke the religious fast. The view that eventually prevailed, that a liquid did not count as food, allowed clergy to consume it freely, and monasteries became some of its most dedicated buyers. For Taddesse, medical and religious approval rather than taste drove the drink's diffusion. Here, I think, the argument goes too far. The surviving treatises largely respond to a habit that was already widespread among the Spanish elite; they explain and justify chocolate's popularity rather than create it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Liisa Kuusisto draws attention to a dimension that both camps have tended to neglect: supply. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the centre of cacao cultivation moved from Mesoamerica to plantations in Venezuela and on the coast of what is now Ecuador, many of them worked by enslaved Africans. The beans from these regions were cheaper and, in the case of the Ecuadorian crop, harsher in flavour. Kuusisto argues that the falling price brought chocolate within reach of artisans and shopkeepers in Spanish towns by the eighteenth century, and suggests that the more bitter beans may themselves have encouraged heavier use of sugar. Her emphasis on the material conditions of production is overdue; debates about taste have too often proceeded as though cacao simply appeared in European ports.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the history of chocolate demonstrates, above all, is that cultural influence in the colonial era did not flow in one direction only. The tastes of the colonised shaped the habits of the colonisers, at least in the first generations of contact, and the image of Europeans improving a primitive foreign food reveals more about the assumptions of later centuries than about the realities of the sixteenth. The solid, sweet bar of the nineteenth century, produced in factories with new machinery, belongs to a quite different story.

area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: persuasive interface design: endless feeds, automatic playback, the loss of stopping cues and whether such features should be regulated
title: Designed Not to Stop
subtitle: Endless feeds and automatic playback are blamed for swallowing users' time, but the case for regulating them is less simple than it appears

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until recently, most media had built-in endings. A newspaper had a last page, a television programme closed with its credits, and even early websites were divided into pages that required a deliberate click to continue. Each of these boundaries served, almost incidentally, as a moment at which the reader or viewer could decide whether to carry on. Over the past fifteen years many digital services have quietly removed them. Feeds now load fresh material continuously as the user moves downwards, and video platforms begin the next episode within seconds of the previous one finishing. To critics, these changes are not neutral improvements in convenience but deliberate attempts to capture time that people would otherwise have spent elsewhere. That charge deserves to be taken seriously, although the evidence for it is more uneven than its loudest advocates tend to admit.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential version of the critique comes from Ingrid Hallgren, who spent several years designing interfaces for a social media company before becoming one of the industry's sharpest critics. Hallgren argues that the disappearance of what she calls 'stopping cues' was driven by commercial metrics: since advertising revenue rises with the time users spend on a service, every feature that extends sessions by even a few seconds is rewarded internally. In her account, designers rarely set out to manipulate anyone; they simply follow dashboards that reward engagement, and the cumulative result is a product that resists being put down. This explanation has the virtue of not depending on villainy. It locates the problem in incentives rather than in individual intentions, which makes it considerably more plausible than the conspiracy-minded accounts of the technology industry that circulate so widely.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Empirical support has come from a group at the Brno Institute of Interaction Design led by Tomas Ruzicka. In a series of experiments, participants browsed a purpose-built news application in which the researchers could switch individual features on and off. When the feed was divided into pages of twenty items, participants spent on average about a quarter less time in the application than when the same items were presented as a continuous stream, and they were also noticeably less accurate when later asked how long they had been reading. Ruzicka regards the second finding as the more important: endless feeds, he suggests, do not merely lengthen sessions but disrupt people's ability to monitor their own behaviour. The experiments were carefully controlled, yet they involved students using an unfamiliar application for a single session, and it remains unclear whether the effect would persist once people had grown accustomed to a service.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That uncertainty lies at the heart of the objection raised by the psychologist Eleni Tsakalidis. She does not dispute that design influences behaviour, but she argues that the language of 'addiction', now routinely applied to these features, is misleading. Clinical addiction involves continued use despite serious harm and a loss of control that persists over time; most heavy users of social media, she points out, reduce their use without difficulty when their circumstances change, for instance during examinations or on holiday. To describe ordinary habits as addiction, in Tsakalidis's view, both trivialises genuine disorders and encourages policymakers to reach for remedies designed for substances rather than for software. Her point about terminology is well made. It does not follow, however, that design is harmless simply because it falls short of producing a clinical condition; a feature can waste a great deal of people's time without making anyone ill.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Legal scholars have begun to consider regulation. Daniel Kiprono of the Centre for Technology Law in Nairobi proposes that platforms should owe their users a 'duty of design care', comparable to the safety obligations that already apply to physical products such as toys and electrical appliances. Under such a duty, a company could be required to demonstrate that features likely to extend use had been assessed for their effects, particularly on younger users. Kiprono deliberately avoids calling for bans on specific features, arguing that lists of prohibited techniques would be out of date almost as soon as they were written, since designers would simply invent alternatives with the same effect. Instead, he favours a principle-based approach, enforced by a regulator with enough technical expertise to judge new designs as they appear.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that intervention is needed. The economist Paul Lamberty contends that automatic playback and continuous feeds persist because many users genuinely like them. Surveys conducted by his team found that a clear majority of respondents would keep such features switched on if offered a simple setting to disable them, and Lamberty argues that regulators should be wary of overriding preferences that people state openly. This argument is weaker than it first appears. A preference expressed in a survey, at a calm moment, says little about how people feel at one o'clock in the morning when they realise they have watched four episodes rather than the one they intended. Moreover, the default setting itself shapes what people choose, as decades of research on pension enrolment and organ donation have shown.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most productive response perhaps lies between these positions. Restoring some form of natural pause, such as a prompt after a given period or a feed that ends unless the user asks for more, would preserve the convenience that Lamberty's respondents value while giving people the moment of decision that older media supplied by default. Measures of this kind will not satisfy those who regard the attention economy as fundamentally exploitative, and they may prove less effective once their novelty wears off. Nonetheless, they address the specific problem that the best available evidence identifies: not that people are powerless, but that they are too rarely invited to choose.

area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: smartphone notifications: the cognitive cost of interruptions, why apps send so many, batching alerts and workplace norms of availability
title: The Price of a Ping
subtitle: Smartphone notifications are widely blamed for fragmenting attention, but researchers disagree about what, if anything, should be done about them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A typical smartphone owner now receives somewhere between fifty and a hundred notifications a day: messages from friends, reminders from calendars, breaking news alerts and a steady flow of invitations from apps to return and see what has changed. Each one is, in effect, a small request for attention, and collectively they have become one of the main instruments through which digital services compete for their users' time. For the companies that send them, notifications are a means of keeping people engaged; for their critics, they are a source of constant distraction that has made sustained concentration increasingly rare. Both descriptions contain some truth, but the debate has too often been conducted as a contest between those two positions alone. The more interesting questions concern not whether notifications are good or bad, but when they arrive and who controls their timing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The cognitive costs of interruption were studied long before the smartphone existed. Claire Fontaneau, who leads a research group at the Lyon Centre for Human-Computer Studies, has examined what happens when people are interrupted during tasks that involve a sequence of steps, such as completing a form or editing a document. Her experiments show that after an interruption participants take several seconds to resume where they left off, and that they are considerably more likely to skip or repeat a step. More strikingly, Fontaneau has found that performance deteriorates even when a notification is merely seen and then dismissed without being opened. The brief act of deciding not to respond appears to leave a trace that lingers in the mind. This is arguably the most important finding in the field, because it implies that ignoring an alert is not a cost-free choice, as many people assume.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why, then, do companies send so many? Hiroshi Nakagome, a behavioural economist who spent several years analysing usage data for app developers before returning to academic work, explains that notifications are judged internally by how many inactive users they bring back. He has also observed that alerts arriving at irregular, unpredictable intervals prompt more people to open an app than those delivered at fixed times, a pattern familiar from research on gambling. Yet Nakagome stresses that firms cannot send unlimited messages. Beyond a certain point, users respond by switching notifications off altogether or deleting the app, a threshold he calls the 'permission cliff'. In his view, this risk gives companies a commercial reason to restrain themselves. The mechanism he describes certainly exists, but it is a feeble safeguard: the extra visits produced by an aggressive campaign appear in this month's figures, whereas the users it drives away are lost gradually and are rarely traced back to their cause.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some of the most useful evidence comes from a field experiment conducted by Adaeze Okeke-Hart and colleagues at the Institute for Digital Wellbeing in Accra. Over two weeks, volunteers were assigned to one of three conditions: some received their notifications as normal, some received them in three bundles at set times each day, and some received none at all. Those in the bundled condition reported feeling more attentive and less stressed than those in the normal condition, and they described a stronger sense of being in charge of their day. The surprise came from the third group. Far from feeling calmer, participants without any notifications reported higher levels of anxiety about missing important information, and many compensated by checking their phones manually more often than before. This result is a serious challenge to the popular advice that the simplest cure for distraction is to silence one's phone completely.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The sociologist Lars Sorensby argues that research of this kind, however carefully designed, places too much emphasis on the individual and the device. Notifications, he contends, are a symptom of wider expectations about availability. In many workplaces, an employee who responds to a message within minutes is regarded as committed, while one who takes several hours is seen as unreliable. Under such conditions, a worker who disables alerts is not so much freeing herself from distraction as accepting a professional penalty. Sorensby's point about social norms is a valuable corrective, yet it should not be taken to mean that design is irrelevant. The settings with which a phone arrives determine what most people experience, since only a minority ever change them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Manufacturers have begun to respond. Most smartphones now offer focus modes that silence alerts during chosen hours, and some can gather non-urgent notifications into a summary delivered at intervals. Usage figures suggest, however, that these tools are taken up by a fairly small proportion of owners. Fontaneau believes the answer is to make bundling the default rather than an option hidden in a settings menu, but she acknowledges that app developers would object strongly, since each would lose the ability to reach users at the moment of its choosing. The companies that build operating systems occupy an awkward position in this argument: they benefit when the apps on their platforms are heavily used, yet they increasingly advertise their devices as tools for protecting users' wellbeing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this suggests that notifications are inherently harmful. A reminder about a medical appointment or a message from a relative in difficulty is precisely the kind of interruption most people would wish to receive. The difficulty lies in a system in which thousands of separate senders each decide independently when to claim a moment of a person's attention. The real question, then, is not whether people should be interrupted at all, but who should have the power to decide when it happens.
