area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: headline A/B testing in online news: optimising for clicks, headline-only readers in social feeds, teasing headlines and trust, platform demotion and subscription incentives
title: Twenty Ways to Say the Same Thing
subtitle: News websites now test rival headlines on live audiences before choosing a winner. What this practice rewards, and what it costs, is fiercely disputed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the history of journalism, the headline above a story was the product of an editor's judgement, made quickly and under pressure, and rarely revisited. Online publishing has turned that judgement into an experiment. Many news websites now write several versions of a headline for the same article and display them, at random, to different readers during the first minutes after publication. Whichever version attracts the most clicks is then shown to everyone. The technique, borrowed from online retailing, is known as A/B testing, and its defenders present it as a triumph of evidence over guesswork. There is nothing inherently objectionable about testing; what deserves scrutiny is the quantity being optimised. A headline chosen because it attracts clicks is not necessarily the one that best informs, and the gap between those two goals lies at the centre of a growing controversy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The stakes are higher than they might appear, because for a large share of the public the headline is no longer a doorway to the news but the news itself. Ingrid Kvaran, a communication researcher at the University of Reykjavik, analysed several million links to news articles that had been posted on social networks and found that the majority were never opened by the people who shared them. Further work by her team showed that most users scrolling through a feed encounter dozens of headlines for every article they actually read. If that is so, a headline which withholds the essential point of a story, or exaggerates it, does not merely fail to attract a reader; it leaves thousands of people with a distorted impression they will never correct. The accuracy of headlines, in other words, has become a question of public understanding rather than simply one of marketing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Supporters of testing assume that it reliably identifies what readers want. Rohan Koirala, who leads a computational journalism group in Kathmandu, was given access to records of more than forty thousand headline tests conducted by a commercial testing service. Certain features did tend to win: headlines phrased as questions, those containing numbers and those using emotionally charged words. Yet the advantages were usually modest, with the winning version typically attracting only a few per cent more clicks than its rivals. More troublingly, Koirala calculated that in a substantial proportion of tests the difference between the leading headlines was too small to be distinguished from random variation, which means that the declared winner had often been chosen by chance. His findings suggest that the confidence many newsrooms place in testing considerably exceeds what the data can support.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Others are concerned less with whether testing works than with what it does to trust. In a series of experiments, the media scholar Thandiwe Mazibuko showed volunteers teasing headlines that promised a surprising revelation and then led to fairly ordinary articles. Readers who felt they had been misled in this way rated the publication as markedly less credible and said they were less likely to visit it again. Mazibuko describes each such headline as a small broken promise: individually trivial, but cumulatively corrosive. She argues that the incentive to make such promises depends heavily on how an outlet earns its money. A website paid according to the number of pages viewed profits from every click, whereas an outlet whose income comes mainly from paying subscribers has strong reasons to avoid disappointing the readers it hopes to retain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that the problem is new or serious. Paolo Laurentis, a former newspaper editor who now teaches journalism, argues that complaints about manipulative headlines are often tinged with snobbery. Printed newspapers, including the most respected, have always used puns, cliffhangers and dramatic phrasing to persuade people to buy them, and many headlines dismissed as manipulative describe their articles perfectly well. For Laurentis, the meaningful line falls between headlines that misrepresent a story and those that merely make it sound intriguing. That distinction is an important one, and critics who condemn every playful headline would do well to observe it. The difficulty is that misrepresentation is a matter of degree, and a test that rewards slightly bolder wording at each stage can carry a newsroom across the line without anyone deciding to cross it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Technology companies have attempted their own remedies. Several social networks have trained automated systems, using examples labelled by human reviewers, to identify headlines that deliberately conceal information, and have reduced the visibility of posts that use them. Publishers adapted within weeks, replacing obvious formulas with less detectable ones that achieved a similar effect. Whatever the intentions behind it, the episode illustrates the limits of purely technical solutions: a classifier can recognise a pattern, but it cannot easily recognise an intention, and those whose income is at stake will always have reason to search for the pattern it has not yet learned.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most promising development may therefore lie not in prohibiting testing but in changing what it measures. A small number of outlets now judge competing headlines by how much of the article readers go on to read, or by whether they return in later weeks, rather than by clicks alone. Such measures reward a headline for accurately signalling what follows, since a misleading one produces readers who abandon the article quickly. Whether these alternatives will spread beyond publishers that depend on subscriptions is uncertain. Nevertheless, they suggest that the tool so often blamed for degrading headlines could, with different goals, be used to improve them.

area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: the 'rabbit hole' debate: whether video recommendation systems push viewers towards extreme content, sock-puppet audits versus real-user browsing data, and researcher data access
title: Following the Recommendations
subtitle: Do video platforms lead viewers step by step towards extreme material, or do viewers find it by themselves?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The story has been told many times. A young person opens a video-sharing site to watch a clip about fitness or video games, accepts a few of the suggestions that appear beside it, and some weeks later is consuming a diet of conspiracy theories and political extremism. In this account, the culprit is the recommendation system, the software that selects which videos to offer next, which is said to push users towards ever more radical material because such material holds their attention. It is a compelling story, and it is not hard to see why journalists and politicians have adopted it. The research, however, tells a more mixed tale, partly because the companies concerned have rarely allowed independent scientists to see how their systems behave.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely cited version of the argument comes from Mira Ondrejka, who worked as an engineer on recommendation software before leaving the industry. Her account, delivered in interviews and a widely read book, gave the theory an insider's authority. She contends that a system rewarded for maximising viewing time will learn, without anyone instructing it to do so, that sensational and emotionally provocative videos keep people watching longer than measured ones. Each recommendation may be only slightly more extreme than the last, but over many sessions the drift accumulates. The mechanism she describes is plausible, but it is worth remembering that her case grew out of her own observations inside one company rather than out of systematic study.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To test such claims, researchers led by Vikram Sundaresan created hundreds of automated accounts, sometimes called 'sock puppets', which started from different videos and then repeatedly followed the platform's suggestions. The design allowed the team to compare hundreds of pathways at once, something no study of human volunteers could achieve. Drift towards more extreme content did occur, but only for accounts that began with certain kinds of political material, and the effect became noticeably weaker after the platform revised its system. For most starting points, the recommendations steered the accounts towards large, mainstream channels instead. Audits of this kind have a clear limitation: automated accounts click whatever they are offered, whereas real viewers ignore most suggestions, so the method cannot by itself show what happens to people.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different approach was taken by the economist Farid Habibi, who obtained the complete browsing histories of several thousand volunteers who had agreed to install monitoring software. Unlike the automated accounts, these were real people making real choices, often across several devices. His results suggest that recommendations are a minor route to extreme videos. Most such viewing began with a link shared on another website, a direct search or a subscription the viewer had already chosen, and it was concentrated among a small minority of viewers with strong prior preferences. Habibi summarises his conclusion as supply meeting existing demand. His evidence is persuasive, yet it does not absolve the platforms entirely: a company that hosts such material, and earns advertising revenue from it, cannot claim to be merely a neutral observer of what its users want.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The media historian Joelle Belcourt places the debate in a longer perspective. Comic books in the 1950s and television violence in the 1970s were each blamed for corrupting the young, and in each case, she argues, the alarm outran the evidence. The rabbit-hole narrative appeals, in her view, because it offers a simple villain and relieves viewers of responsibility for their own choices. This historical perspective is a useful warning against exaggeration, but Belcourt goes too far in treating the concern as little more than a panic. Even if only a small number of people are drawn deeper into extreme content, a handful of radicalised individuals can do a great deal of harm.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Underlying all of this is a problem of access. Lukas Rosmanith, who directs a platform research centre in Graz, points out that recommendation systems are adjusted constantly, sometimes several times a week, so every study is at best a snapshot of a system that no longer exists. Without direct access to the platforms' own data, researchers are left to infer the behaviour of the software from the outside. Some have resorted to collecting data from volunteers' browsers, but such methods are costly, slow and vulnerable to legal challenge from the companies themselves. Rosmanith argues that companies above a certain size should be legally obliged to provide vetted researchers with such access, under safeguards to protect users' privacy. This proposal deserves support, since without it the debate is unlikely ever to be settled.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the evidence so far suggests is that the question itself needs to change. The idea that recommendation systems turn ordinary viewers into extremists finds little support. Equally, the claim that platforms play no part at all is difficult to sustain. The more pressing issue is how these systems serve the minority who arrive already looking for such content, and whether they make that content easier to find and harder to leave. This is a less dramatic question than the one that has dominated public discussion, but it is one that research can realistically answer.

title: The Customers Who Would Have Come Anyway
subtitle: Online advertising was supposed to end the guesswork of marketing. Controlled experiments suggest that much of its apparent success may be an illusion

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A remark often attributed to the merchants of the nineteenth century holds that half the money spent on advertising is wasted, but nobody knows which half. Digital advertising promised to solve that riddle. Unlike a poster or a newspaper page, an online advertisement can be tracked: the platform records who saw it, who clicked on it and, frequently, who went on to buy something. Partly on the strength of that promise, online formats now absorb the majority of advertising expenditure in many economies. Yet the abundance of data has bred a misplaced confidence. The figures supplied to advertisers are remarkably precise, but their precision disguises a basic confusion between what accompanies a purchase and what causes it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The confusion lies in a practice known as attribution. Under the most common method, when a customer makes a purchase, the credit is assigned to the last advertisement on which that customer clicked. The difficulty is that advertisements are not shown at random. They are deliberately aimed at people whom the software judges likely to buy, and those people would often have bought regardless. Someone who types the name of a particular shop into a search engine, for example, has usually decided to visit it already. Oleksandr Goncharuk, a marketing scientist who has studied the problem for over a decade, compares standard attribution to handing out leaflets to people already queuing at a shop door and then counting everyone who enters as a customer won by the leaflet.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the clearest demonstrations of the problem came from an experiment designed by the economist Nadia Marchetti-Lowe in partnership with a large online retailer. The company stopped buying advertisements linked to searches for its own brand name in a selection of regions for several weeks, while continuing them elsewhere for comparison. If the advertisements had been doing the work credited to them, traffic in the affected regions should have fallen sharply. It barely changed. Almost all of the visitors who would previously have clicked the paid link simply clicked the unpaid search result that appeared immediately beneath it. Advertisements bought for general search terms, such as the name of a product category, performed better, but their effect was confined almost entirely to new or infrequent customers; for people who already shopped regularly with the retailer, they made no measurable difference.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most reliable method of measurement is the randomised holdout experiment, in which a campaign's target audience is divided by chance into two groups, only one of which is shown the advertisements; the other sees unrelated material in the same space. Comparing purchases between the groups reveals the effect of the campaign itself. The statistician Dilani Senanayake has analysed dozens of such experiments and reports a sobering pattern. The effects of advertising are generally real, but they are small compared with the ordinary week-to-week fluctuation in a company's sales. Detecting them with confidence can require samples running into millions of people, so that for many campaigns no feasible experiment could distinguish a profitable one from a loss-making one. In Senanayake's view, even very large firms are seldom able to calculate the return on their advertising with any precision.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Advertising platforms and agencies have an answer to such findings. Experiments, they argue, last only a few weeks, whereas the main value of advertising lies in building familiarity and affection for a brand over years, effects that short tests are bound to miss. Paola Annunziata, a former agency strategist, maintains that companies which cut their advertising during recessions have historically lost market share that took a long time to recover. There is probably some truth in this, but the argument has a convenient structure. If the most important effects of advertising are by definition too slow and too diffuse to be measured, then no evidence could ever count against the claim, and belief takes the place of evidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why, then, do so many companies continue to rely on figures that are known to be flawed? The explanation lies less in a shortage of statistical skill than in the incentives within organisations. Marketing departments are typically judged by the sales attributed to their campaigns, and attribution flatters them. Agencies are often paid a percentage of the sums their clients spend, so they gain when budgets grow. The platforms, meanwhile, are both the sellers of advertising and the main suppliers of the data used to evaluate it. None of these parties has much to gain from discovering that a campaign achieved little. The obstacle to better measurement, in short, is institutional rather than technical.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that online advertising is worthless. The experimental evidence suggests that it works best in exactly the situation where it is needed most: when it reaches people who have not yet heard of a product, rather than those who were already on their way to buy it. The lesson of the past two decades is rather one of humility. The ability to count clicks created the impression that marketing had become a science, when in many cases it had simply found more sophisticated ways of measuring the wrong thing.

title: What Is a Feed Worth?
subtitle: Economists have begun paying people to abandon social media for a few weeks. The results complicate both the case for and against the platforms

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Social media services cost their users nothing, and for that reason their contribution to human welfare is largely invisible in conventional economic statistics. National accounts record what people pay for, not what they enjoy for free. One way for economists to estimate the value of such services is to ask how much people would need to be paid to give them up, and then to observe what actually happens when they do. Over the past decade, several research teams have run experiments of exactly this kind. They are among the most revealing studies yet conducted on the subject, although what they reveal has proved more contentious than their authors might have hoped.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best known was organised by the economist Tomasz Lisowski. Using an auction, his team first established the smallest payment at which each volunteer would agree to deactivate their account on a major social network for four weeks; the typical participant demanded a sum roughly equal to a household's weekly food bill. Half of those willing to accept were then chosen at random and paid to stay away. The results were instructive. Those who left spent most of the time they gained offline, with friends and family or watching television, rather than on other websites. They reported small improvements in happiness and slightly lower anxiety. They also knew less about current news, and their views on divisive political questions became somewhat less polarised. Most strikingly, when the four weeks ended, they returned to the platform more slowly and used it less than before, and the sum they said they would need to quit again fell considerably. This suggests that people tend to overestimate how much the service is worth to them, perhaps because habit is easily mistaken for preference.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The psychologist Irina Petrakova urges caution in interpreting the improvements in wellbeing. The changes, she notes, were modest, considerably smaller than those typically produced by established psychological treatments, and they relied entirely on what participants said about themselves. Since volunteers knew that they were being paid and observed, some may have reported the improvements they assumed the researchers expected to see. Petrakova is right that the effects are small and that self-reports have limitations. It does not follow, however, that they are unimportant. A small benefit to each individual, multiplied across the billions of people who use these platforms, could amount to a very large difference in total.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A replication conducted in Kigali by a team under Jean-Paul Rukundo produced a very different picture. There, many participants used social networks and messaging services to run small businesses, advertise goods and stay in touch with relatives working abroad. For these people, four weeks away from the platforms meant lost customers and severed family contact, and their reported wellbeing declined rather than improved. The study suggests that where social media functions as part of a society's commercial infrastructure, rather than mainly as entertainment, the consequences of abandoning it are reversed. This finding is a necessary corrective to a body of research drawn overwhelmingly from wealthy countries, where few people depend on such platforms for their income.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further twist emerged from work by Christos Samaras and his colleagues, who surveyed university students in two ways. First, they asked how much each student would need to be paid to quit a popular platform while everyone else continued to use it; the answers were substantial. Then they asked how much the students would pay for themselves and all of their fellow students to stop using it together. A large proportion said they would gladly pay for such a collective exit. Samaras interprets this as evidence of a 'product trap': many people use the platform not because they enjoy it but because leaving alone would exclude them from the conversations and invitations of their peers. If this interpretation is correct, the figures that individuals demand for giving up a platform measure partly the cost of exclusion rather than the value of the service itself.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The philosopher of economics Hannah Wexley goes further, arguing that payments demanded to quit say nothing reliable about value at all. A heavy smoker, she observes, might demand a large sum to give up cigarettes for a month, yet nobody would conclude that cigarettes therefore improve his life. Wexley's analogy is overstated, since the evidence of harm from social media bears no comparison with the evidence against tobacco. Her underlying point, though, deserves attention, and it is consistent with Lisowski's finding that valuations dropped once the habit had been interrupted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, the experiments suggest that social media provides genuine value, but less than its users believe and distributed very unevenly between different groups and places. They also imply that individual abstinence is a weak remedy for whatever harms the platforms cause. If many people remain only because others do, the more effective responses are likely to be collective ones, such as shared agreements within schools or workplaces, rather than advice addressed to each user alone.

title: Selling the Reader
subtitle: Long before social media, nineteenth-century newspapers discovered that an audience's attention could be sold. Historians disagree about what that discovery changed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 1830s, a daily newspaper in a large American city typically cost six cents, a substantial sum for a labourer, and was sold mainly by annual subscription to merchants and professional men. Within a few years, a new kind of paper had appeared, sold on street corners for a single cent. It could be offered so cheaply because its publishers had discovered that the real source of income was not the reader but the advertiser, who would pay handsomely to reach the tens of thousands of people that a cheap paper could attract. Commentators on today's digital media frequently describe this episode as the birth of the attention economy, the moment at which the audience itself became the product. The comparison is illuminating, but, as with most historical parallels, it becomes misleading if pressed too hard.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The economic historian Piotr Kaczmarski has reconstructed the finances of several of these papers from surviving account books. Such records are rare, since few publishers expected their ledgers to interest anyone, and his reconstruction has therefore attracted considerable attention. He shows that most were sold at a price below the cost of printing them, with the shortfall recovered, and far exceeded, through advertising revenue. Circulation thus became the currency in which papers dealt with advertisers, and publishers began to commission independent counts of the copies they sold and to print the audited figures prominently on their front pages. Competition for readers drove a turn towards crime reports, scandals and human-interest stories. In Kaczmarski's view, the incentives facing a penny publisher were, in all essential respects, the same as those facing the owner of a modern social media platform.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sofia Nikolaidou, a historian of journalism, believes this account omits much of what the penny papers achieved. They brought regular news to working people who had previously had little access to it, and they pioneered the reporting of police courts and city government. Above all, the older six-cent papers had frequently been financed by political parties and served as their mouthpieces; by paying their own way through advertising, the penny papers gained a degree of independence from partisan control that, Nikolaidou argues, made modern journalism possible. This is a vital qualification. The model of selling attention to advertisers clearly encouraged sensationalism, but it also had democratic consequences that any honest assessment must acknowledge. It is worth adding that the party papers had hardly been models of accuracy themselves.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third interpretation stresses material conditions. Arun Ravindran-Holt points out that the penny press emerged at the same moment as steam-driven presses capable of printing thousands of sheets an hour, cheaper paper and the rapid growth of cities full of potential readers. In his account, the new business model was a consequence of these technological and demographic changes rather than an independent invention. The argument is plausible as far as it goes, but technology alone cannot explain the timing. London possessed similar presses and an even larger urban population, yet a heavy tax on newspapers kept prices there high for another two decades. Government policy, in other words, shaped the outcome at least as much as machinery did.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The penny papers' relationship with the truth was not always close. One of them famously published a series of invented reports describing winged creatures living on the moon, and circulation soared. The paper never fully retracted the story, and rival publications were quick to imitate its methods. Margaret Dorrance, who studies popular culture in the period, cautions against treating such episodes as an early version of today's misinformation. Many readers, she suggests, approached these stories as entertainment, enjoying the debate over their authenticity rather than being deceived by them. It is an intriguing claim, but it rests on uncertain foundations. Most of what is known about how readers responded comes from the newspapers themselves, whose editors had every reason to exaggerate both the excitement they caused and the sophistication of their audience.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If there is a decisive difference between the penny press and its digital successors, the media economist Lucía Varela locates it in measurement. A nineteenth-century advertiser bought access to an undifferentiated crowd, knowing only roughly how many copies had been sold. He could not tell whether any particular reader had noticed his announcement at all, let alone acted upon it. A modern platform, by contrast, sells the attention of particular individuals, moment by moment, according to detailed records of their behaviour, and each user sees a feed that no one else sees. Varela's point seems to me the most important of all, because it means that the shared public conversation that the penny papers helped to create is now fragmented into millions of private ones.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, does the history teach? Not that the excesses of an advertising-funded medium are inevitable. The penny papers themselves changed considerably over the following decades. As the century progressed, newspapers that depended on the broadest possible readership increasingly adopted standards of factual accuracy and impartiality, partly because such standards helped them avoid alienating any section of their market. Similar norms could, in principle, emerge in digital media. But they arose in the nineteenth century through a combination of competition, professional organisation and public pressure, and there is no reason to assume they will appear again without similar effort.

area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: parasocial relationships with online video creators and live streamers: loneliness and viewer communities, monetised intimacy and donations, the moral-panic critique, and pressures on creators
title: One-Sided Friendships
subtitle: Millions of viewers feel they know the online creators they watch every day. Is this a new form of loneliness, or an old human habit in a new setting?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1950s, two sociologists studying early television audiences noticed something curious. Viewers spoke about presenters and performers as if they knew them personally, responding to them with the warmth normally reserved for acquaintances, although the performers had no idea who their viewers were. The researchers called this 'parasocial interaction': the illusion of a face-to-face relationship with someone who is in fact a distant figure. Seven decades later, the concept has found a vast new field of application. Creators on video-sharing and live-streaming platforms speak directly into the camera, reply to comments, and broadcast for hours at a time from their bedrooms, and many of their viewers say they feel they know these people as well as they know their friends. Online, the term 'parasocial' has meanwhile become a mild insult, a way of mocking fans for caring too much. That usage is unfair, and it obscures questions that deserve serious attention.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The psychologist Amara Okonjo-Barre has argued that parasocial bonds perform genuine psychological functions. They provide comfort and a sense of familiarity, and they can offer models of behaviour, as when viewers adopt a creator's approach to exercise or study. In a large survey, she found that people with small offline social networks who felt strongly attached to a creator reported lower levels of loneliness than similar people without such attachments. The benefit appeared, however, only among those who also took part in the communities that gather around a creator, chatting with other viewers during broadcasts or in online forums. This suggests that much of the value lies in the community surrounding the creator rather than in the creator alone, which is a less romantic conclusion than many fans would like, but probably a more accurate one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is also an economic dimension. As the media economist Kenji Fujimaki points out, a growing share of creators' income comes not from advertising but directly from viewers, through monthly subscriptions, payments for exclusive content and small donations sent during live broadcasts. These payments, he finds, rise with the intensity of the bond that viewers feel. The platforms' systems for promoting content tend to favour creators who post frequently and reveal details of their personal lives, since such material deepens attachment and keeps audiences returning. Fujimaki describes the result as 'monetised intimacy', and he notes that many creators report exhaustion from the pressure to remain constantly available and disclosing.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Live streaming intensifies these dynamics. When a viewer sends a donation, the creator typically thanks them by name within seconds, sometimes reading out an accompanying message, and the viewer's name may appear on screen for everyone to see. This brief moment of recognition creates the impression of a mutual relationship. According to Fujimaki's data, donations are highly concentrated: on a typical channel, a small fraction of viewers supplies the great majority of the money, and some of them spend more than they can comfortably afford. It is precisely here that the comparison with early television breaks down. A television presenter could not respond to an individual viewer; a streamer can, and that capacity transforms a one-way illusion into something that feels, and to a degree is, reciprocal.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares the concern. The sociologist Rhys Trebilcock argues that worries about parasocial relationships amount to a moral panic. People have always formed attachments to figures they would never meet, from the heroes of novels to radio hosts and religious saints, and Trebilcock finds no convincing evidence that such bonds displace real friendships. Time-use surveys, he notes, show that heavy viewers of online creators spend no less time with friends and family than other people do. Trebilcock is right to resist the temptation to panic, and his historical perspective is a useful one. But displacement is not the only possible harm. Even if most viewers are unaffected, a system that profits most from the minority who are most attached, and who may also be the most isolated, deserves careful scrutiny.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The creators themselves describe a more complicated picture. Elif Sabanci, who interviewed more than sixty full-time streamers, found that many felt a strong sense of obligation to their audiences and struggled to set limits on how much of their lives they shared. Several reported that announcing a break for illness or rest had provoked angry messages from fans who felt they were owed regular broadcasts, and a few described sustained harassment. Such accounts reveal that these relationships are lopsided in knowledge, since viewers know far more about creators than creators know about them, but they are not lopsided in obligation: both sides come to feel that something is owed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Policymakers have begun to consider modest interventions, such as requiring platforms to show viewers how much they have spent on a channel and restricting on-screen prompts to donate when the viewer is a child. Measures of this kind seem sensible. The central point, however, is that parasocial attachment is neither new nor inherently unhealthy. What has changed is the existence of business models designed to deepen such attachments and convert them into revenue, and it is these models, rather than the feelings of viewers, that ought to be the focus of public debate.

area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: news paywalls after the collapse of advertising revenue: metered models, concentration of subscribers, information inequality, effects on editorial priorities and membership or donation alternatives
title: Behind the Wall
subtitle: As advertising has drained away from journalism, news organisations have asked readers to pay. The consequences for who gets informed are only beginning to be understood

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly two decades after newspapers moved online, most of their journalism was available without charge, financed by the advertisements that appeared beside it. That arrangement has largely collapsed. Advertising budgets migrated to search engines and social networks, which could offer advertisers larger audiences and more precise targeting, and news organisations responded by cutting staff, closing local offices and, in many cases, shutting down altogether. The survivors increasingly ask readers to pay, and paywalls of one kind or another now surround much of the most respected journalism in the world. This development is often described as a return to normal, since readers always paid for printed newspapers. That description is misleading. A printed paper was cheap because advertising subsidised it heavily, and its price was a small fraction of what a digital subscription now costs.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Paywalls take several forms. Some publications admit no one who has not paid, while others operate a metered system that allows a certain number of articles each month before asking for a subscription, and still others keep most content open while charging for premium material. The media economist Marc Lefebvre-Akin argues that the metered model has proved the most successful because it allows casual readers to sample a publication while identifying and converting its most loyal users. Even so, he notes, only a few per cent of visitors ever become subscribers. More worryingly, in his view, the economics of subscription favour a small number of national titles that can attract paying readers across an entire country, while regional and local papers, with their smaller potential markets, find it far harder to survive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Survey evidence supports his pessimism. Anni Vähäkangas, who has tracked news consumption in more than a dozen countries for over ten years, finds that the proportion of people paying for online news has remained low and remarkably stable, even as the number of paywalls has multiplied. Those who do pay are disproportionately older, more highly educated and better off than the population as a whole, and most of those who pay subscribe to only one title. Taken together, these findings suggest that the hope that subscriptions will replace advertising as the principal support of journalism in general is unrealistic. Subscriptions can sustain some outlets very well; they are unlikely to sustain most. Vähäkangas also reports that many people who decline to pay say they can find adequate news elsewhere without charge, a belief that is at least partly justified.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The sociologist Darya Toropova has drawn attention to a further consequence. As carefully verified reporting retreats behind paywalls, she argues, misinformation remains free to read, and those who cannot or will not pay are left to rely on sources of lower quality. The result, in her view, is a growing inequality of information that mirrors and reinforces inequalities of income. Toropova's concern is well founded, but it can be overstated. In many countries, public broadcasters provide extensive news coverage without charge, and a number of leading newspapers have removed their paywalls for coverage of public-health emergencies and elections, precisely on the grounds that some information is too important to restrict.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of paywalls argue that they have improved journalism itself. Henrik Nyborg, a former newspaper executive who now advises publishers, contends that when revenue depends on subscribers rather than on clicks, editors have an incentive to invest in depth, investigation and analysis, and to abandon cheap, sensational material that attracts traffic but no loyalty. Figures on subscriber retention, he adds, show publishers what their readers genuinely value, since people cancel when a publication disappoints them. There is some anecdotal support for this view. Yet it carries a risk of its own: if journalism is shaped by the preferences of subscribers, and subscribers are mostly affluent, the concerns of poorer communities may receive steadily less attention.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A number of alternatives have emerged. Grace Kerrigan-Obi, who studies non-profit journalism, has examined outlets that keep all their content free but invite readers to become paying 'members' in order to support the work. Such models succeed, she finds, chiefly where an outlet has a distinctive identity or mission with which readers want to be associated, and they tend to generate less income than paywalls. Their great advantage is that the journalism they fund remains available to everyone, including those who could never afford to contribute. Other proposals include public funding for local reporting and levies on the technology platforms that absorbed journalism's advertising revenue. Each of these approaches has merits and drawbacks, and none appears capable of filling the gap by itself; a combination will almost certainly be required.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The debate is sometimes framed as a question of whether readers ought to pay for journalism, and on that question the answer is surely yes: reporting is expensive, and it cannot be produced indefinitely for nothing. The more difficult question is how to ensure that those who do not pay are not left with only the least reliable information. Paywalls may be a reasonable way for individual publishers to survive. They are not, by themselves, a means of producing a well-informed public, and it would be a mistake to expect the market to deliver one unaided.

area: digital media and the attention economy
topic: the claim that digital media and short-form video are shrinking attention spans: the eight-second statistic, capacity versus habit, task-switching data, short-term carry-over effects and the practice of deep reading
title: Eight Seconds and Counting
subtitle: It is widely believed that digital media have shortened our attention spans. The evidence for that belief is weaker, and more interesting, than its popularity suggests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few statistics about the digital age have travelled as far as the claim that the average human attention span has fallen to eight seconds, one second less than that of a goldfish. It has been repeated in newspaper columns, conference speeches and corporate training courses around the world. Yet attempts to trace it to its source have led only to a marketing report that cited no study at all, and no research on goldfish appears to have been involved. The figure, in short, has no scientific foundation. Its remarkable persistence says more about contemporary anxieties concerning technology than about the workings of the human mind, and that persistence is itself worth explaining.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that 'attention span' is not a single quantity that can be measured like height or weight. The cognitive psychologist Katarína Molnárová distinguishes between at least three different things the phrase is used to describe: the capacity to remain alert during a long, monotonous task; the ability to focus on one source of information while ignoring others; and the willingness to persist with an activity rather than turning to something else. On the first two, she notes, there is little sign of decline. Studies that have given the same laboratory tasks to comparable groups of young adults over a period of three decades find that performance has remained essentially stable. What appears to have changed is the third: how readily people choose to move from one activity to another.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Evidence for that change comes from research on everyday computer use. Lorenzo Sebastiani and his colleagues have installed logging software, with participants' consent, on the computers of office workers and students at intervals since the early 2000s. Over fifteen years, the average time spent on a single screen before switching to another fell from about two and a half minutes to well under one. Sebastiani is careful about what this shows. In his interpretation, the data reveal a change in habits rather than in ability, since the same people who switch tasks constantly at work are perfectly capable of watching an entire series of a drama in one evening or playing a demanding game for hours. The coexistence of restless switching and marathon viewing is, in fact, the strongest evidence against the simple story of a general decline in attention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Short-form video, with clips lasting a few seconds each, has become the latest focus of concern. In an experiment designed by Funmi Oyediran-Holm, volunteers spent twenty minutes either scrolling through short clips or watching a single long documentary, and then completed a reading-comprehension task requiring sustained effort. Those who had watched the short clips performed noticeably worse. However, the difference disappeared entirely after a ten-minute break, and it was no larger among regular users of short-video apps than among people who rarely used them. The results point to a temporary carry-over effect rather than lasting damage. Whether repeated daily exposure over many years might produce something more durable is a question the experiment could not answer, and nobody yet knows.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers find such evidence reassuring. Nikola Jovanović, who studies literacy in secondary schools, points out that teachers in many countries report pupils becoming less willing to tolerate slow-moving texts and periods of boredom, and that surveys document a marked fall in the number of teenagers who read books for pleasure. Whether or not the underlying capacity has changed, he argues, the preference matters, because skills such as following a complex argument across hundreds of pages develop only through sustained practice. This is an important point. If a capacity is rarely used, it may never be fully developed in the first place, so the comforting distinction between what people can do and what they choose to do is less reassuring than it first appears.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Signe Rasmusen, a researcher in human-computer interaction, raises a different objection to the way the debate is usually conducted. By framing the problem as one of shrinking individual attention spans, she contends, commentators place the burden on users while ignoring the environments in which they operate: devices that interrupt constantly, apps designed to be opened compulsively and workplaces that demand instant responses. There is something in this argument, since an environment full of interruptions will produce fragmented behaviour in almost anyone. But it would be wrong to conclude that individuals bear no responsibility for how they spend their attention; habits, after all, are formed by choices as well as by circumstances.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The evidence, then, does not support the claim that human beings have lost the ability to concentrate. It does suggest that patterns of attention are shifting, that people move between activities far more often than they once did, and that some valuable skills may receive less practice as a result. These are real concerns, and they deserve serious study. The goldfish statistic, which has done much to obscure them, should be retired.

topic: sleep and memory consolidation
title: The Night Shift of Memory
subtitle: Scientists agree that sleep matters for learning, but not on what the sleeping brain is actually doing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, sleep was regarded by most psychologists as a passive interlude, a period in which the brain simply rested and nothing of value took place. The observation that people remembered word lists better after a night's sleep than after an equivalent period awake was usually explained in terms of protection: a sleeper, it was argued, is shielded from the new experiences that would otherwise interfere with recently acquired information. This view has now largely been abandoned. Over the past three decades, a growing body of evidence has suggested that the sleeping brain actively reorganises what it learned during the day, strengthening some memories, weakening others and even extracting general rules from specific episodes. What remains fiercely contested is how this happens, and how much it matters outside the laboratory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most influential account centres on a process known as replay. Dr Aurelia Skarsten, a neurophysiologist at the Baltic Institute of Cognitive Science, records the activity of individual neurons in the hippocampus, a structure deep in the brain that is essential for forming new memories of events. When rats explore a maze, particular cells fire in a characteristic sequence as the animal passes through particular locations. During subsequent deep sleep, Skarsten has found, the same sequences reappear, but compressed in time, running perhaps twenty times faster than the original experience. She interprets this replay as the hippocampus 'teaching' the cortex, gradually transferring memories to the outer layers of the brain, where they can be stored for the long term without depending on the hippocampus at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that sleep is primarily about strengthening. Professor Daisuke Bresciani of the Kansai Centre for Sleep Studies argues that waking life leaves the brain's connections, or synapses, in an overloaded state. Every experience strengthens some synapses, and if this continued without limit, the brain would consume ever more energy and lose its ability to distinguish important signals from background noise. Sleep, in Bresciani's view, is the price the brain pays for plasticity: during the night, synapses across the cortex are scaled back in proportion, so that the strongest survive while weak, incidental connections fade. Memory improves after sleep, he suggests, not because anything is added but because irrelevant material has been cleared away. The two theories are often presented as rivals, but this seems to me a false opposition; a brain that both rehearsed valuable memories and pruned trivial ones would be doing exactly what an efficient learning system requires.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most striking evidence that sleep processing can be manipulated comes from a technique called targeted memory reactivation. A research group at the Halvorsen Laboratory in Bergen taught volunteers the locations of objects on a computer screen, with each object paired with a distinctive sound. While the participants were in deep sleep, some of the sounds were played again quietly. On waking, volunteers recalled the positions of the cued objects significantly more accurately than those of objects whose sounds had not been replayed, even though none of them reported hearing anything during the night. The Halvorsen team has since reported similar effects for vocabulary in a foreign language and for simple melodies played on a keyboard.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Such findings have inevitably attracted commercial interest, with several companies now marketing devices that promise to enhance learning by playing sounds to sleepers. This enthusiasm is premature. Laboratory effects of targeted reactivation, though reliable, are typically modest, and they have been obtained under carefully controlled conditions in which participants learn a limited amount of material shortly before sleeping. Dr Rafael Asamoah-Kyei, a cognitive psychologist at the Andean University of Neuroscience, points out that in his own attempts to reproduce the effect in students' homes, the benefit largely disappeared, possibly because domestic noise fragmented sleep in ways that cancelled out any gain. He does not dispute that sleep supports memory; his concern is that the size of the effect has been exaggerated by studies with small samples.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Children may be the group for whom these questions matter most. Dr Folasade Salcedo, who studies development at the Institute for Child Neuroscience in Ibadan, has found that young children spend a far greater proportion of the night in deep sleep than adults do, and that after a nap they are better able to extract general patterns, such as grammatical regularities in an invented language, than after an equal time awake. Salcedo believes that this explains why young children can acquire so much so rapidly, and she has argued that school timetables which shorten sleep, particularly early start times for adolescents, may be undermining the very learning they are designed to promote.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to treat sleep as a remedy that can compensate for poor teaching or insufficient practice. Sleep appears to consolidate what has already been encoded; it cannot create memories of material that was never properly attended to in the first place. The more modest, and more defensible, lesson of this research is that learning is not complete when a lesson ends. A significant part of it takes place hours later, out of sight, and any educational system that ignores this is working with only half of the process.

topic: adult hippocampal neurogenesis and its role in learning
title: New Cells for Old Brains?
subtitle: The question of whether adults grow fresh neurons has divided neuroscience for decades

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, one of the firmest principles of neuroscience held that the adult brain could not produce new neurons. A person was thought to be born with a fixed stock of nerve cells, which could only decline through injury, disease and age. Learning, according to this view, was entirely a matter of changing the connections between existing cells. The principle was so widely accepted that early reports of new neurons in adult rodents, published in the 1960s, were largely ignored for some twenty years. In retrospect, this neglect looks less like scientific caution than a reluctance to question an established doctrine.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: By the 1990s the evidence in animals had become impossible to dismiss. In rodents, and later in monkeys, new neurons were shown to be generated throughout life in the dentate gyrus, a small region of the hippocampus involved in memory. These cells take several weeks to mature, and during a brief window in that period they appear to be unusually excitable, responding to new experiences more readily than older neurons. Animals in which the production of new cells was blocked experimentally performed normally on many simple memory tasks, but struggled with one particular challenge: telling apart two situations that were very similar, such as two cages that differed only in the pattern on one wall.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This ability, known as pattern separation, has become central to theories of what new neurons are for. Dr Ama Owusu-Ansah, who leads a behavioural neuroscience group at the Coastal University of Accra, has shown that mice given access to running wheels produce roughly twice as many new hippocampal cells as inactive mice, and become correspondingly better at distinguishing similar environments. She suggests that young neurons act as a kind of label, allowing memories formed at different times to remain distinct rather than blurring together. Her findings have been widely cited as evidence that physical exercise improves learning, although Owusu-Ansah herself is careful to note that the mice in her studies lived in otherwise unstimulating cages, and that the benefits of running might be far smaller for animals with richer lives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whether any of this applies to humans is another matter. Studying neurogenesis in people is extremely difficult, because the methods used in animals involve injecting chemical markers and then examining brain tissue. For decades, the only direct human evidence came from a handful of patients who had received such a marker for medical reasons and whose brains, examined after death, appeared to contain new hippocampal cells. Such cases, however, were far too few to settle the matter. In 2018, a team led by Dr Yerlan Stavrakis of the Central Asian Neuroscience Consortium examined hippocampal tissue from deceased donors of various ages and reported that the production of new neurons fell sharply in childhood and was virtually undetectable in adults. Their conclusion, that adult human neurogenesis was either absent or too rare to matter, received considerable publicity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Within months, however, Professor Mateus Carvalho of the Paulista Institute of Brain Research published contrasting results. Using tissue that had been preserved within hours of death, he found thousands of immature neurons in the hippocampi of healthy adults, including some in their late seventies. Carvalho argues that the markers used to identify young neurons degrade rapidly after death, and that Stavrakis's samples, some of which had been stored for long periods before processing, would therefore inevitably have underestimated their number. Stavrakis, for his part, responds that some of the markers Carvalho relied on are also found in cells that are not neurons at all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: My own view is that the disagreement is more methodological than fundamental, and that both sides have been too quick to draw sweeping conclusions. Even if Carvalho is correct, the number of new neurons in the adult human brain is almost certainly far smaller, in proportion, than in a young mouse. It does not follow that these cells are unimportant, since a small population of highly excitable neurons could have effects out of proportion to its size. But it does follow that claims made in popular books, which present neurogenesis as the key to lifelong learning, rest on a weaker foundation than their authors suggest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Researchers at the Tartu Centre for Ageing have proposed a way forward. Rather than counting cells in tissue, they are developing brain-imaging techniques intended to detect signs of neurogenesis in living volunteers, which would allow the same person to be studied over many years. If the technique proves reliable, it could finally reveal whether people who produce more new neurons are actually better at learning. The Tartu group readily acknowledges that the signals it measures are indirect, and that they will have to be checked carefully against tissue studies before anyone can be confident about what they show. Until then, the most honest answer to the question that opened this debate is that we still do not know.

topic: dopamine, reward prediction error and motivation in learning
title: The Chemistry of Surprise
subtitle: Dopamine was once called the brain's pleasure molecule. Its real role in learning appears to be stranger, and more contested

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few substances in the brain have acquired as much popular fame as dopamine. In magazine articles and self-help books it is routinely described as a 'pleasure chemical', released whenever we eat chocolate, receive praise or check our phones. Even scientists occasionally use the phrase as convenient shorthand, which has helped it to survive. This description is not merely simplified; it is, according to most researchers in the field, wrong. Over the past few decades, experiments on animals and humans have suggested that dopamine has less to do with enjoying rewards than with learning from them, and in particular with learning from the gap between what we expect and what actually happens.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea emerged from recordings of single neurons in the midbrain of monkeys. Dr Lucía Barrantes of the Valparaíso Institute of Neuroscience trained animals to expect a drop of fruit juice a second after a light appeared. At first, dopamine neurons fired vigorously when the juice arrived. But as the animals learned the association, the response shifted: the neurons now fired when the light came on, and barely responded to the juice itself. Most revealing of all was what happened when the light appeared but the juice was withheld. At the moment the reward should have arrived, the neurons fell briefly silent. Barrantes concluded that these cells do not signal reward as such, but a 'prediction error': positive when things turn out better than expected, negative when they turn out worse, and close to zero when events unfold exactly as predicted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This finding was remarkable because it matched, almost precisely, a mathematical rule that computer scientists had independently developed for training machines to learn by trial and error. In such systems, an artificial agent adjusts its expectations in proportion to how surprised it is by each outcome; once its predictions are accurate, learning stops. The engineers had not set out to imitate the brain; they had simply searched for the most efficient way of learning from experience, which made the apparent rediscovery of their rule inside the skull all the more striking. The convergence of biology and engineering gave the prediction error theory enormous prestige, and it remains, in my judgement, one of the most elegant ideas in modern neuroscience. Elegance, however, is not the same as completeness.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Oluwaseun Bankole of the Midlands Institute of Behavioural Neuroscience has spent much of his career arguing that the theory leaves out something essential. In his experiments, rats whose dopamine systems had been chemically suppressed still showed signs of liking sugar, making the same facial expressions of enjoyment as normal animals, and could still learn which lever produced it. What they lost was the motivation to work for it. Bankole therefore distinguishes between 'liking' and 'wanting', and contends that dopamine's primary role is to make rewards, and the cues that predict them, attractive enough to pursue. Learning, in his account, is a secondary effect rather than the central function.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: More recent work has broadened the debate further. Dr Mirela Constantinescu, who directs the Carpathian Centre for Cognitive Research, has found that the human dopamine system responds not only to food or money but to information itself. In her studies, volunteers who were shown the opening of a trivia question and told they would soon learn the answer displayed increased activity in dopamine-rich regions, and the more curious they reported feeling, the better they remembered the answer a week later. Remarkably, they also remembered unrelated faces shown during the waiting period. Constantinescu interprets curiosity as a state in which the brain anticipates a reward of knowledge, and in which memory in general is temporarily enhanced.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is hardly surprising that educators have seized on such findings. The Learning Games Initiative, a research and development group based in Wellington, has designed classroom software in which correct answers trigger unpredictable rewards, such as points, animations or access to new levels, on the grounds that unpredictability sustains dopamine responses that would otherwise fade. Early trials reported higher levels of engagement. Yet engagement and learning are not the same thing, a point pressed forcefully by Dr Tariq Dahlgren of the Gulf Institute for Education Research. In his comparison of several such programmes, pupils spent more time on tasks but showed no greater gains in understanding than those taught by conventional means, and some became reluctant to attempt work that offered no reward at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Dahlgren's results deserve to be taken seriously, but they do not show that the neuroscience is irrelevant to education. What they show, I would argue, is that its lessons have been drawn too crudely. If dopamine tracks surprise, then the value of a reward lies not in its size but in the expectations it violates, and the most powerful surprises in a classroom may be intellectual ones: a result that contradicts a prediction, a question whose answer is not what pupils assumed. Constantinescu's findings suggest that curiosity of this kind is self-rewarding. Rewards that are attached to learning from outside, by contrast, risk teaching pupils that learning is worth doing only when someone pays for it.

topic: the spacing effect and why spaced practice strengthens memory
title: Why Cramming Fails
subtitle: The benefits of spreading out study have been known for over a century; explaining them, and acting on them, has proved harder

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, students around the world prepare for examinations in much the same way: by concentrating their revision into the final days, or even hours, before the test. The strategy is understandable, and it is not entirely useless. Intensive last-minute study can produce respectable results in an examination taken the next morning. What it rarely produces is lasting knowledge. Material learned in a single concentrated session tends to fade within weeks, whereas the same amount of study divided into shorter sessions separated by days is retained far longer. This phenomenon, known as the spacing effect, was first documented in the late nineteenth century and has since been confirmed in hundreds of experiments, with subjects ranging from sea slugs to medical students. It is, by any reasonable standard, one of the most robust findings in the whole of psychology.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For most of that time, however, nobody could say with confidence why it occurs. Early explanations were largely psychological. One suggested that people simply pay less attention to material they have seen very recently, so that repetitions crammed together are processed superficially. Another held that spaced sessions take place in varied contexts, such as different rooms, moods or times of day, so that the memory becomes linked to a wider range of cues. Both accounts probably contain some truth, but neither explains why the effect appears in animals as simple as sea slugs, whose capacity for attention or for noticing context is extremely limited.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This is where neuroscience has made its most distinctive contribution. Dr Thandiwe Mabuza, a molecular biologist at the Cape Institute of Neuroscience, studies the chemical changes that allow a synapse, the junction between two neurons, to be strengthened over the long term. She has shown that each training session sets off a cascade of molecular events inside the cell, culminating in the production of new proteins that stabilise the connection. Crucially, this process takes time, and while it is under way the synapse appears to be partly unresponsive to further stimulation. Similar delays have been observed in creatures as different as sea slugs and mice, which suggests that the mechanism is very ancient. A second session that arrives too soon, Mabuza argues, is effectively wasted, because the cell is not yet ready to build on what the first one began.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Professor Jarosław Wiśniewski of the Kraków Laboratory for Learning Research accepts these findings but warns against treating them as the whole story. His own work with human volunteers suggests that spacing helps partly because of what happens during the second session. If enough time has passed for a memory to begin fading, retrieving it requires effort, and this effortful recall appears to strengthen the memory far more than easily re-reading information that is still fresh. In Wiśniewski's view, the molecular and psychological accounts are not competitors but descriptions of the same process at different levels. I find this argument convincing, although it raises an awkward practical question: if difficulty is beneficial, how much difficulty is too much?

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Attempts to answer that question have produced surprisingly inconsistent results. Some studies suggest that the ideal gap between sessions is roughly ten to twenty per cent of the period for which information must be remembered, so that material needed in a year should be revisited at intervals of about a month or more. Dr Hamid Bastiaens of the Caspian University of Cognitive Science is sceptical of such formulas. He points out that the optimal interval varies with the type of material, the learner's prior knowledge and even the time of day, and he argues that searching for a single rule is misguided. Bastiaens's point is well taken, but it should not obscure the larger consensus: almost any spacing is better than none.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The real puzzle, then, is why so little of this knowledge has reached the classroom. Dr Paloma Iturriaga of the Basque Centre for Education Science has studied how schools organise their curricula and found that most are built around self-contained units, each taught intensively and assessed shortly afterwards before being set aside for good. Such a structure, she observes, is almost perfectly designed to defeat the spacing effect. Part of the explanation is that spaced learning feels less productive. Students who cram experience a satisfying sense of fluency, while those who return to half-forgotten material feel that they are struggling, and both teachers and learners tend to mistake that struggle for failure.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Changing this will require more than further research. It will mean persuading teachers to revisit old topics when there seems barely enough time for new ones, and persuading students that the discomfort of recall is a sign that learning is taking place. A few schools have begun to experiment, building short weekly reviews of earlier material into their timetables, and the early signs are encouraging, although such initiatives remain the exception rather than the rule. The evidence for doing so has existed for well over a century. What has been lacking is not knowledge but the willingness to organise education around it.

topic: sensitive periods and reopening plasticity in the adult brain
title: Windows That Never Quite Close
subtitle: Is there a deadline for learning, and if so, can the adult brain be persuaded to miss it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1960s, experiments on kittens produced one of the most influential ideas in the science of learning. If one eye was kept closed during the first few months of life, the animal remained permanently unable to see properly through it, even though the eye itself was perfectly healthy. The same treatment applied to an adult cat had almost no lasting effect. The brain, it appeared, had a limited period during which visual experience could shape its wiring; once that period ended, the circuits were fixed. The notion of a 'critical period' soon spread far beyond vision, and it has since been invoked to explain everything from the difficulty adults have in mastering a foreign accent to the claim that the first three years of a child's life determine its future.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some of these extensions were justified; many were not. The term 'critical period' implies an abrupt deadline after which learning becomes impossible, and for most human abilities the evidence simply does not support anything so dramatic. Researchers now generally prefer the phrase 'sensitive period', which describes a time when the brain is especially responsive to certain kinds of experience without implying that the opportunity disappears entirely afterwards. This is more than a matter of vocabulary. Parents who believe that a window has slammed shut may conclude that it is pointless to try, whereas the more accurate picture is one of declining, but rarely vanishing, potential.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What causes the decline? Dr Céline Vautrin of the Lyon Institute for Developmental Neuroscience has identified a set of molecular 'brakes' that accumulate in the brain as it matures. Among the most important are dense mesh-like structures that form around certain neurons towards the end of childhood, physically restricting the growth of new connections. When Vautrin's team used an enzyme to dissolve these structures in adult rats, the animals regained a striking degree of youthful plasticity: visual circuits that had been fixed for months could once again be reshaped by experience. Vautrin is careful to stress that the brakes are not a defect. In her view they exist to protect circuits that have already been refined, and their appearance marks the point at which the brain shifts from building itself to using what it has built.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Language provides the most hotly debated test of these ideas. It is commonly observed that children who move to a new country acquire its language more completely than their parents, and particularly its pronunciation. Professor Rustam Nazarov of the Silk Road University, who has analysed the speech of several thousand immigrants, accepts that age of arrival predicts eventual accent, but disputes the existence of any sharp cut-off. In his data, the ability to acquire native-like pronunciation declines steadily from early childhood into adulthood, with no sudden drop at puberty or at any other age. A sensitive period with a sharp boundary, he argues, should produce a sudden change, and the absence of one is telling.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The Montevideo Bilingualism Project, a long-term study of families who settled in Uruguay, complicates the picture further. Its researchers found that much of the apparent advantage of younger arrivals could be explained by social circumstances rather than biology. Children attended local schools and formed friendships in the new language, whereas their parents often worked and socialised largely within their own communities. When adults were matched with children for the amount and quality of exposure they received, the gap narrowed considerably, though it did not disappear. To my mind, this is the most important finding in the field, because it suggests that the limits we attribute to ageing brains are often, at least in part, limits of opportunity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If biological brakes do play some role, a provocative question follows: could they be released in adult humans? Dr Kalani Akana of the Pacific Institute of Auditory Research reported that adult volunteers given a drug believed to loosen the brakes improved at identifying musical notes by ear, a skill normally thought to be acquired only in early childhood. The effect was small and the sample modest, but the study attracted wide attention. Dr Ji-woo Duchesne of the Hanbit Institute for Brain Ethics has warned against rushing to exploit such results. Plasticity, she points out, cuts both ways: a brain that can be easily rewired for new skills may also be more vulnerable to forgetting old ones, or to the lasting effects of stress and trauma.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Duchesne's caution is sensible, but it should not be overstated. Nobody is proposing to restore a child's level of plasticity in adults wholesale, and targeted, temporary interventions may carry far smaller risks. What the debate makes clear is that the brain's capacity to learn is shaped by a balance between flexibility and stability, and that the balance shifts across a lifetime rather than flipping like a switch. Adults learn differently from children, and often more slowly; they do not, however, stop learning.
