topic: neuromyths among teachers and how to counter them
title: Myths in the Classroom
subtitle: Why do false beliefs about the brain flourish among the very people most committed to learning?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When Dr Annika Ruusmaa of the Tallinn Centre for Educational Research surveyed nearly two thousand teachers across five countries, she expected to find some confusion about how the brain works. She did not expect the scale of it. More than ninety per cent of respondents agreed that individuals learn better when they receive information in their preferred 'learning style', whether visual, auditory or physical. Around half believed that people use only ten per cent of their brains, and a similar proportion thought that differences between 'left-brained' and 'right-brained' learners could help explain individual differences in ability. None of these claims is supported by neuroscience. The survey covered both primary and secondary schools, and the pattern was broadly similar in each. Most striking of all, teachers who reported reading more about the brain were, if anything, more likely to accept such myths than their colleagues.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That last finding is less paradoxical than it first appears. Teachers who are interested in the brain are likely to encounter it through popular books, training courses and commercial programmes rather than through scientific journals, and many of these sources repeat claims that have long been abandoned by researchers. A little knowledge, in this case, may genuinely be a dangerous thing: it supplies the vocabulary of science without the means of evaluating it. A statement such as 'visual learners need images to activate their occipital cortex' sounds authoritative precisely because it contains real anatomical terms, even though the reasoning behind it is false.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The learning styles myth has been tested more thoroughly than any other. Dr Lorenza Bellandi of the Tuscan Centre for Learning Sciences reviewed several dozen experiments in which learners were first classified according to their preferred style and then taught either in a matching or a mismatching way. If the theory were correct, matched learners should consistently outperform the rest. Bellandi found no such pattern. She notes that many of the studies most often cited in support of learning styles never actually tested this prediction; they simply showed that people could describe their preferences, which is a very different matter. People certainly have preferences, and they may enjoy some kinds of presentation more than others, but preference did not predict what helped them learn. What mattered far more was the nature of the material: geography is best learned with maps, music with sound, regardless of who is studying it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards the persistence of such beliefs as a serious problem. Professor Kofi Mensah-Bonsu of the Kumasi Institute of Educational Psychology argues that many myths, though scientifically wrong, lead to harmless or even beneficial practices. A teacher who believes in learning styles may present material in several different ways, and variety itself can sustain attention. On this view, the energy spent correcting myths might be better directed elsewhere. It is a reasonable point, but I think it underestimates the costs. Schools spend considerable sums on programmes based on discredited claims, and pupils labelled as one kind of learner may come to believe that they cannot succeed with other kinds of material.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The obvious response is to teach teachers more neuroscience. Yet some researchers doubt that this is enough, or even that it is the right goal. Dr Anand Krishnaswamy of the Bangalore Institute of Cognitive Education observes that most findings from brain research, however fascinating, have no direct implications for what should happen in a classroom on Monday morning. Knowing which region of the brain is active during reading does not tell a teacher how to teach reading. He compares the situation to that of medicine, where knowledge of cell biology took decades to produce practical treatments, and where clinical trials, rather than laboratory findings, still decide what doctors actually do. In Krishnaswamy's view, the most useful evidence for educators comes from cognitive psychology, which studies learning at the level of behaviour, and neuroscience is valuable mainly when it helps explain why classroom strategies already shown to work actually succeed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different approach has been tried by the Rotterdam Teachers' Research Network, which pairs groups of teachers with researchers and asks them to test claims together in their own schools. Rather than receiving lists of facts, teachers learn how evidence is gathered and how to ask what a study really shows. Early reports suggest that participants become noticeably more sceptical of commercial programmes, although the network has not yet measured whether this changes what pupils learn.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Rotterdam model strikes me as the most promising of the available options, precisely because it treats teachers as professionals capable of judging evidence rather than as passive recipients of scientific conclusions. Myths will never be eliminated entirely; new ones emerge as quickly as old ones are discredited. The goal should therefore not be to supply teachers with a fixed list of correct beliefs, but to equip them with the habits of mind that allow them to recognise a weak claim, however scientific it may sound.

topic: myelin and white matter plasticity in skill learning
title: The Brain's Forgotten Half
subtitle: For decades, research on learning focused on neurons. A fatty substance wrapped around them may matter just as much

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Look at a slice of human brain and two kinds of tissue are immediately visible: a thin outer layer of grey matter and, beneath it, a large region of white. The grey matter contains the bodies of neurons, the cells that process information, and it has long been the focus of research on learning. The white matter, which makes up roughly half of the brain's volume, was for most of the twentieth century regarded as little more than insulation. Its colour comes from myelin, a fatty substance produced by cells called oligodendrocytes, which wrap themselves around the long fibres that carry signals between neurons. Myelin allows electrical impulses to travel up to a hundred times faster than they would along bare fibres. That much was well established; what nobody seriously suspected was that myelin might change as a result of experience.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first hints came from brain imaging. Dr Margarida Fontes of the Atlantic Neuroimaging Centre scanned adults before and after several months of learning to play the piano and reported measurable changes in the white matter connecting regions involved in hearing and movement. The more hours a participant had practised, the greater the change. Remarkably, some of these differences could be detected after only a few weeks of training, far sooner than many researchers would have predicted. Similar findings have since been reported for learners of juggling, of a second language and even of meditation. Fontes argues that these changes reflect an increase in myelin along the pathways that a new skill uses most, and that the brain, in effect, upgrades the cables it relies upon.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Imaging alone cannot establish this, however, and Dr Mehmet Karaca of the Anatolian Centre for Neuroimaging Methods has been one of the most persistent critics of such interpretations. The scanning technique used in most studies does not detect myelin directly; it measures how freely water molecules move through tissue, which is influenced by myelin but also by the density of fibres, the swelling of cells and even the amount of blood flowing through the area. A change in the signal, Karaca insists, could have any of several causes. He is not claiming that myelin does not change, only that human imaging studies have been far more confident than their methods allow. This seems to me a fair criticism, and one that the field was slow to acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence that myelin matters for learning comes instead from animal experiments in which its production can be controlled directly. Professor Gideon Aharoni of the Haifa Institute of Glial Biology genetically modified mice so that they could not produce new oligodendrocytes in adulthood, while their existing myelin remained intact. The mice behaved normally in most respects, but when they were placed on a running wheel with irregularly spaced rungs, a task that requires learning a complex new pattern of movement, they failed to improve, whereas normal mice mastered it within days. Since the modified animals could still run on an ordinary wheel, the problem was not one of movement as such, but of acquiring a new skill. When the genetic change was made only after the mice had already mastered the task, they continued to perform it well, suggesting that new myelin is needed for acquiring skills rather than for retaining them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why should myelin be so important? An intriguing answer has been proposed by Dr Sebastián Rocheleau of the Rosario Institute for Brain Dynamics. Speed alone, he points out, is not the point. Many brain functions depend on signals from different regions arriving at a target at precisely the same moment, and because fibres differ in length, the only way to achieve this is to adjust the speed of transmission along each one. Rocheleau suggests that experience fine-tunes myelin so that the timing of signals becomes synchronised, much as an orchestra's conductor brings players into time. On this view, learning a skill is partly a matter of getting the timing right.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The idea has implications for development. Myelination continues well into a person's twenties, and the frontal regions involved in planning and self-control are among the last to be completed. It has been suggested that the experiences of adolescence may therefore shape these pathways in ways that are difficult to alter later. This is plausible, but the evidence for it is still largely indirect, and the popular claim that teenagers' brains are simply 'unfinished' risks becoming an excuse for low expectations rather than a guide to how they learn best.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the research on myelin has already achieved is to widen the frame. Learning was long imagined as something that happens exclusively at synapses, where neurons meet. It now appears to involve a broader set of changes, including the cells that support and connect neurons rather than the neurons alone. If Aharoni's results are confirmed in other species, one of the oldest assumptions of the field will have to be revised: that the white half of the brain merely carries messages, while the grey half does all the learning.

topic: physical exercise, BDNF and learning in schools
title: Running to Learn
subtitle: Exercise is said to sharpen the mind. The neuroscience is promising, but the classroom evidence is more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many countries, the time devoted to physical education in schools has declined steadily over the past three decades, squeezed out by pressure to raise standards in reading and mathematics. The logic seems straightforward: if pupils are to perform better in academic subjects, they should spend more time studying them. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this reasoning may be self-defeating. Physical activity, it is claimed, does not merely benefit the body; it alters the brain in ways that make learning easier. If that is true, then cutting sport to make room for study may be one of the more counterproductive decisions an education system can make.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the biological case rests on a protein known as brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, which supports the survival of neurons and the strengthening of connections between them. Dr Sigrún Hallgrímsdóttir of the Reykjavík Institute of Exercise Neuroscience has shown that levels of BDNF in the blood rise sharply after a period of aerobic exercise such as running or cycling, and that in mice the increase is particularly marked in the hippocampus, a region essential to memory. The protein appears to encourage the growth of new branches on neurons and to make synapses more responsive to stimulation, both of which are thought to be central to the formation of memories. Animals with access to running wheels learned the layout of a water maze faster than inactive animals, and when Hallgrímsdóttir chemically blocked the action of BDNF, the advantage disappeared. She describes the protein, memorably, as 'fertiliser for the brain'.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The effects are not confined to the young. Dr Takeshi Arakawa of the Sendai Centre for Cognitive Ageing followed several hundred adults over the age of sixty, half of whom took part in a programme of brisk walking three times a week for a year. In the walking group, the hippocampus grew slightly in volume, whereas in the comparison group, which carried out stretching exercises, it shrank by about one per cent, a rate typical of normal ageing. The walkers also performed better on tests of spatial memory. Arakawa is cautious about the size of these benefits, which were modest, but he regards them as evidence that the ageing brain retains a capacity for physical renewal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Timing may matter as much as quantity. Professor Chukwuemeka Jansz of the Niger Delta University of Health Sciences compared groups of students who exercised either before or after studying a list of vocabulary in an unfamiliar language. Those who exercised four hours after studying remembered more words two days later than those who exercised immediately before or immediately after the session. Students who did not exercise at all remembered the fewest words. Jansz speculates that a delayed burst of activity may coincide with the period during which new memories are being stabilised, although he admits that the mechanism remains unclear. His results, if they are replicated, could have practical consequences for how the school day is arranged.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Translating laboratory findings into schools, however, has proved difficult. Dr Ximena Giraudoux of the Andean Institute of Paediatric Research ran a two-year trial in which pupils at forty primary schools received an extra twenty minutes of vigorous activity every day. Teachers reported that pupils were calmer and more attentive in the lessons that followed, but there was no measurable improvement in end-of-year test scores. Giraudoux concludes that exercise may help to create the conditions for learning without guaranteeing that learning takes place. I think this is the right interpretation, and it is a useful corrective to some of the more extravagant claims made by advocates of physical activity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One response has been to combine movement and learning directly. The Ljubljana Movement and Learning Group has developed 'active lessons' in which pupils practise multiplication by jumping between numbered squares or learn spelling through relay games. In their evaluations, children taught this way enjoyed lessons more and made slightly greater progress in mathematics than those taught at their desks. The gains were largest among pupils who had previously shown little interest in mathematics, a result that the group's members regard as especially encouraging. Critics have objected that such lessons take longer to organise and can be chaotic in crowded classrooms, but these seem to me practical problems rather than objections of principle.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that exercise is a shortcut to academic success. Nor should physical education be justified solely by its effect on examination results; it has value for health, enjoyment and social development in its own right. The biological effects are real but modest, and they depend on what pupils do with the brain that exercise has prepared. What the research does show is that the competition between physical education and academic study is largely a false one. A school that removes sport in order to raise test scores is unlikely to achieve its aim, and it may sacrifice something of value in the attempt.

topic: stress hormones and their effects on learning and recall
title: Under Pressure
subtitle: Stress can sharpen memory or sabotage it. Researchers are only beginning to understand which, and when

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask people to recall where they were when they heard some shocking piece of news and many will describe the scene in vivid detail. Ask them what they had for lunch on an ordinary day a week ago and most will struggle. The difference is not accidental. Emotionally charged events trigger the release of stress hormones, chiefly adrenaline and cortisol, and these hormones appear to instruct the brain that an experience is worth remembering. From an evolutionary perspective, this makes obvious sense: an animal that remembered where it had encountered a predator was more likely to survive than one that forgot. Yet the same hormones that engrave some memories can erase others, and the conditions that determine which outcome prevails have proved surprisingly subtle.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The relationship between stress and performance was first described more than a century ago, in experiments in which mice learned to choose between two compartments while receiving mild electric shocks of varying strength. Learning was fastest at intermediate levels of stimulation and slower when the shocks were either very weak or very strong. This pattern, often drawn as an inverted U, has since been observed in many settings. A moderate level of arousal focuses attention and improves learning, whereas too little leaves the learner disengaged and too much overwhelms the capacity to think clearly. The principle is widely cited, but it is a description rather than an explanation, and it says nothing about how the brain produces the effect.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Dr Ilse Vandersteen of the Flemish Institute for Stress Research has spent two decades investigating the biology behind it. Her work centres on the amygdala, a small structure involved in processing emotion, which becomes highly active when stress hormones are released. In rats, Vandersteen found that injecting a stress hormone immediately after training on a task improved memory for that task when the animals were tested a day later, but only if the amygdala was functioning normally; when it was temporarily inactivated, the hormone had no effect. She concludes that the amygdala acts as an amplifier, signalling to the hippocampus and other memory regions that the events just experienced deserve to be stored with particular strength.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Timing, however, turns out to be critical. Professor Farida Darzi of the Maghreb Centre for Behavioural Endocrinology has shown that stress experienced while trying to retrieve information has quite different effects from stress experienced while learning it. In one study, university students learned a list of words and were tested the following day, half of them immediately after giving an unexpected public speech in front of a panel of stern-faced judges. Those who had given the speech recalled roughly a quarter fewer words than the others, and the size of the impairment was related to the rise in their cortisol levels. Darzi argues that this helps explain why well-prepared candidates sometimes go blank in examinations: the information is stored, but the hormonal surge of the moment blocks access to it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Prolonged stress raises a different set of concerns. Dr Oskar Wennerberg of Kattegat University has studied rats exposed to unpredictable stressors daily for several weeks and found that the branching extensions of neurons in the hippocampus, through which they receive signals, became noticeably shorter and less numerous. The animals also performed poorly on tasks requiring spatial memory. Encouragingly, these changes reversed within a few weeks once the stress ended. Wennerberg is careful to point out, however, that recovery appeared slower in older animals, and that similar effects in humans have been inferred mainly from brain-imaging studies of people with long-term stress-related conditions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If stress at the moment of testing is so damaging, can anything be done to reduce its effects? Researchers at the Tāmaki Education Research Unit in Auckland tried a remarkably simple intervention. Before a mathematics examination, some students read a short passage explaining that a racing heart and sweaty palms are signs that the body is preparing to perform well, rather than evidence of impending failure. These students scored significantly higher than a comparison group who received no such information, and the effect was largest among those who had reported the greatest anxiety. Dr Aleksandr Voronin of the Neva Institute of Psychology has questioned whether the result will hold up, noting that similar studies with larger samples have produced smaller effects. His caution is reasonable, but the intervention is so cheap that it would be strange not to test it more widely.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that the common advice to 'stay calm' is incomplete. Some arousal during learning appears to be beneficial, and what matters most may be the way learners interpret the physical sensations of stress rather than whether they experience them at all. The real danger lies at the two extremes: in the sudden overwhelming surge that blocks recall at the worst possible moment, and in the grinding, long-term stress that gradually wears away the brain's capacity to learn.

topic: active forgetting as an adaptive function of memory
title: The Art of Losing
subtitle: Forgetting has long been seen as a failure of memory. A growing number of neuroscientists see it as one of memory's essential functions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Nobody likes to forget. Mislaid keys, forgotten names and vanished facts on the morning of an examination are among the most familiar frustrations of daily life, and an entire industry of memory training, supplements and mobile applications has grown up to help people hold on to more of what they learn. Underlying all of this is an assumption that has shaped psychology for more than a century: that forgetting is simply what happens when memory fails, a passive fading of traces over time, much as ink fades on paper left in the sun. It is an intuitive idea, and for a long time few researchers saw any reason to question it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious challenge came from an unlikely source: the humble fruit fly. Dr Rhiannon Llewellyn of the Severn Institute of Neurobiology trained flies to avoid a particular odour by pairing it with a mild electric shock. Ordinarily, the flies forgot the association within a day or so. But Llewellyn discovered that a small group of neurons releasing dopamine continued to fire after learning, and that this activity was actively dismantling the newly formed memory. When she genetically silenced these neurons, the flies remembered the association for far longer than normal; when she stimulated them, the flies forgot more quickly. Forgetting, in other words, was not merely the absence of remembering. It was a process the brain carried out deliberately, using dedicated machinery.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Why would the brain invest resources in destroying information? Dr Joachim Pardo-Lima of the Graz Institute for Theoretical Neuroscience argues that the answer becomes obvious once memory is seen as a tool for making decisions rather than as an archive. A system that recorded every detail of every experience would, he suggests, be overwhelmed by specifics and unable to recognise what different situations had in common. Engineers who design learning machines face exactly this problem: a program that memorises its training examples too precisely performs well on those examples but fails when faced with anything new. Forgetting irrelevant details, in Pardo-Lima's view, is what allows a learner to extract the general patterns that are actually useful.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This argument strikes me as persuasive, and it helps to explain one of the oldest puzzles in developmental psychology. Adults remember almost nothing of their first three or four years, despite the fact that infants learn at an extraordinary rate. Professor Matías Ferreyra of the Córdoba Centre for Memory Research has proposed that this 'infantile amnesia' is a by-product of the rapid production of new neurons in the young hippocampus. As new cells are wired into existing circuits, he suggests, they disrupt the connections that held older memories. In mice, slowing the production of new neurons in infancy allowed early memories to persist into adulthood, while increasing it in adults caused them to forget recent experiences more rapidly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Humans, too, appear capable of forgetting deliberately. Dr Hoang Thi Lan of the Hanoi Institute of Cognitive Science asks volunteers to learn pairs of words and then, when shown the first word of a pair, either to think of its partner or to actively push it out of mind. Words that participants tried to suppress were later recalled less well than words they had simply not been asked to think about, and brain scans showed that suppression was accompanied by increased activity in the frontal lobes and reduced activity in the hippocampus. Hoang believes this ability may help people to cope with unpleasant experiences, although she acknowledges that her laboratory tasks involve neutral words rather than genuinely distressing memories.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is comfortable with the enthusiasm that these findings have generated. Researchers working with the Leiden Ageing and Memory Cohort, which has followed more than three thousand adults for two decades, warn that celebrating forgetting risks trivialising real memory loss. The forgetting experienced by many older people, they point out, does not selectively remove trivial details while preserving what matters; it affects important and unimportant information alike, and it can be deeply distressing. To describe all forgetting as adaptive is, in their words, to confuse a healthy process with a disease.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The criticism is fair, but it is aimed less at the research itself than at the way it has sometimes been popularised. None of the scientists involved claims that all forgetting is beneficial. What their work demonstrates is that a healthy memory depends on a balance between storing and discarding, and that problems may arise when either side of that balance is disturbed. It is quite possible, indeed, that some forms of memory impairment involve a failure of forgetting as well as a failure of remembering.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: For learners, the implications are reassuring. Forgetting much of what one encounters is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is the price of a memory system designed to keep what is useful. The aim of education should not be to prevent forgetting altogether, an impossible and perhaps undesirable goal, but to ensure that what survives the brain's constant editing is what matters most.

topic: dam removal and the downstream release of stored sediment
title: Letting the River Run
subtitle: Obsolete dams are being dismantled across the world, but what they leave behind is the subject of fierce disagreement

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, building a dam was regarded as an unambiguous sign of progress. Rivers were harnessed for power, irrigation and flood control, and the concrete walls that held them back became symbols of national ambition. Yet alongside the great hydroelectric schemes, hundreds of thousands of smaller barriers were constructed, many of them built to power water mills or to supply factories that closed long ago. In Europe alone, surveys suggest that more than a million barriers of various sizes fragment the continent's rivers, and a significant proportion of them no longer serve any economic function. Over the past three decades, the idea of removing such structures has moved from the margins of conservation thinking into mainstream river management. This change of attitude is long overdue: a dam that has outlived its purpose is not a harmless relic but an ongoing intervention in the life of a river.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principal technical challenge in removing a dam lies not in the structure itself but in what has accumulated behind it. Reservoirs act as traps for the sand, gravel and silt that rivers naturally carry downstream, and a dam that has stood for a century may hold back millions of cubic metres of sediment. When the barrier is taken away, this material is set in motion. Kerstin Brottveit, a geomorphologist at the Bergen Institute of River Dynamics, has tracked sediment movement following the removal of eleven dams in Scandinavia and North America. She reports that in most cases the bulk of the stored sediment was carried away within a few months, and that the river channel had largely regained its natural form within two years. On the basis of this evidence, Brottveit favours removing dams in a single operation rather than lowering them gradually over several seasons, arguing that a short, intense disturbance does less cumulative harm than a prolonged one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone shares her confidence. Amaru Huallpacusi, an aquatic ecologist at the Andean Freshwater Observatory, has documented cases in which a sudden release of fine silt buried the spawning gravels on which salmon and trout depend, and in which populations of insect larvae took far longer to recover than predicted. Huallpacusi points out that most of the rivers in Brottveit's study were steep, fast-flowing channels with enough energy to flush sediment rapidly downstream. Lowland rivers, which move slowly across gentle gradients, may retain fine material in their beds for many years. This distinction deserves more attention than it has received. Rapid removal may well be the best option in mountain streams, but treating conclusions drawn from such rivers as a general rule would be a mistake, and engineers working on slow-moving lowland rivers should be wary of adopting the same approach without careful study.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A further complication arises where dams stood downstream of industrial sites. Sediment that settled in such reservoirs over decades may contain heavy metals, oil residues and other persistent pollutants. Hiroko Tsujimura, an environmental chemist who has analysed sediment cores from more than thirty reservoirs, found contaminant concentrations high enough to pose risks to aquatic life in roughly a quarter of them. Her group recommends that contaminated layers be excavated and safely disposed of before any removal takes place, a step that can multiply the cost of a project several times over. Some local authorities have cited these costs as grounds for leaving old dams where they are. This reasoning, however, is short-sighted. Ageing structures deteriorate, and a dam that is not removed deliberately may eventually fail, causing an uncontrolled release of exactly the pollutants that its preservation was meant to contain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dam removal also has a social dimension that engineers have sometimes underestimated. Millponds and reservoirs are often valued for fishing, boating and scenery, and residents may fear that the loss of open water will lower the value of nearby homes. Femi Ogundimu, a social geographer, has surveyed communities affected by removal projects and found that opposition tended to be strongest before work began and declined considerably once residents could see the restored river. He is careful, however, not to overstate this result. Because many proposals that met fierce resistance were abandoned before construction, his surveys mainly captured communities where removal went ahead, and these may have been more receptive from the outset. Many removals, he adds, are organised by small charities or local agencies working on tight budgets, which rarely have the resources to consult residents in depth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The ecological rewards of removal can be striking. Migratory fish such as salmon, shad and eels have recolonised upstream habitats within a few seasons in several well-documented cases. Yet removal is not automatically beneficial. Radek Szymaniak, a fisheries biologist, has drawn attention to rivers in which old weirs had, entirely by accident, kept non-native predators away from upstream populations of native trout. Once the barriers were gone, these isolated populations declined sharply. Such cases suggest that the decision to remove a dam should rest on a careful assessment of each individual river, rather than on a presumption that any barrier is necessarily harmful.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What unites these debates is a shortage of evidence. Despite the growing number of removals, only a small minority have been followed by monitoring that lasts longer than a year or two, and many have not been studied at all. As a result, disagreements such as that between Brottveit and Huallpacusi remain difficult to resolve. If dam removal is to become a reliable tool of river restoration rather than an act of faith, the funding of long-term monitoring must be treated as an essential part of every project, not as an optional extra to be dropped when budgets are tight.

topic: environmental flows: releasing water from dams to imitate natural river regimes
title: Designer Floods
subtitle: Can water released from dams bring regulated rivers back to life?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the engineers who designed and operated large dams worked from a simple principle: water that flowed past a dam without generating electricity or irrigating crops was water wasted. Reservoirs were managed to smooth out the seasonal rhythms of rivers, storing the floods of the wet season and releasing them steadily through the dry months. The result, below many of the world's large dams, is a river whose flow barely changes from one month to the next. Yet the plants and animals of river systems evolved under quite different conditions, in which floods and low flows alternated in a broadly predictable pattern. The idea that water should be deliberately released from dams to imitate that pattern, known as environmental flows, has spread rapidly since the 1990s. It represents a genuine shift in thinking, and one that deserves to be welcomed: a river is not merely a pipe for delivering water to human users, but a living system with requirements of its own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest attempts to protect rivers below dams took a cruder form. Regulations typically specified a single fixed quantity of water below which the flow must not fall, on the assumption that keeping a river wet was enough to keep it alive. Thandeka Ngcobo, a hydrologist at the Limpopo Basin Institute, regards this approach as fundamentally mistaken. Aquatic ecosystems, she argues, respond not to the volume of water as such but to change: the timing of floods triggers fish to spawn, their size determines whether water spills onto the floodplain, and how often they occur shapes which species can survive. A river held at a constant level, however generous, is in her words 'little more than a canal with fish in it'. Her work has been influential in persuading water authorities to design release schedules that reproduce the variability of natural flows rather than simply guaranteeing a minimum.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some of the most ambitious experiments have involved short, deliberate floods. On several large rivers, managers have opened dam outlets for periods of several days, sending a pulse of water downstream to scour channels and rebuild the sandbars on which riverside vegetation and nesting birds depend. Early results were encouraging, but in a number of cases the newly built sandbars had largely washed away within a year. Inaki Olaizola, a river engineer, attributes this to a problem that water releases alone cannot solve. Because the dam traps the sediment that would once have travelled downstream, an artificial flood can only rearrange what is already in the channel below; it cannot replenish it. Olaizola therefore argues that flow releases must be combined with measures to move sediment past dams. His point is well made, but it should not be taken as evidence that releases are pointless. Even where sediment is scarce, planned floods have reconnected floodplain wetlands and improved conditions for spawning fish.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Environmental flows also carry a price. Water released to benefit a river is water that cannot be used to generate electricity or irrigate farmland, and dam operators are understandably reluctant to give it up. Anouk Verstraeten, an environmental economist, has attempted to set the costs against the gains. Her calculations suggest that, on many rivers, the value of restored fisheries, floodplain grazing and tourism exceeds the revenue lost by power companies. The difficulty, she observes, is that the two do not fall on the same people: the losses are borne by dam operators, while the benefits are spread among downstream communities who have no means of paying for them. Without mechanisms to share costs fairly, she concludes, operators will continue to resist.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The communities living downstream complicate the picture in another way. In parts of Africa and Asia, farmers once planted crops on floodplains as seasonal floods receded, and fishers followed the movements of fish onto flooded land. Researchers with the Riverine Livelihoods Project, working in three river basins, found that in the decades since dams were built many of these households had adjusted their farming calendars and moved their fields to land that no longer floods. For them, a release designed to restore a historical flood could destroy a crop. This finding exposes an awkward truth: once a dam has operated for a generation, the conditions that preceded it can no longer be treated as a neutral goal to which everyone would wish to return.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Climate change adds further uncertainty. Release schedules are usually based on historical flow records, but these records are becoming a less reliable guide to the future. More immediately, environmental allocations tend to be the first to be reduced during dry years, when competition for water is most intense. Unless water for rivers is given the same legal standing as water for agriculture and cities, it will continue to be treated as a luxury to be sacrificed whenever supplies run short.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that environmental flows are a failure. It means rather that they should be understood for what they are: not a restoration of nature as it once was, but a negotiated compromise between ecological needs and human demands. Seen in that light, their limitations are less a sign of weakness than an honest reflection of the choices that any society managing a river must make.

topic: conflict and cooperation over rivers shared by several countries
title: Shared Waters
subtitle: Rivers that cross national borders were once expected to spark wars. The reality has proved more complicated

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: More than three hundred river and lake basins cross national borders, and together they supply water to a substantial share of the world's population. Since the 1980s, commentators have repeatedly warned that competition for these resources would become a leading cause of armed conflict, and the phrase 'water wars' has become a fixture of political journalism. As rising populations, expanding agriculture and a changing climate place growing pressure on shared rivers, the warning has an intuitive appeal. Yet the predictions have so far proved alarmist. Nations that share rivers have argued, threatened and occasionally fired shots, but the large-scale wars fought over water that were once forecast have not materialised, and there is little reason to think they are imminent.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most systematic evidence for this view comes from Ayelet Rozenblum, a political geographer who has spent two decades compiling a database of every recorded interaction between states over shared freshwater. Her analysis of several thousand events, ranging from formal treaties to verbal threats, found that cooperative interactions outnumbered hostile ones by roughly two to one, and that the great majority of disputes were settled through negotiation. Rozenblum argues that this is not a matter of goodwill but of hard logic. A downstream country cannot secure its water simply by defeating its upstream neighbour in battle; to guarantee the flow, it would need to occupy and hold the entire upstream catchment indefinitely, a commitment few governments would contemplate.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kwabena Darkwah, a scholar of international relations, believes such figures paint a misleadingly cheerful picture. Cooperation, he points out, is not the same as fairness. Many water agreements reflect the bargaining power of the stronger party, whether that strength derives from an upstream position or from economic and military weight, and weaker states frequently sign them because the alternative, no agreement at all, would leave them in a still worse position. Darkwah's warning is a valuable corrective: counting treaties tells us very little about whether water is being divided justly. He goes too far, however, when he implies that virtually every agreement is domination in disguise. Several river treaties have continued to function even while their signatories were at war with one another, and have delivered tangible benefits to all the parties involved.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A different weakness has been identified by the international lawyer Mirela Captaru. Many treaties, she notes, divide a river by assigning each country a fixed volume of water per year. These figures were often calculated from flow records gathered during decades that later turned out to be unusually wet, so that the river cannot reliably deliver the quantities promised. In a drought, the upstream country finds itself legally obliged to release water it does not have, and disputes follow. Captaru recommends that allocations be expressed as proportions of whatever flow is available, and that treaties include clauses requiring periodic renegotiation. Her argument is persuasive. In an era of increasingly erratic rainfall, agreements built around fixed quantities are a relic of a more predictable world.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Agreements of either kind depend on reliable information, and here too there are obstacles. Researchers at the Basin Data Collaborative, an international network of hydrologists, have found that many governments treat measurements of river flow as confidential, sometimes classifying them as matters of national security. Without shared figures, each country tends to suspect its neighbours of taking more than their share. The Collaborative advocates jointly operated gauging stations and the open publication of satellite observations, which can now estimate river levels and reservoir volumes from space. Such measures are welcome, but they should not be mistaken for a solution in themselves. Data can narrow disagreements about facts; it cannot by itself create the trust needed to act on them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many shared rivers are now overseen by joint commissions or basin organisations, and their records vary enormously. Some coordinate dam operations, flood warnings and pollution control across several countries; others exist largely on paper. Leopoldina Wamalwa, who has studied more than forty such bodies, attributes the difference mainly to institutional design: organisations with secure funding, a permanent technical staff and clear procedures for settling disputes, she argues, tend to succeed. Design undoubtedly matters, but the evidence suggests that it matters less than the willingness of member governments to cooperate. Commissions created with almost identical structures have flourished in one basin and stagnated in another, depending on the political relationships between the states concerned.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most promising development is a gradual change in what negotiations are about. Rather than arguing over how many cubic metres each country may withdraw, some neighbouring states have begun to discuss how the benefits of a river can be shared: an upstream dam might generate electricity that is sold to downstream countries at reduced prices, while also regulating floods and improving navigation along the river's lower reaches. Such arrangements can turn a contest in which one side's gain is the other's loss into a joint enterprise. They offer no escape, however, from the question Darkwah raises. Benefits can be shared as unequally as water, and the success of this approach will depend on whether weaker states are able to bargain on genuinely equal terms.

topic: managed aquifer recharge: storing surplus water underground
title: Banking Water Underground
subtitle: Storing surplus water in aquifers is attracting growing interest, but its advocates may be promising more than geology can deliver

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Across much of the world, groundwater is being withdrawn faster than it is replenished. Aquifers, the layers of permeable rock, sand or gravel that hold water in the spaces between their grains, supply roughly half of the drinking water used globally and a large share of the water used for irrigation. In some intensively farmed plains, water tables have fallen by tens of metres within a single lifetime. Wells must be drilled ever deeper, pumping costs rise, and in coastal zones sea water seeps inland to replace the fresh water that has been removed. One response that has attracted growing attention is managed aquifer recharge: the deliberate transfer of surplus surface water into the ground so that it can be stored and recovered later. To its supporters, it is the most promising water-storage technology of the century; to its critics, it is an old idea dressed up in new language. The truth, it will be argued here, lies somewhere between these positions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic methods are simple. In the most common approach, water is diverted into shallow basins with sandy floors, where it soaks slowly downwards; in others, it is pumped directly into the aquifer through injection wells. The source may be floodwater from rivers in spate, stormwater collected from city streets or treated wastewater. Haruto Kanzaki, a hydrogeologist at the Institute for Subsurface Hydrology, points out that storing water underground has several advantages over storing it behind a dam. There is almost no loss through evaporation, which in hot climates can remove a quarter or more of a reservoir's volume each year; no valley has to be flooded and no communities displaced; and the passage of water through soil and sediment removes many impurities naturally. Kanzaki has calculated that, in semi-arid regions, the cost of each cubic metre stored in this way is typically less than half that of building new surface reservoirs.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These advantages are real, but they are not universal. Torvald Skjeggestad, who studies groundwater movement at the Bergen Centre for Earth Sciences, stresses that an aquifer is not an empty tank waiting to be filled. Whether recharge succeeds depends on the permeability of the overlying soil, the depth of the water table and the direction in which groundwater naturally flows. In some locations, water that is added at one point simply drains away towards a river or the sea before anyone can recover it. In others, fine particles carried in floodwater gradually seal the floor of the infiltration basin, so that the rate at which water enters the ground falls year after year unless the basins are regularly scraped clean. Skjeggestad estimates that only around a third of the sites proposed for recharge in a recent international survey had the geological conditions needed to make them worthwhile.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Water quality presents a further difficulty. Chidimma Ezeakunne, an environmental chemist at the West African Water Research Institute, has examined schemes that use treated wastewater as their source. She found that while filtration through the ground removed most bacteria and many organic compounds, it could also trigger unexpected chemical reactions. When oxygen-rich water enters an aquifer whose rocks contain certain minerals, it can release naturally occurring arsenic into the groundwater, sometimes at concentrations above drinking-water limits. Ezeakunne does not argue that such schemes should be abandoned. Rather, she insists that each one requires detailed analysis of the local rocks before any water is introduced, and continuous monitoring afterwards. This is sensible advice, although it sits uneasily with the claim that recharge is a cheap alternative to conventional storage, since thorough monitoring is anything but inexpensive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most contentious questions are not technical but legal. Groundwater does not respect property boundaries, and water stored by one user may be pumped out by a neighbour. Itziar Agirrezabala, a specialist in water law at the Bilbao Institute of Resource Governance, has studied regions where farmers' associations invested in recharge only to find that others benefited from their efforts without contributing. In her view, schemes will not attract sustained investment unless the law clearly recognises a right to recover water that one has deliberately stored. Some jurisdictions have created systems of 'recharge credits' for this purpose, which record each deposit and allow it to be withdrawn later. Yet Agirrezabala warns that such accounting can create a misleading sense of precision, since nobody can say exactly how much of the stored water remains where it was placed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters sometimes present managed recharge as a solution to groundwater depletion as a whole. This is surely an exaggeration. In most over-exploited basins, the volume of water withdrawn each year far exceeds any surplus that could realistically be captured and returned to the ground, even in wet years. Recharge can slow decline, and in favourable locations it can reverse it, but it cannot substitute for reducing extraction. Indeed, there is a risk that the promise of recharge will be used to postpone politically difficult decisions about limiting pumping, much as the construction of new dams once allowed governments to avoid confronting rising demand.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the technique should be dismissed. Where geology is favourable, legal rights are clear and water quality is carefully monitored, recharge offers an efficient way of keeping surplus water for times of drought. The lesson of the past few decades, though, is that aquifers have been treated as if they were inexhaustible. It would be unfortunate if, having finally recognised their limits, societies were now to assume that those limits could simply be engineered away.

topic: fish passage structures at dams and their effectiveness for migratory fish
title: Ladders to Nowhere?
subtitle: For more than a century, engineers have tried to help fish past dams. The evidence that they have succeeded is thinner than many assume

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Salmon, shad, sturgeon and eels share a demanding way of life. Each must travel between very different habitats, often hundreds of kilometres apart, in order to feed, grow and reproduce. A dam placed across their route can sever that journey at a stroke. From the late nineteenth century onwards, engineers responded with the fish ladder: a sequence of stepped pools, each slightly higher than the last, up which fish could leap and swim around the barrier. In many countries, such structures eventually became a legal requirement for new dams, and a project that included one was widely regarded as having discharged its ecological obligations. That assumption, however, has rarely been examined with the rigour it deserves, and the data now accumulating suggest that it was, at best, optimistic.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most comprehensive review to date was compiled by Ewa Grzybowska, a fisheries biologist at the Vistula River Ecology Station, who gathered monitoring results from more than a hundred passage structures on several continents. Her central measure was passage efficiency: the proportion of fish that approach a structure and actually get through it. For upstream migration, the median figure she found was below fifty per cent, and for species other than salmon and trout it frequently fell under ten. The explanation, Grzybowska argues, lies in the history of the designs themselves. Most were developed with salmon in mind, and salmon are powerful swimmers capable of leaping considerable heights. Sturgeon, lampreys and many smaller species cannot jump at all and tend to avoid the turbulent water that tumbles through a conventional ladder. As she puts it, engineers have spent a century building for one fish in a river of many.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Low efficiency at a single dam is serious enough, but most large rivers are blocked not once but repeatedly. If each of four successive barriers allows half of the arriving fish to pass, only around six per cent of the original migrants will reach spawning grounds above the last of them. Moreover, the fish that do succeed may pay a hidden price. Aurelio Ferrandis, a physiologist at the Iberian Institute of Aquatic Physiology, tracked individuals that had spent days or weeks searching for the entrance to a fishway. He found that they reached their spawning grounds with markedly depleted fat reserves and, in the case of females, produced fewer eggs than fish that had migrated without obstruction. Such delays are almost never included when the performance of a structure is assessed, and they plainly should be.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If upstream passage has been imperfectly addressed, the downstream journey has been largely neglected. Young salmon heading for the sea, and adult eels returning to the ocean to spawn, must find a way past the same dams, and in practice many are drawn into the turbines of hydroelectric plants. Mortality there varies enormously from site to site, depending on the type of turbine and the speed at which its blades rotate; fish may be struck directly or injured by sudden changes in water pressure. Fine screens can divert them into bypass channels, but screens with a mesh small enough to stop juvenile fish quickly become clogged with leaves and debris and restrict the flow of water to the turbines, reducing the amount of electricity generated. Operators have therefore often been reluctant to install them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts so pessimistic a reading. Lerato Sefularo, a hydraulic engineer with the Southern Rivers Design Consultancy, contends that the disappointing figures reflect obsolete designs and poor maintenance rather than any flaw in the principle of fish passage. She is a leading advocate of so-called nature-like fishways: broad channels lined with boulders and gravel that bypass the dam and imitate the varied currents of a natural stream. Because they offer both fast and slow water, such channels can be used by a far wider range of species, and Sefularo reports efficiencies above seventy per cent at sites she has designed. These results are genuinely encouraging, yet they come almost entirely from low dams on lowland rivers. A nature-like channel needs a great deal of space and a gentle gradient, which makes it all but impossible to build beside a tall dam in a narrow, steep-sided valley.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more radical critique comes from Mahina Kealamakia, an ecologist with the Pacific Watershed Collective. In her view, fish passage has functioned less as a conservation measure than as a licence to build, allowing approval for dams that would otherwise have been rejected on environmental grounds. She maintains that the resources devoted to ever more elaborate fishways would be better spent removing obsolete barriers and protecting the rivers that remain free-flowing. There is considerable force in this argument, but it does little for the fish in rivers whose dams will remain standing for decades to come. For those populations, better passage is not a distraction from the real solution; it is the only realistic help available.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the field most urgently needs is more honest measurement. A fishway should be judged not by its existence, nor even by the number of fish counted through it, but by whether the population upstream of the dam recovers. Few monitoring programmes run for long enough to answer that question, since migratory species may take many years to return from the sea. Until such evidence exists, claims that large dams and healthy populations of migratory fish can coexist should be treated as hypotheses awaiting proof rather than as established facts.

topic: qanats: ancient underground water channels and lessons for sustainable groundwater use
title: Tunnels of Patience
subtitle: Ancient underground channels that still water some desert towns are being reconsidered as models for sustainable water use

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the arid uplands of Iran, and across a broad belt of dry country stretching from Morocco to western China, gently sloping tunnels carry groundwater from the foot of mountains to fields and settlements many kilometres away. Known as qanats in Persian, foggaras in Algeria and aflaj in Oman, these channels are among the oldest water-supply systems still in use. A typical qanat begins at a mother well sunk into an aquifer near the hills. From there, a tunnel barely large enough for a person to crawl through runs downhill at a slight gradient until it emerges at the surface. A line of vertical shafts, resembling a chain of small craters when seen from the air, provides ventilation and access for maintenance. Some systems are thought to be more than two thousand years old.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The engineering is impressive, but what makes qanats interesting to modern water managers is their relationship with the aquifer. Because a qanat relies on gravity alone, it can deliver only the water that flows naturally into it: when the water table falls, the flow diminishes, and when it rises, the flow increases. Parisa Zandieh, a hydrologist at the Kerman Centre for Arid Lands Research, describes this as a built-in brake on overuse. In her view, the qanat imposed sustainability not by rule but by physics, since a community could never take more than the aquifer was able to give. Mechanised wells, by contrast, can keep pumping long after the natural inflow has been exceeded, and their spread since the 1950s has, she argues, been the main cause of the drying up of thousands of qanats.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Zandieh's account is persuasive as far as it goes, but it overlooks the human institutions that made qanats work. Yusuf Karabekir, a historian at the Anatolian Institute for Rural Studies, has examined centuries of water-sharing records from oasis towns. He found that the flow of each qanat was divided among families according to elaborate timetables, often measured with a bowl that sank in water at a fixed rate. Ownership of these time-shares could be bought, sold and inherited, and disputes were settled by an elected water master. For Karabekir, the true achievement was social rather than technical. Without such arrangements, he contends, the channels would have been fought over and neglected long before the first wells arrived.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Maintenance was another collective burden. Tunnels collapse, silt accumulates and roots invade, and a specialist class of diggers, known in Iran as muqannis, cleaned and repaired them, often at considerable personal risk. Some tunnels are so narrow that the diggers must work lying on their sides by lamplight. Hélène Daubigny, an anthropologist at the Lyon Institute of Desert Societies, has interviewed some of the last practitioners of the craft. She reports that it is disappearing not only because the work is dangerous and young people are moving to the cities, but also because the system of payment, once funded jointly by all the holders of water shares, has collapsed as land has been divided into ever smaller plots through inheritance. Her findings suggest that the decline of the qanat is as much an economic story as an environmental one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Recent years have seen a revival of interest. Several governments have funded restoration programmes, and international heritage bodies have recognised some systems as being of outstanding cultural value. In a few places tourism has followed, with visitors guided through short, lit sections of tunnel. Omar al-Tuwaijri, a water engineer with the Gulf Desert Agriculture Programme, has led efforts to restore aflaj in the region and believes that such systems could once again supply a significant share of rural water needs. He points to channels whose flow returned within two years of repairs being completed. These successes are real, but they have come mainly from areas in which the drilling of wells has been restricted. Where pumping nearby continues unchecked, restoration merely refurbishes a tunnel with no water in it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Al-Tuwaijri's optimism should therefore be tempered. Qanats cannot be revived in isolation from the management of the aquifer as a whole, and that requires limiting the very wells on which most modern farming in these regions depends. Nor should the systems be romanticised. Their flow cannot be increased in times of drought, precisely when demand is greatest, and the old water-sharing arrangements often excluded those without inherited rights, including many women and landless labourers. A qanat also runs continuously, day and night, whether or not its water is needed, so that a considerable proportion may flow away unused during the cooler months.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The value of the qanat today, then, lies less in a technology to be copied than in a principle to be learned. Its lesson is that water use remains sustainable only when withdrawal is tied to replenishment, and when the people who depend on a resource share responsibility for its upkeep. Modern societies, equipped with powerful pumps, have largely abandoned both conditions. Restoring them does not require anyone to dig tunnels, but it does require institutions with the authority to insist that some water must be left in the ground. It is a lesson that applies well beyond the deserts where these tunnels were first dug.

topic: greenhouse gas emissions from hydropower reservoirs
title: The Hidden Breath of Reservoirs
subtitle: Hydropower has long been counted as carbon-free. Measurements from flooded valleys are complicating that picture

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Hydropower generates roughly a sixth of the world's electricity, more than all other renewable sources put together. For most of the twentieth century it was assumed that, once a dam had been built, the power it produced came with negligible emissions of greenhouse gases: the water fell, the turbines turned, and nothing was burned. Since the 1990s, however, scientists who have taken measurements on the surface of reservoirs have found that many of them release significant quantities of carbon dioxide and, more worryingly, methane, a gas whose short-term warming effect is many times greater. That reservoirs emit gases is no longer seriously disputed. How much they emit, and how those emissions ought to be counted, are different matters, and the debate on both has been rather more confused than it needed to be.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic mechanism is well understood. When a valley is flooded, the trees, shrubs and soils it contained are submerged, and in the deep water near the bottom of the reservoir, where oxygen is quickly exhausted, their decomposition produces methane rather than carbon dioxide. The process does not end once the original vegetation has rotted away, because the inflowing river continues to deliver leaves, soil and other organic material year after year. Methane escapes in several ways: as bubbles rising from shallow sediments, by slow diffusion across the water surface, and, most strikingly, when water drawn from the depths passes through the turbines. The sudden fall in pressure releases the dissolved gas in much the same way that opening a bottle of fizzy drink releases its bubbles, and emissions can remain elevated for some distance downstream of the dam.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most alarming figures have come from the tropics. Thiago Marangoni, a limnologist at the Amazonian Freshwater Institute, spent six years monitoring fourteen reservoirs in lowland rainforest regions. Several of them, he found, emitted more greenhouse gas for each unit of electricity generated than a modern gas-fired power station. The worst performers shared three characteristics: they were shallow, they covered large areas of former forest, and they generated relatively little power. Emissions were at their highest during the first ten to fifteen years after flooding and declined thereafter, although in none of the reservoirs did they fall to zero. Marangoni argues that no new dam in the lowland tropics should be approved until its likely emissions have been independently assessed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Engineers working in cooler regions have reacted to such findings with some impatience. Halvor Tveitane, of the Nordic Hydropower Research Council, points out that the reservoirs he has studied in boreal and mountain areas emit only a tiny fraction of the quantities reported from the Amazon. Cold water slows decomposition, little vegetation was flooded in the first place, and deep, narrow valleys allow a large amount of power to be produced from each hectare of flooded land. Hydropower, he insists, is not a single technology but thousands of individual sites, and tropical figures should not be used to condemn it as a whole. This is a fair point, but it cuts both ways. If no generalisation is possible, then the industry cannot claim that hydropower in general is clean either; each scheme must demonstrate its own credentials.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A subtler difficulty concerns accounting. Jun-seo Byeon, an environmental scientist at the East Asian Centre for Carbon Accounting, observes that a river and its floodplain were already exchanging carbon with the atmosphere before any dam was built. Wetlands along the valley floor may have been releasing methane naturally, while some of the carbon that settles in reservoir sediments may stay buried for thousands of years. What matters, Byeon argues, is the net change caused by the dam, not the gross quantity of gas observed at the surface afterwards. By his estimate, ignoring both factors may overstate global reservoir emissions by around a third. The principle is sound, but applying it is another matter: establishing what a valley emitted before it was flooded is rarely possible once the water has risen, and few baseline surveys were carried out in advance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Practical remedies do exist. Esi Amoako-Tuffour, a policy analyst at the West African Energy Policy Forum, has compiled a list of measures that developers could adopt. Trees and other vegetation can be cleared before flooding, a costly task that is sometimes partly paid for by selling the timber. Water for the turbines can be drawn from near the surface of the reservoir rather than from the oxygen-poor depths, where dissolved methane accumulates. Above all, new dams can be sited in steep valleys, where a small flooded area supports a large output of power. These measures are welcome, and some are inexpensive. None of them, however, can alter the basic geography of a shallow reservoir spread across a flat lowland plain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The sensible conclusion is that hydropower should be treated neither as automatically green nor as inherently harmful. Some dams produce electricity with emissions lower than almost any alternative; others are, in climate terms, little better than fossil-fuel plants. What is indefensible is the continued practice, in many national inventories, of leaving reservoir emissions out of the official figures altogether. Until those emissions are measured and reported as routinely as those from power stations, decisions about new dams will continue to be made on the basis of an incomplete account.

topic: flood management: raising embankments versus giving rivers room to spread
title: Making Room for Floods
subtitle: After centuries of building ever-higher embankments, some engineers argue that rivers should be allowed to spread out. Not everyone is convinced

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of recorded history, protecting people from rivers has meant building walls of earth along their banks. Embankments, or levees, keep floodwater in the channel and allow towns, roads and farms to occupy the fertile flat land on either side. As settlements grew, the banks were raised, and when a flood overtopped them, they were raised again. Yet despite enormous investment in such defences, the damage caused by river floods has continued to climb in many parts of the world. It is tempting to explain this entirely by pointing to heavier rainfall or to growing populations. Those factors matter, but the fact that ever-stronger defences have coincided with ever-greater losses is not simply a coincidence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Geographers have long described a phenomenon known as the levee effect. Embankments create a sense of security that encourages development in the very areas they protect, so that when a bank eventually fails or is overtopped, far more is lost than would have been at risk without it. Saoirse Cullinane, a geographer at the Shannon Institute for Flood Studies, examined sixty years of building records from floodplain districts and found that, within two decades of an embankment being raised, construction in the protected zone increased by an average of forty per cent. Embankments can also cause harm elsewhere. By confining a river to a narrow channel, they prevent water from spreading across the floodplain as it once did, and the extra volume is pushed further along the river, raising flood levels downstream.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An alternative approach, increasingly popular among engineers in lowland Europe, is to give rivers more space rather than higher walls. Embankments can be moved back from the water's edge, floodplains can be lowered, and bypass channels can be dug to carry surplus water around towns during high flows. Some farmland can be designated as retention areas, to be flooded deliberately when necessary in order to protect cities further downstream. Jorien Kloosterziel, a civil engineer at the Delta Water Engineering Institute, led a modelling study which suggested that a combination of these measures along one major river could lower peak flood levels by up to thirty centimetres at critical points, providing the same degree of safety as raising the banks while also creating wetland habitat and space for recreation. Kloosterziel insists that the approach is not an abandonment of engineering but a different kind of engineering, one that works with the river's natural behaviour.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that space has to come from somewhere, and much of it is currently farmed. Ilinca Drăgulescu, a sociologist at the Danube Rural Studies Centre, interviewed farmers whose fields had been designated as retention areas. Many felt that they were being asked to give up their livelihoods so that city dwellers could stay dry. Compensation for each flood often arrived late and rarely reflected the long-term damage caused when floodwater left behind sand and pollutants on productive soil. Drăgulescu concludes that the main obstacle to such schemes is not hydraulic but a lack of trust, and she notes that plans imposed without genuine negotiation have provoked resistance that delayed them by as much as a decade. She is surely right, and planners have too often treated landowners' objections as a problem of public relations rather than as a legitimate grievance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some economists doubt that the new approach can be applied widely. Kofi Antwi-Boasiako, of the Institute for Infrastructure Finance, observes that giving land back to rivers works best where land is cheap and population sparse. In the densely populated cities that have grown up on the world's great river deltas, there is simply no space to give, and embankments will remain indispensable for the foreseeable future. He also notes that several of the best-known schemes were expensive in relation to the number of people they protected. His objection is valid for the most crowded cities, but it does not follow that embankments should be the default choice everywhere else. In practice, the most successful flood strategies combine both approaches, using walls where land is scarce and space where it is available.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Climate change adds urgency to these choices. Embankments are usually designed to withstand a flood of a particular size, often one expected about once a century, and in many river basins events of that magnitude are now projected to occur far more often. Banks cannot be raised indefinitely: each increase adds weight to soft soils that may subside, and each makes the consequences of a failure more severe. Measures that give rivers room, by contrast, can be extended gradually as conditions change, and this flexibility is arguably their greatest advantage.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The most significant change, however, is in thinking rather than in technique. The older goal of flood control assumed that water could always be kept out; the newer goal of flood management accepts that some flooding is inevitable and asks where it will do the least harm. Answering that question is a political decision as much as an engineering one, because it means choosing whose land will be wet. It is far better for societies to make that choice openly and in advance than to allow a breached embankment to make it for them.
