topic: tradable water rights and water markets in dry river basins
title: Pricing the River
subtitle: Allowing water rights to be bought and sold has been hailed as an answer to scarcity. The experience of the places that have tried it is decidedly mixed

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In most societies, the right to take water from a river has traditionally been tied to the ownership of land, allocated either according to seniority, so that the earliest users had the strongest claims, or through permits issued by officials. Such systems have the merit of stability, but they are notoriously rigid. In a drought, water may continue to be poured onto low-value crops while nearby towns face rationing, simply because the farmers hold older rights. From the 1960s onwards, economists began to argue that rights should be separated from land and made tradable, so that water would move, through voluntary sales, to those who valued it most. Over recent decades, a number of dry regions on several continents have adopted versions of this idea. Their experience offers one of the few genuine opportunities to test in practice a proposition that economists had long debated only in theory.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case for markets rests above all on flexibility. Bronwyn Tregear, an agricultural economist at the Inland Basin Policy Unit, has analysed twenty years of trading records from one large river basin. During a prolonged drought, she found, growers of fruit trees and vines, which die if they are not watered, were able to buy allocations from rice and cotton farmers, who could leave their fields unplanted for a season and recover the following year. By her estimate, the agricultural output lost to the drought was roughly half what it would have been had trade been prohibited. For Tregear, the virtue of the market is not that it creates more water, which of course it cannot, but that it allows a shortage to fall where it causes the least damage.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics concentrate on what markets leave out. Ramón Echevarría-Lutz, a legal scholar at the Andean Water Law Observatory, has studied a country in which water rights were converted into private property several decades ago, with very few restrictions on their sale. Over time, he found, rights became concentrated in the hands of mining companies and large export-oriented farms. Small farmers and indigenous communities who sold during hard times rarely managed to buy their rights back, and some rights were acquired by investors who held them unused in the expectation that prices would rise. Echevarría-Lutz concludes that water should be treated as a public good, with trading allowed only within strict limits set by the state. His evidence is troubling, but it arguably says more about badly designed markets than about markets in general, since the system he studied contained almost no environmental or social safeguards.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A less obvious difficulty lies in the gap between rights on paper and water in the river. Arvid Lindeblad, a hydrologist at the Institute for Basin Hydrology, points out that in many basins the total volume of rights issued exceeds the water that actually flows, because officials once granted permits generously in the knowledge that many would never be exercised. When such dormant rights are sold to active users, total extraction rises even though no new right has been created. Lindeblad also draws attention to return flows. A farmer who irrigates inefficiently allows much of the water to seep back into the river, where users further downstream depend on it. If that water is sold to an efficient user, or transferred out of the basin altogether, downstream flows decline. Markets, Lindeblad contends, require far more sophisticated hydrological accounting than most governments currently possess.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Then there is the environment, which cannot bid for water on its own behalf. In some basins, governments have entered the market as buyers, purchasing rights in order to restore flows to wetlands and floodplain forests. Tadashi Morikubo, an environmental economist with the Pacific Resource Economics Group, compared these purchases with subsidies for infrastructure intended to save water, such as lining canals or installing drip irrigation. He found that buying water directly achieved environmental gains at considerably lower cost, partly because so-called efficiency projects often reduced return flows and so saved less water than claimed. The purchases have nevertheless proved politically contentious, with rural towns blaming them for falling populations. Morikubo notes that in most cases the decline began well before any purchases and owed more to mechanisation and repeated drought.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What emerges from these studies is that markets are neither a cure for scarcity nor a licence for plunder. Their value depends on preconditions: a cap on total extraction based on the water that is really available, accurate metering of what is used, and protection for third parties and for the environment. Where these are absent, trading tends simply to accelerate the over-allocation of rivers that are already overused. Where they are present, it can be an effective way of adjusting to scarcity. The most common mistake has been to introduce trading first and to set limits afterwards, which is precisely the reverse of the order required.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One consequence of markets is rarely discussed. By attaching a price to water, they make visible choices that were previously hidden inside administrative decisions: how much a vineyard is worth compared with a wetland, or a mine compared with a village. Many people find such comparisons distasteful, and their discomfort is understandable. But the fact that a debate is uncomfortable does not make it undesirable, and the alternative is not to avoid such choices but merely to make them out of public view.

topic: daylighting: uncovering urban streams buried in pipes and culverts
title: Rivers Under the Pavement
subtitle: Cities around the world are uncovering streams that were buried a century ago. Whether this amounts to genuine restoration is less certain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As cities expanded during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, thousands of small streams disappeared from view. They were enclosed in brick tunnels or concrete pipes, and roads, railways and buildings were laid on top of them. The motives were understandable. Many urban streams had become little more than open sewers, spreading disease and foul smells, and covering them released valuable land for development. As a result, numerous cities now contain more kilometres of buried watercourse than of visible river. In recent decades, however, a growing number of municipalities have begun to reverse the process, removing the covering and returning streams to open channels, a practice known as daylighting. Such projects are usually presented as a simple act of restoration. The reality is more complicated, and in many ways more interesting.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most celebrated schemes have transformed entire districts. In one East Asian capital, an elevated motorway was demolished to expose the stream beneath it, creating a linear park several kilometres long that now attracts millions of visitors each year. Kenji Utsunomiya, an urban planner at the Institute for Metropolitan Landscape, surveyed fifty daylighting projects and found that the value of homes within half a kilometre of the reopened stream rose by between fifteen and twenty-five per cent within five years. He also recorded summer air temperatures up to three degrees lower beside the open water than in surrounding streets. On the strength of such evidence, Utsunomiya regards daylighting as among the most cost-effective forms of urban regeneration available to city authorities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ecologists are more guarded. Fatou Ndiongue, a freshwater ecologist at the Coastal Cities Ecology Unit, acknowledges that an open channel exposed to sunlight can support algae, insects and eventually fish, whereas a buried pipe is almost lifeless. Her concern is with the water itself. In many cases, the springs that once fed a buried stream have been sealed beneath buildings or diverted into drains, so that the reopened channel would run dry for much of the year. To keep it flowing, authorities pump in water from a larger river or release treated wastewater, sometimes at considerable cost in energy. Ndiongue argues that such projects are better described as ornamental water features than as restored ecosystems. Her judgement is severe, but it is not without foundation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Engineers point to constraints that critics sometimes overlook. Bogdan Ilievski, a hydraulic engineer at the Balkan Urban Water Institute, observes that a naturalistic stream with meanders and gently sloping banks typically requires three to five times the width of a straight channel with stone walls, and such space is rarely available in a crowded city. An open stream must also carry the sudden storm flows previously handled by the culvert, which often means steep sides and a deep bed, and there are legitimate concerns about the safety of children. Ilievski therefore defends hard-edged channels as a realistic compromise. Even an architectural stream, he argues, is a great improvement on a pipe, because it can be inspected and maintained easily, whereas the collapse of ageing brick culverts poses a serious risk to the streets above them. On this point, he is surely right.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some of the most important effects may be social rather than physical. Rosalind Featherstonehaugh, a cultural historian at the Northern School of Urban History, has studied how communities respond to reopened streams. Buried watercourses, she notes, often survive in street names, in local stories and in the dips and curves of old roads. In projects where residents were invited to help research the history of their stream, the finished channel later received more volunteer care and suffered less vandalism than in projects designed entirely by outside experts. Featherstonehaugh suggests that this renewed sense of attachment to place may prove the most durable benefit of daylighting. The idea is plausible, although it is difficult to measure, and the evidence so far comes from a small number of cases.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Less often discussed is the question of who benefits. The rise in property prices that Utsunomiya treats as a measure of success can also signal that long-standing, lower-income residents are being priced out of neighbourhoods that have suddenly become fashionable. It is curious that the same figure is used to proclaim a project's achievement when it may equally indicate displacement, and planners ought to ask whose quality of life a reopened stream is actually improving. Costs, too, are frequently underestimated, since electricity cables, water mains and other services that were laid along the route of a buried stream must often be relocated before any excavation can begin.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that daylighting is misguided. What it cannot do is recreate the stream that was lost: the catchment around it has been transformed beyond recognition, and its springs lie sealed beneath concrete. Yet perhaps it does not need to. What can be achieved is a new kind of urban waterway, one that cools streets, supports some wildlife and reconnects people with the landscape beneath their city. It would be more honest, and ultimately more productive, for planners to promise exactly that, with modest and measurable goals, rather than to claim that a river has been brought back to life.

topic: task-switching costs: reconfiguration versus interference accounts and self-interruption at work
title: The Price of Changing Course
subtitle: Psychologists agree that switching between tasks is costly, but not on why, or on what the finding means for working life

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few claims about modern working life are repeated as confidently as the idea that some people are natural multitaskers, able to answer messages, follow a meeting and draft a document all at once. Laboratory psychology tells a less flattering story. When the tasks in question require deliberate thought, the brain does not perform them simultaneously; it alternates between them, and each alternation carries a price. For this reason, the word 'multitasking' is arguably a misnomer: what it describes is not parallel processing but a sequence of hurried transitions. In a typical experiment, volunteers see a digit or a letter on a screen and must classify it according to one of two rules, such as odd or even, or vowel or consonant. On trials where the rule changes, responses are slower and less accurate than on trials where it stays the same, even when both rules are trivially easy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why should such a switch cost exist at all? The most influential answer, associated with Aino Hirvonen of the Baltic Institute for Cognitive Science, holds that every task depends on a mental 'task set', a configuration of rules, goals and response mappings that must be assembled before the task can be carried out. Changing tasks, on this view, means dismantling one configuration and building another, and that work takes time. Hirvonen's strongest evidence comes from experiments in which participants are told in advance which rule will apply next. Given a warning of half a second or more, they respond considerably faster on switch trials, apparently because they use the interval to prepare. Yet the cost never vanishes entirely. Even with generous preparation time, a stubborn 'residual' delay remains, and Hirvonen concedes that her account struggles to explain why advance knowledge should not be sufficient to complete the reconfiguration.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A rival explanation locates the problem not in the new task but in the old one. Tunde Oyediran of the West African Centre for Behavioural Research, argues that a task set, once activated, does not simply switch off when it is no longer needed. Instead it lingers, competing with the incoming task and having to be actively suppressed. The most compelling support for this idea is a curious asymmetry. When people alternate between a demanding task and a familiar, effortless one, it is the switch back to the easy task that produces the larger delay. Oyediran's interpretation is that the dominant, well-practised task must be strongly inhibited while the difficult one is being performed, and that this inhibition takes time to overcome. It is hard to see how a pure reconfiguration account could predict such a pattern, since setting up a simple task ought to be quicker than setting up a complex one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Marco Pagliarulo, of the Adriatic School of Psychology, regards the dispute as largely artificial. In his view, both preparation and lingering interference contribute to every switch, and the weight of each depends on the circumstances. This compromise is sensible, but it leaves untouched a weakness that both camps share. The tasks used in switching experiments last a fraction of a second and involve a single, clearly defined rule. Real work rarely resembles this. Drafting a report involves holding a complex web of intentions and partial results in mind, and it is the loss of this web, rather than a delay of a few hundred milliseconds, that makes interruptions so damaging. None of this means that laboratory findings should be set aside; they remain the only reliable way of isolating the mechanisms involved. But they cannot, on their own, tell us what switching costs an office.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It is precisely this gap that Gulnara Kurmanbekova, an organisational psychologist at the Central Asian Institute of Work Studies, has tried to fill. Using software that logs which application is active on screen, her team recorded the working days of over two hundred office employees. The average period spent on a single application before moving to another was less than a minute. More surprisingly, roughly half of these changes were not prompted by an incoming message or a colleague's question; employees interrupted themselves, often for no obvious reason. Kurmanbekova also found that those who switched most frequently reported higher levels of stress and time pressure, yet over the month-long study they completed no fewer assigned tasks than their more focused colleagues.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If switching is costly, can people be trained to do it better? A group at the Montreal Laboratory for Applied Attention has examined this question. Participants who spent several weeks alternating between particular pairs of tasks did become markedly faster at switching between them. However, the improvement proved stubbornly specific: when the same participants were asked to switch between unfamiliar tasks, they performed no better than untrained volunteers. This finding should give pause to the many companies that market courses promising to enhance employees' general multitasking capacity. On the evidence currently available, such claims go well beyond what the research can support.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to treat every switch as a small act of self-sabotage, and some commentators recommend eliminating interruptions altogether. That prescription seems to me both impractical and mistaken. Changing activity can relieve fatigue, and a brief move to a different task sometimes allows a stalled problem to be seen afresh. The more useful distinction is not between switching and concentrating but between switches that people choose and switches imposed on them by others. Kurmanbekova's data suggest that much of the fragmentation of modern work is self-generated, which implies that the most effective remedies may lie less in redesigning offices than in helping individuals to recognise and govern their own habits of attention.

topic: inattentional blindness in expert observers such as radiologists and pilots
title: Looking Without Seeing
subtitle: Why trained specialists can miss what is directly in front of their eyes

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In one of the best-known demonstrations in psychology, viewers are asked to watch a short film of people passing a ball and to count the number of passes made by one team. Partway through, a figure in an animal costume strolls across the scene, pauses, and walks off. Remarkably, around half of first-time viewers fail to notice it at all. The phenomenon, known as inattentional blindness, shows that seeing is not simply a matter of having an object in front of one's eyes: what reaches awareness depends heavily on where attention is directed. Such demonstrations are often presented as amusing curiosities, the kind of thing shown at the start of a lecture to wake up an audience. Yet this reputation does them a disservice, because the effect has serious consequences for any profession in which people must search complex scenes for things that matter.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Radiology is an obvious case. Lerato Tlali, a medical imaging specialist at the Southern Highlands Diagnostic Institute, asked experienced radiologists to examine a series of lung scans for signs of cancer. Unknown to them, one scan contained a small cartoon figure, many times larger than a typical tumour, inserted into the lung tissue. More than two-thirds of the radiologists did not report it. More striking still, eye-tracking equipment showed that most of those who missed the figure had looked directly at the place where it appeared. Tlali concludes that expertise offers no protection against the effect and may even intensify it. Years of practice, she argues, teach specialists to search with great efficiency for particular targets, and this efficiency comes at the price of a narrower window of awareness, so that anything falling outside the expected categories is more easily overlooked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts this interpretation. Jerzy Kasprzak of the Vistula Institute of Perception points out that a cartoon figure has no clinical meaning, and that an expert who ignores it is simply doing what expertise requires, namely filtering out information irrelevant to the task. The real question, in his view, is how often radiologists overlook unexpected findings that do matter, such as a fractured rib on a scan ordered for a suspected lung condition. His review of hospital audit data suggests that such omissions, while they certainly occur, are considerably less frequent than the dramatic laboratory figures imply. Kasprzak has a point: memorable demonstrations do give an inflated sense of how often specialists miss significant abnormalities. But his argument underestimates a well-documented hazard. When a radiologist has already found one abnormality, the probability of missing a second rises sharply, as though the discovery brought the search to a premature close. This tendency, sometimes called 'satisfaction of search', has nothing to do with irrelevant cartoons.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Similar concerns arise in aviation. Many modern aircraft are fitted with head-up displays, which project speed, altitude and other flight data onto a transparent screen in the pilot's line of sight, allowing information to be read without looking down at the instruments. In simulator trials run by Somphone Inthavong at the Mekong Aviation Safety Centre, pilots carrying out landings occasionally failed to notice another aircraft that had moved onto the runway ahead of them. Crucially, such failures were more common when the display was switched on than when it was off. Inthavong suggests that placing data on top of the view outside may draw attention towards the symbols and away from the world beyond them, and she is now testing displays that briefly dim when the aircraft is close to the ground.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why do some observers notice the unexpected while others do not? Rosa Delgadillo, a cognitive scientist at the Pacific Coast Laboratory of Attention, initially proposed that people with a greater working memory capacity, who can hold more information in mind at once, would be more likely to spot unexpected objects. Attempts to replicate this link, however, have produced inconsistent results, and Delgadillo herself has shifted her emphasis. Her more recent experiments show that what matters most is the resemblance between the unexpected object and whatever observers are currently attending to. People counting passes made by players dressed in black, for instance, are far more likely to notice a dark intruder than a pale one. Of all the findings in this field, this seems to me the most robust, and it is certainly the most useful for anyone trying to design safer systems.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What follows for practice? The instinctive response is to urge professionals to be more vigilant, but such exhortation is largely futile. Inattentional blindness is not a sign of carelessness; it is a by-product of the very selectivity that allows attention to work efficiently in the first place. More promising are measures built into the structure of the work: checklists that require radiologists to review the whole image once the main question has been answered, for example, or the independent reading of each scan by two specialists. The same reasoning applies to the courts, which still tend to treat a failure to see something obvious as proof of negligence. Legal standards of reasonable care would be fairer if they reflected what research has revealed about the limits of human perception.

topic: the vigilance decrement in sustained monitoring: resource, underload and opportunity-cost explanations
title: The Long Watch
subtitle: Why people who monitor screens and machines for rare events grow steadily worse at it, and what the competing explanations imply

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: During the Second World War, military planners noticed a troubling pattern among the operators who watched radar screens for the faint signals of enemy submarines. Within half an hour of starting a watch, operators were detecting markedly fewer targets, even though nothing about the equipment had changed. This 'vigilance decrement' has since been documented wherever people must monitor for rare and unpredictable events: among airport baggage screeners, lifeguards, security staff scanning banks of camera feeds and inspectors checking products on assembly lines. The phenomenon might seem a relic of an era of primitive technology, but the opposite is true. Automation increasingly leaves human beings with the job of supervising machines that rarely fail, and the more reliable the machine, the rarer the events the human must catch. The problem of the long watch is therefore becoming more pressing, not less.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For several decades the dominant explanation has been that vigilance is far harder work than it looks. Hanta Ravelojaona of the Indian Ocean Institute of Human Factors argues that sustained monitoring draws on a limited pool of mental resources which is gradually depleted, much as a muscle tires under a constant load. Her case rests on two kinds of evidence. When participants complete standard workload questionnaires after a vigilance session, they rate the experience as highly demanding and stressful, scoring it alongside tasks that most people would regard as genuinely difficult. And when blood flow in the brain is measured during such sessions, it declines over time in close parallel with the fall in detection rates.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Armen Ravensworth, an ergonomist at the Caucasus Centre for Work Design, turns this account on its head. In his view, the problem with vigilance tasks is not that they are too demanding but that they are too dull. Faced with long stretches in which nothing happens, the mind drifts away to more interesting matters, and the missed targets are simply the moments when attention happens to be elsewhere. Participants in his studies frequently report that their thoughts wandered during the session. Ravensworth also points to a finding that resource theory struggles to accommodate: when targets are made more frequent, detection improves, even though more targets should mean more work and therefore faster depletion.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It might be tempting to dismiss this disagreement as academic, since both sides accept that performance falls. That would be a mistake, because the two theories point towards opposite remedies. If the decrement reflects exhaustion, operators need lighter workloads and more rest; if it reflects boredom, they need more stimulation. My own view is that neither theory deserves outright victory. Ravensworth's frequency effect is genuine, but the workload ratings that Ravelojaona cites are hard to reconcile with the claim that vigilance is undemanding; people do not normally describe mere boredom as exhausting labour.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A third position, developed by Grace Mukasa at the Great Lakes Cognitive Science Unit, attempts to move beyond the choice between fatigue and boredom. Mukasa proposes that the brain continuously compares the value of the current activity with the value of the alternatives it could be pursuing. As a monotonous task continues, the balance shifts, and attention is gradually redirected, not because resources have run out but because the task no longer seems worth them. Consistent with this, she has shown that the decline can be temporarily reversed when participants are told that the session is nearly over, producing a late surge of accuracy. The theory is elegant, but it carries a risk: an account in which almost any pattern of results can be explained by a change in perceived value may prove difficult to test.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Laboratory sessions, however, are not the same as real watches. Torunn Fagerli, who studies ships' officers for the Nordic Maritime Safety Board, found that the decline among officers on night watch was smaller than laboratory studies would predict, perhaps because the targets they look for, such as small vessels without lights, carry real consequences. Yet she also recorded brief episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds, concentrated in the hours before dawn, suggesting that the body clock can greatly worsen the effects of a long watch.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Efforts to counter the decrement take several forms. At many airports, screening systems project fictional threat images onto the X-ray pictures of real luggage, both to keep screeners alert and to measure how often they detect targets. In road transport, Kenji Kaminaga of the Pacific Rim Transport Research Institute has found that drivers supervising a partly automated car respond markedly more slowly to emergencies after about twenty minutes. He advocates engagement prompts, which require the driver to make occasional small steering or braking inputs. Critics object that such prompts may soon be answered as automatically as the task they were meant to interrupt.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Behind all of these measures lies an uncomfortable conclusion. Human beings are poorly equipped to watch, for long periods, for events that almost never happen. Designs that reduce people to passive observers of automated systems misunderstand the nature of attention, and it would be wiser either to keep operators actively involved in the task or to entrust the monitoring entirely to machines.

topic: hands-free phone conversations while driving: cognitive distraction versus real-world self-regulation
title: The Conversation at the Wheel
subtitle: Why keeping both hands on the steering wheel may not be enough to keep a driver's mind on the road

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In most countries that regulate the use of mobile phones by drivers, the law draws a sharp line between holding a handset and talking through a hands-free kit. The first is typically prohibited, carrying fines and penalty points; the second is permitted and, in some cases, actively promoted by car manufacturers as the responsible alternative. The distinction has an intuitive appeal. A driver who is gripping a phone has one hand fewer on the wheel and may glance down at a screen, whereas a driver using a headset keeps both hands free and eyes on the road. Yet the line rests on an assumption that a growing body of research calls into question: that the principal danger of a phone call lies in what it does to the hands and eyes rather than in what it does to the mind.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most widely cited evidence comes from driving simulators. In a series of experiments at the Danube Institute for Traffic Psychology, Dr Ilona Szatmari asked volunteers to follow a lead vehicle along a simulated motorway while either driving in silence or holding a conversation through a hands-free device. When the lead car braked unexpectedly, conversing drivers took significantly longer to respond, and afterwards they recalled fewer of the roadside signs they had passed. Strikingly, the degree of impairment was almost identical whether the phone was handheld or not. Szatmari interprets this as evidence of what she calls 'cognitive tunnelling': engaged in a demanding exchange, drivers continue to look at the road, but their processing of what they see becomes shallower, so that a hazard may fall on the retina without ever being registered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If conversation itself is the problem, one might expect talking to a passenger to be just as dangerous. It appears not to be. Observational work by Joseph Wanjohi at the Rift Valley Centre for Road Safety found that drivers chatting with an adult passenger performed considerably better than those talking on the phone, and his recordings suggest why. Passengers can see the road. When traffic thickens or a junction approaches, they tend to fall silent, slow the pace of the exchange, or even draw the driver's attention to a hazard. A caller at the other end of a line, by contrast, has no idea that the driver is negotiating a roundabout and keeps talking regardless. Of all the findings in this field, Wanjohi's seems to me the most revealing, because it shows that the difficulty lies less in conversation as such than in conversation that is blind to its circumstances.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that the laboratory picture reflects real roads. Mariela Ahumada, an epidemiologist with the Andean Transport Research Group, points out that although mobile phone ownership has risen enormously over the past three decades, crash rates per kilometre driven have not climbed in step; in several countries they have fallen. Simulators, she argues, overstate the risk because volunteers are instructed to keep talking, whereas real drivers adjust their behaviour: they slow down, leave larger gaps, postpone calls or end them abruptly when conditions become difficult. Ahumada is right that such self-regulation exists, and any honest account of the risk must allow for it. But it would be a mistake to treat it as a safeguard. Drivers are notoriously poor judges of their own impairment, and the same studies that document compensation show that it is weakest among young and inexperienced motorists, the group already most likely to be involved in collisions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The question has acquired fresh urgency with the spread of voice-controlled systems in new vehicles. Manufacturers market these as a way of keeping attention on the road, allowing drivers to dictate messages, change music or set a destination without touching a screen. Research by Kaveh Bakhtiari at the Caspian Human Factors Laboratory complicates this claim. Measuring drivers' reaction times before, during and after voice commands, his team found that mental workload remained elevated for as long as fifteen seconds after a task had been completed, as though the mind needed time to disengage. Systems that misrecognised commands, obliging drivers to repeat themselves, produced the heaviest load of all. Hands-free, in other words, does not mean attention-free.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What should follow for policy? The logical conclusion would be to extend restrictions to hands-free calls, and a few jurisdictions have done so for novice drivers. Enforcement, however, presents an obvious obstacle: a police officer can see a phone pressed to a driver's ear but cannot see a conversation conducted through the car's speakers. For this reason, I suspect that legislation alone will achieve relatively little. More could be gained by changing public understanding. Road safety campaigns still concentrate overwhelmingly on images of drivers typing messages, which reinforces the belief that the danger is manual and visual. Campaigns that explained the cost of divided attention, and that addressed callers as well as drivers, would arguably do more to change behaviour.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Underlying the whole debate is a comforting belief that experienced drivers operate largely on autopilot, leaving the mind free for other activities. There is some truth in this: the routine control of steering and speed does become highly automatic with practice. But detecting the unexpected, such as a child stepping out between parked cars, does not. It is precisely this capacity, rather than the mechanics of handling a vehicle, that a phone conversation erodes, and no amount of hardware placed on the dashboard is likely to restore it.

topic: the attentional blink: bottleneck, gating and awareness accounts of missing a second target in rapid visual streams
title: Half a Second of Darkness
subtitle: A brief lapse that follows every act of noticing is revealing how the mind decides what reaches awareness

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine watching a stream of letters flash up in the same spot on a screen, each visible for about a tenth of a second. Your task is simple: report the two digits hidden among them. If the second digit arrives more than about half a second after the first, most people see both without difficulty. If it arrives between roughly 200 and 500 milliseconds later, however, it frequently vanishes from awareness altogether, even though it was displayed just as clearly as the first. This brief period of functional blindness, known as the attentional blink, has been studied in hundreds of experiments since it was first described in the early 1990s. In my view, it offers one of the clearest windows we have onto the limits of conscious perception, and its importance has been seriously underrated outside the laboratories where it is measured.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The earliest and still most influential explanation treats the blink as a bottleneck. According to Aino Kauppinen of the Baltic Centre for Cognitive Science, a target that has been detected must then be consolidated, that is, transferred into working memory in a stable form that can later be reported. This consolidation stage can handle only one item at a time, and while it is occupied with the first target, the second must wait. Because the display moves on, the waiting item is overwritten by the letters that follow and is lost. The account is elegant, but it faces an awkward anomaly. When the second target appears in the very next position after the first, with no gap between them, it is usually reported quite accurately, a phenomenon known as lag-1 sparing. A strict bottleneck ought to make this the worst position of all, not one of the best. Kauppinen's response is that the two items enter consolidation together as a single episode, but this looks rather like an exception made to save the rule.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more radical proposal comes from Hery Rakotomalala at the Indian Ocean Institute of Neuroscience. In his view, the blink reflects not a shortage of capacity but an excess of caution. When a target is detected, the control system shuts the gate to protect it from the distractors that follow, and anything arriving while the gate is closed is excluded, target or not. The crucial evidence is that when three or four targets appear one after another, without distractors between them, participants report them all with little loss; the gate stays open as long as each new item is relevant. This seems to me the more persuasive of the two explanations, since it accounts naturally for lag-1 sparing, although it remains unclear exactly what triggers the gate to close.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most counterintuitive findings come from Selin Ozbilgin of the Bosporus Laboratory of Perception. She found that participants who listened to background music during the task, or who were asked to think about a recent holiday, showed a smaller blink than those who simply concentrated. Ozbilgin argues that over-investment of attention in the first target makes the gate close more firmly, and that a mild distraction spreads resources more evenly across the stream. The results are intriguing, but the effects she reports are modest, and at least two attempts to reproduce them have failed. It would therefore be premature to turn them into advice for students preparing for examinations.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are also striking differences between individuals. A small minority of people, sometimes called non-blinkers, show almost no blink at all. Tenzin Lhamo, of the Highland Institute for Contemplative Research, has reported that experienced meditators show a reduced blink and that a three-month retreat shrank it further, which he interprets as evidence that attention can be trained to distribute itself more flexibly. Such claims deserve caution. People who devote years to meditation may differ from the general population in ways that have nothing to do with the practice itself, and without random allocation to training it is difficult to know which came first.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recordings of electrical activity in the brain have added a further twist. Aminata Lepage-Oti and colleagues at the West African Centre for Brain Imaging presented words rather than digits and examined the brain responses to second targets that participants claimed not to have seen. These missed words still produced an electrical signature normally associated with the processing of meaning, and the signature was larger when the word was unrelated to the first target. Lepage-Oti concludes that during the blink the brain continues to analyse incoming information; what fails is not perception but access to awareness. If she is correct, the blink is less a gap in seeing than a gate on what can be consciously known.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whether any of this matters beyond the laboratory has been questioned, since everyday scenes rarely consist of items flashed one after another in a single location. The objection has some force, yet there are situations in which the laboratory conditions are closely approximated. A pilot faced with two cockpit warnings in quick succession, or a radiographer scanning a rapid sequence of images, may well be vulnerable. Designers of alarm systems could reduce the risk simply by ensuring that critical alerts are separated by at least half a second, a modest change that seems well worth making.

topic: the irrelevant sound effect: overheard speech, open-plan offices and remedies such as sound masking
title: The Trouble with Overheard Words
subtitle: Why the conversations of colleagues are so hard to ignore, and what might be done about them

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the walls came down in offices across the world in the second half of the twentieth century, the promise was that employees freed from cubicles and corridors would talk more, share ideas and work more collaboratively. Decades later, surveys of open-plan workers consistently place one complaint above all others: not the temperature, nor the lighting, nor the lack of privacy, but the sound of other people talking. Laboratory research suggests that this irritation is well founded. In a typical experiment, participants are shown a sequence of seven or eight digits and asked to recall them in order while recorded speech plays in the background. Their accuracy falls markedly, even when they have been told to ignore the speech, and even when it is in a language they do not understand. This so-called irrelevant sound effect is among the most dependable results in cognitive psychology, and yet it is striking how rarely it has informed the way offices are actually designed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Why should speech be so disruptive? According to Amra Habibovic of the Adriatic Institute of Applied Acoustics, the answer lies not in its meaning but in its structure. Speech consists of a rapid succession of different sounds, each syllable distinct from the last, and it is this 'changing state' that interferes with the mental rehearsal of a sequence. A steady sound, such as the hum of an air-conditioning unit, has almost no effect, and neither does a single tone repeated over and over; a series of tones that vary in pitch, on the other hand, is nearly as harmful as speech itself. Habibovic's account neatly explains the finding that an unfamiliar language disrupts recall: the listener need not understand a word for the brain to register the shifting pattern of sound.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Octavio Ruvalcaba of the Sonoran Centre for Workplace Research accepts this explanation for memory tasks but argues that it is incomplete. Office work, he points out, rarely involves memorising lists of digits; it involves reading, writing and checking documents, activities that draw on the same language-processing systems as listening. In his studies, performance on proofreading declined steadily as background speech became easier to understand, whereas unintelligible babble did comparatively little harm. Ruvalcaba has also drawn attention to the particular disruptiveness of overhearing one side of a telephone call. Because the listener hears only half of the exchange, the brain is drawn into predicting what the unheard speaker is saying. It has sometimes been assumed that the two researchers are in competition, but this seems to me a misreading: their accounts describe different mechanisms that come into play in different kinds of task.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These findings have inspired a range of remedies. The most common is sound masking, in which loudspeakers concealed in the ceiling emit a low, steady background noise that makes nearby conversation harder to follow. Trials conducted by Kavita Saraswat of the Deccan Ergonomics Group found that masking produced modest improvements in concentration tasks, but that the gains disappeared, and complaints increased, when the masking raised the overall sound level too far. Some designers have experimented with absorbent ceiling panels and partitions, which reduce the distance over which speech carries, though in a large open floor their effect is limited. Many employees prefer to solve the problem themselves by wearing headphones. Here, too, the research urges caution: music with lyrics introduces exactly the kind of changing, meaningful sound that does most damage, while instrumental music with a steady tempo is considerably less disruptive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not everyone regards overheard conversation as a straightforward cost. Freja Ostergard of the Nordic Organisational Studies Unit argues that laboratory studies exaggerate the problem, since people tested for an hour have no opportunity to adapt, whereas office workers gradually become accustomed to the voices around them over several months. She also stresses what is gained by overhearing: junior staff, in particular, absorb a great deal of practical knowledge simply by listening to how experienced colleagues handle problems. There is some evidence for habituation, but it is partial at best, and the benefits she describes are unevenly shared. Those who learn most from overhearing are usually not the people whose work demands the deepest concentration, so the advantages for one group are paid for by another.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most promising response is probably not to choose between open and enclosed offices but to provide both, allowing employees to move between collaborative areas and quiet zones according to the task in hand. Such arrangements, however, are only as effective as the norms that support them. A quiet zone in which colleagues feel free to take phone calls is no quieter than the open floor, and managers who expect such zones to work on their own, without discussing and modelling the behaviour they require, are likely to be disappointed. In the end, the problem of overheard speech is as much a matter of workplace culture as of acoustics.

topic: heavy media multitaskers: filtering deficits, replication, causal direction and breadth-of-attention accounts
title: Many Screens, One Mind
subtitle: Does a lifetime of juggling media streams change the way people pay attention, or has the case been overstated?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk into any university library and you will find students who are, by any reasonable definition, doing several things at once: a lecture recording plays in one window, a messaging app flickers in another, and a half-finished essay waits beneath both. For well over a decade, psychologists have asked whether this habit leaves a lasting mark on the mind. The question is not whether people perform worse while they are juggling tasks; on that point the evidence has been consistent for decades. It is whether those who habitually consume several streams of media at once become, over time, different kinds of thinkers even when they are doing only one thing. That is a far more ambitious claim, and it has arguably been accepted too readily by commentators eager for a simple story about technology and decline.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea gained momentum from a laboratory study conducted by Ingrid Haugsdal and her colleagues at the Bergen Institute for Cognitive Science. Participants first completed a questionnaire estimating how many hours per week they spent using two or more media simultaneously, from which the researchers derived a single multitasking score. Those at the top of the scale were then compared with those at the bottom on a series of attention tasks. In one, participants had to judge whether a set of red rectangles had changed orientation while ignoring blue rectangles scattered among them. Heavy multitaskers were noticeably worse at this when the number of blue distractors increased, which led Haugsdal to propose that they had a weaker ability to filter out irrelevant information. Counter-intuitively, they were also slower to switch between tasks, a skill one might expect constant practice to improve.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The findings were widely reported, often with a confidence that the original authors themselves never expressed. Subsequent attempts to reproduce them have produced a more mixed picture. A consortium coordinated by Adaeze Okonjo-Bassey at the University of the Western Highveld pooled data from more than twenty laboratories and several thousand participants. Its analysis found that the relationship between media multitasking and poorer filtering did exist, but that it was small, far smaller than early studies had implied, and that it disappeared altogether in several of the larger samples. Okonjo-Bassey attributes the discrepancy partly to the modest size of the first experiments, which typically compared a few dozen students at each extreme of the scale. Small samples, she notes, are prone to producing striking effects that later shrink. This is a familiar pattern in psychology, and it should make readers wary of any headline built on a single study.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even if a reliable association exists, its direction is far from obvious. The popular interpretation holds that heavy media use damages attention. Yet it is equally possible that people who already find it hard to ignore distractions are drawn to environments full of them. Kenji Oyabu, a developmental psychologist at Kansai Metropolitan University, followed around six hundred adolescents for three years, measuring both their media habits and their performance on attention tasks at regular intervals. He found that poor filtering at the start of the study predicted later increases in multitasking more strongly than early multitasking predicted later declines in filtering. Oyabu is careful not to claim that media use has no effect at all, and his sample was drawn from a single city. Nonetheless, his results seriously weaken the assumption that the causal arrow points in only one direction.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A different challenge comes from researchers who question whether the differences should be described as deficits at all. Raúl Sarmentero of the Andean Centre for Perception Research argues that heavy multitaskers adopt a broader style of attention, spreading their focus across the environment rather than narrowing it to a single target. Such a style is costly in a laboratory task that rewards ignoring everything except the red rectangles, but it may be advantageous elsewhere. In one experiment, heavy multitaskers were better than light multitaskers at detecting a sound that unexpectedly accompanied a visual target, apparently because they were monitoring more than one sense at a time. Sarmentero concedes that this advantage has not yet been demonstrated outside controlled conditions. Even so, his reframing is a valuable corrective: what counts as a weakness depends heavily on what a particular task demands.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are also grounds for doubting the measuring instrument itself. The multitasking score depends on people's recollections of their own behaviour over a typical week, and such estimates are notoriously unreliable. Studies that have compared self-reports with logging software installed on participants' phones and computers find only a moderate correspondence between the two. Moreover, the score treats very different activities as equivalent: listening to music while reading is counted in the same way as switching between a video call and an online game, although the cognitive demands of the two are hardly comparable. It is surprising that so much theorising has rested on so blunt a tool.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the original concern was baseless. Doing two demanding things at once remains a reliable way of doing both of them less well, and nothing in the recent research suggests otherwise. What the evidence does not support is the more dramatic claim that habitual multitasking permanently rewires the brain. Future work would benefit from objective measures of media use, larger and more diverse samples, and tasks that resemble the situations people actually encounter. Until then, the most defensible conclusion is a modest one: the habitually distracted mind is probably a little different, but whether it is damaged, differently skilled, or simply the same mind that was always inclined to wander remains an open question.

topic: mind-wandering: mood, reading comprehension, incubation and the deliberate versus spontaneous distinction
title: Elsewhere in Thought
subtitle: The tendency of attention to drift away from the present is no longer seen simply as a failure of concentration

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few mental activities are as common, or as little noticed, as the drift of attention away from the task in hand. A reader reaches the bottom of a page and realises that not a single sentence has registered; a commuter arrives at work with no memory of the journey. Estimates drawn from studies that interrupt people at random moments during the day suggest that thoughts unrelated to the current activity occupy somewhere between a third and a half of waking life. A habit so pervasive is unlikely to be a mere malfunction, and it is a weakness of much early research that mind-wandering was treated almost exclusively as a failure of concentration.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That research was not without foundation. Liisa Tervahauta, a psychologist at Northern Lakes University, developed a smartphone application that contacted thousands of volunteers at unpredictable times and asked what they were doing, what they were thinking about and how they felt. Her data showed that people reported lower mood when their thoughts had strayed than when they were focused, and that this held even when the activity itself was unpleasant. Tervahauta concluded that a wandering mind is an unhappy one. The pattern is striking, but the conclusion goes further than the data allow. Low mood could just as easily send the mind wandering as result from it, and Tervahauta's own later analyses suggest that pleasant daydreams were associated with no drop in mood at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The costs of inattention are clearer in tasks that demand continuous processing. Mateo Illanes and his team at the Austral Centre for Learning Science asked students to read textbook chapters while occasionally checking whether their minds were on the text. Episodes of wandering were followed by marked declines in comprehension, particularly when students had been unaware that their attention had lapsed until the question came. The effect was larger for difficult chapters than for easy ones. Illanes distinguishes between 'tuning out', in which a person knows that their thoughts have drifted, and 'zoning out', in which they do not. It is the latter, he argues, that causes most of the damage, because a reader who notices a lapse can simply go back and reread the paragraph.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers have stressed what the wandering mind achieves. Farida Noorzai, of the Rotterdam Institute for Creative Cognition, has examined what is known as the incubation effect. Participants who were given a difficult problem and then set to work on an undemanding task that allowed their minds to roam later produced more original solutions than those who spent the same interval either resting or working on something demanding. Noorzai also observes that a large proportion of wandering thoughts concern the future: plans, rehearsals of conversations and anticipated difficulties. On this view, the mind uses idle moments to organise the days ahead, a function that would be impossible if attention were permanently locked to the present. Noorzai is careful to add that incubation appears to help only when a problem has already been thoroughly explored before the break; a mind that has not yet grasped the difficulty has nothing useful to work on while it roams.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A further refinement comes from Bruno Zavattini at the Adriatic Institute of Psychology, who argues that the term covers two distinct phenomena. Some mind-wandering is deliberate: a person chooses to let their thoughts drift during a dull meeting, for instance. Other episodes are spontaneous, arriving uninvited. Zavattini's questionnaire studies indicate that only spontaneous wandering is strongly associated with everyday errors and with symptoms of attention disorders, whereas deliberate wandering seems largely harmless. This distinction deserves wider adoption, since lumping the two together almost certainly exaggerates the costs of mind-wandering in general.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Measurement poses its own difficulties. Nearly all the evidence relies on thought probes, brief questions that interrupt a task to ask where attention was a moment earlier. Probes depend on honest and accurate introspection, and people may not always know where their thoughts have been. More subtly, frequent probes may themselves alter behaviour: participants who expect to be asked about their attention may make an unusual effort to stay focused. Researchers have tried to supplement self-reports with physiological signals such as pupil size and eye movements, though no single measure has yet proved reliable on its own. Some laboratories have instead asked participants to press a button whenever they catch themselves drifting, but this method records only the lapses people notice, which, if Illanes is right, are the least damaging ones.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges is a picture far more balanced than the one that dominated a decade ago. Mind-wandering is costly when a task requires uninterrupted focus and the wanderer fails to notice the lapse; it may be useful, even necessary, at other times. This makes the claims of some commercial attention-training programmes, which promise to eliminate mind-wandering altogether, difficult to take seriously. A more realistic goal is to help people recognise when their thoughts have drifted and to choose more wisely when to allow it. Such a goal is less dramatic than eradication, but it is far more consistent with what the evidence actually shows about a habit that occupies so much of ordinary mental life.

topic: action video games as attention training: cross-sectional versus training studies, expectation effects and transfer
title: The Gamer's Advantage
subtitle: Fast-paced video games have been credited with sharpening visual attention, but separating real benefits from wishful thinking has proved difficult

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the first studies comparing frequent players of fast-paced action video games with non-players appeared in the early 2000s, the results seemed almost too convenient. Players, typically young men who spent at least five hours a week on games in which they had to track several moving targets and respond within fractions of a second, outperformed non-players on a range of laboratory measures of attention. They could keep track of more objects at once, spot a target among clutter more quickly and were less likely to miss a second target that followed closely on the first. To a public accustomed to hearing that screens were harmful, the suggestion that one kind of game might sharpen the mind was irresistible, and it was not long before commercial products were marketed on the strength of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty with such comparisons is that they cannot reveal cause and effect. People who are already quick and visually alert may simply be more attracted to action games, and more likely to persist with them, than those who are not. To address this, Agnieszka Szymborek and her colleagues at the Kraków Institute of Experimental Psychology conducted one of the first training studies. Non-players were randomly assigned either to play an action game for ten hours spread over two weeks or to play a slow-paced puzzle game for the same period. Those in the action group improved more on a test requiring them to locate a briefly flashed object at the edge of their vision. The puzzle game was chosen deliberately as a comparison, since any improvement shared by both groups could then be attributed to practice with the test itself or to the experience of taking part in a study.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Training studies of this kind became the backbone of the field, and several dozen have since been published. A review led by Karim Ouellbani at the Carthage Institute for Cognitive Research found that, taken together, they did point to a genuine benefit of action games, though one considerably smaller than the cross-sectional comparisons had suggested. Ouellbani also noted that studies with larger samples tended to report smaller effects, a warning sign that some of the published literature may have been inflated by the selective reporting of positive results. Of the forty-one studies his team examined, fewer than a third had registered their methods and predictions in advance. Ouellbani's team responded by publishing their own analysis plan before examining a single paper, a practice that remains far from universal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more subtle problem concerns expectations. Participants in the action condition can usually guess what the researchers are hoping for; few people believe that solving puzzles will improve their reaction times, but many believe that shooting games might. Siri Fjellstrand, a methodologist at the Northern Institute of Behavioural Methods, surveyed participants before training began and found that those assigned to action games expected to improve far more on attention tests than those assigned to the comparison games. In medical trials, this kind of imbalance would be controlled by keeping participants unaware of which treatment they had received; in game studies, that is plainly impossible. Fjellstrand does not claim that expectations account for the entire effect, but she argues that until they are measured routinely, the size of the true benefit cannot be known.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even where benefits are found, the question of transfer remains. Improvements on laboratory tasks that closely resemble the demands of the game are one thing; improvements in reading, driving or academic performance are quite another. Here the evidence is sparse. A small study of surgical trainees found that those who played action games made fewer errors on a keyhole-surgery simulator, but the trainees were not randomly assigned and the simulator itself shares many features with a video game. Studies of children with reading difficulties have produced intriguing results, yet most have involved fewer than thirty participants. Nor is it clear how long any benefit lasts. Only a handful of training studies have retested participants several months later, and those that did found that part of the advantage had faded once regular play stopped.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Proponents of game-based training point to its advantages over more conventional forms of practice. Games are engaging, so participants complete the training willingly, and they demand constant shifting between broad and narrow focus, which may be precisely what produces wider benefits. Szymborek has argued that it is the variety and unpredictability of action games, rather than their violent content, that matters, and her group has begun designing non-violent games built around the same demands. If these prove effective, they could be offered to older adults, among whom attentional decline is well documented and in whom the commercial appeal of shooting games is limited.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken as a whole, the research suggests that action games probably do produce modest improvements in certain visual attention skills, at least in young adults. The broader claims made for them, and for many commercial brain-training products, run well ahead of the data. That is not a reason to dismiss the field, which has been more willing than many to scrutinise its own methods, but it is a reason for caution. Progress will depend less on new games than on better studies: larger samples, methods registered in advance, and routine measurement of what participants expect to gain.

topic: the mere presence of a smartphone: 'brain drain' claims, failed replication, anticipated messages and social effects
title: Out of Sight, Still in Mind
subtitle: Can a silent phone that nobody touches really weaken the power of concentration?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people now spend their working days within arm's reach of a smartphone. Even when the device is silent and its screen dark, it remains a gateway to messages, news and social contact, and many users admit to checking it dozens of times a day without any prompt. Surveys suggest that a substantial minority feel uneasy when separated from their phones for even a short period. It is therefore reasonable to ask whether a phone that is doing nothing at all might still exact a cost. The idea that an object can drain attention simply by being present is an intriguing one, but intriguing ideas in psychology have a habit of shrinking under closer examination, and this one has been no exception.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The claim was first set out by Felix Dörrbecker and his colleagues at the Leipzig Laboratory for Applied Cognition. Several hundred students were asked to complete tests of working memory and abstract reasoning, having first been told to leave their phones in one of three places: face down on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in a different room altogether. Those whose phones were in another room performed best, and those with the phone on the desk performed worst, even though nobody actually used their device during the session. The gap was widest among participants who described themselves as most dependent on their phones. Dörrbecker proposed that resisting the pull of the phone requires mental effort, and that this effort draws on the same limited pool of resources needed for demanding thought.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The study attracted enormous attention, partly because its message was so easy to act upon. Yet its samples were divided into fairly small groups, and the differences, though statistically significant, were modest. When Nalani Palakiko of the Pacific Institute for Behavioural Research organised a replication involving more than two thousand participants at eight universities, with the procedures and analyses registered beforehand, the effect on working memory was close to zero, and no reliable effect on reasoning emerged at all. Palakiko interprets this as decisive evidence against the original account. That interpretation may be too hasty. A failed replication shows that an effect is smaller or less consistent than first reported; it does not prove that the effect is absent under all circumstances.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ishaan Varkey, a cognitive scientist at the Kerala Institute of Technology and Learning, has suggested that circumstances may be crucial. In Varkey's view, what matters is not the phone itself but what its owner expects it to deliver. In a field study conducted in university lectures, the visibility of a phone made no measurable difference to the quality of students' notes in general. However, students who were waiting for news they regarded as important, such as the outcome of a job application, took noticeably poorer notes when their phones were in view. A device that is merely present, Varkey argues, is an ordinary object; a device that might deliver something urgent at any moment is a constant temptation. This account has the merit of explaining why laboratory results have proved so inconsistent: few participants in such studies are anticipating anything in particular.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A separate line of research concerns social rather than intellectual effects. Aigerim Zhumabekova, a social psychologist at the Caspian Centre for Social Psychology, has found that strangers who talk with a phone lying on the table between them rate their conversation as less meaningful, and their partner as less empathetic, than those who talk without one. Her findings have been reproduced more consistently than those concerning working memory, perhaps because a visible phone sends a clear social signal: that the conversation might be interrupted at any moment. Even so, most of her studies have involved brief exchanges between strangers, and it is unclear whether the same would be true of close friends.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such findings have been cited in support of policies restricting phones in schools and workplaces. There may well be good reasons for these policies, including concerns about bullying, sleep and the simple annoyance of interruptions. Several countries have already introduced classroom bans, and early reports from teachers describe calmer lessons, although these accounts are anecdotal and difficult to separate from other changes made at the same time. But the evidence that a silent phone damages thinking is too fragile to serve as their main justification, and advocates do their cause no favours by overstating it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What remains is a more nuanced picture than the one that first captured public attention. A phone that is silent and ignored probably costs little in most situations, but one that its owner is anxiously watching may cost a good deal. The practical lesson is less about where the phone is placed than about what its owner is waiting for. For individuals, that might mean dealing with an expected message before sitting down to concentrate, rather than banishing the phone to another room while continuing to wonder what it holds. For researchers, it means paying closer attention to the state of mind that participants bring with them.

topic: Palaeolithic string and cordage as an overlooked early technology
title: The Invisible Thread
subtitle: Some archaeologists suspect that string, not stone, was among the most transformative inventions of early humans

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk into almost any museum gallery devoted to early humans and you will be confronted with row upon row of stone: hand axes, scrapers, blades and the countless flakes struck off in their making. The impression given is of a world in which flint was the defining material, and the very term 'Stone Age' reinforces it. Yet this picture is shaped less by what our ancestors used than by what happened to survive. Wood, leather, sinew and plant fibre decay within years in most soils, while stone endures almost indefinitely. In my view, the label we have inherited for this period is not merely incomplete but actively misleading, because it encourages us to treat the absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The physical traces of early cordage are tiny and easily overlooked. In one cave in the southern Caucasus, excavators recovered hundreds of microscopic flax fibres from layers more than 30,000 years old; some had been twisted, and a few appear to have been coloured with natural pigments. More remarkable still was the discovery, at a rock shelter in southern France, of a fragment of cord less than a millimetre long clinging to a stone flake and attributed to Neanderthals who lived there over 40,000 years ago. Dr Ilse Drabbe, a fibre analyst at the Institute for Prehistoric Materials in Ghent, has examined the fragment under high magnification. It consists of three bundles of fibre, each twisted in one direction and then combined by twisting in the opposite direction. Such a structure, she argues, cannot arise by accident: its maker had to understand how opposing forces lock fibres together and to keep track of pairs and sets while working, which implies a capacity for abstract, almost numerical thought.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For Drabbe, cordage was a foundational technology on which many others depended, from hafted spears to stitched clothing. Perhaps most significantly, it makes nets and snares possible. Drabbe points out that hunting large animals with spears demanded strength, speed and considerable risk, so it was probably confined to a minority of adults. Driving hares or birds into nets, by contrast, is a task in which almost anyone can take part, from children to the elderly. If she is right, the arrival of string altered not only what people ate but who was able to help obtain food.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded that the microscopic evidence can bear so much weight. Tomasz Grzelak, an archaeobotanist at the Silesian Centre for Archaeological Science, warns that plant fibres are abundant in cave sediments, carried in by wind, water and animals, and that some natural fibres twist as they dry. He has proposed strict criteria that a find must meet before it is accepted as deliberate cordage, including a consistent direction of twist along its whole length and the presence of more than one strand. Caution of this kind is healthy in a field where wishful thinking is a constant temptation. Nevertheless, applied without flexibility, Grzelak's standards would exclude almost every specimen ever recovered, since ancient cord rarely survives as more than a broken scrap in which such features are hard to confirm.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Fortunately, string can leave traces in other materials. Aiko Takanobu, of the Kansai Museum of Prehistory, studies fragments of fired clay from settlements in central Europe dating to around 27,000 years ago. Many of these lumps, which were never intended as pottery, carry the clear imprints of woven fabric, knotted nets and fine plaited cords pressed into them while the clay was soft. Takanobu notes that the impressions exist only because the dwellings in which the clay lay were later destroyed by fire, which hardened them by chance. Some of the fabrics she has identified are so even that she believes they were produced on some form of loom, and carved figurines from the same period, apparently wearing woven caps and belts, lend support to her interpretation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A different line of inquiry comes from experimental archaeology. Henrik Lagerqvist and his colleagues at an open-air research station in central Sweden have attempted to make cord using only materials and tools that would have been available in the Palaeolithic, including nettle stems, the inner bark of lime trees and wild flax. Their results suggest that the work is extraordinarily laborious: preparing the fibres and twisting a single metre of strong two-ply cord took an experienced worker more than an hour, and a modest hunting net would have consumed several hundred metres. Lagerqvist concludes that fibre processing may have absorbed more working time than the knapping of flint, and that it required planning across the seasons, since plants had to be gathered when their fibres were at their best. These figures are intriguing, but they should be treated with care. Modern experimenters lack the lifelong practice of people who handled fibres daily, so their times may be considerably longer than those of a skilled prehistoric maker.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What emerges is a picture of the Palaeolithic in which skill, patience and cooperation mattered as much as physical strength. Because spinning and netting have often been associated with women in historical societies, some scholars suggest that the neglect of fibre technology has also obscured women's contributions to early human life. That possibility deserves serious attention, and museums would do well to give perishable technologies a far more prominent place, even if this means relying on reconstructions. However, it would be a mistake to replace the old image of the heroic male hunter with an equally tidy story in which string explains everything. The evidence remains fragmentary, and the most honest account will admit how much has simply rotted away.
