topic: shellfish (murex) purple dye in the ancient Mediterranean: imitation, production scale, colour range and legal exclusivity
title: The Price of Purple
subtitle: New research is questioning the legend of the ancient world's most exclusive colour

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the colours of the ancient Mediterranean world, none carried more prestige than purple. Produced from a secretion of several species of predatory sea snail, collectively known as murex, the dye was associated with kings, magistrates and eventually Roman emperors, some of whom attempted to reserve its finest grades for themselves. Ancient authors repeatedly stressed its cost, and modern textbooks often echo their claims that tens of thousands of snails were required to colour a single garment. Such figures make for a memorable story, but they have been passed from book to book with remarkably little scrutiny. A growing body of scientific and historical work now suggests that the reality of purple was both more varied and more interesting than its legend.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first challenge comes from the laboratory. Eleni Papadakou, an analytical chemist at the Aegean Institute for Heritage Science, has tested dye extracted from more than two hundred textile fragments catalogued in museum collections as 'purple'. Genuine shellfish dye contains a distinctive bromine-bearing compound that no plant can produce, which makes it relatively easy to identify. Papadakou found it in fewer than a third of her samples. The remainder had been coloured with combinations of plant dyes, typically a red root dye applied over a blue one, or with dyes made from lichens. In her view, the extent of this imitation trade shows that true purple was far scarcer than the texts imply, and that a large market existed among buyers who wanted the appearance of prestige without its price.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Archaeology, however, points to production on a remarkable scale. Yusuf Doganay, a zooarchaeologist with the Levant Coastal Survey, has spent a decade measuring mounds of crushed murex shell that line stretches of the eastern Mediterranean shore. Some contain the remains of millions of animals, and the shells are broken at precisely the point needed to reach the gland that holds the dye, indicating a standardised technique. Doganay also argues that the oldest of these deposits, found on Crete, predate the Phoenician cities usually credited with inventing the industry by several centuries. His case for an earlier origin is convincing. It is less clear, though, that the mounds reveal much about annual output, since a heap of a million shells might represent a few intense seasons or the slow accumulation of three hundred years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third perspective comes from those who have tried to make the dye themselves. Lucien Brassac, a textile conservator who has run experimental dyeing workshops on the coast of Brittany for fifteen years, notes that the liquid taken from the snail is initially colourless and changes through yellow and green before reaching its final shade, which depends on the species used and on exposure to sunlight. Under different conditions he has produced colours ranging from deep blue-violet to a red close to crimson. Brassac argues that the ancient words translated as 'purple' therefore described a family of colours rather than a single hue. He also reports that he consistently obtained considerably more dye per snail than the figures quoted in modern handbooks would predict, a result he attributes to reusing the dye bath over many days.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, did purple remain so exclusive? Margit Vadkerti, an economic historian at the Danube School of Humanities, believes the answer lies less in chemistry than in law. Successive rulers issued regulations limiting who could wear purple, in what quantity and on which occasions. Vadkerti points out that the same prohibitions were reissued again and again over several centuries, and she interprets this as proof that they were widely ignored. That reading may be correct, but it is not the only one: new rulers routinely restated existing laws to assert their own authority, and repetition may reflect administrative habit as much as public disobedience.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The trade in purple was also organised in ways that blur the line between luxury and ordinary commerce. Ada Olanipekun, who studies merchant records at the Institute of Ancient Economies in Lagos, has found that the dye usually travelled not as finished garments but as dyed wool sold by weight. Local weavers could then use small quantities for borders and stripes, so that a citizen of modest means might own a tunic with a narrow purple band. Price lists from the late Roman period do value the best grades of purple wool at many times the cost of ordinary wool, and some writers have compared their worth to that of gold. The comparison is striking, yet it is somewhat misleading, because the same lists include cheaper grades within the reach of prosperous households.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that purple's exclusivity was produced as much by social convention as by the difficulty of extracting the dye. The material was costly, certainly, but not impossibly so, and its scarcity was reinforced by laws, by the symbolic weight attached to it and by the stories told about it. If modern accounts have exaggerated its rarity, it is partly because ancient elites had every reason to exaggerate it themselves. None of this diminishes the skill of the dyers who laboured over foul-smelling vats along the shore; it simply reminds us that the value of a colour has never been a purely physical property.

topic: the labour cost of woollen sails in Viking-age Scandinavia and its economic and social consequences
title: Woven Wind
subtitle: The sails of Viking ships have vanished, but reconstructing them reveals the hidden cost of seafaring

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The image of the Viking longship, its square sail swelling above a row of shields, is one of the most familiar in European history. Far less familiar is the sail itself. Whereas timbers from dozens of ships have been excavated from burial mounds and harbour silt, not a single complete sail from the Viking Age has survived, and only small scraps of coarse woollen cloth hint at what they were made of. As a result, histories of Scandinavian seafaring have tended to concentrate on hull design and navigation, treating the sail as a simple accessory. This is a serious oversight. Measured in hours of human labour, the sail was arguably the most expensive single component of the ship, and understanding how it was made changes our picture of the society that launched the fleets.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of what is known comes from reconstruction. Sigrun Kristmundsdottir, a weaver attached to the Coastal Heritage Workshop in western Norway, has spent more than a decade producing woollen sailcloth by hand, using drop spindles and the upright warp-weighted loom known from Viking-age farmsteads. She keeps meticulous records of every stage. For a sail of around ninety square metres, sorting and combing the fleece took several hundred hours and weaving well over a thousand; but spinning the yarn consumed by far the greatest share, more than two-thirds of the total. Because the width of the loom limited each length of fabric to little more than a metre, the finished sail also had to be stitched together from many narrow strips, adding yet more hours of needlework. Her figures suggest that a single sail represented about five years of full-time work for one person.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Making the cloth was only part of the task. Experiments show that untreated woollen fabric allows a surprising amount of air to pass through it, so that much of the wind's force is wasted. Kristmundsdottir and others have therefore coated reconstructed sails with mixtures of animal fat and ochre, which make the cloth almost windproof and give it a reddish colour. Whether Viking sailors did the same is uncertain. The clearest descriptions of such treatments come from Norwegian fishing communities of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and it is risky to project the practices of that period back a thousand years. Still, the problem the coatings solve is so fundamental that it would be surprising if earlier sailors had found no answer to it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The cost of sailcloth may also help to explain a long-standing puzzle. Scandinavians had contact with sail-using peoples, including the Romans, for centuries before they adopted the sail themselves, probably around the seventh or eighth century. Pekka Tiitinen, a maritime historian at the Baltic Institute of Seafaring Studies, rejects the idea that they simply lacked the knowledge. In his view, communities were well aware of sails but could not justify the enormous investment of labour until their farms produced a sufficient surplus of wool. The argument is attractive, but it is probably incomplete. A mast and sail place great strain on a hull, and Scandinavian shipbuilders first had to develop a sturdier keel; technical and economic factors most likely worked together. Some later sails were made of linen instead, but wool remained dominant throughout the period.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the labour estimates are right, the consequences extended well beyond the shipyard. Jakub Jaroszek, an economic historian at the Institute of Northern Studies, has calculated that equipping a fleet of a few hundred vessels, with sails replaced every few years, would have required wool from flocks numbering in the hundreds of thousands. He proposes that demand for sailcloth may have reshaped the landscape, with more land given over to grazing and a preference for breeds whose coarse outer hair was suited to hard-wearing cloth. It is an intriguing hypothesis, but one that can hardly be checked against firm evidence, since bones from excavated farms reveal which animals were eaten, not how many were kept alive for their fleece.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The calculations also bring into focus the people who did the work. In Viking-age Scandinavia, as in most pre-industrial societies, spinning and weaving were overwhelmingly associated with women, and textiles were stored and exchanged as a form of wealth. Kristmundsdottir argues that the labour of women in effect financed the overseas expansion, since without their cloth no fleet could have left harbour. The point is well made, though it requires one qualification. Written sources and the distribution of weaving tools on some estates indicate that enslaved workers, many of them captured in raids, also laboured at the looms, and their contribution should not disappear from the story simply because it is uncomfortable.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes the skill of Viking shipwrights or navigators. It does, however, suggest that a ship was as much a product of the farm as of the boatyard. Maritime histories that count timbers and rivets but ignore spindles and looms have measured only part of the cost of going to sea, and it is time the balance was redressed. The sail may have left almost no physical trace, but the effort that went into it is written into the economy of an entire region.

topic: preservation bias in the archaeology of ancient textiles: burial environments, mineral-preserved cloth on grave metalwork and funerary dress
title: Threads in the Rust
subtitle: Why the surviving record of ancient clothing may tell us more about soil and metal than about the people who wore it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost everything we know about the clothing of the ancient world comes from a handful of unusual places. Textiles are among the most perishable of all human products: in ordinary soils, bacteria and fungi consume wool, linen and cotton within a few decades, leaving nothing behind. Only where these organisms are held at bay, in the extreme dryness of the Egyptian desert or the coastal Andes, in permanently frozen ground, in salt mines or in waterlogged peat, does cloth endure for thousands of years. The result is a map of textile history with a few brightly lit spots and vast areas of darkness. It is tempting to assume that the places with the richest finds were the centres of textile innovation, but in my view this confuses the history of weaving with the history of preservation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Even within those bright spots, survival is selective. Juhan Pihlak, a soil chemist at the Baltic Centre for Conservation Science, has spent years burying modern fabrics in different environments and recovering them at intervals. His results show that the acidity of the surroundings matters as much as the presence of water. In acidic bogs, animal fibres such as wool and silk can survive almost intact, while plant fibres such as linen dissolve; in alkaline soils the pattern is reversed. Pihlak warns that the wealth of woollen garments recovered from northern European bogs may therefore give a false impression that linen was rarely worn there, when it may in fact have been the commonest cloth of all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In recent decades, however, a new source of evidence has emerged from an unexpected place: the surface of corroded metal. When a garment lies against a copper-alloy brooch or an iron buckle in a grave, the corrosion products of the metal can penetrate the fibres and gradually replace them, or form a crust around them that preserves their shape. What remains is a mineral cast of the cloth, known as a pseudomorph, in which the weave can still be seen under a microscope long after every trace of organic material has vanished. Katarina Brezinova, a conservator at the Bohemian Centre for Archaeology, has catalogued several thousand such fragments from early medieval cemeteries across central and western Europe, recording the type of weave, the density of the threads and the direction in which the yarn was spun. Because the metal preserves only the cloth in direct contact with it, each fragment is tiny, often no larger than a fingernail, but the sheer number of examples makes visible patterns that no single bog find could reveal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Brezinova's most ambitious claim concerns that last detail. Yarn can be spun with either a clockwise or an anticlockwise twist, and she argues that mapping the proportions of each across her sites reveals the boundaries of distinct regional weaving traditions, some of which persisted for centuries. The achievement is impressive, and few would dispute the value of the catalogue itself. Yet the evidence has an obvious limitation. Only those buried with metal objects can leave pseudomorphs, and in most early medieval communities these were the better-off. The fabrics Brezinova studies are therefore not a cross-section of society but largely the clothing of its more prosperous members.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Faced with such biases, some researchers have turned to statistics. Hamid Farahbakhsh, who models archaeological data at the Institute for Quantitative Archaeology in Shiraz, proposes weighting each find according to the wealth of the grave in which it was found, so that the few textiles from poorer burials count for more in the overall picture. He believes such methods can reconstruct the dress of ordinary people with reasonable confidence. I am less optimistic. Statistical weighting can correct for material that is under-represented, but it cannot recover what is entirely absent, and the conclusions of any such model are only as reliable as the assumptions on which it is built.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most fundamental challenge, however, comes not from chemistry or statistics but from anthropology. Grace Nantongo, of the East African School of Anthropology, points out that in many societies documented by ethnographers, the dead are not dressed in their everyday clothes but in shrouds or garments made specially for burial, sometimes of a quality that the person never wore in life. If ancient communities followed similar customs, then even a perfectly preserved cemetery would tell us about funerary dress rather than daily wear. Of all the objections raised, this seems to me the hardest to answer, because it applies equally to every grave, however rich or poor its contents.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the study of ancient textiles is futile. Images on pottery and wall paintings, written inventories, and the tools of the trade, such as spindle whorls, loom weights and needles, all offer independent evidence, each with its own distortions. Inventories, for instance, tend to record valuable garments that changed hands, while tools reveal that cloth was made but say little about how it looked or who wore it. Combining them is the only realistic way forward. What the field needs above all is humility: an acknowledgement that the clothing we can reconstruct is a fragment of what people actually wore, and that the fragment was selected not by them but by soil, water and metal.

topic: the emergence of the woolly sheep and the wool economy of Bronze Age Mesopotamia
title: A Revolution in Fleece
subtitle: The woolly sheep was not born but made, and its arrival transformed the economies of the ancient Near East

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When sheep were first domesticated in south-west Asia, some ten and a half thousand years ago, nobody kept them for their wool. Wild sheep, and their earliest domestic descendants, carry a coat of coarse, bristly hair over a thin woolly undercoat that is shed every spring. They were valued for meat, milk and hides. The thick, continuously growing fleece of the modern animal is the product of thousands of years of selective breeding, and its appearance marks one of the most consequential changes in the ancient economy. Yet compared with the domestication of wheat and barley, which fills whole shelves of academic literature, the emergence of the woolly sheep has received surprisingly little attention.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that wool itself almost never survives, so the evidence must be indirect. Neha Bhowmick, a zooarchaeologist at the Institute of Asian Prehistory in Pune, combines two approaches. First, she extracts ancient DNA from sheep bones to look for genetic variants associated with fleece growth. Second, she examines the ages at which animals were slaughtered. A flock raised for meat is usually culled young, once the animals reach their full size, whereas sheep kept for wool are worth more alive and may be retained for six or seven years. At several sites, Bhowmick has found a shift towards older animals beginning in the fifth millennium BC, along with the first appearance of the relevant genetic variants. She concludes that the woolly sheep emerged gradually, over perhaps a thousand years, rather than as a sudden innovation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Obtaining the wool posed problems of its own. Livia Mazzacurati, an experimental archaeologist who keeps a small flock of primitive sheep in the hills of Umbria, points out that early woolly breeds still moulted naturally each year. Their fleece could therefore be gathered by plucking or combing it out as it loosened, a method she has tested extensively. It is slow, but it separates the fine wool from the coarser hair and produces fibre that needs little further sorting. Iron shears, by contrast, do not appear in the archaeological record until the first millennium BC. Their absence for so long strongly suggests that plucking remained the normal practice for several thousand years, and that the continuously growing fleece we now take for granted was a comparatively late development.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: By the late third millennium BC, wool had become the backbone of a vast economy. Liis Ojamets, a specialist in cuneiform texts at the University of Tartu's Centre for Ancient Languages, has studied thousands of clay tablets from the temple and palace archives of southern Mesopotamia. They record flocks numbering in the tens of thousands, monthly rations issued to shepherds, and workshops employing thousands of weavers, most of them women and children. Ojamets has shown that woollen cloth was the region's principal export, traded up the rivers and across the Gulf in exchange for the metal, timber and stone that the alluvial plain entirely lacked.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For Daniel Kasozi, an economic historian at the Kampala School of Economic History, this trade was central to the growth of Mesopotamian cities. Grain, he notes, is bulky, heavy and costly to move any distance, whereas finished cloth is light, durable and easy to store, which makes it ideally suited to long-distance exchange. Kasozi goes further, arguing that the wool economy was the cause of urbanisation itself. Here, I think, he overstates his case. The earliest cities of the region were already well established before the enormous flocks recorded in the archives existed, so wool is better understood as something that strengthened and sustained urban growth than as the force that started it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The tablets are also revealing about the human cost of this system. The weavers received rations of barley, oil and wool that were barely sufficient to live on, and many appear to have been dependants of the temple with little freedom to leave. Some texts record deaths and escapes alongside quantities of cloth produced. It is worth remembering that the archives were written by administrators concerned with quantities, not with lives; they tell us how many garments were woven but almost nothing about how those who wove them experienced their work. The economic achievement was real, but it rested on labour that was often coerced.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There were environmental consequences too. Flocks of the size described in the archives required extensive grazing land, and it is likely that heavy grazing contributed to the loss of vegetation and the erosion of soils on the margins of the cultivated plain. Pollen cores from the surrounding uplands, though still few in number and difficult to date precisely, point in the same direction. The story of the woolly sheep is thus not simply one of technical progress. It is a reminder that a single biological change, achieved slowly by generations of herders, could reshape trade, labour and landscape on a scale that its first breeders could never have imagined.

topic: the origins and spread of silk production: wild versus domesticated silk, reeling technology and the myth of a Chinese silk monopoly
title: The Worm and the Weaver
subtitle: The legend of a closely guarded secret has long shaped the history of silk, but the evidence tells a slower and more tangled story

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than two thousand years, silk was the most coveted fabric in the ancient world, and the story usually told about it is one of jealous secrecy. In the familiar version, China held a monopoly on silk production for millennia, threatening with death anyone who carried silkworm eggs beyond its borders, until two travelling monks smuggled eggs to Constantinople inside hollow canes in the sixth century AD. It is an appealing tale. But the archaeological and genetic evidence gathered over the last three decades points to a far more complicated history, in which silk was made in several places, the knowledge needed to produce it seeped out gradually rather than all at once, and the very idea of a monopoly owes more to the imagination of later chroniclers than to ancient reality.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The domesticated silkworm, Bombyx mori, is a creature wholly dependent on people. Its moths cannot fly, its caterpillars make no attempt to wander, and it would not survive a single season without human care. Tadashi Kumagiri, an insect geneticist at the Kansai Institute of Sericulture, has compared the genomes of domestic silkworms with those of their wild relative, which still feeds on mulberry leaves across eastern Asia. His results suggest that domestication happened only once, probably in the basin of the Yellow River, and that it involved a severe genetic bottleneck: only a small number of wild insects appear to have been brought into captivity at the outset. Kumagiri places the beginning of the process at least five thousand years ago, though he readily acknowledges that molecular clocks of this kind carry wide margins of error.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Physical traces of early silk are scarce, because the protein fibre breaks down quickly in most soils. Zuzana Ostrihonová, a biochemist at the Danube Institute of Archaeological Science, has developed a method that detects silk proteins chemically in earth taken from beneath ancient burials. Working on Neolithic graves in the middle Yellow River valley, her team reported residues of silk protein in deposits thought to be around eight and a half thousand years old, long before the domestic worm is believed to have existed. Ostrihonová concludes that this early silk was obtained from the cocoons of wild moths gathered from trees, and that because it appears only in graves, it probably served a ceremonial purpose rather than an everyday one. Her findings are striking, but the technique is new and has not yet been reproduced by an independent laboratory; until it has, they are best regarded as a promising lead rather than settled fact.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Nor was wild silk a purely Chinese phenomenon. Eskil Brunnhage, a textile historian at the Gotland Centre for Textile Research, has examined threads recovered from settlements of the Indus civilisation, some four and a half thousand years old, and identified them as the product of native wild silk moths. Classical writers, too, describe a fine fabric woven on the Aegean island of Kos from the cocoons of local moths. What distinguished Chinese silk, Brunnhage argues, was not the fibre itself but the technique of reeling. Because the pupa inside a domestic cocoon is killed by heat before it can emerge, the cocoon can be unwound as a single unbroken filament, sometimes more than a kilometre long. Wild cocoons, by contrast, are usually pierced by the escaping moth, so their broken fibres must be spun like wool, producing a coarser and less lustrous yarn. This distinction is, in my view, the key to understanding why Chinese silk commanded such extraordinary prices abroad.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The notion of a monopoly has been challenged most directly by Lucía Echaurren, a historian of ancient trade at the Universidad del Litoral Atlántico. Echaurren points out that the surviving administrative records of early Chinese dynasties are preoccupied with taxing silk and with paying soldiers and foreign rulers in bolts of cloth, but contain almost nothing about forbidding the export of eggs. Sericulture, moreover, had reached the Korean peninsula and the oasis kingdom of Khotan in Central Asia centuries before the monks made their journey; a local legend even credits a princess with carrying eggs to Khotan hidden in her headdress. In Echaurren's account, what kept silk-making concentrated in China was less deliberate concealment than the sheer difficulty of transferring a complex body of skill, from the cultivation of mulberry trees to the precise control of temperature during rearing. This seems to me largely convincing, though it perhaps goes too far in ruling out deliberate protection altogether: a state that paid foreign rulers in silk had obvious reasons not to wish those rulers to produce it for themselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Demand in the Mediterranean was intense. Roman moralists complained that silk garments were indecently transparent and that the trade drained the empire of gold. A team at the Levant Textile Laboratory led by Yara Tabbal has analysed silk fragments from tombs in a Syrian caravan city and found that they fall into two groups: heavy patterned fabrics woven in China, and much lighter cloths made locally, apparently by unpicking imported silk and reweaving the thread to suit Mediterranean taste. Tabbal suggests that this practice allowed a limited supply of raw material to be stretched considerably further.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even after eggs reached Constantinople, the effect was hardly immediate. For several centuries the Byzantine workshops continued to rely heavily on imported raw silk, and domestic production grew only as mulberry plantations matured and expertise accumulated. The tale of the smuggling monks persists because it supplies a single dramatic moment for what was in truth a slow diffusion of knowledge across many generations and many regions. Historians would do well to treat with suspicion any story in which one bold theft is said to transform an entire industry.

topic: cloth as wealth and political instrument in the Inca empire: labour tax, fine cumbi weaving, standardised tunics and tocapu motifs
title: Kingdom of Cloth
subtitle: In the Inca empire, woven textiles did much of the work that coins and precious metals did elsewhere

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When European adventurers reached the Andes in the 1530s, they were dazzled by the gold and silver of the Inca empire. Yet their chronicles also record something that puzzled them: enormous state warehouses filled from floor to ceiling with folded cloth, and reports that retreating Andean armies set fire to such stores rather than allow them to fall into enemy hands. To the newcomers, burning fabric while precious metal lay waiting to be carried off seemed absurd. To the Inca, it was entirely rational, for in their empire it was cloth, more than gold, that represented wealth and power. Only in recent decades have historians begun to take this reversal of values seriously and to see textiles not as a minor craft of the Inca state but as one of its foundations.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The empire recognised two broad grades of cloth. The first, a plain and sturdy fabric for everyday use, was woven by ordinary households as part of the labour they owed the state. Each family received a quantity of llama or alpaca fibre from the state herds and was obliged to return it as finished garments. The second grade, known as cumbi, was something else entirely. Woven in tapestry technique with more than a hundred threads to the centimetre, it was finer than most European tapestry of the same period. Cumbi was produced by full-time specialists: men attached to provincial centres, and women chosen in childhood who lived together in enclosed compounds, cut off from ordinary life, and devoted years to the craft.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Guadalupe Quillaguaman, an ethnohistorian at the Centro de Estudios Andinos in Cusco, has spent much of her career reading colonial lawsuits and property inventories in which Andean witnesses described the old order. From these she has reconstructed a system in which soldiers were rewarded with garments, local lords received cumbi when they swore loyalty, and newborn children and brides were marked by gifts of cloth. In Quillaguaman's view, textiles performed many of the functions that coinage performed in the Old World. Calling cloth a currency is a useful shorthand, but it is also potentially misleading. Cloth was not spent in a marketplace to obtain other goods; it flowed outwards from the ruler as gifts that created obligations, and its value lay as much in who had given it as in its quality.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cloth also helped the state to make its subjects visible. Hendrikus Kortbeek, an archaeologist at the Amstel Institute for Andean Archaeology, has compared tunics recovered from sites hundreds of kilometres apart and found that many share virtually identical designs, among them a black-and-white checkerboard pattern associated with soldiers. He argues that such standardised garments functioned as uniforms, allowing anyone to recognise a wearer's rank or office at a glance. Colonial sources add that conquered peoples were required to continue wearing the distinctive dress and headgear of their home region, and were forbidden to adopt those of others. For Kortbeek, this was not cultural tolerance but administrative control: a population whose origins were displayed on their bodies was far easier to count, tax and move.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most elaborate tunics are covered in small square motifs called tocapu, each containing a geometric figure. Because the Inca had no alphabetic writing, some scholars have proposed that these squares formed a script. Ignacio Valdeavellano, a textile conservator in Lima, catalogued the motifs on more than three hundred surviving garments and found that certain combinations do recur in a fixed order. He nevertheless concludes that this falls well short of proof of writing, and suggests that the squares behaved more like heraldic emblems identifying lineages and offices. I share his caution, although the question is unlikely to be settled until more securely dated garments are found.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more critical view comes from Daudi Ruhumbika, an economic anthropologist at the University of the Great Lakes, who has compared the Inca system with economies elsewhere. Ruhumbika argues that it was strikingly wasteful: vast amounts of labour were poured into cloth that was then stored for years, given away for political ends or simply burned. A system of markets, he contends, would have directed that labour towards more productive uses. This is, I believe, to judge the Inca by the wrong standard. Their economy was never designed to maximise output; it was designed to bind a vast and diverse population to its rulers, and in that respect it succeeded remarkably, sustaining an empire that stretched more than four thousand kilometres within a single century.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Spanish conquest did not end the importance of cloth. The new colonial authorities continued to demand textiles from Andean communities as tribute, and established workshops in which weavers laboured under harsh conditions to supply the colonial economy. A tradition of fine weaving nonetheless survived in highland villages, where it continues today. The garments preserved in museums around the world are usually admired as works of art, and rightly so. But they are also documents of a political system, and they deserve to be read with the same care that historians give to written archives.

topic: linen in ancient Egypt: spliced flax yarn, the labour cost of fine cloth, linen as stored wealth and reused household linen in mummy wrappings
title: Woven Air
subtitle: How the humble flax plant became the hidden engine of the ancient Egyptian economy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The finest linen produced in ancient Egypt was so delicate that later writers described it as woven air. Some surviving fragments contain more than sixty threads to the centimetre, and a few are almost transparent. For most of the twentieth century, scholars assumed that the yarn for these fabrics had been made in much the same way as linen yarn in medieval Europe: by drawing out loose fibres from a bundle and twisting them continuously on a spindle. That assumption has now been overturned, and the consequences reach well beyond the history of craft. If the technique was different, then so was the amount of labour involved, and with it our understanding of what cloth meant to the people who made and owned it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The process began in the fields. Flax pulled while still green yielded the most delicate fibre, whereas plants left to ripen produced material suited to rope and heavy sacking. After the stems had been soaked to loosen the fibres and then beaten and scraped, the workers did not spin the fibre directly. Instead, as Nawal Elkabbany of the Institute of Nile Valley Archaeology has shown, they peeled it into long, narrow strips, which were laid end to end with a short overlap and rolled together between the fingers. Examining yarns from a Middle Kingdom settlement under the microscope, Elkabbany found these overlaps repeated at regular intervals along every thread. The spindle, in her account, served merely to give the finished yarn the torsion that held it together. Painted tomb models of weaving workshops, which show women seated beside bowls of water, make sense in this light: the bowls were used to keep the fibres moist and pliable during the joining process.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Splicing is extraordinarily slow. Bronwyn Murrigan, an experimental archaeologist at the Coral Coast Institute of Experimental Archaeology, has spent several years reproducing Egyptian yarn using flax grown and processed by traditional methods. Her results suggest that preparing enough thread for a single large sheet of fine linen could take a skilled worker many hundreds of hours, and that weaving it added several weeks more. A fine garment, in other words, represented months of human effort. This goes a long way towards explaining why linen appears so often in Egyptian records as a measure of value. Workers were paid partly in cloth, inventories of tomb goods list linen by grade as carefully as they list jewellery, and lengths of fine fabric changed hands in legal settlements.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Nowhere is the value of linen more apparent than in the treatment of the dead. Wrapping a single high-status mummy could consume hundreds of square metres of cloth. Yet much of this cloth was not new. Ylva Lenngren, a textile historian at the Nordic Museum of Antiquities, has catalogued wrappings that bear laundry marks, owners' names, darns and patches, evidently cut from sheets and garments used during life. Lenngren interprets this reuse primarily as a religious choice: cloth that had been worn or slept in carried something of the person's identity and was therefore especially appropriate for protecting the body. The argument is attractive, but it fits elite burials far better than ordinary ones. For the majority of Egyptians, the simpler explanation is surely economic: new linen was too costly to be buried, and worn household cloth was what a family could afford to give up.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The economic dimension has been pursued furthest by Pieter Esterhuysen, a historian of ancient economies at the Karoo Institute for Ancient Studies. Drawing on temple accounts written on papyrus, Esterhuysen argues that linen functioned as a kind of fiscal reserve. Temples received cloth as offerings and as dues from dependent estates, stored it, and later redistributed it as rations to priests and labourers or exchanged it for grain in years of poor harvest. Because good linen keeps for decades if it is stored dry, it was, he suggests, better suited to this role than grain, which spoils, or livestock, which must be fed. His reading of the accounts is persuasive, although it rests on records from a handful of large temples, and it remains uncertain how typical their practices were.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Splicing did not last for ever. During the Greek and Roman periods, the technique of drawing fibres continuously from a prepared bundle, long familiar elsewhere in the Mediterranean, gradually displaced it in Egypt. Draft spinning was considerably faster, and it allowed far more yarn to be produced by the same number of hands. Elkabbany points out, however, that none of the finest fabrics known from Egypt was made in this way; the gain in speed seems to have been paid for with a loss of fineness. Quite why the change happened is still debated. It may reflect the arrival of new settlers with their own habits, or the growth of a market for cheaper everyday cloth.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The study of yarn may seem a narrow specialism, but it opens a window on the whole of Egyptian society. It has been suggested that the total labour devoted to textiles over the course of Egyptian history exceeded that spent on temples, tombs and pyramids combined. Such a figure can never be verified, yet the comparison is less fanciful than it first sounds. Monuments were built in intensive bursts; cloth was made in almost every household, every day, for three thousand years. If we want to understand how ordinary Egyptians spent their working lives, the loom may tell us more than the pyramid.

topic: the origins of footwear: surviving prehistoric sandals and shoes, toe-bone and footprint evidence, and footwear in the settlement of cold regions
title: Underfoot
subtitle: Researchers are piecing together the history of one of humanity's most ordinary and least studied inventions

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of all the objects people have made, few are used as constantly or discarded as casually as footwear. That may be why its history has attracted so little scholarly interest. Shoes wear out, are thrown away and rot, and the handful of prehistoric examples that survive owe their preservation to exceptionally dry or cold conditions. The oldest known are woven sandals from a dry cave in the Great Basin of western North America, made around ten thousand years ago from the bark of sagebrush. A complete leather shoe recovered from a cave in the southern Caucasus is roughly five and a half thousand years old. Yet there are good reasons to think that people protected their feet long before either of these was made, and in my view footwear deserves a far more prominent place in accounts of early human technology than it has generally been given.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Because the objects themselves have vanished, researchers have looked for their effects on the body. Elena Bertolotto, a palaeoanthropologist at the Ligurian Institute of Human Evolution, studies the small bones of the toes. In people who go barefoot, she explains, the lesser toes grip the ground and absorb considerable force with every step, and their bones become correspondingly sturdy. A stiff sole relieves the toes of much of this work, and over a lifetime they grow more slender. Comparing skeletons from many periods, Bertolotto has found a marked thinning of these bones in some human populations from around forty thousand years ago, and she concludes that footwear was in regular use by then. Her reasoning is ingenious, but it is not conclusive. The same thinning could have resulted from other changes in daily life, such as a reduction in the distances people walked, and the skeletal evidence alone cannot distinguish between these possibilities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Fossil footprints offer a different perspective. Hiroshi Nakamaru, who specialises in the study of ancient trackways, has surveyed preserved footprint trails left in mud and volcanic ash across several continents. Even at sites dating from the coldest phases of the last ice age, he notes, the great majority of prints are those of bare feet. Nakamaru does not deny that footwear existed, but he argues that it was probably worn only occasionally, when snow, ice or sharp stone made going barefoot painful or dangerous, rather than as part of everyday life. If he is right, the slender toes identified by Bertolotto may reflect the habits of a few specialised groups rather than of whole populations.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The surviving sandals reveal a great deal about how footwear was made. Ximena Quiahua, an experimental archaeologist at the Escuela de Arqueología Experimental in Puebla, has reproduced several prehistoric designs using plant fibre. The sandals are constructed by twining, the same technique used to make baskets, bags and nets, and this kinship is surely no accident: sandal-making appears to have grown directly out of an older tradition of working with fibre. Quiahua found that an experienced maker could complete a pair in three or four hours, but that the result lasted only a few weeks on stony ground. Footwear, she concludes, was a routine and constantly repeated task rather than a rare achievement. She has also noticed that sandals from different caves differ consistently in the shape of the toe and the pattern of the weave, and that these local styles persisted for thousands of years. In her view, they announced which community the wearer belonged to.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The leather shoe from the Caucasus tells a different story. It was cut from a single piece of hide, laced across the top, and stuffed with grass, which would have provided insulation against the cold. For Tomasz Wierzbinek, a historian of technology at the Wrocław Centre for the History of Technology, such shoes point to a broader truth: without insulated footwear, he argues, humans could never have colonised the cold regions of northern Eurasia, where frostbite would quickly have crippled anyone travelling on foot. This claim seems to me to go too far. Feet can be protected perfectly well with simple wrappings of fur or hide, which would leave no trace, and every shaped shoe yet found is far younger than the earliest human settlement of those regions. Insulation was certainly needed; a shoe of the kind found in the Caucasus was not.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Footwear has also changed the human body in ways that are only now being appreciated. Studies of present-day communities in which some people habitually wear shoes and others do not suggest that the shod develop weaker foot muscles and flatter arches, and may be more prone to certain injuries. Footwear, in other words, has not simply protected the foot; it has gradually reshaped it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to treat shoes as a trivial subject, but the debate surrounding them touches on some of the largest questions in prehistory: how people adapted to new environments, how they expressed identity, and how their technologies altered their own bodies. The humble sandal, it turns out, has a good deal to say.

topic: the multiple independent domestications of cotton, its early use in South Asia, its slow spread with irrigation and the role of mordant dyeing in its value
title: The Fibre Invented Four Times
subtitle: Long before it clothed the industrial world, cotton was domesticated again and again on opposite sides of the globe

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Cotton is now so familiar that it is easy to forget how improbable its history is. The fibre is not a stem or a hair from an animal but a growth on the seed of a shrub, a fluffy coat that in the wild helps seeds to float or to cling to passing animals. Turning that fluff into thread demanded selection over many generations for longer, stronger and more abundant fibres. Remarkably, this was achieved not once but at least four times, by peoples who knew nothing of one another, in South Asia, in Africa or Arabia, in Mesoamerica and on the Pacific coast of South America. There are few clearer examples in the history of technology of the same invention being made independently in widely separated parts of the world, and the reasons for it deserve more attention than they usually receive.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest known cotton comes from an unlikely source. At a Neolithic cemetery in the hills of Baluchistan, on the western edge of the Indian subcontinent, the archaeobotanist Anand Kolhatkar of the Godavari Institute of Archaeobotany examined a copper bead found with a burial dating from around eight thousand years ago. Inside it he identified a few cotton fibres, preserved because the corroding copper had gradually replaced their organic material with minerals. The fibres had evidently formed a thread on which beads were strung. Kolhatkar believes the plant from which they came was already being cultivated, pointing to the regularity of the fibres. The suggestion is plausible, but with so little material it is impossible to rule out the possibility that the thread was made from wild plants gathered nearby.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: By the time the great cities of the Indus civilisation flourished, some four and a half thousand years ago, cotton was unquestionably being grown and woven on a large scale. Impressions of cloth survive on pottery and on clay sealings, and a small fragment of cotton fabric dyed red was found adhering to a silver vessel in one of the principal cities. Some scholars have proposed that cotton cloth was among the goods carried by sea from the Indus to Mesopotamia, where Indus seals and beads have been discovered. No fragment of cotton has so far been identified at any Mesopotamian site, however, and until one is, the idea must remain speculation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Genetics has transformed the picture. Ilse Vandersmissen, a plant geneticist at the Flemish Plant Genome Centre, has compared the genomes of cultivated cottons with those of their wild relatives. Her work confirms that the two Old World species were domesticated separately. The South Asian species has no surviving wild ancestor, which suggests that its wild progenitor has become extinct, whereas the other appears to descend from a wild plant that still grows in the dry scrublands of southern Africa. The two American species are more unusual. Each carries two complete sets of chromosomes, the result of a natural hybridisation, more than a million years ago, between a cotton related to the Old World species and a native American one. Vandersmissen argues that this doubled genome is what allows the American cottons to produce exceptionally long fibres, and it explains why they now account for roughly nine-tenths of the cotton grown commercially across the globe.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In the Old World, cotton spread remarkably slowly. Greek writers of the fifth century BC described Indian plants that bore wool instead of fruit, but the crop was hardly grown around the Mediterranean for another thousand years. Gulnara Zhunusova, a historian of Central Asian trade at the Almaty Institute of Oriental Studies, explains this delay in terms of water. Cotton is a summer crop with a long growing season, and in the dry lands west of India it can flourish only where fields are watered through the hottest months. Zhunusova shows that the expansion of cotton into Iran and Central Asia followed closely behind the construction of large state-sponsored irrigation networks, and that it retreated wherever those networks fell into disrepair. Cotton, in her phrase, travelled along the irrigation frontier.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why was cotton cloth worth the effort? Ritwika Bhattasali, a textile chemist who studies historical dyes, points out that cotton is in fact considerably more difficult to dye than wool or silk, because its fibres do not readily bind with most natural colourants. Indian dyers overcame this by treating cloth with metallic salts known as mordants, which fix dyes to the fibre and allow different colours to be produced from a single dye bath. For Bhattasali, it was this chemistry, and the brilliant, washable colours it made possible, that made Indian cotton so desirable abroad. She is surely right that dyeing was crucial to the cloth's reputation in distant markets. Yet her account underplays a more basic advantage: in hot and humid climates, light cotton was simply more comfortable to wear than wool, and that alone would have ensured steady demand closer to home.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The story of cotton is usually told as the story of the plantation and the factory, of slavery and the industrial mill. That history matters enormously. But it is only the final chapter of a much longer narrative, in which farmers on several continents, working independently over thousands of years, turned an unremarkable seed covering into one of the most valuable materials ever produced.

topic: short-term rental platforms and housing in tourist cities: rent effects, dispersal of visitor spending, 'neighbourhood thinning', night limits versus platform-enforced registration, and the underlying housing shortage
title: Spare Rooms and Empty Streets
subtitle: Home-sharing platforms promised tourism on a human scale. Cities are still arguing about what they actually delivered

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When the first home-sharing websites appeared in the late 2000s, they presented themselves as a modest innovation. A resident with a spare room, or a family going away for the summer, could earn a little extra money by hosting visitors, and travellers would gain access to neighbourhoods that conventional hotels rarely reached. The image was a friendly one: tourism without tower blocks, hospitality on a human scale. Little more than a decade later, that picture bears scant resemblance to what can be observed in the historic centres of many popular destinations. In some districts, entire apartment buildings have been withdrawn from the long-term rental market and turned into what are, in effect, unlicensed hotels. The question now facing city authorities is not whether short-term letting affects local housing, but how much, for whom, and what, if anything, should be done about it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Measuring the effect is harder than it might appear, because rents in attractive cities tend to rise for many reasons at once. Dr Orsolya Kalmanfi, an urban economist at the Danube Institute for Spatial Research, attempted to isolate the platform effect by comparing neighbourhoods that became fashionable with visitors at different times. Her analysis, covering eleven cities over eight years, found that a ten per cent increase in the number of short-term listings in a district was associated with a rise in long-term rents of well under one per cent. Taken by itself, this figure seems trivial, and it has frequently been quoted by the platforms themselves. Kalmanfi insists, however, that it is the cumulative pattern which matters. In the most visited quarters, listings multiplied many times over during her study period, and there the estimated contribution to rent increases was substantial. A small effect repeated often enough, in other words, ceases to be small.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the platforms offer a different reading. Teodoro Ruivaldo, a tourism economist at the Lusitanian Institute of Tourism Studies, argues that home-sharing has dispersed visitor spending well beyond the narrow hotel districts to which it was once confined. Cafés, bakeries and small shops in residential areas, he points out, now receive custom that would otherwise have gone to chain restaurants near the main sights, and many households depend on occasional hosting to meet rising living costs. There is some truth in this, at least on the city's outskirts. Yet the argument rests on an idealised picture of the typical host. Platform data obtained by several municipalities suggest that a minority of operators, each managing multiple properties, earn the majority of the revenue, and these operators are concentrated precisely in the central districts where pressure on housing is most acute.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Rents are only part of the story. The sociologist Lerato Mokoatle, who spent three years interviewing long-standing residents in two southern European old towns, describes a process she calls 'neighbourhood thinning'. As permanent residents leave, the everyday infrastructure that sustained them goes too: hardware shops give way to luggage-storage outlets, a primary school loses enough pupils to close, and the people who remain find themselves surrounded by strangers who change every few days. Mokoatle stresses that, in her interviews, residents complained less about noise or rubbish than about a sense that their district no longer belonged to them. Such losses do not appear in rent statistics, but they arguably do more to erode the character that drew visitors in the first place.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: City governments have experimented with a range of responses. Some limit the number of nights per year for which an entire home may be let; others require hosts to register with the authorities, and a few have banned short-term lets of whole properties in their historic cores altogether. The record of these measures is mixed, largely because enforcement depends on information that cities do not possess. Magnus Nordenfalk, a legal scholar who has compared regulatory regimes in fourteen countries, observes that night limits are almost unenforceable when officials cannot see how often a property is booked. In his view, the decisive factor is whether platforms are legally obliged to remove listings that lack a valid registration number. Where that obligation exists, he found, the number of illegal listings fell sharply within a year; where it does not, even strict rules have had little practical effect.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to treat short-term letting as the root cause of housing problems in tourist cities. In most of the places where the controversy is fiercest, too few homes have been built for decades, and planning restrictions in historic centres make new construction extremely difficult. Platforms have exploited this scarcity rather than created it. Recognising this does not let them off the hook, but it does suggest that a city which suppressed short-term letting entirely, while doing nothing about supply, would probably see rents continue to climb, if more slowly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What the evidence points towards, then, is not prohibition but discrimination in the original sense of the word: the ability to tell different activities apart. A pensioner letting a spare room for a few weekends a year and a company operating forty apartments as a de facto hotel are engaged in fundamentally different businesses, and there is no good reason why the law should treat them alike. The tools for making that distinction already exist. What has often been missing is the political will to insist that the platforms help to apply them.

topic: cruise tourism and port cities: low onshore spending by cruise passengers, congestion from simultaneous dockings, air pollution at berths and shore power, the bargaining power of cruise lines, and resident attitudes
title: Floating Resorts, Crowded Quays
subtitle: Port cities once competed eagerly for cruise ships. Many are now asking what they actually gain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few branches of tourism have grown as quickly, or as conspicuously, as ocean cruising. Over the past three decades the number of passengers has multiplied several times over, and the largest vessels now carry more than six thousand guests. For the port cities on their itineraries, the arrival of these floating resorts was long treated as an unambiguous gift. Municipal authorities dredged harbours and built gleaming terminals, confident that each docking would bring a tide of spending into local shops and restaurants. It is only recently that the assumptions behind this enthusiasm have been examined with any rigour, and the picture that has emerged is considerably less flattering than the brochures suggested.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first assumption to come under scrutiny concerned money. Ingrid Elvebakk, an economist at the Northern Institute of Maritime Studies, interviewed passengers returning to their ships in a dozen European harbours. Her conclusion was that the typical cruise visitor spends barely a third of what an overnight tourist spends in a day, for the simple reason that food, drink and a bed are already paid for on board. Much of what is spent ashore, moreover, never reaches independent local businesses. Excursions sold on the ship are frequently run by a handful of operators that pay a substantial commission to the cruise line, while passengers who do wander into town tend to buy coffee and souvenirs rather than meals. Elvebakk does not claim that cruise visitors bring no benefit; she argues instead that ports have routinely overstated it by applying the spending patterns of conventional tourists to a very different kind of guest.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second problem is one of timing. When three or four large vessels berth on the same morning, a historic centre designed for a few thousand residents can receive more than fifteen thousand day visitors within a few hours. Matías Sandoval-Ruiz, an urban geographer who has mapped pedestrian flows in several such cities, maintains that the root of the difficulty is concentration rather than volume. Spread evenly across the week, he suggests, the same number of passengers would cause little disruption, and he therefore recommends that ports limit the number of ships permitted to dock on any single day. The logic is sound, but the proposal has an obvious weakness: a ship turned away from one harbour is rarely cancelled; it simply calls at a neighbouring port, which may be even less equipped to absorb the crowds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The environmental costs are harder to see but no less significant. While in port, most vessels keep their engines running in order to generate electricity for lighting, air conditioning and kitchens. Hanta Rakotoarisoa, an atmospheric chemist who has placed monitoring stations along several waterfronts, has recorded concentrations of fine particles near cruise berths that rival those found beside busy motorways. The widely promoted remedy is shore power, which allows a docked ship to switch off its engines and draw electricity from the local grid. Rakotoarisoa supports the technology but warns against treating it as a complete answer. The cables and substations are expensive, many older ships lack the necessary connections, and where the grid itself depends on burning coal, the pollution is not eliminated so much as relocated inland. Shore power, in short, is a necessary step, but it would be a mistake to regard its installation as the end of the matter.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Underlying all of these issues is a striking imbalance of bargaining power. A port that has borrowed heavily to build a terminal cannot move, whereas a cruise line can redraw its itineraries from one season to the next. Lukas Brunnhofer, a transport economist, describes cruising as perhaps the most footloose branch of tourism, and argues that this mobility allows companies to play ports against one another, extracting reduced fees and exclusive facilities in return for continued visits. There is much truth in this analysis, yet it can be pushed too far. Cities whose attractions are genuinely irreplaceable, such as a medieval old town or a celebrated fjord, hold more leverage than they generally exercise, because no itinerary in the region would be complete without them. Their reluctance to impose conditions reflects timidity more than weakness.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Public attitudes add a further layer of complexity. A network of researchers known as the Port Cities Observatory surveyed residents in eleven harbour towns and found that hostility towards cruising bore little relation to the number of passengers a town received. Far more important was whether the ships were visible from the historic centre, and whether residents believed that anyone they knew earned a living from the trade. Where vessels loomed over the old quarter and the profits seemed to flow elsewhere, resentment was intense; where the terminal was out of sight and local guides and traders were visibly employed, objections were muted. This suggests that what residents object to is less the presence of visitors than a perceived unfairness in the distribution of costs and rewards.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that ports should turn cruise ships away altogether. The more reasonable lesson is that the terms of the relationship have been set almost entirely by one party. Passenger levies earmarked for the upkeep of public spaces, daily limits agreed among neighbouring ports rather than imposed by each in isolation, and requirements to use shore power where it exists would together begin to correct the balance. Regional coordination of this kind will not be easy to achieve, since every port fears losing business to its rivals. But the alternative, in which each city competes to offer the most generous concessions, has already shown where it leads.

topic: wildlife-watching tourism and its hidden effects on animals: habituation and hidden stress, disease risk to great apes, cumulative disturbance of whales' energy budgets, the conservation-revenue defence, provisioning and weak certification
title: Watching the Watchers
subtitle: Wildlife tourism is often presented as conservation's best friend. The animals may not always agree

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early 1990s, boat trips to see bottlenose dolphins began operating in a sheltered bay on the coast of a small island nation. At first there were two vessels; a decade later there were fourteen. When researchers compared the dolphins' behaviour across that period, they found that the animals were spending markedly less time resting and more time travelling, and that females with calves had begun to avoid the bay during the busiest hours. No single boat trip had caused obvious harm. The effect emerged only gradually, as encounters accumulated. The episode captures a difficulty at the heart of wildlife tourism. The industry has long been promoted as a benign alternative to hunting, one that gives animals an economic value alive rather than dead. That argument has real force, but the assumption that simply watching animals is harmless has proved far too simple.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the confidence rests on a process known as habituation, in which animals that are repeatedly exposed to people without being harmed gradually stop responding to them. To tour operators, a habituated group that continues feeding as visitors approach is evidence of success. Kwame Aboagye, a primatologist at the Centre for Tropical Field Ecology, urges caution in interpreting such calm. His team measured stress hormones in the droppings of habituated and unhabituated primates and found elevated levels in the former on days when visitors were present, even though the animals' outward behaviour showed little change. Habituation, in Aboagye's view, describes what an animal does, not what it feels. It may also carry practical risks: animals that no longer fear humans are more easily approached by hunters, and are more likely to raid crops on neighbouring farms.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For great apes there is a further hazard. Because they are so closely related to humans, gorillas and chimpanzees are susceptible to many of the same respiratory infections, and several outbreaks among habituated groups have been traced to visitors. Most sites therefore limit visits to one hour, require people to stay at least seven metres from the animals and are supposed to turn away anyone who is unwell. Observers report, however, that these rules are frequently relaxed in practice. Guides depend heavily on tips, and tourists who have paid substantial permit fees are understandably eager for close photographs. Some parks have begun to require face masks, a measure that is cheap and sensible but which addresses only one route of transmission.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Marine mammals present a different set of problems. Yelena Lavrentieva, a marine biologist who has tracked humpback whales in their feeding grounds for over a decade, argues that the damage done by whale-watching lies less in any individual encounter than in its cumulative effect on the animals' energy budget. A whale that interrupts feeding to avoid a boat loses only a few minutes; a whale that is approached twenty times a day may lose several hours. Over a feeding season, she calculates, this could reduce the fat reserves that females need to sustain pregnancy. Existing codes of conduct regulate how close boats may come and how fast they may travel, but Lavrentieva believes the more important limit would be on the total number of approaches each animal experiences in a day.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Defenders of the industry respond that criticism of this kind ignores the alternative. Astrid Huitfeldt, a conservation economist, points out that in many regions the land occupied by national parks would be far more profitably used for agriculture or logging if tourism did not generate income from it. Permit fees pay for rangers, and communities that earn money from visitors have reason to protect the animals they come to see. Huitfeldt's argument is persuasive as far as it goes, and it would be naive to imagine that wildlife could be protected on goodwill alone. Yet it does not follow that any level of tourism is acceptable simply because some tourism is beneficial. Moreover, studies of several parks suggest that only a small share of visitor spending reaches the villages nearest to them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Of all the practices associated with wildlife tourism, deliberate feeding is the hardest to defend. In some places, stingrays, monkeys and even sharks are fed regularly so that sightings can be guaranteed. Provisioned animals tend to congregate in unnatural numbers, compete aggressively for food and, in time, become dependent on handouts. Their diets also change in ways that may affect their health. The practice turns a wild encounter into something closer to a performance, and the animals pay the price for the reliability that operators are able to advertise.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of these findings implies that people should stop watching wild animals. The question is not whether, but how much, and under what conditions. Here the industry's response has been disappointing. A growing number of certification schemes award labels to operators who claim to follow responsible practices, but most are voluntary, and few involve independent inspection. Until the rules governing wildlife tourism are monitored as carefully as the animals themselves, visitors will have little way of knowing whether the encounter they have paid for is helping or harming its subject.

topic: economic leakage from tourism in small island economies: unreliable leakage estimates, smallness versus tourism as the cause, all-inclusive resorts and employment, farm-to-hotel linkage schemes, and tax concessions versus foreign ownership
title: Where the Tourist Dollar Goes
subtitle: The idea that island economies lose most of what visitors spend has become an article of faith. It deserves closer inspection

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For every hundred dollars that a tourist spends on a holiday in some small island states, it is often claimed, fewer than thirty remain in the local economy. The rest 'leaks' away: on imported food, fuel and building materials, on profits returned to foreign hotel owners, on the salaries of expatriate managers, and on package holidays that are paid for in the visitor's home country before the journey even begins. Over the past four decades, the notion of leakage has become central to criticism of island tourism, providing a single, memorable number that seems to capture how little a poor destination gains from wealthy visitors. The concept identifies a real problem. The figures attached to it, however, are considerably less reliable than their frequent repetition would suggest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Ravi Ramdhanie, a development economist at the Institute for Island Economies, has compiled published estimates for more than forty destinations and found that they range from around ten per cent to well over seventy. Much of this variation, he argues, reflects differences in what is measured rather than differences between the islands themselves. Some studies count only the imports bought directly by hotels; others also include goods imported by the shops where hotel employees spend their wages, and a few add the interest paid on foreign loans used to build airports. Each approach is defensible, but the results cannot be compared, and the most dramatic figures have been seized on by campaigners without regard to how they were produced. It is difficult not to conclude that leakage has at times served more as a slogan than as a measurement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second objection concerns what leakage is compared with. Lucía Vasconcellos, who studies trade in small states, points out that an island of a few hundred thousand people cannot grow its own wheat, refine its own fuel or manufacture its own lifts and air-conditioning units. Any export industry located there, whether tourism, fishing or financial services, will depend heavily on imported inputs. In her view, high leakage is principally a consequence of smallness rather than a peculiar defect of tourism, and the meaningful question is not how much money flows out but whether a given industry leaves residents better off than the realistic alternatives would.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Nowhere has the leakage argument been deployed more forcefully than against the all-inclusive resort, in which meals, drinks and entertainment are bundled into a single price paid in advance. Kenji Tokuyama, an economist who tracked the spending of guests at resorts on three islands, confirmed that those on all-inclusive packages spent only a fraction as much outside their hotel as other visitors did, to the obvious disadvantage of local restaurants and taxi drivers. Yet his data also showed that such resorts employed considerably more staff per room, since they provide on site the services that other guests buy elsewhere. The all-inclusive model is often caricatured as a sealed bubble from which nothing escapes; Tokuyama's findings suggest that the reality involves a trade-off between fewer business linkages and more direct employment.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If some leakage is unavoidable, the more productive task is to reduce it where possible, and the most promising efforts have focused on food. Anjali Bahadursingh, an agricultural economist, has evaluated schemes intended to connect small farmers with hotel kitchens. The obstacles are considerable: hotels require consistent quality and reliable quantities throughout the season, which individual growers can rarely guarantee, and chefs trained abroad tend to favour ingredients they recognise. Bahadursingh found, however, that where hotels signed purchase agreements with farmers' cooperatives before planting began, the share of fresh produce sourced locally roughly doubled within three years. Programmes of this kind attract far less attention than airport expansions or new resort openings, but they deserve considerably more.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question of ownership is more contentious. Eeva Pihlajamaa, a political scientist who has examined investment agreements across the Caribbean and the Pacific, argues that whether a hotel is foreign-owned matters less than the terms on which it operates. Governments eager to attract international chains have frequently granted tax exemptions lasting ten or twenty years, together with duty-free imports of furnishings and equipment, so that the state receives little revenue from even the most profitable properties. Her emphasis on these concessions is well founded. She is inclined, though, to underestimate the importance of local ownership in another sense: where residents own a share of the tourism industry, they also have a voice in how it develops, and that has a political value which revenue figures do not record.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that leakage is a myth. The money that flows out of island economies is real, and much of it could be retained with better policy. But the ambition of eliminating leakage altogether is unrealistic for economies of this size, and pursuing it can lead governments to neglect more useful goals. A better measure of success would be the proportion of tourism's benefits that reaches the people who live alongside it, which depends on wages, taxes and local enterprise as much as on the origin of the food served at dinner.
