topic: last-chance tourism to disappearing places (retreating glaciers, bleaching reefs, Antarctica): the emissions paradox, visitors' motives, whether travellers become environmental ambassadors, glacier villages selling the story of loss, and the case against a ban
title: See It Before It Goes
subtitle: Travellers are paying to witness landscapes that are vanishing. Is that a tribute or a contradiction?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A new kind of itinerary has appeared in the brochures of adventure travel companies. Visitors are invited to walk on glaciers that are retreating by tens of metres a year, to dive on coral reefs whose colours are fading, and to cross the Southern Ocean to see ice shelves that may not survive the century. Some operators even promise sightings of polar bears on sea ice that now forms weeks later each autumn than it once did. The tourism industry has given the trend a name, 'last-chance tourism', and the numbers suggest that it is flourishing: the number of tourists landing in Antarctica each season has more than doubled in little over a decade. The label began life as a marketing slogan, and it is tempting to dismiss it as one. Yet it describes a genuine contradiction, and one that the people who sell such trips have been slow to acknowledge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The contradiction is simple to state. The places that last-chance tourists travel to see are threatened chiefly by a warming climate, and reaching them generally requires a great deal of fossil fuel. Marina Ivashkina, an environmental scientist at the Polar Policy Unit, has calculated the emissions associated with a typical two-week Antarctic voyage, including flights to the port of departure. Her figure, between five and eight tonnes of carbon dioxide per passenger, is roughly what an average European motorist produces in a year of driving. Because the destinations are by definition remote, she notes, the long-haul flight is rarely optional; the journey itself, rather than the activity at the destination, accounts for the overwhelming share of the impact.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Do the travellers themselves recognise this? Daniel Kilonzo, a tourism researcher, interviewed more than six hundred visitors at a glacier in a national park where the ice front has retreated by over a kilometre since the 1980s. Almost three-quarters cited the wish to see the glacier before it vanished as a principal reason for coming. Only a handful, however, mentioned any connection between their own journey and the melting they had come to witness. Kilonzo interprets this as a familiar form of mental compartmentalisation: people are perfectly capable of regretting a loss while declining to recognise their own small part in it. The pattern, he adds, is hardly unique to tourism; it appears wherever the costs of an individual's choices are distant, diffuse and shared among millions of others.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tour operators have an answer to such criticism. Visitors, they argue, return home as ambassadors, moved by what they have seen to change their habits and to press for action. This is an attractive idea, and Freja Lindahl-Sorensen, a social psychologist, set out to test it. She surveyed Antarctic travellers before departure, on their return and again a year later. Immediately after the voyage, expressions of environmental concern and intentions to act rose sharply. Twelve months on, though, the reported behaviour of most participants, from their flying habits to their charitable giving, was barely distinguishable from what it had been before the trip; only around one in six had made lasting changes. The ambassador argument should not be dismissed altogether, since a committed minority is not nothing, but it has plainly been overstated by those with an interest in promoting it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For the communities that host last-chance tourists, the calculations look different again. Hiroshi Kawaguchi, a geographer who has studied villages beneath retreating Alpine glaciers, observes that the decline of the ice does not necessarily mean the decline of tourism. As the glacier front withdraws up the valley, the walk to reach it lengthens and the spectacle diminishes, but villages have often responded by building visitor centres, guided trails marking the former extent of the ice, and exhibitions on climate change. The attraction, in Kawaguchi's phrase, shifts 'from the ice to the story of its loss'. This adaptability is admirable in one sense, yet it carries a danger. A landscape that earns money as a monument to its own disappearance risks turning environmental loss into a form of entertainment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some critics conclude that such trips should simply be prohibited. This position is understandable but mistaken. A ban would be difficult to enforce, would fall hardest on communities that have come to depend on visitors, and would do little about the far larger emissions of everyday travel. More promising are measures that make the costs of last-chance tourism visible and ensure that some of its revenue serves the places concerned: requiring operators to report the emissions of each trip, capping visitor numbers at the most fragile sites, and directing a portion of every fare towards the monitoring and research on which conservation depends. None of these steps would resolve the contradiction entirely, but each would at least prevent it from being quietly ignored.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the end, last-chance tourism holds up an uncomfortable mirror. It reveals a willingness to treat the degradation of the natural world as one more item on a list of experiences to be collected. Wanting to see remarkable places is nothing to be ashamed of, and many who make these journeys do so with genuine reverence. But the fact that a place is disappearing is a poor reason for going there, and a still poorer one for selling the journey.

topic: tourism's water consumption in dry destinations: guest versus resident use, aquifer over-pumping and saltwater intrusion, hidden water footprints in food and irrigation, golf courses and recycled water, unequal access during shortages, and desalination
title: Thirsty Guests
subtitle: In many sunny destinations, the scarcest resource consumed by visitors is not fuel but water

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A guest at a hotel on a dry coast may use several times as much water each day as the residents of the town beyond its gates. Estimates vary widely, but studies of resorts in the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Caribbean have reported figures of three hundred to eight hundred litres per guest per night, compared with perhaps a hundred and fifty litres for a local household member. The difference lies not only in long showers. Swimming pools must be filled and topped up against evaporation, lawns and flower beds are irrigated through the heat of the day, and towels and bed linen are laundered daily. Worse still, the tourist season in such places generally coincides with the driest months of the year. Discussion of tourism's environmental costs has been dominated by carbon emissions from flights, and that focus is understandable. It has nevertheless allowed water, in many destinations the more immediate constraint, to escape the attention it deserves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Most hotels on small islands and arid coasts draw their water, directly or through municipal supplies, from aquifers, the porous rocks beneath the surface in which groundwater collects. Selin Sertkaya, a hydrogeologist at the Mediterranean Groundwater Institute, has spent a decade monitoring one such aquifer beneath a heavily developed island. When pumping exceeds the rate at which rainfall recharges the rock, she explains, the pressure of fresh water declines and seawater begins to seep inland beneath the coast. Wells that once supplied drinking water become brackish, and because salt is flushed out only slowly, the aquifer may need decades to recover even after pumping is reduced. Sertkaya argues that annual averages disguise the danger: what matters is how much is extracted during the peak tourist months, when demand is highest and recharge is close to zero, compared with what the aquifer receives.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Where, though, does most of this water actually go? Tomás Cárdenas-Ulloa, who specialises in water footprint accounting, argues that the figures quoted for hotel consumption capture only part of the picture. Using a method that traces the water embedded in goods as well as the water drawn from taps, he estimates that direct use in guest rooms accounts for a minority of a resort's total footprint. Far larger shares are absorbed by the irrigation of gardens and sports facilities and, above all, by the production of the food served in the restaurants, much of it grown with irrigation elsewhere. By this measure, the familiar cards inviting guests to reuse their towels address the smallest part of the problem. Such campaigns are not worthless, but it is difficult to avoid the suspicion that their chief attraction for hotels lies in lower laundry bills.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Golf courses occupy a particular place in the debate. A single eighteen-hole course in a hot climate can require as much water in summer as a town of several thousand people. Graham Ollerenshaw, a turf scientist who advises course developers, maintains that the figure is misleading for modern facilities, many of which are irrigated with treated wastewater and planted with drought-tolerant grasses. In his view, such measures can reduce a course's demand for drinking-quality water by more than three-quarters. Yet the claim that recycled water is environmentally costless does not survive scrutiny. Treated wastewater is a resource in its own right, which could otherwise irrigate crops or be returned to depleted aquifers; using it to keep fairways green is a choice with consequences, not a free gift.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Questions of fairness are sharpest where supplies run short. Folake Ajibola, a political ecologist, has documented summer disputes in several resort regions between hotels, farmers and residents. Hotels, she found, are frequently able to secure their supply through private boreholes or by buying water from tanker lorries, while neighbouring households face rationing and interrupted service. In some towns, residents' taps ran dry for days while hotel pools remained full. Ajibola attributes this partly to pricing: in many places hotels pay the same tariff per cubic metre as households, or even less under negotiated contracts. She proposes charges that rise steeply with the volume consumed. Whatever the merits of particular tariffs, an arrangement in which visitors on holiday enjoy secure supplies while residents queue for water is indefensible.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Faced with such pressures, many governments have turned to desalination. Plants that remove salt from seawater can, in principle, free a destination from dependence on rainfall altogether. But they are expensive to build, consume large amounts of energy and discharge concentrated brine that can harm marine life near the outflow. Desalination may well be part of the answer for some islands. There is a risk, however, that its availability will remove any incentive to use water more carefully, allowing consumption to expand until the new supply is itself insufficient.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the greatest obstacle to sensible policy is ignorance. Few hotels meter their consumption in any detail, and fewer still make the figures public; the estimates on which this debate relies are, as a result, assembled from small samples and occasional audits. Until operators are required to measure and report their water use as routinely as they report their occupancy rates, discussion of tourism's thirst will continue to rest more on guesswork than on evidence.

topic: volunteer tourism ('voluntourism') in poorer countries: short-term volunteer teaching, construction projects and 'staged usefulness', orphanage volunteering, fees as the real contribution, and what volunteers learn
title: Helping Hands, Short Stays
subtitle: Paying to volunteer abroad has become a booming industry. Its benefits to host communities are far less certain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each year, hundreds of thousands of young people from wealthy countries pay to spend a few weeks working on projects in poorer ones. They teach English in village schools, help to build classrooms and clinics, survey coral reefs or care for children in orphanages. What began in the mid-twentieth century as a small number of charitable programmes has grown into a commercial industry, with agencies offering packages that combine a short placement with sightseeing and adventure activities. Volunteer tourism, as it has come to be known, is often presented as an antidote to the self-indulgence of conventional holidays. There is little reason to doubt the good intentions of those who take part. Whether their efforts actually help the communities they visit is a different question, and one to which the answer is frequently less encouraging than the agencies' brochures imply.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Teaching provides a revealing example. Thandeka Nakashole, an education researcher, spent two years observing rural primary schools that received a steady stream of short-term volunteer teachers. Because each newcomer arrived without knowledge of what the previous one had covered, lessons on the alphabet, colours and numbers were repeated again and again, while more demanding material was rarely reached. Permanent staff complained that their timetables were constantly disrupted by the need to accommodate visitors. When Nakashole compared pupils' test results with those at similar schools that received no volunteers, she found no measurable difference. Her conclusion, that placements of less than three months contribute little to children's learning, is difficult to dispute. It should be noted, however, that her study concerned untrained volunteers; a qualified nurse or engineer offering specialist skills represents a rather different case.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Construction projects raise similar concerns. Volunteers with no building experience are often employed on tasks that local tradespeople could complete more quickly and to a higher standard, and in doing so they may deprive those tradespeople of paid work. Accounts from several countries describe walls laid by visiting volunteers during the day being quietly taken down and rebuilt by local workers at night. Agnieszka Roszkowska, an anthropologist who has studied volunteer agencies, describes such arrangements as 'staged usefulness': projects designed primarily to give volunteers the satisfying sense of having made a difference, with the needs of the host community a secondary consideration. Agencies, she notes, seldom consult residents about which projects are wanted, relying instead on what sells well to prospective volunteers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most troubling form of volunteer tourism, however, involves orphanages. Investigations in parts of Asia and Africa have found that a large proportion of children living in residential institutions have at least one living parent, and that some institutions actively recruit children from poor families in order to attract volunteers and their donations. Some even stage performances by the children for visiting groups, an arrangement that critics regard as turning vulnerable young people into a tourist attraction. Child development specialists add that a constant succession of short-term caregivers, each of whom forms an attachment and then departs, can damage children's capacity to form stable relationships. Several governments and child-protection organisations now discourage orphanage volunteering altogether. Of all the criticisms levelled at the industry, this is the one that carries the greatest weight.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all researchers take such a bleak view. Rodrigo Quispe-Huamán, a development economist, has surveyed host organisations in a number of countries and argues that critics have misunderstood the transaction. The organisations he studied valued the fees paid by volunteers far more than the volunteers' labour, using the income to pay local staff and fund long-term programmes. Many small charities, he points out, would struggle to survive without this revenue, since grants from larger donors are typically tied to specific projects and rarely cover running costs. Some volunteers, moreover, maintained links with the projects for years afterwards, as donors or advocates. Quispe-Huamán's findings are a useful corrective, but they also imply something the industry is reluctant to say openly: the volunteer is, in effect, a customer, and what is being purchased is an experience rather than a service to others.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If that is so, it is worth asking what the experience teaches. Ilkka Korhonen-Bly, a sociologist, interviewed volunteers before and after their placements. He found that many returned with their stereotypes reinforced rather than challenged, describing the people they had met as 'poor but happy' and showing little awareness of the economic and political causes of the poverty they had witnessed. The exceptions were volunteers whose agencies had provided thorough preparation before departure and structured opportunities for reflection on their return. Korhonen-Bly does not blame the volunteers themselves, most of whom were teenagers on their first journey abroad; responsibility, in his view, lies with agencies that sell the trips as adventures rather than as opportunities to learn.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that volunteer tourism should be abandoned. Longer placements, careful matching of volunteers' skills to genuine needs, the employment of local staff in skilled roles and transparency about how fees are spent would all improve matters. Above all, the industry needs to change the way it measures success. At present, agencies tend to judge their programmes by the satisfaction of returning volunteers. The more meaningful test is whether the communities that receive them are better off as a result.

topic: ski tourism under a warming climate: the snow-reliability rule, the physical limits of artificial snowmaking, closure of small low-altitude resorts and snowmaking subsidies, water abstraction, 'four-season' diversification, and how mountain villages cope when lifts close
title: Snow on Demand
subtitle: Mountain resorts are spending heavily to keep their slopes white. For many, the effort may only delay the inevitable

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the arrival of skiing transformed the economies of mountain valleys across Europe. Villages that had depended on subsistence farming acquired lifts, hotels and ski schools, and in many Alpine districts winter tourism now supports more than half of all local employment. That prosperity rests on a resource that is becoming less dependable. Industry analysts have long used a simple rule of thumb: a resort is regarded as snow-reliable if, in most winters, it has at least thirty centimetres of snow on a minimum of one hundred days between December and April. Since the late nineteenth century, temperatures in the Alps have risen roughly twice as fast as the global average, and resorts below about 1,500 metres are increasingly failing the test. The future of these places is frequently discussed as a technological problem. It is better understood as a matter of altitude and money.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The technology in question is snowmaking. Snow cannons and lances force water and compressed air through nozzles into cold air, where fine droplets freeze before reaching the ground. The process works efficiently only when the air is both cold and dry, generally at a 'wet-bulb' temperature, which combines temperature and humidity, of around minus two degrees Celsius or lower. In several Alpine countries more than two-thirds of pistes are now equipped for artificial snow, supplied by reservoirs constructed high on the mountainside. Matthias Kirchschlager, a snow physicist, points out that machine-made snow is denser than natural snow and therefore more resistant to melting, so a well-prepared base can survive warm spells that would strip a natural snowpack. But he stresses that the machines cannot create cold. At lower altitudes, the number of hours in which conditions allow snow to be made has fallen markedly, and it is in precisely these resorts that the need is greatest.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Snowmaking is also expensive, and its costs fall unevenly. Chiara Valsecchi, an economist who has analysed the accounts of more than two hundred ski areas, finds that investment in snowmaking systems has favoured large, high-altitude resorts with access to capital, while small, low-lying operations, many of them family businesses, have been unable to keep pace. In one region she studied, more than a hundred small lift operations ceased trading between 1990 and 2020. Larger groups, by contrast, have been able to spread the cost of new equipment across several linked ski areas and to raise ticket prices without losing customers, many of whom are attracted precisely by the guarantee of snow. Many local and regional governments have responded by subsidising snowmaking at struggling resorts. Valsecchi is blunt about the policy: in her view, public money spent on artificial snow at low altitudes merely postpones closures that are, in the long run, unavoidable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Environmental objections centre on water. The reservoirs that feed snow cannons alter alpine habitats, and where water is drawn directly from mountain streams, abstraction tends to occur in early winter, when natural flows are already at their lowest. The energy consumed by snowmaking also attracts criticism. Defenders of the industry reply that this energy accounts for only a small fraction of the carbon footprint of a skiing holiday, most of which arises from travel to and from the resort. That is true, but it rather misses the point: the problems caused by abstraction are local, and they are not reduced in the slightest by comparisons with emissions elsewhere.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If winter can no longer be relied upon, the obvious alternative is to attract visitors in other seasons. Many resorts now market themselves as 'four-season' destinations, offering hiking, mountain biking and festivals in summer. Aino Paasilinna, a tourism geographer, has tracked the results in more than thirty resorts. Summer visitors, she found, typically spend considerably less per day than skiers and stay for shorter periods, so that summer income has rarely compensated for losses in winter. Some resorts have nonetheless made the transition successfully, especially those close to large cities. Diversification is clearly necessary, but it has too often been presented as a painless substitute for skiing, which the evidence does not support.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Beyond the balance sheet lies a social dimension. Tomasz Jabłoński, a sociologist who has studied villages in the Alps and the Carpathians after their lifts closed, emphasises that skiing is not merely an industry but part of local identity, sustained by ski clubs, races and generations of instructors. When the lifts stopped, some villages lost many of their young people within a few years as jobs disappeared. Others reinvented themselves, attracting remote workers, spa visitors and enthusiasts for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, activities that need less snow and no lifts at all. The decisive difference, Jabłoński found, lay not in altitude or wealth but in whether planning for the future had begun before closure; communities forced to react afterwards fared far worse.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The likely outcome is a skiing industry that contracts unevenly. Forecasts of how many ski areas will still be operating by the middle of the century differ widely, but few analysts expect the decline to be gradual or evenly shared. High resorts may even gain visitors as lower ones close, while valleys below the snowline will need to find other ways of making a living. Public money has a role to play in that process, but it would be better spent preparing communities for change than keeping lifts turning on slopes where winter is steadily retreating.

topic: dark tourism to sites of death and disaster: the usefulness of the label, a spectrum of 'darker' and 'lighter' sites, visitors' actual motives, photography and behaviour at memorials, survivor-led tours in disaster towns, and commercial facilities
title: Visiting the Places of Sorrow
subtitle: Battlefields, prisons and disaster zones attract millions of tourists. What draws them, and how should such sites respond?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: People have long been drawn to places associated with death and suffering. Medieval pilgrims travelled to the sites of martyrdoms, and in the nineteenth century spectators sometimes picnicked within sight of battles before touring the battlefields once the fighting had ended. Today, former prisons, war cemeteries, disaster zones and memorials to genocide receive millions of visitors each year. The busiest record well over a million admissions annually, and specialist operators now offer holidays devoted entirely to such places. In the 1990s, scholars gave this phenomenon a name, 'dark tourism', and the label has since been taken up enthusiastically by journalists and tour companies alike. It is a memorable phrase, but it has arguably done more to obscure than to illuminate, since it places under a single heading experiences that have very little in common.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Éva Szalkai, a heritage scholar, has attempted to bring some order to the field by placing sites along a spectrum. At the 'darkest' end are places where atrocities actually occurred, which are relatively recent, and whose primary purpose is education and remembrance. At the 'lightest' end are commercial attractions that use death as entertainment, such as theatrical dungeon shows in which actors re-enact historical executions. Applying the same term to a genocide memorial and a horror-themed amusement, Szalkai argues, conceals profound moral differences. Her framework is a genuine advance. Its weakness is that it classifies places rather than people: a single memorial may receive grieving relatives, school groups and holidaymakers who have simply followed their guidebook, and their experiences can differ as much as the sites themselves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What visitors actually seek has been studied by Grace Anyango, a psychologist who surveyed some three thousand people at memorial sites in eight countries. The great majority cited a wish to learn about the past or to pay their respects to the dead. Only a small minority admitted to curiosity about death itself, and a substantial number said they had come mainly because the site was included in a standard itinerary of the city. Many respondents also described feeling uncomfortable during their visit, which, Anyango suggests, indicates engagement with the past rather than indifference to it. She concludes that the popular image of the dark tourist as someone with a morbid fascination for suffering has little basis in evidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Behaviour at such sites is another matter. In recent years, photographs of visitors posing cheerfully at memorials have provoked public anger when shared online, and some site managers have responded by banning photography altogether. Per Mikkelborg, who has advised several memorial museums, regards outright bans as a mistake. For many visitors, he argues, taking photographs is simply how they process and remember an experience, and prohibiting it breeds resentment rather than respect. He prefers to shape behaviour through design: dimmed lighting, narrow passages and quiet zones that signal, without a single printed instruction, that this is a place for reflection. The approach is sensible in most cases, although there are places, such as burial grounds where remains are still being identified, at which a ban is entirely justified.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Places struck by disaster face particular dilemmas. Hélène Lacombe-Vidal, a geographer, has studied five towns that became destinations after natural or industrial catastrophes. In the years immediately after the event, she found, residents tended to resent the arrival of visitors, whom they saw as intruders gazing at their grief. Over time attitudes often softened, especially as tourist spending contributed to rebuilding. The greatest change came where survivors themselves began to lead tours. Telling their own stories gave residents control over how the disaster would be remembered, and visitors reported that such tours were more moving than any museum display. Lacombe-Vidal cautions, however, that survivor-led tours place a heavy emotional burden on the guides, some of whom recount the worst day of their lives several times a week.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Commercial facilities provoke similar unease. Gift shops and cafés at memorial sites are sometimes condemned as attempts to profit from tragedy. Yet the income they generate frequently pays for the conservation of buildings and archives that would otherwise deteriorate, and visitors who have travelled a long way reasonably expect somewhere to eat. Staff at several memorials also report that a café gives visitors somewhere to sit and talk over what they have seen, which many regard as a valuable part of the visit. The real question is not whether such facilities should exist but whether they are run with appropriate restraint; a bookshop selling histories of the event is one thing, a stall selling novelty souvenirs quite another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Supporters of dark tourism frequently claim that visiting such places makes people more tolerant and more determined that past horrors should not be repeated. It is an appealing idea, and it may well be true for some visitors. But the evidence for it remains thin, consisting largely of visitors' own statements as they leave, and few studies have examined whether attitudes change in any lasting way. The case for preserving these sites rests more securely on the duty of remembrance than on promises of moral improvement that have yet to be demonstrated.

topic: the commercialisation of traditional culture for tourists: staged ceremonies and the authenticity debate, tourism reviving dying music, front-stage and back-stage separation, souvenir crafts and factory imitations, and community ownership of performances
title: Performing Tradition
subtitle: When rituals, music and crafts are sold to visitors, are they being destroyed or kept alive?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every evening at half past seven, in the courtyard of a hotel in a highland valley, a troupe of young dancers performs a harvest ceremony. In their grandparents' time the ceremony took place once a year, lasted most of a night and was attended only by members of the village. The version staged for hotel guests lasts twenty minutes, includes a short explanation in three languages and ends with an invitation for the audience to join in. For some observers, this transformation exemplifies everything that is wrong with cultural tourism: a living tradition reduced to a commodity, sold by the hour. For others, it is evidence of a tradition's resilience. The debate is usually framed as a contest between the authentic and the fake. That framing is understandable, but it obscures the question that matters far more, which is who controls the performance and who benefits from it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case against commercialisation has been put most forcefully by Margaux Beaulieu-Tremblay, an anthropologist who has spent two decades working with communities in mountain regions. When a ritual is performed for payment, she argues, its meaning is gradually drained away, and performers begin to see their own culture through the expectations of their audience. She documents one ceremony in which elements regarded as sacred, including a lengthy invocation of ancestors, were dropped at the request of tour operators, who considered them tedious, and replaced with acrobatic sequences that had no place in the original rite. Such cases are troubling, and they should not be dismissed. Yet the argument contains a questionable assumption: that there once existed a fixed and original version of each tradition from which later forms have declined. In reality, ceremonies, songs and crafts have always been modified, borrowed and reinvented, long before any tourist arrived.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is, moreover, evidence that tourism can sustain traditions that would otherwise vanish. Nadia Chaudhry-Lam, an ethnomusicologist, has studied several styles of instrumental music that were on the verge of disappearing in the 1980s, when only a handful of elderly players remained. As visitors began paying to attend concerts, young people took up the instruments, initially as a source of income. What surprised Chaudhry-Lam was what happened next: within a decade, the young musicians were also performing at weddings, funerals and local festivals, occasions from which the music had largely disappeared. Tourist demand, in these cases, did not replace community use but revived it. Chaudhry-Lam is careful not to generalise from these examples, however; elsewhere in her study, concert programmes for visitors gradually narrowed to a few crowd-pleasing pieces, and much of the wider repertoire was forgotten.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Many communities, in any case, draw a careful distinction between what they show visitors and what they keep for themselves. Darius Barzani-Holt, a sociologist, describes this as a division between a public 'front stage', where performances are adapted for outsiders, and a private 'back stage', where ceremonies of religious significance continue unchanged and unseen. In his comparison of fourteen communities, those that had agreed clear rules about which practices could be shown to tourists experienced the least internal conflict over tourism. The arrangement is sensible, but it depends on visitors respecting the boundary, and that cannot be taken for granted. Accounts of photographers slipping into closed ceremonies, or of tour guides promising access to 'secret' rites, are far from rare.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Handicrafts raise similar issues in material form. To appeal to travellers, carvings have become smaller and lighter, textiles have adopted colours that suit foreign tastes, and items once made for household or ceremonial use are now produced chiefly for sale. More damaging, according to Juhani Koskelainen, an economist who has studied craft markets in several countries, is competition from factory-made imitations, often manufactured abroad. In blind tests, he found, most buyers could not tell a handmade piece from a copy costing a fraction of the price. Where producer groups introduced certification labels guaranteeing local, handmade origin, and where those labels were policed, artisans' incomes rose by around a third. Koskelainen also points out that adapting designs is not necessarily a loss: some of the most admired contemporary textiles began as experiments aimed at tourist buyers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings point towards what is arguably the decisive issue. Oksana Ostapenko, who researches community development, argues that the most important variable is not how traditional a performance is but who organises it. Where performances are run by community cooperatives, she found, income remains in the village and residents decide for themselves what is shown and what is withheld. Where hotels or tour companies hire performers directly, wages tend to be low and the content is dictated by what operators believe will sell. Performers in such arrangements, she adds, have little say over when or how often they appear, and some are expected to remain in costume throughout the working day. Ostapenko's analysis is persuasive, and it suggests that much of the energy spent debating authenticity would be better directed at questions of ownership.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even community control, however, does not settle every difficulty. Communities are rarely of one mind: elders may wish to preserve forms that younger members find restrictive, and decisions taken in the name of 'the village' may reflect the interests of its most powerful families. Change in cultural traditions is inevitable, and much of it is welcome. The test is whether such change is chosen by those who live with its consequences or imposed by those who merely profit from it.
